To advance a cause is to further it; to advance money is to provide it ahead of time.

Advantage is a favorable position or circumstance that increases chances of success: {Her experience gave her an advantage over other candidates}. In tennis, advantage is the point scored after deuce. To {take advantage of} something is to make use of it; to take advantage of someone is to exploit them unfairly. The verb advantage means to benefit: {The new policy advantages larger corporations}.

Advantages are favorable conditions or circumstances that give someone a better position than others. You might have the advantage of {experience}, {wealth}, or {location}. In sports, advantage indicates a player or team is ahead. To {take advantage of} something is to exploit it—positively when using an opportunity, negatively when exploiting a person: {He took advantage of her trust}.

Advent refers to the arrival or emergence of something notable or long-awaited: {the advent of the internet}, {the advent of spring}. The word carries a sense of momentousness—you wouldn't use it for ordinary arrivals. It suggests something that changes circumstances or marks a new era. (Capitalized Advent is the Christian season before Christmas.)

Adventure is an exciting or risky undertaking, typically involving the unknown: {an adventure in the mountains}, {her adventures abroad}. The word suggests both danger and possibility—something out of the ordinary that tests you. As a verb, to adventure is to venture forth boldly, though this use is now rare. An {adventure story} features daring exploits. To seek adventure is to court the unpredictable.

An adventurer is someone who seeks out exciting or risky experiences, often involving travel to unfamiliar places: {The adventurers set off into uncharted jungle}. The word can carry romantic connotations of boldness and discovery, but historically it also meant someone who lives by their wits—a fortune hunter or schemer willing to take chances for personal gain. In gaming, adventurer is the standard term for a player character who explores dungeons and completes quests.

Adventurers are people who seek out exciting, risky, or unusual experiences. The word often suggests boldness and a willingness to face danger: {Renaissance adventurers sailed into uncharted waters}. It can carry a negative shade—implying recklessness or fortune-seeking at others' expense: {political adventurers}, {financial adventurers}. In gaming, adventurers are player characters who explore dungeons, complete quests, and battle monsters.

Adventures are exciting or unusual experiences, often involving risk, danger, or the unknown. The word carries a sense of venturing forth—leaving the familiar behind. A person might recount their adventures abroad or seek adventures in the wilderness. Children's stories often center on adventures. In a looser sense, any undertaking with uncertain outcome qualifies: {Starting the business was quite an adventure}. The singular adventure works as both noun and verb: to adventure into unfamiliar territory is to explore it boldly.

Adventuring is engaging in adventures—undertaking risky, exciting, or unusual journeys and activities. The word often appears in fantasy contexts where characters explore dungeons, fight monsters, and seek treasure: {We spent the weekend adventuring through the mountains}. An adventuring party is a group that sets out together on such exploits.

Adventurous describes a willingness to take risks or try new things. An adventurous {traveler} seeks out unfamiliar places; an adventurous {eater} samples exotic cuisines. The word implies excitement rather than recklessness—adventure as opportunity, not danger. {She's always been adventurous, the first to suggest we try something new.}

Adversarial describes a relationship of opposition or conflict between parties. An adversarial {legal system} pits prosecution against defense. Adversarial {negotiations} involve competing rather than cooperating. The word often implies hostility beyond mere disagreement: {The meeting turned adversarial when accusations started flying}. In computing, adversarial attacks deliberately exploit system vulnerabilities.

Adversaries are opponents or enemies—those who stand against you in conflict, competition, or disagreement. The word carries more weight than mere competitors; adversaries actively oppose each other's interests or goals. {The two lawyers were longtime adversaries in the courtroom}. The singular is adversary.

An adversary is an opponent or enemy—someone who stands against you in conflict, competition, or dispute. The word carries more weight than opponent, suggesting genuine opposition rather than mere competition: {The two lawyers were longtime adversaries}. In religious contexts, the Adversary (capitalized) refers to Satan.

Adversity is hardship, difficulty, or misfortune. The word typically describes challenging circumstances rather than momentary setbacks: {She showed remarkable strength in the face of adversity}. People speak of overcoming adversity or thriving despite it. The phrase {in adversity} suggests difficult times generally: {True friends reveal themselves in adversity}.

Advert is British shorthand for advertisement: {I saw an advert for that new restaurant}. As a verb, to advert means to turn attention toward something or refer to it: {She adverted to the matter only briefly}. The verb is formal and uncommon; the noun dominates in everyday British usage.

To advertise is to make something publicly known, typically to promote a product, service, or event: {They advertised the sale in the local paper}. Companies advertise to attract customers; individuals advertise to sell belongings or find jobs. The word extends to unintentional disclosure—you {advertise your intentions} when your behavior reveals them, or {advertise your ignorance} by speaking carelessly.

An advertisement is a public announcement promoting a product, service, or event—typically paid for by whoever wants attention drawn to it. Advertisements appear in newspapers, on television, online, on billboards, and anywhere else people might see or hear them. Often shortened to ad or, in British English, advert. {I saw an advertisement for cheap flights}. The word sometimes extends to anything that showcases qualities: {His behavior was not a good advertisement for the company}.

Advertisements are public notices promoting products, services, or ideas. The word covers everything from television commercials to billboards to sponsored social media posts. Often shortened to ads or, in British English, adverts. {The advertisements during the Super Bowl cost millions per second}. {She skips the advertisements on streaming services}.

An advertiser is a person or organization that pays to promote products, services, or ideas through media channels. The term appears constantly in discussions of journalism, television, and the internet, where advertisers fund content in exchange for audience attention: {The magazine lost several advertisers after the controversial article}. On digital platforms, advertisers target users based on collected data.

Advertisers are companies or individuals who pay to promote products, services, or messages to potential customers. The term often carries slight negative connotations, suggesting manipulation or intrusion: {Advertisers target children with sugary cereal commercials}, {Online advertisers track your browsing habits}. In media contexts, advertisers wield significant power as the primary revenue source for free content.

Advertising is the practice of promoting products, services, or ideas through paid messages in media. The word covers both the industry and its output: {She works in advertising}; {I hate the advertising on this site}. To advertise is to make something publicly known, whether through formal campaigns or casual mention: {He's always advertising his accomplishments}.

An advertorial is an advertisement designed to look like editorial content—a newspaper article, magazine feature, or online post that's actually paid promotion. The format exploits readers' trust in journalism while delivering a sales pitch. Publications typically label them "sponsored content" or "paid advertisement," though the labels are often subtle. {The travel section was half advertorials for cruise lines.}

Advice is most commonly used with verbs of giving, receiving, seeking, and following because that’s what people do with it. Advice has a predictable relationship with its related verb advise for British spellers who have other such pairs, such as license and licence, but this rule does not hold in U.S. English. Advice does not have a plural, so if you need to break it into separate bits, the phrase piece of advice comes in handy.

When you advise someone you give them a recommendation about what to do or not do. In other words, you give them advice. The typical way to use advise is preceding an infinitive phrase: I advise you to shop around before you settle on a doctor. When advise is followed by a clause beginning with a question word, its meaning is not so much about advice as it is simple information: We were advised that the road to the park was still closed. The same is true when an of phrase follows: The suspect was advised of his rights.

Someone who gives advice, especially in a professional or official capacity. An adviser may guide students on academic matters, counsel executives on strategy, or help individuals with finances. The spelling advisor is equally common and carries no difference in meaning. {She served as a foreign policy adviser to three presidents.}

An advisor is someone who gives advice, especially in an official or professional capacity: a financial {advisor}, a campaign {advisor}, a faculty {advisor}. The role implies expertise and ongoing consultation rather than casual suggestion. Also spelled adviser, with no difference in meaning—both are standard.

Advisory describes something that provides advice or recommendations rather than binding decisions: an advisory {committee}, an advisory {opinion}, an advisory {role}. As a noun, an advisory is a bulletin warning of potentially hazardous conditions: a weather {advisory}, a travel {advisory}, a health {advisory}. The distinction matters—advisory panels recommend while governing bodies decide.

Advocacy is the act of publicly supporting or arguing for a cause, policy, or person. An advocacy {group} works to influence public opinion or legislation. The word implies active effort beyond mere agreement—advocates speak up, organize, and push for change: {She devoted her career to advocacy for disability rights}.

Advocate has two pronunciations that distinguish the noun from the verb. The verb has a long ‘a’ in the last syllable. To advocate something, or advocate for something, is to promote it and work for it to succeed or prevail: They advocated the use of force. The organization advocates for pay equality. An advocate (unstressed vowel in the last syllable) is someone who promotes a particular idea, cause, or course of action: Sojourner Truth was a women’s rights advocate. In legal contexts an advocate is someone who pleads the cause of another.

Advocates are people who publicly support or argue for a cause, policy, or person. A defense advocate speaks on behalf of the accused; a patient advocate navigates healthcare systems for others. The verb advocate means to recommend or champion: {She advocates for stricter environmental regulations}. The noun stresses the first syllable; the verb stresses the last.

Advocating is actively supporting or arguing for a cause, policy, or person. Someone advocating for change pushes publicly for it: {She's been advocating for prison reform for years}. The word implies sustained effort rather than mere agreement—advocates speak up, make cases, and try to persuade others.
Adware is software that displays ads in a browser, typically in a pop-up window or a banner.

Aegis originally meant a shield or protective cloak associated with Zeus and Athena in Greek mythology. The word survives almost exclusively in the phrase {under the aegis of}, meaning under the protection, sponsorship, or guidance of: {The project operates under the aegis of the United Nations}. The sense has shifted from physical protection to institutional authority or backing.

An aeon is an immeasurably long period of time, often suggesting eternity or near-eternity. The word appears in religious and philosophical contexts to describe cosmic ages or divine timeframes, and in geology to name the largest divisions of Earth's history. In everyday use, aeon is hyperbolic: {I haven't seen you in aeons.} The spelling eon is more common in American English.

Aeons is the plural of aeon, a vast span of time—an age or era so long it defies ordinary measurement. The word appears most often in the plural to emphasize immensity: {The canyon was carved over aeons}. In geology and cosmology, an eon is a specific unit of deep time. The spelling aeon is more common in British English; eon predominates in American usage.

Aerial describes things relating to the air or atmosphere, or things that occur in the air. An aerial {photograph} is taken from above, typically from an aircraft. Aerial {acrobatics} happen high off the ground. The word also functions as a noun for an antenna, especially in British English: {the TV aerial on the roof}. In sports like skiing and skateboarding, an aerial is a maneuver performed in midair. The adjective can suggest lightness or ethereal quality: {the aerial grace of the dancers}.

An aerialist is a performer who does acrobatics high above the ground—on trapeze, aerial silks, tightrope, or similar apparatus. The term belongs to circus and theatrical performance: {The aerialists rehearsed their routine without a net}. Distinguished from acrobat by the emphasis on height and suspension.

Aerialists are performers who execute acrobatic feats high above the ground—on trapezes, silks, hoops, or tightropes. The term covers circus performers, competitive athletes, and contemporary dance artists who work suspended in the air. {The aerialists soared above the crowd without a safety net.}

Aerials are antennas—devices for transmitting or receiving radio or television signals. British English favors aerial where American English uses antenna: {The aerial on the roof needs adjusting}. In gymnastics and freestyle skiing, aerials are acrobatic maneuvers performed in the air. Aerial as an adjective means relating to the air or atmosphere: {aerial photography}, {aerial warfare}.

An aerie is the nest of a large bird of prey, especially an eagle, typically built high on a cliff or mountaintop. The word extends to any dwelling perched at a height: {Their penthouse aerie overlooked the city}. Also spelled eyrie.
clues: Precipice dwelling for birds of prey

definition: Aerobatics are spectacular maneuvers performed by aircraft—loops, rolls, spins, and dives that push beyond ordinary flight. The term covers both competitive flying and air show entertainment. A pilot who performs aerobatics is an aerobat. The word combines aero- with acrobatics, emphasizing the gymnastic quality of the movements: {The crowd gasped at the aerobatics display}.

Aerobic describes processes or activities that require oxygen. Aerobic exercise—running, swimming, cycling—elevates heart rate and breathing to increase oxygen flow: {I try to do thirty minutes of aerobics every morning}. In biology, aerobic organisms or processes depend on oxygen to function, as opposed to anaerobic ones that don't.

Aerobics is vigorous physical exercise designed to strengthen the heart and lungs by increasing oxygen consumption. The term typically refers to structured workout routines—often set to music—involving sustained rhythmic movement: {She teaches an aerobics class at the gym}. The adjective aerobic describes any activity requiring increased oxygen intake: aerobic {exercise}, aerobic {fitness}.

Aerodynamic describes shapes designed to move through air with minimal resistance. An aerodynamic {car} or {helmet} has smooth, streamlined contours that reduce drag. The term extends to anything sleek and efficient-looking: {The new phone has an aerodynamic profile}. In technical contexts, aerodynamic refers to the physics of air in motion around objects.

Aerodynamics is the study of how air moves around solid objects, especially objects moving through the atmosphere. The field emerged from the need to understand flight: how wings generate lift, how drag slows vehicles, how turbulence affects stability. The principles apply beyond aircraft to cars, buildings, cyclists, and anything else that interacts with moving air. {The car's aerodynamics were designed to reduce fuel consumption.}

Aeronautics is the science and practice of flight through the atmosphere—the design, construction, and operation of aircraft. The field encompasses both the engineering of flying machines and the principles that make flight possible: lift, drag, thrust, propulsion. {She studied aeronautics at MIT}. Aeronautical is the adjective: {aeronautical engineering}.

Aeronauts are people who operate or travel in aircraft, especially balloons or airships. The term evokes early aviation—intrepid figures ascending in wicker baskets beneath silk envelopes: {The aeronauts waved to the crowd as the balloon lifted off}. Modern usage is largely historical or literary, replaced by aviator, pilot, or astronaut depending on context.

An aerosol is a suspension of fine particles or liquid droplets in a gas—mist, fog, and smoke are natural aerosols. The word commonly refers to pressurized containers that release their contents as a spray: {aerosol cans}, {aerosol deodorant}. In scientific contexts, aerosols include airborne particles that can transmit disease or affect climate.

Aerosols are tiny particles or droplets suspended in air or gas. The term covers both natural phenomena—fog, dust, pollen—and manufactured products that spray fine mists: {hairspray}, {insecticide}, {spray paint}. In everyday use, aerosol usually means a pressurized canister that dispenses its contents as a spray: {an aerosol can of deodorant}. Aerosols became controversial when propellants were linked to ozone depletion.

Aerospace refers to Earth's atmosphere and the space beyond it, considered as a single realm for flight and navigation. The term combines aeronautics (atmospheric flight) and astronautics (space travel). As an adjective, it describes the industry, technology, and science of aircraft and spacecraft: {aerospace engineering}, {the aerospace sector}, {aerospace companies like Boeing and SpaceX}.

Aesthetic is a formal adjective that is used mainly to talk about beauty and the role it plays in art. The nouns that keep company with aesthetic are typically abstract, such as value, experience, quality, and appeal. When aesthetic modifies words like theory or principle it is about the various ideas that thinkers have had about how and why it is that we perceive, understand, and appreciate beauty. The spelling esthetic is sometimes used in U.S. English.

Aesthetics is the branch of philosophy concerned with beauty and taste—what makes things pleasing to perceive. More practically, aesthetics refers to the visual principles or style of something: {The restaurant's aesthetics are minimalist}, {She has great aesthetics}. In casual use, aesthetic (singular) now works as both noun and adjective: {That's very aesthetic}, {cottagecore aesthetic}. The word implies attention to how things look and feel rather than how they function.

Aether is an archaic or poetic spelling of ether. In classical and medieval thought, aether was the pure, luminous substance filling the upper regions of space beyond the terrestrial sphere—the fifth element, distinct from earth, air, fire, and water. Nineteenth-century physics proposed a luminiferous aether as the medium through which light waves traveled, a concept abandoned after experiments failed to detect it. The spelling persists in fantasy and science fiction to evoke cosmic or mystical qualities: {The ship sailed through the aether between worlds}.

Afar means at or from a great distance. The word is literary and somewhat archaic, appearing mostly in set phrases: {from afar}, {seen from afar}. It suggests romantic or poetic distance rather than mere physical separation: {She admired him from afar}. The word survives mainly because those phrases have become fixed expressions.

An affair is a matter or concern requiring attention: {affairs of state}, {put your affairs in order}. It can mean an event or social gathering: {The wedding was an elegant affair}. Most distinctively, an affair is a romantic or sexual relationship outside marriage or a committed partnership: {He's having an affair with his secretary}. The word implies something ongoing rather than a single encounter.

Affairs are matters requiring attention or management: {business affairs}, {foreign affairs}, {put your affairs in order}. The word often implies complexity or importance—financial affairs, affairs of state. In the singular, an affair is an event or occasion, often elaborate: {a black-tie affair}. An affair is also a romantic or sexual relationship outside marriage: {He's having an affair with his secretary}.

Like the word it is often confused with (effect), affect can be both a noun and a verb, but unlike effect, affect is usually a verb. It means have an effect or influence on: How does this mutation affect the mice? Affect can also convey contrivance: He affected a British accent in order to appear more refined. When affect is a noun the stress is on the first syllable. The noun affect is used primarily as a technical term in psychology to denote the experience of feeling an emotion.

Affectation is behavior or speech that is deliberately artificial, adopted to impress others rather than expressing genuine feeling or character. Someone with an affectation of British pronunciation didn't grow up speaking that way. The word carries disapproval—affectations are pretentious: {His constant name-dropping was pure affectation}. The plural often refers to specific mannerisms: {She dropped her aristocratic affectations after college}.

Affectations are behaviors, mannerisms, or speech patterns adopted artificially to impress others. The word carries judgment—affectations are pretentious by definition, attempts to seem more sophisticated, cultured, or interesting than one naturally is: {His British accent is pure affectation; he grew up in Ohio}. What reads as affectation to one person may be genuine style to another.

Affected describes something influenced or changed by external forces: {The affected areas were evacuated}. More commonly, affected means artificial or pretentious—behavior or speech that feels put on rather than natural: {an affected British accent}, {Her laugh seemed affected}. The two senses come from different meanings of the verb affect: to influence versus to put on airs.

Affection is warm feeling toward another person—fondness short of passion but beyond mere liking. It implies caring attachment: {She felt deep affection for her grandmother}. The word suggests tenderness expressed through small gestures rather than grand declarations. In older or medical usage, affection could mean any condition affecting the body or mind: {a nervous affection}.

Affectionate describes someone who readily shows warmth and fondness through words, touch, or attention: {an affectionate child}, {an affectionate gesture}. It suggests tenderness without intensity—gentler than passionate, warmer than friendly. {She gave him an affectionate squeeze on the arm.}

Affections are feelings of fondness or tender attachment toward someone or something. The word emphasizes emotional bonds rather than passion: {She had genuine affections for her students}. To win someone's affections is to earn their love or regard. The singular affection names the emotion itself; the plural often suggests the capacity for such feelings or their specific objects: {His affections were divided between two women}.

An affidavit is a written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation, used as evidence in legal proceedings. The person making the statement (the affiant) swears before a notary or other authorized official that the contents are true: {She submitted an affidavit attesting to her whereabouts that night}. Lying in an affidavit constitutes perjury.

Affiliate connects to the idea of adoption into a group or network. An affiliate is an organization or person attached to a larger body: {a local affiliate of the national broadcaster}, {affiliate marketing}. To affiliate is to formally connect or associate: {The hospital affiliated with the university}. Affiliated suggests membership without full absorption—linked but somewhat independent.

Affiliated describes a formal connection or association between entities—typically organizations, institutions, or individuals linked to a larger body. A hospital may be affiliated with a university; a local chapter is affiliated with a national organization. The relationship implies some official recognition or partnership without full merger: {The clinic is affiliated with the medical school}. To affiliate is to establish such a connection: {Several small unions affiliated with the larger federation}.

Affiliates are people or organizations formally connected to a larger entity while maintaining some independence. A company's affiliates might be subsidiaries or partners: {The network and its local affiliates}. In marketing, affiliates earn commissions by promoting others' products. The verb affiliate means to officially attach or associate: {The hospital recently affiliated with the university medical school}.

Affiliation is a connection or association with a group, organization, or institution. A person's political affiliation indicates which party they support or belong to. Religious affiliation identifies one's faith community. The word often appears in formal contexts: {Please list your institutional affiliations}. To affiliate with something is to join or associate with it: {The local chapter affiliated with the national organization}.

Affiliations are the organizations, groups, or causes with which a person or entity is formally connected. The word appears frequently in professional and institutional contexts: {List your affiliations on the application}, {The researcher disclosed no corporate affiliations}. Political or religious affiliations indicate where someone's loyalties or memberships lie. The singular affiliation refers to the state of being connected or the act of joining: {His affiliation with the party began in college}.

Affinities are natural attractions or connections between things. A person may have an affinity for languages, meaning they learn them easily and enjoy them. Chemical substances with affinity for each other bond readily. The word often implies something deeper than preference—a sense of kinship or inherent compatibility: {She felt immediate affinities with her new colleagues}. In biology, affinities indicate evolutionary relationships between species.

In scientific writing, affinity refers to the attractions between substances or particles: The drug has a high affinity for the estrogen receptor. Affinity also is used to characterize attraction or liking for a person, subject, or pursuit: The new composition reflects the composer’s lifelong affinity for Russian music. Perhaps the most modern use of the word is in the compound affinity card, a credit card that provides some benefit for an organization that the card’s user wishes to support.

Affirm means to state positively or declare something to be true: {She affirmed her commitment to the project}. In legal contexts, to affirm is to uphold a lower court's decision or to make a formal declaration without swearing an oath. More broadly, affirm suggests validation or support: {The results affirmed what we already suspected}. To affirm someone is to express approval or encouragement of them.

Affirmation is a statement declaring that something is true, or the act of making such a declaration. In legal contexts, an affirmation serves the same function as an oath but without religious reference, for those who object to swearing. In popular psychology and self-help, affirmations are positive statements repeated to oneself to encourage confidence or change thinking patterns: {She starts each morning with affirmations about her worth}. To affirm something is to state it positively or to validate it.

Affirmations are positive statements repeated to oneself, intended to encourage self-belief or manifest desired outcomes: {She starts each morning with affirmations about her worth}. The practice draws from self-help psychology and New Age thinking. More broadly, an affirmation is any declaration of support or agreement: {The court's ruling was an affirmation of free speech}.

Affirmative means expressing agreement or approval—the opposite of negative. An affirmative {answer} says yes; an affirmative {vote} supports a proposal. In grammar, an affirmative sentence states something as true rather than denying it. As a noun, {the affirmative} is the side arguing in favor of a proposition. As an interjection, affirmative is a formal or military way of saying yes: {Copy that, affirmative}. Affirmative {action} refers to policies favoring groups historically discriminated against.

Affirming describes words or actions that validate, support, or declare something to be true. An affirming {nod} signals agreement. Affirming {feedback} builds confidence. In contemporary usage, affirming often relates to acceptance of identity: {gender-affirming care}, {an affirming community for LGBTQ youth}. To be affirming is to make someone feel recognized and valued.

To afflict is to cause persistent pain, suffering, or distress. Diseases afflict the body; guilt afflicts the conscience; poverty afflicts communities. The word implies ongoing burden rather than momentary harm: {She was afflicted with chronic migraines}. What afflicts someone weighs on them—troubles that don't quickly pass.

Afflicted describes someone suffering from a condition, disease, or persistent hardship: {communities afflicted by poverty}, {patients afflicted with chronic pain}. The word implies ongoing burden rather than momentary trouble. As a noun, {the afflicted} refers collectively to those who suffer: {The charity serves the afflicted}. Something that afflicts causes distress or suffering.

Affliction is suffering or distress, or the condition causing it. The word carries weight—afflictions are serious troubles, not minor inconveniences: {chronic pain was her greatest affliction}, {the afflictions of poverty}. Disease, grief, and hardship are typical afflictions. The word often appears in religious or literary contexts, suggesting trials to be endured.

Afflictions are sources of persistent pain, distress, or suffering. The word typically describes conditions that burden someone over time rather than momentary troubles: chronic illnesses, disabilities, or enduring hardships. {Arthritis and other afflictions of aging limited her mobility.} The term carries a slightly formal or literary tone, often appearing in religious or medical contexts.

Affluence is wealth, especially the comfortable kind that allows for ease and luxury. The word often describes a general state of prosperity rather than specific riches: {suburban affluence}, {an era of affluence}. Someone living in affluence has more than enough money to meet their needs and desires.

Affluent means having plenty of money or resources—wealthy, well-off. An affluent {neighborhood} has expensive homes; an affluent {family} wants for nothing. The word carries connotations of comfortable abundance rather than extreme riches: {affluent suburbs}, {the affluent middle class}. As a noun, an affluent is a tributary stream flowing into a larger one.

Affluenza is a portmanteau of affluence and influenza, treating wealth as a kind of sickness. It describes the psychological malaise supposedly afflicting the wealthy—guilt, lack of motivation, or dissatisfaction despite material comfort. The term gained notoriety in a 2013 legal case where a teenager's lawyers argued his privileged upbringing left him unable to understand consequences: {His defense team claimed affluenza made him incapable of knowing right from wrong}. Often used critically or sarcastically.

Affogato is an Italian dessert of espresso poured over ice cream or gelato—typically vanilla. The word means "drowned" in Italian, describing the ice cream submerged in hot coffee. Served in cafés as both dessert and after-dinner drink: {We split an affogato after dinner}. Sometimes made with liqueur.

Afford means to have enough resources—usually money or time—for something: {Can we afford a vacation this year?} {I can't afford to wait any longer}. The word implies weighing cost against capacity. Afford also means to provide or supply: {The balcony affords a view of the harbor}. This older sense survives mainly in formal contexts.

Affordable means priced within reach—not necessarily cheap, but manageable given one's resources. {Affordable housing} is priced for moderate incomes. {An affordable luxury} is an indulgence that won't break the bank. The word often appears in marketing to suggest value without implying low quality.

An affront is an action or remark that insults or offends, especially one that feels like a deliberate slight to one's dignity: {His dismissive tone was an affront to everyone present}. To affront someone is to offend them openly: {She was affronted by the suggestion that she had cheated}.

Affronts are actions or remarks that insult or offend someone's dignity: {She catalogued the affronts she had suffered}. An affront is typically public or deliberate, a slight that demands acknowledgment. To affront someone is to insult them openly: {His casual dismissal affronted her}. The word carries a formal or literary tone.

An afghan is a knitted or crocheted blanket, typically made of colorful wool in decorative patterns. The word suggests handmade warmth and domestic craft: {She curled up under her grandmother's afghan}. Afghan hounds are tall, slender dogs with long silky coats. (Capitalized Afghan relates to Afghanistan.)

Afghans are soft knitted or crocheted blankets, typically made of wool or acrylic yarn in colorful patterns. They're draped over sofas or beds for warmth and decoration: {She curled up under an afghan to watch television}. The term likely comes from the traditional textiles of Afghanistan. Afghan is also a breed of tall, slender sighthound with long, silky hair. (Capitalized Afghans refers to people from Afghanistan.)

An aficionado is someone with keen interest and knowledge in a particular subject—originally bullfighting, but now applied broadly: {a jazz aficionado}, {an aficionado of fine wines}. The word carries more weight than "fan," suggesting genuine expertise and discriminating taste rather than mere enthusiasm.

Aficionados is the plural of aficionado, a person who is highly knowledgeable and enthusiastic about a particular subject or activity. The word comes from Spanish and carries more weight than mere fan—it suggests deep appreciation and expertise: {wine aficionados}, {jazz aficionados}, {The film attracted aficionados of classic horror}.

Aflame means on fire or lit up with flames: {The building was aflame within minutes}. More often the word is figurative—aflame with passion, desire, or strong emotion: {Her eyes were aflame with anger}. Autumn leaves can set a hillside aflame with color. The word is literary and somewhat old-fashioned; *on fire* or *blazing* serve most contexts.

Afloat means floating on water rather than sunk: {The ship stayed afloat through the storm}. By extension, it describes staying solvent or viable: {The business barely stayed afloat during the recession}. Rumors or ideas that are afloat are circulating: {There's a rumor afloat that the company is being sold}.

Afoot means in motion or underway: {Something strange is afoot}. The word suggests activity that may be secretive or significant—schemes afoot, plans afoot. In its older, more literal sense, afoot means on foot rather than riding or driving: {We set out afoot at dawn}.

Afraid describes the state of feeling fear or apprehension. You can be afraid of something specific {(afraid of heights, afraid of the dark)} or afraid that something will happen {(I'm afraid we'll miss the flight)}. In polite speech, {I'm afraid} softens unwelcome news: {I'm afraid the doctor can't see you today}. Unlike scared, afraid rarely appears before a noun—you wouldn't say "an afraid child."

An afro is a hairstyle in which naturally curly hair—especially Black hair—is grown out and shaped into a rounded mass. The style became a cultural and political statement during the Black Power movement of the 1960s and 70s, signaling pride in natural Black features: {She's been growing out her afro for two years}. The word also functions as an adjective: {afro hairstyle}, {afro pick}.

Afrobeat is a music genre that blends West African musical styles with American funk, jazz, and soul. Nigerian musician Fela Kuti pioneered the sound in the 1960s and 70s, characterized by complex rhythms, extended compositions, and often politically charged lyrics. The genre has influenced contemporary African and global popular music: {The club's DJ mixed afrobeat with electronic dance music}. (Capitalized Afrobeat is an alternate form.)

Afros is the plural of afro, a hairstyle in which tightly curled hair grows out from the head in a rounded shape. The style became a symbol of Black pride and identity in the 1960s and 70s: {The old photos showed everyone rocking afros}. The name comes from African American.

Aft means toward or at the rear of a ship or aircraft—the opposite of fore. As an adjective, it describes things located in that area: the {aft cabin}, the {aft deck}. As an adverb, it indicates direction: {We moved aft to check the engine}. The word belongs almost exclusively to nautical and aviation contexts.

After is frequent in expressions about both time and space. With reference to time, after is similar to past and later than. With reference to space, after is similar to behind. In figurative use, after relates to the idea of a goal, somewhat like at or toward: he came after me with a gun. After is also used to point out similarities between things that came before and things that came after: the boy is named after his grandfather; a painting styled after van Gogh. Though mainly a preposition, after can also be used as a conjunction to introduce a clause describing action before the main clause: She left after we had breakfast.

Afterbirth is the placenta and fetal membranes expelled from the uterus after a baby is born. In humans, medical staff typically dispose of it; in many animals, the mother eats it. The term is straightforward: it's what comes after the birth. {The midwife examined the afterbirth to make sure it was complete.}

Afterburn refers to combustion that continues after the main burning phase. In jet engines, afterburners inject extra fuel into the exhaust to produce additional thrust. In fitness, afterburn describes elevated calorie expenditure following intense exercise—the body continuing to burn energy as it recovers: {The high-intensity workout left her enjoying the afterburn for hours}.

An afterburner is a device in jet engines that injects extra fuel into the exhaust stream, producing additional thrust at the cost of higher fuel consumption. Fighter jets use afterburners for takeoff, rapid acceleration, or combat maneuvers: {The pilot hit the afterburner and climbed steeply}. Figuratively, to {kick in the afterburners} is to accelerate effort dramatically.

Afterburners are components in jet engines that inject additional fuel into the exhaust stream, igniting it to produce a dramatic burst of thrust. Military fighter jets use afterburners for takeoff, combat maneuvers, and supersonic flight, though the massive fuel consumption limits their use to short bursts. The term extends figuratively to describe any sudden surge of power or effort: {She kicked into afterburners for the final stretch of the race}.

Aftercare is the support or treatment provided after a primary intervention. Medical aftercare follows surgery or hospitalization: {The clinic provides aftercare for knee replacement patients}. In BDSM contexts, aftercare refers to the emotional and physical attention partners give each other after intense sexual activity—checking in, cuddling, or tending to any discomfort. The term also applies to services for people leaving institutions like rehab or prison.

An aftereffect is a consequence that follows some time after its cause, especially an unpleasant one that lingers after the main event has passed: {the aftereffects of surgery}, {the aftereffects of the storm}. The word often appears in the plural to describe a cluster of residual symptoms or consequences: {She was still dealing with the aftereffects of chemotherapy}.

Aftereffects are consequences that follow an event or action, especially unpleasant ones that linger after the primary experience has ended. The aftereffects of a medication persist after treatment stops. {She was still dealing with the aftereffects of the accident years later.} The word often implies secondary symptoms or delayed consequences rather than immediate results.

Afterglow is the light remaining in the sky after the sun has set, or the lingering glow from any faded light source. By extension, it describes the pleasant feeling that remains after a positive experience: {basking in the afterglow of victory}, {the afterglow of good sex}. The word suggests warmth slowly fading rather than abruptly ending.

Afterglows is the plural of afterglow—the light that lingers in the sky after the sun has set, when the horizon still holds color though the source is gone. The word extends to any pleasant feeling that remains after an experience has ended: {basking in the afterglow of victory}, {the afterglow of lovemaking}. Multiple sunsets produce multiple afterglows; multiple experiences, multiple lingering pleasures.

Afterhours describes activity occurring after regular business hours, typically late at night: {an afterhours club}, {afterhours trading}. The term often suggests something slightly illicit or underground—venues that stay open past legal closing times, or socializing that extends well beyond when respectable establishments shut down. Also written as two words or hyphenated: after hours, after-hours.

An afterimage is a visual impression that persists after the stimulus has been removed—the ghost of a bright light that floats in your vision after you look away, or the complementary colors you see after staring at a colored shape. {I could still see the afterimage of the camera flash.} The term extends figuratively to any lingering mental impression: {The afterimage of the accident haunted her for weeks}.

Afterimages are visual impressions that persist after the original stimulus has been removed. Stare at a bright light, then look away—the lingering spot you see is an afterimage. They can appear in the same colors as the original (positive) or in complementary colors (negative). The term extends figuratively to any sensory or emotional impression that lingers: {The afterimages of war haunted him for years}.
clues: Lingering impressions from staring too long

definition: The afterlife is existence after death—whatever form that takes in various belief systems. Heaven, hell, reincarnation, and ghostly persistence are all versions of an afterlife. The word also describes a later phase of something's existence: {The building had an afterlife as a community center}. {She didn't believe in an afterlife}.

Afterlives is the plural of afterlife—existence following death, as conceived in religious or spiritual belief. The word extends to what remains after something ends: {The film explores the afterlives of defunct shopping malls}. A work may have multiple afterlives through adaptations, revivals, or reinterpretations: {Shakespeare's plays have had countless afterlives on stage and screen}.

Aftermarket refers to the market for replacement parts, accessories, and services after a product's original sale. Most commonly applied to automobiles: {aftermarket stereo systems}, {aftermarket exhaust pipes}. The term distinguishes third-party or upgraded components from original equipment. In finance, aftermarket describes trading of securities after their initial public offering.

Aftermath originally meant a second crop of grass growing after the first has been mowed—the "after-math" (math being an old word for mowing). Now it refers to the period or consequences following a significant event, usually a destructive or turbulent one: {the aftermath of the hurricane}, {in the aftermath of the scandal}. The word carries connotations of dealing with damage or sorting through what remains.

Afternoon is the part of the day between noon and evening, roughly from 12 PM to 6 PM. It appears in greetings {(good afternoon)} and time expressions {(this afternoon}, {tomorrow afternoon)}. In British English, afternoon tea is a light meal. As an adjective: {the afternoon sun}, {an afternoon nap}.

Afternoons is the plural of afternoon—the hours between midday and evening. As an adverb, it means during the afternoon generally or repeatedly: {She works afternoons}, {I'm usually home afternoons}. The adverbial use is informal and typically American.

Afterparties are gatherings that follow a main event—typically a concert, wedding, premiere, or club night. They tend to be smaller, more informal, and often more exclusive than the primary event: {The real networking happened at the afterparty}. The singular is afterparty.

An afterparty is a gathering that follows a main event—typically held after a concert, wedding reception, awards ceremony, or club closing time. It's usually smaller, more intimate, and less formal than the preceding event: {The real fun happened at the afterparty}. Also spelled as two words: after party.

Afterplay is physical intimacy following sex—the cuddling, caressing, and quiet conversation that comes after orgasm. The term mirrors foreplay, marking the transition from sexual activity back to ordinary closeness. {She values afterplay as much as the sex itself.}

Afterschool describes activities, programs, or care that take place after the school day ends: {afterschool tutoring}, {an afterschool job}, {afterschool snacks}. The term typically refers to the hours between dismissal and when parents return from work. Also spelled as two words: after school, or hyphenated: after-school.

Aftershave is a scented liquid applied to the face after shaving. It typically contains alcohol or other astringents that tighten pores and prevent infection from small cuts. The term covers everything from medicinal-smelling drugstore staples to expensive colognes marketed as aftershave: {He slapped on some aftershave before his date}.

An aftershock is a smaller earthquake that follows a larger one, occurring as the earth's crust adjusts after the main seismic event: {Aftershocks continued for weeks after the initial quake}. Figuratively, aftershocks are the secondary effects or repercussions of any disruptive event: {The political aftershocks of the scandal were still being felt months later}.

Aftershocks are smaller earthquakes that follow a major seismic event, occurring as the earth's crust adjusts to the shift. They can continue for days, weeks, or even months after the initial quake. Figuratively, aftershocks are the secondary effects or repercussions of any disruptive event: {The political aftershocks of the scandal lasted for years}.

An aftershow is an event following a main performance—typically a concert, theater production, or broadcast. Musicians often host aftershows at smaller venues for intimate performances after their main concerts: {We got into the aftershow at a club downtown}. In television, an aftershow is a program that immediately follows and discusses another show: {The aftershow breaks down each episode}.

An aftertaste is a flavor that lingers in the mouth after eating or drinking something: {The wine left a bitter aftertaste}. The word extends to any residual impression or feeling that persists after an experience has ended: {The argument left an aftertaste of resentment}.

An afterthought is something thought of or added later, after the main matter has been settled or completed. The word often carries a dismissive edge—to call something an afterthought suggests it wasn't important enough to consider initially: {The garage was clearly an afterthought, tacked onto the house years later}. A person treated as an afterthought feels overlooked or secondary.

Afterthoughts are ideas or considerations that come only after a decision has been made or an action taken. The word often implies something was overlooked or given insufficient attention: {Safety was an afterthought in the original design}. An afterthought can also be something added belatedly: {The postscript read like an afterthought}.

Afterward means at a later time, following some event or action: {We had dinner and went for a walk afterward}. It suggests sequence rather than a specific interval—the later event could come minutes or years after. Also spelled afterwards, with no difference in meaning. The form afterward is more common in American English, afterwards in British.
clues: At some point down the road

definition: Afterwards means at a later time, following some event or action: {We had dinner and went for a walk afterwards}. It implies sequence rather than simultaneity—something happens, then something else follows. Interchangeable with afterward, though afterwards is slightly more common in British English.

An afterword is a section at the end of a book, typically written by someone other than the author, offering commentary, context, or reflection on the work. Unlike a preface or foreword, which prepares the reader, an afterword assumes the book has been read: {The afterword discusses how the novel was received when first published}.
The core idea of again, an adverb, is more than once. Its other, less frequent uses all grow out of this idea. The common adverbial phrase again and again means repeatedly.

Against conveys the idea of opposition and is the commonest preposition after words suggesting conflict or competition such as game, war, fight, case, charge, and attack. Uses of against that aren’t nuanced with conflict refer to physical contact: lean the ladder against the wall. Against can also be used in comparing and contrasting two things: how do the benefits stack up against the risks?

Agape has two distinct meanings depending on pronunciation. With stress on the second syllable (uh-GAPE), it means wide open, especially of the mouth: {She stood agape at the news}, {His jaw hung agape in disbelief}. With stress on the first syllable (AH-gah-pay), it refers to selfless, unconditional love—particularly the divine love of God for humanity in Christian theology, distinguished from romantic or familial love.

Agate is a semiprecious stone characterized by bands or patterns of color, formed from layers of chalcedony. It comes in many varieties—moss agate, fire agate, blue lace agate—prized for jewelry and decorative objects. In printing, agate is a small type size (about 5.5 points), once standard for classified ads and sports statistics in newspapers.

Agates are semiprecious stones characterized by bands of color, a variety of chalcedony prized for jewelry and decorative objects. The banding creates distinctive patterns—no two agates look alike. In printing, agate is a small type size (5.5 points), used for classified ads and fine print: {The scores were listed in agate type}.

Agave is a genus of succulent plants native to hot, arid regions of the Americas, characterized by thick fleshy leaves arranged in rosettes, often with sharp spines at the tips. Several species are commercially important: blue agave provides the base for tequila, while others yield mezcal, sisal fiber, or agave nectar (a sweetener marketed as a honey alternative). Most agave plants flower only once after many years, then die.

Age is a noun that designates a length of time in which something existed or flourished: the age of dinosaurs, the age of steam engines. The age of a person or object is how old they are in years: At what age did you begin to date? If the unit is not years, it is usually specified: Babies ages newborn to 18 months. Middle age is a vague term applied to people from about 45 to 65 years old. Age or ages can also mean a very long time: We haven’t been back there for ages. As a verb, age refers to allowing something to reach maturity: I don’t think this beef was aged properly. When a person or something else ages, they get older.

Aged describes something that has grown old or been allowed to mature over time. Wine and cheese are aged to develop flavor; aged {beef} hangs to tenderize. An aged {person} is elderly. The word has two pronunciations: one syllable when describing matured products {(aged whiskey)}, two syllables for elderly people {(an aged widow)}. With a number, aged means having reached that age: {a child aged six}.

Ageing is the British spelling of aging—the process of growing older or the changes that come with time. Wine and cheese improve with ageing; skin and joints typically don't. As an adjective, it describes something showing signs of age: {an ageing infrastructure}, {an ageing population}. The spelling with the e is standard in British English and common in scientific literature worldwide.

Ageism is discrimination or prejudice based on a person's age. The term most often describes bias against older people—in hiring, healthcare, or social attitudes—but can apply to any age group: {Mandatory retirement policies are a form of ageism}. The word parallels racism and sexism in structure and meaning.

Ageist describes attitudes, practices, or people that discriminate based on age—typically against older people, though sometimes against the young. An ageist {hiring policy} might favor younger applicants. {That's an ageist assumption about what seniors can do}. The noun ageist refers to someone who holds such views.

Ageless describes something or someone unaffected by age or the passage of time. An ageless {beauty} retains youthful appearance; an ageless {truth} remains valid across generations. The word suggests timelessness—neither old nor young, but somehow beyond such categories: {Her style is ageless}.

Agelessness is the quality of being unaffected by time—neither young nor old, or somehow both at once. It describes people who don't seem to age: {Her agelessness is remarkable; she looks the same as she did twenty years ago}. It also applies to things that remain perpetually relevant or appealing: {the agelessness of Shakespeare's themes}.

Agencies is the plural of agency. An agency is an organization that provides a service or performs a function on behalf of others: {employment agencies}, {travel agencies}, {government agencies}. The word also means the capacity to act or exert power: {human agency}, {moral agency}. When something happens {through the agency of} someone, they serve as the instrument or means.

Agency is the capacity to act or exert power. A person with agency can make choices and influence outcomes: {The new policy gives employees more agency over their schedules}. An agency is also an organization that performs services—a government agency, a talent agency, an advertising agency. These senses connect: an agency acts on behalf of others, exercising delegated power.

An agenda is a list of items to be addressed, typically at a meeting: {What's on the agenda for today?} More broadly, it means a plan or set of goals: {The administration's policy agenda}. When someone is said to have {an agenda} or {a hidden agenda}, the implication is ulterior motives—purposes they haven't openly declared.

Agendas is the plural of agenda—lists of items to be addressed, especially at meetings: {The committee distributed agendas before each session}. The singular agenda, though Latin plural in origin, now takes standard English pluralization. In figurative use, agendas are underlying motives or plans: {Everyone at the table had their own agendas}.

Agender describes someone who experiences no gender identity or feels gender-neutral—neither male nor female nor any other gender category. The term emerged from online LGBTQ+ communities in the early 2010s. As an adjective: {My roommate is agender and uses they/them pronouns}. As a noun: {an agender}.

The many meanings of agent might be summarized as person in charge or doer, and range from general (one who acts, rather than being acted upon) to particular (one who represents an agency). The idea of representation is pervasive, where an organization or other entity is implied by the existence of an agent, or named (real estate agent, FBI agent).

Agents is the plural of agent—someone or something that acts or produces an effect. In business and entertainment, agents represent clients: {Her agents negotiated the contract}. In espionage, agents gather intelligence or conduct operations. Chemical agents cause reactions; cleaning agents remove dirt. In computing and AI, agents are autonomous programs that perform tasks: {The company deployed AI agents to handle customer inquiries}.

Ages is the plural of age, but more commonly appears as an informal intensifier meaning a very long time: {I haven't seen her in ages}, {It took ages to get through security}. The expression suggests duration that feels excessive or noteworthy, though the actual time varies by context—ages might be weeks, months, or years.

Aggravate means to make worse: {The medication aggravated her symptoms}, {His comments only aggravated the situation}. In common usage, aggravate also means to annoy or irritate: {Stop aggravating your sister}. This second sense, though widely used, is considered incorrect by some traditionalists who insist the word should only mean "worsen."

Aggravated intensifies wrongdoing or injury. An aggravated assault involves circumstances that make it more serious than simple assault—use of a weapon, intent to commit another crime, or attack on a protected person. Aggravated can also mean irritated or annoyed: {I was aggravated by the constant delays}. Legal and informal uses coexist, though purists sometimes object to the irritation sense.

Aggravating means making worse or more serious: {Smoking aggravated his asthma}. More commonly, it means annoying or irritating: {an aggravating habit of interrupting}. Purists insist on the first meaning, but the second dominates everyday speech. {Stop being so aggravating!}

Aggravation is the act of making something worse, or the state of being made worse: {The construction noise was an aggravation of an already stressful situation}. More commonly, aggravation means irritation or annoyance: {I don't need this aggravation right now}. The informal sense dominates everyday speech, while the formal sense—worsening of a condition or problem—persists in legal and medical contexts: {aggravation of a preexisting injury}.

Aggravations are things that irritate, annoy, or make a situation worse. The word captures both minor irritants—{the daily aggravations of commuting}—and factors that genuinely worsen a condition or problem. In legal contexts, aggravations are circumstances that increase the severity of a crime or its punishment. The term implies a cumulative quality: one aggravation might be tolerable, but multiple aggravations tend to compound frustration.

Variation in the pronunciation of the last syllable distinguishes the verb aggregate from its noun and adjective counterparts. Common to all meanings is the idea of many collected into one. When you aggregate something, you gather it in one place or under one concept: The analyst will aggregate the survey data. An aggregate substance is composed of smaller parts: Concrete contains fine aggregates, like sand, and coarse aggregates, like gravel.

Aggression is hostile or violent behavior toward others, often unprovoked: {an act of aggression}, {military aggression}. The word implies the aggressor initiates conflict rather than responding to it. In psychology, aggression covers a spectrum from verbal hostility to physical attack. {His aggression on the basketball court earned him technical fouls.}

Aggressive describes behavior that is forceful, hostile, or ready to attack. An aggressive {dog} may bite; an aggressive {driver} cuts people off. The word extends to any pushy or assertive approach: aggressive {marketing}, aggressive {treatment} of a disease. In sports and business, aggressive often carries positive connotations of boldness and competitive drive: {She took an aggressive approach to expanding the company}.

An aggressor is the party who initiates conflict or attack. The term implies fault—the aggressor started it, whether in a schoolyard fight, a war, or a legal dispute. {Russia was widely condemned as the aggressor in the conflict.} International law distinguishes aggressors from those acting in self-defense.

Aggressors are those who initiate an attack or conflict. The term carries moral weight—calling someone an aggressor assigns blame for starting hostilities: {The treaty required aggressors to pay reparations}. In international law, the aggressor nation bears responsibility for war. The word applies beyond warfare to anyone who acts with unprovoked hostility: {She was the aggressor in the argument}.

Aggrieved describes someone who feels wronged or unjustly treated: {The aggrieved party filed a complaint}. It suggests a sense of injury that may or may not be justified—an aggrieved tone can indicate legitimate grievance or self-pity. In legal contexts, an aggrieved party is one whose rights have been violated.

Aggro is aggressive behavior or hostility, often needlessly confrontational: {Why all the aggro? I just asked a question}. Common in British and Australian slang. In gaming, aggro refers to a hostile creature's attention—drawing aggro means becoming its target: {The tank needs to hold aggro so the healer doesn't get hit}.

Aghast means struck with shock, horror, or dismay. The word suggests being frozen or stunned by what you've witnessed: {She stood aghast at the destruction}. It typically follows a linking verb: {He was aghast to learn the truth}. The reaction is stronger than surprised but less physical than horrified—more about being appalled than afraid.

Agile describes quick, nimble movement—the ability to change direction easily and gracefully: {an agile climber}, {agile fingers on the keyboard}. The word extends to mental quickness: {an agile mind} adapts rapidly to new information. In software development, Agile (often capitalized) names a methodology emphasizing iterative progress, collaboration, and flexibility over rigid planning.

Agility is the ability to move quickly and easily, with nimble coordination: {The cat leaped with surprising agility}. The word extends beyond physical movement to mental quickness—the capacity to think and adapt rapidly: {intellectual agility}, {The startup's agility let it outmaneuver larger competitors}. In business contexts, agility often describes organizational flexibility and responsiveness to change.

Aging is the process of growing older or showing the effects of time. Wine ages in barrels; cheese ages in caves. An aging {population} has an increasing proportion of elderly people. The aging {process} refers to biological decline over time. As an adjective, aging describes something or someone showing signs of age: {an aging rock star}, {aging infrastructure}. Also spelled ageing, especially in British English.

Agita is anxiety, heartburn, or general aggravation—the kind of churning discomfort that might be physical, emotional, or both. The word comes from Italian-American slang and suggests a visceral unease: {This project is giving me agita}. It often implies that someone or something is being a source of stress: {Why do you let him cause you so much agita?}

To agitate is to stir up or disturb. You can agitate a liquid by shaking it, agitate a crowd by rousing strong feelings, or agitate for change by persistent advocacy: {Activists agitated for voting rights}. Someone who is agitated is anxious, restless, or emotionally unsettled: {The news left her visibly agitated}.

Agitated describes a state of nervous excitement or troubled restlessness. Someone who is agitated may pace, fidget, or have difficulty staying calm: {The agitated passengers demanded answers about the delay}. The word applies equally to emotional upset and physical disturbance—water can be agitated by stirring, just as a person can be agitated by bad news. In clinical contexts, agitated often describes patients experiencing confusion or distress.

Agitates means to stir up or disturb. You agitate a liquid by shaking or swirling it. A washing machine agitates clothes to clean them. More commonly, agitate describes stirring up emotions or unrest: {The news agitated her}. Someone who agitates for change actively promotes it, often through public advocacy. An agitated person is visibly upset or anxious.

Agitating means stirring up or disturbing. You agitate a liquid by shaking it. To agitate someone is to make them anxious or upset: {The news was agitating her}. To agitate for something is to campaign publicly: {Workers agitated for better conditions}. An agitating person or situation causes unease or irritation: {I found his constant questions agitating}.

Agitation is a state of anxious unrest or troubled excitement. Someone in agitation paces, fidgets, or can't settle down: {She waited in agitation for the test results}. The word also means the act of stirring up—agitation of a liquid keeps particles suspended, while political agitation stirs up public sentiment for change.

An agitator is a person who stirs up public opinion or discontent, especially for political change: {union agitators}, {outside agitators blamed for the protests}. The word often carries negative connotations—implying troublemaking rather than principled activism. In machinery, an agitator is a device that shakes or stirs, as in a washing machine.

Agitators are people who stir up public opinion or sentiment, typically to provoke social or political change. The term often carries negative connotations—suggesting troublemakers rather than reformers: {Outside agitators were blamed for the unrest}. In machinery, an agitator is a device that stirs or shakes contents, as in a washing machine.

Agitprop is political propaganda, especially that which aims to agitate and mobilize rather than simply inform. The term originated in Soviet Russia, where dedicated departments produced art, theater, and literature advancing communist ideology. Now it describes any overtly political creative work, often dismissively: {The film was entertaining despite its agitprop tendencies}. The word combines agitation and propaganda.

An aglet is the small plastic or metal sheath wrapped around the end of a shoelace or drawstring cord. It keeps the fibers from fraying and makes the lace easier to thread through eyelets. The word comes from the French for "needle," which is what an aglet resembles and functions as when you're lacing up shoes.

Agnostic can function as either a noun or an adjective, to denote a person or characterize a belief or point of view. An agnostic is someone who is either not firmly committed to a belief in God, or who holds that God is unknowable. Agnostic is sometimes used in contrast to atheist, which is a firm denial of the existence of God. Outside of religious contexts, agnostic is a way of characterizing their opinion about something that is not known with certainty: He is agnostic about whether early painters might have used mirrors to project images.

Agnosticism is the position that the existence of God or gods is unknown or unknowable. Unlike atheism, which denies the divine, agnosticism suspends judgment: {His agnosticism prevented him from joining either the church or the atheist society}. The term extends beyond religion to any stance of principled uncertainty: {scientific agnosticism about untestable claims}.

Agnostics are people who believe that the existence of God or ultimate reality is unknown or unknowable. Unlike atheists, who deny God's existence, agnostics suspend judgment: {She was raised Catholic but became an agnostic in college}. The term extends beyond religion to anyone who withholds commitment on contested questions: {I'm agnostic about whether remote work improves productivity}.

Ago marks time elapsed from the present backward: {three days ago}, {years ago}, {not long ago}. It always follows the time expression it modifies. The reference point is usually now, but in narrative can shift to a past moment: {She had arrived two hours ago}. {Long ago} reaches into the distant past; {a moment ago} barely precedes the present.

Agonies is the plural of agony—intense physical or mental suffering. The word often appears with emphasis on multiplicity or duration: {the agonies of childbirth}, {the agonies of withdrawal}. To be {in agonies} is to suffer acutely. The phrase {agonies of indecision} describes painful uncertainty when facing a difficult choice.

Agonise is the British spelling of agonize, meaning to suffer intense physical or mental pain, or to struggle with a difficult decision. When you agonise over something, you worry about it excessively, turning it over in your mind: {She agonised for weeks over whether to accept the job offer}. The word suggests prolonged, tortured deliberation rather than quick consideration.

Agonised is the British spelling of agonized. It describes something marked by intense physical or mental suffering: {an agonised cry}, {her agonised expression}. The word often characterizes sounds, looks, or decisions made under great distress. An agonised decision involves painful deliberation, weighing options that all seem costly.
clues: Experienced severe mental or physical torment

definition: Agonising is the British spelling of agonizing. It describes something that causes intense physical or mental suffering: {an agonising wait for test results}, {the agonising pain of a broken bone}. It also characterizes difficult decisions or processes that involve great struggle: {After agonising deliberation, she chose to leave}.

To agonize is to suffer intense mental distress or to struggle painfully with a decision: {She agonized over whether to accept the job offer}. The word emphasizes prolonged inner turmoil rather than physical pain. Someone who agonizes dwells on a problem, turning it over repeatedly without resolution. Agonizing as an adjective describes something that causes such distress: {an agonizing wait for test results}.

Agonized describes something marked by or expressing intense physical or mental suffering. An agonized {scream} conveys extreme pain. An agonized {decision} is one reached only after prolonged inner torment. The word emphasizes visible or audible signs of distress: {She gave him an agonized look before turning away}.

Agonizes is the third-person singular of agonize, meaning to suffer intense mental distress or to struggle painfully with a decision. Someone who agonizes over a choice wrestles with it at length, turning possibilities over and over: {She agonizes over every word in her emails}. The word implies prolonged, sometimes excessive deliberation rather than quick resolution.

Agonizing describes something that causes intense physical or mental suffering: {an agonizing decision}, {agonizing pain}. The word often applies to difficult choices where every option hurts: {After agonizing deliberation, she chose to end the relationship}. Something agonizing may also be unbearably slow or drawn out: {The agonizing wait for test results lasted two weeks}.

Agony is extreme physical or mental suffering—pain so intense it dominates consciousness. A person in agony writhes, cries out, can think of nothing else. The word applies to both bodily torment {the agony of a kidney stone} and emotional anguish {the agony of watching her marriage fall apart}. To {agonize} over a decision is to struggle painfully with it. {The agony of defeat} has become a sports cliché.

An agora is a public gathering place or marketplace, especially in ancient Greek cities. The term extends to any open forum for assembly or exchange of ideas: {The internet has become a global agora for political debate}. In modern usage, agora sometimes describes outdoor markets or public squares. (Capitalized Agora typically refers to the specific ancient marketplace in Athens.)

Agoraphobia is intense fear of situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable—crowded spaces, open areas, public transportation, or being outside the home alone. The condition often develops after panic attacks, leading people to avoid places where attacks occurred. Severe cases may confine someone entirely to their home: {Her agoraphobia kept her housebound for years}.

Agree means to share an opinion or reach a common understanding: {We agreed that the plan was too risky}. Two parties agree when they consent to terms: {They agreed on a price}. Things that agree are consistent or compatible: {Your story doesn't agree with the evidence}. Food that doesn't agree with you causes digestive trouble. In grammar, words agree when they match in number, gender, or case.

Agreeable describes something pleasant or willing to go along. An agreeable {temperature} is comfortable; an agreeable {companion} is easy to be with. A person who is agreeable readily assents: {She was agreeable to the plan}. The word suggests both pleasantness and compliance—sometimes implying someone too eager to please: {He's agreeable to a fault}.

Agreed functions as an affirmation—a way of confirming that parties share the same understanding or have reached consensus: {We meet at noon? Agreed.} As an adjective, it describes something already settled or accepted by all involved: {the agreed price}, {the agreed-upon terms}. The word often closes negotiations or confirms mutual understanding.

Agreement is a state of harmony or accord between parties. When people reach an agreement, they've arrived at a shared understanding or decision: {We finally came to an agreement about the terms}. An agreement can be a formal arrangement—a contract, treaty, or settlement. In grammar, agreement refers to correspondence between words: subjects and verbs agree in number. {There was general agreement that changes were needed.}

Agreements are arrangements in which parties reach a shared understanding or commitment. The word covers everything from informal understandings {We had an agreement to split the cost} to formal contracts {a rental agreement}. Agreement also means the state of being in accord: {The committee reached agreement on the budget}. In grammar, agreement refers to correspondence between words in number, gender, or case.

Agribusiness is farming and related industries treated as a large-scale commercial enterprise rather than a traditional way of life. The term encompasses not just growing crops and raising livestock, but the entire network of seed companies, equipment manufacturers, food processors, and distributors: {Family farms struggle to compete with agribusiness}. The word often carries connotations of industrial scale and corporate ownership.

Agriculture is the practice of cultivating land and raising animals for food, fiber, and other products. It encompasses farming crops, raising livestock, and the broader systems of production that feed populations. {The region's economy depends on agriculture.} Agricultural can describe anything related to farming: {agricultural policy}, {agricultural land}.

Aground describes a boat or ship stuck on the bottom in shallow water, unable to move: {The tanker ran aground on a sandbar}. The word combines the prefix a- (meaning "on" or "in a state of") with ground. Figuratively, plans or projects that run aground have stalled or failed.

People say Aha! when they discover something or learn something, often something that they suspected was true. This has given rise to the expression aha moment, a moment when someone gains a sudden insight or suddenly understands what is happening.

Ahchoo represents the sound of a sneeze, used in writing to indicate someone has sneezed: {Ahchoo! She reached for a tissue}. Like other onomatopoeic words, spelling varies—achoo and atchoo are common alternatives. The word functions as both an interjection and a noun: {That was quite an ahchoo}.

Ahead means in front or in advance of a position. You walk ahead of someone, plan ahead for the future, or get ahead in your career. It suggests forward motion or progress: {The road ahead looks clear}, {She's ahead of schedule}. In competitions, being ahead means winning: {We're ahead by three points}. To go ahead is to proceed: {Go ahead and start without me}.
Ahem is meant to imitate the sound of someone clearing their throat, as when they are about to speak. It nearly always has a negative connotation.
Ahoy is historically associated with sailors but it works on land too. After a noun it indicates that the thing named is within view or on its way: ship ahoy!

Aid is help or assistance, especially of a practical or material kind. Countries send foreign aid—money, food, supplies—to those in need. A hearing aid assists with sound; a visual aid helps explain something. First aid is emergency medical care. To aid someone is to help them: {She aided the investigation}. An aide, spelled differently, is a person who assists.

An aide is a person who assists someone important—typically in government, military, or institutional settings. A presidential aide handles administrative tasks and counsel. A nurse's aide supports medical staff. The word implies a subordinate role with access to power: {The senator's aides drafted the legislation}. Distinguished from aid, which is the assistance itself.

Aides is the plural of aide—people who assist someone in a position of authority. Presidential aides advise on policy. Home health aides help with daily living tasks. The word often appears in political contexts: {White House aides declined to comment}. Not to be confused with AIDS, the disease.
Aids is the plural of aid—things that help: {visual aids}, {hearing aids}. Also the third-person verb: {She aids refugees at the border}. (All-caps AIDS is the disease.)

Aikido is a Japanese martial art focused on redirecting an attacker's energy rather than meeting force with force. Practitioners use joint locks, throws, and circular movements to neutralize aggression without causing unnecessary harm. The discipline emphasizes harmony and self-defense over combat: {She's been studying aikido for years}. Unlike karate or taekwondo, aikido has no competitive sparring—training partners take turns as attacker and defender.

Ail means to trouble or afflict, usually in reference to health or wellbeing: {What ails you?} The word sounds slightly old-fashioned or literary in everyday speech, though it remains common in compounds like ailment. Things other than people can ail: {Whatever ails the economy won't be fixed overnight}.
