The clear gel inside aloe vera leaves is widely used to soothe burns, moisturize skin, and treat minor wounds: {She rubbed aloe on her sunburn}. Aloe appears in countless lotions, drinks, and health products.

Aloft is more often an adverb than a preposition but as a preposition its meaning doesn’t change: it means above, especially up in the air: communications towers aloft the mountain. As an adverb, aloft follows some form of the verb hold more than 90% of the time.

Aloha is used only in Hawaii or in reference to Hawaii. In Hawaiian, aloha has a range of meanings similar to greeting words found in other languages. Colloquially, it can be used to convey a relaxed or festive feeling or appearance associated with a tropical paradise: You’re looking very aloha today.

Alone means without others present or involved. You can be physically alone {(She lives alone)} or emotionally alone {(He felt alone in his grief)}. It also means only or exclusively: {Price alone won't determine the winner}. {Leave me alone} asks for solitude or to stop being bothered. {Let alone} introduces something even less likely: {I can't afford rent, let alone a vacation}.

Along is mainly used in relation to space that can be conceived as a line: we walked along the river or they ran into a storm along the way. The common phrase along the lines of has a meaning very similar to and slightly looser than in accordance with.

Aloof means emotionally distant or uninvolved—standing apart rather than engaging. Someone aloof keeps others at arm's length, whether from shyness, disdain, or self-protection: {She remained aloof from office politics}. The word often carries a whiff of coldness or superiority: {His aloof manner made him hard to approach}.

Aloofness is the quality of being distant, detached, or uninvolved. An aloof person keeps others at arm's length, whether from shyness, arrogance, or deliberate reserve: {Her aloofness made it hard to get to know her}. The word often carries a slight chill—suggesting someone who stands apart when warmth might be expected.

Aloud means in a voice that can be heard, as opposed to silently or in one's head. {She read the poem aloud to the class.} The word emphasizes that sound is produced and audible to others, distinguishing spoken expression from merely thinking or reading silently. To wonder aloud or think aloud is to voice one's thoughts as they occur, often without intending a formal statement.

An alp is a high mountain pasture, particularly in the European Alps where livestock graze during summer months. The word appears most often in its plural form referring to the mountain range itself. In singular lowercase use, it describes any high mountain or peak: {snow-capped alps visible from the valley}. (Capitalized Alp refers to a peak in the Alps range; capitalized Alps is the mountain range.)

An alpaca is a South American mammal related to the llama, domesticated for its soft, luxurious fleece. Smaller and shaggier than llamas, alpacas are raised primarily for fiber rather than as pack animals. The word also refers to the wool itself or fabric made from it: {an alpaca sweater}, {alpaca yarn}.

Alpacas is the plural of alpaca, a domesticated South American mammal related to the llama, raised primarily for its soft, luxurious fleece. Smaller and gentler than llamas, alpacas have become popular on hobby farms: {The alpacas need shearing before summer}. Their fiber is prized for warmth without weight.

Alpenglow is the rosy or golden light that illuminates mountain peaks just before sunrise or after sunset, when the sun is below the horizon but its rays still catch the summits. The effect is particularly striking on snow-covered peaks: {We watched the alpenglow fade from the Rockies}. The word comes from German and is used mainly in mountaineering and nature writing.

An alpenhorn is a long wooden horn, traditionally used by Swiss herders to call cattle or signal across Alpine valleys. The instrument, sometimes called an alphorn, produces deep, resonant tones and has become a symbol of Swiss folk culture: {The sound of an alpenhorn echoed across the mountainside}.

Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, and by extension means the beginning or first of anything. In social dynamics, an alpha is the dominant individual in a group—the alpha {male} or alpha {female} who leads. Tech companies release alpha {versions} as early test software, before beta. In finance, alpha measures investment returns above a benchmark. {He thinks he's the alpha of every room he walks into.} (Capitalized Alpha may refer to specific organizations, products, or code names.)

The alphabet is the complete set of letters used in a writing system, arranged in a fixed order. English uses the Latin alphabet of twenty-six letters. By extension, alphabet refers to basic elements or fundamentals: {the alphabet of music theory}. Learning one's alphabet means learning to read. Alphabet soup describes a confusing jumble of acronyms or initialisms: {The federal government is an alphabet soup of agencies}.

Alphabetical describes an arrangement according to the order of letters in an alphabet, from A to Z in English. Lists, indexes, and directories are commonly organized this way to make items easier to locate: {The contacts are sorted in alphabetical order}. When something is alphabetized, it has been put into alphabetical sequence. The term can also appear as alphabetic, with no difference in meaning.

Alphabets is the plural of alphabet—systems of letters used for writing a language. Each alphabet arranges its characters in a conventional order: the Roman alphabet from A to Z, the Greek from alpha to omega. Different languages use different alphabets: {She learned both the Cyrillic and Arabic alphabets}. Figuratively, alphabets can mean the basics: {the alphabets of diplomacy}.

Alphas is the plural of alpha, the first letter of the Greek alphabet. In discussions of social hierarchy, alphas are dominant individuals—the leaders or top-ranking members of a group: {The alphas in the office always grab the best parking spots}. In software development, alphas are early test versions of programs, preceding betas. In finance, alphas measure investment returns above a benchmark.

An alphorn is a long wooden horn, traditionally used by Swiss herders to call cattle and communicate across mountain valleys. The instrument, typically six to twelve feet long, produces a limited range of deep, resonant tones. Its distinctive sound has become emblematic of Alpine culture: {The alphorn echoed across the valley}.

Alphorns are long wooden horns traditionally used in the Swiss Alps, typically eight to twelve feet long and curved at the bell end. Herders originally used them to call cattle and communicate across mountain valleys. The instrument produces deep, resonant tones and has become a symbol of Swiss folk culture: {The alphorn echoed across the meadow}.

Alpine describes things related to high mountains, particularly those above the tree line where conditions are harsh and vegetation is sparse: {alpine meadows}, {alpine skiing}. The word suggests rugged terrain, thin air, and cold temperatures. In ecology, alpine zones are distinct habitats characterized by low-growing plants adapted to wind and frost. (Capitalized Alpine refers specifically to the European Alps.)

An alpinist is a mountain climber, specifically one who climbs in the Alps or engages in high-altitude mountaineering. The term suggests technical skill and serious commitment to the sport, distinguishing alpinists from casual hikers: {The alpinists prepared for their assault on the north face}.

Already indicates that something has happened before now or before a specified time: {I've already eaten}, {By noon they had already left}. It often emphasizes that something occurred sooner than expected: {Are you leaving already?} In informal American speech, already can express impatience: {Enough already!}, {Let's go already!}

Older usage books often find fault with the spelling alright as a substitute for all right, but it has been in use for 150 years and is arguably no more objectionable than already or altogether. It nearly always expresses a positive emotion.

Alt is a keyboard modifier key (short for alternate) that changes the function of other keys when held down: {Press alt-tab to switch windows}. More broadly, alt describes alternative or non-mainstream versions of things: alt-rock, alt-country, the {alt-right}. An alt account is a secondary account someone maintains online, often for anonymity or separation of identities. In music, alt is the lowest female voice range, also called contralto. (Capitalized Alt is a German surname or a Turkish brand name.)

An altar is a raised structure or table used for religious rituals, sacrifice, or worship. Churches have altars where communion is celebrated; ancient temples had altars where animals were sacrificed to gods. To {lead someone to the altar} is to marry them. To {sacrifice something on the altar of} another thing is to give it up in pursuit of that goal: {He sacrificed his health on the altar of ambition}.

An altarpiece is a work of art—typically a painting, sculpture, or carved panel—placed behind or above an altar in a Christian church. Altarpieces range from simple single panels to elaborate multi-paneled structures called triptychs or polyptychs: {The church's Renaissance altarpiece depicts the Crucifixion flanked by saints}.

Altarpieces are works of art—paintings, sculptures, or carved panels—placed behind or above the altar in a church. They typically depict religious scenes: the crucifixion, the Madonna and child, or the lives of saints. Renaissance altarpieces often featured multiple hinged panels (triptychs or polyptychs) that could be opened for special occasions: {The church's medieval altarpiece was restored after centuries of neglect}.

Altars is the plural of altar, a raised structure or table used for religious rituals, sacrifices, or worship. Churches have altars at the front where communion is administered. Ancient altars received animal offerings to the gods. To {lead someone to the altar} is to marry them. {She was left at the altar} means abandoned at one's own wedding.

An altcoin is any cryptocurrency other than Bitcoin—the term combines "alternative" and "coin." Thousands exist, from major currencies like Ethereum to obscure tokens: {I put some money into altcoins hoping one would take off}. The term often carries connotations of speculation or risk compared to Bitcoin's relative establishment status.

Alter means to change or modify something, usually in a partial rather than complete way. You alter a document by revising it, alter clothing by adjusting the fit, or alter your plans when circumstances change. {The tailor altered the suit to fit perfectly.} The change implied by alter is typically deliberate and measured rather than dramatic or destructive. In some contexts, alter refers specifically to neutering an animal.

Alteration is a change or modification to something existing. A tailor makes alterations to clothing for better fit. Buildings undergo alterations when renovated. {The contract allows minor alterations but not structural changes.} The word implies adjustment rather than replacement—the original thing remains, just modified.

Alterations are changes made to something, especially adjustments to clothing to improve fit: {The tailor charges extra for alterations}. The word implies modification rather than replacement—the original thing remains, just adjusted. In construction, alterations are structural changes to an existing building: {The permit covers interior alterations only}.

Altercations are heated disputes or angry confrontations, typically loud but stopping short of physical violence. The word suggests a quarrel that has escalated beyond calm disagreement: {The altercation between neighbors brought police to the scene}. {What started as a minor disagreement turned into a full-blown altercation}.

Altered means changed from an original state. An altered {document} has been modified, possibly fraudulently. Altered {circumstances} differ from what came before. In reference to animals, altered is a euphemism for neutered or spayed: {The shelter requires all adopted pets to be altered}. An altered state of consciousness is one changed by drugs, meditation, or other means.

Alternate can be an adjective or noun (unstressed vowel in the last syllable) or a verb (long vowel in the last syllable). When two things alternate, they take turns. An alternate is someone who alternates with or substitutes for another, or something used or regarded as a second choice; in other words, an alternative: We took an alternate route to avoid the roadwork. A second meaning of the adjective is every other or alternating: The housekeeper comes on alternate Tuesdays.

Alternates functions as both verb and noun around the idea of taking turns or switching back and forth. To alternate is to occur in succession: {The seasons alternate between wet and dry}. Colors or patterns alternate when they repeat in sequence: {alternating stripes of red and white}. An alternate is a substitute or backup person: {She served as an alternate on the jury}. In American English, alternate often means alternative: {an alternate route}.

Alternating describes something that switches back and forth between two states, positions, or conditions in regular succession. Alternating {current} reverses direction periodically, unlike direct current. An alternating {pattern} of stripes changes color with each stripe. {They worked alternating weekends.} The rhythm implies regularity—not random switching but a predictable back-and-forth.

An alternative is an additional choice. Alternative is closely related to alternate and like it, can be a noun or an adjective (but not a verb). As an adjective it has the same core meanings as alternate: After the flood everyone needed alternative means of transportation. Do we have an alternative in mind if the weather is too hot? A derived use alternative characterizes something that is not mainstream or conventional: Many diseases respond well to therapies using alternative medicine. The story was ignored by the networks but covered in the alternative press.

An alternator is an electrical generator that produces alternating current, typically driven by a belt connected to an engine. In cars, the alternator charges the battery and powers electrical systems while the engine runs: {The mechanic said my alternator needs replacing}. The term distinguishes it from generators that produce direct current.

An altimeter is an instrument that measures altitude—height above a reference point, usually sea level or the ground. Aircraft carry altimeters to show pilots how high they're flying. Hikers and mountaineers use portable altimeters, often built into watches, to track elevation on climbs.

Altitude is height above a reference point, usually sea level or the ground. Aircraft fly at altitude; mountain climbers acclimate to altitude. {The plane cruised at an altitude of 35,000 feet.} In geometry, altitude is the perpendicular distance from a base to the opposite vertex. High altitude affects breathing, cooking times, and athletic performance.

Altitudes is the plural of altitude, meaning height above a reference point, usually sea level or the ground. Aircraft fly at various altitudes; mountain climbers acclimate to high altitudes. The word often implies significant elevation: {At these altitudes, the air is thin and breathing becomes difficult}. In geometry, an altitude is the perpendicular distance from a base to the opposite vertex.

Alto is a singing voice in the range between soprano and tenor, typically the lowest female or highest male voice in choral music. The term also describes instruments in that range: an alto {saxophone}, an alto {flute}. In a choir, the altos sing harmony parts below the melody. {She's been singing alto since high school.}

Altogether means completely or entirely: {The noise stopped altogether}. It also means with everything considered or on the whole: {Altogether, it was a success}. A third sense is in total: {Altogether, there were fifteen of us}. The phrase {in the altogether} is a playful way of saying naked. Not to be confused with all together, which means everyone or everything in one place.

Altos is the plural of alto, a singing voice range between soprano and tenor. In choral music, the altos typically sing the lower harmony parts: {The altos come in on measure twelve}. The term also refers to instruments in this range, like the alto saxophone. {She's been singing with the altos for years}.

Altruism is concern for the welfare of others, often at cost to oneself. The term implies unselfish motivation—helping without expectation of reward: {pure altruism is rare in politics}. In biology, altruism describes behavior that benefits another organism while reducing the actor's own fitness. The adjective is altruistic: {an altruistic gesture}.

An altruist is someone who acts for the benefit of others, often at personal cost. The term implies genuine concern for others' welfare rather than hidden self-interest: {She's a true altruist—she volunteers every weekend at the shelter}. Contrast with egoist.

Altruistic describes concern for others' welfare over one's own. An altruistic act benefits someone else without expectation of reward: {She made an altruistic donation to the shelter}. The word often appears in debates about whether true altruism exists or whether all generosity serves some self-interest. {His motives weren't entirely altruistic.}

Altruists are people who act for the benefit of others rather than themselves. The term carries a sense of genuine selflessness—not just occasional generosity but a consistent pattern of putting others' welfare first: {The charity was founded by altruists who gave up lucrative careers to serve}. The singular is altruist.

Alum is a chemical compound—a double sulfate of aluminum and another metal, typically potassium—used in dyeing, tanning, and water purification. The crystals have astringent properties, once commonly applied to stop bleeding from small cuts. Separately, alum is informal shorthand for alumnus or alumna: {She's an alum of Harvard}. The plural alums avoids the gender distinction of alumni/alumnae.

Aluminium is the British spelling of aluminum, a lightweight silvery metal used in aircraft, cans, foil, and countless other applications. The spelling difference reflects a 19th-century divergence—American English settled on the shorter form while British English retained the extra syllable. Both refer to the same element.

Aluminum is a lightweight, silvery metal—the most abundant metallic element in Earth's crust. It resists corrosion and conducts heat and electricity well, making it useful for everything from beverage cans to aircraft bodies to electrical wiring. The British spelling is aluminium.

Alumni is the plural of alumnus, meaning graduates or former students of a school, college, or university: {The alumni association hosts reunions every five years}. Traditionally, alumni referred to male graduates (with alumnae for women), but the word now commonly applies to graduates of any gender. The singular alum serves as an informal, gender-neutral alternative.

An alumnus is a graduate or former student of a school, college, or university: {Several alumni returned for the reunion}. The Latin plural alumni technically refers to males or mixed groups, with alumna/alumnae for females, but alumni now serves as a general plural regardless of gender. The informal clipping alum sidesteps the issue entirely.

Alums is the plural of alum, an informal shortening of alumnus or alumna—a graduate or former student of a school: {The reunion brought alums from across the country}. The word sidesteps the gendered Latin endings (alumni, alumnae) and serves as a casual, gender-neutral alternative. Alums also pluralizes alum the chemical compound, a class of mineral salts used in dyeing and water purification.

Always means at all times or on every occasion: {She always arrives early}. It can indicate continuous duration: {They had always lived there}. Always also expresses persistent habits or tendencies, sometimes with exasperation: {He's always losing his keys}. In promises or reassurances, always emphasizes permanence: {I'll always love you}. The word can soften suggestions: {You could always try again tomorrow}.

An amalgam is a mixture or blend of different elements. In dentistry, amalgam is the silver-colored alloy used for tooth fillings. More broadly, any combination of diverse things forms an amalgam: {The city's culture is an amalgam of immigrant traditions}. The word often emphasizes that distinct components have merged into something unified.

Amaranth is a plant with broad leaves and dense clusters of tiny flowers, often deep red or purple. Some species are cultivated as grain crops, others as leafy vegetables, and still others as ornamentals for their showy, long-lasting flower heads. The grain, rich in protein, has gained popularity as a health food. Figuratively, amaranth represents something unfading or immortal—the Greek root means "unwithering"—appearing in poetry as an imaginary flower that never dies.

Amaretto is an Italian liqueur with a distinctive almond flavor, though it's typically made from apricot pits or almonds. Sweet and slightly bitter, it's drunk neat, mixed in cocktails like the amaretto sour, or used in desserts and coffee: {She added a splash of amaretto to her tiramisu}. The name comes from the Italian word for "a little bitter."

Amaryllis is a bulbous plant with large, showy trumpet-shaped flowers, typically red, pink, or white. Popular as a winter houseplant, amaryllis bulbs are often given as gifts and forced to bloom indoors around the holidays: {The amaryllis on the windowsill finally opened}. The name is sometimes applied loosely to related plants like the belladonna lily.

To amass is to gather or accumulate a large quantity of something over time: {She amassed a fortune in real estate}, {He had amassed an impressive collection of rare books}. The word implies deliberate acquisition and suggests abundance—you don't amass a little; you amass a lot.

Amassing is gathering or accumulating in large quantities over time. The word emphasizes both the gradual process and the impressive scale of what's collected: {amassing wealth}, {amassing evidence}, {amassing an army}. What gets amassed is usually valuable or powerful—fortunes, followers, data, weapons. {She spent decades amassing one of the finest private art collections in the country.}

An amateur does something for love rather than money—the word comes from Latin for "lover." An amateur photographer pursues it as a hobby, not a profession. The word often implies lack of expertise: {That was an amateur mistake}. Amateur can also describe nonprofessional sports: {amateur boxing}, {amateur athletics}. As an adjective, it modifies nouns directly: {amateur hour}, {amateur dramatics}.

Amateurish describes work or behavior that lacks the skill, polish, or professionalism expected of someone competent in a field. Unlike *amateur*, which can be neutral or even admiring (suggesting passion without pay), amateurish is always critical: {The production values were amateurish}. It implies clumsy execution, inadequate preparation, or failure to meet basic standards: {an amateurish attempt at forgery}.
clues: Showing a clear lack of expertise

definition: Amateurism is the practice or status of doing something without pay, for the love of it rather than as a profession. The term carries different weight depending on context—in sports, amateurism was long idealized as pure competition uncorrupted by money, though critics saw it as a system that exploited athletes. More broadly, amateurism can suggest admirable dedication or, disparagingly, a lack of professional skill: {The production suffered from obvious amateurism}.

Amateurs do something for love rather than money—the word comes from the Latin for lover. An amateur photographer or athlete pursues the activity without professional compensation. The term often carries a dismissive edge: {That's amateur work} suggests incompetence or lack of polish. {The security system was amateur hour} means it was laughably inadequate.
clues: Enthusiasts who do it for love

definition: Amaze means to astonish or fill with wonder. The word suggests surprise at something unexpected or extraordinary: {The magician's trick amazed the children}. Amazing has become so common as a general intensifier that it often means little more than very good: {That restaurant is amazing}. The noun amazement preserves more of the original force: {She stared in amazement}.

Amazed describes being struck with great surprise or wonder. It suggests being momentarily stunned by something unexpected or remarkable: {I was amazed at how quickly she learned}, {He stood amazed at the sight}. The feeling is stronger than surprised but less overwhelming than astonished. To amaze is to cause this reaction: {Her talent amazes me}.

Amazement is overwhelming surprise or wonder—the state of being astonished beyond ordinary reaction. Something that causes amazement leaves you momentarily unable to process what you're experiencing: {She stared in amazement as the magician made the car disappear}. The word suggests being struck speechless or motionless, often with a positive connotation: {To my amazement, he remembered my name after twenty years}.

Amazing describes something that causes wonder or astonishment. The word has weakened through overuse—what once meant genuinely awe-inspiring now often means merely very good or impressive: {The food was amazing}, {She's an amazing person}. Stronger amazement survives in contexts of genuine surprise: {It's amazing anyone survived the crash}.

An amazon is a tall, strong, athletic woman. The word comes from Greek myths about a nation of female warriors who supposedly lived at the edges of the known world. In modern use, calling someone an amazon emphasizes her physical stature and strength, sometimes admiringly, sometimes with an edge of intimidation: {She was an amazon of a woman, towering over everyone in the room}. (Capitalized Amazon is the river, rainforest region, or the company.)

Amazons are the plural of Amazon—tall, strong, athletic women. The term comes from Greek mythology's race of female warriors and extends to any formidable woman: {The volleyball team was a squad of amazons}. In zoology, amazons are green parrots of the genus Amazona, popular as pets for their talking ability. (Capitalized Amazons refers to the mythological warriors or the company's products.)

An ambassador is a diplomatic official of the highest rank, sent by one country to represent it in another: {The ambassador presented her credentials to the president}. The term extends to anyone who represents or promotes something: {a brand ambassador}, {an ambassador for the arts}. To be an ambassador is to embody what you represent, carrying its reputation with you.

Ambassadors are diplomatic officials of the highest rank, sent by one country to represent it in another: {The ambassadors met to discuss the treaty}. By extension, anyone who represents or promotes something can be called an ambassador: {a brand ambassador}, {ambassadors of goodwill}. The term suggests both official authority and the duty to make a favorable impression.

Amber is fossilized tree resin, valued for its warm golden-brown color and sometimes containing preserved insects or plant material. The color amber describes this distinctive yellow-orange hue: {amber waves of grain}, {The traffic light turned amber}. Amber appears in jewelry and decorative objects, prized since ancient times. {She wore an amber pendant with a tiny fly trapped inside.} (Capitalized Amber is a given name.)

Ambergris is a waxy substance produced in the digestive system of sperm whales, found floating in tropical seas or washed ashore. Despite its origin in whale intestines, ambergris develops a sweet, earthy scent as it ages and has been prized for centuries in perfumery as a fixative that helps fragrances last longer. Fresh ambergris smells foul; only after years of oxidation does it become valuable.

Ambiance is the character or atmosphere of a place—the mood created by its lighting, décor, sounds, and overall feel: {The restaurant had a romantic ambiance}. The word is borrowed from French and sometimes spelled ambience. It typically describes environments designed to evoke particular feelings: {soft music added to the ambiance}.

Ambidexterity is the ability to use both hands with equal skill. Most people favor one hand, but the ambidextrous can write, throw, or perform tasks with either: {Her ambidexterity made her a versatile tennis player}. The word extends to general versatility or adaptability: {organizational ambidexterity}, {political ambidexterity}.

Ambidextrous means able to use both hands with equal skill. Most people favor one hand, but ambidextrous individuals write, throw, or perform tasks equally well with either. The word extends figuratively to versatility in other domains: {an ambidextrous politician comfortable with both parties}. In baseball, a switch-hitter bats from either side of the plate, though ambidextrous usually describes throwing ability.

Ambience is the characteristic atmosphere or mood of a place: {The restaurant's dim lighting created an intimate ambience}. It encompasses the sensory and emotional qualities that give a setting its feel—lighting, sound, décor, temperature. In audio, ambient sound or music provides background texture rather than focal content. Also spelled ambiance.

Ambient describes what surrounds or exists in the background of an environment. Ambient {temperature} is the air temperature of a space. Ambient {light} is the general illumination present, distinct from directed sources. Ambient {noise} is background sound. In music, ambient refers to atmospheric electronic compositions meant to create mood rather than demand attention: {ambient music}, {ambient techno}.

Ambiguities are instances where meaning is unclear or open to multiple interpretations. A legal document full of ambiguities invites disputes. A poem's ambiguities may be deliberate, enriching rather than obscuring meaning. {The contract's ambiguities left both parties uncertain of their obligations.} In casual use, ambiguity often signals a problem to fix; in art and literature, it can be a virtue.
clues: Words with more than one meaning

definition: Ambiguity is the quality of being open to more than one interpretation. A sentence with ambiguity can be read different ways: {The sign said "Free Pizza for Students with ID" but the ambiguity left us wondering if the pizza or the students needed identification}. Ambiguity may be unintentional confusion or deliberate evasion—politicians often exploit ambiguity to avoid committing to positions. In literature, ambiguity can enrich meaning by holding multiple interpretations in tension.
clues: A statement open to multiple meanings

definition: People often use ambiguous to mean unclear and with good reason: things that are ambiguous are not clear, but in a particular sense: it has two possible meanings. The kind of meaning can be of many different kinds: an ambiguous term literally has two different meanings. An ambiguous relationship seems to have certain qualities some of the time, and completely different qualities at another time. If something is morally ambiguous it can be construed as right or wrong, depending on the interpreter’s point of view.

Ambition is a strong desire for achievement, success, or distinction. The word often implies eagerness for advancement in status, wealth, or power: {Her ambition drove her to work eighty-hour weeks}. Ambition can be admirable or ruthless depending on context—{blind ambition} suggests reckless pursuit regardless of cost. An ambition is also a specific goal: {His ambition was to climb Everest}.

Ambitions are strong desires for achievement—goals pursued with determination and drive. The word often implies wanting success, power, or recognition: {She had political ambitions from an early age}. Ambitions can be specific {(his ambitions for the company)} or general {(a young man with ambitions)}. The word carries both positive connotations of drive and negative ones of excessive striving.

Ambitious describes someone who has strong desires for success, achievement, or advancement, often in career or social standing. An ambitious person sets high goals and pursues them with determination. The word can carry positive connotations of drive and aspiration, or negative ones suggesting excessive eagerness for power or status. Projects and plans can also be ambitious when they're boldly conceived or require significant effort: {an ambitious renovation}, {an ambitious five-year plan}.

Ambivalence, a noun, and its related adjective (ambivalent) are all about uncertainty of a very particular kind; uncertainty arising out of fluctuation between alternatives: He felt ambivalence about going to the party. If you feel emotional ambivalence you are alternately attracted and repulsed by a person or relationship. Ambivalence began as a technical term in psychiatry but its technical meaning now extends to other fields—such as in acoustics or medicine—and less technical, informal uses. The core meaning of the coexistence of opposites is always present.

Ambivalent describes having mixed or contradictory feelings about something—wanting and not wanting it simultaneously, or seeing both its appeal and its drawbacks: {I'm ambivalent about the promotion; more money but longer hours}. The word implies genuine internal conflict, not mere indifference or uncertainty. Someone ambivalent hasn't decided because they're genuinely pulled in opposing directions.

Amble describes a leisurely, unhurried way of walking—not quite a stroll but definitely not rushed. The word suggests ease and relaxation, often with no particular destination in mind: {We ambled through the park after lunch}. When horses amble, they move at a smooth, easy gait between a walk and a trot. As a noun, an amble is this kind of relaxed walk: {The path was perfect for a morning amble}.

Ambling is walking at a slow, relaxed pace without urgency or fixed purpose. The word suggests ease and leisure rather than destination: {We spent the afternoon ambling through the old quarter}. Horses amble in a specific gait where both legs on one side move together, producing a smooth, unhurried motion.

Ambrosia is the food of the gods in Greek mythology, conferring immortality on those who consume it. By extension, anything exceptionally delicious or fragrant may be called ambrosia: {This chocolate cake is pure ambrosia}. In American cuisine, ambrosia is a sweet fruit salad made with canned fruit, marshmallows, coconut, and whipped cream—a staple at potlucks and holiday meals. The word also names a genus of plants including ragweed, whose pollen causes widespread allergic misery. (Capitalized Ambrosia is the plant genus.)

An ambulance is a vehicle equipped to transport sick or injured people to a hospital, typically staffed with medical personnel who can provide emergency care en route. The word extends to similar vehicles for animals: {a pet ambulance}. To {chase ambulances} is to solicit clients at accident scenes—hence {ambulance chaser} for unscrupulous lawyers.

Ambulances is the plural of ambulance—vehicles equipped to transport sick or injured people to medical facilities, staffed with emergency medical personnel. {Three ambulances responded to the accident}. The word extends to earlier conveyances: horse-drawn ambulances, military field ambulances. To {chase ambulances} is to solicit legal clients from accident victims, hence {ambulance chaser} for unscrupulous lawyers.

An ambush is a surprise attack from a concealed position. Soldiers ambush enemy convoys; predators ambush prey. The word covers both the attack and the position: {They waited in ambush}. Figuratively, any unexpected confrontation qualifies: {The reporter ambushed the senator with questions about the scandal}.

Ambushed is the past tense of ambush—to attack by surprise from a concealed position. Soldiers ambush enemy convoys; predators ambush prey. The word extends to any unexpected confrontation: {She was ambushed by reporters outside the courthouse}. To feel ambushed is to be caught off guard by unwelcome questions or accusations.

Ambushes is the plural of ambush—a surprise attack from a concealed position: {The patrol walked into a series of ambushes}. As a verb form, it means to attack by surprise: {She ambushes him with questions every time he walks in}. The word implies lying in wait, then striking when the target is vulnerable.

Ambushing is attacking from a concealed position. Soldiers ambush enemy convoys; predators ambush prey. The word extends to any surprise confrontation: {Reporters were ambushing celebrities outside the courthouse}. In sports, ambushing means catching an opponent off guard with an unexpected play or sudden aggression.
Amen is a Hebrew word that comes to English from the Bible. As well as being used to end a prayer, it can express strong approval or agreement.

Amend means to change something for the better, typically by correcting errors or making improvements. You amend a document, a contract, or a law: {Congress amended the bill to address privacy concerns}. To {make amends} is to compensate for a wrong you've done. The Constitution has been amended twenty-seven times.

An amendment is a change or addition to a document, law, or agreement. In the U.S., the word most often refers to changes to the Constitution: {the First Amendment}, {the Fifth Amendment}. To amend is to revise or improve: {amend the contract}, {amend your ways}. A friendly amendment is a minor change proposed during deliberation that the original author accepts.

Amendments are formal changes or additions made to a document, law, or agreement. In everyday use, an amendment corrects or improves something already established: {The contract required several amendments before both parties would sign}. In American political discourse, amendments most often refers to the first ten additions to the U.S. Constitution, known as the Bill of Rights, though twenty-seven total amendments exist. People invoke their amendments when asserting constitutional protections: {I'm pleading the Fifth Amendment}.

Amends refers to compensation or reparation for a wrong. The word appears almost exclusively in the phrase {make amends}, meaning to do something to correct or offset a past offense: {He tried to make amends for years of neglect}. Though plural in form, amends functions as a singular concept—you make amends, not an amend.

Amenities are features that provide comfort, convenience, or pleasure. The word appears most often describing what buildings, neighborhoods, or venues offer: {The hotel amenities include a pool and fitness center}. In the plural, amenities also means social courtesies or pleasantries: {After exchanging amenities, they got down to business}.

Amenity refers to a feature that provides comfort, convenience, or pleasure. Hotels advertise amenities like pools, gyms, and room service. Apartments list in-unit laundry and parking as amenities. The word often appears in the plural: {The building lacks basic amenities}. In a broader sense, amenity describes pleasantness or agreeableness of place or manner: {the amenity of the climate}, {social amenities} like polite greetings.

An americano is espresso diluted with hot water, creating a coffee drink similar in strength to drip coffee but with a different flavor profile. The name reflects an origin story—possibly American soldiers in Italy during World War II who found straight espresso too strong. {I'll have an americano with room for cream.} (Capitalized Americano is the same drink, often seen on café menus.)

Amethyst is a purple variety of quartz, prized as a semiprecious gemstone and used in jewelry since ancient times. The color ranges from pale lavender to deep violet, with the most valued stones showing a rich, saturated purple. Amethyst is the traditional birthstone for February. {She wore her grandmother's amethyst ring to the wedding.} The word also functions as a color term for that distinctive purple hue.

Amethysts are purple or violet quartz gemstones, prized since antiquity for jewelry and ornamental use. The color ranges from pale lavender to deep purple, with the most valued specimens showing rich, saturated hues. Amethysts were once considered precious stones on par with diamonds and rubies, but large deposits discovered in the 19th century made them more accessible. {Her grandmother's ring featured a deep purple amethyst surrounded by small diamonds.}

The preposition amid conveys a spatial meaning, and is just a shorthand way to say in the middle of: A voice of reason arose amid the cacophony of the argument. Figuratively it means at the time of or with the accompaniment of. It is especially popular with headline writers and journalists because it’s a short way of conveying all of these phrases.

Amigo is Spanish for friend, borrowed into English as an informal term for a buddy or pal. It appears most often in American English, especially in regions with Spanish influence: {Hey amigo, how's it going?} The word carries a casual, slightly playful tone.

Amigos is Spanish for friends, borrowed into English with a casual, warm tone. It often signals camaraderie or appears in contexts with Latin American flavor: {I'm meeting the amigos for drinks}. The singular amigo works the same way: {He's an old amigo of mine}.

Amiss means wrong, improper, or out of order. It most often appears as a predicate adjective after a linking verb: {Something seemed amiss when the door was left open}. The phrase {take amiss} means to be offended by something, often when no offense was intended: {Don't take my advice amiss}. As an adverb, amiss modifies verbs to indicate something done wrongly or inappropriately: {A little caution wouldn't go amiss}.

Ammo is an informal shortening of ammunition—the projectiles and propellant charges fired from guns: bullets, shells, cartridges. {We're running low on ammo}. Figuratively, ammo is material that can be used against someone: {Don't give them ammo to use in the divorce proceedings}.

Ammonia is a pungent, colorless gas composed of nitrogen and hydrogen, with a sharp smell familiar from cleaning products and cat litter boxes. In household use, ammonia solutions cut through grease and grime. Industrially, it's essential for manufacturing fertilizers, explosives, and plastics. The smell is so distinctive that smelling salts, used to revive someone who has fainted, rely on ammonia's ability to irritate the nasal passages and trigger alertness.

An ammonite is an extinct marine mollusk with a spiral shell, related to modern nautiluses and squids. These fossils are abundant in rocks from the Mesozoic era and are prized by collectors for their distinctive coiled chambers. The name comes from the Egyptian god Ammon, whose ram horns the shells resemble. {She found an ammonite fossil in the limestone cliff.} (Capitalized Ammonite refers to a biblical people.)

Ammonites are extinct marine mollusks with distinctive spiral shells, related to modern nautiluses. Their fossils are among the most recognizable, appearing in rocks from the Devonian through Cretaceous periods. The shells divided into chambers, with the animal occupying only the outermost one. Geologists use ammonite fossils to date rock layers because different species existed during specific time periods. {The cliff face was studded with ammonites.} (Capitalized Ammonites refers to a biblical people.)

Ammunition is the projectiles and explosive charges fired from weapons—bullets, shells, cartridges, missiles. The word often shortens to ammo. Figuratively, ammunition is material that supports an argument or attack: {His past mistakes gave his opponents plenty of ammunition}. The metaphor treats debate as warfare, with facts and evidence as weapons.

Amnesia is memory loss, typically caused by brain injury, illness, or psychological trauma. The loss may be partial or complete, temporary or permanent. Someone with amnesia might forget their past (retrograde amnesia) or be unable to form new memories (anterograde amnesia). The word often appears in fiction, where convenient amnesia erases inconvenient knowledge: {She claimed amnesia about her role in the scandal}.

An amnesiac is a person suffering from amnesia—the inability to remember past experiences or form new memories. The word also works as an adjective describing anything related to such memory loss: {an amnesiac episode}, {amnesiac symptoms}. Figuratively, it can characterize willful forgetting: {The country seemed amnesiac about its colonial past}.

Amnesties are official pardons granted to groups of people, typically for political offenses. Governments declare amnesties to draw a line under past conflicts or violations: {The peace accord included amnesties for rebel fighters}. Tax amnesties allow delinquent filers to come clean without penalty. The word also serves as a verb: {The new regime amnesties political prisoners}.

Amnesty is official forgiveness for offenses, typically granted by a government to a group rather than individuals. Political prisoners may be released under an amnesty; illegal immigrants may be offered amnesty allowing them to remain legally. {The rebels were granted amnesty in exchange for laying down their arms.} Unlike a pardon, which addresses individual cases after conviction, amnesty usually applies broadly and may preclude prosecution entirely.

An amoeba is a single-celled organism that moves by extending temporary projections of its body, flowing into new shapes rather than using fixed appendages. Found in water and soil, amoebas are studied in biology as examples of simple life. Figuratively, something amoeba-like shifts shape or boundaries unpredictably: {The company's structure was amoeba-like, constantly reorganizing}. Also spelled amoeba (American) or amoeba (British).

Amoebas is the plural of amoeba, a single-celled organism that moves by extending temporary projections of its cytoplasm. These microscopic creatures live in water, soil, and as parasites. Figuratively, something amoeba-like lacks fixed shape or direction: {The company's strategy was as formless as an amoeba}. Also spelled amoebae.
clues: They extend false feet to move

definition: Amok appears almost exclusively in the phrase {run amok}, meaning to behave wildly or uncontrollably, often causing damage or chaos. Originally describing a murderous frenzy observed in Southeast Asia, it now applies to anything from children {running amok in the store} to costs {running amok}. Also spelled amuck.

Among means in the middle of or surrounded by. Its object can be physical objects or people, and they needn’t all exist in the same time or place, which makes the meaning of among flexible: a house situated among trees, the most intellectual among all the presidents. If something is divided among a group, each gets an equal share.

Amontillado is a type of sherry—a fortified wine from Spain's Jerez region. It begins as a fino sherry, then undergoes further aging that darkens its color and deepens its flavor to something nutty and dry. The word is familiar to many from Edgar Allan Poe's story "The Cask of Amontillado," where a man is lured to his death with the promise of tasting a rare cask.

Amoral describes someone or something lacking moral sense or unconcerned with right and wrong. An amoral person isn't necessarily immoral—they simply operate outside moral categories altogether: {Nature is amoral; earthquakes don't discriminate between saints and sinners}. The distinction matters: immoral means violating moral standards; amoral means having none to violate.

Amorality is the absence of moral sense or concern—neither moral nor immoral, but outside morality altogether. Where immorality violates ethical standards, amorality simply doesn't recognize them: {The amorality of nature—a tornado destroys without malice or mercy}. The term often describes coldly rational behavior unconstrained by ethical considerations: {corporate amorality}, {the amorality of pure self-interest}.

Amorous describes feelings or behavior relating to romantic or sexual love. An amorous {glance} suggests desire; an amorous {advance} is a romantic overture. The word carries a slightly literary or formal tone, often implying passion that may be unwelcome or excessive: {He grew amorous after a few drinks}. {The amorous couple couldn't keep their hands off each other.}

Amount is a quantity of something, especially something uncountable: {a small amount of sugar}, {the amount of time we have}. Purists insist amount applies only to mass nouns while number applies to countable things, but {a large amount of people} is common in speech. As a verb, to amount to something is to add up to it or be equivalent: {The changes amount to a complete overhaul}.

An amp is a unit of electric current (short for ampere), measuring how much charge flows through a circuit: {a 15-amp fuse}. Amp also shortens amplifier—the device that boosts audio signals: {guitar amp}, {bass amp}. To amp something up is to intensify or energize it: {The crowd was amped for the concert}. (All-caps AMP may be an acronym.)

Amped means excited, energized, or pumped up: {I'm so amped for the concert tonight}. The word comes from amplifier—to be amped is to have your energy turned up. It can also describe being under the influence of stimulants, especially amphetamines, though the excited sense now dominates casual usage.

An ampersand is the symbol &, meaning "and." It appears in company names {Johnson & Johnson}, abbreviations {R&D}, and informal writing {peanut butter & jelly}. The name comes from the phrase "and per se and"—the symbol was once recited at the end of the alphabet as "and, by itself, and."

Amphetamine is a synthetic stimulant drug that affects the central nervous system, increasing alertness, energy, and focus. Prescribed under brand names like Adderall for conditions such as ADHD and narcolepsy, amphetamines are also widely abused as recreational drugs or performance enhancers. Street names include speed, uppers, and bennies. Chronic use can lead to dependency, paranoia, and cardiovascular problems. {The doctor prescribed a low dose of amphetamine for her attention deficit disorder.}

Amphetamines are synthetic stimulant drugs that increase alertness, energy, and focus by affecting the central nervous system. Medically prescribed for conditions like ADHD and narcolepsy, they're also used illicitly for their euphoric effects or to stay awake. Common forms include Adderall and methamphetamine. {He was charged with possession of amphetamines.} Highly addictive with extended use.

An amphibian is a cold-blooded vertebrate that typically begins life in water with gills, then develops lungs for life on land—frogs, toads, salamanders, and newts. The term extends to vehicles or aircraft that operate on both water and land: {an amphibian plane}, {amphibious assault}. As an adjective, amphibian describes anything adapted for both environments.
clues: Vertebrate hatched with gills, later lungs

definition: Amphibians are cold-blooded vertebrates that typically begin life in water with gills, then develop lungs for life on land—frogs, toads, salamanders, and newts. The word comes from Greek roots meaning "both lives," capturing this dual existence. {Amphibians are sensitive to pollution and serve as environmental indicators.} The adjective amphibious describes anything operating in both water and on land: {amphibious vehicles}, {amphibious assault}.

Amphibious describes creatures or operations that function both on land and in water. Frogs and salamanders are amphibious animals. Military amphibious assaults involve forces landing from sea onto shore: {The amphibious invasion required coordination between naval and ground units}. Amphibious vehicles can travel on roads and through water. The word shares a root with amphibian.

An amphitheater is an oval or circular open-air venue with tiered seating rising around a central performance area. The ancient Romans built them for gladiatorial contests and public spectacles; the Colosseum is the most famous. Modern amphitheaters host concerts and outdoor performances. Natural amphitheaters are bowl-shaped landforms with similar acoustic properties: {The canyon formed a natural amphitheater}.

Amphitheaters are oval or circular structures with tiered seating rising around a central open area, designed so audiences can view performances or events from all sides. The ancient Roman Colosseum is the iconic example. Modern amphitheaters are often outdoor venues for concerts, with seating arranged in a semicircle facing a stage: {We saw the band at the amphitheater last summer}.

An amphitheatre is an oval or circular structure with tiered seating rising around a central open area, designed so audiences can view events from all sides. The ancient Romans built amphitheatres for gladiatorial contests and public spectacles; the Colosseum is the most famous example. Modern amphitheatres are typically outdoor venues for concerts and performances, often with seating arranged in a semicircle facing a stage. Also spelled amphitheater.

Amphitheatres is the British spelling of amphitheaters—oval or circular venues with tiered seating rising around a central performance area. The ancient Romans built amphitheatres for gladiatorial contests and public spectacles; modern ones host concerts and sports. Natural amphitheatres are bowl-shaped landforms with similar acoustics: {The valley formed a natural amphitheatre}.

An amphora is a tall ancient Greek or Roman jar with two handles and a narrow neck, used for storing and transporting wine, oil, or grain. The distinctive shape—wide body tapering to a point at the bottom—allowed amphorae to be stacked in ship holds or stood upright in sand. Archaeological finds of amphorae help scholars trace ancient trade routes. The plural is either amphorae or amphoras.

Amping means increasing intensity, energy, or excitement. From amplify, it suggests turning up the volume—literally or figuratively. Someone amping up a crowd is getting them excited; someone amping themselves up is building their own energy before a challenge: {She was amping herself up before the interview}. In drug slang, amping refers to the agitated, hyperactive state from stimulants like amphetamines.

Amphitheatre is a British spelling of amphitheater—an oval or circular structure with tiered seating surrounding a central performance area. Ancient Roman amphitheatres like the Colosseum hosted gladiatorial combat and public spectacles. Modern amphitheatres are typically outdoor venues for concerts and performances: {We saw the symphony at the amphitheatre}. The design ensures sightlines from every seat.

Ample means enough and then some—sufficient with room to spare. An ample {supply} won't run short. Ample {time} allows for delays. The word often suggests generous proportions: an ample {bosom}, an ample {figure}. {There's ample evidence to support the claim.}

Amplification is the act of making something larger, stronger, or more powerful. In electronics, it means increasing the strength of a signal: {The amp provides amplification for the guitar}. In rhetoric, amplification expands on a point through elaboration or repetition for emphasis. DNA amplification creates multiple copies of genetic material. More generally, to seek amplification is to seek greater detail or explanation: {His comments require amplification}.

Amplified means increased in strength, volume, or intensity. Sound is amplified when made louder through electronic equipment: {amplified guitar}, {an amplified voice}. The word extends to anything strengthened or expanded: {amplified concerns}, {amplified effects}. In biology, DNA is amplified when copied repeatedly for analysis. {Her worries were amplified by the news.}

An amplifier is a device that increases the strength of a signal—most commonly an electronic component that boosts audio signals for speakers. In music, amplifier often refers specifically to guitar amps: {He plugged into a vintage tube amplifier}. More broadly, anything that intensifies or magnifies can be called an amplifier: {Social media acts as an amplifier for outrage}.

Amplifiers are devices that increase the strength or magnitude of a signal. In electronics, an amplifier boosts electrical signals—audio amplifiers power speakers, guitar amplifiers shape and project sound: {He cranked the amplifier to eleven}. The term extends to anything that intensifies or magnifies: {Social media serves as an amplifier for outrage}. In scientific contexts, amplifiers increase the amplitude of waves or the gain of signals.

To amplify is to make something larger, stronger, or more intense. An amplifier increases the power of an audio signal; a megaphone amplifies voice. The word extends beyond sound: media amplifies messages, fear amplifies danger, and you might amplify a point by elaborating on it. {The controversy only amplified public interest in the film.}

Amplifying is making something larger, stronger, or more intense. Sound systems amplify audio signals. A spokesperson amplifies a message by repeating and elaborating it. {The media coverage only amplified the controversy.} In electronics, amplifying refers specifically to increasing the strength of an electrical signal.

Amps is the plural of amp, which has two common meanings. An amp is a unit of electrical current (short for ampere): {The circuit draws fifteen amps}. An amp is also an amplifier, especially for musical instruments: {He plugged his guitar into the amp}. As a verb, to amp or amp up means to energize or intensify: {The crowd was amped for the concert}.

To amputate is to cut off a limb or other body part, typically through surgery: {The doctors had to amputate his leg below the knee}. The word implies a deliberate, often medical procedure rather than accidental loss. Figuratively, to amputate is to remove something drastically: {The budget cuts amputated entire departments}.

Amputated describes a limb or body part that has been surgically removed or severed: {His leg was amputated below the knee}. The word applies both to the lost part and to the person who lost it: {an amputated finger}, {amputated veterans}. Figuratively, amputated suggests violent removal of something once integral: {The new highway amputated the neighborhood from downtown}.

Amputation is the surgical removal of a limb or other body part, or the result of such a procedure: {The infection spread so badly that amputation was the only option}. The word extends to any decisive cutting off: {the amputation of funding}, {the amputation of territory after the war}.

An amputee is a person who has lost a limb or part of a limb, whether through surgery, accident, or congenital condition. The word most often refers to those missing an arm or leg: {The clinic specializes in prosthetics for amputees}. Double amputee and triple amputee specify multiple limbs lost.

Amputees are people who have lost a limb or limbs, whether through surgery, accident, or congenital condition. The term covers anyone missing an arm, leg, hand, or foot: {The marathon included several amputees running on prosthetic legs}. Medical contexts distinguish between above-knee and below-knee amputees, upper and lower limb amputees.

An amulet is a small object worn or carried for protection against evil, danger, or disease. Unlike talismans, which are believed to bring good fortune, amulets ward off harm. The term applies to objects from various traditions—a rabbit's foot, a hamsa, a crucifix worn around the neck: {She never traveled without her amulet}.

Amulets are small objects worn or carried for their supposed magical protective powers. Unlike talismans, which are thought to bring good fortune, amulets specifically ward off evil, danger, or disease. They appear across virtually every culture and era—from ancient Egyptian scarabs to medieval crosses to modern lucky charms. {She never traveled without her grandmother's amulet.} The singular amulet is more common, though the plural appears in discussions of folklore, archaeology, or collections.

Amuse means to entertain or hold someone's attention pleasantly: {The magician amused the children for hours}. It can suggest light diversion rather than deep engagement—something that amuses you might make you smile without provoking real laughter. To be amused is to find something mildly funny or entertaining: {I was amused by his attempts to parallel park}. The adjective amusing describes what produces this effect.

Amused describes a state of light entertainment or mild pleasure—finding something funny or diverting without necessarily laughing outright. {She was amused by his attempts at French}. An amused {smile} suggests quiet enjoyment. To {keep someone amused} is to entertain them, often to prevent boredom or complaint. The word can carry a hint of condescension: {He seemed amused by my confusion}.

Amusement is the state of being entertained or finding something funny: {She watched his attempts with quiet amusement}. It also refers to activities that entertain: {The fair offered amusements for all ages}. An amusement park is a commercial venue with rides and attractions. To {do something for one's own amusement} is to do it for personal enjoyment rather than practical purpose.

Amusements are things that entertain or provide enjoyment, particularly activities or diversions that pass time pleasantly. The word often suggests lighter fare—carnival rides, arcade games, or casual pastimes rather than serious pursuits. An {amusement park} is a venue dedicated to such entertainment, featuring rides and attractions. In older usage, amusement could suggest mild interest or detached pleasure: {She watched his fumbling attempts with amusement}.

Amusing means mildly entertaining or funny—enough to hold attention or produce a smile, though not necessarily laughter. An amusing {anecdote} diverts pleasantly. Something can be amusing in an ironic way: {She found his excuses more amusing than convincing}. The word suggests lighter entertainment than hilarious or uproarious.

An anachronism is something that appears outside its proper time period. A wristwatch in a film set in ancient Rome is an anachronism. The term extends to anything outdated or obsolete: {The fax machine has become an anachronism in the age of email}. A person with old-fashioned views or habits may be called an anachronism.

Anachronisms are things appearing outside their proper time period. A wristwatch in a medieval film is an anachronism—an error placing something in the wrong era. The word extends to anything outdated or obsolete: {Typewriters have become anachronisms in modern offices}. Someone with old-fashioned views might be called an anachronism, suggesting they belong to an earlier age.

Anachronistic describes something that belongs to a different time period than the one in which it appears. A rotary phone in a modern office is anachronistic, as is a wristwatch on an actor playing Julius Caesar. The word usually suggests something outdated or old-fashioned that persists into the present: {The monarchy seems increasingly anachronistic in a democratic age.} Less commonly, it can describe something appearing too early, like a sci-fi movie showing technology that doesn't yet exist.

An anaconda is a large South American snake that kills prey by constriction—coiling around and suffocating it. Anacondas are among the world's heaviest snakes and are semiaquatic, often found in swamps and slow-moving rivers. The name sometimes appears figuratively for anything that squeezes or suffocates: {The debt was an anaconda around his finances}.

Anacondas is the plural of anaconda, a large South American snake that kills prey by constriction. The green anaconda is among the heaviest snakes in the world, found in swamps and rivers of the Amazon basin. The word often evokes something massive and powerful: {The line for tickets was an anaconda wrapping around the block}.

Anaesthesia is the loss of sensation, especially the medically induced state that allows surgery without pain. General anaesthesia renders a patient unconscious; local anaesthesia numbs a specific area while the patient remains awake. The spelling with the "ae" is British; Americans write anesthesia. Figuratively, emotional anaesthesia suggests numbness to feeling: {a protective anaesthesia against grief}.

Anaesthetic is a substance that causes loss of sensation, either locally or throughout the body. A local anaesthetic numbs a specific area: {The dentist injected an anaesthetic before drilling}. A general anaesthetic renders a patient unconscious for surgery. The word also works as an adjective: {anaesthetic gas}, {anaesthetic effect}. Spelled anesthetic in American English.

An anagram rearranges the letters of a word or phrase to form a different word or phrase: "listen" becomes "silent," "astronomer" becomes "moon starer." The term also applies to the result itself. Anagrams range from wordplay to puzzle clues to pseudonyms: {Lewis Carroll is an anagram of Charles Lutwidge.}

Anagrams are words or phrases formed by rearranging the letters of another word or phrase, using each letter exactly once. The classic example pairs "listen" and "silent." Creating anagrams is both a word game and a literary device; some anagrammists seek meaningful connections between the original and its rearrangement. {She discovered that "astronomer" anagrams to "moon starer."} The term also applies to the puzzle of finding such rearrangements.

Anal relates to the anus—the opening at the end of the digestive tract. In medicine: {anal fissure}, {anal glands}. Anal sex involves penetration of the anus. In casual speech, anal (from Freudian psychoanalysis) describes someone excessively fussy, orderly, or obsessed with details: {Don't be so anal about the formatting}. The fuller form is anal-retentive.

Analog describes systems that represent information through continuous physical quantities rather than discrete digital values. An analog clock shows time through the position of hands; an analog recording captures sound as continuous grooves or magnetic patterns. The word often contrasts with digital: {I prefer the warmth of analog synths}. As a noun, an analog is something comparable or parallel to something else: {The American West had no true analog in European history}. Also spelled analogue, especially in British English.

Analogies is the plural of analogy—a comparison highlighting similarities between things that are otherwise different. The word often refers specifically to standardized test questions asking you to complete a relationship: {I always struggled with the analogies section}. Drawing analogies helps explain unfamiliar concepts through familiar ones: {He used sports analogies to explain business strategy}.

An analogue is something that corresponds to or resembles something else in function or structure: {The heart is an analogue of a pump}. In technology, analogue describes systems that represent information through continuous physical quantities rather than discrete digital values: {analogue watches}, {analogue signals}. The spelling analog is standard in American English; analogue is British.

An analogy is a comparison highlighting similarities between different things, typically to explain or clarify: {By analogy, the heart is like a pump}. Reasoning by analogy extends known properties of one thing to another that shares relevant features. An analogy may also be the similarity itself: {There is an analogy between computer viruses and biological ones}.
Analyse is a British spelling of analyze.

Analysis is the process, or the result, of taking something apart to see what it’s made of. The thing can be physical (analysis of a chemical compound), physical with an abstract representation (analysis of weather patterns), or completely abstract (analysis of an argument). Analysis for the purpose of discussion or interpretation is common in nearly every sphere of knowledge.

An analyst examines information systematically to draw conclusions or make recommendations. Financial analysts evaluate investments, political analysts interpret events, data analysts find patterns in numbers. In psychoanalysis, analyst is short for psychoanalyst—the person conducting therapy: {She's been seeing her analyst for years}. The word implies careful, methodical examination rather than casual observation.

Analysts are people who examine something systematically to understand its components or meaning. The term appears across fields: financial analysts evaluate investments and markets, political analysts interpret policy and elections, intelligence analysts assess security threats, and data analysts find patterns in information. In psychology, an analyst is a psychoanalyst or therapist: {She's been seeing her analyst twice a week}. Sports analysts break down game strategy and player performance, typically as commentators.

Analytical describes a mind or approach that breaks things down into parts to understand them. An analytical {thinker} examines problems systematically, looking for patterns and logical connections. The word often appears in contexts involving data, research, or careful reasoning: {analytical skills}, {analytical chemistry}. Interchangeable with analytic in most uses.

Analytics is the systematic analysis of data to discover patterns, draw conclusions, and support decision-making. The term usually implies computational methods applied to large datasets: {web analytics}, {business analytics}, {predictive analytics}. In corporate contexts, analytics often refers to the tools and dashboards that track performance metrics: {Let's check the analytics on that campaign}.

To analyze is to examine something methodically by breaking it into parts. You analyze data, evidence, or situations to understand their components and relationships. A chemist analyzes compounds; a therapist analyzes behavior; a critic analyzes films. The noun is analysis: {Her analysis of the problem revealed three underlying causes}. British spelling: analyse.

Analyzing is examining something methodically to understand its parts, structure, or meaning. You analyze data to find patterns, analyze a poem to uncover themes, analyze a problem to identify solutions. The word implies breaking something complex into components: {She spent hours analyzing the financial reports}. In casual use, analyzing can suggest overthinking: {Stop analyzing everything and just enjoy it}.

Anarchic describes a state of disorder or lawlessness, suggesting the absence of governing authority or rules. An anarchic {situation} has no clear structure or control. Anarchic {energy} is wild and unrestrained. The word can be neutral or admiring when applied to art or creativity that rejects conventions: {The film's anarchic humor appealed to younger audiences}.

Anarchism is a political philosophy that rejects centralized authority and advocates for voluntary cooperation without government. It ranges from individualist strains emphasizing personal liberty to collectivist versions favoring worker-controlled communities. {Anarchism influenced labor movements in the early twentieth century.} The word often carries connotations of chaos or disorder, though adherents distinguish their philosophy from mere lawlessness.

An anarchist is someone who rejects governmental authority and advocates for a society organized through voluntary cooperation rather than state control. The term ranges from serious political philosophy to casual dismissal—a teenager who won't follow household rules might be called an anarchist. {The anarchists clashed with police at the summit}. In popular usage, anarchist often implies someone who promotes chaos or disorder, though philosophical anarchists would dispute this characterization.

Anarchists are people who advocate for abolishing government and other coercive hierarchies, believing society can organize itself through voluntary cooperation. The term ranges from serious political philosophy to casual accusation—protesters may call themselves anarchists, while critics use it to mean anyone promoting chaos or lawlessness: {The mayor dismissed the rioters as anarchists}.

Anarchy is the absence of government or organized authority, a state where no ruling power exists to enforce laws or maintain order. Political anarchists advocate for this as an ideal, believing people can organize themselves without coercive institutions. More commonly, anarchy describes any situation of chaos, disorder, or lawlessness: {The city descended into anarchy after the power grid failed}. The adjective anarchic describes conditions resembling this disorder, while an anarchist is someone who promotes or creates such conditions.
clues: When no one is in charge

definition: Anathema is something or someone intensely disliked or loathed: {The idea of compromise was anathema to him}. Originally a formal ecclesiastical curse or denunciation, the word now typically describes anything regarded as utterly unacceptable or detestable. The construction is usually "anathema to": {Such policies are anathema to free-market conservatives}.

Anatomy is the structure of a body or organism, or the scientific study of that structure: {She studied anatomy in medical school}, {the anatomy of a frog}. By extension, anatomy can mean a detailed examination of anything: {an anatomy of political failure}. In older or literary usage, anatomy simply means body: {her

An ancestor is a person from whom one is descended—a parent, grandparent, or anyone further back in a family line. The term extends beyond biology to predecessors in any lineage: {Our ancestors built this country}. Ancestor also applies to earlier versions of things: {The harpsichord is an ancestor of the piano}. The adjective is ancestral.

Ancestors are the people from whom you descend—parents, grandparents, and earlier generations reaching back through time. The word carries weight that "relatives" lacks, suggesting lineage and heritage: {My ancestors came from Ireland during the famine}. In biology, ancestor extends to earlier forms from which organisms evolved. Figuratively, anything that preceded and influenced a later development can be an ancestor: {The telegraph was the ancestor of modern telecommunications}.

Ancestral describes things relating to or inherited from one's ancestors—the family members who came before, often several generations back. An ancestral {home} is where a family has lived for generations; ancestral {lands} are those a family or people have occupied since ancient times. The word carries connotations of lineage, heritage, and connection to the past. In biology, ancestral traits are those present in an organism's evolutionary forebears.

Ancestry is the line of people from whom one descends—parents, grandparents, and earlier generations. It encompasses both the individuals themselves and the broader heritage they represent: {She traced her ancestry back to the 1600s}, {a person of Irish ancestry}. The word often implies connection to ethnic, cultural, or national origins. Ancestry can also apply to things: {the ancestry of an idea}, {a word's linguistic ancestry}.

All meanings of anchor derive from its oldest and most concrete sense: the hook that secures a boat. Figurative anchors, like a news anchor or the anchor store in a shopping mall, hold everything together under a single space, idea, or identity. Anchor baby is used disparagingly to characterize a child who is entitled to birthright citizenship after being born to a mother who is not a citizen of that country.

Anchorage is a place where ships can anchor, or the act of anchoring itself. Harbor fees for this privilege are also called anchorage. The word extends to any secure point of attachment: {The bolts provide anchorage for the scaffolding}. Figuratively, anchorage suggests stability or grounding: {She found anchorage in her faith}. (Capitalized Anchorage is Alaska's largest city.)

Anchored means secured in place, like a ship held by an anchor dropped to the seabed. The word extends to anything fixed or stable: {The tent was anchored with stakes}. Figuratively, anchored suggests being grounded or centered: {Her faith kept her anchored during the crisis}. A news program may be anchored by its lead presenter.

Anchoring is the act of securing something in place, most concretely a boat or ship using an anchor. The term extends to any act of fixing or stabilizing: {The tent stakes are anchoring the corners against the wind.} In psychology and behavioral economics, anchoring describes the cognitive bias where people rely too heavily on the first piece of information they encounter when making decisions—an initial price or number serves as an anchor that influences subsequent judgments.

An anchorman is the principal presenter of a television news broadcast, the person who introduces stories, conducts interviews, and provides continuity between segments. The term derives from the anchor position in relay races—the final, most reliable runner. {Walter Cronkite was the most trusted anchorman of his era.} The gender-neutral anchor or anchorperson now often replaces it.

Anchors are heavy objects dropped from a vessel to grip the bottom and hold the vessel in place. The meaning extends to anything that provides stability or security: {She was my anchor during difficult times}. News anchors hold broadcasts in place, presenting from a fixed position while correspondents report from the field. To anchor is to secure or serve as the foundation: {A strong thesis anchors the essay}. In relay races, the anchor runs the final leg.

Anchovies is the plural of anchovy, small silvery fish prized for their intense, briny flavor. They're sold packed in salt or oil, often used sparingly as a seasoning—in Caesar dressing, on pizza, or mashed into pasta sauces. Their pungent taste polarizes people: {Hold the anchovies} is a common pizza order. Fresh anchovies, milder than preserved, appear in Mediterranean cuisines.

An anchovy is a small, oily fish found in saltwater, typically preserved in salt or oil and used as a flavoring. Anchovies have an intensely salty, savory taste that polarizes people—devotees love them on pizza or in Caesar dressing, while others find them overpowering. The word often appears as an adjective: {anchovy paste}, {anchovy pizza}.

Ancient means very old—belonging to the distant past, especially the civilizations of Greece, Rome, Egypt, and similar eras: {ancient history}, {ancient ruins}, {ancient Greece}. Something ancient has existed for a very long time: {an ancient oak tree}, {ancient traditions}. Informally, ancient exaggerates age: {That computer is ancient}. The ancients are people who lived in ancient times, especially classical scholars and philosophers.

The ancients are people from long-ago civilizations, especially the Greeks and Romans: {The ancients believed the Earth was the center of the universe}.
