Antiracist describes active opposition to racism—not merely the absence of racist beliefs, but deliberate effort to identify and dismantle racist policies and practices. The term gained prominence in discussions emphasizing that neutrality perpetuates existing inequalities: {It's not enough to be "not racist"—you have to be antiracist}. As a noun, an antiracist is someone committed to this work.

An antisemite is a person who harbors hatred or prejudice toward Jewish people. The term covers a spectrum from casual bigotry to murderous ideology: {The antisemites blamed Jewish bankers for the economic collapse}. Someone may be called an antisemite for hostile remarks, discriminatory actions, or subscribing to conspiracy theories about Jewish influence. Also spelled anti-Semite.

Antisemites are people who harbor hostility toward Jews. The term covers a spectrum from those who hold casual prejudices to those who advocate persecution or violence. Antisemites may target Jewish religion, culture, or perceived ethnic characteristics—or all three: {The antisemites blamed Jewish bankers for the economic collapse}. The singular is antisemite.

Antisemitic describes hostility, prejudice, or discrimination directed at Jewish people. The term covers a spectrum from casual stereotyping to systematic persecution, and applies to attitudes, speech, policies, or actions. Someone who holds or expresses such views is an antisemite. {The comedian's antisemitic remarks cost him his television deal.} The word is sometimes hyphenated (anti-Semitic) or capitalized, though the unhyphenated lowercase form has become standard.

Antisemitism is hostility, prejudice, or discrimination against Jewish people. The term covers a spectrum from casual stereotyping to systematic persecution—the Holocaust being its most extreme historical expression. Modern antisemitism may appear as conspiracy theories about Jewish control of finance or media, denial of Israel's right to exist, or outright violence against Jewish communities. Also spelled anti-Semitism.

Antiseptic describes substances or practices that prevent infection by inhibiting the growth of microorganisms. As a noun, an antiseptic is a chemical agent applied to living tissue—skin, wounds, mucous membranes—to kill or stop bacteria and other pathogens. Antiseptic is distinguished from disinfectant, which is used on inanimate surfaces. Figuratively, antiseptic can describe something so clean or sterile as to lack warmth or character: {The hotel lobby had an antiseptic feel}.

Antiseptics are substances that kill or inhibit microorganisms, used to prevent infection on living tissue. Alcohol swabs, iodine, and hydrogen peroxide are common antiseptics applied to wounds or skin before surgery. The term extends figuratively to anything that cleanses or purifies: {His humor served as an antiseptic against despair}. Distinguished from disinfectants, which are used on surfaces rather than skin.

Antislavery describes opposition to the practice of slavery. The term applies to movements, activists, and legislation aimed at abolishing slavery or preventing its spread: {antislavery societies}, {antislavery sentiment in the North}. In American history, antislavery distinguished those who opposed slavery's expansion from outright abolitionists who demanded immediate emancipation.

Antisocial describes behavior or attitudes that avoid or disregard others. Someone antisocial shuns company: {He's been antisocial lately, turning down every invitation}. The word also means hostile to social order—antisocial behavior violates norms or harms others. In clinical use, antisocial personality disorder involves persistent disregard for others' rights. Casually, antisocial often just means preferring solitude: {I'm feeling antisocial tonight}.
clues: Not wanting to be around others

definition: Antithesis is direct opposition or contrast—the exact opposite of something: {His actions were the antithesis of his words}. In rhetoric, antithesis places contrasting ideas in parallel structure for emphasis: "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times." The technique sharpens distinctions by setting opposites against each other.

Antitrust describes laws and policies designed to prevent monopolies and promote competition in business. The "trust" refers to the corporate trusts of the late 19th century—combinations of companies that controlled entire industries: {antitrust legislation}, {an antitrust lawsuit}. The word is primarily American; British English favors "competition law."

Antivax describes opposition to vaccines or vaccination, typically rooted in skepticism about their safety or efficacy: {antivax sentiment}, {antivax movement}. The term gained prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic but predates it. An antivaxxer is a person who holds such views. Often used dismissively by those who support vaccination.

An antivaxer is someone who opposes vaccination, typically believing vaccines are dangerous, ineffective, or part of a conspiracy. The term is usually dismissive, used by those who accept mainstream medical consensus: {My uncle became an antivaxer after reading misinformation online}. Also spelled anti-vaxxer.

Antivaxers are people who oppose vaccination, whether for themselves, their children, or as public health policy. The term carries dismissive connotations, implying the position is irrational or conspiratorial: {The comments section was full of antivaxers spreading misinformation}. Those who hold such views rarely use the label for themselves. Also spelled anti-vaxxers.

Antivaxx describes opposition to vaccines or vaccination, typically based on beliefs that vaccines cause harm or that mandatory vaccination violates personal freedom. The term is usually dismissive or critical: {antivaxx conspiracy theories}, {an antivaxx influencer}. Also spelled anti-vax. Someone holding these views is an antivaxxer.

An antivaxxer is someone who opposes vaccination, whether for themselves, their children, or as public health policy. The term gained prominence during debates over childhood immunizations and intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic. It's typically used dismissively by those who support vaccines: {My uncle became an antivaxxer after reading conspiracy theories online}. Also spelled anti-vaxxer.

Antivaxxers are people who oppose vaccination, typically believing vaccines cause harm or that mandates violate personal freedom. The term emerged during debates over childhood immunizations and gained wider use during the COVID-19 pandemic: {The school board meeting was packed with antivaxxers}. Often used dismissively by those who support vaccination. Also spelled anti-vaxxers.

Antivenom is a medicine used to treat venomous bites and stings, typically from snakes, spiders, or scorpions. It contains antibodies that neutralize the specific toxins in venom. Antivenom is produced by injecting small amounts of venom into animals (usually horses) and harvesting the resulting antibodies. {The hospital administered antivenom within an hour of the snakebite.} Also called antivenin.

Antiviral describes medications, treatments, or substances that work against viruses by inhibiting their ability to replicate or spread within the body. Unlike antibiotics, which target bacteria, antivirals are specifically designed to combat viral infections such as influenza, HIV, or herpes. The term functions as both adjective and noun: {She was prescribed an antiviral for her shingles outbreak}. Antiviral properties may also be found in certain natural compounds and foods.

Antivirus refers to software designed to detect, prevent, and remove malicious programs from computers and other devices. The term functions as both noun and adjective: {antivirus software}, {run an antivirus scan}, {Which antivirus do you use?} Though viruses are just one type of malware, antivirus has become the general term for protection against all such threats.

Antiwar describes opposition to war, especially a specific military conflict: {antiwar protests}, {the antiwar movement}. The term gained prominence during the Vietnam era but applies to opposition to any war. Someone who is antiwar believes a particular conflict—or war generally—is unjust, unnecessary, or too costly in lives and resources.

An antler is a branching bony growth on the head of deer and related animals. Unlike horns, which are permanent, antlers are shed and regrown annually. The branches are called points or tines: {a twelve-point buck}. Antlers appear in hunting trophies, rustic décor, and folk medicine.

Antlers are the branching bony growths on the heads of deer, elk, moose, and related animals. Unlike horns, which are permanent, antlers are shed and regrown annually. The size and number of branches typically increase with age. {The buck's antlers got tangled in the fence}. Antlers appear decoratively on walls, chandeliers, and furniture.

Antlions are insects whose larvae dig conical pits in sandy soil to trap ants and other small prey. The larva waits buried at the bottom, jaws ready, while victims slide down the loose sides. Adults resemble dragonflies but are weaker fliers. The name comes from the larva's predatory relationship with ants.

An antonym is a word with a meaning opposite to another. Antonyms must be the same part of speech. Most speakers agree informally on what word pairs are antonyms, even though there is usually a category of understanding in which antonyms can be considered the same thing, not opposites. Thus go and come are antonyms, even though they’re both verbs of motion, and black and white are antonyms, even though they are both colors.

Antonyms are words with opposite meanings. Hot and cold are antonyms, as are up and down, love and hate. The concept is useful for vocabulary building and word games, though true opposition is rarer than it seems—most words lack clean antonyms. {What's the antonym of "table"?}
clues: Terms that cancel each other out

definition: Ants are small social insects that live in colonies, often underground or in mounds. A colony contains workers, soldiers, and queens, each with distinct roles. Ant colonies can number in the millions. The insects are known for organized labor and collective strength: {The picnic was ruined by ants}. To have {ants in your pants} is to be restless or fidgety.

Antsy means restless, fidgety, or impatient—unable to sit still or wait calmly. The word evokes the sensation of having ants crawling on you: {The kids were getting antsy after two hours in the car}. It can also suggest nervous anxiety: {I'm antsy about the test results}.

The anus is the opening at the end of the digestive tract through which solid waste is expelled from the body. In anatomy, it refers specifically to the external opening of the rectum, controlled by sphincter muscles. The word appears frequently in medical contexts but is also used in casual or vulgar speech. {The doctor examined the patient's anus for signs of hemorrhoids.} Anal is the adjective form, used both anatomically and in the slang sense of being excessively fastidious.

An anvil is a heavy iron or steel block with a flat top on which metal is hammered and shaped. Blacksmiths place hot metal on the anvil and strike it with a hammer to forge tools, horseshoes, and other objects. The characteristic shape—flat working surface with a pointed horn at one end—has remained largely unchanged for centuries. Figuratively, something caught {between the hammer and the anvil} faces pressure from two sides.

Anvils is the plural of anvil, a heavy iron or steel block with a flat top and pointed horn, used by blacksmiths as a surface for shaping heated metal with hammer blows. The anvil's weight and solidity make it a symbol of immovability: {The decision dropped like an anvil}. In cartoons, falling anvils became a staple of slapstick violence.

Anxieties is the plural of anxiety—states of worry, unease, or nervous apprehension about uncertain outcomes. The word often appears when someone has multiple distinct worries: {Her anxieties about money and health kept her awake}. In clinical contexts, anxieties may refer to specific anxiety disorders or recurring patterns of excessive worry. The plural emphasizes that concerns come from different sources rather than forming one general feeling.

Anxiety is a state of unease, worry, or fear about uncertain outcomes. It ranges from mild nervousness to overwhelming dread: {Her anxiety about the interview kept her up all night}. Clinical anxiety disorders involve persistent, excessive worry that interferes with daily life. The word also describes eager anticipation tinged with worry: {He waited with anxiety for the test results}.

Someone who is feeling anxious is experiencing fear, nervousness, or uncertainty about the present or the future. The related noun is anxiety. Occasionally people use anxious with less intensity, where the meaning is closer to enthusiastic or excited: I’m anxious to see what happens to his character in the sequel.
Anybody means any person. It is interchangeable with anyone, which is much more commonly used.

Anymore means from this point forward, typically in negative or questioning contexts: {I don't go there anymore}, {Does anyone use cash anymore?} In some American dialects, especially Midland regions, anymore appears in positive statements meaning "nowadays": {Anymore, everyone works from home}. This positive use sounds wrong to many speakers but is standard in its home territory.

Anyone means any person. It is a pronoun that can stand in place of a name or any noun that designates a person. Anyone doesn’t connote a gender; because of this, most people find it acceptable to use a plural, gender-neutral form after it, even though anyone is singular: Did anyone leave their cell phone by the pool? Anyone is more frequent in questions and negative sentences than someone, but often they are interchangeable: Does someone have a pencil?/Does anyone have a pencil? Anyone is always interchangeable with anybody.

Anything is the sum of its parts: any thing. It is a pronoun or a noun that can stand in place of any noun, except a noun that designates a person (in which case you use anyone or anybody). Anything can stand for both concrete and abstract nouns: Do you need anything from the supermarket? There wasn’t anything wrong with him when I saw him. Anything is typically used in questions and in negations instead of something. Anything has a minor role as an intensifying adverb in the phrase anything like: The hotel wasn’t anything like the one we stayed in last year.

Anytime means at any time or whenever convenient: {Call me anytime}. It also serves as a casual response to thanks, equivalent to "you're welcome": {Thanks for the ride. Anytime.} The single word anytime is an adverb; the two-word phrase any time works as a noun: {Do you have any time to help?}

Anyway is an informal and quicker way of saying in any case or nevertheless. She said she’d ride with us but then took her own car anyway. It is also used, like anyhow, to change the direction of a conversation or to resume a subject that was briefly dropped before. It is better to write two words when what you mean is any way: There isn’t any way that I’m going to be here alone when he comes home.
Anywhere is a compound of any and where and is used to mean to any place or in any place: You can go anywhere you like for your vacation. Is there anywhere I can get a snack around here?

The aorta is the main artery carrying blood from the heart to the rest of the body. It arches from the left ventricle and descends through the chest and abdomen, branching into smaller arteries that supply oxygenated blood to all organs and tissues. {The surgeon repaired a tear in the aorta.}

Apart means separated by distance or not together. Things taken apart are disassembled; people who drift apart grow distant. {They live apart now.} Apart from means except for or in addition to: {Apart from the cost, it's perfect.} To set something apart is to distinguish it: {Her voice sets her apart from other singers.} To tell things apart is to distinguish between them.
clues: No longer in the same place

definition: Apartheid was the system of racial segregation enforced in South Africa from 1948 to 1991, under which the white minority government denied political rights and restricted movement, residence, and economic opportunity for Black South Africans and other non-white groups. The word is Afrikaans for "separateness." Extended to describe any system of rigid racial or ethnic separation: {gender apartheid}, {economic apartheid}.

An apartment is a self-contained living unit within a larger building, typically rented rather than owned. The word is standard in American English; British English prefers flat. An {apartment building} or {apartment complex} contains multiple units. {Studio apartment} denotes a single room serving as both bedroom and living space. {She's looking for a two-bedroom apartment downtown.}

Apartments is the plural of apartment—a self-contained living unit within a larger building, typically rented rather than owned. The word often appears in compound forms: {apartment building}, {apartment complex}, {apartment hunting}. In British English, the equivalent is usually flat.

Apathetic, an adjective, appears to be the opposite of pathetic but usage has transformed its meaning. Apathetic is used to negatively characterize people or attitudes that lack interest and enthusiasm. It carries the connotation that people either should have more enthusiasm, or that they would have under different circumstances: The judge was too apathetic about the case to hand down a fair decision. The related noun apathy has the same negative connotations.

Apathy is a lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern. Where passion or engagement would be expected, apathy offers indifference: {voter apathy}, {public apathy toward the crisis}. The apathetic person doesn't care enough to act—or even to object. {His apathy about his own health worried his family.}

Apatosaurus is a genus of large herbivorous dinosaur that lived during the Late Jurassic period, recognizable by its massive body, long neck, and whip-like tail. For decades it was popularly known as brontosaurus, though paleontologists now treat these as separate genera. {The apatosaurus skeleton dominates the museum's main hall.}

An ape is a large tailless primate—gorillas, chimpanzees, orangutans, and gibbons. Humans are technically apes but rarely called so. To ape is to mimic clumsily: {He aped his teacher's mannerisms}. To {go ape} is to become wildly excited or angry. {Apeshit} intensifies this: {The crowd went apeshit when the band took the stage}.

An apeman is a hypothetical creature intermediate between apes and humans, often invoked in discussions of evolution or depicted in fiction as a brutish, primitive being. The term appears in early evolutionary discourse and pulp adventure stories: {The expedition claimed to have spotted an apeman in the jungle}. It can also be used dismissively for someone perceived as crude or uncivilized.

An aperitif is an alcoholic drink served before a meal to stimulate the appetite. The category includes dry wines, vermouth, champagne, and bitter liqueurs—drinks that aren't sweet or heavy. {We had aperitifs on the terrace before dinner.} The ritual is more common in European dining culture than American.

Aperitifs are alcoholic drinks served before a meal to stimulate the appetite. The category includes dry wines, vermouths, and bitter liqueurs—drinks that aren't sweet enough to dull hunger: {We had aperitifs on the terrace before dinner}. The French tradition contrasts aperitifs with digestifs, which come after eating.

An aperture is an opening or hole, especially one that admits light. In photography and optics, aperture refers specifically to the adjustable opening in a lens that controls how much light reaches the film or sensor: {shooting at a wide aperture for shallow depth of field}. The word appears in technical contexts—telescope apertures, aperture cards in microfilm systems—but always retains the core sense of a gap through which something passes.

Apes are large primates without tails—gorillas, chimpanzees, orangutans, and gibbons, along with humans. In casual use, ape often means any monkey-like creature. To ape someone is to imitate them clumsily or mockingly: {He aped his teacher's mannerisms}. To {go ape} is to become wildly excited or angry.

Apeshit means wildly out of control, usually in the phrase {go apeshit}: {The crowd went apeshit when she walked onstage}. The image evokes primates in chaotic frenzy. It can express excitement, anger, or general mayhem.

The apex is the highest point, peak, or tip of something—literally the top of a triangle, mountain, or structure. Figuratively, it means the culmination or pinnacle: {She reached the apex of her career}. In anatomy, apex refers to the pointed end of organs like the heart or lung. As an adjective, apex describes something at the top of a hierarchy: an {apex predator} sits atop the food chain.

Aphasia is the loss or impairment of the ability to use or understand language, typically caused by brain damage from stroke, injury, or disease. Someone with aphasia may struggle to find words, form sentences, or comprehend speech, though their intelligence remains intact: {After the stroke, her aphasia made conversation exhausting}.

Aphids are tiny soft-bodied insects that feed on plant sap, typically clustering on stems and the undersides of leaves. They reproduce rapidly and can devastate crops and gardens. Gardeners prize ladybugs because they devour aphids. Also called plant lice.

Aphids are tiny soft-bodied insects that feed on plant sap, typically clustering on stems and the undersides of leaves. They reproduce rapidly and can devastate crops and gardens. Gardeners wage constant battle against them: {The roses are covered in aphids}. Ladybugs and lacewings are natural predators. Also called plant lice.

An aphorism is a concise, memorable statement expressing a general truth or principle: {Neither a borrower nor a lender be}. Aphorisms tend toward the literary or philosophical, distinct from proverbs (folk wisdom) or maxims (practical advice). The form rewards compression—the best aphorisms pack large ideas into few words.

Aphorisms is the plural of aphorism, a pithy statement expressing a general truth or observation. Aphorisms are memorable for their compression—wisdom distilled to a sentence: {Neither a borrower nor a lender be}. The term applies to sayings from philosophers, writers, and folk wisdom alike. An aphorism differs from a proverb mainly in having a known author.

An aphrodisiac is a substance believed to arouse sexual desire—foods like oysters and chocolate, drugs, or herbs. Named for Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love. The adjective describes anything that stimulates desire: {the aphrodisiac effect of power}. Most alleged aphrodisiacs lack scientific support, but the belief persists across cultures.

Aphrodisiacs are substances believed to arouse sexual desire or enhance sexual performance. The category includes foods like oysters and chocolate, herbs like ginseng, and various drugs. Scientific evidence for most aphrodisiacs is weak, but the belief in them persists across cultures: {He lit candles and served champagne—the usual aphrodisiacs}.

Aping is imitating someone or something, usually in a way that seems superficial, clumsy, or mocking. The word carries the sense of mimicry without understanding—copying outward behavior rather than grasping its substance: {teenagers aping celebrity fashion}, {a politician aping populist rhetoric}. The term derives from how apes seem to imitate human actions.

Aplomb is self-assured composure and poise, especially in demanding or stressful situations. Someone who handles a crisis {with aplomb} remains calm and confident rather than flustered. The word carries connotations of grace under pressure and unshakable self-possession: {She fielded the hostile questions with remarkable aplomb}. It almost always appears in positive contexts, suggesting admiration for someone's coolness.

Apocalypse originally meant a revelation or unveiling of hidden knowledge, particularly divine truth. The word now primarily refers to a catastrophic destruction of the world or civilization: {zombie apocalypse}, {nuclear apocalypse}, {climate apocalypse}. Capitalized, the Apocalypse refers specifically to the biblical Book of Revelation and its prophecy of end times. The adjective apocalyptic describes catastrophic events or visions of total destruction: {apocalyptic imagery}, {an apocalyptic landscape}.

Apocalypses is the plural of apocalypse, referring to catastrophic events that bring widespread destruction or the end of civilization. The word derives from a Greek term meaning revelation or uncovering, which is why the biblical book of Revelation is also called the Apocalypse. In modern use, apocalypses can be nuclear, environmental, or zombie-related: {Hollywood loves imagining various apocalypses}. The plural suggests multiple scenarios or instances rather than a single definitive end.

Apocalyptic describes total destruction or catastrophic upheaval: {apocalyptic scenes of devastation}, {an apocalyptic wildfire}. The word derives from religious prophecies about the end of the world, particularly the biblical Book of Revelation. Something apocalyptic suggests not just disaster but finality—the collapse of civilization or existence itself. The tone is often dramatic or hyperbolic: {My inbox is apocalyptic right now}.

Apocrypha refers to writings of doubtful authorship or authenticity. More broadly, it describes any works outside an accepted canon—stories, texts, or traditions that circulate alongside official versions but aren't granted the same authority: {Star Wars apocrypha includes novels that aren't considered canon anymore}. The word often carries a sense of the hidden, disputed, or unofficial. (Capitalized Apocrypha refers specifically to biblical texts.)
clues: Documents whose true source remains uncertain

definition: Apogee is the point in an orbit farthest from Earth—the moon's apogee, a satellite's apogee. By extension, apogee means the highest point or peak of anything: {the apogee of her career}, {the apogee of Roman power}. The opposite is perigee.

Apolitical means not interested in or concerned with politics: {He remained stubbornly apolitical throughout the election season}. It can also describe something deliberately kept separate from political considerations: {The organization insists it is apolitical}. The term sometimes carries skepticism—the notion that claiming to be apolitical is itself a political stance.

Apologetic describes someone who is expressing regret or making excuses for a fault or failure: {She was apologetic about arriving late}. The word can also describe a tone or manner that conveys this sense of regret: {an apologetic smile}, {an apologetic shrug}. Someone who is unapologetic shows no regret or remorse. Separately, apologetics refers to the formal defense of a position, especially religious doctrine—not about saying sorry but about making a case.

Apologies is a plural of apology, but it often functions as a standalone expression of regret: {My apologies for the delay}. This usage is slightly more formal than "sorry" and slightly less formal than "I apologize." The phrase {apologies all around} suggests everyone involved owes or receives an apology.

Apologise is the British spelling of apologize—to express regret for a fault or offense: {I apologise for the delay}. The word can range from genuine contrition to mere social lubricant. To apologise for something can also mean to defend it formally, though this sense is rare outside academic contexts.

Apologised is the British spelling of apologized, past tense of apologize—to express regret for a wrong or offense: {She apologised for arriving late}. The word implies acknowledging fault and seeking forgiveness. One can apologise sincerely or perfunctorily, and the quality matters: {He apologised, but it felt hollow}.

Apologising is the British spelling of apologizing—expressing regret or saying sorry for a wrong or offense. The word covers everything from casual {Sorry, my fault} to formal statements of remorse. To apologise for something can also mean to offer a defense or justification, though this sense is rarer: {He spent the essay apologising for colonialism}.

An apologist is someone who argues in defense of a controversial person, idea, or institution. The word often carries negative connotations—calling someone an apologist implies they're making excuses rather than offering legitimate defense: {a corporate apologist}, {an apologist for the regime}. In religious contexts, an apologist defends the faith through reasoned argument, a practice called apologetics.

The verb apologize reduces the three words, say you’re sorry, to one, and also makes the expression slightly more formal: The company publicly apologized for the inappropriate content that appeared briefly on its website. Apologize is weakly used in some formulas and recordings to acknowledge awareness that there is a problem: We apologize for any inconvenience that the closure will cause for our customers.

Apologized is the past tense of apologize—to express regret or say you're sorry for something: {She apologized for being late}. The apology may be sincere or perfunctory. To apologize can also mean to offer a defense or justification, though this sense is rarer: {He apologized for his unconventional methods in the preface}.

Apologizing is expressing regret or asking forgiveness for a wrong or offense. The act ranges from casual acknowledgment {I'm just apologizing for being late} to formal admission of fault. Someone who is always apologizing may be genuinely contrite or merely performing social ritual. To apologize for something can also mean to defend it, though this older sense is rare: {He spent his career apologizing for the regime's excesses}.

An apology is an expression of regret for having done something wrong: {I owe you an apology for what I said}. The word can also mean a defense or justification of a position, though this sense is now rare outside formal contexts. A weak or inadequate example of something is {an apology for}: {The meal was an apology for fine dining}.

Apoplectic means furiously angry—so enraged you might burst a blood vessel. The word comes from apoplexy, an old term for stroke, suggesting anger intense enough to cause medical emergency: {He was apoplectic when he discovered the fraud}. The medical sense is now rare; the anger sense dominates.

Apostasy is the abandonment of a religious faith, political party, or cause one formerly supported. The word carries weight—it's not casual departure but renunciation, often with implications of betrayal: {His apostasy from the Catholic Church shocked his family}. In some religious and legal traditions, apostasy is a serious offense. The person who commits it is an apostate.

An apostate is someone who has abandoned their religion, political party, or other cause they once supported. The word carries weight—it's not casual switching but a renunciation of former beliefs, often viewed as betrayal by those who remain faithful. {The church declared him an apostate after he publicly rejected its teachings.} As an adjective, apostate describes such a person or their actions: {apostate beliefs}.

Apostates are people who have abandoned a religious faith, political party, or other belief system they once held. The term carries strong negative connotations, implying betrayal or disloyalty, and is most often used by those who remain faithful to describe those who have left. In some religious traditions, apostates face formal shunning or worse consequences. {The church elders declared him an apostate after he publicly renounced his beliefs.}

An apostle is someone sent on a mission, originally one of the twelve disciples Jesus chose to spread his teachings. The term extends to any early Christian missionary, especially Paul. More broadly, an apostle is a leading advocate of any cause or movement: {an apostle of free-market economics}, {an apostle of nonviolence}. The word implies passionate, pioneering commitment.

Apostles are the twelve disciples chosen by Jesus to spread his teachings, or more broadly, early Christian missionaries like Paul. The word extends to any pioneering advocates of a cause or movement: {an apostle of free-market economics}, {apostles of the new artistic movement}. The singular apostle follows the same pattern—original disciple or fervent proponent.

An apostrophe is the punctuation mark (') used to indicate possession {the dog's tail}, contractions {don't}, or omitted letters {rock 'n' roll}. Separately, apostrophe is a rhetorical device in which a speaker addresses an absent person or abstract concept as if present: {O Death, where is thy sting?}

Apostrophes is the plural of apostrophe, which has two meanings. The punctuation mark (') indicates possession {(Sarah's book)}, contractions {(don't)}, or omitted letters {(rock 'n' roll)}. In rhetoric, an apostrophe is a dramatic address to someone absent or something abstract: {O Death, where is thy sting?}

Apothecaries is the plural of apothecary, a historical term for a person who prepared and sold medicines—the predecessor of today's pharmacist. The word survives mainly in historical contexts and in the phrase {apothecaries' weight}, an old system of measurement once used for compounding drugs. {The apothecaries of medieval Europe served as both druggists and physicians to common folk.}
clues: Those who once dispensed healing potions

definition: An apothecary is a person who prepares and sells medicines—the historical predecessor of the modern pharmacist. The term also refers to the shop where such preparations were made and sold: {The village apothecary stocked herbs and tinctures}. The word now appears mainly in historical contexts or to evoke old-fashioned charm, as in boutique shops styled as apothecaries selling soaps, candles, or remedies.

App is short for application, specifically software designed for a particular purpose. The word became ubiquitous with smartphones: {I downloaded an app for tracking my runs}. Apps range from games to banking to social media. The term now extends beyond phones to any focused piece of software: {a desktop app}, {a web app}.

To appall is to fill with horror, dismay, or disgust. The word suggests a visceral reaction to something morally shocking or deeply disturbing: {The conditions in the prison appalled investigators}. What appalls someone reveals their values—cruelty appalls the compassionate, waste appalls the frugal. The adjective appalling describes something that provokes this reaction: {appalling neglect}, {appalling behavior}.

Appalled describes a state of shock mixed with horror or disgust at something morally offensive or deeply disturbing. To be appalled is stronger than surprised or disappointed—it suggests visceral revulsion: {I was appalled by the conditions in the factory}. The verb appall produces this state: {The violence appalled everyone who witnessed it}.

Appalling describes something that causes shock, dismay, or horror. The word carries moral weight—appalling conditions suggest not just unpleasantness but wrongness: {The report revealed appalling treatment of prisoners}. It can also express strong disapproval of quality or taste: {Her spelling is appalling}. The participle comes from appall, meaning to dismay or horrify.

An apparatchik is a member of a political organization who follows orders without question—originally applied to Soviet Communist Party functionaries, now used more broadly for any bureaucratic loyalist who prioritizes the organization over principle. The word carries contempt: {The mayor surrounded himself with apparatchiks who never challenged his decisions}. Plural: apparatchiks or apparatchiki.

Apparatchiks is the plural of apparatchik, a member of a political organization who follows orders without question—originally applied to Soviet Communist Party functionaries. The word carries connotations of blind loyalty to bureaucracy and ideology over independent thought: {The policy was crafted by party apparatchiks with no real-world experience}. Now used more broadly for any unthinking organizational loyalist.

Apparatus is equipment or machinery designed for a particular purpose: {laboratory apparatus}, {breathing apparatus}, {the apparatus of government}. The word suggests an assemblage of parts working together as a system. In anatomy, an apparatus is a group of organs performing a related function: the {digestive apparatus}. Plural: apparatus or apparatuses.

Apparent describes something that seems to be true or real based on available evidence. An {apparent} contradiction may dissolve upon closer examination. The {heir apparent} is the one who will inherit unless circumstances change. Apparent also means clearly visible or obvious: {It was apparent she hadn't slept}. The word carries a hint of uncertainty—what's apparent may not be actual.

Apparently signals that something seems to be the case based on available evidence or what others say, though the speaker may not have verified it firsthand: {Apparently they're getting divorced}. It can express mild surprise at learning something: {She's apparently been doing this for years}. Sometimes apparently carries a note of skepticism or irony, suggesting doubt about a claim: {Apparently I'm supposed to just accept this}.

An apparition is something that appears, especially something ghostly or supernatural—a specter, phantom, or vision: {The apparition of a woman in white haunted the old manor}. The word can also describe any sudden or unexpected appearance of a person or thing: {He made a brief apparition at the party before vanishing again}.

Apparitions are ghostly figures or supernatural appearances—spirits of the dead made visible to the living. The word suggests something that appears suddenly and mysteriously: {The apparition vanished as quickly as it came}. More broadly, an apparition can be any strange or unexpected sight: {A lone figure emerged from the fog like an apparition}.

Appeal’s many meanings as both noun and verb fall into the categories of general and legal. A legal appeal is a request for a decision, verdict, or order to be reviewed by a higher court: The plaintiff filed an appeal. An appeal can also be a request for money or help, as well as the quality that makes something attractive: The movie will have appeal for dating teenagers, but few others will be interested. The related verb meaning is followed by for: Police appealed for help from people who may have witnessed the accident.

Appealing describes something that attracts interest or desire, that you find attractive or tempting: {The job offer was appealing, but the location gave me pause}. It also functions as the present participle of appeal, describing the act of making a formal request or legal challenge: {The defendant is appealing the verdict}. An appealing look or gesture is one designed to elicit sympathy or assistance from someone.

Appeals are requests for help, sympathy, or a decision to be reconsidered. A charity makes an appeal for donations. A defendant files an appeal to have a conviction overturned by a higher court. Something that appeals to you attracts or interests you: {The job didn't appeal to me}. Appeal as a noun can mean attractiveness: {The old house had a certain appeal}.

Appear means to come into view or become visible: {A figure appeared in the doorway}. It also means to seem: {She appears tired}, {It appears we were wrong}. To appear somewhere is to show up, whether at an event, in court, or on stage. Published or broadcast material appears when it becomes available: {The article appeared in yesterday's paper}.

Appearance is how something looks or seems to others—the outward aspect rather than the inner reality. {Appearances can be deceiving.} An appearance is also an instance of showing up: a court appearance, a guest appearance on a talk show, a celebrity's public appearances. To {keep up appearances} is to maintain an outward show of prosperity or respectability despite private troubles. To {make an appearance} is to show up, often briefly or as a formality.

Appearances is the plural of appearance, covering looks, acts of showing up, and instances of seeming. {She made several public appearances}. {Appearances can be deceiving} warns that how things look may not reflect reality. To {keep up appearances} is to maintain an outward show of normality or prosperity despite private troubles. {By all appearances} means judging from what can be seen.

To appease is to calm or pacify someone by giving them what they want, often at the cost of principle. You might appease a crying child with candy or appease an angry customer with a refund. The word carries a whiff of capitulation—appeasement of aggressors rarely ends well: {Chamberlain's attempt to appease Hitler failed catastrophically}. To appease hunger or curiosity is simply to satisfy it.

Appeased is the past tense of appease, meaning to calm or pacify someone by giving them what they want. The word often carries a negative connotation of making concessions to avoid conflict rather than addressing underlying problems: {The toddler was appeased with a cookie}. In historical contexts, appeasement famously refers to failed diplomatic efforts to satisfy Hitler's territorial demands before World War II, giving the word a lasting sense of weakness or capitulation.

Appeasement is the act of calming or pacifying someone, especially by giving in to their demands. The word carries a strong negative connotation from its association with British and French efforts to satisfy Hitler's territorial ambitions in the late 1930s, a policy now widely regarded as having enabled rather than prevented war. Today, accusing someone of appeasement suggests they are making dangerous concessions to an aggressor: {Critics called the treaty appeasement rather than diplomacy}.

An appeaser is someone who tries to pacify others by giving in to their demands, typically to avoid conflict. The word carries strong negative connotations from its association with British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain's policy toward Nazi Germany in the 1930s. Calling someone an appeaser suggests they sacrifice principles for a false peace: {Critics called him an appeaser for negotiating with the regime}.

Appeasers are people who try to pacify hostile forces by giving them what they want rather than confronting them. The term carries heavy negative weight from the 1938 Munich Agreement, when European leaders yielded to Hitler's territorial demands. Calling someone an appeaser implies they're trading away principle for a false peace: {The senator dismissed the diplomats as appeasers willing to sacrifice allies for a deal}.

Appeasing means pacifying or calming someone by giving them what they want, often at the cost of principle. The word carries connotations of weakness or capitulation—yielding to demands to avoid conflict rather than standing firm: {an appeasing gesture toward the angry crowd}, {His appeasing tone only emboldened the bully}. The term gained political weight from 1930s British policy toward Nazi Germany, making appeasement a byword for dangerous accommodation of aggressors.

Appendages are parts that extend from a main body or structure. In biology, appendages include limbs, antennae, fins, and other projections that attach to an organism's central body. The term extends to anything that seems added on or subordinate to something larger: {The shed was a ramshackle appendage to the main house.} When applied to people, appendage often suggests someone who merely accompanies another without independent purpose: {She felt like an appendage at her husband's work functions.}

Appendices is the plural of appendix, used for supplementary material at the end of a document: {The appendices contain raw data and interview transcripts}. For the organ, either appendices or appendixes works, though the latter is more common in medical contexts. The Latin plural appendices dominates in academic and publishing usage.

Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, typically causing severe abdominal pain that begins near the navel and shifts to the lower right side. Left untreated, the appendix can rupture, spreading infection through the abdomen. Treatment is usually surgical removal: {She was rushed to the hospital with appendicitis}.

An appendix is supplementary material at the end of a book or document—charts, data, or detailed information that supports but isn't essential to the main text: {The full interview transcripts appear in the appendix}. In anatomy, the appendix is a small tube-shaped pouch attached to the large intestine, vestigial in humans and prone to painful inflammation requiring surgical removal. Plural: appendices or appendixes.

A small dish or drink served before a meal to stimulate the appetite. Appetisers range from simple olives or nuts to elaborate preparations like stuffed mushrooms or shrimp cocktail: {We ordered a few appetisers to share while we looked at the menu}. The spelling is British; American English uses appetizer.

Appetisers is the British spelling of appetizers—small dishes served before the main course to stimulate the appetite. These might be finger foods at a party or a first course at a restaurant: {We ordered some appetisers while we looked at the menu}. The term covers everything from dips and canapés to soup or salad.

Appetising is the British spelling of appetizing, describing food or drink that looks or smells attractive enough to stimulate hunger. Something appetising appeals to the senses and makes you want to eat it: {The roast chicken looked incredibly appetising}. The word extends beyond food to describe anything that seems appealing or inviting, though this figurative use often carries ironic undertones: {The prospect of another three-hour meeting wasn't particularly appetising}.

Appetite is a desire for food, or the capacity to eat: {I worked up an appetite hiking}. The word extends to any strong desire or inclination: {an appetite for risk}, {an appetite for adventure}. Someone with no appetite for something lacks interest in pursuing it. A healthy appetite suggests robust enthusiasm, whether for meals or for life generally.

Appetites is the plural of appetite—a desire or craving, especially for food. The word extends beyond hunger to any strong wanting: sexual appetites, an appetite for risk, an appetite for power. {His appetites got him into trouble}. Someone with large appetites wants much from life; someone who has lost their appetite—literal or figurative—no longer desires what once drew them.

An appetizer is a small portion of food served before the main course of a meal, intended to stimulate the appetite: {We ordered bruschetta and calamari as appetizers}. The term extends to anything that whets interest in what follows: {The trailer was just an appetizer for the film}. British English prefers starter.

Appetizers are small dishes served before a main course to stimulate the appetite. They range from simple fare like cheese and crackers to elaborate preparations: {We ordered appetizers while we waited for our entrees}. At parties, appetizers may constitute the entire spread. The British equivalent is starters. Figuratively, an appetizer is anything that whets interest in what follows: {The trailer was an appetizer for the film}.

Appetizing describes food or drink that looks, smells, or sounds appealing enough to stimulate hunger: {The appetizing aroma of fresh bread filled the kitchen}. By extension, anything attractive or enticing can be appetizing: {The job offer wasn't particularly appetizing}. The negative form unappetizing is equally common, describing things that fail to appeal or actively repel.

To applaud is to clap your hands together to show approval or appreciation, typically at a performance or speech: {The audience applauded enthusiastically}. Extended uses cover any expression of approval: {Critics applauded the decision}. You can applaud someone's courage or applaud their efforts without making a sound.

Applauding is clapping hands to express approval, appreciation, or enthusiasm—what audiences do after performances, speeches, or achievements. The word extends to any expression of praise or endorsement: {Critics are applauding the director's bold choices}. {The crowd stood applauding as she took her bow.}

Applause is the sound of people clapping their hands together to show approval, appreciation, or enthusiasm, typically after a performance, speech, or achievement. It can range from polite and scattered to thunderous and sustained. Figuratively, applause extends to any expression of praise or approval: {The proposal met with applause from environmental groups}. To do something {to applause} is to receive recognition for it.
clues: What standing ovations are made of

definition: Apple, the noun for a tree and the fruit that it bears, is among the oldest words in English, with roots dating from before 900 CE and having relatives in many other Indo-European languages. Apple as the name of a technology company is a phenomenon that arose in the 20th century, but Apple computer is nearly twice as frequent as apple pie in modern text. The ancient history of the apple is evident from its mention in the book of Genesis and in other religious and mythological texts.

An applecart is a cart for selling apples, but the word exists almost entirely in the idiom {upset the applecart}—to disrupt a plan or spoil a satisfactory arrangement. The image is of someone knocking over a vendor's carefully arranged display, ruining their work and scattering produce everywhere.

Applejack is a strong alcoholic drink made from apples, traditionally produced by freezing hard cider and removing the ice to concentrate the alcohol. The technique, called freeze distillation or "jacking," gave the spirit its name. Applejack was especially popular in colonial America when apples were abundant and distillation equipment scarce.

Apples are the round fruit of trees in the genus Malus, typically red, green, or yellow with crisp flesh. Among the most familiar fruits in temperate climates, apples appear in countless varieties and uses—eaten raw, baked into pies, pressed into cider. Figuratively, something is {apples to oranges} when comparisons are invalid. The {apple of your eye} is someone you cherish. {How do you like them apples?} expresses triumph or challenge.

Applesauce is a soft, sweet preparation of cooked apples, typically eaten as a side dish or snack: {The pork chops came with applesauce}. In dated American slang, applesauce means nonsense or insincere flattery: {That's a lot of applesauce}.

An appletini is a cocktail made with vodka and apple-flavored liqueur or juice, typically bright green and served in a martini glass. The drink became popular in the late 1990s and is sometimes associated with a stereotypically feminine or unserious drink order: {He ordered an appletini and the bartender smirked}.

An appliance is a device designed for a specific practical task, especially a household machine like a refrigerator, washing machine, or toaster: {The kitchen came with new appliances}. Small appliances sit on countertops; major appliances are large and often built in. The word sometimes extends to other equipment: {dental appliances}, {orthopedic appliances}.

Appliances are devices designed for specific practical tasks, especially household machines like refrigerators, washing machines, and toasters. The term usually implies electrical or mechanical operation: {The kitchen came with all new appliances}. Small appliances sit on countertops; major appliances are large fixtures. In technical contexts, appliance can mean any apparatus serving a particular function.

An applicant is someone who applies for something—a job, admission to a school, a loan, a permit. The word emphasizes the formal act of requesting consideration: {We received three hundred applicants for the position}. Until accepted, one remains an applicant rather than an employee, student, or member.

Applicants are people who have applied for something—a job, a college admission, a loan, a permit. The word implies a formal process where candidates submit applications and await decisions: {We received three hundred applicants for the position}. An applicant remains one until accepted, rejected, or withdrawn.

Application centers on putting something to use. An application of force achieves a purpose; an application of paint covers a surface. The word extends to focused effort: {She showed great application to her studies}. A job application or college application is a formal request for consideration. In computing, an application (or app) is software designed for a specific task: {a word processing application}.

Applications are formal requests, typically submitted in writing: a job application, a college application, a loan application. The word also names software programs designed for specific tasks—apps on your phone, word processors on your computer. In technical contexts, application refers to putting something to practical use: {the application of scientific principles to engineering problems}. To apply ointment is an application of ointment.
clues: What you fill out seeking employment

definition: Applied describes knowledge or theory put to practical use rather than studied for its own sake. Applied {mathematics} solves engineering problems; applied {physics} builds devices. The distinction separates fields oriented toward real-world problems from their "pure" or theoretical counterparts: {applied research}, {applied science}. As a past tense, applied simply means put into action or submitted: {She applied for the job}.

Appliqué is a decorative technique where pieces of fabric are sewn or attached onto a larger background fabric to create patterns or pictures: {The quilt featured appliqué flowers on each square}. The term covers both the technique and the decorative pieces themselves. Common in quilting, clothing embellishment, and textile arts.

The central meaning of the verb apply always involves contact. When tangible things are involved, the contact is physical; when abstract things are involved, the contact is figurative. When you apply a substance to a surface you put down a layer of it: Apply adhesive to both edges and press them together. When you apply a skill to a problem, you use that skill to try to solve the problem. Applying for something such as a job, a benefit, or a license, you formally request to obtain or be considered for it. If a rule or law applies, it has relevance or force.

Applying is the present participle of apply, covering all that verb's uses. When you apply paint or makeup, you put it on a surface. When you apply for a job or admission, you submit a formal request to be considered. Applying pressure means exerting force, whether physical or figurative. Rules or laws applying to a situation are relevant and enforceable in that context. {She's been applying to graduate programs all month.}

Appoint means to designate someone for a position or duty: {The president appointed her to the Supreme Court}. It implies authority—you appoint someone to a role rather than simply asking them to fill it. Appoint also means to fix or determine: {at the appointed hour}. An appointed room is one furnished or equipped for its purpose.

Appointed describes something that has been designated, assigned, or scheduled: {the appointed time}, {the appointed place}. It also describes someone who has been selected for a position rather than elected: {an appointed official}, {court-appointed attorney}. Well-appointed means elegantly furnished or equipped: {a well-appointed hotel room}.

An appointment is a scheduled meeting or engagement: {I have a doctor's appointment at three}. It also means the act of assigning someone to a position: {Her appointment to the Supreme Court surprised many}. The position itself may be called an appointment. In the plural, appointments refers to furnishings or equipment: {The hotel's appointments were luxurious}.

Appointments are scheduled meetings or engagements, typically with professionals or officials: {a doctor's appointment}, {a hair appointment}. The word also refers to acts of assigning someone to a position: {The president's cabinet appointments drew criticism}. In the plural, appointments can mean furnishings or equipment: {a yacht with luxurious appointments}.

An appraisal is a professional assessment of value or quality. Most commonly, it refers to a formal evaluation of property: {The home appraisal came in higher than expected}. Appraisals also occur in employment contexts, where supervisors evaluate worker performance. More broadly, any careful assessment qualifies: {an honest appraisal of the situation}.

To appraise is to assess the value or quality of something. A professional appraiser determines what property or jewelry is worth: {The house was appraised at $450,000}. More broadly, to appraise is to evaluate or size up: {She appraised the situation before responding}. The word often implies careful, expert judgment.

An appraiser is someone who assesses the value of something—typically property, antiques, or other assets. Real estate appraisers determine what homes are worth for sales or mortgages. Insurance appraisers evaluate damage claims. Art appraisers authenticate and price artwork. {The appraiser valued the estate at two million dollars.}

Appraising means evaluating or assessing something's worth, quality, or nature. An appraising {glance} sizes someone up. A professional appraiser gives an appraising {look} at jewelry or real estate to determine value. The word often suggests a cool, measured judgment: {She gave him an appraising stare before deciding whether to trust him}.

The predominant meanings of the verb appreciate have to do with value and divide roughly along the lines of whether there is an object present or not. When you appreciate someone or something, you value them because they provide some benefit for you. When something appreciates it grows in value, usually slowly and in a predictable way. The first meaning, usually with a personal subject and an object, is far more frequent.

Appreciated describes something recognized for its value or quality, or someone who feels valued by others. {Your help is much appreciated.} {She finally felt appreciated at her new job.} The past tense of appreciate, it often appears in polite expressions of gratitude: {I appreciated the gesture, even if it didn't solve the problem.}

Appreciation is the recognition of something's value, quality, or significance. When you have an appreciation for art or music, you understand and enjoy it; when you show appreciation to someone, you express gratitude for what they've done. {I have a deeper appreciation for her work now that I understand the process.} The word also has a financial sense: appreciation is an increase in value over time, as when real estate or investments appreciate. This contrasts with depreciation, which describes a decrease in value.

Appreciative describes feeling or showing gratitude or pleasure: {an appreciative audience}, {She was appreciative of the help}. It can also mean having good judgment about quality or value: {an appreciative eye for fine art}. The word often appears after linking verbs: {I'm very appreciative of everything you've done}.

Apprehension has two main meanings that seem unrelated but share an underlying sense of grasping or seizing. The more common meaning is anxious unease about something that might happen: {She felt growing apprehension as the interview approached}. The other meaning involves the act of arresting or capturing someone: {The suspect's apprehension followed a three-day manhunt}. A third, more formal sense refers to understanding or perception: {His apprehension of the situation proved accurate}.

Apprehensions are feelings of anxiety or dread about something that might happen: {She had apprehensions about starting the new job}. The word also means acts of arrest or capture: {The apprehensions of the suspects occurred without incident}. Less commonly, apprehension refers to understanding or grasping an idea, though this sense has faded from everyday use.

Apprehensive describes a state of worry or unease about something that might happen: {She was apprehensive about the interview}. The word suggests anticipatory anxiety rather than immediate fear—you're apprehensive before the results come in, not while the building is on fire. {He gave an apprehensive glance toward the door}.

An apprentice is a person, usually young, in a program that enables him or her to learn a trade. Before another noun, apprentice indicates a tradesperson who is still in training (apprentice electrician). To apprentice someone (or yourself) is to enter a program of such training. When capitalized as The Apprentice, the phrase refers to a global reality TV franchise in which contestants are eliminated one by one as they fail to impress a boss.

Apprentices are people learning a trade or craft under the guidance of a skilled practitioner. The arrangement typically involves hands-on training in exchange for labor: {The master craftsman took on two apprentices}. Figuratively, anyone new to a field learning from experienced practitioners: {We were all apprentices once}.

An apprenticeship is a period of training under a skilled practitioner, combining hands-on work with formal instruction. Traditionally associated with trades like plumbing, carpentry, and electrical work, apprenticeships have expanded into technology, healthcare, and other fields. The term also applies figuratively to any formative period of learning: {His years as a junior reporter were an apprenticeship in hard news}.

Whether used as a noun or verb, approach always involves two people or things and some notion of decreasing distance between them. An airplane will approach the runway when it has permission from air traffic control. The approach of the army alarmed the villagers. Outside the physical world, approach has more leeway in its meanings. We say that a holiday approaches when its time is near on the calendar. Your approach to a problem is a particular manner of trying to arrive at a solution.

Approachability is the quality of being easy to talk to or deal with. An approachable person seems friendly and open, not intimidating or standoffish: {Her approachability made students comfortable asking questions}. The word applies equally to people, organizations, or even ideas—anything that doesn't put up barriers to engagement.
clues: How easy someone is to talk to

definition: Approachable describes someone easy to talk to or deal with—not intimidating, not standoffish: {She's very approachable; just knock on her door}. The word also applies to places that can be reached or entered: {The cabin is approachable only by foot}. An approachable subject or text is accessible to newcomers rather than forbiddingly complex.

Approaches names the methods or strategies for dealing with something: {different approaches to teaching}, {a hands-on approach}. As a verb, to approach is to move toward something in space or time: {Winter approaches}, {The car approached the intersection}. You approach a person to initiate contact, or approach a problem to begin working on it. Approach also means to come close to without quite reaching: {temperatures approaching ninety degrees}.

Approaching describes movement toward something in space or time. A storm is approaching; a deadline is approaching. It also means nearly reaching a level or condition: {She's approaching forty}. {The temperature is approaching freezing}. As a preposition, approaching means close to: {a fortune approaching ten million dollars}.

As an adjective, by far the most common use, appropriate is a near synonym of suitable, to which it adds the idea of correct or best: The most appropriate time to prune this tree is in the fall. It’s not appropriate for you to take this problem over your supervisor’s head. As a verb, appropriate has a long vowel in the last syllable and a meaning not closely related to the adjective. To appropriate something (typically money or property) means to seize it for a particular use: The government has sought to appropriate the land for a nature preserve.

Appropriated is the past tense of appropriate, meaning to take something for one's own use, often without permission or right. Governments appropriate funds by allocating them: {Congress appropriated $50 million for the project}. In cultural contexts, to appropriate is to adopt elements from another culture, sometimes controversially: {Critics argued the fashion line appropriated Indigenous designs}. The word can suggest both legitimate allocation and unauthorized taking.

Appropriating is taking something for one's own use, often without permission or right. Governments appropriate funds by setting aside money for specific purposes: {Congress appropriated $50 million for disaster relief}. The more contentious sense involves adopting elements from another culture: {Critics accused her of appropriating Indigenous traditions}. This cultural appropriation debate centers on whether such borrowing constitutes theft, homage, or something in between.

Appropriation is the act of taking something for one's own use. Governments appropriate funds by setting aside money for specific purposes: {The appropriation for defense exceeded last year's budget}. In broader use, appropriation suggests taking without permission or right. Cultural appropriation refers to adopting elements of another culture, especially when a dominant group borrows from a marginalized one: {Critics called the headdress cultural appropriation}. In art, appropriation means incorporating existing images or objects into new work.

Appropriations are funds officially set aside for a specific purpose, especially by a legislative body. Government budgets move through appropriations committees that allocate money to departments and programs: {The defense appropriations bill passed the Senate}. The singular appropriation can mean any act of taking something for one's own use, sometimes without permission: {the appropriation of indigenous cultural symbols}.

Approval is favorable acceptance or agreement. To give approval is to sanction or endorse: {The board gave its approval to the merger}. Official approval often implies formal permission: {The drug received FDA approval}. Seeking approval suggests wanting validation or acceptance from others: {She craved her father's approval}.

To approve is to regard favorably or give formal consent. You might approve of someone's choices, or a committee approves a proposal. {The board approved the budget unanimously.} Approval often implies authority—a manager approves expenses, a parent approves a request. {I don't approve of his methods} expresses moral or personal disapproval without formal power.

Approved describes something that has received official acceptance or authorization: {an approved vendor}, {FDA-approved medications}. It signals that something has passed scrutiny or met required standards. In casual use, approved can simply mean sanctioned or endorsed by someone whose opinion matters: {mother-approved boyfriend}.

Approximate means close but not exact. An approximate {figure} or {estimate} is near the true value but not precise. As a verb, to approximate is to come close to something: {His description approximates the truth}. Two things that approximate each other are similar: {The color approximates what I had in mind}. The adjective stresses "ah-PROK-sih-mit," the verb "ah-PROK-sih-MATE."

An approximation is something close to but not exactly right—a value, estimate, or representation that comes near the target without hitting it precisely. In math and science, approximations are often necessary when exact answers are impractical or impossible: {Pi is irrational, so any decimal is an approximation}. More broadly, any rough version counts: {The sketch was a crude approximation of the final design}.

Approximations are estimates or values that come close to something without being exact. In math and science, approximations substitute manageable numbers for unwieldy ones: {Pi is about 3.14, but that's only an approximation}. More broadly, anything that resembles but doesn't perfectly match something else: {These rough sketches are approximations of the final design}.

Apps is the plural of app, short for application—software designed to perform specific tasks. The term became ubiquitous with smartphones: {I have too many apps on my phone}. Apps range from games and social media to productivity tools and utilities. The word has largely displaced "program" in casual speech about consumer software.

An apricot is a small, soft fruit with fuzzy yellowish-orange skin, sweet flesh, and a large pit. The color apricot—a pale orange with peachy undertones—takes its name from the fruit: {apricot walls}, {an apricot dress}. Apricots are eaten fresh, dried, or preserved.

Apricots are small, soft stone fruits with fuzzy orange-yellow skin and sweet flesh. Related to peaches but smaller and slightly tart. Fresh apricots bruise easily and don't travel well, so many people know them mainly dried or in jam. {We picked apricots from the tree in the backyard.}

An apron is a protective garment worn over the front of the body, tied at the waist and sometimes the neck, to shield clothing from spills and stains while cooking or working. The word extends to any protective or covering surface: the paved area where aircraft park, the strip of stage extending toward the audience, or the skirt around machinery. To be tied to someone's {apron strings} is to be overly dependent on them, especially a mother.

Aprons are protective garments worn over clothing, typically tied at the waist and covering the front of the body. Cooks wear aprons to shield against spills and stains; craftspeople wear them for protection from tools and materials. The word extends to protective or covering surfaces: the apron of a stage is the area in front of the curtain, and an airport apron is the paved area where aircraft park and load.

Apropos means relevant or appropriate to the situation: {That comment was hardly apropos}. It also introduces a topic related to what was just mentioned: {Apropos of your question, I have some thoughts}. The phrase {apropos of nothing} signals a sudden change of subject—bringing up something unconnected to the conversation.

Apt means appropriate or fitting: {an apt comparison}, {an apt reply}. It also means having a tendency toward something: {He's apt to forget appointments}. A person who is apt at something learns or performs it readily: {She proved apt at languages}. The word suggests a natural suitability or quickness. (Capitalized APT is an acronym.)

Aptitude is natural ability or talent for learning something: {She showed an aptitude for languages from an early age}. An aptitude test measures potential rather than acquired knowledge—what someone could become good at, not what they already know. The word implies innate capacity that can be developed with training.

Aqua is a blue-green color, the shade of tropical seawater or swimming pools. As a prefix or combining form, it relates to water: {aquarium}, {aquatic}, {aqueduct}. In chemistry and pharmacy, aqua simply means water, appearing in terms like aqua regia (a mixture of acids that dissolves gold).

An aqualung is a portable breathing apparatus for underwater diving, consisting of compressed air tanks worn on the back connected to a mouthpiece. The word is largely synonymous with scuba gear, though aqualung was the original trade name: {Jacques Cousteau co-invented the aqualung in 1943}. Now often lowercase and generic.

Aquamarine is a pale blue-green color, named for the gemstone that resembles seawater. The gem itself is a variety of beryl, prized in jewelry for its clear, watery hue. As a color term, aquamarine describes things with that distinctive blue-green tint: {aquamarine eyes}, {an aquamarine swimming pool}.

Aquamarines is the plural of aquamarine, a pale blue-green gemstone that takes its name from its seawater color. The word also describes the color itself: {Her eyes were the palest aquamarines}. Aquamarine is a variety of beryl, related to emerald but valued for its cool, watery hue rather than deep green.

An aquanaut is a person who lives and works in an underwater habitat for extended periods, conducting research or exploration beneath the sea. The term parallels astronaut, substituting water for the stars: {The aquanauts spent two weeks in the undersea laboratory}. Sometimes used more loosely for any deep-sea diver or underwater explorer.

Aquanauts are people who work or live underwater for extended periods, typically in underwater habitats or research stations. The term parallels astronaut, substituting water for the cosmos. Aquanauts conduct marine research, test diving equipment, or explore ocean environments that require prolonged submersion beyond what standard diving allows. {The aquanauts spent two weeks living in the undersea laboratory studying coral reef ecosystems.}

Aquaplaning is what happens when a layer of water builds between a vehicle's tires and the road surface, causing the tires to lose contact with the pavement. The driver temporarily loses steering and braking control: {The car started aquaplaning on the flooded highway}. Also called hydroplaning, especially in American English.

Aquaponics is a farming system that combines aquaculture (raising fish) with hydroponics (growing plants in water). Fish waste provides nutrients for the plants, while the plants filter the water for the fish—a closed loop that uses less water than conventional agriculture. {The restaurant sources herbs from its rooftop aquaponics setup.}

An aquarium is a glass or plastic tank for keeping fish and other aquatic creatures. The word also applies to buildings housing such exhibits: {We took the kids to the aquarium}. Home aquariums range from simple fishbowls to elaborate setups with filters, heaters, and live plants.

Aquariums is the plural of aquarium—a water-filled tank or enclosure for keeping fish and other aquatic creatures. The word also refers to public facilities housing such displays: {We took the kids to the aquariums in both cities}. The Latin plural aquaria appears in formal or scientific contexts, but aquariums dominates in everyday use.

Aquatic describes things relating to water—especially life in or on it. Aquatic {plants} grow in water. Aquatic {animals} live there. Aquatic {sports} like swimming and water polo take place in pools or open water. An aquatic {center} is a facility with pools. The word applies to fresh and salt water alike.

An aqueduct is a channel or conduit built to carry water over long distances, typically from a source to a city or agricultural area. The term often evokes the arched stone bridges the Romans built to maintain water flow across valleys: {The ancient aqueduct still stands outside the city}. Any artificial channel for water transport qualifies, including modern pipelines and canals.

Aqueducts are channels or conduits built to carry water over long distances, typically from a source to a city or agricultural area. The word often evokes the arched stone structures of ancient Rome, though aqueducts may also run underground or at ground level. Modern aqueducts supply water to cities like Los Angeles and Phoenix: {The California Aqueduct stretches over 400 miles}.

An aquifer is an underground layer of rock or sediment that holds water and allows it to flow through. Wells and springs draw from aquifers, making them crucial sources of freshwater. {The Ogallala Aquifer supplies irrigation water across eight Great Plains states.} Aquifers can be depleted faster than rainfall replenishes them.

Aquifers are underground layers of rock or sediment that hold and transmit groundwater. Wells tap into aquifers to supply drinking water and irrigation. {The Ogallala Aquifer supplies water to farms across eight states.} Aquifers can be depleted faster than rainfall replenishes them, making groundwater management a growing concern.

An arabesque is an ornate decorative design of intertwining flowing lines, typically featuring stylized leaves, flowers, and geometric patterns. The style originated in Islamic art, where religious prohibitions discouraged figurative representation. In ballet, an arabesque is a pose where the dancer stands on one leg with the other extended straight behind and arms outstretched: {She held the arabesque for several counts}. The term extends to any elaborate, intricately patterned design or flourish.

Arabesques are ornate decorative patterns featuring intertwining flowing lines, leaves, and scrollwork—characteristic of Islamic art, which traditionally avoided human figures. In ballet, an arabesque is a pose where the dancer stands on one leg with the other extended straight behind. The word suggests graceful, intricate elegance: {The skater traced arabesques across the ice}.

Arabica is the most widely cultivated species of coffee, prized for its smooth, nuanced flavor compared to the harsher robusta. The word typically appears as a modifier: {arabica beans}, {100% arabica}. Coffee shops and roasters use it to signal quality, though growing conditions matter as much as species.

Arachnids are eight-legged invertebrates including spiders, scorpions, ticks, and mites. They belong to a class distinct from insects, which have six legs. The term appears most often in scientific or educational contexts: {The exhibit featured arachnids from around the world}. Many people use arachnid as a fancier way to say spider, though the class is broader.

Arachnophobia is an intense, irrational fear of spiders. It ranks among the most common specific phobias, triggering anxiety responses ranging from unease to full panic at the sight—or even thought—of spiders: {Her arachnophobia was so severe she couldn't enter the basement}. The fear typically exceeds any actual danger the creatures pose.

An arbiter is someone with the power or authority to decide a dispute or settle a matter. Judges and referees are arbiters in formal contexts. More broadly, an arbiter is anyone whose judgment carries weight in determining standards or outcomes: {the arbiters of fashion}, {an arbiter of good taste}. The word suggests final authority—what the arbiter decides, stands.

Arbitrage is the practice of exploiting price differences for the same asset across different markets, buying where it's cheap and selling where it's more expensive to pocket the difference. In finance, this might mean purchasing a stock on one exchange and simultaneously selling it on another where the price is slightly higher. The term has extended beyond trading to describe any strategy of taking advantage of inefficiencies or discrepancies: {retail arbitrage involves buying clearance items to resell online at a markup}.

Arbitrary has a meaning similar to random but it is often used with a negative connotation. An arbitrary decision is one made because of personal preference or prejudice. An arbitrary system is one that probably treats someone unfairly.
