The word implies aggression and initiative, positioning someone as the one who starts the conflict or action.

Attackers are people or entities that initiate aggression against others. The word applies across contexts: physical assailants {The attackers fled when police arrived}, military forces launching offensives, or digital threats {Attackers exploited a vulnerability in the system}. In sports, attackers are offensive players whose role is to score rather than defend.

Attacking describes an aggressive, offensive approach—moving forward to challenge or confront rather than defend. In sports, an attacking {style} or attacking {player} prioritizes scoring over protection: {The team played an attacking game from the opening whistle}. The word applies similarly to criticism, argument, or any assertive initiative: {Her attacking tone put him on the defensive}.

Attacks is most often the verb: one person or group attacks another, a disease attacks the body, critics attack a policy. The noun attack names the act itself—a military attack, an asthma attack, a panic attack. To be {under attack} is to face aggression or criticism. {The attacks on her character were relentless.}
Attagirl is a sound spelling of an informal pronunciation of that’s a girl. It is used to give encouragement or to convey approval to females.

An attempt is an effort to do something, especially something difficult or uncertain: {Her attempt to climb Everest ended at base camp}. The verb means to try: {He attempted to explain but gave up}. An attempt on someone's life is an effort to kill them. Unlike try, attempt suggests formality or seriousness—you try a new restaurant but attempt a summit.

Attend means to be present at something: {She attended the conference}, {Will you attend the wedding?} It also means to pay attention to or take care of: {Attend to your studies}, {A nurse attended the patient}. To attend to a matter is to deal with it. An attendant is someone who assists or accompanies.

Attendance is the act of being present somewhere, or the number of people present: {Attendance at the rally exceeded expectations}. To {take attendance} is to record who has shown up. School attendance may be mandatory; church attendance voluntary. The word often implies obligation or expectation—you attend classes, meetings, court dates. Poor attendance suggests chronic absence from somewhere you should be.

An attendant is someone whose job involves waiting on, serving, or assisting others in a particular setting: flight {attendant}, parking lot {attendant}, {pool attendant}. The word also works as an adjective meaning accompanying or connected with something else: {the responsibilities attendant upon parenthood}. Attendant circumstances or conditions are those that exist alongside a main event or situation. The noun can also refer simply to someone who attends or is present at an event.

An attendee is someone who attends an event—a conference, meeting, wedding, or concert. The word emphasizes presence rather than participation: {Conference attendees received name badges at registration}. Unlike participant, attendee implies showing up without necessarily taking an active role.

Attending describes being present at something or giving attention to it: {the attending physician}, {all attending members voted}. In medical settings, an attending is a fully licensed doctor who oversees residents and has primary responsibility for patient care—distinct from trainees still in supervision. The word carries connotations of both physical presence and focused care.

Attention is the mental focus you direct toward something. To {pay attention} is to concentrate; to {call attention to} something is to make others notice it. {Attention!} commands soldiers to stand alert and ready. In the plural, attentions are acts of courtesy or romantic interest: {unwanted attentions}. Something that {comes to your attention} enters your awareness.

Attentive means paying close attention or being alert and watchful: {an attentive audience}, {attentive to every detail}. It also describes someone who is considerate and responsive to others' needs: {an attentive host}, {He was attentive to her throughout the evening}. The word suggests focused awareness, whether directed at information or at people.

An attic is the space directly under a roof, typically used for storage. Unlike a finished upper floor, an attic is usually unheated and accessed by a ladder or narrow stairs. Attics accumulate forgotten belongings: {We found old photographs in the attic}. The word also describes anything relating to this space: {attic insulation}, {attic fan}. (Capitalized Attic relates to ancient Athens.)

Attics is the plural of attic, the space directly below a roof and above the ceiling of the top floor. Attics serve as storage for items not in regular use: {boxes of old photographs in the attic}, {We found the Christmas decorations in the attic}. In older homes, attics were sometimes converted to bedrooms or living spaces.

Attire is clothing, especially when considered as a whole outfit or style of dress: {formal attire}, {business attire}, {wedding attire}. The word sounds slightly elevated compared to clothes or outfit, appearing often on invitations and dress codes. As a verb, to attire oneself is to dress: {She was attired in silk}.

Your attitude toward or about something is the way you feel about it, as reflected in your behavior. Attitudes can be positive, negative, or neutral, but often when people talk about attitude without characterizing it, they mean a bad attitude: He had such an attitude when he came in this morning that no one wanted to talk to him. This usage may explain why one of the most frequent verbs that precedes attitude is change: The community has slowly changed its attitude and now seems very welcoming to newcomers. You can also use attitude to talk about posture or physical position: Several statues of the Buddha show him in a reclining attitude.
clues: Your typical way of regarding something

definition: Attitudes are settled ways of thinking or feeling about something, often reflected in behavior: {Her attitude toward work changed after the promotion}. The word commonly implies a negative disposition: {Don't give me attitude}. In physical contexts, attitude describes body position or posture, especially in dance, gymnastics, or aviation where aircraft orientation matters.

An attorney is a person legally appointed to act on another's behalf, particularly a lawyer authorized to represent clients in legal matters. In American usage, attorney and lawyer are nearly interchangeable, though attorney often sounds more formal: {The defendant's attorney filed a motion to dismiss}. An attorney-in-fact holds power of attorney to handle someone's affairs without necessarily being a lawyer.

Attorneys is the plural of attorney, a person legally authorized to act on another's behalf or, in American usage, a lawyer. {The attorneys filed a motion to dismiss}. An attorney-at-law practices law in court; an attorney-in-fact holds power of attorney to handle someone's affairs. {She hired three attorneys to handle the case}.

To attract is to draw something toward oneself. A magnet attracts iron filings. A person may attract attention, criticism, or romantic interest. Attractive places or opportunities draw people to them. The word suggests a pull rather than a push—something about the object creates the drawing force: {The smell of coffee attracted me to the kitchen}. {She attracts controversy wherever she goes}.

Attracted is the past tense of attract, meaning drawn toward something by appeal, interest, or force. A person can be attracted to another romantically or sexually: {I've always been attracted to confident people}. The word also applies to non-romantic pull: {She was attracted to the idea of working abroad}. In physics, particles or objects are attracted by magnetic or gravitational forces.

Attraction is a force that draws things together—whether physical objects, people, or interest. Gravity is an attraction between masses; magnetism attracts iron. Between people, attraction usually means romantic or sexual interest: {I felt an immediate attraction to her}. A tourist attraction draws visitors. The word covers anything that pulls attention or desire toward itself.

Attractions are things that draw interest or visitors. Tourist attractions are places people travel to see: {The Grand Canyon is one of Arizona's main attractions}. The attractions of a job or lifestyle are its appealing qualities. An attraction between people is a pull toward each other, often romantic or sexual: {There was an obvious attraction between them}. In entertainment, attractions are featured performances or exhibits.

Attractive describes something that draws interest or attention. An attractive person is pleasing to look at; an attractive offer appeals to your interests. The word implies a pull toward something: {She found the idea of moving abroad attractive}. What's attractive exerts a kind of magnetism—whether physical beauty, favorable terms, or appealing qualities.

Attractiveness is the quality of being pleasing or appealing. Physical attractiveness draws romantic or sexual interest: {Her attractiveness was undeniable}. But the word applies beyond appearance—a job offer's attractiveness might depend on salary and location, an investment's attractiveness on potential returns. The word often implies a pull toward something desirable.

Attribute can be a noun (first syllable stressed) or a verb (second syllable stressed). When you attribute something you name the person or thing that is responsible for it or the cause of it: The plague of insects is being attributed to an unusually mild winter. When text or a work of art is attributed to someone, that person is identified as its author or creator. An attribute is one among a number of qualities of something. For me the most important attributes in a partner are fidelity, intelligence, and humor. In a computing environment, an attribute is a variable that provides additional information about something.

Attributes are qualities or characteristics that belong to something or someone: {patience and kindness are her best attributes}, {the attributes of a good leader}. In computing, attributes are properties assigned to data elements or objects. The verb attribute means to credit or assign a cause: {She attributed her success to hard work}, {a quote attributed to Einstein}.

Attribution is the act of assigning a cause, source, or origin to something. In academic and creative contexts, it means crediting a work or idea to its creator: {The painting's attribution to Vermeer remains disputed}. In psychology, attribution theory examines how people explain behavior—whether they attribute actions to character or circumstance. Online, attribution often refers to citing sources or linking to original creators: {The image was used without proper attribution}.

Attrition is gradual reduction through sustained pressure or loss. In warfare, a war of attrition wears down the enemy through continuous losses rather than decisive victory. In business, attrition refers to workforce reduction through resignation or retirement rather than layoffs: {We'll reduce headcount through natural attrition}. The word implies slow erosion—of numbers, strength, or resolve—rather than sudden elimination.

Attuned describes a state of being sensitively aware of or responsive to something. If you are attuned to someone's needs, you readily perceive and understand them. Musicians attune their instruments to a standard pitch; by extension, people attune themselves to situations, moods, or cultural shifts. {After years of marriage, she was finely attuned to his moods.} The word suggests a kind of harmonious alignment, whether with another person, an environment, or a set of expectations.

Attunement is the state of being in harmony with something—receptive to its signals, responsive to its rhythms. A therapist develops attunement to a patient's emotional states. A musician achieves attunement with fellow performers. The word suggests sensitivity that comes through sustained attention: {Her attunement to shifts in office politics was uncanny}. To attune is to bring into harmony or make receptive.

Aubergine is the British English term for eggplant—the glossy, typically dark purple fruit used as a vegetable in cooking. The word comes from French and is standard in British recipes and supermarkets where Americans would say eggplant. Aubergine also names the deep purple color of the fruit's skin: {an aubergine sweater}, {aubergine lipstick}.

Auburn is a reddish-brown color, typically describing hair. The shade falls between brown and red, often with copper or chestnut tones: {She had long auburn hair that caught the light}. The word appears almost exclusively in descriptions of hair color, though it can technically describe anything with that warm, brownish-red hue. (Capitalized Auburn refers to cities or universities.)

An auction is a public sale where items go to the highest bidder. Bidders compete by offering progressively higher amounts until no one will bid more: {The painting sold at auction for three million dollars}. To auction something is to sell it this way: {They auctioned off the estate's contents}. Auction extends to any competitive bidding process: {The government auctioned wireless spectrum licenses}.

An auctioneer is a person who conducts auctions, calling out bids and managing the sale of goods to the highest bidder. The role requires a distinctive rapid-fire speaking style: {The auctioneer's chant rattled off numbers too fast to follow}. To auctioneer is to work in this capacity or to sell something at auction.

Auctioneers conduct auctions—sales where items go to the highest bidder. The auctioneer announces bids, encourages higher offers, and declares items sold, traditionally with a gavel strike. The role requires rapid speech and showmanship: {The auctioneer's chant rattled off bids faster than I could follow}. Auctioneers work at estate sales, livestock markets, art houses, and charity events.

Auctions are sales where goods go to the highest bidder. Participants compete by offering progressively higher prices until no one will bid more. The verb auction means to sell this way: {They auctioned off the estate's contents}. Auctions range from livestock sales to fine art at Sotheby's to eBay listings. To {auction off} suggests disposing of items, often to settle debts or clear inventory.

Audacious describes bold willingness to take risks or defy convention. An audacious plan might seem reckless to cautious minds: {an audacious heist}, {an audacious debut novel}. The word can carry admiration for daring or disapproval of presumption, depending on context. {She made the audacious decision to quit her job and sail around the world.}

Audacity is bold daring, often with a hint of recklessness or disregard for normal limits. It can be admirable—the audacity to challenge authority, to attempt what others won't. But it frequently carries disapproval, suggesting presumption or impudence: {He had the audacity to ask for a raise after missing three deadlines}. The word implies that someone has crossed a line others would respect.

Audible means capable of being heard. An audible {sigh} is loud enough to reach nearby ears. {The music was barely audible over the noise of the crowd.} In American football, an audible is a play called at the line of scrimmage, changing the planned play—the quarterback literally makes it audible to teammates. To {call an audible} has spread to general use for any last-minute change of plan.

Audibles is the plural of audible, which as a noun refers to sounds that can be heard or, in American football, a play called at the line of scrimmage to replace the originally planned play: {The quarterback called three audibles in the fourth quarter}. The verb audible means to call such a change, and has extended to mean changing plans on the fly: {We had to audible when the restaurant was closed}.

An audience is the group of people who watch, listen to, or read something. A performer has an audience, as does a book or podcast. The word also means a formal meeting with an important person: {She was granted an audience with the Pope}. In marketing and media, audience refers to a target demographic: {The show skews toward a younger audience}.

Audiences is the plural of audience—groups of people who watch, listen to, or receive some form of performance, presentation, or communication. A play draws audiences, a podcast builds audiences, a politician addresses audiences. The word emphasizes the collective nature of reception: {The film found audiences worldwide}. In marketing, audiences are demographic segments targeted for messaging: {We're trying to reach younger audiences}.

Audio refers to sound, especially as recorded, transmitted, or reproduced electronically. It covers the range of frequencies humans can hear. Audio works as both noun and adjective: {The audio was terrible on that call}, {audio equipment}, {audio file}. In video contexts, audio is the sound component as distinct from the visual: {We have picture but no audio}.

An audiobook is a recording of someone reading a book aloud. Once distributed on cassette tapes and CDs, audiobooks now stream or download digitally. They range from single-narrator readings to full productions with voice actors and sound effects: {I listened to the audiobook on my commute}.

Audiobooks are books read aloud and recorded for listening rather than reading. Once distributed on cassette tapes and CDs, they now come primarily as digital files. Audiobooks allow consuming literature while commuting, exercising, or doing chores: {I listened to the audiobook on my drive to work}. Professional narrators or sometimes the authors themselves perform the readings.

An audiophile is someone passionate about high-fidelity sound reproduction. Audiophiles invest in quality speakers, amplifiers, and headphones, often spending considerable sums pursuing sonic perfection: {He's such an audiophile he can hear the difference between cable types}. The term can carry mild mockery when applied to those obsessed with imperceptible improvements.

Audiophiles are people passionate about high-quality sound reproduction. The term suggests someone who invests in premium audio equipment and can discern subtle differences in sound quality that casual listeners might miss: {The audiophiles debated whether vinyl really sounds warmer than digital}. The word sometimes carries connotations of obsessiveness or snobbery about gear.

Audiotape is magnetic tape used to record and play back sound. Before digital formats, audiotape was the standard medium for music distribution and voice recording: {The interview was preserved on audiotape}. As a verb, to audiotape is to make such a recording: {They audiotaped the entire deposition}.

An audit is a formal examination of records, accounts, or practices to verify accuracy or compliance. Auditors review financial statements, tax returns, or organizational procedures: {The IRS audited her returns for the past three years}. To audit a college course is to attend without receiving credit. The verb and noun share the same form.

Auditing is the systematic examination of records, accounts, or processes to verify accuracy and compliance. Financial auditing checks that a company's books reflect reality: {The firm conducts an annual audit of our finances}. Auditing extends to other formal reviews—security audits, energy audits, compliance audits. To audit a college course is to attend without receiving credit, observing rather than formally participating.

An audition is a trial performance where an actor, musician, or other performer demonstrates their abilities for a role or position: {She auditioned for the lead in the school play}. The verb works both ways—performers audition for parts, and directors audition performers. The process typically involves prepared pieces or cold readings from a script.

Auditioning is the process of trying out for a role or position by performing for those making the selection. Actors audition for parts, musicians audition for orchestras, dancers audition for companies. The word works as both a present participle and a gerund: {She's auditioning for the lead} or {Auditioning is nerve-wracking}.

Auditions are tryouts where performers demonstrate their abilities for a role or position. Actors audition for parts in plays and films, musicians audition for orchestras, dancers for companies. The word works as both noun and verb: {She auditioned for the lead} or {The auditions lasted all day}. A {callback} is a second audition for those who passed the first.

An auditor is someone who examines records to verify their accuracy. Most often this means a financial auditor—an accountant who reviews a company's books to ensure they're correct and compliant: {The auditors found discrepancies in the quarterly reports}. Government auditors may examine tax returns or agency spending. In academic settings, an auditor attends a course without receiving credit: {She audited the philosophy seminar just for interest}.

An auditorium is a large room or building designed to seat an audience for performances, lectures, or public gatherings. The term emphasizes the space where listeners sit rather than the stage: {The auditorium filled quickly before the concert}. Schools, theaters, and convention centers all have auditoriums.

Auditors examine financial records to verify their accuracy and compliance. External auditors work independently to certify that a company's accounts are truthful; internal auditors check for fraud, waste, and procedural failures within an organization. The IRS employs auditors to review tax returns. Beyond finance, auditors may evaluate any system: {safety auditors}, {environmental auditors}. In academic settings, an auditor attends a course without receiving credit.

Audits are official examinations of records, accounts, or practices to verify accuracy or compliance. Financial audits check that books reflect reality; tax audits scrutinize returns for errors or fraud. The IRS can audit individuals or businesses. Beyond finance, audits evaluate systems: {a security audit}, {an energy audit}. To audit a class is to attend without receiving credit.

An auger is a tool with a helical shaft for boring holes in wood, ice, or earth. Hand augers have a T-shaped handle; powered versions drill through frozen lakes for ice fishing or into soil for fence posts. The spiral design pulls material up and out of the hole as it turns: {He used an auger to dig postholes for the new fence}.

Augers are tools for boring holes, typically featuring a helical shaft that pulls material away as it cuts. A hand auger drills into wood; larger augers bore into earth for fence posts or ice fishing holes. The word also names the screw mechanism inside grain elevators and snow blowers that moves material along: {The combine's auger jammed with wet corn}.

Augmentation is the act of making something larger or more substantial, or the result of that increase. A budget augmentation adds funds; breast augmentation adds volume surgically. In music, augmentation stretches a melody by lengthening its note values. The word implies deliberate enhancement rather than natural growth: {The company approved augmentation of the security team}.

Augmentations are additions or enhancements that increase something's size, value, or capability. The word appears most often in technical contexts: surgical augmentations like breast implants, digital augmentations to photographs, or character augmentations in video games that boost abilities. {The cyberpunk genre features characters with mechanical augmentations.}

Augmented means made larger or enhanced by addition. An augmented {staff} has extra members. An augmented {chord} in music has a raised fifth. Augmented {reality} overlays digital information onto the physical world through a screen or headset—the real environment enhanced with computer-generated elements.

Auguries are signs or omens, especially ones interpreted as predicting the future. The word comes from ancient Roman practice, where priests called augurs read divine will in the flight patterns of birds. Now augury appears mostly in literary contexts: {The auguries were not favorable for the expedition}. The singular augury can also mean the practice of reading such signs.

August means dignified, grand, and inspiring reverence or admiration. The word describes people, institutions, or settings that command respect through their importance or solemnity: {the august halls of Congress}, {an august assembly of scholars}. It suggests weight and gravitas rather than mere fame. (Capitalized August is the month.)

An aunt is the sister of one's parent, or the wife of one's parent's brother (an uncle). The term extends to women who fill aunt-like roles without biological connection, such as close family friends. {My aunt always sends a card on my birthday.} In some communities, aunt is used as a respectful address for older women generally. The informal auntie or aunty conveys affection or familiarity.

Auntie is an informal or affectionate form of aunt, used especially by children or when addressing one's aunt directly: {Can I have another cookie, Auntie?} The term extends beyond blood relatives to familiar older women in a child's life, such as close family friends. In some cultures, particularly South Asian and African communities, auntie is a respectful form of address for any older woman, regardless of relation.

Aunties is the plural of auntie, an affectionate or informal form of aunt. The word carries warmth that the formal aunt sometimes lacks: {The aunties gathered in the kitchen to gossip}. In many cultures, aunties extends beyond blood relatives to include older women in a community who offer guidance, food, or unsolicited opinions about your life choices.

Aunts is the plural of aunt—the sisters of one's parents, or the wives of one's uncles. The word appears in contexts involving family gatherings or inheritance: {My aunts always brought the best dishes to Thanksgiving}. An aunt by marriage may be distinguished from a blood aunt, though both are simply aunts in everyday use.

Aunty is an informal spelling of aunt, used especially in British English and Commonwealth countries. It often carries a warmer, more familiar tone than the standard spelling: {Aunty came over for tea}. In some cultures, aunty extends beyond blood relations to address older women with affection or respect. Also spelled auntie.

An aura is an atmosphere or quality that seems to surround a person or thing: {an aura of mystery}, {an aura of calm}. The word suggests something intangible yet perceptible—a presence you sense rather than see. In New Age contexts, auras are supposedly visible energy fields around living beings. In medicine, an aura is a sensory warning that precedes a migraine or seizure.

Auras is the plural of aura—a distinctive atmosphere or quality surrounding a person, place, or thing: {The old library had an aura of quiet scholarship}. In New Age and spiritual contexts, auras are fields of colored light said to emanate from living beings, visible to some: {She claimed to see auras around people}. In medicine, an aura is a sensory warning before a migraine or seizure.

Aurora refers to the natural light displays in polar skies—the aurora borealis (northern lights) and aurora australis (southern lights)—caused by charged particles from the sun interacting with Earth's atmosphere. The term extends to any similar atmospheric glow. In literary or poetic use, aurora means dawn itself: {The aurora crept over the eastern hills}. (Capitalized Aurora is the Roman goddess of dawn or a given name.)

Auroras are luminous displays in the night sky caused by charged particles from the sun interacting with Earth's atmosphere, producing curtains and ribbons of colored light. They appear near the poles—aurora borealis in the north, aurora australis in the south. The singular aurora can also mean dawn or the Roman goddess of dawn, from whom the phenomenon takes its name.

Auspicious describes something that suggests favorable prospects or good fortune ahead. An auspicious {beginning} or auspicious {sign} points toward success. The word carries a slightly formal tone, often appearing in contexts like ceremonies or major undertakings: {The clear weather seemed an auspicious start to the voyage}. The opposite is inauspicious.

Austere describes something severely simple, stripped of comfort or ornament. An austere room has bare walls and minimal furniture. An austere person is strict, self-disciplined, and unindulgent—perhaps forbiddingly so. Austere measures or budgets involve harsh restrictions: {The company adopted austere cost-cutting policies}. The word carries connotations of both admirable discipline and cold severity.

Austerity is primarily used in the context of an economy and scarcity of something: money, goods, or jobs. It is a term that governments and economists like to use to characterize difficult times. Governments may impose austerity measures, policies, programs, or packages in order to reduce spending. The underlying adjective, austere, is closely related and characterizes severity, strictness, and abstinence.

An auteur is a filmmaker whose personal vision and artistic control are so distinctive that they're considered the primary creative force behind their work, like a novelist or painter. The term emerged from French film criticism to argue that directors—not screenwriters or studios—are the true authors of their films. {Hitchcock was the quintessential auteur.} The concept now extends beyond cinema to any creative domain where individual vision dominates: {She's the auteur of her own fashion label}.

Authentic means genuine or real, not counterfeit or copied: {an authentic Picasso}, {authentic Mexican cuisine}. Something authentic is true to its origins or claims. A person described as authentic is sincere and unpretentious—their behavior matches their true self rather than being performed for others: {She appreciated his authentic personality}. The word often signals approval, implying integrity and trustworthiness.

To authenticate is to verify that something is genuine or that someone is who they claim to be. Documents, artworks, and signatures are authenticated to confirm they're not forgeries: {Experts authenticated the painting as a genuine Vermeer}. In computing, authentication confirms user identity through passwords, biometrics, or security tokens. The adjective authentic and noun authentication are more common than the verb.

Authentication is the process of verifying that someone or something is who or what they claim to be. In computing, authentication typically involves passwords, biometric scans, or security tokens: {two-factor authentication}, {The app requires authentication before granting access}. Beyond digital contexts, authentication confirms the genuineness of documents, artworks, or artifacts: {The painting underwent authentication by three experts}.

Authenticity is the quality of being genuine or real rather than fake or imitation. A document's authenticity determines whether it's original or forged. A person's authenticity means they act according to their true self rather than performing for others: {I admire her authenticity—she never pretends to be someone she's not}. In philosophy and psychology, authenticity often describes living in accordance with one's values despite social pressure.

An author is someone who writes—especially books, articles, or other substantial works. The term carries more weight than "writer," suggesting completed, published work: {the author of three novels}, {a best-selling author}. Author also extends to anyone who creates or originates something: {the author of the plan}. As a verb, to author is to write or create: {She authored the report}.

Authoring is the act of creating content, especially written works. While author as a verb works for any text {She authored the report}, authoring appears most often in computing contexts: authoring {software}, authoring {tools}. These are programs for creating multimedia content, websites, or interactive materials without requiring traditional programming skills.

Authorisation is the British spelling of authorization—the act of granting permission or official approval for something to proceed. It refers both to the process of approving and to the document or credential that proves approval: {You'll need written authorisation from the department head}. In computing, authorisation determines what actions a user is permitted to perform after their identity has been verified.

Authorised is the British spelling of authorized, meaning officially approved or given permission. Someone authorised to act has been granted authority to do so: {Only authorised personnel may enter}. A company can be an authorised dealer, a document can be authorised for release. The spelling with -ise is standard in British English, while American English uses -ize.

Authoritarian describes a system or person demanding strict obedience to authority at the expense of personal freedom. An authoritarian {government} concentrates power and limits dissent. An authoritarian {parent} enforces rigid rules without explanation. As a noun, an authoritarian is someone who favors or exercises such control: {The new CEO governed like an authoritarian}.

Authoritarianism is a political system or philosophy in which a central authority holds power and limits individual freedoms, often suppressing opposition and controlling many aspects of public and private life. Unlike totalitarianism, authoritarianism may tolerate some social institutions operating independently, provided they don't challenge state power. The term also describes attitudes or behaviors that demand strict obedience to authority at the expense of personal freedom: {The company's authoritarianism drove away talented employees who valued autonomy}.

Authoritarians are people who favor or enforce strict obedience to authority at the expense of personal freedom. The term describes both leaders who concentrate power and suppress dissent, and followers who prefer strong hierarchical control: {The regime was run by authoritarians who tolerated no opposition}. As an adjective, authoritarian describes systems, tendencies, or personalities marked by this preference for unquestioning compliance.

Authoritative describes something or someone possessing recognized authority or expertise. An authoritative {source} is reliable and trustworthy. An authoritative {tone} conveys confidence and command—sometimes warranted, sometimes not. An authoritative {account} is considered definitive: {the authoritative biography of Lincoln}. The word can suggest either genuine expertise or merely the manner of it.

Authorities are people or institutions with official power to make decisions, enforce rules, or control others. Police, government agencies, and regulatory bodies are {the authorities}: {He was questioned by authorities}. The word often implies legitimate power that demands compliance. An authority on a subject is an expert whose knowledge commands respect: {She's an authority on medieval history}. In the singular, authority is the power itself: {Who has authority here?}

Authority is the power to determine or judge things, or the right to control or command: In our house, only our father had absolute authority. A person or institution who has this power or right can also be called an authority: Authorities have issued a warning of very severe weather tonight. Almost any government department or organization can be called an authority in a particular area. If you are an authority about a subject, you know a lot about it and others may come to you for advice or information: The book has made her an international authority on mineral nutrition.

Authorization is official permission or approval to do something: {You'll need authorization from the department head}. In computing and security, authorization determines what actions a user is permitted to perform after their identity has been verified. The verb authorize and the act of granting permission share this sense of sanctioned access or action.

To authorize is to give official permission or approval for something to happen. A manager authorizes expenses, a government authorizes military action, a cardholder authorizes a transaction. The word carries formal weight—you don't authorize a friend to borrow your pen, but you might authorize a contractor to begin work. {She wasn't authorized to release that information.} An authorized dealer or biography has official sanction from the source.

Authorized means officially permitted or sanctioned. An authorized {dealer} has formal approval to sell a product. An authorized {biography} is written with the subject's cooperation and blessing. To be authorized is to have proper credentials or permission: {Only authorized personnel may enter}. The word implies legitimacy granted by someone with the power to grant it.

Authors are people who write—books, articles, essays, or other texts. The term carries more weight than "writer," suggesting completed, published work: {the author of three novels}. Author also means originator more broadly: {the author of the plan}. As a verb, to author is to write or create: {She authored the report}. In academic contexts, authors are credited contributors to research papers.

Authorship is the state of being the author of something—having written or created a work. Questions of authorship ask who wrote what: {The authorship of several Shakespeare plays has been disputed}. The term also refers to the occupation or practice of writing: {She pursued authorship after retiring from law}.

Autism is a neurological condition characterized by differences in social communication, sensory processing, and patterns of behavior or interests. It exists on a spectrum, meaning autistic people vary widely in how the condition affects them—some need significant daily support while others live independently with few accommodations. The clinical term is autism spectrum disorder (ASD), though many in the autistic community reject framing it as a disorder. {My son was diagnosed with autism at age three.} {She's autistic and advocates for neurodiversity acceptance.}

Autistic describes someone with autism, a neurological condition affecting social interaction, communication, and sensory processing. The condition exists on a spectrum—some autistic people need significant support while others live independently. The word also appears as informal slang for obsessive focus or social awkwardness: {I went full autistic on spreadsheets this weekend}. This casual use is controversial.

Auto is a prefix meaning self or automatic: {autocorrect}, {autopilot}, {autobiography}. As a standalone word, auto is a somewhat dated informal term for automobile: {auto insurance}, {auto mechanic}, {the auto industry}. In photography and electronics, auto refers to automatic settings: {Switch the camera to auto}.

An autobahn is a highway in a German-speaking country, particularly Germany's federal motorway system famous for having no general speed limit on many stretches. The word is German for "car road." English speakers often use it with a sense of high-speed driving: {He was doing 150 on the autobahn}. The plural is autobahns or autobahnen.

Autobiographies are books in which people tell the stories of their own lives. The word distinguishes self-written life accounts from biographies, which are written by someone else about their subject. {She's reading the autobiographies of jazz musicians}. An autobiography typically covers a full life or significant portion of it, while a memoir may focus on particular events or themes.

An autobiography is a person's account of their own life, written by themselves. The term distinguishes such works from biographies, which are written by others. Autobiographies typically cover significant portions of a life and reflect on formative experiences: {She published her autobiography at seventy}. A memoir is similar but usually focuses on specific periods or themes rather than a full life story.

Autocomplete is a software feature that predicts and suggests completions as you type, based on common patterns or previous entries. Search engines autocomplete queries; phones autocomplete words and phrases. The feature saves keystrokes but can suggest embarrassing or unwanted options: {The autocomplete revealed his search history}. As a verb: {My phone autocompleted "love" to "love you" and I sent it to my boss}.
clues: Predicts what you're about to type

definition: Autocorrect is software that automatically fixes typing errors or suggests corrections as you type. It catches misspellings and typos but sometimes "corrects" words you meant to type, producing unintended—often embarrassing—substitutions: {Autocorrect changed "coming" to "cumming" in my text to grandma}. The term also works as a verb: {My phone autocorrected it}.

Autocorrected describes text that has been automatically changed by software attempting to fix spelling or typing errors. The corrections often miss the mark, substituting unintended words: {I meant to type "duck" but it autocorrected to something else}. The term implies the change happened without the writer's intent, often as an excuse for embarrassing messages.

Autocorrects is the third-person singular of autocorrect, the feature on phones and computers that automatically changes typed text to what it guesses you meant. The feature catches genuine typos but notoriously substitutes wrong words, creating unintended meanings: {My phone autocorrects "duck" to something else entirely}. As a noun, autocorrects are the changes themselves: {I had to fix three autocorrects in that message}.

Autocracies is the plural of autocracy—a system of government in which one person holds absolute power, unchecked by laws or other institutions. The term also describes nations governed this way: {The region's autocracies have resisted democratic reforms}. Unlike democracies, autocracies concentrate authority rather than distributing it.

Autocracy is government by a single person with unlimited power. The autocrat's authority faces no constitutional checks—no legislature, judiciary, or electorate constrains their decisions. The term often carries negative connotations, implying tyranny or oppression: {The country slid from democracy into autocracy}. Autocracy can also describe any organization where one person holds absolute control: {He runs the company as an autocracy}.

An autocrat is a ruler with absolute power, unchecked by laws or other governing bodies. The term extends to anyone who wields authority in a domineering, unilateral way: {My boss is a complete autocrat—she never consults anyone}. Autocratic describes this style of rule or behavior.

Autocratic describes rule by a single person with absolute power, or behavior that resembles such rule. An autocratic {government} concentrates authority in one leader who tolerates no opposition. The word extends to anyone who acts domineering or dictatorial: {an autocratic boss}, {an autocratic management style}. The tone is almost always critical—autocratic leaders don't consult others or share decision-making.

Autocrats are rulers who hold absolute power, governing without meaningful checks from legislatures, courts, or citizens. The term applies to dictators, absolute monarchs, and anyone who wields unchallenged authority: {The autocrats of the 20th century left millions dead}. In looser usage, autocrat describes anyone who acts domineering or brooks no dissent: {My boss is a total autocrat}.

Autofill is a software feature that automatically completes form fields or text entries based on previously stored information. Browsers and phones remember names, addresses, passwords, and credit card numbers to save typing: {My browser autofilled the shipping address}. The word works as noun or verb: {Turn off autofill for passwords}, {It autofilled the wrong email}.

Autofocus is a camera system that automatically adjusts the lens to bring subjects into sharp focus, freeing the photographer from manual focusing. Most modern cameras and smartphones use autofocus by default. The term also works as a verb: {The camera autofocused on her face}. As an adjective: {an autofocus lens}.

An autograph is a person's signature, especially a famous person's, sought as a memento: {She waited outside the stadium to get autographs from the players}. The word also means any document written in the author's own hand—the original manuscript rather than a copy. As a verb, to autograph is to sign something: {He autographed my baseball}.

Autographed means signed by the person in question, typically someone famous: {an autographed copy of her novel}, {autographed baseballs}. The signature adds value or sentimental worth because it represents direct contact with the celebrity or author. Items may be autographed in person or through the mail.

Autographs are signatures, especially those of famous people collected as keepsakes or sold as memorabilia: {She got autographs from the entire cast}. The verb means to sign something for a fan or collector: {He autographed baseballs for an hour after the game}. An autograph can also mean any document in the author's own handwriting.

An automaker is a company that manufactures automobiles. The term typically refers to major corporations like Ford, Toyota, or Volkswagen rather than small custom builders: {Japanese automakers dominated the market for fuel-efficient cars}. Also spelled as two words: auto maker.

An automat is a type of restaurant where food and drink are dispensed from coin-operated machines behind small glass doors. The customer inserts coins, opens the door, and retrieves the item. Popular in American cities from the early to mid-20th century, automats offered quick, inexpensive meals without waitstaff: {We grabbed sandwiches at the automat between shows}. The word comes from the same root as automatic. The format has largely disappeared, surviving mainly as nostalgia.

Automata is the plural of automaton—self-operating machines or mechanisms designed to follow a predetermined sequence of operations. The term appears most often in technical contexts: cellular automata in mathematics, finite automata in computer science. In older usage, automata were mechanical figures that mimicked living creatures: {The 18th-century automata could write, draw, and play music}.

To automate is to convert a process so machines or computers perform it without human intervention. Factory assembly lines were automated; now software automates data entry, scheduling, and countless other tasks. {We automated our email responses.} The goal is usually efficiency, though automation often displaces workers.

Automated describes processes or systems that operate with minimal human intervention, typically through machinery or computers. An automated {factory} runs largely without workers. Automated {emails} send themselves when triggered. To automate is to convert something to such a system: {We automated the billing process last year}.

Automatic describes actions or processes that happen without conscious effort or human intervention. An automatic {door} opens by sensor. An automatic {transmission} shifts gears without driver input. Automatic {breathing} continues without thought. The word also suggests inevitability: {Membership comes with automatic renewal}. As a noun, an automatic is a self-loading firearm or a car with automatic transmission.

Automatically means without deliberate thought or intervention. A machine that runs automatically operates on its own once started. Actions performed automatically happen by reflex or habit: {I automatically reached for my phone when I woke up}. The word often implies efficiency—something handled without requiring attention—but can suggest lack of consideration: {She automatically assumes the worst}.

Automating is the process of making something operate automatically, without continuous human intervention. You automate tasks by setting up systems—mechanical, electronic, or software—to perform them independently: {We're automating the invoice process}, {automating customer responses}. The goal is typically efficiency, consistency, or freeing humans for other work.

Automation is the use of machines, computers, or technology to perform tasks with minimal human involvement. What once required hands now requires only switches, sensors, or software. Factory automation replaced assembly-line workers; home automation lets you control lights and thermostats from your phone. The word often surfaces in debates about jobs: {Automation threatens to eliminate millions of positions in the service sector.} To automate a process is to convert it from manual to automatic operation.

An automaton is a machine that operates by itself, especially one designed to imitate human or animal actions. The word often suggests mechanical, unthinking movement—a robot following its programming. Figuratively, someone who acts like an automaton behaves without emotion or independent thought: {He moved through his workday like an automaton}. Plural: automata or automatons.

Automatons is a plural of automaton—a self-operating machine, especially one designed to imitate human or animal actions. Early automatons were mechanical marvels: clockwork figures that wrote, played music, or performed tricks. The word extends to people who act mechanically, without thought or feeling: {The workers moved like automatons on the assembly line}. The alternate plural automata appears in technical and academic contexts.

Automats were coin-operated self-service restaurants, most popular in American cities from the early to mid-twentieth century. Patrons inserted coins into slots beside small glass compartments to access prepared foods like sandwiches, pie, and coffee. The Horn & Hardart chain made automats iconic in New York and Philadelphia. The term also applies more broadly to any vending machine or automated food-dispensing device. {The automat offered a quick, cheap lunch for office workers.}

An automobile is a self-propelled passenger vehicle, typically with four wheels and an internal combustion or electric engine—a car. The word emphasizes the machine's ability to move under its own power rather than being pulled by horses. Automobile sounds more formal than car and appears often in industry contexts: {the automobile industry}, {automobile insurance}. As a verb, rarely used, it means to travel by car.

Autonomous means self-governing or independent—able to act or function without external control. An autonomous {region} has political self-rule. An autonomous {vehicle} operates without a human driver. The word emphasizes freedom from outside authority or intervention: {The department operates as an autonomous unit within the university}. In philosophy and psychology, autonomy refers to the capacity for self-directed choice and action.

Autonomy is the capacity to govern oneself—to make decisions and act according to one's own judgment rather than external control. Nations seek political autonomy from colonial powers. Individuals value personal autonomy in medical decisions: {The patient has autonomy over her treatment}. In philosophy, autonomy is central to moral agency—the ability to choose freely makes ethical responsibility possible. Autonomous vehicles and systems operate without human intervention.

Autopay is a payment arrangement where charges are automatically deducted from a bank account or credit card on a recurring basis: {I set up autopay for my utilities so I never miss a payment}. Most subscription services and bills offer autopay as an option. The system eliminates manual payments but requires monitoring to catch errors or unwanted charges.

Autopilot is a system that controls a vehicle—originally aircraft, now also cars and ships—without continuous human input. The pilot or driver can disengage to let the machine maintain course, altitude, or speed. Figuratively, to be {on autopilot} is to act mechanically, without conscious thought: {I was so tired I drove home on autopilot}.

Autoplay is a feature that automatically starts playing media—video, audio, or the next episode in a series—without requiring the user to click play. {I disabled autoplay because videos kept blasting in my headphones.} Websites and apps use autoplay to keep users engaged, though many find it intrusive. The term also functions as a verb: {The next episode autoplayed before I could stop it.}

Autopsies is the plural of autopsy, a medical examination of a corpse to determine cause of death. The procedure involves systematic inspection of organs and tissues, performed by a pathologist. Autopsies may be required by law in suspicious deaths or requested by families seeking answers: {The autopsies revealed traces of poison}.

An autopsy is an examination of a dead body to determine the cause of death. A medical examiner or pathologist performs it by dissecting the corpse and examining organs, tissues, and fluids. Autopsies may be required by law in cases of suspicious or unexplained death: {The autopsy revealed traces of poison}. Figuratively, an autopsy is any after-the-fact analysis of a failure: {The team conducted an autopsy of the failed product launch}.

An autorickshaw is a small three-wheeled vehicle used as a taxi, common in South Asia and other parts of the developing world. It typically has a motor scooter front, a cabin for passengers, and an open or canvas-covered frame. Also called a tuk-tuk, auto, or rickshaw: {We hired an autorickshaw to get across town}.

Autosave is a software feature that automatically saves your work at regular intervals, protecting against data loss from crashes, power outages, or forgetting to save manually. Most word processors, spreadsheets, and creative applications now include autosave, often syncing to cloud storage. {I didn't lose anything when my laptop died because autosave had my back.} As a verb, to autosave means to save automatically without user intervention.

Autotune is audio processing software that corrects pitch in vocal and instrumental performances, snapping notes to the nearest correct tone. Used subtly, it's invisible; used aggressively, it creates a robotic, warbling effect that became a signature sound in pop and hip-hop: {That song is autotuned to death}. The verb means to apply this effect: {They autotuned her voice}. Often used dismissively to suggest a singer lacks natural talent.

Autotuned describes audio, especially vocals, that has been processed through pitch-correction software to achieve perfect or near-perfect intonation. The effect can be subtle, smoothing out minor imperfections, or pushed to extremes for a distinctive robotic, warbling quality associated with pop and hip-hop: {That chorus is so autotuned it sounds like a robot singing}. Figuratively, autotuned can describe anything artificially polished or lacking authentic character.

Autotuning is the process of automatically adjusting parameters for optimal performance. In audio production, Auto-Tune (the software) corrects pitch in vocal recordings, smoothing imperfect notes or creating a distinctive robotic effect heard in pop and hip-hop: {Her voice was obviously autotuned}. In computing, autotuning lets software optimize itself for specific hardware configurations.

Autoworkers are people employed in the automobile manufacturing industry, typically in factories that produce cars, trucks, and their components. The term often appears in discussions of labor unions, trade policy, and industrial economics: {The autoworkers went on strike for better wages}. {Detroit autoworkers faced layoffs when production moved overseas}.

Autumn is the season between summer and winter, when temperatures cool and deciduous trees shed their leaves. In North America, *fall* is the more common term; *autumn* sounds slightly more formal or literary. The word extends to periods of decline or maturity: {the autumn of her career}, {an autumn romance}. As an adjective: {autumn leaves}, {autumn colors}.

Autumnal means relating to or characteristic of autumn: {autumnal colors}, {autumnal equinox}. The word often carries connotations of decline, melancholy, or late maturity—the waning phase before winter: {an autumnal mood}, {the autumnal years of his career}. It's more literary than simply saying "fall."

Availability is the state of being accessible or obtainable. A product's availability determines whether you can buy it; a person's availability determines whether they can meet. The word often implies readiness for use or action: {Check the doctor's availability for next week}. In dating contexts, availability suggests being single or open to romantic interest.

Available describes something ready for use or accessible when needed. A product is available if it's in stock; a person is available if free to meet or, in dating contexts, not in a relationship: {Is she available?} {The report will be available next week.} {No rooms were available.} Something that {avails} itself to you presents itself for your use.

An avalanche is a mass of snow, ice, and debris sliding rapidly down a mountainside. The word extends to any overwhelming quantity arriving suddenly: {an avalanche of mail}, {an avalanche of criticism}. As a verb, to avalanche is to descend or accumulate like an avalanche: {Letters avalanched into the office}.

Avalanches is the plural of avalanche—a mass of snow, ice, and debris sliding rapidly down a mountainside. The term extends to any sudden overwhelming quantity: {an avalanche of emails}, {an avalanche of criticism}. As a verb form, avalanches describes the action: {Snow avalanches down the slope when conditions are right}.

Avarice is extreme greed for wealth or material gain. The word carries a moralizing tone, suggesting not just wanting money but an excessive, almost obsessive desire to accumulate it: {His avarice knew no bounds}. Avarice appears more in literary or religious contexts than everyday speech, where greed serves the same purpose.

An avatar is a digital representation of a person in virtual spaces—video games, chat rooms, social media. Users customize avatars to represent themselves or create alternate identities: {My avatar has purple hair and wings}. The word comes from Hindu mythology, where an avatar is the earthly incarnation of a deity, particularly Vishnu descending to earth in human or animal form. This religious sense persists in discussions of Hinduism and occasionally in figurative use for someone who perfectly embodies a quality: {He was the avatar of cool}.

Avatars is the plural of avatar, which has meanings that connect through the idea of embodiment or manifestation. In Hindu tradition, an avatar is a deity descended to earth in physical form—Vishnu's avatars include Krishna and Rama. The word extends to any embodiment of a concept or quality: {She was the avatar of elegance}. In computing, an avatar is a digital representation of a user—a character, icon, or image that stands in for you in games, forums, or virtual worlds: {Players customize their avatars before entering the game}.

To avenge is to inflict harm or punishment in return for a wrong done to oneself or another: {She vowed to avenge her brother's murder}. Unlike revenge, which centers on personal satisfaction, avenge carries a sense of justice or righting a wrong. The person avenged is typically the victim, not the one acting: {He avenged his fallen comrades}.

Avenged is the past tense of avenge, meaning to inflict punishment or harm in retaliation for a wrong done to oneself or another: {She avenged her father's murder}. Unlike revenge, which often implies personal spite, avenge carries a sense of justice or righteous retribution. {The defeat was avenged in the rematch}.

An avenger is someone who inflicts harm or punishment in return for a wrong done to themselves or others. The word carries overtones of righteous retribution: {He styled himself an avenger of the oppressed}. In superhero contexts, avengers are heroes who fight injustice, though the original sense implies retaliation rather than prevention.

Avengers are people who inflict punishment or harm in return for a wrong done to themselves or others. The word carries a sense of righteous retaliation rather than mere revenge: {The avengers tracked down the men who had killed their father}. An avenger acts on behalf of justice, often outside legal channels. (Capitalized Avengers refers to the Marvel superhero team.)

Avenging describes the act of taking revenge or inflicting punishment on behalf of oneself or another. An avenging {angel} brings divine retribution. An avenging {hero} seeks justice for wrongs done. The word carries connotations of righteous payback rather than mere retaliation: {She returned as an avenging force against those who had betrayed her family}.

Avenue is a broad street, often tree-lined or otherwise distinguished from ordinary roads. In city grids, avenues typically run perpendicular to streets: {Fifth Avenue}, {Park Avenue}. Figuratively, an avenue is a means of approach or access: {We've explored every avenue}. The word suggests a path toward something—whether physical or abstract.

Avenues is the plural of avenue, a wide street or road, often lined with trees or leading to an important destination. The word extends to figurative paths or approaches: {We explored every avenue before making a decision}. In cities, avenue often distinguishes streets running one direction from those running perpendicular.

Common elements of meaning can be found in uses of average, whether as noun, verb, or adjective. The core meaning is a single value that represents a summary of a range of unequal values: The average of 4, 6, and 20 is 10. When derived mathematically, that number is technically called the mean, but colloquially, it’s known as the average. To average a set of values is to find their mean. Anything designated as average is intermediate in value or quality: The movie was just average; the baby’s length is average for his age.

Averages functions as both noun and verb forms of average. As a noun, averages are typical or middle values calculated from a set of numbers: {batting averages}, {grade point averages}. The verb means to calculate such a value or to achieve as a typical amount: {She averages six hours of sleep}. To {average out} is to reach an equilibrium over time: {Some days are better than others, but it averages out}.

Averaging is finding the mean of a set of numbers—adding them together and dividing by how many there are. The term extends to any process of finding a typical or central value: {Averaging across all participants, the treatment showed modest improvement}. In finance, {averaging down} means buying more shares as a price falls to reduce your average cost per share.

Aversion is a strong dislike or disinclination toward something: {She has an aversion to public speaking}. The word suggests turning away—you avoid what you find distasteful or repellent. An aversion can be mild preference or visceral disgust: {His aversion to needles made blood draws difficult}. Risk-averse investors avoid uncertainty; the averse person steers clear of what bothers them.

Aversions are strong dislikes or feelings of repugnance toward something. The word captures active avoidance rather than mere indifference: {She had an aversion to crowds}. People speak of aversions to foods, social situations, or ideas that provoke visceral distaste: {His aversions included small talk and fluorescent lighting}.

To avert is to turn away or prevent. You avert your {eyes} or {gaze} from something you don't want to see. More commonly, avert means to ward off or prevent something undesirable: {avert disaster}, {avert a crisis}, {avert war}. The word suggests deflecting what's coming rather than stopping it directly.

Averted is the past tense of avert, meaning turned away or prevented. You avert your eyes or gaze by looking elsewhere: {She averted her eyes from the accident scene}. To avert disaster, crisis, or danger is to prevent it from happening: {Quick action averted a catastrophe}. Both senses share the idea of steering something away from its course.

An aviary is a large enclosure for keeping birds, typically allowing them space to fly. Unlike cages, aviaries are sized for the birds rather than for convenient display: {The zoo's tropical aviary houses dozens of species}. The word shares its root with aviation—both derive from the Latin for bird.

Aviation encompasses the design, development, operation, and use of aircraft, particularly heavier-than-air machines like airplanes and helicopters. The term covers both the technical aspects of flight and the broader industry surrounding it, including commercial airlines, military air forces, and private flying. Someone who works in aviation might be a pilot, engineer, air traffic controller, or flight attendant. {She pursued a career in aviation after getting her pilot's license.}

An aviator is a person who flies aircraft—a pilot. The term carries a slightly formal or historical tone, often evoking early aviation pioneers or military flyers: {Amelia Earhart was a celebrated aviator}. Aviator sunglasses, with their teardrop shape and thin metal frames, were designed for pilots and remain a popular style.

Aviators are sunglasses with large teardrop-shaped lenses and thin metal frames, originally designed for pilots to reduce glare. The style remains popular for its classic look: {He pushed his aviators up on his head}. Aviator can also simply mean a pilot, though this use sounds dated or formal.

Avid describes eager enthusiasm or intense interest: an avid {reader}, an avid {collector}, avid {fans}. The word suggests sustained dedication rather than passing curiosity—someone avid about something pursues it with genuine appetite. {She's an avid hiker who hits the trails every weekend.}

Avocado is a fruit with buttery green flesh and a large pit. The word comes from Nahuatl, the Aztec language, where {ahuacatl} meant both the fruit and, because of its shape, testicle. People eat avocados mashed into guacamole, sliced on toast, or blended into smoothies. {I'll have the avocado toast.}

Avocados is the plural of avocado, the pear-shaped fruit with green or blackish skin, creamy pale-green flesh, and a large pit. Native to Mexico and Central America, avocados are eaten raw—in guacamole, on toast, in salads, or sliced into sandwiches. {The avocados at the market were finally ripe.}

To avoid something is to stay away from it or prevent it from happening: {Avoid the freeway during rush hour}, {She avoided eye contact}. The word suggests deliberate effort to not encounter or experience something unwanted. You can avoid a person, a topic, a collision, or a mistake. To avoid doing something is to refrain from it: {He avoided answering the question directly}.

Avoidable describes something that can be prevented or escaped. An avoidable {accident} is one that didn't have to happen. Avoidable {costs} are expenses that can be eliminated. The word often carries implicit criticism—calling something avoidable suggests someone should have prevented it: {His death was entirely avoidable}.

Avoidance is the act of staying away from something or preventing it from happening. You might practice {avoidance of conflict} or {tax avoidance}—legal strategies to minimize what you owe. The word often carries a slight judgment: {His avoidance of the topic was obvious}. In psychology, avoidance behavior means steering clear of situations that trigger anxiety.

Avoidant describes a tendency to avoid—particularly in psychology, where it characterizes people who withdraw from emotional closeness or social interaction. An avoidant {attachment style} develops in childhood and shapes adult relationships. Someone avoidant in relationships may pull away when intimacy deepens: {He gets avoidant whenever we talk about the future}.

Await means to wait for something expected: {We await your decision}. It's slightly more formal than wait for, common in official or written contexts: {The suspect awaits trial}. What awaits you is what lies ahead: {No one knows what awaits us}. In computing, await pauses code execution until an asynchronous operation completes.

Awake means not asleep, or to stop sleeping. You can lie awake at night, be wide awake at dawn, or stay awake through a boring lecture. To awaken is to wake up or to rouse: {The noise awoke him}. Figuratively, awake suggests alertness or awareness: {awake to the dangers}, {a rude awakening}. The adjective pairs with to: {I'm awake to the possibilities}.

Awaken means to wake up or rouse from sleep: {A noise awakened me at three in the morning}. It extends to stirring any dormant state—awakening memories, suspicions, or desires. The word carries a slightly more literary or dramatic tone than wake: {The experience awakened something in her}. A spiritual or political awakening marks a profound shift in consciousness or understanding.

Awakened is the past tense and past participle of awaken—to wake up or rouse from sleep: {She awakened at dawn}. Figuratively, it means having become aware or spiritually conscious: {an awakened sense of justice}, {spiritually awakened}. In New Age and Buddhist contexts, awakened describes someone who has achieved enlightenment or heightened consciousness: {an awakened master}.

Awakening is the act of waking up or becoming aware. The literal sense involves rousing from sleep: {The baby's awakening came earlier than usual}. More often it describes a new awareness or realization: {a spiritual awakening}, {a political awakening}. An awakening can be pleasant—discovering a passion—or harsh: {a rude awakening} is an unpleasant confrontation with reality.

Awakenings are instances of waking up or becoming aware. The word often carries spiritual or intellectual weight—moments when someone gains new understanding or consciousness: {The book describes her series of political awakenings}. A single dramatic awakening may transform someone's worldview, while gradual awakenings accumulate into changed perspective.

An award is something given in recognition of achievement or merit—a prize, medal, or honor: {She won the award for best director}. Awards are also sums granted by official decision: {The jury's award exceeded what the plaintiff sought}. To award is to grant or bestow: {The committee awarded her the scholarship}. {The contract was awarded to the lowest bidder}.

Awards are honors or prizes given in recognition of achievement, merit, or victory: {She won three awards at the ceremony}, {The film swept the awards season}. To award is to grant such recognition, or more broadly, to give officially: {The jury awarded damages to the plaintiff}. Award can also mean something granted by decision rather than negotiation: an arbitration award, a contract award.

Aware means having knowledge or consciousness of something: {I wasn't aware you were coming}. It implies perception or realization: {She became aware of footsteps behind her}. Someone who is aware of current events or social issues stays informed. The word often pairs with prepositions: aware {of} dangers, aware {that} time is short.

Awareness is the state of knowing or perceiving something. You can have awareness of your surroundings, of a problem, or of your own thoughts and feelings. The word often implies conscious attention: {She had no awareness that anyone was watching}. Awareness campaigns aim to inform the public about issues: {breast cancer awareness}, {climate awareness}. Self-awareness is understanding your own character and motivations.

Awash means covered or flooded with water, especially so that water washes over the surface: {The deck was awash in the storm}. The word extends to any overwhelming abundance: {The office was awash in paperwork}, {a city awash with tourists}. Something awash is inundated, swamped, unable to stay above the tide of whatever surrounds it.

Away indicates distance or separation from a reference point—usually here, now, or the speaker. Someone who is away is not present: {She's away on business}. To move away is to increase distance: {He walked away without looking back}. Away can mean into storage or safekeeping: {Put the dishes away}. It also suggests continuous action: {They talked away the afternoon}. In sports, an away game is played at the opponent's venue. {Right away} and {straight away} mean immediately.

Awe is a feeling of reverential wonder mixed with fear or admiration, inspired by something vast, powerful, or sublime: {We stood in awe of the mountain}. The word suggests being overwhelmed—rendered small or speechless by what you're witnessing. To be in awe of someone is to regard them with profound respect. Awesome originally meant inspiring awe; now it's casual praise for anything good. Awful once meant the same but shifted to mean very bad. Awe-inspiring retains the original force.

Awed describes the state of feeling awe—a mixture of wonder, reverence, and sometimes fear in the presence of something grand or powerful. You might stand awed before a cathedral, a mountain range, or an act of extraordinary courage. {The crowd fell silent, awed by the display}. To be awed is to feel small in the best sense.

Until the late 20th century, awesome was used mainly for things that genuinely inspired awe and it was often used in a religious context. It is a frequent word in Bible translations: Before our own eyes, the Lord performed great and awesome deeds of power against Egypt, Pharaoh, and his entire dynasty. Today, awesome has much wider and weaker use and is synonymous with such words as great, remarkable, or fantastic: You get Friday off? Awesome!

Awesomeness is the quality of being awesome—impressive, excellent, or worthy of admiration. The word follows the trajectory of awesome itself, which shifted from genuine awe (as before God or nature) to casual enthusiasm. Now awesomeness usually describes anything cool or excellent: {The sheer awesomeness of that guitar solo}, {Rate this movie's awesomeness on a scale of one to ten}.
clues: The trait of being truly impressive

definition: Awestruck describes being filled with awe—a mix of wonder, reverence, and sometimes fear in the presence of something vast or powerful. Someone might stand awestruck before the Grand Canyon, a great work of art, or a display of extraordinary talent: {The audience sat awestruck as she played}. Also spelled awe-struck.

Awful describes something extremely bad, unpleasant, or of poor quality: {The weather was awful all week}. It intensifies negative states—you might feel awful when sick or guilty. Informally, awful works as an intensifier meaning "very" or "a great deal of": {an awful lot of people showed up}. The word originally meant "inspiring awe," a sense now largely obsolete except in the related adverb awfully, which can mean either terribly or very: {I'm awfully sorry}.

Awkward describes something clumsy, ungainly, or lacking grace. An awkward {movement} is physically ungraceful. An awkward {silence} is socially uncomfortable—people don't know what to say. An awkward {situation} puts someone in a difficult position: {It was awkward running into my ex at the party}. The word often captures that cringe-inducing feeling when something doesn't flow naturally. An awkward {angle} or awkward {shape} is hard to manage or maneuver around.

Awkwardness is the quality of being uncomfortable, clumsy, or socially uneasy. Physical awkwardness shows in ungainly movement: {the awkwardness of a newborn foal}. Social awkwardness involves discomfort in interactions: {There was an awkwardness between them after the breakup}. A situation's awkwardness comes from tension or embarrassment that no one quite knows how to dispel.

An awning is a roof-like covering, usually of canvas or similar material, extending over a doorway, window, or outdoor area to provide shade or shelter from rain. Awnings on storefronts often display the business name. {The café's striped awning shaded the sidewalk tables.}

Awnings are roof-like coverings that extend over windows, doors, or outdoor spaces to provide shade or shelter from weather. They attach to buildings and project outward, often made of canvas or metal: {The café's striped awnings shaded the sidewalk tables}. Retractable awnings can be rolled up when not needed.

Awoke is the past tense of awake. Someone who awoke at dawn woke up then. The word extends to figurative awakening: {She awoke to the dangers of complacency}. Awoken is the past participle: {I had awoken before sunrise}.

Awoken is the past participle of awake, used with helping verbs: {I had awoken before dawn}, {She was awoken by thunder}. The simple past is awoke: {He awoke suddenly}. Awoken also appears in figurative contexts about becoming aware: {They had awoken to the reality of their situation}. The forms awake, awoke, and awoken parallel wake, woke, and woken.
clues: No longer in a sleeping state

definition: Awooga imitates the sound of a loud, old-fashioned horn or klaxon—the kind heard in submarines or vintage cars. Online, it expresses cartoonish attraction or excitement, often accompanying exaggerated reactions to someone attractive: {awooga awooga *eyes pop out of head*}. The spelling varies: awoooga, awooooga.

Awry means turned or twisted to one side, not straight: {His tie was slightly awry}. More commonly, it describes plans or situations that have gone wrong: {Something went awry with the delivery}. The word carries a sense of deviation from what was intended or expected—not catastrophic failure, just things not quite right.

Aww is an exclamation of sympathetic or sentimental response, typically to something endearing, cute, or touching: {Aww, look at the puppy!} It can also express mild disappointment or sympathy: {Aww, that's too bad}. The spelling stretches to match the sound—more w's for more feeling.

An axe is a tool with a heavy metal blade on a wooden handle, used for chopping wood or felling trees. The figurative axe is a cutting instrument of a different sort—to {get the axe} is to be fired or eliminated, and to {have an axe to grind} is to have a personal agenda. In music slang, an axe is a guitar. Also spelled ax.

Axed is the past tense of axe. To axe something is to cut it with an axe, but the word more often means to eliminate or cancel abruptly: {The network axed the show after one season}. People get axed when they're fired: {Half the department got axed in the layoffs}. The word suggests swift, decisive removal.

An axel is a figure skating jump: the skater launches from the forward outside edge of one skate, rotates in the air, and lands on the back outside edge of the other. Unlike other jumps, the axel takes off while moving forward, adding an extra half-rotation. A single axel is one and a half turns; a double is two and a half; a triple, three and a half. Named for Norwegian skater Axel Paulsen.

An axeman is someone who wields an axe, whether a woodcutter felling trees or a firefighter breaking through doors. The term extends to executioners who beheaded condemned prisoners.
