In music slang, an axeman is a guitarist, especially one known for aggressive or virtuosic playing: {The band's axeman shredded through a ten-minute solo}. Also spelled axman.

Axemen is the plural of axeman—someone who wields an axe, whether for felling trees, splitting wood, or combat. The term extends to slang for a guitarist, especially one known for aggressive or virtuosic playing: {The band's axeman shredded through a ten-minute solo}. In Australian rules football, the Axemen are a team nickname.

Axes is the plural of two different words. An axe is a tool with a heavy blade on a handle, used for chopping wood or, historically, as a weapon. To axe something is to eliminate it: {The network axed three shows}. An axis is a line around which something rotates or a reference line on a graph: {the x and y axes}. Someone with {an axe to grind} has a grievance or selfish motive.

Axing is removing, cutting, or terminating—from the tool that chops. A company axes jobs during layoffs. A network axes a show that underperforms. A budget committee axes programs to reduce spending. {The whole department got axed.} The spelling axeing also appears, particularly in British English.

An axiom is a statement accepted as true without proof, serving as a starting point for reasoning. In mathematics and logic, axioms are foundational assumptions from which other truths are derived: {Euclid's axioms form the basis of plane geometry}. More loosely, an axiom is any self-evident truth or established principle: {It's an axiom of politics that all campaigns need money}.

Axioms are statements or principles accepted as true without requiring proof, serving as starting points for reasoning or argument. In mathematics and logic, axioms form the foundation from which theorems are derived: {Euclid's axioms underpin classical geometry}. More broadly, an axiom is any self-evident truth or established principle that people take for granted: {It's an axiom of politics that all campaigns promise more than they deliver}.

An axis is an imaginary straight line around which something rotates or is symmetrically arranged. The Earth spins on its axis once every twenty-four hours. In geometry and graphs, axes are reference lines used to locate points in space: {the x-axis and y-axis of a coordinate plane}. The word extends to any central line or organizing principle: {the axis of a debate}. In World War II, the Axis referred to Germany, Italy, Japan, and their allies.

An axle is a rod or shaft on which wheels rotate. In vehicles, axles connect opposite wheels and transmit power from the engine to the road: {The rear axle needs replacing}. The word extends to any central shaft around which something turns. To {wrap around the axle} is to become excessively tangled in a problem.

Axles is the plural of axle, a rod or shaft on which wheels rotate. A vehicle's axle connects two wheels and may transmit power from the engine: {The truck's rear axle snapped under the load}. Axles bear the weight of the vehicle and its cargo, making them critical structural components.

An axman is a person who wields an ax, whether for felling trees, chopping wood, or combat. The term extends to anyone who cuts ruthlessly—a corporate axman eliminates jobs or departments: {The new CEO brought in his axman to slash the budget}. In music slang, an axman is a guitarist, from the slang term ax for guitar.

Axmen is the plural of axman—a person who wields an ax, whether for felling trees, splitting wood, or combat. The term extends to anyone who cuts ruthlessly: corporate axmen eliminate jobs and departments. In music slang, an axman plays guitar, the instrument being his ax.

An axolotl is a salamander native to Mexico that remains in its aquatic larval form throughout life, retaining external gills and a finned tail. Unlike most amphibians, it never undergoes metamorphosis to become land-dwelling. Axolotls are studied for their remarkable ability to regenerate limbs and organs, and are kept as aquarium pets.

Axolotls is the plural of axolotl, a salamander native to Mexico that remains in its aquatic larval form throughout life, retaining its feathery external gills rather than developing lungs and moving to land. This trait, called neoteny, makes axolotls unusual among amphibians. They're popular in laboratories and as exotic pets: {She keeps axolotls in a tank in her bedroom}.

Ayahuasca is a psychoactive brew traditionally prepared by indigenous peoples of the Amazon basin, made from the ayahuasca vine combined with other plants containing DMT. The drink induces intense hallucinogenic experiences lasting several hours, often accompanied by vomiting and emotional catharsis. It has become popular in spiritual tourism and alternative therapy circles: {She traveled to Peru for an ayahuasca ceremony}. Also called yagé.

An ayatollah is a high-ranking Shiite Muslim cleric, particularly in Iran. The title indicates significant religious authority and scholarly achievement in Islamic jurisprudence. Since the 1979 Iranian Revolution, the term has become familiar in Western news, often associated with political as well as spiritual leadership: {The ayatollah issued a ruling on the matter}. Sometimes used loosely to describe any stern religious authority figure.

Ayatollahs are high-ranking Shia Muslim clerics, particularly in Iran, who have achieved advanced religious scholarship and authority to interpret Islamic law. The title literally means "sign of God" in Arabic. Since Iran's 1979 Islamic Revolution, ayatollahs have wielded significant political as well as spiritual power, with the Supreme Leader holding ultimate authority. {The ayatollahs issued a ruling on the matter.} In Western usage, the term sometimes carries connotations of rigid religious conservatism.

Aye means yes, used in parliamentary voting {all in favor say aye}, nautical contexts {aye aye, captain}, and some British and Scottish dialects. The ayes are the affirmative votes or those who cast them: {The ayes have it}. A separate word aye, pronounced differently, means always or forever, now archaic except in {for aye}.

Ayurveda is a traditional system of medicine originating in India, emphasizing balance among body, mind, and spirit through diet, herbal remedies, yoga, and lifestyle practices. The term comes from Sanskrit words meaning "knowledge of life." In Western contexts, ayurveda appears in discussions of alternative medicine and wellness: {She consulted an ayurveda practitioner about her digestive issues}. The lowercase form is less common than the capitalized version. (Capitalized Ayurveda is the standard form.)

An azalea is a flowering shrub in the rhododendron family, prized for its showy clusters of blooms in spring. The flowers come in pinks, reds, whites, and purples. Azaleas thrive in acidic soil and partial shade, making them popular in woodland gardens: {The azaleas are spectacular this year}.

Azaleas is the plural of azalea, a flowering shrub in the rhododendron family prized for its showy spring blooms. The flowers come in pinks, reds, whites, and purples, often blanketing yards in the American South: {The azaleas are stunning this year}. Azaleas prefer acidic soil and partial shade.

Azure is a bright blue color, the blue of a clear sky at midday. In heraldry, azure denotes blue on a coat of arms. The word appears often in poetry and elevated prose to describe skies, seas, and eyes: {The azure waters of the Mediterranean stretched before us}. As an adjective, it simply means bright blue: {azure tiles}, {azure eyes}.

Baa is the bleating sound a sheep makes, or a representation of that sound. As a verb, to baa is to make this sound: {The lamb baaed for its mother}. The word is onomatopoeic—it sounds like what it describes. {Baa, baa, black sheep} begins a familiar nursery rhyme.

Babble is rapid, incoherent speech—the sounds a baby makes before learning words, or what adults produce when excited, confused, or delirious: {The fever had him babbling nonsense}. A brook babbles when it makes continuous murmuring sounds over stones. Babble can also mean idle chatter or gossip: {office babble}, {the babble of the crowd}.

Babbled is the past tense of babble—to talk rapidly and continuously in a way that's hard to follow or makes little sense. Babies babble before they can form words. Adults babble when excited, nervous, or incoherent: {She babbled on about her vacation plans}. Water babbles when it flows with a continuous murmuring sound: {The brook babbled over the rocks}.

Babbles is the third-person singular of babble, meaning to talk rapidly and continuously in a way that is foolish, excited, or difficult to understand. Babies babble before they can form words, producing streams of sounds that approximate speech. Water babbles when it makes the continuous murmuring sound of a brook flowing over rocks. {She babbles on about nothing in particular.} The noun babble refers to such speech or sound.

Babbling describes continuous, rapid talk that's hard to follow—either because it lacks sense or because too much comes at once: {The witness was babbling incoherently}. Babies babble before they can speak, producing streams of meaningless but speech-like sounds. A brook babbles when water tumbles over stones, making a continuous murmuring sound.

Babe is an affectionate term for a baby or small child, now somewhat old-fashioned in that sense. More commonly, babe is a term of endearment for a romantic partner: {Hey babe, how was your day?} It also refers to an attractive person, especially a woman: {She's a total babe}. The phrase {babe in the woods} describes someone naive or inexperienced. (Capitalized Babe is a given name or nickname.)

A babel is a confused mixture of sounds, especially many voices speaking at once so that nothing is intelligible: {The meeting dissolved into a babel of competing opinions}. The word comes from the biblical Tower of Babel, where God confounded human speech into mutually incomprehensible languages. Any scene of noise and confusion qualifies. (Capitalized Babel refers to the biblical story.)

Babies is the plural of baby—human infants or the very young of other species. The word extends to anyone treated as immature or helpless: {Don't be such babies about it}. Projects or creations someone feels protective of become their babies: {This startup is my baby}. As a term of endearment, babies addresses multiple loved ones: {Hey babies, I'm home}.

Babka is a rich, yeasted cake of Eastern European Jewish origin, typically featuring swirls of chocolate or cinnamon throughout a soft, brioche-like dough. The loaf is usually braided or twisted before baking, creating distinctive ribbons of filling. Once a humble Sabbath bread, babka gained mainstream American popularity after being featured in a celebrated *Seinfeld* episode debating chocolate versus cinnamon. {We picked up a chocolate babka from the bakery for brunch.}

A baboon is a large, ground-dwelling monkey native to Africa and Arabia, known for its dog-like snout, prominent canine teeth, and often brightly colored rear. Baboons live in hierarchical social groups and have a reputation for aggression. As an insult, baboon suggests someone crude, stupid, or brutish: {Don't be such a baboon}.

Baboons are large, ground-dwelling monkeys native to Africa and Arabia, recognizable by their dog-like snouts, powerful jaws, and prominent canine teeth. They live in hierarchical social groups and have a reputation for aggressive, opportunistic behavior. As an insult, calling someone a baboon suggests they're crude, loud, or stupid: {Those baboons in the back row won't stop talking}.

A babushka is a headscarf folded into a triangle and tied under the chin, traditionally worn by older women in Russia and Eastern Europe. The word is Russian for grandmother, and the scarf carries associations with elderly peasant women: {She wrapped a babushka around her head against the cold}. In American English, babushka sometimes refers to the grandmother herself.

Babushkas is the plural of babushka, a Russian word for grandmother. In English, babushka typically refers to a headscarf tied under the chin, the style associated with elderly Eastern European women: {She wrapped a babushka around her head against the cold}. The word can also refer to an old woman herself, especially one of Slavic background.

Baby is the standard and most frequent term for a newborn human. That core meaning informs all other uses, which partake of some qualities of real babies. Any newborn or very young animal can be called a baby, and it is also a term of endearment, typically used between people who are intimate with each other. Less frequently, baby is used appreciatively to designate inanimate things in small sizes (baby carrots). To baby someone is to either nurture them or treat them inappropriately, as if they were a baby.

Babydaddy is informal slang for the biological father of a woman's child, especially when he is not her husband or current partner. The term often implies an informal or complicated relationship: {My babydaddy is supposed to pick up the kids this weekend}. Also spelled baby daddy or baby's daddy. The parallel term is babymama.

A babydoll is a short, loose-fitting nightgown or negligee, typically ending above the knee and often trimmed with lace or ruffles. The style became popular in the 1950s and remains associated with feminine sleepwear and lingerie. Babydoll can also describe a style of dress with a similar silhouette—fitted at the bust and flowing loosely below. As a term of endearment, babydoll addresses someone affectionately, suggesting sweetness or attractiveness: {Come here, babydoll}.

A babyface is a face with soft, youthful features—round cheeks, smooth skin, large eyes—that make someone look younger than their age: {He's thirty but still has a babyface}. In professional wrestling, a babyface (or simply face) is a heroic character the audience is meant to cheer for, contrasted with the heel or villain.

Babyfaced describes someone whose face looks younger than their actual age—typically smooth, round, and lacking sharp angles or lines. The term can be neutral or slightly dismissive, suggesting someone appears too young for their role: {The babyfaced CEO looked barely old enough to drive}. Also spelled baby-faced.

Babygirl is a term of endearment, originally directed at young female children but now commonly used between romantic partners regardless of the recipient's age or sometimes gender. In contemporary slang, especially online, babygirl has expanded to describe someone—often a male celebrity or fictional character—who appears emotionally vulnerable, sensitive, or deserving of protection and affection: {He's not a villain, he's my babygirl}. This newer usage carries an ironic or affectionate tone and signals the speaker's devotion to the person described.

Babying is treating someone as if they were a baby—with excessive care, protection, or indulgence. The word usually carries criticism: {Stop babying him; he needs to learn to handle things himself}. Parents baby their children, coaches refuse to baby players, and people accuse others of babying themselves when they avoid discomfort.

A babymoon is a vacation taken by expectant parents before their baby arrives—a last hurrah of couple time before the demands of parenthood begin. The term echoes honeymoon, substituting baby for the romantic occasion: {We're planning a babymoon to the coast before the due date}. Less commonly, babymoon refers to a period of seclusion after birth, when new parents bond with their infant.

Babymooning is taking a vacation before a baby arrives—a last getaway for expectant parents before the demands of newborn care begin. The term blends baby with honeymoon, suggesting a romantic trip, though the focus is less on the relationship than on rest and relaxation: {We went babymooning in Hawaii during my second trimester}.

A babymoon is a vacation taken by expectant parents before their baby arrives—a last trip as a couple before the demands of parenthood set in. The term echoes honeymoon, suggesting a celebratory getaway: {We're planning a babymoon to the coast before the due date}. Less commonly, babymoon refers to a quiet period of bonding immediately after birth.

Babyproof means designed or modified to prevent injury to infants and toddlers. Parents babyproof a home by covering electrical outlets, securing cabinets, and padding sharp corners. As a verb, to babyproof is to make something safe for babies: {We need to babyproof the kitchen before she starts crawling}. Also spelled baby-proof.

Babyproofing is the process of making a home or space safe for infants and toddlers by removing or securing potential hazards. This typically involves installing cabinet locks, covering electrical outlets, padding sharp corners, and gating stairs. The term can extend metaphorically to any effort to make something foolproof or protected against careless handling: {We spent the weekend babyproofing the living room before the twins started crawling}.

To babysit is to look after someone else's children, typically for a few hours while the parents are out: {Can you babysit on Saturday night?} The term extends to watching over anything requiring supervision: {I spent the afternoon babysitting the printer}. A babysitter is usually a teenager or young adult earning pocket money, though the verb applies regardless of who's doing it.

Babysits is the present tense of babysit—to watch over children temporarily while their parents are away: {She babysits for the neighbors every Saturday}. The term extends to watching over anything that needs supervision: {He babysits the servers overnight in case something crashes}.

A babysitter is someone hired to look after children while parents are away, typically for a few hours at a time. The term usually implies a teenager or young adult rather than a professional caregiver: {We need to find a babysitter for Saturday night}. By extension, anyone tasked with watching over something that shouldn't need supervision: {I'm not here to babysit the new hires}.

Babysitters are people hired to look after children while parents are away, typically for short periods like an evening out. The term implies temporary, informal care rather than professional childcare: {We need to find a babysitter for Saturday night}. Figuratively, to babysit can mean supervising anyone or anything that shouldn't need it: {I'm not here to babysit the interns}.

Babysitting is watching over children while their parents are away, typically for a few hours. A babysitter handles basic care—feeding, entertainment, bedtime—without the deeper responsibilities of parenting. The term extends to temporary oversight of anything: {I'm babysitting my neighbor's plants while she's on vacation}. To babysit someone can imply they need excessive supervision: {I shouldn't have to babysit you through every step}.

Babyspeak is the simplified, high-pitched way adults talk to infants—short words, exaggerated intonation, and terms like {mama}, {baba}, and {night-night}. The style extends to how people address pets: {Who's a good boy?} Babyspeak can also describe immature or overly cutesy language from adults: {Spare me the babyspeak and just tell me what happened}.

A babystep is a small, cautious advance—the kind a toddler takes when learning to walk. The term usually appears in contexts of gradual progress: {We're taking babysteps toward reform}. Often plural: {babysteps in the right direction}. The emphasis is on incremental movement rather than bold action.

Small, tentative movements forward—literally the tottering steps of a toddler learning to walk, but almost always used figuratively for cautious, incremental progress: {We're taking babysteps toward reconciliation}. The word implies deliberate restraint, advancing slowly to avoid failure or overwhelm. Often appears in self-help contexts or when someone urges patience with gradual change.

Babytalk is the simplified speech adults use when addressing infants—higher pitch, exaggerated intonation, simple words, and repeated syllables: {Who's a good boy? Yes you are!} The term also describes an adult's immature or cutesy way of speaking: {Stop with the babytalk and tell me what happened}. Children's early attempts at speech may also be called babytalk.

Babywearing is carrying an infant or young child in a sling, wrap, or structured carrier worn on the body. The practice keeps the baby close while freeing the caregiver's hands: {She's really into babywearing—says it helps with bonding}. Advocates cite benefits for infant development and parental convenience.

Baccarat is a casino card game where players bet on whether the "player" or "banker" hand will have a point total closer to nine. Face cards and tens count as zero, and only the last digit of a total matters. The game requires no skill—players simply place bets and watch the dealer draw cards according to fixed rules. {The high rollers were at the baccarat table}. James Bond famously plays baccarat in several novels and films.

A bacchanal is a wild, drunken celebration—the kind where restraint dissolves and revelry takes over. The word comes from Bacchus, the Roman god of wine. It can describe either the event itself or a participant in such festivities: {The office party devolved into a bacchanal}. The adjective bacchanal or bacchanalian describes anything marked by uninhibited indulgence.

Bacchanalia were ancient Roman festivals honoring Bacchus, god of wine, marked by drunken revelry and orgiastic rites. The word now refers to any wild, unrestrained celebration involving excessive drinking and uninhibited behavior: {The office party devolved into a bacchanalia}. The singular bacchanal works similarly, and bacchanalian serves as the adjective: {bacchanalian excess}.

Bacchanals are wild, drunken celebrations—revelries marked by uninhibited drinking and carousing. The word comes from Bacchus, the Roman god of wine. A bacchanal can be either the event itself or a participant in such festivities: {The office party devolved into a bacchanal}. The singular bacchanalian works as an adjective describing anything characterized by riotous excess.

Bachata is a style of music and dance that originated in the Dominican Republic. The music features guitar-driven melodies with romantic or melancholic lyrics, often about heartbreak. The dance is characterized by a side-to-side pattern with hip movements and a distinctive tap on the fourth beat: {We took bachata lessons before the wedding}. Once associated with lower-class bars and brothels, bachata gained mainstream acceptance in the 1990s and has since spread internationally.

A bachelor is an unmarried man, particularly one who has never married. The word often implies someone living independently and perhaps enjoying single life: {He's a confirmed bachelor}. A bachelor's degree is the first level of university degree, and a bachelor apartment (or bachelor pad) is a small dwelling suited for one person. In older usage, a bachelor was also a young knight serving under another's banner.

A bachelorette is an unmarried woman, formed as a feminine counterpart to bachelor. The word appears most often in {bachelorette party}—a celebration for a woman about to be married, typically involving her female friends. Outside this context, bachelorette sounds dated or playful; unmarried women are more often called single.

Bachelorettes is the plural of bachelorette, an unmarried woman. The word mirrors bachelor but carries a more playful or dated tone. A bachelorette party is a celebration for a bride-to-be before her wedding: {The bachelorettes hit the bars in matching sashes}. The term also names the female contestant on certain reality dating shows.

Bachelorhood is the state of being an unmarried man. The word carries connotations of freedom and independence, sometimes with a hint of immaturity or reluctance to commit: {He clung to his bachelorhood well into his forties}. The term has become less common as marriage patterns shift and "single" becomes the neutral descriptor for unmarried people of any gender.

Bachelors is the plural of bachelor—unmarried men, or holders of a four-year undergraduate degree. {The bachelors at the party outnumbered the married men}. {Three bachelors of science graduated with honors}. A bachelor's degree is sometimes called simply a bachelors: {She earned her bachelors in engineering}.

Back, as adverb, adjective, noun, and verb, is the opposite of front and roughly synonymous with rear. When time is involved, back refers to the past: I wrote the letter back in 2010. When space is involved, back is the direction behind you, or behind the speaker or subject at hand: She walked back three steps. Your back is the rear side of your torso, where your spine is: I strained my back when I bent over. The back of a building or physical object is the side opposite the front: They left through the house’s back door. In some sports, a back plays behind the front line of players: The running back scored a touchdown. To back is to move backwards: Please back the car out of the garage.

A dull, persistent pain in the back, especially the lower back. Backache is among the most common physical complaints, often caused by muscle strain, poor posture, or prolonged sitting: {I've had this backache ever since I helped them move}.

Backasswards is a humorous intensification of backwards, formed by transposing the first syllables of "back" and "ass" to create a deliberate spoonerism. It emphasizes doing something in completely the wrong order or in a thoroughly illogical way. {You've got the whole thing backasswards—start with the data, then draw conclusions.} The variant bass-ackwards achieves the same effect while sounding slightly less vulgar.

A backbeat is the emphasis on beats two and four in a four-beat measure, characteristic of rock, R&B, and most popular music. The snare drum typically provides it: {The drummer laid down a heavy backbeat}. Music without a backbeat—emphasizing beats one and three—sounds square or old-fashioned to modern ears.

Backbeats are the emphasized beats on the second and fourth counts in a four-beat measure, characteristic of rock, funk, and most popular music. The drummer typically marks backbeats with the snare drum, creating the driving pulse that makes music feel like it wants to move forward: {The song's heavy backbeats got everyone dancing}.

Backbench refers to the rear seats in a parliament or legislature, occupied by rank-and-file members rather than party leaders or ministers. A backbencher holds no official position in government or opposition leadership: {She spent years on the backbench before being appointed to cabinet}. The term implies distance from power—backbenchers vote but rarely shape policy.

A backbencher is a legislator who holds no ministerial or leadership position, sitting on the back benches of the chamber rather than the front rows reserved for party leaders and cabinet members. The term is most common in British and Commonwealth parliamentary systems. Backbenchers may have less influence but more freedom to vote independently: {A backbencher rebellion threatened the prime minister's bill}.

A backbend is a gymnastic or yoga position in which the body arches backward, typically with hands and feet on the ground and the torso curved upward: {She held a perfect backbend for ten seconds}. The move requires flexibility in the spine and shoulders.

Backbiters are people who speak maliciously about others behind their backs. The term carries moral weight, suggesting not just gossip but deliberate harm to someone's reputation when they aren't present to defend themselves. {The office backbiters had already spread rumors before she even started the job.} The word appears frequently in religious and literary contexts where betrayal of trust is condemned.

Backbiting is speaking maliciously about someone who isn't present to defend themselves. The word emphasizes the cowardly or treacherous nature of the criticism—attacking from behind rather than face to face: {Office backbiting poisoned the whole team's morale}. The verb is backbite; the agent noun is backbiter.

A backboard is a flat vertical surface, typically rectangular, that supports and frames a basketball hoop. Shots that bank off the backboard and into the basket use the {glass} or {board} strategically. In medical contexts, a backboard is a rigid board used to immobilize and transport patients with suspected spinal injuries.

Backboards are the vertical boards behind basketball hoops, off which shots can be banked into the basket. The term also refers to flat boards used to immobilize patients with potential spinal injuries during transport: {Paramedics strapped him to a backboard before moving him}.

Backbone is the spine—the column of vertebrae running down the center of the back in humans and other vertebrates. Figuratively, backbone means courage, determination, or moral strength: {She showed real backbone standing up to them}. It also means the central supporting structure of something larger: {Small businesses are the backbone of the economy}. In computing, a backbone is the main high-capacity network line that smaller networks connect to.

Backbones is the plural of backbone—the spine, the column of vertebrae running down the center of the back. Figuratively, backbone means courage or resolve: {Those senators lack the backbones to stand up to their party}. Backbone also refers to the main supporting structure of something: {Small businesses are the backbones of local economies}.

Backbreaker refers to any task or burden so demanding it could figuratively break your back—exhausting physical labor, an overwhelming workload, or a crushing financial obligation: {Moving all that furniture was a real backbreaker}. In wrestling, a backbreaker is a move where one wrestler drops an opponent's spine across their knee.
clues: A job that leaves you spent

definition: Backbreakers are tasks or burdens so demanding they could figuratively break your back—exhausting physical labor or overwhelming challenges: {Moving all that furniture up five flights was a backbreaker}. In wrestling, a backbreaker is a move where an opponent is dropped across the wrestler's knee or shoulder, bending the spine painfully.

Backbreaking describes work so physically demanding it could break your back—heavy labor requiring intense exertion: {backbreaking work in the coal mines}, {the backbreaking task of hauling stones}. The term emphasizes grueling effort, though it extends to any exhausting undertaking: {the backbreaking process of editing a manuscript}.

Backburner, usually appearing as two words or hyphenated, refers to a state of reduced priority or temporary neglect. The metaphor comes from cooking: pots on the back burners of a stove receive less attention than those in front. To put something {on the backburner} means to postpone dealing with it while attending to more urgent matters. As a verb, to backburner a project or issue is to deprioritize it: {We had to backburner the expansion plans until funding came through}.

A backchannel is an unofficial or informal route for communication, often running parallel to official channels: {Diplomats used backchannels to negotiate before the formal talks began}. In conversation, backchannels are the small responses—"uh-huh," "right," "mm-hmm"—that signal you're listening without interrupting. As a verb, to backchannel is to communicate through such informal routes.

Backchannels are unofficial or informal routes of communication, typically running parallel to official ones. Diplomats use backchannels to negotiate sensitive matters away from public scrutiny: {The two governments maintained backchannels even during the crisis}. In conversation, backchannels are the small verbal cues—{uh-huh}, {right}, {mm-hmm}—that signal you're listening without interrupting.

Backchat is impudent or cheeky talk in response to authority—what Americans more often call back talk. A child gives backchat when answering a parent's instruction with attitude: {Don't give me any backchat, young lady}. The term is more common in British English and suggests defiance without outright rebellion.

Backcountry is remote, undeveloped land far from towns and roads—wilderness areas where you're largely on your own. The term appears often in outdoor recreation: {backcountry skiing}, {backcountry camping}, {backcountry hiking}. It implies terrain without marked trails, lodges, or easy rescue access. In some regions, backcountry simply means rural or sparsely settled areas away from population centers.

In basketball, the backcourt is the half of the court containing a team's own basket—the area they defend and must advance the ball out of within ten seconds. By extension, backcourt refers collectively to a team's guards (point guard and shooting guard): {The Lakers have one of the best backcourts in the league}. In tennis, the backcourt is the area near the baseline, behind the service boxes.

To backdate something is to put an earlier date on it than when it was actually created or signed: {The contract was backdated to make it appear valid during the audit period}. Backdating is sometimes legitimate—applying a policy retroactively—but often implies fraud or deception, making documents appear to have existed before they did.

Backdated describes something, typically a document or agreement, that has been assigned an earlier date than when it was actually created or signed. The practice may be legitimate—such as making an insurance policy effective from a prior date—or fraudulent, as when backdating stock options to secure a more favorable price. {The contract was backdated to the first of the month.} As a verb, to backdate is to apply such a date.

Backdating is assigning an earlier date to a document than when it was actually created or signed. The practice ranges from innocent—dating a check for the day you meant to write it—to fraudulent: backdating stock options to a more favorable price, or contracts to create false paper trails. {The executive was convicted of backdating options grants.}

A backdoor is a rear or secondary entrance, but the word usually carries connotations of secrecy or circumvention. A backdoor {deal} happens through unofficial channels. In computing, a backdoor is a hidden method of bypassing normal authentication—sometimes built in by developers, sometimes installed by hackers. As an adjective: {backdoor access}, {backdoor negotiations}. Also spelled back door or back-door.

Backdoored describes software or systems that have been compromised with a hidden access point, allowing unauthorized entry while bypassing normal security. A backdoored program may function normally while secretly transmitting data or awaiting commands: {The update was backdoored—hackers had access for months}. The term extends to any situation where someone has been secretly undermined or bypassed: {He got backdoored out of the promotion}.

Backdoors names hidden methods of bypassing normal security or authentication in a computer system. Programmers sometimes build them in deliberately for maintenance access; hackers install them to maintain secret entry after a breach. The term extends to any covert way around official channels: {The lobbyist found a backdoor into the senator's office}. As a verb, to backdoor is to gain access through such means. In basketball, a backdoor play sends a player cutting behind the defense toward the basket.

A backdraft is an explosive surge of fire that occurs when oxygen suddenly enters a confined space where flames have depleted the air supply. The superheated gases ignite violently when a door or window opens. Firefighters are trained to recognize warning signs—bowing windows, smoke-stained glass, pulsing smoke—before entering burning buildings.

Backdrafts is the plural of backdraft, a dangerous phenomenon in firefighting where a fire starved of oxygen suddenly reignites when fresh air enters the space. Opening a door or window to a smoldering room can trigger an explosive backdraft as superheated gases ignite: {The firefighters vented the roof to prevent backdrafts}.

Backdraught is a dangerous phenomenon in firefighting where a fire starved of oxygen suddenly reignites explosively when fresh air enters—through an opened door or broken window. The inrush of oxygen causes accumulated combustible gases to ignite at once: {The firefighters checked for signs of backdraught before breaching the door}. Also spelled backdraft, especially in American English.

A backdrop is a painted cloth or screen hung at the back of a stage, creating the visual setting for a performance. The term extends to any background: {The mountains provided a stunning backdrop for the ceremony}. Figuratively, backdrop describes the circumstances or context surrounding events: {The negotiations took place against a backdrop of rising tensions}.

Backdrops is the plural of backdrop—a painted cloth or screen hung at the back of a stage, or any background setting. The singular extends to figurative contexts: {The treaty was signed against a backdrop of rising tensions}. As a verb, to backdrop is to provide such a background: {Mountains backdropped the ceremony}.

Backed means supported or assisted. A backed candidate has endorsements; a backed claim has evidence. To be backed into a corner is to be forced into a difficult position. Backed also describes physical support: a chair may be high-backed or low-backed. In compounds, backed indicates what's behind something: {a plastic-backed mirror}, {a rubber-backed rug}.

Backend refers to the part of a system that users don't directly see or interact with—the behind-the-scenes machinery. In computing, the backend handles data storage, server logic, and processing: {She works on the backend while her partner builds the user interface}. More generally, backend describes any operational infrastructure hidden from public view: {the backend of a retail operation}. Often written as two words or hyphenated: back end, back-end.

A backer is someone who supports a person, project, or cause—usually with money, but also with endorsement or influence. {The startup found a backer willing to invest two million}. {She couldn't have won without her political backers}. In crowdfunding, backers pledge money in exchange for early access or rewards.

Backers are people who support a person, project, or cause—usually with money, but sometimes with influence or endorsement. A political candidate has backers who fund campaigns. A startup seeks backers to provide capital. On crowdfunding platforms, backers pledge money to bring projects to life: {The film found enough backers to begin production}.

The backfield is the area of a football field behind the line of scrimmage, or collectively, the players who line up there—typically the quarterback and running backs on offense, or the safeties and cornerbacks on defense. {The team's backfield was decimated by injuries}. A handoff or pass that goes backward happens {in the backfield}.

Backfill is material used to refill an excavated hole or trench, or the act of refilling it: {They backfilled the foundation with gravel}. In business contexts, to backfill a position is to hire someone to replace a departed employee: {We need to backfill the marketing director role}. The term extends to retroactively adding data or completing work that should have been done earlier.

Backfire originally describes an engine's premature combustion, producing a loud bang when fuel ignites in the exhaust or intake rather than the cylinder. The figurative use now dominates: when a plan backfires, it produces the opposite of the intended result. {Her attempt to make him jealous backfired spectacularly.} A backfire is also a controlled burn set to stop an advancing wildfire by depriving it of fuel.

Backfired is the past tense of backfire. An engine backfires when fuel ignites in the wrong place, producing a loud bang. A plan backfires when it produces the opposite of its intended result: {The smear campaign backfired spectacularly—it only made her more popular}. The metaphor captures how something meant to propel you forward instead explodes in your face.

Backfires is the third-person singular of backfire. An engine backfires when combustion occurs in the wrong place or at the wrong time, producing a loud bang: {The old truck backfired as it pulled away}. More commonly now, a plan or action backfires when it produces the opposite of its intended result: {Her attempt to make him jealous backfired spectacularly}.

Backfiring is when something produces the opposite of its intended effect. A plan backfires when it fails in a way that harms the person who made it: {Her attempt to make him jealous backfired spectacularly}. The term comes from engines—a backfire is a loud bang caused by fuel igniting at the wrong time, either in the intake or exhaust system.

A backflip is an acrobatic move where you leap and rotate backward, landing on your feet. Gymnasts, divers, and cheerleaders perform backflips; so do skateboarders and parkour practitioners, often off obstacles. Figuratively, to do a backflip is to reverse position dramatically: {The senator did a backflip on the tax bill}.

Backflips are acrobatic maneuvers in which someone rotates backward through the air, typically landing on their feet. Gymnasts, divers, and cheerleaders perform backflips as technical elements. Figuratively, to do backflips is to go to extreme lengths or express excessive enthusiasm: {The company did backflips to accommodate the client}. Also spelled as two words.

Backgammon is a board game for two players, each moving fifteen pieces according to dice rolls along a track of twenty-four triangular points. The goal is to move all your pieces around the board and off before your opponent does. One of the oldest known board games, it combines luck and strategy: {We played backgammon on the beach}.

Background is what lies behind something more prominent. A painting has figures in the foreground and scenery in the background. A person's background is their history—education, experience, family origins: {She has a background in finance}. Background music or noise exists without being the focus of attention. To background something is to make it less prominent. {In the background} means present but not central: {He prefers to stay in the background}.

Backgrounds is the plural of background, referring to what lies behind something more prominent. A photograph's background contains elements behind the main subject. A person's background encompasses their education, experience, and origins: {Candidates from diverse backgrounds applied for the position}. In computing, background processes run while you work on other tasks. To run a background check is to investigate someone's history.

A backhand is a stroke in tennis and similar sports made with the back of the hand facing the direction of movement—the opposite of a forehand. The term extends to any swing or blow delivered this way: {a backhand slap across the face}. As a verb, to backhand is to strike with this motion. Backhanded can mean indirect or ambiguous: a backhanded {compliment} carries an insult within apparent praise.

Backhanded describes something done with the back of the hand facing forward—a backhanded {stroke} in tennis, a backhanded {slap}. The figurative sense dominates: a backhanded {compliment} seems positive but contains an insult or criticism: {Saying she's "pretty smart for a blonde" is backhanded}. Backhanded can also mean indirect or underhanded: {backhanded methods}.

A backhander is a bribe or illicit payment, especially one given discreetly to secure favorable treatment: {The contract went to whoever paid the biggest backhander}. The term is primarily British. Separately, a backhander is a stroke made with the back of the hand—in tennis, a backhand shot; in fighting, a slap delivered with the knuckles facing forward.

Backhanding is striking with the back of the hand rather than the palm, a motion used in tennis, slapping, and other contexts requiring a reverse swing. Figuratively, to backhand someone is to deliver a backhanded compliment—praise that carries an insult: {She backhanded me by saying I looked good "for my age"}.

Backhands is the plural of backhand, which refers to a stroke in tennis and similar racket sports made with the back of the hand facing the direction of movement. The term extends to any similar sweeping motion, such as a backhanded slap across the face. To backhand someone is to strike them this way. In hockey, a backhand shot is taken with the blade curved away from the puck. {She backhands every insult that comes her way.}

A backheel is a kick in soccer where the player strikes the ball backward with their heel, often to pass to a teammate behind them. The move is flashy and somewhat risky—useful for surprising defenders when a forward pass isn't available: {He flicked a backheel to his teammate at the edge of the box}. As a verb, to backheel is to execute such a kick.

A backhoe is a piece of excavating equipment with a hinged bucket on the end of a jointed arm, used for digging trenches and foundations. The bucket digs by pulling toward the machine—hence "back." Most backhoes combine a front loader bucket with the rear excavator arm: {The contractor brought in a backhoe to dig the foundation}.

Backing is support or assistance, whether financial, political, or moral: {The project has backing from several major investors}. It also refers to material placed behind something for reinforcement or support—the backing on a mirror, the backing on carpet. In music, backing refers to the instrumental or vocal accompaniment behind a lead performer: {backing vocals}, {backing track}.

Backlash is a strong negative reaction against a change or trend, typically from people who feel threatened by it: {The policy provoked immediate backlash}, {backlash against feminism}. The word comes from machinery—the jarring backward motion when gears or chains have too much play. The social sense captures that same sudden, forceful recoil.

A backlight is a light source positioned behind a subject or display. In photography and film, backlighting creates silhouettes or glowing outlines: {The sunset backlit the mountains}. In screens—phones, monitors, TVs—the backlight illuminates the display from behind, making images visible. As a verb, to backlight is to illuminate from behind: {The photographer backlit the model's hair}.

Backlighting is illumination from behind a subject, creating silhouettes or glowing edges. In photography and film, backlighting separates subjects from backgrounds and produces dramatic rim effects: {The backlighting made her hair glow}. On screens and displays, backlighting provides the light source that makes images visible: {The keyboard backlighting helps me type in the dark}.

Backline refers to the amplifiers, speakers, and other large equipment positioned at the back of a stage during a live music performance. Venues or promoters often provide backline so touring musicians don't have to transport heavy gear: {The club's backline includes a drum kit and bass amp}. In sports like rugby, the backline is the row of players behind the forwards.

Backlit describes something illuminated from behind. A backlit screen has light shining through it from the rear, making it visible in darkness. A backlit photograph shows a subject silhouetted against a bright background: {The backlit figure stood in the doorway}. The past tense of backlight.

Backload means to concentrate weight, effort, or obligations toward the end rather than the beginning. A backloaded schedule has most of its demands near the finish. Backloaded payments defer costs to later periods: {The contract backloads the bonuses into the final year}. The opposite is frontload.

A backlog is an accumulation of unfinished work or unfilled orders: {We have a six-month backlog of customer requests}. The word implies tasks waiting in queue, often more than can be handled promptly. In software development, a backlog is a prioritized list of features or fixes to be addressed. The original meaning—a large log placed at the back of a fire to burn slowly—is now rare.

Backlogged describes having accumulated work, orders, or tasks waiting to be processed. A company backlogged with orders has more demand than it can currently fulfill. A court backlogged with cases has a queue of matters awaiting hearing. {We're so backlogged that new orders won't ship for six weeks.} The word implies delay caused by volume exceeding capacity.

Backlogs are accumulations of unfinished work or unfilled orders. A company with more orders than it can immediately fulfill has a backlog—often a positive sign of demand. But backlogs of paperwork, emails, or maintenance suggest falling behind: {The court system has a massive backlog of cases}. In software development, a backlog is a prioritized list of features or tasks awaiting implementation.

A backlot is the outdoor area of a movie studio where large sets are built—city streets, Western towns, medieval villages. These permanent or semi-permanent structures allow filming without location travel: {Half of old Hollywood was shot on the backlot}. The term evokes classic studio-era filmmaking, when major productions rarely left the lot.

A backorder is an order for goods that are temporarily out of stock, to be filled when inventory becomes available. As a verb, to backorder is to place or accept such an order: {The laptop is backordered until next month}. The term implies a delay rather than a cancellation—the customer waits rather than going elsewhere.

A backpack is a bag with shoulder straps designed to be carried on the back, leaving hands free. Students carry books in them; hikers carry gear. As a verb, to backpack is to travel or hike while carrying one's belongings this way: {We backpacked through Europe after graduation}. Also called a rucksack or knapsack.

A backpacker is someone who travels with their belongings in a backpack, typically on a budget and for extended periods. The term suggests youth hostels, trains, and flexible itineraries rather than package tours: {We met some backpackers from Australia at the hostel}. Backpacker also describes anyone hiking with a loaded pack: {The backpackers set up camp near the ridge}.

Backpackers are travelers who carry their belongings in a backpack, typically associated with budget-conscious, independent travel. The term suggests hostels over hotels, flexibility over fixed itineraries: {The hostel was full of backpackers from all over Europe}. Backpackers also refers to hikers on extended wilderness trips, carrying everything needed for multiday treks.

Backpacking is traveling with belongings carried in a backpack, typically on a budget and for extended periods. It suggests independence and mobility—staying in hostels, using public transit, moving frequently: {We spent six months backpacking through Southeast Asia}. Backpacking also means hiking with overnight camping gear: {a backpacking trip in the Sierra Nevada}.

Backpacks are bags carried on the back, supported by shoulder straps and often a waist belt. Designed to distribute weight comfortably, they range from small daypacks to large frames for hiking and camping. Students carry books in backpacks; travelers live out of them. As a verb, to backpack is to travel with one's belongings on one's back: {We backpacked through Europe after college}.

Backpay is wages owed for work already performed but not yet paid. It typically arises when an employer has underpaid, withheld wages, or when a raise is applied retroactively: {The settlement included two years of backpay}. Also spelled as two words: back pay.

To backpedal is to pedal a bicycle backward or, in sports like boxing, to move backward quickly while facing an opponent. The figurative sense dominates: to retreat from a previous position or statement. Politicians backpedal when their remarks prove unpopular; companies backpedal on controversial policies. {After the backlash, she backpedaled on her earlier comments.}

Backpedaled is the past tense of backpedal. To backpedal is literally to pedal backward on a bicycle, but the figurative sense dominates: retreating from a position or reversing course on something previously stated. {After the backlash, the company backpedaled on its new policy.} The word suggests reluctant withdrawal under pressure rather than a genuine change of heart.

Backpedaling is moving backward while facing forward, literally by pedaling a bicycle in reverse or by taking steps backward. The word is far more common in its figurative sense: retreating from a position, commitment, or statement one has previously made. Politicians backpedal when their remarks prove unpopular; companies backpedal on policies that generate backlash. {After the public outcry, the mayor started backpedaling on her proposed budget cuts.} The spelling backpedalling is preferred in British English.

Backpedalling is reversing course—literally pedalling backward on a bicycle, or figuratively retreating from a position or statement. Politicians backpedal when their remarks prove unpopular: {After the backlash, she started backpedalling on her earlier comments}. The spelling with double L is British; American English prefers backpedaling.

A backrest is the part of a chair, seat, or bench that supports the sitter's back. Car seats, office chairs, and park benches have backrests; stools and ottomans typically don't. The term also applies to portable supports that prop up someone sitting in bed: {She adjusted the backrest to read more comfortably}.

A backroad is a minor road, typically rural, that winds through countryside away from main highways. Backroads suggest slower travel, scenic routes, and places off the beaten path: {We took the backroads to avoid traffic}. The term evokes a kind of unhurried exploration—{backroad driving through small towns}.

Backroads are secondary roads through rural or less-traveled areas, away from highways and main routes. The term evokes countryside driving, scenic detours, and places off the beaten path: {We took the backroads to avoid traffic}. Figuratively, backroads suggests the overlooked or hidden parts of something: {the backroads of American music history}.

A backronym is an acronym created after the fact by assigning words to existing letters. Unlike true acronyms, where the phrase comes first and gets abbreviated, backronyms work backward—taking an established word or abbreviation and inventing a phrase to fit it. Some are folk etymologies: the claim that "golf" stands for "gentlemen only, ladies forbidden" is a backronym, not the word's actual origin. Others are deliberate coinages: the USA PATRIOT Act was named to spell out a word.

A backroom is a private space away from public view, typically behind a main area where business is conducted. As an adjective, it describes activities done secretly or unofficially: {backroom deals}, {backroom politics}. The implication is often of decisions made by insiders without public scrutiny or accountability.

The backrooms are hidden or private areas where real decisions get made, away from public scrutiny: {The deal was struck in the backrooms of Congress}. Backroom as an adjective describes such secretive dealings: {backroom negotiations}, {backroom politics}. In internet lore, the Backrooms are a creepypasta concept—an infinite maze of empty, liminal spaces resembling generic office interiors, supposedly accessible by "noclipping" out of reality.

A backrub is a massage of the back, typically informal and brief compared to professional massage. The term often carries intimate connotations—offering someone a backrub can be a prelude to romance: {He offered her a backrub after dinner}. Also spelled as two words: back rub.
clues: What sore shoulders are asking for

definition: Backs is the plural of back—the rear surface of the human body from shoulders to waist, or the corresponding part of animals, chairs, books, or buildings. In sports, backs are players positioned behind the front line: {The backs carried the ball on most plays}. To back someone is to support them; backs as a verb means supports: {She backs her team no matter what}. Something that backs onto a place faces it from the rear: {The house backs onto a park}.

A backscratcher is a long-handled tool with a curved or clawed end, designed to reach spots on your back that your own hands cannot. The handles are typically made of wood, plastic, or bamboo, often with a hand-shaped scratching end. Figuratively, a backscratcher is someone who exchanges favors with another person for mutual benefit, as in the expression {you scratch my back, I'll scratch yours}.

Backscratching is the exchange of favors, especially in politics or business—you help me, I'll help you. The metaphor comes from the literal act: scratching someone's back feels good but requires another person to reach. {The bill passed through backscratching between committee members.} The related expression is {you scratch my back, I'll scratch yours}.

The backseat is the rear seat in a vehicle, behind the driver. By extension, a backseat position is one of lesser importance or authority. To {take a backseat} is to assume a secondary role: {Career took a backseat once the baby arrived}. A {backseat driver} offers unwanted advice from a position of no responsibility.

The backside is the rear surface of something, or the side opposite the front: {the backside of the building}, {flip it over to see the backside}. Most commonly, backside is a mild or polite term for the buttocks: {She fell right on her backside}. In surfing and snowboarding, backside describes maneuvers where the rider faces away from the wave or slope.

Backsies is children's slang for taking back something given or reclaiming a previous position. The word appears almost exclusively in the negative: {no backsies} means a gift, trade, or decision is final and cannot be reversed. Adults use it playfully to seal informal agreements.

Backslap refers to hearty, often performative camaraderie—the kind expressed through literal slaps on the back. The verb describes engaging in such jovial physical congratulation or, more broadly, exchanging effusive mutual praise: {The executives spent the meeting backslapping each other over the quarterly results}. The tone is usually skeptical, suggesting the warmth is superficial or self-congratulatory.

A backslapper is someone who greets others with exaggerated friendliness—literally slapping backs, shaking hands vigorously, remembering names. The word usually carries a note of suspicion: backslappers seem to be working the room for their own benefit. {The convention was full of grinning backslappers angling for connections.}

Backslapping is hearty, demonstrative friendliness—the kind expressed through literal slaps on the back. The term usually carries a hint of skepticism, suggesting the warmth is excessive, performative, or politically motivated: {The convention was full of backslapping and empty promises}. As an adjective, it describes people or atmospheres marked by this boisterous camaraderie: {a backslapping good-old-boy network}.

A backslash is the punctuation mark \, slanting from upper left to lower right—the reverse of the forward slash /. In computing, backslashes separate elements in file paths: {C:\Users\Documents}. The symbol has no traditional use in ordinary writing; it exists almost entirely in technical contexts.

Backslid is the past tense of backslide, meaning to relapse into bad habits, sinful behavior, or a worse condition after a period of improvement. The word comes from religious contexts describing someone who has fallen away from faith: {He backslid into drinking after two years sober}. The past participle can be backslid or backslidden.

To backslide is to slip back into bad habits, sinful behavior, or a less desirable state after making progress. The term originated in religious contexts—a backslider has fallen away from faith—but now applies broadly: {He backslid into drinking after six months sober}. The past tense is backslid or backslided.

A backslider is someone who has fallen away from a commitment, especially religious faith or moral standards. The term carries judgment—a backslider hasn't just drifted but has returned to old sins or bad habits after a period of reform: {The preacher warned against becoming a backslider}. Common in evangelical Christian contexts.

Backsliders are people who have lapsed from a commitment, particularly a religious faith or moral standard. The word carries a tone of disapproval, implying weakness or moral failure: {The preacher warned backsliders to return to the fold}. In secular contexts, backsliders are those who revert to bad habits after a period of improvement: {The support group welcomed backsliders without judgment}.

Backslides is the third-person singular of backslide, meaning to revert to bad habits or sinful behavior after a period of improvement. The word comes from religious contexts—a reformed sinner who backslides returns to former ways: {He backslides every time he visits his old neighborhood}. The past tense is backslid or backslided.

Backsliding is reverting to bad habits, sinful behavior, or a worse condition after a period of improvement. The term originates in religious contexts, where it describes someone who has fallen away from faith or moral discipline, but it applies broadly to any regression: {After six months sober, one bad weekend sent him backsliding}. A backslider is someone prone to such lapses. The word carries a tone of moral judgment—it implies not just failure but a kind of weakness or betrayal of progress already made.

Backspace is the key on a keyboard that deletes the character to the left of the cursor, moving the insertion point backward. The verb means to use this key: {I backspaced over the typo}. On typewriters, backspace moved the carriage back without erasing, allowing overtyping for corrections or accents.

Backspin is rotation of a ball opposite to its direction of travel, imparted by striking or throwing it in a way that makes the top spin backward. In tennis and golf, backspin causes the ball to stop quickly or bounce back upon landing. In pool and basketball, it affects how the ball behaves after contact: {She put backspin on the cue ball to draw it back after the shot}.

A backsplash is a protective surface installed on the wall behind a sink, stove, or countertop to guard against water damage and food splatter. Typically made of tile, stone, or glass, backsplashes have become a decorative element in kitchen and bathroom design: {We chose a subway tile backsplash for the renovation}.

To backstab is to betray someone who trusts you, especially by attacking their reputation or undermining them secretly: {She backstabbed her best friend to get the promotion}. The image is of a literal knife in the back—harm delivered when the victim can't see it coming. As a noun, a backstab is such an act of betrayal.

Backstabbed is the past tense of backstab—to betray someone who trusted you, especially by attacking their reputation or undermining them secretly: {I can't believe she backstabbed me after everything I did for her}. The image is of stabbing someone in the back while they face away, unaware of the threat.

A backstabber is someone who pretends friendship while working against you—the image is of attacking someone from behind while embracing them. The word implies betrayal by a trusted person: {I thought she was my ally, but she turned out to be a backstabber}. The verb is backstab; the act is backstabbing.
clues: One who feigns loyalty, then betrays

definition: Backstabbers are people who betray others while pretending to be friendly or loyal. The image is of someone attacking from behind—striking when the victim can't see it coming. The word implies deceit and cowardice: {Watch out for backstabbers in that office}. A backstabber smiles to your face while undermining you to others.

Backstabbing is betraying someone who trusts you, especially by criticizing or undermining them when they're not present. The image is of attacking from behind—a cowardly strike against someone who considers you an ally. {The office was full of backstabbing and petty rivalries.} As an adjective: {a backstabbing colleague}. One who does this is a backstabber.

Backstabs is the verb form of backstab, meaning to betray someone who trusts you, especially by acting friendly while secretly working against them. The metaphor evokes a literal knife in the back—an attack from someone positioned as an ally: {She backstabs everyone who helps her}. The noun backstabber describes someone who habitually does this.

Backstage is the area of a theater hidden from the audience—dressing rooms, wings, and work spaces where performers prepare and crew operates. As an adverb or adjective, it describes what happens in these spaces: {She went backstage to meet the actors}. Figuratively, backstage refers to any behind-the-scenes activity concealed from public view: {backstage negotiations}, {backstage maneuvering}.

Backstairs refers to a secondary staircase, originally one used by servants to move through a house without being seen by the family. The figurative sense dominates modern usage: backstairs means secret, underhanded, or conducted through unofficial channels. {Backstairs deals}, {backstairs intrigue}, and {backstairs influence} all suggest maneuvering that avoids proper procedures or public scrutiny.

A backstop is a barrier that prevents something from going too far—originally the fence or screen behind home plate in baseball that stops wild pitches and foul balls. The meaning extends to any safeguard or fallback: {The emergency fund serves as a financial backstop}. To backstop is to provide such protection: {The government backstopped the failing banks}.

Backstops are barriers that prevent something from going too far—literally or figuratively. In baseball, the backstop is the fence behind home plate that stops wild pitches and foul balls. More broadly, backstops are safeguards or fallback measures: {The federal reserve acts as a backstop for failing banks}. A backstop can also be a person providing backup support.

Backstories are the histories behind characters, situations, or events—the background that explains how things came to be. In fiction, a character's backstory includes formative experiences that shaped their personality: {The villain's tragic backstory made him almost sympathetic}. The term extends beyond fiction to anything with a hidden history worth knowing: {Every antique in her shop has a backstory}.

A backstory is the history behind a character, situation, or narrative—events that occurred before the main story begins. In fiction, backstory explains motivations and relationships: {The villain's backstory reveals childhood trauma}. The term extends beyond fiction to any context where understanding the past illuminates the present: {What's the backstory on this merger?}

A backstreet is a minor road away from main thoroughfares, often in older or less prosperous parts of town. As an adjective, backstreet suggests something hidden, unofficial, or illicit: a backstreet {abortion}, a backstreet {deal}. The connotation is of activities conducted away from public scrutiny.

Backstreets are the smaller, quieter roads away from a town's main thoroughfares. The term often carries connotations of seediness or poverty—the parts of town tourists don't see: {He grew up in the backstreets of Naples}. Backstreet as an adjective suggests something hidden or illicit: a {backstreet abortion}, a {backstreet deal}.

The backstretch is the straight section of a racetrack opposite the homestretch—the part farthest from the grandstand and finish line. By extension, backstretch refers to the stable area where horses are housed and workers live: {He grew up on the backstretch, mucking stalls before school}. The term also describes the later middle portion of any extended effort: {We're on the backstretch of this project}.

Backstroke is a swimming stroke performed while lying face-up, arms alternating in backward circular motions while legs kick. It's one of the four competitive swimming strokes: {She won the 100-meter backstroke}. The term can also mean any backward stroke or movement, as in rowing or tennis.

The backswing is the initial backward movement of a club, bat, racket, or arm before striking. In golf, tennis, and baseball, the backswing stores energy for the forward swing: {He took a long backswing before driving the ball}. A restricted backswing limits power but may improve control.

Backtalk is impudent or argumentative response to someone in authority—a child answering back to a parent, a soldier to an officer. The word implies disrespect through the very act of responding: {Don't give me any backtalk}. To backtalk is to respond this way: {She backtalked the teacher and got detention}.

To backtrack is to retrace your steps—returning along the path you came. Hikers backtrack when they've gone the wrong way: {We had to backtrack half a mile to find the trail}. Figuratively, backtrack means to reverse position on a statement or commitment: {The senator backtracked on her promise to oppose the bill}. The noun backtrack is the path itself.

Backtracked is the past tense of backtrack, meaning to retrace one's steps or reverse course. Literally, it's returning along the same path: {We backtracked to find the lost keys}. Figuratively, it means withdrawing from a position or statement: {The senator backtracked on her earlier comments after public backlash}.

Backtracking is reversing course to return the way you came, whether literally on a trail or figuratively in conversation: {We had to backtrack two miles to find the turnoff}. In argument or negotiation, to backtrack is to retreat from a position: {The senator backtracked on her earlier comments}. In computing, backtracking is an algorithmic method that abandons partial solutions when they prove unworkable, returning to try alternative paths.

Backtracks means to reverse course, either literally by retracing one's steps or figuratively by withdrawing from a position or statement. Politicians backtrack on campaign promises; hikers backtrack when they realize they've taken a wrong turn. {After the public outcry, the company backtracked on its new pricing policy.} The word implies going back over ground already covered, often reluctantly or under pressure.

Backup is a copy kept in case the original is lost or damaged: {Make sure you have a backup of your files}. The word extends to anything held in reserve as a substitute: a backup {plan}, a backup {generator}, backup {singers}. As a verb (usually two words: back up), it means to create such a copy or to provide support. A backup can also be an accumulation causing delay: {a backup on the freeway}.

Backups are copies of data stored separately from the original, kept as protection against loss or corruption: {Make sure you have backups before updating the system}. The term extends to anything held in reserve—backup {plans}, backup {generators}, backup {singers}. In traffic, a backup is congestion or blockage: {There's a backup on the highway}.

In its most frequent use as an adverb, backward refers to movement in the direction opposite to forward and it is found most frequently in the company of action verbs (step backward, bend backward, slide backward, stumble backward). This meaning extends to adjectival use (backward glance, backward motion). Figurative use of backward is pejorative, suggesting lack of sophistication, development, or intelligence. In expressions of time, backward refers to the past.

Backwards means in the reverse direction—opposite to usual forward motion or sequence. You can walk backwards, count backwards from ten, or play a video backwards. It also describes something oriented the wrong way: {You've got your shirt on backwards}. Figuratively, backwards suggests being behind the times or underdeveloped: {a backwards town}. The adverb form backward is interchangeable, though backwards is more common in British English.

Backwash is water pushed backward, especially the wave that retreats after breaking on shore or the turbulent water churned behind a moving boat or propeller. By extension, backwash describes any aftermath or residual effect: {the political backwash of the scandal}. In casual use, backwash is the liquid that flows back into a container after someone drinks from it: {I don't want your backwash}.

Backwashing is reversing the flow of water through a filter to flush out accumulated debris. Pool and aquarium filters require periodic backwashing to maintain effectiveness: {The pool guy comes weekly to backwash the filter}. In a different sense, backwashing is the flow of liquid from mouth back into a container while drinking—generally considered disgusting: {Don't backwash into the milk carton}.

A backwater is a part of a river where the water is stagnant or flows backward, cut off from the main current. The figurative sense dominates: a backwater is an isolated place untouched by progress or new ideas. {The town remained a cultural backwater}. The word usually carries a dismissive tone—suggesting somewhere dull and behind the times.

Backwaters are bodies of water cut off from the main current—stagnant pools fed by a river but lying aside from its flow. The term extends to any place or condition characterized by stagnation and isolation from progress: {a cultural backwater}, {an economic backwater}. The singular backwater works the same way: {The town remained a backwater until the highway came through}.

Backwoods refers to remote, heavily forested, or sparsely settled rural areas far from cities and towns: {a cabin in the backwoods of Maine}. The term often carries connotations of isolation, lack of sophistication, or resistance to modern ways: {backwoods culture}, {a backwoods accent}. As an adjective, it describes things characteristic of such regions: {backwoods hospitality}, {backwoods ignorance}.

A backwoodsman is someone who lives in remote, heavily forested, or sparsely settled frontier regions—historically the American wilderness beyond established settlements. The term suggests self-reliance and rough living, sometimes with connotations of being unsophisticated or uncultured: {He had the practical skills of a backwoodsman}. In British parliamentary usage, a backwoodsman is a member of the House of Lords who rarely attends sessions.

A backyard is the outdoor area behind a house, typically private and enclosed. Americans hold barbecues, let children play, and keep dogs in their backyards. Figuratively, something {in your own backyard} is close to home or within your sphere: {They opposed the landfill—not in my backyard}. As an adjective, backyard suggests informal or amateur: {backyard mechanic}, {backyard wrestling}.

Backyards are the areas behind houses, typically enclosed or bounded by fences. In American English, the backyard is where children play, families gather for barbecues, and dogs run. Figuratively, something {in your own backyard} is close to home or within your sphere of concern: {The scandal was happening in their own backyard}.

Bacon is cured meat from a pig, typically from the belly or back, sliced thin and fried until crisp. It's a breakfast staple in American and British cuisine, prized for its salty, smoky flavor and satisfying crunch. Bacon has become something of a cultural phenomenon, appearing in everything from desserts to novelty items: {bacon-wrapped dates}, {maple bacon donuts}. To {bring home the bacon} is to earn a living or achieve success. To {save someone's bacon} is to rescue them from trouble. (Capitalized Bacon is a surname.)

Bacteria are microscopic single-celled organisms found virtually everywhere—in soil, water, air, and living bodies. Some cause disease; others are essential for digestion, decomposition, and ecological balance. The word is technically plural (singular: bacterium), though {the bacteria is spreading} appears in casual speech. {Good bacteria in yogurt aid digestion.}

A bacterium is a single-celled microorganism, the simplest form of life. Bacteria exist nearly everywhere—in soil, water, air, and inside other organisms. Some cause disease; others are essential for digestion, decomposition, and countless industrial processes. The plural is bacteria, which often appears incorrectly as a singular: {The bacteria is spreading} should technically use "are."

Though less frequent than its usual opposite good, bad has a wide range of meanings that grow out of its core function of characterizing something or someone as lacking good or desirable qualities. The large number of adjectives that may be considered as synonyms of bad in various contexts are all words with a negative connotation. To the consternation of many, bad developed a slang meaning in the late 20th century that is its opposite; in some limited contexts, bad means good.
A badass is someone tough, intimidating, or impressively skilled: {She's a total badass on the guitar}. As an adjective, badass describes something formidable or cool: {That was a badass move}.

Badassery is the quality or display of being a badass—tough, fearless, impressively skilled, or defiantly cool. The word celebrates audacious competence or swagger: {That stunt was pure badassery}. It often carries admiration for someone who breaks rules or defies expectations while looking good doing it.
Badasses is the plural of badass, describing tough or impressively skilled people: {The squad was full of badasses}.

Baddest is the superlative of bad in its slang sense of impressively good, tough, or formidable: {the baddest dude on the block}, {the baddest guitar player in town}. The nonstandard form signals the slang meaning—using "worst" would lose the swagger. The word carries admiration for someone's skill, style, or dominance.

A baddie is a villain or antagonist, especially in movies, TV shows, or stories. The term is informal and often playful, used when the villain isn't particularly menacing: {The kids cheered when the superhero defeated the baddie}. In recent slang, baddie has taken on a second meaning: an attractive, confident person, usually a woman, who projects a bold or fierce persona on social media. {She posted her vacation pics looking like a total baddie}.

Baddies is the plural of baddy, an informal word for villains or antagonists—the bad guys in a story, game, or conflict: {The hero fought off the baddies}. In recent slang, baddie has flipped to mean an attractive, confident woman, often one who knows she looks good: {She posted photos looking like a total baddie}. Context usually makes the meaning clear.

A baddy is a villain or antagonist, especially in fiction: {The movie's baddy gets defeated in the final scene}. The word is informal and slightly playful, often used when discussing entertainment or when speaking to children. Also spelled baddie.

A badge is a small object worn or displayed to indicate membership, authority, or achievement: a police badge, a scout badge, a name badge. The word extends to any visible marker of identity or status: {Carrying a tote bag became a badge of the educated class}. To badge in or out is to use an identification card for access.
