To {go berserk} is to lose control violently or become wildly agitated: {She went berserk when she found out}.

Berserking is the act of going berserk—fighting or behaving with wild, uncontrolled fury. The term derives from Norse warriors called berserkers who reportedly fought in a trance-like rage. In gaming, berserking often refers to a combat mode or ability where a character trades defense for increased attack power or speed. {The boss kept berserking whenever his health dropped below half.} Outside gaming, it describes any frenzied, out-of-control behavior.

Berserks is the plural of berserk as a noun—a person in a state of uncontrolled fury or violent frenzy. The word comes from Norse warriors said to fight in trance-like rage: {The berserks charged without regard for their own safety}. The adjective berserk, meaning wildly out of control, is far more common today: {The crowd went berserk}.

Berth originally meant sufficient space for a ship to maneuver, which led to its meaning of a place where a ship can dock or anchor: {The ferry pulled into its berth}. From nautical use, berth extended to sleeping accommodations on ships and trains—a built-in bed or bunk. More broadly, berth can mean any position or slot: {She earned a berth on the Olympic team}. To give someone a wide berth is to keep your distance from them.

Berths are sleeping accommodations on ships, trains, or other vehicles—narrow beds built into walls or stacked in tiers: {The cabin had two berths}. A berth is also a ship's designated spot at a dock: {The vessel pulled into its berth}. In sports, a berth is a position or slot: {The team clinched a playoff berth}. To {give someone a wide berth} is to keep your distance from them.

Beseeching means asking urgently or imploringly, with earnest pleading: {She gave him a beseeching look}. The word suggests desperation or emotional vulnerability—someone beseeching isn't just requesting but appealing to another's compassion or mercy. The verb beseech is literary and old-fashioned; beseeching survives mainly as an adjective describing eyes, glances, or tones.

Beset means to trouble persistently or attack from all sides. Problems beset a project; doubts beset a decision-maker; dangers beset a traveler. The word suggests being surrounded or hemmed in by difficulties: {The expedition was beset by storms and equipment failures}. Something that besets you won't leave you alone.

The root of beside is evident in its spelling and in its meaning: the word side. The simple relationship of being adjacent is the most frequent idea that beside conveys. A minor sense of beside, seen mainly in the phrase beside the point, is not relevant to. It can also be used in the same way that besides is used.

Though it differs by only one letter from its source beside, besides has a different meaning: it means other than or except, as in No one besides me wanted to go. With a slight twist of meaning, you can also use besides to express the idea of together with: Besides my brothers I also have some step siblings.

To besiege is to surround a place with armed forces, cutting off supplies and escape routes to force surrender: {The army besieged the fortress for three months}. Extended uses describe being overwhelmed by demands or requests: {The senator was besieged by reporters}. Someone besieged with problems faces them from all sides at once.

Besieged describes being surrounded by hostile forces or overwhelmed by persistent demands. A city under siege is besieged by enemy troops. More commonly, the word describes being inundated: {besieged by reporters}, {besieged with phone calls}, {a besieged customer service department}. The past participle often functions as an adjective suggesting embattlement or exhaustion from constant pressure.

Besieging is surrounding a place with armed forces to cut off supplies and force surrender. Armies besiege fortified cities; protesters may besiege government buildings. The word extends to persistent pressure or overwhelming attention: {Fans besieged the actor outside the theater}. {She was besieged by doubts about her decision}.

Besmirched means stained or tarnished, usually referring to reputation or honor rather than physical surfaces. To besmirch someone's name is to damage it through accusation or association with wrongdoing: {His reputation was besmirched by the scandal}. The word carries a literary or formal tone, suggesting dishonor that clings like dirt.

Besotted means infatuated to the point of foolishness—so enamored that judgment is impaired: {He was completely besotted with her}. The word carries a slightly mocking tone, suggesting the person's devotion is excessive or undignified. Less commonly, besotted can mean stupefied by drink, connecting to its older sense of being made sottish or foolish.

Bespoke means custom-made, originally referring to clothing tailored to a specific customer's measurements: {a bespoke suit from Savile Row}. The word has spread from tailoring to describe anything made to order rather than off the shelf: {bespoke furniture}, {bespoke software}. In marketing, bespoke often signals premium quality or personalized service, sometimes to the point of pretension.

Best is the superlative of good—the highest quality, most desirable, or most suitable among options: {She's the best player on the team}. As a noun, the best refers to what exceeds all else: {He gave it his best}. To best someone is to defeat them: {She bested him in the debate}. {At best} concedes limited expectations; {make the best of it} means accept circumstances and proceed optimally.

Bestiaries are medieval illustrated texts cataloging real and imaginary animals, each entry pairing description with moral or religious allegory. The lion represented Christ's resurrection; the pelican, self-sacrifice. Modern usage extends to any compendium of creatures: {a bestiary of mythological beasts}, {a video game's monster bestiary}. Singular: bestiary.

A bestiary is a medieval illustrated book cataloging real and imaginary animals, typically describing each creature's appearance, habits, and symbolic or moral significance. The term now applies to any compendium of beasts, especially in fantasy literature and games: {The author included a bestiary at the back of the novel}. A writer's bestiary might be their collected monster creations.

A bestie is a best friend—someone you're especially close to. The word is casual and affectionate, common among younger speakers: {She's been my bestie since middle school}. It often appears in social media and texting, sometimes playfully: {brunch with the besties}.

Besties is an affectionate term for best friends, typically used among younger speakers or in casual contexts: {We've been besties since middle school}. The word carries a playful, intimate tone—adults using it often do so with ironic self-awareness or genuine warmth: {brunch with my besties}.

Bestow means to give or confer something, typically something valuable or honorable: {The university bestowed an honorary degree upon her}, {Nature has bestowed great beauty on this region}. The word carries formal or elevated overtones—you bestow honors, titles, gifts, or blessings rather than ordinary objects. It implies the giver has authority or abundance to share.

A bestseller is a book that sells in very large numbers, typically appearing on ranked lists compiled by newspapers or retailers: {Her memoir hit the bestseller list within a week}. The term extends to other products that outsell competitors: {That model became our bestseller}. As an adjective, bestselling: {a bestselling author}.

Bestsellers are books or other products that sell in very large numbers. The term typically refers to books appearing on ranked lists compiled by newspapers and trade publications: {Three of her novels became bestsellers}. A bestseller may indicate commercial success without implying literary quality. The singular bestseller can also describe an author: {She's a bestselling novelist}.

Bestselling describes something that has sold more copies than competitors in its category: a bestselling {novel}, a bestselling {author}. The term appears most often with books but applies to music, games, and other products. What qualifies as bestselling varies—it may mean topping charts nationally, within a genre, or on a particular platform.

A bet is a wager—an agreement where the parties risk something (usually money) on an uncertain outcome: {I put a bet on the home team}. To bet is to make such a wager: {He bet fifty dollars on the race}. Extended, bet means to rely confidently on something: {I wouldn't bet on it}. In casual speech, {you bet} means certainly or you're welcome. As slang, bet is an affirmation meaning agreed, okay, or sounds good: {Want to meet at eight? Bet.}

Beta, β, is the second letter of the Greek alphabet, with a sound like B, which occupies the same place in the Roman alphabet. With the advent of the computer age, beta has taken on new meanings, many of them associated with second, reflecting beta’s ordinal status. Beta testing is a second phase of software development when users can report bugs. Something that is in beta is at this stage, not quite ready for official launch or release.

Betcha is an informal spelling of "bet you," representing how the phrase sounds in rapid speech: {Betcha can't catch me}, {I betcha he forgot}. It often implies confident prediction or friendly challenge. The standalone {betcha} or {you betcha} means "certainly" or "you can count on it."

To betray is to be disloyal to someone who trusts you—revealing secrets, breaking faith, or acting against their interests: {He betrayed his country by passing documents to foreign agents}. The word extends to unintentional disclosure: a trembling voice betrays nervousness, a glance betrays hidden feelings. To betray a cause or principle is to abandon it: {The compromise betrayed everything we stood for}.
clues: Turn against one you swore to

definition: Betrayal is the violation of trust or loyalty. When someone betrays you, they break faith—revealing secrets, abandoning commitments, or acting against your interests despite an implicit or explicit bond. The word carries heavy emotional weight: {The betrayal stung more than the loss itself}. Betrayal can be personal (a cheating spouse, a backstabbing friend) or political (treason, defection). It implies a relationship that made the treachery possible—strangers can't betray you.

Betrayals is the plural of betrayal—acts of disloyalty or breaking trust. A betrayal violates an expectation of faithfulness, whether in relationships, alliances, or principles. The word carries emotional weight: {The betrayals of her closest friends left her unable to trust anyone}. Small betrayals accumulate; large ones shatter: {a history of betrayals}, {the betrayals that ended their marriage}.

Betrayed is the past tense of betray, meaning to be disloyal to someone who trusted you. A betrayed {spouse} has been cheated on. A betrayed {secret} has been revealed. Someone who feels betrayed has had their trust violated: {She felt betrayed when her best friend spread the rumor}. Betrayed can also mean inadvertently revealed: {His accent betrayed his origins}.

A betrayer is someone who breaks faith with another—violating trust, loyalty, or confidence. The word carries moral weight: a betrayer isn't merely disloyal but has actively harmed someone who trusted them. {Judas is history's most famous betrayer}. The term applies to personal relationships, political alliances, or any situation where trust is weaponized against the one who gave it.

Betraying is being disloyal to someone who trusts you—revealing secrets, breaking faith, or acting against their interests. A spy betraying their country passes information to enemies. A friend betraying a confidence shares what was told privately. Betraying can also mean unintentionally revealing: {Her trembling voice was betraying her fear}. Things betray when they fail you: {His legs betrayed him on the final hill}.

Betrothal is a formal agreement to marry—an engagement, but with older and more ceremonial overtones. The word appears in historical and literary contexts where marriages were arranged or announced with ritual significance: {The betrothal was celebrated with a feast}. Someone betrothed to another is formally pledged to marry them.

Betrothed means engaged to be married. The word is formal or old-fashioned: {They were betrothed in a ceremony at the palace}. As a noun, one's betrothed is one's fiancé or fiancée: {He introduced his betrothed to the family}. The related noun betrothal names the engagement itself.

Bets is the plural of bet—a wager on an uncertain outcome. When someone bets, they stake money or reputation on a prediction: {She bets on horses every weekend}. The plural often appears in figurative expressions: {All bets are off} means previous assumptions no longer hold. {Hedging your bets} is protecting yourself by not committing fully to one position.

Better is the comparative form of good—an improvement or advantage over something else. {She's a better cook than I am.} {I feel better today.} To better something is to improve or surpass it: {He bettered his previous record.} A better is also one who bets. {You'd better} means you should, with implied consequence: {You'd better hurry or we'll be late.} To get the better of someone is to defeat or outwit them. {For better or worse} acknowledges uncertainty about outcomes.

Betting is wagering money or something of value on an uncertain outcome—a game, race, election, or any event where the result isn't known. The term covers both the activity {illegal betting operations} and the industry {sports betting has exploded since legalization}. {I'm betting he doesn't show up} expresses confident prediction without actual stakes.

The –tween part of between has the same root as the word two, and between is properly used in reference to two things only, as in a house between two trees. Some writers object to the use of between instead of among when more than two things are involved, even though such sentences have long been standard: cultural exchanges between many nations, sing the chorus between every verse.

A bevel is an angled edge or surface—one that's neither perpendicular nor parallel to adjacent faces. Picture the slanted edge of a mirror or the chamfered corner of a piece of wood. To bevel is to cut or shape such an angle: {bevel the edges before joining the boards}. A bevel is also the tool used to measure or mark angles, sometimes called a bevel square.

A beverage is a drink—any liquid intended for consumption. The word is slightly formal, appearing more often on menus and in official contexts than in casual speech: {The airline offers complimentary beverages}. Where you'd say {Can I get you a drink?} a sign might read "Food and Beverages."
clues: What you order at a café

definition: Beverages are drinks—liquids prepared for human consumption. The word is slightly formal, appearing more often on menus and in commerce than in casual speech: {The café offers a full range of hot and cold beverages}. Nobody asks a friend to grab a beverage from the fridge; they ask for a drink.

A bevy is a group or gathering, especially of women or girls: {a bevy of bridesmaids}, {a bevy of beauties}. The word originally referred to a flock of quail, and it retains that technical use among hunters. In general usage, bevy suggests an attractive or impressive collection: {a bevy of options}, {a bevy of celebrities}.

Beware is a warning to be cautious or watchful. It takes a direct object without a preposition: {Beware the dog}, {Beware false prophets}. The word appears mainly in warnings and commands rather than ordinary statements—you rarely hear {I beware} or {she bewared}. {Buyer beware} (caveat emptor) warns that purchases are at one's own risk.

To bewilder is to confuse thoroughly, leaving someone disoriented or at a loss. A bewildering situation offers too many options, contradictions, or unfamiliar elements to process easily: {The sheer variety of choices bewildered her}. Unlike simple confusion, bewilderment suggests being lost—unable to find your bearings amid complexity or strangeness.

Bewildered describes a state of confusion or disorientation, as if lost in a wilderness without bearings. Someone bewildered by events can't make sense of what's happening: {She looked bewildered by the sudden change in plans}. The feeling suggests being overwhelmed rather than simply puzzled—too much information, too fast, with no clear path forward.

Bewildering describes something that confuses or disorients through complexity, strangeness, or overwhelming variety. A bewildering {array of choices} leaves you unsure where to start. Bewildering {instructions} make no sense no matter how many times you read them. The word suggests being mentally lost rather than merely puzzled—surrounded by things that don't add up.

Bewilderment is a state of confused disorientation—the feeling of being mentally lost or unable to make sense of what's happening. It suggests more than simple confusion; there's often an element of being overwhelmed or stunned: {She stared at the contract in bewilderment}, {His sudden departure left everyone in bewilderment}. The word implies a temporary inability to process or respond.

Bewilders is the third-person singular of bewilder, meaning to confuse or perplex deeply. Something bewilders when it leaves you unable to understand or respond: {The complexity of the tax code bewilders most people}. What bewilders doesn't just puzzle—it disorients, leaving you uncertain how to proceed.

To bewitch is to cast a spell on someone—to enchant or hex them through magic. The word now appears most often in its figurative sense: to captivate utterly, as if by supernatural means. A performer bewitches an audience; a landscape bewitches a traveler. {He was bewitched by her smile.} The adjective bewitching describes irresistible charm: {a bewitching melody}.

Bewitched describes someone or something under the influence of magic or enchantment—literally cursed or charmed by a witch. More commonly, it means captivated or entranced: {He was bewitched by her smile}. The word suggests being so fascinated that rational thought fails, as if under a spell.

Bewitches is the third-person singular of bewitch, meaning to cast a spell on someone or something. More commonly, it means to captivate or enchant: {Her voice bewitches everyone who hears it}. The word carries connotations of irresistible charm, often with a hint of danger or the supernatural.

Bewitching describes something so captivating it seems to cast a spell. A bewitching smile or bewitching beauty entrances the observer, suggesting an almost magical power to attract: {She had a bewitching way of tilting her head when she listened}. The word carries romantic or admiring connotations, implying enchantment rather than literal witchcraft.

Bewitchment is the state of being under a spell or magical influence, or the act of casting such a spell. The word extends naturally to any powerful fascination or enchantment: {He fell under the bewitchment of her voice}. It suggests being captivated beyond rational control, held by something mysterious or irresistible.

You can easily see the relationship to the dialectal word yonder in beyond and their meanings are related. Beyond means on the far side of in its most literal sense. From this it developed the meaning outside the scope or limit of, as in these equations are beyond my understanding. Beyond can also mean superior to: talent beyond others in her class.

A bezel is the grooved ring or rim that holds something in place—the glass of a watch, a gemstone in its setting, or the screen of a phone or monitor. The word often appears in technical contexts: {The diamond sits in a bezel setting}. On watches, a rotating bezel may track elapsed time or time zones.

Bhaji is an Indian snack of vegetables—often onion, potato, or spinach—mixed with spiced chickpea batter and deep-fried. The crispy fritters are popular as street food and appetizers in South Asian cuisine: {We ordered onion bhajis as a starter}. Also spelled bhajia or bhajiya.

Bhangra is a style of popular music combining Punjabi folk traditions with Western dance beats. The genre emerged from the celebratory harvest dances of the Punjab region, later fused with electronic music by South Asian communities in Britain during the 1980s. {The DJ mixed bhangra tracks into the set.}

Meanings that have grown out of the earliest use of bias now far outnumber its original noun use: to denote a line or cut in fabric that is diagonal to the weave. Today bias, whether as noun or verb, is used primarily as a near synonym of prejudice to talk about representations that are false or skewed because of people’s views, or because of incorrect use of data or statistics: The judge was thought to have a liberal bias. The exclusion of this data seriously biased the results. The participle biased is often used as an adjective: biased findings.

Biased means having a prejudice or inclination that prevents fair judgment. A biased {jury} cannot weigh evidence impartially. A biased {news source} favors one perspective. The word often implies unfairness: {The hiring process was biased against older applicants}. Someone can be biased toward something they favor or biased against something they oppose.

Biases is the plural of bias—preconceptions or inclinations that favor or disfavor something. Everyone has biases, whether conscious or unconscious: {We all carry biases that affect our judgment}. In statistics, bias is systematic error that skews results. The verb form means to influence unfairly: {Media coverage biases public opinion}.

Biathlon is a winter sport combining cross-country skiing with rifle marksmanship. Competitors ski between shooting stations, where they must hit targets before continuing—elevated heart rates from skiing make the precision shooting more difficult. The sport features prominently in the Winter Olympics. {She trained for years to compete in the biathlon.}

A bib is a cloth or plastic covering tied around a child's neck during meals to protect clothing from spills and dribbles. Adults wear bibs for messy foods like lobster or barbecue. The upper front part of an apron or overalls is also called a bib. To bib is an archaic verb meaning to drink, usually alcohol.

Bibimbap is a Korean dish of rice topped with seasoned vegetables, meat, a fried egg, and chili pepper paste, served in a bowl and mixed together before eating. The name means "mixed rice." When served in a hot stone bowl ({dolsot bibimbap}), the rice develops a crispy crust at the bottom.

Bibimbop is a Korean dish of rice topped with sautéed vegetables, meat, a fried egg, and chili paste, served in a hot stone bowl and mixed together before eating. The ingredients create a variety of textures and flavors—crispy rice forms where it contacts the heated bowl. Also spelled bibimbap. {I ordered bibimbop with extra gochujang.}

A bible is any book considered the definitive authority on its subject: {the baker's bible}, {a fisherman's bible}. The term implies comprehensive, trusted guidance that practitioners consult repeatedly. (Capitalized Bible is the Christian scriptures.)

Bibles is the plural of Bible, the sacred scriptures of Christianity comprising the Old and New Testaments. Extended to mean authoritative reference works in any field: {The Chicago Manual of Style is the bible for editors}. Someone might own multiple bibles—different translations, study editions, or family heirlooms: {She collected antique bibles}.

Biblical means relating to or derived from the Bible, the sacred scriptures of Christianity and Judaism. A biblical {reference} draws on scriptural text. {Biblical proportions} describes something of enormous, catastrophic scale—floods, plagues, disasters echoing Old Testament narratives: {The hurricane caused destruction of biblical proportions}. Biblical can also mean very old or traditional in a mildly humorous way.

A bibliography is a list of sources—books, articles, websites—cited or consulted in preparing a written work. It typically appears at the end: {Check the bibliography for further reading}. Bibliography also means the study of books as physical objects, examining their production, history, and classification. A bibliography of an author is a comprehensive list of their published works.

A bibliophile is a person who loves books—not just reading them, but collecting, handling, and appreciating them as objects. The term suggests someone drawn to fine editions, rare volumes, and the physical pleasures of book ownership: {a bibliophile's library filled with first editions}. It's more elevated than bookworm, which emphasizes reading rather than collecting.

Bibs is the plural of bib—a cloth or plastic covering worn over the chest to protect clothing, especially during meals. Babies wear bibs to catch drool and food; adults might wear them while eating lobster or getting a haircut. Bib overalls, often called just bibs, are work pants with a chest panel and shoulder straps: {He pulled on his bibs and headed to the barn}.

Bicentennial refers to a two-hundredth anniversary or its celebration: {the bicentennial of American independence}. As an adjective, it describes events or things marking such an occasion: {bicentennial commemorations}, {bicentennial coins}. The 1976 U.S. bicentennial made the word especially familiar to Americans.

Bicep is the informal singular of biceps, treating the Latin plural form as if it were regular English. The biceps is the large muscle at the front of the upper arm that flexes the elbow: {He flexed his bicep for the camera}. Though technically biceps is already singular (one biceps, two biceps), bicep has become common in casual usage.

The biceps is the large muscle at the front of the upper arm, responsible for bending the elbow and rotating the forearm. Though biceps ends in *s*, it's singular—one biceps, two biceps: {My left biceps is sore from yesterday's workout}. The word also names the corresponding muscle at the back of the thigh (biceps femoris). Flexing one's biceps is a classic display of strength.

To bicker is to argue in a petty, persistent way—squabbling over small matters rather than having a serious dispute. Siblings bicker, couples bicker, coworkers bicker. The word suggests irritation more than genuine conflict: {They bickered about whose turn it was to do the dishes}. Bickering tends to be ongoing and tiresome rather than brief or intense.

Bickering is petty, prolonged quarreling over trivial matters. Unlike a full argument, bickering involves back-and-forth sniping without resolution: {The siblings' constant bickering drove their parents crazy}. It suggests irritation more than genuine conflict—the kind of squabbling that wears people down rather than clearing the air.

Bickers is the third-person singular of bicker, meaning to quarrel over petty matters. People who bicker engage in small, persistent arguments rather than serious fights: {The couple bickers constantly about whose turn it is to do dishes}. The word suggests irritating repetition—squabbling that recurs without resolution.

Bicoastal describes someone or something connected to both the east and west coasts, typically of the United States. A bicoastal lifestyle involves splitting time between cities like New York and Los Angeles: {She's bicoastal—apartment in Manhattan, house in Malibu}. The term often suggests wealth or professional demands that require presence on both coasts.

Bicurious describes someone who identifies as heterosexual or homosexual but is curious about sexual experiences with people of a different gender than they're usually attracted to. The term suggests openness to experimentation without commitment to a bisexual identity: {I've always been straight, but lately I've been bicurious}. Often a transitional label.

A bicycle is a two-wheeled vehicle propelled by pedaling. The rider sits on a seat and steers with handlebars while turning cranks connected to the rear wheel by a chain. Bicycles serve transportation, exercise, and sport. As a verb, to bicycle is to ride one: {We bicycled through the countryside}. Often shortened to bike.

Bicycles are two-wheeled vehicles powered by pedaling, with a frame, handlebars for steering, and a seat. The word works as both noun and verb—to bicycle is to ride one: {She bicycles to work every day}. Bicycle appears in compounds: {bicycle lane}, {bicycle rack}, {bicycle shorts}. Often shortened to bike.

Bicycling is riding a bicycle—a two-wheeled vehicle powered by pedaling. The term covers transportation, recreation, and competitive sport: {She's been bicycling to work for years}, {We went bicycling along the coast}. In American English, biking is more common in casual speech, though bicycling remains standard in formal contexts.

A bid is an offer, especially one stating a price you're willing to pay: {The highest bid wins the auction}. To bid is to make such an offer, or in card games, to declare how many tricks you intend to take. A bid can also be an attempt to achieve something: {a bid for power}, {a bid to break the record}. The past tense is bid (for offers) or bade (for farewells and commands, as in {She bade him farewell}). (Capitalized BID is an acronym in specialized fields.)

A bidder is someone who makes an offer, especially at an auction or in competition for a contract. The {highest bidder} wins the item being sold. In business contexts, bidders compete for projects or acquisitions: {Three bidders submitted proposals for the construction contract}. The {lowest bidder} often wins service contracts where cost is the deciding factor.

Biddies is the plural of biddy, an informal and often dismissive term for an older woman, especially one perceived as fussy, meddlesome, or set in her ways: {a group of old biddies gossiping at the coffee shop}. The word carries condescending overtones. Biddy can also mean a hen or young chicken, though this sense is rare outside rural dialect.

Bidding is the act of making offers or bids, especially at an auction: {The bidding started at five hundred dollars}. It also means a command or invitation: {I came at her bidding}. To {do someone's bidding} is to carry out their wishes or orders. A bidding war occurs when competing parties drive prices up through successive offers.

Biddy is a mildly dismissive term for a woman, typically suggesting someone fussy, gossipy, or meddlesome. It often appears with modifiers: {old biddy}, {nosy biddy}. The word can also mean a hen or chick, which likely influenced its application to women. In older usage, Biddy was a nickname for Bridget, once stereotypically associated with Irish servant women.

Bide means to wait or remain in a place. The word is old-fashioned except in the phrase {bide your time}, meaning to wait patiently for the right moment: {She bided her time until the opportunity arose}. In Scottish and some regional dialects, bide retains its older sense of dwell or stay: {He bides in Edinburgh}.

A bidet is a low bathroom fixture designed for washing the genitals and anal area after using the toilet. It resembles a toilet but has a faucet or spray nozzle. Common throughout Europe and parts of Asia, bidets remain rare in American bathrooms, though bidet attachments for standard toilets have gained popularity.

A bidet is a low bathroom fixture for washing the genitals and anal area after using the toilet. Traditional bidets resemble a shallow basin you straddle; modern versions are often toilet attachments that spray water. Common in Europe and Asia, bidets remain relatively uncommon in American homes: {The hotel bathroom had both a toilet and a bidet}.

Bids are offers, typically of money. At an auction, bids compete until the highest wins. In contracting, companies submit bids to win projects. In card games like bridge, a bid declares how many tricks you intend to take. To make a bid for something is to attempt to obtain it: {a bid for power}, {a bid for freedom}. Someone who bids you farewell wishes you well on departure.

Biff is a punch or blow, typically not too serious: {He gave me a biff on the arm}. As a verb, to biff someone is to hit them: {She biffed him with her purse}. In British and Australian slang, to biff something is to throw it carelessly: {Just biff it in the bin}.

Bifocals are eyeglasses with lenses divided into two sections—typically the upper part for distance vision and the lower part for reading. The design lets wearers see clearly at different distances without switching glasses: {She peered over her bifocals at the fine print}. The term can suggest middle age, when close-up vision typically begins to weaken.

Big is the most common all-purpose adjective for characterizing something that is larger, more important, or more significant than average. Starting in the 19th century it jumped the part-of-speech barrier to operate as an adverb as well, though it is always considered somewhat informal in this context: think big or talk big.

A bigamist is a person who marries someone while still legally married to another. The term is legal and disapproving—bigamy is a crime in most jurisdictions: {The bigamist had maintained separate households for years before being discovered}.

Bigamy is the crime of marrying someone while already legally married to another person. The offense lies in the legal act of marriage, not in maintaining two relationships—that's polygamy or simply infidelity. {He was charged with bigamy after his first wife discovered the second marriage.}

Bigger is the comparative form of big—larger in size, amount, or importance. {The bigger house costs more}. {She's got bigger problems than money}. To have {bigger fish to fry} is to have more important matters to attend to. Something can be bigger physically or figuratively: a bigger crowd, a bigger impact, a bigger deal.

Biggest is the superlative of big—the largest in size, amount, or importance among three or more things: {the biggest house on the block}, {my biggest fear}, {the biggest mistake of his life}. It often carries emphasis beyond literal measurement: {That's the biggest load of nonsense I've ever heard}.

Biggie is informal for something big or important: {It's no biggie} dismisses something as trivial. A biggie can be a major player or significant item in any category: {one of the biggies in tech}, {That exam is a biggie}. The word has a playful, casual tone.

Biggies is the plural of biggie, an informal term for something important or significant: {Don't sweat the small stuff—focus on the biggies}. Often appears in the phrase {no biggie}, meaning it's not a problem or not a big deal: {You forgot to call? No biggie}.

Bigheaded means conceited or excessively proud of oneself, often to the point of arrogance. Success can make someone bigheaded: {Don't let the promotion make you bigheaded}. The image is of a head swollen with self-importance. Also spelled big-headed.

Bighearted means generous and kind, especially in giving help or showing compassion to others. A bighearted person gives freely of their time, money, or sympathy: {She made a bighearted donation to the shelter}. The word suggests warmth and openness rather than calculation.

A bighorn is a wild sheep native to the mountains of western North America, named for the male's massive curved horns. The full name is bighorn sheep: {We spotted a bighorn on the cliff face}. The horns can weigh up to thirty pounds and are used in dramatic head-butting contests during mating season.

Bighorns are wild sheep native to the mountainous regions of western North America, named for the large, curved horns on the males. The animals are prized by hunters and have become symbols of rugged wilderness. Bighorn also names places where these sheep are found: {the Bighorn Mountains}, {the Bighorn River}.

A bigmouth is someone who talks too much, especially revealing secrets or speaking boastfully. The word implies indiscretion—a bigmouth can't keep confidences: {Don't tell her anything; she's a bigmouth}. As an adjective, bigmouthed describes loud, indiscreet, or boastful behavior: {his bigmouthed bragging}.

A bigot is someone who holds strong, intolerant views toward a particular group without reasonable foundation. The target of many bigots’ view are ethnic or racial groups, making bigot effectively a synonym of racist, but bigot can also be used of anyone who holds particularly narrow views, for example on gender equality. There is no related verb for bigot but the adjective form bigoted is used: a bigoted police commissioner.

Bigoted describes someone who holds rigid, intolerant views toward people of different groups—whether based on race, religion, politics, or other characteristics. A bigoted person refuses to consider other perspectives and treats their prejudices as self-evident truths: {His bigoted remarks about immigrants cost him his job}. The word implies not just holding biased views but being stubbornly attached to them.

Bigotry is stubborn, unreasonable prejudice against people based on their membership in a group—whether defined by race, religion, sexuality, or other characteristics. Unlike casual bias, bigotry implies active hostility or contempt: {The policy was rooted in bigotry, not public safety}. A bigot holds such views; bigoted describes them.

Bigots are people who hold obstinate, unreasonable attachment to their own opinions and prejudices, especially regarding race, religion, or other group identities. The word implies not just holding biased views but refusing to consider alternatives: {The bigots shouted down anyone who disagreed}. Unlike broader terms for prejudiced people, bigot emphasizes the stubborn, closed-minded quality of the intolerance.

A bigshot is an important or influential person, often used with slight mockery or resentment: {He thinks he's such a bigshot now that he got promoted}. The term suggests someone who wields power or acts self-important. Also spelled as two words: big shot.

Bigshots are important or influential people, typically used with a note of irreverence or resentment: {The bigshots in corporate don't care what happens to us}. The term suggests someone who wields power or commands attention, often implying they're self-important or out of touch with ordinary people. Also spelled as two words: big shots.

Bigtime, usually written as two words (big time), works as both noun and adverb. As a noun, the big time refers to the highest level of achievement or prominence in a field: {She finally made it to the big time}. As an adverb, it means to a great degree or extensively: {That decision backfired bigtime}. The adjective big-time describes something operating at that top level or something significant in scale: {a big-time Hollywood producer}.

A bigwig is an important or influential person, especially one with authority in a particular field or organization: {The bigwigs from corporate are visiting next week}. The term carries a slightly mocking tone, suggesting the person takes their own importance seriously. It alludes to the elaborate wigs once worn by judges and aristocrats.

Bigwigs are important or influential people, especially those in positions of power: {The corporate bigwigs flew in for the meeting}. The term carries a slightly mocking tone, suggesting the people in question may be pompous or out of touch. It derives from the large wigs once worn by people of high rank.

A bike is a bicycle—a two-wheeled vehicle propelled by pedaling. The word also applies to motorcycles and, more recently, electric scooters. To bike is to ride one: {I bike to work most days}. A biker rides motorcycles; a cyclist rides bicycles, though the terms blur.

A biker is someone who rides a motorcycle, especially as a lifestyle rather than mere transportation. The term often evokes leather jackets, long rides, and motorcycle clubs: {a group of bikers pulled into the bar}. Biker can also mean a cyclist, though this usage is less common in American English.

Bikers are people who ride motorcycles, especially as a lifestyle or group identity. The term often suggests leather jackets, long rides, and motorcycle clubs: {a bar popular with bikers}. Biker can also mean cyclist, though this use is less common in American English, where cyclist or bike rider typically fills that role.

Bikes is the plural of bike, a common shortening of bicycle—a two-wheeled vehicle powered by pedaling. The term extends to motorcycles and motorbikes as well. As a verb, bikes means travels by bicycle: {She bikes to work every day}. Biking culture has spawned compounds like {bike lane}, {bike share}, and {bike messenger}.

Bikeshare is a system where bicycles are available for short-term rental, typically from automated stations throughout a city. Users pick up a bike at one location and return it to any station in the network: {I used bikeshare to get to the meeting}. Also called bike-sharing or bike share.

Biking is riding a bicycle, whether for transportation, exercise, or recreation. The word covers everything from commuting to work to mountain biking on trails: {We went biking along the river path}. In some contexts, biking can also refer to motorcycling, though cycling or riding usually clarifies the distinction.

A bikini is a two-piece swimsuit for women, with separate pieces covering the breasts and groin. The design has varied from modest to minimal since its mid-twentieth-century debut. By extension, bikini describes other two-part configurations: a {bikini wax} removes pubic hair outside the swimsuit line; {bikini briefs} are low-cut underwear. (Capitalized Bikini is the Pacific atoll.)

Bikinis is the plural of bikini, a two-piece swimsuit for women consisting of a bra-like top and brief bottoms. The garment takes its name from Bikini Atoll, where atomic bomb tests occurred in 1946—the year the swimsuit debuted, marketed as explosively daring. {She packed three bikinis for the beach trip.} A bikini wax removes pubic hair that would show beyond the swimsuit's edges.

Bile is a bitter yellow-green fluid produced by the liver that aids digestion, particularly of fats. The word extends figuratively to bad temper or bitterness: {His essay was full of bile toward his critics}. Someone described as bilious is irritable or ill-tempered, though the older medical sense referred to disorders of bile production.

Bilge is the lowest internal part of a ship's hull, where water collects. By extension, bilge water is the foul liquid that accumulates there—a mixture of seawater, oil, and waste. Figuratively, bilge means nonsense or rubbish: {That's absolute bilge}. The word carries a sense of something worthless, polluted, or contemptible.

Bilingual means able to speak two languages with native or near-native fluency: {She's bilingual in English and Spanish}. The term also describes things involving two languages: {bilingual education}, {bilingual signage}. Someone raised speaking two languages from childhood is a native bilingual; others become bilingual through study or immersion.

Bilingualism is the ability to speak two languages with fluency, or the regular use of two languages in a community or region. Individual bilingualism develops through upbringing, education, or immersion: {Her bilingualism made her invaluable as a translator}. Societal bilingualism describes places where two languages have official or widespread status: {Canada's official bilingualism}. The term sometimes extends loosely to multilingualism.

Bilinguals are people who speak two languages fluently. The term encompasses those who grew up with two languages from birth and those who acquired a second language later. Research on bilinguals often examines cognitive effects of dual-language use: {Bilinguals may switch between languages mid-sentence}. The singular bilingual works as both noun and adjective.

B-i-l-l represents four words in English, of which only two are common. The most frequent meaning of bill is for a document that records a monetary transaction (heating bill), that represents currency (five dollar bill), or that details legislation (education bill). The other common kind of bill is the jaws of a bird, along with the horny part called the beak. The visor of a cap that resembles this is also a bill.

A billabong is a stagnant pool or backwater formed when a river changes course, leaving a section of its former channel cut off. The term is Australian, evoking the outback landscape: {We camped near a billabong thick with water lilies}. Billabongs fill during floods and may dry up in drought, serving as crucial water sources for wildlife in arid regions.

Billabongs are stagnant pools or backwaters formed when a river changes course, leaving behind an isolated stretch of water. The term comes from Australian English, where billabongs are distinctive features of the outback landscape: {The cattle gathered at the billabong during the drought}. The word appears famously in "Waltzing Matilda," Australia's unofficial anthem.

A billboard is a large outdoor advertising structure, typically placed along highways or in urban areas where many people will see it. The word extends to any prominent display surface: {The building's side became a billboard for political messages}. As a verb, to billboard something is to advertise it prominently or give it heavy promotion. (Capitalized Billboard is the music industry magazine.)

Billboards are large outdoor advertising signs, typically mounted along highways or on buildings where they'll catch the attention of passing traffic. The format has become a unit of cultural visibility—a song "tops the Billboard charts" because the magazine tracking music sales took its name from this form of advertising. To billboard something is to advertise it prominently: {The company billboarded its new product across the city}.

Billed describes something that has been advertised, announced, or scheduled: {The concert was billed as a once-in-a-lifetime event}. A performer billed as a headliner gets top promotion. Billed also means having received an invoice: {We were billed for services we never received}. In zoology, billed describes birds by their beaks: {a yellow-billed cuckoo}.

Billiard relates to billiards, the game played on a cloth-covered table by striking balls with a cue stick: {billiard table}, {billiard room}, {billiard ball}. The game itself is almost always billiards, with the singular form appearing mainly as a modifier. A billiard can also name a specific shot where the cue ball strikes two other balls in succession.

Billiards is a family of games played on a cloth-covered table, where players use a long stick called a cue to strike balls into pockets or against other balls. The term covers pool, snooker, and carom billiards, though in American English billiards often means specifically the pocketless carom game: {We played billiards at the club}. The word takes a singular verb despite its plural form.

Billing is the process of preparing and sending invoices for goods or services: {The hospital's billing department handles insurance claims}. In entertainment, billing refers to the prominence of a performer's name in credits or advertisements—top billing means your name appears first and largest: {She received second billing behind the lead actor}. As a compound, billing appears in terms like {billing cycle} and {billing address}.

A billion is a thousand million—the number 1,000,000,000, or 10⁹. In older British usage, billion meant a million million (10¹²), but American usage now dominates globally. The word commonly expresses vast quantities: {billions of stars}, {The company is worth billions}. A billionaire has wealth exceeding one billion dollars.

A billionaire is a person whose wealth amounts to at least one billion dollars, euros, or other major currency unit. The term emerged in the twentieth century as fortunes grew beyond the millionaire threshold. Billionaires often appear in discussions of inequality, philanthropy, and political influence: {Tech billionaires have reshaped how we communicate}. The word sometimes carries connotations of excess or detachment from ordinary life.

Billionaires are people whose net worth exceeds one billion dollars or equivalent currency. The term carries connotations beyond mere wealth—billionaires are often discussed as a class wielding outsized influence on politics, media, and public policy: {Billionaires shouldn't exist}, {tech billionaires buying up newspapers}. Whether admired as visionaries or criticized as symptoms of inequality, the word rarely appears neutrally.

Billions is the plural of billion, a quantity of one thousand million (1,000,000,000). The word often indicates an imprecisely large number: {The universe contains billions of stars}. {Billions of dollars in aid} suggests vast sums without exact accounting. As a count, billions means multiple units of a billion: {The company is worth several billions}.

A billow is a large, rolling wave or surge, especially of the sea. The word extends to anything that swells and rolls similarly: {billows of smoke}, {billows of fabric}. As a verb, to billow is to swell outward with air or movement: {The curtains billowed in the wind}, {Her dress billowed as she walked}.

Billowed is the past tense of billow—to swell outward or rise in waves. Fabric billows in the wind; smoke billows from a chimney. The word suggests volume and movement, something filling with air or expanding dramatically: {Her dress billowed as she ran}, {Clouds of dust billowed behind the truck}.

Billowing describes something swelling outward and undulating, typically from air or wind filling it. Sails billow when wind catches them; curtains billow through open windows; smoke billows from a chimney. The word captures both the outward expansion and the wavelike motion. As a noun, billowing refers to this swelling movement itself. {Her dress was billowing in the breeze.} {Billowing clouds of dust rose from the dirt road.}

Billows are large, rolling waves of water, or masses of something that surge and swell like waves: {billows of smoke}, {billows of fabric}. The verb billow describes this swelling motion—sails billow in the wind, curtains billow through open windows, clouds billow upward. The word emphasizes soft, voluminous movement rather than sharp or violent action.

Billowy describes something that swells, undulates, or puffs out like a wave or a sail filled with wind. Clouds are billowy when they mass in soft, rounded heaps. Fabric is billowy when it flows loosely rather than lying flat: {a billowy white dress}, {billowy curtains}. The word suggests gentle fullness and movement.

Bills are statements of money owed: {The bills are piling up}. A bill is also paper currency: {a twenty-dollar bill}. In legislation, a bill is a proposed law before it becomes an act. A bird's bill is its beak. To bill someone is to send them an invoice, or in entertainment, to advertise: {She was billed as the next big thing}. To {fit the bill} is to meet requirements.

Billy is informal for a billy club—a short, heavy stick carried by police officers for striking: {The cop reached for his billy}. In Australian English, a billy or billy can is a metal pot used for boiling water over a campfire, especially for making tea: {Put the billy on}. (Capitalized Billy is a given name, often short for William.)

A billygoat is a male goat, especially an adult one. The term emphasizes the animal's sex, often evoking the stereotypical traits of male goats: beards, pungent smell, and aggressive or stubborn behavior. {The old billygoat butted anyone who came near the fence.} Also spelled billy goat. The female counterpart is a nanny goat.

Bimbo is a derogatory term for a woman perceived as attractive but unintelligent or vacuous. The word implies someone who trades on physical appearance rather than intellect, often with connotations of sexual availability. Though historically applied to men (meaning a foolish fellow), modern usage targets women almost exclusively. {She hated being dismissed as just another bimbo.} The male equivalent, when used, is sometimes *himbo*.

Bimbos is the plural of bimbo, a derogatory term for a woman perceived as attractive but unintelligent or vapid: {The movie was full of bimbos in bikinis}. The word implies that looks and brains are mutually exclusive. Male equivalents like himbo exist but are rarer and often used more playfully.

A bin is a container for storage or disposal—a trash bin, recycling bin, bread bin. In British English, bin is the standard word for what Americans call a garbage can or wastebasket. To bin something is to throw it away: {Just bin those old magazines}. In computing, a bin folder holds executable files.

Binaries are things that come in pairs or involve two parts. In computing, binaries are executable files—compiled code ready to run, as opposed to source code: {Download the binaries from the release page}. The term also refers to binary star systems, where two stars orbit each other. In discussions of gender or politics, binaries are either/or frameworks that some argue oversimplify reality: {rejecting the male-female binary}.

Binary means composed of two parts or involving a choice between two options. In computing, binary is the base-2 number system using only 0 and 1—the fundamental language of digital machines. Binary code underlies all computer operations. More broadly, binary describes any either/or framework: {binary thinking}, {a binary choice}. Gender is increasingly discussed as non-binary, rejecting the traditional male/female division.

The core meaning of bind, primarily a verb, is to secure by tying: Bind his hands with cord. The idea of securing so as to be integrated or connected extends to other meanings of bind, as in the binding of books, of molecules to receptors, or of parties to an agreement. If you are in a bind, you’re in a situation in which there are few or no desirable choices.

A binder is something that holds things together. A ring binder holds loose papers. A binder in cooking—egg, breadcrumbs—holds ingredients together. In publishing, a binder assembles printed pages into books. A binder is also a chest compression garment worn to flatten breasts, used by some transgender men and nonbinary people: {I need to take off my binder—I've been wearing it too long}.

Binders are covers or folders that hold loose papers together, typically with rings or clips that open to add or remove pages: {a three-ring binder}. The word extends to anything that binds—an adhesive agent in paint, a substance that holds ingredients together in cooking. In transgender contexts, binders are compression garments worn to flatten the chest: {He wore a binder under his shirt}.

A bindi is a decorative dot worn on the forehead, traditionally by Hindu women. Placed between the eyebrows at the site of the "third eye," it has spiritual significance in South Asian cultures, though it's also worn as fashion. The term extends to the adhesive gems or stickers sold for this purpose: {She chose a red bindi to match her sari}.

Binding describes something that holds together or obligates. A binding agreement is legally enforceable—you can't back out without consequences. Book binding holds pages together; a ski binding attaches boot to ski. As a noun, binding is the material covering a book's spine or edging fabric on a quilt. {The contract is binding once both parties sign.}

Bindings are what hold things together or in place. Ski bindings attach boots to skis. Book bindings hold pages together. In programming, bindings connect a name to a value or link software components: {The Python bindings let you call the C library}. A binding agreement or contract is one that obligates the parties to its terms.

Bindis are small decorative dots worn on the forehead, traditionally by Hindu women at the spot considered the seat of wisdom. The bindi originated as a religious symbol but has become fashionable adornment across South Asia and beyond. In Western contexts, bindis worn as fashion accessories have drawn criticism as cultural appropriation: {She stuck a bindi between her eyebrows before the music festival}.

Binds is the third-person singular of bind, meaning to tie, fasten, or hold together. Rope binds a prisoner's wrists; a contract binds parties to its terms. What binds can also unite: {Music is what binds us together}. As a noun, binds are difficult situations: {I'm in a real bind here}.

A binge is a period of excessive indulgence—eating, drinking, spending, or consuming entertainment without restraint: {a weekend binge}, {a Netflix binge}. The verb means to engage in such excess: {I binged the entire series in two days}. Binge eating and binge drinking specifically describe consuming large amounts in short periods, often compulsively. {Binge-watch} has become standard for consuming multiple episodes consecutively.

Bingeable describes entertainment—usually a TV series—that's so compelling you want to consume multiple episodes or installments in one sitting. The word emerged with streaming services that release entire seasons at once: {The show is incredibly bingeable}. A bingeable series typically has strong narrative hooks and cliffhangers that pull you into the next episode.

Binged is the past tense of binge—to indulge in something excessively, especially in a concentrated period. Originally about food or alcohol: {She binged on chocolate after the breakup}. Now commonly describes consuming media in extended sessions: {I binged the entire series in one weekend}. Also spelled bingeing or binging for the present participle.

Bingeing is indulging in something to excess in a single session. The word originally described uncontrolled eating or drinking: {a bingeing episode that left her sick}. Now it commonly describes watching multiple episodes of a show consecutively: {I spent Sunday bingeing the new season}. Also spelled binging.

Binges is the plural noun and third-person singular verb form of binge. A binge is a period of unrestrained indulgence in something, most often eating, drinking alcohol, or consuming media: {Her weekend binges left her feeling sluggish on Monday}. When someone binges, they engage in this kind of excess: {He binges true crime documentaries every time a new series drops}. The word often carries connotations of loss of control or later regret, though binge-watching has normalized the term somewhat.

To bingewatch is to watch multiple episodes of a television series in rapid succession, often consuming an entire season or more in one sitting. The practice became widespread with streaming services that release full seasons at once: {I bingewatched the whole series over the weekend}. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated.
clues: Consume a series in one sitting

definition: Bingewatching is consuming multiple episodes of a television series in rapid succession, often in a single sitting. The practice became widespread with streaming services that release entire seasons at once: {I spent the whole weekend bingewatching that new crime drama}. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated: binge watching, binge-watching.

Bingeworthy describes entertainment—usually a TV series—compelling enough to watch multiple episodes in one sitting. The word emerged with streaming services that release entire seasons at once, enabling marathon viewing sessions. {Is the new season bingeworthy, or should I wait?} Something bingeworthy hooks you and doesn't let go.

Binging is indulging in something to excess, typically in a concentrated period. The word applies to eating, drinking, or consuming media: {binging on Halloween candy}, {a weekend of binging TV shows}. The spelling bingeing also appears, preserving the silent e from binge. Netflix popularized {binge-watching}, making binging the default verb for consuming entire seasons at once.

From its use in the game of bingo to signal that you have won, Bingo! has become a general interjection that expresses something realized suddenly, such as a discovery or sudden insight. It can also be used to acknowledge someone else’s sudden understanding.

A binkie is a baby's pacifier—the nipple-shaped device infants suck for comfort. The term comes from a brand name but has become generic in American English: {The baby won't sleep without her binkie}. Binkie can also refer to any comfort object a child clings to, like a favorite blanket or stuffed animal.

Binkies has two distinct meanings. A binky is a baby's pacifier—a brand name that became generic: {The baby dropped her binky}. Separately, binkies are the joyful leaps rabbits make when excited, twisting and kicking in midair: {My rabbit does binkies every morning when I let her out}.

A binky is a baby's pacifier—the rubber or silicone nipple infants suck for comfort. The word is nursery talk, often used by parents and young children. Separately, a binky is the excited jump a rabbit makes when happy, twisting in midair with a kick: {The bunny did a binky when I let her out of her cage}.

Binocular means involving both eyes: {binocular vision}. The noun binoculars (almost always plural) refers to a handheld optical device with two eyepieces for viewing distant objects: {She watched the birds through binoculars}. A single unit is occasionally called {a binocular} or {a pair of binoculars}.

Binoculars are a handheld optical device with two barrels, one for each eye, used to magnify distant objects. They function like a pair of small telescopes mounted side by side: {She watched the birds through binoculars}. Field glasses and opera glasses are types of binoculars. The word is almost always plural, though a single unit is occasionally called a binocular.

Bins are containers for storing or discarding things—storage bins hold items, trash bins hold waste. In British English, bin is the standard word for what Americans call a garbage can or wastebasket: {Put it in the bin}. To bin something is to throw it away: {I binned the old magazines}. In data analysis, bins are ranges into which values are grouped for statistical purposes.

Bio is an informal shortening of biography, referring to a brief account of someone's life or background. On social media and professional platforms, your bio is the short self-description in your profile: {Her Twitter bio says she's a writer and cat enthusiast}. Bio also clips biological or biology: {bio class}, {bio major}.

A biochemist is a scientist who studies the chemical processes and substances that occur within living organisms. The field bridges biology and chemistry, examining molecules like proteins, DNA, and enzymes to understand how life works at the molecular level. {Biochemists developed the COVID vaccine.}

Biochemistry is the branch of science that studies chemical processes within living organisms—the molecular mechanisms of metabolism, genetics, and cellular function. It bridges biology and chemistry, examining how proteins fold, how enzymes catalyze reactions, how DNA replicates. {She majored in biochemistry before medical school.}

Biodad is informal for biological father—the man whose genetic material contributed to a child's conception, as distinguished from a stepfather, adoptive father, or other father figure. The term often appears in contexts involving adoption, blended families, or absent fathers: {My biodad left when I was three, but my stepdad raised me}. Also spelled bio-dad or bio dad.

Biodegradable describes materials that can be broken down by bacteria, fungi, or other living organisms into natural substances like water, carbon dioxide, and organic matter. The term appears constantly in environmental discussions: {biodegradable packaging}, {biodegradable detergent}. Marketing often stretches the word—something technically biodegradable may take decades to decompose, or require industrial composting conditions rarely available.

To biodegrade is to break down naturally through the action of living organisms, especially bacteria and fungi. Organic materials biodegrade over time, returning to the earth: {Banana peels biodegrade in weeks; plastic bags take centuries}. The term appears frequently in environmental discussions about waste and packaging.

Biodiesel is a renewable fuel made from vegetable oils, animal fats, or recycled cooking grease, used as an alternative to petroleum-based diesel. It can power diesel engines directly or be blended with conventional diesel: {The city's buses run on biodiesel}. Unlike fossil fuels, biodiesel is biodegradable and produces fewer emissions.

Biodiversity is the variety of life in a particular environment or on Earth as a whole—the range of species, genetic variation within species, and diversity of ecosystems. The term emerged in conservation science to name what's lost when habitats shrink: {Deforestation threatens biodiversity}. High biodiversity generally indicates ecosystem health; low biodiversity signals vulnerability.

A biodome is a large enclosed structure designed to replicate a natural environment, typically housing plants and animals from specific ecosystems under controlled conditions. The dome shape maximizes interior space while providing structural efficiency. Biodomes serve as research facilities, conservation centers, or public attractions where visitors can experience tropical rainforests, deserts, or other biomes regardless of local climate: {The biodome recreates four distinct ecosystems under one roof}.

A bioengineer applies engineering principles to biological systems—designing medical devices, artificial organs, prosthetics, or genetically modified organisms. The field bridges biology and technology: {Bioengineers developed the artificial heart valve}. As a verb, to bioengineer is to create or modify something through such methods: {Scientists bioengineered bacteria to produce insulin}.

Biofeedback is a technique for learning to control normally involuntary body functions—heart rate, blood pressure, muscle tension—by monitoring them with electronic sensors and receiving real-time feedback. The idea is that awareness enables conscious influence: {She used biofeedback to manage her chronic pain}. The practice bridges medicine and self-regulation training.

Biofuel is fuel derived from organic matter rather than fossil sources—typically plant materials like corn, sugarcane, or soybeans, but also algae, animal waste, or used cooking oil. Ethanol and biodiesel are the most common types. Biofuels are promoted as renewable alternatives to petroleum, though debates persist about their environmental benefits when accounting for land use and production costs.

Biofuels are fuels derived from organic matter rather than fossil sources. Ethanol from corn or sugarcane and biodiesel from vegetable oils are the most common types. Proponents argue biofuels are renewable and carbon-neutral since plants absorb CO2 while growing. Critics point to land use, food supply impacts, and energy-intensive production: {The biofuels mandate drove up corn prices}.

A biographer is a person who writes an account of someone else's life. The biographer researches their subject through interviews, letters, diaries, and historical records, then shapes this material into narrative: {His biographer spent eight years tracking down sources}. Unlike autobiographers, biographers write about others, not themselves.

Biographies are accounts of people's lives written by others. A biography covers its subject from birth to death or to the present, distinguishing it from memoirs or autobiographies written by the subjects themselves. The term also refers to the genre: {She reads mostly biography}. A short biography summarizing someone's background is often called a bio.

A biography is an account of someone's life written by another person. The term covers everything from scholarly works to popular celebrity profiles: {She's writing a biography of Lincoln}. A biography written by its subject is an autobiography. The shortened form bio typically refers to brief professional summaries: {Update your bio for the conference program}.

A biohacker is someone who experiments with biology outside traditional institutional settings—often in home labs or community spaces. The term covers a wide range: DIY geneticists modifying organisms, people implanting chips or magnets in their bodies, or health enthusiasts optimizing their own biology through diet, supplements, and self-tracking. {She considers herself a biohacker after years of experimenting with nootropics and sleep protocols.}

Biohackers are people who experiment with biology outside traditional institutions—often in home labs or community spaces. The term covers a spectrum: some optimize their own bodies through diet, supplements, or implanted devices; others conduct DIY genetic engineering or citizen science. {Biohackers have been experimenting with CRISPR in garage labs}. The movement blends tech culture's hacker ethos with biological tinkering.

Biohacking is the practice of modifying one's own biology through self-experimentation, often outside traditional medical or scientific institutions. It ranges from relatively mainstream interventions like optimizing sleep, diet, and supplements to more radical measures: implanting microchips under the skin, DIY gene editing, or experimental nootropics. {He got into biohacking after reading about people implanting magnets in their fingertips.} The term carries both tech-optimist enthusiasm and concerns about unregulated experimentation.

A biohazard is a biological substance that poses a threat to human health—infectious agents, toxins, or contaminated materials. The term appears on warning labels for medical waste, laboratory specimens, and areas where dangerous pathogens are handled: {The samples were marked with the biohazard symbol}. Biohazardous materials require special disposal protocols.

Biohazards are biological materials that pose a threat to human health or the environment—infectious agents, toxins, medical waste, or contaminated materials. Laboratories display the distinctive biohazard symbol to warn of dangerous pathogens. The term covers everything from used needles to weaponized anthrax: {The cleanup crew wore full protective gear due to potential biohazards}.

Biological relates to living organisms and the science of life. It distinguishes natural processes from artificial ones: a biological {parent} versus an adoptive one, biological {weapons} versus chemical ones. In casual speech, biological often appears in phrases about bodily functions: {I need to take a biological break}. The noun biology is the scientific study of life.

A biologist studies living organisms—their structure, function, growth, evolution, and distribution. The field spans from molecular biology to ecology, from microbes to whales. {Marine biologists tagged the whale for tracking}. {The biologist spent years documenting beetle species in the rainforest}.

Biology is the scientific study of living organisms—their structure, function, growth, evolution, and distribution. The word covers everything from molecular processes within cells to ecosystems spanning continents. A person's biology refers to their physical nature: {Her biology made her susceptible to the disease}. In casual use, biology often means innate rather than learned characteristics: {It's just biology}.

Bioluminescence is light produced by living organisms through chemical reactions in their bodies. Fireflies, deep-sea fish, and certain jellyfish and fungi generate their own glow. The phenomenon serves various purposes—attracting mates, luring prey, or confusing predators. {The bioluminescence of the waves at night was otherworldly.}

Bioluminescent describes organisms that produce their own light through chemical reactions in their bodies. Fireflies, deep-sea fish, and certain jellyfish are bioluminescent. The glow serves various purposes—attracting mates, luring prey, or confusing predators. {The bioluminescent plankton made the waves glow blue at night.}

A biome is a large-scale ecological community defined by its climate and dominant vegetation: {tropical rainforest}, {desert}, {tundra}, {grassland}. Each biome supports characteristic plant and animal life adapted to its conditions. The term appears frequently in ecology, climate science, and video games where players explore distinct environmental zones.

Biomes are large-scale ecological regions defined by their climate and dominant plant and animal life. The major terrestrial biomes include tundra, desert, grassland, and various forest types. Aquatic biomes cover freshwater and marine environments. The term appears most often in biology education and environmental science: {Students learned about the rainforest biome}. Each biome supports characteristic species adapted to its conditions.

Biometric refers to measurements of biological characteristics used to identify individuals—fingerprints, facial features, iris patterns, voice prints. Security systems use biometric data for authentication: {The phone unlocks with biometric verification}. As a noun, a biometric is any such measurable trait: {The border agent collected several biometrics}.

Biometrics is the measurement and analysis of unique physical characteristics for identification purposes. Fingerprints, iris patterns, facial geometry, and voiceprints can verify identity more reliably than passwords or cards. {The airport uses biometrics for passport control.} The field also encompasses broader biological measurement—heart rate, gait, typing rhythm—increasingly used in security systems and personal devices.

Biomimicry is the practice of designing technology, materials, or systems by imitating structures and processes found in nature. Velcro famously drew from burrs that cling to fur; bullet train noses borrowed from kingfisher beaks to reduce noise. The field assumes that evolution has already solved many engineering problems: {Researchers are using biomimicry to develop self-cleaning surfaces based on lotus leaves}.

A biomom is a biological mother—the woman who gave birth to a child, as distinguished from adoptive, step, or foster mothers. The term appears most often in contexts involving adoption, blended families, or assisted reproduction: {She's been in touch with her biomom since turning eighteen}. Also spelled bio mom or bio-mom.

Bionic describes body parts or organisms that have been enhanced or replaced by electromechanical components. A bionic arm or bionic eye integrates technology with biology to restore or augment natural function. The term gained popular currency through 1970s television shows featuring characters with superhuman abilities derived from artificial implants. In casual use, bionic often suggests extraordinary capability: {After my coffee, I feel bionic.}

Bionics is the science of designing artificial systems modeled on biological ones—mechanical limbs that mimic natural movement, sensors inspired by animal vision. The field bridges engineering and biology: {researchers in bionics developed a prosthetic hand with sensory feedback}. In popular usage, bionic suggests superhuman enhancement: {a bionic arm}, {the bionic man}.

A biopic is a film dramatizing the life of a real person, usually someone famous or historically significant. The word blends "biographical" and "picture." Biopics typically compress and reshape events for narrative effect: {The biopic took liberties with the timeline of her early career}.

Biopics are biographical films dramatizing the life of a real person, typically focusing on key episodes rather than comprehensive coverage. The genre favors subjects with dramatic arcs—artists, athletes, musicians, historical figures: {Oscar season always brings a crop of biopics}. The word blends "biographical" and "picture."

Bioprinting is a form of 3D printing that uses living cells and biological materials to build tissue structures layer by layer. The technology aims to create functional human organs for transplant, though current applications focus on simpler tissues for research and drug testing: {Scientists bioprinted a patch of cardiac tissue}. The verb is bioprint.

A biopsy is a medical procedure in which a small sample of tissue is removed from the body for examination, typically to determine the presence or extent of disease. The tissue is usually examined under a microscope by a pathologist. Biopsies are commonly performed to diagnose cancer but are also used to identify infections, inflammatory conditions, and other abnormalities. {The doctor recommended a biopsy after finding a suspicious lump.} As a verb, to biopsy means to perform this procedure on tissue or an organ.

The biosphere is the part of Earth where life exists—the thin zone encompassing oceans, land surfaces, and lower atmosphere where organisms live and interact. It includes all living things and the environments they inhabit, from deep-sea vents to mountain peaks. Scientists study the biosphere as an interconnected system: {Human activity is altering the biosphere at an unprecedented rate}.

Biotech is short for biotechnology—the use of living organisms or biological systems to develop products and processes. The term often refers to the industry itself: {She works in biotech}, {a biotech startup}. Biotech companies typically focus on pharmaceuticals, genetic engineering, or agricultural applications. As an adjective: {biotech stocks}, {biotech research}.

Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or biological systems to develop products and processes. The field spans medicine (genetically engineered insulin, gene therapy), agriculture (drought-resistant crops, pest-resistant seeds), and industry (biofuels, enzyme production). {Biotechnology firms led the stock rally}. The term often suggests genetic manipulation, though it encompasses older techniques like fermentation and selective breeding.

Bioterrorism is the deliberate release of viruses, bacteria, or other biological agents to cause illness or death in people, animals, or crops. The intent is to create fear, disrupt society, or achieve political aims: {The anthrax letters of 2001 were an act of bioterrorism}. Bioterrorism exploits the invisibility and contagiousness of pathogens, making detection and containment difficult.

Bioterrorists are people who use biological agents—viruses, bacteria, or toxins—as weapons to cause mass harm, fear, or political pressure. The term emerged in the late twentieth century as concerns grew about weaponized anthrax, smallpox, and other pathogens: {Federal agencies track potential bioterrorists}. The word combines the clinical precision of biology with the political violence of terrorism.

Biowarfare is warfare using biological agents—bacteria, viruses, or toxins—to harm enemy populations, livestock, or crops. The term covers both the practice and the broader category of weapons: {international treaties banning biowarfare}. Also called biological warfare or germ warfare.

A bioweapon is a biological agent—such as a bacterium, virus, or toxin—weaponized to cause disease or death in humans, animals, or crops. Bioweapons are banned under international law but remain a concern in warfare and terrorism: {Intelligence agencies warned of potential bioweapon attacks}. Also called biological weapon.

Bioweapons are biological agents—bacteria, viruses, toxins, or other pathogens—weaponized to cause disease or death in humans, animals, or crops. They range from anthrax spores to engineered viruses.
