International treaties ban their development and use, though nations and terrorist groups have pursued them: {The facility was suspected of producing bioweapons}. Also called biological weapons.

Bipartisan describes political action or agreement involving cooperation between two opposing parties, especially Democrats and Republicans in American politics: {a bipartisan bill}, {bipartisan support for the measure}. The word often carries positive connotations of compromise and working across the aisle, though critics sometimes use it to suggest politicians are ignoring their base.

Bipartisanship is cooperation between two political parties, especially in the United States between Democrats and Republicans. The term implies setting aside partisan differences to achieve shared goals: {The bill passed with unusual bipartisanship}. Politicians often invoke bipartisanship as an ideal while accusing opponents of blocking it. The adjective is bipartisan: {a bipartisan effort}, {bipartisan support}.

Biphobia is prejudice, hostility, or discrimination directed at bisexual people. It can come from straight communities or from within LGBTQ+ spaces, where bisexuality is sometimes dismissed as confusion, a phase, or fence-sitting: {She encountered biphobia from both her conservative family and some gay friends who questioned her identity}.

A biplane is an aircraft with two sets of wings, one positioned above the other, connected by struts. This design was standard in early aviation because the dual wings provided greater lift and structural strength than a single wing could achieve with the materials available at the time. Biplanes dominated military and civilian aviation through World War I and into the 1930s before being largely replaced by monoplanes. Today they appear mainly in aerobatic displays and crop dusting.

Biplanes is the plural of biplane—an aircraft with two sets of wings stacked one above the other. Biplanes dominated early aviation through the 1930s, when monoplanes proved faster and more efficient. Today biplanes are mainly used for aerobatics and crop dusting: {We watched the biplanes loop and roll at the air show}.

Bipolar describes something with two poles or extremes. In geography and physics, it refers to opposite ends: {bipolar electrodes}. In psychiatry, bipolar disorder involves cycles between manic highs and depressive lows—formerly called manic depression. Informally, bipolar describes erratic mood swings or contradictory behavior: {The weather has been totally bipolar this week}.

Birch is a deciduous tree with distinctive pale bark that peels in papery layers. The wood is pale and fine-grained, used for furniture and plywood. A birch is also a bundle of birch twigs used for flogging—to birch someone is to beat them with such a rod: {The schoolmaster birched the boys for misbehavior}. This sense is now historical.

Birchbark is the papery outer bark of birch trees, which peels off in thin, flexible sheets. Indigenous peoples of North America used it extensively—for canoes, containers, and writing surfaces. The word often appears as a modifier: {birchbark canoe}, {birchbark basket}. Also spelled birch bark.

Birches is the plural of birch, a deciduous tree known for its distinctive pale, often papery bark that peels in horizontal strips. Birch trees are common in northern temperate and boreal regions and valued for their wood, which is used in furniture and plywood. The word also appears as a verb form: to birch someone is to strike them with a birch rod as punishment, a practice now largely historical. {White birches lined the path to the lake.}

Bird is the most general and ordinary term for creatures that have wings and feathers, that have beaks instead of teeth, that lay eggs, and that may fly. Bird also has informal meanings with less obvious relationships to the feathered kind; it can designate a person (an odd bird), a young woman, an airplane, or a vulgar sign made with the middle finger. Bird abounds in idioms and proverbs, most of which have something to do with the behavior of actual birds: birds of a feather flock together. As a verb, bird means to look for and observe birds, as a hobby, or to hunt game birds.

A birdbath is a shallow basin, usually on a pedestal, placed outdoors and filled with water for birds to drink and bathe in. It's a common garden ornament: {She watched sparrows splashing in the birdbath}.

Birdbaths are shallow basins, usually on pedestals, filled with water for birds to drink and bathe in. They're a common feature in gardens, attracting songbirds and adding a decorative element: {The robins splashed in the birdbath all morning}.

A birdbrain is a stupid person—someone whose brain is supposedly as small as a bird's. The adjective is birdbraned: {What kind of birdbrained scheme is this?} Despite the insult, many birds are remarkably intelligent; crows use tools and parrots solve puzzles.

Birdbrained means stupid or scatterbrained: {Some birdbrained driver cut me off}. The insult assumes birds have tiny brains and therefore limited intelligence—though research suggests many birds are surprisingly clever. Someone who is birdbrained lacks focus or good judgment: {It was a birdbrained scheme from the start}.

Birdbrains is a playful insult for people considered stupid or scatterbrained, based on the assumption that birds have small brains and limited intelligence: {Those birdbrains forgot to lock up again}. The singular birdbrain works the same way.

A birdcage is an enclosure of wire or bars for keeping pet birds. The structure—a framework of thin vertical elements—extends to things resembling it: a birdcage veil covers part of the face with netting, and an elevator's open metalwork shaft is sometimes called a birdcage. {She draped a cloth over the birdcage at night.}

Birdcages are enclosures for keeping birds, typically made of wire or bars with enough spacing to contain the bird while allowing light and air. Pet birds live in cages; wild birds are trapped in them. The structure suggests confinement generally: {She felt her marriage had become a birdcage}.

A birdcall is the sound a bird makes, or an imitation of that sound. Birdcalls may be natural vocalizations—songs, chirps, warning cries—or human-made sounds used to attract birds for hunting or observation. A birdcall is also a small device that produces such sounds: {He used a wooden birdcall to lure the ducks}.

A birddog is a dog bred to locate and retrieve game birds for hunters—pointers, setters, and retrievers. The verb means to watch closely or pursue doggedly: {He birddogged the lead until the story broke}. In sales, to birddog is to scout prospects for someone else, usually for a finder's fee. Also spelled bird dog.

A birder is someone who observes wild birds as a hobby, tracking species, keeping lists, and often traveling to spot rare birds. The term emphasizes active pursuit and expertise, distinguishing serious enthusiasts from casual {bird-watchers}: {Birders arrived at dawn hoping to see the migrating warblers}.

A birdfeeder is a container placed outdoors to supply food for wild birds. Birdfeeders come in various designs—tube feeders, platform feeders, suet cages—each attracting different species. {She hung a birdfeeder outside the kitchen window}. Also spelled as two words: bird feeder.

A birdhouse is a small wooden structure with an entrance hole, mounted outdoors to provide nesting shelter for birds. Also called a nesting box. The design typically includes a sloped roof and drainage holes: {We hung a birdhouse in the backyard and wrens moved in within weeks}.

Birdhouses are small structures designed to provide nesting sites for birds, typically mounted on poles or hung from trees. They have an entrance hole sized for specific species and a cavity where birds can lay eggs and raise young. Building and placing birdhouses is a common backyard hobby: {We put up birdhouses to attract bluebirds}.

A birdie is a small bird, used affectionately or when speaking to children: {Look at the little birdie!} In golf, a birdie is a score of one stroke under par for a hole—a good result. The verb means to score a birdie: {She birdied the ninth}. In badminton, birdie is informal for shuttlecock.

Birdies is the plural of birdie. A birdie is a little bird, used affectionately or when speaking to children: {Look at the birdies!} In golf, a birdie is a score of one stroke under par on a hole—a good result worth celebrating. To birdie a hole is to achieve this score: {She birdied three holes on the back nine}.

Birding is the hobby of observing wild birds in their natural habitat, typically with binoculars and field guides. The activity ranges from casual backyard watching to serious pursuits involving travel and life lists—records of every species spotted. {We went birding at the refuge this morning}. Birding and birdwatching are interchangeable, though enthusiasts sometimes prefer birding as the more active term.

A birdman is someone closely associated with birds—a person who keeps, trains, or studies them. The term also applies to early aviation pioneers and daredevils who attempted flight with wing-like contraptions: {The birdmen of the early 1900s risked their lives testing crude flying machines}. In comics and folklore, a birdman is a winged humanoid creature.

Birdmen is the plural of birdman—someone associated with birds or flight. A birdman might be an aviator, especially an early or daring one: {The birdmen of the early twentieth century risked their lives in flimsy aircraft}. It can also mean someone who keeps or studies birds. In mythology and comics, birdmen are winged humanoid creatures.

Birds is the plural of bird, designating the class of warm-blooded, feathered vertebrates that typically fly. Beyond this literal meaning, birds appears in several expressions: {the birds and the bees} is a euphemism for basic sex education given to children. {A little bird told me} suggests information from an unnamed source. In British slang, birds can refer informally to women or girls, though this usage strikes many as dated or mildly sexist.

Birdseed is seed or a mixture of seeds sold for feeding birds, typically in backyard feeders or birdhouses. Common ingredients include sunflower seeds, millet, and cracked corn. {She filled the feeder with birdseed every morning}.

Birdshot is the smallest size of lead or steel pellets used in shotgun shells, designed for hunting birds and small game. The pellets scatter widely when fired, increasing the chance of hitting fast-moving targets. Birdshot causes less damage at range than larger buckshot: {He was hit with birdshot but survived}.

Birdsong is the musical vocalization of birds, especially the complex, melodious calls used to attract mates or establish territory. The word often evokes pleasant natural sounds: {We woke to birdsong}. It can suggest peace, early morning, or rural settings: {The only sound was distant birdsong}.

Birdwatch is the activity of observing wild birds in their natural habitats, typically as a hobby. The verb means to engage in this pursuit, often involving binoculars, field guides, and travel to locations where particular species can be spotted. {We spent the morning birdwatching at the nature reserve.} Enthusiasts may keep life lists documenting every species they've seen. Also spelled as two words: bird watch.

A birdwatcher is someone who observes wild birds as a hobby, typically using binoculars and field guides to identify species in their natural habitats. The activity ranges from casual backyard observation to dedicated expeditions seeking rare species. Also called a birder, though some enthusiasts distinguish between casual birdwatchers and serious birders.

Birdwatchers are people who observe birds as a hobby or pursuit. The activity ranges from casual backyard observation to dedicated travel in search of rare species. Serious birdwatchers keep life lists—records of every species they've seen: {The birdwatchers gathered at dawn, hoping to spot the elusive warbler}.

Birdwatching is the hobby of observing wild birds in their natural habitats, typically with binoculars and field guides for identification. Enthusiasts may keep life lists—records of every species they've spotted: {We went birdwatching at the nature reserve}. Also called birding, though some consider birding the more serious pursuit.

Biriani is an Indian rice dish layered with spiced meat, fish, or vegetables, then baked or steamed. The rice is typically colored with saffron or turmeric, and the dish often includes nuts, raisins, and fried onions. Regional variations abound: {chicken biriani}, {lamb biriani}, {vegetable biriani}. Also spelled biryani.

Biriyani is a South Asian rice dish in which meat, vegetables, or both are layered with spiced basmati rice and slow-cooked. The dish originated in the Indian subcontinent and varies by region—Hyderabadi biriyani differs from Lucknowi or Kolkata styles. Also spelled biryani. {We ordered chicken biriyani and naan.}

Birria is a Mexican stew traditionally made from goat meat, though beef has become common. The meat is braised in a rich, spiced chile broth until tender and falling apart. Originally from Jalisco, birria has spread widely, especially as {birria tacos}—tortillas dipped in the cooking fat and filled with the meat, served with consommé for dipping.

Birth is the emergence of offspring from its mother's body, marking the beginning of independent life. The word extends to origins generally: {the birth of a nation}, {the birth of an idea}. To give birth is to bear young. Birth also indicates circumstances of origin: {noble birth}, {American by birth}. As a verb, to birth means to deliver or bring into existence.

A birthday is the annual anniversary of one's birth: {What do you want for your birthday?} Children's birthdays typically involve parties, cake, and gifts. The word extends to anniversaries of other beginnings: a nation's birthday, a company's birthday. {Birthday suit} means nakedness—the condition you were born in.

Birthdays is the plural of birthday, the annual anniversary of one's birth. The word usually implies celebration: {What do you want for your birthday?} {We're throwing her a surprise birthday party}. Birthday also marks anniversaries of events or institutions: {the company's fiftieth birthday}. In your {birthday suit} means naked—wearing only what you were born in.

Birthed is the past tense of birth used as a verb, meaning to give birth to or bring into existence. While *gave birth to* remains more common, birthed appears in both literal and figurative contexts: {She birthed three children at home}, {The movement birthed a new political party}. The usage strikes some as awkward or needlessly novel, though it has a long history.

Birthing is the process of giving birth, used as a noun or adjective: {a birthing center}, {birthing classes}, {the birthing process}. The term gained currency in the late twentieth century as natural childbirth movements sought warmer, less clinical language than delivery or parturition. {She was in the birthing suite for six hours}.

A birthmark is a colored spot or blemish on the skin that is present from birth or appears shortly after. Birthmarks vary widely in size, shape, and color—from pale patches to deep red or brown marks—and may be flat or raised. Most are harmless and permanent, though some fade over time. {She had a small birthmark on her shoulder.} Folk traditions once attributed birthmarks to events during pregnancy, but they result from variations in skin pigmentation or blood vessels.

Birthmarks are distinctive marks on the skin present from birth or appearing shortly after. They vary widely—some are flat discolorations, others raised; some fade with time, others persist for life. Common types include port-wine stains and café-au-lait spots. Folklore once attributed birthmarks to maternal experiences during pregnancy, and some cultures still attach superstitious significance to their shapes or locations.

A birthmother is a woman who has given birth to a child but does not raise that child—typically because the child was placed for adoption. The term distinguishes biological parentage from the social and legal role of parenting: {She searched for years before finding her birthmother}. Also spelled as two words: birth mother.

Birthpangs are the sharp, rhythmic pains of labor contractions during childbirth. The term appears most often in figurative contexts, describing the difficult early stages of something new emerging: {the birthpangs of democracy}, {the birthpangs of a new era}. The metaphor suggests that creation requires suffering.

A birthparent is a biological parent, especially one who has given up a child for adoption. The term distinguishes the genetic parent from adoptive parents: {She decided to search for her birthparents when she turned eighteen}. Also spelled as two words: birth parent.

Birthparents are the biological mother and father of a child, especially one who has been adopted. The term distinguishes genetic parents from adoptive parents: {She decided to search for her birthparents when she turned eighteen}. Also spelled as two words: birth parents.

A birthplace is the location where someone was born, whether a specific building or a broader geographic area: {Her birthplace was a small hospital in rural Kansas}, {He returned to his birthplace after forty years}. By extension, birthplace refers to where something originated: {New Orleans is the birthplace of jazz}.

Birthrate is the number of births in a population over a given period, typically expressed per thousand people per year. It serves as a key demographic indicator: {The birthrate has been declining in developed countries}. High birthrates strain resources; low birthrates raise concerns about aging populations and workforce shortages.

Birthrates measure how many babies are born in a population over a given period, typically expressed as births per thousand people per year. The term appears frequently in discussions of demographics, economics, and social policy: {Birthrates in developed countries have been declining for decades}. Also spelled as two words: birth rates.

A birthright is something you're entitled to simply by being born—whether into a particular family, nation, or circumstance. The firstborn's birthright to inherit was once paramount: {Esau sold his birthright for a bowl of stew}. More broadly, birthright suggests inherent entitlement: {Freedom of speech is our birthright as Americans}. The word often appears in debates about citizenship and privilege.

Birthrights are privileges or possessions that belong to someone by virtue of their birth. The term often refers to inheritance rights of firstborn sons in traditional societies, as in the biblical story of Esau selling his birthright to Jacob. More broadly, birthrights are entitlements claimed simply by being born: {Freedom of speech is our birthright}. The word carries weight—losing or selling one's birthright suggests trading something precious for short-term gain.

Births is the plural of birth—the emergence of offspring from a parent. It typically refers to multiple instances of being born: {The hospital recorded three hundred births last month}. Births often appears in demographic contexts: {birth rates}, {live births}, {births per capita}. As a verb form, births means delivers or brings forth: {She births her calves in the spring pasture}.

A birthstone is a gemstone associated with a particular month of the year, traditionally believed to bring luck or special qualities to people born in that month. The practice of wearing one's birthstone as jewelry remains popular: {She received a ring with her birthstone for her sixteenth birthday}. The twelve birthstones include garnet for January, amethyst for February, and diamond for April, though assignments vary by tradition.

Birthstones are gemstones associated with each month of the year, traditionally worn by people born in that month. The practice of assigning specific stones to birth months became standardized in the early twentieth century: garnet for January, amethyst for February, diamond for April, and so on. {She wears her birthstone in a pendant}.

Biryani is a South Asian rice dish made by layering spiced meat, vegetables, or both with partially cooked basmati rice, then slow-cooking them together until the flavors meld. The dish originated in the Indian subcontinent and varies by region—Hyderabadi biryani is known for its aromatic spices, while Lucknowi biryani tends to be milder. {We ordered chicken biryani from the new Indian place.} The spelling varies; biriyani and biriani are also common.

Biscotti are Italian cookies baked twice—first as a log, then sliced and baked again until dry and crunchy. The double baking makes them hard enough to dip in coffee or dessert wine without falling apart. Though biscotti is already plural in Italian, English speakers often say {a biscotti} for one cookie and {biscottis} for several.

A biscuit is a small baked bread, though what counts as one varies by region. In American English, a biscuit is a soft, flaky quick bread served with meals: {biscuits and gravy}. In British English, a biscuit is what Americans call a cookie or cracker—something crisp and often sweet. A biscuit color is a pale tan or beige. In ceramics, biscuit refers to pottery that has been fired once but not glazed.

Biscuits is the plural of biscuit, a small baked bread product. In American English, biscuits are soft, fluffy, and leavened—served with breakfast or as a side: {biscuits and gravy}, {buttermilk biscuits}. In British English, biscuits are what Americans call cookies—crisp, sweet, and often dunked in tea. The word also appears in figurative expressions: {that takes the biscuit} (British for something outrageous).

Bisexual describes sexual attraction to both men and women, or more broadly, to people of one's own gender and other genders. As a noun, a bisexual is a person with such attractions: {She came out as bisexual in college}. The shortened form bi is common: {He's bi}. Bisexual also has a biological sense meaning having both male and female reproductive organs, though hermaphrodite is more precise for that usage.

Bisexuality is sexual attraction to both men and women, or more broadly, to people of one's own gender and other genders. The term covers a spectrum—some bisexual people experience equal attraction to multiple genders, others lean one direction. {She's been open about her bisexuality since college}. Unlike homosexuality or heterosexuality, bisexuality often faces skepticism from both straight and gay communities.

Bisexuals are people sexually attracted to both men and women. The term serves as both noun and identity label: {The bar welcomes gays, lesbians, and bisexuals}. Some bisexuals prefer "bi" in casual speech. The word can also function as a plural adjective: {bisexuals rights}, though {bisexual rights} is more standard.

A bishop is a senior member of the Christian clergy, typically overseeing a diocese or regional group of churches. The rank sits above priest and below archbishop in traditions that maintain episcopal hierarchy. In chess, a bishop is a piece that moves diagonally across the board, its pointed top suggesting a bishop's mitre. The word also names a mulled wine drink sweetened with citrus. {The bishop confirmed the young parishioners.} (Capitalized Bishop is a surname.)

Bishops is the plural of bishop. In Christianity, a bishop is a senior clergy member who oversees a diocese or group of churches. In chess, bishops are pieces that move diagonally across the board; each player starts with two, one on light squares and one on dark. {The bishops controlled the center of the board.}
clues: Pieces that slide corner to corner

definition: A bison is a large, shaggy-haired bovine with a massive head and humped shoulders. Two species exist: the American bison, nearly exterminated in the 19th century but now partially recovered, and the smaller European bison. American bison are sometimes called buffalo, though true buffalo are different animals found in Africa and Asia.

Bisque is a rich, creamy soup, traditionally made from shellfish like lobster or crab, with the shells ground and strained to produce a smooth texture: {lobster bisque}, {She ordered a cup of the tomato bisque}. The term has broadened to include other pureed soups with a velvety consistency. Separately, bisque refers to unglazed ceramic ware with a matte finish, fired but not yet coated: {bisque porcelain}, {The figurines were left in bisque}.

A bistro is a small, casual restaurant, typically serving simple, moderately priced food in an informal atmosphere. The word comes from French and carries connotations of Parisian charm—intimate seating, handwritten menus, unpretentious fare: {We found a little bistro near the hotel}. American usage sometimes stretches to any cozy neighborhood eatery.

Bistros is the plural of bistro, a small, casual restaurant or café serving simple, moderately priced food. The term evokes a cozy, unpretentious atmosphere, often with French associations: {The neighborhood has several bistros where you can grab a quick lunch}. Bistros fall somewhere between fast food and fine dining.

Three separately derived English words have the spelling bit. The most common by far is the noun denoting a small but significant quantity of something: a bit of cheese, a bit of extra time. If you describe someone as a bit of a liar, you are either being polite (and he is a terrible liar) or factual (and he has been known to lie occasionally). Bit is used before an adjective to lessen its force: it’s a bit cold in here. The second bit is related to bite and has meanings inspired by teeth, such as the bit that horses hold in their mouths, or a drill bit. The third bit is a blend of “binary digit” and represents the smallest unit of computational information, which may be 1 or 0, on or off, yes or no.

The original meaning of bitch is an adult female dog, still used in technical contexts like breeding and dog shows. More commonly, bitch is a vulgar term for a difficult or unpleasant woman—though between friends it can be affectionate: {You bitch, I can't believe you didn't tell me!} As a verb, to bitch is to complain: {Stop bitching about the weather}. A bitch can also be a complaint: {My one bitch with this place is the parking}. The word appears in expressions like {son of a bitch}, {life's a bitch}, and {bitch and moan}.

Bitches is the plural of bitch—female dogs, difficult women, or complaints. It's also the third-person singular verb meaning to complain: {He bitches about everything}. In casual speech among friends, bitches can be a rough term of endearment: {What's up, bitches?}

A bitchfest is a session of prolonged complaining or venting, typically among friends: {The lunch turned into a bitchfest about our terrible boss}. The term implies mutual griping rather than constructive discussion—participants take turns airing grievances. Mildly vulgar.

Bitching works two ways. As a verb form, it means complaining: {He's always bitching about something}. As a slang adjective, bitching means excellent or impressive: {That's a bitching guitar}. The adjective was popular in the 1980s and 90s and now sounds somewhat dated.

A bitchslap is an open-handed slap across the face, meant to humiliate more than injure—the kind of slap stereotypically delivered to a hysterical person or an insolent subordinate. The term implies contempt and dominance: {He bitchslapped the guy who owed him money}. Figuratively, to bitchslap is to defeat or rebuke decisively: {The judge bitchslapped that argument}.

Bitchy describes behavior that is spiteful, petty, or snappish: {She gets bitchy when she's tired}. The word implies mean-spirited sharpness rather than outright hostility—gossip, snark, social manipulation. Though applied more often to women, men get called bitchy too.

Bite is something that creatures, including humans, do with their piercing mouth parts. If the thing being bitten is alive, a bite usually inflicts pain. An instance of biting or the result of biting is also called a bite (insect bite, bite of an apple). Figuratively, if something inanimate bites, it might inflict some pain or damage: The handcuffs are biting my wrists. Or, it might add something desirable: The lime zest gave the cookies a tangy bite. A bite out of something is a significant reduction of it: That car repair really took a bite out of my paycheck.

A biter is someone or something that bites. The word appears in compounds: {nail-biter}, {ankle-biter}. In slang, a biter is someone who copies another's style or work without credit—common in hip-hop and graffiti culture: {He's a biter who stole my flow}. The phrase {the biter bit} describes someone harmed by their own scheme.

Bites is the plural of bite and the third-person singular verb. A bite is an act of cutting into something with teeth: {The dog's bites left marks on his arm}. Extended to amounts: a bite of food, a bite of your paycheck. Something that bites can sting, grip, or take hold: {The cold really bites today}. {That bites} expresses that something is disappointing or unfair.

Bitesize describes something small enough to consume in one bite, or by extension, something brief and easily digestible: {bitesize pieces of chocolate}, {bitesize lessons for busy learners}. The word suits content designed for quick consumption—short videos, condensed summaries, manageable chunks of information. Also spelled bite-size or bite-sized.

Biting describes something that cuts or stings. A biting wind is sharply cold. Biting remarks are harsh and critical, intended to wound: {Her biting sarcasm left him speechless}. The word captures both physical sensation—teeth sinking in, cold penetrating—and verbal sharpness that feels similarly piercing.

A bitmap is an image stored as a grid of individual pixels, each with its own color value. The term contrasts with vector graphics, which store images as mathematical shapes. Bitmap formats like JPEG, PNG, and BMP lose quality when scaled up because enlarging reveals the pixel grid. As a verb, to bitmap is to convert an image to this format.

Bits is the plural of bit, a small piece or amount: {bits of broken glass}, {bits of information}. In computing, bits are the fundamental units of digital data—binary digits representing 0 or 1. To {blow something to bits} is to destroy it completely. To do your bit is to contribute your share. {Bits and pieces} are miscellaneous small items or fragments.

Bitten is the past participle of bite. Someone who has been bitten bears the marks of teeth or fangs: {She was bitten by a dog}. The word extends to any sharp sensation: {bitten by frost}, {bitten by the cold}. To be bitten by something like ambition or curiosity is to be seized by it. {Once bitten, twice shy} warns that a bad experience breeds caution.

Bitter is one of the basic tastes—sharp, acrid, often unpleasant, like coffee without sugar or unsweetened chocolate. The taste extends to emotional states: bitter {disappointment}, bitter {resentment}, a bitter {enemy}. Someone bitter harbors lasting anger or grief: {She grew bitter after the divorce}. Bitter {cold} is harsh and piercing. A bitter {pill} is hard to accept. In British usage, bitter is also a style of pale ale with a hoppy flavor.

Bitterness is one of the basic tastes—sharp, acrid, and often unpleasant, like unsweetened coffee or quinine. Extended to emotion, bitterness describes deep resentment or lasting anger over perceived wrongs: {Years later, she still spoke of the divorce with bitterness}. The word captures both the sharp quality of the taste and the lingering, hard-to-swallow nature of the feeling.

Bitters is a concentrated alcoholic preparation flavored with herbs, roots, bark, or fruit, used in small quantities to add depth to cocktails: {a dash of bitters in an old fashioned}. The plural form is standard even for a single bottle. Angostura and Peychaud's are well-known brands. The bitter taste comes from botanicals like gentian root or quinine.

Bittersweet describes experiences that blend pleasure with pain or happiness with sadness: {a bittersweet farewell}, {bittersweet memories of childhood}. The word captures the recognition that joy and sorrow often arrive together—a graduation, a last visit, a love that didn't work out. Bittersweet is also a climbing vine with bright orange berries, and a type of chocolate with minimal sugar.

Bitty means very small or tiny, often with a note of affection or dismissiveness: {a bitty little apartment}, {itty-bitty pieces}. The word is informal and frequently appears in the reduplicated form {itty-bitty} or {itsy-bitsy}. In British slang, {a bit bitty} describes something fragmented or disjointed rather than small.

A bivouac is a temporary camp, especially one set up by soldiers or mountaineers without tents or elaborate shelter: {We made a bivouac in the lee of the ridge}. The verb means to camp in such conditions: {The troops bivouacked in the forest overnight}. The word suggests roughing it—sleeping under minimal cover in exposed terrain.

Bizarre describes something strikingly unusual, odd, or unexpected in a way that catches attention or defies easy explanation. The word suggests more than mere strangeness—there's often an element of the unsettling or absurd. {The whole situation was too bizarre to believe.} A bizarre coincidence or a bizarre outfit stands out precisely because it deviates so dramatically from the ordinary.

Bizarro describes something strange, surreal, or absurdly different from the norm. The word suggests not just unusual but weirdly so, often with a sense of inverted or distorted reality: {It was like some bizarro version of my childhood home}. The term carries a comic-book flavor, frequently appearing in phrases like {bizarro world} to describe situations where normal expectations are reversed: {In this bizarro election, the frontrunner is avoiding debates}.

Blab means to reveal secrets or talk too freely about things that should be kept private: {She blabbed to everyone about the surprise party}. A blab can also be a person who talks too much or can't keep confidences. The word suggests careless disclosure rather than deliberate betrayal—someone who blabs usually lacks discretion rather than malice.

Blabber means to talk excessively or indiscreetly, revealing things that should be kept quiet: {She blabbered the secret to everyone}. As a noun, a blabber is someone who talks too much or can't keep confidences. The word suggests mindless chatter rather than deliberate betrayal—more loose lips than malice.

Blabbering is talking at length without saying much of substance, or revealing things better kept quiet. The word suggests someone who can't stop themselves from running their mouth: {She kept blabbering on about her ex}. A blabbermouth is someone prone to this, especially one who spills secrets.

A blabbermouth is someone who talks too much, especially about things that should be kept secret. The word carries mild contempt—a blabbermouth can't be trusted with confidential information: {Don't tell Sarah anything; she's a total blabbermouth}. The related verb blab means to reveal secrets carelessly.

Blabbermouths are people who talk too much, especially those who can't keep secrets or speak indiscreetly: {Don't tell her anything—she's a blabbermouth}. The word combines blab (to reveal carelessly) with mouth, emphasizing that the problem is uncontrolled speech. Someone who blabs has a blabbermouth.

Blabbing is talking too much, especially revealing things that should be kept private. Someone who blabs shares secrets or sensitive information carelessly: {Who's been blabbing to the press?} {She blabbed about the surprise party}. The word suggests indiscretion rather than malice—loose lips rather than deliberate betrayal.

Blabs means talks too much or reveals secrets carelessly. Someone who blabs shares information they shouldn't: {She blabbed about the surprise party}. The word suggests loose lips and indiscretion rather than malicious intent. A blab or blabbermouth is a person who can't keep quiet.

Black is called a color but it is really the absence of color and light. Many things that are black or near black in color are also called black. Native Africans, African Americans, South Asians, and Australian Aborigines are often called Black because of their dark skin color. Black also carries many connotations of gloom, pessimism, evil, and misfortune, because of its status as the opposite of white and light.

To blackball someone is to exclude them from a group or organization, typically by secret vote. The term comes from the practice of casting black balls into a ballot box to register opposition. Now it applies broadly to any rejection or ostracism: {He was blackballed from the country club after the scandal}. As a noun, a blackball is such a negative vote.

Blackballed means rejected or excluded by secret ballot, from the practice of voting with balls—white to approve, black to deny. A single black ball could veto a candidate's admission to a club or society. The term now applies broadly to exclusion from any group or opportunity: {He was blackballed from the industry after the scandal}. {She suspected she'd been blackballed by the hiring committee}.

Blackballing is the act of excluding someone from a group or organization by secret ballot, traditionally by placing a black ball in a voting box. The term now applies broadly to any deliberate exclusion or rejection: {She was blackballed from the sorority}, {After the scandal, he was blackballed from the industry}. The practice suggests collective shunning rather than individual rejection.

Blackballs is the plural of blackball and the third-person singular verb form. To blackball someone is to reject them from membership in a club or organization, or more broadly to exclude or ostracize them: {The committee blackballed his application}. The term comes from the practice of voting with colored balls—a black ball signifying rejection.

A blackbelt is someone who has achieved advanced rank in martial arts like judo, karate, or taekwondo, marked by wearing a black belt. The term extends to any high level of expertise: {She's a blackbelt in Excel spreadsheets}. Also spelled as two words: black belt.

Blackberries are the dark purple-black fruit of a thorny bramble, composed of small drupelets clustered around a core. They grow wild in hedgerows and are cultivated for eating fresh, in jams, and in desserts: {We picked blackberries along the fence line}. The plural also refers to the plants themselves: {The blackberries have taken over the back corner of the yard}.

A blackberry is a dark purple, edible fruit composed of small drupelets clustered around a core. The thorny brambles that produce them grow wild in temperate regions and are also cultivated. Blackberries are eaten fresh, baked into pies and cobblers, or made into jam: {We picked blackberries along the fence line}. (Capitalized BlackBerry was a brand of smartphone.)

Blackberrying is the activity of gathering wild blackberries, typically from hedgerows or woodland edges in late summer: {We spent the afternoon blackberrying along the country lanes}. The word evokes a pastoral, leisurely pursuit—filling baskets or containers while wandering through brambles, often getting scratched and stained in the process.

A blackbird is any of several species of dark-plumaged birds. In Europe, the common blackbird is a thrush; in North America, blackbirds include grackles, cowbirds, and red-winged blackbirds. The word also has historical uses referring to enslaved or exploited laborers, particularly Pacific Islanders forced into labor in the 19th century: {blackbirding ships preyed on island populations}.

Blackbirds is the plural of blackbird—any of several species of dark-plumaged birds. In North America, blackbirds include red-winged blackbirds, grackles, and cowbirds. In Britain, the blackbird is a thrush species, the male entirely black with an orange beak. {A flock of blackbirds descended on the field.}

A blackboard is a dark, smooth surface for writing on with chalk, traditionally found in classrooms. The teacher writes, students copy. Despite the name, blackboards are often green. The word persists even as whiteboards and digital screens replace them: {The professor covered the blackboard with equations}.

Blackboards are large dark surfaces, traditionally slate or painted wood, designed for writing with chalk. Once ubiquitous in classrooms, they've largely been replaced by whiteboards and digital displays, though the term persists: {The professor covered the blackboard with equations}. Figuratively, a clean blackboard suggests a fresh start.

A blackbox is a system whose internal workings are hidden or unknown—you see inputs and outputs but not what happens between them. The term comes from engineering, where flight recorders (actually orange) became known as black boxes. In computing and machine learning, blackbox describes algorithms or models that produce results without revealing their reasoning: {The AI's decision-making process is a complete blackbox}. To blackbox something is to treat it as opaque, ignoring internal mechanics. Also spelled black box.

Blackcurrant is a small, dark purple berry with a sharp, tangy flavor, used in jams, juices, cordials, and liqueurs like cassis. The shrub that produces it grows widely in Europe but was long banned in parts of the United States for harboring a fungus that damaged pine trees. The flavor is common in British sweets and drinks but relatively unfamiliar to Americans: {blackcurrant jam}, {Ribena is a blackcurrant drink}.

Blackcurrants are small, dark purple berries that grow in clusters on shrubs. They have a tart, intensely flavored taste and are commonly used in jams, cordials, and liqueurs like cassis. More popular in Europe than North America, where cultivation was once restricted: {The recipe calls for a handful of blackcurrants}.

Blacken means to make or become black or dark: {Smoke blackened the ceiling}, {The sky blackened before the storm}. The word extends to reputation—to blacken someone's name is to damage it through slander or accusation: {The scandal blackened his reputation for years}. In cooking, blackened refers to a Cajun technique of coating fish or meat with spices and searing it until the exterior chars: {blackened catfish}.

Blackened describes something that has become black or very dark, typically through burning, charring, or exposure to smoke: {blackened ruins}, {blackened toast}. In cooking, blackened refers to a Cajun technique where fish or meat is coated in spices and seared at high heat until the coating chars: {blackened catfish}, {blackened chicken}. Figuratively, a blackened reputation has been damaged or tarnished.

Blackening refers to the process of becoming black or making something black, whether through burning, charring, decay, or applied coating. In cooking, blackening is a Cajun technique where fish or meat is coated with spices and cooked in a very hot cast-iron skillet until a dark, flavorful crust forms: {I'm blackening some catfish for dinner}. The term also describes damage or discoloration: {The blackening of the walls from smoke took weeks to clean}.

Blackface is dark makeup worn by a non-Black performer to caricature Black people. The practice was central to American minstrel shows of the 19th and early 20th centuries, where white actors exaggerated features for racist comedy. Today blackface is widely recognized as deeply offensive, though it occasionally resurfaces in Halloween costumes or ill-conceived performances, invariably provoking outrage: {The politician resigned after photos of him in blackface surfaced}.

Blackfish is a common name for several dark-colored marine animals. It most often refers to pilot whales or killer whales—the latter made famous by a 2013 documentary of this name about captive orcas. The term also applies to certain dark fish species, including the tautog found along the Atlantic coast: {We caught three blackfish off the jetty}.

Blackfishing is when a white person alters their appearance to seem Black or mixed-race—through tanning, makeup, hairstyles, or photo editing. The term draws on "catfishing" (online identity deception) and implies appropriation of Black aesthetics for social media clout or commercial gain while avoiding the discrimination Black people face: {She was accused of blackfishing after her Instagram photos surfaced}.

Blackfly refers to small biting flies of the family Simuliidae, found near running water where they breed. The females feed on blood and can transmit diseases. In British usage, blackfly also means aphids that infest plants, particularly beans: {The roses are covered in blackfly}.

A blackhat is a hacker who breaks into computer systems for malicious purposes—stealing data, spreading malware, or causing damage. The term comes from old Western films where villains wore black hats. In broader tech usage, blackhat describes any unethical practice that violates rules for personal gain: {blackhat SEO tricks can get your site banned from Google}. Contrast with whitehat (ethical hacker) and greyhat (ambiguous ethics).

A blackhead is a small plug of dark-colored material clogging a pore in the skin—a mild form of acne. The dark color comes not from dirt but from oxidized oil and dead skin cells exposed to air. {She squeezed the blackheads on her nose.} Blackhead also names a bacterial disease affecting turkeys and other poultry.

Blackheads are small dark spots on the skin caused by clogged hair follicles. The dark color comes not from dirt but from oxidized oil and dead skin cells exposed to air. They appear most commonly on the face, especially the nose and chin: {She squeezed the blackheads on her nose}. Blackheads are a mild form of acne.

Blackhearted describes someone wicked, malevolent, or thoroughly cruel. The word draws on the ancient association of black with evil and the heart as the seat of character. A blackhearted villain feels no remorse; a blackhearted betrayal is one committed with full awareness of the harm it causes. The term is literary and somewhat old-fashioned: {The blackhearted scoundrel left them to die}.

Blackjack is a casino card game where players try to reach 21 without going over, also called twenty-one. The name comes from a bonus paid for an ace with a black jack (spades or clubs). Blackjack also refers to a short, leather-covered club used as a weapon, typically filled with lead: {The mugger carried a blackjack}. As a verb, to blackjack someone is to strike them with such a weapon or to coerce them.

Blackjacked is the past tense of blackjack, meaning to strike someone with a blackjack—a small, leather-covered club weighted with lead, designed to knock a person unconscious. {The guard was blackjacked from behind and never saw his attacker.} By extension, blackjacked can mean coerced or forced into something through intimidation or unfair pressure: {They blackjacked him into signing the contract.}

A blacklight is a lamp that emits ultraviolet light, which makes certain materials glow fluorescent while remaining largely invisible itself. Used to detect counterfeit currency, authenticate documents, reveal bodily fluids at crime scenes, and create visual effects at clubs and parties: {The blacklight made the poster glow}. Also spelled as two words.

Blacklights are lamps that emit ultraviolet light, making certain materials glow while producing little visible illumination. They're used to detect substances invisible under normal light—bodily fluids at crime scenes, security marks on currency, stamps at club entrances. The purple glow is iconic at parties and in haunted houses, where it makes white clothing and teeth appear to fluoresce.

A blacklist is a list of people, organizations, or things to be excluded, avoided, or punished. During the McCarthy era, Hollywood maintained a blacklist of suspected communists who couldn't find work. The verb means to place on such a list: {The company was blacklisted after the scandal}. In computing, a blacklist blocks specific email addresses, IP addresses, or websites.

Blacklisted describes someone or something that has been placed on a list of those to be excluded, shunned, or denied privileges. A blacklisted person may be barred from employment, membership, or participation: {Several writers were blacklisted during the McCarthy era}. The term extends to entities like companies, countries, or IP addresses that are blocked or banned from access. To blacklist is to add someone to such a list. The practice implies organized, often institutional exclusion rather than individual rejection.

Blacklisting is the practice of putting someone on a list of people to be excluded, denied employment, or otherwise punished. The term evokes the Hollywood blacklist of suspected Communist sympathizers in the 1950s, but applies broadly: {The company was accused of blacklisting union organizers}. In computing, blacklisting blocks specific addresses or programs while allowing everything else—the opposite of whitelisting.

Blacklists are lists of people, organizations, or things that are banned, excluded, or denied privileges. Employers might blacklist workers who organize unions; email systems blacklist known spam addresses. The term carries connotations of unfair exclusion: {She was blacklisted from the industry after speaking out}. To blacklist is to add someone or something to such a list.
clues: People you won't do business with

definition: Blackmail is the crime of demanding money or other benefits in exchange for not revealing damaging information about someone: {He paid thousands in blackmail to keep the affair secret}. The verb means to commit this act or, more loosely, to pressure someone through threats: {She blackmailed him into signing the contract}. Emotional blackmail manipulates through guilt rather than explicit threats.

Blackmailed is the past tense of blackmail—to demand money or favors by threatening to reveal damaging information. Someone who has been blackmailed was coerced through such threats: {She was blackmailed into silence}. The word extends to any coercive pressure: {He blackmailed me into going to the party by threatening to tell Mom}.

A blackmailer is someone who extorts money or favors by threatening to reveal damaging information. The threat might involve exposing secrets, crimes, or embarrassing details: {The blackmailer demanded fifty thousand to keep quiet about the affair}. Blackmailer implies ongoing coercion—the victim pays to prevent disclosure, often repeatedly.

Blackmailing is the act of extorting money or favors by threatening to reveal damaging information about someone. The threat typically involves exposure of secrets, scandals, or compromising material: {He was blackmailing her with photos from the affair}. The word covers both the demand and the ongoing pressure to comply with it.

Blackmails is the third-person singular verb form of blackmail, meaning to demand money or other benefits from someone by threatening to reveal damaging information about them. {She blackmails her former employer with evidence of tax fraud.} The term extends to any coercive leverage, not just literal demands for payment: {He blackmails his sister into silence by threatening to tell their parents.}

Blackness is the quality or state of being black—the absence of light or color. More significantly, blackness refers to Black racial identity, culture, and experience: {The novel explores themes of blackness in America}, {She wrote about her blackness with pride}. The term carries political and cultural weight, encompassing shared history, aesthetics, and community. Blackness can also describe darkness of mood or outlook: {a blackness of spirit}.

A blackout is a loss of light or consciousness. Power blackouts plunge areas into darkness; memory blackouts leave gaps you can't recover. During wartime, blackouts meant extinguishing lights to avoid enemy detection. In media, a blackout blocks coverage or broadcast: {a news blackout}, {The game is blacked out in the local market}. To black out is to lose consciousness or to suppress information.

Blackouts are periods when something goes dark or blank. A power blackout cuts electricity to an area. A news blackout suppresses information. A blackout in wartime means extinguishing lights to hide from enemy aircraft. Personal blackouts are episodes of memory loss, typically from alcohol or head trauma: {I drank so much I had blackouts}. In theater, a blackout ends a scene by cutting all lights.

Blackshirts were members of fascist paramilitary organizations, named for their uniform. The term originally referred to Mussolini's Italian fascist squads in the 1920s, later extending to similar groups elsewhere, including Oswald Mosley's British Union of Fascists in the 1930s. The word now evokes fascist thuggery generally: {The blackshirts beat protesters in the streets}.

A blacksmith is a craftsperson who shapes iron and steel by heating the metal in a forge until it's soft enough to hammer into tools, horseshoes, gates, and other objects. The work requires both strength and precision, as the smith must strike while the metal is hot and malleable. Historically, blacksmiths were essential to every community, producing everything from nails to weapons. The trade still exists today, though often focused on decorative metalwork or farriery.

Blacksmithing is the craft of forging and shaping iron or steel by heating it in a forge and hammering it on an anvil. The blacksmith makes or repairs metal objects—tools, horseshoes, gates, hardware. The term distinguishes general metalwork from specialized trades like farriery (horseshoeing) or bladesmithing. {He took up blacksmithing as a hobby after retiring.}

Blacksmiths is the plural of blacksmith, a craftsperson who forges and shapes iron and steel by heating metal in a forge and hammering it on an anvil. Before industrialization, blacksmiths were essential to every community, making horseshoes, tools, weapons, and hardware. The trade survives in farriery and artisanal metalwork: {The blacksmiths at the Renaissance fair demonstrated traditional techniques}.

Blackthorn is a thorny shrub native to Europe, bearing white flowers in early spring before its leaves appear, followed by small blue-black fruits called sloes. The dense, dark wood has traditionally been used for walking sticks and cudgels. {A blackthorn winter} refers to a cold snap when the shrub is in bloom.

Blacktop is asphalt paving, the dark surface material used for roads, driveways, and parking lots. The word often refers to the paved surface itself: {kids playing basketball on the blacktop}, {miles of empty blacktop stretching ahead}. As a verb, to blacktop is to pave with asphalt: {They blacktopped the driveway last summer}.
clues: Dark surface of a parking lot

definition: Blacktops is the plural of blacktop, referring to asphalt-paved surfaces—roads, driveways, parking lots, or playgrounds. The term emphasizes the dark color of the material: {The summer heat radiates off the blacktops}. In American usage, blacktop often specifically means a school playground: {Kids played basketball on the blacktop}.

Blackwater refers to wastewater containing fecal matter and urine—the sewage from toilets, as distinct from greywater from sinks and showers. In environmental contexts, blackwater also describes dark-stained water in swamps and slow-moving rivers, colored by tannins from decaying vegetation: {We paddled through the blackwater cypress swamp}. (Capitalized Blackwater was a private military company.)

A bladder is a flexible sac in the body that holds liquid, especially the urinary bladder that stores urine until it's released. The word extends to similar containers: a football's inner bladder, a wine bladder. Bladder suggests something that fills and empties, expanding and contracting with its contents: {I need to find a restroom—my bladder is about to burst}.

A blade is something flat, thin, long, and often sharp (blade of grass, knife blade, razor blade, shoulder blade, wiper blade). A few blades that have some cutting or separating function don’t have the characteristic shape but still get the name (snowplow blade). Blade is also an informal and dated term for a fashionable young man.

A bladerunner is someone who smuggles or illegally sells surgical instruments, particularly scalpels and other blades, often for black-market medical procedures. The term gained wider currency from the 1982 science fiction film *Blade Runner*, where it refers to a police officer who hunts down and "retires" rogue androids. In popular usage, the film sense dominates: {He's basically a bladerunner, tracking down rogue AI}.

Blades is the plural of blade—the flat cutting part of a knife, sword, or tool, or anything with a similar thin, flat shape: {grass blades}, {fan blades}, {shoulder blades}. In skating, blades are the metal runners on ice skates. Slang uses blades for inline skates themselves: {Let's go hit the park on blades}.

A bladesmith is a metalworker who forges blades—knives, swords, axes, and other edged tools or weapons. The term distinguishes this specialty from general blacksmithing: {He apprenticed with a bladesmith in Japan}. Bladesmiths work primarily through forging rather than stock removal, shaping heated metal with hammer and anvil.

Bladesmithing is the craft of forging knives, swords, and other edged tools. It involves heating metal, shaping it through hammering, and heat-treating the finished blade for hardness and durability. The term distinguishes this specialty from general blacksmithing: {He studied bladesmithing to make custom hunting knives}.

Bladework is the technique and skill of using a blade—whether sword, fencing foil, knife, or similar weapon. The term appears in martial arts, stage combat, and historical fencing: {Her bladework was precise and economical}. In sports like fencing, bladework encompasses the movements, parries, and attacks executed with the weapon itself, distinct from footwork.

Blading is skating on inline skates—rollerblades. The term emerged when inline skating became popular in the 1990s, distinguishing it from traditional quad roller skating: {We went blading in the park}. Less commonly, blading refers to using a blade for any purpose, from ice skating to surgical cutting.

Blah expresses boredom, indifference, or dismissive vagueness. It can stand in for words not worth saying: {He went on about taxes, responsibilities, blah blah blah}. As an adjective, blah describes something dull or uninspired: {The movie was pretty blah}. Feeling blah means feeling listless or mildly unwell. The blahs are a state of low spirits or malaise: {I've got the blahs today}.

The blahs is a state of feeling listless, uninspired, or mildly depressed without any particular cause. It suggests a general malaise rather than acute unhappiness—the kind of low-grade funk where nothing seems wrong but nothing feels right either. {I've had the blahs all week and can't seem to shake them.} The word mimics the sound of bored, uninterested speech, as if even talking feels like too much effort.

Blame is holding someone responsible for something wrong or undesirable. You can blame a person, blame circumstances, or blame yourself: {I blame the delay on poor planning}. As a noun, blame is the responsibility itself: {He took the blame for the mistake}. To be {to blame} is to be at fault. {Don't blame me} deflects responsibility, sometimes defensively.

Blamed is a mild oath used as a euphemistic intensifier, substituting for damned: {I can't find my blamed keys}, {That blamed dog got into the trash again}. It appears in expressions of frustration or emphasis, now sounding old-fashioned or folksy. The past tense and past participle of blame also take this form: {They blamed him for the accident}.

Blameless describes someone or something free from fault or responsibility for wrongdoing. A person who is blameless has done nothing wrong and deserves no criticism or punishment. {The investigation found her completely blameless in the matter.} The word often appears in contexts where guilt or fault is being assigned to others, emphasizing that this particular person bears no share of it. A blameless life or record suggests consistent moral uprightness.
clues: Having done nothing at all wrong

definition: Blameshifting is deflecting responsibility for a mistake or wrongdoing onto someone else. Rather than accepting fault, the blameshifter redirects attention: {When confronted about the failed project, he immediately started blameshifting to his colleagues}. The term appears frequently in discussions of toxic relationships and workplace dysfunction. Also written as two words: blame shifting.

Blaming is the act of holding someone or something responsible for a fault or wrong. It's the present participle of blame, used both as a verb form {She was blaming him for the accident} and as an adjective {a blaming tone}. Blaming often carries a negative connotation, suggesting accusation rather than neutral assessment of responsibility. Self-blaming describes the tendency to fault oneself, often excessively.

Blanch means to turn white or pale, often from shock or fear: {She blanched at the news of the accident}. In cooking, to blanch is to briefly immerse food in boiling water, then plunge it into ice water—a technique used to loosen skins, set colors, or partially cook vegetables before freezing. The cooking sense connects to the core meaning: blanched almonds have had their brown skins removed, leaving them white.

Blanched describes something that has turned white or pale, whether from shock, fear, or deliberate treatment. A face blanches when blood drains from it: {She blanched at the news}. In cooking, to blanch is to briefly plunge vegetables or nuts into boiling water, often to loosen skins or preserve color before freezing. Blanched almonds have had their brown skins removed.

Blanching is briefly immersing food in boiling water, then plunging it into ice water to stop the cooking. The technique softens vegetables while preserving color, loosens skins for peeling, or prepares food for freezing. Blanching also describes losing color from shock or fear: {She blanched at the news}. The connection is paleness—blanched almonds are white, a blanched face has gone pale.

Bland describes something lacking strong flavor, character, or interest. Food that is bland has little taste or seasoning: {The hospital food was nutritious but bland}. Applied to people or their manner, bland suggests an unremarkable pleasantness that fails to make an impression: {His bland smile revealed nothing}. Music, writing, or entertainment called bland is safe and forgettable, stripped of anything that might provoke strong reactions. The word often carries mild criticism, implying that something could benefit from more distinctiveness or edge.

The various meanings of blank can be connected under the idea of vacancy where you expect to find something. If you leave a space blank, you do not write in it. A blank stare or expression does not convey an emotion or mien. If you draw a blank, you fail to supply or think of needed information. A blank is also a gun cartridge with powder but no bullet. To blank is to fail to retrieve from memory: I’m blanking on his name.

A blanket is a large piece of soft fabric used as a covering for warmth, especially on beds. The word extends to anything that covers like a blanket: a blanket of {snow}, a blanket of {fog}. As an adjective, blanket means comprehensive or all-inclusive: a blanket {ban}, a blanket {statement}. To blanket something is to cover it completely: {Snow blanketed the valley}.

Blanketed means covered as if with a blanket—completely or uniformly spread over a surface. Snow blanketed the {valley}. Fog blanketed the {city}. The word suggests thorough, even coverage: {The town was blanketed in silence after the news broke}. It can also mean wrapped in an actual blanket: {She blanketed the sleeping child}.

Blankets are soft coverings used for warmth, typically on beds or wrapped around the body. The word extends to anything that covers like a blanket: {a blanket of snow}, {a blanket of fog}. As an adjective, blanket means comprehensive or all-inclusive: a blanket {ban}, a blanket {statement}. To blanket something is to cover it completely: {Smoke blanketed the valley}.
clues: What you pull up when cold

definition: A blankie is a child's security blanket—a soft, familiar object carried for comfort. The diminutive form reflects baby talk and the affection attached to such objects: {She won't sleep without her blankie}. Adults sometimes use the term playfully or nostalgically.

Blanking is forgetting or failing to recall something, especially suddenly or under pressure: {I kept blanking on her name}. It also means ignoring someone deliberately, treating them as if they don't exist: {She's been blanking me all week}. In manufacturing, blanking is cutting flat shapes from sheet metal. To {blank out} is to lose awareness momentarily or to obscure something: {The censor blanked out the profanity}.

Blankly describes doing something with a blank expression—showing no emotion, comprehension, or recognition. Someone stares blankly when their face reveals nothing: {She looked at me blankly, as if we'd never met}. The word often suggests confusion or mental absence: {He blankly repeated the question}.

Blanks is the plural of blank—empty spaces waiting to be filled in: {Fill in the blanks on the form}. To draw blanks is to fail repeatedly to find or remember something. Blanks are also cartridges loaded with powder but no projectile, used for theatrical gunfire, training, or starting races: {The pistol was loaded with blanks}.

Blare is a loud, harsh, often unpleasant sound—typically from horns, sirens, or speakers: {Car horns blared in the traffic jam}, {Music blared from the open window}. The word suggests both volume and a grating quality. As a noun, it's the sound itself: {the blare of trumpets}.

Blared is the past tense of blare, meaning to sound loudly and harshly. Horns blare, sirens blare, music blares from speakers. The word suggests an intrusive, often unpleasant volume: {The television blared in the background}. {Headlines blared the scandal across every front page}.

Blaring describes loud, harsh sound that demands attention and often grates on the nerves. A blaring horn, blaring music, or blaring television fills a space aggressively: {The blaring alarm woke the whole building}. The word suggests not just volume but an unpleasant, intrusive quality—sounds that blast rather than flow.

Blarney is smooth, flattering talk designed to persuade or charm—often with a hint of insincerity. Someone full of blarney knows how to sweet-talk their way through situations: {Don't give me that blarney; I know what you're really after}. The word suggests clever manipulation wrapped in friendliness rather than outright deception. To blarney someone is to coax them with such flattery. (Capitalized Blarney refers to the Irish village and its famous stone.)

Blasé describes a jaded indifference born from overexposure. Someone blasé about fine dining has eaten at enough good restaurants that another one barely registers. The word suggests world-weariness rather than simple disinterest—you're blasé about things others find exciting because you've seen too much: {She was blasé about meeting celebrities after years in Hollywood}.

To blaspheme is to speak irreverently about God or sacred things—cursing, mocking, or showing contempt for what others hold holy. The word carries weight in religious contexts where such speech is considered sinful or even criminal: {He was accused of blaspheming against the Prophet}. Extended to secular use, blaspheme describes violating any deeply held belief: {To question the founder's vision was to blaspheme}.

A blasphemer is someone who speaks irreverently about God or sacred things. The term carries strong religious weight—in some traditions and legal systems, blasphemy remains a serious offense. More loosely, blasphemer can describe anyone who violates what others hold sacred: {To wine purists, he was a blasphemer for adding ice cubes}.

Blasphemers are people who speak irreverently or contemptuously about God, sacred things, or religious beliefs. The term carries strong negative connotations and is used primarily by religious communities to condemn those who mock or disrespect what they hold holy. In some religious traditions and legal systems, blasphemers face severe punishment. The word also gets applied more loosely to anyone who challenges orthodoxy or speaks against revered institutions: {The old guard considered reformers blasphemers against tradition}.

Blaspheming is speaking irreverently about God or sacred things. The word implies deliberate disrespect toward religious beliefs—cursing God, mocking holy texts, or profaning sacred names. In looser use, blaspheming can mean violating anything held sacred: {To a purist, adding ice to single malt is blaspheming}. The noun is blasphemy; the adjective, blasphemous.

Blasphemous describes speech or acts that show contempt for God or sacred things: {a blasphemous remark}, {blasphemous imagery}. The term belongs primarily to religious contexts, where it carries serious weight. More loosely, blasphemous can mean deeply offensive to cherished beliefs or institutions: {To some fans, trading the star player was blasphemous}.

Blasphemy is speech or action that insults or shows contempt for God or sacred things. In religious contexts, it's a serious sin; in some countries, a crime. The word extends to any irreverent treatment of something held sacred: {To a jazz purist, smooth jazz is blasphemy}. The adjective is blasphemous; to commit blasphemy is to blaspheme.

The qualities of a blast are suddenness, violence, and great force (atomic blast, shotgun blast). A blast of air or wind is one that carries great force. Colloquially, a blast is also a very enjoyable and lively experience: I had a blast at the concert. The core meaning of blast as a verb is to strike with great force. This notion informs other meanings, like blasting music (playing it very loud) or blasting the president (criticizing him vigorously).

Blasted works as a mild expletive expressing annoyance or frustration: {This blasted printer won't work}, {Where are my blasted keys?} It's a softer alternative to damned or cursed. Separately, blasted describes something destroyed or withered by blast, blight, or supernatural force: {a blasted heath}, {blasted hopes}. As slang, blasted means extremely drunk or high.

A blaster is a device that produces a powerful burst of something—sound, air, or energy. A boom box may be called a {ghetto blaster}. In science fiction, blaster is the generic term for a handheld energy weapon: {Set your blasters to stun}. Someone who blasts is also a blaster—a demolitions worker or a critic who tears something apart.

Blasters is the plural of blaster, a device that projects force or material—a sand blaster strips paint, a boom blaster plays loud music. In science fiction, blasters are handheld energy weapons that fire concentrated beams or bolts: {The stormtroopers raised their blasters}. The term often appears in video games and toy marketing.

Blasting is the present participle of blast, carrying forward its senses of explosive force and loud sound. Workers are blasting rock at a construction site. Music is blasting from speakers. Someone blasting an opponent is attacking them harshly: {The senator spent the debate blasting her rival's record}. In gaming and internet slang, blasting can mean moving fast or acting recklessly: {I was just blasting through the level}.

Blastoff is the moment a rocket or spacecraft launches, when engines ignite and the vehicle leaves the ground. Countdown sequences traditionally end with {blastoff!} The word captures both the explosive force and the instant of departure. Figuratively, blastoff marks any dramatic beginning: {The campaign's blastoff exceeded expectations}.

Blasts is the plural of blast and the third-person singular verb form. A blast is an explosion or a powerful rush of air: {bomb blasts}, {a blast of cold wind}. To blast is to explode, to criticize harshly, or to play music loudly: {She blasted the report as misleading}. A blast can also be a great time: {We had a blast at the party}.

A blastwave is the wave of intensely compressed air that radiates outward from an explosion. The blastwave from a nuclear detonation can level buildings miles from ground zero. Also spelled as two words: blast wave.

Blatant means offensively obvious or unashamed: {a blatant lie}, {blatant disregard for the rules}. The word implies something that should be hidden or restrained but instead flaunts itself openly. A blatant error is one anyone can see; blatant favoritism makes no effort to appear fair. The adverb blatantly intensifies accusations: {He blatantly ignored the warning}.

Blather is empty, foolish talk—words without substance or direction. Someone who blathers goes on at length without saying much: {He blathered on about his weekend plans}. The noun names such talk: {I couldn't follow his blather}. Blatherskite adds emphasis, naming either the talk itself or the person producing it.

Blathering is talking at length without saying much of substance. The word suggests rambling, foolish speech that tests the listener's patience: {He kept blathering on about his golf game}. As an adjective, it intensifies fool or idiot: {You blathering idiot!}

Blaxploitation refers to a genre of American films from the early 1970s featuring Black actors in action roles, often with funk soundtracks and urban settings. The term blends "Black" and "exploitation," acknowledging that while these films provided rare leading roles for Black performers, they frequently traded in stereotypes of pimps, drug dealers, and street violence. Titles like *Shaft*, *Super Fly*, and *Foxy Brown* defined the style. The term now applies broadly to media that exploits Black culture for profit: {The show's portrayal of inner-city life felt like blaxploitation}.

Blaze has two main senses unified by intensity. A blaze is a bright, fierce fire: {Firefighters battled the blaze for hours}. By extension, a blaze of color or light is vivid and striking. To blaze is to burn brightly or shine intensely. A trail blazer marks a path by cutting marks into trees—blazes—hence {blaze a trail} means to pioneer. Separately, a blaze is a white marking on an animal's face.

Blazed means burned brightly or with intensity: {The fire blazed through the night}. Blazed also means marked with a blaze—a trail marker cut into a tree, or a white marking on an animal's face: {The path was blazed through the forest}. {The horse had a blazed forehead}. In slang, blazed means very high on marijuana: {I got so blazed I couldn't move}. The connection is to {blaze}, slang for smoking marijuana.

A blazer is a lightweight jacket, typically single-breasted with metal buttons, worn as part of a uniform or as smart casual dress. Originally associated with British schools, rowing clubs, and yacht clubs, blazers now appear in business and social settings: {He threw on a navy blazer for the interview}. Unlike suit jackets, blazers are usually worn with non-matching trousers.

Blazers are lightweight, tailored jackets, typically solid-colored or with bold stripes. Originally associated with British sports clubs and schools, they now serve as smart-casual attire: {He threw on a navy blazer for the interview}. The name likely comes from the bright, "blazing" colors of early examples. (Capitalized Blazers refers to the Portland Trail Blazers.)

Blazes appears mainly in emphatic expressions of surprise, frustration, or intensity: {What the blazes is going on?}, {Run like blazes}, {Hot as blazes}. The word serves as a mild euphemism for hell in these constructions. On its own, blazes is the plural of blaze—large flames or intense fires: {The firefighters battled multiple blazes across the county}.

Blazing describes something burning intensely with bright flames: {a blazing fire}. Extended uses emphasize extreme heat or brightness: {blazing sun}, {blazing headlights}. Figuratively, blazing conveys intensity of any kind—speed, anger, passion: {blazing fast}, {a blazing argument}, {blazing talent}. As an intensifier, it's a milder British alternative to "bloody": {a blazing idiot}.

Whether noun or verb, meanings of bleach share the idea of losing color or force, and moving towards white. Chemical bleach removes color. To bleach something (clothes, flour, coral) is to deprive it of color, and sometimes of vigor. Bleaching strips are used to whiten the teeth. In language, the meaning of a word or expression is bleached if it becomes weaker or less specific over time.

Bleached describes something that has been whitened or had its color removed, usually through chemical treatment or exposure to sunlight. Hair can be bleached blonde, fabric bleached white, coral bleached by warming seas. {Her bleached jeans had that worn-in look.} Figuratively, bleached suggests something drained of vitality or character: {a bleached, sanitized version of history}.

A bleacher is a long bench for spectators, typically backless and arranged in rising tiers at sporting events or outdoor venues. Almost always plural: {the bleachers}, {sitting in the bleachers}. Bleacher seats are the cheap seats—uncovered, exposed to sun and weather, far from the action. The term comes from the bleaching effect of sun on the wooden planks and on spectators sitting in them. Separately, a bleacher is a person or chemical that bleaches—whitens fabric, paper, or hair.

Bleachers are tiered bench seating, typically without backs, found at outdoor sports fields and stadiums. The term comes from the bleaching effect of sun exposure on both the wooden benches and the spectators sitting in them. Bleacher seats are usually the cheapest in a venue: {We sat in the bleachers at the baseball game}. The singular bleacher appears mainly as a modifier: {bleacher seats}, {bleacher creature}.

Bleaching is the process of removing color or whitening something, typically using chemicals or sunlight. Hair bleaching lightens natural pigment; bleaching clothes removes stains. Coral bleaching occurs when stressed corals expel the algae that give them color, often a sign of environmental damage. {The sun had bleached the curtains}.

Bleak describes something bare, exposed, and uninviting. A bleak landscape is windswept and treeless. Bleak weather is cold and gray. The word extends naturally to emotional or situational hopelessness: {The outlook for peace talks is bleak}. A bleak {future} offers little promise; a bleak {assessment} finds nothing encouraging.

Bleakness is the quality of being bleak—cold, bare, and unwelcoming. It most often describes landscapes or weather that offer no comfort or shelter: {the bleakness of the moor in winter}. The word extends naturally to emotional and psychological states, suggesting hopelessness or despair: {A sense of bleakness settled over her after the diagnosis}. Bleakness can also characterize situations, outlooks, or prospects that seem grim and without promise.
