The name also refers to the Portuguese man-of-war, a jellyfish-like creature with a painful sting, common in Australian waters: {The beach was closed because of bluebottles}. In British slang, bluebottle is old-fashioned for a police officer, from the blue uniform.

Blue-chip describes investments, companies, or stocks considered reliable and prestigious—financially sound with a strong track record. The term comes from poker, where blue chips traditionally hold the highest value. Extended to anything first-rate or top-tier: {a blue-chip prospect}, {blue-chip credentials}. Also spelled blue chip or bluechip.

Bluecoats is a historical term for soldiers wearing blue uniforms, most often Union troops during the American Civil War: {The bluecoats advanced on the Confederate position}. The term also referred to police officers, whose uniforms were traditionally blue. Both uses are now dated, appearing mainly in historical contexts or period fiction.

Bluefin is a large species of tuna prized for its rich, fatty flesh. Bluefin tuna are among the largest and fastest fish in the ocean, and their meat commands premium prices in sushi markets: {A single bluefin sold for three million dollars at the Tokyo auction}. Overfishing has made them increasingly scarce.

A bluegill is a freshwater sunfish native to North America, common in lakes and ponds. Named for the bluish coloring on its gill covers, it's a popular target for recreational fishing—easy to catch and good eating. {We spent the afternoon catching bluegills off the dock.}

Bluegills are small freshwater sunfish native to North America, popular with anglers and commonly found in ponds, lakes, and slow streams. Named for the blue-black flap on the gill cover, they're often a child's first catch: {We spent the afternoon catching bluegills off the dock}. Singular: bluegill.

Bluegrass is a style of American country music characterized by acoustic string instruments—banjo, fiddle, mandolin, guitar, and upright bass—with tight vocal harmonies and rapid tempos. The genre emerged in the 1940s, named after Bill Monroe's band the Blue Grass Boys. {We caught some bluegrass at the festival}. Separately, bluegrass is a type of grass common in lawns and pastures, named for its blue-green tinge when allowed to seed. Kentucky is called the Bluegrass State.

A bluejay is a crested North American bird with bright blue, white, and black plumage, known for its loud, harsh calls and bold personality. Bluejays are intelligent and sometimes aggressive, raiding other birds' nests. They're common at backyard feeders: {A bluejay chased the sparrows away}. Usually spelled as two words: blue jay.

Bluejays is the plural of bluejay, a crested North American bird with bright blue and white plumage, known for its loud, harsh calls and bold behavior at feeders: {The bluejays chased the smaller birds away from the sunflower seeds}. Also spelled as two words: blue jays.

Bluejeans are casual pants made of denim, typically blue. The word is often shortened to jeans, which has become the dominant form. Originally workwear for laborers and cowboys, bluejeans became universal casual dress in the twentieth century. {She threw on a pair of bluejeans and a T-shirt.}

Blueline refers to one of the two blue lines on an ice hockey rink that divide it into three zones—the lines marking where the offensive and defensive zones begin. A player is offside if they cross the blueline into the attacking zone before the puck: {He was a step ahead of the puck at the blueline}. In publishing, a blueline is a proof print made from photographic negatives, used for final review before printing—named for the blue color of the image.

A blueprint is a technical drawing showing the design of a building, machine, or other structure—originally printed as white lines on blue paper. The term now applies to any detailed plan or scheme: {a blueprint for success}, {the blueprint for healthcare reform}. As a verb, to blueprint something is to plan it in detail.

Blueprints are detailed technical drawings showing plans for buildings, machines, or other constructions. The name comes from an older printing process that produced white lines on blue paper. The term extends to any detailed plan or scheme: {a blueprint for success}, {the blueprint for economic reform}. To blueprint something is to plan it in detail.

Blues is a feeling of melancholy or depression: {I've got the blues today}. The blues is also a genre of American music originating among Black communities in the Deep South, characterized by expressive vocals, bent notes, and call-and-response patterns. The musical and emotional senses intertwine—the music often expresses sorrow, longing, or hard times: {She sang the blues like she'd lived every word}. Blues can modify other nouns: {blues guitar}, {blues singer}. (Capitalized Blues typically refers to sports teams.)

Bluescreen refers to the blue background used in film and video production that allows editors to replace it with other imagery—a technique called chroma key compositing: {They filmed the actors against a bluescreen, then added the spaceship digitally}. In computing, bluescreen (or blue screen) is shorthand for the "blue screen of death," the error display indicating a critical Windows system crash: {My laptop bluescreened in the middle of my presentation}.

Bluescreening is a film and video technique where actors perform in front of a solid blue background, which is later replaced digitally with other imagery: {The entire battle scene was shot with the actors bluescreening in a warehouse}. Green screens now dominate, but the term persists. Also refers informally to a computer crashing and displaying the Windows "blue screen of death": {My laptop keeps bluescreening during updates}.

A bluesman is a male musician who plays or sings the blues. The term evokes the tradition of solo performers—often guitarists—who emerged from the American South: {Robert Johnson remains the archetypal Delta bluesman}. It carries connotations of authenticity, hardship, and musical credibility that "blues musician" lacks.

Bluesmen are musicians who perform blues music, particularly the traditional or classic styles rooted in African American musical traditions. The term evokes an image of guitar-playing singers performing emotionally raw, often improvised music: {The old bluesmen of the Mississippi Delta shaped rock and roll}. The singular is bluesman.

Bluestockings are intellectual or literary women, originally referring to members of 18th-century London salons where serious conversation replaced card games. The term arose when a male attendee wore informal blue worsted stockings instead of formal black silk. It later became mildly derisive, suggesting a woman more interested in books than in feminine pursuits: {She was dismissed as a bluestocking by those who found her learning threatening}.

A blueswoman is a female blues musician, typically a singer. The term parallels bluesman and emphasizes women's significant role in the genre: {Bessie Smith remains the most celebrated blueswoman of the classic era}. While less common than the masculine form, it specifically honors the tradition of female blues artists from Ma Rainey to contemporary performers.

Bluesy describes music or performance that evokes the blues—soulful, melancholy, with bent notes and emotional rawness. A song can be bluesy without being a blues song proper: {The track has a bluesy guitar riff}. The word extends to moods and atmospheres suggesting wistful sadness: {a bluesy late-night vibe}.

Bluey is Australian and New Zealand slang for several things united by color. A bluey is a blue-heeler cattle dog, a red-haired person (ironic Australian nickname), a summons or traffic ticket (from the blue paper), or a swag or blanket roll traditionally wrapped in blue cloth. The word also names a popular Australian animated television series about a cartoon blue heeler puppy.

Bluff has two main threads. One involves deception: to bluff is to mislead others about your position, especially in poker or negotiation. {She called his bluff and he folded}. A bluff is the act itself or the person doing it. The other thread is geographical: a bluff is a steep cliff or riverbank with a broad face. As an adjective, bluff describes a person who is direct and good-naturedly abrupt in manner—hearty rather than subtle.

Bluffing is pretending to have strength, knowledge, or intentions you don't actually possess. The term comes from poker, where players bet aggressively on weak hands to intimidate opponents into folding: {He was bluffing with a pair of twos}. The concept extends to any situation involving strategic deception: {She's bluffing about having another job offer}.

Bluffs works across two unrelated words. From one: a bluff is a steep cliff or riverbank with a broad face, and the plural names such features: {the bluffs overlooking the Missouri River}. From the other: to bluff is to deceive by false confidence, especially in poker, and bluffs are instances of this—attempts to mislead about what you hold or intend: {He called her bluffs and won the pot}.

A blunder is a careless or stupid mistake, typically one with consequences: {a tactical blunder}, {a diplomatic blunder}. The word suggests the error was avoidable—someone should have known better. To blunder is to make such a mistake, or to move clumsily and uncertainly: {He blundered through the dark room}, {She blundered into the wrong meeting}.

A blunderbuss is an old-fashioned firearm with a short barrel and flared muzzle, designed to scatter shot at close range. The wide mouth made loading easier and spread projectiles in a broad pattern—effective for defense but wildly inaccurate. Figuratively, a blunderbuss approach is crude and indiscriminate: {His blunderbuss management style alienated half the staff}.

Blundered is the past tense of blunder, meaning to make a serious mistake through carelessness or stupidity: {He blundered when he sent the email to the wrong person}. It can also mean to move clumsily or stumble: {She blundered into the furniture in the dark}.

Blundering describes clumsy, mistake-prone action—stumbling through tasks without skill or care. A blundering {fool} makes obvious errors. A blundering {attempt} fails through incompetence rather than bad luck. The word emphasizes awkwardness and lack of grace: {The blundering waiter spilled wine on three guests}.

Blunders are serious mistakes, typically caused by carelessness or poor judgment rather than ignorance. The word suggests clumsiness—stumbling into error rather than being misled: {a series of diplomatic blunders}, {The company's marketing blunders cost them millions}. To blunder is to make such mistakes, or to move clumsily: {He blundered through the dark room}.

Blunt describes something with a dull edge or point—the opposite of sharp. A blunt {knife} cuts poorly. Figuratively, blunt speech is direct and unsparing of feelings: {She was blunt about his chances}. A blunt {instrument} in detective fiction is any heavy object used to bludgeon. To blunt something is to dull it: {The setback blunted his enthusiasm}. A blunt is also slang for a marijuana cigar, typically rolled in tobacco leaf.

Blunted describes something that has lost its edge or sharpness. A blunted knife cuts poorly. Figuratively, blunted applies to diminished intensity or sensitivity: {His enthusiasm was blunted by repeated rejection}. In drug slang, blunted means high from smoking a blunt (a marijuana cigar): {We got blunted and watched movies all night}.

Bluntly means in a direct, straightforward manner without softening or diplomacy: {She told him bluntly that his work wasn't good enough}. Speaking bluntly prioritizes honesty over tact—sometimes refreshingly, sometimes rudely. {To put it bluntly, you're fired}.

Bluntness is directness of speech without softening or tact. Someone known for bluntness says what they mean plainly, even if it stings: {Her bluntness about his cooking hurt his feelings}. The quality can be valued as honesty or criticized as rudeness, depending on context and audience. The word extends from the physical sense of blunt—a blunt knife lacks a sharp edge, just as blunt speech lacks diplomatic edges.

Blunts are cigars that have been hollowed out and refilled with marijuana, named after Phillies Blunts, a brand of inexpensive cigars commonly used for this purpose. The tobacco leaf wrapper adds a slight buzz to the high. {We rolled up some blunts and watched the game.} As a verb form, blunts means makes less sharp or intense: {Time blunts the pain of loss.}

Blur is indistinctness—the loss of sharp edges or clear boundaries. A photograph can be blurry, and so can vision or memory: {The details have blurred over time}. To blur is to make something indistinct or to become so: {Tears blurred her vision}, {The line between work and life has blurred}. A blur of motion suggests speed that defeats perception: {The days passed in a blur}.

A blurb is a short promotional description, typically found on book jackets, movie posters, or product packaging. Blurbs praise the work in breathless terms: {Critics are calling it a masterpiece}. The word was coined by humorist Gelett Burgess in 1907, mocking the extravagant endorsements that adorned book covers.

Blurbs are short promotional descriptions, typically found on book jackets, movie posters, or product packaging. A blurb praises and summarizes, aiming to entice: {The blurbs on the back cover promised a gripping thriller}. Publisher-solicited endorsements from other authors are also blurbs. The word was coined by American humorist Gelett Burgess in 1907.

Blurred describes something with unclear edges or outlines, as if seen through fog or tears: {The photo came out blurred}. Vision blurs when eyes lose focus. Distinctions blur when boundaries become indistinct: {The line between work and life has blurred}. A blurred memory is one whose details have faded or merged together.

Blurring is the process of making something less distinct or clear. An image loses sharpness through blurring. Boundaries undergo blurring when distinctions fade: {the blurring of lines between work and personal life}. Vision blurring can signal eye strain or medical conditions. The word captures both physical indistinctness and conceptual ambiguity.

Blurry describes something indistinct or out of focus, lacking sharp edges or clear definition. A blurry {photograph} failed to capture a crisp image. Blurry {vision} may indicate you need glasses. The word extends to anything vague or unclear: {My memory of that night is blurry}.

Blurt means to say something suddenly and impulsively, usually without thinking first. The word almost always appears with out: {She blurted out the secret before she could stop herself}. What gets blurted is typically something that should have been kept private or at least delivered more carefully—a confession, an insult, an awkward truth. The spontaneity implied by blurt suggests the speaker immediately regrets the utterance or at least didn't intend to make it.
clues: Utter before your brain catches up

definition: Blurted is the past tense of blurt, meaning to say something suddenly and without thinking, often revealing what you meant to keep quiet: {She blurted out the secret before she could stop herself}. The word suggests impulsiveness—words escaping before the speaker can filter them.

Blurting is saying something suddenly and impulsively, often without thinking: {She kept blurting out the answers before anyone else could respond}. The word suggests words escaping before you can stop them—embarrassing secrets, inappropriate comments, or thoughts better left unspoken. {He has a habit of blurting whatever comes to mind.}

Blurts is the third-person singular of blurt, meaning to say something suddenly and without thinking, often revealing something meant to stay hidden: {She blurts out the answer before anyone else can respond}. The word suggests impulsiveness—words escaping before the speaker can stop them.

Blush is the reddening of the face from embarrassment, shame, or modesty: {She felt a blush creep up her cheeks}. The verb means to redden this way: {He blushed when she caught him staring}. By extension, blush describes any rosy tint—a blush {wine} is pale pink, and blush as a cosmetic adds color to cheeks. {At first blush} means on initial impression: {At first blush, the plan seemed reasonable}.

Blushed is the past tense of blush—to redden in the face from embarrassment, shame, or modesty. {She blushed when he complimented her}. The word extends to anything taking on a rosy tint: {The sky blushed pink at dawn}. A blushing bride is traditionally modest; to make someone blush is to embarrass or flatter them.

Blusher is cosmetic powder or cream applied to the cheeks to add color or create the appearance of a healthy flush: {She dusted blusher across her cheekbones}. The term is more common in British English; Americans typically say blush. Blusher can also mean someone who blushes easily.

Blushes is the plural of blush and the third-person singular verb form. A blush is a reddening of the face from embarrassment, shame, or modesty: {Her blushes betrayed her feelings}. To blush is to redden in this way: {He blushes easily}. Something done {at first blush} happens upon initial impression, before deeper consideration.

Blushing is the involuntary reddening of the face from embarrassment, shame, or self-consciousness. The word works as both verb and adjective: {She was blushing furiously} or {the blushing bride}. A blushing person is modest or easily embarrassed. By extension, things tinged pink or red may be described as blushing: {blushing peaches}, {a blushing sky at dawn}.

Bluster is loud, aggressive talk that lacks substance—empty threats or boastful claims meant to intimidate or impress: {His bluster couldn't hide his inexperience}. As a verb, to bluster is to speak or behave this way. Wind also blusters when it blows in strong, noisy gusts. The noun and verb share the sense of forceful noise without follow-through.

Blustered is the past tense of bluster, meaning to speak or act with noisy, empty aggression. Someone who blustered made loud threats or boasts without substance behind them: {He blustered about taking legal action but never followed through}. Weather that blustered blew in violent, turbulent gusts.

Blusters is the verb form of bluster—to speak or act with loud, aggressive blowing. Wind blusters against windows; a bully blusters threats he may not carry out. The word suggests more noise than substance: {He blusters about lawsuits but never files them}. Someone who blusters is trying to intimidate or conceal weakness through sheer volume.

Blustery describes weather marked by strong, gusty winds, often with rain or snow: {a blustery November afternoon}. The word suggests unpredictable gusts rather than steady gales. Extended to people, blustery means loudly aggressive or boastful but without real substance—all bluster: {His blustery threats didn't intimidate anyone}.

A boa is a large snake that kills prey by coiling around it and squeezing—a constrictor. The term covers various species, most famously the boa constrictor of Central and South America. A boa is also a long, fluffy scarf made of feathers or fur, worn draped around the neck and shoulders: {She wore a pink feather boa to the party}. The garment takes its name from its snake-like shape and the way it wraps around the wearer.

A boar is a male pig, especially an uncastrated one kept for breeding. Wild boar refers to the tusked ancestor of domestic pigs, native to Eurasia and hunted as game: {Wild boar have returned to parts of Britain}. The word often evokes something fierce or brutish.

The many meanings of the noun board can be roughly divided in three: a rigid piece of wood, longer than it is wide (2’ x 4’ board); a group of persons with a particular authoritative function (board of directors); and daily meals, provided for pay (room and board). Things like a circuit board grow out of the first meaning. The verb board is related to the first and third meanings. You can board up a building (cover it with boards), or you can board at a hotel (get your meals there).

A boarder is someone who pays for lodging and meals at another person's residence: {The widow took in boarders to make ends meet}. In schools, a boarder lives on campus rather than commuting—the opposite of a day student. The word also refers to someone who boards a vessel, whether legitimately or by force, and to practitioners of board sports: {snowboarder}, {skateboarder}.

Boarders are people who pay for regular meals and lodging at someone's home or an establishment. A boarding house takes in boarders. Students at boarding schools are boarders, living on campus during the school year: {The school housed three hundred boarders}. Separately, a boarder is someone who boards a ship or vehicle—either passengers or, in maritime contexts, hostile forces attempting to seize a vessel.

A boardgame is a game played on a marked surface—a board—with pieces, cards, dice, or other components. Chess, Monopoly, and Scrabble are classic examples. The term distinguishes tabletop games from card games, video games, or sports. Also spelled as two words: {board game}.

Board games are games played on a marked surface—a board—typically with pieces, cards, or dice. The category ranges from ancient strategy games like chess and Go to family games like Monopoly and Scrabble to modern designer games with complex rules and themes. {We spent the evening playing board games.} Often written as two words: board games.

Boarding is the act of getting onto a vehicle for travel—a plane, ship, train, or bus. Airlines announce boarding by zones; cruise passengers await boarding times. Boarding also means covering with boards: {They boarded up the windows before the hurricane}. In hockey, boarding is the penalty for violently checking an opponent into the boards. A boarding school provides room and board for students who live on campus.

A boardinghouse is a residence where paying guests receive lodging and meals. Unlike hotels, boardinghouses typically offer longer-term arrangements—weeks or months rather than nights. Residents often share common spaces and eat together. The term evokes an earlier era when such establishments were common for workers, students, and travelers: {She rented a room at a boardinghouse near the factory}.

A boardroom is a room where the board of directors of a company meets to conduct business, make decisions, and set policy. By extension, boardroom often refers to corporate leadership itself or the culture of high-level business decision-making: {The deal was hammered out in the boardroom}. Boardroom politics suggests the maneuvering and power dynamics among executives, while boardroom diversity addresses representation at the highest levels of corporate governance.

Boardrooms are the rooms where a company's board of directors meets to make high-level decisions. The word often stands for corporate leadership itself: {The decision came from the boardroom}. Boardroom discussions concern strategy, executive appointments, and major financial matters. The singular boardroom can refer to corporate power generally: {She fought her way into the boardroom}.

Boards are flat, rigid pieces of material—typically wood cut into planks for construction or other purposes: {The floor boards creaked underfoot}. Board extends to any flat surface serving a function: a cutting board, a circuit board, a board game's playing surface. A board is also a group that governs or advises: {board of directors}, {school board}. To tread the boards is to perform on stage, from the wooden planks of theater floors. In hockey, the boards are the walls surrounding the rink.

A boardwalk is a walkway made of wooden planks, typically found along beaches or through marshy areas where the ground is unstable or prone to flooding. The term especially evokes the famous promenades at seaside resorts—Atlantic City's boardwalk being the most iconic—lined with shops, amusements, and carnival attractions: {We strolled the boardwalk eating saltwater taffy}. The boardwalk in Monopoly references Atlantic City's.

Boardwalks is the plural of boardwalk—a walkway made of wooden planks, typically found along beaches or through marshy areas. Seaside boardwalks often feature shops, games, and amusements: {the Atlantic City boardwalk}, {We strolled the boardwalk eating cotton candy}. Nature boardwalks protect fragile ecosystems while allowing foot traffic through wetlands or forests.

Boars are male pigs, especially uncastrated ones raised for breeding. The word also refers to wild pigs—the tusked ancestors of domestic swine that still roam forests in Europe, Asia, and parts of the Americas: {Wild boars have been spotted in the hills outside town}. A boar is larger and more aggressive than a castrated male, which is called a barrow.

Boas is the plural of boa, which names two quite different things. A boa constrictor is a large snake that kills prey by squeezing rather than biting. A feather boa is a fluffy scarf made of feathers or similar material, worn as a fashion accessory or costume piece: {She draped a pink boa around her shoulders}. Both wrap around things—one fatally, one decoratively.

To boast is to speak with excessive pride about one's accomplishments, possessions, or abilities: {He boasted about his promotion to anyone who would listen}. The word carries a whiff of disapproval—boasting suggests self-praise that crosses into bragging. A boast is also the thing claimed: {His boast that he could beat anyone proved hollow}. A place or thing can boast a feature, meaning it possesses something noteworthy: {The hotel boasts a rooftop pool}.

Boastful describes someone who brags or speaks with excessive pride about themselves or their accomplishments. A boastful person draws attention to their own success, wealth, or abilities: {He was boastful about his promotion}. The word carries a negative connotation—boasting is generally seen as off-putting rather than confident.
clues: Never missing a chance to crow

definition: Boasting is talking with excessive pride about oneself or one's achievements. The word carries a negative connotation—someone who boasts isn't just sharing good news but doing so in a way that feels self-aggrandizing or tiresome to others: {His constant boasting about his salary alienated his coworkers}. A boast can sometimes prove hollow: {All that boasting, and he came in last}.

A boat is a watercraft—a vessel for traveling on water. Boats are generally smaller than ships, though the line is imprecise. You can boat across a lake or down a river. To {be in the same boat} is to share circumstances with others. To {rock the boat} is to disturb a stable situation. To {miss the boat} is to lose an opportunity.

A boater is a stiff straw hat with a flat crown and brim, once standard summer attire for men: {He wore a boater and a striped blazer}. The style persists mainly in period costumes and barbershop quartet uniforms. Separately, a boater is someone who boats—a person engaged in recreational boating.

A boathouse is a structure built at the water's edge for storing boats. Boathouses range from simple sheds to elaborate buildings with living quarters above: {The old boathouse had fallen into disrepair}. College rowing programs often use boathouses as headquarters for their teams.

Boathouses are structures built at the water's edge to shelter boats. They typically stand on pilings or a dock, with an opening that allows boats to float in directly from the water. Some boathouses include upper levels for storage or living space: {The lakefront property came with a private boathouse}.

Boating is the activity of traveling on water in a boat for recreation or sport. The term covers everything from casual rowing on a pond to sailing, motorboating, and yachting. {We spent the afternoon boating on the lake.} Someone who enjoys boating regularly might be called a boating enthusiast, and areas with marinas and waterways often develop boating communities around the pastime.

A boatlift is an emergency evacuation or mass transport of people by boat, typically from a country in crisis. The term evokes images of improvised flotillas—fishing boats, pleasure craft, anything seaworthy—carrying refugees across water: {the Mariel boatlift brought 125,000 Cubans to Florida in 1980}. The word combines the urgency of airlift with maritime improvisation.

Boatlifts are organized evacuations or migrations by sea, typically involving large numbers of people fleeing political upheaval or disaster. The term evokes images of crowded vessels and humanitarian crisis: {the Mariel boatlift brought 125,000 Cubans to Florida in 1980}. A boatlift may be government-sanctioned or improvised by desperate civilians.

A boatload is the amount a boat can carry—passengers, cargo, or fish. By extension, a boatload means a large quantity of anything: {We made a boatload of money on that deal}. The figurative sense is informal and emphatic, suggesting abundance without specifying an exact amount.

Boatloads means a large quantity or amount of something: {They made boatloads of money on that deal}. The literal sense—the cargo capacity of a boat—exists but rarely appears. The figurative use dominates, always suggesting abundance: {boatloads of homework}, {boatloads of fans showed up}.

A boatman is someone who operates, rows, or otherwise manages a small boat, typically for hire or as an occupation. The term evokes traditional watercraft like rowboats, ferries, or punts rather than large vessels with engines. Boatmen have historically transported passengers and goods across rivers, lakes, and harbors. {We hired a boatman to take us across the river.} The word carries a somewhat old-fashioned or literary flavor, though it remains in use where such work continues.

Boatmen is the plural of boatman—a person who operates, rows, or works on a boat. The term typically suggests small watercraft rather than large ships: ferrymen, river guides, or those who rent out rowboats. {The boatmen waited at the dock for tourists.} In some contexts, boatmen are figures of folklore who ferry passengers across mythic waters.

Boat people are refugees who flee their country by sea, often in overcrowded or unseaworthy vessels. The term became prominent during the exodus from Vietnam after 1975, when hundreds of thousands risked drowning and piracy to escape: {The boat people faced harrowing journeys across the South China Sea}. Now applied to any maritime refugees, the term can carry dismissive or dehumanizing overtones depending on context.

Boats are watercraft—vessels that float and move across water. The word typically suggests smaller craft: rowboats, sailboats, motorboats. Larger vessels are usually called ships, though the line blurs. To boat is to travel by boat or to transport something in one: {We boated across the lake}. {In the same boat} means sharing circumstances, usually unfortunate ones.

A boatswain is a ship's officer responsible for the deck crew, rigging, anchors, and general maintenance. Often pronounced "bosun" and sometimes spelled that way. The boatswain supervises sailors in their daily work and ensures the vessel's equipment stays in good order: {The boatswain piped the crew to stations}.

A boatyard is a place where boats are built, repaired, or stored. Unlike a marina, which focuses on docking and services for boats in the water, a boatyard typically has facilities for hauling vessels out and working on them on land: {We had the hull repainted at the boatyard}.

Several words have settled on the spelling b-o-b in English. The most common is the verb, indicating a quick up-and-down movement: Let’s bob for apples. The noun bob indicates an instance of this. A bob is also a kind of short women’s haircut; it is the result when you bob your hair. In British slang, a bob is shilling, and still notes a quantity of money even though the shilling is obsolete: I lent him a few bob. When capitalized, Bob is a standard nickname for Robert.

Boba is a tea-based drink featuring chewy tapioca pearls, originating in Taiwan. The pearls settle at the bottom and are sucked up through an oversized straw. Boba can refer to the drink itself or just the pearls: {Let's get boba}, {I love the boba in this}. Also called bubble tea. The drink comes in countless flavors, from classic milk tea to fruit blends.

Bobbed describes something cut short, especially hair trimmed to hang evenly around the head: {She wore her hair bobbed at chin length}. The word comes from the verb bob, meaning to cut short or move with a quick up-and-down motion. A bobbed tail on a dog or horse has been docked or is naturally short.

A bobber is a float used in fishing, attached to the line to suspend bait at a desired depth and signal when a fish bites by dipping or moving. The word also names a style of stripped-down motorcycle with fenders and other parts removed for a minimalist look: {He rides a custom bobber}.

Bobbies is the plural of bobby, British slang for a police officer. The term comes from Sir Robert Peel, who established London's Metropolitan Police in 1829. It remains common in British English and sounds quaint or old-fashioned to American ears: {The bobbies patrolled the neighborhood on foot}.

A bobbin is a small spool or cylinder around which thread, yarn, or wire is wound. In sewing machines, the bobbin holds the lower thread that interlocks with the upper thread to form stitches: {I need to wind a new bobbin before I can finish this seam}. Bobbins also appear in lacemaking, weaving, and electrical work.

Bobbing is repeated quick up-and-down or side-to-side movement. A cork bobs on the water. A head bobs in agreement or to music. {She kept bobbing her head to the beat.} Bobbing for apples is the Halloween game of catching floating apples with your teeth. The word suggests light, buoyant motion rather than deliberate action.

Bobbins are small spools that hold thread or yarn, used in sewing machines, lace-making, and weaving. The thread feeds from the bobbin as the machine stitches. In British slang, bobbins means rubbish or nonsense: {That film was absolute bobbins}.

A bobble is a small, soft ball of material, often decorative—the kind found on winter hats or curtain trim. In British usage, a bobble is also a hair tie. As a verb, to bobble is to fumble or handle clumsily: {He bobbled the catch and the ball rolled away}. A bobblehead is a figurine with an oversized head on a spring that wobbles when touched.

Bobbled is the past tense of bobble, meaning to fumble or handle clumsily. In sports, a fielder who bobbles a ball fails to catch or control it cleanly: {He bobbled the grounder and the runner reached first}. More broadly, anything mishandled or bungled can be bobbled: {The company bobbled the product launch}.

A bobblehead is a collectible figurine with an oversized head attached by a spring, causing it to wobble when touched or jostled. Most depict athletes, celebrities, or fictional characters, often given away at sporting events: {I got a free bobblehead at the baseball game}. The nodding motion can suggest mindless agreement: {Don't be a bobblehead—think for yourself}.

Bobbleheads are figurines with oversized heads attached by springs, causing them to wobble when touched or jostled. They typically depict athletes, celebrities, or cartoon characters and are popular as collectibles and promotional giveaways at sporting events: {I have a whole shelf of baseball bobbleheads}. The term sometimes describes people who nod along agreeably without independent thought.

Bobbles are small decorative balls, typically fuzzy or pom-pom-like, attached to fabric or clothing: {a hat with bobbles}, {a bobble-trimmed curtain}. In British usage, bobbles also refers to the small fiber balls that form on worn fabric—what Americans call pills or fuzz. To bobble something is to fumble or mishandle it, especially in sports: {He bobbled the catch and dropped the ball}.

A bobby is a British police officer, a term deriving from Sir Robert Peel, who established London's Metropolitan Police in 1829. The word is informal but not disrespectful: {The bobby on the corner gave us directions}. Though still understood, it sounds increasingly old-fashioned in contemporary British speech. (Capitalized Bobby is a given name.)

Bobbysocks are ankle-length socks, typically white and often worn cuffed, associated with teenage girls in 1940s and 1950s America. The term evokes the era of sock hops and early rock and roll. A bobbysoxer was a teenage girl of that period, especially one who swooned over crooners like Frank Sinatra.

A bobcat is a wild cat native to North America, named for its short, stubby tail. About twice the size of a house cat, bobcats have tufted ears and spotted coats. They're solitary, nocturnal hunters found from southern Canada through Mexico: {We spotted a bobcat crossing the trail at dusk}.

Bobcats are wild cats native to North America, named for their short, bobbed tails. Smaller than lynxes but larger than housecats, they're adaptable predators found from Canadian forests to Mexican deserts. {A bobcat was spotted near the hiking trail}. The term also refers to a brand of compact construction equipment: {We rented a Bobcat to grade the driveway}.

A bobsled is a racing sled with runners, a steering mechanism, and brakes, used to hurtle down an ice-covered track. Teams of two or four push the sled at the start, then jump in and navigate banked curves at high speeds. The sport features in the Winter Olympics. Also called bobsleigh, especially in British English.

Bobsledding is the winter sport of racing down an ice-covered track in a bobsled—a streamlined sled with runners, steering mechanism, and brakes. Teams of two or four push the sled at the start, then jump in and hurtle down a twisting chute at high speeds. {She took up bobsledding after her track career ended.}

Bobsleds are racing sleds designed to carry two or four people down an ice-covered track at high speeds. The sled has a streamlined body, runners, and a steering mechanism. The sport derives its name from early racers who bobbed their heads to gain speed. As a verb, to bobsled is to ride or race in one: {We went bobsledding in Switzerland}.

A bobsleigh is a racing sled used on ice tracks, typically crewed by two or four people who steer and shift their weight through banked curves at high speeds. The sport originated in Switzerland in the late 19th century. Also spelled bobsled, which is more common in American English: {The Jamaican bobsleigh team became unlikely Olympic heroes}.
Bobsleigh is the most frequently used spelling for the winter sport of bobsled.

Bobtails are animals with docked or naturally short tails—especially horses and dogs. The Old English Sheepdog is sometimes called a bobtail. The word extends to anything similarly shortened or truncated. In the song "Jingle Bells," {bells on bobtails ring} refers to horses with cropped tails pulling the sleigh.

Bocce is an Italian ball game in which players take turns tossing larger balls toward a smaller target ball, trying to land closest to it. The game is played on a long, narrow court, often in parks or backyards: {We played bocce on the lawn after dinner}. Also spelled bocci or boccie.

Bocci is an Italian lawn game where players toss balls toward a smaller target ball, trying to land closest to it. Also spelled bocce or boccie. The game resembles French pétanque and English bowls: {We played bocci in the backyard after dinner}. Popular at Italian-American gatherings and in parks with dedicated courts.

Boccie is an Italian bowling game played on a long, narrow court. Players take turns tossing or rolling balls, trying to land them closest to a smaller target ball called the pallino. Popular in Italian-American communities, it's often played casually in parks and backyards: {We set up boccie in the backyard for the cookout}. Also spelled bocce or bocci.

Bodacious means bold, audacious, or remarkable—often with admiration for something impressively brazen or excellent. The word blends *bold* and *audacious* and carries a Southern American flavor: {That was a bodacious lie}. It can describe physical impressiveness, especially curves: {a bodacious figure}. The tone is usually playful or enthusiastic rather than serious.

A bodega is a small neighborhood grocery store, especially in Hispanic communities in the United States. The word is Spanish for "warehouse" or "wine cellar." In urban areas like New York City, bodegas typically sell everyday essentials—snacks, drinks, cigarettes, lottery tickets—and often stay open late: {I ran to the bodega for milk}. The term carries cultural weight, evoking corner-store convenience and neighborhood character.

Bodegas are small grocery or convenience stores, especially in Latino neighborhoods of American cities. The word is Spanish for storeroom or wine cellar. In urban areas like New York, a bodega typically stocks basics—milk, bread, beer, cigarettes, lottery tickets—and stays open late: {I'm running to the bodega for some eggs}. The term carries neighborhood familiarity; your bodega is the one on your corner.

Bodge is British slang for a hasty, clumsy repair or makeshift fix—something done carelessly or without proper skill. To bodge a job is to patch it together rather than do it properly: {He bodged the plumbing and now it leaks worse than before}. A bodge job may hold temporarily but lacks craftsmanship. The word overlaps with botch, though bodge emphasizes improvisation while botch emphasizes failure.

In Buddhism, a bodhisattva is a being who seeks enlightenment not just for themselves but for all sentient creatures. In Mahayana Buddhism especially, the bodhisattva delays their own entry into nirvana to help others along the path. The term extends loosely to anyone who embodies selfless compassion: {She's a bodhisattva, always putting others first}. The Dalai Lama is considered an incarnation of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.

A bodice is the fitted upper part of a woman's dress, covering the torso from shoulders to waist. Historically, it was a separate garment worn over a blouse or chemise, often laced at the front. The term appears frequently in romance novels, where bodices are famously ripped: {a bodice-ripper} is a romance novel featuring passionate seduction scenes.

Bodied describes having a body of a particular kind, almost always with a modifier: {full-bodied wine}, {able-bodied sailors}, {a long-bodied insect}. In recent slang, to get bodied means to be dominated or humiliated, especially in competition or conflict: {He got bodied in that rap battle}. The slang sense suggests being reduced to a mere body—defeated so thoroughly you're left lifeless.

Bodies is the plural of body—physical forms of humans, animals, or objects. The word often implies corpses: {They found three bodies in the wreckage}. Bodies can be collective groups: governing bodies, bodies of water, bodies of work. In casual speech, body positivity movements have made {bodies} a term for celebrating physical diversity: {All bodies are beautiful}.

Bodily means of or relating to the physical body: {bodily functions}, {bodily harm}, {bodily fluids}. As an adverb, it means physically or in person, often with a sense of forceful movement: {He was carried bodily from the room}. The word distinguishes physical from mental or spiritual: {bodily needs versus spiritual ones}.

The core meaning of body is the physical part of living things—the part that decays when life ends. In a narrower sense, body may refer to the torso. By extension, body often refers to the main or surrounding part of something that has ancillary or interior parts. The body of a car is the exterior, exclusive of its mechanical parts. The body of a document or book is the main part, exclusive of indices, appendices, or front matter. In expressions where body is followed by an of prepositional phrase, the thing designated is a physically separate or separately conceived entity: a body of water, a body of knowledge.

A bodybag is a zippered bag, usually made of heavy plastic or rubber, used to transport human corpses. They are standard equipment for military personnel, emergency responders, and morgue workers. The term sometimes appears in aggressive contexts to suggest killing someone: {They'll be leaving in bodybags}. Bodybag can also function as a slang verb meaning to defeat someone decisively, especially in gaming or sports: {Our team got bodybbagged in the finals}.

A bodyboard is a short, lightweight foam board used for riding waves while lying prone or sometimes kneeling. Unlike surfboards, bodyboards are designed to be ridden with the body flat against the deck, with the rider using swim fins for propulsion and control. The sport of bodyboarding developed in the 1970s and remains popular at beaches worldwide. {She grabbed her bodyboard and headed for the shore break.}

Bodyboarding is a water sport in which a rider lies prone on a short, rectangular foam board and rides breaking waves toward shore. Unlike surfing, where you stand, bodyboarding keeps you flat or propped on your elbows: {We spent the afternoon bodyboarding at the beach}. The board itself is called a bodyboard or boogie board.

A bodybuilder is someone who develops their muscles through weight training and diet, typically for competition or aesthetic display. The sport emphasizes symmetry, definition, and size, with competitors posing to showcase their physiques: {Professional bodybuilders follow strict training regimens}. The term also applies to serious recreational lifters pursuing muscular development.

Bodybuilders are people who develop their muscles through weight training and diet, typically for competition or aesthetic goals. The sport emphasizes muscular size, symmetry, and definition, with competitors posing to display their physiques: {The bodybuilders backstage were applying oil before going onstage}. The term can also describe anyone serious about building muscle mass.

Bodybuilding is the practice of developing muscle size and definition through weight training, diet, and exercise. Competitive bodybuilders display their physiques in poses before judges who evaluate symmetry, proportion, and muscular development. The activity exists on a spectrum from casual gym-goers seeking to {build muscle} to professionals using rigorous regimens and sometimes performance-enhancing drugs.

A bodycam is a small video camera worn on the body, typically by police officers to record interactions with the public. The footage serves as evidence and accountability: {The bodycam captured the entire arrest}. Also spelled body cam or body-cam.

Bodycams are small video cameras worn on the body, typically by police officers to record interactions with the public. The footage serves as evidence and accountability: {The bodycam footage contradicted the officer's account}. Also spelled as two words (body cams) or hyphenated (body-cams).

A bodycheck is a defensive move in ice hockey and lacrosse where a player uses their body to block or knock an opponent off the puck or ball. The contact must target the torso rather than the head or legs to be legal: {He delivered a hard bodycheck at center ice}. As a verb, to bodycheck is to execute such a hit.

Bodychecked is the past tense of bodycheck, a hockey move where a player uses their body to block or knock an opponent off the puck. The term extends to any forceful physical collision used to impede someone: {He bodychecked me into the wall as he rushed past}. The move is legal in hockey under certain conditions but can draw penalties if excessive.

Bodychecking is the act of using one's body to block or knock down an opponent, especially in hockey and lacrosse. It's a legal defensive tactic when executed within the rules—targeting an opponent with the puck or ball. Outside sports, bodychecking describes any deliberate physical collision: {He bodychecked me into the wall on his way out}.

Bodychecks is the plural of bodycheck, a deliberate collision in hockey or lacrosse where a player uses their body to block or disrupt an opponent. The move is legal within rules but can be penalized if excessive. As a verb, to bodycheck is to deliver such a hit: {He bodychecks anyone who comes near the goal}.

A bodyguard is a person hired to protect someone from physical harm. Bodyguards accompany their clients in public, watch for threats, and intervene if danger arises. The term applies to individual protectors and to security details: {The celebrity traveled with two bodyguards}. By extension, anything that shields or defends can serve as a bodyguard: {The lawyer acted as a bodyguard against legal threats}.

Bodyguards are people employed to protect someone from physical harm or unwanted contact. The term typically suggests close personal protection rather than general security work: {The celebrity traveled with two bodyguards}. A single protector is a bodyguard; the plural often refers to a protective detail or team.

A bodypillow is an elongated pillow designed to support the full length of the body while sleeping, typically measuring four to five feet long. Side sleepers often use them to align the spine and relieve pressure on hips and knees. In anime and gaming culture, bodypillows with printed character images—called dakimakura—have become collectible items, sometimes carrying romantic or sexual connotations. {He ordered a bodypillow cover featuring his favorite character.}

A bodyshamer is someone who mocks, criticizes, or humiliates others for their physical appearance, especially their weight or body shape. The term emerged from online discourse about bullying and self-acceptance: {She called out the bodyshamers in her comments section}. The verb is bodyshame; the practice is bodyshaming.

A bodyshop is a garage that repairs vehicle bodies—fixing dents, repainting panels, and restoring cars after collisions. In business slang, a bodyshop is a staffing agency that supplies contract workers, especially in IT: {They're just a bodyshop that farms out programmers}. The term implies commodified labor rather than specialized talent.

A bodyslam is a wrestling move where one wrestler lifts an opponent and throws them forcefully to the mat. Outside wrestling, it describes any forceful takedown or collision: {He bodyslammed the guy into the wall}. The verb bodyslam means to execute such a move: {She bodyslammed him onto the couch}. Figuratively, it can mean to defeat decisively: {The bill got bodyslammed in committee}.

Bodyslammed is the past tense of bodyslam, a wrestling move where you lift an opponent and throw them forcefully to the ground. Outside the ring, it describes any similarly aggressive physical takedown: {The bouncer bodyslammed him onto the sidewalk}. Figuratively, it means to defeat or overwhelm decisively: {We got bodyslammed in the quarterly review}.

Bodyslamming is the act of lifting and forcefully throwing someone to the ground, a signature move in professional wrestling. The term extends to any aggressive physical takedown: {Security bodyslamming protesters made the evening news}. Figuratively, it describes overwhelming defeat or forceful criticism: {The committee bodyslamming the proposal surprised no one}.

Bodyslams is the plural of bodyslam, a wrestling move where one lifts an opponent and throws them forcefully to the mat. Outside wrestling, it describes any forceful physical takedown: {The linebacker bodyslams quarterbacks for a living}. Figuratively, it means to defeat or overwhelm decisively: {The critic bodyslammed the new film}.

A bodysnatcher is someone who steals corpses, historically from graves to sell to medical schools for anatomical study. The practice was common in the 18th and 19th centuries when legal sources of cadavers were scarce. The term now applies more loosely to anyone who illicitly removes bodies: {The funeral home director was arrested as a bodysnatcher for selling body parts}.

Bodysnatchers are people who steal corpses, historically from graves to sell to medical schools for dissection. The practice was common in the 18th and 19th centuries when legal cadavers were scarce. The term extends to science fiction, where bodysnatchers are aliens who take over human bodies: {Invasion of the Body Snatchers}. Informally, a bodysnatcher is anyone who recruits people away from their current positions.

Bodysnatching is the practice of stealing corpses from graves, historically to sell them for medical dissection when legal cadavers were scarce. The term extends to any unauthorized removal of a body. Figuratively, it describes taking someone away from a group or organization: {Corporate bodysnatching of university researchers has become common}.

A bodysuit is a one-piece garment that covers the torso and snaps or fastens at the crotch. Women wear bodysuits as tops that stay tucked in, since they can't ride up: {She wore a black bodysuit with high-waisted jeans}. In dancewear and athletics, bodysuits may extend to cover the limbs. Infant onesies are essentially bodysuits.

Bodysuits are one-piece garments that cover the torso and fasten at the crotch, worn as underwear, athletic wear, or as tops tucked into pants or skirts. The snap closure keeps the garment from riding up or bunching. Infant bodysuits (onesies) serve a similar function for babies. {She wore a black bodysuit under her blazer.}

Bodysurfed is the past tense of bodysurf, meaning to ride waves toward shore using only your body—no board or other equipment. The swimmer catches a wave and glides on its momentum: {We bodysurfed until the sun went down}. It requires timing the wave's break and positioning the body to plane across the water's surface.

Bodysurfing is riding waves without a board, using only the body to catch and glide on breaking waves. The swimmer positions themselves at the wave's crest and extends arms forward to plane across the water's surface: {We spent the afternoon bodysurfing at the beach}. It requires timing and technique but no equipment beyond swim fins, which are optional.
clues: Using your form to catch waves

definition: A bodyswap is a fictional scenario in which two characters exchange bodies, each inhabiting the other's physical form while retaining their own consciousness and personality. The premise appears across science fiction, fantasy, comedy, and romance, often used to explore identity, empathy, or humor arising from characters navigating unfamiliar bodies and social situations. {The movie's bodyswap between father and daughter forces them to understand each other's lives.}

Bodywork refers to the outer shell of a vehicle—the panels, doors, and frame that form its exterior: {The car runs fine but needs bodywork after the accident}. In a different sense, bodywork means therapeutic practices involving physical manipulation or touch: massage, chiropractic adjustment, and similar treatments. {She specializes in bodywork for chronic pain.}

Boffin is British slang for a person engaged in scientific or technical research, especially one who is highly knowledgeable but perhaps socially awkward or obsessively focused on their work. The term emerged during World War II to describe scientists working on military projects and carries a mixture of respect and gentle mockery. {The boffins in the lab finally cracked the encryption problem.} It remains primarily British, with Americans more likely to say nerd or egghead.

Boffins is British slang for scientists or technical experts, especially those doing research or working behind the scenes on complex problems. The term carries a slightly affectionate, slightly dismissive tone—suggesting brilliant but socially awkward people in lab coats: {The boffins have developed a new vaccine}. Originally wartime slang for military scientists.

A bog is wet, spongy ground, a kind of wetland. If you get bogged down, it’s possible that you are stuck in a bog, but more likely that you have stopped making progress because of obstacles or impediments. Bog is a slang term for toilet in British English.

To bogart is to selfishly take or keep something that should be shared—originally marijuana in a smoking circle: {Don't bogart that joint}. The term comes from Humphrey Bogart, whose film persona often featured a cigarette dangling from his lips. The meaning has broadened to any greedy monopolizing: {He's bogarting the remote again}.

To bogart something is to selfishly keep it to oneself, especially when sharing is expected: {Don't bogart the joint—pass it around}. The term comes from Humphrey Bogart's habit of letting cigarettes dangle from his lips in films. Originally marijuana slang, it now applies to anything someone monopolizes: {She's bogarting the remote}.

A bogey in golf is a score of one stroke over par on a hole. Beyond the links, bogey names something undesirable or troublesome—a persistent problem or source of worry. In military contexts, a bogey is an unidentified aircraft, presumed hostile until proven otherwise. British English also uses bogey for the dried nasal mucus that children (and some adults) pick from their noses. As a verb, to bogey a hole means to complete it one over par.

A bogeyman is a frightening imaginary creature used to scare children into obedience: {The bogeyman will get you if you don't behave}. By extension, any object of dread or fear, often one exaggerated or fabricated: {Communism was the bogeyman of Cold War politics}. Also spelled boogeyman or bogyman.

Bogeymen is the plural of bogeyman, a frightening imaginary creature used to scare children into good behavior. Parents might warn that the bogeyman will come if a child doesn't go to sleep or stop misbehaving. The term extends to any person or thing used as a source of fear or an object of blame, often exaggerated or imaginary: {Politicians love to invoke bogeymen to rally their base}. The spelling bogeyman is more common in American English, while boogeyman is a frequent variant.

Bogeys is the plural of bogey, which has several meanings. In golf, a bogey is a score of one stroke over par on a hole: {He finished with three bogeys and two birdies}. A bogey is also an unidentified aircraft, especially a potentially hostile one on radar. In British usage, a bogey can be a piece of dried nasal mucus, or a frightening specter—the bogeyman. To bogey a hole in golf is to score one over par on it.
Boggart is a dialectal British word for a mischievous spirit. It is used in the Harry Potter series for a spirit that takes on the appearance of whatever will frighten the observer.

Boggarts are mischievous household spirits in English folklore, particularly from Northern England. They attach themselves to homes or families, causing milk to sour, objects to disappear, and doors to slam. Unlike some spirits, boggarts supposedly follow families who try to escape them by moving. The term appears in fantasy literature, sometimes with altered meanings: {The boggart in the wardrobe turned into whatever you feared most}.

Bogged means stuck or slowed down, from the image of sinking into a bog. A vehicle gets bogged in mud; a project gets {bogged down} in bureaucracy. The phrase {bogged down} is nearly universal—without it, bogged sounds incomplete. {We got bogged down in details and missed the deadline.}

To boggle is to hesitate or waver, usually from astonishment or alarm: {The mind boggles at the scale of the universe}. Something that boggles the mind overwhelms comprehension. The word suggests a moment of mental stumbling—you encounter something so strange or vast that thought itself falters. Boggle is also a word game where players find words in a grid of lettered dice.

Boggled is the past tense of boggle, meaning to be overwhelmed or staggered, usually by something hard to comprehend: {My mind boggled at the complexity}. The phrase {the mind boggles} expresses astonishment at something difficult to believe or process. To be boggled is to be mentally stymied or dumbfounded: {I was boggled by the sheer amount of paperwork}.

Boggles is the third-person singular of boggle—to be overwhelmed or staggered by something hard to comprehend: {The mind boggles at the scale of the universe}. What boggles usually boggles the mind or imagination. The word suggests a moment of mental hesitation when confronting something too vast, strange, or complex to process easily.

Boggling describes something that overwhelms or astounds the mind—usually appearing as {mind-boggling}: {The scale of the universe is mind-boggling}. The word comes from boggle, meaning to hesitate or be startled, as if the mind recoils from something too vast or strange to process. {The boggling complexity of the tax code left him paralyzed}.

A bogie is a wheeled undercarriage assembly that swivels beneath a railway car or locomotive, allowing it to negotiate curves. The term extends to similar assemblies on tanks and other tracked vehicles. In golf, bogie (usually spelled bogey) means one stroke over par. In military slang, a bogie is an unidentified aircraft, potentially hostile.

Bogies is the plural of bogie, which has several meanings depending on context. In golf, a bogie (usually spelled bogey) is one stroke over par: {He finished with three bogies on the back nine}. In British English, a bogie is a wheeled undercarriage beneath a railway car. Bogie also means a ghostly or mischievous spirit, related to boogeyman. In military slang, a bogie is an unidentified aircraft, potentially hostile: {Radar picked up two bogies approaching from the north}.

Bogs are wetlands characterized by soft, waterlogged ground composed largely of decomposing plant matter, especially sphagnum moss. The verb bog, nearly always followed by down, means to become stuck or mired, whether literally in mud or figuratively in complications: {The project got bogged down in committee}. In British slang, bog is a crude term for a toilet, giving rise to expressions like {bog roll} for toilet paper.

Bogus means fake, counterfeit, or not genuine. Originally applied to counterfeit money, it now describes anything fraudulent or without merit: {a bogus insurance claim}, {bogus credentials}. In casual speech, bogus can simply mean bad or disappointing: {That's totally bogus}.
clues: Pretending to be the real thing

definition: Bogyman is an alternative spelling of bogeyman—a frightening imaginary creature used to scare children into obedience: {The bogyman will get you if you don't behave}. More broadly, any object of fear or dread, often exaggerated or imaginary: {Inflation has become the bogyman of economic policy}.

A bohemian is someone who lives an unconventional, artistic life, rejecting bourgeois values in favor of creative freedom and casual attitudes toward money and social norms. The term evokes artists, writers, and musicians living cheaply in garrets, prioritizing art over respectability: {She fell in with a bohemian crowd in the Village}. As an adjective, bohemian describes this lifestyle or aesthetic: {a bohemian apartment full of mismatched furniture and half-finished canvases}. (Capitalized Bohemian refers to the Czech region or its people.)

Bohemians are people who live unconventional lives, often artists, writers, or musicians who reject mainstream values and social norms in favor of creative freedom and nonconformity: {The café attracted bohemians and intellectuals}. The term evokes a lifestyle of artistic pursuit over material comfort, often associated with urban neighborhoods like Greenwich Village or Montmartre. (Capitalized Bohemians are people from Bohemia.)

Boho is short for bohemian—the unconventional, artistic lifestyle associated with writers, artists, and free spirits. As an adjective, it describes a style mixing vintage, ethnic, and handcrafted elements: {boho chic}, {a boho wedding}. The aesthetic favors flowing fabrics, earth tones, layered jewelry, and an effortlessly eclectic look.

To boil is to heat liquid until it bubbles and turns to vapor, or to cook something in boiling water: {Boil the pasta for eight minutes}. Water boils at 212°F at sea level. Emotions boil when they reach an intense state: {His anger boiled over}. To {boil down} is to reduce to essentials. A boil is also a painful, pus-filled skin infection—unrelated to the cooking sense.

Boiled describes something cooked in boiling water or other liquid: {boiled eggs}, {boiled potatoes}. The past tense of boil, it extends to anything subjected to intense heat or agitation. Figuratively, boiled can mean extremely angry: {I was boiled when I found out}. In older slang, boiled means drunk: {He came home boiled at 3 a.m.}

A boiler is a large tank or vessel in which water is heated, typically to produce steam for heating buildings or powering engines. Industrial boilers generate steam for manufacturing processes or electricity generation. In domestic settings, a boiler heats water for radiators or household use. The term also applies informally to a chicken too old and tough for roasting, suitable only for long, slow cooking in liquid—hence {boiler} as opposed to {broiler}.

A boilermaker is a worker who makes or repairs boilers and other heavy metal structures—tanks, vats, ships. The term also names a drink: a shot of whiskey followed by or dropped into a glass of beer. {He ordered a boilermaker and downed it in one go.} The drink may take its name from the workers who favored it.

A boilermaker is a worker who makes or repairs boilers and other heavy metal equipment—historically demanding, dangerous industrial work. In drinking, a boilermaker is a shot of whiskey served with or dropped into a glass of beer: {We ordered boilermakers at the dive bar}. The drink's name suggests the rough-and-ready workers who favored it.

Boilerplate is standardized text used repeatedly without change—contract clauses, legal disclaimers, or form letters. The term comes from the metal plates newspapers once used for syndicated content, which arrived ready to print. In computing, boilerplate is template code that appears in many programs with little modification. The word often carries a dismissive tone: {Skip the boilerplate and get to the actual terms}.

Boilerplate originally referred to the rolled steel plates used to make boilers, then came to mean syndicated newspaper content distributed as metal printing plates. Today boilerplate most often designates standardized text that can be reused without much change—the generic legal language in contracts, the standard paragraphs in press releases, the template code programmers drop into new projects. {The lawyer added the usual boilerplate about liability limitations.} The term often carries a slightly dismissive tone, suggesting text that's functional but unoriginal.

A boilersuit is a one-piece garment covering the torso and legs, typically worn as protective clothing for manual labor. The British term corresponds to American coveralls or jumpsuit. Originally designed for workers maintaining boilers and other dirty machinery, it zips or buttons up the front: {He pulled on his boilersuit before crawling under the truck}.

Boiling describes liquid heated to the point where it churns with bubbles and produces steam—water boils at 212°F at sea level. The word extends to intense heat generally: {It's boiling outside}. Figuratively, boiling describes barely contained anger: {She was boiling with rage}. As an intensifier, boiling hot emphasizes extreme temperature.

Boils covers both the verb and the noun. Water boils when heated to the point where it bubbles and turns to vapor. To boil something is to cook it in boiling water: {boil the pasta for ten minutes}. Figuratively, emotions boil when they reach an intense point: {His anger boiled over}. To {boil down} is to reduce to essentials. A boil is also a painful, pus-filled skin infection—an inflamed swelling that eventually ruptures.

Boing represents the sound of something springy bouncing or rebounding—a diving board, a coiled spring, a trampoline. The word is onomatopoeic, imitating the twangy vibration of elastic recoil: {The ball hit the rim and—boing—bounced away}. It often appears in cartoon contexts or playful speech.

Boink is informal for having sex, often with a playful or casual tone: {They've been boinking for months}. The word sounds cartoonish, like a sound effect, which gives it a lighthearted quality compared to cruder alternatives. Boink can also mean to hit or bump something, though the sexual sense dominates in contemporary usage.

Boisterous describes noisy, energetic, and slightly unruly behavior—the kind that comes from high spirits rather than malice. A boisterous {crowd} cheers loudly; boisterous {children} run and shout; a boisterous {party} keeps the neighbors awake. The word suggests exuberance that's barely contained, energetic but not quite out of control. Weather can also be boisterous: {boisterous winds}, {boisterous seas}.

A bola is a throwing weapon consisting of weights attached to interconnected cords. When hurled at an animal or person, the cords wrap around the target's legs or body, entangling and immobilizing them. Bolas were traditionally used by South American gauchos for hunting and catching livestock, and remain associated with that region. The weapon appears occasionally in video games and action films as an exotic restraint device.

Bold describes willingness to take risks or face challenges without fear: {a bold move}, {a bold strategy}. It can shade toward audacious or presumptuous: {That was bold of you to ask}. In design and typography, bold means visually prominent—heavy strokes that stand out: {Set the title in bold}. Bold flavors are strong and distinct. To be {bold as brass} is to act with shameless confidence.

Boldly means in a daring or confident manner, without hesitation or fear: {She boldly asked for a raise}. It can also mean strikingly or conspicuously: {The colors clashed boldly}. The phrase {to boldly go} became famous from Star Trek, making it the most recognized split infinitive in English.

Boldness is the quality of being willing to take risks or act with confidence despite potential consequences. It suggests courage that borders on audacity: {Her boldness in challenging the CEO surprised everyone}. Boldness can be admirable or reckless depending on context—a bold move might be praised as visionary or criticized as foolhardy.

A bolero is a short jacket that ends at or above the waist, often worn open and with no fastening. The garment takes its name from the bolero, a Spanish dance in triple time characterized by sharp turns and sudden pauses, typically accompanied by castanets and guitar. The dance gave rise to a musical form, most famously Ravel's orchestral piece of the same name. In Latin America, bolero also refers to a slow, romantic style of song that emerged in Cuba.

Boleros names two distinct items of clothing and music. The garment is a short jacket ending above the waist, often worn open over a dress or blouse. The dance is a slow, romantic Latin ballroom style originating in Spain and popular throughout Latin America, or the music accompanying it. {She paired the black bolero with her evening gown.} {They danced a bolero under the stars.}

A bollard is a short, sturdy post set into the ground to control traffic or protect areas from vehicles. Bollards line sidewalks, guard storefronts, and mark boundaries in parking lots. On ships and docks, a bollard is a post for securing mooring lines: {The crew looped the rope around the bollard}.

Bollards are short, sturdy posts set in the ground to control traffic or protect areas from vehicles. They line sidewalks, guard storefronts, and block cars from pedestrian zones: {The city installed bollards after the attack}. On ships and docks, a bollard is a thick post for securing mooring lines.

Bollocked can mean severely reprimanded: {I got bollocked for missing the deadline}. In slang, it also means drunk or ruined: {We got completely bollocked last night}. {The whole project is bollocked now}.

A bollocking is a severe reprimand, a harsh dressing-down: {He got a bollocking from his manager}. The word implies real anger and consequences, not just mild criticism. To give someone a bollocking is to tear into them verbally: {She bollocked him in front of the whole team}.

Bollocks is vulgar British slang for testicles. More commonly, bollocks means nonsense or rubbish: {That's complete bollocks}. As an exclamation, it expresses frustration or disbelief: {Oh bollocks, I left my wallet at home}. {Bollocks to that} is dismissive refusal. Confusingly, {the dog's bollocks} means something excellent—the best of its kind: {That curry is the dog's bollocks}. The word is versatile, vulgar, and quintessentially British.

A bolo is a large single-edged knife used in the Philippines and other parts of Southeast Asia, similar to a machete, used for cutting vegetation and as a weapon. In American usage, a bolo tie (or bolo) is a cord necklace with a decorative clasp, worn as Western-style neckwear: {He wore a silver bolo with his suit jacket}. In law enforcement slang, BOLO is an acronym for "be on the lookout."

Bologna is a seasoned smoked sausage made from finely ground meat, typically beef and pork. In American usage, it's the familiar pink lunch meat sliced for sandwiches: {a bologna and cheese sandwich}. The word is often spelled and pronounced "baloney." Separately, bologna is slang for nonsense or lies: {That's a load of bologna}—though "baloney" is the more common spelling for this sense. (Capitalized Bologna is the Italian city.)

Bolognaise is a meat sauce for pasta, originating from Bologna, Italy. The authentic version (ragù alla bolognese) is a slow-cooked mixture of ground meat, tomatoes, wine, and aromatics, traditionally served with tagliatelle. Outside Italy, bolognaise typically means any tomato-meat sauce served over spaghetti: {spaghetti bolognaise}. Also spelled bolognese.

Bolognese is a meat sauce originating from Bologna, Italy, typically made with ground beef, tomatoes, onions, and wine, simmered slowly. It's the traditional sauce for tagliatelle and lasagna: {spaghetti bolognese}, {I made a bolognese from scratch}. The term also describes anything in the style of Bologna's cuisine.

Boloney is nonsense or foolish talk: {That's a load of boloney}. The word likely derives from bologna, the sausage—something processed and of questionable composition. The spelling boloney emphasizes the slang sense, while bologna typically refers to the lunch meat, though both spellings work for either meaning.

Bolshie (also bolshy) is British slang for deliberately uncooperative or rebellious: {She got bolshie when they asked her to work late}. The word derives from Bolshevik but has lost most of its political edge, now describing anyone stubbornly resistant to authority or requests. It carries a tone of exasperated affection rather than genuine hostility.

A bolster is a long cylindrical pillow or cushion, typically placed under other pillows or used for back support. The word extends to any structural support—a bolster beneath a beam, a bolster in a saddle. The verb dominates modern usage: to bolster is to strengthen, support, or prop up: {The new evidence bolstered her case}. You bolster confidence, bolster defenses, bolster an argument. The physical prop becomes metaphorical reinforcement.

Bolsters means supports or strengthens, often in an abstract sense: {The new evidence bolsters her argument}, {Extra funding bolstered the program}. A bolster is also a long pillow or cushion, typically placed across a bed for support. The verb sense extends from this physical propping up to metaphorical reinforcement of ideas, confidence, or positions.

A bolt may be a threaded fastener (nuts and bolts), an arrow (shoot a bolt), a flash of lightening, or a sliding mechanism: Pull on the bolt to unlock the door. One sense of the verb bolt is related to these meanings: to bolt is to move or depart rapidly: He bolted from the scene of the crime. If a plant bolts, it produces seed earlier than is desired. A different verb bolt is used only of flour; if you bolt flour, you sift it through a cloth or sieve.

Boltcutters are heavy-duty hand tools with long handles and short, powerful jaws designed to cut through padlocks, chains, bolts, and wire fencing. The long handles provide leverage to shear metal that ordinary pliers can't touch. Associated with both legitimate work and breaking into places: {Someone had taken boltcutters to the chain-link fence}.

Bolted describes something secured with a bolt—a metal fastener or sliding bar: {a bolted door}, {bolted to the floor}. More commonly, bolted means having fled suddenly: {The horse bolted when the gun fired}, {She bolted from the room}. To bolt food is to eat it hastily, so bolted can describe food gulped down without chewing. In plant terminology, bolted describes vegetables that have prematurely gone to seed: {The lettuce bolted in the heat}.

A bolthole is a place of escape or refuge—somewhere to retreat when things get difficult. The term comes from holes that allow rabbits and other burrowing animals to bolt from predators. In British usage especially, it describes a private hideaway: {She kept a cottage in Wales as a bolthole from London life}. Also spelled bolt-hole.

Boltholes is the plural of bolthole—a place of escape or refuge, somewhere you can retreat when things get difficult. The term originally referred to a hole through which an animal could bolt to safety. Now it usually describes a secondary residence or hideaway: {They kept a cottage in Cornwall as a bolthole from London life}. The word is more common in British than American English.

Bolting covers several actions united by sudden movement or securing. A horse bolts when it runs off unexpectedly; a person bolts from a room in alarm or haste. To bolt food is to swallow it quickly without chewing: {He bolted his lunch and ran}. Bolting also means fastening with a bolt—a metal pin or bar: {bolting the door shut}. In gardening, bolting describes plants that shoot up prematurely to produce seeds, usually ruining the crop: {The lettuce is bolting in this heat}.

Bolts are threaded metal fasteners used with nuts to hold things together, or sliding bars that secure doors and windows. A bolt of lightning is a sudden discharge of electricity. A bolt of fabric is a roll. To bolt is to secure with a bolt, to run suddenly {The horse bolted}, or to eat quickly {He bolted his dinner}. Someone who {bolts upright} snaps suddenly to attention. To {make a bolt for} something is to dash toward it.

A bomb is primarily an explosive device, usually used as a weapon. The bomb is the atomic bomb, specifically in contexts of whether a country has one or not. As a verb, bomb means drop bombs on. All extended meanings of bomb reference the destructive nature of the core meaning and the inevitable negative result. A work of art or performance is a bomb when it fails spectacularly. By contrast, the slang expression da bomb characterizes something that is wildly successful or appealing: Her newest movie is really da bomb.

To bombard is to attack with artillery fire or bombs—a sustained assault: {Allied forces bombarded the fortifications for three days}. The word extends to any overwhelming barrage: bombarded with {questions}, bombarded with {emails}, bombarded with {information}. In physics, to bombard is to direct a stream of particles at a target.
