The spelling brake is also used for some archaic and infrequent words in English, the commonest of which is a kind of fern.

Brakes are devices that slow or stop motion, typically by applying friction to wheels or axles. A car's brakes press pads against rotating discs; a bicycle's brakes squeeze the wheel rim. To brake is to apply brakes: {She braked hard at the yellow light}. Figuratively, to {put the brakes on} something is to slow or halt it: {The recession put the brakes on expansion plans}.

Braking is the act of slowing or stopping by applying brakes. The term appears in contexts involving vehicles, machinery, or any system with brakes: {The truck's braking distance increases on wet roads}. Braking can be gradual or sudden: {Hard braking caused the tires to skid}. The word also appears in compound forms: {braking system}, {regenerative braking}.

A bralette is a lightweight, unstructured bra—typically wireless, unpadded, and made of soft fabric or lace. Bralettes prioritize comfort and aesthetics over support, often designed to be seen under or instead of clothing: {She wore a lace bralette under an open cardigan}. They're popular for lounging, layering, or as alternatives to traditional bras.

Bramble refers to prickly shrubs of the rose family, especially blackberries and raspberries, or the tangled thickets they form. The thorny, scrambling growth makes brambles difficult to navigate: {We pushed through the brambles at the edge of the field}. Figuratively, a bramble suggests something thorny or entangled: {a bramble of legal complications}.

Brambles are thorny, sprawling shrubs—especially blackberries and raspberries—or the prickly thickets they form. The word evokes wild, tangled growth that catches at skin and clothing: {We pushed through the brambles at the edge of the field}. Bramble can refer to a single plant or to the whole mass of intertwined growth.

Bran is the outer layer of cereal grains—wheat, oats, rice—removed during milling to produce refined flour. It's high in fiber and often added back to foods for nutritional value: {bran muffins}, {oat bran cereal}. What was once discarded as animal feed is now marketed as a health food.

A branch is a limb extending from a tree's trunk, or any similar division from a main body. Rivers have branches, as do roads, families, and organizations: {The company opened a new branch in Denver}. Fields of study branch into specializations. To branch out is to expand into new areas: {She branched out from acting into directing}.

Branches are limbs extending from a tree trunk or main stem. The word extends to anything that divides from a main body: a river branch, a branch of government, a bank branch, a branch of study. To branch is to divide or spread outward: {The road branches ahead}. To {branch out} is to expand into new areas: {The company branched out into software}.

Branching describes something that divides into separate paths or parts, like tree limbs or blood vessels. In computing, branching is when code takes different paths based on conditions, or when developers create parallel versions of a project: {The branching logic handles errors differently}. Figuratively, branching suggests spreading outward: {Her research kept branching into new areas}.

Various meanings of brand can be summarized under the idea of distinguishing mark. A brand on an animal is an enduring mark made by its owner: The brand on this cow means it’s from the Lazy Z Ranch. Such an animal has been branded. A brand is also a distinct product or line of products that share a name and other distinctive marks, such as a logo: I’m loyal to the General Motors brand. A product or service that has been branded has been distinguished in this way by its maker. When brand is attributed to a person, it refers to their reputation, character, and style.

Branded describes something marked with a brand—a distinctive symbol burned or stamped to show ownership or origin. Cattle are branded to identify their owner. Branded products carry a company's name or logo, distinguishing them from generic alternatives: {branded merchandise}, {branded content}. In marketing, branded emphasizes association with a recognizable identity. Historically, criminals and enslaved people were branded on the skin as permanent marks of status or punishment.

Branding is the practice of creating a distinctive identity for a product, company, or organization through names, logos, design, and messaging. Originally literal—burning a mark into cattle or goods to show ownership—branding now refers to shaping public perception: {The company invested heavily in branding}. A brand is both the identity itself and the reputation it carries.

To brandish is to wave or flourish something, especially a weapon, in a threatening or dramatic way: {He brandished a knife at the security guard}. The gesture is meant to intimidate or display aggression. Figuratively, someone might brandish credentials or authority to make a point: {She brandished her PhD whenever anyone questioned her expertise}.

Brandished is the past tense of brandish, meaning to wave or flourish something—usually a weapon—in a threatening or dramatic way: {He brandished a knife at the cashier}. The gesture is meant to intimidate or display aggression. Figuratively, someone might brandish credentials or evidence to make a forceful point: {She brandished her diploma at anyone who questioned her expertise}.

Brandishing is waving or flourishing something, typically a weapon, in a threatening or excited manner: {He was arrested for brandishing a knife}. The gesture is meant to intimidate or signal readiness to use force. Figuratively, people brandish credentials, statistics, or arguments—displaying them aggressively to make a point: {She brandished her PhD at anyone who disagreed}.
clues: Flourishing something in a threatening way

definition: Brands are distinctive names, symbols, or designs that identify products or services and distinguish them from competitors. A brand encompasses not just visual identity but also reputation and the emotional associations consumers have with it—{brand loyalty}, {brand recognition}. Companies invest heavily in building and protecting their brands. As a verb, brand means to mark with an identifying symbol, originally by burning a mark onto livestock or, punitively, onto human skin. To be branded a {traitor} or {liar} is to be publicly labeled as one.

Brandy is a spirit distilled from wine or fermented fruit juice. Grape brandy is the standard; fruit brandies specify their source: {apple brandy}, {cherry brandy}. The drink is traditionally sipped after dinner or used in cooking. {She warmed the brandy in her hands before drinking.} (Capitalized Brandy is a given name.)

Bras is the plural of bra, the undergarment that supports a woman's breasts. {She tried on several bras before finding one that fit}. The word is a shortened form of brassiere, now the standard term in everyday speech.

Brash describes behavior that is bold to the point of rudeness—confident but lacking tact or restraint. A brash young executive might interrupt senior colleagues or dismiss their ideas. The word suggests impulsiveness and insufficient respect for others: {His brash manner alienated potential allies}. Brash can also describe things that are loud or garish: {brash colors}, {brash music}.

Brashness is bold, assertive behavior that borders on reckless or insensitive. It suggests acting without proper consideration for consequences or others' feelings: {His brashness in the meeting alienated potential allies}. The quality can read as confidence or rudeness depending on context—what strikes some as refreshing directness strikes others as tactless aggression.

The metal alloy (made of copper and zinc) called brass is present, literally or figuratively, in most of its meanings. Wind instruments made of metal are collectively called brass. The top officials of a military or other organization are called the brass, a metonym for the decorations they wear. Aside from this, brass does not share any of the prestigious associations that gold and silver have. Informally, brass is a brazen attitude, or another term for money.

A brasserie is a French-style restaurant or café serving simple, hearty meals in an informal atmosphere. Unlike more formal French restaurants, brasseries typically offer a limited menu of traditional dishes—steak frites, onion soup, roast chicken—served throughout the day: {We grabbed a late lunch at the brasserie on the corner}.

Brassy describes something loud, bold, and somewhat harsh—like the sound of brass instruments. A brassy voice or laugh is strident and unrefined. Brassy colors have the yellowish gleam of brass. Applied to people, especially women, brassy suggests aggressive confidence that borders on vulgarity: {a brassy blonde}, {her brassy manner}. The word carries a whiff of cheapness or showiness.

A brat is a child who behaves badly—whiny, demanding, or spoiled: {Their kids are such brats}. The word carries affectionate exasperation as often as genuine criticism. In adult contexts, brat describes someone acting childishly entitled. A brat is also a type of sausage, short for bratwurst. In BDSM, a brat is a submissive who playfully defies their dominant. (Capitalized Brat refers to the 2024 Charli XCX album and cultural phenomenon.)

Brats is the plural of brat—a child who behaves badly or gets whatever they want: {Those brats broke my window}. The word carries affection when parents use it about their own children. A military brat is someone who grew up in a military family, moving frequently between bases. Brats is also short for bratwurst, the German sausage: {We grilled brats for the cookout}.

Bratty describes behavior typical of a brat—spoiled, demanding, or petulant. A bratty child whines when denied candy; a bratty adult sulks when they don't get their way. The word often carries affectionate exasperation rather than genuine condemnation: {She's being bratty because she's tired}. In kink contexts, bratty describes a submissive who playfully defies or provokes their dominant.

Bratwurst is a German sausage made from pork, beef, or veal, typically seasoned with spices like nutmeg, ginger, and caraway. The sausage is usually grilled or pan-fried and served in a bun with mustard and sauerkraut: {We grilled bratwursts for the cookout}. Often shortened to brat.

Bravado is a bold or swaggering display of confidence, often masking fear or uncertainty. It suggests performance rather than genuine courage—the loud boasting before a fight, the defiant pose when cornered: {His bravado crumbled when they called his bluff}. The word carries a note of skepticism about whether the boldness is real.

Brave describes a willingness to face danger, pain, or difficulty without giving way to fear. A brave {soldier} charges into battle; a brave {decision} risks consequences for the sake of principle. The word suggests courage that's active rather than passive—not just enduring hardship but confronting it. To brave something is to face it boldly: {She braved the storm to reach the hospital}. The noun brave, now dated, referred to a Native American warrior.
clues: Bold in the face of peril

definition: Braved is the past tense of brave, meaning to face or endure something dangerous, difficult, or unpleasant with courage. {She braved the storm to get home.} {Protesters braved tear gas and rubber bullets.} The word implies deliberate confrontation with adversity rather than mere survival of it—you brave something when you choose to face it despite knowing the risks.

Bravehearts are people who show courage, especially in difficult or dangerous circumstances. The term carries a romantic or admiring tone, evoking warriors or heroes who act boldly despite fear: {The bravehearts who stormed the beach changed history}. Sometimes used ironically for minor acts of daring.

Bravery is the quality of facing danger, pain, or difficulty without giving way to fear. It suggests deliberate courage rather than mere recklessness: {The firefighters showed remarkable bravery}. Bravery can be physical or moral—standing up for principles requires bravery too: {It took bravery to speak out against her own party}.

Braves is the third-person singular of brave as a verb, meaning to face or endure something dangerous or unpleasant with courage: {She braves the cold every morning to walk her dog}. As a plural noun, braves is a dated and now offensive term for Native American warriors, surviving mainly in the name of the Atlanta Braves baseball team.

Bravo is an exclamation of approval and admiration, shouted especially after a performance: {The audience cried bravo as the soprano finished her aria}. It comes from Italian and retains associations with opera and classical music, though it can be used for any impressive feat. The NATO phonetic alphabet uses bravo for the letter B. (Capitalized Bravo is a cable television network.)

Bravura is brilliant, showy skill—especially in musical or artistic performance. A bravura {passage} demands virtuoso technique; a bravura {performance} dazzles with technical mastery. The word extends beyond the arts: {a bravura display of diplomatic maneuvering}. Bravura suggests confidence bordering on flamboyance, execution so assured it invites admiration.

A brawl is a noisy, chaotic fight involving multiple people—the kind that breaks out in bars or at sporting events: {A brawl erupted in the stands after the game}. Unlike a duel or boxing match, a brawl is disorderly and unregulated. To brawl is to engage in such fighting. The word can extend to heated verbal disputes.

A brawler is someone who fights, especially in rough, disorderly scuffles rather than formal combat. The word suggests a person prone to or skilled at physical altercations: {He was a barroom brawler in his younger days}. In video games, a brawler is a fighting game or a character class built for close-quarters combat.

Brawlers is the plural of brawler—someone who engages in rough, physical fights, typically spontaneous and unrefined rather than organized combat. The word suggests scrappy aggression: {The bar was full of brawlers looking for trouble}. In gaming, brawlers often refers to fighting games or characters built for close-range combat.

Brawling describes noisy, rough fighting—the kind that spills out of bars or erupts at sporting events. It suggests physical combat that's chaotic rather than organized: {brawling fans}, {brawling in the streets}. The word can also describe anything loud and turbulent: {a brawling stream}.

Brawls are noisy, disorderly fights, typically involving multiple people in a public place: {A brawl broke out in the parking lot after the game}. The word suggests chaotic physical conflict rather than organized combat—bar brawls, street brawls, bench-clearing brawls in sports. To brawl is to engage in such fighting.

Brawn refers to muscular strength and power, especially of the kind developed through physical labor or training. It often appears in contrast with brain, suggesting a distinction between physical and intellectual capability: {The job requires more brawn than brains}. In British usage, brawn is also a cold cut made from the meat of a pig's head set in gelatin—what Americans call head cheese. Someone described as brawny has well-developed muscles and appears physically powerful.

Bray is the loud, harsh cry of a donkey—that distinctive hee-haw sound. The word extends to similarly grating noises: {His laugh was more of a bray}. To bray is to make such a sound, whether you're a donkey or a person speaking loudly and unpleasantly: {He brayed his opinions at anyone who would listen}.

Braying is the harsh, loud cry of a donkey—that distinctive hee-haw sound. The word extends to any similarly grating noise, especially unpleasant human sounds: {braying laughter}, {braying voices}. To describe someone as braying suggests they're loud, obnoxious, and oblivious to how unpleasant they sound.

Brays are the harsh, loud cries of a donkey—that distinctive hee-haw sound. The word extends to any similarly harsh or grating noise: {the brays of car horns in traffic}, {brays of laughter from the back of the room}. As a verb form, brays describes the act of making such sounds: {The donkey brays at dawn}.

Brazen describes behavior that is bold and shameless, showing no attempt to hide wrongdoing or impropriety. A brazen {lie} is one told without apparent guilt; a brazen {thief} operates openly rather than covertly. The word originally meant "made of brass," and this metallic sense survives in phrases like brazen {trumpets}. To brazen something out is to face a difficult situation with defiant confidence rather than backing down: {She decided to brazen it out despite the accusations}.

Brazenly means in a bold, shameless manner—openly doing something typically hidden or disapproved of: {She brazenly lied to the committee}, {He brazenly cheated on the exam while the teacher watched}. The word implies not just wrongdoing but a refusal to conceal it, suggesting defiance or indifference to judgment.

Brazenness is bold, shameless audacity—behaving without embarrassment or apology when others might expect contrition. The word carries disapproval: {The brazenness of the theft shocked everyone}. Someone acting with brazenness doesn't try to hide wrongdoing or minimize it; they proceed as if entitled to do exactly as they please.

A brazier is a metal container for holding burning coals or charcoal, used for cooking or heating. Historically, braziers provided warmth in rooms without fireplaces or chimneys. Modern braziers are typically outdoor fixtures for grilling or ambiance: {We gathered around the brazier on the patio}. The word is unrelated to brassiere, though the spelling invites confusion.

Braziers are metal containers for holding burning coals or charcoal, used for heating or cooking. Before central heating, braziers warmed rooms and outdoor spaces: {Workers huddled around a brazier to keep warm}. The word also refers to people who work with brass, though this sense is rare.

A breach is a break or gap in something—a wall, a barrier, a defense. The word extends to violations of agreements or duties: a breach of {contract}, a breach of {trust}, a breach of {etiquette}. To breach is to break through or violate: {Whales breached the surface}; {The company breached its agreement}. A security breach means unauthorized access. To {step into the breach} is to fill a gap left by someone's absence.

Breached is the past tense of breach—to break through, violate, or fail to uphold. A wall can be breached by attackers, a contract breached by a party who doesn't fulfill its terms, trust breached by betrayal. {Hackers breached the company's security systems.} {The whale breached and crashed back into the water}—here meaning to leap above the surface.

A breacher is someone who breaches—breaks through barriers or violates boundaries. In military and law enforcement contexts, a breacher specializes in forced entry, using explosives, battering rams, or other tools to break down doors and walls: {The breacher blew the hinges and the team moved in}. The term also applies to anyone who breaches rules, contracts, or security.

Breaches is the plural of breach, a gap or break in something that should be continuous or intact. A breach in a wall, a breach in security, or a breach of protocol all suggest something has been broken through or violated. {The storm caused several breaches in the levee.} As a verb form, breaches means to break through or violate: {The company routinely breaches its own privacy policy.} A whale that breaches leaps dramatically out of the water.

Breaching is the act of breaking through or violating something. Security forces breach walls or doors to gain entry. Whales breach when they leap from the water. A contract is breached when its terms are violated: {The company was sued for breaching the agreement}. A breach in a dam or defensive wall is a dangerous opening.

Bread is a staple food made from flour and water, typically leavened with yeast and baked. It comes in countless varieties—sliced sandwich bread, crusty loaves, flatbreads, rolls. {Breaking bread} with someone means sharing a meal. Bread is also slang for money: {I need to make some bread}. The verb means to coat food with breadcrumbs before cooking: {breaded chicken cutlets}.

Breadbasket has meanings centered on providing bread or holding it. A breadbasket is a container for serving bread at the table. By extension, a breadbasket is a region that produces large quantities of grain: {Ukraine was once the breadbasket of Europe}. Informally, breadbasket means stomach or belly—where the bread goes: {He took a punch to the breadbasket}.

A breadboard is a board for slicing bread, or a prototype board used in electronics. The electronics sense dominates: a breadboard has a grid of holes for inserting component leads and wires, allowing circuits to be assembled and tested without soldering. {I built my first amplifier on a breadboard before committing to a printed circuit.} To breadboard is to prototype this way.

Breadboards are flat boards used for constructing experimental electronic circuits without soldering. Components and wires push into a grid of holes connected by metal strips underneath, allowing quick assembly and modification: {I prototyped the amplifier on a breadboard before designing the PCB}. The name comes from an earlier sense—a wooden board for slicing bread—which hobbyists once used as bases for mounting components.

A breadbox is a container, usually kept on a kitchen counter, for storing bread to keep it fresh. The standard American breadbox—roughly a cubic foot—serves as an informal unit of comparison for size: {It's about as big as a breadbox}. This phrase became a cliché through the guessing game Twenty Questions, where "Is it bigger than a breadbox?" was a stock opening move.

A breadcrumb is a small fragment of bread, the kind that falls from a loaf when sliced or accumulates at the bottom of a toaster. In the plural, breadcrumbs are used for coating foods before frying: {chicken coated in breadcrumbs}. Figuratively, breadcrumbs are small hints or pieces of information left as a trail—from the fairy tale where children mark their path through the forest. In web design, breadcrumbs are navigational links showing your location within a site's hierarchy. To breadcrumb someone is to string them along with sporadic, minimal attention: {He kept breadcrumbing her with occasional texts}.

Breadcrumbing is sending occasional, noncommittal messages to keep someone interested without genuine intention of pursuing a relationship. The term evokes Hansel and Gretel's trail—just enough to lead someone on: {He texts me once a week but never makes plans. Classic breadcrumbing}. Common in dating contexts but applies to any situation where someone strings another along with minimal effort.

Breadcrumbs are small pieces of dried or toasted bread, used as coating for fried foods or as a topping: {chicken cutlets dredged in breadcrumbs}. In computing and web design, breadcrumbs are a navigation trail showing your path through a site's hierarchy, letting you retrace your steps. The term alludes to the trail Hansel and Gretel left in the forest. To {leave breadcrumbs} is to drop hints or clues leading somewhere.

Breaded describes food that has been coated in breadcrumbs before cooking, typically by dipping first in egg or another binding liquid. The coating creates a crispy exterior when fried or baked. {Breaded chicken cutlets are a weeknight staple.} Almost any protein or vegetable can be breaded, from shrimp to zucchini, though the technique is most associated with fried foods like schnitzel or fish sticks.

Breadfruit is a large, round, starchy fruit from a tropical tree native to the Pacific islands. When cooked, its pale flesh has a texture and mild flavor reminiscent of bread or potatoes, making it a dietary staple in many tropical regions: {roasted breadfruit}, {breadfruit curry}. The tree itself is also called breadfruit.

Breading is a coating of breadcrumbs or similar dry ingredients applied to food before frying or baking. The process typically involves dipping in flour, then egg, then crumbs: {The chicken needs breading before it goes in the fryer}. Breading creates a crispy outer layer that seals in moisture.

A breadline is a queue of people waiting to receive free food, typically bread, from a charity or government agency during times of economic hardship. The image of breadlines became iconic during the Great Depression. The phrase {on the breadline} means living in poverty, barely able to afford basic necessities: {Many families are just one paycheck away from the breadline}.

Breadlines are queues of people waiting to receive free food, typically bread or basic provisions, distributed by charities or government agencies during times of economic hardship. The term evokes images of the Great Depression, when unemployed workers lined up for handouts. Today breadlines appear both literally, at food banks and soup kitchens, and figuratively to suggest widespread poverty or economic collapse: {If this policy continues, we'll all be standing in breadlines}.

A breadstick is a long, thin piece of bread, typically crisp and dry, served as an appetizer or alongside meals at restaurants, especially Italian ones. Breadsticks range from pencil-thin and crunchy to soft and chewy, sometimes brushed with garlic butter or topped with seeds. {The waiter brought a basket of breadsticks while we looked at the menu.}

Breadsticks are long, thin sticks of crispy or soft bread, often served as an appetizer or alongside meals at Italian restaurants. They may be plain, salted, or flavored with garlic or herbs. {The waiter brought a basket of breadsticks to the table.}

Breadth is width—the measurement of something from side to side: {the breadth of the river}. More often, breadth describes range or scope: {breadth of knowledge}, {breadth of experience}. Where depth suggests going deep into one area, breadth suggests covering wide ground. {The curriculum lacks breadth.} A {hair's breadth} is an extremely small distance or margin.

A breadwinner is the person whose income supports a household. The term evokes traditional family structures where one spouse—historically the husband—earned money while the other managed the home: {She became the family's breadwinner after her husband's injury}. The word remains common even as dual-income households have become the norm.

Breadwinners are the members of a household who earn money to support the family. The term evokes the image of bringing home bread—basic sustenance. Traditionally applied to fathers in single-income households, it now describes anyone whose earnings are primary: {Both parents are breadwinners in most families today}. A sole breadwinner carries the full financial burden.

Break is highly varied in its noun and verb meanings and it also forms the foundation of several frequent phrasal verbs, such as break down, break in, and break off. The ideas common to all meanings of break are discontinuity or separation. You might think that the things most often broken are tangible, like windows or vases, but the words that most often follow the verb break are abstract, such as law, record, rule, and heart. The most popular meaning of break as a noun is not about things being broken; it’s about discontinuity in time or activity: Take a break to think about it.

Breakable describes something capable of being broken—fragile enough that impact or pressure could shatter, crack, or damage it. The word often appears as a warning or consideration: {Pack the breakables separately}. As a noun, breakables are fragile items requiring careful handling: glassware, ceramics, delicate ornaments.

Breakaway describes something that separates or breaks off from a larger group. A breakaway faction splits from a political party; a breakaway republic declares independence. In sports, a breakaway is a sudden rush toward the goal, having broken free from defenders: {She scored on a breakaway}. As an adjective, breakaway also describes objects designed to break apart on impact for safety: {breakaway glass}, {breakaway bases}.

Breakaways are the plural of breakaway—something that separates from a larger group or entity. In politics, a breakaway faction splits from an established party: {The breakaways formed their own caucus}. In sports, breakaways are fast attacks where a player gets past defenders toward the goal. Breakaways can also be objects designed to separate on impact, like theatrical props or safety equipment.

Breakbeat is electronic dance music built around syncopated drum patterns—typically sampled from the "break" sections of funk and soul records where percussion takes the spotlight. The chopped, looped rhythms give breakbeat its driving, irregular feel, distinguishing it from the steady four-on-the-floor pulse of house or techno. The style spawned genres like drum and bass, jungle, and big beat.

Breakbeats are drum patterns sampled from the instrumental breaks of funk, soul, and R&B records—the moments when other instruments drop out and the drummer plays alone. These looped rhythms became the foundation of hip-hop, jungle, drum and bass, and other electronic genres. The most famous is the "Amen break," a six-second drum solo sampled thousands of times. {The producer chopped up breakbeats to create the track's backbone.}

Breakdance is a style of street dance that emerged from hip-hop culture, characterized by acrobatic moves performed close to the ground—spins, freezes, and power moves like headspins and windmills. As a verb, to breakdance is to perform this style: {He learned to breakdance in the '80s}. Also spelled break-dance or written as two words.

A breakdancer is someone who performs breakdancing—an acrobatic street dance style originating in 1970s New York hip-hop culture. Breakdancers execute spins, freezes, and floor work, often in competitive battles or ciphers: {The breakdancers took turns in the center of the circle}.

Breakdancers are people who perform breakdancing—an acrobatic street dance style that emerged from hip-hop culture in the 1970s. The term covers anyone from casual practitioners to competitive professionals: {Breakdancers gathered in the park to battle}. The dance involves spins, freezes, and athletic floor work.

Breakdancing is an acrobatic style of street dance that emerged from hip-hop culture, featuring athletic moves performed close to the ground—spins, freezes, and fluid footwork. Dancers (b-boys and b-girls) often compete in battles, taking turns showing off increasingly difficult combinations: {He learned to breakdance in the park}. Also called breaking.

Breakdown is a failure or collapse—of machinery, negotiations, relationships, or mental health. A car has a breakdown when it stops working; a person has a breakdown when stress overwhelms them. Breakdown also means analysis by components: {a breakdown of costs}, {a breakdown of the vote by demographic}. In compounds, it becomes break down: {Let me break down the numbers for you}.

Breakdowns are failures or collapses. A mechanical breakdown stops a machine from working. A breakdown in communication means people aren't understanding each other. A nervous breakdown is a period of severe mental distress. The word also means an analysis that separates something into parts: {Give me a breakdown of the costs}. In some contexts, breakdowns are energetic dance moves or musical passages.

A breaker is something that breaks, in any of that verb's many senses. A wave that breaks on the shore is a breaker. A circuit breaker interrupts electrical flow when current exceeds safe levels. In CB radio culture, "breaker" announces someone wanting to join a conversation: {Breaker, breaker, anyone got eyes on traffic ahead?} Compound forms like lawbreaker, dealbreaker, and icebreaker specify what's being broken or disrupted.

Breakers are waves that crash onto shore, their crests collapsing into foam as they meet shallow water or obstacles. The term extends to anything that breaks: a circuit breaker interrupts electrical flow; a breaker at a salvage yard dismantles ships. In CB radio slang, {breaker, breaker} announces someone seeking to join a conversation.

Breakeven is the point at which gains equal losses, resulting in neither profit nor loss. A business reaches breakeven when revenue covers all costs: {We need to sell 500 units to break even}. As an adjective, it describes this threshold: {breakeven point}, {breakeven analysis}. Often written as two words when used as a verb phrase.

Breakfast is the first meal of the day, typically eaten in the morning. The word reflects the idea of breaking the overnight fast. Breakfast foods vary by culture but often include eggs, bread, cereal, or pastries: {We grabbed a quick breakfast before work}. As a verb, to breakfast is to eat this meal: {They breakfasted on the terrace}.

Breakfasts is the plural of breakfast, the first meal of the day, typically eaten in the morning. It can refer to multiple instances of the meal or to different types of morning fare: {The hotel offers both continental and full English breakfasts}. As a verb in the third person singular, breakfasts means eats breakfast: {She breakfasts early before her commute}.

Breaking is the act of causing something to separate into pieces, or the moment when something gives way. It extends to violations ({breaking the law}), interruptions ({breaking news}), and transitions ({breaking free}, {day is breaking}). In hip-hop culture, breaking is a style of acrobatic street dance, also called breakdancing.

Breakneck describes a dangerously fast pace or speed, suggesting recklessness that could result in a broken neck. It appears almost exclusively before the noun it modifies: {The project proceeded at breakneck speed}. Despite the violent imagery, breakneck is often used with a hint of admiration for ambitious velocity rather than genuine warning.

A breakout is an escape, especially from confinement: {a prison breakout}. The word extends to any sudden emergence from constraint—a disease breakout spreads rapidly, a breakout {session} at a conference splits from the main group. In entertainment and sports, a breakout {role} or breakout {season} marks someone's transition from obscurity to prominence. As an adjective, breakout describes unexpected success: {a breakout hit}, {a breakout star}.

Breakouts are instances of breaking out—escaping confinement, emerging suddenly, or erupting. A prisoner might attempt a breakout from jail. In skin care, a breakout is an outbreak of acne or blemishes: {I always get breakouts when I'm stressed}. In business and finance, a breakout occurs when a stock price moves beyond an established trading range, signaling potential momentum. The term also describes separating into smaller groups for focused discussion: {We'll do breakouts after the main presentation}.

A breakpoint is a marker set by a programmer that tells a debugger to pause execution at a specific line of code, allowing inspection of variables and program state: {I set a breakpoint to see why the loop was failing}. In responsive web design, breakpoints are the screen widths at which a layout changes to accommodate different devices. More generally, a breakpoint is any threshold where behavior changes significantly.

A breakroom is a designated space in a workplace where employees can rest, eat lunch, or take breaks from their duties. It typically contains tables, chairs, a refrigerator, and a microwave: {Someone left fish in the breakroom microwave again}. Also spelled as two words: break room.

Breaks is the plural of break—pauses, interruptions, or fractures: {We took several breaks during the hike}, {breaks in the clouds}. In music and dance, breaks are rhythmic passages where instruments drop out, leaving drums or bass exposed—the foundation of breakdancing and hip-hop sampling. {Give me a break} asks for leniency or expresses disbelief. {That's the breaks} accepts misfortune philosophically.

A breakthrough is a sudden advance or important discovery that overcomes an obstacle or barrier. The word suggests a decisive moment when progress that was blocked finally occurs: {a breakthrough in cancer research}, {a major diplomatic breakthrough}. Scientists, negotiators, and researchers all pursue breakthroughs. The term can describe anything from solving a stubborn problem to a personal moment of clarity.

Breakthroughs are significant advances or discoveries that overcome obstacles previously blocking progress. The term implies a barrier that has been penetrated—whether in science, medicine, technology, or personal development. {Researchers announced a breakthrough in cancer treatment.} A breakthrough can also describe a sudden moment of understanding or success after prolonged effort: {After months of therapy, she finally had a breakthrough.} The word carries connotations of hard-won achievement rather than gradual improvement.

A breakup is the ending of a romantic relationship: {The breakup was hard on both of them}. The term extends to any dissolution or separation—the breakup of a {company}, of the {Soviet Union}, of {ice} on a frozen river in spring. To break up is to end such a relationship or to separate into pieces.

Breakups are endings of romantic relationships. The term implies emotional weight—a clean split rather than a gradual fade. A breakup can be mutual or one-sided, amicable or bitter: {She's still not over the breakup}. The word extends to any dissolution: {the breakup of the Soviet Union}, {the breakup of a business partnership}.

A breakwater is a barrier built to protect a harbor or shoreline from the force of waves. Breakwaters are typically made of stone, concrete, or timber, extending into the water to create calmer conditions for boats and prevent erosion: {The fishing boats sheltered behind the breakwater during the storm}.

Breakwaters are barriers built to protect harbors, beaches, or shorelines from the force of waves. Typically constructed of stone, concrete, or timber, they absorb or deflect wave energy before it reaches what lies beyond: {The breakwaters kept the marina calm even during storms}. The singular breakwater refers to one such structure.

A few words have an uncomfortable edge because they combine ordinary meanings with others that are taboo in certain contexts. Breast is certainly one of these words. The core meaning is to denote either of the pair of lactating glands in mature female primates (including humans). Discussion of women’s breasts in a non-medical context is associated with sexuality and arousal. No such issue arises in talk about chicken breasts, where the word denotes the mound of flesh on the front of a game bird.

Breastfed is the past tense of breastfeed—to nurse a baby at the breast rather than with a bottle. The word appears in discussions of infant nutrition and parenting: {She breastfed both children for a year}. Also spelled breast-fed.

To breastfeed is to feed an infant milk directly from the breast. The mother breastfeeds the baby; the baby breastfeeds from the mother—both constructions are standard. {She breastfed her daughter for eighteen months.} The practice is also called nursing. Breastfeeding in public remains socially contested in some places despite legal protections.

Breastfeeding is the practice of nursing an infant at the breast, providing milk directly from mother to child. The term covers both the act and the broader experience: {She's still breastfeeding}, {breastfeeding in public}, {the challenges of breastfeeding}. It can modify other nouns: {breastfeeding mother}, {breastfeeding support group}. The hyphenated form breast-feeding also appears.

Breastmilk is the milk produced by a woman's mammary glands to feed an infant. It provides complete nutrition for newborns and contains antibodies that help protect against infection. Also spelled as two words: breast milk. {She pumped breastmilk to leave with the babysitter.}

A breastplate is a piece of armor covering the chest, worn historically by soldiers and knights for protection in battle. The term extends to similar protective gear worn by modern police or military personnel, and to the decorative chest piece worn by horses in ceremonial contexts. In Jewish tradition, a breastplate refers to the jeweled vestment worn by the high priest, set with twelve stones representing the tribes of Israel.

Breastplates are pieces of armor covering the chest, protecting the heart and lungs in combat. Knights wore breastplates as part of a full suit of armor. The term extends to ceremonial or decorative chest pieces worn by soldiers on parade. In some religious contexts, a breastplate is an ornamental vestment worn by priests.

Breasts are the pair of soft, rounded organs on the front of a woman's chest that contain mammary glands for producing milk to feed infants. The word applies to the corresponding area on men as well, though male breasts lack the same development. Breast also refers to the chest area more generally, especially in older or literary usage: {He clutched the letter to his breast}. In poultry, the breast is the cut of meat from this part of the bird. To breast something is to face or push against it: {breast the waves}.

Breaststroke is a swimming stroke performed face-down, with the arms pushing forward together then sweeping outward while the legs execute a frog-like kick. It's the slowest of the competitive strokes but often the first taught to beginners: {She prefers breaststroke because she can keep her head above water}.

Breath is the air taken into and expelled from the lungs. A single instance is also a breath: {Take a deep breath}. By extension, breath suggests life itself—to draw breath is to be alive, and a dying breath is a final one. Breath can mean a slight movement of air: {not a breath of wind}. To {hold your breath} is to wait anxiously. Something {under your breath} is spoken very quietly. {In the same breath} means almost simultaneously, often of contradictory statements.

Breathable describes materials that allow air or moisture to pass through: {breathable fabric}, {breathable mesh}. Athletic and outdoor gear emphasizes breathability to prevent sweat buildup. Air that is breathable contains enough oxygen to sustain life: {The atmosphere on Mars is not breathable}.

A breathalyser is a device that measures blood alcohol content from a breath sample. Police use breathalysers during traffic stops to determine whether drivers are legally impaired: {He failed the breathalyser and was arrested for drunk driving}. Also spelled breathalyzer, especially in American English.

To breathalyze someone is to test their breath for alcohol content using a device called a breathalyzer. Police breathalyze drivers suspected of drunk driving: {She was breathalyzed at the checkpoint and blew over the legal limit}. Also spelled breathalyse in British English.

A breathalyzer is a device that measures blood alcohol content from a breath sample. Police use breathalyzers during traffic stops to determine if drivers are legally intoxicated: {He failed the breathalyzer and was arrested for DUI}. The word comes from breath plus analyzer, originally a trademark now used generically.

Breathalyzers are devices that measure blood alcohol content from a breath sample. Police use them to test suspected drunk drivers—you blow into a tube, and the device estimates how much alcohol is in your bloodstream. The term comes from the brand name Breathalyzer, now used generically for any such device. {He failed the breathalyzer and was arrested for DUI.}

To breathe is to draw air into the lungs and expel it—the fundamental act of respiration. Extended uses preserve the sense of air moving: fabrics that breathe allow air to pass through, wine breathes when exposed to air. To breathe a word is to speak very softly or not at all: {Don't breathe a word of this}. To {breathe down someone's neck} is to monitor them oppressively. {Breathe easy} means relax.

A breather is a brief pause or rest from activity: {Let's take a breather before we start the next section}. The word suggests catching one's breath—a short recovery period rather than an extended break. Someone who breathes is also a breather, though this use is uncommon outside phrases like {mouth breather}, which can be literal or insulting slang for someone dim or socially oblivious.
clues: A pause to catch your wind

definition: Breathes is the act of drawing air into and expelling it from the lungs. All animals that breathe do so to sustain life, making the word extend naturally to being alive: {As long as she breathes, there's hope}. Something that breathes can also admit air or allow circulation: {This fabric breathes}. Wine breathes when exposed to air before drinking. To breathe a word is to speak quietly or at all: {Don't breathe a word of this}.

Breathing is the process of drawing air into and expelling it from the lungs. As an adjective, it means alive: {Every breathing creature on earth}. A breathing {space} or breathing {room} is a pause or margin that allows relief from pressure. {Heavy breathing} suggests exertion, fear, or sexual arousal. {Fire-breathing} describes dragons and aggressive people alike.

Breathless describes being out of breath, as after exertion: {She arrived breathless from running up the stairs}. It extends to states of intense emotion—excitement, anticipation, or awe—that feel like they stop your breath: {breathless with anticipation}, {The view left us breathless}. Breathless prose or narration moves rapidly without pause, creating urgency. Something breathless can also be airless or still: {the breathless summer heat}.

Breathlessly describes doing something while short of breath, whether from physical exertion or emotional intensity. A runner finishes a race breathlessly. More often the word conveys eager excitement or rapt anticipation: {The crowd waited breathlessly for the announcement}. News reported breathlessly carries a sense of overwrought urgency.
clues: Speaking while completely out of air

definition: Breathlessness is the state of being out of breath—gasping or struggling to get air, whether from exertion, illness, or strong emotion. {She paused on the stairs, overcome by breathlessness.} The word also captures the quality of intense anticipation or excitement that seems to suspend normal breathing: {the breathlessness of first love}, {a breathlessness in his voice as he described the discovery}.

Breathtaking describes something so striking it seems to momentarily stop your breath—stunning beauty, unexpected news, or overwhelming experience: {The view from the summit was breathtaking}. The word implies sudden impact rather than gradual appreciation. A breathtaking performance astonishes; a breathtaking fall terrifies. The intensity has softened through overuse, sometimes meaning merely impressive.

Breathwork is the practice of using controlled breathing techniques to affect mental, emotional, or physical states. The term covers a range of methods—from ancient yogic practices to contemporary therapeutic approaches—used for stress relief, meditation, or altered consciousness: {I started doing breathwork to help with my anxiety}. Some forms involve rapid breathing patterns; others emphasize slow, deliberate rhythm.

Breathy describes a voice or vocal quality with audible breath mixed into the sound—soft, intimate, not fully resonant. A breathy whisper, a breathy singer. The effect suggests vulnerability, seduction, or exhaustion: {She answered in a breathy voice}. {His breathy delivery made every lyric sound like a confession}.

Bred is the past tense and past participle of breed. Something bred has been raised or produced through controlled reproduction: {a horse bred for racing}, {born and bred in Texas}. It extends to upbringing and training: {well-bred} suggests good manners, {ill-bred} the opposite. In combinations, bred indicates origin or development: {purebred}, {crossbred}, {inbred}.

Breech refers to the back or rear part of something. In firearms, the breech is the rear of the barrel where ammunition is loaded—a breech-loading rifle loads from the back rather than the muzzle. In anatomy, breech describes a baby positioned bottom-first rather than head-first in the womb: {a breech birth}, {The baby was breech}. The plural breeches are trousers that extend to just below the knee, once standard menswear, now mainly worn for horseback riding.

Breeches are trousers that end just below the knee, typically fastened with buttons or buckles. Once standard men's attire, they now appear mainly in equestrian contexts, historical costume, and ceremonial dress. The word survives in phrases like {too big for your breeches}, meaning arrogantly overconfident, and {breeches buoy}, a rescue device. Breeches is always plural; a single garment is still {a pair of breeches}.

Breed refers to a distinct variety within a species, especially domestic animals developed through selective breeding: {a rare breed of cattle}, {What breed is your dog?} The verb means to produce offspring or raise animals for particular traits. Extended uses cover anything that generates or fosters: {Familiarity breeds contempt}. A breed of person shares distinctive characteristics: {a new breed of politician}. Well-bred and ill-bred describe manners and upbringing.

A breeder is someone who raises animals or plants for reproduction, typically to produce offspring with desirable traits: {a dog breeder}, {a horse breeder}. In nuclear technology, a breeder reactor produces more fissile material than it consumes. In gay slang, breeder is a mildly disparaging term for a heterosexual person, emphasizing their capacity for reproduction.

Breeders are people who breed animals or plants, selecting for desirable traits: {dog breeders}, {horse breeders}, {rose breeders}. In gay slang, breeders refers dismissively or humorously to heterosexuals—people who reproduce: {The bar was full of breeders on a Friday night}. The term inverts the usual direction of reproductive-based insults.

Breeding is the process of mating animals or plants to produce offspring, especially to develop desired traits: {selective breeding}, {a breeding program for endangered species}. The breeding season is when animals mate. Breeding also means upbringing and manners—someone of good breeding behaves with refinement and social grace. A breeding ground is where animals reproduce, or figuratively, where something develops: {a breeding ground for crime}.

Breeds functions as both noun and verb around the idea of producing offspring or types. A breed is a distinct variety within a species, developed through selective reproduction: {dog breeds}, {cattle breeds}. To breed is to produce offspring or to raise animals for particular traits. Figuratively, familiarity breeds contempt, and certain conditions breed problems. A person's breeding refers to their upbringing and manners: {good breeding}, {ill-bred}.

A breeze is a light, gentle wind—stronger than still air but not forceful enough to be called wind proper: {A cool breeze came off the lake}. Figuratively, a breeze is something effortless: {The exam was a breeze}. To breeze through is to accomplish something with casual ease. To breeze in or out is to arrive or leave in a carefree manner: {She breezed into the meeting ten minutes late}.

Breezed is the past tense of breeze, meaning to move in a quick, effortless manner. Someone who breezed through a task completed it with ease: {She breezed through the exam}. To breeze in or out suggests casual, unhurried arrival or departure: {He breezed into the meeting twenty minutes late}.

Breezes are gentle winds, light movements of air that feel pleasant rather than forceful: {Ocean breezes cooled the afternoon}. To breeze somewhere is to move casually and confidently: {She breezed into the meeting twenty minutes late}. To breeze through something is to accomplish it with ease: {He breezed through the exam}.

A breezeway is a covered passage, open on the sides, that connects two buildings or two parts of the same building. The design allows air to flow through freely, providing shade and shelter while maintaining ventilation—hence the name. Breezeways commonly link a house to a garage or connect wings of a school or office complex. {We stored the bikes in the breezeway between the house and garage.}

Breezing is moving quickly and effortlessly, like a breeze passing through: {She came breezing into the office twenty minutes late}. To breeze through something is to complete it with ease: {He breezed through the exam}. The word suggests casual confidence, sometimes to the point of carelessness.

Breezy describes weather with a light, pleasant wind—stronger than calm but gentler than windy. The word extends to manner and tone: a breezy {attitude} is casual, carefree, cheerful. Breezy {conversation} flows easily without heaviness. The connotation is usually positive, though it can suggest someone is too casual for the situation: {Her breezy dismissal of the complaint annoyed him}.

Brekkie is informal, chiefly British and Australian slang for breakfast: {What are you having for brekkie?} The word has a casual, cheerful tone suited to everyday conversation rather than formal contexts.

Brekky is informal, chiefly British and Australian slang for breakfast: {What are you having for brekky?} The word has a casual, familiar tone, typically used among friends or family rather than in formal settings.

Brethren is an archaic plural of brother, now used almost exclusively in religious or fraternal contexts: {Dearly beloved brethren, we are gathered here today}. It suggests fellowship among members of a group united by shared faith, purpose, or identity. Outside ceremonial language, brethren sounds deliberately old-fashioned or ironic.

Brevity is shortness, especially of expression. A speaker known for brevity uses few words. {Brevity is the soul of wit} suggests concise expression is more effective than lengthy elaboration. The word applies to duration as well: {the brevity of summer}, {the brevity of life}.

Brew originally means to make beer—steeping grain, fermenting, producing alcohol. The process extends to tea and coffee: {Let the tea brew for five minutes}. A storm brews when it gathers force; trouble brews when it develops. As a noun, a brew is any beverage made by brewing, or informally any drink: {a cold brew}, {What's your favorite brew?}

Brewed is the past tense of brew, which means to make beer or other fermented drinks, or to prepare tea or coffee by steeping or boiling. {She brewed a fresh pot of coffee}. Figuratively, something brewed has been developing or forming gradually: {Trouble had been brewing for months}. {A storm brewed on the horizon}.

A brewer is someone who brews beer or ale, either professionally or as a hobbyist. The term applies to individuals and by extension to companies: {Anheuser-Busch is one of the world's largest brewers}. A brewer's yeast is the strain used in fermentation, also sold as a nutritional supplement.

Breweries is the plural of brewery, a facility where beer is produced. The word covers operations from small craft breweries making limited batches to industrial plants producing millions of barrels annually. {The city's old breweries have been converted to apartments.} {Local breweries often offer tours and tastings.}

Brewers are people or companies that brew beer or other fermented beverages. The term covers everything from craft brewery owners to industrial beverage manufacturers: {Local brewers have transformed the city's warehouse district}. Brewer's yeast is the strain used in fermentation, also sold as a nutritional supplement. (Capitalized Brewers refers to the Milwaukee baseball team.)

A brewery is a facility where beer is made. The term covers operations of all sizes, from industrial plants producing millions of barrels to small craft breweries and brewpubs that serve their beer on-site. {We toured a local brewery and sampled their seasonal ales.}

Brewing is the process of making beer or ale by steeping, boiling, and fermenting grain and hops. The term extends to making tea or coffee by steeping: {The coffee is brewing}. Figuratively, something brewing is developing or gathering force, usually something ominous: {There's trouble brewing}, {A storm is brewing on the horizon}.

A brewmaster is the person in charge of brewing operations at a brewery, responsible for recipe development, quality control, and overseeing production. The title suggests expertise and authority—a brewmaster has typically spent years learning the craft. {The brewmaster walked us through their new seasonal ale.} Sometimes used more loosely for any skilled homebrewer.

A brewpub is a restaurant or bar that brews its own beer on the premises. Unlike a standalone brewery, a brewpub serves food alongside its house-made beers, combining dining with craft brewing: {We tried the seasonal IPA at the new brewpub downtown}. The term emerged with the American craft beer movement of the 1980s.

Brewpubs are restaurants or bars that brew their own beer on the premises. Unlike standalone breweries that primarily produce and distribute, brewpubs emphasize the drinking and dining experience alongside small-batch production: {We tried the seasonal IPA at a local brewpub}. The term emerged in the 1980s as craft brewing gained popularity.

Brews is the plural of brew and the third-person singular verb form. A brew is a batch of beer or other fermented drink, or any concoction that has steeped: {local craft brews}, {a witch's brew}. To brew is to make such drinks, or more broadly to develop or gather strength: {A storm is brewing}, {Trouble brews when those two get together}.

Brewskies is casual slang for beers, used when the mood is relaxed and social: {Let's grab some brewskies after work}. The playful suffix gives the word a lighthearted, buddy-comedy tone. Also spelled brewskis.

A briar is a prickly shrub, especially wild roses or brambles with thorny stems. The word suggests tangled, difficult-to-penetrate undergrowth: {We hacked through the briars}. A briar is also a tobacco pipe made from the root of a Mediterranean shrub—the briar tree—whose dense wood resists burning. Also spelled brier.

Briars are thorny shrubs, especially wild roses and brambles, or the prickly stems themselves. A briar patch is a dense tangle of such growth—difficult to navigate and useful for creatures seeking refuge from predators. Briars also refers to pipes made from briarwood, the root of a Mediterranean shrub prized for heat resistance. {His jacket snagged on the briars.}

A bribe is money or something else of value given to influence someone's actions, especially to make an official act corruptly: {The judge accepted bribes from defendants}. The verb bribe means to offer such inducements: {They tried to bribe the inspector}. Lighter uses describe small rewards for cooperation: {I bribed the kids with ice cream to behave}.

Bribed is the past tense of bribe—to offer money or favors to influence someone's actions, especially to get them to act dishonestly or against their duties: {The official was bribed to approve the permit}. Someone who has been bribed has accepted such an inducement: {The jury was bribed}.

Bribery is the act of offering, giving, or accepting something of value to influence someone's actions—especially an official's decisions. The bribe might be money, gifts, or favors: {The senator was convicted of bribery}. Bribery corrupts institutions by substituting private incentives for public duty. The word covers both sides of the transaction: giving and receiving.

Bribes are payments or favors offered to influence someone's actions, typically to get them to act dishonestly or against their duties: {The official accepted bribes from contractors}. The singular bribe works as both noun and verb—to bribe someone is to offer such inducement. Bribes range from cash to gifts to promises of future benefit. The word carries inherent disapproval; people rarely describe their own payments as bribes.

Bribing is offering money, gifts, or favors to influence someone's actions, especially to get them to act improperly or illegally. The word implies corruption—inducing someone to betray a duty or trust: {He was caught bribing a judge}. Bribing can be playful when the stakes are low: {I'm bribing the kids with ice cream to behave}.

A brick is a rectangular block of fired clay used for building walls, paths, and other structures. Bricks are laid in rows and bonded with mortar, and the term extends to anything brick-shaped: a brick of cheese, a brick of cash. As slang, brick describes a failed shot in basketball that clangs off the rim, or an electronic device so broken it's useful only as a paperweight. To brick a phone is to render it unusable. Calling someone a brick means they're dependable and solid.

A brickbat is a piece of brick, especially one used as a weapon or missile. The word extends to harsh criticism or insults hurled at someone: {The proposal drew brickbats from both sides of the aisle}. Political commentary often pairs it with bouquets—brickbats for criticism, bouquets for praise.

Brickbats are harsh criticisms or verbal attacks. The word comes from the literal sense—a piece of broken brick used as a weapon or missile—but now almost always appears figuratively: {The proposal drew brickbats from both sides of the aisle}. Often paired with bouquets to contrast criticism and praise: {The film received both brickbats and bouquets from critics}.

Bricked describes an electronic device rendered completely unusable—as functional as a brick. A phone, game console, or computer becomes bricked when a failed software update, botched modification, or corrupted firmware leaves it unable to start: {I tried to jailbreak my phone and bricked it}. The term emerged from tech communities where tinkering sometimes produced expensive paperweights.

Bricking is rendering an electronic device completely unusable—as functional as a brick. It typically happens when a software update goes wrong, firmware gets corrupted, or someone attempts an unauthorized modification: {I was jailbreaking my phone and ended up bricking it}. A bricked device won't boot or respond to inputs. Some bricking is reversible; some is permanent.

A bricklayer is a tradesperson who builds walls, structures, and other constructions using bricks and mortar. The work requires skill in laying bricks level and plumb, mixing mortar to the right consistency, and maintaining consistent joints. {The bricklayers finished the garden wall in two days.}

Bricklayers are workers who build structures by laying bricks in mortar. The trade requires skill in maintaining level courses, cutting bricks to fit, and working efficiently before mortar sets. {The bricklayers started on the foundation at dawn.} The term extends to anyone who does careful, methodical construction work.

Bricklaying is the craft of building structures by setting bricks in mortar. The work requires skill in maintaining level courses, consistent spacing, and proper bonding patterns. A bricklayer constructs walls, chimneys, patios, and other masonry features: {He learned bricklaying from his uncle}.

Bricks are rectangular blocks of fired clay used for building walls, paths, and structures. The standard shape makes them stackable and easy to handle. Figuratively, to {shit bricks} is to be terrified. A {brick} can be a dependable person, or a phone or device rendered useless: {I updated the firmware and bricked my phone}.

Brickwork is construction made of bricks—walls, chimneys, facades, or decorative elements built by laying bricks in mortar. The term covers both the structure itself and the craft of creating it: {The old brickwork needs repointing}. Brickwork can be ornamental, with patterns created by varying brick orientation or color.

Bridal means relating to a bride or wedding: {bridal gown}, {bridal shower}, {bridal party}. The word functions almost exclusively as an adjective, though it occasionally appears as a noun for wedding festivities. Despite sounding identical to bridle (the horse equipment), the words have different origins and meanings.

A bride is a woman on her wedding day or in the period just before and after marriage. The term applies from engagement through the ceremony and briefly beyond: {The bride wore her grandmother's veil}. Bridal relates to brides and weddings: {bridal shower}, {bridal party}. A bride-to-be is an engaged woman.

A bridegroom is a man about to be married or recently married. The word appears most often in formal contexts—wedding invitations, ceremony programs, news announcements: {The bride and bridegroom exchanged vows at sunset}. In casual speech, groom is more common.

Brides is the plural of bride, a woman about to be married or recently married. The word appears frequently in contexts involving wedding planning, ceremonies, and the wedding industry. A bridal party typically includes bridesmaids who attend to the bride. {The brides were all smiles as they posed for photos after the ceremony.} In same-sex weddings, both partners may be referred to as brides if they are women.

A bridesmaid is a woman who attends the bride at a wedding, typically helping with preparations and standing alongside her during the ceremony. Bridesmaids traditionally wear matching dresses chosen by the bride. The phrase {always a bridesmaid, never a bride} describes someone who helps others succeed but never achieves success themselves.

Bridesmaids are women who attend a bride at her wedding, typically friends or relatives who participate in the ceremony and help with preparations. They traditionally wear matching dresses and stand beside the bride during the vows: {She asked her college roommate to be one of her bridesmaids}. The singular bridesmaid refers to one such attendant.

A bridesman is a male attendant chosen by the bride to be part of her wedding party, the counterpart to a bridesmaid. The role parallels that of a groomsman but serves the bride rather than the groom: {Her brother stood as her bridesman}. The term reflects shifting wedding customs as couples move away from strictly gender-divided attendant parties.

Bridesmen is the plural of bridesman, a male attendant chosen by the bride in a wedding party. The role mirrors that of bridesmaids but is filled by a man—typically a close friend or relative of the bride. The term has gained currency as wedding parties become less rigidly gendered: {Her two bridesmen wore suits that matched the bridesmaids' dresses}.

A bridezilla is a bride-to-be who becomes obsessively demanding or difficult while planning her wedding. The blend of bride and Godzilla suggests someone who has transformed into a monster, terrorizing vendors, bridesmaids, and family members with unreasonable expectations: {My sister turned into a total bridezilla—she screamed at the florist for twenty minutes}. The term is usually disparaging but sometimes used self-deprecatingly.

A bridge is a structure that carries a road or path over water or some other obstacle or depression. This connecting feature in the meaning of bridge gives rise to many other meanings that share an element of joining or spanning two things that would otherwise be separate: The halfway house serves a bridge between addiction and the return to society. Bridge can also denote an anatomical feature, a dental appliance, or a passage in music, all of which form important connections. As a verb, bridge means to connect: a grant that will bridge the gap in funding. The name of the card game bridge is separately derived.

Bridged is the past tense of bridge, meaning to span or connect across a gap. A structure bridged a river; a compromise bridged differences between factions. In electronics, bridged describes components connected in a specific circuit configuration. {The new highway bridged the bay}. {Her research bridged neuroscience and psychology}.

A bridgehead is a fortified position on the enemy's side of a river or other obstacle, established by troops crossing over to secure passage for forces following behind. The term extends to any initial foothold in hostile territory: {The landing established a bridgehead on the coast}. Figuratively, a bridgehead is any secured starting position for further advance: {The company's new office serves as a bridgehead into the Asian market}.

Bridgeheads is the plural of bridgehead, a military position secured on the enemy's side of a river or other obstacle. Forces establish a bridgehead to protect a crossing point and allow reinforcements to advance: {Allied troops secured bridgeheads along the Rhine}. Figuratively, any initial foothold that enables further progress: {The company established bridgeheads in Asian markets}.

Bridges is the plural of bridge—structures spanning gaps to allow passage across rivers, valleys, or other obstacles. Beyond physical crossings, bridges metaphorically connect disparate things: {building bridges between communities}, {bridges between disciplines}. In dentistry, a bridge is a false tooth anchored to adjacent teeth. In music, a bridge is a passage connecting two sections of a song.

Bridging is the act of spanning a gap or creating a connection between two things. A bridging loan provides temporary financing between transactions. In construction, bridging refers to structural supports between joists. Figuratively, bridging describes efforts to connect divided groups or ideas: {The mediator focused on bridging their differences}. The word emphasizes transition and connection across separation.

A bridle is the headgear used to control a horse, consisting of straps, bit, and reins. The rider uses it to direct the animal's movement. To bridle a horse is to put this gear on. Figuratively, to bridle something is to restrain or control it: {She bridled her temper}. To bridle at something is to react with indignation, like a horse jerking its head back: {He bridled at the suggestion that he'd cheated}.

A bridle is the headgear used to control a horse, consisting of straps, a bit, and reins. The verb bridle means to put a bridle on a horse, or more commonly, to restrain or control something: {She bridled her temper during the meeting}. When someone bridles at something, they show resentment or indignation, typically by throwing back the head and drawing in the chin—a gesture reminiscent of a horse reacting to the bit.

Brie is a soft French cheese with a white edible rind and creamy interior. It ripens from the outside in, becoming increasingly runny as it ages. Brie is typically served at room temperature, often with crackers or fruit: {We brought a wheel of brie to the party}.

All meanings of brief contain the underlying idea of shortness, either in length or duration. A brief report is short. When you brief someone, you convey necessary information. The information may be called a brief, especially if it is in written form. In law, a brief is a statement of a case. Briefs are a kind of underwear that fit closer to the body than boxers and do not cover the leg.

A briefcase is a flat, rectangular case with a handle, used for carrying documents, papers, and other work-related materials. The term evokes professional or business contexts, and briefcases are associated with lawyers, executives, and office workers. Modern briefcases may include compartments for laptops and other electronics. {He grabbed his briefcase and headed to the meeting.}

Briefcases is the plural of briefcase, a flat rectangular bag with a handle for carrying documents and papers. The word evokes professional work—lawyers, businesspeople, commuters: {Executives filed into the meeting, briefcases in hand}. With the shift to laptops and backpacks, traditional hard-sided briefcases have become less common, though the word persists for any professional carrying bag.

Briefed is the past tense of brief, meaning to give someone essential information or instructions before a task or event. Officials brief reporters, lawyers brief clients, commanders brief troops: {The ambassador was briefed before the meeting}. To be briefed is to be brought up to speed on what you need to know.

A briefing is a meeting or document in which essential information is conveyed, typically to prepare someone for an action or decision. The term suggests efficiency and purpose—briefings are meant to be brief. Government officials hold press briefings to update journalists, military commanders conduct mission briefings before operations, and executives receive briefings before important meetings. {The intelligence briefing lasted twenty minutes.} To brief someone is to give them such information.

Briefings are meetings or documents that provide concise, essential information about a situation, typically to prepare someone for a task or decision. The term implies distilled content—key facts without excess detail: {daily intelligence briefings}, {press briefings}, {mission briefings}. A briefing brings someone up to speed quickly on what they need to know.

Briefly means for a short time or in a few words. Something that happens briefly doesn't last long: {She paused briefly before continuing}. To put something briefly is to summarize: {Briefly, here's what happened}. The word signals conciseness—you're not going to elaborate.

Briefs are short, close-fitting underpants without leg extensions—the classic underwear style as opposed to boxers. The word also refers to short written summaries, especially legal documents outlining arguments for a case: {The lawyer filed a brief with the court}. To brief someone is to give them essential information before an event or task: {The general briefed the troops on the mission}.

A brig is a two-masted sailing vessel with square sails on both masts. In naval and military usage, a brig is a jail or detention facility, especially one aboard a ship or at a military installation: {They threw him in the brig for insubordination}. The prison sense likely derives from the practice of confining offenders on such vessels.

A brigade is a military unit, typically comprising several battalions and forming part of a division. The term extends to organized groups working toward a common purpose: {fire brigade}, {bucket brigade}. It can describe any coordinated team effort: {The cleanup brigade tackled the mess after the party}. To brigade is to form into a brigade or group together.

Brigades are military units, typically comprising several battalions under a brigadier or colonel. The term extends to organized groups working toward a common purpose: {fire brigades}, {bucket brigades}. In political contexts, brigade can describe coordinated groups acting in concert, sometimes disparagingly: {the outrage brigades on social media}. To brigade is to organize into such groups or to coordinate attacks, especially online harassment campaigns.

A brigadier is a military officer ranking above a colonel and below a major general. In the British army and many Commonwealth forces, brigadier is a one-star rank; the American equivalent is brigadier general. The rank typically commands a brigade—a unit of several thousand soldiers: {The brigadier inspected the troops before deployment}.

Brigading is coordinated action by a group to flood a platform with votes, comments, or reports—typically to manipulate rankings, suppress content, or harass users. The term comes from online communities, especially Reddit, where users from one subreddit might collectively downvote posts in another: {The thread got brigaded by people who disagreed with the article}. The practice violates most platform rules.

Brigands are bandits or outlaws who rob travelers, typically in remote areas like mountains or forests. The word carries a romantic, old-world flavor—you're more likely to encounter brigands in historical fiction or fantasy than in news reports: {The mountain pass was notorious for brigands who preyed on merchant caravans}.

Bright describes something that gives off or reflects strong light: {a bright sun}, {bright colors}, {a bright smile}. The word extends to intelligence—a bright student is quick and clever. Bright can mean cheerful or promising: {a bright future}, {looking on the bright side}. To arrive {bright and early} is to show up promptly, alert and ready.

Brighten means to make or become lighter, more luminous, or more vivid. The sun brightens a room when clouds part; a fresh coat of paint brightens dull walls. The word extends naturally to mood and demeanor: {Her face brightened when she heard the news.} To brighten up a space is to add light, color, or cheerful touches. Things that brighten your day lift your spirits or improve your outlook.

Brightest is the superlative of bright—the most luminous, vivid, or intelligent in a group. The brightest star in the sky, the brightest student in the class, the brightest idea anyone had. {She was the brightest of her siblings.} {The brightest colors catch the eye first.}

Brightness is the quality of emitting or reflecting light. A room has brightness when sunlight floods it; a screen's brightness can be adjusted. The word extends to vividness of color and to mental quickness: {the brightness of her smile}, {a student of unusual brightness}. Brightness also describes cheerfulness or optimism: {Despite everything, she maintained her brightness}.

Brigs are two-masted sailing vessels with square sails on both masts, commonly used for trade and naval purposes from the 18th through 19th centuries. The term also refers to prison cells or detention areas on naval ships, where sailors who violated regulations were confined. This nautical jail sense extends to military prisons generally: {He spent a week in the brig for going AWOL}.

Brilliance is exceptional brightness or radiance: {the brilliance of the summer sun}, {diamonds prized for their brilliance}. Extended to mental qualities, it means outstanding intelligence or talent: {Her brilliance in mathematics was evident early}. A brilliant performance or idea displays remarkable skill or insight. The word carries connotations of dazzling effect—something that impresses or even overwhelms.
clues: What makes diamonds and minds shine

definition: Brilliant describes intense light or exceptional quality. A brilliant sun blazes; brilliant diamonds catch and scatter light. Extended to intellect, brilliant means exceptionally clever or talented: {a brilliant scientist}, {a brilliant idea}. British speakers use it as an enthusiastic term of approval: {That's brilliant!} The noun brilliance covers both radiance and mental sharpness.

The brim is the projecting edge of a hat, the part that shades your face. More generally, a brim is the upper edge of a container: {The cup was filled to the brim}. To brim is to be full to the point of overflowing: {Her eyes brimmed with tears}. {He was brimming with enthusiasm}.

Brimful means filled to the brim—the very top edge of a container: {a cup brimful of coffee}. The word extends naturally to abstract fullness: {brimful of confidence}, {eyes brimful of tears}. Also spelled brim-full.

Brimming describes something filled to the very edge, ready to overflow. A cup brimming with coffee has no room for more. The word extends naturally to abundance of any kind: {eyes brimming with tears}, {a report brimming with good news}, {brimming with confidence}. The sense is always of fullness pressing against limits.
