Cardiologists handle conditions like heart failure, arrhythmias, and coronary artery disease: {My doctor referred me to a cardiologist after the stress test}. Some cardiologists perform procedures like catheterizations; others focus on prevention and medication management.

A cardroom is a room or establishment where card games are played, typically for money. In casinos, the cardroom is the area dedicated to poker and other table games, distinct from slot machines. Standalone cardrooms operate as licensed businesses where players compete against each other rather than the house: {The local cardroom hosts tournaments every weekend}.

Cards are small flat pieces of stiff paper or plastic used for countless purposes. Playing cards come in decks and are used for games and magic tricks. Credit cards and debit cards facilitate purchases. Business cards identify people professionally. Greeting cards convey messages for occasions. ID cards verify identity. To be {in the cards} means something is likely to happen. If you {play your cards right}, you handle a situation skillfully to your advantage.

A cardshark is someone highly skilled at card games, especially one who uses that skill to win money from less experienced players. The term carries a hint of sharp dealing or hustling—a cardshark may not cheat outright but plays with predatory cunning: {He lost three hundred dollars to some cardshark at the casino}. Also spelled card shark.

Cardsharks are people who cheat at card games, typically for money. The term combines skill with deception—a cardshark knows the game intimately but uses that knowledge to fleece opponents through marked cards, sleight of hand, or rigged deals. Also spelled card sharks or cardsharp. {He lost his savings to cardsharks in a backroom poker game.}

A cardsharp is someone who cheats at card games, especially for profit. The word implies skill and cunning rather than crude deception—a cardsharp manipulates cards or exploits opponents through sleight of hand, marked decks, or psychological tactics: {The riverboat was notorious for cardsharps fleecing naive travelers}. Also spelled cardsharper.

Cardsharps are people who cheat at card games, typically for money. The term suggests professional skill in deception—sleight of hand, marked cards, or other tricks. A cardsharp differs from a mere cheater by the implication of practiced expertise: {The riverboat was notorious for its cardsharps}. Also spelled card sharps or cardsharpers.

Care centers on attention and concern. To care about something is to regard it as important; to care for someone is to look after them. A caregiver provides care. {I don't care} dismisses something as unimportant. {Take care} means be careful or, as a farewell, stay well. {Handle with care} warns of fragility. Cares are worries or burdens: {the cares of the world}. {Couldn't care less} expresses total indifference—though {could care less}, logically backward, means the same thing.

Carebear is internet and gaming slang for someone perceived as overly friendly, conflict-averse, or soft. The term derives from the 1980s cartoon characters known for spreading kindness. In online games, a carebear avoids player-versus-player combat, preferring cooperative or non-competitive play: {The server's full of carebears who won't fight back}. More broadly, it disparages anyone seen as too sensitive or unwilling to engage in harsh environments.

Careen means to tilt, sway, or lurch while moving at speed: {The taxi careened around the corner}. Originally a nautical term for tilting a ship on its side for cleaning or repair, it now describes any wild, uncontrolled motion. In American English, careen has largely absorbed the meaning of career (to rush headlong), though purists maintain the distinction.

Careening describes wild, uncontrolled movement—lurching from side to side while moving fast: {The car came careening around the corner}, {He careened through the crowd}. The word suggests both speed and instability. Originally a nautical term for tilting a ship on its side for cleaning or repair, that sense survives mainly in historical contexts.
clues: Moving fast and out of control

definition: Career is the arc of one's working life, especially in a particular field: {a career in medicine}, {a career politician}. It implies progression and commitment rather than just a job. The older sense—rapid movement or rushing—survives in the verb: {The car careered off the road}. To career through something is to move fast and somewhat out of control.

Careerism is the prioritization of professional advancement over other values—ethics, relationships, or the work itself. The term is almost always pejorative, suggesting someone who climbs the ladder without regard for who they step on: {His careerism alienated colleagues who once admired him}. A careerist pursues status and promotion as ends in themselves.

A careerist is someone who prioritizes professional advancement above other considerations—personal relationships, ethics, or broader purpose. The term carries a critical edge, suggesting ruthless ambition or shallow striving: {He's a careerist who'd step over anyone to get promoted}. The adjective careerist describes this orientation: {careerist ambitions}, {careerist motives}.
clues: Person prioritizing professional success above all

definition: Careers is the plural of career, referring to long-term professional paths or occupations: {She counseled students on their careers}. The verb careers means to move swiftly and erratically: {The car careered down the hillside}. This sense is more common in British English; Americans typically use careen for uncontrolled motion.

Carefree means without worry or responsibility. A carefree attitude takes things lightly; a carefree summer lacks obligations. The word suggests pleasant lightness rather than recklessness: {She had a carefree childhood}, {those carefree days before the diagnosis}. Someone carefree isn't necessarily careless—just unburdened.

Careful means taking care to avoid mistakes, damage, or harm. A careful driver watches the road attentively. A careful reader notices details others miss. {Be careful with that vase—it's fragile.} The word can also mean thorough and deliberate: {careful analysis}, {careful planning}. To be careful about something is to give it proper attention and consideration.

Carefully means with care—paying close attention to avoid mistakes, damage, or harm. You might {carefully proofread an email} or {carefully carry a full cup of coffee}. The word suggests deliberate attention rather than casual action: {She carefully considered her options before responding}.

A caregiver is someone who looks after another person who cannot fully care for themselves—typically a child, elderly person, or someone with illness or disability. The term covers both paid professionals and unpaid family members: {Her daughter became her primary caregiver after the stroke}. Caregiving often involves physical assistance, emotional support, and managing medical needs.

Caregivers is the plural of caregiver—a person who provides care for someone unable to fully care for themselves. The term typically refers to those who tend to children, the elderly, or people with disabilities or chronic illness. Caregivers may be family members providing unpaid care or professionals: {Her mother's caregivers rotate in twelve-hour shifts}. The word emphasizes the ongoing, often demanding nature of the work.

Caregiving is the work of looking after someone who cannot fully care for themselves—typically the elderly, chronically ill, or disabled. The term encompasses both professional care and the unpaid labor of family members: {She left her job to focus on caregiving for her mother}. Caregiving often implies sustained, demanding responsibility rather than occasional help.

Careless means lacking attention or concern. A careless driver fails to notice hazards. A careless remark is made without thinking of consequences. Careless can also suggest ease and freedom from worry: {a careless summer afternoon}. The word implies negligence when stakes are high but relaxed indifference when they're not.

Carelessness is a lack of attention or caution, the quality of not being careful. It suggests negligence through inattention rather than deliberate disregard: {The accident was caused by carelessness}. Carelessness can range from minor oversights to serious lapses with real consequences: {His carelessness with the company's finances cost him his job}.

A carer is someone who looks after a person unable to care for themselves fully—typically an elderly, disabled, or chronically ill family member. The term is primarily British; Americans more often say caregiver. {She became her mother's carer after the stroke.} Professional carers provide similar support for pay.

Carers is the British term for what Americans call caregivers—people who look after someone unable to fully care for themselves, whether due to age, illness, or disability. The word covers both professional workers and unpaid family members: {Carers often neglect their own health while tending to others}. {The charity supports carers of dementia patients}.

Cares are worries or concerns that weigh on the mind: {free from cares}, {the cares of the world}. To have cares is to carry burdens. The word often appears in expressions about releasing worry: {without a care}, {not a care in the world}. As a verb form, cares indicates concern or interest: {She cares deeply about the environment}, {Who cares?}

A caress is a gentle, affectionate touch—stroking someone's hair, brushing fingers along a cheek. The verb means to touch in this tender way: {He caressed her face}. Caress extends to anything that touches lightly and pleasantly: {A warm breeze caressed the curtains}. The word implies intimacy, tenderness, or sensuality rather than mere contact.

Caressed is the past tense of caress, meaning to touch or stroke gently and lovingly. The word implies tenderness and affection—you caress a lover's face, a child's hair, a pet's fur. Figuratively, things that touch softly may caress: {A warm breeze caressed her skin}. The noun caress is the touch itself.

Caresses is the plural of caress—gentle, loving touches meant to show affection. A caress is tender rather than forceful, often romantic or sensual: {She felt his caresses on her skin}. The verb caress means to touch this way: {He caressed her cheek}. Figuratively, things that touch lightly may caress: {A breeze caressed the curtains}.

Caressing is touching gently and affectionately, usually with slow, stroking movements: {She sat caressing the cat in her lap}, {His hand caressing her cheek}. The word suggests tenderness and intimacy. Figuratively, things that touch softly may caress: {A breeze caressing the curtains}, {Sunlight caressing the hillside}.

A caretaker looks after something in the owner's absence or incapacity—a property, an estate, a person. In British English, a caretaker maintains a building; Americans would say janitor or custodian. As an adjective, caretaker describes someone holding a position temporarily until a permanent replacement is found: {a caretaker government}, {a caretaker manager}.

Caretakers are people who look after something or someone. A caretaker may tend to property: {The caretakers live in a cottage on the estate}. Or caretakers may provide care for children, the elderly, or the ill—though caregiver is more common for this sense in American English. A caretaker government or administration is temporary, holding power until a permanent one takes over.

Caretaking is the work of looking after someone or something—a child, an elderly parent, a property, an institution. The term emphasizes ongoing responsibility rather than one-time assistance: {She balanced caretaking duties with her career}. Caretaking can also describe temporary management: {The caretaking government held elections within six months}.

Careworn describes a face or appearance showing the effects of prolonged worry, stress, or hardship. The word suggests visible weariness—lines deepened by anxiety, a tired expression from carrying burdens too long: {Her careworn face softened when she saw her children}. It's somewhat literary, often appearing in descriptions of people who have endured difficult circumstances.

Cargo is goods transported by ship, plane, truck, or train—freight in bulk rather than individual packages. The word emphasizes commercial transport: {cargo ship}, {cargo hold}, {cargo plane}. Cargo pants have large pockets on the thighs, originally for carrying tools or supplies. {The ship arrived with a cargo of grain}.
clues: Merchandise transported by ship or plane

definition: A carhop is a server at a drive-in restaurant who brings food to customers in their parked cars. The job was most common in mid-twentieth-century America, when drive-in restaurants flourished: {The carhop brought our burgers on a tray that hooked to the car window}. Some carhops famously wore roller skates. The word combines car with hop, from the sense of a bellhop or someone who hops to serve.

Carhops are restaurant servers who bring food to customers waiting in parked cars. The term emerged with American drive-in restaurants in the mid-twentieth century, where carhops—often on roller skates—would take orders and deliver trays that hooked onto car windows. The practice has largely disappeared, though a few chains preserve it: {The carhops at Sonic still skate out with your order}.

Caribou is a large deer native to Arctic and subarctic regions of North America, known for its broad hooves and large antlers carried by both sexes. The same animal is called reindeer in Europe and Asia. Caribou migrate in vast herds across tundra and boreal forest: {The caribou crossed the frozen river by the thousands}.

A caricature is a portrait that exaggerates distinctive features for comic or satirical effect—a politician's prominent nose made enormous, a celebrity's quirk amplified. The term extends beyond visual art: any depiction that distorts through oversimplification becomes a caricature. {The villain was a caricature of corporate greed.} To caricature someone is to portray them this way.

Caricatures are exaggerated representations that distort distinctive features for comic or satirical effect. A caricature artist at a fair might enlarge a subject's nose or ears. The term extends beyond visual art: {His portrayal of the CEO was a caricature, reducing her to a handful of quirks}. To caricature someone is to depict them this way, emphasizing traits to the point of absurdity.

Caricaturing is the act of depicting someone or something with exaggerated features for comic or satirical effect. Political cartoonists make their living caricaturing public figures. The word extends beyond visual art: {The film caricatures small-town life}, {He was caricaturing her accent}. To caricature is to simplify while amplifying what's distinctive.

Caring describes genuine concern for someone's wellbeing and the willingness to act on it. A caring {parent} attends to a child's needs; a caring {friend} checks in during hard times. The word implies warmth and attentiveness rather than mere obligation. As a noun, caring refers to the work of looking after someone: {the challenges of caring for elderly relatives}.

To carjack is to steal a vehicle by force or threat while the driver is present—distinguished from ordinary auto theft by the element of confrontation. The carjacker typically approaches at a stoplight or parking lot and demands the keys at gunpoint: {She was carjacked outside the grocery store}. The noun carjacking names the crime.

Carjacked means having had one's vehicle stolen by force or threat while present. The term combines car with hijacked: {She was carjacked at a stoplight}. Someone who carjacks is a carjacker, and the crime is carjacking. Unlike ordinary auto theft, carjacking involves confronting the driver or occupants directly.

A carjacker is someone who steals a vehicle by force or threat while the driver is present—distinguishing carjacking from ordinary auto theft, which typically targets unoccupied cars. {The carjacker pulled a gun and ordered her out of the vehicle.}

Carjackers are people who steal vehicles by force or threat, typically while the driver is present—distinguishing carjacking from ordinary auto theft. The term combines car with hijacker: {The carjackers pulled him from the vehicle at gunpoint}. Carjacking often occurs at traffic lights, parking lots, or gas stations.

Carjacking is stealing a vehicle by force or threat while the driver is present—distinguished from ordinary auto theft by the element of confrontation. The term emerged in the early 1990s as such crimes increased in American cities: {He was convicted of carjacking after pulling a gun on a woman at a gas station}. The verb is carjack.

Carjacks is the verb form of carjack—to steal a vehicle by force or threat while someone is in or near it. Unlike ordinary auto theft, carjacking involves confrontation: {He carjacked her at a stoplight}. The crime typically occurs when drivers are stopped or entering their vehicles. (As a noun, a carjack is a device for lifting a car.)

Carmine is a vivid red color with a slight purple tinge, deeper than cherry but brighter than crimson. The word names both the color and the pigment that produces it, derived from crushed cochineal insects. As an adjective, it describes things of this hue: {carmine lips}, {carmine robes}. The color appears in cosmetics, food dye, and fine art.

Carnage is the killing of many people, especially in war or violence. The word emphasizes brutal, bloody destruction—bodies and devastation left behind: {The battlefield was a scene of carnage}. Extended to any severe destruction: {The stock market crash left financial carnage in its wake}.

Carnal means relating to the physical body and its appetites, especially sexual desires. The word carries connotations of earthly pleasures as opposed to spiritual concerns: {carnal desires}, {carnal knowledge}. Legal language uses {carnal knowledge} as a formal term for sexual intercourse. {The sermon warned against carnal temptations.}

A carnation is a flowering plant with fringed petals in white, pink, red, or yellow, widely cultivated for bouquets and boutonnieres. Carnations are traditional for Mother's Day and proms. The flowers have a spicy-sweet fragrance. The color carnation is a light pinkish-red, like the most common variety of the flower.

Carnations are flowering plants prized for their ruffled, fragrant blooms that come in white, pink, red, yellow, and purple varieties. They are among the most popular cut flowers for bouquets, corsages, and boutonnieres, often appearing at weddings, funerals, and on Mother's Day. Different colors carry traditional meanings: red for love, white for luck, pink for gratitude. {She pinned a carnation to his lapel before the dance.}

Carney is a variant spelling of carny—a carnival worker or the carnival world itself. The term carries connotations of transience, showmanship, and mild seediness: {The carney running the ring toss had been working fairs for thirty years}. Sometimes used as an adjective: {carney tricks}, {carney life}.

Carneys is the plural of carney, an informal term for carnival workers—the people who operate rides, run games, and work the booths at traveling fairs and amusement shows. The word carries connotations of a rough, transient lifestyle and sometimes implies untrustworthiness: {The carneys packed up overnight and moved to the next town}. Also spelled carnies.

A carnie is someone who works at a carnival, especially traveling fairs with rides, games, and sideshows. The term often carries connotations of rough living, transience, and insider knowledge of rigged games: {The carnie running the ring toss made it look easy}. Also spelled carny.

Carnies are the workers who operate carnival rides, games, and attractions. The term carries connotations of transience and seediness—carnies travel from town to town, live in trailers, and have a reputation (fair or not) for running rigged games and living rough: {The carnies were setting up the Ferris wheel when we arrived}. Sometimes used dismissively for anyone who seems shabby or untrustworthy.

Carnitas is a Mexican dish of pork that has been braised or simmered until tender, then shredded and often crisped. The word is Spanish for "little meats." Carnitas typically appears as a taco filling or in burritos: {I'll have the carnitas tacos with extra salsa}.

A carnival is a traveling amusement show with rides, games, and sideshows, typically set up temporarily in towns and fairgrounds. The word also refers to a period of public festivity before Lent, especially the elaborate celebrations in places like Rio de Janeiro and New Orleans: {Carnival season brings parades and costumes}. By extension, any wild, chaotic scene can be called a carnival: {The press conference turned into a carnival}.

Carnivals is the plural of carnival, a traveling amusement show with rides, games, and sideshows, or a festival of public celebration, often before Lent. The word carries connotations of bright lights, noise, and slightly seedy entertainment: {State fairs and carnivals came through every summer}. Figuratively, any chaotic or colorful spectacle: {The trial became a media carnival}.

A carnivore is an animal that eats meat—lions, wolves, sharks. The term also applies to meat-eating plants like the Venus flytrap. In casual use, carnivore describes a person who loves meat or eats it enthusiastically: {I'm a carnivore—I need steak at least twice a week}. The opposite is herbivore.

Carnivores are animals that eat meat—predators like lions, wolves, and sharks, or scavengers like vultures and hyenas. The term also applies to carnivorous plants that trap insects. In taxonomy, Carnivora is an order of mammals including cats, dogs, bears, and seals. Informally, carnivore describes any enthusiastic meat-eater: {I'm a carnivore—I need steak at least once a week}.

Carnivorous describes organisms that eat meat. Carnivorous animals—lions, wolves, sharks—hunt and consume other animals. Carnivorous plants like Venus flytraps trap and digest insects to supplement nutrients from poor soil. The word can describe eating habits more loosely: {I'm feeling carnivorous tonight—let's get steak}.

A carny is a person who works at a carnival, typically operating rides or running games on the midway. The word carries connotations of seediness—carnies are stereotyped as drifters, con artists, or rough characters: {The carny running the ring toss looked like he hadn't slept in days}. Also spelled carnie. The word can also refer to carnival culture or lifestyle generally.

Carob is a pod from a Mediterranean evergreen tree, dried and ground into a powder used as a chocolate substitute. It has a naturally sweet, somewhat earthy flavor without caffeine or the bitterness of cocoa: {carob chips}, {carob brownies}. Health food stores stock carob products for those avoiding chocolate, though devotees of real chocolate rarely find it satisfying.

A carol is a joyful song, especially one sung at Christmas: {We went caroling through the neighborhood}. The word applies to any celebratory hymn, though Christmas carols dominate modern usage. To carol is to sing such songs, typically in a group moving from house to house. {The choir caroled late into the evening.} (Capitalized Carol is a given name.)

A caroler is a person who sings carols, especially someone who goes door to door singing Christmas songs during the holiday season. The activity is typically done in groups: {Carolers gathered on the porch singing "Silent Night"}. Also spelled caroller.

Carolers are people who sing carols, especially groups who go door to door singing Christmas songs during the holiday season: {Carolers came by last night with "Silent Night"}. The tradition involves neighbors or church groups spreading seasonal cheer, often collecting donations for charity. Also spelled carollers.

Caroling is the act of singing carols, especially Christmas songs, often in a group going door to door: {We went caroling through the neighborhood}. The tradition involves visiting homes or public spaces to spread holiday cheer through song. Also spelled carolling.

A caroller is someone who sings carols, especially Christmas songs performed in groups going door to door or gathering in public spaces: {The carollers came by last night singing "Silent Night"}. Also spelled caroler.

Carollers are people who sing carols, especially those who go door to door singing Christmas songs. The tradition involves small groups visiting neighborhoods, often collecting donations for charity. {Carollers gathered on the porch, their breath visible in the cold air.} Also spelled carolers.

Carolling is the act of singing carols, especially Christmas songs, often in a group going door to door: {We went carolling through the neighborhood on Christmas Eve}. The word evokes a festive, old-fashioned tradition of spreading holiday cheer through song. Also spelled caroling.

Carols are joyful songs, especially those sung at Christmas: {We went caroling through the neighborhood}, {The choir sang traditional carols}. The word once applied to any celebratory song accompanied by dancing, but now Christmas carols dominate usage. To carol is to sing such songs, typically going door to door during the holiday season.

A carousel is a rotating amusement ride with seats, often shaped like horses or other animals, that move up and down as the platform spins: {The children begged for another ride on the carousel}. The term extends to any rotating mechanism—a luggage carousel at an airport, a slide carousel for projectors. In digital interfaces, a carousel is a display element that cycles through images or content horizontally.

Carousels are rotating platforms, most commonly the amusement park ride with decorated horses and other animals that move up and down as the platform spins. The term extends to any rotating mechanism: a luggage carousel at an airport, a slide carousel for a projector. In digital interfaces, a carousel is a display element that cycles through images or content: {Swipe through the carousel to see more photos}.

Carousing is drinking and merrymaking in a loud, uninhibited way, typically with others: {They spent the night carousing at the pub}. The word suggests boisterous revelry that may go on too long or too late. To carouse is the verb; a carouse is an instance of such drinking.

Carp is a large freshwater fish, often bottom-feeding, found in ponds and slow rivers. Common carp are farmed for food in many parts of the world; koi are ornamental carp bred for their colors. Separately, to carp is to complain or find fault in a petty, nagging way: {He carped about every little thing}.

Carpaccio is a dish of raw meat or fish sliced paper-thin and served as an appetizer, typically drizzled with olive oil, lemon juice, and seasonings. The classic version uses beef, though tuna and salmon carpaccio have become equally common: {The restaurant is known for its beef carpaccio with arugula and shaved parmesan}.

A carpark is a designated area for parking vehicles, either an open lot or a multi-story structure. The term is standard in British English and Commonwealth countries; Americans say parking lot or parking garage. {The carpark was full by nine o'clock.}

A carpenter is a skilled worker who builds and repairs wooden structures—framing houses, installing cabinets, constructing furniture. The trade divides into rough carpentry (structural framing) and finish carpentry (trim, moldings, fine detail work). {We hired a carpenter to build the deck.} As a verb, to carpenter is to do such work, though the noun dominates.

Carpenters are skilled workers who build and repair wooden structures—framing houses, installing cabinets, constructing furniture. The trade divides roughly into rough carpentry (structural framing) and finish carpentry (trim, molding, visible surfaces). To carpenter is to do such work: {He carpentered his way through college}.

Carpentry is the craft of cutting, shaping, and joining wood to build or repair structures and objects. A carpenter builds houses, frames walls, installs doors and cabinets. The term covers rough work like framing and finish work like trim and molding. {He learned carpentry from his father.}

Carpet is a thick floor covering of woven or felted fabric, typically extending wall-to-wall rather than as a smaller rug. To carpet a room is to install this covering. Carpet extends to anything resembling such a covering: {a carpet of wildflowers}. To carpet someone (British) is to reprimand them severely, from being called to stand on the boss's carpet. To {sweep under the carpet} is to hide something inconvenient.

A carpetbag is a type of travel bag made from carpet fabric, popular in the 19th century. The word survives mainly in carpetbagger—a derogatory term for an outsider who moves somewhere to exploit local opportunities, especially for political gain. The original carpetbaggers were Northerners who went South after the Civil War: {He was dismissed as a carpetbagger who didn't understand the district}.

A carpetbagger is an outsider who moves to a new area seeking political or economic advantage. The term originated after the American Civil War for Northerners who went South during Reconstruction, supposedly carrying all their belongings in a carpetbag. Now it applies broadly to any opportunist exploiting a place where they have no roots: {The candidate was dismissed as a carpetbagger who'd only moved to the district six months before the election}.

Carpetbaggers were Northerners who went to the South after the American Civil War, supposedly carrying all their belongings in a bag made of carpet fabric—implying they were opportunists with no real stake in the region. The term now describes any outsider who moves somewhere to exploit local opportunities, especially political ones: {The candidate was dismissed as a carpetbagger who'd only lived in the district for six months}.

Carpetbagging is exploiting a place or situation where one has no genuine roots or stake. The term comes from Northerners who moved to the South after the Civil War, carrying their belongings in carpet bags, to profit from Reconstruction. Now it often describes politicians who run for office in districts where they don't truly live: {She accused her opponent of carpetbagging into the district just to win a seat}. The word implies opportunism and lack of authentic connection.

Carpets is the plural of carpet—thick textile floor coverings that span a room or area. Unlike rugs, carpets typically cover an entire floor and are often installed permanently. To carpet is to cover with carpet or to reprimand severely: {The boss carpeted him for missing the deadline}. To {sweep something under the carpet} is to hide a problem rather than address it.

A carpool is an arrangement where people share rides to a common destination, typically work or school, rotating drivers or splitting costs: {We started a carpool to save on gas}. The verb means to participate in such an arrangement: {I carpool with three coworkers}. A carpool lane on highways is reserved for vehicles carrying multiple passengers.

Carpooling is sharing a car ride with others traveling the same route, typically to work or school: {We started carpooling to split the cost of gas}. The arrangement reduces expenses, traffic, and environmental impact. A carpool lane on highways is reserved for vehicles carrying multiple passengers. Also spelled car-pooling or car pooling.

Carpools are arrangements where people share rides in a single vehicle, typically for commuting to work or school. The practice reduces costs, traffic, and environmental impact. As a verb, to carpool is to participate in such an arrangement: {We carpool to save on gas}. Many highways have carpool lanes reserved for vehicles with multiple occupants.

A carport is a shelter for a car, typically a roof supported by posts attached to or near a house. Unlike a garage, a carport has no walls or door—it protects vehicles from sun and rain but not from theft or wind-blown debris. {We pulled into the carport during the storm.}

A carriage is a wheeled vehicle, especially one drawn by horses for transporting people. The word extends to anything that carries or conveys: a baby carriage, the carriage of a typewriter (the part that moves), or a railway carriage (British for a passenger car). Carriage also means bearing or posture—how someone carries themselves: {She has the carriage of a dancer}. The carriage of goods is their transport, and carriage charges are shipping fees.

Carriages is the plural of carriage—a wheeled vehicle, historically horse-drawn, for transporting people: {The carriages lined up outside the estate}. In British usage, a carriage is a passenger car on a train: {We found seats in the first carriage}. The word also denotes bearing or posture: {She was admired for her elegant carriage}.

Carried is the past tense of carry—to transport something from one place to another: {She carried the groceries inside}. Beyond physical transport, carried extends to bearing responsibility {(He carried the weight of the family)}, winning {(The motion carried)}, reaching {(His voice carried across the room)}, or sustaining {(The melody carried the song)}. To get {carried away} is to lose restraint through enthusiasm or emotion.

A carrier is someone or something that transports goods or people—a mail carrier, an aircraft carrier, a common carrier like a trucking company. In medicine and genetics, a carrier harbors a disease or gene without showing symptoms: {She's a carrier of the sickle cell trait}. Telecommunications carriers provide phone or internet service. In physics and electronics, a carrier wave transmits a signal.

Carriers is the plural of carrier—a person or thing that transports something. Shipping carriers move packages; aircraft carriers launch planes; disease carriers transmit pathogens without showing symptoms themselves. In genetics, carriers have a gene for a condition they don't express but can pass to offspring. In telecommunications, a carrier is a company providing phone or data service: {Which carriers offer coverage in your area?}

Carries is the third-person singular of carry, which means to move something from one place to another while supporting it: {She carries her laptop everywhere}. Beyond physical transport, carry extends to bearing weight or responsibility {The job carries a lot of stress}, transmitting {Mosquitoes carry disease}, or having as a feature {The crime carries a ten-year sentence}. To carry yourself is to hold your body in a particular way. A voice that carries travels well across distance.

Carrion is the decaying flesh of dead animals. Vultures, crows, and other scavengers feed on carrion. The word often carries connotations of rot and disgust: {The battlefield reeked of carrion}. As an adjective, it describes creatures that eat the dead: {carrion birds circled overhead}.

A carrot is an orange root vegetable, long and tapered, eaten raw or cooked. Carrots appear in the phrase {carrot and stick}—reward paired with punishment—from the image of luring a donkey forward with a dangled carrot while threatening it from behind. A carrot alone is any promised incentive: {They dangled a promotion as a carrot}.

Carrots are orange root vegetables, long and tapered, eaten raw or cooked. They're a common side dish and salad ingredient, often associated with good eyesight. A carrot dangled before someone is an incentive or reward: {The promotion was the carrot that kept her working late}. The phrase {carrot and stick} pairs reward with punishment as motivational tools.

Carry shares core ideas with another frequent verb, bring. When used literally, the subject of carry is a person or thing that is capable of holding or transporting an object, and the object so held would probably not be moving on its own: Ask the porter to carry your bags to the car. When used figuratively, carry includes the idea of accompaniment that may also be present with bring: a crime that carries the death penalty. Without a direct object, carry may include the idea of succeed or pass: the motion carried on a vote of 23-7.

Carrying is the present participle of carry—moving something while supporting its weight. You can be carrying groceries, carrying a child, or carrying a weapon. Extended uses include bearing responsibility {carrying the team}, maintaining something {carrying insurance}, or being pregnant {She's carrying twins}. In sports, carrying often means advancing the ball: {He's averaging four yards per carry}.

Carryover is something that persists or transfers from one period, situation, or context into another. In accounting and taxes, a carryover is an amount—such as a loss or unused credit—that can be applied to a future year's calculations. More generally, it describes any remnant or continuation: {The tension in the room was a carryover from yesterday's argument}. As a modifier, it describes things retained beyond their original timeframe: carryover {funds}, carryover {inventory}.

Cars are motor vehicles designed to carry passengers on roads—the dominant form of personal transportation in developed countries. The word is the standard informal term for automobiles: {We took two cars to the airport}. Cars also refers to railroad vehicles: {freight cars}, {passenger cars}. In an elevator, the car is the enclosure that moves.

Carsick describes the nausea and discomfort some people feel while riding in a car, caused by the disconnect between what the eyes see and what the inner ear senses. Reading or looking at screens often makes it worse. {I get carsick if I sit in the back seat.} Similar terms exist for other vehicles: seasick, airsick.

Carsickness is nausea and discomfort caused by the motion of riding in a vehicle. It results from a mismatch between what the eyes see and what the inner ear senses. Children are particularly susceptible. {She always got carsickness on winding mountain roads.} The adjective is carsick.

A cart is a vehicle for hauling goods, typically with two wheels and pulled by an animal or pushed by hand. Shopping carts and golf carts extend the sense to wheeled conveyances in retail and recreation. To cart something is to transport it, often with effort or complaint: {I carted all those boxes up three flights of stairs}. To {put the cart before the horse} is to do things in the wrong order.

A cartel is a group of independent businesses or nations that coordinate to control prices, limit competition, or dominate a market. OPEC is perhaps the most famous cartel, controlling oil production. The term also refers to criminal organizations, particularly Latin American drug trafficking syndicates: {The Sinaloa cartel controls much of the border region}. More loosely, cartel suggests any powerful coalition acting in concert against outside interests.

Cartels are groups of independent entities—typically businesses or nations—that collude to control prices, limit competition, or divide markets. Oil-producing nations form cartels to regulate supply. Companies form illegal cartels to fix prices: {The Justice Department broke up the cartel}. Drug cartels are criminal organizations that control narcotics trafficking, often wielding military-level power: {Mexican cartels fighting for territory}.

A carthorse is a large, heavy horse bred for pulling carts, wagons, and plows rather than for riding or racing. Draft breeds like Clydesdires and Percherons are typical examples. Figuratively, calling someone a carthorse suggests they're sturdy and hardworking but perhaps lacking grace or speed: {She felt like a carthorse next to the ballerinas}.

Cartilage is the firm, flexible connective tissue found throughout the body—in joints, the ear, the nose, between vertebrae. It provides structure and cushioning without the rigidity of bone. Sharks have skeletons made entirely of cartilage. In meat, cartilage is the gristle you might cut around or chew through.

A cartographer is a person who makes maps. The work combines geographic knowledge with design skills to represent spatial information visually. Modern cartographers often use satellite imagery and digital tools, though the term covers mapmakers across all eras and methods: {The cartographer spent years surveying the coastline}.

Cartographers are people who make maps. The term covers both the craft of drawing and designing maps and the science of accurately representing geographic information. Modern cartographers work with satellite imagery and digital tools as much as pen and paper: {The cartographers updated the flood zone boundaries after the survey}.

Cartography is the science and art of making maps. The term covers everything from ancient hand-drawn charts to modern satellite-based mapping systems. A cartographer studies geography, surveys terrain, and represents spatial relationships on paper or screen. {The cartography of the region was unreliable until aerial photography became available.}

A carton is a lightweight container, typically made of cardboard or paperboard: a {carton of eggs}, a {carton of milk}, a {carton of cigarettes}. The word suggests something boxlike and disposable, distinct from heavier containers like crates or permanent packaging like bottles.

Cartons are containers, typically made of cardboard or paperboard, used for packaging and transporting goods. Milk and juice come in cartons; so do eggs. A carton of cigarettes contains multiple packs. The word suggests something lighter and more disposable than a box: {She carried the cartons up to her new apartment}.

A cartoon is a drawing, typically humorous or satirical, often with captions or speech bubbles. Editorial cartoons comment on politics; comic strips are cartoon sequences. The word extended to animated films—motion pictures made from drawings—and now covers any animation: {Saturday morning cartoons}, {a Pixar cartoon}. Cartoon also means a simplified or exaggerated version of something: {He's a cartoon villain}.

Cartooning is the art and practice of creating cartoons, whether single-panel drawings, comic strips, or animated sequences. The term covers both the drawing itself and the broader creative process of developing characters, gags, and visual storytelling. Someone who does cartooning professionally is a cartoonist. {She studied cartooning at art school before landing a job at a newspaper.}

Cartoonish describes something resembling a cartoon—exaggerated, simplified, or lacking realistic nuance. A cartoonish {villain} has no subtlety or complexity. Cartoonish {features} are oversized or distorted. The word usually carries a dismissive tone, suggesting something is too silly or broad to take seriously: {The film's cartoonish violence kept it from feeling genuinely disturbing}.

A cartoonist is someone who draws cartoons—whether single-panel comics, comic strips, editorial illustrations, or animated sequences. The term covers a range from newspaper cartoonists producing daily strips to political cartoonists commenting on current events: {The cartoonist captured the senator's arrogance in a few lines}.

Cartoonists are artists who draw cartoons—whether single-panel gags, comic strips, editorial illustrations, or animated sequences. The term covers newspaper cartoonists, political cartoonists, and those who create comics for magazines or the web. {The cartoonists at the newspaper worked under tight deadlines.}

Cartoons are drawings, typically humorous or satirical, often published in newspapers and magazines. Political cartoons comment on current events through caricature and visual metaphor. The word also refers to animated films or television shows: {Saturday morning cartoons}, {cartoon characters}. A cartoon can be a preliminary sketch for a painting or fresco, though this sense is now rare outside art history.

A cartridge is a container holding material ready to be fed into a device. A gun cartridge contains propellant and usually a bullet, designed to be loaded and fired as a unit. Ink cartridges slot into printers; game cartridges into consoles. The word implies a standardized, replaceable unit: {I need to buy new toner cartridges for the copier}.

Cartridges is the plural of cartridge, a self-contained unit designed to be loaded into a device. The oldest sense is ammunition—a casing holding a bullet, powder, and primer: {The rifle holds five cartridges}. The concept extends to replaceable containers for ink, toner, or video games: {I need to buy new printer cartridges}. A cartridge simplifies reloading by packaging components together.

Carts is the plural of cart—a wheeled vehicle for transporting goods, typically pushed or pulled by hand or drawn by animals. Shopping carts hold groceries; golf carts ferry players across courses. In computing, a cart (short for cartridge) holds game software: {old Nintendo carts}. Online, carts hold items selected for purchase: {I have three things in my cart}.

A cartwheel is a sideways flip where hands and feet touch the ground alternately, arms and legs extended like spokes of a wheel. Children turn cartwheels on lawns; gymnasts perform them in routines. The word extends to any wheel-like rotation: {The plane cartwheeled across the runway}. A cartwheel is also slang for a large coin, especially the old silver dollar.

Cartwheeling is performing cartwheels—the acrobatic move where you turn sideways with arms and legs extended like wheel spokes. The term extends to any spinning or tumbling motion: {The car went cartwheeling off the cliff}. Figuratively, something cartwheeling moves wildly or dramatically: {Stock prices went cartwheeling after the announcement}.

Cartwheels are acrobatic movements where the body rotates sideways with arms and legs extended like wheel spokes, hands and feet touching the ground in sequence. Children do cartwheels on lawns; gymnasts perform them in routines. Figuratively, to do cartwheels is to express exuberant joy: {When she got the acceptance letter, her heart did cartwheels}.
clues: Hands and feet touch ground alternately

definition: Carve is to cut into a solid material with a blade or sharp tool. You carve wood, stone, or ice to create shapes or designs: {She carved a figure from a block of oak}. At the dinner table, to carve is to slice meat from a larger piece: {Who's going to carve the turkey?} To carve out something—a career, a niche, a territory—is to establish it through sustained effort. To carve up is to divide: {The victors carved up the defeated empire among themselves}.

Carved describes something that has been shaped by cutting away material—typically wood, stone, or ice. A carved {statue} shows the marks of deliberate shaping. Carved {initials} in a tree trunk are cut into the bark. Figuratively, features can look carved: {Her face was carved from granite}. Something deeply carved feels permanent, etched, established.

A carver is someone who carves—shaping wood, stone, or other materials by cutting away pieces: {a master carver of wooden decoys}. In dining contexts, the carver is the person who cuts and serves meat at table, or the large knife used for that purpose: {He took up the carver and began slicing the roast}.

Carvers are people who carve—shaping wood, stone, or other materials by cutting away pieces: {The carvers worked on the totem pole for months}. In a dining context, carvers are the utensils used to carve meat, typically a long knife and matching fork. A carver can also be a dining chair with arms, traditionally reserved for the head of the table.

A carvery is a restaurant or buffet where roasted meats are sliced to order, typically by a chef stationed at a carving table. The term is primarily British, often describing a section within a pub or hotel where diners choose from joints of beef, turkey, ham, or lamb: {Sunday lunch at the carvery}.

Carves is the third-person singular of carve. To carve is to cut into a solid material—wood, stone, meat—with deliberate strokes. A sculptor carves a figure from marble. Someone carves a turkey at Thanksgiving. To carve out a niche or career is to establish one through sustained effort: {She carved out a reputation as a tough negotiator}. To carve up is to divide, often aggressively: {The colonial powers carved up Africa}.

Carving is the act of cutting into a solid material to shape it—wood, stone, meat. A carving is the result: a decorative object cut from wood or stone, or a slice of meat from a roast. The carving knife is the large blade used at the table: {Who's doing the carving this Thanksgiving?}

Carvings are objects or designs shaped by cutting away material—typically wood, stone, or ice. The word emphasizes the finished products rather than the process: {ancient carvings on temple walls}, {intricate carvings decorating the mantelpiece}. Carvings range from folk art to fine sculpture, and the term often suggests handcraft and traditional technique.

A carwash is a facility where vehicles are cleaned, either by automated machinery or by hand. Drive-through carwashes pull cars along a track through sprayers, brushes, and dryers. A carwash can also mean the act of washing a car: {The team held a carwash to raise money for new uniforms}.

A casbah is the old fortified quarter of a North African city, typically featuring narrow winding streets, traditional architecture, and dense residential areas. The term often evokes images of labyrinthine markets and ancient walls: {We got lost in the casbah of Algiers}. Sometimes spelled kasbah.

A cascade is a waterfall, especially one of several falling in stages down a rocky slope. The word extends to anything that flows or falls in a similar pattern: {a cascade of auburn hair}, {a cascade of events}. In technical contexts, cascade describes processes that trigger subsequent processes in sequence—a cascade of failures, a cascade effect in electronics. As a verb, things cascade when they pour or tumble downward in stages: {Water cascaded over the rocks}. (Capitalized Cascade refers to the mountain range.)

Cascades are waterfalls, especially a series of small falls or water flowing over rocks in stages. The word extends to anything that falls or flows in succession: {a cascade of curls}, {a cascade of events}. In computing, cascading describes how styles or effects pass down through hierarchies. As a verb, to cascade is to fall or flow in this tumbling, sequential way: {Errors cascaded through the system}.

Cascading describes something falling or flowing in stages, like water over a series of rocks. Each level triggers the next: {cascading waterfalls}, {cascading failures in the power grid}. In computing, cascading style sheets (CSS) apply formatting rules that flow down through nested elements. The word emphasizes succession and accumulation—effects that multiply as they descend.

Case is really two words with a single spelling, a fact that partly explains its high frequency. One kind of case is a physical object that encloses or contains something; the other case is abstract and stands for a set of circumstances, a situation requiring action, or a matter in a court of law. The relatively infrequent verb case is derived from the first meaning. The second kind of case is frequently used idiomatically in the phrase in case.

A casefile is a collection of documents, records, and evidence relating to a particular case, whether legal, medical, investigative, or administrative. Police detectives maintain casefiles on ongoing investigations; lawyers keep casefiles on their clients; doctors may have casefiles on patients with complex conditions. The term suggests organized documentation that can be referenced, updated, and eventually closed when the matter is resolved. {The detective pulled the casefile from the cabinet and began reviewing the witness statements.}

A caseload is the number of cases handled by a professional at any given time—typically a social worker, lawyer, doctor, or judge. The term implies ongoing responsibility: {Her caseload increased to forty clients}. Heavy caseloads strain workers and can compromise quality of care or attention.

Cases is the plural of case, covering all its senses. A case can be a container {a glasses case}, an instance or example {a case of mistaken identity}, a legal matter {the case goes to trial}, or a medical situation {confirmed cases of flu}. In grammar, case refers to the form a noun or pronoun takes based on its function in a sentence.

A caseworker is a professional who manages individual cases in social services, healthcare, or similar fields. They assess needs, coordinate resources, and advocate for clients—whether helping families access benefits, monitoring child welfare, or guiding patients through treatment programs. {The caseworker visited the home twice a month to check on the children.}

Caseworkers is the plural of caseworker, a professional who manages individual cases in social services, healthcare, or similar fields. Caseworkers assess needs, coordinate resources, and advocate for clients—whether children in foster care, hospital patients, or welfare recipients. {The caseworkers were overwhelmed by their caseloads.}

Cash is money in physical form—coins and paper currency rather than checks, cards, or digital transfers: {Do you have cash or should I put it on the card?} To cash a check is to exchange it for currency. To {cash in} on something is to profit from it. To {cash out} is to convert assets to money, often when leaving a game or investment.

Cashback is money returned to a buyer as an incentive. Credit cards offer cashback as a percentage of purchases: {I get 2% cashback on groceries}. Retail promotions may advertise cashback on specific items. At checkout, cashback also means withdrawing cash from your bank account while paying with a debit card: {Would you like any cashback with that?}

A cashew is an edible kidney-shaped nut that grows attached to the bottom of a fleshy fruit called the cashew apple. The nut is sold roasted and often salted: {a bowl of cashews}, {cashew butter}. Cashews are native to Brazil but now cultivated widely in tropical regions. The shell contains a caustic oil that must be removed before eating.

Cashews are kidney-shaped nuts that grow from the bottom of cashew apples, native to Brazil but now cultivated across the tropics. They're always sold shelled because the shell contains a caustic oil. Cashews appear in stir-fries, curries, and trail mixes, and are processed into dairy substitutes: {cashew milk}, {cashew cheese}.

Cashflow is the movement of money into and out of a business, account, or household over time. Positive cashflow means more coming in than going out; negative cashflow means the reverse. A business can be profitable on paper but fail due to poor cashflow—bills come due before payments arrive. {We're waiting on invoices to clear up our cashflow problems.}

A cashier is a person who handles payments at a store, bank, or other business, receiving money and making change. The word also functions as a verb meaning to dismiss someone from a position, especially in disgrace: {The officer was cashiered for misconduct}. This sense carries connotations of formal discharge with dishonor, used particularly in military contexts.

Cashiers is the plural of cashier, a person who handles payments at a store, bank, or other business: {The cashiers were overwhelmed during the holiday rush}. As a verb, to cashier means to dismiss someone from service, especially military service, in disgrace: {The officer was cashiered for misconduct}. This sense is formal and uncommon.

Cashless describes transactions or systems that don't involve physical currency—paper bills or coins. A cashless payment uses credit cards, debit cards, or digital transfers instead: {The festival is completely cashless}. A cashless society would eliminate physical money entirely, conducting all commerce electronically.

Cashmere is a luxuriously soft, lightweight wool made from the undercoat of cashmere goats, originally from the Kashmir region. The fiber is prized for warmth without bulk: {a cashmere sweater}, {cashmere scarf}. Because genuine cashmere is expensive, the word connotes quality and refinement. Fabrics blended with cashmere or imitating it may also be called cashmere.

Cashout is the act of converting assets, chips, or accumulated value into actual money. In gambling, you cashout when you exchange your chips for currency or withdraw winnings from an account. The term extends to finance and business, where cashing out means liquidating investments or selling one's stake in a company. In video games and apps, cashout refers to redeeming points or virtual currency for real money or prizes. {I hit a lucky streak and decided to cashout before losing it all.}

Casing is an outer covering or container that encloses something. A sausage casing holds the meat. A door casing is the frame surrounding it. In construction, casing refers to the finished molding around windows and doors. Bullet casings are the metal shells ejected after firing. To case a place is to examine it before a robbery: {They cased the joint for a week before the heist}.

Casings are outer coverings or enclosures. Bullet casings are the metal shells ejected after firing. Sausage casings hold the meat mixture in shape—traditionally intestine, now often synthetic. Door and window casings are the trim frames surrounding openings. The word emphasizes containment: whatever's inside needs wrapping, housing, or structural support.

A casino is an establishment where people gamble, typically featuring games like blackjack, poker, roulette, and slot machines. Casinos range from massive resort complexes in Las Vegas and Macau to modest riverboat operations. The word extends to card games played at home: {We're having a casino night}. Casino is also a specific card game involving capturing cards that match or sum to cards on the table.

Casinos are establishments where gambling takes place—typically offering games like blackjack, poker, roulette, and slot machines. The word evokes places like Las Vegas or Monte Carlo, where gambling is the main attraction surrounded by hotels, restaurants, and entertainment. {The casino floor was packed on Saturday night.} Online casinos have expanded gambling beyond physical venues.

A cask is a barrel-shaped container, typically wooden, used for storing and aging liquids—especially wine, whiskey, and beer. The word suggests craftsmanship and tradition: {aged twelve years in oak casks}. Cask-strength spirits are bottled directly from the barrel without dilution. A casket was originally a small cask.

A casket is a box for storing or displaying valued objects, or more commonly in American English, a coffin—the box in which a dead body is buried or cremated. The burial sense dominates modern usage, though the older meaning of a small ornamental box for jewelry or keepsakes persists in some contexts. {The family chose a mahogany casket for the funeral.} Casket tends to sound more euphemistic and genteel than coffin, which may explain its preference in American funeral industry language.

Caskets are containers for burial—coffins, typically rectangular with a hinged lid. The word sounds gentler than coffin, which is why American funeral homes prefer it. Originally, a casket was a small ornamental box for jewelry or keepsakes, and this sense survives: {a casket of love letters}. The burial meaning arose in 19th-century America.

Casks are barrel-shaped containers, typically made of wooden staves bound by metal hoops, used for storing and aging liquids—especially wine, whiskey, and beer. The wood imparts flavor during aging: {The bourbon aged twelve years in charred oak casks}. Cask can also refer to the quantity a cask holds, or any barrel-like container.

Cassava is a starchy root vegetable native to South America, now a dietary staple across tropical regions of Africa, Asia, and Latin America. The plant's large tuberous roots are processed into flour, tapioca, and various other food products. Raw cassava contains compounds that can release cyanide, so it must be properly prepared before eating. {Cassava flour has become popular as a gluten-free alternative in baking.}

A casserole is a deep dish used for slow-cooking in an oven, and by extension, the food cooked in it—typically a one-pot meal combining meat or vegetables with a starchy binder like rice, pasta, or potatoes: {tuna casserole}, {green bean casserole}. The dish is associated with home cooking and potlucks. To casserole something is to cook it this way.

Casseroles is the plural of casserole—a deep dish used for slow-cooking in an oven, or the food prepared in such a dish. A casserole typically combines meat, vegetables, and starch in a sauce, baked until the flavors meld: {She brought three casseroles to the potluck}. The dish is associated with home cooking and communal meals, often appearing at funerals and family gatherings.

A cassette is a small plastic case containing magnetic tape for audio or video recording and playback. Audio cassettes dominated music distribution from the 1970s through the 1990s before CDs displaced them: {I found my old cassette collection in the attic}. Cassette tapes could be recorded at home, enabling mixtapes and bootlegs. The format survives mainly in nostalgia and lo-fi aesthetics.

Cassettes are small plastic cartridges containing magnetic tape, used for recording and playing audio or video. Audio cassettes dominated music distribution from the 1970s through the 1990s before CDs displaced them: {I found a box of old cassettes in the attic}. Videocassettes (VHS, Betamax) served the same function for film. The format has nostalgic appeal and a small revival among audiophiles and indie musicians.

A cassock is a long, close-fitting robe worn by clergy in certain Christian traditions, typically reaching to the ankles and buttoned down the front. Black is standard for most priests and ministers, while bishops may wear purple, cardinals red, and the pope white. The garment is worn for liturgical services and sometimes as everyday clerical dress: {The priest's cassock rustled as he walked up the aisle}.

Cassowaries is the plural of cassowary, a large flightless bird native to New Guinea and northeastern Australia. Related to emus and ostriches, cassowaries are distinctive for their black plumage, bright blue necks, and bony helmet-like crests. They can be aggressive when threatened and are considered among the world's most dangerous birds.

A cassowary is a large flightless bird native to New Guinea and northern Australia. Second only to ostriches in size, cassowaries have distinctive bony crests on their heads and bright blue necks. They can be dangerous—powerful legs ending in dagger-like claws have killed humans. {We spotted a cassowary in the rainforest.}

Cast, a busy and complex word, is most frequent as a verb literally meaning throw (cast a fishing line) and figuratively, cause to be felt or present (cast doubt, cast a shadow, cast a spell). Noun meanings are also extremely varied and many of them have an associated, specific verb meaning. The cast of a play or movie consists of the actors in it. When you cast a film, you choose these people. A cast is also something formed by molding (a copper cast of the statue), and to cast something is to mold it: The company cast a bell for city hall. A protective covering for a broken limb is also called a cast; the medical professional casts the limb.

Castanets are a percussion instrument consisting of two small concave shells of wood or plastic, clicked together rhythmically in the palm. Strongly associated with Spanish flamenco dancing, they're held in each hand and clapped by the fingers to produce a sharp, rattling sound that accents the music: {The dancer's castanets punctuated each step}.

Castanets are a percussion instrument consisting of two shell-shaped pieces of wood or plastic, held in the hand and clicked together rhythmically. They're associated with Spanish flamenco dancing and music: {The dancer's castanets punctuated every turn}. The clicking sound itself may be called castanets.

A castaway is a person stranded in an isolated place, typically after a shipwreck: {The castaways survived on coconuts and rainwater}. The word evokes Robinson Crusoe scenarios—someone marooned on a deserted island. More broadly, castaway describes anyone abandoned or rejected by society, cast away like refuse.

Castaways are people stranded in a remote place, typically after a shipwreck. The word evokes someone washed ashore on a deserted island, surviving on coconuts and signal fires: {The castaways built a raft from driftwood}. By extension, a castaway is anyone abandoned or rejected by society—an outcast left to fend for themselves.

Caste is a rigid social class determined by birth, most associated with the Hindu system in India, where hereditary groups are ranked hierarchically and traditionally dictate occupation, marriage, and social interaction. The term extends to any society with similar stratification: {America's racial caste system}. In biology, caste describes specialized groups within social insects—worker bees, soldier ants. The {caste system} implies inherited inequality that individuals cannot escape through achievement or effort.

A caster is a small swiveling wheel attached to furniture or equipment, allowing it to roll: {The desk chair has five casters}. A caster is also one who casts—a person throwing fishing line, pouring molten metal, or in gaming, a character who casts spells. A caster may also be a small container with holes for sprinkling sugar or spices.

Casters are small wheels mounted in swiveling frames, attached to furniture or equipment so it can roll easily: {office chairs with casters}, {hospital beds on casters}. The swivel lets the object change direction smoothly. Also spelled castors. Separately, casters are people who cast—fishing lines, metal, spells, or live commentary on video game streams.

Castes are hereditary social classes, especially the rigid divisions of traditional Hindu society that determine occupation, marriage eligibility, and social standing. The system historically ranged from Brahmins (priests) at the top to "untouchables" at the bottom. More broadly, caste describes any fixed social stratification: {Hollywood has its own caste system}. The singular caste refers to the system itself or one's position within it.

Casting is the process of selecting actors for roles in a play, film, or other production: {The casting took three months}. A casting {director} oversees auditions. In manufacturing, casting means pouring liquid material into a mold to create a shape—metal casting, plaster casting. A casting is also the object produced by this process. To cast a fishing line is to throw it; the noun casting can refer to this action or the tackle used.

Castings are objects formed by pouring molten material into a mold and letting it harden—metal castings, plaster castings. The word also refers to what's discarded: anglers speak of castings (the line thrown out), and earthworm castings are the soil particles worms excrete. In film and theater, castings are auditions or the selections made from them: {The castings for the new production were announced yesterday}.

A castle is a large fortified building or complex, typically from medieval Europe, designed for defense and as a residence for nobility. Castles feature thick stone walls, towers, moats, and battlements. The word extends to grand residences generally, even without fortifications, and to the rook in chess. The phrase {a man's home is his castle} asserts that people have absolute authority within their own dwelling. To castle in chess is to move the king and rook simultaneously in a specific defensive maneuver.

Castles are fortified residences built for medieval nobility, combining defensive architecture with living quarters. Thick walls, towers, moats, and drawbridges characterized these structures. The word extends to grand or imposing buildings: {Her mansion was practically a castle}. In chess, castle is an informal name for the rook, and to castle is to move the king and rook simultaneously in a protective maneuver. To build {castles in the air} is to indulge in fanciful, impractical dreams.

Castling is a special move in chess where the king and a rook move simultaneously. The king shifts two squares toward the rook, and the rook jumps to the square the king crossed. It's the only move where two pieces move at once, used to protect the king while activating the rook: {I castled queenside to get my rook into play}.

A castmate is a fellow member of a theatrical, film, or television cast—someone you perform alongside in a production. The word follows the pattern of classmate, roommate, and teammate: {She remained close friends with her castmates long after the show ended}. Also spelled as two words: cast mate.

Castmates are fellow performers in a theatrical production, film, or television show. The term emphasizes the collaborative relationship among actors working together on the same project: {She remained close friends with her castmates long after the show ended}. Sometimes spelled as two words: cast mates.

A castoff is something discarded or rejected, especially clothing passed along to someone else: {The younger siblings wore their older brother's castoffs}. As an adjective, castoff describes things thrown away or abandoned: {castoff furniture}, {castoff lovers}. In knitting, casting off is the technique for finishing an edge and removing work from the needles.

Castoffs are things discarded or rejected as no longer useful or wanted. The term often applies to clothing passed along after the original owner has finished with it: {She dressed in her older sister's castoffs}. It extends to people who have been rejected or abandoned: {a team built from castoffs nobody else wanted}. Also spelled cast-offs.

To castrate a male animal or human is to remove or destroy the testicles, eliminating the ability to reproduce and drastically reducing testosterone. The practice has been applied to livestock for centuries to make animals more docile and improve meat quality, and historically to humans to create eunuchs or as punishment. Castrate also works figuratively: to castrate a proposal or argument is to strip it of force or effectiveness. {The committee castrated the bill before it reached the floor.}

Castrated describes a male animal or person whose testicles have been removed or destroyed, eliminating reproductive capacity and reducing testosterone. Livestock are commonly castrated to make them more docile and improve meat quality. The term extends figuratively to anything stripped of force or vitality: {The amendment castrated the bill}. A castrated man is also called a eunuch.

Castrating is removing the testicles of a male animal or person, eliminating reproductive capacity and reducing testosterone. Farm animals are routinely castrated to make them more docile and improve meat quality. Figuratively, to castrate someone is to deprive them of power, strength, or vitality: {She accused the committee of castrating the proposal}. The metaphor suggests emasculation—rendering someone ineffective or weak.

Castration is the removal or destruction of the testicles, eliminating male reproductive capacity and testosterone production. The term applies to humans and animals alike—livestock are routinely castrated to control breeding and behavior. Figuratively, to castrate someone is to deprive them of power or vigor: {The amendments castrated the bill}. The adjective castrating describes someone who undermines another's confidence, especially a man's sense of masculinity.
clues: Making a male unable to reproduce

definition: A castrato was a male singer castrated before puberty to preserve his high vocal range into adulthood. The practice produced voices of unusual power and flexibility, prized in Italian opera from the 17th through 19th centuries. The plural is castrati. The term now appears mainly in historical discussions of Baroque music.

Casts is the plural of cast in its noun senses and the third-person singular in its verb senses. A cast is something shaped by pouring material into a mold—a bronze cast, a plaster cast for a broken limb. A cast is also the group of actors in a production: {The cast takes a bow}. To cast is to throw, project, or assign: cast a {fishing line}, cast a {shadow}, cast a {vote}, cast an {actor} in a role. {She casts doubt on his story}. {The foundry casts engine blocks}.

Casual describes what is relaxed, informal, or not serious. Casual {dress} is everyday clothing, not formal attire. A casual {acquaintance} is someone you know slightly. Casual {sex} happens without commitment. A casual {remark} is offhand, not carefully considered. Casual {work} is irregular or temporary. The word implies ease and lack of intensity: {He adopted a casual tone to hide his nervousness}.

Casually means in a relaxed, informal, or unconcerned manner. Someone dressed casually wears everyday clothes rather than formal attire: {He showed up casually in jeans and a t-shirt}. To mention something casually is to bring it up offhandedly, without apparent emphasis: {She casually mentioned she'd been offered a promotion}. The word can suggest deliberate nonchalance masking actual interest or effort.

Casuals are clothes suitable for informal occasions—jeans, t-shirts, comfortable shoes rather than business attire or formalwear: {I packed mostly casuals for the trip}. In British usage, casuals can also refer to workers employed on a temporary or irregular basis, or to soccer hooligans who dress in designer sportswear to avoid police detection.

Casualties are people killed, injured, or otherwise lost in war, disaster, or accident. Military reports distinguish between killed in action and total casualties, which include the wounded, captured, and missing. The word extends to anything damaged or destroyed by circumstance: {Local businesses were casualties of the economic downturn}. A single victim is a casualty: {She was a casualty of the restructuring}.

A casualty is someone killed, injured, or otherwise lost in war or disaster. Military reports count casualties—the wounded alongside the dead. The meaning extends to anything damaged or destroyed by circumstance: {Truth is the first casualty of war}. A casualty of budget cuts might be a beloved program. In British usage, casualty also means an emergency room.

Cat is the general term for the family of mammals that includes domestic kitties, lions, tigers, jaguars, pumas, lynxes, and the like—more technically speaking, felines or felids. Without modification or other contextual clues, cat refers to the domestic animal kept as a pet. It also has many slang and technical meanings that have no obvious connection with felines. Cat can designate a man (a cool cat) or disparagingly, a malicious woman. Cats figure in several idioms including let the cat out of the bag (reveal a secret), and like herding cats (difficult to organize successfully).

A cataclysm is a violent upheaval or disaster on a massive scale. The word applies to catastrophic natural events—floods, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions—and to social or political convulsions: {The French Revolution was a cataclysm that reshaped European politics}. The adjective cataclysmic describes anything sudden, violent, and transformative: {cataclysmic climate change}, {cataclysmic consequences}.

Cataclysmic describes events of violent, large-scale destruction or upheaval. A cataclysmic earthquake levels cities; a cataclysmic flood reshapes landscapes. The word often appears in geological or cosmic contexts: {the cataclysmic asteroid impact that killed the dinosaurs}. Figuratively, it applies to any sudden, devastating change: {a cataclysmic defeat}, {cataclysmic consequences for the economy}.

Cataclysms are sudden, violent upheavals that cause massive destruction or change. The word applies to natural disasters—floods, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions—and to catastrophic events in human affairs: wars, revolutions, economic collapses. {The cataclysms of the twentieth century reshaped the world order.} A cataclysm implies not just destruction but transformation; things cannot return to what they were before.

A catacomb is an underground cemetery, typically consisting of tunnels and chambers with recesses cut into walls for burial. The word usually appears in the plural—the catacombs beneath Rome or Paris are famous examples, holding remains of millions. By extension, any dark, winding underground passage might be called a catacomb: {We explored the catacombs beneath the old city}.

Catacombs are underground passages or tunnels containing graves or burial chambers, typically cut into rock. The term comes from the subterranean cemeteries beneath Rome where early Christians buried their dead. By extension, catacombs can describe any network of underground tunnels or chambers, even without burials: {We explored the catacombs beneath the old city}. The word usually appears in plural form.

A catalog is a systematic list or record of items, typically organized for easy reference. Libraries maintain catalogs of their holdings; retailers publish catalogs displaying merchandise available for purchase. The verb catalog means to create such a list or to add items to one: {She spent the afternoon cataloging her vinyl collection}. In extended use, catalog can describe any comprehensive enumeration: {a catalog of complaints}. The spelling catalogue, with the silent -ue ending, is preferred in British English.

Cataloging is the act of organizing items into a systematic list or record. Libraries catalog books by author, title, and subject. Museums catalog their collections. The word implies methodical classification rather than simple listing: {She spent weeks cataloging her grandmother's photographs}. Also spelled cataloguing.

Catalogs is the plural of catalog, a systematic list or collection of items—books in a library, products for sale, courses at a university. To catalog something is to organize it into such a list: {She spent months cataloging the museum's collection}. The word extends to any comprehensive enumeration: {He cataloged her faults one by one}. Also spelled catalogues.

Catalogue is the British spelling of catalog—a systematic list of items, typically with descriptions: a library catalogue, an auction catalogue. As a verb, to catalogue is to compile such a list or to record systematically: {She spent years cataloguing the museum's collection}. The word extends to any comprehensive enumeration: {a catalogue of complaints}, {a catalogue of errors}.

A catalyst is something that triggers or accelerates change without being consumed by it. The term comes from chemistry, where a catalyst speeds up reactions while remaining chemically unchanged. The figurative sense now dominates: {The assassination was the catalyst for war}. A person can be a catalyst: {She was the catalyst who finally got the team working together}.

Catalysts are agents that cause or accelerate change. In chemistry, a catalyst speeds up a reaction without being consumed by it. The figurative sense dominates general usage: {The assassination was the catalyst for war}. A catalyst sets things in motion or brings latent tensions to a head. The singular is catalyst.
