Centred is the British spelling of centered. Something centred is placed in the middle or has a specified focus: {The discussion centred on budget cuts}. A person who is centred feels balanced and emotionally grounded: {She seemed calm and centred despite the chaos}. Self-centred describes someone focused mainly on themselves.

A centrefold is the middle spread of a magazine, designed as a single large image when the pages are unfolded. The term typically refers to a nude or sexually suggestive photograph, especially of a woman, featured in such spreads: {a Playboy centrefold}. By extension, a centrefold is the person pictured. The spelling centerfold is American; centrefold is British.

Centrefolds is the British spelling of centerfolds—the middle pages of a magazine that fold out to reveal a larger image, typically a photograph of a nude or seminude model. By extension, a centrefold is the person pictured: {She was a centrefold in the 1990s}. The term evokes glossy men's magazines like Playboy.

A centrepiece is a decorative object placed in the middle of a table, typically for formal occasions: {The florist created an elaborate centrepiece for the wedding reception}. By extension, centrepiece describes anything that serves as the central or most important element: {The tax cut was the centrepiece of his economic plan}. British spelling; Americans write centerpiece.

A centrifuge is a machine that spins rapidly to separate substances of different densities. The spinning creates centrifugal force that pushes heavier materials outward while lighter ones stay closer to the center. Laboratory centrifuges separate blood components or isolate DNA; industrial centrifuges extract honey or dry laundry. As a verb, to centrifuge is to subject something to this process: {We centrifuged the samples at high speed}.

Centrism is a political stance that avoids the extremes of left and right, favoring moderate or middle-ground positions. A centrist might support some progressive social policies while endorsing fiscal conservatism. Critics from both sides often characterize centrism as fence-sitting or lacking conviction: {His centrism pleased no one during the primary}.

A centrist holds political views in the middle of the ideological spectrum, avoiding the extremes of left and right. The term can be neutral description or mild criticism—centrists may be seen as pragmatic moderates or as lacking conviction. {She positioned herself as a centrist to appeal to swing voters.} As an adjective: {centrist policies}, {centrist Democrats}.

Centrists occupy the political middle ground, rejecting what they see as extremes on both left and right. The term can be self-applied with pride or used dismissively by critics who view centrism as fence-sitting or lack of conviction: {Centrists in Congress held the deciding votes}. In polarized times, centrist positions may be characterized as either reasonable compromise or spineless moderation, depending on who's talking.

Cents is the plural of cent, the smallest monetary unit in the United States and other countries—one hundredth of a dollar. The word appears constantly in prices: {The total comes to twelve dollars and fifty cents}. To {put in your two cents} is to offer an opinion, often unsolicited.

Centuries is the plural of century, a period of one hundred years. The word appears constantly in historical writing: {The practice dates back centuries}. Numbered centuries count from year one: the 1900s were the twentieth century, a source of perpetual confusion. {It took centuries to build the cathedral.}

A centurion was an officer in the ancient Roman army commanding a century—nominally one hundred soldiers, though in practice often fewer. The rank was roughly equivalent to a modern captain or senior sergeant. Centurions formed the backbone of Roman military discipline and appear frequently in historical accounts and biblical narratives: {The centurion said to Jesus, "Lord, I am not worthy"}. The word now evokes Roman military imagery in historical fiction, games, and metaphorical use for authoritative leadership.

Centurions were officers in the ancient Roman army, each commanding a century—nominally one hundred soldiers, though typically fewer in practice. The term now appears in historical contexts and as a name for sports teams, military units, or products evoking Roman martial discipline: {The centurion barked orders to his men}.

A century is a period of one hundred years. The word often refers to specific hundred-year spans counted from a base date: {the twentieth century}, {eighteenth-century architecture}. In cricket, a century is a score of one hundred runs by a single batsman. The term extends to any count of one hundred: {He's pitched six centuries of wins}.

A cephalopod is a marine mollusk with a prominent head and tentacles—octopuses, squids, cuttlefish, and nautiluses. The name means "head-foot," describing how the tentacles attach directly to the head. Cephalopods are known for intelligence, camouflage abilities, and jet propulsion: {The aquarium's cephalopod exhibit features a giant Pacific octopus}.

Cephalopods are marine mollusks with tentacles attached to their heads—octopuses, squid, cuttlefish, and nautiluses. The name means "head-foot," describing their distinctive anatomy. They're known for intelligence, camouflage abilities, and jet propulsion. Unlike their shelled mollusk relatives, most cephalopods have reduced or lost their shells entirely.

Ceramic refers to materials made by shaping clay or similar substances and hardening them with heat. The word covers everything from ancient pottery to modern tiles, porcelain, and industrial components. As an adjective, ceramic describes objects made this way: {ceramic tiles}, {ceramic cookware}. The plural ceramics names both the art of making such objects and the objects themselves: {She studied ceramics in college}.

Ceramics are objects made from clay that has been shaped and hardened by heat—pottery, tiles, bricks, porcelain. The term covers both the objects themselves and the art of making them: {She's taking a ceramics class}. As a material science, ceramics includes non-metallic solids used in electronics, aerospace, and medicine, valued for heat resistance and durability.

Cereal is a grass cultivated for its edible grain—wheat, rice, corn, oats, barley. The word also means the processed breakfast food made from these grains: {a bowl of cereal with milk}. Cereal grains form the foundation of human agriculture and diet worldwide. As an adjective, cereal describes things relating to grain: {cereal crops}, {cereal production}.

Cereals are grains used for food—wheat, rice, corn, oats, barley—or the breakfast foods made from processed grains: {a bowl of cereal with milk}. The singular cereal typically means the breakfast food, while cereals as a plural often refers to the grain crops themselves: {Cereals account for most of the world's agricultural output}.

Cerebral relates to the brain or intellect. A cerebral {hemorrhage} involves bleeding in the brain. More often, cerebral describes something that appeals to the mind rather than the emotions: a cerebral {film}, a cerebral {approach to music}. Calling someone cerebral suggests they favor thinking over feeling—sometimes admiringly, sometimes implying they're cold or overly analytical.

Ceremonial describes things relating to or used in ceremonies—formal rituals or observances: {ceremonial robes}, {ceremonial duties}, {a ceremonial sword}. Something ceremonial emphasizes formality and tradition over practical function. As a noun, a ceremonial is the system of rites for a particular occasion: {the ceremonial of a state funeral}. Ceremonial overlaps with ceremonious, though ceremonious more often describes excessively formal behavior.

Ceremonies is the plural of ceremony—formal events marking significant occasions. Weddings, graduations, and inaugurations are ceremonies. The word often appears in phrases: {master of ceremonies} (the host who guides an event), {stand on ceremony} (insist on formality). {Without further ceremonies} means dispensing with preliminaries to get to the point.

A ceremony is a formal act or series of acts performed according to established rules or customs, especially to mark significant occasions: {a wedding ceremony}, {a graduation ceremony}. The word extends to elaborate formality in general: {the ceremony of a state dinner}. To {stand on ceremony} is to insist on formalities; without ceremony means unceremoniously or abruptly.

Certain means sure or definite. If you're certain about something, you have no doubt: {I'm certain I locked the door}. Certain facts are established beyond question. The word also picks out unspecified particulars: {certain people}, {a certain charm}. This vagueness can be pointed—{a certain someone} hints at knowledge withheld. {To a certain extent} means partly but not completely.

Certainly expresses strong affirmation or agreement: {Will you help me?} {Certainly.} It can emphasize confidence in a statement: {She certainly knows her stuff}. The word sometimes carries a note of concession—acknowledging a point before pivoting: {He's certainly talented, but he lacks discipline}. In formal contexts, certainly sounds more measured than definitely or absolutely.

Certainties is the plural of certainty—things known or believed to be true beyond doubt. Life offers few certainties, though {death and taxes} are proverbial exceptions. In philosophy and science, certainties are propositions held to be absolutely true, though such claims invite skepticism. {The old certainties no longer apply.}

Certainty is the state of being sure or confident about something, free from doubt. When you have certainty, you feel no hesitation or wavering: {I can say with certainty that she was home that night}. A certainty is something that is sure to happen or be true: {Death is the only certainty in life}. The phrase {for a certainty} means definitely or without question. Certainty often contrasts with probability or possibility, where doubt remains.

Certifiable means able to be certified or officially confirmed: {The diamond came with certifiable proof of its origin}. More commonly, certifiable describes someone whose mental state warrants commitment to an institution—legally insane: {He's absolutely certifiable}. This psychiatric sense has loosened into informal use for anyone acting crazy or irrational: {You'd have to be certifiable to swim in that water}.

A certificate is an official document attesting to some fact, qualification, or status: a birth {certificate}, a teaching {certificate}, a {certificate} of authenticity. To certificate or certify someone is to formally recognize their qualifications. In finance, a certificate of deposit (CD) is a savings instrument with a fixed term. {She framed her certificate and hung it on the wall.}

Certificates are official documents attesting to facts, qualifications, or completion of requirements. A birth certificate records when and where someone was born. Educational certificates confirm completion of courses or programs. Professional certificates verify competency in a field. In computing, certificates authenticate identity for secure connections. The verb certify produces the noun: {She received certificates for completing all three levels}.

Certification is official confirmation that something meets a standard or that someone has achieved a qualification. A certification may be a document attesting to this: {She earned her yoga teacher certification}. The process of certifying is also certification: {The product is undergoing certification}. Professional certifications verify competency in fields from accounting to welding.

Certifications are official documents or credentials confirming that a person, organization, or product meets specific standards or qualifications. Professional certifications verify expertise: {She earned her project management certification}. Product certifications indicate compliance with safety or quality standards. The term often appears in job listings specifying required credentials: {CPR certification required}.

Certified means officially verified or guaranteed to meet certain standards. A certified {accountant} or certified {nurse} has credentials from a recognized authority. Certified {mail} provides proof of delivery. Certified {organic} products meet regulatory requirements. In slang, certified intensifies: {That song is a certified banger}. Something certified is authenticated, validated, confirmed as genuine.

To certify is to formally confirm or attest that something meets a standard or is true: {The inspector certified the building as safe}, {certified organic produce}. Officials certify documents, boards certify professionals, and agencies certify compliance. A certified {check} has bank-guaranteed funds. To certify someone can also mean to declare them legally insane—committed by official determination.

Cerulean is a shade of blue—specifically the deep, vivid blue of a clear sky. The word appears mostly in literary or artistic contexts: {cerulean waters}, {a cerulean gaze}. In everyday speech, people usually just say blue or sky blue.
clues: The color above on clear days

definition: The cervix is the narrow, lower portion of the uterus that connects to the vagina. It dilates during childbirth to allow passage of the baby. Medical exams check the cervix for abnormalities; a Pap smear screens for cervical cancer. More broadly, cervix means any neck-like anatomical structure, though the uterine cervix dominates modern usage.
clues: Cylindrical tissue connecting womb, birth canal

definition: A cesarean is a surgical procedure to deliver a baby through an incision in the mother's abdomen and uterus, bypassing the birth canal: {The baby was breech, so they scheduled a cesarean}. Often called a cesarean section or C-section. Also spelled caesarean, especially in British English.

A cesspit is a pit or tank for collecting sewage or waste—essentially a hole in the ground where filth accumulates. The word extends figuratively to any place of moral corruption or concentrated unpleasantness: {The comment section became a cesspit of hatred}. Also called a cesspool, though technically a cesspool allows drainage while a cesspit is sealed.

Cesspits are holes or tanks for collecting sewage or waste, typically underground. The word appears in literal contexts—properties with cesspits instead of modern plumbing—but more often as a metaphor for places of moral filth or corruption: {The forum had become a cesspit of conspiracy theories}. Cesspool means the same thing.

A cesspool is a pit or tank for collecting sewage or waste. The word extends naturally to anything foul or corrupt: a cesspool of {crime}, a cesspool of {misinformation}. The figurative use emphasizes moral filth and concentrated corruption: {Social media can be a cesspool}.

Cesspools are underground tanks or pits for collecting sewage and wastewater. Unlike septic systems, cesspools have no outlet—waste simply accumulates and slowly seeps into surrounding soil. The word extends to anything foul or corrupt: {The city had become a cesspool of crime and vice}. A cesspool of corruption, a cesspool of disease.

Ceviche is a Latin American dish of raw fish or seafood cured in citrus juice, typically lime or lemon. The acid denatures the proteins, giving the fish a firm, opaque texture similar to cooking. Usually mixed with onions, cilantro, and chili peppers, ceviche is served cold as an appetizer: {We ordered ceviche and margaritas}. Also spelled seviche or cebiche.

Chad is a small piece of paper or cardboard punched out from a card or tape—the tiny debris left over from hole-punching. The word gained fame during the 2000 U.S. presidential election, when partially detached chads on Florida ballots ({hanging chads}, {dimpled chads}) became the center of a recount controversy. In internet slang, a chad is a stereotypically attractive, confident, socially dominant man—often used ironically or in contrast to less successful types: {He walked in like a total chad}. (Capitalized Chad is a country or a given name.)

Chafe is to rub against something, causing irritation or soreness. Skin chafes from friction—a collar against the neck, thighs rubbing together. The word extends to emotional irritation: to chafe at restrictions is to feel restless under them, as though they're wearing at you. {He chafed under his father's rules.} {The rope chafed her wrists raw.}

Chafed describes skin that has become sore, raw, or irritated from repeated rubbing or friction. Runners often get chafed thighs, and ill-fitting shoes leave feet chafed and blistered. The word extends to emotional irritation as well: someone chafed by constant criticism feels worn down and annoyed by it. {He was visibly chafed by the delay.} If you chafe at restrictions or rules, you feel restless and resentful under them.

Chafes means rubs in a way that causes irritation or soreness. Skin chafes against rough fabric; a tight collar chafes the neck. Figuratively, to chafe is to feel irritated or restless under constraints: {She chafed at the bureaucratic delays}. You can also chafe something to warm it by rubbing: {He chafed her cold hands between his own}.

Chaff is the husks and other debris separated from grain during threshing—the worthless material left after extracting what's valuable. The word extends to anything trivial or worthless: {separating the wheat from the chaff}. To chaff someone is to tease them good-naturedly. In military contexts, chaff is strips of metal foil released to confuse radar.

Chafing is skin irritation caused by repeated friction—typically where skin rubs against skin or clothing during physical activity: {The marathon runner applied petroleum jelly to prevent chafing}. Extended to objects, chafing means wearing away through rubbing. Figuratively, to chafe is to feel irritated or restless under constraints: {He chafed at the bureaucratic delays}. A chafing dish keeps food warm over a small flame.

Chagrin is distress or embarrassment caused by failure, disappointment, or humiliation. It suggests wounded pride more than simple sadness: {Much to her chagrin, she wasn't invited}. The phrase {to my chagrin} introduces an admission of embarrassment. As a verb, chagrin means to cause such feelings, usually in passive form: {He was chagrined to discover his error}.

Chagrined means feeling distressed or embarrassed by failure, disappointment, or humiliation. The emotion combines wounded pride with frustration: {She was chagrined to discover her zipper had been down the whole time}. {He looked chagrined when his prediction proved spectacularly wrong}. The noun chagrin names this feeling; chagrined is its adjectival form.

Chai is tea, borrowed from Hindi. In American English, chai usually means a spiced milk tea with cinnamon, cardamom, ginger, and cloves—what Indians call masala chai: {I'll have a chai latte}. The phrase "chai tea" is redundant but common. In much of the world, chai simply means tea of any kind.

The archetypal chain—a series of sturdy interlocking metal links—is so useful that its name has come to characterize many things capable of linking items or holding them together. Chain is the word of choice to characterize any series of connected items that can be conceived as one while each constituent maintains its own identity: a supply chain, a chain of events, a mountain chain. Chain also characterizes businesses with multiple, functionally equivalent locations: a chain of restaurants. When something is chained, it is connected to another thing by a literal or figurative chain.

Chained means fastened or secured with a chain, or figuratively bound and restricted. A chained {dog} is tethered; a chained {bicycle} is locked. The figurative sense suggests constraint or bondage: {chained to a desk}, {chained to debt}. In computing, chained operations or commands execute in sequence, each triggered by the previous: {chained API calls}.

A chaingun is an automatic weapon that uses an external power source—typically an electric motor driving a chain mechanism—to cycle the action, rather than relying on the recoil or gas pressure of fired rounds. This makes chainguns exceptionally reliable and capable of sustained high rates of fire. The term often appears loosely in video games and action movies to describe any rapid-fire mounted weapon: {The helicopter's chaingun tore through the building}.

A chaingun is a machine gun or automatic cannon that uses an external motor-driven chain to cycle the weapon's action—loading, firing, and ejecting rounds. The chain mechanism makes them more reliable than gas-operated guns. Chainguns appear on military vehicles, helicopters, and aircraft: {The Apache's 30mm chaingun can fire 625 rounds per minute}.

Chaining is linking things together in sequence, like links in a chain. In computing, chaining connects commands or functions so output from one becomes input to the next: {method chaining}, {promise chaining}. In psychology, chaining breaks complex behaviors into linked steps, teaching them one at a time. The word implies sequential connection where each element depends on the previous.

Chainlink refers to a type of fencing made from wire woven into a diamond pattern, creating a durable mesh barrier. It's common around schoolyards, construction sites, and backyards—functional but not decorative: {The baseball diamond was surrounded by chainlink}. Also spelled as two words: chain link.

Chainmail is armor made of small metal rings linked together in a mesh pattern, worn for protection in combat from ancient times through the medieval period. The interlocking rings allowed flexibility while deflecting sword cuts and arrow strikes. Modern chainmail appears in specialty applications like shark-resistant diving suits and butcher's gloves. The word is also spelled as two words, chain mail, and sometimes refers to chain letters or spam emails forwarded repeatedly.

Chains is the plural of chain—a series of connected links, typically metal. Physical chains restrain or secure: {The dog strained against its chains}. Figuratively, chains represent bondage or oppression: {break the chains of poverty}, {chains of addiction}. Snow chains wrap around tires for traction on ice. In retail, chains are businesses with multiple locations under one brand: {fast-food chains}, {hotel chains}. To chain is to fasten or confine: {She chained her bike to the rack}.

A chainsaw is a portable power saw with teeth set on a continuous chain that loops around a guide bar. Chainsaws cut through wood quickly—used for felling trees, trimming limbs, and cutting firewood. The verb means to cut with one: {We chainsawed the fallen oak into manageable pieces}. Figuratively, to chainsaw something is to cut it drastically or brutally.

Chainsaws are power tools with a toothed chain rotating around a guide bar, used for cutting wood. They fell trees, trim branches, and slice logs. The word evokes raw power and danger—chainsaws appear in horror films as instruments of terror. Figuratively, to chainsaw through something is to cut aggressively without finesse: {He chainsawed through the budget proposal}.

Chainsmoking is smoking cigarettes one after another in rapid succession, lighting each new one from the last. The term captures the linked, continuous nature of the habit: {He sat chainsmoking by the window, the ashtray overflowing}. A person who does this is a chainsmoker. Also spelled chain-smoking and chain smoking.

The familiar piece of furniture designed for one person to sit upon inspires all other meanings of chair. The human predilection to conduct business while seated may have led to people being characterized as chairs when they are in charge: the department chair, the chair of the board. Even without the person in it, chair can characterize an office or position: the orchestra needs a cello first chair. When you chair a meeting, committee, or panel, you are the person who directs it.

A chairlift is a series of chairs suspended from a moving cable, used to transport people up a slope—typically skiers and snowboarders at mountain resorts. Passengers sit on open-air seats that travel continuously in a loop: {We rode the chairlift to the summit}. Similar systems appear at scenic attractions and amusement parks.

Chairlifts are aerial transport systems that carry passengers in suspended chairs along a cable, typically up and down mountains. Ski resorts use them to move skiers uphill: {We rode the chairlift to the summit}. Chairlifts also appear at scenic attractions for sightseeing. The singular chairlift can refer to the system or an individual chair.

A chairman is the person who presides over a meeting, committee, board, or organization. The chairman leads discussions, maintains order, and often has authority to make procedural decisions or cast tie-breaking votes. In corporate settings, the chairman of the board holds significant power over company direction and executive appointments. {The chairman called the meeting to order.} The term is increasingly replaced by the gender-neutral chair or chairperson, though chairman remains common in formal and traditional contexts.

Chairs is the plural of chair—seats with backs, typically for one person. Beyond furniture, chairs can be people who preside over meetings or organizations: {The committee chairs met to discuss the agenda}. As a verb, to chair is to lead such a body: {She chairs the department}.

A chairwarmer is someone who occupies a position without doing meaningful work—they warm a chair but contribute little else. The term is mildly disparaging, suggesting the person is redundant or unproductive: {Half the department are chairwarmers collecting a paycheck}. Sometimes used self-deprecatingly: {I'm just a chairwarmer until I figure out what I'm doing}.

A chaise is a light horse-drawn carriage, typically with two wheels and a folding hood. The word also refers to a chaise longue—a reclining chair with an extended seat for the legs—though in American English this is often shortened to just chaise: {She stretched out on the chaise by the pool}.

Chakra comes from a Sanskrit word meaning wheel or circle. In Hindu and Buddhist traditions, chakras are energy centers in the body, typically counted as seven, aligned along the spine from base to crown. Each governs different aspects of physical and spiritual well-being: {Her yoga teacher talked about opening the heart chakra}. The concept has been widely adopted in Western alternative medicine and New Age spirituality, often with simplified or adapted meanings.

Chakras are energy centers in the body according to Hindu and Buddhist traditions. The standard system identifies seven chakras aligned along the spine, from the base to the crown of the head, each associated with different qualities—survival, creativity, power, love, expression, intuition, and spiritual connection. In Western wellness culture, chakras appear in yoga, meditation, and alternative healing: {She said my throat chakra was blocked}. The singular is chakra.

A chalet is a wooden house or cottage with a sloping roof and wide eaves, originally associated with the Swiss Alps. The term now applies broadly to any vacation dwelling in a mountainous or ski resort area, regardless of architectural style. {We rented a chalet for the weekend.} In some contexts, chalet refers to a small cabin or lodge within a larger resort property.

Chalets are houses or cottages with wide eaves and a sloping roof, originally associated with the Swiss Alps. The style features wooden construction and exposed beams. The term extends to any rustic vacation dwelling, particularly in mountain or ski resort settings: {We rented a chalet for the weekend}. In some contexts, chalet refers to a small cabin at a holiday camp or beach.

A chalice is a goblet or cup, typically with a stem and base, used for drinking wine. The word carries ceremonial weight—in Christian worship, the chalice holds wine for communion. Outside religious contexts, chalice sounds literary or archaic: {He raised the golden chalice to his lips}. A poisoned chalice is something that appears desirable but brings harm.

Chalices is the plural of chalice, a goblet or drinking cup, especially an ornate one used in religious ceremonies. The communion chalice holds wine in Christian services. The word carries associations of ritual and reverence: {The priest raised the chalice}. Figuratively, a chalice may contain something bitter—a {poisoned chalice} is an assignment or gift that seems desirable but brings harm.

Chalk is a soft, white limestone composed of ancient marine shells, or a stick of this material used for writing on blackboards and sidewalks. The powdered form dusts gymnasts' hands and pool players' cues for grip. As a verb, to chalk is to mark with chalk: {She chalked the score on the board}. To {chalk something up} is to attribute it: {Chalk it up to inexperience}. Things that differ {like chalk and cheese} are fundamentally unlike despite surface similarities.

A chalkboard is a dark, smooth surface for writing on with chalk, traditionally found in classrooms. The term emerged as schools shifted from slate boards to green or black painted surfaces, and later as a synonym for blackboard regardless of color. {The teacher wrote the equation on the chalkboard.} Now largely replaced by whiteboards and digital displays.

Chalkboards are smooth, dark surfaces designed to be written on with chalk. Traditional chalkboards were made of slate; modern ones are typically green or black synthetic material. Found in classrooms for generations, they've largely been replaced by whiteboards and digital displays, though the term persists: {back to the chalkboard}. The singular chalkboard names one such surface.

Chalked is the past tense of chalk, meaning marked or written with chalk: {She chalked the score on the board}. In billiards, to chalk a cue is to apply chalk to its tip for better grip. To {chalk something up} is to attribute or ascribe it: {Chalk it up to experience}. In sports betting, chalked describes heavily favored outcomes.

Chalking is marking or writing with chalk, or the marks themselves: {chalking messages on the sidewalk}, {chalking up the score}. In billiards, chalking means applying chalk to a cue tip for better grip. On surfaces, chalking describes the powdery residue that forms when paint or other coatings degrade: {The old fence showed signs of chalking}.

Chalky describes something resembling chalk—pale, powite, and powdery. Chalky skin looks unnaturally pale, often suggesting illness. A chalky texture feels dry and slightly gritty, like calcium deposits on a faucet or residue from an antacid tablet. Chalky taste has that distinctive mineral dryness: {The wine had a chalky finish}.

Challah is a braided Jewish bread, typically enriched with eggs and slightly sweet, traditionally eaten on Shabbat and holidays. The distinctive braided shape and golden, glossy crust come from an egg wash applied before baking. {We tore off pieces of challah and dipped them in honey for Rosh Hashanah.}

Challenge works as both a verb and a noun with related meanings. When you challenge a person, you invite them to compete or to prove or to demonstrate something. If you challenge a fact, you call its truth into question. If something challenges you, it requires you to exert effort in order to succeed. All of these actions can be called challenges. If you face or meet a challenge, you do what is required to overcome it or be successful. You can describe something as challenging if it requires you to be patient, alert, or persevering in your efforts.

Challenged means confronted or disputed: {She challenged his assumptions}. In compounds, it functions as a euphemism for disabled or deficient: {physically challenged}, {mentally challenged}. This usage emerged from well-meaning attempts to avoid words like handicapped, but has spawned ironic formations mocking the pattern: {vertically challenged} for short, {follically challenged} for bald.

A challenger is someone who competes for a position or title currently held by another—the opposite of a champion or incumbent. In boxing and politics alike, the challenger seeks to unseat whoever holds power: {The challenger landed a decisive blow in the third round}. More broadly, anyone who disputes or contests something: {challengers to the traditional theory}. (Capitalized Challenger refers to the space shuttle.)

Challengers are people or things that compete against established holders of titles, positions, or claims. In sports, a challenger faces the reigning champion: {The challenger knocked out the defending titleholder in the third round}. In politics, challengers run against incumbents. The word implies an underdog status—someone seeking to take what another currently holds.

Challenges are difficulties that test ability or resolve: {the challenges of raising teenagers}, {financial challenges}. The word often softens harsher alternatives—a company facing challenges may be struggling or failing. As a verb, to challenge is to question or dispute something, or to invite competition: {She challenged him to a rematch}. A challenge can also be a formal objection: {a challenge to the verdict}.

Challenging describes something that tests your abilities or demands significant effort: {a challenging hike}, {a challenging exam}. The word carries a positive connotation—challenges are difficult but surmountable, even rewarding. To call work challenging is to frame difficulty as opportunity rather than obstacle. A challenging person or behavior is one that provokes or defies: {She found his attitude challenging}.

A chalupa is a Mexican dish—a fried or toasted tortilla shaped like a small boat, filled with meat, cheese, lettuce, salsa, and other toppings. The name comes from the Spanish word for a small boat, reflecting the vessel-like shape. In American fast food, particularly Taco Bell, chalupa refers to a specific menu item with a thick, fried shell.

Chalupas are a Mexican food consisting of a fried masa shell shaped like a small boat, typically topped with meat, cheese, lettuce, and salsa. The name comes from the Spanish word for small boats, which the shells resemble. In the United States, Taco Bell popularized a version that uses a flatbread shell rather than the traditional fried corn base, making the term familiar even to those unfamiliar with authentic Mexican cuisine.

A chamber is an enclosed space or room, often one with a specific purpose: a {burial chamber}, a {torture chamber}, a {gas chamber}. Legislative bodies meet in chambers, and the body itself may be called a chamber: {the upper chamber of Congress}. A chamber in the body is a hollow space: the {chambers of the heart}. In firearms, the chamber holds the cartridge before firing. To chamber a round is to load it into position. A chambered nautilus has compartmented shells.

A chamberlain is an official who manages a royal or noble household, overseeing domestic affairs and often controlling access to the sovereign. The title appears in historical contexts and survives in ceremonial roles: {The Lord Chamberlain attended the coronation}. By extension, any high-ranking household manager or treasurer. (Capitalized Chamberlain is a surname.)

A chambermaid is a woman employed to clean and maintain bedrooms, particularly in hotels or large private households. The term dates to an era when domestic service was rigidly organized by task and location within a house. In modern usage, chambermaid has largely given way to housekeeper or room attendant, though it persists in British English and in period literature. {The chambermaid had already turned down the beds by the time we returned from dinner.}

A chamberpot is a bowl kept in a bedroom for urinating or defecating, used before indoor plumbing became standard. The name comes from its use in private chambers rather than outdoor privies. Now largely obsolete except as antiques or in places without modern facilities: {The museum displayed Victorian chamberpots alongside washbasins}.

Chamberpots are portable containers kept in bedrooms for urination and defecation, used before indoor plumbing became standard. Typically ceramic or metal bowls with handles, they were stored under beds or in bedside cabinets and emptied each morning. The term now appears mostly in historical contexts: {The museum displayed Victorian chamberpots alongside other domestic artifacts}.

Chambers are enclosed spaces or rooms, especially ones designated for specific purposes. A judge's chambers are the private office where legal matters may be discussed away from the courtroom. Legislative bodies meet in chambers: {The bill passed both chambers of Congress}. In anatomy, the heart has four chambers. A chamber can also be the part of a gun that holds the cartridge. To chamber a round is to load it into position. (Capitalized Chambers is a surname.)

A chameleon is a lizard known for changing color to match its surroundings. The ability makes chameleon a metaphor for adaptability or inconsistency—someone who shifts personality, opinions, or appearance to fit different situations: {He's a political chameleon, adjusting his views to whatever audience he's addressing}. The word can be neutral or critical depending on whether the adaptation seems skillful or unprincipled.

Chameleons is the plural of chameleon, a lizard known for changing color to match its surroundings. The ability extends metaphorically to people who shift their behavior, opinions, or appearance to fit different situations: {Politicians are chameleons who say whatever their audience wants to hear}. The word usually carries a hint of distrust—adaptability shading into inauthenticity.

Chamomile is an aromatic plant with small daisy-like flowers, used primarily for herbal tea. The tea is associated with relaxation and sleep: {I drink chamomile before bed}. Chamomile also appears in skin products and essential oils for its soothing properties. Also spelled camomile.

Champ works two ways. As a noun, it's an informal shortening of champion: {the reigning champ}, {a champ at solving puzzles}. The verb champ means to bite or chew noisily, especially with impatience—horses champ at the bit, and people {champ at the bit} when eager to get started. The spelling chomp has largely displaced this verb sense.

Champagne is sparkling white wine, originally and most prestigiously from the Champagne region of France. The word often refers to any sparkling wine in that style: {We popped the champagne at midnight}. Champagne is associated with celebration and luxury—toasts, weddings, victories. {Champagne taste on a beer budget} describes wanting expensive things one can't afford. As an adjective, champagne describes a pale golden-beige color. (Capitalized Champagne is the French region.)

A champion is the winner of a competition or the holder of first place: {the defending champion}, {world heavyweight champion}. The word extends to anyone who fights for or defends a cause: {a champion of civil rights}, {a champion of the poor}. As a verb, to champion something is to support or advocate for it vigorously. As an adjective, champion means excellent or first-rate, though this use sounds old-fashioned outside British dialect: {That's champion}.

Championed is the past tense of champion, meaning to vigorously support or defend a cause, person, or idea. Someone who championed civil rights fought publicly for equality. {She championed affordable housing throughout her career.} The word implies active advocacy rather than passive agreement—championing requires effort and visibility.

Champions are winners of competitions or those who have proven themselves the best in their field. The word carries connotations of sustained excellence rather than a single lucky victory. Champion also functions as a verb meaning to support or defend a cause vigorously: {She championed workers' rights throughout her career}. As an adjective, particularly in British English, champion means excellent or first-rate.

A championship is a competition to determine a champion—the best in a sport, game, or other contest: {the world chess championship}, {the NBA championship}. It also refers to the status or title itself: {She held the championship for three consecutive years}. The word can describe the quality of being a champion: {His championship of free speech earned him admirers and enemies alike}.

Championships are contests that determine supremacy in a sport or competition, or the titles won by victors. A team may compete in the championships (the event) or win the championship (the distinction): {The Lakers won three consecutive championships}. Championship as an adjective describes the highest competitive level: {championship round}, {championship game}.

Champs is informal for champions—winners of a competition or the best in their field: {The champs defended their title}, {We're the champs!} The word carries celebratory energy, often appearing in sports contexts or playful boasting. Separately, champs is also a form of the verb champ, meaning to bite or chew noisily: {The horse champs at the bit}.

Chance refers to the way things happen without apparent cause or design—the unpredictable element in events. If something happens {by chance}, it wasn't planned or intended. A chance is also an opportunity or possibility: {Give me a chance to explain}. The adjective describes things occurring without intention: a {chance encounter}. To chance something is to risk it: {I'll chance the rain and leave my umbrella}. If you {chance upon} something, you discover it accidentally.

Chancellor is a title for high-ranking officials whose specific role varies by context. In government, a chancellor may be the head of state, as in Germany, or a senior minister, as the UK's Chancellor of the Exchequer who oversees financial matters. In American universities, a chancellor typically leads the institution, equivalent to a president. In British universities, the chancellor is largely ceremonial while the vice-chancellor handles administration. {The chancellor announced sweeping budget reforms.}

Chancellors is the plural of chancellor, a title for high-ranking officials in various contexts. In government, a chancellor may head a state (Germany's chancellor) or oversee finances (Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer). In American universities, chancellors typically lead individual campuses within larger systems. In law, chancellors preside over courts of equity. {The chancellors of the state university system met to discuss tuition increases.}

Chances are possibilities or probabilities—the likelihood that something will happen: {What are the chances of rain?} The plural often emphasizes multiple opportunities: {You've had your chances}. To {take chances} is to accept risk. {Chances are} introduces a probability: {Chances are he's already left}. The singular chance covers the same ground but emphasizes a single opportunity or occurrence.

A chandelier is a decorative light fixture that hangs from the ceiling, typically with multiple branching arms holding bulbs or candles. Chandeliers are associated with elegance and formal spaces—ballrooms, dining rooms, theater lobbies. They range from ornate crystal designs to minimalist modern interpretations: {The crystal chandelier cast prismatic light across the room}.

Change, a noun and verb, encompasses the core concept of difference between two things or states. A change may be about different clothing (change clothes), money left over from a purchase (get change from a dollar), a deviation from routine (change things up), or a switch in transportation (change trains). You can change a baby (put on a clean diaper) or change horses (exchange one for another).

Changeable describes something that shifts or can be altered. Changeable weather is unpredictable; changeable moods swing from one state to another. A changeable situation remains unsettled: {The schedule is still changeable}. The word can suggest either flexibility or instability, depending on context—a changeable policy might be adaptable or simply inconsistent.

Changed describes something that has become different from what it was before. A changed {person} has undergone significant transformation in character or outlook. A changed {landscape} looks notably different. The word often implies the change is substantial or permanent: {She's a changed woman since the accident}. Changed can also simply mark completion: {I've changed my clothes}.
clues: Switched from one state to another

definition: A changeling is a child secretly substituted for another—specifically, in folklore, a fairy or elf child left in place of a stolen human infant. The word now applies figuratively to any person or thing that seems mysteriously altered or replaced: {He came back from college a changeling, unrecognizable to his parents}. In fantasy fiction, changelings are often shapeshifters who can assume others' appearances.

Changelings are creatures from European folklore—fairy children secretly swapped for human infants. The term extends to any child believed to have been exchanged, or more broadly, a person given to unpredictable change: {She was a changeling, never the same from one day to the next}. In fantasy fiction, changelings are often shapeshifters who can assume different forms.

A changemaker is someone who actively works to create positive social change—an activist, innovator, or community organizer who identifies problems and takes initiative to address them. The term emerged from nonprofit and social entrepreneurship circles: {The foundation supports young changemakers tackling climate issues}. It carries an optimistic, empowering tone, though critics find it vague or self-congratulatory.

A changeover is a shift from one system, method, or situation to another: {the changeover from manual to automated production}, {the changeover to digital broadcasting}. The word emphasizes the transition period itself rather than the end state. In sports, a changeover is the pause when players switch sides of the court.

Changes are alterations or modifications—things becoming different from what they were before. The word covers everything from minor adjustments to complete transformations: {We made a few changes to the contract}, {climate change}, {a change of heart}. To change is to make or become different. Change also means coins rather than bills, or money returned when you pay more than owed: {Keep the change}. A change of clothes is a fresh set to put on.

A changeup is a baseball pitch designed to deceive the batter by looking like a fastball but arriving much slower. The pitcher uses the same arm motion as a fastball while gripping the ball deeper in the palm, reducing its speed. This disrupts the batter's timing. Outside baseball, changeup describes any unexpected shift in approach or tempo: {The detective's friendly questioning was a changeup from his earlier interrogation style}.

Changing is the act of becoming or making different. As a participle, it describes something in the process of transformation: {changing weather}, {changing times}, {the changing seasons}. A changing room is where you switch clothes. {I'm changing} can mean switching outfits or altering plans. The word emphasizes flux—nothing changing has settled into its final form.
clues: Moving from one state to another

definition: Channel is related to canal and that sense conveys many of its meanings. A channel was originally a conduit for water; today, the word is more frequently encountered when it’s a conduit for a signal or information (satellite sports channel) or a conduit for chemical transfer (the cell’s potassium channel). When you channel something, you direct the flow or expression of it in a particular way: The wealthy benefactor channeled her money into charities working to alleviate hunger.

Channeled is the past tense of channel, meaning directed through or as if through a channel. Water is channeled through irrigation ditches; energy is channeled into productive work. A medium who has channeled a spirit claims to have served as a conduit for communication from the dead. {She channeled her anger into activism.} Also spelled channelled in British English.

Channeling is directing something through a particular course or medium. You might channel water through pipes, channel funds into a project, or channel energy toward a goal: {She channeled her anger into activism}. In spiritual contexts, channeling means serving as a conduit for spirits or supernatural entities, supposedly allowing them to speak through you. More loosely, to channel someone is to evoke their style or essence: {He's really channeling his inner James Dean}.

Channelled is a British spelling of channeled, the past tense of channel. To channel is to direct something through a particular path or medium: {She channelled her anger into activism}, {Funds were channelled through offshore accounts}. The spelling with double L follows British convention for verbs ending in a consonant.

Channelling is the British spelling of channeling, the present participle of channel. To channel is to direct something through a particular course or medium: {channelling resources into education}, {channelling her anger into activism}. In spiritual contexts, channelling refers to serving as a medium for spirits or otherworldly entities: {She claimed to be channelling an ancient Egyptian priest}.

Channels are pathways for flow or transmission. Water moves through river channels; television broadcasts arrive through channels. A channel can be a frequency band, a means of communication {diplomatic channels}, or a groove that guides movement. To channel is to direct flow: {She channeled her anger into activism}. A medium channels spirits. The Channel, unmodified, usually means the English Channel.

A chant is a rhythmic, repetitive vocalization—words or phrases spoken or sung in unison, often with a simple melody or monotone pitch. Religious traditions use chants in worship: {Gregorian chant}, {Buddhist chanting}. Crowds chant at protests and sporting events: {The fans chanted his name}. To chant is to produce such sounds. The word suggests group participation and hypnotic repetition.

Chanterelle is an edible wild mushroom prized for its golden color, funnel shape, and fruity aroma. Chanterelles grow in forests near trees and are foraged rather than cultivated, making them expensive and seasonal: {We found chanterelles under the oaks}. They have a delicate, peppery flavor and appear frequently in European cuisine.

Chanterelles are wild mushrooms prized in cooking, with a distinctive funnel shape and golden-orange color. They have a fruity, peppery flavor and meaty texture that holds up well in sautés and cream sauces. Chanterelles grow in forests across Europe and North America, typically foraged rather than cultivated: {We found chanterelles under the oaks after the rain}.

A chantey (also spelled shanty) is a song traditionally sung by sailors while performing rhythmic work aboard ships, such as hauling ropes or raising anchors. The songs feature a call-and-response structure that helped coordinate group labor and maintain morale during long voyages. {The crew broke into a chantey as they hoisted the sails.} Though working sail ships have largely disappeared, chanteys remain popular in folk music and maritime festivals.

Chanties is the plural of chanty, a variant spelling of shanty—a work song sung by sailors to coordinate group labor like hauling ropes or raising anchors. The rhythmic call-and-response structure helped synchronize physical effort: {The crew sang chanties as they weighed anchor}. Also spelled chanteys or shanties.

Chanting is the rhythmic, repetitive vocalization of words or sounds, often in a group. Religious chanting—monks intoning prayers, congregations reciting scripture—aims to focus the mind or invoke the sacred. Crowds chant at protests and sporting events: {The chanting grew louder as the team took the field}. The repetition creates unity and intensity.

Chants are words or phrases repeated rhythmically, often in unison. Religious chants—Gregorian, Buddhist, Hindu—use melodic repetition for spiritual practice. Crowds chant at protests and sporting events: {The fans chanted his name}. To chant is to speak or sing in this repetitive, rhythmic way: {Protesters chanted slogans outside the courthouse}.

Chaos is complete disorder and confusion—a state where nothing follows predictable patterns. The word describes situations where normal structure has collapsed: {The office was in chaos after the merger announcement}, {Traffic chaos followed the power outage}. Chaos can also refer to the formless void that existed before the universe took shape, a sense preserved in cosmology and philosophy. In mathematics and physics, chaos theory studies systems that appear random but follow underlying rules sensitive to initial conditions—the famous "butterfly effect." (Capitalized Chaos is the primordial deity in Greek mythology.)

Chaotic describes a state of complete disorder or confusion, where things lack any organizing principle: {The office was chaotic after the merger announcement}. Traffic, situations, and environments can be chaotic. In casual use, chaotic often just means hectic or disorganized: {My morning routine is chaotic}. The phrase {chaotic energy} describes someone whose unpredictable behavior is entertaining or unsettling.

Chap has two unrelated meanings. One is a crack or roughness in the skin, especially from cold or wind: {My lips are chapped}. The verb means to become cracked or rough. The other chap is British informal for a man or fellow: {He's a decent chap}. This sense is friendly and slightly old-fashioned, often heard in {old chap} as a form of address.
clues: What harsh weather does to lips

definition: A chapati is a round, flat unleavened bread from South Asian cuisine, made from whole wheat flour and cooked on a griddle. Thinner and simpler than naan, chapatis are a staple at Indian and Pakistani meals, torn into pieces and used to scoop up curries and other dishes: {She made fresh chapatis to go with the dal}. Also spelled chapatti or chappati.

Chapatis are unleavened flatbreads from South Asian cuisine, made from whole wheat flour, water, and salt, then cooked on a dry griddle. They're a staple accompaniment to curries and other dishes, used to scoop up food. Also spelled chapatti or chapati. {She tore off a piece of chapati to eat with the dal.}

A chapatti is a thin, round flatbread from South Asian cuisine, made from whole wheat flour and cooked on a dry griddle. It's a staple food in India, Pakistan, and neighboring regions, typically served alongside curries and other dishes: {She tore off a piece of chapatti to scoop up the dal}. Also spelled chapati or chappati.

Chapattis are thin, round flatbreads made from whole wheat flour, water, and salt, cooked on a dry griddle without oil. A staple food across South Asia, particularly in India and Pakistan, they accompany curries, lentils, and vegetable dishes, used to scoop up food in place of utensils. The singular is chapatti or chapati, with various spellings reflecting different transliterations from Hindi and Urdu.

A chapel is a small place of worship, either a standalone building or a room within a larger structure like a hospital, prison, or university. Chapels are typically simpler and more intimate than churches. The word also refers to a section of a larger church containing its own altar: {the Lady Chapel in the cathedral}. In British usage, chapel can mean a nonconformist Protestant congregation, distinct from the Church of England.

Chapels is the plural of chapel, a small place of worship. A chapel may be a freestanding building smaller than a church, or a room within a larger structure—a hospital chapel, a prison chapel, an airport chapel. Some denominations use chapel for their main worship spaces. A wedding chapel specializes in marriage ceremonies. In British universities, chapel refers to the daily religious service: {Chapel is at eight}.

A chaperon is a person who accompanies and supervises others, especially young people, to ensure proper behavior. Traditionally, a chaperon was an older woman accompanying an unmarried young woman in public to preserve her reputation. The role now extends to adults supervising groups on outings: {parent chaperons on a school field trip}. The verb means to serve in this capacity: {She chaperoned the prom}. Also spelled chaperone.

A chaperone is someone who accompanies and supervises others, especially young people at social events: {Parent chaperones attended the school dance}. Traditionally, a chaperone was an older woman ensuring a young unmarried woman's propriety in mixed company—a role now largely obsolete. The verb means to act as such a supervisor: {She chaperoned the field trip}. Also spelled chaperon.

Chaperoned means accompanied by a chaperone—someone who supervises or watches over others, especially young people in social situations. A chaperoned {dance} has adults present to maintain order. Chaperoned {visits} are monitored, whether for safety or propriety: {The teenagers were chaperoned by her mother}.

Chaperones are people who accompany and supervise others, ensuring proper behavior or safety. Traditionally, a chaperone was an older woman who accompanied a young unmarried woman in public to guard her reputation. Now the term usually refers to adults supervising children on school trips or at events: {We need parent chaperones for the field trip}. The verb means to act as such a supervisor: {She chaperoned the prom}.

Chaperoning is accompanying someone to provide supervision or guidance. Traditionally, a chaperone was an older woman who accompanied a young unmarried woman in public to ensure propriety. Now the term usually means an adult supervising children or teenagers on outings: {I'm chaperoning the field trip tomorrow}. The word can carry a slightly weary tone—implying obligation rather than choice.

A chaplain is a member of the clergy attached to an institution rather than a parish—a hospital, prison, military unit, or university. Chaplains provide spiritual guidance and conduct religious services for people in these settings: {The hospital chaplain visited patients on the oncology ward}. The role has expanded to include secular counselors who offer emotional support regardless of religious affiliation.

Chaplains are clergy or spiritual advisors attached to institutions rather than congregations—military units, hospitals, prisons, universities, or legislatures. They provide religious services, counseling, and pastoral care to people in settings where a traditional church isn't available: {The hospital chaplain visited patients regardless of their faith}. Military chaplains hold officer rank and deploy with troops.
clues: Priests serving in the armed forces

definition: A chappati is a thin, round flatbread made from whole wheat flour, cooked on a griddle without oil. It's a staple of South Asian cuisines, particularly Indian and Pakistani, served alongside curries and other dishes. Also spelled chapati or chapatti: {She tore off a piece of chappati to scoop up the dal}.

Chapped describes skin that has become dry, rough, and cracked from exposure to cold, wind, or dry air. Lips and hands are most commonly affected: {My lips are chapped from the winter wind}, {chapped hands from washing dishes}. Chap as a verb means to cause such cracking, though the adjective form dominates everyday use.

Chaps are protective leather leggings worn over trousers, covering the front of the legs while leaving the seat open. Cowboys and ranchers wear them for protection against brush and rope burns; motorcycle riders wear them against wind and road debris. In British informal speech, chaps means fellows or men: {The chaps from the office are meeting for drinks}. This British sense is old-fashioned and somewhat upper-class, often used with mild affection or irony.

A chapter is a main division of a book, typically numbered or titled: {I read three chapters before bed}. Extended to comparable divisions—a chapter of one's life, a local branch of an organization {(the Boston chapter of the Red Cross)}. To {close the chapter on} something is to consider it finished. In religion, a chapter is a governing body of clergy or the meeting itself.

Chapters are the main divisions of a book, typically numbered or titled, each covering a distinct portion of the narrative or subject matter. Beyond books, chapter extends to any distinct phase or period: {a new chapter in her life}, {the final chapter of the Cold War}. A chapter is also a local branch of an organization: {the Seattle chapter of the Sierra Club}.

Char has several unrelated meanings. To char is to burn something until blackened, or to become blackened by fire: {The edges of the paper were charred}. A char is also British slang for a cleaning woman or charwoman, and for tea—from the Chinese word for tea leaf. In computing, char (rhymes with "car") is short for character, a data type representing a single letter or symbol.

Character is the qualities that make someone or something distinctive. A person's character is their moral nature: {She has good character}. A character is a person in a story, film, or play, or an eccentric person: {He's quite a character}. Character also means a letter, number, or symbol in a writing system. To {act out of character} is to behave unexpectedly; to {stay in character} is to maintain a role.

Characterisation is the British spelling of characterization—the way a writer creates and develops characters in a story, or the way someone describes or portrays a person or thing. A novel might be praised for its rich characterisation, or you might object to someone's characterisation of your actions: {That's an unfair characterisation of what happened}.

A characteristic is a distinguishing feature or quality—something that marks a person, thing, or group as recognizable: {Stubbornness was his defining characteristic}. As an adjective, characteristic means typical or representative: {She answered with characteristic bluntness}. The word often appears with "of": {Such generosity is characteristic of him}.

Characterization is the way someone or something is portrayed or described. In fiction, it refers to the techniques writers use to develop characters—through dialogue, action, appearance, or direct description: {The novel's characterization of the villain felt thin}. More broadly, any depiction or representation: {His characterization of the meeting as hostile seemed unfair}. To call something a characterization often implies it's one interpretation among possible others.

Characters are the people, animals, or figures that populate stories, plays, films, and games—the cast of a narrative. The word extends to distinctive individuals in real life: {He's quite a character}. Character also means the qualities that define someone's nature—moral fiber, integrity, personality: {a person of good character}, {character assassination}. Letters, numerals, and symbols in writing systems are characters: {The password must contain eight characters}. A reference attesting to someone's reputation is a character reference.

A charade is a pretense or absurd falsity that everyone recognizes but goes along with: {The trial was a charade—the verdict was decided before it began}. In the plural, charades is a party game where players act out words or phrases without speaking while others guess. The singular sometimes refers to one such acted clue.

Charades is a parlor game where players act out words or phrases without speaking while teammates guess. One person pantomimes while others call out guesses until someone gets it right. The word also describes an obvious pretense or absurd facade: {The trial was a charades—the verdict was decided before it began}. The singular charade usually carries this figurative sense of empty show.

Charbroiled means cooked over an open flame or hot coals, producing a distinctive smoky flavor and characteristic grill marks. The term appears most often on restaurant menus to suggest food prepared with more care than standard grilling: {charbroiled burgers}, {charbroiled chicken}. Also spelled char-broiled.

Charcoal is wood or other organic matter burned in limited oxygen until only carbon remains. It burns hotter and cleaner than wood, making it ideal for grilling and metalworking. Artists use charcoal sticks for drawing, producing soft black lines that smudge easily. As a color, charcoal is a dark gray approaching black: {charcoal suit}, {charcoal walls}.

Charcuterie refers to prepared meat products—typically cured, smoked, or preserved pork items like salami, prosciutto, pâté, and sausages. The term also describes the craft of preparing such meats and the shops that sell them. In contemporary usage, a charcuterie board or charcuterie platter is an arrangement of cured meats, cheeses, crackers, and accompaniments served as an appetizer or shared meal. {We put together a charcuterie board for the party.}

Chard is a leafy green vegetable with broad, crinkly leaves and thick stalks that come in white, red, or yellow varieties. Also called Swiss chard, it belongs to the beet family but is cultivated for its leaves rather than its root. The leaves can be prepared like spinach while the stalks are often cooked separately, similar to celery. {I sautéed the chard with garlic and olive oil.}

Chardonnay is a white wine grape variety and the wine made from it. Chardonnay wines range from crisp and unoaked to rich and buttery, depending on production methods: {I'll have a glass of chardonnay}. The grape originated in Burgundy but is now grown worldwide, making it one of the most popular white wines.

Charge is extremely frequent as both a noun and a verb, and has a wide range of meanings. The most common meaning is to request or demand payment, but is also frequently used in the legal sense, in which police charge someone with a crime. A third meaning is to supply or endow with electric potential, as when you charge a battery. As a noun, charge is often plural when it refers to money or crime: she appeared in court to face charges. There were several charges on my credit card bill that I didn’t recognize. Charge is also used to identify the electric potential of something: electrons have a negative charge.

A chargeback is a reversal of a credit card transaction, initiated when a cardholder disputes a charge with their bank. The bank withdraws funds from the merchant's account and returns them to the customer. Chargebacks protect consumers from fraud or unsatisfactory purchases, but merchants view them as costly: {We lost three hundred dollars to chargebacks last month}. The verb is to charge back.

Charged describes something loaded with energy, intensity, or significance. An electrically charged particle carries positive or negative charge. A charged {atmosphere} crackles with tension or emotion. Charged {language} carries strong connotations that may provoke reaction. In law, someone charged with a crime has been formally accused. A charged {battery} holds stored power, ready for use.

A charger is a device that restores power to a battery: a phone charger, a laptop charger. The word also means a large flat dish for serving food, and historically, a horse ridden into battle—a warhorse. {He forgot his charger at home}. {The knight mounted his charger}.

Chargers is the plural of charger, covering several meanings. A charger is a device that restores power to batteries: {phone chargers}, {laptop chargers}. A charger is also a large flat serving dish, or a horse ridden in battle or ceremony. The Los Angeles Chargers are a professional football team.

Charges covers accusations, costs, and electrical states. Criminal charges are formal allegations: {The charges were dropped}. Charges on a bill are fees for services: {bank charges}, {delivery charges}. An electrical charge is positive or negative. To bring charges is to accuse formally. When someone charges forward, they rush aggressively. {She charges her phone every night.}

Charging is the act of supplying power to a battery or device: {My phone is charging}. It also means rushing forward aggressively, as in battle or sports: {The bull came charging at us}. To charge someone is to formally accuse them of a crime, or to demand payment: {They're charging fifty dollars for parking}. Charging can describe an intense, energetic quality: {a charging guitar riff}.

A chariot is a two-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle used in ancient warfare and racing. The driver stood upright, pulled by one or more horses at high speed. Chariots appear throughout ancient history—Egyptian, Greek, Roman—and figure prominently in mythology and religious texts: {Elijah ascended to heaven in a chariot of fire}. The word now evokes antiquity or poetic grandeur.

A charioteer is someone who drives a chariot—the ancient two-wheeled vehicle drawn by horses. The term appears mainly in historical and mythological contexts: {The charioteer urged his horses forward}, {Greek charioteers competed in the Olympic games}. Figuratively rare, but occasionally used for anyone who guides or drives with skill and command.

Charioteers are drivers of chariots—the two-wheeled horse-drawn vehicles of ancient warfare and racing. The term evokes classical antiquity: Roman charioteers competing in the Circus Maximus, Egyptian warriors charging into battle. Figuratively, anyone who drives or controls something with skill and speed might be called a charioteer: {He was the charioteer of the company's rapid expansion}.

Chariots is the plural of chariot, a two-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle used in ancient warfare and racing. Greek and Roman chariots carried warriors or competed in arenas. The word now appears mostly in historical contexts or metaphorically: {swing low, sweet chariot}. A chariot of fire suggests divine or transcendent conveyance.

Charisma is a compelling personal magnetism that inspires devotion or enthusiasm in others. A leader with charisma attracts followers through force of personality rather than rational argument: {Her charisma energized the crowd}. The word originally meant a divinely granted gift or power, and retains a sense of something beyond ordinary charm—an almost inexplicable quality that makes people want to follow, believe, or be near someone.

Charismatic describes someone with a compelling personal magnetism that attracts and inspires others. A charismatic {leader} draws followers through force of personality rather than position alone. The word derives from charisma, originally a divine gift of grace. In religious contexts, charismatic refers to Christian movements emphasizing spiritual gifts like speaking in tongues and faith healing: {a charismatic church}, {charismatic worship}.

Charitable describes generosity toward those in need, whether through donations, volunteer work, or organizations devoted to helping others: {a charitable foundation}, {charitable contributions}. The word extends to kindness in judgment—a charitable interpretation gives someone the benefit of the doubt: {Let's take a charitable view of his motives}. Charitable can also mean lenient: {The reviews were not charitable}.

Charities is the plural of charity—organizations devoted to helping those in need or advancing causes like education, health, or the arts. People donate to charities, volunteer for them, or run marathons to raise money for them: {She supports several charities focused on childhood hunger}. Charity work and charitable giving are associated with altruism, though charities vary widely in effectiveness and overhead costs.

Charity is giving money, goods, or help to those in need, or the organizations that do so: {She donated to several charities}. The word can also mean kindness or generosity of spirit—a willingness to judge others favorably: {Have some charity; he's doing his best}. In religious contexts, charity often means love for others, especially as a Christian virtue.

A charlatan is someone who pretends to be something they are not, usually in order to gain an advantage: He was a charlatan who pretended to be a doctor in order to make money. A religious charlatan is someone who appears to be quite devout while secretly engaging in activities that are forbidden. The verb most likely to precede charlatan is expose, which should perhaps be a warning to anyone who is tempted to become one!

Charlatanism is the practice of claiming expertise or abilities one doesn't possess, especially to deceive others for profit or prestige. The term carries strong connotations of fraud and quackery: {The medical board investigated him for charlatanism}. It suggests not just ignorance but deliberate imposture—the charlatan knows they're faking it.

Charlatans is the plural of charlatan—a person who falsely claims to have special knowledge or skills, especially in medicine or other fields requiring expertise. The word implies deliberate deception for profit or prestige: {The wellness industry attracts its share of charlatans}. A charlatan may have superficial charm but lacks substance beneath the performance.

Charm is the power to please or attract. A person with charm draws others in effortlessly: {She has a natural charm that puts people at ease}. Charm also names a small ornament worn on a bracelet or necklace, and a magical spell or object believed to bring luck or ward off evil: {a good luck charm}. To charm is to delight or enchant, or to influence as if by magic: {He charmed his way into the party}. The phrase {works like a charm} means something succeeds perfectly.

Charmed describes someone or something under a spell of good fortune or protection: {He leads a charmed life}. More commonly, it expresses delight at meeting someone or receiving news: {Charmed to meet you}. This social use sounds formal or slightly old-fashioned. A charmed particle in physics has a specific quantum property called charm.

A charmer is someone with an appealing, persuasive manner—able to win people over through personality rather than argument: {He's a real charmer when he wants something}. The word can be sincere or ironic, suggesting either genuine likability or manipulative smoothness. A snake charmer handles serpents, traditionally by playing music to entrance them.

Charming describes someone or something that delights through appeal, grace, or pleasing manner. A charming person wins others over with warmth and social ease: {He was charming enough to talk his way out of trouble}. A charming village or cottage has quaint, picturesque appeal. The word can carry a note of suspicion—charm may be calculated or manipulative: {a charming con artist}. Used sarcastically, charming expresses displeasure: {Oh, charming—they've canceled my flight}.

Charmless means lacking appeal, warmth, or engaging qualities. A charmless person fails to win others over—cold, graceless, or simply dull. A charmless building or town offers nothing inviting: {The hotel was charmless but cheap}. The word carries mild contempt, suggesting not just absence of charm but a kind of off-putting blankness.

Charms are objects, words, or actions believed to have magical power—a lucky charm, a charm bracelet, a spoken charm to ward off evil. The word extends to personal magnetism: someone with charm captivates others effortlessly. {She charmed everyone at the party.} To charm is to enchant or delight, whether through supernatural means or sheer appeal. A charmed {life} is one blessed with unusual good fortune.

A charnelhouse is a building or vault where corpses or bones are deposited. Before modern cemetery practices, churchyards would overflow, and older remains were moved to charnelhouses to make room for fresh burials. The word now appears mostly in figurative contexts describing scenes of death and horror: {The battlefield was a charnelhouse}. Also spelled charnel house.

Charred describes something burned black on the surface, reduced to carbon by intense heat. Wood becomes charred in a fire; meat gets charred on a grill. The word suggests transformation by flame—not fully consumed, but darkened and often brittle: {charred remains of the building}, {The edges of the paper were charred}.

Charring is the process of burning something partially so that it blackens on the surface without being consumed entirely. Wood, meat, and vegetables can all be charred, sometimes intentionally for flavor or preservation, sometimes accidentally. {The grill left a nice charring on the peppers.} Charring also refers to the residue left behind—the blackened, carbonized material that remains after partial combustion.

A chart is a visual display of information—a diagram, graph, or table that organizes data for quick comprehension: {a pie chart}, {a flow chart}, {an organizational chart}. In navigation, a chart is a map showing coastlines, depths, and hazards: {nautical chart}. The charts are ranked lists of popular music: {The song topped the charts for three weeks}. To chart is to map, record, or plan: {chart a course}, {chart your progress}.

Charted is the past tense of chart—to map, record, or plan a course. A ship charts its route; a doctor charts a patient's progress; a song charts when it appears on music rankings. {The expedition charted previously unknown territory.} {The single charted at number three.} Not to be confused with chartered, which involves hiring or licensing.

A charter is a formal document granting rights, privileges, or authority—a city charter establishes municipal government, a corporate charter creates a company. The Magna Carta was a charter limiting royal power. To charter is to hire exclusively: {We chartered a bus for the trip}, {a chartered flight}. A charter member is an original founder. Charter schools operate under agreements that exempt them from some public school regulations.

Chartered describes something that has been hired or leased for exclusive use: a chartered {bus}, a chartered {flight}, a chartered {yacht}. It also describes professionals or institutions that have received an official charter—a formal grant of rights or recognition: a chartered {accountant} (British), a chartered {bank}. The verb charter means to hire a vehicle or grant such authorization.

Charters is the plural of charter—a document granting rights, privileges, or establishing an organization. A city operates under its charter; a company has articles of incorporation that function similarly. Charter also means to hire or lease: {We chartered a boat for the day}. Charter schools operate under agreements with public authorities but with more autonomy than traditional schools.

Charting is the activity of making charts—visual representations of data or navigational maps. In medical contexts, charting means recording patient information: {The nurse spent an hour charting after her shift}. In music, charting refers to a song's placement on popularity rankings: {The single is charting in twelve countries}. Stock traders speak of charting when analyzing price movements through graphs.

Chartreuse is a yellow-green color, somewhere between lime and olive on the spectrum. The name comes from a French liqueur of that distinctive hue: {The bridesmaids wore chartreuse dresses}.
