The spelling chile (from Spanish) is standard in the American Southwest and Mexico, while chili dominates elsewhere in American English. Chiles range from mild to extremely hot, measured on the Scoville scale: {Habanero chiles are among the hottest varieties}. (Capitalized Chile is the South American country.)

Chili is a hot pepper of the genus Capsicum, or the powder made from dried peppers. Chili also names a spiced stew of meat and beans—or just meat, if you're a Texan purist: {a bowl of chili}, {chili con carne}. The spelling varies: chili, chile, and chilli all appear, with regional preferences. {I added extra chili powder to the pot.}

A chilidog is a hot dog topped with chili con carne, typically served in a bun and often garnished with cheese, onions, or mustard. It's a staple of American casual dining, available at diners, ballparks, and fast-food chains: {We grabbed chilidogs at the game}.

Chilies are the spicy fruits of plants in the capsicum family, used fresh, dried, or powdered to add heat and flavor to food. The spelling varies by region—Americans tend to write chili or chile, while the British prefer chilli—but all refer to the same fiery pods. Varieties range from mild bell peppers to blistering habaneros and ghost peppers. {I added a few dried chilies to the stew for extra kick.}

Chilis is the plural of chili, referring to hot peppers of the capsicum family or dishes made with them. The spelling varies: chili predominates in American English, chile in the Southwest and Mexico, chilli in British English. {She added fresh chilis to the salsa.} {The restaurant serves five different chilis, from mild to volcanic.}

Chill, a noun, adjective, and verb, is associated with coldness, but has recently taken on some informal positive associations, like cool did before it. To chill something is to reduce the temperature of it. A chill is a reduction in temperature, or a reduction in friendly feelings. If you want to chill, however, you want to relax in a low-stress environment, and a chill dude is a relaxed guy.

Chillax blends chill and relax, meaning to calm down or take it easy. The word emerged in the 1990s as casual slang, often directed at someone who's tense or overreacting: {Dude, chillax—it's not a big deal}. It can also describe deliberately unwinding: {I'm just going to chillax this weekend}.

Chilled means cooled, typically to a temperature below ambient but above freezing: {chilled wine}, {chilled soup}. The word extends to people who feel cold: {I'm chilled to the bone}. In informal use, chilled (or chilled out) describes a relaxed, easygoing state: {We just chilled at home all weekend}. A chilling effect discourages action through fear or intimidation.

A chiller is something that chills. In refrigeration, it's a machine that cools water or other fluids for industrial or building climate control. In entertainment, a chiller is a horror story or thriller designed to make your blood run cold: {We watched an old chiller from the 1950s}. The word suggests suspense and creeping dread rather than outright gore.

Chilli is a hot pepper of the capsicum family, or the spicy powder made from dried peppers. The spelling with double-l is standard in British English; Americans typically write chili. Chilli appears in countless dishes and sauces worldwide: {Thai chilli paste}, {chilli con carne}. The heat comes from capsaicin, concentrated in the seeds and white membranes.

Chillies is the British English spelling of the plural of chilli, the hot pepper fruit of plants in the genus Capsicum. These peppers range from mildly warm to extremely hot, with heat measured on the Scoville scale. Chillies appear in cuisines worldwide, adding spice to dishes from curries to salsas. {I added a few chillies to the stir-fry for extra kick.} The American spelling is chilies or chilis.

Chillin is slang for relaxing or taking it easy, often doing nothing in particular: {Just chillin at home tonight}. The dropped g reflects casual pronunciation, matching the laid-back attitude the word describes. It can also mean hanging out: {We're just chillin, watching the game}.

Chilling describes something that causes fear or dread—a cold sensation running through the body: {a chilling account of the massacre}, {chilling implications for democracy}. The connection to cold is metaphorical; fear makes us feel cold. Separately, chilling is the relaxed present participle of chill: {We're just chilling at home}.

Chillis is the plural of chilli, the British spelling of chili—hot peppers of the capsicum family. The spelling with double l appears in British English and throughout former British colonies: {The recipe calls for two fresh chillis}. Americans typically write chilies or chilis.

Chillout describes music, spaces, or activities designed for relaxation after intense stimulation—especially the ambient electronic music played in club lounges where dancers recover between sessions on the floor. A chillout {room}, chillout {zone}, or chillout {playlist} offers calm respite: {We found a chillout area away from the main stage}. As a verb phrase, chill out means to relax or calm down.

Chills are episodes of shivering and feeling cold, often accompanying fever or illness as the body tries to raise its temperature. The word also describes the creepy, tingling sensation that runs through you during fear or excitement—{that horror movie gave me chills}. In a positive sense, something can {give you chills} when it moves you deeply, like a powerful piece of music or an emotional speech.

Chilly means moderately cold—not freezing, but cool enough to cause discomfort: {It's getting chilly out here}. The word often prompts reaching for a sweater or jacket. Figuratively, chilly describes an unfriendly atmosphere or reception: {She gave him a chilly look}. {The meeting got off to a chilly start}.

Chimaeras is a spelling variant of chimeras—mythological creatures combining parts from different animals, or by extension, impossible fantasies and wild illusions. In biology, a chimera is an organism with genetically distinct cells. The spelling chimaera, closer to the Greek original, appears more often in British English and scientific contexts, particularly for the cartilaginous fish also called ratfish or ghost sharks.

A chime is a bell or set of tuned bells, or the sound they produce—typically a clear, resonant tone: {the chime of the grandfather clock}, {wind chimes on the porch}. To chime is to ring or sound melodically. Clocks chime the hour. To {chime in} is to join a conversation, often uninvited: {She chimed in with her opinion}.

Chimed is the past tense of chime. Bells chime when they ring melodically, often marking the hour: {The clock chimed twelve}. To chime in is to join a conversation, sometimes uninvited: {She chimed in with her opinion}. When things chime with each other, they harmonize or agree: {His views chimed with hers}.

A chimera is a creature from Greek myth—a fire-breathing monster with a lion's head, goat's body, and serpent's tail. The word now means any fanciful hybrid or impossible fantasy: {His plan for the company was a chimera}. In biology, a chimera is an organism containing genetically distinct cells, whether from mutation, grafting, or embryonic fusion. In genetics, chimeric DNA combines sequences from different sources.

Chimeras are creatures composed of parts from different animals—in Greek mythology, a fire-breathing monster with a lion's head, goat's body, and serpent's tail. The word now applies to any hybrid or fantastical combination: {genetic chimeras}, {architectural chimeras}. More broadly, a chimera is an illusion or impossible fancy: {His dreams of wealth proved to be chimeras}. In biology, a chimera is an organism containing cells from two distinct genetic sources.

Chimes are a set of tuned bells or metal tubes struck to produce musical tones. Wind chimes hang outdoors and ring when the breeze moves them. Door chimes sound when someone arrives. A clock chimes the hour. The verb extends to voices joining in: {Several others chimed in with their opinions}. Things that chime together harmonize or agree: {Her views chimed with mine}.

A chimichanga is a deep-fried burrito—a flour tortilla wrapped around a filling of meat, beans, cheese, or other ingredients, then fried until crispy. The dish originated in Mexican-American cuisine, likely in Arizona. {I ordered a beef chimichanga with sour cream and guacamole.}

Chimichangas are deep-fried burritos—flour tortillas filled with meat, beans, cheese, or other ingredients, then fried until crispy. The dish is Tex-Mex or Southwestern American, often served smothered in salsa or sour cream: {I ordered the beef chimichanga with extra guacamole}. Singular: chimichanga.

Chimichurri is a vibrant green sauce from Argentina and Uruguay, made with parsley, garlic, vinegar, oil, and oregano. It's the traditional accompaniment to grilled meats, especially steak: {The asado came with a bowl of chimichurri on the side}. Unlike most sauces, it's uncooked—fresh and sharp rather than rich.

A chiminea is a freestanding outdoor fireplace, typically made of clay or cast iron, with a bulbous body and a vertical chimney that directs smoke upward. Originally from Mexico, chimineas are used for warmth and ambiance on patios and in backyards. {We gathered around the chiminea on cool autumn evenings.} The enclosed design makes them safer than open fire pits, though clay versions can crack if exposed to sudden temperature changes.

Chiming is the sound of bells or bell-like tones ringing in harmony or sequence: {the chiming of church bells}, {a clock chiming midnight}. It extends to any melodious ringing sound: {wind chimes chiming in the breeze}. To chime in is to join a conversation, often uninvited: {He kept chiming in with his opinions}.

A chimney is a vertical structure that channels smoke and gases from a fire or furnace up and out of a building. By extension, chimney applies to any similar passage—a volcanic chimney, a glass chimney around a lamp flame, or a narrow vertical cleft in rock that climbers ascend by bracing against opposite walls. {Smoke poured from the chimney.}

Chimneys is the plural of chimney—vertical structures that vent smoke and gases from fireplaces, furnaces, or industrial processes. A house may have multiple chimneys for different heating sources. In climbing, a chimney is a narrow vertical cleft in rock that a climber ascends by bracing against opposite walls: {We chimneyed up through a gap in the cliff face}.

Chimp is an informal shortening of chimpanzee, the highly intelligent African ape that shares about 98% of its DNA with humans. Chimps live in social groups, use tools, and communicate through vocalizations and gestures. The word appears frequently in casual contexts where the full form would sound overly scientific: {The chimps at the zoo were playing with cardboard boxes}. To chimp out is a vulgar and offensive slang expression meaning to lose control in a fit of rage.

A chimpanzee is a great ape native to the forests of central and west Africa, closely related to humans genetically. Chimpanzees live in social groups, use tools, and display complex behaviors that make them subjects of extensive research into cognition and evolution. Often shortened to chimp: {The chimp picked up a stick and poked it into the termite mound}.

Chimpanzees are great apes native to African forests, humanity's closest living relatives. They share roughly 98% of human DNA and display remarkable intelligence—using tools, solving problems, and communicating through gestures and vocalizations. Chimpanzees live in complex social groups with hierarchies, alliances, and occasional violence. {The chimpanzees at the zoo drew crowds with their antics.}

Chimps is the informal plural of chimpanzee, the African great ape most closely related to humans. The shortened form dominates casual speech and writing: {The chimps at the zoo were playing with cardboard boxes}. Scientific contexts tend to prefer the full word.

The chin is the front part of the lower jaw, the point of the face below the mouth. To {take it on the chin} is to endure hardship stoically. To {keep your chin up} is to stay positive through difficulty. {Chin up} alone serves as encouragement. As a verb, to chin yourself is to pull your body up on a bar until your chin clears it.

China is porcelain or ceramic dinnerware, typically fine and delicate, often decorated with intricate patterns. The term derives from the country where such ceramics were first perfected and exported to Europe. People distinguish between everyday dishes and their "good china," which is reserved for special occasions and often passed down through families. {We use the good china for holidays and dinner parties.} {She inherited her grandmother's china set.} (Capitalized China is the country.)

A chinchilla is a small South American rodent prized for its exceptionally soft, dense fur. The animals were hunted nearly to extinction for their pelts, which remain among the most expensive in the fur trade. Chinchillas are also kept as pets. The word extends to the luxurious gray fur itself and to garments made from it: {a chinchilla coat}.

Chinchillas are small, soft-furred rodents native to the Andes Mountains of South America, prized for their exceptionally dense, silky coats. They are kept as exotic pets and historically were hunted nearly to extinction for their fur, which remains among the most valuable in the world. {Our chinchilla loves to take dust baths.} The word also refers to the fur itself or to garments made from it.
clues: South American pets with velvet coats

definition: Chinless describes someone whose chin recedes weakly into the neck, giving the face an indistinct lower profile. The physical trait extends to a figurative sense: weak, ineffectual, lacking backbone. British usage often pairs it with "wonder" to describe upper-class men perceived as feckless: {a chinless wonder from the Home Counties}.

Chino is a sturdy cotton twill fabric, typically in khaki or tan colors, used for casual trousers. The trousers themselves are called chinos: {He wore chinos and a blazer to the interview}. The fabric originated as military uniform material but became standard casual wear. Chinos occupy the space between jeans and dress pants—presentable but not formal.

A chinook is a warm, dry wind that blows down the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains, capable of raising temperatures dramatically in winter: {A chinook came through and melted a foot of snow overnight}. The word also refers to a type of large Pacific salmon, prized by sport fishers and commercially important. (Capitalized Chinook refers to the Indigenous people or the military helicopter.)

Chinos are casual trousers made from a lightweight twill cotton fabric, typically in khaki, tan, or olive colors. Originally military wear, they now occupy the middle ground between jeans and dress pants—acceptable in business casual settings where denim wouldn't be: {He wore chinos and a button-down to the interview}.

Chins is the plural of chin, the front of the lower jaw below the mouth. People may have multiple chins—folds of flesh beneath the jawline associated with weight gain or aging: {He's developed a few extra chins over the years}. As a verb form, chins means performing chin-ups: {She chins herself on the bar every morning}.

Chintz is a cotton fabric with a glazed finish, typically printed with bright floral patterns. Originally imported from India, it became popular for curtains, upholstery, and clothing. The adjective chintzy means cheap or stingy, reflecting how the once-prized fabric came to seem gaudy or tasteless: {The hotel lobby had a chintzy feel with its faded floral couches}.

Chintzy means cheap, stingy, or tastelessly showy. The word comes from chintz, a printed cotton fabric once associated with gaudy, inexpensive décor. A chintzy gift disappoints with its obvious cheapness: {He gave her some chintzy earrings from the airport gift shop}. A chintzy person is unwilling to spend money: {Don't be so chintzy—tip the guy}.

Chinwag is British informal for a friendly, casual conversation—the kind of unhurried chat people have over tea: {We had a lovely chinwag about the old days}. Used as both noun and verb: {Come over for a chinwag}, {They chinwagged for hours}.

Common to various meanings of chip is the idea of something small, sometimes flat, and being one of a number of like things, perhaps formerly attached to something larger. A single potato will yield many chips, which are extremely thin and flat if you’re in the U.S., and sticklike if you’re in the UK. A chip may break off of something, such as a piece of crockery. A poker chip is a small disk with some value assigned to it for betting. To chip something is to remove chips from it, or reduce it to chips.

A chipmaker is a company that designs or manufactures semiconductor chips—the tiny integrated circuits that power computers, phones, and countless electronic devices. The term appears frequently in business and technology news: {Chipmakers are struggling to meet global demand}. Also spelled chip maker.

Chipmaking is the process of manufacturing semiconductor chips—the tiny integrated circuits that power computers, phones, and countless electronic devices. The industry requires extraordinarily precise fabrication facilities and has become geopolitically significant as nations compete for chipmaking capacity: {Taiwan dominates global chipmaking}.

A chipmunk is a small, striped rodent related to squirrels, native to North America and parts of Asia. Chipmunks have distinctive markings—light and dark stripes running along the back and face—and characteristically stuff their cheek pouches with seeds and nuts. They live in underground burrows and are commonly seen in wooded areas and suburban yards.

Chipmunks is the plural of chipmunk, a small striped rodent of the squirrel family found mainly in North America. They have characteristic stripes along their backs and cheeks that expand to store food: {Chipmunks were raiding the bird feeder}. The animated Chipmunks—Alvin, Simon, and Theodore—have been pop culture fixtures since the 1950s.

A chipotle is a dried, smoked jalapeño pepper, giving dishes a deep, smoky heat distinct from fresh chiles. Common in Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking, chipotles often come canned in adobo sauce: {Add a chipotle or two for some kick}. The flavor is earthy and complex rather than just hot. (Capitalized Chipotle is the restaurant chain.)

Chipotles is the plural of chipotle, a dried and smoked jalapeño pepper used in Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking. The peppers have a distinctive smoky heat and appear whole, ground, or packed in adobo sauce: {I added a couple of chipotles to the stew}. The name comes from Nahuatl.

Chipped describes something with a small piece broken off its edge or surface: a chipped {tooth}, a chipped {mug}, chipped {paint}. Chipped potatoes are British for french fries—potatoes cut into pieces. In sports, a chipped shot or pass is lofted with a short, sharp stroke: {He chipped it over the goalkeeper}.

Chipper means cheerful and lively, often with a suggestion of energetic good spirits: {She seemed surprisingly chipper for a Monday morning}. The word can carry a faint note of skepticism—someone described as chipper may seem more upbeat than circumstances warrant. Separately, a chipper is a machine that reduces wood to chips.

Chipping is the act of breaking off small pieces from a surface, or the small pieces themselves. Paint chips from walls, teeth chip from impact, ice chips off glaciers. In golf, a chip shot is a short, lofted stroke near the green—chipping gets the ball up and over obstacles. To be {chipping away} at something is to make gradual progress: {She's been chipping away at her dissertation for months}.

Chippy has several distinct meanings depending on region. In British English, a chippy is a fish-and-chip shop: {We grabbed dinner at the chippy}. In American slang, chippy describes someone irritable or quick to take offense—often used of athletes playing aggressively: {The game got chippy in the third period}. Older American slang used chippy for a promiscuous woman or prostitute, though this sense has faded. In British and Australian usage, a chippy is also a carpenter.

Chips are thin, flat pieces—usually crisp and edible. In American English, chips are thin slices of potato fried until crunchy: {a bag of chips}, {chips and dip}. In British English, chips are thick-cut fried potatoes (American French fries): {fish and chips}. Chips also means small fragments broken off something larger: {wood chips}, {paint chips}. In gambling, chips are tokens representing money: {poker chips}, {cash in your chips}. In computing, chips are integrated circuits: {computer chips}, {microchips}. To have a {chip on your shoulder} is to carry a grudge. When the {chips are down}, circumstances are dire. (Capitalized CHIPS is an acronym.)

A chip shot is a short, low-trajectory shot in golf played near the green, intended to pop the ball briefly into the air before it rolls toward the hole. The term has extended to other sports, particularly soccer and hockey, where it describes a shot lofted over a goalkeeper or defender. Figuratively, chip shot describes any task that's easy or nearly effortless: {Getting him to agree was a chip shot}.

Chiptune is electronic music made using the sound chips from vintage video game consoles and computers—the Nintendo Entertainment System, Game Boy, Commodore 64, and similar hardware. The genre embraces the lo-fi, 8-bit aesthetic of early gaming, with its characteristic bleeps, square waves, and arpeggios. Modern chiptune artists may use original hardware, emulators, or software that recreates those distinctive synthesized sounds: {The chiptune scene has a devoted following at gaming conventions}.

Chiptunes are electronic music created using the sound chips from vintage video game consoles and early computers—particularly 8-bit systems like the Nintendo Entertainment System or Commodore 64. The genre embraces the bleepy, lo-fi quality of these processors as an aesthetic choice rather than a limitation. Modern chiptune artists often use original hardware or software that emulates those iconic sounds: {The soundtrack has a chiptune vibe}.

Chiropractic is a system of treatment based on the theory that disease results from misalignment of the spine. Chiropractors manipulate the spine and joints to relieve pain, particularly back and neck problems. The field occupies contested ground between mainstream medicine and alternative therapy: {My doctor referred me to a chiropractor}, but also {Chiropractic is pseudoscience}.

A chiropractor is a practitioner of chiropractic, a system of treatment based on the belief that many health problems stem from misalignments of the spine. Chiropractors manipulate the spine and joints, often producing audible cracks: {My chiropractor adjusted my lower back}. The practice occupies contested ground between mainstream medicine and alternative therapy.

Chiropractors are practitioners of chiropractic, a form of alternative medicine focused on diagnosing and treating musculoskeletal problems, especially of the spine. They perform manual adjustments—manipulating joints with controlled force—to relieve pain and improve function: {The chiropractor cracked my back and I felt immediate relief}. Chiropractors are licensed healthcare providers in most jurisdictions but remain controversial in mainstream medicine, with debate over the efficacy of spinal manipulation for conditions beyond back pain.

Chirp is the short, high-pitched sound made by small birds and insects: {sparrows chirping outside the window}, {crickets chirping at dusk}. The word imitates the sound. To chirp is to make such sounds, or by extension, to speak in a bright, cheerful manner. In slang, to chirp someone is to taunt or trash-talk them, especially in sports: {The bench was chirping the opposing goalie all game}.

Chirped is the past tense of chirp—to make a short, high-pitched sound like a small bird or cricket. People chirp when they speak in a bright, cheerful tone: {She chirped a greeting as she walked in}. Electronics chirp too: {The smoke detector chirped all night}.

Chirping is the short, high-pitched sounds made by small birds and insects like crickets. The word extends to any similar sharp, repetitive sounds: {The smoke detector won't stop chirping}. People chirp when they speak in quick, cheerful bursts. In sports slang, chirping means trash-talking opponents: {The players were chirping at each other all game}.

Chirps are the short, high-pitched sounds made by small birds and insects. Crickets chirp; sparrows chirp. By extension, any brief, bright sound or remark: {Her phone chirped with notifications}. To chirp is to make such sounds, or to speak in a cheerful, almost annoyingly upbeat way: {He was chirping about his promotion all morning}.

Chirpy describes a cheerfully upbeat manner—bright, perky, and talkative. The word evokes the quick, high-pitched sounds of small birds. Someone chirpy seems energetically positive, sometimes annoyingly so: {She's too chirpy for this early in the morning}. The word is more common in British than American English.
clues: Like a morning person greeting strangers

definition: A chisel is a hand tool with a sharp beveled blade at one end, used for cutting or shaping wood, stone, or metal. A woodworker drives it with a mallet; a sculptor uses one to carve marble. To chisel is to cut or shape with this tool. In slang, to chisel someone is to cheat or swindle them: {He chiseled me out of fifty bucks}.

Chiseled describes something cut or shaped with a chisel—a tool for carving wood, stone, or metal. The word usually appears figuratively to describe features that look precisely carved: {chiseled cheekbones}, {a chiseled jaw}. The implication is sharp, well-defined lines suggesting strength or classical beauty, often applied to male faces and physiques.

A chiseler is someone who cheats or swindles, especially through petty schemes or by shaving small amounts off what's owed to others: {That chiseler shortchanged me again}. The term derives from the tool—a chisel chips away bit by bit, just as a chiseler nibbles away at money or trust. Also spelled chiseller.

Chiseling is cutting or shaping with a chisel, the sharp-edged tool used for carving wood, stone, or metal. Figuratively, chiseling means cheating or swindling someone out of money through petty fraud: {He's been chiseling customers for years}. Someone who chisels is a chiseler. Also spelled chiselling.

Chiselled describes something shaped or cut with a chisel—or appearing as if it were. The word most often applies to facial features, especially a man's jaw or cheekbones, suggesting sharp, well-defined angles: {his chiselled features}, {a chiselled jawline}. The spelling with double L is British; American English uses chiseled.

Chisels are hand tools with a sharpened metal blade used for cutting or shaping wood, stone, or metal. The blade is driven by striking the handle with a mallet or by hand pressure. To chisel is to cut with such a tool, or figuratively, to cheat or swindle someone: {He chiseled me out of fifty bucks}. A chiseled face or body has sharply defined features, as if carved from stone.

A chit is a short written note, especially one serving as a receipt, voucher, or record of a debt: {Sign the chit and we'll settle up later}. The word appears in phrases like {chit system} for informal credit arrangements. Separately, chit is a slightly old-fashioned or dismissive term for a young woman or girl: {a mere chit of a thing}.

Chitchat is light, informal conversation about trivial matters—small talk that fills silence without addressing anything substantial: {We made chitchat while waiting for the meeting to start}. The word can also function as a verb: {They chitchatted about the weather}. The reduplication suggests the back-and-forth rhythm of casual exchange.

Chitlins are pig intestines prepared as food, typically cleaned, boiled, and then fried or stewed. A staple of Southern American cuisine, particularly soul food, they require extensive preparation to remove their strong odor. Usually appears in the plural: {a plate of chitlins}. Also spelled chitterlings, the more formal variant.

Chitlings is an alternate spelling of chitterlings—the small intestines of a pig, cleaned and prepared as food. The dish has deep roots in Southern American and African American cuisine, traditionally slow-cooked until tender: {Grandma's chitlings were always the highlight of the holiday table}. Also spelled chitlins.

Chitlins is a shortened form of chitterlings—the small intestines of a pig, cleaned and cooked as food. A staple of Southern American cooking and soul food, chitlins require extensive preparation to remove impurities and have a distinctive, pungent smell when cooking: {Grandma always made chitlins for New Year's Day}.

Chitter is the rapid, high-pitched sound made by small birds or insects—a series of short, sharp notes in quick succession. Squirrels and chipmunks chitter when alarmed or excited. The word is imitative, close to chirp and twitter but suggesting a faster, more fragmented quality: {Sparrows chittered in the hedgerow}.

Chittering describes the rapid, high-pitched sounds made by small animals—squirrels, birds, insects, or rodents: {Squirrels were chittering in the branches overhead}. The word suggests quick, repetitive vocalizations, often conveying agitation or excitement. It can apply to human speech that resembles such sounds—rapid, nervous chatter: {The children were chittering with excitement}.

Chitterlings are the small intestines of a pig, cleaned and prepared as food. Usually plural: {We're having chitterlings for New Year's}. The dish has deep roots in Southern American and African American cuisine, often slow-cooked or fried. Also spelled chitlins or chitlings.

Chitterlings are the small intestines of a pig, prepared as food. They require extensive cleaning and long cooking, typically boiling or frying. A traditional dish in Southern American and soul food cooking, often called chitlins: {Grandma always made chitterlings for New Year's Day}.

Chivalrous describes conduct associated with the medieval code of knighthood—brave, honorable, and courteous, especially toward women. A chivalrous man opens doors, offers his coat, or stands when a woman enters. The term can carry a whiff of old-fashioned gender roles: {His chivalrous gesture felt patronizing to her}. More broadly, chivalrous applies to any gallant or magnanimous behavior: {a chivalrous offer to let the opponent rest before continuing}.

Chivalry was the medieval code governing knights—courage in battle, loyalty to one's lord, protection of the weak. The word now usually refers to courteous behavior, especially by men toward women: holding doors, offering seats, paying for meals. Whether such gestures are admirable or patronizing depends on who you ask. {Chivalry isn't dead.}

Chive is an herb in the onion family, grown for its slender, hollow green leaves. The mild onion flavor makes chives a common garnish for baked potatoes, soups, and cream-based dishes. Usually plural: {a sprinkle of fresh chives}. The plant produces edible purple flowers.

Chives are a mild-flavored herb related to onions and garlic, with thin, hollow, grass-like leaves. They're typically snipped into small pieces and used as a garnish or flavoring, especially on potatoes, eggs, and cream-based dishes: {baked potato with sour cream and chives}. The word is almost always plural; a single blade is rarely called "a chive."

Chlamydia is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by bacteria. It often produces no symptoms, making testing important for sexually active people. Left untreated, it can cause serious reproductive complications including infertility. {She got tested for chlamydia after her annual checkup}. The word also names the bacterial genus responsible for several diseases, including some eye infections.

Chlorine is a greenish-yellow gas with a sharp, suffocating odor—one of the chemical elements. It's highly reactive and toxic in concentrated form but essential in diluted compounds: chlorine disinfects drinking water and swimming pools, bleaches fabrics, and appears in table salt (sodium chloride). {The pool smells strongly of chlorine.}

Chloroform is a colorless liquid with a sweet smell, once widely used as an anesthetic. It became notorious as a tool for incapacitating people—the cliché of a rag soaked in chloroform pressed over someone's face persists in fiction, though it works far slower than movies suggest. As a verb, to chloroform someone is to render them unconscious with the substance: {The kidnapper chloroformed his victim}.

Chlorophyll is the green pigment in plants that captures light energy for photosynthesis, the process by which plants convert sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into food. It gives leaves and stems their characteristic green color. When chlorophyll breaks down in autumn, other pigments become visible, producing the reds and yellows of fall foliage. The word combines Greek roots meaning "green" and "leaf."

A chocaholic is someone with an excessive craving for chocolate, treating the fondness as if it were an addiction. The word playfully combines chocolate with alcoholic: {I'm such a chocaholic—I can't walk past a bakery without buying something}. Also spelled chocoholic.

A chock is a wedge or block placed against something to prevent movement—typically under wheels or around cargo: {Put chocks under the tires before you jack up the car}. As a verb, to chock is to secure with such blocks. The adverb chock means tightly packed or completely full, appearing mainly in combinations: {chock-full}, {chock-a-block}.

Chockablock means packed tightly together, crammed full: {The shelves were chockablock with old books}. Originally a nautical term describing blocks of a tackle drawn so close together they touch. Often intensified as {chock-full} or used with "with": {The street was chockablock with tourists}. Sometimes spelled chock-a-block.

Chockful means completely filled, packed to capacity: {The attic was chockful of old photographs}. The word emphasizes abundance to the point of overflow. Also spelled chock-full. {A book chockful of practical advice.}

Chockfull means completely full, packed to capacity: {The attic was chockfull of old photographs}. The word emphasizes abundance to the point of overflow. Also spelled chock-full. {Her speech was chockfull of promises.}

A chocoholic is someone with an excessive fondness for chocolate, often humorously described as an addiction. The word playfully borrows the -aholic suffix from alcoholic to suggest compulsive consumption. {I'm such a chocoholic that I keep emergency chocolate in my desk drawer.} The term is almost always lighthearted rather than clinical, acknowledging chocolate's status as a socially acceptable indulgence.

Chocolate is a food made from roasted cacao beans, typically sweet and brown. It appears as candy bars, baking chips, hot drinks, and flavoring for countless desserts. Dark chocolate contains more cacao and less sugar; milk chocolate adds dairy; white chocolate contains cocoa butter but no cocoa solids. {I'll have the chocolate cake.} As a color, chocolate is a deep reddish-brown. A {box of chocolates} contains assorted individual candies, often given as gifts.

Chocolates are individual pieces of chocolate candy, typically with fillings like cream, caramel, nuts, or liqueur, often presented in decorative boxes: {a box of chocolates}, {Valentine's Day chocolates}. The plural distinguishes these confections from chocolate as a substance or drink. {Life is like a box of chocolates.}

A chocolatier is a person who makes or sells chocolate confections, especially high-quality artisanal pieces. The term suggests craft and expertise beyond mass production: {The chocolatier hand-dipped each truffle}. A shop specializing in fine chocolates may also be called a chocolatier.

Chocolatiers are people who make or sell chocolate, especially fine confections. The term suggests artisanal craft rather than industrial production—a chocolatier hand-dips truffles and tempers ganache, while a factory churns out candy bars. {The chocolatier's display case featured sea salt caramels and champagne bonbons.}

Choice is the act of selecting among options, or the thing selected: {It was a difficult choice}, {She made her choice}. It also means the range of options available: {The menu offered little choice}. As an adjective, choice means of high quality or carefully selected: {choice cuts of beef}, {choice words}. A few choice words usually means pointed or cutting ones.

Choices is the plural of choice—the options available or the decisions made among them. To {have choices} is to face multiple possibilities. The word often emphasizes agency or responsibility: {You made your choices, now live with them}. {We have limited choices here.}

A choir is a group of singers who perform together, typically in a church, school, or concert hall. Church choirs sing hymns and anthems during services; school choirs perform at assemblies and competitions. The word also refers to the section of a church where such singers sit. {She joined the choir in seventh grade.} To {preach to the choir} is to advocate to those already convinced.

A choirboy is a boy who sings in a church or cathedral choir. The term often appears figuratively to describe someone notably innocent, pure, or well-behaved: {He's no choirboy} suggests a person has a questionable past or isn't as virtuous as they might appear.

Choirboys are boys who sing in a choir, especially in a church or cathedral setting. The singular choirboy often appears figuratively to suggest innocence or moral purity: {He's no choirboy} means someone has a checkered past or questionable character. The image draws on the traditional association of church choirs with wholesomeness and propriety.

A choirmaster is the director of a choir, responsible for conducting rehearsals and performances. The role involves selecting music, training singers, and leading the group during services or concerts. Churches, schools, and community organizations all have choirmasters. The term is somewhat old-fashioned; {choir director} is now more common in American usage.

Choirs is the plural of choir—a group of singers who perform together, typically in a church or concert setting. The word extends to sections of singers within a larger ensemble: {The sopranos and altos sat on opposite sides of the choir loft}. Choirs also names groups of similar things, especially in the phrase {choirs of angels}, referring to the traditional ranks of heavenly beings.

Meanings of choke share the idea of obstructing a flow. If you choke, your breathing becomes obstructed. If you choke someone (by compressing their throat, for example), it’s their breathing that’s affected. If weeds or dust choke a place, they are the predominant and undesirable things there. A choke is an instance of choking, but on a motor, the choke controls the flow of air.

Choked is the past tense of choke—to have one's airway blocked or constricted: {He choked on a piece of steak}. Figuratively, to choke is to fail under pressure: {She choked in the final round}. Choked can also describe something constricted or clogged: {roads choked with traffic}, {a voice choked with emotion}. In British slang, choked means upset or disappointed: {I was absolutely choked when they cancelled}.

A chokehold is a restraining grip around someone's neck, used to subdue or immobilize them. In wrestling and martial arts, it's a legitimate technique. When applied by police, chokeholds have caused deaths and sparked controversy: {The officer placed him in a chokehold}. Figuratively, a chokehold is any tight, controlling grip: {The corporation has a chokehold on the market}.

A chokehold is a restraining technique in which pressure is applied to someone's neck, typically from behind, to restrict breathing or blood flow. Chokeholds are used in wrestling, martial arts, and by law enforcement, though their use by police has become increasingly controversial due to deaths in custody. The term also works figuratively: a corporation might have a chokehold on an industry, meaning it dominates so completely that competitors can barely survive.

A chokepoint is a narrow passage where movement becomes restricted—a geographic bottleneck that concentrates traffic or forces. The Strait of Hormuz and the Suez Canal are strategic chokepoints where naval traffic can be controlled or blocked. The term extends to any critical juncture where flow is constrained: {The security checkpoint became a chokepoint during rush hour}. In networks and supply chains, a chokepoint is a vulnerable node whose failure disrupts the whole system.

Chokepoints are narrow passages where movement is restricted and easily blocked. The term originates in geography and military strategy—the Strait of Hormuz and Panama Canal are classic chokepoints where naval traffic can be controlled or cut off. The meaning extends to any bottleneck: {Supply chain chokepoints delayed production for months}. In gaming, chokepoints are defensible positions where enemies must funnel through.

A choker is a necklace or band worn tight around the neck: {She paired the black choker with a simple dress}. The word extends to anything that encircles snugly at the throat—a close-fitting collar, a clerical collar. In logging, a choker is a cable looped around logs for dragging. Informally, a choker is a decisive failure under pressure, especially in sports: {He's a choker—he always misses the clutch shots}.

Chokers is the plural of choker, a close-fitting necklace or band worn snugly around the neck. The style has cycled in and out of fashion, from Victorian ribbon chokers to 1990s black velvet bands to modern statement pieces: {She collected vintage chokers}. In other contexts, a choker is someone who fails under pressure—who chokes when it matters: {He's a choker in big games}.

Chokes is the verb form of choke—to have breathing obstructed, or to obstruct another's breathing: {He chokes every time he eats too fast}, {She chokes up when she talks about her late father}. In sports, to choke is to fail under pressure: {He always chokes in the playoffs}. As a noun, chokes are devices that restrict flow—in engines, the choke limits air intake; in shotguns, it narrows the shot pattern. Artichoke hearts are surrounded by the choke, the inedible fibrous center.

A chokeslam is a professional wrestling move where a wrestler grabs an opponent by the throat, lifts them up, and slams them down onto the mat. The move was popularized by wrestlers like The Undertaker and Kane. Outside wrestling, chokeslam describes any forceful takedown: {He got chokeslammed into the pavement}.

Choking is the obstruction of airways that prevents breathing: {The baby was choking on a grape}. By extension, choking describes anything constricted or overwhelmed: {choking traffic}, {a voice choking with emotion}. In sports and performance contexts, choking means failing under pressure—freezing when the stakes are high: {He choked in the finals}.

Chola is a Latina woman or girl associated with a particular urban subculture, often marked by distinctive style—dark lip liner, thin eyebrows, flannel shirts, hoop earrings. The term originated in Mexican-American communities and can be neutral, affectionate, or derogatory depending on who uses it and how: {She's got that chola aesthetic down}. The male equivalent is cholo.

Cholera is a severe bacterial infection of the small intestine, spread through contaminated water and causing violent diarrhea and dehydration. Without treatment, it can kill within hours. Cholera outbreaks occur where sanitation is poor, often following natural disasters or in refugee camps. {A cholera epidemic swept through the city.}

Cholesterol is a waxy substance found in blood and cell membranes, essential for producing hormones and vitamin D. The term usually appears in health contexts distinguishing HDL ("good cholesterol") from LDL ("bad cholesterol"): {My doctor wants me to lower my cholesterol}. High cholesterol levels increase risk of heart disease, making it a common target of dietary intervention and medication.

Cholo is a term for a Mexican American man, particularly one associated with a distinctive urban style—baggy khakis, flannel shirts, shaved head, tattoos. The word carries different weight depending on who's using it: among Chicanos it can signal cultural pride or neighborhood identity, while outsiders using it often intend or convey disrespect. The female equivalent is chola. {He dressed cholo style in high school.}

Chomp is to bite or chew vigorously, often noisily: {The horse chomped on an apple}. To {chomp at the bit} is to be restless or impatient, like a horse chewing its harness while waiting to run. A chomp is a single bite: {He took a big chomp out of the sandwich}.

Chomper is informal for a tooth, almost always in the plural: {Nice chompers!} The word emphasizes the biting function—teeth as tools for chomping. It appears most often in casual speech about dental appearance or dentures: {Grandpa took out his chompers for the night}.

Chompers is informal, often playful slang for teeth: {Nice chompers!} The word emphasizes teeth as tools for chewing or biting. It can refer to natural teeth or dentures: {Grandpa took out his chompers for the night}.

Chomping is chewing or biting down on something with noisy, vigorous movements. It often suggests impatience or restlessness, as in the expression {chomping at the bit}, where a horse bites impatiently at its harness while waiting to run. This phrase extends to people eager to begin something: {The team was chomping at the bit to start the project}. Chomping is a variant of champing, with chomping now more common in American English.

Chomps is the third-person singular of chomp, meaning to bite or chew vigorously, often noisily: {The horse chomps on its bit}. Someone who {chomps at the bit} is impatient to begin. The word suggests enthusiastic, sometimes aggressive eating: {He chomps his food like he hasn't eaten in days}.

Choochoo is a child's word for a train, imitating the sound of a steam locomotive. It appears in baby talk and children's books: {Do you want to ride the choochoo?} Adults use it playfully or nostalgically. Also spelled choo-choo.

Choose is to pick from among options, selecting one or more while leaving others behind. The word implies agency and deliberation: {Choose your words carefully.} You can choose a career, a partner, or what to have for dinner. When something is chosen, it has been selected with intent; {the chosen few} are a select group. To choose between options is to weigh them; to choose not to do something is a deliberate decision to abstain. {I chose the red one} records a completed selection.

Choosing is the act of selecting from alternatives. The word often emphasizes the process or moment of decision: {Choosing a college is stressful}, {I'm having trouble choosing between them}. As a noun, choosings appears in phrases like {slim choosings}, meaning few options available.
clues: The act of making a decision

definition: Choosy means particular or selective, unwilling to accept just anything: {She's choosy about her friends}. The word often implies pickiness that others find excessive or unwarranted: {You can't afford to be choosy in this job market}. Also spelled choosey.

Chop is most frequently encountered as a verb signifying a cutting action. In cooking, to chop is to reduce something to small pieces: Please chop the garlic. To chop with something larger, such as an ax, means to sever smaller pieces from a larger one (chop wood). A chop may be an instance of chopping, or the result of it. Chief among resultants is a cut of meat containing a section of rib (lamb chop, pork chop).

A chophouse is a restaurant specializing in meat dishes, particularly chops and steaks. The term dates to an era when such establishments served straightforward fare—grilled cuts of beef, lamb, or pork—in no-frills settings. Modern chophouses often position themselves as upscale steakhouses: {We celebrated at the old chophouse downtown}.

Chopped describes something cut into pieces, usually with a blade: {chopped onions}, {chopped wood}. In car culture, a chopped vehicle has had its roof lowered by removing a horizontal section—a modification associated with hot rods and custom builds. Chopped can also mean eliminated or cut from consideration: {The project got chopped from the budget}.

A chopper is something that chops—a cleaver, an ax, or a food processor blade. In informal use, chopper most often means a helicopter, from the chopping motion of the rotor blades: {The chopper lifted off at dawn}. A chopper is also a customized motorcycle with high handlebars and an extended front fork, associated with outlaw biker culture. In British slang, choppers are teeth.

Choppers is informal for teeth, especially large or prominent ones: {Nice choppers—you must have had braces}. The word also refers to helicopters, from the chopping motion of rotor blades: {News choppers circled the scene}. Less commonly, choppers are people or tools that chop, or a style of custom motorcycle with extended front forks.

Chopping is cutting something into pieces with repeated sharp blows, typically using a knife or axe: {chopping onions}, {chopping wood}. The word emphasizes the forceful, rhythmic motion rather than precision. Choppy water has short, irregular waves—as if the surface were being struck repeatedly. A {chopping block} is where butchers cut meat or, figuratively, where jobs and budgets get eliminated.

Choppy describes something broken into short, irregular segments. Choppy water has small, rough waves that make for an uncomfortable boat ride. Choppy prose lacks smooth transitions between ideas. A choppy signal cuts in and out. {The helicopter hit choppy air over the mountains.} The word suggests disruption of what should flow continuously.

Chops are the jaws or the area around the mouth, especially on an animal: {The dog licked its chops}. In music, chops means technical skill, particularly on an instrument: {That guitarist has serious chops}. The meaning extends to competence in any field: {She has the chops to run the department}. A chop is also a cut of meat with bone attached, typically from the rib or loin: {pork chops}, {lamb chops}. To bust someone's chops is to tease or criticize them persistently.

Chopsticks are a pair of slender sticks used as eating utensils, held in one hand and manipulated to pick up food. They originated in East Asia and remain the primary utensil in Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese cuisine. The singular chopstick is rare—they function as a pair: {I never learned to use chopsticks properly}.

Chopsticks are a pair of slender sticks used as eating utensils, held in one hand and manipulated to pick up food. They originated in East Asia and remain the standard implements for eating in Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese cuisines. Chopsticks are typically made of wood, bamboo, plastic, or metal. Learning to use them takes practice: {I still can't eat rice with chopsticks}.

A chord is three or more musical notes sounded together, forming the harmonic foundation of most Western music. Guitar players strum chords; pianists voice them. In geometry, a chord is a straight line connecting two points on a curve. The phrase {strike a chord} means to resonate emotionally or trigger recognition: {Her speech struck a chord with the audience}. The spelling chord also appears in {spinal cord} and {vocal cords}, though these derive from a different word meaning string or rope.

Chords is the plural of chord, which has two distinct meanings. In music, a chord is three or more notes sounded together harmoniously; to strike a chord with someone is to evoke an emotional response, as if their feelings were strings being played. In geometry and anatomy, a chord is a straight line connecting two points on a curve—the vocal cords (often spelled chords) are membranes that vibrate to produce sound. {She strummed a few chords on the guitar.}

A chore is a routine task, especially a household duty like washing dishes or taking out the trash. The word carries a sense of obligation rather than pleasure—something that must be done: {Saturday mornings were for chores}. By extension, any tedious but necessary task becomes a chore: {Commuting is such a chore}.

To choreograph is to design and arrange movements for dance or other staged performances. A choreographer decides where dancers go, what steps they execute, and how movement flows with music. The word extends to orchestrating any complex sequence: {She choreographed the entire product launch}, {a carefully choreographed photo op}. The figurative use often implies calculated staging that might otherwise seem spontaneous.

Choreographed describes movement that has been planned and arranged in advance, originally for dance performances: {a beautifully choreographed ballet}. The term extends to any carefully coordinated sequence of actions: {a choreographed publicity campaign}, {The whole event felt choreographed}. The implication is deliberate staging rather than spontaneity—sometimes admiringly, sometimes suggesting artificiality.

A choreographer creates and arranges dance movements for performances. The role extends beyond dance to any staged movement—fight scenes in films, marching band formations, or synchronized sequences in theater. {The choreographer worked with the cast for weeks before opening night.} Figuratively, someone who orchestrates complex coordination: {She was the choreographer of the entire merger.}

Choreographers are people who create and arrange dance movements for performances. The term extends beyond dance to anyone who plans and coordinates complex sequences of movement or action: {the choreographers of the military operation}, {She served as one of the choreographers for the opening ceremony}. A choreographer may work in ballet, theater, film, music videos, or figure skating.

Choreographies is the plural of choreography—the art of designing dance movements, or the sequences themselves. A ballet company may perform several different choreographies over a season. The word extends to any carefully coordinated sequence: {the choreographies of political campaigns}, {the complex choreographies of a film's fight scenes}.

Choreographing is composing or arranging dance movements for a performance: {She spent months choreographing the ballet}. The word extends to any careful orchestration of complex elements: {choreographing a military operation}, {choreographing a product launch}. The implication is deliberate coordination of many moving parts into a unified sequence.

Choreographs means designs and arranges the movements of a dance or performance: {She choreographs for the city ballet}. The term extends to any careful orchestration of complex sequences: {He choreographs every detail of his product launches}. The word implies deliberate, artistic control over how elements move and interact.

Choreography is the art of designing and arranging dance movements, or the movements themselves as composed for a particular performance. A choreographer creates sequences of steps, gestures, and spatial patterns that dancers then execute. The term extends beyond dance to describe any carefully planned sequence of movements or actions: {The choreography of the heist required split-second timing.} Political events, ceremonies, and even sports plays may be described as having choreography when their coordination seems deliberate and rehearsed.

Chores are routine tasks, especially household duties like cleaning, laundry, and taking out the trash. The word often implies tedium—things that must be done but aren't enjoyed: {I spent Saturday morning doing chores}. Children are commonly assigned chores to teach responsibility. Any tedious obligation can be called a chore: {Filling out the form was a real chore}.

Chorizo is a highly seasoned pork sausage. Spanish chorizo is cured and firm, colored deep red by smoked paprika, often sliced and eaten cold or added to cooked dishes. Mexican chorizo is fresh and crumbly, typically removed from its casing and fried: {Scrambled eggs with chorizo}. The two types aren't interchangeable in recipes.

Chortle is a verb meaning to laugh in a breathy, gleeful way, typically with a snorting or chuckling quality. Lewis Carroll coined the word in *Through the Looking-Glass*, likely blending chuckle and snort. The term suggests amused satisfaction rather than uproarious laughter: {He chortled at his own cleverness}. As a noun, a chortle is an instance of such laughter.

Chortled is the past tense of chortle, a word Lewis Carroll invented by blending chuckle and snort. To chortle is to laugh in a breathy, gleeful way, often with satisfaction or triumph: {He chortled at his own cleverness}. The word has outlived its literary origins and appears in ordinary speech.

Chortling is laughing in a breathy, gleeful way—a chortle blends a chuckle with a snort. The word was coined by Lewis Carroll in *Through the Looking-Glass*, where the hero slays the Jabberwock and comes "chortling" back. It suggests smug or self-satisfied amusement: {He sat chortling over his rival's misfortune}.

A chorus is a group of people singing together, or the part of a song they sing—typically the repeated section between verses: {Everyone joined in on the chorus}. In theater, a chorus comments collectively on the action. Figuratively, a chorus is any unified response: {a chorus of criticism}, {a chorus of boos}. The verb means to say something in unison.

Choruses is the plural of chorus. A chorus is a group singing together, or the refrain of a song that repeats between verses: {The choruses were catchy enough to sing along}. In theater, a chorus comments on the action collectively. Multiple choruses may perform at a festival or competition. The word also appears as a verb—when people chorus something, they say it simultaneously: {The children chorused their thanks}.

Chosen is the past participle of choose, used as an adjective to describe something or someone that has been selected: {the chosen candidate}, {a chosen few}. It often implies special status or divine favor: {the chosen people}, {the chosen one}. As a noun, {the chosen} refers to a select group: {Only the chosen were admitted}.

Chotchke is a small decorative object of little value—a trinket, knickknack, or bauble. From Yiddish, the word often carries affectionate dismissiveness: {Her shelves were covered with chotchkes from yard sales}. The spelling varies widely: tchotchke, tsatske, and other forms all appear. In theater and film, a chotchke is a prop an actor handles during a scene.

Chotchkes are small decorative objects or trinkets, often of little value—the knickknacks that accumulate on shelves and mantels: {Her apartment was cluttered with chotchkes from every vacation}. From Yiddish, the word carries a slight dismissiveness, suggesting the items are more kitsch than art. Also spelled tchotchkes.

Chow is informal for food or a meal: {Let's grab some chow}, {The chow in the mess hall was terrible}. To chow down is to eat, often heartily or quickly. Separately, a chow or chow chow is a stocky dog breed with a thick coat and blue-black tongue, originally from China.

Chowder is a thick, chunky soup, typically made with seafood or vegetables in a milk or cream base. New England clam chowder is the classic version—creamy, with potatoes and salt pork. Manhattan clam chowder uses tomatoes instead of cream. Corn chowder skips the seafood entirely. {We ordered bowls of chowder at the waterfront restaurant.}

A chowderhead is a stupid person—someone whose head seems full of mush rather than brains. The word is mildly insulting but old-fashioned, more likely to appear in old movies or comic strips than contemporary speech: {Don't be such a chowderhead}.

Chowderheads is the plural of chowderhead, a mildly insulting term for a stupid or foolish person. The insult suggests someone whose head is as thick and lumpy as chowder: {Those chowderheads in accounting lost the invoice again}. The word has an old-fashioned, almost affectionate quality—more exasperated than vicious.

Chowders is the plural of chowder, a thick, hearty soup typically made with seafood or vegetables in a milk or cream base. New England clam chowder is the most famous variety, though Manhattan-style uses tomatoes instead of cream. {The restaurant offered three different chowders on their winter menu.}

A chowhound is someone with an enthusiastic, even obsessive interest in food—not just eating it, but seeking out the best, most authentic, or most interesting examples: {He's a real chowhound who knows every taco stand in the city}. The term suggests adventurous eating and strong opinions about where to find good food, distinguishing it from mere gluttony.

To christen is to baptize, especially an infant, and give them a Christian name. The word extends to any ceremonial naming: {The queen christened the ship by breaking a bottle of champagne against its bow}. More casually, to christen something is to use it for the first time: {Let's christen the new grill with some burgers}.

Christened is the past tense of christen, meaning to baptize or formally name. A child is christened in a religious ceremony that welcomes them into the faith: {She was christened Elizabeth after her grandmother}. More loosely, to christen something is to use it for the first time: {We christened the new grill with burgers and corn}.

A christening is a Christian ceremony in which a person, typically an infant, is baptized and given a name. The word extends to any formal naming or inaugural use: {the christening of a ship}, {We christened the new grill with burgers}. To christen something informally is simply to use it for the first time.

Christenings are ceremonies in which infants or converts are baptized and given a Christian name. The word extends to any formal naming or inaugural use: {the christening of a new ship}, {We haven't christened the new grill yet}. To christen something informally is simply to use it for the first time.

Christlike describes qualities or behavior resembling those attributed to Jesus Christ—compassion, humility, forgiveness, self-sacrifice. The word appears almost exclusively in Christian religious contexts: {She showed christlike patience with the difficult child}. Usually capitalized as Christlike.

Chrome is the shiny, mirror-like finish produced by electroplating metal with chromium: {chrome bumpers}, {chrome faucets}. The word often describes anything with that bright, reflective appearance. In computing, chrome refers to the visual interface elements surrounding content—toolbars, buttons, borders: {The browser has too much chrome}. As a verb, to chrome is to apply such a finish.

A chromosome is a thread-like structure in cells that carries genetic information. Chromosomes contain DNA organized into genes, which determine inherited traits. Humans typically have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs, with the final pair determining biological sex—XX in females, XY in males. {The condition results from an extra chromosome.}

Chromosomes is the plural of chromosome, a thread-like structure in cells that carries genetic information. Each chromosome contains DNA organized into genes. Humans typically have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs. {The test revealed an extra chromosome.} Chromosome abnormalities can cause genetic disorders like Down syndrome.

Chronic describes conditions that persist over long periods, especially medical ones: {chronic pain}, {chronic fatigue}, {chronic inflammation}. The word contrasts with acute, which describes sudden, severe, short-term conditions. Extended to habits or problems, chronic suggests ongoing and seemingly intractable: {chronic unemployment}, {a chronic liar}. In British slang, chronic means very bad: {The service was chronic}.

Chronically means in a persistent, long-lasting way. Medical conditions are chronic when they continue indefinitely rather than resolving quickly: {chronically ill}, {chronic pain}. The word extends to any ongoing problem: {chronically underfunded schools}, {chronically late}. In casual speech, chronically emphasizes frequency or severity: {I'm chronically online}, {chronically exhausted}.

A chronicle is a record of events in the order they happened, typically covering a significant span of time. Medieval chronicles documented the histories of kingdoms and monasteries. The word now applies broadly to any sequential account: {a chronicle of the civil rights movement}, {a family chronicle spanning four generations}. To chronicle is to record events this way: {She chronicled her travels in a series of essays}.

A chronicler is someone who records events in order, typically as a historical narrative. The term suggests a methodical, often firsthand account of happenings over time, as opposed to analysis or interpretation. Medieval chroniclers documented the deeds of kings and the progress of wars. In modern use, chronicler often describes journalists, historians, or writers who thoroughly document a particular subject or era: {She became the chronicler of small-town American life}.

Chroniclers are people who record events, especially historical ones. The term suggests methodical documentation over time rather than interpretation or analysis. Medieval chroniclers recorded the deeds of kings; modern chroniclers might document a neighborhood's transformation or a movement's rise. {The band's unofficial chroniclers have preserved every setlist since 1987.}

Chronicles are records of events arranged in order of time, typically covering historical or significant happenings: {the chronicles of medieval England}. The word suggests ongoing documentation rather than a single account. To chronicle something is to record it systematically: {She chronicled her travels in a series of letters}. Chronicles often appears in titles of newspapers and historical works.

Chronicling is the act of recording events in order, typically as they unfold over time. A journalist might be chronicling a political campaign; a biographer might be chronicling someone's life. The word suggests thorough, ongoing documentation rather than a single snapshot: {She spent years chronicling the rise and fall of the empire}.

Chronological means arranged in order of time, from earliest to latest: {a chronological account of the war}, {listed in chronological order}. Events presented chronologically unfold as they actually occurred. Chronological age is how old someone is in years, as opposed to mental or developmental age.

Chronology is the arrangement of events in the order they occurred. A chronology of the war lists battles and treaties by date. The word also refers to the study of establishing such sequences, particularly in history and geology. {The detective worked out the chronology of the crime}. Something is chronological when ordered by time: {List your jobs in chronological order}.
clues: Events listed by when they happened

definition: A chronometer is a precision timepiece designed for exceptional accuracy, especially one used for navigation at sea. Determining longitude required knowing the exact time at a reference point, so marine chronometers were built to withstand motion and temperature changes. The term now applies to any highly accurate clock or watch: {The observatory's chronometer lost only two seconds per year}.

A chrysalis is the hard protective case enclosing a butterfly or moth during its pupal stage—the phase between caterpillar and winged adult. Inside, the insect undergoes complete transformation. Figuratively, chrysalis describes any transitional state of development or protection before emergence: {The startup remained in chrysalis while they refined the product}.

A chrysanthemum is a flowering plant with dense, layered petals radiating from a central disk, cultivated in countless varieties and colors. Native to East Asia, chrysanthemums hold cultural significance in China and Japan, where they symbolize autumn and longevity. Often shortened to *mum* in casual speech: {I picked up some mums for the porch}.

Chrysanthemums is the plural of chrysanthemum, a flowering plant with dense, layered blooms in colors ranging from white to deep burgundy. Often shortened to mums, they're associated with autumn gardens and are traditional funeral flowers in many European cultures. {She arranged chrysanthemums in a vase on the table.}

Chubby describes someone who is plump or slightly overweight, typically in a way that suggests softness and roundness rather than obesity. The word often carries affectionate or diminutive connotations, especially when applied to babies and young children: {Look at those chubby cheeks!} When used of adults, chubby is gentler than fat but can still cause offense depending on context. Chubby {bunny} is a game where players stuff marshmallows in their mouths.

Unrelated nouns and verbs share the spelling c-h-u-c-k. To chuck something is to toss it lightly or throw it away: Chuck the wrapper in the garbage. If you chuck someone on the cheek, you tap them gently. When chickens chuck, they make their characteristic clucking sound. A chuck is a fixed machine part around which something else moves. A cut of beef that includes the neck and shoulders is also called chuck. When capitalized, Chuck is a common nickname for men whose given name is Charles.

Chucked is the past tense of chuck, a casual verb for throwing something, usually with a light or careless motion: {He chucked the ball to his friend}. It also means to discard or get rid of: {She chucked all her old magazines}. In British English, if you've chucked someone, you've ended a romantic relationship with them. To be chucked out is to be expelled or ejected from a place.

Chucking is the act of throwing something casually or carelessly: {He was chucking stones into the pond}. In British slang, chucking someone means ending a romantic relationship: {She's chucking him}. The word can also mean discarding: {I'm chucking all these old magazines}.

A chuckle is a quiet, suppressed laugh—softer than a full laugh, often expressing mild amusement or private satisfaction: {He chuckled at the memory}. To chuckle is to laugh this way. The word suggests warmth and gentleness rather than ridicule.

Chuckled is the past tense of chuckle—a quiet, suppressed laugh expressing mild amusement or satisfaction. A chuckle is softer than a laugh, often private or half-concealed: {She chuckled at his joke}. It suggests genuine but restrained pleasure, the kind of laugh that doesn't demand attention.

A chucklehead is a fool or blockhead—someone whose judgment or intelligence you're mocking, usually with more amusement than malice. The word sounds old-fashioned and playful: {Don't be such a chucklehead}. It belongs to a family of "-head" insults (bonehead, knucklehead) that question someone's mental capacity without real venom.

Chuckleheads is a playful insult for stupid or foolish people. The word is old-fashioned and mild, more affectionate than cutting—something you'd call friends who made a dumb mistake: {Those chuckleheads locked themselves out again}. It carries the same gentle mockery as blockheads or boneheads.

Chuckles are quiet, suppressed laughs—softer and more contained than full laughter. The word suggests amusement rather than hilarity: {The joke got a few chuckles from the audience}. As a verb, to chuckle is to laugh this way: {He chuckled to himself while reading}. The tone is often private or knowing, as if enjoying something without wanting to make a scene.

Chuckling is laughing quietly, usually with the mouth closed—a sound of mild amusement rather than hilarity. A chuckle suggests private enjoyment or gentle humor: {He sat chuckling at his phone}. Someone might chuckle at an inside joke, a clever turn of phrase, or their own thoughts.

Chucks is informal for Chuck Taylor All-Stars, the iconic canvas sneakers with rubber toe caps: {She wore her favorite pair of chucks to the concert}. The term comes from the shoes' association with basketball player Chuck Taylor, whose name appears on the ankle patch. Chucks also serves as the plural of chuck in its various senses—a cut of beef, a mechanical grip, or a casual toss.

A chuckwagon is a horse-drawn wagon equipped as a mobile kitchen, used to feed cowboys and ranch hands on cattle drives and roundups. The rear of the wagon featured a hinged lid that dropped down to form a work surface, with compartments holding cooking supplies and provisions. The term now often refers to cookouts or outdoor dining with a Western theme: {chuckwagon supper}, {chuckwagon barbecue}.

Chuckwagons are wagons equipped with cooking facilities, originally used to feed cowboys during cattle drives across the American West. The chuck wagon carried food supplies, utensils, and a fold-down counter for meal preparation on the trail. The term now also applies to food trucks or outdoor cooking setups at rodeos and western-themed events: {The chuckwagon served biscuits and beans to hungry ranch hands}.

Chuffed is British slang for pleased or delighted: {I was dead chuffed when they offered me the job}. The word carries a warm, informal tone—you're chuffed about good news, a compliment, or an unexpected success. Confusingly, chuffed has also meant displeased in some dialects, though the positive sense now dominates.

Chug is the repetitive sound of an engine laboring steadily: {The old truck chugged up the hill}. By extension, to chug along is to move or progress steadily if not quickly: {The project chugs along}. Separately, to chug a drink is to swallow it continuously without pausing for breath: {He chugged the entire beer in seconds}.

Chugged is the past tense of chug. A train chugs when its engine makes rhythmic puffing sounds: {The locomotive chugged up the mountain}. To chug a drink is to consume it in continuous gulps without pausing: {He chugged his beer and ordered another}. Things that move steadily but slowly chug along: {The project chugged along despite setbacks}.

Chugging describes the sound or motion of something moving in steady, rhythmic pulses—like a train engine or an idling motor: {The old locomotive came chugging up the hill}. To chug a drink is to swallow it continuously without pause, often as a social challenge: {He chugged the entire beer in seconds}. Something that chugs along proceeds steadily if not impressively: {The project keeps chugging along}.

Chugs is the third-person singular of chug. A train chugs along, making rhythmic puffing sounds. An engine chugs when it labors. To chug a drink is to gulp it down steadily without pausing: {He chugs his beer like he's in a frat movie}. Things that chug move with effort but persistence: {The project chugs along despite setbacks}.

Chum has two distinct origins in English. One chum is a close friend or companion, probably from chamber-fellow (a roommate): {We've been chums since college}. The verb means to be friendly or hang out: {chumming around with the neighbors}. The adjective chummy describes warm friendliness, sometimes with a hint of excessive familiarity. The other chum is chopped fish and other matter thrown into water to attract fish. To chum is to scatter such bait: {chumming for sharks}.

Chumming is scattering fish parts, blood, or oily bait into the water to attract fish to a boat or fishing area. The technique draws fish by appealing to their sense of smell: {We spent an hour chumming before the first shark appeared}. Figuratively, chumming describes any attempt to lure a target by spreading attractive bait: {The company was chumming for investors with promises of quick returns}.

Chummy means friendly in a familiar, easygoing way: {They got chummy over drinks}. The word often carries a hint of suspicion—that the friendliness is calculated or inappropriate: {The mayor seemed awfully chummy with the developers}. To be chummy with someone suggests closeness that others might find questionable or exclusive.

A chump is a foolish or gullible person, easily deceived or taken advantage of: {Don't be a chump—read the contract before you sign}. The word suggests someone lacking street smarts rather than intelligence. A chump is also a thick cut of meat, especially from the loin: {chump chop}.

Chumps is the plural of chump—a fool or someone easily deceived. The word carries mild contempt: {Those chumps fell for the oldest trick in the book}. A chump is gullible, not necessarily stupid, but naive enough to be taken advantage of. {Don't be a chump—read the contract before you sign}.

Chums is the plural of chum—close friends or companions, especially in British usage: {We've been chums since boarding school}. The word has an old-fashioned, slightly precious quality. In American fishing, chum is bait made of chopped fish scattered to attract game fish, and chums is its verb form: {He chums the water before casting}.

A chunk is a thick, solid piece of something, usually broken or cut off from a larger mass: {a chunk of bread}, {a chunk of ice}. By extension, chunk refers to any substantial portion: {A good chunk of my paycheck goes to rent}. In computing, a chunk is a segment of data processed as a unit. To chunk is to divide into chunks, or in British slang, to throw: {He chunked the ball across the yard}.

Chunking is breaking something into smaller, manageable pieces. In psychology and education, it refers to grouping information to aid memory—remembering a phone number as three chunks rather than ten digits. In linguistics, it means parsing language into meaningful units. The verb chunk means to divide this way: {I chunked the project into weekly tasks}.

Chunks are thick, solid pieces, usually irregularly shaped: {chunks of ice}, {pineapple chunks}, {a chunk of cheese}. The word suggests substance and heft. A chunk of time or money is a considerable amount: {That project took a big chunk of my day}. In computing, chunks are segments of data processed together. To chunk is to divide into pieces or, informally, to throw: {He chunked the ball across the yard}.

Chunky describes something thick and substantial, often with visible pieces or lumps: {chunky peanut butter}, {chunky salsa}. Applied to people, chunky is a softer way of saying stocky or slightly overweight: {He was a chunky kid}. Chunky knit sweaters have thick, prominent stitches. The word suggests solid bulk rather than smooth uniformity.

A chupacabra is a creature from Latin American folklore said to attack livestock—especially goats—and drain their blood. The name translates from Spanish as "goat-sucker." Reports emerged from Puerto Rico in the 1990s and spread throughout the Americas. The chupacabra occupies the same cultural space as Bigfoot or the Loch Ness Monster: a cryptid that believers insist is real despite lack of scientific evidence. {They blamed the dead chickens on a chupacabra.}

Chupacabras is a creature from Latin American folklore, supposedly responsible for killing livestock by draining their blood. The name is Spanish for "goat-sucker." Sightings began in Puerto Rico in the 1990s and spread throughout the Americas.
