Clawing is scratching or tearing with claws or fingernails, or moving by digging in with them: {The cat was clawing at the furniture}. Figuratively, to be clawing at something is to struggle desperately for it: {clawing for a foothold in the market}. To be {clawing your way} somewhere is to advance through difficult effort.

A clawmark is a scratch or gouge left by an animal's claws—on tree bark, furniture, skin, or any surface that yields to sharp nails. The word usually appears in the plural: {The door was covered in clawmarks from the dog}. Clawmarks serve as evidence of animal presence or struggle, whether from a house cat or something more dangerous.

Claws are the sharp, curved nails found on the feet of birds, reptiles, and many mammals, used for gripping, climbing, scratching, and capturing prey. The term extends to similar grasping appendages on crustaceans like crabs and lobsters. To claw is to scratch or tear at something: {The cat clawed the furniture}. If you claw your way somewhere, you advance through determined struggle: {She clawed her way to the top of the industry}.

Clay is fine-grained earth that becomes pliable when wet and hardens when heated—the basis of pottery, bricks, and ceramics. Clay soil drains poorly and sticks to garden tools. Figuratively, clay suggests raw material to be shaped: {young minds of clay}. {Feet of clay} describes a hidden weakness in someone admired. The {clay courts} of tennis are made from crusite brick. (Capitalized Clay is a surname or given name.)

Claymation is stop-motion animation using clay or plasticized figures. Each frame captures the figures in slightly different positions; when played in sequence, they appear to move. The technique requires painstaking manipulation between shots. *Wallace and Gromit* and early *Gumby* episodes are classic examples. The term blends "clay" and "animation."

Claymations are animated films or sequences made using clay figures that are repositioned and photographed frame by frame to create the illusion of movement. The technique, also called stop-motion clay animation, produces a distinctive handcrafted look: {Wallace and Gromit are classic claymations}. The singular claymation can refer to the technique itself or a single such production.
clues: Films made frame by sculpted frame

definition: A claymore is a large two-handed sword historically used by Scottish Highlanders, characterized by its long blade and cross-shaped hilt. The word now more commonly refers to a type of directional antipersonnel mine used by military forces: {The patrol set up claymores along the perimeter}. The mine's casing famously reads "FRONT TOWARD ENEMY."

Claymores names two different weapons. The Scottish claymore was a large two-handed broadsword used in the Highlands from the 15th to 18th centuries—the word comes from Gaelic for "great sword." The modern claymore is a directional antipersonnel mine that sprays steel balls in a lethal arc when detonated: {The patrol set up claymores along the perimeter}. The mine's casing bears the infamous instruction "FRONT TOWARD ENEMY."

Clean things are free of soil, dirt, filth, or contamination. Figuratively, freedom from anything illegal, immoral, or unethical is also clean. When you clean something, you remove impurities and pollutants from it. This activity can be called a clean in British English. A derivative adverb clean means completely: The ball went clean through the window. If you clean your plate, you eat all of the food on it.

A cleaner is a person who cleans, especially one employed to clean buildings: {The office cleaner comes in after hours}. Cleaner also means a substance or device used for cleaning: {window cleaner}, {pipe cleaner}, {vacuum cleaner}. A cleaner or cleaners is a dry cleaning establishment: {I need to pick up my suit from the cleaner's}. To {take someone to the cleaners} is to swindle them thoroughly or defeat them decisively.

Cleaners is the plural of cleaner—a person or substance that cleans. A cleaner might be a janitor, a housekeeping professional, or a product like a bathroom cleaner. The plural often refers to a dry-cleaning establishment: {I need to pick up my suit from the cleaners}. To {take someone to the cleaners} is to swindle them thoroughly or defeat them decisively.

Cleaning is the act of removing dirt, mess, or unwanted material from something. A cleaning can be a particular instance: {The house needs a good cleaning}. Professional cleanings happen at the dentist. To {take someone to the cleaners} is to cheat them out of money or defeat them thoroughly. A {cleaning lady} or {cleaning woman} is hired to clean homes or offices.

Cleanliness is the state of being clean—free from dirt, contamination, or impurities. The word applies to physical hygiene {personal cleanliness}, tidy environments {the cleanliness of the kitchen}, and sanitary conditions {hospital cleanliness standards}. The proverb "cleanliness is next to godliness" elevates the concept to a moral virtue. Cleanliness can also describe precision or lack of messiness: {the cleanliness of his technique}.

Cleanrooms are controlled environments where airborne particles, dust, and contaminants are kept to extremely low levels through specialized filtration and strict protocols. Used in semiconductor manufacturing, pharmaceutical production, and aerospace assembly, cleanrooms require workers to wear protective garments: {The chip fabrication takes place in a Class 100 cleanroom}. The classification number indicates maximum particles per cubic foot.

Cleanse means to clean thoroughly, often with connotations of purification or ritual. You cleanse a wound before bandaging it. A detox program claims to cleanse the body of toxins. Religious traditions speak of cleansing the soul. {She cleansed her face before bed.} The word carries more formality and thoroughness than simple cleaning—scrubbing dishes is cleaning; purging impurities is cleansing.

Cleansed is the past tense of cleanse, meaning to make thoroughly clean or pure. Where cleaned suggests removing dirt, cleansed often implies deeper purification—spiritual, moral, or ritualistic: {She felt cleansed after confession}, {The wound was cleansed with antiseptic}. Ethnic cleansing is the forced removal or killing of a population.

A cleanser is a substance used for cleaning, particularly skin or surfaces. The word emphasizes gentle or specialized formulas: {facial cleanser}, {cream cleanser}. While cleaner suggests industrial or household products, cleanser tends toward personal care and cosmetics. {She uses a gentle cleanser morning and night.}

Cleanses is the third-person singular of cleanse, meaning to make thoroughly clean or pure. The word implies more than ordinary washing—a deeper or more complete purification: {This tonic cleanses the skin of impurities}, {The ritual cleanses the spirit}. Cleanse often appears in contexts involving toxins, sins, or spiritual renewal.

Cleanshaven describes a man whose face is free of beard or stubble—smooth from recent shaving. The word often distinguishes someone from bearded alternatives: {The suspect was described as cleanshaven, about six feet tall}. Also spelled clean-shaven.

Cleansing is the act of making something clean or pure. The word carries more weight than simple cleaning—it suggests thoroughness or ritual significance. A cleansing {diet} purges toxins from the body. {Ethnic cleansing} is the forced removal or extermination of a population. Cleansing {cream} removes makeup; a cleansing {breath} restores calm.

Cleantech refers to technologies, products, and services designed to reduce environmental impact—renewable energy, electric vehicles, water purification, waste reduction. The term emerged in the early 2000s as both an industry category and investment sector: {Venture capital is pouring into cleantech startups}. Sometimes spelled as two words or hyphenated.

Cleanup is the act of making a place clean or orderly: {The cleanup after the party took hours}. It extends to any effort to remove unwanted elements—a cleanup of government corruption, a cleanup of contaminated soil. In baseball, the cleanup hitter bats fourth, positioned to drive in runners and "clean up" the bases. As an adjective: {cleanup crew}, {cleanup hitter}.

All senses of clear are easily relatable to the core adjectival sense of transparent or free from darkness. Applied in the abstract, it means easily understood: clear thinking. With tangible items, it characterizes a quality that is perceptible by sight or hearing: clear sky, clear signal. As a verb, clear can be a synonym for empty (clear the table), for open (clear a path), or for authorize (clear the items for export). As an adverb, clear is sometimes used interchangeably with clearly and sometimes shares a meaning with entirely: You drove clear to Kansas City in one day?

Clearance is permission or authorization to proceed—security clearance grants access to classified information, clearance to land allows a plane to touch down. The word also means the space between objects: {The bridge has twelve feet of clearance}. In retail, clearance refers to selling off inventory at reduced prices: {clearance sale}, {on clearance}. To clear customs or obtain official approval is to get clearance.

Clearances is the plural of clearance, covering its various senses. A clearance is permission or authorization, especially official approval to access classified information: {He finally got his security clearances}. It also means the space between objects—the gap allowing passage: {Check the clearances under the bridge}. A clearance sale offers goods at reduced prices to move inventory: {The store advertised holiday clearances}.

Clearcut describes something sharply defined with no ambiguity or blurred edges. A clearcut {distinction} or clearcut {case} leaves no room for doubt or interpretation. The word also refers to a logging practice where every tree in an area is felled, leaving bare ground rather than selectively harvested forest. Both uses share the sense of complete removal of anything that might obscure or complicate—whether conceptual fuzziness or standing timber. {The evidence made it a clearcut victory for the prosecution.}

Clearcuts are areas of forest where all or nearly all trees have been felled at once, leaving bare or stubbled land. The term carries environmental weight—clearcuts represent the most aggressive form of timber harvesting, criticized for destroying habitat and causing erosion: {The hillside was a patchwork of clearcuts and regrowth}. As a verb, to clearcut is to harvest timber this way.

Clearcutting is a logging practice where all trees in an area are harvested at once, leaving the land bare. The method is efficient for timber production but controversial for its environmental impact—destroying habitat, causing erosion, and leaving stark landscapes: {The hillside was scarred by clearcutting}. Also spelled clear-cutting.

Cleared is the past tense of clear, carrying its meanings of removal, passage, and approval. A table is cleared of dishes; a path is cleared of obstacles. When someone is cleared of charges, suspicion has been removed: {She was cleared of all wrongdoing}. Cleared also means authorized or given permission: {The plane was cleared for takeoff}. A check clears when funds transfer successfully.

Cleareyed describes someone who sees things accurately, without illusion or sentimentality: {a cleareyed assessment of the risks}, {She remained cleareyed about her chances}. The literal sense—having bright, unclouded eyes—is less common than the figurative meaning of perceptive and realistic. Also spelled clear-eyed.

Clearheaded means thinking clearly, not confused or impaired. A clearheaded person can assess situations rationally and make sound decisions: {Despite the chaos, she remained clearheaded}. The term often implies freedom from influences that cloud judgment—alcohol, emotion, fatigue: {I need to be clearheaded for tomorrow's meeting}.

A clearing is an open space in a forest or wooded area where trees have been removed or never grew: {We found a small clearing and set up camp}. The word also refers to the process of making something clear or empty, and in banking, to the settlement of checks and other financial instruments between institutions.

Clearings is the plural of clearing—an open space in a forest or woods where trees have been removed or never grew. Clearings appear naturally or through deliberate cutting, creating gaps in otherwise dense woodland: {We found a small clearing and set up camp}. In banking, clearings refers to the process of settling transactions between financial institutions.

Clearly means in a way that is easy to perceive or understand: {She spoke clearly so everyone could hear}. It also signals obviousness or certainty: {Clearly, we need a new approach}. When someone says {clearly} at the start of a sentence, they're asserting that what follows should be apparent to any reasonable person—though this sometimes masks less certainty than the speaker admits.

A clearout is the act of removing unwanted items from a space, typically a room, closet, or building: {We're having a clearout of the garage this weekend}. The term is more common in British than American English. A clearout can also refer to a removal of people—staff dismissed or tenants evicted: {The new management conducted a clearout of the old guard}.

A cleat is a piece of hardware with projecting arms or ends, used to secure ropes by winding them in a figure-eight pattern: {She tied off the halyard on the cleat}. On shoes, cleats are studs or spikes on the sole that grip turf or soft ground—and by extension, the shoes themselves: {Don't forget your cleats for practice}. A cleat can also be a strip of wood or metal fastened to a surface to provide support or prevent slipping.

Cleats are projections that provide grip or secure attachment. On shoes, cleats are studs on the sole that dig into turf or soft ground—athletes wear cleats for football, soccer, and baseball. On boats, a cleat is a T-shaped fitting for fastening ropes. The common thread is something that grips or holds fast: {I need to buy new cleats for the season}.

Cleavage is a division or split along natural lines. In geology, minerals cleave along planes determined by their crystal structure. In biology, cells divide through cleavage. The word also refers to the visible division between a woman's breasts, especially as revealed by low-cut clothing: {That dress shows a lot of cleavage}. More abstractly, cleavage describes any sharp division: {the cleavage between political factions}.

Cleave is two opposite verbs spelled the same way. One means to split or divide forcefully: {The axe cleaved the log in two}. The other means to cling or adhere faithfully: {She cleaved to her principles}. Context usually clarifies which is meant—splitting involves objects and tools, clinging involves loyalty or attachment.

Cleaved is the past tense of cleave, a verb with two opposite meanings. To cleave something is to split it apart: {The axe cleaved the log in two}. But to cleave to something is to cling or hold fast: {She cleaved to her principles}. Context usually makes the sense clear. The past tense clove and past participle cloven survive in phrases like {cloven hoof}.

A cleaver is a large, heavy knife with a broad rectangular blade, used for chopping through meat and bone: {The butcher brought the cleaver down on the joint}. The weight of the blade does most of the work, making it effective for cutting through tough material that would dull a thinner knife. (Capitalized Cleaver is a surname.)

Cleaves is a verb with two opposite meanings from different roots. One cleave means to split or divide forcefully: {The axe cleaves the wood}, {Lightning cleaved the sky}. The other cleave means to cling or adhere faithfully: {She cleaves to her principles}, {a man shall cleave unto his wife}. Context usually makes the intended sense clear—splitting involves objects, clinging involves loyalties or relationships.

Cleaving names two opposite actions that share a shape. To cleave is to split or divide forcefully: {The axe cleaved the log in two}. But cleave also means to cling or adhere: {She cleaved to her faith through hardship}. The splitting sense dominates modern usage; the clinging sense survives mainly in religious and literary contexts.

A clef is a symbol placed at the beginning of a musical staff to indicate which pitches the lines and spaces represent. The treble clef (G clef) and bass clef (F clef) are most common; together they form the grand staff used for piano music. Other clefs exist for specific instruments and vocal ranges. {She learned to read both clefs}.

Clefs are the symbols placed at the beginning of a musical staff to indicate the pitch of written notes. The treble clef (G clef) and bass clef (F clef) are most common; the alto and tenor clefs (C clefs) appear in orchestral music. Each clef assigns a specific pitch to one line of the staff, from which all other notes are read.

A cleft is a split or fissure—a narrow opening in rock, wood, or flesh. A cleft in a cliff face offers a handhold; a cleft palate is a birth defect where the roof of the mouth hasn't fully closed. Cleft also serves as the past tense of cleave: {The axe cleft the log in two}. To be {caught in a cleft stick} is to face a dilemma with no good options.

Clemency is mercy or leniency, especially from someone in authority who could impose harsher treatment. A governor grants clemency to a death row inmate by commuting the sentence. A judge shows clemency by giving probation instead of prison. The word implies the power to punish fully but choosing restraint: {The defendant's family pleaded for clemency}.

A clementine is a small citrus fruit, a variety of mandarin orange with smooth, glossy skin that peels easily and sweet, seedless flesh. Clementines are popular as snacks and in children's lunchboxes: {She packed a clementine and some crackers}. (Capitalized Clementine is a given name.)

Clementines are small citrus fruits, a variety of mandarin orange with smooth, glossy skin that peels easily and segments that separate cleanly. They're seedless or nearly so, sweeter and less acidic than regular oranges: {The kids went through a whole box of clementines in two days}. Often sold in small wooden crates during winter months.

Clench means to close or grip tightly. You clench your fist by curling fingers firmly into the palm. You clench your teeth or jaw by pressing them together hard—often from anger, determination, or pain: {She clenched her jaw and said nothing}. The word suggests tension and force held in check. Something clenched stays closed through muscular effort: {His hands were clenched at his sides}.

Clenched describes something tightly closed or gripped, especially hands or teeth. A clenched {fist} is closed hard, often in anger or determination. Clenched {teeth} or a clenched {jaw} suggests tension, pain, or suppressed emotion: {She spoke through clenched teeth}. The word implies muscular effort and emotional intensity.

Clergy are the ordained officials of a religion—priests, ministers, rabbis, imams, and the like. The term is collective, referring to religious leaders as a class rather than to individuals: {The clergy opposed the new legislation}. A single person is a member of the clergy or, more naturally, a clergyman or clergywoman. The clergy stands in contrast to the laity, the ordinary members of a religious community.

A clergyman is an ordained religious leader—a priest, minister, rabbi, or imam. The term applies across faiths but sounds somewhat dated; clergy or member of the clergy now serves where clergyman once did. {The clergyman performed the wedding ceremony.}

A cleric is a member of the clergy—a priest, minister, rabbi, imam, or other religious leader. The term is neutral and spans traditions: {Several clerics spoke at the interfaith service}. In fantasy gaming, a cleric is a character class combining religious devotion with healing magic and combat ability.

Clerical has two distinct senses. One relates to clergy—priests, ministers, and other religious officials: {clerical robes}, {clerical collar}. The other relates to office work, especially routine administrative tasks like filing, typing, and record-keeping: {clerical duties}, {clerical error}. A clerical error is a minor mistake in paperwork, not a moral failing.

Clerics are members of the clergy—priests, ministers, rabbis, imams, or other religious officials. The term covers religious leaders across faiths: {Several clerics spoke at the interfaith gathering}. In fantasy games and fiction, a cleric is a character class that wields divine magic and often serves as a healer: {Our party needs a cleric}.

A clerk is someone who handles records, accounts, or administrative tasks—a bank clerk, a file clerk, a clerk of the court. In American usage, clerk also means a retail salesperson: {The clerk rang up my purchase}. Law clerks assist judges with legal research. To clerk is to work in such a position: {She clerked for a federal judge after law school}.

Clerks is the plural of clerk—a person who performs routine office or administrative tasks, handles records, or assists customers. A store clerk works the counter; a file clerk manages documents; a law clerk assists a judge. In religious contexts, clergy were once called clerks, which survives in expressions like {clerks in holy orders}. The verb means to work as a clerk: {She clerked for a federal judge}.

Clever describes quick mental ability—the capacity to learn fast, solve problems, or devise resourceful solutions. A clever {student} grasps concepts readily. A clever {plan} shows ingenuity. The word sometimes carries a faint suggestion of superficiality or cunning rather than deep wisdom: {too clever by half} implies someone outsmarting themselves. Clever can also describe things that are neatly designed or skillfully made: {a clever gadget}, {a clever bit of engineering}.

Cleverness is the quality of being quick-witted, resourceful, or mentally agile. It suggests finding smart solutions or showing ingenuity: {Her cleverness got us out of a tight spot}. Unlike wisdom, cleverness implies speed and sharpness rather than depth—and can carry a faint whiff of being too smart for one's own good: {His cleverness will catch up with him someday}.

A cliche is an expression or idea so overused it has lost its force or originality: {avoid cliches like the plague}, {at the end of the day}, {it is what it is}. The word extends to any tired or predictable element—a cliched plot twist, a cliched character type. What begins as vivid or insightful becomes cliche through repetition.

Cliched describes something that has become stale through overuse—a phrase, idea, or artistic choice that was once fresh but now feels tired and unoriginal. A cliched {love story} follows predictable beats. Cliched {dialogue} relies on expressions everyone has heard too many times. Also spelled clichéd, preserving the French accent.

Cliches are expressions so overused they've lost their force: {avoid clichés like the plague}, {at the end of the day}, {it is what it is}. The term extends to any tired idea or predictable element: {The movie was full of action-movie clichés}. What begins as vivid language becomes cliché through repetition. Also spelled without the accent: cliches.

A click is a short, distinct sound, like the click of a mouse button, and most meanings derive from this. If you click something, you generate this sound, and often also accomplish something else: Click on the link. Click languages, found in Africa, include a clicking sound that is made with the tongue. Click can also convey compatibility. If two people click, they like each other immediately and get along well. If an idea clicks with people, they like it and adopt it.

Clickbait is online content designed to lure clicks through sensational or misleading headlines: {You Won't Believe What Happened Next}. The term is almost always disparaging—clickbait promises more than it delivers, exploiting curiosity to generate ad revenue. As an adjective: {clickbait headlines}, {clickbait thumbnails}.

Clicked is the past tense of click—a short, sharp sound like a latch closing or fingers snapping. A door clicked shut, a camera clicked. In computing, clicking means pressing a mouse button or tapping a touchscreen: {I clicked the link but nothing happened}. Figuratively, when something clicks, it suddenly makes sense or works smoothly: {After weeks of practice, it finally clicked}. When people click, they connect instantly: {We clicked from the moment we met}.

A clicker is anything that clicks—a device that makes a clicking sound when pressed. The term covers TV remote controls, handheld counters used to track attendance or repetitions, and small noisemakers used to train animals: {Use the clicker when the dog performs the behavior correctly}. In gaming, a clicker may be a game requiring rapid, repetitive clicking, or a type of enemy that navigates by echolocation.

Clickers are small handheld devices that produce a clicking sound, used for various purposes. Dog trainers use clickers to mark desired behaviors during conditioning. In classrooms, clickers are response devices students use to answer questions electronically. The term also applies to TV remote controls and the tally counters used to track attendance or inventory: {The bouncer kept count with a clicker}.

Clicking is the act of making or producing a click—a short, sharp sound like a latch closing or a tongue against the roof of the mouth. With computers, clicking means pressing a mouse button or tapping a touchscreen: {Keep clicking until something happens}. When things are clicking, they're working smoothly or falling into place: {Everything just clicked for us that season}.

Clicks is the plural of click—a short, sharp sound, or the act of making one. A click of the tongue, a click of heels, the click of a mouse button. In digital contexts, clicks measure engagement: {The ad generated thousands of clicks}. To {get clicks} is to attract online attention, sometimes through sensationalism: {Headlines designed to get clicks rather than inform}.

Clicktivism is political or social activism conducted through low-effort online actions—signing petitions, sharing posts, changing profile pictures. The term is usually dismissive, implying that clicking replaces meaningful engagement: {Clicktivism makes people feel good without accomplishing anything}. Defenders argue such actions raise awareness and can spark broader movements.

A client is a person or organization that pays for professional services—from a lawyer, accountant, consultant, or similar provider. The word implies an ongoing relationship rather than a single transaction: {She's been my client for years}. In computing, a client is a program or device that requests services from a server. Social services use client for those receiving assistance, softening older terms like patient or case.

Clientele is the body of customers or clients that patronizes a business or professional: {The restaurant attracts an upscale clientele}, {a lawyer's clientele}. The word carries a slightly more refined tone than "customers," suggesting an established, ongoing relationship between provider and patrons.

Clients is the plural of client—people or organizations that hire professionals for services. Lawyers, consultants, therapists, and designers have clients rather than customers, the distinction suggesting an ongoing relationship requiring expertise: {The firm represents several corporate clients}. In computing, a client is software or a device that requests services from a server.

A cliff is a steep rock face, especially one at the edge of the sea or forming one side of a mountain. The word evokes height and danger—falling from a cliff is usually fatal. A cliffhanger is a story that leaves you in suspense, as if dangling from a cliff's edge. {The path wound along the cliff above the ocean.} (Capitalized Cliff is a given name.)

A cliffhanger is a story or situation that leaves you in suspense at a critical moment. The term comes from serialized fiction where episodes would end with a character literally hanging from a cliff—tune in next week. Now it applies to any dramatic pause before resolution: {The season finale was a cliffhanger}, {The election remained a cliffhanger into the night}.

Cliffhangers are stories or episodes that end at a moment of suspense, leaving the outcome unresolved. The term comes from serialized fiction where a character might literally be left hanging from a cliff until the next installment. Now it applies to any dramatic situation with an uncertain outcome: {The election was a cliffhanger}, {The season finale ended on a cliffhanger}.

Cliffs is the plural of cliff—a steep rock face, especially one rising from water or at the edge of a plateau. The word often appears in place names: {the White Cliffs of Dover}, {the cliffs of Big Sur}. Figuratively, a cliff suggests a sharp drop or sudden change: {fiscal cliff}, {cliff-hanger}.

The side or face of a cliff, or the area immediately adjacent to it. Cliffside typically describes locations perched at the edge of a steep drop: {cliffside homes with ocean views}, {a cliffside trail along the gorge}. The word emphasizes proximity to the precipice and often implies dramatic scenery or precarious positioning.

The top of a cliff—the relatively level ground at the edge before it drops away. Used as both noun and adjective: {a clifftop path}, {houses perched on the clifftop}. The word evokes dramatic coastal or mountain scenery, often with implied danger or sweeping views.

Climate is the long-term weather patterns of a region—its typical temperatures, rainfall, humidity, and seasons over years or decades. {The Mediterranean climate features mild, wet winters and hot, dry summers.} Climate also describes prevailing conditions or atmosphere in other domains: the political {climate}, the business {climate}, a {climate of fear}. Climate change refers to shifts in global weather patterns, particularly warming attributed to human activity.

Climates is the plural of climate—the typical weather patterns of a region over time. Different climates support different ecosystems: {tropical climates}, {arid climates}, {temperate climates}. The word extends to prevailing conditions or atmospheres: {political climates}, {business climates}. {The economic climates of various countries affect investment decisions.}

A climatologist is a scientist who studies climate—the long-term patterns of temperature, precipitation, and atmospheric conditions in a region or globally. Climatologists analyze historical data, model future scenarios, and investigate phenomena like ice ages and global warming: {Climatologists warn that current emissions trajectories will produce catastrophic warming by century's end}.

Climax is the point of highest intensity or the decisive moment in a sequence of events. A story builds to its climax before resolution. A musical piece reaches a climax before subsiding. Sexual climax is orgasm. To climax is to reach that peak: {The argument climaxed with her walking out}. In ecology, a climax community is the stable endpoint of succession—a forest that has reached its mature state.

Climaxed is the past tense of climax, meaning reached a peak or culmination. A story climaxes at its most intense moment: {The film climaxed with a rooftop chase}. Events build toward resolution: {Months of tension climaxed in a shouting match}. In sexual contexts, climaxed means reached orgasm.

Climaxes is the plural of climax—the point of greatest intensity or the decisive moment in a sequence of events. A story builds to its climax; a career reaches its climax. In sexual contexts, climax means orgasm: {She climaxes easily}. The verb form appears here too: {The film climaxes with a spectacular chase scene}.

Climb is to move upward, typically using effort—up a ladder, a mountain, a tree. The word implies progression against gravity: {We climbed three flights of stairs}. Prices climb, temperatures climb, careers climb. A climb is the act itself or the route taken: {a steep climb to the summit}. To {climb down} is to descend, or figuratively, to back away from a position: {The senator climbed down from her earlier statements}.

A climbdown is a retreat from a stated position, especially an embarrassing or reluctant one. The word implies backing away from something you publicly committed to: {The minister's climbdown on the tax proposal surprised her supporters}. British usage favors the noun; Americans more often use the verb phrase {climb down}.

Climbed is the past tense and past participle of climb. To climb is to move upward, typically using effort or exertion, whether scaling a mountain, ascending a ladder, or working your way up a corporate hierarchy. {We climbed three flights of stairs to reach the apartment.} Prices climb, temperatures climb, and ambitious people climb their way to success. When something has climbed, it has risen from a lower position to a higher one.

A climber is someone or something that climbs. The word most often refers to a person who scales mountains or rock faces as sport: {an experienced climber}, {rock climber}, {mountain climber}. In botany, a climber is a plant that grows upward by attaching to supports—ivy, vines, climbing roses. Figuratively, a {social climber} aggressively pursues higher status.

Climbers are plants that grow upward by attaching to surfaces or supports—ivy climbing a wall, vines winding up a trellis. The word also names people who climb: mountaineers scaling peaks, or social climbers seeking status. In either sense, climbers ascend by gripping whatever's available: {The climbers reached base camp by nightfall}.

Climbing is the act of ascending something—a ladder, a mountain, a tree—using hands, feet, or equipment. As a sport, climbing encompasses rock climbing, ice climbing, and mountaineering. The word also works as an adjective: a climbing {wall}, climbing {gear}, a climbing {rose} that grows upward by attaching to surfaces.

To clinch is to secure something decisively—a deal, a victory, a playoff spot: {The home run clinched the championship}. In boxing and wrestling, to clinch is to hold an opponent close, limiting their movement. A clinch is also an embrace, especially a passionate one: {The lovers were locked in a clinch}. As hardware, a clinch is a fastening made by bending over a nail or bolt after it passes through material.

Clinched is the past tense of clinch, meaning to secure or settle decisively. A boxer clinches by holding an opponent close to prevent punches. You clinch a deal, a victory, or a playoff spot by making the outcome certain: {The home run clinched the championship}. A clinched fist is tightly closed, though clenched is more common for that sense.

A clincher is the decisive fact, argument, or event that settles a matter: {The DNA evidence was the clincher}. In cycling, a clincher is a tire that hooks onto the rim with a bead, the standard type for most bikes. In construction, a clincher is a nail or bolt bent over after driving to secure it.

Clinchers are decisive factors that settle a matter or win an argument. A salesperson saves the clincher for last—the point that closes the deal: {The low price was nice, but the lifetime warranty was the clincher}. In cycling, a clincher is a tire that hooks onto the rim rather than using an inner tube, the most common type for road bikes.

Clinches is the verb form of clinch, meaning to secure or settle decisively: {She clinches the deal}, {That argument clinches it}. In boxing, a clinch is when fighters hold each other at close range to prevent punches—to clinch is to enter this position. A clinch is also a tight embrace, especially a romantic one: {The movie ended with the lovers in a clinch}.

Clinching is securing or settling something decisively. A team clinches a playoff spot by winning enough games. A lawyer clinches an argument with irrefutable evidence. In boxing, clinching is when fighters hold each other at close range to prevent punches—a defensive maneuver that referees break up. {That last goal clinched the championship.}

Cling means to hold on tightly, resisting separation. A child clings to a parent's leg. Wet clothes cling to the body. The verb extends to emotional attachment: {She clings to the hope that he'll return}. Someone clingy is excessively dependent or needy. Cling wrap adheres to surfaces. {The smell of smoke clung to his jacket for days.}

Clinging describes something that holds tightly or adheres closely. A clinging {vine} wraps around its support; a clinging {dress} follows the body's contours. Applied to people, clinging suggests excessive emotional dependence: {a clinging child}, {a clinging ex-boyfriend}. The word carries slightly negative connotations when describing adults—neediness rather than affection.

Clingy describes something or someone that clings—holds on tightly and won't let go. Clingy fabric sticks to the body. A clingy child won't leave a parent's side. Most often the word describes emotionally dependent behavior in relationships: {My ex was way too clingy}. The connotation is usually negative, suggesting excessive neediness or lack of independence.

A clinic is a medical facility smaller than a hospital, typically focused on outpatient care or specialized treatment: {a dental clinic}, {an urgent care clinic}, {a fertility clinic}. The word extends to instructional sessions where experts demonstrate techniques: {a basketball clinic}, {a writing clinic}. When someone dominates a competition so thoroughly it becomes educational, they're said to have {put on a clinic}.

Clinical describes what happens in direct contact with patients—a clinical {examination}, clinical {trials}, clinical {experience}. The word extends to anything resembling a medical setting: clean, efficient, emotionally detached. A {clinical} approach to a problem is coolly analytical, stripped of sentiment. In sports, a {clinical} finish is precise and ruthless—no wasted motion, no drama, just results.

A clinician is a healthcare professional who works directly with patients—diagnosing, treating, or managing their care. The term distinguishes hands-on practitioners from researchers or administrators: {The study was designed by scientists but carried out by clinicians}. Doctors, nurses, psychologists, and physical therapists all qualify as clinicians when engaged in patient care.

Clinics are healthcare facilities that provide outpatient medical services, typically more specialized or limited in scope than hospitals. A clinic might focus on a particular type of care—a dental clinic, a fertility clinic, a walk-in clinic for minor ailments. The word also describes group instruction sessions where experts teach skills: {a basketball clinic}, {a writing clinic}. When someone "puts on a clinic," they demonstrate masterful skill at something, as if teaching by example.

Clink is the short, sharp sound of hard objects striking together—glasses touching in a toast, coins dropping, keys jingling: {They clinked their champagne flutes}. The word imitates the sound it describes. Separately, the clink is slang for jail or prison, from a famous London prison called the Clink: {He spent six months in the clink}.

Clinked is the past tense of clink, meaning to make a light, sharp ringing sound, typically when hard objects strike each other: {They clinked glasses and drank to his health}. The word often appears in toasting contexts. Clink can also refer to the sound itself, or slang for jail—from the name of a London prison.

Clinking describes the sharp, light metallic sound made when hard objects strike together—glasses touching in a toast, coins jangling in a pocket, keys rattling on a ring. The word captures that bright, high-pitched quality: {the clinking of ice cubes in a glass}, {clinking champagne flutes}. As British slang, clinking means excellent or first-rate, though this use is dated.

Clinks is the plural of clink—short, sharp metallic sounds, like glasses touching in a toast or coins hitting each other: {The clinks of champagne flutes filled the room}. As a verb form, clinks describes making such sounds: {She clinks her spoon against the mug to get everyone's attention}.

Clip represents two verbs and their derivative nouns. If you clip one thing to another, you attach it, as you might do with a paper clip. If you clip something using a sharp instrument, you cut it, usually with the result of leaving it shorter: It’s time to clip your toenails. This clip can also refer to a hit or blow, especially an unintentional one: I clipped a light pole when I was backing out. Something happening at a good clip is happening agreeably fast.

Clipart is pre-made images designed to be inserted into documents, presentations, or other media. The term emerged with desktop publishing software, when users could "clip" graphics from collections and paste them into projects. Clipart tends toward simple, generic illustrations—office workers, handshakes, globes—often with a dated or cheesy quality: {The presentation was full of terrible clipart}.

A clipboard is a rigid board with a spring clip at the top for holding papers in place while writing. The design lets you write without a desk. In computing, a clipboard is temporary storage for cut or copied data—text, images, files—waiting to be pasted elsewhere: {Copy the link to your clipboard}. {She walked through the store with a clipboard, taking inventory}.

A clipboard is a rigid board with a spring clip at the top for holding papers in place while writing. The word extends to computing: a clipboard is temporary storage for cut or copied data, letting you move text or images between locations. {Copy the text to your clipboard and paste it into the document.}

Clipped describes something cut short or trimmed. A clipped hedge has been shaped by shears. Clipped speech is brief and curt, with words or syllables cut off: {She answered in clipped tones}. A clipped accent—especially British—sounds precise and abbreviated. In linguistics, a clipped word is shortened from a longer form: phone from telephone, flu from influenza.

A clipper is a tool for cutting or trimming—nail clippers, hair clippers, hedge clippers. The word usually appears in plural even for a single implement. A clipper was also a fast sailing ship of the 19th century, designed for speed with tall masts and sharp lines: {the great tea clippers racing from China}. In basketball, the Clippers are the Los Angeles team.

Clippers are cutting tools with two blades that meet, used for trimming hair, nails, or hedges: {nail clippers}, {hair clippers}, {hedge clippers}. Electric clippers buzz through hair quickly. Historically, clippers were fast sailing ships with sharp bows designed to "clip" through waves: {The tea clippers raced from China to London}.

Clipping is cutting something short—trimming hedges, snipping coupons, or cutting articles from newspapers. A clipping is what you've cut: {a newspaper clipping}, {grass clippings}. In linguistics, clipping shortens words: phone from telephone, flu from influenza. In audio and video, clipping is distortion from signal levels exceeding capacity, producing harsh, flattened peaks.

Clippings are pieces cut or trimmed from something larger. Newspaper clippings are articles cut from publications and saved: {She kept a scrapbook of clippings about her daughter's tennis career}. Grass clippings are what the mower leaves behind. Nail clippings, hair clippings—the word covers any small bits removed by cutting.

Clips are small fastening devices that grip or hold things together—paper clips, hair clips, binder clips. A clip is also a container holding ammunition for quick loading into a firearm. In media, a clip is a short segment extracted from longer footage: {Did you see that clip from the interview?} To clip is to cut or trim: {clip the hedges}, {clip coupons}. A clip can also be a sharp blow: {a clip on the ear}. At a good clip means at a brisk pace.

A clique is a small, exclusive group of people who associate closely and tend to exclude outsiders. The word carries negative connotations of snobbishness and insularity: {the popular clique in high school}, {Washington's political cliques}. Members of a clique may not see themselves as exclusionary, but those left out usually do.

Cliques are small, exclusive groups whose members share common interests and tend to exclude outsiders. The word carries a negative connotation—it suggests the group is insular and perhaps snobbish: {High school cliques can be brutal to anyone who doesn't fit in}. A clique differs from a circle of friends mainly in its perceived exclusivity and unwelcoming attitude toward newcomers.

Cliquey describes people or groups that form tight, exclusive circles and aren't welcoming to outsiders. A cliquey workplace or school has social clusters that are difficult to break into. The word carries a negative connotation, suggesting snobbishness or deliberate exclusion rather than mere close friendship. {The department was so cliquey that new hires ate lunch alone for months.} Also spelled cliquish.

Cliquish describes people or groups that form tight, exclusive circles and resist outsiders. A cliquish {office} divides into factions that don't mix. Cliquish {behavior} involves shutting out those who don't belong: {The department was so cliquish that new hires struggled to break in}. The word carries disapproval—cliquishness suggests pettiness and social gatekeeping.

The clitoris is a small, sensitive organ at the front of the vulva, above the vaginal opening. Though only a small portion is externally visible, most of its erectile tissue extends internally. Its sole function is sexual pleasure—the clitoris has more nerve endings than any other part of the human body. {clitoral stimulation}, {clitoral orgasm}.

A cloak is a loose outer garment without sleeves, fastened at the neck and hanging from the shoulders—the kind worn in medieval times or fantasy settings. The word extends to anything that conceals or covers: {a cloak of secrecy}, {under the cloak of darkness}. To cloak something is to hide or disguise it: {The organization cloaked its true purpose in charitable language}.

Cloaked means covered or concealed, as if hidden beneath a cloak. The word usually appears figuratively: a town {cloaked in fog}, motives {cloaked in secrecy}, an operation {cloaked in mystery}. In fantasy and science fiction, cloaked often describes invisibility technology: {The ship remained cloaked until it was too late}.

Cloaking is the act of concealing or disguising something. In science fiction, a cloaking device renders spacecraft invisible. In computing, cloaking is a deceptive technique where a website shows different content to search engines than to human visitors—typically to manipulate search rankings. The word suggests technological or deliberate concealment rather than simple hiding.

A cloakroom is a room where coats and other outer garments can be left temporarily, typically at a theater, restaurant, or public building: {Check your coat at the cloakroom}. In British usage, cloakroom is also a polite term for a bathroom or toilet. In legislative buildings, the cloakroom is a private area adjacent to the chamber where members gather informally.

Cloaks are loose outer garments that hang from the shoulders, typically without sleeves—the kind of dramatic wrap you see in period films or fantasy settings. The word extends to anything that conceals: {a cloak of secrecy}, {under the cloak of darkness}. To cloak something is to cover or hide it: {The project was cloaked in mystery}. A {cloaking device} renders something invisible.

Clobber means to strike hard or defeat decisively: {The team got clobbered in the semifinals}. It suggests overwhelming force—you don't clobber someone in a close match. In computing, to clobber a file is to overwrite it, destroying the original contents. British slang uses clobber as a noun meaning clothing or personal belongings: {Get your clobber and let's go}.

Clobbered is the past tense of clobber, meaning to hit hard or defeat decisively. Someone gets clobbered in a fight, a team gets clobbered in a game, or stocks get clobbered in a market crash: {We got clobbered by the competition}. In computing, to clobber a file is to overwrite it, destroying its previous contents.

Clobbering is the act of hitting or defeating someone or something decisively and often violently. In physical contexts, it suggests a heavy, forceful blow: {He took a clobbering in the ring}. The word extends readily to competitive situations where one side dominates: {Our team took a clobbering in the playoffs}. In computing, clobbering refers to accidentally overwriting data or files.

Clobbers is the third-person singular form of the verb clobber, which means to strike heavily or defeat decisively. You might clobber someone in a fight, or a team might clobber their opponents in a lopsided game. In computing, clobber has a specific technical meaning: to overwrite data, often unintentionally or destructively. {The update clobbers any custom settings you've configured.} The word carries a sense of force and thoroughness in all its uses.

A cloche is a close-fitting, bell-shaped women's hat, popular in the 1920s, that hugs the head and sits low on the forehead: {She wore a felt cloche pulled down over her bobbed hair}. The word comes from the French for bell, which also gives us the gardening sense—a bell-shaped glass or plastic cover placed over plants to protect them from frost or hasten growth.

The timekeeping device that we call a clock is the source of most other meanings of the word. If you clock something, you time it. Something or someone that clocks achieves a certain timing or level: The website has clocked six million hits this month. If your job requires you to clock in, you use a time clock that records your arrival. If you’re on the clock, you’re at work. Unrelatedly, if you clock someone, you hit them hard.

Clocked is the past tense of clock, which has several distinct uses. To clock someone or something is to time them: {She clocked his mile at 4:32}. To clock in or out is to record arrival or departure at work. In slang, to clock someone is to hit them hard: {He clocked the guy right in the jaw}. More recently, to clock someone means to notice or recognize them, especially to identify a transgender person as trans: {I got clocked at the store}.

Clocking is the present participle of clock, covering all its verb senses. You clock your hours at work, or clock a fast time in a race. In British slang, to clock someone is to notice or spot them: {I clocked him across the room immediately}. In trans and drag communities, clocking means recognizing someone as transgender or in drag, often when they're trying to pass: {She was worried about getting clocked at the interview}.

A clockmaker is a person who makes or repairs clocks. The trade requires precision mechanical skills—cutting gears, fitting springs, adjusting escapements. Historically, clockmakers were among the most skilled artisans, and their techniques contributed to early manufacturing precision: {The village clockmaker also repaired watches and music boxes}.

Clocks are devices that measure and display time—from grandfather clocks to alarm clocks to the clock on your phone. To clock something is to time it or to notice it: {I clocked his lap at under a minute}, {Did you clock her new haircut?} To clock in or out is to record arrival or departure from work. In slang, to clock someone can mean to hit them hard or to recognize something they're trying to hide: {She got clocked immediately}.

A clocktower is a tall structure, often freestanding or part of a building, with a large clock face visible from a distance. Clocktowers served as public timekeepers before watches became common, and many remain landmarks in town squares and civic buildings: {The clocktower struck noon}. {We agreed to meet beneath the clocktower}.

A clockwatcher is someone who watches the clock, eager for work to end. The term is mildly derogatory, implying the person lacks engagement or motivation: {Don't be such a clockwatcher—we've still got things to finish}. The related noun clockwatching describes this behavior.

Clockwatchers are people who watch the clock, waiting for the workday to end. The term implies minimal engagement—doing just enough to get by while counting minutes until quitting time. {The office was full of clockwatchers by Friday afternoon.} The singular clockwatcher and the verb clockwatch share this sense of disengaged timekeeping.

Clockwatching is the habit of repeatedly checking the time, especially when waiting for work to end or an event to arrive. The term implies impatience, boredom, or lack of engagement: {The meeting dragged on and everyone started clockwatching}. A clockwatcher is someone who does this habitually—often used disparagingly for employees who care more about quitting time than their work.

Clockwise describes rotation in the direction a clock's hands move—rightward at the top, leftward at the bottom. {Turn the dial clockwise to increase the volume.} The opposite is counterclockwise (or anticlockwise in British English). The term extends to any circular or spiral motion: {The dancers moved clockwise around the floor.}

Clockwork is the internal mechanism of a clock—gears, springs, and wheels working in precise coordination. The term extends to any intricate mechanical system operating with similar regularity. {Like clockwork} describes anything happening with perfect predictability and timing: {The trains run like clockwork}. Clockwork as an adjective describes mechanical devices powered by wound springs rather than electricity: {a clockwork toy}, {a clockwork orange}.

A clod is a lump of earth or clay, the kind you might break up when preparing soil for planting. By extension, clod refers to a stupid or clumsy person—someone as dense and unrefined as a lump of dirt. {Don't be such a clod; watch where you're stepping.} The word shares this insulting sense with related terms like clodhopper, which suggests a rustic, awkward person.

A clodhopper is a large, heavy shoe or boot—the kind that might tramp over clods of earth in a field. The word extends to the person wearing such footwear: a rustic, unsophisticated person, especially a clumsy farmer or country bumpkin. {Get your clodhoppers off the couch.}

Clodhoppers are large, heavy shoes or boots—the kind suited for tramping through plowed fields, where you'd be hopping over clods of dirt. The word is mildly derisive, suggesting footwear that's clunky and graceless: {Take off those clodhoppers before you come inside}. By extension, a clodhopper is a clumsy rustic or bumpkin.

Clods are lumps of earth or clay, the kind that break up when you work soil: {He broke up the clods with a hoe}. By extension, a clod is a dull, stupid, or insensitive person—someone as dense as a lump of dirt: {Don't be such a clod}. The insult suggests clumsiness and lack of refinement.

A clog is a shoe with a thick wooden sole, traditionally worn in the Netherlands and other parts of Europe. The word extends to anything that blocks or obstructs: a clog in a drain, a clog in the system. To clog is to block or become blocked: {Hair clogged the drain}. Arteries clog with plaque. Bureaucracy clogs progress.

Clogged describes something blocked or obstructed, preventing normal flow. A clogged drain won't empty; clogged arteries restrict blood flow; clogged pores lead to acne. The word suggests accumulated matter—hair, grease, debris—that has built up over time: {The sink is clogged with food scraps}. Figuratively, a clogged system or process has become sluggish from overload.

Clogging is a form of folk dance characterized by rhythmic footwork that strikes the floor to create percussive sounds. The dancer wears hard-soled shoes, often with metal taps. Clogging has roots in Appalachian and Irish traditions and remains popular at folk festivals and competitions: {She's been clogging since she was six}. Separately, clogging is the process of becoming blocked or obstructed: {Hair clogging the drain caused the backup}.

Clogs are shoes with thick wooden soles, traditionally worn for protection or warmth. The rigid base elevates the foot above wet or dirty ground. Dutch wooden shoes are the iconic example, though clogs appear across cultures. As a verb, to clog means to block or obstruct: {Hair clogged the drain}. Something that clogs up becomes jammed or congested: {Traffic clogged the highway}.

A cloister is a covered walkway around a courtyard, especially in a monastery or convent, with arched openings on one side. By extension, cloister refers to any place of religious seclusion or monastic life itself: {She entered the cloister at nineteen}. To cloister is to seclude or shelter from the outside world: {He cloistered himself in his study}. A cloistered life suggests withdrawal from worldly concerns, whether literal or figurative.

Cloistered means secluded from the outside world, originally describing religious communities living in a cloister—an enclosed monastery or convent. The word extends to any sheltered, protected existence: {a cloistered academic life}, {cloistered from the harsh realities of the world}. It often implies naivety or unworldliness resulting from limited exposure.

Cloisters are covered walkways surrounding a courtyard, typically in monasteries or churches, with arched openings on one side. The architecture creates enclosed, contemplative spaces for walking and meditation. By extension, a cloister is any place of religious seclusion: {She spent her youth in the cloister}. To cloister is to seclude or shelter from the world: {He cloistered himself in his study}.

Clomp is to walk heavily and noisily, making dull, thudding sounds with each step: {He clomped down the stairs in his work boots}. The word suggests footwear with hard soles—boots, clogs, or heels—striking a surface with more force than grace. A clomp is one such heavy footfall.

Clomping is walking with heavy, loud footsteps, suggesting boots or hard-soled shoes striking a surface: {I heard her clomping up the stairs}. The word captures both the sound and the graceless quality of the movement. Someone who clomps isn't trying to be quiet or elegant.

A clone is a genetically identical copy of an organism, produced either naturally (as with identical twins) or artificially through laboratory techniques. The term extends to any exact duplicate: {a clone of the original software}, {cheap clones of designer handbags}. In computing, to clone a hard drive is to copy its entire contents. Informally, someone who closely imitates another may be called a clone: {He's basically a clone of his father}.

Cloned describes something produced as a genetically identical copy of another organism or, by extension, any exact duplicate. A cloned sheep shares its donor's DNA. In computing, a cloned hard drive contains an exact copy of another's data. Figuratively, cloned suggests mass-produced sameness: {The strip mall was lined with cloned storefronts}.

Clones are genetically identical copies of a living thing—produced naturally (as with identical twins) or artificially through laboratory techniques. The word extends to any close copy: {The company released a series of iPhone clones}. In science fiction, clones are often artificially grown duplicates of humans. To clone is to create such copies: {Scientists cloned the sheep from adult cells}.

Cloning is creating a genetically identical copy of an organism or cell. In biotechnology, cloning produces organisms with the same DNA as a parent—Dolly the sheep was cloned from an adult cell. The term extends to exact duplication generally: cloning a hard drive, cloning a credit card. To clone is to make such a copy; a clone is the copy itself.

Clonk is the dull, resonant sound of one solid object striking another—heavier than a clink, duller than a clang: {The wrench clonked against the pipe}. As a verb, to clonk is to make this sound or to hit something producing it: {She clonked him on the head with a book}. The word is onomatopoeic, imitating the sound it describes.

Clonked is the past tense of clonk, meaning to hit something with a dull, heavy sound: {He clonked his head on the low beam}. The word suggests impact without sharpness—more thud than crack. Something can also clonk down or clonk along, making that characteristic hollow noise: {The old radiator clonked all night}.

Clop is the sharp, hollow sound of a horse's hoof striking pavement or hard ground. The word imitates the sound itself. As a verb, to clop is to make this sound: {The horse clopped down the cobblestone street}. By extension, any hard-soled footwear can clop: {She clopped across the wooden floor in her heels}.

Close, when pronounced with an “s” sound, is an adjective, noun, or adverb, representing one group of meanings relating to proximity and confinement. Close with a “z” sound is a noun or a verb with other meanings relating to termination and obstruction. Anything that can be thought of as open in some sense is a typical object of close: close the door/window/gap. A close friend or relative is one who may be geographically distant but intimately connected. As a noun, close is similar to end: He spoke at the close of the service. #

Closed describes something not open—a door, a store, a case. A closed shop requires union membership for employment. A closed meeting excludes outsiders. A closed mind won't consider new ideas. When something is closed to discussion, the matter is settled: {The subject is closed}. A closed system has no outside input. In math, a set is closed under an operation if applying it yields another member of the set.

Closeknit describes a group whose members are tightly bound by shared interests, loyalty, or affection: {a closeknit family}, {a closeknit community}. The metaphor comes from fabric woven with threads lying close together. Usually hyphenated as close-knit, though the solid form appears increasingly.

Closeness is the state of being near—physically, emotionally, or in degree. Physical closeness is proximity: {the closeness of the houses made privacy impossible}. Emotional closeness is intimacy: {I value the closeness I have with my sister}. Closeness can also describe similarity: {the closeness of their test scores surprised the teacher}. A close race or close call has closeness—a narrow margin.

A closeout is a sale of remaining merchandise at reduced prices, typically when a store is clearing inventory or going out of business: {Everything's 50% off—it's a closeout sale}. The term also applies to the final settlement of a financial account or position. As a verb, to close out means to conclude or liquidate: {We need to close out this project by Friday}.

Closeouts are items sold at deep discounts because a store or manufacturer is discontinuing them, clearing inventory, or going out of business. The term also names the sales themselves: {The furniture store is having a closeout}. Closeout merchandise may be last season's stock, excess inventory, or products from bankrupt companies—perfectly good goods that simply need to move.

Closer describes something nearer in distance, time, or relationship—the comparative form of close. As a noun, a closer is someone who finishes things: a relief pitcher who closes out games, a salesperson who seals deals, or the final act at a concert. In real estate and law, a closer handles the final steps of transactions. A closer can also be the concluding element itself: {That song was the perfect closer for the album}.

Closers are people who finalize deals or bring things to completion. In sales, the closer is the person who gets customers to sign—the one who seals the transaction: {Send in the closers}. In baseball, a closer is the relief pitcher who finishes games, typically entering in the ninth inning to preserve a lead. The word carries connotations of skill under pressure and the ability to finish what others started.

Closest is the superlative of close—nearest in distance, time, or relationship. The closest {store} is the one requiring the least travel. Your closest {friend} is your most intimate one. In competitions, the closest {result} is the one with the smallest margin. {That was the closest I've ever come to quitting.}
clues: Best friends are this to you

definition: A closet is a small room or enclosed space for storage, especially for clothes. In American English, closets are built into bedrooms; in British English, the term more often refers to a wardrobe or small storage room. Closet also describes something private or secret: a {closet smoker} hides the habit; to {come out of the closet} is to reveal one's homosexuality publicly. To closet yourself is to withdraw into privacy: {She closeted herself in her study}. A {skeleton in the closet} is a shameful secret.

Closeted describes someone who keeps a significant aspect of their identity hidden, especially being gay or otherwise LGBTQ+: {He was closeted for years before coming out to his family}. The metaphor is of hiding in a closet—concealed from public view. Extended to other secrets: {a closeted conservative in a liberal workplace}. The opposite is out or openly: {She's been out since college}.

Closets are small enclosed spaces used for storage, most often for clothing and household items. In American homes, a closet typically refers to a built-in storage area with a door, while British English more often uses wardrobe or cupboard. The phrase {in the closet} or {closeted} describes someone hiding an aspect of their identity, especially their sexuality, from others. To closet oneself is to withdraw into privacy, often for private conversation or work. {They closeted themselves in the study to discuss the matter.}

A closeup is a photograph, film shot, or view taken at close range, showing detail: {The director called for a closeup of the actor's face}. By extension, any detailed or intimate examination: {a closeup of life in rural America}. Also spelled close-up.

Closeups is the plural of closeup, a camera shot taken at close range, showing a subject in detail—typically a face filling the frame. In film and photography, closeups create intimacy or draw attention to important details: {The director called for closeups of the actor's hands}. The term extends to any detailed examination: {a closeup of the scandal}.

Closing is the act of shutting, ending, or concluding something. A closing {door}, a closing {argument}, the closing {minutes} of a game. In real estate, the closing is the final meeting where property transfers and documents are signed: {We're scheduled for closing on Friday}. Closing can also describe something that comes at the end: {closing remarks}, {closing credits}.

Closure is the act of closing something or the state of being closed. A road closure blocks traffic; a factory closure ends operations. Emotionally, closure means resolution after a difficult experience—the sense that a painful chapter has ended: {She needed closure after the breakup}. In legislation, closure (or cloture) is a procedure to end debate and force a vote.
clues: The feeling of finally moving on

definition: Closures is the plural of closure—acts or instances of closing something down or bringing it to an end. Road closures block traffic; factory closures eliminate jobs; school closures cancel classes. The word also names the psychological resolution people seek after traumatic events: {She needed closure after the breakup}. In programming, a closure is a function that retains access to variables from its surrounding scope even after that scope has closed.

A clot is a thickened mass formed when liquid—especially blood—coagulates: {a blood clot in his leg}, {clots formed in the wound}. The verb means to form such a mass: {The blood clotted quickly}. In British slang, a clot is a stupid person: {Don't be such a clot}.

Cloth is fabric—material made by weaving, knitting, or felting fibers together. A cloth is a piece of such material used for a specific purpose: a {tablecloth}, a {washcloth}, a {dish cloth}. {The cloth} refers collectively to the clergy, from their distinctive garments. {Cut from the same cloth} means made alike, sharing essential qualities.

To clothe is to provide with clothing or cover as if with clothing: {She clothed herself in silk}; {Fog clothed the valley}. The past tense is clothed or the archaic clad. Clothe often appears in passive constructions: {clothed in rags}, {clothed in mystery}. The word carries a slightly formal or literary tone compared to dress.

Clothed means wearing clothes, covered with garments: {The children were warmly clothed against the cold}. It often appears in contrast to nakedness or in descriptions of how someone is dressed: {clothed in white}, {fully clothed}. The past tense of clothe, it functions primarily as an adjective in modern usage.

Clothes are garments worn on the body—shirts, pants, dresses, and the like. The word covers everything from underwear to outerwear: {Put on some clothes before you answer the door}. Clothes often appears with modifiers indicating purpose or quality: {work clothes}, {dress clothes}, {designer clothes}. To change clothes is to put on different garments.

A clotheshorse is a frame, usually foldable, on which clothes are hung to dry or air out indoors. The term also describes a person excessively devoted to fashionable dress—someone who treats their wardrobe as seriously as a horse might carry its rider. {She's such a clotheshorse that her closet takes up an entire room.} The figurative sense is mildly disparaging, suggesting vanity or superficiality about appearance.

A clothesline is a rope or wire strung between two points for hanging laundry to dry: {She hung the sheets on the clothesline}. In sports, especially football and hockey, to clothesline someone is to strike them across the neck or chest with an extended arm, knocking them down—the motion resembling running into a taut line.

Clotheslined describes being struck across the neck or upper chest by an outstretched arm, knocking you backward off your feet—as if you'd run into a taut clothesline at full speed. The move is common in wrestling and football, often illegal in the latter: {The defender clotheslined the receiver and drew a flag}. Figuratively, anything that stops you abruptly: {I was clotheslined by the news}.

Clotheslines are ropes or wires strung between posts or buildings for hanging laundry to dry outdoors. The term also serves as a verb in sports and fighting: to clothesline someone is to strike them across the neck or chest with an extended arm, knocking them backward as if they'd run into a clothesline at speed.

Clotheslining is a move where you strike someone across the neck or chest with an extended arm while they're moving toward you, knocking them down—like running into a clothesline at neck height. Common in wrestling and football, where it's usually illegal: {He got flagged for clotheslining the receiver}. The term extends to any sudden horizontal takedown.

A clothespin is a clip for fastening wet laundry to a line for drying. The traditional type has two wooden prongs joined by a spring; simpler versions are just slotted pegs. {She hung the sheets with clothespins.} The British term is clothes peg.

Clothespins are small clips used to secure wet laundry to a line for drying. The traditional design has two wooden prongs joined by a spring; simpler versions are single pieces of wood with a slot. {She hung the sheets on the line with clothespins.} Though less common with the rise of electric dryers, they remain useful for outdoor drying and craft projects.

Clothing is the collective term for garments worn on the body—shirts, pants, dresses, coats, and the like. Unlike clothes, which tends toward the concrete and countable, clothing functions as a mass noun and often appears in more formal or commercial contexts: {a clothing store}, {protective clothing}, {winter clothing}. The word emphasizes the category or type rather than specific items. {She packed enough clothing for a week.}

Clots are lumps formed when liquid thickens or coagulates. Blood clots form to stop bleeding but can be dangerous when they block vessels: {a clot in his lung}. Clots also form in milk, paint, or other liquids that congeal. In British slang, a clot is a stupid person: {Don't be such a clot}.

Clotting is the process by which a liquid, especially blood, thickens into a semi-solid mass. Blood clotting stops bleeding from wounds; without it, even minor cuts would be dangerous. Clotting can also be harmful when it blocks blood vessels: {The medication prevents clotting in the arteries}. The word applies to other liquids that coagulate or curdle.

The clouds you see in the sky inspire the many other meanings of this word, all of which relate to a quality associated with the airborne water vapor. Today’s commonest uses are inspired by the cloud associated with the Internet, where data storage and processing takes place far from people’s own devices but immediately available to them. The verbal meanings of cloud mostly draw on the ability of clouds to block the sun: anything that darkens, obscures, or occludes can be said to cloud: A look of distress clouded his features.

A cloudburst is a sudden, intense rainstorm—a downpour so heavy it seems a cloud has split open and dumped its contents all at once. The term suggests brief but extreme rainfall: {We got caught in a cloudburst and were soaked within seconds}. Unlike steady rain, a cloudburst arrives without warning and overwhelms.

Clouded means obscured or made unclear, as if covered by clouds. A clouded {sky} is overcast; a clouded {judgment} is impaired by emotion or bias. Clouded {water} or {glass} has lost its transparency. The word suggests something that was once clear has become difficult to see through: {His memory of the event was clouded by time}.

Cloudless describes a sky without clouds—completely clear and unobstructed: {a cloudless summer day}, {The stars were brilliant against the cloudless night}. The word suggests ideal weather conditions and often carries connotations of brightness or optimism.

Clouds are visible masses of water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the atmosphere. They form when moist air cools and condenses around tiny particles. Beyond weather, clouds describe anything that obscures or darkens: {a cloud of dust}, {a cloud of suspicion}. To cloud is to make unclear: {Emotions clouded her judgment}. In computing, {the cloud} refers to remote servers accessed via the internet for storage and processing.

A cloudscape is a view or picture of clouds, especially a dramatic or picturesque arrangement across the sky. The word parallels landscape and seascape, framing clouds as a subject for contemplation or artistic representation: {The sunset cloudscape turned orange and purple}. Photographers and painters speak of capturing cloudscapes.

Cloudy describes a sky covered or partly covered with clouds: {a cloudy afternoon}, {cloudy with a chance of rain}. The word extends to anything lacking clarity or transparency—cloudy water is murky, cloudy thinking is confused, and a cloudy future is uncertain. Cloudy emotions suggest sadness or gloom: {Her expression turned cloudy when she heard the news}.

Clout is influence or power, especially in political or social contexts: {She has clout with the mayor}, {His endorsement carries real clout}. The word suggests the ability to make things happen through connections or reputation rather than formal authority. In its older sense, a clout is a heavy blow: {He gave him a clout on the ear}. To clout is to hit hard. Among younger speakers, clout increasingly refers to social media fame or cultural cachet: {chasing clout}, {clout chaser}.

Clouts is the plural of clout, which has two main senses. A clout is a blow or strike: {He gave the ball a good clout}. More commonly now, clout means influence or power, especially in politics or business: {She has clout with the mayor}. In internet slang, clout is social media influence or fame—someone {chasing clouts} seeks attention and followers.

Clove has two unrelated meanings. The spice clove is the dried flower bud of a tropical tree, pungent and aromatic, used in cooking and baking: {ham studded with cloves}, {a pinch of ground clove}. Separately, a clove of garlic is one of the segments that make up a garlic bulb: {Mince three cloves of garlic}.

Cloven means split or divided into two parts. The word is the past participle of cleave and appears almost exclusively in {cloven hoof}—the divided foot of cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, and deer. Because the devil is traditionally depicted with cloven hooves, the word carries diabolical associations: {cloven-footed}, {a cloven hoof beneath the robe}.

Clover is a low-growing plant with distinctive three-lobed leaves, common in lawns and pastures. Finding a four-leaf clover is considered lucky because the mutation is rare. To be {in clover} is to live in comfort or prosperity, from the plant's value as rich fodder for livestock.

A cloverleaf is a highway interchange where two roads cross at different levels, with curving ramps that form a shape resembling a four-leaf clover when viewed from above. Traffic flows continuously without stopping, looping around to change direction or merge onto the crossing road. {Take the cloverleaf onto the interstate.} The word also describes the shape itself: a cloverleaf pattern, a cloverleaf roll.

Clovers is the plural of clover, the low-growing plant with three-lobed leaves common in lawns and fields. Finding a four-leaf clover is considered lucky, making it a symbol of good fortune. {The yard was covered in clovers and dandelions.} To be {in clover} is to live in comfort or prosperity.

Cloves are the dried flower buds of a tropical tree, used as a pungent spice in cooking and baking. Their intense, warm flavor appears in spiced drinks, ham glazes, and pumpkin pie. Whole cloves look like small dark nails—the name comes from the Latin word for nail. Clove oil, extracted from the buds, has traditional uses as a dental analgesic. A clove of garlic is an unrelated sense: one of the segments that make up a garlic bulb.

A clown is a comic performer, traditionally in colorful costume and exaggerated makeup, who entertains through slapstick, jokes, and physical comedy—originally in circuses, now at children's parties and other venues. Clown extends to anyone who acts foolishly or seeks attention through buffoonery: {Stop clowning around}. To clown on someone is to mock or ridicule them. In slang, calling someone a clown dismisses them as incompetent or unserious: {That guy's a complete clown}.

Clownery is foolish or absurd behavior, the kind of antics you'd expect from a clown. The word carries mild disapproval—someone engaged in clownery isn't being taken seriously: {I'm tired of his clownery; we have work to do}. It can describe deliberate buffoonery or unintentional foolishness that invites ridicule.

Clownfish are small, brightly colored tropical fish known for their orange bodies with distinctive white bands outlined in black. They live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones in a mutually beneficial relationship—the fish gains protection while helping clean and defend the anemone.
