The animated film *Finding Nemo* made them widely recognizable. Also called anemonefish.

Clowning is acting in a silly, playful, or attention-seeking way. Children clown around in class; adults clown at parties. The word carries a mild note of disapproval—clowning implies the behavior is excessive or inappropriate to the situation: {Stop clowning and pay attention}. It can also refer to the art of performing as a clown.

Clownish describes behavior that resembles a clown's—silly, awkward, or buffoonish. The word usually carries mild criticism, suggesting someone is acting foolishly or without dignity: {His clownish antics embarrassed the other guests}. It can describe appearance as well as behavior: {a clownish grin}, {clownish oversized shoes}.

Clowns are comic performers, typically in exaggerated makeup and costumes, who entertain through slapstick, physical comedy, and buffoonery. The circus clown is the archetype, but clowns appear at children's parties, in theater, and in horror films that play on their unsettling appearance. Informally, a clown is someone who acts foolishly: {Stop clowning around}. To clown is to joke or behave playfully: {We were just clowning}.

Cloying describes sweetness so excessive it becomes unpleasant or nauseating. The word applies literally to overly sugary foods and drinks, but more often figuratively to sentimentality, flattery, or affection that feels suffocating: {The movie's cloying sentimentality made it hard to watch}. What begins as pleasant curdles into too much.

A club is a heavy stick used as a weapon, thick at one end for striking. From this come specialized clubs—the golf club, the billy club. Playing cards have a suit marked with a three-lobed symbol called clubs. A club is also a group organized around shared interests: {a book club}, {a chess club}. The place where such groups meet is also a club, which extends to venues for drinking, dancing, or entertainment: {nightclub}, {strip club}, {comedy club}. To club is to strike with a club, or to combine resources: {We clubbed together to buy her a gift}.

Clubbed is the past tense of club, meaning to strike with a heavy object or to beat repeatedly: {The seal was clubbed to death}. Clubbed also describes something shaped like a club—thick at one end: {clubbed fingers} are swollen at the tips, a medical sign of certain heart or lung conditions.

Clubbers are people who frequent nightclubs, especially as a regular social activity. The term suggests enthusiasm for club culture—dancing, music, late nights: {The clubbers spilled onto the street at 3 a.m.} A clubber may also be someone who wields a club as a weapon, though this sense is rare.

Clubbing is going to nightclubs, typically for dancing and drinking: {We went clubbing every weekend that summer}. The activity implies loud music, late hours, and often a scene built around fashion or social display. Separately, clubbing can mean beating with a club or heavy object: {the clubbing of baby seals}.

Clubby describes an atmosphere of exclusive intimacy, like a private club where members share unspoken understanding. A clubby {restaurant} feels like an insiders' gathering place. The word often carries a whiff of criticism—clubby {networks} and clubby {boards} suggest decisions made by cozy elites rather than on merit: {The industry remains clubby and hard to break into}.

Clubgoers are people who frequent nightclubs—venues for dancing, drinking, and socializing, typically with loud music and late hours. The term appears in discussions of nightlife culture, drug use, or urban entertainment: {Clubgoers lined up outside the venue}, {The new policy affects clubgoers and bar patrons alike}.

A clubhouse is a building where members of a club gather for meetings, socializing, and activities. Sports teams have clubhouses where players change, shower, and relax before and after games—these are also called locker rooms. Golf courses typically have clubhouses serving as social hubs for members. In children's usage, a clubhouse might be a backyard fort or treehouse where kids hold secret meetings. {The team celebrated their victory in the clubhouse.}

Clubhouses are buildings or rooms where clubs meet—places for members to gather, socialize, and conduct activities. Sports teams have clubhouses where players change and relax: {The manager addressed the team in the clubhouse after the game}. Golf courses typically have a clubhouse serving as social hub and administrative center. Children build clubhouses for secret meetings and play.

Clubs is a suit in playing cards, marked by a black three-lobed symbol resembling a clover. In the standard deck, clubs rank alongside spades, hearts, and diamonds. The word also refers to the cards themselves: {I'm out of clubs}. Separately, clubs are the plural of club—organizations, venues, or blunt implements used as weapons.

Clubwear is clothing designed for nightclubs and similar venues—typically bold, body-conscious, and attention-grabbing. The category includes tight dresses, crop tops, platform heels, and anything with sequins, mesh, or metallic fabric. {She changed into clubwear before hitting the dance floor.} The term distinguishes going-out clothes from everyday or office attire.

Cluck is the short, throaty sound a chicken makes, especially a hen calling her chicks. The verb means to make this sound, or by extension, to express fussy disapproval: {She clucked her tongue at the mess}. A cluck or dumb cluck is a stupid person—someone with a chicken's brain.

Clucking is the short, repetitive sound a hen makes, especially when brooding or calling chicks. The word extends to any similar sound: {the clucking of tongues}. To cluck over someone is to fuss disapprovingly or with excessive concern: {My mother was clucking over my messy apartment}. A clucking sound made with the tongue expresses disapproval or sympathy.

Clucks are the short, throaty sounds chickens make—a series of low, repetitive notes. By extension, clucks describe similar sounds of disapproval or sympathy from humans: {She made little clucks of concern}. To cluck is to make these sounds, or to express fussy disapproval: {The neighbors clucked about the overgrown lawn}.

A clue is a piece of evidence or information that helps solve a mystery, puzzle, or problem: {The detective found a clue at the crime scene}. In crosswords and games, clues are hints that point toward answers. To clue someone in is to inform them: {Can you clue me in on what happened?} Someone clueless lacks awareness or understanding.

Clueless means lacking understanding or awareness about something. Someone clueless about fashion doesn't know what looks good. The word often implies obliviousness that others find obvious or frustrating: {He's completely clueless about how his comments affect people}. It can shade toward innocent naïveté or willful ignorance depending on context.

Cluelessness is the state of having no idea what's going on or how to handle a situation. It implies obliviousness rather than mere ignorance—someone clueless doesn't just lack information but fails to pick up on obvious signals: {His cluelessness about her feelings was painful to watch}. The word often carries mild contempt.

Clues is the plural of clue—pieces of evidence or information that help solve a puzzle, mystery, or problem. Detectives follow clues to catch criminals; crossword solvers work from clues to fill in answers. {The detective gathered clues at the crime scene}. To be {clueless} is to lack understanding entirely.

A clump is a compact mass or cluster of things grouped together: a clump of {trees}, a clump of {dirt}, a clump of {hair} in the drain. The word suggests irregular, natural grouping rather than deliberate arrangement. To clump is to gather into such masses, or to walk with heavy, thudding steps: {He clumped up the stairs in his boots}.

Clumping is the process of forming into clumps—masses or clusters that stick together. Cat litter that clumps makes cleanup easier. Hair clumps when wet or greasy. Cells clump in certain medical conditions. The word also describes a heavy, noisy way of walking: {She clumped up the stairs in her boots}.

Clumps are irregular groupings or masses of things pressed or growing together: {clumps of dirt}, {clumps of grass}, {clumps of hair in the drain}. The word suggests thickness and unevenness—mascara clumps, sauce clumps. To clump is to gather in such masses, or to walk with heavy, noisy steps: {She clumped up the stairs in her boots}.
clues: Dense gatherings of dirt or hair

definition: Clumpy describes something that forms clumps or lumps rather than staying smooth or evenly distributed. Gravy goes clumpy when flour isn't whisked properly. Mascara gets clumpy with age. Soil can be clumpy after rain. Hair styled with too much product looks clumpy. The word suggests unwanted texture—things that should flow or spread but stick together instead.

Clumsiness is a tendency to move awkwardly or handle things without grace, often resulting in dropped objects, stumbles, or minor accidents. The word implies a lack of coordination rather than intent: {His clumsiness around the house meant broken dishes were routine}. Extended to speech or social behavior, clumsiness suggests tactlessness or inelegance: {the clumsiness of his apology made things worse}.

Clumsy describes someone who moves awkwardly and tends to knock things over or drop them: {a clumsy waiter spilling drinks}. It extends to anything lacking grace or skill—a clumsy {attempt} at humor, a clumsy {apology}. The word suggests unintentional awkwardness rather than incompetence: {My clumsy fingers couldn't manage the tiny buttons}.

Clung is the past tense and past participle of cling. To cling is to hold tightly or stick closely to something: {She clung to the railing as the boat rocked}. The word often suggests desperation or emotional attachment: {He clung to the hope that she'd return}. Things that adhere—wet clothes to skin, vines to walls—also cling.

Clunk is a dull, heavy sound—the noise of metal hitting metal or something solid dropping: {The car door shut with a clunk}, {I heard a clunk from the engine}. As a verb, to clunk is to make or move with such a sound: {He clunked the wrench down on the workbench}. A clunker is an old, unreliable car prone to making such noises.

A clunker is an old, unreliable machine—typically a car in poor condition: {He drove that clunker until the engine finally gave out}. The term extends to anything that fails or performs badly: a joke that doesn't land, a movie that bombs, a line of dialogue that thuds. The word suggests something heavy, graceless, and past its usefulness.

Clunkers is the plural of clunker—an old, worn-out, or poorly functioning machine, especially a car: {He drove that clunker until the transmission finally gave out}. By extension, clunker applies to anything that fails or performs badly: a joke that lands with a thud, a movie that flops, an awkward sentence in otherwise good prose.

Clunking describes a dull, heavy sound—the noise of something solid striking or falling: {The clunking of the old radiator kept me awake}. As an adjective, it characterizes things that make such sounds: {clunking machinery}, {clunking footsteps on the stairs}. Figuratively, clunking suggests awkwardness or gracelessness: {clunking dialogue}, {clunking prose}.

Clunky describes something awkward, heavy, or lacking grace. Clunky shoes are bulky and inelegant. Clunky prose reads clumsily. Clunky software has an unintuitive interface: {The app works, but the navigation is clunky}. The word suggests something functional but unrefined—it gets the job done without finesse.

A cluster is a group of similar things gathered or growing close together: a cluster of {grapes}, a cluster of {stars}, a cluster of {buildings}. The word emphasizes natural or loose grouping rather than rigid arrangement. Things cluster when they bunch together: {Fans clustered around the entrance}. In computing, a cluster is a group of connected computers or storage units working as a single system.

Clustered describes things grouped closely together. Grapes grow in clusters; houses may be clustered around a village green; stars cluster in galaxies. {Clustered around the fire, they shared stories}. In computing, clustered servers or databases are linked systems that work together, sharing resources or data for performance and reliability.

A clusterfuck is a situation gone chaotically wrong through a combination of incompetence, poor planning, or cascading failures. The military slang origin suggests multiple people fucking up simultaneously, creating a mess worse than any single mistake could produce: {The evacuation was a complete clusterfuck}. The word is vulgar but widely used when ordinary terms like "disaster" or "fiasco" feel inadequate.

Clusterfucked describes a situation that has become hopelessly chaotic, disorganized, or mismanaged—the state of being in a clusterfuck. The term is military slang that spread to general use, typically describing operations, plans, or events gone catastrophically wrong through incompetence or poor coordination: {The whole project got clusterfucked when three departments started working at cross-purposes}. Vulgar.

Clustering is the act of gathering or forming into clusters—groups of similar things positioned close together. In computing and data science, clustering is a technique for grouping data points by similarity without predefined categories: {The algorithm uses clustering to identify customer segments}. People cluster around interesting displays; ideas cluster around themes; stars cluster in galaxies.

Clusters are groups of similar things positioned close together. Grapes grow in clusters. Stars form clusters in the night sky. Data analysts look for clusters in their datasets—natural groupings that emerge from proximity or similarity. The verb means to gather or form such groups: {Fans clustered around the stage}. A {cluster bomb} disperses smaller munitions over a wide area. A {clusterfuck} (vulgar) is a situation gone chaotically wrong.

A clutch is a tight grip or grasp: {She held the railing in a desperate clutch}. To clutch is to grab or hold tightly: {He clutched the steering wheel}. In machinery, a clutch connects and disconnects rotating shafts—notably in manual-transmission vehicles, where the clutch pedal disengages the engine from the drivetrain. A clutch of eggs is a batch laid together; a clutch of anything is a small group. In sports slang, clutch describes performance under pressure: {He hit a clutch three-pointer with seconds left}. A clutch bag is a small handbag without straps, held in the hand.

Clutched is the past tense of clutch, meaning to grasp or hold tightly, often with urgency or desperation: {She clutched the railing as the boat rocked}. The word suggests intensity—you clutch something you're afraid to lose or reaching for anxiously: {He clutched at any excuse}. In sports, clutched describes performing well under pressure: {She really clutched that last shot}.

Clutches is the plural of clutch, most often appearing in the figurative phrase {in the clutches of}, meaning under someone's control or power: {She fell into the clutches of a cult leader}. The image derives from clutching hands or claws gripping tightly. A clutch is also a group of eggs or chicks, and the pedal that engages a vehicle's transmission.

Clutching is the present participle of clutch—to grip tightly, often desperately or anxiously. Someone clutching a handbag holds it close; someone clutching at straws grasps for any slim hope. The word suggests tension or urgency: {She sat clutching the armrest during takeoff}. Clutching can also describe possessive or controlling behavior: {a clutching parent who won't let go}.

Clutter is a disordered accumulation of things, typically in a space where they shouldn't be: {The desk was buried under clutter}. The word suggests mess without purpose—stuff that crowds out what matters. To clutter is to fill a space this way: {Magazines cluttered the coffee table}. Figuratively, clutter can crowd the mind: {too much clutter to think straight}.

Cluttered describes a space filled with too many things in a disorganized way: {a cluttered desk}, {a cluttered apartment}. The meaning extends to anything overwhelmed by excess—a cluttered {mind} has too many competing thoughts, a cluttered {schedule} has too many commitments. To clutter is to fill a space this way: {Don't clutter up the counter with appliances}.

A coach is a person who trains athletes or teams: {a basketball coach}, {a life coach}. The word extends to anyone who guides development—vocal coaches, executive coaches. As a verb, to coach is to instruct or prepare someone: {She coached him through the interview}. Coach also means the economy section of an airplane or train, or a large enclosed carriage. A coach bag or purse refers to the luxury brand.

Coachable describes someone receptive to instruction and willing to improve. A coachable athlete listens to feedback and adjusts accordingly. The term appears in sports, business, and education contexts: {She's talented and coachable—that's a rare combination}. Being coachable implies humility and a growth mindset, valuing guidance over ego.

Coached is the past tense of coach, meaning to train, instruct, or prepare someone for a performance or challenge. Athletes are coached for competition, executives for interviews, witnesses for testimony. The word can imply legitimate guidance {She coached him through the presentation} or improper prompting {The lawyer was accused of coaching the witness}.

Coaches is the plural of coach. A coach is someone who trains athletes or teams: {The coaches met to discuss strategy}. In education, coaches guide improvement in specific skills: {literacy coaches}, {executive coaches}. Coach also means a bus for long-distance travel, a train car, or economy-class seating on an airplane. The verb means to train or instruct: {She coaches the debate team}.

Coaching is the work of guiding someone toward improvement in a skill, sport, or area of life. A coach provides instruction, feedback, and encouragement: {She's been coaching youth soccer for ten years}, {He hired a life coach to help with career decisions}. The term covers everything from athletic training to executive development to personal growth work.

A coachman is a person who drives a horse-drawn coach, typically as paid employment. The term belongs to an era when coaches were primary transportation for the wealthy. {The coachman waited outside while the guests dined.} Now largely historical, appearing in period fiction and formal carriage services.

Coachmen is the plural of coachman, a person who drives a horse-drawn coach or carriage. The term belongs to an era before automobiles, when coaches were the primary means of passenger transport for those who could afford them: {The coachmen waited outside the theater for their employers}. The word persists mainly in historical contexts.

Coal is a black or brownish-black solid fuel formed from ancient plant matter compressed over millions of years. It burns to produce heat and has powered industrial economies since the 1800s. To {rake someone over the coals} is to criticize them harshly. {Coals to Newcastle} describes something pointlessly redundant—Newcastle was England's coal-mining center.

The coalface is the exposed surface of coal in a mine where extraction actually happens—where miners physically cut into the seam. Figuratively, {at the coalface} means doing the practical, hands-on work of an enterprise rather than managing or theorizing about it: {nurses at the coalface of healthcare}, {teachers at the coalface}. The metaphor emphasizes direct contact with difficult reality. More common in British than American English.

A coalition is a temporary alliance of distinct groups or parties pursuing a common goal. Political coalitions form when no single party holds a majority: {The coalition government collapsed after six months}. The term applies beyond politics to any strategic partnership where separate entities join forces while retaining their identities: {a coalition of environmental groups}.

Coalitions are temporary alliances formed by distinct groups or parties to achieve a shared goal. Political coalitions unite parties that lack enough votes to govern alone: {The coalition government collapsed after six months}. The term applies beyond politics—military coalitions, business coalitions, coalitions of advocacy groups. What distinguishes a coalition from a merger is its provisional nature; members retain separate identities and may part ways once the objective is met or abandoned.

A coalmine is an underground excavation or system of tunnels where coal is extracted from the earth. Surface operations that strip away overlying rock are usually called strip mines rather than coalmines. {His grandfather worked in the coalmines of West Virginia}. A {canary in a coalmine} is an early warning sign—from the practice of bringing canaries underground to detect toxic gases.

A coalminer is a person who works in a coal mine, extracting coal from underground deposits. The work is physically demanding and historically dangerous, associated with black lung disease, cave-ins, and explosions. {His grandfather was a coalminer in West Virginia.} Also spelled as two words: coal miner.

Coalminers are workers who extract coal from underground or surface mines. The occupation shaped industrial economies and labor movements, with coalminers' unions among the most powerful in history. The work is physically demanding and historically dangerous, associated with black lung disease and mine collapses: {The coalminers emerged from the shaft covered in coal dust}. Usually spelled as two words: coal miners.

Coalmines are underground excavations where coal is extracted. The word is usually written as two words (coal mines) or hyphenated (coal-mines), but the solid form appears in older texts and British usage. {The coalmines employed thousands of workers in the region.}

Coalmining is the extraction of coal from underground deposits. The industry shaped regions like Appalachia, Wales, and the Ruhr Valley, creating distinct working-class cultures. Coalmining carries associations of dangerous labor, black lung disease, and labor struggles. Also spelled as two words: coal mining.

Coals are pieces of coal or, more commonly, glowing fragments of burned wood or fuel. A fire burns down to coals when flames subside but heat remains: {We roasted marshmallows over the coals}. To {rake someone over the coals} is to criticize them harshly. To {carry coals to Newcastle} is to bring something where it's already abundant—Newcastle being a historic coal-mining center. {Hot coals} appear in expressions about walking on fire or enduring discomfort.

Coarse describes texture that is rough, unrefined, or composed of large particles: {coarse sand}, {coarse fabric}, {coarse salt}. The word extends to manner and speech—coarse language is crude or vulgar, and a coarse person lacks refinement or delicacy. {His coarse jokes made everyone uncomfortable.} The opposite is fine in matters of texture, refined in matters of behavior.

Coarseness is the quality of being rough in texture, manner, or refinement. A fabric's coarseness comes from thick, uneven threads. In speech or behavior, coarseness suggests vulgarity or crudeness—lacking delicacy or tact: {The coarseness of his jokes made her uncomfortable}. Coarseness can also describe granular texture: {the coarseness of sea salt versus table salt}.

definition: A coast is the land along the edge of a sea or ocean: {the California coast}, {a drive down the coast}. To coast is to move without applying power—a bicycle coasting downhill, a car coasting to a stop. By extension, coasting means getting by with minimal effort: {He coasted through his senior year}. {The coast is clear} means no one is watching and it's safe to proceed.

Coastal describes things relating to or located near the coast—the land along an ocean or sea: {coastal erosion}, {coastal communities}, {a coastal highway}. The word often implies proximity to the sea without being directly on it. In American politics, coastal sometimes carries cultural overtones, contrasting densely populated ocean-bordering states with the interior: {coastal elites}.

Coasted is the past tense of coast. To coast is to move without effort or power—a car coasting downhill, a bike coasting after you stop pedaling. The word extends to getting by with minimal effort: {He coasted through the semester on natural talent}. The implication is often that more effort could or should have been applied.

A coaster is a small mat placed under a glass or cup to protect the surface beneath from moisture or heat. The word extends to things that coast: a roller coaster, a ship engaged in coastal trade, or a sled for coasting downhill. In casual use, someone coasting through life—expending minimal effort—might be called a coaster.

Coasters are small mats placed under drinking glasses to protect surfaces from moisture, heat, or scratches. They come in countless materials and designs—cork, cardboard, ceramic, novelty shapes. Separately, coasters are amusement park rides: roller coasters. A coaster can also be a ship that travels along coastlines rather than across oceans.

A coastguard is a maritime organization that patrols coastal waters, performing search and rescue, enforcing maritime law, and protecting borders. In the US, the Coast Guard is a branch of the armed forces. The term also refers to an individual member of such a service: {The coastguard spotted the capsized vessel}. Also spelled as two words: coast guard.

Coastguards is the plural of coastguard—members of a maritime organization responsible for coastal defense, search and rescue, and enforcing maritime laws. In the U.S., the Coast Guard is a branch of the armed forces; in Britain, it's a civilian rescue service. {The coastguards responded to the distress signal within minutes.}

Coasting is moving without applying power—a car coasting downhill, a bicycle coasting after you stop pedaling. The word extends to any situation where momentum carries you forward without effort: {He's been coasting on his early success}. This figurative use often implies criticism—that someone capable of more is settling for the minimum: {She coasted through the semester}.

A coastline is the boundary where land meets the sea—the outline of a coast as seen on a map or from above. The term often emphasizes shape and extent: {California's rugged coastline}, {the coastline stretches for hundreds of miles}. Coastlines shift with tides and erosion, making precise measurement famously difficult.

Coastlines is the plural of coastline—the boundary where land meets sea. A coastline traces the edge of a landmass: {The Pacific coastlines of North and South America run for thousands of miles}. Coastlines can be rocky, sandy, or marshy, and their lengths vary dramatically depending on how finely you measure their irregular edges.

Coasts is the plural of coast—the land along the sea. The coasts of a country are its shorelines: {The hurricane threatened both coasts}. As a verb form, coasts means to move without effort or propulsion: {She coasts downhill on her bicycle}, {He coasts through life on charm}. To coast is to rely on momentum rather than active exertion.

A coat is an outer garment with sleeves, typically worn for warmth or protection: {She grabbed her coat before heading out}. The word extends to any covering layer—a coat of {paint}, a coat of {fur} on an animal, a coat of {dust}. To coat something is to cover it with a layer: {Coat the pan with butter}.

A coathanger is a device for hanging clothes, typically a curved frame of wire, wood, or plastic with a hook at the top. Coathangers keep garments from wrinkling when stored in closets. Wire coathangers have grim associations with self-induced abortions before the procedure was legal. Also spelled as two words: coat hanger.

A coating is a layer of material applied to cover a surface—paint on walls, chocolate on candy, wax on a car. The term emphasizes the thinness and evenness of the layer: {a protective coating}, {a coating of dust}. To coat something is to apply such a layer: {The pills are coated with a smooth finish}.

A coatroom is a room where coats and other outerwear are checked or stored, typically at restaurants, theaters, or event venues: {We left our jackets at the coatroom}. Also called a cloakroom or checkroom.

Coats is the plural of coat—outer garments worn for warmth or protection, or layers covering a surface. A closet holds winter coats; a painter applies multiple coats. The verb form means to cover with a layer: {The chef coats the chicken in breadcrumbs}. {Sugar coats the pills to make them easier to swallow}.

A coattail is the back flap of a formal coat, extending below the waist. The plural coattails appears most often in the phrase {ride someone's coattails}, meaning to benefit from another's success or influence without earning it independently. In politics, a popular candidate's coattails can carry lesser-known running mates to victory: {She won on the governor's coattails}.

Coattailing is riding someone else's success or momentum. The image is of grabbing onto another's coattails to be pulled along. In politics, a lesser-known candidate coattails on a popular one's appeal: {She won by coattailing on the governor's landslide}. In investing, coattailing means copying the trades of successful investors rather than doing independent analysis.

Coattails are the two flaps at the back of a formal coat, hanging below the waist. The word appears most often in the figurative phrase {on someone's coattails}, meaning benefiting from another's success or popularity: {She rode into office on the president's coattails}. The image is of someone literally clinging to a more powerful person's coat as they advance.

A coauthor is someone who writes something jointly with another person. The term applies most often to books, academic papers, and screenplays: {She coauthored the study with three colleagues}. As a verb, to coauthor is to share authorship: {They coauthored a bestseller}. Also spelled co-author.

To coax is to persuade gently through patience, flattery, or persistent encouragement: {She coaxed the cat out from under the bed}. You coax a reluctant child into eating vegetables, coax information from someone hesitant to share. The word implies gradual success through soft persistence rather than force or demand. Things can also be coaxed into working: {He coaxed the old engine back to life}.

Coaxed is the past tense of coax, meaning to persuade gently through patience, flattery, or persistent effort. You coax a reluctant child into eating vegetables, coax a secret out of someone, or coax a stubborn engine into starting. The word implies careful, gradual persuasion rather than force: {She coaxed the cat out from under the bed}.

Coaxing is gentle, persistent persuasion—the kind that works through patience rather than force. You coax a reluctant child into eating vegetables, coax a car engine to turn over on a cold morning, coax information from someone who's hesitant to share. The word suggests a soft touch: {With some coaxing, she agreed to sing}. As an adjective, a coaxing tone or manner is warm and encouraging.

Cob collects several unrelated meanings. The most familiar is the central core of an ear of corn, the part that remains after the kernels are removed: {corn on the cob}. A cob is also a stocky, short-legged horse, or a male swan. In building, cob refers to a mixture of clay, straw, and water used to construct walls, an ancient technique still practiced today. A cobnut is a type of hazelnut, sometimes shortened to cob.

Cobalt is a hard, silvery-blue metallic element used in alloys, batteries, and blue pigments. The distinctive deep blue color it produces in glass and ceramics has made cobalt blue a standard color name: {a cobalt sky}, {cobalt eyes}. As an adjective, cobalt describes this vivid blue shade.

Cobble works as both noun and verb around the idea of rough assembly. A cobble is a rounded stone, larger than a pebble but smaller than a boulder, historically used for paving streets—hence cobblestone and cobbled streets. To cobble is to pave with such stones, or to make or mend shoes. More commonly now, to {cobble together} something is to assemble it roughly or hastily from available materials: {We cobbled together a proposal overnight}.

Cobbled describes a surface paved with cobblestones—rounded stones set into the ground to create a road or path: {We walked down the cobbled streets of the old town}. The word evokes historic European cities and charming antiquity. Separately, to cobble something together is to assemble it roughly or hastily from whatever materials are available: {He cobbled together a proposal the night before the deadline}.

A cobbler is a person who repairs shoes, or formerly, one who makes them. The word also names a type of deep-dish fruit dessert with a thick biscuit or cake topping: {peach cobbler}, {blackberry cobbler}. In British English, a load of cobblers means nonsense—from rhyming slang (cobbler's awls = balls).

Cobblers has two distinct meanings in English. A cobbler is someone who repairs shoes, or a baked fruit dessert with a thick crust: {peach cobbler}, {berry cobbler}. Separately, cobblers is British slang for nonsense or rubbish: {That's a load of cobblers}. This slang derives from rhyming slang "cobbler's awls" for balls.

Cobbles are rounded stones, larger than pebbles but smaller than boulders, historically used to pave streets. Cobblestone streets survive in old European city centers and historic districts. To cobble is to pave with such stones, or more commonly, to put something together roughly: {She cobbled together a meal from leftovers}. A cobbler repairs shoes—or makes fruit pies with a rough, stone-like crust.

A cobblestone is a naturally rounded stone used for paving roads and walkways, common in European cities before modern asphalt. The stones fit together to create durable but uneven surfaces: {The carriage rattled over the cobblestones}. Cobblestoned streets evoke historic charm or, for cyclists and pedestrians, an ankle-twisting nuisance.

Cobblestones are rounded stones used to pave streets and walkways, fitted together to create a durable surface. The term evokes old European city centers and historic districts: {We walked along the cobblestone streets of Prague}. Cobblestone roads are charming but notoriously rough on feet, wheels, and suspensions.

Cobbling is the work of making or repairing shoes, an old trade now largely replaced by mass manufacturing. The word also describes assembling something hastily from available parts: {We spent the afternoon cobbling together a proposal from old documents}. This improvised quality often implies the result is functional but inelegant.

A cobra is a venomous snake native to Africa and Asia, known for spreading its neck ribs into a hood when threatened. Cobras are iconic in snake charming, though the snake responds to movement rather than music. The king cobra is the world's longest venomous snake. Figuratively, cobra may describe something dangerous or poised to strike.

Cobras are venomous snakes known for their distinctive hood—a flattened neck region they spread when threatened. Native to Africa and Asia, they're iconic in snake charmer performances and appear widely in mythology and popular culture. The plural covers various species in the family Elapidae: {king cobras}, {spitting cobras}. {The cobra raised its hood and hissed.}

Cobs is the plural of cob, which has several unrelated meanings. Most commonly, a cob is the cylindrical core of an ear of corn: {corn on the cob}, {We threw the cobs to the pigs}. A cob is also a stocky, short-legged horse, or a male swan. In British dialect, a cob can be a round bread roll.

A cobweb is a spider's web, especially an old or dusty one found in neglected corners: {She brushed the cobwebs from the attic rafters}. Figuratively, cobwebs suggest mental dullness or confusion from disuse: {A morning walk helps clear the cobwebs}. Something cobwebby is thin, delicate, or gauzy.

Cobwebs are the dusty, abandoned webs of spiders, typically found in neglected corners and unused spaces. The word evokes disuse and neglect: {The attic was thick with cobwebs}. Figuratively, to {blow away the cobwebs} is to clear one's mind or refresh oneself after stagnation: {A morning walk blows away the cobwebs}.

Coca is a South American shrub whose leaves contain alkaloids including cocaine. Indigenous peoples have chewed coca leaves for centuries as a mild stimulant and to suppress hunger and altitude sickness. The plant is also the source of flavoring for Coca-Cola, though the cocaine has been removed since the early twentieth century. {Coca cultivation remains legal in Bolivia and Peru for traditional use.}

Cocaine is a powerful stimulant drug extracted from coca leaves. It produces intense euphoria and energy, followed by a sharp crash. Cocaine is typically snorted as a white powder, though it can be injected or smoked in crystalline form (crack). The drug is highly addictive and illegal in most countries. {He had a cocaine habit that cost him his job}.

A cock is a rooster—the adult male of domestic fowl. The word appears in compounds like {cockfight}, {cockcrow}, and {cockerel} (a young rooster). Cock also means a device for controlling liquid flow (a stopcock), or a slight tilt: {the cock of his hat}. The verb cock means to tilt or prepare: cock a {gun}, cock an {eyebrow}. If you cock up (British), you make a serious mistake. Cock is also vulgar slang for a penis, which makes the word ripe for double entendre and has gradually displaced its innocent uses in American speech.

Cockadoodledoo is the conventional English spelling of a rooster's crow—the loud call made at dawn or to assert territory. The word is onomatopoeic, imitating the sound itself. It appears most often in children's contexts: nursery rhymes, picture books, farm stories. {The rooster went cockadoodledoo and woke the whole farmyard.}

Cockamamie means ridiculous, implausible, or nonsensical: {What kind of cockamamie scheme is this?} The word dismisses ideas or plans as absurd or poorly thought out. It's informal and often affectionate in its mockery—used more for eye-rolling exasperation than genuine contempt. Also spelled cockamamy.

A cockatiel is a small Australian parrot with a distinctive crest and orange cheek patches, popular as a pet. Cockatiels are known for their whistling ability and can learn to mimic tunes and simple words. They're smaller and generally easier to care for than their cockatoo relatives: {The cockatiel bobbed its head when I walked in}.

Cockatiels is the plural of cockatiel, a small crested parrot native to Australia, popular as a pet. They're known for their distinctive orange cheek patches, whistling ability, and relatively gentle temperament compared to larger parrots: {The cockatiels in the pet shop were all singing}.

A cockatoo is a large parrot native to Australia and nearby islands, typically white or pale-colored with a distinctive crest of feathers that rises when the bird is excited or alarmed. Cockatoos are popular as pets, known for their intelligence, loud calls, and long lifespans: {The cockatoo shrieked whenever someone entered the room}.

Cockatoos are large parrots native to Australia and nearby islands, distinguished by their curved bills and prominent head crests that rise when the bird is alarmed or excited. Most species are white, though some are black or pink. They're popular as pets but notoriously loud and demanding. {The cockatoo shrieked whenever anyone entered the room.}

A cockatrice is a mythical creature, typically depicted as a two-legged dragon or serpent with a rooster's head. Medieval bestiaries described it as hatched from a cock's egg by a serpent, with a gaze or breath that could kill. The word now appears mainly in fantasy literature and games: {The party encountered a cockatrice in the dungeon}.

To cockblock is to interfere with someone's attempt to have sex or pursue a romantic connection. A cockblock is a person who does this, whether intentionally or obliviously: {My roommate totally cockblocked me last night}. The term is vulgar but common in casual speech, especially among younger people. It extends to any interference with someone's plans or goals: {Don't cockblock me on this promotion}.

Cockblocked is the past tense of cockblock—to interfere with someone's attempt to pursue a sexual or romantic connection. The blocking may be deliberate or accidental: {I was about to get her number when my drunk friend cockblocked me}. The term extends to any frustrating interference with someone's plans or desires.

A cockblocker is someone who interferes with another person's attempt to pursue a sexual or romantic connection. The interference may be intentional—a jealous friend, a protective sibling—or oblivious: {Her roommate was such a cockblocker, always hanging around}. The term is vulgar but common in casual speech, especially among younger people. The verb is cockblock.

Cockblocking is interfering with someone's attempt to pursue a romantic or sexual connection. A friend who monopolizes conversation when you're trying to flirt is cockblocking. The term originated in male contexts but applies broadly: {She kept cockblocking me every time I tried to talk to him}. Can describe intentional sabotage or oblivious interference.

Cocked is the past tense of cock, meaning tilted or prepared. A cocked {gun} is ready to fire. A cocked {hat} sits at an angle. To be half-cocked is to be poorly prepared—from a gun whose hammer isn't fully back and may misfire: {Don't go off half-cocked}.

A cockerel is a young rooster—a male chicken less than a year old. The word distinguishes immature males from full-grown cocks: {The cockerel was just starting to crow}. In British usage especially, cockerel remains common where Americans might simply say rooster.

A cockfight is a blood sport in which roosters fight each other, typically to the death, while spectators bet on the outcome. The birds are often fitted with metal spurs to inflict maximum damage. Cockfighting is illegal in most Western countries but persists in parts of Latin America, Southeast Asia, and elsewhere. {They raided an illegal cockfight in the warehouse district.}

Cockfighting is a blood sport in which roosters, often fitted with metal spurs, fight each other until one is killed or incapacitated. The practice has ancient roots and continues in parts of Latin America, Southeast Asia, and elsewhere, though it is illegal in most Western countries. Spectators typically gamble on the outcome.

Cockfights are organized contests in which roosters, often fitted with metal spurs, fight each other until one is killed or incapacitated. Once widespread entertainment, cockfighting is now illegal in most countries due to animal cruelty concerns, though it persists underground and in some cultures where it holds traditional significance: {Police raided an illegal cockfight in a rural barn}.
Cockiness is swaggering self-confidence, often excessive or unearned: {His cockiness rubbed people the wrong way}. The word suggests strutting bravado—the rooster who thinks he rules the yard.

A cockle is a small edible saltwater clam with a distinctive ribbed, heart-shaped shell. The shells wash up on beaches and have long been collected for decoration. The phrase {warm the cockles of your heart} means to give you a feeling of deep contentment or affection—the cockles here being an old anatomical term for the heart's ventricles, which resemble the bivalve's shell. As a verb, cockle means to pucker or wrinkle: {The paper cockled from the humidity}.

Cockles are small, heart-shaped bivalve mollusks with ribbed shells, gathered as food along sandy shores. The phrase {warm the cockles of one's heart} means to produce feelings of deep contentment or affection—the cockles here being the heart's ventricles, which the shell's shape resembles.

A cockleshell is the ridged, heart-shaped shell of a cockle—a small edible bivalve mollusk. The word evokes something small and fragile, particularly a tiny boat: {They crossed the channel in a cockleshell}. The nursery rhyme "Mary, Mary, Quite Contrary" features cockleshells as garden ornaments.

A cockney is a working-class Londoner, traditionally one born within earshot of the bells of St Mary-le-Bow church in the East End. The term also refers to their distinctive accent and dialect, marked by dropped H's, glottal stops, and rhyming slang where {apples and pears} means stairs and {dog and bone} means phone. {He spoke in broad cockney.} (Capitalized Cockney is interchangeable.)

A cockpit is the compartment where a pilot sits to control an aircraft, or where the driver sits in a racing car. On boats, the cockpit is a recessed area in the deck where the helmsman steers. The word originally meant a pit for cockfighting—a small enclosed space where combat takes place—which extended to any cramped area of intense activity: {the cockpit of Europe}, meaning a region of frequent warfare.

Cockpits is the plural of cockpit, which originally meant an arena for cockfighting. The enclosed, confined sense carried over to the pilot's compartment in an aircraft, the driver's area in a racing car, or the helmsman's station on a boat. A cockpit may also be any scene of intense conflict: {the cockpit of war}.

A cockroach is a flat-bodied insect with long antennae, known for infesting buildings and scavenging on food scraps. Cockroaches are notoriously hard to kill and associated with filth, though they thrive in clean environments too. Their survival skills make them symbols of resilience and disgust in equal measure: {The apartment had cockroaches}. To call someone a cockroach is to suggest they're repulsive or unkillable.

Cockroaches are insects of the order Blattodea, known for their flat, oval bodies, long antennae, and remarkable resilience. They thrive in warm, dark environments and are commonly associated with unsanitary conditions, though most species live outdoors and pose no threat to humans. A few species have adapted to human dwellings and are notoriously difficult to eliminate, giving rise to their reputation as survivors of nearly anything. {The apartment had a cockroach problem that no exterminator could solve.}

Cocks is the plural of cock—roosters, flow-control devices, or tilts. It's also vulgar slang for penises. The verb form means tilts or prepares: {She cocks her head when she's thinking}. The rooster sense remains standard in farming and cooking contexts, though speakers often reach for rooster to avoid snickering.

Cocksucker is a vulgar and offensive insult, literally meaning someone who performs oral sex on a penis but used as a general term of contempt: {That cocksucker stole my promotion}. The word is particularly harsh and can carry homophobic overtones when directed at men.

Cocksure means completely confident, often to the point of arrogance. Someone cocksure acts certain they're right, sometimes without justification: {He was cocksure he'd get the job}. The word carries a negative edge—cocksure people tend to be overconfident or smug. Despite appearances, the word has no vulgar origin; it likely derives from an old sense of cock meaning "secure" or "set."

A cocktail is a mixed alcoholic drink, typically combining spirits with other ingredients like juice, soda, or bitters: {She ordered a cocktail before dinner}. The word extends to other mixtures: a {shrimp cocktail} is an appetizer, a {cocktail of drugs} combines multiple medications. As an adjective, cocktail describes things associated with semiformal drinking occasions: {cocktail dress}, {cocktail party}, {cocktail hour}.

Cocktails are mixed alcoholic drinks combining spirits with other ingredients—juices, syrups, bitters, liqueurs. The term covers everything from a simple gin and tonic to elaborate creations requiring specialized equipment. A cocktail party is a social gathering where such drinks are served with light appetizers. Figuratively, cocktail describes any mixture: {a cocktail of medications}, {a toxic cocktail of stress and exhaustion}.

A cockup is a mistake or blunder, chiefly British: {The whole project was a complete cockup}. The verb form is cock up: {They really cocked up the arrangements}. The term is mildly vulgar but common in casual speech. Americans more often say fuckup or screw-up.

Cockups is the plural of cockup, a British slang term for a mistake or blunder, especially one that causes embarrassment or creates a mess of things. The word is mildly vulgar but widely used in casual British speech and writing. {There were several cockups in the planning stages that delayed the whole project.} {The IT department's cockups left us without email for two days.}

Cocky describes someone arrogant and overly self-confident, strutting like a rooster: {He's gotten cocky since his promotion}. The word implies swagger and bravado, often unearned. A cocky attitude might be charming in small doses but grating in excess.

Cocoa is the powder made from roasted cacao beans, used to make chocolate drinks and baked goods: {a cup of hot cocoa}, {cocoa powder}. The word also refers to the drink itself, typically served hot with milk: {The children warmed up with cocoa after sledding}. Cocoa and cacao refer to the same plant, though cacao often designates the raw form.

A coconspirator is someone who conspires alongside another—a partner in a plot or scheme. The term appears most often in legal contexts, where prosecutors charge defendants and their coconspirators with jointly planning crimes: {Her coconspirator testified against her in exchange for a lighter sentence}. Outside courtrooms, it can describe any collaborator in mischief or secret plans.

Coconut is the large seed of a tropical palm, with a hard brown shell, white flesh, and liquid center. The flesh is eaten fresh or dried (as copra), and coconut milk and oil are cooking staples. The fibrous outer husk yields coir for rope and matting. As a slur, coconut describes someone seen as betraying their ethnic identity—brown outside, white inside: {accused of being a coconut for assimilating}.

Coconuts are the large, hard-shelled fruits of the coconut palm, containing white flesh and a liquid called coconut water or coconut milk. The outer husk is fibrous, the inner shell woody, and the meat inside can be eaten fresh, dried, or processed into oil, cream, and flour. Coconut is a staple ingredient across tropical cuisines. In vulgar slang, coconuts refers to a woman's breasts or, offensively, to a person of color perceived as culturally assimilated to whiteness—brown on the outside, white on the inside.

A cocoon is the silky protective case spun by certain insect larvae, especially silkworms, as they transform into adults. The word extends to anything that wraps or shelters: {She cocooned herself in blankets}. To cocoon is to wrap protectively or to withdraw into comfortable isolation: {We spent the weekend cocooning at home}.

Cocooned means wrapped up snugly or protectively, like a caterpillar in its silk casing. The word usually suggests comfortable isolation from the outside world: {She spent the weekend cocooned in blankets}, {cocooned from the harsh realities of life}. The image is of being enclosed in something soft and safe, though it can imply excessive sheltering or withdrawal.

Cocooning is withdrawing into the comfort and privacy of one's home, avoiding social interaction with the outside world. The term evokes a caterpillar wrapped in protective silk. It gained currency in the 1980s to describe a cultural trend toward home-centered entertainment and domestic retreats: {After months of travel, I'm ready for some serious cocooning}.

Cocoons are the protective silk casings that caterpillars spin around themselves during metamorphosis into moths or butterflies. The word extends to any snug, protective wrapping: {She cocoons herself in blankets}. To cocoon is to wrap protectively or to withdraw into sheltered domesticity: {We spent the winter cocooning at home}.

Cod is a large cold-water fish prized for its mild white flesh, historically one of the most important commercial fish in the Atlantic. Cod fishing shaped economies and diets across northern Europe and North America for centuries. The word also appears in British slang: a cod accent or cod philosophy is fake or mocking, a parody of the real thing. {The cod was so plentiful they said you could walk across the sea on their backs.}

A coda is the concluding passage of a piece of music, distinct from the main structure and bringing the work to a close. By extension, any concluding section that rounds off a larger work: {The final chapter serves as a coda to the trilogy}. In linguistics, the coda is the consonant sound or sounds that end a syllable, following the vowel.

Codas is the plural of coda, a concluding passage or section. In music, a coda brings a piece to its close, often marked in scores with a special symbol. The term extends to any concluding element: {The film's coda showed the characters years later}. In linguistics, a coda is the consonant sound ending a syllable.

To coddle is to treat with excessive care or tenderness, often implying overprotection: {She coddled him through every minor illness}. The word carries a slight criticism—coddling someone may prevent them from developing resilience. Coddle also means to cook eggs gently in water just below boiling, though this culinary sense is far less common than the pampering one.

Coddled describes someone treated with excessive care or protection, shielded from difficulty or discomfort: {coddled children who can't handle criticism}, {the coddled rich}. The word carries disapproval—coddling produces weakness. A coddled egg is gently cooked in water just below boiling, the culinary sense from which the metaphor extends.

Coddles means to treat with excessive care or indulgence, often implying overprotection: {She coddles her youngest child}. The word carries a note of criticism—coddling someone may prevent them from developing resilience or independence. Coddle also means to cook eggs gently in water just below boiling, though this culinary sense is less common than the pampering one.

Coddling is treating someone with excessive care or protection, shielding them from difficulty or discomfort. The word carries a note of criticism—coddling implies the care is unwarranted or weakening: {Stop coddling him; he needs to learn responsibility}. Parents coddle children, institutions coddle students, critics accuse governments of coddling criminals. Separately, coddling is a gentle cooking method—eggs coddled in barely simmering water.

Code suggests a medium of communication that is at least one step removed from ordinary language, such as the instructions a computer uses to execute a program. When you code, you convert some message or information into a code. The related verb codify is helpful for remembering some other meanings of code, such as a systematic body of laws. A code may also be a short sequence of letters that has a particular function, like a coupon code.

A codebase is the complete collection of source code for a software project—all the files, scripts, and configurations that make up an application or system. Developers speak of working within a codebase, contributing to it, or learning their way around it: {It took me months to understand this codebase}. Large codebases may span millions of lines across thousands of files.

A codebook is a reference document that pairs encoded signals with their meanings—originally used for translating messages in cipher or military communications. In research, a codebook defines how data should be categorized or scored: {The codebook specifies how to code each survey response}. The term suggests systematic, authoritative translation between one system and another.

A codebreaker is someone who deciphers encrypted messages or cracks secret codes. The term evokes wartime cryptanalysts like those at Bletchley Park who broke the Enigma cipher. More broadly, codebreaker applies to anyone who solves puzzles or figures out hidden patterns: {She's a natural codebreaker—solved the riddle in seconds}.

Codebreakers are people who decipher encrypted messages or crack secret codes. The term evokes wartime cryptanalysts—those who broke enemy ciphers at places like Bletchley Park. More broadly, codebreaker applies to anyone who solves puzzles or unravels hidden patterns: {The codebreakers worked around the clock to decrypt the intercepted transmissions}.

Codebreaking is the work of deciphering encrypted messages or solving secret codes, typically without having the key that was used to create them. The term evokes wartime cryptanalysis, particularly the famous efforts at Bletchley Park during World War II, but it applies equally to modern cybersecurity and puzzle-solving. Someone engaged in codebreaking is a codebreaker. {The codebreaking team worked around the clock to intercept enemy communications.}

A codec is software or hardware that compresses and decompresses digital media—audio, video, or both. The term blends "coder" and "decoder." Different codecs optimize for different purposes: some prioritize file size, others quality, others speed. {The video won't play because you're missing the right codec.} Common examples include MP3 for audio and H.264 for video.

Coded means converted into a system of symbols or signals: {coded messages}, {coded data}. More commonly now, coded describes language that conveys meaning indirectly or to a particular audience while maintaining plausible deniability: {coded racism}, {coded appeals to voters}. A {coded message} might be encrypted, or it might simply mean one thing on the surface and another underneath.

Codeine is an opioid pain reliever derived from opium, weaker than morphine but effective for mild to moderate pain and cough suppression. It appears in prescription medications and some over-the-counter cough syrups, depending on the country. Like other opioids, codeine carries risks of dependence and is a controlled substance in most places.

A codename is a word or phrase used to conceal the true identity of a person, project, or operation. Military operations receive codenames to maintain secrecy: {Operation Overlord} for the D-Day invasion. Software companies use codenames during development before official product names are announced. Intelligence agencies assign codenames to agents and sources. The verb is to codename: {The project was codenamed Phoenix}.

Codenamed means designated by a secret or unofficial name, typically for military operations, intelligence projects, or confidential initiatives: {the codenamed operation to capture the fugitive}, {a codenamed surveillance program}. The past participle works as an adjective before what's being named: {a mission codenamed Neptune}.

Codenames are secret or substitute names used to conceal identity or purpose. Spies operate under codenames; military operations receive them to maintain secrecy: {Operation Overlord was the codename for the D-Day invasion}. In casual use, codename can mean any unofficial label: {Her codename for the annoying coworker was "The Interrupter"}. Also spelled as two words.

Codependence is a pattern in relationships where one person's sense of identity and worth becomes excessively tied to caring for or controlling another—often someone with an addiction or other dysfunction. The codependent person enables harmful behavior while neglecting their own needs: {Her codependence kept her in the marriage long after it became destructive}. Originally from addiction psychology, the term now applies broadly to any relationship marked by unhealthy emotional reliance.

Codependency is an unhealthy reliance on another person, especially one with addiction or behavioral problems. The codependent person's self-worth becomes tied to caring for, rescuing, or controlling the other: {Her codependency kept her in the marriage long after it turned abusive}. Originally from addiction recovery contexts, the term now applies broadly to any relationship where one person enables another's dysfunction while neglecting their own needs.

Codependent describes a relationship dynamic where one person's sense of identity or emotional wellbeing depends excessively on another, often someone with an addiction or dysfunction. The codependent partner enables harmful behavior while neglecting their own needs: {She realized she'd been codependent, making excuses for his drinking for years}. As a noun, a codependent is someone caught in this pattern. The term emerged from addiction recovery circles but now applies broadly to any relationship marked by unhealthy emotional reliance.

A coder is someone who writes computer code—a programmer. The term is slightly informal and often suggests hands-on work with actual code rather than higher-level software design or architecture: {We need a coder who knows Python}. In casual usage, coder and programmer are interchangeable, though some distinguish coders as more junior or task-focused.

Coders are people who write computer code—programmers who create software, websites, or applications. The term is informal and often implies hands-on technical work rather than high-level architecture: {We need more coders on this project}. Coder culture celebrates problem-solving, late nights, and caffeine.

Codes are systems of symbols, words, or rules that convey meaning. A building code establishes construction standards; a dress code sets clothing expectations; a moral code guides behavior. In computing, code is the instructions that make software run—programmers write code, debug code, break code. To code is to write such instructions or to encode information: {The message was coded to prevent interception}. A code can also be a secret system for communication: {They spoke in code so no one would understand}.

Codeswitch is to shift between languages, dialects, or registers depending on context—speaking one way at home, another at work, another with friends. The term originated in linguistics but has expanded to describe any situational adjustment of speech, behavior, or presentation: {She codeswitches effortlessly between her professional voice and her neighborhood slang}. The phenomenon is especially discussed regarding people from minority backgrounds navigating majority-culture spaces.

Codeswitching is alternating between languages, dialects, or registers within a conversation or even a single sentence. A bilingual speaker might switch from English to Spanish mid-thought; someone might shift from professional jargon to casual slang depending on audience. The term extends beyond language to any adaptive shift in behavior or presentation across social contexts: {She's codeswitching between her work persona and her weekend self}.

A codetalker is someone who transmits military messages in a language the enemy cannot understand. The term refers specifically to Native American soldiers—most famously Navajo—who used their indigenous languages as unbreakable codes during World War I and II: {The Navajo codetalkers were essential to American operations in the Pacific}.

Codetalkers were Native American military personnel who used their indigenous languages as unbreakable codes during wartime, most famously Navajo speakers in World War II. The languages' complexity and lack of written form made them impenetrable to enemy cryptanalysts. {The codetalkers transmitted tactical messages that Japanese intelligence never deciphered.} Also spelled code talkers.

A codeword is a word or phrase with a secret or prearranged meaning, used to communicate without others understanding: {The codeword for the operation was "Neptune"}. In espionage or military contexts, codewords classify sensitive information. More loosely, codeword describes any term that signals membership or shared understanding: {"States' rights" became a codeword for racial segregation}.

Codewords are words or phrases with secret meanings known only to certain people. Spies use codewords to conceal information; {the codeword for the operation was "Neptune"}. More loosely, codewords are terms that signal shared understanding within a group—political codewords like "family values" or "law and order" communicate specific positions to those attuned to them while seeming innocuous to others.

A codex is an ancient manuscript in book form, with bound pages rather than a scroll. The term typically refers to handwritten texts from classical antiquity or the medieval period: {the Codex Sinaiticus}, {a Mayan codex}. In modern usage, codex sometimes appears in gaming and fiction to mean a compendium of lore or rules.

A codger is an old man, usually with a note of affection or amusement: {The old codger still walks three miles every morning}. The word suggests someone set in their ways, perhaps eccentric or curmudgeonly, but essentially harmless. It's rarely used without "old" in front of it.

Codgers is the plural of codger, an informal and usually affectionate term for an old man, especially one who is quirky or set in his ways. The word nearly always appears with old: {a couple of old codgers playing chess in the park}. It suggests eccentricity more than feebleness.

Coding is the activity of writing computer programs—translating instructions into a language machines can execute. The term emphasizes the practical, hands-on work of programming: {She spent the weekend coding a new app}. In medical contexts, coding refers to a patient going into cardiac arrest: {The patient is coding}.

A codpiece is a pouch or flap covering the crotch in men's clothing, prominent in 15th- and 16th-century European fashion. Originally functional—allowing men to urinate without removing tight hose—codpieces evolved into elaborate, padded displays meant to emphasize the genitals. The term now appears mostly in historical contexts or costume design, though it sometimes surfaces as a joke about masculine vanity.

A codpiece is a pouch or flap covering the male genitals, attached to the front of men's breeches. Prominent in 15th- and 16th-century European fashion, codpieces evolved from practical garment closures into exaggerated, padded displays of masculinity. The word survives mainly in historical costume discussions and as a comic image of male vanity: {His ego needs its own codpiece}.

Codswallop is British slang for nonsense or rubbish—talk that's patently untrue or worthless: {That's a load of codswallop}. The word carries a dismissive, mildly comic tone, often used to reject an argument or excuse as ridiculous. It remains more common in British than American English.

Coed (also co-ed) describes something involving both sexes together, especially in education: {a coed dormitory}, {the school went coed in 1975}. As a noun, coed is a dated term for a female college student, from when women were the newcomers to previously all-male institutions. The noun now sounds quaint or condescending.

A coelacanth is a large, primitive fish once thought to have been extinct for millions of years until a living specimen was discovered in 1938. The fish has fleshy, limb-like fins and represents an ancient lineage that predates dinosaurs. Finding a living coelacanth was among the most dramatic zoological discoveries of the twentieth century.

To coerce is to force someone to do something through threats, pressure, or intimidation. The force isn't physical but psychological—compelling action against someone's will: {They coerced him into signing the contract}. In legal contexts, coercion can invalidate agreements made under duress. In computing, to coerce is to convert data from one type to another.

Coerced is the past tense of coerce, meaning forced or compelled through pressure, threats, or intimidation. Someone coerced into signing a contract did so unwillingly: {She claimed she was coerced into confessing}. A coerced confession is legally suspect because it wasn't given freely. The word implies the absence of genuine choice.

Coercing is using force, threats, or pressure to make someone do something against their will. The word implies compulsion rather than persuasion—the target complies not from agreement but from fear of consequences: {They accused the police of coercing confessions from suspects}. Governments coerce through law enforcement; individuals coerce through intimidation or manipulation.

Coercion is the use of force, threats, or pressure to compel someone to act against their will. It implies a lack of free choice—the coerced person complies because the alternative is worse: {The confession was obtained through coercion}. Legal and political contexts distinguish coercion from persuasion or consent. To coerce is the verb.

Coercive describes the use of force, threats, or intimidation to compel behavior. A coercive {regime} maintains power through fear. Coercive {tactics} in negotiations pressure someone into agreement against their will. The word implies illegitimate pressure—persuasion becomes coercive when it crosses into manipulation or compulsion: {The contract was signed under coercive circumstances}.

Coexist means to exist at the same time or in the same place, especially when the parties involved might otherwise be in conflict. Nations with different ideologies may coexist peacefully. Species coexist in an ecosystem. The word often implies tolerance despite differences: {Art and commerce can coexist}, {She learned to coexist with her chronic pain}.

Coexistence is the state of existing together, especially when the parties involved might otherwise be in conflict or competition. The term gained prominence during the Cold War as peaceful coexistence, describing the uneasy but nonviolent relationship between capitalist and communist nations. More broadly, it applies to any situation where different groups, species, or ideas occupy the same space without one eliminating the other: {The coexistence of wolves and livestock remains controversial in ranching communities.}

Coexisting describes things that exist together at the same time or in the same space. The term often implies peaceful or functional simultaneity despite differences: {coexisting species in an ecosystem}, {coexisting beliefs within a society}. It can suggest tension held in balance: {The two communities have been coexisting uneasily for decades}.

Coffee is the roasted and ground seeds of a tropical shrub, brewed into a bitter, caffeinated drink. The beverage is so central to daily life that coffee can mean a cup of it: {I need my morning coffee}. Coffee also names the social occasion: {Let's get coffee sometime}. As a modifier, coffee describes a medium brown color. A {coffee table} sits low before a sofa.

A coffeecake is a sweet cake meant to accompany coffee, typically eaten at breakfast or brunch. It's usually a single-layer cake with a crumbly streusel topping or swirl of cinnamon, sometimes with fruit or nuts: {She brought a coffeecake to the morning meeting}. Despite the name, coffeecake contains no coffee.

A coffeehouse is an establishment serving coffee and other beverages, often with light food. Coffeehouses have historically been gathering places for conversation, reading, and intellectual exchange—17th-century London coffeehouses functioned as early social clubs and business centers. Modern coffeehouses range from independent cafés to chains like Starbucks: {We met at a coffeehouse to discuss the project}.

Coffeehouses are establishments serving coffee and other beverages, often with light food. They function as social spaces for conversation, work, or relaxation: {We met at a coffeehouse to discuss the project}. Historically, coffeehouses served as centers of intellectual exchange and political discussion. The term feels slightly old-fashioned; *coffee shop* or *café* is now more common in everyday speech.

A coffeemaker is an appliance that brews coffee, typically by heating water and passing it through ground beans held in a filter. The term covers everything from simple drip machines to elaborate espresso setups: {The office coffeemaker runs all day}. Also spelled as two words.

A coffeepot is a container for brewing or serving coffee, typically with a handle and spout. The design varies from stovetop percolators to glass carafes that sit on warming plates. {She grabbed the coffeepot and refilled everyone's mug.}

A coffeeshop is a casual establishment serving coffee and often light food, similar to a café. The single-word spelling is particularly associated with Dutch establishments in the Netherlands, where coffeeshops are licensed venues that sell cannabis products alongside coffee—distinct from regular cafés or coffee bars. Outside this Dutch context, coffeeshop and coffee shop are used interchangeably for any place primarily serving coffee. {We stopped at a coffeeshop in Amsterdam.}

Coffeeshops are establishments that serve coffee and light refreshments. The term typically describes casual cafés where people gather to drink coffee, work, or socialize: {I spent the afternoon writing at a coffeeshop}. In the Netherlands, coffeeshops are licensed establishments where cannabis is sold and consumed—distinct from coffee houses, which serve only beverages.

A coffer is a strongbox or chest for storing valuables, especially money. In the plural, coffers refers to an organization's financial reserves: {The scandal drained the company's coffers}. In architecture, a coffer is a recessed panel in a ceiling or dome, typically square or octagonal, creating a grid pattern: {The coffered ceiling of the Pantheon}.

Coffers are chests or strongboxes for storing valuables, especially money. The word almost always appears in the plural, referring to financial reserves or treasury funds: {The scandal drained the party's coffers}, {The tax cut would add billions to corporate coffers}. A coffer is also a recessed panel in a ceiling or dome, used decoratively in architecture.

A coffin is a box in which a dead body is buried or cremated. The word traditionally refers to the six-sided, shoulder-tapered shape, while casket describes the rectangular style common in American funerals—though the terms are often used interchangeably. To coffin is to place in a coffin. {The final nail in the coffin} is the last in a series of problems that ensures failure.

Coffins are boxes designed to hold a dead body for burial or cremation. The word evokes the traditional elongated hexagonal shape—wider at the shoulders, tapering toward the head and feet—though rectangular caskets are now more common in American funeral practice. Coffin also works as a verb: to coffin a body is to place it in one. The phrase {nail in the coffin} refers to something that contributes to an eventual failure or downfall.

A cofounder is someone who establishes an organization or enterprise together with one or more others. The term appears most often in startup and tech contexts: {She was a cofounder of the company before it went public}. Also spelled co-founder.

A cog is one of the teeth or projections on the rim of a gear or wheel that meshes with another gear to transmit motion. By extension, cog refers to a person who is just one small part of a large organization or system, usually with the implication that they are unimportant or replaceable: {I'm just a cog in the machine}. The phrase captures the feeling of being a minor, interchangeable component in something much bigger than oneself.

Cognac is brandy distilled from wine in the Cognac region of France. The name is protected—only brandy from this area can legally be called cognac. It's aged in oak barrels and graded by age: VS, VSOP, XO. Cognac has become associated with luxury and celebration: {He poured two glasses of cognac after dinner}. The word sometimes appears generically for any fine brandy, though purists object.

Cognition is the mental process of acquiring knowledge and understanding through thought, experience, and the senses. It encompasses perceiving, reasoning, remembering, and problem-solving—the full range of mental activities by which we make sense of the world. {The study examined cognition in aging adults.} Cognitive is the adjective: {cognitive development}, {cognitive decline}.

Cognitive is a somewhat technical but very useful adjective to characterize things that happen in your mind. Cognitive ability refers to the mental activities that most people share, such as the ability to recognize and integrate input from your senses and act appropriately based on what you experience. Cognitive impairment is a term used to describe a temporary or permanent inability to do such things effectively: His high blood alcohol content caused cognitive impairment.

Cogs are the teeth on a gear wheel that mesh with other teeth to transmit motion. By extension, a cog is a small but necessary part of a larger system: {just a cog in the machine}. The phrase suggests being replaceable and insignificant within a vast mechanism—useful but interchangeable.

Cohabitation is living together, especially as an unmarried couple in a romantic relationship: {They chose cohabitation over marriage}. The word carries a slightly formal or legal tone—everyday speech more often says {living together}. Cohabitation can also describe any arrangement where people share a dwelling: {the uneasy cohabitation of three generations under one roof}.

Cohabiting means living together in the same residence, typically referring to an unmarried couple sharing a home as romantic partners. The term carries a slight formality, often appearing in legal or demographic contexts: {cohabiting couples}, {They've been cohabiting for three years}. It can also simply mean sharing living quarters without romantic implication, though this use is less common.

Coherence is the quality of fitting together logically and consistently. An argument has coherence when its parts connect and support each other. A story lacks coherence when events seem random or contradictory. The word applies to writing, thought, speech, or any system where unity matters: {The essay lacked coherence—ideas jumped around without transitions}. In physics, coherent light waves maintain a fixed phase relationship, as in lasers.

Coherent describes things that hold together logically and make sense as a unified whole. A coherent argument or explanation has parts that connect clearly and don't contradict each other. A person who is coherent speaks or thinks in a way that others can follow and understand: {After the accident, he was shaken but coherent}. In physics, coherent light consists of waves that maintain a constant phase relationship, as in a laser beam.

Cohesion is the quality of sticking together or forming a unified whole. In physics, it's the force that holds molecules of the same substance together—water's cohesion creates surface tension. More commonly, cohesion describes how well parts work as a unit: {The team lacked cohesion after the trade}. A cohesive argument holds together logically; a cohesive group acts in concert.

A cohort is a group of people sharing a common characteristic or experience, especially for purposes of study or analysis: {the 1990 birth cohort}, {a cohort of first-year medical students}. In ancient Rome, a cohort was a military unit of several hundred soldiers.
