The word now sometimes means companion or associate, though this use draws criticism from traditionalists: {The mayor and his cohorts dominated city politics}.

Cohorts are groups of people sharing a common characteristic, especially for research purposes: {The study followed a cohort of patients over ten years}. In demographics, a birth cohort shares an approximate birth year. The word often appears in academic and medical contexts. Informally, cohorts can mean companions or associates: {He arrived with his usual cohorts}.

A cohost shares hosting duties with another person. Television and radio programs often have cohosts who divide interviewing, commentary, and audience interaction: {She's been my cohost for three seasons}. The term extends to podcasts, events, and parties. To cohost is to serve in this role: {We're cohosting a fundraiser next month}.

Coiffed describes hair that has been styled or arranged, typically with care: {her perfectly coiffed blonde waves}, {a freshly coiffed look for the gala}. The word often implies professional styling or deliberate effort, and can carry a slightly formal or old-fashioned tone. Well-coiffed suggests polished appearance; elaborately coiffed suggests excess.

A coil is something wound in a spiral or series of loops—a coil of rope, a coil of wire, the coils of a snake. To coil is to wind into such a shape: {The snake coiled around the branch}. Coils appear in electrical and mechanical devices: the coils of a motor, a heating coil. An IUD is sometimes called a coil. {Mortal coil}, from Hamlet, refers to the troubles of earthly life—a different word meaning turmoil.

Coiled describes something wound in loops or spirals—a snake coiled to strike, a rope coiled on a deck, a spring coiled tight. The shape suggests stored energy or compact arrangement: {Her hair was coiled at the nape of her neck}. To coil is to wind into such a shape: {He coiled the hose after watering}.

Coils are loops or spirals formed by winding something flexible—rope, wire, a snake's body. A coil of rope sits wound in circles; a snake coils around its prey. Electrical coils are wound wire used in motors, transformers, and inductors. The word works as both noun and verb: {She coiled the hose after watering}. Metaphorically, something coils when it tightens with tension: {Fear coiled in her stomach}.

The basic meaning of coin, a metallic disk used as money, gives rise to many common expressions. Two sides of the same coin are two perspectives or aspects of the same thing. A coin toss is a way of deciding something, based on which side of a coin is facing up after tossing it into the air. If you coin a word or expression, you invent it to suit some occasion.

Coinage is the process of making coins, or coins collectively: {gold coinage}, {the coinage of ancient Rome}. By extension, coinage means the invention of new words or phrases, or the words themselves: {The term "nerd" is a relatively recent coinage}. The connection is that both coins and words are minted—stamped into standard form for circulation.

Coincide means to occur at the same time or occupy the same space. Events coincide when they happen together: {The conference coincides with my vacation}. Views or opinions coincide when they match or align: {Our interests happen to coincide}. The word often suggests chance rather than planning—things that coincide weren't necessarily meant to.

A coincidence is the occurrence of events that seem meaningfully connected but happen by chance. Two old friends booking the same flight without coordinating is a coincidence. The word often carries a sense of improbability or wonder: {What a coincidence that we both wore the same dress!} In more neutral usage, coincidence simply means things happening at the same time or place: {a coincidence of interests}.

Coincidences are events that occur together in a way that seems meaningful but lacks any apparent causal connection. The plural often emphasizes accumulation—one coincidence is unremarkable, but multiple coincidences invite suspicion or wonder: {Too many coincidences for my taste}. {The coincidences kept piling up until she couldn't ignore them}.

Coincidental describes things that happen or exist together by chance rather than design. Two events are coincidental when their co-occurrence is accidental: {It was purely coincidental that we showed up wearing the same dress}. The word often deflects suspicion of intention: {The timing was coincidental, not planned}. Something coincidental may seem meaningful but lacks causal connection.

Coined means newly created or invented, especially of words and phrases: {Who coined the term "robot"?} The metaphor comes from minting coins—stamping new money into existence. A {newly coined expression} has just entered the language. Something {freshly coined} suggests recent invention, while a {well-coined phrase} implies successful creation that caught on.

A coinflip is the act of tossing a coin and letting chance determine the outcome based on which side lands facing up. Because a fair coin has only two equally likely outcomes—heads or tails—a coinflip has become the standard method for making a random binary decision or settling a dispute impartially. {We decided who would go first with a coinflip.} Figuratively, calling something a coinflip means the odds are roughly fifty-fifty.

Coining is the process of creating new words or phrases: {The tech industry is constantly coining new terms}. The word comes from making coins—stamping metal into currency—and extends to stamping language into new forms. To coin a phrase introduces a new expression, though the formula {to coin a phrase} now often precedes clichés ironically.

Coins are small flat pieces of metal used as money, typically round and stamped with official designs. The word covers both the objects and the act of making them—governments coin currency, and by extension, to coin a phrase is to invent new language. {She flipped a coin to decide}. {The term was coined in the 1990s}. The other side of the coin refers to an alternative perspective on a situation.

Cojones is Spanish for testicles, borrowed into English as slang for courage or nerve—the same metaphorical leap as "balls." It often carries a tone of grudging admiration: {You have to admit, it took cojones to stand up to the boss like that}. The Spanish pronunciation (roughly co-HO-nays) is usually preserved.

Coke is the solid carbon residue left after coal is heated to drive off gases and tar. It burns hotter than coal and is essential in steelmaking for smelting iron ore in blast furnaces. To coke coal is to convert it through this heating process. Coke also serves as informal shorthand for cocaine: {He was caught with coke in his pocket}. (Capitalized Coke is the soft drink.)

A cokehead is a person who habitually uses cocaine, especially someone whose use has become compulsive or defining. The term is dismissive or contemptuous: {He turned into a cokehead in the eighties}. Like other -head formations (pothead, crackhead), it reduces a person to their drug of choice.

Cokeheads are habitual cocaine users. The term is informal and mildly disparaging, suggesting someone whose drug use has become a defining characteristic: {The club was full of cokeheads and party girls}. Like other -head compounds (pothead, crackhead), it implies regular use rather than occasional experimentation.

Cola is a carbonated soft drink flavored with kola nuts, citrus, vanilla, and spices—though the exact recipes of major brands remain proprietary secrets. Coca-Cola and Pepsi dominate the category, making cola nearly synonymous with soda in some regions: {Want a cola?} The word also refers to the kola nut itself, a caffeine-rich seed from African trees.

Colada most often appears in piña colada, the sweet rum cocktail made with pineapple juice and coconut cream. The Spanish word means strained, describing how the drink is prepared. Outside that phrase, colada rarely appears in English, though some Cuban coffee drinks use the term for coffee meant to be shared from a single cup.

A colander is a bowl-shaped kitchen utensil with holes or perforations, used for draining liquid from food—typically pasta, vegetables, or washed produce. The holes allow water to escape while retaining the solids: {She dumped the spaghetti into the colander in the sink}.

Cold is the go-to adjective when for the opposite of hot. Humans provide the conventional reference point for what is cold, namely a temperature that is too low for comfort. The common viral infection called a cold has no causal connection with things that are cold, other than people stay indoors when it’s cold outside and infect each other more easily. As an adverb, cold carries an idea of absoluteness or completeness: he was knocked out cold in the third round.

Coldblooded describes animals whose body temperature varies with their environment—reptiles, fish, amphibians. The figurative sense dominates: a coldblooded act is calculated and merciless, done without emotion or hesitation: {a coldblooded killer}, {coldblooded murder}. The spelling varies: cold-blooded, coldblooded, cold blooded.

To coldcock someone is to knock them out with a single punch, typically unexpected and to the head. The blow comes without warning—cold because the victim never saw it coming: {He coldcocked the guy before anyone could react}. Sometimes spelled as two words.

To coldcock someone is to knock them out with a sudden, hard punch, typically without warning. The blow usually lands on the head or jaw: {He coldcocked the guy before he even saw it coming}. The word emphasizes the abruptness and force of the hit—the victim goes down cold.

Coldhearted describes someone who lacks warmth, sympathy, or compassion toward others. A coldhearted person remains unmoved by suffering or appeals for help: {It was coldhearted of him to evict the family right before Christmas}. The word implies deliberate emotional distance rather than mere indifference.

Coldly describes doing something in a manner lacking warmth or friendliness. A person who speaks coldly shows no emotion or sympathy: {She coldly informed him the relationship was over}. The word suggests deliberate detachment—not passionate anger, but icy control: {He coldly calculated his next move}.

Coldness is the quality of being cold—low temperature or lack of warmth. More often, coldness describes emotional distance or unfriendliness: {There was a coldness in her voice that made him uneasy}. The coldness of a response, a stare, or a relationship suggests deliberate detachment or hostility rather than mere indifference.

Colds is the plural of cold, the common viral infection affecting the nose and throat: {She catches several colds every winter}. The phrase {out in the cold} means excluded or neglected. To {leave someone out in the cold} is to abandon or ignore them. {I've had three colds this year already.}

Coleslaw is a salad made from shredded raw cabbage, typically dressed with mayonnaise or a vinegar-based dressing. It often includes other ingredients like carrots, onions, or celery seed. Coleslaw is a staple side dish in American cuisine, appearing alongside barbecue, fried chicken, and sandwiches. {The pulled pork came with a generous helping of coleslaw.} The word comes from Dutch *koolsla*, meaning cabbage salad.

Colic is severe abdominal pain caused by spasms in the intestines or other organs. In adults, it often describes pain from gallstones or kidney stones: {renal colic}. Most commonly, colic refers to unexplained bouts of intense crying in otherwise healthy infants: {The baby has colic and screams for hours every evening}. The adjective is colicky.

A coliseum is a large stadium or arena for sports, concerts, or other public events. The word derives from the Colosseum in Rome, the ancient amphitheater where gladiatorial contests were held. Modern coliseums host everything from basketball games to rock concerts: {The band sold out the coliseum three nights in a row}.

Collab is informal for collaboration, especially a creative partnership between artists, brands, or content creators: {The album features a collab with a rising hip-hop artist}. As a verb, to collab is to work together on such a project: {We should collab sometime}. The word belongs to social media and entertainment industry vocabulary.

Collaborate means to work together toward a shared goal. Scientists collaborate on research, musicians collaborate on albums, writers collaborate on screenplays. The word carries positive connotations of pooling talents and resources: {We collaborated on the project for months}. During wartime, however, to collaborate is to cooperate treasonously with an enemy occupier—a collaborator aids the opposition.

Collaborating is working together with others toward a shared goal. The term is neutral in most contexts—artists collaborate on projects, scientists collaborate on research. But it carries a dark historical sense: during wartime, collaborating often meant cooperating with enemy occupiers, especially Nazi forces: {He was accused of collaborating with the Germans}. Context usually makes clear which sense is intended.

Collaboration is working together toward a shared goal. The word emphasizes joint effort and contribution: {The project was a collaboration between three universities}. In creative fields, a collaboration typically means a work produced by two or more artists: {Their collaboration resulted in a Grammy-winning album}. During wartime, collaboration takes on a darker sense—cooperating with enemy occupiers: {accused of collaboration with the Nazis}.

Collaborations are instances of people or groups working together toward a shared goal. The word emphasizes joint effort and pooled resources rather than individual achievement. In creative fields, a collaboration typically produces something neither party could have made alone: {The album features several collaborations with hip-hop artists.} Business collaborations may involve formal partnerships or informal cooperation. The term can carry positive connotations of synergy or, in contexts like wartime, negative ones suggesting complicity with an enemy.

A collaborator is someone who works jointly with others on a project or enterprise: {She was my collaborator on the research paper}. The word carries a second, darker meaning: one who cooperates with an enemy, especially an occupying force. A French collaborator during World War II aided the Nazis. Context usually makes clear which sense applies—creative partnership or treasonous cooperation.

Collaborators are people who work together on a shared project or goal. Scientists, artists, and writers often have collaborators: {She and her collaborators published the findings together}. The word carries a darker sense when applied to those who cooperate with an enemy or occupying force: {Nazi collaborators faced prosecution after the war}. Context usually makes clear which meaning applies.

Collabs is the plural of collab, informal shorthand for collaborations—joint creative projects between artists, brands, or creators. The term dominates social media and entertainment: {She's done collabs with every major YouTuber}, {The brand announced collabs with three designers}. Musicians release collab tracks; influencers post collab videos. The word signals casual, often commercial partnerships rather than deep artistic union.

A collage is an artwork made by gluing various materials—paper, photographs, fabric, found objects—onto a surface. The technique emphasizes juxtaposition and layering. By extension, any composite of disparate elements: {The film is a collage of interviews, archival footage, and animation}. The verb means to create such a composition.

Collagen is the main structural protein in connective tissue—the most abundant protein in mammals. It forms the fibrous framework of skin, tendons, cartilage, bones, and blood vessels. Collagen gives tissue its strength and elasticity. As we age, collagen production decreases, leading to wrinkles and joint stiffness. Collagen supplements and skincare products claim to restore what time depletes: {collagen peptides}, {collagen cream}.

Collages are works of art made by assembling diverse materials—paper, photographs, fabric, found objects—onto a surface. The technique emphasizes juxtaposition and layering: {She made collages from old magazines and ticket stubs}. Figuratively, anything assembled from disparate elements may be called a collage: {The film was a collage of documentary footage and interviews}.

Collapse is a sudden loss of structure or support. Buildings collapse when they give way; people collapse when they fall or faint. Systems, governments, and negotiations collapse when they fail completely. A collapsed lung has lost its ability to inflate. To collapse into something—a chair, tears, laughter—is to surrender to it suddenly: {She collapsed onto the sofa after work}. Figuratively, things collapse when distinctions between them disappear: {The two categories collapse into one}.

Collapsed is the past tense of collapse—to fall down or inward suddenly, to fail or break down. A building collapses under structural failure. A person collapses from exhaustion or illness. An argument collapses when its logic fails. {She collapsed into the chair after the long shift.} {The talks collapsed over disagreements about funding.}

Collapses is the verb and noun plural of collapse. To collapse is to fall down or cave in suddenly: {The roof collapses under the weight of snow}. A person collapses from exhaustion, illness, or shock. Systems, negotiations, or markets collapse when they fail abruptly: {The deal collapses without funding}. As a noun, a collapse is such a failure or breakdown: {a series of collapses in the housing market}.

Collapsible describes something designed to fold or compress into a smaller, more compact form: a collapsible {umbrella}, a collapsible {stroller}, collapsible {furniture}. The word implies intentional design—a collapsible item can be restored to full size, unlike something that merely collapses from weakness or damage.

Collapsing is the present participle of collapse—falling in on itself, giving way, or failing suddenly. A building may be collapsing under its own weight. A person collapsing is falling down, often from exhaustion or illness. Markets, negotiations, and governments can be collapsing when they fail rapidly: {The economy was collapsing around them}.

A collar is the part of a garment that encircles the neck. Other things that do this also get the name, like jewelry worn around the neck, or a bird’s differently colored neck feathers. Dogs wear collars around their necks for identification, or as a point of attachment for a leash. When police collar someone, they arrest them, sometimes by restraining them at the neck. If you collar someone, you compel them to address a topic that they may have been avoiding.

The collarbone is the bone that runs horizontally from the shoulder to the base of the neck, connecting the shoulder blade to the breastbone. Anatomists call it the clavicle. It's one of the most commonly broken bones in the body, typically from falls or impacts: {She fractured her collarbone in the cycling accident}.

Collarbones are the pair of long, slender bones extending horizontally from the base of the neck to the shoulders. Anatomically called clavicles, they connect the shoulder blades to the breastbone. Prominent collarbones are sometimes considered attractive: {She had striking collarbones that showed above her neckline}.

Collard is a leafy green vegetable with thick, slightly bitter leaves, closely related to kale and cabbage. Collard greens—often just called collards—are a staple of Southern American cooking, traditionally slow-cooked with ham hocks or bacon: {She made collards and cornbread for Sunday dinner}. The plant tolerates frost well and is harvested through winter in mild climates.

Collards are leafy green vegetables with thick, slightly bitter leaves, a staple of Southern American cooking. The leaves are typically slow-cooked with smoked meat: {She simmered collards with ham hocks for hours}. Also called collard greens. Related to kale and cabbage, collards tolerate heat better than most cool-weather greens.

Collared describes something fitted with or caught by a collar. A collared {shirt} has a band of fabric around the neck. A collared {dog} wears identification. In wildlife contexts, collared animals wear tracking devices: {collared wolves in Yellowstone}. Informally, to get collared is to be grabbed or arrested: {The cops collared him outside the bar}.

Collars are bands that encircle the neck. A shirt collar frames the face; a dog collar holds tags and a leash. The word extends to anything ring-shaped that encircles: a pipe collar, a bearing collar. To collar someone is to grab them by the collar or, more broadly, to apprehend: {Police collared the suspect outside the bank}. A collar can also mean an arrest itself. Blue-collar and white-collar distinguish manual laborers from office workers, based on traditional work attire.

Collateral is something pledged as security for a loan—if you default, the lender takes it: {The house serves as collateral for the mortgage}. The adjective means accompanying or secondary: {collateral damage} refers to unintended harm, especially civilian casualties in military operations. Collateral also means parallel or side-by-side: a {collateral branch} of a family descends from the same ancestor but through a different line.

A colleague is someone with whom you work, either in the same physical location or profession. Occasionally, colleague is used to describe people who simply belong to the same organization, such as a political party. Colleague is typically used by those who work at universities, making its relationship with college obvious—you just have to remember where the two extra vowels go.

Colleagues are people you work with professionally. The term implies a peer relationship—shared occupation, organization, or field—without suggesting close friendship: {I'm meeting some colleagues for drinks after work}. Unlike coworkers, which emphasizes shared workplace, colleagues can extend to others in your profession generally: {Her colleagues in academia respected her research}.

Collect means to gather or bring together. You collect stamps, debts, or your thoughts. A collector gathers items systematically; a collection is what's gathered. To collect someone is to pick them up: {I'll collect you at eight}. To collect yourself is to regain composure. A collect call charges the recipient rather than the caller. As an adverb, collect means with charges paid by the receiver: {Call collect}.

Collectable, also spelled collectible, describes items considered worth collecting, typically because of rarity, age, craftsmanship, or nostalgic appeal. As a noun, a collectable is such an item: {vintage toys and other collectables}. The term spans everything from stamps and coins to sports memorabilia and limited-edition figurines. What qualifies as collectable often depends on market trends and collector communities rather than inherent worth.

Collected describes a state of calm composure, especially under pressure: {She remained collected during the crisis}. Someone collected has gathered their thoughts and emotions rather than letting them scatter. The word also means brought together: {his collected works}, {the collected essays of James Baldwin}. To collect oneself is to regain composure after being rattled.

Collectible describes items valued and sought by collectors: {collectible coins}, {collectible cards}, {vintage collectible toys}. As a noun, a collectible is such an item—anything people accumulate as a hobby or investment, from stamps to sneakers to Star Wars memorabilia. The appeal often lies in rarity, nostalgia, or condition. Also spelled collectable.

Collectibles are items valued and sought by collectors—often for rarity, nostalgia, or potential appreciation rather than practical use. The category spans sports cards, coins, stamps, vintage toys, and limited editions. The term often suggests mass-produced items marketed to collectors, as opposed to antiques or fine art: {The shop sells comics and other collectibles}. Also spelled collectables.

Collecting is the activity of gathering objects of a particular type, typically as a hobby: {stamp collecting}, {She's been collecting vintage postcards for years}. The word emphasizes the ongoing practice rather than a single act of acquisition. What you accumulate becomes a collection.

Collection is the verbal noun of collect and denotes the activity, instance, or result of collecting. In some contexts, collection refers to the activity of trying to satisfy overdue debts, which is the work of collection agencies that send out collection letters. A group of objects that someone has collected is a collection and the holdings of a museum, a published anthology, and a recording or set of recordings may all be called this.

Collections are groups of objects gathered together, often systematically: {stamp collections}, {art collections}, {a collection of essays}. In retail, a collection is a designer's seasonal offerings. The word also means the act of gathering: {garbage collection}, {debt collection}. In computing, collections are data structures that group multiple elements.

Collective describes things done by or belonging to a group acting together: {collective bargaining}, {collective responsibility}, {collective memory}. A collective is a cooperative enterprise owned and operated by its members. In grammar, collective nouns name groups—*team*, *flock*, *committee*—that can take singular or plural verbs depending on whether the group acts as a unit.

Collectives are groups of people organized around shared ownership, decision-making, or purpose—especially those operating without traditional hierarchy. An artists' collective shares studio space and resources. A workers' collective owns the business jointly. The term often carries countercultural or leftist connotations: {The farm was run as a collective}. In grammar, collective nouns name groups: *flock*, *committee*, *jury*.

Collectivisation is the process of consolidating individual holdings into collective or state ownership, especially agricultural land. The term is most associated with Soviet policy under Stalin, when peasant farms were forcibly merged into collective farms (kolkhozes), resulting in widespread famine and millions of deaths. The spelling with -s- is British; American English uses collectivization.

Collectivism is a political and economic philosophy that prioritizes the group over the individual, emphasizing shared ownership, communal decision-making, and collective responsibility. It stands in opposition to individualism, which centers personal autonomy and private property. The term appears in discussions of socialism, communism, and cooperative movements, though critics use it pejoratively to suggest suppression of individual rights. {The commune operated on principles of collectivism, with all major decisions made by vote.}

Collectivization is the process of consolidating individual holdings—typically farms or businesses—into collective ownership, usually under state control. The term is most associated with Soviet agricultural policy in the 1930s, when peasant farms were forcibly merged into large collective farms (kolkhozy), resulting in widespread famine. {Stalin's collectivization campaign killed millions.} The word carries connotations of coercion and ideological rigidity.

A collector is someone who gathers objects of a particular type, typically for study, display, or personal satisfaction: {a stamp collector}, {an art collector}, {a collector of rare books}. The term extends to anyone or anything that collects: a {bill collector} pursues unpaid debts, a {tax collector} gathers revenue, and a {dust collector} is either a device or something that sits unused. In electronics, a collector is a terminal in a transistor.

Collectors is the plural of collector—people who gather objects of a particular type, whether for personal interest, investment, or professional purposes. Art collectors, stamp collectors, and coin collectors pursue their acquisitions with varying degrees of obsession: {Collectors drove the price to absurd heights at auction}. The term also covers those who collect debts or payments: {The collectors started calling within days of the missed payment}.

College has different meanings in different English-speaking countries, but its commonest meaning designates an institution of learning, usually one for post-secondary education: He’ll attend college in the fall. Occasionally, college designates people who come together for a specific, and usually specified purpose, as the Electoral College, which elects the U.S. president and vice president.

Colleges is the plural of college, an institution of higher education. In the United States, colleges grant undergraduate degrees and are often smaller than universities: {She visited several colleges before deciding where to apply}. In Britain, colleges may be secondary schools or constituent parts of universities. The word also names professional bodies: {the College of Cardinals}, {the Electoral College}.

Collegiate means relating to a college or its students: {collegiate athletics}, {collegiate life}. The word often describes the particular culture of undergraduate education—sports rivalries, campus traditions, social organizations. A collegiate atmosphere suggests youthful energy and academic community. Collegiate can also describe institutions organized like a college, with shared governance among members.

Collide means to strike against something with force, typically while both objects are in motion: {The two cars collided at the intersection}. The word extends to any forceful coming together—schedules collide when they conflict, ideas collide when they clash. Particles collide in physics experiments; cultures collide when they meet with friction.

Collided is the past tense of collide—to crash into something or someone. Vehicles collide on highways, particles collide in accelerators, people collide rounding corners. The word extends to abstract clashes: {Their ambitions collided}, {The deadline collided with the holiday}. When interests or schedules collide, they conflict in ways that create problems.

A collider is a device or thing that collides with something else. In physics, a particle collider accelerates subatomic particles to near light speed and smashes them together, revealing fundamental properties of matter: {The Large Hadron Collider discovered the Higgs boson}. In video games and software, a collider is an invisible boundary that detects when objects touch or overlap.

Collides is the third-person singular form of collide, which means to crash into something with force. Two objects collide when they strike each other while in motion: {The cars collided at the intersection}. The word extends to abstract conflicts as well—ideas, interests, or schedules can collide when they come into opposition or cannot coexist: {My work obligations collided with my vacation plans}. In physics, collide describes particles or bodies meeting with transfer of energy or momentum.

Colliding is the present participle of collide, describing objects or forces that crash into each other. Cars collide on highways, particles collide in accelerators, and air masses collide to create weather fronts. The word extends naturally to abstractions: {colliding interests}, {colliding worldviews}. When schedules or appointments are colliding, they overlap in a way that creates conflict. A collision course puts two things on track to collide, literally or figuratively.

A collie is a breed of herding dog with a long, pointed snout and thick coat, originally from Scotland. The rough collie has a luxuriant mane; the smooth collie has shorter fur. Collies are known for intelligence and trainability: {The collie rounded up the sheep with minimal commands}. The breed gained fame through Lassie, the fictional dog of film and television.

Collies are a breed of herding dog originating in Scotland, known for their intelligence, loyalty, and distinctive long, flowing coats. The breed comes in two varieties: the rough collie with its luxurious mane, and the smooth collie with shorter fur. Collies gained widespread popularity through the fictional character Lassie, cementing their image as devoted family dogs. {Our collie rounds up the kids like they're sheep.}

A collision is an impact between moving objects—two cars, two particles, two people rounding a corner. The word emphasizes forceful contact: {The collision totaled both vehicles}. Extended uses describe conflicts between incompatible things: a collision of {ideas}, a collision of {cultures}, {scheduling collisions}. In computing, a collision occurs when two pieces of data compete for the same space or identifier.

Collisions are instances of objects striking each other, often with force: {The collision totaled both cars}. The word extends to any clash or conflict—a collision of ideas, cultures, or interests. In computing, a collision occurs when two pieces of data compete for the same space or identifier. {They were on a collision course from the start.}

To collude is to cooperate secretly for deceptive or illegal purposes. The word implies conspiracy—working together while hiding the collaboration: {The companies colluded to fix prices}. Collude often appears in legal and political contexts: {evidence that the campaign colluded with foreign agents}. The noun is collusion.

Colluded is the past tense of collude, meaning to cooperate secretly for fraudulent or illegal purposes. The word implies deliberate conspiracy, often between parties who appear to be independent or even adversarial: {The contractors colluded to fix prices}, {Officials colluded with organized crime}. Collusion is the noun.

Colludes means secretly cooperates with others for a deceptive or illegal purpose. The word implies conspiracy—working together while hiding the partnership from those who would object: {The executives colluded to fix prices}. Someone who colludes is a party to collusion: {investigators alleged the campaign colluded with foreign agents}.

Colluding is cooperating secretly for fraudulent or deceptive purposes. The word implies conspiracy—working together while hiding the collaboration from those who would object: {The companies were colluding to fix prices}. Unlike legitimate cooperation, colluding carries inherent disapproval, suggesting the parties are cheating someone or subverting fair dealing.

Collusion is secret cooperation between parties for a deceptive or fraudulent purpose. The word implies wrongdoing—you don't collude to plan a surprise party. Legal contexts often involve collusion to fix prices, rig bids, or manipulate markets. Political collusion suggests covert coordination with foreign powers or adversaries: {The investigation found no evidence of collusion with Russia}.

Cologne is a type of scented liquid worn on the body, lighter and less concentrated than perfume. Originally associated with men's fragrances, though the distinction has blurred: {He splashed on some cologne before the date}. The word comes from the German city where it was first made. (Capitalized Cologne is the city.)
clues: What he dabs on after shaving

definition: Colognes is the plural of cologne, a lightly scented liquid applied to the skin. Cologne is less concentrated than perfume, typically containing 2-5% fragrance oils. The word comes from Cologne, Germany, where a distinctive citrus-based scent was first produced. Men's fragrances are often marketed as colognes regardless of concentration: {He had too many colognes on his bathroom shelf}.

A colon is the punctuation mark (:) used to introduce what follows—a list, an explanation, or an elaboration of what precedes it. In biblical and time notation, colons separate chapter from verse and hours from minutes: {John 3:16}, {4:30 PM}. The other colon is the large intestine, the final section of the digestive tract leading to the rectum.

A colonel is a military officer rank, typically below general and above lieutenant colonel. The word's spelling preserves its Italian origin while the pronunciation (/KER-nuhl/) reflects a different historical form. In American usage, colonel appears as an honorary title in some Southern states, and {Colonel Sanders} made it familiar as a corporate mascot. {The colonel addressed the troops at dawn.}

Colonial relates to colonies—territories under the political control of a distant nation. Colonial {architecture}, colonial {rule}, colonial {history}. The word often carries critical weight, implying exploitation or cultural imposition: {a colonial mindset}. In American usage, colonial describes the period before independence or its distinctive style: {colonial furniture}, {a colonial-era farmhouse}. A colonial is a person living in a colony, especially a settler from the ruling nation.

Colonialism is the practice of acquiring and maintaining control over foreign territories, typically exploiting their resources and people for the benefit of the colonizing power. European colonialism from the 15th through 20th centuries reshaped much of the world, leaving lasting effects on borders, economies, and cultures. The adjective colonial describes this era or its remnants: {colonial architecture}, {colonial attitudes}. In extended use, colonialism describes any relationship of domination and exploitation: {cultural colonialism}, {digital colonialism}.

A colonialist supports or participates in colonialism—the policy of acquiring and maintaining control over foreign territories and their peoples. The term carries strong negative connotations, implying exploitation and cultural domination: {colonialist attitudes}, {colonialist powers}. As a noun, it describes someone who advocates or benefits from colonial rule: {The colonialists extracted resources while suppressing local traditions}.

Colonialists are people who support or participate in colonialism—the policy of establishing control over foreign territories and peoples. The term typically describes Europeans who settled in or administered colonies in Africa, Asia, and the Americas: {The colonialists imposed their language and customs on the indigenous population}. In contemporary use, colonialist often carries critical weight, implying exploitation or cultural domination.

Colonies is the plural of colony. A colony is a territory controlled by a distant power, or a group of people who settle in such a territory: {the thirteen colonies that became the United States}. Colonies also refers to groups of organisms living together: {ant colonies}, {colonies of bacteria}. In casual use, colonies of anything cluster in one place: {colonies of artists in Greenwich Village}.

Colonisation is the British spelling of colonization—the act of establishing control over a territory and its people. A nation colonises by sending settlers, extracting resources, and imposing its laws and culture on indigenous populations. The term now carries heavy connotations of exploitation and cultural destruction: {the colonisation of Africa by European powers}. Extended uses describe any takeover or spread: {the colonisation of the gut by bacteria}, {corporate colonisation of public space}.

Colonise is the British spelling of colonize. To colonise is to establish control over a territory and its people, typically by settling there and imposing outside governance: {Britain colonised much of Africa in the 19th century}. The word extends to any takeover or spreading occupation: {Weeds colonised the abandoned lot}. In biology, organisms colonise new habitats when populations establish themselves there.

Colonised is the British spelling of colonized, the past tense of colonize. To colonize is to establish control over a territory and its people, typically by a foreign power: {India was colonised by the British for nearly two centuries}. The word extends to any takeover or spread: bacteria colonise a wound, invasive species colonise new habitats. In contemporary discourse, colonised often carries critical weight, highlighting exploitation and cultural erasure.

A coloniser is a person or nation that establishes control over a foreign territory, typically exploiting its resources and imposing authority over indigenous populations. The term carries strongly negative connotations in contemporary usage, emphasising the harm done to colonised peoples through displacement, cultural destruction, and extraction of wealth. In modern discourse, coloniser often appears as a pointed accusation: {The protesters called the developers colonisers for displacing longtime residents}. This is the British spelling; American English uses colonizer.

Colonisers is the British spelling of colonizers—people who establish control over foreign territory and its inhabitants. The term carries strong negative connotations, evoking exploitation, displacement of indigenous peoples, and cultural destruction: {The colonisers imposed their language and religion on the native population}. In contemporary discourse, coloniser often appears as an accusation or insult.

Colonising is the British spelling of colonizing—establishing control over a foreign territory and its people, typically by settlement and exploitation of resources. European powers colonised much of Africa, Asia, and the Americas. The word extends to any takeover: {Invasive species are colonising the lake}. To colonise can also mean simply to establish a presence: {Bacteria colonise the gut within hours of birth}.

A colonist is a person who settles in a colony—a territory claimed and controlled by a distant power. The term applies both to early settlers who establish colonies and to later inhabitants who maintain them: {The colonists struggled through their first winter}. Unlike immigrant, colonist emphasizes the extension of one nation's authority over another land, often displacing indigenous peoples.

Colonists are people who settle in a new territory while maintaining ties to their country of origin. The term applies both to those who establish colonies and to their descendants who continue living there: {The colonists declared independence from Britain}. The word carries different weight depending on perspective—colonists saw themselves as settlers and pioneers; indigenous peoples experienced them as invaders.

Colonization is the process of establishing control over a foreign territory and its people. A nation sends settlers to occupy land, extract resources, and impose its political and cultural systems. European colonization of Africa and the Americas reshaped global demographics and power structures. The term extends to any takeover of space: bacterial colonization of a wound, colonization of Mars. In postcolonial discourse, colonization often emphasizes exploitation and displacement of indigenous peoples.

Colonize means to establish a colony—a settlement of people from one country in foreign territory. European powers colonized much of Africa and the Americas, displacing indigenous populations. The word extends to any takeover of space: {Weeds colonized the abandoned lot}. Bacteria colonize surfaces. In contemporary discourse, colonize often carries critical weight, implying exploitation or cultural imposition: {Tech companies colonizing public spaces with advertising}.

Colonized describes a place or people that have been brought under the control of a foreign power. A colonized {territory} is settled and governed by outsiders. Colonized {peoples} have had their land, resources, or governance taken over. The term extends to cultural domination: {colonized minds} have internalized the values of their colonizers. In biology, a surface colonized by bacteria has been populated by them.

A colonizer is someone who establishes control over a foreign territory and its people, typically through settlement, exploitation, or displacement of indigenous populations. The term carries strong negative connotations, emphasizing the harm done to colonized peoples: {The colonizers seized land that had been inhabited for centuries}. In contemporary discourse, colonizer often appears as a pointed critique of historical injustice and its ongoing effects: {You're on colonizer land}. It may be used loosely to describe anyone perceived as appropriating or dominating spaces where they don't belong.

Colonizers are people who establish control over foreign territories and their populations. The term carries strong negative connotations, emphasizing exploitation and displacement of indigenous peoples: {The colonizers imposed their language and religion on the native population}. In contemporary usage, colonizer often appears as a pointed criticism of historical and ongoing power imbalances: {You can't just show up and take over—don't be a colonizer}.

Colonizes is the third-person singular of colonize, meaning to establish control over a territory and its people. A nation colonizes when it sends settlers to occupy foreign land: {Britain colonized much of North America}. The word extends to biological contexts—bacteria colonize a wound, invasive species colonize an ecosystem. Figuratively, something colonizes when it spreads to dominate: {Corporate jargon has colonized everyday speech}.

Colonizing is the act of establishing control over a territory and its people, typically by a foreign power. Settlers colonize lands by displacing or subjugating indigenous populations: {European powers spent centuries colonizing Africa and the Americas}. The term extends to any takeover of space: bacteria colonizing a wound, invasive species colonizing an ecosystem. In contemporary discourse, colonizing often carries critical weight, implying exploitation or cultural erasure.

A colonnade is a row of columns supporting a roof, entablature, or series of arches, typically forming a covered walkway or portico. Colonnades appear frequently in classical architecture, lining the exteriors of temples, government buildings, and grand public spaces. {The museum's colonnade provided welcome shade on hot afternoons.} The term can also describe any imposing row of upright forms, such as a colonnade of trees lining a formal garden path.

Colonnades is the plural of colonnade, a row of columns supporting a roof or series of arches. Colonnades appear in classical architecture—temples, palaces, covered walkways—where they create shaded passages and impressive visual rhythm: {The colonnades of St. Peter's Square embrace visitors approaching the basilica}. The term extends to any similar arrangement of evenly spaced vertical elements.

A colonoscopy is a medical procedure in which a flexible camera is inserted through the rectum to examine the colon for polyps, cancer, or other abnormalities. The patient undergoes bowel preparation beforehand—typically a liquid diet and strong laxatives. Colonoscopies are standard screening for adults over fifty: {My doctor scheduled me for a colonoscopy}.

A colony is a territory controlled by a distant country, with settlers or administrators sent to govern it: {Britain's American colonies declared independence in 1776}. The word extends to groups of organisms living together—a colony of ants, a colony of bacteria, a leper colony. Artists or writers may form colonies, gathering in a shared location to work.

Color (colour in British English) is a visual quality of objects, owing to distinctions our eyes perceive in various wavelengths of light. Put more simply, a color is any of the many named variations of this light that we distinguish, such as red, gold, orange, or blue. When you color something, you add one or more colors to it. Color may also describe emotional qualities. Prejudice colored his account means that his account was influenced by prejudice.

Colorblind describes inability to distinguish certain colors, most commonly red from green. The condition is usually inherited and more common in men. Figuratively, colorblind means deliberately ignoring distinctions of race or ethnicity: {a colorblind society}, {colorblind hiring policies}. Critics argue such approaches can overlook systemic inequalities. Also spelled colour-blind.

Colorblindness is the inability to distinguish certain colors, most commonly red and green. The condition is usually inherited and far more prevalent in men. Figuratively, colorblindness means disregarding racial or ethnic distinctions: {The company claims colorblindness in its hiring practices}. Critics argue such colorblindness can ignore real inequities rather than transcending them.

Colored describes something that has color, especially color that's been added: {colored pencils}, {brightly colored fabric}. As a past tense, it means influenced or affected: {His judgment was colored by personal experience}. As a noun or adjective referring to people, colored was once a standard American term for Black people but is now dated and offensive in most contexts, though it persists in organizational names like the NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People). In South Africa, Coloured (capitalized) remains an official demographic category for people of mixed ancestry.

Colorful describes something with many colors, especially bright or vivid ones: {a colorful garden}, {colorful illustrations}. By extension, colorful applies to anything lively or striking: a colorful {personality}, a colorful {past}. Colorful {language} is profane or obscene—the expression is often euphemistic: {The coach was known for his colorful vocabulary}.

Coloring is the application of color to something, or the colors themselves: {the coloring of autumn leaves}, {artificial coloring in food}. A person's coloring is their skin tone, hair, and eye color considered together: {She has her mother's coloring}. A coloring book contains outline drawings for children to fill in with crayons or markers. Figuratively, coloring suggests influence or bias: {His account was colored by resentment}.

Colorism is discrimination based on skin tone, typically favoring lighter skin over darker skin within the same racial or ethnic group. Unlike racism, which operates between racial categories, colorism creates hierarchies within them: {She faced colorism from her own family for being darker than her siblings}. The phenomenon appears across many cultures and often intersects with standards of beauty, economic opportunity, and social status.

A colorist is someone who works professionally with color. In film and photography, the colorist adjusts and enhances the color palette of images in post-production: {The colorist gave the film its distinctive blue-gray look}. In comic books and animation, a colorist adds color to line art. In hair salons, a colorist specializes in dyeing and highlighting. A colorist may also be someone who discriminates based on skin color, particularly within racial groups—favoring lighter or darker complexions.

Colorization is the process of adding color to black-and-white images, particularly photographs or films. The practice became controversial in the 1980s when studios began colorizing classic movies: {Turner's colorization of Casablanca sparked outrage among film purists}. Digital tools have made colorization increasingly sophisticated, applied to historical photos to make the past feel more immediate.

Colorize means to add color to something originally in black and white, especially photographs or films. The process uses digital or manual techniques to transform monochrome images: {They colorized classic Hollywood movies for modern audiences}. The practice is sometimes controversial among film purists who prefer original black-and-white cinematography. Also spelled colourise in British English.

Colorized describes black-and-white film or photographs that have had color added digitally or through other techniques: {the colorized version of Casablanca}, {colorized footage from World War II}. The practice emerged in the 1980s and sparked debate among film purists who considered it a violation of the original work's artistic integrity.

Colorless describes something lacking color—transparent, neutral, or dull. Water and glass are colorless. A colorless {personality} or colorless {prose} lacks vividness or interest. The word implies absence where color might be expected or welcomed: {The winter landscape looked colorless and bleak}. British spelling: colourless.

Colors are the visual qualities we perceive through differences in light wavelength—red, blue, green, yellow, and so on. The word extends to any distinguishing visual element: {The team wore their colors proudly}. To color is to apply pigment or, figuratively, to influence: {His past colored his judgment}. A {person of color} is non-white. To {show your true colors} is to reveal your real character. {With flying colors} means with complete success.

Colossal means extremely large—beyond ordinary bigness into the realm of the monumental. The word evokes ancient statues of impossible scale: {a colossal statue}, {colossal columns}. It extends readily to abstractions: {a colossal mistake}, {colossal arrogance}, {colossal waste of time}. The emphasis is on impressiveness or excess, not mere measurement.

Colossi is the plural of colossus—gigantic statues or figures, or by extension, anything of enormous size or power. The word evokes ancient monumental sculpture: {the colossi of Memnon}, {colossi guarding the temple entrance}. Figuratively, it describes dominant entities: {the colossi of the tech industry}. The anglicized plural colossuses is also used.

A colossus is something enormous in size, power, or importance. The word originally referred to a giant statue, especially the Colossus of Rhodes—a bronze figure of the sun god that stood at the harbor entrance in ancient Greece. Now it describes anything of overwhelming scale: {a colossus of industry}, {an intellectual colossus}. The plural is colossi or colossuses. (Capitalized Colossus may refer to specific statues, machines, or fictional characters.)

Colour (color in American English) is a visual quality of objects, owing to distinctions our eyes perceive in various wavelengths of light. Put more simply, a colour is any of the many named variations of this light that we distinguish, such as red, gold, orange, or blue. When you color something, you add one or more colors to it. Colour may also describe emotional qualities. Prejudice coloured his account means that his account was influenced by prejudice.
clues: Property that distinguishes red from blue

definition: Colourblind describes the inability to distinguish certain colours, most commonly red and green. The condition is usually inherited and more prevalent in men. Figuratively, colourblind means deliberately ignoring differences, especially racial ones: {a colourblind society}, {colourblind hiring practices}. This figurative use is sometimes criticized for implying that noticing race is itself problematic. British spelling of colorblind.

Colourblindness is the inability to distinguish certain colours, most commonly red from green. The condition is usually inherited and far more prevalent in men than women. Figuratively, colourblindness means disregarding race or ethnicity: {The judge claimed colourblindness in her rulings}. This figurative sense is now contested—critics argue it ignores systemic inequalities. Also spelled colorblindness.

Colourful describes things with many colours or vivid hues: {a colourful garden}, {colourful fabrics}. Figuratively, it means lively, interesting, or distinctive: {a colourful character}, {colourful language}. The latter phrase often euphemizes profanity or vulgarity. British spelling of colorful.

Colouring is the British spelling of coloring. It refers to the process of adding colour to something, or to the colours themselves: {the bird's distinctive colouring}. Colouring also means complexion or skin tone. A colouring book contains outlined drawings for children to fill in. Food colouring is dye added to alter appearance.

Colourism is discrimination or prejudice based on skin tone, typically favoring lighter skin over darker skin within the same racial or ethnic group. Unlike racism, which operates between racial groups, colourism creates hierarchies within communities—lighter-skinned individuals often receive preferential treatment in employment, dating, and social status. The phenomenon appears across many cultures worldwide. {She wrote about colourism in the Black community and how it affects self-esteem.} The spelling colorism is standard in American English.

A colourist is someone who works professionally with colour. In film and photography, a colourist adjusts and grades images to achieve a particular look: {The colourist gave the film its distinctive blue-gray palette}. In publishing, a colourist adds colour to illustrations, particularly comic books. In hair salons, a colourist specializes in dyeing and highlighting. British spelling of colorist.

Colours is the British spelling of colors—the visual qualities of objects produced by different wavelengths of light. The word covers the same range of meanings: literal hues {the colours of the rainbow}, figurative associations {show your true colours}, and military flags {trooping the colours}. In British usage, colours appears in {colour film}, {colour scheme}, and {colourful language}.

A colt is a young male horse, typically under four years of age. The term extends to young males of related animals like donkeys and zebras. Figuratively, colt describes an inexperienced young man or a rookie athlete: {The team's colts showed promise in preseason}. A colt may also be a young, spirited person of either sex. (Capitalized Colt is the firearms manufacturer.)

Colts is the plural of colt, a young male horse typically under four years old. The term extends to young or inexperienced people, especially in sports: {The colts on the junior varsity showed promise}. A colt revolver is a firearm made by the Colt company. {Three colts grazed in the pasture.} (Capitalized Colts usually refers to the Indianapolis NFL team.)

Columbine is a flowering plant with distinctive spurred petals, common in gardens and mountain meadows. The flowers have an unusual shape—five petals with backward-projecting spurs—often in blue, purple, pink, or white. {Wild columbine grew along the rocky trail.} The name comes from a Latin word for dove, which the flower supposedly resembles. (Capitalized Columbine refers to a stock character in commedia dell'arte, or to the 1999 school shooting in Colorado.)

A column is a vertical structural pillar that supports weight in buildings, or any similarly shaped upright object. The word extends to vertical arrangements of text, numbers, or data on a page or screen: {newspaper columns}, {spreadsheet columns}. A column of soldiers or vehicles is a formation moving in a line. In journalism, a column is a regular feature by a particular writer expressing opinions or covering a specific topic: {She writes a weekly advice column}. The person who writes such a feature is a columnist.

A columnist is a writer who contributes a regular series of articles to a newspaper, magazine, or website. Unlike reporters who cover breaking news, columnists offer analysis, opinion, or specialized commentary on topics like politics, sports, or advice: {a syndicated columnist}, {She's been the paper's food columnist for fifteen years}.

Columnists are writers who regularly contribute signed opinion pieces or commentary to newspapers, magazines, or websites. Unlike reporters who present news objectively, columnists offer personal perspectives, analysis, or expertise on topics ranging from politics to sports to lifestyle: {The paper's columnists weighed in on the scandal}. A columnist typically has a recurring slot or "column."

Columns are vertical structural supports—pillars holding up a building or monument. The term extends to anything arranged vertically: a column of {soldiers} marching in formation, a column of {numbers} in a spreadsheet, or a column of {text} on a page. In newspapers and magazines, a column is also a regular feature by a particular writer: {She writes a weekly advice column}.

A coma is a state of deep unconsciousness from which a person cannot be awakened. It results from severe injury, illness, or poisoning affecting the brain: {He remained in a coma for three weeks after the accident}. Separately, coma is an astronomy term for the hazy envelope surrounding a comet's nucleus.

Comas is the plural of coma, a state of deep unconsciousness from which a person cannot be awakened. Comas result from severe injury, illness, or drug overdose: {Patients in comas may still hear voices around them}. Separately, coma names the hazy envelope surrounding a comet's nucleus, or an optical aberration causing blurred images—both pluralize the same way.

Comatose describes someone in a coma—a state of deep unconsciousness from which they cannot be roused. More loosely, it describes extreme lethargy or unresponsiveness: {After Thanksgiving dinner, we were all comatose on the couch}. The figurative use suggests being so sluggish as to be effectively unconscious.

A comb is a toothed implement for untangling and styling hair. To use this implement is to comb. To comb a place is to examine it very carefully, usually because you are looking for something. One thing that slightly resembles a comb also gets the name: the fleshy growth on the heads of some birds and reptiles. A comb that doesn’t resemble any others is the mass of hexagonal cells built by honeybees – that is, the honeycomb.

Combat is fighting, especially organized armed conflict between military forces. The word carries more formality than fight: {hand-to-hand combat}, {combat troops}, {combat zone}. As a verb, to combat something is to fight against it: {measures to combat inflation}, {combating misinformation}. A combat can also be a struggle or contest between opposing forces or ideas.

A combatant is someone engaged in combat—a fighter in a war or armed conflict. International law distinguishes combatants from civilians, with combatants being legitimate military targets who may also be held as prisoners of war. The term extends to anyone actively fighting in any struggle: {The combatants in the custody battle hired expensive lawyers}.

Combatants are people engaged in fighting, especially soldiers or others actively participating in armed conflict. The term distinguishes those who fight from civilians or noncombatants: {The treaty protected combatants who surrendered}. In broader use, combatants are any parties in a dispute or contest: {Both combatants in the debate scored points}.

Combative describes someone eager to argue or fight. A combative {witness} challenges every question. A combative {stance} signals readiness for conflict. The word suggests aggression that may be excessive or unwarranted: {She got combative when I asked about the missing funds}. Less negatively, it can mean spirited or pugnacious in competition.

Combination is what you get when you join separate things together. A combination of {factors} led to the crisis. In reference to a lock, the combination is the specific sequence of numbers that opens it. Combination underwear is a single garment covering both torso and legs. To work {in combination} is to work together: {Diet and exercise work in combination}.

Combinations is the plural of combination—things joined or mixed together. A combination of factors produced the result. Combinations are also one-piece undergarments covering the torso and legs, now old-fashioned: {He stripped down to his combinations}. In mathematics, combinations are selections of items where order doesn't matter, unlike permutations.

To combine is to bring things together into a unified whole: {Combine the ingredients in a bowl}, {The two companies combined to form a conglomerate}. Things that combine merge or join forces. A combine is also a large farm machine that harvests grain—so called because it combines the operations of cutting, threshing, and cleaning in one pass.

Combined describes things joined or merged together to form a single unit or work toward a common effect. A {combined effort} pools resources from multiple sources. {Combined income} totals what two or more people earn. The word emphasizes unity from previously separate elements: {Their combined weight exceeded the elevator limit}. As a verb form, combined means brought together: {We combined our savings to buy the house}.

Combing is the act of drawing a comb through hair to smooth, untangle, or arrange it. The word extends to any thorough, methodical search: {Police are combing the area for evidence}. Combings are the loose hairs collected in a comb after use.

Combo is short for combination, typically referring to a grouped set offered together. In restaurants, a combo meal bundles items at a reduced price: {I'll have the burger combo}. In music, a combo is a small jazz or dance band. In video games, a combo is a rapid sequence of attacks chained together for extra damage. The word keeps its casual, clipped feel across all uses.

Combos is the plural of combo, an informal clipping of combination. A combo meal bundles a main dish with sides and a drink. In music, a combo is a small jazz or dance band. In video games, a combo is a rapid sequence of moves executed together for amplified effect: {I finally landed that 12-hit combo}. The word appears wherever things are bundled or chained together.

A combover is a hairstyle that attempts to cover a bald spot by growing hair long on one side and combing it across the scalp. The style rarely fools anyone and often invites ridicule: {His combover flapped in the wind}. Also spelled comb-over.

A combover is a hairstyle that drapes hair from one side of the head across a bald spot to create the illusion of coverage. The attempt rarely fools anyone: {His combover lifted in the wind, exposing what he'd tried to hide}. The style has become a symbol of male vanity and denial about hair loss.

Combs is the plural of comb—a toothed implement for arranging hair or fiber. Combs also names the fleshy red crests atop roosters' heads. As a verb, combs means to draw a comb through: {She combs her daughter's hair each morning}. To comb through something is to search it thoroughly: {He combs through job listings daily}.

To combust is to catch fire or burn. The word appears most often in scientific or technical contexts describing ignition: {The fuel combusts at high temperatures}. Spontaneous combustion occurs without an external spark. Figuratively, someone might combust from rage or embarrassment—an exaggerated image of internal explosion: {I thought my mother was going to combust when she saw the mess}.

Combustion is the process of burning—a chemical reaction between a substance and oxygen that produces heat and light. A car engine runs on internal combustion, igniting fuel in enclosed cylinders. {Spontaneous combustion} occurs when materials ignite without an external spark. Figuratively, combustion describes explosive emotional states or volatile situations.

Come is among the most common verbs in English, indicating movement toward the speaker or a destination: {Come here}. {She came to the party}. Come conveys arrival, occurrence, or result: {Spring has come}. {It came as a surprise}. {Come what may}. The word appears in countless expressions: {come and go}, {come to terms}, {come of age}, {come clean}. In vulgar slang, come means to have an orgasm: {She came twice}. As a noun (often spelled cum), it means semen or orgasm: {There was come on the sheets}.

A comeback is a return to prominence after a period of absence or decline: {The singer staged a remarkable comeback after years out of the spotlight}. In conversation, a comeback is a quick, clever reply to criticism or an insult—the retort you wish you'd thought of in the moment. To {make a comeback} or {mount a comeback} is to recover from a losing position, especially in sports.

Comebacks are returns to prominence after a period of decline or absence. An aging athlete stages a comeback; a politician mounts one after scandal. The word also means quick, clever replies to criticism or insult: {I couldn't think of a good comeback until hours later}. Both senses share the idea of answering something—adversity or an opponent.

A comedian is someone who performs comedy—telling jokes, doing impressions, or otherwise trying to make audiences laugh. Stand-up comedians work alone on stage with a microphone. The word also applies more broadly to anyone who habitually cracks jokes: {He's the comedian of the family}. In older usage, comedian meant any comic actor, especially in theater.

Comedians are performers whose craft is making people laugh, whether through stand-up routines, sketch comedy, improvisation, or comedic acting. The term applies broadly—from club comics working small rooms to household names filling arenas. {My favorite comedians are the ones who find humor in everyday absurdities.} Someone might be called a comedian outside professional contexts when they're being funny or, sarcastically, when they think they're funnier than they are: {Nice try, comedian.}
clues: People paid to make audiences laugh

definition: Comedies is the plural of comedy—works intended to amuse or entertain, typically with happy endings. The term covers stage plays, films, television shows, and literary works: {Shakespeare wrote comedies as well as tragedies}. In classical usage, comedy contrasted with tragedy; today it broadly encompasses anything meant to be funny, from romantic comedies to stand-up specials.

A comedown is a decline in status, importance, or intensity—a letdown after something better: {Working retail after running my own company was quite a comedown}. In drug slang, a comedown is the period of fatigue and depression following a high: {The comedown from ecstasy hit her hard the next morning}.

Comedowns are declines or letdowns from elevated states. After drug-induced highs, the comedown brings fatigue, depression, or irritability as the body readjusts: {The comedown from ecstasy lasted two days}. More broadly, any deflating return to ordinary reality after excitement or success: {Returning to work after the trip was a real comedown}.

Comedy is entertainment designed to amuse—plays, films, or performances meant to provoke laughter. The term contrasts with tragedy and drama: {I'm in the mood for a comedy tonight}. A comedy of errors involves absurd mishaps. Beyond entertainment, comedy describes any ludicrous situation: {The meeting devolved into comedy}. Stand-up comedy features a solo performer delivering jokes to a live audience.

A comer is someone who arrives or approaches: {all comers welcome}. More often, comer describes someone showing promise or gaining momentum—a rising talent: {She's a real comer in the tech industry}. The phrase {first come, first served} treats arrivals by order; {all comers} means anyone who shows up.

A comet is a celestial body that orbits the sun, distinguished by a glowing tail of gas and dust that streams behind it when near the sun. Comets appear periodically—Halley's comet returns roughly every 76 years. Figuratively, someone who rises to sudden prominence and fades quickly might be called a comet: {She blazed through Hollywood like a comet}.

Comets are icy bodies that orbit the sun, developing glowing tails of gas and dust as they approach it. Ancient observers saw them as omens. Unlike planets, which follow predictable paths, comets appear irregularly—some returning on cycles of decades or centuries, others passing through the solar system only once. {Halley's Comet won't return until 2061.}

Comeuppance is a deserved punishment or misfortune that befalls someone who has behaved badly. The word carries a sense of poetic justice—the idea that wrongdoers eventually face consequences for their actions. {After years of cheating investors, the CEO finally got his comeuppance when he was arrested.} It's almost always used with "get" or "have" and appears most often when the speaker takes satisfaction in someone's downfall.

Comeuppances is the plural of comeuppance, a deserved punishment or misfortune that befalls someone who has behaved badly. The word implies justice catching up with wrongdoers: {After years of cheating investors, he finally got his comeuppance}. Usually singular—multiple comeuppances suggests several people each receiving their due: {The film ends with the villains all getting their comeuppances}.

Comfort is a state of ease and contentment, free from pain or anxiety. Physical comfort comes from soft chairs, warm blankets, adequate food. Emotional comfort comes from reassurance and support: {She found comfort in her friend's words}. To comfort someone is to console them. A comfort is something that provides ease: {the comforts of home}. Cold comfort is consolation so slight it hardly helps.
clues: State of being at peaceful ease

definition: Comfortable describes a state of physical or mental ease. A comfortable chair supports the body well. A comfortable room has pleasant temperature and furnishings. Comfortable extends to psychological states: {I'm not comfortable with that decision}. Someone who is comfortable financially has enough money to live without worry. The word implies adequacy rather than luxury—comfortable is less than lavish but more than merely tolerable.

Comfortably is the adverb form of comfortable, describing actions done with physical ease, adequate resources, or psychological security. If you sit comfortably, your body is at ease; if you live comfortably, you have enough money to meet your needs without strain. {She settled comfortably into the chair.} The word often implies a margin of safety or excess: winning comfortably means winning by more than enough. Someone comfortably numb has dulled their senses to avoid discomfort.

A comforter is a thick, quilted bedcover filled with down or synthetic material, used for warmth. In British usage, the same item is often called a duvet. Comforter also means one who provides comfort: {She was a comforter to the grieving family}. In religious contexts, the Comforter refers to the Holy Spirit.

Comforters are thick, quilted bed coverings filled with down, synthetic fibers, or batting—the top layer that provides warmth. In older or religious usage, a comforter is one who gives comfort or consolation; the Holy Spirit is sometimes called the Comforter. {She pulled the comforter up to her chin and fell asleep.}

Comforting describes something that provides solace or eases distress: {a comforting thought}, {comforting words from a friend}. Food or activities can be comforting when they restore a sense of security or well-being: {There's something comforting about a bowl of soup on a cold day}. The word often carries warmth and reassurance rather than mere relief.

Comforts are things that provide physical ease or emotional solace. The word often appears with modifiers: {creature comforts} are material pleasures like good food and soft beds; {cold comfort} is consolation that fails to console. {Home comforts} are the familiar amenities of domestic life. To take comfort in something is to find reassurance there: {She took comfort in the routine}.

Comfy is informal for comfortable, almost always referring to physical ease—a comfy {chair}, comfy {clothes}, a comfy {bed}. The word has a cozy, casual quality that formal *comfortable* lacks. {I'm getting comfy on the couch}. It rarely describes emotional comfort or financial security the way *comfortable* can.

Comic describes something intended to provoke laughter or amusement: a comic {novel}, a comic {performance}. A comic is a person who performs comedy, or a publication featuring sequential illustrated panels—what longer form becomes a comic {book}. The plural comics refers to the newspaper section containing comic strips: {I always read the comics first}. Comic overlaps with comical, though comical more often describes things unintentionally funny.

Comical describes something that provokes laughter or amusement, often through absurdity or incongruity: {The dog's comical expression made everyone laugh}. It differs slightly from comic—comical emphasizes the effect of being funny, while comic can describe intent or genre. Something comical is often unintentionally amusing: {His comical attempts at dancing}.

Comics are sequential images, usually with text, that tell a story or convey humor—from newspaper strips to graphic novels to superhero serials. The form ranges from single-panel gags to elaborate narratives. Comic also works as an adjective meaning funny or related to comedy, and as a noun for a comedian: {She's a stand-up comic}. The phrase {the comics} typically refers to the comics section of a newspaper.

Coming is the present participle of come. It describes approaching, arriving, or imminent occurrence: {The train is coming}. {The coming year looks promising}. In vulgar usage, coming means approaching orgasm: {I'm coming!}

A comma is a punctuation mark (,) indicating a pause or separation between elements in a sentence. Commas set off clauses, separate items in lists, and clarify meaning: {Let's eat, Grandma} versus {Let's eat Grandma}. In numbers, commas mark groups of three digits: {1,000,000}. A comma can also be a brief pause or interval in music or speech.

All meanings of command suggest power, authority, or advantage. Command is the right or authority to order, and if you have it, you can issue commands. Computers respond to commands, that is, instructions it receives from a program or user. Command of a skill is mastery of it. When you command someone or something, your expectation is that your wish will be satisfied. If a place commands a view, it is situated so as to provide one.

A commandant is the commanding officer of a military installation, training facility, or prison camp. The term carries formal authority: {the commandant of the Marine Corps}, {the camp commandant}. It appears frequently in military academy contexts and historical accounts of prisoner-of-war camps.

Commanded is the past tense of command, meaning to give an authoritative order or to hold a position of control. A general commanded troops; a view commanded attention. {She commanded them to stop}. {The hill commanded the valley below}. The word carries weight and formality—you command when you have the authority to expect obedience.

Commandeer means to seize something for official or military use, typically without permission: {The army commandeered civilian vehicles during the evacuation}. More loosely, it means to take control of something for your own purposes: {My sister commandeered the TV remote}. The word carries a sense of authority or forcefulness, whether legitimate or playfully asserted.

Commandeered is the past tense of commandeer, meaning to seize something for official or military use, or more loosely, to take control of something without asking: {The police commandeered a civilian's car to chase the suspect}. The word often carries a sense of urgent necessity or casual entitlement: {She commandeered the remote and changed the channel}.

Commandeering is seizing property or personnel for military or official use. Soldiers commandeer vehicles, buildings, or supplies during wartime.
