In pharmacy, compounding is preparing customized medications by mixing ingredients. The word also describes making something worse: {His lies only compounded the problem}.

Compounds are things made by combining two or more elements. In chemistry, a compound is a substance formed when atoms of different elements bond together—water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. In grammar, a compound word joins existing words: {blackbird}, {mother-in-law}. A compound sentence links independent clauses. As a verb, to compound means to combine or intensify: {His lies only compounded the problem}. A compound can also be an enclosed area containing buildings: {a military compound}, {a prison compound}—this sense comes from a different word entirely.

Comprehension is the ability to understand something: Children with good language comprehension learn to read earlier than others do. The word is used in the same way as a countable noun to describe a test of comprehension: The reading comprehension was very difficult. Comprehension has a second meaning with a different emphasis: the ability to appreciate the full range of something. In this sense it is typically used in the phrase beyond comprehension: The damage that was done was beyond comprehension.

Comprehensive is primarily an adjective that characterizes something as being complete, wide in scope, or all-embracing: The comprehensive plan is intended to steer the city’s growth for the next five years. An independent panel conducted a comprehensive review of the case. As a noun, comprehensive is usually short for comprehensive exam, an academic exam that is intended to measure students’ progress or competence. In British English, a comprehensive is a school that admits pupils of all abilities.

To compress is to press or squeeze together, reducing volume or size. Air compresses in a cylinder; files compress for storage. A compress (noun, stressed on the first syllable) is a pad applied to the body for therapeutic purposes: {a cold compress on the swelling}. Figuratively, to compress information is to condense it: {She compressed three chapters into one}.

Compressed means reduced in size or volume by pressure. Air can be compressed into tanks; files can be compressed to save storage space. Compressed {schedules} pack more into less time. The word suggests something squeezed tighter than its natural state: {compressed lips}, {a compressed summary}. In audio and video, compressed formats sacrifice some quality for smaller file sizes.

Compression is the act of pressing or squeezing something into a smaller space. In physics, compression is the opposite of tension—force that pushes inward rather than pulling apart. Digital compression reduces file sizes by eliminating redundant data: {audio compression}, {video compression}. In medicine, compression applies pressure to an injury or body part: {compression bandage}, {compression socks}. Engine compression refers to the squeezing of fuel and air before ignition.

Compressions are acts of pressing or squeezing together, reducing volume or space. In CPR, compressions are the rhythmic pressing on a patient's chest to manually pump the heart: {She performed thirty compressions before giving rescue breaths}. Data compression reduces file size. Physical compressions can refer to bandaging that applies pressure to injuries, or geological forces compacting rock layers.

A compressor is a machine that increases the pressure of a gas by reducing its volume: {The air compressor powers the pneumatic tools}. In audio engineering, a compressor reduces the dynamic range of a signal, making quiet sounds louder and loud sounds quieter—essential for radio broadcasting, music production, and podcasts. Refrigerators and air conditioners use compressors to circulate coolant.

Compressors are machines that reduce volume by applying pressure. An air compressor forces air into a smaller space, storing it under pressure for tools and equipment. A gas compressor moves natural gas through pipelines. In audio, a compressor reduces the dynamic range of sound, evening out loud and quiet passages: {The vocals need more compression}. Refrigerators and air conditioners use compressors to circulate coolant.

Compromise is an agreement reached when each side gives up something it wanted. To compromise is to settle by mutual concession: {They compromised on the price}. Compromise also means to expose to risk or suspicion: {The leak compromised national security}. A compromised {immune system} is weakened. To find oneself in a {compromising position} is to be caught in circumstances that suggest misconduct.

Compromised describes something whose integrity, security, or effectiveness has been damaged or undermined. A compromised {immune system} can't fight infections properly. A compromised {password} has been exposed to unauthorized parties. A compromised {position} is one weakened by revelation or circumstance: {His authority was compromised when the emails leaked}. The word often implies vulnerability that wasn't immediately apparent—the breach may have happened before anyone noticed.
clues: Integrity has been called into question

definition: Compromises are settlements reached by mutual concession—each side gives up something to resolve a dispute. The word also names things that fall short of an ideal: {The design was a compromise between cost and quality}. To compromise is to reach such an agreement, or to damage reputation or security: {The leak compromised the investigation}. A compromised {system} has been breached.

Compromising describes something that exposes a person to suspicion, disgrace, or damage to reputation. A compromising {position} suggests sexual impropriety—being caught in circumstances that look bad. Compromising {evidence} or {photos} could be used against someone. The word implies vulnerability to blackmail or scandal: {The leaked emails contained compromising information about several executives}.

Comps is short for several things depending on context. In gambling, comps are complimentary perks—free rooms, meals, or drinks casinos offer to keep players gambling: {The casino comped our hotel room}. In real estate, comps are comparable sales used to estimate property value: {The comps in this neighborhood suggest we're priced right}. In publishing or events, comps are complimentary copies or tickets. To comp something is to provide it free.

Compulsion is an irresistible urge to do something, often against one's better judgment. The word carries a sense of being driven by forces beyond conscious control: {She felt a compulsion to check the locks again}. In psychology, compulsions are repetitive behaviors performed to relieve anxiety, as in obsessive-compulsive disorder. Compulsion also means the act of compelling—forcing someone to do something: {They acted under compulsion, not by choice}.

Compulsions are urges to perform certain actions, especially repetitive behaviors driven by anxiety or obsessive thoughts. In clinical contexts, compulsions pair with obsessions in OCD—the obsessive fear of contamination produces compulsive handwashing, for instance. More loosely, a compulsion is any strong, hard-to-resist impulse: {She felt a compulsion to check her phone every few minutes}.

Compulsive describes behavior driven by an irresistible urge rather than rational choice. A compulsive {liar} lies even when truth would serve better. A compulsive {gambler} can't stop despite mounting losses. The word suggests psychological compulsion—the person feels unable to control the behavior. As a noun, a compulsive is someone who acts this way: {He's a compulsive when it comes to cleaning}.

Compulsory describes something that is required or mandatory, leaving no room for choice. Compulsory {education} laws require children to attend school; compulsory {military service} means citizens must serve in the armed forces. The word often appears in legal, educational, and governmental contexts where compliance is enforced rather than optional. {Attendance at the safety training is compulsory for all employees.}

Computation is the process of calculating or processing information, especially by mathematical or logical operations. In its broadest sense, any systematic transformation of data counts as computation—from mental arithmetic to what happens inside a computer. {The computation took several hours on older hardware.} Computational methods now pervade fields from biology to linguistics.

To compute is to calculate or determine by mathematical or logical means: {Let me compute the total cost}. The word suggests systematic processing—computers compute, but so do people working through problems step by step. Figuratively, something that {doesn't compute} fails to make sense or be understood.

A computer is a machine that processes information according to programmed instructions. Originally the word meant a person who performs calculations—a sense now obsolete. Modern computers range from pocket-sized smartphones to warehouse-scale data centers. {My computer crashed and I lost an hour of work.} {She's good with computers.}

To computerize is to convert a process, system, or operation to computer control or management. A business computerizes its records by moving from paper files to digital databases. A factory computerizes by replacing manual operations with automated systems. The word gained currency in the 1960s as organizations began adopting electronic data processing: {The library computerized its catalog in the 1990s}.

Computerized means performed or controlled by computer rather than by human effort or mechanical means. What was once done manually—calculations, record-keeping, scheduling—becomes computerized when software takes over: {The library computerized its catalog in the 1990s}. A computerized system stores and processes information digitally: {computerized medical records}, {computerized testing}.

Computers are electronic machines that process information according to instructions. The term once meant people who performed calculations—human computers—but now refers almost exclusively to the devices. Desktop computers, laptop computers, and the computers in smartphones all share the essential function: taking input, processing it, and producing output. {My computer crashed during the update.}

Computing is the use of computers to process information, solve problems, or perform calculations. The term covers both the activity and the field: {She works in computing}, {cloud computing has transformed how businesses store data}. Computing power refers to a machine's capacity for processing: {The simulation required massive computing power}.

A comrade is a companion or fellow member of a group, especially one sharing a common purpose or hardship. Soldiers call their fellow soldiers comrades; activists address each other the same way. The word carries a socialist or communist connotation from its use as a form of address in leftist movements: {Comrade Lenin}, {Hello, comrade}.

Comradery is an alternate spelling of camaraderie—the spirit of friendship and mutual trust among people who spend time together, especially colleagues or teammates. The spelling reflects how many English speakers pronounce the word, dropping the second *a*: {There was real comradery among the crew}. Both spellings are accepted, though camaraderie remains more common in edited writing.

Comrades are companions united by shared activity, purpose, or circumstance—fellow soldiers, fellow workers, fellow travelers. The word implies equality and mutual commitment: {comrades in arms}, {comrades in the struggle}. Because of its prominence in socialist and communist movements, comrade carries political connotations in English, often suggesting leftist solidarity or used ironically to mock it.

Comradeship is the bond between comrades—people who share work, struggle, or purpose. It emphasizes solidarity and mutual support rather than mere friendship: {the comradeship of soldiers who served together}, {a spirit of comradeship among the workers}. The word carries connotations of shared hardship and collective identity.

Con has two distinct origins. One means against: the pros and cons of a decision. The other comes from confidence—a con is a swindle that exploits trust, and to con someone is to deceive them: {He conned her out of her savings}. A con artist runs such schemes. Con is also short for convict: {an ex-con}. As a prefix, con- means with or together: connect, congregate.

Concave describes a surface that curves inward, like the inside of a bowl or a cave. The opposite of convex. A concave mirror curves inward and can focus light to a point; a concave lens is thinner at the center than at the edges. {The concave surface collected rainwater.}

To conceal is to hide something or keep it from being seen or known. You might conceal a weapon under a coat, conceal evidence of wrongdoing, or conceal your true feelings. The word often implies deliberate secrecy: {She couldn't conceal her disappointment}. Concealed suggests hidden from view; {concealed carry} refers to carrying a weapon out of sight.

Concealed means hidden from view or kept secret. A concealed {weapon} is carried out of sight. Concealed {evidence} has been deliberately suppressed. The word implies intentional hiding rather than accidental obscurity: {She barely concealed her disappointment}. What's concealed could be revealed—the hiddenness is imposed, not inherent.

Concealer is a cosmetic product used to hide blemishes, dark circles, or other skin imperfections. Thicker than foundation, it provides targeted coverage for specific areas: {She dabbed concealer under her eyes before the interview}. The term extends to anything that hides or masks: {The shrubs acted as a concealer for the ugly fence}.

Concealing is hiding something from view or knowledge. You might conceal a weapon under a coat, conceal evidence of a crime, or conceal your true feelings behind a smile. {She did her best at concealing her disappointment.} The word emphasizes deliberate effort to keep something hidden.

Concealment is the act of hiding something or keeping it secret. A concealment of evidence obstructs justice; a concealment of assets cheats creditors. The word emphasizes deliberate hiding rather than accidental obscurity: {The investigation revealed years of concealment by company executives}. Concealment can also mean a hiding place, especially in hunting or military contexts.

To concede is to admit something reluctantly or under pressure: {I concede that you have a point}. In competitions, to concede is to acknowledge defeat before the final result is official: {The candidate conceded the election}. Concede also means to yield or grant something: {The company conceded several demands to the union}. A goal conceded is one allowed by the defending team.

Conceded is the past tense of concede, meaning to acknowledge something reluctantly or admit defeat. You concede a point in an argument when you accept its validity: {She conceded that he had a point}. In competitions, to concede is to accept loss before the final result: {The candidate conceded the election}. To concede something to an opponent is to yield it: {They conceded two goals in the first half}.

Conceding is acknowledging something reluctantly or under pressure. You might concede a point in an argument when you can no longer defend it, or concede defeat when victory becomes impossible. In elections, the losing candidate concedes by publicly acknowledging the winner: {He called to concede after the results came in}. Conceding can also mean granting or yielding something: {conceding territory}, {conceding an advantage}.

Conceit is an excessively high opinion of oneself—vanity or self-importance: {His conceit was insufferable}. In literary criticism, a conceit is an elaborate or unusual metaphor, especially one that draws surprising comparisons: {The poem's central conceit compares the lovers to a compass}. The two senses connect through the idea of something conceived in the mind—whether flattering self-regard or imaginative invention.

Conceited describes someone who has an excessively high opinion of themselves, their abilities, or their appearance. A conceited person assumes others share their self-admiration and may talk about themselves constantly or dismiss others' accomplishments. {He's so conceited he checks his reflection in every window.} The word carries strong disapproval—unlike confident or self-assured, conceited implies the self-regard is unwarranted or obnoxious.

Conceits are self-flattering beliefs or affectations, often unjustified: {He has conceits about his importance}. In literature, a conceit is an elaborate or extended metaphor—a fanciful comparison that structures a poem or passage: {The metaphysical poets were known for their conceits}. More neutrally, conceits can be artistic devices or imaginative notions: {the conceits of romantic comedy}.

Conceive means to form something in the mind—an idea, a plan, an image. {I can't conceive of a reason to refuse.} The word also means to become pregnant: {They conceived their first child that summer.} The connection is generative: whether mental or physical, conceive is about bringing something new into being.

Conceived most often means formed in the mind—an idea, plan, or belief that someone thought up: {The project was conceived as a way to reduce waste}. It also means to become pregnant: {She conceived after years of trying}. The passive construction {conceived in} describes origins: {a nation conceived in liberty}. Something {poorly conceived} was badly planned from the start.

Conceiving is the present participle of conceive. To conceive is to form an idea or plan in the mind: {I can't conceive of a reason to stay}. It also means to become pregnant: {They had trouble conceiving}. The mental and biological senses share the notion of something coming into being—whether a thought or a child.

Concentrate means to focus attention or effort on a single point: {I can't concentrate with all this noise}. It also means to gather or collect in one place: {Power concentrated in the capital}. As a verb in chemistry and cooking, concentrate removes water or diluting substances, making something stronger or more intense. The noun concentrate is the resulting product—orange juice concentrate, protein concentrate. To concentrate troops is to mass them in one location.
clues: Mental effort aimed at one thing

definition: Concentrated describes something made stronger or denser by removing diluting elements. Concentrated orange juice has had water removed. A concentrated solution holds more solute per volume. The word extends to mental focus: {concentrated effort}, {concentrated attention}. Concentrated also describes things gathered into a small area: {concentrated fire}, {concentrated population}.

Concentrates works as both verb and noun around the idea of bringing things together or intensifying. To concentrate is to focus mental attention: {I can't concentrate with all this noise}. It also means to gather in one place: {Wealth concentrates in few hands}. To concentrate a liquid is to remove water, making it stronger. As a noun, concentrates are substances reduced to their essence—frozen orange juice concentrate, cannabis concentrates, mineral concentrates for smelting.

Concentrating is giving full attention to something, gathering mental focus on a single task or subject: {I can't think with all this noise—I'm trying to concentrate}. The word also describes making something more dense or potent by removing diluting elements: {concentrating the sauce by simmering}. Both senses share the idea of drawing scattered things toward a center.

Concentration is the focusing of attention or effort on a single thing: {The job requires intense concentration}. It also means a gathering or accumulation in one place: {a concentration of troops near the border}, {high concentrations of lead in the water}. In chemistry, concentration measures how much of a substance is dissolved in a solution. A concentration camp is a facility for mass detention, most notoriously the Nazi death camps of World War II.
clues: Keeping your mind on one thing

definition: A concept is an idea, especially one that arises by generalizing from many instances or characteristics: Democratic concepts arose in reaction to the despotic rule of kings and tyrants. The concept of a concrete thing is an idea that includes all of its particular characteristics: The concept of a creator God is present, with some variation, in many different cultures. When used as an adjective, concept designates something that is built around a single idea or is intended to illustrate a concept, such as a concept car or a concept building.

Conception is the moment when a new life begins—the fertilization of an egg by sperm. From this biological sense comes the broader meaning of bringing something into existence: the conception of an {idea}, the conception of a {plan}. A conception is also an understanding or mental picture of something: {Her conception of justice differs from mine}. The word bridges physical creation and mental formation.

Conceptions are ideas, notions, or ways of understanding something: {Her conception of justice differs from mine}. The word often implies a mental framework or interpretation rather than simple knowledge. Conception also refers to the moment when pregnancy begins—when sperm fertilizes egg. A grand conception is an ambitious creative vision: {The architect's original conception proved too expensive to build}.

Concepts are mental categories or abstract ideas that organize understanding. A concept of justice differs from any particular just act—it's the underlying principle. Scientific concepts like gravity or entropy frame how we interpret phenomena. To {grasp a concept} is to understand an abstraction. Concept also describes preliminary designs: {concept art}, {concept car}. Something {in concept} exists as an idea but not yet in practice.

When one thing concerns another, it is related to it in an important way. A matter that concerns you is one to which you must attend or pay attention. A movie that concerns three orphans is about them. If something does not concern you, you are not involved or interested in it. A concern is a matter that is important to someone: Those attending the meeting were able to air their concerns. If something causes concern, it makes people worry that something bad may happen if action is not taken.

Concerned means worried or troubled about something: {I'm concerned about your health}. It also means interested or involved: {All concerned parties should attend the meeting}. The phrase {as far as I'm concerned} introduces a personal opinion or perspective: {As far as I'm concerned, the matter is closed}. To be concerned with something is to deal with or relate to it: {The book is concerned with climate change}.

Concerning morphed in function from being a participle that had to agree with the subject in a sentence to working like a preposition, where it can have different points of attachment to mean the same thing as about or with regard to: There hasn’t been any decision concerning the new appointments yet.

Concerns, as a noun, are matters that engage someone's attention, interest, or care, often because they involve worry or responsibility. A business or organization may also be called a concern. The verb concern means to relate to or affect someone: {This matter doesn't concern you}. If something concerns you, it causes worry or unease. To concern yourself with something is to take an active interest in it. Concerned can mean worried {I'm concerned about her health} or involved {all concerned parties were notified}.

A concert is a live musical performance, typically by one or more musicians or groups playing for an audience. Concerts range from intimate acoustic sets to massive stadium events, and the word applies across genres from classical to rock to hip-hop. {We got tickets to the concert downtown.} The phrase {in concert} means working together in coordination: {The agencies acted in concert to address the crisis.}

A concertina is a small handheld instrument similar to an accordion, with bellows and buttons on each end. To concertina is to collapse or fold in accordion-like pleats: {The car concertinaed on impact}. Concertina wire is razor wire coiled in expandable spirals, used as a barrier.

Concertinas are small handheld musical instruments related to the accordion, with bellows and buttons on each end that produce notes when pressed while squeezing or expanding. The word also describes things that fold or collapse in accordion-like fashion: a concertina {file}, concertina {wire} (coiled razor wire used as a barrier). As a verb, to concertina is to compress or crumple in zigzag folds: {The car concertinaed on impact}.

The concertmaster is the principal first violinist in an orchestra, seated nearest the conductor. The concertmaster leads the string section, coordinates bowing among the violins, and serves as a liaison between conductor and musicians. Before a performance, the concertmaster signals the oboe to sound the tuning note. The British term is leader.

A concerto is a musical composition for orchestra featuring one or more solo instruments. The soloist and orchestra engage in dialogue—sometimes the soloist takes the spotlight while the orchestra accompanies, sometimes they play in conversation: {a piano concerto}, {a violin concerto}. The form emerged in the Baroque period and remains central to classical repertoire. Plural: concertos or concerti.

Concerts are live performances of music before an audience, typically featuring one or more musicians or groups playing for an extended period. The word covers everything from symphony orchestras in formal halls to rock bands in arenas to jazz combos in clubs. {We got tickets to the concert downtown.} As a verb, concert means to arrange or plan together, and appears most often in the adjective concerted, meaning coordinated or done in combination: {a concerted effort to raise funds.}

A concession is something yielded or granted, often reluctantly. In an argument, you make a concession by acknowledging a point for the other side: {I'll make one concession—the data isn't perfect}. A concession can be a right or privilege granted by an authority: {mining concessions}, {logging concessions}. In American English, a concession is also a vendor's right to sell goods at a venue—hence {concession stand} at stadiums and theaters. To {concede} is the verb.

Concessions are things yielded or granted, often reluctantly. In negotiation, making concessions means giving ground: {Both sides made concessions to reach a deal}. At stadiums and theaters, concessions are the snacks and drinks sold to patrons, or the stands selling them: {The concessions at the arena are overpriced}. A concession can also be a right granted to operate a business within a larger property.

A conch is a large spiral-shelled sea snail, or the shell itself. The shells have been used as trumpets, decorative objects, and symbols of the ocean. In *Lord of the Flies*, the conch represents order and authority. Conch meat is eaten in Caribbean cuisine: {conch fritters}, {conch salad}. Pronounced with a hard k or as "konch."

Conchas are Mexican sweet bread rolls topped with a crunchy sugar shell scored to resemble a seashell—the name means "shells" in Spanish. The topping comes in vanilla, chocolate, or other flavors, creating a distinctive striped pattern. Conchas are a staple of Mexican bakeries and breakfast tables: {We picked up conchas from the panadería}.

Conches is the plural of conch, a large spiral-shelled marine mollusk. The shell itself is also called a conch, prized for its pink interior and used as decoration, horn, or material for cameos. {She collected conches on the beach}. In the Florida Keys, longtime residents call themselves Conchs.

A concierge is a staff member at a hotel or apartment building who assists guests or residents with services—making reservations, arranging transportation, securing tickets, recommending restaurants. The role combines doorman, information desk, and personal assistant. In healthcare, a concierge practice offers enhanced access to a physician for an annual fee: {concierge medicine}.

Conciliation is the act of making peace or restoring goodwill after conflict or disagreement. It emphasizes soothing hurt feelings and finding common ground: {The meeting was an attempt at conciliation after months of hostility}. Unlike arbitration, conciliation focuses on repairing relationships rather than imposing solutions. A conciliatory gesture signals willingness to end a dispute.

Conciliatory describes words or actions intended to make peace or reduce hostility: {a conciliatory gesture}, {a conciliatory tone}. Someone being conciliatory is trying to appease an angry party or smooth over conflict rather than escalate it. The word often implies a willingness to compromise or acknowledge fault: {She made conciliatory remarks after the heated exchange}.

Concise means expressing much in few words—brief but complete. A concise {summary} captures essential points without excess. A concise {writer} wastes no words. The term implies skillful compression rather than mere shortness; something concise lacks padding, not substance.

A conclave is a private meeting, especially one where participants deliberate in secret. The word is most associated with the gathering of Catholic cardinals to elect a new pope—historically locked in isolation until they reach a decision. More broadly, any closed-door meeting of insiders qualifies: {The party leaders met in conclave to choose their candidate}.

Conclaves are private or secret meetings, especially ones where participants are secluded until reaching a decision. The word is most associated with the assembly of cardinals that elects a new pope, locked away until white smoke signals their choice. By extension, any exclusive gathering of insiders deliberating important matters: {The party leaders met in conclave to choose their candidate}.

Conclude means to bring something to an end or to reach a final point: {The meeting concluded at noon}, {She concluded her speech with a call to action}. It also means to arrive at a judgment or decision through reasoning: {The jury concluded that he was guilty}, {What can we conclude from these findings?} To conclude an agreement is to finalize it formally. In formal writing, "in conclusion" signals a summary or final remarks.

A conclusion is the end or final part of something—a speech, an essay, a negotiation. It also means a judgment reached through reasoning: {The detective arrived at a startling conclusion}. To {jump to conclusions} is to decide without sufficient evidence. A {foregone conclusion} is an outcome that seems inevitable. In formal contexts, to {bring something to a conclusion} is simply to finish it.

Conclusions are judgments or decisions reached through reasoning. After weighing evidence, you {draw a conclusion} or {reach a conclusion}. A conclusion is also the end or final part of something—the conclusion of a speech, a novel's conclusion. To {jump to conclusions} is to decide without sufficient evidence. {In conclusion} signals a summary or final remarks.

Conclusive means settling a matter beyond doubt or dispute. Conclusive evidence leaves no room for alternative interpretations. A conclusive victory is decisive, not narrow. The word often appears in legal and scientific contexts where certainty matters: {The DNA results were conclusive}. If something is inconclusive, the question remains open.

To concoct is to make something by combining ingredients or elements. You concoct a sauce from what's in the fridge, or concoct a plan from available resources. The word often implies improvisation or creativity: {She concocted a story to explain her absence}. Concoct frequently carries a whiff of deception or scheming—concocted alibis and concocted excuses rarely hold up under scrutiny.

Concocted is the past tense of concoct, which means to prepare by mixing ingredients or to devise through imagination. You concoct a {sauce} or a {potion} in the kitchen, or you concoct a {story}, {scheme}, or {excuse} in your mind. The word often carries a whiff of fabrication or implausibility: {a concocted alibi}, {a hastily concocted explanation}.

Concocting is preparing something by combining ingredients or elements. You concoct a meal, a drink, or a potion. The word often implies improvisation or scheming: {She was concocting an excuse for being late}. A concocted story is fabricated, invented rather than true.

A concoction is something made by mixing various ingredients together, often with a suggestion of improvisation or dubious results: {She whipped up some concoction of leftover vegetables and rice}. The word can describe drinks, potions, remedies, or dishes, and extends to elaborate schemes or fabricated stories: {His alibi was an obvious concoction}.

Concoctions are things mixed together from various ingredients, often with a suggestion of improvisation or dubious results. The word applies to drinks, potions, foods, or figuratively to stories and schemes: {She handed me some herbal concoction that was supposed to cure headaches}. A concoction implies creativity, but sometimes also suspicion about what went into it.

Concocts means to make something by combining various ingredients or elements. The word most often applies to food or drink preparation, especially when the mixture is unusual or improvised: {She concocts a smoothie from whatever's in the fridge}. It extends naturally to creating stories, excuses, or schemes, often with a suggestion of fabrication or deception: {He concocted an elaborate alibi}. The noun form is concoction.

Concord is agreement or harmony between people or groups. Treaties establish concord between nations; families strive for domestic concord. In grammar, concord refers to agreement between words—subject and verb, noun and pronoun. In music, concord describes notes sounding together pleasantly, the opposite of discord. {The two sides finally reached concord after months of negotiation.} (Capitalized Concord is a place name or grape variety.)

A concourse is a large open space where people gather or pass through, especially in public buildings like train stations or airports: {We agreed to meet at the main concourse}. The word also means a crowd or gathering of people, or the act of coming together: {a concourse of protesters outside the courthouse}.

Concrete in its oldest sense means solid and real, as opposed to abstract: {concrete evidence}, {concrete proposals}. The word extends to the building material—a mixture of cement, sand, gravel, and water that hardens into stone-like mass. Concrete dominates modern construction: sidewalks, foundations, highways. To concrete something is to cover or set it in this material. The jungle metaphor describes urban environments dominated by concrete structures.

A concubine is a woman who lives with a man in a sexual relationship without being his wife, typically in cultures or historical periods where such arrangements had recognized social status. Unlike a mistress, whose relationship is usually secret, a concubine often held an acknowledged position in the household, though inferior to that of a wife. The term appears frequently in historical and biblical contexts, where men of wealth or power maintained multiple concubines alongside their legal wives.

Concubines is the plural of concubine—a woman who lives with a man in a sexual relationship without being his legal wife. Historically, concubines occupied a recognized but subordinate status in households where polygamy or informal unions were accepted: {The emperor's concubines lived in a separate wing of the palace}. The term now appears mainly in historical or biblical contexts.

Concussed describes having suffered a concussion—a brain injury caused by a blow to the head. Someone concussed may experience confusion, headache, dizziness, or memory problems: {The player was clearly concussed after the collision}. The term appears in medical contexts and sports coverage, where head injuries receive increasing attention.

A concussion is a brain injury caused by a blow to the head, typically producing temporary symptoms like confusion, headache, or memory problems. The word also means a violent shaking or jarring impact: {the concussion from the blast rattled windows}. In sports medicine, concussion protocols now govern when athletes can return to play after head trauma.

Concussions is the plural of concussion, a brain injury caused by a blow to the head. The impact causes the brain to move within the skull, resulting in temporary impairment: {He suffered two concussions playing football}. Symptoms include headache, confusion, and memory problems. The term has gained prominence as awareness of sports-related brain injuries has grown. Concussion can also mean violent shaking from an impact: {the concussion of the blast}.

Condemn means to express strong disapproval or to declare something wrong or evil: {The senator condemned the attack}. Courts condemn prisoners to punishment—especially death. Buildings are condemned when declared unsafe for use. To condemn someone to a fate is to doom them to it: {His injury condemned him to a life of chronic pain}. The word carries weight and finality.

Condemnation is strong disapproval or censure: {The policy drew condemnation from human rights groups}. It also refers to official judgment that something is unfit—a building condemned as unsafe, meat condemned as diseased. In legal contexts, condemnation is the formal seizure of private property for public use. A condemnation can also be a sentence of punishment: {The judge's condemnation was swift}.

Condemned describes something officially declared unfit, guilty, or destined for destruction. A condemned building is too dangerous for occupation. A condemned prisoner awaits execution. The word carries finality—what is condemned has been judged and found wanting: {The condemned man ate his last meal}. To feel condemned is to feel doomed or beyond redemption.

Condensation is the process by which gas or vapor turns to liquid, typically when warm air meets a cooler surface: {condensation on the bathroom mirror}, {condensation forming on a cold glass}. The word also means the act of making something shorter or more compact—condensing a long report into a summary. A condensation is the result: {a condensation of the novel}.

Condense means to make denser or more compact. Steam condenses into water droplets when it cools. A condensed book or report has been shortened. Condensed milk has had water removed. To condense an argument is to compress it into fewer words: {Let me condense this into three points}. The opposite is expand or dilute.

Condensed means reduced in volume, length, or scope while retaining essential content. Condensed {milk} has had water removed. A condensed {version} of a book or article is shortened. In physics, condensed matter is material in a dense state—liquids and solids rather than gases. The word implies compression without loss of substance: {a condensed summary of the main points}.

Condensing is making something more compact or concentrated. You condense a report by cutting unnecessary material. Water vapor condenses into liquid droplets when it meets a cold surface. {The editor spent hours condensing the manuscript}. Condensing can also describe the emotional weight of compression: {Years of resentment came condensing into that single look}.

To condescend is to act as though you're lowering yourself to someone else's level—implying superiority while appearing gracious. The word almost always carries negative connotations: {She condescended to explain the basics, as if I were a child}. Someone who condescends may offer help or attention in a way that emphasizes the gap in status rather than bridging it. Less commonly, condescend can simply mean to do something beneath one's dignity: {The CEO rarely condescends to attend staff meetings}.

Condescending describes behavior that implies superiority over the person being addressed—a patronizing tone that suggests the other person is less intelligent, capable, or worthy of respect: {Don't be so condescending; I understand the basics}. The word carries strong negative judgment; calling someone condescending is never a compliment. A condescending {smile}, condescending {explanation}, or condescending {attitude} all suggest the person thinks they're doing you a favor by engaging at your level.

Condescension is an attitude of superiority that shows in how someone speaks or behaves toward others. A condescending person talks down to people, often while appearing gracious: {His condescension was obvious in the way he explained basic concepts to the expert}. The word usually implies the superiority is unearned or the manner offensive, though historically it could mean a gracious willingness to lower oneself to others' level.

A condiment is a substance added to food to enhance its flavor—ketchup, mustard, mayonnaise, relish, hot sauce. Condiments are typically applied at the table rather than during cooking, distinguishing them from spices and seasonings. {Pass the condiments, please.} The word can extend to pickles, chutneys, and similar accompaniments.

Condiments are flavorings added to food at the table or during preparation—mustard, ketchup, mayonnaise, relish, hot sauce. The term covers a wide range from simple salt and pepper to elaborate sauces. Unlike spices used in cooking, condiments are typically applied by the eater to suit personal taste: {Pass the condiments, please}.

A condition is the state something is in (weather condition, market condition). An illness that lingers or requires attention is euphemistically called a condition. If conditions are attached to an agreement, they stipulate what you must do or accept. If you condition someone to something, you get them used to it. If you condition yourself, you get in shape. If you condition your hair or some other physical thing, you treat it with a substance that improves it.

Conditional means depending on certain conditions being met. A conditional {offer} or {approval} takes effect only if requirements are satisfied: {The job offer was conditional on passing a background check}. In grammar, conditional structures express hypotheticals: {If it rains, we'll cancel}. In logic and programming, conditionals test whether something is true before proceeding. As a noun, a conditional is such a statement or clause.

Conditioned describes something that has been trained, treated, or modified to respond in a particular way. A conditioned {response} is learned through repeated association—Pavlov's dogs salivating at a bell. Hair or leather can be conditioned by applying substances that soften or protect. Air is conditioned when mechanically cooled or heated. More broadly, we are all conditioned by our upbringing and culture: {Years of poverty had conditioned her to hoard food}.
clues: Prepared to respond a certain way

definition: Conditioner is a product that improves the condition of something. Hair conditioner softens and detangles after shampooing. Fabric conditioner (or softener) makes laundry feel less stiff. Leather conditioner keeps hides supple. Air conditioners don't condition air in this sense—they cool it—but the name stuck from early claims about improving air quality. {My hair is dry without conditioner.}

Conditioning is preparation or training that shapes behavior, skills, or physical capacity. Athletes undergo conditioning to build strength and endurance. In psychology, conditioning refers to learned associations between stimuli and responses—Pavlov's dogs salivating at a bell being the classic example. Hair conditioner and air conditioning share the root sense of bringing something into proper condition. {Years of conditioning made her flinch at raised voices.}

Conditions are the circumstances or factors that affect a situation: {working conditions}, {weather conditions}, {living conditions}. A condition can also be a requirement that must be met: {The loan came with strict conditions}. As a verb, to condition is to train or accustom someone to respond in a particular way, or to treat something to improve its state: {condition your hair}, {condition your muscles}. A medical condition is an ailment or health problem. {On condition that} means only if: {I'll go on condition that you come with me}.

A condo is a housing unit in a building or complex where each unit is individually owned, while common areas are shared. Short for condominium. The term emphasizes the ownership structure rather than the physical building: {They bought a condo downtown}. Condos typically come with association fees and rules governing the property.

Condolence is an expression of sympathy for someone experiencing grief or misfortune, especially after a death. The word appears most often in the plural: {Please accept my condolences}. To {offer condolences} or {pay condolences} is to express sympathy formally, whether in person, by card, or at a funeral.

Condolences are expressions of sympathy offered to someone grieving a loss, especially a death: {Please accept my condolences}, {We sent our condolences to the family}. The word appears almost exclusively in this plural form and in formal contexts—cards, funeral visits, official statements. To {offer condolences} or {extend condolences} is to express sorrow for another's misfortune.

A condom is a thin sheath worn over the penis during sex to prevent pregnancy and reduce transmission of sexually transmitted infections. Most are made of latex, though polyurethane and lambskin versions exist. The female condom is inserted into the vagina. {Do you have a condom?}

A condominium is a building divided into individually owned units, or one such unit itself: {They bought a condominium downtown}. Owners hold title to their units while sharing ownership of common areas—hallways, pools, grounds. Often shortened to condo. The term originally meant joint sovereignty over a territory by multiple nations, a sense that survives in legal and diplomatic contexts.

Condoms are thin sheaths worn over the penis during sex to prevent pregnancy and reduce transmission of sexually transmitted infections. They're typically made of latex, though polyurethane and lambskin versions exist. {Do you have a condom?} The word also appears in safer-sex campaigns: {No condom, no sex}.

Condone means to accept or overlook behavior that is wrong or objectionable, often by failing to take action against it. It does not imply approval so much as a willingness to let something slide: {The school cannot condone cheating, even when students are under pressure}. Condone often appears in negative constructions emphasizing what someone refuses to tolerate: {I don't condone violence, but I understand the frustration}.

Condoning is accepting or allowing behavior that others might consider wrong or objectionable. The word implies passive approval rather than active encouragement—you condone something by not objecting to it: {Silence can be seen as condoning the abuse}. The term often appears in denials: {I'm not condoning what he did, but I understand why}.

A condor is a very large vulture of the Americas, among the largest flying birds in the world. The Andean condor inhabits South American mountain ranges; the California condor, once nearly extinct, survives through conservation efforts. Condor sometimes appears figuratively for something that circles or looms: {Creditors hovered like condors over the failing business}.

Condors are very large New World vultures with wingspans exceeding ten feet—among the largest flying birds. The Andean condor inhabits South American mountains; the California condor, nearly extinct by the 1980s, has been slowly recovering through captive breeding programs. Both species are scavengers, feeding on carrion.

Condos is the plural of condo, an informal shortening of condominium—an individually owned unit within a larger residential building or complex. Unlike apartments, condos are purchased rather than rented, though owners pay fees for shared amenities and maintenance: {She's looking at condos downtown}. {The beach condos sell out every summer}.

Conduct as a noun (first syllable stressed) is a near synonym of behavior and usually includes the idea of propriety: The teachers received compliments on the conduct of the schoolchildren. When used as a verb (second syllable stressed), conduct has meanings that all involve the idea of leadership. If you conduct an orchestra or choir you lead it when it rehearses or performs. If you conduct an investigation, you carry it out, either alone or in a leadership role. When no agent is identified, conduct just means carry out: a study was conducted to determine how many trees were infected.

Conducted is the past tense of conduct, covering its main senses. To conduct an investigation, survey, or experiment is to carry it out: {The study was conducted over three years}. To conduct oneself is to behave: {She conducted herself with dignity}. To conduct music is to direct performers. To conduct electricity or heat is to transmit it. A guide conducts visitors through a space.

Conducting is directing or leading, especially an orchestra or other musical ensemble. A conductor uses gestures to guide tempo, dynamics, and expression. Beyond music, conducting means carrying out or managing: {conducting research}, {conducting business}, {conducting a survey}. Materials that are conducting allow electricity or heat to pass through them.

Conduction is the transfer of heat or electricity through a material without visible movement of the material itself. Heat conducts through a metal pan from flame to handle. Electrical conduction moves current through wires. The term extends to how nerve impulses travel along fibers. {Copper's excellent conduction makes it ideal for wiring.}

A conductor leads an orchestra or chorus, directing performers through gesture and expression. The word extends to anyone who guides or directs: a tour conductor, a train conductor who manages passengers and tickets. In physics, a conductor is a material that allows heat or electricity to pass through it—copper is an excellent conductor, rubber a poor one. The underlying sense is something that leads or carries forward.

Conductors is the plural of conductor, which centers on leading or conveying. An orchestra conductor directs musicians, interpreting the score and coordinating performance. A train conductor manages passengers and operations aboard the cars. In physics, a conductor is a material that transmits heat or electricity: {Copper and silver are excellent conductors}. The word implies something that channels flow—whether of music, passengers, or electrons.

Conducts covers leading, guiding, or carrying through. An orchestra conductor conducts the musicians. A scientist conducts an experiment. A guide conducts tourists through a museum. Someone conducts themselves well or poorly—behaves in a certain manner. Materials that conduct electricity or heat allow it to pass through: {Copper conducts better than aluminum}. The word implies directed movement or managed activity.

A conduit is a channel or pipe through which something flows or is conveyed, typically water, electrical wires, or other utilities. The word extends naturally to figurative uses: a person or organization can serve as a conduit for information, money, or influence, channeling it from one place to another. {The nonprofit acted as a conduit for donations to reach disaster victims.} The emphasis is always on transmission—something passes through a conduit rather than originating there.

Conduits are channels or pipes through which something flows—water, electrical wiring, or other substances that need to be directed from one place to another. The word extends to anything that serves as a means of transmission: {The aide served as a conduit between the senator and lobbyists}. A person can be a conduit for information, influence, or resources, connecting parties who might not otherwise communicate directly.

A cone is a three-dimensional shape that tapers smoothly from a flat circular base to a point called the apex. This geometric form appears throughout daily life: ice cream cones, traffic cones, pine cones, and the cones in your eyes that detect color. The verb cone means to shape something into a cone or to mark off an area with traffic cones: {Police coned off the accident scene}. In casual use, to cone can mean to eat ice cream from a cone.

Coneflower is a North American wildflower with a distinctive raised central cone surrounded by drooping petals, typically purple or yellow. The plants are hardy perennials popular in gardens and prairie restoration. Echinacea, used in herbal remedies, is a type of coneflower: {The coneflowers attract butterflies all summer}.

Cones are three-dimensional shapes with a circular base tapering to a point: {traffic cones}, {ice cream cones}, {pine cones}. The shape extends to anything cone-like—a volcano's peak, a megaphone, the paper holder for soft serve. In anatomy, cones are photoreceptor cells in the retina responsible for color vision, distinguished from rods that detect light and dark. To {cone off} an area is to mark it with traffic cones.

A confab is an informal conversation or discussion, often a brief chat: {We had a quick confab about the schedule}. It also serves as a verb meaning to converse casually: {They confabbed in the hallway between meetings}. The word carries a friendly, relaxed tone—more casual than conference, less formal than consultation.

A confection is a sweet food, especially one made with sugar or chocolate, like candy, pastries, or elaborate desserts. The word often suggests something crafted with care or artistry: {The bakery's confections were almost too beautiful to eat}. By extension, confection can describe anything elaborate or frivolous, particularly in fashion or entertainment: {The dress was a pink confection of ruffles and lace}. To confect something is to make or put it together, often with a hint of artifice.

A confectioner is a person who makes or sells confections—candies, sweets, and other sugar-based treats. The term extends to the shop itself: {the old confectioner on Main Street}. A confectioner's sugar is finely powdered sugar used in frostings and delicate pastries.

Confectionery is candy and sweets collectively, or the art of making them. A confectionery is also a shop where such items are sold: {The old confectionery on Main Street still makes fudge by hand}. The word covers chocolates, hard candies, pastries, and similar sugary creations.

Confections are sweet foods, especially candy and other sugary treats made with skill or artistry: {a shop full of chocolate confections}, {delicate confections from the pastry chef}. The word suggests something elaborate or fanciful—extending to non-food creations that seem light or decorative: {Her hat was a frothy confection of lace and ribbons}.
clues: Desserts made with lots of sugar

definition: A confederacy is an alliance or league, especially of states or groups united for a common purpose. The term implies a looser bond than a federation—members retain more independence. {The confederacy of tribes controlled trade routes throughout the region.} Any group joined in common cause, even informally, may be called a confederacy: {a confederacy of dunces}. (Capitalized Confederacy refers to the Confederate States of America.)

A confederate is an ally or accomplice—someone joined with others in a common purpose, often with overtones of conspiracy or secrecy: {The detective suspected the witness was a confederate of the accused}. To confederate is to unite in a league or alliance. As an adjective, confederate describes things joined together or relating to a confederation. (Capitalized Confederate relates to the American Civil War.)

Confederates are allies or accomplices joined in a common purpose, often with secretive or conspiratorial overtones: {The thief and his confederates planned the heist}. The verb means to unite or band together. In American history, Confederates were those who supported or fought for the Confederate States during the Civil War. (Capitalized Confederate specifies the Civil War context.)

A confederation is a loose alliance of states, organizations, or groups that join together for common purposes while retaining their individual autonomy. Unlike a federation, where central authority is strong, a confederation keeps power largely with its members: {The Articles of Confederation created a weak central government that struggled to function}. The term applies beyond politics to any alliance of independent entities: {a confederation of labor unions}, {a confederation of tribes}. (Capitalized Confederation often refers to specific historical alliances.)

Confederations are unions of states, organizations, or groups that join together for a common purpose while retaining significant independence. The term often describes loose political alliances where member entities keep more autonomy than in a federation: {The Articles of Confederation preceded the U.S. Constitution}. Sports confederations govern regional competitions: {the Asian Football Confederation}. The word implies cooperation without full merger—partners working together while maintaining separate identities.

A conference is a formal meeting where people gather to discuss a shared subject—typically a professional, academic, or political one. Business conferences bring together industry members; academic conferences present research papers. Conference also names a grouping of sports teams that compete against each other: {the Western Conference}. To conference is to meet and discuss, often by phone: {Let's conference in the marketing team}.

Conferences is the plural of conference—formal meetings where people gather to discuss shared interests or concerns. Academic conferences bring scholars together to present research. Business conferences assemble professionals for networking and industry updates. Press conferences let public figures address journalists: {The coach held a press conference after the game}. In sports, conferences are groups of teams that compete primarily against each other.

To confess is to admit something you've concealed—typically a wrongdoing, secret, or uncomfortable truth: {He confessed to the crime}, {I have to confess I never liked her}. In religious contexts, to confess is to acknowledge sins to a priest or to God. A confession may be coerced or voluntary, formal or casual. {I confess} often introduces reluctant admissions: {I confess I haven't read the book}.

Confessed describes something openly acknowledged, especially wrongdoing or something potentially embarrassing. A confessed {murderer} has admitted to the crime. A confessed {romantic} owns the label. The word often carries a sense of admission against interest—you confess to things that might reflect poorly on you, not to virtues.

Confesses is the third-person singular of confess—to acknowledge something one has concealed, especially a wrongdoing or secret: {She confesses to eating the last cookie}. The word carries weight from its religious sense, where one confesses sins to a priest. Someone confesses guilt, love, ignorance, or doubt. {He finally confesses that he never read the book}.

Confessing is admitting to something, usually something wrong or hidden. A suspect confesses to a crime; a person confesses sins to a priest; someone confesses feelings they've kept secret: {I have to confess, I never liked him}. The word implies reluctance overcome—you confess what you'd rather not reveal.

A confession is an admission of something concealed—typically wrongdoing, guilt, or an uncomfortable truth. In religious contexts, confession is the formal acknowledgment of sins to a priest: {She went to confession every Saturday}. Police seek confessions from suspects. More casually, confession introduces personal revelations: {I have a confession—I've never seen that movie}. The word implies disclosure of something the speaker might prefer to hide.

A confessional is a small enclosed booth in a Catholic church where a priest hears confessions—typically a wooden structure with a partition separating priest from penitent. As an adjective, confessional describes writing or speech that reveals intimate personal details: {confessional poetry}, {a confessional memoir}. The tone suggests unburdening private thoughts or admitting uncomfortable truths.

Confessionals are the small enclosed booths in Catholic churches where priests hear confessions, typically with a screen or grille separating priest from penitent. The term extends to any private space for intimate disclosure. In reality television, confessionals are the segments where participants speak directly to camera about their thoughts and feelings: {The best drama happens in the confessionals}.

Confessions are admissions of wrongdoing, guilt, or secret information. In legal contexts, a confession is a statement acknowledging criminal responsibility: {The police obtained a confession after hours of interrogation}. In religious practice, confession is the ritual acknowledgment of sins to a priest. The word also applies to intimate revelations generally: {late-night confessions about past relationships}. A confession can be a public declaration of faith or belief. As a literary genre, confessions are autobiographical works revealing private thoughts and experiences, after Augustine's *Confessions*.

A confessor is a priest who hears confessions and grants absolution in the Catholic tradition: {She spoke to her confessor about her doubts}. The term also applies to anyone who confesses or to whom confessions are made. Historically, a confessor was someone who suffered for their faith without being martyred—distinguished from martyrs who died for it.

Confetti is small pieces of colored paper thrown during celebrations—weddings, parades, New Year's Eve. The pieces flutter down over the honorees or revelers. Confetti was originally small candies thrown at Italian carnivals; the paper version is cheaper and less painful. {The newlyweds emerged from the church amid a shower of confetti.}

A confidant is someone you trust with private matters—a person to whom you confide secrets, fears, or sensitive information. The relationship implies intimacy and discretion: {She had been his confidant for years}. The feminine form confidante exists but is increasingly rare; confidant now serves for any gender.

A confidante is a person, especially a woman, to whom secrets are entrusted. The word implies deep trust and intimacy—a confidante knows what others don't: {She had been my confidante since college}. The masculine form is confidant, though confidante now often applies regardless of gender.

Confidantes is the plural of confidante, a person—especially a woman—to whom secrets or private matters are entrusted. The word implies deep trust and intimacy: {She was one of the queen's closest confidantes}. Confidant is the masculine or gender-neutral form, though confidante increasingly applies regardless of gender.

Confidants are people to whom one tells secrets or private matters. The word implies deep trust—a confidant receives information you wouldn't share widely. {She had been his confidant for years, knowing things even his wife didn't}. The feminine form confidante exists but confidant now serves for any gender.

To confide is to share something private or secret with someone you trust: {She confided her fears to her sister}, {He confided that he was thinking of leaving}. The word implies both intimacy and discretion—you confide in someone, expecting them to keep your confidence. To confide something to someone's care is to entrust it to them.

Confided is the past tense of confide, meaning to share something private or secret with someone you trust: {She confided her fears to her sister}, {He confided that he was thinking of quitting}. The word implies intimacy and discretion—you confide in someone you believe will keep the information safe.

Confidence is trust or faith in something—a person, an outcome, or especially oneself. {She spoke with confidence}. A confident person believes in their own abilities; overconfidence tips into arrogance. To confide is to share secrets, so a confidence is something told in trust: {He took me into his confidence}. A confidence game or con exploits misplaced trust. A vote of confidence affirms faith in leadership; a vote of no confidence withdraws it.

Confidences is the plural of confidence, but the word typically appears in this form only in certain senses. Someone who shares their confidences reveals private matters: {She told me things in confidence, and I've kept her confidences ever since}. To {exchange confidences} is to share secrets mutually. The sense of self-assurance rarely pluralizes—you don't usually have multiple confidences in yourself.

Confident describes assurance in oneself or certainty about something. A confident person believes in their own abilities: {She gave a confident presentation}. You can be confident about outcomes: {I'm confident we'll win}. The word suggests composure without arrogance, though overconfidence tips into hubris. A confidant (different spelling) is someone you trust with secrets.

Confidential describes information meant to be kept private or shared only with authorized people. A confidential {document} contains sensitive material. A confidential {source} provides information on condition of anonymity. {This is strictly confidential.} The word implies trust—breaking confidentiality means betraying someone who shared something in confidence.

Confidentiality is the state of being kept private or secret, especially regarding sensitive information shared in trust. Doctors, lawyers, and therapists owe confidentiality to their clients. A {confidentiality agreement} legally binds parties not to disclose certain information. {Patient confidentiality prevents me from discussing the case.}

Confides is the present-tense form of confide, meaning to share private thoughts or secrets with someone trusted: {She confides in her sister about everything}. The word implies intimacy and trust—you confide in people you believe will keep your confidence. To confide something to someone is to entrust them with sensitive information: {He confided his fears to no one}.

Confiding describes someone who readily shares personal thoughts or secrets, often implying a trusting or naive openness: {She had a confiding manner that made strangers tell her things}. A confiding tone suggests intimacy and trust. The word can carry a hint of vulnerability—someone confiding may be too willing to trust.

Configuration is an arrangement of parts or elements in a particular form or pattern. A computer's configuration specifies its hardware and software settings. The configuration of furniture in a room is how pieces are positioned relative to each other. In chemistry, configuration describes the spatial arrangement of atoms in a molecule. The word often implies that the arrangement can be changed: {The software allows you to save multiple configurations}.

Configurations are particular arrangements of parts or elements. A configuration determines how something is set up—the configuration of furniture in a room, the configuration of stars in a constellation, the configuration of a computer system. In technical contexts, configurations specify settings that control how software or hardware behaves: {Check your network configuration}. The word emphasizes that the arrangement is one of many possibilities.

Configure means to arrange or set up according to specific requirements. The word appears most often in technical contexts—you configure software settings, configure a computer network, or configure a device before first use. The underlying sense is adjusting components or options to work together properly: {I need to configure the router before we can get online}. Configuration is the noun for either the process or the resulting arrangement.

To confine someone or something is to limit movement or freedom. You might confine a dangerous dog to a cage, or confine your remarks to the main point. If a pregnant woman is confined, she is nearing delivery. Confines are any boundaries that limit movement or freedom. The word has a negative connotation and is often used to criticize something that is considered too limited: The judge’s decision did not go beyond the confines of established law.

Confined means restricted to a limited space or area. A confined {space} is enclosed and cramped—basements, tanks, crawlspaces. Someone confined to {bed} or confined to a {wheelchair} cannot move beyond it. Prisoners are confined to cells. The word suggests enclosure that restricts movement: {She felt confined in the small apartment}. In older usage, a woman who was confined was in the late stages of pregnancy or childbirth—restricted to home or bed.

Confinement is the state of being restricted to a place or enclosed space. A prisoner serves time in confinement. Someone ill or injured may be confined to bed: {The doctor ordered strict confinement for two weeks}. In an older sense, confinement referred specifically to the period surrounding childbirth, when women were expected to remain indoors. Solitary confinement isolates a prisoner from all human contact.

Confines are boundaries or limits that restrict movement or activity. The word usually appears in phrases like {within the confines of} or {beyond the confines of}: {within the confines of the law}, {beyond the confines of the classroom}. Physical confines are enclosing walls or borders; abstract confines are constraints on thought or behavior. The stress falls on the first syllable, distinguishing the noun from the verb confine.

Confining describes something that restricts movement or freedom. A confining {space} is too small or cramped. Confining {rules} limit what you can do. The word often carries a sense of discomfort—people feel trapped or hemmed in by confining circumstances: {The job felt confining after a few months}.

Confirm means to establish something as true, valid, or definite. You confirm a suspicion by finding evidence, confirm a reservation by calling ahead, confirm an appointment by showing up. In religious contexts, confirmation is a rite affirming one's faith or membership: {She was confirmed in the Catholic Church at fourteen}. To confirm someone in a position is to formally approve their appointment.

Confirmation is verification that something is true, accurate, or settled: {We're waiting for confirmation of the booking}, {The blood test was confirmation of what we already suspected}. In Christianity, confirmation is a rite admitting a baptized person to full church membership, typically in adolescence. The ritual confirms the faith commitment made at baptism. In government, confirmation is the formal approval of an appointment: {Senate confirmation of the nominee}.

Confirmed means verified or established as true: {The airline confirmed my reservation}. It also describes something firmly settled or habitual: a confirmed {bachelor}, a confirmed {skeptic}. In religious contexts, confirmed refers to someone who has undergone confirmation, the rite admitting them to full church membership. {We're still waiting for confirmed reports from the scene.}
clues: Checked and found to be true

definition: To confiscate is to take possession of something by authority, typically as a penalty or for security reasons. Teachers confiscate phones, customs agents confiscate contraband, governments confiscate assets. The word implies official power—a thief steals, but a principal confiscates: {The guard confiscated my water bottle at the gate}.

Confiscated describes something seized by authority—typically by government, police, or officials acting under legal power. Contraband gets confiscated at borders; a teacher confiscates a student's phone. The past tense of confiscate: {Police confiscated the weapons}. As an adjective: {the confiscated goods were destroyed}.

Confiscating is seizing property by authority—typically government or institutional power taking something from someone, often as a penalty or for security reasons. Teachers confiscate phones, customs agents confiscate contraband, governments confiscate assets from criminals: {The officer was confiscating weapons at the checkpoint}. The action implies the original owner loses possession, usually permanently.

Confiscation is the act of seizing property by authority—typically by government or officials. Customs agents confiscate contraband. Schools confiscate phones. The noun emphasizes the taking itself: {The confiscation of his assets left him penniless}. Unlike forfeiture, which may be voluntary, confiscation implies seizure without the owner's consent.

Confit is a method of cooking meat slowly in its own fat, then storing it submerged in that fat—traditionally a preservation technique. Duck confit is the classic example: {duck leg confit with crispy skin}. The term now extends to anything slow-cooked in fat or oil, including garlic confit or tomato confit, where the preservation aspect matters less than the tender, rich result.

Conflab is an informal word for a chat or discussion, typically one that's relaxed and conversational rather than formal. It can also serve as a verb meaning to engage in such talk. {We had a quick conflab about the weekend plans.} The word is a shortened form of confabulation, though it lacks that word's clinical associations with false memory.

A conflagration is a large, destructive fire: {The conflagration consumed three city blocks before firefighters brought it under control}. The word is formal and often appears in news reports or historical accounts. Figuratively, it can describe any widespread destructive outbreak: {The assassination sparked a conflagration that engulfed the entire region}.

Conflict as a noun (first syllable stressed) denotes a state of antagonism, incompatibility, or opposition between two things or parties: He is wracked by internal conflict. The conflict arose over an argument about borders. When used as a verb (second syllable stressed), conflict is frequently followed by with and means to show antagonism, opposition, or incompatibility: The report conflicts with statements made by the police last month. The concert date conflicts with the religious holiday and will probably be moved.

Conflicted describes the state of having incompatible feelings, desires, or loyalties pulling in different directions. Someone conflicted about a decision sees merit on both sides: {I'm conflicted about taking the job—the money is great but I'd have to relocate}. The word implies genuine internal struggle rather than simple indecision.

Conflicting describes things that cannot both be true or cannot coexist peacefully. Conflicting reports offer different versions of events. Conflicting interests pull in opposite directions. Conflicting emotions—like loving someone you're furious with—create inner tension: {I had conflicting feelings about leaving home}.

Conflicts are clashes between opposing forces, interests, or ideas. A conflict may be armed warfare, a dispute between people, or an internal struggle: {conflicts in the Middle East}, {a conflict with my landlord}, {the conflict between ambition and family}. To conflict is to be incompatible: {The meetings conflict with each other}. A conflict of interest arises when competing obligations compromise impartiality.

Confluence is where two or more things flow together, most often rivers: {the confluence of the Ohio and Mississippi}. The word extends to any meeting or merging: {a confluence of events}, {a confluence of influences}. In technical contexts, Confluence is also a widely used collaboration software platform.

Confluences is the plural of confluence, which refers to a place where streams or rivers flow together and merge: {The city sits at the confluence of two rivers}. Extended to abstract situations, it means a coming together of people, ideas, or factors: {a rare confluence of talent and opportunity}, {the confluence of several economic trends}.

To conform is to act in accordance with prevailing standards, expectations, or rules: {Students are expected to conform to the dress code}. The word often carries a whiff of pressure or loss of individuality—someone who conforms goes along with the group rather than standing apart. Things that conform match or fit a pattern: {The building conforms to safety regulations}. To conform can also mean to make similar or bring into harmony: {She conformed her behavior to local customs}.

Conformed is the past tense of conform—to comply with rules, standards, or expectations, or to match a particular shape or pattern. Someone who conformed to social norms behaved as expected: {She conformed to her parents' wishes}. A document conformed to requirements met all specifications. {The data conformed to the predicted model.}

Conforming means matching expectations, standards, or norms. A conforming {loan} meets criteria set by lending agencies. Conforming {behavior} follows social rules. The word often carries a slightly negative shade—suggesting compliance over originality: {She spent her youth conforming to her parents' expectations}. Something nonconforming deviates from the standard.

A conformist is someone who follows prevailing standards, attitudes, or practices rather than thinking or acting independently. The word often carries a negative connotation, suggesting a lack of originality or courage: {He dismissed them as conformists who never questioned authority}. As an adjective, conformist describes behavior or attitudes that align with social expectations: {conformist tendencies}, {a conformist culture}.

Conformists are people who follow established norms, conventions, or expectations rather than acting independently. The term often carries mild disapproval, suggesting someone who lacks originality or courage: {The conformists went along with whatever management wanted}. The opposite is nonconformists—those who resist prevailing standards or forge their own path.

Conformity is the state of acting in accordance with prevailing standards, attitudes, or practices. It often carries a slightly negative connotation, suggesting someone has abandoned their individuality to match what others do or expect: {The suburbs were criticized for their stifling conformity}. In a neutral sense, conformity simply means compliance with rules or specifications: {The building was inspected for conformity with safety codes}. To be in conformity with something is to match or agree with it.

Conforms means to act in accordance with established rules, standards, or expectations. A building that conforms to code meets all requirements. A person who conforms adjusts their behavior to match social norms: {She conforms to avoid standing out}. The word often carries a slight negative charge, suggesting loss of individuality or mere compliance rather than genuine agreement.

Confound means to confuse or perplex someone, often by presenting them with something unexpected or contradictory. In older or more formal usage, it can mean to defeat or overthrow: {The rebels confounded the king's forces}.
