Confound also appears as a mild oath expressing frustration: {Confound it, I've lost my keys again!} In research contexts, a confounding variable is one that distorts results by influencing both the independent and dependent variables.

Confounded means confused or perplexed: {The puzzle left me completely confounded}. More commonly, it serves as a mild oath expressing frustration or annoyance, a euphemism for "damned": {That confounded dog dug up my garden again}. The euphemistic use sounds old-fashioned but persists in exasperated speech.

Confounding describes something that baffles or defeats understanding: {a confounding mystery}, {confounding results}. It can also mean something that frustrates expectations or plans: {The team's confounding loss ended their championship hopes}. In research and statistics, confounding refers to variables that distort the apparent relationship between factors being studied.

To confront is to face directly, especially something difficult or threatening. You confront a problem by addressing it head-on rather than avoiding it. You confront a person by challenging them or forcing an encounter: {She confronted him about the missing money}. To be confronted with something is to have it placed unavoidably before you: {Detectives confronted him with the evidence}.

A confrontation is a face-to-face meeting between opposing parties, typically hostile or tense in nature. The word emphasizes direct engagement rather than avoidance: {The confrontation between protesters and police turned violent}. It can describe anything from a diplomatic standoff between nations to a personal dispute between neighbors. To have a confrontation with someone is to challenge or oppose them directly, though the encounter need not be physical—verbal confrontations are equally common.

Confrontational describes a person, manner, or approach that is aggressively challenging or provocative, tending toward conflict rather than cooperation. A confrontational {tone} or confrontational {style} suggests someone who is eager to argue or challenge others directly. {His confrontational attitude made negotiations difficult.} The word often carries negative connotations, implying that the person or behavior is unnecessarily hostile or combative when a more diplomatic approach might work better.

Confrontations are face-to-face encounters marked by conflict or opposition. The word implies direct engagement rather than avoidance: {The meeting devolved into confrontations between union leaders and management}. Confrontations can be verbal or physical, ranging from tense arguments to violent clashes. Someone who seeks out such encounters is confrontational.

Confronted is the past tense of confront, meaning to face directly or come up against. You might be confronted by an angry neighbor, confronted with difficult choices, or confronted by evidence of wrongdoing. The word implies something challenging or uncomfortable that demands a response: {When confronted, he admitted everything}.

To confuse is to make unclear or difficult to understand: {The instructions only confused me further}. You can confuse a person by bewildering them, or confuse a situation by muddling it. To confuse one thing with another is to mistake them for each other: {People always confuse the twins}. Confused describes both the mental state and the thing causing it: {a confused old man}, {a confused explanation}.

Confused describes a state of mental disorientation or uncertainty—unable to think clearly or understand what's happening. A confused {expression} shows bewilderment. You might feel confused by contradictory instructions or wake up confused about where you are. Things can also be confused, meaning mixed up or disordered: {a confused jumble of papers}, {confused memories of the accident}.

Confusing describes something that creates uncertainty or makes understanding difficult. A confusing {explanation} leaves you unsure what was meant. Confusing {instructions} are hard to follow. The word applies to situations, statements, or anything that muddles clarity: {The signs were confusing, so we took the wrong exit}.

Confusion is the state of being unclear or bewildered—unable to think clearly or understand what's happening. A confusing explanation creates confusion in the listener. Confusion can also mean disorder or mixing things up: {There was some confusion about which room to use}. In the confusion of a crowd, things get lost. To {throw into confusion} is to disrupt or disorient.
clues: When nothing seems to make sense

definition: A conga is a tall, narrow drum of Cuban origin, played with the hands and typically used in Latin music. It also names the dance performed to such drums—a line dance where participants form a chain, hands on the hips of the person ahead, stepping in unison with periodic kicks: {The wedding reception ended with everyone doing the conga around the dance floor}.

Congas are tall, narrow drums of Cuban origin, played with the hands. They typically come in sets of two or three with different pitches and are essential to Latin music, salsa, and jazz. The conga is also a line dance where participants form a chain, hands on the hips of the person ahead, moving to a syncopated beat: {The whole party joined the conga line}.

Congealed describes something that has thickened or solidified, especially a liquid that has cooled or clotted: {congealed bacon grease}, {congealed blood on the wound}. The word often carries a slightly unpleasant connotation—food that has congealed has usually sat too long and become unappetizing. Figuratively, ideas or plans that have congealed have taken fixed form after a period of uncertainty.

Congealing is the process of becoming thick, solid, or semi-solid—typically through cooling or chemical change. Blood congeals as it clots. Fat congeals on the surface of cold soup. The word extends to abstract things that solidify or coalesce: {His vague suspicions were congealing into certainty}.

Congee is a rice porridge common across East and Southeast Asia, made by boiling rice in large amounts of water until it breaks down into a thick, creamy consistency. It serves as comfort food, breakfast staple, or sustenance for the sick. Congee is typically plain and mild, dressed up with toppings like preserved eggs, pickled vegetables, or sliced meat: {She made congee for her grandmother when she had the flu}.

Congeniality is a warm, friendly disposition that makes someone pleasant to be around. A congenial person gets along easily with others: {Her congeniality made her popular at work}. The word often appears in contexts of social ease—the "Miss Congeniality" award at pageants honors the contestant others most enjoyed spending time with.

Congested means overcrowded or blocked, impeding normal flow. Traffic becomes congested when too many vehicles clog the roads. Airways become congested when mucus accumulates during illness: {My sinuses are completely congested}. A congested city center has more people or cars than it can comfortably handle. The noun is congestion.

Congestion is overcrowding that impedes flow. Traffic congestion slows vehicles to a crawl. Nasal congestion blocks breathing passages with swollen tissue and mucus. Network congestion occurs when data traffic exceeds capacity. The word always implies too much of something in too little space: {The congestion downtown was unbearable during rush hour}.

A conglomerate is a collection of diverse things gathered into one mass. In business, it's a corporation composed of multiple companies in unrelated industries: {The conglomerate owns hotels, film studios, and insurance companies}. In geology, conglomerate is rock formed from rounded fragments cemented together. To conglomerate is to gather into such a mass.

Conglomerates are things composed of heterogeneous parts clustered together. In geology, a conglomerate is rock made of rounded fragments cemented in a finer matrix. In business, a conglomerate is a corporation combining multiple unrelated companies under one ownership: {The conglomerate owns everything from media networks to insurance companies}. To conglomerate is to gather into such a mass.

Congrats is an informal shortening of congratulations, used to express pleasure at someone's achievement or good fortune: {Congrats on the promotion!} The clipped form suits casual speech and text messages, while the full word remains standard in formal contexts.

To congratulate is to express pleasure at someone's success, achievement, or good fortune: {Let me congratulate you on your promotion}. The word implies shared happiness—you acknowledge that something good has happened to them. People congratulate newlyweds, new parents, graduates, and winners. To {congratulate yourself} is to feel self-satisfied, sometimes smugly: {He congratulated himself on his foresight}.

Congratulations is an expression of praise or good wishes for someone's achievement, success, or happy occasion: {Congratulations on your promotion!} The word acknowledges that something worth celebrating has happened. It works equally for major milestones like graduations and weddings and for smaller wins: {Congratulations, you finally beat that level}.

A congregation is a group of people gathered together, especially for religious worship. The word emphasizes collective assembly—a congregation fills a church, listens to a sermon, sings hymns together. {The congregation rose for the blessing.} Beyond religion, congregation can describe any gathering: {a congregation of protesters}, {a congregation of birds at the feeder}.

Congregations is the plural of congregation, a group of people gathered together, especially for religious worship. A church's regular attendees form its congregation: {The minister addressed the congregation}. The word can also describe any assembled group: {Congregations of tourists crowded the plaza}. In Catholicism, a congregation may be a religious community or a Vatican administrative division.

A congressman is a member of a congress, especially the United States Congress. The term applies to members of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, though in practice it usually refers to representatives: {My congressman voted against the bill}. The gender-neutral congressperson exists but sees limited use; congresswoman is the standard feminine form.

Congressmen is the plural of congressman, referring to male members of a congress, particularly the United States Congress. While congressman can technically apply to members of either the Senate or House of Representatives, it most commonly designates House members, with senators typically called by that title instead. The term has increasingly given way to the gender-neutral congresspeople or members of Congress in formal contexts, though congressmen remains common when referring specifically to male representatives.

A congresswoman is a female member of a congress, especially the United States Congress. The term applies to members of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, though senators are more often called senators: {The congresswoman from California introduced the bill}. The gender-neutral representative or congressperson now appears in formal contexts.

Congruence is the state of being in agreement, harmony, or correspondence. In geometry, congruent figures have identical shape and size—they match exactly when superimposed. More broadly, congruence describes alignment between things: {There was congruence between her values and her actions}. In psychology, congruence refers to consistency between one's feelings and outward expression.

A conifer is a tree or shrub that bears cones and typically has needle-shaped or scale-like leaves that remain green year-round. Pines, spruces, firs, cedars, and redwoods are all conifers. Most conifers are evergreen, though a few like larches shed their needles seasonally. Conifers dominate cold and mountainous regions and are major sources of timber and paper pulp. {The forest was thick with conifers that blocked out the winter sun.}

Conifers are cone-bearing trees and shrubs—pines, spruces, firs, cedars, and their relatives. Most are evergreen with needle-like or scale-like leaves, though a few like larches shed their needles seasonally. Conifers dominate cold and mountainous regions and include some of the world's oldest and tallest trees. {The forest was thick with conifers.}

Conjecture is a conclusion reached without firm evidence—an educated guess or tentative theory. Scientists form conjectures before gathering data to test them. In mathematics, a conjecture is an unproven proposition believed to be true: {Goldbach's conjecture remains unproven after nearly three centuries}. The verb means to guess or speculate: {We can only conjecture about their motives}.

Conjoined means joined together or united. The word appears most often in {conjoined twins}—siblings born physically connected, sharing tissue or organs. Outside this medical context, conjoined sounds formal or literary: {Their fates were conjoined from that moment}.

A conjunction is an important part of speech used in linking. In tradition grammar, conjunctions are of two kinds: those that link sentence elements of equal rank are called coordinating conjunctions, and those that introduce a dependent clause are called subordinating conjunctions. Some conjunctions work in pairs, such as either and or, both and and. Grammatical meanings aside, conjunction means an act or instance of things being conjoined.

Conjuration is the act of summoning something through magic or ritual—especially spirits, demons, or supernatural forces. A conjurer performs conjurations. The word extends to any seemingly magical production: {With a conjuration of hand gestures, she produced a coin from behind his ear}. In fantasy games and fiction, conjuration is often a school of magic focused on summoning creatures or objects from other planes.

To conjure is to summon or produce as if by magic: {The magician conjured a rabbit from his hat}. The word extends to any impressive act of bringing forth: {She conjured a meal from nearly empty cupboards}. To {conjure up} is to evoke or call to mind: {The smell conjured up memories of childhood}. A name {to conjure with} belongs to someone powerful or influential.

Conjured is the past tense of conjure, which means to summon or produce as if by magic: {The wizard conjured a fireball}. More commonly, conjure means to evoke or call to mind: {The smell conjured memories of childhood summers}. To {conjure up} an image or feeling is to create it vividly in the imagination. {She conjured a solution out of nothing} suggests resourceful creation from limited materials.

A conjurer performs magic—either the stage variety involving sleight of hand and illusion, or the supernatural kind involving summoning spirits or casting spells. The word carries a slightly old-fashioned flavor, evoking traveling performers and medieval sorcerers alike: {The conjurer produced a rabbit from his hat}. Also spelled conjuror.

Conjurers are people who perform magic tricks or, in older usage, summon spirits through incantation. The word carries theatrical associations—a conjurer pulls rabbits from hats, makes cards appear and vanish: {The conjurer amazed the children at the party}. In fantasy contexts, conjurers summon creatures or objects through supernatural power.

Conjures is the third-person singular of conjure, which means to summon or bring forth, originally by magic or supernatural means: {The wizard conjures spirits from the deep}. More commonly now, conjure means to evoke or call to mind: {The smell conjures memories of childhood summers}. To {conjure up} is to produce as if by magic: {She conjured up a feast from an empty refrigerator}.

Conjuring is the performance of magic tricks—sleight of hand, illusions, making things appear or disappear. A conjurer pulls rabbits from hats and coins from behind ears. The word extends to any act of summoning or producing as if by magic: {conjuring spirits}, {conjuring memories of childhood}. To conjure up is to evoke or bring vividly to mind: {The smell conjured up my grandmother's kitchen}.

A conjuror is someone who performs magic tricks or illusions for entertainment—pulling rabbits from hats, making objects disappear. The older sense refers to someone who summons spirits or performs supernatural feats through incantation. The spelling conjurer is equally common. {The conjuror astounded the children with card tricks.}

Conk has several informal meanings united by suddenness or impact. To conk out is to fall asleep abruptly or stop working: {The engine conked out on the highway}. A conk on the head is a blow, and to conk someone is to hit them. In older slang, conk also meant to straighten kinky hair with chemicals, or the hairstyle itself—now largely historical.

Conked is the past tense of conk, meaning to hit on the head or to break down suddenly. If you {conked your head on the cabinet}, you struck it. If the car {conked out}, it stopped working. To {conk out} also means to fall asleep suddenly: {I conked out on the couch after dinner}.

A conker is the hard, shiny brown seed of the horse chestnut tree, especially as used in the British children's game of the same name. In conkers, players thread seeds on strings and take turns striking their opponent's seed until one breaks: {My conker smashed his on the third hit}. The word is primarily British.

Conkers is a British children's game in which players swing horse chestnuts on strings, trying to smash their opponent's nut. The chestnuts themselves are also called conkers. Players take turns striking until one conker breaks: {My conker's a sixer—it's beaten six others}. The game is a schoolyard autumn tradition in Britain.

A conman is a person who swindles others through deception, gaining their trust before exploiting it for money or advantage. The term is short for confidence man—one who wins confidence to abuse it: {The conman posed as a financial advisor and bilked retirees of their savings}. Con artist is a near-synonym.

Conmen is the plural of conman—a person who swindles others through deception, typically by gaining their trust before exploiting it. The term comes from confidence man, reflecting how these schemers depend on winning confidence before the fraud: {The conmen posed as investment advisors and bilked retirees of their savings}. Also spelled con men.

Connect means to join or link things together. Wires connect to terminals, roads connect cities, flights connect through hubs. People connect when they form relationships or find common ground: {We really connected at the conference}. To connect the dots is to perceive relationships between separate facts. A connecting flight gets you from one leg of a journey to another.

Connected describes things that are joined or linked. Physical connections attach objects: {connected rooms}, {connected cables}. Abstract connections link ideas, people, or events: {The two crimes are connected}. A well-connected person has influential relationships or contacts. To feel connected is to experience belonging or emotional closeness: {I've never felt so connected to another person}. In technology, connected means online or networked: {Make sure you're connected to Wi-Fi}.

Connectedness is the state of being linked or joined to something else. The term appears in discussions of social bonds, emotional intimacy, and belonging: {a sense of connectedness to the community}, {the connectedness she felt with her grandmother}. In mathematics and network theory, connectedness describes whether points or nodes can reach one another through continuous paths.

Connection is a link or relationship between things. Physical connections join objects: {The connection between the pipe and the faucet was leaking}. Abstract connections link ideas, people, or events: {I see no connection between the two crimes}. A connection can be a person who provides access or advantage: {She has connections in the industry}. In travel, a connection is a transfer between vehicles: {We missed our connection in Chicago}. To {make a connection} with someone is to establish rapport or understanding.

Connections are relationships or links between people, things, or ideas. A connection may be physical: {The plumber checked the pipe connections}. Social connections are people you know who might help you: {She got the job through connections}. Mental connections link ideas: {I'm not seeing the connection between those two points}. A travel connection is a transfer between routes: {We missed our connection in Chicago}.

Connectivity is the state of being connected, especially to communication networks or the internet: {The cabin had no cell connectivity}. The word also describes how well things link together—transportation connectivity between cities, or social connectivity within communities. In biology, connectivity refers to how ecosystems or habitats are linked, allowing species movement between them.

A connector is something that joins or links things together. In physical contexts, it's a device that couples wires, pipes, or components: {The USB connector was bent}. In language, connectors are words or phrases that link ideas: "however," "therefore," "in addition." A person who connects others—facilitating introductions or relationships—may also be called a connector.

Conned is the past tense of con, meaning to deceive or swindle someone through a confidence trick—a scheme that exploits trust: {He conned her out of her life savings}, {I got conned into buying a worthless timeshare}. The victim believes they're dealing with someone trustworthy, which is what makes the deception work.

Conning is the present participle of con in its sense of swindling or deceiving: {He's been conning old ladies out of their savings}. Separately, conning relates to directing a ship's steering—the conning tower on a submarine is where navigation commands originate. The two words have different origins.

A conniption is a fit of rage, panic, or hysterics—an exaggerated emotional outburst: {My mother will have a conniption when she sees this mess}. The word is informal and often humorous, suggesting the reaction is disproportionate to its cause. Also appears as {conniption fit}, which is slightly redundant but common.

Conniptions are fits of rage, panic, or hysterical emotion—usually appearing in the phrase {have conniptions} or {throw conniptions}. The word is informal and often hyperbolic, describing an exaggerated reaction to something upsetting: {My mother will have conniptions when she sees this mess}. The singular conniption appears less often but means the same thing.

Conniving describes someone who schemes or plots, typically through dishonest means. A conniving person manipulates situations for personal advantage, often by secretly cooperating with others in wrongdoing: {a conniving business partner}, {She's conniving to get the inheritance}. The word carries strong negative connotations of sneakiness and moral untrustworthiness.

A connoisseur is someone with expert knowledge and refined taste in a particular field, especially the arts, food, or wine. The word implies not just expertise but discriminating judgment—the ability to distinguish quality from mediocrity: {a connoisseur of fine whiskey}, {a connoisseur of Renaissance painting}. It can be used seriously or with light irony: {He fancies himself a connoisseur of cheap beer}.

Connoisseurs are people with expert knowledge and refined taste in a particular field, especially the arts, food, or wine. The word implies discriminating judgment developed through experience: {a connoisseur of fine whiskey}, {jazz connoisseurs recognized his genius before critics did}. Sometimes used ironically for obsessive expertise in trivial matters: {a connoisseur of bad movies}.

Connotation is the emotional or cultural baggage a word carries beyond its literal meaning. {Home} denotes a dwelling but connotes warmth and belonging. {Cheap} and {inexpensive} mean the same thing, but cheap connotes low quality. Writers and speakers choose words partly for their connotations—{slender} flatters where {skinny} might not.

Connotations are the associations and implications a word carries beyond its literal meaning. {The word "home" has warm connotations that "house" lacks.} While denotation is what a word directly refers to, connotations are the feelings, judgments, or cultural baggage it brings along. Writers choose words partly for their connotations: "slender" and "skinny" denote the same thing but suggest different attitudes toward it.

To conquer is to defeat and take control of, typically through military force: {Alexander conquered most of the known world}. The word extends to overcoming obstacles or fears: {She conquered her addiction}, {He finally conquered his fear of heights}. A conquering personality or smile wins people over through charm or force of will.

Conquered is the past tense of conquer, meaning to defeat and take control of by force. Armies conquer territories; nations conquer other nations: {The Romans conquered Gaul}. Extended uses describe overcoming challenges or obstacles: {She conquered her fear of heights}. To be conquered is to be subdued or won over: {He was conquered by her charm}.

Conquering is the act of defeating and taking control—of enemies, territories, or challenges. A conquering army seizes land; a conquering hero returns victorious. The word extends to overcoming obstacles: {conquering your fears}, {conquering a mountain}. Someone conquering hearts wins them over through charm or appeal.

A conqueror is someone who defeats and takes control of people, territory, or obstacles. The word carries overtones of military victory and domination: {William the Conqueror invaded England in 1066}. Extended uses describe anyone who overcomes challenges or achieves mastery: {a conqueror of fears}, {conquerors of Everest}.

Conquerors are those who defeat and take control through force—of territories, peoples, or rivals. The word carries historical weight: {Spanish conquerors brought disease to the New World}. It extends to anyone who overcomes great obstacles: {conquerors of Everest}, {conquerors of their own fears}. William the Conqueror established the template.

Conquest is the act of taking control of a place or people through military force, or the territory so acquired. The Norman Conquest of England in 1066 is the most famous example in English-speaking history. Beyond warfare, conquest extends to any decisive victory or successful effort to overcome: {the conquest of disease}, {the conquest of space}. In romantic contexts, a conquest is someone whose affections have been won, often implying pursuit and triumph rather than mutual attraction.

Conquests are acts of conquering—taking control of territory, people, or resources through force or sustained effort. Military conquests expand empires; romantic conquests are people seduced or won over: {He boasted of his conquests}. The word can describe any hard-won achievement: {her conquest of the literary establishment}. See also conquest.

A conquistador is a Spanish or Portuguese conqueror, specifically the soldiers and explorers who invaded and colonized the Americas in the sixteenth century. Cortés, Pizarro, and their contemporaries subjugated the Aztec and Inca empires, often with brutal efficiency. The term now applies figuratively to anyone who conquers aggressively: {corporate conquistadors expanding into new markets}.

Conquistadors were the Spanish soldiers and explorers who conquered much of the Americas in the 16th century, toppling the Aztec and Inca empires and claiming vast territories for Spain. The word is Spanish for "conquerors." Figuratively, conquistador suggests aggressive conquest or domination: {Silicon Valley conquistadors reshaping entire industries}.

Cons are disadvantages or arguments against something, typically weighed against pros: {Let's consider the pros and cons before deciding}. A con is also a swindle or confidence trick, and to con someone is to deceive them for gain: {He conned her out of her savings}. A con is also informal for a convict: {an ex-con}. In programming, cons is a function that constructs data structures.

Conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong that guides behavior and produces guilt when violated. It functions as a moral compass: {My conscience wouldn't let me keep the money}. A {guilty conscience} troubles someone who has done wrong. To do something {in good conscience} is to act without moral conflict. {Conscience} can also mean conscientiousness: {a conscience about returning calls}.

Conscientious describes someone who takes their duties seriously and performs them carefully and thoroughly. A conscientious {worker} pays attention to details and follows through on commitments. A conscientious {objector} refuses military service based on moral or religious principles—the conscience won't allow it. The word suggests internal motivation rather than external pressure: {She was conscientious about recycling long before it became popular}.

Conscientiousness is the quality of being thorough, careful, and attentive to duty. A conscientious person takes their responsibilities seriously and follows through on commitments: {Her conscientiousness made her the most reliable employee on the team}. In psychology, conscientiousness is one of the Big Five personality traits, associated with self-discipline, organization, and goal-directed behavior.
clues: The trait of being reliably thorough

definition: Conscious means awake and aware—able to perceive and respond to surroundings. An unconscious person lacks this awareness; a conscious one has it. The word extends to deliberate attention: a {conscious effort}, a {conscious decision}. To be {conscious of} something is to notice or consider it: {She was conscious of being watched}. {Self-conscious} describes heightened awareness of oneself, often uncomfortably so.

Consciousness is the state of being aware—of yourself, your surroundings, your thoughts. At its most basic, it distinguishes waking from sleep or coma: {The patient regained consciousness after surgery}. More abstractly, consciousness is subjective experience itself—what philosophers call the "hard problem" of explaining why physical processes produce inner awareness at all. A consciousness can also mean a particular mindset or awareness: {class consciousness}, {environmental consciousness}. To {raise consciousness} is to increase awareness of social or political issues.

A conscript is a person compelled by law to serve in the military—a draftee rather than a volunteer. The verb means to enlist someone by compulsion: {They conscripted thousands of young men during the war}. Conscript armies contrast with professional or volunteer forces. The term extends to any forced recruitment: {The regime conscripted civilians into labor brigades}.

Conscripted means compelled into military service by government authority rather than volunteering. The word applies to soldiers drafted during wartime: {My grandfather was conscripted in 1942}. It extends to any forced enrollment or labor: {Workers were conscripted to build the railroad}. The tone often emphasizes lack of choice: {I was conscripted into helping with the move}.

Conscription is compulsory military service—the government's power to require citizens to serve in the armed forces. Countries institute conscription during wartime or maintain it permanently. The term often carries negative connotations that voluntary enlistment doesn't: {He fled to Canada to avoid conscription}. Also called the draft.

Conscripts are people compelled by law to serve in the military, as opposed to volunteers. The term carries connotations of unwillingness or inexperience: {an army of poorly trained conscripts}. To conscript is to draft someone into service. The word extends beyond military contexts to forced participation generally: {conscripted into helping with the move}.

To consecrate is to declare something sacred or dedicate it to a religious purpose: {The bishop consecrated the new cathedral}. The word extends to any solemn dedication: {She consecrated her life to the cause}. Something consecrated is set apart from ordinary use, made holy or venerable. The adjective describes what has undergone this transformation: {consecrated ground}.

Consecrated describes something that has been formally dedicated to sacred or religious purposes. A consecrated church, altar, or burial ground has undergone ritual blessing that sets it apart from ordinary use. The word extends to anything solemnly devoted to a high purpose: {consecrated to the service of others}. Ground where significant sacrifice occurred may be called consecrated: {We cannot consecrate this ground; the brave men who struggled here have consecrated it}.

Consecration is the act of making something sacred or dedicating it to a holy purpose. In religious contexts, it refers to rituals that set apart objects, places, or people for divine service: {the consecration of a church}, {the consecration of bread and wine in the Eucharist}. A bishop's consecration formally installs them in office. More broadly, consecration can mean solemn dedication to any cause: {She viewed her work as a consecration to justice}.

Consecutive describes things that follow one after another without interruption: {three consecutive wins}, {consecutive days of rain}. The word emphasizes unbroken sequence—if you miss a day, the count resets. {She served four consecutive terms in office.}

Consensual describes something done with the agreement of all parties involved. The word appears most often in contexts where consent matters legally or ethically—sex, medical procedures, contracts: {consensual sex}, {a consensual relationship}. If something is consensual, everyone affected has agreed to it.

Consensus means general agreement or agreement among all. When people reach a consensus, they come to agree about something, even if the agreement is a small part of a larger issue: After much debate, a consensus emerged to allocate funds for the initial phase of the project. When there is no consensus, members of a group cannot come to even a modicum of agreement. Since consensus is about opinion, it is redundant to say consensus of opinion, and since consensus is by definition general, it is redundant to say general consensus. Despite that, both phrases are very common.

When you consent to something, you agree to do it: More than 500 volunteers consented to participate in the study. You can give your consent about an action that doesn’t involve you directly: Students are required to get their parents’ consent in writing before using the facilities. The participle consenting is used to talk about activities, usually involving two people, in which both of them consent to what they are doing—that is, neither is acting by compulsion: consenting partners.

Consenting describes someone who gives permission or agreement, especially in contexts where consent matters legally or ethically. A {consenting adult} can make their own choices about sex, medical treatment, or risky activities. The phrase {consenting adults} often appears in arguments that private behavior between willing participants shouldn't be regulated: {What consenting adults do in their bedroom is their own business}.

A consequence is what follows from an action or condition—the result, outcome, or effect. {The scandal had consequences for his career.} To face the consequences is to accept responsibility for outcomes, usually negative ones. A person of consequence has importance or distinction; something of no consequence doesn't matter. In consequence means as a result.

Consequences are the results or effects that follow from an action, condition, or decision. The word often carries a negative weight—{actions have consequences} typically warns of unpleasant outcomes rather than rewards. {Face the consequences} means accepting responsibility for what follows. Something {of consequence} matters; something {of no consequence} doesn't. The phrase {truth or consequences} names a game where refusing to answer honestly results in a penalty.

A conservancy is an organization dedicated to protecting natural resources, wildlife, or land from development and degradation: {The Nature Conservancy}, {the local conservancy manages three thousand acres of wetlands}. The term also refers to the act of conservation itself, or to a commission overseeing a port or river. British usage favors conservancy where Americans might say conservation.

Conservation is the act of preserving, protecting, or carefully managing something to prevent its loss, waste, or destruction. The term applies most often to natural resources and wildlife—{conservation efforts helped the bald eagle recover}—but extends to energy, water, and cultural heritage like historic buildings or artworks. In physics, conservation refers to principles stating that certain quantities (energy, momentum, mass) remain constant in a closed system. A conservation area is land set aside for environmental protection. The word emphasizes thoughtful stewardship rather than mere non-use.

A conservationist is someone who advocates for or works to protect natural environments, wildlife, and resources from destruction or depletion. The term emphasizes preservation and sustainable use rather than exploitation: {Conservationists fought to save the wetlands from development}. The word often appears in contexts of wildlife protection, forest management, and habitat restoration.

Conservationists are people who advocate for protecting natural resources, wildlife, and ecosystems from destruction or depletion. The term applies broadly—from scientists studying endangered species to activists opposing development in wilderness areas: {Conservationists have fought to preserve the wetlands for decades}. Conservation emphasizes careful management and sustainable use rather than strict preservation.

Conservatism is a political philosophy favoring tradition, established institutions, and gradual rather than radical change. Conservatives typically emphasize individual liberty, limited government, free markets, and traditional social values. The word also describes any disposition toward preserving existing conditions: {His conservatism about investing meant he avoided risky stocks}. What counts as conservative shifts with time and place—today's mainstream was often yesterday's radical reform.

Conservative describes a disposition toward preserving existing conditions and institutions, or being cautious about change. In politics, conservatives generally favor traditional values, limited government, and free markets. A conservative {estimate} is deliberately low to avoid overstatement. Conservative {dress} is modest and conventional. A conservative {approach} avoids unnecessary risk. {She's conservative with her money.} (Capitalized Conservative refers to specific political parties.)

Conservatives are people who favor traditional values and institutions, resist rapid change, and prefer gradual reform over sweeping transformation. In politics, conservatives typically support limited government, free markets, and established social norms: {Conservatives opposed the new spending bill}. The term is relative—what counts as conservative shifts across eras and cultures. American conservatives often emphasize individual liberty and religious values; British Conservatives (capitalized) belong to the specific political party.

A conservator is a person responsible for preserving and protecting something valuable. In museums, conservators repair and maintain artworks and artifacts: {The conservator carefully cleaned the Renaissance painting}. In law, a conservator is appointed by a court to manage the affairs of someone unable to do so themselves—handling finances, property, or personal care for the incapacitated person.

Conservatories is the plural of conservatory, which has two main senses. A conservatory is a school devoted to music or other performing arts: {She studied violin at the conservatory}. It is also a greenhouse or glass-enclosed room attached to a house, used for growing plants or as a sunroom: {The conservatory was filled with orchids}.

Conservators are professionals who preserve and restore cultural artifacts, artworks, or historical objects. A conservator might stabilize a deteriorating painting, repair ancient textiles, or prevent further decay in archaeological finds: {The museum's conservators spent months restoring the damaged fresco}. In legal contexts, a conservator is someone appointed by a court to manage the affairs of a person deemed unable to do so themselves—handling finances, property, or personal care decisions: {The court appointed a conservator for her elderly father}.

A conservatorship is a legal arrangement in which a court appoints someone to manage the affairs of another person deemed unable to do so themselves—typically due to age, illness, or disability. The conservator may control finances, make medical decisions, or both. Conservatorships are meant to protect vulnerable people but can become controversial when the person under protection disputes their incapacity: {Britney Spears fought for years to end her conservatorship}. The term is roughly equivalent to guardianship, though usage varies by jurisdiction.

Conservatorships are legal arrangements in which a court appoints someone to manage another person's affairs—typically finances, healthcare decisions, or both. Courts establish them when someone is deemed unable to care for themselves due to age, illness, or disability. The appointed conservator has significant authority over the protected person's life: {The family sought a conservatorship after their father's dementia diagnosis}. High-profile cases have drawn scrutiny to how conservatorships can restrict autonomy even when the person under protection disagrees.

A conservatory is a glass-enclosed room attached to a house, used for growing plants or as a sunlit living space. The term also refers to a school devoted to training in music or other performing arts: {She studied violin at the conservatory}. The botanical and musical meanings both suggest cultivation—of plants or of talent.

Conserve means to protect from loss, waste, or decay. You conserve energy by using less of it, conserve water during a drought, or conserve natural resources for future generations. Conservation efforts protect endangered species and wild habitats. As a noun, conserve is a fruit preserve, typically with whole or large pieces of fruit: {a jar of strawberry conserve}.

Conserved describes something that has been kept, preserved, or protected from loss or change. In science, particularly biology, conserved refers to features—genes, proteins, or structures—that have remained largely unchanged across species or over evolutionary time because they serve essential functions: {The gene sequence is highly conserved across mammals}. In physics, quantities like energy or momentum are conserved when they remain constant in a closed system. More generally, conserved suggests careful stewardship: {Resources were conserved for future generations}.

When you consider an abstract issue or option, you think about it or agree to think about it. When you consider a person for something, you regard them as a candidate: Only applicants with industry experience were considered for the job. Consider can also convey your opinion about someone or something: I considered the case closed after I received the check. We consider him to be the most valuable member of this community.

Considerate is an adjective that characterizes someone who is thoughtful in a way that shows concern for others. Though the word is always a compliment, it may be used sarcastically when someone’s behavior is inconsiderate, that is, they fail to show concern for others: It was very considerate of you to park in front of the driveway! Considerate is used predicatively (she is considerate) but also attributively with some nouns: considerate, parents, considerate behavior.

Consideration is careful thought before deciding or acting: {After much consideration, she accepted the job}. It also means regard for others' feelings or circumstances—thoughtfulness: {Show some consideration for your neighbors}. In law, consideration is something of value exchanged between parties to make a contract binding. To {take into consideration} is to factor something in. {Under consideration} means being thought about but not yet decided.

Considered describes something arrived at through careful thought: a {considered opinion}, a {considered response}. It implies deliberation rather than impulse—you've weighed the matter before speaking or acting. {After much debate, she gave her considered judgment}. To be {well-considered} is to be thoughtfully planned; {ill-considered} suggests the opposite.
Considering is used to introduce a fact or condition that makes the information in the main clause seem surprising or noteworthy: There really wasn’t much damage considering how windy it was.

A consigliere is an advisor or counselor, especially one who serves as a trusted confidant to a powerful figure. The term comes from Italian and is most associated with organized crime—the consigliere advises the boss on strategy and mediates disputes: {He served as consigliere to the don for twenty years}. The word entered mainstream English largely through *The Godfather* and now applies broadly to any behind-the-scenes advisor: {She's been his political consigliere since his first campaign}.

Consignment is sending goods somewhere, especially for sale or delivery. In retail, goods sold {on consignment} remain the property of the supplier until sold—the shop takes a cut only after a sale occurs. A consignment is also the batch of goods itself: {a consignment of leather goods from Italy}. Consignment shops sell secondhand items this way.

Consistency is the quality of staying the same or holding together. A substance has consistency—thick, thin, smooth, lumpy: {Beat the batter to a smooth consistency}. Behavior has consistency when it doesn't vary: {Her consistency in meeting deadlines made her invaluable}. Arguments have consistency when their parts don't contradict each other. The word implies reliability, though critics might call the same quality rigidity.
clues: Doing it the same way always

definition: Consistent means staying the same over time or across instances. A consistent performer delivers reliable results; consistent behavior follows the same pattern. Something consistent with something else aligns or agrees with it: {The evidence is consistent with her account}. Inconsistency is the failure to maintain this steadiness—changing standards, contradicting oneself, or producing uneven results.

Consolation is comfort received after a loss or disappointment. A {consolation prize} goes to a loser—something, but not what they wanted. The word often carries a sense of inadequacy: {It was small consolation that others had failed too}. To console someone is to offer such comfort, though the comfort may fall short of actually helping.

Consolations are things that provide comfort during disappointment or grief—the silver linings, the compensating factors, the sources of solace. When something goes wrong, you look for consolations: {The team lost, but the consolation was that everyone played well}. A consolation prize goes to losers as a token gesture. {Small consolations} often aren't enough: {It was cold consolation to know others had it worse}.

Console unites several meanings around the idea of comfort and support. To console someone is to offer comfort during distress or grief: {Nothing could console her after the loss}. A console is a cabinet or panel housing controls—for a stereo system, a car's dashboard, or a video game system. In computing and gaming, console refers both to the physical hardware and to a text-based interface for entering commands. The word also names a decorative bracket or a narrow table designed to stand against a wall.

Consoled is the past tense of console, meaning to comfort someone in grief or disappointment. The word implies offering emotional support during distress: {She consoled him after the loss of his father}. To be consoled is to receive such comfort, though the phrase {I'm not consoled} suggests the effort failed to help.

Consoles is the verb form of console, meaning to comfort someone in distress or grief: {She consoles him after the loss}. As a plural noun, consoles are control panels or cabinets housing electronic equipment—particularly video game systems: {The kids were glued to their gaming consoles}. A console table is a narrow decorative table against a wall.

Consolidate means to combine separate things into a unified whole, or to strengthen by bringing together. Companies consolidate when they merge operations: {The firm consolidated its three regional offices into one}. You consolidate power by securing control, or consolidate debt by combining multiple loans. The word suggests both unification and strengthening—scattered resources become more manageable or effective when consolidated.

Consolidating is the process of combining separate things into a unified whole. Companies consolidate by merging operations: {They're consolidating three regional offices into one}. Debts consolidate into a single payment. Power consolidates when it becomes concentrated: {The regime spent years consolidating control}. The word suggests strengthening through unification—making something more solid or secure.

Consolidation is the act of combining separate things into a unified whole. Businesses undergo consolidation when they merge operations or acquire competitors: {The airline industry has seen massive consolidation}. Debt consolidation combines multiple loans into one. In a more physical sense, consolidation means strengthening or solidifying: {consolidation of power}, {the consolidation of wet concrete}. The word implies making something more compact, stable, or manageable.

Consoling means offering comfort to someone in distress or grief. A consoling word, gesture, or presence helps ease another's pain or disappointment: {She put a consoling hand on his shoulder}. The word can also describe things that provide indirect comfort: {The only consoling thought was that it could have been worse}.

A consonant is a speech sound produced by obstructing airflow—with the lips, tongue, or throat—as opposed to a vowel, which flows freely. The letters representing these sounds are also called consonants: B, C, D, F, and so on. As an adjective, consonant means in agreement or harmony: {His actions were consonant with his beliefs}. The opposite is dissonant.

Consonants are speech sounds produced by obstructing airflow—with lips, tongue, teeth, or throat—as opposed to vowels, which flow freely. The term also refers to the letters representing these sounds: in English, all letters except a, e, i, o, u, and sometimes y. {The word "strength" has eight consonants and one vowel.}

A consort is a spouse, particularly of a monarch: {prince consort}, {queen consort}. The word suggests partnership without equal status—the consort doesn't rule independently. To consort with someone is to associate or keep company with them, often with disapproving overtones: {He was seen consorting with known criminals}. A consort can also be a group of musicians playing together, especially early music ensembles.

A consortium is a group of organizations or individuals joining together for a common purpose, typically a large project requiring resources beyond any single member's capacity: {a consortium of banks financing the development}, {a research consortium pooling data across universities}. The arrangement is usually temporary and focused on a specific undertaking. Plural: consortia or consortiums.

Consorts functions as both noun and verb around the idea of companionship. A consort is a spouse, especially of royalty: {the prince consort}, {the queen consort}. To consort with someone is to keep company with them, often with disapproving overtones: {He was known to consort with criminals}. A consort can also be a group of musicians playing together, especially early music ensembles.

Conspicuous means clearly visible or attracting attention. Something conspicuous stands out from its surroundings: {a conspicuous stain on his shirt}, {Her absence was conspicuous}. The word often implies unwanted visibility—being conspicuous can mean being exposed or obvious when discretion would be preferable. {Conspicuous consumption} refers to lavish spending meant to display wealth.

Conspiracies is the plural of conspiracy—a secret plan by multiple people to do something harmful or illegal, or the act of planning together in secret. The word often appears in {conspiracy theories}, explanations attributing events to hidden plots rather than official accounts: {She doesn't believe the conspiracies about the moon landing}. A conspiracy can also be a legal charge: {conspiracy to commit fraud}.

A conspiracist is someone who believes in or promotes conspiracy theories—explanations that attribute events to secret plots by powerful groups rather than to ordinary causes. The term often carries skeptical connotations, implying the person's beliefs lack credible evidence: {The forum was full of conspiracists convinced the moon landing was faked}.

A conspiracy is a secret plan by two or more people to do something harmful or illegal: {a conspiracy to overthrow the government}, {conspiracy to commit fraud}. The word also describes the group doing the planning or the act of planning itself. A {conspiracy theory} alleges that powerful hidden forces orchestrate events—often without solid evidence: {conspiracy theories about the moon landing}. To {conspire} is to participate in such plotting, or more loosely, for circumstances to combine toward some end: {Everything conspired against us}.

A conspirator is someone involved in a conspiracy—a secret plan with others to do something harmful or illegal. The word emphasizes active participation in plotting: {The conspirators met in secret to plan the assassination}. Unlike mere accomplices, conspirators are in from the beginning, helping devise the scheme rather than just carrying it out.

Conspiratorial describes behavior suggesting secret plotting or shared secrecy. A conspiratorial {whisper} implies hidden plans; a conspiratorial {glance} signals unspoken understanding between people. The word can describe actual conspiracies or just the appearance of them: {They huddled in conspiratorial conversation}. Often the secrecy is playful rather than sinister: {She gave me a conspiratorial wink}.

Conspirators are people who secretly plan together to do something harmful or illegal. The word carries connotations of treachery and hidden schemes—political conspirators plot coups, criminal conspirators plan heists. {The conspirators met in secret to finalize their plan.} Unlike mere accomplices, conspirators implies active participation in the plotting itself.

To conspire is to plan something secretly with others, usually something harmful or illegal: {They conspired to overthrow the government}. The word carries connotations of scheming and hidden motives. Events or circumstances can also conspire when they seem to combine against someone: {Everything conspired to ruin the picnic}. A conspiracy is the noun form.

Conspired is the past tense of conspire, meaning to plan secretly with others toward some end, often unlawful or harmful: {They conspired to overthrow the government}. The word carries undertones of shadowy coordination. Figuratively, circumstances can conspire when multiple factors align to produce an outcome: {Everything conspired against us that day}.

Conspires is the third-person singular of conspire, meaning to plan secretly with others toward some end, usually harmful or illegal: {He conspires with his brother to defraud investors}. The word can also describe circumstances that seem to work together toward an outcome, as if by design: {Everything conspires against us finishing on time}.

Conspiring is plotting secretly with others, typically to do something harmful or illegal: {They were conspiring to overthrow the government}. The word carries implications of secrecy and shared intent. More loosely, circumstances or events can conspire against someone when multiple factors combine unfavorably: {Everything seemed to be conspiring against us that day}.

A constable is a police officer, especially one of low rank. In Britain, constable is the basic title for uniformed officers. In the U.S., constables are typically minor officials with limited law enforcement duties—serving warrants, providing courthouse security. Historically, a constable was any officer responsible for keeping the peace in a parish or township.

Constables are law enforcement officers, though the title carries different weight depending on where you are. In the UK, constable is the basic rank of police officer, and the word appears in formal titles like {chief constable}. In the US, constables are typically minor officials with limited jurisdiction, often serving court papers or providing security for local courts. Historically, the term designated a high military or household officer, but that sense survives mainly in period dramas.

Constancy is the quality of staying the same over time—remaining faithful, steady, or unchanging. It most often describes loyalty in relationships {her constancy through his long illness} or persistence in purpose {the constancy of his devotion to the cause}. The word carries positive connotations of reliability and commitment, suggesting someone or something you can count on not to waver. In scientific contexts, constancy refers to variables that remain stable under changing conditions.

Constant describes something that doesn't change or stop. A constant {temperature} stays the same. Constant {interruptions} keep coming. In science, a constant is a value that remains fixed—the speed of light is a physical constant. The word can suggest reliability {(a constant companion)} or relentlessness {(constant pain)}. Constantly means continuously or repeatedly.

Constants are values that remain fixed and unchanging. In math and science, a constant is a quantity that doesn't vary—pi is always approximately 3.14159, the speed of light never wavers. In programming, constants are variables set once and never modified: {The API key is stored as a constant}. Figuratively, constants are the reliable elements in life: {Through all the chaos, her friendship was a constant}.

A constellation is a group of stars that form a recognizable pattern in the night sky, typically named after mythological figures, animals, or objects. Ancient cultures identified these patterns to navigate and mark seasons, and astronomers still use 88 officially recognized constellations to map the celestial sphere. The word extends figuratively to any cluster of related things, especially notable people or qualities: {a constellation of Hollywood talent gathered for the premiere}.

Constellations are groups of stars that form recognizable patterns in the night sky, named after mythological figures, animals, or objects: {Orion}, {the Big Dipper}, {Scorpius}. Astronomers have formally designated 88 constellations that divide the celestial sphere into regions. Figuratively, a constellation is any cluster of related things: {a constellation of symptoms}, {a constellation of talent}.

Consternation is a state of anxiety or dismay, typically caused by something unexpected or confusing. It suggests being thrown off balance—not quite panic, but troubled bewilderment: {The announcement caused consternation among the staff}. {To her consternation, the door was locked}.

Constipated describes difficulty emptying the bowels—infrequent or painful defecation. The word extends to anything blocked or sluggish: {constipated prose} is stilted and unflowing, a {constipated bureaucracy} moves nothing through. Someone emotionally constipated has trouble expressing feelings: {He's too constipated to say he loves her}.

Constipation is difficulty emptying the bowels, typically from hard, dry stool. The condition ranges from occasional discomfort to chronic problems requiring medical attention. Figuratively, constipation describes any state of being blocked or stuck: {emotional constipation}, {creative constipation}. The adjective constipated works similarly: {The bureaucracy was constipated with paperwork}.

Constituencies are groups of voters or supporters, especially those represented by an elected official. A politician's constituency is the district they represent or, more broadly, the people whose interests they serve: {The senator's rural constituency opposed the bill}. The word extends to any group with shared interests that an organization must satisfy: {The university balances the constituencies of students, faculty, and donors}.

A constituency is a body of voters represented by an elected official, or the district those voters inhabit: {She won her constituency by a narrow margin}. More broadly, constituency means any group of supporters or stakeholders whose interests someone serves: {The proposal appeals to the governor's core constituency}. Politicians speak of building, losing, or appealing to constituencies.

A constituent is a component part that makes up a larger whole. In chemistry and cooking alike, constituents are the ingredients or elements that combine to form something: {Water's constituents are hydrogen and oxygen}. In politics, constituents are the voters who make up an elected official's district—the people a representative is supposed to serve. The adjective use emphasizes this part-of-whole relationship: {constituent parts}, {constituent elements}. A constituent assembly is one convened specifically to draft or adopt a constitution.

Constituents are the parts that make up a whole: {the chemical constituents of the compound}, {the constituents of a balanced diet}. In politics, constituents are the voters in a particular district—the people a representative serves: {She met with constituents to discuss the proposed legislation}. The word works as an adjective meaning component or essential: {constituent parts}, {a constituent assembly}.

Constitution refers to the fundamental makeup of something—its essential character and composition. A person's constitution is their physical or mental nature: {She has a strong constitution}, {His nervous constitution couldn't handle the stress}. The word also means the act of establishing or forming something: {the constitution of a new committee}. More commonly, it refers to the basic principles and laws governing an organization or nation, typically written in a founding document: {The club's constitution requires annual elections}. (Capitalized Constitution refers to a specific national founding document, especially the U.S. Constitution.)

Constitutional describes what relates to or is established by a constitution—the fundamental principles governing a nation or organization: {constitutional rights}, {constitutional law}, {a constitutional amendment}. A constitutional monarchy limits royal power through founding documents. Something constitutional to a person belongs to their physical or mental makeup: {a constitutional weakness}. As a noun, a constitutional is an old-fashioned word for a health-promoting walk: {taking one's morning constitutional}.

Constitutions are the fundamental principles and laws that establish a government's structure and powers. Most nations have a written constitution as their supreme legal document: {The U.S. Constitution established three branches of government}. Constitution also means a person's physical or mental makeup: {She has a strong constitution}, {His delicate constitution couldn't handle the stress}. The plural often refers to the founding documents of organizations or the varying health and temperaments of different individuals.
clues: Documents establishing governmental rules and rights

definition: To constrain is to restrict, limit, or hold back. Physical constraints confine movement: {The straitjacket constrained his arms}. Abstract constraints limit options: {Budget constraints forced us to cut the project}. To feel constrained is to feel restricted or obligated: {She felt constrained to accept the invitation}. The word implies external pressure rather than voluntary restraint.

Constrained means restricted or limited by external forces or conditions. A constrained {budget} limits spending options. Constrained {movement} suggests physical restriction. Someone acting in a constrained manner appears stiff or unnatural, holding back their true feelings or impulses: {Her smile seemed constrained}. In technical contexts, a constrained system operates within defined boundaries or rules.

A constraint is a limitation or restriction on what is possible. Physical constraints like gravity or material strength determine what can be built. Budget constraints limit what can be purchased. Time constraints restrict how much can be accomplished. In technical contexts, constraints are conditions that a solution must satisfy: {The design had to work within tight constraints}. To act {under constraint} is to act without free choice, compelled by circumstances or force.

Constraints are limitations or restrictions that bound what's possible. Physical constraints govern what materials can do; budget constraints limit spending; time constraints restrict how long you have. The word implies external forces rather than personal choices: {We're working under tight constraints}. In technical fields, constraints are conditions a solution must satisfy.

Constrict means to make narrower or tighter, usually by squeezing or compressing. Blood vessels constrict in cold temperatures. A boa constrictor kills by constricting its prey until it suffocates. The word extends to anything that limits or restricts: {Budget cuts constricted the program's scope}. A constricted throat may come from fear or emotion.

Constricted means made narrower or tighter, squeezed inward. Blood vessels constrict, throats constrict with emotion, pupils constrict in bright light. The word often implies uncomfortable restriction: {Her chest felt constricted with anxiety}. Figuratively, a constricted life or worldview is one hemmed in, lacking room to expand.

Constriction is the act of squeezing, tightening, or narrowing. Blood vessels undergo constriction when they contract. A constriction in a pipe reduces flow. The word applies to physical sensations—{a constriction in her chest}—and figurative limits: {the constrictions of small-town life}. Something that constricts creates constriction.

A constrictor is a snake that kills prey by coiling around it and squeezing until the animal suffocates—boas and pythons are constrictors. The term extends to any muscle that tightens or compresses a body part: {the constrictor muscles of the throat}. More loosely, anything that squeezes or restricts: {The debt felt like a constrictor around his finances}.

To construct is to build or put together from parts: {construct a building}, {construct an argument}. The noun construct (stress on first syllable) refers to something built, especially an abstract idea or theoretical framework: {Gender is a social construct}. In grammar, a construct is a phrase or clause arrangement. The word emphasizes deliberate assembly rather than organic development.

Constructed is the past tense of construct, meaning built or put together from parts. A building is constructed from materials; an argument is constructed from evidence. Something that feels constructed seems artificial or deliberately assembled rather than natural: {Her excuse sounded constructed}. In linguistics, a constructed language (like Esperanto) is one deliberately created rather than evolved naturally.

As the verbal noun from construct, construction has numerous meanings related to the action of putting something together or forming a whole. Construction is commonly associated with the industry whose job is to build houses, buildings, and the infrastructure that supports them. In a more abstract way, construction can represent something put together in the mind, or with words. A grammatical construction is a group of words that derives its meaning partly from the order in which words are put together.

Constructions are things that have been constructed—buildings, bridges, or other structures: {New construction lined the highway}. The word also refers to the act or process of building: {The bridge is under construction}. In grammar, a construction is an arrangement of words: {a passive construction}. More abstractly, constructions are interpretive frameworks: {You could put a sinister construction on his silence}.

Constructive describes actions, attitudes, or criticism that aim to improve or build something rather than tear it down. Constructive {feedback} helps someone get better; constructive {dialogue} moves toward resolution. The word implies usefulness and positive intent, even when addressing problems. In legal contexts, constructive has a technical sense meaning "implied by law rather than explicit": constructive {dismissal} occurs when an employer makes conditions intolerable enough that an employee feels forced to quit.

Constructs works as both verb and noun around the idea of building or assembling. To construct is to build something by putting parts together: {They constructed a bridge across the river}. A construct is something built or created, often abstract—a mental framework or theoretical idea: {Gender is largely a social construct}. In grammar, a construct is a group of words forming a phrase or clause.

A consul is an official appointed by a government to live in a foreign city and protect the interests of citizens from the home country. Consuls handle visas, passports, and assist nationals abroad: {The American consul helped us replace our stolen passports}. A consulate is a consul's office. In ancient Rome, consuls were the two chief magistrates who shared executive power for one-year terms.

A consulate is the office or residence of a consul—a government official stationed in a foreign city to assist citizens and promote commercial interests. Unlike an embassy, which handles diplomatic relations at the national level, consulates serve regional functions: issuing visas, helping stranded travelers, registering births abroad. {The nearest consulate is in Chicago.} Major cities often host consulates from dozens of countries.

Consulates is the plural of consulate, a government office in a foreign city that serves citizens abroad and handles visas and trade matters. Consulates differ from embassies, which are larger diplomatic missions located in capital cities: {The nearest consulate is in Shanghai, but the embassy is in Beijing}. A country may have multiple consulates throughout another nation.

Consuls are government officials stationed in foreign cities to assist their country's citizens and promote commercial interests. Unlike ambassadors, who represent their nation to another government, consuls handle practical matters: issuing visas, helping travelers in trouble, supporting trade. {The American consuls in Shanghai processed thousands of visa applications.} In ancient Rome, consuls were the two highest elected magistrates who jointly held executive power for one-year terms.

To consult is to seek information or advice from a source—a person, book, or reference: {I consulted a lawyer before signing}. Professionals who consult offer expert guidance, often as outside advisors rather than employees: {She consults for several tech firms}. A consultation is such an exchange. To consult with someone suggests a more mutual discussion: {The president consulted with his cabinet}.

A consultancy is a firm that provides expert advice in a specialized field: {a management consultancy}, {an IT consultancy}. The word also refers to the practice or business of consulting: {She left corporate work to set up her own consultancy}. More common in British than American English, where consulting firm is preferred.

A consultant is someone hired to provide expert advice in a particular field. Companies bring in consultants for specialized knowledge they lack internally—management consultants, IT consultants, legal consultants. The term can suggest expensive outside help: {They paid consultants millions to tell them what employees already knew}. In some contexts, consultant is a euphemism for someone between jobs or working freelance.

Consultants are people hired to give expert advice in a particular field. Companies bring in consultants for specialized knowledge they lack internally: {management consultants}, {IT consultants}, {political consultants}. The term can carry a whiff of skepticism—consultants are sometimes seen as expensive outsiders who state the obvious or avoid accountability for their recommendations. {We hired a consultant to streamline operations.}

Consultation is the act of seeking advice or information from someone with expertise: {a consultation with a lawyer}, {a medical consultation}. It also means a meeting where parties discuss options before making decisions: {The policy was developed in consultation with stakeholders}. The word implies deliberation rather than action—you consult, then decide.

Consultations are meetings where advice or information is sought, typically from professionals or experts. A doctor schedules consultations with patients; a lawyer offers initial consultations to potential clients. The word implies a formal exchange where one party has expertise the other needs: {After consultations with tribal leaders, the agency revised its proposal}. In business and government, consultations often precede decisions, gathering input from stakeholders.

Consulting is the business of providing expert advice professionally. A consulting {firm} employs specialists who advise organizations on management, strategy, technology, or other matters. As an adjective, it describes someone who gives professional advice rather than holding a permanent position: a consulting {physician}, a consulting {engineer}. {She left her corporate job to start consulting independently.}

Consume means to use up or take in completely. You consume food and drink by eating and drinking them. A fire consumes what it burns. Time, energy, and resources are consumed by activities that deplete them: {The project consumed most of our budget}. To be consumed by an emotion is to be overwhelmed by it: {consumed with jealousy}. In economics, consumers are those who purchase and use goods and services.

Consumed is the past tense of consume, meaning to use up, eat, drink, or destroy completely. Fire consumes fuel; people consume food and beverages; industries consume resources. The word extends powerfully into emotional territory: to be consumed by grief, rage, or jealousy suggests being overwhelmed to the point where the feeling dominates everything else. {She was consumed with worry about the test results.} In economics, consumed goods are those purchased and used by end consumers rather than businesses.

A consumer is someone who buys or uses goods and services. The term emphasizes the end user rather than the producer or seller, making it central to economics and marketing: {Consumer spending drives the economy}. Consumer protection laws shield buyers from fraud and unsafe products. In ecology, consumers are organisms that obtain energy by eating other organisms rather than producing their own food through photosynthesis. The word often appears in compounds like {consumer goods}, {consumer confidence}, and {consumer debt}.

Consumerism is the preoccupation with acquiring goods and services, or the belief that personal happiness comes through consumption. The term often carries critical weight, implying excessive materialism: {Holiday consumerism starts earlier every year}. In a neutral sense, consumerism can mean advocacy for consumer rights and protections against deceptive business practices.

Consumerist describes attitudes, behaviors, or systems that emphasize acquiring goods and services as central to personal satisfaction or economic health. As a noun, a consumerist is someone who prioritizes consumption or who advocates for consumer rights and protections. The term often carries critical undertones when applied to societies or individuals seen as excessively materialistic: {The holiday season has become overwhelmingly consumerist}. {Consumer advocates and consumerists pushed for stronger product safety laws.}

Consumers are people who buy and use goods or services. The term frames people through their economic activity—what they purchase rather than what they produce or create. {Consumer confidence drives the economy}. In ecology, consumers are organisms that eat other organisms rather than producing their own food. {Consumer protection laws} shield buyers from unfair practices.

Consumes is the third-person singular of consume, meaning to use up or eat. Fire consumes fuel, worry consumes energy, and a person consumes food. {The project consumes most of her time.} What consumes you occupies your attention completely: {Jealousy consumes him.} A consuming passion is one that dominates everything else.

Consuming describes something that dominates attention or energy so completely that little remains for anything else. A consuming {passion} or consuming {interest} absorbs a person fully. Consuming {flames} devour everything in their path. The word emphasizes totality—whatever consumes leaves nothing untouched: {Her consuming ambition left no room for relationships}.

Consummate works as both verb and adjective around the idea of completion or perfection. To consummate is to bring something to completion, especially a marriage through sexual intercourse or a deal through final agreement: {The merger was consummated last week}. As an adjective, consummate means supremely skilled or complete: {a consummate professional}, {a consummate liar}. The adjective stresses CON-, the verb stresses -MATE.

Consummated means brought to completion or fulfillment. A marriage is consummated when the couple first has sexual intercourse, making the union legally binding in traditional contexts: {The marriage was never consummated}. More broadly, consummated describes anything brought to its intended end: {They finally consummated the deal after months of negotiation}.

Consummation is the act of bringing something to completion or fulfillment. A marriage is consummated when the couple first has sexual intercourse, legally completing the union. More broadly, consummation marks the culmination of any process or achievement: {the consummation of years of negotiation}, {the consummation of her lifelong dream}.

Consumption is the act of consuming—using up resources, eating or drinking, or purchasing goods. In economics, consumption drives demand: {Consumer spending accounts for most of the economy}. The word once commonly referred to tuberculosis, from how the disease seemed to consume the body: {She died of consumption at twenty-three}. This medical sense is now archaic.

When two things touch or make a connection, they contact. Eye contact happens when people’s eyes meet. Physical contact happens when their bodies touch.
