If you’re in contact with someone, you are able to communicate with them. All such people collectively can be called your contacts. When you contact someone, you establish a channel of communication with them. Contacts may also be short for contact lenses, which rest in direct contact with your eyeballs.

Contactless describes transactions or interactions that don't require physical touch. A contactless payment uses near-field communication to transmit data when you tap or wave a card or phone near a reader: {I tapped my card at the contactless terminal}. The term gained currency during the COVID-19 pandemic for delivery and service options minimizing human contact: {contactless pickup}, {contactless check-in}.

Contacts are people you know, especially those useful for business or information: {She has contacts in the industry}. The word also refers to contact lenses—thin corrective discs worn directly on the eye: {I need to put my contacts in}. As a verb, to contact someone is to get in touch with them: {Contact me if you have questions}.

Contagion is the transmission of disease through direct or indirect contact. By extension, it describes anything that spreads from person to person like an infection—fear, panic, laughter, or financial instability: {The contagion of enthusiasm swept through the crowd}. In epidemiology, contagion specifically means spread requiring physical contact, distinguished from airborne transmission.

Contagions are things that spread by contact—diseases transmitted from person to person, or influences that pass through populations. The word covers both literal infection and figurative spread: {financial contagions}, {social contagions}. Fear, panic, and enthusiasm are often described as contagions, capturing how emotions ripple through crowds.

Contagious describes diseases that spread from person to person through direct or close contact: {Measles is highly contagious}. The word extends to anything that spreads readily from one person to another—laughter, enthusiasm, fear, yawning: {Her excitement was contagious}. Contagious emphasizes transmission between individuals, while infectious (often used interchangeably) technically refers to diseases caused by pathogens.

To contain is to hold something within limits or boundaries. A jar contains pickles; a building contains offices; a report contains findings. The word extends to restraint: {She could barely contain her excitement}. To contain a threat, disease, or fire is to prevent it from spreading. In math, a set contains its elements.

Contained describes something kept within limits or boundaries. A contained {fire} stays where it is. A contained {spill} doesn't spread. A contained person keeps emotions in check—measured, restrained, not given to outbursts: {She remained contained throughout the interview}. The word suggests control, whether physical or emotional.

A container is anything that holds something else—a box, jar, bottle, can, bag, or similar receptacle: {Store leftovers in airtight containers}. In shipping, a container is a large standardized metal box for transporting goods by truck, train, or ship. In computing, a container is a lightweight package that bundles software with everything needed to run it.

Containers are objects designed to hold other things—boxes, bottles, jars, bags, cans. The word emphasizes the holding function rather than the material or shape: {shipping containers}, {food storage containers}. In computing, containers are lightweight virtualization units that package software with its dependencies, allowing applications to run consistently across different environments.

Containment is the act of keeping something within limits—preventing it from spreading or escaping. The word applies to physical substances {containment of the oil spill}, diseases {containment measures slowed transmission}, and abstract threats. In Cold War policy, containment was the U.S. strategy of preventing the spread of Soviet communism without direct military confrontation. Nuclear containment structures house reactors to prevent radiation leaks.

A contaminant is something that makes another substance impure or unsuitable for its intended use. The term appears most often in environmental and industrial contexts: {Water samples showed elevated levels of contaminants}. Air, soil, food, and blood can all contain contaminants. The word emphasizes unwanted presence rather than inherent harm—a contaminant in one context may be harmless in another.

Contaminants are substances that make something impure or unsafe. The term typically appears in contexts of environmental or health concern: {The water supply tested positive for contaminants}, {industrial contaminants in the soil}. Food, air, water, and blood can all harbor contaminants. The word implies unwanted presence rather than deliberate addition.

To contaminate something is to make it impure or unsuitable by introducing a harmful or unwanted substance. Water supplies can be contaminated by industrial runoff, food by bacteria, and crime scenes by careless handling of evidence. The word extends beyond physical pollution to abstract corruption: {His judgment was contaminated by personal bias}. Contaminated materials require decontamination before they're safe to use or consume again.

Contaminated describes something made impure or unsafe by the introduction of unwanted substances. Water becomes contaminated when pollutants enter it; food becomes contaminated with bacteria. The word extends beyond physical impurity: {contaminated evidence} has been compromised by mishandling, and {contaminated data} contains errors that undermine its reliability. The past participle of contaminate, it functions as both verb form and adjective.

Contamination is the presence of something unwanted that makes a substance impure or unsafe. Water contamination renders it undrinkable; radioactive contamination makes an area uninhabitable. The term extends beyond physical substances: {cross-contamination of evidence} compromises a crime scene, and ideas can suffer contamination from bias. In scientific contexts, contamination invalidates experiments by introducing foreign variables.

To contemplate is to look at or think about something carefully and at length. You might contemplate a painting, contemplate your options, or contemplate the meaning of life. The word suggests unhurried, serious reflection: {She sat contemplating the view}. To contemplate doing something is to consider it as a possibility: {He's contemplating a move to Portland}.

Contemplates means to look at or think about something carefully and at length. You might contemplate a painting, contemplate your options, or contemplate the meaning of life. The word suggests quiet, sustained attention—not a quick glance or passing thought: {She sat by the window, contemplating the garden}. To contemplate doing something is to consider it seriously: {He's contemplating a career change}.

Contemplating is considering something carefully and at length. You might be contemplating a {career change}, contemplating the {meaning of life}, or contemplating {whether to say yes}. The word suggests sustained, serious thought rather than quick decision-making. To contemplate something can also mean simply to gaze at it thoughtfully: {She sat contemplating the mountains}.

Contemplation is deep, focused thought—the act of considering something carefully and at length. It suggests a calmer, more reflective mode than mere thinking: {She sat in quiet contemplation of the mountains}. The word often carries spiritual connotations, describing meditative attention to the divine or transcendent. In religious traditions, contemplation is distinguished from prayer or study as a more passive receptivity to insight.

Contemplative describes a disposition toward deep, sustained thought—especially quiet reflection on profound matters. A contemplative {mood} is introspective and unhurried. In religious contexts, contemplative life emphasizes meditation and prayer over active service: {contemplative orders of monks and nuns}. As a noun, a contemplative is someone devoted to such reflection.

Contemporaries are people living or active during the same period. The term often emphasizes shared historical moment: {Shakespeare and his contemporaries}, {She was more radical than her contemporaries}. It can also mean people of roughly the same age: {He seemed older than his contemporaries at school}. The singular contemporary doubles as an adjective meaning modern or current.

Contemporary is primarily used as an adjective to characterize one thing that exists at the same time as another: Analysis determined that the two manuscripts were contemporary with each other. A secondary meaning is belonging to the present time: Contemporary art leaves me cold. As a noun, contemporary designates a person who lives at the same time as another: At six feet, the skeleton found in the cave would have been much taller than his contemporaries.

Contempt is a negative feeling or attitude towards something that is considered worthless, low, and offensive. It may be combined with feelings of hatred, ridicule, or anger. Various prepositions can follow contempt but the most common is for: The locals consider themselves descendants of saints and often show contempt for outsiders. Contempt has a special meaning in law: Contempt of court is willful disobedience or open disrespect for the rules of a court.

Contemptible means deserving contempt—worthy of scorn or disdain. A contemptible act is morally low or despicable: {His treatment of the workers was contemptible}. The word judges character or behavior as beneath respect. Not to be confused with contemptuous, which describes someone showing contempt rather than deserving it.

Contemptuous describes an attitude of scorn or disdain toward something considered worthless or beneath consideration. A contemptuous {glance} conveys that the person being looked at doesn't merit respect. {She was contemptuous of his excuses.} The word implies active dismissal rather than mere indifference—contempt made visible.

Contend means to struggle or compete against opposition. If you contend for a title or position, you actively vie for it: {Three candidates are contending for the nomination}. You can also contend with difficulties or challenges, meaning you deal with them: {We had to contend with bad weather the whole trip}. In argument or debate, to contend is to assert or maintain a position: {The defense contends that the evidence was obtained illegally}.

A contender is someone competing for something—a title, prize, or position. The word implies genuine possibility of winning: a contender for the {championship}, a contender for the {nomination}. Someone who isn't a serious contender is {not in contention}. A {pretender to the throne} claims it; a contender actually has a shot.

Contenders is the plural of contender—those competing for a position, title, or prize. The word implies serious candidacy: not everyone in a race is a contender, only those with a realistic chance of winning. {The two leading contenders for the nomination squared off in tonight's debate.} A {pretender to the throne} claims legitimacy; a contender actually fights for it.

Contending describes people or groups competing against each other, often for the same prize or position: {the contending teams}, {contending factions within the party}. It can also describe ideas or forces in opposition: {contending theories about the origin of the universe}. Someone contending with something is struggling against it or dealing with difficulty: {She's contending with a lot right now}.

Stress on the first syllable of content means it’s a noun; on the second syllable, it’s an adjective or verb, or possibly a noun with different meaning. These days, content (noun, first syllable stress) is the most frequently encountered form because it designates what we see and listen to on web pages. A distant second in terms of frequency is the adjective content (second syllable stress), which characterizes a feeling of comfort and satisfaction. The verb content is related to this meaning: I’m contented with my marriage and my job.

Contented means satisfied with one's situation or circumstances—not striving for more, not restless. It suggests a quiet, settled happiness rather than excitement: {a contented sigh}, {She seemed contented with her modest life}. The word overlaps with content but carries a slightly warmer, more complete sense of ease.

Contention is disagreement or dispute: {The main point of contention was who would pay}. It also means a position argued for: {Her contention is that the policy causes more harm than good}. In competition, to be {in contention} is to have a realistic chance of winning. {Out of contention} means eliminated from consideration.

Contentious describes something that causes or is likely to cause disagreement: {a contentious issue}, {a contentious election}. A contentious person is argumentative, quick to dispute or quarrel. The word often signals that reasonable people hold opposing views: {The proposal proved contentious among committee members}.

Contentment is a state of peaceful satisfaction with one's circumstances. Unlike happiness, which may spike with joy, contentment suggests a quieter, more settled feeling—not wanting more than you have: {She found contentment in her small garden and simple routines}. The adjective content describes someone in this state: {I'm content to stay home tonight}.

Contents refers to what is inside something—the contents of a box, a stomach, a document. For written works, contents specifically means the list of chapters or sections at the front of a book: {Check the table of contents}. The word always appears plural in these senses, though the singular content refers to substance or meaning: {the content of his speech}.

A contest is a competition in which participants vie against each other to win a prize or determine superiority: {a beauty contest}, {a writing contest}. The word works as both noun and verb, with stress shifting accordingly—CONtest for the noun, conTEST for the verb. To contest something is to challenge or dispute it: {She plans to contest the will}. A contested election is one where the outcome is disputed or closely fought. Something uncontested faces no opposition or challenge.

A contestant is someone who competes in a contest—a game show, a beauty pageant, an athletic competition. The word emphasizes participation rather than skill level; both frontrunners and longshots are contestants. {Three contestants remain in the final round.} {She was a contestant on Jeopardy.}

Contestants are people who compete in a contest—a game show, talent competition, election, or other competitive event. The word emphasizes participation rather than victory: all who enter are contestants, whether they win or lose. {Three contestants remain in the final round.} {The contestants lined up at the starting block.}

Contested describes something disputed or challenged. A contested election has results that one side refuses to accept. A contested divorce involves disagreement over terms. In sports, a contested shot faces defensive pressure. The word implies active opposition rather than mere doubt: {The will was contested by the disinherited nephew}. Uncontested is the opposite.

Contesting is the act of challenging or disputing something. You might be contesting a will, contesting election results, or contesting a parking ticket. The word implies active opposition rather than passive disagreement: {Several parties are contesting the outcome}. In amateur radio, contesting refers to competitive events where operators try to make as many contacts as possible within a time limit.

Contests are competitions where participants vie for a prize, title, or recognition: {a beauty contest}, {a writing contest}. The word also covers disputes or challenges: {a contest over the will}, {no contest} in legal pleas. To contest something is to compete for it or to challenge its validity: {She contested the election results}. {The divorce was uncontested.}

Context is a noun whose parts reveal its meaning: con- is “together” and text refers to words. Context is the neighboring text of a word or expression that can shed light on its meaning. A natural extension of this sense of context is the conditions in which something exists, occurs, or is considered: The context of their very formal relationship meant that feelings were rarely expressed openly. The author introduces the characters without any historical context, so their actions seem strange.

A continent is one of the large continuous landmasses that make up most of Earth's dry land—traditionally counted as seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. The boundaries between continents are somewhat arbitrary, following convention rather than strict geological criteria. As an adjective, continent means exercising self-restraint, particularly regarding bodily functions or sexual urges: {The patient was continent and ambulatory}. The opposite, incontinent, is more commonly encountered.

Continental means relating to or characteristic of a continent—a large landmass. In European contexts, continental usually means mainland Europe as distinct from Britain: {continental cuisine}, {a continental breakfast} (the light morning meal of pastries and coffee typical of France or Italy). Continental can also describe climate or scale: {continental weather} features temperature extremes; {continental drift} refers to the movement of landmasses. In American history, the Continental Congress and Continental Army date from the Revolutionary War period.

Continents are the large landmasses of Earth—Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. The count varies by convention; some combine Europe and Asia into Eurasia, others count the Americas as one. Continental describes things pertaining to a continent: {continental drift}, {continental breakfast}. Continent as an adjective, a different word, means exercising self-restraint, especially regarding bodily functions or sexual urges.

Contingencies are possible future events or circumstances that cannot be predicted with certainty. Planning accounts for contingencies—things that might happen and would require a response: {The budget includes a fund for contingencies}. In contracts and negotiations, a contingency is a condition that must be met before an agreement takes effect: {The offer is subject to financing contingencies}.

A contingency is something that might happen but isn't certain—a possible future event that must be planned for. Insurance covers contingencies like fire or theft. A {contingency plan} prepares for scenarios that may never occur. In contracts, a contingency is a condition that must be met: {The sale is contingent on financing}. The adjective contingent means dependent on circumstances or conditional.

Contingent means dependent on something uncertain or conditional: {Our plans are contingent on the weather}. A contingent is also a group representing a larger body: {the California contingent at the convention}, {a military contingent}. The adjective sense emphasizes that outcomes hinge on factors not yet determined; the noun sense emphasizes a subset drawn from a whole.

Continual is a near synonym of continuous and in many sentences the two adjectives are interchangeable, meaning continuing indefinitely without interruption. There’s no significant difference between continual bombardment and continuous bombardment. Continuous is often used to talk about both time and space, but continual is used primarily to talk about things that happen in time: The dogs have shown continual improvement since they were rescued from the farm.

Continuation is the act or state of continuing—carrying on without stopping or resuming after an interruption. A sequel is a continuation of an earlier story. A continuation of talks means negotiations have resumed. The word often implies that something extends beyond an expected endpoint: {The meeting ran late, so we scheduled a continuation for tomorrow}. In technical contexts, a continuation may be a supplementary document or installment.

Continue means to keep doing something without stopping, or to resume after an interruption: {The rain continued through the night}, {We'll continue this discussion tomorrow}. Something that continues extends in space or time: {The path continues beyond the ridge}. In legal contexts, to continue a case is to postpone it to a later date.

Continuing describes something that persists or goes on without stopping: {continuing education}, {continuing coverage of the crisis}. It emphasizes duration and ongoingness rather than completion. A continuing {relationship} remains active; a continuing {problem} hasn't been resolved. The word often appears in formal or institutional contexts: {continuing medical education}, {continuing resolution}.

Continuity is unbroken connection or consistency over time. A story has continuity when its details remain consistent across scenes; a business maintains continuity when operations persist despite changes in leadership. In film and television, continuity refers to consistency in props, costumes, and settings between shots: {The continuity error showed her glass full in one frame, empty in the next}. More abstractly, continuity suggests smooth persistence rather than abrupt change: {There's remarkable continuity between her early and late work}.
clues: What keeps a narrative internally consistent

definition: Continuous describes something that goes on without interruption or breaks. A continuous {line} has no gaps. Continuous {rain} falls steadily. Continuous {improvement} happens gradually over time. The word emphasizes unbroken duration or connection, distinguishing it from continual, which suggests repeated occurrence with pauses between.

A continuum is an unbroken sequence or range in which adjacent elements are barely distinguishable but the extremes are quite different: {Gender exists on a continuum}, {the continuum from amateur to professional}. The word emphasizes gradual transition rather than discrete categories. In physics, the space-time continuum treats space and time as unified dimensions.
clues: Smooth gradient from end to end

definition: To contort is to twist or bend out of normal shape, often violently or painfully. A face contorts in agony; a body contorts to fit through a narrow space. The word suggests distortion beyond comfortable limits: {She contorted herself into a pretzel shape}. Figuratively, logic or truth can be contorted—twisted to serve a purpose: {He contorted the facts to support his argument}.
clues: Force into a strained, unnatural shape

definition: Contorted means twisted or bent out of shape, often violently or unnaturally. A contorted {face} is screwed up in pain or intense emotion. A contorted {body} is bent into an awkward position. Contorted {logic} or contorted {reasoning} is strained and unconvincing—twisted to reach a desired conclusion: {His contorted explanation convinced no one}.

Contorting is twisting or bending something severely out of its normal shape. A gymnast contorts her body into impossible positions. A face contorts in pain or rage. The word often suggests distortion that looks unnatural or strained: {He was contorting himself to reach the switch behind the couch}. Figuratively, someone contorts facts or logic when they twist them to fit a purpose.
clues: Bending a body or object grotesquely

definition: Contortion is the act of twisting or bending something, especially the body, into an unusual or unnatural shape. The word often describes the extreme flexibility of circus performers: {The contortionist's contortions amazed the audience}. Faces contort in pain or disgust. Arguments can be contorted—twisted to mean something they don't: {His contortions of logic convinced no one}.

A contortionist is a performer who twists their body into extreme positions—bending backward until their head touches their feet, folding into impossibly small spaces. The word extends to anyone who achieves difficult flexibility, literal or figurative: {The administration's contortionist explanations grew less convincing by the day}.

Contortionists are performers who bend and twist their bodies into extreme positions—folding themselves into boxes, wrapping limbs around their torsos, or bending backward until their head touches their feet. The skill requires unusual flexibility, often developed from childhood training. Figuratively, someone doing {mental contortions} or {verbal contortions} is twisting logic or language to justify a position: {The lawyer's contortions to explain the discrepancy convinced no one}.

Contortions are twisting movements that distort the body or face into unnatural positions. A circus contortionist performs extreme bends and stretches. The word extends to strained efforts: {the verbal contortions of a politician avoiding a direct answer}, {mental contortions to justify a bad decision}. The singular contortion works the same way but emphasizes a single instance.

Contorts means twists or bends out of normal shape. A face contorts in pain or anger. An acrobat contorts her body into impossible positions. The word often suggests distortion that looks unnatural or strained: {His features contorted with rage}. Figuratively, someone might contort an argument or the truth—twisting it to serve their purposes.

Contour is the outline or shape of something, especially as defined by its edges or curves: {the contour of the coastline}, {the contours of her face}. Contour lines on a map connect points of equal elevation, revealing terrain. As a verb, to contour is to shape something to follow curves: {seats contoured to the body}. Contour farming follows the natural slopes of land to prevent erosion.

Contouring is the practice of using light and dark shades to create the illusion of depth and dimension. In makeup, contouring sculpts facial features—defining cheekbones, slimming noses, sharpening jawlines: {She spent twenty minutes contouring before the photo shoot}. The technique also applies to mapmaking, where contour lines trace elevation, and to cosmetic procedures that reshape the body.

Contours are the lines that define a shape's outline or the curves of a surface. The word often describes terrain: {the contours of the hillside}, {a contour map showing elevation}. It extends to bodies: {the contours of her face}. Figuratively, contours are the general shape or character of something: {the contours of the argument}, {the contours of foreign policy}. To contour is to shape along natural lines, as in contouring makeup to emphasize facial structure.
Contra is a Latin borrowing that has infrequent use as a preposition meaning “in opposition or comparison to.” Outside of law and debate, it is usually considered jargon.

Contraband is goods that are illegal to import, export, or possess—smuggled items that cross borders or prison walls in violation of law. The word often appears in legal and military contexts: {The border agents seized contraband worth millions}. Contraband can also function as an adjective: {contraband weapons}, {contraband cigarettes}. Anything forbidden by regulation might be called contraband, even informally: {The camp counselor confiscated contraband candy from the cabin}.

Contraception is the prevention of pregnancy through deliberate means. Methods include barrier devices like condoms, hormonal treatments like the pill, intrauterine devices, and surgical sterilization. {They discussed contraception before becoming sexually active.} The word covers both the practice and the various methods themselves.

A contraceptive is a device, drug, or method used to prevent pregnancy. Condoms, birth control pills, IUDs, and spermicides are all contraceptives. As an adjective, contraceptive describes things related to preventing conception: {contraceptive methods}, {contraceptive failure}. The shortening {the pill} refers specifically to oral contraceptives.

Contraceptives are devices, drugs, or methods used to prevent pregnancy. The category includes condoms, intrauterine devices, birth control pills, and spermicides, among others. {She keeps her contraceptives in the bathroom cabinet.} The adjective contraceptive describes anything serving this purpose: {contraceptive methods}, {contraceptive effectiveness}.

Contract follows the sound pattern of many Latinate words in distinguishing the noun (stress on first syllable) from the verb (stress on second syllable) for some meanings. As a noun, contract represents a formal, enforceable, binding agreement between parties. Verb uses of contract related to this meaning have the same pronunciation: We contracted with a roofer for the job. When used as a verb with any other meaning, the stress is on the second syllable: contract tuberculosis (to shrink or incur), contracting “it is” gives us “it’s” (to shorten).

Contracted describes something that has been made smaller, shortened, or drawn together. Muscles contract when they tense. A contracted form shortens words: {can't} for {cannot}, {I'll} for {I will}. Contracted also means bound by agreement: {a contracted employee}, {contracted services}. To have contracted an illness is to have caught it: {She contracted pneumonia during the outbreak}.

A contraction is a shortening—of words, muscles, or time intervals. In grammar, contractions combine words by omitting letters: {can't}, {won't}, {I'm}. Muscles contract when they tighten or shorten. The contractions of childbirth are periodic tightenings of the uterus. An economic contraction is a period of decline. All senses share the idea of drawing inward or becoming smaller.

Contractions are shortened forms created by combining words and omitting letters, marked by an apostrophe: {can't}, {won't}, {I'm}, {they're}. In physiology, contractions are the tightening of muscles—particularly the rhythmic uterine contractions of labor: {Her contractions were five minutes apart}. Any shortening or shrinking can be called a contraction: {economic contraction}, {the contraction of a cooling metal}.

A contractor is a person or company hired to perform work under contract—typically construction, renovation, or other services requiring specialized skills. General contractors oversee entire projects and hire subcontractors for specific tasks: {We're meeting with contractors to get bids on the kitchen remodel}. The term extends to independent workers in any field who work on contract rather than as employees, and to private firms providing services to government: {defense contractors}, {military contractors}.

Contractors are people or companies hired to perform work under contract, typically for a specific project or period rather than as permanent employees. A building contractor manages construction projects; an independent contractor works freelance rather than on staff. Government contractors provide goods or services to federal agencies. {We hired contractors to renovate the kitchen.} The term often implies skilled trades—plumbing, electrical, roofing—but extends to any contracted work.

Contracts covers both the verb and noun forms built on the idea of drawing together. A contract is a binding agreement between parties—legal documents {sign a contract}, but also informal ones {We had a contract: I cook, you clean}. To contract is to enter such an agreement, or to shrink and tighten: muscles contract, pupils contract in bright light. You can also contract a disease, drawing it into yourself. The opposite motion appears in expand and relax.

A contradance is a folk dance in which two lines of dancers face each other and execute figures as couples, progressing down the line to dance with new partners. Also spelled contra dance or contredanse. The form thrives in American folk communities: {We go to the contradance every Saturday night}. The caller announces each figure before it occurs.

To contradict is to assert the opposite of what someone has said, or to deny the truth of a statement: {She contradicted his account of events}. Evidence or facts can contradict claims: {The data contradicts the theory}. To contradict oneself is to say something inconsistent with what you said before. The word implies direct opposition, not mere disagreement.

Contradiction is a statement or situation in which elements conflict or cancel each other out. Two claims contradict when both cannot be true: {His alibi was full of contradictions}. A contradiction in terms is a phrase whose parts oppose each other, like "deafening silence." To say something is {a contradiction} suggests internal inconsistency or logical impossibility.

Contradictions are statements or facts that conflict with each other, making both impossible to accept simultaneously. Logic treats contradiction as fatal—if a claim contradicts itself, it cannot be true. In everyday use, contradictions often reveal complexity rather than error: {She was a contradiction—fiercely independent yet desperate for approval}. To {speak in contradictions} is to say incompatible things. A {contradiction in terms} is a phrase that defeats itself, like "deafening silence."

Contradictory describes things that cannot both be true at the same time. Two statements are contradictory when affirming one means denying the other: {His testimony was contradictory—he said he was home, then said he was at the bar}. People can be contradictory when their words or actions don't align: {She's so contradictory, telling me to relax while piling on more work}. As a noun, a contradictory is a proposition that negates another.

A contrail is the white streak left in the sky by aircraft at high altitude. Short for condensation trail—hot exhaust meets cold air, water vapor condenses and freezes into ice crystals. Contrails may dissipate quickly or linger for hours depending on atmospheric conditions: {The sky was crisscrossed with contrails}.

Contrails are the white streaks that form behind aircraft at high altitudes, created when hot exhaust meets cold air and water vapor condenses into ice crystals. Short for condensation trails. They dissipate quickly or linger depending on atmospheric conditions: {The sky was crisscrossed with contrails}.

A contraption is a machine or device that appears awkward, complicated, or improvised. The word carries a tone of skepticism or bemusement about whether the thing will actually work: {He built some kind of contraption to keep squirrels off the bird feeder}. Contraptions are often homemade or jury-rigged, assembled from whatever parts were available rather than professionally engineered.

Contraptions are mechanical devices, usually makeshift, improvised, or unnecessarily complicated. The word carries a slightly dismissive tone—suggesting something cobbled together or overly elaborate for its purpose: {What's this contraption supposed to do?} {He built some contraption out of spare parts to open the gate automatically}. Often used when the speaker doesn't know or care what something is properly called.

A contrarian takes positions opposed to prevailing opinion, often deliberately. The term applies especially in investing, where contrarians buy when others sell and vice versa, betting that the crowd is wrong. More broadly, someone contrarian habitually argues the opposite side: {He's such a contrarian—if you say it's hot, he'll insist it's cold}.

Contrarianism is the practice of taking positions opposed to prevailing opinion, often reflexively. A contrarian opposes consensus views on principle, whether in politics, investing, or everyday matters. The stance can reflect genuine independent thinking or mere stubbornness: {His contrarianism meant he'd argue the opposite of whatever you said}. In finance, contrarian investors buy when others sell.

Contrarians are people who take opposing positions, especially when those positions go against popular opinion or conventional wisdom. The term appears often in investing, where contrarian investors buy when others sell and sell when others buy: {The contrarians were loading up on tech stocks during the crash}. More broadly, it describes anyone who habitually disagrees or argues the unpopular side: {Leave it to the contrarians to defend the most hated policy}.

Contrariness is the quality of being contrary—stubbornly oppositional or perversely inclined to disagree. A child's contrariness shows in refusing whatever is offered: {Out of sheer contrariness, she said no to every suggestion}. The word can describe either a temporary mood or a settled disposition toward obstinacy.

Contrary describes opposition or reversal. A contrary wind blows against you; a contrary opinion opposes yours. {Contrary to what you might expect, the experiment succeeded.} Someone described as contrary is stubbornly disagreeable, inclined to oppose whatever others say. {On the contrary} introduces a statement that reverses what came before. The noun contrary refers to the opposite: {I believe the contrary}.

Contrast is about difference—specifically, the kind that becomes visible or meaningful when things are placed side by side. You might contrast two candidates' positions, or notice the contrast between someone's public persona and private behavior. In visual contexts, contrast refers to the degree of difference between light and dark areas: {Turn up the contrast on your monitor}. The word works as both noun and verb, with stress on the first syllable for the noun (CONtrast) and often on the second for the verb (conTRAST), though this distinction is fading.

Contrasts are differences made visible by comparison. A photographer adjusts contrast to sharpen the distinction between light and dark. {The contrast between wealth and poverty was stark.} To contrast things is to set them against each other to highlight differences: {She contrasted his calm demeanor with her own anxiety.} Something that contrasts with another thing differs noticeably from it. {By contrast} or {in contrast} introduces an opposing point.

To contribute is to give something—money, effort, ideas—toward a shared purpose or collection: {She contributed fifty dollars to the fund}, {Everyone contributed to the discussion}. The word implies adding to something larger than oneself. One can contribute to a cause, a publication, or a problem: {Stress contributes to heart disease}. A contributor gives; a contribution is what's given.

Contributing is the present participle of contribute, functioning as both a verb form and an adjective. When you are contributing to something, you are giving money, effort, ideas, or other resources toward it: {She's been contributing articles to the magazine for years}. As an adjective, contributing identifies something as one of several causes or factors: {Smoking was a contributing factor in his illness}. A contributing member participates actively rather than passively.

A contribution is something given or done to help achieve a goal or support a cause. The word covers both material gifts—money, goods, time—and less tangible offerings like ideas or effort. {Her contribution to the discussion changed the direction of the project.} In financial contexts, contributions often refer to payments into retirement accounts, insurance plans, or charitable organizations. The word can also acknowledge someone's role in a larger outcome: {His contributions to the field earned him lasting recognition.}

Contributions are things given or done to help a common effort. You make contributions to a retirement fund, to a charity, or to a group project. The word covers money, effort, ideas, or creative work: {Her contributions to the field were groundbreaking}. In online contexts, contributions often means user-generated content—edits, comments, or donations to platforms and creators.

A contributor is someone who gives something to a shared effort or cause. The word applies to donations {a major contributor to the campaign}, creative work {a regular contributor to the magazine}, and collaborative projects {open-source contributors}. A contributing factor is one among several causes: {Stress was a contributor to his illness}.

Contrition is deep remorse for wrongdoing, especially moral or spiritual offenses. The word carries religious weight—in Catholic tradition, contrition is essential for valid confession and absolution. Outside religious contexts, contrition suggests genuine, heartfelt regret rather than mere embarrassment at being caught: {His apology showed no real contrition}. The adjective is contrite.

A contrivance is something cleverly made or devised, often suggesting ingenuity or artifice. The word can describe a mechanical device or gadget, especially an improvised one: {The garage was full of strange contrivances he'd built from spare parts}. It also refers to schemes or plans, sometimes with a negative connotation of being overly clever or manipulative: {The plot relied on an unlikely contrivance to bring the characters together}. In literary criticism, contrivance often implies forced or artificial plot devices.

Contrived describes something that feels forced, artificial, or overly engineered rather than natural or spontaneous. A contrived plot relies on unlikely coincidences. A contrived excuse sounds rehearsed. Contrived dialogue doesn't sound like real speech. The word carries criticism—what's contrived lacks the ease of the genuine: {The ending felt contrived}, {a contrived attempt at humor}.

Control is the power to direct or restrain something. You control a car by steering it, control your temper by holding it in check, control a meeting by deciding who speaks. Controls are the buttons, levers, or switches that operate a machine: {the controls of an aircraft}. A control group in an experiment receives no treatment, providing a baseline for comparison. To be {in control} is to have command of a situation; to be {out of control} is to have lost it. {Everything is under control.}

Controlled describes something kept in check, regulated, or restrained. A controlled {substance} is legally restricted. A controlled {experiment} holds variables constant. A controlled {burn} is deliberately set and managed. Someone who remains controlled stays calm under pressure: {Her voice was controlled despite her anger}. The word often implies discipline or deliberate limitation rather than natural freedom.

A controller is a person or device that controls something. In organizations, a controller (also comptroller) is an executive who oversees financial operations and accounting. In gaming and computing, a controller is a handheld device for giving input: {She grabbed the controller and started a new game}. In engineering, controllers are components that regulate systems—a temperature controller maintains desired heat levels.

Controllers are people or devices that direct, regulate, or manage something. An air traffic controller guides aircraft. A game controller is a handheld device for input. In business, a controller (also comptroller) is the chief accounting officer who oversees financial operations. {The controllers approved the budget revision.}

Controlling describes the exercise of power or influence over something or someone. A controlling {interest} in a company is enough ownership to direct decisions. A controlling {personality} dominates others, often to an unhealthy degree—managing their choices, monitoring their behavior, demanding compliance. The word carries negative connotations when applied to people: {Her ex was controlling and jealous}.

Controls are mechanisms for operating or regulating something—the controls of an aircraft, the controls on a stereo. The word extends to any means of restraint or direction: {parental controls}, {price controls}, {border controls}. In experiments, controls are comparison groups left untreated to measure the effect of intervention. A control freak insists on managing everything.

Controversial describes something that provokes strong disagreement or public debate. A controversial {decision}, {figure}, or {topic} divides opinion and invites argument. The word often signals that reasonable people hold opposing views: {The film proved controversial for its graphic violence}. Something can be controversial without being wrong—it simply means people fight about it.

Controversies is the plural of controversy—public disputes where people hold strong opposing views. Controversies arise around politics, religion, science, and public figures: {The book sparked controversies that lasted for years}. Unlike simple disagreements, controversies typically involve sustained debate and often media attention.

Controversy is public disagreement or debate over a matter that provokes strong opposing views. A controversy surrounds something when people argue about whether it's right, true, or acceptable: {The film sparked controversy for its graphic violence}. Controversial topics invite dispute; controversial figures attract criticism. The word can describe anything from political scandals to disputes over pineapple on pizza.

A conundrum is a problem that does not have a solution, or whose apparent solution only creates another problem: Workers faced the conundrum of being unable to live on their wages while knowing that a raise would bankrupt the company. An older meaning of conundrum is a riddle whose answer involves a pun or a play on words, but this meaning is rarely employed today.

Conundrums is the plural of conundrum—a puzzling question or problem, especially one without a clear answer. A conundrum often involves a dilemma where every option has drawbacks: {The committee faced several conundrums about how to allocate the budget}. The word can also mean a riddle whose answer involves a pun.

Convalescence is the gradual recovery of health and strength after illness, injury, or surgery. The period emphasizes rest and recuperation rather than active treatment—the body healing itself over time. {After her operation, she spent three weeks in convalescence at her sister's house.} A convalescent home provides care for people in this recovery phase.

Convalescing is the present participle of convalesce, meaning to recover gradually from an illness, injury, or medical procedure. Someone who is convalescing is in the period between acute sickness and full health, typically resting and regaining strength. {She spent three weeks convalescing at her sister's house after the surgery.} The word implies a slow, progressive return to normal function rather than an instant cure.

Convenience is ease of access or use—whatever makes something simpler or more comfortable. A {convenience store} stays open late for easy access. Modern {conveniences} are amenities that reduce effort: running water, electricity, appliances. Something done {at your convenience} happens when it suits you. A {marriage of convenience} serves practical purposes rather than love. As an adjective, convenience describes ready-made products: {convenience foods}, {convenience meals}.

Convenient describes what suits your needs or saves effort. A convenient {location} is easy to reach. A convenient {time} works well with your schedule. Something convenient is ready at hand when you need it: {I keep a flashlight in a convenient spot}. The word can carry a faint suggestion of being too easy or suspiciously well-timed: {a convenient excuse}, {a convenient memory lapse}.

A convent is a community of nuns living under religious vows, or the building where they reside. The term sometimes extends to communities of monks or friars, though monastery is more common for men. {She entered a convent at nineteen.} Convent schools are educational institutions run by nuns.

Convention centers on agreement and gathering. A convention is a large formal assembly—political parties hold conventions to nominate candidates, and industries hold conventions to network and exhibit: {the annual comic book convention}. Convention also means an established practice or custom accepted by general consent: {social conventions}, {the conventions of the genre}. What's conventional follows these norms; to flout convention is to defy them. In contracts, a convention is a formal agreement between parties, especially nations.

Conventional describes what follows established customs, standards, or accepted practices. A conventional {approach} does things the expected way. Conventional {weapons} are non-nuclear. Conventional {wisdom} is what most people believe, whether true or not. The word often carries a faint dismissiveness—conventional implies safe, unimaginative, or conformist: {Her taste in art is utterly conventional}.

Conventions are established practices or customs that groups follow without formal rules requiring them. Writing has its conventions (spelling, punctuation), as do social situations (shaking hands, saying "bless you"). A convention is also a large gathering of people with shared interests: {the annual comic book convention}, {the Democratic National Convention}. In art, conventions are accepted techniques or devices: {the conventions of the detective genre}.

Convents are communities of religious women living under vows, or the buildings housing them. Nuns in convents follow a rule of life—prayer, work, and communal living. The word sometimes extends to communities of friars or monks, though monastery is more common for men. {She entered a convent at nineteen.}

To converge is to come together toward a single point. Roads converge at an intersection. Lines converge where they meet. People converge on a location when they arrive from different directions: {Protesters converged on the capitol}. Ideas or trends converge when they move toward agreement or similarity. The opposite is diverge.

Convergence is the act or process of coming together toward a single point. Lines converge at a vanishing point; opinions converge when people reach agreement. In biology, convergent evolution produces similar traits in unrelated species. In technology, convergence describes formerly separate systems merging: {the convergence of television and the internet}. The opposite is divergence.

Converging describes things moving toward a common point or coming together. Roads converge at an intersection; converging {lines} meet at a vanishing point. Ideas, interests, or technologies can converge when they move toward agreement or similarity: {converging opinions on the matter}. In mathematics and optics, converging rays or series approach a limit or focus.

Conversation is spoken exchange between people. The word emphasizes back-and-forth interaction rather than one-way speech: {We had a long conversation about her future}. A {conversation starter} is something that prompts discussion. To {make conversation} is to chat politely, often to fill silence. In computing, conversational interfaces respond to natural language.

Conversational describes speech or writing that resembles ordinary, informal talk between people: {a conversational tone}, {conversational English}. The word often signals accessibility—a conversational style avoids stiffness or jargon. Someone who is conversational is easy to talk to or skilled at casual exchange. In language learning, conversational ability means practical fluency for everyday communication rather than formal mastery.

A conversationalist is someone skilled at conversation—able to engage others, keep discussion flowing, and make talk enjoyable. The word usually carries positive connotations: {She's a brilliant conversationalist who puts everyone at ease}. A {good conversationalist} listens as much as they speak.

Conversations is the plural of conversation—verbal exchanges between two or more people. A conversation involves back-and-forth dialogue, distinguishing it from speeches or monologues. {We had several conversations about the project}. The word extends to any ongoing exchange of ideas: {national conversations about race}, {the conversation around climate change}.

Converse means to talk with someone, to engage in conversation: {We conversed for hours over coffee}. The word is slightly formal—people more often say "talk" or "chat." As an adjective and noun, converse describes something reversed or opposite: {the converse is also true}, {the converse of a proposition}. In logic, a converse swaps the subject and predicate of a statement. (Capitalized Converse is the sneaker brand.)

Conversion is turning one thing into another. A religious conversion changes a person's faith or commitment. In football, a conversion adds points after a touchdown. Converting a file changes its format; converting currency exchanges one for another. A conversion van has been modified from a standard vehicle. The word implies transformation—something becomes what it wasn't before.

Conversions are acts of changing something from one form, state, or purpose to another. A loft conversion transforms attic space into living quarters. Religious conversion means adopting a new faith. In sports, a conversion is scoring additional points after a touchdown or try. In computing and marketing, conversions measure when users complete desired actions: {Our conversion rate improved after redesigning the checkout page}. The word covers any successful transformation from one category to another.

When convert is stressed on the last syllable, it’s a verb that conveys changing from one thing to another (convert dollars into euros, convert the old church into apartments). Less commonly, when the stress is on the first syllable, convert is a noun and designates a person who has adopted a new religion (Catholic convert). This is the usual meaning if a person converts.

Converted describes something that has been changed from one form, function, or state to another. A converted {warehouse} is now apartments; a converted {atheist} now believes. The word often implies the change is complete and the original purpose abandoned. In religion, a convert has adopted a new faith. As a football term, a converted {try} or {field goal} successfully scored after a touchdown or penalty.

Converters are devices or things that change one form into another. A catalytic converter transforms exhaust pollutants into less harmful gases. A converter box changes digital television signals for older analog sets. In computing, file converters translate documents between formats. The word applies broadly to anything that converts: {currency converters}, {unit converters}, {power converters}.
clues: Devices that alter input to output

definition: Convertible describes something that can be changed from one form or state to another. A convertible {sofa} becomes a bed. A convertible {currency} can be exchanged for other currencies. Most commonly, a convertible is a car with a roof that folds down or detaches: {We drove along the coast with the top down in her convertible}. In finance, convertible {bonds} or convertible {notes} can be exchanged for company stock.

Convertibles are things that can be transformed from one state to another. Most commonly, a convertible is a car with a roof that folds down or detaches: {We drove along the coast in a convertible}. In finance, convertible bonds or securities can be exchanged for stock. A convertible sofa becomes a bed. The singular convertible usually means the car.

Converting is the act of changing something from one form, function, or state to another. A factory might be converting to solar power; a person might be converting to a new religion. In sports, converting means successfully completing a scoring opportunity: {She's converting free throws at 90 percent}. Converting files changes them from one format to another.

Converts functions as both verb and noun around the idea of change or transformation. To convert is to change something from one form, function, or belief to another: {They converted the garage into a studio}, {She converted to Islam}. In sports, to convert is to score after an opportunity: {He converted the penalty kick}. A convert is someone who has adopted a new religion, belief, or cause—often with the zeal associated with fresh conviction: {a recent convert to veganism}.

Convex describes a surface that curves outward, like the exterior of a sphere or the back of a spoon. The opposite of concave. A convex {lens} is thicker in the middle than at the edges, bending light outward. In geometry, a convex shape has no indentations—any line drawn between two points on the boundary stays inside the shape.

The verb convey is somewhat formal and overlaps partly with the meanings of two much more common verbs: carry and send. If you convey a message to someone, you take it to them; but if you say that a painting conveys a message of tranquility, you mean that you feel tranquil when looking at the painting. In law, the meaning of convey is closer to transfer: when someone conveys property to another, ownership changes hands.
clues: Carry from one place to another

definition: A conveyor is a mechanical system that moves materials or objects from one place to another, typically using a continuous belt, rollers, or chain. The word almost always appears in the phrase conveyor {belt}, which has become a metaphor for any repetitive, assembly-line process: {The job felt like being on a conveyor belt}. In industrial settings, conveyors transport everything from packages to coal to sushi.

A convict is a person found guilty of a crime and serving a prison sentence. The word carries a harsher edge than "prisoner" or "inmate," often implying serious offenses: {escaped convicts}, {a gang of convicts breaking rocks}. As a verb (stress on second syllable), to convict is to find guilty in court: {The jury convicted him of murder}. A conviction is the resulting judgment.

Convicted describes someone found guilty of a crime by a court: {a convicted felon}, {convicted of murder}. The word carries the weight of official judgment—not merely accused or suspected, but determined guilty through legal process. As a verb, to convict is to deliver that guilty verdict: {The jury convicted him on all counts}.

Convicting is finding someone guilty of a crime or wrongdoing. A jury convicts by returning a guilty verdict; evidence convicts by proving guilt beyond doubt. The word also applies to self-judgment: {His own conscience was convicting him}. Convicting evidence is the kind that seals a case.

Conviction carries two distinct meanings united by the idea of firmness. In law, a conviction is a formal declaration that someone is guilty of a crime: {His conviction on fraud charges ended his political career}. The other sense refers to a strong, unwavering belief: {She spoke with conviction about the need for reform}. Someone with deep convictions holds firm principles they're unlikely to abandon. To carry conviction means to be persuasive or believable.

Convictions are firmly held beliefs or opinions: {a woman of strong convictions}, {Nothing could shake his political convictions}. A conviction is also a formal declaration of guilt in court—the outcome when someone is found guilty of a crime: {His prior convictions made bail unlikely}. To speak {with conviction} is to speak with certainty and confidence.

Convicts functions as both noun and verb. A convict is a person found guilty of a crime, especially one serving a prison sentence: {The convicts worked on a chain gang}. To convict someone is to find them guilty in court: {The jury convicted him of fraud}. The noun stresses the first syllable, the verb the second.

To convince someone is to bring them to belief or agreement through argument, evidence, or persuasion: {She convinced me that the project was worth pursuing}. You can also convince someone to do something: {They convinced him to stay}. A convinced person holds firm belief: {a convinced vegetarian}. Convincing evidence or arguments are persuasive enough to produce belief.

Convinced means firmly believing something to be true or right. When you're convinced of a fact, you feel certain: {I'm convinced she's lying}. Someone who is a convinced {atheist} or convinced {socialist} holds their position as settled belief, not tentative opinion. To become convinced is to move from doubt to certainty.

Convincing describes something that produces belief or agreement. A convincing argument persuades you; a convincing performance makes you believe the character. The word often implies overcoming initial doubt: {The evidence was convincing enough to change my mind}. A convincing victory is decisive, leaving no question about the outcome.

Conviviality is the quality of being friendly, lively, and enjoyable in company—the warm atmosphere of good food, drink, and conversation shared among people who are happy to be together. The word suggests festive sociability rather than mere politeness: {The conviviality of the dinner party lasted well past midnight}. A convivial person or gathering puts others at ease and encourages merriment.

Convoluted means intricately folded or twisted, like the convolutions of the brain. The word usually describes something unnecessarily complex or hard to follow: a convoluted {plot}, convoluted {reasoning}, convoluted {bureaucratic procedures}. {The tax code is so convoluted that even experts disagree on its interpretation.}

Convolutions are twists, folds, or coils—the intricate windings of something complex. The brain's surface has convolutions, as does a tangled argument or bureaucratic process. The word often suggests unnecessary complexity: {The plot's convolutions made the movie hard to follow}. In mathematics and signal processing, convolution is a specific operation combining two functions.

A convoy is a group of vehicles or ships traveling together, typically for protection or mutual support. Military convoys move troops and supplies under armed escort. Civilian convoys form for safety or solidarity: {a convoy of aid trucks}, {a convoy of truckers protesting fuel prices}. To convoy is to travel in or escort such a group.

Convoys is the plural of convoy—a group traveling together for protection or efficiency. Military convoys move troops and supplies under armed escort. Truck convoys coordinate long-haul journeys. Ship convoys were crucial in wartime, crossing dangerous waters in formation: {Allied convoys crossed the Atlantic despite U-boat attacks}. The verb convoys means accompanies protectively.

Convulsed describes violent, uncontrollable physical movement—muscles contracting spasmodically, a body shaking with seizure or shock. The word extends naturally to emotional extremes: {convulsed with laughter}, {convulsed with grief}. Societies and nations can be convulsed by upheaval: {The country was convulsed by civil war}. The past tense of convulse, it often functions as an adjective describing the shaking state itself.

Convulsing is undergoing violent, involuntary muscular contractions—the body seizing and shaking uncontrollably: {The patient was convulsing on the floor}. Extended uses describe any violent shaking or upheaval: {The building was convulsing from the explosion}, {a nation convulsing with political unrest}. To be convulsed with laughter is to shake uncontrollably from it.

A convulsion is a violent, involuntary contraction of the muscles—the body seizing and shaking uncontrollably. Medical convulsions occur with epilepsy, high fevers, or other conditions. The word extends to any violent upheaval: political convulsions, convulsions of laughter. {The country was racked by convulsions following the coup.} {She went into convulsions of giggles.}

Convulsions are violent, involuntary muscle contractions that shake the body uncontrollably. The word most often describes seizures: {The child went into convulsions from the high fever}. It extends to any violent shaking—convulsions of laughter, convulsions of grief, political convulsions that shake a nation. {The economy went through convulsions after the crash.}

Coo is the soft, murmuring sound a dove or pigeon makes. By extension, people coo when speaking in soft, gentle tones, especially to babies or lovers: {She cooed over the newborn}. The word captures affectionate, soothing vocal expression. As a noun, it's the sound itself: {the coo of mourning doves at dawn}.

Cooing is the soft, murmuring sound doves and pigeons make—a gentle, repetitive vocalization. By extension, cooing describes any soft, affectionate talk: {The couple sat cooing at each other}. Parents coo at babies; lovers coo endearments. The word suggests tenderness bordering on saccharine excess: {Stop your cooing and get to work}.

Cook is the most common verb for the activity of preparing food using heat. A person who does this is a cook, especially if it’s a job or profession. If food is cooking, it has been prepared and is being heated. The verb has several informal uses. What’s cooking? is a way of asking what is happening. If you cook up something, you fabricate it to deal with the situation at hand. Someone who cooks the books does dishonest and illegal bookkeeping.

A cookbook is a book containing recipes and instructions for preparing food. The term extends to any collection of procedures: {a cookbook for laboratory protocols}, {a cookbook approach to software development}. The adjective cookbook suggests following instructions mechanically rather than understanding underlying principles: {cookbook chemistry}.

Cookbooks are books containing recipes and instructions for preparing food. The term covers everything from comprehensive culinary references to specialized collections focused on particular cuisines, ingredients, or dietary approaches: {a shelf full of cookbooks}, {She collects vintage cookbooks}. Many cookbooks go uncooked-from, functioning more as aspirational reading or kitchen décor than practical guides.

Cooked describes food that has been heated to prepare it for eating: {a cooked breakfast}, {cooked vegetables}. Beyond the kitchen, cooked means ruined or doomed—if you're cooked, your situation is hopeless: {Once the evidence came out, he was cooked}. In Australian slang, cooked describes someone exhausted, intoxicated, or mentally fried: {I'm absolutely cooked after that shift}.

A cooker is an appliance for cooking food, particularly in British English where it refers to what Americans call a stove or range: {a gas cooker}, {an electric cooker}. In American usage, cooker typically appears in compounds: {pressure cooker}, {rice cooker}, {slow cooker}. Something described as a cooker can also be intensely hot: {Today's going to be a cooker}.

A cookhouse is a building or room used for cooking, especially in a military camp, on a ranch, or at a remote work site. The term suggests a separate structure dedicated to food preparation, distinct from where people sleep or work: {The crew gathered at the cookhouse for breakfast before dawn}.

A cookie is a small, sweet baked treat, typically flat and round: {chocolate chip cookies}, {sugar cookies}. In computing, a cookie is a small file stored by a website on your device to track preferences or activity. To {toss one's cookies} is slang for vomiting. Someone described as a {tough cookie} or {smart cookie} is resilient or clever.

Cookies are sweet baked treats, typically small, flat, and crisp or chewy: {chocolate chip cookies}, {oatmeal raisin cookies}. In British English, these are called biscuits. In computing, a cookie is a small file stored by a website on your device to track preferences or activity: {Accept cookies?} The phrase {that's the way the cookie crumbles} expresses resignation about how things turn out.

Cooking is the practice of preparing food by applying heat—boiling, frying, baking, roasting, grilling. The term extends to the whole process of meal preparation: {I do most of the cooking in our house}. Someone's cooking is their characteristic style or skill: {Her cooking reminds me of my grandmother's}. Figuratively, if something is cooking, it's developing or happening: {What's cooking?} To cook the books is to falsify financial records.

A cookoff is a cooking competition where participants prepare dishes to be judged, often featuring a specific ingredient or cuisine: {the annual chili cookoff}. The format ranges from casual community events to televised contests. Also spelled cook-off. Separately, a cook-off in military contexts is the unintended discharge of ammunition due to heat buildup in the weapon's chamber.

Cookoffs are cooking competitions where participants prepare dishes to be judged against each other. The format ranges from casual neighborhood events to televised contests: {The annual chili cookoff draws competitors from three states}. A cook-off tests skill under pressure, often with time limits or required ingredients.

A cookout is an outdoor meal where food is grilled or barbecued, typically in a backyard or park. The word emphasizes the social gathering as much as the cooking: {We're having a cookout for the Fourth of July}. Cookout is more common in American English, where it overlaps with but is more casual than barbecue.

Cookouts are outdoor gatherings where food is grilled or barbecued, typically in a backyard or park. The term emphasizes the social occasion as much as the cooking method—friends and family assembling for burgers, hot dogs, and conversation. Cookouts are associated with warm weather and American holidays like the Fourth of July and Labor Day: {We're having a cookout this weekend}.

Cooks is the plural of cook, a person who prepares food: {Too many cooks spoil the broth}. As a verb, cooks means prepares food by heating: {She cooks dinner every night}. Extended uses include falsifying records {(cooks the books)} and progressing well {(Now we're cooking)}. Something that cooks is also being planned or developed: {What's cooking?}

Cool is mainly a designation of a usually comfortable place between warm and cold. Cool relations or a cool reception, however, are uncomfortable because they are better when they’re warm. To cool something is to reduce its temperature. This is especially positive when it applies figuratively to tempers or emotions. The adjective cool is a frequent, informal way to express approval or appreciation: He’s a cool dude.

Coolant is a liquid or gas that absorbs and transfers heat away from machinery, engines, or industrial processes. The most familiar is the antifreeze mixture circulating through a car's engine and radiator: {The mechanic said I was low on coolant}. Nuclear reactors, air conditioners, and computer systems all rely on coolants to prevent overheating.

A cooldown is a period of reduced activity after exertion—light stretching after a workout, easy jogging after a sprint. In gaming, cooldown is the waiting period before a skill or ability can be used again: {The spell has a thirty-second cooldown}. More broadly, any enforced pause before something can happen again: {There's a cooldown between login attempts}.

Cooldowns are periods of waiting before something can be used again. In video games, abilities or items often have cooldowns—after casting a spell, you must wait before casting it again: {The healing skill has a thirty-second cooldown}. In exercise, a cooldown is a period of lighter activity after intense exertion, allowing heart rate and breathing to return to normal. The singular cooldown works as both noun and modifier: {cooldown period}, {cooldown timer}.

Cooled is the past tense of cool. Something cooled has lost heat or become less warm: {The soup cooled on the counter}. Emotions and relationships that have cooled have become less intense or friendly: {Their enthusiasm cooled after the first setback}. {Things between them had cooled since the argument}.

A cooler is an insulated container for keeping food and drinks cold, typically portable: {We packed the cooler with ice and beer for the picnic}. Cooler also refers to any device that lowers temperature: an {air cooler}, a {wine cooler}. In slang, the cooler is jail or a solitary confinement cell: {They threw him in the cooler for the night}. As an adjective, cooler is the comparative form of cool.

Coolers are insulated containers that keep food and beverages cold, typically portable boxes used for picnics, camping, or tailgating: {Pack the coolers with ice and beer}. A cooler can also be a cold drink, especially wine mixed with fruit juice or soda: {wine cooler}. In slang, the cooler is a jail or solitary confinement cell.

Coolheaded describes someone who stays calm and thinks clearly under pressure. A coolheaded {negotiator} doesn't let emotions derail the process. The quality is prized in emergencies, crises, and high-stakes decisions where panic would make things worse: {She remained coolheaded throughout the ordeal}.

Cooling is the process of becoming or making something less warm. It describes temperature reduction {Leave the pie out for cooling} or systems that manage heat {the cooling system in a car}. Figuratively, cooling applies to diminishing intensity—a cooling economy slows down, cooling enthusiasm wanes, and a cooling-off period lets tempers settle before resuming negotiations.

Coolness is the quality of being cool—either in temperature or in manner. A room's coolness provides relief from summer heat. Personal coolness can mean calm composure {She handled the crisis with admirable coolness} or emotional distance {There was a coolness between them after the argument}. In casual use, coolness describes social appeal or stylishness: {His effortless coolness made everyone want to be around him}.
clues: What makes someone seem effortlessly collected

definition: A coonhound is a breed of American hunting dog developed to track and tree raccoons. These hounds have exceptional scenting ability and a distinctive baying voice that carries through woods at night. Major varieties include the Black and Tan, Redbone, Bluetick, and Treeing Walker. {The coonhound treed three raccoons before midnight.} Though bred for raccoon hunting, coonhounds also track larger game like bear and mountain lion.

A coop is a small enclosure for poultry, especially chickens: {We built a chicken coop in the backyard}. The word extends to any cramped or confining space: {Their apartment felt like a coop}. To coop someone up is to confine them in a small space: {The kids were cooped up inside all winter}. Separately, coop is short for cooperative—a jointly owned enterprise: {a food coop}, {a housing coop}.

Cooped appears almost exclusively in the phrase {cooped up}, meaning confined in a small or cramped space. The image comes from a coop—a cage for poultry. People feel cooped up when stuck indoors too long or restricted in their movement: {After three days cooped up in the hotel room, we were desperate to get outside}.

To cooperate is to work together toward a shared goal or to comply with a request. Nations cooperate on trade agreements; witnesses cooperate with investigators. The word implies willingness—cooperation under duress is coercion. {The children refused to cooperate}. {If everyone cooperates, this will go smoothly}.

Cooperation is working together toward a shared goal. The word emphasizes willing participation rather than coerced effort: {The project succeeded through cooperation between departments}. Cooperation can also mean compliance or assistance: {We need your cooperation to complete the investigation}. The adjective cooperative describes both the attitude and organizations owned jointly by members.

Cooperative describes willingness to work with others toward a shared goal: {The witness was cooperative with investigators}. A cooperative venture involves collaboration rather than competition. As a noun, a cooperative (or co-op) is an organization owned and operated by its members for mutual benefit—housing cooperatives, food cooperatives, worker cooperatives. Members share costs, decisions, and profits.

Cooperatives are businesses or organizations owned and operated by their members, who share in the benefits and decision-making. Members might be workers, consumers, or producers: worker cooperatives divide profits among employees, food cooperatives give members access to bulk goods, agricultural cooperatives help farmers market crops collectively. {The dairy cooperative negotiates better prices than individual farms could.} Often shortened to co-ops.

Coops is the plural of coop, a small enclosure for poultry: {The farmer built several coops for the new chickens}. To coop is to confine in a small space, usually with "up": {We were cooped up inside all weekend}. In informal use, coop can also mean a cooperative, especially a housing co-op: {She's looking at coops in Brooklyn}.

To coopt is to absorb or take over something, usually by appropriating it for a different purpose than originally intended. A movement coopts symbols from another cause; a corporation coopts countercultural language for marketing. The word often carries a note of disapproval—what's coopted loses its original meaning or power. Also spelled co-opt. {The establishment coopted the revolutionary rhetoric.}

Coopted means recruited or absorbed into a group, often with the implication of undermining original independence or principles. A movement gets coopted when its energy is channeled toward purposes different from its founders' intentions: {The grassroots campaign was coopted by corporate interests}. Someone coopted onto a committee has been brought in as a member, typically by existing members rather than election.

Coopting is bringing someone or something into your group or system, often by absorbing potential opposition. A political party coopts rivals by offering them positions. A corporation coopts critics by hiring them. The word carries a hint of strategic absorption—neutralizing a threat by incorporating it: {The movement was coopted by mainstream politicians who diluted its message}.

Coordinate means to arrange elements so they work together harmoniously. You coordinate {schedules}, {outfits}, or {efforts} between teams. The verb implies bringing multiple parts into proper relation. As an adjective, coordinate describes things of equal rank or importance: {coordinate clauses} in grammar. As a noun, coordinates are numbers that specify a position—map coordinates locate a point on Earth, and in fashion, coordinates are matching separates designed to go together.

Coordinated describes things working together smoothly and efficiently, whether body parts, people, or systems. A coordinated {effort} involves multiple parties acting in harmony toward a common goal. Someone who is physically coordinated moves with grace and control, while someone uncoordinated tends toward clumsiness. Coordinated also describes items that match or complement each other aesthetically: {Her outfit was perfectly coordinated}. The verb coordinate means to bring elements into proper relation or to organize joint action.

Coordinates are numbers that identify a position in space—on a map, a graph, or the earth's surface. GPS coordinates pinpoint locations using latitude and longitude: {I'll send you the coordinates}. In math, coordinates specify points on axes. The word also names matching separates in clothing: {a set of coordinates in navy and cream}.

Coordination is the organization of different elements to work together effectively. In physical movement, coordination means controlling body parts smoothly: {She has excellent hand-eye coordination}. In planning, it means arranging activities so they don't conflict: {The project required coordination between three departments}.
