The word implies bringing separate things into harmonious operation—whether muscles, schedules, or people.

Coos are the soft, murmuring sounds doves and pigeons make—low, gentle, repetitive calls. By extension, people coo when speaking in soft, affectionate tones, especially to babies or lovers: {She cooed at the newborn}. The word captures both the sound itself and the tender intimacy it conveys.

A coot is a dark waterbird with a distinctive white bill, found on lakes and ponds. The bird's bold, somewhat comical behavior likely inspired the informal sense: an eccentric or foolish person, especially an elderly man. {That old coot has been feeding pigeons in the park for thirty years.}

Cooties are imaginary germs or parasites that children attribute to members of the opposite sex—or anyone deemed undesirable—to justify avoiding contact: {Don't touch him, he has cooties!} The word originated as World War I slang for body lice. The childhood sense treats contamination as a game, with elaborate rituals like "cootie shots" providing immunity.

Cooties are imaginary germs or parasites that children claim someone has—usually to justify avoiding them: {Don't touch him, he has cooties!} The concept functions as playground currency for social exclusion, with elaborate rituals like "cootie shots" to protect against contamination. Originally, cooties was World War I slang for body lice.

Coots are dark waterbirds with white bills, found on lakes and ponds. They bob their heads as they swim and have lobed toes rather than webbed feet. An {old coot} is an eccentric or grumpy elderly person, usually a man: {That old coot has been yelling at kids to stay off his lawn for thirty years}.

A cop is a police officer, from an old slang verb meaning to catch or seize—cops catch criminals. The word is informal but not disrespectful: {The cops showed up within minutes}. To cop something is to get or take it, sometimes illicitly: {cop a feel}, {cop a plea}. To {cop out} is to avoid responsibility or commitment. To {cop to} something is to admit it: {He copped to stealing the car}.

A coparent is someone who shares parenting responsibilities with another person, typically after divorce or separation. The term emphasizes cooperation between parents who are no longer romantically involved: {We coparent pretty well despite everything}. Coparenting can also describe arrangements between friends or others who choose to raise a child together without being a couple.

Coparenting is the shared raising of a child by two or more adults, typically parents who are divorced or separated. The term emphasizes cooperation and coordination between caregivers who don't live together: {We've worked out a coparenting arrangement that gives the kids stability}. It can also describe arrangements between unmarried parents or non-romantic partners who choose to raise a child together.

Coparents are two people who share parenting responsibilities for a child, typically after divorce or separation. The term emphasizes cooperative child-rearing despite the parents no longer being romantically involved: {The coparents agreed to alternate weeks with the kids}. It also applies to unmarried couples who have children together, or to arrangements where friends or relatives share parenting duties.

A copay is a fixed amount a patient pays for a medical service, with insurance covering the rest. Unlike deductibles or coinsurance, copays don't vary with the total cost—a doctor visit might be a $30 copay whether the visit costs $100 or $300: {My copay for prescriptions just went up}.

Cope is mainly a verb that means deal with effectively, and is used of people in relation to challenging situations: How does she cope with four kids and a full-time job? Other words spelled c-o-p-e are infrequent and only likely to be encountered in older or specialized literature. One kind of cope is an ecclesiastical garment. In woodworking, to cope is to fit two pieces of wood together by cutting a miter joint.

Copied is the past tense of copy—to reproduce or duplicate something. You might have copied a file, copied someone's homework, or copied a painting. In digital contexts, copied often refers to placing text or data on a clipboard for pasting elsewhere: {I copied the address but forgot to paste it}. To say someone copied you is to accuse them of imitation.

A copier is a machine that makes copies of documents, short for photocopier. The word also means someone who copies—either neutrally {a fast copier of notes} or negatively, implying imitation without originality: {He's just a copier, not a real artist}.

Copies are reproductions or duplicates of an original, whether physical objects like documents and artworks or digital files. A copy of a book or magazine is one of many identical items produced for distribution. To copy something is to make a reproduction of it, or to imitate someone's behavior or style: {She copied his homework} or {He copies everything his older brother does}. In computing, copy places data on a clipboard for pasting elsewhere.

A copilot is the second pilot in an aircraft, assisting the captain and capable of taking command if needed. The term extends to any assistant who shares control: {My wife was copilot on our road trip, handling navigation}. In computing, copilot now names AI assistants that help with coding or other tasks.

Copilots are the secondary pilots in an aircraft, trained to assist the captain and take over if needed. The term has expanded beyond aviation to describe any assistant who shares control or responsibility with a primary operator. In computing, copilot now commonly refers to AI assistants that work alongside users, suggesting collaboration rather than replacement: {The AI copilot helped me draft the report}. The plural form simply indicates multiple such assistants or secondary pilots.

Coping is the cap or covering on top of a wall, designed to shed water and protect the masonry beneath. The term extends to any protective top edge. Separately, coping refers to the psychological strategies people use to manage stress, difficulty, or trauma: {Her coping mechanisms include exercise and journaling}. The verb cope means to deal with challenges: {He's coping with the loss}.

Copium is internet slang for the imaginary substance people consume when clinging to false hope or making excuses after disappointment. A blend of "cope" and "opium," it suggests someone is numbing themselves to reality rather than accepting an unfavorable outcome: {He's huffing copium if he thinks they'll get back together}. The term originated in gaming and political communities, often used mockingly when someone rationalizes a loss or refuses to acknowledge defeat.

A copout is an evasion of responsibility or commitment, typically one that disappoints others who were counting on you. Someone who backs out of a difficult situation or avoids taking a stand when one is expected may be accused of copping out. {Blaming the weather was such a copout.} The term carries connotations of weakness or dishonesty—taking the easy way out rather than facing consequences or honoring obligations.

Copouts are excuses or evasions used to avoid responsibility or difficulty. The term carries accusation—calling something a copout implies the person took an easy way out when they should have followed through: {His apology was just a copout}. A copout can also be a person who backs down or fails to commit. Also spelled cop-outs.

Copped is the past tense of cop, meaning to get, take, or catch. To cop something is to obtain it, often illicitly or opportunistically: {He copped some weed from his roommate}. To {cop a feel} is to grope someone. To {cop a plea} is to plead guilty to a lesser charge. To {cop to} something is to admit it: {She finally copped to breaking the vase}.

Copper is a reddish-brown metallic element, valued since ancient times for conducting heat and electricity. Copper wire runs through buildings; copper pipes carry water. The color copper describes that distinctive brownish-red. Coppers are copper coins or British slang for police officers—from the verb cop, to catch. {The old pennies were solid copper.}

A copperhead is a venomous pit viper native to eastern North America, named for its copper-colored head. The snake is responsible for more snakebites than any other North American species, though bites are rarely fatal. {Watch where you step—copperheads blend right into the leaf litter.} (Capitalized Copperhead is a historical term for a Northern Democrat who opposed the Civil War.)

Copperheads are venomous pit vipers native to eastern North America, named for their copper-colored heads. The term also refers to Northern Democrats who opposed the Civil War and advocated peace with the Confederacy—their enemies compared them to the snake that strikes without warning. {The copperhead was coiled under the woodpile.}
clues: North American snakes with metallic names

definition: Copperplate is a polished copper sheet used for engraving, or a print made from such a plate. The term more commonly describes a style of elegant, formal handwriting with fine lines and flowing curves—the kind taught in penmanship classes and seen on diplomas and wedding invitations: {Her copperplate script was impeccable}. As an adjective, it describes this refined lettering style: {copperplate calligraphy}.

Coppers is the plural of copper—the reddish-brown metal, or coins made from it. In British usage, coppers specifically means low-denomination coins: {I've got a few coppers in my pocket}. Coppers is also informal for police officers, from the verb cop meaning to catch or seize: {The coppers showed up and broke up the party}.

A coppersmith is a person who makes or repairs objects from copper—pots, pipes, decorative metalwork. The trade is ancient but now rare, largely replaced by industrial manufacturing. Coppersmith also names a barbet, a colorful Asian bird whose call sounds like metal being hammered.

Copping is getting or obtaining something, often with a suggestion of acquisition that's quick, opportunistic, or illicit: {copping drugs on the corner}, {copping a feel}. To cop to something is to admit it: {He finally copped to the theft}. {Copping a plea} means accepting a plea bargain. To {cop out} is to avoid responsibility or take the easy way out.

Cops is the common informal term for police officers. The word carries no inherent disrespect—it's simply casual: {The cops showed up within minutes}. To cop is to get or take: {cop a plea}, {cop an attitude}, {cop a feel}. A cop-out is an evasion of responsibility.

A copse is a small group of trees growing close together, typically in open country or at the edge of a field. The word suggests something smaller and more compact than a wood or forest—a cluster you could walk through in a minute: {We picnicked in the shade of a copse}. The variant coppice has the same meaning.

The idea uniting all meanings of copy is duplication. A copy of a letter, software program, or painting is a duplicate that can fill some or all functions of the original. When you copy something tangible, you make a copy of it. If you copy someone’s behavior, you imitate some or all aspects of what they did. In publishing, journalism, and increasingly in the world of online content, copy refers to text that is being prepared for or is ready for publication or broadcast: Their press release came to us as camera-ready copy.

A copycat imitates someone else's actions, style, or work—often with the suggestion of lacking originality. The term appears frequently as an attributive noun: a copycat {crime} mimics an earlier one, copycat {products} knock off successful brands. Children use it as a taunt: {Copycat, copycat!} The verb means to imitate: {She's just copycatting what the cool kids do}.

Copycats is the plural of copycat—someone who imitates another's behavior, work, or style, often without originality. The term carries mild disapproval, suggesting the imitation lacks creativity: {The success spawned dozens of copycats}. Copycat also works as an adjective: a copycat {crime} replicates methods from an earlier offense.

A copyeditor reviews written material for errors in grammar, spelling, punctuation, and style before publication. The role falls between writing and proofreading—copyeditors don't create content but do more than catch typos, improving clarity and consistency: {The copyeditor flagged three inconsistencies in how we spelled the company name}. Also spelled copy editor.

Copying is making a duplicate or reproduction of something. Students copy notes from the board; software copies files. To copy someone's work without permission is plagiarism; to copy a product is counterfeiting. In casual speech, copying someone means imitating their behavior or style: {She's always copying her older sister}. In radio communication, {copy that} confirms a message was received.

Copypasta is a block of text copied and pasted repeatedly across the internet, often to the point of becoming a recognizable meme. The term blends "copy-paste" with "pasta," suggesting text that gets served up again and again. Copypastas range from absurdist humor to fake warnings to elaborate jokes: {Someone posted the Navy Seal copypasta in the comments again}. The repetition is the point—recognition triggers the humor or annoyance.

Copypastas are blocks of text copied and pasted repeatedly across the internet, often for humorous or ironic effect. They range from absurdist nonsense to fake outrage to intentionally cringeworthy monologues. Some become recognizable memes: {He posted the Navy Seal copypasta in response}. The humor often lies in the incongruity of encountering the same overwrought text in wildly different contexts.

Copyright is the legal right to control reproduction and distribution of creative work—books, music, films, software, images. The creator or rights holder can authorize or prohibit copying: {The photograph is protected by copyright}. To copyright something is to secure this protection: {She copyrighted her designs}. Copyright infringement is unauthorized use of protected material.

Copyrights is the plural of copyright—legal protections giving creators exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, and profit from their original works. Literature, music, film, and software all fall under copyright. The term also works as a verb: {She copyrights all her photographs before posting them online}. To infringe copyrights is to use protected material without permission.

A copywriter writes text for advertising, marketing, and promotional materials. The copy in copywriter refers to written content destined for publication—headlines, slogans, product descriptions, website text, email campaigns. {She works as a copywriter for an ad agency}. Distinguished from copyright, which concerns legal ownership of creative works.

Copywriting is writing text for advertising, marketing, or promotional purposes. The goal is persuasion—getting readers to buy something, sign up, or take action. Copy refers to the text itself: {Who wrote the copy for this ad?} A copywriter crafts headlines, slogans, product descriptions, and sales pages. Not to be confused with copyrighting, which involves legal protection of creative work.

A coquette is a woman who flirts playfully or teasingly, often without serious romantic intent. The word suggests someone who enjoys attention and uses charm strategically: {She played the coquette, keeping all her suitors guessing}. The adjective coquettish describes this flirtatious manner. Though the word can carry negative connotations of manipulation, it often suggests lighthearted romantic gamesmanship rather than genuine deception.

Coquettes are women who flirt playfully or teasingly, often without serious romantic intent. The word carries a whiff of the old-fashioned—a coquette attracts admirers through charm and coy behavior, keeping them interested without committing. The singular coquette can describe a personality type: {She was a born coquette}. The adjective is coquettish.

Coral refers to marine invertebrates that build hard calcium carbonate skeletons, forming reefs in warm shallow seas. A coral reef is an ecosystem of extraordinary biodiversity. The word also names the pinkish-orange color of certain coral species: {coral lipstick}, {a coral sunset}. As a modifier, coral describes this distinctive hue or things made from coral: {coral jewelry}, {coral beads}.

Corals are marine invertebrates that build hard skeletons, forming reefs in tropical waters. A single coral is one such organism or a piece of its skeleton, often used decoratively. Coral also names the pinkish-orange color of these skeletons: {coral lipstick}, {a coral dress}. Coral reefs support extraordinary biodiversity and face threats from warming oceans.

A cord is a length of flexible material—thicker than string, thinner than rope—used for tying, binding, or connecting: {Pull the cord to close the blinds}. Electrical cords carry power to devices. Anatomically, the spinal cord runs through the vertebrae, and the umbilical cord connects fetus to placenta. To {cut the cord} is to sever a dependent relationship. A cord is also a unit of firewood measuring 128 cubic feet, typically a stack four feet by four feet by eight feet.

Cordial describes warmth and friendliness, especially the polite kind shown to guests or acquaintances: {a cordial greeting}, {cordial relations between the two countries}. The warmth is genuine but measured—cordial suggests civility more than deep affection. As a noun, a cordial is a sweet liqueur or, in British usage, a concentrated fruit drink diluted with water.

Cordials are sweet, often fruit-flavored liqueurs served in small glasses, typically after dinner. The word extends to any sweet, concentrated drink—medicinal or otherwise—meant to stimulate or comfort: {The doctor prescribed a cordial for her nerves}. In British usage, a cordial is a concentrated syrup diluted with water to make a drink: {elderflower cordial}. The sweetness connects to the broader sense of cordial as warm and heartfelt.
clues: Sweetened spirits served in small glasses

definition: Cordite is a smokeless explosive used as a propellant in ammunition, replacing black powder in the late 19th century. The name comes from its cord-like appearance—thin cylindrical strands. In fiction, characters often smell cordite after gunfire, though modern ammunition typically uses different propellants: {The air smelled of cordite and gun smoke}.
clues: What replaced black powder in cartridges

definition: Cordless describes devices that operate without a connecting electrical cord, typically powered by rechargeable batteries: a cordless {phone}, a cordless {drill}. The term emerged as portable battery technology made wirelessness notable—before that, most tools and appliances were simply assumed to have cords. {I need to charge the cordless vacuum.}

A cordon is a line or ring of people, typically police or soldiers, positioned to prevent access to or from an area. The term extends to any barrier or boundary that controls movement: {Police set up a cordon around the crime scene.} To cordon off an area is to establish such a barrier. In cooking, cordon bleu refers to a dish of meat wrapped around cheese and ham, or more broadly to food preparation of the highest standard—literally "blue ribbon" in French.

Cords are trousers made of corduroy—a ridged cotton fabric with vertical wales. The word is always plural when referring to the garment: {He wore brown cords and a sweater}. The singular cord refers to rope, string, or flexible insulated wire, or the spinal cord. A cord of wood is a stack measuring 4 × 4 × 8 feet.

Corduroy is a durable cotton fabric with distinctive raised parallel ridges called wales. The texture comes from cut pile woven in lengthwise rows. Corduroy pants were once standard schoolboy wear; now the fabric suggests casual or vintage style: {a corduroy jacket with elbow patches}. As an adjective, corduroy describes roads made of logs laid crosswise over swampy ground—the ridges resembling the fabric's texture.

Corduroys are trousers made from corduroy—a cotton fabric with distinctive raised parallel ridges. The texture is created by cut pile woven in vertical lines called wales. The plural form typically refers to the pants rather than the fabric: {He wore brown corduroys and a sweater}. The fabric appears in other garments, but corduroys almost always means the trousers.

Cordwood is firewood cut into short lengths, typically four feet, and stacked for measurement or sale. A cord—the standard unit—is a pile measuring 4 by 4 by 8 feet, or 128 cubic feet. The term extends to any wood processed this way, whether for fuel, pulp, or other uses. {We spent the afternoon stacking cordwood for winter.}

The core of something is its innermost part. The cores of some things – like apples – are dispensable. When you core an apple, you remove its core. The core of something abstract is usually taken to be the most important, essential part: What is the core of your argument? In computing, a core is an element of hardware used in memory.

Cores is the plural of core—the central, essential part of something. Apple cores hold the seeds. The cores of planets are their innermost layers. In computing, processor cores are independent processing units: {My laptop has eight cores}. To core fruit is to remove its center, so cores also works as a verb: {She cores the apples before baking}.

A corgi is a small herding dog with a long body, short legs, and large upright ears. The breed originated in Wales, where two varieties developed: the Pembroke and the Cardigan. Corgis gained wider recognition as the favored dogs of Queen Elizabeth II. Despite their size, they're energetic working dogs bred to herd cattle by nipping at their heels.

Corgis is the plural of corgi, a small herding dog with short legs, a long body, and pointed ears. The breed originated in Wales, where two varieties exist: Pembroke Welsh and Cardigan Welsh. Corgis became widely associated with British royalty through Queen Elizabeth II's lifelong affection for them: {The Queen's corgis had the run of Buckingham Palace}.

Coriander is an herb whose leaves and seeds are used in cooking. The plant is also called cilantro, though in American usage coriander typically refers to the dried seeds while cilantro means the fresh leaves. The seeds have a warm, citrusy flavor used in curries, pickling, and baking: {toast the coriander before grinding}. The leaves are pungent and polarizing—some people taste soap.

Cork is the buoyant, spongy bark of a Mediterranean oak tree, used to make bottle stoppers, flooring, bulletin boards, and other products. A cork is specifically the stopper itself: {Pull the cork on that wine}. To cork is to seal with a cork. Corked wine has been contaminated by a faulty cork, giving it a musty taste. In baseball, a corked bat has been illegally hollowed and filled with cork to make it lighter. (Capitalized Cork is a city in Ireland.)

A corkboard is a board made of compressed cork, used for posting notes, photos, and papers with pushpins or tacks. Common in offices, classrooms, and kitchens as an informal bulletin board: {She pinned the schedule to the corkboard}. The soft, porous surface grips pins easily and self-heals after removal.

Corked describes wine that has been contaminated by a faulty cork, giving it a musty, moldy taste. A corked bottle is ruined regardless of quality or price: {Send it back—it's corked}. Separately, corked means sealed with a cork, and in baseball slang, a corked bat has been illegally hollowed and filled with cork to make it lighter.

A corker is something remarkable or outstanding, usually in a positive sense. The word comes from the idea of a cork that seals something so completely that nothing more can be said—a decisive finishing touch. Someone might call an impressive performance, a stunning goal, or an exceptionally good joke a corker. {That last question was a real corker.} The term is somewhat dated but still appears in British English and Australian English.

Corks is the plural of cork—the lightweight, buoyant bark of the cork oak tree, or stoppers made from it. Wine bottles are sealed with corks; to cork a bottle is to close it this way. Cork also describes anything made from the material: cork {flooring}, cork {board}. As an exclamation, corks is a mild, old-fashioned oath: {Oh corks, I've forgotten my wallet!}

A corkscrew is a tool for removing corks from wine bottles, typically featuring a pointed metal spiral that twists into the cork and a mechanism for pulling it out. The spiral shape gives the word its extended uses: corkscrew {curls}, a corkscrew {staircase}. As a verb, to corkscrew is to move in a twisting spiral: {The plane corkscrewed toward the ground}.

Corkscrewing describes a spiraling, twisting motion like the metal spiral of a corkscrew. A plane corkscrewing toward earth spins as it descends. A punch can corkscrew into its target with a rotating twist. Hair corkscrewing in tight ringlets winds in helical curls. {The ball went corkscrewing through the air.}

Corkscrews are devices for removing corks from bottles, consisting of a pointed metal spiral attached to a handle. The spiral shape extends to anything with tight helical turns: {corkscrew curls}, {a corkscrew staircase}. As a verb, to corkscrew is to move in a twisting spiral: {The plane corkscrewed toward the ground}.

A cormorant is a large, dark waterbird with a long neck and hooked bill, found near coasts and inland waters worldwide. Cormorants dive to catch fish and are often seen perched with wings spread to dry—their feathers lack the waterproofing of most aquatic birds. In some Asian cultures, trained cormorants have been used for fishing. The word sometimes suggests greed or voracity: {a cormorant appetite for wealth}.

Cormorants is the plural of cormorant, a large dark waterbird with a long neck and hooked bill. Cormorants dive underwater to catch fish and are often seen perched with wings spread to dry. In some Asian fishing traditions, trained cormorants catch fish for their handlers. {Cormorants lined the rocky shore, drying their wings in the sun.}

Corn is a tall grain plant with kernels growing in rows on a cob, a staple crop in the Americas. In British English, corn means grain generally—wheat, barley, oats. Corny jokes or sentiments are trite and unsophisticated, evoking rural simplicity. A corn is also a painful hardening of skin on the foot, unrelated to the grain.

Cornball describes something unsophisticated, overly sentimental, or awkwardly old-fashioned—the kind of humor or behavior that makes people cringe or roll their eyes: {His cornball jokes embarrassed his teenagers}. As a noun, a cornball is a person who acts this way. The word suggests trying too hard to be wholesome or funny and landing somewhere between endearing and painful.
clues: Someone who loves saccharine, dated humor

definition: Cornballs are people considered unsophisticated, overly sentimental, or cloyingly old-fashioned in their humor or manner. The term derives from corny, suggesting someone who traffics in stale jokes or wholesome earnestness that others find embarrassing. {Those cornballs actually think dad jokes are peak comedy.} The word carries affectionate contempt—cornballs are annoying but harmless, more cringe-worthy than offensive.

Cornbread is a quick bread made from cornmeal, a staple of Southern American cooking. It's typically baked in a cast-iron skillet and served alongside beans, greens, or barbecue. Regional variations abound—Southern cornbread is usually unsweetened and crusty, while Northern versions tend sweeter and cakier: {She crumbled cornbread into her bowl of chili}.

A corncob is the cylindrical core of an ear of corn, the woody part that remains after the kernels are removed. Corncobs have been used as fuel, as scrubbing tools, and historically as toilet paper. A corncob pipe is carved from a dried cob: {He sat on the porch smoking his corncob pipe}.

A corncrib is a ventilated structure for storing and drying ears of corn. The slatted walls allow air circulation while keeping out animals. Traditional corncribs are narrow buildings raised off the ground, a familiar sight on American farms: {The old corncrib behind the barn was falling apart}.

A corndog is a hot dog coated in cornmeal batter and deep-fried on a stick. It's classic American fair and carnival food, though widely available frozen. The stick makes it portable finger food: {We grabbed corndogs at the state fair}. Also spelled corn dog.

A corndog is a hot dog on a stick, coated in cornmeal batter and deep-fried. It's quintessential American fair food, sold at carnivals, amusement parks, and state fairs: {We got corndogs and funnel cake at the county fair}. Also spelled as two words: corn dog.

A corner is where two lines, edges, or surfaces meet at an angle. Rooms have corners, pages have corners, streets have corners. To corner someone is to trap them where escape is difficult: {The reporter cornered the senator after the hearing}. To corner a market is to gain control of a commodity's supply. Something done {on the corner} happens at a street intersection. To {cut corners} is to take shortcuts, often sacrificing quality. {Around the corner} means nearby or imminent: {Spring is just around the corner}.

A cornerback is a defensive player in American and Canadian football who lines up on the outer edges of the formation, primarily responsible for covering wide receivers and preventing pass completions. Cornerbacks need speed and agility to match receivers stride for stride: {The cornerback jumped the route and intercepted the pass}. Along with safeties, they make up the secondary.

Cornerbacks are defensive players in American football who cover wide receivers and defend against passes. They typically line up near the sidelines, opposite the offensive receivers they're assigned to guard. The position demands speed, agility, and the ability to read plays quickly. A cornerback's main responsibilities include preventing receptions, breaking up passes, and intercepting throws: {Their cornerbacks shut down our passing game all night}.

Cornered describes being trapped or forced into a position with no escape. A cornered {animal} is most dangerous because it has nowhere to flee. Someone cornered in an argument has no good response left. To have something cornered—or to {corner the market}—is to control it completely, leaving others no access.

Cornering is maneuvering through a turn, especially at speed: {The sports car handles cornering beautifully}. It also means trapping someone in a position where they must respond: {She cornered him after the meeting to demand answers}. In markets, cornering means gaining control of a commodity's supply to manipulate prices: {cornering the silver market}.

A cornerman is a boxer's assistant who works from the corner of the ring between rounds—applying ice, stopping cuts, offering water and tactical advice. The term extends to anyone providing close support during a difficult situation: {He's been my cornerman through every crisis}. In some contexts, a cornerman is a lookout or assistant in street-level drug dealing.

Corners is the plural of corner—the points where edges meet, or the angles they form. Streets have corners where they intersect; rooms have corners where walls join. To corner someone is to trap them where escape is difficult. To cut corners is to take shortcuts, often by skimping on quality or effort: {They cut corners on safety to save money}. In commerce, to corner a market is to gain controlling influence over it.

A cornerstone is literally a stone at the corner of a building's foundation, often ceremonially laid to mark construction's beginning. Figuratively, it means the fundamental element on which something depends: {Trust is the cornerstone of any relationship}. The word implies both foundational importance and structural necessity—remove it and everything built upon it weakens.

Cornerstones are the foundation stones placed at the corner of a building, traditionally the first stones laid and often ceremonially marked with dates or inscriptions. From this literal meaning comes the more common figurative use: the essential elements upon which something is built or depends. {Trust is the cornerstone of any good relationship.} {The cornerstones of democracy include free speech and voting rights.} When something is called a cornerstone, it's being identified as fundamental and indispensable.

A cornet is a brass instrument similar to a trumpet but with a more compact shape and mellower tone, commonly used in brass bands and jazz. The word also refers to a cone-shaped container, particularly in British English for the wafer cone holding ice cream: {She ordered a strawberry cornet from the seaside vendor}. Historically, a cornet was a piece of women's headwear or a cavalry officer of the lowest commissioned rank who carried the colors.

Cornfed describes someone or something raised on corn, especially livestock fattened for market. Applied to people, it suggests a robust, wholesome, rural American look—healthy and well-nourished but perhaps unsophisticated: {a cornfed Iowa farm boy}, {cornfed cheerleaders}. The term can be affectionate or mildly condescending depending on context.

A cornfield is a field where corn is grown. In American English, this means maize; in British English, it typically means wheat or other cereal grains. The word evokes rural agricultural landscapes: {We drove past miles of cornfields}. A cornfield can serve as a setting for hide-and-seek, horror movies, or getting lost.

Fields where corn is grown. In American English, cornfields are planted with maize—the tall stalks with yellow ears. In British English, they may contain wheat or other cereal grains. Cornfields evoke rural farmland and agricultural heartland: {We drove past miles of cornfields in Iowa}. {Children of the Corn} made them briefly sinister.

A cornflake is a small, flat flake of toasted corn, typically eaten as breakfast cereal with milk. Usually plural: {a bowl of cornflakes}. Cornflake can describe a thin, crispy coating: {cornflake-crusted chicken}.

Cornflakes are a breakfast cereal made from toasted flakes of corn, typically eaten with milk: {a bowl of cornflakes}. The word often appears generically for any similar flaked cereal, regardless of brand. Cornflakes have become emblematic of plain, wholesome breakfast fare—something reliable but unremarkable.

Cornflower is a wildflower with bright blue, fringed petals, traditionally found growing among grain crops. The blue is distinctive enough that cornflower serves as a color name—a medium blue, lighter than navy but more vivid than powder blue: {a cornflower blue dress}, {eyes the color of cornflowers}.

Cornflowers are wildflowers with bright blue, fringed petals, traditionally found growing among grain crops. The distinctive blue has become a color term: {cornflower blue}. Also called bachelor's buttons, they're used in dried flower arrangements and occasionally as edible garnish.

Cornhole is a lawn game where players toss beanbags at a slanted wooden board with a hole in it, scoring points when bags land on the board or pass through the hole. Popular at tailgates and backyard gatherings: {We set up cornhole at the cookout}. Separately, cornhole is vulgar slang for anal sex or the anus itself.

Cornholes functions as both a noun and a verb. As a noun, it refers to the holes in a cornhole board—the tilted wooden platforms used in the popular lawn game where players toss bean bags, aiming to land them in the circular opening for points. The verb cornhole, from which this derives, is vulgar slang meaning to penetrate someone anally. {We set up the cornhole boards and took turns tossing bags at the cornholes.}

The cornhusk is the leafy outer covering of an ear of corn, peeled away before eating. Dried cornhusks are used to wrap tamales and other foods for cooking. They also serve as material for crafts—cornhusk dolls were traditional toys in many cultures. {She soaked the cornhusks before wrapping the tamales.}

A cornhusker is a person or machine that removes the husks from ears of corn. Before mechanization, cornhusking was labor-intensive work done by hand, often as a communal activity. The term is most associated with Nebraska, whose residents are called Cornhuskers, and whose state university athletic teams bear the name. {The old cornhusker could strip an ear in seconds.}

Cornhuskers are people who remove the husks from ears of corn, or machines designed for that task. Before mechanization, cornhusking was labor-intensive work often done communally at harvest time. The term evokes rural American life and agricultural tradition: {The cornhuskers worked through the night to finish before the frost}.

A cornice is a horizontal molding that projects from a wall or building, typically where the wall meets the roof or ceiling. In architecture, it crowns a structure or divides it into sections: {an ornate cornice runs along the top of the building}. In mountaineering, a cornice is an overhanging mass of snow or ice formed by wind at a ridge or cliff edge—dangerous because it can break off: {The climber tested the cornice before crossing}.

Cornices are decorative horizontal moldings that project along the top of a building, wall, or piece of furniture. In architecture, a cornice caps an entablature or runs beneath a roofline: {The building's ornate cornices had begun to crumble}. In mountaineering, a cornice is an overhanging mass of hardened snow at a ridge crest, formed by wind—dangerous because it can break off unexpectedly.

Cornmeal is dried corn ground into a coarse flour, used in baking and cooking. It's the base for cornbread, polenta, and grits, and can coat foods before frying: {catfish dredged in cornmeal}. Cornmeal ranges from fine to coarse grind and may be white, yellow, or blue depending on the corn variety.

Cornpone is cornbread made without milk or eggs, baked or fried in simple cakes—traditional fare in the rural American South. As an adjective, cornpone describes something unsophisticated, folksy, or stereotypically Southern: {cornpone humor}, {a cornpone accent}. The term can be affectionate or dismissive depending on context.

Cornrows are a hairstyle in which the hair is braided flat against the scalp in narrow, raised rows, typically running from front to back. The style originated in Africa and remains culturally significant in Black communities. As a verb, to cornrow is to braid hair this way: {She cornrowed her daughter's hair for the first day of school}.

Cornrowing is the act of braiding hair into tight, raised rows that lie flat against the scalp, creating geometric patterns. The technique, rooted in African traditions, involves weaving three strands in an underhand motion while adding hair progressively: {She spent hours cornrowing her daughter's hair for the first day of school}.

Cornrows are a hairstyle in which the hair is braided flat against the scalp in narrow, raised rows, typically running from front to back. The style has deep roots in African cultures and remains popular in Black communities worldwide. Creating cornrows requires sectioning hair and weaving it tightly in continuous, attached braids: {She sat for hours getting her cornrows done}. The name comes from the rows' resemblance to planted corn.

Cornsilk is the mass of fine, silky threads that emerge from the top of an ear of corn, each strand connected to a kernel inside. When corn is fresh, the silk is pale and glossy; it dries and darkens as the ear matures. {She pulled the cornsilk away before boiling the ears.} Cornsilk is also used in herbal remedies, traditionally as a mild diuretic.

A cornstalk is the stem of a corn plant, typically growing several feet tall with a jointed structure that supports the leaves and ears. In agricultural regions, cornstalks dominate the landscape during growing season and remain as dry stubble after harvest. The dried stalks are sometimes used for autumn decorations, animal fodder, or incorporated back into the soil. {The scarecrow stood among the cornstalks.}

Cornstarch is a fine white powder extracted from corn kernels, used primarily as a thickening agent in cooking. It thickens sauces, gravies, and puddings when heated with liquid: {Add a tablespoon of cornstarch to thicken the gravy}. Outside the kitchen, cornstarch appears in cosmetics and as a base for baby powder. Called cornflour in British English.

A cornucopia is a horn-shaped container overflowing with fruits, vegetables, and flowers—a symbol of abundance associated with harvest festivals and Thanksgiving decorations. The image extends to any overflowing plenty: {a cornucopia of options}, {a cornucopia of delights}. The word comes from Latin for "horn of plenty."

Cornucopias is the plural of cornucopia, a horn-shaped container overflowing with fruits, vegetables, and flowers—a symbol of abundance and plenty. The image comes from classical mythology and appears frequently in harvest imagery and Thanksgiving decorations: {Paper cornucopias spilled across the table}. Figuratively, any generous supply: {a cornucopia of delights}.

Corny describes something so sentimental, outdated, or obvious that it feels trite or embarrassing—a corny {joke}, a corny {pickup line}, a corny {movie}. The word suggests excessive sweetness or predictability: {I know it sounds corny, but I really do believe in true love}. Something corny isn't necessarily bad—it can be endearing in its earnestness—but it lacks sophistication or originality.

Corona is Latin for crown, and its English senses branch from that image. In anatomy, a corona is a crown-like structure—most often the rounded rim of the glans penis. In astronomy, the corona is the luminous halo visible around the sun during an eclipse. Corona became shorthand for coronavirus during the COVID-19 pandemic: {I had corona twice in 2021}. Corona is also a brand of Mexican beer.

A coronation is the ceremony of crowning a monarch. The ritual typically involves religious rites, the placing of a crown on the sovereign's head, and formal investiture with symbols of power: {The coronation drew millions of television viewers}. Figuratively, coronation describes any formal elevation to a position of dominance or acclaim: {The tournament was supposed to be his coronation as the sport's next superstar}.

Coronations are ceremonies in which monarchs are formally crowned and invested with royal authority. The ritual typically involves religious rites, the placing of a crown on the sovereign's head, and oaths of office: {The coronation of King Charles III drew global attention}. By extension, coronation describes any formal elevation to power or status, sometimes ironically: {Critics called the nomination process a coronation rather than a real contest}.

A coronavirus is any of a family of viruses named for the crown-like spikes on their surface. Coronaviruses cause respiratory infections ranging from common colds to severe diseases. The word became ubiquitous during the COVID-19 pandemic, often used interchangeably with COVID-19 itself: {The coronavirus shut down schools worldwide}, {coronavirus restrictions}, {Did you get coronavirus?} Scientists distinguish specific coronaviruses like SARS-CoV-2, but in everyday speech, {the coronavirus} means the one responsible for the pandemic.

A coroner is a public official who investigates deaths, particularly those that are sudden, violent, or unexplained. The coroner determines cause of death and whether an inquest or autopsy is needed. In some jurisdictions, the role requires medical training; in others, it's an elected position that may not. {The coroner ruled the death a homicide.}

Coroners are public officials who investigate deaths, particularly those that are sudden, violent, or unexplained. The coroner determines cause of death and whether an inquest or autopsy is needed. In some jurisdictions, the role requires medical training; in others, it's an elected position without such requirements. {The coroner ruled the death a homicide.}

A coronet is a small crown, typically worn by nobility ranking below a monarch. The design varies by rank—a duke's coronet differs from a baron's. By extension, coronet describes any crown-like ornament or headpiece: {a coronet of flowers}, {a coronet braid}. In anatomy, the coronet is the part of a horse's hoof where horn meets skin.

Corpo is slang for a large corporation or someone who works for one, typically carrying connotations of soulless corporate culture, profit-over-people mentality, or bland conformity. The term gained currency through cyberpunk fiction and gaming, where corporations wield dystopian power: {The corpos control everything in this city}. As an adjective: {That's such a corpo response}.

Corporal has two distinct sources. One means of the body: {corporal punishment} is physical discipline like spanking or caning. The other corporal is a military rank—the lowest grade of noncommissioned officer, above private and below sergeant. A corporal typically leads a small unit of soldiers.

Corporate relates to corporations—business entities legally distinct from their owners. As an adjective, it describes things belonging to or characteristic of such organizations: {corporate headquarters}, {corporate culture}, {corporate responsibility}. The word often carries connotations of impersonal bureaucracy or profit-driven priorities: {The decision felt very corporate}. Used disparagingly, corporate suggests bland conformity or soulless efficiency: {The neighborhood lost its character after all the corporate chains moved in}.

Corporatese is the jargon-laden, vague language characteristic of business communication. It favors abstraction over clarity: {leverage synergies}, {circle back}, {move the needle}, {align stakeholders}. The term is usually disparaging, implying empty buzzwords that obscure meaning rather than convey it. {The memo was pure corporatese—I couldn't tell what they actually wanted.}

Corporatespeak is the jargon and buzzwords characteristic of business communication, often criticized for being vague, evasive, or needlessly complicated. It favors abstract nouns, euphemisms, and trendy phrases: {Let's leverage our synergies}, {We need to right-size the organization}. The term is usually dismissive, suggesting language designed to obscure rather than clarify.

A corporation is a business entity legally separate from its owners, who hold shares of ownership. This structure shields shareholders from personal liability—if the corporation fails, they lose only their investment. Corporations can own property, enter contracts, and sue or be sued in their own name. {She works for a large corporation.} The word often carries connotations of impersonal bigness: {faceless corporations}, {corporate greed}.

Corporations are businesses organized as legal entities separate from their owners. This structure limits owners' liability—shareholders can lose their investment but not personal assets if the corporation fails. Corporations can own property, enter contracts, and sue or be sued in their own name. The word often carries connotations of faceless bureaucracy or profit-driven indifference: {You can't fight the corporations}.

Corporatism is a system of organizing society where major interest groups—business, labor, agriculture, professions—are formally incorporated into political decision-making. Rather than competing through elections or lobbying, these groups negotiate directly with the state. The term often carries negative connotations, suggesting cozy arrangements between government and powerful industries that exclude ordinary citizens: {Critics accused the administration of corporatism, letting energy companies write their own regulations}.

Corporatization is the process of restructuring a government agency or public institution to operate like a private corporation—adopting business practices, profit motives, and management structures typical of the private sector. The term often carries critical connotations, suggesting that values like public service or education are being subordinated to efficiency metrics and bottom-line thinking: {the corporatization of universities}, {the corporatization of healthcare}.

Corporatocracy describes a society or system where corporations hold dominant political and economic power, influencing or controlling government policy to serve business interests over public welfare. The term is almost always critical, suggesting that democratic institutions have been captured by corporate influence: {We don't live in a democracy anymore—it's a corporatocracy}. Compare plutocracy and oligarchy.

A corps is an organized group acting as a unit, especially a military formation comprising multiple divisions under a single commander. The word extends to any disciplined body working together: the {press corps}, the {diplomatic corps}, a {corps de ballet}. The final *s* is silent in both singular and plural—one corps, two corps.

A corpse is a dead body, especially a human one. The word carries a clinical or literary tone—news reports prefer {body}, while {corpse} appears in crime fiction, horror, and formal contexts. In theater slang, to corpse is to break character by laughing uncontrollably during a performance.

Corpses is the plural of corpse—dead bodies, especially of humans. The word appears in contexts ranging from crime scenes to battlefields to horror fiction: {Corpses littered the field after the battle}. Unlike "bodies," which can refer to living people, corpses are unambiguously dead.

A corral is an enclosure for confining livestock—horses, cattle, sheep. The word comes from Spanish and remains common in the American West and Southwest. To corral animals is to drive them into such an enclosure. Figuratively, to corral is to gather or round up: {She corralled the kids for dinner}. {He corralled enough votes to pass the bill}.

Corralling is the act of gathering and confining livestock into a corral—a fenced enclosure. The word extends to any effort to round up or contain: {Police spent hours corralling the escaped animals}. Figuratively, it means bringing scattered things or people together: {She's been corralling votes for the bill}, {corralling the kids for dinner}.

Corrals are enclosures for confining livestock, typically horses or cattle, made of fencing or rails. The verb means to gather animals into such an enclosure, and by extension, to round up or gather people or things: {She corralled the kids into the car}. To corral resources or votes is to secure them through effort: {He corralled enough support to pass the bill}.

Correct means free from error or conforming to fact, standard, or convention: {the correct answer}, {correct spelling}, {politically correct}. As a verb, to correct is to fix what's wrong—correcting a mistake, correcting a child's behavior, correcting course. A correction in financial markets is a decline that adjusts inflated prices. To {stand corrected} is to acknowledge you were wrong.

Correcting is the act of fixing errors or making something right. A teacher correcting papers marks mistakes and provides feedback. Correcting someone's pronunciation or grammar can be helpful or annoying depending on context: {Stop correcting me in front of other people}. Self-correcting means adjusting one's own errors: {She kept correcting herself mid-sentence}.

Correction is the act of making something right or accurate. A teacher's corrections mark errors on student work. A correction to a news story fixes a mistake. In finance, a market correction is a significant decline after prices have risen too high. Corrections can also mean punishment intended to reform: {a house of correction}, {the department of corrections}.

Corrections refers to changes made to fix errors or improve accuracy: {The editor marked corrections in red}. In institutional contexts, corrections is the system of prisons, jails, and supervision programs that handle convicted offenders: {He worked in corrections for twenty years}, {the Department of Corrections}. A corrections officer is a prison guard.

Correctness is the quality of being accurate, proper, or free from error. A solution has mathematical correctness if it follows valid logic. In computing, correctness means a program behaves as specified. The word often carries social or political overtones: {political correctness} refers to language and behavior that avoids offense to particular groups—a concept praised by some as respectful and derided by others as excessive.

Correlation is a relationship or connection between things, especially one where changes in one accompany changes in another: {There's a strong correlation between smoking and lung cancer}. In statistics, correlation measures how closely two variables move together. A positive correlation means both rise or fall together; a negative correlation means one rises as the other falls. Crucially, correlation doesn't imply causation—two things can move together without one causing the other.

Correspond has two main senses. First, to match or be equivalent: {The punishment should correspond to the crime}. Second, to exchange letters or messages: {They corresponded for years before meeting}. Things that correspond are in agreement or harmony; people who correspond communicate in writing. A correspondent is someone who corresponds—or a journalist reporting from a particular location.

Correspondence is the exchange of letters or messages between people: {They maintained a correspondence for years}. The word also means agreement or similarity between things: {a close correspondence between the two accounts}. In mathematics, correspondence describes a relationship where elements in one set map to elements in another.

Correspondences is the plural of correspondence, which covers two main ideas: communication by letter or email, and the quality of matching or being similar. A collection of letters exchanged between people is their correspondence: {The museum acquired the writer's correspondences with her editor}. In more abstract use, correspondences are points of similarity or agreement between things: {scholars have noted correspondences between the two ancient texts}. The word appears frequently in mystical and esoteric contexts to describe symbolic relationships between different realms of existence.

A correspondent is someone who exchanges letters or messages with another: {pen pals are correspondents}. More commonly, a correspondent is a journalist who reports from a particular location or on a specific subject: {a war correspondent}, {a White House correspondent}. As an adjective, correspondent means matching or analogous, though corresponding is more common in this sense.

Correspondents is the plural of correspondent—someone who exchanges letters or messages with another, or a journalist reporting from a particular location. A {pen pal} is a correspondent in the first sense. News organizations station {foreign correspondents} in major cities, and {war correspondents} report from conflict zones. The word implies ongoing communication from a distance.

A corridor is a long, narrow passage in a building, typically with rooms opening off it on both sides: {The hotel corridor stretched endlessly ahead}. The word extends to any narrow strip of land, especially one providing access: an {air corridor}, a {wildlife corridor}, a {corridor of power}. The plural {corridors of power} refers to the inner circles where political decisions are made.

Corridors is the plural of corridor—long, narrow passageways connecting rooms or parts of a building: {hospital corridors}, {hotel corridors}. Extended to strips of land or airspace: a {wildlife corridor} allows animals to move between habitats; an {air corridor} is a designated flight path. The {corridors of power} refers to the halls of government buildings where decisions get made, and by extension, the people and processes within them.

Corroboration is evidence or testimony that confirms or supports something already claimed. A witness provides corroboration when their account matches another's. In legal contexts, certain claims require corroboration—independent evidence beyond a single person's word: {The prosecution lacked corroboration for the accusation}. The verb is corroborate.

To corrode is to gradually destroy or be destroyed by chemical action, especially oxidation. Metal corrodes when exposed to moisture and air; acid corrodes stone. The word extends to gradual deterioration of any kind: {Resentment corroded their friendship}. What corrodes eats away slowly from within or without, leaving damage that accumulates over time.

Corroded describes something that has been gradually worn away or destroyed by chemical action. Metal corrodes when exposed to moisture and oxygen, producing rust or other oxidation: {The corroded pipes finally burst}. Figuratively, trust or relationships can be corroded by neglect or betrayal: {Years of lies had corroded their marriage}.

Corrodes is the third-person singular of corrode, meaning to wear away gradually through chemical action. Rust corrodes metal; acid corrodes stone. The word extends to anything that deteriorates through persistent attack: {Resentment corrodes a marriage}. {Cynicism corrodes public trust}. What corrodes is slowly destroyed from within or without.

Corroding is the present participle of corrode—to eat away gradually through chemical action. Metal corrodes when exposed to moisture and air; rust is corroded iron. The word extends to anything that deteriorates through persistent attack: {Resentment was corroding their marriage}. A corroding influence weakens or destroys over time.

Corrosion is the gradual destruction of material, especially metal, through chemical reaction with its environment. Rust is the most familiar form—iron corroding through exposure to oxygen and moisture. The word extends to any slow wearing away: {the corrosion of trust}, {the corrosion of democratic institutions}. What corrodes doesn't shatter; it degrades incrementally.

Corrosive describes substances that chemically destroy or eat away at materials they contact. Strong acids and bases are corrosive to metals, skin, and eyes: {corrosive chemicals require special handling}. Figuratively, corrosive describes things that gradually damage or undermine: {corrosive cynicism}, {a corrosive influence on public trust}. The noun names the substance itself.

Corrugated means shaped into parallel ridges and grooves, like a washboard. The pattern adds strength and rigidity: {corrugated cardboard}, {corrugated metal roofing}. The ridges create air pockets for insulation and allow flexibility without breaking. Almost always describes manufactured materials rather than natural surfaces.

Corrupt describes something tainted, dishonest, or morally degraded. A corrupt official abuses power for personal gain. Corrupt {data} has been damaged and is unreliable. Corrupt {practices} involve bribery or fraud. To corrupt is to make something impure or to pervert its original state: {Power corrupts}. A corrupting {influence} leads others toward wrongdoing. The word implies decay from a better original condition.

Corrupted describes something altered from its original, proper, or pure state—usually for the worse. Data becomes corrupted when errors make files unreadable: {The hard drive crashed and corrupted my photos}. Text is corrupted when copying errors distort it over time. A corrupted official has been morally compromised, typically through bribery. The word implies decay from something once sound or whole.
Corruptible is mainly used to describe people who are susceptible to bribery or to other influences that will make them dishonest.

Corrupting describes the process of degrading, tainting, or morally undermining something or someone. A corrupting {influence} leads others toward dishonesty or depravity. Power is often called corrupting because it tempts abuse. Data or files can be corrupting when they damage other files they interact with. {The investigation revealed corrupting payments to local officials.}

Corruption is the decay of integrity or proper functioning. In its most common use, corruption involves abuse of entrusted power for private gain—bribery, embezzlement, or exploiting public office: {The mayor was convicted of corruption}. Data corruption means files have been damaged or altered. Moral corruption suggests a degraded character. The word implies something once sound has been spoiled or perverted from its original state.

Corruptions is the plural of corruption, which denotes the process or result of something being made impure, debased, or morally degraded. Political corruptions involve abuse of power for personal gain, while textual corruptions are errors or alterations that creep into manuscripts over time. The word also applies to degraded forms of language or data: {The file showed several corruptions after the failed transfer}. Each corruption represents a departure from an original, pure, or intended state.

Corrupts is the verb form of corrupt, meaning to degrade, spoil, or make dishonest. Power corrupts those who wield it unchecked. Money corrupts political systems. In computing, data corrupts when files become damaged or unreadable: {The virus corrupted my hard drive}. A corrupting influence leads others toward moral decay or wrongdoing.

A corsage is a small bouquet of flowers worn on the body, typically pinned to a dress or worn on the wrist. Corsages are traditional accessories for formal occasions like proms and weddings: {He picked up her corsage from the florist before the dance}. The word originally referred to the bodice of a dress, where such flowers were pinned.

Corsages is the plural of corsage, a small arrangement of flowers worn on a woman's dress or wrist for formal occasions. Corsages are most associated with American high school dances—proms and homecomings—where a date traditionally presents one: {He picked up the corsage from the florist before the dance}. They also appear at weddings, usually worn by mothers of the bride and groom.

A corsair is a pirate, especially one operating in the Mediterranean. The term also applies to a pirate ship itself. Corsair carries a slightly romantic or swashbuckling connotation compared to the blunter pirate: {The corsairs of the Barbary Coast terrorized European shipping for centuries}.

Corsairs are pirates or privateers, especially those who operated in the Mediterranean. The word carries a slightly romantic or historical flavor compared to plain pirate: {Barbary corsairs raided European coastal towns for slaves}. Corsair can also refer to the fast ships these raiders sailed.

A corset is a close-fitting undergarment stiffened with boning and tightened with laces, designed to shape the torso—typically narrowing the waist and supporting the bust. Once standard women's wear, corsets fell from everyday use in the early twentieth century but persist in fashion, costume, and fetish contexts: {She laced her corset tight for the period drama}. To corset is to confine or restrict: {corset-like regulations}.

Corseted describes someone wearing a corset, the stiff undergarment traditionally used to shape the torso and cinch the waist. The term often evokes Victorian-era fashion, when tightly laced corsets were standard for women. Figuratively, corseted suggests being constrained or restricted, whether physically or socially: {She felt corseted by the expectations of her conservative family}. The word can also describe anything shaped or compressed as if by a corset.

Corsets are close-fitting undergarments stiffened with boning to shape the torso, traditionally worn by women to narrow the waist and support the bust. Once standard foundation garments, they fell from everyday use in the early twentieth century but persist in fashion, costume, and fetish contexts. The verb corset means to confine tightly: {a bureaucracy corseted by regulations}.

The cortex is the outer layer of an organ or structure, distinguished from its interior. In anatomy, it most often refers to the cerebral cortex—the folded outer surface of the brain responsible for higher functions like thought, perception, and memory: {damage to the prefrontal cortex}. Plants have cortex too: the tissue between bark and the woody core. The adrenal cortex is the outer portion of the adrenal gland, producing hormones like cortisol.

A corvette is a small, fast warship, typically used for escort duty or patrol. Historically, corvettes were sailing vessels smaller than frigates. In modern navies, the term describes lightly armed ships suited for coastal operations. {The corvette intercepted the smuggling vessel.} (Capitalized Corvette is the sports car.)

Corvettes are small, fast warships—lighter than destroyers, typically used for patrol, convoy escort, or coastal defense. The term dates to sailing navies but was revived for World War II escort vessels. Separately, a Corvette is a Chevrolet sports car, an American icon since 1953: {He restored a '63 Corvette}.

Corvids are birds of the crow family, including crows, ravens, jays, magpies, and rooks. They are known for exceptional intelligence among birds—using tools, recognizing faces, and solving complex problems. {Corvids have demonstrated the ability to plan for future events.} The group is found worldwide except Antarctica.

Cosign means to sign a document jointly with another person, typically to guarantee a loan or contract: {My father cosigned my first car loan}. The cosigner accepts responsibility if the primary party defaults. In slang, cosign means to endorse or vouch for something: {I cosign that recommendation completely}.

Cosigned is the past tense of cosign, meaning to sign a document alongside another person, typically to guarantee a loan or contract. A cosigner agrees to take responsibility if the primary signer defaults: {Her father cosigned the car loan}. In slang, cosigned means endorsed or agreed with: {I cosigned everything she said in that meeting}.

A cosigner is someone who signs a document alongside another person, sharing legal responsibility for its terms. Most often this refers to loans: a cosigner guarantees repayment if the primary borrower defaults. Parents commonly cosign for children who lack credit history: {My dad had to cosign on my first car loan}. The cosigner takes on risk without receiving the loan proceeds.

Cosigning is vouching for someone or backing them up, especially in informal contexts: {I'm cosigning everything she just said}. The term comes from the formal sense of co-signing a loan—taking shared legal responsibility for someone else's debt—but has spread to mean any endorsement or agreement: {I can't cosign that behavior}.

Cosiness is the quality of being cosy—warm, comfortable, and pleasantly snug. A room with soft lighting, blankets, and a fire has cosiness. The word extends to atmospheres and relationships that feel intimate and secure: {the cosiness of a small village}, {the cosiness between old friends}. British spelling; Americans write coziness.

Cosleeping is the practice of parents and young children sleeping in close proximity—either in the same bed or the same room. Advocates argue it facilitates breastfeeding and bonding; critics raise concerns about infant safety. The term appears frequently in parenting debates: {We practiced cosleeping until she was two}. Also spelled co-sleeping.

Cosmetic refers to products or procedures meant to beautify the face and body: {cosmetic surgery}, {the cosmetics industry}. The word extends to anything superficial or surface-level—changes that improve appearance without addressing underlying substance: {The renovations were purely cosmetic}. A cosmetic fix makes something look better without solving the real problem.

Cosmetics are substances applied to the body, especially the face, to enhance appearance or alter skin condition. The category includes makeup like lipstick and foundation, as well as skincare products, lotions, and perfumes. As an adjective, cosmetic describes something superficial or intended only to improve appearance without addressing underlying issues: {The renovations were purely cosmetic.} A cosmetic procedure in medicine improves looks rather than treating disease or injury.

A cosmetologist is a professional trained in beauty treatments—hair styling, skincare, nail care, and makeup application. The term distinguishes someone with formal training and licensing from casual practitioners. {She went to cosmetology school before opening her salon.} A cosmetologist works in salons, spas, or film and theater productions.

Cosmic relates to the cosmos—the universe as an ordered whole. It describes things pertaining to outer space: {cosmic rays}, {cosmic dust}. More often, cosmic conveys vastness or profound significance: {cosmic questions about existence}, {a discovery of cosmic importance}. Something can be cosmically {insignificant} or a {cosmic coincidence}. The word suggests scale beyond ordinary human concerns.

Cosmo is an informal clipping of cosmopolitan, usually referring to the cocktail—a pink drink of vodka, triple sec, cranberry juice, and lime: {She ordered a cosmo at the bar}. Less commonly, it shortens cosmopolitan in its sense of worldly or sophisticated. Cosmo also appears as a given name and as shorthand for Cosmopolitan magazine.

A cosmologist is a scientist who studies the origin, structure, and evolution of the universe. The field draws on physics, astronomy, and mathematics to address questions about the Big Bang, dark matter, and the ultimate fate of the cosmos. {Stephen Hawking was perhaps the most famous cosmologist of his generation.}

Cosmology is the study of the universe as a whole—its origin, structure, and eventual fate. The term applies both to scientific cosmology, which uses physics and astronomy to model the Big Bang and cosmic expansion, and to philosophical or religious accounts of creation and cosmic order. {Modern cosmology suggests the universe is about 13.8 billion years old.}

A cosmonaut is a Russian astronaut—a person trained to travel and work in space as part of the Russian (formerly Soviet) space program. The distinction is purely national: Americans are astronauts, Russians are cosmonauts, though both do the same work. {Yuri Gagarin became the first cosmonaut to orbit Earth in 1961.}

Cosmonauts is the plural of cosmonaut, a Russian space traveler—the equivalent of an American astronaut. The term comes from Russian and reflects the Soviet space program's parallel development during the Cold War space race: {Yuri Gagarin was the first cosmonaut to orbit Earth}. The distinction persists today, with cosmonauts typically referring to those in the Russian space program.

Cosmopolitan describes someone or something at home in many countries and cultures, free from local prejudices or national limitations. A cosmopolitan city like New York draws people from everywhere. A cosmopolitan person has broad international experience and outlook: {She's thoroughly cosmopolitan—educated in Paris, working in Tokyo}. The noun means such a person, or the vodka-and-cranberry cocktail popular since the 1990s.

Cosmopolitanism is the idea that all human beings belong to a single global community, regardless of national or cultural boundaries. The cosmopolitan feels at home anywhere in the world and values exposure to diverse peoples and customs. The term can describe a philosophical stance, a lifestyle, or an urban sensibility: {Her cosmopolitanism showed in everything from her reading habits to her dinner parties}. Critics sometimes use it pejoratively to suggest rootlessness or disloyalty to one's own nation.

Cosmopolitans is the plural of cosmopolitan, which works as both noun and adjective. A cosmopolitan is a person who has lived in and knows about many different parts of the world, carrying an air of sophistication and worldly experience. As an adjective, it describes places or attitudes characterized by diversity and international influence: {New York has always been a cosmopolitan city}. A cosmopolitan is also a cocktail made with vodka, triple sec, cranberry juice, and lime—often shortened to cosmo.

Cosmos refers to the universe as an ordered, harmonious whole—the opposite of chaos. Ancient Greek philosophers used the term to describe a reality governed by natural laws rather than arbitrary forces. {The cosmos stretches beyond what we can observe.} More modestly, cosmos can mean any complete, self-contained system: {the cosmos of medieval thought}. Cosmos is also a garden flower with delicate, daisy-like petals.

Cosplay is dressing up as a character from fiction, video games, anime, or other media—the word blends "costume" and "play." What distinguishes cosplay from ordinary costume-wearing is the culture around it: cosplayers often make elaborate outfits, attend conventions, and pose for photos in character. The verb means to engage in this practice: {She cosplays as Sailor Moon}.

Cosplayed is the past tense of cosplay—to dress up as a character from fiction, video games, anime, or other media. The word blends "costume" and "play." Cosplaying ranges from casual fan activity to elaborate craftsmanship: {She cosplayed as Sailor Moon at the convention}. {He's cosplayed dozens of characters over the years}.

A cosplayer is someone who dresses up as a character from fiction, gaming, or popular culture—the word blends "costume" and "player." Cosplayers create elaborate outfits to wear at conventions, competitions, or photo shoots: {The cosplayers at Comic-Con were incredible this year}. The practice ranges from casual fan tribute to intricate craftsmanship requiring months of work.

Cosplayers are people who dress in costumes to portray specific characters, typically from anime, video games, comics, or films. The practice—cosplay—blends costume and roleplay, ranging from casual fan appreciation to elaborate craftsmanship competitions. Cosplayers gather at conventions, photo shoots, and online communities: {The cosplayers at Comic-Con spent months on their outfits}.

Cosplaying is the activity of dressing up as a character from fiction, video games, anime, or other media, often with elaborate costumes and accessories crafted by the wearer. The term blends "costume" and "play," and practitioners take pride in accuracy and craftsmanship. Cosplaying is most visible at fan conventions, where participants pose for photos and compete in costume contests. {She spent months cosplaying as her favorite anime character.}

Cosplays is the plural of cosplay, the practice of dressing as characters from fiction, video games, anime, or other media. People cosplay at conventions, Halloween, or for social media content. As a verb, cosplays means engages in this activity: {She cosplays obscure anime characters}. The word blends "costume" and "play."

Cost is what must be given up to obtain something—usually money, but also time, effort, or sacrifice. The cost of a car is its price; the cost of success might be years of work. Costs in business are expenses: {operating costs}, {labor costs}. To cost is to require payment or loss: {The mistake cost him his job}. At all costs means regardless of what must be sacrificed.

A costar is a performer who shares top billing with another in a film, play, or television show. The word implies roughly equal prominence—neither is supporting the other. As a verb, to costar is to appear alongside another lead: {She costars with him in the new thriller}. Also spelled co-star.

Costarring describes a performer who shares top billing with another in a film, play, or show: {a romantic comedy costarring two former sitcom leads}. The term appears in credits and promotional material to indicate actors of roughly equal prominence in a production. Also spelled co-starring.

Costars are the performers who share leading roles in a production. The term implies rough equality of billing—neither is the sole star, but both are prominent: {The film's costars had great chemistry}. As a verb, to costar is to appear alongside another performer in a principal role: {She costars with him in the new series}.

Costly means expensive or requiring significant resources: {a costly renovation}, {a costly mistake}. The word emphasizes the burden of the expense rather than just the price—something costly depletes what you have. Costly errors aren't just expensive in money; they may cost time, reputation, or opportunity. {The delay proved costly to the campaign}.

Costs are expenses—the money, effort, or resources required to obtain or accomplish something. In business, costs include materials, labor, and overhead: {We need to cut costs}. Legal costs are fees for litigation. The phrase {at all costs} means regardless of sacrifice required. To cost is to require expenditure: {The renovation cost us fifty thousand}.

A costume is clothing worn to portray a character or disguise identity—for Halloween, theater, or themed events: {She made her own witch costume}. The word also describes the characteristic dress of a particular time, place, or group: {period costume}, {national costume}. As a verb, to costume is to provide with or dress in such clothing. Costume jewelry is decorative but made of inexpensive materials.

Costumes are clothing worn to transform appearance, typically for theatrical performances, Halloween, or costume parties. Actors wear costumes to become their characters; partygoers wear costumes to become pirates, zombies, or celebrities for a night. {The kids picked out their Halloween costumes in September}. A costume drama or costume piece is set in a historical period, with actors dressed accordingly. As a verb, to costume is to provide or dress in such attire: {She costumed the entire production herself}.

Costuming is the art or practice of designing, making, or selecting costumes, especially for theatrical productions, films, or other performances. The term covers both the creative process and the finished work: {The costuming in that period drama was impeccable}. It also applies to dressing up generally: {Halloween costuming has become increasingly elaborate}.

Cosy describes warm, comfortable snugness—a quality of sheltered intimacy: {a cosy cottage}, {a cosy evening by the fire}. The word suggests pleasant smallness rather than cramped space. A cosy is also a padded cover that keeps a teapot warm. To cosy up to someone is to ingratiate yourself or become friendly, often with ulterior motives. British spelling; Americans write cozy.

A cot is a small, portable bed with a collapsible frame, typically used for camping or as temporary sleeping arrangements: {We set up cots for the overnight guests}. In British English, cot refers to what Americans call a crib—a baby's bed with raised sides. A cot may also be a simple bed in a military barracks or summer camp.

Cots is the plural of cot—a lightweight, portable bed with a frame and fabric stretched across it, used for camping or as temporary sleeping arrangements: {The Red Cross set up cots in the gymnasium for evacuees}. In British English, a cot is a baby's crib. A finger cot is a protective covering for an injured finger.

A cottage is a small, simple house, typically in a rural or semi-rural setting. The word evokes quaintness and charm: {a cottage in the woods}, {a thatched cottage}.
