Crests are the topmost parts or highest points of things. A wave has a crest just before it breaks. A hill's crest is its summit. A bird's crest is the tuft of feathers on its head; a rooster's is its fleshy comb. Heraldic crests are emblems displayed on shields or above them. To crest is to reach the top: {The river crested at twelve feet}. {We crested the ridge at dawn}.

Cretin is an insult meaning a stupid person. The word originated as a medical term for severe developmental disability caused by thyroid deficiency, now called congenital hypothyroidism. That clinical sense is obsolete, and cretin survives only as an epithet: {What kind of cretin parks across two spaces?} The tone ranges from contemptuous to playfully exasperated.

Cretins is the plural of cretin, an insult for a stupid or foolish person: {Those cretins left the gate open and the dog got out}. The word originally denoted someone with severe physical and mental impairment caused by congenital thyroid deficiency—a medical sense now obsolete and offensive. The insult use, while harsh, is common in informal speech.

A crevasse is a deep crack or fissure, especially in a glacier or ice sheet. Crevasses form when ice moves over uneven terrain, creating gaps that can be hundreds of feet deep and sometimes hidden by snow bridges. The word also applies to breaches in levees or riverbanks: {The flood waters poured through a crevasse in the levee}. Distinguished from crevice, which is smaller and typically in rock.

Crevasses are deep cracks or fissures, especially in glacial ice. Climbers and explorers must watch for crevasses, which can be hidden under snow bridges and pose serious danger: {Two members of the expedition fell into a crevasse}. The word also applies to breaches in levees or riverbanks during floods. Not to be confused with crevices, which are narrow cracks in rock.

A crevice is a narrow opening or crack, especially in rock or a wall: {Water seeped through crevices in the stone}. The word suggests a gap deep enough to hide things or allow passage of small creatures: {Lizards disappeared into crevices in the cliff face}.

Crevices is the plural of crevice, a narrow opening or crack in a surface, especially in rock or a wall. Things hide or get lost in crevices: {Crumbs fell into the crevices of the couch cushions}. The word often appears with nooks: {They searched every nook and crevice of the old house}.

A crew is a group of people cooperating on a common task or goal (cleanup crew, flight crew). In entertainment, the crew are people involved in a production who are not part of the cast (lighting crew, sound crew). Less precisely, crew may designate any group of people to characterize them (strange crew, crew of buddies). Crew is also the sport of rowing. The relatively infrequent verb crew means to be a member of a working crew: He crewed on the sailboat. In archaic use, crew is the past tense of crow.

A crewcut is a short hairstyle in which the hair is cut close to the scalp, typically slightly longer on top. The style originated in American collegiate rowing teams and became associated with military servicemen and clean-cut conformity: {He got a crewcut before basic training}. Also spelled crew cut.

Crewcuts are very short haircuts in which the hair stands upright on top, typically trimmed to uniform length. The style originated in American athletics—rowing crews, hence the name—and became associated with clean-cut, conventional masculinity: {He still wore the same crewcut he'd had since high school}. Also spelled crew cuts or crew-cuts.

A crewmate is a fellow member of a crew—someone who works alongside you on a ship, aircraft, or team. The word gained widespread currency through the video game Among Us, where players identify as crewmates trying to complete tasks while imposters sabotage them: {One of us is not a real crewmate}.

A crewneck is a garment—typically a sweater or T-shirt—with a round, close-fitting neckline that sits at the base of the throat. The style contrasts with V-necks, turtlenecks, and collared shirts: {He threw on a gray crewneck and jeans}. Also used as an adjective: {a crewneck sweater}.

Crewnecks are sweaters or shirts with a round, close-fitting neckline that sits at the base of the neck without a collar. The style contrasts with v-necks and turtlenecks. A crewneck is also the neckline itself: {I prefer crewnecks to collared shirts}.

Crews is the plural of crew—groups of people who work together on a ship, aircraft, film set, or other coordinated endeavor. It also refers to informal groups or gangs: {rival crews battled for territory}. As a verb, crews means to serve as crew: {She crews on a racing yacht every summer}.

A bed for a baby with high, protective sides is called a crib in American English. Some containers that look like this in some way are called cribs (corn crib). Informally, a crib is someone’s house or the place where they sleep. If you crib information, you plagiarize. A crib or crib sheet is a collection of notes intended to aid the bearer in passing a test, or less sinisterly, a written or pictorial aid to help you understand something difficult.

Cribbage is a card game for two to four players, typically played with a distinctive wooden board used for scoring. Players form combinations of cards to earn points, which are tracked by moving pegs along the board's holes. The game involves strategy in discarding cards to a "crib"—an extra hand that alternates between players: {We played cribbage at the cabin every summer}.

Cribs is the plural of crib, a bed with high slatted sides for infants. The word extends to any small confined space—a storage bin for grain, a manger, or in British slang, an apartment or home: {Nice cribs in this neighborhood}. In academic contexts, cribs are unauthorized notes used for cheating, or translations used as study aids. To crib is to copy dishonestly or to confine.

A cribsheet is a set of notes used for quick reference, especially one smuggled into an exam for cheating. More innocently, it's any condensed summary of key information: {I made a cribsheet of keyboard shortcuts}. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated.

A crick is a painful stiff feeling in the neck or back, typically from sleeping in an awkward position or sudden movement: {I woke up with a crick in my neck}. The word is informal and primarily American. Separately, crick is a dialectal pronunciation of creek in parts of the American South and Midwest.

Cricket names two things. The insect is a small, chirping creature related to grasshoppers, known for the rhythmic sound males produce by rubbing their wings: {The only sound was crickets}. That silence extends to a joke or question met with no response: {I asked for volunteers and got crickets}. The sport is a bat-and-ball game played on a grass oval, dominant in Britain and its former colonies. Something that's {not cricket} violates fair play or proper conduct.

A cricketer is a person who plays cricket, the bat-and-ball sport popular in Britain, Australia, India, and other Commonwealth nations. The term applies to professionals and amateurs alike: {He dreamed of becoming a professional cricketer}. In American English, where cricket is uncommon, the word sounds formal or foreign.

Cricketers are people who play cricket, the bat-and-ball sport popular in Britain and former British colonies. The term applies to professionals and amateurs alike: {The cricketers took the field after lunch}. In countries where cricket dominates, cricketers enjoy celebrity status comparable to football or basketball players elsewhere.

Crickets are jumping insects known for the chirping sound males produce by rubbing their wings together. The plural also serves as slang for silence or lack of response, especially awkward silence following a joke or announcement that falls flat: {I asked if anyone had questions and got crickets}. The slang derives from the quiet of empty spaces where only insects can be heard.

Cried is the past tense of cry. Most often it means wept—shed tears from emotion: {She cried when she heard the news}. It also means called out or exclaimed: {Help! he cried}. Things that {cried out} for attention demanded it urgently. If you {cried wolf}, you raised a false alarm.

A crier is someone who cries out—announcing, proclaiming, or calling attention to something. The town crier was once an official who walked through streets announcing news and proclamations: {Hear ye, hear ye!} The role is mostly ceremonial now, though court criers still call courtrooms to order. More generally, a crier is simply someone who cries or weeps.

Cries is the plural of cry—utterances of distress, alarm, or strong emotion: {The cries of the wounded filled the night}. Also the third-person singular verb: {She cries every time she watches that movie}. A cry can be a shout, a weeping spell, or an animal's call. {Battle cries}, {cries for help}, {cries of joy}—the word covers the full range of vocal intensity.

Crikey is one of several interjections inspired by the word Christ as a slightly less offensive alternative. It is mainly used in British and Australian English to express surprise or a negative emotion.

Crime is an act that violates the law and is punishable by the state—theft, assault, murder, fraud. The word extends to serious moral wrongs even without legal violation: {a crime against humanity}, {It's a crime to waste such talent}. In casual use, crime emphasizes that something is regrettable or outrageous: {It would be a crime to miss this opportunity}.

A crimebuster is someone who fights or solves crimes, especially with notable success or zeal. The term has a comic-book flavor, evoking masked vigilantes and hard-boiled detectives: {The new police chief styled himself as a crimebuster who would clean up the city}. Often used with a hint of exaggeration or irony.

A crimefighter is someone who combats crime—typically a police officer, detective, or prosecutor, but the term carries a heroic, often sensationalized connotation from comic books and action films. Batman and Superman are crimefighters; so is a district attorney who prosecutes organized crime. The word suggests active pursuit rather than mere enforcement: {The mayor promised to be a crimefighter, not just an administrator}.

Crimefighters are people who work to prevent or combat crime, whether as law enforcement officers, vigilantes, or fictional superheroes. The term carries a slightly dramatic or nostalgic quality, evoking comic book heroes and old-time radio dramas as much as actual police work. {Batman and other masked crimefighters patrolled the city streets.} In serious contexts, crimefighter often describes particularly dedicated or effective law enforcement personnel.

Crimefighting is the work of preventing, investigating, or combating crime. The term applies to police work but also to vigilante justice in fiction—Batman and other superheroes are crimefighters. As an adjective, it modifies related nouns: {crimefighting efforts}, {crimefighting technology}. Also spelled as two words.

A crimelord is the leader of a criminal organization—someone who controls illegal operations like drug trafficking, gambling, or extortion. The term evokes organized crime hierarchies: {The crimelord ran the city's underworld from his nightclub}. Also spelled as two words: crime lord.

Crimelords are the leaders or bosses of organized criminal enterprises, wielding power over illegal operations like drug trafficking, gambling, or protection rackets. The term emphasizes their authority and territorial control, suggesting a feudal-like dominion over criminal networks. {The city's crimelords controlled everything from the docks to the gambling dens.} While crime lord as two words is more common, the single-word form appears in journalism and fiction depicting underworld hierarchies.

Crimes is the plural of crime—acts that violate the law and are punishable by the state. The word covers everything from petty theft to murder. {Crimes against humanity} are atrocities so severe they offend universal moral standards. {Fashion crimes} and {crimes against good taste} are hyperbolic complaints about aesthetic offenses.
clues: What detectives are paid to solve

definition: A crimewave is a sudden increase in criminal activity within a particular area or time period. The term suggests a surge that rises and eventually subsides, like a wave: {The city experienced a crimewave in the early 1990s}. Often used in news coverage and political rhetoric about public safety. Also spelled as two words: crime wave.

Criminal describes people, actions, or matters relating to crime and its prosecution. A criminal act violates laws that can result in punishment by the state; criminal law is the body of law dealing with such offenses, distinct from civil law. As a noun, a criminal is someone who has committed a crime. The word extends figuratively to characterize anything outrageously wrong or wasteful: {It's criminal how much food gets thrown away}. {The criminal justice system needs reform.} {He has no criminal record.}

Criminalisation is the process of making something illegal or treating it as a crime. It refers to laws or policies that designate previously legal activities as criminal offenses: {the criminalisation of drug use}, {the criminalisation of homelessness}. The term often appears in debates about whether punishment is the appropriate response to social problems. British spelling of criminalization.

To criminalise is to make something illegal by law, turning an act into a crime: {The new legislation criminalises possession of certain weapons}. It can also mean to treat someone as a criminal or cast them in that light: {Policies that criminalise poverty}. British spelling of criminalize.

Criminality is the quality or state of being criminal—involvement in illegal activity or the tendency toward it. The word often implies a pattern rather than a single act: {The neighborhood struggled with poverty and criminality}. It can also describe something's illegal nature: {The criminality of the scheme was obvious to investigators}.

Criminalization is the act or process of making something illegal—turning conduct that was previously lawful or tolerated into a criminal offense. The term often appears in policy debates: {the criminalization of marijuana}, {the criminalization of homelessness}. It can also describe treating people as criminals: {Critics argue that immigration enforcement has led to the criminalization of asylum seekers}.

To criminalize something is to make it illegal—to declare by law that an action constitutes a crime: {The state criminalized possession of certain drugs}. The term often appears in debates about whether prohibiting something is wise or just: {Should we criminalize homelessness?} The opposite is decriminalize.

Criminalized means made illegal by law: {Marijuana possession was criminalized in the 1930s}. The term often appears in debates about whether certain acts should be crimes at all: {Should drug use be criminalized or treated as a public health issue?} To say something has been criminalized emphasizes that illegality is a policy choice, not an inherent quality of the act.

Criminally means in a way that violates the law: {He was criminally charged with assault}. It also serves as an intensifier for something shockingly bad or wrong: {criminally negligent}, {criminally underrated}. The emphatic use suggests the situation is so egregious it ought to be illegal, even when it isn't: {That restaurant is criminally overpriced}.

Criminals is the plural of criminal—people who have committed crimes or engage in criminal activity. The word labels rather than describes: once applied, it tends to stick regardless of rehabilitation or circumstance. {The program helps former criminals reenter the workforce.} {Career criminals rarely reform.} Used attributively: {a criminals' code of silence}.

A criminologist is a scholar who studies crime—its causes, patterns, prevention, and social effects. The field draws on sociology, psychology, law, and statistics. Criminologists analyze data on criminal behavior, evaluate justice policies, and may advise lawmakers or law enforcement: {The criminologist testified about recidivism rates}.

Criminology is the scientific study of crime, criminals, and the criminal justice system. It draws on sociology, psychology, and law to examine why people commit crimes, how societies respond, and what policies might reduce criminal behavior. A criminologist might study recidivism rates, the effectiveness of rehabilitation programs, or patterns in violent crime.
Criminy is one of several interjections inspired by the word Christ as a slightly less offensive alternative. It is mainly used to express surprise or a negative emotion.

Crimp describes a tight wave, bend, or fold pressed into something. Hair can be crimped into zigzag patterns; metal can be crimped to join pieces together; pie crust edges get crimped decoratively. The verb means to create such a shape, often by pinching or pressing with a tool. Figuratively, to put a crimp in something is to hinder or obstruct it: {The rain really put a crimp in our plans}. A crimp is also someone who tricks or coerces people into service, especially historically as sailors.

Crimped describes something pressed into small folds, waves, or ridges. Hair that has been crimped shows tight, zigzag waves: {She crimped her hair for the party}. Metal or pastry edges are crimped by pinching or pressing to seal or decorate: {crimped pie crust}. Crimped wire or cable has been compressed to form a connection. The word suggests artificial shaping—something bent from its natural form.

Crimping is pressing or pinching something into tight folds, waves, or ridges. You crimp the edge of a pie crust to seal it, crimp hair with a heated tool to create waves, or crimp a wire connector to secure it. In fishing, a crimp secures line to hooks or leaders. To {put a crimp in} something is to hinder or obstruct it: {The rain put a crimp in our plans}.

Crimps are tight waves or ridges pressed into something—hair styled with a crimping iron, or the bent edges that seal a pie crust. In climbing, crimps are small holds gripped with bent fingers. To crimp is to create such ridges or bends, or figuratively to restrict: {Budget cuts crimped our expansion plans}. A crimp in something is an obstacle or limitation.

Crimson is a deep, vivid red with a slight blue tinge—darker and richer than scarlet. The color of arterial blood, certain roses, and autumn leaves. As a verb, to crimson is to blush or flush red: {Her cheeks crimsoned with embarrassment}. Harvard University's athletic teams are the Crimson, and the color appears in their branding.

Cringe is to shrink back or flinch, usually from fear, disgust, or embarrassment: {She cringed when he started singing}. The reaction can be physical or purely emotional. As slang, cringe describes something painfully awkward or embarrassing: {That video is so cringe}. Cringeworthy and cringey are related adjectives. To cringe at a memory is to wince at your past self.

Cringed is the past tense of cringe—to shrink back or flinch, typically from fear, disgust, or embarrassment. Someone cringes physically when recoiling from a blow or unpleasant sensation: {She cringed as the needle went in}. More often now, cringing is an internal reaction to something awkward or embarrassing: {I cringed at my old photos}. The word has gained currency describing secondhand embarrassment at others' behavior.

A cringefest is an event, performance, or situation so awkward or embarrassing that it's painful to witness. The word combines cringe with the suffix -fest (suggesting an abundance of something): {The awards ceremony was a total cringefest}. Often used for social media posts, speeches, or interactions that provoke secondhand embarrassment.

Cringeworthy describes something so awkward, embarrassing, or socially painful that it makes you cringe—that involuntary wince when witnessing someone else's humiliation or your own past mistakes: {I found some cringeworthy poems I wrote in high school}. Often shortened to cringe as an adjective: {That speech was so cringe}.

Cringey describes something that provokes secondhand embarrassment or discomfort, usually because it's awkward, try-hard, or socially tone-deaf. The word emerged from internet culture alongside the noun cringe, which names that visceral wince you feel watching someone humiliate themselves. {His attempts at flirting were painfully cringey.} Also spelled cringy.

Cringing describes the act of recoiling or shrinking back, whether physically from fear or pain, or emotionally from embarrassment or disgust. Someone cringing at a horror movie flinches at the scary parts; someone cringing at an awkward speech feels secondhand embarrassment. In contemporary usage, cringing often appears in response to social media posts or public behavior deemed painfully awkward: {I couldn't stop cringing at his attempt to seem relatable}.

Cringy describes something that provokes secondhand embarrassment or discomfort—the feeling of witnessing someone else's awkwardness or failed attempt at being cool. Often applied to social media posts, jokes that don't land, or desperate bids for attention: {That video of him rapping at the wedding was so cringy}. Also spelled cringey.

Crinkle describes the formation of small creases, wrinkles, or wavy folds. Paper crinkles when crushed; skin crinkles around the eyes when smiling. The word works as both verb and noun: {She crinkled the wrapper} and {the crinkles in the foil}. Crinkle suggests lighter, finer texture than wrinkle—more delicate folds, often with a rustling sound.

Crinkles are small wrinkles, folds, or creases—the fine lines that form when something flexible is compressed or aged. Paper crinkles when crushed, skin crinkles around the eyes when smiling. The verb means to form such creases: {She crinkled her nose in disgust}. The word suggests something lighter and more delicate than a full wrinkle, often with a slightly pleasing quality: {the crinkle of cellophane}, {crinkles of laughter around his eyes}.

Crinkling is the act of making small creases or wrinkles, or the rustling sound that accompanies it. Paper crinkles when crushed; skin crinkles around the eyes when someone smiles. The word captures both the visual texture and the soft, crackling noise: {the crinkling of cellophane}, {the crinkling at the corners of her eyes}.

Crinkly describes something with small creases, wrinkles, or folds—a surface that isn't smooth but rippled or rumpled: {crinkly wrapping paper}, {crinkly skin around her eyes}. The word suggests texture you can see or feel, often with an implicit sound—paper and cellophane crinkle when handled. {His crinkly smile made him look friendly}.

Crippled describes someone or something severely impaired in function. Traditionally it meant physically disabled, especially unable to walk: {He was crippled in the accident}. The term is now considered offensive when applied to people—disabled or specific terms are preferred. It remains standard for things: {crippled by debt}, {a crippled economy}, {The storm crippled the power grid}.

Crippling describes something that causes severe damage or disability. A crippling {injury} leaves someone unable to function normally. Crippling {debt} is so overwhelming it prevents financial recovery. Crippling {fear} paralyzes action. The word implies not just harm but impairment so severe that normal functioning becomes impossible: {The sanctions had a crippling effect on the economy}.

Crises is the plural of crisis—a point of danger, difficulty, or decisive change. A single crisis demands attention; multiple crises can overwhelm: {The administration faced overlapping crises in health care, housing, and foreign policy}. The word retains its Greek plural form, though "crisises" occasionally appears in informal speech.

A crisis is a turning point—a crucial moment when things could go either way. The word often describes emergencies or periods of intense difficulty: {a financial crisis}, {a hostage crisis}, {the Cuban Missile Crisis}. A {midlife crisis} is a period of anxiety about aging and accomplishment. In medicine, a crisis is the point when a patient either begins to recover or declines. The plural is crises.

Crisp is most frequently an adjective for a desirable quality of food (crisp lettuce leaves), fabrics (crisp linen), or images (crisp graphics). Crisp air is the kind you find on a cool autumn morning. The noun crisp is used in British English for the food that Americans call potato chips. The relatively infrequent verb crisp means to make something crisp: Crisp the celery by putting it in water.

Crispbread is a thin, dry, crunchy cracker made from rye or other grains. It originated in Scandinavia as a long-lasting staple and remains popular as a light alternative to bread: {She topped the crispbread with cheese and smoked salmon}. The texture is brittle and snaps cleanly.

Crispness is the quality of being crisp. In food, it suggests a satisfying snap or crunch: {the crispness of fresh lettuce}, {the crispness of bacon}. In air or weather, crispness means cool and invigorating: {autumn crispness}. The word extends to anything sharp and clean—the crispness of a new dollar bill, the crispness of well-pressed linens, the crispness of someone's diction.

Crisps is the British term for what Americans call potato chips—thin slices of potato fried until crisp and salted or flavored: {a packet of crisps}, {cheese and onion crisps}. The word also serves as the plural of crisp in its other senses, or as the verb form meaning to make something crispy: {The bacon crisps in the pan}.

Crispy describes food with a pleasingly firm, brittle texture that breaks with a slight crunch: {crispy bacon}, {crispy fried chicken}, {The edges got nice and crispy}. It suggests a thin, delicate crispness rather than deep crunchiness—potato chips are crispy, raw carrots are crunchy. The word carries appetizing connotations that crisp sometimes lacks.

Crisscross describes a pattern of lines crossing each other at angles, forming X shapes or a grid: {crisscross marks on the pavement}, {a crisscross of hiking trails}. As a verb, to crisscross is to move back and forth across an area: {We crisscrossed the country looking for the best barbecue}. The word can also describe movement or arrangement in intersecting directions: {Cables crisscross overhead}.

Crisscrossed describes a pattern of lines or paths that cross each other repeatedly, forming an X or grid-like arrangement: {The countryside was crisscrossed with ancient stone walls}. It can describe physical marks, routes, or movement: {She crisscrossed the country on her book tour}. The pattern suggests intersection and overlap rather than parallel arrangement.

Crisscrosses refers to patterns of lines crossing each other at angles, or the act of creating such patterns. Roads crisscross the countryside; loyalties crisscross political boundaries. The word works as both noun and verb: {The quilt featured crisscrosses of colorful thread}; {Hiking trails crisscross the mountain}.

Crisscrossing describes lines, paths, or movements that cross each other repeatedly in different directions, forming a pattern of intersections: {Hiking trails go crisscrossing through the valley}. It suggests multiple crossings rather than a single intersection. Someone crisscrossing a country travels back and forth across it: {She spent the summer crisscrossing Europe by train}.

Criteria is the plural of criterion, meaning standards or principles used to judge, evaluate, or decide something. When you apply for a job, you're measured against hiring criteria; when judges score a competition, they follow established criteria. Though criteria is grammatically plural, it increasingly appears with singular verbs in casual use: {What's the criteria for admission?} Purists insist on {What are the criteria?} and reserve criterion for the singular.

A criterion is a standard or rule for judging something—for example, whether a thing can be considered a member of a class on the basis of its characteristics. Few things are judged by a single criterion, and so the irregular plural criteria is much more frequently used. The verb that typically precedes criteria is meet: Before they are officially approved, laboratories must meet the criteria for each analysis.

A critic is someone who judges or evaluates, especially professionally. Film critics review movies; literary critics analyze books. The word often carries negative weight—to be {a critic} of something is to find fault with it, and {critics} in news headlines usually means opponents: {Critics say the bill doesn't go far enough}. Critical can mean either analytical or disapproving.

Critical centers on careful judgment and evaluation. A critical analysis examines something closely to assess its merits and flaws. A critic offers such assessments, so critical can mean disapproving or fault-finding: {She was critical of his work habits}. Critical also means essential or decisive: a critical moment, critical infrastructure, {This next step is critical}. In medicine, a critical condition is precarious—the patient may not survive. A critical mass is the minimum amount needed to sustain a reaction, literal or figurative.

Critically means in a way that involves careful analysis and judgment: {Read the sources critically before citing them}. It also means in a way that expresses disapproval or finds fault: {She spoke critically of his work habits}. In medical contexts, critically means dangerously or severely: {critically ill}, {critically injured}. Something critically important is essential—failure would be decisive.

Criticise is the British spelling of criticize. To criticise is to point out faults or flaws: {The report criticised the government's handling of the crisis}. It can also mean to evaluate or analyse, especially in artistic or literary contexts: {She criticised the novel for a literary journal}. The negative sense—finding fault—dominates everyday usage.

Criticism is the expression of disapproval based on perceived faults or mistakes: {The proposal drew criticism from environmental groups}. In a more neutral sense, criticism refers to the analysis and evaluation of creative or intellectual works—literary criticism, film criticism—where the aim is assessment rather than fault-finding. A critic engages in criticism professionally or habitually. The verb criticize can lean toward either sense but more often implies finding fault.

To criticize is to point out faults or shortcomings: {Critics criticized the film for its slow pacing}. The word often implies negative judgment, though criticism can be constructive: {She asked him to criticize her essay before submission}. In formal contexts, criticize can mean simply to evaluate or analyze, without necessarily finding fault: {The committee criticized the proposal on its merits}.

Criticized is the past tense of criticize, meaning to find fault with or express disapproval of something or someone: {The report was widely criticized for its methodology}. Criticism can be constructive or hostile—a teacher criticizes a student's essay to help them improve, while a politician criticizes opponents to undermine them. {She criticized his decision to leave}.

Criticizing is pointing out faults or flaws in something or someone. The word carries a negative connotation—to criticize usually means to find fault rather than to evaluate neutrally: {She's always criticizing my driving}. Critics professionally evaluate art and performance, but even there, criticizing often implies unfavorable judgment: {He spent the whole review criticizing the director's choices}.

Critics are people who evaluate and pass judgment on works of art, literature, music, film, or other creative efforts. Professional critics write reviews for publications; amateur critics share opinions everywhere. The word often carries a negative edge—{critics of the policy demanded changes}—suggesting fault-finding rather than fair assessment. {The critics loved the film, but audiences stayed home.}

Critique is a detailed analysis and assessment of something, typically a creative work or intellectual argument. Unlike simple criticism, critique implies systematic evaluation of both strengths and weaknesses: {The professor offered a thorough critique of my thesis}. As a verb, to critique is to provide such analysis: {We'll critique each other's drafts in workshop}. The word carries more academic weight than criticize, which tends toward finding fault.

Critiquing is the act of offering a critique—a detailed analysis and evaluation of something, especially a creative work. The word emphasizes the process of assessment: {She spent the afternoon critiquing student portfolios}. Unlike criticizing, which often implies finding fault, critiquing suggests balanced evaluation that may include both strengths and weaknesses.

Critter comes from creature but feels more informal and affectionate. Any animal can be called a critter, though the word implies familiarity or harmlessness rather than danger. {We're going out to feed the critters.} Critter also works for creatures we can't or don't identify: {Hey, there's a critter on your shirtsleeve.}

Critters is an informal, often affectionate term for creatures—typically small animals, insects, or wildlife: {We've got critters living under the porch}. The word carries a rural or folksy tone. It can refer to any animal, but usually suggests pests, wildlife, or farm animals rather than pets: {The barn cats keep the critters out of the feed}.

Croak is the deep, harsh sound a frog or raven makes. By extension, to croak is to speak in a rough, strained voice: {She croaked out a few words through her sore throat}. In slang, croak means to die: {The old man finally croaked}. As a noun, a croak is an instance of such a sound.

Croaked is the past tense of croak. A frog croaked by the pond. A voice that croaked was harsh and raspy. In slang, someone who croaked has died: {He croaked before the ambulance arrived}. To croak someone is to kill them.

Croaking is the harsh, low-pitched sound frogs and ravens make, or any similar rough vocalization. Someone with a sore throat speaks in a croak. Figuratively, to croak is to complain pessimistically or, in slang, to die: {The old man finally croaked}. As an adjective, croaking describes the sound itself: {croaking frogs filled the night air}.

Croaks is the plural of croak, the low, hoarse sound a frog makes. Extended to any rough, guttural vocalization: {His voice came out in croaks after the surgery}. As a verb form, croaks means to make such a sound, or in slang, to die: {The old man finally croaks in the third act}.

Croc is an informal shortening of crocodile, the large aquatic reptile: {We spotted a croc sunning on the riverbank}. In the plural, Crocs refers to the brand of rubber clogs with ventilation holes, distinctive for their chunky appearance and comfort: {She wore her Crocs to the beach}.

Crochet is a method of knitting in which loops are pulled through each other using a hook. To crochet is to use this method to make something. The product of crocheting is also called crochet. A crochet hook is the tool used in the process.

Crocheted describes something made by crochet—the craft of creating fabric by interlocking loops of yarn with a hooked needle: {a crocheted blanket}, {crocheted doilies}. The word often evokes handmade, homespun quality: {She wore a crocheted shawl her grandmother made}. Pronounced with two syllables (cro-SHAYED) or three (cro-SHAY-ed).

Crocheting is the craft of creating fabric by interlocking loops of yarn or thread with a hooked needle. Unlike knitting, which uses two needles, crocheting builds each stitch independently, making it easier to correct mistakes. The term covers both the activity and its products: {She took up crocheting during the pandemic}, {The baby blanket is her own crocheting}.

A crock is a thick earthenware pot or jar, traditionally used for storing food or fermenting: {a crock of pickles}, {a crock of butter}. The word also means nonsense or rubbish, especially in the phrase {a crock of shit}—something worthless or untrue: {His alibi was a complete crock}. As a verb, to crock out is to break down or fail, and a crock can be a decrepit person or thing.

Crockery is dishes, plates, bowls, and cups collectively—the everyday tableware used for serving and eating meals. The term is more common in British than American English, where people tend to say dishes or dinnerware: {Be careful unpacking that box—it's full of crockery}.

A crockpot is an electric cooking appliance that simmers food at low temperatures over several hours, producing tender stews, roasts, and soups with minimal attention. The name comes from the ceramic pot (crock) that holds the food. Though Crock-Pot is a trademark, the lowercase form has become generic: {I threw everything in the crockpot before work}.

A crocodile is a large aquatic reptile with a long snout, powerful jaws, and armored skin, found in tropical rivers and swamps. Crocodiles are distinguished from alligators by their narrower snouts and visible lower teeth. {Crocodile tears} are insincere displays of grief—from the old belief that crocodiles weep while devouring prey.

Crocodiles is the plural of crocodile, a large aquatic reptile with a long snout, powerful jaws, and armored skin. Found in tropical rivers and wetlands, crocodiles are ambush predators—patient and deadly. {Crocodiles basked on the riverbank}. Crocodile tears are false displays of sorrow, from the old belief that crocodiles weep while eating prey.

A crocus is a small flowering plant that blooms in early spring, often pushing through snow. The cup-shaped flowers appear in purple, yellow, white, or striped varieties. Crocuses are among the first signs of spring in temperate climates: {The crocuses are up already}. Saffron comes from the stigmas of one crocus species.

Crocuses is the plural of crocus, a small flowering plant that blooms in early spring or autumn. The flowers emerge close to the ground in purple, yellow, white, or striped varieties. Spring crocuses are among the first signs of the season's change: {The crocuses are up—winter's almost over}.

A croissant is a crescent-shaped pastry made from buttery, flaky dough that puffs into thin layers when baked. The word is French for "crescent." Croissants are a breakfast staple, eaten plain or filled with chocolate, ham and cheese, or almond paste: {She grabbed a croissant and coffee on her way to work}.

Croissants are crescent-shaped pastries made from buttery, flaky, laminated dough. The dough is repeatedly folded and rolled to create dozens of thin layers that puff apart during baking, producing the characteristic airy texture. Though associated with French cuisine, the pastry has Austrian origins. Croissants are typically eaten at breakfast, either plain or filled with chocolate, almond paste, or ham and cheese. {I grabbed a croissant and coffee on my way to work.}

A crone is an old woman, especially one who is thin, ugly, or unpleasant. The word is almost always derogatory: {The old crone muttered curses at passersby}. In some feminist and pagan contexts, crone has been reclaimed as a term honoring elder women's wisdom, but the negative connotations dominate general usage.

Crones is the plural of crone, an old woman—especially one considered ugly, withered, or sinister. The word carries negative connotations of decrepitude and menace: {The fairy tale featured three crones stirring a cauldron}. In some feminist and pagan circles, crone has been reclaimed as a positive term for wise elder women who have passed through maiden and mother stages of life.

Cronies are close friends or companions, but the word almost always carries negative connotations—implying favoritism, corruption, or mutual back-scratching among insiders. Politicians reward their cronies with appointments and contracts. The singular crony exists but appears less often than the plural: {The mayor filled city hall with his cronies}.

A crony is a close friend or companion, especially one who receives special favors. The word nearly always carries negative connotations—cronies benefit from connections rather than merit: {The mayor appointed his cronies to city positions}. Cronyism describes the practice of favoring friends in hiring or contracts.

Cronyism is the practice of favoring friends and associates, especially in political appointments or business dealings. A leader who fills positions with loyal pals rather than qualified candidates practices cronyism. The word carries strong negative connotations—it suggests corruption, incompetence, and closed circles of power: {The administration was plagued by cronyism and nepotism}.

Crook is contained in crooked and that’s a good way to remember its two seemingly divergent meanings. One crook is a liar, thief, or criminal; the other crook is a bend in a linear thing: A small crook in the river. A shepherd’s or bishop’s staff, which has a bend, is also called a crook. If you crook something, especially a body part, you bend it: She crooked her neck to hold the phone to her ear.

Crooked means bent, curved, or not straight: {a crooked path through the woods}, {a crooked smile}. The word extends to dishonest or corrupt behavior: {a crooked politician}, {a crooked deal}. Something crooked deviates from what's expected—whether a physical line or a moral one.

Crooks is the plural of crook—people who engage in dishonest or criminal activity: {The company was run by crooks}. A crook is also a hooked staff, especially the curved implement carried by shepherds, which gives us the crook of the arm (the inside bend of the elbow) and the verb crook, meaning to bend: {She crooked her finger to beckon him over}.

Croon is to sing or hum in a soft, soothing voice—the kind used for lullabies or romantic ballads: {She crooned to the baby until he fell asleep}. The word evokes intimacy and gentleness. Crooners were mid-twentieth-century male vocalists like Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra who sang in this smooth, subdued style.

Crooned is the past tense of croon, meaning to sing or hum in a soft, low, soothing voice. The word often suggests romantic or sentimental delivery: {He crooned love songs into the microphone}. Crooning became associated with mid-twentieth-century pop singers like Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra, who used intimate vocal styles suited to radio and recording.

A crooner is a singer, especially a male vocalist, who sings sentimental songs in a soft, smooth style. The term evokes the intimate microphone technique that emerged in the 1930s and 1940s, associated with performers like Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra: {He fancies himself a crooner at karaoke night}.

Crooners are singers, especially male vocalists, known for a smooth, sentimental style of singing popular songs. The term evokes the intimate, microphone-dependent vocal technique that emerged in the 1930s and 40s with performers like Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra: {the great crooners of the swing era}. Someone might be called a crooner affectionately or dismissively, depending on whether the speaker values that polished, romantic style.

Crooning is singing softly and sentimentally, often in a low, smooth voice. The style is associated with intimate ballads and romantic songs: {He was crooning love songs into the microphone}. The term can also describe any gentle, murmuring vocalization: {She sat crooning to the baby}.

The handful of noun meanings of crop is dominated by its use to designate a cultivated plant raised for food or profit. But a crop is also an enlarged area in a bird’s gut for holding food; a short whip used in horse riding; and a collection of things: A crop of new comedies. As a verb, to crop most often means to trim or cut something back. When you crop a photo, you cut off its edges.

A cropduster is a small aircraft used to spray pesticides, herbicides, or fertilizers over agricultural fields. The pilot who flies such a plane is also called a cropduster. As slang, a cropduster is someone who passes gas while walking through a crowd, leaving others to discover it: {He cropdusted the whole meeting room}.

Cropdusters are aircraft used to spray pesticides, herbicides, or fertilizers over agricultural fields. The planes fly low, releasing chemicals in a fine mist across crops. By extension, cropduster can describe the pilot who operates such a plane. In crude slang, cropdusting means passing gas while walking through a space, leaving others to encounter the smell: {He cropdusted the whole office on his way out}.

Cropped means cut short or trimmed. A cropped photograph has had its edges removed to improve composition or focus: {I cropped the image to center the subject}. Cropped hair is cut close to the head. Cropped pants or a cropped top are cut shorter than standard length, ending above where they normally would: {She wore a cropped jacket that showed her waist}.

Cropping is the act of cutting away unwanted outer portions—most often from photographs or images to improve composition or focus on a subject: {The cropping removed the distracting background}. In agriculture, cropping refers to cultivating crops or the cycle of planting and harvesting: {crop rotation}, {continuous cropping}. Hair or ears may be cropped short.

Crops are plants cultivated for food, fiber, or other uses: {corn crops}, {cash crops}, {crop rotation}. A crop is also a yield or harvest: {This year's crop of graduates}. To crop is to cut short—cropping hair, cropping a photograph. A riding crop is a short whip. An animal's crop is a pouch in its digestive tract where food is stored before digestion.

A croquembouche is a French dessert consisting of cream puffs stacked into a cone and bound with threads of caramelized sugar. The name means "crunch in the mouth." Traditional at French weddings and celebrations, it serves as an elaborate centerpiece: {The pastry chef assembled a towering croquembouche for the reception}.

Croquet is a lawn game in which players use mallets to drive wooden balls through a series of wire hoops called wickets. The game rewards strategy and precision over athleticism. To croquet an opponent's ball is to strike your own ball, placed against theirs, so that yours stays put while theirs flies away—a satisfying tactical move.

A croquette is a small roll or patty of minced meat, fish, or vegetables, coated in breadcrumbs and deep-fried until crisp: {potato croquettes}, {salmon croquettes}. The word comes from French for "crunch." Croquettes appear across many cuisines as a way to use leftover ingredients in an appealing form.

Croquettes are small portions of food—typically mashed potato, minced meat, or fish—shaped into cylinders or balls, coated in breadcrumbs, and deep-fried until crispy. The word comes from French for "crunch." They appear across many cuisines: {potato croquettes}, {ham croquettes}, {the Japanese korokke}. Usually served as appetizers or side dishes.

The many meanings of cross all arise from the one made famous by Jesus of Nazareth: an object formed by placing one straight beam or line on another, intersecting in a right angle at their midpoints. The notion of two things meeting in a particular way persists in the cross that is a hybrid animal or plant, and in a boxing punch where the arm passes over the opponent’s arm. When one thing crosses another, it goes from one side to the other, typically at a right angle, as when a bridge crosses a river. If you cross something out, you draw a line or lines through it to obscure it.

A crossbar is a horizontal bar connecting two upright posts or supports. In sports, it's the bar joining the goalposts in football, soccer, or hockey—a shot that hits the crossbar narrowly misses: {The ball struck the crossbar and bounced away}. Bicycles have a crossbar connecting the seat post to the handlebars. Any horizontal structural element bridging two verticals may be called a crossbar.

Crossbars are horizontal bars that span between two upright supports. A crossbar connects the goalposts in football or soccer—a shot that hits the crossbar narrowly misses. Crossbars also appear on bicycles (the bar between seat and handlebars) and as roof rack components on vehicles: {We strapped the kayak to the crossbars}.

Crossbody describes something worn diagonally across the torso, typically a bag or purse with a strap that goes over one shoulder and rests on the opposite hip: {She switched to a crossbody bag so she could keep her hands free}. The style distributes weight evenly and keeps belongings secure while walking or traveling.

Two bones depicted in an X shape, almost always paired with a skull to form the skull and crossbones symbol. This image appears on poison labels, pirate flags, and anywhere death or danger needs signaling. The bones represent human femurs or tibiae crossed beneath a grinning skull: {The bottle was marked with a skull and crossbones}.

A crossbow is a weapon consisting of a bow mounted horizontally on a stock, with a mechanism to hold the drawn string and release it by trigger. Unlike traditional bows requiring continuous arm strength to hold at full draw, a crossbow stays cocked until fired: {He aimed the crossbow and squeezed the trigger}. Crossbows are used for hunting and target shooting.

A crossbow is a weapon that shoots projectiles using a bow mounted horizontally on a stock, drawn and held by a mechanical catch until released by a trigger. Unlike traditional bows requiring sustained arm strength, crossbows can be aimed and fired like guns: {The hunter loaded his crossbow}. They remain popular for hunting and target shooting.

Crossbred describes an animal or plant produced by mating or crossing two different breeds, varieties, or species: {a crossbred dog}, {crossbred cattle}. The term applies both to the offspring and to the process: something can be crossbred deliberately for desired traits. As a noun, a crossbred is the resulting hybrid: {The crossbreds showed better disease resistance than purebreds}.

Crossbreed refers to an animal or plant produced by mating or crossing two different breeds, varieties, or species: {The dog is a crossbreed of a poodle and a labrador}. As a verb, to crossbreed is to produce such offspring deliberately: {Farmers crossbreed cattle to improve disease resistance}. The term applies to both the process and the result.

Crossbreeding is mating animals or plants of different breeds, varieties, or species to produce offspring with combined traits. Farmers crossbreed cattle to improve milk production or disease resistance. The term extends to any deliberate mixing: {a crossbreeding of musical styles}. The verb is crossbreed; the offspring is a crossbreed.

Crossbreeds are offspring produced by mating parents of different breeds, varieties, or species. The term applies most often to dogs and other domesticated animals: {The shelter had several crossbreeds available for adoption}. As a verb, to crossbreed is to produce such offspring, often intentionally to combine desirable traits from each parent stock.

Crosscheck means to verify information by comparing it against another source or using a different method. If you crosscheck facts, you confirm their accuracy by consulting multiple references. In hockey, a crosscheck is an illegal move where a player shoves an opponent using the shaft of their stick held horizontally. {I always crosscheck flight times on the airline's website.} The word emphasizes the idea of intersecting verification—checking across rather than just checking once.

Crosschecking is verifying information by comparing it against another source or method: {She was crosschecking the figures against last year's report}. The practice is standard in journalism, accounting, and research—anywhere accuracy matters. In hockey, crosschecking is an illegal hit using the shaft of the stick held horizontally against an opponent.

Crosschecks is plural of crosscheck, the act of verifying something by using an alternative source or method: {She crosschecks every invoice against the original purchase order}. In hockey, a crosscheck is an illegal move where a player shoves an opponent using the shaft of the stick held horizontally. The verb means to perform either action.

A crosscurrent is a current flowing across or against another current, whether in water or air. The word extends naturally to conflicting forces or tendencies: {crosscurrents of public opinion}, {political crosscurrents that made consensus impossible}. The plural often describes competing influences within a single situation: {The negotiations were complicated by crosscurrents of regional rivalry}.

Crosscurrents are conflicting forces or tendencies moving in opposition to each other. The literal sense is water or air flowing against the main current: {Crosscurrents made swimming dangerous}. More often the word describes competing influences in politics, culture, or opinion: {The legislation faced crosscurrents from both progressives and conservatives}. The plural dominates; the singular crosscurrent appears but is less common.
clues: Waters or ideas pulling opposite ways

definition: Crosscut describes cutting across the grain rather than along it. A crosscut {saw} has teeth designed to sever wood fibers perpendicular to their direction. The term extends to any diagonal or transverse cut. In film, to crosscut is to alternate between two scenes happening simultaneously, building tension or showing parallel action: {The director crosscut between the chase and the ticking bomb}.

Crosscuts are cuts made across the grain of wood, perpendicular to the fibers—the opposite of ripping, which follows the grain. A crosscut saw has teeth designed for this purpose. The term extends to any diagonal or transverse cut. In film, crosscutting alternates between scenes happening simultaneously: {The director crosscuts between the chase and the ticking bomb}.

To crossdress is to wear clothing typically associated with the opposite sex. The practice may be for personal comfort, sexual arousal, theatrical performance, or gender expression. Someone who crossdresses is a crossdresser: {He crossdresses on weekends}. The term is neutral, though attitudes toward the practice vary widely.

A crossdresser is a person who wears clothing typically associated with the opposite sex. The practice may be for comfort, self-expression, entertainment, or erotic pleasure. Crossdresser has largely replaced the older term transvestite, which acquired clinical or pejorative overtones: {He's been a crossdresser since his twenties}. Crossdressing doesn't necessarily indicate anything about sexual orientation or gender identity.

Crossdressers are people who wear clothing typically associated with a different gender. The practice may be occasional or regular, for comfort, self-expression, performance, or sexual pleasure. Crossdressing doesn't necessarily indicate anything about sexual orientation or gender identity—many crossdressers are heterosexual and identify with their birth gender. {The support group welcomed crossdressers and their partners.}

Crossdressing is wearing clothing typically associated with the opposite sex. The practice may be for entertainment, self-expression, sexual arousal, or simply comfort. A man wearing women's clothing is the more common image, though women crossdress too—less remarked upon since women's fashion already borrows freely from men's. {He was crossdressing long before he came out as trans.}

Crossed describes lines or paths that intersect, or limbs placed one over another: {She sat with her legs crossed}. Crossed wires—literal or figurative—create confusion through miscommunication: {We got our wires crossed about the meeting time}. A crossed check has lines drawn across it, restricting how it can be cashed. To be crossed in love is to be thwarted. Star-crossed lovers are fated for misfortune.

Crosses is the plural of cross—the shape formed by two intersecting lines, the Christian symbol of crucifixion, or a hybrid of two things: {genetic crosses between species}. As a verb form, crosses means to traverse {(she crosses the street)}, to intersect {(where the railroad crosses the highway)}, or to oppose someone {(don't cross him)}. A person who crosses a line violates a boundary, literal or figurative.

Crosseyed describes eyes that turn inward toward the nose, so they appear to look at each other rather than straight ahead. The condition, called strabismus medically, may be constant or intermittent. Figuratively, crosseyed can mean confused or disoriented: {I've been staring at spreadsheets so long I'm going crosseyed}.

A crossfade is a smooth audio or video transition where one element fades out while another fades in, the two briefly overlapping. DJs crossfade between tracks to maintain continuous music. In video editing, a crossfade dissolves one scene into the next. The verb describes performing this transition: {She crossfaded into the next song}.

Crossfaded describes being simultaneously intoxicated by alcohol and high on marijuana. The term comes from audio mixing, where crossfading blends two tracks together. The combined effect can be disorienting or intensified: {I got way too crossfaded at the party and had to lie down}. Sometimes spelled as two words.

Crossfading is the technique of smoothly transitioning between two audio or video sources by fading one out while fading the other in simultaneously. DJs crossfade between tracks to maintain continuous music. Video editors crossfade between scenes for seamless transitions. In slang, crossfading means being intoxicated on both alcohol and marijuana at the same time: {I got way too crossfaded at that party}.

Crossfire is gunfire from multiple directions that intersects in a zone, creating extreme danger for anyone caught there. The term extends to any situation where someone is caught between opposing forces: {She was caught in the crossfire between her feuding parents}. A crossfire of questions or criticism comes from multiple sources at once.

Crossfires is the plural of crossfire—gunfire coming from multiple directions that intersects at a point. The term appears most often in the figurative phrase {caught in the crossfire}, describing someone harmed by a conflict they weren't part of: {Civilians were caught in the crossfires of rival gangs}. The plural emphasizes distinct, separate incidents of intersecting fire.

To crossfit is to engage in high-intensity functional fitness training that combines weightlifting, cardio, and gymnastics movements. The lowercase form appears as a generic verb or descriptor for this style of workout, though the branded form dominates: {I've been crossfitting for about six months now}. (Capitalized CrossFit is the trademarked fitness brand.)

Crosshairs are the thin intersecting lines in the center of an optical instrument—a rifle scope, telescope, or camera viewfinder—used to aim or focus precisely. The singular crosshair refers to one of these lines or to the intersection point itself. To have someone {in your crosshairs} is to target them, literally or figuratively: {The prosecutor has the CEO in her crosshairs}.

Crosshairs are the pair of fine lines—one vertical, one horizontal—intersecting at the center of a gun sight, telescope, or other optical instrument, used to aim precisely at a target. Figuratively, to be {in the crosshairs} is to be targeted for criticism, attack, or close scrutiny: {The company found itself in the crosshairs of federal regulators}.

Crosshatch refers to a pattern of intersecting parallel lines, used in drawing and engraving to create shading or texture. The closer the lines, the darker the area appears. As a verb, to crosshatch is to shade using this technique: {She crosshatched the shadows beneath the figure's chin}. The pattern also appears in design and security printing.

Crosshatches are intersecting sets of parallel lines that create a grid-like pattern. In drawing and engraving, crosshatching produces shading—the denser the lines, the darker the area: {She crosshatched the shadows beneath the tree}. The term extends to any crisscrossing pattern: {Tire tracks crosshatched the muddy field}.

Crosshatching is a shading technique using sets of parallel lines that cross each other at angles to create depth, texture, or tonal variation. Artists and illustrators use it in drawing, engraving, and printmaking—the closer the lines, the darker the area appears: {The etching used fine crosshatching to suggest shadow}. The verb is crosshatch.

Crossing is the act of going from one side to another, or a place where paths intersect. A pedestrian crossing marks where people may walk across a street. A border crossing is where you pass between countries. A railroad crossing is where tracks cross a road. The word also names a voyage: {an Atlantic crossing}. In biology, a crossing is the mating of different varieties to produce hybrids.

Crossings are places where paths, roads, or routes intersect or where passage from one side to another is possible: {pedestrian crossings}, {railroad crossings}, {border crossings}. The word also names instances of traversing something: {Atlantic crossings}, {river crossings}. A crossing can be perilous or routine depending on what's being crossed and under what conditions.

Crosslegged describes sitting with legs crossed at the ankles or knees, typically on the floor: {The children sat crosslegged during story time}. The position is associated with informal settings, meditation, and yoga. Also spelled cross-legged.

Crossover describes movement from one category, domain, or audience to another. A crossover hit appeals beyond its original genre: {The song was a country-to-pop crossover}. A crossover vehicle blends car and SUV features. In fiction, a crossover brings characters from different stories together. The word works as noun or adjective: {crossover appeal}, {crossover episode}. A physical crossover is a place where paths or tracks intersect.

Crossovers are points or instances where things cross from one category, domain, or audience to another. A musical crossover reaches listeners outside its primary genre: {The country song became a pop crossover hit}. In fiction, a crossover brings characters from separate works together. Crossover vehicles blend car and SUV features. The word also names physical crossing points—a pedestrian crossover, or a basketball move faking one direction before crossing to another.

Crossplay is cosplay in which the performer dresses as a character of a different gender—a woman portraying a male anime hero, a man as a female video game character. The term blends "cross-dressing" with "cosplay." Common at anime conventions and gaming events: {She's crossplaying as Link from Zelda}.

To crosspollinate is to transfer pollen from one plant to fertilize another of a different variety or species, producing hybrid offspring. Bees and other insects crosspollinate flowers as they move between them. Figuratively, crosspollination describes the mixing of ideas, influences, or methods across fields: {The conference let scientists and artists crosspollinate}. Also spelled cross-pollinate.

Crosspollination is the transfer of pollen from one plant to fertilize another of the same species, producing genetic variety in offspring. The figurative sense dominates casual use: the productive mixing of ideas, methods, or influences across different fields or groups. {The crosspollination between jazz and hip-hop created new sounds.} Also spelled cross-pollination.

To crosspost is to share the same content across multiple online platforms or forums simultaneously. A message crossposted to several subreddits or social media accounts reaches different audiences without rewriting. The practice can spread information efficiently but risks being seen as spam: {She crossposted her announcement to Twitter, Instagram, and Facebook}.

A crossroad is a place where two roads intersect. The plural crossroads, though grammatically plural, often functions as singular: {We came to a crossroads and turned left}. Figuratively, a crossroads is a critical point requiring decision: {She's at a crossroads in her career}. The image suggests choosing among diverging paths.

A crossroads is a place where two or more roads meet and cross each other. The word usually appears singular: {We stopped at a crossroads to check the map}. Figuratively, a crossroads is a decisive point—a moment requiring choice between different paths forward: {The company is at a crossroads}. The plural crossroads refers to multiple such intersections.

Crosstown describes movement or position across a city rather than toward or away from its center: a crosstown {bus}, a crosstown {rival}. The word implies horizontal transit through urban geography, often suggesting the difficulty of east-west travel in cities where north-south routes dominate: {The crosstown trip took an hour in traffic}.

Crosstraining is practicing multiple sports or exercise disciplines rather than specializing in one. Athletes crosstrain to build overall fitness, prevent overuse injuries, and avoid burnout: {She crosstrains with swimming and cycling during the off-season}. The term extends to workplaces where employees learn multiple roles: {We crosstrain everyone so someone can always cover the front desk}.

A crosswalk is a marked path across a street where pedestrians have the right of way. White stripes or painted lines typically indicate the boundaries: {Use the crosswalk at the corner}. The term is chiefly American; British English prefers pedestrian crossing or zebra crossing.

Crosswalks is the plural of crosswalk, a marked section of road where pedestrians have the right of way to cross: {Use the crosswalk at the intersection}. Crosswalks are typically painted with white stripes, sometimes called zebra crossings in British English. {The city added crosswalks near the school after parents complained}.

A crosswind blows perpendicular to the direction of travel, making it harder to hold a straight course. Pilots landing in crosswinds must angle into the wind, then straighten at the last moment. Cyclists and truck drivers feel it pushing them sideways: {The crosswind nearly blew us off the bridge}.

Crosswinds are winds blowing perpendicular to a direction of travel. Pilots and drivers must compensate for crosswinds to maintain course: {The plane landed safely despite strong crosswinds}. Figuratively, crosswinds are forces that complicate progress toward a goal: {The project faced political crosswinds from both parties}.

A crossword is a word puzzle consisting of a grid of white and black squares, where solvers fill in words based on numbered clues. Words intersect horizontally and vertically, sharing letters at their crossing points. The crossword puzzle became a newspaper staple in the early twentieth century and remains popular in print and digital formats: {I do the crossword with my morning coffee}.

Crosswords are word puzzles consisting of a grid of white and black squares, where solvers fill in words based on numbered clues. Words intersect horizontally and vertically, with shared letters providing hints. {She does the crossword every morning with her coffee}. The difficulty ranges from casual newspaper puzzles to notoriously challenging cryptic crosswords favored in British tradition.

Crostini are small slices of toasted or grilled bread, typically brushed with olive oil and topped with various ingredients—tomatoes, cheese, liver pâté, or spreads. The singular is crostino, though English speakers rarely use it. Crostini appear as appetizers or accompaniments to soups and salads: {We started with crostini topped with fresh ricotta and honey}.

The crotch is where something forks into two parts. On the human body, it's the area where the legs meet the torso: {He took a knee to the crotch}. On clothing, it's the corresponding seam area: {The crotch of these jeans is wearing thin}. A tree's crotch is where a branch diverges from the trunk.

Crotchety describes someone who is irritable, grumpy, and quick to complain—especially an older person set in their ways. A crotchety neighbor yells at kids on the lawn; a crotchety relative grumbles about everything at dinner. The word suggests chronic ill temper rather than a passing bad mood: {The crotchety old man refused to return the ball that landed in his yard}.

To crouch is to lower the body by bending the knees, typically while keeping the torso relatively upright—a position between standing and sitting. Animals crouch before pouncing; humans crouch to hide, to examine something at ground level, or to make themselves smaller targets: {She crouched behind the car}. The noun crouch names this position: {He waited in a crouch}.

Crouched describes a lowered body position with bent knees and hunched posture, typically close to the ground: {She crouched behind the wall}. The stance suggests hiding, readiness to spring, or making oneself smaller. Animals crouch before pouncing; people crouch to avoid detection or to examine something low: {He crouched to tie his shoe}.

Crouches is the verb crouch in the third person singular or its plural noun form. To crouch is to lower the body by bending the knees, often in preparation for movement or to avoid being seen: {The cat crouches before it pounces}. As a noun, a crouch is the position itself: {He waited in a crouch behind the wall}.

Crouching describes the posture of bending low with knees bent and body compressed, typically while remaining on one's feet. Animals crouch before pouncing; humans crouch to hide, to examine something on the ground, or to spring into action. {A crouching figure waited in the shadows.}

A croupier is the casino employee who runs a gambling table—dealing cards, spinning the roulette wheel, collecting losing bets, and paying out winners. The word comes from French, where it originally meant someone who rides behind on a horse's croup. {The croupier slid the chips across the felt with practiced efficiency.}

A crouton is a small cube of toasted or fried bread, typically seasoned, used as a topping for salads and soups. The crisp texture contrasts with softer ingredients: {Caesar salad with garlic croutons}. Croutons are usually store-bought but can be made from stale bread.

Croutons are small cubes of bread that have been toasted or fried until crisp, typically seasoned with herbs, garlic, or butter. They add texture to salads and soups: {Caesar salad with croutons}, {a bowl of tomato soup topped with croutons}. Homemade croutons use stale bread; packaged versions are a supermarket staple.

A crow is a large black bird known for intelligence and harsh cawing calls. Crows appear in idioms: {as the crow flies} means in a straight line; {eat crow} means to admit humiliating error. To crow is to make a rooster's call, or to boast triumphantly: {He crowed about his victory for weeks}. A crowbar, despite the name, relates to the prying tool's beak-like shape.

A crowbar is a heavy metal bar with a flattened, curved end, used as a lever for prying things apart or open: {He used a crowbar to remove the boards}. The tool appears frequently in contexts of forced entry, demolition, and improvised weapons. To crowbar something is to force it open or, figuratively, to force something into a tight space: {They crowbarred another meeting into the schedule}.

Crowbars is the plural of crowbar, a metal bar with a flattened, curved end used for prying things apart or open. The tool appears in contexts from construction to burglary: {The thieves used crowbars to force the door}. To crowbar something is to pry it open or force it into place: {They crowbarred an extra clause into the contract}.

Themes common to many meanings of crowd are large numbers and inadequate space. A large number of assembled people is a crowd; if they don’t have much room to move, they are crowded. A group of people who share a characteristic, no matter how large the group, can also be called a crowd: the Wall Street crowd. If people crowd a place, they go in large numbers, or press in closely. With abstract objects, crowd suggests more items than time or space allows: Silly meetings keep crowding my schedule.

Crowded describes a space filled with more people or things than is comfortable or convenient. A crowded {room} or crowded {train} has limited space to move around. The word often carries connotations of discomfort or unpleasantness: {The bar was so crowded we couldn't find seats}. When applied to time or schedules, crowded suggests being packed with activities: {a crowded agenda}. Things crowd together when they press or gather closely.

To crowdfund is to raise money for a project or venture by collecting small contributions from a large number of people, typically through the internet: {They crowdfunded the documentary through Kickstarter}. The practice allows creators, entrepreneurs, and individuals to bypass traditional financing by appealing directly to potential supporters or customers.

Crowdfunded describes something financed through small contributions from many people, typically gathered online: {Their crowdfunded documentary exceeded its goal in three days}. The model bypasses traditional investors or publishers, letting creators appeal directly to potential audiences. Projects range from albums and films to gadgets and medical bills.

Crowdfunding is raising money by collecting small contributions from a large number of people, typically through online platforms. A filmmaker might crowdfund a documentary, offering backers early access or credits in return for pledges: {We crowdfunded the album and hit our goal in two weeks}. The practice has expanded from creative projects to medical bills, startups, and political campaigns.

Crowding is the condition of being too full or packed together. A crowded room has too many people; crowding on public transit makes commutes uncomfortable. The term extends beyond physical spaces: {crowding in the schedule left no time for lunch}. To accuse someone of crowding you is to say they're pressing too close or being too insistent.

A crowdpleaser is something designed to appeal to popular taste and generate enthusiastic response—an entertainer, performance, or product that reliably wins over audiences. The term often carries a faint suggestion of playing it safe rather than taking artistic risks: {The encore was a crowdpleaser, not their best song}. Also spelled crowd-pleaser.

Crowdpleasers are things designed to appeal to popular taste—songs, jokes, performances, or dishes that reliably win approval from a broad audience. The term often carries a hint of calculation: a crowdpleaser may sacrifice originality or depth for safe appeal. {The DJ closed with a few crowdpleasers.} {Her lemon bars are real crowdpleasers at potlucks.}

Crowds is the plural of crowd—large groups of people gathered in one place. The word often implies density and anonymity: {Crowds filled the stadium}, {I lost her in the crowds}. As a verb, crowds means presses together or encroaches: {The furniture crowds the room}, {Don't let anxiety crowd out the joy}.

Crowdsource means to obtain work, ideas, or funding by soliciting contributions from a large group of people, typically online. Companies crowdsource product designs, researchers crowdsource data collection, and entrepreneurs crowdsource startup capital: {The project was crowdsourced through Kickstarter}. The word blends crowd with outsource—distributing tasks to a dispersed public rather than a defined contractor.

Crowdsourced describes work, information, or funding gathered from a large number of people, typically via the internet. A crowdsourced project draws on distributed contributions rather than traditional employees or experts: {The map was crowdsourced from thousands of volunteer editors}. Crowdsourcing harnesses collective effort—whether for encyclopedia entries, product designs, or startup capital.

Crowdsources means to obtain something—ideas, funding, labor, content—from a large group of people, typically via the internet. The crowd replaces traditional sources like employees or experts: {The company crowdsources product ideas from its customers}. Crowdsourcing harnesses distributed effort, whether for Wikipedia articles, Kickstarter campaigns, or identifying objects in photos.

Crowdsourcing is obtaining work, ideas, or funding by soliciting contributions from a large group of people, typically online. Rather than hiring employees or contractors, a company or individual puts out an open call: {The project was crowdsourced to volunteers worldwide}. Crowdfunding is a specific type where money is raised from many small contributors. The practice harnesses collective effort for tasks ranging from encyclopedia writing to product design to scientific research.

Crowdsurfing is being passed hand-over-hand above a densely packed audience, typically at a rock concert or punk show. You launch yourself from the stage or get hoisted up by nearby concertgoers, then ride atop the crowd on outstretched hands: {She crowdsurfed all the way to the back of the venue}. The practice carries risks—gropers, drops, and collisions—but remains a staple of live music culture.

Crowdsurfed is the past tense of crowdsurf—to be passed hand-over-hand across a crowd at a concert or similar event, typically after diving or being lifted from the stage. The practice emerged from punk and metal scenes: {She crowdsurfed all the way to the back of the venue}. It requires a dense, cooperative audience willing to keep the surfer aloft.

A crowdsurfer is someone who rides atop a concert audience, passed hand-to-hand across the crowd. The practice is common at rock and punk shows, where performers or fans launch themselves from the stage to be carried by the sea of raised hands: {Security pulled another crowdsurfer over the barrier}.

Crowdsurfers are concertgoers who ride atop the outstretched hands of the audience, passed along from person to person above the crowd. The practice typically occurs at rock, punk, and metal shows, where fans launch themselves from the stage or are lifted up from the floor: {Security pulled crowdsurfers over the barrier one after another}.

Crowdsurfing is being passed hand-to-hand over the heads of a packed audience at a concert or festival. A performer or audience member dives or is hoisted up, then rides atop the crowd's raised hands, propelled toward the stage or across the venue: {She went crowdsurfing during the encore}. The practice carries risk of being dropped or groped.

Crowed is the past tense of crow. A rooster crows at dawn—the loud, distinctive call that announces morning. People crow when they boast or gloat triumphantly: {He crowed about his promotion for weeks}. The word captures both the sound and the self-satisfied quality of the rooster's call.

Crowing is the loud, distinctive call a rooster makes, especially at dawn. By extension, crowing describes boastful or triumphant speech—announcing one's success with excessive pride: {He was crowing about his promotion all week}. The word carries a note of gloating, suggesting the person is making more noise than the achievement warrants.

A crown is the top of something. Fancy headwear for royalty is typically a crown, but you may be awarded a crown for a victory in a competition: The spelling champ was accorded the division crown.
