The term has expanded to anyone who thoughtfully assembles content: a curator of playlists, a curator of online images. The underlying idea is discriminating selection—choosing what belongs and what doesn't. {The gallery's curator specializes in contemporary sculpture.}

A curb is the raised edge along a street, separating roadway from sidewalk. By extension, curb means any restraint or check: {curbs on spending}, {curb your enthusiasm}. To curb something is to hold it back or keep it in check: {She curbed her temper}. To {kick someone to the curb} is to reject or discard them.

Curbs is the plural of curb—the raised edge along a street separating roadway from sidewalk: {Cars lined up along the curbs}. The verb sense also pluralizes: one curbs impulses, appetites, or excesses. {She curbs her spending during lean months}. In British English, the spelling is kerb for the concrete edge, while curb covers the restraint sense.

Curbside refers to the edge of a street where the curb meets the pavement. As an adjective, it describes services or activities conducted at this location without leaving one's vehicle: {curbside pickup}, {curbside recycling}, {curbside check-in at the airport}. The term gained prominence with the rise of drive-through culture and expanded dramatically during the COVID-19 pandemic when businesses offered curbside service to minimize contact.

Curd is the thick, soft substance that forms when milk coagulates—the solid part that separates from the liquid whey. Curds are the basis for cheese-making and appear in dishes like curds and whey. Bean curd is tofu. The verb means to form curds: {The milk curdled in the heat}.

Curdle describes liquid—typically milk or cream—separating into solid curds and watery whey. This happens intentionally in cheesemaking or unintentionally when milk sours or acid is added: {The lemon juice curdled the cream}. Figuratively, something that curdles your blood fills you with horror or dread: {a scream that curdled my blood}.

Curdled describes milk or other liquids that have separated into lumps and watery liquid, usually through spoilage or acid: {The milk had curdled in the heat}. Figuratively, something that curdles has gone sour or wrong: {His enthusiasm curdled into resentment}. To make someone's blood curdle is to horrify them.

Curdles is the third-person singular form of the verb curdle, which describes the process of milk or another liquid separating into lumps or solid masses, typically through souring or the addition of acid. {The lemon juice curdles the cream if you add it too quickly.} Blood curdles in horror contexts, where the expression {blood-curdling} describes something terrifying enough to make one's blood feel as if it has thickened or congealed from fear.

Curdling is the process of separating into curds—the clumping that happens when milk sours or when acid meets dairy. The word extends to anything that thickens unpleasantly or inspires visceral dread: {a blood-curdling scream}, {The thought of public speaking was enough to curdle my stomach}. What curdles loses its smooth consistency, literally or figuratively.

Curds are the solid lumps that form when milk coagulates, separating from the liquid whey. They're the basis of cheese-making and appear in dishes like cottage cheese. {Curds and whey} is the classic pairing, familiar from the nursery rhyme about Little Miss Muffet. Cheese curds—fresh, squeaky, unaged—are a regional delicacy in Wisconsin and Quebec.

A cure is what marks or brings about the end of illness or undesirable condition: We need a cure for the common cold. If you take a cure, you take the medicine or treatment intended to end your suffering. To cure an illness or condition is to provide treatment intended to end it: The doctor cured Sheila’s chronic back pain. But you can also cure some foods, such as meat, with salt or chemicals in order to preserve them for later use.

Cured describes something that has been preserved or treated. Meat and fish are cured with salt, smoke, or drying to prevent spoilage: {cured ham}, {cured salmon}. A cured illness has been eliminated: {The infection was completely cured}. Cured concrete or resin has hardened through a chemical process. A cured hide has been processed into leather.

Cures is the plural of cure—remedies or treatments that restore health or solve problems: {Modern medicine has cures for many diseases that were once fatal}. As a verb, cures means heals or preserves: {Time cures most wounds}. Meat or fish cures when preserved by salting, smoking, or drying: {The ham cures in the smokehouse for several weeks}.

A curfew is a regulation requiring people to remain indoors during specified hours, typically at night. Governments impose curfews during emergencies or unrest; parents set curfews for teenagers: {Her curfew was eleven on school nights}. The word originally referred to a bell signaling time to extinguish fires and retire for the evening.

Curfews is the plural of curfew—a regulation requiring people to be indoors or off the streets by a specified time. Governments impose curfews during emergencies, wars, or civil unrest. Parents set curfews for teenagers: {Her curfew was midnight on weekends}. The word originally referred to the evening bell signaling time to extinguish fires and retire for the night.

Curing is the process of preserving or preparing something through treatment. Meat and fish are cured with salt, smoke, or chemicals to prevent spoilage: {home-cured bacon}, {cured salmon}. Concrete cures as it hardens and strengthens over time. Rubber cures through vulcanization. Tobacco leaves cure by controlled drying. The word also covers the process of healing: {The doctor is focused on curing her patients}.

A curio is a small object valued for its novelty, rarity, or aesthetic interest—the sort of thing displayed on a shelf or in a cabinet. The word is short for curiosity in its sense of something unusual that arouses interest: {The shop was full of curios from around the world}. A curio cabinet is a piece of furniture with glass panels for displaying such items.

Curios are objects valued for their unusual, rare, or exotic qualities rather than practical use—the kind of things that fill antique shops and collectors' shelves: {The cabinet displayed curios from her travels}. The word is the plural of curio, a shortened form of curiosity in its sense of an object that arouses interest.

Curiosities is the plural of curiosity, covering both senses: instances of wanting to know something, and objects that attract interest because they're unusual or rare. The second sense dominates in the plural—a cabinet of curiosities holds strange artifacts, a shop sells curiosities and antiques. {The museum displayed curiosities from around the world.}

Curiosity is the desire to know or learn something. It drives exploration and discovery: {Her curiosity about the natural world led her to biology}. A curiosity is also an unusual or rare object that attracts interest: {The shop was full of curiosities from around the world}. To satisfy one's curiosity is to find the answer to something that has been nagging at you.

Curious describes an eager desire to know or learn something: {I'm curious what she said about me}. A curious person asks questions and investigates. The word also means strange or unusual: {a curious smell}, {a curious coincidence}. These senses connect—oddities attract attention and provoke questions. {Curiously enough} introduces surprising information.

Curiously works as an adverb in two directions. It can describe manner—doing something with curiosity: {She curiously examined the artifact}. More often it comments on a whole sentence, marking something as strange or unexpected: {Curiously, he never mentioned the money}. In this second use, curiously is close to oddly or strangely.

The idea of a curve or roundedness is present in meanings of curl. Hair, eyelashes, toes, and lips are all subject to curling, though only the first two are beauty treatments. When you curl your body, you bring it into a fetal-like position. A curl is the result of curling, especially of hair. If you’re doing curls at the gym, you’re bending a limb with weight attached. To curl is also to participate in the sport of curling.

A curler is a small cylinder around which hair is wound to create curls: {She slept in curlers}. The term also refers to someone who plays curling, the sport of sliding stones across ice toward a target. In both cases, the word derives from the action of curling—wrapping hair or directing a stone's curved path.

Curlers are cylindrical objects around which hair is wound to create curls or waves: {She slept in curlers}. They come in various materials—foam, plastic, heated ceramic. The word also refers to people who play curling, the ice sport where players slide stones toward a target: {The curlers swept the ice furiously}.

A curlew is a large wading bird with long legs and a distinctive long, curved bill, found in wetlands, mudflats, and coastal areas. Curlews are known for their haunting, melodic calls. Several species exist worldwide, with some populations declining due to habitat loss: {We spotted a curlew probing the mud for invertebrates}.

A curlicue is a decorative curl or spiral, especially in handwriting or ornamental design. Fancy signatures often end with curlicues. The word suggests something playful or elaborate—flourishes that serve style rather than function: {The wrought-iron gate was covered in curlicues}.

Curlicues are decorative spiral or curling shapes—the flourishes in ornate handwriting, the scrollwork on wrought iron, the swirls piped onto a cake. The word suggests something fanciful and perhaps excessive: {Her signature ended in elaborate curlicues}. Curlicue can also verb: {Vines curlicued up the trellis}.

Curling is a winter sport played on ice, where teams slide heavy granite stones toward a target while teammates sweep the ice with brooms to control the stone's path and speed. The sweeping reduces friction and guides the stone's curl—its gradual curve across the ice. {Olympic curling has gained a devoted following.} Separately, curling is the present participle of curl: {She's curling her hair}.

Curls are spiraling or coiling shapes, especially in hair. Someone with naturally wavy hair {has curls}, while others use heat or rollers to create them. The word extends to anything with that winding form: {curls of smoke}, {wood curls from a plane}. In weightlifting, a curl is an exercise that bends the arm to lift weight toward the shoulder: {bicep curls}.

Curly describes hair or other material that forms curves, spirals, or ringlets rather than lying straight: {She has naturally curly hair}. The word extends to anything with similar winding shapes: {curly fries}, {curly brackets}. As a nickname, Curly often refers affectionately to someone with curly hair—or ironically to someone bald.

A curlycue is a decorative spiral or fancy curved flourish, especially in handwriting or ornamental design: {Her signature ended with an elaborate curlycue}. The word suggests something playful or whimsical rather than functional. Also spelled curlicue.

Curlycues are decorative spiral or curling shapes—the flourishes in fancy handwriting, the scrollwork on wrought iron, the swirls piped onto a cake. The word suggests something ornamental and perhaps excessive: {Her signature was full of curlycues}. Also spelled curlicues.

A curmudgeon is a bad-tempered, difficult person, especially an older man who's chronically irritable or stubbornly set in his ways: {The old curmudgeon yelled at kids for cutting across his lawn}. The word often carries a hint of grudging affection—curmudgeons may be cantankerous, but they're frequently seen as characters rather than villains.

Curmudgeonly describes someone ill-tempered, stubborn, and inclined to complain—the manner of a curmudgeon. The word often carries a hint of affection, suggesting grumpiness that's more cantankerous than truly mean-spirited: {a curmudgeonly old professor}, {He gave a curmudgeonly grunt and returned to his newspaper}.

Curmudgeons is the plural of curmudgeon—a bad-tempered, difficult person, especially an older man who grumbles about modern life or other people's behavior. The word carries a note of affection; curmudgeons are cantankerous but often endearing: {The old curmudgeons at the diner complained about everything but showed up every morning}.

A currant is a small dried grape used in baking, darker and smaller than a raisin: {currant scones}, {hot cross buns studded with currants}. Currant also names several shrubs of the genus Ribes and their tart berries—red, black, or white—used in jams, jellies, and liqueurs like cassis.
clues: Dried grape in hot cross buns

definition: Currants are small dried grapes used in baking—darker and smaller than raisins. {Currant scones}, {hot cross buns with currants}. Separately, currants are small berries that grow in clusters on shrubs: red currants, black currants, white currants. Black currant is the dominant flavor in many European fruit drinks and preserves.

Currencies is the plural of currency, which is money in circulation within a country or economic zone: {The euro and dollar are the world's most traded currencies}. Currency also means general acceptance or prevalence: {The idea gained currency in academic circles}. Foreign currencies fluctuate in value against one another, creating exchange rates that matter for trade and travel.

Currency is money in circulation within an economy—coins, bills, or digital equivalents: {foreign currency}, {The local currency is the peso}. More broadly, currency means general acceptance or prevalence: {The idea gained currency among economists}. Something that has currency is in common use or widely acknowledged as valid: {outdated theories that no longer have currency}.

Current describes what flows or what exists now. Water currents and electrical currents move through channels; air currents move through atmosphere. The currency of money flows through economies. What is current is happening in the present moment: {current events}, {the current issue of a magazine}, {my current address}. A currant, spelled differently, is a small dried grape or berry.

Currents is the plural of current—flows of water, air, or electricity moving in a particular direction. Ocean currents carry warm or cold water across vast distances. Electrical currents power devices. The word also covers prevailing trends or movements: {the currents of public opinion}, {political currents sweeping the nation}.

A curriculum is the set of courses and content that make up a program of study. Schools design curricula; teachers implement them. The word often appears in debates about what students should learn: {The district added financial literacy to the curriculum}. A curriculum vitae (CV) is a summary of one's educational and professional history—literally, the course of one's life.

Curried describes food prepared with curry—a blend of spices common in South Asian cooking: {curried chicken}, {curried lentils}. The flavor profile typically includes turmeric, cumin, coriander, and chili. Separately, curried is the past tense of curry, meaning to groom a horse with a currycomb, or in the phrase {curry favor}, to seek approval through flattery.

Curries is the plural of curry, a dish of meat or vegetables cooked in a spiced sauce, originating in South Asian cuisines: {We ordered three different curries}. As a verb form, curries means to prepare food with curry spices, or to groom a horse with a currycomb. To {curry favor} is to seek approval through flattery—a phrase unrelated to the spice.

Curry is a dish or sauce seasoned with a blend of spices—turmeric, cumin, coriander, chili—originating in South Asian cuisines but now global. The word also names the spice blend itself: {curry powder}. To curry favor is to seek approval through flattery, from an unrelated word meaning to groom a horse. A currycomb is a grooming tool with metal teeth. {We ordered chicken curry and naan.}

A curse is a spoken wish for harm or misfortune to befall someone, often invoking supernatural power: {She put a curse on the family}. The word extends to the harm itself—an affliction or source of persistent trouble: {Flooding has been the curse of this region}. To curse is to utter such a wish, or more commonly, to swear or use profanity: {He cursed under his breath}. Cursed describes something afflicted by a curse or, informally, something frustrating: {This cursed printer never works}.

Cursed means under a curse—afflicted by supernatural misfortune or divine punishment: {The tomb was said to be cursed}. Extended uses describe anything plagued by persistent bad luck: {a cursed project that kept failing}. In internet slang, cursed describes images or content that feel deeply unsettling or wrong in ways hard to articulate: {That photo of a hairless cat in a sweater is cursed}. As an adjective before a noun, cursed can simply mean damned or detestable: {this cursed weather}.
Curses, simply the plural of curse, is a mild oath used to express surprise or some undesirable emotion. It is often used ironically.

Cursing is the act of uttering curses—swear words, profanity, or wishes of harm. Someone who is cursing may be swearing in anger {Stop your cursing!} or invoking supernatural punishment {The old woman stood cursing the thieves who robbed her}. The word covers both casual profanity and formal malediction.

Cursive is a style of handwriting in which letters connect fluidly within words, allowing the pen to stay on the paper. The style developed for speed and efficiency before typing became dominant. Cursive writing is still taught in schools, though less universally than before: {Her cursive is elegant but hard to read}. The term also applies to typefaces that mimic this connected, flowing style.

A cursor is a movable indicator on a computer screen showing where the next action will occur—where typed text will appear, or where a click will land. The blinking vertical line in a text field is a cursor; so is the arrow you move with a mouse. The word originally meant a sliding part on a measuring instrument, from Latin for "runner."

Cursors is the plural of cursor, the movable indicator on a computer screen showing where the next action will occur—typically a blinking line in text or an arrow for navigation. The cursor tracks mouse movement or marks typing position: {I lost track of my cursors across three monitors}. The word comes from Latin for "runner."

Curt describes speech or manner that is abrupt and terse, often to the point of rudeness. A curt reply gives the minimum necessary information without warmth or elaboration: {She gave a curt nod and walked away}. The word suggests impatience or dismissiveness rather than mere brevity.

A curtain is a piece of fabric hung to cover a window, divide a space, or conceal something behind it. Theater curtains separate stage from audience; shower curtains keep water contained. Figuratively, a curtain obscures: {a curtain of fog}, {the iron curtain}. To curtain is to provide or conceal with curtains. {Curtains} as slang means the end, especially death: {If they find us, it's curtains}.

Curtains are pieces of fabric hung to cover windows, block light, or provide privacy. They also hang at the front of a stage, opening and closing to mark acts. From this theatrical use comes the slang meaning: the end, especially death or ruin. {If they find out, it's curtains for us.} To draw the curtains can mean either to open or close them.

A curtsey is a formal gesture of respect made by bending the knees and lowering the body, traditionally performed by women and girls. It's the feminine counterpart to the bow, used when greeting royalty or in formal ceremonies: {She curtsied before the queen}. The verb and noun share the spelling, with curtsy as a common variant.

Curtseying is the present participle of curtsy, describing the act of performing a formal gesture of respect in which a person, typically a woman or girl, bends their knees while keeping the back straight, often with a slight bow of the head. The gesture is traditionally made before royalty or other dignitaries. {She was curtseying to the queen when her heel caught on her gown.}

Curtsied is the past tense of curtsy, the formal greeting in which a woman or girl bends her knees and lowers her body briefly while keeping the upper body straight. The gesture historically showed deference to royalty or social superiors: {She curtsied before the queen}. Now largely ceremonial or theatrical.

Curtsies is the plural of curtsy, a formal greeting in which a woman or girl bends her knees and lowers her body briefly, traditionally performed before royalty or as a sign of respect: {The young dancers practiced their curtsies before the recital}. Also a verb form: {She curtsies whenever she meets the queen}.

A curtsy is a gesture of respect or greeting in which a woman or girl bends her knees while keeping her back straight, often with a slight bow of the head. Traditionally performed before royalty or in formal settings: {She curtsied to the queen}. The male equivalent is a bow. Also spelled curtsey.

Curtsying is the act of making a curtsy—a formal gesture of respect in which a woman or girl bends her knees while bowing her head slightly. The gesture traditionally acknowledges royalty or social superiors: {She practiced curtsying before meeting the queen}. Also spelled curtsying or curtseying.

Curvaceous describes a woman's body with pronounced, attractive curves—full hips, bust, and a defined waist. The word carries appreciative connotations, suggesting sensual appeal rather than clinical measurement: {a curvaceous blonde}, {her curvaceous figure}. Occasionally applied to winding roads or sinuous designs, but the human female form remains the primary reference.

Curvature is the degree to which something curves or bends away from being straight or flat. In geometry, curvature measures how sharply a line or surface deviates from a straight line or plane: {the curvature of the Earth}, {spinal curvature}. The word appears in technical contexts—optics, mathematics, medicine—but also describes any gentle bending: {the curvature of her smile}.

A curve is a line that bends smoothly, without angles. Roads curve through mountains, rivers curve across plains. The word extends to anything with such a shape: the curve of a hip, a curve in the road. To curve is to bend or follow such a path. A curveball in baseball breaks unexpectedly; to {throw someone a curve} is to surprise them with something difficult. To {grade on a curve} adjusts scores relative to class performance. {Ahead of the curve} means anticipating trends before others do.

A curveball is a baseball pitch thrown with spin that causes it to curve as it approaches the batter, making it harder to hit. The figurative meaning dominates everyday usage: an unexpected development that catches someone off guard. {Life threw me a curveball when I lost my job}. To {throw someone a curveball} is to surprise them with something difficult or unforeseen.

Curveballed means caught off guard by something unexpected, from the baseball pitch designed to deceive batters by curving unpredictably. If life curveballed you, it threw you an unwelcome surprise: {I was curveballed by the layoff announcement}. The past tense works as verb or adjective: {We got completely curveballed by the new regulations}.

Curveballs are unexpected difficulties or surprises that disrupt plans or expectations. The term comes from baseball, where a curveball is a pitch that breaks sharply as it approaches the batter, making it hard to hit. Figuratively, life throws curveballs: {Just when I thought everything was settled, the company threw me a curveball with the layoffs}.

Curved describes something that bends or arcs rather than following a straight line. A curved {path} winds through the garden. A curved {blade} has an arc to it. The word applies to anything with a smooth, continuous bend—from {curved glass} to {curved hips}. As the past tense of curve, it describes the action of bending: {The road curved sharply left}.

Curves is the plural of curve—a line or surface that bends smoothly, or a rounded shape on a body. As a verb, curves means to bend or follow a curved path: {The road curves sharply ahead}. In informal use, curves refers specifically to a woman's figure, emphasizing hips and bust: {She's got curves in all the right places}.

Curving describes something that bends or follows a curved path rather than a straight line: {a curving road through the mountains}, {the curving arc of a thrown ball}. As a present participle, it captures motion in progress: {The river was curving gently toward the sea}. In slang, curving someone means rejecting or ignoring their romantic advances: {She's been curving him for weeks}.

Curvy describes something with curves—not straight or angular. A curvy {road} winds through hills. Curvy {handwriting} has flowing loops. Applied to bodies, curvy typically describes women with prominent bust, hips, and waist: {She has a curvy figure}. The term is generally complimentary, suggesting shapeliness rather than thinness.

A cushion is a soft pad used for sitting, kneeling, or resting against—typically a fabric case stuffed with foam, feathers, or other yielding material. Cushion extends to anything that absorbs impact or provides a buffer: {a cushion of air}, {a financial cushion}. To cushion is to soften a blow or protect from harsh effects: {Savings cushioned the loss of her job}.

Cushioned describes something softened or protected by padding, or figuratively shielded from impact or hardship. A cushioned {seat} has padding for comfort. A cushioned {landing} is softened by something absorbing the blow. A cushioned {existence} is protected from life's difficulties: {Her inheritance cushioned her from financial worry}.

Cushioning is the material or effect that absorbs impact or provides softness. A shoe's cushioning protects joints from hard surfaces. {The packaging needs more cushioning}. The term extends to anything that softens a blow, literal or figurative: {Savings provide cushioning against financial setbacks}. In dating slang, cushioning means maintaining backup romantic options while in a relationship—keeping "cushions" to land on if things fail.

Cushions are soft pads used for comfort or decoration—on sofas, chairs, or floors. A cushion absorbs impact: {The snow cushioned her fall}. To cushion something is to soften or protect it from shock: {Savings can cushion the blow of job loss}. A cushion can also be a protective margin: {We built in a two-week cushion before the deadline}.

Cushy means comfortable, easy, or involving little effort. A cushy {job} pays well without demanding much work. A cushy {assignment} poses no real challenge. The word often carries a hint of envy or resentment—implying someone has it easier than they deserve: {He landed a cushy position through connections}.

A cusp is a pointed end where two curves meet—the cusps of a crescent moon, the cusps of teeth. In astrology, a cusp is the boundary between zodiac signs. The most common use is figurative: to be {on the cusp} of something is to be at the point just before it begins or changes: {on the cusp of adulthood}, {on the cusp of a breakthrough}.

Cuss is an informal American word for curse in both noun and verb senses. A cuss is a swear word: {He let out a string of cusses}. To cuss is to swear: {She cussed him out good}. Cuss also means a person, usually with an adjective: {He's a stubborn old cuss}. The tone is folksy and rural.

Cussing is the act of using profane or vulgar language, synonymous with cursing or swearing. The term is informal and somewhat folksy, more common in American English and regional dialects. Someone who cusses a lot might be described as having a {cussing habit}, and a parent might scold a child for {cussing in front of grandma}. To cuss someone out is to berate them with profanity.

Custard is a creamy dessert or sauce made from milk or cream thickened with eggs, sugar, and often vanilla. It can be poured over fruit or cake, baked into pies, or served on its own. The texture ranges from pourable to firmly set depending on preparation. {She drizzled custard over the warm apple crumble.}

Custards is the plural of custard, a creamy dessert or sauce made from eggs, milk or cream, and sugar, cooked until thickened. The texture ranges from pourable ({vanilla custard over bread pudding}) to firm enough to slice ({baked custard}). Custards form the base for many desserts: crème brûlée, flan, and pastry cream are all custards.

A custodian is someone responsible for the care and protection of something. In American English, custodian often means a janitor—the person who maintains and cleans a building: {The custodian unlocked the gym for us}. More broadly, a custodian guards assets or records: a {custodian} of financial accounts, a {custodian} of cultural heritage. The role implies stewardship rather than ownership.

Custodians are people responsible for looking after something. A custodian of a building maintains and cleans it—the term often serves as a formal or euphemistic title for janitor. A custodian of records or assets has charge of their safekeeping. More abstractly, someone can be a custodian of traditions or values: {We see ourselves as custodians of the land for future generations}.

Custody is the state of being held or kept somewhere, especially under guard. A suspect is {taken into custody} by police. In legal contexts involving children, custody refers to the right and responsibility to care for a child: {She has full custody of the kids}, {They share joint custody}. A custodian is someone who has custody of something—whether a prisoner, a child, or a building.

Custom is a habitual practice or long-established tradition within a group: {It's our custom to open presents on Christmas Eve}. Customs in the plural refers to duties levied on imported goods, or the government agency that collects them: {We went through customs at the airport}. As an adjective, custom means made to order rather than mass-produced: {custom furniture}, {a custom suit}. The adjective often compounds: custom-built, custom-made.

A customer is someone who buys goods or services from a business. The word emphasizes the transaction: a person browsing is a shopper, but once they buy, they become a customer. {The customer is always right} reflects the commercial principle of deferring to buyers. Regular customers may be called regulars. In informal speech, customer can describe any person you're dealing with: {He's a tough customer}.

Customers is the plural of customer—people who buy goods or services from a business. The word emphasizes the commercial relationship: {The store opens early to accommodate customers}. Customer also appears in expressions like {tough customer} (someone difficult to deal with) or {ugly customer} (someone dangerous or unpleasant).

Customise is the British spelling of customize, meaning to modify or build something according to individual specifications or preferences. You customise a car with aftermarket parts, customise software settings, or customise a wedding cake. The word implies tailoring something standard to particular needs: {I customised my phone's home screen}.

Customizable describes something that can be modified to suit individual preferences or requirements. Software is customizable when users can adjust settings, layouts, or features: {The app offers a highly customizable interface}. Products, services, and experiences marketed as customizable allow buyers to select options or make changes from a standard version.

Customization is the act of modifying something to suit individual preferences or requirements. A product or service can be customized to meet specific needs: {The software allows extensive customization of the interface}. Mass customization refers to producing goods tailored to individual customers while maintaining efficiency. The British spelling is customisation.

To customize is to modify something to fit particular preferences or requirements. You customize a car with aftermarket parts, customize software settings, or order a customized {birthday cake}. The word implies personal choice—making something yours rather than accepting the default: {You can customize your homepage layout}.

Customized means modified to suit individual preferences or requirements. A customized {car} has been altered from factory specifications. Customized {software} is tailored to a client's needs. The word implies personal choice and specificity—not off-the-shelf but made or adjusted for someone in particular: {a customized workout plan}, {customized search results}.

Customs has two main uses. One refers to the practices and traditions of a group or culture: {local customs}, {wedding customs}. The other refers to the government agency that inspects goods and people entering a country, or the place where this happens: {We got held up at customs}. Customs duties are taxes on imported goods.

The verb cut is frequent and has many meanings, all of which spring from its original and core definition: penetrate (and often separate) with a sharp-edged instrument. From this you might expect that the most frequent subject of cut is knife, but figurative meanings have far overtaken the original. Today, cut is most often used to mean reduce, as if by cutting: governments cut programs, companies cut prices. The noun cut simply names an instance of what the verb does: Recent cuts resulted in the area losing its bus service. She fell and got a cut on her leg.

A cutaway is a coat with the front cut away from the waist, tapering to tails at the back—formal morning dress. In film and television, a cutaway is a shot that breaks from the main action to show something else: a reaction, a detail, a clock on the wall. Technical illustrations use cutaways to reveal interior structures by removing part of the outer surface: {a cutaway view of the engine}.

A cutback is a reduction, especially in spending, production, or personnel: {The company announced cutbacks in its workforce}. Budget cutbacks trim expenses; cutbacks in oil production reduce output. In surfing, a cutback is a sharp turn back toward the breaking part of a wave. To cut back is to reduce or prune.

Cutbacks are reductions in something, especially spending, services, or staff levels. Organizations announce cutbacks when they need to reduce costs or scale down operations. {The company's cutbacks meant laying off three hundred workers.} Budget cutbacks often affect programs that serve the public. The word carries negative connotations since cutbacks typically mean people lose jobs or access to services they previously had.

Cute describes something appealing in a delicate or endearing way—a cute baby, a cute puppy, a cute outfit. The word often implies smallness or youthfulness. Applied to adults, cute usually means attractive in a fresh, approachable way rather than strikingly beautiful: {He's cute, but not my type}. Cute can also mean cleverly contrived, sometimes dismissively: {Don't get cute with me}. A cute trick or cute idea may be too clever for its own good.

Cuteness is the quality of being attractive in an endearing, often childlike way. Babies, kittens, and small things with large eyes trigger cuteness responses. The word can be dismissive when applied to attempts at cleverness: {Enough with the cuteness—just give me a straight answer}. Something done {for the cuteness} prioritizes charm over substance.

Cutesy describes something excessively or affectedly cute, often to the point of being annoying or cloying: {The movie's cutesy dialogue made me cringe}. The suffix -sy adds a dismissive or mocking tone, suggesting the cuteness is overdone or insincere: {cutesy baby talk}, {cutesy decorations}. What's cute charms; what's cutesy tries too hard.

Cuticle most commonly refers to the thin strip of skin at the base of a fingernail or toenail, the part that manicurists push back or trim. In biology, cuticle has broader application: it's any protective outer layer covering an organism, such as the waxy coating on plant leaves that prevents water loss, or the tough external layer of insects and other arthropods. {She pushed back her cuticles before applying nail polish.}

Cuticles are the thin layers of skin at the base of fingernails and toenails, where the nail meets the finger. Manicurists push back or trim cuticles for a cleaner look: {She soaked her hands before pushing back the cuticles}. In biology, cuticle refers more broadly to any protective outer layer—the waxy coating on leaves, the tough exterior of insects.

Cutie is an informal term of endearment for someone or something considered attractive, charming, or appealing in a sweet way. It's applied to people, animals, and occasionally objects: {What a cutie that puppy is!} The word often carries playful or affectionate connotations and is especially common when addressing or describing children, romantic interests, or anything deemed adorable. The diminutive form cutie pie intensifies the sweetness.

Cuties is the plural of cutie—people or things considered adorable or attractive. It's an affectionate term, often for children or romantic interests: {Look at those cuties in their Halloween costumes}. Cuties is also a brand name for small, seedless mandarin oranges.

A cutlass is a short, broad sword with a slightly curved blade, associated especially with sailors and pirates of the 17th and 18th centuries. The design suited close combat in the cramped quarters of ships. The word now evokes romanticized piracy: {The pirate brandished his cutlass}.

Cutlery refers to eating utensils—knives, forks, and spoons used at the table. In British usage, cutlery covers all these implements; Americans more often say silverware or flatware. The word also extends to cutting instruments generally, especially knives: {a cutlery set}, {a shop selling fine cutlery}.

A cutlet is a thin slice of meat, typically from the leg or rib, often breaded and fried: {veal cutlet}, {pork cutlet}. The term extends to similarly shaped preparations of ground meat, fish, or vegetables: {chicken cutlet}, {vegetable cutlet}. In American usage, a cutlet is sometimes a boneless chicken breast pounded thin.

Cutlets are thin, boneless pieces of meat, typically from the leg or rib section of veal, pork, lamb, or chicken. The meat is often pounded flat for quick cooking—breaded and fried, or sautéed: {chicken cutlets}, {veal cutlets}. The term also applies to similar preparations made from ground meat or vegetables shaped into flat patties: {vegetable cutlets}.

A cutman is a cornerman in boxing or mixed martial arts who specializes in treating cuts and swelling between rounds. The cutman applies pressure, uses ice, and deploys coagulants like adrenaline chloride to stop bleeding and reduce swelling so the fighter can continue: {The cutman worked frantically to close the gash above his eye}.

A cutoff is a point where something stops or is no longer included: {The cutoff for applications is Friday}. A cutoff can be a shortcut that cuts across a longer route, or a device that stops flow. Cutoffs are jeans cut off at the knee or higher. As an adjective, cutoff marks a limit: {cutoff date}, {cutoff score}.

Cutoffs are jeans or other pants that have been cut short to make them into shorts, typically with a raw, frayed edge rather than a finished hem. The term also refers to points or levels at which something stops or is excluded: {The cutoff for applications is Friday at midnight}. A cutoff can be a shortcut or a road that branches from a main route, or a device that stops a flow of liquid or gas.

A cutout is something cut from a larger piece—a shape removed from paper or cardboard, a hole cut in a wall, or a magazine figure snipped for a scrapbook. A cardboard cutout is a life-sized figure of a person, often a celebrity, used for display or photos. In espionage, a cutout is an intermediary who shields communication between agents: {The handler never met the asset directly—everything went through a cutout}. A cutout can also be a device that interrupts an electrical circuit.

Cutouts are shapes or figures cut from paper, cardboard, or other material. A life-size cardboard cutout of a celebrity stands in a store display. In espionage, a cutout is an intermediary who shields communication between agents: {The handler never met the operative directly—they used a cutout}. Cutout also describes clothing with sections removed to reveal skin: {a dress with side cutouts}.

Cutpurses is the plural of cutpurse, an old term for a thief who stole by cutting purses from belts—the historical method before pockets became common. The word survives mainly in historical fiction and period dramas: {The market was thick with cutpurses and pickpockets}. Now largely synonymous with pickpocket, though cutpurse sounds more archaic and literary.

Cuts is the plural of cut, covering the noun's many senses: wounds from sharp objects, portions of meat, reductions in amount or size, or versions of a film. In music, cuts are individual tracks: {The album has some great cuts}. Someone's cuts at the gym are their visible muscle definition. To make the cut is to qualify; to not make it is to be eliminated.

A cutscene is a non-interactive sequence in a video game that advances the story or provides exposition. During cutscenes, players watch rather than play—the game takes control to show dialogue, plot developments, or cinematic moments: {I always skip the cutscenes and get straight to the gameplay}. Some games let players skip them; others don't.

Cutscenes are non-interactive sequences in video games that advance the story, provide exposition, or reward the player between segments of gameplay. They range from simple text screens to elaborate cinematic productions with voice acting and motion capture. Players sometimes skip cutscenes to get back to the action, while others watch every one for the narrative experience. {I grabbed a snack during the cutscene.}

A cutter is a person or tool that cuts. The word appears in compounds describing specific functions: {box cutter}, {wire cutters}, {cookie cutter}. A cutter is also a small, fast boat—originally one that cuts through water. In baseball, a cutter is a fastball that breaks sharply. In self-harm contexts, a cutter is someone who cuts their own skin.

Cutthroat describes ruthless competition where participants show no mercy: {cutthroat business practices}, {a cutthroat industry}. The image is of someone willing to slit throats to win. As a noun, a cutthroat is a murderer or assassin. Cutthroat trout, a species native to western North America, has red markings under its jaw resembling a slashed throat.

Cutthroats are people willing to kill or destroy others to get what they want—murderers, ruthless competitors, or anyone who operates without moral restraint. The word suggests cold-blooded self-interest: {The industry is full of cutthroats who'd ruin you for a nickel}. A cutthroat trout is a species marked by red slashes under the jaw, as if its throat had been cut.

Cutting describes the act of dividing something with a blade or sharp edge, or the result of such action. A cutting remark is sharply hurtful: {Her cutting words left him speechless}. Cutting-edge technology is at the forefront of innovation. In horticulture, a cutting is a piece of plant removed for propagation. The adjective describes cold that seems to slice through clothing: {a cutting wind}.

Cuttings are pieces cut from something larger. In gardening, cuttings are sections of stem or leaf removed from a plant to propagate new growth: {She rooted the cuttings in water}. In journalism, cuttings are clipped articles, especially in British usage: {a scrapbook of newspaper cuttings}. Cuttings also refers to material removed during excavation or editing—earth from a trench, footage from a film.

A cuttlefish is a marine mollusk related to squid and octopus, with eight arms, two tentacles, and an internal shell called a cuttlebone. Cuttlefish are known for their ability to rapidly change color and texture for camouflage or communication. The cuttlebone, rich in calcium, is often given to pet birds to sharpen their beaks.

A cutup is someone who clowns around or acts silly to get laughs, especially in settings where seriousness is expected: {He was always the cutup in class}. The term is mildly affectionate rather than critical. As two words, cut up means to slice into pieces or, informally, to behave in this joking manner: {Stop cutting up and pay attention}.

Cyan is a vivid blue-green color, positioned between blue and green on the spectrum. In printing and digital displays, cyan is one of the primary colors in the CMYK model, combined with magenta, yellow, and black to produce full-color images. The color appears in nature in tropical waters and certain gemstones: {The Caribbean shimmered in shades of cyan}.

Cyanide is a rapidly acting poison that prevents cells from using oxygen. The term covers several compounds containing a carbon-nitrogen group—most notoriously hydrogen cyanide (the gas used in Nazi death chambers) and potassium cyanide (the crystalline salt of spy capsules and murder mysteries). Despite its lethal reputation, cyanide has industrial uses in mining, metallurgy, and chemical synthesis. {The detective suspected cyanide when he smelled bitter almonds.}

Cyber is a prefix or adjective relating to computers, digital technology, and the internet. It appears in compounds: {cybersecurity}, {cybercrime}, {cyberspace}, {cyberattack}. Standing alone, cyber often refers to online threats or warfare: {The Pentagon is investing heavily in cyber}. In casual use, it can sound dated or bureaucratic—a relic of 1990s internet terminology that persists mainly in government and security contexts.

A cyberattack is a malicious attempt to damage, disrupt, or gain unauthorized access to computer systems, networks, or data. Cyberattacks range from individual hackers stealing personal information to state-sponsored operations targeting critical infrastructure: {The cyberattack knocked out the power grid for three days}. Common forms include ransomware, phishing, and denial-of-service attacks.

Cyberattacks are malicious attempts to damage, disrupt, or gain unauthorized access to computer systems, networks, or data. They range from phishing schemes targeting individuals to sophisticated operations against government infrastructure. Common forms include ransomware, denial-of-service attacks, and data breaches: {The company suffered a cyberattack that exposed millions of customer records}. Also styled as two words.

Cyberbullied is the past tense and past participle of cyberbully, meaning to harass, threaten, or humiliate someone through digital means such as social media, text messages, or online forums. Unlike traditional bullying, cyberbullying can follow victims everywhere and persist indefinitely as harmful content spreads or remains accessible. {She was cyberbullied throughout middle school after a classmate created a fake account in her name.}

Cyberbullies are people who harass, threaten, or intimidate others through digital channels—social media, text messages, online forums, or gaming platforms. The term emerged as bullying migrated from schoolyards to screens: {The cyberbullies posted humiliating photos of her}. As a verb, to cyberbully is to engage in such harassment: {He was cyberbullied relentlessly after the video went viral}.

To cyberbully is to harass, intimidate, or humiliate someone through digital channels—social media, text messages, online forums. Unlike schoolyard bullying, cyberbullying follows victims home and can spread rapidly to wide audiences. As a noun, a cyberbully is someone who engages in this behavior: {The cyberbullies created fake accounts to torment her}.

Cyberbullying is harassment, intimidation, or cruelty conducted through digital channels—social media, text messages, online forums, or gaming platforms. Unlike schoolyard bullying, it follows victims home and can spread rapidly to wide audiences: {The cyberbullying got so bad she deleted all her accounts}. It often involves public shaming, spreading rumors, or sharing embarrassing content without consent.

A cybercafe is a business where customers pay to use computers with internet access, often while drinking coffee or other beverages. The concept flourished in the 1990s and early 2000s before smartphones and widespread home internet made them largely obsolete in wealthy countries, though they remain common in developing regions: {I checked my email at a cybercafe in Bangkok}.

Cyberchondria is health anxiety amplified by internet searching. Someone with mild symptoms researches them online, encounters worst-case diagnoses, and spirals into escalating worry: {I looked up my headache and now I'm convinced I have a brain tumor}. The word blends cyber with hypochondria. Unlike general health anxiety, cyberchondria specifically involves the feedback loop of symptom-searching and catastrophizing.

Cybercrime is illegal activity conducted through computers or the internet. It ranges from hacking and identity theft to online fraud, ransomware attacks, and distribution of illegal content. {The FBI's cybercrime division investigates data breaches affecting millions of users.} The term covers both crimes unique to digital technology and traditional crimes committed through digital means.

Cybercrimes are illegal activities conducted through computers or the internet. The category includes hacking, identity theft, fraud, ransomware attacks, and distribution of illegal content. {The FBI investigates cybercrimes that cross state lines.} Also spelled as two words: cyber crimes.

A cybercriminal is someone who commits crimes using computers or the internet—hacking, fraud, identity theft, ransomware attacks, and similar offenses. The term covers everyone from lone hackers to members of organized criminal networks: {Cybercriminals stole millions of credit card numbers from the retailer's database}.

Cybercriminals are people who commit crimes using computers or the internet—hacking, fraud, identity theft, ransomware attacks, and similar offenses. The term covers everyone from lone hackers to organized networks: {Cybercriminals stole millions of customer records from the database}. Unlike hackers, which can be neutral or positive, cybercriminals always implies illegal activity.

Cyberespionage is spying conducted through computer networks—stealing classified information, trade secrets, or intelligence by hacking into systems rather than planting human agents. Nation-states engage in cyberespionage against rival governments and corporations: {The breach was attributed to Chinese cyberespionage}. Also spelled cyber-espionage or cyber espionage.

Cybernetic relates to systems that regulate themselves through feedback—the way a thermostat adjusts temperature or a body maintains balance. The term comes from a Greek word for steering or governing. In popular use, cybernetic often suggests the integration of biology and technology: {cybernetic implants}, {a cybernetic organism}. The field of cybernetics studies communication and control in machines and living things.

Cybernetics is the study of communication and control systems in both machines and living organisms. The field emerged in the mid-twentieth century, examining how systems regulate themselves through feedback loops—a thermostat adjusting temperature, a body maintaining balance, a guided missile correcting its course. Cybernetics influenced early computing, artificial intelligence, and systems theory, though the term now sounds somewhat dated: {The conference covered robotics, cybernetics, and neural networks}.

Cyberpunk is a science fiction genre set in dystopian futures where advanced technology—especially computing and cybernetics—coexists with social decay. The aesthetic combines high tech with low life: hackers, megacorporations, neon-lit slums, and body modification. {Blade Runner} and {Neuromancer} defined the genre. The term extends to the subculture and visual style it spawned.

Cyberpunks are people immersed in the culture surrounding cyberpunk—a science fiction genre focused on high technology and social decay, typically featuring hackers, artificial intelligence, and corporate dystopias. The term also describes real-world tech enthusiasts, hackers, or activists who embrace the genre's rebellious, anti-establishment ethos: {The cyberpunks gathered at the convention to discuss digital privacy}.

Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computer systems, networks, and data from digital attacks, unauthorized access, and damage. It encompasses everything from password protocols to firewalls to encryption. As more of life moves online, cybersecurity has become a major concern for individuals, corporations, and governments alike: {The company hired a cybersecurity firm after the breach}.

Cybersex is sexual activity conducted through digital communication—exchanging erotic messages, images, or engaging in mutual stimulation while connected online. The term emerged with internet chat rooms in the 1990s and now covers texting, video calls, and virtual reality encounters: {We had cybersex over video chat}. Also called *cyber* for short.

Cybersleuths are people who investigate mysteries or gather information using the internet. The term evokes amateur detectives who piece together clues from social media posts, public records, and digital footprints: {Cybersleuths identified the hit-and-run driver from dashcam footage posted online}. The word can carry admiring or critical overtones depending on whether the investigation seems helpful or invasive.

Cyberspace is the notional environment where digital communication and online activity occur—the interconnected realm of computers, networks, and the internet experienced as a place rather than infrastructure. {Kids today spend half their lives in cyberspace.} The term emerged from science fiction but now appears in serious contexts like cybersecurity policy and international law. It implies a space you enter or navigate, distinct from physical reality.

Cyberstalk is to harass or obsessively monitor someone online—tracking their social media, sending unwanted messages, or gathering personal information. The behavior mirrors physical stalking but uses digital tools: {He cyberstalked his ex through fake accounts}. Cyberstalking is a crime in many jurisdictions, though enforcement varies.

A cyberstalker is someone who harasses, monitors, or threatens another person using digital technology—tracking their online activity, sending repeated unwanted messages, or gathering personal information to intimidate. The behavior mirrors physical stalking but operates through email, social media, and other electronic channels: {Her cyberstalker created fake accounts to keep contacting her after she blocked him}.

Cyberstalkers are people who use the internet, social media, or other digital technologies to repeatedly harass, monitor, or threaten others. Unlike traditional stalkers who physically follow their targets, cyberstalkers exploit online tools—tracking someone's posts, sending unwanted messages, hacking accounts, or spreading harmful information. The behavior ranges from obsessive monitoring of an ex-partner's social media to coordinated harassment campaigns. {The cyberstalkers created fake accounts to continue contacting her after she blocked them.}

Cyberstalking is the use of digital technology to harass, monitor, or threaten someone—typically through repeated unwanted contact, tracking online activity, or sending threatening messages. Unlike casual online annoyance, cyberstalking implies a pattern of behavior that makes the target fear for their safety: {She filed a police report about the cyberstalking after he created fake accounts to follow her everywhere online}.

Cyberterrorism is the use of computer attacks to cause fear, disruption, or harm for political or ideological purposes—targeting infrastructure, financial systems, or government networks. The term blends the digital realm with terrorism's intent to intimidate: {The power grid failure raised fears of cyberterrorism}. Whether a particular hack qualifies as cyberterrorism or mere cybercrime often depends on the attacker's motives and targets.

A cyberterrorist is someone who uses computer networks and digital technology to attack infrastructure, disrupt services, or create fear for political or ideological purposes. Unlike ordinary hackers who might seek profit or notoriety, cyberterrorists aim to cause widespread harm or panic, targeting systems like power grids, financial networks, or government databases. {Authorities arrested the cyberterrorist who had threatened to shut down the city's water treatment systems.}

Cyberterrorists are people who use computer networks to carry out attacks intended to cause fear, disruption, or harm for political or ideological purposes. The term covers a range of actors—from state-sponsored hackers targeting infrastructure to lone extremists defacing websites. {Cyberterrorists could cripple the power grid.} The label often gets applied loosely to any malicious hacker, though purists insist true cyberterrorism requires a political motive beyond mere criminality.

A cyberthreat is any potential danger to computer systems, networks, or digital infrastructure—malware, hacking attempts, data breaches, ransomware attacks. The term covers both the actors (hackers, hostile governments) and their methods. {The company hired consultants to assess cyberthreats to their payment systems.} Often written as two words: cyber threat.

Cyberwar is warfare conducted through digital attacks on computer systems, networks, and infrastructure. Nations engage in cyberwar to disrupt enemy communications, steal intelligence, or sabotage critical systems like power grids and financial networks. The term often blurs into cyber espionage and cyberattacks that fall short of traditional armed conflict: {The line between cyberwar and routine hacking grows increasingly unclear}.

Cyberware refers to technological devices implanted in or integrated with the human body, typically to enhance physical or mental capabilities. The term comes from cyberpunk fiction and gaming, where characters upgrade themselves with artificial eyes, neural interfaces, or mechanical limbs: {She had enough cyberware to set off every metal detector in the building}. As real-world technology advances—cochlear implants, brain-computer interfaces—the word occasionally appears in serious discussion of human augmentation.

Cyberwarfare is hostile action between nations or groups conducted through computer networks—attacking infrastructure, stealing intelligence, or disrupting communications. Unlike conventional warfare, cyberwarfare can be difficult to attribute and may blur lines between military and civilian targets: {The power grid went down in what officials suspected was an act of cyberwarfare}. Also spelled cyber warfare.

A cyberwarrior is someone who engages in digital warfare—attacking or defending computer systems, networks, and infrastructure. The term covers government hackers, military cyber units, and sometimes security professionals or hacktivists: {The Pentagon is recruiting cyberwarriors to counter foreign threats}. The word carries a dramatic, militarized tone that some find overblown.

Cyberwars are conflicts conducted through digital attacks on computer systems, networks, and infrastructure. Nations or groups wage cyberwar by hacking, deploying malware, or disabling critical systems rather than using conventional weapons. The term covers both actual state-sponsored attacks and hypothetical large-scale digital warfare: {Experts warn that future cyberwars could cripple power grids}.

A cyberweapon is software or code designed to damage, disrupt, or gain unauthorized access to computer systems, networks, or infrastructure. Unlike ordinary malware, cyberweapons are typically developed by nation-states or sophisticated actors for strategic purposes: espionage, sabotage, or warfare. {The Stuxnet virus that targeted Iranian nuclear facilities is considered the first major cyberweapon.} The term emphasizes the military or geopolitical nature of the attack rather than criminal profit.

A cyborg is a being that combines organic and mechanical parts—a human or other organism enhanced with technological components. The term blends "cybernetic" and "organism." Science fiction imagines cyborgs with robotic limbs or computer-integrated brains, but in a looser sense, anyone with a pacemaker or cochlear implant qualifies: {We're all becoming cyborgs, glued to our devices}.

Cyborgs are beings that combine organic and mechanical parts—humans enhanced with technological implants or machines given biological components. The term blends "cybernetic" and "organism." In science fiction, cyborgs range from humans with prosthetic limbs to figures more machine than flesh: {The villain was a cyborg with a mechanical arm}. The concept extends to anyone deeply integrated with technology: {We're all cyborgs now, dependent on our phones}.

Cycle is closely related to circle. A typical cycle is abstract and has the quality of repetitiveness or ebbing and flowing (business cycle, cycle of seasons). A set of artistic works with separate, related parts is called a cycle (song cycle). Something that cycles repeats: The phases of the moon cycle each month. A person who cycles to work rides a bicycle.

Cycles is the plural of cycle—a series of events that repeats in the same order: {the cycles of the seasons}, {business cycles}, {sleep cycles}. In exercise, cycles often refers to stationary bikes or spinning equipment: {The gym just got new cycles}. As a verb form, cycles means to ride a bicycle or to move through phases: {She cycles to work}, {The thermostat cycles on and off}.

Cyclical describes something that moves in cycles—recurring in regular patterns or intervals. Economic cycles of boom and bust are cyclical. Seasonal changes are cyclical. {The industry is notoriously cyclical, with layoffs every few years.} Often interchangeable with cyclic, though cyclical appears more in economic and business contexts.

Cycling is the activity of riding a bicycle, whether for transportation, exercise, or sport. As a sport, it encompasses road racing, track racing, mountain biking, and BMX, with events like the Tour de France drawing global attention. The term also describes any process that moves through repeated phases or stages: {the cycling of nutrients through an ecosystem}. In everyday use, someone who cycles commutes or exercises by bike.

A cyclist is a person who rides a bicycle. The term applies to casual riders and competitive racers alike: {Cyclists filled the bike lane during rush hour}. In traffic contexts, cyclist often distinguishes bicycle riders from motorists and pedestrians.

Cyclists are people who ride bicycles. The term applies broadly—from commuters biking to work to competitive racers in the Tour de France. In traffic discussions, cyclists often appear as a distinct category of road user: {The new lane is reserved for cyclists}. {Cyclists and motorists don't always get along.}

A cyclone is a large-scale rotating storm system, with winds spiraling inward around a low-pressure center. In the Indian Ocean and South Pacific, cyclone names what's called a hurricane in the Atlantic or typhoon in the western Pacific—all the same phenomenon. More loosely, cyclone describes any violent rotating windstorm: {The cyclone tore through the trailer park}. Figuratively, a person or force that moves with destructive energy: {She swept through the office like a cyclone}.

Cyclones are large-scale weather systems characterized by rotating winds around a low-pressure center. In the Northern Hemisphere they spin counterclockwise; in the Southern Hemisphere, clockwise. The term covers tropical storms and hurricanes as well as the broader atmospheric disturbances that bring unsettled weather to temperate regions. Colloquially, cyclone may refer to any violent windstorm, including tornadoes, though meteorologists distinguish between them. {The cyclone made landfall with devastating winds.}

A cyclops is a one-eyed giant from Greek mythology—creatures who forged Zeus's thunderbolts and whom Odysseus famously outwitted. The image extends to anything with a single central eye or lens: a cyclops {camera}, a cyclops {fish}. In biology, Cyclops is a genus of tiny one-eyed crustaceans. Plural: cyclopes or cyclopses.

A cylinder is a three-dimensional shape with straight parallel sides and circular ends of equal size, like a soup can or a drinking glass. The term extends to any object with this form, from engine cylinders where pistons move to the rotating cylinders of a revolver that hold cartridges. {The engine runs on four cylinders.} In casual speech, saying something is {firing on all cylinders} means it's operating at full capacity or performing optimally.

Cylinders are three-dimensional shapes with parallel circular ends connected by a curved surface—like a can or a pipe. In engines, cylinders are the chambers where pistons move up and down: {a four-cylinder engine}, {The car was only firing on three cylinders}. That mechanical sense extends figuratively—to operate {on all cylinders} is to perform at full capacity.
clues: What rolling pins and pipes share

definition: A cymbal is a round metal plate that produces a ringing or crashing sound when struck or clashed against another cymbal. Cymbals come in pairs for hand-clashing or mount singly on stands for drumsticks and brushes. They're essential to drum kits, orchestras, and marching bands: {The drummer hit the cymbal at the song's climax}.

Cymbals are a pair of brass percussion instruments, circular plates that produce a crashing or shimmering sound when struck together or hit with a drumstick. They appear in orchestras, marching bands, and drum kits. The singular cymbal usually refers to one mounted on a stand: {a ride cymbal}, {a crash cymbal}, {hi-hat cymbals}.

A cynic believes people act from self-interest and distrusts claims of altruism or sincerity. The attitude ranges from healthy skepticism to corrosive distrust: {Don't be such a cynic—she might actually want to help}. Cynical describes the outlook; cynicism names it. A cynic sees the price of everything and the value of nothing.

Cynical, an adjective, is used to characterize people who are pessimistic or who are ready to believe the worst about others. Opinions of such people are also characterized with cynical: His cynical view of human nature is evident in all of his films. If you are cynical about someone’s motives or actions, you think they have a self-serving agenda, despite what they may say. If you are cynical about something abstract—politics, for example—you don’t expect good results.

Cynicism is a disposition to distrust others' motives and dismiss claims of sincerity or goodness. A cynic assumes people act from self-interest and that idealistic talk masks baser intentions: {Her cynicism about politics kept her from voting}. The word can describe a general worldview or a reaction to specific disappointments: {Years in corporate law had bred a deep cynicism about justice}.

Cynics are people who doubt the sincerity of others' motives, assuming self-interest underlies apparent goodness: {The cynics said she only donated for the tax break}. The word suggests world-weary skepticism, sometimes justified, sometimes reflexive. A cynic may be right about human nature or may simply be unable to recognize genuine virtue. (Capitalized Cynics were ancient Greek philosophers who rejected conventional desires for wealth and status.)

Cypher is an alternate spelling of cipher, used interchangeably in most senses. It refers to a secret code or method of encryption, a person of no importance {a mere cypher}, or the numeral zero. In hip-hop culture, a cypher is a circle of rappers taking turns freestyling, each building on what came before: {We formed a cypher in the parking lot after the show}.

Cypress is a type of evergreen conifer with dark foliage and a distinctive tall, narrow shape. The trees grow in warm climates and are associated with Mediterranean landscapes and American swamps, where bald cypress trees rise from standing water. Cypress wood is valued for its durability and resistance to rot. The trees have ancient associations with mourning and cemeteries: {A row of cypress lined the path to the grave}.

Cypresses are evergreen coniferous trees with scale-like leaves and a distinctive columnar or pyramidal shape. They're associated with Mediterranean landscapes and, since antiquity, with cemeteries and mourning—their dark, upright forms line graveyards throughout Southern Europe. {Tall cypresses flanked the villa's entrance.}

A cyst is an abnormal sac in the body containing fluid, air, or semisolid material. Cysts form in various tissues—ovarian cysts, sebaceous cysts on the skin, cysts in the kidneys. Most are benign but may require drainage or removal if they grow large or cause pain. {The doctor said the cyst was nothing to worry about.}

Czar was the title of Russian emperors until 1917, from a word meaning Caesar. The spelling tsar is closer to the Russian. In American English, czar commonly refers to someone given broad authority over a particular domain: {drug czar}, {energy czar}, {climate czar}. These appointed officials typically coordinate policy across agencies.

A czarina is the wife of a czar—the empress consort of Russia under the old imperial system. The term extends to any woman wielding great power in a particular domain: {She was the czarina of New York fashion}. Also spelled tsarina.

Czars is the plural of czar, the title of Russian emperors before the 1917 revolution. The word derives from Caesar. In American politics, czar denotes an official with broad authority over a particular policy area: {drug czar}, {energy czar}, {border czar}. These appointments typically lack formal power but signal political priority. The spelling tsar is preferred in British English.

Daal, also spelled dal or dhal, is a staple of South Asian cuisine consisting of dried legumes—typically lentils, split peas, or beans—cooked until soft, often with spices like turmeric, cumin, and coriander. The word refers both to the raw ingredient and the finished dish, which is usually served as a thick, soupy accompaniment to rice or flatbread. {We ordered daal with naan for the table.}

A dab is a small amount or portion of something: I’ll take a dab of butter. A quick, small motion involving some purpose is also a dab. This dab is frequently encountered as a verb: Dab the sponge gently around the wound. The fixed expression smack dab in the middle (or center) means exactly in the middle. A concentrated form of cannabis is called dab and using this for recreational purposes is called dabbing.

Dabbed is the past tense of dab, meaning to touch lightly or apply with quick, gentle strokes: {She dabbed at her eyes with a tissue}, {He dabbed ointment on the cut}. In cannabis culture, dabbed refers to having consumed a dab—a concentrated dose of marijuana extract vaporized and inhaled: {I dabbed before the concert}.

Dabbing is a dance move where you tuck your face into a bent elbow while extending the other arm outward, as if sneezing into your sleeve while pointing. The move became a viral celebration gesture in the mid-2010s, especially in sports and hip-hop culture: {He scored and started dabbing}. Separately, dabbing refers to inhaling vaporized cannabis concentrates called dabs.

To dabble is to splash or play in water with hands or feet, like a child at the edge of a pool. Ducks dabble when they feed in shallow water, tipping forward to reach below the surface. The word extends to casual or superficial involvement in an activity: {She dabbles in painting but never commits to it}. A dabbler tries things without serious dedication.

Dabbled is the past tense of dabble. To dabble is to splash or play in water, usually with hands or feet: {The children dabbled their toes in the stream}. More commonly, dabble means to take up an activity casually or superficially, without serious commitment: {She dabbled in painting but never pursued it}. {He dabbled in stocks before losing interest}.

A dabbler engages in an activity superficially rather than seriously or professionally. The word carries mild dismissiveness—a dabbler in painting never commits to mastering the craft, a dabbler in stocks trades casually without deep knowledge. {He's just a dabbler, not a real photographer.} The implication is of someone who samples without dedicating themselves.

Dabblers are people who engage in activities superficially rather than seriously or professionally. A dabbler in painting might take a weekend class but never commit to the craft. The word carries mild dismissiveness—suggesting dilettantism rather than dedication: {The conference attracted serious researchers and dabblers alike}. Ducks that feed by tipping forward in shallow water are also called dabblers.
clues: People who never go beyond basics

definition: Dabbles is the third-person singular of dabble. To dabble is to splash or play in water with hands or feet: {The child dabbled her fingers in the fountain}. More commonly, dabble means to take part in something casually or superficially without serious commitment: {He dabbles in photography}, {She dabbles in the stock market}. A dabbler never goes deep.

Dabbling is casual, shallow engagement with something—trying it without serious commitment. Someone dabbles in painting or dabbles in stocks without dedicating themselves fully: {He's been dabbling in photography lately}. The word carries a mild dismissiveness, suggesting amateur status. Literally, to dabble is to splash about in shallow water, as ducks do when feeding at the surface.

Dabs are small, quick touches or applications: {a dab of butter}, {a few dabs of paint}. To dab is to press lightly and repeatedly, as when dabbing a wound with gauze. In cannabis culture, dabs are concentrated doses of THC extract, typically vaporized and inhaled—potent enough that the noun became a verb: {We dabbed all afternoon}. Separately, the dab is a brief dance move where one drops the head into a bent elbow.

A dachshund is a small dog breed with a long body, short legs, and droopy ears—originally bred in Germany for hunting badgers in their burrows. The distinctive elongated shape has earned them nicknames like "wiener dog" and "sausage dog." Dachshunds come in standard and miniature sizes, with smooth, longhaired, or wirehaired coats: {Her dachshund tunneled under every blanket in the house}.

Dachshunds are a breed of dog with a distinctively long body and short legs, originally bred in Germany to hunt badgers and other burrowing animals. Their elongated shape earned them the nickname "wiener dog" or "sausage dog." Dachshunds come in standard and miniature sizes, with smooth, longhaired, or wirehaired coats. They are known for being spirited, curious, and sometimes stubborn companions.
clues: Dogs bred to pursue burrowing prey

definition: Dad is an informal word for father, used both as a term of address and a general noun: {Dad, can I borrow the car?}, {My dad taught me to fish}. Dad joke refers to corny, pun-based humor stereotypically favored by fathers. The word carries warmth and familiarity compared to the more formal father. (Capitalized Dad is used when addressing one's father directly or as a name substitute.)

Dada is baby talk for father, one of the earliest words many children produce. The reduplicated syllables are easy for infants to articulate, making dada and mama universal across languages. Adults use it when speaking to small children: {Say dada!} {Where's dada?} (Capitalized Dada is the early 20th-century art movement.)

Dadaism is the artistic and literary movement that emerged during World War I, characterized by deliberate irrationality, absurdity, and rejection of conventional aesthetics. The movement embraced chance, nonsense, and anti-art as protests against bourgeois culture and the rationalism blamed for the war's horrors: {Her collages have a dadaism quality—random newspaper clippings glued over fashion ads}. (Capitalized Dadaism is the more common form.)

A dadbod is the physique of a middle-aged man who was once fit but has softened—carrying extra weight around the midsection without being obese. The term emerged as a gentle, sometimes affectionate way to describe this common body type: {He's got a dadbod now but he used to run marathons}. The concept gained traction partly as pushback against idealized male fitness standards.

Dadbods are the physiques of men who've let their bodies soften into middle age—not obese, but carrying extra weight around the middle, with diminished muscle tone. The term emerged as a counterpoint to idealized male fitness, sometimes celebrated as approachable and unpretentious: {He's not hitting the gym anymore, just embracing the dadbod}. Often spelled as two words: dad bod.

Daddies is the plural of daddy, the informal word for father. Beyond the familial sense, daddies can refer to older men in relationships with younger partners, particularly in gay contexts: {sugar daddies}, {leather daddies}. The term carries connotations of authority, provision, or sexual dominance depending on context.

Daddio is a casual, somewhat dated form of address for a man, used the way one might say "buddy" or "pal." It emerged from mid-20th-century jazz and beatnik culture: {What's the word, daddio?} The term sounds deliberately retro today, often used for comic effect or nostalgic flair.

Daddy is a child's word for father, often the first form children use before graduating to dad. Adults may use it affectionately or nostalgically: {I still call him Daddy}. In sexual contexts, daddy refers to an older male partner, often implying dominance or a provider role: {Who's your daddy?} A {sugar daddy} is a wealthy older man who lavishes gifts on a younger partner. Informally, daddy can mark someone as the best or most dominant in a field: {He's the daddy of all quarterbacks}.

Dadgummit is a mild oath expressing frustration or annoyance, a euphemistic substitution for "goddammit." It has a folksy, rural flavor—the kind of thing a grandfather might say when he drops his wrench: {Dadgummit, I can't find my glasses anywhere}. Also spelled dad-gummit or daggummit.

Dads is the plural of dad, an informal word for father. The term appears in contexts discussing fathers collectively: {Dads today are more involved in childcare than previous generations}. It also labels social groups: {a support group for new dads}, {soccer dads}. In direct address, Dad typically remains singular even with multiple fathers present.

A daemon is a background process in computing that runs without direct user interaction, handling system tasks like printing, email, or network services. The spelling distinguishes these programs from the older sense of daemon (also spelled daimon), a spirit or supernatural being in Greek thought—neither good nor evil, but an intermediary force. The computing sense plays on this: daemons work invisibly, attending to tasks behind the scenes. {The mail daemon processes incoming messages automatically.}
