The word originally referred to a line around a military prison that prisoners crossed at risk of being shot, but this origin has faded from modern awareness. Deadlines structure work, school, journalism, and bureaucracy: {I work better under deadline pressure}.

Deadlines are the times or dates by which something must be completed. The term originated in American prisons as a line beyond which inmates would be shot—now it survives only in its figurative sense of a cutoff point. A deadline may be firm or soft, depending on consequences for missing it: {The deadline for applications is Friday}. To {meet a deadline} is to finish in time; to miss one is to fail.

A deadlock is a standstill where opposing forces block each other and neither can move forward: {Contract negotiations reached a deadlock}. In computing, deadlock occurs when two processes each wait for resources the other holds, freezing both. The verb means to bring to such an impasse: {The jury was deadlocked}.

Deadlocked describes a situation where opposing sides are stuck, unable to move forward or reach agreement. A jury is deadlocked when members cannot achieve the required consensus for a verdict. Negotiations become deadlocked when neither party will compromise: {Peace talks remained deadlocked over territorial disputes}. The image is of a lock that won't open—progress completely blocked.

Deadlocks are situations where no progress can be made because opposing parties or forces are stuck waiting on each other. In computing, a deadlock occurs when two processes each hold a resource the other needs, so neither can proceed: {The system crashed due to a deadlock between competing threads}. In negotiations or disputes, a deadlock is an impasse: {Contract talks reached a deadlock over wages}. The singular deadlock serves as both noun and verb—to deadlock is to bring to a standstill.

Deadly means capable of causing death: a deadly {weapon}, a deadly {disease}, a deadly {poison}. It extends to anything extremely harmful or dangerous: deadly {serious}, deadly {accurate}. In informal British usage, deadly can mean excellent or thrilling: {That concert was deadly}. The adverb form means in a way suggesting death: deadly {pale}, deadly {quiet}.

A deadname is the birth name of a person who has since changed their name, especially a transgender person's pre-transition name. The term implies the old name is no longer valid—socially dead. To deadname someone is to call them by that former name, whether intentionally or not: {Her coworker kept deadnaming her in meetings}. Deliberate deadnaming is widely considered disrespectful or hostile.

Deadnamed describes being called by a name one no longer uses, particularly a birth name abandoned after a transgender person's transition. To deadname someone is to use their former name, whether intentionally or carelessly: {She was repeatedly deadnamed by coworkers who refused to acknowledge her transition}. The practice is considered disrespectful and potentially harmful.

Deadnames is the plural of deadname, which refers to the birth name or former name of a transgender person who has since adopted a different name to match their gender identity. Using someone's deadname, especially intentionally, is considered disrespectful and invalidating. The term also functions as a verb: {Don't deadname me}. A related noun, deadnaming, describes the act of using someone's former name against their wishes.

Deadnaming is calling a transgender person by a name they no longer use—typically their birth name before transitioning. The practice is considered disrespectful because it denies someone's identity: {She accused the journalist of deadnaming her in the article}. The term emerged from transgender communities in the 2010s, where an abandoned former name is called a deadname.

Deadpan describes a deliberately expressionless manner, especially when delivering humor. A deadpan face shows no emotion; deadpan comedy relies on the contrast between absurd content and flat delivery: {She told the joke completely deadpan}. The word works as adjective, adverb, noun, and verb: {He deadpanned the punchline}.

Deadpanned is the past tense of deadpan, meaning to deliver something—usually humor—with a completely expressionless face and flat tone: {She deadpanned the punchline so perfectly that half the audience missed the joke}. The effect relies on contrast between serious delivery and absurd content.

Deadpanning is delivering humor, sarcasm, or absurdity with a completely expressionless face and flat tone—as if you're serious. The contrast between the ridiculous content and the blank delivery creates the comedic effect: {She kept deadpanning about her cat's political opinions until someone finally cracked}. The technique works precisely because it refuses to signal that a joke is happening.

Deadpans is the verb form of deadpan, meaning to deliver something—usually humor—with a completely expressionless face and flat tone: {She deadpans the punchline so perfectly that half the audience doesn't realize it's a joke}. The effect relies on contrast between absurd content and emotionless delivery.

Deadset functions as an intensifier meaning absolutely or completely: {I'm deadset against it}, {She was deadset on leaving}. The phrase suggests unwavering determination or conviction. In Australian slang, deadset also means genuine or serious, often as an exclamation: {Deadset, that actually happened}. Also spelled dead set.

Deadweight is a heavy, inert mass that is difficult to move—literally, weight that is dead rather than animate. A person who is unconscious or uncooperative becomes deadweight when you try to carry or move them. The term extends to anything that burdens without contributing: {The committee was carrying too much deadweight}. In shipping, deadweight tonnage measures the total weight a vessel can safely carry, including cargo, fuel, and crew.

Deadwood is wood that is dead—branches or trees no longer living. In forestry, clearing deadwood reduces fire risk. Figuratively, deadwood refers to people or things that are no longer useful or productive: {The new CEO promised to cut the deadwood from upper management}. The word implies dead weight that burdens an organization. (Capitalized Deadwood is a place name.)

A deadzone is an area where something fails to register or function. In gaming, it's the range of joystick movement that produces no response—a buffer against drift. In driving, it's the slack in a steering wheel before the wheels turn. Dead zones in bodies of water lack oxygen to support marine life. More loosely, a deadzone is any space of absence or unresponsiveness: {My apartment is a WiFi deadzone}.

Deadzones are areas where something expected to function doesn't work. In gaming, a deadzone is the range of joystick movement that produces no response—a threshold before input registers. In telecommunications, deadzones are spots with no signal: {There's a deadzone in the basement where my phone gets nothing}. In ecology, deadzones are oxygen-depleted water areas where marine life cannot survive.

Deaf describes the inability to hear, whether total or partial. Someone deaf in one ear has hearing loss on that side. The deaf as a group are those with significant hearing loss. Figuratively, deaf means refusing to listen: {My complaints fell on deaf ears}. To be {deaf to} something is to ignore it willfully. Capitalized Deaf often refers specifically to the cultural community of deaf people who use sign language.

Deafblind describes a person with significant loss of both hearing and vision. The combination creates unique challenges distinct from either condition alone, as the senses cannot compensate for each other. Communication methods vary—some use tactile sign language, others Braille or adapted devices. Also spelled deaf-blind.

Deafened means made deaf, whether permanently or temporarily. A sudden explosion can leave you deafened for hours. {I was deafened by the roar of the crowd.} Figuratively, to be deafened to something is to be made unable or unwilling to hear it: {Years of political rhetoric had deafened him to genuine appeals for help.}

Deafening describes sound so loud it overwhelms hearing—a deafening {roar}, deafening {applause}. The word is nearly always hyperbolic; truly deafening noise would cause hearing damage. Paradoxically, {deafening silence} describes an absence of sound so conspicuous it feels overwhelming.

Deafness is the inability to hear, ranging from partial to complete. It may be present from birth or acquired through age, illness, or injury. The Deaf community—capitalized—refers to those who identify culturally with sign language and deaf institutions. Figuratively, deafness suggests willful refusal to listen: {His deafness to criticism ultimately cost him the job}.

Deaging is the digital process of making someone appear younger, typically an actor in film or television. Visual effects artists smooth wrinkles, tighten skin, and restore youthful features frame by frame: {The deaging in that movie was so good I forgot he's actually seventy}. Sometimes spelled de-aging.

Deal centers on distribution and arrangement. To deal cards is to distribute them; a dealer handles this task. The meaning extends to distribution generally: {Who's dealing?} A deal is an agreement or transaction: {We made a deal}, {What's the deal with parking?} To deal with something is to handle or address it: {I'll deal with this later}. A great deal or good deal means a large amount: {a great deal of trouble}. As an adjective, deal refers to pine or fir wood, especially planks—a separate word from the same spelling.

A dealbreaker is something that causes a negotiation, agreement, or relationship to fail. In business contexts, it's a condition one party cannot accept: {The salary was fine, but no remote work was a dealbreaker}. In dating, dealbreakers are traits or behaviors that make someone unacceptable as a partner: {Smoking is a dealbreaker for me}. Also spelled deal-breaker or deal breaker.

Dealbreakers are conditions or flaws that make something unacceptable, ending negotiation or consideration. In relationships, a dealbreaker is a trait or behavior you won't tolerate in a partner: {Smoking is a dealbreaker for me}. In business, it's a term that kills a deal. The singular dealbreaker is more common than the plural.

A dealer is someone who buys and sells goods, especially as a business: a car dealer, an antiques dealer, a dealer in rare books. In card games, the dealer distributes cards to players. Without further context, dealer often means a person who sells illegal drugs: {Her son got the stuff from a dealer in the neighborhood}. A dealer may also be a firm that trades securities for its own account rather than as a broker for clients.

Dealers are people who buy and sell goods, typically as a business. The term applies across contexts: a car dealer sells automobiles, an antiques dealer trades in collectibles, and a drug dealer sells illegal substances. In card games, the dealer is the person who distributes cards to the other players. {The dealers at the casino work in shifts.} {She found a reputable art dealer to appraise the painting.}

A dealership is a business authorized to sell a particular manufacturer's products, especially vehicles: {a Ford dealership}, {a motorcycle dealership}. The term implies an official franchise relationship with the brand, distinguishing it from independent sellers. Dealerships typically also provide service, repairs, and financing.

Dealerships are businesses authorized to sell products on behalf of manufacturers, most commonly automobiles. A car dealership holds franchise agreements with specific brands: {Ford dealerships}, {Toyota dealerships}. The term extends to other industries—boat dealerships, motorcycle dealerships—but without qualification usually means car lots. {We visited three dealerships before finding the right price.}

Dealing most often refers to conducting business or transactions, especially of an illicit kind: {drug dealing}, {arms dealing}. The plural dealings covers interactions or business relations with others: {I've had no dealings with him since the lawsuit}. Dealing also names the act of distributing cards in a game. To be {dealing with} something is to handle or address it.
clues: What poker players take turns doing

definition: Dealings are interactions or transactions between parties, especially in business or official contexts: {I've had dealings with that company before}, {Their financial dealings came under scrutiny}. The word often carries a slight whiff of suspicion—shady dealings, secret dealings, backroom dealings. To {have dealings with} someone is to conduct business or maintain a relationship with them.

A dealmaker is someone skilled at negotiating and closing agreements, especially in business or politics. The term often carries connotations of pragmatism and transactional thinking—a dealmaker focuses on getting to yes rather than on principles or ideology: {He styled himself a dealmaker, not an ideologue}. The word can be admiring or dismissive depending on context.

Dealmakers are people who negotiate and close agreements, especially in business, politics, or diplomacy. The term suggests skill at bringing parties together and finding terms everyone will accept. A dealmaker may broker mergers, treaties, or contracts: {The mayor fancied himself a dealmaker who could get unions and management to the table}. The word often carries connotations of pragmatism over principle.

Dealmaking is the process of negotiating and closing agreements, especially in business, politics, or diplomacy. The term emphasizes the skill and maneuvering involved: {His dealmaking brought the two companies together}. A dealmaker is someone adept at brokering such agreements, often implying shrewdness or transactional thinking: {She built her reputation as a dealmaker in commercial real estate}.

Deals covers agreements, transactions, and the act of distributing. A deal is an arrangement between parties: {We made a deal}. In commerce, a deal is a bargain or special offer: {I got a great deal on flights}. To deal cards is to distribute them to players. To deal with something is to handle or address it: {I'll deal with this later}. A dealer sells goods, often with connotations of illicit trade: {drug dealer}, {arms dealer}. {What's the deal?} asks what's happening or what the situation is. {Big deal} dismisses something as unimportant.

Dealt is the past tense and past participle of deal. Cards are dealt to players. A blow can be dealt to an opponent, literally or figuratively: {The scandal dealt a serious blow to his campaign}. If you've dealt with something, you've handled it: {I've already dealt with that problem}.

A dean is an administrator in a college or university, typically overseeing a school or division: {the dean of the law school}, {dean of students}. The term extends to the senior or most respected member of any group: {the dean of American sportswriters}. In church contexts, a dean heads a cathedral chapter or group of parishes. {She was appointed dean of the medical school last year.} (Capitalized Dean is a given name.)

Deans is the plural of dean, an academic administrator who oversees a college, faculty, or division within a university: {The deans met to discuss budget cuts}. Dean also means the senior member of a group: {the dean of American sportswriters}. In ecclesiastical contexts, a dean heads a cathedral chapter or group of parishes.

Dear and oh dear are mild exclamations used to signal that something is not as it should be or as someone would like it to be. Dear is also used as a term of endearment or affection: Of course, dear. Many consider them old-fashioned expressions.

Dearest is a superlative form of dear, used as both adjective and noun. As an adjective, it means most beloved: {my dearest friend}, {her dearest wish}. As a noun, it's a term of endearment for someone deeply loved: {Come here, dearest}. The word appears often in letter salutations: {Dearest Mother}. Dearest can also mean most expensive, though this use is uncommon.

Dearie is an affectionate term of address, a diminutive of dear. It's used toward children, close friends, or romantic partners: {Come here, dearie}. The word can also carry condescension when directed at strangers, particularly from older speakers to younger ones: {That's not how it works, dearie}.

Death is the end of life—the permanent cessation of biological functions. It extends to the end of anything: {the death of a friendship}, {the death of an era}. To {be the death of} someone is to cause them extreme distress or amusement: {You'll be the death of me with these jokes}. A {death blow} or {death knell} signals the end of something. To {do something to death} is to overuse it until it loses meaning. {At death's door} means near dying. (Capitalized Death is the personification.)

A deathbed is the bed where someone dies or lies dying. The word usually appears in contexts about final moments: a {deathbed confession}, a {deathbed conversion}, {deathbed wishes}. To be {on one's deathbed} is to be dying or very close to death. The term evokes solemnity—last words spoken, final reconciliations attempted, wills amended at the last moment.

A deathbed is the bed where someone dies or is dying. The word usually appears in contexts surrounding final moments: a deathbed {confession}, a deathbed {conversion}, a deathbed {promise}. These carry special weight—statements made when someone has nothing left to lose or gain by lying. {He gathered his children around his deathbed.}

A deathblow is a strike or action that kills, or more often, something that destroys or ends something definitively: {The scandal dealt a deathblow to his campaign}. The word usually appears figuratively—the final, decisive blow that finishes off something already weakened.

A death camp is a prison facility designed for mass killing, most commonly referring to Nazi extermination camps like Auschwitz and Treblinka during World War II. Distinguished from concentration camps, which were primarily for detention and forced labor, death camps existed specifically to murder prisoners—predominantly Jews—on an industrial scale. The term now applies to any facility where systematic killing occurs: {reports of death camps in the region}.

A deathcap is a highly poisonous mushroom (*Amanita phalloides*) with a pale greenish-yellow cap, white gills, and a bulbous base enclosed in a cup-like structure called a volva. Native to Europe but now found worldwide, it is responsible for most fatal mushroom poisonings, as its toxins cause severe liver and kidney damage. The deathcap's danger lies partly in its bland appearance and delayed symptoms, which can emerge hours after ingestion when organ damage is already underway.

Deathless means immortal or undying—not subject to death. The word appears most often in literary contexts describing fame or achievements that will endure: {deathless prose}, {deathless glory}. It can be used ironically for work that falls short of such permanence: {his deathless contributions to the company newsletter}.

Deathly means resembling or suggestive of death. A deathly {pallor} is the pale color of a corpse. Deathly {silence} is the absolute stillness of the grave. As an adverb, deathly intensifies certain adjectives: {deathly quiet}, {deathly afraid}, {deathly ill}. The word emphasizes extremity through association with death's finality.

A deathmatch is a competitive video game mode where players fight to kill each other, typically with the winner being whoever reaches a kill count first or has the most kills when time expires. The format emphasizes individual combat over team objectives: {I spent hours in deathmatch perfecting my aim}. The term extends to any chaotic free-for-all competition: {The meeting devolved into a deathmatch over the budget}.

Deathmatches are competitions where participants fight until one side is eliminated—literally in combat sports, figuratively in video games. In gaming, a deathmatch is a free-for-all mode where players respawn after being killed and compete for the most kills: {We played deathmatches until 3 a.m.} In professional wrestling, a deathmatch involves extreme weapons and intentional bleeding.

A deathray is a fictional or hypothetical weapon that emits a concentrated beam of energy capable of killing or destroying targets at a distance. The concept appears throughout science fiction: {The alien ship's deathray vaporized the city}. In real-world contexts, deathray typically describes proposed but never-realized directed-energy weapons. Also spelled death ray.

Deaths is the plural of death, meaning instances of dying or the ends of lives. A disease might cause thousands of deaths. In statistics and reporting, deaths often appears as a count: {The accident resulted in three deaths}. Death in the singular names the state or concept; deaths names specific occurrences.

A deathtrap is a place or structure so dangerous it could kill you—a building with blocked fire exits, a car with failed brakes, a mine with no ventilation. The word implies negligence or disregard for safety: {That old elevator is a deathtrap}. Often used hyperbolically for anything perceived as hazardous: {I'm not getting on that deathtrap of a roller coaster}.

Deathtraps are places, vehicles, or situations so dangerous they seem likely to cause death. A building with blocked fire exits is a deathtrap. An old car with failing brakes is a deathtrap. The word emphasizes negligence or poor design rather than inherent danger: {That rickety staircase is a deathtrap}.

Deathwatch is a compound noun with two meanings. The more common one is a vigil, either private or public, that is maintained as someone dies or is about to be executed. In a related meaning, a deathwatch is a guard that is mounted for someone who is about to die or be executed. This meaning is sometimes used in extended senses to talk about the anticipation of the death of something other than a living thing, like a business or a project: The company’s board is on deathwatch, waiting for the CEO to resign. The other meaning of deathwatch is for a kind of beetle that infests wood and that makes a noise that is considered a harbinger of death.

A deathwish is a conscious or unconscious desire for one's own death, or behavior so reckless it suggests such a desire: {Riding a motorcycle without a helmet? You have a deathwish}. Often used hyperbolically for any foolhardy risk-taking. Also spelled as two words: death wish.

A debacle is a sudden, complete disaster or failure—often one that's embarrassing or humiliating. The word suggests not just defeat but collapse, a situation falling apart spectacularly: {The product launch was a debacle from start to finish}. Unlike mere setbacks, a debacle implies something that went catastrophically wrong in a way that's hard to recover from.

Debacles is the plural of debacle, a sudden and complete disaster or humiliating failure. The word suggests not just defeat but collapse—plans falling apart spectacularly, organizations imploding publicly: {a series of debacles that ended his political career}, {the debacles of the 2008 financial crisis}. A debacle implies something that should have been avoidable.

Debased means lowered in quality, value, or character. Currency is debased when precious metal content is reduced. A debased {version} of something has been corrupted from its original form. The word carries moral weight—debased {conduct} suggests degradation or corruption: {The scandal debased the office of the presidency}. Something debased has fallen from a higher state.

Debasement is the act of lowering something in quality, value, or dignity. Currency debasement historically meant reducing precious metal content while maintaining face value; now it often refers to inflation eroding purchasing power. More broadly, debasement describes any degradation or corruption: {the debasement of public discourse}, {a debasement of artistic standards}. Self-debasement is humiliating oneself, whether through groveling behavior or degrading acts.

Debasing is lowering something in quality, value, or character. Currency is debased by reducing precious metal content. A person debases themselves through shameful behavior: {He wouldn't debase himself by begging}. Standards, traditions, and institutions can all be debased by corruption or neglect: {debasing the democratic process}.

Debatable describes something open to argument or dispute. A debatable {point} invites disagreement; reasonable people might conclude differently. The word often signals that a claim isn't settled: {Whether the policy helps is debatable}. Sometimes used dismissively to suggest something is wrong without saying so directly: {That's debatable}.

A debate is a formal argument between opposing sides, typically following structured rules: {a presidential debate}, {a debate over immigration policy}. To debate is to argue a position or consider alternatives: {I'm debating whether to take the job}. The word carries a sense of weighing options or exchanging views rather than simply quarreling.

Debates are formal discussions where opposing sides present arguments on a topic, typically following structured rules about time and turn-taking. The format appears in politics, academics, and competitive speaking circuits. More loosely, any sustained back-and-forth disagreement can be called a debate: {There's ongoing debate about whether remote work hurts productivity}. The verb debate means to engage in such discussion or to deliberate internally: {I'm still debating whether to go}.

To debauch is to corrupt or lead astray, especially into excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures—drinking, sex, or other dissipation. The word carries moral weight: you debauch someone's character or innocence. As a noun, a debauch is a bout of such indulgence: {After a weekend debauch, he swore off alcohol}. The related noun debauchery names the lifestyle.

Debauched describes someone given over to excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures—drinking, sex, drugs, or general dissolution. A debauched {lifestyle} suggests moral corruption and a lack of restraint. The word carries strong connotations of degradation and excess beyond mere enjoyment: {The debauched aristocrats spent their fortunes on wine and women}. Someone debauched has abandoned conventional standards of behavior, usually in ways that damage themselves or others.

Debauchery is behavior that shows a lack of self-control and that is aimed at gratifying sensual desires: Parents were dismayed to learn that evenings of drunken debauchery were not uncommon in dormitories. The word has a strongly negative connotation, except when use ironically. Debauchery (the word) has been declining steadily in frequency since the late 18th century, perhaps because people find less old-fashioned words to describe the same phenomenon.

Debilitating describes something that weakens or impairs, draining strength or vitality. A debilitating {illness} leaves you unable to function normally. Debilitating {debt} cripples financial freedom. The word emphasizes severity—not merely inconvenient but significantly impairing: {The team suffered a debilitating loss of their star player}.

Debit is a charge against an account—money withdrawn or owed. In accounting, debits record what goes out or what's owed, balancing against credits. A debit card draws directly from a bank account rather than borrowing: {The charge appeared as a debit on my statement}. To debit an account is to subtract from it.

Debonair describes a man who is suave, charming, and confident in manner—sophisticated without seeming to try. The word suggests effortless elegance and worldly polish: {He had a debonair smile that put everyone at ease}. A debonair person moves through social situations with grace and self-assurance, often with a hint of playful wit.

To debrief is to question someone after a mission, operation, or significant event to gather information about what happened. Intelligence officers debrief agents returning from the field; researchers debrief study participants. The noun debrief refers to this questioning session itself: {We'll hold a debrief after the exercise}. The word reverses the direction of brief, which means to inform someone beforehand.

Debriefed is the past tense of debrief, meaning to question someone after a mission, operation, or experience to gather information about what happened. Military personnel are debriefed after combat operations; astronauts after space flights; witnesses after incidents. The word reverses the original briefing that prepared them: {The agents were debriefed as soon as they returned from the field}.

Debriefing is the process of questioning someone after a mission, operation, or experience to gather information about what happened. Intelligence agencies debrief spies returning from assignments; researchers debrief study participants after experiments. The term implies systematic extraction of knowledge: {The pilot underwent debriefing after the reconnaissance flight}. More casually, any post-event discussion: {We had a quick debriefing after the meeting}.

Debris is scattered fragments or remains, especially from something destroyed or discarded. After a storm, debris litters the streets—fallen branches, broken glass, torn shingles. The word applies to wreckage of any kind: {rescue workers searched through the debris}, {space debris orbits Earth}. It can also describe accumulated refuse or rubbish: {Clear the debris from the yard}.

Debt is money owed to another party. You incur debt by borrowing—through loans, credit cards, or unpaid bills. Debt can also be non-financial: {I owe you a debt of gratitude}. To be {in someone's debt} is to owe them for a favor. A debt {collector} pursues payment on behalf of creditors.

A debtor is a person or entity that owes money to another. The term appears most often in legal and financial contexts: {The debtor defaulted on the loan}. A debtor may owe money through loans, credit purchases, or court judgments. The opposite is a creditor—the one owed money.

Debtors are people or entities that owe money to others. The term appears most often in legal, financial, and accounting contexts: {The company's debtors failed to pay on time}. A debtor owes; a creditor is owed. In biblical and religious usage, debtors may owe moral or spiritual obligations: {Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors}.

Debts are amounts of money or obligations owed to others. The word covers everything from credit card balances and mortgages to money borrowed from friends. Beyond financial obligations, debt extends to abstract owing: {I owe you a debt of gratitude}. To be {in debt} is to owe money; to be {in someone's debt} is to feel obligated to them for a favor or kindness. Debts can be repaid, forgiven, or—if you're lucky—written off.

In video games, a debuff is a negative effect applied to a character that weakens their abilities, slows their movement, or otherwise hampers their performance. It is the opposite of a buff, which enhances abilities. As a verb, to debuff means to apply such an effect: {The mage debuffed the boss before we attacked}. The term has spread beyond gaming to describe anything that diminishes someone's effectiveness or energy: {This hangover is a serious debuff}.

To debug is to find and fix errors in a system—originally in computer programs, where bugs are flaws in code: {I spent three hours debugging the script}. The term extends to any troubleshooting process: {We need to debug our hiring process}. To debug a room is to remove hidden surveillance devices.

Debugged is the past tense of debug, meaning to find and remove errors from computer code or electronic systems: {I finally debugged that script after three hours}. The term extends to any process of identifying and fixing problems: {We debugged the registration process before the conference}. Something debugged has had its flaws corrected and should now work properly.

A debugger is a software tool that helps programmers find and fix errors in code. It allows you to pause a program's execution, step through it line by line, inspect variables, and observe how data changes as the code runs. The term also applies to a person who debugs: {She's the best debugger on the team—nothing gets past her}. In either sense, the debugger's job is to locate the source of unexpected behavior and correct it.

Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors in computer code or other systems. The term comes from early computing, when an actual moth trapped in a relay caused a malfunction. Now it applies broadly: {I spent three hours debugging the script}. By extension, debugging can mean troubleshooting any complex problem: {We're still debugging the new workflow}.

To debunk is to expose something as false, exaggerated, or unfounded—puncturing claims that have gained undeserved acceptance. You debunk myths, conspiracy theories, or pseudoscience by showing the evidence doesn't support them: {The study debunked the idea that vaccines cause autism}. The word implies the target had pretensions to truth that careful examination deflates.

Debunked describes something that has been exposed as false or exaggerated. A debunked {myth} or debunked {theory} has been shown to lack evidence or validity: {The claim that vaccines cause autism has been thoroughly debunked}. The word often appears in discussions of misinformation, conspiracy theories, and pseudoscience.

A debunker is someone who exposes false claims, myths, or popular misconceptions. The term carries a slightly dismissive edge—debunkers often position themselves as rational skeptics cutting through nonsense: {The debunker showed how the psychic used cold reading techniques}. Science communicators, fact-checkers, and skeptics frequently wear the label.

Debunkers are people who expose false claims, myths, or exaggerated beliefs. The term carries a slightly dismissive edge—debunkers don't just disprove, they deflate, treating the original claim as pretentious nonsense. {Professional debunkers target pseudoscience and conspiracy theories.} The word implies both skepticism and a certain relish in dismantling what others believe.

Debunking is exposing false or exaggerated claims—showing that something widely believed or promoted is actually untrue, misleading, or overblown. The word implies active investigation and public correction: {The documentary debunks several myths about the moon landing}. Debunking often targets conspiracy theories, pseudoscience, and urban legends.

A debut is a first public appearance or performance—an actor's debut on Broadway, a singer's debut album, an athlete's professional debut. The word extends to any notable first: {the debut of a new product line}. As a verb, to debut is to make such an appearance: {The show debuts next week}. The stress falls on the second syllable.

A debutante is a young woman making her formal introduction to society, traditionally at a ball or similar event marking her eligibility for marriage. The custom belongs to upper-class and aristocratic circles: {The debutantes curtsied before the queen}. More broadly, debutante describes anyone new to a field or activity, though this use is less common.

Debutantes are young women making their formal entrance into society, traditionally at a ball or similar event marking their eligibility for marriage. The practice originated among aristocratic families and persists in some social circles: {The debutantes curtsied before the assembly}. By extension, any newcomer to a field might be called a debutante, though the word retains its feminine, upper-class associations.

Debuting is making a first appearance or being introduced for the first time. A singer debuts at Carnegie Hall, a product debuts at a trade show, a film debuts in theaters. The word applies to people, creative works, and things entering public awareness: {The company is debuting its new logo next month}. Pronounced either deh-BYOO-ing or day-BYOO-ing.

Debuts is the plural of debut—first public appearances or performances. A singer debuts at Carnegie Hall; a product debuts at a trade show. The word works as both noun and verb: {The company's new models had their debuts at the auto show}; {The series debuts next month}. Pronounced with stress on either syllable.
clues: Shows up for the first time

definition: A decade is a period of ten years and is most typically used to refer to a period of time that begins with a year ending in zero and ends with a year ending in nine. Decade is also used to refer to a person’s age in the same way that century is used to refer to a person’s age when they are over 100. If someone is in their fifth decade, they are in their forties. Decade is also used to refer to any ten-year period in someone’s life: The two decades between the time I graduated from college and my retirement were the most productive of my life.

Decadence is moral or cultural decline, especially one marked by excessive indulgence in pleasure. The word often describes societies or periods seen as having abandoned earlier virtues: {the decadence of late Rome}, {fin-de-siècle decadence}. In everyday use, decadence suggests luxurious self-indulgence without the moral judgment: {the decadence of a chocolate lava cake}. The adjective is decadent.
clues: Too much pleasure, too little virtue

definition: Decadent describes something characterized by excessive indulgence, luxury, or moral decline. A decadent dessert is sinfully rich; a decadent society has abandoned the virtues that once made it strong. The word carries a whiff of disapproval but also a guilty pleasure—calling something decadent often means you're about to enjoy it anyway. {The chocolate cake was absolutely decadent.} As a noun, a decadent is someone who embraces such excess, or a member of the late 19th-century artistic movement that prized aesthetic pleasure over moral convention.

Decades is the plural of decade, a period of ten years. Most often it refers to the named divisions of a century—the twenties, the sixties, the nineties: {Fashion from the decade I grew up in is back in style}. Decades also conveys a long but vague stretch of time: {I haven't seen her in decades}.

Decaf is coffee or tea that has had most of its caffeine removed, or a cup of such a beverage: {I'll have a decaf, please}. The word also works as an adjective: {decaf espresso}. Decaf emerged as an option for people who enjoy coffee's taste but want to avoid caffeine's stimulating effects, though trace amounts typically remain. It sometimes carries connotations of being less potent or exciting: {the decaf version of rock and roll}.

A decal is a design or image printed on special paper that can be transferred to another surface—glass, metal, wood, or skin. The paper is soaked in water or pressed with heat to release the image. Decals appear on car windows, skateboards, laptops, and children's temporary tattoos: {She covered her water bottle with decals}.

Decals are designs or images printed on special paper that can be transferred to another surface. They stick to windows, cars, walls, and other smooth surfaces: {The laptop was covered in band decals}. Unlike stickers, decals typically transfer only the image itself, leaving no backing material visible. Short for decalcomania.

A decanter is a glass vessel, typically elegant and often ornamental, used to hold wine or liquor after it has been transferred from its original bottle. The practice of decanting wine serves to separate it from sediment and allow it to breathe, improving flavor. Decanters for spirits like whiskey or brandy are primarily decorative and keep the contents readily accessible for serving. {She poured the aged port into a crystal decanter before dinner.}

Decanters are glass vessels, typically with a stopper, used to hold wine or spirits after they've been transferred from their original bottles. The practice of decanting serves two purposes: it separates wine from any sediment that has formed, and it allows the wine to breathe, releasing its aromas and softening its flavors. Decanters range from simple and functional to ornate crystal pieces displayed as tableware. {The whiskey decanters on the sideboard had belonged to his grandfather.}

To decapitate is to cut off someone's head. The word applies to executions, accidents, and violence: {The guillotine decapitated thousands during the French Revolution}. Figuratively, to decapitate an organization is to remove its leadership: {The raid decapitated the cartel}.

Decapitated means having had the head cut off. A decapitated body is headless, whether from execution, accident, or violence: {The decapitated corpse was found near the railroad tracks}. Figuratively, an organization is decapitated when its leadership is suddenly removed: {The raid decapitated the cartel's command structure}.

Decapitation is the act of cutting off someone's head. The term applies to executions, accidents, and surgical procedures alike. Historically, decapitation by sword or axe was considered an honorable death reserved for nobility: {The queen faced decapitation at the Tower}. Figuratively, to decapitate an organization is to remove its leadership.

Decapitations are acts of cutting off heads. The word appears in contexts of execution, warfare, and violent crime: {The regime carried out public decapitations}. Figuratively, decapitation can mean removing leadership: {The raid was meant to decapitate the organization}.

Decarbonisation is the process of reducing or eliminating carbon dioxide emissions, especially from energy production and industrial processes. The term dominates climate policy discussions: {The decarbonisation of the power grid requires massive investment in renewables}. Also spelled decarbonization. The verb is decarbonise.

Decarbonization is the process of reducing or eliminating carbon dioxide emissions, especially from energy production and industrial processes. The term dominates climate policy discussions: {The decarbonization of the power grid requires massive investment in renewables}. Industries, economies, and entire nations pursue decarbonization to slow global warming. Also spelled decarbonisation in British English.

Decarbonize means to reduce or eliminate carbon dioxide emissions, typically from industrial processes, energy production, or transportation. The term dominates climate policy discussions: {We need to decarbonize the economy by 2050}. To decarbonize a sector is to shift it away from fossil fuels toward renewable energy sources. Also spelled decarbonise in British English.

A decathlete is an athlete who competes in the decathlon, a grueling two-day track and field competition comprising ten events: sprints, hurdles, jumps, throws, and a distance race. The word emphasizes versatility over specialization—decathletes must be competent across radically different disciplines. {She trained as a decathlete throughout college.}

A decathlon is an athletic competition consisting of ten track and field events, completed by the same competitor over two days. Events include sprints, distance running, hurdles, jumping, and throwing disciplines. The decathlon tests all-around athletic ability: {He won the Olympic decathlon}. By extension, any grueling multi-part challenge: {The interview process was a decathlon}.

Decathlons is the plural of decathlon, an athletic competition comprising ten track and field events contested over two days. The events test speed, strength, and endurance: sprints, hurdles, jumps, throws, and a distance run. By extension, any grueling multi-part challenge might be called a decathlon: {The job interview was a decathlon of tests and panels}.

Decay is the process of rotting, breaking down, or deteriorating. Organic matter decays after death; teeth decay without care. The noun names either the process or its result: {the decay of fallen leaves}, {urban decay}. Extended meanings cover any gradual decline: {moral decay}, {the decay of democratic institutions}. In physics, radioactive decay is the spontaneous breakdown of unstable atomic nuclei.

Decayed describes something that has rotted, deteriorated, or broken down over time. Organic matter decays: {decayed teeth}, {decayed wood}, {the decayed remains of a animal}. The word extends to non-physical decline—a {decayed neighborhood} has fallen into disrepair, a {decayed empire} has crumbled from its former greatness.

Decaying describes the process of rotting, deteriorating, or breaking down. Organic matter decays after death: {the smell of decaying leaves}, {a decaying corpse}. Buildings and infrastructure decay from neglect: {decaying factories in the Rust Belt}. The word extends to abstract decline—decaying institutions, decaying standards, a decaying empire. In physics, radioactive materials decay as unstable atoms emit particles over time.

Decays is the verb decay in the third person singular. To decay is to break down gradually through natural processes—organic matter rots, buildings crumble, radioactive elements lose particles over time. The noun decay names this deterioration: {tooth decay}, {urban decay}, {the decay of old institutions}. What decays loses integrity, structure, or vitality: {The abandoned house decays a little more each year}.

Deceased means dead. The word appears most often in legal, medical, and formal contexts where "dead" might seem too blunt: {the deceased's estate}, {notify the next of kin of the deceased}. As a noun, the deceased refers to the dead person or persons: {The deceased left no will}. It's the preferred term in official documents, obituaries, and funeral contexts.

Deceit is the act or practice of deceiving—making someone believe what isn't true. It suggests deliberate dishonesty and cunning: {The scheme was built on deceit from the start}. Deceit implies sustained or strategic deception rather than a single lie. A person full of deceit is deceitful; what they do is deceptive.

Deceitful describes someone or something given to deception—deliberately misleading others through lies, trickery, or false appearances. A deceitful {person} makes a habit of dishonesty; a deceitful {smile} masks true intentions. The word suggests not just a single lie but a pattern or disposition: {He proved deceitful in all his business dealings}.

To deceive is to cause someone to believe something false—through lies, misleading statements, or strategic omission. You can deceive others or yourself: {She deceived herself into thinking everything was fine}. Appearances deceive when they create false impressions: {The calm surface deceived us about the current beneath}. Unlike lying, deception doesn't require explicit false statements—silence or misdirection suffices.

Deceived is the past tense of deceive, meaning to cause someone to believe something false. A deceived person has been misled or tricked: {She felt deceived when she learned the truth}. The word often carries emotional weight—being deceived implies a betrayal of trust, not just an error in information.

A deceiver is someone who misleads others through lies, false appearances, or manipulation. The word carries stronger moral weight than *liar*—a deceiver may use truth strategically or create elaborate illusions rather than simply stating falsehoods: {He was a master deceiver who had fooled everyone for years}. The term often appears in religious or literary contexts referring to tempters or con artists.

Deceivers are people who mislead others through lies, trickery, or false appearances. The word carries moral weight—deceivers act deliberately, not accidentally: {History's great deceivers understood human psychology}. A deceiver may be a con artist, an unfaithful spouse, or anyone who cultivates false impressions for personal gain.

Deceiving is the present participle of deceive, meaning to cause someone to believe something false. The word works as a verb form {He's been deceiving his wife for years} and as an adjective {deceiving appearances}. What's deceiving leads you away from truth—whether through outright lies, omissions, or misleading impressions.

Decency is behavior that conforms to accepted standards of propriety and morality. It encompasses respect for others, appropriate conduct, and basic human consideration: {Have the decency to call if you're going to be late}. The decencies are the requirements of respectable behavior. Decency also means modesty regarding the body—covering what shouldn't be exposed: {She waited until he had a towel on for decency's sake}.

Decent means meeting an acceptable standard—not excellent, but satisfactory: {The food was decent}. It describes behavior that conforms to moral standards or propriety: {a decent person}, {the decent thing to do}. Decent also means adequate or sufficient: {a decent salary}, {decent weather}. In casual use, {Are you decent?} asks whether someone is clothed enough to be seen.

Decentralisation is the distribution of power, authority, or functions away from a central location or governing body. Governments decentralise when they shift decision-making to regional or local authorities. Organisations decentralise by giving departments more autonomy. In technology, decentralised systems like blockchain operate without central control: {The movement toward decentralisation challenged traditional power structures}. Also spelled decentralization.

Decentralised is the British spelling of decentralized. To decentralise power, authority, or operations is to distribute them away from a single centre: {The company decentralised its management structure}. In technology, decentralised systems like blockchain operate without central control, with functions distributed across many nodes rather than concentrated in one authority.

Decentralization is the distribution of power, authority, or functions away from a central location or governing body. A company might pursue decentralization by giving regional offices more autonomy. In politics, decentralization shifts control from national to local governments. In technology, decentralized systems like blockchain operate without a central authority: {The appeal of cryptocurrency lies partly in its decentralization}.

To decentralize is to distribute power, functions, or resources away from a central authority. A government decentralizes when it shifts control to regional bodies. A company decentralizes by giving divisions more autonomy. In technology, decentralized systems like blockchain operate without central servers: {The currency is fully decentralized—no bank controls it}. The opposite of centralize.

Decentralized describes systems or organizations where control is distributed rather than concentrated in a single authority. A decentralized {government} shares power among regional bodies. Decentralized {currency} like Bitcoin operates without a central bank. The structure implies resilience—no single point of failure—but often slower decision-making: {The company's decentralized management made coordination difficult}.

Deception is the act of making someone believe something false. It covers lies, tricks, misdirection, and concealment—anything that leads another person away from the truth. A magician's deception entertains; a con artist's deception defrauds. {The deception was so complete that no one suspected him for years.} Self-deception is the trick of fooling yourself.

Deceptions are acts of deceiving—misleading someone into believing something false. The word covers everything from white lies to elaborate frauds: {The investigation revealed a series of financial deceptions}. A deception can also be the false impression itself: {The calm surface was a deception; underneath, the current was treacherous}.

Deceptive describes something that misleads or creates a false impression. A deceptive {appearance} conceals true nature; deceptive {advertising} makes products seem better than they are. Something can be deceptive without intent—{The calm surface was deceptive; strong currents ran beneath}. Deceptively is often ambiguous: a {deceptively simple} problem may be either harder or easier than it looks.

A decibel is a unit measuring the intensity of sound. The scale is logarithmic—each ten-decibel increase represents a tenfold increase in sound energy. Normal conversation runs about 60 decibels; a jet engine at close range exceeds 140. Decibels also measure signal strength in electronics and telecommunications: {The antenna boosts the signal by three decibels}.

Decibels are units for measuring the intensity of sound or the power of an electrical signal. The scale is logarithmic—each increase of ten decibels represents a tenfold increase in intensity. Normal conversation runs about 60 decibels; a rock concert might hit 120. Beyond technical use, decibels often just means volume or noise level: {Can you turn down the decibels?}

To decide is to make a choice or reach a conclusion after considering options: {I've decided to take the job}. The word implies settling a matter that was previously uncertain. A judge decides cases; a goal decides a match. Something that decides an outcome is the determining factor: {One vote decided the election}. The adjective decided means clear or unmistakable: {a decided advantage}.

Decided describes something clear and unmistakable, leaving no room for doubt: {a decided advantage}, {a decided improvement}. The word emphasizes definiteness—a decided opinion is firm, a decided tone brooks no argument. As the past tense of decide, it simply means a choice was made: {We decided to leave early}.

Decides is the third-person singular of decide—to make a choice or reach a conclusion after consideration. Someone decides what to do, where to go, or which option to take. A judge decides a case. The word often appears with whether or if: {She decides whether to stay or leave}. What decides an outcome is what settles or determines it: {One vote decides the election}.

Deciding functions as the present participle of decide, used both as a verb form and as an adjective meaning determinative or conclusive. A deciding {factor} tips the balance one way. The deciding {vote} breaks a tie. A deciding {game} determines the winner of a series. {We're still deciding where to eat.}

Deciduous describes trees and shrubs that shed their leaves annually, typically in autumn: {The deciduous forest blazed with color before winter}. The term contrasts with evergreen. In anatomy, deciduous teeth are baby teeth—the set that falls out to make way for permanent ones. The underlying idea is something designed to be shed.

Decimal relates to the base-ten number system, where each position represents a power of ten. A decimal point separates whole numbers from fractional parts: {The price was $19.99, two decimal places}. As a noun, a decimal is a number expressed this way: {Convert the fraction to a decimal}. Decimal can also mean proceeding by tens: {the decimal system of currency}.

Decimals is the plural of decimal, a number expressed in the base-ten system using a point to separate whole numbers from fractional parts: {The answer came out to three decimals}. In everyday speech, decimals often refers specifically to the digits after the decimal point: {Round to two decimals}, {The price is $19.99—just ignore the decimals}.

Decimate originally meant to kill one in ten—a Roman military punishment where soldiers drew lots and the unlucky tenth was executed by his comrades. Modern usage has drifted far from that precision. Now decimate means to destroy a large portion of something: {The plague decimated the population}. Purists object to this loosening, but the "destroy heavily" sense dominates contemporary English.

Decimated means severely reduced or destroyed. The word originally referred to the Roman military punishment of killing one in ten soldiers, but modern usage ignores this ratio—something decimated has been devastated, not reduced by exactly ten percent. {The population was decimated by disease.} {Budget cuts decimated the department.} Pedants insist on the historical meaning, but common usage has long since won.

Decimating is destroying or killing a large portion of something. The word originally meant executing one in ten soldiers as punishment, but modern usage has shifted toward near-total destruction: {The plague decimated the population}. Despite objections from traditionalists, decimating now typically suggests severe damage rather than precisely ten percent loss.

Decimation is severe destruction or reduction of something. The word originally referred to the Roman military practice of killing one in ten soldiers as collective punishment, but modern usage has shifted toward near-total destruction: {The decimation of the rainforest continues unchecked}. Purists object to this evolution, but the looser sense now dominates.

To decipher is to convert coded or obscured text into understandable form. You decipher encrypted messages, ancient scripts, or illegible handwriting. The word extends to making sense of anything puzzling: {I couldn't decipher his motives}. {She finally deciphered the doctor's scrawl on the prescription}.

Deciphered is the past tense of decipher, meaning to convert coded or obscure text into understandable form. Cryptographers deciphered enemy messages during wartime. The word extends to making sense of anything difficult to read or understand: {I finally deciphered his handwriting}, {Scientists deciphered the ancient inscription}.

Deciphering is the act of figuring out something obscure or hard to read. You might spend time deciphering a friend's handwriting, an ancient inscription, or someone's true intentions. The word implies working through confusion to extract meaning: {I spent an hour deciphering the instructions}. To decipher a code is to crack it—converting encrypted text back into readable form.

A decision is a choice made after consideration: {The decision to move was difficult}. It can also mean the act of deciding: {We need a decision by Friday}. Decision implies resolution—reaching a conclusion that ends deliberation. In sports, a decision is a victory determined by judges rather than knockout. Someone with decision acts firmly and without hesitation.

Decisions are choices made after consideration. The word emphasizes the act of settling on one option among alternatives: {We need to make a decision by Friday}. A decision can be formal and binding—a court decision, a business decision—or personal and everyday: {Her decision to move surprised everyone}. To reach a decision implies deliberation; to hand down a decision implies authority.

Decisive describes actions or people that settle matters conclusively. A decisive {victory} leaves no doubt about the outcome. A decisive {moment} determines what follows. A decisive person makes choices quickly and firmly, without wavering: {She's decisive—once she decides, she acts}. The opposite is indecisive or hesitant.

Decisiveness is the quality of being able to make decisions quickly and firmly. A decisive person doesn't waffle or second-guess—they assess the situation and commit to a course of action. {Her decisiveness in the crisis saved the company}. The trait is generally admired in leaders, though it can shade into recklessness when speed trumps deliberation.
clues: The trait of choosing without wavering

definition: A deck is a flat surface or platform. On a ship, the deck is the floor-like covering of the hull. A deck attached to a house is an outdoor platform, usually wooden. A deck of cards is a complete set, so named because cards were once stacked flat like ship planking. To deck someone is to knock them to the ground—to flatten them like a deck. To deck something out is to adorn it: {The hall was decked out for the holidays}. In music and broadcasting, a deck is equipment for playing recordings: {tape deck}, {cassette deck}.

Deckbuilding is the process of assembling a personalized deck of cards for a game, selecting from a larger pool to create a coherent strategy. The term appears in two contexts: constructing a deck before play begins {I spent hours deckbuilding for the tournament}, and games where building the deck is the central mechanic, with players acquiring cards during play itself. The practice blends preparation, strategy, and personal expression.

A deckchair is a portable folding chair with a fabric seat stretched between a wooden or metal frame, designed for lounging outdoors. Originally associated with ocean liners, deckchairs now appear on beaches, patios, and lawns. {We set up deckchairs in the garden}. To {rearrange the deckchairs on the Titanic} is to make futile gestures while disaster looms.

Deckchairs are folding chairs with a wooden frame and fabric seat, designed for lounging outdoors—originally on the decks of ocean liners, now common at beaches and in gardens. The phrase {rearranging deckchairs on the Titanic} describes futile efforts to address minor details while ignoring catastrophic problems.

Decked has two main senses. To be decked is to be adorned or decorated: {The halls were decked with holly}. In informal use, to deck someone is to knock them down with a punch: {He decked the guy with one hit}. The past tense works both ways—festively decorated or flat on the ground.

A deckhand is a crew member on a ship or boat who performs general labor on deck—handling lines, maintaining equipment, assisting with cargo, and keeping the vessel clean. The position is entry-level in maritime work: {He started as a deckhand on a fishing boat before earning his captain's license}.

Deckhands are crew members who perform manual labor on a ship or boat. They handle lines, maintain equipment, clean decks, and assist with cargo or fishing operations. The term applies broadly from commercial fishing vessels to cruise ships to oil rigs. {The deckhands secured the mooring lines as we pulled into port.}

Decking is the material used to build a deck—the flat outdoor platform attached to a house. The term covers both the planks themselves and the surface they create: {composite decking}, {We need to replace the decking}. Separately, decking is slang for punching someone hard enough to knock them down: {He got arrested for decking a bouncer}.

Decks is the plural of deck and the third-person singular verb form. A deck is a flat surface—the floor-like platform on a ship, a wooden structure attached to a house, or a pack of playing cards. To deck someone is to knock them down with a punch: {He decked him with one blow}. To deck something out is to decorate it: {The halls were decked with holly}.

A declaration is a formal announcement or statement, often with official or legal weight: {a declaration of war}, {the Declaration of Independence}. To make a declaration is to state something clearly and deliberately, whether in court, at customs, or in everyday speech: {She made a declaration of her intentions}. The word implies something spoken or written with purpose, not casually mentioned.

Declarations are formal statements or announcements, often with official weight. A {declaration of war} announces hostilities. A {declaration of independence} proclaims sovereignty. In legal contexts, declarations are sworn statements or assertions of fact. In programming, a declaration introduces a variable or function to the compiler. The word often implies something proclaimed publicly and with conviction: {a declaration of love}.

To declare is to state something formally or emphatically: {declare war}, {declare bankruptcy}, {declare your love}. At customs, you declare goods you're bringing into a country. In card games, you declare by announcing what you'll play or bid. A declarative statement asserts rather than questions. {I have nothing to declare but my genius.}

Declared describes something openly stated or officially announced. A declared {major} is one formally registered with a university. A declared {candidate} has publicly announced their intention to run. The word often implies commitment or formality: {a declared enemy}, {a declared state of emergency}. Self-declared means proclaimed by oneself rather than recognized by others: {a self-declared expert}.

Declaring is the act of announcing or stating something formally or emphatically. You might be declaring independence, declaring bankruptcy, or declaring your love. At customs, declaring means reporting goods you're bringing into a country. In card games, declaring names the trump suit or announces a winning hand: {After declaring hearts, she laid down her cards}.

Declassification is the removal of secret or confidential status from government documents, making them available to the public. The process typically follows set procedures and time periods: {The declassification of Cold War files revealed decades of covert operations}. Declassified materials often generate news when they expose previously hidden government actions.

Declassified describes information, documents, or materials that were once secret but have been officially released for public access. Governments declassify records after a set period or when secrecy is no longer deemed necessary: {The CIA declassified files from the Cold War era}. The opposite is classified.

To declassify is to remove the classification status from a document or piece of information, making it available to the public. Governments classify materials as secret, top secret, or confidential; declassification reverses that designation. {The CIA declassified thousands of Cold War documents}. The noun is declassification.

To declaw is to surgically remove an animal's claws, most commonly a cat's. The procedure is controversial—critics call it painful and unnecessary, akin to amputation. Figuratively, to declaw someone or something is to render them harmless by removing their power or means of resistance: {The new regulations effectively declawed the oversight committee}.

Declawed describes an animal, typically a cat, that has had its claws surgically removed. The procedure is controversial—banned in many countries as inhumane since it amputates the last bone of each toe. Figuratively, declawed means rendered harmless or stripped of power: {The amendment left the bill declawed}. A declawed critic or opponent has lost their ability to do damage.

Declawing is the surgical removal of an animal's claws, most commonly performed on cats. The procedure actually amputates the last bone of each toe, not just the nail. Once routine, declawing is now widely considered inhumane and has been banned in many countries and some U.S. jurisdictions. Veterinary organizations increasingly oppose it except for rare medical necessity. {The shelter won't adopt cats to people who plan on declawing them.}

Decline is movement downward or away from a peak. A civilization declines, health declines, prices decline. To decline an invitation or offer is to turn it down: {She declined to comment}. As a noun, decline names the downward trend itself: {the decline of the Roman Empire}, {a decline in sales}. In grammar, to decline a noun or adjective is to list its inflected forms—cases, genders, numbers.

Declined is the past tense of decline, covering all its senses. Something that declined went downward or diminished: {Sales declined sharply in the fourth quarter}. To have declined an offer or invitation is to have refused it politely: {She declined to comment}. In grammar, a noun or adjective that declined was inflected for case, number, or gender.

Declines covers refusal and downward movement. To decline an invitation or offer is to say no politely: {She declined to comment}. Declines also names downward trends—a decline in {health}, in {profits}, in {influence}. {The Roman Empire's decline took centuries}. As a verb, to decline is to diminish or deteriorate: {His strength declined after the surgery}.

Declining describes something growing smaller, weaker, or less vital over time. A declining {population} is shrinking; declining {health} is worsening. To decline is to refuse politely: {She declined the invitation}. A decline is the process or state of diminishing: {the decline of the Roman Empire}, {a decline in sales}.

To declutter is to remove unnecessary items from a space, making it tidier and more organized: {I spent Saturday decluttering the garage}. The word extends beyond physical spaces to mental or digital cleanup: {declutter your inbox}, {declutter your schedule}. Decluttering often implies not just tidying but deciding what to keep and what to discard.

Decluttered describes a space that has had excess items removed, leaving it organized and uncluttered: {The decluttered closet felt spacious again}. As a verb form, it means performed the act of clearing out unnecessary possessions: {She decluttered her apartment over the weekend}. The concept has gained currency alongside minimalism and organizational movements.

Decluttering is the process of removing unnecessary items from a space—clearing out closets, drawers, garages, or entire homes. The word emerged alongside minimalist lifestyle trends and organizing methods: {I spent the weekend decluttering the garage}. It extends to non-physical domains: decluttering your schedule, your inbox, your mind.

Deco is an informal shortening of art deco, the decorative style of the 1920s and 30s characterized by bold geometric forms, rich colors, and lavish ornamentation: {The building has gorgeous deco details}, {a deco lamp}. The clipped form appears frequently in design and real estate contexts. (Capitalized Deco is a variant spelling.)

To decode is to convert something from a coded form back into its original or understandable form—the opposite of encode. You decode a secret message, a scrambled signal, or encrypted data. The meaning extends to interpreting anything obscure or puzzling: {I'm still trying to decode what she meant by that comment}. A decoder is a device or person that decodes.

Decoded is the past tense of decode—to convert something from coded form back to its original meaning. A spy decodes an encrypted message; a scientist decodes DNA sequences; software decodes compressed files. Figuratively, to decode something is to interpret or make sense of it: {I'm still trying to decode what she meant by that comment}.

A decoder is a device or program that converts encoded information back into its original form. A cable decoder unscrambles television signals. An audio decoder processes compressed sound files. In electronics, a decoder converts coded inputs into distinct outputs. The term extends to anything that interprets or makes sense of obscure information: {He was a decoder of ancient scripts}.

Decoders are devices or programs that convert encoded information back into usable form. A cable decoder unscrambles television signals. In computing, audio and video decoders translate compressed files into playable media. A person who interprets coded messages or complex information is also a decoder: {cryptographers and decoders worked around the clock}. The term extends to anything that helps make sense of obscure content: {a decoder ring for corporate jargon}.

Decoding is the process of converting encoded information back into its original or usable form. A computer decodes data; a spy decodes intercepted messages; a reader decodes words on a page into meaning. The term applies broadly—from cryptography to linguistics to simply interpreting signals: {I'm still decoding what she meant by that comment}.

Decolletage is the low-cut neckline of a dress or top, or the area of the neck, shoulders, and upper chest it exposes. The word is French and carries a sense of elegance or formality: {Her decolletage was adorned with a pearl necklace}. The term often appears in fashion writing or when describing evening wear.

Decolonisation is the process by which colonies gain independence from colonial powers, or more broadly, the dismantling of colonial systems and their lasting effects. The term covers both the historical wave of independence movements in the mid-twentieth century and ongoing efforts to undo colonial legacies in institutions, culture, and thought: {decolonising the curriculum}, {the decolonisation of Africa}. Also spelled decolonization.

Decolonise (also decolonize) means to free from colonial status—granting independence to a territory previously ruled by a foreign power. The term extends to removing colonial influence from institutions, curricula, or ways of thinking: {efforts to decolonise the university curriculum}, {decolonising the mind}. This broader sense involves questioning whose perspectives, histories, and values are centred in any system.

Decolonization is the process by which colonies gain independence from imperial powers, or more broadly, the dismantling of colonial systems and their effects. The term covers both political independence—{African decolonization accelerated in the 1960s}—and ongoing efforts to undo colonial legacies in institutions, education, and culture: {decolonization of the curriculum}, {decolonization of museums}. The word implies not just ending foreign rule but actively reversing its lasting impacts.

Decolonize means to free from colonial status—when a territory gains independence from an occupying power: {Algeria decolonized from France in 1962}. More recently, the word has extended to removing colonial influences from institutions, curricula, or ways of thinking: {efforts to decolonize the museum's collection}, {decolonize your bookshelf}. This newer sense is sometimes criticized as overreach.

Decolonizing is the process of undoing colonial influence—politically, culturally, or intellectually. A colony decolonizes when it gains independence from imperial rule. More recently, the term describes efforts to remove colonial perspectives from institutions: {decolonizing the curriculum}, {decolonizing the museum}. This newer sense focuses on centering indigenous or non-Western knowledge and dismantling assumptions inherited from colonial power structures.

To decommission something is to officially remove it from active service—typically military equipment, nuclear facilities, or industrial infrastructure. A decommissioned {aircraft carrier} may become a museum; a decommissioned {power plant} must be safely dismantled. The process often involves extensive protocols: {The reactor took fifteen years to fully decommission}.

Decommissioned describes something officially removed from active service or operation. Military equipment gets decommissioned when no longer needed: {a decommissioned aircraft carrier}. Nuclear plants are decommissioned through careful dismantling. The term implies formal retirement rather than simple abandonment—paperwork and procedures, not just walking away.

Decommissioning is the process of taking something out of active service—typically military equipment, nuclear facilities, or industrial infrastructure. A decommissioned warship is retired from duty. Decommissioning a nuclear plant involves shutting it down, removing fuel, and managing radioactive materials: {The decommissioning process will take decades and cost billions}.

To decompose is to break down into simpler components. Organic matter decomposes through bacterial action: {The body had been decomposing for weeks}. In chemistry, compounds decompose into their constituent elements. The word extends to analysis: mathematicians decompose problems into manageable parts. Decomposition is the noun.

Decomposed describes organic matter that has broken down through decay. A decomposed body has rotted; decomposed leaves become soil. The word applies to anything that has undergone decomposition: {The remains were too decomposed to identify}. In technical contexts, decomposed can mean broken into component parts: {The signal was decomposed into its frequencies}.

A decomposer is an organism that breaks down dead organic matter—bacteria, fungi, and certain insects that feed on decaying plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil. In ecology, decomposers are essential to nutrient cycling: {Without decomposers, dead matter would accumulate endlessly}. The term extends loosely to anything that breaks down complex material into simpler components.

Decomposers are organisms that break down dead organic matter, returning nutrients to the soil. Bacteria, fungi, and certain invertebrates like earthworms and beetles perform this role in ecosystems. Without decomposers, dead plants and animals would accumulate and essential elements would remain locked in unusable forms: {Decomposers are nature's recyclers}.

Decomposes means to break down into simpler parts or elements. Organic matter decomposes through bacterial action: {The fallen leaves decompose into rich soil}. In chemistry, compounds decompose into constituent elements. The word also applies to analysis—decomposing a problem into manageable pieces. A decomposing body is one in the process of decay.

Decomposing describes the process of breaking down into simpler components. Organic matter decomposes through bacterial action: {The body was already decomposing when they found it}. The word applies to any gradual disintegration—a decomposing marriage, decomposing infrastructure. In technical contexts, decomposing means separating into constituent parts: {decomposing a complex problem into manageable steps}.

Decomposition is the process of breaking down into component parts or simpler substances. Organic matter decomposes after death—bacteria and fungi reduce dead plants and animals to basic elements: {The body was in an advanced state of decomposition}. In chemistry and mathematics, decomposition means separating a compound or problem into constituents. The verb is decompose.

To decompress is to release pressure or return to normal pressure after being compressed. Divers decompress gradually when ascending to avoid the bends. Files decompress when extracted from compressed formats like ZIP. Figuratively, to decompress is to relax after stress or intensity: {I need a few hours to decompress after that meeting}.

Decompressed describes something that has been released from pressure or compression. Data files are decompressed when restored to their original size after being compressed for storage or transfer: {Wait for the files to be decompressed before opening them}. Physically, a diver who has decompressed has undergone gradual pressure reduction to prevent the bends. Informally, someone who has decompressed has unwound after stress: {I decompressed with a long bath after the interview}.

Decompressing is the process of returning to normal pressure or releasing built-up tension. Divers decompress gradually to avoid the bends. Compressed digital files decompress when opened. Most commonly, decompressing means unwinding after stress: {I spent the weekend decompressing after finals}. The word suggests a necessary period of recovery before resuming normal activity.

Decompression is the release or reduction of pressure. Divers must decompress slowly when surfacing to avoid dangerous gas bubbles forming in the blood. The word extends to any process of releasing built-up tension: {I need some decompression time after that meeting}. In computing, decompression is the restoration of compressed files to their original size.

A decongestant is a medication that relieves nasal congestion by shrinking swollen blood vessels in the nasal passages.
