In older slang, to dig something means to understand or appreciate it: {I really dig jazz}. A dig can be a critical remark: {He got in a few digs about her cooking}. In archaeology, a dig is an excavation site.
Digeridoo, originally spelled didgeridoo, is a word that arose from the sounds that the instrument makes.

Digest centers on breaking down and absorbing. The body digests food, extracting nutrients. The mind digests information, processing it into understanding: {Give me time to digest this news}. As a noun, a digest is a condensed summary of longer material—already broken down for easier consumption: {a weekly news digest}, {Reader's Digest}.

Digesting is the process of breaking down food in the body so nutrients can be absorbed. The word extends to mental processing: {I'm still digesting the news}. Something difficult to accept is {hard to digest}. A digest is a summary or compilation of information, condensed for easier absorption—the same idea applied to text rather than food.

Digestion is the body's process of breaking down food into nutrients that can be absorbed and used. The stomach and intestines handle most digestion, converting what you eat into energy and building blocks for cells. The word extends to mental processing: {I need time for digestion of all this new information}. Something's digestibility is how easily it can be digested.

Digestive relates to the process of breaking down food in the body so it can be absorbed and used for energy. The digestive {system} includes organs from mouth to intestines. A digestive {biscuit}, common in British English, is a slightly sweet whole-wheat cookie originally marketed as an aid to digestion, though it has no special digestive properties. Something that aids digestion may also be called a digestive: {an after-dinner digestive}.

Digestives are a type of British biscuit, round and semi-sweet, made with whole wheat flour. Originally marketed in the 19th century with claims about aiding digestion—claims now considered dubious—they remain enormously popular in the UK, often enjoyed with tea or coated in chocolate. The term also functions as an adjective relating to digestion: {digestive enzymes}, {digestive tract}. As a noun in this sense, a digestive is something that aids digestion, such as an after-dinner drink.

Digests works as both verb and noun around the idea of breaking down and absorbing. The body digests food, extracting nutrients. The mind digests information, processing it into understanding: {Give me time to digest the news}. A digest is a condensed summary—information broken into manageable form: {a weekly news digest}, {Reader's Digest}.

A digger is a person or machine that digs—excavates earth or other material. Gold diggers once dug for gold; now the term usually means someone who pursues relationships for money. In Australian and New Zealand English, digger is an informal term for a soldier, originally from World War I, and extends to a friendly form of address between men: {How ya going, digger?}

Diggers are people who dig—whether laborers excavating earth, archaeologists uncovering artifacts, or anyone working with a shovel. In Australian and New Zealand slang, digger is an informal term for a soldier, originally from World War I, now extended to mean friend or mate: {G'day, digger}. Gold diggers seek gold, or metaphorically, wealthy partners.

Digging is the act of breaking up and moving earth or other material, typically with a shovel or hands. The word extends to any vigorous excavating motion: {digging through old boxes in the attic}. In informal use, digging can mean strongly liking or appreciating something: {I'm really digging this new album}.

A digit is a finger or toe—humans have twenty digits total. Because we count on our fingers, digit also means any numeral from 0 through 9: {a four-digit PIN}, {the last four digits of your phone number}. The digital age takes its name from the discrete digits that encode all computer data.

Digital relates to fingers or to numerical digits. In computing, digital describes information stored as discrete numerical values—typically ones and zeros—as opposed to analog's continuous signals. Digital technology has transformed how we create, store, and share information: {digital photography}, {digital music}, {the digital age}. A digital clock displays numerals rather than hands. In medicine, a digital exam uses fingers: {a digital rectal exam}.

Digitize means to convert something into digital form—translating analog information into the ones and zeros that computers can process. You digitize old photographs by scanning them, vinyl records by recording them as audio files, paper documents by creating PDFs. The process preserves and often improves access: {The library is digitizing its entire archive}. Digitization has transformed how we store, share, and interact with information.

Digitizing is converting information into digital form—turning analog sources like paper documents, photographs, film, or audio recordings into computer-readable data. Libraries digitize archives for preservation and access. Musicians digitize vinyl records. The process involves scanning, sampling, or encoding: {We're digitizing all our old family photos}. Also spelled digitising in British English.

Digits are the fingers and toes—the ten appendages at the ends of hands and feet. In mathematics, digits are the numerals 0 through 9, the basic symbols for writing numbers. The connection is ancient: humans counted on their fingers. In slang, {Can I get your digits?} asks for a phone number.

Dignified describes someone or something showing calm self-respect and seriousness of manner. A dignified {response} to criticism doesn't stoop to pettiness. A dignified {ceremony} maintains appropriate gravity. The word suggests composure and restraint—not flashy or attention-seeking, but quietly commanding respect: {She made a dignified exit despite the chaos}.

To dignify something is to give it dignity or importance, often more than it deserves. {I won't dignify that question with a response} implies the question is too absurd or offensive to merit serious engagement. A dignified manner is calm, composed, and worthy of respect. To dignify an event is to honor it with one's presence: {The mayor dignified the ceremony by attending}.

Dignitaries are people of high rank or distinction, especially those holding official positions of authority. The term typically applies to government officials, diplomats, religious leaders, or other VIPs at formal events: {Foreign dignitaries attended the state funeral}. The word carries a ceremonial quality—you're more likely to hear it at summits and galas than in everyday conversation.

A dignitary is a person who holds a high rank or office, especially in government, religion, or diplomacy. The word emphasizes the formal importance of the position rather than the individual: {Foreign dignitaries attended the state funeral}. Dignitaries typically receive special treatment at official events—reserved seating, formal introductions, security details. The term can sound slightly stiff or ceremonial, which is why it appears more often in news coverage than in casual conversation.

Dignity is the quality of being worthy of respect or honor. It suggests composed self-possession and seriousness of manner: {She accepted the award with dignity}. To stand on one's dignity is to insist on being treated respectfully. Dignity also names the inherent worth of human beings: {human dignity}, {die with dignity}. Something beneath your dignity is too lowly for you to do.

To digress is to wander from the main subject in speech or writing: {I digress, but this reminds me of a story}. The word acknowledges a temporary departure before returning to the point. A digression is such a departure—sometimes apologized for, sometimes deliberately indulged: {Allow me a brief digression}.

Digressing is departing from the main subject in speech or writing, wandering into tangential territory before (usually) returning to the point: {I'm digressing, but this reminds me of something}. The participle often appears as a self-aware aside: {Digressing for a moment, let me mention...} A person who digresses frequently may lose their audience or never finish a thought.

A digression is a departure from the main subject in speech or writing. Someone telling a story might pause to explain background, then say {But I digress} before returning to the point. Digressions can enrich or derail, depending on their length and relevance. The verb is digress.

Digressions are departures from the main subject in speech or writing. A lecturer might wander into personal anecdotes before returning to the topic; a novel might include chapters that stray from the central plot. The word carries mild disapproval—digressions waste time—but some are welcome: {His digressions were more interesting than his main points}.

Digs is informal for lodgings or living quarters, especially rented rooms: {I found some new digs near campus}, {Nice digs you've got here}. The word often carries a casual, temporary connotation—student housing, a first apartment. In British usage particularly, digs traditionally meant rented rooms in a private house with meals provided by the landlady.

A dike is an embankment built to hold back water and prevent flooding, especially in low-lying coastal areas: {The Dutch have maintained dikes for centuries}. Dike also means a long mass of igneous rock that cuts through other rock formations. As a verb, to dike is to build such barriers. Separately, dyke (also spelled dike) is slang for a lesbian, often derogatory when used by outsiders but sometimes reclaimed within the community.

Dikes are embankments built to hold back water and prevent flooding, especially along rivers or coastlines: {The dikes of the Netherlands reclaim land from the sea}. A dike can also be a ditch or channel for drainage. In geology, a dike is a sheet of rock that cuts across existing formations. The spelling dyke is common outside American English. (Lowercase dykes as slang for lesbians is covered separately.)

Dilapidated describes something fallen into disrepair through age or neglect. Buildings are most often dilapidated—roofs sagging, paint peeling, foundations crumbling: {a dilapidated farmhouse at the edge of town}. The word suggests decay over time rather than sudden damage, and carries a sense of former solidity now compromised.

Dilapidation is the state of being run-down or fallen into disrepair through neglect or age. Buildings, infrastructure, and other structures fall into dilapidation when maintenance stops: {The old factory had reached an advanced state of dilapidation}. The word suggests gradual decay rather than sudden damage—a process of deterioration over time.

Dilation is the act of expanding or widening something, or the state of being expanded. In medicine, it typically refers to the enlargement of an opening or hollow structure: {The doctor checked for cervical dilation during labor}, {The eye drops cause pupil dilation}. In mathematics, dilation is a transformation that enlarges or reduces a figure while preserving its shape. The word can also describe expansion more broadly: {time dilation in physics}, {the dilation of blood vessels}.

A dildo is a penis-shaped object used for sexual penetration. Dildos are typically made of silicone, rubber, glass, or other materials and come in various sizes. The word is straightforward rather than vulgar—it's the standard term used in sex shops, medical contexts, and casual conversation alike: {She bought a dildo online}. As an insult, dildo calls someone stupid or contemptible: {Don't be such a dildo}.

Dildos is the plural of dildo, a sex toy shaped like an erect penis, designed for vaginal or anal penetration. Dildos come in various sizes, shapes, and materials, and unlike vibrators, they don't typically have motorized components. The word is also used as a vulgar insult to call someone stupid or contemptible: {Those dildos couldn't find their way out of a paper bag}.

A dilemma is a situation requiring a choice between two options, both of which are undesirable or mutually exclusive. The classic dilemma forces you to pick the lesser of two evils: {She faced the dilemma of reporting her friend's theft or staying silent and being complicit}. In casual use, dilemma often just means a difficult decision or problem, though purists insist the word should involve exactly two alternatives. The phrase {on the horns of a dilemma} captures the sense of being caught between two equally painful choices.

Dilemmas is the plural of dilemma—a situation requiring a choice between equally undesirable alternatives. A classic dilemma offers two options, both with significant drawbacks: {She faced the dilemma of telling the truth and hurting her friend, or lying to protect her}. The word has loosened to mean any difficult decision: {I'm in a dilemma about which job offer to accept}.

A dilettante dabbles in a field—usually the arts—without serious commitment or deep expertise. The word carries condescension: a dilettante lacks the discipline of a true practitioner. {He dismissed her as a dilettante who'd never put in the work}. Originally more neutral, suggesting a lover of the arts, the modern sense emphasizes superficiality.

Diligence is careful, persistent effort toward a task or goal. It suggests thoroughness and steady attention rather than bursts of enthusiasm: {She reviewed the contract with diligence}. Due diligence is the reasonable investigation expected before entering a business transaction or making a decision: {The investors conducted due diligence before the acquisition}.
clues: The habit of thorough, sustained labor

definition: Diligent describes someone who works with careful, persistent effort. A diligent student does assignments thoroughly; a diligent researcher checks every source. The word implies conscientiousness rather than mere speed—steady attention to detail over time: {Through diligent practice, she mastered the piano}. Diligence is the noun.

Dill is an herb with feathery leaves and a distinctive tangy flavor, used fresh or dried in cooking. It pairs especially well with fish, pickles, and potatoes: {dill pickles}, {salmon with dill}. The seeds are also used as a spice. Dill weed refers specifically to the leaves.

To dillydally is to waste time through indecision or aimless dawdling: {Stop dillydallying and make up your mind}. The word suggests puttering about when you should be acting—not quite laziness, but a failure to get on with things. Also spelled dilly-dally.

Dillydallying is wasting time through indecision or aimless delay. The word suggests puttering, hesitating, or dawdling when action is needed: {Stop dillydallying and get dressed—we're going to be late}. It carries a mildly scolding tone, often directed at children or anyone moving too slowly.

To dilute is to make something weaker by adding water or another substance: {dilute the juice with water}, {dilute the paint until it flows smoothly}. The word extends to weakening anything: dilute someone's {influence}, dilute the {impact} of a message. As an adjective, dilute describes something already weakened: {a dilute solution}, {a dilute version of the original proposal}.

Diluted describes something weakened by the addition of water or another substance. A diluted {solution} has less active ingredient per volume than a concentrated one. The word extends to anything diminished in force or intensity: diluted {authority}, diluted {impact}. {The scandal diluted his influence in the party.}

Diluting is making something weaker or less concentrated by adding another substance, typically water or another liquid: {diluting the juice with water}, {diluting the paint to the right consistency}. The term extends to weakening anything: diluting someone's influence, diluting the impact of a message, diluting a brand by overextension.

Dilution is the process of making something weaker or less concentrated by adding more of a solvent, typically water: {The dilution of the chemical made it safe to handle}. The term extends to anything that gets watered down or diminished in strength—{dilution of voting power}, {dilution of brand value}. In finance, share dilution occurs when a company issues new stock, reducing existing shareholders' ownership percentage.

Dim describes low light—not dark, but poorly illuminated: {a dim hallway}, {the dim glow of a candle}. By extension, dim applies to things hard to perceive or remember: {a dim outline}, {dim memories of childhood}. A dim view is unfavorable: {She takes a dim view of his excuses}. Calling someone dim suggests they're slow-witted. To dim is to reduce brightness: {Dim the lights}.

A dime is a U.S. coin worth ten cents, one-tenth of a dollar. Because it's the smallest U.S. coin in circulation, dime suggests something tiny or insignificant: {a dime a dozen} means common and cheap. To {turn on a dime} is to change direction instantly. To {drop a dime} is to make a phone call, especially to inform on someone—from the days when pay phones cost ten cents.

Dimension is a measurable extent—length, width, height, depth, or time. The dimensions of a room are its measurements. In physics, the fourth dimension is time; in science fiction, alternate dimensions are parallel realities. Figuratively, dimension means an aspect or facet: {The scandal added a new dimension to the campaign}. Something with dimension has depth or substance: {a character with real dimension}.

Dimensions are measurable extents—length, width, height, depth. A box has three dimensions; a line has one. The dimensions of something are its measurements: {What are the dimensions of the room?} Figuratively, dimensions are aspects or facets: {The scandal took on new dimensions}. A fourth dimension typically means time, or in fiction, a parallel realm.
Dimes is the plural of dime, the name for a ten-cent coin in the U.S. and Canada.
clues: Ten of these make one dollar

definition: Dimestore refers to a type of variety store that sold inexpensive merchandise, originally for five or ten cents. These stores—Woolworth's being the most famous—were retail fixtures in American towns through most of the twentieth century. As an adjective, dimestore suggests cheapness or shoddiness: {dimestore jewelry}, {a dimestore novel}. The word carries nostalgic connotations even as it implies low quality.

Dimestores, also spelled dime stores, are retail shops selling inexpensive merchandise—the kind where nothing costs much. The term comes from stores where items originally sold for five or ten cents. As an adjective, dimestore suggests something cheap or inferior: {dimestore psychology}, {a dimestore novel}. The format has largely given way to dollar stores.

To diminish is to make or become smaller, fewer, or less important. Light diminishes at dusk. Pain diminishes over time. Authority can be diminished by scandal. The word often implies gradual reduction rather than sudden loss: {His influence diminished as rivals gained power}. To diminish someone is to belittle them or make them seem less significant.

Diminished means reduced or made smaller in size, importance, or intensity. A diminished {role} carries less significance than before; diminished {capacity} suggests impaired ability. In music, a diminished chord or interval has been lowered by a half step. The word often implies something once greater: {His influence was greatly diminished after the scandal}.

Diminishing describes something becoming smaller, fewer, or less significant over time. A diminishing {supply} is running low. The law of diminishing {returns} holds that adding more of something eventually yields smaller gains. Diminishing can suggest gradual decline toward insignificance: {His influence was diminishing by the day}.

Diminuendo is a musical term for a gradual decrease in volume—the opposite of crescendo. As a direction in sheet music, it tells performers to get progressively softer. The word extends to any gradual fading or tapering off: {The argument ended in a diminuendo of muttered complaints}. Also used as a noun for a passage played this way.

Dimmed describes light or brightness that has been reduced or softened. A dimmed {lamp} casts less light; dimmed {headlights} are set to low beam. The word extends to anything that has lost intensity or clarity: dimmed {hopes}, dimmed {memories}, a dimmed {reputation}. Eyes can be dimmed by tears or age. {The theater lights dimmed before the show began.}

A dimmer is a device that controls the brightness of a light, typically a dial or sliding switch that reduces the electrical current: {Install a dimmer in the dining room for ambiance}. As an adjective, dimmer is the comparative form of dim—less bright, less clear, or less intelligent: {The stars grew dimmer as dawn approached}, {not the dimmer of the two students}.

Dimming is the process of becoming or making less bright. Lights dim at the theater before a show; stars dim as dawn approaches. The word extends to anything that fades or lessens in intensity: {dimming hopes}, {dimming memories}, {the dimming of her enthusiasm}. As a noun, it often refers to controlled light reduction: {smart dimming}, {automatic dimming}.
clues: Gradually becoming less and less bright

definition: A dimple is a small natural indentation in the flesh, especially the kind that appears in the cheeks or chin when someone smiles. The word extends to any small depression in a surface: {dimples on a golf ball}, {dimples in sheet metal}. As a verb, to dimple is to form such indentations: {Her cheeks dimpled when she laughed}.

Dimpled describes something marked by small natural indentations, especially in skin or a surface. A dimpled {smile} shows the slight depressions that form in some people's cheeks. A dimpled {chin} has a small cleft. Golf balls are dimpled to improve aerodynamics. The word suggests charm when applied to faces: {her dimpled cheeks}.

Dimples are small natural indentations in the flesh, most often in the cheeks or chin. Cheek dimples appear when smiling and are generally considered attractive: {Her dimples showed when she laughed}. The word extends to any small depression in a surface—golf balls have dimples to improve aerodynamics. As a verb, to dimple is to form such indentations: {The rain dimpled the pond's surface}.

A dimwit is a stupid person—someone whose mental light burns low. The word is insulting but relatively mild, more dismissive than vicious: {Don't be such a dimwit}. The adjective dimwitted describes slow or foolish thinking: {a dimwitted plan}.

Dimwits is the plural of dimwit—a person regarded as stupid or slow-witted. The word combines dim (not bright) with wit (intelligence), making the insult transparent. It's milder than harsher terms for stupidity, often used with exasperated affection: {Those dimwits left the gate open again}.

Din is a loud, prolonged, and unpleasant noise—the kind that makes conversation difficult or thought impossible. A {din of voices} filled the crowded restaurant. Construction creates a din. Unlike mere loudness, din suggests confusion or chaos in the sound. To din something into someone is to instill it through constant repetition: {My parents dinned good manners into me}.

Dine means to eat a meal, typically dinner, often with connotations of formality or leisure. You dine at a restaurant rather than grab a quick bite; you dine with colleagues rather than eat with them. {We dined at a lovely French bistro.} To dine out is to eat at a restaurant rather than at home. If you dine on something, you eat it as a meal: {We dined on fresh lobster.} The phrase dine and dash describes leaving a restaurant without paying.

A diner is a person who dines, but the word more often names a type of American restaurant—informal, inexpensive, serving simple fare like burgers, eggs, and coffee. The classic diner has a long counter with stools, booths along the windows, and operates long hours: {We stopped at a diner for breakfast at 3 a.m.}

Diners is the plural of diner—a person eating a meal, especially at a restaurant: {The diners complained about the slow service}. A diner is also a small, informal restaurant, typically with counter seating and an extensive menu of American comfort food: {We stopped at a roadside diner for coffee and pie}. The classic American diner often occupies a converted railroad car or imitates that aesthetic.

A dinette is a small dining area, typically a nook or alcove in a kitchen or apartment too small for a full dining room. The term also refers to a compact table-and-chairs set designed for such spaces: {The breakfast dinette seats four}. In recreational vehicles and boats, a dinette is a booth-style seating arrangement that often converts to a bed.

Ding is the sound of a bell or similar metallic ring—short, clear, and high-pitched: {The elevator gave a ding}. It extends to any brief alert tone: {My phone dinged with a notification}. To ding something is to make a small dent or nick: {I dinged the car door in the parking lot}. A ding can also be a minor negative mark against someone: {That mistake was a ding on his record}.

A dingaling is a foolish or scatterbrained person—someone not quite all there: {Don't be such a dingaling}. The word evokes the light, empty sound of a small bell, suggesting a head with nothing solid inside. It remains a mild, almost affectionate insult, more playful than cutting. Also spelled ding-a-ling.

A dingbat is a stupid or scatterbrained person: {Don't be such a dingbat}. The word is mildly dismissive rather than harsh. In typography, dingbats are decorative symbols and ornaments—stars, arrows, checkmarks—used to embellish or separate text. The connection between the meanings is unclear; both emerged in American English in the early twentieth century.

Dingbats are typographical ornaments and symbols—stars, arrows, pointing hands, decorative flourishes—used to separate sections or add visual interest to printed text. The term also means a foolish or scatterbrained person: {Don't be such a dingbat}. In architecture, a dingbat is a boxy, unadorned apartment building, common in mid-20th-century Los Angeles.
clues: Those with heads full of air

definition: Dingdong imitates the sound of a bell, especially a doorbell: {Dingdong! Trick or treat!} As a noun, it's a ringing sound or, informally, a foolish person: {Don't be such a dingdong}. A dingdong battle or argument is one where advantage shifts back and forth, like a bell swinging between strikes.

Dinged is the past tense of ding, which means to make a light ringing sound or to cause minor damage. A car gets dinged in a parking lot when it picks up a small dent or scratch. More broadly, dinged means damaged or penalized: {My credit score got dinged when I missed a payment}. {The report dinged the company for poor safety practices}.

A dinger is a home run in baseball—the ball leaves the park with a satisfying crack: {He hit three dingers in last night's game}. The term likely comes from the ringing sound of a solid hit. Outside baseball, dinger can mean anything impressive or emphatic, or in Australian slang, the buttocks or anus.

Dinghies is the plural of dinghy, a small boat. A dinghy may be an inflatable raft, a small sailboat, or a tender used to ferry passengers between a larger vessel and shore: {We took the dinghy to the beach}. The word comes from Hindi.

A dinghy is a small boat, typically used as a tender to ferry passengers and supplies between a larger vessel and shore. The term also covers small recreational sailboats and inflatable rubber boats: {We rowed the dinghy to the beach}. The word comes from Hindi.

Dingleberries are small clumps of fecal matter clinging to hair around the anus—common in dogs and sheep, occasionally in humans. The word extends to any small dangling object, like the pom-poms on a sombrero or decorative fringe. As slang, dingleberry means a foolish or annoying person: {Don't be such a dingleberry}.

A dingo is a wild dog native to Australia, typically tawny-colored with a bushy tail. Dingoes are descended from domestic dogs brought to Australia thousands of years ago but have lived feral ever since. They hunt alone or in packs and are known for preying on livestock, which has made them controversial among ranchers. {A dingo took my baby} became a cultural catchphrase after a famous 1980 case.

Dingoes are wild dogs native to Australia, characterized by their sandy-yellow coat, erect ears, and bushy tail. They are Australia's largest land predator and have lived on the continent for thousands of years, likely introduced by early human migrants. Dingoes hunt both solo and in packs, preying on kangaroos, rabbits, and livestock—which has made them controversial among farmers. {Dingoes howl rather than bark like domestic dogs.}

Dingos is the plural of dingo, a wild dog native to Australia. Dingos are lean, tawny-coated canines that hunt alone or in packs, preying on kangaroos, rabbits, and livestock. The dingo holds cultural significance for Indigenous Australians. {Dingos howled in the distance as the sun set over the outback.}

Dings is the plural of ding—small dents or nicks, typically in a surface: {The car had a few dings in the door}. Dings can also mean minor charges or penalties: {My credit report has a couple of dings on it}. As a verb form, dings means to damage slightly or to penalize: {Every late payment dings your score}.

A dingus is a thing whose name you can't remember or don't know: {Hand me that dingus over there}. It's a placeholder word like thingamajig or whatchamacallit. Dingus also describes a foolish or inept person: {What kind of dingus forgets their own phone number?}

Dingy describes something that looks dirty, dull, or shabby from neglect or wear. A dingy apartment has grimy walls and faded paint. Dingy clothes have lost their brightness through repeated washing. The word suggests accumulated grime rather than fresh dirt—a gradual descent into drabness: {The once-grand hotel had become dingy and depressing}.

Dining is eating, especially in a formal or social context. You dine at restaurants, not at home over the sink. A dining {room} or dining {table} is where meals are served. To {dine out} is to eat at a restaurant; to {dine on} something is to eat it: {We dined on fresh lobster}. Fine dining implies upscale restaurants with elaborate service.

A dink is a soft, delicate shot in sports like tennis, pickleball, or volleyball—one that barely clears the net and drops quickly, making it hard to return: {She dinked it just over the net}. In American slang, dink is a mildly derisive term for someone perceived as insignificant or foolish. It can also mean to waste time or dawdle: {quit dinking around}. As an acronym, DINK stands for "dual income, no kids," describing a household where both partners work and have no children.

Dinky means small and often insignificant or unimpressive: {a dinky little apartment}, {some dinky town in the middle of nowhere}. The word carries a dismissive tone—something dinky isn't just small, it's inadequately so. In British English, dinky can mean attractively small or neat, nearly the opposite connotation: {a dinky little sports car}.

Dinner is the main meal of the day, typically eaten in the evening. In some regions and older usage, dinner refers to a midday meal, with supper being the evening one. The word also describes formal meals or banquets: {a state dinner}, {a dinner party}. {What's for dinner?} is among the most common household questions.

Dinners is the plural of dinner, the main meal of the day, typically eaten in the evening. The timing varies by culture and household—some families have dinner at midday, others at six or eight. Dinners can refer to multiple such meals or to formal dining events: {The charity hosts several dinners each year}. {TV dinners} are prepackaged frozen meals.

Dinnertime is the hour when dinner is typically eaten. The actual time varies by culture, region, and household—anywhere from late afternoon to late evening. {Is it dinnertime already?} The word often signals a transition in the day's activities: work stops, family gathers, screens get put away.

Dino is informal for dinosaur, used especially by children or when speaking to them: {Look at the dinos!} The word appears in contexts where the full term feels too formal or cumbersome: {dino toys}, {dino nuggets}. Adults use it casually or nostalgically.

Dinosaurs are a group of reptiles that dominated Earth for over 160 million years before going extinct about 66 million years ago. They ranged from chicken-sized to the largest land animals ever. Calling someone a dinosaur suggests they're outdated or unable to adapt: {He's a dinosaur who still refuses to use email}. The word comes from Greek for "terrible lizard."

Dinosaurs is the plural of dinosaur—the group of reptiles that dominated Earth for over 160 million years before going extinct roughly 66 million years ago. The word now applies to anything outdated or unable to adapt: {These mainframe computers are dinosaurs}. Someone called a dinosaur is behind the times: {He's a dinosaur when it comes to social media}.

A diorama is a three-dimensional miniature scene, typically displayed in a box or case with a painted background. Museum dioramas show animals in recreated habitats or historical moments frozen in time. Children build dioramas for school projects: {She made a diorama of the rainforest in a shoebox}. The word sometimes describes any elaborate miniature display.

Dioramas are three-dimensional miniature scenes, typically displayed in a box or case with a painted background. Museums use dioramas to recreate historical moments or natural habitats—taxidermied animals posed against painted landscapes. Children build dioramas for school projects: {She made a diorama of the rainforest in a shoebox}. The form creates an illusion of depth and reality in miniature.

For a short word, the noun and verb dip has somewhat complex associations. It often suggests downward motion, and there is sometimes liquid involved, as when you take a dip (go for a swim). If you dip a spoon into a pan, you put it in and bring it out again. If a surface dips (dip in the road) it descends suddenly and perhaps unexpectedly. The thick-ish food that you dip chips into is called – what else – dip!

Diplodocus is a genus of enormous plant-eating dinosaurs that lived during the late Jurassic period, roughly 150 million years ago. Distinguished by its extraordinarily long neck and whip-like tail, it is among the longest land animals ever discovered, with some specimens exceeding 80 feet in length. The name, meaning "double beam," refers to distinctive chevron-shaped bones on the underside of its tail. Diplodocus remains a staple of natural history museums and dinosaur books.

A diploma is an official document certifying that someone has completed a course of study or earned a degree: {She framed her high school diploma}. The word can refer to the physical certificate or to the qualification itself. In American usage, diploma often specifically means a high school credential, while college completion yields a degree—though both come with diplomas.

Diplomacy is the conduct of relations between nations through negotiation rather than force. Diplomats represent their countries in foreign capitals, managing treaties, trade agreements, and conflicts. Extended to personal dealings, diplomacy means tact and skill in handling sensitive situations: {She handled the family dispute with diplomacy}. The adjective is diplomatic.

Diplomas is the plural of diploma, a document certifying that someone has completed a course of study or earned a degree. Schools award diplomas at graduation: {She framed her diplomas and hung them in her office}. The word can also refer to official documents conferring honors or privileges.

A diplomat is an official who represents their country in relations with other nations, typically stationed at an embassy or consulate. Diplomats negotiate treaties, manage crises, and maintain communication between governments. By extension, anyone skilled at handling sensitive situations tactfully may be called a diplomat: {She was the family diplomat, smoothing over every argument}.

Diplomatic describes conduct or speech that is tactful and sensitive to others' feelings, especially in delicate situations: {She gave a diplomatic answer that avoided offending anyone}. The word derives from diplomacy—the art of managing international relations—where careful communication prevents conflict. A diplomatic person navigates social tensions skillfully. In its literal sense, diplomatic refers to official relations between nations: {diplomatic immunity}, {diplomatic channels}.

Diplomats are officials who represent their country in foreign nations, conducting negotiations and maintaining international relationships. The work requires tact and careful communication—hence the adjective diplomatic, which describes anyone skilled at handling sensitive situations without giving offense: {She was diplomatic about declining the invitation}. A diplomat navigates competing interests while preserving goodwill.

Dipped is the past tense and past participle of dip, conveying brief immersion or downward movement. You dipped your toe in the water, dipped a chip in salsa, or dipped your headlights for oncoming traffic. In slang, dipped means left quickly: {We dipped before the cops showed up}. Someone who is dipped may be dressed stylishly or, in older usage, slightly crazy. Dipped in gold or chocolate describes a coating applied by brief immersion.

A dipper is a ladle or cup with a long handle, used for scooping liquids: {She used a dipper to serve the punch}. The word extends to birds that dive into water for food, and to anything that dips. A skinny-dipper swims naked. In carnival slang, a dipper is a pickpocket. (Capitalized Dipper refers to star formations.)

Dipping is the act of briefly submerging something in liquid: {dipping chips in salsa}, {dipping a brush in paint}. It extends to any quick downward motion—a bird dipping toward water, prices dipping before recovering. In American slang, dipping means using dip tobacco: {He started dipping in high school}. To be dipping into something is to take from it gradually: {dipping into savings}.

Dippy means silly, scatterbrained, or slightly crazy in a harmless way: {She's a bit dippy but everyone loves her}. The word is informal and affectionate rather than harsh—it suggests endearing eccentricity more than genuine mental deficiency. {He had some dippy idea about starting a llama farm}.

Dips is the plural of dip—downward movements, brief immersions, or creamy foods for dunking. {She did fifty dips on the parallel bars}. {We brought chips and dips to the party}. In slang, dips are pickpockets, from their habit of dipping into pockets. In finance, buying the dips means purchasing assets after price drops: {I'm buying the dips on tech stocks}.
Dipshit is a vulgar insult for a stupid or foolish person: {Some dipshit parked in my spot}.
Dipshits is the plural of dipshit, a vulgar insult for stupid or foolish people: {The dipshits in marketing approved that disaster of an ad}.

A dipstick is a rod used to measure the level of liquid in a container, especially the oil in a car engine: {Check the dipstick before a long trip}. By extension, dipstick is mild slang for a stupid or incompetent person—someone whose mental level comes up short: {Don't be such a dipstick}.

Dipsticks is the plural of dipstick, a rod used to measure fluid levels—especially engine oil. You pull it out, check the mark, and know whether to add more. The singular has become slang for a stupid person, someone whose mental gauge reads low: {Those dipsticks forgot to lock the door}.

Dire means extremely serious, urgent, or dreadful. A dire situation threatens catastrophe: {dire consequences}, {dire warnings}, {dire need}. The word emphasizes gravity and often implies that action is required to prevent disaster. Something in dire straits faces desperate circumstances. Dire can also simply mean terrible: {The movie was dire}.

Direct means straight, without deviation or intermediary. A direct {route} takes you there without detours. A direct {answer} addresses the question without evasion. Direct {sunlight} reaches you unobstructed. To direct is to guide or aim: direct {traffic}, direct a {film}, direct your {attention}. A director oversees; directions tell you how to get somewhere or how to proceed. Someone who is direct speaks plainly, without softening or hedging—a quality that can be refreshing or blunt depending on context.

Directed describes something that has been guided, aimed, or controlled toward a specific target or purpose. A directed {effort} focuses on a particular goal. A directed {question} is aimed at someone specific. In film and theater, a production is directed by whoever oversaw its creation: {a film directed by Spielberg}. Self-directed means independently guided: {self-directed learning}.

Directing is guiding something toward a destination or purpose. You direct traffic, direct attention, direct a question to someone. In film and theater, directing means overseeing the creative vision of a production—working with actors, making artistic decisions, shaping the final work: {She's been directing commercials for ten years}. A person directing others exercises authority over their actions.

Direction is the course along which something moves or faces, or the point toward which it is oriented. {Which direction is north from here?} {The wind changed direction.} Direction extends to guidance or instruction: following {directions} to assemble furniture, or working under someone's {direction}. In film and theater, direction is the creative oversight a director provides to shape a production. If something is moving {in the right direction}, it is progressing favorably toward a goal.

Directionless means lacking a clear aim, purpose, or course. A directionless person drifts without goals or plans: {After graduation, he felt directionless}. A directionless policy or organization has no coherent strategy. The word suggests aimless wandering—whether literal movement or figurative lack of purpose in life.

Directions are instructions for reaching a destination or accomplishing a task. You ask for directions when lost, or follow directions on a recipe or medicine bottle. The word implies sequential steps: {Read the directions before assembling}. Directions also refers to the ways something can go—north, south, up, down: {The wind shifted directions}. A sense of direction is the ability to orient oneself spatially.

A directive is an official instruction or order, typically issued by an authority: {The CEO issued a directive banning personal phone use during meetings}. In computing, directives are commands that guide how code should be processed. The adjective directive describes something that provides direction or guidance: {directive leadership}, {directive counseling}.
clues: Mandate issued by those in charge

definition: Directives are official instructions or orders issued by an authority. A government issues directives to agencies; a supervisor gives directives to staff. The word implies formal communication requiring compliance: {The directive came down from headquarters}. In computing, directives are instructions that guide how code is processed. The singular directive works as both noun and adjective: {a directive tone}, {EU directive on data privacy}.

A director is someone who guides, manages, or controls. In film and theater, the director shapes the creative vision—choosing how scenes are staged, how actors perform: {The director called for another take}. In business, a director sits on a board overseeing company policy. A director of an organization heads a department or division: {director of marketing}, {museum director}. The word implies authority over some enterprise or activity.

Directors are people who direct—who guide, manage, or oversee something. A film director shapes a movie's creative vision. A company's board of directors governs corporate decisions. A director of a department or organization leads its operations: {She was named director of the research institute}. The title suggests authority over a defined domain.

A directory is a listing of names, addresses, or other information organized for reference: a telephone directory, a business directory, a membership directory. In computing, a directory is a folder containing files or other folders—a way of organizing data hierarchically: {Navigate to the home directory}. Directory assistance connects callers with phone numbers.

A direwolf is an extinct species of large wolf that roamed North America during the Pleistocene epoch, significantly larger than modern wolves. The term gained contemporary currency through George R.R. Martin's fantasy series, where direwolves are massive, intelligent wolves bonded to the Stark children: {Each of the Stark kids had their own direwolf}.

Direwolves is the plural of direwolf, an extinct species of large wolf that roamed North America during the Pleistocene epoch. The term gained wide currency through fantasy fiction, particularly *Game of Thrones*, where direwolves are massive, intelligent wolves bonded to the Stark family: {Each of the Stark children received a direwolf pup}.

A dirge is a slow, mournful song or piece of music, especially one performed at a funeral or in commemoration of the dead. The word extends to any lamenting expression: {The wind made a dirge through the empty house}. A dirge for something lost or ended need not be musical: {His memoir reads as a dirge for small-town America}.

Dirges are slow, mournful songs or pieces of music, typically performed at funerals or to commemorate the dead. The word extends to any solemn lament: {The wind through the abandoned house sounded like a dirge}. Something dreary or tediously sorrowful might be called a dirge: {His speech was a dirge of complaints}.

A dirigible is a large, steerable aircraft kept aloft by gas—distinguished from free-floating balloons by its ability to be directed. The term covers both rigid airships like the Hindenburg and non-rigid blimps. As an adjective, dirigible means capable of being steered or directed, though this use is rare outside technical contexts.

Dirigibles are lighter-than-air aircraft that can be steered and propelled—unlike free-floating balloons. The term covers both rigid airships with internal frameworks (like the Hindenburg) and non-rigid blimps. The word comes from Latin for "steerable," distinguishing these craft from balloons at the mercy of winds: {The dirigibles floated majestically over the fairgrounds}.

A dirk is a long dagger, historically associated with Scottish Highlanders and sailors. The blade is typically straight and double-edged, designed for thrusting. {He wore a dirk at his belt.} The word survives mainly in historical contexts and fantasy fiction.

Dirt is loose earth or soil: {The kids were playing in the dirt}. Extended to any substance that makes something unclean—dust, grime, mud tracked indoors. Figuratively, dirt is scandalous or damaging information about someone: {They're digging up dirt on the candidate}. To {treat someone like dirt} is to show them no respect. {Dirt cheap} means extremely inexpensive.

A dirtbag is a contemptible or worthless person—someone dishonest, sleazy, or generally lowlife: {Her ex-boyfriend turned out to be a total dirtbag}. The term is mildly vulgar but common. In a separate sense, dirtbag describes a minimalist outdoor lifestyle, especially among climbers who live cheaply to maximize time on the rock: {dirtbag climbing}.

Dirtbags are people considered worthless, contemptible, or morally low—roughly synonymous with scumbags or lowlifes: {Those dirtbags stole my bike}. The term suggests someone grimy in character, not just behavior. In outdoor and climbing culture, dirtbag has been reclaimed to describe someone who lives cheaply and unconventionally to pursue their passion: {She spent three years as a dirtbag climber, living out of her van}.

A dirtbike is a lightweight motorcycle designed for off-road riding on rough terrain—dirt trails, mud, hills, and motocross tracks. Dirtbikes have knobby tires for traction, long suspension travel, and minimal bodywork. {He spent weekends racing dirtbikes in the desert.} Also spelled as two words: dirt bike.

Dirtbikes are lightweight motorcycles designed for off-road riding on rough terrain—dirt trails, hills, and tracks. They feature knobby tires, high ground clearance, and rugged suspension. The term covers both motocross racing bikes and recreational trail bikes: {We spent the weekend riding dirtbikes in the desert}. Also spelled as two words: dirt bikes.

In its most literal use, the adjective dirty suggests the presence of dirt, and the less frequent verb dirty means make dirty. There are many figurative uses, mostly with the negative connotations of the literal use. Anything dishonorable, illegal, improper, or immoral can be called dirty. A dirty little secret is one that is probably damaging to someone’s reputation. It can also express a sense of distortion or impurity that may or may not be desirable: a dirty color is less vibrant but dirty guitar playing can be a hallmark of certain music.

Dis is slang for disrespect, used as both noun and verb: {Don't dis me like that}, {That was a serious dis}. The word emerged from hip-hop culture in the 1980s and spread into mainstream speech. To dis someone is to insult, criticize, or show contempt for them. Also spelled diss.

Disabilities are physical, mental, or developmental conditions that limit a person's movements, senses, or activities. The word covers a wide spectrum—from mobility impairments requiring wheelchairs to cognitive differences affecting learning. {The building was retrofitted for accessibility to accommodate people with disabilities.} In legal and social contexts, disability often determines eligibility for accommodations, benefits, or protections against discrimination.

Disability is a physical or mental condition that limits a person's movements, senses, or activities. The word covers a vast range—from blindness and paralysis to chronic illness and cognitive differences. Legal definitions matter: a recognized disability may entitle someone to accommodations, benefits, or protections. {She has a learning disability}. {The building lacks disability access}. In disability communities, the term is neutral and preferred over euphemisms like "differently abled."

Disable means to make something unable to function or to deprive someone of ability. You disable a device by turning off its power or removing a component: {Disable notifications in settings}. A person may be disabled by injury or illness, losing physical or mental capacity. The adjective disabled describes people with lasting impairments, though preferences vary on whether to say {disabled people} or {people with disabilities}. To disable a security system is to deactivate it.
clues: Take away its ability to function

definition: Disabled describes someone with a physical, mental, or sensory condition that limits major activities—movement, sight, hearing, cognition. The word functions as both adjective and collective noun: {services for the disabled}, {a disabled veteran}. A disabled vehicle or machine is one that has been rendered inoperable. Some prefer "person with a disability" to emphasize the person before the condition, though many in disability communities embrace disabled as a neutral descriptor rather than a euphemism to avoid.

A disadvantage is an unfavorable condition or circumstance that makes success harder: {Growing up poor is a disadvantage in many ways}. It can also mean a weakness relative to others: {Her lack of experience was a disadvantage in the interview}. To disadvantage someone is to put them in an unfavorable position. At a {disadvantage} means in a weaker position than competitors or opponents.

Disadvantaged describes people or groups lacking the resources, opportunities, or social position that others enjoy: {programs for disadvantaged youth}, {economically disadvantaged communities}. The term is a euphemism that emerged as earlier words like underprivileged fell out of favor. It implies systemic barriers—poverty, discrimination, poor schools—rather than personal failing, though critics note it still defines people by what they lack.

Disadvantages are unfavorable conditions or drawbacks that put someone or something at a relative weakness: {The disadvantages of rural living include limited access to healthcare}. To disadvantage someone is to place them in an unfavorable position: {The new policy disadvantages small businesses}. Often paired with advantages in weighing decisions: {We discussed the advantages and disadvantages of each option}.

To disagree is to hold a different opinion or to differ in judgment: {We disagree about politics, but we're still friends}. People disagree with each other or with statements and ideas. Things that disagree fail to match or correspond: {The two accounts disagree on key details}. When food or climate disagrees with you, it causes discomfort or illness: {Spicy food disagrees with me}.

Disagreement is a difference of opinion or failure to agree: {There was some disagreement about how to proceed}. It can range from mild difference to open conflict. A disagreement between accounts or stories means they don't match up. The word often softens what might otherwise be called an argument or dispute: {We had a minor disagreement}.

Disagreements are instances of differing opinions or failure to agree. The word covers everything from minor disputes to serious conflicts: {We had a few disagreements about the budget}, {philosophical disagreements between the two camps}. A disagreement can be a single clash or an ongoing state of discord.

Disapparate is a verb from the Harry Potter series meaning to vanish instantly from one location, typically to reappear elsewhere through apparition. The word blends "disappear" with "apparate," the magical teleportation in J.K. Rowling's universe: {With a loud crack, she disapparated}. Outside fan contexts, the word sees little use.

To disappear is to pass out of sight or cease to exist. A person disappears around a corner, into a crowd, or without a trace. Things disappear when lost, stolen, or consumed: {My keys have disappeared}, {The cake disappeared in minutes}. In sinister contexts, to disappear someone is to abduct or kill them secretly, often by state actors: {The regime disappeared thousands of dissidents}.

Disappearance is the act of vanishing or ceasing to be visible or present. A person's disappearance may be voluntary or mysterious: {Police are investigating her disappearance}. Things undergo disappearance when they're removed or fade away: {the disappearance of small farms}, {the gradual disappearance of cash transactions}. The word often carries undertones of concern or loss.

Disappearances are instances of vanishing or ceasing to be visible. The word often carries ominous weight—{the disappearances of several hikers in the region}, {political disappearances under the regime}. It can describe mundane losses: {the mysterious disappearances of socks from the dryer}. Or broader phenomena: {the disappearance of traditional crafts}, {the gradual disappearance of small farms}.

Disappeared is the past tense of disappear—to vanish or cease to be visible: {The magician's assistant disappeared behind the curtain}. Something can disappear gradually {(The fog disappeared by noon)} or suddenly {(My wallet disappeared from my pocket)}. In political contexts, disappeared often describes people who vanish under state violence—detained, killed, or abducted without official acknowledgment: {Thousands disappeared during the dictatorship}.

Disappearing describes something in the process of vanishing or becoming invisible. A disappearing {act} is a magic trick—or someone's sudden, unexplained departure. Disappearing {ink} fades after writing. Species are disappearing from ecosystems. The word often carries urgency about loss: {a disappearing way of life}, {disappearing glaciers}.

To disappoint is to fail to meet expectations or hopes. A movie disappoints when it doesn't live up to its trailer. A person disappoints by not coming through: {I hate to disappoint you, but I can't make it}. The disappointed person feels let down; the disappointing thing or person caused that feeling. {The team's performance disappointed everyone who'd believed in them}.

Disappointed describes the feeling when expectations or hopes aren't met. You're disappointed in a person who let you down, disappointed with a result that fell short, disappointed by news you didn't want to hear. The emotion ranges from mild letdown to profound deflation: {I was disappointed but not surprised}. A disappointed {sigh} or {look} expresses this feeling nonverbally.
clues: When reality falls short of hopes

definition: Disappointing describes something that fails to meet expectations or hopes. A disappointing {meal} leaves you unsatisfied; a disappointing {performance} falls short of what you anticipated. The word implies a gap between what was promised or hoped for and what actually arrived: {The sequel was disappointing compared to the original}.

Disappointment is the feeling when expectations or hopes go unmet. You feel disappointment when something turns out worse than anticipated: {The movie was a disappointment after all the hype}. A person or thing that disappoints can itself be called a disappointment: {He felt like a disappointment to his parents}. The word covers a spectrum from mild letdown to crushing defeat.

Disappointments are things that fail to meet expectations—events, outcomes, or people that let you down. The word carries emotional weight: disappointments aren't just neutral failures but ones that leave you feeling deflated or sad. {The movie was one of the year's biggest disappointments.} {She's had her share of disappointments in love.}

Disapproval is an unfavorable opinion or judgment of something or someone. It ranges from mild reservation to outright condemnation: {Her parents made no secret of their disapproval}. A {look of disapproval} signals displeasure without words. To disapprove is to hold or express such a view: {He disapproved of her career choice}.

To disapprove is to regard something unfavorably or consider it wrong: {Her parents disapproved of the relationship}. The word often implies moral or social judgment rather than mere preference. You can disapprove silently or express disapproval openly. In formal contexts, to disapprove a request or proposal is to reject it officially: {The board disapproved the budget amendment}.

Disapproving describes an attitude of criticism or disfavor toward something or someone: {a disapproving glance}, {disapproving parents}. The word often characterizes looks, tones, or silences that communicate judgment without words: {She gave him a disapproving look when he reached for a third slice of cake}.

To disarm is to remove weapons from someone or something: {The police disarmed the suspect}. Nations may disarm by reducing military arsenals. Figuratively, to disarm someone is to defuse their hostility or suspicion, often through charm or unexpected warmth: {Her candor disarmed the critics}. A disarming smile puts people at ease.

Disarmament is the reduction or elimination of military weapons and forces. The term usually applies to nations reducing their arsenals through treaties or agreements: {nuclear disarmament}, {multilateral disarmament talks}. It can also describe the act of taking weapons from individuals or groups: {the disarmament of rebel forces}. The word often appears in contexts of peace negotiations and international security.

Disarmed is the past tense and participle of disarm, which means to remove weapons from someone or to reduce military forces. Beyond the literal sense, disarmed often describes having one's defenses lowered emotionally or socially: {Her candor completely disarmed me}. Someone who is disarmed in this figurative sense has had their suspicion, hostility, or resistance neutralized, often by charm or unexpected kindness.

Disarming describes something that overcomes suspicion or hostility by being unexpectedly charming or sincere. A disarming {smile} puts people at ease. A disarming {honesty} catches you off guard in a pleasant way. The word suggests defenses being lowered—as if emotional weapons were being set aside: {His disarming manner made it hard to stay angry}.

Disarray is a state of disorder or confusion—things scattered, plans disrupted, organization broken down. Clothes in disarray are disheveled or partially removed. An army in disarray has lost its formation. {The scandal threw the campaign into disarray.} {She arrived with her hair in disarray.} The verb means to throw into disorder.
clues: When nothing is where it belongs

definition: A disaster is a sudden event causing widespread destruction or suffering—floods, earthquakes, plane crashes. The word extends to anything that goes catastrophically wrong: {The dinner party was a complete disaster}. A disaster can also be a person who's hopelessly disorganized or prone to failure: {She's a disaster in the kitchen}.

Disasters are sudden events causing widespread destruction, suffering, or loss of life. Natural disasters include earthquakes, floods, hurricanes, and wildfires. Human-caused disasters include industrial accidents, oil spills, and acts of terrorism. The word extends to any serious failure or fiasco: {The dinner party was a complete disaster}. {Disaster struck when the levee broke}.

Disastrous describes something that causes or constitutes a disaster—a catastrophic failure or calamity. A disastrous {flood} destroys homes; a disastrous {decision} leads to ruin. The word often carries a sense of irreversibility: {The merger proved disastrous for both companies}. In casual use, disastrous can mean merely very bad: {a disastrous haircut}, {a disastrous first date}.

Disavowal is the act of denying responsibility, connection, or approval. A politician issues a disavowal of controversial remarks made by a supporter. A company publishes a disavowal of its former CEO's conduct. The word carries formal weight—stronger than mere denial, it actively repudiates any association: {His disavowal of the conspiracy theories came too late to matter}.

Disavowed is the past tense of disavow, meaning to deny responsibility for or association with something. A government might disavow knowledge of a covert operation; a politician might disavow earlier statements. {The agency disavowed any involvement in the scandal.} The word carries more force than simply denying—it suggests actively distancing oneself from something potentially damaging.

To disband is to break up an organized group, ending its existence as a unit. Bands disband, armies disband, committees disband. The word applies to groups that were formally constituted: {The task force disbanded after completing its investigation}. Members scatter; the collective identity dissolves.

Disbanded describes a group that has broken up and ceased to exist as an organized unit. Bands disband, military units disband, committees disband. The word implies formal dissolution rather than gradual fading: {The band disbanded in 1995 after creative differences}. Once disbanded, the group no longer functions collectively, though members may reunite later.

Disbanding is the act of breaking up a group or organization so that it no longer exists as a unified entity. When a band disbands, its members go their separate ways; when an army disbands, soldiers are released from service. The word applies to any organized group—committees, teams, militias, clubs—that formally dissolves rather than simply becoming inactive. {The committee voted to disband after completing its investigation.}

To disbar is to expel a lawyer from the legal profession, revoking their license to practice law. Disbarment typically follows serious misconduct—fraud, criminal conviction, or gross ethical violations: {He was disbarred after embezzling client funds}. The bar in question is the legal profession itself, from the railing that historically separated court officers from spectators.

Disbarment is the revocation of a lawyer's license to practice law, typically as punishment for professional misconduct or ethical violations. A disbarred attorney can no longer represent clients or appear in court: {He faced disbarment after mishandling client funds}. The term comes from the bar, meaning the legal profession collectively.

Disbarred means expelled from the legal profession, stripped of the right to practice law. A lawyer is disbarred for serious ethical violations—fraud, theft from clients, criminal conduct. The term comes from the bar, the legal profession itself: {He was disbarred after embezzling client funds}. Being disbarred is usually permanent, unlike suspension.

Disbelief is the state of not believing something, often because it seems impossible or shocking: {She stared in disbelief at the wreckage}. To {suspend disbelief} is to temporarily accept the impossible premises of a story or performance. Disbelief can also mean rejection of religious faith, though unbelief is more common for that sense.

Disc is a variant spelling of disk, preferred in British English and in specific technical contexts. Compact disc and disc brake use this spelling by convention. In anatomy, the pads between vertebrae are usually spinal discs. American English generally favors disk for computing contexts: {hard disk}, {floppy disk}. The spellings are often interchangeable, though consistency within a document matters more than which you choose.

Discard means to throw away or get rid of something no longer wanted or useful: {She discarded the worn-out shoes}. In card games, to discard is to remove a card from your hand, placing it in a discard pile. The noun refers to something thrown away or the act itself: {The pile of discards grew}.

Discarded describes something thrown away or abandoned as no longer useful or wanted: {discarded packaging littered the street}, {a pile of discarded clothes}. The word often implies rejection after consideration—something once had value or purpose but has been cast aside: {discarded ideas}, {discarded lovers}.

Discarding is throwing something away or getting rid of it. The word implies deliberate removal of what's unwanted or no longer useful: {discarding old newspapers}, {discarding outdated ideas}. In card games, discarding means removing cards from your hand, usually to the discard pile: {She kept the ace while discarding the rest}.

Discards are things thrown away or rejected as unwanted. In card games, discards are cards a player has chosen to remove from their hand: {The discard pile was getting tall}. The term extends to anything set aside as useless or no longer needed: {The factory floor was littered with discards}.

To discern is to perceive or recognize something, especially when it requires effort or careful attention. You might discern a pattern in data, discern someone's true motives, or discern a faint shape in the fog. The word suggests seeing through surface appearances to grasp what lies beneath: {I couldn't discern whether she was joking}. Discerning as an adjective describes someone with good judgment or refined taste.

Discerning describes someone with keen judgment and the ability to distinguish quality or truth from inferior alternatives. A discerning {eye} notices subtle differences others miss. A discerning {palate} detects nuances in food and wine. Discerning {readers} or {viewers} have refined taste and high standards. The word implies discrimination in the positive sense—choosing wisely rather than accepting indiscriminately.

Discernment is the ability to perceive differences or judge wisely. Someone with discernment notices subtle distinctions others miss: {She showed real discernment in choosing her advisors}. The word implies careful evaluation rather than snap judgment, often in matters of taste, character, or moral complexity. {His discernment of quality wines impressed even the sommelier}.

Meanings of the noun and verb discharge vary according to whether associated with a person, an abstraction, or an object. To discharge a weapon is to fire it. To discharge a person is to fire them or relieve them of duty. To discharge a debt is to excuse it. The noun discharge represents an instance of any of these, such as an honorable discharge from military service. A discharge from a body orifice is usually something gooey, like nasal discharge.

Discharged means released from an obligation, duty, or confinement. A soldier is discharged from the military when service ends—honorably or dishonorably. A patient is discharged from a hospital when well enough to leave. A debtor is discharged from bankruptcy when obligations are cleared. Discharged also describes the release of energy or matter: {The gun discharged}, {The wound discharged pus}, {The battery discharged overnight}.

Discharges are releases or emissions—things sent out from a source. A factory discharges waste into a river. A wound discharges pus. Electrical discharges release stored energy. A soldier receives a discharge when released from military service: {honorable discharge}, {dishonorable discharge}. To discharge a debt is to pay it off; to discharge a duty is to fulfill it.

Discharging is the present participle of discharge, covering all that verb's meanings. A wound discharges pus; a factory discharges waste into a river. A soldier is discharged from service; a patient is discharged from the hospital. A battery discharges its stored energy. A gun discharges when fired. {The ship was discharging cargo at the dock.}

A disciple is a follower who accepts and helps spread the teachings of a leader or philosophy. The word most often appears in religious contexts—the twelve disciples of Jesus, or disciples of Buddha. More broadly, anyone devoted to learning from a master qualifies: {She became a disciple of the minimalist architect}. A disciple differs from a mere student in the depth of commitment implied.

Disciples are followers or students of a teacher, leader, or philosophy. The term most often refers to the twelve followers of Jesus in Christian tradition, but extends to devoted adherents of any influential figure or movement: {a disciple of Freud}, {disciples of minimalist design}. A disciple implies committed study and personal allegiance, not casual interest.

Discipleship is the state or practice of being a disciple—a devoted follower who learns from and commits to a teacher, leader, or set of teachings. The term appears most often in religious contexts, particularly Christianity, where it describes the process of following Jesus and growing in faith. {The church offered a discipleship program for new believers.} More broadly, discipleship can refer to any relationship of dedicated learning and imitation between mentor and student.

A disciplinarian is someone who enforces strict rules and order, especially in raising children or managing institutions. The word often carries a stern connotation: {Her father was a strict disciplinarian who tolerated no backtalk}. It can be neutral or approving when discipline is seen as beneficial, but frequently suggests harshness or inflexibility.

Discipline is a noun and a verb with a range of loosely related meanings. Discipline in a classroom is behavior in accordance with rules or order. A field of study can also be called a discipline: disciplines of the humanities. Training undertaken to improve skills can also be called discipline. When you discipline someone, you take steps to bring them under control, either as a part of their training or as a form of punishment: They expect nannies to provide quality care but then do not allow them to discipline the children.

Disciplined describes someone who exercises control and follows a regimen consistently: {a disciplined athlete}, {a disciplined approach to saving money}. It suggests the ability to resist temptation or distraction in pursuit of goals. Disciplined can also mean having received correction or punishment: {The employee was disciplined for repeated tardiness}.

Disciplines are fields of study or practice with their own methods and standards: academic disciplines like physics or philosophy, artistic disciplines like ballet. The word also means controlled behavior and the training that produces it: {Military discipline kept the troops calm under fire}. To discipline someone is to punish or correct them, especially children. Self-discipline is the ability to make yourself do difficult things. As a verb, discipline also means to train systematically: {She disciplined herself to write every morning}.

Disciplining is applying discipline—training, correcting, or punishing to enforce rules or improve behavior. Parents discipline children; managers discipline employees. The word suggests structured correction rather than random punishment: {The school was disciplining students who violated the dress code}. Self-disciplining means imposing order on your own habits or impulses.

A disclaimer is a statement that limits responsibility or denies connection to something. Legal disclaimers appear before potentially controversial content or risky activities: {The views expressed are those of the author and do not reflect the opinions of this network}. Product disclaimers warn of dangers: {Results may vary}. To disclaim is to deny or renounce.

Disclaimers are statements that limit responsibility or liability, or that clarify the scope of what's being offered. Legal disclaimers appear on products, websites, and contracts: {The disclaimer said past performance doesn't guarantee future results}. In casual speech, a disclaimer is any qualifying statement made before saying something potentially problematic: {Disclaimer: I'm not a doctor, but...}

Disclosure is the act of revealing information that was previously hidden or unknown. Companies make financial disclosures to investors; individuals disclose conflicts of interest. In legal contexts, disclosure refers to the required sharing of relevant documents between parties: {The defense requested full disclosure of the evidence}. A disclosure can also be the information itself: {The senator's disclosure shocked the committee}.

Disco is a style of dance music that emerged in the 1970s, characterized by a steady four-on-the-floor beat, lush orchestration, and pulsing bass lines. The term also names the nightclubs where people danced to this music: {We're going to the disco tonight}. As a verb, to disco is to dance to such music or frequent such clubs. The disco era peaked in the late 1970s, and the word now carries nostalgic or retro connotations: {disco ball}, {disco fever}.

A discography is the complete catalog of recordings by a particular artist or composer, or on a particular label: {The Beatles' discography spans thirteen studio albums}. The term also refers to the study of recorded music as a field. In medical contexts, discography is a diagnostic procedure involving spinal disc imaging.

Discoloration is a change in color, usually for the worse—a stain, spot, or faded area where the original color has been altered. Skin shows discoloration from bruises, sun damage, or medical conditions. Fabrics develop discoloration from age or improper washing. {The water damage left discoloration on the ceiling.} Also spelled discolouration in British English.

Discombobulated means confused, flustered, or thrown off balance. The word describes a state of disorientation where someone can't quite collect their thoughts or composure: {I was completely discombobulated after the time zone change}. Despite its playful, invented-sounding quality, discombobulated has been in use since the nineteenth century. The shorter form discombobulate works as a verb: {The contradictory instructions discombobulated everyone}.

Discombobulating means confusing or disorienting someone, leaving them flustered and off-balance: {The sudden change in plans was discombobulating}. The word has a playful, mock-formal sound that often makes it the comedic choice over simpler alternatives like confusing or unsettling. Something discombobulating throws you into a state of discombobulation.

Discombobulation is a state of confusion or disorientation—being thrown off balance mentally. The word sounds playful and slightly absurd, which suits its use for befuddlement that isn't too serious: {The time zone change left me in complete discombobulation}. It's the noun form of discombobulate, itself a fanciful 19th-century American coinage.

Discomfort is mild physical or psychological unease—not quite pain, but not comfort either. A hard chair causes discomfort; so does an awkward silence. The word often appears where stronger terms would overstate: {I felt some discomfort during the procedure}. To discomfort someone is to make them uneasy, though this verb sounds formal or old-fashioned.

Disconcerting describes something that disturbs composure or unsettles expectations. A disconcerting silence follows a question no one wants to answer. {It was disconcerting to find the door unlocked}. The word suggests unease rather than alarm—something feels off without being outright threatening.

To disconnect is to sever a connection—unplugging a cable, ending a phone call, or cutting off a utility: {They'll disconnect your power if you don't pay}. The noun disconnect describes a gap between things that should align: {There's a disconnect between what politicians say and what they do}. To feel disconnected is to feel isolated or out of touch.

Disconnected describes things no longer linked or joined. A disconnected {phone line} has been cut off from service. Disconnected {thoughts} lack logical flow between them—they don't hang together coherently. A person who feels disconnected experiences emotional distance from others or from their surroundings: {I've felt disconnected from my family since the move}. The word implies that a connection once existed or should exist.

Disconnecting is the act of breaking a connection—physical, electrical, or social. You disconnect a cable from a device, disconnect from the internet, or disconnect from a conversation. The word often describes the process rather than the completed action: {I'm disconnecting the old wires before installing the new ones}. Figuratively, disconnecting can mean emotionally withdrawing: {She's been disconnecting from her friends lately}.

Disconnection is the state of being separated or cut off from something. A phone line or utility service undergoes disconnection when terminated. The word often describes emotional or social severance: {a growing disconnection between politicians and voters}, {She felt a disconnection from her old friends}. In technical contexts, it refers to breaking a link or circuit.

Disconnects functions as both verb and noun. To disconnect is to sever a connection—unplugging a device, ending a call, or cutting off service: {The power company disconnects customers who don't pay}. Figuratively, to disconnect is to disengage mentally or emotionally. As a noun, a disconnect is a gap between things that should align: {There's a disconnect between what politicians promise and what they deliver}.
