Discontent is dissatisfaction with one's circumstances—a restless unhappiness that something isn't as it should be. {The workers' discontent grew as wages stagnated}. As an adjective, discontent means dissatisfied: {She was discontent with the arrangement}. The noun often appears with modifiers suggesting it might lead to action: {simmering discontent}, {growing discontent}, {the winter of our discontent}.

Discontents are people who are dissatisfied or disgruntled, especially with existing conditions or authority: {The new policy only emboldened the discontents}. The word also names the grievances themselves—the things causing dissatisfaction: {the discontents of modern life}, {winter of our discontent}. Less commonly, discontents is the verb form meaning makes unhappy.

Discontinued describes something that is no longer being made, sold, or provided. Manufacturers discontinue products that aren't selling well or that have been replaced by newer versions; services get discontinued when they're no longer viable. {They discontinued my favorite shampoo, so now I have to find a new one.} The word often appears in retail contexts where customers learn a desired item is simply no longer available.

A discontinuity is a break or gap in something that should be continuous. In mathematics, it's a point where a function jumps or becomes undefined. In geology, a discontinuity marks where rock layers or properties change abruptly. More broadly, any interruption in a sequence or pattern: {The war created a discontinuity in the city's development}. The word emphasizes that something expected to flow smoothly doesn't.

Discord is lack of harmony or agreement—whether between people, factions, or musical notes. {Discord among the partners doomed the business.} The word suggests ongoing tension rather than a single disagreement. A discordant note clashes with others; discordant opinions clash similarly. To sow discord is to deliberately create conflict. (Capitalized Discord is a communication platform.)

Discordant means lacking harmony or agreement. Discordant sounds clash unpleasantly—notes that don't belong together, voices that grate against each other. The word extends to any jarring mismatch: {a discordant note in an otherwise cheerful gathering}, {discordant opinions among the committee members}. Something discordant disrupts an expected unity.

Discos is the plural of disco, the dance music and nightclub culture that dominated the late 1970s. Disco featured synthesizers, steady four-on-the-floor beats, and orchestral flourishes. The venues themselves were also called discos: {We hit three discos that night}. The word survives in compounds like {disco ball} and {disco nap}—a pre-evening rest before going out.

A discotheque is a nightclub where people dance to recorded music rather than live bands. The word, borrowed from French in the 1960s, has largely given way to its shortened form disco, though discotheque retains a retro or European flavor: {The old discotheque had a mirrored ball and flashing lights}.

Discotheques are nightclubs where people dance to recorded music, typically with a DJ selecting and mixing tracks. The word is French, literally "record library," and was borrowed into English in the 1960s. The shortened form disco largely replaced it, especially during the disco era of the 1970s. Discotheque now sounds dated or deliberately retro: {The hotel advertised a discotheque in the basement}.

A discount is a reduction from the usual price: {The store offers a 20% discount on clearance items}. To discount something is to reduce its price, or more broadly, to diminish its importance or credibility: {Don't discount her opinion just because she's young}. A discount {rate} is a reduced price or, in finance, the interest rate central banks charge for loans. Something done {at a discount} comes cheaper than expected, sometimes implying lower quality.

Discounts are reductions from a standard price or value. A store offers discounts to move inventory; a seller discounts merchandise that isn't selling. To discount something figuratively is to diminish its significance: {I wouldn't discount the possibility}. A story or claim can be discounted if it seems unreliable. At a discount means below face value or, figuratively, undervalued: {His opinions are held at a discount around here}.

To discourage is to diminish someone's confidence or enthusiasm: {Don't let setbacks discourage you}. It also means to try to prevent something by expressing disapproval or creating obstacles: {The high price discourages impulse buying}, {Her parents discouraged the relationship}. A discouraged person feels disheartened; a discouraging situation dampens hope or motivation.

Discouraged describes a state of having lost confidence, enthusiasm, or hope, typically after setbacks or criticism. Someone who feels discouraged has had their motivation dampened: {After months of rejection letters, she was discouraged but kept applying}. The word can also describe something that has been actively opposed or dissuaded: {Smoking is discouraged on hospital grounds}. This second sense comes from the verb discourage, meaning to persuade someone against a course of action or to make something less likely to happen.

Discouragement is the feeling of having lost confidence or enthusiasm—the deflation that follows setbacks or criticism. It can also mean the act of trying to prevent something: {Despite discouragement from her parents, she pursued acting}. A discouragement is anything that dampens spirits or deters effort: {The long commute was a major discouragement}.

Discouraging describes something that diminishes confidence, hope, or enthusiasm. A discouraging {result} makes you want to give up. A discouraging {sign} suggests things won't improve. {The early reviews were discouraging, but she kept writing anyway.} The word can also describe a person who dampens others' aspirations: {My parents were discouraging about my music career.}

Discourse is a somewhat formal word that describes particular aspects or examples of language. A discourse is also a detailed or scholarly talk or essay about a subject. Discourse also has technical meanings related to speech and conversation, and in fact a conversation can be called a discourse. As a subject matter in linguistics, discourse is a unit of connected speech that is longer than a sentence

Discover means to find or learn something for the first time. You discover a new restaurant, a hidden talent, or that your keys were in your pocket all along. The word often implies uncovering what already existed but was unknown: {Columbus didn't discover America—people already lived there}. Scientists discover cures; explorers discover lands; you discover the truth. To be discovered is to be found by someone who recognizes your potential: {She was discovered singing in a café}.

Discovered is the past tense of discover—to find something previously unknown or hidden. Columbus discovered America (from a European perspective). Scientists discover cures. You might discover a talent you didn't know you had: {I discovered I was good at chess}. To be discovered often means to be found out: {The affair was discovered by her husband}.

A discoverer is someone who finds or becomes aware of something previously unknown or unrecognized. The term applies to explorers who reach new lands, scientists who identify phenomena, and anyone who uncovers what was hidden: {Columbus is often credited as the discoverer of America, though others arrived earlier}. Discovery implies being first—you discover what no one knew before, or at least what you yourself didn't know.

Discoveries is the plural of discovery, denoting things that have been found or learned for the first time. The word applies across domains: scientific discoveries advance human knowledge, archaeological discoveries reveal the past, and personal discoveries shape individual understanding. {Recent discoveries in genetics have transformed medicine.} Discovery also has a legal sense referring to the pretrial process where parties exchange relevant information and evidence.

Discovering is finding or learning something previously unknown or unnoticed. You might discover a shortcut, discover that someone lied, or discover a talent you didn't know you had. The word emphasizes the moment of revelation: {I'm still discovering new things about this city after ten years}.

Discovery is the act of finding or learning something for the first time: {the discovery of penicillin}, {a voyage of discovery}. It extends to the thing found: {The cave paintings were an astonishing discovery}. In law, discovery is the pretrial process where opposing parties exchange relevant information and evidence: {The emails emerged during discovery}. A discovery can also be a person whose talent is newly recognized: {The young actress was the director's discovery}.

To discredit something is to damage its credibility or reputation: {The leaked emails discredited the entire investigation}. You can discredit a person, theory, or institution by exposing flaws or casting doubt. As a noun, discredit is the state of diminished trust or respect: {The scandal brought discredit on the department}. To someone's discredit means reflecting poorly on them.

Discredited describes something that has lost credibility or been shown to be unreliable. A discredited {theory} has been disproven or rejected by experts. A discredited {politician} has lost public trust, usually through scandal or exposed dishonesty. The word implies that reputation or authority once existed but has been undermined: {a discredited witness}, {discredited claims}.

Discrediting is the act of damaging someone's reputation or undermining the credibility of something. You discredit a witness by exposing lies, discredit a theory by presenting contrary evidence, discredit an opponent by revealing scandal. {The leaked emails were aimed at discrediting the candidate}. The goal is to make people doubt or dismiss what they previously trusted.

Discredits is the verb discredit in third-person singular. To discredit is to damage someone's reputation or cause doubt about something's validity: {The scandal discredits his claims to moral leadership}. Evidence that discredits a theory undermines its credibility. A person who discredits a witness makes their testimony seem unreliable.

The adjective discreet must not be confused with another adjective, discrete, which is a homonym but not related in meaning. Someone who is discreet shows good judgment and tact with regard to privacy or other people’s feelings or reputations: We made discreet inquiries and learned that the family did not have a place to stay. When concrete things are described as discreet it usually means that they are unobtrusive and do their job without calling attention to themselves: The room’s discreet lighting makes for a pleasant dining experience.

Discrepancies are differences between things that should match or agree. An accountant finds discrepancies between reported and actual figures. A detective notices discrepancies in witness statements. The word implies that the mismatch matters—it suggests error, inconsistency, or something requiring explanation: {There were significant discrepancies between his two accounts of the evening}.

A discrepancy is a difference between things that should match or agree but don't. You might find a discrepancy between two accounts of the same event, or between the amount of cash in a register and what the receipts show. {There's a discrepancy between what he said and what actually happened.} The word often implies that something is wrong or needs explanation—discrepancies in financial records, for instance, suggest errors or possible fraud.

Discrete means individually separate or distinct, not connected to others: {The course is divided into twelve discrete modules}. The word often emphasizes that things which might seem continuous are actually divided into distinct units: {discrete categories}, {discrete steps in a process}. In mathematics and computing, discrete refers to values that are countable and separate rather than continuous. Often confused with discreet, which means careful or unobtrusive—the two words share an origin but have diverged completely in meaning.

Discretion is the freedom to make decisions according to one's own judgment: {The judge has discretion in sentencing}. It also means the quality of being careful about what you say or do, especially to avoid embarrassment or offense: {I trust your discretion with this information}. The phrase {at your discretion} leaves the choice entirely to you. {Discretion is the better part of valor} suggests knowing when to hold back is wiser than rushing in.

To discriminate is to recognize or make distinctions. A wine expert discriminates among vintages; a person of discriminating taste notices fine differences. But discriminate more often carries negative weight—to treat people unfairly based on group membership: {The company was found to have discriminated against women in hiring}. The neutral sense (perceive differences) and the charged sense (act on prejudice) coexist, though the latter now dominates.

Discriminated is the past tense of discriminate, which has two distinct directions. To discriminate can mean to perceive or make fine distinctions: {a discriminated palate}, {She discriminated between subtle shades of meaning}. More commonly now, it means to treat people unfairly based on group membership: {The company discriminated against older workers}. The neutral sense has faded as the prejudicial sense has dominated.

Discrimination is the activity or the result of making a judgment about difference: Discrimination improved considerably when subjects were given more time to study the objects. The core meaning of discrimination is neutral but in usage, it often refers to the unfair effects of judgment about differences: The study found that racial discrimination in housing is still widespread in the city. Discrimination is sometimes used positively to talk about someone’s judgment: Her discrimination during interviews gave us a very good field of candidates.

Discriminatory describes actions, policies, or attitudes that treat people unfairly based on characteristics like race, sex, age, or religion: {discriminatory hiring practices}, {The law was ruled discriminatory}. The word carries negative connotations—calling something discriminatory implies it's unjust, not merely that it makes distinctions.

Discs is the plural of disc, the British English spelling of disk. Both forms refer to flat, circular objects or shapes. In British usage, discs commonly describes vinyl records, CDs, DVDs, and similar media: {I found a box of old discs in the attic}. The spelling also appears in anatomical contexts like spinal discs and in disc brakes. American English generally prefers disk, though compact disc uses the British spelling universally.

A discus is a heavy disk thrown as an athletic event, one of the oldest Olympic sports. The thrower spins in a circle to build momentum before releasing. The shape extends to anything disk-like: {a discus fish}, {a discus-shaped UFO}. The event itself is also called the discus: {She competed in the discus}.

Discuss means to talk about something with others, typically to share information, examine different perspectives, or work toward understanding. The word implies more depth and exchange than casual conversation—you discuss {politics}, discuss {options}, or discuss {a problem} when you want to explore it thoroughly. In academic and professional settings, discuss often appears as an instruction: {Discuss the implications of the study's findings}. The noun form is discussion.

Discussing is the present participle of discuss, meaning to talk about something with others, examining it from various angles. It implies exchange rather than one-way communication: {We were discussing the merger when the boss walked in}. Discussing can also work as a gerund: {Discussing politics at dinner rarely ends well}.

Discussion is the exchange of ideas through conversation, often to reach understanding or make decisions: {We need to have a discussion about the budget}. Unlike debate, discussion implies collaborative exploration rather than opposing sides. The word covers everything from casual talks to formal meetings: {The matter is still under discussion}. To table something {for discussion} is to put it on the agenda.

Disdain is a feeling of contempt or scorn toward something considered beneath one's dignity or unworthy of respect: {She regarded his excuses with disdain}. The verb means to look down on or reject as unworthy: {He disdained to answer the accusation}. Disdain carries a note of superiority—not merely disliking something but considering it too low to merit serious attention.

Disdainful describes an attitude of contempt or scorn toward something considered beneath one's dignity or unworthy of respect. A disdainful {glance} conveys superiority; a disdainful {tone} suggests the speaker finds the subject undeserving of serious attention. The word implies looking down from a position of assumed superiority: {She was disdainful of their small-town concerns}.

Disdains is the verb form of disdain, meaning to regard something as beneath one's dignity or unworthy of consideration. The word carries a sense of contemptuous superiority: {She disdains small talk}, {He disdains anyone who disagrees with him}. To disdain something is stronger than merely disliking it—it implies looking down on it.

Disease is a condition in which the body or mind functions abnormally, causing discomfort, dysfunction, or distress. Diseases may be caused by infection, genetics, environment, or lifestyle: {heart disease}, {infectious disease}, {Alzheimer's disease}. The word extends to unhealthy conditions in plants, animals, or systems. Figuratively, disease describes corrupting social problems: {Racism is a disease}.

Diseased describes something affected by disease—abnormal, unhealthy, corrupted by illness. A diseased {organ} has pathology; a diseased {tree} is dying from infection. The word extends to minds and societies: {a diseased imagination}, {a diseased political system}. Unlike "sick," which can be temporary, diseased suggests something fundamentally wrong, often progressive or chronic.

Diseases are conditions that impair normal functioning of the body or mind. The word covers everything from infectious illnesses like influenza to chronic conditions like diabetes to mental disorders like depression. Something that spreads harmfully may be called a disease metaphorically: {Corruption is a disease eating away at the institution}. To be diseased is to be afflicted with illness or decay.

To disembark is to leave a ship, aircraft, or other vehicle: {Passengers began to disembark as soon as the plane reached the gate}. The word carries a slightly formal tone, more common in travel announcements than casual speech. The opposite is embark.

Disembodied means separated from or existing without a body. A disembodied {voice} or {spirit} has no visible physical source—it seems to come from nowhere. The word often describes sounds that feel eerily detached from their origin: {A disembodied laugh echoed through the empty hallway}. Figuratively, something disembodied lacks grounding or tangible form: {disembodied ideas}, {disembodied data}.

To disembowel is to cut open and remove the internal organs, especially the intestines. The word appears in contexts of butchering animals, graphic violence, or historical execution methods: {The hunter disemboweled the deer}. Figuratively, to disembowel something is to gut it of essential content: {Budget cuts disemboweled the program}.

Disemboweled means having had the intestines or internal organs removed, whether by violence, surgery, or butchering. A disemboweled corpse has been cut open and gutted. Figuratively, something disemboweled has been stripped of its essential contents: {The budget cuts left the program disemboweled}. Also spelled disembowelled in British English.

Disemboweling is the act of removing the internal organs, especially the intestines, from a body. The term applies to gutting animals for butchering or taxidermy, to gruesome violence in combat or torture, and to horror fiction: {The killer disemboweled his victims}. Figuratively, to disembowel something is to gut it of essential contents: {Budget cuts disemboweled the program}. Also spelled disembowelling.

Disembowelment is the removal of the bowels or internal organs from a body. The term appears in descriptions of torture, execution methods, animal butchery, and gory fiction: {The coroner noted signs of disembowelment}. Figuratively, disembowelment describes thorough gutting of anything: {the disembowelment of the federal budget}.

To disenchant is to free from illusion or false belief—to strip away the magic, as it were. Someone disenchanted with a job or relationship has lost their earlier enthusiasm: {She became disenchanted with corporate life after ten years}. The word implies a shift from naive hopefulness to clear-eyed disappointment, though not necessarily bitterness.

Disenchanted describes someone who has lost faith, enthusiasm, or idealized belief in something—the spell is broken. A disenchanted voter no longer trusts the political process. A disenchanted employee has seen through the company's promises. {After three years of broken promises, she grew disenchanted with the organization.} The word implies previous enchantment: you can only become disenchanted with something you once believed in.

Disenchanting describes something that causes disappointment by revealing reality to be less appealing than expected. A disenchanting experience strips away illusion or idealism: {The internship was disenchanting—I learned the industry runs on nepotism}. The word implies a loss of magic or wonder, leaving someone more cynical or realistic than before.

Disenchantment is the loss of illusion or idealism about something once admired or believed in. The word suggests a spell being broken—what once seemed magical or promising now appears ordinary or flawed: {Her disenchantment with corporate life led her to quit}. Political disenchantment describes voter cynicism toward institutions. The feeling often follows enthusiasm: {The disenchantment set in after the first year of marriage}.

To disenfranchise is to deprive someone of a right or privilege, especially the right to vote. Laws that disenfranchise felons bar them from elections. The word extends beyond voting to any exclusion from participation or belonging: {Economic policies that disenfranchise the poor}. The noun is disenfranchisement. Also spelled disfranchise.

Disenfranchised means deprived of rights or privileges, especially the right to vote. Historically, various groups were disenfranchised by law: {Black voters were systematically disenfranchised through poll taxes and literacy tests}. The word now extends to anyone made to feel excluded or powerless within a system: {disenfranchised youth}, {economically disenfranchised communities}. To feel disenfranchised is to feel shut out from participation or belonging.

Disenfranchisement is the removal or denial of rights, especially voting rights. Laws requiring identification or restricting polling hours may result in the disenfranchisement of certain groups. The word extends beyond voting to any loss of privilege or voice: {the disenfranchisement of workers from company decisions}. The feeling of being excluded or powerless is also disenfranchisement: {Economic inequality breeds disenfranchisement among the young}.

Disenfranchising means depriving someone of a right or privilege, especially the right to vote. Voter ID laws have been criticized as disenfranchising poor and minority citizens. The word extends beyond voting to any exclusion from participation or belonging: {Corporate mergers left longtime employees feeling disenfranchised}.

To disengage is to release from connection or involvement. Gears disengage when they separate; soldiers disengage when they withdraw from combat; a person disengages from a conversation by tuning out or walking away. The word implies a deliberate uncoupling: {She disengaged her hand from his grip}. Disengaged describes someone emotionally detached or uninvolved: {The students seemed completely disengaged}.

Disengaged means withdrawn or detached from involvement. A disengaged student sits in class without participating. A disengaged employee does the minimum. The word suggests mental or emotional absence rather than physical: {He seemed disengaged during the entire meeting}. In mechanical contexts, disengaged means disconnected or released from contact: {The clutch is disengaged}.

Disengagement is the act of withdrawing from involvement or commitment. Military forces disengage when they pull back from combat. A country's disengagement from a region means reducing its presence or intervention there. The word applies to personal withdrawal too: {His emotional disengagement from the marriage was obvious long before the divorce}. In psychology, disengagement describes detachment from situations that once commanded attention or investment.

Disengaging is the act of withdrawing or separating from something previously connected. You might be disengaging from a conversation, a commitment, or a mechanical coupling. The word suggests a deliberate pulling back: {She found herself disengaging from the argument before it escalated}. In military contexts, disengaging means breaking contact with enemy forces.

To disentangle is to separate things that have become twisted, knotted, or interwoven. You disentangle headphone cords, fishing line, or a child's hair. Figuratively, to disentangle is to sort out something complicated: {disentangling fact from fiction}, {disentangling the company's finances}. To disentangle yourself from something is to extract yourself from an unwanted involvement: {She's trying to disentangle herself from that relationship}.

Disentangled means freed from tangles, knots, or confusion. Hair gets disentangled with a comb; a mystery gets disentangled through investigation. The word suggests patient unraveling of something complex: {It took months to disentangle the company's finances}. To be disentangled from something is to be separated or extricated from it: {She finally disentangled herself from the relationship}.

To disfigure is to spoil the appearance of something, especially by damaging or marring its surface or form. The word most often applies to faces and bodies: {The accident left him badly disfigured}. It extends to landscapes, buildings, and other things whose visual integrity has been compromised: {Graffiti disfigured the monument}. The damage implied is usually permanent or at least lasting.

Disfigured describes something whose appearance has been damaged or marred, especially a face or body that bears visible scars, burns, or deformities: {The acid attack left her permanently disfigured}. The word implies that the original form was altered in a way that makes it less attractive or harder to recognize. It applies beyond bodies—a disfigured landscape has been scarred by mining or development.

Disfigurement is damage to appearance, especially to the face or body, that leaves lasting visible marks. Burns, scars, and birth defects can cause disfigurement. The word carries weight in legal contexts, where {permanent disfigurement} may affect compensation claims. Disfigurement can also describe damage to landscapes or buildings: {the disfigurement of the coastline by industrial development}.

Disfigures means mars or spoils the appearance of something. A scar disfigures a face; graffiti disfigures a monument. The word implies damage to something that was once whole or attractive: {The accident disfigured him permanently}. The damage need not be physical—scandal disfigures a reputation.

Disfiguring means causing damage that mars appearance, especially to a face or body: {a disfiguring scar}, {disfiguring burns}. The word emphasizes visible, lasting harm rather than internal injury. Disfiguring can also describe anything that spoils the look of something: {disfiguring graffiti on the monument}.

Disgrace is a state of shame or dishonor, often public: {He resigned in disgrace}. A disgrace is also something that brings shame: {The condition of these roads is a disgrace}. To disgrace someone is to bring shame upon them: {She disgraced the family name}. To be in someone's disgrace is to have lost their favor.

Disgraced describes someone who has lost respect or reputation through shameful conduct. A disgraced {politician} resigned after the scandal. A disgraced {doctor} lost her license. The word implies a fall from a previous position of honor or trust—you can only be disgraced if you once had grace to lose.

Disgraceful describes conduct or conditions that bring shame or dishonor: {a disgraceful display of cowardice}, {The state of the facilities was disgraceful}. The word carries moral weight—something disgraceful isn't merely bad but worthy of contempt or public disapproval. It often implies that someone should be ashamed: {His treatment of the staff was disgraceful}.

Disgracing is bringing shame or dishonor upon someone or something. A scandal disgraces a politician; misconduct disgraces a profession. You can disgrace yourself through your own actions or disgrace others by association: {He's disgracing the family name}. The word implies a fall from a previously respected position.

Disgruntled means annoyed, dissatisfied, or resentful, usually because of unfair treatment or unmet expectations. The word often describes workers or customers who feel wronged: {disgruntled employees filed a complaint}, {a disgruntled voter}. Despite appearances, there is no common verb "disgruntle" or opposite "gruntled"—the word exists mainly in this form.
clues: In a mood of petty resentment

definition: A disguise is an altered appearance meant to conceal identity—a costume, wig, or false beard that makes someone unrecognizable. To disguise yourself is to put on such a covering. The word extends to anything that masks true nature: {a blessing in disguise}, {thinly disguised contempt}. To disguise a voice is to alter it so the speaker can't be identified.

Disguised describes something altered to conceal its true identity or nature. A person in disguise wears different clothes or makeup to avoid recognition: {She arrived at the party disguised as a pirate}. The word extends to anything hidden behind a false appearance: {a blessing disguised as a setback}, {criticism disguised as concern}. Thinly disguised suggests the concealment is unconvincing: {a thinly disguised attempt to take credit}.

Disguises are outward alterations meant to conceal identity—costumes, masks, wigs, or changes in appearance that make someone unrecognizable: {The spy traveled under various disguises}. The word extends to anything that obscures true nature: {His friendliness was a disguise for ambition}. As a verb form, disguises means to conceal or misrepresent: {She disguises her accent when she's nervous}.

Disguising is concealing identity or true nature by altering appearance or presentation. A spy disguising herself as a tourist adopts clothing and mannerisms to blend in. The word extends beyond physical transformation: {He couldn't help disguising his disappointment}. Disguising often implies deliberate deception, though the motive may be protective rather than malicious.

Disgust is a strong feeling of revulsion or distaste, often physical in origin—the response to rotting food, bodily fluids, or foul smells. The feeling extends to moral repugnance: {His behavior disgusted everyone}. As a verb, to disgust is to provoke this reaction: {The corruption disgusts me}. {She left in disgust.}

Disgusted describes a strong feeling of revulsion or distaste. The reaction can be physical—triggered by foul smells, rotting food, or bodily fluids—or moral, provoked by behavior that offends one's values: {I'm disgusted by the way they treated her}. The word often implies contempt alongside the revulsion: {He gave a disgusted sigh and walked out}.

Disgusting describes something that provokes revulsion or strong distaste—a visceral reaction of wanting to turn away. The feeling can be physical, as with rotting food or bodily fluids, or moral, as with cruelty or corruption: {The conditions in the factory were disgusting}. The word often expresses emphatic disapproval: {His behavior at the funeral was disgusting}.

Dish is the most generic term for a food container, especially one you eat out of or off of. Dishes are what you wash when all the eating is done. Before the eating, dishes are all the different things that have been prepared to eat. When you dish out food, you remove individual servings from a pot (or dish). In slang use, a dish is someone sexually attractive. To dish the dirt is to gossip.

To dishearten is to cause someone to lose confidence, hope, or enthusiasm. Bad news disheartens; repeated failures dishearten. {She was disheartened by the rejection letter.} The adjective disheartening describes what causes this effect: {a disheartening lack of progress}. Disheartened describes the resulting state.

Disheartened means having lost hope, enthusiasm, or confidence. Someone becomes disheartened when setbacks or disappointments drain their motivation: {She felt disheartened after her third rejection letter}. The word suggests spirits that have sunk rather than broken entirely—a disheartened person might rally with encouragement.

Disheartening describes something that causes a loss of hope, confidence, or enthusiasm. A disheartening defeat makes you question whether to keep trying. {The news from the doctor was disheartening}. The word implies discouragement without complete despair—setback rather than devastation.

Dishes are plates, bowls, cups, and other containers used for serving and eating food. The term often refers specifically to dirty tableware needing washing: {Whose turn is it to do the dishes?} A dish is also a prepared food item: {a traditional Mexican dish}. To dish is to serve food or, informally, to gossip: {She's always dishing about her coworkers}.

Disheveled describes hair, clothing, or general appearance that is untidy, rumpled, or in disarray: {She arrived looking disheveled after running for the bus}. The word suggests carelessness or the aftermath of activity rather than deliberate styling—someone who just woke up, came through a storm, or has been too busy to attend to their appearance.

Dishevelled describes a person or their appearance as untidy, unkempt, or in disarray—hair uncombed, clothes rumpled, looking like you've just rolled out of bed or been caught in a windstorm: {He arrived dishevelled and out of breath}. The word suggests disorder that happened to someone rather than deliberate carelessness. Also spelled disheveled.

Dishing is sharing gossip or juicy information, often with enthusiasm: {She was dishing about the office drama}. The phrase {dish it out} means to deliver criticism or punishment freely, often paired with the observation that someone {can dish it out but can't take it}. Dishing also describes serving food or creating a concave shape in a surface.

Dishonest describes someone who lies, cheats, or deceives—or actions characterized by such behavior. A dishonest {person} can't be trusted. A dishonest {answer} conceals or distorts the truth. {It would be dishonest to pretend I didn't know}. The word carries moral weight: dishonesty isn't just inaccuracy but deliberate deception.

Dishonesty is the quality of being untruthful or deceptive—lying, cheating, or misrepresenting facts. It covers everything from small lies to systematic fraud: {intellectual dishonesty}, {financial dishonesty}, {a pattern of dishonesty}. The word often implies a character trait rather than a single act: {His dishonesty finally caught up with him}.

Dishonor is the loss or absence of honor—a state of shame or disgrace. To dishonor someone is to bring shame upon them or treat them disrespectfully: {He dishonored his family's name}. To dishonor a commitment is to fail to fulfill it. A dishonored check is one the bank refuses to pay. The word carries weight in contexts where reputation matters: military conduct, family standing, broken promises.

Dishonorable describes conduct or character that lacks honor—actions that are shameful, deceitful, or morally degrading: {a dishonorable betrayal of trust}. A dishonorable discharge from the military is the most severe form, given for serious offenses like desertion or assault. The word carries weight because it implies not just wrongdoing but a fundamental failure of integrity.

Dishonored describes someone or something that has lost honor or been disgraced. A dishonored soldier has been stripped of standing through misconduct or failure. A dishonored {check} has been refused by a bank—it bounces. {He returned home dishonored after the scandal}. To be dishonored is to have one's reputation or commitments rejected.

Dishonors is the third-person singular of dishonor, meaning to bring shame or disgrace upon someone or something: {He dishonors his family's name with such behavior}. It can also mean to fail to honor an obligation or agreement—a bank dishonors a check when it refuses payment due to insufficient funds.

Dishonour is the British spelling of dishonor—loss of reputation or respect, or the act of bringing shame upon someone or something. To dishonour a person is to disgrace them; to dishonour a commitment is to fail to keep it. A bank dishonours a cheque when it refuses payment: {The cheque was dishonoured due to insufficient funds}.

Dishonourable describes conduct or character lacking honour or integrity—shameful, disgraceful, or morally compromised. A dishonourable {discharge} from military service marks serious misconduct. Dishonourable {intentions} suggest deceit or exploitation. The word carries weight in contexts where honour matters: military, professional, or personal reputation. {His dishonourable behaviour cost him everything.} British spelling; American English uses *dishonorable*.

Dishonoured is the British spelling of dishonored—the past tense of dishonour, meaning to bring shame upon or fail to honor. A dishonoured {promise} was broken. A dishonoured {cheque} was rejected by the bank for insufficient funds. A dishonoured {soldier} has lost reputation through misconduct or cowardice.

A dishpan is a large, shallow basin used for washing dishes by hand, typically made of plastic or metal. Before the widespread adoption of kitchen sinks with built-in basins, dishpans were essential household items placed on counters or tables and filled with soapy water. The term survives in {dishpan hands}, describing dry, rough skin from prolonged exposure to dish soap and water.

A dishwasher is a machine that washes dishes, or a person employed to wash dishes in a restaurant kitchen. The machine sense now dominates in everyday speech: {We need to run the dishwasher}. The human sense persists in food service: {He started as a dishwasher and worked his way up to line cook}.

Dishwashers is the plural of dishwasher, which has two meanings. The older sense is a person who washes dishes, typically as a job in a restaurant kitchen: {He started as a dishwasher and worked his way up to head chef}. The newer sense is the household appliance that cleans dishes automatically. Both senses remain common, though context usually clarifies which is meant.

Dishwashing is the task of cleaning dishes, utensils, and cookware after meals. It can be done by hand in a sink or by machine. The term often appears as a modifier: {dishwashing liquid}, {dishwashing gloves}. Dishwashing duty is a household chore often assigned or negotiated: {Whose turn is it to do the dishwashing?}

Dishwater is the water used for washing dishes, typically soapy and containing food residue. The word appears mainly in unflattering comparisons: coffee or soup that tastes like dishwater is weak and unpleasant. {Dull as dishwater} describes something or someone utterly boring.

Disillusion is to strip away false beliefs or naive ideals, revealing a harsher reality. The noun names this state of lost innocence: {His disillusion with politics came after years of broken promises}. The related disillusionment is more common as a noun. Someone disillusioned has had their hopeful expectations shattered—not necessarily wiser, but certainly less trusting.

Disillusioned describes the state of having lost faith or belief in something once admired or trusted. The word implies a painful awakening—discovering that a person, institution, or ideal isn't what you thought: {She became disillusioned with politics after the scandal}. Someone disillusioned with their job has lost the enthusiasm or hope they once had. The feeling combines disappointment with a sense of having been naive.

Disillusioning describes something that destroys naive beliefs or pleasant illusions: {It was disillusioning to learn how the sausage gets made}. The word implies a painful but often necessary confrontation with reality—the discovery that a hero has flaws, an institution is corrupt, or a cherished idea doesn't hold up to scrutiny.

Disillusionment is the disappointment that comes from discovering something isn't as good, noble, or true as you believed. It follows the collapse of an illusion—about a person, institution, or ideal: {Her disillusionment with politics came after years of broken promises}. The feeling often carries a bitter edge, the sense of having been naïve or deceived.

To disinfect something is to clean it with chemicals or other agents that kill germs, bacteria, and viruses. The goal is to make a surface or object safe by eliminating microorganisms that could cause disease. You disinfect a kitchen counter after handling raw meat, or disinfect a wound before bandaging it. Disinfecting is more thorough than ordinary cleaning but less extreme than sterilizing, which aims to destroy all microbial life.

A disinfectant is a substance that kills germs, bacteria, or viruses on surfaces. Unlike antiseptics, which are safe for living tissue, disinfectants are typically too harsh for skin and are used on countertops, floors, and equipment: {Wipe down the handles with disinfectant}. Bleach and alcohol solutions are common disinfectants.

Disinfectants are substances that kill or neutralize harmful microorganisms on surfaces and objects. Common disinfectants include bleach, alcohol, and hydrogen peroxide. Unlike antiseptics, which are safe for living tissue, disinfectants are typically too harsh for skin: {The hospital uses industrial disinfectants on floors and equipment}. The term extends to anything that eliminates contamination: {Sunlight is nature's disinfectant}.

Disinfection is the process of killing or removing harmful microorganisms from surfaces, objects, or environments. It differs from sterilization, which eliminates all microbial life; disinfection targets pathogens that pose health risks while potentially leaving harmless organisms behind. {The hospital's disinfection protocols were updated after the outbreak.} Common disinfection methods include chemical agents like bleach, ultraviolet light, and heat treatment.

Disinfo is a clipped form of disinformation—false information spread deliberately to deceive. The shortened form appears in casual speech and online: {The article was pure disinfo}. Unlike misinformation, which may be spread unknowingly, disinfo implies intentional manipulation.

Disinformation is false information deliberately created and spread to deceive. Unlike misinformation, which may be shared innocently, disinformation implies intent—someone knows it's false and spreads it anyway: {Russian disinformation campaigns targeted the election}, {The report was pure disinformation}. The word entered English from Russian dezinformatsiya, a Soviet intelligence term.

Disingenuous means not straightforward or candid—feigning ignorance or innocence while knowing more than you let on. A disingenuous question pretends to seek information but actually makes a point: {Asking "Have you considered the consequences?" was disingenuous—she knew he hadn't}. The word suggests calculated insincerity rather than outright lying.

To disinherit someone is to cut them out of an inheritance they would otherwise receive, typically by excluding them from a will. Parents may disinherit children who have disappointed or estranged them: {After the scandal, his father threatened to disinherit him entirely}. The term can also apply figuratively to any situation where someone is denied a legacy or birthright they might have expected.

Disinheritance is the act of cutting someone out of an inheritance, or the state of being cut out. A parent might threaten disinheritance to control a child's behavior: {She lived in fear of disinheritance if she married outside the faith}. The term extends beyond wills to any deprivation of expected legacy or birthright.

Disinherited describes someone who has been cut off from an inheritance, typically by a parent's deliberate exclusion from a will: {His father disinherited him after the scandal}. The word extends to anyone denied something they might naturally expect to receive—rights, opportunities, or cultural belonging: {the disinherited masses}, {feeling disinherited from her own heritage}.

Disinheriting is cutting someone out of an inheritance, typically by excluding them from a will. Parents may disinherit children who disappoint them or estrange themselves: {He was disinherited after the scandal}. The term extends to any denial of what someone might expect to receive by right or tradition.

To disintegrate is to break apart into smaller pieces or fragments. Physical objects disintegrate through decay, explosion, or erosion: {The old book disintegrated in my hands}. The word extends to abstract things that fall apart: {Their marriage disintegrated over the following year}. In physics, disintegrate describes radioactive decay or particle breakdown.

Disintegrated means broken apart into fragments or components. Physical objects disintegrate when their structure fails: {The old book disintegrated in my hands}. Organizations, relationships, and plans disintegrate when they fall apart: {Their marriage disintegrated after the affair}. In physics, atoms disintegrate through radioactive decay. The past tense and past participle of disintegrate.

Disintegrating describes something breaking apart into smaller pieces or losing its structural integrity. A disintegrating building crumbles over time; a disintegrating marriage falls apart through accumulated strain. The word captures the process of coming undone: {The old manuscript was disintegrating in my hands}. Figuratively, anything cohesive can disintegrate—plans, alliances, composure.

Disintegration is the process of breaking apart into smaller pieces or components, often to the point of destruction or collapse. Physical objects disintegrate when their structure fails—a crumbling building, a decaying body, a spacecraft burning up on reentry. The word extends to abstractions: the {disintegration of a marriage}, the {disintegration of social order}. In physics, it refers specifically to radioactive decay, where atomic nuclei break down spontaneously.

A disintegrator is a device or agent that breaks something into fragments or causes it to fall apart. The word appears most often in science fiction, where a disintegrator ray or disintegrator gun reduces targets to atoms or dust: {The alien raised his disintegrator}. In industrial contexts, disintegrators are machines that grind or pulverize materials.

Disinterest has two meanings that usage guides have long tried to keep separate. The traditional sense is impartiality—freedom from bias or personal stake: {A judge must maintain disinterest in the outcome}. The disputed sense, now very common, means lack of interest or indifference: {She showed complete disinterest in the proposal}. The verb disinterest means to free from interest or concern. Many careful writers still distinguish disinterest (impartiality) from uninterest (not caring), but the merger is well advanced.

Disinterested means impartial or free from personal stake in an outcome: {A disinterested judge should hear the case}. The word is frequently used to mean uninterested or indifferent, though careful writers maintain the distinction. Someone disinterested in a dispute has no stake in it; someone uninterested simply doesn't care about it.

Disinvited means to have had an invitation rescinded. Someone who was disinvited was initially invited to an event or gathering, then told not to come: {She was disinvited from the wedding after the argument}. The word often implies social awkwardness or conflict—you don't disinvite someone without reason.

Disjointed means lacking connection or coherence—the parts don't fit together smoothly. A disjointed {conversation} jumps erratically between topics. A disjointed {argument} fails to build logically from one point to the next. The word suggests something that should be unified but isn't: {His speech was disjointed and hard to follow}.

A disk is a flat, circular object—or something shaped like one. The sun appears as a bright disk in the sky. In anatomy, spinal disks cushion the vertebrae. In computing, a disk stores data: {hard disk}, {floppy disk}. The spelling disc is British and appears in specific terms like {compact disc} and {disc brake}, while disk dominates American usage and computing contexts.

Disks is the plural of disk, a flat circular object or shape. Computer disks store data magnetically or optically: {She backed up her files onto several disks}. Spinal disks cushion the vertebrae. In American English, disk is the standard spelling, while British English often prefers disc, especially for music recordings and anatomy.

Dislike is a mild aversion or lack of fondness for something or someone. It falls well short of hate or loathing—more a preference against than active hostility: {I dislike getting up early}, {She took an instant dislike to him}. As a noun, dislike names the feeling itself: {his dislike of crowds}, {likes and dislikes}.

To dislocate is to force something out of its proper position. Most commonly, this refers to joints: a dislocated {shoulder}, a dislocated {hip}. The bone shifts from its socket, causing pain and immobility. More abstractly, to dislocate is to disrupt or throw into disorder: {The pandemic dislocated supply chains worldwide}. Something dislocated is displaced, unsettled, out of alignment.

Dislocated describes something forced out of its normal position. A dislocated {shoulder} or {hip} has been displaced from its joint socket—painful and requiring medical attention to reset. The word extends to anything thrown out of proper arrangement: dislocated {plans}, a dislocated {economy}, lives dislocated by war. The sense is of violent or unwelcome displacement rather than gentle movement.

Dislocation is displacement from a proper position. In medicine, a dislocated joint has bones forced out of alignment: {She suffered a shoulder dislocation in the fall}. More broadly, dislocation describes any severe disruption of normal arrangement or function: {the economic dislocation caused by the pandemic}, {the dislocation of communities during wartime}. The word captures both physical displacement and the disorder that follows.

To dislodge is to force something from a fixed position—physically knocking it loose or displacing it from where it was settled: {The impact dislodged a tooth}, {We couldn't dislodge the cork}. The word extends to removing people or things from established positions: {rebel forces dislodged from the hills}, {Nothing could dislodge the idea from his mind}.

Disloyal describes someone who fails to maintain allegiance or commitment where it's expected—to a person, group, cause, or country. A disloyal {friend} betrays confidences. A disloyal {employee} undermines the company. The word implies a relationship that should command faithfulness: {She felt disloyal for even considering the competitor's offer}.

Disloyalty is the failure to remain faithful to a person, group, or cause that has a claim on your allegiance. It implies betrayal or abandonment of a bond—to a spouse, employer, country, or team: {The general was executed for disloyalty to the crown}. Disloyalty suggests not just distance but active breach of trust.

Dismal describes something dreary, gloomy, or depressingly inadequate. A dismal day is gray and cheerless. A dismal performance falls far short of expectations. Dismal prospects offer little hope. The word carries emotional weight beyond mere badness—it suggests something that dampens the spirit: {The team's dismal record left fans despairing}.

To dismantle something is to take it apart piece by piece: {They dismantled the scaffolding after the project finished}. The word implies methodical deconstruction rather than destruction—you dismantle a machine to repair it or a tent to pack it away. Figuratively, to dismantle is to systematically undo: {The new administration dismantled environmental regulations}.

Dismantled is the past tense of dismantle, meaning to take apart piece by piece. You dismantle machinery, structures, or systems: {They dismantled the scaffolding after construction}. The word extends to abstract things—dismantling an argument, an organization, or a policy: {The new administration dismantled environmental regulations}. Something dismantled has been systematically broken down or abolished.

Dismantling is taking something apart piece by piece, whether a machine, a structure, or a system. You might dismantle scaffolding after construction or dismantle a corrupt institution through reform. The word implies methodical deconstruction rather than destruction: {The crew began dismantling the stage after the concert}. Dismantling suggests the parts may remain intact even as the whole ceases to function.

Dismay is a feeling of distress or discouragement when facing something unexpected or daunting. It suggests being thrown off balance: {To her dismay, the files had been deleted}. The verb means to cause this feeling: {The test results dismayed the doctors}. Dismay implies a sudden loss of confidence or hope rather than simple disappointment.

Dismayed describes feeling sudden discouragement or distress when confronted with something daunting or disappointing. It suggests being thrown off balance by unwelcome news or circumstances: {She was dismayed to learn the project had been canceled}, {He looked dismayed when he saw the bill}. The feeling combines shock with a sinking sense that things have gone wrong.

To dismember is to cut or tear the limbs from a body, or more broadly, to divide something into pieces: {The killer dismembered the corpse}. The word extends to separating parts from any whole: {The empire was dismembered after the war}. The violence of the literal sense colors figurative uses.

Dismembered describes a body that has had its limbs or other parts cut off or torn away. The word applies to corpses—victims of violence, accidents, or deliberate mutilation: {Police found the dismembered remains in a shallow grave}. Figuratively, dismembered can describe anything broken into pieces: {the dismembered empire}, {a dismembered organization}.

Dismembering is cutting, tearing, or pulling the limbs from a body. The word applies to humans, animals, or figuratively to organizations and territories: {The empire was dismembered after the war}. In crime contexts, dismembering typically refers to cutting up a corpse: {He was convicted of dismembering the victim}.

Dismemberment is the act of cutting, tearing, or pulling the limbs from a body. The term applies to deliberate acts of violence, torture, or execution, as well as to accidental trauma: {The coroner noted signs of postmortem dismemberment}. Figuratively, dismemberment describes breaking apart any unified whole: {the dismemberment of the empire after the war}.

Dismiss means to send away or allow to leave: {Class dismissed}. It extends to ending employment: {She was dismissed after three warnings}. More commonly, dismiss means to reject something as unworthy of consideration: {He dismissed her concerns as paranoia}. To dismiss a legal case is to end it without a verdict. A dismissive attitude treats others or their ideas as unimportant.

Dismissal is the act of sending someone away or ending their employment. A worker receives dismissal when fired; a case receives dismissal when a judge terminates proceedings. The word carries finality—something has been judged unworthy of further attention or continuation: {Her dismissal of his concerns hurt him deeply}. A dismissive attitude treats something as beneath consideration.

Dismissals is the plural of dismissal, which names the act of sending someone away or ending their employment. In workplace contexts, dismissal is often a formal or euphemistic term for firing: {The company announced mass dismissals following the merger}. In legal settings, a dismissal ends a case or removes charges: {The judge granted a dismissal of all charges}. Dismissals can also refer to casually rejecting ideas or concerns: {Her dismissals of his suggestions became a pattern}.

Dismissed is the past tense of dismiss, meaning sent away or released from duty, attention, or consideration. A class is dismissed when the teacher ends it; an employee is dismissed when fired. {The judge dismissed the case} means it was thrown out, not allowed to proceed. To feel dismissed is to feel brushed off—your concerns treated as unworthy of serious attention.

Dismissing is the act of sending someone away, ending their employment, or rejecting something as unworthy of consideration. When you're dismissing an idea, you're treating it as not worth serious attention: {She kept dismissing my concerns as overblown}. A judge dismissing a case is formally ending it, usually because the evidence is insufficient. The word carries connotations of authority—the person doing the dismissing typically has power over what or whom they dismiss.

Dismissive describes treating something or someone as unworthy of serious attention. A dismissive {wave of the hand} brushes aside an idea. A dismissive {tone} signals that what's being said doesn't matter. The attitude ranges from casual disregard to contemptuous rejection: {She was dismissive of his concerns about the project}.

To dismount is to get off something you're riding—a horse, bicycle, or motorcycle. The word suggests a deliberate, controlled descent rather than falling. In gymnastics, the dismount is the final move off an apparatus: {She stuck the dismount}. In computing, to dismount a drive is to disconnect it from the operating system before removal.

Disobedience is the act of refusing to obey rules, commands, or authority. A child's disobedience might mean ignoring a parent's instructions; civil disobedience is the deliberate, nonviolent breaking of laws to protest injustice: {Thoreau's essay on civil disobedience influenced Gandhi and King}. The word implies willful defiance rather than mere failure to comply.

Disobedient describes someone who refuses to follow rules or obey authority: {a disobedient child}, {disobedient to his commanding officer}. The word implies willful defiance rather than mere failure—you can't be disobedient by accident. It applies mostly to children, soldiers, pets, and others expected to submit to direction.

To disobey is to fail or refuse to follow a rule, order, or authority. Children disobey parents, soldiers disobey commanders, citizens disobey laws: {She disobeyed her doctor's orders and went back to work}. The word implies willful defiance rather than mere failure—you can't accidentally disobey.

Disorder is a lack of order—things out of place, systems not functioning properly, or conditions deviating from normal. A room in disorder is messy; civil disorder is public unrest. In medicine, disorder names conditions that disrupt normal function: {anxiety disorder}, {eating disorder}, {sleep disorder}. The verb means to disturb arrangement or health: {The news disordered his thoughts}.

Disorderly means lacking order or control. A disorderly room is messy; a disorderly crowd is unruly. In legal contexts, disorderly conduct is behavior that disturbs the peace—public drunkenness, fighting, or causing a commotion: {He was arrested for disorderly conduct outside the bar}. A disorderly person acts in violation of public order.

Disorders is the plural of disorder—conditions marked by disruption of normal function. Medical disorders affect body or mind: {anxiety disorders}, {eating disorders}, {sleep disorders}. The term often replaces older, more stigmatizing language: what was once called madness becomes a mood disorder. Beyond medicine, disorders are states of confusion or disarray: {civil disorders}, {public disorders}. To disorder something is to throw it into confusion.

Disorganised is the British spelling of disorganized—lacking order, structure, or systematic arrangement. A disorganised person struggles to keep track of things: {My desk is a disaster; I'm so disorganised}. A disorganised effort lacks coordination: {The response to the crisis was completely disorganised}.

Disorganization is the state of lacking order or structure. A disorganized office has papers scattered everywhere; a disorganized person struggles to keep track of appointments or belongings. The word can describe both physical chaos and mental confusion: {The disorganization of his thoughts showed in his rambling speech}. In organizational contexts, it suggests failed systems rather than mere messiness.

Disorganized describes a lack of order, structure, or planning. A disorganized desk is cluttered and chaotic. A disorganized person struggles to keep things in order or manage time effectively: {I'm too disorganized to run a business}. Disorganized efforts lack coordination: {The rescue attempt was disorganized and ineffective}.

To disorient is to cause someone to lose their sense of direction or position—literally or figuratively. A blow to the head disorients. So does waking in an unfamiliar room, or receiving shocking news. The disoriented person doesn't know where they are, what's happening, or how to proceed. {The fog disoriented the hikers.} {I was completely disoriented after the time change.}

Disorientation is the state of being confused about where you are, what time it is, or what's happening around you. It can be physical—the disorientation of waking in an unfamiliar room—or psychological: {The rapid changes left employees in a state of disorientation}. Medical professionals assess disorientation as a symptom of concussion, dementia, or intoxication.
clues: Unable to tell which way's up

definition: Disoriented means confused about where you are, what time it is, or what's happening around you. The word suggests losing your bearings—literally or figuratively. A head injury can leave someone disoriented. Jet lag disorients travelers. {She woke up disoriented, unsure what city she was in.} In British English, the spelling is usually disorientated.

Disorienting describes something that causes confusion about direction, position, or situation. A disorienting {maze} makes you lose your bearings. A disorienting {experience} leaves you uncertain what's happening or how to respond. The word often describes sudden changes—waking in an unfamiliar place, jet lag, or contradictory information that upends what you thought you knew.

To disown someone is to reject any connection with them, especially to renounce a family member: {His parents disowned him when he came out}. The word suggests a formal, often permanent severing of ties. You can also disown actions, statements, or beliefs—refusing to acknowledge them as yours: {She disowned her earlier comments}.

Disowned is the past tense of disown, meaning to reject or sever ties with someone or something previously acknowledged as one's own. Parents who disown children cut them off emotionally and often financially: {His father disowned him when he dropped out of law school}. One can also disown beliefs, actions, or statements: {She disowned her earlier remarks}.

Disowning is the act of refusing to acknowledge a connection to someone or something. Parents may disown children who violate their values, severing financial and emotional ties: {After she came out, her family disowned her}. You can also disown ideas, statements, or past actions: {He disowned his earlier comments when they became controversial}.

Disowns is the act of rejecting association with someone or something, typically a family member or one's own past actions. A parent who disowns a child cuts off the relationship entirely, often removing them from inheritance: {Her father disowns her for marrying outside the faith}. One can also disown statements, beliefs, or earlier versions of oneself: {He disowns his youthful radicalism}.

Disparities are differences, especially ones that seem unfair or shouldn't exist. The word usually appears in discussions of inequality: {racial disparities in healthcare}, {income disparities between regions}. Unlike neutral terms like "differences" or "variations," disparities implies the gap is problematic and worth addressing. The singular disparity is less common but works the same way.

Disparity is a significant difference or inequality between things being compared: {the disparity between rich and poor}, {racial disparities in healthcare outcomes}. The word implies the gap is measurable and often unjust or troubling. Where difference is neutral, disparity suggests the difference matters and may need addressing.

As a verb (second syllable stressed), dispatch has a meaning similar to send in the sense of send someone to do something: An elite SWAT team was dispatched to intervene in the standoff. As a noun (first syllable stressed), dispatch designates a message or an update about a situation. Dispatch can also mean the act of sending something (Dispatch of the documents was delayed), or it can stand for promptness and efficiency (She handled the difficult project with dispatch).

Dispatched is the past tense of dispatch, meaning sent off quickly to a destination or for a purpose: {The package was dispatched yesterday}, {Emergency crews were dispatched to the scene}. It also means dealt with promptly or efficiently: {She dispatched the paperwork in an hour}. In a grimmer sense, to dispatch someone is to kill them swiftly: {The assassin dispatched his target without hesitation}.

A dispatcher is a person who coordinates and directs the movement of vehicles, personnel, or resources. Emergency dispatchers receive 911 calls and send police, fire, or ambulance services. Trucking dispatchers assign drivers to routes. The role involves rapid decision-making and communication: {The dispatcher radioed all available units to the scene}.

Dispatchers are people who coordinate the movement of vehicles, personnel, or resources. Emergency dispatchers answer 911 calls and send police, fire, or ambulance units. Trucking companies employ dispatchers to route drivers and track shipments. The role requires quick decisions and clear communication: {The dispatcher sent two units to the scene}.

Dispatches works as both noun and verb around the idea of sending something off with urgency or purpose. To dispatch a messenger is to send them on a mission; to dispatch an enemy is to kill them swiftly. A dispatch is an official message or report sent from the field: {war dispatches from the front}. The plural dispatches often refers to news reports or communications collectively. {She dispatches her duties with impressive efficiency.}

Dispatching is the act of sending something or someone off to a destination or for a purpose: {The company handles dispatching of emergency vehicles}. It can also mean killing or finishing off quickly: {The hunter was efficient in dispatching the wounded animal}. In logistics and emergency services, dispatching refers to coordinating and directing personnel or resources from a central location.

To dispel is to drive away or scatter something unwanted, typically something intangible: {The president's speech failed to dispel doubts about the economy}, {Sunlight dispelled the morning fog}. The word suggests clearing away darkness, confusion, fear, or illusion—replacing uncertainty with clarity or gloom with light.

Dispelled is the past tense of dispel, meaning to drive away or cause to vanish. You dispel things that hang in the air—fog, clouds, doubts, fears, rumors, illusions: {Her explanation dispelled any concerns I had}. The word suggests scattering something that had gathered or accumulated.

Dispelling is driving away or causing to vanish. You dispel doubts, fears, rumors, or myths—things insubstantial that dissolve under scrutiny or effort: {Her calm explanation dispelled any concerns about the procedure}. The word suggests scattering something that had gathered, like wind dispelling fog.

Dispensaries are establishments where medicines or medical supplies are prepared and distributed. The term traditionally referred to clinics providing free or low-cost healthcare to the poor. In contemporary American usage, dispensaries are often retail locations licensed to sell cannabis products: {There's a new dispensary on the corner}. The singular is dispensary.

A dispensary is a place where medicines or medical supplies are given out. In older usage, it referred to charitable clinics providing free care to the poor. Today the term most commonly describes a retail shop licensed to sell cannabis: {There are three dispensaries within walking distance of my apartment}.

Dispensation is permission to do something that is normally not allowed, especially an exemption granted by a religious or official authority: {The priest obtained a dispensation to marry the couple during Lent}. In theology, it refers to a divinely ordered system or era in religious history. More broadly, dispensation can mean the act of distributing or administering something: {the dispensation of justice}. The word often implies that rules exist but exceptions can be made by those with proper authority.

To dispense is to distribute or give out, typically in measured portions: {The machine dispenses tickets}, {a nurse dispensing medication}. A pharmacist dispenses prescriptions. To dispense with something is to do without it or set it aside: {Let's dispense with the formalities}. A dispenser is a device that releases items on demand.

A dispenser is a device that releases measured amounts of something: a soap dispenser, a paper towel dispenser, a candy dispenser. The word extends to people who provide things: {a dispenser of wisdom}, {a dispenser of justice}. Vending machines are sometimes called dispensers. In pharmacy, the dispenser is the person who fills prescriptions.

Dispirited means dejected or discouraged, having lost enthusiasm or hope. Someone dispirited has had the spirit taken out of them: {The team looked dispirited after the crushing defeat}. The word suggests a deflation of morale rather than deep sadness—more defeated than grieving.

Dispiriting describes something that drains enthusiasm or hope: {The team's losing streak was dispiriting}. A dispiriting situation makes you feel defeated or discouraged before you've even tried. The word suggests a slow deflation of spirit rather than sudden devastation: {After months of dispiriting job interviews, she finally got an offer}.

To displace is to move something from its usual place or position: {The earthquake displaced thousands of families}. Water displaced by an object rises equal to the object's volume—Archimedes' insight. People displaced by war or disaster become refugees. To displace can also mean to replace or supplant: {Streaming has displaced physical media}. The noun is displacement.

Displaced describes something moved from its proper or usual position. A displaced {vertebra} has shifted out of alignment. More commonly, it refers to people forced from their homes by war, disaster, or persecution: {millions of displaced refugees}, {displaced families seeking shelter}. To feel displaced is to feel out of place or unsettled: {She felt displaced after moving to the new city}.

Displacement is the act of moving something from its usual place or position. People experience displacement when forced from their homes by war, disaster, or development: {The flooding caused mass displacement of residents}. In physics, displacement measures the volume of fluid pushed aside by an object—a ship's displacement is the weight of water it displaces. In psychology, displacement is redirecting emotions toward a safer target: anger at your boss becomes snapping at your spouse. The word captures both physical removal and the sense of something being where it doesn't belong.

Displacing is taking the place of something or moving it from its usual position. Water displaces air when filling a container; a new technology displaces an old one. People are displaced by war or disaster, forced from their homes. {The rising floodwaters were displacing thousands of residents.} In psychology, displacing refers to redirecting emotions toward a safer target: {He was displacing his anger at his boss onto his family.}

Display centers on showing something visibly for others to see. A museum displays artifacts, a store displays merchandise, a peacock displays its feathers. The word suggests deliberate presentation—you display confidence, display affection, display ignorance. As a noun, it's both the act of showing and the thing shown: {a fireworks display}, {a display of strength}. In computing, a display is a screen: {The display went dark}. Display often implies performance or ostentation: {His generosity was just for display}.

Displeased means annoyed or dissatisfied, though not strongly so—it suggests mild irritation rather than anger. {She was displeased with the service}. The word often appears in formal or restrained contexts where someone is unhappy but maintaining composure: {The queen was displeased}.

Displeasure is mild to moderate dissatisfaction or annoyance, typically felt by someone in a position of authority or judgment: {The king made his displeasure known}. It suggests controlled disapproval rather than outright anger—more formal than annoyance, less intense than fury. {She expressed her displeasure with a frown}.

Disposability is the quality of being designed or intended to be thrown away after use. The concept applies most directly to physical products like razors, diapers, and plastic utensils, but extends metaphorically to relationships, workers, and cultural products that are treated as easily replaceable. {The disposability of fast fashion contributes to environmental waste.} The term often carries critical connotations, suggesting a troubling readiness to discard rather than repair, retain, or value.

Disposable describes something designed to be used once or briefly, then discarded: {disposable razors}, {disposable diapers}, {disposable income}. The last phrase means money available after necessities are paid—income you can "throw away" on wants rather than needs. Applied to people, disposable suggests they're treated as expendable or easily replaced: {The company views its workers as disposable}.

Items designed to be used once or briefly and then thrown away. Disposable diapers, razors, and plastic utensils are disposables—convenient but environmentally costly. In darker contexts, disposables can refer to people treated as expendable: {To the company, temp workers were just disposables}.

Disposal is the act of getting rid of something: {waste disposal}, {the disposal of hazardous materials}. A garbage disposal is a device in a kitchen sink that grinds food scraps. At your disposal means available for your use: {I'm at your disposal if you need anything}. Disposal can also mean the arrangement or settlement of a matter: {the disposal of the estate}.

Dispose means to arrange or settle matters, or to get rid of something. You dispose of {waste}, dispose of {assets}, or dispose of {a problem}. To be disposed toward something is to be inclined or willing: {She was favorably disposed to the idea}. A person's disposition is their temperament or tendency. At your disposal means available for your use.

Disposed means inclined or willing: {I'm not disposed to help after what happened}. With "of," it means gotten rid of: {The evidence was disposed of}. Someone well-disposed toward you is favorably inclined; ill-disposed means the opposite. A disposed person has a particular temperament: {a cheerfully disposed child}.

Disposition has two jobs, corresponding to the primary meanings of its underlying verb dispose. Someone’s disposition is the way they tend to be, or the way they are habitually: Sheila has such a sunny disposition. Your disposition toward something is your attitude toward it. Disposition can also mean the disposing of something—that is, the getting rid of it or the dealing with it: An official will oversee the disposition of the company’s assets.

Dispossessed describes people who have been deprived of their home, land, or property, often by force or legal action. The term carries connotations of injustice and powerlessness, frequently applied to groups displaced by war, colonization, or economic exploitation. As a noun, {the dispossessed} refers collectively to such people as a class: {The revolution promised land reform for the dispossessed}. To dispossess someone is to strip them of what they rightfully had.

Dispossession is the act of depriving someone of property, land, or belongings—typically by force or legal action. The term often describes the taking of homes or territory from people who lack power to resist: {the dispossession of indigenous peoples from their ancestral lands}. It can extend to losing intangible things: {a dispossession of rights}, {cultural dispossession}.

Disproportionate means out of proportion—too large or too small relative to something else. A disproportionate {response} exceeds what the situation warrants. A disproportionate {share} of the burden falls on one group when others contribute less. The word often implies unfairness or imbalance: {The punishment was disproportionate to the crime}.

To disprove something is to show it to be false or incorrect. You disprove a theory by presenting evidence that contradicts it, or disprove an accusation by demonstrating it couldn't have happened: {The alibi disproved the prosecution's timeline}. Disprove is stronger than doubt or question—it implies decisive refutation.

Disproven is the past participle of disprove, meaning shown to be false or invalid. A theory is disproven when evidence contradicts it: {The hypothesis was disproven by subsequent experiments}. Disproved is equally correct and more common in formal writing, but disproven appears frequently in speech and casual prose.

A dispute is a disagreement or argument, often one that persists: {a property dispute}, {a labor dispute}, {The facts are not in dispute}. To dispute something is to challenge or contest it: {She disputed the charges on her bill}. To dispute with someone is to argue with them. {Beyond dispute} means undeniable.

Disputed describes something that is contested, challenged, or subject to disagreement. A disputed {territory} is claimed by multiple parties.
