Unlike fictional narratives, documentaries aim to inform, persuade, or explore actual phenomena: {a documentary about climate change}, {a true-crime documentary}. As an adjective, documentary means consisting of or based on documents or factual records: {documentary evidence}, {documentary proof}.

Documentation is written material that explains, records, or provides evidence of something. Software documentation describes how programs work and how to use them. Legal or official documentation consists of papers that verify identity, ownership, or authorization: {You'll need documentation to cross the border}. The word can also mean the act of creating such records: {Her documentation of the process was thorough}.
clues: Written materials explaining how things work

definition: Documented means recorded in writing or other media, creating an official or verifiable record. A documented {immigrant} has legal papers establishing their status. A documented {case} has evidence supporting it. To say something is {well-documented} means abundant records exist: {The health risks of smoking are well-documented}. The word implies proof or authentication—what's documented can be checked.

Documenting is the process of creating a record or account of something. You document events by writing them down, photograph scenes to document conditions, or compile files to document a case. The emphasis is on creating evidence or reference material: {She spent months documenting human rights abuses}. In software, documenting means writing explanations of how code works.

Documents are written or printed records that provide information or evidence: birth certificates, contracts, legal filings, identification papers. To document something is to record it systematically: {She documented every expense}. In computing, a document is any file containing text or data that a user creates or edits. {Do you have the documents I need to sign?}

A docuseries is a documentary presented as a series of episodes rather than a single film. The format allows deeper exploration of complex subjects—true crime cases, historical events, celebrity profiles—across multiple installments: {The streaming service released a docuseries about the cult}. Also called a documentary series.

To dodge is to move quickly to avoid something—a blow, a ball, or a person. By extension, dodge means to evade or escape through cleverness or trickery: {dodge taxes}, {dodge the draft}, {dodge a question}. A dodge can also be a scheme or trick: {It's just a dodge to avoid responsibility}. The word suggests nimble evasion, whether physical or figurative. (Capitalized Dodge is the automobile brand.)

Dodgeball is a game where players throw balls at opponents while trying to avoid being hit themselves. Getting struck eliminates you; catching a thrown ball may eliminate the thrower or revive a teammate. The game is associated with school gymnasiums and playground culture: {We played dodgeball in P.E.} To dodge is to evade—the sport's essential skill.

Dodged is the past tense of dodge, meaning to move quickly out of the way to avoid something: {She dodged the ball}. Figuratively, to dodge is to evade or avoid by cunning or trickery: {He dodged the question}, {They dodged taxes for years}. A {dodged bullet} is a narrow escape from harm or misfortune.
clues: Slipped aside at the last moment

definition: Dodgem is the British term for a bumper car—a small electric vehicle driven around an enclosed arena at amusement parks, where the point is to bump into other cars: {The kids spent all their tokens on the dodgems}. Americans usually say bumper cars. The name comes from dodging, though colliding is half the fun.

Dodgems is the British term for bumper cars—the amusement park ride where small electric vehicles are driven around an enclosed arena, deliberately crashing into one another: {We spent half our tickets on the dodgems}. The name comes from the futile attempt to dodge collisions. Americans say bumper cars.

A dodger is someone who evades or avoids something—often an obligation or responsibility. A {draft dodger} avoids military conscription; a {fare dodger} rides without paying. The word implies craftiness or evasion rather than direct refusal. In baseball, the Dodgers took their name from Brooklyn pedestrians who dodged streetcars.

Dodgers is the plural of dodger—someone who evades or avoids something: {draft dodgers}, {tax dodgers}. The word suggests deliberate evasion of obligations or responsibilities. In baseball, the Dodgers refers to the Los Angeles team, originally the Brooklyn Dodgers—named for pedestrians who dodged the city's trolley cars.

Dodges is the plural of dodge and its verb form. A dodge is a quick evasive movement—a way of avoiding something coming at you. By extension, a dodge is any clever trick or scheme to avoid obligation: {a tax dodge}, {draft dodges}. To dodge is to evade: {She dodged the question}. {He dodges responsibility whenever possible}.

Dodging is the act of avoiding something by moving quickly aside or out of the way: {He kept dodging punches}. The word extends to evasion more broadly—dodging questions, dodging responsibilities, dodging the draft. In photography, dodging is a darkroom technique of selectively reducing exposure in parts of a print to lighten them.

Dodgy is British slang for something questionable, unreliable, or potentially dangerous. A dodgy {character} seems untrustworthy. A dodgy {deal} might be fraudulent. A dodgy {knee} gives trouble. The word suggests something not quite right without specifying exactly what's wrong: {The whole situation felt a bit dodgy}.

A dodo was a large flightless bird native to Mauritius, hunted to extinction by the late 17th century. The dodo's inability to fly or flee made it easy prey, and it has become a symbol of obsolescence and extinction. To call someone a dodo is to call them stupid or hopelessly out of touch: {Don't be a dodo}. The phrase {dead as a dodo} means completely extinct or defunct.

Dodos are flightless birds that became extinct in the late 17th century, native to Mauritius. Unable to fly and unafraid of humans, they were easily hunted to extinction—making the dodo a symbol of obsolescence and vulnerability. To call someone a dodo is to call them stupid or hopelessly out of touch: {Those old dodos in management don't understand the internet}.

A doe is an adult female deer. The term extends to females of related animals—antelopes, rabbits, and hares. {A doe and her fawns emerged from the treeline.} The word appears in the phrase {doe-eyed}, describing large, gentle, innocent-looking eyes. (Capitalized Doe is a placeholder surname.)

A doer is someone who acts rather than merely talks or plans. The word carries approval—doers get things done while others deliberate: {We need fewer thinkers and more doers on this project}. In compound forms, doer specifies what kind of action: {evildoer}, {wrongdoer}.

Doers is the plural of doer—people who take action rather than merely talking or planning. The word often appears in contrast to thinkers, dreamers, or talkers: {We need fewer planners and more doers}. A {doer of good deeds} performs charitable acts. In religious contexts, {doers of the word} are those who live their faith rather than simply professing it.

Dog is a native English word that denotes the domesticated form of canine that is descended from the gray wolf. Dog combines with many other words to form compounds such as bulldog and sheepdog. It is also frequently modified by adjectives, since there are so many kinds of dogs and they serve so many different purposes: police dog, attack dog, and stray dog. As a slang word, dog can mean feet (my dogs are tired) or it can designate a person, as in You lucky dog!

A dogcatcher is a local government employee who captures stray or unlicensed dogs. The job is often invoked as the lowest rung of public office: {He couldn't get elected dogcatcher}. The formal title is usually animal control officer.

Doge is a title for the elected chief magistrate in the former republics of Venice and Genoa, holding office for life. The word comes from Latin dux, meaning leader. {The Doge's Palace still stands in Venice.} In internet culture, doge refers to a Shiba Inu dog meme featuring broken English captions like "much wow" and "very excite," which inspired the Dogecoin cryptocurrency. (Capitalized Doge is the historical title.)

A dogear is a folded corner of a page, used to mark one's place in a book. The crease resembles a floppy dog's ear. To dogear a page is to fold it this way: {She dogeared the recipe she wanted to try}. Some readers consider dogearing a mild form of book abuse; others find it practical. Also spelled dog-ear or dog's ear.

Dogeared describes pages with corners folded down to mark a place, and by extension, anything worn from heavy use. A dogeared {paperback} shows signs of being read and reread. Dogeared {notes} have been consulted many times. The term suggests something well-loved rather than merely damaged: {Her dogeared copy of the cookbook was full of marginal notes}.

Dogearing is the practice of folding down the corner of a page to mark one's place in a book. The fold resembles a floppy dog ear. Some readers consider it practical; others view it as mistreating books: {I caught her dogearing my first edition}. The term extends to any similar corner-folding.

Dogears are the folded corners of book pages, turned down to mark one's place. The fold resembles a floppy dog's ear. To dogear a page is to make such a fold: {She dogeared the recipe she wanted to try}. A dogeared book shows heavy use—its pages creased and worn from repeated handling.

A dogfight is aerial combat between fighter aircraft at close range, characterized by rapid maneuvering as pilots try to get behind their opponents. The term evokes the chaotic, snarling quality of dogs fighting. By extension, dogfight describes any fierce, close-quarters struggle or intensely competitive situation: {The election turned into a real dogfight in the final weeks}. As a verb, to dogfight is to engage in such combat.

A dogfighter is someone who engages in dogfighting—either aerial combat between fighter pilots or the illegal blood sport of setting dogs against each other. Military use celebrates skill and bravery: {He was one of the best dogfighters in the squadron}. The animal-fighting sense carries strong criminal connotations, as organized dogfighting is a felony in most jurisdictions.

Dogfighters are people who engage in dogfighting—either the illegal blood sport of setting dogs against each other in combat, or aerial combat between military aircraft. The first sense carries strong criminal connotations: {Police arrested several dogfighters in the raid}. The second is military: {World War I dogfighters became legendary aces}.

Dogfighting is the blood sport of pitting dogs against each other in fights, typically to the death or serious injury. It's illegal in most countries but persists underground, with gambling on outcomes. Separately, dogfighting refers to close-range aerial combat between military aircraft: {The pilots engaged in a dogfight over the channel}.

Dogfights are aerial battles between fighter aircraft at close range, involving tight maneuvers as pilots try to gain position on opponents: {The skies over Britain were filled with dogfights during the Blitz}. The term comes from the chaotic, swirling nature of fighting dogs. Dogfights also names the cruel practice of setting dogs against each other for sport, now illegal in most places.

Dogfish is a name applied to various small sharks, especially the spiny dogfish common in coastal waters. The name likely comes from their habit of hunting in packs. Dogfish were once considered trash fish by commercial fishermen but are now marketed as "rock salmon" or "flake" in fish and chips. {We caught nothing but dogfish all day.}

Dogfood is food formulated for dogs. In tech slang, to dogfood (or eat your own dogfood) means to use your own product internally before releasing it: {We're dogfooding the new app this week}. The practice tests real-world performance and signals confidence in what you're building.

Dogged means stubbornly persistent, continuing despite difficulty or discouragement: {dogged determination}, {a dogged pursuit of the truth}. The word suggests tenacity that borders on obstinacy—someone who won't give up even when others might. {She showed dogged resistance to the proposed changes.} Pronounced with two syllables: DOG-id.

Doggedness is stubborn persistence—the quality of refusing to give up despite difficulty or discouragement. It emphasizes determination through sheer will rather than talent or cleverness: {Her doggedness eventually wore down the opposition}. The word carries a hint of inelegance, suggesting success through grinding effort rather than grace.

Doggie is an affectionate or childish word for a dog. It appears in baby talk, pet-directed speech, and casual conversation: {Who's a good doggie?} The spelling doggy is equally common. Doggie bag originally referred to restaurant leftovers supposedly taken home for the dog, though usually eaten by the humans.

Doggo is internet slang for dog, used affectionately and often in deliberately childish or playful contexts: {Look at that fluffy doggo}. The term emerged from online culture alongside similar cutesy animal vocabulary like pupper and birb. Separately, to {lie doggo} is an older British expression meaning to stay hidden or keep quiet.

Doggone is a mild oath expressing frustration, annoyance, or emphasis—a euphemism for "goddamn": {Doggone it, I left my wallet at home}, {That's the doggonedest thing I ever saw}. It functions as an adjective, adverb, or interjection. The word sounds folksy and old-fashioned, more likely from a grandfather than a teenager.
clues: What grandpa says instead of cursing

definition: Doggy is a childish or affectionate word for a dog: {Look at the cute little doggy!} As an adjective, it means resembling or relating to dogs: {a doggy smell}, {doggy treats}. Doggy style (or doggie style) refers to a sexual position where one partner enters from behind while the other is on hands and knees.

A doghouse is a small outdoor shelter for a dog. The phrase {in the doghouse} means in disfavor or trouble with someone, as if banished from the comfort of home: {He forgot their anniversary and ended up in the doghouse}.

Doghouses is the plural of doghouse, a small outdoor shelter built to house a dog. The phrase {in the doghouse} means to be in disfavor or trouble with someone, as if banished from the comfort of the main house to sleep outside with the dog. {After forgetting our anniversary, I was in the doghouse for a week.}

A dogleg is a sharp bend or angle, like the crook of a dog's hind leg. The word appears most often in golf, where a dogleg is a hole that bends left or right between tee and green: {The seventh is a dogleg left around the pond}. Roads, pipes, and hallways can also dogleg. As a verb: {The trail doglegs through the woods before reaching the summit}.

Doglegs are sharp bends or angles in a path, road, or structure—named for resembling the angular shape of a dog's hind leg. In golf, a dogleg is a hole where the fairway turns sharply left or right: {The seventh is a dogleg right around the trees}. Stairs may have doglegs where they change direction at a landing. The verb means to bend at such an angle: {The trail doglegs around the cliff face}.

Dogma is a set of principles laid down by an authority as incontrovertibly true. Religious dogma comprises official doctrines that believers must accept: {the dogma of papal infallibility}. Outside religion, dogma often carries a negative connotation—rigid beliefs held without evidence or openness to question: {economic dogma}, {political dogma}. Someone who clings to dogma is dogmatic.

Dogmas are doctrines or beliefs held as authoritative and not open to question. Religious dogmas are official teachings of a faith: {the dogma of papal infallibility}. The word often carries negative connotations—suggesting rigid, unexamined beliefs imposed without evidence: {They clung to economic dogmas long after the evidence contradicted them}. Someone who insists on dogmas without tolerance for dissent is dogmatic.

Dogmatic describes someone who asserts opinions as unquestionable truth, refusing to consider alternatives: {He was dogmatic about his political views}. The word implies rigidity and closed-mindedness—a dogmatic person states beliefs as if they were established facts. In theology, dogmatic refers to official church doctrine, but the everyday sense carries negative connotations of arrogance and inflexibility.

Dogmatism is the tendency to assert opinions as absolute truths without consideration of evidence or other viewpoints. A dogmatic person refuses to entertain doubt or alternative perspectives: {His dogmatism made productive debate impossible}. The term carries negative connotations—suggesting closed-mindedness rather than principled conviction.

To dognap is to steal someone's dog. The word follows the pattern of kidnap, substituting the victim. Dognappers may demand ransom or sell stolen pets. {Their French bulldog was dognapped from the front yard.}

A dognaper is someone who steals dogs, whether for ransom, resale, or other purposes. The term parallels kidnapper but applies to canines: {The dognaper demanded five thousand dollars for the poodle's return}. Also spelled dognapper.

A dognapper is someone who steals dogs, typically for ransom, resale, or to sell to research laboratories. The term combines dog with kidnapper, treating the theft of a pet with the gravity usually reserved for abducting people: {The dognapper demanded five hundred dollars for the poodle's return}.

Dognappers are people who steal dogs, whether for ransom, resale, or other purposes. The term parallels kidnapper but applies to pets: {The dognappers demanded five thousand dollars for the purebred's return}. Also spelled dog-nappers.

Dognapping is the theft of a dog, formed on the model of kidnapping. The crime has increased with the rising value of certain breeds: {The French bulldog was recovered three days after the dognapping}. Dognapper is the agent noun.

Dogpaddle, also written as dog paddle or dog-paddle, is a basic swimming stroke in which a person stays mostly upright and moves the arms and legs in a paddling motion beneath the water's surface, resembling how a dog swims. It's often the first stroke children learn because it keeps the head above water and requires no formal technique. As a verb, to dogpaddle means to swim using this stroke: {We dogpaddled across the shallow end}.

A dog park is a fenced outdoor area where dogs can run off-leash and socialize with other dogs. Most are public spaces in urban or suburban settings, offering city dogs rare freedom to roam: {We take her to the dog park every morning}. Also spelled as two words: dog park.

A dogpile is a heap of people piling on top of one person, often in celebration or roughhousing: {The team formed a dogpile on the pitcher after the final out}. Figuratively, to dogpile is to join others in attacking or criticizing someone: {Everyone dogpiled on him after his controversial tweet}. The image comes from dogs piling together.

Dogpiled means overwhelmed by a sudden rush of people or responses, from the literal image of multiple people jumping onto someone in a heap. Online, it describes being flooded with criticism, replies, or attacks: {She made one unpopular tweet and got dogpiled}. In sports or play, it's the physical pile-on after a big moment: {The team dogpiled the pitcher after the final out}.
A dogpile is either a literal or figurative heap of people or things. If you dogpile, you take part in the activity of piling up on someone or something.

Dogpiling is ganging up on someone, especially online—when multiple people attack, criticize, or mock a single target in rapid succession. The image is of dogs piling onto prey or each other. {She posted one controversial opinion and got dogpiled by hundreds of strangers}. The noun dogpile refers to the heap itself or the act of joining one.

Dogs are domesticated canines kept as pets, working animals, or companions. The word extends to related animals (prairie dog, wild dog) and mechanical gripping devices. Informally, dogs are feet: {My dogs are killing me}. To dog someone is to follow persistently: {Bad luck dogged him for years}. Something that {goes to the dogs} falls into ruin.

Dogsbodies is the plural of dogsbody, British slang for a person assigned menial or tedious tasks—a general assistant expected to do whatever needs doing. The term originated in naval slang, where it referred to junior sailors. {The interns are treated as dogsbodies, fetching coffee and making copies.}

A dogsbody is a person assigned menial tasks or drudge work, especially in a workplace hierarchy. The term is primarily British: {I spent my internship as a dogsbody, fetching coffee and making copies}. It implies being at everyone's beck and call, doing whatever unpleasant jobs others don't want.

Dogshit is feces from a dog, the stuff you step in on sidewalks and scrape off your shoe. As an adjective, it means worthless or terrible: {The service at that restaurant was dogshit}. The term is vulgar but emphatic—stronger than "bad," more dismissive than "crappy."

To dogsit is to look after someone else's dog while they're away, the canine equivalent of babysitting: {I'm dogsitting for my neighbor this weekend}. The term covers everything from staying at the owner's home to hosting the dog at your own place. Also appears as dog-sit.

A dogsitter is someone who cares for a dog while its owner is away, whether for a few hours or an extended period. Unlike a dog walker, who provides brief exercise outings, a dogsitter typically stays with the dog or hosts it in their own home, handling feeding, companionship, and overnight care. {We hired a dogsitter for the week we were in Hawaii.}

Dogsitting is caring for someone else's dog while they're away, typically in your own home or theirs. Unlike professional boarding, dogsitting usually implies a personal arrangement: {My neighbor is dogsitting while we're on vacation}. The person doing it is a dogsitter.

A dogsled is a sled pulled by a team of dogs, used for transportation across snow and ice. Dogsleds were essential to Arctic and subarctic peoples and later to polar explorers. The verb means to travel by dogsled: {We dogsledded across the frozen lake}. Also spelled dog sled.

Dogsledding is the activity of traveling over snow or ice on a sled pulled by a team of dogs, typically huskies or malamutes. It originated as transportation in Arctic regions and remains both a practical method of winter travel and a competitive sport: {We went dogsledding in Alaska}. The verb is dogsled; the vehicle is a dogsled or dog sled.

Dogsleds are sleds pulled by teams of dogs, traditionally used for transportation across snow and ice in Arctic regions. The dogs, typically huskies or malamutes, are harnessed in pairs or a fan formation. Dogsled racing remains popular in northern climates: {The Iditarod is Alaska's famous dogsled race}. As a verb, to dogsled is to travel by this method.

A dogtag is a metal identification tag worn by military personnel, typically on a chain around the neck. The tags bear essential information—name, service number, blood type—for identifying casualties. The name comes from their resemblance to pet identification tags. In extended use, dogtag applies to any similar identification tag: {The gym requires members to scan their dogtags at entry}.

Dogtags are metal identification tags worn around the neck by military personnel, stamped with name, serial number, blood type, and other vital information. The tags help identify soldiers who are wounded or killed in combat. The term extends to any similar identification tag: {The gym requires members to scan their dogtags at the entrance}. Also spelled dog tags.

A dogwhistle is a signal that is intended to be heard or understood by a particular audience. In politics, this may be a reference to an earlier statement or event that is understood by those familiar with the earlier context. The idea behind the term is that only dogs can hear dogwhistles; similarly, only those for whom a dogwhistle is intended can understand it.

Dogwhistles are coded messages that appear innocent to general audiences but carry specific meaning to a targeted group. The term comes from ultrasonic whistles only dogs can hear. In politics, a dogwhistle signals alignment with particular views—often controversial or prejudiced—without stating them explicitly: {Critics accused the candidate of using racial dogwhistles}. The verb is to dogwhistle.

Dogwood is a flowering tree or shrub of the genus *Cornus*, prized for showy spring blossoms that are actually modified leaves surrounding tiny flowers. The wood is dense and hard, historically used for tool handles, weaving shuttles, and golf club heads. {The dogwoods were in full bloom along the mountain road.}

Dogwoods are flowering trees and shrubs of the genus Cornus, prized for their showy spring blossoms—typically white or pink bracts surrounding small flowers. The wood is exceptionally hard and dense. {The dogwoods are blooming early this year.} Native to temperate regions, they're popular ornamental plants in gardens and along streets.
Doh and duh are used ironically to signal that you, or someone else, have been very slow to understand something obvious.

Doiley is a variant spelling of doily—a small decorative mat, usually made of lace or paper with an ornate pattern. Doilies are placed under vases, plates, or other objects to protect surfaces or add a delicate, old-fashioned touch: {The cake sat on a paper doiley}.

Doilies is the plural of doily, a small ornamental mat typically made of lace or paper with decorative cutout patterns. Doilies are placed under vases, plates, or other objects to protect surfaces or add a dainty, old-fashioned touch: {The antique shop had doilies under every lamp}. The word often evokes fussy, grandmother-style decor.

A doily is a small decorative mat, typically made of lace, paper, or linen, placed under dishes, vases, or other objects to protect surfaces or add ornamentation. Doilies evoke Victorian domesticity and grandmother's parlors—either charming or fussy depending on your taste: {The cake sat on a paper doily}.

Doink is a playful word for a light impact or the sound it makes—something bouncing off a surface or bonking gently: {The ball doinked off the rim}. It can also mean a small mistake or blunder: {I made a real doink on that form}. In crude slang, doink sometimes means to have sex.

A dojo is a training hall for martial arts—judo, karate, aikido, and similar disciplines. The Japanese word literally means "place of the way," suggesting a space for learning and practice. In figurative use, dojo extends to any space dedicated to intensive skill development: {a coding dojo}, {a writer's dojo}.

Dojos is the plural of dojo, a training hall for martial arts like judo, karate, or aikido. The word comes from Japanese and literally means "place of the way." Extended to coding dojos—spaces where programmers practice skills collaboratively: {There are several coding dojos in the city}.

The doldrums are a state of stagnation or listlessness: {The economy has been in the doldrums for months}, {She's been in the doldrums since the breakup}. The word comes from a region near the equator where sailing ships could be becalmed for weeks in still air—the original doldrums were geographical before becoming psychological.

Dole is money or goods distributed to the needy, particularly government unemployment benefits in British usage: {He's been on the dole for six months}. To dole something out is to distribute it in small portions, often grudgingly or sparingly: {She doled out the remaining supplies}. The word carries connotations of charity and meagerness. (Capitalized Dole is a surname or brand name.)

A doll is a small figure of a human, typically a toy for children. Dolls range from simple cloth figures to elaborate collectibles. The word extends to attractive people, especially women: {She's a real doll}. To {doll up} is to dress elaborately or apply heavy makeup. Calling someone a doll can be affectionate or condescending depending on context.

A dollar is the basic unit of currency in the United States, Canada, Australia, and several other countries. The word often stands for money generally: {I don't have a dollar to my name}. A {dollar store} sells cheap goods. To {look like a million dollars} is to look fantastic. {The sixty-four-thousand-dollar question} is the crucial one everyone wants answered.

Dollars is the plural of dollar, the basic unit of currency in the United States and several other countries. Beyond counting money, dollars appears in expressions about value and cost: {That painting is worth big dollars}. To {look like a million dollars} is to look fantastic. {Dollars to donuts} expresses high confidence in a bet.

Dollface is an affectionate term of address, usually for a woman or girl considered attractive: {Hey, dollface, can I buy you a drink?} The term evokes the smooth, symmetrical features of a porcelain doll. It can sound flirtatious, dated, or patronizing depending on context—charming from a 1940s film noir detective, creepy from a stranger on the street.

A dollhouse is a miniature model of a house, typically furnished with tiny furniture and figures, used as a child's toy or adult collectible. The scale and detail vary from simple play sets to elaborate replicas. Figuratively, dollhouse describes anything diminutive or precious: {The cottage was a perfect little dollhouse}. Also spelled doll's house, especially in British English.

Dollhouses are miniature model houses, typically furnished with small-scale furniture and accessories, used as children's toys or adult collectibles. The appeal lies in creating and controlling a complete domestic world in miniature: {She spent hours arranging the tiny furniture in her dollhouse}. Elaborate dollhouses with handcrafted details can be serious hobbies for adults. Also spelled as two words: doll houses.

Dollies is the plural of dolly. A dolly is a child's word for a doll—a toy figure of a person. In film and television, a dolly is a wheeled platform for moving a camera smoothly; to dolly is to move the camera this way: {The director called for the camera to dolly in}. A dolly is also a small wheeled cart for moving heavy objects: {We loaded the boxes onto dollies}.

A dollmaker is someone who creates dolls, whether as a craft, art form, or profession. The term covers hobbyists who sew cloth dolls at home and artisans who sculpt elaborate porcelain figures: {The dollmaker's studio was filled with tiny glass eyes and miniature wigs}. Dollmaker sometimes appears in horror contexts, where creating lifelike human replicas carries sinister undertones.

A dollop is a small, soft lump or blob of something, typically food: {a dollop of whipped cream}, {a dollop of sour cream on the baked potato}. The word suggests an imprecise, casually applied portion rather than a measured amount. Figuratively, a dollop of something is a small quantity: {The story needs a dollop of humor}.

Dollops is the plural of dollop, a soft, shapeless lump or blob of something, typically food: {dollops of whipped cream}, {a dollop of sour cream on the baked potato}. By extension, dollop means a small amount of anything: {The story needed a dollop of humor}. As a verb, to dollop is to serve in such portions: {She dolloped the mashed potatoes onto each plate}.

Dolls are figures resembling humans or animals, typically used as children's toys. A doll can be simple or elaborate—from rag dolls to porcelain collectibles to action figures. To {doll up} is to dress elaborately or apply heavy makeup. Calling someone a doll is dated slang for an attractive person or a term of endearment: {Thanks, you're a doll}.

A dolly is a small platform on wheels used for moving heavy objects: {We loaded the refrigerator onto a dolly}. In film and television, a dolly is a wheeled platform that carries a camera for smooth tracking shots—to dolly is to move the camera this way: {The director wanted to dolly in slowly on the actor's face}. Dolly is also a child's word for a doll. (Capitalized Dolly is a given name.)

Dolma is a family of stuffed dishes common in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Central Asian cuisines. The most familiar version consists of grape leaves wrapped around a filling of rice, herbs, and sometimes ground meat, though the term covers any vegetable—peppers, zucchini, eggplant, tomatoes—that has been hollowed out and stuffed. Dolmas may be served hot as a main dish or cold as an appetizer, often with yogurt or lemon.

Dolmas are grape leaves stuffed with a mixture of rice, herbs, and sometimes ground meat, then rolled into small cylinders and cooked. A staple of Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines, they're served warm or cold, often with lemon or yogurt: {We ordered dolmas as an appetizer}. Also spelled dolmades. Singular: dolma.

Dolphins are marine mammals known for their intelligence, playfulness, and streamlined bodies adapted for swift swimming. They breathe air through a blowhole, live in social groups called pods, and communicate through clicks and whistles. Dolphins appear frequently in human culture as symbols of friendliness and grace, and some species are trained for entertainment or research. In nautical contexts, a dolphin is also a mooring post or buoy cluster used to secure boats.

Dolphins are marine mammals known for their intelligence, playfulness, and streamlined bodies. They breathe air through a blowhole, travel in social groups called pods, and communicate through clicks and whistles. Dolphins appear frequently in mythology and popular culture as friendly, even mystical creatures. The Miami Dolphins are an NFL team. {We watched dolphins leaping alongside the boat.}

A dolt is a stupid person—someone slow-witted or dense. The word is old-fashioned and literary, carrying less sting than modern insults: {Don't be such a dolt}. It suggests foolishness rather than malice.

Dolts is the plural of dolt—a slow-witted or stupid person. The word carries a tone of exasperated dismissal rather than clinical diagnosis: {Those dolts in accounting lost my paperwork again}. It's milder than stronger insults but still contemptuous.

A domain is an area, either physical or abstract, that is separate from others because of unique qualities. The public domain includes everything freely available to or concerning the public. A domain expert is someone who is an authority on a particular topic. Historically, a domain was all the territory governed by a particular ruler. Today, we encounter domain most frequently in connection with the internet: The company has purchased a group of domain names in preparation for its launch.

Domains are areas of territory, knowledge, or activity over which someone or something has control or influence: {the king's domain}, {the domain of physics}, {that's outside my domain of expertise}. In computing, a domain is a distinct subset of the internet identified by a common address suffix: {.com}, {.org}, {.edu}. The word often implies ownership or sovereignty—a domain is yours to govern.

A dome is a rounded vault forming a roof or ceiling, typically hemispherical: {the dome of the Capitol building}. The shape extends to anything dome-like—a bald head, the sky, or a stadium roof. To dome in gaming slang is to shoot someone in the head: {He domed me from across the map}.

Domes is the plural of dome—a rounded vault forming a roof or ceiling, typically hemispherical: {The domes of the cathedral gleamed in the sunlight}. Dome extends to anything dome-shaped: the dome of the skull, a sports stadium with a domed roof. In slang, domes means heads: {Use your domes, people}.

Domestic relates to the home, household, or family life: {domestic chores}, {domestic bliss}. It also means within one's own country rather than foreign: {domestic flights}, {domestic policy}. A domestic is a household servant. Domestic animals are tamed species that live alongside humans. In law enforcement, a domestic is a call involving household members in conflict—often a {domestic dispute} or {domestic violence} situation.

To domesticate an animal or plant is to adapt it over generations for human use—breeding wolves into dogs, wild grasses into wheat. The process implies taming, but goes further: domesticated species depend on humans and differ genetically from wild ancestors. Figuratively, to domesticate someone is to make them more settled or conventional: {Marriage domesticated him}. To domesticate an idea is to make it familiar or acceptable: {The show domesticated Buddhism for Western audiences}.

Domesticated describes animals or plants that have been bred over generations to live alongside humans and serve human purposes. Dogs, cats, and cattle are domesticated; wolves, wildcats, and bison are wild. The word extends to people who have settled into conventional home life: {Marriage has domesticated him—he does dishes now}. A domesticated person has traded wilder ways for comfortable routines.

Domesticating is the present participle of domesticate, which means to tame wild animals or plants for human use and companionship. The process typically spans generations, breeding organisms for traits that make them more useful or docile: {Humans began domesticating dogs thousands of years ago}. Figuratively, domesticating can describe making something more familiar or manageable, or settling someone into home life: {Marriage had a way of domesticating him}.

Domestication is the process of taming wild animals or plants for human use over generations. Dogs emerged through domestication of wolves; wheat through domestication of wild grasses. The term extends to cultural adaptation: {the domestication of foreign customs}. To speak of someone's domestication is to suggest they've been trained for household life: {Marriage completed his domestication}.

Domesticity is the quality of being focused on home and family life. It suggests comfort with household activities—cooking, cleaning, caring for children—and contentment with staying home rather than pursuing outside ambitions. The word can be neutral or carry a whiff of judgment: {She surprised everyone by settling into domesticity} may imply something lost. {The domesticity of the scene} evokes warmth and familiarity.

Dominance is control or power over others, or the state of being dominant. In animal behavior, dominance describes hierarchical relationships where some individuals have priority access to resources: {The alpha wolf maintained dominance over the pack}. The word applies to competitive situations—market dominance, military dominance—and to personality traits: {Her dominance in meetings intimidated colleagues}. In genetics, dominance describes how one allele masks another.

Dominant describes what prevails, controls, or stands above others. A dominant {trait} in genetics masks recessive ones. A dominant {player} overpowers competitors. The dominant {theme} of a novel is its most prominent. In music, the dominant is the fifth note of a scale. In BDSM, a dominant (or dom) is the partner who takes control.

To dominate is to exert control or power over something or someone. A dominant team dominates its opponents. A dominant personality dominates conversations. {The cathedral dominates the skyline}—it towers over everything else, commanding attention. Market domination means controlling a large share: {Three companies dominate the industry}. To be dominated by a fear or obsession is to be ruled by it.

Dominated is the past tense of dominate, meaning to have control, power, or commanding influence over something or someone. A team that dominated a game won decisively; a figure who dominated a field shaped it more than anyone else. {The empire dominated the region for centuries.} {She dominated the conversation.} In sexual contexts, particularly BDSM, dominated describes being under the control of a dominant partner.

Dominating describes exerting control or influence over others, or standing out as the most prominent or powerful: {a dominating presence in the room}, {the dominating figure in twentieth-century physics}. In sports, a dominating performance is one where superiority is obvious and sustained. The word can suggest forcefulness that borders on overbearing: {His dominating personality made collaboration difficult}.

Domination is control or power over others. A country achieves domination over a region through military conquest or economic leverage. A team's domination of a sport means consistent, overwhelming superiority. In BDSM, domination refers to the role of exercising control over a submissive partner: {She's into domination}. To seek {world domination} is to aim for global control—often used hyperbolically or in fiction.

A dominator is someone or something that dominates—exercises control, holds power, or surpasses all rivals. The word appears in contexts ranging from sports {The team was the dominator of the league for a decade} to technology, where a dominator in graph theory is a node that must be passed through to reach another. In BDSM, a dominator is the controlling partner in power-exchange dynamics.

A dominatrix is a woman who takes the dominant role in BDSM activities, typically as a professional service. She controls and sometimes humiliates submissive partners, often using restraints, commands, or corporal punishment. The term evokes a specific aesthetic—leather, latex, high heels, whips: {She worked as a dominatrix in a Manhattan dungeon}. Plural: dominatrices or dominatrixes.

Domineering describes someone who asserts control over others in an overbearing way. A domineering {boss} micromanages every decision. A domineering {parent} dictates rather than guides. The word emphasizes not just authority but its aggressive, suffocating exercise—the kind that leaves little room for others to act or think independently.

Dominion is supreme authority or control over something: {The king held dominion over the realm}. It can also mean the territory subject to such rule: {the vast dominions of the empire}. In theology, dominion often refers to God's sovereignty over creation, or humanity's granted authority over the natural world. The word carries a formal, sometimes archaic tone, appearing in legal and religious contexts more than everyday speech.

Dominions are territories or realms under sovereign control: {the British dominions}, {the king's dominions}. The word suggests lands ruled rather than merely governed—a monarch holds dominion over dominions. Historically, Dominion designated self-governing nations within the British Empire, like Canada and Australia. In Christian angelology, Dominions are an order of angels exercising divine authority.

A domino is a small rectangular tile marked with dots on one face, used in games where players match ends with equal values. A set of these tiles is called dominoes, as is the game itself. The domino effect describes a chain reaction where one event triggers the next: {Defaults spread through the banking system like dominoes falling}. Separately, a domino is a loose hooded cloak worn at masquerades, or the mask that accompanies it.

Dominoes is a game played with rectangular tiles divided into two squares, each marked with dots (pips) indicating value. Players match ends with equal pip counts, building chains across a table. The tiles themselves are also called dominoes. A single tile is a domino. The {domino effect} describes a chain reaction where one event triggers others in sequence—like toppling dominoes stood on end.

Dominos is the plural of domino, referring to the rectangular game pieces marked with dots, or to the game played with them. The word also names a loose hooded cloak with a half-mask, worn at masquerades—though this sense is now rare. {We played dominos until midnight.} (Capitalized Domino's is the pizza chain.)

To don something is to put it on—usually clothing or equipment: {He donned his coat and hat}. The word is literary and somewhat old-fashioned, the opposite of doff. Don also appears as a title of respect in Spanish-speaking contexts, placed before a man's first name: {Don Miguel}. In British university slang, a don is a senior member of a college, especially at Oxford or Cambridge. (Capitalized Don is a given name.)

To donate is to give something—usually money, blood, or goods—to a cause, organization, or person in need. Unlike ordinary giving, donate implies generosity without expectation of return: {She donated her old clothes to charity}, {He donates blood regularly}. The word often appears in formal or institutional contexts: {Please donate to our campaign}.

Donated is the past tense of donate, meaning to give something—usually money, goods, or time—to a charitable cause or organization without expecting payment in return. {She donated blood at the community center.} {The billionaire donated millions to the university.} The word implies generosity and voluntary giving, distinguishing it from mere transfer or sale.

Donating is giving something—usually money, blood, or goods—to a charitable cause or person in need. The word implies generosity without expectation of return: {She's been donating to the food bank for years}, {He spent the morning donating blood}. Unlike simply giving, donating carries connotations of civic virtue or philanthropy.

A donation is something given to a cause, charity, or person in need—typically money, but also goods, blood, or organs. The word implies voluntary giving without expectation of return: {Please consider making a donation to the food bank}. To donate is to give in this way. A donor is one who donates.

Donations are things given to a cause, charity, or person in need—typically money, but also goods, blood, or organs. The word emphasizes voluntary giving without expectation of return: {The shelter relies on donations from the community}. A donation to a political campaign may be called a contribution instead, perhaps to downplay the one-sidedness of giving.

Done indicates completion or finish. When something is done, it has reached its end state—a task is done when completed, food is done when fully cooked, and a person is done when they've had enough: {I'm done with this conversation}. The expression {done and dusted} emphasizes finality. In informal speech, done often replaces finished: {Are you done with the bathroom?} When someone says {I'm done}, context determines whether they mean finished with a task or exhausted by a situation.

Doneness is how thoroughly something has been cooked. The term appears most often with meat, where doneness ranges from rare through medium to well-done: {The steak was cooked to perfect doneness}. With baked goods, doneness simply means fully cooked through: {Test the cake for doneness with a toothpick}.

Doner is meat—typically lamb, beef, or chicken—cooked on a vertical rotisserie and shaved off in thin slices. The word comes from Turkish and appears in doner kebab, the dish that inspired Greek gyros and Middle Eastern shawarma. In British English especially, a doner kebab is late-night street food, often eaten after drinking: {We grabbed a doner on the way home from the pub}.

Donezo is slang meaning finished, done, or over with—often with a note of finality or resignation. It can describe completed tasks {I'm donezo with my homework}, exhausted states {After that hike, I was completely donezo}, or relationships and situations that have ended {We broke up—totally donezo}. The -zo suffix adds casual emphasis, making it sound more definitive or dramatic than plain "done."

A dongle is a small hardware device that plugs into a computer or other electronic equipment. Originally dongles were copy-protection keys required to run certain software. Now the term covers any small plug-in device: USB adapters, Bluetooth receivers, streaming sticks, or cables that convert one port type to another. {I need a dongle to connect my headphones to the new laptop.}

Dongles are small hardware devices that plug into a computer or other electronic equipment. Originally, dongles were copy-protection keys required to run certain software. Now the term covers any small plug-in adapter: USB dongles for wireless mice, Bluetooth dongles, HDMI adapters, or devices that add functionality to a port. {I need a dongle to connect my laptop to the projector.}

A donkey is a domesticated animal related to the horse but smaller, with longer ears and a bray instead of a neigh. Donkeys are known for stubbornness and surefootedness, making them useful as pack animals in rough terrain. Calling someone a donkey suggests they're foolish or stubborn: {Don't be a donkey about this}.

Donkeys are domesticated members of the horse family, smaller and with longer ears than horses. They're known for stubbornness and sure-footedness, traditionally used as pack animals. A donkey can also mean a stupid person. {Donkey's years} means a very long time. In British slang, {donkey work} is tedious labor.

Donkeywork is the hard, tedious labor that requires effort but little skill—the unglamorous tasks that must be done before anything interesting can happen. The donkey carries the load while others ride. {I spent three weeks doing the donkeywork before the actual analysis could begin.} Also spelled as two words.

A donor is someone who gives something—typically blood, organs, money, or time—without receiving payment. Blood donors supply hospitals. Organ donors provide kidneys or hearts for transplant. Donors to charities or political campaigns give money: {The museum's largest donor got a wing named after him}. A sperm donor or egg donor contributes genetic material for reproduction.

Donors are people who give something—typically money, blood, or organs—to help others or support a cause. A blood {donor} gives blood for transfusions; an organ {donor} provides organs for transplant. In charitable contexts, donors contribute money: {The museum honored its major donors at a gala}. A sperm or egg donor provides genetic material for reproduction.

Dons is the third-person singular of don, meaning to put on clothing or gear: {She dons her lab coat before entering the clean room}. The word is slightly formal, often used for ceremonial or specialized attire—robes, armor, uniforms. Dons also pluralizes don, a British term for a university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge.

Donut is a variant spelling of doughnut—a small, sweet fried cake, typically ring-shaped with a hole in the center or filled with jam or cream. The simplified spelling dominates in American commercial contexts: {Dunkin' Donuts}, {a dozen donuts}. In driving, to do donuts is to spin a vehicle in tight circles, leaving circular tire marks.

Donuts is the spelling preferred by the food industry for doughnuts—ring-shaped fried dough, typically glazed or frosted. The simplified spelling gained traction through chains like Dunkin' Donuts. {I grabbed a dozen donuts for the office}. In automotive slang, doing donuts means spinning a car in tight circles, leaving circular tire marks.

A doobie is a marijuana cigarette—a joint. The term emerged in American slang in the 1960s and remains in casual use: {We smoked a doobie on the back porch}. It has a slightly dated, mellow connotation compared to newer slang.

A doodad is a small object whose name you don't know or can't recall—a placeholder word like thingamajig or whatchamacallit: {What's this doodad for?} It often refers to gadgets, parts, or decorative items: {The shelf was cluttered with doodads}. The word is casual and typically dismissive, suggesting the object is minor or unimportant.

Doodads are small objects or gadgets, especially ones whose names you don't know or can't recall: {What's that doodad on the dashboard?} The word also covers decorative trinkets or ornamental bits: {The shelves were cluttered with doodads}. Synonyms include thingamajig, whatchamacallit, and doohickey.

Doodah is a placeholder word for something whose name you can't recall or don't bother to specify—similar to thingamajig or whatchamacallit: {Hand me that doodah over there}. In British slang, {all of a doodah} means flustered or agitated. The word also appears in the minstrel song refrain "Camptown Races": {Doo-dah, doo-dah}.

A doodle is an aimless drawing made while the mind is elsewhere—during a phone call, a boring meeting, a lecture. The verb means to make such drawings: {She doodled in the margins of her notebook}. By extension, to doodle can mean to waste time or putter around without purpose.

Doodlebug has several unrelated meanings. It's a common name for the larva of an antlion—a small insect that digs conical pits in sand to trap prey. In British slang during World War II, doodlebug referred to German V-1 flying bombs, probably from the buzzing sound they made. In American regional use, a doodlebug is any small vehicle, especially a rail car used for light duties. The word also appears as a term of endearment for a child: {Come here, doodlebug}.

Doodled is the past tense of doodle, meaning to draw absent-mindedly, usually while attention is elsewhere: {She doodled in the margins during the meeting}. Doodles are typically simple sketches—shapes, patterns, faces—made without much thought. The word can extend to any idle, unfocused activity: {He doodled around on the guitar}.

Doodles are casual, absentminded drawings made while attention is elsewhere—during phone calls, lectures, or meetings. The verb doodle means to make such sketches: {She doodled in the margins of her notebook}. Doodles range from geometric patterns to rough figures, typically unplanned and idle rather than deliberate artwork.

Doodling is drawing idly, usually while attention is elsewhere—during a phone call, a lecture, a meeting. The drawings themselves are doodles: absent-minded sketches, shapes, or patterns in the margins of notebooks. {She filled the page with doodling while waiting on hold.} Despite its association with distraction, doodling may actually aid concentration and memory.
clues: What bored students do in margins

definition: Doodoo is a childish term for feces, used by small children or adults speaking to them: {Did you make doodoo in your diaper?} The reduplicated form makes it less harsh than shit. By extension, doodoo means trouble: {You're in deep doodoo now}.

A doofus is a fool or idiot—someone who acts stupidly or clumsily. The word is mildly insulting but usually affectionate, suggesting bumbling incompetence rather than malice: {Don't be such a doofus}. {He locked his keys in the car again—what a doofus}.

A doohickey is a thing whose name you don't know or can't recall—a gadget, device, or small mechanical part: {Hand me that doohickey over there}. The word belongs to a family of informal placeholder terms including thingamajig, whatchamacallit, and gizmo, used when the proper name escapes you or when the object seems too minor to name precisely.

Doohickeys are gadgets or small mechanical devices whose proper names you don't know or can't recall: {Hand me that doohickey over there}. The word belongs to a family of placeholder terms—thingamajig, whatchamacallit, gizmo—used when the real name escapes you or doesn't matter. Plural of doohickey.

Doom is fate or destiny, especially when terrible or unavoidable. The word carries weight—not just misfortune but inescapable ruin: {a sense of impending doom}, {the doom of civilization}. To doom someone is to condemn them to a grim fate: {The expedition was doomed from the start}. Doomsday is the day of final judgment or catastrophic destruction. In gaming, Doom became iconic as a pioneering first-person shooter, lending the word associations with demonic combat and heavy metal aesthetics.

Doomed means fated to fail, die, or meet disaster. Something doomed cannot be saved: {The ship was doomed from the moment it left port}. A doomed relationship has no future. The doom in question is usually death or destruction, though it can mean any inevitable bad outcome: {Their plan was doomed to fail}. To doom is to condemn to such a fate.

A doomer is someone who believes catastrophe is inevitable—whether ecological collapse, societal breakdown, or personal failure—and dwells on that belief. The term emerged from internet culture, often describing those who've given up hope about climate change or civilization's trajectory: {He's such a doomer about the economy}. Doomers may embrace their pessimism as clear-eyed realism or wear it with ironic detachment.

Doomers are people who believe catastrophe is inevitable or imminent—environmental collapse, societal breakdown, economic ruin. The term carries mild derision, suggesting excessive pessimism or even a perverse satisfaction in predicting disaster: {The doomers have been saying civilization will collapse for decades}. Climate doomers believe environmental damage is already irreversible. In internet culture, doomer describes someone resigned to hopelessness, often depicted as a withdrawn figure in memes.

Dooming is condemning to a grim fate or inevitable failure. The word implies sealing someone's destiny, usually badly: {His confession was dooming him to a life sentence}. In internet slang, dooming (or doomscrolling) describes obsessively consuming negative news: {I spent the evening dooming on Twitter}.

Doomposting is sharing relentlessly negative content online, especially about climate change, politics, or societal collapse. The poster may be genuinely distressed or seeking validation through pessimism. Related to doomscrolling, but active rather than passive: {My feed is nothing but doomposting about the election}. The practice often draws criticism for being unproductive or emotionally draining to others.

Dooms is the verb form of doom, meaning to condemn someone or something to a terrible fate or certain failure. When circumstances doom a project, they make its failure inevitable: {The lack of funding dooms the initiative from the start}. People can also be doomed by their own choices or by forces beyond their control: {His stubbornness dooms him to repeat the same mistakes}. The word carries a sense of finality and inescapability.

A doomsayer is someone who predicts disaster, catastrophe, or the end of the world. The term typically carries a dismissive tone, suggesting the person's warnings are exaggerated or unwarranted. {Climate doomsayers have been predicting imminent collapse for decades.} Doomsayers may turn out to be right, but the label usually implies skepticism about their dire forecasts.

Doomsayers are people who predict disaster or catastrophe, especially those who do so habitually or with apparent relish. The term usually carries a dismissive tone, suggesting the predictions are exaggerated or unfounded: {The doomsayers warned the economy would collapse, but it recovered}. Climate skeptics call environmentalists doomsayers; environmentalists say the doomsayers were right all along.

Doomsaying is predicting disaster or catastrophe, often with an implication that the predictions are exaggerated or unwelcome. A doomsayer warns of collapse, ruin, or apocalypse—economic, environmental, or otherwise: {Despite the doomsaying, the company survived}. The term usually carries skepticism toward the prediction rather than the predictor's sincerity.

Doomscrolling is compulsively consuming negative news or social media content, typically on a phone, despite the anxiety it causes. The term emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic when people found themselves unable to stop scrolling through upsetting headlines: {I stayed up until 3 a.m. doomscrolling}. The noun doomscroll refers to such a session.

Doomscrolled is the past tense of doomscroll—to compulsively consume negative news or social media content, typically late at night or during crises. The behavior is recognized as unhealthy but hard to stop: {I doomscrolled for three hours after the election results came in}. The word emerged in the early 2020s amid pandemic anxiety and political turmoil.

A doomscroller is someone who compulsively scrolls through negative news or social media content, unable to stop despite the anxiety it causes. The term emerged in the early 2020s as people found themselves endlessly consuming bleak headlines about pandemics, political crises, and disasters: {I've become such a doomscroller—I spent three hours reading about climate collapse last night}.

Doomscrolling is the habit of compulsively scrolling through bad news online, especially on social media, despite the emotional toll. The term emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic when people found themselves unable to stop consuming distressing content: {I stayed up until 3 a.m. doomscrolling through Twitter}. Also spelled doom-scrolling or doom scrolling.

Doomsday is the end of the world—the day of final judgment or catastrophic destruction. Religious traditions speak of a literal day when God judges humanity; secular usage extends to any civilization-ending catastrophe: nuclear doomsday, a {doomsday scenario}. A {doomsday clock} measures how close humanity stands to annihilation. A {doomsday prepper} stockpiles supplies for societal collapse.

A door is a movable barrier that opens and closes an entrance—to a room, building, vehicle, or cabinet. Doors provide privacy, security, and climate control. By extension, a door is any means of access: {The internship opened doors for her}. To {show someone the door} is to dismiss them. {Behind closed doors} means in private. To {darken someone's door} is to visit, usually unwelcome.

A doorbell is a button near an entrance that rings a bell or chime inside, alerting occupants to a visitor: {Ring the doorbell}. Modern doorbells often include cameras and speakers for remote communication. The word also names the sound itself: {I heard the doorbell}.

Doorbells are devices mounted near the entrance of a home or building that visitors press to announce their arrival, typically producing a chime, buzz, or melody inside. The classic doorbell connects a button to an electric bell or speaker, though modern smart doorbells often include cameras and two-way audio, letting homeowners see and speak with visitors remotely. {The doorbell rang just as we sat down to dinner.}

A doorbuster is a deeply discounted item offered to draw customers into a store, especially during sales events like Black Friday. The term evokes crowds so eager they might bust down the doors: {The TV was a doorbuster special at $199}. By extension, doorbuster describes any sale featuring such deals.

Dooring is a collision that occurs when someone opens a vehicle door into the path of an oncoming cyclist or pedestrian. The term emerged from urban cycling advocacy: {She was doored on her morning commute}. Dooring can cause serious injuries and is a traffic violation in many jurisdictions.

A doorknob is a rounded handle that you grip and turn to open a door. The knob operates a latch mechanism that releases when twisted. Doorknobs are being replaced in many settings by lever handles, which are easier for people with limited grip strength. {She rattled the doorknob but the door was locked}. To say someone is {dumb as a doorknob} is to call them profoundly stupid.

Doorknobs are the round handles you turn or grip to open a door. The knob operates a latch mechanism that holds the door closed. Doorknobs come in various styles—from simple brass spheres to ornate crystal or ceramic designs. {The old doorknob rattled when she tried to turn it.} In the phrase {dumb as a doorknob}, the object represents total lack of intelligence.

A doorknocker is a hinged metal fixture on a door, meant to be struck against a plate to announce a visitor's presence. Traditional designs include rings, lion heads, and decorative shapes. The word sometimes appears as slang for a woman's breasts, especially large ones that swing or bounce.

A doorman is an attendant stationed at the entrance of a building—typically an upscale apartment building, hotel, or club—who opens doors, greets visitors, monitors access, and assists with packages or taxis. The position suggests a certain level of service and security: {The doorman hailed a cab for us}. {He slipped the doorman a twenty}.

A doormat is a mat placed at a doorway for wiping shoes before entering. Figuratively, a doormat is a person who lets others walk all over them—someone too passive or submissive to stand up for themselves: {Don't be a doormat; tell him what you really think}.

Doormats are mats placed at doorways for wiping shoes before entering. The plural also refers to people who let others walk all over them—those too passive to resist mistreatment: {She's tired of being a doormat in that relationship}. The metaphor connects literally to the object's function and placement.

Doormen is the plural of doorman—a person stationed at the entrance of a building, typically a hotel, apartment building, or club. Doormen greet visitors, assist with packages, hail taxis, and control access: {The doormen at her building know everyone by name}. The role combines service with security.

Doors is the plural of door—a hinged or sliding barrier that closes an opening in a wall, vehicle, or piece of furniture. The word often appears in phrases about access or opportunity: {behind closed doors} means in private, {open doors} suggests new possibilities. {Doors open at seven} announces when a venue admits the public. To {show someone the door} is to dismiss them.

A doorstep is the step or platform at a building's entrance, just outside the door. By extension, something {on your doorstep} is very close or immediately accessible: {The beach is right on our doorstep}. As a verb, chiefly British, to doorstep is to approach someone at their home uninvited, typically for journalism or canvassing: {Reporters doorstepped her for days after the scandal broke}.

Doorsteps are the steps leading up to a door, especially the single step or threshold directly outside an entrance. Something {on your doorstep} is very close by or easily accessible. To doorstep someone (British) is to approach them uninvited at their home, typically as a journalist or canvasser seeking comment: {Reporters doorstepped the minister all morning}.

A doorstop is a device that holds a door open or prevents it from swinging too far. Common types include wedges placed under the door, weighted objects set against it, and spring-mounted bumpers attached to walls or baseboards. Figuratively, a doorstop is something heavy and useless: {That old computer is just a doorstop now}.

A doorstopper is a device that holds a door open or prevents it from swinging shut—a wedge, a weighted object, or a spring-mounted bumper attached to the wall or floor. Informally, a doorstopper is any thick, heavy book: {That biography is a real doorstopper}.

A doorway is the opening or passage that a door closes off, or the space immediately around and including a door. People stand in doorways, pause in doorways, and block doorways. {She appeared in the doorway holding a cup of coffee.} Figuratively, doorway suggests an entry point or threshold to something new: {College was a doorway to opportunities she'd never imagined.}

Doorways is the plural of doorway—the opening or passage through which a door closes, or the area immediately surrounding it. People stand in doorways, linger in doorways, or pass through them: {She paused in the doorway before entering}. Figuratively, doorways suggest points of transition or opportunity: {doorways to new possibilities}.

Doo-wop is a style of vocal rhythm and blues that emerged in the 1950s, characterized by close harmonies, nonsense syllables, and a cappella or lightly accompanied arrangements. The name itself mimics the backing vocals typical of the genre. Groups like the Platters and the Drifters exemplified the sound, which influenced later pop and rock music. {My grandmother still listens to her old doo-wop records.}

A doozie is something outstanding or remarkable of its kind—usually something impressively large, difficult, or extreme: {That last exam was a doozie}, {We've had some bad storms, but this one's a doozie}. The word carries a tone of wry admiration, acknowledging that something exceeds normal expectations, often unpleasantly.

Doozies is the plural of doozy—something outstanding, remarkable, or extreme of its kind. The word carries a note of impressed surprise, often at something impressively bad: {That last question was a doozy}, {We've had some storms, but this one's a doozy}. The spelling doozie also appears.
clues: Things that make you say wow

definition: A doozy is something remarkable or outstanding of its kind—usually something impressive, difficult, or extreme: {That last exam was a doozy}. The word can describe positive or negative extremes: an exceptional performance, a particularly bad hangover, or an unusually difficult problem. {We've had some storms this year, but last night's was a real doozy.}

Dopamine is a neurotransmitter—a chemical messenger in the brain associated with pleasure, reward, and motivation. It plays a role in how we experience satisfaction and pursue goals. In popular usage, dopamine often serves as shorthand for the brain's reward system: {Social media is designed to trigger dopamine hits}. The term appears frequently in discussions of addiction, habit formation, and what makes activities feel rewarding.

Dope began as a thick liquid or paste—a lubricant, a preparation, or a drug in viscous form. From there it branched. Dope means a narcotic drug, especially heroin or marijuana: {They found dope in his car}. A dope is a stupid person: {What a dope I was}. As an adjective, dope is slang for excellent or cool: {That's a dope jacket}. The verb means to administer drugs: {The horse had been doped}. To {dope out} something is to figure it out. The {dope} on a subject is inside information: {What's the dope on the new boss?}

Doped describes something that has been treated with a substance to alter its properties. In electronics, doped silicon has had impurities added to change its conductivity. In sports, a doped athlete has taken performance-enhancing drugs: {The doped cyclists were stripped of their medals}. Informally, doped can mean drugged or intoxicated: {He was too doped up to drive}.

Dopeheads is the plural of dopehead—a person who habitually uses drugs, especially marijuana or hard drugs. The term is informal and usually derogatory: {A bunch of dopeheads hanging around the park}. It carries connotations of addiction and wasted potential, though some use it self-deprecatingly.

Dopers is the plural of doper—someone who uses drugs, particularly in contexts where drug use is prohibited or frowned upon. In sports, dopers are athletes who use banned performance-enhancing substances: {The cycling world was rocked by revelations about dopers in the peloton}. More casually, dopers are simply people who smoke marijuana or use recreational drugs.

Dopes is the plural of dope, a word with meanings that cluster around two ideas: stupidity and drugs. A dope is a stupid person, and dopes are stupid people. Dope is also a slang term for marijuana or other illegal drugs, so dopes can refer to multiple quantities or types of these substances. The verb dope means to administer drugs to someone, typically without their knowledge: {Someone doped their drinks at the party}. As slang, dope can also mean excellent or cool: {Those sneakers are dope}.

Dopesick describes the state of withdrawal from opioids or other addictive drugs—the sweating, nausea, pain, and desperate craving that come when an addict's body lacks its expected dose. {He was dopesick and shaking, willing to do anything for a fix.} The term gained wider recognition through coverage of the American opioid epidemic.

Dopey describes someone sluggish, drowsy, or mentally slow—as if sedated or half-asleep: {I was still dopey from the anesthesia}. It also means foolish or dim-witted: {a dopey grin}, {What a dopey thing to say}. The word connects to dope in its sense of a stupefying drug, though the association has faded. Also spelled dopy.

Doping is the practice of administering performance-enhancing drugs to athletes or animals, especially in competitive sports where such substances are banned: {The cyclist was stripped of his title after doping allegations}. The term also applies in electronics, where doping means introducing impurities into a semiconductor to alter its electrical properties. To dope something is to add a substance to it—whether drugs to a person, additives to fuel, or impurities to silicon.

A doppelganger is a person who looks strikingly like someone else—an uncanny double or lookalike. The German word literally means "double-goer." In folklore, seeing one's own doppelganger was an omen of death. Today the word usually describes any remarkable resemblance: {I saw your doppelganger at the grocery store}. Also spelled doppelgänger.

Doppelgangers are look-alikes—people who closely resemble each other despite being unrelated. The word comes from German meaning "double-goer." In folklore, a doppelganger is a ghostly double of a living person, often an omen of misfortune. Modern usage is usually lighter: {Everyone says my doppelganger works at the coffee shop downtown}. Also spelled doppelgängers.
A doppelganger is a ghostly double of a living person. The word is borrowed from German. A less common use of doppelganger refers to a double, counterpart, or alter ego.

Doppler is informal shorthand for Doppler radar or the Doppler effect—the phenomenon where waves change frequency as the source moves toward or away from an observer. Weather forecasters use doppler to track storms by measuring how precipitation moves: {The doppler shows rain moving in from the west}. Medical ultrasounds use doppler technology to measure blood flow. (Capitalized Doppler refers to the physicist.)

A dork is a socially awkward or unfashionable person, someone out of step with what's cool: {He was such a dork in high school}. The word is mildly insulting but often affectionate—you might call a friend a dork for an embarrassing enthusiasm or clueless moment. Dork is also slang for penis, though this sense has faded as the social-misfit meaning took over.

Dorks are people perceived as socially awkward, unfashionable, or obsessively interested in niche subjects. The word carries less sting than similar terms—a dork is more endearingly clueless than genuinely contemptible: {We were such dorks in high school}. Many wear the label proudly now, especially fans of comics, gaming, or tech. Dork originally meant penis, but that sense has faded almost entirely.

Dorky describes someone or something socially awkward, unfashionable, or enthusiastically uncool—often in an endearing way. A dorky {laugh}, dorky {glasses}, or dorky {dance moves} suggest harmless awkwardness rather than genuine offense. The word is gentler than its cousins nerdy and geeky, implying lovable clumsiness: {He made a dorky joke that somehow worked}.

A dorm is a dormitory—a building with rooms for sleeping, typically at a college or university. The word implies shared living spaces for students: {I lived in the dorms my freshman year}. Dorm can also modify related nouns: {dorm room}, {dorm life}, {dorm mate}.

Dormancy is a state of reduced activity or suspended development. Seeds remain in dormancy until conditions favor germination. Animals enter dormancy to survive harsh seasons. The word extends to anything temporarily inactive: {The volcano has been in dormancy for centuries}, {The project fell into dormancy during the funding gap}. Dormant is the adjective form.

Dormant describes something inactive but capable of becoming active again. A dormant volcano hasn't erupted in recorded history but isn't extinct. Seeds lie dormant until conditions favor germination. A dormant bank account sees no transactions. Animals enter dormancy to survive harsh seasons. {The disease can remain dormant for years before symptoms appear.}

A dormer is a window that projects vertically from a sloping roof, creating additional headroom and light in an attic or upper floor. The structure includes its own small roof, typically gabled or hipped. Dormers are both functional and architectural features: {The old Victorian had three dormers across the front}. {We converted the attic into a bedroom and added dormers}.

Dormers are windows that project vertically from a sloping roof, each housed in its own small roofed structure. They add light and headroom to attic spaces: {The old farmhouse had three dormers across the front}. The singular dormer can refer to either the window or the entire projecting structure containing it.

Dormice is the plural of dormouse, a small European rodent known for hibernating through winter. The name likely comes from a word meaning "to sleep," fitting for an animal that spends much of its life in torpor. The dormouse appears memorably in *Alice in Wonderland*, dozing at the Mad Hatter's tea party.

Dormitories are residential buildings where many people sleep, typically in shared or small private rooms. The word most often refers to college housing: {Freshmen are required to live in the dormitories}. Dormitory can also mean a large room with multiple beds, as in boarding schools or hostels. Usually shortened to dorm in casual speech.

A dormitory is a building providing sleeping quarters for many people, especially at a school or university. Students live in dormitories during the academic year, often sharing rooms: {My freshman dormitory had communal bathrooms}. Informally shortened to dorm. A dormitory can also be a large room with multiple beds, as in a hostel. In British usage, a dormitory town or suburb is a residential area whose inhabitants commute elsewhere to work.

A dormouse is a small European rodent resembling a mouse but with a furry tail, known for hibernating through winter. The name likely comes from a word meaning "sleep"—dormice can hibernate for six months or more. {The Dormouse kept falling asleep} at the Mad Hatter's tea party. Plural: dormice.

Dorms is the informal plural of dormitory, referring to residential buildings where students live at colleges and universities. Each student typically has a small room, often shared with a roommate, with communal bathrooms and common areas on each floor. {Freshman are usually required to live in the dorms.} The word extends to any institutional group housing, such as for workers or athletes during training camps.

A dory is a small, flat-bottomed fishing boat with high, flaring sides, traditionally used by commercial fishermen off the Atlantic coast. Dories are light enough to be stacked on a larger vessel and launched individually: {The schooner carried a dozen dories for the cod fishery}. The word also names the John Dory, an edible fish with a distinctive dark spot on each side.

Dosa is a thin, crispy South Indian crepe made from fermented rice and lentil batter. It's a staple of South Indian cuisine, typically served for breakfast or as a snack, accompanied by chutneys and sambar. The most popular variety is masala dosa, which comes stuffed with spiced potatoes. {We ordered dosas at the new Indian restaurant downtown.}
