Dosage is the amount of a medicine, drug, or other substance to be taken at one time or over a period: {The recommended dosage is two tablets daily}. It can also refer to the administration schedule: {Dosage varies by age and weight}. In broader use, dosage applies to any measured quantity of something administered or experienced: {a healthy dosage of skepticism}.

A dose is a measured quantity of something, especially medicine or a drug, meant to be taken at one time: {The doctor prescribed a higher dose of the antibiotic}. By extension, dose applies to any portion of experience, particularly unpleasant ones: {a healthy dose of reality}, {a dose of his own medicine}. As a verb, to dose someone is to administer medicine to them, or to add a substance to something in measured amounts.

Doses is the plural of dose—measured quantities of medicine, radiation, or other substances administered at one time: {The doctor prescribed smaller doses for children}. By extension, doses can be portions of any experience: {healthy doses of skepticism}, {daily doses of exercise}. As a verb form, doses means to administer medicine: {She doses the cat with antibiotics twice daily}.

Dosing is the act of measuring out and administering a dose, typically of medicine or a drug: {The nurse handled the dosing of painkillers}. It also refers to the schedule or regimen of doses: {The dosing instructions say twice daily with food}. In casual use, dosing can mean secretly giving someone a drug: {Someone dosed his drink}.

A dossier is a collection of documents about a particular person, subject, or case. The word suggests thoroughness—intelligence agencies compile dossiers on persons of interest, lawyers assemble dossiers of evidence, journalists build dossiers on investigative subjects. {The FBI maintained a dossier on the civil rights leader.} A dossier implies organized information gathered over time, often with an element of surveillance or scrutiny.

Dossiers is the plural of dossier, a collection of documents about a particular person, event, or subject. Intelligence agencies keep dossiers on persons of interest. Human resources maintains personnel dossiers. The word carries a slight flavor of surveillance or investigation: {The FBI had compiled a thick dossier on the activist}.

A dot is a small round mark or spot. It appears in punctuation (the period), in digital displays (the dot-matrix printer), and in web addresses where {dot-com} became synonymous with internet business. To dot is to mark with dots or to scatter: {Farms dotted the landscape}. To {dot the i's and cross the t's} is to attend to every detail. {On the dot} means exactly at the specified time: {She arrived at noon on the dot}. (Capitalized DOT is the Department of Transportation.)

Dotcom refers to a company that does business primarily on the internet, from the ".com" suffix in web addresses: {She works for a dotcom startup}. The term emerged in the 1990s during the explosive growth of internet commerce. The dotcom {bubble} or dotcom {bust} describes the rapid rise and crash of internet stock valuations around 2000. Also spelled dot-com.

Dotcoms are internet-based companies, named for the ".com" in their web addresses. The term emerged during the late 1990s tech boom and is most associated with that era's speculative bubble: {Many dotcoms went bust when the bubble burst in 2000}. The word can describe either the companies themselves or the period: {the dotcom era}, {dotcom millionaires}.

To dote is to lavish excessive affection or attention, usually on someone: {She dotes on her grandchildren}. The word implies fondness taken to an indulgent extreme—a doting parent may spoil a child. An older sense, now rare, means to be feeble-minded from age: {The old man had begun to dote}.

Doted is the past tense of dote, meaning to lavish excessive affection or attention on someone: {She doted on her grandchildren}. The word suggests fond indulgence, sometimes to the point of spoiling. An older sense, now rare, meant to be feeble-minded or senile from age.

Doting describes excessive, uncritical affection—the kind that overlooks faults and indulges every whim. A doting {grandmother} spoils her grandchildren. Doting {parents} can't see their child's flaws. The word carries a gentle criticism: the love is real but perhaps blinds the doting person to reality.

Dots are small round marks or points. A dot marks the end of a sentence (period) or sits above the letter i. Polka dots are a pattern of evenly spaced circles on fabric. To dot is to mark with dots or to scatter across a surface: {Cottages dotted the hillside}. {On the dot} means exactly on time. (Capitalized DOTS refers to braille software.)
clues: What polka patterns are made of

definition: Dotted describes something marked or covered with dots: a {dotted line}, {dotted swiss} fabric. A dotted line on a document indicates where to sign—hence {sign on the dotted line} means to commit formally to an agreement. In music, a dotted note is lengthened by half its value. To dot is to mark with dots or scatter across a surface: {Farms dotted the valley}.

Dotty means slightly eccentric or scatterbrained, often in a harmless, endearing way: {My dotty aunt collects vintage teapots and talks to her plants}. In British usage especially, it can describe someone who's mildly crazy or obsessed: {He's dotty about cricket}. The word carries affection rather than harsh judgment—dotty people are charmingly odd, not genuinely disturbed.

Double implies two, sometimes for things with a counterpart that is called single. If you double a number, you add it to itself. Double digits means some number from 10 to 99. A double standard is two expectations that apply separately and unfairly. A competition of doubles involves teams of two. In baseball, hitting a double will get you to second base. A double bed or a double room has space for two. Double the expense means twice as much.
clues: Increase something by one hundred percent

definition: To doublecheck is to verify something by checking it a second time: {I doublechecked the address before we left}. The word implies careful attention—making sure you haven't made a mistake. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated: double-check, double check.

To doublecross someone is to betray them after gaining their trust, especially by secretly working against an agreement or alliance. The noun doublecross is the act itself: {The heist fell apart because of a doublecross}. The word implies deliberate deception—not merely backing out, but actively undermining someone who believed you were on their side.

Doublecrossed means betrayed by someone you trusted, especially a partner in crime or scheme who turned against you: {We had a deal, but he doublecrossed me and took the money}. The double suggests a cross within a cross—pretending loyalty while planning treachery. Also spelled double-crossed.

Doublecrossing is betraying someone who trusts you, especially after pretending to be loyal or cooperative. The word implies deliberate deception—agreeing to one thing while secretly planning another: {She suspected her business partner was doublecrossing her}. A doublecrossing friend or ally is particularly treacherous because the victim never sees it coming.

Doubled means multiplied by two or made twice as great: {The company doubled its profits}. It also describes something folded over on itself: {doubled fabric}. In acting, to double is to play two roles in the same production. If you're {doubled over}, you're bent sharply at the waist, usually from pain or laughter.

Doubledealing is deception through pretending loyalty to two opposing sides, or saying one thing while doing another. A doubledealing business partner might secretly negotiate with competitors while promising exclusivity. The word emphasizes betrayal of trust through duplicity: {His doubledealing cost him every friendship he'd ever had}. Usually hyphenated: double-dealing.

A doubledecker is something with two levels stacked vertically. The term most commonly describes buses with an upper and lower passenger deck, iconic in London: {We rode the doubledecker through the city}. It extends to sandwiches made with three slices of bread creating two layers of filling, and to any two-tiered structure: {a doubledecker bunk bed}.

A doubleheader is two games played consecutively between the same teams on the same day, originally and still most commonly in baseball: {The Yankees swept the doubleheader}. The term extends to any two events scheduled back-to-back: {a doubleheader of horror films}. Also spelled double-header.

Two games played back-to-back between the same teams on the same day, typically in baseball: {The Yankees swept the doubleheader}. The term extends to any paired events in sequence. A single game that counts for two in scheduling terms may also be called a doubleheader.

To doublepark is to park a vehicle alongside one already parked at the curb, blocking it in. The practice is illegal in most places but common in congested cities where parking is scarce: {I'll just doublepark for a minute while you run in}. Also spelled double-park and double park.

Doubleparked describes a vehicle parked alongside another that's already occupying a legitimate space, blocking it in or obstructing traffic. The practice is illegal in most places but common in dense urban areas: {I'll just be a minute—I'm doubleparked}. Often hyphenated or written as two words.

Doubles is a plural that takes several directions from double. In sports, doubles is a format with two players per side: {mixed doubles in tennis}. A doubles match contrasts with singles. In darts or dominoes, doubles are tiles or throws with matching numbers. The bartender meaning—a second pour of the same drink—also pluralizes: {He ordered two doubles}.

Doublespeak is language designed to obscure, disguise, or reverse meaning—making the unpleasant sound acceptable or the simple sound profound. It encompasses euphemisms, jargon, and deliberately ambiguous phrasing: {The company announced a "workforce reduction" of 2,000 employees}. Unlike straightforward lies, doublespeak technically says something while meaning another. The term derives from George Orwell's concepts of "doublethink" and "newspeak" in *1984*.

A doubletake is a delayed reaction where someone looks at something, looks away, then looks back sharply upon realizing what they saw. The word captures that moment of belated recognition: {I did a doubletake when I saw my ex at the party}. Often spelled as two words: double take.

A doubletake is a delayed reaction where someone looks at something, looks away, then looks back as the significance registers. The term comes from film acting, where the technique conveys dawning surprise or recognition. In everyday use: {I did a doubletake when I saw my ex across the room}.

Doubletalk is deliberately evasive or ambiguous language designed to confuse or mislead. Politicians engage in doubletalk when they want to seem responsive without committing to anything: {His answer was pure doubletalk—ten minutes of talking without saying a thing}. The word can also mean rapid nonsense speech mixing real words with gibberish, performed for comic effect.

Doubletap (also double-tap) refers to firing two shots in rapid succession at the same target—a technique emphasizing speed and accuracy in shooting. The term extends to touchscreen interfaces, where a doubletap is tapping twice quickly to zoom, select, or activate: {Doubletap the image to like it}. On social media, doubletapping often means liking a post: {I doubletapped her vacation photos}.

Doublethink is the mental capacity to hold two contradictory beliefs simultaneously and accept both as true. George Orwell coined the term in *1984* to describe how totalitarian regimes condition citizens to embrace logical impossibilities: war is peace, freedom is slavery. The word now applies broadly to any willful self-deception or cognitive dissonance that allows someone to ignore contradictions in their own thinking: {The company's doublethink lets them claim environmental leadership while expanding oil drilling}.

Doubletime means twice the normal speed or rate. In military contexts, it's a marching cadence of 180 steps per minute—double the standard pace: {The sergeant ordered them to doubletime across the field}. In music, doubletime doubles the tempo or rhythmic density. As a verb, to doubletime is to move at this accelerated pace. Doubletime pay is twice the regular hourly wage, typically for overtime or holiday work.

Doubletiming means moving at twice the normal pace, originally a military term for marching at double speed. It extends to any rushed activity: {We were doubletiming it to make the flight}. Doubletiming also means cheating on a romantic partner—seeing someone else on the side: {She found out he'd been doubletiming her for months}.

A doublewide is a manufactured home made of two sections joined together, roughly twice the width of a standard mobile home. The term often carries class connotations, evoking rural or lower-income housing: {They grew up in a doublewide on the edge of town}. Also spelled double-wide.

Doubling is the act of making something twice as large or twice as many: {The company announced a doubling of its workforce}. In film and theater, doubling means one actor playing two roles. A doubling can also be a fold or layer: {a doubling of fabric for reinforcement}.

A doubloon is a Spanish gold coin that circulated from the sixteenth through nineteenth centuries, worth about two escudos. The word appears most often in pirate stories and treasure-hunting contexts: {a chest full of doubloons}, {buried doubloon}. Outside historical or fictional settings, doubloon sometimes means any gold coin or, loosely, money.

Doubloons were Spanish gold coins that circulated widely from the 16th through 19th centuries, particularly in the Americas and Caribbean. The word now evokes pirate treasure and adventure fiction more than actual currency: {a chest full of doubloons}, {pieces of eight and doubloons}. Informally, doubloons can mean money generally, usually with a playful or ironic tone: {I don't have the doubloons for that}.

Doubt is uncertainty about whether something is true, will happen, or is the right choice. To doubt is to question or disbelieve: {I doubt he's telling the truth}. A doubt is an instance of such uncertainty: {I have my doubts about this plan}. {Beyond a reasonable doubt} is the legal standard for criminal conviction. {No doubt} concedes a point or expresses near-certainty: {No doubt you're right}. To give someone {the benefit of the doubt} is to trust them despite uncertainty.

A doubter is someone who questions or remains unconvinced. The word often carries a slightly dismissive tone—doubters are those who fail to believe what others accept: {The doubters were proven wrong when the project succeeded}. A doubter may be skeptical by temperament or simply uncertain about a particular claim.

Doubters are people who question, disbelieve, or remain unconvinced. The word usually implies skepticism toward something others accept: {The doubters said it couldn't be done}. Doubters may be proven right or wrong—the term itself is neutral, though context often casts them as obstacles to be overcome or vindicated skeptics.

Doubtful describes uncertainty or skepticism. A doubtful outcome is uncertain; a doubtful claim invites skepticism. Someone who is doubtful has reservations: {I'm doubtful we'll finish on time}. The word can also mean unlikely to be true or genuine: {evidence of doubtful authenticity}. A doubtful look conveys visible skepticism.

Doubting is the state of being uncertain or skeptical about something. A doubting {mind} questions rather than accepts. {Doubting Thomas} refers to someone who requires proof before believing—from the apostle who doubted Christ's resurrection until he touched the wounds himself.

Doubts are feelings of uncertainty or lack of conviction. When you have doubts about something, you're not sure it's true, wise, or likely to succeed: {I have my doubts about this plan}. To doubt is to question or feel uncertain: {I doubt he'll show up}. {Beyond a reasonable doubt} is the legal standard for criminal conviction—near certainty. {No doubt} means certainly or very probably: {No doubt she's already heard the news}.

A douche is a device for washing out a body cavity with a stream of water or other solution, used medically for cleansing wounds or, historically, for vaginal hygiene: {Vaginal douches are now discouraged by doctors}. The word comes from French for shower. To douche is to wash with such a device. As slang, douche (short for douchebag) is an insult for an arrogant, obnoxious, or contemptible person—typically a man: {That guy is such a douche}. The insult implies someone offensive and oblivious about it.

A douchebag is literally the bag component of a douche used for vaginal irrigation. As an insult, douchebag describes an arrogant, pretentious, or obnoxious person—almost always a man: {What a douchebag, parking his BMW across two spaces}. The insult implies someone aggressively unpleasant and unaware of it, often with overtones of privilege and entitlement. Frequently shortened to douche.
Douchebags is the plural of douchebag—either the literal feminine hygiene devices or, more commonly, arrogant obnoxious men: {The party was overrun with douchebags talking about crypto}.
Douches is the plural of douche—cleansing devices or, in slang, arrogant obnoxious people: {The pharmacy sells disposable douches}. {The club was full of douches in expensive shirts}.

Douchey is an adjective meaning characteristic of a douche—arrogant, obnoxious, and obliviously self-impressed: {That was a douchey thing to say}. {He drives a douchey sports car and talks about it constantly}. The word implies someone aggressively uncool while trying hard to be cool.
Douchiness is the quality of being douchey—arrogant, obnoxious behavior combined with obliviousness: {The douchiness of his pickup lines was almost impressive}.

Dough is a thick mixture of flour and liquid, worked into a mass for baking bread, pastries, or other foods. {She kneaded the dough until it was smooth.} The texture—soft, pliable, substantial—makes dough natural slang for money: {He's got plenty of dough}.

A doughboy is an American infantryman, especially one who served in World War I. The term predates the war but became strongly associated with the American Expeditionary Forces in Europe from 1917 to 1918. Various explanations exist for the nickname—from the flour used to whiten uniforms to the dumplings soldiers ate—but none is certain. {My grandfather was a doughboy in France.} The word has largely been replaced by GI for later conflicts.

Doughboys were American infantrymen, especially those who served in World War I. The term predates that war—it appeared during the Mexican-American War and possibly earlier—but its origin is uncertain. Theories involve flour-dusted uniforms, adobe dust, or doughy brass buttons, but none is conclusive. {My grandfather was a doughboy in France.}

A doughnut is a small fried cake of sweetened dough, typically ring-shaped with a hole in the center, though filled varieties are solid. The ring shape comes from how the dough cooks—centers would remain raw without the hole. In driving, a doughnut is a tight circular skid performed intentionally: {He did doughnuts in the parking lot}. Also spelled donut.

Doughnuts are sweet fried cakes, typically ring-shaped with a hole in the center, though filled varieties are solid. The hole allows even cooking and has become iconic—{doughnut hole} names both the missing center and the small round pastries made from that dough. In automotive slang, to {do doughnuts} is to spin a car in tight circles, leaving circular tire marks. Also spelled donut.

Doughy describes something with the soft, pale, yielding texture of raw bread dough. Flesh that is doughy lacks firmness or healthy color: {his doughy face}, {doughy arms}. The word often carries unflattering connotations of being unfit or unhealthy-looking. Bread or pastry that is doughy remains undercooked—soft and dense rather than properly baked through.

A doula is a trained companion who provides emotional and physical support during childbirth, though not medical care. Unlike midwives or nurses, doulas focus on comfort measures, breathing techniques, and advocacy for the mother's wishes: {Our doula helped us navigate the hospital experience}. Some doulas also assist during pregnancy or the postpartum period.

A doula is a trained professional who provides emotional support and physical comfort to a woman during pregnancy, labor, and the postpartum period. Unlike midwives, doulas don't deliver babies or provide medical care—they offer continuous presence, encouragement, and practical help like massage or positioning suggestions. {Our doula helped us feel calm throughout the birth.} Postpartum doulas assist with newborn care and household tasks after delivery.

Douse means to drench with liquid or to extinguish: {douse the flames}, {douse the lights}. You might douse a campfire with water or douse yourself with cologne. The word suggests sudden, thorough application. To douse can also mean to lower quickly, as with a sail. The spelling dowse typically refers to searching for water with a divining rod—a different word.

Doused is the past tense of douse, meaning to drench with liquid or to extinguish. You douse a fire with water, or douse yourself in cologne. {The protesters were doused with pepper spray}. {She doused the flames before they could spread}. The word suggests thorough soaking or complete extinguishing.

Douses is the verb douse in third-person singular present tense. To douse is to drench with liquid or to extinguish: {She douses the campfire before leaving}, {He douses himself in cologne}. The word suggests thorough soaking or sudden quenching—you douse flames, douse lights, or douse someone with a bucket of water.

Dousing is pouring liquid over something, typically to drench or extinguish: {dousing the campfire with water}, {The protesters were doused with pepper spray}. To douse lights is to extinguish them quickly. Dousing also refers to the practice of using a forked stick or rod to locate underground water or minerals—also called dowsing or water witching.

Dove is the past tense of dive in American English: {She dove into the pool}. British English prefers dived. As a noun, a dove is a bird in the pigeon family, typically smaller and more delicate than what we call pigeons. Doves symbolize peace and gentleness—a political dove favors negotiation over military action, opposite of a hawk. {The administration's doves urged diplomatic solutions.} (Capitalized Dove is a brand name.)

A dovecote is a structure built to house domesticated pigeons or doves, typically a small tower or wooden house with many nesting compartments. Historically kept for meat, eggs, and fertilizer, dovecotes are now mainly decorative or for hobbyist pigeon-keeping. To {flutter the dovecotes} is to cause a stir among calm or complacent people.

Doves are birds of the pigeon family, typically smaller species with pointed tails. The word carries connotations of gentleness, peace, and purity—a dove with an olive branch symbolizes peace, and white doves appear at weddings and memorials. In politics, doves favor diplomacy over military action, contrasted with hawks: {The administration was split between doves and hawks on intervention}.

Dovetail names a joint where wedge-shaped projections on one piece interlock with matching notches on another, creating a strong connection without nails—common in fine woodworking and cabinetry. The verb means to fit together neatly: {Her skills dovetail with his}. Plans or schedules that dovetail align conveniently: {The meetings dovetailed perfectly with my travel}.

Dovetailed describes things that fit together precisely and seamlessly, like the interlocking joints in fine woodworking from which the term derives. The dovetail joint, shaped like a dove's spread tail, locks pieces of wood together without fasteners. Extended to any context, dovetailed means combined or coordinated in a way that creates a unified whole: {Her research dovetailed nicely with the team's existing work}. {We dovetailed our vacation schedules so someone was always in the office}.

Dovetailing is the fitting together of separate things so they work as one. The word comes from carpentry, where dovetail joints interlock like spread fingers. In wider use, it describes how schedules, plans, or ideas connect smoothly: {Her research dovetails with mine}, {We dovetailed our vacation days to cover the whole month}. The present participle often functions as a noun for this kind of integration.

Dovetails names a type of interlocking joint used in woodworking, where fan-shaped projections on one piece fit into corresponding notches on another—creating a strong, elegant connection without nails. The figurative verb dominates modern usage: things that dovetail fit together neatly or complement each other: {Her skills dovetail with his perfectly}. {The two schedules dovetail nicely}.

Dovish describes a preference for peace, diplomacy, and negotiation over military action or aggressive measures. The term comes from the dove as a symbol of peace, contrasting with hawkish. In economics and finance, dovish describes policymakers who favor lower interest rates and prioritize employment over inflation control: {The Fed chair's dovish comments sent markets higher}.

A dowager is a widow who holds a title or property inherited from her deceased husband, particularly in aristocratic contexts. The term traditionally distinguished a widow from the current holder of a title—the {dowager duchess} being the previous duke's widow, distinct from the current duke's wife. More loosely, dowager describes any dignified elderly woman of wealth or high social standing, sometimes with connotations of formality or old-fashioned grandeur.
clues: Widow retaining her late husband's title

definition: Dowdy describes clothing, style, or a person that looks dull, unfashionable, or frumpy. The word suggests outdated rather than intentionally plain—a dowdy outfit isn't just modest, it's behind the times: {She felt dowdy in her mother's hand-me-downs}. The noun dowdy, now rare, once meant a plain or unstylish woman.

A dowel is a cylindrical rod, typically wooden, used to join pieces of material together or serve as a peg. Furniture makers insert dowels into aligned holes to connect boards without visible fasteners: {The shelf is held in place by wooden dowels}. Dowels also serve as hanging rods, axles for craft projects, or supports in baking when stacking cakes.

Dowels are cylindrical rods, usually wooden, used to join pieces of material together or reinforce joints. A furniture maker drills matching holes in two boards and inserts dowels with glue to create a strong bond without visible fasteners. Dowels also serve as pegs, axles, or structural elements: {The shelf rests on wooden dowels}. To dowel is to fasten with such pins.

Down is much less frequently used than its opposite up, mainly from having fewer extended and figurative uses. Its core meaning, lower, is present in most of its uses having to do with space, but not all: down the street doesn’t mean to a lower place on the street. Down is far more frequent as an adverb and adjective than as a preposition, where it has many extended meanings that are usually the opposite of the figurative meanings of up.

Downbeat has two distinct meanings. In music, the downbeat is the first beat of a measure—the strong beat where a conductor's hand moves downward. More commonly, downbeat describes a gloomy or pessimistic mood or tone: {The report struck a downbeat note about the economy}. The musical and emotional senses share a quality of heaviness or descent.

Downbeats are the first beats of musical measures—the moments when a conductor's baton moves downward. These beats typically receive the strongest emphasis in a piece. Figuratively, downbeats can mean low points or depressing moments: {The film's few downbeats are offset by its overall optimism}.

Downcast describes eyes or a gaze directed toward the ground, often signaling sadness, shame, or dejection: {She sat with downcast eyes, unwilling to meet anyone's gaze}. By extension, downcast describes a person's mood—dejected or dispirited: {He seemed downcast after the rejection}. The word pairs physical posture with emotional state.

Downcourt describes movement or position toward the opposite end of a basketball or tennis court from where a team is defending. It functions as both an adverb and adjective: a player moves downcourt on a fast break, or throws a downcourt pass to a teammate ahead of the play. The term mirrors downfield in football, orienting action toward the opponent's goal. {She sprinted downcourt before the defense could set up.}

Downdrafts are currents of air moving downward. In meteorology, they occur within thunderstorms when rain-cooled air descends rapidly, sometimes producing dangerous wind shear near airports. In architecture, downdrafts happen when cold air sinks through chimneys or ventilation systems: {The fireplace kept smoking because of downdrafts}. Figuratively, a downdraft describes a decline: {The stock market hit a downdraft in March}.

Downed is the past tense of down used as a verb, meaning brought down or consumed quickly. A pilot downed behind enemy lines has been shot down. A downed power line has fallen. To down a drink is to consume it in one motion: {He downed three beers before dinner}. To down an opponent is to defeat or tackle them.

A downer is something that dampens spirits or causes sadness or disappointment: {The news about layoffs was a real downer}. The word also refers to a depressant drug, such as a barbiturate or tranquilizer, that slows bodily functions and produces sedation—the opposite of an upper. Someone described as a downer is persistently negative or gloomy, the kind of person who brings down the mood of a gathering.

Downers are drugs that depress the central nervous system, producing sedation, relaxation, and reduced anxiety—the opposite of uppers or stimulants. Barbiturates, benzodiazepines, and opioids all qualify as downers. Outside pharmacology, a downer is anything that dampens mood or spirits: {The news about layoffs was a real downer}. A person who habitually kills the mood might be called a downer as well.

Downfall is a sudden loss of power, status, or success—the collapse of someone or something that was once high. A politician's downfall may come from scandal, a company's from mismanagement. The word often implies that the fall was caused by a specific weakness or error: {Pride was his downfall}. It can also mean heavy rain or snow, though this sense is rare.

Downfalls is the plural of downfall—a sudden loss of power, status, or success, or the cause of such a loss. A politician's downfall might be a scandal; a company's downfall might be poor management. {Pride and arrogance were his downfalls.} The word often appears in cautionary contexts about what leads to ruin.

Downfield refers to the direction toward the opponent's goal in football and similar field sports. A quarterback throws downfield; receivers run downfield routes. The term works as both adverb and adjective: {He threw the ball downfield}, {a downfield pass}. The opposite is upfield, toward one's own goal.

Downforce is the aerodynamic pressure that pushes a vehicle toward the ground, increasing tire grip at high speeds. Racing cars generate downforce through wings, spoilers, and body shape, allowing faster cornering: {The new front wing produces more downforce}. The tradeoff is increased drag, which reduces top speed on straightaways.

To downgrade is to reduce in rank, status, or quality. A storm may be downgraded from hurricane to tropical storm. Software gets downgraded when you install an older version. Airlines downgrade passengers from business to economy. As a noun, a downgrade is a descent or decline: {The stock was on a downgrade}. A literal downgrade is a downward slope in a road or track.

Downgrades are reductions in status, rating, or quality. Analysts issue downgrades when they lower their assessment of a stock or bond: {The downgrades sent shares tumbling}. Airlines downgrade passengers from first class to coach. Software downgrades revert to earlier versions. Credit agencies downgrade nations whose debt becomes riskier. The verb downgrade works the same way: {They downgraded the storm from a hurricane to a tropical storm}.

Downhearted means dispirited or discouraged, having lost hope or enthusiasm. The word suggests a sinking feeling, as if the heart has dropped: {Don't be downhearted—there will be other opportunities}. It's gentler than devastated but stronger than disappointed.

Downhill describes movement toward lower ground, following a slope's descent: {The trail runs downhill for two miles}. As an adjective, it modifies things oriented toward the bottom: a downhill {ski run}, a downhill {race}. Figuratively, downhill suggests decline or deterioration: {Everything went downhill after she left}. But {it's all downhill from here} can mean either easier going or worsening conditions, depending on context.

Downhome (also styled down-home) evokes the unpretentious, simple qualities associated with rural Southern American life. As an adjective, it describes things that feel authentic, folksy, and warmly familiar: {downhome cooking}, {downhome hospitality}. The term carries positive connotations of genuineness and lack of affectation, suggesting comfort rather than sophistication. It can also function as an adverb or noun referring to one's place of origin or roots: {He never forgot his downhome ways}.

To download is to transfer data from a remote system to your own device—the opposite of upload. You download files, apps, music, movies: {The download took forever on this connection}. As a noun, a download is the file itself or the act of transferring it. Figuratively, to download information to someone is to brief them thoroughly: {Let me download you on what happened at the meeting}.

Downloading is the transfer of data from a remote computer or server to your own device. You download files, apps, movies, music. The opposite is uploading. Figuratively, downloading means absorbing information rapidly: {Let me download everything that happened at the meeting}. As a noun, a download is either the act or the thing transferred: {The download took forever}.

Downloads are files transferred from a remote server to a local device, or the act of transferring them: {My downloads folder is full of PDFs}. The term covers music, software, documents, videos—anything pulled from the internet or network. As a verb form, downloads describes this retrieval: {The app downloads updates automatically}. Download speed measures how fast data arrives.

Downlow (also down-low or down low, often abbreviated DL) describes something kept secret or discreet: {Keep this on the downlow}. The term gained specific currency for men who have sex with men while publicly maintaining heterosexual identities: {He's on the DL}. This sense emerged from Black American vernacular and carries connotations of hidden behavior, particularly around sexuality.

Downmarket describes goods, services, or establishments positioned at the cheaper, less prestigious end of a range. A downmarket {hotel} offers basic accommodations; a downmarket {tabloid} prioritizes sensation over substance. The word can describe movement: {The brand has gone downmarket to attract budget shoppers}. More common in British than American English, where downscale serves similar purposes.

A downpayment is an initial partial payment toward a larger purchase, with the remainder to be paid later. Most commonly used for real estate and vehicles: {They saved for years to make a downpayment on a house}. The downpayment reduces the amount financed and demonstrates buyer commitment. Also spelled as two words: down payment.

To downplay something is to minimize its significance or importance: {The company downplayed the security breach}. It suggests deliberately making something seem less serious, dramatic, or noteworthy than it actually is—often to avoid alarm, criticism, or unwanted attention: {He downplayed his role in the project}.

Downplayed is the past tense of downplay, meaning to make something seem less important, serious, or significant than it actually is. Officials might downplay risks to avoid panic, or someone might downplay their accomplishments out of modesty. {She downplayed her role in the project's success.} The word suggests a deliberate minimizing, whether for strategic reasons, self-deprecation, or deception.

Downplaying is minimizing the significance or severity of something. You downplay bad news to avoid alarm, downplay your own achievements out of modesty, or downplay a scandal to protect your reputation. {Officials downplayed the health risks}. {She downplayed her role in the project's success}. The opposite is playing something up.
clues: Acting like it's no big deal

definition: Downplays is the third-person singular form of downplay, meaning to minimize the importance or significance of something. Someone who downplays a problem treats it as less serious than it may be: {The company downplays safety concerns}. The word often implies deliberate understatement: {She downplays her achievements}.
clues: Acts like it's no big deal

definition: A downpour is a sudden, heavy rain—the kind that soaks you in seconds: {We got caught in a downpour on the way home}. The word emphasizes intensity and volume, as if rain were being poured from above rather than falling in drops.

Downpours is the plural of downpour—a sudden, heavy rainfall. The word emphasizes intensity and volume: rain coming down in sheets rather than drops. {We got caught in one of those summer downpours}. Figuratively, a downpour can describe any sudden deluge: {a downpour of criticism}, {a downpour of emails}.

Downrange means in the direction a weapon is aimed or a projectile travels—away from the firing point toward the target area. Military bases have downrange zones where bullets and shells land. The term extends to aerospace: a rocket's downrange distance is how far it travels horizontally from launch. {The target is two hundred meters downrange.}

Downright intensifies what follows, emphasizing thoroughness or completeness: {downright rude}, {downright dangerous}, {a downright lie}. It typically modifies negative qualities, though not exclusively: {downright delicious}. The word suggests something unambiguous and undeniable—no hedging, no qualification. As an adjective, it means absolute or utter: {a downright refusal}.

Downriver means in the direction a river flows, toward the mouth: {The canoe drifted downriver}. As an adjective, it describes locations further along that course: {the downriver towns}. The opposite is upriver or upstream.

Downs functions as a verb and noun from the word down. To down something is to consume it quickly, especially a drink: {He downed three beers}. To down an opponent is to bring them to the ground. In football, a down is one of four attempts to advance the ball; to down the ball is to end a play. The downs are also rolling grassy hills, especially chalk uplands in southern England: {the South Downs}.

Downshift means to shift to a lower gear in a vehicle, typically to slow down or gain power for climbing: {She downshifted as she approached the curve}. Figuratively, to downshift is to reduce pace or intensity, especially in work or lifestyle: {After the heart attack, he downshifted to part-time consulting}. The noun describes such a shift: {a downshift in consumer spending}.

Downshifting is shifting to a lower gear in a vehicle, typically to slow down or gain more power on hills. The term extends to a lifestyle choice of voluntarily reducing work hours, income, or consumption in favor of more time, less stress, and simpler living. Someone who downshifts their career might move from a high-powered job to something less demanding. {After the heart attack, he started downshifting—fewer hours, more time with family.}

The downside is the negative aspect or disadvantage of something: {The upside is more money, but the downside is longer hours}. It pairs naturally with upside in weighing pros and cons. In finance, downside refers to potential losses or declining value: {downside risk}, {limit your downside}.

Downsides are the negative aspects or disadvantages of something, the unfavorable consequences that balance against benefits: {The job pays well, but the downsides include long hours and frequent travel}. The word implies weighing pros and cons—every decision has its downsides.

Downsize means to make smaller, especially to reduce a company's workforce or to move to a smaller residence. Corporations downsize by laying off employees: {The company downsized and eliminated three hundred positions}. People downsize their living situations, typically after children leave or in retirement: {After the kids moved out, we downsized to a condo}. The word emerged as corporate euphemism for firing but has lost some of that evasive quality.

Downsized means reduced in size, especially through corporate layoffs. A company downsizes by eliminating positions: {The firm downsized from 500 employees to 300}. The term emerged as a corporate euphemism—being downsized sounds less harsh than being fired or laid off. It also applies to scaling back generally: {They downsized to a smaller house after the kids moved out}.

Downsizing is reducing something's size or scale, especially a company's workforce through layoffs: {The merger led to significant downsizing}. The term emerged as corporate euphemism—firing people sounds harsh, downsizing sounds strategic. It also applies to individuals choosing smaller living spaces, often in retirement: {After the kids left, we started downsizing}.

Downstage is the part of a theater stage closest to the audience. As an adverb or adjective, it describes movement or position toward the front: {She moved downstage for her monologue}. The term comes from the historical raking of stages, which sloped down toward the audience for better sightlines.

Downstairs refers to the lower floor or floors of a building, or the direction toward them: {I left my phone downstairs}, {She ran downstairs to answer the door}. As a noun, it names that area: {The downstairs needs painting}. In British period contexts, the downstairs was where servants worked, distinct from the family's upstairs quarters.

Downstream describes the direction water flows in a river or stream—toward the mouth, away from the source: {The canoe drifted downstream}. By extension, it means later in a sequence or process: {downstream effects of the policy}, {downstream in the supply chain}. In oil and gas, downstream refers to refining and distribution rather than extraction. The opposite is upstream.

A downswing is a downward movement or trend—the opposite of an upswing. In golf, it's the portion of the swing where the club moves down toward the ball. In economics or business, it describes a decline: {The company struggled during the market's downswing}. The word implies a phase within a larger cycle, suggesting an eventual reversal.

Downtempo describes electronic music with a slow, relaxed pace—typically under 100 beats per minute. The genre emphasizes atmospheric textures and mellow grooves over dancefloor energy: {perfect downtempo playlist for a lazy Sunday morning}. The term contrasts with uptempo and emerged from electronic music scenes in the 1990s alongside related styles like trip-hop and ambient.

Downtime is time when something isn't operating or productive. Machines have downtime for maintenance; websites have downtime during outages. For people, downtime means leisure or rest between activities: {I need some downtime after this project}. The word implies a pause in normal function—whether scheduled, forced, or welcomed.

Downtown is the central business district of a city—where offices, shops, and commercial activity concentrate. As an adverb or adjective, it indicates direction toward or location in this area: {I'm heading downtown}, {a downtown apartment}. In American usage, downtown often implies urban energy and density, contrasting with residential neighborhoods and suburbs.

Downtrodden describes people who have been oppressed or treated harshly by those with power over them: {the downtrodden masses}, {giving voice to the downtrodden}. The image is of being trampled underfoot. The word appears almost exclusively as an adjective, though it began as a past participle of the now-rare verb downtread.

A downturn is a decline in economic or business activity. The word typically describes periods when growth slows, profits fall, or markets contract: {The company laid off workers during the downturn}. It implies a temporary dip rather than permanent collapse—downturns eventually reverse. The term applies beyond economics to any measurable decline: {a downturn in her health}.

Downturns is the plural of downturn, a decline or reduction in economic activity, business performance, or general conditions. The word implies a reversal from a previous upward or stable trend: {The company weathered several downturns in the market}. Economic downturns may range from brief slumps to prolonged recessions.

A downvote is a negative vote on social media or online forums, used to express disapproval or disagreement with a post or comment. The opposite of an upvote. As a verb, to downvote is to cast such a vote: {I downvoted the comment because it was misleading}. On platforms like Reddit, accumulated downvotes push content lower in visibility.

Downvoted describes content that has received negative votes on social platforms like Reddit, where users can upvote or downvote posts and comments. A downvoted comment has been judged unhelpful, wrong, or objectionable by the community: {His comment got downvoted into oblivion}. Being heavily downvoted often hides content from view.

Downvotes are negative ratings users give to content on platforms like Reddit, indicating disapproval or that something doesn't contribute to discussion. The opposite of upvotes. Content with many downvotes may be hidden or pushed to the bottom: {The comment was downvoted into oblivion}. To downvote is to cast such a vote: {I downvoted that post for misinformation}.

Downvoting is clicking a button to register disapproval of online content—a post, comment, or reply. On platforms like Reddit, downvotes push content lower in visibility, while upvotes raise it. The practice lets communities collectively judge quality: {Stop downvoting me just because you disagree}. Heavy downvoting can bury a comment or damage a user's reputation score.

Downward describes movement or direction toward a lower position: {The path led downward into the valley}. It applies to physical descent and figurative decline: a downward {trend} in prices, a downward {spiral} into addiction. As an adverb, downwards is equally common: {She glanced downwards}. The adjective form only takes downward: {a downward slope}.

Downwind means in the direction the wind is blowing—the opposite of upwind. If you stand downwind of a campfire, smoke blows toward you: {We positioned ourselves downwind of the deer so it couldn't catch our scent}. The word works as both adverb and adjective: {The downwind leg of the flight was faster}.

Downy describes something soft and fluffy like down—the fine, insulating feathers found beneath a bird's outer plumage. A baby bird is downy before its adult feathers grow in. The word extends to anything similarly soft: {downy hair on a peach}, {the baby's downy head}. Downy suggests delicate texture and gentle touch.

Dowries is the plural of dowry, the money, property, or goods a bride's family provides to the groom or his family upon marriage. The practice varies across cultures and eras: {Dowries were negotiated months before the wedding}. In some traditions, dowries secured a woman's financial standing; in others, they functioned as payment to the groom's family.

A dowry is money, property, or goods that a bride's family gives to her husband or his family upon marriage. The practice, ancient and widespread across cultures, ranges from symbolic gifts to substantial wealth transfers. In societies where dowries persist, they can create financial pressure on the bride's family and have been linked to domestic abuse when payments are deemed insufficient. The reverse arrangement—payment from the groom's family—is called a bride price.

A dowser is someone who practices dowsing—the folk art of locating underground water, minerals, or other hidden substances using a forked stick, pendulum, or bent rods. The dowser walks slowly until the instrument supposedly dips or twitches, indicating what lies beneath. Though scientifically unproven, dowsing persists in rural areas: {They hired a dowser to find where to dig the well}.

Dowsing is the practice of searching for underground water, minerals, or other hidden things using a forked stick or pair of rods that supposedly move when passed over the target. The dowser holds the instrument and walks until it dips or twitches, indicating where to dig a well or find buried objects. Despite centuries of use, dowsing has no scientific basis—controlled studies show dowsers perform no better than chance. Also called water witching or divining.

Dox is internet slang meaning to publicly reveal someone's private information—real name, address, phone number, workplace—typically with malicious intent. The word comes from "docs" (documents). Doxing is often used as harassment or intimidation: {Someone doxed her after she criticized the game online}. The threat of being doxed can silence people from speaking publicly.

Doxed means having had one's private information—real name, home address, phone number, workplace—publicly exposed online without consent, typically with malicious intent. The spelling varies: doxed, doxxed. The practice weaponizes personal data, often to enable harassment or threats: {She was doxed after posting a controversial opinion}. From "docs" (documents).

A doxer is someone who engages in doxing—researching and publicly releasing private information about a person, typically with malicious intent. The information might include home addresses, phone numbers, workplace details, or family members' identities. Doxers often operate to harass, intimidate, or enable others to do so: {The doxer posted her home address after she criticized him online}.

Doxers are people who dox—who dig up and publicly release someone's private information without consent. The information typically includes real names, home addresses, phone numbers, or workplaces. Doxing is usually malicious, intended to harass, intimidate, or enable others to do so: {The doxers posted her address and she had to move}.

Doxes is the third-person singular form of dox, meaning to publicly reveal someone's private information online—real name, address, phone number, workplace—typically with malicious intent. The term comes from "docs" (documents). Doxing is often used to harass, intimidate, or enable real-world targeting of the victim: {She doxes people who disagree with her on Twitter}.

Doxing is publicly revealing someone's private information online—real name, home address, workplace, phone number—typically with malicious intent. The practice weaponizes personal data, often to enable harassment or intimidation: {After she criticized the game, trolls doxed her and she had to leave her apartment}. Also spelled doxxing.

To doxx someone is to publicly reveal their private information online—real name, home address, phone number, workplace—typically with malicious intent. The word comes from "docs" (documents). Doxxing is a form of harassment, often used to intimidate, enable stalking, or incite others to target the victim: {She was doxxed after her tweet went viral}. Also spelled dox.

Doxxed means having had one's private information—real name, home address, phone number, workplace—publicly exposed online, typically with malicious intent. The term comes from "docs" (documents). Being doxxed often leads to harassment, threats, or stalking: {She was doxxed after her tweet went viral}. The verb is dox or doxx.

A doxxer is someone who doxxes—who searches out and publicly reveals another person's private information, typically with malicious intent. The term comes from "dropping docs" (documents). Doxxers often target people for harassment, exposing home addresses, phone numbers, or workplace details: {The doxxer posted her personal information after she criticized him online}.

Doxxers are people who publish someone's private information online without consent—real name, home address, phone number, workplace. The practice, called doxxing, is typically meant to harass, intimidate, or expose the target to real-world consequences: {Doxxers revealed her address and she started getting death threats}. The term comes from "docs" (documents).

Doxxes is the third-person singular of dox or doxx, meaning to publicly reveal someone's private information online—real name, home address, phone number, workplace—typically with malicious intent. The act weaponizes personal data, often to enable harassment or intimidation: {She doxxes anyone who criticizes her}. From "docs" (documents).

Doxxing is publicly revealing someone's private information online—real name, home address, phone number, workplace—typically with malicious intent. The term comes from "dropping docs" (documents). Someone might be doxxed as punishment, harassment, or to enable others to threaten them: {She was doxxed after her tweet went viral, and strangers started showing up at her house}.

Doze is a light, intermittent sleep—the kind you drift into without meaning to. You doze in a chair, doze through a lecture, doze off during a movie. A doze is briefer and shallower than proper sleep: {I caught a quick doze on the train}. To doze is to hover at the edge of consciousness, not fully asleep but not alert.

Dozed is the past tense of doze, meaning to sleep lightly or drift in and out of sleep: {She dozed on the couch while the movie played}. Often appears with off to mark the moment of falling asleep: {He dozed off during the lecture}.

A dozen is twelve of something: {a dozen eggs}, {a dozen roses}. The word functions as a convenient unit for counting, especially in commerce. In the plural, dozens indicates a large but indefinite number: {I've told you dozens of times}. A {baker's dozen} is thirteen—traditionally an extra item to avoid accusations of shortchanging customers.

Dozens means an indefinitely large number, roughly in the range of twenty-four to perhaps a hundred: {Dozens of people showed up}. The literal meaning—multiples of twelve—rarely applies; the word simply conveys "many" with a sense of scattered abundance. {Playing the dozens} is a form of ritualized insult exchange, especially in Black American culture, where participants trade escalating put-downs about each other's mothers.

Dozing is light, intermittent sleep—the kind where you drift in and out of awareness. Unlike deep sleep, someone dozing can be easily roused: {He was dozing in front of the television when the phone rang}. To doze off is to fall into this state unintentionally: {I dozed off during the lecture}.

Dozy means drowsy or half-asleep: {I was still dozy from my afternoon nap}. In British usage, dozy also means slow-witted or inattentive, often as mild criticism: {You dozy thing, you left the door wide open}. The word carries an affectionate edge even when chiding.

Drab describes something dull, colorless, or cheerless—lacking vibrancy or interest. A drab {office} has beige walls and flickering fluorescent lights. Drab {weather} is gray and dreary. The word often suggests monotony: {Her days had become drab and routine}. As a noun, drab is a yellowish-brown color, or a coarse cloth of that shade.

A drachma is an ancient Greek unit of currency, and later the modern Greek monetary unit until replaced by the euro in 2002. The word sometimes appears in historical or biblical contexts: {Thirty drachmas would have been a modest sum}. In ancient times, a drachma was also a unit of weight, roughly the mass of the silver coin.

Draconian describes laws, measures, or punishments that are excessively harsh or severe: {draconian budget cuts}, {draconian sentencing guidelines}. The word comes from Draco, an ancient Athenian lawgiver whose legal code prescribed death for even minor offenses. The sense has broadened to any rules or actions considered unreasonably strict or cruel.

Draconic means relating to or resembling a dragon—used in fantasy literature, games, and mythology: {draconic magic}, {draconic ancestry}. The word also means extremely harsh or severe, from the Athenian lawmaker Draco, whose legal code prescribed death for minor offenses. In this sense, draconian is more common: {draconian measures}, {draconian penalties}.

Draft, noun, verb, and adjective, has seemingly unrelated meanings, most of which are spelled draught in British English. The most frequent meaning concerns writing: a draft is a non-final version of a document, subject to revision: The author submitted her draft manuscript to the publisher. When you draft a text, you write a version of it that will probably be modified later. Draft legislation is a preliminary version of it. A draft is also many other things: an unwelcome gust of air (draft through an open window); a process by which a selection is made (first-round draft pick); and an instance of drinking (take a long, cool draft of beer). If a team drafts a player, it selects them for the team. If you get drafted, you are conscripted for military service.

Drafted is the past tense of draft, covering its various senses. Someone drafted into military service was conscripted: {He was drafted during the Vietnam War}. A document that's been drafted has been written in preliminary form: {The contract was drafted by our lawyers}. In sports, a player drafted was selected by a team: {She was drafted third overall}. In racing or cycling, someone drafted used another's slipstream to reduce wind resistance.

A draftee is someone who has been drafted—conscripted into military service rather than volunteering. The term is most associated with wartime mobilization: {My grandfather was a draftee in World War II}. Draftee can also refer to someone selected in a sports draft, though this usage is less common than the military sense.

Draftees are people who have been conscripted into military service rather than volunteering. The term is most associated with wartime mobilization, particularly during the Vietnam War era: {Many draftees opposed the war they were forced to fight}. The word carries connotations of reluctance or compulsion that distinguish draftees from career soldiers or willing enlistees.

Drafting is the act of creating preliminary versions of documents, plans, or designs. A lawyer drafts contracts; an architect drafts blueprints. The word implies work subject to revision: {I'm still drafting the proposal}. In racing and cycling, drafting means following closely behind another vehicle or rider to reduce wind resistance. The draft in professional sports—selecting new players—makes drafting the verb for that selection process.

Drafts are preliminary versions of written work, meant to be revised before reaching final form. The term extends to other kinds of rough plans or sketches. A draft is also a current of air moving through an enclosed space, or the act of drawing liquid from a container—hence draft beer, drawn directly from a keg. In American English, the draft refers to compulsory military service, and to draft someone is to select them for duty or, in sports, for a team. {I'm still working on early drafts of the manuscript.}

A draftsman creates technical drawings—architectural plans, engineering blueprints, mechanical diagrams. The work requires precision and spatial understanding, translating three-dimensional designs into two-dimensional representations. The term also applies to someone who drafts documents: {The senator's draftsman prepared the bill}. In chess, British English uses draughtsman for a checker piece. Also spelled draughtsman.

Drafty describes a space where unwanted currents of air flow through: {a drafty old farmhouse}, {The window was drafty}. The word suggests discomfort—cold air seeping through gaps in walls, windows, or doors. British spelling: draughty.

Drag implies movement, often along the ground, and often somewhat slowed by friction. When you drag something, you pull on it, unless you drag and drop with your mouse on a computer screen. Drag is the force that resists movement through air or water: The drag of the current prevented the swimmer from reaching shore. In slang use, drag is dressing in clothes associated with a gender not assigned at birth. A boring person or activity is a drag. The main drag of a town is its principal street. If you take a drag of a cigarette, you inhale from it.

Dragged is the past tense of drag—to pull something along a surface, typically with effort or resistance: {She dragged the heavy suitcase across the floor}. To be dragged into something is to be reluctantly involved: {I got dragged into their argument}. In slang, to drag someone is to mock or criticize them harshly, so {She got dragged on social media} means she faced public ridicule.

Dragging is the present participle of drag, carrying all its senses—pulling something along a surface, moving slowly, or extending tediously: {The meeting kept dragging on}. In internet slang, dragging someone means publicly criticizing or mocking them, often at length: {Twitter was dragging him for that take}. Drag-and-drop computing uses dragging to move files or objects across a screen.

A dragnet is a net dragged along the bottom of a body of water to catch fish. The word extends to any systematic search or coordinated effort to catch criminals or gather suspects: {Police set up a dragnet across the city}. The figurative sense suggests sweeping up everything in a wide area, sometimes indiscriminately.

Dragnets are nets dragged along the bottom of a body of water to catch fish, or nets drawn through an area to capture game. The word extends to systematic searches by police or military forces, sweeping through an area to find suspects or contraband: {The dragnet caught three of the escaped prisoners}. A dragnet catches whatever falls within its reach, wanted or not.

A dragon is a mythical creature typically depicted as a giant, fire-breathing reptile with wings, scales, and claws. Western dragons are usually fearsome beasts to be slain by heroes; Eastern dragons tend to be benevolent symbols of power and wisdom. Figuratively, a dragon is a fierce or formidable person, especially a stern older woman: {Her grandmother was a real dragon}. In computing, {dragon} sometimes refers to speech recognition software.

A dragonboat is a long, narrow racing vessel paddled by a team of twenty or more rowers, with a drummer at the bow keeping rhythm. The boats feature ornate dragon-head prows and are central to festivals originating in Chinese tradition but now held worldwide: {Our company entered a team in the dragonboat races}.

Dragonborn is a fantasy race originating in Dungeons & Dragons—humanoid creatures with draconic features like scales, claws, and the ability to breathe fire or other elemental attacks. The term gained wider recognition through the video game Skyrim, where the Dragonborn is a prophesied hero with the power to absorb dragon souls and speak their language. {The Dragonborn can shout enemies off cliffs.}

Dragonfire is fire breathed by a dragon in fantasy literature, games, and film. The word evokes extreme, mythical destructive power—hotter and more devastating than ordinary flame: {The castle walls melted under the dragonfire}. It appears in fantasy franchises like Game of Thrones and Dungeons & Dragons, where dragonfire often has magical properties that make it unstoppable by normal means.

Dragonflies is the plural of dragonfly, a large flying insect with an elongated body, two pairs of transparent wings, and prominent eyes. Dragonflies hunt mosquitoes and other small insects in flight, often hovering near water where they breed. {Dragonflies darted over the pond.}

A dragonfly is a large flying insect with a long slender body, two pairs of transparent wings, and enormous multifaceted eyes. Dragonflies are often seen near ponds and streams, where they hunt mosquitoes and other small insects in flight with remarkable speed and agility. They hover, dart, and change direction instantly—capabilities that have inspired drone and helicopter designs. Despite their fierce appearance and name, dragonflies are harmless to humans.

Dragonfruit is a tropical fruit with bright pink or yellow skin covered in green-tipped scales, suggesting a dragon's appearance. The white or magenta flesh inside is dotted with tiny black seeds and has a mild, slightly sweet flavor. Also called pitaya, it grows on climbing cacti native to Central America but now cultivated widely in Southeast Asia: {The smoothie bowl was topped with dragonfruit and coconut}.

Dragonhide is the skin or leather of a dragon, appearing in fantasy games and fiction as a prized material for armor and magical items. The word implies exceptional toughness and resistance: {dragonhide boots}, {dragonhide gloves}. In the Harry Potter universe, dragonhide is used for protective clothing worn by wizards working with dangerous creatures.

A dragonlord is a figure who commands or rules over dragons, appearing in fantasy fiction, games, and mythology. The term suggests mastery over these powerful creatures—whether through magic, bond, or conquest: {The dragonlord surveyed his kingdom from the mountain peak}. In gaming contexts, it often denotes a boss character or high-level title: {She finally defeated the dragonlord after dozens of attempts}.

Dragonlords are powerful figures in fantasy fiction who command or ride dragons—typically rulers, warriors, or nobles whose authority derives from their bond with these creatures. The term appears across novels, games, and films: {The dragonlords of Valyria conquered an empire}. In gaming contexts, a dragonlord may be a boss character or player class with dragon-related powers.

A dragonrider is a person who rides a dragon, a stock figure in fantasy fiction. The term gained prominence through Anne McCaffrey's Pern novels, where dragonriders form telepathic bonds with their mounts and defend their world from deadly spores. The concept appears across fantasy games, books, and films: {She dreamed of becoming a dragonrider}.

Dragonriders are people who ride dragons, typically as bonded partners rather than mere mounts. The term appears almost exclusively in fantasy fiction, where dragonriders often form elite warrior classes or hold special status: {The dragonriders of Pern defended the planet from Thread}. The bond between rider and dragon is usually portrayed as telepathic and lifelong.

Dragons are mythical creatures typically depicted as large, reptilian beasts capable of flight and breathing fire. They appear across cultures—menacing villains in European folklore, benevolent symbols of power in East Asian tradition. In fantasy fiction and gaming, dragons are often the ultimate adversary or a source of ancient wisdom. To {chase dragons} is to pursue something elusive; in drug slang, {chasing the dragon} refers to inhaling heroin vapor.

A dragonslayer is someone who kills dragons—a heroic figure in mythology and fantasy literature. The term extends to anyone who defeats a seemingly invincible opponent or overcomes an enormous challenge: {She became a dragonslayer when she took down the corrupt CEO}. In gaming, dragonslayer often names legendary weapons or achievements.

Dragonslayers are those who kill dragons, whether in myth, fantasy literature, or games. The term evokes heroic figures from legend—Saint George being perhaps the most famous—who defeat monstrous serpents threatening kingdoms or hoarding treasure. In gaming contexts, dragonslayer often appears as a character class, achievement, or weapon type. Figuratively, a dragonslayer is someone who conquers seemingly insurmountable challenges: {She's the dragonslayer who finally fixed our legacy codebase}.

A dragoon is a mounted infantry soldier, historically one who could fight on horseback or on foot. The verb to dragoon means to coerce or force someone into doing something, from the practice of using dragoons to suppress civilian populations: {They dragooned him into helping with the move}. The coercive sense now dominates everyday usage.

Dragoons were originally mounted infantry soldiers who could fight on horseback or on foot, though the term later came to designate cavalry units in various European armies. The verb dragoon means to coerce or pressure someone into doing something, often through harassment or intimidation—a sense that developed from the historical practice of using dragoons to suppress civilian populations. {The government dragooned citizens into compliance through military force.} {She was dragooned into organizing the company picnic.}

Drags is the third-person singular of drag—to pull something heavy or unwilling along a surface: {She drags the suitcase up the stairs}. Time drags when it passes slowly. The plural noun drags can mean puffs on a cigarette: {He took a few drags and stubbed it out}. In drag culture, drags refers to performances or costumes: {The club hosts weekend drags}.

A dragster is a vehicle built or modified for drag racing—short, straight-line acceleration contests. Purpose-built dragsters are long, narrow machines with oversized rear tires and powerful engines, designed purely for speed off the line: {The dragster covered the quarter mile in under four seconds}. The term also applies to street cars modified for racing.

Dragsters are vehicles built or modified for drag racing—straight-line acceleration contests over a short distance, typically a quarter mile. The term covers everything from street cars modified for weekend racing to purpose-built machines with massive engines and parachutes for braking: {The dragsters lined up at the starting line}. A dragster can also mean the person who races one.

A dragstrip is a straight, paved track designed for drag racing—typically a quarter-mile long with timing equipment at both ends. Cars launch side by side and race in a straight line to the finish. The term extends to any stretch of road used informally for the same purpose: {They turned the abandoned airfield into a makeshift dragstrip}.

Dragstrips are straight, paved tracks designed for drag racing—acceleration contests between vehicles over a short distance, typically a quarter mile. The word combines drag (racing slang for a race between vehicles) with strip (a narrow stretch of pavement). Also spelled as two words: {drag strips}.

A drain is a pipe or channel that carries away water or waste. To drain is to draw liquid off or out: {drain the pasta}, {drain the swamp}. What drains away gradually disappears: energy drains, resources drain. A drain on something depletes it: {Commuting is a drain on my time}. If something goes {down the drain}, it's wasted or lost.

Drainage is the process of water or other liquid draining away, or a system designed to carry it off: {The field has poor drainage}, {a drainage ditch}. In medicine, drainage removes fluid from a wound or body cavity. The word also refers to an area from which water flows into a river system: {the Mississippi drainage basin}.

Drained describes something emptied of liquid or resources. A drained pool has no water; a drained battery has no charge. When applied to people, drained means exhausted—depleted of energy or emotion: {I felt completely drained after the meeting}. The word implies something has been drawn out, leaving emptiness behind.
clues: Like a battery with no charge

definition: Draining describes something that depletes energy, resources, or emotional reserves: {Taking care of my mother is draining}, {a draining commute}. The word captures gradual exhaustion rather than sudden collapse—the slow emptying of a sink rather than pulling a plug. Physically draining tasks tire the body; emotionally draining ones wear on the spirit.

A drainpipe is a pipe that carries water away from a roof or other surface, typically running vertically down the side of a building. The word also describes a style of very tight, narrow trousers: {drainpipe jeans}, {drainpipe trousers}—the leg shape resembling the pipe.

Drainpipes are pipes that carry water away from a building, typically running vertically down exterior walls to channel rainwater from gutters to the ground. The word also describes a style of very tight, narrow trousers that hug the legs like pipes: {He wore black drainpipes and pointed boots}. This fashion sense, popular in various youth subcultures since the 1950s, is sometimes shortened to drainpipe as an adjective: {drainpipe jeans}.

Drains are channels or pipes that carry away unwanted water or waste. A drain in a sink or tub leads to the sewer; a drain in a field carries off excess rainwater. To drain something is to empty it of liquid: {Drain the pasta}. Energy, resources, or money can drain away: {The lawsuit drained our savings}. Something that depletes you is a drain: {Commuting is such a drain}.

A drake is an adult male duck. The word is less common than the female counterpart "duck," which serves for both sexes in casual speech, but appears in nature writing and among hunters: {The drake's iridescent head distinguished it from the drab hen}. Drake is also an archaic or poetic term for a dragon. (Capitalized Drake is a surname or given name.)

Drakes is the plural of drake, an adult male duck. The term appears in contexts distinguishing male from female waterfowl: {The pond had several drakes and a few hens}. Drake also survives in the compound firedrake, an archaic word for a fiery dragon or meteor.

Drama is a form of storytelling performed by actors, typically on stage—plays, theater, the dramatic arts. By extension, drama describes intense emotional situations or conflict: {There was so much drama at the office today}. The informal sense often carries dismissiveness—unnecessary emotional excess or attention-seeking behavior: {I don't need this drama in my life}, {She's always stirring up drama}.

Dramas is the plural of drama—serious works of theater, film, or television distinguished from comedy by their weighty subject matter and emotional intensity. The word extends to real-life situations fraught with tension or conflict: {I can't deal with all this family drama}. Someone prone to exaggerating emotional situations is said to create drama or be dramatic.

Dramatic describes what relates to drama or theater: a dramatic {performance}, dramatic {arts}. More commonly, it means striking, vivid, or emotionally intense—the qualities that make good theater: a dramatic {entrance}, dramatic {improvement}, dramatic {scenery}. Someone who is dramatic tends toward heightened emotion or exaggerated expression: {She's so dramatic about everything}.

Dramatics refers to theatrical performance or the study of acting and stagecraft: {She majored in dramatics}. More commonly, it describes exaggerated emotional behavior meant to draw attention or sympathy: {Save the dramatics for someone who cares}. The theatrical origin carries into the figurative—someone indulging in dramatics is performing rather than genuinely feeling.

Dramatisation is the British spelling of dramatization—the act of adapting something for dramatic presentation, or the result of that adaptation: {The BBC's dramatisation of the novel won critical acclaim}. It also describes making something seem more dramatic or exciting than it is: {His account was pure dramatisation}.

Dramatise is the British spelling of dramatize. To dramatise is to adapt something for theatrical performance: {The novel was dramatised for the stage}. More commonly, it means to present events in an exaggerated or emotional way: {She tends to dramatise every minor setback}. The word implies making something more vivid, theatrical, or sensational than it might otherwise appear.

Dramatization is the act of adapting something for dramatic presentation, or the resulting work: {The film is a dramatization of the 1969 moon landing}. More loosely, dramatization means exaggerating for effect—making something seem more serious, emotional, or significant than it is: {His account of the accident was pure dramatization}.

Dramatize means to adapt something for dramatic presentation—turning a novel into a play or film: {The book was dramatized for television}. More commonly, it means to present something in an exaggerated, theatrical way, making events seem more exciting or serious than they are: {She tends to dramatize every minor setback}. The noun is dramatization.

Dramatized means presented in dramatic form or with dramatic effect. A story dramatized for television has been adapted into a script with actors, dialogue, and scenes. More loosely, to dramatize is to exaggerate or make something seem more exciting or serious than it is: {She dramatized every minor setback into a crisis}. A dramatized account may be based on true events but embellished for effect.

Dramatizing is making something more dramatic or theatrical than it needs to be—exaggerating events or emotions for effect: {Stop dramatizing, it's just a scratch}. It also means adapting something for dramatic presentation: {They're dramatizing the novel for television}. The first sense carries a note of criticism; the second is neutral.

Dramedy blends drama and comedy, referring to films, television shows, or plays that mix serious subject matter with humorous elements. The term emerged in the 1980s as television began experimenting with shows that didn't fit neatly into either category. A dramedy might tackle heavy themes like illness or family dysfunction while maintaining a lighter tone or incorporating comic relief. {The show walks the line between tearjerker and sitcom—a true dramedy.}

Drank is the past tense of drink: {I drank too much last night}, {She drank her coffee black}. In some dialects, drank also serves as the past participle where standard English uses drunk: {I had drank three beers} instead of {I had drunk three beers}. Separately, drank is slang for a codeine-based cough syrup mixed with soda, associated with hip-hop culture: {sipping on some drank}.

Drape means to hang or arrange fabric loosely: {She draped a shawl over her shoulders}, {Curtains draped the windows}. The word suggests graceful, flowing folds rather than tight arrangement. To drape yourself over something is to sprawl or lean languidly: {He draped himself across the couch}. As a noun, drape refers to the way fabric hangs, or in the plural, to curtains themselves.

Draped describes something hanging or arranged in loose, flowing folds. Fabric draped over furniture falls gracefully rather than lying flat. A figure draped in silk wears it loosely arranged.
