The word suggests casual elegance—curtains draped across a window, a shawl draped over shoulders: {She sat with one arm draped across the back of the couch}.

Drapery is cloth arranged in loose folds, especially as decoration or clothing. The word often refers to heavy curtains: {The drapery blocked out the morning light}. In art, drapery describes the representation of fabric and its folds in painting or sculpture. The term can also mean fabric goods collectively, or a shop selling them.

Drapes are heavy curtains, typically hanging in folds from a rod over a window. The word is more common in American English, where it often suggests something more substantial or formal than simple curtains: {She pulled the drapes closed against the afternoon sun}. Drapes can also refer to the way fabric hangs: {the drapes of a toga}.

Draping is the act of arranging fabric so it hangs or falls in loose folds. The term applies to covering something with cloth {draping furniture before painting} or to how fabric naturally falls on a body or form. In fashion and design, draping refers to the technique of positioning fabric directly on a mannequin to create garments: {She learned draping before she learned to work from patterns}.

Drastic describes actions or measures that are severe, extreme, or far-reaching in effect. A drastic change is sudden and dramatic; drastic measures are aggressive responses to serious problems: {The company took drastic steps to cut costs}. The word often implies necessity—drastic action suggests the situation demanded nothing less.
Drat is a little-used and old-fashioned exclamation that expresses a sudden, negative emotion.

Draught, pronounced like draft, is the British spelling of draft for particular meanings. A draught is a current of cool air, a single act of drinking, or the depth of water needed to float a ship. As an adjective, draught is used to denote beer or cider served from a tap in a barrel, or to denote an animal used for pulling loads. U.S. English uses draft for all of these meanings. British English also uses draft for certain meanings, including a preliminary version of a document and a written order to pay money (a bank draft).

Draughts is the British name for the board game Americans call checkers—two players moving round pieces diagonally across a checkered board, capturing by jumping over opponents. {Fancy a game of draughts?} The singular draught has other meanings: a current of air, a drink taken in one swallow, or the depth a ship sits in water.

Draughty describes a space where unwanted currents of cold air blow through: {a draughty old farmhouse}, {The windows made the room draughty}. The word is the British spelling; Americans write drafty. Both come from draught/draft in its sense of a current of air.

Draw, a verb and noun, is very frequent and highly varied in its meanings. When you draw a picture you create a likeness. If you draw a load, you pull it. If you draw a liquid, you cause it to come out of a container. If you draw something from your pocket, you take it out. In sports, a draw is a game that ends without a winner. More generally, a draw is an instance of most of the verbal meanings of the word; for example you can draw a card (pick it up) in a card game, and that act is called a draw.

A drawback is a disadvantage or negative aspect of something that is otherwise appealing or beneficial. It often appears in evaluations where pros and cons are weighed: {The main drawback of the apartment is its distance from public transit}. Unlike a flaw, which suggests something inherently wrong, a drawback implies a trade-off—an acceptable downside to an otherwise desirable thing.

Drawbacks are disadvantages or negative aspects that offset something's benefits. Every option has its drawbacks: {The apartment is perfect except for one drawback—no parking}. The word implies weighing pros and cons, acknowledging that even good things come with downsides. A drawback doesn't disqualify something entirely but deserves consideration.

A drawbridge is a bridge that can be raised, lowered, or drawn aside to allow passage beneath or to prevent crossing. Medieval castles had drawbridges over moats, raised to keep invaders out. Modern drawbridges span waterways and lift to let boats pass: {Traffic backed up waiting for the drawbridge to lower}.

Drawbridges is the plural of drawbridge, a bridge designed to be raised, lowered, or drawn aside to allow or prevent passage. Medieval castles used drawbridges over moats for defense—raised to keep enemies out, lowered for friendly entry. Modern drawbridges span waterways, lifting to let boats pass: {Traffic backed up while the drawbridge was raised for a sailboat}.

A drawcard is something that attracts people or attention—a main attraction or selling point. The term is primarily Australian and British: {The festival's biggest drawcard was the headline act}. A star performer, special feature, or compelling offer can serve as a drawcard for an event or business.

Drawdown is a reduction or withdrawal, especially of military forces from a region or funds from an account. In finance, it measures the decline from a peak value to a subsequent low: {The portfolio suffered a 15% drawdown during the market correction}. Environmental contexts use drawdown for lowering water levels in reservoirs or aquifers. The word emphasizes gradual depletion rather than sudden removal.

A drawer is a sliding compartment in a piece of furniture—a desk, dresser, or cabinet—that pulls out for access and pushes back in for storage: {She rummaged through the junk drawer}. Drawers (plural) is an old-fashioned or humorous term for underpants. A drawer is also one who draws—an artist who sketches, or the person who writes a check or draft.

Drawers are undergarments covering the lower body—what Americans now usually call underwear or underpants. The term sounds old-fashioned or humorous today: {He stood there in his drawers}. Drawers is also simply the plural of drawer, the sliding compartment in furniture: {She rummaged through the desk drawers}.

Drawing is the act of making marks on a surface to create images, or the image itself: {a pencil drawing}, {a child's drawing of a house}. The word extends to any pulling or extracting motion—drawing water from a well, drawing a weapon, drawing conclusions. A drawing is also a selection by chance: {The raffle drawing is tonight}.

Drawings are pictures or diagrams made with a pen, pencil, or other marking instrument, typically without paint. A drawing can be a rough sketch or a finished work of art. The word also refers to selections made by chance: a lottery drawing, a drawing of names from a hat. {The architect presented her drawings to the committee.}

A drawl is a way of speaking in which vowels are stretched and words come out slowly, giving speech a lazy or relaxed quality. The term often describes Southern American accents: {He spoke with a Texas drawl}. As a verb, to drawl is to speak this way: {She drawled her greeting}.

Drawn is the past participle of draw, covering all that verb's meanings: a picture drawn in charcoal, curtains drawn shut, a bath drawn, a gun drawn, a conclusion drawn. As an adjective, drawn describes a face showing strain or exhaustion—features tight and haggard, as if pulled taut by worry or fatigue: {She looked pale and drawn after the ordeal}.

Draws is the third-person singular and plural form of draw, carrying its many meanings. Someone draws a picture, draws a conclusion, draws a weapon, or draws a crowd. A fireplace draws when it pulls air properly. In games, draws are ties—neither side wins: {The match ended in a series of draws}. Draws can also mean attractions: {The band was one of the festival's biggest draws}.

A drawstring is a cord or ribbon threaded through a casing in fabric, pulled to tighten or close an opening. Drawstring waistbands adjust fit without buttons or zippers: {drawstring pants}, {drawstring bag}. The cord cinches the material when pulled and loosens when released.

Dread is intense fear or apprehension, especially about something anticipated: {She felt a growing dread as the court date approached}. To dread something is to fear or be reluctant to face it: {I dread going to the dentist}. As an adjective, dread means feared or fearsome—mostly literary now: {the dread pirate}, {dread disease}. Dreaded serves the same function in everyday speech: {the dreaded Monday meeting}.

Dreaded describes something regarded with great fear or apprehension: {the dreaded phone call finally came}, {my dreaded in-laws are visiting}. The word often carries a touch of hyperbole or dark humor, dramatizing ordinary unpleasantness: {the dreaded Monday morning meeting}, {the dreaded blank page}.

Dreadful means causing dread or fear, though it now more commonly expresses strong disapproval or poor quality: {a dreadful mistake}, {dreadful weather}, {The food was absolutely dreadful}. The word has softened from its literal sense—something truly dread-inducing—to general intensified negativity. British speakers use it more freely as an emphatic: {I'm dreadfully sorry}.

A dreadhead is a person who wears dreadlocks—the hairstyle of matted, rope-like strands. The term is neutral or affectionate, used especially within Black communities and among fans of reggae culture: {The festival was full of dreadheads dancing to roots music}. Sometimes shortened to dread.

Dreading is anticipating something with anxiety or dread—expecting the worst and feeling unsettled about it: {I've been dreading this conversation all week}. The word suggests ongoing apprehension rather than a single moment of fear. You can dread an event, a task, or even a person's reaction: {She's dreading telling her parents}.

A dreadlock is a ropelike strand of hair formed by matting or braiding and not combing out. The style has roots in Rastafarian culture and various African traditions, though it has spread widely. Usually plural: {She's been growing her dreads for years}. The shortened form dreads is common in casual speech.

Dreadlocks are a hairstyle in which the hair is allowed to mat and twist into long, ropelike strands. The style has roots in various cultures but is most associated with Rastafarian culture and reggae music. Often shortened to dreads: {She's been growing her dreads for three years}. The style can form naturally or be cultivated through various techniques.

A dreadnaught is a powerful battleship, named after HMS *Dreadnought* (1906), whose design—featuring uniform heavy guns and steam turbines—rendered all previous warships obsolete. The word originally meant someone who fears nothing, from "dread naught." Now it suggests anything formidable or dominant in its class: {The company became a dreadnaught in the tech industry}. Also spelled dreadnought.

Dreadnaughts are battleships of a type that dominated naval warfare in the early twentieth century, named after HMS *Dreadnought* (1906), whose design made all previous battleships obsolete. The word extends to anything formidable or fearless—a dreadnaught was originally someone who dreaded nothing. A dreadnought is also a large-bodied acoustic guitar, and dreadnought fabric is a thick, tightly woven wool.

A dreadnought is a type of battleship that revolutionized naval warfare in the early twentieth century, named after HMS Dreadnought, launched in 1906. Its design—heavy guns of uniform caliber and steam turbine propulsion—made all previous battleships obsolete overnight. The term now applies more broadly to anything massive and formidable, or specifically to a large-bodied acoustic guitar with a deep, powerful sound: {He preferred a dreadnought for its bass response}. The word originally meant someone who fears nothing.

Dreadnoughts were a class of early 20th-century battleships that made all previous warships obsolete overnight. Named after HMS *Dreadnought* (1906), they featured uniform heavy guns and steam turbine propulsion. The term now applies to anything formidable or revolutionary in its field: {The new stadium was a dreadnought of modern architecture}.

Dreads is short for dreadlocks—rope-like strands of matted or braided hair. The style has roots in Rastafarian culture but has spread widely: {She's been growing her dreads for three years}. Dreads also serves as the plural of dread, meaning fears or anxieties: {Sunday night dreads kicked in before the work week}.

A dream is a series of thoughts and images experienced by sleepers, sometimes recalled in narrative form on awakening. When you dream you have this experience. By extension, and building on the sometimes-hopeful aspect of this, a dream is a vague plan or wish for the future. Figuratively, when you dream of something, you long to do it, even though it might be unrealistic. A person or situation characterized as a dream is extremely attractive.

A dreamboat is someone extremely attractive or romantically ideal—the kind of person you might dream about. The term emerged in mid-20th-century American slang and retains a slightly dated, playful quality: {She thought the new teacher was an absolute dreamboat}. It can also describe anything considered ideal or wonderful, though this use is less common.

Dreamboats is the plural of dreamboat, a slang term for an extremely attractive or desirable person: {All the dreamboats in high school ignored me}. The word evokes mid-twentieth-century romantic idealism, now often used with nostalgic or ironic inflection.

A dreamcatcher is a handcraft of Native American origin, traditionally a willow hoop with a woven net and hanging feathers. In Ojibwe tradition, dreamcatchers hung above sleeping children filter dreams—good ones pass through while nightmares catch in the web. Now widely commercialized as decorative objects: {She hung a dreamcatcher from her rearview mirror}.

Dreamcatchers are handmade objects traditionally crafted by some Native American peoples, consisting of a woven web inside a hoop, often decorated with feathers and beads. According to tradition, they filter dreams—letting good ones pass through while trapping nightmares. Mass-produced versions have become popular decorations, hung in bedrooms, cars, and dorm rooms: {She bought a dreamcatcher at the craft fair}.

Dreamed is the past tense and past participle of dream. It refers to experiencing images and sensations during sleep, or to imagining something desired: {I dreamed about flying last night}, {She dreamed of becoming a doctor}. Also spelled dreamt, though dreamed is more common in American English. {I never dreamed it would actually happen} expresses surprise at an outcome once thought impossible.

A dreamer is someone who dreams—either literally during sleep or figuratively through imagination and aspiration. The word often carries a gentle criticism: dreamers indulge in fantasy rather than practical action. {He's a dreamer who never follows through}. But it can also suggest visionary qualities: {Every great invention started with a dreamer}. The tension between impractical and idealistic runs through most uses.

Dreamers are people who dream—whether in sleep or in imagination. The word often carries a gentle criticism: dreamers have impractical hopes, heads in the clouds rather than feet on the ground. {He's a dreamer who never follows through.} But dreamers also envision what others can't: {Every great invention started with a dreamer.} In American political discourse, Dreamers (often capitalized) refers to undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children, from the proposed DREAM Act legislation.

A dreamgirl is an idealized romantic partner—the woman someone imagines as perfect for them. The term suggests fantasy and longing: {She was his dreamgirl, but he never worked up the courage to ask her out}. Often used nostalgically or wistfully about an unattainable crush. The compound emphasizes that the person exists more in imagination than reality.

A dreamhouse is one's ideal home, real or imagined—the house you fantasize about owning: {They finally bought their dreamhouse on the coast}. The term often appears in discussions of aspirational living, real estate marketing, and childhood play (as in Barbie's Dreamhouse). Sometimes spelled as two words: dream house.

Dreaming is the experience of images, sensations, and narratives during sleep. As an adjective, it describes someone lost in thought or fantasy: {a dreaming child gazing out the window}. The word carries connotations of imagination and aspiration—someone dreaming of success envisions a desired future. {I must have been dreaming} dismisses an unrealistic expectation.

Dreamland is the imaginary realm of sleep and dreams, or any place of fantasy and unreality. It often describes a state of pleasant obliviousness: {She was off in dreamland during the meeting}. The word can refer to an idealized place: {a dreamland of endless summer}. Parents use it when coaxing children to sleep: {Time to head off to dreamland}.

Dreamlike describes something having the quality of a dream—hazy, surreal, or disconnected from ordinary reality. A dreamlike {state} suggests altered consciousness; a dreamlike {quality} in film or art evokes the strange logic of dreams. The word often implies something beautiful but elusive: {The whole evening had a dreamlike feel, as if it might dissolve at any moment}.

Dreampop is a style of alternative rock characterized by hazy, atmospheric production, ethereal vocals, and shimmering guitars heavy with reverb and delay. The sound evokes a gauzy, half-conscious state—melodic but diffuse, pretty but detached. Cocteau Twins and Beach House exemplify the genre. {I've been on a dreampop kick lately.}

Dreams are the images, sensations, and narratives that unfold in the mind during sleep—often vivid, sometimes bizarre, rarely remembered in full. The word extends to waking life for hopes and aspirations: {She had dreams of becoming a doctor}. To dream is to experience these visions or to imagine possibilities: {I never dreamed it would actually happen}. Something dreamlike has the quality of dreams—hazy, surreal, detached from ordinary reality.

A dreamscape is an imaginary landscape resembling a dream—surreal, fluid, distorted. The word appears most often in art criticism and literary description: {The painter's dreamscapes blend melting clocks with impossible architecture}. It can describe actual dream imagery or any scene with dreamlike qualities: {The fog turned the harbor into a dreamscape}.

Dreamscapes are imaginary landscapes, the kind of surreal or fantastical settings that appear in dreams or evoke that quality. The word describes visual art, literature, film, or music that creates an otherworldly atmosphere: {The album's ambient tracks conjure hazy dreamscapes}. A dreamscape may be beautiful, unsettling, or both—logic suspended, imagery vivid but strange.

Dreamsicle is a frozen treat consisting of vanilla ice cream or ice milk coated with flavored ice, typically orange—a creamy core inside a fruity shell. The word often appears as a flavor descriptor for anything evoking that orange-vanilla combination: {dreamsicle cake}, {dreamsicle smoothie}. Sometimes spelled Creamsicle, which is a trademark.

Dreamt is a past tense and past participle of dream, used interchangeably with dreamed. British English favors dreamt; American English tends toward dreamed, though both are correct everywhere. {I dreamt of flying last night.} {She never dreamt it would end this way.}

Dreamtime is a state of reverie or abstraction, when someone seems mentally elsewhere: {She drifted into dreamtime during the meeting}. The word suggests a pleasantly unfocused mental state, neither fully asleep nor fully present. (Capitalized Dreamtime refers to Australian Aboriginal cosmology.)

A dreamwalker is someone who can enter or navigate dreams—either their own with unusual awareness and control, or other people's dreams entirely. The term appears in fantasy fiction, video games, and certain spiritual traditions where practitioners claim to move through dreamscapes at will: {The dreamwalker slipped into the sleeping king's nightmare}. Related to lucid dreaming but implies greater agency or supernatural ability.

Dreamwalkers are people who navigate or enter dreams—either their own or others'. The term appears in fantasy and supernatural fiction for characters with the ability to move through dreamscapes, often influencing events or communicating across the boundary of sleep: {The dreamwalkers gathered in the shared vision}. In some spiritual traditions, dreamwalkers practice lucid dreaming or shamanic journeying.

Dreamwalking is the supposed ability to enter or navigate through another person's dreams, a concept from folklore and fantasy fiction. A dreamwalker might communicate with sleepers, observe their subconscious, or influence dream events. The term also describes a state of moving through waking life as if in a trance: {She went through the day dreamwalking, barely aware of her surroundings}.

A dreamweaver is someone who crafts dreams or weaves together imaginative visions—used literally for mythical figures who create or control dreams, and figuratively for storytellers, artists, or visionaries who shape compelling narratives or experiences: {The novelist was a dreamweaver, spinning tales that felt more real than waking life}. Also the name of Adobe's web design software.

A dreamworld is an imaginary realm experienced during sleep or created by fantasy—a place detached from reality where normal rules don't apply. The term often carries connotations of escapism or delusion: {He's living in a dreamworld if he thinks that plan will work}. It can describe any idealized mental landscape where wishes come true and harsh realities don't intrude. (Capitalized Dreamworld is a theme park.)

Dreamworlds are imaginary realms—the landscapes of sleep, fantasy, or escapist fiction. The term often carries a note of unreality or delusion: {He lives in a dreamworld where consequences don't exist}. In gaming and entertainment, dreamworlds are constructed fantasy environments players or viewers inhabit temporarily: {The game's dreamworld blends medieval castles with alien technology}.

Dreamy describes a soft, hazy quality suggestive of dreams. A dreamy expression suggests someone lost in thought or reverie: {She had a dreamy look in her eyes}. Dreamy music or lighting is gentle and ethereal. In casual speech, dreamy means attractively appealing: {He's so dreamy}. A dreamy person tends toward fantasy and impracticality.

Dreary describes something depressingly dull, bleak, or cheerless. A dreary day is gray and dispiriting. A dreary landscape offers nothing to lift the spirits. The word applies equally to weather, places, tasks, or moods: {a dreary commute}, {dreary office walls}, {the dreary routine of daily chores}. Dreary suggests not just unpleasantness but a wearing monotony.

Dreck is worthless trash or rubbish, especially in reference to artistic or commercial products of low quality. From Yiddish, it literally means excrement but usually serves as a dismissive judgment: {The studio keeps churning out dreck}. {Most of what passes for television drama is pure dreck}.

Dredge has two distinct meanings. One is to scoop up material from the bottom of a body of water, either to deepen it or to search for something: {They dredged the river for the missing weapon}. To {dredge up} old memories or grievances is to bring them back to the surface. The other dredge is a cooking term—to coat food lightly in flour, breadcrumbs, or sugar before cooking: {Dredge the chicken in seasoned flour before frying}.

Dredged is the past tense of dredge, which has two distinct meanings. One involves clearing or deepening waterways by scooping up mud, silt, or debris from the bottom: {They dredged the harbor to accommodate larger ships}. If you dredge up something, you bring it to the surface, often unpleasant memories or forgotten information: {Why dredge up the past?} The other dredge belongs to cooking: to coat food lightly in flour, breadcrumbs, or sugar before frying or baking.

Dredges is the plural of dredge, a machine or vessel used to scoop mud, sand, and debris from the bottom of waterways—essential for keeping harbors and channels navigable. To dredge is to clear or deepen using such equipment, or more broadly to drag something up from below. In cooking, to dredge means to coat food lightly in flour or breadcrumbs before frying. If you {dredge up} old memories or grievances, you bring them back to the surface, often unwelcomely.

Dredging is the process of scooping sediment, debris, or other material from the bottom of a body of water. Channels are dredged to keep them navigable; harbors are dredged to deepen them. The verb dredge also means to coat food lightly with flour or breadcrumbs before cooking: {Dredge the chicken in seasoned flour}. To dredge up is to bring something unpleasant back to attention: {Why dredge up old grievances?}

Dregs are the sediment that settles at the bottom of a liquid—the bits of solid matter in wine, coffee, or tea that sink to the vessel's floor. By extension, dregs refers to the last remaining portion of something: {She drained the dregs of her coffee}. Figuratively, the dregs of society are people considered the lowest or most worthless: {the dregs of humanity}. The singular dreg appears occasionally but dregs dominates.

Dregs are the sediment that settles at the bottom of a liquid—the bits of grounds left in a coffee cup, the residue in a wine bottle. By extension, dregs means the least valuable remnants of anything: {the dregs of society}, {drinking the dregs of his savings}. The word almost always appears in plural form.

A dreidel is a four-sided spinning top used in a Hanukkah game. Each side bears a Hebrew letter, and players spin to determine whether they win or lose tokens from a central pot. The game is especially popular among children during the Jewish holiday season. {The kids played dreidel for chocolate coins.}

Dreidels is the plural of dreidel, a four-sided spinning top used in a traditional Jewish game played during Hanukkah. Each side bears a Hebrew letter, and players spin to determine whether they win or lose tokens from a central pot. {The children played with dreidels after lighting the menorah.}

A dreidl is a four-sided spinning top used in a traditional Hanukkah game. Each face bears a Hebrew letter, and players spin to determine whether they win or lose tokens from a shared pot. Children play for coins, nuts, or chocolate gelt. Also spelled dreidel.

A dreidle is a four-sided spinning top used in a traditional Jewish game played during Hanukkah. Each side bears a Hebrew letter, and players spin to determine whether they win or lose tokens from a central pot. Also spelled dreidel. {The children played dreidle for chocolate coins.}

Dreidles is the plural of dreidel, a four-sided spinning top used in a traditional Hanukkah game. Each side bears a Hebrew letter, and players spin to determine whether they win or lose from a pot of coins, candy, or nuts. Also spelled dreidels. {The children played with their dreidles after lighting the menorah.}

To drench is to soak thoroughly with liquid, usually water: {The sudden downpour drenched us}. Something drenched is completely saturated—not merely damp but soaked through. The word often suggests being caught unprepared by rain or waves. Figuratively, light or sound can drench a space by filling it completely: {Sunlight drenched the room}.

Drenched means thoroughly soaked, completely saturated with liquid. The word almost always describes wetness from water or rain: {We got drenched in the downpour}, {Her clothes were drenched with sweat}. Figuratively, something can be drenched in light, color, or atmosphere: {a room drenched in afternoon sun}. The past participle of drench, it functions primarily as an adjective.

Drenching is a thorough soaking—the kind that leaves something completely wet. Rain can give you a drenching, or you can give plants a drenching with the hose. The word implies saturation, not just dampness: {We got a drenching walking back from the car}. In veterinary contexts, a drenching is the forced administration of liquid medicine to an animal.
clues: What storms do to the unprepared

definition: Verbal uses of dress are about putting one thing on another, such as clothes on a person, medicine on a wound, or condiments on a salad. If you simply dress, you put clothes on yourself, which results in the state of being dressed. As a noun, dress divides its meanings between countable and uncountable uses. Dress, generally, characterizes the clothes that people wear: ceremonial dress, casual dress. A dress, on the other hand, is a one-piece garment for women.

Dressage is a form of competitive horseback riding in which horse and rider perform a series of precise, choreographed movements. The discipline emphasizes the horse's natural athletic ability and willingness to respond to subtle cues from the rider. {She's been training in dressage for years.} The word comes from French for training.

Dressed means wearing clothes, especially with care or formality: {She was dressed for the occasion}. To get dressed is to put on clothes. Dressed can specify the type of attire: {dressed in black}, {dressed as a clown}. A dressed wound has been cleaned and bandaged. Dressed meat has been prepared for cooking—cleaned, trimmed, and readied. A dressed stone or board has been smoothed or finished.

A dresser is a piece of bedroom furniture with drawers for storing clothes, typically with a mirror attached. In British English, dresser refers to a kitchen sideboard with shelves for displaying dishes. A dresser is also someone who dresses in a particular way: {a stylish dresser}, {a sloppy dresser}. In theater, a dresser helps performers with costumes and quick changes.

Dressers are pieces of furniture with drawers for storing clothes, typically found in bedrooms. In American usage, a dresser often has a mirror attached; in British usage, a dresser may be a kitchen sideboard with shelves for displaying dishes. The word also refers to people who dress in a particular way: {a stylish dresser}, {a sloppy dresser}. In theater, dressers help performers with costume changes.

Dresses is the plural of dress—a one-piece garment with a bodice and skirt, typically worn by women and girls: {She tried on several dresses before finding the right one}. The verb dresses means puts on clothing or prepares something: {He dresses quickly in the morning}, {She dresses the salad with vinaigrette}. To dress a wound is to clean and bandage it.

Dressing covers things applied to other things. Salad dressing coats greens. A wound dressing covers an injury. Dressing on a turkey is stuffing—seasoned bread mixture applied inside the bird. Window dressing makes storefronts attractive, and figuratively means superficial embellishment: {The policy changes were just window dressing}. A dressing-down is a severe scolding.

A dressmaker is a person who makes women's clothing, especially dresses, typically as a trade or profession. The term suggests custom work—measuring, cutting, fitting, and sewing garments for individual clients—rather than factory production. {She apprenticed with a dressmaker in Paris before opening her own shop.}

Dressy describes clothing or occasions that call for elegant or formal attire rather than casual wear: {a dressy restaurant}, {That outfit is too dressy for a barbecue}. The word occupies a middle ground—fancier than everyday clothes but often short of black-tie formal. {She changed into something dressier for the party}.

Drew is the past tense of draw, covering all that verb's meanings. You drew a picture, drew a bath, drew a crowd, drew a conclusion, drew a weapon, or drew the short straw. {She drew the curtains and sat down}. {The game drew thousands of fans}. (Capitalized Drew is a given name.)

A dreydel is a four-sided spinning top used in a traditional game played during Hanukkah. Each face bears a Hebrew letter—nun, gimel, he, and shin—representing the phrase "a great miracle happened there." Players spin the dreydel and win or lose tokens based on which letter lands face up. Also spelled dreidel.

A dreydl is a four-sided spinning top used in a Hanukkah gambling game. Each side bears a Hebrew letter, and players spin to determine whether they win or lose from a pot of coins, nuts, or chocolate. The spelling dreidel is more common. {The children played dreydl after lighting the menorah.}
clues: Spun during the Festival of Lights

definition: Dribble describes liquid falling or flowing in small drops or a thin stream: {Water dribbled from the faucet}. A person dribbles when saliva escapes the mouth uncontrolled—common in infants and the infirm. In basketball, to dribble is to bounce the ball repeatedly while moving; in soccer, to advance the ball with short kicks. The noun covers any of these: {a dribble of sauce}, {a dribble down the court}.

Dribbled is the past tense of dribble, which has meanings related to liquid falling in drops or a thin stream: {Water dribbled from the faucet}. In basketball, to dribble is to bounce the ball while moving; in soccer and hockey, it means to move the ball or puck with short, controlled touches. A baby dribbles when saliva runs from its mouth. If something dribbles out or in, it comes gradually in small amounts: {Details about the scandal dribbled out over several weeks}.

Dribbles is the third-person singular of dribble. Liquid dribbles when it flows in a thin, irregular stream: {Water dribbled from the faucet}. A person dribbles when saliva escapes their mouth uncontrollably. In basketball and soccer, to dribble is to advance the ball with short, controlled bounces or kicks. As a noun, dribbles are small amounts trickling out: {dribbles of information}, {dribbles of funding}.

Dribbling is the present participle of dribble—letting liquid fall in drops or a thin stream, or moving a ball with repeated short touches. In basketball, dribbling means bouncing the ball while moving; in soccer, it means advancing with light kicks. A baby dribbling has saliva trickling from its mouth. {He was dribbling the ball up the court.}

Dried is the past tense and past participle of dry, used as a verb or adjective. As a verb, it describes the completion of removing moisture: {I dried the dishes and put them away}. As an adjective, it characterizes something from which moisture has been removed, often for preservation: {dried fruit}, {dried herbs}, {sun-dried tomatoes}. Dried flowers are preserved for decorative purposes. If tears or a well has dried up, the moisture is completely gone.

Drier is the comparative form of dry: {This towel is drier than that one}. A drier is also a machine or substance that removes moisture—a hair drier, a clothes drier, an additive that speeds paint drying. The spelling dryer is equally common for the appliance, less so for the comparative.

Driest is the superlative of dry—the most lacking in moisture, wetness, or humidity: {Death Valley is the driest place in North America}. It extends to other senses of dry: the driest humor shows the least emotion, the driest wine has the least residual sugar, the driest county has the strictest alcohol laws.

When something drifts, it moves somewhat slowly and not always in a consistent direction. When a conversation drifts, it moves gradually from one topic to another. Drift is an instance of such movement (continental drift). If you get the drift of what someone is saying, you understand their underlying message. Genetic drift is the process by which the genomes of a population change through gain and loss of genes.

Drifted is the past tense of drift—to move slowly without direction or control. Snow drifted against the fence. A boat drifted downstream. Figuratively, someone who drifted off fell asleep gradually, and a conversation that drifted moved from topic to topic without purpose: {We drifted from politics to old movies to whether dogs dream}.

A drifter is someone who moves from place to place without a fixed home, job, or purpose—a person who drifts through life rather than putting down roots. The term carries connotations of rootlessness and sometimes aimlessness, though it can also suggest freedom from conventional obligations. {A drifter came through town looking for odd jobs.} In fishing, a drifter is a boat that uses drift nets.

Drifters are people who move from place to place without fixed purpose or destination. The word carries connotations of rootlessness and lack of ambition—someone who drifts through life rather than directing it: {The town attracted drifters looking for seasonal work}. In older crime narratives, drifters often appear as suspects precisely because they have no ties to the community.

Drifting is moving slowly without direction or purpose, carried by currents of water, air, or circumstance. Snow drifts into piles; a boat drifts downstream; a conversation drifts to other topics. Someone who drifts through life lacks clear goals: {He spent his twenties drifting from job to job}. In driving, drifting is a technique of intentionally oversteering to slide through turns while maintaining control—a motorsport style that emerged in Japan.

Drifts are accumulations of snow, sand, or other material piled up by wind: {The drifts blocked the road}. The word also names the plural of drift in its other senses—a gradual movement or shift {(the drifts of public opinion)}, the general meaning of speech {(I catch your drift)}, or a state of aimless wandering {(He fell into one of his drifts)}. As a verb form, drifts describes slow, undirected movement: {The boat drifts downstream}, {Her attention drifts during meetings}.

Driftwood is wood that has been washed ashore by waves, tides, or currents. It typically comes from fallen trees, broken branches, or shipwrecks, weathered smooth and bleached pale by sun and salt water. Driftwood is collected for decoration, furniture, or fuel: {The beach was littered with driftwood after the storm}. Figuratively, driftwood suggests someone adrift or rootless: {He felt like driftwood, carried wherever life took him}.

The main meanings of drill, noun and verb, fall into two categories. First, a drill is a tool with a cutting attachment that makes holes. When you drill, you use one of these. By extension, when you figuratively drill into or drill down on something, you get past the surface of it to look at it in greater detail. Second, drill is an activity that is repeated for mastery or reinforcement (fire drill). When you drill, you take part in such an activity (drill Spanish verbs, drill multiplication tables).

Drilled is the past tense of drill. To drill is to bore a hole using a rotating tool, or to train through repetitive practice: {The sergeant drilled the recruits until they moved as one}. Students are drilled on multiplication tables; dentists drill teeth. In slang, to drill someone is to shoot them or, vulgarly, to have sex with them.

Drilling is the act of making holes with a rotating tool, or the repetitive practice of skills through exercises: {The coach had the team drilling plays all afternoon}. Military drilling involves marching and maneuvers in formation. In textiles, drilling is a sturdy twilled cotton fabric used for workwear and uniforms.

A drillmaster is someone who instructs others in military drill or marching exercises, enforcing precise, synchronized movements through repetition and discipline. The term extends to any strict trainer or instructor who demands rigorous practice and adherence to form, whether in athletics, music, or other fields requiring technical precision. {The band's drillmaster had them rehearsing formations until well after dark.} The word often carries connotations of harshness or inflexibility.

Drills are exercises repeated for mastery—military drills, fire drills, spelling drills. The repetition builds automatic response. A drill is also a tool that bores holes by rotating, or the act of boring: {Drill through the wall carefully}. To drill someone is to train them through repetition or to question them intensely: {The lawyer drilled the witness}. A drill is also a sturdy cotton fabric used for workwear.

Drink is to take liquid into the mouth and swallow it. Without specification, drink often implies alcohol: {Do you drink?} {She doesn't drink anymore}. A drink is a serving of liquid, especially an alcoholic beverage: {Let me buy you a drink}. To drink to someone is to toast them. To {drink in} a sight is to absorb it eagerly. {Drink the Kool-Aid} means to accept something uncritically.

A drinker is someone who drinks, almost always referring to alcohol. The word usually implies regular consumption: {He's a heavy drinker}, {She's not much of a drinker}. Without qualification, drinker often suggests problem drinking, though modifiers like social or moderate soften this. A drinker can also be a container designed for animals to drink from.

Drinkers are people who drink, almost always referring specifically to those who consume alcohol. The word often implies regular or habitual consumption: {The bar attracts serious drinkers}. A {heavy drinker} consumes to excess; a {social drinker} drinks only in company. Without qualifiers, drinkers typically suggests people for whom alcohol is a notable habit rather than an occasional indulgence.

Drinking is the act of consuming liquids, but used alone it almost always means consuming alcohol: {She doesn't approve of drinking}. A drinking {problem} is alcoholism. Drinking {water} is water safe to consume. A drinking {buddy} is someone you regularly drink alcohol with. {We stayed out drinking until two in the morning.}

Drinks are beverages—liquids meant for consumption. The word often implies alcoholic beverages specifically: {Let's grab some drinks after work}, {The drinks are on me}. A drinks menu at a restaurant lists what you can order to sip. As a verb, drinks is the third-person singular: {She drinks too much coffee}.

When a liquid, body part, or a device drips, drops fall (from it). A drip is an instance, or the sound of this. In a hospital, a drip is a device for introducing a liquid slowly into a patient’s bloodstream. Drip coffee is coffee made by letting hot water slowly drip through ground coffee beans. In slang use, a drip is an annoyingly stupid person. If someone is dripping in something, they have a needless excess of it: He was dripping with money.

Dripped is the past tense of drip—to fall or let fall in drops. Liquid drips from a faucet, sweat drips from a brow, wax drips down a candle. {Water dripped from the ceiling onto the floor.} Figuratively, something can drip with a quality: {His voice dripped with contempt.}

Dripping describes liquid falling in drops: {a dripping faucet}, {dripping wet from the rain}. Something dripping with a quality has it in excess: {dripping with sarcasm}, {dripping with jewels}. As a noun, dripping is the fat rendered from roasting meat, used in British cooking for frying or spreading on bread.

Drippings are the fat and juices that collect in the pan when meat is roasted or fried. Cooks save drippings to make gravy, baste the meat, or use as cooking fat: {Yorkshire pudding is traditionally made with beef drippings}. The singular dripping appears mainly in British English.

Drippy describes something that drips or tends to drip: {a drippy faucet}, {drippy candle wax}. Figuratively, drippy means excessively sentimental or mawkish: {a drippy love song}, {drippy greeting card verse}. The insult extends to people who are weak, boring, or lacking substance: {He's kind of drippy—no personality at all}.

Drips is the plural of drip, referring to drops of liquid falling or the sound they make. As a verb form, it describes liquid falling in drops: {Water drips from the faucet}. The noun extends to medical contexts where an IV drip delivers fluids slowly into a patient's bloodstream. In slang, drip means stylish clothing or accessories, and drips can describe someone with impressive style: {He's got serious drips}. Calling someone a drip, however, means they're dull or boring.

Drive, noun and verb, is about directional and usually intentional movement (drive a car). A drive may be an instance of driving a vehicle, or it could be a directed movement of animals (a cattle drive). A fundraising drive is an activity aimed at raising money. Drive is also a motivational force: This job requires a lot of drive. If you drive someone to do something, you compel them: Her love of mathematics drives her to succeed. In computers, a drive is a device that stores data.

A driveby is a shooting from a moving vehicle, typically gang-related: {Two teenagers were killed in a driveby last night}. The term extends to any quick, passing action—especially a brief, dismissive comment online: {He left a driveby insult and never responded to replies}. As an adjective, driveby describes something done hastily or superficially: {driveby journalism}, {driveby diagnosis}.

Drivel is foolish, meaningless talk or writing—nonsense that wastes the listener's time: {I couldn't sit through another minute of that drivel}. The word suggests not just wrongness but emptiness, speech without substance. As a verb, to drivel is to talk this way, or in older usage, to let saliva dribble from the mouth—the image behind the metaphor.

Driven describes someone powerfully motivated to achieve, often to an unusual degree: {She's incredibly driven—works eighteen-hour days}. The word suggests ambition that comes from within, sometimes obsessively. As a past participle of drive, driven also describes things propelled or operated by a force: {wind-driven turbines}, {a character-driven story}, {snow driven sideways by the wind}.

A driver is someone who operates a vehicle: a taxi driver, a truck driver, a getaway driver. The word extends to golf clubs designed to hit the ball far off the tee. In computing, a driver is software that enables hardware to communicate with an operating system. Figuratively, a driver is anything that propels or motivates: {Consumer spending is a key driver of economic growth}. A backseat driver offers unwanted advice.

Driverless describes a vehicle that operates without a human driver, using sensors, software, and automation to navigate: {driverless cars}, {driverless trucks}. The term appears most often in discussions of autonomous vehicle technology and its implications for transportation, safety, and employment.

Drivers is the plural of driver—people who operate vehicles or other things that drive. A driver is someone behind the wheel: {taxi drivers}, {drunk drivers}. In golf, a driver is the club for long-distance shots off the tee. In computing, drivers are software programs that allow hardware to communicate with an operating system: {You need to update your graphics drivers}. A driver can also be a motivating factor: {Cost was the main driver of the decision}.

Drives is the plural of drive and the third-person singular verb form. A drive is a journey by car, a paved path to a house, or inner motivation: {She has incredible drives—ambition, curiosity, hunger for success}. Computer drives store data. In sports, a drive is a powerful shot or sustained offensive push. To drive is to operate a vehicle, propel forward, or compel: {What drives you?} {Ambition drives her}. {He drives me crazy.}

A driveshaft is a rotating rod that transmits power from an engine to the wheels or other moving parts. In rear-wheel-drive vehicles, the driveshaft connects the transmission to the rear axle, running underneath the car: {The mechanic said the vibration was coming from a worn driveshaft}. Also called a propeller shaft.

A driveway is a private road leading from a street to a house, garage, or other building. Unlike public roads, driveways belong to the property: {The kids were playing basketball in the driveway}. In American suburbs, the driveway often serves as overflow parking, workspace, or gathering spot.

Driveways is the plural of driveway, a private road or paved surface connecting a house or building to a public street. Driveways provide access for vehicles to garages, carports, or parking areas: {The neighborhood driveways were lined with basketball hoops}. They range from short suburban strips to long rural lanes.

Driving is operating a vehicle, especially a car: {I learned driving at sixteen}. As an adjective, driving describes forceful, propelling motion: {driving rain}, {driving rhythm}. A driving force is what pushes something forward—the main cause or motivation: {She was the driving force behind the project's success}.

Drizzle is light rain falling in fine, scattered drops—heavier than mist but gentler than a steady rain: {We walked through the drizzle without umbrellas}. As a verb, to drizzle is to rain lightly, or to pour a thin stream of liquid over food: {Drizzle olive oil over the salad}. The cooking sense suggests a slow, controlled pour rather than a splash.

Drizzles is light rain falling in fine droplets, or the act of pouring a thin stream of liquid: {The recipe says she drizzles olive oil over the salad}. Weather drizzles when it rains gently. A chef drizzles sauce for presentation. {It drizzles most mornings in Seattle}.

Drizzling describes light rain falling in fine, scattered drops—more than mist but less than a steady rain. Weather reports distinguish drizzling from heavier precipitation: {It's just drizzling; you won't need an umbrella}. In cooking, drizzling means pouring a thin stream of liquid over food: {drizzling olive oil over the salad}, {drizzling chocolate over the cake}.

Droid is science fiction slang for a robot or android—a mechanical being, often humanoid, with artificial intelligence. The term was popularized by Star Wars, where droids serve various functions from protocol to astromech. Outside fiction, droid sometimes describes any automated system or person who acts mechanically: {He's a total droid—just follows orders without thinking}.

Droids are robots, especially humanoid ones. The term comes from android and was popularized by the Star Wars films, where droids serve as servants, translators, and companions. Outside that franchise, droid often carries a playful or science-fiction flavor: {These aren't the droids you're looking for}. It can describe anyone acting mechanically or without independent thought.

A drone is an unmanned aircraft, typically remote-controlled or autonomous: {Drones delivered packages to rural areas}. The word comes from the male honeybee, which makes no honey and exists only to mate with the queen—hence drone for a person who does tedious work or lives off others' labor. The bee's deep humming sound gives us the verb drone, meaning to make a low continuous sound or to speak monotonously: {He droned on about quarterly projections}. A drone is also a sustained bass note in music, especially from bagpipes.

Drones are unmanned aircraft, typically controlled remotely or by onboard computers. Military drones conduct surveillance and airstrikes; consumer drones take aerial photos or race. The word comes from the male honeybee, which doesn't work—so a drone is also a person who does tedious labor or lives off others. A drone can be a monotonous humming sound, or to speak in such a tone: {He droned on about quarterly projections}.

Droning describes a continuous, low, monotonous sound—the hum of bees, the buzz of machinery, or a voice that never varies in pitch or intensity. A droning {engine} produces steady background noise. A droning {speaker} puts listeners to sleep. The word suggests tedium: something that goes on and on without relief or variation.

Drool is saliva that flows uncontrollably from the mouth. Babies drool; so do sleeping adults and people who've had dental work. The verb means to let saliva escape: {The dog drooled on the carpet}. Figuratively, to drool over something is to desire it intensely: {He was drooling over the sports car}.

Drooling is letting saliva flow from the mouth, whether involuntarily (as babies and some elderly or ill people do) or from eager anticipation: {The dog was drooling over the steak}. Figuratively, to drool over something is to desire it openly and perhaps excessively: {He was drooling over the new sports car}.

Drools is the third-person singular of drool—to let saliva dribble from the mouth. Babies drool; so do sleeping adults. Figuratively, to drool over something is to desire it intensely: {He drools over sports cars}. As a plural noun, drools would be instances of drooling, though this usage is rare.

Droop describes a downward sag or hang, typically from weakness, fatigue, or lack of support. Flowers droop when they need water; eyelids droop when someone is tired; shoulders droop in defeat or exhaustion. The word works as both verb and noun: {The droop of his head suggested he'd fallen asleep}. Things that droop lack the stiffness or energy to remain upright, giving the word connotations of wilting, flagging spirits, or physical decline.

Drooped is the past tense of droop, meaning to sink, hang, or bend downward from weakness or exhaustion. Flowers droop without water. Shoulders droop with fatigue or dejection. Eyelids droop when someone is tired. {Her head drooped as she fell asleep}. {The flag drooped in the still air}.

Drooping describes something that hangs or sags downward, lacking the strength or structure to stay upright: {drooping flowers}, {drooping eyelids}, {a drooping mustache}. The word often suggests weariness, neglect, or decline. Spirits can droop as readily as physical things: {His shoulders were drooping with exhaustion}.

Droops is the third-person singular of droop, meaning to sag, sink, or hang downward from weakness or lack of support. Flowers droop without water. Eyelids droop with fatigue. Spirits droop under disappointment. {Her shoulders drooped when she heard the news.} {The flag droops in the still air.}

Droopy describes something that hangs or sags downward, lacking firmness or rigidity: {droopy eyelids}, {a droopy mustache}, {droopy flowers that need water}. The word often suggests tiredness, sadness, or neglect. A droopy demeanor conveys low energy or dejection: {He looked droopy after the bad news}.
clues: Bent over from its own weight

definition: Drop is mainly a verb, with the noun meanings derived from the verb meaning of descending to a lower place. The thing dropping can be an object (Helicopters dropped relief supplies) or an abstraction (The price of gas dropped five cents today). If you drop an activity, you stop doing it: I dropped physics because it was too hard. A drop is a sudden descent: The first drop over the ridge made the skiing treacherous. A tiny quantity of liquid that falls as a round mass is also called a drop.

A dropdown is an interface element that expands to reveal a list of options when clicked or tapped: {Select your country from the dropdown}. The term comes from the menu appearing to drop down from a button or field. Also written as two words or hyphenated. Dropdown menus are ubiquitous in software and web forms for selecting from predefined choices.

A dropkick is a kick executed by dropping a ball and kicking it just as it bounces off the ground—still legal but rare in American football and rugby. In wrestling and martial arts, a dropkick is an aerial attack where you jump, kick with both feet, and land on your back: {He dropkicked his opponent into the ropes}. Informally, to dropkick something is to punt it decisively: {I'd dropkick that idea right now}.

Dropkicked is the past tense of dropkick—a kick where the ball is dropped and struck just as it bounces, or in wrestling and fighting, a jumping kick with both feet. Figuratively, to dropkick something is to reject or dismiss it forcefully: {I dropkicked that idea the moment I heard it}. {He dropkicked the proposal into oblivion.}

Dropkicking is delivering a kick where the ball is dropped and struck just as it bounces, or in wrestling and fighting, jumping to kick an opponent with both feet. The term extends to forceful rejection or removal: {I'm dropkicking that idea from the proposal}. The gerund form of dropkick, used as verb or noun.

Dropkicks are kicks delivered after dropping a ball and striking it as it bounces, used in rugby and Australian football. In wrestling, a dropkick is an aerial attack where the wrestler jumps and kicks with both feet. The term also works as a verb: {He dropkicks the ball downfield}. In Australian slang, dropkick is an insult for a worthless or incompetent person.

A droplet is a very small drop of liquid: {droplets of rain on the window}, {respiratory droplets spread the virus}. The diminutive suffix emphasizes tininess—droplets are smaller than ordinary drops, often fine enough to hang suspended in air or mist.

Droplets is the plural of droplet—tiny drops of liquid. The word appears frequently in scientific and medical contexts: {respiratory droplets}, {droplets of moisture}. During the COVID-19 pandemic, droplets became ubiquitous in discussions of airborne transmission: {The virus spreads through droplets expelled when an infected person coughs or sneezes}.

A dropoff is a place where something is left or delivered: a {package dropoff}, a {daycare dropoff}. It also names a sharp descent or decline—a cliff has a steep dropoff, and business might experience a dropoff in sales. The verb form is two words: {I need to drop off the kids at school}.

A dropout is someone who quits school before completing their degree or program: {a high school dropout}, {college dropout}. The term carries connotations of failure or giving up, though some famous dropouts have succeeded spectacularly. Dropout also describes the act of leaving: {the dropout rate}. In electronics and audio, a dropout is a brief loss of signal.

Dropouts are people who leave school, a program, or an activity before completing it. The term most often refers to those who quit high school or college without graduating: {High school dropouts face limited job prospects}. It extends to anyone who withdraws from conventional society or mainstream expectations, carrying connotations of failure or nonconformity depending on context. In technical contexts, a dropout can also mean a brief loss of signal or data.

Dropped is the past tense of drop. Something dropped has fallen or been released: {She dropped her keys}. A dropped call disconnects unexpectedly. A dropped charge is no longer being pursued. In music, dropped tuning lowers one or more guitar strings. To get dropped is to be removed from a team, label, or roster: {He got dropped from the squad}.

A dropper is a small tube with a squeezable rubber bulb at one end, used to dispense liquid in drops: {an eye dropper}, {a medicine dropper}. The term extends to anyone or anything that drops: a {name-dropper} casually mentions important acquaintances, and a {jaw-dropper} is something astonishing. In drug contexts, a dropper may be someone who delivers contraband.

Dropping is the present participle of drop, used for actions in progress: {I keep dropping my phone}. As a noun, a dropping is animal excrement, usually in the plural: {bird droppings}, {mouse droppings}. The term is slightly more polite than saying shit or feces directly.

Droppings are the feces of animals, especially birds and small mammals. The term is almost always plural and typically refers to waste found where it falls—on sidewalks, windowsills, in barns, or scattered across fields. {The car was covered in bird droppings.} Unlike more clinical terms like feces or excrement, droppings suggests small, discrete pellets or spots rather than larger deposits.

Drops is the plural of drop—small amounts of liquid that fall or hang in rounded masses: {A few drops of rain hit the windshield}. Eye drops and ear drops are medicinal liquids applied in small quantities. In theater and film, drops are large painted backdrops. To {do drops} in certain contexts means to deliver packages, often drugs, to multiple locations.

To dropship is to sell products that ship directly from a manufacturer or wholesaler to the customer, bypassing the seller's inventory. The seller never handles the goods: {She dropships jewelry from suppliers in China}. The model is popular in e-commerce because it requires minimal upfront investment. A dropship is also a fictional spacecraft designed to deploy troops or cargo from orbit to a planet's surface.

Dropshipping is a retail method where the seller doesn't keep products in stock. Instead, when a customer orders, the seller purchases the item from a third party—usually a wholesaler or manufacturer—who ships it directly to the customer. The seller never handles the merchandise: {She started a dropshipping business selling phone cases from Chinese suppliers}. The model requires little upfront investment but offers thin margins and limited quality control.

Dropships function in two distinct domains. In retail, to dropship is to sell products that ship directly from the manufacturer or wholesaler to the customer, bypassing the seller's inventory entirely. {She built her online store around dropshipping so she never had to handle merchandise.} In science fiction and video games, dropships are spacecraft designed to rapidly deploy troops or cargo from orbit to a planet's surface, combining the roles of transport and tactical insertion vehicle.

A dropshot is a shot in tennis, badminton, or similar racket sports that barely clears the net and falls sharply, landing close to it on the opponent's side. The goal is to catch an opponent off guard, especially one positioned deep in the court: {She won the point with a perfect dropshot}. In fishing, dropshot refers to a rigging technique where the weight hangs below the hook.

Dropshots are a type of soft plastic fishing lure designed for the dropshot rig, where the weight hangs below the hook rather than above it. This setup keeps the bait suspended off the bottom, presenting it naturally to fish. The term also refers to shots in racket sports that barely clear the net and drop quickly, minimizing bounce: {Her dropshot caught him flat-footed at the baseline}.

A droptop is a convertible car—one with a roof that folds down or detaches: {cruising the coast in a droptop}. The term emphasizes the open-air experience, appearing frequently in hip-hop and car culture. Also spelled drop-top or drop top.

Droptops are convertible cars—vehicles with roofs that fold down or retract. The term emphasizes the lowered roof as a defining feature: {cruising in droptops}, {summer's for droptops}. Common in hip-hop and casual speech as a marker of status or carefree living. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated.

A dropzone is a designated area where something is released from above—originally where paratroopers or supplies land after being dropped from aircraft. The term extends to any spot designated for depositing things: a {dropzone for keys and mail} by the front door. In computing and interface design, a dropzone is an area where users can drag and drop files or content: {Drag your images into the dropzone to upload}.

Dross is the scum or impurities that form on molten metal and are skimmed off during smelting. The word extends to anything worthless, trivial, or of poor quality: {sifting through the dross to find something worth reading}. It often implies waste material left after the valuable part has been extracted.

A drought is an extended period of abnormally low rainfall, causing water shortages and crop failure. The word extends to any prolonged absence or scarcity: {a drought of new ideas}, {The team's scoring drought lasted three games}. In some regions, drought also means thirst or dryness generally.

Droughts is the plural of drought—prolonged periods of abnormally low rainfall causing water shortages and crop failure. The word extends to any sustained scarcity: {a drought of new ideas}, {The team's scoring drought lasted three games}. Droughts can last months or years and may trigger famine, migration, and economic crisis.

Drove is the past tense of drive, but it also stands alone as a noun meaning a group of animals being driven together: {a drove of cattle}. By extension, drove describes any large moving group: {Droves of tourists descended on the city}. The phrase {in droves} emphasizes large numbers arriving or departing together.

Droves is the plural of drove, which originally meant a herd of animals being driven somewhere—cattle, sheep, pigs moving along a road. Now droves almost always appears in the phrase {in droves}, meaning in large numbers: {Fans left in droves after the third quarter}. The word emphasizes mass movement, usually of people arriving or departing together.

To drown is to die by submersion in water, unable to breathe. The verb works both ways: a person drowns, or water drowns them. Figuratively, to drown is to be overwhelmed: {drowning in debt}, {drowning in paperwork}. To {drown out} is to overpower with louder sound: {The music drowned out our conversation}. To {drown your sorrows} is to drink alcohol to forget troubles.

Drowned is the past tense of drown—to die by submersion in water, unable to breathe: {Three swimmers drowned in the flood}. Extended uses describe overwhelming quantities: {drowned in debt}, {drowned out by noise}. A drowned landscape is submerged or waterlogged. {Her voice was drowned by the crowd's roar.}

Drowning is death by suffocation in water or other liquid. The lungs fill with fluid, preventing oxygen from reaching the body. Someone who is drowning struggles at the surface before going under. Figuratively, to be drowning is to be overwhelmed: {I'm drowning in paperwork}. {She was drowning in debt}.

Drowsiness is the state of being sleepy or half-asleep—that heavy-lidded feeling when alertness fades. It suggests a pull toward sleep rather than full wakefulness: {The medication's side effects include drowsiness}. Warning labels caution against operating machinery if drowsiness occurs. The word implies a gentle, gradual onset rather than sudden exhaustion.

Drowsy means sleepy or inclined toward sleep: {The warm afternoon made me drowsy}. It suggests a pleasant, heavy-lidded state rather than exhaustion. Drowsy extends to things that induce sleepiness: {a drowsy summer afternoon}, {the drowsy hum of bees}. Warning labels caution that medications may cause drowsiness.

A drubbing is a thorough beating or defeat. The word appears most often in sports coverage, where a lopsided loss becomes a drubbing: {The team took a drubbing in the playoffs}. It can also mean a physical beating, though this sense is less common now. To drub is to beat soundly.

A drudge is someone who does hard, tedious, or menial work: {She felt like a drudge, scrubbing floors while others relaxed}. The word emphasizes monotony and lack of recognition rather than skill. To drudge is to labor at such tasks. Drudgery is the work itself—exhausting, unglamorous toil that must simply be done.

Drudgery is hard, tedious, unpleasant work—the kind that feels endless and offers no satisfaction beyond its completion. The word emphasizes monotony and lack of reward: {the drudgery of data entry}, {household drudgery}. Unlike labor, which can be fulfilling, drudgery suggests work that dulls the spirit.

Drudges is the plural of drudge—a person who does hard, tedious, or menial work. The word suggests someone trapped in unglamorous labor: {office drudges filing paperwork}, {kitchen drudges scrubbing pots}. As a verb, to drudge is to toil at such work: {She drudges away at a job she hates}.

A drug is a substance that alters body function, whether for medical treatment or intoxication. Prescription drugs treat illness; recreational drugs produce altered states. The line between medicine and drug depends on context and legality—the same substance might be either. To drug someone is to administer a substance without consent: {Someone drugged my drink}. To {drug up} is to take medications or intoxicants heavily.

Drugged describes a state of being under the influence of drugs, especially when administered without consent or for incapacitation: {She felt drugged and couldn't keep her eyes open}. It also describes something that has had drugs added to it: {a drugged drink}, {drugged food}. The word often implies impairment, sedation, or vulnerability.

A druggie is an informal, usually disparaging term for someone who habitually uses illegal drugs or is addicted to them. The word carries connotations of irresponsibility or being strung out: {A couple of druggies were hanging around the parking lot}. It's less clinical than "addict" and more dismissive, often used to distance the speaker from the person described.

Druggies is informal, often disparaging, for people who use drugs habitually—especially illegal ones. The term suggests addiction or a lifestyle centered on drug use: {The park had become a hangout for druggies}. Less harsh than "junkie" but still dismissive, carrying connotations of irresponsibility or social marginality.

Drugging is the act of administering drugs to someone, typically without their knowledge or consent. The term most often appears in contexts of crime or assault: {She suspected someone had been drugging her drinks}. It can also refer to the ongoing use of sedatives on patients or animals: {The constant drugging left him groggy and disoriented}.

A druggist is a person who prepares and sells medicines—a pharmacist. The term is somewhat old-fashioned in American English, where pharmacist now dominates, but remains in use: {The druggist filled my prescription}. A druggist may also refer to someone who owns or operates a drugstore.

A druglord is a high-ranking leader of a drug trafficking organization, typically controlling production, distribution, and territory through a combination of wealth, corruption, and violence. The term evokes powerful figures in the illegal narcotics trade: {Colombian druglords of the 1980s}, {Mexican druglords who control border smuggling routes}. Also spelled as two words: drug lord.

Drug lords are the kingpins of illegal narcotics operations—the bosses who control production, distribution, and profit at the highest levels. The term evokes figures who command cartel empires, bribe officials, and order violence to protect their territories: {Colombian drug lords of the 1980s}, {The drug lord controlled routes through three countries}. Often used in journalism and crime narratives about international trafficking.

Drugs are substances that alter the body's chemistry—whether to treat illness, relieve pain, or produce intoxicating effects. The word covers everything from prescription medications to illegal narcotics, though in casual speech {drugs} usually means the illicit kind: {He got into drugs in high school}. To drug someone is to administer a substance without their knowledge or consent: {Someone drugged her drink}.

A drugstore is a retail store where medicines and prescriptions are dispensed, typically alongside everyday household items, toiletries, and convenience goods. The term is primarily American; British English prefers chemist or pharmacy. Unlike a pure pharmacy, a drugstore usually sells snacks, magazines, cosmetics, and sundries. {I picked up my prescription and some toothpaste at the drugstore.}

Drugstores are retail stores that sell prescription medications, over-the-counter remedies, and personal care products. In American usage, drugstores typically also stock convenience items, cosmetics, and household goods—functioning as general stores anchored by a pharmacy counter. The British equivalent is chemist or chemist's shop.

A druid was a member of the learned priestly class among ancient Celtic peoples, serving as religious leaders, judges, and keepers of oral tradition. Modern druids practice nature-based spirituality loosely inspired by these ancient figures: {The druids gathered at Stonehenge for the summer solstice}. In fantasy games and fiction, a druid is typically a magic user with powers over nature and shapeshifting abilities.

Druids are members of the priestly class of ancient Celtic peoples, associated with nature worship, oak groves, and sacred rituals. Modern druids belong to neo-pagan movements that revive or reimagine these traditions: {The druids gathered at Stonehenge for the summer solstice}. In fantasy games and fiction, druids are magic users with power over nature and animals. (Capitalized Druids emphasizes the historical priesthood.)

A drum is a percussion instrument—a hollow body with a membrane stretched over one or both ends, struck with hands or sticks to produce sound. Drums extend to cylindrical containers: an oil {drum}, an {eardrum}. To drum is to play drums or tap rhythmically: {She drummed her fingers on the table}. To {drum up} support or business is to generate it through effort. To {drum something into} someone is to teach it through repetition.

A drumbeat is the sound made by striking a drum, or the rhythmic pattern produced by repeated strikes. In figurative use, drumbeat often describes a persistent, repetitive message or campaign pushing toward a particular outcome: {the drumbeat of criticism}, {a drumbeat for war}. The word emphasizes relentlessness—like an actual drum, the message keeps pounding until it can't be ignored.

Drumbeats are the sounds produced by striking a drum, or the rhythmic pattern they create. The word often appears figuratively for insistent, repeated messaging: {the drumbeats of war}, {drumbeats for reform}. Like an actual drum's steady pulse, these metaphorical drumbeats build pressure toward action.

The taut membrane stretched over one or both ends of a drum, struck to produce sound. Drumheads were traditionally made of animal skin but are now often synthetic. The term extends to things resembling this surface: a {drumhead court-martial} is a summary military trial conducted in the field, originally held around an upturned drum.

A drumkit is the complete set of drums, cymbals, and hardware that a drummer plays as a single instrument. The standard kit includes a bass drum operated by foot pedal, a snare, tom-toms, hi-hat cymbals, and various crash and ride cymbals, all arranged for one seated player. Also spelled as two words: drum kit.

A drumline is the percussion section of a marching band, typically arranged in a line formation during performances. The term refers both to the group of drummers and to the music they play—heavy on snares, bass drums, and cymbals. Drumlines perform intricate, synchronized rhythms and are central to halftime shows and drum corps competitions: {The drumline brought the crowd to its feet}.

Drumlines are the percussion sections of marching bands, typically arranged in a line formation during performances. They include snare drums, bass drums, tenor drums, and cymbals, providing rhythmic foundation for the ensemble: {The drumlines competed at the state championship}. Separately, a drumline is a fishing apparatus—a long line with baited hooks suspended from floats, used commercially or for shark control near beaches.

A drummer is a person who plays drums, whether in a band, orchestra, or solo: {The drummer kept perfect time throughout the set}. Historically, drummers signaled commands in military units. A drummer can also be a traveling salesperson—one who "drums up" business—though this sense is now dated. To {march to the beat of a different drummer} is to follow one's own path.

Drummers are people who play drums, especially as musicians in bands or orchestras. The word extends to anyone who beats a drum—military drummers keeping time for marching troops, or a child with a toy drum. In older usage, a drummer was a traveling salesman who drummed up business by going door to door.

Drumming is the act of playing drums or making rhythmic percussive sounds. It extends to any repeated beating or tapping: {the drumming of rain on the roof}, {He drummed his fingers on the table}. In nature, drumming describes the rapid bill-beating of woodpeckers or the wing-beating displays of grouse. To drum something into someone is to instill it through repetition: {They drummed the rules into us}.

A drumroll is a sustained sound produced by rapid, continuous beats on a drum, creating a rolling effect. Drumrolls traditionally precede announcements, dramatic revelations, or climactic moments: {And the winner is—drumroll please—Sarah Chen!} The word often appears figuratively to signal that something significant is about to be revealed, sometimes ironically for trivial announcements.

Drumrolls is the plural of drumroll—a rapid succession of beats on a drum, creating a sustained rumbling sound. Drumrolls build anticipation before announcements, reveals, or dramatic moments: {And the winner is—drumroll please—Sarah Chen!} The word often appears figuratively to signal that something important is coming: {After much drumroll, the company finally unveiled its new product}.

Drums are percussion instruments—hollow cylinders with membranes stretched over one or both ends, played by striking with sticks or hands. The term covers everything from a child's toy to a concert timpani. A drum kit or drum set is also called drums: {She plays drums in a band}. To drum is to beat rhythmically, whether on an instrument or impatiently on a table. To {drum up} support or business is to generate it through effort. To {drum something into} someone is to teach through repetition.

A drumstick is a stick used to strike a drum, typically wooden with a padded or rounded tip. Drumsticks also refers to the lower leg of a chicken or turkey, resembling a drum mallet in shape: {I saved the drumsticks for the kids}. The dual meaning comes from the shared silhouette—a knob at one end tapering to a handle.

Drumsticks are sticks used to strike drums and cymbals, typically wooden with a rounded tip. The word also refers to the lower leg of a chicken or turkey, shaped like a club—the dark meat portion often eaten by hand: {The kids always fight over the drumsticks at Thanksgiving}.

Drunk describes the state of impairment from alcohol—coordination falters, speech slurs, judgment wavers. The word works as adjective {(He was too drunk to drive)} and noun {(The drunk stumbled home)}. A drunk is also someone who habitually drinks to excess. Drunk doubles as the past participle of drink: {I've drunk three cups of coffee}. To be drunk on something besides alcohol is to be intoxicated by it: {drunk on power}, {drunk with success}.

A drunkard is a person who habitually drinks to excess—not someone who got drunk once, but someone whose life is marked by repeated drunkenness. The word carries moral judgment and sounds somewhat old-fashioned: {The old drunkard stumbled home from the tavern}. Modern usage often prefers clinical terms like alcoholic.

Drunkards is the plural of drunkard—a person who habitually drinks to excess. The word carries a tone of moral disapproval that alcoholic, the clinical term, avoids. Drunkard sounds old-fashioned and judgmental: {The preacher warned against becoming drunkards}. It appears in older literature and religious contexts more than in contemporary speech.

Drunken describes the state of intoxication or things associated with it: {a drunken sailor}, {drunken revelry}, {a drunken stupor}. The word functions only as an adjective before a noun—you say someone is drunk, not drunken, but a drunken {brawl} or drunken {driving}. Drunken often carries connotations of disorder or excess.
