Drunkenness is the state of being drunk—impaired by alcohol to the point where coordination, judgment, and speech are affected. The word covers everything from mild intoxication to complete incapacitation: {arrested for public drunkenness}, {His drunkenness cost him his marriage}. It can describe a pattern of behavior as much as a single episode.

Drunks is the plural of drunk, a person who is intoxicated or who habitually drinks to excess. The noun carries more judgment than the adjective—calling someone {a drunk} suggests a pattern, not just a state: {The bar was full of drunks by closing time}. {Staggering drunks spilled onto the sidewalk}.

Druthers means personal preference or choice, almost always appearing in the phrase {if I had my druthers}: {If I had my druthers, we'd skip the meeting entirely}. The word comes from a dialectal contraction of "I'd rather"—what you'd rather do if given the choice. It's informal and slightly folksy.

Dry means without moisture or liquid. A dry {towel} absorbs water; a dry {climate} receives little rain. Dry {wine} lacks sweetness. Dry {humor} is deadpan and understated. A dry {cough} produces no phlegm. To go dry or be {dry} can mean abstaining from alcohol, or a place where alcohol sales are prohibited. To dry is to remove moisture: {Dry your hands}. If inspiration or supply runs out, it {dries up}.

A dryad is a tree nymph in Greek mythology—a spirit inhabiting and guarding a tree, typically an oak. The term appears in fantasy literature and games for woodland spirits or tree-dwelling creatures: {The dryad emerged from the ancient oak to speak with the travelers}. Dryads are usually depicted as beautiful female figures bound to their trees.

Dryads are tree spirits in Greek mythology—nymphs who inhabit and protect trees, particularly oaks. Each dryad's life was bound to her tree; if the tree died, so did she. The word appears in fantasy literature and games for woodland spirits or tree-dwelling creatures: {The forest was said to be protected by dryads}.

A drycleaner is a business that cleans clothes and fabrics using chemical solvents rather than water, or a person who operates such a business. Items that might shrink, bleed, or lose shape in water—suits, silk blouses, wool coats—go to the drycleaner: {I need to pick up my suits from the drycleaner}. Also spelled dry cleaner.

A drydock is an enclosure that can be drained of water, allowing ships to be built, repaired, or inspected below the waterline. The vessel enters while the dock is flooded, then the water is pumped out, leaving the hull accessible. As a verb, to drydock a ship is to put it in such a facility: {The destroyer was drydocked for hull repairs}.

Drydocked describes a ship that has been placed in a drydock—a basin that can be drained to expose the hull for repair, cleaning, or inspection. Figuratively, drydocked means sidelined or out of commission: {The quarterback was drydocked with a knee injury}. The term implies temporary removal from action, with return expected.

Drydocks are structures for building or repairing ships out of water. A drydock is a basin that can be flooded to float a vessel in, then drained to expose the hull for work below the waterline. As a verb, to drydock a ship is to place it in such a facility: {The carrier was drydocked for maintenance}.

A dryer is a machine or device that removes moisture. The clothes dryer tumbles wet laundry in heated air. A hair dryer blows hot air. Dryer also works as the comparative form of dry: {The climate here is dryer than back east}. The spelling drier is equally valid for both uses.

Drying is the process of removing moisture or becoming dry. It functions as both verb form and adjective: {The drying laundry hung on the line}. A drying agent absorbs moisture. Drying time is how long something takes to dry completely. Paint, concrete, and nail polish all have drying times that matter.

Drystone describes a method of construction using stones fitted together without mortar. The technique relies on careful selection and placement of stones that interlock under their own weight. Drystone walls are common in rural Britain, where they mark field boundaries and contain livestock: {The drystone walls crisscrossing the hillside were centuries old}. Also spelled dry-stone or dry stone.

Drywall is the standard interior wall material in modern construction, consisting of gypsum plite pressed between paper sheets. It replaced plaster-and-lath construction because it's faster and cheaper to install—you screw or nail the panels to studs, tape the seams, and apply joint compound. As a verb, to drywall means to install this material: {We spent the weekend drywalling the basement}. Also called wallboard, gypsum board, or by the brand name Sheetrock.

Dual means consisting of two parts or having a twofold nature. A dual {citizenship} grants belonging to two countries. A dual {purpose} serves two functions. Dual {carriageways} have lanes running in both directions. The word emphasizes pairing or doubling: {She led a dual life as teacher and spy}. In grammar, some languages have a dual number for exactly two of something, distinct from singular and plural.

Dualism is the division of something into two opposed or contrasting aspects. In philosophy, it often refers to the view that mind and body are fundamentally different substances—{Cartesian dualism}. Religious dualism posits opposing forces of good and evil. The term appears wherever thinkers emphasize binary division rather than unity or multiplicity: {the dualism of nature and culture}.

Duality is the state or quality of having two parts, aspects, or natures, often ones that contrast or complement each other. Philosophers speak of mind-body duality, the idea that mental and physical existence are fundamentally different. In physics, wave-particle duality describes how light behaves as both wave and particle depending on how it's observed. More loosely, duality refers to any pairing of opposing forces or ideas: {the duality of good and evil}, {the duality of public persona and private self}.

A duathlon is an endurance race combining two disciplines, typically running and cycling. The standard format is run-bike-run: athletes run a set distance, cycle a longer segment, then finish with another run. Unlike a triathlon, which includes swimming, a duathlon stays on land: {She switched from triathlons to duathlons after a shoulder injury}.

Despite low frequency, dub has several meanings that don’t overlap. Most frequent is the verb that is about giving names and titles to people and things: He dubbed the pastry chef “Bakemaster.” Another dub verb means to add or replace the audio part of a video presentation: The film was dubbed in English. The most frequent noun use of dub today is for a genre of music with irregular and unexpected sounds: Dubstep is the epitome of electronic dance music.

Dubbed means named or given a title, often informal or descriptive: {The media dubbed him "the king of pop"}. The word carries a sense of bestowing identity through declaration rather than formal process. Separately, dubbed describes audio that has been replaced or added—a dubbed {film} has dialogue recorded in a different language from the original, or dubbed {music} has vocals layered over a track.

Dubbing is the process of adding or replacing sound in a film or recording. Most often this means replacing dialogue in one language with another: {The movie was dubbed into Spanish}. Dubbing also covers adding sound effects, music, or voiceover to video. The related sense of copying recordings—{dubbing a tape}—comes from the same studio practice of layering audio tracks.

Dubious expresses doubt or uncertainty. A dubious claim is one you're not sure you believe; a dubious expression shows skepticism: {She gave him a dubious look when he explained his whereabouts}. Something of dubious quality or value is questionable, probably not good: {a dubious honor}, {dubious accounting practices}. The word often implies something is suspect or shady rather than merely uncertain.

Dubs is slang with several distinct meanings. In audio and film, dubs are dubbed versions—foreign dialogue replaced with another language, or music remixed: {I prefer subs over dubs for anime}. In cannabis culture, a dub is a twenty-dollar bag of weed. In sports, dubs means wins (from the W): {The team got three dubs this week}. The Golden State Warriors are nicknamed the Dubs.

Dubstep is a genre of electronic dance music that emerged from UK garage in the early 2000s, characterized by heavy bass, syncopated rhythms, and the signature "wobble bass"—a low-frequency oscillation that sounds like machinery grinding or tearing. The tempo typically hovers around 140 beats per minute. {The dubstep drop hit and the whole club went crazy.}

Ducats were gold coins used across Europe for centuries, particularly in Venice and other Italian states. The word survives mainly in informal use meaning money: {I don't have the ducats for that}. Shakespeare's Shylock famously laments his stolen ducats. The plural form appears far more often than the singular.

A duchess is a woman who holds the highest hereditary rank below princess in British and European nobility, either in her own right or as the wife of a duke. The title carries significant social prestige and traditionally comes with ceremonial duties and estates. {The Duchess of Cambridge attended the charity gala.} In informal usage, duchess can be an affectionate or ironic term of address for a woman perceived as acting grand or imperious.

A duchy is a territory ruled by a duke or duchess. The term belongs to European feudal history, when duchies were significant political units below kingdoms: {the Duchy of Normandy}, {the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg}. Some duchies persist as ceremonial or administrative regions, though few retain political power.

There are three English words spelled d-u-c-k. Most frequent is a noun for a family of swimming birds that are often hunted and sometimes eaten (mallard duck). As a verb, duck is the motion of lowering your head or body, especially quickly in order to avoid an obstacle or projectile: He ducked through the doorway. A related meaning is push underwater: I ducked my head into the river to cool off. Figuratively, it is to evade (duck out of the party, duck responsibility for the project). Duck is also a noun for a heavy cotton fabric used for clothing and especially pants.

A duckboard is a wooden slatted platform laid over wet or muddy ground to provide footing. The term comes from World War I, when soldiers used them in flooded trenches: {We laid duckboards across the worst of the mud}. They're still used in showers, saunas, and anywhere standing water collects.

Duckface is a facial expression made by pursing the lips outward, creating a pout that vaguely resembles a duck's bill. The pose became ubiquitous in selfies during the 2010s, intended to make lips appear fuller and cheekbones more defined. Often used mockingly: {She made a duckface for the camera}. {Every photo from that era features someone doing duckface}.

Duckie is an affectionate term of address, chiefly British: {Thanks, duckie}. It carries a warm, slightly old-fashioned tone, similar to "dear" or "love." The word also refers to a small rubber duck toy, the kind children play with in the bath. The spelling ducky is more common in American English.

Duckies is an affectionate plural for small rubber ducks or toy ducks, especially those used in bathtubs: {The baby loves playing with her duckies}. It can also be a playful term of endearment for people, typically children or close friends: {How are my little duckies doing today?}

A duckling is a young duck, typically one still covered in down rather than adult feathers. The word often evokes images of fluffy yellow hatchlings following their mother. In the fairy tale "The Ugly Duckling," a bird thought homely becomes a swan—making {ugly duckling} a term for someone whose potential isn't yet apparent.

Ducklings are young ducks, typically covered in soft downy feathers before developing adult plumage. The word evokes images of fluffy, vulnerable creatures following their mother in a line—a behavior so iconic it appears in children's stories and wildlife documentaries alike. {The ducklings waddled behind their mother toward the pond.} Figuratively, someone's ducklings might be the people they guide or mentor, especially in a group setting.

Ducks are waterfowl with broad flat bills, webbed feet, and waterproof feathers. They float, dive, and waddle—the archetypal pond bird. To duck is to lower your head or body quickly to avoid something: {She ducked under the branch}. By extension, to duck a question or responsibility is to evade it. As a term of endearment, duck is British: {Thanks, duck}. A duck in cricket is a score of zero.

A ducktail is a men's hairstyle popular in the 1950s where the hair is slicked back on both sides to meet at the center back of the head, resembling a duck's tail feathers. The style became associated with greasers and early rock and roll culture: {He combed his ducktail in the mirror}. Also called a duck's ass or D.A.

A duckwalk is a way of moving while squatting, waddling forward with knees bent and body low to the ground—mimicking a duck's gait. It appears in exercise routines, military training, and children's games. The move became iconic in rock and roll through Chuck Berry, who duckwalked across stages while playing guitar: {He duckwalked through the entire solo}.

Duckwalked is the past tense of duckwalk—to walk in a squatting position with knees bent, waddling like a duck. It's associated with physical training exercises and childhood games, but most famously with Chuck Berry's signature stage move: {He duckwalked across the stage while playing his guitar solo}.

Duckwalking is walking in a squatting position with knees bent, waddling forward like a duck. It appears in exercise routines, military training, and children's games. The term also describes the signature stage move pioneered by Chuck Berry—shuffling across a stage while crouched low, guitar in hand: {He duckwalked across the stage during his solo}.

Duckweed is a tiny aquatic plant that floats on still water, forming dense green mats on ponds and slow-moving streams. The plants are among the smallest flowering species, each consisting of a simple leaf-like frond with dangling roots. Ducks and other waterfowl feed on it, hence the name. {The pond was completely covered in duckweed.}

Ducky means satisfactory or fine, usually with a note of irony or sarcasm: {Well, isn't that just ducky}. The word sounds deliberately cute, which is why sincere use is rare—it typically signals the opposite of genuine approval. As a noun, ducky is a term of endearment, especially British: {Hello, ducky}. Also a child's word for a duck or rubber duck toy.

A duct is a tube or channel that conveys something from one place to another. In buildings, ducts carry air for heating and cooling systems. In the body, ducts transport fluids: {tear ducts}, {bile ducts}, {milk ducts}. To duct is to channel through such a passage. Duct tape, despite the name, is rarely used on actual ductwork.

Ducts are tubes or channels that convey something from one place to another. Air ducts carry heated or cooled air through buildings. Tear ducts drain fluid from the eyes. In anatomy, ducts transport secretions: {bile duct}, {milk duct}. To duct is to channel through such passages, though the verb is uncommon outside technical contexts.

A dud is something that fails to work as expected. Originally a bomb or shell that doesn't explode, the term now applies broadly to anything disappointing: a movie that flops, a product that malfunctions, a firework that fizzles. {The new phone was a complete dud.} As an adjective, dud means defective or worthless: {a dud battery}.

Dude is an informal term for a man or guy, used especially as a casual form of address: {Dude, you're not going to believe this}. Originally 19th-century slang for a fastidious man overly concerned with dress, it evolved through surfer and skater culture into a general exclamation of surprise, enthusiasm, or emphasis. The word now transcends gender in casual speech—women address other women as dude. A dude ranch is a Western-style vacation resort where guests can play cowboy.

A dudebro is a young man characterized by aggressive masculinity, often associated with fraternity culture, sports enthusiasm, and performative confidence. The term combines the casual address "dude" with "bro" to suggest someone who embodies a particular type of male bonding culture—heavy on gym talk, beer pong, and chest-bumping camaraderie. Usually mildly derogatory: {Some dudebro kept trying to explain football to me}.

Dudes is the plural of dude, a casual term for a man or guy. Originally 19th-century slang for a dandy or city slicker unfamiliar with rural life, dude evolved into a general-purpose word for any male person: {The dudes at the gym were hogging the weights}. In relaxed speech, dudes can address or refer to a mixed-gender group: {What's up, dudes?} The word carries an informal, friendly tone and appears frequently in youth and surf culture.

Duds has two distinct meanings. The original sense is clothing, especially casual or work clothes: {I threw on some old duds}. The other meaning is things that fail to work as intended—fireworks that don't explode, products that disappoint: {Half the batch turned out to be duds}. A single dud is a failure or disappointment.

The small but important word due can be a noun or an adjective. All of its meanings are related to the idea of debt, obligation, or the timing of an event. When a bill is due, it is time to pay it. When a baby is due, it is time for it to be born. When a library book is due, it is time to return it. If you give someone their due, you give them what they are owed or what they deserve. Before a noun, due carries the idea of something that is required, expected, or necessary, as in due diligence.

A duel is a prearranged combat between two people, traditionally fought with matched weapons to settle a point of honor. The practice is now largely historical, though some cultures retain ritualized forms. Figuratively, any intense one-on-one contest is a duel: {The debate became a duel of wits}. To duel is to engage in such combat: {They dueled at dawn}.

Dueled is the past tense of duel—to fight a formal combat between two people, traditionally with swords or pistols to settle a point of honor: {They dueled at dawn}. The word extends to any intense one-on-one contest: {The two guitarists dueled for twenty minutes}. Also spelled duelled.

Dueling is the act of fighting a formal combat between two people, traditionally with matched weapons like swords or pistols, often to settle a point of honor. The practice was once common among aristocrats and military officers but is now illegal virtually everywhere. The word extends to any intense one-on-one contest: {dueling guitarists}, {dueling op-eds}. Politicians or lawyers with competing agendas may have {dueling press conferences}. The spelling duel**l**ing is standard in British English.

A duelist is someone who fights duels—formal combats between two people, traditionally to settle disputes of honor. The term evokes an earlier era of swords at dawn and pistols at ten paces: {He fancied himself a duelist, though he'd never held a rapier}. In gaming contexts, a duelist is a player who specializes in one-on-one combat.

A duelist is a person involved in a duel, a formalized fight between two people armed with weapons. Duelists can also be players in a card game known as Duelist, in which players try to win cards from each other.

Duelled is the past tense of duel—to fight a formal combat between two people, typically with weapons and witnesses. Historically, duels settled disputes of honor: {They duelled at dawn with pistols}. The word extends to any intense one-on-one contest: {The lawyers duelled over every point}. Also spelled dueled.

Duelling is the British spelling of dueling—fighting a formal combat between two people, typically with weapons, to settle a point of honor. The practice was once common among aristocrats and military officers: {He was killed in a duelling accident}. The word extends to any intense one-on-one contest: {duelling pianos}, {duelling headlines}.

A duellist is someone who fights duels—formal combat between two people, typically with swords or pistols, to settle a point of honor. The term evokes an era when gentlemen resolved insults through ritualized violence: {Hamilton died a duellist, shot by Aaron Burr}. Also spelled duelist.

Duels are formal, prearranged fights between two people, historically conducted with swords or pistols to settle a matter of honor or resolve a dispute. The practice was once a socially accepted way for gentlemen to defend their reputations, though it was often illegal and frequently fatal. Today the word extends to any intense one-on-one contest: {The two candidates engaged in a verbal duel during the debate}. As a verb, to duel is to fight or compete in this manner.

Dues are regular payments required for membership in an organization: {union dues}, {club dues}, {membership dues}. The word is almost always plural. To {pay your dues} is to earn your place through hard work or difficult experience before enjoying success: {She paid her dues playing small clubs before hitting it big}.

A duet is a performance by two musicians or singers, or a piece of music composed for two performers: {They sang a duet at the wedding}. The term extends to any collaborative effort between two people: {The comedy duo's verbal duets were legendary}. In dance, a duet is a pas de deux.

Duets is the plural of duet, a musical performance by two people—singers or instrumentalists—or the composition written for such a performance. The term extends to any collaborative effort between two: {The film featured several duets between the lead actors}. A duet implies coordination and harmony between partners.

Duff has several unrelated meanings. It's the decaying organic matter on a forest floor—leaf litter, fallen needles, decomposing debris. In British slang, duff means worthless or broken: {The information turned out to be duff}. Your duff is your backside: {Get off your duff and help}. To duff up someone is to beat them. In cooking, a duff is a boiled or steamed pudding.

Duffel is a coarse, heavy woolen fabric, or a bag made from it—typically a large cylindrical bag with a drawstring or zipper closure, carried by a shoulder strap: {She packed her duffel for the weekend trip}. Duffel bags are associated with military gear, gym clothes, and travel. Also spelled duffle.

A duffer is someone incompetent at a particular activity, especially golf: {The course was full of weekend duffers}. The word suggests amateur bumbling rather than serious failure—a duffer isn't dangerous, just not very good. In British and Australian slang, duffer can also mean a stupid or useless person generally.

Duffers are people who are incompetent or clumsy at something, especially golf. A duffer hacks around the course without much skill: {The course was full of weekend duffers}. The term is mildly dismissive but usually good-natured—duffers know they're duffers. British English also uses duffer for any inept or stupid person.

Duffle is a coarse woolen fabric with a thick nap, originally from Duffel, Belgium. The word now most often refers to items made from or associated with this material: a duffle bag is a large cylindrical bag of heavy cloth, and a duffle coat is a hooded toggle-fastened coat. The spelling duffel is equally common.

Dufus is a mildly insulting term for someone who is stupid, clueless, or socially inept: {Don't be such a dufus}. The word suggests bumbling incompetence rather than malice—a dufus is more laughable than threatening. Also spelled doofus, which is more common.

Dug is the past tense and past participle of dig. You dug a hole yesterday; you have dug many holes in your life. Separately, a dug is an udder or teat, especially of a domestic animal—now archaic or dialectal: {The calf nuzzled at the cow's dug}.

A dugong is a large marine mammal found in warm coastal waters from East Africa to Australia. Related to manatees, dugongs are slow-moving herbivores that graze on seagrass, earning them the nickname "sea cow." Unlike manatees, dugongs have a fluked tail like a whale's and spend their entire lives in saltwater.

A dugout is a shelter or space created by digging into the ground or a hillside, or by hollowing out a log. The term most commonly refers to two things: a canoe made from a hollowed tree trunk, and the covered bench area in baseball where players and coaches sit when not on the field. {The team watched nervously from the dugout as the final inning began.} Dugouts also historically served as primitive shelters or military positions dug into embankments.

Dugouts are shelters dug into the ground or a hillside, often used for military protection or basic habitation. In baseball, a dugout is the sunken bench area where players and coaches sit when not on the field: {The manager paced the dugout}. A dugout canoe is a boat carved from a single log, hollowed out to form the hull.
Duh and doh are used ironically to signal that you, or someone else, have been very slow to understand something obvious.

Dui is an informal, lowercase rendering of DUI, the acronym for "driving under the influence"—operating a vehicle while impaired by alcohol or drugs. In casual writing, the lowercase form appears frequently: {He got a dui last year}, {two dui convictions}. The term functions as both noun and modifier: {dui laws}, {dui checkpoint}. (DUI is the standard capitalized form.)

A duke is the highest rank of nobility below royalty in European aristocracies, ruling over a duchy. The title appears in fairy tales and period dramas: {The duke summoned his advisors}. In American slang, dukes means fists: {Put up your dukes}. To duke it out is to fight or compete intensely: {The two candidates duked it out in the debate}. (Capitalized Duke is a name or university.)

Dukes is slang for fists, especially when raised and ready to fight. The expression {put up your dukes} is a challenge to engage in a fistfight. This sense likely derives from Cockney rhyming slang, where "Duke of Yorks" meant forks, which was itself slang for fingers or hands. Outside of this idiom, dukes simply refers to multiple noblemen ranking just below princes. {He put up his dukes and told the bully to back off.}

A dulcimer is a stringed musical instrument. The hammered dulcimer has wire strings stretched over a trapezoidal sounding board and is played by striking with small mallets. The Appalachian or mountain dulcimer is an hourglass-shaped fretted instrument held across the lap and plucked or strummed: {She learned to play dulcimer from her grandmother in the hollers of eastern Kentucky}.

Dulcimers are stringed musical instruments, typically with a trapezoidal wooden body. The hammered dulcimer has strings struck with small mallets, while the Appalachian or mountain dulcimer is a fretted instrument held on the lap and plucked or strummed: {She played old folk tunes on her dulcimer}. The sound is delicate and resonant, associated with folk and traditional music.

Dull describes something lacking sharpness, brightness, or intensity. A dull knife doesn't cut well; a dull color lacks vibrancy; a dull ache persists without being acute. Applied to people or things, dull means boring or uninteresting: {The lecture was so dull I nearly fell asleep}. A dull mind is slow to understand. Weather can be dull—gray and overcast. To dull something is to make it less sharp or intense: {Time dulls the pain}.

Dulled describes something that has lost its sharpness, brightness, or intensity. A dulled knife no longer cuts cleanly. Pain can be dulled by medication. Senses become dulled by repetition or fatigue: {Years of factory noise had dulled his hearing}. Emotions dull too: {Grief had dulled her capacity for joy}.

Dullness is the quality of being dull—lacking sharpness, brightness, or interest. A knife's dullness makes it struggle to cut. The dullness of a lecture puts students to sleep. {The dullness of the gray sky matched her mood.} Dullness can describe mental slowness, sensory flatness, or simple boredom.

Dullsville is slang for a boring place, situation, or state of affairs. The -ville suffix treats dullness as a destination you've arrived at or are stuck in: {This party is dullsville—let's get out of here}. Sometimes capitalized as if it were an actual town. The coinage spawned similar formations: squaresville, deadsville.

Dumb originally meant unable to speak—a meaning that persists in {deaf and dumb} and {struck dumb with amazement}. The sense shift to stupid now dominates casual usage: {That was a dumb idea}, {Don't be dumb}. This evolution has made the original meaning problematic, as calling a mute person dumb now risks implying stupidity. To {dumb down} is to simplify for a less sophisticated audience.
clues: Unable to speak, in older usage

definition: Dumbass is a vulgar insult for a stupid person: {I felt like a dumbass for locking my keys in the car}. It can be affectionate among friends.

Dumbassery is the quality or practice of being a dumbass—behaving in ways that are stupid, reckless, or thoughtlessly foolish. The word covers both individual acts and a general pattern: {That was pure dumbassery} describes a specific incident, while {I've had enough of your dumbassery} suggests ongoing idiocy. The -ery suffix gives it a mock-formal ring, as if stupidity were a craft or trade.
Dumbasses is the plural of dumbass, a vulgar term for stupid people: {Those dumbasses forgot to book the venue}.

A dumbbell is a short bar with weights at each end, held in one hand for exercise: {She grabbed a pair of dumbbells for bicep curls}. The word also means a stupid person—someone whose head is as useful as a bell that makes no sound: {Don't be such a dumbbell}.

Dumbbells are handheld weights used for exercise, consisting of a short bar with a weight at each end. They're lifted repeatedly to build strength and muscle: {She grabbed the dumbbells for her arm workout}. The name comes from an older device for practicing bell-ringing that made no sound—a "dumb" (silent) bell. By extension, a dumbbell is a stupid person.

Dumbfound means to astonish so thoroughly that someone is left speechless. The word combines dumb (unable to speak) with a sense of being struck or confounded: {The verdict dumbfounded everyone in the courtroom}. Also spelled dumfound. The adjective dumbfounded is more common than the verb.

Dumbfounded means utterly astonished—so shocked or surprised that you're momentarily speechless. The word combines dumb (unable to speak) with confounded (bewildered): {She stood dumbfounded when they announced her name}. Unlike mere surprise, dumbfounded suggests being rendered temporarily incapable of response.

Dumbfounds is the third-person singular present tense of dumbfound, meaning to astonish or bewilder someone to the point where they are momentarily speechless. The word combines dumb (in its older sense of unable to speak) with confound. {The jury's verdict dumbfounds legal experts.} Something that dumbfounds leaves you stunned, struggling to process what just happened.

A dumbfuck is an extremely stupid person. The word combines two vulgar terms for emphasis, suggesting someone whose stupidity is so profound it deserves special contempt: {What kind of dumbfuck leaves their car unlocked in this neighborhood?} As an adjective, it describes idiotic actions or ideas: {That was a dumbfuck move}.

Dumbfuckery is spectacularly stupid behavior or decisions, especially when repeated or systematic: {The whole project collapsed due to management dumbfuckery}. The word implies not just incompetence but a kind of aggressive, almost willful stupidity. It often describes institutional failures or bureaucratic absurdity: {I can't deal with this dumbfuckery anymore}.

Dumbo is informal for a stupid person—someone perceived as slow or dim-witted: {Don't be such a dumbo}. The insult derives from dumb in its sense of unintelligent, with the -o suffix adding a mocking, dismissive tone. It's relatively mild, often used playfully among friends or directed at oneself after a foolish mistake. (Capitalized Dumbo is the Disney elephant character.)

A dumbphone is a basic mobile phone without smartphone capabilities—no touchscreen, no apps, no internet browsing. The term arose as a retronym after smartphones became standard, often used affectionately by those who prefer simpler devices: {I switched back to a dumbphone to cut my screen time}.

Dumbphones are basic mobile phones that lack the advanced features of smartphones—no touchscreen, no apps, no internet browsing beyond rudimentary functions. They make calls, send texts, and little else. The term emerged as a retronym after smartphones became standard: {I switched back to a dumbphone to reduce screen time}. Some users choose them deliberately to avoid digital distraction.

Dumbstruck means so shocked or astonished that you're rendered speechless. The dumb here is the old sense meaning mute, not stupid—you're literally struck silent by surprise, disbelief, or overwhelming emotion: {She stood dumbstruck when she saw the damage}. Also spelled dumfounded or dumbfounded.

A dumbwaiter is a small elevator used to move food, dishes, or other items between floors—typically from a kitchen to a dining room above. The name comes from its function as a silent servant. In older usage, a dumbwaiter could also be a wheeled serving table or tiered stand for holding dishes.

A dumbwaiter is a small freight elevator used to move food, dishes, or other items between floors—typically connecting a kitchen to a dining room above or below. The name reflects that it performs a waiter's task silently, without the need for human servants on stairs. In older homes, dumbwaiters were often built into walls; in restaurants and hotels, they remain practical for moving supplies. {The cook sent the plates up on the dumbwaiter.}

Dumdum has two meanings. A dumdum bullet is designed to expand on impact, causing greater tissue damage—named after an arsenal near Calcutta. Separately, dumdum is informal for a stupid person: {Don't be such a dumdum}. The insult reduplicates "dumb" for childish emphasis, common in schoolyard taunts.

Dummies is the plural of dummy—a figure representing a human body, as in a ventriloquist's dummy or a crash-test dummy. A dummy is also a stupid person: {Those dummies left the door unlocked}. The "For Dummies" book series popularized the self-deprecating phrase: {I need a guide for dummies}. In card games, the dummy is the exposed hand played by the declarer's partner.

A dummy is a model or replica that substitutes for the real thing—a ventriloquist's dummy, a crash-test dummy, a dressmaker's dummy. The word extends to anything serving as a placeholder: a dummy {corporation} exists only on paper, a dummy {variable} holds a position in code. Informally, dummy means a stupid person: {Don't be such a dummy}. As a verb, to dummy up is to remain silent or to create a mock-up: {We dummied up a prototype}.

Dump is most frequently a verb about getting rid of things, often in a way that shows no affection for them. If you dump a boyfriend or girlfriend, you end the relationship summarily. If you dump your possessions somewhere, you drop them carelessly. Someone may dump a lot of trash by the side of the road. It would be more desirable, however, if they took it to the dump, informal for a landfill. To take a dump is an informal and somewhat vulgar expression for emptying your bowels.

Dumped is the past tense of dump—to drop or unload something, often unceremoniously: {She dumped the laundry on the bed}. To dump someone is to end a romantic relationship abruptly: {He got dumped right before prom}. Data gets dumped when transferred in bulk or output for analysis. Dumped goods are sold cheaply abroad, often below cost.

A dumper is a person or thing that dumps. In relationships, the dumper is the one who ends things, as opposed to the one being dumped: {It's easier to be the dumper than the dumpee}. A dumper can also be a vehicle designed to tip its load—a dump truck or similar equipment used in construction. In Australian and British slang, a dumper is a powerful wave that crashes swimmers into the sand.

Dumping is getting rid of something, often carelessly or in large quantities: {They were caught dumping waste in the river}. In commerce, dumping means selling goods in a foreign market below cost to undercut competitors—a practice often subject to trade penalties. To dump someone is to abruptly end a romantic relationship: {She dumped him right before prom}.

A dumpling is a small mass of dough, often filled with meat or vegetables, cooked by boiling, steaming, or frying. Dumplings appear across cuisines—Chinese jiaozi, Polish pierogi, Southern American chicken and dumplings. The word extends affectionately to a chubby or endearing person: {Come here, my little dumpling}.

Dumplings are pieces of dough cooked by boiling, steaming, or frying. The simplest are balls of flour and water dropped into soups or stews. Many cuisines wrap dough around savory or sweet fillings: {We ordered pork dumplings}, {apple dumplings for dessert}. The term covers a vast range—from pierogi to potstickers to gnocchi—united by the dough-based structure.

Dumps is a state of low spirits or depression, appearing almost exclusively in the phrase {down in the dumps}: {He's been down in the dumps since he lost his job}. The word has no singular form in this sense—you're never in just one dump. Separately, dumps is the plural of dump (a place for discarding waste, or an act of dumping).

A dumpster is a large metal container for trash, typically with a hinged lid, designed to be lifted and emptied by a garbage truck. The word comes from Dempster, the brand name of the company that patented the design. To {dumpster dive} is to scavenge discarded items from such containers—for food, furniture, or other usable goods.

Dumpsters are large metal containers for trash, typically found behind businesses and apartment buildings. The word comes from the Dempster Dumpster, a trademarked waste container, though the lowercase form now functions as a generic term. To {dumpster dive} is to search through dumpsters for discarded items—whether for food, furniture, or sellable goods.

A dumptruck is a heavy vehicle with a hinged bed that tilts to unload loose materials—sand, gravel, dirt, debris. The bed dumps its contents out the back or side. In slang, dumptruck describes a person with a notably large rear end: {She's got a dumptruck}.

Dumpy describes someone or something short and squat—thick in proportion to height. The word carries unflattering connotations when applied to people: {a dumpy little man in a rumpled suit}. Buildings and objects can be dumpy too: {a dumpy concrete bunker}. The word suggests ungainliness rather than mere compactness.

A dunce is a person regarded as slow-witted or stupid, especially someone who struggles to learn. The word often implies repeated failure despite instruction: {He felt like a dunce in math class}. A dunce cap—the tall conical hat once used to humiliate slow students—survives as an image of public shaming for stupidity.

Dunces is the plural of dunce, a slow learner or stupid person. The word carries a tone of contempt or exasperation: {The committee was run by dunces}. A dunce cap—the tall conical hat once used to shame struggling students—survives as a symbol of stupidity even though the practice has vanished from schools.

A dune is a hill or ridge of sand shaped by wind. Dunes form along coastlines and in deserts, constantly shifting as wind moves grains from one side to the other. Beach dunes protect inland areas from storm surges. {The children ran up and down the dunes.} Sand dunes can grow to hundreds of feet tall in places like the Sahara. (Capitalized Dune is the science fiction novel and franchise.)

Dunes are hills or ridges of sand shaped by wind. They form along coastlines and in deserts, where wind piles loose sand into characteristic slopes—gentle on the windward side, steeper where sand cascades down. Dunes migrate slowly as wind moves sand from one face to the other. {We climbed the dunes to watch the sunset over the beach.}

Dung is animal excrement, especially from large herbivores like cattle, horses, and elephants. The word sounds more rural and agricultural than *shit* or *feces*: {dung beetle}, {cow dung}, {dung heap}. Dung has been used for millennia as fertilizer and, when dried, as fuel. The verb means to spread dung on fields.

Dungaree is a coarse cotton fabric, originally from India, used for work clothes and sails. In the plural, dungarees are pants or overalls made from this material—sturdy garments associated with manual labor: {He wore dungarees and a flannel shirt}. The word now often refers to denim jeans or bib overalls generally.

Dungarees are sturdy work pants or overalls made of coarse cotton fabric, typically denim. The term is somewhat old-fashioned in American English, where jeans now dominates, but remains current in British English for casual trousers: {She wore dungarees and a striped shirt}. The word comes from a Hindi term for the coarse fabric itself.

A dungeon is an underground prison cell, especially in a medieval castle—dark, damp, and often used for torture or indefinite confinement. The word evokes historical cruelty: {The prisoner was thrown into the dungeon and forgotten}. In fantasy games and fiction, dungeons are underground labyrinths filled with monsters and treasure to be conquered: {We spent the weekend crawling through dungeons in the new RPG}.

A dungeonmaster is the person who runs a tabletop role-playing game, especially Dungeons & Dragons. The dungeonmaster creates the world, controls non-player characters, narrates events, and referees the rules while players make decisions for their characters. Often abbreviated DM. The role requires improvisation, storytelling ability, and managing group dynamics: {Our DM spent weeks preparing the campaign}. Outside gaming, dungeonmaster occasionally appears in BDSM contexts for someone who oversees activities in a dungeon space.

Dungeons are dark underground prison cells, typically in castles or fortresses. The word evokes medieval settings—damp stone chambers where prisoners were confined and sometimes tortured. In fantasy games and literature, dungeons are underground complexes filled with monsters, traps, and treasure to be explored: {We spent the weekend playing Dungeons & Dragons}. A dungeon may also be a BDSM space equipped for bondage activities.

To dunk is to dip something briefly into liquid—a doughnut into coffee, a cookie into milk. In basketball, a dunk is a shot where a player thrusts the ball directly through the hoop from above, and to dunk is to score this way: {He dunked on three defenders}. Internet slang extends this to verbal takedowns: {She dunked on him with one tweet}.

Dunked is the past tense of dunk. To dunk is to dip something briefly into liquid: {She dunked her donut in coffee}. In basketball, to dunk is to slam the ball down through the hoop from above: {He dunked on the defender}. Figuratively, to dunk on someone is to humiliate or decisively refute them, especially online: {She dunked on him with receipts}.

Dunking is the act of dipping something into liquid—a donut into coffee, a cookie into milk. In basketball, dunking means slamming the ball downward through the hoop: {He's famous for his powerful dunks}. The slang sense of dunking on someone means humiliating them, especially online, derived from the dominance a basketball dunk displays over a defender.

Dunks is the plural of dunk—a forceful basketball shot where a player thrusts the ball down through the hoop. Highlight-reel dunks showcase athleticism and power: {He had three dunks in the first quarter}. Outside basketball, dunks are acts of dipping something briefly into liquid: {a few dunks of the cookie into milk}.

Dunno is an informal spelling of "don't know," representing casual or rapid speech where the words blur together: {I dunno, maybe we should just stay home}. It appears mainly in dialogue, text messages, and informal writing to convey a shrug or uncertainty.

A duo is a pair, especially two people who perform or work together: {a comedy duo}, {a musical duo}. The word emphasizes partnership or collaboration more than simply counting two of something. It can also describe any twosome: {The duo spent the afternoon plotting their next move}.

A duopoly is a market dominated by two sellers. The term parallels monopoly (one seller) and extends to any situation where two entities hold overwhelming control: {The duopoly of Coke and Pepsi}, {a political duopoly of two major parties}. The word often carries critical undertones, suggesting limited choice or collusion.

Duos is the plural of duo, a pair or twosome. Musical duos perform together: {The festival featured several acoustic duos}. The word applies to any collaborative pair: {comedy duos}, {figure skating duos}. In video games, duos often names a two-player team mode: {Let's play duos}.

A dupe is someone who has been deceived or tricked, often implying they were gullible or naive enough to fall for it: {The investors were dupes in an elaborate Ponzi scheme}. As a verb, to dupe someone is to deceive them, usually for personal gain. In casual usage, dupe also functions as a shortened form of duplicate, referring to a copy or knockoff: {This lipstick is a dupe for the high-end brand}.

Duped means deceived or tricked into believing something false. Someone who has been duped was taken in by a lie, scam, or manipulation: {Investors were duped by promises of guaranteed returns}. The word implies the victim was made to look foolish—you feel duped when you realize you've been had.

Dupes are people who have been deceived or tricked—victims of a con, scam, or manipulation: {The fraudster's dupes lost their life savings}. The word carries a note of foolishness; dupes are seen as gullible, not just unlucky. As a verb, to dupe is to deceive: {They duped him into signing the contract}. In casual usage, dupes also means duplicates, especially cheaper alternatives to expensive products: {These lipsticks are dupes for high-end brands}.

Duping is the act of deceiving or tricking someone into believing something false: {They're duping customers into paying for services they don't need}. The word implies the victim is made a fool of—a dupe. In gaming slang, duping also refers to exploiting glitches to duplicate items: {He got banned for duping rare weapons}.

Duplex describes something with two parts or layers. A duplex is a building divided into two separate living units, typically side by side or stacked: {They bought a duplex and rent out the other half}. In telecommunications, duplex refers to two-way transmission—full duplex allows simultaneous sending and receiving, half duplex alternates. Duplex paper is printed on both sides.

Duplexes is the plural of duplex, a building divided into two separate living units, typically side by side or stacked vertically, each with its own entrance. In American real estate, duplexes occupy a middle ground between single-family homes and apartment buildings, often appealing to owners who live in one unit and rent out the other. {The neighborhood has a mix of single-family homes and duplexes.} The term extends to telecommunications, where duplex refers to systems allowing simultaneous two-way transmission.

Duplicate means to make an exact copy of something, or the copy itself: {duplicate the file}, {a duplicate key}. As an adjective, it describes things that are identical copies: {duplicate receipts}. Something done {in duplicate} exists in two identical versions. The word can also mean to repeat unnecessarily: {We don't want to duplicate effort}.

Duplicates are copies or exact matches of something else. The word works as both noun and verb: you might find duplicates in a photo library, or duplicate a key at the hardware store. To {remove duplicates} is to eliminate redundant items from a set. A duplicate can also be a person who closely resembles another: {She's a duplicate of her mother}.

Duplicitous describes someone who deceives by pretending to have one set of intentions while actually pursuing another—saying one thing while meaning or doing something else. The word implies deliberate two-facedness rather than simple dishonesty: {a duplicitous ally who fed information to both sides}, {His duplicitous nature eventually caught up with him}.

Duplicity is deliberate deception—saying one thing while meaning or doing another. Unlike simple lying, duplicity implies a sustained pattern of two-facedness: {His duplicity was revealed when the emails surfaced}. The word suggests calculated betrayal of trust rather than momentary dishonesty. A person acting with duplicity maintains one appearance while secretly pursuing contrary ends.

Durability is the ability to withstand wear, pressure, or damage over time. A product's durability determines how long it lasts under normal use: {The durability of this fabric makes it ideal for outdoor furniture}. The quality extends beyond physical objects—a relationship's durability, an idea's durability. Durable goods are items expected to last years rather than be quickly consumed.

Durable means able to withstand wear, pressure, or damage over time. A durable {fabric} holds up through repeated washing. Durable {goods} are products expected to last years rather than be quickly consumed—appliances, furniture, vehicles. The word emphasizes longevity and resilience: {a durable friendship}, {a durable peace agreement}.

A durag is a close-fitting cloth head covering, typically made of silky material, tied at the back. Originally worn by Black men to protect and compress hair—especially to maintain waves or braids—it has become a fashion item and cultural symbol in hip-hop and Black American style: {He put on his durag before bed to keep his waves fresh}. Also spelled do-rag.

A durag is a close-fitting cloth head covering, typically made of silky material, tied at the back. Worn primarily by Black men and women, durags compress and protect hairstyles—especially waves and braids—while sleeping or between styling sessions. They've become a fashion statement and cultural symbol beyond their practical function: {He never leaves the house without his durag}.

Duration is how long something lasts—the span of time from beginning to end. A movie has a duration; so does a war, a battery charge, or a headache. {The duration of the flight was three hours.} The phrase {for the duration} means for as long as something continues, often implying an indefinite or extended period: {We're stuck here for the duration.}

Duress is compulsion or constraint, especially when it involves threats, violence, or imprisonment. When someone acts under duress, they do so because they have been forced or coerced, not of their own free will. {She signed the contract under duress.} In legal contexts, proving duress can invalidate agreements or serve as a defense against criminal charges, since the law recognizes that people cannot be held fully responsible for actions they were compelled to take.

Durian is a large tropical fruit native to Southeast Asia, notorious for its powerful odor—often described as sewage-like or rotten—that gets it banned from hotels and public transit in the region. Those who tolerate the smell find the custard-like flesh rich and complex. The spiky husk can weigh several pounds. {Durian is an acquired taste.}

Durians are large tropical fruits with a thick, spiky husk and soft, creamy flesh. Native to Southeast Asia, they're prized for their rich, custard-like texture but notorious for an intensely pungent smell that many find repulsive—banned from hotels and public transit in several Asian countries. Fans consider them the "king of fruits." Singular: durian.

Unusual among prepositions ending in –ing, during has no use in modern English other than as a preposition. Its meaning is always connected with time and its object is typically a divisible period of time: practices that began during the Middle Ages, a disturbance during the night.

Dusk is the time just after sunset when daylight fades but darkness hasn't fully arrived—the transitional period between day and night. It's dimmer than twilight's beginning but not yet night: {We walked home at dusk}. The word can also describe the dim light itself or, figuratively, a period of decline: {the dusk of an empire}.

Dust is fine particles of matter that are ubiquitous in the human environment. Before another noun, dust means either consisting of it (dust storm, dust cloud) or for protection from it (dust jacket, dust mask). As a verb, dust means remove dust from surfaces where it settles. Dust can also mean sprinkle with a fine powder: Dust the cake with powdered sugar.

Dustbin is the standard British English term for what Americans call a trash can or garbage can—a container for household waste. The word combines dust (once a common term for refuse) with bin (a container). In figurative use, the dustbin of history refers to the fate of forgotten or discredited ideas and movements: {Communism was supposed to end up in the dustbin of history.}

A dustbowl is a region where drought and poor land management have stripped away topsoil, leaving barren, wind-eroded terrain. The term comes from the 1930s Dust Bowl, when severe drought devastated the American Great Plains, creating massive dust storms and displacing thousands of farmers. Figuratively, any parched, desolate area: {The yard was a dustbowl by August}.

Dusted is the past tense of dust, which cuts two ways: to remove dust {She dusted the shelves} or to apply a fine coating {He dusted the cake with powdered sugar}. In slang, dusted means defeated or killed: {We dusted them in the playoffs}. Someone dusted on PCP is intoxicated with the drug, from "angel dust."

A duster is a cloth or brush for removing dust from surfaces. In the American West, a duster was a long, light coat worn to protect clothing from trail dust—now mostly seen in period films. A duster can also be a crop-dusting aircraft. In baseball, a duster is a pitch thrown deliberately close to the batter, meant to make them back off the plate.

Dusters are tools or garments designed for removing dust. A feather duster or cloth duster whisks dust from surfaces. A duster is also a lightweight coat, originally worn to protect clothing from road dust during open-air automobile travel. In baseball, a duster is a pitch thrown close to the batter to back them off the plate. {She grabbed the duster and cleaned the blinds.} {The pitcher's duster sent him sprawling.}

Dusting is light cleaning to remove dust from surfaces, or the thin layer of something scattered over a surface: {a dusting of snow}, {a dusting of powdered sugar}. The word suggests a minimal amount—just enough to coat. In another sense, a dusting is a beating or defeat: {Our team took a dusting}.

A dustjacket is the removable paper cover wrapped around a hardcover book, protecting the binding while displaying the title, author, and promotional material. Also called a dust cover or book jacket. Collectors prize books with intact original dustjackets: {The first edition is worth more with its dustjacket}.

A dustman is a British term for a garbage collector—someone employed to remove household waste. The word reflects older usage when ash and dust from coal fires comprised much of what was discarded: {The dustman comes on Thursdays}. Americans say garbage man or sanitation worker.

A dustpan is a flat, handled scoop used to collect dirt and debris swept from a floor. You hold it at an angle while brushing material into it with a broom: {She swept the broken glass into a dustpan}. Most have a short handle requiring you to bend down, though long-handled versions attach to upright brooms.

A duststorm is a weather event in which strong winds lift loose sand or dirt from dry ground and carry it through the air, reducing visibility and coating everything in grit. Duststorms occur in arid regions and can travel hundreds of miles: {The duststorm turned the sky brown and forced drivers off the road}. Also spelled as two words: dust storm.

Duststorms are weather events in which strong winds lift loose, dry soil into the air, reducing visibility and sometimes darkening the sky. They occur in arid regions where drought or land degradation has left topsoil exposed: {Duststorms plagued the Great Plains during the 1930s Dust Bowl}. A single event is a duststorm.

A dustup is a quarrel, fight, or commotion—typically brief and not too serious: {There was a dustup at the bar last night}, {The meeting turned into a dustup over budget cuts}. The word suggests something loud and messy but ultimately minor, more scuffle than brawl.

Dusty describes something covered with or full of fine dry particles—the kind that accumulate on surfaces left undisturbed: {a dusty shelf}, {dusty old books in the attic}. By extension, dusty suggests neglect, staleness, or being out of date: {dusty ideas}, {a dusty corner of the archive}. A dusty color is muted or grayish, as if seen through a film of dust: {dusty rose}, {dusty blue}.

Duties are obligations or responsibilities—things you're expected or required to do. A soldier's duties include following orders; a parent's duties include caring for children. Duty also refers to taxes on imports: {customs duties}, {duty-free shops}. The phrase {on duty} means actively working, while {off duty} means not: {The officer was off duty when the accident occurred}.

Dutiful describes someone who fulfills their obligations reliably, especially out of a sense of duty rather than enthusiasm. A dutiful {son} visits his aging parents regularly. A dutiful {employee} completes tasks without complaint. The word often carries a faint suggestion of going through the motions—doing what's expected without genuine feeling: {She made the dutiful phone call to her mother-in-law}.

Dutifully means in a manner that fulfills obligations or expectations, often with a sense of conscientiousness rather than enthusiasm. Someone who dutifully {attends every meeting} or {calls their parents every Sunday} does so because they feel they should, not necessarily because they want to. The word can carry a faint note of resigned compliance.

Duty is an obligation—something you must do because of your role, position, or moral code. A soldier has duties, as does a nurse, a citizen, or a child. {Jury duty} is compulsory service. To be {on duty} is to be working; {off duty} means free from responsibilities. Duty also refers to a tax on imports: {customs duty}, {duty-free}. The phrase {do one's duty} can mean anything from fulfilling basic responsibilities to a euphemism for using the toilet.

A duvet is a soft, thick bed covering filled with down, feathers, or synthetic material, used in place of blankets and a top sheet. Common in European bedding traditions, duvets typically have removable covers for washing: {I need to change the duvet cover}. Americans sometimes call them comforters, though duvets are usually fluffier and designed with covers.

A duvet is a thick, blanket-like covering for a bed that is enclosed in a removable cover. Duvets are typically filled with down or feathers but may also be filled with wool, silk, or synthetic materials.

A DVR (digital video recorder) is a device that records television programs to a hard drive for later viewing. Unlike the VCRs it replaced, a DVR can pause and rewind live broadcasts, skip commercials, and store many hours of content. The verb DVR means to record something: {I'll DVR the game and watch it tonight}. TiVo was the brand that popularized DVRs in the late 1990s.

A dwarf is a person of unusually small stature, or in folklore, a small humanoid creature often associated with mining, metalwork, and underground realms. The word extends to anything notably smaller than typical: a dwarf {planet}, dwarf {varieties} of fruit trees. As a verb, to dwarf something is to make it seem small by comparison: {The skyscraper dwarfs the surrounding buildings}. The plural is dwarfs or dwarves, the latter popularized by Tolkien's fantasy novels.

Dwarfed means made to appear small by comparison. A towering building dwarfs the houses around it; a celebrity's salary dwarfs an average worker's. The word comes from dwarf—the mythical small creature—and implies that something large or significant has been reduced to seeming insignificant: {The skyscraper dwarfed everything on the block}. Less commonly, dwarfed describes something actually stunted in growth: {a dwarfed bonsai tree}.

Dwarfing describes something that makes another thing seem small by comparison. A skyscraper dwarfs neighboring buildings. An achievement can dwarf previous accomplishments. {The mountain range, dwarfing everything around it, dominated the horizon.} In horticulture, dwarfing refers to techniques or rootstocks that limit plant growth: {a dwarfing rootstock for apple trees}.

Dwarfism is a medical condition resulting in unusually short stature, typically defined as an adult height under 4'10". The most common form, achondroplasia, affects bone growth and produces characteristic proportions. People with dwarfism are called dwarfs or little people; the latter term is now generally preferred. {Her dwarfism was diagnosed at birth.}

Dwarfs is the plural of dwarf—a person of unusually short stature, a mythological small humanoid, or anything markedly smaller than typical: {dwarf planets}, {dwarf varieties of fruit trees}. As a verb, dwarfs means to make something appear small by comparison: {The skyscraper dwarfs the surrounding buildings}. The alternate plural dwarves, popularized by Tolkien, appears mainly in fantasy contexts.

Dwarven describes things relating to dwarves—the stout, bearded, mine-dwelling folk of fantasy literature and games: {dwarven armor}, {dwarven ale}, {a dwarven stronghold}. The word follows the pattern of elven, serving as the adjectival form where dwarfish might sound dismissive. It appears almost exclusively in fantasy contexts.

Dwarves is a plural of dwarf, used especially for the mythological beings—short, bearded, skilled in mining and metalwork—found in Norse legend and modern fantasy: {The dwarves forged magical weapons in their mountain halls}. Tolkien popularized this spelling over the older dwarfs. For people of short stature, dwarfs remains standard; dwarves may seem to equate real people with fantasy creatures.

Dwarvish describes things relating to dwarves—the short, sturdy, often bearded fantasy race known for mining, metalwork, and underground kingdoms. Most commonly refers to their language: {The runes were written in Dwarvish}. The word belongs to fantasy literature and gaming, particularly works following Tolkien's tradition. Also spelled dwarfish, though that form more often means simply small or stunted.

A dweeb is a socially awkward, unfashionable person—someone perceived as boring, studious, or out of touch with what's cool. The term emerged in 1980s American slang alongside nerd and geek, though dweeb carries more contempt and less suggestion of technical competence: {Don't be such a dweeb}. The insult has softened over time but remains mildly derogatory.

Dweebs is the plural of dweeb, a mildly derisive term for someone perceived as socially awkward, unfashionable, or obsessively studious. Unlike nerd or geek, which have acquired positive connotations, dweeb remains dismissive: {Those dweebs are always in the computer lab}. The word emerged in American slang in the 1980s.

Dweeby describes someone or something nerdy, socially awkward, or uncool in a harmless way. A dweeby person might wear unfashionable clothes, obsess over obscure hobbies, or lack social grace: {He had a dweeby charm that grew on her}. The word is mildly teasing rather than truly insulting—more affectionate than cruel.
clues: Studious but not at all cool

definition: Dwell means to live or reside somewhere, though the word sounds literary or old-fashioned for everyday use: {They dwelt in a cottage by the sea}. More commonly, dwell appears with "on" or "upon" to mean lingering mentally on something, usually unpleasantly: {Don't dwell on the past}. {She dwelt on every mistake she'd made}.

Dwelled is the past tense of dwell, meaning to live or reside somewhere: {They dwelled in a small cottage by the sea}. More often, dwell appears in figurative contexts—to dwell on something is to think about it at length, usually excessively: {She dwelled on the mistakes she'd made}. Dwelt is an equally common past tense form.

Dwellers are people who live in a particular place or type of environment. The word almost always appears with a modifier specifying the habitat: {city dwellers}, {cave dwellers}, {apartment dwellers}, {forest dwellers}. It emphasizes ongoing residence rather than temporary presence—dwellers belong to a place in some sustained way.

A dwelling is a place where someone lives—a house, apartment, or any structure serving as a residence. The word is formal and appears mainly in legal, administrative, or literary contexts: {The ordinance prohibits more than four unrelated persons in a single dwelling}. In everyday speech, people say home, house, or place.

Dwellings is the plural of dwelling, a somewhat formal word for places where people live. The term encompasses houses, apartments, caves, tents—any structure serving as a residence. It appears often in legal, bureaucratic, and real estate contexts: {The zoning permits single-family dwellings only}. {Census workers counted all dwellings in the district}.

Dwells means lives or resides in a place: {She dwells in a cottage by the sea}. The word sounds literary or old-fashioned compared to "lives." To dwell on something is to think or talk about it at length, often excessively: {Don't dwell on past mistakes}. The noun dwelling is more common than the verb in modern usage.

Dwindle means to shrink or diminish gradually over time. Supplies dwindle, populations dwindle, hopes dwindle. The word emphasizes slow decline rather than sudden loss: {Her savings dwindled to nothing}. Unlike decrease, dwindle carries a sense of fading away toward insignificance or exhaustion.

Dwindling describes something gradually shrinking, diminishing, or becoming less. Resources dwindle, populations dwindle, hopes dwindle: {Their dwindling savings forced them to sell the house}. The word emphasizes slow decline rather than sudden loss—a candle burns down, a crowd thins out, enthusiasm fades. {She watched her dwindling options with growing alarm}.

Dye is a substance used to color materials—fabric, hair, food, or other things that absorb it. Unlike paint, which coats a surface, dye penetrates and bonds chemically: {She dyed her hair purple}. The verb and noun share spelling with die, but the continuous forms disambiguate: dying versus dyeing. {A dye job} is a hair coloring, sometimes implying it's obvious or poorly done.

Dyed describes something that has had its color changed by soaking in a coloring substance: {dyed fabric}, {dyed hair}, {dyed Easter eggs}. The phrase {dyed in the wool} means thorough or complete—from the practice of dyeing wool before spinning, which produces deeper, more permanent color: {a dyed-in-the-wool conservative}.

Dyes are substances used to color materials—fabrics, hair, food, or other surfaces. Unlike paints, dyes penetrate and bond with the material rather than coating it. The verb means to apply such coloring: {She dyed her hair purple}. The past tense dyed distinguishes it from died.

Dying is the process of ceasing to live, the transition toward death. Someone dying of cancer is in their final decline. The word extends to things fading or ending: {a dying art}, {dying embers}, {her dying wish}. To be {dying to} do something is to want it intensely: {I'm dying to know what happened}. To be {dying for} something is to crave it: {I'm dying for a cup of coffee}.
Dyke is the British spelling of dike and represents all meanings of that word that represent structures, natural or built. Dyke is also a slang and sometimes disparaging word for a lesbian.

Dynamic describes things characterized by energy, motion, or change. A dynamic {personality} is forceful and engaging. A dynamic {economy} grows and evolves. In physics, dynamics is the study of forces and motion, as opposed to statics. Dynamic contrasts with static—what's dynamic moves, shifts, or develops rather than staying fixed. In computing, dynamic content changes based on user input or conditions.
clues: Characterized by constant change or activity

definition: Dynamics refers to forces that produce motion or change. In physics, it's the branch of mechanics dealing with motion and the forces causing it. More broadly, dynamics describes the interacting forces within any system: {group dynamics}, {family dynamics}, {market dynamics}. In music, dynamics means the variation in loudness—the contrast between soft and loud passages. The word nearly always appears in plural form.

Dynamism is energy and vigor in action or expression. A leader with dynamism inspires others through force of personality. The word suggests forward momentum and vitality: {The startup lost its early dynamism after the founders left}. In philosophy, dynamism is the theory that phenomena arise from force or energy rather than matter alone.

Dynamite is a powerful explosive made from nitroglycerin absorbed into a stabilizing material. Invented by Alfred Nobel, it revolutionized mining, construction, and demolition—and warfare. Figuratively, dynamite describes anything explosive or sensational: {That story is dynamite}. As slang, dynamite means excellent or exciting: {The band was dynamite last night}. To dynamite is to blow something up.

Dynamiting is the use of dynamite to blast or destroy something. The word appears in contexts of demolition, mining, and terrorism: {They were arrested for dynamiting the bridge}. Figuratively, to dynamite something is to wreck it completely: {The scandal dynamited his campaign}.

A dynamo is a machine that converts mechanical energy into electrical current—an early term for what's now usually called a generator. Figuratively, a dynamo is a person with exceptional energy or drive: {She's a dynamo—runs three businesses and still volunteers on weekends}. The figurative sense dominates contemporary usage.

Dynamos is the plural of dynamo—a machine that converts mechanical energy into electrical current, or figuratively, a person with exceptional energy and drive. The literal sense is now largely historical, replaced by generator: {The factory's old dynamos have been converted to museum pieces}. The figurative use remains common: {She's a dynamo who transformed the department in six months}.

Dynastic describes things relating to a dynasty—a sequence of rulers from the same family or a family that maintains power across generations. A dynastic {marriage} unites powerful families. Dynastic {succession} passes rule from parent to child. The word extends beyond royalty to any family that dominates a field: {the dynastic ambitions of political families}, {a dynastic sports franchise}.

Dynasties is the plural of dynasty, a sequence of rulers from the same family line who maintain power across generations. The term appears most often in historical contexts—the Ming dynasty, the Romanov dynasty—but extends to any family that dominates a field over time: {political dynasties like the Kennedys} or {sports dynasties like the Manning family}. In casual use, dynasty can describe any team or organization that sustains dominance: {The Patriots built a dynasty in the 2000s}.

A dynasty is a sequence of rulers from the same family line, each inheriting power from predecessors: {the Ming dynasty}, {the Habsburg dynasty}. The word extends to any family that maintains prominence across generations in business, politics, or entertainment: {a banking dynasty}, {a Hollywood dynasty}. In sports, dynasty describes teams that dominate their league over multiple seasons.

Dysentery is a severe intestinal infection causing bloody diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and fever. It spreads through contaminated food or water and can be caused by bacteria or parasites. Historically a major killer of soldiers and travelers, dysentery remains dangerous in areas with poor sanitation: {Half the expedition died of dysentery before reaching the coast}.

Dysfunction is impaired or abnormal functioning. A bodily dysfunction affects an organ or system: {erectile dysfunction}, {kidney dysfunction}. Family dysfunction describes unhealthy relationship patterns. Organizational dysfunction means a workplace or institution operates poorly. The adjective dysfunctional appears more often than the noun: {a dysfunctional family}, {dysfunctional communication}.

Dysfunctional describes something that fails to function properly or healthily. Most often applied to families or relationships marked by poor communication, conflict, or harmful patterns: {She grew up in a dysfunctional household}. The word extends to organizations, systems, or governments that don't work as they should: {a dysfunctional Congress}, {dysfunctional management}. Sometimes used loosely for anything messy or problematic.

Dyslexia is a learning disorder that affects reading, writing, and spelling despite normal intelligence. The brain processes written language differently, making it difficult to connect letters with sounds or recognize words fluently. Someone with dyslexia might reverse letters, read slowly, or struggle with spelling: {Her dyslexia wasn't diagnosed until college}. The condition is lifelong but manageable with specialized instruction.

Dyslexic describes someone with dyslexia, a learning difference affecting reading, writing, and spelling. The brain processes written language differently, often reversing or scrambling letters: {My dyslexic son reads slowly but has exceptional spatial reasoning}. As a noun, a dyslexic is a person with this condition. The word has largely replaced older terms like "word-blind."

Dysmorphia is a distorted perception of one's own body or a body part. In body dysmorphic disorder, someone fixates on perceived flaws others don't notice or consider minor. Muscle dysmorphia involves seeing oneself as insufficiently muscular despite evidence otherwise. The term appears most often in clinical and psychological contexts: {Her therapist diagnosed her with body dysmorphia}.

Dysphoria is a state of profound unease, dissatisfaction, or discomfort with one's situation or self. The opposite of euphoria, it describes emotional distress that goes beyond ordinary unhappiness. In clinical contexts, {gender dysphoria} refers to distress arising from incongruence between one's gender identity and assigned sex. {The medication's side effects included anxiety and dysphoria.}

Dystopia is an imagined society characterized by oppression, suffering, or injustice—the opposite of utopia. The word typically describes fictional worlds where authoritarian control, environmental ruin, or technological excess has created nightmarish conditions: {Orwell's 1984 remains the quintessential dystopia}. Dystopian as an adjective extends beyond fiction to describe real conditions that feel oppressively bleak: {The abandoned factory district had a dystopian quality}.

Dystopian describes an imagined society characterized by oppression, suffering, or degradation—the opposite of utopian. Dystopian fiction depicts futures gone wrong: totalitarian control, environmental collapse, technological enslavement. {The novel paints a dystopian vision of surveillance capitalism.} The word also describes real situations that feel ominously like such fiction: {The abandoned factory district looked dystopian.}

Dystopias are imagined societies characterized by oppression, suffering, and dehumanization—the opposite of utopias. In fiction, dystopias typically feature authoritarian governments, environmental catastrophe, technological control, or social collapse. The word gained currency through twentieth-century novels like *1984* and *Brave New World*. People also use dystopia loosely to describe real-world conditions they find oppressive or nightmarish: {This airport feels like a dystopia.}

Eager describes strong enthusiasm or impatient desire for something anticipated: {eager to please}, {eager for news}, {an eager student}. The word suggests positive energy and readiness rather than passive waiting. An {eager beaver} is someone who shows excessive enthusiasm, sometimes annoyingly so.

Eagerly means with keen interest or impatient desire. Someone who waits eagerly for news anticipates it with enthusiasm: {She eagerly accepted the job offer}. The word suggests active wanting rather than passive willingness—you don't just agree to something eagerly, you want it.

Eagerness is enthusiastic readiness or impatience to do something. It suggests forward-leaning energy—wanting something to happen and wanting it now: {Her eagerness to help was obvious}, {He accepted with an eagerness that surprised me}. The word carries positive connotations of vitality and genuine interest, though excessive eagerness can seem desperate or naive.

An eagle is a large bird of prey with powerful wings, keen eyesight, and a hooked beak—apex predators that hunt fish, small mammals, and other birds. The bald eagle serves as the national symbol of the United States, appearing on currency and official seals. In golf, an eagle is a score of two under par on a hole: {She made eagle on the par five}. As a verb, to eagle a hole is to achieve this score. {Eagle-eyed} means having sharp vision or keen attention to detail.

Eagles are large birds of prey known for their keen eyesight, powerful talons, and soaring flight. The word typically appears as the plural of eagle, referring to multiple birds: {Bald eagles have rebounded since DDT was banned}. In golf, eagles are scores of two under par on a hole. The term also applies to various coins bearing an eagle image, particularly the American gold eagle. (Capitalized Eagles refers to sports teams or the rock band.)

An eaglet is a young eagle, especially one still in the nest or not yet able to fly. The word follows the pattern of other diminutive animal names like piglet or owlet: {The eaglets waited in the nest for their mother to return with food}.

Any part of the organ of hearing, from the innermost to the outermost part, can be called the ear; context usually reveals which particular part or parts is meant. When an adjective that characterizes shape or size precedes ear (pointy/floppy/rounded/huge), the reference is to the visible parts of the ear, as opposed to the “hearing” parts. Ear has figurative use with reference to hearing, listening, and understanding: He has the ear of the President, lend me your ears, in one ear and out the other.

An earache is pain in the ear, typically caused by infection, pressure changes, or inflammation. The word describes the symptom rather than a specific condition: {I woke up with a terrible earache}. Like headache and stomachache, it names discomfort by location.
