An earbud is a small speaker designed to fit inside or just outside the ear canal, typically used in pairs for listening to audio from phones, computers, or music players. Unlike over-ear headphones, earbuds are compact and portable: {I lost one of my earbuds on the subway}. Wireless earbuds have largely replaced wired versions.

Earbuds are small headphones that fit inside or just outside the ear canal, typically connected by a cord or wirelessly via Bluetooth. They're compact and portable, favored for listening to music or taking calls while commuting, exercising, or working: {I can't find my earbuds anywhere}. Also called earphones or in-ears.

The eardrum is the thin membrane inside the ear that vibrates in response to sound waves, transmitting them to the inner ear. Loud noises or sudden pressure changes can rupture it: {The explosion burst his eardrum}. Also called the tympanic membrane.

Eardrums are the thin membranes inside the ear that vibrate in response to sound waves—the mechanism that makes hearing possible. Loud noises, pressure changes, or infection can damage or rupture an eardrum: {My eardrums were ringing after the concert}. Also called the tympanic membrane.

An earful is a large amount of talk, usually unwelcome—a scolding, complaint, or lengthy lecture: {I got an earful from my mother about coming home late}. Less commonly, it can mean as much as one can absorb: {That concert was quite an earful}.

Eargasm is slang for intense auditory pleasure—the experience of hearing something so satisfying it feels almost physical: {That bass drop gave me an eargasm}. The word blends ear with orgasm, suggesting music or sounds that produce a rush of sensation. Common in discussions of headphones, audio equipment, and favorite songs.

Earl is a British noble rank, falling between marquess and viscount in the peerage hierarchy. The title corresponds to count in other European systems—a countess is an earl's wife. Earls were originally royal officials governing shires, though the title became hereditary. {The Earl of Sandwich}, {the Earl of Essex}.

Earlier is the comparative form of early, indicating something that comes before in time or sequence. It often refers to a previous point in the same day or period: {I saw her earlier this morning}, {As mentioned earlier in the report}. Earlier can also compare two events or versions: {The earlier model lacked these features}.

The earlobe is the soft, fleshy lower part of the outer ear that hangs below the cartilage. Earlobes are commonly pierced for earrings. Some people have attached earlobes that connect directly to the head; others have free-hanging lobes—a classic example in genetics teaching.

Earlobes are the soft, fleshy lower parts of the outer ear, hanging below the cartilage. They have no biological function but serve as common sites for piercing: {She had three studs in each earlobe}. Earlobes vary in shape—some hang free, others attach directly to the head.

Earls is the plural of earl, a British title of nobility ranking below marquess and above viscount. The title is ancient, predating the Norman Conquest, and remains in use today: {The earls gathered for the ceremony}. An earl's wife is a countess, and his domain is an earldom.

Early can function as an adjective or adverb with a range of related meanings, most of which are the opposite of late. Early is typically associated with concepts such as before, soon, and beginning, just as late is connected with after and end. In anything that develops over time, early suggests a form or stage that is relatively primitive, immature, or undeveloped.

An earmark is a distinguishing mark, originally the notch cut into an animal's ear to identify ownership. By extension, earmark means to set aside for a specific purpose: {funds earmarked for education}, {She earmarked the afternoon for writing}. In U.S. politics, an earmark is a provision directing government spending to a particular project, often inserted by legislators to benefit their home districts.

Earmarked means designated or set aside for a specific purpose. Money is commonly earmarked: {Congress earmarked funds for highway repairs}. The term comes from the practice of notching livestock ears to indicate ownership. Beyond finances, anything reserved for a particular use can be earmarked: {She had earmarked the afternoon for reading}.

Earmarking is designating something for a particular purpose. Money is earmarked for specific projects; funds earmarked for education can't be spent on roads. The term comes from the practice of notching animals' ears to identify ownership. In politics, earmarking often refers to congressional provisions directing money to specific local projects: {Critics called it earmarking; supporters called it constituent service}.

Earmarks are distinguishing characteristics that identify something: {The proposal had all the earmarks of a scam}. The term comes from the practice of notching or marking animals' ears to show ownership. In American politics, earmarks are provisions inserted into legislation to direct funds toward specific projects, often benefiting a lawmaker's home district: {Critics called the bridge an earmark for a powerful senator}. To earmark money is to set it aside for a particular purpose.

Earmuffs are a pair of soft pads connected by a band, worn over the ears for warmth or noise protection. Winter earmuffs keep ears from freezing; industrial earmuffs block harmful sound levels. The singular earmuff occasionally appears but the plural dominates: {I left my earmuffs in the car}.

Earmuffs are a pair of soft coverings worn over the ears, connected by a band that passes over the head. They provide warmth in cold weather or muffle loud sounds in noisy environments: {She pulled on her earmuffs before heading out into the snow}. Protective earmuffs for noise reduction are bulkier than the fuzzy kind worn for warmth.

To earn is to receive something in exchange for work or effort: {She earns a good salary}, {He earned his degree after years of night classes}. The word implies deserving what you get—earned income differs from inherited wealth, and an earned victory differs from a lucky one. Earn extends to intangibles: {earn someone's trust}, {earn a reputation}. Interest or investments earn returns.

Earned is the past tense of earn—to receive something through effort, work, or merit. Money is earned through labor: {She earned sixty thousand last year}. Respect, trust, and reputation are earned over time. {Earned} often emphasizes that something was deserved rather than given freely: {He earned every bit of that promotion}. In sports, an earned run scores without fielding errors.

Earnest describes serious intent and sincere conviction. An earnest {student} applies genuine effort. An earnest {plea} comes from the heart. To begin {in earnest} is to start with full commitment after preliminary steps: {After months of planning, construction began in earnest}. The word suggests authenticity but can imply a lack of humor or lightness—calling someone earnest isn't always a compliment.

Earnestness is the quality of being serious, sincere, and deeply committed to what one says or does. It suggests genuine conviction rather than casual interest or performance: {Her earnestness about climate change convinced even the skeptics}. The word carries mostly positive connotations of authenticity, though excessive earnestness can seem naive or humorless. It stands in contrast to irony, flippancy, and detachment.

Earning is the act of gaining something through effort, work, or merit. Most often it refers to money received for labor: {She's earning good money at her new job}. But earning extends to non-monetary rewards—you earn respect, trust, or a reputation through your actions. The plural earnings refers to income or profits: {quarterly earnings}, {lifetime earnings}.

Earnings are money received for work or from investments. In personal finance, earnings usually means wages or salary: {Her earnings increased after the promotion}. In business contexts, earnings refers to profits—revenue minus expenses: {The company reported strong quarterly earnings}. The word nearly always appears in plural form.

Earns is the third-person singular of earn—to receive payment or reward for work or effort: {She earns a good salary}. Beyond wages, one earns respect, trust, or reputation through actions that merit them: {He earned their loyalty over years of fair dealing}. Interest or investments earn returns. To earn one's keep is to contribute enough to justify one's place.

An earphone is a small speaker worn in or over the ear to listen to audio privately. Earphones connect to phones, computers, or audio players. The singular usually refers to one of a pair: {I lost an earphone on the train}. The plural covers the set: {These earphones have great sound quality}.

Earphones are small speakers designed to be worn in or over the ears, connected to an audio device by wire or wirelessly. The term covers both earbuds that sit in the ear canal and larger headphones that cover the entire ear, though some reserve *headphones* for the latter: {I forgot my earphones on the train}.

An earpiece is the part of a device designed to be held against or inserted into the ear. On eyeglasses, the earpieces are the arms that hook over the ears to hold the frames in place. On a telephone or headset, the earpiece is the speaker portion that delivers sound. In professional settings, an earpiece often refers to a small, discreet receiver worn in the ear canal for private communication: {The Secret Service agent adjusted her earpiece}.

Earpieces are the parts of a device that fit in or over the ears. On eyeglasses, the earpieces are the arms extending from the frame to hook behind the ears. On headphones or hearing aids, earpieces are the components that deliver sound. A single earpiece often refers to a small speaker worn in one ear for private communication: {The Secret Service agent adjusted his earpiece}.

An earplug is a small object inserted into the ear canal to block sound or water. Foam earplugs expand to fit the canal and reduce noise—worn at concerts, construction sites, or for sleeping: {I can't sleep without earplugs}. Silicone plugs keep water out while swimming.

Earplugs are small devices inserted into the ear canal to block sound or water. They're worn for sleeping, swimming, or protecting hearing in loud environments: {I forgot my earplugs at the concert}. Materials range from foam to silicone to custom-molded plastic.

An earring is a piece of jewelry worn on the ear, typically attached through a pierced hole in the earlobe or clipped to the edge. Earrings come in countless styles—studs, hoops, dangles, cuffs. They may be worn singly or in pairs, and multiple piercings allow for several at once: {She wore three earrings in each ear}.

Earrings are jewelry worn on the ears, typically attached through pierced holes in the earlobes or clipped onto them. They range from simple studs to elaborate dangles: {She wore diamond earrings to the gala}. Earrings appear across cultures and genders, though Western conventions have historically associated them more with women.

Ears are the organs of hearing, located on either side of the head. The visible outer part catches sound waves; the inner structures convert them to signals the brain interprets. Ears also govern balance. Figuratively, an ear is attention or receptiveness: {lend an ear}, {have someone's ear}. A good ear for music or language means natural aptitude for hearing distinctions. To {play it by ear} is to improvise rather than follow a plan.

Earshot is the distance within which sounds can be heard. If you are within earshot of something, you are close enough to hear it; if you are out of earshot, you are too far away. The word appears almost exclusively in these two phrases: {Let's wait until we're out of earshot before we talk about the surprise party.}

Earsplitting describes sounds so loud they seem capable of damaging the ears: {an earsplitting shriek}, {earsplitting feedback from the speakers}. The word is hyperbolic—the sound rarely poses actual danger, but it's painfully loud nonetheless.

Earth is the name for the planet we inhabit; this is nearly always the meaning if the word is capitalized. Earth can also mean land (in contrast to air or sea) or soil: I planted seeds in the loamy earth. Some fixed expressions using earth are not to be taken literally, like cost the earth (cost a lot) or I felt the earth move (I was deeply impressed). In British English, earth (noun and verb) has the same meaning as ground in American English as it applies to electrical connections.
clues: What gardeners dig their hands into

definition: Earthbound means headed toward or bound for Earth, as a spacecraft returning from orbit: {The earthbound capsule entered the atmosphere}. It also means tied to earthly concerns, unable to rise above mundane matters or limitations: {earthbound thinking}, {earthbound creatures who cannot fly}. The word can suggest being stuck or grounded when flight or transcendence is desired. (Capitalized EarthBound is a video game.)

Earthenware is pottery made from porous clay fired at relatively low temperatures. It's the oldest and most basic form of ceramic, softer and more fragile than stoneware or porcelain. Earthenware must be glazed to hold liquids: {terracotta pots}, {rustic earthenware bowls}. The word also works as an adjective: {an earthenware jug}.

Earthiness is the quality of being earthy—connected to soil, the body, or unrefined reality. It can describe a flavor reminiscent of dirt or mushrooms: {The wine had an earthiness from the terroir}. More often it suggests unpretentious frankness, especially about physical or sexual matters: {Her earthiness made guests comfortable talking about anything}.
clues: Quality of being raw and real

definition: Earthling means an inhabitant of Earth—a human being. The word appears almost exclusively in science fiction contexts, where it distinguishes humans from extraterrestrials: {The aliens demanded to speak with the earthlings' leader}. Outside fiction, earthling sounds deliberately playful or ironic, adopting an outsider's perspective on humanity.

Earthlings are inhabitants of Earth—human beings, as distinguished from extraterrestrials or celestial beings. The word appears almost exclusively in science fiction contexts, where aliens or space travelers use it to address humans: {Take me to your leader, earthlings}. Outside fiction, it's used humorously to suggest an outsider's perspective on humanity.

Earthly means belonging to or characteristic of the earth and physical existence, as opposed to heaven or the spiritual realm: {earthly pleasures}, {no earthly reason}. The phrase {no earthly} intensifies negation—{no earthly use}, {no earthly chance}—suggesting something so unlikely it couldn't exist anywhere in the physical world.

An earthquake is a sudden, violent shaking of the ground caused by movement of rock beneath the earth's surface. Earthquakes range from imperceptible tremors to catastrophic events that destroy cities. The scale of destruction depends on magnitude, depth, and proximity to populated areas. {The earthquake leveled most of the downtown.} Figuratively, an earthquake is any event that fundamentally disrupts the status quo: {a political earthquake}.

Earthquakes is the plural of earthquake—a sudden shaking of the ground caused by shifting tectonic plates or volcanic activity. The term extends to any major upheaval: {political earthquakes}, {earthquakes in the financial markets}. {California experiences frequent earthquakes along the San Andreas Fault.}

Earthshaker typically refers to a being or force powerful enough to make the ground tremble. In Greek mythology, Poseidon bore this epithet—god of the sea and earthquakes. The word extends to anything with tremendous impact: {an earthshaker of a speech}, {The announcement was an earthshaker in the industry}. In gaming, earthshaker often names characters or abilities that cause seismic damage.

Earthshakers are people or things powerful enough to cause major upheaval—literally or figuratively. The word evokes seismic force: {The tech giants are the earthshakers of modern commerce}. In mythology, earthshaker was an epithet for Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes. The term applies to anyone whose actions fundamentally alter their domain.

Earthshaking describes something of enormous significance or impact—momentous enough to shake the foundations of how things are. The word is often used ironically or in the negative: {The discovery wasn't exactly earthshaking}, {Nothing earthshaking happened at the meeting}. Genuinely earthshaking events—revolutions, scientific breakthroughs—reshape the world.

Earthshattering describes events or revelations of enormous significance—momentous enough to shake the foundations of what came before. The word is often used hyperbolically: {It's not exactly earthshattering news that teenagers like to sleep late}. Genuinely earthshattering developments change how we understand something fundamental. Also spelled earth-shattering.

Earthshine is the faint glow visible on the dark portion of the moon, caused by sunlight reflecting off Earth's surface onto the lunar face. It's most noticeable when the moon is a thin crescent: {You could see the whole disk outlined by earthshine}. Also called earthlight.

Earthwork refers to large-scale excavation and movement of soil, especially in construction and engineering: {The earthwork for the new highway took months}. In military contexts, earthworks are defensive fortifications made from mounded earth—trenches, ramparts, and embankments: {Civil War earthworks still scar the Virginia landscape}. Archaeological earthworks include ancient mounds and ditches shaped by human activity.

Earthworks are large-scale constructions made by moving and shaping soil—defensive fortifications like ramparts and trenches, or ancient ceremonial mounds. Military earthworks provided protection before concrete bunkers: {The soldiers dug earthworks through the night}. The term also covers modern earth-moving projects: excavation, grading, and landscaping that reshape terrain for construction.

An earthworm is a long, segmented worm that burrows through soil, aerating it and breaking down organic matter. Earthworms are familiar to gardeners and children alike—pinkish-brown, soft-bodied, emerging after rain. They lack eyes and limbs but can regenerate lost segments. {We dug up earthworms for fishing bait.}

Earthworms are segmented worms that live in soil, aerating it as they burrow and enriching it with their castings. They're the familiar wriggling creatures that surface after rain and get threaded onto fishhooks as bait. Gardeners prize them as indicators of healthy soil: {The compost bin was full of earthworms}.

Earthy describes qualities associated with soil or the ground—an earthy {smell} after rain, an earthy {color} palette of browns and ochres. Extended to people and art, earthy means unrefined, direct, and unpretentious: {Her earthy humor made everyone feel at ease}. Earthy jokes or language tend toward the crude or sexual without being genuinely vulgar—more robust than delicate, more peasant than aristocrat.

Earwax is the yellowish waxy substance secreted in the ear canal. It traps dust and debris, protecting the eardrum. The formal term is cerumen, but earwax dominates ordinary speech: {The doctor removed a buildup of earwax}.

An earwig is a slender insect with pincers at its tail end. The name comes from an old superstition that they crawl into people's ears—they don't, though they do favor dark, tight spaces. To earwig is to eavesdrop or whisper insinuatingly: {He earwigged their conversation from the next booth}.

Earwigs are slender insects with pincers at the rear of their abdomen, commonly found in gardens and damp places. Despite folklore that they crawl into human ears, they pose no such threat. The pincers look menacing but are mostly harmless to humans. As a verb, to earwig is British slang for eavesdropping: {She was earwigging on their conversation}.

An earworm is a catchy piece of music that gets stuck in your head, repeating involuntarily: {I've had that jingle stuck as an earworm all day}. The term captures how these melodic fragments seem to burrow into consciousness and resist dislodging. Earworm also refers to various moth larvae that damage corn and other crops by boring into the ears.

An earworm is a catchy piece of music that is easy to remember and that people like to sing or hum. When people use the word earworm they are usually talking about a song that they themselves have stuck in their head that they can’t get rid of.

The various noun and verb uses of ease do not travel far from the related adjective easy. When you ease an unpleasant condition (congestion, tension, pressure, strain), you diminish its force and make it more bearable. When something eases, such as wind or rain, it diminishes in strength. As a noun, ease is a condition or state in which little or no effort is required and there is freedom from discomfort: Retirement led to a life of ease.

Eased is the past tense of ease, meaning to make or become less difficult, painful, or intense. Pain eases when it subsides; restrictions ease when they're relaxed. To ease into something is to proceed gradually: {She eased into the cold water}. To ease out of a role is to withdraw gently. Something eased into position was moved there carefully.

An easel is a freestanding frame, typically with three legs, used to hold a canvas or board upright while an artist paints. Easels range from small tabletop versions to large studio models, and some fold flat for portability. The word extends to any similar stand used to display artwork, posters, or presentation boards. {She set up her easel in the park to paint the landscape.}

Easels are upright frames for supporting an artist's canvas, a display board, or a flip chart. The typical easel is a tripod of wooden or metal legs that holds a surface at a convenient angle for painting or viewing. {She set up her easel in the garden to paint the roses.}

Easing is the gradual lessening of something—pain, tension, restrictions, or pressure. Economic policy might involve the easing of interest rates. Physical therapy brings easing of stiffness. In animation and user interface design, easing refers to the acceleration curve of motion—how an element speeds up or slows down rather than moving at constant speed: {The button uses ease-in-out easing for a smoother feel}.

East is the direction where the sun rises, one of the four cardinal points of the compass, opposite to west. As a noun or adjective, it describes this direction or regions lying in that direction: {The sun comes up in the east}; {the east side of town}. When capitalized, East often refers to specific regions—the Eastern Hemisphere, East Asia, or the eastern United States—and carries cultural weight in phrases like {East meets West}. The adverb form describes movement toward that direction: {We drove east for hours}.

Eastbound means traveling or heading toward the east: {the eastbound lane}, {an eastbound train}. The word functions as both adjective and adverb: {Traffic was eastbound on the highway}. Like its directional siblings westbound, northbound, and southbound, it appears most often in transportation contexts—highways, railways, flights.

Eastern describes location or direction toward the east—where the sun rises. An eastern {exposure} faces that direction; the eastern {states} lie on the Atlantic coast. Capitalized, Eastern often refers to Asia or Asian culture ({Eastern philosophy}, {Eastern medicine}) or to the Orthodox churches of Christianity. During the Cold War, {Eastern bloc} meant Soviet-aligned nations.

Easy describes something requiring little effort, presenting few difficulties, or causing no discomfort. An easy {test} doesn't challenge much. An easy {chair} is comfortable. Easy can suggest relaxed or unhurried: {Take it easy}. Someone {easy to talk to} is approachable. In older slang, an easy woman was sexually available—a usage now recognized as sexist. {Easy come, easy go} dismisses losses that arrived without effort.

Easygoing describes someone relaxed and tolerant, not easily upset or bothered by difficulties. An easygoing person doesn't sweat the small stuff: {He's pretty easygoing about deadlines}. The word can also describe atmospheres or situations that feel casual and unstressed: {an easygoing workplace}, {an easygoing pace of life}.

Eat is to take food into the body through the mouth, chew, and swallow. The word extends to gradual consumption or destruction: rust eats metal, guilt eats at you. To eat something is also to absorb or accept it: {I'll eat the cost}. If something is {eating you}, it's bothering you persistently. {Eat your words} means to retract a statement, usually with embarrassment. In vulgar slang, to eat someone out is to perform oral sex.

Eaten is the past participle of eat, used with helping verbs to form perfect tenses: {I have eaten}, {The leftovers had been eaten}. It also works as an adjective: {half-eaten sandwich}, {moth-eaten sweater}. To be {eaten up} by something is to be consumed by it: {She was eaten up with guilt}.

An eater is someone or something that eats. The word usually appears with a modifier indicating what or how: {a picky eater}, {a meat eater}, {a big eater}. Compound forms name creatures by their diet: anteater, beefeater. A {world eater} in fantasy suggests something that consumes on a cosmic scale.

Eating is the act of consuming food—taking it into the mouth, chewing, and swallowing. The word covers everything from basic sustenance to pleasure: {We were eating dinner when she called}. Eating often implies the manner or context: {clean eating}, {emotional eating}, {eating out}. To {eat someone alive} is to overwhelm or destroy them. Something that's {eating at you} is troubling you persistently.

Eats is an informal noun for food or a meal: {Let's grab some eats before the movie}. It appears frequently in casual speech and in names of restaurants or food establishments. The word carries a relaxed, unpretentious tone that suggests simple, satisfying fare rather than fine dining.

The eave is the part of a roof that overhangs the wall, providing some protection from rain and directing water away from the foundation. Almost always plural: {Water dripped from the eaves}. {Birds nested under the eaves}. Eaves connect to eavesdrop—originally standing under the eaves to listen at windows.

Eaves are the edges of a roof that overhang the walls of a building, projecting outward to direct rainwater away from the structure. The word is almost always plural, even when referring to a single roof edge. To eavesdrop originally meant to stand within the eavesdrop—the strip of ground where water drips from the eaves—close enough to a building to secretly listen to conversations inside.

To eavesdrop is to listen secretly to a private conversation. The word comes from the practice of standing under the eaves of a building—where rainwater drips—to overhear what's said inside. {I couldn't help eavesdropping on their argument}. The noun eavesdropper describes someone who habitually listens in.
clues: Hear what isn't meant for you

definition: An eavesdropper is someone who secretly listens to private conversations. The word comes from the practice of standing under the eaves of a building—where rainwater drips—to overhear what's happening inside. {The eavesdropper pressed her ear to the wall}. The verb is eavesdrop; the activity is eavesdropping.

Eavesdroppers are people who secretly listen to private conversations. The term comes from standing under the eaves of a building—where rainwater drips—to overhear what's said inside. An eavesdropper might press an ear to a wall, linger near a doorway, or tap a phone line: {The eavesdroppers recorded hours of incriminating conversations}.

Eavesdropping is secretly listening to private conversations. The word comes from the practice of standing under the eaves of a house to hear what's said inside. Now it applies to any covert listening—through walls, on phone calls, or via electronic surveillance: {The NSA's eavesdropping programs sparked controversy}. To eavesdrop is to engage in such listening: {I couldn't help eavesdropping on their argument}.

Eavesdrops means secretly listens to a private conversation. The word comes from the practice of standing under the eaves of a building—where rainwater drips—to overhear talk inside. Someone who eavesdrops on neighbors, colleagues, or phone calls is listening without the speakers' knowledge or consent: {She eavesdrops on her roommate's calls}. The connotation is sneaky and intrusive.

Ebb is the receding of the tide as water flows back out to sea, opposite of flow. The tide ebbs twice daily. By extension, anything that diminishes or declines ebbs: {Her enthusiasm began to ebb}. The phrase {ebb and flow} describes natural cycles of increase and decrease. At a low ebb means at a weakened or depleted state: {Morale was at a low ebb}.

Ebbed is the past tense of ebb, meaning to recede or flow back, originally describing the tide withdrawing from shore. By extension, anything that diminishes or fades away ebbs: {Her enthusiasm ebbed as the project dragged on}, {His strength ebbed in his final days}. The opposite of ebbed is flowed or surged.

Ebbing describes something gradually receding or declining. The term comes from the ebb tide—water retreating from shore between high tides. By extension, anything can be ebbing: {His strength was ebbing}, {ebbing enthusiasm}, {the ebbing light of dusk}. The word suggests slow, steady diminishment rather than sudden loss.

Ebbs is the verb form of ebb, meaning to recede or flow back. The tide ebbs when it retreats from shore. By extension, anything that diminishes or fades ebbs: {Her enthusiasm ebbs as the project drags on}, {His strength ebbs with each passing day}. The noun ebb describes this receding state—{at low ebb} means at the weakest point.

An ebike is a bicycle with an electric motor that assists pedaling. The motor typically engages when the rider pedals, providing extra power for hills or distance. Some models include a throttle for motor-only propulsion. Also spelled e-bike. {I commute on my ebike now—no more showing up to work sweaty.}

Ebikes are bicycles equipped with an electric motor that assists pedaling, making hills easier and extending range. The motor typically engages when you pedal, providing a boost rather than full propulsion. Most have rechargeable batteries and multiple power levels. Also spelled e-bikes or electric bikes. {She commutes on an ebike to avoid arriving sweaty.}

Ebony is a dense, dark hardwood prized for its deep black color and fine grain. It's used for piano keys, chess pieces, and decorative objects. The word extends to anything sharing that distinctive black color: {ebony hair}, {ebony skin}. As an adjective, ebony describes this rich, lustrous black: {an ebony finish on the cabinet}. (Capitalized Ebony is a name or the magazine.)

An ebook is a book in digital format, readable on computers, tablets, dedicated e-readers, or phones. The term covers everything from novels to textbooks to self-published works distributed electronically. Ebooks can be purchased, borrowed from libraries, or downloaded free: {I bought the ebook version since it was cheaper}. Also spelled e-book.

Ebooks are books in digital format, readable on computers, tablets, e-readers, or phones. The term covers any electronic text file designed for reading—from novels to textbooks to self-published works. Ebooks can be downloaded, shared, and stored without physical space: {I switched to ebooks when I ran out of shelf room}. The format allows adjustable text size, searchability, and instant access. Also spelled e-books or eBooks.

Eccentric describes something or someone deviating from the norm, especially in behavior or personality. An eccentric person has unusual habits or unconventional ways: {My eccentric aunt collects vintage typewriters and talks to her plants}. The word carries affection more than criticism—eccentricity suggests harmless oddity rather than troubling deviance. In technical contexts, eccentric means off-center: an eccentric wheel doesn't rotate around its middle. As a noun, an eccentric is a person known for peculiar behavior: {The neighborhood eccentric fed pigeons at exactly 3 PM daily}.
clues: Someone who zigs when others zag

definition: Eccentricities are unusual habits, behaviors, or qualities that deviate from what's considered normal or conventional. The word carries affection or tolerance rather than harsh judgment—an eccentric person is odd but harmlessly so, perhaps even charmingly: {His eccentricities included wearing mismatched socks and talking to plants}. {The old professor was known for her eccentricities}.

Eccentricity is deviation from conventional or expected behavior—the quality of being odd or unconventional: {His eccentricity charmed some colleagues and alienated others}. The word carries a gentler connotation than similar terms; an eccentric person is quirky rather than disturbed. In geometry and astronomy, eccentricity measures how much an ellipse deviates from a perfect circle: {The comet's high eccentricity gives it an elongated orbit}.

Eccentrics are people who behave in unconventional or peculiar ways—those who deviate from social norms in dress, habits, or thought. The term carries affection or admiration more often than criticism: {The neighborhood had its share of harmless eccentrics}. In mechanical contexts, an eccentric is a disk or wheel mounted off-center, used to convert rotary motion to reciprocating motion.

An echelon is a level or rank within an organization or hierarchy: {the upper echelons of management}, {the highest echelons of government}. The word implies distinct tiers of authority or prestige. In military usage, an echelon is a formation of troops, ships, or aircraft arranged in parallel lines, each offset from the one ahead—like a staircase viewed from above.

Echelons are levels or ranks within a hierarchy, especially in military or organizational contexts. The word often appears with modifiers indicating position: {the upper echelons of management}, {the lower echelons of the army}. In military usage, an echelon is also a formation where units are arranged in a staggered diagonal pattern, like steps.

An echidna is a spiny egg-laying mammal native to Australia and New Guinea, sometimes called a spiny anteater. Echidnas have long snouts and tongues for feeding on ants and termites, and their bodies are covered with coarse hair and sharp spines. Along with platypuses, they are the only surviving monotremes—mammals that lay eggs. {We spotted an echidna waddling through the underbrush.} (Capitalized Echidna is the monster of Greek mythology.)

Echidnas is the plural of echidna, a spiny egg-laying mammal native to Australia and New Guinea. Also called spiny anteaters, echidnas have long snouts and feed on ants and termites. Along with platypuses, they are the only surviving monotremes—mammals that lay eggs rather than bearing live young.

Echinacea is a genus of flowering plants native to North America, commonly called coneflowers for their distinctive raised central cones. The plants are widely used in herbal supplements believed to boost immune function and shorten colds, though scientific evidence for effectiveness remains mixed: {I take echinacea at the first sign of a sore throat}.

A literal echo is the reflection of sound off a surface after some delay; when sound does this, it is said to echo. The most frequent use of echo is figurative, to characterize things that repeat. If you echo a sentiment or opinion, you express the same one as someone else. Some sounds that are said to echo, such as footsteps, merely repeat. If you hear or find an echo of some idea, you come across another instance of it.

Echoed is the past tense of echo. A sound echoes when it bounces off a surface and returns: {Her voice echoed through the empty hall}. By extension, words or ideas echo when they're repeated or reflected: {His concerns echoed those of many voters}. A place echoes with sound when it reverberates: {The stadium echoed with cheers}.

Echoes is the plural of echo—sound waves that bounce back from a surface and return to the listener. The word extends to any repetition or reverberation: {echoes of the past}, {Her words found echoes in his own experience}. As a verb, echoes means repeats or reflects: {The canyon echoes with birdsong}, {His speech echoed the president's remarks}.

Echoing describes sounds that repeat or reverberate, bouncing back from surfaces: {Her footsteps went echoing through the empty hall}. It extends to things that repeat or imitate something else: {His words, echoing his father's advice, stayed with me}. An echoing space is one where sounds reverberate: {the echoing chamber of the cathedral}.

Echolocation is a biological sonar system used by certain animals—bats, dolphins, some whales—to navigate and locate prey in darkness or murky water. The animal emits sounds and interprets the returning echoes to map its surroundings. {Bats use echolocation to catch insects in flight.} The term also applies to similar technology in submarines and robotics.

An eclair is an oblong pastry made from choux dough, filled with cream or custard, and topped with chocolate icing. The shape distinguishes it from round cream puffs, which use the same light, airy dough. {She ordered a chocolate eclair with the coffee.}

Eclairs are oblong pastries made from choux dough, filled with cream or custard, and topped with chocolate icing. The shape distinguishes them from round cream puffs, which use the same dough. {She picked up an eclair from the bakery case.}

Eclectic is an adjective used to characterize something that contains elements drawn from many different sources. It is similar in meaning to diverse and heterogeneous. Groups of objects can be characterized as eclectic, such as an eclectic collection of modern art or an eclectic group of actors. If someone has eclectic tastes, they like a number of different but related things equally, such as different kinds of music or food.

The relatively rare celestial event called an eclipse, in which one astronomical object is obscured by another, inspires more frequent use of the word. If one thing eclipses another, the first thing diminishes the importance or prominence of the second. If a celestial body is in eclipse, it is obscured by another; but if your hopes are in eclipse, they don’t have much chance of success. Eclipse plumage is exhibited by birds after the mating season, when they shed their bright features.

Eclipsed means overshadowed or surpassed, from the astronomical event where one celestial body blocks light from another. A star's performance can be eclipsed by a newcomer's brilliance. A company's achievements may be eclipsed by scandal. {Her early work was eclipsed by her later masterpieces.} The literal sense describes a sun or moon during an eclipse: {The moon eclipsed the sun.}

Eclipses is the plural of eclipse—an astronomical event where one celestial body passes into the shadow of another, as when the moon blocks the sun or enters Earth's shadow. The word extends to any overshadowing: {Her later work eclipses her early novels}. To eclipse someone is to surpass them so completely they seem diminished by comparison.

Eclipsing describes something that passes in front of another, blocking it from view—or more commonly, something that overshadows or surpasses another in importance or achievement. {Her later novels ended up eclipsing her early work.} An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars that periodically block each other's light as seen from Earth.

Eco is a prefix meaning ecological or environmentally friendly: {eco-tourism}, {eco-friendly}, {eco-warrior}. Standing alone, eco works as an adjective or noun for environmental consciousness: {The company is trying to go eco}. {All that eco stuff is just greenwashing}.

Ecoanxiety is distress or dread about environmental degradation and climate change. Unlike general worry, it describes a chronic unease about ecological collapse, species extinction, or an uninhabitable future: {Her ecoanxiety spiked every time she read about wildfires}. The term gained currency in the 2010s as climate concerns intensified. Also spelled eco-anxiety.

Ecocide is the deliberate destruction of the natural environment, especially on a massive scale. The term frames environmental devastation as a crime comparable to genocide—the killing of ecosystems rather than peoples. Advocates push for ecocide to be recognized under international law: {The oil spill was an act of ecocide}. The word appears in discussions of deforestation, industrial pollution, and climate policy.

Ecofriendly describes products, practices, or behaviors that minimize harm to the environment: {ecofriendly packaging}, {ecofriendly cleaning supplies}. The term often appears in marketing, where its meaning can range from genuinely sustainable to vaguely green-sounding. Also spelled eco-friendly.

Ecological relates to ecology—the study of how organisms interact with each other and their environment. An ecological {crisis} threatens natural systems. An ecological {footprint} measures human impact on the planet. The word often signals environmental concern: {ecological sustainability}, {ecological damage}. Something ecologically sound works in harmony with natural systems rather than against them.

An ecologist is a scientist who studies the relationships between organisms and their environments. The field examines how living things interact with each other and their surroundings—from individual species to entire ecosystems. {Marine ecologists warned that rising temperatures were bleaching the coral reefs.}

Ecology is the study of how living things relate to each other and their environment—the web of interactions between organisms and the systems they inhabit. The term extends to any complex of such relationships: {the ecology of a coral reef}, {the ecology of the human gut}. Figuratively, ecology describes interconnected systems more broadly: {the ecology of social media}, {the media ecology}. The related adjective ecological appears in phrases like {ecological balance} and {ecological disaster}.

Ecommerce, also written e-commerce, is the buying and selling of goods and services over the internet. The term covers everything from massive online marketplaces to small businesses selling handmade items through their websites. {Most of our ecommerce sales come from mobile users.} The rise of ecommerce has transformed retail, enabling consumers to shop from anywhere while forcing traditional brick-and-mortar stores to adapt or close.

An econobox is a small, inexpensive, fuel-efficient car—typically a compact or subcompact with modest power and few frills. The term carries mild derision, suggesting the vehicle prioritizes economy over style, performance, or comfort: {I drove an econobox through college}. The word blends "economy" with "box," evoking the boxy shape common to such cars.

Economic relates to the economy—the system of producing, distributing, and consuming goods and services. Economic {policy}, economic {growth}, economic {crisis}. The word also means financially practical or efficient: {It wasn't economic to repair the old car}. This second sense overlaps with economical, though economical more often describes thrifty behavior while economic connects to larger systems.

Economical means avoiding waste, whether of money, resources, or effort. An economical {car} uses fuel efficiently. An economical {writing style} conveys meaning without unnecessary words. The term often implies getting good value: {It's more economical to buy in bulk}. Economical differs subtly from economic, which relates to economics or the economy rather than thriftiness.

Economics is the study of how societies allocate scarce resources—how goods and services are produced, distributed, and consumed. The field divides into microeconomics (individual choices, markets, firms) and macroeconomics (national output, unemployment, inflation). As a modifier, economic describes things relating to the economy: {economic growth}, {economic policy}. The plural form economics takes a singular verb when referring to the discipline: {Economics is called the dismal science}.

Economies is the plural of economy. A country's economy is its system of producing and distributing goods and services: {emerging economies}, {the world's largest economies}. Economies also means instances of saving money or resources: {We found economies in the production process}. {Economies of scale} are cost reductions achieved by producing in larger quantities.

An economist is a person who studies or specializes in economics—the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services. Economists analyze data, develop theories, and advise governments and businesses on policy: {The economist predicted a recession}. The term can carry skepticism about the gap between economic models and real-world outcomes: {Economists disagreed, as usual}.

Economists study how societies allocate scarce resources—production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services. They analyze markets, develop theories about economic behavior, and advise governments and businesses. The profession spans academic researchers, policy advisors, and financial analysts. Economists are sometimes mocked for disagreeing with each other or for predictions that don't pan out: {Ask three economists, get four opinions}.

Economy centers on the management of resources—money, goods, labor, time. A country's economy is its system of production, distribution, and consumption: {The economy grew by three percent}. To practice economy is to avoid waste: {She ran the household with strict economy}. An economy {car} or economy {class} offers basic service at lower cost. The adjective economical means thrifty or efficient: {an economical use of space}. In writing, economy of language means expressing ideas with minimal words.

An ecosystem is a community of living organisms together with their physical environment, functioning as an interconnected system: {the marine ecosystem}, {a forest ecosystem}. The term extends to any complex network of interdependent elements: {the startup ecosystem}, {the Apple ecosystem of devices and services}. Disrupting one part affects the whole.

Ecosystems are communities of living organisms interacting with their physical environment—the plants, animals, microbes, soil, water, and climate of a particular place functioning as a unit. A pond is an ecosystem; so is a rainforest. The term extends to any complex system of interdependent elements: {the startup ecosystem}, {the media ecosystem}. Damage to one part affects the whole.

Ecoterrorism is the use of violence, sabotage, or intimidation in the name of environmental causes. Acts range from spiking trees to injure loggers, to burning construction sites, to attacks on research facilities: {The FBI classified the arson as ecoterrorism}. The term is contested—activists may call it direct action while opponents and law enforcement call it terrorism.

An ecoterrorist is someone who commits violent or destructive acts in the name of environmental protection—sabotaging logging equipment, burning construction sites, or targeting industries perceived as harming nature. The term is often applied by critics; those labeled ecoterrorists may see themselves as activists or defenders of the earth. {The FBI classified the arson as ecoterrorism.}

Ecoterrorists are people who commit acts of violence, sabotage, or intimidation in the name of environmental causes. The term is applied to those who destroy property, spike trees to injure loggers, or bomb facilities they view as harming the environment. {The FBI classified the arson at the ski resort as the work of ecoterrorists.} The label is controversial—supporters of such activists may call them radical environmentalists instead, while opponents use ecoterrorist to delegitimize the broader environmental movement.

Ecotourism is travel to natural areas that aims to conserve the environment and benefit local communities. The term combines ecological awareness with tourism, emphasizing minimal impact and education: {The Costa Rican rainforest draws ecotourism from around the world}. In practice, ecotourism ranges from genuinely sustainable travel to conventional tourism with a green veneer.
clues: Visiting wild places while protecting them

definition: An ecovillage is an intentional community designed around principles of environmental sustainability and low-impact living. Residents typically share resources, grow food collectively, use renewable energy, and build with eco-friendly materials. The term gained currency in the 1990s as both a practical model and an idealistic alternative to conventional suburban development. {They left the city to join an ecovillage in rural Oregon.}

Ecstasy is intense joy or rapture—a state of being overwhelmed by emotion, often to the point of losing ordinary self-awareness. Religious mystics describe ecstatic visions; lovers speak of ecstasy in intimate moments. The word implies being transported beyond normal experience: {She listened in ecstasy as the orchestra reached its climax}. Ecstasy (or E) is also slang for MDMA, a drug that induces euphoria and emotional openness.
clues: That soaring feeling beyond mere contentment

definition: Ecstatic describes overwhelming joy or delight—emotion so intense it seems to transport you beyond ordinary experience. {She was ecstatic when she got the job offer.} The word implies more than happiness; it suggests being carried away by feeling. Ecstasy is the noun form.

Ectoplasm is a supernatural substance supposedly exuded by mediums during séances—a luminous, gelatinous material through which spirits manifest. The concept flourished in 19th-century spiritualism, though "ectoplasm" proved consistently to be cheesecloth or other fakery when examined. In biology, ectoplasm is the outer layer of a cell's cytoplasm. The ghostly slime in *Ghostbusters* popularized the word beyond its spiritualist origins.

Eczema is a skin condition causing patches of inflamed, itchy, red, and sometimes cracked or blistered skin. The term covers several related conditions, with atopic dermatitis being the most common form. Flare-ups may be triggered by irritants, allergens, stress, or dry weather: {Her eczema gets worse in winter}.

Edam is a mild, slightly salty Dutch cheese with a pale yellow interior and distinctive red or yellow wax coating. It's named after the town where it originated. The cheese has a semi-hard texture and subtle nutty flavor that intensifies with age: {The cheese board included edam, brie, and cheddar}. (Capitalized Edam is the Dutch town.)

Edamame are immature soybeans, typically served in the pod and eaten as a snack or appetizer. The pods are boiled or steamed, often salted, and the beans squeezed out with the teeth. Common in Japanese cuisine and now widespread at sushi restaurants and in frozen food aisles: {We ordered edamame while we waited for our rolls}.

Eddies are circular currents moving against the main flow—water swirling behind a rock in a stream, or air curling in the wake of a building. The singular eddy also works as a verb: {Leaves eddied in the wind}. Figuratively, anything that moves in similar patterns eddies: {Rumors eddied through the office}.

An eddy is a circular movement of water or air that runs counter to the main current, forming a small whirlpool or vortex: {Leaves spun in the eddy near the riverbank}. The verb means to move in such a pattern: {Smoke eddied around the chimney}. By extension, anything that swirls or circles back on itself eddies: {Rumors eddied through the office}. (Capitalized Eddy is a given name.)

Edelweiss is a small Alpine plant with woolly white flower heads, native to high mountain regions of Europe. The plant has become a symbol of the Alps and mountain climbing, prized for growing in difficult, rocky terrain. It appears in Austrian and Swiss folk culture, most famously in the song from *The Sound of Music*.

Present in many of the uses of edge are the ideas of a boundary and a linear feature (house on the edge of town, feathers edged in red). The edge of a blade is the sharp part. Figuratively, an edge may be an advantage (height is an edge in basketball) or a state of nervousness or agitation: Traffic puts me on edge. When you edge or edge an object, you move (yourself) or move the object slowly closer in a specified direction: She edged closer to him on the bench.

Edged describes something with an edge or border, often of a particular kind: {a lace-edged tablecloth}, {gilt-edged stationery}. It also means having a cutting edge: an edged {weapon} like a sword or axe. Figuratively, edged suggests sharpness of tone: {Her voice had an edged quality that made him uneasy}.

An edgelord is someone who deliberately adopts shocking, offensive, or transgressive views to appear provocative or gain attention online. The term is always disparaging, suggesting the person's edginess is performative rather than genuine—a pose of dark sophistication that impresses no one: {He's just being an edgelord with all that nihilist talk}.

Edgelording is deliberately saying shocking, offensive, or provocative things online to get a reaction—typically dark humor about taboo subjects, contrarian political views, or casual cruelty presented as honesty. The behavior seeks attention through transgression rather than substance: {He's just edgelording in the comments, ignore him}. An edgelord is someone who does this habitually, often a young man performing toughness or cynicism for an audience.

Edgelords are people who deliberately say shocking, offensive, or provocative things online to get attention or seem darkly sophisticated. The term is dismissive—it mocks those who mistake being transgressive for being interesting: {The comments section was full of edgelords posting racist jokes}. The singular edgelord describes an individual practitioner of this posturing.

Edges are the outermost boundaries or sharp borders of things—where a surface ends or two surfaces meet at an angle. A knife's edge is its cutting line; a cliff's edge is where land drops away. To edge is to move gradually: {She edged toward the door}. Figuratively, edge suggests sharpness or advantage: a competitive edge, an edge in your voice. On edge means tense or irritable. To be on the edge of something is to be close to it: {on the edge of bankruptcy}. Edgy describes something nervously tense or provocatively unconventional.

Edgewise means with the edge forward or facing outward, rather than flat: {Stack the plates edgewise to save space}. The word appears most often in the expression {get a word in edgewise}, meaning to find an opportunity to speak when someone else dominates the conversation: {She talked so fast I couldn't get a word in edgewise}.

Edginess is a state of nervous tension or irritability: {There was an edginess to her voice that made me uneasy}. The word also describes a quality of being provocatively unconventional or pushing boundaries—the edginess of avant-garde art, transgressive comedy, or fashion that courts discomfort. Something with edginess feels sharp, unsettled, or deliberately confrontational.

Edging is the process of creating or trimming a border or boundary—the edge of a lawn, a garden bed, a garment. As a noun, edging is material used for such borders: decorative edging, brick edging. In sexual slang, edging is the practice of bringing oneself or a partner close to orgasm repeatedly without completion, prolonging arousal: {He's been edging for an hour}.
clues: Slowly moving forward, bit by bit

definition: Edgy describes someone or something tense, nervous, or irritable—on edge: {She's been edgy since the layoffs were announced}. The word also means daringly unconventional or provocatively avant-garde: {an edgy film}, {edgy humor}. Online, edgy often carries ironic dismissal of content that tries too hard to shock or seem cool: {Wow, so edgy}.

Edible means safe or suitable to eat. The word distinguishes what can be consumed from what cannot: {The berries looked tempting but weren't edible}. Edible doesn't imply appetizing—something can be technically edible but unpleasant. As a noun, edibles often refers to cannabis-infused foods: {She prefers edibles to smoking}.

Edibles are things fit to be eaten—food, broadly. The word often distinguishes what's safe to consume from what isn't: {foraging for edibles in the forest}, {Are these berries edible?} In contemporary usage, edibles frequently refers specifically to food products containing cannabis: {She brought edibles to the party}, {I prefer edibles to smoking}.

An edict is an official order or decree issued by someone in authority. The word suggests commands handed down from above—historically from monarchs or governments, now from any powerful figure: {The CEO's edict banned personal phones in meetings}. Edicts are pronouncements, not requests; they expect compliance.

Edicts are official orders or decrees issued by an authority. The word suggests formal pronouncements that must be obeyed: {The king's edicts were read aloud in every village square}. In looser usage, edict describes any authoritative command: {My mother's edict was clear—no phones at the dinner table}.

An edifice is a large, imposing building—typically one of architectural significance like a cathedral, government building, or palace: {the grand edifice of the opera house}. The word carries connotations of permanence and grandeur. Figuratively, an edifice is any elaborate structure or system: {the edifice of modern democracy}, {His argument was an intellectual edifice built on shaky foundations}.

To edit is to prepare written or recorded material for publication or presentation—correcting, revising, selecting, or arranging content. An editor edits manuscripts, films, or broadcasts. The word extends to any modification: {I edited my comment before posting}, {She edited him out of the photo}. An edit is an instance of such revision. In computing, edit mode allows changes to a document or file.

Edited describes something that has been revised, corrected, or prepared for publication or presentation. An edited {manuscript} has undergone changes for clarity, accuracy, or style. An edited {video} has been cut, rearranged, or otherwise modified from raw footage. The word can suggest improvement or, sometimes, selective omission: {an edited version of events} implies details were left out.

Editing is the process of revising and refining written, visual, or audio material. An editor cuts, rearranges, corrects, and polishes: {She spent the weekend editing her manuscript}. In film and video, editing means assembling footage into a coherent sequence. The word covers everything from fixing typos to reshaping a work's entire structure.

An edition is a particular version of something published or produced. A book's first edition is its original printing; later editions may be revised or expanded. Newspapers have morning and evening editions. A limited edition restricts the number of copies: {a limited edition print}. Special editions of products feature added content or packaging: {the collector's edition of the game}.

An editor is someone who prepares written material for publication—selecting, revising, correcting, and arranging content. A newspaper editor decides what stories run; a book editor shapes manuscripts. In film and video, an editor assembles footage into a coherent whole. Editor also names software for creating or modifying files: {a text editor}, {a photo editor}. To edit is to perform this work.

Editorial describes material expressing opinion rather than reporting facts. An editorial is a newspaper or magazine article stating the publication's official position: {The Times ran an editorial opposing the bill}. As an adjective, editorial distinguishes opinion from news: {editorial content}, {editorial page}. It also relates to the editing process: {editorial decisions}, {editorial staff}.

To editorialize is to express opinions rather than report facts objectively. The word comes from journalism, where editorials are opinion pieces distinct from news coverage. A reporter who editorializes lets personal views color what should be neutral reporting: {The anchor couldn't help editorializing about the verdict}. More broadly, it means injecting commentary where it wasn't asked for: {Just tell me what happened without editorializing}.

Editorializing is injecting opinion into what should be neutral reporting or description. A journalist editorializes by letting personal views color a news story. The term is usually critical—accusing someone of editorializing suggests they've abandoned objectivity: {The anchor was editorializing instead of just reading the news}. More broadly, it means offering unsolicited opinions or commentary.

Editors are people who prepare written material for publication. A book editor shapes a manuscript, suggesting revisions and corrections. A newspaper or magazine editor selects and organizes content, or oversees a section: {the sports editor}. A film or video editor assembles footage into a finished product. In computing, an editor is software for creating or modifying files: {a text editor}, {a photo editor}.

Edits are changes made to improve or correct something—a document, video, photograph, or other work. The word covers everything from fixing typos to restructuring entire sections: {The editor sent back the manuscript with extensive edits}. In computing, edits are modifications to files or data. As a verb form, edits means performs editing: {She edits the local newspaper}.

To educate is to develop someone's knowledge, skills, or character through instruction or experience. Schools educate children in academic subjects; parents educate them in values. The word implies systematic development rather than casual learning: {She was educated at Oxford}. To educate yourself is to pursue knowledge independently. An educated guess draws on relevant knowledge rather than pure speculation.

Educated describes someone who has received formal schooling or training, especially at advanced levels: {an educated woman}, {a Harvard-educated lawyer}. More broadly, it suggests knowledge, refinement, or good judgment—an educated {guess} is informed rather than random. To educate is to teach or develop understanding: {The campaign educated voters about climate change}.
clues: Having completed a course of study

definition: Educating is the process of teaching or providing instruction. Parents and schools share responsibility for educating children. The word extends beyond formal schooling to any effort at informing or raising awareness: {The campaign focused on educating voters about climate change}. To educate oneself is to learn independently: {She spent years educating herself on wine}.

In its most common meaning, education is the action or process of instructing learners in the knowledge, skills, or information that they need. Education encompasses formal learning experiences for people from childhood to adulthood; the various stages are designated with compound terms such as primary education, secondary education, and higher education. When someone talks about their education, they may mean the entire process or the last part of it. But education can be used outside of a formal instructional setting. If you say that an experience was an education, you mean that you learned something important.

Educational describes things designed to teach or inform: an educational {program}, educational {materials}, an educational {experience}. The word emphasizes learning value over entertainment, though {edutainment} tries to combine both. Something educational imparts knowledge or develops skills: {The museum offers educational tours for schoolchildren}.

An educator is someone who teaches, especially as a profession. The term is broader than teacher—it encompasses administrators, curriculum designers, and others involved in formal instruction. Educator carries a note of dignity or officialdom: {Educators gathered to discuss policy changes}. It appears frequently in institutional contexts where teacher might sound too informal.

Edutainment blends education with entertainment—media designed to teach while being enjoyable. The term covers educational video games, children's television programs, museum exhibits, and apps that make learning feel like play: {The science center's edutainment approach keeps kids engaged}. Often used skeptically by those who doubt whether entertainment-first content actually teaches anything.

Eejit is the Irish and Scottish spelling of idiot, reflecting regional pronunciation. It functions as a mild, often affectionate insult—closer to fool or dummy than a serious accusation of stupidity: {Don't be such an eejit}. The word carries warmth that its standard English equivalent lacks, making it suitable for teasing friends or chiding oneself: {I locked my keys in the car like a complete eejit}.
Eek!, often used ironically, is mainly an expression of sudden fear or alarm.

An eel is a long, slender fish with a snakelike body, typically lacking scales and covered in slippery mucus. Eels live in both fresh and salt water, with some species migrating between the two. The slipperiness makes them hard to grasp, giving rise to {slippery as an eel} for someone evasive or hard to pin down.

Eels are long, snakelike fish found in both fresh and salt water. Most species have smooth, scaleless skin and lack pelvic fins. Some, like the moray eel, are marine; others migrate between rivers and oceans to spawn. Eels are notoriously slippery—hence {slippery as an eel} for someone evasive or hard to pin down.

Eerie describes something strange and unsettling, suggesting supernatural or inexplicable forces. An eerie {silence} feels unnatural. An eerie {glow} seems otherworldly. The word captures that specific unease when something feels wrong in ways you can't quite name: {The abandoned hospital had an eerie atmosphere}. Eerie differs from merely scary—it emphasizes the uncanny rather than outright fear.

Eerily describes something done in a way that inspires unease or a sense of the uncanny. An {eerily quiet} street feels wrong in its silence. Something {eerily similar} to another thing suggests a disturbing coincidence. The word often signals that something ordinary has taken on a strange, unsettling quality: {The abandoned house was eerily intact}.

Eeriness is the quality of being eerie—strange, unsettling, and suggestive of the supernatural or inexplicable. It describes the atmosphere of places, sounds, or situations that produce a sense of unease or creeping dread. {The eeriness of the abandoned hospital made everyone reluctant to enter.} Unlike outright horror, eeriness works through subtle wrongness—something feels off without an obvious source of danger.

Like the word it is often confused with (affect), effect can be both a noun and a verb. Unlike affect, effect is usually a noun. An effect is a noticeable change or result from some action or condition: What effect will the disease have on the child’s development? When something takes effect it becomes active or operational: The new law will take effect January 1st. Effect is used infrequently as a verb to mean bring about: Organizers felt that the campaign had effected positive changes.

Effective means producing the intended result. An effective {treatment} works; an effective {leader} gets things done. Something effective has the power to accomplish its purpose: {The new policy proved effective at reducing wait times}. Effective also marks when something takes force: {The changes become effective January 1}. The distinction from efficient is that effective concerns results while efficient concerns resources—a method can be effective but wasteful.

Effectiveness is the degree to which something achieves its intended purpose. An effective treatment cures the disease; its effectiveness is how well and reliably it does so. The word emphasizes results over process—a plan may be elegant or efficient, but its effectiveness is measured by whether it works: {The effectiveness of the new policy remains to be seen}.

Effects are belongings or possessions, especially personal items: {She gathered her effects and left}. The word often appears in legal or formal contexts—someone's {personal effects} are collected after death or hospital stays. Effects also names the technical elements that create illusions in film and theater: {special effects}, {sound effects}, {practical effects}.

Effervescence is the bubbling or fizzing that occurs when gas escapes from a liquid, as when you open a bottle of champagne or drop an antacid tablet in water. The word extends naturally to describe a bubbly, lively quality in people or atmospheres: {Her effervescence made every party more fun}. Someone with effervescence radiates enthusiasm and high spirits. The adjective effervescent applies to both fizzy drinks and sparkling personalities.

Effervescent describes liquids that release bubbles of gas—champagne, soda water, antacid tablets dissolving in water. The fizzing action extends to personality: an effervescent person is lively, enthusiastic, and bubbly in manner. {Her effervescent charm made everyone feel welcome.} The noun is effervescence.

Efficiency is accomplishing something with minimal waste of time, effort, or resources. An efficient {engine} extracts more work from its fuel; an efficient {worker} produces more in less time. The word implies optimization—getting the maximum output from given inputs. {We need to improve efficiency in the warehouse.} In physics, efficiency is the ratio of useful work performed to total energy expended.

Efficient describes achieving results with minimal waste of time, effort, or resources. An efficient {engine} extracts more power from less fuel. An efficient {worker} completes tasks quickly without unnecessary steps. The word implies optimization—getting the most output from the least input. {She found a more efficient route to work.}

Effigies is the plural of effigy—a sculptured or stuffed likeness of a person. Stone effigies of nobles lie atop medieval tombs. The word most often appears in {burn in effigy} or {hang in effigy}, where crowds destroy a crude figure representing someone they despise: {Protesters burned the dictator in effigy}. The ritual expresses contempt without harming the actual person.

An effigy is a sculpture or model of a person, typically made to be destroyed as an act of protest or contempt: {Protesters burned the dictator in effigy}. The phrase {in effigy} distinguishes symbolic destruction from actual harm to a person. Effigies also appear in neutral contexts—carved stone figures on medieval tombs, or stuffed dummies burned on Guy Fawkes Night.

Effing is a direct euphemism for fucking, spelling out the initial letter: {I don't give an effing damn}. {Shut the eff up}. The euphemism is thin—everyone knows what it means—but it allows use in contexts where the actual word would offend. {Effing and blinding} (British) means swearing profusely.

Effort is the energy or exertion applied toward accomplishing something. Physical effort involves bodily strain; mental effort involves concentration and will. An effort is also a particular attempt: {Her effort to quit smoking lasted three weeks}. Something that requires {no effort} comes easily. To {make an effort} is to try, often implying the attempt matters more than the outcome.

Effortless describes something done with apparent ease, without visible struggle or strain: {Her effortless grace on the dance floor}. The word often implies skill so refined that difficulty becomes invisible—what looks effortless usually required considerable effort to master. {He made the complicated maneuver look effortless}.

Effortlessly means without apparent effort or strain—smoothly, naturally, easily. Someone who speaks effortlessly in public makes it look simple. {She effortlessly switched between three languages}. The word often implies skill or talent that conceals the work behind it: what looks effortless usually isn't.

Efforts is the plural of effort—exertions of physical or mental energy toward a goal. The word often appears where a single "effort" might suffice, perhaps because multiple attempts or contributors are implied: {conservation efforts}, {fundraising efforts}, {efforts to reduce costs}. Someone's efforts are their work or contributions: {We appreciate your efforts}.

Egalitarian describes a belief in or commitment to the principle that all people deserve equal rights, opportunities, and treatment. As an adjective, it characterizes systems, societies, or attitudes that reject hierarchies based on class, wealth, or status: {The commune operated on egalitarian principles, with everyone sharing work equally}. As a noun, an egalitarian is someone who holds these views. The word often appears in political and philosophical discussions about how societies should be organized.

Egalitarianism is the belief that all people are fundamentally equal and deserve equal rights, opportunities, and treatment. The term applies to political philosophies advocating social equality, economic systems opposing class hierarchies, and moral frameworks holding that every person's interests matter equally. {Her egalitarianism made her uncomfortable with inherited wealth.}

An egg is the reproductive body produced by female birds, reptiles, fish, and insects—a rounded structure containing an embryo and nutrients enclosed in a shell or membrane. Most commonly, egg refers to a chicken egg used as food: {scrambled eggs}, {egg salad}. To egg someone on is to urge or provoke them. Egg also appears in compounds describing shapes: {egghead} (an intellectual), {egg-shaped}. To have {egg on your face} is to be embarrassed by a mistake.

An eggbeater is a handheld kitchen tool with rotating blades used to beat eggs, whip cream, or mix batters. The classic design has two interlocking beaters turned by a hand crank. Electric versions are now more common. In slang, eggbeater refers to a helicopter, from the resemblance of its rotor blades: {The eggbeater touched down on the hospital roof}.

Egged is the past tense of egg, meaning to urge or incite someone toward action, almost always followed by "on": {They egged him on until he jumped}. The word comes from an Old Norse term meaning to sharpen or goad. Separately, egged describes something pelted with eggs as vandalism or protest: {Someone egged my car last night}.

An egghead is an intellectual or highly educated person, usually with a hint of mockery—suggesting someone so absorbed in books and ideas that they lack common sense or social grace. The bald or egg-shaped head supposedly reflects a brain-heavy life: {Don't listen to those eggheads in Washington}.

Eggheads is a mildly disparaging term for intellectuals or highly educated people, especially those perceived as out of touch with practical matters or common sense. The word suggests someone whose head is all brain—smooth, oval, and fragile like an egg: {The eggheads in Washington don't understand what real Americans need}. It often carries anti-intellectual overtones.

Egging is the act of throwing eggs at something—typically a house, car, or person—as a prank or act of vandalism: {The kids went egging on Halloween night}. The word also serves as the present participle of egg in its verb sense of urging or inciting: {She kept egging him on until he finally agreed}.

Eggnog is a rich, creamy drink made from eggs, milk or cream, sugar, and usually alcohol—traditionally rum, brandy, or bourbon. It's associated with winter holidays, particularly Christmas and New Year's: {We spiked the eggnog with bourbon}. The nonalcoholic version is popular with children. Store-bought eggnog appears seasonally alongside other holiday foods.

Eggplant is a large, egg-shaped vegetable with glossy purple skin and spongy white flesh. It's a staple in Mediterranean and Asian cuisines—baba ghanoush, ratatouille, eggplant parmesan. The flesh absorbs oil readily and turns creamy when cooked. In British English, the vegetable is called aubergine. As slang, the eggplant emoji suggests a penis.

Eggplants are the plural of eggplant—a large, usually purple-skinned vegetable with spongy white flesh, commonly used in Mediterranean and Asian cooking: {grilled eggplants with tahini}, {I picked up two eggplants at the market}. The emoji 🍆 has become widely recognized as a phallic symbol in digital communication.

An eggroll is a fried appetizer in American Chinese cuisine—a wheat wrapper encasing shredded cabbage, pork, and other fillings, rolled into a cylinder and deep-fried until crispy. The wrapper blisters during frying, giving it a bubbly texture. Eggrolls are served with duck sauce or hot mustard: {We ordered eggrolls to start}.

Eggrolls is the plural of eggroll, a fried appetizer in American Chinese cuisine. A cylindrical wrapper—made from wheat flour and egg—encases a filling of cabbage, pork, or other ingredients, then deep-fried until crispy. Distinguished from spring rolls by their thicker, bubblier wrapper. {We ordered eggrolls to start.}

Eggs are the reproductive cells produced by female animals, enclosed in protective shells or membranes. Most commonly, eggs refers to chicken eggs used as food—scrambled, fried, boiled, or in baking. To {egg someone on} is to encourage them, usually toward mischief. To {put all your eggs in one basket} is to risk everything on a single venture. {Walking on eggshells} means being extremely careful not to upset someone. In slang, eggs can mean testicles.

Eggshell is the hard outer covering of an egg, thin and brittle. The word extends to things sharing these qualities: eggshell {paint} has a slight sheen between flat and satin; an eggshell {finish} is delicate and easily damaged. To {walk on eggshells} is to act with extreme caution to avoid upsetting someone. As a color, eggshell is off-white with a faint yellow or cream tint.

Eggshells are the hard outer covering of eggs, thin and brittle once dried. They break easily and leave sharp fragments—hence {walking on eggshells}, meaning to act with extreme caution around someone easily upset or offended. The image is of tiptoeing through a kitchen floor covered in broken shells.

An egirl is a young woman whose persona is shaped by and for internet culture, particularly gaming, streaming, and social media platforms like TikTok and Twitch. The aesthetic typically includes dyed hair (often pink or black), heavy eyeliner, and anime-influenced style. The term can be neutral or slightly dismissive, sometimes implying performative quirkiness for male attention online: {She's got the whole egirl look going}. Compare eboy for the male equivalent.

Egirls are young women who cultivate a distinctive aesthetic on social media and streaming platforms—typically featuring dyed hair, heavy eyeliner, and alternative fashion blending goth, anime, and gamer influences.
