The term emerged from gaming and internet culture, sometimes carrying dismissive undertones suggesting performative femininity for male attention: {She's got that whole egirl look going on}. The male counterpart is eboy.

Ego is one's sense of self—personal identity, self-image, and self-importance. In everyday use, ego often implies excessive self-regard: {His ego won't let him admit he was wrong}. A {big ego} suggests arrogance; a {bruised ego} means wounded pride. In Freudian psychology, the ego mediates between primitive drives and moral constraints. {Check your ego at the door.}

Egocentric describes someone who views the world primarily through the lens of their own experience, needs, and interests. The term is less harsh than selfish—it suggests a limited perspective rather than moral failing. Children are naturally egocentric before developing awareness of others' viewpoints. {He was too egocentric to notice she was upset.} In psychology, egocentrism is a stage of cognitive development.
clues: Thinks the world revolves around them
Sees everything through their own lens

definition: Egocentrism is the tendency to see the world primarily from one's own perspective, often with difficulty imagining how others might think or feel differently. In developmental psychology, it describes a normal stage in children who assume everyone shares their viewpoint. In adults, it suggests self-absorption: {His egocentrism made him oblivious to how his decisions affected the team}. Distinct from egotism, which implies arrogance—egocentrism is more about limited perspective than inflated self-regard.

Egoism is the ethical theory or personal stance that self-interest is the foundation of morality and the proper goal of all action. Unlike egotism, which suggests excessive self-regard or boastfulness, egoism is more philosophical—it holds that acting in one's own interest is rational and justified. {Rational egoism argues that pursuing your own good is always reasonable.} In everyday use, egoism sometimes overlaps with selfishness, though philosophers distinguish between ethical egoism (how one should act) and psychological egoism (the claim that people always do act from self-interest).

An egoist is someone who acts primarily from self-interest or believes self-interest is the proper basis for action. The term can be neutral—describing a philosophical position that all motivation is ultimately selfish—or critical, suggesting excessive self-centeredness: {He's such an egoist he can't imagine anyone disagreeing with him}. Distinguished from egotist, which emphasizes boastfulness rather than self-serving behavior.

Egomania is obsessive preoccupation with oneself—an extreme, pathological form of self-centeredness. Unlike ordinary egotism, egomania suggests a compulsive quality, an inability to see beyond one's own importance: {His egomania made collaboration impossible}. The term is used loosely for anyone excessively self-absorbed, though psychiatry reserves it for more severe conditions.

An egomaniac is a person with an obsessive preoccupation with their own importance, abilities, or desires. The term implies not just ordinary self-centeredness but a pathological inability to consider others: {He's such an egomaniac he can't even ask how your day was}. Unlike clinical narcissism, egomaniac is informal—an insult rather than a diagnosis.

Egomaniacal describes someone obsessively self-centered, consumed by their own importance to a pathological degree. The word implies more than ordinary vanity—an egomaniacal person genuinely believes the world revolves around them: {His egomaniacal leadership style alienated everyone on the team}. The noun is egomaniac.

Egomaniacs is the plural of egomaniac—a person with an obsessive preoccupation with their own importance, achievements, or desires. The word suggests self-absorption beyond ordinary vanity, approaching pathological levels: {The office was run by egomaniacs who couldn't share credit}. Unlike narcissist, which has clinical overtones, egomaniac remains firmly colloquial.

Egos is the plural of ego, a person's sense of self-importance or self-esteem. When egos clash, competing personalities create conflict: {Too many egos in the room made collaboration impossible}. A bruised ego has suffered a blow to pride. Someone with a big ego thinks highly of themselves, often excessively.

Egotism is excessive preoccupation with oneself—talking about yourself too much, steering conversations back to your own experiences, assuming others share your interest in your affairs. An egotist believes they're the main character. The word overlaps with egoism, though egoism more often refers to a philosophical position that self-interest is the basis of morality. {His egotism made every dinner party exhausting.}
clues: Believing the world revolves around you

definition: An egotist is someone excessively focused on themselves—their own importance, achievements, or concerns. The word implies not just self-interest but a tendency to talk about oneself and steer conversations back to one's own experiences: {He's such an egotist that every story becomes about him}. Egotist overlaps with egoist, though egoist leans more toward selfishness in action while egotist emphasizes self-absorption in speech and thought.

Egotistical describes someone excessively focused on themselves—their achievements, opinions, or importance. An egotistical person talks about themselves constantly, assumes others share their fascination, and often dismisses others' contributions: {He was too egotistical to consider anyone else's ideas}. The word carries more disapproval than simply confident or self-assured.

Egregious is an adjective that characterizes something as conspicuously bad: Her insult to the professor was an egregious example of disrespect. His speech is full of egregious grammatical errors. Most uses of egregious are about mistakes and things that go wrong, and use of the word often implies criticism.

An egret is a wading bird with white plumage and long decorative feathers, typically found near water. Egrets are herons, distinguished mainly by their breeding plumage—the elegant, wispy feathers once prized for hat decorations: {A snowy egret stalked the shallows}.

Egrets are long-legged wading birds with white plumage, found near water in warm regions worldwide. They belong to the heron family and are known for their elegant appearance and slender necks. During breeding season, many species display ornamental plumes called aigrettes, which were once hunted nearly to extinction for hat decoration: {A snowy egret stood motionless in the shallows}.

Eiderdown is the soft, fine feathers from the eider duck, prized for exceptional insulating properties. These down feathers fill high-end quilts, comforters, and jackets. By extension, eiderdown refers to a thick, warm quilt or comforter itself, especially in British usage: {She pulled the eiderdown up to her chin}.

Eight is the number between seven and nine, represented as 8. It appears throughout measurement and culture: eight ounces in a cup, eight bits in a byte, a figure eight, behind the eight ball. To be {behind the eight ball} is to be in a difficult position, from the pool ball that blocks clean shots.

An eightball is the black ball numbered 8 in pool, pocketed last to win—or first to lose, if sunk prematurely. To be {behind the eightball} is to be in a difficult position, from the disadvantage of having the eightball between cue ball and target. In drug slang, an eightball is an eighth of an ounce of cocaine or methamphetamine.

Eighteen is the number between seventeen and nineteen, written 18. It marks legal adulthood in many countries—the age when one can vote, sign contracts, or buy cigarettes: {She turned eighteen last month}. An eighteen-wheeler is a large truck with that many wheels.

Eighteenth is the ordinal form of eighteen—the position after seventeenth in a sequence. It names a birthday marking legal adulthood in many countries: {She's turning eighteen, so we're throwing a big party for her eighteenth}. An eighteenth is one of eighteen equal parts: {an eighteenth of the estate}.

Eighth is the ordinal form of eight, indicating position number eight in a sequence: {the eighth day}, {her eighth birthday}, {eighth in line}. As a noun, an eighth is one of eight equal parts—one-eighth of a pizza, an eighth of an inch. In drug slang, an eighth is an eighth of an ounce, a common quantity for purchasing cannabis.

The eighties refers to the decade from 1980 to 1989, or to the numbers 80 through 89. Someone in their eighties is between 80 and 89 years old. When the temperature is in the eighties, it falls within that range. {The music of the eighties is making a comeback.} {My grandmother is in her eighties but still plays tennis.}

Eights is the plural of eight, the number between seven and nine. In rowing, an eight is a racing shell with eight rowers and a coxswain—the largest standard crew boat: {The eights final is the marquee event at Henley}. To be {behind the eight ball} is to be in a difficult position, from the pool game where sinking the eight ball prematurely loses.

Eighty is the cardinal number between seventy-nine and eighty-one, equal to eight tens. {She lived to be eighty years old.} The eighties refers to the decade from 1980 to 1989, or to temperatures or ages in that range: {The heat wave kept us in the eighties all week.}

Ejaculate means to discharge suddenly. The primary sense is sexual: to expel semen during orgasm. The noun ejaculate refers to the fluid itself. In older literature, ejaculate meant to exclaim abruptly: {"Good heavens!" he ejaculated}. This non-sexual usage has largely disappeared, now reading as unintentionally comic.

Ejaculation has two distinct meanings. The older sense, now somewhat dated, refers to a sudden exclamation or outcry, especially a short prayer or emotional utterance: {His ejaculations of surprise startled the room}. The more common modern meaning is the discharge of semen from the male reproductive organs during orgasm. The verb ejaculate covers both senses, though the exclamatory use now risks unintended double entendre and is largely avoided.

Eject means to force or throw out. A pilot ejects from a crashing plane; a bouncer ejects a rowdy patron; a machine ejects a disc. The word suggests sudden, forceful removal: {He was ejected from the game for fighting}. To eject can also mean to push out mechanically: {Press the button to eject the cartridge}.

Ejected is the past tense of eject, meaning forcibly expelled or thrown out. A pilot who ejected launched from a crashing aircraft. A fan who was ejected got removed from a venue for bad behavior. A disc that ejected popped out of its slot. {Security ejected the heckler from the concert}. {The cartridge ejected smoothly after each shot}.

Ejecting is forcing something or someone out, often suddenly or forcefully. A pilot ejects from a crashing plane. A bouncer ejects rowdy patrons. A machine ejects a disc. {The umpire ejected three players for fighting.} The word implies expulsion with some energy behind it—you don't gently eject anything.

Ejection is the act of forcing something or someone out. A pilot triggers an ejection seat to escape a failing aircraft. A bouncer handles ejections from a bar. In sports, ejection removes a player or coach for misconduct: {The coach earned an ejection for arguing with the referee}. Ejection can also describe expulsion of matter: the ejection of volcanic ash, the ejection of a disc from a drive.

When pronounced with an unstressed final vowel, elaborate is an adjective that means richly detailed or complex: The tribal elders wore elaborate headgear. They unveiled an elaborate plan for taking over the department. The verb elaborate has a long final vowel and means to expand something in detail: An audience member asked the mayor to elaborate on the implications of the new zoning rules.

Elaboration is the act of developing something in greater detail or complexity. A basic idea gains elaboration through explanation, ornamentation, or refinement: {The proposal needs further elaboration}. In writing or speech, elaboration adds supporting details to a point: {Her elaboration on the theory took twenty minutes}. The word also describes ornate decoration or intricate workmanship: {the elaboration of Gothic cathedrals}.

Elastic describes materials that stretch under force and return to their original shape—rubber bands, waistbands, bungee cords. The noun elastic refers to such material, especially fabric woven with rubber threads: {The elastic in these socks has lost its stretch}. Figuratively, elastic means flexible or adaptable: {elastic interpretation of the rules}, {elastic demand} in economics. The opposite is rigid or inelastic.

Elasticity is the ability to stretch or compress and then return to original form. Rubber bands have elasticity; clay does not. The concept extends to economics, where elasticity measures how sensitive one variable is to changes in another: {price elasticity of demand} describes how much buying behavior shifts when prices change. Figuratively, elasticity suggests flexibility or adaptability: {the elasticity of youth}, {elasticity in scheduling}.

Elated means extremely happy, often with a sense of triumph or relief. The feeling typically comes from good news or achievement: {She was elated when she got the job offer}. Elated suggests a buoyant, soaring quality—happiness that lifts you up rather than simply pleases.

Elation is a feeling of intense happiness and excitement, often following success or good news. It suggests being lifted up emotionally—a buoyant, energized joy rather than quiet contentment: {She felt a surge of elation when she got the acceptance letter}. The feeling is typically intense but temporary.

The elbow is the joint connecting the upper and lower arm, where the arm bends. By extension, elbow refers to anything shaped like a bent arm, such as a pipe fitting or a sharp turn in a road. To elbow someone is to push or nudge them with your elbow, often to get past: {She elbowed her way through the crowd}. Elbow grease is vigorous physical effort, especially scrubbing or polishing. If you rub elbows with someone, you associate with them socially.

Elbowing is using the elbow to push, nudge, or strike. In crowds, people elbow their way through: {She was elbowing past the other shoppers}. In sports, elbowing is a foul—using the elbow against an opponent. Figuratively, elbowing suggests aggressive competition for position or attention: {Startups elbowing for market share}.

Elbowroom is space to move freely, literally enough room to extend your elbows without bumping into things: {The tiny kitchen didn't give her much elbowroom}. More often figurative—freedom to act without restriction: {The new policy gives managers more elbowroom to make decisions}. Also spelled as two words.

Elbows are the joints connecting the upper and lower arm, where the arm bends. The word extends to angular bends in pipes or corridors. To elbow is to push or nudge with one's elbow: {She elbowed her way through the crowd}. {Elbow grease} means vigorous physical effort. To {rub elbows} with someone is to mingle with them socially.

Elder means older, used when comparing ages within a family or group: {my elder brother}, {the elder of the two sisters}. As a noun, an elder is someone older and often wiser—elders command respect in many cultures and hold formal authority in some churches and tribal communities. The elder tree or elderberry is unrelated, named for a different root entirely.

Elderberries are the small, dark purple berries of the elder tree, used in wines, syrups, jams, and folk remedies. They're toxic when raw but safe when cooked. The word appears in a famous taunt from *Monty Python and the Holy Grail*: {Your mother was a hamster and your father smelt of elderberries!}

Elderberry is the small, dark purple berry of the elder tree, used in wines, jams, syrups, and folk medicine. The berries grow in clusters and have long been valued for supposed immune-boosting properties: {elderberry syrup for cold season}. Raw elderberries are mildly toxic and must be cooked before consumption.

Eldercare is the provision of assistance and support to aging adults, especially those who can no longer live independently. The term covers a range of services—from in-home help with daily tasks to nursing facilities and hospice care. {The rising cost of eldercare strains many families.} Also styled as elder care.

Elderflower refers to the small, creamy-white blossoms of the elder tree, prized for their delicate, floral fragrance. The flowers are widely used to make cordials, liqueurs, and teas, lending a sweet, slightly musky flavor. Elderflower cordial diluted with sparkling water is a popular summer drink in Britain and Scandinavia. {The cocktail was garnished with elderflower and a twist of lemon.} The flowers are also battered and fried as fritters in some European cuisines.

Elderflowers are the small, creamy-white blossoms of the elder tree, harvested in late spring. They have a delicate, floral fragrance and are used to make cordials, wines, liqueurs, and teas: {elderflower cordial}, {St-Germain elderflower liqueur}. The flowers can also be battered and fried into fritters. Elderberries come from the same plant.

Elderly means old, especially referring to people past middle age. The word is somewhat formal and often appears in institutional contexts: {elderly care}, {the elderly population}. Some consider it more respectful than "old," though others find it euphemistic or patronizing. {My elderly neighbor needs help with yard work.} As a noun, {the elderly} refers to old people collectively.

Elders are people who are older, especially those deserving respect or holding authority by virtue of their age and experience. In many cultures and religious traditions, elders serve as leaders, advisors, or custodians of wisdom: {The tribal elders gathered to settle the dispute.} The term implies not just advanced age but earned standing within a community. Elder can also refer to certain shrubs or small trees of the genus Sambucus, whose berries are used in wines and preserves.

Eldest means oldest among a group, typically siblings: {the eldest of four children}, {my eldest daughter}. Unlike older, which compares two, eldest usually implies three or more. The word is somewhat formal; oldest serves the same function in casual speech. Eldest can also describe the senior member of any group: {the eldest statesman in the room}.

Eldorado is an imagined place of fabulous wealth or opportunity. The name comes from Spanish for "the gilded one," originally a legendary South American city of gold that lured conquistadors and explorers. Now it describes any place where riches or success seem guaranteed: {Silicon Valley was the eldorado for tech entrepreneurs}. Often capitalized El Dorado.

Eldritch means weird, eerie, or supernatural in a way that inspires fear. The word is literary and archaic, surviving mainly through horror fiction and fantasy: {an eldritch shriek}, {eldritch horrors from beyond the stars}. It suggests something uncanny and otherworldly—not merely frightening but fundamentally alien or unnatural.

Elect means to choose, especially by voting: {We elected a new mayor}. To elect to do something is to decide on that course: {She elected to stay home}. As an adjective, elect follows a title to indicate someone chosen but not yet serving: {the president-elect}. The elect, as a noun, refers to a select group—in religious contexts, those chosen by God for salvation.

Electability is a candidate's perceived ability to win an election. The concept is circular—voters often support candidates they believe others will support, making electability partly self-fulfilling. {She has the experience, but voters question her electability}. The term appears most often in primary campaigns, where partisans weigh ideological preference against pragmatic calculation about who can beat the opposing party.

Elected describes someone chosen by vote for a position or office: {the newly elected mayor}, {an elected official}. It can also describe choices more broadly—an elected course of study is one chosen rather than required. To say someone is elected but not yet serving, use {president-elect} or similar constructions with the hyphenated suffix.

An election is a formal process by which people vote to choose a person or decide an issue: {presidential election}, {local election}, {election day}. The word also means the act of choosing more broadly: {her election to stay home surprised everyone}. In theology, election refers to God's selection of individuals for salvation.

Electioneering is actively campaigning to win votes in an election—canvassing neighborhoods, making speeches, distributing literature, and persuading voters. The term often carries a slightly cynical edge, suggesting the calculated, sometimes manipulative side of political campaigns: {The senator spent October electioneering in swing states}. Laws typically prohibit electioneering within a certain distance of polling places.

Elections are formal processes by which people vote to choose leaders or decide issues. The word typically appears in plural because voting happens across multiple offices, districts, or cycles: {midterm elections}, {local elections}, {presidential elections}. An election can also refer to a single contest: {She won the election by twelve points}. The verb elect means to choose by voting, and by extension, to choose generally: {He elected to stay home}.

Elective describes something chosen rather than required. An elective course is one students select freely, as opposed to mandatory ones: {I took ceramics as an elective}. In medicine, elective procedures are scheduled in advance rather than performed as emergencies: {elective surgery}. In politics, elective office is filled by voting rather than appointment. The word emphasizes optionality—the power to choose.

Electives are courses students choose freely rather than having them required. In American education, electives contrast with core curriculum—required math, English, science—and let students explore interests: {I'm taking photography as an elective}. The term extends to anything optional within a structured system: {elective surgery} is scheduled by choice, not emergency.

An elector is someone who votes or has the right to vote in an election: {registered electors}. In the United States, an elector specifically refers to a member of the Electoral College—the body that formally elects the president: {Each state appoints electors equal to its congressional delegation}. Historically, certain German princes were called electors because they chose the Holy Roman Emperor.

Electoral is an adjective relating to elections or electors—the people who vote. It most commonly modifies nouns like {process}, {system}, {college}, {vote}, and {reform}. In American politics, the Electoral College is the body of electors who formally cast votes for president, making {electoral votes} distinct from the popular vote. Electoral fraud refers to illegal interference with elections. The word appears frequently in political and journalistic contexts but rarely in everyday conversation.

An electorate is the body of people entitled to vote in an election: {The electorate rejected the incumbent}. In some countries, particularly Australia, an electorate is also a geographic voting district—what Americans call a congressional district or constituency. The word emphasizes voters as a collective political force rather than as individuals.

Electors are people who vote in elections, or more specifically, members of an electoral body that formally chooses a leader. In the United States, electors are the members of the Electoral College who cast the official votes for president: {The candidate won the popular vote but lost among electors}. Historically, certain German princes were electors who chose the Holy Roman Emperor.

Electric describes phenomena involving electricity—the flow of charged particles that powers modern life. An electric {current} moves through wires; an electric {car} runs on batteries rather than gasoline. Figuratively, electric describes an atmosphere charged with excitement or tension: {The crowd was electric}. Electric also distinguishes powered instruments from acoustic ones: an electric {guitar}, an electric {piano}.

Electrical describes things relating to or powered by electricity. An electrical {engineer} works with electrical systems; an electrical {outlet} provides power. The word overlaps considerably with electric, though electrical tends toward the technical or systemic: electrical {wiring}, electrical {current}, electrical {equipment}. Electric more often suggests the dramatic or energizing: an electric {atmosphere}, electric {guitar}.

An electrician is a tradesperson who installs, maintains, and repairs electrical wiring and equipment. Electricians work in residential, commercial, and industrial settings, handling everything from household outlets to complex building systems. The trade typically requires apprenticeship and licensing: {We called an electrician to rewire the basement}.

Electricians is the plural of electrician, a tradesperson who installs, maintains, and repairs electrical wiring and equipment. Electricians work in residential, commercial, and industrial settings, handling everything from outlets and lighting to complex power systems. {The electricians rewired the whole house.} {We need to call the electricians about the circuit breaker.}

Electricity is a form of energy resulting from charged particles, harnessed to power lights, machines, and devices. It flows through wires as current and can be generated from various sources: coal, nuclear reactions, wind, sunlight. The word also describes the scientific study of electrical phenomena. Figuratively, electricity means excited tension or energy: {There was electricity in the air before the concert}.

Electrification is the process of bringing electrical power to something that previously lacked it. A region undergoes electrification when power lines and infrastructure are installed: {Rural electrification transformed American farm life in the 1930s}. Electrification also refers to converting systems from other power sources to electricity: {the electrification of the rail network}, {vehicle electrification}. The word increasingly appears in discussions of climate policy, where electrification of transportation and heating is seen as key to reducing fossil fuel dependence.

Electrified describes something supplied with or affected by electricity. An electrified {fence} delivers a shock to deter animals or intruders. A railroad may be electrified when it converts from steam or diesel to electric power. Figuratively, electrified means thrilled or galvanized: {The crowd was electrified by her speech}. The word suggests sudden, intense energy—whether literal current or emotional charge.

Electrifies means to charge with electricity or supply electrical power to: {The rural electrification program electrified remote villages}. More commonly, it describes thrilling or exciting someone intensely: {Her performance electrifies audiences}. The metaphor captures the sudden, jolting quality of powerful excitement—as if energy were literally coursing through a crowd or person.

To electrify is to charge with electricity or convert to electric power: {The railroad was electrified in the 1930s}. More commonly, electrify means to thrill or excite intensely: {Her performance electrified the audience}. The metaphor captures how strong emotion seems to jolt through a person like current through a wire.

Electrifying describes something that generates intense excitement or sudden energy, as if delivering an electric shock to the senses. An electrifying {performance} thrills an audience; electrifying {news} jolts people to attention. The word captures that quality of being powerfully stimulating: {The atmosphere in the stadium was electrifying}.

Electro is a style of electronic dance music that emerged in the early 1980s, characterized by drum machines, synthesizers, and robotic vocals. The term later broadened to describe various electronic music genres: {electro house}, {electro pop}. As a prefix, electro- attaches to words to indicate electrical involvement: {electroshock}, {electromagnetism}. Standing alone, electro usually means the music genre: {The DJ played electro all night}.

To electrocute is to kill or seriously injure by electric shock. The word blends "electric" and "execute," originally referring to death by electric chair, but now covers any fatal or severe electrical injury: {He was electrocuted while repairing the power line}. Loosely, people use it for any electric shock, even minor ones: {I electrocuted myself on the outlet}.

Electrocuted means killed or severely injured by electric shock. The word blends electric and executed, originally referring specifically to death by electric chair. Usage has loosened—people now say {I almost got electrocuted} to mean any significant shock, though purists insist the word requires death or near-death. {The worker was electrocuted when he touched a live wire.}

Electrocuting is killing or seriously injuring by electric shock. The word combines electric with execute—originally referring specifically to death by electric chair. Usage has loosened to include any severe shock: {He nearly electrocuted himself fixing the wiring}. Purists insist electrocution requires death, but common usage includes non-fatal shocks.

Electrocution is death or serious injury caused by electric shock. The word blends electric and execution, reflecting its origin in the electric chair. Usage has loosened—people now say they were {electrocuted} when they received a painful shock but survived, though purists insist electrocution requires death. {The faulty wiring nearly electrocuted him.}

An electrode is a conductor through which electric current enters or leaves a substance—typically a battery, electrolytic solution, or vacuum tube. The two electrodes in a circuit are the anode (positive) and cathode (negative). Electrodes appear in medical devices like pacemakers and EKG machines, where they contact the body to deliver or detect electrical signals: {The technician attached electrodes to his chest}.

Electrodes are conductors through which electric current enters or leaves a medium—whether a battery, a welding arc, or living tissue. Medical electrodes attach to the body to monitor heart rhythms or brain activity: {The technician placed electrodes on his chest for the EKG}. In welding and electroplating, electrodes deliver current to complete a circuit.

An electrolyte is a substance that conducts electricity when dissolved in water or melted, because it separates into charged particles called ions. In everyday usage, electrolytes usually refers to minerals like sodium, potassium, and magnesium that regulate fluid balance in the body: {Sports drinks replenish electrolytes lost through sweat}. {The doctor said my electrolytes were low.}

Electrolytes are minerals that carry an electrical charge when dissolved in bodily fluids—sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium among them. They regulate nerve and muscle function, hydration, and blood pressure. Sports drinks advertise electrolyte replacement for athletes who lose them through sweat: {You need to replenish your electrolytes}. The term also applies in chemistry and battery technology.

An electromagnet is a magnet created by running electric current through a coiled wire, typically wrapped around an iron core. Unlike permanent magnets, electromagnets can be switched on and off and their strength adjusted by varying the current. They power everything from doorbells and MRI machines to junkyards cranes that lift scrap metal.

Electromagnetism is the branch of physics dealing with the relationship between electricity and magnetism—forces that turn out to be aspects of a single phenomenon. Electric currents generate magnetic fields; changing magnetic fields generate electric currents. This unity underlies electric motors, generators, radio waves, and light itself. {The course covered electromagnetism and quantum mechanics.}

Electromagnets are magnets created by running electric current through a coil of wire, usually wrapped around an iron core. Unlike permanent magnets, they can be switched on and off and their strength adjusted by varying the current. They power electric motors, generators, MRI machines, and scrapyard cranes that lift cars. {The junkyard crane uses a powerful electromagnet to move metal.}

An electron is a subatomic particle carrying a negative electric charge. Electrons orbit the nucleus of an atom and are fundamental to chemical bonding, electricity, and magnetism. In everyday contexts, electron appears in compounds: {electron microscope}, {electronics}, {free electron}. The flow of electrons through a conductor is electric current.

Electronic describes devices or systems that use circuits and components to control electrical current—transistors, microchips, semiconductors. An electronic {keyboard} differs from an electric {guitar} in complexity of circuitry. Electronic also describes communication or transactions conducted through such devices: electronic {mail}, electronic {payments}. The plural electronics refers both to the technology as a field and to consumer devices: {the electronics section of the store}.

Electronica is a broad term for electronic dance music and related genres that emerged in the 1990s—encompassing techno, house, ambient, drum and bass, and other styles produced primarily with synthesizers, drum machines, and computers. The term gained currency as electronic music moved from underground clubs to mainstream audiences: {The festival lineup was heavy on electronica}. In American usage, electronica often distinguishes this music from earlier electronic experiments, suggesting something more danceable and commercially accessible.

Electronics is the branch of physics and engineering dealing with the flow of electrons through circuits—the technology behind computers, televisions, radios, and countless devices. The term also refers collectively to such devices: {the electronics aisle at the store}, {consumer electronics}. Electronic as an adjective describes anything operating on these principles: {electronic music}, {electronic funds transfer}.

Electrons are subatomic particles carrying negative electric charge, orbiting the nucleus of an atom. The flow of electrons through a conductor constitutes electric current. In everyday contexts, electrons appear in discussions of electronics, static electricity, and chemical bonding: {The battery works by moving electrons from one terminal to the other}.

Electropop is a style of popular music that foregrounds synthesizers, drum machines, and other electronic instruments while maintaining accessible pop song structures. The genre emerged in the late 1970s and early 1980s with acts like Gary Numan and Depeche Mode, then experienced revival in the 2000s: {Her new album has a distinct electropop sound}. The term emphasizes catchiness over the experimental edge of broader electronic music.

Electroshock is the application of electric current to the body, especially to the brain as a psychiatric treatment. Electroshock therapy (also called electroconvulsive therapy or ECT) induces seizures to treat severe depression and other mental disorders. The term often carries negative connotations from its history of misuse: {They threatened him with electroshock}.

Electroshocks are jolts of electricity delivered to the body, most often in the context of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), a psychiatric treatment for severe depression and other conditions: {The patient received electroshocks twice weekly}. The term also covers electric shocks from other sources—stun guns, faulty wiring, or medical defibrillators. As a verb, to electroshock is to administer such treatment.

Elegance is refined grace and tasteful simplicity—the quality of being pleasingly ingenious yet understated. An elegant solution to a problem achieves much with little: {The proof was elegant in its simplicity}. Elegant dress, manners, or surroundings suggest sophistication without excess: {She moved through the room with quiet elegance}. The word implies that beauty and effectiveness arise from restraint rather than elaboration.

Elegant describes something refined, graceful, and tastefully understated. An elegant {solution} achieves its goal with surprising simplicity. An elegant {dress} or elegant {room} shows sophistication without excess. The word suggests quality achieved through restraint rather than elaboration—nothing wasted, nothing lacking: {The proof was elegant in its brevity}.

Elegies are poems or songs of mourning, typically lamenting someone's death. The form has ancient roots and follows conventions of grief, praise, and consolation: {Milton's elegies for deceased friends}. More broadly, an elegy can be any mournful reflection on loss—of a person, a place, a way of life: {The film is an elegy for small-town America}.

An elegy is a mournful poem or song, typically one written to honor someone who has died. The form has ancient roots and traditionally features reflective, sorrowful meditation on loss, mortality, or the passage of time. While elegies most often commemorate the dead, the term extends to any literary work with a tone of grief or lamentation: {Gray's "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" remains a classic of the form}. The adjective elegiac describes anything expressing sorrow or nostalgia.

Element denotes one constituent of a thing composed of many, or an irreducible constituent, such as a chemical element. In its original use, element comprised only four things—earth, air, fire, and water. Science has now determined that these are not irreducible, and has transferred the meaning of element to things that are (such as silicon, lead, or krypton). More generally, element refers to something that can be isolated or abstracted from its context and identified: elements of a good play, the game has an element of luck.
clues: What atoms of one kind form

definition: Elemental means relating to the basic forces or components of something. The elemental {power of the storm} suggests nature's raw, fundamental energy. In chemistry, elemental refers to a substance in its pure, uncombined form: {elemental carbon}, {elemental iron}. The word often carries overtones of primal force—something stripped to its essence, unrefined and powerful: {an elemental struggle for survival}.

Elementals are supernatural beings embodying or inhabiting natural forces—earth, air, fire, and water. The concept comes from Renaissance occult philosophy, which assigned spirits to each element: gnomes to earth, sylphs to air, salamanders to fire, undines to water. The term appears frequently in fantasy fiction and games, where elementals are creatures summoned or encountered as manifestations of raw elemental power: {The wizard conjured a fire elemental to guard the passage}.

Elementary means basic, fundamental, or introductory—concerned with first principles rather than advanced concepts: {elementary arithmetic}, {elementary school}, {an elementary course in physics}. Something elementary is simple or rudimentary: {The mistake was elementary}. In chemistry, elementary refers to a single element: {elementary particles}, {elementary substances}.

Elements are the basic parts or components that make up something larger. Chemical elements are pure substances that cannot be broken down further—hydrogen, oxygen, carbon. The elements of a skill or subject are its fundamentals: {She's learning the elements of music theory}. The elements also refers to weather, especially harsh conditions: {exposed to the elements}. To be {in your element} is to be in circumstances where you thrive.

An elephant is a massive land mammal with thick gray skin, a long trunk, and large ears, native to Africa and Asia. Elephants are the largest living land animals. The phrase {elephant in the room} describes an obvious problem everyone ignores. A {white elephant} is a burdensome possession or an expensive gift of little use. To {have a memory like an elephant} is to remember everything.

Elephants is the plural of elephant, the largest living land animal—a massive mammal with a long trunk, tusks, and large ears. African and Asian elephants are the surviving species. The phrase {the elephant in the room} describes an obvious problem everyone avoids discussing. {Pink elephants} are hallucinations associated with drunkenness. {White elephants} are burdensome possessions or gifts.

Elevate means to raise something higher—physically or figuratively. A platform elevates speakers above the crowd. To elevate someone is to promote them: {She was elevated to partner}. Elevated language or style is formal and refined. An elevated heart rate is higher than normal. The word often suggests improvement or enhancement: {Good design elevates the ordinary}.

Elevated means raised above a normal level. An elevated {platform} sits higher than the ground; elevated {blood pressure} exceeds healthy ranges. The word often suggests improvement or refinement: elevated {discourse}, elevated {taste}. In American cities, {the elevated} or {the el} is a railway built on an overhead structure. Someone in an elevated {mood} feels unusually happy or excited.

Elevating describes something that raises—literally or figuratively. An elevating platform lifts objects; an elevating experience lifts the spirit or mind. The word often carries connotations of moral or intellectual improvement: {an elevating conversation}, {elevating literature}. When used ironically, it suggests pretension: {How elevating of you to say so}.

Elevation is height above a reference point, usually sea level: {The city sits at an elevation of 5,000 feet}. It also means the act of raising something or someone to a higher position—physical or metaphorical: {his elevation to the Supreme Court}. In architecture, an elevation is a flat drawing showing one face of a building. An elevated mood or style has a lofty, dignified quality.

An elevator is a platform or compartment that moves vertically to transport people or goods between floors of a building. The British term is lift. Elevator also names various mechanical devices that raise things: a grain elevator stores and moves grain; a small flap on an airplane's tail controls pitch. To give someone an {elevator pitch} is to deliver a brief persuasive summary—short enough for an elevator ride.

Elevators are enclosed platforms or compartments that move vertically to transport people or goods between floors of a building. The term is American; British English prefers lift. An elevator can also be a hinged surface on an aircraft's tail that controls pitch. In agriculture, a grain elevator is a tall structure for storing and moving grain. Elevator shoes have thick soles to make the wearer appear taller.

Eleven is the number after ten, written 11. It's the first number that English doesn't construct from smaller parts—unlike thirteen (three + ten) or twenty-one. In sports, eleven often names a team's starting lineup, especially in soccer and cricket: {the starting eleven}. {Eleven o'clock} marks late morning or late night. The adjective eleventh indicates position in sequence: {the eleventh hour} means the last possible moment.

Elevenses is a British term for a light snack or refreshment taken around eleven o'clock in the morning—tea or coffee with biscuits, typically. The word captures the institutionalized mid-morning break in British culture: {Shall we stop for elevenses?} Less common in American English, where the practice exists but lacks a dedicated name.

Elevensies is a mid-morning snack or light meal taken around eleven o'clock, similar to a coffee break. The word is chiefly British and somewhat old-fashioned, associated with rural or working-class custom: {Time for elevensies—put the kettle on}. It gained wider recognition through Tolkien's hobbits, who treat elevensies as one of several daily meals between breakfast and lunch.

Eleventh is the ordinal form of eleven, indicating position number eleven in a sequence. As a noun, an eleventh is one of eleven equal parts. The phrase {at the eleventh hour} means at the last possible moment before a deadline, referencing the parable of workers hired late in the day who still received full wages.

An elf is a small supernatural being from Germanic folklore, typically depicted with pointed ears and magical powers. In traditional tales, elves could be mischievous or malevolent; modern fantasy has largely reimagined them as noble, immortal beings skilled in archery and magic. Santa's elves are cheerful workshop helpers. {She dressed as an elf for the Renaissance faire.}

Elfin describes something small, delicate, and otherworldly—suggestive of elves or fairies. It typically applies to facial features or body types: {an elfin face}, {her elfin frame}. The word carries connotations of charm and mischief alongside diminutiveness. Elfin ears are pointed; an elfin smile is impish and knowing.

Eligibility is the state of meeting requirements to qualify for something. You might check your eligibility for a loan, a scholarship, or a program. Rules determine who is eligible: {Eligibility depends on income level}. Sports leagues set eligibility standards for players. The word often appears in bureaucratic contexts where specific criteria must be satisfied before someone can participate or receive benefits.

Eligible means qualified or entitled to be chosen. Someone eligible for a position meets the requirements: {All citizens over eighteen are eligible to vote}. An eligible bachelor is unmarried and considered a desirable match—available and worth pursuing. The word implies both meeting criteria and being available for selection.

Eliminate means to remove or get rid of something completely. You eliminate {errors} from a document, eliminate {candidates} from consideration, or eliminate {foods} from your diet. In sports, a team eliminated from a tournament can no longer advance. The euphemistic sense—to kill—appears in crime and espionage contexts: {The target was eliminated}.

Eliminated is the past tense of eliminate, meaning to remove, get rid of, or rule out. A suspect is eliminated from an investigation when evidence clears them. A team eliminated from a tournament can no longer advance. In clinical language, to eliminate is to expel waste from the body. {We've eliminated several possibilities.}

Elimination is the act of removing or getting rid of something. In competitions, elimination means being knocked out—unable to continue: {single-elimination tournament}, {process of elimination}. The word applies to bodily waste functions in medical or polite contexts: {bowel elimination}. To work through possibilities by elimination is to rule them out one by one until only the answer remains.

An eliminator is a person or thing that removes, destroys, or excludes something. In competitive contexts, an eliminator is a contest or round that knocks out losing participants: {The semifinal serves as an eliminator before the championship}. Products marketed as eliminators promise to get rid of unwanted things like odors, pests, or stains. The word appears frequently in sports brackets and tournament structures where single losses end a competitor's run.

Elite refers to a select group regarded as superior—the best, most powerful, or most privileged within a larger population. The elite may be defined by wealth, talent, education, or social standing: {political elite}, {academic elite}, {elite athletes}. As an adjective, elite describes things associated with or reserved for such groups: {an elite private school}, {elite military units}. The word can carry either admiration or resentment, depending on whether excellence or exclusivity is emphasized.

Elites are the people at the top of a hierarchy—those with the most power, wealth, influence, or skill in a given domain. Political elites shape policy; cultural elites set taste; athletic elites dominate their sports. The word often carries suspicion: {The elites don't understand ordinary people}. Elite as an adjective means top-tier or exclusive: {elite universities}, {an elite fighting force}.

Elitism is the belief that society should be led by a select group of superior individuals, or the sense of entitlement that comes from belonging to such a group. The word is almost always pejorative—accusing someone of elitism suggests they look down on ordinary people or favor the privileged few: {The candidate was accused of coastal elitism}. Elitist works as both noun and adjective: {an elitist attitude}, {Silicon Valley elitists}.

Elitist describes someone who believes certain people deserve more power, influence, or resources based on superior ability, education, or status. The word is almost always pejorative, accusing someone of looking down on ordinary people: {His elitist attitude alienated voters}. As a noun, an elitist is a person who holds such views. The related noun elite refers to a select group at the top of a hierarchy—elitist suggests excessive devotion to that group or contempt for those outside it.

Elitists are people who believe certain individuals deserve special treatment or influence based on superior ability, wealth, education, or taste. The term is almost always disparaging, suggesting someone who looks down on ordinary people or dismisses popular preferences: {Those elitists in Washington don't understand real Americans}. Politicians frequently deploy the accusation against opponents regardless of actual class background.

An elixir is a magical or medicinal potion, especially one believed to cure all ailments or grant immortality: {the elixir of life}. Medieval alchemists sought an elixir to turn base metals into gold. More broadly, any solution or remedy that seems to work wonders: {Exercise became her elixir}. In pharmacy, an elixir is a sweetened liquid used to deliver medication.

Elixirs is the plural of elixir, a magical or medicinal potion. In medieval alchemy, the elixir of life promised immortality. Modern use is often figurative or playful: {coffee is my morning elixir}. Pharmaceutical elixirs are sweetened liquid medicines: {cough elixirs}. The word suggests something with transformative or restorative powers.

Elk is a large deer native to North America, known for its impressive antlers on males and its bugling call during mating season. In British English, elk refers to what Americans call a moose. The animal is prized by hunters and figures prominently in the iconography of the American West. The Elks, formally the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks, is a fraternal organization whose lodges are found throughout the United States.

An ellipse is an oval shape—a closed curve like a circle stretched along one axis. In geometry, it's defined as the set of points whose distances from two fixed points (foci) sum to a constant. Planetary orbits are ellipses. In writing, ellipse sometimes substitutes for ellipsis, the three dots indicating omitted text, though this usage is disputed.

Ellipses is the plural of ellipsis. An ellipsis is a set of three dots (...) indicating omitted words or a trailing off: {Her voice faded into ellipses}. In geometry, ellipses are oval shapes—closed curves where the sum of distances from two focal points remains constant. The punctuation and the shape share a Greek root meaning "falling short."

An ellipsis is the omission of words from speech or text, or the punctuation mark (three dots: ...) indicating such an omission. In quoted material, ellipsis shows where words have been left out: {The report stated that "ichthyosaurs... gave birth to live young"}. In casual writing, ellipsis creates trailing-off effects, hesitation, or dramatic pauses: {I don't know...} The plural is ellipses.

Elliptical describes the shape of an ellipse—an oval or flattened circle: {the elliptical orbit of a planet}. In language, elliptical means leaving out words that can be understood from context, creating compressed or incomplete expression: {His elliptical style frustrated readers expecting clear explanations}. An elliptical machine is exercise equipment with an oval stride pattern.

An elm is a large deciduous tree with serrated leaves and rough bark, common in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Elms were once a defining feature of American streets and parks until Dutch elm disease devastated populations in the mid-20th century. The wood is valued for its strength and resistance to splitting.

Elms are large deciduous trees with serrated leaves and a distinctive vase-shaped canopy. Once common along American streets, most were devastated by Dutch elm disease in the mid-20th century. The wood is tough and water-resistant, traditionally used for coffins, wheel hubs, and boat keels. {The old elm shaded the entire yard.}

To elope is to run away secretly, typically to get married without parental consent or public ceremony. The word suggests romantic urgency and often disapproval from family: {They eloped to Vegas over the weekend}. More broadly, elope can mean to slip away or abscond: {The couple eloped with the company funds}, though the marriage sense dominates modern usage.

Eloped is the past tense of elope, meaning to run away secretly to get married, typically without parental consent or an elaborate ceremony: {They eloped to Vegas last weekend}. The word often implies spontaneity or avoiding family disapproval. More broadly, to elope can mean to run off with a lover, married or not.

Elopement is the act of running away secretly, typically to get married without parental consent or public ceremony: {Their elopement shocked both families}. The word implies haste and secrecy, often romantic urgency. In healthcare settings, elopement refers to a patient—especially one with dementia—leaving a facility without authorization: {The nursing home installed alarms to prevent elopement}.

Elopements is the plural of elopement—instances of running away secretly, typically to get married without parental consent or public ceremony. The word carries romantic connotations of couples escaping social constraints: {The judge had performed dozens of elopements over the years}. In healthcare settings, elopement refers to a patient leaving a facility without authorization, particularly concerning with dementia patients or psychiatric wards.

Elopes is the third-person singular of elope—to run away secretly to get married, typically without parental consent: {She elopes with her boyfriend next week}. The word once meant any secret escape but now centers on marriage. Extended uses describe sudden departures with romantic partners even when marriage isn't the goal.

Eloping is running away secretly to get married, typically without parental consent or a formal wedding: {They eloped to Las Vegas}. The word once meant any secret escape, especially a wife leaving her husband for a lover, but now almost exclusively refers to impromptu marriages. By extension, eloping can mean slipping away from any expected situation: {We eloped from the party early}.

Eloquence is the power to speak or write in a way that moves, persuades, or delights. It combines fluency with force—not just smooth delivery but language that lands: {His eloquence swayed the jury}. The word implies a natural gift, though eloquence can be cultivated. Someone eloquent makes complex ideas clear and ordinary ideas memorable.

Eloquent describes speech or writing that is fluent, persuasive, and powerfully expressive. An eloquent speaker moves audiences through skillful use of language, while an eloquent essay makes its case with grace and precision. The word can also apply to nonverbal expression: {Her eloquent silence spoke volumes.} Something eloquent conveys meaning or emotion with unusual effectiveness, whether through words or gestures.

Elote is Mexican street corn—a grilled ear of corn on the cob slathered with mayonnaise, cotija cheese, chili powder, and lime juice. The word is Spanish for corn on the cob generally, but in American English it specifically means this popular street food preparation: {We grabbed elote from a vendor at the festival}.

Else is an important function word that also carries the idea of other or alternative. As an adjective it is placed after a word beginning with some- or any-: Does anyone else want to go with us? I would really like to live somewhere else. The combinations anything else and nothing else are used talk about any or no additional thing: Is there anything else you need from the store? Or else introduces a necessary alternative if what comes before it does not work: Hurry up or else we’ll go without you.

Elsewhere means in or to another place: {The book you want isn't here—try looking elsewhere}. It suggests an unspecified alternative location: {If you're not happy with our service, take your business elsewhere}. The word often implies that something exists or is happening, just not in the current context: {Elsewhere in the building, a meeting was underway}.

Elude means to escape or avoid, typically through cleverness or skill. A fugitive eludes capture; a word eludes you when you can't quite recall it. {The answer eluded me until I stopped trying so hard.} What eludes you stays just out of reach—success, sleep, understanding. Not to be confused with allude, which means to refer to indirectly.

Eluded is the past tense of elude, meaning to escape or avoid, often by cleverness or agility. A suspect eludes capture; an answer eludes someone who can't quite remember. {The meaning of the poem eluded me}. {He eluded his pursuers by ducking into an alley}. What eludes you stays just out of reach.

Eludes means escapes or avoids, often through cleverness or elusiveness. A fugitive eludes capture; a name eludes you when you can't recall it. The word suggests something slipping away despite effort: {The answer eludes me}. What eludes comprehension remains beyond understanding: {The meaning of the poem eludes most readers}.

Elusive describes something difficult to catch, find, or pin down. An elusive {criminal} evades capture. An elusive {answer} stays just out of reach. The word often suggests something that seems almost within grasp but slips away: {Sleep proved elusive that night}. Elusive memories, meanings, or qualities resist clear definition or recall.

Elven describes things related to elves—the graceful, immortal beings of fantasy literature and mythology: {elven archers}, {elven kingdoms}, {elven magic}. The word gained wide currency through Tolkien's work, where it distinguishes the language and culture of his Elves. Elvish serves the same function and is equally common.

Elves are mythical beings of folklore and fantasy, typically depicted as human-like but with pointed ears, magical powers, and exceptional longevity. In older traditions, elves ranged from mischievous household spirits to dangerous supernatural creatures. Modern fantasy, shaped by Tolkien, usually portrays them as tall, graceful, and wise. {Santa's elves} are the industrious toymakers of Christmas lore—a quite different image. Elf is the singular.
clues: Small magical folk with pointy ears

definition: Elvish describes things resembling or relating to elves—the small, magical creatures of folklore and fantasy. Something elvish has a mischievous, otherworldly, or delicately supernatural quality: {an elvish grin}, {elvish features}. The word carries connotations of playfulness and enchantment. In fantasy literature and gaming, elvish often refers to the culture, appearance, or languages of elves: {elvish architecture}, {speaking elvish}. (Capitalized Elvish typically refers to Tolkien's constructed languages.)

Elysium is a state or place of perfect happiness and bliss. The word comes from Greek mythology, where the Elysian Fields were the final resting place of the heroic and virtuous after death—a paradise reserved for those favored by the gods. In modern use, elysium describes any idyllic condition or setting: {The garden was her personal elysium}. The adjective elysian means blissful or heavenly. (Capitalized Elysium may refer to specific places or works named after the mythological realm.)

Emaciated describes extreme thinness from starvation, illness, or neglect—beyond merely thin or underweight, suggesting visible bone structure and wasting: {The emaciated prisoners could barely stand}. The word applies to humans and animals alike. Figuratively rare, but a landscape or budget might be called emaciated to suggest severe depletion.

Email is electronic mail—messages sent and received through computer networks, primarily the internet. As a noun, it refers both to the system itself and to individual messages: {I'll send you an email} or {Check your email}. As a verb, it means to send such a message: {Email me when you get a chance}. Though the hyphenated e-mail was once standard, the solid form now dominates in everyday use.

Emails are electronic messages sent between computers over networks. The word works as both noun and verb: {I have three hundred unread emails}, {She emails me every morning}. Email has largely replaced letters for routine correspondence, though the conventions of letter-writing—greetings, sign-offs, formal registers—linger in professional contexts. The plural often refers to the accumulated mass: {drowning in emails}.

To emancipate is to set free from bondage, oppression, or legal restriction. The word carries historical weight from slavery and liberation movements: {Lincoln's proclamation emancipated enslaved people in Confederate states}. It extends to any release from constraining authority—a minor may be legally emancipated from parental control, or someone might feel emancipated from outdated traditions: {Leaving home emancipated her from her family's expectations}.

Emancipated means freed from restraint or control. The word applies most often to legal liberation: an emancipated {slave}, an emancipated {minor} who gains adult rights before turning eighteen. More broadly, emancipated describes anyone released from limiting circumstances or conventions: {She felt emancipated after leaving the restrictive community}. The past participle functions as an adjective suggesting independence and self-determination.

Emancipation is the act of freeing someone from bondage, oppression, or legal restriction. The word is most associated with the abolition of slavery—Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people in Confederate states to be free. More broadly, emancipation applies to liberation from any constraining authority: {the emancipation of women}, {emancipation from parental control}. In law, an emancipated minor gains adult rights before reaching the age of majority.

An emancipator is someone who sets others free from bondage, oppression, or restriction. The term most often appears in historical contexts involving slavery—Abraham Lincoln is called "the Great Emancipator" for the Emancipation Proclamation. More broadly, anyone who liberates others from constraint: {an emancipator of the human mind}.

To emasculate is to deprive of masculine qualities or vigor. The literal meaning is to castrate, but the word almost always appears figuratively: an emasculated {bureaucracy}, emasculated {leadership}. To emasculate a man is to make him feel less manly, often through domination or criticism: {She emasculated him in front of his friends}. The word carries assumptions about what masculinity should look like.

Emasculated means weakened or stripped of power, vigor, or authority. The word literally refers to castration but appears almost exclusively in its figurative sense—describing something or someone made ineffectual: {an emasculated opposition party}, {He felt emasculated by her constant criticism}. The term carries gendered freight, implying that strength and capability are inherently masculine.

Emasculating describes something that undermines a man's sense of masculinity or makes him feel weak, powerless, or inadequate. The term derives from the literal meaning of emasculate—to castrate—but is almost always used figuratively to describe experiences, comments, or situations that diminish male confidence or authority. {He found it emasculating to be corrected by his wife in front of his friends.} The word carries assumptions about what masculinity should look like, so its use can reveal as much about the speaker's values as about the situation being described.

Emasculation is the removal of male genitals, or more broadly, the stripping away of masculine qualities or power. The literal sense appears in medical and veterinary contexts. The figurative sense dominates everyday use: {The budget cuts were an emasculation of the agency's enforcement powers}. To describe a man as emasculated suggests he has been weakened, humiliated, or rendered ineffectual—often by a woman or by circumstances that undermine traditional masculine authority.

To embalm is to preserve a corpse from decay, typically by replacing blood with preservative fluids. The practice prepares bodies for viewing at funerals or for long-term preservation. Figuratively, to embalm something is to preserve it unchanged: {His letters embalm the spirit of that era}. The word suggests arrested decay—something kept from natural deterioration.

Embalmed describes a corpse that has been preserved from decay, typically through chemical treatment. Funeral homes embalm bodies for viewing: {The embalmed body lay in the open casket}. Figuratively, something embalmed is preserved but lifeless—frozen in time rather than allowed to change: {embalmed traditions}, {a culture embalmed in nostalgia}.

An embalmer is a person who preserves corpses for burial or display, typically by draining blood and replacing it with preservative fluids. Embalmers work in funeral homes, preparing bodies for viewing and slowing decomposition. The work requires technical skill and comfort with the dead: {The embalmer made her grandmother look peaceful}.

Embalmers are people who preserve corpses, typically by replacing blood with chemical solutions to delay decay. The practice allows time between death and burial for viewing, transport, or legal requirements. Embalmers work in funeral homes and must be licensed in most jurisdictions. {The embalmers prepared the body for the open-casket service.}

Embalming is the process of preserving a dead body from decay, typically by replacing blood with chemical solutions like formaldehyde. Funeral homes embalm corpses to allow viewing before burial: {The embalming took several hours}. The practice dates to ancient Egypt, where it was essential to mummification. As a participle, embalming also describes anything that preserves: {the embalming cold of the arctic}.

An embankment is a raised bank of earth or stone, typically built to hold back water or carry a road or railway above the surrounding level. Rivers have embankments to prevent flooding; trains run along embankments to maintain grade. {The path along the embankment offered views of the river below.}

A misspelling of embarrassed—note the double r and double s. The word means feeling self-conscious, awkward, or ashamed, typically from social discomfort: {I was embarrassed when I tripped on stage}. The spelling trips people up because the double letters fall in unexpected places.

An embargo is an official ban on trade or commerce with a particular country, or a government order prohibiting ships from entering or leaving ports. More broadly, it means any prohibition or restriction: {The court placed an embargo on publishing the documents}. To embargo something is to impose such a ban: {The administration embargoed all Cuban imports}.

Embargoes are official restrictions on commerce or communication. A government may impose an embargo on trade with a hostile nation, prohibiting imports, exports, or both. The word also applies to information: {The press release was under embargo until noon}. To embargo something is to place such a restriction on it. Singular: embargo.

Embargos is the plural of embargo, an official ban on trade or other activity with a particular country or entity: {The embargos against Cuba have lasted decades}. Governments impose embargos as economic or political pressure. The word also applies to restrictions on releasing information: {news embargos}. Also spelled embargoes.

To embark is to board a ship, aircraft, or other vessel for a journey: {We embarked at dawn}. The word extends naturally to beginning any significant undertaking: {She embarked on a new career}, {They embarked on a journey of self-discovery}. The sense of setting out on something consequential—with its mix of anticipation and uncertainty—carries through both literal and figurative uses.

Embarked is the past tense of embark, meaning to board a ship or aircraft: {We embarked at dawn}. More often, embarked appears with "on" or "upon" to indicate beginning a journey, venture, or undertaking: {She embarked on a new career}, {They embarked upon an ambitious project}. The word carries a sense of setting forth into something significant.

Embarking is the present participle of embark, meaning to board a ship, aircraft, or other vessel: {passengers embarking on the cruise liner}. More commonly, embarking describes beginning a journey, project, or new phase: {embarking on a career in medicine}, {embarking on married life}. The word carries a sense of setting out into something significant or unknown.

To embarrass is to make someone feel self-conscious, awkward, or ashamed, usually in front of others: {Don't embarrass me in front of my friends}. The feeling can range from mild discomfort to acute mortification. You can also embarrass yourself through your own actions. Extended uses describe situations that create difficulty or inconvenience: {The leak embarrassed the administration}. Financial embarrassment means being short of money.

Embarrassed describes the self-conscious discomfort of being exposed to others' judgment—whether from a mistake, awkward situation, or unwanted attention. The feeling ranges from mild sheepishness to acute shame: {I was embarrassed when I forgot her name}, {He felt embarrassed about asking for help}. Someone can also be embarrassed on another's behalf, cringing at their missteps.

Embarrassing describes something that causes self-consciousness, awkwardness, or shame—typically by exposing a flaw, mistake, or private matter to others. An embarrassing {moment} might involve tripping in public or forgetting someone's name. The word can also characterize situations that reflect poorly on someone: {The leaked emails were embarrassing for the company}. What counts as embarrassing varies by person and culture, though bodily functions, social blunders, and being caught in lies are near-universal triggers.

Embarrassingly describes doing something in a way that causes self-consciousness or shame, or to a degree that should cause it. {He embarrassingly mispronounced her name during the toast}. Often used to intensify an admission: {The movie was embarrassingly bad}, {I'm embarrassingly unfamiliar with her work}. The word can signal the speaker's own discomfort or highlight how something ought to make someone uncomfortable.

Embarrassment is the uncomfortable self-consciousness that comes from being exposed to others' judgment—whether from a social blunder, public mistake, or unwanted attention. {I could die of embarrassment.} An embarrassment can also be something that causes this feeling: {His drunk uncle was an embarrassment at the wedding}. An {embarrassment of riches} is an overabundance, so much of a good thing that it becomes awkward to manage.

Embassies is the plural of embassy—the official headquarters of an ambassador in a foreign country, or the diplomatic staff working there. Embassies handle relations between governments, issue visas, and assist citizens abroad. {The embassies were evacuated when fighting broke out.} By extension, any formal delegation sent to negotiate may be called an embassy.

An embassy is the official residence and offices of an ambassador in a foreign country, or the diplomatic mission itself: {The protesters gathered outside the American embassy}. By extension, embassy can mean the ambassador's staff collectively. To seek refuge at an embassy is to request diplomatic protection on what is technically foreign soil.

Embattled describes someone or something under sustained attack or pressure. A military force may be embattled by enemy troops, but the word now more often describes organizations or leaders facing criticism, scandal, or opposition: {the embattled CEO}, {an embattled administration}. In heraldry, embattled describes a line with battlements like a castle wall.

To embed is to fix something firmly within a surrounding mass. A splinter embeds in skin; fossils embed in rock. The meaning extends to anything inserted as an integral part: {The video is embedded in the article}. An embed is a journalist attached to a military unit, traveling with and reporting from within it. In computing, embedded systems are computers built into devices they control.

Embedded means fixed firmly within a surrounding mass or context. A splinter is embedded in skin; a journalist is embedded with military troops, living and traveling with them. In computing, embedded code or media sits within a larger document or system: {an embedded video in a webpage}, {an embedded chip in a device}. The word suggests something so integrated it can't easily be separated from its context.

Embedding is the act of placing something firmly within a surrounding mass or context. A journalist may be embedded with military troops, living and traveling alongside them. In computing and machine learning, an embedding is a numerical representation that captures meaning—words, images, or concepts transformed into vectors that position similar things close together in mathematical space: {The model uses embeddings to understand semantic relationships}.

To embellish is to add decorative details or ornamentation: {an embellished manuscript}, {a dress embellished with beads}. More often, embellish means to enhance a story or account with invented or exaggerated details: {He couldn't resist embellishing the tale}. The word carries a hint of skepticism—embellished accounts may be entertaining but aren't entirely trustworthy.

Embellished means decorated or adorned, often with elaborate detail: {an embellished gown}, {embellished with gold trim}. More commonly, embellished describes a story or account that has been enhanced with exaggerated or invented details: {His version of events was heavily embellished}. The word suggests additions that may improve appearance or entertainment value while straying from plain truth.

Embellishing is adding decorative details or flourishes to something. You might embellish a story with colorful exaggerations, embellish a dress with beadwork, or embellish a melody with ornamental notes. The word often carries a whiff of suspicion—embellished accounts may be less than truthful: {I think he's embellishing a bit}.

Embellishment is decoration or ornamentation added to make something more attractive or interesting: {The dress featured embellishments along the neckline}. The word extends to stories and accounts—an embellishment is an added detail that enhances the narrative but may stretch the truth: {His version of events contained a few embellishments}. To embellish is to add such flourishes.

Embellishments are decorative additions that enhance or beautify something. A dress might have embellishments of lace or beading. In music, embellishments are ornamental notes added to a melody. The word often implies excess or falsification: {His story contained a few embellishments}. To embellish a tale is to add details that may not be strictly true.

An ember is a glowing piece of wood or coal in a dying fire. Embers retain heat long after flames have gone out, capable of reigniting fuel or causing burns. Figuratively, embers represent what remains of something once intense: {the embers of a former passion}, {stirring the embers of an old rivalry}. The plural embers often describes the final stage of a fire: {We sat watching the embers}.

Embers are the glowing remains of a fire after flames have died down—small pieces of wood or coal that stay hot and faintly luminous. You can {stir the embers} to rekindle a fire or {watch the embers fade}. Figuratively, embers suggest something nearly extinguished but not quite dead: {the embers of their romance}, {embers of hope}.

To embezzle is to steal money or property entrusted to your care, typically from an employer or organization. Unlike robbery, embezzlement involves betraying a position of trust—a treasurer who siphons funds, an accountant who diverts payments. {She embezzled half a million dollars over five years before anyone noticed.}

Embezzled describes money or property that has been stolen by someone entrusted with it. An accountant embezzles company funds; a treasurer embezzles from the organization. The word implies betrayal of trust rather than theft by an outsider: {He embezzled thousands before anyone noticed the discrepancies}.

Embezzlement is the theft of money or property by someone entrusted with it—an employee skimming from the register, an accountant diverting company funds, a trustee misappropriating assets. The crime requires a breach of trust: the embezzler had legitimate access before stealing. {She was convicted of embezzling three million dollars from the nonprofit.}

An embezzler is someone who steals money or property entrusted to their care, typically from an employer or organization. The crime involves betrayal of trust—a bookkeeper skimming funds, a treasurer diverting donations: {The embezzler had siphoned off millions before anyone noticed}.

Embezzlers are people who steal money or property entrusted to their care, typically from an employer or organization. The crime requires a position of trust—accountants, treasurers, or executives who divert funds they're authorized to handle: {The embezzlers had siphoned off millions before anyone noticed the discrepancy}.

Embezzles is the act of stealing money or property entrusted to one's care, typically from an employer or organization. The crime involves a breach of trust—a bookkeeper who embezzles isn't robbing strangers but siphoning funds they were authorized to handle: {She embezzles small amounts each month, hoping no one will notice}.

Embezzling is the act of stealing money or property entrusted to your care, typically from an employer or organization. The crime involves breach of trust rather than breaking and entering—an accountant embezzling company funds, a treasurer embezzling from a charity: {She was caught embezzling from the nonprofit where she'd worked for years}.

Embittered describes someone made resentful or cynical by negative experiences. An embittered person carries lasting bitterness from disappointment, betrayal, or perceived injustice: {an embittered ex-employee}, {embittered by years of broken promises}. The word suggests the bitterness has settled in and shaped their outlook, not just a passing mood.
