Emblazoned means decorated with a coat of arms, heraldic device, or other prominent design: {shields emblazoned with the family crest}. More broadly, it describes anything boldly displayed or inscribed across a surface: {a banner emblazoned with the company logo}, {his name emblazoned across the marquee}. The word suggests conspicuous, deliberate display.

An emblem is a symbol or design representing an idea, organization, or identity: {The eagle is the emblem of the United States}. Unlike a logo, which may be abstract, an emblem typically depicts something recognizable—an animal, object, or figure. Emblems appear on flags, shields, uniforms, and official documents. Figuratively, anything serving as a symbol qualifies: {She became an emblem of resistance}.

Emblematic means serving as a symbol or representative example of something larger. An emblematic image captures the essence of an era, movement, or idea: {The photo of sailors kissing in Times Square became emblematic of V-J Day}. Something emblematic stands for the whole: {Her rise from poverty to CEO is emblematic of the American dream}.

Emblems are symbols or designs that represent something larger—a nation, organization, or idea. A country's flag is an emblem of national identity; a logo serves as a corporate emblem. The word suggests official or formal representation: {The eagle is the emblem of the United States}. Emblems can also be abstract: {The dove has long been an emblem of peace}.

Embodied means given a body or physical form. Abstract concepts become embodied when made concrete or tangible: {The constitution embodied the founders' ideals}. A person can embody qualities they represent fully: {She embodied grace under pressure}. In philosophy and cognitive science, embodied cognition holds that thinking is shaped by having a physical body, not just a brain.

To embody something is to give it physical form or concrete expression. A constitution embodies the principles of a nation. A person can embody grace, courage, or evil—their presence makes the abstract quality visible and tangible: {She embodies everything I aspire to be}. The word suggests completeness: not just displaying a quality, but being its living manifestation.

Embodiment is a physical form given to something abstract. A person can be the embodiment of a quality: {She was the embodiment of grace}. A document or system can be the embodiment of principles: {The Constitution is the embodiment of democratic ideals}. The word suggests that an abstraction has become concrete and visible—incarnated in a particular person, object, or form.

Embody means to give a body to something abstract or intangible, making it concrete or visible. A person can embody a quality like grace or courage by expressing it so fully that they seem to be its physical form: {She embodies everything I admire about the profession}. Ideas, principles, or values can be embodied in documents, institutions, or works of art: {The Constitution embodies the founders' vision of democracy}. To embody also means simply to include or contain: {The report embodies all our findings from the past year}.

Embodying is the present participle of embody—to give physical or concrete form to something abstract. A constitution embodies the principles of a nation. A person can embody grace, evil, or the spirit of an era: {She was the embodiment of elegance}. The word suggests that an idea or quality has found its fullest expression in a particular form: {The building embodies everything wrong with modern architecture}.

To embolden is to give someone courage or confidence to act: {Emboldened by the crowd's cheers, she spoke up}. Success emboldens further risk-taking; so does anonymity, alcohol, or backing from powerful allies. The word implies overcoming hesitation—you embolden someone who might otherwise hold back.

Emboldened means made bolder or more confident, typically by some encouraging circumstance: {Emboldened by her early success, she took on bigger challenges}. The word usually describes someone who, having received validation or perceived weakness in opposition, now acts with greater daring than before: {The protesters, emboldened by the lack of police response, pushed past the barricades}.

To emboss is to raise a design or pattern from a surface, creating a three-dimensional effect you can see and feel. Letters, logos, or decorative patterns are embossed on leather, paper, metal, or fabric: {The invitation was embossed with gold lettering}. The opposite technique—pressing a design into a surface—is debossing.

Embossed describes a surface with a raised design or pattern pressed into it from behind or below. The technique creates dimensional decoration that stands out from the background: {embossed leather}, {embossed stationery}, {an embossed seal on the diploma}. The opposite effect—pressed inward—is debossed.

Embossing is the process of creating raised designs on a surface by pressing from behind or using dies. Paper, leather, metal, and fabric can all be embossed: {The wedding invitation featured elegant embossing}. The technique produces texture you can feel—letters, patterns, or images that stand out from the material. The opposite process, creating indented designs, is debossing.

To embrace is to hold someone in your arms, typically as a greeting or expression of affection: {They embraced at the airport}. The noun is the act itself: {a warm embrace}. Figuratively, to embrace something is to accept or adopt it willingly: {embrace change}, {embrace a new philosophy}. An embrace can also mean inclusion: {a theory that embraces multiple disciplines}.

Embraced is the past tense of embrace. To embrace is to hold someone in your arms, typically as a greeting or expression of affection: {They embraced at the airport}. Figuratively, to embrace something is to accept or adopt it willingly: {She embraced the opportunity}, {He embraced minimalism}. An embraced idea or practice has been warmly accepted.

Embraces are acts of holding someone closely in one's arms, typically expressing affection, greeting, or comfort: {They shared a long embrace before parting}. The word extends to acceptance or adoption: {her embrace of minimalism}, {the company's embrace of new technology}. As a verb form, embraces means either hugs or willingly accepts: {She embraces challenges}.

Embracing is the act of holding someone in your arms, typically as a sign of affection or greeting. More often, embracing describes accepting or adopting something willingly: {embracing change}, {embracing new technology}, {embracing uncertainty}. The figurative sense suggests welcoming rather than resisting: {The company is embracing remote work}.

Embroider is to decorate fabric with needlework, creating patterns or images by stitching thread into cloth. The craft ranges from simple monograms to elaborate tapestries. The figurative sense extends naturally: to embroider a story is to add decorative details that weren't originally there, enhancing it beyond plain truth. {She tends to embroider her childhood memories.} The noun embroidery covers both the craft and its products.

Embroidered describes fabric decorated with needlework—patterns or images stitched into cloth: {an embroidered pillowcase}, {embroidered flowers on the collar}. Figuratively, an embroidered story or account has been elaborated with invented details, often to make it more interesting or flattering: {His war stories grew more embroidered with each telling}.

Embroidering is the act of decorating fabric with needle and thread, creating patterns or images through stitching. The figurative sense means adding invented details to a story or account: {He couldn't help embroidering the tale with each retelling}. Both senses share the idea of adding ornamental flourishes to something that exists.

Embroiders is the third-person singular of embroider. To embroider is to decorate fabric with needlework—stitching patterns, designs, or images onto cloth: {She embroiders pillowcases with flowers}. Figuratively, to embroider is to embellish a story with invented details: {He embroiders the truth until it's unrecognizable}.

Embroidery is decorative needlework—patterns or pictures stitched onto fabric with thread. The craft ranges from simple monograms on handkerchiefs to elaborate tapestries. Figuratively, embroidery means adding fanciful details to a story: {His account of the fishing trip included considerable embroidery}.

Embroiled means deeply involved in a conflict, dispute, or difficult situation. The word suggests being caught up in something messy and hard to escape: {The company became embroiled in a legal battle}. You don't choose to be embroiled—you find yourself that way, often through circumstances beyond your control.

An embryo is an organism in its earliest stage of development, before it has taken recognizable form. In humans, the term applies from fertilization through about eight weeks, after which it becomes a fetus. The word extends to anything in an undeveloped state: {The plan was still in embryo}. Embryonic means rudimentary or just beginning: {an embryonic democracy}.

Embryonic describes something in its earliest stage of development, like an embryo. An embryonic {idea} or embryonic {plan} exists only in rudimentary form, not yet fully shaped: {The project is still embryonic—we haven't worked out the details}. In biology, embryonic refers specifically to the embryo stage of development: {embryonic stem cells}, {embryonic tissue}.

Embryos is the plural of embryo—an organism in its earliest stages of development, before birth or hatching. In humans, the term applies from fertilization through about eight weeks, after which it becomes a fetus. The word appears frequently in discussions of fertility treatment {frozen embryos}, stem cell research, and abortion debates. Figuratively, something in embryo exists only in rudimentary form: {The plan was still in embryo}.

An emcee is the host or master of ceremonies at an event—someone who introduces performers, makes announcements, and keeps things moving: {The emcee warmed up the crowd before the main act}. In hip-hop, emcee (also MC) specifically means a rapper. The spelling reflects the pronunciation of the initials M.C. As a verb, to emcee is to serve in this role.

Emceed is the past tense of emcee, meaning to act as master of ceremonies—introducing performers, keeping an event moving, and engaging the audience. The verb comes from pronouncing the initials M.C.: {She emceed the awards show last night}. {He's emceed dozens of weddings}.

Emceeing is serving as master of ceremonies—hosting an event, introducing performers, and keeping things moving. The term comes from pronouncing the abbreviation MC. {She's been emceeing comedy shows for years.} The role requires stage presence, quick wit, and the ability to manage transitions between acts or segments.

Emcees is the plural of emcee, a person who hosts an event or introduces performers—the master of ceremonies. The term comes from pronouncing the initials M.C. In hip-hop, an emcee is a rapper, someone who delivers rhymes over beats. As a verb, to emcee is to serve as host: {She emcees the annual awards show}.

Emerald is a precious green gemstone, a variety of beryl colored by trace amounts of chromium. The color itself—a vivid, slightly bluish green—is called emerald: {emerald waters}, {emerald eyes}. Ireland is the Emerald Isle for its lush green landscape. In printing, emerald was a size of type between minion and nonpareil.

Emeralds is the plural of emerald, a green precious gemstone prized since antiquity. The color emerald green takes its name from the stone. Figuratively, emeralds can describe anything of that distinctive deep green: {The emeralds of the Irish countryside stretched before us}.

To emerge means to appear as a new phenomenon, or to become obvious or prominent: Problems emerged when we tried to start the engine. When emerge is followed by an adjective it works as a linking verb to show a result or outcome: The Greeks emerged victorious from the battle. Today, the participle emerging is often used in economic contexts to characterize growing financial systems: The fund is invested entirely in Asian emerging markets.

Emergence is the act or process of coming into view, existence, or notice. A celebrity makes a public emergence after years of seclusion. A butterfly's emergence from its cocoon marks its transformation. In philosophy and science, emergence describes how complex properties arise from simpler components—consciousness emerging from neural activity, or traffic patterns from individual drivers. {The emergence of social media changed political discourse.}

Emergencies is the plural of emergency—urgent situations requiring immediate action. The word appears in contexts where multiple crises exist or might occur: {emergency room staff see all kinds of emergencies}, {the kit contains supplies for emergencies}. An emergency {fund} or emergency {plan} prepares for such situations generally.

An emergency is a serious, unexpected situation requiring immediate action. Medical emergencies threaten life or health. A {state of emergency} grants governments special powers during crises. Emergency serves as an adjective for things used in urgent situations: emergency {exit}, emergency {room}, emergency {fund}. {In case of emergency, break glass.}

Emergent describes something in the process of coming into being or becoming visible. An emergent {democracy} is newly forming. Emergent {technologies} are just appearing. In philosophy and science, emergent properties arise from complex systems but cannot be predicted from their components alone—consciousness emerging from neurons, traffic jams from individual drivers. {Emergent behavior in the flock surprised researchers.}

Emerging describes something in the process of coming into view or existence. An emerging {trend} is just becoming noticeable. Emerging {markets} are economies transitioning from developing to developed status. An emerging {artist} is gaining recognition but not yet established. The word captures that moment between obscurity and prominence—visible but not yet fully formed.

An emigrant is a person who leaves their country to settle elsewhere. The word emphasizes departure—you're an emigrant from the place you leave, an immigrant to the place you arrive. {My grandfather was an emigrant from Poland.} The term often appears in historical contexts: {The emigrants crossed the prairie in covered wagons.}

Emigrants are people who leave their home country to settle elsewhere. The word emphasizes departure rather than arrival—the same person is an emigrant from one country and an immigrant to another. {The emigrants boarded ships bound for America.} {Many emigrants never saw their homeland again.}

To emigrate is to leave one's country to settle permanently in another. The word emphasizes departure from the homeland rather than arrival at the destination: {My grandparents emigrated from Poland in 1923}. Compare with immigrate, which emphasizes entering the new country. People emigrate from somewhere and immigrate to somewhere, though the distinction blurs in casual usage.

Emigrating is leaving one's country to settle permanently in another. The word emphasizes departure from the homeland rather than arrival at the destination—you emigrate *from* somewhere: {My grandparents emigrated from Poland in 1920}. Compare immigrate, which emphasizes arrival, and migrate, which is neutral about direction.

Emigration is the act of leaving one's country to settle in another. The word emphasizes departure rather than arrival—you emigrate *from* somewhere: {Her grandparents' emigration from Poland saved them from the Holocaust}. Compare immigration, which focuses on entering a new country. Mass emigrations often follow war, famine, or political upheaval.

An emigre is someone who has left their home country, typically for political reasons. The word carries connotations of forced departure or exile rather than voluntary relocation: {Russian emigres who fled after the Revolution}, {Cuban emigres in Miami}. The term suggests maintaining cultural ties to the homeland while living abroad. Also spelled émigré.

Emigres are people who have left their home country, typically for political reasons. The term carries connotations of exile or flight rather than voluntary relocation—emigres often cannot safely return. Originally applied to French aristocrats fleeing the Revolution, it now describes any politically displaced group: {Cuban emigres in Miami}, {Russian emigres in Paris}. Also spelled émigrés.

Eminence is a position of superiority or distinction, especially in a particular field: {a scholar of great eminence}, {She achieved eminence in her profession}. The word can also mean a piece of high ground—a hill or rise. As a title of address, {Your Eminence} or {His Eminence} refers to a Roman Catholic cardinal.

An emir is a Muslim ruler, prince, or military commander. The title has been used across the Islamic world for leaders of varying rank—from provincial governors to heads of state. Today it most commonly refers to rulers of certain Gulf states: {the Emir of Kuwait}, {the Emir of Qatar}. Also spelled amir.

An emirate is a territory ruled by an emir—an Islamic prince or commander. The term appears most often in reference to the United Arab Emirates, a federation of seven such territories on the Arabian Peninsula. Historically, emirates were common political units across the Islamic world: {The emirate maintained its independence for two centuries}.

Emirates is the plural of emirate, a territory ruled by an emir—an Arab prince or commander. The term appears most often in the United Arab Emirates, a federation of seven emirates on the Arabian Peninsula: {Dubai is one of the emirates}. Emirates also refers to the Dubai-based airline, one of the world's largest carriers.

Emissaries are people sent on a mission, typically to represent or advance the interests of a government, organization, or leader. The word carries a sense of official delegation: {The president dispatched emissaries to negotiate a ceasefire}. Emissaries may operate openly as diplomats or quietly as intermediaries. The singular is emissary.

An emissary is a person sent on a mission to represent or advance the interests of another—typically a government, organization, or leader. The role suggests diplomacy and negotiation: {The president dispatched an emissary to negotiate the ceasefire}. Unlike an ambassador with permanent posting, an emissary usually handles a specific task or message.

Emission is the act of sending something out or the thing that is sent out. The word appears most often in environmental contexts, where emissions refers to gases and particles released into the atmosphere, especially from vehicles and industrial processes: {The new regulations aim to reduce carbon emissions}. In physics, emission describes the release of energy, light, or particles from a source. The verb emit produces this noun, and both share the sense of something flowing outward from an origin point.

Emissions are substances released into the environment, especially gases discharged into the atmosphere. The word appears most often in environmental contexts: {carbon emissions}, {greenhouse gas emissions}, {vehicle emissions}. Emissions standards regulate what factories and cars can release. The singular emission refers to any act of sending something out—light, sound, radiation, or bodily fluids.

To emit is to send forth or give off. Light sources emit light, factories emit pollutants, speakers emit sound. The word applies to anything released outward from a source: {The engine emitted a strange grinding noise}. Emit suggests continuous or repeated release rather than a single burst—radiation emits steadily, a person emits a gasp only in the moment.

Emmental is a mild Swiss cheese with characteristic large holes formed by gas bubbles during aging. The pale yellow cheese has a slightly nutty, buttery flavor and melts well, making it popular in fondue and sandwiches. Named for the Emme Valley in Switzerland, it's sometimes spelled emmenthal or called Swiss cheese generically: {a slice of emmental on rye}. (Capitalized Emmental refers to the Swiss region.)

Emo is a style of rock music characterized by emotional, confessional lyrics and a melodic punk sound that emerged in the 1980s and peaked in mainstream popularity in the 2000s. The term extends to the associated subculture—dark clothing, side-swept hair, eyeliner, and an aesthetic embracing melancholy and sensitivity: {She went through an emo phase in high school}. Often used dismissively for anything perceived as overly emotional or dramatic: {Stop being so emo about it}.

An emoji is a small digital image used in electronic communication to convey emotion, tone, or meaning—a smiley face, a thumbs up, a heart. The term comes from Japanese for "picture character." Unlike emoticons made from punctuation :), emojis are standardized graphics built into keyboards and platforms. They range from facial expressions to animals, foods, flags, and abstract symbols: {She responded with three crying-laughing emojis}. Plural: emoji or emojis.

Emojis is the plural of emoji—the small pictographic characters used in digital communication to convey emotion, tone, or meaning: {She replied with a string of emojis}. Hearts, faces, and hand gestures are among the most common. Emojis help signal intent where text alone might seem flat or ambiguous: {Added some emojis so she'd know I was joking}.

Emos is the plural of emo, referring to people associated with the emo subculture—characterized by emotional sensitivity, introspective or melancholic music, and a distinctive aesthetic featuring dark clothing, side-swept hair, and heavy eyeliner. The term often carries dismissive or mocking overtones: {The emos were hanging out behind the school}.

To emote is to express emotion, especially in an exaggerated or theatrical way: {The actor emoted wildly during the death scene}. The word often carries a faintly mocking tone, suggesting performative rather than genuine feeling. In online contexts, an emote is a small image or animation expressing emotion—a smiley face, a dancing figure, a crying emoji.

Emotes are small images or animations used in online communication, especially on gaming platforms and streaming services like Twitch. They function like emoji but are platform-specific and often feature faces, characters, or inside jokes from internet culture: {Chat was spamming emotes during the stream}. The verb emote means to express emotion dramatically, often with theatrical exaggeration: {She emoted wildly during her monologue}.

An emoticon is a small picture made from keyboard characters to express emotion in text, such as :-) for a smile or :-( for sadness. The term blends "emotion" and "icon." Emoticons emerged in early internet communication when text lacked tone cues. They've been largely supplanted by emoji—actual images rather than character combinations—though the terms are often confused.

Emoticons are combinations of keyboard characters used to convey emotion or tone in text, typically read sideways: :-) for a smile, :-( for a frown, ;-) for a wink. The term blends *emotion* and *icon*. Emoticons emerged in early internet communication to clarify intent where tone of voice was absent. They've been largely supplanted by emoji—actual pictographic images—though the terms are often confused.

Emoting is acting out emotions in an exaggerated or theatrical way, often with the suggestion of insincerity or overperformance: {She spent the whole scene emoting rather than acting}. The word carries a faintly dismissive tone—genuine feeling doesn't need to be performed. In online spaces, emoting refers to using emotes or emoticons to express reactions.

Emotion is a mental state arising in response to circumstances—joy, anger, fear, sadness, love, disgust. Emotions are distinguished from thoughts (which are cognitive) and sensations (which are physical), though all three intertwine. Someone {full of emotion} is visibly moved. An {emotional person} feels things strongly or expresses feelings readily. To {show emotion} is to let inner states become visible; to {hide emotion} is to suppress that display.

Emotional describes something relating to or arising from feelings rather than reason: {an emotional response}, {emotional support}. A person who is emotional experiences feelings intensely or expresses them readily—sometimes admirably ({She gave an emotional speech}), sometimes dismissively ({Don't get so emotional}). The word can suggest someone is being irrational, particularly when applied to women, where it often carries sexist undertones.

Emotionless describes someone or something showing no emotion—no joy, anger, fear, or sadness. An emotionless {face} reveals nothing. An emotionless {voice} stays flat and uninflected. The word often suggests coldness or detachment: {She delivered the news in an emotionless tone}. Robots and psychopaths are stereotypically emotionless.
clues: Like a face carved in stone

definition: Emotions are feelings that arise in response to experiences, thoughts, or situations—joy, anger, fear, sadness, love, disgust. The word often distinguishes feeling from thinking: {Don't let your emotions cloud your judgment}. Someone {in touch with their emotions} acknowledges and understands their feelings. To {show emotion} is to display feeling outwardly, especially in contexts where restraint is expected.

An empanada is a pastry turnover with a savory or sweet filling, folded and sealed before baking or frying. Fillings vary by region—beef, chicken, cheese, vegetables, or fruit. The dish is ubiquitous across Latin America and Spain, with each country claiming distinctive versions: {We grabbed empanadas from the food truck}.

Empanadas are pastries made by folding dough around a filling and baking or frying. The filling varies by region—beef, chicken, cheese, vegetables, or fruit. Common throughout Latin America and Spain, each country has distinctive styles: Argentine empanadas differ from Chilean, which differ from Colombian. {We ordered a dozen empanadas for the party.}

An empath is someone who feels others' emotions intensely, as if absorbing them. The term gained currency in science fiction and New Age spirituality, describing people who claim heightened sensitivity to others' mental states: {As an empath, crowded rooms exhaust me}. Often used loosely for anyone highly attuned to others' feelings.

Empathetic describes someone who feels or understands what another person is experiencing—who can put themselves in someone else's position: {She's an empathetic listener}. The word overlaps almost entirely with empathic, though empathetic is more common in everyday speech. {He gave me an empathetic nod when I described my frustration}.

Empathise is the British spelling of empathize—to understand and share another person's feelings or perspective. To empathise requires imaginative effort: {I tried to empathise with what she was going through}. The word implies emotional connection rather than mere intellectual understanding.

To empathize is to understand and share another person's feelings—to imaginatively enter their emotional experience. Unlike sympathy, which observes suffering from outside, empathy attempts to feel it from within: {I could empathize with her frustration after going through something similar}. The ability to empathize is considered fundamental to human connection and moral behavior.

Empathizing is the act of understanding or sharing another person's feelings—putting yourself in their position emotionally. It differs from sympathizing, which maintains more distance: you can sympathize with someone's loss without feeling their grief yourself. {She spent the afternoon empathizing with her friend's frustration.} Also spelled empathising in British English.

Empaths are people who believe they absorb or directly feel the emotions of others, beyond ordinary empathy. The term comes from science fiction but has been adopted by self-help and spiritual communities to describe those who consider themselves unusually sensitive to emotional atmospheres: {As an empath, I find crowds exhausting}. Skeptics regard the concept as pseudoscientific, noting that everyone experiences some emotional contagion.

Empathy is a noun describing the ability to imagine another person’s feelings or attitudes, based on your experience of your own feelings. It is thought to be a key component of being human and people who are unable to feel empathy are usually regarded as pathological or developmentally disabled. The most common preposition after empathy is for, but with and toward are also seen: Her empathy for her subjects makes her photographs compelling. The nearest synonym of empathy is compassion.

An emperor is the male ruler of an empire—a sovereign who reigns over multiple territories or peoples. The title historically ranked above king, suggesting broader dominion: {the Roman emperor}, {the Emperor of Japan}. Emperor can describe anyone exercising supreme power in a domain: {He was emperor of his own little kingdom}. The emperor penguin is the largest penguin species.

Emperors is the plural of emperor, a male sovereign who rules an empire—a domain larger or more powerful than a kingdom. Historically, emperors held supreme authority over vast territories: {the emperors of Rome}, {Chinese emperors}. The emperor penguin, the largest penguin species, takes its name from this sense of supremacy.

Emphasis is special stress or importance given to something. In speech, emphasis falls on particular words or syllables to highlight meaning: {She put emphasis on the word "never"}. In writing, emphasis comes through italics, repetition, or structure. More broadly, emphasis indicates where attention or priority lies: {The company's emphasis on customer service}, {with emphasis on practical skills}.

Emphasise is the British spelling of emphasize, meaning to give special importance or prominence to something. You emphasise a point by stressing it, repeating it, or calling attention to it: {She emphasised the need for caution}. The word works for verbal stress, written highlighting, or any form of drawing attention to something significant.

When you emphasize something, you stress its importance: All speakers emphasized the need for us to decide the matter today. When the subject of emphasize is not a person or other agent, it means to show the importance or truth of: These victories emphasize the fact that the team has overcome its earlier difficulties with defense.

Emphatic means strongly expressed or showing emphasis. An emphatic {denial} leaves no room for doubt. An emphatic {victory} is decisive, not narrow. The word describes both the manner of expression and the person expressing it: {She was emphatic that we arrive on time}. To do something emphatically is to do it with force or conviction.

An empire is most strictly the domain under the rule of an emperor. In common usage, an empire is any extensive territory under single rule that is not geographically continuous, such as the one-time British Empire. When empire is capitalized, it is typically preceded or contextualized by a specifying adjective (the Roman Empire). Figuratively, an empire is any vast entity that exerts great influence: Amazon has a global business empire. Empire is also a women’s fashion style featuring a waistline under the bust.

Empires is the plural of empire—a group of nations or territories under a single authority, typically an emperor or empress. The word evokes vast scale and central control: {the Roman Empire}, {the British Empire}. Empire extends to dominant commercial entities: {a real estate empire}, {a media empire}. {Empires rise and fall.}

Empirical is an adjective that means based on or derived from observation of facts. It can be contrasted with theoretical (based on ideas) or speculative (based on imagination). Empirical is an important word in science and often precedes the word evidence, even though that combination is somewhat redundant: Empirical evidence shows that farmers often adopt parts of new technology rather than the whole. An empirical study or empirical research is based on experiments designed to allow for observation of facts.

Empiricism is the philosophical position that knowledge comes from sensory experience rather than innate ideas or pure reason. The doctrine holds that we learn about the world through observation and experiment, not through armchair speculation. Empiricism underlies the scientific method and opposes rationalism, which trusts reason over experience. {British empiricism shaped Enlightenment thought.}

To employ is to put something to use or to hire someone for work. You employ {strategies}, {methods}, or {tools} to accomplish tasks. An employer employs workers; those workers are employees in that employer's employ. {The factory employs three hundred people.} {She employed every trick she knew to win him over.}

Employed means having a job or being put to use. Someone who is employed works for wages or salary: {She's been employed at the hospital for ten years}. The word also describes things being utilized: {Every available resource was employed in the search}. The employed, as a noun, refers collectively to people who have jobs, often contrasted with the unemployed.

An employee is a person who works for another person or organization in exchange for wages or salary. The term implies a formal arrangement: employees typically have set hours, receive benefits, and work under supervision, distinguishing them from contractors or freelancers. {The company has over five hundred employees.} {She's been an employee here for ten years.}

An employer is a person or organization that hires workers and pays them for their labor. The term emphasizes the relationship from the hiring side: {Her employer offers good benefits}. Employer appears frequently in legal and HR contexts—employer contributions, employer liability, employer of record. The relationship implies ongoing work arrangements rather than one-time transactions.

Employers are people or organizations that hire workers and pay them for their labor. The term emphasizes the relationship from the hiring side: {Employers must withhold taxes from employee paychecks}. It appears frequently in legal and workplace contexts: {The employer violated safety regulations}. A single business is an employer; collectively, employers shape labor markets and working conditions.

Employment is the state of having paid work, or the work itself: {She found employment at a law firm}. It also refers to the act of using something: {the employment of new teaching methods}. The term often appears in economic and policy contexts: {employment rate}, {full employment}, {employment opportunities}.

An emporium is a large retail store offering a wide variety of goods. The word suggests abundance and old-fashioned commercial grandeur—think of a Victorian department store or a merchant's trading house. Today it often appears in shop names aiming for nostalgic charm: {Hank's Hardware Emporium}. The plural is emporia or emporiums.

Empower means to give someone authority or power to do something: {The new law empowers regulators to impose fines}. More commonly, it describes building confidence or capability in people who lack it: {The program empowers young women to pursue careers in science}. This second sense became prominent in self-help and social justice contexts during the late twentieth century, sometimes attracting criticism for overuse.

Empowered describes having been given power, authority, or confidence. Someone empowered to act has official authorization: {The board empowered her to negotiate on their behalf}. More often, empowered suggests a psychological state—feeling capable and in control: {The workshop left participants feeling empowered}. This softer sense dominates contemporary usage, appearing in self-help, marketing, and corporate contexts until the word risks meaning little more than "good about oneself."

Empowering describes something that gives people confidence, authority, or capability to act on their own behalf. An empowering {experience} builds self-assurance; empowering {legislation} grants rights or resources to marginalized groups. The word often appears in contexts of personal development, social justice, and workplace culture: {She found the workshop empowering}. Sometimes overused to the point of losing meaning.

Empowerment is the process of gaining power, authority, or confidence—or of granting these to others. The word appears frequently in discussions of social justice, workplace dynamics, and self-help: {women's empowerment}, {employee empowerment}, {personal empowerment}. Critics sometimes dismiss the term as corporate or political jargon, but it remains widely used to describe giving people control over their own circumstances.

An empress is a female sovereign ruling an empire, or the wife or widow of an emperor. The title historically carried immense power and prestige: {Catherine the Great was empress of Russia}. Figuratively, empress describes a woman who dominates her sphere: {She was the empress of Broadway during its golden age}.

Empresses is the plural of empress, a woman who rules an empire or the wife of an emperor. The term appears in historical contexts—{the empresses of Russia}, {the empresses of Rome}—and occasionally in figurative use for women who dominate their domains: {the empresses of fashion}.

Emptiness is the state of containing nothing or being devoid of content. A room's emptiness strikes you when the furniture is gone. The word extends to emotional hollowness—the emptiness after a loss, the emptiness of a meaningless routine. {She felt a profound emptiness after her children left home.} Emptiness can also describe futility: {the emptiness of his promises}.

Empty describes something with nothing inside. An empty {container}, {room}, or {stomach} lacks contents. Empty {streets} have no people. Empty {words} or {promises} lack substance or sincerity. To empty is to remove contents: {She emptied her pockets}. Figuratively, to {feel empty} is to experience emotional hollowness or absence of meaning.

Emptyhanded means without bringing or taking anything. You arrive emptyhanded at a party when you forget to bring a gift. You leave emptyhanded when a search or negotiation yields nothing: {The police searched the house but came away emptyhanded}. Also spelled empty-handed.

An emu is a large flightless bird native to Australia, second only to the ostrich in size. Emus have shaggy gray-brown plumage, long necks, and powerful legs built for running. They're farmed for meat, oil, and leather: {Emu oil is marketed as a skin treatment}. (Uppercase EMU is the European monetary union.)

Emulate means to try to equal or surpass by imitation. A young athlete might emulate a sports hero's training regimen. The word suggests admiration—you emulate those you respect: {She emulated her mentor's teaching style}. In computing, to emulate is to replicate another system's functions, allowing software designed for one platform to run on another.

Emulated is the past tense of emulate, meaning to imitate with effort to equal or surpass. A younger sibling might have {emulated an older one's success in school}. In computing, emulated describes software or hardware that mimics another system: {The program emulated a vintage arcade machine}.

Emulating is trying to match or surpass someone or something admired. A young player emulating a sports hero copies their technique and approach. In computing, emulating means mimicking another system's functions—software that emulates a vintage game console lets you play old games on modern hardware. {She grew up emulating her older sister's style.}

Emulation is the effort to match or surpass someone or something, usually through imitation of their qualities or achievements. A young athlete might study a champion's technique in emulation of their success. In computing, emulation refers to software or hardware that mimics another system, allowing programs designed for one platform to run on a different one: {I use an emulator to play old Nintendo games on my laptop}. The verb emulate captures both senses—striving to equal and technically replicating.

An emulator is software or hardware that mimics another system, allowing programs designed for one platform to run on a different one. Video game emulators let you play old console games on modern computers: {I use an emulator to play Nintendo 64 games on my laptop}. The term extends to anyone who emulates—imitates or tries to equal—another person, though this sense is less common.

Emulators are software programs that mimic other systems, allowing one device to behave like another. A Super Nintendo emulator lets you play old cartridge games on a modern computer. Phone emulators let developers test apps without physical devices. The term extends to hardware that replicates other hardware's functions. {I downloaded an emulator to play GameBoy games on my laptop.}
clues: Software pretending to be something else

definition: Emus are large flightless birds native to Australia, second only to ostriches in size. They have shaggy gray-brown feathers, long necks, and powerful legs built for running. The plural follows standard English rules: {We spotted several emus in the outback}. Singular: emu.

Enable means to make something possible or give someone the ability to do something: {The scholarship enabled her to attend college}. It often appears in technical contexts—enabling a feature turns it on. In psychology, to enable someone is to facilitate their harmful behavior, especially addiction, by removing consequences or providing resources that allow the behavior to continue.

Enabled is the past tense and participle of enable, meaning to make something possible or to give someone the ability or authority to do something. In technology contexts, enabled describes a feature or setting that has been switched on or made active: {Make sure Bluetooth is enabled}. The word often appears in compound forms like {voice-enabled} or {Wi-Fi-enabled} to indicate built-in capability. Someone who is enabled has been given the means or permission to act, though in psychological contexts, enabling someone often carries negative connotations of supporting harmful behavior.

An enabler is someone who makes something possible, often with the connotation of facilitating harmful behavior. In psychology and addiction contexts, an enabler shields someone from the consequences of destructive actions—covering for an alcoholic spouse, lending money to a gambler: {His mother was his chief enabler, bailing him out every time}. The term can also be neutral, describing anyone who helps others accomplish goals: {a great enabler of young talent}.

Enablers are people or things that make something possible. The word carries a negative connotation when describing those who facilitate destructive behavior—particularly addiction—by shielding someone from consequences: {His family were enablers who kept bailing him out}. In neutral contexts, enablers simply allow or support an activity: {Technology has been an enabler of remote work}.

Enabling means making something possible or giving someone the power to do something: {The grant enabled her to finish her research}. In psychology, enabling describes behavior that allows someone to continue destructive patterns—particularly addiction—by shielding them from consequences: {His parents kept enabling him by paying his rent}. Enabling technology or legislation creates conditions for further development.

To enact is to make into law: {Congress enacted new tax legislation}. The word emphasizes the formal, official process of passing legislation rather than merely proposing it. Enact also means to act out or perform: {The children enacted scenes from their favorite movie}. This theatrical sense connects to the legal one—both involve bringing something into being through formal action.

Enactment is the process of passing a law or the law itself once passed: {The enactment of new regulations took months}. More broadly, enactment means acting something out—performing or representing it: {a dramatic enactment of the battle}, {the enactment of a ritual}. Both senses share the idea of making something real through formal action.

Enamel is a hard, glossy coating. The outermost layer of teeth is enamel—the hardest substance in the human body. Enamel is also a glassy coating fused onto metal, pottery, or glass by heat, used decoratively or for protection: {enamel jewelry}, {enamel cookware}. Enamel paint dries to a similar hard, shiny finish. To enamel is to coat with enamel.

Enamels are glossy, hard coatings—either the vitreous material fused onto metal, glass, or pottery by heat, or the paint that dries to a similar hard finish: {She painted the trim with white enamel}. Tooth enamel is the hard outer layer protecting the crown. As a verb, to enamel is to coat with such a finish: {enameled jewelry}, {enameled cookware}.

Enamored means filled with love or deep admiration. You can be enamored of a person, idea, or thing: {She was enamored of the old house from the moment she saw it}. The word suggests strong attraction that may cloud judgment—being enamored doesn't guarantee the feeling is warranted. Often used with "of" or "with": {He's not enamored with the idea of moving}.

Enamour means to inspire love or strong affection in someone. The word appears almost exclusively in passive constructions: {She was enamoured of the old house}, {He became enamoured with the idea of sailing around the world}. The prepositions of and with both work. Enamour is the British spelling; Americans write enamor.

Enamoured means filled with love or deep admiration for someone or something. The word usually appears with "of" or "with": {He was enamoured of her from their first meeting}, {She's not enamoured with the idea of moving}. The British spelling uses -our; American English prefers enamored. The word carries a slightly literary or formal tone, suggesting infatuation or strong attraction rather than mere liking.

Enby is a phonetic spelling of NB, short for nonbinary—a person whose gender identity falls outside the male/female binary. The term emerged from online communities as a noun parallel to boy and girl: {I'm not a guy or a girl, I'm an enby}. Some nonbinary people embrace the label; others find it too cutesy or infantilizing.

An encampment is a place where a group of people have set up tents or temporary shelters, whether for military purposes, protest, or because they lack permanent housing. Military encampments are temporary bases established during operations or training. The term increasingly describes gatherings of unhoused people in urban areas or protest camps like those on college campuses. {The encampment grew to over a hundred tents within a week.}

Encampments are places where groups of people have set up temporary shelter, typically tents or improvised structures. The word carries a military flavor from its original use for army camps, but now commonly describes homeless camps in urban areas or protest sites where demonstrators have established a presence. {Police cleared the encampments from the park.} {The refugee encampments stretched for miles along the border.} An encampment suggests something more established than simply camping—there's an implication of duration and collective purpose.

To encapsulate is to enclose something in a capsule or protective covering. The word extends readily to abstractions: to encapsulate an idea is to express it in condensed form, capturing its essence: {The phrase encapsulates everything wrong with modern politics}. In computing, encapsulation bundles data with the methods that operate on it, hiding internal complexity behind a simpler interface.

To encase is to enclose something completely in a covering or container: {The fossil was encased in rock}, {wires encased in plastic}. The word suggests tight, protective, or permanent enclosure—something sealed in rather than simply placed inside. Also spelled incase.

Encased means enclosed or surrounded by a covering, shell, or outer layer. Something encased is contained within a protective or decorative exterior: {The wires were encased in plastic tubing}, {a diamond encased in gold}. The word often suggests complete surrounding rather than partial coverage: {His leg was encased in a plaster cast}.

Enchant originally meant to cast a spell on someone, from the Latin for singing or chanting magical words. The literal sense persists in fantasy contexts: {The witch enchanted the prince}. More commonly now, enchant means to delight or captivate thoroughly: {The children were enchanted by the puppet show}. Someone enchanting possesses irresistible charm.

Enchanted describes something magical or under a spell: an enchanted {forest}, an enchanted {castle}. More commonly, it means delighted or captivated: {I was enchanted by the old town's narrow streets}. The formal phrase {enchanted to meet you} expresses pleasure at an introduction, though it sounds old-fashioned or affected in casual settings.

An enchanter is someone who casts spells or charms, typically in fantasy and folklore contexts: {The enchanter transformed the prince into a frog}. The word carries connotations of mysterious power and seduction rather than malevolence—enchanters beguile and captivate. Figuratively, anyone who charms or fascinates might be called an enchanter: {He was an enchanter on the piano}.

Enchanters are people who cast enchantments—magical spells that bewitch or captivate. The word appears most often in fantasy literature and fairy tales: {The enchanters gathered in the forest clearing}. By extension, anyone who charms or fascinates others might be called an enchanter: {He was one of the great enchanters of the silver screen}.

Enchanting describes something that captivates or delights as if by magic: {an enchanting smile}, {an enchanting melody}. The word suggests charm that holds attention and stirs wonder. A place, person, or performance can be enchanting when it produces a spell-like effect on the observer. The related verb enchant means to cast such a spell, literally or figuratively.

Enchantment is the state of being under a magical spell, or the act of casting one. Fairy tales feature enchantments that transform princes into frogs or put princesses to sleep. Extended to ordinary life, enchantment means captivated delight: {The garden held a certain enchantment at dusk}. To fall under someone's enchantment is to be utterly charmed by them.

Enchantments are magic spells or the states they produce—being under a spell, bewitched, charmed. The word extends to anything that captivates completely: {the enchantments of Paris}, {the enchantment of first love}. Something possessing enchantment holds you spellbound, whether through actual magic or metaphorical allure. In gaming, enchantments are magical properties applied to weapons or items.

An enchantress is a woman who casts spells or practices magic—a sorceress or witch. The word extends to any woman with an almost magical power to captivate: {She was an enchantress who held the whole room spellbound}. The suggestion is of irresistible allure or charm rather than literal sorcery.

An enchilada is a Mexican dish consisting of a tortilla rolled around a filling—typically meat, cheese, or beans—and covered with chili sauce. The phrase {the whole enchilada} means everything, the entire matter: {They wanted the whole enchilada, not just a partial settlement}. A {big enchilada} is an important person.

Enchiladas are a Mexican dish of tortillas rolled around a filling—typically meat, cheese, or beans—and covered with chili sauce. The dish is baked until the sauce soaks into the tortillas. {We ordered chicken enchiladas with green sauce.} The {whole enchilada} means the entirety of something: {They wanted the whole enchilada—house, furniture, everything}.

To encircle is to form a circle around something, surrounding it completely: {Enemy troops encircled the city}. The word suggests containment or embrace—arms encircle a loved one, mountains encircle a valley. It can imply entrapment or protection depending on context.

Encircled means surrounded or ringed, forming a circle around something: {The castle was encircled by a moat}. It often implies containment or being hemmed in: {Enemy forces encircled the town}. The word can describe physical arrangement or metaphorical situations: {encircled by admirers}, {encircled by debt}.
clues: Bounded by something on all sides

definition: An enclave is a territory entirely surrounded by another territory—a pocket of one country within another's borders, or a distinct area within a larger region. The word extends to any group or space set apart from its surroundings: {an ethnic enclave in the city}, {an enclave of wealth in a poor neighborhood}. The defining feature is isolation or distinctiveness within a surrounding whole.

Enclaves are distinct areas enclosed within larger, different surroundings. In geography, an enclave is territory entirely surrounded by another country: {Vatican City is an enclave within Italy}. The word extends to any community or district set apart by ethnicity, culture, or class: {an enclave of artists in the warehouse district}, {wealthy enclaves in the suburbs}. The defining feature is separation—a pocket of difference within a dominant whole.

Enclose means to surround or close in on all sides. A fence encloses a yard; mountains enclose a valley. To enclose something in a container is to put it inside: {She enclosed a check with the letter}. The word often appears in correspondence to indicate an attachment: {Please find the documents enclosed}. An enclosed space is shut off from the outside.

Enclosed means surrounded or contained within boundaries. An enclosed space has walls or barriers around it: {an enclosed porch}, {an enclosed courtyard}. When something is enclosed with a letter or package, it's included inside: {Please find the invoice enclosed}. The past participle often functions as an adjective describing spaces that feel contained or shut in.

An enclosure is a space that has been fenced or walled off: {The animals were kept in a large enclosure}. The word also refers to something included with a letter or package: {Please find the enclosure with your policy documents}. To enclose is to surround, contain, or include something within.

Enclosures are spaces bounded by walls, fences, or other barriers—a pen for livestock, a fenced yard, a walled garden. The word also refers to documents or objects included with a letter or package: {Please see the enclosures for more details}. In British history, the Enclosures were the legal process of converting common lands into private property, transforming rural life in the 18th and 19th centuries.

To encode is to convert information into a particular form or code. Data is encoded for transmission or storage; a message may be encoded to keep it secret. In computing, encoding translates characters into a format computers can process: {The file was encoded in UTF-8}. More broadly, experiences or meanings can be encoded in memory, symbols, or DNA. The opposite is decode.

Encoded means converted into a coded form. Information is encoded when transformed into a different format for transmission, storage, or secrecy: {The message was encoded before being sent}. DNA encodes genetic instructions. A video file is encoded for streaming. The word implies that decoding—reversing the process—is possible for those with the right key or method.

Encoding is the process of converting information from one form to another. In computing, encoding transforms data into a specific format—text into binary, video into a compressed file: {The encoding took several hours}. Character encoding determines how text is represented digitally (UTF-8, ASCII). More broadly, encoding refers to how the brain converts experiences into memory, or how messages get translated into signals for transmission.

The interjection Encore! is a request for continuation of a performance. When it succeeds, the audience gets an encore. By extension, encore is used to characterize actions that are viewed as a repetition or continuation of what has gone before: Fans are hoping for an encore of the previous score when the team plays next week. As a verb, encore usually means perform an encore: The band encored with new material.

Encores are additional performances given after the scheduled program ends, demanded by enthusiastic applause. The word comes from French for "again." At concerts, the encore is often anticipated—artists leave the stage knowing they'll return for one or two more songs. {The crowd cheered until the band came back for an encore.} Figuratively, an encore is any repeat performance: {Her second novel was an encore to her debut success.}

Encounter means to meet or come upon, often unexpectedly or in the course of doing something else. You might encounter an old friend at the grocery store or encounter difficulties while renovating your house. The noun encounter denotes such a meeting or experience: {a chance encounter with a celebrity}, {a close encounter with a bear}. In gaming and fantasy contexts, an encounter is a specific confrontation or battle that players must face.

Encounters are meetings or experiences, often unexpected or notable. You might have a {chance encounter} with an old friend, or a {close encounter} with danger. The word suggests something worth remarking on—routine interactions rarely qualify. As a verb, to encounter is to meet or come upon: {We encountered resistance at every turn}. An {encounter group} is a form of therapy emphasizing direct emotional exchange.
clues: Comes upon others without prior arrangement

definition: Encourage means to give someone confidence, hope, or support to do something: {Her teacher encouraged her to apply to medical school}. It can also mean to foster or promote: {Warm weather encourages plant growth}. The word suggests helping something along rather than forcing it—a gentle push rather than a shove.

Encouraged is the past tense of encourage, meaning to give someone confidence, hope, or support to do something. A teacher encourages a struggling student; a doctor encourages a patient to exercise more. To be encouraged is to feel hopeful or optimistic: {I'm encouraged by the early results}. Encouraged can also describe behavior that has been promoted or fostered: {The company encouraged innovation through flexible policies}.

Encouragement is support or confidence given to someone, boosting their resolve or spirits: {A few words of encouragement helped her get through the interview}. It can also mean something that promotes or fosters an activity: {Tax breaks served as encouragement for small businesses}. To give encouragement is to hearten; to offer it is often simply to approve.

Encouraging means giving hope, confidence, or support. An encouraging {word} lifts spirits; encouraging {news} suggests things may turn out well. To be encouraging is to foster someone's efforts: {Her teacher was encouraging about her writing}. Encouraging results or signs point toward a positive outcome: {The early data is encouraging}.

To encroach is to advance beyond proper limits, gradually intruding on someone else's territory, rights, or time. The word suggests creeping transgression rather than sudden invasion: {Development has encroached on the wetlands}. You can encroach on someone's privacy, on a neighbor's property, or on time reserved for other things. The noun is encroachment.

Encroached is the past tense of encroach, meaning to gradually intrude on someone's territory, rights, or time. The word implies a slow, often unnoticed advance beyond proper boundaries: {The sea had encroached on the coastline over decades}. {Work encroached on his weekends until he had no time left for family}.

Encroaching describes something that gradually intrudes or advances beyond proper limits. Development encroaches on wetlands; darkness encroaches as evening falls. The word often carries negative connotations of unwelcome intrusion: {the encroaching influence of social media on daily life}, {encroaching weeds threatening the garden}. What encroaches takes territory that isn't rightfully its own.

Encroachment is gradual intrusion into territory or rights that belong to someone else. A neighbor's fence encroaches when it crosses the property line. Government power encroaches on civil liberties. The sea encroaches on the coastline. In American football, encroachment is a penalty when a defensive player crosses the line of scrimmage before the snap. {The encroachment of development on wetlands continues despite regulations.}

Encrusted describes something covered with a hard layer or coating, typically built up over time. Jewels may be encrusted with smaller gems; a pan becomes encrusted with burnt residue; barnacles encrust a ship's hull. The coating is usually uneven, rough, or textured: {The old pipe was encrusted with mineral deposits}. The word often suggests neglect or age.

To encrypt is to convert information into a coded form that only authorized parties can read. The process protects sensitive data—passwords, messages, financial transactions—from interception: {The app encrypts all messages end-to-end}. Encrypted files require a key or password to decrypt and access. The adjective encrypted describes data in this protected state.

Encrypted describes information that has been converted into code to prevent unauthorized access. Digital communications, files, and storage devices are encrypted to protect sensitive data: {The messages were end-to-end encrypted}. Something encrypted requires a key or password to decode. The term applies broadly to any scrambled or encoded content: {an encrypted hard drive}, {encrypted emails}.

Encrypting is the process of converting information into a coded form that unauthorized parties cannot read. When you encrypt a file, message, or data stream, you transform it using an algorithm so that only someone with the proper key or password can decrypt it back to its original form. {Make sure you're encrypting sensitive documents before sending them.} The term applies broadly to digital security but also to any systematic scrambling of information to protect it from unwanted access.

Encryption is the process of encoding information so only authorized parties can read it. Data is transformed using an algorithm and key, rendering it unintelligible to anyone who intercepts it without the corresponding decryption key. Encryption protects everything from text messages to financial transactions: {The app uses end-to-end encryption}. {Make sure the website has encryption before entering your credit card}.

Encyclopaedias is the British spelling of the plural of encyclopaedia—comprehensive reference works containing articles on a wide range of subjects or on one field of knowledge: {The library had several encyclopaedias covering everything from art to zoology}. The American spelling is encyclopedias.

An encyclopedia is a comprehensive reference work containing articles on a wide range of subjects or covering one field in depth. Traditional encyclopedias arranged entries alphabetically across multiple volumes; digital versions now dominate. The word suggests authoritative, systematically organized knowledge: {She's a walking encyclopedia of baseball statistics}. {I looked it up in the encyclopedia}.

Encyclopedias are reference works containing articles on a wide range of subjects or on many aspects of a single field, typically arranged alphabetically. Before the internet, a set of encyclopedias—often sold door-to-door—was a household's primary research resource: {We looked it up in the encyclopedia}. Wikipedia has largely displaced print encyclopedias for general reference.

Encyclopedic describes knowledge that is vast and comprehensive, covering many subjects or one subject in exhaustive detail: {She has an encyclopedic knowledge of baseball statistics}. The word suggests the breadth and thoroughness of an encyclopedia. An encyclopedic {work} or {survey} aims to be complete and authoritative.

End is a very frequent noun and verb with several meanings corresponding to ideas of stop, last, and boundary: I was dead tired at the end of the day. Tie one end of the rope to a tree. She ended the service with a prayer. If you put or make an end to something, you cause it to stop: Peacekeeping troops were unable to put an end to the rioting. When you reach the end of something in time or space, you come to the point where there is no more.

To endanger is to put at risk of harm, damage, or destruction. The word often appears in contexts of safety and conservation: {Reckless driving endangers lives}. Species facing extinction are called endangered: {The bald eagle was once endangered but has recovered}.

Endangered describes something at serious risk of extinction or disappearance. The term applies most often to species whose populations have declined to critical levels: {The giant panda is no longer classified as endangered}. Conservation laws protect endangered animals and plants. The meaning extends to anything threatened with loss: {endangered languages}, {an endangered way of life}.

Endeared is the past tense of endear, meaning to cause someone to be loved or cherished. To endear yourself to someone is to win their affection, often through charm or kindness: {She endeared herself to the staff with her generosity}. Something that endears a person makes them more likable: {His self-deprecating humor endeared him to audiences}.

Endearing describes qualities that inspire affection or fondness in others. An endearing {smile}, an endearing {habit}, an endearing {awkwardness}—something that makes you like a person more, not less. The word often applies to minor flaws or quirks that charm rather than annoy: {His tendency to mispronounce words was oddly endearing}.

An endearment is a word or phrase expressing affection: {honey}, {sweetheart}, {my love}. The word also refers to the feeling itself or acts that inspire it: {small endearments that sustained their marriage}. Terms of endearment range from the universal to the private—couples often develop their own.

Endearments are words or phrases expressing affection. Terms of endearment include {honey}, {sweetheart}, {darling}, {baby}, and countless pet names couples invent for each other. The word also covers affectionate gestures more broadly: {whispered endearments}, {small endearments that kept the marriage alive}.

Endeavor is a formal word that is roughly synonymous with attempt and try. Like those two words, endeavor can act as a noun or a verb: Didn’t you endeavor to contact her again? We will take better equipment on our next endeavor to reach the summit. In referring to a project, endeavor can mean the equivalent of undertaking: They have a lot of venture capital supporting their latest endeavor. The British spelling of endeavor is endeavour.

Endeavors are earnest attempts or efforts to achieve something, typically requiring sustained work over time. The word carries a tone of seriousness and purpose that distinguishes it from casual trying: {Her endeavors in medical research spanned three decades}. As a verb, endeavor means to make a serious effort or attempt: {We will endeavor to respond within 48 hours}. The word appears more often in formal contexts and tends toward the aspirational rather than the mundane.

Endeavour is the British spelling of endeavor—to try earnestly or make a serious effort toward a goal: {We shall endeavour to finish by Friday}. As a noun, it refers to a purposeful undertaking or field of activity: {scientific endeavour}, {a worthy endeavour}. The word carries a slightly formal or literary tone, suggesting sustained effort rather than casual attempt.

Endeavours is the British spelling of endeavors, the plural noun and third-person verb form of endeavor. An endeavour is a serious attempt or effort toward a goal: {artistic endeavours}, {scientific endeavours}. To endeavour is to try earnestly: {She endeavours to treat everyone fairly}. The word carries a formal, slightly elevated tone compared to simply "try" or "effort."

Endgame is the final stage of a chess game, when few pieces remain and victory depends on precise maneuvering. The word extends to any concluding phase of a process, especially one involving strategy: {What's your endgame here?} {The negotiations entered their endgame}. It implies that earlier moves have shaped what's now possible.

Endgames is the plural of endgame—the final stage of a chess match when few pieces remain, or more broadly, the concluding phase of any strategic situation: {We're in the endgames of these negotiations}. The term implies that outcomes are becoming clearer and decisive moves are imminent.

An ending is the final part of something—a story, a relationship, a journey. It marks termination or conclusion: {The movie had a satisfying ending}, {the ending of an era}. In grammar, an ending is a suffix attached to a word: the -ing ending, the -ed ending. The ending of a word can signal tense, number, or part of speech.

Endings are the concluding portions of stories, events, or periods of time: {The movie's ending surprised everyone}. In grammar, an ending is a suffix that changes a word's form—the -ed that marks past tense, the -s that marks plural. Nerve endings are the terminal points where sensory nerves detect stimuli. Happy endings resolve satisfyingly; unhappy ones don't.

Endive is a leafy vegetable in the chicory family, eaten raw in salads or cooked. The term covers two distinct plants: curly endive, with frilly, slightly bitter leaves, and Belgian endive, a pale, torpedo-shaped head grown in darkness to keep it mild. {She added endive to the salad for some crunch.}

Endives are leafy vegetables of the chicory family, with a slightly bitter taste. The word covers two distinct plants: Belgian endive, a pale, torpedo-shaped head of tightly packed leaves grown in darkness, and curly endive (also called frisée), with frilly, loose leaves. Both appear in salads or can be braised. {She arranged the endive leaves around the dip.}

Endless means having no end—continuing indefinitely or seemingly forever. An endless {road} stretches beyond sight. Endless {possibilities} are unlimited. Often the word conveys weariness or frustration: {endless meetings}, {endless paperwork}, {the endless wait}. Something can be literally endless (a loop) or just feel that way.

Endlessly means without stopping or limit. Something that continues endlessly goes on indefinitely: {The meeting dragged on endlessly}. It often carries a sense of tedium or exhaustion—what feels endless may not literally be so: {She endlessly rehearsed the same arguments}. Endlessly can also suggest boundless capacity: {endlessly creative}, {endlessly patient}.

Endorphins are chemicals produced by the body that reduce pain and create feelings of pleasure or euphoria. The brain releases them during exercise, excitement, pain, or orgasm. The term comes from "endogenous morphine"—morphine made within. {Runner's high comes from endorphins.} {The massage triggered a rush of endorphins.}

Endorphins are chemicals produced naturally in the brain that reduce pain and create feelings of pleasure or euphoria. The body releases them during exercise, laughter, sex, and other activities—hence the term {runner's high}. They function similarly to opioid drugs but are manufactured internally: {My endorphins kicked in around mile three}.

To endorse is to give public approval or support: {The union endorsed the Democratic candidate}. Originally, to endorse meant to sign the back of a check or document, transferring rights or confirming receipt—a meaning that persists in banking. The extended sense of backing or recommending now dominates: {She endorsed the new policy}, {celebrity endorsements}. An endorsed product carries someone's public approval, often for payment.

Endorsed is the past tense of endorse, which means to give public approval or support to something or someone. Politicians seek endorsed status from newspapers, unions, and influential figures during campaigns. Products are endorsed by celebrities who lend their reputation to marketing efforts. A check is endorsed when the payee signs the back, authorizing its deposit or transfer. {The committee endorsed the proposal unanimously.} {She endorsed the check and handed it to the teller.}

Endorsement is approval or support, especially public backing of a person, product, or idea. A politician seeks endorsements from unions; a celebrity gives an endorsement to a brand. In business, endorsement also means signing the back of a check to transfer or deposit it: {She wrote her account number below her endorsement}. An insurance endorsement is an amendment to a policy.

Endorsements are statements of approval or support. A political endorsement is a public declaration backing a candidate: {The senator's endorsement boosted the campaign}. Product endorsements involve celebrities promoting brands for pay. On documents like checks, an endorsement is a signature authorizing transfer. In insurance, an endorsement modifies a policy's terms or coverage.

Endorses is the third-person singular of endorse, meaning to express public approval or support: {The senator endorses the proposed legislation}. A celebrity endorses a product by lending their name to it. To endorse a check is to sign the back, authorizing its transfer or deposit. The word implies putting one's reputation behind something.

Endorsing is expressing public support or approval for something or someone: {The union is endorsing the Democratic candidate}. It can also mean signing the back of a check to cash or deposit it, or adding one's signature to a document to validate it. A celebrity endorsing a product lends their name and reputation to promote it.

To endow is to provide with a quality, ability, or asset. Nature endows some people with unusual gifts: {She was endowed with a beautiful singing voice}. The word also means to fund permanently, especially institutions: endow a {university chair}, endow a {scholarship}. An endowment is both the act and the resulting fund. {Well-endowed} is a common euphemism for having large breasts or, of men, a large penis.

Endowed means provided with a quality, ability, or asset. Nature or circumstance does the providing: {She was endowed with a beautiful singing voice}, {a man generously endowed by nature}. When used alone about people, endowed often implies physical attributes—large breasts in women, a large penis in men. Institutions are endowed when given permanent funding: {an endowed professorship}, {a well-endowed university}.

An endowment is something given to provide ongoing support—typically a fund whose principal remains intact while its interest or returns fund an institution: {The university's endowment exceeds two billion dollars}. More broadly, endowment refers to natural gifts or qualities someone possesses: {Her musical endowment was evident from childhood}. In insurance, an endowment policy pays out after a set term or upon death. Informally, endowment is a euphemism for the size of a man's penis: {He's not lacking in the endowment department}.

Endowments are gifts or grants, typically money or property, given to an institution like a university or hospital to provide ongoing support. The principal remains invested while income funds operations: {The university's endowment grew to three billion dollars}. More broadly, endowments are natural qualities or talents someone possesses: {her intellectual endowments}. In informal use, endowments refers euphemistically to a woman's breasts or a man's genitals, usually implying impressive size.

Ends are the points where something terminates—the physical extremities of an object or the conclusion of an event: {the end of the road}, {the end of the movie}. Ends also means purposes or goals: {a means to an end}, {to what end?} To make ends meet is to earn enough to cover expenses. In football, ends are players positioned at the edge of the offensive or defensive line.

The endtimes are the final days of the world, particularly in religious traditions that prophesy apocalyptic events preceding divine judgment. Christian usage draws heavily on Revelation: {Many believe we're living in the endtimes}. The term appears in both sincere eschatological discourse and ironic commentary on current events: {This news cycle feels very endtimes}. Also spelled end times or end-times.

Endurance is the capacity to withstand hardship, strain, or prolonged effort without giving way. Physical endurance lets athletes complete marathons; mental endurance gets people through grief or tedious work. {Her endurance impressed everyone on the team.} Endurance events test how long participants can last rather than how fast they can go. The word implies not just surviving difficulty but maintaining function throughout it.

Endure means to bear something difficult or painful without giving way: {She endured years of chronic pain}. It also means to last or continue existing: {Their friendship endured for decades}. The two senses connect—what endures has withstood time or hardship. An enduring legacy persists; an enduring marriage survives its trials.

Endured is the past tense of endure, meaning to bear something difficult or painful over time. What is endured is typically unpleasant—hardship, suffering, criticism, boredom: {She endured years of chronic pain}. The word suggests persistence through adversity rather than passive suffering. Something that has endured has lasted or survived: {Their friendship endured despite the distance}.

Endures is the third-person singular form of endure, which means to continue existing despite hardship or to tolerate something difficult. When something endures, it lasts through time or adversity: {Their friendship endures after all these years}. When someone endures something, they bear it with patience: {She endures the pain without complaint}. The word suggests persistence in the face of difficulty rather than mere passive existence.

Enduring means lasting through time or hardship. An enduring {friendship} survives years and difficulties. An enduring {legacy} remains influential long after its origin. The word suggests not just duration but resilience—something that endures has withstood challenges: {Her enduring optimism surprised everyone who knew what she'd been through}.

The endzone is the area at each end of an American football field where touchdowns are scored. A player must carry or catch the ball in the opponent's endzone to score. The term extends to similar scoring areas in other sports like rugby and ultimate frisbee. Usually spelled as two words: {end zone}.

End zones are the rectangular areas at each end of an American or Canadian football field, extending ten yards beyond the goal line. Teams score touchdowns by carrying or catching the ball in the opponent's end zone. The term occasionally appears in other sports or metaphorically for any final destination: {We're in the end zone now—just need to close the deal}.
