An enema is a procedure in which liquid is injected into the rectum to stimulate bowel movement or deliver medication. The liquid itself is also called an enema. The practice serves medical purposes—relieving constipation, preparing for surgery or examination—but also appears in sexual contexts: {The nurse administered an enema before the colonoscopy}.

Enemies is the plural of enemy—those who oppose, threaten, or wish harm. The word covers personal antagonists {She made enemies at work}, military adversaries {The enemies surrounded the city}, and abstract forces {Stress and poor sleep are enemies of good health}. Unlike rivals, who compete for the same goal, enemies actively work against each other's interests.

An enemy is someone who opposes, threatens, or seeks to harm you. The term applies to personal adversaries, military opponents, or hostile nations: {They were childhood friends who became bitter enemies}. Enemy extends to abstract threats: {Sugar is the enemy of good health}. As an adjective, enemy describes hostile forces: {enemy territory}, {enemy fire}. The enemy can refer collectively to opposing forces in conflict.

Energetic describes someone or something full of energy, vigor, or enthusiasm. An energetic {person} tackles tasks with vitality; an energetic {performance} crackles with intensity. The word applies to activities requiring sustained effort: {an energetic workout}, {an energetic campaign}. In physics, energetic refers to high energy levels: {energetic particles}, {energetic radiation}.
clues: Like a battery that never drains

definition: Energies is the plural of energy, used when distinguishing types or sources: {renewable energies}, {creative energies}. Someone who {devotes their energies} to a cause directs sustained effort toward it. In physics, different energies—kinetic, potential, thermal—are measured separately. In spiritual contexts, energies may refer to forces or vibrations: {The room had strange energies}.

Energize means to give energy or vitality to something. Coffee energizes the tired, a speech energizes a crowd, and solar panels energize electrical systems. The word works for both physical and figurative invigoration: {The good news energized the team}. In technical contexts, to energize a circuit or device is to supply it with electrical power.

Energized means filled with energy or vitality. Someone who feels energized is alert, motivated, and ready to act: {I felt energized after my morning run}. The word often describes renewed vigor after rest, exercise, or inspiration. To energize something is to supply it with power or to invigorate it: {The rally energized the campaign}.

An energizer is anything that gives energy, vitality, or renewed vigor. The term applies to people who invigorate others, substances that boost alertness, or activities that restore enthusiasm: {Coffee is my morning energizer}. In some contexts, it refers to battery chargers or devices that restore power to rechargeable cells. (Capitalized Energizer is the battery brand.)

Energy is the capacity for doing work or producing change—the fundamental currency of physics. In everyday use, energy describes vitality and vigor: {I don't have the energy to argue}. A person with energy is lively and active. Energy also refers to power sources: {renewable energy}, {nuclear energy}. To {put energy into} something is to apply sustained effort.

To enforce is to compel compliance with a rule, law, or obligation—to make sure it's actually followed rather than merely stated. Police enforce laws, referees enforce rules, parents enforce bedtimes. The word implies authority backed by consequences: {The contract is unenforceable without penalties}. Enforce can also mean to impose by force: {enforce one's will on others}.

Enforced describes something compelled or imposed by authority rather than chosen voluntarily. An enforced {curfew} is one backed by official power. Enforced {silence} or enforced {absence} suggests someone had no choice in the matter. The word often carries a sense of unwillingness on the part of those subject to the enforcement.

Enforcement is the act of compelling compliance with a law, rule, or obligation. Police handle law enforcement; agencies pursue enforcement of regulations. The word implies authority and consequences: {Enforcement of the new policy begins Monday}. Without enforcement, rules have no teeth. An enforcer is someone who ensures compliance, sometimes through intimidation.

An enforcer is someone who compels compliance with rules or demands, often through intimidation or force. The term appears in sports for players who protect teammates through physical aggression, and in organized crime for those who collect debts or punish disloyalty: {The mob sent their enforcer to deliver a message}. More broadly, any person or mechanism that ensures rules are followed: {The IRS acts as the chief enforcer of tax law}.

Enforcers are people who ensure rules or laws are followed, often through intimidation or force. In organized crime, an enforcer threatens or commits violence on behalf of a boss: {The mob sent their enforcer to collect the debt}. In hockey, an enforcer is a player whose role is to fight and physically intimidate opponents. More broadly, anyone who compels compliance—a strict teacher, a regulatory agent—might be called an enforcer.

Enforcing is ensuring compliance with a rule, law, or standard—making sure it's actually followed rather than merely stated. Police enforce laws, referees enforce rules, parents enforce bedtimes. {The city is finally enforcing the parking regulations.} The word implies authority and the power to compel: you can only enforce what you have standing to enforce.

Enfranchisement is the granting of rights, especially voting rights. The term appears most often in historical contexts—the enfranchisement of women, the enfranchisement of formerly enslaved people. More broadly, it can mean liberation from any form of restriction or servitude: {The movement sought the enfranchisement of the working class}. The opposite is disenfranchisement.
clues: Being granted the right to vote

definition: Engage means to occupy attention or involve actively. You engage someone in conversation, engage with difficult material, or engage the services of a lawyer. Gears engage when their teeth interlock; a clutch engages when it connects. To be engaged is to be busy, already committed, or pledged to marry: {They got engaged last summer}. In military use, to engage the enemy is to enter combat.

Engaged describes being occupied or committed. Someone engaged in conversation is absorbed in it. An engaged employee is invested in their work. The word often signals a formal commitment to marry: {They got engaged last spring}. A busy signal means a phone line is engaged. Gears engage when they mesh and transfer power.

Engagement centers on the idea of involvement or commitment. To have an engagement is to have an appointment or obligation that demands your presence: {I have a prior engagement}. A couple's engagement is their promise to marry, usually formalized with a ring. In military contexts, an engagement is an armed encounter or battle. The broader sense describes active participation or connection: {student engagement in the classroom}, {social media engagement}. To engage is to participate, attract attention, or interlock, as gears do.

Engagements are commitments or appointments that claim your time: {I have several engagements this week}. An engagement to marry is a formal agreement to wed. Military engagements are battles or skirmishes between forces. The word carries a sense of being bound or occupied—whether by social obligation, romantic promise, or combat.

Engages is the third-person singular of engage, a verb with meanings that cluster around connection and involvement. A speaker engages an audience by capturing their attention. Gears engage when their teeth mesh. Someone engages in an activity by participating in it: {She engages in volunteer work on weekends}. To engage an enemy is to enter combat. An engaged couple has agreed to marry.

Engaging describes something that captures and holds attention—a quality of being interesting, charming, or absorbing. An engaging {speaker} draws you in; an engaging {smile} invites connection. The word suggests active involvement rather than passive observation: {The documentary was engaging from start to finish}. To engage is to occupy attention or involve oneself, and engaging is its natural adjective.

An engine converts one kind of energy into another, like the engine in a car that converts fossil fuel to motion. Until the late 20th century, engines were mostly thought of as heavy metal things with moving parts. Thanks to search engines, that idea is changing. In even more figurative use, engine can refer to a person or group who supply the energy or force to make something happen: She was the engine behind the suffragist movement in the Northeast.

An engineer designs, builds, or maintains structures, machines, or systems—from bridges to software. The word covers a vast range of specializations: civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical, software. An engineer also operates engines or technical equipment: a railroad engineer drives trains, a sound engineer manages audio. To engineer something is to skillfully arrange or bring about: {She engineered his downfall}.

Engineered describes something deliberately designed or constructed, typically with technical skill: {an engineered solution}, {genetically engineered crops}. The word often implies careful planning or manipulation—sometimes with negative connotations suggesting artificiality or contrivance: {The whole controversy felt engineered to distract from the real issues}. {A beautifully engineered bridge.}

Engineering is the application of scientific and mathematical principles to design, build, and maintain structures, machines, systems, and processes. Civil engineering deals with infrastructure; mechanical with machines; electrical with circuits and power; software with computer systems. The verb engineer means to design or construct, or more broadly to bring something about through skillful planning: {She engineered a meeting between the two rivals}. An engineer is a practitioner of the field, or someone who operates an engine—particularly a locomotive.

Engineers design, build, and maintain complex systems—bridges, software, engines, electrical grids. The word covers many specialties: civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical, software. To engineer something is to design or bring it about through skillful planning: {She engineered the merger}. The verb often implies cleverness or manipulation: {He engineered his rival's downfall}.

Engines are machines that convert energy into motion. The term originally meant any mechanical device (as in {siege engines} or {engines of war}), but now usually refers to motors that power vehicles or equipment: {car engine}, {jet engine}, {search engine}. A steam engine converts heat to mechanical force. A fire engine is the truck, not just its motor. Figuratively, something can be an engine of change or growth—a driving force.

English in lowercase is rare in edited prose but appears in certain contexts. In billiards, english refers to spin imparted to a ball to control its path after striking: {He put english on the cue ball}. The term likely derives from a technique associated with English players. To put english on something can also mean to add spin or a particular slant to a story or presentation. (Capitalized English is the language or nationality.)

Engorged means swollen with fluid, typically blood. The word appears most often in medical contexts—engorged blood vessels, engorged breasts during lactation—and in descriptions of feeding parasites: {The tick was engorged with blood}. Extended uses describe anything swollen to capacity: {rivers engorged with snowmelt}.

To engrave is to cut or carve a design into a hard surface—metal, glass, stone, wood. The technique produces decorative items, printing plates, and personalized objects: {a watch engraved with his initials}, {an engraved invitation}. Figuratively, something engraved on your memory or heart is permanently fixed there: {That moment is engraved in my mind}.

Engraved describes something with designs or letters cut into its surface: {an engraved silver bracelet}, {engraved wedding invitations}. The image of cutting into material extends to memory and emotion—something engraved {on your heart} or {in your mind} is permanently fixed there, impossible to forget.

Engraves is the third-person singular of engrave, meaning to cut or carve designs, letters, or patterns into a hard surface. The work is typically done on metal, glass, stone, or wood: {She engraves wedding rings for a living}. Figuratively, something deeply memorable engraves itself on the mind or heart: {The image engraves itself in memory}.

Engraving is the art or process of cutting designs into a hard surface—metal, wood, glass, or stone—using sharp tools or acid. The term also refers to the product: a print made from an engraved plate, or the incised design itself. {The museum displayed Renaissance engravings}. {The engraving on the watch read "To my beloved."}

Engravings are images or designs cut into a hard surface, or prints made from such surfaces. The term covers both the carved original and the reproductions pulled from it: {The museum displayed Renaissance engravings}. An engraving may also be decorative work incised into metal objects like jewelry or trophies: {The watch had a personal engraving on the back}.

Engrossed means completely absorbed in something, with attention so fully captured that other things fade from awareness: {She was engrossed in her book and didn't hear me come in}. The word suggests deep, willing concentration rather than mere distraction. You become engrossed in novels, conversations, or work that genuinely holds your interest.

Engrossing means fully absorbing one's attention. An engrossing {book} or {conversation} captures you so completely that time passes unnoticed and distractions fade away. The word carries positive connotations—being engrossed is usually pleasant, a state of focused immersion rather than anxious preoccupation.

To engulf is to swallow up completely or surround entirely. Fire engulfs a building, waves engulf a swimmer, darkness engulfs a landscape. The word carries a sense of being overwhelmed or consumed: {Grief engulfed her after the funeral}. {The scandal threatened to engulf the entire administration}.

Engulfed describes being completely surrounded or swallowed up by something overwhelming. Flames engulf a building; floodwaters engulf a town. The word works for abstract forces too: {She was engulfed by grief}. {The scandal engulfed the administration}. Something engulfed has been overtaken entirely, often suddenly.

Engulfing describes something that completely surrounds, swallows, or overwhelms. Flames engulf a building; grief engulfs a person. The word suggests total consumption—whatever engulfs doesn't merely touch or affect but wholly envelops: {The darkness was engulfing}, {an engulfing sense of dread}. In financial charts, an engulfing pattern is a candlestick formation where one bar completely contains the previous one.

Engulfs is the third-person singular of engulf, meaning to swallow up or overwhelm completely. Fire engulfs a building, flames consuming it entirely. Floodwaters engulf a town. The word works figuratively too: {Grief engulfed her}, {The scandal engulfed the administration}. The sense is of something surrounded and overcome on all sides.

When you enhance something you make it better: The research team is dedicated to enhancing the quality of our products. Enhancing something is generally perceived as good, but sometimes the word has slightly negative connotation, with the suggestion that the improvement is in appearance only, temporary, or insubstantial: The exercise was designed merely to enhance the philanthropic reputation of the couple. The participle enhancing is used often today in the term performance-enhancing drugs to characterize substances used by athletes to gain an unfair advantage in competition.

Enhanced describes something that has been improved, intensified, or augmented beyond its original state. The word often implies technological or artificial improvement: {enhanced graphics}, {enhanced security features}, {enhanced interrogation} (a euphemism for torture). In food labeling, enhanced may indicate added ingredients: {enhanced with vitamins}. Enhanced suggests deliberate upgrading rather than natural development.

Enhancement is the act of improving or intensifying something, or the improvement itself. Software receives security enhancements. Photos undergo digital enhancement to sharpen details or adjust colors. {The new lighting was a real enhancement to the room}. Performance-enhancing drugs boost athletic ability. Enhancement suggests augmentation of existing qualities rather than fundamental transformation.

An enigma is something puzzling or mysterious—a riddle that resists easy explanation. The word often describes people whose motives or character remain opaque: {He was an enigma to everyone who knew him}. It extends to any baffling situation or phenomenon: {The disappearance remains an enigma}. Something enigmatic invites interpretation but withholds clear answers.
clues: A person no one figures out

definition: Enigmas is the plural of enigma—people, things, or situations that are mysterious or difficult to understand. An enigma resists explanation: {The case remains one of history's great enigmas}. A person who seems unknowable is an enigma: {She was an enigma to her colleagues, friendly but utterly private}.

Enigmatic describes someone or something mysterious, puzzling, or difficult to interpret. An enigmatic {smile} hints at hidden meaning. An enigmatic {figure} remains unknowable despite scrutiny. The word suggests deliberate inscrutability—not mere confusion, but a quality that invites interpretation while resisting it: {She gave an enigmatic reply that left us all guessing}.

Enjoy means to take pleasure in something: {I really enjoyed the concert}, {Enjoy your meal}. It can also mean to have the benefit of: {She enjoys good health}, {They enjoy certain privileges}. The imperative {enjoy!} has become a standalone wish, especially from servers delivering food. To {enjoy yourself} is to have a good time.

Enjoyable describes experiences, activities, or things that give pleasure or satisfaction. Something enjoyable is worth doing or having because it brings happiness or contentment: {We had an enjoyable evening at the concert}. The word carries lighter connotations than pleasurable, suggesting wholesome or uncomplicated satisfaction rather than intense delight. It appears frequently in polite conversation and reviews, sometimes as faint praise when stronger endorsement isn't warranted.

Enjoying is the present participle of enjoy, meaning to take pleasure or satisfaction in something. It describes the ongoing experience of finding something pleasurable: {I'm really enjoying this book}, {They were enjoying the warm weather}. To be enjoying yourself is to be having a good time.

Enjoyment is the pleasure or satisfaction derived from something: {She took great enjoyment from her garden}. The word emphasizes the experience itself rather than the source—you find enjoyment in activities, not just from them. Legal usage refers to the use and benefit of property or rights: {quiet enjoyment of the premises}.

To enlarge is to make or become larger: {We enlarged the kitchen}, {The pupil enlarges in dim light}. The word applies to physical expansion, photographic prints, scope of projects, or abstract concepts: {enlarge the scope of the investigation}. To {enlarge upon} a topic is to expand on it with more detail.

To enlighten is to give someone knowledge or understanding they lacked: {The documentary enlightened me about the history of redlining}. The word suggests illumination—bringing light to darkness, clarity to confusion. In spiritual contexts, enlightenment is a state of profound wisdom or awakening: {The Buddha became enlightened under the Bodhi tree}. To enlighten can also mean simply to inform: {Would you care to enlighten us about your plans?}

Enlightened describes someone who has gained wisdom, understanding, or freedom from ignorance. An enlightened {ruler} governs with reason and compassion. The term often implies progressive thinking: {enlightened views on education}. In spiritual contexts, particularly Buddhism, enlightenment is a state of awakening or liberation from suffering—one who has achieved this is enlightened. The word can also be used ironically for those who consider themselves superior: {our enlightened critics}.

Enlightening describes something that provides insight, clarity, or understanding—illuminating what was previously unclear or unknown. The word implies genuine learning or revelation: {The documentary was enlightening}. An enlightening conversation leaves you knowing more than before. The term carries positive connotations, suggesting valuable knowledge gained rather than mere information received.

Enlightenment is the state of gaining deep understanding or insight, often after confusion or ignorance: {Reading that book was a moment of enlightenment for me}. The word suggests clarity breaking through—a light turning on in the mind. In Buddhism, enlightenment is the ultimate spiritual awakening, liberation from the cycle of suffering and rebirth. More casually, enlightenment is simply being informed: {I'd appreciate some enlightenment on what happened at the meeting}. (Capitalized Enlightenment is the 18th-century intellectual movement.)

Enlightens means to give knowledge or understanding to someone, to illuminate what was previously dark or unclear. A teacher enlightens students about history; an investigation enlightens the public about corruption. The word carries connotations of bringing someone from ignorance into clarity: {The documentary enlightens viewers about the refugee crisis}. In spiritual contexts, to be enlightened suggests profound awakening or wisdom.

To enlist is to join the armed forces voluntarily, as opposed to being drafted: {He enlisted in the Marines right after high school}. Extended uses apply the same idea of signing up for a cause or effort. To enlist someone's help is to recruit their support: {She enlisted her neighbors to search for the missing dog}. An enlisted soldier holds a rank below officer.

Enlisted describes military personnel who are not officers—the ranks that form the bulk of armed forces. Someone enlisted holds a position entered through enlistment rather than commission: {enlisted men}, {enlisted ranks}. The past tense of enlist, it also means joined or recruited: {She enlisted in the Navy}, {He enlisted his friends to help move}.

Enlistment is the act of joining a military service or the period of service that follows: {His enlistment in the Navy lasted four years}. The term extends to recruiting support for any cause: {The campaign focused on enlistment of local volunteers}. An enlistment bonus is money offered to attract recruits.

Enmeshed means caught up in something difficult to escape, like a fish tangled in a net. The word usually describes complicated situations rather than physical entrapment: {enmeshed in bureaucracy}, {enmeshed in a web of lies}. In psychology, enmeshed relationships lack healthy boundaries—family members so intertwined they can't function independently.

Enmity is deep-seated hostility or hatred between people or groups. Unlike casual dislike, enmity suggests a lasting, often mutual antagonism: {The enmity between the two families went back generations}. The word appears frequently in discussions of feuds, rivalries, and historical conflicts where animosity has hardened into something durable.

An enneagram is a nine-pointed geometric figure, but the word almost always refers to a personality typing system that categorizes people into nine interconnected types based on core motivations and fears. The system draws from various spiritual and psychological traditions and is popular in self-help, workplace training, and relationship counseling: {I'm a Type Four on the enneagram}. Critics question its scientific validity.

Ennui is a listless weariness born of boredom or dissatisfaction—not mere boredom, but a deeper spiritual fatigue when nothing seems worth doing. The word retains its French flavor and tends toward the literary or dramatic: {Summer ennui had set in by July}. It suggests privileged dissatisfaction, the malaise of those with too much leisure and too little purpose.

Enoki is a type of mushroom with long, thin white stems and tiny caps, grown in clusters. Popular in East Asian cuisine, enoki mushrooms have a mild, slightly fruity flavor and a crisp texture. They appear in soups, stir-fries, and hot pot dishes: {Add the enoki in the last minute of cooking}.

Enormity traditionally refers to extreme wickedness or moral outrage, not merely large size: {the enormity of the crime shocked even seasoned detectives}. However, enormity is now widely used to mean immense scale or magnitude, especially of problems or tasks: {the enormity of the refugee crisis}. Purists object to this second sense, preferring enormousness for sheer size, but the usage is well established. Context usually clarifies whether moral weight or scale is intended.

Enormous means extremely large in size, extent, or degree. The word carries more weight than big or large but less than colossal or gargantuan: {an enormous house}, {enormous pressure}, {an enormous mistake}. Enormous often suggests something impressively or problematically oversized rather than merely big.

Enough can operate as an adjective, adverb, or pronoun to convey the idea of sufficiency: Make sure there’s enough food for everyone. Do you need more time or is that enough? Enough is also one of a handful of frequent words in English in which the letters gh are pronounced as /f/.

Enquiries is the plural of enquiry, a chiefly British spelling of inquiry. It refers to questions or requests for information: {Direct all enquiries to the front desk}. An enquiries desk or office handles such requests. In British usage, enquiry often applies to routine questions while inquiry suggests formal investigation, though this distinction isn't strict.

To enrage someone is to make them extremely angry—not just annoyed or irritated, but furious. The word emphasizes the intensity and suddenness of the anger provoked: {The verdict enraged protesters who had gathered outside the courthouse}. Unlike anger, which can build slowly, enrage suggests a rapid escalation to rage. The adjective enraged describes someone in this state of fury: {an enraged mob}, {enraged customers demanding refunds}.

Enraged means filled with rage—intensely, visibly angry. The word suggests anger that has built to a peak: {The enraged crowd stormed the gates}. Unlike merely angry or upset, enraged implies a loss of composure, someone pushed past the point of restraint.

Enraptured means filled with delight or overwhelmed with joy—transported by intense pleasure or admiration. The word suggests being seized by emotion so completely that everything else fades: {She stood enraptured before the painting}. {The audience was enraptured by his performance}. More literary than simply delighted or thrilled.

To enrich something is to make it richer—more valuable, more nutritious, more interesting. You can enrich soil with compost, enrich a curriculum with new courses, or enrich someone's life with friendship. Enriched flour has nutrients added back after processing. Enriched uranium has a higher concentration of fissile isotopes, used in nuclear reactors or weapons.

Enriched describes something that has been made richer or more valuable by adding desirable elements. Food products are enriched when nutrients are added back after processing has removed them: {enriched flour} has B vitamins and iron restored. Soil can be enriched with fertilizer, and a curriculum enriched with new courses. The term often implies improvement or enhancement beyond a basic state. Enriched uranium has had its concentration of fissile isotopes increased for use in reactors or weapons.

Enrichment is the process of making something richer or more valuable. Soil enrichment adds nutrients. Cultural enrichment expands knowledge or experience: {The museum offers enrichment programs for children}. In nuclear contexts, uranium enrichment increases the concentration of fissile isotopes. Animal enrichment provides stimulation to captive creatures: {The zookeepers designed enrichment activities for the primates}.

To enroll is to sign up officially—for a class, a program, or an institution: {She enrolled in the nursing program}, {The school enrolled 500 new students this fall}. Enrollment implies formal registration and often a commitment. In British English, spelled enrol.

Enrolled is the past tense of enroll, meaning to have officially registered or signed up for something: {She enrolled in a pottery class}, {He enrolled at the university last fall}. The word implies formal entry onto a list or into an institution—schools, programs, courses, insurance plans. In British English, spelled enrolled or enroled.

Enrolling is the act of registering or signing up for something—a school, a program, a course, an insurance plan: {She's enrolling in community college this fall}. The word implies formal entry onto a list or roster. Someone enrolling others is adding them to such a list: {The campaign was enrolling new voters}.

Enrollment is the act of registering or being registered for something—a school, a program, an insurance plan. It also refers to the total number of people registered: {Enrollment at the university increased by twelve percent}. The enrollment period is when registration is open. British spelling: enrolment.

An ensemble is a group of things considered as a whole, especially performers who work together: a jazz ensemble, a theater ensemble. In fashion, an ensemble is a coordinated outfit—pieces selected to complement each other: {She wore a stunning ensemble to the gala}. The word emphasizes unity and harmony among parts, whether musicians, actors, or garments.

Ensembles is the plural of ensemble, a group whose parts work together as a unified whole. A musical ensemble is a group of performers—a jazz ensemble, a string ensemble. In fashion, an ensemble is a coordinated outfit: {She wore a stunning black ensemble}. The word emphasizes coherence among components rather than individual elements.

To enshrine something is to preserve it as sacred or inviolable. The literal sense—placing in a shrine—rarely appears; the figurative dominates: rights enshrined in a constitution, principles enshrined in law, memories enshrined in tradition. {The First Amendment enshrines freedom of speech.} What gets enshrined is protected from casual change or challenge.
clues: Place in a position of honor

definition: Enshrined means preserved or protected as sacred or inviolable. Rights enshrined in a constitution have formal protection. A memory enshrined in the heart is cherished and guarded. The word carries connotations of reverence—what's enshrined isn't merely stored but honored: {The principle of free speech is enshrined in the First Amendment}. Athletes are enshrined in halls of fame.

Enshrining is preserving something in a place of honor or protection. Laws enshrine rights by formally establishing them: {The First Amendment enshrines freedom of speech}. Memories can be enshrined in monuments, traditions in rituals. The word suggests both reverence and permanence—what gets enshrined is meant to last and be respected.

An ensign is a flag or banner, especially one flown on a ship to indicate nationality: {the White Ensign of the Royal Navy}. In the U.S. Navy and Coast Guard, ensign is the lowest commissioned officer rank, equivalent to a second lieutenant in the Army. The word can also mean any badge or emblem of office or authority.

To enslave is to make someone a slave—to strip them of freedom and hold them in bondage. The word applies literally to the historical practice of slavery and figuratively to anything that dominates or controls: {enslaved by addiction}, {enslaved to debt}. The figurative use can seem tone-deaf given slavery's brutal reality.

Enslaved describes people held in bondage—forced to work without freedom or compensation. The term has largely replaced "slave" as a noun in historical writing, emphasizing that slavery was a condition imposed on people rather than an identity: {enslaved Africans}, {enslaved workers}. This framing recognizes humanity first, captivity second.

Enslavement is the act of making someone a slave—reducing a person to property that can be bought, sold, and forced to labor. The word covers both the historical institution and individual acts of subjugation: {the enslavement of captured peoples}, {her enslavement to an abusive employer}. Figuratively, enslavement describes being controlled by something: {enslavement to debt}, {enslavement to addiction}.

An enslaver is a person who holds others in slavery—who claims ownership over human beings and compels their labor. The term has gained currency in historical writing as a more direct alternative to "slaveholder" or "slave owner," emphasizing the active role in subjugation: {Thomas Jefferson was an enslaver who held over six hundred people in bondage over his lifetime}.

Enslavers are people who hold others in slavery. The term has gained currency in historical writing as a replacement for "slaveholders" or "slaveowners," which some argue normalize the institution by framing it as mere property ownership. Enslaver emphasizes the active role in creating and maintaining bondage: {The enslavers of colonial Virginia built their wealth on tobacco and human suffering}.

Enslaves is the third-person singular of enslave, meaning to make someone a slave or to dominate completely. A conquering army enslaves a population. Figuratively, anything that controls you enslaves: {She was enslaved by her addiction}. The word carries the full weight of forced servitude—loss of freedom, ownership by another, compelled labor.

Enslaving is the act of making someone a slave—depriving them of freedom and forcing them into servitude. The word extends to anything that dominates or controls completely: {enslaving debt}, {an enslaving addiction}. Work that consumes all your time and energy can feel enslaving: {The job was enslaving—I had no life outside it}.

To ensnare is to catch in a snare or trap. The word appears most often in figurative contexts—being ensnared by debt, ensnared in a web of lies, ensnared by an attractive stranger. {She found herself ensnared in office politics she wanted no part of.} The sense is of entrapment that's difficult to escape.

Ensnared is the past tense and past participle of ensnare, meaning caught in a snare or trap. The word applies literally to animals captured by hunters but appears far more often in figurative contexts describing people caught up in situations they cannot easily escape: {She found herself ensnared in a web of lies}. Someone ensnared by debt, scandal, or a manipulative relationship is trapped by circumstances rather than physical restraints.

Ensnares means to catch in a snare or trap, literally or figuratively. The word usually describes situations where someone becomes entangled in something difficult to escape: {The detective ensnares the suspect with careful questioning}, {She was ensnared by debt}. The sense is of being caught unawares and held fast.

Ensnaring is catching or trapping, literally or figuratively. A hunter ensnares prey; a con artist ensnares victims. The word emphasizes the trap aspect—something that catches and holds: {an ensnaring web of lies}, {ensnaring melodies that stuck in my head for days}. See also snare and ensnarement.

A room, especially a bathroom, directly connected to and accessible only from a bedroom: {The master bedroom has an ensuite}. Also used as an adjective: {an ensuite bathroom}. The term comes from French meaning "in sequence" and is more common in British, Australian, and Canadian English than American.

To ensure something means to make it secure, certain, or safe: Can you ensure the well-being of the party as they cross the border? In modern usage ensure is usually followed by a ‘that’ clause, although the ‘that’ is not always present: It’s important to ensure that their diet has adequate vitamin D. Before calling, ensure you are using the latest version of the software. In North American English, insure is sometimes used for these meanings of ensure, as well as the meanings of insure that have to do with indemnification.

To entangle is to catch or twist something in a way that makes it difficult to separate. Fishing line entangles in kelp; a bird becomes entangled in netting. Figuratively, to be entangled is to be caught up in something complicated or compromising: {entangled in a web of lies}, {romantically entangled with a coworker}. The noun entanglement describes such situations, or in physics, a quantum phenomenon where particles remain connected across distance.

Entangled describes things twisted together in a way that's difficult to separate. Hair becomes entangled, fishing line becomes entangled, and so do people in complicated relationships or situations: {She got entangled with the wrong crowd}. In physics, entangled particles remain connected across distance, their states linked regardless of separation. To be entangled in something is to be caught up in it, often unwillingly: {entangled in a legal dispute}.

Entanglement is the state of being tangled up in something—caught, ensnared, or complicated by involvement. A physical entanglement might be fishing line wrapped around a propeller. More often the word describes messy involvements: {a romantic entanglement}, {legal entanglements that delayed the project}. In physics, quantum entanglement describes particles whose states remain correlated regardless of distance—a phenomenon Einstein called "spooky action at a distance."

Entanglements are situations or relationships that are difficult to get out of or that complicate one's life. The word suggests being caught up in something messy, like a net or web: {His romantic entanglements made headlines}. Military entanglements refer to involvement in foreign conflicts that prove hard to exit. In physics, quantum entanglement describes particles whose states remain correlated regardless of distance—a phenomenon Einstein famously called "spooky action at a distance."

Entangling describes something that catches, ensnares, or complicates. Fishing line becomes entangling when it wraps around things. An entangling {alliance} draws nations into unwanted conflicts—a phrase from Washington's farewell address warning against foreign commitments. Entangling {roots} trip hikers; entangling {regulations} trap businesses in red tape.

Enter is to go or come into a place: {She entered the room without knocking}. The word extends to beginning participation: enter a {competition}, enter a {profession}, enter into {negotiations}. To enter data is to input it into a system. The enter key on a keyboard submits commands or creates line breaks. {It never entered my mind} means something never occurred to you.

Enterprise is a project or undertaking, especially one requiring effort or boldness: {a risky enterprise}, {a commercial enterprise}. The word also names the quality itself—initiative and resourcefulness: {She showed real enterprise in building her business}. An enterprise is often a business venture or company: {a state-owned enterprise}, {free enterprise}. The word carries connotations of ambition and scale.

Enterprises is the plural of enterprise, which names ambitious undertakings or projects requiring effort and initiative: {The whole enterprise was doomed from the start}. Enterprise also means boldness and resourcefulness—the spirit of entrepreneurship. In business contexts, an enterprise is a company or organization, especially a large one: {small and medium-sized enterprises}, {enterprise software}. The word often appears in formal company names.

Enterprising describes someone who shows initiative and readiness to undertake new ventures, especially in business. An enterprising person spots opportunities and acts on them: {An enterprising teenager started a lawn care business in the neighborhood}. The word carries positive connotations of energy, ambition, and resourcefulness, though it can shade toward cunning when the venture pushes ethical boundaries.

Entertain covers a range of activities that share the idea of holding attention or holding in mind. To entertain guests is to receive and accommodate them, keeping them engaged and comfortable. To entertain an audience is to provide them with amusement or diversion: {The comedian entertained the crowd for two hours}. More abstractly, to entertain an idea or proposal is to consider it, holding it in your mind without necessarily accepting it: {I won't even entertain that suggestion}.

Entertained is the past tense of entertain. To entertain is to hold someone's attention pleasurably—through performance, conversation, or diversion: {The magician entertained the children for an hour}. It also means to receive guests hospitably: {They entertained frequently at their country house}. To entertain an idea is to consider it seriously: {She refused to entertain the possibility of failure}.

An entertainer is someone who performs for an audience—singers, comedians, magicians, dancers, actors. The term is broad enough to cover anyone whose job is to amuse or engage others professionally. {She was a natural entertainer, commanding the room effortlessly.} The word often implies versatility or showmanship rather than mastery of a single art form.

Entertainers are people who perform for an audience—singers, comedians, dancers, magicians, actors. The term emphasizes the goal of amusing or delighting rather than educating or informing: {The cruise ship hired several entertainers for the evening shows}. Entertainer can sound slightly old-fashioned compared to more specific terms like performer or artist.

Entertaining describes something that holds attention and provides enjoyment or amusement. An entertaining {movie} or entertaining {speaker} keeps you engaged rather than bored. The word also functions as a noun for the activity of hosting guests: {She does a lot of entertaining during the holidays}. What counts as entertaining varies wildly by person—one viewer's entertaining documentary is another's tedious lecture.

Entertainment is anything that holds attention in an enjoyable way—a movie, a concert, a party trick. The word covers both the activity and the industry that produces it: {the entertainment business}, {That's entertainment!} To entertain guests is to host them; entertainment in this sense means hospitality, including food and drink provided.

To enthrall is to captivate completely, holding someone's attention as if by a spell: {The documentary enthralled viewers for two hours}. The word carries a sense of pleasurable captivity—you're held, but willingly. Originally it meant to enslave, and that older sense of being held in thrall survives in the modern meaning's intensity. Also spelled enthral.
clues: Seize someone's attention and keep it

definition: Enthralled means captivated or spellbound, completely absorbed by something fascinating. The word suggests being held in place by wonder or interest: {The children sat enthralled by the magician's tricks}. Someone enthralled by a book or performance can't look away. The older sense—literally enslaved—survives mainly in fantasy literature.

To enthrone is to place someone on a throne, literally or figuratively—installing them in a position of authority or honor. Monarchs are enthroned at coronations; bishops at investitures. By extension, anything elevated to a place of supreme importance can be enthroned: {Modern culture has enthroned convenience above all else}.

Enthroned means placed on or occupying a throne, either literally or figuratively. A monarch is enthroned at coronation. More broadly, anything given supreme status or positioned in a place of honor can be enthroned: {The portrait hung enthroned above the fireplace}. {Money sits enthroned in American culture}.

Enthronement is the ceremony or act of placing a monarch, religious leader, or other dignitary on a throne, formally investing them with authority. The word extends to any installation in a position of power or honor: {the enthronement of a new archbishop}, {his enthronement as CEO}. Figuratively, it describes elevating something to supreme status: {the enthronement of profit above all other values}.

Enthusiasm is eager interest or excitement about something: {Her enthusiasm for the project was contagious}, {He spoke with great enthusiasm about his travels}. The word implies energy and wholehearted engagement rather than passive approval. Someone who lacks enthusiasm is indifferent or going through the motions. An enthusiast is a person with strong interest in a particular subject: {a car enthusiast}, {a wine enthusiast}.

An enthusiast is someone with intense interest or passion for a particular subject or activity: {a car enthusiast}, {wine enthusiasts gathered for the tasting}. The word implies deep engagement beyond casual interest—enthusiasts collect, study, discuss, and advocate for their chosen pursuit. It's often used attributively: {enthusiast forums}, {enthusiast-grade equipment}.

Enthusiastic describes someone showing eager interest or intense enjoyment. An enthusiastic {supporter} backs a cause wholeheartedly. An enthusiastic {response} signals genuine excitement. The word suggests energy and positivity rather than mere approval—you can be supportive without being enthusiastic, but enthusiasm implies active engagement: {She wasn't just willing to help; she was enthusiastic about it}.

Enthusiasts are people who have a strong and eager interest in a particular activity, subject, or pursuit. The word carries connotations of dedication and passion that go beyond casual interest: car enthusiasts know their engines, wine enthusiasts study their vintages, and outdoor enthusiasts spend weekends on trails. {The forum attracts enthusiasts from around the world.} Unlike hobbyist, which emphasizes leisure, enthusiast suggests genuine devotion and often considerable expertise.

To entice is to attract or lure someone toward something, usually by making it seem appealing or desirable: {The smell of fresh bread enticed customers into the bakery}. The word often implies temptation—drawing someone toward pleasure, opportunity, or sometimes trouble. You entice with promises, rewards, or charm: {They enticed him away from his old job with a bigger salary}.

Enticement is something that attracts or tempts, often by appealing to desire or self-interest. The word carries a slightly manipulative connotation—an enticement isn't just an offer but something designed to lure: {The free trial was an enticement to sign up for the full subscription.} What distinguishes enticement from mere attraction is the suggestion of deliberate persuasion, sometimes toward something questionable. To entice is the corresponding verb.

Entices is the third-person singular of entice, meaning to attract or tempt someone toward something, often by offering pleasure or advantage. The word carries a hint of seduction or manipulation—enticement appeals to desire rather than reason: {The smell of fresh bread entices customers into the bakery}. {He entices investors with promises of quick returns}.

Enticing means tempting or alluring, drawing someone toward something desirable: {The smell of fresh bread was enticing}. What entices appeals to appetite or interest, promising pleasure or reward. An enticing {offer} is hard to refuse. An enticing {glimpse} makes you want to see more.

Entire means whole or complete, with nothing left out or excluded. An entire {day} passes from morning to night. You can read an entire {book} or eat an entire {pizza}. The word emphasizes completeness more strongly than whole: {The entire population was evacuated}. In technical contexts, entire can mean unbroken or uncastrated, as with horses.

Entities are things that exist as distinct units. The word often appears in contexts requiring precision about what counts as a separate item: {The database tracks three types of entities}. Legal and business entities are organizations recognized as having their own identity—corporations, governments, trusts. In philosophy and fiction, entity can mean any being or creature: {a supernatural entity}, {an alien entity}. The singular form entity is more common than the plural.

To entitle is to give someone a right or claim to something: {The ticket entitles you to one free drink}. A person who feels entitled expects privileges without earning them. Entitle also means to give a title to a book, film, or other work: {She entitled her memoir "Starting Over"}. The passive {entitled} often just means named or called.

Entitled means having a right or claim to something: {She's entitled to half the estate}. A book or article entitled something has that as its title: {a memoir entitled "My Life in Paris"}. The word has developed a strongly negative sense describing someone who believes they deserve special treatment without earning it: {entitled customers demanding refunds}, {an entitled attitude}. This pejorative use now dominates casual speech.

Entitlement is a right to something—benefits, privileges, or treatment. Government entitlements are programs like Social Security or Medicare that qualifying citizens receive by law. The word often carries negative connotations: someone with {a sense of entitlement} expects special treatment without earning it. {The entitlement of that generation is astounding.} The adjective entitled works the same way: an entitled person believes they deserve more than others.

Entitlements are benefits or rights one is owed, especially government programs like Social Security or Medicare that citizens qualify for automatically: {Entitlement spending dominates the federal budget}. The word often carries negative connotations of undeserved expectation: {Kids these days have such a sense of entitlement}. In computing, entitlements are permissions granted to software.

An entity is something that exists as a distinct, separate unit—a being or thing with its own identity. The word often appears in legal, corporate, or philosophical contexts where precision about boundaries matters: {The company operates as a separate legal entity}. Entities can be concrete (a person, a corporation) or abstract (a soul, a concept). In databases and information systems, an entity is any object about which data can be stored.
clues: A thing with its own boundaries

definition: To entomb is to place in a tomb or burial chamber: {The pharaohs were entombed with treasures for the afterlife}. More broadly, it means to bury or trap completely: {Miners were entombed by the collapse}. The word carries a sense of permanent enclosure—something entombed is sealed away, often beyond recovery.

Entombed means placed in a tomb or buried, often with connotations of permanence or finality: {The pharaohs were entombed with their treasures}. Figuratively, it describes being trapped or sealed within something: {The miners remained entombed for days before rescue}. The word suggests enclosure that is complete and difficult to escape.

Entombing is the act of placing in a tomb or sealing away as if in one. The word carries connotations of permanence and finality: {Workers spent months entombing the damaged reactor in concrete}. Figuratively, anything buried or enclosed beyond easy retrieval can be described as entombed: {manuscripts entombing secrets for centuries}, {memories entombing grief}.

Entombment is the act of placing a body in a tomb. The word appears most often in religious and art-historical contexts—{the entombment of Christ} is a common subject in Renaissance painting. More broadly, entombment can describe any burial or the state of being sealed away: {the entombment of miners after the collapse}.

An entomologist is a scientist who studies insects. The field covers insect biology, behavior, ecology, and classification, with practical applications in agriculture, disease control, and forensics: {The entomologist identified the beetle destroying the crops}. Amateur entomologists often focus on collecting and cataloging specimens.

An entourage is a group of attendants or associates who accompany an important person: {The celebrity arrived with her entourage of stylists, assistants, and bodyguards}. The word carries connotations of status and sometimes excess—having an entourage signals that someone is important enough to require a supporting cast.

Entourages is the plural of entourage—the group of attendants, assistants, or followers surrounding an important person. A celebrity's entourage might include managers, bodyguards, stylists, and hangers-on: {The rapper arrived with his entourage of twenty}. The word carries connotations of status and sometimes excess.

The internal organs of an animal, especially the intestines. Almost always plural: {The hunter removed the entrails before carrying the deer out}. Entrails appear in contexts of butchering, sacrifice, and divination—ancient priests read entrails to predict the future. Figuratively, entrails can mean the innermost parts of anything: {the entrails of the ship}.

Entrails are the internal organs of an animal, especially when removed during butchering or sacrifice. The word typically refers to intestines and other abdominal organs: {The hunter cleaned the deer and left the entrails for scavengers}. Figuratively, entrails can mean the innermost parts of anything: {the entrails of the ship}, {the entrails of the bureaucracy}.

Entrance has two distinct meanings depending on pronunciation. With stress on the first syllable, an entrance is a way in—a door, gate, or opening that allows access: {the entrance to the building}, {the main entrance}. It also means the act of entering: {She made a grand entrance}. With stress on the second syllable, to entrance is to fill with wonder or delight, to captivate completely: {The magician entranced the audience}. Someone entranced is spellbound, as if in a trance.

Entranced means captivated or spellbound, as if under a magical influence. Someone entranced by a performance is so absorbed they forget their surroundings: {She stood entranced before the painting}. The word suggests being held in a kind of pleasant paralysis, unable or unwilling to look away.

Entrances serves two words. The noun entrance (stress on the first syllable) is a way in or the act of entering: {The building has two entrances}; {She made a dramatic entrance}. The verb entrance (stress on the second syllable) means to fill with wonder or delight: {The magician entranced the children}. The plural entrances belongs to the noun; the verb form appears in {The music entrances anyone who hears it}.
clues: Where you go in, or mesmerizes

definition: Entrancing means captivating or spellbinding—holding attention as if by magic. The word suggests being so charming or beautiful that one can't look away: {an entrancing melody}, {She found the city entrancing}. From the verb entrance, meaning to fill with wonder or delight, not the noun meaning doorway.
clues: Making you unable to look away

definition: Entrapment is the act of luring someone into a compromising situation, especially when law enforcement induces a person to commit a crime they wouldn't otherwise have committed. It serves as a legal defense: {The defendant claimed entrapment, arguing the undercover officer pressured him into the sale}. More broadly, entrapment describes any situation where someone is tricked or manipulated into a trap.

An entree is a dish served as the main course of a meal in American usage: {The entrees include steak, salmon, and a vegetarian option}. In formal dining and much of the world outside the United States, an entree is a course served before the main dish—closer to an appetizer. The spelling entrée, with the accent, is also common.

Entrees are the main courses of a meal—the substantial dishes that follow appetizers. In American usage, the entree is the centerpiece: {We ordered entrees of salmon and steak}. Confusingly, the French word originally meant the dish that "enters" before the main course, and this older sense persists in formal European dining. The spelling entrées, with the accent, also appears.

To entrench is to establish something so firmly that it becomes difficult to change or remove. The word comes from digging trenches for military defense, and that sense of protected position carries into figurative use: {entrenched interests}, {entrenched beliefs}, {deeply entrenched habits}. What's entrenched has dug in and won't easily be dislodged. The reflexive {entrench oneself} means to settle into a defensive position, literal or figurative.

Entrenched describes something firmly established and resistant to change. An entrenched {position} or {belief} has been held so long it seems immovable. Entrenched {interests} are powerful groups protecting their advantages. The military origin—troops dug into defensive trenches—survives in the sense of being dug in, fortified against attack: {The opposition remains deeply entrenched}.

Entrenchment is the state of being firmly established and resistant to change. An entrenched position—whether military, political, or ideological—is dug in and difficult to dislodge: {The entrenchment of special interests makes reform nearly impossible}. The word carries connotations of rigidity and defensiveness, suggesting something has become so fixed that removing it would require considerable effort.

An entrepreneur is someone who takes a financial risk and launches a new business. In market economies, entrepreneur usually has positive connotations. Someone who simply owns or runs a business is not usually called an entrepreneur, unless they also started the business.

Entrepreneurial describes qualities associated with starting and running businesses—initiative, risk-taking, and resourcefulness. An entrepreneurial {spirit} drives someone to identify opportunities and act on them. The word applies beyond business: an entrepreneurial {approach} to problem-solving emphasizes innovation and self-direction over following established paths.

Entrepreneurs are people who start and run their own businesses, typically taking on financial risk in pursuit of profit. The term implies initiative and innovation—entrepreneurs don't just manage existing operations but create new ventures: {Tech entrepreneurs flocked to Silicon Valley}. The word carries connotations of ambition and self-reliance, though it's sometimes used loosely for anyone self-employed.

Entrepreneurship is the activity of starting and running businesses, typically with initiative and risk. The word emphasizes the process and mindset rather than a single venture: {She studied entrepreneurship in college}, {The city's culture encourages entrepreneurship}. It often carries connotations of innovation, self-reliance, and economic ambition.

Entries is the plural of entry. An entry is an act of going in, or a place for entering: {The back door is the only entry}. It also means a recorded item—in a ledger, dictionary, or database: {She added an entry to the spreadsheet}. In competitions, an entry is a submitted item or the act of submitting: {The contest received over a thousand entries}.

Entropy is a measure of disorder or randomness in a system. In thermodynamics, it quantifies the energy unavailable for useful work—systems tend toward higher entropy over time, which is why heat flows from hot to cold and not the reverse. In information theory, entropy measures uncertainty or unpredictability in data. Figuratively, entropy suggests inevitable decline into chaos or disorganization: {The project descended into entropy once the manager quit}.

To entrust is to give someone responsibility for something valuable or important, placing confidence in their care: {She entrusted her children to her sister}, {He was entrusted with the company's finances}. The word implies both trust in the recipient and the significance of what's being handed over. You entrust tasks, secrets, possessions, or people to someone you believe will handle them properly.

Entrusted is the past tense of entrust, meaning to give someone responsibility for something valuable or important. You entrust a task to a capable person, or entrust a person with a task: {She entrusted her savings to a financial advisor}. The word implies confidence in the recipient's reliability or discretion: {He was entrusted with the company's most sensitive documents}.

Entrusting is the act of placing something valuable—whether physical, like money or possessions, or abstract, like responsibility or secrets—into someone else's care with the expectation they will protect or manage it faithfully. The word implies confidence in the recipient: {She's entrusting her children to her sister while she travels}. You entrust something to someone, or entrust someone with something.

Entry is the act of going in or the place where you go in: {The entry to the building was blocked}. It extends to items entered somewhere—an entry in a ledger, a dictionary entry, an entry in a competition. Entry also names the right or ability to enter: {She was denied entry to the country}. In law, unlawful entry is entering property without permission.

An entryway is a passage or area through which you enter a building or room—the space just inside or leading to a door. In homes, the entryway is where you hang coats, remove shoes, and greet visitors: {We installed hooks in the entryway for jackets}. The word emphasizes the transitional function of the space.

To entwine is to twist or wind together, like vines climbing a trellis or fingers interlacing: {Their arms entwined as they walked}. The word often suggests intimacy or inseparability—lives, fates, or stories can become entwined. {Her history was deeply entwined with the town's.}

Entwined means twisted or woven together, like vines climbing a trellis or fingers interlaced. The word often describes things physically wrapped around each other: {Their arms were entwined}. Figuratively, entwined suggests deep connection or inseparability: {Their fates were entwined from the beginning}, {a story entwined with themes of loss and redemption}.

Entwining is wrapping or weaving together, twisting around something or each other: {vines entwining the trellis}, {their fingers entwining}. The word suggests intimate, often beautiful connection—lovers' limbs, intertwined fates, stories that wind together. What entwines becomes difficult to separate.

Enunciation is the act of pronouncing words clearly and distinctly. Good enunciation means articulating each syllable so listeners can understand: {Her enunciation was so precise that even the back row heard every word}. The word also applies to formal statements or declarations: {the enunciation of a new policy}.

To envelop is to wrap, surround, or cover completely. Fog envelops a city; flames envelop a building; darkness envelops the landscape. The word suggests something closing in from all sides: {She was enveloped in his arms}. Envelop is the verb; envelope (with an e) is the noun for the paper sleeve that holds a letter.

An envelope is a flat paper container for a letter or document, typically with a flap that folds over and seals. The word extends to any wrapper or covering: the {envelope of gas surrounding a star}. To {push the envelope} is to test limits or boundaries—originally aviation slang for exceeding a plane's performance parameters.

Envelopes are flat paper containers for letters or documents, with a flap that folds over and seals. The word extends to any enclosing layer: {the envelope of atmosphere surrounding Earth}. To {push the envelope} is to test limits—from aviation, where the flight envelope defines a plane's safe operating range. The verb envelope (no s) means to surround completely: {Fog enveloped the city}.

Enveloping describes something that surrounds or wraps completely, creating a sense of being enclosed or immersed: {an enveloping darkness}, {the enveloping warmth of a blanket}. The word suggests thorough coverage—not just touching but containing from all sides. An enveloping hug draws someone fully in; an enveloping fog obscures everything.

Enviable describes something desirable enough to provoke envy in others: an enviable {position}, enviable {success}, an enviable {reputation}. The word carries a note of admiration—what's enviable isn't just good but notably, visibly good in a way others recognize and want for themselves.

Envied is the past tense of envy—to feel resentful longing for what someone else has. The object of envy can be a person or a possession: {She envied her sister's easy confidence}, {He envied the promotion his colleague received}. To be envied is to possess something others covet: {Her talent was widely envied}.

Envious describes wanting what someone else has—their possessions, qualities, or advantages. {She was envious of her sister's natural talent.} The feeling ranges from mild longing to bitter resentment. Envious often implies awareness that the desire is somewhat shameful, distinguishing it from the more neutral admiring or the harsher covetous.

Environment is a multipurpose word, but its meaning always relates to surroundings or conditions. Without qualification, environment often refers to the complex factors that make life possible on earth, including living things themselves. A specific environment means the surroundings and factors that have an influence on a person or place: The environment in my office gets increasingly stressful toward the end of the week.

Environmental relates to the surroundings or conditions in which people, animals, or plants live. It often concerns the natural world and human impact on it: {environmental protection}, {environmental damage}, {an environmental activist}. The word also applies to any setting or context: {environmental factors in child development}. An {environmental impact assessment} evaluates how a project might affect its surroundings.

Environmentalism is advocacy for protecting the natural world from pollution, resource depletion, and human destruction. The term covers a spectrum from mainstream conservation efforts to radical activism. An environmentalist might support recycling programs, oppose offshore drilling, or chain themselves to trees. {Her environmentalism began with childhood hikes and grew into a career in climate policy.}

An environmentalist is someone who advocates for protecting the natural world from pollution, habitat destruction, and climate change. The term can describe casual supporters of conservation or dedicated activists: {Environmentalists protested the pipeline}. It sometimes carries political connotations, used admiringly by allies or dismissively by opponents: {Those environmentalists want to shut down the whole industry}.

Environmentalists are people who advocate for protecting the natural world from pollution, habitat destruction, and climate change. The term ranges from casual supporters of conservation to committed activists who chain themselves to trees or blockade pipelines. {Environmentalists pushed for stricter emissions standards.} Critics sometimes use the label dismissively to suggest impractical idealism.

Environments is the plural of environment—the surroundings or conditions in which something exists or operates. Physical environments include natural settings like forests or deserts, and built spaces like offices or homes. Abstract environments describe conditions for activity: {hostile work environments}, {learning environments}, {competitive business environments}. In computing, an environment is a configured system where software runs: {development environment}, {testing environment}.

Envision means to form a mental picture of something, especially something that doesn't yet exist or that you hope to bring about. It's the verb of choice when describing imaginative planning or forward-looking thought: {She envisioned a future where everyone had access to clean water}. Unlike simply imagining, envision often carries a sense of purpose or intention—you envision outcomes you're working toward, not just idle fantasies.

An envoy is a messenger or representative sent on a mission, especially a diplomatic one. The term typically refers to someone dispatched by a government to conduct negotiations or deliver communications: {The president sent a special envoy to broker peace talks}. An envoy ranks below an ambassador but carries similar authority for specific assignments.

Envoys are official representatives sent on diplomatic missions, typically to deliver messages or negotiate on behalf of a government or organization. The term suggests a formal emissary with specific duties rather than a permanent ambassador: {The president dispatched envoys to negotiate a ceasefire}. Envoys may also represent non-governmental entities in formal contexts.

Envy is resentful longing for what someone else has—their possessions, qualities, or good fortune. Unlike jealousy, which fears losing what you have, envy wants what belongs to another: {I envy her ability to speak five languages}. The feeling can be mild admiration or bitter covetousness. As a verb, to envy is to feel this way: {Don't envy the rich; they have their own troubles}. One of the seven deadly sins in Christian tradition.

An enzyme is a protein that speeds up chemical reactions in living organisms without being consumed in the process. Enzymes are essential to digestion, metabolism, and virtually every biological function. Each enzyme typically acts on a specific substance: {Lactase breaks down lactose in milk}. Outside biology, enzymes appear in detergents and food processing.

Enzymes are proteins that accelerate chemical reactions in living organisms. They act as biological catalysts—speeding up processes without being consumed themselves. Digestive enzymes break down food; other enzymes copy DNA, build muscle, or detoxify the liver. Each enzyme typically acts on a specific molecule: {lactase breaks down lactose}. Industrial applications include laundry detergents and food processing.

An eon is an immensely long period of time. In geology, it's the largest division of Earth's history, spanning hundreds of millions of years. In everyday use, eon is hyperbolic: {I haven't seen you in eons}. The word suggests time so vast it becomes almost abstract. Also spelled aeon, especially in British English.

Eons is a vast stretch of time, typically spanning millions or billions of years. In geology, an eon is the largest division of Earth's history. More loosely, eons describes any period that feels immeasurably long: {I haven't seen her in eons}, {It took eons for the food to arrive}. Also spelled aeons.

An epaulet is an ornamental shoulder piece on a military uniform, typically featuring braided cord or fringe. Epaulets indicate rank and add ceremonial formality. The term extends to any decorative shoulder attachment on clothing: {a jacket with gold epaulets}. Also spelled epaulette.

Epaulets are ornamental shoulder pieces on military uniforms or formal jackets—fringed or braided fabric that sits on each shoulder, indicating rank or regiment. The term extends to any decorative shoulder detail on clothing: {a jacket with gold epaulets}. Also spelled epaulettes.

An epaulette is an ornamental shoulder piece on a military uniform, typically featuring braided cord, fringe, or metallic embellishments that indicate rank or regiment. Originally functional—securing shoulder straps for carrying gear—epaulettes became purely decorative markers of military status. The term extends to similar decorative shoulder features on civilian clothing, particularly jackets and coats with buttoned flaps or raised padding at the shoulders.

Epaulettes are ornamental shoulder pieces on military uniforms, typically featuring fringe or braiding that indicates rank. They originated as functional armor protection but evolved into purely decorative insignia: {The general's epaulettes gleamed with gold braid}. The term extends to any decorative shoulder detail on clothing. Also spelled epaulets.

An epee is a fencing sword with a stiff, narrow blade and a blunted tip. Unlike the foil or sabre, the epee allows touches anywhere on the body, making it the weapon closest to actual dueling. The word comes from French for sword. {She won gold in the individual epee event.}

Ephemera are things meant to last only briefly—printed materials like tickets, pamphlets, postcards, and posters that weren't designed for preservation. Collectors prize vintage ephemera precisely because so little survives: {The auction featured Victorian trade cards and other ephemera}. The word extends to anything transient or short-lived: {the ephemera of daily life}, {social media ephemera}. The singular ephemeron is rare; ephemera serves for both.

Ephemeral describes things that last only briefly—a day, a moment, a season. Mayflies are the classic example: their adult lives span hours. The word applies to anything transient: {ephemeral pleasures}, {ephemeral fame}, {the ephemeral beauty of cherry blossoms}. What's ephemeral passes quickly and cannot be held.

Genuine epics, that is, long poems about legendary heroes, such as The Iliad and The Odyssey, are not common. Things characterized as epic are a dime a dozen and include any enjoyable or out of the ordinary phenomenon or experience: That sunset was epic! Something of epic proportions is impressively large or grand. Novels of great length with a historical setting are frequently called epics, especially by their publishers.

The epicenter is the point on Earth's surface directly above where an earthquake originates: {The epicenter was located twelve miles offshore}. By extension, epicenter means the focal point or center of any activity or phenomenon: {Silicon Valley remains the epicenter of tech innovation}. The figurative use sometimes draws criticism when center would suffice, but it emphasizes intensity or impact.

Epicenters is the plural of epicenter, the point on Earth's surface directly above an earthquake's origin: {The epicenters of both quakes were offshore}. Figuratively, an epicenter is the focal point of activity or crisis: {Several cities became epicenters of the outbreak}. The figurative use sometimes draws criticism for imprecision, but it's well established.

Epicentre is the point on the earth's surface directly above the origin of an earthquake. The seismic waves radiate outward from this location, making it the area of greatest intensity. Figuratively, epicentre describes the central point of any activity or phenomenon: {Paris was the epicentre of the art world}, {The tech company found itself at the epicentre of the scandal}. Also spelled epicenter.

Epics are long narrative works centered on heroic deeds and grand events—the *Iliad*, *Beowulf*, *Paradise Lost*. The term extends to any ambitious, sweeping story: an epic film, an epic novel. Informally, epic describes anything impressively large or memorable: {That party was epic}. {We're planning an epic road trip across the country}.

Epicurean describes devotion to sensory pleasure, especially fine food and drink. An epicurean {meal} features carefully prepared dishes; an epicurean {lifestyle} prioritizes refined enjoyment. The word derives from the Greek philosopher Epicurus, though his actual philosophy emphasized moderate pleasures and freedom from anxiety—quite different from the indulgent connotations the word now carries. {She had epicurean tastes in wine.}

An epidemic is a widespread occurrence of disease in a community or region during a particular period, affecting many people at once. When diseases spread across multiple countries or continents, they become pandemics rather than epidemics. The word extends beyond medicine to describe any rapid spread or sudden increase: {an epidemic of violence}, {the opioid epidemic}. As an adjective, epidemic describes something spreading rapidly and extensively: {Fear had reached epidemic proportions}.
clues: When sickness takes a whole community

definition: Epidemics are outbreaks of disease that spread rapidly through a population, affecting many people at once: {The flu epidemic swept through the school}. The term extends to any widespread occurrence of something undesirable: {an epidemic of gun violence}, {an epidemic of misinformation}. As an adjective, epidemic describes such rapid spread: {Violence had reached epidemic proportions}.

An epidural is an injection of anesthetic into the space around the spinal cord, numbing the lower body while keeping the patient conscious. Most commonly administered during childbirth to manage labor pain: {She decided to get an epidural after six hours of contractions}. Also used for certain surgeries and chronic pain management.

Epidurals are injections of anesthetic into the space around the spinal cord, used to block pain in the lower body. The term most commonly refers to epidural anesthesia given during childbirth: {She decided to get an epidural during labor}. Epidurals also manage chronic back pain or provide anesthesia for certain surgeries.

An epigram is a short, witty statement that makes a pointed observation, often with a twist: {Oscar Wilde was a master of the epigram}. The form prizes compression and cleverness—a memorable phrase that captures something true or paradoxical. In poetry, an epigram is a brief poem with a similar punch: sharp, polished, ending with a sting.

Epigrams are short, witty statements that make a pointed observation, often with a clever twist or paradox. The form originated in ancient Greece as brief inscriptions, but evolved into a literary genre prized for its compression and sting. Oscar Wilde's quips exemplify the modern epigram: {I can resist everything except temptation}. An epigrammatic style favors concise, memorable phrasing over elaboration.

Epilepsy is a neurological condition characterized by recurring seizures—episodes of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Seizures range from brief lapses in awareness to full-body convulsions. The condition is chronic but often manageable with medication. Someone with epilepsy is epileptic, though many prefer "person with epilepsy."

Epilog is a variant spelling of epilogue—a concluding section of a book, play, or other work that provides closure or reflects on what came before. The spelling without the -ue is less common but acceptable, particularly in American English: {The epilog revealed what happened to the characters ten years later}.

An epilogue is a concluding section that comes after the main action of a story ends. In novels and films, it often shows what happened to characters years later: {The epilogue revealed they'd stayed married for fifty years}. In plays, an actor may deliver an epilogue directly to the audience, commenting on the story's meaning.
