More broadly, any concluding event or period can be called an epilogue: {The treaty was an epilogue to decades of conflict}.

Epilogues is the plural of epilogue—a concluding section that comes after the main narrative ends. In literature and drama, an epilogue wraps up loose ends or reflects on the story's events: {The epilogues of Shakespeare's plays often address the audience directly}. Epilogues may also appear in film and television, showing what became of the characters.

Epiphanies is the plural of epiphany—moments of sudden insight or revelation when something becomes clear. The word originally referred to the manifestation of a divine being, and the Christian feast of Epiphany celebrates the revelation of Christ to the Magi. In secular use, an epiphany is any flash of understanding: {She had a series of epiphanies about her career}. Writers use the term for moments when characters suddenly grasp something essential about themselves or their situation.

A sudden realization is often called an epiphany when it is sparked by an event or when it is especially helpful or important. The most common epiphanies are personal, religious, or spiritual; that which is realized is of interest only to the person himself: After years in therapy, he experienced an epiphany about his motivations. Epiphany, when capitalized, is a day in the Christian calendar relating to the birth of Jesus.

An episode is a distinct event or period within a larger series. Television shows are divided into episodes—individual installments of a continuing narrative. In life, an episode is a notable incident or stretch of time: {a brief episode of happiness}, {an embarrassing episode from my youth}. Medical episodes are occurrences of illness or symptoms: {a psychotic episode}, {an episode of chest pain}. The word suggests something bounded—with a beginning and end—set against a longer backdrop.

Episodes are individual installments of a serialized work—distinct segments of a television series, podcast, or other ongoing narrative: {I've only watched the first three episodes}. More broadly, an episode is any distinct event or period within a larger experience: {a brief episode of unemployment}, {an episode of chest pain}. The word suggests bounded incidents within a continuing story.

An epitaph is an inscription on a tomb or gravestone commemorating the person buried there. By extension, it can be any brief statement honoring the dead, or a fitting final summation of someone's life or work: {His last failed venture was a fitting epitaph for his career}. The related word epithet is sometimes confused with epitaph.

Epitaphs is the plural of epitaph—an inscription on a tomb or gravestone commemorating the dead. By extension, any brief statement honoring someone who has died: {The obituary served as his epitaph}. Figuratively, a final judgment or summation: {That loss was the epitaph for their championship hopes}.

An epithet is a word or phrase used to characterize someone or something: {Alexander the Great}, {Richard the Lionheart}, {the wine-dark sea}. In modern usage, epithet often means an abusive or contemptuous term: {The protesters hurled epithets at police}. The word carries a suggestion of name-calling, though historically it simply meant a descriptive label attached to a name.

Epithets is the plural of epithet, a word or phrase characterizing someone or something. Epithets range from honorific ({Alexander the Great}, {the Iron Lady}) to descriptive ({wine-dark sea}) to abusive. In modern usage, epithet often implies a slur or insult: {The crowd hurled racial epithets at the players}. The singular appears in {ethnic epithet}, {racial epithet}.

The epitome of something is the perfect example or embodiment of it: {She was the epitome of grace}. The word implies that the person or thing fully represents a quality or type. Less commonly, epitome refers to a summary or condensed version of a longer work—a meaning now mostly found in academic contexts.

To epitomize something is to be a perfect example of it—to embody its essential qualities: {She epitomizes elegance}. A thing that epitomizes a category represents it so fully that it could stand for the whole: {That building epitomizes brutalist architecture}. Less commonly, to epitomize is to summarize or condense.

An epoch is a distinct period of time, especially one marked by notable events or characteristics: {the epoch of industrialization}, {the Victorian epoch}. In geology and astronomy, epoch has precise technical meanings for divisions of time. The word suggests a significant era rather than just any stretch of time—epochs are memorable, defining periods that shape what follows.

Epochs are extended periods of time, typically marked by distinctive characteristics, events, or developments: {the Victorian epoch}, {the epoch of space exploration}. In geology, an epoch is a subdivision of a period, spanning millions of years. In computing and astronomy, an epoch is a reference point from which time is measured—Unix systems count seconds from the epoch of January 1, 1970.

Epoxy is a type of strong adhesive or resin that hardens when two components are mixed together. The resulting bond is exceptionally durable and resistant to heat and chemicals, making epoxy popular for industrial applications, crafts, and repairs: {I used epoxy to fix the broken handle}. As a verb, to epoxy something is to glue it with this adhesive.

Equal describes things that match in quantity, degree, or status. Two halves are equal portions. {All men are created equal} asserts equivalent moral standing. To equal something is to match it: {Nothing equals a home-cooked meal}. An equal is a peer: {She treats her employees as equals}. Equal also means capable of meeting a challenge: {Are you equal to the task?}

Equalise is the British spelling of equalize—to make things equal or uniform. In sports, especially football, to equalise is to score a goal that ties the match: {They equalised in the 89th minute}. The word applies broadly to balancing levels or amounts: {The new policy aims to equalise pay across departments}.

An equaliser is British spelling of equalizer. In sports, especially football, an equaliser is a goal that ties the score: {They scored an equaliser in the 89th minute}. In audio, an equaliser adjusts frequency levels. More broadly, something that equalises removes advantages or levels differences: {Death is the great equaliser}.

Equality is the condition of being equal—having the same status, rights, opportunities, or value as others. In social and political contexts, equality typically refers to the principle that all people deserve the same treatment regardless of characteristics like race, gender, or wealth: {The movement fought for equality under the law.} Mathematical equality means two expressions have the same value. The word often appears in debates about whether formal equality (same rules for everyone) achieves genuine fairness.

To equalize is to make things equal or uniform. You might equalize pressure between two chambers, equalize pay across departments, or equalize the volume on different audio tracks. In sports, to equalize is to tie the score: {They equalized in the final minute}. An equalizer is a device—especially in audio—that adjusts frequencies to achieve balance.

Equalized means made equal or brought into balance. Audio that has been equalized has had its frequency levels adjusted: {The engineer equalized the mix to bring out the vocals}. In sports, a team that has equalized has tied the score: {They equalized in the 89th minute}. The word implies correction—something was uneven and has been leveled out.

An equalizer is something that levels a playing field or neutralizes an advantage. A gun is sometimes called {the great equalizer}—it lets a smaller person match a larger one. In audio, an equalizer adjusts frequency levels to balance sound: {She boosted the bass on the equalizer}. In sports, an equalizer is a goal or score that ties the game.

Equals functions as verb and noun around the idea of sameness or equivalence. Two plus two equals four. To equal something is to match it: {Nothing equals the thrill of a live performance}. As a noun, an equal is someone of the same rank or ability: {She treats everyone as equals}. The phrase {first among equals} describes nominal leadership within a group of peers.

Equanimity is mental calmness and composure, especially in difficult situations. The word suggests an evenness of temperament—neither elated by good fortune nor crushed by bad: {She accepted the diagnosis with remarkable equanimity}. It implies not indifference but a steady, balanced response to whatever comes.

To equate two things is to treat them as equivalent or identical: {She equates money with success}. The word often carries skepticism—when someone equates A with B, we may doubt the comparison holds: {Critics say the policy equates dissent with disloyalty}. In mathematics, to equate is to set expressions equal to each other. The noun is equation.

An equation is a mathematical statement that two expressions are equal, connected by an equals sign: {2 + 2 = 4}. Solving an equation means finding values that make it true. Outside mathematics, equation describes a complex situation where multiple factors must balance: {the political equation}, {factoring climate change into the equation}. To say something is {part of the equation} acknowledges it as one element among several that matter.

Equations are mathematical statements asserting that two expressions are equal, connected by an equals sign: {The equation x + 2 = 5 has the solution x = 3}. Beyond math, equation can mean any complex situation with multiple factors to balance: {the political equation}, {factoring childcare into the equation}. To equate things is to treat them as equivalent.

The equator is an imaginary line circling Earth at its widest point, equidistant from the North and South Poles. It divides the planet into Northern and Southern Hemispheres and marks zero degrees latitude. Countries {on the equator} experience roughly equal day and night year-round. The term extends to similar lines on other celestial bodies or any central dividing line: {the celestial equator}.

Equestrian relates to horseback riding or horse riders. An equestrian {statue} depicts someone on horseback. Equestrian {sports} include dressage, show jumping, and polo. As a noun, an equestrian is a person who rides horses: {She's been an equestrian since childhood}. The word carries connotations of formality and tradition—casual trail riders are less often called equestrians.

Equestrians are people who ride horses, particularly those skilled in horsemanship or involved in competitive riding sports like dressage, show jumping, or eventing. The word also works as an adjective describing anything related to horseback riding: {equestrian events}, {equestrian sports}, {an equestrian statue} depicting a figure mounted on horseback.

Equilibrium is a state of balance between opposing forces or influences. In physics, a body is in equilibrium when forces acting on it cancel out, producing no net change. In chemistry, equilibrium occurs when a reaction proceeds equally in both directions. The word extends to mental or emotional steadiness: {She recovered her equilibrium after the shock}. Economic equilibrium describes markets where supply meets demand. {The ecosystem remained in delicate equilibrium until the invasive species arrived.}

An equinox is either of two moments each year when the sun crosses the celestial equator, making day and night approximately equal in length worldwide. The vernal equinox occurs around March 20, marking spring in the Northern Hemisphere; the autumnal equinox falls around September 22, marking fall. {The equinox signals the changing of seasons.}

Equinoxes are the two moments each year when the sun crosses the celestial equator, making day and night approximately equal in length worldwide. The vernal equinox occurs around March 20, marking the start of spring in the Northern Hemisphere; the autumnal equinox falls around September 22, beginning fall. {The equinoxes signal seasonal transitions.}

To equip is to supply with what's needed for a particular purpose—tools, gear, knowledge, or skills. You equip a soldier with weapons, a kitchen with appliances, a student with critical thinking. {The expedition was fully equipped for arctic conditions}. To be {well-equipped} for something is to have adequate resources or preparation. Equipment is the noun.

Equipment is the set of tools, gear, or supplies needed for a particular purpose: {camping equipment}, {medical equipment}, {gym equipment}. The word is uncountable—you don't have "an equipment" or "equipments," but rather a piece of equipment. Equipment can also refer to mental or emotional resources: {He lacks the emotional equipment to handle criticism}.

Equipped means supplied with what is needed for a particular purpose. A kitchen is equipped with appliances; a soldier is equipped with weapons and gear. The word extends beyond physical objects: {She wasn't emotionally equipped to handle the news}. To be well-equipped or ill-equipped is to be prepared or unprepared for what lies ahead.

Equity is fairness or justice in how people are treated. In finance, equity is ownership value—what remains after debts are subtracted: {home equity}, {shareholder equity}. Equity in a company means ownership shares, distinct from debt. In recent usage, equity often appears alongside diversity and inclusion, emphasizing fair outcomes rather than merely equal treatment: {The policy aims for equity, not just equality}.

Equivalence is the state of being equal or interchangeable in value, function, or meaning. Two things have equivalence when they can substitute for each other: {The course has equivalence with the required prerequisite}. In logic and mathematics, equivalence describes a relationship where statements or expressions yield the same result. {There's no real equivalence between the two situations.}

Equivalent describes things equal in value, function, or meaning, though not necessarily identical in form. A dollar is equivalent to one hundred cents. A nod can be equivalent to saying yes. As a noun, an equivalent is the thing that matches another: {What's the English equivalent of that French word?} {She earns the equivalent of fifty thousand dollars a year.}

Equivalents is the plural of equivalent—things equal in value, function, or meaning. You might ask for the equivalent of a cup in milliliters, or seek the French equivalent of an English idiom. {The generic drug is the equivalent of the brand name}. In chemistry, equivalents measure reactive capacity between substances.

Equivocating is speaking in deliberately vague or ambiguous terms to avoid committing to a position. Someone who equivocates uses slippery language that could be interpreted multiple ways, often to evade direct questions or escape accountability: {The witness kept equivocating about what he saw that night}. Politicians are frequently accused of equivocating when they want to please opposing constituencies.

Equivocation is the use of ambiguous language to mislead without outright lying. A politician asked about raising taxes might equivocate by discussing fiscal responsibility in general terms. The word implies deliberate vagueness—exploiting multiple meanings to avoid commitment: {His answer was pure equivocation}. To equivocate is to speak this way.

An era is a distinct period of time marked by particular characteristics, events, or developments. Eras are defined by what makes them different from what came before: {the Victorian era}, {the digital era}, {the end of an era}. In geology, an era is a major division of time containing multiple periods. The word often signals historical or cultural turning points: {We're entering a new era in medicine}.

Eradicate means to destroy completely or eliminate entirely. The word implies thorough removal—not just reduction but total elimination: {eradicate poverty}, {eradicate disease}, {eradicate corruption}. Weeds are eradicated from gardens, pests from crops, errors from manuscripts. The goal is leaving no trace behind.
clues: Destroy so nothing at all remains

definition: Eradicated means completely destroyed or eliminated, as if pulled up by the roots. Diseases are eradicated when no cases remain anywhere. Pests, weeds, and social problems can be eradicated—though the word often overstates what's actually achieved: {The program claims to have eradicated poverty in the region}. The past participle works as an adjective: {an eradicated species}.

Eradication is complete elimination or destruction—wiping something out entirely. The word applies most often to diseases, pests, or social problems: {the eradication of smallpox}, {efforts toward poverty eradication}. Unlike control or reduction, eradication implies total removal with no trace remaining.

Eras are distinct periods of time marked by particular characteristics, events, or figures. History divides into eras: the Victorian era, the Cold War era, the digital era. The word works at any scale—geological eras span millions of years, while someone might speak of {the Jordan era} in basketball or {the end of an era} when a favorite restaurant closes.

Erase means to remove something, typically marks from a surface. You erase pencil with a rubber eraser, chalk from a blackboard, files from a hard drive. The word extends to removing anything as if by rubbing out: {erase the memory}, {erase all doubt}. To erase someone from history is to eliminate their record or legacy entirely.

Erased means rubbed out or removed. Pencil marks are erased with an eraser; digital files are erased with a keystroke. The word extends to anything eliminated or made to disappear: {The scandal erased years of goodwill}. To feel erased is to feel ignored or rendered invisible, as though your presence or identity doesn't register.

An eraser is a piece of rubber or similar material used to remove pencil marks from paper. In British English, the same object is called a rubber. Erasers also appear on digital devices as tools that remove pixels or strokes: {Use the eraser to clean up the edges of your drawing}.

Erasers is the plural of eraser—a tool for removing marks, typically pencil marks from paper. The most familiar is the rubber or vinyl block found at the end of pencils or sold separately. Erasers also remove chalk from blackboards and dry-erase marker from whiteboards. {I keep a pack of erasers in my desk drawer.}

Erases is the present tense of erase, meaning to remove marks, data, or traces of something. You erase pencil marks with a rubber eraser, digital files with a keystroke. Figuratively, to erase is to eliminate or make something as if it never existed: {The scandal erased years of goodwill}. {Time erases painful memories}.

Erasing is removing marks, writing, or recorded material. You erase pencil marks with a rubber eraser, chalkboard writing with a felt pad, digital files with a keystroke. The word extends to anything eliminated or obliterated: {erasing all traces of the previous tenant}, {erasing the memory from her mind}. In basketball, erasing a deficit means overcoming it.

Erasure is the act of erasing or the state of being erased—the removal of marks, records, or traces. You might correct an erasure on a form or notice erasures in a ledger. The word extends to figurative removal: the erasure of someone's {contributions from history}, the erasure of {cultural identity}. In critical theory, erasure describes the systematic omission or marginalization of groups from discourse or representation.

Erasures is the plural of erasure—acts of erasing or the marks left behind when something has been rubbed out. You can see erasures on a document where someone corrected mistakes. The word extends to deliberate removal from history or discourse: {the erasures of women's contributions to science}, {cultural erasure of indigenous peoples}. In poetry, erasure is a technique of selectively removing words from an existing text to create new meaning.

An ereader is a portable electronic device designed primarily for reading digital books and documents. Unlike tablets or phones, ereaders typically use e-ink displays that mimic the appearance of paper and are easier on the eyes for extended reading. They can store thousands of books and often connect to online bookstores for purchasing and downloading content. {I loaded my ereader with novels before the trip.}

Erect means upright or standing straight up. An erect {posture} is tall and rigid. A structure that has been erected has been built or raised into position: {They erected a monument in the town square}. Erect also describes body parts that have stiffened and risen—most often the penis during arousal, but also nipples or ears: {The dog's ears were erect}.

Erected is the past tense of erect, meaning built or constructed: {They erected a monument in his honor}, {A fence was erected along the property line}. It also means raised to an upright position: {The flagpole was erected at dawn}. In reference to body parts, especially the penis, erected describes becoming rigid and engorged with blood.

An erection is the state of being erect—stiff, upright, or raised. Most commonly, the word refers to the engorgement of the penis with blood, causing it to become rigid: {He woke up with an erection}. The word also applies to the act of constructing something: {the erection of a monument}, {the erection of trade barriers}. A structure itself may be called an erection, though this use sounds dated.

Erections is the plural of erection. Most commonly, an erection is the stiffening of the penis when engorged with blood, typically from sexual arousal: {He woke up with an erection}. The word also means the act of building or assembling something, or a structure that has been erected: {the erection of a monument}, {steel erections dotted the construction site}.

Ergonomic describes design intended to minimize physical strain and maximize efficiency for the human body. An ergonomic {chair} supports proper posture; an ergonomic {keyboard} reduces wrist strain. The term applies broadly to workspaces, tools, and equipment shaped around how people actually move and work: {The office underwent an ergonomic assessment}.

Ergonomics is the study of designing equipment, workspaces, and systems to fit human bodies and capabilities. The goal is efficiency and comfort while reducing strain or injury: {The company invested in ergonomics—adjustable desks, better chairs}. The adjective ergonomic describes things designed with these principles: {an ergonomic keyboard}, {ergonomic office furniture}.

Ermine is a stoat in its white winter coat, or the fur from such animals. The white fur with black tail tips became associated with royalty and high office—judges' robes and monarchs' capes traditionally feature ermine trim. By extension, ermine can refer to the office or dignity itself: {the ermine of a peer}. The animal is also called a short-tailed weasel.

Ermines is the plural of ermine, a stoat in its white winter coat or the fur itself. Ermine fur, prized for its pure white color with distinctive black tail tips, traditionally trimmed the robes of royalty and judges: {The king's cape was lined with ermines}. In heraldry, ermine is a pattern of black spots on white.

Erode means to wear away gradually through natural forces—water erodes rock, wind erodes soil. The word extends to any slow deterioration: {Inflation erodes purchasing power}, {Trust between them had eroded over the years}. What erodes doesn't collapse suddenly but diminishes bit by bit until significantly reduced or gone.

Eroded describes something that has been gradually worn away or diminished. Water erodes rock; wind erodes soil. The past participle works as an adjective for the result: {eroded cliffs}, {eroded coastline}. Figuratively, trust, support, or rights can be eroded—weakened slowly over time: {Public confidence in the institution has eroded}.

Erodes is the third-person singular of erode, which describes the gradual wearing away of something through persistent action. Wind erodes rock formations; waves erode coastlines; acid erodes metal. The word extends naturally to abstract contexts: {Constant criticism erodes confidence}, {Inflation erodes purchasing power}. Whether physical or figurative, erosion implies slow, steady deterioration rather than sudden destruction.

Eroding is the present participle of erode, describing the gradual wearing away of something. Physically, wind and water erode rock and soil: {The coastline is eroding at an alarming rate}. Figuratively, things erode when they diminish slowly over time: {Public trust in institutions is eroding}, {eroding profit margins}. The word emphasizes process rather than result—something actively being worn down.

Eros is sexual love or desire, particularly in its passionate, romantic dimension—distinguished from other Greek love concepts like philia (friendship) or agape (selfless love). In psychoanalytic theory, eros refers to the life instinct, the drive toward survival, pleasure, and reproduction. The term appears in discussions of art, literature, and psychology: {The film explores the tension between eros and duty}. (Capitalized Eros is the Greek god of love.)

Erosion is the gradual wearing away of material by natural forces—wind, water, ice, or gravity. Rivers erode canyons, waves erode coastlines, glaciers erode valleys. The word extends to any slow deterioration: {the erosion of civil liberties}, {erosion of trust}, {erosion of purchasing power}. Soil erosion from poor farming practices remains a global concern.

Erotic describes what arouses sexual desire or relates to sexual love. Erotic {literature}, erotic {art}, erotic {dreams}. The word carries more refinement than sexual or sexy—it suggests aestheticized or elevated sensuality rather than crude arousal. {The film's erotic tension built slowly}. Erotica refers to sexually stimulating creative works, distinguished from pornography by artistic intent.

Erotica is literature, art, or other media depicting sexual desire and activity, intended to arouse. Unlike pornography, erotica suggests artistic merit or emotional depth beyond mere titillation: {She writes erotica exploring female desire}. The distinction is subjective—one person's erotica is another's porn.

Eroticism is sexual desire or the quality of arousing it. The term applies to art, literature, and imagery that depicts or evokes sensuality: {The film's eroticism made censors nervous}. Unlike pornography, eroticism often implies aesthetic intent or subtlety—suggestion rather than explicitness. The word can also describe a general atmosphere or quality: {an air of eroticism}.

To err is to make a mistake or be incorrect: {To err is human, to forgive divine}. The word is somewhat formal or literary. It can also mean to stray from a standard: {err on the side of caution} means to make the safer choice when uncertain. The pronunciation with a short "e" (like "air") is traditional; rhyming with "fur" is now equally common.

An errand is a short trip to accomplish a specific task, usually routine: picking up dry cleaning, mailing a package, buying groceries. {I have to run a few errands this afternoon.} The word implies going somewhere and returning, often on behalf of someone else or a household. A {fool's errand} is a pointless or hopeless task.

Errands are short trips to accomplish specific tasks, usually routine ones like picking up groceries, dropping off dry cleaning, or mailing a package. The word implies minor obligations that take you out of the house: {I have to run some errands this afternoon}. Errands are distinguished from more significant outings by their mundane, practical nature.

Erratic describes movement or behavior that is irregular, unpredictable, or inconsistent: {erratic driving}, {erratic mood swings}, {The stock has been erratic all week}. The word implies deviation from a steady or expected pattern—not merely unusual, but varying without apparent logic. In geology, an erratic is a boulder transported by glacial ice and deposited far from its origin.

Error is a mistake—a deviation from what is correct, accurate, or intended. An error in {judgment} is a bad decision. An error in {calculation} produces a wrong result. In baseball, an error is a fielder's misplay that allows a batter or runner to advance. In computing, error messages indicate something has gone wrong. {Trial and error} is learning by making mistakes and correcting them. To {err} is the verb form.

Errors are mistakes—deviations from what is correct, accurate, or intended. The word covers everything from typos to moral failings: {a spelling error}, {an error in judgment}, {human error}. In sports, an error is a fielding mistake that allows a batter or runner to advance. In computing, error messages signal that something has gone wrong. {Trial and error} describes learning through repeated attempts and failures.

Ersatz describes something serving as a substitute, usually an inferior one. The word came from German during wartime shortages, when ersatz {coffee} might be made from acorns and ersatz {rubber} from synthetic materials. The connotation is of something artificial or second-rate that fails to match the original: {ersatz sentiment}, {ersatz leather}, {an ersatz version of democracy}.

Erupt means to burst forth suddenly and violently. Volcanoes erupt, sending lava and ash into the air. The word extends to any sudden outbreak: violence erupts, applause erupts, a crowd erupts in cheers. Skin erupts in a rash. Teeth erupt when they break through the gums. {Fighting erupted in the streets}. {She erupted in anger when she heard the news}.

Erupted is the past tense of erupt. A volcano erupts when it expels lava, ash, and gases. The meaning extends to any sudden, forceful emergence: {Violence erupted in the streets}, {The crowd erupted in applause}, {A rash erupted on her skin}. Teeth erupt when they break through the gums. Emotions erupt when they can no longer be contained.

Erupting describes something in the act of bursting forth violently. A volcano erupts when it expels lava, ash, and gas. Skin erupts with a rash. A crowd erupts in cheers or anger. Violence erupts when it breaks out suddenly. {The volcano was erupting when we arrived}. {Protests were erupting across the country}.

An eruption is a sudden, violent release—typically of lava and ash from a volcano, but also of emotion, conflict, or physical symptoms. Crowds erupt in anger, violence erupts in a region, rashes erupt on skin. The word emphasizes the abruptness and force of the outbreak: {The eruption sent ash clouds miles into the atmosphere}. {An eruption of applause followed the finale}.

Eruptions are sudden, violent releases—lava from a volcano, pus from a wound, anger from a person. The word captures both the physical event and its abruptness: {The eruption sent ash clouds miles into the atmosphere}. Skin eruptions are outbreaks of rashes or blemishes. Figuratively, eruptions describe any sudden outburst: {eruptions of violence}, {eruptions of applause}.

Erupts describes sudden, forceful release. A volcano erupts when it expels lava and ash. Violence or applause erupts when it breaks out abruptly: {Fighting erupted in the streets}, {The crowd erupted in cheers}. A person erupts when emotion bursts forth: {She erupted in anger}. Skin erupts when a rash or blemish appears suddenly.

Escalate means to increase in intensity, scope, or severity. A disagreement escalates into a fight. Costs escalate beyond projections. {The conflict escalated when both sides brought in reinforcements.} The word often implies a progression through stages—each step raising the stakes. To escalate something can also mean to refer it to a higher authority: {I'd like to escalate this complaint to your supervisor.}

Escalated is the past tense of escalate, meaning to increase in intensity, scope, or severity. A disagreement escalates into a fight. Costs escalate beyond projections. {The situation escalated quickly} suggests rapid loss of control. To escalate something is to raise it to a higher level of authority or urgency: {She escalated the complaint to management}.

Escalating describes something increasing in intensity, scope, or severity. Conflicts escalate when they grow more serious: {escalating tensions between the two countries}. Costs escalate when they rise beyond expectations. The word implies a progression—each stage worse or more extreme than the last: {The argument kept escalating until they were both shouting}.

Escalation is an increase in intensity, scope, or severity—typically of conflict, tension, or costs. What begins as a minor disagreement may undergo escalation into something serious: {The border skirmish threatened escalation into full-scale war}. The term implies a step-by-step progression upward, each move prompting a larger response. De-escalation is its opposite.

Escalations are increases in intensity, scope, or severity. The word appears most often in contexts of conflict or complaint: military escalations raise the stakes of war, while customer service escalations move problems up the chain to supervisors with more authority. {The recent escalations along the border have diplomats worried.} {I handle escalations when regular agents can't resolve the issue.}

An escalator is a moving staircase—a mechanized set of steps that carries people between floors in buildings. Escalators loop continuously, with steps flattening at top and bottom for easy boarding. The word began as a trademark but became generic. To escalate is to increase or intensify, often gradually: {The argument escalated into a shouting match}.

Escalators are moving staircases—continuously circulating steps that carry people between floors in buildings. They're standard in shopping malls, airports, and subway stations. The singular escalator also works as a general term for anything that increases or intensifies: {an escalator clause} in a contract automatically raises prices or wages under certain conditions.

An escapade is a reckless adventure or wild prank—something exciting that flirts with trouble or breaks from routine: {youthful escapades}, {a drunken escapade that landed him in jail}. The word often carries a tone of amused indulgence, as if the misbehavior were forgivable or even charming in retrospect.

Escapades are daring, reckless, or unconventional adventures, often with a hint of mischief or rule-breaking. The word suggests excitement and perhaps a touch of irresponsibility—the kind of exploits that make good stories later. {Their college escapades became legendary among younger students.} Escapades can range from harmless pranks to genuinely risky behavior, but the word typically carries a tone of affectionate indulgence rather than serious condemnation. A romantic escapade usually implies an affair or fling.

Escape, noun and verb, is about getting away from an undesirable person, place, or thing – sometimes in order to avoid hardship or danger. If a prisoner escapes, he gets free of detention or prison. This might enable him to escape punishment. Something that escapes detection goes unnoticed. An escape is an instance of escaping. An escape clause is a feature of a contract that allows for avoiding an obligation. In computers, escape is a character generated by a keystroke that has various functions.

Escaped is the past tense of escape—having gotten away from confinement, danger, or an undesirable situation. An escaped {prisoner} has broken free from custody. Escaped also describes things that have gotten loose: {an escaped zoo animal}, {escaped gas from a pipeline}. What has escaped your notice went undetected: {The error escaped everyone's attention}.

An escapee is someone who has escaped, especially from confinement or custody: {Police are searching for two escapees from the county jail}. The word applies most often to prisoners, though it extends to anyone who has fled an undesirable situation: {escapees from the hurricane zone}.

Escapes is the plural of escape—instances of getting away from confinement, danger, or unpleasant situations: {The prison had three escapes last year}. It also refers to diversions from routine or stress: {weekend escapes to the country}. As a verb, escapes is the third-person singular: {Nothing escapes her notice}.

Escaping is the act of getting away from confinement, danger, or something unpleasant. A prisoner escaping custody breaks free; someone escaping notice avoids being seen. The word often implies urgency or relief: {We barely made it out—escaping felt like a miracle}. In computing, escaping refers to using special characters to change how text is processed.

Escapism is the tendency to seek distraction from unpleasant realities through entertainment, fantasy, or other absorbing activities. The term usually carries mild disapproval, suggesting avoidance rather than engagement: {Video games are pure escapism for him}. But escapism can also be defended as necessary mental relief: {Sometimes you need a little escapism}.

Escapist describes something designed to distract from reality or unpleasant circumstances, or a person who seeks such distraction. Escapist {fiction}, escapist {fantasy}, and escapist {entertainment} offer temporary refuge from everyday concerns. As a noun, an escapist is someone who habitually avoids facing problems: {He's an escapist who buries himself in video games}.

Escapists are people who habitually seek distraction from reality through entertainment, fantasy, or imagination. The term usually carries mild criticism, implying avoidance of responsibilities or difficult truths: {The novel appeals to escapists who want to forget their troubles}. An escapist seeks refuge in movies, books, games, or daydreams rather than confronting the real world.

An escapologist is a performer who specializes in escaping from restraints—handcuffs, straitjackets, locked containers, or elaborate physical traps. The term is more common in British English; Americans tend to say escape artist. Harry Houdini remains the most famous practitioner. Figuratively, someone skilled at evading difficult situations: {He's an escapologist when it comes to household chores}.

Escapology is the art or practice of escaping from physical restraints—handcuffs, straitjackets, locked containers, or other confinements. The term is associated with stage performers like Houdini who made escapes into theatrical spectacle. An escapologist specializes in these feats: {The escapologist freed himself from chains while submerged in a water tank}.

Escargot is the French word for snail, used in English specifically to mean edible land snails prepared as food. The dish is particularly associated with French cuisine, where the snails are typically cooked in garlic butter and herbs, then served in their shells. {We ordered escargot as an appetizer.} The word retains its French pronunciation and plural form in English usage.

Escargots is the French word for snails, used in English specifically for edible land snails prepared as food. The dish is associated with French cuisine, typically served cooked in garlic butter and herbs: {We ordered escargots as an appetizer}. The singular escargot appears occasionally but the plural dominates English menus and usage.

An escort accompanies someone for protection, guidance, or courtesy. A dignitary travels with a police escort; a guest is escorted to their table. The term extends to paid companions—sometimes implying sexual services, sometimes not. Escort services often use the word as a euphemism for prostitution, though many escorts provide only companionship: {She worked as an escort for wealthy businessmen}.

Escorting is the act of accompanying someone, typically for protection, guidance, or courtesy: {Security was escorting him from the building}. The term also refers to working as a paid companion, often a euphemism for prostitution: {She made money escorting on weekends}.

Escorts are people who accompany others, whether for protection, guidance, or companionship. A military escort guards a convoy; a funeral escort leads a procession. The verb means to accompany: {Security escorted him from the building}. Escort also refers to a paid companion for social events, and euphemistically to a prostitute—hence {escort service}, which may offer either.

Escrow is a financial arrangement where a third party holds money or property until specific conditions are met. In real estate, an escrow account holds the buyer's deposit until closing: {The house is in escrow}. The term extends to any situation where something is held pending fulfillment of terms. To escrow funds is to place them in such an account.

The esophagus is the muscular tube connecting the throat to the stomach, through which food and liquid pass when swallowed. It's roughly ten inches long in adults. {The doctor examined her esophagus with a scope.} Also spelled oesophagus in British English.

Esoteric is an adjective that characterizes knowledge of subjects that are known or understood by only a few. Esoteric is primarily associated with the law, academia, and religious or spiritual matters: Tribal elders and medicine men are revered for their esoteric knowledge of the afterlife. The opposite of esoteric is the little-used technical word exoteric.

An espadrille is a casual flat shoe with a canvas or cotton upper and a flexible sole made of braided rope, typically jute. Originally from the Pyrenees region, espadrilles are associated with warm weather and beach settings: {She packed her espadrilles for the trip to Barcelona}. Some styles have wedge heels wrapped in the same rope material.

Espadrilles are casual flat shoes with canvas or fabric uppers and flexible soles made of braided rope, typically jute. Originally Mediterranean peasant footwear, they became summer fashion staples: {She packed espadrilles for the beach vacation}. Some styles have wedge heels. The singular is espadrille.

Espionage is the practice of spying—gathering secret information about a government, organization, or competitor through covert means. The word usually implies state-level intelligence operations: {Cold War espionage}, {industrial espionage}. An espionage {agent} works undercover; an espionage {ring} is a network of spies. {He was convicted of espionage and sentenced to life in prison.}

An esplanade is a long, open, level stretch of pavement or grass, typically along a waterfront or outside a fortification, designed for walking or promenading. The word suggests a scenic public space meant for leisurely strolling: {We walked along the esplanade at sunset}, {cafés lined the esplanade overlooking the harbor}.

Esport is competitive video gaming at a professional or organized level, typically with spectators and prize money: {League of Legends is the biggest esport in Asia}. The term is modeled on sport, treating gaming as athletic competition. Also spelled e-sport or eSport. The plural esports often refers to the industry as a whole: {She works in esports}.

Esports refers to competitive video gaming at a professional or semi-professional level, with organized tournaments, teams, and spectators. Players compete in games like League of Legends, Counter-Strike, or Fortnite for prize money and sponsorships. The industry has grown to include leagues, arenas, and broadcast coverage rivaling traditional sports: {She made a career in esports commentary}.

Espresso is coffee brewed by forcing hot water through finely ground beans under pressure, producing a concentrated shot with a layer of crema on top. It serves as the base for drinks like lattes, cappuccinos, and Americanos. The word comes from Italian, suggesting coffee made expressly for the customer. The common misspelling "expresso" appears frequently enough that some dictionaries acknowledge it, though purists consider it an error.

An essay is a short piece of writing on a particular subject, typically expressing the author's perspective or argument: {a five-paragraph essay}, {an essay on climate change}. The form ranges from academic assignments to personal reflections. As a verb, to essay something is to attempt it—a formal or literary usage: {She essayed a smile}.

An essayist is a writer of essays—typically short prose pieces exploring ideas, observations, or arguments in a personal voice. The term suggests someone who writes essays as a primary or serious pursuit rather than occasionally: {Montaigne was the first great essayist}. Unlike journalists or scholars, essayists prize reflection and style alongside substance.

Essayists are writers who compose essays—short prose works exploring ideas, observations, or arguments in a personal voice. The form ranges from formal academic pieces to informal reflections. {Montaigne and Bacon were among the first modern essayists.} {Contemporary essayists often blend memoir with cultural criticism.}

Essays are short pieces of prose writing on a particular subject, typically presenting the author's own perspective or argument. The word carries a sense of attempt or exploration—an essay tries out ideas rather than settling them definitively. As a verb, to essay something is to attempt it: {She essayed a smile despite her grief}. The noun also appears in phrases like {photo essay}, where images rather than words explore a theme.

Essence is the fundamental nature of something—what makes it what it is. The essence of a {contract} is agreement between parties. In cooking and perfumery, an essence is a concentrated extract: {vanilla essence}, {essence of rose}. The phrase {in essence} means fundamentally or at its core: {In essence, we agree}. Something {of the essence} is critically important: {Time is of the essence}.

Essences is the plural of essence—the fundamental nature or most important quality of something: {The essences of their arguments were identical, despite different rhetoric}. In perfumery and cooking, essences are concentrated extracts: {vanilla essence}, {essential oils}. The word often appears in philosophical or spiritual contexts discussing what makes something what it truly is.

Essential describes what is absolutely necessary or fundamental to something's nature. An essential {ingredient} cannot be left out. Essential {oils} contain the concentrated essence of plants. The essentials are basics you can't do without: {We packed only the essentials}. Something's essential {character} is its core identity stripped of incidentals.

Essentials are the things you absolutely need—the basics without which something cannot function or survive. Food, water, and shelter are essentials for human life. {We packed only the essentials for the trip.} The word often appears in product marketing to suggest necessity: {kitchen essentials}, {summer essentials}. As an adjective, essential means fundamentally necessary: {Sleep is essential for good health}.

Establish means to set up or bring into being on a firm, lasting basis. You establish a business, a rule, a precedent, or a reputation. To establish something as true is to demonstrate it beyond doubt: {The investigation established that no crime had occurred}. Once established, something is accepted, settled, or entrenched: {an established tradition}, {the established order}. To {establish yourself} somewhere is to settle in securely.

Established describes something that has been set up and made permanent or stable. An established {business} has operated long enough to prove its viability. An established {fact} is accepted as true. The established {order} refers to existing social or political structures that have become entrenched. To become established is to gain recognition or secure footing: {She established herself as an authority on the subject}.

An establishment is a place of business or an institution: {a dining establishment}, {an educational establishment}. The word often implies permanence and formality. With the definite article, the establishment refers to the dominant group controlling politics, business, and cultural institutions—those invested in maintaining existing power structures. To be {anti-establishment} is to oppose these entrenched interests. Establishment also names the act of establishing: {the establishment of diplomatic relations}.

Establishments are institutions or organizations, especially businesses or places of commerce: {The health department inspects food establishments}. The word often implies formality or permanence. *The establishment* (singular, with the article) refers to the dominant group in society—those who hold power and resist change: {She spent her career fighting the establishment}. The term carries connotations of entrenched authority and conventional thinking.
clues: Organizations set up for specific purposes

definition: Estate centers on property and standing. In its primary sense, an estate is a large piece of landed property, often with a substantial house: {The family estate has been in our hands for generations}. Estate also means the total property someone owns, especially at death: {His estate was divided among three heirs}. In British usage, an estate (or housing estate) is a residential development. The word extends to social rank—the three estates of medieval society were clergy, nobility, and commoners. A {real estate} agent deals in property; an {estate sale} liquidates a deceased person's belongings.

Estates is the plural of estate, covering its various meanings. Real estate encompasses land and property: {She manages several estates in the countryside}. A person's estate is everything they own, especially at death: {The estates were divided among the heirs}. In historical and legal contexts, estates are classes of society with political standing—clergy, nobility, and commoners were the three estates of pre-revolutionary France. The fourth estate is journalism, wielding influence comparable to those formal powers.

Esteem is respect and admiration for someone or something: {She held her mentor in high esteem}. The verb means to regard favorably or value highly: {His colleagues esteem him for his integrity}. Self-esteem is one's sense of personal worth. To esteem something can also mean to consider or judge it: {I esteem it an honor to be asked}.

An esthetician is a licensed skincare specialist who performs cosmetic treatments on the skin—facials, exfoliation, hair removal, and similar services. The spelling with an initial "e" reflects the Greek root; "aesthetician" is an alternate spelling. Estheticians work in spas, salons, and dermatology offices: {My esthetician recommended a new moisturizer}.

An estimate is a rough calculation or judgment about quantity, size, cost, or value when exact figures aren't available: {The contractor gave us an estimate of twelve thousand dollars}. To estimate is to form such a judgment: {I estimate we'll arrive around noon}. Estimates acknowledge uncertainty—they're informed guesses, not guarantees. An {estimated} crowd size or {estimated} time of arrival signals approximation.

Estimation is the act of forming an approximate judgment about something's value, size, or nature. A cost {estimation} calculates expected expenses. In someone's {estimation}, a thing is good or bad based on their personal assessment. Estimation also means regard or opinion: {He rose in my estimation after that speech}. The word often implies calculation without precise measurement.

To estrange is to turn someone from closeness to distance—emotionally, socially, or both. The word implies a relationship that once existed: {She became estranged from her parents after the divorce}. Estranged spouses are separated but not yet divorced. An estranged friend or family member is one you no longer speak to. The noun is estrangement.

Estranged describes a relationship that has become distant or hostile, typically between family members or spouses who were once close: {her estranged husband}, {estranged from his father for years}. The word implies a breach that may or may not be permanent—more serious than distant, less final than divorced or disowned.

Estrangement is the condition of being alienated or cut off from someone or something once close. Family estrangement describes relatives who no longer speak: {His estrangement from his father lasted decades}. The word implies a relationship that existed before distance grew—you can't be estranged from a stranger. Estrangement can also describe disconnection from institutions, beliefs, or one's own feelings.

Estrogen is the primary female sex hormone, responsible for developing and regulating the reproductive system and secondary sex characteristics like breasts and body fat distribution. The ovaries produce most estrogen, though smaller amounts come from fat tissue and the adrenal glands. Estrogen levels fluctuate through the menstrual cycle and drop sharply at menopause. Synthetic estrogens appear in birth control pills, hormone replacement therapy, and gender-affirming treatment for transgender women. Also spelled oestrogen in British English.

Estuaries is the plural of estuary—a coastal body of water where a river meets the sea. The mixing of fresh and salt water creates a distinctive brackish environment that supports diverse ecosystems: {Estuaries serve as nurseries for many fish species}. Major estuaries include the Chesapeake Bay and the mouth of the Thames.

An estuary is a body of water where a river meets the sea, creating a zone where fresh and salt water mix. Estuaries are typically wide, shallow, and tidal, with distinctive ecosystems supporting species adapted to brackish conditions. {The Thames estuary}, {Chesapeake Bay is North America's largest estuary}.

Eta is the seventh letter of the Greek alphabet (Η, η), used in mathematics, physics, and engineering to represent various quantities like efficiency or viscosity. Outside technical contexts, eta appears mainly in fraternity and sorority names. (Capitalized ETA is the acronym for estimated time of arrival.)

To etch is to cut into a surface using acid or a sharp tool, creating lines or designs. The technique is central to printmaking, where acid eats into metal plates to hold ink. By extension, etch describes any sharp, precise rendering: {The skyline was etched against the sunset}. Something deeply memorable is {etched in memory}.

Etched describes something cut or engraved into a surface, originally through acid on metal or glass. The word usually appears as a past participle: an etched {design}, etched {glass}. Figuratively, something etched in memory or etched on the mind is vividly and permanently fixed there: {The image of her face was etched in his memory forever}.

Etches is the third-person singular form of etch, meaning to cut lines into a surface using acid or a sharp tool. The technique is common in printmaking and metalwork. Figuratively, something etched in memory or etched on someone's face is deeply marked or permanently fixed: {Grief was etched on her features}. {The image etches itself into your mind}.

Etching is a printmaking technique where an image is incised into a metal plate using acid, then inked and pressed onto paper. The resulting print is also called an etching. The verb etch means to create such marks, or more broadly, to engrave or impress deeply: {The scene was etched in her memory}. {His face was etched with worry}.

Etchings are prints made from metal plates into which designs have been incised with acid. The artist draws through a wax coating, acid bites into the exposed metal, and ink fills the grooves for printing. The phrase {come up and see my etchings} became a cliché for luring someone to one's apartment with romantic intent—the pretense of viewing art masking seduction.

Eternal means lasting forever, without beginning or end. Religious and philosophical contexts speak of eternal {life}, eternal {damnation}, the eternal {soul}. More loosely, eternal describes anything that seems to go on indefinitely: {the eternal wait at the DMV}, {eternal optimism}. The Eternal City is Rome. Eternally is the adverb: {I'm eternally grateful}.

Eternities is the plural of eternity—infinite or unending time. In practical use, eternities almost always appears hyperbolically to describe periods that feel interminably long: {We waited for eternities in that line}, {It seemed like eternities before she responded}. The plural intensifies the exaggeration, suggesting not just one endless stretch but multiple.

Eternity is time without end—infinite duration extending forever into the future, the past, or both. In religious contexts, eternity is the timeless realm where God exists or where souls go after death: {eternal life}, {spending eternity in heaven}. Colloquially, an eternity is any period that feels interminably long: {We waited an eternity for the results}. {It seemed like an eternity before she answered}.

Ether names something rarefied or intangible. In old physics, the ether was a hypothetical substance filling all space, through which light waves traveled. In chemistry, ethers are volatile organic compounds; the most familiar is diethyl ether, once used as an anesthetic: {The patient was put under with ether}. Figuratively, voices or signals travel {through the ether}—the airwaves, the atmosphere, the vague medium of transmission. {The announcement vanished into the ether.}

Underlying the adjective ethereal is the noun ether, which provides an important clue to its meaning. Ether was once thought to be the substance or element that filled the heavens, and ethereal conveys intangibility or lacking material substance. It may also have a connotation of delicacy or exquisiteness, especially in writing about the arts. People use ethereal today when they can’t pinpoint specifics: The ethereal beauty of her voice filled the concert hall. Ethereal is usually complimentary.

Ethernet spelled with a lowercase e is occasionally seen in casual or technical writing, though the capitalized form is standard. The technology is a system for connecting computers in a local area network using cables and standardized protocols. It remains the dominant wired networking technology in offices and homes: {The ethernet port on my laptop stopped working}. (Capitalized Ethernet is the standard spelling.)

An ethic is a moral principle that motivates people to behave in a particular way. The most common use of the word is in the term work ethic, which is a respect and appreciation for the value of hard work: All of the farm hands have a strong work ethic. Ethic can also be used to describe a particular value: Caring is an ethic grounded in a teacher’s commitment to professionalism.

Ethical means conforming to accepted standards of right and wrong conduct: {an ethical business practice}, {ethical treatment of animals}. It also describes things relating to ethics as a field of study: {ethical philosophy}, {ethical dilemmas}. Someone who is ethical acts with integrity and moral principle. The word often implies careful consideration of consequences and fairness, not just following rules.

Ethically means in a manner consistent with moral principles or standards of right conduct. Someone who behaves ethically follows accepted rules of fairness and integrity: {The company claims to source its products ethically}. The word often implies adherence to professional or institutional codes: {ethically questionable research practices}, {Is it ethically permissible to lie to protect someone?}

An ethicist is someone who studies or specializes in ethics—the branch of philosophy concerned with right and wrong conduct. Ethicists work in academic settings but also advise institutions on moral questions: {The hospital consulted its ethicist about end-of-life care}. A bioethicist focuses specifically on ethical issues in medicine and biological research.

Ethics are a set of values that guides a particular endeavor, or when no context is specified, the general values held by a group or society that help people decide what is right and wrong: The committee is tasked with developing research ethics that will serve the institution in the 21st century. Anthropologists struggle to recreate the code of ethics of societies that left no written records. An ethics committee in a legislature or other institution is one that develops rules of conduct or examines breaches of conduct.

Ethnic relates to groups of people who share cultural characteristics such as language, religion, customs, or ancestry. It often appears in phrases like ethnic {food}, ethnic {music}, or ethnic {neighborhood}, where it signals traditions from a particular cultural group, often one that is a minority in a given context. Ethnic {cleansing} refers to the forced removal or extermination of a population based on their ethnicity. As a noun, ethnic can refer to a member of an ethnic minority, though this usage strikes some as dated or dismissive.

Ethnicities is the plural of ethnicity—distinct cultural or ancestral groupings based on shared heritage, language, traditions, or national origin. Forms and surveys often ask respondents to identify their ethnicities: {The study collected data on participants' ethnicities}. A person may claim multiple ethnicities through mixed ancestry or cultural identification.

Ethnicity refers to shared cultural identity—common ancestry, language, traditions, or national origin that bind a group: {Her ethnicity is Korean}, {a neighborhood with diverse ethnicities}. Unlike race, which categorizes by physical features, ethnicity emphasizes cultural heritage and group affiliation. Someone may identify with multiple ethnicities or none at all. Forms and surveys often ask about ethnicity alongside race, treating them as distinct categories.

Ethos is the characteristic spirit or guiding beliefs of a community, culture, or movement: {the Protestant work ethic}, {the ethos of Silicon Valley startups}. It captures the underlying values and attitudes that shape how a group thinks and acts. In rhetoric, ethos refers specifically to a speaker's credibility or moral character as a persuasive tool—distinct from logos (logic) and pathos (emotion).

Etiquette is the set of unwritten rules governing polite behavior in social or professional settings. It covers everything from table manners to email conventions to how you address royalty. Etiquette varies by culture and era—what's proper in one context may be rude in another. {Business etiquette requires a prompt reply.} {The etiquette of formal dining can be intimidating.}

Etouffee is a Cajun and Creole dish of shellfish—usually crawfish or shrimp—smothered in a thick, seasoned sauce and served over rice. The name comes from a French word meaning smothered or suffocated, describing how the main ingredient is cooked slowly in its own juices with onions, peppers, and spices: {We ordered the crawfish etouffee}.

An etude is a musical composition designed to develop a specific technical skill in the performer. Though originally practice pieces, many etudes—especially those by Chopin and Liszt—are artistically substantial enough for concert performance. The word comes from French for "study," and etude occasionally appears in non-musical contexts meaning a focused exercise or study piece.

Etudes are musical compositions designed primarily as technical exercises, meant to develop a performer's skill on an instrument. The best etudes transcend mere practice pieces to become concert works: {Chopin's etudes are as beautiful as they are demanding}. The French word, meaning "studies," extends occasionally to exercises in other arts.

Etymology is the study of word origins—where words come from and how their meanings have changed over time. The etymology of a particular word is its history: {The etymology of "salary" traces back to Roman soldiers being paid in salt}. Linguists and lexicographers use etymology to explain why words mean what they do and how unrelated-seeming meanings connect.

Eucalyptus is a genus of trees native to Australia, known for aromatic leaves that produce a pungent oil used in medicines and cleaning products. The trees grow tall with distinctive peeling bark. Koalas feed almost exclusively on eucalyptus leaves. The oil clears congestion: {eucalyptus cough drops}, {a few drops of eucalyptus in the humidifier}.

Euchre is a trick-taking card game played with a deck of 24 or 32 cards, popular in the American Midwest and parts of Canada and Britain. Four players in two partnerships try to win at least three of five tricks, with the trump suit determined each hand. To euchre someone is to prevent them from winning—and by extension, to cheat or swindle them: {They euchred us out of our share}.

Eugenics is the idea of improving human populations through selective breeding—encouraging reproduction among people deemed genetically "fit" while discouraging or preventing it among those deemed "unfit." The term now carries heavy stigma due to its association with forced sterilization programs and Nazi racial policies. {Eugenics was taught as legitimate science in American universities into the 1930s.} The adjective is eugenic.

Eulogies is the plural of eulogy, a speech or written tribute praising someone who has died. Eulogies are delivered at funerals and memorial services, celebrating the deceased's life and character: {The eulogies painted a picture of a generous, funny man}. The word can extend to high praise for the living, though this use is less common.

A eulogy is a speech honoring someone who has died, typically delivered at a funeral or memorial service. The speaker recounts the deceased's life, character, and impact on others: {She gave a moving eulogy for her father}. More broadly, eulogy can mean high praise for anyone or anything: {The book is a eulogy to small-town life}.

A eunuch is a man who has been castrated, historically to serve as a harem guard, court official, or singer whose high voice was preserved. The practice was common in ancient China, the Ottoman Empire, and Byzantine courts. Figuratively, eunuch suggests someone ineffectual or powerless: {a political eunuch with no real influence}.

Eunuchs is the plural of eunuch, a man who has been castrated. Historically, eunuchs served as harem guards, court officials, or religious figures in various cultures—their inability to father children making them trusted in positions near women or power. The term sometimes extends figuratively to any man perceived as weak, ineffectual, or lacking virility.

A euphemism is a mild or indirect word substituted for one considered too harsh, blunt, or offensive. {Passed away} softens death, {let go} softens firing, {restroom} avoids toilet. Euphemisms often cluster around taboo subjects—death, sex, bodily functions, violence—allowing speakers to reference uncomfortable realities without naming them directly.

Euphemisms are mild or indirect expressions substituted for ones considered too harsh, blunt, or offensive. Death becomes {passing away}, firing becomes {letting go}, and lies become {misinformation}. The impulse to euphemize touches nearly every sensitive domain—bodily functions, sex, death, money, and politics. Euphemisms can soften difficult conversations or obscure uncomfortable truths.

Euphoria is a state of intense happiness, elation, or well-being that goes beyond ordinary good feelings. It can arise from positive life events, success, or love, but also from drugs, mental health conditions, or physical exertion like runner's high. The feeling is characteristically powerful but often temporary. {The team was in a state of euphoria after winning the championship.} Something that produces this feeling is euphoric.

Euphoric describes a state of intense happiness, elation, or well-being—often beyond what circumstances might warrant. The feeling may come from achievement, drugs, or brain chemistry: {The runners described a euphoric high after the marathon}. Something that produces this state is euphoric or euphoriant. The noun is euphoria.

In ancient Greek eureka means “I have found.” It was reportedly uttered by Archimedes on making a great discovery, and has been used since then for the same purpose. It is often associated with an exclamation by miners who found a vein of gold.

The euro is the official currency of most European Union countries, introduced in 1999 and symbolized by €. It replaced national currencies like the German mark and French franc. The word functions as both singular and plural in financial contexts: {The euro fell against the dollar}, {That costs fifty euro}. Outside the eurozone, euros is the standard plural. (Capitalized Euro- appears in compounds relating to Europe.)

Euros is the plural of euro, the official currency of most European Union member states. The eurozone comprises countries that have adopted the euro as their primary currency: {The meal cost twenty euros}. In casual speech, euros sometimes refers broadly to European money or the European economy: {How are euros doing against the dollar?}

The eurozone is the group of European Union member countries that have adopted the euro as their official currency. It functions as a monetary union with shared fiscal policies: {Greece's debt crisis threatened the entire eurozone}. Also spelled euro zone or euro-zone. (Capitalized Eurozone is an alternate form.)

Euthanasia is the practice of painlessly bringing about the death of people or animals who are so ill or injured that they have no possibility of a useful or enjoyable life. Euthanasia is widely practiced with domestic animals but is illegal in relation to humans. Euthanasia law is a misnomer for a law permitting physician assisted suicide for people who are terminally ill.

To euthanise is to kill painlessly, typically to end suffering from terminal illness or severe injury. The word applies most often to animals: {We had to euthanise the dog after the cancer spread}. For humans, euthanise appears in debates about assisted dying and end-of-life care. Also spelled euthanize.

To euthanize is to kill painlessly, typically to end suffering from illness or injury. The term applies primarily to animals: {We had to euthanize our cat after the cancer spread}. When applied to humans, euthanize usually refers to physician-assisted death in jurisdictions where it's legal, though some use it critically to characterize such practices.

Euthanized is the past tense of euthanize, meaning to kill painlessly, especially to end suffering. The term applies primarily to animals: {The vet recommended we have the dog euthanized}. When applied to humans, it refers to medically assisted death for the terminally ill, legal in some jurisdictions. The word carries clinical distance—a gentler way to describe a difficult act.

Evac is a clipped form of evacuation or evacuate, used in military and emergency contexts: {We need an evac now}, {Call for evac}. The shortened form conveys urgency and appears in compounds like {medevac} (medical evacuation). Common in action films, video games, and situations where brevity matters.

Evacuate means to leave or empty a place, especially in response to danger. Authorities evacuate buildings during fires, cities before hurricanes, civilians from war zones. The word implies urgency and organized departure: {We had to evacuate when the gas leak was detected}. In medical contexts, evacuate means to empty the bowels or bladder. Figuratively, to evacuate is to remove or withdraw: {The army evacuated its troops from the region}.

Evacuated is the past tense of evacuate, meaning to leave or remove from a place, typically because of danger. People evacuate buildings during fires, cities during hurricanes, civilians during wartime: {The town was evacuated before the flood}. In technical contexts, evacuated describes a container from which air has been removed: {an evacuated chamber}.

Evacuating is removing people or things from a dangerous place, or leaving such a place yourself. Authorities evacuate buildings during bomb threats; residents evacuate ahead of hurricanes. The word also means emptying the bowels—a clinical term for defecation. {They're evacuating the coastal areas}, {The patient had difficulty evacuating}.

Evacuation is the act of leaving or removing people from a dangerous place. During fires, floods, or other emergencies, authorities order evacuations to move populations to safety: {The hurricane prompted a mandatory evacuation of coastal areas}. In medical contexts, evacuation refers to emptying the bowels or bladder. Military evacuations remove troops or civilians from combat zones.

Evacuations are instances of emptying out or withdrawing. The word most often refers to organized removals of people from dangerous areas: {Evacuations began as the wildfire approached}. In medical contexts, evacuation means emptying the bowels or bladder. The military uses evacuation for withdrawing troops or removing casualties from combat zones.

An evacuee is a person who has been evacuated from a dangerous place. The word typically appears in contexts of war, natural disasters, or other emergencies: {Evacuees from the flooded parish were sheltered in a nearby gymnasium}. Unlike refugee, evacuee emphasizes the act of organized removal rather than flight.

Evacuees are people who have been evacuated—removed from a dangerous place to somewhere safer. The term appears most often during wars, natural disasters, and other emergencies: {Evacuees from the hurricane filled the shelters}. The word carries a sense of displacement and vulnerability, emphasizing the people rather than the process.

To evade is to avoid or escape, especially through cleverness or deception. You can evade capture, evade detection, or evade a question by steering around it. To evade taxes is to illegally avoid paying them—distinct from tax avoidance, which uses legal means. {He evaded her questions about where he'd been.}

Evades means avoids or escapes, especially through cleverness or trickery. A suspect evades police by slipping through alleys. Someone evades a question by changing the subject. You can evade taxes, responsibilities, or detection. The word suggests active effort to stay out of reach: {He evaded capture for three years}. What evades you remains just beyond your grasp: {Sleep evaded her}.

Evading is the present participle of evade—to escape or avoid, especially through cleverness or deception. Someone evading capture stays one step ahead of pursuers. Evading a question means deflecting rather than answering directly. {He was arrested for evading taxes.} The word implies active effort to slip away from something that's pursuing or pressing.

When you evaluate someone or something, you investigate with a view to making a judgment about value or worth: The experiment will evaluate the effects of various dietary restrictions on dairy cattle. The purpose of evaluating is usually to arrive at a practical decision, such as whether to continue an activity, hire or promote a person, or assign a value or grade: We need to evaluate the risks involved in making such an investment.

Evaluation is the process of judging the quality, value, or condition of something. Teachers write evaluations of students; employees receive performance evaluations from supervisors. The word often implies systematic assessment against criteria: {The evaluation found the program effective but underfunded}. To evaluate is to make such a judgment.

Evaluations are assessments of quality, value, or performance. The word appears constantly in educational and professional contexts: {annual performance evaluations}, {course evaluations}, {program evaluations}. An evaluation judges how well something or someone meets standards or expectations. Unlike casual opinions, evaluations typically follow criteria and may have consequences: {The employee's raise depends on her evaluation}.

Evangelical describes Christians who emphasize personal conversion, biblical authority, and spreading the faith. An evangelical {church} prioritizes these commitments. The word often appears in political contexts, where evangelicals form a significant voting bloc in the United States: {Evangelical voters supported the candidate}. More broadly, evangelical describes zealous advocacy for any cause: {She's evangelical about veganism}.

Evangelicalism is a Protestant Christian movement emphasizing personal conversion (being "born again"), the authority of the Bible, and active efforts to spread the faith. The term covers a broad spectrum—from mainline denominations to charismatic megachurches. In American politics, evangelicals became a significant voting bloc in the late 20th century, often associated with conservative positions on social issues: {the evangelical vote}, {white evangelicalism}.
clues: Protestant movement emphasizing conversion and scripture

definition: Evangelicals are Christians who emphasize personal conversion, the authority of the Bible, and actively sharing their faith with others. The term comes from a Greek word meaning "good news" or "gospel." In American usage, evangelicals often refers specifically to Protestant Christians associated with conservative social and political positions, though the movement is theologically diverse. {Evangelicals turned out in large numbers for the election.} The singular evangelical works as both noun and adjective.

Evangelise is the British spelling of evangelize—to spread religious faith, especially Christianity, by preaching or personal testimony. The word extends to any fervent advocacy: {She evangelises for open-source software}. An evangelist promotes something with missionary zeal, whether the Gospel or a new technology.

Evangelism is zealous preaching or advocacy, originally and still primarily associated with spreading the Christian gospel. The word implies active persuasion rather than passive belief: {street evangelism}, {door-to-door evangelism}. The meaning has expanded to enthusiastic promotion of any cause or product: {brand evangelism}, {tech evangelism}. {His evangelism for the new framework converted several skeptical developers.}

An evangelist is someone who spreads a message with missionary zeal. Originally and still commonly, the term refers to Christian preachers who seek converts, especially through revivals or public campaigns: {a televangelist}, {Billy Graham was America's most famous evangelist}. The four Evangelists—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—wrote the Gospels. In secular use, an evangelist champions any cause or product with fervent advocacy: {a technology evangelist}, {an evangelist for clean energy}.

Evangelists are people who spread a message with fervent conviction. The word comes from Greek for "bringer of good news," and its oldest sense refers to those who preach the Christian gospel—particularly the authors of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. More broadly, an evangelist promotes any cause or product with missionary zeal: {a tech evangelist}, {an evangelist for clean energy}. The term implies not just belief but active persuasion.

Evangelize means to spread a message with missionary zeal. The core sense is religious—to preach the Christian gospel and seek converts: {She spent years evangelizing in rural communities}. The meaning has broadened to promoting any cause or product with fervent enthusiasm: {He evangelizes for open-source software}. Tech companies hire "evangelists" to champion their platforms.
