Unlike internal bones, exoskeletons must be shed periodically as the animal grows. The term also applies to wearable mechanical frameworks that enhance human strength or mobility: {The factory workers use powered exoskeletons to lift heavy parts}.

An exosuit is a wearable mechanical framework that augments the wearer's strength, endurance, or mobility. Powered versions use motors or hydraulics to amplify human movement; unpowered ones use springs and cables to reduce strain. Exosuits appear in military applications, industrial labor, and rehabilitation medicine: {The warehouse workers wore exosuits to prevent back injuries}. In science fiction, exosuits are often armored and weaponized.

Exosuits are wearable mechanical frameworks that augment human strength, endurance, or mobility. Unlike rigid exoskeletons, exosuits typically use soft materials—fabric, cables, motors—that move with the body rather than encasing it. Military and industrial applications help workers lift heavy loads; medical versions assist people with mobility impairments: {The exosuit helped her walk again after the stroke}. The term appears frequently in science fiction and video games, where exosuits grant superhuman abilities.

Exotic describes something strikingly unusual because it originates from a distant place or unfamiliar culture: {exotic spices}, {exotic birds}, {an exotic accent}. The word carries connotations of allure and fascination—the appeal of the foreign and rare. It can shade into fetishizing difference: calling a person exotic often reduces them to their otherness. An exotic dancer is a stripper, the adjective serving as euphemism.

Exotica refers to objects, cultural products, or experiences that seem unusual, foreign, or intriguingly different from one's own culture. The term often carries connotations of the romanticized or fetishized "other," particularly items from distant lands marketed for their perceived strangeness or allure. In music, exotica specifically denotes a mid-20th-century genre featuring lush orchestration and sounds meant to evoke tropical or Polynesian atmospheres. {The shop was filled with exotica from Southeast Asia.}

Expand means to make or become larger, wider, or more extensive. A business expands by opening new locations. Lungs expand when filling with air. To expand on an idea is to develop it further, adding detail or explanation: {Could you expand on that point?} The opposite is contract or shrink.

Expanded describes something that has been made larger, broader, or more extensive. An expanded {edition} includes additional content. An expanded {role} involves more responsibilities. The word often appears with abstract nouns: expanded {access}, expanded {coverage}, expanded {powers}. In physical contexts, materials expand when heated; expanded {foam} has been aerated to increase volume.

Expands is the third-person singular form of expand, meaning to increase in size, scope, or extent. Something that expands grows larger or spreads out: {Metal expands when heated}. A company expands by opening new locations or entering new markets. When someone expands on a topic, they elaborate or provide more detail: {She expanded on her earlier remarks during the Q&A}. The word suggests outward movement from a center or an increase from an established baseline.

An expanse is a wide, open area stretching out before you—typically of land, water, or sky: {a vast expanse of desert}, {the blue expanse of the Pacific}. The word emphasizes unbroken continuity and scale. It can extend to abstract domains: {an expanse of time}, {the expanse of human knowledge}.

Expanses is the plural of expanse—wide, open stretches of something, typically land, water, or sky. The word emphasizes breadth and unbroken continuity: {vast expanses of desert}, {the dark expanses between stars}. It often conveys a sense of scale that dwarfs human presence.

Expansion is the act of becoming larger or more extensive, or the state that results. A company undergoes expansion when it opens new locations. The expansion of a gas fills available space. Urban expansion pushes city boundaries outward. An expansion can also be an extended version of something: {The director's cut is a two-hour expansion of the original film}. In gaming, an expansion adds new content to an existing game.

Expansionism is the policy or practice of extending a nation's territory or influence, typically through military conquest, colonization, or economic domination. The term usually carries critical connotations, suggesting aggressive or unjustified growth: {19th-century American expansionism pushed westward to the Pacific}. It applies to empires, ideologies, or corporations seeking to enlarge their reach.

Expansionist describes a policy, ideology, or person favoring territorial or economic expansion, typically of a nation or empire. An expansionist government seeks to extend its borders or influence: {expansionist ambitions}, {expansionist foreign policy}. The term often carries negative connotations, suggesting aggression or imperialism. As a noun, an expansionist is someone who advocates such policies.

Expansions are increases in size, scope, or extent. The word applies to physical growth ({the expansion of the universe}), territorial acquisition ({westward expansion}), economic development ({business expansion into new markets}), and elaboration of ideas ({an expansion on earlier themes}). In gaming and software, an expansion is additional content that extends the original product. The plural often appears in technical contexts discussing multiple instances or phases of growth.

Expansive describes things that are wide-ranging, extensive, or capable of expansion. An expansive {view} stretches across a broad area; an expansive {mood} is one of openness and generosity. People with expansive {personalities} are outgoing and communicative, sometimes excessively so. In technical contexts, expansive may describe materials or forces that tend to expand: {expansive soils} swell when wet. The word often carries positive connotations of abundance and possibility, though it can also suggest excess or lack of restraint.

An expat is someone living outside their native country, typically for work or lifestyle reasons rather than as a refugee or immigrant. The term carries connotations of choice and often privilege—retirees in Costa Rica, executives in Singapore, writers in Paris. {She's been an expat in Barcelona for fifteen years.} Short for expatriate.

An expatriate is someone living outside their native country, whether by choice or circumstance. The term often implies a prolonged stay rather than brief travel: {a community of American expatriates in Paris}. As a verb, to expatriate is to leave one's country or to banish someone from theirs. The clipped form expat is common in casual use.

Expatriates are people living outside their native country, whether temporarily or permanently. The term often implies choice rather than forced displacement—professionals working abroad, retirees in warmer climates, artists seeking creative freedom: {a community of American expatriates in Paris}. As a verb, to expatriate is to leave one's country or to banish someone from theirs. The informal clipping expat is more common in speech.

Expats is the plural of expat, a clipped form of expatriate—someone living outside their native country. The term usually implies a voluntary, often privileged relocation: {a community of American expats in Paris}, {British expats retiring to Spain}. Unlike immigrant or refugee, expat suggests choice and often temporary residence, though many stay permanently.

To expect is to consider something likely or certain to happen: {I expect it'll rain tomorrow}. Expect also means to anticipate or await: {We're expecting guests}. When you expect something of someone, you believe they should deliver it: {They expect too much from their employees}. A woman who is expecting is pregnant.

Expectancy is the state of expecting or anticipating something, often with eagerness: {There was a sense of expectancy in the air as the curtain rose}. It also refers to statistical likelihood, especially in {life expectancy}—the average number of years a person can expect to live. The word carries more formality than expectation and often suggests hopeful waiting.

Expectant describes someone waiting for something to happen, especially with hope or anticipation: {an expectant hush fell over the crowd}, {expectant faces turned toward the stage}. Most specifically, expectant describes a woman who is pregnant: {an expectant mother}. The word carries a sense of readiness—something is about to arrive or occur.

Expectation is what you anticipate will happen or what you believe should happen. You can have expectations about outcomes {(The movie didn't live up to expectations)} or about behavior {(There are certain expectations that come with the job)}. Expectations may be realistic or unrealistic, and they shape how we experience what actually occurs—met expectations satisfy, exceeded ones delight, and unmet ones disappoint.

Expectations are what you anticipate or believe will happen. The word often implies a sense of entitlement or standard: {She had high expectations for the project}. Expectations can be hopes {(against all expectations, he survived)} or demands {(The job didn't meet my expectations)}. To {manage expectations} is to temper what others believe they'll receive. Social expectations are unwritten rules about behavior: {There were certain expectations about how a lady should dress}.

Expected describes what is anticipated or considered likely to happen. An expected {guest} is one whose arrival is planned. Expected {results} are those predicted beforehand. The word often implies a standard or norm: {expected behavior}, {expected performance}. When something falls short of expectations, it's {less than expected}; when it exceeds them, {better than expected}. To be expecting usually means to be pregnant.

Expecting means anticipating or looking forward to something: {I'm expecting a package today}, {We're expecting rain this afternoon}. When used without an object, expecting is a euphemism for pregnant: {She's expecting}, {They're expecting their first child in June}. The pregnant sense has become so common that {expecting} alone usually implies pregnancy rather than general anticipation.

Expediency is the quality of being useful or advantageous for achieving a particular purpose, often with the implication that ethics or principles are being set aside. When someone acts out of expediency, they're choosing what works over what's right: {The decision was made purely out of political expediency}. The word carries a note of moral compromise—expedient solutions get results but may cut corners or ignore longer-term consequences.

An expedition is a journey undertaken for a specific purpose, especially exploration, research, or military action: {a polar expedition}, {a scientific expedition to the Amazon}. The word also refers to the group making such a journey: {The expedition set out at dawn}. By extension, expedition can describe any organized outing: {a shopping expedition}. The formal noun expedience shares a root but has diverged in meaning.

Expeditions are journeys undertaken for a specific purpose, typically exploration, research, or military action. The word suggests organized effort and planning: {a polar expedition}, {a scientific expedition to the Amazon}. By extension, any purposeful outing can be called an expedition, often with mild humor about its ambition: {a shopping expedition}, {an expedition to the grocery store}.

Expel means to force out or drive away. A student expelled from school is permanently removed for misconduct. A country expels diplomats by ordering them to leave. The body expels waste. Lungs expel air. {The protesters were expelled from the building.} The word implies authority or force behind the removal.

Expelled is the past tense of expel, meaning to force out or eject. A student expelled from school is permanently removed for misconduct. A country may expel diplomats during political disputes. The word also applies to physical ejection: {The volcano expelled ash and lava}. Being expelled carries a sense of formal, often punitive removal rather than casual departure.

Expendable describes something or someone considered acceptable to sacrifice or use up for a larger goal. Supplies are expendable when they're meant to be consumed. More starkly, soldiers or workers are called expendable when those in charge view their loss as tolerable: {In war, infantry are often treated as expendable}. The word carries a cold, utilitarian edge.

Expendables are people or things considered acceptable to sacrifice or use up in pursuit of a goal. The term often appears in military contexts for soldiers assigned to high-casualty missions, or for equipment not expected to survive deployment. More broadly, it describes workers or resources treated as replaceable: {The company viewed temp workers as expendables}. The noun derives from the adjective expendable, meaning not worth preserving.

An expense is money spent or cost incurred. Business expenses include rent, salaries, and supplies. Personal expenses cover daily living costs. The plural often appears in set phrases: {travel expenses}, {medical expenses}, {at the company's expense}. To expense something is to charge it to an account or claim reimbursement: {I expensed the client dinner}. Figuratively, {at someone's expense} means to their detriment or as the butt of a joke: {They laughed at his expense}.

Expenses are costs incurred in doing something—running a business, completing a project, or traveling for work. The term often appears in phrases like {business expenses}, {operating expenses}, or {travel expenses}. To expense something is to record it as a cost or submit it for reimbursement: {I'll expense the hotel}. An {expense account} covers work-related costs.

Expensive means costing a lot of money: {an expensive restaurant}, {an expensive mistake}. The word implies a price high enough to give pause or strain a budget. What counts as expensive varies by context—expensive for a meal differs from expensive for a house. Something can be expensive in a good way (worth the cost) or bad (overpriced): {It's expensive, but you get what you pay for}.

As a noun, experience has two related meanings. One is the internal residue of events in your life: Her experience as a lawyer makes her question people’s motives. The other is an event in which you take part and which has an effect on you: I once had a harrowing experience on the New York subway. The verb experience simply means to have an encounter of some kind: People who have never experienced hunger cannot imagine its long-term effects on the mind.

Experienced describes someone who has gained knowledge or skill through practice and exposure over time. An experienced {surgeon} has performed many operations; an experienced {traveler} knows how to navigate airports and foreign cities. The word implies competence earned through doing, not just studying. It can also describe events that have been felt or undergone: {the worst pain I've ever experienced}.

Experiences is the plural of experience, referring to events or occurrences that leave an impression on someone or contribute to their knowledge. The word often emphasizes the subjective or personal nature of what happens: {Her experiences abroad shaped her worldview}. As a verb form, experiences indicates someone undergoing or encountering something: {She experiences anxiety before public speaking}. The noun frequently appears in marketing contexts to describe curated activities or encounters: {The resort offers unique dining experiences}.

An experiment is a test designed to discover something unknown or verify a hypothesis. Scientists conduct experiments by controlling variables and observing outcomes: {The experiment confirmed that the drug reduced symptoms}. The word extends to any deliberate trial of something new: {an experiment in open marriage}, {The restaurant is experimenting with a new menu}. To experiment is to try things out, often with an implication of risk or novelty.

Experimental describes something done as an experiment—testing an idea, method, or product that isn't yet established. An experimental {drug} is still being evaluated. Experimental {music} or {film} breaks from convention to try new forms. The word often signals that results are uncertain or that something exists as a trial rather than a finished product: {The program is still experimental}.

Experimentation is the process of trying things out to see what happens—testing ideas, methods, or substances through trial and observation. In science, experimentation follows systematic procedures to test hypotheses: {The drug underwent years of experimentation before approval}. More broadly, it suggests exploring possibilities without guaranteed outcomes: {Her early work shows bold experimentation with form}. The word often implies willingness to risk failure in pursuit of discovery.

Experimenting is trying things out to see what happens. Scientists experiment with controlled variables; cooks experiment with ingredients; teenagers experiment with identity, drugs, or sexuality. The word suggests openness to outcomes rather than commitment: {We're just experimenting with the relationship}. To experiment is to test possibilities without knowing where they'll lead.

Experiments are tests or trials designed to discover something unknown, demonstrate something known, or examine a hypothesis. Scientists conduct experiments to gather empirical evidence, but the word extends beyond labs: {I've been experimenting with different recipes}. The verb experiment means to carry out such tests, often implying a willingness to try new approaches. {The band experimented with electronic sounds on their latest album.} An experimental treatment or method is one still being tested rather than established.

An expert possesses deep knowledge or skill in a particular field, acquired through study or experience. The word works as both noun and adjective: {She consulted a tax expert}; {expert advice}. Expertise implies mastery beyond ordinary competence—experts are who you call when the problem exceeds normal ability. {He's no expert, but he knows enough to get by}.
clues: Person who truly knows their field

definition: Expertise is specialized knowledge or skill in a particular field, typically gained through training and experience. An expert has expertise; a novice lacks it. The word often appears in professional contexts: {legal expertise}, {technical expertise}, {We brought in a consultant for her expertise in cybersecurity}. Unlike mere familiarity, expertise implies depth sufficient to make authoritative judgments.

Experts are people with specialized knowledge or skill in a particular field. The word implies authority—an expert's opinion carries weight that a novice's doesn't. {We brought in experts to assess the damage.} Someone can be an expert {in} or {on} a subject: {an expert in constitutional law}, {an expert on butterflies}. The word often appears attributively: {expert witness}, {expert advice}, {expert opinion}.

Expiration is the act of coming to an end or the moment when something ceases to be valid. A driver's license has an expiration {date}. A contract reaches expiration. Food past its expiration may be unsafe. In physiology, expiration is the act of breathing out—exhaling air from the lungs. The related verb is expire.

Expire means to come to an end or cease to be valid. A driver's license expires after a set period. A deadline expires when the time runs out. The word also means to die—to breathe one's last breath: {He expired peacefully in his sleep}. Food and medications expire when they pass their safe-use date. {My membership expired last month.}

Expired means no longer valid, usable, or alive. Food past its expiration date has expired. A passport or license that's no longer current has expired. {My membership expired last month.} When someone dies, especially in formal or euphemistic contexts, they expire: {The patient expired at 3:47 AM.} A lease expires when its term ends. Expired breath is air breathed out.

Expires means reaches the end of validity or usefulness. A passport expires after ten years. A coupon expires on a certain date. Food past its expiration date has expired. The verb also means to breathe out, and by extension, to die—though this sense now sounds literary or clinical: {He expired peacefully in his sleep}.

Expiring describes something reaching the end of its valid period or coming to a close. A passport or coupon that is expiring will soon no longer be accepted: {Check for expiring medications in your cabinet}. The word also applies to breath being released, or in literary contexts, to dying: {With his expiring breath, he whispered her name}.

To explain is to make something clear or understandable by describing it in detail or revealing relevant facts: {Let me explain how this works}, {She explained the procedure step by step}. You explain concepts, reasons, or circumstances. To explain away is to minimize or dismiss with justification: {He tried to explain away his absence}. An explanation that accounts for behavior may excuse it: {That explains everything}.

An explainer is a piece of content—article, video, or graphic—designed to clarify a complex topic for a general audience. News outlets publish explainers on intricate policy issues or unfolding events: {Here's an explainer on the debt ceiling crisis}. The format prioritizes accessibility over depth, answering basic questions readers might hesitate to ask.

Explaining is making something clear or understandable to someone else. You explain a concept, a process, a decision, or your reasoning: {Let me explain how this works}, {She explained why she was late}. Explaining often involves breaking down complexity or filling gaps in someone's knowledge. To have {some explaining to do} is to owe someone an account of your actions.

An explanation is a statement or account that makes something clear or understandable. You might offer an explanation for being late, or seek an explanation of how something works. The word covers both justifications {(What's your explanation for this mess?)} and clarifications {(The teacher's explanation helped)}. To explain is to provide one.

Explanations are statements or accounts that make something clear or understandable. An explanation answers why or how: {Her explanation of the delay satisfied no one}. The word implies more than mere description—it addresses causes, reasons, or mechanisms: {The detective's explanation tied all the evidence together}. To {owe someone an explanation} is to be accountable for your actions.

Expletive has two distinct meanings. In grammar, an expletive is a word that fills a syntactic position without adding meaning, like "it" in {it seems unlikely} or "there" in {there are problems}. More commonly, expletive refers to a swear word or obscenity, especially one uttered in anger or frustration. News reports often note that someone's tirade was {laced with expletives} or that {expletives were deleted} from a transcript.

Expletives are words or phrases used to express strong emotion, especially anger or frustration. The term most often refers to profanity or swear words: {The coach let loose a string of expletives after the bad call}. In grammar, expletive has a technical meaning: a word that fills a syntactic slot without adding meaning, such as "it" in {it is raining} or "there" in {there are problems}. These grammatical expletives are sometimes called dummy subjects or placeholder words.

Explicit is an adjective meaning clearly or directly stated: The report contains no explicit statement of what the authors believe. Explicit can also be used to mean “containing direct references to sex”: Parents are concerned that the explicit material on the website will be damaging to children. The opposite of explicit is implicit.

Explode means to burst violently outward with sudden release of energy: {The bomb exploded}. Things that expand rapidly or dramatically also explode: {The population exploded after the war}. A person explodes when anger or laughter erupts uncontrollably: {She exploded at him}. To explode a theory or myth is to disprove it decisively—to blow it apart.

Exploded describes something that has burst apart violently or suddenly: {The bomb exploded}. Beyond physical blasts, it applies to rapid expansion or increase: {The population exploded}. A person who explodes loses their temper suddenly: {She exploded when she heard the news}. An exploded diagram shows components separated but arranged to reveal how they fit together.

Explodes is a form of explode—to burst violently outward with sudden release of energy: {The bomb explodes on impact}. Things that expand rapidly or dramatically also explode: {The population exploded after the war}. A person explodes when emotion erupts suddenly: {She exploded with rage}. To explode a myth or theory is to prove it false—to blow it apart.

Exploding describes something in the act of bursting violently apart, or figuratively, undergoing rapid expansion or intense expression. An {exploding bomb} detonates; an {exploding population} grows dramatically; someone {exploding with rage} releases sudden, forceful emotion. The word captures the moment of rupture or release: {The exploding fireworks lit up the sky}.

To exploit something is to make use of it, often skillfully or to maximum advantage: {exploit natural resources}, {exploit a market opportunity}. The word carries a double edge—it can mean smart utilization or selfish manipulation. To exploit workers is to take unfair advantage of them. An exploit as a noun is a notable deed or feat, especially a bold or daring one: {tales of military exploits}, {the exploits of legendary heroes}. In computing, an exploit is code that takes advantage of a security vulnerability.

Exploitation is the act of using something or someone for benefit—often with connotations of unfairness or extraction. Natural resources are exploited for profit; workers may be exploited through low wages and poor conditions. The word can be neutral {exploitation of new technology} but more often suggests taking advantage: {corporate exploitation of cheap labor}. In film, exploitation refers to low-budget movies emphasizing sensational content: {blaxploitation}, {sexploitation}.

Exploitative describes actions or systems that unfairly use others for profit or advantage, typically by taking more than is given: {exploitative labor practices}, {an exploitative relationship}. The word carries strong moral judgment—calling something exploitative implies the powerful are benefiting at the expense of the vulnerable. Industries, employers, and personal relationships can all be exploitative.

Exploited describes something or someone that has been used, often unfairly or selfishly. An exploited {worker} is taken advantage of—underpaid or overworked for someone else's gain. Exploited {resources} have been extracted or depleted: {The region's oil reserves were heavily exploited}. The word carries connotations of imbalance: one party benefits while another bears the cost.

An exploiter is someone who takes advantage of a person, resource, or situation for their own benefit, often unfairly or unethically. The word carries negative connotations of selfishness and disregard for others: {He was an exploiter of vulnerable workers}. In neutral contexts, exploiter can simply mean one who makes productive use of something: {an exploiter of market opportunities}.

Exploiting is making use of something for one's own benefit. The word carries a range of moral weight depending on context. Exploiting natural resources or market opportunities is neutral: {The company is exploiting a gap in the market}. But exploiting people suggests taking unfair advantage of their vulnerability or labor: {accused of exploiting undocumented workers}. The noun exploitation follows the same pattern.

Exploits works in two directions. As a noun (with stress on the first syllable), exploits are bold or daring deeds—adventures worthy of recounting: {His wartime exploits became legendary}. As a verb (stress on the second syllable), to exploit is to make use of something, often unfairly or selfishly: {The company exploits cheap labor overseas}. In computing, an exploit is code that takes advantage of a software vulnerability.

Exploration is the act of traveling through unfamiliar territory to learn what's there. Early European exploration mapped coastlines and trade routes. The word extends to any systematic investigation of the unknown: {space exploration}, {exploration of new ideas}, {oil exploration}. To explore a topic is to examine it thoroughly. Exploratory describes preliminary investigation: {exploratory surgery}, {exploratory talks}.

Exploratory describes investigation or examination undertaken to learn more about something unknown or uncertain. An exploratory {committee} gauges interest before a political campaign launches. Exploratory {surgery} opens the body to assess what's happening inside. The word emphasizes that outcomes remain undetermined—the purpose is discovery, not confirmation.

To explore is to travel through unfamiliar territory to learn about it: {We spent a week exploring the Scottish Highlands}. The word extends to any systematic examination of the unknown—exploring options, exploring ideas, exploring feelings. In medicine, exploratory surgery investigates what's happening inside the body. Children explore their surroundings; adults explore possibilities. {Let's explore that further.}

Explored is the past tense of explore—to travel through unfamiliar territory, examine something systematically, or investigate possibilities. The word often appears in passive constructions describing what has been investigated: {The region remains largely unexplored}. It can describe physical journeys {We explored the caves} or intellectual inquiry {The documentary explored themes of identity}.

An explorer is a person who travels to unfamiliar regions to discover what's there—historically mapping unknown territories, now often investigating remote or extreme environments: {Arctic explorers}, {cave explorers}. The word extends to anyone who investigates the unfamiliar: {an explorer of ideas}, {urban explorers} who document abandoned buildings. Explorer can also name vehicles or tools designed for investigation. (Capitalized Explorer is a Microsoft web browser or a Ford SUV model.)

Explorers is the plural of explorer—people who travel to unfamiliar places to discover or investigate. The word applies both to historical figures who mapped unknown territories {the Spanish explorers of the Americas} and to anyone venturing into uncharted areas, whether physical, intellectual, or creative: {explorers of the deep sea}, {explorers of consciousness}.

Exploring is the activity of investigating unfamiliar territory or subjects. You might spend an afternoon exploring a new city, or years exploring the limits of human knowledge. The word suggests curiosity and openness to discovery: {We're still exploring our options}. Children explore their surroundings; scientists explore hypotheses; couples explore each other's bodies.

An explosion is a sudden, violent release of energy—a bomb detonating, a gas tank rupturing, a chemical reaction going wrong. The word extends to any rapid, dramatic increase: {an explosion of interest in AI}, {a population explosion}. Something explosive can literally blow up or figuratively erupt: an explosive {temper}, explosive {growth}.

Explosions is the plural of explosion—a sudden, violent release of energy, typically with a loud noise and rapid expansion of gases. Bombs cause explosions; so do chemical reactions and pressure buildups. The word extends to any sudden outburst: {an explosion of laughter}, {a population explosion}, {an explosion of color across the canvas}.

Explosive describes something capable of exploding—detonating with sudden, violent force. An explosive device contains materials that combust rapidly. As a noun, an explosive is such a material: dynamite, C-4, gunpowder. The meaning extends to anything that erupts suddenly or intensely: an explosive {temper}, explosive {growth}, an explosive {situation}. In sports, explosive describes powerful, sudden movement: {explosive speed off the line}.

Explosives are substances or devices that undergo rapid chemical reactions releasing large amounts of gas and energy, producing violent expansion. The term covers everything from dynamite and TNT to plastic explosives and improvised bombs. {The building was demolished with explosives}. Explosive can also function as an adjective: {explosive materials}, {an explosive temper}.

Expo is short for exposition, meaning a large public exhibition or trade show: {the world expo}, {a home and garden expo}. The informal clipping has largely replaced the fuller form in everyday speech. Expos showcase products, industries, or innovations, typically running for several days and drawing crowds from various regions.

An exponent is someone who advocates or represents something: {a leading exponent of free-market economics}. In mathematics, an exponent is the superscript number indicating how many times a base multiplies itself—in 2³, the exponent is 3. The mathematical sense extends metaphorically: someone can be an exponent of a skill, embodying it at a high power.

Exponential describes growth or change that accelerates at a rate proportional to the current amount—the larger it gets, the faster it grows. In mathematics, exponential functions involve a constant raised to a variable power. Loosely, exponential just means rapid or dramatic: {Housing prices have grown exponentially}. This casual use irritates mathematicians, but it's well established.

Exponentially describes growth or increase at a rate proportional to current size—each step multiplies rather than adds. In mathematics, exponential functions increase by a constant factor: 2, 4, 8, 16. In casual use, exponentially often just means dramatically or rapidly: {The problem grew exponentially worse}. This looser sense irritates mathematicians but dominates everyday speech.

Exponents are numbers or symbols indicating how many times a base number multiplies itself: in 2³, the exponent 3 means 2 × 2 × 2. Beyond mathematics, an exponent is someone who advocates or exemplifies something: {She was an early exponent of minimalist design}. The word suggests active promotion or skilled demonstration of an idea, style, or method.

Export means to send goods or services to another country for sale or trade: {Coffee is Brazil's major export}. The word extends to sending data out of one program or format into another: {Export the file as a PDF}. As a noun, an export is a product sent abroad, or the act of sending it. To export an idea or practice is to spread it elsewhere: {Hollywood exports American culture worldwide}.

Exporters are businesses or countries that sell goods or services to foreign markets. The term often appears in economic discussions about trade balances and international commerce: {China is among the world's largest exporters of manufactured goods}. An exporter may also be an individual who ships products abroad: {She works as an exporter of handmade textiles}.

Exporting is sending goods or services to another country for sale or trade. The term extends to any transfer outward: exporting data moves it from one program or system to another, exporting jobs shifts employment overseas. {The region's economy depends on exporting timber}. {Export the file as a PDF}.

Exports are goods or services sent to another country for sale. A nation's exports represent what it sells abroad, as opposed to imports, which come in: {Oil is their primary export}. The verb export means to send products out of a country or, more broadly, to spread something outward: {Hollywood exports American culture worldwide}. In computing, to export is to convert data for use in another program.

Expos is the plural of expo, short for exposition—a large public exhibition or fair showcasing products, industries, or ideas: {trade expos}, {tech expos}, {home and garden expos}. The word often appears in event names. Capitalized Expos was also the Montreal Expos, a former Major League Baseball team.

Expose means to uncover or make visible something that was hidden or protected. You expose skin by removing clothing, expose film by letting in light, expose a lie by revealing truth. To expose someone to something is to subject them to it: {children exposed to violence}, {patients exposed to the virus}. An exposé (with the accent) is a journalistic revelation of wrongdoing. To expose oneself is to display one's genitals publicly—a criminal act in most jurisdictions.

Exposed means uncovered or unprotected—open to view, harm, or the elements. An exposed {wire} lacks insulation. An exposed {hillside} has no shelter from wind. To feel exposed is to feel vulnerable, whether physically or emotionally: {Standing at the podium, she felt completely exposed}. In photography, exposed film has been subjected to light. A scandal exposes wrongdoing; the wrongdoer is then exposed.

Exposes is the verb expose in the present tense: to uncover, reveal, or make visible what was hidden or protected. You expose skin to sunlight, expose a secret to the public, expose film to light. {The investigation exposes corruption at the highest levels.} To expose someone is to reveal damaging information about them. Exposés (with the accent) are the noun form—investigative reports that expose wrongdoing.

Exposing is the act of making something visible or known that was previously hidden or covered. You might be exposing skin to sunlight, exposing film to light, or exposing corruption to public scrutiny. The word often implies revelation of something concealed: {The investigation ended up exposing years of fraud}. To expose oneself is to display one's genitals publicly—a criminal act in most jurisdictions.

Exposition is the act of explaining or setting forth ideas clearly. In writing and drama, exposition provides background information—character histories, settings, prior events—that audiences need to understand what follows: {The first chapter is mostly exposition}. An exposition is also a large public exhibition showcasing products, industries, or achievements: {the World's Fair exposition of 1893}.

Exposure is the state of being unprotected or uncovered. You can die of exposure to cold, or suffer exposure to harmful substances. Public exposure means being seen or known: {The scandal brought unwanted exposure}. Media exposure can build a career. In photography, exposure is the amount of light reaching the film or sensor, or a single frame: {I have a few exposures left on this roll}. To expose oneself is to display one's genitals publicly—indecent exposure.

Exposures is the plural of exposure, which centers on being uncovered or revealed. In photography, an exposure is a single frame—one instance of light hitting film or sensor: {She took several exposures of the sunset}. In finance, exposures are vulnerabilities to risk: {The bank's exposures to subprime mortgages proved catastrophic}. Medical exposures refer to contact with pathogens, radiation, or harmful substances: {Workers tracked their daily exposures to asbestos}.

The noun and adjective express have to do with rapid movement; the verb express means to manifest in some communicable or understandable form (express an opinion, express anger). Things are characterized with the adjective express to distinguish them from slower things: The restaurant offered express delivery. As a noun, express may designate a mode of fast service, or a vessel: Take the 5 o’clock express.

Expressed is the past tense of express, meaning communicated or conveyed outward. Thoughts, feelings, or ideas that were expressed have been put into words, gestures, or other forms others can perceive: {She expressed her gratitude}. Expressed also describes something squeezed out: {expressed juice from the oranges}. In genetics, an expressed gene is one that has been activated to produce its protein.

Expression is the act of conveying thought, feeling, or meaning outward—through words, art, gestures, or facial movements. A {pained expression} crosses someone's face. Freedom of {expression} protects speech and creative work. In mathematics, an expression is a combination of symbols representing a value: {algebraic expression}. To do something {as an expression of} gratitude or love is to communicate that feeling through action.

A broad approach in art, literature, music, and drama that emphasizes subjective emotional experience over realistic representation. The artist distorts or exaggerates reality to express inner feelings rather than depict outward appearances. The term applies loosely to any work prioritizing emotional intensity: {The painting had a raw expressionism that unsettled viewers}. (Capitalized Expressionism refers to the specific early 20th-century movement.)

An expressionist is an artist who works in the expressionist style—prioritizing emotional intensity and subjective experience over realistic representation. The term applies especially to early 20th-century German painters and filmmakers who used distorted forms, vivid colors, and dramatic contrasts: {The expressionists rejected naturalism}. As an adjective, expressionist describes work in this tradition: {expressionist theater}, {an expressionist woodcut}.

Expressionists are artists or writers associated with expressionism, a movement emphasizing emotional experience over realistic representation. The term applies most often to early 20th-century German painters who used distorted forms and intense colors to convey inner states: {The expressionists rejected naturalism in favor of psychological truth}. It extends to practitioners in theater, film, literature, and music who prioritize subjective feeling over external reality.

Expressionless describes a face or voice showing no emotion—blank, unreadable, impossible to interpret. An expressionless {stare} reveals nothing of what the person is thinking or feeling. The word often suggests deliberate concealment: {Her face remained expressionless as she heard the verdict}.

Expressions are outward manifestations of inner states. A facial expression reveals emotion—joy, disgust, surprise. An expression is also a word or phrase: {That's an odd expression}. In mathematics, an expression is a combination of symbols representing a value. To express is to convey meaning outward, and expressions are what results. {Her expression said everything her words didn't}.

Expressive describes something that effectively conveys meaning, feeling, or character. An expressive {face} reveals emotion readily. Expressive {language} communicates vividly. An expressive {performance} moves the audience. The word often implies emotional transparency or artistic power: {Her eyes were remarkably expressive}. In linguistics, expressive language is the ability to produce speech, contrasted with receptive language (comprehension).

An expressway is a high-speed divided highway designed for through traffic, with limited access points and no intersections at grade level. The term is more common in American English, where it often overlaps with freeway and highway: {Take the expressway to avoid downtown traffic}. Unlike toll roads, expressways are typically free to use.

Expulsion is the act of forcing someone or something out. A student faces expulsion from school for serious misconduct. A country may order the expulsion of foreign diplomats. The word applies to physical ejection too: {the expulsion of air from the lungs}, {the expulsion of waste from the body}. Where dismissal might be voluntary, expulsion implies forcible removal.

Expulsions are acts of forcing someone or something out. A student faces expulsion from school for serious misconduct. A country may order the expulsion of foreign diplomats. The body's expulsion of waste is a natural process. {The expulsions followed the failed coup attempt.}

Exquisite describes something of exceptional beauty, craftsmanship, or refinement—the kind that rewards close attention: {exquisite embroidery}, {an exquisite wine}. The word often implies delicacy or intricacy: {exquisite detail}. Exquisite can also intensify sensations, pleasant or not: {exquisite pleasure}, {exquisite pain}. The underlying sense is something so finely wrought it stands apart from the ordinary.

Extend means to stretch out or make longer. You extend an {arm}, extend a {deadline}, extend a {road}. The meaning broadens to offering: extend an {invitation}, extend {credit}, extend {sympathy}. Something that extends covers a certain distance or duration: {The forest extends for miles}. Extended means lengthened or prolonged: an extended {warranty}, an extended {stay}.

Extended means stretched out in space or time. An extended {family} includes relatives beyond the nuclear unit. An extended {warranty} lasts longer than standard coverage. An extended {stay} is prolonged beyond the usual. Extended {arms} reach outward. The word often suggests something enlarged or expanded from a basic form: an extended {version} of a film includes additional footage.

Extension is the act of stretching something out or the state of being stretched. A limb held straight is in extension. An extension cord lengthens an electrical connection. A deadline extension grants more time. A phone extension connects to the main line. A building extension adds space. In computing, a file extension (like .pdf or .jpg) indicates format. Hair extensions add length. The word covers anything that extends—literally or figuratively—the reach of something else.

Extensions are things added to lengthen or expand something original. Hair extensions add length. A file extension (.pdf, .jpg) identifies format. Browser extensions add functionality. A phone extension routes calls within an organization. An extension cord extends electrical reach. To get an extension on a deadline is to receive more time: {I asked for an extension on my paper}.

Extensive means covering a large area, scope, or amount. An extensive {search} is thorough and wide-ranging. Extensive {damage} affects much of something. Extensive {experience} spans many years or situations. The word emphasizes breadth rather than depth—an extensive reading list covers many topics but may not exhaust any single one.

Extent is how far something reaches or stretches—in space, time, or degree. {The full extent of the damage wasn't clear until morning.} You might know something {to some extent} or {to a certain extent}, meaning partially. {The extent to which} introduces degree questions: {The extent to which he was involved remains unknown.}

Exterior refers to the outer surface or appearance of something, as opposed to its interior: {the exterior of the building}, {exterior walls}. It extends to outward manner or behavior that may not reflect inner reality: {His calm exterior hid considerable anxiety}. As an adjective, exterior describes what is outside or outward-facing: {exterior paint}, {exterior lighting}.

Exteriors are outer surfaces or appearances—the outside of buildings, vehicles, or people. In film and television, exteriors are scenes shot outdoors: {We filmed the exteriors in Vancouver}. The word often contrasts with what lies beneath: {His calm exterior hid considerable anxiety}. As an adjective, exterior describes what's on the outside: {exterior walls}, {exterior paint}.

To exterminate is to destroy completely, especially to kill off an entire population of pests or people. Exterminators eliminate rats and roaches; genocides exterminate ethnic groups. The word implies thoroughness—not just killing some, but wiping out all: {The regime sought to exterminate its political opponents}. Extermination carries clinical coldness, suggesting systematic rather than passionate violence.

Exterminated means completely destroyed or killed off. The word applies to deliberate, thorough elimination—of pests, populations, or groups: {The invasive species was exterminated from the island}. When applied to people, exterminated carries the cold efficiency of genocide or mass killing: {Millions were exterminated in the camps}.

Exterminating is the act of completely destroying or killing off a population—typically pests, vermin, or unwanted organisms: {The exterminator is coming Tuesday for the roaches}. The word implies thoroughness, eliminating every last member of a group. Applied to people, exterminating carries the weight of genocide or mass murder: {The regime's policy of exterminating ethnic minorities}.

Extermination is the complete destruction or elimination of something, especially a population. The word typically describes killing on a mass scale: the extermination of pests, the extermination of indigenous peoples, the extermination of Jews in Nazi death camps. {The landlord called for extermination of the roaches}. The clinical tone can mask horror when applied to humans.

An exterminator is a person or company that kills pests—insects, rodents, or other unwanted creatures in homes and buildings. The work involves traps, poisons, and pesticides: {We called the exterminator about the roaches}. The term also applies more broadly to anyone who destroys or eliminates something completely.

Exterminators are people or companies hired to eliminate pests—insects, rodents, or other unwanted creatures—from buildings or properties. The term emphasizes killing rather than removal: {We called the exterminators about the termites}. Figuratively, an exterminator destroys or eliminates anything systematically: {an exterminator of hope}.

External refers to what lies outside or on the surface of something, as opposed to internal. External {walls} face outward; external {hard drives} connect from outside a computer. External {forces} come from beyond a system or organization. The word often distinguishes outward appearance from inner reality: {external calm}, {external symptoms}. In academic contexts, an external {examiner} comes from another institution.

Extinct describes something that no longer exists. A species becomes extinct when its last member dies: {Dinosaurs went extinct millions of years ago}. The word extends to anything that has disappeared entirely—extinct languages, extinct volcanoes (no longer active), extinct customs. To be extinct is to be gone permanently, beyond recovery.

Extinction is the state of no longer existing—when every member of a species has died, leaving none alive: {The dodo was hunted to extinction}. The word extends beyond biology: extinction of a debt means paying it off completely, and behavioral extinction occurs when a response disappears after reinforcement stops. To face extinction is to face complete elimination: {Without intervention, the language faces extinction within a generation}.

Extinctions is the plural of extinction, which denotes the complete dying out of a species or the end of something's existence. Scientists track mass extinctions in Earth's history, such as the one that killed the dinosaurs. The term extends beyond biology to describe the disappearance of languages, cultures, or practices. {Human activity has accelerated the rate of extinctions worldwide.} In psychology, extinction refers to the gradual weakening of a conditioned response when reinforcement stops.

To extinguish is to put out a fire or light: {Extinguish all campfires before leaving}. The word extends to ending or eliminating anything: extinguish a {debt}, extinguish {hope}, extinguish a {species}. To extinguish a right is to terminate it legally. The formal tone makes extinguish more common in official contexts than everyday speech—you put out a cigarette but extinguish a blaze.

Extinguished describes something that has been put out or ended. A fire is extinguished with water; a candle is extinguished by blowing. The word extends to anything that ceases to exist: {an extinguished species}, {extinguished hopes}. A debt that has been paid off is extinguished. {The last embers were finally extinguished by morning}.

An extinguisher is a device for putting out fires, typically a portable canister that sprays water, foam, or chemical agents: {Every kitchen should have a fire extinguisher}. The full term is fire extinguisher, but context usually makes the shortened form clear.

Extinguishing is the act of putting out a fire or light: {firefighters extinguishing the blaze}, {extinguishing the candles before bed}. The word extends to ending or eliminating anything: extinguishing a debt, extinguishing hope, extinguishing a species. What's extinguished no longer burns, glows, or exists.

To extort is to obtain something—usually money—through force, threats, or abuse of power. The threat may be physical harm, exposure of secrets, or misuse of official authority: {The gang extorted protection money from local businesses}. Extortion differs from robbery in relying on intimidation rather than direct taking. Someone who extorts is an extortionist.

Extorted is the past tense of extort—to obtain something, typically money, through force, threats, or intimidation. The word implies coercion rather than voluntary exchange: {He extorted thousands from local businesses by threatening violence}. What's extorted is usually money or favors, and the extorter typically exploits a position of power or knowledge of damaging secrets.

Extorting is obtaining something—usually money—through threats, intimidation, or abuse of power. The threat might be physical harm, exposure of damaging information, or misuse of official authority: {The gang was extorting local businesses for protection money}. Extorting differs from robbery in relying on coercion rather than direct force.

Extortion is obtaining money, property, or cooperation through threats or coercion. The threat might be violence, exposure of damaging information, or abuse of official power. Unlike robbery, which takes by force, extortion compels the victim to hand something over: {The gang ran an extortion racket on local businesses}. Blackmail is extortion through threatened exposure.

An extortionist obtains money or other benefits through threats, coercion, or intimidation. The term applies both to criminals who threaten violence or exposure and to anyone perceived as demanding unreasonable payment: {The mechanic quoted three thousand dollars—what an extortionist}. Also extortioner.

Extorts is the third-person singular of extort—to obtain something, especially money, through force, threats, or abuse of power. The victim pays or complies to avoid harm: {He extorts money from local businesses by threatening violence}. Extortion typically involves blackmail, intimidation, or leveraging authority: {The official extorts bribes from contractors seeking permits}.

Extra means beyond what is usual, expected, or necessary. An extra blanket provides additional warmth; extra credit offers bonus points. As a noun, an extra is something added—a car with all the extras—or a person hired to appear in the background of a film. As an adverb, extra intensifies: {extra large}, {extra careful}. In recent slang, extra describes someone being excessive or dramatic: {She's being so extra right now}.

Extract centers on the idea of pulling something out from a larger whole. You extract a tooth from a jaw, a confession from a suspect, data from a database. The noun extract is the concentrated substance drawn from something—vanilla extract, plant extract. A literary extract is a passage pulled from a longer work. The process often implies effort or force: {extracting information from reluctant witnesses}, {extracting meaning from a difficult text}.

Extraction is the act of removing or pulling something out—often with effort or specialized methods. A dentist performs a tooth extraction. In chemistry, extraction separates a substance from a mixture. Military forces conduct extractions to retrieve personnel from dangerous areas. Extraction also refers to ancestry or origin: {a family of Italian extraction}.

An extractor is a device or tool that removes something from where it's lodged or contained. A juice extractor separates liquid from fruit. A bullet extractor removes projectiles from wounds. In firearms, the extractor is the mechanism that pulls spent cartridges from the chamber. The term extends to software that pulls data from files or databases: {The PDF extractor grabbed all the text from the document}. A person who extracts information, especially through interrogation, may also be called an extractor.

Extracts functions as both verb and noun around the idea of pulling something out. To extract a tooth is to remove it; to extract a confession is to obtain it through pressure. An extract is something drawn out—a passage from a book, a concentrated substance from a plant: {vanilla extract}, {The article includes extracts from her diary}. The noun stresses what's been separated from a larger whole.

Extracurricular describes activities outside the regular academic curriculum—sports, clubs, theater, volunteer work: {Her extracurricular activities helped her college application}. The word extends to anything outside one's main duties or commitments. {Extracurricular affairs} is a euphemism for adultery, suggesting activity outside the marriage.

Extracurriculars are activities pursued outside the regular academic curriculum—sports, clubs, theater, volunteer work. The term appears most often in discussions of college admissions, where a strong roster of extracurriculars supposedly demonstrates a well-rounded applicant: {Her extracurriculars include debate team and community organizing}. Sometimes used loosely for any side pursuits beyond one's main obligations.

To extradite is to surrender a person accused or convicted of a crime to the jurisdiction where the offense occurred. Governments extradite based on treaties and formal requests: {The U.S. extradited the suspect to face trial in Mexico}. Countries sometimes refuse extradition on political grounds or when the accused might face the death penalty.

Extradited is the past tense of extradite, meaning to surrender a person accused or convicted of a crime to the jurisdiction where the offense occurred. The process typically involves legal proceedings between governments: {He was extradited to France to face murder charges}. Someone can also be extradited from one state to another within a country.

Extradition is the legal process of surrendering a person from one jurisdiction to another to face criminal charges or serve a sentence. Countries negotiate extradition treaties specifying which offenses qualify and what protections apply. {The U.S. sought his extradition from Mexico on drug trafficking charges.} A person who flees to a country without an extradition treaty may avoid prosecution.

Extraditions are formal processes by which one jurisdiction surrenders a person to another for prosecution or punishment. Countries negotiate extradition treaties specifying which crimes qualify and what protections apply. {The extraditions of the suspected terrorists took months to arrange.} Political considerations often complicate extraditions, particularly when the accused claims persecution or faces the death penalty.

Extramarital describes sexual or romantic activity outside of marriage—specifically, one's own marriage. An extramarital {affair} involves a married person and someone other than their spouse. The word carries moral weight, implying betrayal of marital vows: {Evidence of extramarital relationships emerged during the divorce proceedings}.

Extraordinary means beyond the ordinary—exceptional, remarkable, or surpassing what is usual. An extraordinary {talent} stands out from the crowd. Extraordinary {measures} go beyond normal procedures. The word can intensify almost any noun: extraordinary {beauty}, extraordinary {circumstances}, extraordinary {luck}. In formal contexts, extraordinary may indicate something outside regular arrangements: an {ambassador extraordinary}, an {extraordinary session} of Congress.

Extrapolating is extending known data or experience into unknown territory—projecting trends, patterns, or conclusions beyond what has been directly observed. Scientists extrapolate from experimental results to predict future outcomes. {Extrapolating from current growth rates, the population will double by 2050.} The word often carries a note of caution: extrapolation involves assumptions that may not hold.

Extrapolation is the act of extending known data or experience into unknown territory—projecting a trend, estimating beyond measured values, or inferring what might be true based on what is known. {Based on current growth, extrapolation suggests the population will double by 2050.} The term appears in statistics, science, and everyday reasoning. Unlike interpolation, which estimates between known points, extrapolation ventures beyond them, making it inherently riskier.

Extras are additional items beyond what's standard or expected. A movie's extras are the unnamed performers who populate background scenes. In cricket, extras are runs scored without the batsman hitting the ball. On a bill, extras are charges beyond the base price. The word often implies optional additions: {The car comes with leather seats and other extras}. In film production, to work as an extra is entry-level acting work requiring no lines.

Extraterrestrial means originating or existing outside Earth or its atmosphere. As an adjective, it describes phenomena beyond our planet: {extraterrestrial life}, {extraterrestrial intelligence}. As a noun, an extraterrestrial is a being from another world—the alien of science fiction. The word is often shortened to ET: {The search for ET continues}.

Extraterrestrials are beings from beyond Earth—life forms originating on other planets or in outer space. The word appears most often in discussions of whether such life exists and whether it has visited Earth: {Do you believe in extraterrestrials?} As an adjective, extraterrestrial describes anything originating outside Earth: {extraterrestrial intelligence}, {extraterrestrial life}.

Extravagance is spending or behavior that exceeds what's reasonable or necessary. The word carries a sense of excess—too much money, too much flair, too much of anything: {The wedding was an extravagance they couldn't afford}. An extravagance can be a specific indulgent purchase: {The sports car was his one extravagance}. The term sometimes suggests admirable boldness rather than wastefulness: {the extravagance of her imagination}.

Extravagant means exceeding reasonable limits, especially in spending money: {an extravagant lifestyle}, {extravagant gifts}. The word suggests excess beyond what's necessary or prudent. Extravagant praise or claims are exaggerated or overblown. An extravagant production is elaborate and costly. The noun extravagance covers both the quality and specific instances: {such extravagance!}, {We can't afford these extravagances}.

An extravaganza is a spectacular, elaborate production—typically entertainment on a grand scale with lavish sets, costumes, and effects: {The halftime show was a musical extravaganza}. The word implies excess and showiness, sometimes with a hint of overindulgence: {a shopping extravaganza}, {a fireworks extravaganza}. Any event designed to impress through sheer scale or abundance qualifies.

Extravaganzas is the plural of extravaganza, an elaborate and spectacular entertainment or production. The word suggests lavish excess—expensive sets, large casts, dramatic effects: {Broadway extravaganzas}, {holiday shopping extravaganzas}. The term often carries a note of irony or criticism when applied to events that seem excessive or overproduced: {The wedding was a three-day extravaganza}.

Extraversion is the personality trait of directing energy outward—toward people, activities, and external stimulation rather than inward reflection. Extraverts typically feel energized by social interaction and may find solitude draining. The term comes from psychology, particularly the work of Carl Jung, and remains central to personality models. Also spelled extroversion, which is now more common in American English.

Extraverts are people who gain energy from social interaction and external stimulation. The term comes from psychology, describing those oriented toward the outer world of people and activity rather than inward reflection. Extravert is the original spelling, though extrovert has become more common: {Extraverts thrive at parties that exhaust introverts}.

Extreme marks the farthest possible point on a scale or spectrum. An extreme {temperature} is very hot or very cold. Extreme {measures} go beyond what's normal or moderate. An {extreme sport} involves exceptional risk. As a noun, extremes are the outermost limits: {the extremes of wealth and poverty}. To {go to extremes} is to act excessively. {In the extreme} means to the highest degree: {The situation was dangerous in the extreme}.

Extremes are the farthest points on a spectrum or the most intense versions of something. In temperature, the extremes are scorching heat and bitter cold. In politics, the extremes are radical positions at opposite ends. To {go to extremes} is to take excessive action: {She went to extremes to prove her point}. The phrase {in the extreme} means to the highest degree: {The situation was dangerous in the extreme}.

Extremism is holding political, religious, or ideological views far outside the mainstream, especially views that advocate radical action or reject compromise. The term is almost always applied by outsiders—few call themselves extremists: {The government cracked down on religious extremism}. What counts as extreme shifts with time and context; yesterday's extremism sometimes becomes tomorrow's orthodoxy.

An extremist holds views far outside the mainstream, typically in politics or religion, and often advocates radical action to advance them. The term is almost always applied by opponents rather than claimed by the people it describes: {The government labeled the protesters extremists}. As an adjective, it describes such views or groups: {extremist ideology}, {extremist factions}.

Extremists are people who hold radical political, religious, or ideological views far outside the mainstream. The term implies not just strong beliefs but willingness to pursue them through uncompromising or violent means: {The group was infiltrated by extremists}. Whether someone counts as an extremist depends heavily on the speaker's own position—one person's extremist is another's freedom fighter.

Extremities are the parts farthest from the center—most often the hands and feet, or sometimes all four limbs. Cold weather affects the extremities first as the body prioritizes warming vital organs. The word also applies to extreme measures or conditions: {driven to extremities by desperation}. In the singular, extremity can mean the farthest point or edge of something, or an extreme degree: {the extremity of his grief}.

Extremity refers to the outermost or farthest point of something, particularly the limbs of the body—hands, feet, arms, and legs are collectively called the extremities. Beyond anatomy, extremity describes the furthest degree or limit of anything: {the extremity of his grief}, {driven to extremity by circumstances}. In this sense it suggests an intense or dire condition, often implying desperation or crisis. The word captures both physical endpoints and the outer bounds of experience or emotion.

Extroversion is a personality trait marked by outward focus—drawing energy from social interaction, external stimulation, and engagement with the world. An extrovert thrives in company and may feel drained by too much solitude. The term comes from psychology, where it pairs with introversion as opposite ends of a spectrum: {Her extroversion makes her a natural networker}. Also spelled extraversion, especially in technical contexts.

An extrovert is a person who draws energy from social interaction and external stimulation, typically outgoing and talkative. The term comes from psychology but now appears in everyday speech: {She's a total extrovert—parties energize her}. The spelling extravert appears in technical contexts. The opposite is introvert.

Extroverted describes someone who draws energy from social interaction and external stimulation. An extroverted person tends to be outgoing, talkative, and comfortable in groups: {She's too extroverted to enjoy working from home}. The opposite is introverted. Also spelled extraverted, especially in psychology.

Extroverts are people who gain energy from social interaction and external stimulation. The term comes from psychology, contrasting with introverts. Extroverts tend to be outgoing, talkative, and energized by being around others: {The extroverts at the party were still going strong at midnight}. The spelling extravert appears in clinical contexts but extrovert dominates in everyday use.

Exuberance is lively, unrestrained enthusiasm or energy: {youthful exuberance}, {the exuberance of the crowd}. It suggests abundance spilling over—too much vitality to contain. The word extends to luxuriant growth: {the exuberance of tropical vegetation}. Alan Greenspan famously warned of {irrational exuberance} in financial markets—enthusiasm untethered from reality.

Exuberant describes overflowing energy, enthusiasm, or abundance. An exuberant {greeting} is effusively warm. An exuberant {personality} bubbles with vitality. The word applies equally to people and to lush, unrestrained growth: {exuberant foliage}, {exuberant prose}. There's always a sense of something spilling beyond normal bounds—not reckless, but irrepressibly full.

Exultation is triumphant joy—the feeling of elation that comes from victory, success, or vindication. It suggests celebration that's hard to contain: {The crowd erupted in exultation when the final whistle blew}. The word carries more intensity than mere happiness; exultation implies you've overcome something or achieved what seemed uncertain.

Exulting is rejoicing triumphantly, feeling or expressing great elation at success or victory. The word suggests open, unrestrained celebration: {The fans were exulting in the streets after the championship win}. Someone exulting doesn't just feel happy—they feel vindicated, victorious, perhaps even gloating.

An exurb is a prosperous community beyond a city's suburbs—farther out, more rural in character, but still within commuting distance. Exurbs typically feature larger properties and lower density than suburbs, attracting residents who want space while maintaining economic ties to an urban center: {The exurbs kept expanding as remote work became common}.

Exurbs are the prosperous communities beyond a city's suburbs—farther from urban centers but still within commuting range. Where suburbs border cities directly, exurbs lie past them, typically characterized by larger lots, newer developments, and residents who accept longer commutes for more space and lower density: {Housing prices in the exurbs have skyrocketed as remote work becomes common}.

Eye denotes the light-sensitive organ with which humans and other organisms process visual stimuli. From this meaning a number of other meanings have developed that are connected with sight or vision. Other physical structures that bear a resemblance to the eye are also called eye, such as the eye of a storm or the eye of a needle. Eye occurs as often in the plural as the singular, reflecting the fact that most organisms have two.

Eyebags are the puffy or swollen areas beneath the eyes, typically caused by fluid retention, lack of sleep, aging, or genetics. The skin under the eyes is thin and delicate, making any swelling or discoloration there particularly visible. Dark circles often accompany eyebags, though they're technically distinct conditions. {I woke up with terrible eyebags after staying up all night.} Cosmetics, cold compresses, and various treatments claim to reduce their appearance.

An eyeball is the spherical organ of sight, housed in the eye socket. The term often emphasizes the physical globe itself: {His eyeballs darted back and forth}. To eyeball something is to look at it directly or estimate by sight rather than measurement: {She eyeballed the distance at about ten feet}. To be {up to your eyeballs} in something is to be overwhelmed by it.

Eyeballed is the past tense of eyeball, meaning to look at something closely or to estimate by sight rather than measurement: {She eyeballed the distance and figured it was about thirty feet}. To eyeball someone is to stare at them, often with suspicion or hostility: {The bouncer eyeballed us as we walked in}.

Eyeballing is estimating or measuring something by sight alone, without instruments or precise calculation: {I was just eyeballing the distance—maybe fifty feet?} The term suggests rough approximation rather than accuracy. Eyeballing can also mean looking at someone or something intently, often with suspicion or interest: {He kept eyeballing me from across the room}.

Eyeballs are the spherical organs of sight that sit in the eye sockets. The word emphasizes the physical, globular nature of the eye rather than the sense of vision itself. In informal usage, eyeballs often means attention or views: {We need more eyeballs on this website}. To eyeball something is to look at it carefully or to estimate by sight rather than measurement: {I eyeballed the distance at about fifty feet}.

Eyeblack is the dark grease or adhesive strips athletes apply under their eyes to reduce glare from sunlight or stadium lights. Most associated with American football and baseball, where players smear it in distinctive patterns: {The quarterback's eyeblack had Bible verses written on it}. Whether it actually improves vision is debated, but it remains a fixture of game-day ritual.

The eyebrow is the arch of hair above each eye. Eyebrows protect the eyes from sweat and debris, but their expressive function dominates: raised eyebrows signal surprise or skepticism, furrowed brows suggest concentration or anger. To {raise an eyebrow} is to express doubt or disapproval. Something that {raises eyebrows} causes surprise or mild shock.

Eyebrows are the strips of hair growing above each eye, following the curve of the brow bone. They help keep sweat and debris from the eyes and play a major role in facial expression—raised eyebrows signal surprise, furrowed ones concentration or anger. To {raise eyebrows} is to cause surprise or mild shock: {Her comments raised a few eyebrows at the meeting}.

An eyedropper is a small glass or plastic tube with a rubber bulb at one end, used to dispense liquid in drops. Squeeze the bulb, dip the tip into liquid, release to draw it up, then squeeze again to release drops. Originally for applying medicine to eyes, eyedroppers now measure small quantities of any liquid: {Add three eyedroppers of food coloring}.

Eyedrops are liquid medication or solution applied directly to the eye, typically from a small squeeze bottle with a narrow tip. They treat conditions like dryness, allergies, infections, or glaucoma, or simply rinse debris from the eye: {The doctor prescribed eyedrops for my pink eye}. Also spelled as two words: eye drops.

An eyeful is as much as the eye can take in at once. The word usually appears in the phrase {get an eyeful}, meaning to see something remarkable—often something you weren't supposed to see, particularly someone naked or scantily dressed: {The towel slipped and he got an eyeful}. An eyeful can also be a strikingly attractive person.

Eyeglasses are lenses in a frame worn on the face to correct vision. The word is standard in American English, where the shortened form glasses is more common in casual speech. British English prefers spectacles. {I need new eyeglasses—these are scratched}. The singular eyeglass typically refers to a monocle or a lens for one eye.

Eyeing is looking at something with sustained attention or interest. You might eye a dessert you're considering, or eye someone suspiciously across the room. The word often implies assessment or desire: {She was eyeing the last slice of pizza}. Also spelled eying.

An eyelash is one of the short hairs that grow along the edge of the eyelid. Eyelashes help protect the eye from dust and debris. They figure in expressions of narrow margins: {She won by an eyelash}. To {bat one's eyelashes} is to flutter them flirtatiously or in feigned innocence.

Eyelashes are the short hairs that grow along the edge of the eyelids, curving outward from the eye. They help protect the eye from dust and debris. Long or thick eyelashes are considered attractive, prompting various enhancement methods: {She wore false eyelashes to the gala}. To {bat one's eyelashes} is to flutter them flirtatiously.

An eyelet is a small hole reinforced with metal or stitching, designed for a cord or lace to pass through: {She threaded the laces through the eyelets of her boots}. Eyelets appear on shoes, corsets, sails, and tarps. The term also applies to small decorative holes in embroidery or fabric, creating patterns through absence.

Eyelets are small holes reinforced with metal or stitching, designed for laces or cords to pass through. Shoes and corsets have eyelets. The term also applies to small holes in fabric for decorative effect or ventilation. An eyelet can be the metal ring itself that reinforces the hole: {She replaced the rusted eyelets on her hiking boots}.

An eyelid is the fold of skin that covers and protects the eye when closed. Humans have upper and lower eyelids, though the upper does most of the work in blinking and sleeping. To {not bat an eyelid} is to show no reaction to something surprising or disturbing.

Eyelids are the folds of skin that close over the eyes. They protect the eye and spread moisture across its surface with each blink. Heavy eyelids signal drowsiness: {I could barely keep my eyelids open}. Drooping eyelids may indicate fatigue, aging, or medical conditions. Cosmetics and surgery often focus on the eyelids as expressive features of the face.

Eyeliner is a cosmetic applied along the edges of the eyelids to define or accentuate the eyes. It comes in pencil, liquid, gel, and felt-tip forms, each producing different effects from soft and smudged to sharp and dramatic: {She applied a thin line of eyeliner to her upper lid}. Winged eyeliner extends past the outer corner of the eye.

An eye-opener is something that reveals a surprising or previously unrecognized truth: {The documentary was a real eye-opener about factory farming}. It shifts perspective, making you see things differently than before. In older usage, an eye-opener was also an early morning alcoholic drink—something to open the eyes and start the day.

Eyeopeners are things that reveal surprising truths or provide unexpected insight: {The documentary was a real eyeopener about factory farming}. The term suggests having one's eyes opened to something previously unseen or misunderstood. Separately, an eyeopener is a drink of alcohol taken early in the morning—something that literally opens the eyes.

An eyepatch is a covering worn over one eye, held in place by a strap or cord around the head. Eyepatches protect injured eyes or conceal missing ones.
