Fanfics is the plural of fanfic, itself a clipped form of fan fiction—stories written by fans using characters, settings, or worlds from existing media. Fanfics range from short sketches to novel-length works and circulate online in dedicated communities: {She's written dozens of Harry Potter fanfics}. The term covers everything from innocent reimaginings to explicit romantic or sexual scenarios.

Fanfiction is fiction written by fans using characters, settings, or worlds from existing stories—novels, films, TV shows, video games. It ranges from short scenarios to novel-length works, often exploring relationships or plotlines the original didn't pursue: {She writes Harry Potter fanfiction where Draco is the hero}. The genre thrives online in dedicated communities. Also spelled fan fiction or shortened to fanfic.

Fanfictions are stories written by fans using characters, settings, or worlds from existing media—novels, films, TV shows, video games. The genre thrives online, ranging from short vignettes to novel-length works. Writers explore alternative storylines, romantic pairings, or scenarios the original creators never addressed: {She's been posting Harry Potter fanfictions since middle school}. Also spelled as two words or shortened to fanfic.

A fang is a long, pointed tooth. Venomous snakes have hollow fangs that inject poison; dogs and wolves have fangs for tearing meat. The word extends to fang-like things: the prongs of a fork, the root of a tooth. Vampires sink their fangs into victims' necks. {The dog bared its fangs and growled.}

A fangame is a video game created by fans based on an existing commercial franchise, made without official authorization from the original creators. Fangames range from simple tributes to ambitious reimaginings: {The Pokémon fangame community has produced dozens of original regions}. They exist in legal gray areas—copyright holders sometimes tolerate them, sometimes issue takedown notices.

A fangirl is a female fan whose enthusiasm borders on obsession—typically for a band, actor, fictional character, or media franchise. The term suggests intense emotional investment, from collecting merchandise to defending the object of devotion online: {She's been fangirling over that K-pop group for years}. As a verb, to fangirl is to express such enthusiasm: {I fangirled so hard when I met him}. Originally dismissive, the word has been reclaimed by many who embrace passionate fandom. The male equivalent is fanboy.

Fangirling is expressing enthusiastic, often excessive admiration for a celebrity, fictional character, band, or other object of devotion. The term captures the intense, gushing quality of fan behavior—squealing, obsessing, collecting merchandise, attending events: {I was fangirling so hard when I met the cast}. Though derived from girl, the verb applies regardless of gender. The noun fangirl denotes someone who engages in such behavior.

Fangirls are female fans who express intense, often obsessive enthusiasm for a celebrity, fictional character, band, TV show, or other cultural phenomenon. The term captures both devoted appreciation and the stereotype of emotional excess—screaming at concerts, collecting memorabilia, writing fan fiction, and defending their favorite against criticism. {The fangirls lined up overnight for concert tickets.} Though sometimes dismissive, fangirl has been reclaimed by many who embrace passionate fan culture. It also works as a verb: {She fangirls over every post he makes.}

Fangs are the long, pointed teeth that certain animals use to bite, grip, or inject venom. Snakes have hollow fangs that deliver poison; dogs and wolves have fangs for tearing flesh. In vampire lore, fangs are the signature feature that allows blood-drinking. Figuratively, if someone {bares their fangs}, they show aggressive intent. The word occasionally describes any prominent or sharp tooth: {The kid's fangs came in crooked}.

Fanmade describes creative works produced by fans rather than official creators or rights holders: {fanmade videos}, {fanmade merchandise}, {a fanmade sequel to the game}. The term applies to art, fiction, music, costumes, and other productions inspired by existing media franchises. Fanmade content exists in a gray area of copyright law but thrives in online communities.

Fanmail is correspondence sent by admirers to celebrities, athletes, writers, or other public figures expressing appreciation or enthusiasm for their work. The term covers everything from handwritten letters to digital messages: {She hired an assistant just to handle the fanmail}. Also written as two words: fan mail.

Fanned is the past tense of fan. To fan is to move air toward something, originally with a handheld fan: {She fanned herself in the heat}. By extension, to fan flames is to intensify them—literally or figuratively: {The rumors fanned public outrage}. To fan out is to spread in a widening pattern: {The search party fanned out across the field}.
Fannies is the plural of fanny. In American English, it refers to buttocks: {Get your fannies in the car}. In British English, it's vulgar slang for female genitals, and considerably more offensive.

Fanning is waving something back and forth to create a breeze or spread air: {She was fanning herself with a magazine}. Fire can be fanned to make it burn hotter. Figuratively, to fan is to intensify: {fanning the flames of controversy}. In baseball, fanning means striking out: {He's been fanning a lot this season}.

Fanny means different things depending on where you are. In American English, fanny is a mild, almost childish term for the buttocks: {She fell on her fanny}. In British English, fanny is vulgar slang for the female genitals—not a word to use casually. This regional split makes fanny a minefield for travelers: a {fanny pack} in America is a {bum bag} in Britain for good reason.

Fans are devices that move air for cooling or ventilation, from handheld folding fans to electric ceiling fans. The blades spread out from a central point, which gives us the verb: to fan out is to spread in a widening pattern. To fan flames—literal or figurative—is to intensify them by directing air. Separately, a fan is an enthusiastic devotee: sports fans, music fans, {I'm a big fan of her work}. This sense is short for fanatic.

Fanservice is material included in media primarily to please devoted fans rather than serve the story. In anime and manga, it typically means gratuitous shots of attractive characters in revealing poses or states of undress: {The show has a good plot but too much fanservice}. More broadly, it can mean any crowd-pleasing callback, cameo, or reference inserted to delight the audience: {The finale was pure fanservice for longtime viewers}.

A fansite is a website created by enthusiasts dedicated to a particular celebrity, band, TV show, video game, or other cultural phenomenon. Fansites typically aggregate news, images, discussion forums, and fan-created content: {I found rare concert photos on a fansite}. They range from simple tribute pages to elaborate archives rivaling official sources.

A fantail is a fan-shaped tail or tail-like structure. The word appears in several contexts: a breed of domestic pigeon with tail feathers that spread into a semicircle, small flycatcher birds of Australasia that fan their tails while foraging, and the overhanging stern of certain ships. Anything with a spreading, radiating shape may be called a fantail: {a fantail of cards}, {a fantail burner} on a gas lamp.

A fantasia is a musical composition with an improvisatory character, free in form rather than following strict structures like sonata or fugue. The term suggests imaginative, fanciful work that follows the composer's whim: {Bach's Chromatic Fantasia and Fugue}. Extended to other arts, fantasia describes any work characterized by free-flowing imagination rather than formal constraints.

Fantasies are imagined scenarios, especially pleasurable or wishful ones. The word covers daydreams about success or romance, sexual imaginings, and elaborate fictional worlds. A fantasy can be harmless escapism or a worrying detachment from reality: {He had fantasies of quitting his job and sailing around the world}. In the plural, fantasies often suggests recurring or indulgent imaginings: {She kept her fantasies to herself}.

Fantasise is the British spelling of fantasize—to indulge in daydreams or imagine desirable scenarios. The fantasies may be idle wishes, creative visions, or sexual imaginings: {She fantasised about quitting her job and sailing around the world}. To fantasise about something is often to desire it without realistic expectation of having it.

Fantasising is the British spelling of fantasizing—imagining scenarios that are pleasant, improbable, or impossible. The word covers everything from idle daydreaming to elaborate mental narratives: {She caught herself fantasising about quitting her job}. Sexual fantasising involves imagining erotic encounters: {He'd been fantasising about her for months}.

Fantasize means to imagine something desirable, often something unlikely or impossible. The word frequently implies sexual daydreaming: {He fantasized about his coworker}. But fantasizing can be about any wish: {She fantasized about quitting her job and moving to Paris}. The tone often suggests the vision is impractical or self-indulgent.

Fantasized is the past tense of fantasize, meaning to imagine or daydream about something desired or unlikely: {She fantasized about quitting her job and traveling the world}. The word often carries sexual connotations: {He fantasized about his coworker}. Fantasized scenarios range from harmless daydreams to elaborate wish fulfillment.

Fantasizing is imagining things you desire or find pleasurable—scenarios that may be unlikely, impossible, or simply not present. The word often carries sexual connotations: {She caught him fantasizing about his coworker}. But fantasizing applies broadly to any wishful imagining: {He spent the meeting fantasizing about quitting}. Unlike daydreaming, fantasizing usually involves specific desires rather than idle mental wandering.

Fantastic originally meant existing only in fantasy—imaginary or unreal: {fantastic creatures}, {fantastic tales}. The word shifted to mean extraordinarily good or impressive: {The concert was fantastic}. This positive sense now dominates casual speech, though the older meaning persists in contexts emphasizing imagination or implausibility: {fantastic claims}, {fantastic voyage}. Something fantastic may also be bizarre or grotesque: {fantastic rock formations}.

Fantastical describes something extravagantly fanciful or bizarre, often with a dreamlike or imaginary quality: {fantastical creatures}, {a fantastical landscape}. It carries more whimsy and strangeness than simply fantastic—less about excellence and more about wild imagination or improbability: {The story grew increasingly fantastical as she embellished it}.

Fantasy is imagination unrestrained by reality. A fantasy can be a daydream, a wishful scenario, or an elaborate imagined world: {She indulged in fantasies of early retirement}. Sexual fantasies are erotic scenarios that arouse. As a genre, fantasy fiction features magic, mythical creatures, and invented worlds—distinct from science fiction's technological basis. Fantasy sports leagues let participants build imaginary teams from real players. To fantasize is to indulge in such imaginings: {He fantasized about quitting his job}.

A fantasyland is any place or situation characterized by unrealistic thinking or wishful imagination rather than practical reality. Often used dismissively to suggest someone is out of touch: {His economic proposals come straight from fantasyland}. The word implies pleasant delusion—expectations untethered from how things actually work. (Capitalized Fantasyland is a themed area in Disney parks.)

Fanwork is creative content made by fans based on existing media—fiction, art, videos, or music inspired by movies, TV shows, books, games, or celebrities. Unlike official productions, fanworks are typically shared freely in fan communities: {She wrote fanwork exploring what happened after the series ended}. The term encompasses fanfiction, fan art, fan videos, and similar amateur creations.

Fanworks are creative works produced by fans based on existing media—fiction, art, videos, music, or other content inspired by books, films, TV shows, games, or celebrities. The term encompasses fanfiction, fan art, fan videos, and similar amateur productions: {She posted her fanworks on Archive of Our Own}. Fanworks exist in a legal gray area regarding copyright but thrive in online fan communities.

A fanzine is an amateur magazine produced by and for enthusiasts of a particular interest—originally science fiction, later punk rock, sports teams, or any niche passion. The word blends "fan" and "magazine." Fanzines are typically photocopied or cheaply printed, distributed informally, and valued for their grassroots authenticity: {She discovered the band through a local punk fanzine}.

Fanzines are amateur publications created by enthusiasts of a particular subject, typically science fiction, music, comics, or sports. The term blends "fan" and "magazine," and the format emerged in the 1930s among science fiction communities before spreading to punk rock and other subcultures. Unlike professional publications, fanzines are usually photocopied or cheaply printed, distributed informally, and produced for passion rather than profit. {She discovered several rare punk fanzines at the record shop.}

Faq is an informal, sometimes jocular rendering of FAQ, the abbreviation for "frequently asked questions." The lowercase spelling treats the acronym as a word rather than initials, often pronounced as a single syllable rhyming with "back": {Check the faq before posting}. (Capitalized FAQ is the standard form.)

Far indicates great distance in space, time, or degree. A far {country} is remote; the far {future} is distant in time. Far often appears with comparatives: {far better}, {far worse}, {far more likely}. As an adjective, it typically means the more distant of two: the far {end} of the room, the far {side} of the moon. {So far} means until now; {by far} emphasizes degree; {far and away} means by a great margin.

Faraway means distant in space or time: {a faraway land}, {faraway memories of childhood}. A faraway look or expression suggests someone lost in thought, mentally distant from their surroundings: {She had a faraway look in her eyes}. The word carries a slightly dreamy or romantic quality that distant lacks.

A farce is a comedy built on absurd situations, improbable coincidences, and physical humor—mistaken identities, doors slamming, people hiding in closets. The genre values chaos over wit. Extended to any situation that's absurdly inadequate or a mockery of what it should be: {The trial was a farce}. To farce, rarely used, is to stuff—the original meaning, surviving in "forcemeat."

Farces is the plural of farce—a type of comedy built on absurd situations, improbable coincidences, and physical humor rather than wit or character development. Farces feature mistaken identities, slamming doors, and characters hiding in closets. Extended to non-theatrical contexts, farce describes any situation that has become laughably absurd: {The trial was a farce}. {Bedroom farces dominated the West End for decades.}

Farcical describes something absurdly ridiculous, as if belonging to a farce—a comedic theatrical genre built on improbable situations and exaggerated misunderstandings. A farcical situation strains belief through sheer preposterousness: {The trial descended into farcical chaos when three witnesses gave identical alibis}. The word often carries a note of contempt, suggesting something that should be serious has become laughable.

Fare is the price of transportation—what you pay to ride a bus, taxi, train, or plane: {The fare to the airport is thirty dollars}. A fare is also the passenger who pays it, especially in taxi driving: {The cabbie picked up a fare downtown}. Fare extends to food, particularly what's offered or served: {pub fare}, {simple fare}. As a verb, fare means to get along or manage: {How did you fare on the exam?} To fare well or poorly is to experience good or bad fortune.

Fares are the prices charged for transportation—what you pay to ride a bus, train, taxi, or airplane. A fare can also mean a paying passenger, especially in a taxi: {The cabbie picked up three fares that hour}. The verb fare means to get along or manage: {How did you fare on the exam?} To fare well or poorly is to experience good or bad fortune. Farewell preserves this older sense of wishing someone a good journey through life.

Farewell is a formal or literary way of saying goodbye, often implying a final or long-term parting: {They bade farewell to their homeland}. As a noun, it's the act of leaving or the occasion of departure: {a farewell party}, {a fond farewell}. The word carries more weight than casual goodbyes—you don't say farewell when leaving for lunch.

Farewells are acts of parting or leave-taking—the goodbyes exchanged when people separate. The word covers everything from casual waves to tearful airport scenes: {We said our farewells and promised to write}. A farewell can also be a formal occasion marking someone's departure: {The office threw her a farewell party}. To bid farewell is slightly literary.

Farfalle is a type of pasta shaped like bow ties or butterflies, with pinched centers and ruffled edges. The shape catches chunky sauces well: {farfalle with peas and pancetta}. The name comes from the Italian word for butterflies.

Farfetched describes something unlikely or hard to believe—an explanation, theory, or story that seems too improbable to accept: {His alibi was farfetched at best}. The word suggests someone has reached too far for a connection or conclusion. Also spelled far-fetched.

The most frequent use of farm is an area of land, bigger than a garden, that is set aside for agricultural use. The archetypal farm includes a barn and a house, the farmhouse, where the farmer and his family live. Farms are sometimes characterized by their product, which may or may not be related to agriculture: pig farm, wind farm. Someone who farms makes a living in agriculture. Something that is farmed out is assigned to another: the company farms out its hiring efforts to an agency.

A farmboy is a young man who lives or works on a farm. The term often carries connotations of rural innocence, simple upbringing, or lack of worldly sophistication: {He's just a farmboy from Iowa}. In fiction, farmboys frequently appear as unlikely heroes—ordinary young men destined for adventure: {Every farmboy dreams of leaving home}.

Farmboys is the plural of farmboy—a boy or young man raised on a farm. The term often carries connotations of rural innocence, hard work, and lack of worldly sophistication: {Just a farmboy from Iowa who'd never seen a city}. In fiction and folklore, the farmboy is a common archetype for unlikely heroes who rise from humble origins.

Farmed describes something raised or cultivated through agriculture rather than found in the wild: {farmed salmon}, {farmed shrimp}. The distinction matters for food—farmed fish are raised in controlled environments, while wild-caught are harvested from natural waters. Farmed land has been worked for growing crops. {They farmed the land for three generations}.

A farmer is someone who works the land, raising crops or livestock. The term covers everything from small family operations to industrial agriculture. Farmer often implies ownership or management rather than hired labor: {My grandfather was a dairy farmer in Wisconsin}. The word extends metaphorically to anyone who cultivates something systematically: {a fish farmer}, {a server farmer}.

Farmers are people who work the land, raising crops or livestock for food, fiber, or other products. The term covers a wide range—from small family operations to managers of industrial agricultural enterprises. {Local farmers sell produce at the weekend market.} {Farmers in the region shifted from tobacco to soybeans.} Figuratively, farmer suggests rural simplicity or lack of sophistication.

A farmhand is a person hired to do manual labor on a farm—feeding livestock, mending fences, operating machinery, harvesting crops. The term suggests someone employed by a farm's owner rather than a family member or the farmer themselves: {The ranch employed three farmhands during calving season}.

Farmhands are workers hired to do manual labor on a farm—tending livestock, operating equipment, harvesting crops. The term suggests physical, often seasonal work rather than farm ownership or management: {The ranch employed a dozen farmhands during harvest season}.

A farmhouse is the main dwelling on a farm, typically where the farmer and family live. The word evokes rural architecture—sturdy, practical houses often with large kitchens and wraparound porches. As a modifier, farmhouse describes a rustic aesthetic popular in interior design: {farmhouse style}, {farmhouse sink}, {farmhouse table}. The look emphasizes natural materials, distressed wood, and vintage touches.

Farming is the practice of cultivating land and raising animals for food, fiber, or other products. The word covers everything from small family operations to industrial agriculture. Beyond agriculture, farming describes any systematic harvesting: {wind farming}, {fish farming}, {click farming}. To farm out work is to delegate it to others.

Farmland is land used or suitable for agriculture—growing crops or raising livestock. The term often appears in discussions of development, conservation, or real estate: {Developers are buying up farmland outside the city}. Prime farmland has especially fertile soil and favorable growing conditions.

Farms are areas of land used for growing crops or raising animals. A farm typically includes cultivated fields, pastures, or facilities for livestock. The word extends to specialized operations: fish farms, wind farms, server farms. To farm is to work the land or raise animals. To farm something out is to delegate it to others: {They farmed out the design work to contractors}.

A farmstand is a small roadside retail outlet where farmers sell produce directly to customers, typically featuring seasonal fruits, vegetables, eggs, and sometimes baked goods or preserves. Unlike farmers' markets, which operate on scheduled days at designated locations, farmstands are permanent or semi-permanent structures located on or near the farm itself. They range from simple tables with an honor-system cash box to staffed wooden structures. {We stopped at a farmstand for fresh corn and tomatoes.}

A farmstead is a farm property including its buildings—the house, barns, sheds, and surrounding land as a unit. The word emphasizes the physical place rather than the agricultural operation: {The old farmstead had been in the family for generations}. It often evokes rural permanence or heritage.

A farmworker is a person employed to do agricultural labor—planting, harvesting, tending livestock, or maintaining equipment. The term often refers specifically to hired hands rather than farm owners or family members: {Farmworkers harvested the strawberry fields before dawn}. In American usage, farmworker frequently describes migrant or seasonal laborers.

Farmworkers are people employed to do agricultural labor, typically on farms or in fields harvesting crops, tending livestock, or operating machinery. The term often carries connotations of seasonal, physically demanding work performed by hired laborers rather than farm owners. In American usage, farmworkers frequently refers specifically to migrant agricultural workers, many of whom travel to follow harvest seasons. {The farmworkers started picking strawberries at dawn.}

A farmyard is the area immediately surrounding farm buildings—the barn, stables, and outbuildings—typically enclosed or partially enclosed. It's where daily farm activity concentrates: animals fed, equipment stored, vehicles parked. {Chickens scratched in the farmyard.} The word evokes rural life and its characteristic sounds and smells.

A farrier is a craftsperson who trims and shoes horses' hooves. The work combines blacksmithing skills—forging and fitting metal horseshoes—with knowledge of equine anatomy and hoof care. Though less common since horses gave way to motorized transport, farriers remain essential for working horses, police mounts, and competitive equestrian animals. {The farrier comes every six weeks to check the horses' feet.}

Farsighted describes a condition in which distant objects are seen more clearly than nearby ones, the opposite of nearsighted. This literal meaning extends to people who plan wisely for the future: {Her farsighted investments paid off decades later}. A farsighted leader anticipates problems before they arise. The word can also be spelled far-sighted, and the condition itself is called farsightedness.

Farsightedness is a condition of the eyes in which distant objects can be seen more clearly than nearby ones, the opposite of nearsightedness. The term also describes the quality of being able to anticipate future needs or consequences and plan accordingly. {Her farsightedness in investing early paid off decades later.} Someone with farsightedness in this figurative sense shows wisdom and prudent judgment about what lies ahead.
clues: Close objects appear out of focus

definition: A fart is an expulsion of intestinal gas through the anus, or the sound or smell it produces. The verb means to release such gas: {Who farted?} The word is mildly vulgar but common in casual speech. To {fart around} is to waste time or act aimlessly. An {old fart} is a boring or out-of-touch older person.

Farted is the past tense of fart—to expel gas from the anus. The word is mildly vulgar but common in casual speech: {Who farted?} {The dog farted and cleared the room}. Figuratively, to {fart around} is to waste time on trivial things.

Farther is the comparative form of far, indicating greater physical distance: {The store is farther down the road than I thought}. In American English, farther typically refers to measurable distance, while further handles abstract extension: {further discussion}, {nothing could be further from the truth}. British English uses further for both. As a verb, to farther means to advance something, though further dominates this use.

Farthest is the superlative of far, indicating the greatest distance: {the farthest reaches of the galaxy}, {Who can throw the ball farthest?} It works for both physical and figurative distance: {the farthest thing from my mind}. Furthest is interchangeable in most contexts, though farthest tends toward literal distance while furthest leans abstract.

A farthing was a British coin worth one quarter of a penny—the smallest denomination in circulation until 1961. The word now appears mainly in historical contexts or idioms suggesting trivial amounts: {I don't care a farthing what he thinks}. {She hadn't a farthing to her name}.

Farting is the act of expelling gas from the digestive system through the anus. The word is mildly vulgar but universal—everyone farts, and the term appears freely in casual speech: {The dog kept farting during dinner}. Farting around means wasting time or goofing off.

Farts are expulsions of intestinal gas through the anus, typically with an audible sound. The word is mildly vulgar but common in casual speech. To fart is to release such gas: {Who farted?} Figuratively, to {fart around} is to waste time on trivial activities. An {old fart} is a boring or out-of-touch older person.

To fascinate is to capture and hold someone's attention completely, often with an element of wonder or compelling interest. A speaker fascinates an audience; a mystery fascinates investigators. The word carries a hint of its original meaning—to bewitch or cast a spell—though modern usage is almost always positive: {I'm fascinated by how languages evolve}. Something fascinating draws you in and holds you there.

Fascinated describes being intensely captivated or absorbed by something. The word suggests more than casual interest—a fascinated person is held almost spellbound: {She was fascinated by the magician's sleight of hand}, {He sat fascinated as the documentary unfolded}. Originally tied to bewitchment, the modern sense retains that quality of being unable to look away.

Fascinating describes something that captures and holds attention through strong interest or curiosity. A fascinating {book} engrosses the reader; a fascinating {person} commands attention. The word implies more than mere interest—something fascinating exerts a kind of pull, drawing you in and making it hard to look away. {I find the history of medicine fascinating.}

Fascination is intense interest or attraction—the state of being captivated by something. A subject holds fascination when it commands attention almost involuntarily: {She developed a fascination with deep-sea creatures}. The word suggests something compelling, even slightly obsessive: {His fascination with true crime worried his mother}. What fascinates often combines curiosity with a hint of the mysterious or forbidden.

A fascinator is a decorative headpiece, typically a small ornamental design mounted on a comb or clip, worn at formal occasions like weddings and horse races. Unlike full hats, fascinators perch on the head at an angle, often featuring feathers, netting, or flowers: {She wore a fascinator to the Kentucky Derby}. The term comes from the idea of something that fascinates or catches the eye.

Fascinators are decorative headpieces, typically small and ornamental, worn at formal events like weddings and horse races. Unlike full hats, fascinators attach to the hair with clips or combs and often feature feathers, netting, or sculptural elements: {She wore a fascinator with peacock feathers to the Kentucky Derby}. The term also applies to lightweight knitted scarves or shawls, though this usage is old-fashioned.

Fascism, especially when capitalized, refers to a 20th century political movement in Italy and Germany that valued the country and a particular ethnic group above the individual. When used today, and not capitalized, fascism is used loosely and pejoratively to characterize any political movement, idea, or action that is seen as concentrating power in a single individual or group in ways that are detrimental to ordinary people: The militia’s seizure of power is being criticized as a huge step towards fascism.

In the mid-20th century, a Fascist was someone who was a member of or supported the autocratic governments of Hitler in Germany or Mussolini in Italy. Today, fascist is used loosely as an insulting way to characterize the ideas or behavior of anyone who is perceived as trying to exercise strict control over people using undemocratic and sometimes violent or terroristic means: The state media now appears to be under the control of religious fascists.

Fascists are adherents of fascism—an authoritarian political ideology emphasizing nationalism, dictatorial power, and suppression of opposition. The term originated with Mussolini's movement in 1920s Italy. In strict usage, fascists support specific far-right ideologies: {The fascists marched through the streets}. More loosely, fascist is an epithet for anyone perceived as authoritarian or intolerant: {Don't be such a fascist about the dress code}.

Fashion is the prevailing style in dress, behavior, or way of life at a given time. What's in fashion changes constantly—{last year's fashion is this year's embarrassment}. The word extends beyond clothing to any domain with trends: {the fashion for open floor plans}. As a verb, to fashion something is to make or shape it: {She fashioned a crown from wildflowers}. {After a fashion} means in a rough or imperfect way.

Fashionable means in accordance with current style or popular taste. Fashionable {clothes}, fashionable {neighborhoods}, fashionable {ideas}—all suggest what's currently in vogue among those who set trends. The word carries slight connotations of superficiality or transience: what's fashionable today may not be tomorrow. {It became fashionable to dismiss his early work.}

A fashionista is someone intensely devoted to fashion—following trends, curating their wardrobe, and often working in the fashion industry. The term can be admiring or gently mocking, depending on context: {She's a total fashionista who never wears the same outfit twice}. It suggests enthusiasm bordering on obsession.

Fashionistas are people intensely devoted to fashion—following trends, knowing designers, and caring deeply about style. The term can be admiring or gently mocking, depending on context: {The fashionistas descended on Milan for fashion week}. A fashionista might be a professional in the industry or simply someone whose wardrobe choices are central to their identity.

Fashions serves as both noun and verb forms of fashion. As a plural noun, fashions are the prevailing styles in clothing, behavior, or way of life at any given time: {Paris fashions dominated the runway}. The word also encompasses broader cultural trends and customs that gain temporary popularity. As a verb, fashions means to shape or create something, often by hand or with deliberate effort: {She fashions jewelry from recycled materials}. This creative sense connects to the noun's underlying idea of giving form to something.

The adjective and adverb fast are distinct from the noun and verb. The main meanings of the adjective and adverb are firmly fixed (held fast in a trap) and quick or quickly (a fast train, how fast can you get here?). Less frequent meanings are unlikely to fade (color fast) and very loyal (hold fast to your faith). The verb fast means go without food. A fast is a period of conscious abstention from eating: The monk undertook a seven-day fast.

A fastback is a car body style where the roof slopes continuously downward to the rear, creating a single smooth line from roof to tail rather than a distinct trunk. The design became popular in the 1960s on muscle cars and sports cars: {The Mustang fastback was the sportiest model in the lineup}. The term also describes any car with this styling.

A fastball is a pitch in baseball thrown at maximum velocity with minimal spin variation, relying on speed rather than movement to challenge the batter. It's the most basic and common pitch type, typically clocked between 90 and 100 miles per hour at the professional level. Figuratively, to {throw someone a fastball} is to give them something straightforward rather than tricky.

Fastballs is the plural of fastball, a baseball pitch thrown at maximum speed with minimal spin or movement. The fastball is the most fundamental pitch in a pitcher's arsenal, relying on velocity rather than deception: {He threw nothing but fastballs in the first inning}. Figuratively, a fastball is something direct and unsubtle: {The prosecutor came at him with fastballs}.

A fastbreak is a rapid offensive push in basketball, moving the ball upcourt before the defense can set up. Teams get fastbreak opportunities after steals, rebounds, or quick inbounds passes: {They scored twelve points on fastbreaks in the first quarter}. The term applies similarly in hockey and other sports. Also spelled fast break.

Fasten means to attach, secure, or close something firmly. You fasten a seatbelt, fasten a button, fasten a lock. The word implies making something fixed or immovable: {Fasten the boards together with screws}. To fasten onto something is to grip it tightly or focus on it intently: {The detective fastened onto a single detail in the testimony}.

Faster is the comparative form of fast—moving or happening at greater speed than something else: {She runs faster than her brother}. It can describe acceleration: {My heart beat faster}. Figuratively, faster applies to any process: {News travels faster than ever}. The adverb and adjective share the form: {a faster car}, {drive faster}.

Fasting is the practice of abstaining from food, drink, or both for a period of time. Religious fasting appears across traditions—Muslims fast during Ramadan, Jews on Yom Kippur, Christians during Lent. Medical fasting prepares patients for procedures or blood tests. Intermittent fasting has gained popularity as a health practice: {I've been fasting sixteen hours a day}. The adjective fasting describes the state: {fasting blood sugar}.

Fastpitch is a style of softball in which the pitcher delivers the ball with a windmill motion at high speed, as opposed to slowpitch softball's gentle arc. The term usually modifies softball: {She played fastpitch softball in college}. Fastpitch is the form used in competitive and Olympic play, demanding quick reflexes from batters.

Fasts is the plural of fast—a period of abstaining from food, often for religious or health purposes. Muslims observe fasts during Ramadan; Catholics traditionally keep fasts before Easter. Medical fasts precede certain procedures. The verb fasts means to abstain from eating: {She fasts every Monday for weight management}.

Fat is first an adjective, secondly a noun, with closely related meanings. A fat person has a relatively high percentage of body fat. Fat is the general term for two things: a greasy substance that is insoluble in water, and animal tissue that contains a lot of this substance. Fat can have positive associations: a fat paycheck, a fat contract.

Fatal means causing death or destruction: a fatal {accident}, a fatal {disease}, a fatal {blow}. The word extends to anything that causes ruin or failure: a fatal {flaw}, a fatal {error}, a fatal {mistake}. Something fatal is decisive in a way that can't be undone—the consequences are final and irreversible.

Fatalism is the belief that events are fixed in advance and human effort cannot change them. A fatalist accepts outcomes as inevitable: {With a fatalist's shrug, she said whatever happens, happens}. The term often carries connotations of passive resignation or refusal to struggle against circumstances. Fatalistic describes this attitude: {His fatalistic outlook kept him from even trying}.

A fatalist believes that events are predetermined and human effort cannot change outcomes. The term carries connotations of passive resignation—a fatalist accepts whatever happens rather than fighting against it: {He was a fatalist about his health, refusing to see doctors}. Fatalism can be philosophical conviction or simply a temperament that shrugs at circumstance.

Fatalistic describes an attitude of resignation to fate—a belief that events are predetermined and resistance is futile. A fatalistic person accepts outcomes as inevitable rather than fighting to change them: {She had a fatalistic view of her illness}. The word often carries a negative connotation, suggesting passivity or defeatism: {His fatalistic shrug suggested he'd already given up}.

Fatalists believe that events are predetermined and beyond human control. The term usually carries a negative connotation—fatalists accept outcomes passively rather than trying to change them: {The fatalists on the team had already given up before the game started}. A fatalist might shrug at bad news, seeing resistance as pointless.

Fatalities is the plural of fatality—deaths resulting from accidents, disasters, violence, or war. News reports tally fatalities from earthquakes, car crashes, and military operations: {The storm caused twelve fatalities}. The word carries clinical distance, preferred in official contexts over more direct terms like deaths or people killed.

A fatality is a death, particularly one resulting from an accident, disaster, or violent incident. The word emphasizes the fatal outcome rather than the circumstances: {The crash caused three fatalities.} Traffic reports, military briefings, and emergency services favor this clinical term over more emotionally charged alternatives like deaths or casualties. Fatality can also refer to the quality of being destined or inevitable, though this philosophical sense is now rare outside academic contexts.

Fatally means in a way that causes or results in death: {He was fatally wounded in the crash}. The word extends to anything that proves ruinous or decisive: {a fatally flawed argument}, {fatally undermined by scandal}. In both cases, fatally suggests an outcome that cannot be reversed or recovered from.

A fatass is a fat person, used as an insult emphasizing excess weight and lack of self-control: {Get off the couch, fatass}. The term doubles as a general insult implying laziness or gluttony even when the target isn't particularly overweight. As an adjective, it describes someone or something excessively large: {his fatass SUV}.

Fatback is a layer of fat from a pig's back, used in Southern American cooking to season vegetables, beans, and greens. Unlike bacon, it comes from higher on the animal and contains little or no meat. It's typically salt-cured and sliced thin, then rendered to flavor dishes: {She added a piece of fatback to the collard greens}.

A fatberg is a large mass of congealed fat, grease, wet wipes, and other non-biodegradable waste that accumulates in sewer systems. These blockages form when cooking oils poured down drains combine with flushed items that don't break down, hardening into rock-like obstructions that can weigh several tons and stretch hundreds of feet. The term blends fat with iceberg, suggesting both the mass and the hidden-beneath-the-surface danger. {The city spent millions removing a fatberg that had blocked the Victorian-era pipes.}

A fatcat is a wealthy, privileged person, especially one seen as using money for political influence or living comfortably off others' labor. The term carries connotations of greed and corruption: {fatcat donors}, {fatcat executives}. Often written as two words: fat cat.

Fate is the force or power believed to determine what happens—the idea that events are fixed in advance and beyond human control. Your fate is your destiny, the outcome awaiting you: {He accepted his fate}. The fates, in Greek mythology, were three goddesses who spun, measured, and cut the thread of each life. To be fated is to be destined: {They were fated to meet}. A fateful decision has momentous consequences. To fate something is rare; the passive dominates: {It was fated from the start}.

Fated describes something destined to happen, as if determined by fate: {They were fated to meet}. It often carries a sense of inevitability, whether fortunate or tragic: {a fated encounter}, {fated to fail}. An ill-fated venture is doomed from the start. Fated suggests forces beyond human control have already decided the outcome.

Fateful describes something that determines or reveals fate—a turning point with significant consequences. A fateful {decision} shapes everything that follows. A fateful {day} is one when destiny unfolds. The word carries a sense of inevitability, as if larger forces are at work. Fateful moments are usually serious, often ominous: {That fateful meeting changed the course of history}.

Fates is the plural of fate, referring to destinies or outcomes beyond human control. People speak of the fates of individuals, nations, or enterprises: {The fates of the two brothers diverged wildly}. To leave something to the fates is to abandon it to chance or providence. (Capitalized Fates refers to the mythological goddesses.)

Fatfingered describes a typing error caused by hitting the wrong key or multiple keys at once, usually on a small keyboard or touchscreen: {I fatfingered the password three times and got locked out}. The verb fatfinger means to make such an error: {He fatfingered the trade and accidentally sold a million shares}. The image is of fingers too large for the keys they're pressing.

A fathead is a stupid person—someone whose head seems stuffed with fat rather than brains: {Don't be such a fathead}. The insult is mild and somewhat dated, more likely heard in old movies than modern conversation. Fathead also names several species of fish, including the fathead minnow commonly used as bait.

Father means male parent—the man whose genetic material or parental role produced a child. The term extends to founding figures: {the Founding Fathers}, {the father of modern physics}. To father a child is to sire one, though the word increasingly implies active parenting rather than mere biological contribution. {My father taught me to fish.} (Capitalized Father is a religious or clerical title.)

Fatherhood is the state of being a father—having a child for whom you are responsible. The word encompasses both the biological fact and the social role: {He wasn't ready for fatherhood}. Fatherhood often carries connotations of duty, provision, and guidance that go beyond mere procreation: {Fatherhood changed him completely}.

Fatherland is one's native country, especially when viewed with patriotic attachment. The term emphasizes ancestral connection to the land—where one's fathers lived and are buried. {He returned to the fatherland after decades abroad.} Though neutral in most languages, fatherland in English carries associations with Nazi Germany, where *Vaterland* featured prominently in nationalist rhetoric. Motherland and homeland are often preferred.

Fatherless describes someone whose father is absent, dead, or unknown. The term emphasizes lack rather than mere absence—a fatherless child lacks paternal guidance, support, or connection: {He grew up fatherless in rural Tennessee}. The word carries emotional weight, suggesting vulnerability or deprivation in ways that "without a father" does not.

Fatherlessness is the state of being without a father—whether through death, abandonment, divorce, or absence. The term often carries sociological weight, appearing in discussions of poverty, crime, and childhood development: {Studies link fatherlessness to higher dropout rates}. It can describe literal absence or emotional unavailability: {He grew up with fatherlessness despite his dad living in the same house}.

Fatherly describes qualities associated with a good father—protective, caring, wise, and gently authoritative. A fatherly {smile} conveys warmth and approval. Fatherly {advice} comes from experience and genuine concern for someone's wellbeing. The word typically carries positive connotations, suggesting benevolent guidance rather than stern control: {He took a fatherly interest in the young apprentice}.

Fathers is the plural of father—male parents. Beyond biology, fathers extends to founders or originators: {the founding fathers}, {the fathers of the church}. The verb fathers means to sire offspring or to create something: {He fathered three children}. {Einstein fathered modern physics}.

Fathom is a unit of water depth equal to six feet, used in nautical contexts: {The harbor was only three fathoms deep}. More commonly, fathom means to understand or comprehend something difficult or mysterious: {I can't fathom why she would do that}. The connection is probing depths—whether of water or meaning. The negative is especially common: {unfathomable}, {I couldn't fathom it}.

Fathomed is the past tense of fathom, meaning to understand something difficult or mysterious: {I never fathomed why she left}. The word comes from a nautical term—a fathom is six feet of depth, measured by the span of outstretched arms. To fathom water was to measure its depth; to fathom a problem is to get to the bottom of it.

Fathomless means too deep to measure. A fathom is a unit of depth (six feet), so the fathomless cannot be fathomed—literally bottomless. The word appears most often in figurative contexts: {fathomless grief}, {fathomless mystery}, {eyes of fathomless blue}. It suggests depth beyond comprehension, something that resists being fully known or understood.

Fathoms is the plural of fathom, a unit of measurement equal to six feet, used primarily for measuring water depth. Sailors and maritime charts still use fathoms: {The wreck lies at twelve fathoms}. The verb fathom means to measure depth, but its figurative sense—to understand or comprehend something difficult—is now more common: {I can't fathom why she quit}. If something is unfathomable, it's too deep or complex to grasp.

Fatigue is weariness from exertion—physical, mental, or emotional. {The fatigue of a long day set in}. Materials also fatigue: metal fatigue is weakening from repeated stress. In the military, fatigues are work uniforms, and fatigue duty is menial labor. The verb means to tire: {The climb fatigued us all}.

Fatigues are the durable, typically camouflage work uniforms worn by military personnel for everyday duties rather than dress occasions. The term comes from fatigue duty—menial labor assigned to soldiers—for which these practical clothes were originally worn. {He showed up in army fatigues}. The singular fatigue also means physical or mental exhaustion.

Fatphobia is prejudice or discrimination against fat people, ranging from social stigma and mockery to systemic disadvantages in healthcare, employment, and public spaces. The term frames negative attitudes toward fatness as a form of bigotry rather than justified concern: {The fatphobia in dating culture is exhausting}. Also fatphobic (adjective).

Fatphobic describes prejudice, discrimination, or hostility directed at fat or overweight people. The term emerged from body-positive and fat acceptance movements to name bias that ranges from individual attitudes to institutional practices: {fatphobic comments about her weight}, {fatphobic hiring practices}. Someone who holds such views is a fatphobe. Like other -phobic formations (homophobic, transphobic), it frames the prejudice as irrational fear or aversion.

Fats are oily substances found in animal tissue and plant seeds, solid at room temperature unlike oils. In nutrition, fats form one of the three macronutrients alongside proteins and carbohydrates: {healthy fats}, {saturated fats}, {trans fats}. Fat also refers informally to overweight people, though this use is often considered rude: {a bunch of fats sitting around}.

Fatso is a derogatory term for a fat person, used as an insult or cruel nickname: {Hey fatso, why don't you skip dessert?} The word is playground-level mean—deliberately hurtful but unsophisticated. Occasionally used self-deprecatingly or affectionately among close friends.

Fatten means to make or become fat. Farmers fatten livestock before slaughter. A person fattens up after a period of good eating. Figuratively, to fatten something is to make it larger or more substantial: {fatten your savings account}, {fatten the profit margins}. The phrase {fatten up} emphasizes the process: {She's trying to fatten him up with home cooking}.

Fattening describes food or habits that tend to cause weight gain: {Avoid fattening snacks if you're watching your weight}. The word implies high calories, often from fats or sugars. Something fattening isn't necessarily unhealthy, but the connotation leans toward indulgence: {The pasta was delicious but fattening}.

Fatty describes something containing or resembling fat: {fatty tissue}, {fatty acids}, {fatty foods}. As a noun, fatty is an insulting term for an overweight person—childish but hurtful: {Hey fatty, want another donut?} The word carries a mocking, playground quality that makes it particularly demeaning.

A fatwa is a formal legal opinion or ruling issued by an Islamic scholar on a point of religious law. Though fatwas address everyday matters like diet, prayer, and commerce, Western media often associate the term with death sentences—particularly after Iran's 1989 fatwa calling for the killing of author Salman Rushdie. A fatwa is advisory, not automatically binding, and its authority depends on the scholar's standing and the legal traditions of a given Muslim community.

Fatwas is the plural of fatwa, a formal ruling or opinion on Islamic law issued by a recognized religious authority. A fatwa interprets how religious principles apply to specific situations—from dietary questions to financial transactions. In Western media, the word gained prominence from the 1989 fatwa calling for Salman Rushdie's death, which has skewed popular understanding toward death sentences, though most fatwas address mundane matters of religious practice.

A faucet is a valve with a handle or knob that controls the flow of water from a pipe, typically at a sink or bathtub: {Turn off the faucet}. Americans say faucet; the British say tap. The word extends to any similar spigot controlling liquid flow.

Faucets is the plural of faucet, a valve controlling water flow from a pipe, typically found at sinks and bathtubs. Most have separate handles for hot and cold water, though single-lever designs mix both: {The plumber replaced all the faucets in the bathroom}. In British English, the word is tap.

A fault is a deviation from perfection, correctness, or integrity: We all have our faults. If you are at fault, you are responsible for something that’s gone wrong. A geological fault is a break in the earth’s crust that is subject to further movement: The earthquake’s epicenter was along the San Andreas Fault. The phrase to a fault means to a great degree. To fault is to criticize or blame: The report faulted all of the directors. To fault is also to make a mistake, especially in sports: The tennis player faulted when she served.

Faultfinding is the habit of pointing out flaws, errors, or shortcomings in others. The term carries a negative connotation—a faultfinding person looks for problems rather than stumbling upon them: {His constant faultfinding made everyone defensive}. As an adjective, it describes someone prone to criticism: {a faultfinding supervisor}.

A faultline is a fracture in the earth's crust where tectonic plates meet and shift, causing earthquakes. The figurative sense dominates contemporary usage: a faultline is any deep division likely to cause conflict or rupture. {The debate exposed faultlines within the party.} {Economic inequality remains a major faultline in American society.} Also spelled fault line.

Faultlines are fractures in the earth's crust where tectonic plates meet and shift, causing earthquakes. The figurative sense dominates contemporary usage: divisions or tensions that could rupture into open conflict. {The debate exposed faultlines within the party.} {Economic faultlines run through the region.} Also spelled as two words: fault lines.

Faults are defects, flaws, or imperfections—things wrong with something or someone. A person's faults are their shortcomings: {His biggest fault is impatience}. In geology, a fault is a fracture in the earth's crust where rock masses have shifted. In tennis and volleyball, a fault is a serve that fails to land in bounds. To fault someone is to criticize them: {You can't fault her for trying}. To be {at fault} is to bear responsibility for something that went wrong.

Faulty means having faults or defects—not working properly or containing errors. A faulty {appliance} malfunctions. Faulty {wiring} is dangerous. Faulty {logic} or faulty {reasoning} contains flaws that undermine an argument. The word implies something that should work correctly but doesn't: {The recall was due to a faulty ignition switch}.

A faun is a creature from Roman mythology with a human upper body and the legs and horns of a goat. Fauns inhabit forests and are associated with wildness, revelry, and pastoral life. They appear frequently in fantasy literature and art: {The children discovered a faun in the snowy wood}. Often confused with satyrs, their Greek counterparts.

Fauna refers to the animal life of a particular region, time period, or environment: {the fauna of the Amazon rainforest}, {prehistoric fauna}. The term pairs with flora (plant life) in scientific and ecological contexts: {The island's flora and fauna remain largely undisturbed}. Fauna can also describe a catalog or study of such animals.

Fauns are creatures from Roman mythology with a human upper body and the legs, horns, and tail of a goat. Associated with forests, fertility, and rustic revelry, they appear in classical art and literature as playful, lustful nature spirits. The faun is often conflated with the Greek satyr, though satyrs were traditionally more goat-like and wild.

Faustian describes a bargain or arrangement in which someone sacrifices something of lasting value—typically their integrity, soul, or moral principles—in exchange for immediate power, success, or gratification. The term comes from the legend of Faust, a scholar who sold his soul to the devil. A {Faustian bargain} implies the exchange will ultimately prove disastrous, even if initially attractive. The word suggests willful self-destruction disguised as ambition.

Faux means fake or artificial, borrowed from the French word for false. It often describes imitation materials: faux {leather}, faux {fur}, faux {marble}. The term can suggest deliberate artifice rather than deception—a faux finish is meant to look decorative, not to fool anyone. A faux {pas} is a social blunder, literally a false step.

A fauxhawk is a hairstyle that mimics the look of a mohawk without shaving the sides of the head. The hair is styled to stand up in a ridge along the center of the scalp, often using gel or other products, while the sides are simply combed or slicked down rather than buzzed off. The style offers the edgy appearance of a mohawk with less commitment and easier maintenance. {He spiked his fauxhawk before heading out to the club.}

A fauxhawk is a hairstyle that mimics the mohawk's central ridge without shaving the sides. The hair is styled upward in the middle—often with gel or pomade—while the sides are merely shorter, not bare: {He spiked his fauxhawk for the concert}. The style offers mohawk aesthetics with office-acceptable practicality.

A fauxpology is an apology that isn't really an apology—a statement that mimics the form of apologizing while avoiding genuine accountability. Classic markers include "I'm sorry if anyone was offended" or "I'm sorry you feel that way," which shift blame to the recipient's reaction rather than acknowledging wrongdoing. {His statement was a fauxpology that satisfied no one.}
Fav is informal for favorite, used as both noun and adjective: {What's your fav?}, {my fav song}. Common in texting and social media, where brevity matters. The spelling fave is equally common.

Fava is a broad bean—a large, flat legume eaten fresh or dried. Common in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines: {fava bean soup}, {fava with olive oil}. The pods are thick and velvety; the beans inside have a slightly bitter, earthy flavor. Often simply called favas: {I'm making favas for dinner}.

Fave is an informal shortening of favorite, used as both noun and adjective: {She's my fave}, {my fave band}. The word is casual and slightly playful, common in everyday speech and social media but rarely in formal writing.

A favela is a Brazilian slum or shantytown, typically built on hillsides around major cities like Rio de Janeiro. The communities are characterized by densely packed, improvised housing and limited infrastructure. Favelas have developed distinct cultures and are often portrayed in media as sites of both poverty and vibrant community life: {The favela overlooked the wealthy beach neighborhoods below}.

Favelas are densely populated informal settlements found primarily in Brazilian cities, characterized by makeshift housing, narrow passageways, and limited access to public services. Originally built by poor residents on unoccupied land, often hillsides, these communities developed outside official city planning and property systems. Though sometimes associated with poverty and crime, favelas are vibrant neighborhoods with distinct cultures, and many have become increasingly integrated into urban life. {The favelas of Rio de Janeiro have become tourist destinations.}

Favor centers on kindness, approval, or preference. A favor is an act of goodwill: {Can you do me a favor?} To favor someone is to prefer or support them: {The rules favor the wealthy}. To be {in favor of} something is to support it. {In someone's favor} means to their advantage. To favor a body part is to protect it by limiting use: {She's favoring her left knee}. Favor also means to resemble: {The child favors her mother}. A party favor is a small gift for guests.

Favorable describes conditions, circumstances, or opinions that support or benefit someone or something. A favorable {review} praises the work; favorable {weather} suits your plans; a favorable {outcome} is the one you hoped for. When someone looks favorably on a proposal, they're inclined to approve it. The word suggests advantage or approval without implying enthusiasm—favorable is positive but measured, more practical than passionate.

Favored describes someone or something that receives preferential treatment or is regarded with special approval. A favored {candidate} has advantages others lack, whether through connections, luck, or genuine merit. The word also indicates likelihood of success: the favored {team} is expected to win. In older or more formal usage, favored can describe physical appearance, as in {ill-favored} (ugly) or {well-favored} (attractive). To be favored {with} something is to be granted it as a privilege or blessing.

Favorite is what you prefer above all others of its kind: a favorite {song}, a favorite {restaurant}, {Who's your favorite?} The British spelling is favourite. A favorite is also the competitor expected to win: {The Lakers are heavy favorites}. To play favorites is to show unfair preference. As a verb, to favorite something—especially on social media—is to mark it for later or signal approval.

Favorites are things preferred above others—people, places, songs, foods. A favorite child receives preferential treatment. In sports, the favorite is expected to win: {The home team was a heavy favorite}. On computers and phones, favorites are bookmarked links or saved items for quick access. The spelling favourites is British.

Favoritism is the practice of giving unfair preferential treatment to one person or group over others. It implies partiality where impartiality is expected: {The coach's favoritism toward his own son frustrated the other players}. The word carries a negative charge—no one admits to favoritism, only accuses others of it.

Favors are acts of kindness or assistance done for someone: {Can you do me a favor?} The word also covers small gifts given at parties: {wedding favors}, {party favors}. To favor something is to prefer it or give it advantage: {The rules favor incumbents}. A favorable outcome works in your benefit. To favor a body part is to protect it: {She's favoring her left knee}. Someone's favor is their approval or goodwill: {to curry favor}, {in favor with the boss}.

Favour is the British spelling of favor. As a noun, it denotes approval, support, or a kind act done for someone: {Could you do me a favour?} To curry favour is to seek approval through flattery. As a verb, favour means to prefer or give advantage to: {The rules favour experienced players}. Party favours are small gifts given to guests. If something is in your favour, it benefits you; if you're in favour of something, you support it.

Favourable is the British spelling of favorable, meaning positive, approving, or advantageous. A favourable {review} praises its subject. Favourable {conditions} support success. A favourable {impression} is a good one. To look favourably on something is to regard it with approval: {The committee looked favourably on her application}.

Favoured is the British spelling of favored. To be favoured is to be preferred or treated with special advantage: {She was the favoured candidate}. A favoured few receive benefits others don't. Something ill-favoured is unattractive or unpromising. {Fortune favoured the bold.}

Favourite is the British spelling of favorite. It describes what is preferred or most liked: {chocolate is my favourite flavour}. As a noun, a favourite is a preferred person, thing, or competitor expected to win: {She's the favourite to take gold}. To play favourites is to show unfair preference toward certain people.

Favourites is the British spelling of favorites—things or people preferred above others. Your favourites might be songs, books, foods, or teams you support. In computing, favourites are bookmarked websites or saved items for quick access: {I added the page to my favourites}. The spelling with -ou- is standard in British, Australian, and Canadian English.

Favouritism is the practice of giving unfair preferential treatment to one person or group over others. A manager who promotes friends over more qualified candidates shows favouritism. The word carries negative connotations—it implies the preference is undeserved or unjust: {accusations of favouritism}, {The teacher's favouritism toward certain students was obvious}. Spelled favoritism in American English.

Favours is the British spelling of favors. It covers the plural noun (doing someone multiple favours, handing out party favours) and the verb form indicating preference or advantage: {The system favours those with connections}. The spelling difference is purely regional—meaning and usage are identical.

A fawn is a young deer, typically in its first year. The soft tan color of a young deer's coat gives the color name: {fawn-colored upholstery}. Separately, to fawn is to seek favor through excessive flattery or attention: {assistants fawning over the celebrity}. The two words share a spelling but not an origin.

Fawning describes excessive flattery or affection, typically motivated by a desire to gain favor or approval. Someone who fawns over a celebrity or authority figure showers them with obsequious praise and attention. The word carries negative connotations—fawning behavior suggests insincerity and servility rather than genuine admiration. {The fawning coverage made the candidate seem beyond criticism.} The term derives from the behavior of dogs, who demonstrate eager submission by wagging tails and licking faces.

Fawns are young deer, typically less than a year old, known for their spotted coats that provide camouflage in dappled forest light. The word also functions as a verb meaning to show affection or seek favor through excessive flattery and attention, much like a young animal might nuzzle its parent. {The politician's aides fawned over every word he said.} Someone who fawns behaves in an obsequious, servile manner that often comes across as insincere.

A fax is a document transmitted electronically over telephone lines and printed at the receiving end, or the machine that sends and receives such documents. The word is clipped from facsimile. To fax is to send a document this way: {I'll fax you the contract}. Once essential to business communication, fax machines have been largely displaced by email and scanning.

Faxes are documents sent electronically over telephone lines, reproduced as paper copies at the receiving end. The technology dominated business communication in the 1980s and 1990s before email largely displaced it, though faxes persist in medicine, law, and government where signatures matter. As a verb, faxes is the third-person singular: {She faxes the contract to the lawyer}.

To faze is to disturb or disconcert someone's composure: {The criticism didn't faze her}. Nearly always appears in negative constructions—people are unfazed, nothing fazes them, they weren't fazed. Often confused with phase, which means a stage or to introduce gradually.

Fazed means disturbed or unsettled, almost always appearing in negative constructions: {She wasn't fazed by the criticism}, {Nothing fazes him}. The word suggests someone remains calm or unflustered when you might expect otherwise. Often confused with phased, which relates to stages or timing.

Fealty is the loyalty and allegiance that a vassal owed to a feudal lord, formalized through an oath of service and obedience. The term now appears mainly in historical contexts or as a somewhat literary way of describing devoted loyalty to a person, cause, or institution. {The knights swore fealty to the king.} {She questioned whether the party still commanded her fealty.} Unlike simple loyalty, fealty carries overtones of formal obligation and hierarchical submission.

Fear is the feeling of dread or alarm in response to danger or threat. You might fear heights, fear failure, or fear for someone's safety. Fear can be warranted or irrational—reasonable caution or crippling phobia. As a verb, to fear is to be afraid of something: {I fear the worst}. To fear God is to hold reverent awe. {No fear} dismisses a concern as unlikely.

Feared is the past tense of fear, meaning to be afraid of something or someone. More distinctively, feared functions as an adjective describing someone or something that inspires fear in others: {a feared warlord}, {the most feared hitter in baseball}. A feared opponent commands respect through intimidation or demonstrated power.

Fearful means full of fear or causing fear. A fearful {child} is afraid; a fearful {storm} is one that inspires dread. The word can also mean timid by disposition: {She was too fearful to speak up}. In informal use, fearful intensifies: {a fearful mess}, {a fearful racket}—suggesting something extreme or impressive, though this usage is now somewhat old-fashioned.

Fearless describes someone who shows no fear—bold, brave, unafraid to take risks. A fearless {leader} confronts challenges directly. A fearless {journalist} pursues dangerous stories. The word often carries admiration: {Her fearless honesty won people over}. It can shade toward reckless when the absence of fear seems unwise.

Fearlessness is the quality of being without fear—bold, unafraid, undaunted. It may describe genuine absence of fear or the ability to act despite it: {Her fearlessness in the face of criticism was remarkable}. The word often carries admiration, suggesting courage rather than recklessness, though context determines whether the fearlessness is wise or foolish.

A fearmonger is someone who deliberately spreads alarming information to provoke anxiety or panic, often for political or personal gain. The term is always pejorative—it implies the fear being spread is exaggerated or manipulative: {Critics called him a fearmonger for his dire predictions about immigration}. The verb fearmonger and noun fearmongering follow the same pattern as warmonger and rumormonger.

Fearmongering is the deliberate spreading of frightening or exaggerated information to influence public opinion or behavior. Politicians and media figures are often accused of fearmongering when they emphasize worst-case scenarios about immigration, crime, or public health to rally support or boost ratings. {Critics dismissed the campaign ad as pure fearmongering.} The related noun fearmonger describes someone who engages in this practice.

Fearmongers are people who deliberately spread alarming information to provoke anxiety or panic, often for political or personal gain. The term is almost always pejorative—accusing someone of fearmongering suggests their warnings are exaggerated or manipulative rather than legitimate: {Critics dismissed the senators as fearmongers exploiting public anxiety about immigration}.

Fears functions as both noun and verb around the core idea of being afraid. As a noun, fears are things that frighten or worry someone: {She confronted her fears}, {His fears proved groundless}. As a verb, it's the third-person form of fear: {He fears the worst}, {She fears for her children's safety}. The plural noun often suggests anxieties about what might happen rather than immediate terror.

Fearsome describes something that inspires fear or dread—a fearsome {opponent}, a fearsome {reputation}, a fearsome {storm}. The word suggests the thing itself is formidable, not merely frightening in appearance. A fearsome creature poses real danger; a scary costume just looks alarming. {The dog had a fearsome bark but was gentle with children.}

Feasibility is the quality of being achievable or practical. A feasibility {study} examines whether a proposed project can actually be accomplished given available resources, time, and constraints. The word implies realistic assessment rather than wishful thinking: {We need to evaluate the feasibility of expanding into new markets before committing funds}.

Feasible means capable of being done or accomplished: {Is it feasible to finish by Friday?} The word suggests practical possibility—not just theoretical but achievable given real constraints of time, money, or resources. A feasible plan is one that could actually work. {The engineers determined that the bridge design was feasible.}

A feast is a large, elaborate meal, often for many people and marking a celebration: {The wedding feast lasted for hours}. A feast can also be any abundant supply of something enjoyable: {a feast for the eyes}. To feast is to eat abundantly or to take great pleasure in something: {We feasted on fresh crab}, {She feasted her eyes on the view}. A feast day is a religious holiday commemorating a saint or sacred event.

Feasted is the past tense of feast—to eat abundantly and with pleasure, typically at a celebratory meal: {They feasted on turkey and ham}. The word suggests indulgence beyond ordinary eating. Figuratively, to feast on something is to take great pleasure in it: {She feasted her eyes on the view}.

Feasting is eating and drinking lavishly, typically at a celebratory gathering. The word suggests abundance and pleasure beyond ordinary meals: {The wedding guests spent the evening feasting and dancing}. Figuratively, feasting can mean indulging richly in any experience: {feasting your eyes on the view}.

Feasts is the plural of feast—elaborate ceremonial meals marking celebrations, holidays, or religious occasions. The word suggests abundance and communal eating: {wedding feasts}, {holiday feasts}. As a verb, feasts means to eat lavishly or to take great pleasure: {She feasts her eyes on the sunset}. {The village feasts for three days after the harvest}.

A feat is an achievement requiring skill, strength, or courage—something difficult that not everyone could accomplish. The word often appears with adjectives emphasizing impressiveness: {a remarkable feat of engineering}, {an athletic feat}, {no mean feat}. To accomplish something {no mean feat} is to do something genuinely difficult.

The growths forming the outer covering of birds and constituting their plumage are feathers. All other more specific meanings arise from this. Feather is common in idioms such as birds of a feather (like things or people) and a feather in your cap (an achievement of distinction). Verb uses of feather are mainly technical and specific to various skill domains: The hairdresser feathered her hair. To feather your nest is to enrich yourself unethically or illegally.

A featherbed is a thick mattress or mattress topper stuffed with feathers, traditionally goose down, providing luxurious softness and warmth. The verb featherbed means to pamper or coddle someone, or more specifically in labor contexts, to require employers to hire more workers than necessary or to maintain inefficient practices that protect jobs. {The union was accused of featherbedding to preserve outdated positions.} The adjective featherbed describes such protective arrangements: {featherbed rules in the contract}.

A featherbrain is a scatterbrained or frivolous person—someone whose head seems filled with feathers rather than substance. The word is mildly dismissive rather than harsh: {Don't be such a featherbrain; focus!} The adjective featherbrained describes the quality: {another featherbrained scheme}.

Feathered means covered with or having feathers: {a feathered friend}, {brightly feathered birds}. It extends to things resembling feathers in appearance or arrangement: {feathered arrows}, {feathered bangs}. To {feather one's nest} is to enrich oneself, often through questionable means. {Tar and feather} was a punishment involving hot tar and feathers applied to the body.

Feathering is the act of giving something a feathered edge—a gradual transition rather than a sharp boundary. In painting and graphic design, feathering softens edges by blending them into the background: {Feathering the selection made the cutout look natural}. In aviation, feathering a propeller turns the blades edge-on to reduce drag. In rowing, it's rotating the oar blade flat between strokes. The word also describes the arrangement of feathers on a bird or the decorative plumage on certain dog breeds.

Feathers are the light, flat structures that cover birds' bodies, providing insulation, enabling flight, and displaying colors for mating or camouflage. Each feather consists of a central shaft with soft barbs branching off. The word extends to similar structures: feathers on arrows stabilize flight, and to feather oars is to turn them flat between strokes. If you {ruffle someone's feathers}, you irritate them. A {feather in your cap} is an achievement worth noting. To {feather your nest} is to enrich yourself, often through dubious means.

Featherweight is a boxing division for fighters at the lighter end of the scale, typically around 126 pounds. By extension, featherweight describes anything notably light in weight or, figuratively, lacking substance or importance: {a featherweight laptop}, {His arguments were featherweight compared to hers}. The term often carries a dismissive edge when applied to people or ideas.

Featherweights is the plural of featherweight—a boxing weight class for fighters up to 126 pounds, or more broadly, anyone or anything notably light or insignificant. In figurative use, featherweights lack power or influence: {The committee was stacked with political featherweights}. The term can describe objects as well as people: {These laptops are featherweights compared to older models}.

Feats is the plural of feat, an accomplishment requiring skill, strength, or daring: {feats of engineering}, {athletic feats}, {feats of endurance}. The word suggests something impressive enough to be remarked upon—not routine tasks but achievements that stand out: {The rescue was a remarkable feat of coordination}.

A feature is an identifiable part of an object that makes it distinct from other objects of roughly the same kind, or of a different kind: What features can be used to identify members of the willow family? He always has to have a phone with the latest features. A person’s features are the parts of their face, taken together. As a verb, feature means to have or make a prominent attribute: All rooms feature a mini-fridge and a microwave. The evening edition features a story about the daring rescue.

Featured describes something given special prominence or attention. A featured {article} receives top billing; a featured {guest} gets highlighted treatment. In compound forms, it describes physical characteristics: {fine-featured}, {sharp-featured}. Something that features a particular element includes it as a notable component: {a phone featured in the ad}.

Featureless describes something lacking distinctive characteristics or variation—uniform and blank. A featureless {landscape} stretches flat and empty to the horizon. A featureless {face} offers nothing memorable to fix in memory. The word emphasizes monotony or absence where you might expect texture, detail, or distinguishing marks.
