A flatfish is a fish with a flattened body that swims on its side and has both eyes on one side of its head—flounder, sole, halibut, and turbot are flatfish. They lie camouflaged on the ocean floor, nearly invisible to prey and predators. The term also describes anything flat and fish-shaped.

Flatfoot has two main meanings. One is a foot condition where the arch is flattened, allowing the entire sole to touch the ground: {The army rejected him for flatfoot}. The other is slang for a police officer, especially one walking a beat—the connection being hours spent pounding pavement. The plural for the condition is flatfeet; for cops, flatfoots.

Flatfooted describes feet with collapsed arches that rest flat on the ground, or a person with such feet. More commonly, flatfooted means unprepared or caught off guard: {The question caught him flatfooted}. In sports, being flatfooted means standing with weight on the heels rather than the balls of the feet, unable to move quickly. To come out flatfooted is to state something bluntly and without hedging.

Flathead describes something with a flat top surface. A flathead screwdriver has a single flat blade that fits into slotted screws, as opposed to a Phillips head. A flathead engine has cylinders and valves arranged in a flat configuration. Flathead is also a category of freshwater catfish with distinctively flattened heads, prized by anglers: {He caught a thirty-pound flathead}.

A flatiron is a flat-bottomed iron that was heated on a stove or fire and used to press wrinkles from clothing before electric irons became standard. The word now more commonly refers to a hair-straightening tool with heated plates that clamp sections of hair flat. The Flatiron Building in New York City, a famous early skyscraper, takes its name from its distinctive triangular shape resembling the household tool.

Flatirons are dramatic, slanted rock formations that rise at steep angles from the ground, resembling old-fashioned flat irons used for pressing clothes. The term is most associated with the iconic sandstone slabs outside Boulder, Colorado: {We hiked to the base of the Flatirons at sunrise}. Lowercase flatiron can also mean a clothes iron with a flat metal base, heated on a stove—the predecessor to electric irons.

Flatland is terrain without hills or mountains—level ground that extends to the horizon. Often plural: {the flatlands of Kansas}, {miles of flatland stretched before us}. The term can carry connotations of monotony or emptiness, though residents may prize the open sky and unobstructed views. (Capitalized Flatland is the novella.)

A flatlander is someone from flat terrain, typically used by mountain or hill dwellers to describe outsiders unfamiliar with elevated geography. The term often carries mild condescension—implying the person lacks experience with slopes, altitude, or rugged country: {The flatlanders from Kansas struggled on the hiking trails}. In some regions, it's simply descriptive; in others, it marks someone as an outsider who doesn't belong.

Flatline refers to the straight horizontal line on a monitor that indicates the absence of electrical activity, particularly in a heart monitor showing cardiac arrest. As a verb, to flatline means to die or to show no vital signs: {The patient flatlined twice during surgery but was resuscitated}. The term extends figuratively to anything that shows no activity, growth, or variation: {Sales have flatlined since the new competitor entered the market}. Something that flatlines goes completely still or ceases to function.

Flatlined comes from the flat line on a heart monitor when cardiac activity stops. Literally, to flatline is to die or experience cardiac arrest: {The patient flatlined twice during surgery}. Figuratively, it describes anything that has stopped progressing or gone completely inactive: {Sales flatlined after the initial buzz}, {The project flatlined when funding dried up}.

A flatliner is someone whose vital signs have gone flat—whose heart has stopped, producing the horizontal line on a cardiac monitor rather than peaks and valleys. Medical dramas use the term for patients who've coded: {We've got a flatliner in room three}. Extended to mean someone showing no activity or response: {The project's been a flatliner since January}. The verb flatline works similarly—to die or to stagnate completely.

Flatliners are people whose heart has stopped, producing the flat line on a cardiac monitor that indicates no electrical activity. The term gained currency from the 1990 film about medical students who deliberately induce death to explore the afterlife. Outside medical contexts, a flatliner is someone or something showing no activity or response: {The stock's been a flatliner all year}.

Flatlines refers to the flat horizontal line on a heart monitor when electrical activity stops—meaning clinical death. By extension, anything that flatlines fails completely or goes to zero: {The project flatlined after funding was cut}, {Ratings flatlined in the second season}. In medical contexts, to flatline is to experience cardiac arrest, though it's often used loosely for any critical decline.

Flatlining originally describes the flat line on a heart monitor when cardiac activity stops—the patient is dying or dead. The term extends to anything showing no activity or movement: {Sales have been flatlining for months}, {The project is flatlining}. To flatline is to show this pattern, whether literally in a medical crisis or figuratively for stagnant performance.

A flatmate is someone you share a rented flat with—the British equivalent of roommate. Unlike a housemate, the term specifically implies an apartment rather than a house: {I found a flatmate through an online listing}. The relationship is typically practical rather than intimate; flatmates split rent and utilities but may keep largely separate lives.

Flatmates are people who share an apartment or flat, typically splitting rent and living expenses. The term is British; Americans say roommates. Flatmates may be friends, strangers matched through listings, or acquaintances of convenience: {I found my flatmates through an online ad}. The singular flatmate refers to one such person.

Flatness is the quality of being flat—level, smooth, or without variation. A surface has flatness when it lacks bumps or curves. The word extends to anything lacking dimension or interest: the flatness of a {performance}, the flatness of the {prairie}, the flatness of {stale beer}. In technical contexts, flatness measures how closely a surface approaches a perfect plane.

Flatpack describes furniture or other items sold disassembled in a flat box, designed for home assembly: {We spent the afternoon wrestling with flatpack bookshelves}. The term is strongly associated with IKEA and similar retailers. As a noun, it refers to the item itself or its packaging: {The flatpack arrived with missing screws}.

Flatpacks are furniture or equipment sold unassembled in flat boxes, designed for the buyer to put together at home. The format reduces shipping costs and storage space, though assembly can test patience: {We spent the whole afternoon building flatpacks from IKEA}. As a verb, to flatpack is to package something this way. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated.

Flats are shoes without elevated heels, worn for comfort or practicality: {She changed from heels into flats for the walk home}. The word also refers to level expanses of land, especially wetlands: {salt flats}, {mud flats}, {tidal flats}. In theater, flats are lightweight framed panels used as scenery. In music, flats are notes lowered by a half step, or the symbol indicating this. In British English, flats are apartments.

A flatscreen is a television or monitor with a thin, flat display panel rather than the bulky cathode-ray tube of older sets. The term emerged in the late 1990s as LCD and plasma technology replaced traditional televisions. Now that nearly all screens are flat, the word increasingly sounds dated—what was once a selling point has become the default.

A flatshare is a living arrangement where people who aren't family share a rented apartment, splitting costs and common spaces. The term is primarily British, corresponding to American "roommate situation." It can also refer to the flat itself: {I found a flatshare near the station}. As a verb, to flatshare is to live this way: {I flatshared with strangers throughout my twenties}.

Flatten means to make flat or flatter—to compress, level, or smooth something out. You flatten dough with a rolling pin, flatten a box for recycling, or flatten your hair against your head. Extended uses follow naturally: a storm flattens crops, an army flattens a city, bad news flattens your mood. To flatten someone can mean to knock them down or defeat them decisively: {He flattened his opponent in the third round}.

Flattened describes something that has been made flat or pressed down from its original shape. A flattened cardboard box takes up less space. {The crops lay flattened after the storm}. Figuratively, to be flattened is to be defeated or exhausted: {I was absolutely flattened by the news}.

Flattening is the process of making something flat or flatter. A rolling pin flattens dough. Economic flattening levels hierarchies or reduces growth curves. In data structures, flattening converts nested elements into a single level: {flattening a nested list}. The word often implies reduction or compression—eliminating variation, dimension, or complexity.

To flatter is to praise someone, often insincerely or excessively, usually to win favor or manipulate: {He flattered her to get the promotion}. Flattery may also be genuine admiration: {I'm flattered you asked}. To say something flatters a person means it makes them look good: {That dress flatters your figure}. To {flatter yourself} is to hold an inflated self-opinion.

Flattered describes the pleased feeling when someone's attention or praise suggests you matter to them. To feel flattered is to be gratified by a compliment or honor: {I'm flattered you remembered my birthday}. It can also acknowledge praise while deflecting it: {I'm flattered, but I really don't deserve the credit}. Sometimes it signals suspicious pleasure—flattery implies possible insincerity.

A flatterer is someone who gives excessive or insincere praise, typically to gain favor or advantage. The word carries negative connotations—a flatterer isn't genuinely complimentary but strategic: {Beware of flatterers who tell you only what you want to hear}. Unlike someone who simply gives compliments, a flatterer has an agenda.

Flattering describes something that makes a person look or feel more attractive, capable, or admirable than they might otherwise appear. A flattering {photograph} captures someone at their best; a flattering {dress} accentuates favorable features while minimizing less desired ones. Flattering remarks or attention may be sincere compliments or may be exaggerated praise designed to win favor. When someone is described as flattering, it often carries a hint of insincerity or ulterior motive.

Flattery is excessive or insincere praise, usually offered to gain favor or manipulate. Unlike genuine compliments, flattery has an agenda—the flatterer wants something. {She saw through his flattery immediately.} The line between flattery and sincere admiration depends on motive and proportion: {A little flattery never hurts, but don't overdo it.}

A flattop is a haircut where the hair on top is cut to form a flat horizontal surface, typically with closely cropped sides. The style was popular among military personnel and became a 1950s fashion. Flattop also refers to an aircraft carrier, whose deck forms a flat surface for planes to land on.

Flattops are aircraft carriers, named for their flat flight decks. The word also refers to a style of haircut where the hair is cut short on the sides and back but left longer on top, trimmed to create a flat, level surface: {He's worn a flattop since his Marine Corps days}. Less commonly, a flattop is any flat-topped surface or structure.

Flatulence is the presence of gas in the digestive system, or the expulsion of that gas through the anus—farting. The term is slightly clinical, often used to discuss the condition rather than individual instances: {Certain foods cause flatulence}. Extended to mean empty, pompous speech: {political flatulence}.

Flaunt means to display something ostentatiously, usually to provoke admiration or envy: {She flaunted her new diamond ring}, {He likes to flaunt his wealth}. The word implies showing off deliberately rather than simply being visible. Flaunt is often confused with flout (to openly disregard), but they're distinct: you flaunt possessions, you flout rules.

Flaunted is the past tense of flaunt, meaning to display something ostentatiously or with excessive pride: {She flaunted her wealth at every opportunity}. The word carries a whiff of disapproval—flaunting suggests showing off rather than simply showing. Often confused with flouted, which means to openly disregard rules or conventions.

Flaunting is showing something off ostentatiously, displaying it to attract attention or admiration: {flaunting her new diamond ring}, {flaunting his wealth}. The word carries a note of disapproval—flaunting suggests excess or poor taste. Often confused with flouting, which means openly defying rules or conventions.

Flautas are a Mexican dish of tightly rolled tortillas filled with meat or other ingredients, then fried until crisp. The name means "flutes" in Spanish, describing their long, thin shape. They're typically served with salsa, guacamole, or sour cream: {We ordered flautas and a plate of nachos}.

Flavor is the distinctive taste of something, the sensation produced when food or drink meets the tongue and nose: {The soup had a rich, savory flavor}. Extended, flavor means a characteristic quality or style: {The neighborhood has an old-world flavor}. In physics, flavor distinguishes types of quarks and leptons. To flavor something is to add taste to it. Flavors can be literal (vanilla, chocolate) or figurative (flavors of political conservatism).

Flavoring is a substance added to food or drink to give it a particular taste. The term covers both natural extracts and artificial compounds: {vanilla flavoring}, {artificial flavoring}. In American English, flavoring; in British English, flavouring. The word can also describe the act of adding such substances: {The flavoring of the sauce took several attempts}.

Flavors are the distinctive tastes that characterize foods, drinks, and other substances we put in our mouths. The word extends beyond literal taste to describe varieties or versions of things: {The software comes in several flavors}. In physics, flavor distinguishes types of quarks and leptons. As a verb, to flavor something is to add taste to it, and figuratively, experiences can flavor our perceptions: {His time in the military flavored his approach to management}.

Flavour is the British spelling of flavor. The taste of something, or more precisely the combination of taste and smell that makes food distinctive: {The soup had a rich, earthy flavour}. Extended to any distinctive quality or character: {The town retains its medieval flavour}. In physics, flavour distinguishes types of quarks and leptons. To flavour food is to add seasoning or enhance its taste.

Flavours is the British spelling of flavors. A flavour is the distinctive taste of something—the flavour of {vanilla}, the flavour of {fresh basil}. Extended uses describe character or quality: {The town has an old-world flavour}. To flavour food is to season it. Something that flavours a situation gives it a particular quality: {Her skepticism flavoured the entire discussion}.

A flaw is an imperfection that diminishes quality or value. A diamond has a flaw if it contains a visible inclusion. A flaw in an argument is a weakness in its logic. A character flaw is a personal failing: {His temper was his fatal flaw}. To flaw something is to mar it, though flawed as an adjective is more common: {a deeply flawed study}.

Flawed means having a flaw—an imperfection, defect, or weakness. A flawed {diamond} has visible impurities. A flawed {argument} contains logical errors. A flawed {character} has moral shortcomings. The word often acknowledges imperfection without total condemnation: {He was flawed but fundamentally decent}. Deeply flawed or fatally flawed signal more serious problems.

Flawless means without any imperfection or defect. A flawless {diamond} has no visible inclusions. A flawless {performance} contains no errors. The word often carries hyperbolic force—praising something as ideal or beyond criticism: {Her logic was flawless}. In casual use, flawless has become enthusiastic approval: {That outfit is flawless}.

Flaws are imperfections or defects—features that mar something otherwise sound. A diamond has flaws if it contains visible inclusions. A plan has flaws if it contains weaknesses that could cause failure. Character flaws are personal shortcomings: {His fatal flaw was pride}. The verb means to introduce such defects: {A single error flawed the experiment}.

Flax is a plant grown for its fiber and seeds. The fiber, extracted from the stem, is spun into linen thread and woven into fabric. The seeds yield linseed oil, used in paints and wood finishes, and are eaten for their nutritional value. Flax also describes the pale yellowish color of the plant's dried fiber: {flaxen hair}.

Flaxseed is the small, flat, oval seed of the flax plant, used as a dietary supplement and food ingredient. Rich in omega-3 fatty acids and fiber, flaxseed appears in health foods, cereals, and smoothies: {She sprinkles ground flaxseed on her yogurt}. Also called linseed, especially when pressed for oil used in paints and wood finishes.

To flay is to strip the skin from a body, typically by cutting or whipping. The image is visceral—executioners flayed criminals, hunters flay game. Figuratively, to flay someone is to criticize them harshly, as if peeling away their defenses: {The critics flayed his latest novel}. A flaying review leaves nothing intact.

Flayed means stripped of skin. Literally, to flay is to remove the skin from a body, whether as butchery, torture, or punishment—an image of extreme pain and exposure. Figuratively, to be flayed is to be harshly criticized or verbally attacked: {The critics flayed her performance}. {He felt flayed by her words}.

Flaying is the act of stripping skin from a body, whether animal or human. Hunters flay game to prepare hides; in historical contexts, flaying was a method of torture and execution. Figuratively, to flay someone is to criticize them harshly: {The critics flayed his latest novel}.

A flea is a tiny wingless insect that feeds on blood, jumping between hosts with powerful hind legs. Fleas infest dogs, cats, and other mammals, causing itching and sometimes transmitting disease. A {flea market} is an outdoor bazaar selling secondhand goods—the name suggesting items might carry fleas. A {flea bag} or {fleabag} is a shabby hotel.

A fleabag is a shabby, run-down place—typically a cheap hotel or rooming house: {We spent the night in some fleabag motel off the highway}. The word suggests a place so dirty it might harbor fleas. It can also refer to a mangy animal, especially a dog or cat, or more loosely to any decrepit thing or disreputable person.

Fleabags are shabby, run-down places—typically cheap hotels or motels in poor condition: {We checked into some fleabag on the edge of town}. The term suggests a place so neglected it might harbor fleas. It also applies to mangy animals, especially dogs, or disparagingly to unkempt people.

Fleabitten describes something shabby, worn, or run-down: {a fleabitten motel on the edge of town}. The image is of a mangy dog covered in flea bites. Applied to horses, fleabitten describes a white or gray coat speckled with small reddish-brown spots—the coloring actually resembling flea-bite marks.

A fleapit is a rundown, shabby movie theater or other entertainment venue, suggesting a place so decrepit it might be infested with fleas. The term is used mainly in British English and carries affectionate contempt—people might fondly recall the fleapit where they watched films as children while acknowledging its seediness. {We caught the late show at that old fleapit on the corner.} The word can extend to any dilapidated building or cheap accommodation.

Fleas are tiny wingless insects that feed on the blood of mammals and birds. They're infamous for infesting pets and homes, jumping remarkable distances relative to their size. A flea market sells secondhand goods—the name suggests you might find items that have been around long enough to harbor parasites. To {put a flea in someone's ear} is to give them a sharp rebuke or unwelcome hint.

A fleck is a tiny spot, speck, or patch of something, often color or light, that contrasts with its surroundings: {flecks of gold in the granite}, {flecks of gray in his beard}. The word suggests smallness and scattered distribution rather than concentration. As a verb, fleck means to mark with such spots: {Blood flecked the windshield}. The adjective flecked describes surfaces bearing these small marks: {a flecked tweed jacket}.

Flecks are small spots or specks, typically of color or light: {flecks of gold in her eyes}, {flecks of paint on the floor}. The word suggests scattered, irregular marks rather than a pattern. To fleck is to mark with such spots: {Gray flecked his beard}.

Fled is the past tense and past participle of flee. To flee is to run away from danger or pursuit: {They fled the burning building}, {The suspect fled on foot}. Fled also applies to leaving a place urgently due to threat or hardship: {Refugees fled the war zone}, {She fled an abusive marriage}.

Fledgeling is a British spelling of fledgling—a young bird that has just grown flight feathers and is learning to fly. By extension, it describes anything new and inexperienced: a fledgeling {company}, a fledgeling {democracy}, a fledgeling {writer}. The spelling with an e is less common than fledgling, even in British English.

A fledgling is a young bird that has recently grown its flight feathers and is learning to fly. From this concrete image comes the more common figurative use: anything new and inexperienced, especially a person or organization just starting out. {The fledgling company struggled to find investors.} As an adjective, fledgling characterizes things that are new, immature, or just beginning to develop: {a fledgling democracy}, {fledgling efforts at reform}.

Fledglings are young birds that have developed enough feathers to leave the nest but are still learning to fly and fend for themselves. The term extends to any inexperienced person or thing just starting out: {The company hired several fledglings fresh out of college}. A fledgling business or fledgling democracy is one in its early stages of development, not yet fully established or proven.

To flee is to run away from danger or unpleasantness. You flee a burning building, a war zone, or an uncomfortable conversation. The past tense is fled: {They fled the country when the regime changed}. Flee suggests urgency—you don't flee casually. Things can also flee figuratively: {All hope fled when we saw the damage}.

Fleece is the woolly coat of a sheep, or the wool sheared from one: {The shepherd sold the fleece at market}. By extension, fleece names soft fabric that mimics wool's warmth: {a fleece jacket}. To fleece someone is to swindle them—shearing them of their money as a sheep is shorn of wool: {The con artist fleeced tourists out of thousands}.

Fleeced means swindled or overcharged—stripped of money the way a sheep is stripped of wool. Someone who paid three hundred dollars for a counterfeit watch got fleeced. The word implies the victim was naive or the swindler particularly skilled: {Tourists get fleeced at that market}. Less commonly, fleeced describes fabric with a soft napped surface.

Fleeces is the plural of fleece—the woolly coat of a sheep, or the material shorn from it. By extension, fleece names any soft, fuzzy fabric or garment: {She packed two fleeces for the camping trip}. As a verb, fleece means to swindle or overcharge: {The scam fleeces elderly victims out of their savings}.

Fleecing is cheating or swindling someone, typically by charging excessive prices or extracting money through deception: {tourists getting fleeced by street vendors}, {The casino fleeced him for everything he had}. The image comes from shearing a sheep—stripping away what covers someone, leaving them exposed and poorer.

Fleeing is the act of running away from danger, threat, or an undesirable situation. The word captures active escape in progress: {Residents were photographed fleeing the wildfire}, {refugees fleeing persecution}. It emphasizes urgency and often fear—you flee what threatens you, not merely what inconveniences you.

Fleet describes a group of vehicles or vessels with a common purpose or mission. All of the vehicles owned by a company for their own use may be called a fleet, just as all the ships of a nation are. As an adjective, fleet is seen mainly in literary use meaning fast, in the expressions fleet of foot and a fleet horse.

Fleeting describes something that passes quickly or lasts only a moment: a fleeting {glimpse}, a fleeting {thought}, fleeting {happiness}. The word emphasizes how briefly something exists before vanishing. What's fleeting may be precious precisely because it doesn't last: {Their time together was fleeting but unforgettable}.

Fleets is the plural of fleet—groups of ships, vehicles, or aircraft operating together under common ownership or command: {The company operates fleets of delivery trucks across three states}. A nation's naval fleet is its warships collectively. Fleet also works as an adjective meaning swift, and as a verb meaning to pass quickly, though these uses are literary and uncommon.

Flesh refers to skin (typically of humans) or other soft tissue (typically of animals). Flesh is also a common metaphor for humankind and its vulnerabilities. Flesh and blood may designate your blood relatives, the human body, or human nature. If you flesh out an idea, you add more detail or information about it. Things appreciatively described as fleshed out have all needed information or features available.

Fleshy describes something with abundant soft tissue or pulp. A fleshy {arm} is plump or corpulent. A fleshy {fruit} like a peach has thick, soft matter surrounding the seed. Fleshy {leaves} are thick and succulent. The word can suggest sensuality or excess: {fleshy lips}, {fleshy thighs}. It emphasizes substance you can sink into.

Flew is the past tense of fly. A bird flew overhead. Time flew by. She flew into a rage. He flew to Chicago. The ball flew over the fence. In each case, flew describes movement through air or rapid motion that has already occurred.

Flex means to bend or contract a muscle, showing its shape and strength: {He flexed his biceps in the mirror}. By extension, to flex is to demonstrate power or capability: {The company flexed its market dominance}. In slang, flex means to show off or boast, especially about wealth or status: {She's always flexing on Instagram}. As a noun, a flex is an act of showing off: {Buying that car was a flex}.

Flexed is the past tense of flex, meaning to bend or contract a muscle to display its size and strength: {He flexed his biceps in the mirror}. Figuratively, to flex is to show off power, wealth, or status: {She flexed on everyone with her new car}. The slang sense has made flexed common in casual speech about any kind of boastful display.

Flexes is the plural of flex and the third-person singular verb form. To flex is to bend or contract a muscle, showing its shape and strength: {He flexes his biceps in the mirror}. In slang, to flex is to show off or boast, especially about wealth, status, or achievements: {She's always flexing her new car on social media}. The noun flex is an instance of showing off: {That watch is a flex}.

Flexibility is the ability to bend without breaking, whether physical or figurative. A gymnast has flexibility; so does a schedule that accommodates changes. Flexible arrangements adapt to circumstances: {We need some flexibility on the deadline}. The word implies willingness to adjust rather than rigid adherence to fixed plans or positions.

Flexible means able to bend without breaking: {flexible plastic}, {a flexible wire}. The word extends naturally to anything that can adapt or adjust. A flexible schedule accommodates changes. A flexible person is open to new ideas or willing to compromise. Flexible thinking allows for creative problem-solving. The opposite is rigid, whether describing materials or mindsets.

Flexing is contracting a muscle to make it bulge, the way bodybuilders do to display their physiques. The meaning extends to any show of strength or capability: {Russia is flexing its military power}. In slang, flexing is showing off wealth, status, or possessions: {He's always flexing his new watch on Instagram}. The slang usage often carries a note of disapproval—suggesting the display is excessive or insecure.

A flexitarian follows a mostly vegetarian diet but occasionally eats meat or fish. The term blends "flexible" with "vegetarian," describing someone who reduces rather than eliminates animal products: {I'm flexitarian—vegetarian at home but I'll have a burger at a cookout}. The approach prioritizes plant-based eating without strict prohibition.

Flextime is a work arrangement allowing employees to choose their own hours within limits set by the employer. Workers might arrive early and leave early, or start late and finish late, so long as they complete required hours and cover core periods when everyone must be present: {The company offers flextime, so I work seven to three}. Also spelled flex-time or flexi-time.

A flick is a quick, light motion—a snap of the fingers, a flip of a switch, a brush of the wrist: {She flicked a crumb off the table}. To flick through something is to browse it rapidly: {flicking through channels}, {flicking through a magazine}. In casual speech, a flick is a movie: {We caught a flick last night}. A chick flick targets female audiences.

Flicker describes unsteady, wavering light or movement—a candle flame disturbed by a draft, a dying lightbulb, an old film projection. The noun names such movement or a brief instance of something: {a flicker of hope}, {a flicker of recognition crossed her face}. To flicker is to move or shine in this unstable way. A flicker is also a North American woodpecker with a distinctive undulating flight.

Flickered is the past tense of flicker, meaning to shine unsteadily or waver rapidly between states. A candle flame flickered in the draft. Lights flickered during the storm. The word extends to quick, intermittent movements or expressions: {A smile flickered across her face}. {Hope flickered briefly, then died}.

Flickering describes light or flame that wavers unsteadily, alternating rapidly between brightness and dimness: {flickering candles}, {the flickering glow of the television}. The word suggests instability or impermanence. A flickering hope or interest is one that appears and fades, uncertain whether it will sustain itself or die out entirely.

Flickers names the action of flickering—unsteady light that wavers or pulses irregularly: {The candle flickers in the draft}. Eyes flicker when they move rapidly or blink; a smile flickers across a face when it appears briefly. As a noun, flickers are instances of this wavering: {flickers of light}, {flickers of hope}. A flicker is also a North American woodpecker with spotted plumage.

Flicking is making a quick, sharp movement, usually with the finger or wrist. You flick a light switch, flick lint off a jacket, flick through TV channels. The motion is brief and snapping: {She kept flicking her hair out of her eyes}. Flicking through pages means browsing rapidly without close attention.

Flicks is informal for movies or the cinema: {Let's catch a flick}, {going to the flicks}. The term comes from the flickering of early film projectors. Flicks is also the plural of flick—a quick, light motion or strike: {flicks of the wrist}, {flicks of a light switch}. To flick is to move something with such a motion: {She flicked a crumb off the table}.

A flier is someone or something that flies—a pilot, a flying creature, or a fast-moving vehicle. The word also means a small printed advertisement distributed by hand: {They handed out fliers for the concert}. To {take a flier} on something is to take a risk or make a speculative attempt. Also spelled flyer, with no difference in meaning.

Fliers is the plural of flier. A flier is a person or thing that flies—a pilot, a passenger on an aircraft, or a flying creature. A flier is also a printed handbill for advertising or announcements: {They handed out fliers for the concert}. To {take a flier} is to take a speculative risk. Also spelled flyers.

Flies is the plural of fly in its noun senses—the common insect, the zipper flap on trousers {your flies are undone}, or the space above a theater stage. As a verb, flies is the third-person singular: {She flies to Boston every week}, {Time flies}. In baseball, a player flies out by hitting a ball caught in the air.

Flight is a noun closely related to the verb fly, which explains most of its meanings. It denotes the ability to fly, or an act or instance of flying. Flight can also mean escape: fight or flight, flight of the Israelites out of Egypt. A flight of steps is the group of stairs from one level to another: I didn’t know she lived five flights up! Today, the most frequent use of flight is to designate the journeys of aircraft. This is also true when flight comes before another noun: flight attendant, flight path, flight recorder.

Flightless describes birds and insects that cannot fly, despite belonging to groups that typically can. Penguins, ostriches, and kiwis are flightless birds—their wings have evolved for other purposes or atrophied. {The dodo was a flightless bird native to Mauritius.} The term sometimes extends figuratively to anything grounded or unable to take off.

Flights is the plural of flight, covering all its senses. A bird takes flight; you book flights to distant cities; flights of stairs connect floors. A flight can be a group moving together: {a flight of geese}, {a flight of arrows}. Flights of fancy are imaginative excursions, sometimes impractical ones. In drinking, a flight is a sampler of several varieties: {a flight of wines}, {a beer flight}.

A flightsuit is a one-piece garment worn by pilots and aircrew, typically made of fire-resistant material. The design allows freedom of movement while providing pockets for equipment and protection in emergencies. Military flightsuits are usually olive drab or tan; civilian versions vary. The garment has become iconic in aviation imagery: {She zipped up her flightsuit before the preflight briefing}.

Flighty describes someone who is impulsive, changeable, or not serious-minded. A flighty person shifts attention or affections unpredictably: {She was too flighty to commit to anything long-term}. The word often carries a dismissive tone, especially when applied to women, suggesting frivolousness or emotional instability. A flighty {horse} is skittish and easily startled.

Flimflam is nonsense or deceptive talk, especially when used to swindle someone. A flimflam is a confidence trick or petty fraud: {The whole investment scheme was a flimflam}. To flimflam is to cheat through fast talk or misdirection: {He flimflammed tourists out of their cash}. The word has an old-fashioned, almost playful ring despite describing dishonesty.

Flimflammed is the past tense of flimflam, meaning to swindle or deceive someone through a confidence trick or elaborate deception. If you've been flimflammed, someone has cheated you out of money or tricked you into believing something false, typically through charm or fast talk rather than force. {The tourists got flimflammed by a street hustler running a shell game.} The word has a playful, old-fashioned quality that can soften the accusation of fraud.

Flimsy describes something weak, thin, or insubstantial—easily torn, broken, or seen through. A flimsy {excuse} won't hold up to scrutiny. Flimsy {curtains} let light through. Flimsy {construction} suggests poor quality that won't last. The word carries connotations of cheapness or inadequacy: {The evidence against him was flimsy at best}.

Flinch is a quick, involuntary movement away from something painful or startling—a wince, a recoil: {She flinched when the nurse inserted the needle}. Figuratively, to flinch is to shrink from difficulty or unpleasantness: {He didn't flinch from telling her the truth}. The noun names the movement itself: {a visible flinch}.

Flinched is the past tense of flinch, meaning to make a quick, involuntary movement away from something painful or frightening: {She flinched when the nurse inserted the needle}. Figuratively, to flinch is to shrink from difficulty or unpleasantness: {He didn't flinch from telling her the truth}.

Flinches is the verb flinch in third person or its plural noun form. To flinch is to make a quick, involuntary movement away from something painful or startling: {She flinches every time he raises his voice}. Figuratively, to flinch is to shrink from difficulty or unpleasantness: {He never flinches from hard truths}. A flinch is an instance of such recoiling.

Flinching is the act of drawing back or wincing, typically as an instinctive response to anticipated pain or discomfort: {He couldn't help flinching when the needle went in}. The word extends to any involuntary shrinking from something unpleasant or difficult: {She kept reading without flinching at the gruesome details}.

Fling emphasizes force and carelessness in throwing: {She flung the door open}, {He flung his coat on the chair}. The word extends to any abrupt, energetic action: {fling yourself into work}, {fling accusations}. A fling is also a brief romantic or sexual affair, implying something casual and temporary: {a summer fling}. To {have a fling} at something is to give it a try.

Flings is the plural of fling and the third-person singular verb form. A fling is a brief, carefree episode—especially a short romantic or sexual relationship: {We had a fling one summer}. To fling is to throw with force or abandon: {She flung open the door}. A {final fling} or {last fling} is one more indulgence before settling down or giving something up.

Flint is a hard, fine-grained stone that produces sparks when struck against steel. This property made flint essential for starting fires and firing early guns—a flintlock rifle uses a piece of flint to ignite gunpowder. The word extends to anything that sparks or ignites: the flint in a lighter, or figuratively, a person with a {heart of flint}—cold and unyielding.

A flintlock is an old firing mechanism that uses a flint striking steel to create sparks, igniting gunpowder to discharge the weapon. By extension, flintlock refers to any gun using this mechanism—muskets, pistols, and rifles from roughly the 17th through mid-19th centuries: {a pair of dueling flintlocks}, {The militia carried flintlock muskets}.

Flintlocks are firearms that use a flint striking steel to create sparks that ignite gunpowder. The mechanism dominated from the 17th through early 19th centuries before percussion caps replaced it. A flintlock is also the firing mechanism itself. The term evokes colonial America, pirates, and Revolutionary War muskets: {The militia shouldered their flintlocks}.

Flinty describes something hard and unyielding, like flint—the stone that produces sparks when struck. A flinty {expression} or flinty {gaze} reveals no warmth or sympathy. Flinty {determination} suggests tough resolve. The word often characterizes people who are stern, unsparing, or emotionally guarded: {a flinty New England grandmother who never hugged anyone}.

Flip captures a quick, snapping motion—turning something over with a flick: flip a {coin}, flip a {pancake}, flip through {pages}. A flip is also a backward somersault. To flip out is to lose control emotionally: {She flipped when she saw the mess}. To flip someone off is to extend the middle finger as an insult. Flip as an adjective means casually disrespectful: {a flip remark}. In real estate, to flip a property is to buy and quickly resell it for profit.

A flipbook is a small book with a series of images that, when pages are rapidly flipped with the thumb, create the illusion of animation. Each page shows a slightly different position, so the sequence appears to move: {She made a flipbook of a stick figure doing a backflip}. The format demonstrates the basic principle behind film and animation. Also spelled flip book.

A flipbook is a small book with a series of images that, when pages are rapidly thumbed, create the illusion of motion—a primitive form of animation. The technique exploits persistence of vision: {She made a flipbook of a stick figure doing a backflip}. Digital flipbooks are electronic documents designed to simulate page-turning.

A flipchart is a large pad of paper mounted on an easel, used for presentations or brainstorming sessions. Pages flip over the top as each is filled, revealing a fresh sheet beneath. Common in meeting rooms and classrooms before digital displays became standard: {She sketched the timeline on the flipchart}.

A flipflop is a flat sandal held on by a Y-shaped strap between the toes, named for the sound it makes when walking. The word also describes a reversal of position or opinion, especially in politics: {The senator's flipflop on immigration cost him votes}. As a verb, to flipflop is to reverse course: {She keeps flipflopping on whether to take the job}. Also spelled flip-flop.

Flipflopped is the past tense of flip-flop, meaning to reverse position or change one's stance, especially on a political issue: {The senator flipflopped on immigration reform}. The term carries a negative connotation, suggesting inconsistency or opportunism rather than thoughtful reconsideration. Also spelled flip-flopped.

Flipflopping is reversing position on an issue, especially in politics. The term implies opportunism or inconsistency rather than thoughtful reconsideration: {Critics accused the senator of flipflopping on immigration}. Someone who flipflops may be called a flipflopper. The word evokes the back-and-forth motion of a flipflop sandal.

Flipflops are flat sandals with a Y-shaped strap that passes between the big toe and second toe, named for the sound they make when walking. Also spelled flip-flops or flip flops. Separately, a flipflop is a reversal of position, especially in politics: {The senator's flipflop on immigration cost her votes}. The verb flipflop means to change stance abruptly or repeatedly.

Flippancy is a lack of proper seriousness or respect, treating weighty matters with casual disregard: {His flippancy during the funeral offended everyone}. The word implies inappropriate levity—joking when gravity is called for. Someone accused of flippancy isn't being funny; they're being thoughtlessly dismissive.

Flippant describes a lack of appropriate seriousness—treating something grave or important with casual disregard: {His flippant remarks about the accident upset everyone}. The word implies the speaker knows better but chooses levity anyway, distinguishing it from mere ignorance. A flippant tone can signal disrespect, defensiveness, or deliberate provocation.

Flipped is the past tense of flip, covering all its senses. Something flipped has been turned over quickly: {She flipped the pancake}. A coin flipped determines chance outcomes. Someone who flipped has lost composure or changed sides abruptly: {He totally flipped when he heard the news}. A flipped house has been renovated for quick resale. To be flipped out is to be shocked or excited.

A flipper is a broad, flat limb adapted for swimming—the appendages of seals, sea turtles, penguins, and whales. Rubber flippers worn by divers mimic this shape to improve propulsion. In pinball, flippers are the paddle-like levers players use to keep the ball in play. Informally, a flipper is someone who buys property to renovate and quickly resell for profit: {House flippers drove up prices in the neighborhood}.

Flippers are the broad, flat limbs that marine mammals like seals and dolphins use for swimming, and by extension, the rubber foot attachments that human swimmers and divers wear to propel themselves through water. The word also names the paddle-like controls on a pinball machine used to bat the ball back into play. In casual use, someone might call their own hands or feet flippers, especially if they're clumsy: {I can't text with these flippers}.

Flipping is a British euphemism for fucking, used as a mild intensifier: {I can't find my flipping keys}. {That's flipping ridiculous}. The word is safe for general audiences while still conveying frustration.

Flips is the plural of flip and the third-person singular verb form. A flip is a quick rotating motion—a pancake flip, a gymnastic flip, a coin flip. To flip is to turn over rapidly: {She flips through channels}, {He flips burgers for a living}. To flip out is to lose composure from excitement or anger. A flip response is dismissive or glib. Flip-flops are sandals that flip against the heel.

The flipside is the reverse or opposite aspect of something. Originally the B-side of a vinyl record—the back of the disc, often featuring a lesser-known track. Now used figuratively for any alternative perspective or consequence: {The flipside of fame is loss of privacy}. Also spelled as two words: flip side.

To flirt is to behave playfully toward someone in a way that suggests romantic or sexual interest, often without serious intent: {She was flirting with the bartender}. A flirt is someone who does this habitually. The word extends to casual engagement: to {flirt with danger} or {flirt with an idea} is to toy with it without full commitment.

Flirtation is playful romantic or sexual attention without serious intent. A flirtation may be a brief exchange of glances and banter, or a longer dalliance that stops short of full involvement: {What started as harmless flirtation became something more}. The word extends to any casual engagement with an idea or activity: {her brief flirtation with vegetarianism}.

Flirtations are instances of playful romantic or sexual attention—the teasing glances, suggestive remarks, and lighthearted advances that signal interest without commitment. The word often implies something superficial or passing: {Their flirtations never developed into anything serious}. A flirtation can also be a brief involvement with an idea or activity: {his flirtation with socialism in college}.

Flirtatious describes behavior that playfully suggests romantic or sexual interest without serious commitment. A flirtatious {smile}, a flirtatious {comment}, a flirtatious {tone}. The word can describe people who habitually flirt or specific actions meant to charm: {She gave him a flirtatious wink}. Someone flirtatious may be genuinely interested or simply enjoying the game.

Flirted is the past tense of flirt—to behave in a playfully romantic or sexually suggestive way without serious intent: {She flirted with him at the party}. Flirted also describes brief engagement with ideas or risks: {He flirted with danger}, {She flirted with the idea of moving abroad}.

Flirting is behaving in a playfully romantic or sexually suggestive way toward someone, typically to gauge or spark their interest. It involves teasing, compliments, eye contact, or light touching: {She was flirting with the bartender all night}. Flirting can be serious pursuit or harmless fun. To {flirt with} an idea or danger is to consider it casually or court it recklessly: {He's been flirting with the idea of quitting}.

Flirts is the plural of flirt and its third-person singular verb form. To flirt is to behave playfully or suggestively toward someone, signaling romantic or sexual interest without serious intent: {She flirts with everyone at parties}. Flirt extends to toying with ideas or risks: {He's been flirting with the idea of moving abroad}, {flirting with danger}. A flirt is someone who flirts habitually.

Flirty describes behavior that playfully suggests romantic or sexual interest without serious commitment. A flirty {smile}, flirty {banter}, a flirty {text message}. The word can describe people, their manner, or things associated with light seduction: {a flirty summer dress}. The tone is usually lighthearted rather than aggressive.

Flit means to move quickly and lightly from place to place, often with a sense of restlessness or impermanence. Birds flit from branch to branch; a thought flits across your mind. In British informal use, to do a flit is to leave hurriedly, especially to avoid paying rent or debts: {They did a flit in the middle of the night}. The word suggests darting, brief movements rather than sustained travel.
clues: Pass swiftly from place to place

definition: Flitting is quick, light movement from place to place—a butterfly flitting among flowers, eyes flitting across a page, thoughts flitting through the mind. The word suggests brief stops without settling: {She flitted from guest to guest at the party}. In Scottish and Northern English dialect, to flit also means to move house, especially hastily or secretly to avoid paying rent.
clues: Moving lightly from place to place

definition: When something floats, it is lighter than what is below it and thus does not seem subject to gravity. Boats float on water, and balloons float in the air. If you float a proposal or idea, you communicate it in order to gauge a reaction. If rumors are floating, people are exchanging them in conversation. If a currency floats, its value is variable. A float is something that is buoyant in water (fishing float, pool float), a soft drink with ice cream (root beer float), and a platform that is part of a parade: The class rode on the float they had decorated.

Floated is the past tense of float. Something floated if it rested on or moved across a liquid surface without sinking: {A leaf floated downstream}. Ideas and rumors float when they circulate informally: {Someone floated the possibility of a merger}. A company floats when it offers shares publicly for the first time. To float a loan is to obtain one.

A floater is something that floats—on water, in air, or in suspension. The word has accumulated specific uses across domains. In the eye, floaters are specks or strands drifting across vision. In insurance, a floater covers property that moves between locations. A floater is a corpse found in water, or a stool that doesn't sink. In workplace slang, a floater is an employee without a fixed assignment who fills in where needed. In politics, a floater is a voter without fixed party loyalty.

Floaters are things that float. In the eye, floaters are small specks or threads that drift across your vision—bits of debris in the vitreous fluid casting shadows on the retina. A floater in a toilet is unflushed feces. In politics, a floater is a voter without fixed party loyalty. In insurance or banking, a floater is a policy or instrument with variable terms. An employee who floats between departments is also a floater.

A floatie is an inflatable device that keeps you buoyant in water—the arm bands children wear while learning to swim, or a pool toy you lounge on. The word is casual and often childish: {Don't forget your floaties!} In toilet humor, a floatie is a piece of feces that won't flush.

Floaties are inflatable armbands worn by children learning to swim, providing buoyancy to keep them afloat: {Don't forget your floaties before you get in the pool}. The term can extend to any small flotation device. Informally, floaties also describes the bits of debris or sediment floating in a liquid: {There are floaties in my water}.

Floating describes something resting on or suspended in liquid, air, or space without sinking or falling: {a floating leaf}, {floating debris}. Extended meanings involve lack of fixed position—a floating {population} moves around, a floating {exchange rate} fluctuates with market forces, and a floating {holiday} falls on different dates. In computing, floating-point numbers handle decimals. Something that floats drifts without anchor: {a floating feeling of unreality}.

A floatplane is an aircraft equipped with pontoons instead of wheels, allowing it to take off from and land on water. Unlike flying boats, which have boat-shaped hulls, floatplanes are conventional aircraft with floats attached beneath the fuselage: {The floatplane taxied across the lake to the dock}. Common in remote areas with many lakes and few runways.

Floats are things that rest on a liquid's surface without sinking. A parade float is a decorated platform on wheels—originally so-called because early versions were pulled through flooded streets. A float is also a buoyant device: {The fishing line had a float to signal bites}. In beverages, a float is ice cream bobbing in soda: {root beer float}. The verb covers staying buoyant, moving gently, or letting currency values fluctuate freely. {Whatever floats your boat} means whatever pleases you.

Floaty describes something light and airy, tending to drift or hover rather than sink or settle. A floaty dress billows gently; a floaty feeling suggests pleasant lightness or dreaminess. The word often carries a whimsical quality: {She felt floaty after the massage}. In British slang, floaties are inflatable armbands children wear while learning to swim.

A flock is a group of animals, especially birds or sheep, that stay together: {a flock of geese}, {a flock of sheep}. The word extends to groups of people, particularly those under spiritual guidance—a pastor's flock. To flock is to gather or move as a group: {Tourists flock to the beaches in summer}. Separately, flock refers to tufts of fiber used for stuffing or creating textured surfaces on wallpaper and fabric.

Flocked describes a surface covered with soft, velvety fibers to create texture. Flocked wallpaper has a raised fuzzy pattern. Flocked Christmas trees are coated with artificial snow. The technique involves applying short fibers to an adhesive-covered surface: {flocked velvet}, {flocked gift boxes}. Separately, flocked is the past tense of flock—to gather in a crowd: {Tourists flocked to the beach}.

Flocking describes the behavior of creatures moving together as a group—birds flocking to a feeder, tourists flocking to a new attraction. The word captures both the gathering and the collective movement: {Fans flocked to the stadium}. In manufacturing, flocking is a technique of applying short fibers to a surface to create a velvet-like texture: {the flocking on a jewelry box}.

Flocks is the plural of flock—groups of birds, sheep, or goats that move together. By extension, any group moving or gathering as one: {Tourists arrived in flocks}. A pastor's congregation is also a flock. The verb means to gather or move in crowds: {Fans flocked to the stadium}.

A floe is a sheet of floating ice, typically broken off from a larger mass such as a glacier or ice shelf. Floes range from small fragments to enormous platforms spanning miles, drifting with ocean currents and winds. The term appears most often in the phrase {ice floe} and in discussions of polar regions, where floes provide habitat for seals and polar bears. {The expedition's ship navigated carefully through the floes.}

Floes is the plural of floe, a sheet of floating ice. Ice floes drift on polar seas, ranging from small fragments to vast expanses miles across. {The ship navigated carefully between the floes.} The word appears almost exclusively in descriptions of arctic or antarctic waters.

Flog means to beat severely, typically with a whip or rod as punishment: {The sailor was flogged for desertion}. The word extends to any harsh criticism or relentless pushing: {Don't flog a dead horse}. In British slang, to flog something is to sell it, often aggressively or illicitly: {He's flogging watches down at the market}.

Flogged is the past tense of flog, meaning to beat severely with a whip or rod as punishment: {The sailor was flogged for insubordination}. Figuratively, to flog something is to promote it relentlessly: {She's been flogging her new book on every podcast}. In British slang, to flog is to sell, often hastily or cheaply: {He flogged his old car for a few hundred quid}.

A flogger is a multi-tailed whip used for striking, with origins in corporal punishment but now most commonly associated with BDSM practices. The tails—usually leather, suede, or rubber—deliver sensation ranging from light sting to heavy thud depending on material and force. In historical contexts, floggers were instruments of discipline on ships and in prisons. A flogger is also simply one who flogs: {a flogger of dead horses}, {a flogger of stolen goods}.

Flogging is beating someone with a whip, rod, or cane, typically as punishment. Historically common in military and naval discipline, flogging remains a legal penalty in some countries. The word extends to any severe beating: {The team took a flogging in the semifinals}. In British slang, to flog something is to sell it, often aggressively or illicitly: {He was flogging watches on the corner}.

Floggings are beatings administered as punishment, typically with a whip, rod, or cane. The term evokes historical contexts—naval discipline, colonial justice, slavery—where such corporal punishment was routine: {The captain ordered twenty lashes; floggings were common for minor infractions}. Figuratively, a flogging is any severe defeat or harsh criticism: {The team took a flogging in the semifinals}.

A flood is an overflow of water that submerges normally dry land. Rivers flood when rainfall or snowmelt exceeds their banks. The word extends to any overwhelming quantity: a flood of {refugees}, a flood of {emails}, a flood of {emotions}. To flood is to inundate or overwhelm: {Orders flooded in after the commercial aired}. {The flood} often refers to the biblical deluge survived by Noah.

Flooded describes something overwhelmed by water or, figuratively, by abundance. A flooded basement has water where it shouldn't be. A flooded market has too much supply. To be flooded with requests or emotions is to receive more than you can handle: {My inbox is flooded}. A flooded engine has too much fuel to start properly.

A floodgate is a gate controlling water flow, especially one that holds back a river or reservoir. Opening the floodgates releases a rush of water. The figurative use dominates: {The ruling opened the floodgates to lawsuits}. To open the floodgates is to remove a barrier that had been holding something back, typically unleashing an overwhelming quantity.

Floodgates are gates controlling water flow from a reservoir, dam, or canal—opened to release excess water, closed to hold it back. The figurative sense dominates modern usage: to {open the floodgates} is to remove barriers that were holding something back, typically unleashing an overwhelming quantity: {The ruling opened the floodgates to lawsuits}.

Flooding is an overflow of water onto normally dry land. Rivers flood when rainfall exceeds their capacity; coastal areas flood from storm surges. The word extends to any overwhelming influx: {The company was flooded with applications}. In psychology, flooding is a therapeutic technique that confronts patients with intense exposure to what they fear.

A floodlight is a powerful lamp that casts broad, intense illumination over a wide area. Floodlights illuminate outdoor spaces—stadiums, parking lots, building facades, construction sites. To floodlight is to illuminate with such lights: {The cathedral was floodlit at night}. Figuratively, to turn the floodlights on something is to subject it to intense scrutiny.

Floodlights are powerful lamps that cast broad, intense illumination over a wide area. They light up sports fields, construction sites, building facades, and outdoor stages. To floodlight something is to illuminate it with such lights: {The stadium was floodlit for the night game}. Security floodlights often activate by motion sensor.

A floodplain is the flat land along a river that naturally floods when water levels rise. Rivers deposit sediment here over time, creating fertile soil that attracts agriculture despite the flooding risk. {They built the house on the floodplain, so insurance was expensive.} Floodplains serve as natural overflow areas, and developing them increases flood damage downstream.

Floodplains are flat lands adjacent to rivers that periodically flood when water levels rise. These areas absorb overflow during heavy rains or snowmelt, acting as natural buffers. Floodplains are typically fertile from deposited sediment, making them attractive for agriculture despite the risk: {Houses built on floodplains often require special insurance}.

Floods are overflows of water onto normally dry land—rivers breaching banks, storm surges swamping coasts, heavy rains overwhelming drainage. The word extends to any overwhelming quantity: {a flood of emails}, {a flood of memories}. To flood is to inundate: {Light flooded the room}. {The market was flooded with cheap imports}. The biblical Flood was the deluge survived by Noah.

Floodwaters are the waters that spread over normally dry land during a flood, whether from overflowing rivers, storm surges, or heavy rainfall that overwhelms drainage systems. The term emphasizes the destructive, uncontrolled nature of the water—it's not just water but water out of place, threatening homes, roads, and lives. {Floodwaters reached the second floor of many downtown buildings.} {Residents were warned not to walk through floodwaters due to hidden hazards.}

The basic and original meaning of floor is still the most prevalent: the lower, flat, horizontal surface of a room. Words that precede floor usually tell us something about its composition (marble floor, bamboo floor), its level in a multistory building (second floor, ninth floor), or its function (trading floor, dance floor). Figurative uses of floor usually draw on its quality of being at the bottom of something (ocean floor), or the lower limit of something, such as a price or bid. Someone who has the floor has the right to address a meeting or assembly. If you floor someone, you confound or surprise them. #

A floorboard is one of the long wooden planks that make up a floor. The word often appears in plural: {The old floorboards creaked underfoot}. In a car, the floorboard is the floor of the passenger compartment: {She found the lost earring under the floorboard}. To {put the pedal to the floorboard} is to accelerate fully.

Floorboards are the long wooden planks that form a floor. In older houses, floorboards may creak or develop gaps. The term often appears in contexts of concealment—money hidden {under the floorboards}, or the telltale heart beneath them. In a car, the floorboard is the floor of the passenger compartment: {He floored it, pressing the accelerator to the floorboard}.

Floored is the past tense of floor, with meanings that follow from knocking someone to the ground. To be floored by a punch is to be knocked down. More commonly, floored describes being stunned or astonished: {I was absolutely floored when she said yes}. The overwhelming surprise leaves you metaphorically flat on your back.

Flooring is material used to cover a floor—hardwood, tile, carpet, vinyl, or laminate. The term covers both the material itself and the finished surface: {We're putting in new flooring throughout the house}. Flooring also names the work of installing it. In boxing or fighting, flooring someone means knocking them to the ground.

A floorplan is a diagram showing the layout of a building or room as viewed from above, with walls, doors, windows, and fixtures drawn to scale. Real estate listings typically include floorplans so buyers can visualize the space: {The floorplan showed an open kitchen flowing into the living area}. Also spelled as two words: floor plan.

Floors are the surfaces you walk on inside a building—the ground level of each story. A floor is also a story itself: {the third floor}. The floor of a legislative chamber is where members sit and debate; to {have the floor} is to be recognized to speak. A floor can be a minimum level: {wage floor}, {price floor}. To floor someone is to knock them down, or to stun them completely: {The news floored me}. To floor it means to press a vehicle's accelerator to the floor.

A floorshow is live entertainment performed on the floor of a nightclub, cabaret, or restaurant rather than on a raised stage—singers, dancers, comedians, or specialty acts performing among or near the diners. The format peaked mid-twentieth century but persists in venues offering dinner theater or cabaret nights: {The jazz club's floorshow starts at ten}.

A floozie is a woman considered promiscuous or of loose morals, often one who pursues men for money or favors. The term is mildly derogatory and old-fashioned, carrying a whiff of 1940s slang: {He was seen around town with some floozie}. Also spelled floozy.

Floozies is the plural of floozy, a dated and mildly derogatory term for a woman considered promiscuous or of loose morals. The word carries a lighthearted, almost campy tone compared to harsher alternatives: {He spent his evenings with floozies and ne'er-do-wells}. It suggests disapproval without real venom.

A floozy is a woman considered sexually promiscuous or of loose morals. The term is mildly derogatory and old-fashioned, suggesting someone cheap or disreputable: {He was seen around town with some floozy half his age}. Sometimes spelled floosie or floosy.

Flop captures the motion and sound of something falling heavily and loosely: {The fish flopped on the deck}, {She flopped onto the couch}. Things that flop are limp, ungraceful, or exhausted. A flop is also a complete failure—a movie, play, or product that performs far below expectations: {The film was a box-office flop}. To flop is to fail this way: {The sequel flopped despite heavy marketing}. In poker, the flop is the first three community cards dealt face-up.

A flophouse is a cheap lodging house offering minimal accommodations—often just a bed or cot in a shared room—typically catering to transients, the homeless, or those down on their luck. The term suggests squalid conditions: {He spent a week in a flophouse before finding work}. Now somewhat dated, as such establishments have largely disappeared.

Flophouses are cheap lodging houses offering minimal accommodations—typically just a bed in a shared room—for transients, vagrants, and the down-on-their-luck. The term evokes Skid Row districts and Depression-era poverty: {He spent his last dollar on a flophouse bed}. The singular flophouse remains more common.

Flopped is the past tense of flop. Something that flopped fell or dropped heavily and loosely: {He flopped onto the couch}. A project, performance, or product that flopped failed conspicuously: {The movie flopped at the box office}. In poker, the flop is the first three community cards dealt, so flopped describes what appeared: {She flopped a full house}.

A flopper is someone or something that flops. In sports, especially basketball and soccer, a flopper is a player who dramatically falls or feigns injury to draw a foul: {He's such a flopper—barely got touched and hit the floor like he'd been shot}. The term carries contempt, suggesting the player lacks integrity. More generally, flopper can describe anything that flops physically or fails commercially.

Flopping is falling or dropping heavily and loosely: {He came home and flopped on the couch}. A fish flops when pulled from water. Something that flops fails badly: {The movie flopped at the box office}. In basketball and soccer, flopping is exaggerating contact to draw a foul—falling dramatically when barely touched.

Floppy means soft and hanging loosely, tending to flop or fall limply: {a floppy hat}, {floppy ears on a basset hound}. The word suggests something flexible rather than rigid, often endearingly so. A floppy disk—now largely obsolete—was a thin, flexible magnetic storage medium, distinguished from hard drives by its bendable casing.

Flops is the plural of flop—a heavy, flopping fall or movement, or something that fails badly. A movie that bombs at the box office is among the flops of the year. Flip-flops are often shortened to flops: {I packed my flops for the beach}. As a verb, flops is the third-person singular: {He flops onto the couch after work}. (All-caps FLOPS is a computing term.)

Flora is plant life, especially all the plants of a particular region or period: {the flora of the Amazon basin}, {intestinal flora}. The term pairs with fauna (animal life) when describing an ecosystem's living things: {the flora and fauna of the Galápagos}. In medicine, flora refers to microorganisms living in or on the body: {gut flora}. (Capitalized Flora is the Roman goddess of flowers or a given name.)

Floral describes things relating to or resembling flowers. A floral {arrangement} is a display of cut flowers. Floral {patterns} feature flower designs on fabric, wallpaper, or other surfaces. A floral {scent} smells of flowers—perfumes and wines often have floral notes. {The bridesmaids wore floral dresses.}

Florentine as a common adjective describes a style of cooking involving spinach, typically with eggs or in a cream sauce: {eggs florentine}, {chicken florentine}. The dish is served on a bed of spinach or incorporates it prominently. A florentine is also a thin cookie made with nuts and candied fruit, often coated with chocolate on one side. (Capitalized Florentine relates to Florence, Italy.)

A floret is one of the small flowers that make up a composite flower head, or one of the small branchlike pieces of broccoli or cauliflower: {Break the broccoli into florets before steaming}. The word is simply a diminutive of flower.
clues: One piece of a broccoli head

definition: Florets are the small individual flowers that make up a larger flower head, or the small pieces into which broccoli and cauliflower naturally divide. In botany, a sunflower head contains hundreds of tiny florets. In cooking, you cut broccoli into florets for even cooking: {Steam the florets until tender}.

A florist is a person who sells flowers and arranges them into bouquets, corsages, and decorative displays. Florists work from shops that also sell houseplants, vases, and related gifts: {I ordered a dozen roses from the florist}. The term can refer to either the person or the business itself.

Florists are people who sell flowers and floral arrangements, or the shops where they work. A florist designs bouquets, corsages, and decorative displays for weddings, funerals, and other occasions: {I ordered the centerpieces from a florist downtown}. The singular florist refers to the person or the business.

Floss is thin thread used to clean between teeth, or the act of using it: {I need to floss more often}. The word extends to anything similarly wispy—candy floss (British for cotton candy), silk floss from certain seed pods. In slang, to floss means to show off wealth or status, displaying expensive possessions conspicuously: {He was flossing his new watch on Instagram}.

Flossing is cleaning between teeth with dental floss—a thin thread worked back and forth to remove food particles and plaque. The verb also describes a showy display of wealth or success: {He's always flossing his new watch on Instagram}. This slang sense, from hip-hop culture, suggests polishing oneself to a shine, like teeth.

A flotilla is a small fleet of ships or boats, typically naval vessels operating together: {a flotilla of destroyers patrolled the coast}. The word often suggests a modest or informal grouping rather than a grand armada. It extends to any collection of small watercraft: {a flotilla of kayaks set out from the marina}.

Flotillas is the plural of flotilla, a small fleet of boats or ships. The term often describes naval squadrons or groups of small vessels moving together: {A flotilla of fishing boats headed out at dawn}. It extends to any collection of watercraft: {The harbor was crowded with a flotilla of yachts and sailboats}.

Flotsam is debris floating on water after a shipwreck—cargo, wreckage, or other materials cast overboard or washed away. In legal and maritime contexts, flotsam technically refers to goods lost accidentally, distinguished from jetsam (deliberately thrown overboard). The phrase {flotsam and jetsam} has become a fixed expression for any miscellaneous debris, rubbish, or odds and ends: {The garage was full of flotsam and jetsam from decades of neglect}. Figuratively, flotsam can refer to people cast adrift by circumstance: {the flotsam of war}.

Flounce has two unrelated meanings. One is a dramatic, exaggerated movement expressing annoyance or impatience: {She flounced out of the room}. The motion suggests swishing skirts and theatrical displeasure. The other flounce is a wide ruffle or gathered strip of fabric attached to clothing or furnishings: {a skirt with three flounces}.

Flounced is the past tense of flounce, meaning to move with exaggerated, impatient motions—typically expressing anger or indignation: {She flounced out of the room after the argument}. The word suggests dramatic, attention-seeking movement. Separately, flounced describes fabric trimmed with a flounce—a wide ruffle or gathered strip: {a flounced skirt}.

Flounces names both a movement and a decoration. To flounce is to move with exaggerated, impatient motions—storming off dramatically: {She flounced out of the room when no one agreed with her}. A flounce is also a wide ruffle or gathered strip of fabric sewn to a skirt or curtain, adding fullness and movement. The connection may be visual—both involve emphatic swishing.

Flouncing is moving with exaggerated, dramatic motions that broadcast displeasure or self-importance. Someone who flounces out of a room wants everyone to notice their exit: {She went flouncing off after the argument}. Online, flouncing describes announcing a dramatic departure from a community or platform, often with grievances: {He made a big flouncing post about leaving Twitter}. Separately, flouncing is attaching decorative ruffled fabric strips to clothing or furnishings.

Flouncy describes something decorated with flounces—ruffled strips of fabric that create a frilly, layered effect: {a flouncy skirt}, {flouncy sleeves}. The word often carries connotations of feminine excess or theatrical flair. Applied to behavior or movement, flouncy suggests exaggerated, dramatic gestures: {She made a flouncy exit}.

Flounder works as both noun and verb with unrelated origins. The noun is a flatfish with both eyes on one side of its head, prized as food. The verb means to struggle clumsily or proceed with difficulty: {The company floundered after losing its biggest client}. Someone who flounders thrashes about ineffectively, whether literally in water or figuratively in conversation, business, or life. Often confused with founder, which means to sink or fail completely.

Floundered is the past tense of flounder, meaning to struggle clumsily or proceed with difficulty. A person flounders when wading through mud, speaking without preparation, or trying to manage an unfamiliar situation: {She floundered through the interview questions}. The word suggests awkward, ineffective effort rather than complete failure. Not to be confused with foundered, which means sank or collapsed entirely.

Floundering is struggling awkwardly or making clumsy attempts without clear direction. A fish flounders when pulled from water; a person flounders when overwhelmed or unprepared: {The candidate floundered when asked about foreign policy}. The word suggests helpless, ineffective effort—thrashing rather than progressing. Not to be confused with foundering, which means sinking or collapsing entirely.

Flounders are flatfish that live on the ocean floor, with both eyes on one side of their bodies. Several species go by the name. As a verb, to flounder is to struggle clumsily—thrashing about like a fish out of water: {The company floundered after losing its CEO}. Not to be confused with founder, which means to sink or fail completely.

Flour is grain that has been ground into powder, typically wheat, used as the foundation for breads, pastries, and countless baked goods. Different grains produce different flours—rice flour, corn flour, almond flour—each with distinct properties for cooking. All-purpose flour handles most kitchen tasks, while bread flour has more protein for chewier results and cake flour less for tender crumb. As a verb, to flour means to dust a surface or food with flour: {Flour the pan before pouring in the batter}.

To flourish is to thrive, grow well, or succeed. Plants flourish when they have the right combination of light, water, and soil nutrients. Trade flourishes when economic and social conditions promote it. Your career flourishes when you obtain successive advancements. To flourish an object is to display or handle it so as to attract attention. A flourish is an instance of this, or in music or architecture, a small decorative element: Four ruffles and flourishes precede the playing of “Hail to the Chief.”

Flourished is the past tense of flourish, meaning to thrive, prosper, or be at the peak of activity and influence. The word appears most often in biographical and historical contexts to indicate when someone lived or when something was most active: {The philosopher flourished in fifth-century Athens}. When exact dates are unknown, flourished (often abbreviated fl.) gives an approximate period: {fl. 1450}.

Flourishes connects to thriving and decorative display. Plants flourish when they grow vigorously; people flourish when they prosper. The word also names showy gestures or ornamental additions: a {signature with flourishes}, a {trumpet flourish}, a speech delivered {with rhetorical flourishes}. To do something {with a flourish} is to add dramatic flair: {He opened the door with a flourish}.

Flourishing describes vigorous growth and success—thriving in a way that suggests health, vitality, and abundance. Plants flourish in good soil; businesses flourish in favorable markets; artists flourish when given creative freedom. The word carries more energy than merely surviving: {The garden is flourishing after all this rain}. As a noun, a flourishing refers to a period of prosperity or peak development.

Flouting is openly disregarding or treating with contempt—usually rules, conventions, or authority: {flouting the dress code}, {flouting international law}. The word implies brazenness rather than mere violation; someone who flouts doesn't just break the rules but does so conspicuously. Often confused with flaunting, which means showing off.

Flow is related to fluid, which provides a good way to connect its various meanings, since fluids, by their nature, flow. Anything that moves continuously in a natural way, propelled by gravity or some other force, can be said to flow. The noun flow describes an instance of this, or the phenomenon of flowing generally:, as in the flow of a river, of music, or of emotions. Cash flow usually designates a readily available money that assures solvency.
