If a process is flowing, the connotation is usually positive, suggesting that things are proceeding in an easy and desirable way.

A flowchart is a diagram that maps out a process or system using shapes connected by arrows. Rectangles typically represent steps, diamonds represent decision points, and arrows show the sequence of operations. Flowcharts are standard tools in programming, business analysis, and project planning: {The flowchart showed where the approval process was getting stuck}.

Flowcharts are diagrams that map out a process or system using shapes connected by arrows. Rectangles typically represent steps or actions, diamonds represent decision points, and arrows show the sequence of flow. They're used in programming, business planning, and technical documentation to visualize workflows: {The flowchart shows what happens when a user clicks submit}. To flowchart something is to diagram it this way.

Flowed is the past tense of flow. Liquids flow when they move smoothly and continuously: {Water flowed from the tap}. Traffic, electricity, and conversation flow when they move without obstruction. Ideas flow when they come easily: {The words flowed onto the page}. Hair or fabric flows when it hangs loosely and gracefully.

The showy part of a plant that bears reproductive organs is called the flower. In less technical usage, flower designates such plant parts, severed from their roots, that are appreciated for their color, scent, and attractiveness: I sent Mom some flowers for Mother’s Day. In gardening, flowers are attractive, flowering plants” Why don’t you plant some flowers out front? The verb flower, when a plant is the subject, means to produce flowers: are the day lilies flowering yet? Other things may be said to flower when they develop in a desirable way: Their unlikely friendship flowered into love.

A flowerbed is a plot of ground, usually in a garden or yard, where flowers or ornamental plants are cultivated. Flowerbeds are typically bordered or edged to separate them from lawns or pathways: {She planted tulips along the flowerbed by the front walk}. Also spelled as two words: flower bed.

Flowerbeds are cultivated plots of ground where flowers are grown, typically in gardens or landscaped areas. They're usually bordered by lawn, stone, or edging to define their shape: {She planted tulips along the flowerbeds in front of the house}. Also spelled as two words: flower beds.

Flowering describes plants that are producing flowers, or the process itself: {The flowering of the cherry trees draws crowds each spring}. Figuratively, flowering marks the period when something reaches full development or peak expression: {the flowering of the Renaissance}, {the flowering of her talent}. As an adjective, it distinguishes plants that bloom from those that don't: {flowering shrubs}.
clues: In the stage of producing blossoms

definition: A flowerpot is a container, typically made of clay or plastic, used for growing plants. The drainage hole at the bottom distinguishes it from decorative planters. {She repotted the orchid into a larger flowerpot.}

Flowerpots are containers for growing plants, typically made of clay, plastic, or ceramic with a drainage hole at the bottom. The term usually implies a modest-sized vessel for a single plant, distinguishing it from larger planters or garden beds: {She lined the windowsill with flowerpots of herbs}.

Flowers are the reproductive structures of flowering plants, typically colorful and fragrant to attract pollinators. Cut flowers serve as gifts and decorations: {She brought flowers to the hospital}. To flower is to bloom or flourish: {The cherry trees flowered early this year}. Figuratively, the flower of something is its finest part or period: {the flower of youth}.

Flowery describes something covered with or resembling flowers: {a flowery meadow}, {flowery wallpaper}. More often, flowery characterizes language or style that is elaborately ornate—full of decorative words and figures of speech: {flowery prose}, {a flowery speech}. The implication is usually unfavorable, suggesting excess or insincerity rather than eloquence.

Flowing describes continuous, smooth movement like water in a stream. A flowing river moves steadily; flowing robes or hair hang loose and move gracefully. Flowing prose or conversation proceeds without interruption or awkwardness. The word suggests ease and naturalness: {Her flowing handwriting filled the page}. Traffic can be flowing or stopped.

Flown is the past participle of fly. It appears with auxiliary verbs: {I've never flown first class}, {The birds had flown south}. Something that has flown the coop has escaped or departed. Time flies, and before you know it, years have flown by.

Flows is the third-person singular of flow, describing smooth continuous movement. Water flows downhill, traffic flows through intersections, conversation flows naturally. In music and hip-hop, flows refers to a rapper's rhythmic delivery and cadence: {Her flows are unmatched}. Cash flow describes money moving through a business. When something flows, it moves without interruption or resistance.

Flu is short for influenza, a contagious viral infection affecting the respiratory system. Symptoms include fever, body aches, fatigue, and coughing. The word often appears loosely for any illness with similar symptoms: {I think I'm coming down with the flu}. Flu season peaks in winter months. The {stomach flu} is a different illness—gastroenteritis rather than influenza.

Flub means to bungle or botch something, especially a performance or action that should go smoothly: {She flubbed her lines during the live broadcast}. As a noun, a flub is the mistake itself—a fumbled catch, a mispronounced word, a missed cue. The word suggests minor embarrassment rather than serious failure.

Flubbed is the past tense of flub, meaning to botch or bungle something—to make a clumsy mistake in performance or execution. An actor flubs a line by forgetting or mangling it. A politician flubs a speech. {He flubbed the easy catch and the runner scored.} The word suggests minor, embarrassing error rather than serious failure.

Flubbing is making a clumsy mistake, especially in performance or speech—botching a line, fumbling a catch, bungling a presentation. The word suggests minor incompetence rather than serious failure: {She kept flubbing her lines during rehearsal}. A flub is the mistake itself: {His flub on the candidate's name went viral}.

Flubs are mistakes or blunders, especially clumsy ones in performance or speech. An actor flubs a line by forgetting or stumbling over it. A politician flubs a question by answering poorly. The word suggests minor, embarrassing errors rather than serious failures: {The interview was full of flubs}. {He flubbed the punchline}.

Fluctuate means to rise and fall irregularly, to shift back and forth between states or values. Prices fluctuate with market conditions. Weight fluctuates throughout the day. Moods fluctuate. The word implies repeated variation rather than a single change—not a permanent shift but ongoing instability: {Her confidence fluctuated wildly during the interview}.

Fluctuation is a rise and fall or back-and-forth movement, especially when irregular or unpredictable: {fluctuations in temperature}, {market fluctuations}, {mood fluctuations}. The word emphasizes variation over time rather than a single change—prices don't just drop, they fluctuate up and down. Minor fluctuations are normal; wild fluctuations suggest instability.

Fluctuations are irregular rises and falls in level, amount, or intensity. Stock prices experience daily fluctuations. Body weight shows natural fluctuations. {The fluctuations in her mood made her hard to work with.} The word implies movement within a range rather than a steady trend in one direction—variation around some norm or average.

A flue is a duct or channel that carries smoke, hot air, or exhaust gases from a fireplace, furnace, or boiler to the outside: {The chimney flue needs cleaning}. By extension, flue refers to any passage for conveying heat, as in a heat exchanger. A flue can also be the pipe of an organ or the fishing net called a flue net.

Fluency is smooth, effortless flow—especially in language. A fluent speaker of French produces speech without halting or searching for words. Fluency extends beyond languages to any skill performed with ease: {She played the sonata with remarkable fluency}. Reading fluency combines speed, accuracy, and proper expression. The word implies not just competence but grace in execution.

Fluent describes smooth, effortless flow. A fluent speaker of a language uses it with ease and naturalness: {She's fluent in Mandarin}. Fluent speech or writing moves without hesitation or awkwardness. The word extends to any graceful, uninterrupted movement: {fluent brushstrokes}, {fluent gestures}. Fluency implies mastery sufficient to operate without conscious effort.

Fluently describes doing something with smooth, effortless skill—especially speaking or writing a language: {She speaks French fluently}. The word implies not just competence but ease, without hesitation or struggle. Beyond language, fluently applies to any practiced ability performed without apparent effort: {He reads music fluently}.
clues: As if born to the language

definition: Fluff is soft, light, airy material—the downy stuff that gathers under furniture or floats off dandelions. To fluff a pillow is to shake it loose and full. Fluff also means trivial or insubstantial content: {The article was mostly fluff}. To fluff lines is to bungle them during a performance. {She fluffed her entrance cue}.

A fluffball is something small, round, and covered in soft fur or fibers—a kitten, a pom-pom, a dust bunny. The term is affectionate when applied to animals: {Our new puppy is just a little fluffball}. It can also describe a person who seems soft, harmless, or lacking substance.

Fluffballs are small, soft, rounded masses of fluffy material—lint, fur, or fiber that collects in pockets, under furniture, or in dryer vents. The term extends affectionately to anything similarly round and soft: a kitten, a pomeranian, a baby chick. {Look at that little fluffball!} The singular fluffball is more common.

Fluffed is the past tense of fluff, meaning to shake or puff something up to make it softer and fuller: {She fluffed the pillows before the guests arrived}. In performance contexts, to fluff a line is to bungle or forget it: {He fluffed his opening monologue}. In British slang, fluffed can mean botched generally: {They fluffed the presentation}.

A fluffernutter is a sandwich made with peanut butter and marshmallow fluff, typically on white bread. The combination is sweet, sticky, and nostalgic—a childhood favorite in American homes: {I packed a fluffernutter for my kid's lunch}. The word blends fluff (the Marshmallow Fluff brand) with peanut butter.

Fluffing is shaking or patting something to make it fuller and softer: {fluffing the pillows}, {fluffing her hair}. Extended uses describe padding or inflating: {fluffing up a résumé}, {fluffing the numbers}. In pornography, fluffing refers to keeping male performers aroused between takes—a job sometimes assigned to a dedicated person called a fluffer.

Fluffs is the verb form of fluff—to shake or puff something to make it fuller or softer: {She fluffs the pillows before guests arrive}. An actor who fluffs a line delivers it badly or forgets it. As a noun, fluffs are bits of soft, downy material or minor mistakes: {lint fluffs on his jacket}, {a few fluffs in an otherwise solid performance}.

Fluffy describes something soft, light, and airy—covered with or resembling soft fibers or down: {a fluffy kitten}, {fluffy clouds}, {fluffy towels fresh from the dryer}. Food that's fluffy has been aerated to lightness: {fluffy scrambled eggs}, {fluffy pancakes}. Figuratively, fluffy content lacks substance or depth: {The article was entertaining but fluffy}.

Fluid describes something that flows—liquids and gases are fluids, distinguished from solids by their ability to move and change shape. The word extends to anything similarly flowing or changeable: a fluid {motion}, fluid {boundaries}, a fluid {situation}. Fluid can also mean not fixed or settled: {The plans are still fluid}. Gender fluid describes identity that shifts rather than remaining constant.

Fluidity is the quality of flowing or moving smoothly, like a liquid. The term applies to physical substances—the fluidity of water versus honey—but extends to anything that shifts easily: fluidity of {movement}, fluidity of {thought}, {gender fluidity}. The opposite is rigidity. Where flexibility suggests bending without breaking, fluidity suggests continuous, unimpeded change.

Fluids are substances that flow—liquids and gases, as opposed to solids. The term appears often in medical and mechanical contexts: {Drink plenty of fluids}, {Check your car's fluids}. Body fluids include blood, urine, and saliva. The adjective fluid describes smooth, uninterrupted movement or flexibility: {fluid motion}, {a fluid situation}.

Fluke has two distinct origins in English. One fluke is a stroke of luck—an outcome achieved by chance rather than skill: {It was a total fluke that we ran into each other}. A fluke can also be a lucky shot in billiards or a fortuitous catch in fishing. The other fluke refers to flat, pointed structures: the triangular blade of an anchor, the lobe of a whale's tail, or a parasitic flatworm that infests livers and intestines.

Flukes names several unrelated things. The flat triangular parts of an anchor are flukes. The lobes of a whale's tail are flukes. A flatworm parasite—especially one infecting livestock livers—is a fluke. And a fluke is a stroke of luck, usually good: {It was a fluke that we met}. Something achieved by chance rather than skill is fluky.

Flukey describes something achieved or occurring by luck rather than skill—a flukey {goal}, a flukey {win}. The word carries a slightly dismissive tone, suggesting the outcome was undeserved or unrepeatable. Also spelled fluky. Both derive from fluke, a stroke of luck.

Fluky describes something achieved or occurring by luck rather than skill or design: {a fluky shot that bounced off the post and in}, {a fluky win}. The word suggests the outcome was improbable or undeserved—more accident than accomplishment. Also spelled flukey.

A flume is an artificial channel for directing water, typically a wooden trough or chute used in mining, logging, or irrigation. Water flumes once carried logs down mountainsides. At amusement parks, a flume is a water ride where boats travel through such channels: {The log flume splashed everyone in the front row}. A flume can also be a natural gorge with a stream running through it.

A flume is an artificial channel for conveying water, typically a wooden or metal trough used to transport logs, carry water for mining operations, or direct flow in industrial settings. The term also applies to water park rides that send riders sliding down steep, winding channels. Natural ravines with streams running through them are sometimes called flumes as well. {The old mining flume still clings to the mountainside.}

To flummox is to bewilder or confuse someone so thoroughly they don't know how to respond: {The question completely flummoxed him}. The word suggests being thrown off balance, left speechless or unable to proceed. Flummoxed captures that state of bewildered paralysis: {I was flummoxed by the instructions}.

Flummoxed means bewildered or confused, typically by something unexpected or hard to understand. The word has a slightly old-fashioned, whimsical quality: {I was completely flummoxed by the instructions}. To flummox someone is to perplex them thoroughly.

Flummoxing is the present participle of flummox, meaning to confuse or perplex completely. Something flummoxing bewilders you, leaves you unable to proceed or respond: {The instructions were flummoxing—I couldn't make sense of them}. The word has an informal, slightly comic tone.

Flung is the past tense and past participle of fling. To fling is to throw forcefully or carelessly: {She flung open the door}. The word suggests sudden, often emotional action—you fling yourself onto a bed, fling accusations at someone, or fling caution to the wind.

Flunk means to fail, especially an academic test or course: {I flunked chemistry twice}. A teacher can flunk a student by giving a failing grade. To {flunk out} is to be dismissed from school for poor performance. The word is informal and predominantly American. It carries a blunt, slightly shameful connotation that "fail" lacks.

Flunked is the past tense of flunk, meaning to fail an examination or course: {I flunked the midterm}, {She flunked out of college}. To flunk someone is to give them a failing grade: {The professor flunked half the class}. The word is informal and predominantly American.

A flunkey is a servant, especially one in livery who performs minor duties. The word extends to anyone who does someone else's bidding in a servile way: {The CEO surrounded himself with flunkeys who never challenged his decisions}. The spelling flunky is equally common. The tone is always dismissive—flunkeys lack independence or dignity.

Flunkeys is the plural of flunkey, a variant spelling of flunky. A flunkey is a servant in livery, or more broadly, someone who performs menial tasks for another. The word often carries contempt, suggesting excessive subservience or slavish devotion to a powerful person: {The CEO surrounded himself with flunkeys who never challenged his decisions}.

A flunkie is a person who does menial or trivial tasks for someone more important—an assistant or lackey, often one perceived as servile or sycophantic: {He surrounded himself with flunkies who never challenged him}. The term is dismissive, suggesting someone who lacks independence or self-respect. Also spelled flunky.

Flunkies is the plural of flunky, a person who does menial tasks or follows someone slavishly. The word carries contempt—flunkies lack independence and do others' bidding: {The CEO surrounded himself with flunkies who never challenged him}. Originally it meant a liveried servant, which explains the dismissive tone. Also spelled flunkeys.

Flunking is failing, especially failing a test or course in school: {I'm flunking algebra}, {She flunked out of college}. To flunk someone is to give them a failing grade. The word is informal and primarily American. Outside academics, flunking means failing to meet any standard: {He flunked the interview}.

A flunky is a person who performs menial tasks or follows orders without question—a servant, lackey, or subordinate. The term is usually dismissive, suggesting someone who lacks independence or dignity in their service: {The CEO surrounded himself with flunkies who never challenged him}. Also spelled flunkey.

Fluorescence is the emission of light by a substance that has absorbed radiation, where the emitted light typically has a longer wavelength than the absorbed light. The effect is immediate and stops when the light source is removed, distinguishing it from phosphorescence, which continues to glow. Many materials fluoresce under ultraviolet light, producing vivid colors invisible under normal lighting. {The fluorescence of the minerals was spectacular under the black light.}

Fluorescent describes things that glow by absorbing light at one wavelength and emitting it at another—typically producing bright, vivid colors. Fluorescent lights use this principle, converting ultraviolet radiation into visible light. The word often describes the harsh, flat quality of such lighting: {the fluorescent glare of the office}. Fluorescent colors are intensely bright, almost glowing: {fluorescent yellow highlighters}, {fluorescent pink}.

Fluoride is a compound containing the element fluorine. The term appears most often in discussions of dental health—fluoride in toothpaste and water supplies helps prevent tooth decay by strengthening enamel. {Does your city add fluoride to the water?} Water fluoridation has been controversial since its introduction, with opponents raising health concerns despite scientific consensus on its safety at recommended levels.

Flurries are brief, light snowfalls—scattered flakes that don't accumulate much: {The forecast calls for flurries this afternoon}. By extension, a flurry is any sudden burst of activity or commotion: {a flurry of emails}, {a flurry of punches}. The singular flurry is more common for figurative uses; flurries typically means snow.

A flurry is a brief, light snowfall or a sudden gust of wind carrying snow. The word extends to any brief burst of activity or commotion: {a flurry of emails arrived after the announcement}. In finance, a flurry describes a sudden spike in trading activity. The verb flurry means to agitate or confuse, though this use is less common than the noun.

One meaning of the verb flush signifies a sudden and noticeable flow of various things. You can flush a toilet (cause water to flow through it) or your cheeks can flush (suddenly fill with color from rushing blood). A flush is a flow of this kind. Another flush is mainly an adjective meaning forming a continuous plane: The door is flush with the wall. Yet another flush adjective means wealthy. In cards, a flush is a hand with cards all of one suit.

Flushed describes a face or skin reddened by emotion, exertion, or heat: {Her cheeks were flushed with embarrassment}. The flush may come from excitement, fever, alcohol, or physical effort. Figuratively, flushed extends to emotional states—{flushed with success}, {flushed with victory}—suggesting the warm glow of triumph. As past tense of flush, it means forced out of hiding {flushed the birds from cover} or cleared by rushing water {flushed the pipes}.

Flushes are sudden rushes of blood to the skin, causing redness and warmth, especially in the face: {hot flushes during menopause}, {flushes of embarrassment}. The word also names acts of flushing—cleaning with water, driving game from cover, or poker hands where all cards share a suit: {She won with two flushes in a row}.

Flushing is the action of cleaning or clearing something with a rush of water or other liquid. You flush a toilet, flush debris from a wound, or flush a cooling system. Extended senses involve driving out or revealing: {Police flushed the suspect from hiding}. Flushing also describes the reddening of skin from emotion, exertion, or heat: {Her face was flushing with embarrassment}. A flush of something is a sudden surge: {a flush of pride}, {a flush of new growth}.

Fluster is a state of agitated confusion, or to put someone in that state. A flustered person is rattled, unable to think clearly: {The unexpected question flustered her}. The word suggests mild panic rather than complete breakdown—being thrown off balance but still functioning: {Don't get flustered; just take your time}.

Flustered describes a state of agitated confusion, typically from being rushed, embarrassed, or caught off guard. Someone flustered struggles to think clearly or act composedly: {She got flustered during the interview and forgot her prepared answers}. The word suggests visible discomfort—blushing, stammering, or fumbling.

To fluster someone is to make them agitated, confused, or nervous, typically through unexpected pressure or attention. The state itself is also called a fluster: {She was in such a fluster before the interview that she forgot her portfolio}. People get flustered when they're put on the spot, caught off guard, or overwhelmed by competing demands. The word often implies visible signs of discomfort—blushing, stammering, or losing one's train of thought.

A flute is a woodwind instrument played by blowing across a hole near one end while fingering keys along its length. The orchestral flute is held sideways; recorders and similar instruments are held vertically. Flute also names a tall narrow glass for champagne, and a decorative groove carved into a column or other surface. To flute is to play the flute, speak in flutelike tones, or carve such grooves.

Fluted describes something with parallel grooves or channels running along its length. Classical columns are often fluted, their vertical ridges catching light and shadow. A fluted {pie crust} has decorative crimped edges. A fluted {glass} has lengthwise ridges. The word comes from the flute—an instrument whose early forms had grooved finger holes.

Flutes are woodwind instruments consisting of a tube with holes and keys, played by blowing across an opening near one end. The transverse flute held horizontally is the orchestral standard, though recorders and pan pipes are also flutes. The word extends to any long, narrow groove or channel, particularly the vertical channels carved into classical columns or the decorative ridges pressed into pie crusts and fabric. Champagne flutes are tall, narrow glasses designed to preserve bubbles. To flute is to play the instrument or to create such grooves.

Fluting refers to parallel grooves or channels, especially the vertical ones carved into classical columns. The word extends to any similar decorative pattern of rounded channels: {the fluting on a pie crust}, {fluted glassware}. As a musical term, fluting describes high, clear tones resembling a flute: {the fluting call of a songbird}.

Flutter is rapid, irregular movement—the motion of wings beating quickly, a flag rippling in wind, or a heart skipping beats. To flutter is to move this way: {Butterflies fluttered around the garden}, {Her eyelashes fluttered}. A flutter of excitement is a nervous, agitated feeling. In British slang, to have a flutter is to place a small bet: {I had a flutter on the horses}.

Fluttering describes rapid, light, irregular movement—the motion of wings, flags, or leaves stirring in a breeze: {curtains fluttering in the wind}. A fluttering heart beats rapidly from excitement or anxiety. Eyelashes flutter when batted coyly. The word captures movement that is quick but gentle, never heavy or forceful.

Flux is a state of continuous change or flow. Situations {in flux} are unsettled, still shifting. In physics, flux measures the rate at which something passes through a surface—magnetic flux, heat flux. In metallurgy and soldering, flux is a substance that promotes the fusion of metals by preventing oxidation. The word suggests movement rather than stability: {The company's policies remain in flux}.

From the original verb designating the act of moving through the air with wings, fly has developed other meanings that borrow an element from the original. The wings don’t have to be your own, as when you fly from one place to another in an aircraft. If a flag is what’s flying, wings are not even necessary. Fly is always irregular (flew, flown), except in baseball, where the past tense is flied: He flied into the bleachers. The most common noun use of fly designates any of various insects, especially the housefly. In baseball, a fly is a hit ball that is caught by a fielder.

Flyaway describes hair that is fine, wispy, and difficult to control—strands that lift and drift with static or wind: {Her flyaway hair refused to stay in the braid}. The word also applies to things ready to fly or seemingly about to take flight: a flyaway {kite}, a flyaway {imagination}. As a noun, a flyaway can be a stray strand of hair or, in broadcasting, a portable satellite transmission system.

Flyaways are fine strands of hair that won't stay in place, standing up or sticking out from an otherwise smooth style: {She smoothed down the flyaways with a bit of hairspray}. Static electricity and dry conditions make them worse. The term also applies to loose threads or fibers on fabric that resist lying flat.

Flyball is a dog sport where teams of dogs race relay-style over hurdles to retrieve a ball from a spring-loaded box. The dogs trigger the box, catch the ball, and race back so the next dog can go. Speed and precision matter: {Their border collie is a flyball champion}. In baseball, a fly ball (two words) is a ball hit high into the air.

Flyballs is the plural of flyball, a baseball term for a ball hit high into the air. Fielders track flyballs to make catches; batters hope flyballs carry over the fence. A routine flyball is an easy out, while a deep flyball might become a home run or a sacrifice fly: {He caught three flyballs in center field}.

Flyboy is informal slang for a pilot, especially a military aviator. The term carries a hint of swagger or recklessness—the cocky fighter pilot archetype: {He had that flyboy attitude}. It can be affectionate or slightly dismissive depending on context.

Flyboys is an informal, slightly dated term for military pilots, especially fighter pilots. The word carries a mix of admiration and gentle mockery—acknowledging their daring while suggesting cockiness or swagger: {The flyboys thought they were invincible}. It evokes World War II and the era of leather jackets and aviator sunglasses.

A flyby is a flight passing close to a target without landing or stopping. Spacecraft make flybys of planets to gather data: {The probe completed a flyby of Jupiter}. Aircraft perform flybys as ceremonial displays or shows of force. Also spelled fly-by.

Flybys is the plural of flyby, a flight path that passes close to a target without stopping. In space exploration, a flyby allows a spacecraft to observe a planet or moon without entering orbit or landing: {The probe conducted several flybys of Jupiter's moons}. In aviation, a flyby is a ceremonial or demonstration pass over spectators: {The jets performed a flyby at the air show}.

A flyer is a printed sheet distributed to advertise or announce something: {Someone was handing out flyers on the corner}. A flyer is also someone or something that flies—a pilot, a passenger, or a fast-moving person or vehicle: {She's a frequent flyer}. To {take a flyer} is to take a risk or make a speculative gamble. Also spelled flier.

Flyers is the plural of flyer—printed sheets distributed as advertisements or announcements: {They handed out flyers for the concert}. Flyers also names people or things that fly: frequent flyers, high flyers. In American sports, the word often appears in team names. (Capitalized Flyers usually refers to the Philadelphia hockey team.)

To flyfish is to fish using an artificial fly as bait, casting with a specialized weighted line that carries the nearly weightless lure. The technique requires skill in casting and reading water. Flyfishing is associated with trout and salmon in streams and rivers: {We spent the weekend flyfishing in Montana}. Also spelled fly-fish.

Flyfishing is a method of angling that uses an artificial fly as bait, cast with a specialized weighted line rather than a heavy lure. The technique requires skill in casting and "presenting" the fly to mimic natural insect behavior on or below the water's surface. Flyfishing has a reputation as a contemplative, almost meditative pursuit: {He took up flyfishing to decompress from work}. Also spelled fly-fishing or fly fishing.

Flying is moving through the air, whether by wings, engines, or being thrown. Birds fly, planes fly, and so does a frisbee. The adjective describes things airborne or moving swiftly: a flying {leap}, flying {debris}, {flying colors}. To pass with flying colors is to succeed brilliantly. A flying {visit} is brief and hurried. {He came in flying through the door.}

A flyleaf is a blank page at the beginning or end of a book, between the cover and the title page or final text. Authors often sign flyleaves, and owners write inscriptions there: {For Sarah, with love—Dad}. The plural is flyleaves.

A flyover is a bridge carrying one road over another, called an overpass in American English. In aviation, a flyover is a ceremonial flight passing over a location—military jets at a stadium, planes honoring a funeral. As an adjective, flyover describes the middle of the United States that coastal travelers fly over rather than visit: {flyover country}, {flyover states}. The term often carries condescension.

Flyovers are the parts of a country passed over during air travel between major destinations—typically rural or less populated regions. In American usage, flyover country often carries dismissive connotations, suggesting places coastal elites ignore: {Politicians only visit flyover states during election years}. In British English, a flyover is an overpass—a bridge carrying one road over another.

Flypaper is a strip of paper coated with sticky, often poisonous substance, hung to catch and kill flies. The insects land on it and can't escape. Figuratively, something that attracts and traps: {The casino was flypaper for desperate gamblers}. To {stick like flypaper} is to cling persistently.

A flypast is a ceremonial flight of aircraft over a specific location, typically to mark a special occasion or honor someone: {The coronation concluded with a flypast of military jets}. The term is chiefly British; Americans usually say flyover. Flypasts often feature at air shows, national holidays, and state funerals.

A flyswatter is a handheld device for killing flies and other insects, typically a flat perforated paddle on a long handle. The holes reduce air resistance, allowing faster swings. The word also appears as two words (fly swatter) or hyphenated (fly-swatter). {She grabbed the flyswatter and chased the wasp around the kitchen.}

Flytipping is the illegal dumping of waste in unauthorized locations—roadsides, fields, vacant lots. The term is primarily British. The fly- prefix suggests doing something hastily or on the sly, as in {fly-by-night}. {Flytipping has become a serious problem in rural areas.} Also spelled fly-tipping.

A flytrap is a device or plant that catches flies. The most famous is the Venus flytrap, a carnivorous plant with hinged leaves that snap shut when triggered by an insect. Artificial flytraps use sticky surfaces, bait, or light to attract and trap flies. Figuratively, anything that lures victims into a trap: {The bar was a flytrap for lonely tourists}.

Flyweight is a boxing weight class for the lightest fighters, typically capped at 112 pounds. By extension, flyweight describes anything small, slight, or lacking substance: {a flyweight intellect}, {flyweight competition}. In software design, a flyweight is a pattern that minimizes memory use by sharing data across similar objects.

Flyweights are boxers in one of the lightest weight classes, typically capped around 112 pounds. The term extends to anyone or anything notably small or lightweight. Figuratively, a flyweight lacks influence or significance: {He's a political flyweight who won't last long in Washington}. In computing, a flyweight is a design pattern that minimizes memory by sharing data across similar objects.

A flywheel is a heavy rotating wheel that stores kinetic energy and smooths out power delivery in engines and machinery. Once spinning, its mass resists changes in speed, evening out the pulses of an engine's combustion strokes. Figuratively, a flywheel is any self-reinforcing cycle that builds momentum: {Once the business flywheel started turning, growth accelerated}.

Flywheels are heavy rotating wheels that store kinetic energy and smooth out mechanical motion. In engines, a flywheel's momentum carries pistons through non-power strokes, preventing jerky operation. The concept extends to business strategy, where a flywheel is a self-reinforcing cycle that builds momentum over time: {Once the flywheel starts spinning, growth compounds}.

A foal is a young horse, typically under one year old. The term applies to both males and females, though a male foal is also called a colt and a female a filly. To foal is to give birth to a horse: {The mare foaled in early spring}.

Foals are young horses, typically under one year old. The term applies to both colts (males) and fillies (females) before they mature. To foal is to give birth: {The mare foaled in early spring}. The word extends to young donkeys and zebras as well.

Foam is a mass of small bubbles formed on or in liquid—the froth on ocean waves, the head on beer, the lather from soap. Foam also names lightweight materials with a bubbly structure: {foam rubber}, {foam insulation}, {styrofoam}. To foam is to produce bubbles: {The rabid dog foamed at the mouth}. To {foam at the mouth} figuratively means to rage uncontrollably.

Foaming describes something producing or covered with foam—a mass of small bubbles. Beer foams when poured, waves foam as they break, a rabid dog foams at the mouth. Figuratively, foaming suggests extreme agitation or rage: {He was foaming at the mouth over the decision}. The image of uncontrolled frothing conveys loss of composure.

Foams is the plural of foam and the third-person singular verb. Foam is a mass of bubbles formed in or on liquid—beer foam, sea foam, the foam at a rabid dog's mouth. As a material, foam is light and spongy, full of air pockets: {foam rubber}, {foam padding}, {memory foam}. To foam is to produce bubbles: {The waves foamed against the rocks}. To {foam at the mouth} is to be furiously angry.

Foamy describes something covered with or resembling foam—the mass of small bubbles that forms on liquids. A foamy cappuccino has a thick layer of frothed milk. Ocean waves are foamy where they break against rocks. Beer poured too fast becomes foamy. The word suggests lightness and aeration: {a foamy mousse}, {foamy bath bubbles}.

A fob is a small ornament or charm attached to a watch chain or keychain, or the short chain or ribbon itself. The word now commonly refers to a small electronic device that controls access—a key fob unlocks a car remotely, a security fob grants building entry. To fob someone off is to dismiss them with evasions or excuses, or to pass off something inferior as acceptable: {He tried to fob off the broken watch as an antique}. (Capitalized FOB is an acronym.)

Focaccia is an Italian flatbread, typically rectangular or round, characterized by its dimpled surface and generous coating of olive oil. The dough is similar to pizza dough but yields a thicker, softer result with a chewy interior and crisp exterior. Focaccia is often topped simply with coarse salt and herbs like rosemary, though variations include olives, tomatoes, or onions. {We ordered focaccia as an appetizer.}

The original noun meaning of focus—a point at which rays converge or concentrate—informs all of its other meanings. The most common use of focus today is to indicate a thing receiving the most attention or effort: A small farm in Kansas is now the focus of the recent salmonella outbreak. The common term focus group is a group assembled for the purpose of gathering opinions on a topic or product. When you focus a camera, you adjust the lens in order to capture a sharp image. When you focus your attention, you put it on something and try to minimize distractions.

Focused means having attention concentrated on a single point or purpose. A focused {student} works without distraction. A focused {effort} channels energy toward one goal. The word implies clarity and deliberate direction—the opposite of scattered or diffuse. In optics, focused light converges at a point rather than spreading. Also spelled focussed, especially in British English.

Focusing is the act of directing attention, effort, or optical equipment toward a specific point or subject. When you focus a camera or your eyes, you adjust to achieve clarity; when you focus your mind, you concentrate on one thing while filtering out distractions. {I'm focusing on finishing this project before the deadline.} The spelling focussing, with the doubled consonant, is a legitimate variant more common in British English.

Fodder is food for livestock, especially dried hay or straw fed to cattle and horses. The word extends to anything consumed in bulk or used as raw material: {cannon fodder} (soldiers treated as expendable), {fodder for gossip}, {fodder for late-night comedians}. The implication is abundance without much value—plentiful stuff to be processed or used up.

A foe is an enemy or adversary. The word is literary and somewhat old-fashioned in everyday speech, though it remains common in certain phrases: {friend or foe}, {a foe of tyranny}. Foe applies to personal rivals, military opponents, or abstract adversaries: {Procrastination is the foe of productivity}.

Foes is the plural of foe—enemies or adversaries. The word appears more often in literary, historical, or dramatic contexts than in everyday speech: {The knight faced his foes on the battlefield}, {political foes united against the bill}. Where enemy sounds neutral, foe carries a slightly archaic or elevated tone.

Foetus is the British spelling of fetus—an unborn mammal after it has developed past the embryonic stage. In humans, this occurs around eight weeks after conception. The spelling with -oe- remains standard in British medical and legal contexts, while American English uses fetus exclusively.

Fog, noun and verb, suggests obstruction of clear view. Fog near the ground is like a cloud come down to earth. If your windshield or glasses fog up they become occluded with water droplets. In figurative use, a fog is anything that hampers clarity, as in the fog of war or brain fog. If something fogs your mind or thinking, you are unable to think or reason clearly. Things made for use in fog include fog lights and foghorns.

Fogbound describes something unable to move or operate because of fog. A fogbound ship sits anchored in harbor, waiting for visibility to improve. A fogbound airport delays or cancels flights. The word can extend figuratively to mental states—someone fogbound by confusion or uncertainty cannot see their way forward.
clues: Unable to sail through thick gray

definition: A fogey is someone with old-fashioned attitudes, resistant to change or new ideas. Usually appears as {old fogey}, though the "old" is nearly redundant—fogey already implies someone set in their ways: {Don't be such a fogey; try the new restaurant}. The word is mildly dismissive rather than deeply insulting. Also spelled fogy.

Fogeys is the plural of fogey, an old-fashioned or stuffy person resistant to new ideas. Usually appears as {old fogeys}: {Those old fogeys on the board will never approve anything innovative}. The spelling fogy is also common. Despite the typical pairing with old, the word sometimes describes younger people with conservative attitudes: {young fogeys}.

Fogged describes something obscured by fog or a fog-like film. A fogged {windshield} has condensation blocking the view. Fogged {glasses} steam up when you enter a warm room. Camera film can be fogged by accidental light exposure. Figuratively, a fogged {mind} or fogged {memory} lacks clarity: {My brain was completely fogged from lack of sleep}.

Foggy describes conditions of limited visibility due to fog: {a foggy morning}, {foggy weather}. Extended to mental states, foggy means unclear or confused: {My memory is foggy on the details}, {I woke up feeling foggy}. A foggy notion is vague or uncertain. To not have the foggiest means to have no idea at all: {I haven't the foggiest what she meant}.

A foghorn is a loud, low-pitched horn used on ships and at coastal stations to warn of obstacles in fog. The deep, penetrating sound carries well through dense air. Figuratively, someone with a foghorn voice speaks in booming, unmistakable tones: {Her foghorn of a mother could be heard three rooms away}.

Foghorns are loud, low-pitched horns used to warn ships in foggy conditions. Lighthouses and vessels sound foghorns to signal their presence when visibility is poor. The deep, mournful sound carries well through fog. Figuratively, someone with a foghorn voice speaks in a loud, penetrating tone: {She announced dinner in her foghorn voice}.

A fogie, also spelled fogy, is an old-fashioned or conservative person, typically someone older who is out of touch with current trends or resistant to new ideas. The word almost always appears with old in front of it: {Don't be such an old fogie—try the new restaurant.} Despite the mild derision it carries, fogie is more affectionate than truly insulting, often used self-deprecatingly by people acknowledging their own outdated preferences.

Fogies is the plural of fogy, a mildly disparaging term for an old-fashioned or conservative person, especially an older one resistant to new ideas or change. The phrase {old fogy} is common, though technically redundant since fogy already implies age or outdated thinking. {The fogies on the committee rejected every proposal for modernizing the system.} The spelling fogey is equally acceptable.

A fogy is a person with old-fashioned attitudes, resistant to new ideas or change. Usually appears with *old*: {Don't be such an old fogy—try the new software}. The word carries mild contempt, suggesting someone stuck in their ways. Also spelled fogey.

A fohawk is a hairstyle that mimics the mohawk but without shaving the sides completely—instead, the hair on the sides is cut short while the center strip is left longer and often styled upward. The name blends "faux" and "mohawk," reflecting that it's a tamer, more workplace-acceptable version of the punk original. {He asked the barber for a fohawk because his office wouldn't allow a real mohawk.}

A foible is a minor weakness or quirk in someone's character—not a serious flaw, but an endearing or at least forgivable eccentricity. {His foible for collecting vintage lunch boxes amused his friends.} The word carries a gentle, tolerant tone; we speak of foibles when we're inclined to excuse rather than condemn. Everyone has their foibles, and acknowledging them is part of accepting human imperfection.

Foibles are minor weaknesses or quirks in someone's character—small flaws that don't rise to the level of serious faults. The word carries an affectionate or tolerant tone: {We learn to accept each other's foibles}. Everyone has foibles; acknowledging them suggests gentle self-awareness rather than harsh judgment.

Foil is metal in very thin sheets, especially made of aluminum and used in food preparation and storage. A different kind of foil is a person or thing that makes another seem (even) better by contrast: Strong beer is the perfect foil for good cheese. If you foil an attempt or plot, you act in a way that prevents it from succeeding. If you are foiled, something has blocked your success. A foil is also a sword used in fencing.

Foiled means thwarted or frustrated in one's plans. The word typically describes efforts that were stopped before succeeding: {The robbery was foiled by an alert security guard}. It often appears in melodramatic or mock-dramatic contexts: {Curses, foiled again!} The underlying image is of a fencing move deflected—a thrust turned aside before it lands.

Foiling is the act of thwarting or preventing something from succeeding: {The detective kept foiling the villain's schemes}. The phrase {Curses, foiled again!} has become a theatrical cliché for frustrated antagonists. Separately, foiling refers to applying thin metal sheets as decoration or backing, or in sailing and water sports, riding above the water on a hydrofoil.

Foils is the plural of foil, which has several distinct meanings. Thin sheets of metal are foils: {aluminum foil}, {gold foil}. In fencing, a foil is a light, flexible sword with a blunted tip. A foil is also a character who contrasts with another, making their qualities more apparent: {Watson serves as a foil to Holmes}. The verb foil means to thwart or frustrate: {The hero foiled the villain's plan}. As a verb form, foils continues this sense: {She foils every attempt to surprise her}.

To foist something on someone is to impose it on them against their will or without their knowledge. The word carries a sense of deception or unfairness—passing off something unwanted, inferior, or false: {They tried to foist the blame on the new employee}. {The salesman foisted a lemon on the unsuspecting buyer}. You can foist responsibilities, opinions, or substandard goods.

To fold something is to lay one part over another, thereby reducing dimensions and sometimes forming creases (fold a letter, fold clothes). If you fold one ingredient into another in cooking, you carefully add one to the other. If a business folds, it fails and shuts down. If you fold in a poker game, you withdraw from play and lose what you have wagered. A fold is created anytime that you fold something tangible, like the fold in the center of a newspaper.

Folded describes something bent over on itself, creating layers: {a folded napkin}, {folded arms}. In poker and figuratively, folded means having given up or withdrawn: {The company folded after three years}. Folded can also describe something incorporated by gentle mixing: {She folded the egg whites into the batter}.

A folder is a container for holding loose papers, typically made of folded cardboard or plastic with a crease down the middle. In computing, a folder is a virtual container for organizing files—the graphical equivalent of a directory. {Create a new folder on your desktop.} {She kept all her receipts in a manila folder.}

Folders are containers for organizing loose papers or documents, typically made of cardboard or plastic and designed to hold materials flat. In computing, folders are virtual containers that organize files within a directory structure—the icon deliberately mimics the physical object. The verb form means to put into folders: {She spent the afternoon foldering client documents}.

Folding describes something designed to collapse into a more compact form: a folding {chair}, a folding {table}, a folding {knife}. The term implies portability or storage convenience—the object folds flat or smaller when not in use. As a noun, folding can refer to the act itself: {The folding of the laundry took an hour}.
clues: What chairs do to save space

definition: Folds are bends or creases made by doubling material over itself: {the folds of a curtain}, {a letter's folds}. A fold in terrain is a gentle depression or ridge. To fold is to bend something flat, or to collapse: fold laundry, fold a business, fold in poker. A fold is also an enclosure for sheep—and figuratively, a community of believers: {return to the fold}.

Foley is the art of creating sound effects for film and television by recording everyday objects and movements in sync with the action on screen. A foley artist might crinkle cellophane for fire, clap coconut shells for hoofbeats, or walk on gravel to match an actor's footsteps: {The foley work in that film was incredible—every punch sounded brutal}. Named for sound pioneer Jack Foley, the term has become generic in film production. (Capitalized Foley is a surname.)

Foliage refers to the leaves of plants, especially when considered as a mass or visual feature. We talk about the foliage of a particular plant, or the foliage of an entire forest. The word is most common in autumn, when the foliage of deciduous trees turns red, orange, and yellow: {We drove through Vermont to see the fall foliage.}

A folio is a large sheet of paper folded once to make two leaves (four pages) of a book, or a book made of such sheets—the largest standard book format. Shakespeare's plays were first collected in the First Folio of 1623. More broadly, folio refers to a page number in a book, or a leaf in a manuscript: {The passage appears on folio 47}. In law and accounting, a folio may be a fixed number of words used as a unit for measuring document length.

Folk means people, especially as a collective group sharing common traits, traditions, or origins. Your folks are your family, particularly parents: {My folks are visiting this weekend}. Folk as an adjective describes things arising from ordinary people rather than experts or institutions: folk {music}, folk {art}, folk {medicine}, folk {wisdom}. These suggest traditions passed down through communities rather than formal training. Folks is a casual way to address a group: {Listen up, folks}.

A folkdance is a traditional dance that developed among ordinary people of a region or culture, typically passed down through generations rather than formally choreographed. The term covers dances performed at community gatherings, celebrations, and festivals: {square dancing}, {polka}, {Irish step dancing}. As a verb, to folkdance is to perform such dances. Also spelled folk dance.

A folkie is someone devoted to folk music—either a performer in the genre or an enthusiastic fan. The term carries affectionate connotations of acoustic guitars, coffeehouses, and earnest singer-songwriters: {The folkies gathered at the open mic every Thursday}. Sometimes used dismissively by those outside the scene to suggest naïveté or excessive earnestness.

Folkies are fans or performers of folk music, especially those associated with the acoustic, often politically conscious folk revival of the mid-twentieth century. The term can be affectionate or mildly dismissive, depending on context: {The folkies gathered at the coffee house for open mic night}. Someone might be called a folkie for their musical tastes, their earnest style, or both.

Folklore is the traditional beliefs, customs, stories, and practices passed down through generations within a community or culture. It encompasses myths, legends, fairy tales, folk songs, proverbs, and superstitions—the unofficial knowledge that exists alongside formal education and official religion. {Local folklore warns against swimming in the lake at night.} Folklore often reflects a community's values and attempts to explain natural phenomena or teach moral lessons.

Folks is a warm, informal word for people—often a specific group you're addressing or referring to. {Hey folks, dinner's ready.} {Some folks just don't listen.} Your folks are your parents or family: {I'm visiting my folks this weekend.} The word carries a down-to-earth, unpretentious tone, making it popular with politicians and public speakers seeking connection with ordinary people.

A folksinger is a performer of folk music—traditional songs passed down through generations or contemporary songs written in that style. The term often carries associations with acoustic instruments, particularly guitar, and with social or political consciousness: {She started as a folksinger in Greenwich Village coffeehouses}. Also spelled folk singer.

Folksingers are performers of folk music—traditional songs passed down through generations or contemporary songs written in that style. The term evokes acoustic instruments, especially guitars, and lyrics about ordinary people, social issues, or historical events. {The folksingers of the 1960s revival sang about civil rights and war.} The word carries associations with authenticity and grassroots culture rather than commercial polish.
clues: They strum and sing old songs

definition: Folksinging is the performance of folk songs—traditional music passed down through communities, often with acoustic instruments like guitars and banjos. The term also covers the folk revival style of the mid-20th century, when artists wrote new songs in traditional modes. A folksinger performs this music: {She spent her college years folksinging in coffeehouses}.

A folksong is a traditional song passed down orally within a community, typically of unknown authorship: {She learned old folksongs from her grandmother}. The term also covers modern songs written in that style, especially those with acoustic instrumentation and lyrics about ordinary people or social issues. Also spelled as two words: folk song.

Folksongs are traditional songs passed down orally within a community, typically of unknown authorship. They often tell stories of everyday life, work, love, or historical events: {We learned old folksongs around the campfire}. The term extends to modern songs written in traditional style, especially those associated with acoustic instruments and social movements. Also spelled as two words: folk songs.

Folksy describes a manner that is informal, unpretentious, and characteristic of rural or small-town life. A folksy politician cultivates an approachable image with homespun sayings and casual charm: {His folksy demeanor made voters feel like they were chatting with a neighbor}. The word can be genuine or calculated—sometimes both at once.

A folktale is a traditional story passed down orally through generations within a culture. Folktales include fairy tales, fables, legends, and myths—stories featuring stock characters, simple morals, or supernatural elements: {The Brothers Grimm collected German folktales}. The term distinguishes stories arising from collective tradition rather than individual authorship.

Folktales are traditional stories passed down orally through generations—fairy tales, fables, legends, and myths that belong to a culture rather than an individual author. They typically feature archetypal characters and situations: clever tricksters, wicked stepmothers, magical transformations. {Cinderella appears in folktales across dozens of cultures.} The singular folktale works as both noun and adjective: {a folktale tradition}.

Follies is the plural of folly—acts of foolishness or costly mistakes: {the follies of youth}, {the follies of war}. Follies also names a type of theatrical revue featuring elaborate costumes, music, and comedy sketches, popularized in the early twentieth century: {the Ziegfeld Follies}. In architecture, follies are ornamental buildings serving no practical purpose, built for decoration or whimsy in gardens and estates.

Follow means to go or come after, whether physically, temporally, or logically. A dog follows its owner; dessert follows dinner; a conclusion follows from premises. To follow instructions is to act according to them. To follow someone on social media is to subscribe to their updates. To follow a story or argument is to understand its progression: {I couldn't follow what he was saying}. A following is a group of supporters or fans.

A follower is someone who follows—trailing behind a leader, subscribing to a belief system, or tracking someone's posts on social media: {She has two million followers on Instagram}. A follower of a religion or philosophy accepts its teachings: {followers of Buddhism}. The word often implies subordination or lack of originality: {He's a follower, not a leader}.

Followers are people who follow—physically, ideologically, or digitally. A leader has followers. A religion has followers. On social media, followers are users who subscribe to someone's content: {She has two million followers on Instagram}. The word can suggest subordination or passive allegiance, unlike supporters or fans, which imply more active engagement.
When it is followed by a noun phrase, following can be interpreted as a preposition where it means the same thing as after: There will be a speech following dinner.

Follows is the third-person singular of follow, meaning to come after or go behind: {She follows him everywhere}. To follow instructions or rules is to obey them. To follow a story or argument is to understand it as it unfolds. On social media, to follow someone is to subscribe to their updates: {He follows three hundred accounts but rarely posts}.

Followup is something that comes after an initial action to continue, check on, or reinforce it. A doctor schedules a followup {appointment} after surgery. A salesperson makes a followup {call} after a pitch. As a verb (usually hyphenated or two words): {I'll follow up with you next week}. The word implies persistence or due diligence—making sure something doesn't slip through the cracks.

Folly is foolishness or lack of good judgment: {the folly of youth}, {It would be folly to ignore the warning signs}. The word carries a sense of recklessness or ill-advised action rather than mere stupidity. In architecture, a folly is an ornamental building with no practical purpose—a decorative whim, often elaborate and extravagant.

Fond means having affection or warm regard for something or someone: {She's fond of her nephew}, {I'm quite fond of that old sweater}. It can also describe cherished but perhaps unrealistic attitudes: {a fond hope}, {fond memories}. To be fond of an activity is to enjoy it habitually: {He's fond of long walks}. The word carries gentler warmth than love—affection without intensity.

Fondant is a smooth, pliable sugar paste used in candy-making and cake decorating. Rolled fondant covers cakes in a flawless, almost sculptural finish: {She draped the wedding cake in white fondant}. Poured fondant is softer and coats petit fours or fills chocolates. The texture is divisive—some find it cloyingly sweet, others appreciate how it takes color and holds intricate shapes.

To fondle is to touch or stroke affectionately, often with sexual undertones. The word implies lingering, gentle contact—caressing rather than grabbing: {He fondled her hair as they talked}. In sexual contexts, fondle typically describes touching intimate areas: {They fondled each other in the back seat}. The word often appears in accounts of unwanted contact, carrying connotations of inappropriate touching.

Fondling is touching or stroking in an affectionate or sexual way. The word often appears in contexts of inappropriate or unwanted contact: {He was charged with fondling a minor}. In innocent use, it suggests gentle, lingering touch: {She sat fondling the cat in her lap}. A fondling is also an archaic term for a person treated with excessive affection.

Fondly means with affection or tender feeling: {She looked fondly at her sleeping child}, {He spoke fondly of his college years}. The word can also mean naively or with misplaced optimism, as in {fondly imagining} that something will work out when it probably won't—though this sense is becoming rare.
clues: The way sweethearts gaze at each other

definition: Fondness is affection or warm regard for someone or something: {She developed a fondness for her neighbor's cat}. It also describes a liking or taste: {His fondness for sweets}, {a fondness for old movies}. The word suggests gentle, steady attachment rather than intense passion.

Fondue is a Swiss dish in which diners dip food into a communal pot of melted substance—traditionally cheese melted with wine, into which cubes of bread are dipped. Chocolate fondue uses melted chocolate for dipping fruit or pastries. Fondue bourguignonne involves cooking meat in hot oil. The word comes from French for "melted." {We had cheese fondue for dinner.}

A font is a complete set of type in one size and style—the characters a printer or computer uses to render text. In digital contexts, font and typeface blur together, though purists distinguish them: a typeface is the design (Helvetica), while a font is a specific instance (Helvetica Bold 12pt). {Choose a font that's easy to read.} Separately, a font is a basin in a church holding water for baptism.

Fonts are the distinct visual designs for displaying letters and characters. In typography, a font originally meant a specific size and style of a typeface, though font and typeface are now used interchangeably: {What font is that?} Digital fonts are files containing character designs: {Install the font on your computer}. {Comic Sans is an overused font.}

Food is what living things eat to sustain themselves—any substance that provides nourishment when consumed. The word covers everything from raw ingredients to prepared meals: {We need to pick up food for the week}, {The food at that restaurant is excellent}. Food extends metaphorically to anything that sustains or stimulates: {food for thought}, {food for the soul}. As a modifier, it describes things related to eating: food {chain}, food {poisoning}, food {court}.

A foodbank is an organization that collects and distributes food to people who cannot afford to buy enough. Donations come from individuals, grocery stores, and manufacturers; the food goes to those facing hunger or financial hardship. {The local foodbank serves hundreds of families each month.} Also spelled as two words: food bank.

Foodbanks is the plural of foodbank, a charitable organization that collects and distributes food to people who cannot afford to buy enough. Donors give packaged goods; volunteers sort and distribute them to individuals and families facing hunger: {The local foodbanks saw record demand during the recession}. Also spelled as two words: food banks.

A foodie is someone with an enthusiastic interest in food—not just eating it, but seeking out quality ingredients, new restaurants, and culinary experiences. The term emerged in the 1980s as a less pretentious alternative to "gourmet": {The foodies in the group insisted we try the new ramen place}. It can carry a hint of mockery, suggesting someone who treats dining as a personality trait.

Foodies are people with an enthusiastic interest in food—its preparation, presentation, and cultural dimensions. The term suggests someone who seeks out exceptional meals, follows culinary trends, and treats eating as more than mere sustenance: {The restaurant caters to foodies willing to pay for a tasting menu}. Unlike gourmand or epicure, foodie carries a slightly self-deprecating casualness.

A fool is a person who lacks good sense or judgment. To call someone a fool is to say they've acted stupidly: {Don't be a fool—take the money}. The verb means to trick or deceive: {You can't fool me}. To {fool around} is to waste time or, sometimes, to engage in casual sexual activity. {Fool's gold} looks valuable but isn't. A court fool or jester entertained royalty, so fool can suggest playful absurdity rather than genuine stupidity.

Fooled is the past tense of fool—to deceive or trick someone into believing something false: {I was fooled by the knockoff}. To be fooled is to have been taken in: {Don't be fooled by his friendly manner}. The phrase {could have fooled me} expresses skeptical disbelief: {He says he's qualified? Could have fooled me}.

Foolhardy describes reckless bravery—boldness without adequate consideration of danger or consequences. Where courage weighs risks, foolhardiness ignores them: {a foolhardy attempt to climb without ropes}, {It would be foolhardy to invest your savings in a single stock}. The word combines fool with hardy (bold), suggesting courage that crosses into stupidity.

Fooling is playful, joking behavior—not meant to be taken seriously: {We were just fooling around}. To fool someone is to deceive them, so fooling can also mean tricking: {You're not fooling anyone with that excuse}. The phrase {no fooling} emphasizes sincerity: {No fooling, I really saw it}.

Foolish describes behavior or thinking that shows poor judgment or lack of sense. A foolish {mistake} is one that should have been avoided. A foolish {person} acts without considering consequences. The word is milder than stupid—it suggests momentary lapses rather than permanent deficiency: {I felt foolish for believing him}. Foolish can also mean trivial or frivolous: {foolish distractions}.

Foolishness is the quality of lacking good sense or judgment, or behavior that demonstrates such a lack. It covers a spectrum from mild silliness to serious lapses in wisdom. {The foolishness of youth often gives way to the caution of age.} Someone might dismiss an idea as foolishness, meaning it's not worth serious consideration. Unlike stupidity, which implies limited capacity, foolishness suggests poor choices despite knowing better.

Foolproof describes something designed so simply or reliably that even a fool couldn't misuse it or cause it to fail: {a foolproof plan}, {foolproof instructions}. The word implies that failure has been engineered out—no skill or intelligence required. {The system isn't foolproof, but it catches most errors.}

Fools is the plural of fool—people who lack good judgment or sense. The word appears in expressions where the singular wouldn't work: {Fools rush in where angels fear to tread}. To {suffer fools gladly} is to tolerate stupid people with patience—usually negated: {She doesn't suffer fools gladly}. April Fools' Day invites harmless deception.

Foosball is a tabletop game simulating soccer, played by manipulating rows of miniature players mounted on rotating rods to strike a ball toward the opponent's goal. The game is a fixture in bars, game rooms, and break rooms: {We played foosball in the basement all afternoon}. Also called table football or table soccer.

The structure at the lower end of the vertebrate leg inspires all other meanings of foot, including another very common meaning, a unit of measure in the imperial system equal to 12 inches. That kind of foot often relies heavily on context for its exact interpretation: someone who is “6 foot” is six feet tall. Someone who lives at 9,000 feet lives at an elevation of 9,000 feet above sea level. Foot can also refer to an inanimate object that either supports something above it (the feet of a table), or is at the bottom (the foot of the bed). If you foot a bill, you pay the cost of something.

Footage is video or film material, measured historically in feet of film but now applied to any recorded visual content: {security footage}, {news footage}, {behind-the-scenes footage}. The word implies raw or unedited material more often than finished productions. Footage also refers to length or area measured in feet: {the square footage of a house}.

The ambiguity of football arises from the word representing different games in different parts of the world. To Americans, football is a passing, running, and kicking game played on a 100-yard field with teams of 11 players. A game in Australia with some similarities is Australian rules football, or footie to many of the locals. In most of the rest of the world, football is Association football, that is, soccer.

A footballer is someone who plays football, whether professionally or recreationally. In British English and most of the world, this means a soccer player; in American English, it typically refers to someone who plays American football, though the term is less common there than {football player}. Professional footballers at the highest levels are among the world's most recognized and highly paid athletes.

Footballers are people who play football professionally or seriously. In British usage, footballers play association football (soccer): {Premier League footballers earn millions}. In American contexts, the word typically refers to American football players, though it's less common than simply "football players."

Footballs is the plural of football—the inflated ball used in various sports, or the sports themselves. In American English, a football is the pointed oval used in gridiron football; in British English, it's the round ball used in soccer. {We need more footballs for practice.} The nuclear football, a briefcase carried near the U.S. president containing launch codes, takes its name from the ball's shape.

Footbinding was a Chinese practice of tightly wrapping young girls' feet to prevent growth, breaking bones to achieve a shape considered beautiful and sexually desirable. The process caused permanent disability, limiting women's mobility. Bound feet, ideally around three inches long, were called "lotus feet." The practice was outlawed in the early twentieth century but persisted in rural areas for decades.

A footbridge is a narrow bridge designed for pedestrians rather than vehicles. Footbridges span rivers, ravines, highways, or railroad tracks, providing safe passage for people on foot. They range from simple wooden planks to elaborate architectural structures. {The old footbridge swayed as we crossed the gorge.}

Footdragging is deliberate slowness or reluctance to act, especially when someone is expected to move forward on something: {The committee's footdragging on the proposal frustrated everyone}. The image is of someone shuffling their feet rather than walking with purpose. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated: foot-dragging, foot dragging.

Footfall is the sound or act of a foot striking the ground: {She heard footfalls in the corridor}. The word often appears in contexts suggesting stealth or atmosphere—quiet footfalls, approaching footfalls. In British commercial usage, footfall means the number of people entering a store or area: {The new location increased footfall by thirty percent}.

Footfalls are the sounds of feet striking the ground while walking or running. The word appears most often in literary or atmospheric contexts, suggesting measured or ominous approach: {She heard footfalls in the hallway}. Runners and biomechanics researchers also use it technically to describe each foot strike during a stride.

A foothill is a low hill at the base of a mountain or mountain range, marking the transition from flat land to higher elevations. Foothills typically appear in clusters: {a house in the foothills of the Rockies}, {vineyards spread across the Sierra foothills}. The word almost always appears in the plural.

Foothills are the low hills at the base of a mountain or mountain range, forming a transition zone between flatland and peaks: {a ranch in the foothills of the Rockies}. The term usually appears in plural, treating the terrain as a collective feature rather than individual elevations.

A foothold is a place where you can securely plant your foot, especially when climbing: {She found a foothold in the rock face}. Figuratively, it's any secure position from which to advance or operate: {The company gained a foothold in the Asian market}. To {establish a foothold} is to secure an initial position before expanding.

A foothold is a place where you can securely place your foot while climbing, such as a ledge or crack in a rock face. By extension, foothold refers to any secure position from which further progress can be made: {The company gained a foothold in the Asian market}. Military forces establish footholds in enemy territory as a base for advancing. The word nearly always appears in contexts of advancement or progress, whether literal climbing or figurative expansion.

Footie is informal British slang for football (soccer): {We're watching the footie tonight}, {a footie match}. The diminutive suffix gives it a casual, affectionate quality. In North America, footie more often refers to footie pajamas—one-piece sleepwear with enclosed feet, typically for children.

Footing is the position of your feet on a surface, especially regarding stability: {She lost her footing on the wet rocks}. From this comes the figurative sense of one's standing or basis: {The company regained its financial footing}. To be on equal footing is to have the same status or advantages. In construction, a footing is the concrete base that supports a foundation.

A footlight is a light placed along the front edge of a stage floor, aimed upward to illuminate performers. Usually plural: {the footlights}. The term serves as a metonym for the theater itself or for a career in acting: {She was drawn to the footlights from childhood}. {The footlights cast dramatic shadows on his face.}

Footlights are a row of lights set into the floor at the front edge of a theater stage, casting upward illumination on performers. The term often stands for the theater profession itself: {She was drawn to the footlights from childhood}. To be {in the footlights} is to be onstage or in the public eye.

A footlocker is a sturdy rectangular trunk, typically placed at the foot of a bed, used for storing personal belongings. The term is most associated with military barracks, where each soldier keeps uniforms, gear, and personal items in a standard-issue footlocker: {He stowed his letters in his footlocker}. Summer camps and boarding schools use them similarly.

Footlong describes something measuring twelve inches, or one foot, in length. Most commonly encountered as a noun for a sandwich of that size: {I ordered a footlong from Subway}. The term appears in other contexts where the twelve-inch measurement matters: {footlong hot dog}, {footlong ruler}. Often hyphenated as foot-long when used as an adjective before a noun.

Footloose means free from obligations or ties, able to go wherever one pleases. Someone footloose has no commitments—no job, family, or mortgage—holding them in place: {After graduation, I spent a footloose summer backpacking through Europe}. The word often pairs with fancy-free to emphasize complete freedom from responsibility.

A footman is a uniformed male servant in a household, traditionally one who attends to the door, waits at table, and accompanies carriages. The term evokes the era of grand estates with elaborate domestic staffs, where footmen were often selected for their height and appearance. In modern usage, footman appears mainly in period dramas and historical fiction. {The footman announced each guest as they entered the ballroom.}

Footmen is the plural of footman, a uniformed male servant in a wealthy household. The footman's duties included answering doors, serving at table, and attending to guests. The term evokes aristocratic estates and formal service: {The footmen stood at attention as guests arrived}. In historical contexts, footmen were also foot soldiers, as distinct from cavalry.

A footnote is a note at the bottom of a page providing additional information, citation, or commentary on something in the main text, typically marked with a superscript number or symbol. Footnotes handle material too detailed or tangential for the main argument: {See footnote 3 for the full citation}. Figuratively, a footnote is something minor or incidental: {He'll be a footnote in history}.

Footnotes are notes at the bottom of a page, keyed to specific passages in the main text by numbers or symbols. They provide citations, clarifications, or supplementary information without interrupting the flow of reading: {The footnotes run longer than the chapter itself}. Figuratively, a footnote is something minor or incidental: {He became a footnote in music history}.

A footpath is a narrow path for walking, especially one through countryside or parks. Unlike roads or sidewalks, footpaths are typically unpaved trails meant for pedestrians only: {We followed the footpath along the river}. In British usage, footpath also refers to what Americans call a sidewalk.

A footprint is the impression left by a foot or shoe on a surface: {footprints in the sand}, {muddy footprints on the floor}. The term extends to any mark of presence or impact. A building's footprint is the ground area it occupies. A carbon footprint measures environmental impact. In computing, a program's footprint is the memory or storage it requires. To {follow in someone's footprints} is to imitate their path.

Footprints are the marks left by feet on a surface—in sand, snow, mud, or dust. The word extends to any trace of presence or passage: a carbon footprint measures environmental impact, a digital footprint tracks online activity. {The footprints in the snow led to the back door.} {We need to reduce our carbon footprint.}

A footrace is a competition in which participants run a set distance on foot, the winner being whoever crosses the finish line first. Footraces range from short sprints to marathons and ultramarathons. {She entered the footrace on a whim and finished third}.

Footsie is playful touching of feet, usually under a table, as flirtation or intimate communication: {They were playing footsie during dinner}. By extension, {play footsie with} describes secretive or improper collaboration: {The senator was accused of playing footsie with lobbyists}.
