In finance, gamma measures the rate of change in an option's delta. In photography and computing, gamma describes the relationship between input signal and displayed brightness: {Adjust the gamma settings on your monitor}. Informally, a gamma male ranks below alpha and beta in pop-psychology hierarchies of male dominance.

Gammon is cured or smoked ham, typically from the hind leg of a pig, popular in British cooking and often served in thick slices. In backgammon, a gammon is a victory where the losing player hasn't removed any pieces from the board. British slang has added a newer meaning: gammon describes a red-faced, middle-aged white man perceived as holding reactionary political views, the ruddy complexion suggesting both anger and heavy drinking. {The comments section was full of gammons complaining about immigration.}

Gamut is the complete range or scope of something: {the whole gamut of human emotions}, {Her music runs the gamut from folk to electronica}. The word comes from medieval music theory, where it named the full range of notes. To {run the gamut} is to cover an entire spectrum from one extreme to another.

Ganache is a rich mixture of chocolate and cream, used as a filling, frosting, or glaze for cakes and pastries. The proportions vary—more cream yields a pourable glaze, more chocolate a thicker truffle filling. {She whipped the ganache until it was light and fluffy.} The texture is smooth and glossy when properly made.

A gander is an adult male goose. The informal phrase {take a gander} means to take a look: {Let me take a gander at those numbers}. This sense likely comes from the way a goose stretches its neck to see.

Ganders is the plural of gander, an adult male goose. The word also appears in the informal expression {take a gander}, meaning to take a look: {Let me take a gander at that menu}. This sense likely comes from the way geese crane their necks to see.

Gang usually refers to a group of people (gang of friends, gang of thieves). Before another noun, gang references criminal gang activity (gang warfare, gang violence). If you gang up on someone, you join with others to exert pressure, oppose, or criticize. To gang together is positive, as animals might do to protect each other.

A gangbanger is a member of a street gang, typically one involved in violent or criminal activity. The term emerged from American urban slang and carries connotations of youth violence, turf wars, and drug trafficking: {Police arrested three suspected gangbangers after the shooting}. Sometimes shortened to banger.

Gangbangers are members of street gangs, especially those involved in violent criminal activity. The term carries strong associations with urban crime, drugs, and turf warfare: {Police arrested three suspected gangbangers after the shooting}. Used primarily in American English, often by law enforcement and media. The word can function as a slur when applied broadly to young men of color regardless of actual gang affiliation.

Gangbuster originally meant a law enforcement officer who aggressively pursued organized crime. The word now appears almost exclusively in the phrase {like gangbusters}, meaning with great energy, speed, or success: {Sales took off like gangbusters}. As an adjective, gangbuster describes something impressively successful or forceful: {gangbuster profits}, {a gangbuster performance}.

Gangbusters refers to law enforcement officers who aggressively pursue organized crime. The word survives mainly in the phrase {like gangbusters}, meaning with great energy, speed, or success: {The new product is selling like gangbusters}. {The economy came roaring back like gangbusters}. The expression derives from a 1930s radio drama about FBI agents.

Gangland refers to the world of organized crime and criminal gangs, or the territory they control. The word appears most often as an adjective: a gangland {slaying}, a gangland {boss}, gangland {violence}. It evokes a shadowy underworld with its own rules, hierarchies, and brutal methods of settling disputes.

A gangleader is the person in charge of a gang, whether a criminal organization, a prison clique, or a group of young people who engage in antisocial behavior together. The term emphasizes authority and control over the group's activities and members. {Police arrested the suspected gangleader in connection with a series of robberies.} The word is sometimes written as two words: gang leader.

A ganglord is the leader of a criminal gang or organized crime operation. The term emphasizes power and hierarchy—a ganglord commands loyalty and directs illegal activities like drug trafficking, extortion, or racketeering. {The neighborhood had been under the ganglord's control for decades.} Also spelled as two words: gang lord.

Ganglords is the plural of ganglord—a leader or boss of a criminal gang or organized crime operation. The term suggests significant power and territory: {The city's ganglords controlled entire neighborhoods}. It appears in journalism, crime fiction, and discussions of urban violence or drug trafficking.

Gangly describes a tall, thin person whose limbs seem loosely jointed and awkward in movement. The word suggests adolescent ungainliness—someone who hasn't quite grown into their body: {a gangly teenager all elbows and knees}. Also spelled gangling, with the same meaning.

A gangplank is a movable board or ramp used to bridge the gap between a ship and a dock, allowing people to board or disembark. The term evokes the age of sailing ships and pirate lore—prisoners forced to {walk the plank} were sent off a similar board into the sea. Modern equivalents are usually called gangways.

Gangplanks is the plural of gangplank, a movable bridge or ramp used to board or disembark from a ship. The plank typically extends from the vessel's deck to the dock or shore: {Passengers streamed down the gangplanks onto the pier}. The term appears in nautical contexts and occasionally as a metaphor for any transitional passage.
clues: Movable bridges from dock to vessel

definition: Gangrene is the death and decay of body tissue, usually caused by loss of blood supply or bacterial infection. The affected flesh turns black and may spread if untreated, often requiring amputation: {The wound became gangrenous and they had to take the leg}. Figuratively, gangrene describes corruption spreading through an institution or system.

Gangs is the plural of gang—a group united by common purpose or identity. The word ranges from innocent to sinister: a {gang of kids} playing together, a work {gang} on a construction site, or a criminal organization controlling territory through violence. {Street gangs} and {biker gangs} carry connotations of lawlessness. As a verb, to gang up on someone is to unite against them: {They ganged up on the new kid}.

Gangsta is a hip-hop spelling of gangster, reflecting African American pronunciation. It emerged with West Coast rap in the late 1980s and 1990s, particularly in the subgenre {gangsta rap}, which depicted street life, crime, and gang culture. The spelling marks authentic connection to that musical and cultural moment: {He's got that gangsta swagger}. Outside hip-hop contexts, it often signals ironic or playful toughness.

Gangstas is the plural of gangsta, a hip-hop spelling of gangster that emerged from rap culture in the 1980s. The spelling reflects African American Vernacular English pronunciation and signals street authenticity rather than old-school organized crime: {Real gangstas don't snitch}. Gangsta rap glorifies or narrates the violent realities of gang life.

A gangster is a member of an organized criminal group. The term evokes images of prohibition-era mobsters in pinstripe suits, but applies to any era's organized crime figures: {The gangsters ran numbers rackets throughout the neighborhood}. In hip-hop culture, gangster (often spelled gangsta) describes a street-tough persona or lifestyle. As an adjective, gangster can mean impressively bold or ruthless: {That was a gangster move}.

Gangsterism is the methods, behavior, and culture of organized criminal groups—intimidation, violence, extortion, and loyalty to the gang above the law. The term often appears in discussions of urban crime or political corruption: {The city was plagued by gangsterism in the 1920s}. It can describe any thuggish tactics used to maintain power or control.

Gangsters are members of criminal organizations, typically involved in activities like racketeering, drug trafficking, or extortion. The term evokes organized crime figures of the Prohibition era—suited men with tommy guns—but applies broadly to anyone operating in a criminal gang: {The neighborhood was controlled by local gangsters}. Gangster also works as an adjective: {gangster rap}, {gangster movies}.

A gangway is a passageway, especially a temporary or movable one that allows people to board or leave a ship, aircraft, or other vessel. The term extends to any narrow walkway or aisle, particularly in British English where it refers to the passage between sections of seats in a theater or the House of Commons. As an exclamation, gangway! is a command to clear the way, demanding that people step aside to let someone through. {Gangway! Coming through!}

Ganja is marijuana, especially in forms associated with Rastafarian culture or Caribbean origin. The word comes from Hindi and entered English through Jamaican usage: {He was smoking ganja on the porch}. It appears in reggae lyrics and cannabis culture generally, carrying a slightly more exotic or countercultural flavor than plain *marijuana* or *weed*.

Ganked is gaming slang for being ambushed or killed unfairly, typically by a much stronger player or group attacking without warning: {I got ganked by a level 60 while I was questing}. The term originated in multiplayer online games but has spread to mean getting robbed, cheated, or screwed over more generally: {Someone ganked my lunch from the break room fridge}.

Ganking is video game slang for ambushing or killing another player, especially when they're vulnerable—outnumbered, low-level, or caught off guard. The term originated in multiplayer online games where experienced players would prey on weaker ones: {I got ganked by a level 60 while I was just trying to quest}. Extended to mean attacking someone unfairly or unexpectedly: {Three of them ganked me in the parking lot}.

A gannet is a large seabird with a long neck and pointed bill, known for plunge-diving into the ocean to catch fish. The bird's voracious feeding habits give rise to the informal British sense: a greedy person who eats excessively. {Don't be such a gannet—save some for the rest of us.}

Gannets are large seabirds known for their spectacular plunge-diving, folding their wings and dropping from height to catch fish. They're white with black wingtips and have a wingspan approaching two meters. In British slang, a gannet is a greedy person who eats voraciously: {Don't be such a gannet—save some for everyone else}.

A gap is an opening, difference or separation; the word is related to the much less frequent verb gape. The gender gap refers to differences in attitudes by and about, and opportunities for, males and females: By voting in large numbers, women created a gender gap that elected the progressive candidate. A budget gap is the difference between how much is available and how much is needed or wanted. To bridge a gap is to supply whatever missing thing resulted in there being a gap. Physical gaps might include one between a person’s front teeth, or between two mountains.

Gape means to stare with the mouth open, usually in wonder, surprise, or stupidity: {Tourists gaped at the cathedral's vaulted ceiling}. It also describes something wide open—a gaping wound, a gaping hole. The noun gape refers to this open-mouthed stare or the width of an opening: {the gape of a bird's beak}.

Gaped is the past tense of gape, meaning to stare with one's mouth open, typically in surprise or wonder: {She gaped at the enormous diamond}. It can also describe something opening wide or standing ajar: {A hole gaped in the fence where the boards had rotted away}.

Gaping describes something wide open, especially a mouth or wound: {a gaping hole in the wall}, {He stared with gaping mouth}. The word emphasizes the size or conspicuousness of an opening. A gaping {chasm} yawns before you. Figuratively, a gaping {flaw} in an argument is one impossible to miss.

Gaps is the plural of gap—empty spaces or intervals where something is missing or incomplete. Physical gaps are openings or breaks: {gaps in the fence}, {gaps between teeth}. Abstract gaps are deficiencies or disconnects: {gaps in knowledge}, {gaps in the fossil record}, {the gap between rich and poor}. To fill or close gaps is to address what's lacking.

A garage is a building or enclosed structure for housing vehicles, typically attached to or near a home. It often doubles as storage space or a workshop. In British usage, a garage is also a gas station or auto repair shop. To garage a vehicle is to put it in a garage: {We garage the car in winter}. A garage sale offers household items for sale, typically in the driveway.

Garb is clothing, especially when distinctive or characteristic of a particular group or role: {prison garb}, {surgical garb}, {priestly garb}. The word suggests a complete outfit rather than individual items. To garb someone is to dress them, usually in something specific: {garbed in ceremonial robes}.

Garbage is waste material, especially household refuse: {Take out the garbage}. The word extends to anything worthless or of poor quality: {That movie was garbage}, {garbage in, garbage out}. In computing, garbage refers to corrupted or meaningless data. To garbage something is to discard it, though this use is less common than simply throwing it away.

A garbageman is a worker who collects and hauls away household trash. The term is giving way to more formal alternatives like sanitation worker or waste collector: {The garbagemen come on Tuesdays}. Also spelled as two words: garbage man.

Garbagemen is the plural of garbageman—a worker who collects trash from residences and businesses. The term is giving way to gender-neutral alternatives like garbage collector or sanitation worker: {The garbagemen come on Tuesdays}. In figurative use, someone who cleans up messes others leave behind.

Garbanzo is a round, beige legume with a firm texture and nutty flavor, widely used in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cooking. Also called chickpea. Garbanzo appears most often in the phrase {garbanzo bean}, though this is technically redundant since garbanzo already means the bean.

To garble is to distort or scramble something—typically speech, a message, or information—so that it becomes unclear or misleading. A bad phone connection garbles voices. Rumors get garbled as they pass from person to person. {The witness garbled the details of what happened.} A garbled message retains fragments of the original but loses coherent meaning.

Garbled describes communication that has become confused, distorted, or incomprehensible—whether through poor transmission, faulty memory, or deliberate scrambling. A garbled {message} arrives with words missing or jumbled. Garbled {instructions} are impossible to follow. {The recording was so garbled I couldn't make out what she said.} Information can become garbled as it passes from person to person.

A garden is a plot of land where plants are cultivated—flowers, vegetables, herbs, or ornamental shrubs. British English uses garden where Americans say yard: {The children played in the garden}. To garden is to tend such a space. {Garden-variety} means ordinary or unremarkable. To {lead someone down the garden path} is to deceive them gradually.

A gardener is someone who tends a garden—planting, weeding, watering, and cultivating plants. The term covers both hobbyists who maintain home gardens and professionals hired to care for others' landscapes: {We hired a gardener to handle the yard work}. A {master gardener} has completed horticultural training, often through extension programs.

A gardenia is a fragrant flowering shrub with glossy dark leaves and waxy white or cream-colored blooms. Native to tropical and subtropical regions, gardenias are prized for their intensely sweet scent and are popular in gardens, corsages, and perfumery: {The gardenia's perfume filled the room}.

Gardenias are flowering shrubs prized for their creamy white blooms and intensely sweet fragrance. Native to tropical and subtropical regions, they're cultivated as ornamentals and used in perfumery. The flowers are associated with romance and formal occasions—often worn as corsages or boutonnieres: {She pinned a gardenia to her dress}.

Gardening is the activity of cultivating plants—flowers, vegetables, herbs, or ornamental shrubs—typically in a yard or designated plot. It encompasses planting, watering, weeding, pruning, and tending soil. The word covers everything from casual weekend puttering to serious horticultural pursuit: {She took up gardening after retirement}. Someone with {a green thumb} has a knack for it.

Gardens are plots of land cultivated for growing plants—flowers, vegetables, herbs, or ornamental shrubs. A garden may be a small backyard patch or an elaborate public space: {the botanical gardens}, {a rooftop garden}. The verb means to tend such a space: {She gardens every weekend}. Figuratively, to {tend your own garden} is to focus on your own affairs rather than meddling in others'.

Gargantuan means enormous or immense, typically beyond what seems normal or expected. The word comes from Gargantua, the giant king in Rabelais's sixteenth-century satire who had an appetite to match his size. While any synonym for huge will do in most contexts, gargantuan often carries connotations of excess or grotesque scale: {a gargantuan meal}, {gargantuan debts}. It suggests not just bigness but bigness that strains credulity or propriety.

Gargle is to rinse the mouth and throat by holding liquid in the back of the throat and agitating it with exhaled breath: {Gargle with salt water for a sore throat}. The word imitates the bubbling sound produced. As a noun, a gargle is the act itself or a liquid used for gargling: {The doctor recommended a medicated gargle}.

Gargled is the past tense of gargle—to rinse the throat by holding liquid in the back of the mouth and agitating it with exhaled air, producing a bubbling sound. The practice is typically medicinal: {She gargled with salt water for her sore throat}. Figuratively, a voice that sounds gargled has a wet, throaty quality.

Gargling is the act of holding liquid in the back of the throat and agitating it with exhaled air, usually for medicinal purposes: {Gargling with salt water can soothe a sore throat}. The word imitates the bubbling sound produced. Figuratively, a voice that gargles has a wet, throaty quality.

A gargoyle is a carved stone figure, typically grotesque or monstrous, projecting from a building's roofline to channel rainwater away from the walls. The term extends to any grotesque carved figure on a building, even decorative ones without drainage function. By extension, gargoyle describes an ugly person: {He sat in the corner like a gargoyle}.

Gargoyles is the plural of gargoyle, a carved stone figure projecting from a building's roofline. True gargoyles are waterspouts—the grotesque faces channel rainwater away from walls. Similar decorative figures without drainage function are technically called grotesques, though gargoyle covers both in casual use. The creatures are usually monstrous or demonic: {Stone gargoyles leered down from the cathedral}.

Garish describes something tastelessly bright, showy, or overdone—colors that clash, decorations that overwhelm, lighting that glares. The word carries judgment: what's garish isn't just vivid but aggressively so, demanding attention without earning it. {The casino's garish neon signs lit up the strip.} {She thought the bridesmaids' dresses were garish.}

A garland is a wreath or decorative chain of flowers, leaves, or other materials, typically hung as decoration or worn on the head: {garlands of holly}, {a garland of roses}. To garland something is to adorn it with such decoration: {The victors were garlanded with laurels}. The word suggests festivity, honor, or celebration. (Capitalized Garland is a proper name.)

Garlands are decorative wreaths or chains of flowers, leaves, or other materials, typically hung as festive ornaments or draped around something: {The hall was hung with garlands for the wedding}. To garland is to adorn with such decorations: {They garlanded the winner with flowers}. Figuratively, garlands can mean honors or praise: {the garlands of literary fame}.

Garlic is a pungent bulb used as seasoning in cooking worldwide. The bulb divides into segments called cloves, which are peeled, minced, or crushed to release their sharp, aromatic flavor. Raw garlic is more intense than cooked. Garlic appears in countless dishes and is said to ward off vampires—and, less fancifully, to repel people with its lingering smell on the breath.

A garment is a piece of clothing. The word is somewhat formal, appearing more in fashion, retail, and manufacturing contexts than in everyday speech: {garment industry}, {garment worker}, {garment bag}. You're more likely to hear someone say "clothes" or "outfit" than "garments" in casual conversation.

Garments are articles of clothing. The word is somewhat formal or literary—more common in fashion industry contexts, legal documents, and older texts than in everyday speech. You might read about {garment workers} or the {garment district}, but you'd rarely tell someone you like their garments. The singular garment appears in phrases like {a garment bag} for transporting clothes.

Garnet is a group of hard silicate minerals occurring in various colors, most commonly deep red. Prized as gemstones and used industrially as abrasives, garnets appear in jewelry and sandpaper alike: {a garnet ring}, {garnet paper for finishing wood}. The deep reddish-brown color itself is called garnet. (Capitalized Garnet is a given name.)

Garnets are a group of hard, glassy minerals occurring in many colors, most commonly deep red. Prized as semiprecious gemstones, they appear in jewelry and also serve industrial purposes as abrasives: {a garnet ring}, {garnet sandpaper}. The deep reddish-brown color itself is called garnet.

Garnish means to decorate or embellish, most commonly food: {The chef garnished the plate with parsley and a lemon wedge}. A garnish is such a decoration—something added for visual appeal rather than substance. In legal contexts, to garnish wages is to withhold money from someone's paycheck to satisfy a debt, typically by court order: {The IRS garnished his wages until the back taxes were paid}.

Garnished is the past tense of garnish, meaning decorated or embellished—most often food presented with an added element for visual appeal: {The plate arrived garnished with parsley and a lemon wedge}. In legal contexts, garnished describes wages or accounts that have been seized to satisfy a debt: {His paycheck was garnished to cover child support}.

Garnishes are decorative additions to food or drink, meant to enhance appearance or add a finishing touch: {a cocktail with citrus garnishes}, {parsley garnishes on the entrées}. As a verb form, garnishes means to add such decoration: {She garnishes each plate with a sprig of mint}. In legal contexts, garnishes refers to the seizure of wages or assets to satisfy a debt.

A garotte is a wire, cord, or metal collar used to strangle someone, typically from behind. The word also refers to execution by strangulation, historically practiced in Spain. As a verb, to garotte is to kill or attack by this method: {The assassin garotted the guard before he could raise an alarm}. Also spelled garrote or garrotte.

A garret is a small room or space directly beneath the roof of a house, typically cramped and poorly finished. The word carries associations with poverty and artistic struggle—the proverbial starving artist lives in a garret: {He spent years writing in a cold Parisian garret}. Distinguished from attic mainly by connotation: attics store things; garrets house people, usually reluctantly.

A garrison is a body of troops stationed at a military post, or the post itself: {The garrison held out for three weeks}. To garrison a place is to station troops there for defense. The word suggests permanent or semi-permanent military presence rather than troops passing through. A {garrison town} is one where soldiers are regularly stationed.

Garrisons are military troops stationed at a particular location, or the fortified places where they're stationed. The word works both ways: soldiers garrison a fort, and a fort is garrisoned by soldiers. {The garrison held out for three months}. {They garrisoned the border towns against invasion}. By extension, any group posted somewhere to maintain control: {a garrison of security guards}.

A garrote is a device for strangling—traditionally a cord, wire, or metal collar tightened around the victim's neck. The word also refers to execution by this method, once practiced in Spain. As a verb, to garrote is to strangle someone this way: {The assassin garroted the guard from behind}. Also spelled garrotte.

A garrotte is a device for strangling someone, typically a cord, wire, or metal collar tightened around the neck. Historically, it was an execution method in Spain—the condemned sat in a chair while an executioner twisted a metal band until death. As a verb, to garrotte is to strangle someone this way: {The victim had been garotted with piano wire}. Also spelled garotte or garrote.

A garter is a band worn around the leg to hold up a stocking. Before elastic waistbands, garters were essential undergarments; now they appear mainly in formal or erotic contexts. A {garter belt} is a piece of lingerie with straps that attach to stocking tops. The Order of the Garter is Britain's highest order of chivalry. A garter snake is a harmless North American snake with lengthwise stripes.

Garters are bands worn around the leg to hold up stockings or socks. Before elastic waistbands, garters were essential undergarments—either simple bands below the knee or straps attached to a belt or corset. Modern garters are mostly decorative, associated with lingerie or wedding traditions: {The groom removed the bride's garter and tossed it to the groomsmen}.

The most general use of gas is to designate one of the primary states of matter: one in which molecules move about randomly and would expand infinitely in the absence of containment or pressure. Gas is also used as shorthand for some common fossil fuels—some of which actually are gasses, such as natural gas. In American English, the petroleum distillate that is used to power internal combustion engines (petrol in British English) is gas. If a person has gas, they are experiencing indigestion that is accompanied by the release of gas through belching or flatulence. As a verb, gas may mean to fuel a vehicle (gas up the car) or to subject a person or animal to a harmful or lethal gas: The shelter was reportedly gassing surplus animals.

A gasbag is a bag that holds gas, such as the inflatable compartment of a balloon or airship. The figurative sense dominates: a gasbag is a person who talks excessively without saying much of substance. {Uncle Frank is a gasbag—he'll corner you for an hour about nothing.}

Gasbags is the plural of gasbag—a container holding gas, as in a balloon or airship. More commonly, gasbag describes a person who talks excessively without saying much of substance: {The meeting dragged on because a few gasbags wouldn't stop pontificating}. The metaphor captures how such people seem inflated with hot air.

Gases is the plural of gas—substances like air, helium, or methane that expand to fill any container. The word covers both natural phenomena {(greenhouse gases)} and practical applications {(anesthetic gases)}. In informal use, gases can mean instances of flatulence. The verb form gases means supplies with gas or, informally, talks idly: {He gases on about nothing}.

A gash is a long, deep cut or wound, typically jagged or ragged rather than clean: {The fall left a nasty gash on his forehead}. The word extends to similar cuts in materials: {a gash in the leather seat}. As a verb, to gash is to make such a cut: {He gashed his knee on the rocks}. In British slang, gash is vulgar for female genitalia, and by extension, a crude term for women generally.

Gashed describes something that has been cut or slashed, leaving a deep wound or opening: {His gashed forehead needed stitches}, {The gashed hull took on water}. The word implies a jagged, violent cut rather than a clean incision.

Gashes is the plural of gash—a deep, long cut or wound, typically jagged rather than clean: {The fall left gashes on his knees}. Gash extends to any deep slash or opening: {gashes in the hull}, {gashes in the earth}. As a verb form, gashes means inflicts such wounds: {The broken glass gashes his palm}.

A gasket is a shaped piece of rubber, metal, or other material that seals the junction between two surfaces, preventing leakage of fluids or gases: {The mechanic replaced the blown head gasket}. To {blow a gasket} is to lose your temper explosively—from the dramatic failure when engine gaskets rupture under pressure.

To gaslight someone is to manipulate them into doubting their own perceptions, memory, or sanity. The term comes from a 1938 play in which a husband dims the gas lights while denying any change, making his wife question her grip on reality. Gaslighting is a form of psychological abuse: {He gaslit her for years, insisting her concerns were imaginary}. The word has broadened to describe any attempt to make someone distrust their own judgment: {The company tried to gaslight customers about the defective product}.

Gaslighted is the past tense of gaslight, meaning to manipulate someone psychologically so they question their own memory, perception, or sanity. The term comes from a 1944 film in which a husband dims the gas lights while denying any change, making his wife doubt her reality. Someone who has been gaslighted has experienced sustained psychological manipulation designed to make them distrust themselves: {She realized she'd been gaslighted for years when friends confirmed what she'd always suspected}. The alternate past tense gaslighted competes with gaslit.

A gaslighter is someone who manipulates another person into doubting their own perceptions, memories, or sanity. The term comes from a 1938 play in which a husband dims the gaslights while denying any change, making his wife question her grip on reality. Gaslighters deny events that happened, dismiss concerns as overreactions, or insist their victims are imagining things: {My ex was a gaslighter—he'd say cruel things and then swear I'd misheard him}.

Gaslighters are people who manipulate others into questioning their own perception, memory, or sanity. The term comes from a 1944 film in which a husband dims the gas lights while denying any change, making his wife doubt her own observations. Someone who gaslights typically denies events that occurred, dismisses feelings as overreactions, or insists their victim misremembers things. {Her therapist helped her recognize that her ex had been one of the worst gaslighters she'd ever encountered.}

Gaslighting is a form of psychological manipulation where someone makes another person question their own memory, perception, or sanity. The manipulator denies events that happened, dismisses the victim's feelings, or insists their recollections are wrong: {He kept gaslighting her about the argument until she wondered if it had even occurred}. The term comes from the 1944 film *Gaslight*, where a husband dims the gas lights while insisting his wife is imagining it. Now widely applied to any sustained attempt to undermine someone's grip on reality.

Gaslights can be lamps that burn gas for illumination, the kind that lit streets and homes before electricity. More commonly now, gaslights is the verb form of gaslight—to manipulate someone into questioning their own perception or sanity: {He gaslights her by denying conversations that happened}. The psychological sense comes from the 1944 film *Gaslight*, where a husband dims the gas lamps while telling his wife she's imagining it.

Gaslit describes someone who has been manipulated into doubting their own perceptions, memories, or sanity. The term comes from a 1944 film in which a husband dims the gas lights while denying any change, making his wife question her reality. To be gaslit is to have experienced this psychological manipulation: {I thought I was going crazy, but I was being gaslit}. The verb gaslight and noun gaslighting are now common in discussions of abusive relationships and political rhetoric.

A gasmask is a device worn over the face to protect against poisonous gases, smoke, or airborne contaminants. It typically covers the nose and mouth with a filter or connects to an air supply. Gasmasks became iconic in World War I when chemical warfare made them essential for soldiers. Also spelled gas mask.

Gas masks are protective devices worn over the face to filter harmful gases, chemicals, or particles from breathed air. The sealed mask covers nose and mouth, sometimes the entire face, with replaceable filter canisters. Associated with chemical warfare, industrial hazards, and apocalyptic imagery: {Soldiers donned gas masks as the shells landed}. Also spelled as two words.

Gasoline is a flammable liquid fuel refined from petroleum, used primarily to power internal combustion engines in cars and other vehicles. Americans say gasoline or gas; the British say petrol. {Gas prices are up again}. The shortened form gas dominates casual speech, though it invites confusion with gaseous substances.

A gasp is a sudden, sharp intake of breath, typically triggered by surprise, shock, pain, or exertion. To gasp is to take such a breath or to struggle for air: {She gasped when she saw the price tag}. Someone at their last gasp is near death or exhaustion. If you gasp for something, you desperately need or want it: {I'm gasping for a coffee}. Gasp also functions as an interjection conveying mock surprise or drama in informal writing.

Gasping is breathing in short, labored bursts, usually from exertion, shock, or lack of air: {She came up gasping for breath}. It suggests desperate or involuntary inhalation. Figuratively, to be gasping for something is to crave it urgently: {I'm gasping for a cup of tea}. This figurative use is more common in British English.

Gasps is the plural of gasp—a sudden, sharp intake of breath, typically from shock, surprise, or exertion: {The audience let out gasps when the magician disappeared}. As a verb form, gasps describes this breathing: {She gasps for air after running}. To be at one's {last gasps} is to be near death or exhaustion.

Gassed has several distinct meanings. To be gassed is to be exposed to poison gas or anesthetic—soldiers were gassed in the trenches, patients gassed before surgery. In slang, gassed means intoxicated or, more recently, excited and energized: {I'm so gassed for this concert}. To get gassed up is to be hyped or flattered: {Don't get too gassed—stay humble}.

Gassing covers several meanings united by gas in motion. To gas someone is to expose them to poison gas—a method of execution or warfare. Gassing also means idle chatter: {We were just gassing about nothing}. In car culture, gassing it means accelerating hard. Someone gassing you up is flattering or hyping you, sometimes insincerely.

Gastronomy is the art and science of good eating, encompassing not just cooking but the entire culture surrounding food—its preparation, presentation, and appreciation. The term elevates food beyond mere sustenance to a subject worthy of serious study and connoisseurship. A gastronomist or gastronome is someone who cultivates refined taste in food and drink. {The city has become a destination for gastronomy tourists seeking authentic regional cuisine.}

A gastropub is a bar or pub that serves high-quality food rather than typical pub fare. The concept emerged in 1990s Britain, combining the casual atmosphere of a traditional pub with restaurant-caliber cooking: {The gastropub had craft beers on tap and duck confit on the menu}. The food tends toward elevated comfort dishes rather than fine dining.

Gastropubs are pubs that serve high-quality food, blending the casual atmosphere of a traditional British pub with refined cuisine. The term emerged in 1990s London as some pubs began offering restaurant-caliber dishes alongside their beer: {We found a gastropub with an amazing wine list and duck confit}. The concept has since spread internationally, though the word retains its British flavor.

A gasworks is a facility where gas is manufactured, historically from coal, for distribution as fuel for lighting and heating. The term typically refers to the industrial plants that supplied cities before natural gas pipelines became common: {The old gasworks was converted into a park}. Usually treated as singular despite the plural form.

A gate is a passage through a fence or wall that can be opened and closed. This meaning is extended to computing, where a gate is a logical pathway that has two settings, on or off. A place that is gated is accessible only through a gate. The combining form -gate arises from Watergate, the name of a Washington, DC, hotel that was the kernel of the Nixon political scandal in the 1970s. From this, -gate is appended to other words to designate official wrongdoing, like “Irangate” or “Travelgate.”

To gatecrash is to enter a party or event without an invitation or ticket. The term evokes pushing past the gate of a private gathering. A gatecrasher is someone who does this habitually or on a particular occasion: {Three gatecashers showed up at the wedding reception}. The word can extend to any uninvited intrusion into exclusive spaces or situations.

Gatecrashed is the past tense of gatecrash—to enter a party, event, or private gathering without an invitation or ticket: {We gatecrashed the wedding reception and no one noticed}. The term evokes slipping past the gate, though modern gatecrashing rarely involves actual gates. A gatecrashed event is one that's been infiltrated by uninvited guests.

A gatecrasher is someone who enters a party, event, or venue without an invitation or ticket. The term implies deliberate intrusion rather than innocent mistake: {Security removed several gatecrashers from the reception}. The verb is gatecrash: {We gatecrashed the after-party}.

Gatecrashers are people who enter an event without invitation or payment. The term evokes someone literally crashing through the gate—forcing entry where they're not wanted. A gatecrasher at a wedding wasn't on the guest list; at a concert, they slipped past security. {The bouncers caught three gatecrashers trying to sneak in the back.}

Gatecrashes is the verb form of gatecrash, meaning to enter a party, event, or venue without an invitation or ticket. The term evokes physically pushing past a gate or entrance: {She gatecrashes every industry event in town}. Someone who does this is a gatecrasher.

Gatecrashing is entering an event without an invitation or ticket—showing up at a party you weren't asked to, slipping into a concert without paying. The term evokes literally crashing through a gate. Someone who does this is a gatecrasher: {Security caught three gatecrashers at the wedding reception}. The verb is gatecrash: {We gatecrashed the afterparty}.

Gated describes something controlled by a gate or barrier. A gated community restricts entry to residents and approved visitors. In electronics and computing, gated signals pass only when a control condition is met. Gated content online requires action before access—signing up, paying, or completing a form: {The full article is gated behind a paywall}.

A gatehouse is a building at or over a gate, typically controlling entrance to a larger property, estate, or enclosed area. Historically, gatehouses defended castle entrances; today they're more often small structures where security guards check visitors: {The guard waved us through at the gatehouse}. A gatehouse may also serve as living quarters for a gatekeeper.

Gatekeep means to control access to something—resources, communities, or cultural spaces. The term often carries negative connotations, suggesting someone is arbitrarily deciding who belongs or what counts as authentic: {Stop gatekeeping—let people enjoy things}. A gatekeeper traditionally guards an entrance, but gatekeeping now frequently describes policing the boundaries of fandoms, identities, or hobbies: {He was gatekeeping the music scene, dismissing anyone who discovered the band after 2010}.

A gatekeeper controls access to something—originally the person who guards a gate, now usually figurative. Gatekeepers decide who gets in: editors gatekeep publication, administrators gatekeep resources, fans gatekeep fandoms by challenging newcomers' credentials. {The interview is just the first gatekeeper}. To gatekeep is to restrict access, often with connotations of elitism or excessive control: {Stop gatekeeping—let people enjoy things}.

Gatekeepers are people who control access to something—originally literal gates, now usually figurative. A gatekeeper decides who gets in: {The editor served as gatekeeper for what got published}. The term often carries skepticism about whether such control is legitimate: {Self-appointed gatekeepers of the art world}. In medicine, a gatekeeper is a primary care physician who must approve referrals to specialists.

Gatekeeping is controlling access to something—resources, communities, or information. A gatekeeper decides who gets in and who doesn't. The term often carries negative connotations, especially online, where it describes excluding people from fandoms or identities based on arbitrary standards: {Stop gatekeeping—let people enjoy things}. But gatekeeping can be neutral or positive when it means maintaining quality or protecting boundaries: {Editors do necessary gatekeeping}.

Gatekept is the past tense of gatekeep—to control access to something, deciding who gets in and who doesn't. Originally literal (guards at gates), it now describes restricting entry to communities, professions, or cultural spaces: {The industry was gatekept by a handful of executives}. In internet usage, gatekeeping often carries negative connotations of elitism or exclusion: {She gatekept the fandom by quizzing newcomers on obscure trivia}.

Gates are movable barriers controlling passage through walls, fences, or other boundaries. A gate swings open; a door slides or lifts. Gates also control flow in other systems: a gate at an airport terminal, a logic gate in electronics, a gate controlling water in a dam. To gate is to restrict access: {The community is gated}. In skiing, gates are pairs of poles marking a course. (Capitalized Gates often refers to Bill Gates.)

A gateway is an entrance or passage through a barrier—a gate in a wall, fence, or hedge, or the structure framing it. By extension, gateway means a point of entry or access to something larger: {St. Louis was the gateway to the West}. A gateway {drug} is one thought to lead users toward harder substances. In computing, a gateway is a device or software that connects different networks, translating between protocols.

Gateways are openings or passages that allow entry—literal or figurative. A gateway is an entrance through a wall or fence, or the structure framing it. More often, gateway describes something that provides access to a larger domain: {a gateway to success}, {a gateway drug}. In computing, a gateway connects different networks, translating between protocols. The plural emphasizes multiple points of access: {international gateways}, {payment gateways}.

Gather means to bring together into one place or group. You gather firewood, gather your thoughts, gather people for a meeting. Cloth gathers when it's drawn into folds or puckers: {The skirt gathered at the waist}. To gather something is also to conclude or infer: {I gather you're not coming}. A gathering is an assembly of people. Things gather gradually—dust gathers, clouds gather, momentum gathers.

Gathered is the past tense of gather, meaning to bring together or collect. People gather berries, information, or courage. Fabric that is gathered has been drawn into folds or pleats: {a gathered skirt}. If you've gathered correctly, you've understood through inference: {I gathered from her tone that she was upset}.

A gatherer is someone who collects things, whether systematically or casually. The word most often appears in the phrase {hunter-gatherer}, describing societies that subsist by hunting animals and gathering wild plants rather than farming. Outside this context, gatherer describes anyone who accumulates: {a gatherer of rare books}, {a gatherer of information}.

Gatherers are people who collect things, whether food, information, or objects. The term appears most often in the phrase {hunter-gatherers}, describing societies or ancestors who survived by hunting animals and gathering plants rather than farming. Outside anthropology, gatherer describes anyone whose role involves bringing things together: {news gatherers}, {intelligence gatherers}. The word emphasizes the act of seeking out and accumulating rather than producing or creating.

A gathering is a group of people who have come together in one place: {a family gathering}, {a gathering of world leaders}. The word can emphasize either the assembly itself or the act of assembling. To gather is to bring things together—gather firewood, gather information, gather your thoughts. Fabric gathers when it's drawn into folds or pleats. {Clouds gathered on the horizon} suggests accumulation and often impending change.

Gatherings is the plural of gathering—instances where people come together in one place. The word covers everything from small {family gatherings} to large {public gatherings}. A gathering can also be a collection of things brought together: {a gathering of dust}, {a gathering of clouds on the horizon}.

Gathers are small folds or pleats in fabric, created by drawing material together along a line of stitching to add fullness: {The gathers at the waist give the skirt its shape}. In sewing, gathering allows a wider piece of fabric to fit a narrower one while creating soft, controlled bunching.

Gating is the process of controlling access or flow through a checkpoint. In electronics, gating controls when a signal passes through a circuit. In scientific research, gating filters data by excluding results outside set parameters. In gaming and media, gating restricts content until players complete requirements or pay: {The best weapons are gated behind a paywall}. The word implies a barrier that opens selectively.

Gator is an informal shortening of alligator—the large reptilian predator native to the American Southeast and China. The clipped form appears in casual speech and regional contexts: {Watch out for gators in that swamp}. It's also a common nickname and mascot, most notably for the University of Florida athletic teams.

Gators is informal for alligators—the large reptiles of the American Southeast: {Watch out for gators in that swamp}. The word also refers to shoes or overshoes made from alligator leather, or rubber overshoes that protect dress shoes from wet weather. Capitalized, Gators is the nickname for University of Florida athletic teams.

Gauche describes behavior or manner that is socially awkward, tactless, or lacking grace. Someone gauche says the wrong thing at dinner parties, makes guests uncomfortable, or handles delicate situations clumsily: {It would be gauche to ask how much they paid for the house}. The word carries a whiff of unsophistication—not outright rudeness, but a failure to read the room.

A gaucho is a South American cowboy, particularly from the grasslands of Argentina, Uruguay, and southern Brazil. Gauchos herded cattle on the pampas and became romanticized as rugged, independent figures—similar to how Americans mythologize the cowboy. The word also describes a style of wide-legged, calf-length pants: {gaucho pants}.

Gauchos are the horsemen and cattle herders of the South American pampas, particularly Argentina and Uruguay—roughly equivalent to American cowboys. The term evokes a romanticized figure of rugged independence and skilled horsemanship. Gauchos are also wide-legged trousers that end at mid-calf, named for their resemblance to traditional gaucho dress: {She wore gauchos and boots}.

Gaudy means tastelessly showy or excessively ornate—bright colors, flashy decorations, or elaborate designs that lack refinement: {gaudy jewelry}, {gaudy Christmas decorations}. The word suggests trying too hard to impress: {The casino's gaudy interior featured gold-painted columns and velvet everywhere}. Something gaudy draws attention but not admiration.

Gauge, sometimes spelled gage, is a noun and verb with meanings related to measurement. A gauge is a device with an indicator and a range of values (pressure gauge, rain gauge). Gauge can also indicate a particular standard (12- gauge shotgun, narrow gauge railway). To gauge something is to get a measurement of it, or to estimate its intensity: He gauged interest by polling the group.

Gauges are instruments that measure or display quantities—fuel gauges, pressure gauges, temperature gauges. The word also refers to standard measurements or dimensions: the gauge of wire indicates its thickness, the gauge of a shotgun its bore diameter, and railroad gauge is the distance between rails. To gauge something is to measure or estimate it: {It's hard to gauge public opinion}. The spelling gage appears in some technical contexts.

Gauging is the act of measuring, estimating, or assessing something. You gauge distance, temperature, or pressure with instruments. More often, gauging is approximate—judging reactions, situations, or feelings: {She paused, gauging his mood before continuing}. The spelling gage appears in technical contexts but gauging dominates in general use.

Gaunt describes a person or animal that is extremely thin in a way that suggests illness, exhaustion, or prolonged hardship. The word conveys more than mere slenderness—it implies a haggard, worn appearance where bones are visible and flesh seems stretched tight. {His gaunt face showed the toll of months in the hospital.} Applied to landscapes or buildings, gaunt suggests a bleak, desolate bareness: {gaunt cliffs rising from the sea}.

A gauntlet is a heavy protective glove, especially the armored kind worn by medieval knights or the thick leather gloves used in industrial work. To {throw down the gauntlet} is to issue a challenge—from the medieval custom of flinging one's glove to provoke a duel. To {take up the gauntlet} is to accept such a challenge. To {run the gauntlet} means to endure attacks from all sides, originally a military punishment where the condemned passed between two rows of soldiers who struck him as he ran. This gauntlet comes from a different word meaning "lane" or "passage."

Gauntlets are armored gloves, part of a knight's suit of armor protecting the hands and wrists. The word extends to any heavy protective gloves: {welding gauntlets}, {falconer's gauntlets}. To {throw down the gauntlet} is to issue a challenge, from the medieval custom of tossing one's glove to provoke a duel. To {run the gauntlet} is to endure attacks from both sides—originally a military punishment where the condemned passed between two rows of soldiers who struck him as he ran.

Gauze is a thin, loosely woven fabric with an open mesh structure. Medical gauze serves as bandaging material: {The nurse wrapped the wound in gauze}. The same weave appears in curtains and theatrical scrims. Figuratively, gauze suggests haziness or obscurity: {a gauze of fog}, {memories seen through gauze}.

Gauzy describes something thin, light, and translucent, like gauze fabric. A gauzy curtain filters light without blocking it. The word extends to anything hazy or vague: {gauzy memories of childhood}, {gauzy promises from politicians}. There's often a romantic or dreamlike quality implied—soft edges rather than sharp definition.

Gave is the past tense of give. Where give covers transferring possession, providing, or yielding, gave places these actions in the past: {She gave him the keys}, {The bridge gave way under the weight}, {He gave a speech at the conference}. The word appears in countless idioms: {gave it my all}, {gave up}, {gave in}, {gave birth}.

A gavel is a small wooden mallet used by a presiding officer to call for attention or signal decisions. Judges use gavels in courtrooms, auctioneers use them to mark sales, and chairpersons use them to maintain order in meetings: {The judge banged her gavel and called for silence}. To gavel is to strike with or as if with a gavel: {He gaveled the meeting to a close}.

A gavel is the small wooden mallet used by judges and presiding officers to call for order or signal decisions. The sharp rap of a gavel commands attention in courtrooms, legislatures, and auctions. To gavel is to use one, often in the phrase {gavel in} or {gavel out} a session. The gavel has become a symbol of judicial and parliamentary authority, appearing in logos and imagery even when the actual implement isn't used.

To gawk is to stare openly and stupidly, usually at something unusual or shocking: {Drivers slowed to gawk at the accident}. The word implies slack-jawed curiosity without social awareness—gawkers don't realize or care that they're being rude. A gawk can also be an awkward, clumsy person, though this use is dated.

Gawked is the past tense of gawk, meaning to stare openly and stupidly at something, usually with one's mouth hanging open. The word suggests a lack of sophistication or self-awareness in the observer. {Tourists gawked at the celebrities outside the restaurant.} Unlike glanced or observed, gawking implies rudeness or social awkwardness—you gawk at accidents, oddities, or spectacles rather than at things deserving respectful attention.

A gawker is someone who stares openly, usually at something sensational or disturbing—an accident scene, a celebrity, a public spectacle. The word carries a note of disapproval, suggesting idle or intrusive curiosity rather than legitimate interest: {Gawkers slowed traffic to a crawl past the wreck}. (Capitalized Gawker was a media website.)

Gawkers are people who stare openly, usually at something sensational or disturbing. The word carries disapproval—gawkers slow traffic at accident scenes, crowd around celebrity sightings, or linger at disasters without helping: {Police pushed back the gawkers to let paramedics through}. Unlike spectators or onlookers, gawkers suggest idle, intrusive curiosity.

Gawking is staring openly, usually with slack-jawed curiosity or rudeness. The word implies a lack of sophistication—you gawk at car accidents, celebrities, or anything that draws vulgar attention: {Tourists stood gawking at the mansion}. To gawk is the verb; a gawker is someone who does it.

Gawks is the third-person singular of gawk, meaning to stare stupidly or rudely. The word suggests slack-jawed, open-mouthed staring—more vacant than a glare, more intrusive than a glance: {He gawks at every pretty woman who walks by}. As a noun, gawks are awkward or foolish people, though this use is uncommon.

Gawky describes someone who is awkward and clumsy, especially in their movements or physical presence. The word often applies to adolescents going through growth spurts, when limbs seem too long and coordination hasn't caught up: {He was a gawky teenager, all elbows and knees}. Gawky suggests ungainliness rather than mere clumsiness—there's a lanky, uncoordinated quality to it.

Gawp is British slang meaning to stare stupidly or rudely, mouth agape: {Tourists gawped at the palace guards}. It suggests slack-jawed wonder or dim incomprehension rather than focused attention. The word is informal and mildly derisive—you gawp at spectacles, not at things deserving contemplation. American English prefers gawk.

Gawping is British and Irish English for gaping or staring stupidly, mouth hanging open: {Tourists stood gawping at the castle}. The word suggests slack-jawed wonder or vacant curiosity. Americans typically say gawking, which carries the same connotations.

Gay originally meant lighthearted, carefree, and happy: {a gay melody}, {gay spirits}. By the mid-20th century, it became the preferred term for homosexual, largely replacing older clinical or pejorative terms. This sense is now primary. In late 20th-century slang, particularly among young people, {that's so gay} meant stupid, lame, or undesirable—usage now widely condemned as homophobic even when speakers claim no anti-gay intent. The carefree sense survives in historical contexts ({the Gay Nineties}) but is otherwise obsolete.

A gayborhood is an urban neighborhood with a high concentration of LGBTQ residents, businesses, and culture. Cities like San Francisco, New York, and Philadelphia have recognized gayborhoods with rainbow crosswalks and gay-owned shops and bars: {We're meeting at a club in the gayborhood}. The term blends "gay" and "neighborhood."

Gayborhoods are urban neighborhoods known for their concentration of LGBTQ+ residents, businesses, and culture. These areas often feature gay bars, rainbow flags, and Pride events, serving as social hubs and historically as safer spaces for queer communities: {The Castro in San Francisco is one of America's most famous gayborhoods}. The term blends "gay" with "neighborhood."
clues: Urban areas with many queer residents

definition: Gaydar is the supposed intuitive ability to recognize whether someone is gay, a blend of "gay" and "radar." The term is often used playfully or self-deprecatingly: {My gaydar must be broken—I had no idea he was gay}. Whether gaydar reflects genuine perception of subtle cues or just stereotype-matching remains debated.

Gays is the plural of gay, referring to homosexual people, especially men. The noun form is common in journalism and advocacy: {gays and lesbians}, {rights for gays}. Some prefer "gay people" or "gay men" to the noun, finding {the gays} reductive or clinical, though context and tone matter more than the word itself.

Gaze is a steady, prolonged look—more intent than a glance, less aggressive than a stare. You gaze at something that holds your attention: {She gazed out the window}, {He couldn't tear his gaze away}. The noun names this kind of looking: {under the gaze of the crowd}, {averting her gaze}. In academic contexts, the gaze refers to the way a viewer regards what's viewed, often with implications of power: {the male gaze}, {the colonial gaze}.

A gazebo is a freestanding outdoor structure with a roof and open sides, typically found in gardens or parks. Usually hexagonal or octagonal, it provides shade and a place to sit while enjoying the surrounding landscape: {The wedding ceremony took place in the gazebo}. Gazebos are often decorative, with latticework or railings.

Gazebos is the plural of gazebo, a freestanding roofed structure open on all sides, typically found in gardens or parks. Gazebos provide shade and a place to sit while enjoying outdoor surroundings: {The wedding ceremony was held in the gazebo}. They range from simple wooden frames to elaborate Victorian designs.

Gazed is the past tense of gaze, meaning to look steadily and intently at something, usually for an extended moment. The word suggests absorption or contemplation rather than a quick glance: {She gazed out the window}, {He gazed at the stars}. Gazing often implies wonder, longing, or deep thought.

A gazelle is a slender, swift antelope native to Africa and Asia, known for its graceful build and large dark eyes. The animal's elegance makes it a common symbol of beauty and grace: {She moved with the grace of a gazelle}. Gazelles are often depicted bounding across savannas, their speed and agility legendary among prey animals.

Gazelles are slender, swift antelopes native to Africa and Asia, known for their graceful movement and large, dark eyes. The word often evokes speed and elegance: {She moved with the grace of a gazelle}. Various species exist, typically tan or brown with distinctive markings. In tech slang, a gazelle is a fast-growing startup company.

A gazette is an official journal or newspaper, especially one published by a government containing public notices, appointments, and legal announcements: {The appointment was published in the official gazette}. Historically, gazettes were among the earliest newspapers. The word now appears mainly in the names of established newspapers: {The Phoenix Gazette}, {The Montreal Gazette}.

Gazillion is a playful invented number meaning an impossibly large, uncountable quantity: {I've told you a gazillion times}. Like bajillion and zillion, it borrows the suffix from actual large numbers (million, billion) to create hyperbolic effect. The word is informal and never refers to an actual mathematical value.

A gazillionaire is an extremely wealthy person—a playful exaggeration suggesting wealth beyond counting. The word substitutes the nonsense prefix "gazillion" for "million" or "billion," emphasizing cartoonish abundance rather than actual net worth: {He lives like a gazillionaire}. Often used humorously or by children.

Gazillions is the plural of gazillion, a playful term for an impossibly large, unspecified number: {I've told you gazillions of times}. Like millions or billions but deliberately exaggerated and imprecise, it emphasizes overwhelming quantity rather than actual count. The word belongs to a family of made-up -illion numbers including bajillion and zillion.

Gazing is looking steadily at something, usually with sustained attention or absorption. Where glancing is quick and looking is neutral, gazing suggests duration and focus: {She stood gazing out the window}, {tourists gazing at the cathedral}. The word often carries a contemplative or admiring quality.

Gazpacho is a cold Spanish soup made from raw blended vegetables—typically tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, onions, and garlic—with olive oil and vinegar. It's served chilled, often in summer: {We started with gazpacho and crusty bread}. The soup originated in Andalusia and has become a staple of Mediterranean cuisine.

Gear refers to equipment or apparatus for a particular activity: fishing gear, camping gear, climbing gear. In machinery, gears are toothed wheels that mesh to transmit motion: {The car ground its gears}. To gear up is to prepare: {We're gearing up for the holiday rush}. Something geared toward a purpose is designed for it. In British slang, gear can mean clothing or illegal drugs.

A gearbox is an enclosed system of gears that transmits power from an engine to wheels or other moving parts, allowing changes in speed and torque. In vehicles, shifting gears engages different gear ratios within the gearbox. The term applies broadly to any cased gear assembly in machinery: {The tractor's gearbox needs rebuilding}.

Geared describes something designed or adjusted for a particular purpose or audience: {The program is geared toward beginners}, {a economy geared for growth}. From the literal sense of fitting with gears—the toothed wheels that transmit motion in machinery. A car's gears determine how engine power translates to wheel speed; similarly, something geared to a task has been calibrated for it.

A gearhead is someone obsessively interested in machinery, especially cars or motorcycles. The term suggests hands-on enthusiasm—someone who tinkers with engines, knows technical specifications, and enjoys talking shop: {My brother's a total gearhead; he's rebuilt three transmissions this year}. The word can extend to any technical enthusiast: audio gearheads, computer gearheads.

Gearheads are enthusiasts obsessed with mechanical things, especially cars and motorcycles. The term combines gear (machinery) with the slang suffix -head (devotee), suggesting someone whose mind is always on engines, horsepower, and technical specifications. {The gearheads spent all weekend rebuilding the transmission}. The word can extend to anyone deeply absorbed in technical equipment or gadgetry.

Gearing refers to a system of gears or the way gears are arranged to transmit motion: {The gearing on this bicycle needs adjustment}. In finance, gearing (British) means the ratio of a company's debt to its equity—what Americans call leverage: {The company's high gearing made investors nervous}. To gear up or gear down is to shift into higher or lower gears, literally or figuratively preparing to increase or decrease effort.

Gears are toothed wheels that mesh with other toothed wheels to transmit motion or change speed and torque in machinery. The plural often refers to a system of such wheels: {The gears in the transmission}. In vehicles, gears are the different speed ratios: {shift gears}, {low gear}, {high gear}. To gear up is to prepare: {We're gearing up for the holidays}. Something geared toward a purpose is designed or adjusted for it: {a program geared toward beginners}.

A gearshift is the lever or mechanism used to change gears in a vehicle, typically located on the floor console or steering column. Manual transmissions require the driver to operate the gearshift along with a clutch pedal; automatic transmissions shift themselves but still use a gearshift to select drive, reverse, park, and neutral. {She moved the gearshift into reverse.}

A gecko is a small lizard found in warm climates worldwide, known for its ability to climb smooth vertical surfaces and even walk upside down on ceilings. This remarkable grip comes from millions of tiny hair-like structures on their toe pads. Geckos are often welcomed in homes because they eat insects, and unlike most lizards, many species are vocal, producing distinctive chirping or clicking sounds. {We found a gecko on the bedroom wall last night.}

Geckos is the plural of gecko, a small lizard found in warm climates worldwide. Geckos are known for their ability to climb smooth vertical surfaces—even glass—using specialized toe pads. Many species are nocturnal and vocal, making distinctive chirping sounds. {The geckos scattered when I turned on the porch light.}

Gee is a mild exclamation, a euphemism for Jesus: {Gee, that's great!} {Gee whiz}. It's also a command to turn right for horses and other draft animals: {Gee! Haw!} The exclamation is old-fashioned and wholesome.

A geek is someone obsessively devoted to a particular interest or field, especially one considered niche or technical: {a computer geek}, {a film geek}, {a history geek}. The word once meant a carnival performer who did bizarre acts, then shifted to mean any socially awkward person. Now it's often worn proudly—geek culture celebrates passionate expertise in gaming, comics, technology, and similar pursuits. To {geek out} is to enthusiastically discuss or engage with one's obsession.

Geekdom is the world of geeks—the community, culture, and shared interests of people deeply passionate about technology, gaming, comics, science fiction, or similar pursuits. It can refer to the state of being a geek: {She embraced her geekdom proudly}. The term carries affection rather than stigma, reflecting how geek identity has shifted from insult to badge of honor.

Geeked means excitedly enthusiastic, often to an almost excessive degree: {I'm so geeked for this concert}. The word emerged from hip-hop and youth slang, suggesting the jittery intensity of a geek obsessing over something. In drug slang, geeked can mean high on stimulants, especially cocaine or methamphetamine—wired and hyperalert.

Geekery is enthusiastic, sometimes obsessive engagement with niche interests—particularly technology, gaming, comics, or science fiction. The term embraces what was once dismissive: {I spent the weekend deep in Star Wars geekery}. It can describe both the activity and the culture surrounding it: {The convention was a celebration of geekery in all its forms}.

A geekfest is a gathering or event dominated by enthusiastic discussion of niche interests—technology, gaming, comics, science fiction, or similar subjects. The term can be affectionate or mildly dismissive depending on context: {The conference turned into a total geekfest}. It may also describe any prolonged indulgence in geeky pursuits: {We had a Star Wars geekfest last weekend}.

Geeking is obsessing over or enthusiastically diving into something, typically a niche interest: {I've been geeking out over vintage synthesizers all week}. The term comes from geek culture, where passionate expertise is celebrated rather than mocked. In drug slang, geeking can mean being high on stimulants, especially crack cocaine, or the jittery, paranoid behavior that accompanies such use.

A geekout is an episode of intense, enthusiastic engagement with a niche interest—someone talking at length about vintage synthesizers or comic book continuity is having a geekout. As a verb, to geek out is to indulge this enthusiasm: {We geeked out over the new Star Wars trailer}. The term is affectionate, celebrating rather than mocking the passion.

Geeks are people intensely devoted to specialized interests, especially in technology, gaming, or pop culture. The word once meant a carnival performer who bit the heads off live animals—a sideshow freak. That sense of being outside mainstream society persisted as geek became an insult for socially awkward obsessives. But as tech culture gained status, geek shifted toward pride: {I'm a total computer geek}, {theater geeks}, {history geeks}. To geek out is to enthusiastically immerse yourself in such interests.

Geekspeak is technical jargon or insider terminology used by specialists—originally computer enthusiasts, now anyone deep in a particular field. The term implies language that excludes outsiders: {Sorry for all the geekspeak, but basically your hard drive is toast}. Often used self-deprecatingly or as mild criticism of communication that prioritizes precision over accessibility.

Geeky describes someone or something characterized by intense, often obsessive interest in niche subjects—especially technology, science fiction, gaming, or comics. Originally disparaging, suggesting social awkwardness, the term has softened as geek culture gained mainstream acceptance: {Her geeky enthusiasm for board games is actually charming}. Something can be geeky without the person being a geek: {a geeky hobby}, {geeky glasses}.

Geese is the plural of goose—large waterfowl with long necks, found wild and domesticated. The irregular plural follows the same pattern as feet and teeth. {A flock of geese flew overhead}. Someone's {goose is cooked} when they're in trouble, but the plural doesn't appear in that idiom.

Geez is a euphemism for Jesus, used as a mild exclamation of surprise or frustration: {Geez, give me a break}. {Oh geez, not again}. Less old-fashioned than gee or golly, geez remains common in everyday speech. Also spelled jeez.

A geezer is an old man, often one who's somewhat eccentric or crotchety: {The old geezer yelled at kids to get off his lawn}. In British slang, geezer simply means a man or guy, without the age connotation: {He's a proper geezer}. The American sense carries mild affection or gentle mockery rather than real insult.

Geezers is the plural of geezer—an old man, especially one perceived as eccentric or out of touch. The word carries mild contempt or affection depending on context: {A couple of old geezers were playing chess in the park}. In British slang, geezer can mean any man, without the age connotation: {He's a proper geezer}.

A geisha is a Japanese woman trained in traditional arts—music, dance, conversation, tea ceremony—who entertains guests at private gatherings. Geishas are not prostitutes, though Western misconceptions often conflate the two. The role requires years of apprenticeship and represents a respected cultural tradition: {The geisha played shamisen while guests dined}.

Gel is a semisolid substance with a jelly-like consistency—firmer than liquid but yielding to pressure. Hair gel holds styles in place. Shower gel is liquid soap. The verb means to form a gel, but more often appears figuratively: plans gel when they come together, teams gel when members start working well as a unit. {It took a few weeks for the new lineup to gel.}

Gelatin is a protein derived from collagen, extracted by boiling animal bones, skin, and connective tissue. It dissolves in hot water and sets into a firm, translucent jelly when cooled—the basis for desserts, gummy candies, and aspics. Gelatin also appears in capsules, photographic film, and cosmetics. As an adjective, gelatin describes things made from or resembling the substance: {gelatin capsules}, {gelatin molds}.

Gelatine is an alternative spelling of gelatin, the translucent protein derived from collagen—extracted from animal bones, skin, and connective tissue. It dissolves in hot water and sets into a wobbly solid when cooled, used to thicken desserts, jellies, and capsules. The spelling gelatine is more common in British English.

Gelatinous describes something with the consistency of gelatin or jelly—thick, viscous, and somewhat wobbly. The word applies to substances that are neither fully solid nor liquid, like the {gelatinous mass of a jellyfish} or {a gelatinous blob of hair gel}. It often carries slightly unpleasant connotations, suggesting something slimy or unappetizingly gooey: {The soup had cooled into a gelatinous puddle}.

Gelato is Italian-style ice cream, denser and silkier than American varieties because it contains less air and typically less cream. Served at a slightly warmer temperature, it has an intense, concentrated flavor. Gelato shops ({gelaterias}) often display it in metal tubs with the surface sculpted into peaks: {We stopped for pistachio gelato}.

A gelding is a castrated male horse. Castration makes horses calmer and easier to handle, so most male horses not kept for breeding are gelded. The term extends to other castrated equines like donkeys and mules. {The ranch keeps three geldings and two mares.}

Geldings are castrated male horses. The plural of gelding, the term applies to horses neutered to make them calmer and more manageable for riding or work. Geldings lack the temperamental unpredictability of stallions while retaining their size and strength: {The stable keeps mostly geldings for trail rides}.

Gelled describes something that has formed into a gel—a substance between liquid and solid. Hair gel makes hair gelled. Figuratively, when plans or ideas gel, they come together and take shape: {The project finally gelled after months of discussion}. A gelled team has found its chemistry. The spelling jelled is equally common.

Gelling is the process of becoming a gel—thickening from liquid to a more solid, cohesive state. Gelatin gels as it cools. The term extends to groups or ideas coming together: {The team is finally gelling}, {The plan started gelling in my mind}. Also spelled jelling.

Gels is the third-person singular verb form of gel. When a liquid gels, it thickens into a semi-solid state: {The mixture gels as it cools}. When a plan or group gels, it comes together and begins working effectively: {The team finally gelled after a few rough weeks}. Gels is also the plural of gel—hair gels, shower gels, the colored filters placed over stage lights.

Gelt is money or profit, from Yiddish. The word appears most often in connection with Hanukkah, where chocolate coins wrapped in gold foil are given to children: {The kids fought over the gelt}. Outside this context, gelt sounds dated or deliberately ethnic: {He made some serious gelt on that deal}.

A gem is a precious or semiprecious stone, especially one that has been cut and polished for use in jewelry: {a ring set with gems}. By extension, gem describes anything of exceptional quality or value: {This restaurant is a hidden gem}, {Her new assistant is a real gem}. A gem of a thing is small but excellent: {a gem of a short story}.

Gems are precious or semiprecious stones, especially when cut and polished for jewelry: diamonds, rubies, emeralds. Figuratively, a gem is anything of exceptional quality or beauty: {That little café is a real gem}, {gems of wisdom}. The word carries connotations of rarity and value—something worth seeking out or treasuring.

A gemstone is a mineral or other material prized for its beauty, durability, and rarity, typically cut and polished for use in jewelry. Diamonds, rubies, emeralds, and sapphires are the most valued gemstones. Semi-precious stones like amethyst, turquoise, and opal command lower prices but remain popular. {She inherited a ring set with a deep blue gemstone.}

Gemstones are minerals or other materials prized for their beauty, durability, and rarity, cut and polished for use in jewelry or ornamentation. Diamonds, rubies, emeralds, and sapphires are the traditional "precious" gemstones; others like amethyst, opal, and jade are called "semiprecious," though the distinction is more commercial than scientific. {She inherited a collection of loose gemstones from her grandmother.}

A gendarme is a member of a military force employed in police duties, particularly in France and other French-speaking countries. The term distinguishes these officers from civilian police: gendarmes typically patrol rural areas and highways, while regular police handle urban zones. In mountaineering, a gendarme is a rock pinnacle on a ridge that blocks easy passage—an obstacle standing guard over the route.

Gender classifies people, animals, or grammatical forms into categories—most commonly male and female, though contemporary usage increasingly recognizes additional identities beyond this binary. In grammar, gender is a system for classifying nouns and pronouns that may or may not correspond to biological sex. The distinction between gender (as social or psychological identity) and sex (as biological category) has become important in modern discourse: {Gender is a spectrum, not a binary}. Gender also appears in compounds like {gender roles}, {gender expression}, and {gender identity}.

Genderbend is to reimagine a character, person, or figure as a different gender than their original presentation. Common in fan fiction, fan art, and cosplay, where creators depict male characters as female or vice versa: {a genderbent version of Sherlock Holmes}, {She genderbent Link for her costume}. The noun genderbend refers to such a reimagining. Also appears as gender-bend or gender bend.

A genderbender is a person who defies conventional expectations about gender presentation—through clothing, behavior, appearance, or identity. The term emerged in the 1980s and can describe drag performers, androgynous dressers, or anyone whose gender expression crosses traditional boundaries: {She's always been a bit of a genderbender}. Also spelled gender-bender or gender bender.

Genderbenders are people who deliberately blur or cross traditional gender boundaries in appearance, behavior, or identity. The term emerged in the 1980s for those who mixed masculine and feminine presentation—androgynous fashion, makeup on men, masculine dress on women.
