Informally, gourd means head: {Use your gourd!} If someone is {out of their gourd}, they're crazy or intoxicated.

Gourds are hard-shelled fruits of the cucumber family, typically inedible but valued for their shapes. Dried gourds serve as containers, birdhouses, musical instruments, and decorations—pumpkins and squash at harvest festivals, carved jack-o'-lanterns at Halloween. In slang, {out of one's gourd} means crazy or intoxicated, gourd standing in for head.

A gourmand is someone who loves food and eats heartily—an enthusiastic eater rather than a picky one. The word occupies middle ground between foodie and glutton: a gourmand appreciates good food but the emphasis falls on quantity and gusto rather than refined taste. {He's a gourmand who can't resist seconds}. Compare gourmet, which stresses discriminating palate over appetite.

Gourmet describes food, cooking, or dining of especially high quality and refinement: {a gourmet restaurant}, {gourmet coffee}. As a noun, a gourmet is someone with cultivated taste in food and drink—a connoisseur who appreciates fine cuisine. The word can shade into pretension: {He's such a gourmet he won't eat at chain restaurants}. Marketing has diluted the term; "gourmet" now appears on everything from frozen pizzas to dog food.

Gourmets are people with refined taste in food and drink who appreciate fine cuisine and culinary excellence. The term suggests sophisticated palates and discriminating judgment about what constitutes quality eating, distinguishing gourmets from mere enthusiasts or heavy eaters. {The restaurant caters to gourmets willing to pay premium prices for exceptional ingredients.} A gourmet, as an adjective, describes food or cooking of high quality: {gourmet coffee}, {gourmet kitchen}.

Gout is a painful form of arthritis caused by uric acid crystals accumulating in joints, especially the big toe. Historically associated with rich food and drink, it was called "the disease of kings." The word also has an archaic meaning of a drop or splash, surviving mainly in heraldry: {gouttes of blood}.

To govern is to exercise authority over a political unit—a country, state, or city. A governing body makes and enforces rules: {The council governs the township}. Beyond politics, govern means to control or regulate: {Supply and demand govern prices}. What governs your decisions influences or determines them. A governor controls speed in machinery, preventing runaway acceleration.

Governance is the system or process by which an organization, institution, or society is directed and controlled. It encompasses the rules, practices, and structures through which decisions are made and authority is exercised: {corporate governance}, {good governance in developing nations}. The term often implies accountability and transparency—qualities that distinguish legitimate governance from mere rule.

A governess is a woman employed to educate and care for children in a private household. Unlike a nanny, who focuses primarily on childcare, a governess provides formal instruction—teaching reading, languages, music, and deportment. The role was common among middle- and upper-class families in the 18th and 19th centuries, often filled by educated women of reduced circumstances. {Jane Eyre worked as a governess at Thornfield Hall.} The word now sounds historical or British.

Governesses is the plural of governess, a woman employed to teach and care for children in a private household. The role was common among middle-class women in the 18th and 19th centuries—respectable but precarious, as governesses occupied an awkward social position between family and servants. {The governess taught the children French and deportment.} The term now sounds historical or literary.

Governing describes the act of exercising authority or control over something—a nation, organization, or system. A governing {body} makes official decisions. Governing {principles} are the fundamental rules that shape how something operates. The word emphasizes ongoing direction rather than one-time decisions: {The governing party faces criticism over its economic policies}.

Government is the system or group that holds authority over a territory and its people—making laws, enforcing them, and managing public affairs. It can refer to a specific administration {the current government}, the abstract institution {government exists to serve the people}, or the act of governing {democratic government}. Forms range from democracies to dictatorships, federal systems to city councils.

Governments is the plural of government—the systems or bodies that exercise authority over states, nations, or organizations. It often emphasizes variety or comparison: {Governments around the world responded differently to the pandemic}. The word also refers to successive administrations: {Three governments have fallen since the crisis began}.

Most uses of governor are for an elected or appointed official. In the U.S., the elected head of every state is the governor. In British English, governor is more likely to refer to someone in charge of a prison or other large institution: Write to the governors of the BBC. On some kinds of motors, the governor maintains a constant speed with variable loads by regulating the supply of fuel.

Governors is the plural of governor—those who govern. Most often these are elected chief executives of states or provinces: {The governors met to discuss the new federal policy}. A governor can also be a device that regulates speed or flow, as in an engine governor that prevents overspeeding. In institutional contexts, a board of governors oversees an organization: {The Federal Reserve's board of governors sets monetary policy}.

Governorship is the office or position of governor, or the period during which someone holds that office: {She announced her candidacy for the governorship}. {During his governorship, the state balanced its budget for the first time in decades}. The term applies to executives of states, provinces, or institutions like central banks.

Governorships is the plural of governorship—the office, term, or jurisdiction of a governor. The word typically refers to multiple such positions considered together: {Three governorships are up for election this year}. It can also refer to successive terms: {His two governorships spanned twelve years}.

A gown is a long, flowing garment. For women, a gown is a formal dress: {evening gown}, {ball gown}, {wedding gown}. For professionals, it's a loose outer robe indicating status or function: a judge's gown, a graduation gown, a hospital gown. The verb means to dress in a gown: {gowned and ready for surgery}.

Gowns are loose, flowing garments. A gown may be a woman's formal dress {an evening gown}, a robe worn for official ceremonies {academic gowns at graduation}, or a simple covering worn in medical settings {a hospital gown}. The word carries associations of formality, elegance, or institutional function depending on context.

Goy is a Yiddish and Hebrew word for a non-Jewish person, plural goyim or goys. Among Jews, the term ranges from neutral to mildly dismissive depending on tone and context: {The goyim don't understand why we can't eat that}. The adjective goyish describes things characteristic of non-Jewish culture: {Skiing is so goyish}. Non-Jews sometimes adopt the term self-deprecatingly.

Goyim is the Hebrew plural of goy, meaning non-Jews collectively. The word is neutral in Jewish religious and legal contexts but carries dismissive or contemptuous undertones in casual speech, implying outsiders who don't understand Jewish culture or concerns: {The goyim wouldn't get it}. Some speakers use it affectionately or ironically.

Grab means to take hold of something quickly or forcefully: {He grabbed her arm}. It suggests urgency or lack of ceremony—you grab a snack, not a formal dinner. To grab attention is to seize it suddenly. Something {up for grabs} is available to anyone who wants it. As a noun, a grab is a quick snatch: {She made a grab for the phone}.

A grabbag is a container filled with small items from which you draw without seeing what you'll get—common at fairs and fundraisers. By extension, grabbag describes any miscellaneous assortment: {The album is a grabbag of styles}. Also spelled grab bag or grab-bag.

Grabby describes someone or something that grabs—reaching out to seize or clutch. A grabby child snatches toys from others. Grabby hands won't leave things alone. The word often carries a negative tone, suggesting greed or presumptuousness: {The grabby headline was designed to get clicks}. {He got a little grabby after a few drinks.}

Grace in a secular sense denotes elegance combined with beauty, movement, or form: The dancer leapt across the stage with grace. The sacred sense of grace is the loving generosity of God towards humans. If you say grace before a meal, you say a short prayer for the occasion. A grace period is a time after a particular deadline when no penalty will be assessed for failure to meet the deadline. When capitalized, Grace may be an old-fashioned female name, or a title for various nobility or church officials.

Graced is the past tense of grace. To grace something is to bring elegance or honor to it: {She graced the cover of Vogue}. The word often carries a note of condescension—someone important deigning to appear: {He finally graced us with his presence}. In religious contexts, to be graced is to receive divine favor.

Graceful describes movement or form that is smooth, elegant, and pleasing to watch—suggesting effortless control and coordination: {a graceful dancer}, {the graceful arc of a diving bird}. The word extends to behavior and expression: a graceful {apology} handles an awkward situation with tact and dignity. To make a graceful {exit} is to leave without causing disruption or embarrassment.

Gracefully means with grace—smoothly, elegantly, without awkwardness. A dancer moves gracefully across the stage. The word extends beyond physical movement to any action performed with poise or dignity: {She gracefully declined the invitation}, {He gracefully accepted defeat}. To age gracefully is to accept growing older without fighting it desperately.

Graces is the plural of grace, covering its range of meanings. Someone's good graces are their favor or approval: {She worked to stay in her boss's good graces}. Social graces are the polite behaviors expected in company. In Christianity, graces may be prayers of thanks before meals. One graces an occasion by attending it: {The duchess graced the charity gala with her presence}.

Gracious describes someone who is kind, courteous, and generous in manner—particularly toward those of lower status or in difficult situations: {a gracious host}, {She was gracious in defeat}. The word often implies elegance or refined charm: {gracious living}. As an exclamation, {goodness gracious} expresses mild surprise or dismay—a euphemistic oath avoiding "God."

Graciousness is warmth, courtesy, and generosity of spirit in dealing with others. A gracious host makes guests feel welcome and at ease. The quality suggests elegance without stiffness—kindness that comes naturally rather than from obligation: {She accepted the criticism with graciousness}. Graciousness can also describe physical charm or divine favor: {the graciousness of the old estate}, {God's graciousness toward sinners}.

A grackle is a medium-sized North American blackbird with iridescent plumage that shifts between purple, green, and bronze in sunlight. Grackles are gregarious and noisy, often gathering in large flocks that descend on lawns, parking lots, and bird feeders. Their harsh, creaking calls and bold scavenging make them familiar—and to some, unwelcome—suburban birds.

Grackles are medium-sized blackbirds common across North America, known for their iridescent plumage and harsh, creaking calls. They gather in large, noisy flocks, often in parking lots and suburban areas, where their bold scavenging and cacophonous chatter make them hard to ignore: {The grackles descended on the picnic table the moment we turned away}.

Grad is informal for graduate—someone who has completed a degree: {a college grad}, {a recent grad}. It also shortens gradient in technical contexts, particularly in mathematics and physics. As an adjective, grad modifies academic contexts: {grad school}, {grad student}.

Gradations are small, incremental degrees or stages in a sequence. The word implies fine distinctions rather than sharp breaks: {gradations of color from pale pink to deep crimson}, {subtle gradations of meaning}. A gradient shows gradation—smooth transition rather than abrupt change. The singular gradation refers to one such step or to the process of arranging things by degree.

Grade, in all of its uses, implies a range or continuum of values or degrees of quality. In the U.S., grade denotes any of the 12 years of compulsory education (first grade, eighth grade), and also the evaluative marks received by students for their work: My math grade is an A. Many commodities and foods are distinguished in quality by grade (Grade A sheepskin). When you grade something, you assign it a degree of quality on a scale; in other words, a grade. The grade of a road is the degree to which it slopes.

A gradebook is a record where teachers track students' scores on assignments, tests, and overall performance. Traditionally a physical ledger, it now usually refers to digital systems within educational software: {I need to update the gradebook before report cards go out}. Students and parents often have access to view grades online.

Graded describes something arranged in levels, stages, or degrees of intensity. A graded {assignment} has been evaluated and scored. A graded {exercise program} increases difficulty progressively. Graded {readers} are books calibrated to specific skill levels. Land that has been graded has been leveled or smoothed: {The construction crew graded the lot before pouring the foundation}.

A grader is someone or something that grades. A teacher grading papers is a grader; so is automated software that scores tests. In construction, a grader is heavy equipment that levels earth for roads and foundations. In American schools, grader combines with ordinals to indicate a student's year: {a third grader}, {an eighth grader}.

Graders are students in a particular school year: {third graders}, {eighth graders}. The term is American, corresponding to British "year" students. A grader is also a person who grades papers or exams, or a machine that levels ground—a road grader or motor grader pushes earth to create flat surfaces for construction.

Grades are levels or ranks on a scale. In education, grades are marks indicating quality of work—letter grades run from A to F, with A being excellent. Grade also means a year of schooling: {My son is in fourth grade}. The grade of a road is its slope or incline. To grade is to assign a rank or to level ground: {Workers graded the site for construction}. To {make the grade} is to meet a standard.

A gradient is a rate of change across distance or space. In mathematics and physics, it measures how steeply something rises or falls—a road's gradient indicates its slope. Temperature gradients show how heat varies across a surface. In design, a gradient is a gradual transition between colors: {The sky faded in a gradient from orange to purple}. In machine learning, gradient descent is an optimization technique that adjusts parameters by following the steepest path toward minimum error.

Gradients describe rates of change across a distance or dimension. In its most concrete sense, a gradient is a slope – the steepness of a road or hill measured as the ratio of vertical rise to horizontal distance. This extends to any gradual transition: a {temperature gradient} shows how heat changes across a space, a {color gradient} blends smoothly from one hue to another. In machine learning, gradients are mathematical values that guide how neural networks adjust during training.

Grading is the act of assigning grades or ratings to evaluate quality, performance, or rank. Teachers grade student work; inspectors grade meat or produce. Grading also means leveling or smoothing a surface: {The crew finished grading the lot before construction began}. In construction and landscaping, grading ensures proper drainage and foundation stability.

Gradual means happening slowly, by degrees rather than all at once. A gradual {increase} in temperature differs from a sudden spike. Gradual {change} accumulates over time, often imperceptibly in the moment but noticeable in retrospect. The word implies steady progression without abrupt shifts: {a gradual slope}, {gradual improvement}.
clues: Happening little by little over time

definition: Gradualism is the principle that change happens slowly and incrementally rather than through sudden transformation. In politics, gradualists favor reform over revolution: {The party embraced gradualism rather than radical upheaval}. In geology and evolutionary biology, gradualism holds that major changes result from accumulated small steps over vast time periods, contrasting with theories of punctuated or catastrophic change.

Gradually means by small degrees over time, not all at once. Change that happens gradually is slow and incremental: {The sky gradually lightened}. {She gradually came to understand his point of view}. The word implies a process smooth enough that any single moment seems barely different from the one before.

Graduate centers on completion and advancement. To graduate is to complete a course of study and receive a degree or diploma: {She graduated from medical school last spring}. The noun is someone who has done so: {a Harvard graduate}. As an adjective, graduate describes advanced academic work beyond a bachelor's degree: {graduate school}, {graduate students}. Graduate also means to mark with degrees or divisions—a graduated cylinder has measurement lines. More broadly, to graduate is to progress through stages: {The program graduates participants from basic to advanced levels}.

Graduated describes something marked with units of measurement: a graduated {cylinder}, a graduated {measuring cup}. It also means arranged in stages or degrees: graduated {tax rates} increase as income rises. Most commonly, graduated is the past tense of graduate—to complete a course of study and receive a degree: {She graduated from college last spring}.

Graduates are people who have completed a course of study, especially at a school or university: {This year's graduates faced a tough job market}. The verb graduate means to complete such a course and receive a diploma or degree: {She graduated from medical school in May}. Graduate also works as an adjective for advanced academic work: {graduate studies}, {graduate student}. To graduate something like a measuring cup is to mark it with degrees or increments.

Graduating is the process of completing a course of study and receiving a degree or diploma: {She's graduating from medical school in June}. It also means progressing through stages or levels: {The program uses graduating levels of difficulty}. To graduate something is to mark it with incremental measurements, as on a thermometer or measuring cup.

Graduation is the completion of an academic program and the ceremony marking it: {Her graduation from medical school took six years}. The word extends to any movement through stages or levels—graduation from training wheels to a real bike, or the gradual progression of colors in a sunset. Graduations are also the marks on a measuring instrument indicating units or degrees.

Graduations are the marks or lines indicating measurement on an instrument—the small divisions on a ruler, thermometer, or measuring cup. The word also refers to ceremonies marking completion of an academic program: {She attended three graduations this spring}. More abstractly, graduations can mean gradual stages or degrees of change: {subtle graduations of color in the sunset}.
clues: Events where diplomas get handed out

definition: Graffiti is writing or drawings scrawled on public surfaces—walls, subway cars, buildings, bridges. The word is Italian and technically plural, though English treats it as a mass noun: {The graffiti was removed overnight}. Graffiti ranges from crude tags and obscenities to elaborate murals. Whether it constitutes art or vandalism depends on who you ask and who owns the wall.

Graft has two distinct origins yielding different meanings. One graft is a shoot or bud inserted into another plant to grow there, or tissue transplanted surgically: {a skin graft}, {a bone graft}. The verb means to attach in this way: {graft a branch onto the rootstock}. The other graft is corrupt use of a position for personal gain, especially in politics: {The mayor's administration was riddled with graft}. In British slang, graft also means hard work: {It took years of graft to build the business}.

Grafted is the past tense of graft, which means to join a shoot or bud from one plant onto another so they grow as one: {She grafted apple branches onto the rootstock}. In medicine, grafted describes tissue transplanted from one site to another: {The surgeon grafted skin from his thigh onto the burn}. Figuratively, something grafted onto an existing structure has been attached or added: {New traditions were grafted onto old customs}.

A grafter is someone who works hard, especially at manual or tedious labor—British slang for a diligent worker: {He's a proper grafter, never takes a day off}. In American usage, grafter more often means someone who engages in graft—political corruption or petty swindles. The two meanings are essentially opposite: one earns honestly through effort, the other dishonestly through schemes.

Grafters are people who work hard, especially at physical or tedious labor—a usage more common in British English: {Those grafters have been at it since dawn}. In American English, grafters typically means people who obtain money or advantage through dishonest means, particularly political corruption or swindling: {The reformers promised to clean out the grafters at city hall}. In horticulture, grafters are those who join plant tissues to propagate varieties.

Grafting is joining plant tissue from one specimen to another so they grow as one—typically attaching a cutting (the scion) to an established root system (the rootstock). Orchardists graft to propagate fruit varieties that won't breed true from seed. The technique extends metaphorically: {grafting new ideas onto old traditions}. In medicine, grafting transfers tissue—skin grafts cover burns. In British slang, grafting means working hard, especially at seduction: {He's been grafting on her all night}.

Grafts covers two unrelated words. One involves attachment: a graft is tissue transplanted from one site to another, or a shoot inserted into a plant to grow there. Surgeons perform skin grafts; gardeners graft branches onto rootstock. The other graft means corrupt acquisition of money through political position—bribery, kickbacks, backroom deals. {The mayor's administration was riddled with graft.}

A grail is an object of prolonged quest or ultimate aspiration—something pursued with devotion despite difficulty: {For decades, room-temperature superconductivity has been the grail of physics}. The word comes from the Holy Grail of medieval legend, the cup Christ used at the Last Supper, sought by knights as the supreme spiritual prize. The lowercase form emphasizes the secular sense of any ardently pursued goal.

Two main meanings of grain inspire nearly all uses of the word. One is to designate a small, hard seed that might be used as food (grain of rice) or something resembling that (grain of sand). The other denotes the pattern in a surface, especially of wood, where the grain means the general direction in which fibers are oriented. Something that goes against the grain is contrary to what is wanted or expected. A grain of truth or some other thing is a very small but meaningful quantity of it.

Grains are the edible seeds of cereal plants like wheat, rice, corn, and oats—staple foods that form the foundation of diets worldwide. The word extends to any small, hard particle resembling these seeds: grains of {sand}, grains of {salt}. A grain is also a tiny amount: {There's a grain of truth in what she says}. In woodworking and textiles, grain refers to the directional pattern of fibers: {Sand with the grain, not against it}. To go {against the grain} is to act contrary to one's nature or prevailing expectations.

Grainy describes a texture of small particles or granules, like sand or coarse salt. A grainy photograph or video has visible specks or pixels that reduce sharpness—sometimes an unwanted flaw, sometimes a deliberate aesthetic: {The old footage had that grainy look}. Grainy can also describe food texture: {The sauce turned out grainy instead of smooth}.

A gram is a unit of mass in the metric system, equal to one thousandth of a kilogram—roughly the weight of a paperclip. In drug slang, a gram typically refers to that quantity of an illegal substance: {He bought a gram of coke}. The abbreviation is g or gm.

Gramma is an informal, affectionate term for grandmother, used especially by young children or when speaking to them: {Go give gramma a hug}. The spelling reflects childish pronunciation. Also spelled grandma.

Grammar is the system of rules governing how words combine into sentences—how they inflect, agree, and arrange themselves. Native speakers internalize grammar without formal study; what schools teach as "grammar" is largely style and usage conventions. {Her grammar is impeccable.} Grammar also refers to a book describing such rules: {a Latin grammar}.

A gramophone is an early device for playing recorded sound, using a needle that traces grooves in a rotating disc. The word is largely historical now, replaced by record player and turntable, though it survives in the Grammy Awards (short for Gramophone Awards) and in British English as an old-fashioned term for any phonograph.

Gramophones are early record players—devices that play sound recordings from rotating discs. The word is dated in American English, where phonograph and then record player replaced it, but remains current in British English. {My grandmother's gramophone still works.} The term evokes the horn-shaped speaker of early twentieth-century machines.

Gramps is an informal, affectionate term for one's grandfather: {Gramps taught me to fish}. It's casual and familiar, typically used by grandchildren speaking to or about their grandfather directly. The word can also refer to any elderly man in a familiar or slightly condescending way: {Hey gramps, you're holding up the line}.

Grams is the plural of gram, a metric unit of mass equal to one thousandth of a kilogram. Small quantities are commonly measured in grams: {The recipe calls for 200 grams of flour}. In drug contexts, grams often refers to quantities of illegal substances: {He was caught with ten grams of cocaine}.

Granaries are buildings for storing grain after harvest. The word appears most often in plural because farms and regions typically have multiple storage structures. Figuratively, a granary is any region that produces abundant grain: {The Midwest is America's granary}. The singular granary refers to a single storage building or, abstractly, to a supply of grain.

A granary is a building or room for storing grain after harvest. By extension, granary describes any region that produces large quantities of grain: {Ukraine was once called the granary of Europe}. The word suggests abundance and agricultural wealth.

Grand means large, impressive, or magnificent in scale or ambition: a {grand staircase}, {grand plans}, a {grand gesture}. It can describe something ambitious or elevated: {the grand scheme of things}. In informal use, grand is a noun meaning a thousand dollars or pounds: {The car cost twenty grand}. A grand {total} is the final sum. A grand {jury} investigates potential crimes. Family terms with grand— {grandmother}, {grandson}—indicate a generation removed.

Grandad is an informal spelling of granddad—one's grandfather. The spelling with one *n* is common in British English: {My grandad fought in the war}. Like granddad, it can address or refer to any elderly man, though this risks condescension.

Grandaddy is an informal spelling of granddaddy, meaning grandfather or, more broadly, the oldest or most venerable example of something: {the grandaddy of all rock festivals}. The spelling without the second "d" reflects casual pronunciation. Used affectionately for elderly patriarchs or to emphasize something's foundational status in its category.

A grandchild is the child of one's son or daughter. The term encompasses both grandsons and granddaughters: {She has four grandchildren}. The relationship extends through any number of generations with the prefix great-: a great-grandchild is the child of one's grandchild.

Grandchildren are the children of one's children—the generation two steps down from oneself. The word combines the familial relationships: your son's daughter is your granddaughter, your daughter's son is your grandson, and collectively they are your grandchildren. {She has six grandchildren, ages three to fifteen.}

Granddad is an informal word for grandfather—your parent's father. The spelling granddad is more common than grandad, though both appear. Like other grandparent terms, it often drops the first syllable in speech and casual writing: {My grandad taught me to fish}.

Granddaddy is an informal term for grandfather, used especially by children or in Southern American speech: {My granddaddy taught me to fish}. Extended, it means the earliest, largest, or most respected example of something: {the granddaddy of all rock festivals}, {the granddaddy of horror films}. Also spelled grandaddy.

Granddads is the plural of granddad, an informal word for grandfather. The term appears in contexts involving multiple people's grandfathers or grandfathers collectively: {Our granddads fought in the same war}. It can also refer metaphorically to older men or predecessors: {the granddads of rock and roll}.

A granddaughter is the daughter of one's son or daughter. The relationship spans two generations: {My granddaughter just started kindergarten}. Like other family terms, it can be modified to show further remove: great-granddaughter, great-great-granddaughter.

Grandeur is impressive greatness in scale, appearance, or character. The word applies to physical things—the grandeur of the {Grand Canyon}, of {Versailles}—and to abstract qualities: grandeur of {vision}, of {ambition}. {Delusions of grandeur} are fantasies of one's own importance or power. The word carries a note of nobility or magnificence that mere bigness lacks.

A grandfather is your parent's father. The word extends to any male ancestor further back: {My grandfather immigrated from Poland; his grandfather fought in the Napoleonic Wars}. Grandfather also works as a verb meaning to exempt from new rules based on prior status: {Existing tenants were grandfathered in under the old rent policy}. A grandfather clock is a tall freestanding pendulum clock.

Grandfathered describes something exempted from new rules because it existed before those rules took effect. A grandfathered {policy} or {property} continues under old terms while new acquisitions must comply with current regulations: {Our building was grandfathered in, so we don't need the updated permits}. The term comes from post-Civil War voting laws that exempted men whose grandfathers could vote—a device to disenfranchise Black Americans while protecting illiterate whites.

Grandfathering is exempting existing cases from new rules or requirements. When regulations change, those already engaged in an activity may be grandfathered in—allowed to continue under the old rules: {The new licensing requirements don't apply to current practitioners; they're grandfathered in}. The term comes from post-Civil War voting restrictions that exempted men whose grandfathers could vote, effectively excluding Black citizens while protecting white ones.

Grandfatherly describes qualities associated with a kindly grandfather—gentle, patient, warmly protective, often with an air of aged wisdom. A grandfatherly man might offer advice without judgment or show indulgent affection toward younger people: {He took a grandfatherly interest in the new hires}. The word suggests benevolence without authority, warmth without intensity.

Grandfathers is the plural of grandfather—the father of one's parent. The word also functions as a verb: to grandfather something is to exempt it from new rules based on prior status. Old practices or people are {grandfathered in} when regulations change: {Existing tenants were grandfathered in at the old rent}. This usage derives from post-Civil War "grandfather clauses" that exempted white voters from literacy tests if their grandfathers had voted.

Grandiose describes something impressive in scale or ambition—or something that tries too hard to be. A grandiose {palace} genuinely impresses; grandiose {plans} may or may not succeed. The word often carries a whiff of excess or self-importance: {His grandiose speeches promised more than he could deliver}. When applied to people, grandiose usually suggests inflated self-regard bordering on delusion.

Grandiosity is an inflated sense of one's own importance, abilities, or status. The word carries clinical weight in psychology, where it describes a symptom of conditions like narcissistic personality disorder or bipolar mania: {His grandiosity made him believe he was destined for world leadership}. Outside clinical contexts, grandiosity suggests pretension or delusion—ambitions or self-assessments that exceed reality: {The grandiosity of the plan was matched only by its eventual failure}.

A grandkid is a grandchild—the son or daughter of one's own child. The word is informal and affectionate, common in casual speech: {I've got three grandkids now}. The plural grandkids appears more often than the singular.

Grandkids is the informal plural of grandchild—the children of one's children. The word is common in casual speech: {I'm babysitting the grandkids this weekend}. The singular grandkid exists but is less frequent than the plural.

Grandma is an informal word for grandmother—the mother of one's parent. It's among the most common terms children use for this relationship, along with grandpa for grandfather. {Grandma's coming for Thanksgiving}. The spelling grandma reflects casual pronunciation; the more formal grandmother preserves both syllables.
clues: Cookies and stories at her house

definition: Grandmas is the plural of grandma, an informal and affectionate term for grandmother. It appears in contexts involving multiple grandmothers or grandmothers collectively: {Both my grandmas are coming to Thanksgiving this year}. The word carries warm, familiar connotations and is common in casual speech and writing, contrasting with the more formal grandmother.
clues: Parents of your mom or dad

definition: A grandmaster is a chess player who has achieved the highest title awarded by the World Chess Federation, requiring exceptional tournament performance against other top players. The term extends to masters of other pursuits—martial arts, competitive gaming, or any domain where hierarchical ranks exist: {He's a grandmaster of Go}. Sometimes used loosely for anyone with supreme skill: {a grandmaster of negotiation}.

Grandmasters is the plural of grandmaster, a title for those who have achieved the highest level of skill in a field. In chess, grandmaster is the supreme title awarded by FIDE to elite players: {Three grandmasters competed in the final round}. The term extends to martial arts, where grandmasters head schools or styles, and to any domain where mastery is formally recognized.

A grandmother is the mother of one's parent—either father's mother or mother's mother. The word often carries associations of nurturing, wisdom, and family tradition: {My grandmother taught me to bake}. Informal variants include grandma, granny, nana, and nanna. To {teach your grandmother to suck eggs} is to presumptuously offer advice to someone more experienced.
clues: The one who always bakes cookies

definition: Grandmotherly describes qualities associated with grandmothers—warmth, gentle affection, patience, and nurturing care. A grandmotherly {woman} might offer comfort and homemade cookies; a grandmotherly {manner} suggests kind, indulgent attention. The word can apply to anyone, regardless of whether they actually have grandchildren: {The grandmotherly librarian helped the children pick out books}.

Grandmothers is the plural of grandmother—the mother of one's parent. The word often carries connotations of warmth, wisdom, and family tradition: {My grandmothers both immigrated from Poland}. To {teach your grandmother to suck eggs} is to presume to instruct someone more experienced than yourself.

Grandpa is an informal term for grandfather—a father's or mother's father. It's a child's word that persists into adulthood as an affectionate form of address or reference: {Grandpa taught me to fish}. The variant grandpapa is old-fashioned. Grandpa can also refer to any elderly man, sometimes dismissively: {Some grandpa was holding up traffic}.

A grandparent is the parent of one's parent—a grandmother or grandfather. The term encompasses both maternal and paternal sides: {My grandparents on my mother's side lived in Ohio}. Grandparents often occupy a special role in family life, associated with spoiling children and passing down traditions. The verb grandparent means to act in that capacity: {She grandparents three kids}.

Grandparents are the parents of one's parents—maternal grandparents on the mother's side, paternal on the father's. The term often carries associations of wisdom, indulgence, and family history: {My grandparents spoiled me rotten}. Grandparents may serve as primary caregivers when parents are absent or unable.

Grandpas is the plural of grandpa, an informal word for grandfather. The term carries warm, familiar connotations: {Both my grandpas served in World War II}. Like grandpa itself, grandpas suggests affection rather than formality—you'd say grandpas at a family gathering, grandfathers in a legal document.

A grandson is a son of one's son or daughter—the male child one generation removed. {My grandson is starting kindergarten this fall.} The relationship implies the perspective of grandparents looking down the family tree.

A grandstand is a large, often covered seating structure for spectators at stadiums, racetracks, and fairgrounds, typically with tiered rows facing the action. To grandstand is to perform or speak in a way calculated to impress an audience rather than achieve substance: {The senator was grandstanding for the cameras}. The adjective grandstand describes showy plays or catches made with flair: {a grandstand catch in center field}.

A grandstander is someone who behaves dramatically to impress an audience rather than accomplish anything substantive. The term comes from the grandstand—the main seating area at a stadium—and implies playing to the crowd: {He dismissed the senator as a grandstander who cared more about cable news clips than legislation}. The verb is grandstand; the behavior is grandstanding.

People who grandstand—who perform actions or make statements designed to attract attention and impress an audience rather than to accomplish anything substantive. The term is dismissive, implying that someone's apparent principles or outrage are really just posturing: {The senators questioning the witness were grandstanders playing to the cameras}.

Grandstanding is behaving in a way designed to attract attention or impress others rather than to accomplish anything substantive. Politicians grandstand when they make speeches aimed at voters rather than colleagues. The term comes from the grandstand—the main seating area at a stadium—where spectators sit watching. To grandstand is to play to that crowd: {He accused the senator of grandstanding during the hearing}.

Grandstands are tiered seating structures for spectators at sporting events, races, or parades—typically large, open-air, and facing the action. The verb grandstand means to perform showily to impress an audience rather than accomplish something substantive: {He's just grandstanding for the cameras}. A grandstander seeks attention over results.

A grange is a farm with its associated buildings, especially a large or impressive country estate. The term often suggests agricultural property belonging to a substantial household. In American usage, Grange refers to a fraternal organization for farmers founded in 1867, formally called the National Grange of the Order of Patrons of Husbandry: {The local Grange held a harvest supper}. Members meet at a grange hall. (Capitalized Grange often refers to the farmers' organization.)

Granite is a coarse-grained igneous rock, typically gray or pink, composed mainly of quartz and feldspar. It forms deep underground as magma cools slowly, creating the visible crystalline texture. Granite is prized for its hardness and durability in construction—countertops, monuments, building facades. Figuratively, something {set in granite} is unchangeable, and a {granite jaw} suggests stern determination.

Grannies is the plural of granny, an informal word for grandmother. The term extends to any elderly woman, sometimes affectionately, sometimes dismissively. Granny glasses are small, round spectacles. A granny flat is a small secondary dwelling, often for an aging parent. A granny knot is a square knot tied incorrectly. {The grannies sat knitting on the porch.}

Granny is an informal word for grandmother, suggesting warmth and familiarity. It extends to any elderly woman: {a little granny in a rocking chair}. A granny knot is tied incorrectly, the way a grandmother supposedly might. Granny Smith is a variety of green apple. A granny flat is a small dwelling for an aging relative, typically on adult children's property.

Granola is a breakfast food or snack made from oats, nuts, honey, and other ingredients, baked until crunchy. It's eaten as cereal with milk or yogurt, or formed into bars. As slang, granola describes someone with earthy, health-conscious, environmentally aware sensibilities—the kind of person who might eat granola: {She's pretty granola—composting, hiking, the whole thing}.

Granpappy is an informal, folksy term for grandfather, associated with rural or Southern American speech. It suggests affection and down-home warmth: {My granpappy taught me to fish}. The word often evokes nostalgia for simpler times or older generations. Also spelled grandpappy.

To grant is to give something formally—permission, a request, a wish, money. Governments grant rights, foundations grant scholarships, genies grant wishes. A grant is something given this way, especially funding for research or projects: {She received a grant to study climate change}. To {take for granted} is to assume something without question or fail to appreciate what you have. {Granted} concedes a point: {Granted, he's difficult, but he's also brilliant}. (Capitalized Grant is a surname or given name.)

Granted functions mainly in two expressions. To {take something for granted} is to assume it without question, or to fail to appreciate what you have: {We take clean water for granted}. As a sentence opener, granted concedes a point before pivoting: {Granted, it's expensive, but it's worth it}. The past tense of grant appears in phrases like {granted permission} or {wish granted}.

Granting is used as a conjunction to acknowledge a point while simultaneously limiting its force or introducing a contrast. If you say {granting that the weather was bad, we still should have tried}, you concede the weather but don't let it excuse inaction. It functions much like "even if" or "although," allowing a speaker to appear fair-minded before pivoting to their main argument.

Grants are sums of money given by governments, institutions, or organizations for specific purposes—typically research, education, or projects serving public benefit. Unlike loans, grants don't require repayment: {She received a grant to study climate change}. To grant is to give or allow: {The judge granted the motion}. By extension, granting something in argument means conceding a point: {Granted, it's not perfect, but it works}.

A grape is a small, round fruit that grows in clusters on vines, eaten fresh or dried as raisins and crushed to make wine and juice. Grapes come in varieties from deep purple to pale green. {Sour grapes} describes disparaging something you can't have, from Aesop's fable of the fox who couldn't reach the grapes.

Grapefruit is a large citrus fruit with a thick yellow or pinkish rind and tart, slightly bitter flesh that ranges from pale yellow to deep pink or red. It grows in clusters on the tree, which may explain the name—though the fruit itself resembles an oversized orange more than a grape. Grapefruit is eaten fresh, juiced, or used in salads and desserts. {I have half a grapefruit for breakfast most mornings.} The fruit is known for interacting with certain medications, affecting how drugs are metabolized.

Grapefruits is the plural of grapefruit, a large citrus fruit with yellow skin and pink, red, or white flesh that's tart and slightly bitter. The name comes from how the fruit grows in clusters, like grapes. {She ate half a grapefruit for breakfast.} {The grapefruits from Texas are sweeter than the ones from Florida.}

Grapes are small, round fruits that grow in clusters on woody vines. They come in green, red, purple, and black varieties, eaten fresh or dried into raisins. Grapes are the source of wine—the fermented juice of the fruit. {Sour grapes} describes dismissing something you can't have, from the Aesop fable about a fox who couldn't reach the grapes.

Grapeshot is a type of artillery ammunition consisting of small iron balls packed together, which scatter upon firing like pellets from a shotgun. Used from the 17th through 19th centuries, it was devastating against massed infantry at close range: {Napoleon ordered grapeshot fired into the crowd}. The term occasionally appears in historical fiction or figurative descriptions of overwhelming force.

A grapevine is a climbing plant that produces grapes. More commonly, the grapevine is an informal network through which rumors and information spread: {I heard through the grapevine that they're getting divorced}. The metaphor suggests news traveling along interconnected pathways, passing from person to person like tendrils linking one vine to the next.

Grapevines are the climbing plants that produce grapes, trained on trellises or arbors for wine production and table fruit. The singular grapevine also names an informal channel for rumors and gossip: {I heard through the grapevine that they're getting divorced}. The image is of information traveling along interconnected social paths, like tendrils spreading vine to vine.

A graph is a diagram showing the relationship between variables, typically with values plotted along horizontal and vertical axes: {The graph showed sales declining over time}. In mathematics, graph theory studies networks of points connected by lines. To graph something is to represent it in such a diagram. Graph also appears as a suffix meaning something written or recorded: {photograph}, {telegraph}, {seismograph}.

Graphic describes something visual or vividly detailed. A graphic {designer} works with images and layout. A graphic {novel} tells its story through sequential art. When describing violence, sex, or disturbing content, graphic means explicit and detailed—nothing left to imagination: {The documentary contained graphic footage of the aftermath}. As a noun, a graphic is an image or visual element: {The presentation needs better graphics}.

Graphics refers to visual images, designs, or representations—especially those produced by computers. The term covers everything from simple charts and diagrams to elaborate digital artwork and video game visuals. A graphics {card} processes visual data; graphics {design} arranges visual elements for communication. The singular graphic works as both noun and adjective: {a graphic showing population trends}, {graphic violence}.

Graphite is a soft, gray-black form of carbon used in pencil cores, lubricants, and batteries. Despite being pure carbon like diamond, graphite's layered molecular structure makes it slippery and conductive rather than hard. The "lead" in pencils is actually graphite mixed with clay—the more graphite, the darker and softer the mark.

Graphs are visual representations of data or mathematical relationships. A line graph tracks change over time; a bar graph compares quantities. In mathematics, a graph plots points and lines on coordinate axes to show how variables relate: {The graph of y = x² forms a parabola}. To graph something is to represent it this way. In technical contexts, a graph is also a network of nodes connected by edges.

Grappa is an Italian brandy distilled from pomace—the grape skins, seeds, and stems left over from winemaking. It's typically clear, high in alcohol, and ranges from harsh and fiery to smooth and refined depending on quality. Traditionally served as a digestivo after meals: {We finished dinner with a glass of grappa}.

Grapple means to seize and struggle with something at close quarters. Wrestlers grapple, as do people fighting for control of an object: {They grappled for the gun}. The word extends to mental struggle: {grappling with a difficult decision}, {grappling with grief}. A grapple or grappling hook is a multi-pronged device for catching and holding.

Grappled is the past tense of grapple, which means to seize and struggle with someone at close quarters: {The two wrestlers grappled on the mat}. More often, grapple describes wrestling mentally with something difficult: {She grappled with the decision for weeks}. A grappling hook is a device thrown to catch and hold.

A grappler is someone who grapples—who seizes and struggles at close quarters. The word appears most often in wrestling and martial arts, where grapplers specialize in holds, locks, and throws rather than strikes: {He's a skilled grappler who prefers to take fights to the ground}. By extension, anyone wrestling with a difficult problem might be called a grappler.

Grapples covers both physical and mental wrestling. To grapple is to seize and struggle with someone in close combat, or to wrestle with a difficult problem: {She grappled with the decision for weeks}. A grapple or grappling hook is a device with claws for grabbing and holding—thrown to catch a ledge or drag something closer.

Grappling is close-quarters fighting that involves grabbing, holding, and wrestling rather than striking. Wrestlers and martial artists grapple for position and control. Figuratively, to grapple with something is to struggle with it mentally: {She's been grappling with the decision for weeks}. Grappling hooks catch and hold surfaces for climbing.

Grasp means to seize and hold firmly with the hand: {She grasped the railing to steady herself}. The word extends naturally to mental holding—to grasp an idea is to understand it: {I finally grasped what she was trying to say}. A grasp is both a grip and the capacity to comprehend: {a good grasp of the fundamentals}. Something {within your grasp} is attainable; something {beyond your grasp} exceeds your reach or understanding.

Grasping describes someone excessively eager to acquire money or possessions—greedy, avaricious. A grasping {landlord} squeezes every penny from tenants. The word carries strong disapproval, suggesting someone who clutches at wealth without generosity or scruple: {His grasping nature alienated everyone who tried to help him}.

The general, nonspecific use of grass is to denote any member of the plant family Poaceae: plants with single seed leaves that are usually called blades. Types of grass that are planted for ornamental purposes in lawns are also simply called grass: Keep your dog off the grass. When are you going to mow the grass? A pasture for grazing, or a field that will be harvested for hay might also be said to contain grass, and grass is also a dated slang term for marijuana. In British slang, to grass on someone is to inform the police of their illegal activity.

A grasshopper is a jumping insect with long hind legs, known for leaping through grass and fields. Grasshoppers chirp by rubbing their legs against their wings. In large numbers they become locusts, devouring crops. Figuratively, a grasshopper is someone who lives for the moment without planning ahead, from Aesop's fable of the improvident grasshopper and the industrious ant.

Grasshoppers are jumping insects with powerful hind legs, found in fields and meadows worldwide. They're known for their chirping sounds and occasional swarming as locusts. Figuratively, a grasshopper is someone who lives for the moment without planning ahead—from Aesop's fable contrasting the carefree grasshopper with the industrious ant: {Don't be a grasshopper; save for retirement}.

Grassland is open terrain where grasses dominate rather than trees or shrubs. The term covers both natural ecosystems—prairies, savannas, steppes—and land maintained for grazing or hay production. {The ranch sprawled across miles of grassland.} Grasslands support distinct wildlife and play important roles in carbon storage and agriculture.

Grasslands are large open areas where grasses are the dominant vegetation, with few trees or shrubs. These ecosystems occur on every continent and go by regional names: prairies in North America, steppes in Eurasia, savannas in Africa, pampas in South America. Grasslands typically receive moderate rainfall—enough to support grasses but not dense forests—and provide habitat for grazing animals and the predators that hunt them.

Grassroots describes activity originating from ordinary people rather than leaders or institutions. A grassroots {movement} or {campaign} builds support from the ground up—local volunteers, small donors, community organizing—rather than from established power structures. {The candidate relied on grassroots fundraising}. The word evokes organic growth, like grass spreading across a field. As a noun, the grassroots are the common people, especially as a political base: {The party has lost touch with its grassroots}.

A grate is a framework of metal bars—in a fireplace to hold burning fuel, or over a drain or window as a cover. To grate is to reduce something to small pieces by rubbing against a rough surface: {grate some cheese}. Grating also produces harsh scraping sounds, and by extension, harsh effects on the nerves: {Her voice grates on me}.

Grated describes something reduced to small particles by rubbing against a rough surface: {grated cheese}, {grated lemon zest}. A grated window or opening has a grate—a framework of parallel or crossed bars—covering it. Separately, grated is the past tense of grate, meaning to irritate: {Her voice grated on my nerves}.

Grateful describes feeling or expressing thanks for something received or experienced: {I'm grateful for your help}, {She gave him a grateful smile}. The word implies recognition that something good has come from outside oneself—a gift, a kindness, an outcome. To be grateful to someone is to feel indebted to them; to be grateful for something is to appreciate having it.

A grater is a kitchen tool with a surface of sharp-edged holes or slits, used to shred food into small pieces by rubbing it against the surface: {a cheese grater}, {Grate the carrots with a box grater}. Different hole sizes produce different textures, from fine zest to coarse shreds.

Grates covers both the noun and verb. A grate is a framework of metal bars—in a fireplace holding burning fuel, or over a drain or window. To grate is to reduce something to shreds by rubbing against a rough surface: {grated cheese}, {grated ginger}. The other verb grate means to irritate or annoy: {His voice grates on me}. A harsh sound grates; so does an unpleasant personality.

Gratification is the pleasure that comes from having a desire fulfilled or a need satisfied. The word often appears in discussions of delayed versus immediate gratification—whether to take a smaller reward now or wait for a larger one later: {She chose instant gratification over long-term savings}. Sexual gratification refers specifically to sexual pleasure or release.

Gratified means pleased or satisfied, especially when a desire or expectation has been fulfilled. The word carries a formal, measured tone—less effusive than delighted, more dignified than happy: {I was gratified to learn that my work had made a difference}. It often implies that satisfaction was earned or deserved rather than simply received.
clues: Left with a sense of satisfaction

definition: Gratifying describes something that gives pleasure or satisfaction, especially when it fulfills a desire or validates effort: {It's gratifying to see your hard work pay off}. The word often appears when results match hopes or expectations: {The response to her speech was gratifying}. Related to gratify, which means to give pleasure or indulge.

Gratin is a cooking technique that produces a browned, crispy top—typically achieved by broiling breadcrumbs, cheese, or butter over a dish. The term also names dishes prepared this way: {potato gratin}, {gratin dauphinois}. {Au gratin} means prepared with this crust: {cauliflower au gratin}. The golden, bubbling top is the defining feature.

Grating describes sounds or sensations that are harsh, irritating, or abrasive: {Her grating voice made it hard to concentrate}, {the grating screech of metal on metal}. A grating personality wears on you through repeated annoyance. As a noun, a grating is a framework of parallel or crossed bars—a drain cover, a ventilation screen, or a barrier over a window.

Gratitude is the feeling of appreciation for something received or experienced—a gift, a kindness, an unexpected good turn. It implies recognition that the benefit came from outside oneself: {She expressed her gratitude to the doctors who saved her life}. Gratitude can be fleeting or cultivated as a disposition: {He kept a gratitude journal}.

Gratuitous means given freely, without payment or obligation—but this neutral sense has largely been overtaken by a negative one: unnecessary, uncalled for, serving no purpose. A gratuitous {insult} is one that didn't need to be made. Gratuitous {violence} in a film exists for shock value rather than narrative necessity: {The gore felt gratuitous}.

Grave covers both noun and adjective territory with quite different meanings. The noun grave is a burial site, typically a hole dug in the earth to receive a corpse, or the mound or marker above it. {She visits her father's grave every year.} The adjective grave means serious or solemn, suggesting weighty concern: {The doctor's expression was grave.} A grave situation or grave danger is one requiring urgent attention. As a verb, grave is an archaic term meaning to carve or engrave.

A gravedigger is someone who digs graves for burial. The work is manual labor, traditionally done with a shovel, though modern cemeteries often use machinery. Gravedigger carries associations with death and darkness—the figure appears in folklore and literature as someone comfortable among corpses, most famously in the scene from *Hamlet*. {The gravediggers had the plot ready by morning.}

Gravediggers are workers who dig graves for burial. The job involves preparing burial plots in cemeteries, typically using shovels and backhoes. Figuratively, gravediggers are those who contribute to something's demise: {the gravediggers of democracy}, {Critics called the new policies the gravediggers of the welfare state}.

Gravedigging is the work of digging graves for burial. The gravedigger is a stock figure in literature and film—earthy, philosophical, unbothered by death. Figuratively, gravedigging suggests unearthing what should stay buried: {The journalist's gravedigging into the scandal cost him his job}. In sports, gravedigging describes actions that seal an opponent's defeat.

A gravekeeper is a person who maintains a cemetery—mowing grass, tending graves, and sometimes digging them. The role overlaps with sexton and groundskeeper, though gravekeeper emphasizes the burial ground itself rather than church duties. In fiction and games, gravekeepers often appear as solitary, eerie figures who know the secrets of the dead.
clues: One who tends the dead's rest

definition: Gravel is a loose collection of small stones and rock fragments, coarser than sand but smaller than cobbles. It forms naturally in riverbeds and is manufactured for construction—driveways, paths, roadbeds. A gravel {road} or {driveway} is surfaced with it. To gravel someone is to irritate or perplex them, though this use is old-fashioned. A gravelly {voice} is rough and low-pitched, as if full of small stones.

Gravelly describes something containing or resembling gravel—small loose stones: {a gravelly path}, {gravelly soil}. More commonly, it describes a voice that is rough, harsh, and low-pitched, as if the speaker has stones in their throat: {His gravelly voice made everything sound like a threat}. The quality often suggests age, tobacco use, or natural raspiness.

A graverobber is someone who digs up corpses from graves, historically to sell bodies to medical schools for dissection or to steal valuables buried with the dead. The term extends to anyone who profits from the dead or their legacy: {These estate lawyers are just graverobbers in suits}. Also spelled as two words.

Graverobbers are people who dig up corpses or steal from graves. Historically, graverobbers supplied cadavers to medical schools for dissection, or looted burial sites for valuables. The term extends to anyone who profits from the dead or desecrates their memory: {Those estate lawyers are nothing but graverobbers}. Also spelled as two words.

Graverobbing is the act of stealing from graves—whether taking valuables buried with the dead or the corpses themselves. Historically, bodies were stolen to supply medical schools with cadavers for dissection. The term extends to any distasteful exploitation of the deceased or their legacy: {Critics called the posthumous album release pure graverobbing}.

Graves are holes dug in the earth for burying the dead, or the mounds marking such burial sites. The word extends to any final resting place: {a watery grave}, {mass graves}. To dig your own grave is to cause your own downfall. Something carries weight {from beyond the grave} when it influences events after the person's death. To work yourself {into an early grave} is to harm your health through overwork. (Capitalized Graves is a surname.)

Graveside refers to the area immediately beside a grave, especially during a burial ceremony. A graveside {service} takes place at the burial site rather than in a church or funeral home. {Mourners gathered at the graveside as the casket was lowered.} The word functions as both noun and adjective.

A gravestone is a stone marker placed at a burial site, inscribed with the deceased person's name, dates, and sometimes an epitaph. The terms gravestone, headstone, and tombstone overlap considerably, though headstone specifically marks the head of a grave and tombstone may refer to a larger monument. {We found our ancestor's gravestone in the old cemetery.}

Gravestones are stone markers placed at graves, typically inscribed with the deceased's name, dates of birth and death, and sometimes an epitaph or decorative carving. The terms gravestone, tombstone, and headstone are largely interchangeable, though headstone specifically marks the head of a grave. {We walked through the old cemetery reading the gravestones.}

A graveyard is a burial ground for the dead, typically adjacent to a church. The term is largely interchangeable with cemetery, though cemetery often implies a larger, independent burial ground. Figuratively, a graveyard is where things go to die or be forgotten: {a graveyard of abandoned projects}, {the elephants' graveyard}. The graveyard shift is the late-night work shift, roughly midnight to 8 a.m.

Graveyards are burial grounds, places where the dead are interred. The term originally referred specifically to churchyards—land surrounding a church used for burials—while cemetery denoted any burial ground. This distinction has largely faded: {The old graveyard behind the church dates to the 1700s}. Figuratively, a graveyard is where things go to die or be forgotten: {a graveyard for failed startups}. The graveyard shift is the overnight work shift, roughly midnight to 8 a.m.

Gravitas is dignified seriousness of manner or bearing. The word suggests weight and substance—the quality that makes people take someone seriously. A leader with gravitas commands respect through presence rather than force: {She brought gravitas to the role}. The term often appears in discussions of politicians or executives who either possess or conspicuously lack it.

To gravitate is to be drawn toward something, as if by gravity. The word usually describes attraction to people, places, or ideas rather than physical force: {She gravitates toward quiet, intellectual types}, {The conversation gravitated toward politics}. In physics, gravitate refers to actual gravitational attraction between masses, but this technical sense is far less common than the figurative one.

Gravitated is the past tense of gravitate, meaning to be drawn toward something as if by gravitational pull. The word usually describes attraction to people, places, or ideas rather than literal physics: {She gravitated toward the quiet corner of the party}, {He's always gravitated to jobs that let him work outdoors}. The movement implied is gradual and natural rather than deliberate.
clues: Moved as if by invisible force

definition: Gravitating is moving toward something as if pulled by gravity. Objects gravitate toward massive bodies; people gravitate toward ideas, places, or other people they find attractive: {She found herself gravitating toward the quieter guests at the party}. The word implies natural, almost inevitable movement rather than deliberate choice.

Gravity is the force, not completely understood by science, which causes objects with mass to attract each other. That is the most frequent use of the word, but gravity is also the verbal noun of the adjective grave (meaning extremely serious), so gravity also means that state or condition of being. This use typically occurs in phrases such as the gravity of the situation.

Gravy is a sauce made from meat juices, typically thickened with flour and served over meat, potatoes, or biscuits. Beyond the kitchen, gravy means easy money or unexpected profit—something extra beyond what's needed or earned: {The base salary covers expenses; bonuses are gravy}. A {gravy train} is a situation providing effortless income or benefits.

Gray is the color between black and white, the color of ash, overcast skies, and aged hair. It suggests neutrality, ambiguity, or dullness: {a gray area}, {gray weather}. To gray is to become gray, especially of hair with age. Gray matter is brain tissue, and by extension, intelligence. Also spelled grey, especially in British English.

A graybeard is an old man, the term referencing the gray or white facial hair that comes with age. By extension, graybeard describes someone with long experience or seniority in a field: {The graybeards in the department remember when everything was done on paper}. In computing, graybeard often refers specifically to veteran programmers or system administrators who learned their craft in earlier technological eras. The spelling greybeard is preferred in British English.

Graybeards are old men, especially those viewed as wise or venerable elders: {The graybeards on the committee favored caution}. The term can be respectful, suggesting accumulated wisdom, or dismissive, implying outdated thinking: {The graybeards in management don't understand the new technology}. In some contexts, graybeard refers specifically to senior experts or veterans in a field.

Graying describes the process of becoming gray, especially of hair losing its pigment with age: {His temples were graying}. The term extends to populations or institutions growing older on average: {the graying of America}, {a graying workforce}. Something graying may also be fading or becoming dull: {graying memories of childhood}.

Grayscale refers to images or displays using only shades of gray, from white through black, without color. A grayscale photograph strips away hue, leaving only tonal values: {Convert the image to grayscale}. In design and printing, grayscale simplifies production and focuses attention on form rather than color. The term also describes any spectrum between two extremes: {Ethics isn't black and white—it's grayscale}.

Graze has two distinct meanings. One involves feeding: cattle graze on grass, moving across a field eating as they go. By extension, people graze when they eat small amounts throughout the day rather than sitting down to meals: {I grazed on snacks all afternoon}. The other graze means to scrape lightly in passing—a bullet grazes an arm, a car grazes a fence. A graze is also the resulting scrape or abrasion: {She cleaned the graze on her knee}.

Grazed is the past tense of graze, which has two distinct meanings. One graze describes animals feeding on growing grass or vegetation: {The cattle grazed in the meadow all afternoon}. The other graze means to scrape or touch lightly in passing: {The bullet grazed his shoulder}. A grazed knee is one that has been scraped, typically from a fall. Both uses share a sense of light, surface-level contact.

A grazer is an animal that feeds on grass and other low-growing vegetation—cattle, sheep, and horses are classic grazers. The term extends to browsing humans: someone who eats small amounts throughout the day rather than full meals, or who samples food while wandering through a kitchen or market. {She's a grazer—never sits down for a proper dinner.}

Grazers are animals that feed on grass and other low-growing plants, as opposed to browsers, which eat leaves from trees and shrubs. Cattle, sheep, and horses are classic grazers. The term extends to people who eat small amounts throughout the day rather than full meals: {I'm more of a grazer—I never sit down for proper dinners}.

Grazes covers two related ideas. The first is feeding: cattle graze on grass, and people graze when they snack lightly throughout the day rather than eating full meals. The second is light contact: a bullet that grazes your arm just barely touches it, and a graze is the superficial wound it leaves. {The sheep grazed in the meadow}. {She grazed her knee on the pavement}.

Grazing is the act of animals feeding on growing grass or other vegetation in a field or pasture: {cattle grazing on the hillside}. The word extends to human eating habits—nibbling small amounts throughout the day rather than eating full meals: {She spent the afternoon grazing on snacks}. A grazing wound or impact barely touches the surface, passing by with only light contact.

Grease is thick, oily substance used for lubrication or produced by cooking fatty foods. Mechanics apply grease to moving parts; bacon leaves grease in the pan. To grease something is to apply this substance: {grease the axle}, {grease the baking pan}. To {grease someone's palm} is to bribe them. Grease also refers to oily buildup in hair or on skin. As slang, grease can mean to kill: {The hitman greased him outside the restaurant}.

Greased means coated with grease or oil, typically to reduce friction or prevent sticking: {a greased baking pan}, {greased axles}. Figuratively, greased suggests something made smoother or easier: {The deal went through like a greased pig}. To {grease someone's palm} is to bribe them. {Greased lightning} describes something extremely fast.

Greasepaint is thick, waxy makeup used by actors, especially in theater, where stage lighting demands heavy coverage. The term evokes old-fashioned theatrical tradition—the world of the stage, costume, and performance: {the smell of greasepaint and sawdust}. By extension, greasepaint can stand for the acting profession itself.

A greaser is a person who greases machinery, especially on ships or in factories. The term also denotes a young man of a 1950s subculture marked by slicked-back hair, leather jackets, and motorcycles or hot rods: {The greasers hung out at the drive-in}. As ethnic slur, greaser is a derogatory term for a person of Mexican or Latin American descent.

Greasers were members of a 1950s-60s youth subculture characterized by slicked-back hair (hence the name), leather jackets, and working-class swagger. The look was associated with rock and roll, motorcycles, and a rebellious attitude: {The greasers hung out by the gas station}. The term is now mostly historical or nostalgic. Separately, greaser is an old ethnic slur for Mexicans or other Latin Americans.

Greasing is the act of applying grease or lubricant to something—machinery, baking pans, or moving parts: {The mechanic was greasing the axle}. Figuratively, greasing can mean facilitating through bribery or favors: {greasing palms}, {greasing the wheels of bureaucracy}. The word sometimes appears in contexts of making things run smoothly, literally or otherwise.

Greasy describes something coated or saturated with grease or oil: {greasy fingers from the fried chicken}, {greasy hair}. Food that's greasy has excessive fat: {a greasy spoon} is a cheap diner serving such fare. Figuratively, greasy suggests something slick and untrustworthy: {a greasy salesman}, {greasy charm}. The word carries connotations of uncleanliness or moral slipperiness.
Great is mainly an approving adjective and as an interjection it also expresses a positive response or feeling—except when used ironically.

A greatcoat is a long, heavy overcoat, typically of wool, worn for warmth in cold weather. The term evokes military or formal styles from earlier centuries—double-breasted, often with a cape or shoulder flaps: {He pulled his greatcoat tighter against the wind}. The word sounds old-fashioned now, largely replaced by overcoat.

Greatcoats is the plural of greatcoat, a heavy overcoat designed for warmth in severe weather. The garment is associated especially with military dress from the 18th through early 20th centuries, worn by soldiers over their uniforms: {Officers in greatcoats stamped their boots against the cold}. The word sounds historical or formal today.

Greater is the comparative form of great, indicating a larger degree, extent, or importance: {the greater good}, {greater New York}. When modifying place names, greater refers to a metropolitan area including suburbs and surrounding regions: {Greater London}, {Greater Boston}. In math, greater than means larger in value.

Greatest is the superlative of great—the most great among a group. It describes whatever surpasses all others in size, extent, or importance: {the greatest threat to democracy}, {the greatest basketball player of all time}. In casual speech, greatest often expresses enthusiastic approval: {This is the greatest!} The phrase {greatest of all time} has spawned the acronym GOAT.

A greatgrandfather is the father of one's grandfather or grandmother—three generations back. The term extends predictably: a great-greatgrandfather is four generations back, and so on. {My greatgrandfather immigrated from Poland in 1902.} Also spelled great-grandfather.

A greatgrandson is the son of one's grandchild—three generations removed. The relationship extends further with additional "great" prefixes: a great-great-grandson is four generations down. {Her greatgrandson visited every Sunday.}

Greatness is the quality of being great—exceptional, distinguished, or remarkably superior in some domain. It applies to achievements, abilities, or character that rise well above the ordinary: {She never doubted his greatness as a composer}. Greatness can describe historical significance, moral stature, or sheer excellence in a field. The word often carries weight and formality, invoked when ordinary praise falls short: {Some are born to greatness, others achieve it}.
clues: The state of being truly remarkable

definition: Greats is the plural of great used as a noun—the outstanding figures in a field: {one of the all-time greats}, {She studied the greats of jazz piano}. At Oxford University, Greats refers to the classics curriculum covering ancient Greek and Roman literature, history, and philosophy, or the final examinations in that program.

A greatsword is a large two-handed sword, typically four to six feet long, requiring both hands to wield effectively. The term appears most often in fantasy games and fiction, where greatswords are prized for their reach and devastating power: {The barbarian hefted her greatsword}. Historical equivalents include the Scottish claymore and German Zweihänder.

Greed is excessive desire for more than one needs or deserves, especially money or possessions. The word carries moral weight—greed isn't just wanting things but wanting them beyond reasonable measure, often at others' expense. {Corporate greed}, {greed for power}. The greedy hoard what they have while craving what they don't.

Greedflation is the theory that corporate price gouging, rather than supply-chain disruptions or increased costs, drives inflation. The term blends greed with inflation, suggesting companies exploit economic uncertainty to raise prices beyond what rising costs would justify: {Critics blame greedflation for grocery prices that stayed high even after supply chains recovered}. The word carries a political charge, typically used by those skeptical of corporate motives.

Greedy describes an excessive desire for more than one needs or deserves—typically food, money, or possessions. A greedy {child} wants all the candy; a greedy {corporation} maximizes profits at others' expense. The word carries moral judgment: greed is one of the seven deadly sins. In computing, a greedy {algorithm} takes the largest available option at each step without considering long-term consequences.

The color adjective green designates things that are the usual color of living leaves and grass. Its many figurative meanings differ greatly across languages, but in English, green can stand for inexperience, envy, jealousy, youth, vigor, and nausea. In politics, green indicates an agenda of environmental issues, and in fact many countries have a Green Party that puts the environment first. Green occurs frequently in food names (green onion, green salad, green bean, green pepper) and characterizes places dominated by plant life, such as a green belt. In golf, a green is the area immediately around the pin and cup.

A greenback is a piece of U.S. paper currency, named for the green ink on the reverse side. The term dates to Civil War–era banknotes but remains common informal usage: {I've got a few greenbacks in my wallet}. In the plural, greenbacks means cash generally: {He's always chasing greenbacks}.
