In law, hearsay is an out-of-court statement offered as evidence, generally inadmissible because the original speaker isn't available for cross-examination.

A hearse is a vehicle for transporting a coffin to a funeral or burial site. Modern hearses are typically long, black automobiles with a rear compartment visible through side windows: {The hearse led the procession to the cemetery}. The word sometimes extends metaphorically to anything associated with death or funerals.

Hearses is the plural of hearse, the specialized vehicle used to transport a coffin to a funeral or burial site. Hearses are typically long, black, and solemn in appearance, designed to accommodate a casket in the rear compartment. {A procession of hearses moved slowly through the cemetery gates.}

Heart designates the blood-pumping vital organ in vertebrates, but it is used to talk about emotional or moral feelings (as distinct from intellect). Two frequent collocations are win someone’s heart (succeed in attracting their love), and break someone’s heart (withdraw your love or affection from them when they don’t want this). The expression at heart means essentially or in essence: She’s a country girl at heart. The heart of something is the most central or vital part of it.

Heartache is emotional anguish, especially from grief or disappointed love. The word locates suffering in the chest, where strong emotions register physically: {the heartache of losing a child}, {all the heartache she'd been through}. It suggests deep, lingering pain rather than sudden shock.

Heartaches is the plural of heartache—deep emotional pain, especially from romantic disappointment or loss. The word suggests suffering that feels physical, located in the chest: {She's had her share of heartaches}. Country and blues music trade heavily in heartaches, treating them as the inevitable cost of loving.

A heartbeat is one complete cycle of the heart's contraction and relaxation, pumping blood through the body. The word often refers to the rhythmic sound or sensation: {I could feel my heartbeat racing}. Figuratively, someone or something can be the heartbeat of a place or movement—its vital center: {Small businesses are the heartbeat of the local economy}. In a heartbeat means instantly or without hesitation: {I'd do it again in a heartbeat}.

Heartbeats are the rhythmic contractions of the heart that pump blood through the body. The term often emphasizes the individual pulses: {I could feel my heartbeats quicken}. Figuratively, heartbeats measure tiny increments of time: {The election could have gone the other way in a heartbeat}. The heartbeat of something is its vital center or driving force: {Small businesses are the heartbeat of the local economy}.

Heartbreak is the crushing emotional pain that follows loss—especially the end of a romantic relationship or the death of someone loved. The word captures how grief can feel physical, as if the heart itself has been damaged. A heartbreak can also be any devastating disappointment: {It was a heartbreak to see the old theater torn down}.

A heartbreaker is someone who causes romantic disappointment or emotional pain, typically by ending a relationship or failing to return affection: {She's a heartbreaker—left a trail of broken hearts across three states}. The word can also describe a devastating loss or near-miss: {That last-second field goal was a real heartbreaker for the home crowd}.

Heartbreakers is the plural of heartbreaker—someone or something that causes emotional pain, especially by ending a romantic relationship or failing to return affection. A person known for leaving a trail of disappointed lovers is a heartbreaker: {She dated a string of heartbreakers in her twenties}. The term also applies to devastating losses or near-misses: {The team has played too many heartbreakers this season}.

Heartbreaking describes something that causes intense emotional pain or grief. A heartbreaking {story} moves you to tears; heartbreaking {news} delivers devastating information. The word applies to situations that evoke deep sympathy or sorrow: {It was heartbreaking to watch her say goodbye}. Unlike merely sad, heartbreaking suggests something that pierces you emotionally.

Heartbreaks is the plural of heartbreak—instances of deep emotional pain, typically from loss or disappointment in love. The word suggests grief intense enough to feel physical: {She's had her share of heartbreaks}. Beyond romance, heartbreaks can come from any crushed hope: {the heartbreaks of a long political career}.

Heartbroken describes the devastation of profound emotional loss—the end of a relationship, the death of someone loved, the collapse of a cherished hope. The heart is imagined as literally broken, unable to function normally: {She was heartbroken when he left}. The noun is heartbreak; the adjective heartbreaking describes what causes such pain.

Heartburn is a burning sensation in the chest caused by stomach acid rising into the esophagus. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with the heart—the discomfort just occurs in that general area. Spicy food, overeating, and lying down after meals commonly trigger it. {I shouldn't have had that second helping—now I've got heartburn.}

To hearten is to give someone courage or confidence, to lift their spirits when they're discouraged: {The team was heartened by their first win of the season}. The opposite is dishearten. Something heartening provides encouragement or hope: {heartening news}, {a heartening sign}.

Heartened means encouraged or filled with renewed hope and confidence. Someone who is heartened feels their spirits lifted after receiving good news or witnessing positive signs: {I was heartened to see so many young people at the rally}. The opposite is disheartened.

Heartening means encouraging or giving hope: {The early test results were heartening}. Something heartening lifts the spirits or restores confidence after doubt or difficulty. {It was heartening to see so many people volunteer after the disaster.}

Heartfelt describes emotions or expressions that are deeply sincere and genuine: {a heartfelt apology}, {heartfelt thanks}, {heartfelt condolences}. The word implies that feeling comes from somewhere essential rather than being performed or obligatory. Something heartfelt may be simple or inarticulate but carries authentic emotional weight.

A hearth is the floor of a fireplace, typically made of stone or brick, extending into the room. By extension, hearth represents home and domestic life: {hearth and home}, {defending hearth and family}. The word evokes warmth, safety, and the traditional center of household gathering.

Hearthfire is the fire burning in a hearth—the fireplace at the center of a home. The word carries connotations of warmth, domesticity, and familial comfort: {We gathered around the hearthfire on winter evenings}. It appears in fantasy literature and historical fiction to evoke premodern settings where the hearth was central to household life.

Hearths is the plural of hearth, the floor of a fireplace or the area immediately surrounding it. The hearth was traditionally the center of home life—where families gathered for warmth and cooking. This makes it a symbol of domesticity: {hearths and homes}, {defending their hearths}. The word extends to the floor of furnaces and forges in metalworking.

A hearthstone is the flat stone forming the floor of a fireplace, or more broadly, the area in front of a hearth. Figuratively, it represents home and domestic life—the center of household warmth and gathering: {They returned to the family hearthstone after years abroad}. The word evokes traditional images of home fires and family bonds. (Capitalized Hearthstone is a video game.)

Hearties is the plural of hearty used as a noun, meaning comrades or friends—especially in nautical contexts. A ship's captain might address the crew as {me hearties}, though this usage now sounds theatrical or piratical, more likely encountered in costume than on actual vessels.

Heartland refers to the central or most important part of a country or region, especially one considered essential to its character or identity. In American usage, the heartland typically means the rural Midwest, evoking images of farms, small towns, and traditional values distinct from coastal urban centers. {Politicians love to campaign in the heartland.} The term can apply to any nation's core territory, or metaphorically to the essential center of anything: {the heartland of conservative thought}.
clues: The nation's agricultural and cultural center

definition: The heartlands are the central, essential regions of a country or territory—areas considered culturally representative or economically vital. In American usage, {the heartland} typically means the rural Midwest, evoking traditional values and agricultural life: {Politicians love to invoke heartland voters}. The term can also describe the core territory of any movement, industry, or phenomenon: {the heartland of the auto industry}.

Heartless means lacking compassion or feeling—cruel, unfeeling, indifferent to others' suffering. A heartless {decision} disregards human cost. A heartless {person} shows no sympathy. The word implies coldness rather than active malice: {It was heartless to fire her on Christmas Eve}. Something heartless treats people as if they don't matter.

Heartlessness is the quality of being cruel, unfeeling, or indifferent to others' suffering. Where *cruelty* suggests active harm, heartlessness emphasizes absence—a void where compassion should be: {The heartlessness of the policy left families homeless}. Someone acting with heartlessness shows no mercy or emotional response to distress.

Heartrending describes something that causes overwhelming grief or anguish—the kind of sorrow that feels like it might tear you apart: {a heartrending goodbye}, {heartrending images of the famine}. The word applies to things witnessed rather than experienced directly; you watch something heartrending, you don't feel heartrending yourself.

Hearts are the plural of heart—the organ, the shape, or the seat of emotion. In cards, hearts is one of the four suits, marked by red heart symbols. Hearts is also a trick-taking card game where players try to avoid winning hearts and especially the queen of spades: {Let's play hearts after dinner}. (Capitalized Hearts may refer to the Scottish football club.)

Heartsick describes deep emotional distress—the ache of grief, disappointment, or longing. Someone heartsick over a breakup or a death feels the pain almost physically, as if the heart itself were afflicted: {She was heartsick when she learned he had married someone else}. The word is slightly literary but still current.

Heartsickness is deep emotional anguish, especially from grief, longing, or romantic disappointment. The word evokes a physical sensation—as if sorrow has settled in the chest: {She was overcome with heartsickness after he left}. More literary than everyday, it suggests sustained melancholy rather than momentary sadness.

Heartsong is the deeply personal expression that defines someone's spirit or emotional core—what moves them most fundamentally. The term appears in spiritual and self-help contexts to describe authentic inner voice or calling: {She finally found her heartsong after years of searching}. It also names the songs emperor penguins use to identify mates and family members.

A heartstopper is something so surprising, thrilling, or beautiful that it figuratively stops the heart—a moment of breathless shock or awe. The word often describes dramatic moments in sports or entertainment: {The last-second goal was a real heartstopper}. It can also refer to a person of stunning attractiveness: {She's an absolute heartstopper}.

Heartstopping describes something so intense, shocking, or suspenseful that it feels like your heart might stop—a moment of extreme excitement or fear: {a heartstopping finish to the race}, {heartstopping footage of the near-collision}. The word implies a brief, involuntary physical response to something dramatic or dangerous.

Heartstrings are the deepest feelings of love or compassion. The word appears almost exclusively in the plural and with a possessive: {The documentary tugged at my heartstrings}. To tug, pull, or pluck at someone's heartstrings is to evoke strong emotion, especially sympathy or tender sentiment. The image suggests invisible cords connecting the heart to what it loves.

Heartstrings are the deep emotions, especially love, sympathy, or sentimental attachment. The word appears almost exclusively in the phrase {tug at the heartstrings} or {pull at the heartstrings}, describing something that evokes tender feelings: {The documentary about orphaned animals really tugged at my heartstrings}. The image is of emotions as strings that can be plucked or pulled.

A heartthrob is a celebrity or public figure who inspires romantic admiration, especially among young fans: {He was a teen heartthrob in the nineties}. The term evokes the quickened pulse of infatuation. It typically describes actors, musicians, or other performers known for their physical appeal.

Heartthrobs is the plural of heartthrob—a celebrity or public figure who inspires romantic infatuation, especially among young fans: {teen heartthrobs of the 1990s}, {The actor was a heartthrob before becoming a serious dramatic performer}. The word evokes the quickened pulse of adolescent crushes.

Heartwarming describes something that evokes tender, positive emotions—a feeling of warmth in the chest associated with affection, gratitude, or restored faith in human goodness. The word typically applies to stories, gestures, or moments: {a heartwarming reunion}, {a heartwarming tale of kindness}. It suggests emotional uplift without sentimentality tipping into saccharine.

Heartwood is the dense inner wood of a tree trunk, no longer carrying sap. As a tree grows, the older central wood darkens and hardens while the outer sapwood remains light and active. Heartwood provides structural strength and is prized in woodworking for its durability and rich color: {The table was made from walnut heartwood}.

Heartworm is a parasitic roundworm that infests the hearts and pulmonary arteries of dogs, cats, and other mammals. The worms are transmitted by mosquitoes and can grow to a foot long, causing serious cardiovascular damage. {The vet recommended monthly heartworm prevention.} Heartworm disease is fatal if untreated.

Heartwrenching describes something that causes intense emotional anguish or distress, typically sadness or grief. A heartwrenching {story} or heartwrenching {scene} evokes deep sympathy or sorrow in the audience. The word suggests an almost physical sensation of the heart being twisted or torn by powerful emotion. It applies to experiences, narratives, or images that move people to tears or profound compassion: {The documentary included heartwrenching footage of families separated at the border}.

Hearty describes something robust, vigorous, or wholehearted. A hearty {meal} is substantial and satisfying. A hearty {laugh} comes from deep within. Hearty {congratulations} are warm and sincere. A hearty {welcome} is enthusiastic. The word often suggests physical vigor or abundance: {hearty appetite}, {hale and hearty}. In nautical tradition, {me hearties} addresses fellow sailors.

Heat, a verb and noun, is related to the adjective hot. When you heat something, you make it warmer. Heat has the same figurative meanings as hot that are associated with anger and passion. If a discussion heats up, it becomes more intense. When a female animal is in heat, it is receptive to pregnancy. If someone is applying heat, they are bringing pressure in order to achieve a result.

Heated describes something with elevated temperature: {heated seats}, {a heated pool}. More often, heated refers to emotional intensity, especially anger or passionate disagreement: {a heated argument}, {The discussion grew heated}. Both senses share the idea of energy applied—whether thermal or emotional. The verb heat produces this past participle, which functions mainly as an adjective.

A heater is a device that produces warmth, typically for indoor spaces during cold weather. Space heaters warm single rooms while central heating systems warm entire buildings. In baseball slang, a heater is a fastball thrown at high velocity: {He blew a heater right past the batter}. Informally, heater can also mean a handgun, especially in older crime fiction and film noir contexts.

Heaters is the plural of heater—devices that produce warmth. Space heaters warm rooms; water heaters supply hot water. In baseball slang, a heater is a fastball: {He threw nothing but heaters in the ninth}. In street slang, a heater is a handgun, from the heat of firing: {He was carrying a heater under his jacket}.

Heath is an area of open, uncultivated land, typically covered with low shrubs like heather and gorse. The word evokes wild British landscapes—moorlands, commons, and coastal stretches where the soil is too poor for farming: {We walked across the heath at sunset}. Heath also names the low-growing plants that thrive in such terrain, especially heathers and related species. (Capitalized Heath is a surname or given name.)

Heathen originally meant someone who didn't follow Christianity, Judaism, or Islam—a pagan or unbeliever. The word carries connotations of being uncivilized or irreligious: {The missionaries sought to convert the heathens}. In casual use, heathen often appears humorously to describe someone lacking manners or culture: {Were you raised by heathens?} The adjective form describes pagan practices or beliefs: {heathen rituals}.

Heathens is the plural of heathen—people who don't follow one of the major religions, especially Christianity. The term originally distinguished pagans and polytheists from monotheists. In contemporary use, it's often playful or ironic: {Time to civilize these heathens}, a parent might joke about rowdy children. Calling someone a heathen suggests they lack refinement or proper upbringing rather than literal religious difference.

Heather is a low-growing shrub with small purple, pink, or white flowers, native to moorlands and heaths of Europe. It thrives in poor, acidic soil and covers vast stretches of Scottish and English highlands: {The hillside was purple with heather}. The grayish-purple color of heather flowers is also called heather. (Capitalized Heather is a given name.)

Heathers is the plural of heather, the low-growing shrub with purple or pink flowers that covers moorlands and hillsides, especially in Scotland and northern England. The word often evokes wild, windswept landscapes: {The heathers were in bloom across the moor}. (Capitalized Heathers refers to the 1988 dark comedy film.)

Heathland is open, uncultivated land dominated by low-growing shrubs like heather and gorse, typically on acidic, nutrient-poor soil. Common in Britain and northern Europe, heathlands are often windswept and treeless: {We walked across miles of purple heathland}. The term overlaps with moorland, though moors tend to be wetter and higher in elevation.

Heaths are areas of open, uncultivated land covered with low-growing shrubs—especially heather, gorse, and similar plants. The terrain is typically sandy or peaty, found across Britain and northern Europe. {The wind swept across the heaths.} Heath also names the plants themselves, particularly heather and related species in the Ericaceae family.

Heating is the process of making something warmer, or a system that warms a building: {The heating broke down in January}, {central heating}. In British English, heating often stands alone where Americans would say heat: {Turn up the heating}. As an adjective, it describes something that produces warmth: {heating element}, {heating pad}.

A heatmap is a data visualization that uses color gradients to represent values across a two-dimensional surface. Areas of high intensity appear in warm colors (red, orange), while low-intensity areas appear cool (blue, green). Heatmaps show website user behavior, geographic population density, or any data where spatial patterns matter: {The heatmap showed most clicks concentrated in the upper left corner}.

Heatmaps are visual representations that use color gradients to show the intensity or frequency of data across a surface. In web analytics, a heatmap reveals where users click, scroll, or hover on a page—hot colors indicating high activity, cool colors indicating low. The technique applies wherever spatial patterns matter: {The heatmap showed most touches clustered near the basket}.
clues: Warm spots glow, cold stays dark

definition: Heats is the plural of heat, referring to multiple instances of warmth, intensity, or competitive rounds: {The qualifying heats determine who advances to the finals}. In animal breeding, heats are periods of fertility: {The mare goes through several heats per season}. As a verb, heats means warms or intensifies: {She heats the soup on the stove}, {The debate heats up as election day approaches}.

A heatseeker is a missile that tracks targets by their heat signatures, locking onto engine exhaust or other thermal emissions: {The jet deployed flares to confuse the heatseeker}. Figuratively, someone described as a heatseeker pursues attention, popularity, or the spotlight with similar single-minded determination.

Heatseekers are missiles or other projectiles that track targets by detecting infrared radiation—the heat signature of jet engines or exhaust: {The pilot deployed flares to confuse the heatseekers}. Figuratively, a heatseeker is someone or something drawn relentlessly toward a goal, especially attention or success: {She's a heatseeker for controversy}.

A heatsink is a device that absorbs and disperses heat from electronic components, preventing overheating. Typically made of metal with fins or ridges to maximize surface area, heatsinks are essential in computers, where they draw heat away from processors: {The CPU heatsink needs fresh thermal paste}. Often paired with fans for active cooling.

Heatstroke is a dangerous condition caused by prolonged exposure to high temperatures, in which the body loses its ability to regulate heat. Core temperature rises to dangerous levels, causing confusion, loss of consciousness, and potentially death if untreated. Unlike heat exhaustion, heatstroke is a medical emergency requiring immediate cooling and professional care.

A heatwave is a prolonged period of unusually hot weather, typically lasting several days or more. Meteorologists define it variously—often as temperatures exceeding the average by a certain threshold for a set number of consecutive days. {The heatwave broke temperature records across Europe}. The term also describes any surge of intense heat: {A heatwave from the oven hit her face}.

Heatwaves are prolonged periods of abnormally hot weather, typically lasting several days or longer. The term also describes the visible shimmering distortion of air rising from hot surfaces like pavement or desert sand: {Heatwaves rippled across the highway}. In physics, heat waves are infrared radiation. The spelling varies: {heat wave} or {heatwave}.

The verb heave suggests movement requiring significant force or weight: Heave the couch up the stairs. Heave is often used to suggest the movement caused by deep breathing: Brian’s shoulders heaved when he gasped. If you heave a sigh of relief, you expel lots of breath. The noun heave designates an act of heaving and is used especially to characterize the movement of waves. As slang, heaves are associated with vomiting: She had the dry heaves.

Heaved is the past tense and past participle of heave, which means to lift, throw, or pull with considerable effort. {She heaved the suitcase onto the bed.} When your chest or stomach heaves, it rises and falls dramatically, often from exertion or nausea. To heave a sigh is to exhale deeply and audibly, usually expressing relief or weariness. In nautical contexts, a ship heaves when it rises and falls with the waves, and heaved or hove are both used as past forms.

Heaven is a general term denoting a notional place in many religions that is the destination of the virtuous after death. This meaning inspires far more frequent figurative use in expressions like seventh heaven and hog heaven, both delightful states experienced by the living. Heaven also figures in many mild oaths (heaven forbid, for heaven’s sake, good heavens).

Heavenly describes things belonging to or characteristic of heaven—the divine realm of gods, angels, and the blessed afterlife: {heavenly hosts}, {heavenly father}. More commonly, heavenly expresses that something is wonderful or deeply pleasurable: {This chocolate cake is heavenly}. The word suggests an experience so good it seems to transcend the ordinary: {a heavenly massage}, {heavenly weather}.
Heavens! and Good heavens! are old-fashioned and mild interjections that express a passing emotion.

Heaves functions as both verb and noun. As a verb, it's the third-person singular of heave—to lift with effort, to throw, or to rise and fall rhythmically: {The ship heaves in the swell}, {She heaves the bag onto the counter}. As a noun, the heaves refers to a chronic respiratory condition in horses causing labored breathing, or to the dry heaves—retching without vomiting: {I had the dry heaves all morning}.

Heavier is the comparative form of heavy—weighing more than something else or more than expected: {This box is heavier than it looks}. The word extends to figurative weight: heavier {burdens}, heavier {responsibilities}, a heavier {heart}. In casual speech, heavier can describe intensity: {The traffic gets heavier after five}.

Heavies is the plural of heavy used as a noun. A heavy is a large, intimidating person, especially one employed as a bodyguard or enforcer: {The boss sent his heavies to collect the debt}. In film and theater, the heavy is the villain or antagonist. The heavies can also refer to serious newspapers or influential figures in an industry: {the heavies of Silicon Valley}.

Heaviness is the quality of weighing a lot or feeling weighty. Physical heaviness makes things difficult to lift: {the heaviness of the stone}. The word extends to sensations of burden or oppression: {a heaviness in her chest}, {the heaviness of grief}. Heavy eyelids suggest fatigue; heavy hearts suggest sorrow. Heaviness can also describe density or thickness: {the heaviness of the fog}.

Heaving describes intense, rhythmic motion—rising and falling, swelling and subsiding. A heaving chest moves dramatically with labored breathing; a heaving sea rolls with powerful waves. When crowds are heaving, they're packed tight and surging together. The word also covers the physical act of lifting or throwing something heavy with effort: {We spent the morning heaving boxes into the truck}. In British slang, a heaving pub is absolutely packed with people.

The adjective heavy denotes a number of qualities that are nearly all the opposite of those characterized as light. Heavy may describe something physically weighty, something burdensome and oppressive, something serious, or something morose. It may also mean loud or deep (heavy metal music), fatty and hard to digest (heavy meal), or high in volume (heavy rain). A heavy informally designates a person or character that is important, influential, or malevolent: Al Pacino played the heavy in the movie. In dated slang, heavy is an appreciative adjective conveying profundity: Wow, man, that’s heavy.

Heavyhanded describes excessive force or lack of subtlety. A heavyhanded {crackdown} uses more force than necessary. Heavyhanded {criticism} is harsh and unsparing. A heavyhanded {approach} lacks finesse or delicacy. The word implies bluntness where restraint or tact would serve better: {The director's heavyhanded symbolism left nothing to interpretation}. Also spelled heavy-handed.

Heavyhearted means weighed down by sadness, grief, or worry. The word evokes a physical sensation—as if sorrow has actual mass pressing on the chest: {She left the funeral heavyhearted}. It suggests a sustained emotional burden rather than a fleeting mood. The opposite is lighthearted.

Heavyweight denotes the heaviest category in combat sports like boxing and wrestling, or a competitor in that class. By extension, a heavyweight is anyone with significant influence or importance in their field: {a heavyweight in Democratic politics}, {an intellectual heavyweight}. The word can also simply describe something heavy: {heavyweight fabric}.

Heavyweights are people or things of great importance, influence, or ability in their field: {The conference attracted heavyweights from across the tech industry}. The term comes from boxing's highest weight class, where fighters exceed a certain limit. A heavyweight carries authority and commands attention: {She's a heavyweight in constitutional law}.

Heck is a mild euphemism for hell, used to avoid profanity: {What the heck is going on?} {Oh heck, I forgot}. The word allows speakers to express frustration without the religious offense of invoking hell. {Heck of a} means remarkable: {That was a heck of a game}. Heck is safe for all audiences, though some consider it slightly corny.

To heckle is to interrupt a speaker or performer with hostile or mocking comments: {Protesters heckled the senator throughout her speech}. The word implies persistent disruption rather than a single outburst. Comedians often develop skills for handling hecklers, turning interruptions into material. A heckler is someone who heckles.

Heckled is the past tense of heckle, meaning to interrupt and harass a speaker or performer with hostile comments or questions. The word originated in textile work—to heckle flax was to comb it with sharp metal teeth—but now lives almost entirely in its figurative sense of verbal aggression: {The comedian was heckled throughout her set}, {Protesters heckled the senator at the town hall}.

A heckler is someone who interrupts a public speaker or performer with taunts, hostile questions, or disruptive comments. Comedians develop techniques for handling hecklers; politicians learn to deflect them. The verb is heckle: {Someone in the crowd heckled the mayor during her speech}.

Hecklers are people who interrupt a public speaker or performer with hostile or mocking comments. The term comes from heckling—originally combing flax fibers, then metaphorically "combing through" someone's words to find fault. Comedians face hecklers in clubs; politicians face them at rallies. {The hecklers were escorted out after drowning out the candidate's speech.}

Heckles are the hackles—the erectile hairs along an animal's back that rise when threatened or agitated. The spelling heckles appears mainly in the phrase {raise someone's heckles}, meaning to provoke irritation or defensiveness: {His dismissive tone raised my heckles}. The standard spelling is hackles.

Heckling is the act of interrupting a speaker or performer with hostile or mocking comments. A comedian deals with hecklers; a politician faces heckling at a rally. The intent is to unsettle, challenge, or derail: {Security removed him after repeated heckling}. To heckle is to engage in this behavior.

Hectic describes frantic, rushed activity with too much to do and too little time: {a hectic morning getting the kids to school}, {My schedule has been hectic lately}. The word implies barely controlled chaos—not quite overwhelming, but close. Originally a medical term for the flushed fever of tuberculosis, that sense survives only in technical contexts.

To hector is to bully or badger someone with aggressive, persistent pressure: {Stop hectoring me about the deadline}. The word implies relentless intimidation rather than physical violence—a boss hectoring employees, a parent hectoring a child about grades. The hectoring person wears down resistance through sheer persistence. (Capitalized Hector is the Trojan hero.)

A hedge is a row of bushes or shrubs planted close together, typically forming a boundary or barrier between properties or along roadsides. This core meaning extends to anything that serves as a barrier or means of protection against loss: a financial hedge is an investment made to offset potential losses elsewhere. To hedge is to protect yourself against risk, often by avoiding commitment: {He hedged when asked about his plans}. If you hedge your bets, you spread risk across multiple options rather than committing to one.

Hedged describes something qualified or guarded against risk. A hedged statement avoids full commitment: {His answer was hedged with caveats}. In finance, a hedged position is protected against loss through offsetting investments. A hedged bet covers multiple outcomes. Something hedged in is enclosed or confined: {a garden hedged by boxwoods}.

A hedgehog is a small nocturnal mammal covered in stiff spines, which it erects by rolling into a ball when threatened. Native to Europe, Asia, and Africa, hedgehogs root through underbrush eating insects and small creatures. They've become popular as pets: {Our hedgehog likes to burrow under blankets}. In military usage, a hedgehog is a defensive position bristling with obstacles or weapons in all directions.

Hedgehogs is the plural of hedgehog, a small nocturnal mammal covered in spines that rolls into a ball when threatened. Native to Europe, Asia, and Africa, hedgehogs eat insects and small invertebrates. They've become popular as exotic pets: {We got two hedgehogs for the kids}. The name comes from their pig-like snouts and habit of rooting through hedges.

A hedgerow is a row of bushes or small trees forming a boundary or barrier, typically between fields or along roadsides. Common in the British countryside, hedgerows serve as property lines, windbreaks, and wildlife habitat. They're denser and more deliberately maintained than natural thickets: {The hedgerows were alive with birdsong}.

Hedgerows are dense rows of shrubs and small trees forming boundaries between fields or along roads, especially in the British countryside. They serve as natural fences, windbreaks, and wildlife corridors. The word evokes pastoral English landscapes: {The hedgerows were thick with blackberries in late summer}. A hedgerow is a single such boundary.

Hedges are rows of shrubs or small trees planted close together to form a boundary or barrier: {a hedge of boxwood}. The verb hedge means to enclose with such a barrier, or more commonly, to limit risk by taking offsetting positions: {hedge your bets}, {hedge against inflation}. Financial hedges protect against losses. To hedge in speech is to qualify statements, avoiding commitment: {She hedged when asked directly}.

Hedging is protecting against risk by taking offsetting positions. In finance, you hedge a bet or investment by also betting the other way, limiting potential losses: {The fund hedged its stock positions with put options}. More broadly, hedging means avoiding commitment or direct answers: {She kept hedging when asked about her plans}. To {hedge your bets} is to avoid putting all your resources behind one outcome.

Hedonism is the pursuit of pleasure as the primary goal in life. In philosophy, it's the doctrine that pleasure is the highest good. In everyday use, hedonism suggests indulgence in sensual pleasures without regard for consequences: {a weekend of pure hedonism}. The word often carries a judgmental edge, implying excess or shallow priorities.

A hedonist is someone who pursues pleasure as the highest good. The term can be neutral—describing a philosophical position that pleasure and happiness are life's proper aims—or mildly disapproving, suggesting someone devoted to sensory indulgence: {He's a hedonist who spends his weekends at wine tastings and spas}. The related adjective is hedonistic.

Hedonistic describes devotion to pleasure as the chief good in life. A hedonistic lifestyle prioritizes sensory enjoyment—food, drink, sex, comfort—over duty or discipline: {After the divorce, he embraced a hedonistic phase of travel and indulgence}. The word often carries a note of disapproval, implying excess or selfishness, though it can be neutral or even admiring depending on context.

Hedonists are people who pursue pleasure as their primary aim in life. The term derives from a Greek word for pleasure and can be used neutrally to describe followers of the philosophical position that pleasure is the highest good, but more often it carries a judgmental tone, suggesting someone excessively devoted to sensual gratification and self-indulgence. {The resort caters to hedonists seeking endless luxury and entertainment.}

A state of nervousness, anxiety, or unease—often with a physical component like jitters or shivers: {That creepy house gives me the heebiejeebies}. The word is playful and informal, typically describing mild dread rather than serious fear. Also spelled heebie-jeebies.

A state of nervous anxiety or the creeps, usually with *the*: {That old house gives me the heebyjeebies}. The word is playful and informal, often describing an irrational unease rather than genuine fear. Also spelled heeby-jeebies or heebie-jeebies.

Heed means to pay attention to something, especially advice or warning: {She failed to heed the doctor's instructions}. The noun form appears in phrases like {pay heed} and {take heed}, both meaning to give careful attention: {Take heed of what I'm telling you}. To give no heed is to ignore completely.

Heeded is the past tense of heed, meaning to pay attention to advice, a warning, or a request—and act accordingly. To heed is more than just hearing; it implies taking something seriously enough to respond: {She heeded her doctor's advice and quit smoking}. {Had they heeded the warnings, the disaster might have been avoided}.

Heedless means paying no attention, especially to potential consequences or warnings: {heedless of the danger}, {heedless of her mother's advice}. The word implies carelessness or recklessness—someone heedless isn't just unaware but fails to give proper consideration. {They rushed heedlessly into the burning building.}

Meanings of heel are inspired by the original and core meaning, namely the back part of the human foot. Besides this, heel denotes the part of a sock or shoe that fits over the heel. Heels (also high heels) are women’s shoes with an elevated heel. Other things called heel include the end of a loaf of bread and an inconsiderate man. Heel occurs in many idioms with variable meaning but often involving the meaning of following closely, as in at one’s heels.

A heeler is a dog that herds livestock by nipping at their heels—the Australian cattle dog is the classic example. In American politics, a heeler is a low-level party operative who does whatever the boss needs: canvassing, delivering votes, running errands. The political sense suggests someone who follows at heel like a trained dog. {The ward heeler rounded up votes on election day.}

A heelflip is a skateboarding trick where the rider kicks the board with their heel to make it flip laterally while airborne, then lands back on it. The motion uses the heel edge of the front foot, distinguishing it from a kickflip, which uses the toes: {He landed a clean heelflip off the curb}.
A heelflip is a trick in skateboarding in which the skateboarder jumps into the air while the skateboard spins 360 degrees on its longitudinal axis.

Heelies are sneakers with a wheel embedded in each heel, allowing the wearer to roll by shifting weight to the back of the foot. Popular among children in the early 2000s, they blur the line between footwear and skating: {He rolled through the mall in his Heelies}. A trademark that functions as a common noun.

Heels are shoes with elevated backs that raise the wearer's heel above the toe. The term usually refers to women's high heels—shoes with thin, tall heels worn for style rather than comfort: {She kicked off her heels after the party}. To be {head over heels} is to be completely smitten. Someone {on your heels} follows closely behind. To {dig in your heels} is to refuse to budge.

Hefeweizen is a German wheat beer, cloudy and unfiltered, with a distinctive yeasty flavor and notes of banana and clove. The name means "yeast wheat" in German. Hefeweizens are typically light-bodied and refreshing, often served in tall, curved glasses: {I'll have a hefeweizen with the bratwurst}.

Heft is weight, especially weight you can feel by lifting: {The heft of the book surprised me}. To heft something is to lift it, often to judge its weight: {He hefted the melon in his hand}. Figuratively, heft means substance or influence: {His opinion carries some heft around here}. The adjective hefty means heavy or substantial.

Hefting is lifting something briefly to judge its weight: {She picked up each melon, hefting it before choosing one}. The action tests heft—how heavy something feels in the hand. By extension, hefting can mean considering or weighing mentally: {He spent the morning hefting his options}.

Hefty means large, heavy, or substantial. A hefty {box} requires effort to lift. A hefty {fee} is considerable. A hefty person is big and solidly built—not necessarily fat, but with bulk and presence. The word carries a sense of impressive weight or force: {He landed a hefty punch}. Hefty portions are generous; hefty problems are serious.

Hegemony implies the existence of a group whose status is nominally equal but where one member has dominance or authority: Several companies battle for hegemony in the cell phone market. Hegemony can also designate the authority that one person or other entity exercises: In the colonial period, France established hegemony in much of West Africa. The related adjective is hegemonic.

A heifer is a young female cow that has not yet borne a calf. Once she gives birth, she becomes a cow. The distinction matters in cattle farming, where heifers are raised for breeding or eventually for beef. In slang, heifer is a rude term for a woman, implying she is fat or unpleasant: {Don't be calling me a heifer}.

Heifers is the plural of heifer, a young cow that has not yet given birth to a calf. The term is standard in cattle farming, distinguishing unbred females from cows that have calved: {The ranch sold fifty heifers at auction}. Used of women, heifer is insulting—implying heaviness or coarseness.

Height is vertical extent—how tall something is or how far above a reference point it sits: {What's your height?}, {the height of the ceiling}. Heights are high places: {afraid of heights}, {the Golan Heights}. Figuratively, height marks an extreme or peak: {the height of summer}, {the height of fashion}, {the height of stupidity}.

Heighten means to make higher or more intense. You can heighten a wall by adding to it, but more often the word applies to abstractions: heighten {awareness}, heighten {tension}, heighten {security}. Senses may be heightened by alertness or drugs. {The approaching storm heightened our anxiety.} The intransitive form appears less often: {Excitement heightened as the deadline approached}.

Heightened means intensified or increased beyond the normal level. Heightened {awareness} is sharper than usual; heightened {security} involves extra precautions; heightened {emotions} run stronger than typical. The word implies elevation above a baseline: {The pandemic created a heightened sense of vulnerability}. Something heightened has been raised, not just high.

Heights are elevated places—hilltops, cliffs, tall buildings. The word often appears with a proper name for neighborhoods or districts on high ground: {Washington Heights}, {Golan Heights}. Fear of heights is acrophobia. Figuratively, heights represent peaks of achievement or intensity: {the heights of fame}, {new heights of absurdity}. To scale the heights is to reach the top of something difficult.

Heinous describes acts so wicked or shocking they provoke moral outrage: {a heinous crime}, {heinous acts of violence}. The word is reserved for the most reprehensible offenses—murder, torture, atrocities. It carries a formal, often legal tone, appearing frequently in news reports and courtroom language. Pronounced HAY-nuss.

An heir is someone entitled to inherit property, a title, or a position when the current holder dies: {She was heir to a vast fortune}, {the heir to the throne}. Extended uses describe anyone who continues or receives something from a predecessor: {heirs to the civil rights movement}, {intellectual heirs of Marx}. An heir apparent has a guaranteed claim; an heir presumptive can be displaced by a closer relative.

An heiress is a woman who stands to inherit or has inherited substantial wealth or property. The term typically implies considerable fortune—you wouldn't call someone inheriting a modest sum an heiress. {The heiress to the hotel fortune} suggests glamour and privilege. The word has an old-fashioned ring; heir now often covers both sexes.

An heirloom is a valuable object passed down through generations of a family: {The ring was a family heirloom from her great-grandmother}. The word implies both age and sentimental worth—items treasured for their history rather than monetary value. Heirloom varieties of plants are old cultivars preserved through open pollination rather than commercial hybridization: {heirloom tomatoes}.

Heirlooms are possessions passed down through generations of a family, valued for their history and sentimental significance rather than monetary worth: {The ring was a family heirloom from my great-grandmother}. Heirloom varieties of plants are older cultivars preserved through open pollination rather than modern hybridization: {heirloom tomatoes}, {heirloom seeds}. Both senses emphasize continuity with the past.

Heirs are those who inherit—property, titles, or legacy—from someone who dies. The term is legal but extends to anyone positioned to receive what another leaves behind: {She was heir to a banking fortune}, {the heir to the throne}. Figuratively, heirs continue traditions or ideas: {heirs to the civil rights movement}. An heir apparent has a secure claim; an heir presumptive could be displaced by a closer relative.

A heist is a robbery, especially a dramatic or carefully planned one: {a bank heist}, {a jewelry heist}. The word carries a sense of audacity or cleverness—heists involve schemes, not simple muggings. As a verb, to heist is to steal in this manner. The term appears frequently in crime fiction and film, where elaborate heists drive the plot.

Heists is the plural of heist—a robbery or burglary, typically one that's elaborately planned: {a string of bank heists}, {jewel heists}. The word carries a slightly glamorous connotation, evoking skilled criminals and clever schemes rather than crude theft. Heist films and heist novels are genres built around such capers.

Held is the past tense and past participle of hold. Something held is grasped, maintained, or kept in position: {She held the baby close}. Beliefs and opinions are held: {He held that taxes were too high}. Events are held when they take place: {The meeting was held on Tuesday}. A person held is detained or kept somewhere: {Police held him overnight}.

A helicopter is an aircraft that generates lift from horizontally spinning rotor blades, allowing it to take off and land vertically, hover in place, and fly in any direction. Unlike fixed-wing planes, helicopters need no runway. To helicopter is to transport by helicopter or, informally, to hover anxiously over someone: {helicopter parents} monitor their children's every move.

Helicoptering is hovering over someone with excessive attention or supervision. The term usually describes parents who monitor their children's every move, swooping in to solve problems or prevent difficulties: {Her helicoptering made it hard for him to develop independence}. The behavior extends beyond parenting to any overprotective oversight: {The manager's helicoptering killed team morale}.

Helicopters is the plural of helicopter—an aircraft that lifts off vertically using overhead rotating blades. Unlike airplanes, helicopters can hover in place, fly backward, and land without runways: {News helicopters circled the scene}, {Medical helicopters airlifted the injured}. As a verb, to helicopter is to transport by helicopter or, informally, to hover anxiously over someone: {helicopter parents}.

Heliocentrism is the astronomical model placing the sun at the center of the solar system, with Earth and other planets orbiting around it. The term usually appears in contrast to geocentrism, the older belief that Earth occupied the center. Copernicus proposed the heliocentric model in the 16th century, and it became foundational to modern astronomy: {The shift from geocentrism to heliocentrism transformed our understanding of the cosmos}.
clues: Model with orbiting planets, central star

definition: A helipad is a designated landing area for helicopters—a flat, marked surface where they can take off and land. Helipads appear on hospital roofs for emergency medical transport, on offshore oil platforms, and atop tall buildings. Unlike a heliport, which is a full facility with services, a helipad is just the landing surface itself.

Helipads are designated landing surfaces for helicopters, typically marked with a large H or circle. They appear on hospital roofs, offshore oil platforms, yacht decks, and military installations. A helipad is smaller and simpler than a heliport, which offers fueling and other services. {The medical helicopter touched down on the rooftop helipad.}

A heliport is a small airport designed for helicopters, typically featuring one or more landing pads rather than runways. Heliports often serve hospitals, corporate buildings, or offshore platforms where conventional aircraft cannot land: {The executive helicopter touched down at the rooftop heliport}.

Helium is a chemical element, a colorless, odorless gas that is lighter than air. It's best known for making balloons and blimps float. Helium is also used in welding, deep-sea diving tanks, and to cool superconducting magnets. Because it's inert—it doesn't react with other elements—helium is safe around flames and in sensitive equipment. Inhaling helium temporarily raises the pitch of your voice, a party trick that can be dangerous in excess.

A helix is a three-dimensional spiral curve, like a corkscrew or the threads of a screw. The shape appears throughout nature and technology: DNA's famous double helix, spiral staircases, coiled springs. The plural is helices or helixes. Helical is the adjective: {a helical staircase}, {helical motion}.

Hell is the place of eternal punishment in many religious traditions, where the wicked suffer after death: {The sermon described the torments of hell}. By extension, hell describes any place or situation of misery: {War is hell}. {The commute was hell today}. As an exclamation, hell expresses surprise, frustration, or emphasis: {What the hell is going on?} {Hell, I don't care}. Common expressions include {all hell broke loose} (chaos erupted), {hell to pay} (serious consequences), {when hell freezes over} (never), {a snowball's chance in hell} (no chance at all), and {go to hell} (a curse or dismissal).

Hella is California slang, originally from the Bay Area, meaning very or extremely: {That movie was hella good}, {We waited hella long}. It also functions as a quantifier meaning a lot of: {There were hella people at the party}. The word has spread beyond its regional origins through internet culture and media, though it still carries a distinctly West Coast flavor.

Hellacious is slang for extreme or overwhelming, usually in a negative sense: {a hellacious commute}, {hellacious traffic}, {a hellacious hangover}. It can also express grudging admiration for something impressively intense: {She threw a hellacious punch}. The word blends hell with a Latin-style suffix, giving informal speech a mock-grandiose edge.

A hellbender is a large aquatic salamander native to eastern North America, reaching up to two feet long. It lives under rocks in clear, fast-flowing streams and has a flattened body with loose, wrinkled skin along its sides. The name likely reflects its strange appearance—early settlers may have thought the creature looked like it crawled out of hell.

Hellbent means recklessly determined, stubbornly committed to a course of action regardless of consequences: {She's hellbent on getting that promotion}. {He was hellbent on self-destruction}. The word implies dangerous single-mindedness—someone so determined they'd go to hell to achieve their goal.

Hellbound describes someone or something destined for hell—either literally in religious contexts or figuratively suggesting a path toward ruin or damnation. A preacher might warn that sinners are hellbound; a reckless lifestyle might be called a {hellbound journey}. The word often carries a tone of moral condemnation or dramatic foreboding: {That hellbound fool won't listen to reason}.

A hellcat is a fierce, ill-tempered woman—someone wild, shrewish, or given to violent outbursts. The word combines the fury of hell with the scratching aggression of a cat: {His ex-wife was a hellcat who made his life miserable}. More broadly, hellcat can describe anyone dangerously aggressive or reckless.

Hellcats are fierce, aggressive women—the kind who fight without restraint or decorum. The term often carries grudging admiration: {She turned into a hellcat when they threatened her kids}. In military history, the Hellcat was a World War II fighter aircraft. The word combines hell's fury with a cat's claws.

Hellfire is the fire of hell, the flames in which the damned supposedly suffer for eternity. It appears in phrases describing punishment or condemnation: {The preacher threatened hellfire and brimstone}. Figuratively, hellfire describes intense anger or fierce energy: {She came at him with hellfire in her eyes}.

Hellfires is the plural of hellfire—the fires of hell, understood as eternal punishment for the damned. The word appears most often in religious contexts warning of damnation: {The preacher thundered about hellfires awaiting sinners}. Hellfire also names the AGM-114 missile used by U.S. military aircraft.

A hellhole is a thoroughly miserable, unpleasant, or squalid place—somewhere so awful it resembles hell: {That prison was a hellhole}. {We worked in a hellhole of a factory}. The word suggests not just discomfort but real suffering or degradation.
Hellholes is the plural of hellhole, describing thoroughly miserable places: {He'd worked in hellholes across three continents}.

A hellhound is a demonic dog from folklore, typically depicted as a fierce, fire-eyed creature guarding the gates of the underworld or serving as an omen of death. The most famous example is Cerberus from Greek mythology. In modern usage, hellhound can describe any vicious or relentless pursuer: {The debt collectors were hellhounds who wouldn't leave him alone}. It also appears in fantasy games and horror fiction as a standard monster type.

Hellhounds are supernatural dogs from folklore, typically black, fiery-eyed, and associated with death, the underworld, or the devil. They appear across mythologies as guardians of the afterlife or omens of doom. In contemporary use, hellhound often describes any fierce, relentless pursuer: {Creditors were on him like hellhounds}.

A hellion is a rowdy, mischievous, or unruly person—typically a child or young person who causes trouble. The word carries a tone of exasperated affection rather than genuine condemnation: {Those hellions trampled my flower bed again}. A hellion is wild and hard to control, but the trouble is usually minor.

Hellions are wild, unruly troublemakers—typically children or young people who cause mischief or chaos: {Those little hellions trampled my flower beds}. The word carries a tone of exasperated affection more often than genuine condemnation, suggesting energetic misbehavior rather than true malice.

Hellish means resembling or characteristic of hell—extremely unpleasant, torturous, or difficult: {The traffic was hellish}. {We had a hellish time getting the project finished}. The word suggests suffering beyond normal complaint, though it's often used hyperbolically for everyday frustrations.

A hellmouth is any entrance to hell or place of damnation, especially as depicted in medieval art and drama—a gaping monster's maw through which damned souls pass. The word has been revived in fantasy fiction and gaming to describe portals through which demons or evil forces enter the world: {The town was built on a hellmouth, which explained a lot}.
Hello is the standard greeting on the telephone and is the default face-to-face greeting for people who don’t use a more informal expression.

A hellraiser is someone who causes trouble, behaves wildly, or lives recklessly: {He was a hellraiser in his youth}. The word suggests rowdy, disruptive behavior—partying hard, breaking rules, causing chaos—but often with a note of admiration for the energy involved.
Hellraisers is the plural of hellraiser, describing people who cause trouble or live wildly: {The band were notorious hellraisers who trashed hotel rooms}.

Hellraising is wild, disruptive behavior—causing trouble, making noise, raising hell. A hellraiser acts out boisterously, often with drinking and rowdiness involved: {His hellraising days ended when he got married}. The term suggests energetic defiance of decorum rather than serious wrongdoing, though it can shade into genuine destructiveness.

A hellscape is a landscape resembling hell—devastated, nightmarish, or apocalyptic. The word describes both literal scenes of destruction {The wildfire left behind a hellscape of ash and charred trees} and metaphorical ones {Twitter became a hellscape of misinformation}. It conveys not just damage but a sense of horror or hopelessness about what remains.

Hellscapes are nightmarish, devastated landscapes—places that evoke hell through their desolation, destruction, or hostile conditions. The word applies to war zones, environmental disasters, dystopian wastelands, or any terrain that appears apocalyptic: {Wildfires turned the hillsides into hellscapes}. In gaming and fantasy, hellscapes are literally infernal realms. Figuratively, any unbearable situation: {The commute was an absolute hellscape}.

Hellspawn refers to a creature or being supposedly originating from hell—a demon, devil, or their offspring. The term appears in fantasy, horror, and religious contexts: {The heroes battled the hellspawn threatening the village}. Used figuratively as an insult for someone considered evil or monstrous, or hyperbolically for misbehaving children: {Her little hellspawn terrorized the neighborhood}.

A hellstorm is a violent, chaotic onslaught—literal or figurative. The word evokes fire, destruction, and overwhelming force: {The city endured a hellstorm of artillery fire}. It applies to any intense barrage: a hellstorm of {criticism}, a hellstorm of {controversy}. The compound intensifies storm with infernal imagery, suggesting something not just severe but apocalyptic.

Helluva is an informal spelling of "hell of a," used as an intensifier meaning remarkable or extreme: {That was a helluva game}. It can express admiration {(a helluva singer)} or emphasize difficulty {(a helluva time finding parking)}. The spelling captures casual pronunciation.

A helm is the steering apparatus of a ship—the wheel or tiller that controls direction. By extension, helm refers to a position of control or leadership: {She took the helm of the company during a difficult period}. To helm is to steer or lead: {He helmed the project from start to finish}. Separately, helm is an archaic or literary word for helmet.

Helmed means led or directed, typically said of creative projects or organizations: {The film was helmed by a first-time director}. The word derives from helm, the wheel or tiller used to steer a ship. Someone who helms a project guides it, as a captain guides a vessel. The usage is common in entertainment journalism and corporate announcements.

A helmet is a hard protective covering for the head, worn by soldiers, motorcyclists, construction workers, athletes, and others facing head-injury risk. The word extends to helmet-shaped things: the upper lip of certain flowers, a shell structure in some mollusks. {Always wear a helmet when cycling.}

Helmets are protective head coverings, typically hard-shelled, worn to guard against impact. Different activities require different designs: motorcycle helmets, football helmets, bicycle helmets, combat helmets. {Always wear a helmet when riding.} Figuratively, to {put on your helmet} is to prepare for conflict or difficulty.

Helming is steering or directing—from the helm, a ship's wheel or tiller. The word appears most often in discussions of film and television, where a director helms a production: {Spielberg is helming the sequel}. It suggests being at the controls, guiding something through its course.

A helmsman is the person who steers a ship, operating the helm or wheel. The term extends to anyone who guides or directs an organization or enterprise: {He served as helmsman of the company through turbulent years}. The figurative use suggests steady guidance through difficulty, as a ship's helmsman navigates through storms.

Whether as a verb or a noun, help has many synonyms but it is the most general and the most frequent word we use for the act of or an instance of doing something that makes someone else’s life or work easier: Can you help me with this math problem? My nephews weren’t much help on moving day. If you need help, you face a task that you do not feel able to do alone. If you can’t help doing something, you can’t restrain or prevent yourself from doing it: I can’t help thinking that they turned down the invitation because they’re broke.

A helpdesk is a service that provides technical support or answers questions, typically for computer systems or software. The term can refer to the physical location, the team staffing it, or the function itself: {Call the helpdesk if you can't log in}. Also spelled as two words: help desk.

A helper is someone or something that assists with a task or provides support. The word emphasizes a secondary role—the helper aids the primary person doing the work: {I need a helper in the kitchen}, {Santa's helpers}. Helper can also describe things that facilitate: {a helper function in programming}, {a memory helper}. In some contexts, helper suggests informal or volunteer assistance rather than professional expertise.

Helpful describes someone or something that provides assistance or makes a task easier. A helpful {neighbor} offers to carry groceries. Helpful {advice} actually solves the problem. The word can carry slight condescension when applied to unsolicited contributions: {Thanks, that's very helpful} sometimes means the opposite.

A helping is a portion of food served to one person: {She took a second helping of mashed potatoes}. The word implies a single serving from a larger dish. By extension, helping can describe any portion or share: {a generous helping of criticism}.

Helpings is the plural of helping, a portion of food served to one person: {She had two helpings of mashed potatoes}. The word implies abundance or appetite—asking for seconds suggests the food was good or the eater was hungry. {The helpings were generous}.

Helpless means unable to act, defend oneself, or manage without assistance. A helpless {infant} depends entirely on caregivers. Someone in a helpless {situation} lacks the power or resources to change it. The word often carries emotional weight—helplessness in the face of tragedy suggests both inability and anguish: {We watched helplessly as the house burned}.

Helplessly describes doing something without the ability to prevent or control it. Someone who watches helplessly as disaster unfolds can do nothing to stop it: {She stood helplessly as the fire spread}. The word often conveys a sense of powerlessness or futility: {He shrugged helplessly}, {They were helplessly lost}.

Helplessness is the state of being unable to act effectively or protect oneself. It may be situational—{the helplessness of watching someone you love suffer}—or a deeper psychological condition. Learned helplessness describes giving up after repeated failures, even when action might succeed. The word carries connotations of vulnerability and dependence: {She hated the helplessness of being bedridden}.

A helpline is a telephone service providing information, advice, or support on specific issues. Organizations operate helplines for crisis intervention, consumer complaints, technical support, or health concerns: {Call our 24-hour helpline for assistance}. The term sometimes extends to online chat services serving similar functions.

Helplines are telephone services providing information, advice, or emotional support on specific issues. They typically focus on crisis intervention, health concerns, or consumer assistance: {suicide prevention helplines}, {domestic abuse helplines}. The term emphasizes accessibility—someone is available to help when you call. Also spelled as two words: help lines.
Like hmm and um, hem represents a vocalization made by someone who is hesitating or doesn’t know what to say next.

A hemisphere is half of a sphere—any globe-shaped object divided in two. Most commonly, the word refers to halves of Earth: the Northern and Southern Hemispheres (divided by the equator) or the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. In anatomy, the brain's two cerebral hemispheres control opposite sides of the body: {a stroke in the left hemisphere}.

Hemispheres are halves of a sphere. The term most often refers to the Earth's northern and southern hemispheres (divided by the equator) or eastern and western hemispheres (divided by meridians). In anatomy, the brain's left and right hemispheres control different functions: {The left hemisphere processes language in most people}. Any rounded half qualifies: {the hemisphere of a dome}.

A hemline is the lower edge of a garment, especially a skirt or dress, where the hem falls: {Hemlines rose dramatically in the 1960s}. The term often refers to where that edge sits on the body—at the knee, mid-thigh, or ankle. Fashion commentary frequently tracks hemlines as cultural indicators.

Hemlines is the plural of hemline—the bottom edge of a garment, especially a skirt or dress. The word typically appears in discussions of fashion trends, where hemlines rise and fall with changing tastes: {Hemlines dropped dramatically in the 1930s}. The hemline index is a playful economic theory suggesting skirt lengths correlate with market conditions.

Hemlock is a poisonous plant of the parsley family, notorious since antiquity—Socrates was executed by drinking hemlock extract. The name also applies to a group of evergreen trees unrelated to the poison plant, valued for timber and ornamental use: {a stand of eastern hemlock}. The tree's feathery foliage supposedly resembled the poisonous herb's leaves.

Hemlocks are coniferous evergreen trees with short needles and small cones, native to North America and Asia. Hemlock also refers to a poisonous plant in the carrot family—the one famously used to execute Socrates. The two plants are unrelated; the tree was named for the similar smell of its crushed foliage. {The cabin was shaded by towering hemlocks.}

Hemmed is the past tense of hem, which means to fold and sew the edge of fabric to create a finished border that won't unravel. Beyond sewing, hemmed appears most often in the phrase {hemmed in}, meaning surrounded or confined in a way that restricts movement or options: {We felt hemmed in by all the new regulations}. The expression suggests being trapped or boxed in, unable to escape or maneuver freely.

Hemming is the act of creating a hem—folding and sewing the edge of fabric to prevent fraying: {She spent the afternoon hemming curtains}. To be hemmed in is to be surrounded or confined: {The protesters found themselves hemmed in by police}. Hemming also describes hesitant speech, usually paired with hawing: {After much hemming and hawing, he finally agreed}.

Hemorrhage is severe, uncontrolled bleeding—blood escaping rapidly from ruptured vessels. The term applies to internal bleeding {a brain hemorrhage} or external wounds. Figuratively, hemorrhage describes rapid, damaging loss: {The company was hemorrhaging cash}. As a verb, to hemorrhage is to bleed profusely or lose something at an alarming rate.

Hemorrhaged is the past tense of hemorrhage, meaning to bleed severely or uncontrollably, especially from a ruptured blood vessel: {The patient hemorrhaged during surgery}. Figuratively, it describes rapid, massive loss: {The company hemorrhaged cash for three quarters straight}. The spelling haemorrhaged appears in British English.

Hemorrhaging is heavy, uncontrolled bleeding—the kind that's dangerous or fatal if not stopped. The word applies literally to medical emergencies: {The patient was hemorrhaging internally}. Figuratively, it describes rapid, alarming loss: a company hemorrhaging {money}, a campaign hemorrhaging {voters}. The spelling haemorrhaging appears in British English.

A hemorrhoid is a swollen vein in or around the anus, causing discomfort, itching, or bleeding. Usually plural: {I've been dealing with hemorrhoids since the pregnancy}. The condition is common but rarely discussed openly. Figuratively, calling someone a hemorrhoid means they're a persistent irritation: {My boss is a real hemorrhoid}.

Hemorrhoids are swollen blood vessels in and around the anus, causing discomfort, itching, and sometimes bleeding. Nearly everyone develops them at some point, typically from straining during bowel movements, pregnancy, or prolonged sitting. The word often appears in plural even when referring to a single swollen vein: {The doctor said it's just hemorrhoids}. Also spelled haemorrhoids in British English.

Hemp is a variety of the cannabis plant grown for industrial uses rather than intoxication. Its fibers make rope, textiles, and paper; its seeds yield oil and food products. Hemp cultivation was once common but became restricted alongside marijuana, though legal distinctions have reemerged: {hemp-derived CBD products}. The word appears in compounds like {hempfield} and {hemp rope}.

Hems is the plural of hem—the finished edges of fabric, folded and sewn to prevent fraying: {She checked the hems on all the curtains}. As a verb form, hems appears in {hem in}, meaning to surround or confine: {The crowd hems in the speaker}. The hesitation sound hem also takes this form: {He hems and haws whenever I ask about money}.

A hen is an adult female chicken, distinguished from a rooster (male) and chick (young). The term extends to females of other birds: {a hen pheasant}, {a hen turkey}. Informally, hen describes a fussy or gossipy woman, now somewhat dated. A {hen party} is a women-only gathering, especially before a wedding. To {hen-peck} is to nag persistently.

A henchman is a loyal follower or supporter, especially one who carries out unpleasant or illegal tasks for a powerful person. The word nearly always appears in negative contexts, suggesting someone who does dirty work without questioning orders. Villains in fiction typically have henchmen who do their bidding, and the term extends to real-world politics and crime: {The mob boss sent his henchmen to collect the debt.} The word implies blind loyalty and a willingness to act as an instrument of someone else's will.

Henchmen is the plural of henchman—a loyal follower who carries out orders, often unsavory ones. The word almost always appears in contexts of villainy or corruption: a crime boss's henchmen, a dictator's henchmen. {The supervillain dispatched his henchmen to capture the hero.} The singular henchman exists but the plural dominates, perhaps because villains rarely travel with just one.

A henchwoman is a female loyal follower who carries out someone's bidding, especially a villain's. The word parallels henchman but sees far less use, appearing mainly in fiction and journalism: {The crime boss sent his henchwoman to deliver the threat}. Like henchman, it implies willing participation in wrongdoing rather than mere employment.

A henge is a prehistoric circular earthwork consisting of a ring-shaped bank with an internal ditch, typically enclosing a ritual or ceremonial space. The term comes from Stonehenge, though Stonehenge itself is atypical—its famous standing stones are a separate feature from the earthwork. Henges are found primarily in Britain and Ireland: {The area contains several Bronze Age henges}.

Henges is the plural of henge, a type of prehistoric monument found mainly in Britain—a circular area enclosed by a ditch with an external bank. Stonehenge is the most famous, though ironically its prominent stones make it atypical; most henges were earthwork enclosures without major stone structures. The term comes from Stonehenge itself, extracted backward from that site's name.

A henhouse is a small building or shelter where chickens are kept, particularly for roosting and laying eggs. The expression {the fox guarding the henhouse} describes someone untrustworthy given responsibility over what they might exploit.

Henna is a reddish-brown dye derived from the leaves of a tropical shrub, used for centuries to color hair and create temporary body art. The intricate designs painted on hands and feet, especially for weddings and celebrations in South Asian and Middle Eastern cultures, are also called henna or mehndi. {She got henna done for her sister's wedding.} The plant itself shares the name. As a verb, to henna means to dye with this substance: {I henna my hair every few months}.

To henpeck is to nag or dominate, said of a wife toward her husband. A henpecked husband is one whose wife criticizes him constantly and controls his behavior. The image is of a hen pecking at something persistently. The term carries old-fashioned, mildly sexist overtones: {His friends joked that he was too henpecked to join them for poker night}.

Henpecked describes a man whose wife constantly nags, criticizes, or dominates him: {a henpecked husband}. The image is of a hen pecking at a smaller bird. The word is old-fashioned and carries sexist assumptions about marriage dynamics, but remains in use for men seen as submissive to their wives.

Henpecking is persistent nagging or domineering by a wife toward her husband. The image comes from hens pecking at roosters or each other in the barnyard. A henpecked husband is one whose wife controls him through constant criticism or demands: {After years of henpecking, he'd stopped offering opinions at all}.

Hens is the plural of hen—adult female chickens, kept primarily for eggs. The word extends to females of other birds: {The hens guard the nest while the rooster patrols}. A hen party or hen night is a women-only gathering, especially a pre-wedding celebration for the bride. To be as {scarce as hen's teeth} is to be extremely rare, since hens have no teeth.

Hentai is Japanese animated pornography, typically featuring explicit sexual content with exaggerated or fantastical elements. The genre often includes scenarios impossible in live-action porn—tentacles, transformations, supernatural beings. In Japanese, the word means "pervert" or "abnormal," but English uses it specifically for the genre: {He's into hentai}. Sometimes used attributively: {hentai manga}.

Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver, typically caused by viral infection. The major types—hepatitis A, B, and C—differ in transmission and severity. A spreads through contaminated food or water, while B and C spread through blood and bodily fluids. Hepatitis can also result from alcohol abuse, toxins, or autoimmune conditions. Symptoms include jaundice, fatigue, and abdominal pain, though some forms remain asymptomatic for years.
clues: A, B, or C variety illness

definition: A heptathlon is an athletic competition consisting of seven events, typically completed over two days. The women's heptathlon in track and field includes the 100-meter hurdles, high jump, shot put, 200 meters, long jump, javelin, and 800 meters. Points are awarded for each event, and the highest combined score wins: {She won the Olympic heptathlon}.

You use her before a noun to show that it belongs to or is associated with a female that you have named or indicated: Barbara forgot her purse. I’ve met Martha but I don’t know her husband. Her is also the objective form of she: Please give this to Cindy when you see her.

A herald was originally a royal official who made proclamations, carried messages between rulers, and oversaw ceremonies—especially the protocols of tournaments and the granting of coats of arms. The word now means anyone or anything that announces what's coming: {The robin is a herald of spring}. To herald something is to signal or announce its arrival: {Critics heralded the album as a masterpiece}. The verb often carries a note of celebration or significance. (Capitalized Herald often appears in newspaper names.)

Heralded means announced or greeted with enthusiasm, often suggesting something significant or long-awaited: {The discovery was heralded as a breakthrough}. Something much-heralded has received considerable advance praise or attention: {The much-heralded sequel disappointed fans}. The word carries a note of ceremony or fanfare, from heralds who once proclaimed royal news.

Heralding is announcing or signaling the arrival of something. A herald was historically a messenger who proclaimed important news, so heralding suggests formal or significant announcement: {Robins heralding spring}, {a discovery heralding a new era in medicine}. The word often implies that what follows will be momentous or transformative.

Heraldry is the system of designing, displaying, and regulating coats of arms and other armorial bearings. It developed in medieval Europe as a way to identify knights in armor and has its own vocabulary of terms and rules. By extension, heraldry refers to any ceremonial display of symbols or pageantry: {the heraldry of a royal wedding}, {corporate heraldry}. The adjective is heraldic.

Heralds are announcers or messengers, originally officials who made royal proclamations and managed ceremonies. The word extends to anything that signals what's coming: {Robins are heralds of spring}. To herald something is to announce or foreshadow it: {The discovery heralded a new era in medicine}. A herald can also proclaim praise: {Critics heralded the film as a masterpiece}.

An herb is a plant used for flavoring, medicine, or fragrance—basil, mint, thyme, rosemary. In botany, herb refers more broadly to any plant with soft rather than woody stems. Informally, herb is slang for marijuana. The word is pronounced with a silent H in American English, with a sounded H in British English. (Capitalized Herb is a given name.)

Herbal describes things made from or relating to herbs, especially plants used for medicinal or culinary purposes. An herbal {remedy} or herbal {tea} uses plant materials rather than synthetic compounds. As a noun, an herbal is a book describing plants and their uses, particularly for healing—a genre popular from medieval times through the Renaissance. The word appears frequently in marketing for products positioned as natural alternatives: herbal {supplements}, herbal {shampoo}.
