Humbug is deceptive or dishonest talk, behavior, or practices—especially pretentious nonsense meant to impress or mislead: {The whole ceremony was pure humbug}. A humbug is also a person who deceives through false claims or pretenses. As an exclamation, it dismisses something as fraudulent or absurd—famously Scrooge's {Bah, humbug!} in response to Christmas cheer. In British usage, a humbug is also a hard striped peppermint candy.

Humbugs can be hard candy—in Britain, striped peppermint sweets; in parts of the US, chocolate-coated caramels. But a humbug is also a fraud or impostor, and humbug as a mass noun means deceptive nonsense: {Bah, humbug!} To humbug someone is to deceive them with false pretenses.

A humdinger is something remarkable or outstanding of its kind—a real standout: {That storm was a humdinger}. The word carries informal, slightly old-fashioned enthusiasm, suggesting impressed admiration: {She told a humdinger of a story}. Often used for things impressively large, intense, or memorable.

Humdingers are remarkable or outstanding things—impressive examples of their kind. The word carries informal enthusiasm: {That storm was a real humdinger}. A humdinger can be a person, event, or object that stands out for excellence, intensity, or impact: {She told some humdingers of stories}.

Humdrum describes what is dull, monotonous, and lacking variety—the tedious routine of everyday life. {The humdrum of office work wore him down.} As an adjective: {a humdrum existence}, {humdrum tasks}. The word itself mimics the droning quality it describes.

Humid describes air that contains a lot of water vapor. Humid weather feels heavy and often uncomfortable because perspiration doesn't evaporate easily: {The humid summer made everything feel sticky}. Tropical climates are typically humid, while deserts are arid. A {humid} greenhouse keeps plants moist.

A humidifier is a device that adds moisture to the air, typically used indoors to combat dryness from heating systems or arid climates. People use humidifiers to ease respiratory discomfort, prevent dry skin, or protect wooden furniture: {The pediatrician recommended running a humidifier in the baby's room}.

Humidity is the amount of moisture in the air. High humidity makes hot weather feel more oppressive because sweat evaporates slowly; low humidity dries out skin and nasal passages. {The humidity today is unbearable.} Relative humidity expresses moisture as a percentage of what the air could hold at that temperature.

A humidor is a container designed to maintain constant humidity, used primarily for storing cigars and pipe tobacco. The controlled moisture prevents tobacco from drying out and losing flavor. Humidors range from small desktop boxes to walk-in rooms: {He kept his Cubans in a cedar humidor}.

To humiliate someone is to make them feel ashamed or foolish, often publicly. The act attacks their dignity or self-respect: {He humiliated her in front of the whole office}. Humiliation can be deliberate cruelty or an unintended consequence: {Losing so badly humiliated the team}. The feeling lingers—humiliation cuts deeper than mere embarrassment.

Humiliated describes the state of having one's dignity or pride stripped away, often publicly. To be humiliated is to feel diminished, shamed, or made to look foolish: {He was humiliated when his lies were exposed in front of everyone}. The feeling lingers—humiliation cuts deeper than mere embarrassment.

Humiliates is the third-person singular of humiliate—to make someone feel ashamed, foolish, or stripped of dignity, often publicly. The act implies a power imbalance: a boss humiliates an employee, a bully humiliates a victim. {He humiliates her in front of their friends.} Unlike embarrassment, humiliation suggests deliberate cruelty or deep degradation.

Humiliating describes something that causes a painful loss of dignity or self-respect. A humiliating {defeat} is one that exposes weakness publicly. A humiliating {experience} leaves you feeling diminished or shamed: {It was humiliating to be corrected in front of everyone}. The word emphasizes the social dimension—humiliation typically involves witnesses or an audience, real or imagined.

Humiliation is the experience of being made to feel ashamed, foolish, or stripped of dignity—usually publicly. It differs from embarrassment in intensity and from shame in its external source: someone or something humiliates you. {The humiliation of being fired in front of coworkers stayed with him for years.} To humiliate is to inflict this feeling; humiliating describes what causes it.

Humiliations are experiences of being made to feel ashamed, foolish, or stripped of dignity. The word emphasizes the depth of embarrassment—not minor awkwardness but genuine degradation: {the daily humiliations of poverty}, {She never forgot the humiliations of her first job}. Public humiliations carry special weight because they involve witnesses to one's diminishment.

Humility is the quality of being modest about one's abilities or importance—the opposite of arrogance or pride. It implies an accurate, unpretentious assessment of oneself: {She accepted the award with humility}. Humility can be genuine self-awareness or a strategic posture: {His humility seemed calculated to disarm critics}.

Hummable describes a melody simple and catchy enough to hum easily. A hummable tune sticks in your head after one hearing: {The song isn't complex, but it's incredibly hummable}. The quality suggests accessible, memorable music—often used as praise for pop songs or criticism of music that prioritizes catchiness over depth.

A hummer is something that hums—a person humming a tune, or more commonly, a hummingbird. In slang, a hummer is something excellent or remarkable: {That new song is a real hummer}. Vulgar slang uses hummer for oral sex performed on a man, from the humming vibration sometimes involved. (Capitalized Hummer is the vehicle brand.)

Humming is producing a continuous low sound with closed lips, often while breathing out a tune: {She was humming to herself in the kitchen}. A place that's humming is full of activity and energy: {The restaurant was humming on Saturday night}. Things that hum mechanically produce a steady drone: {the humming of the refrigerator}.

A hummingbird is a tiny, brightly colored bird native to the Americas, named for the humming sound its rapidly beating wings produce. Hummingbirds hover in place while feeding on flower nectar, their wings beating up to eighty times per second. They are the only birds capable of sustained backward flight.
clues: Wings beat too fast to see

definition: Hummingbirds are tiny, brightly colored birds of the Americas known for their ability to hover in place by beating their wings rapidly—fast enough to produce the humming sound that gives them their name. They feed on flower nectar, their long bills adapted to reach deep into blossoms. {The hummingbirds returned to the feeder in early spring.}

Hummus is a thick Middle Eastern spread or dip made from mashed chickpeas blended with tahini, lemon juice, garlic, and olive oil. It's typically eaten with pita bread or vegetables: {We ordered hummus and falafel}. The word comes from Arabic for "chickpeas." Also spelled houmous or hommos.

Humongous means extremely large—bigger than huge, enormous, or gigantic would suggest: {a humongous portion of fries}, {The project turned into a humongous mess}. The word is informal and emphatic, often chosen for comic effect or childlike exaggeration. Also spelled humungous.

Humor is the quality that makes something funny or amusing, or the ability to perceive and enjoy what's funny: {She has a great sense of humor}. It also means a mood or state of mind: {He was in good humor after the promotion}. To humor someone is to indulge them, going along with what they want even if you disagree: {Just humor me and try it}. In older medical theory, the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile—were bodily fluids thought to determine temperament, which is why humor came to mean mood.

Humoring is going along with someone's wishes, ideas, or whims to keep them satisfied, even when you don't take them seriously. A parent humors a child's fantasy; a nurse humors a difficult patient. The word implies tolerance without genuine agreement: {I was just humoring him when I said his plan might work}.

A humorist is someone who creates humor professionally—a writer, performer, or speaker known for witty, amusing work. The term suggests sophistication rather than slapstick: Mark Twain and Dorothy Parker were humorists, not comedians. {The magazine published essays by humorists and satirists.}

Humorous means funny or amusing, characterized by humor: {a humorous story}, {a humorous take on everyday life}. It often suggests wit or cleverness rather than slapstick: {His humorous observations about office culture made the presentation memorable}. A humorous person has a talent for finding or creating amusement.

Humors has two main senses. The bodily humors were four fluids in ancient medicine—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance supposedly determined health and temperament. Someone {of choleric humor} had too much yellow bile. The singular humor meaning mood or disposition descends from this: {She was in a foul humor}. To humor someone is to indulge their whims: {Just humor me and try it}.

Humour is the British spelling of humor, covering all the same meanings: the quality of being amusing or comic, a person's mood or temperament, and the ability to appreciate what's funny. {She has a wicked sense of humour.} The word traces to medieval medicine's four bodily humours—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance supposedly determined temperament. To humour someone is to indulge their wishes or go along with their whims, even if you disagree.

Humouring is the British spelling of humoring—going along with someone's wishes or ideas to keep them happy, even when you don't agree or take them seriously. You might humour a child's fantasy or humour a difficult colleague to avoid conflict: {She was just humouring him when she said the painting was good}.

Humourless describes someone who lacks the ability to appreciate or express humour—serious to a fault, unable to laugh at themselves or find amusement in situations others find funny. A humourless {response} takes literally what was meant as a joke. {Her humourless boss made meetings unbearable.} The American spelling is humorless.

Humours is the British spelling of humors. In medieval and Renaissance medicine, the four humours—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were bodily fluids thought to determine temperament and health. An imbalance caused illness or mood disorders, which is why we still speak of being {in good humour} or {out of humour}. To humour someone is to indulge them: {She humoured his eccentricities}.

A hump is a rounded protuberance—the hump on a camel's back, a speed bump in the road, a mound of earth: {The camel stores fat in its hump}. {Slow down for the humps}. To hump is to carry something heavy on one's back, bending under the load: {They humped their packs through the jungle}. Wednesday is hump day—the middle of the workweek, after which you're "over the hump." In vulgar slang, to hump is to have sex, especially with thrusting motions: {They humped on the couch}. The sex sense is crude but common.

A humpback is a rounded deformity of the back, or a person with such a condition—now considered offensive when applied to people. The word more commonly refers to the humpback whale, a large baleen whale known for its acrobatic breaching and complex songs: {We watched humpbacks feeding off the coast}. As an adjective, humpbacked describes anything with a humped shape: {a humpbacked bridge}.

Humpbacks are humpback whales—large baleen whales known for their long pectoral fins, knobbed heads, and elaborate songs. The name comes from the arched appearance of their backs when diving. {We spotted humpbacks breaching off the coast}. The term can also refer to humpbacked individuals or things, though this use is uncommon.

Humpday is informal slang for Wednesday—the middle of the traditional Monday-through-Friday work week. The metaphor treats the week as a hill: once you're over the hump of Wednesday, the weekend is in sight. {Happy humpday, everyone!} The term is workplace casual, often appearing in social media posts celebrating midweek survival.
Humph is a spelling that is supposed to be imitative of a grunt. It is used to show contempt or disbelief.

Humping is the present participle of hump—carrying a heavy load or, in slang, having sex: {The soldiers were humping gear through the jungle}. {He was humping sixty pounds of equipment}. {The dog was humping my leg}.

Humps is the plural of hump—rounded protuberances like those on camels or in roads: {A Bactrian camel has two humps}. {The road is full of humps and potholes}. As a verb, humps means carries heavily or, in slang, has sex: {He humps his bag up four flights of stairs every day}. {The dog humps everything in sight}.

Hums is the sound of humming—a low, steady, continuous tone made with closed lips: {the hum of bees}, {the hum of machinery}. To hum is to produce this sound, often while singing a melody without words: {She hummed softly while she worked}. A place that hums is busy with activity: {The office was really humming today}.

Humungous means extremely large or enormous, with a playful, emphatic quality: {a humungous slice of cake}, {The spider was humungous}. The word emerged in American slang in the 1960s, probably blending huge and monstrous or tremendous. Also spelled humongous.

Hun is a casual, affectionate term of address, a shortened form of honey: {Thanks, hun}, {You okay, hun?} It's common in American speech, especially from service workers to customers or between friends and romantic partners. The tone ranges from genuinely warm to perfunctory depending on context. (Capitalized Hun refers to the ancient nomadic people.)

A hunch is an intuitive feeling or suspicion not based on evidence: {I had a hunch she wasn't telling the truth}. To hunch is to arch or draw up: {He hunched his shoulders against the cold}. A hunch can also be a rounded lump, as in hunchback—someone with a curved spine.

A hunchback is a person with a pronounced curvature of the upper spine, creating a rounded or humped back. The term is old-fashioned and now considered offensive when applied to people—medical language prefers kyphosis for the condition. The word persists mainly through literary references: {The Hunchback of Notre Dame}.

Hunchbacks is the plural of hunchback, a person with a pronounced curvature of the upper spine causing a rounded or humped back. The term is now considered offensive; medical contexts prefer kyphosis for the condition. The word evokes literary figures like Quasimodo from *The Hunchback of Notre-Dame*: {The cathedral's famous fictional bell-ringer is among literature's most sympathetic hunchbacks}.
clues: Those with severely curved upper backs

definition: Hunched describes a posture with the shoulders raised and the back curved forward, typically suggesting cold, discomfort, or dejection: {He sat hunched over his desk}. Someone who hunches draws their body inward protectively. A hunched figure appears smaller, contracted: {She walked hunched against the wind}.

Hunches is the plural of hunch in its noun sense—an intuitive feeling or suspicion not based on evidence: {I had a hunch she was lying}. To {play a hunch} is to act on intuition rather than logic. The verb hunch means to bend or curve the body forward: {He hunched over his desk}. Hunched shoulders suggest tension or cold.

Hunching is drawing up or rounding the body, especially the shoulders and back, into a cramped or curved posture. People hunch over desks, hunch against the cold, or hunch their shoulders when tense or defensive: {She sat hunching over her laptop for hours}. The word suggests protective contraction or poor posture.

Hundred is the number 100, ten times ten. It serves as a basic unit for counting and measuring: {a hundred dollars}, {a hundred years}. In the plural, hundreds indicates a large but indefinite quantity: {Hundreds of people showed up}. {A hundred percent} means completely or totally: {I'm a hundred percent certain}. Historically, a hundred was also an administrative subdivision in English counties.

Hundreds is the plural of hundred, referring to multiple groups of one hundred or to quantities in the range of 100-999. It often indicates an imprecise but substantial number: {Hundreds of people showed up}. The hundreds place is the third digit from the right in a numeral. In the plural, it can specify a century: {the seventeen hundreds} means the 1700s.

Hundredth describes something in the position numbered one hundred in a sequence: {the hundredth anniversary}, {her hundredth birthday}. As a noun, a hundredth is one of a hundred equal parts: {A centimeter is one hundredth of a meter}. The word often signals a milestone or emphasizes repetition: {I've told you for the hundredth time}.

Hung is the past tense and past participle of hang in most senses: {She hung the picture on the wall}, {The fog hung over the valley}. The exception is execution by hanging, which uses hanged: {The murderer was hanged at dawn}. Separately, hung is slang for having a large penis: {hung like a horse}. A hung jury cannot reach a verdict.

Hunger is the bodily sensation of needing food—the discomfort or weakness that comes from not eating. Extended, it describes severe food scarcity: {Millions face hunger in the region}. Figuratively, hunger is intense desire or craving: {a hunger for success}, {hunger for knowledge}. To hunger for something is to yearn for it deeply.

Hungover describes the unpleasant physical state following heavy alcohol consumption—headache, nausea, fatigue, sensitivity to light. {I was so hungover I couldn't get out of bed until noon.} The noun form is hangover. Someone perpetually hungover might be called a drunk; someone occasionally hungover had a rough night.

Hungry describes the physical sensation of needing food—the body signaling it wants to eat. Beyond literal hunger, it expresses strong desire or eagerness: {hungry for success}, {hungry for attention}. A hungry look suggests intense longing. Athletes described as hungry are driven and ambitious, not yet satisfied with their achievements.

A hunk is a large piece of something, typically torn or cut off roughly: {a hunk of bread}, {a hunk of cheese}. The word suggests irregular shape and substantial size. In informal use, a hunk is an attractive, well-built man: {She thinks the new lifeguard is a real hunk}.

To hunker is to squat or crouch low, typically on the balls of the feet: {He hunkered by the campfire}. The posture suggests settling in or bracing yourself. To {hunker down} is to take shelter, dig in, or prepare to wait something out: {We hunkered down for the storm}. The phrase implies endurance—staying put through difficulty rather than fleeing.

Hunkered is the past tense of hunker, meaning to crouch or squat low to the ground, often in a defensive or settled posture. The phrase {hunkered down} is far more common than hunkered alone, suggesting someone has settled in firmly to wait something out or concentrate intensely: {We hunkered down for the storm}. It can also imply stubborn resistance to change or outside pressure.

Hunkering is the act of crouching down on one's heels or squatting low to the ground. The word often implies settling in or waiting something out: {We spent the storm hunkering in the basement}. To hunker down suggests bracing for difficulty or digging in stubbornly: {The team is hunkering down for a long negotiation}.

Hunks is the plural of hunk. A hunk is a large, thick piece of something: {hunks of bread}, {hunks of cheese}. Informally, a hunk is an attractive, muscular man: {She thinks the new lifeguard is a total hunk}. The plural often appears in this sense: {a calendar full of hunks}.

Hunky describes a man who is muscularly attractive—broad-shouldered, well-built, sexually appealing: {a hunky lifeguard}, {She thinks he's hunky}. The word is informal and slightly playful, used more often by women describing men. Separately, hunky is an older ethnic slur for a person of Hungarian or Eastern European descent, now rarely encountered.

Hunkydory means fine, satisfactory, or going well. The word is informal and slightly old-fashioned, often appearing in assurances that everything is under control: {Don't worry, everything's hunkydory}. It sometimes carries a hint of irony when things clearly aren't fine: {He acts like it's all hunkydory while the business is failing}.

Hunt is to pursue and try to capture or kill, especially game animals: {They hunted deer every fall}. The noun is an instance of hunting or a group that hunts together. Hunt extends to any determined search: {hunting for a job}, {hunting for the car keys}. To {hunt down} is to pursue until caught. A {witch hunt} is a campaign against people considered undesirable, often with flimsy evidence.

Hunted describes someone or something being pursued, especially by hunters or those seeking to capture or kill: {the hunted fox}, {a hunted fugitive}. The word carries connotations of fear and desperation—a hunted {look} in someone's eyes suggests they feel watched or threatened, unable to relax: {She had the hunted expression of someone always looking over her shoulder}.

A hunter is a person who hunts—pursuing and killing wild animals for food, sport, or pest control. The term extends to anyone who searches persistently: {a bargain hunter}, {a job hunter}, {a bounty hunter}. Hunter also names a type of horse bred for fox hunting, and a style of tall waterproof boot. {The hunters returned at dusk with two deer.} (Capitalized Hunter is a given name.)

Hunters is the plural of hunter—people who pursue and kill wild animals for food, sport, or wildlife management. The term extends to anyone who seeks something persistently: {job hunters}, {bargain hunters}, {bounty hunters}. In nature, hunters are predatory animals: {Wolves are pack hunters}. {The hunters returned with two deer}.

Hunting is the pursuit and killing of wild animals, typically for food, sport, or population control. The word extends to any determined search: {a job hunt}, {house hunting}, {hunting for my keys}. A hunting dog or hunting rifle is designed for the activity. To go hunting is to engage in the pursuit: {We went hunting every fall}.

A huntress is a female hunter—a woman who pursues and kills wild game. The word appears more often in mythology and fantasy than in contemporary usage, where hunter serves for any gender: {Artemis was the huntress of Greek myth}. Huntress can also describe a woman who pursues anything with predatory intensity.

Hunts is the third-person singular of hunt. To hunt is to pursue animals for food or sport, or to search persistently for something: {She hunts for bargains every weekend}. A hunt is the activity itself or an organized hunting party. Hunts as a noun refers to multiple such pursuits or groups: {Fox hunts were once common in the English countryside}.

A huntsman is a person who hunts, particularly one who manages hounds during a fox hunt or similar pursuit. The term carries a traditional, slightly formal tone—you're more likely to encounter it in British contexts or period literature than in casual American speech: {The huntsman sounded his horn to call the hounds}. A huntsman spider is a large, fast-moving spider found in warm climates.

Huntsmen is the plural of huntsman—a person who hunts, especially one who manages hounds during a fox hunt. The term carries traditional or formal connotations: {The huntsmen gathered at dawn with their horses and dogs}. It appears in fairy tales and period literature more often than in contemporary usage, where hunters is the standard plural.

A hurdle is a barrier to be jumped over, especially the lightweight frames used in track-and-field races. By extension, a hurdle is any obstacle or difficulty that must be overcome: {The biggest hurdle was getting funding}. To hurdle is to leap over something while running: {She hurdled the fence and kept going}.

A hurdler is an athlete who competes in hurdle races, sprinting down a track while leaping over a series of barriers called hurdles. The term applies to competitors in both track and field events and equestrian steeplechase. By extension, hurdler can describe anyone who overcomes obstacles: {She's been a hurdler all her life, never letting setbacks stop her}.

Hurdlers are athletes who compete in hurdle races—track events requiring runners to leap over evenly spaced barriers. The term applies to both sprinters running short hurdle distances and those in longer steeplechase events. By extension, a hurdler is anyone who overcomes obstacles: {She's a hurdler in life, never letting setbacks stop her}.

Hurdles are barriers to be jumped over, originally in track-and-field races where runners leap a series of them. The sport itself is called hurdles or the hurdles: {She won gold in the 400-meter hurdles}. By extension, any obstacle or difficulty becomes a hurdle: {We still have a few hurdles to clear before the deal closes}. To hurdle is to jump over something while running.

Hurdling is the track-and-field event of running a course with hurdles—barriers that athletes must leap over at speed. The term covers both the activity and the sport: {She took up hurdling in high school}. By extension, hurdling can describe overcoming any series of obstacles: {hurdling bureaucratic requirements}.

Hurl means to throw with great force: {He hurled the ball across the field}, {She hurled insults at her opponent}. The violence of the motion distinguishes hurling from ordinary throwing—you hurl something when you want it to travel fast or hit hard. Informally, hurl also means to vomit: {I thought I was going to hurl}.

Hurled is the past tense of hurl, meaning to throw something with great force: {He hurled the ball across the field}, {She hurled insults at her opponent}. The word implies violent or aggressive motion—you don't hurl something gently. To hurl can also mean to vomit: {He was so sick he hurled all night}.

A hurler is someone who hurls—throws with force. The word appears most often in baseball contexts, where it's a slightly colorful synonym for pitcher: {The hurler struck out twelve batters}. In Irish sports, a hurler plays hurling, the traditional field game played with sticks and a ball.

Hurling is an Irish sport played with wooden sticks and a small ball, resembling a fast-paced combination of field hockey and lacrosse. Teams score by hitting the ball into or over the goal. The sport has ancient origins and remains central to Irish athletic culture: {The hurling match drew thousands to Croke Park}. Separately, hurling is the present participle of hurl—to throw forcefully.

Hurls is the third-person singular of hurl, meaning to throw something with great force: {She hurls the ball across the field}. The word often carries a sense of violence or aggression—you hurl insults, accusations, or abuse at someone. To hurl can also mean to vomit: {He hurled after drinking too much}.
Hooray, variously spelled, is a standard exclamation to express appreciation of a victory, gain, or advantage.

Hurrahs are shouts of joy, approval, or celebration—the plural of hurrah. The word captures enthusiastic cheering: {The crowd's hurrahs echoed through the stadium}. A final hurrah (or last hurrah) is a concluding effort or triumph before retirement or decline: {The album was the band's last hurrah}.
Hurray, variously spelled, is a standard exclamation to express appreciation of a victory, gain, or advantage.

A hurricane is a powerful tropical storm with sustained winds of at least 74 miles per hour, forming over warm ocean waters. Hurricanes bring destructive winds, heavy rain, and storm surges to coastal areas. The term applies specifically to such storms in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific; elsewhere they're called typhoons or cyclones. Figuratively, a hurricane of activity or emotion suggests overwhelming intensity: {a hurricane of criticism}.

Hurricanes is the plural of hurricane, a powerful tropical storm with sustained winds of at least 74 miles per hour, rotating around a calm central eye. Hurricanes form over warm ocean waters and can cause catastrophic damage through wind, rain, and storm surge: {Three hurricanes hit the Gulf Coast that season}. The term applies specifically to such storms in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific; equivalent storms elsewhere are called typhoons or cyclones.

Hurried describes something done quickly, often with a sense of urgency or insufficient time. A hurried {breakfast} is eaten in haste. A hurried {glance} is brief and cursory. The word often implies carelessness or lack of thoroughness: {Her hurried response contained several errors}. Someone who looks hurried appears rushed or pressed for time.

Hurry is urgent haste—moving or acting faster than comfortable pace allows. You hurry to catch a train, hurry through a meal, hurry someone along. {What's the hurry?} asks why speed is necessary. {No hurry} signals patience. To be {in a hurry} is to feel pressed for time. {I won't do that again in a hurry} means not anytime soon.

Hurrying is the present participle of hurry, capturing the act of moving or acting with speed, often because time is short. Someone who is hurrying rushes through tasks or toward a destination: {She was hurrying to catch her train}. The word can also function as a noun for the activity itself: {All this hurrying around is exhausting}. Hurrying often carries a sense of pressure or urgency that mere quickness does not.

Hurt covers physical pain and emotional distress. Something hurts when it causes pain: {My back hurts}, {That hurts!} To hurt someone is to injure or wound them, literally or figuratively: {I didn't mean to hurt your feelings}. As an adjective, hurt describes the injured state: {a hurt expression}, {deeply hurt by the betrayal}. The noun is the pain itself: {the hurt in her eyes}. Things that {wouldn't hurt} are advisable: {It wouldn't hurt to ask}.

Hurtful describes words, actions, or behavior that cause emotional pain or distress to someone. A hurtful {remark} wounds feelings; a hurtful {decision} may damage a relationship. The word implies intent or at least carelessness—something hurtful could have been avoided. It tends to describe interpersonal slights rather than physical harm: {What you said about her weight was really hurtful.}

Hurting describes being in pain, whether physical or emotional: {My back is hurting}, {She's still hurting from the breakup}. As an adjective, it characterizes someone or something in a bad state: {a hurting team}, {hurting for cash}. To be {hurting for} something is to need it badly. The word carries more immediacy than simply saying something hurts—it emphasizes ongoing distress.
clues: What a wound does to you

definition: Hurtle means to move with great speed and force, often recklessly or out of control: {The car hurtled down the mountain road}, {Debris hurtled through the air}. The word suggests dangerous momentum—things that hurtle may crash. To hurtle something is to throw or propel it violently, though this active use is less common than the intransitive.

Hurtled is the past tense of hurtle, meaning to move with great speed and often reckless force: {The car hurtled down the mountain road}, {Debris hurtled through the air}. The word emphasizes violent momentum—things that hurtle seem barely under control, careening toward impact or disaster.

Hurtling is moving at high speed, typically with a sense of recklessness or unstoppable momentum: {a boulder hurtling down the mountainside}, {hurtling toward disaster}. The word implies something large or heavy in rapid motion, often on a collision course. Unlike merely speeding, hurtling suggests force and consequence.

Hurts is the third-person singular and plural form of hurt, covering both physical pain and emotional distress. Something hurts when it causes or feels pain: {My back hurts} or {It hurts to watch him struggle}. As a noun, hurts are injuries or sources of pain, though this usage is less common than the verb. The word applies equally to stubbed toes and wounded feelings, making no sharp distinction between bodily sensation and emotional anguish.

A husband is a man in a marriage—the male counterpart to a wife. The word carries connotations of commitment, partnership, and domestic responsibility: {her husband of thirty years}, {a devoted husband and father}. As a verb, to husband means to manage resources carefully and economically: {They husbanded their supplies through the winter}.

Husbandry is the care and cultivation of crops and livestock—the work of farming: {animal husbandry}, {crop husbandry}. The word extends to careful management of resources generally: {good husbandry of the organization's funds}. Despite appearances, the word connects to household management, not to husbands specifically, though both share the same root.

Husbands is the plural of husband, a man to whom someone is married. The word can also function as a verb meaning to manage resources carefully and economically: {She husbanded her savings through the lean years}. This sense connects to the older meaning of husband as one who manages a household, though that usage is now archaic outside of compounds like animal husbandry.

Hush calls for silence or quiet. As an interjection, it's a gentle command: {Hush, the baby's sleeping}. The verb means to make or become quiet: {She hushed the children}. A hush is a period of silence: {A hush fell over the crowd}. To hush something up is to suppress it, keeping it from becoming known: {They tried to hush up the scandal}. Hushed describes quiet, subdued tones: {They spoke in hushed voices}.

Hushed means quiet, silent, or subdued. A hushed {voice} is lowered to avoid being overheard. A hushed {room} has fallen silent, often in anticipation or reverence. The word suggests deliberate quieting rather than mere absence of sound: {The crowd fell hushed as the ceremony began}. Hushed {tones} implies secrecy or solemnity.

Hushes is the third-person singular of hush, meaning to make or become quiet. Someone hushes a crying baby, or hushes up a scandal to keep it secret. A crowd hushes when the speaker approaches the microphone. {She hushes the children whenever the phone rings.}

Hushpuppies are small, deep-fried balls of cornmeal batter, a staple of Southern American cooking typically served alongside fried fish or barbecue. The name supposedly comes from cooks tossing scraps to quiet barking dogs: {Hush, puppies}. {The catfish platter came with coleslaw and hushpuppies.} (Capitalized Hush Puppies is a shoe brand.)

A hushpuppy is a small, deep-fried ball of cornmeal batter, a staple of Southern American cooking often served alongside fried fish or barbecue. The name supposedly comes from tossing scraps to quiet barking dogs: {Hush, puppy}. Also spelled hush puppy. (Capitalized Hush Puppies is a shoe brand.)

A husk is the dry outer covering of a seed or fruit—corn husks, coconut husks. To husk corn is to strip away this covering. Figuratively, a husk is an empty shell of what once held life: {After the divorce, he was just a husk of his former self}. The adjective husky, meaning dry-throated or rough-voiced, derives from the same image.

Huskies is the plural of husky, a breed of sled dog developed in Arctic regions. These dogs are known for their thick coats, endurance, and wolf-like appearance: {The huskies pulled the sled across the frozen tundra}. Husky also means a person or thing that is big and sturdy, so huskies can refer to multiple such individuals. (Capitalized Huskies refers to sports teams.)

Husks are the dry outer coverings of seeds, grains, or fruits—the papery sheaths around corn kernels, the rough casings of wheat. To husk corn is to strip away these layers. Figuratively, a husk is what remains when substance is gone: {He was a husk of his former self}. The word suggests emptiness, something hollowed out.

Husky has two unrelated origins. One comes from husk—husky corn has its husk on, and a husky voice is rough and dry like a husk. This extends to sturdy or burly: {a husky farmhand}. The other husky is a sled dog bred for Arctic conditions, probably from a shortening of Eskimo. {A team of huskies pulled the sled across the ice.}

Hussy is an insulting term for a woman considered sexually promiscuous or brazenly improper. The word is old-fashioned and somewhat theatrical: {That hussy stole my husband!} It originated as a neutral contraction of housewife but shifted entirely to contempt. Today it appears mostly in period pieces or ironic use among friends.

Hustle centers on energetic, often aggressive activity. To hustle is to move quickly or push someone along: {The guards hustled him out of the building}. It means to work hard and fast, especially to make money: {She's been hustling to pay rent}. In American English, hustle often implies swindling—a hustle is a scam, and a hustler is someone who deceives for profit, whether at pool or on the street. The noun also names a disco-era line dance. {Side hustle} is a secondary job or income source.

Hustled is the past tense of hustle, which carries several related meanings around energetic, forceful movement. To hustle is to move quickly or push someone along: {We hustled to catch the train}, {Security hustled him out of the building}. It also means to work hard and aggressively to get something done or make money. In American slang, to hustle someone is to swindle them, especially through a scam that appears fair: {He got hustled at pool by a guy who pretended not to know the game}.

A hustler is someone who pursues money or success aggressively, often through dubious means. The word carries a spectrum of meanings from admiring to criminal. A street hustler might sell stolen goods or run scams. A pool hustler pretends to play poorly, then wins big bets. In sex work, a hustler is typically a male prostitute. More positively, calling someone a hustler can praise their tireless drive and resourcefulness: {She's a real hustler—started three businesses before she was thirty}. (Capitalized Hustler is the magazine.)

Hustlers is the plural of hustler—someone who pursues money or success aggressively, often through questionable means. A hustler might be a swindler running scams, a pool shark feigning incompetence, or simply someone with relentless drive: {She admires hustlers who built empires from nothing}. In some contexts, hustler means prostitute, especially a male sex worker.

Hustles covers energetic effort and deceptive schemes. To hustle is to move quickly or push aggressively: {She hustled the kids out the door}. In sports, hustle means relentless effort: {He's not the most talented, but he hustles}. The shadier sense involves swindling or aggressive selling: {street hustlers}, {hustling pool for money}. As a noun, a hustle is a scheme or scam, or the daily grind of making money: {the side hustle}.

Hustling is energetic, aggressive activity toward a goal. In sports and work, it means giving maximum effort: {I admire his hustling on defense}. Hustling also means pursuing money through aggressive salesmanship, schemes, or fraud: {He's been hustling tourists on the boardwalk}. It can specifically mean working as a prostitute or soliciting customers for sex.
Hut and hup, along with hep, are used to set the pace for people, especially soldiers, who are marching. It is also a small, simple house or shelter.

A hutch is a cage or enclosed pen for small animals, especially rabbits: {The children fed the rabbits in their hutch}. The word extends to a piece of furniture—typically a cabinet with open shelves on top of an enclosed base, used for storing and displaying dishes: {grandmother's china hutch}. Both senses share the idea of a compartmented enclosure.

Hutches is the plural of hutch, a small enclosed structure for keeping animals, especially rabbits: {The children fed the rabbits in their hutches}. Hutch also refers to a piece of furniture—typically a cabinet or cupboard with open shelves above a closed base, used for storing and displaying dishes: {The china hutches were filled with her grandmother's collection}.

Huts is the plural of hut—a small, simple dwelling or shelter, typically rough or temporary: {fishermen's huts along the shore}, {a Quonset hut}. Hut suggests something more primitive than a cabin and less permanent than a house. Pizza Hut notwithstanding, the word carries connotations of poverty or rusticity.

Huzzah is an old-fashioned exclamation of joy, approval, or triumph—a cheer: {Huzzah! The king approaches!} It sounds deliberately archaic, often used playfully or ironically to celebrate minor victories: {I finally fixed the printer. Huzzah!} Renaissance fairs and period dramas keep it alive.

A hyacinth is a bulb flower known for its dense clusters of fragrant, bell-shaped blooms in purple, pink, white, or blue. Native to the eastern Mediterranean, hyacinths are spring garden staples: {The hyacinths are finally blooming}. The word also names a reddish-orange gemstone, a variant of zircon. (Capitalized Hyacinth is a given name from Greek mythology.)

Hyacinths are bulbous flowering plants with dense clusters of fragrant blooms in spring, typically blue, pink, white, or purple. The name comes from Greek mythology—Hyacinthus was a youth beloved by Apollo, from whose blood the flower supposedly sprang. {The scent of hyacinths filled the garden}. In the plural, hyacinths often refers to the cut flowers or bulbs themselves: {She planted hyacinths along the walkway}.

A hybrid combines elements from different sources. In biology, a hybrid is offspring from two different species or varieties: a mule is a hybrid of horse and donkey. The term extends to anything of mixed origin: hybrid {cars} use both gasoline and electric power, hybrid {work} splits time between office and home. {The film is a hybrid of comedy and horror.}

Hybrids is the plural of hybrid—something produced by combining two different elements. A hybrid plant or animal has parents of different species or varieties: {mules are hybrids of horses and donkeys}. A hybrid car uses both gasoline and electric power. The word extends to anything mixed: {The course was a hybrid of lecture and seminar}.

A hydra is a many-headed serpent from Greek mythology that grew two heads for each one cut off—making it nearly impossible to kill. The word now describes any problem that multiplies when you try to solve it: {Every time we fix one bug, two more appear—it's a hydra}. In biology, hydra refers to tiny freshwater organisms with remarkable regenerative abilities, named for the mythical creature. (Capitalized Hydra is the specific mythological monster or a constellation.)

A hydrangea is a flowering shrub with large, showy clusters of blossoms in shades of blue, pink, purple, or white. The color often depends on soil acidity—more acidic soil produces bluer flowers. Hydrangeas are popular in gardens and as cut flowers: {The hydrangeas along the fence were in full bloom}.

Hydrangeas is the plural of hydrangea, a flowering shrub prized for its large, showy clusters of blooms in shades of blue, pink, purple, or white. The flowers' color often depends on soil acidity—a quirk gardeners exploit. {The hydrangeas along the fence were in full bloom.} Common in temperate gardens and floral arrangements.

A hydrant is a connection point for drawing water from a main supply, typically a short post with valves and outlets found along streets for firefighters to attach hoses: {The truck pulled up next to the hydrant}. Fire hydrant is the full term, though hydrant alone usually means the same thing. {Don't park in front of a hydrant.}

Hydrants are outlets in a water-supply system, typically the upright pipes with valves found along streets for firefighters to connect hoses: {The car was towed for parking in front of a hydrant}. Fire hydrants are the familiar red or yellow fixtures; other hydrants provide water for street cleaning or irrigation.

Hydras are the plural of hydra, a genus of small freshwater organisms with tubular bodies and tentacles, notable for their regenerative abilities—cut one apart and each piece regrows into a complete animal. The name comes from the Hydra of Greek mythology, a many-headed serpent that sprouted two new heads whenever one was severed. Figuratively, a hydra is any problem that multiplies when attacked: {Every regulation they cut spawned two new loopholes—a bureaucratic hydra}.

To hydrate is to supply water or moisture. The most common use is bodily: {Stay hydrated during your workout}. You can also hydrate skin with lotion or hydrate dried foods by soaking them. As a noun, a hydrate is a chemical compound containing water molecules. The opposite is dehydrate.

Hydrated means having adequate water or moisture. The term appears most often in contexts of health and chemistry. To {stay hydrated} is to drink enough fluids. In chemistry, a hydrated compound has water molecules incorporated into its structure. Skin can be hydrated with moisturizer. The opposite is dehydrated.

Hydration is the process of absorbing or supplying water. The body needs hydration to function—{Drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated}. Athletes and health-conscious people track their hydration levels. In chemistry, hydration refers to water molecules bonding with other substances. Skincare products promise to improve skin hydration.

Hydraulic describes systems that use pressurized liquid—typically oil or water—to transmit force and do work. A hydraulic {lift} raises cars by pumping fluid into cylinders. Hydraulic {brakes} stop vehicles through fluid pressure. The word also applies to anything relating to water in motion or under pressure: hydraulic {engineering}, hydraulic {fracturing}. Hydraulic systems multiply force efficiently, which is why heavy machinery relies on them.

Hydraulics is the branch of engineering and physics concerned with the mechanical properties of liquids, especially water, and how they can be harnessed to do work. Hydraulic systems use pressurized fluid to generate force and motion—powering everything from car brakes to construction equipment. {The excavator runs on hydraulics.} The singular hydraulic functions as an adjective: hydraulic {lift}, hydraulic {pressure}.

Hydro is a combining form meaning water, appearing in countless English words: hydrogen, hydroelectric, hydrant, dehydrate. In Canadian slang, hydro means electricity—from the prevalence of hydroelectric power—so {the hydro bill} is the electric bill. In British slang, hydro can refer to hydroponically grown cannabis.

Hydroelectric describes electricity generated from the energy of moving water. Dams are the most common hydroelectric infrastructure, using falling water to spin turbines: {The region gets most of its power from hydroelectric plants}. Run-of-river systems harness natural flow without large reservoirs. Hydroelectric power is renewable but can disrupt ecosystems and displace communities.

A hydrofoil is a boat fitted with wing-like structures beneath the hull that lift the vessel above the water at speed, reducing drag and allowing faster travel. The term also refers to the foil structure itself—the underwater fin that generates lift as water flows over it: {The ferry's hydrofoils raised it clear of the waves}.

Hydrofoils are wing-like structures mounted beneath a boat's hull that lift the vessel above the water at speed, reducing drag and increasing efficiency. The term also refers to boats equipped with these structures: {The hydrofoil skimmed across the harbor}. As the craft accelerates, the foils generate lift like airplane wings, raising the hull clear of the surface.

Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe, a colorless, odorless gas that combines with oxygen to form water. Its name means "water-former." Hydrogen appears in countless compounds and serves as a fuel source: {hydrogen fuel cells}, {the hydrogen bomb}. In chemistry, hydrogen has atomic number 1.

A hydroplane is a boat designed to skim across the water's surface at high speed, its hull lifting almost entirely out of the water. The term also names a horizontal fin that controls a submarine's depth. As a verb, hydroplane describes a vehicle losing traction when water builds between tires and road surface: {The car hydroplaned on the wet highway and spun out}.

Hydroplaned is the past tense of hydroplane—to skim across water or lose traction when a layer of water separates tires from the road surface. The term comes from boats designed to skim at high speed, but now appears mostly in driving contexts: {The car hydroplaned on the wet highway and spun out}. The experience is brief and terrifying—the steering goes slack as the vehicle glides uncontrolled.

Hydroplanes functions as both noun and verb, united by the idea of skimming across water. A hydroplane is a boat designed to skim the surface at high speed, its hull rising to reduce drag. Racing hydroplanes compete in speed events. The verb describes a vehicle losing traction on wet pavement as tires ride atop a film of water rather than gripping the road: {The car hydroplaned on the flooded highway}. Aircraft fitted with floats for water landings are also called hydroplanes.

Hydroplaning is when a vehicle's tires lose contact with the road surface due to a layer of water, causing loss of traction and steering control. The tires essentially skim across the water rather than gripping pavement: {The car started hydroplaning and I couldn't brake}. The same phenomenon affects aircraft landing on wet runways. Also called aquaplaning.

Hydroponics is the practice of growing plants without soil, using water-based nutrient solutions instead. Roots may be suspended directly in liquid or supported by inert materials like gravel or perlite. The method allows precise control over growing conditions and is used in commercial greenhouses, urban farms, and home setups: {a hydroponic lettuce operation}, {hydroponic tomatoes}.

Hydropower is electricity generated from the energy of flowing or falling water. Dams are the most common source, using turbines turned by released water to produce power. Hydropower is renewable and produces no direct emissions, making it attractive for clean energy: {The region gets most of its electricity from hydropower}. Also called hydroelectric power.

A hyena is a carnivorous mammal native to Africa and Asia, known for its sloping back, powerful jaws, and distinctive vocalizations—the spotted hyena's call sounds like laughter, giving rise to {laughing hyena}. Hyenas are scavengers and hunters, often traveling in packs. Figuratively, a hyena is someone who profits from others' misfortune or laughs cruelly.

Hyenas are carnivorous mammals native to Africa and Asia, known for their powerful jaws, sloping backs, and distinctive vocalizations—the spotted hyena's call sounds like cackling laughter. Despite their doglike appearance, they're more closely related to cats. Figuratively, a hyena is someone who laughs cruelly or preys on others' misfortune: {The paparazzi descended like hyenas}.

Hygiene is the practice of keeping oneself and one's surroundings clean to maintain health and prevent disease. Personal hygiene includes bathing, handwashing, and dental care. The word extends to anything kept clean or uncontaminated: {code hygiene}, {sleep hygiene}. {Good hygiene habits start in childhood.}

Hygienic means clean and free from disease-causing agents, or designed to promote cleanliness: {hygienic food preparation}, {hygienic conditions}. The word often describes practices or environments that meet health standards: {The kitchen wasn't exactly hygienic}. Something unhygienic poses contamination risks.

A hygienist is a specialist in hygiene—the science of preserving health through cleanliness. In practice, the word almost always means dental hygienist, a licensed professional who cleans teeth, takes X-rays, and educates patients about oral care: {The hygienist scraped the plaque off my teeth before the dentist came in}.

Hygienists are professionals who specialize in maintaining cleanliness and health standards. Most commonly, the term refers to dental hygienists—licensed practitioners who clean teeth, take X-rays, and educate patients about oral care: {The hygienist scraped the tartar off my teeth before the dentist came in}. Industrial hygienists assess workplace hazards like chemical exposure or noise levels.

A hymn is a song of praise or worship, especially one sung in religious services: {The congregation sang a hymn}. By extension, any expression of devoted praise can be called a hymn: {The film is a hymn to small-town America}. To hymn something is to praise it effusively, though this use is literary and uncommon.

A hymnal is a book containing hymns for use in religious services. Churches often provide hymnals in pews so congregations can sing together: {She opened the hymnal to page 47}. The word functions as both noun and adjective: {a hymnal collection}.

Hymnals are books containing hymns—religious songs meant for congregational worship. Churches keep hymnals in pew racks for services, though many congregations now project lyrics on screens instead. {She found her grandmother's handwritten notes in the margins of the old hymnal.}

Hymns are religious songs, typically sung in worship by a congregation. The word usually implies traditional compositions with multiple verses, as opposed to contemporary praise music. A hymnal or hymnbook collects these songs. Figuratively, anything that praises effusively might be called a hymn: {His speech was a hymn to free enterprise}.

Hype is extravagant publicity or promotion, often exceeding what the thing deserves: {The movie couldn't live up to the hype}. To hype something is to promote it aggressively: {They've been hyping the new product for months}. Hyped or hyped up can mean excited or agitated: {The kids were all hyped up on sugar}. Something overhyped has been promoted beyond its merits.

A hypebeast is someone obsessively devoted to acquiring trendy, often expensive streetwear and sneakers—less for personal style than for status and social media clout. The term is usually disparaging, suggesting someone who chases whatever brands or products are currently hyped rather than developing genuine taste: {He's such a hypebeast, camping out for every Supreme drop}.

Hyped means excited or full of anticipation, often with the suggestion of being worked up beyond what's warranted: {I'm so hyped for this concert}. Something hyped has been heavily promoted or publicized: {The movie was hyped for months before release}. The word carries a hint of inflation—hype often exceeds reality. {Don't believe the hype.}

A hypeman is someone who builds excitement and energy, especially as a supporting performer who hypes up the crowd at concerts or introduces the main act. In hip-hop, the hypeman backs up the lead rapper with ad-libs, call-and-response, and crowd engagement. The term extends beyond music to anyone whose role is generating enthusiasm: {Every sales team needs a hypeman to keep morale up.} {He's basically her hypeman, always talking up her work to the boss.}

Hyper describes a state of being overly energetic, excitable, or wound up. It's often applied to children or pets who can't seem to settle down: {The kids got hyper after eating all that candy}. As a prefix, hyper- means excessive or above normal, appearing in words like hyperactive, hypersensitive, and hyperlink. The standalone adjective hyper is informal and typically carries a mildly negative connotation, suggesting someone is too amped up for the situation.

Hyperactive describes excessive activity or restlessness beyond normal levels. A hyperactive child can't sit still in class. The term has clinical weight—attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is characterized by hyperactive behavior—but casual use is common: {My brain gets hyperactive at night}. An overactive immune system or imagination might also be called hyperactive.

Hyperactivity is excessive physical movement and restlessness, particularly the kind that makes it difficult to sit still or focus. The term appears most often in clinical contexts—attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)—but applies broadly to anyone unusually energetic or fidgety: {The kids were bouncing off the walls with hyperactivity after eating all that candy}.

Hyperbole describes exaggeration for obvious (I’ve told you a million times) or subtle (the dawn of a new era) effect. Not meant to be taken literally, hyperbole is an impactful literary device in poetry and speechwriting.
clues: Saying a million when meaning many

definition: Hyperbolic means wildly exaggerated or overstated: {His hyperbolic claims about the product's benefits strained credibility}. The word describes language that goes beyond what's reasonable or accurate for effect. In mathematics, hyperbolic refers to curves and functions related to the hyperbola—a technical sense unrelated to exaggeration.

A hypercar is an extremely high-performance automobile that exceeds even supercars in speed, power, and price. These are the rarest and most technologically advanced production vehicles, often limited editions costing millions of dollars: {The Bugatti Chiron and McLaren P1 are iconic hypercars}. The category emerged in the 2010s as manufacturers pushed beyond what "supercar" could describe.

Hyperconsumerism is excessive consumption of goods beyond practical need, driven by advertising, status-seeking, or compulsive buying. The term implies criticism—that consumer culture has gone too far, prioritizing acquisition over wellbeing or sustainability: {Hyperconsumerism has turned shopping into a lifestyle}. Related to but stronger than consumerism, suggesting pathological or environmentally destructive levels.

Hyperconsumption is consumption at excessive or unsustainable levels, typically in discussions of environmental impact or consumer culture. The term implies buying and discarding goods beyond what's needed or healthy—for individuals, societies, or the planet: {Hyperconsumption in wealthy nations drives resource depletion}. It often carries critical connotations about materialism and waste.

Hyperdrive is a fictional faster-than-light propulsion system that allows spacecraft to travel across vast interstellar distances almost instantaneously. Popularized by science fiction franchises like Star Wars, it typically works by propelling a ship into an alternate dimension or "hyperspace" where normal physics don't apply. Outside of fiction, hyperdrive describes any state of extreme speed, intensity, or productivity: {The whole team went into hyperdrive to meet the deadline}.

Hyperdrives are propulsion systems in science fiction that allow spacecraft to travel faster than light, typically by entering an alternate dimension or warping space itself. The concept appears across franchises from *Star Wars* to *Babylon 5*, each with its own rules: {The hyperdrive failed and left them stranded}. In figurative use, hyperdrive suggests maximum speed or intensity: {The campaign kicked into hyperdrive after the debate}.

Hyperfixated describes being intensely, sometimes obsessively focused on a single subject, activity, or interest to the exclusion of other things. The term comes from psychology, particularly discussions of ADHD and autism, where hyperfixation names this pattern of deep absorption: {I've been hyperfixated on this video game for weeks}. The focus feels compulsive rather than chosen, and shifting attention away can be difficult.

Hyperfixation is intense, consuming focus on a single interest, activity, or topic—often to the exclusion of other responsibilities or needs. The term originated in discussions of ADHD and autism, where such episodes are common: {I've been in hyperfixation mode on this video game for three days}. Unlike casual enthusiasm, hyperfixation implies difficulty disengaging even when you want or need to.

Hyperfixations are intense, consuming preoccupations with a particular subject, activity, or interest—often to the exclusion of other responsibilities or needs. The term emerged from discussions of ADHD and autism, where such fixations are common: {My latest hyperfixation is Victorian death photography}. Unlike casual hobbies, hyperfixations tend to be all-consuming but temporary, eventually fading or being replaced by new obsessions.

Hyperfocus is intense, sustained concentration on a single task or subject, often to the exclusion of everything else. The term appears frequently in discussions of ADHD, where it describes the paradoxical ability to focus deeply on engaging activities while struggling with routine tasks: {I was in hyperfocus mode and didn't notice three hours had passed}. The verb hyperfocus follows naturally: {She hyperfocuses on puzzles but can't sit through a meeting}.

Hyperfocused describes a state of intense, sustained concentration on a single task or subject, often to the exclusion of everything else. The term appears frequently in discussions of ADHD, where hyperfocus can be both asset and liability—productive when directed well, problematic when someone can't disengage: {I got hyperfocused on the project and forgot to eat}. Outside clinical contexts, it simply means extremely focused.

Hyperfocusing is concentrating so intensely on something that everything else fades away—time, surroundings, other obligations. The term comes from discussions of ADHD, where the ability to lock onto engaging tasks contrasts with difficulty sustaining attention on boring ones: {I was hyperfocusing on the game and missed three texts}. The state can be productive or problematic depending on what captures attention.

Hyperinflation is runaway inflation so extreme that a currency loses value faster than people can spend it. Prices may double daily or weekly, making savings worthless and forcing people to use wheelbarrows of cash for basic goods: {The Weimar hyperinflation of the 1920s saw Germans papering walls with worthless banknotes}. Hyperinflation typically signals economic collapse or severe political instability.

Hyperjump is science fiction terminology for instantaneous or near-instantaneous travel across vast distances of space, bypassing normal physical limitations: {The ship made a hyperjump to the outer rim}. The concept appears across space opera franchises with varying names—hyperspace jump, warp, fold. In video games, hyperjump may describe any rapid teleportation or boosted leap ability.

Hyperjumps are instantaneous or near-instantaneous jumps through space, a staple of science fiction. Spacecraft equipped with hyperdrive technology can hyperjump between star systems, bypassing the limitations of conventional travel: {The fleet made three hyperjumps before reaching the outer colonies}. The term implies faster-than-light movement through some dimension beyond normal space.

A hyperlink is a reference in a digital document that, when clicked or tapped, takes you to another location—either elsewhere in the same document or to an entirely different webpage or file. The term combines hyper (suggesting extended capability beyond ordinary text) with link (a connection). Hyperlinks are the fundamental navigational mechanism of the World Wide Web, typically appearing as underlined or colored text. {Click the hyperlink to access the full report.} As a verb, to hyperlink is to create such a connection.

Hyperparenting is an intense, overinvolved approach to raising children—scheduling every activity, monitoring every interaction, shielding from every disappointment. The term is critical, suggesting parents who hover anxiously and intervene excessively: {Hyperparenting produces kids who can't handle setbacks}. Related to helicopter parenting, though hyperparenting emphasizes the driven, perfectionist quality of the involvement.

Hyperpop is a loosely defined genre of popular music that exaggerates and distorts the conventions of mainstream pop—pushing auto-tune, synthesizers, and digital production to abrasive or cartoonish extremes. The sound often features pitched-up vocals, glitchy beats, and maximalist layering: {Her new album leans hard into hyperpop}. The term emerged in the late 2010s, associated with internet-based artists and the PC Music collective.

Hyperrealism is an art movement producing work so detailed it resembles high-resolution photography. Paintings and sculptures depict subjects with precision beyond what the eye naturally perceives—every pore, reflection, and texture rendered with obsessive clarity. The effect can be uncanny, making viewers question whether they're looking at art or reality. The term extends to anything that seems more real than real: {The video game's hyperrealism was unsettling}.

Hyperrealistic describes art or imagery so detailed it appears more vivid than reality itself. The term applies especially to painting and sculpture that mimics photographs with uncanny precision: {The hyperrealistic portrait captured every pore and wrinkle}. In digital contexts, it describes computer-generated images approaching photographic quality. The word also applies figuratively to any depiction intensified beyond naturalism.

Hypersensitive describes an excessive or exaggerated response to something, whether physical or emotional. In medical contexts, it refers to an immune system that overreacts to substances most people tolerate, as in allergies or autoimmune conditions. More broadly, hypersensitive characterizes someone who takes offense easily or reacts strongly to criticism: {She's hypersensitive about her weight, so don't mention it}. The word implies that the sensitivity exceeds what the situation warrants.

Hypersensitivity is an exaggerated or excessive response to something. In medicine, it describes an immune system overreaction to substances that are normally harmless—allergies are hypersensitivity reactions. More broadly, it means being easily offended or emotionally reactive: {His hypersensitivity to criticism made feedback sessions difficult}. The word often carries a faintly dismissive tone, suggesting the reaction is disproportionate to the cause.
clues: When minor triggers cause major responses

definition: Hypersexualized describes something presented with exaggerated sexual characteristics or appeal, often beyond what's natural or appropriate. The term typically carries critical weight, pointing to media portrayals, advertising, or cultural pressures that impose adult sexuality onto contexts where it seems excessive or exploitative: {hypersexualized depictions of women in video games}, {the hypersexualized marketing of children's clothing}.

Hypersleep is a science fiction concept referring to a state of suspended animation used during long-distance space travel, allowing passengers to remain unconscious and age slowly or not at all while their spacecraft crosses vast distances. The term combines hyper- (suggesting something beyond normal) with sleep, though the state is more like medically induced hibernation than ordinary rest. {The crew entered hypersleep for the twenty-year journey to the colony planet.} It appears frequently in films, novels, and video games set in space.

Hyperspace is a theoretical higher-dimensional space through which spacecraft can travel faster than light, a staple of science fiction: {The ship jumped into hyperspace}. The concept sidesteps relativity by having ships exit normal space rather than exceed light speed within it. In mathematics, hyperspace refers to any space of more than three dimensions.

Hyperspeed is speed beyond normal limits—faster than anything conventionally possible. The term comes from science fiction, where it describes spacecraft traveling faster than light: {The ship jumped to hyperspeed}. Outside fiction, hyperspeed suggests extreme rapidity: {Technology is advancing at hyperspeed}. The prefix hyper- intensifies speed past its usual boundaries.

Hypertext is text displayed on a computer that contains links to other text, allowing readers to jump between related documents or sections. The term captures how digital text transcends the linear structure of printed pages—you can follow connections in any direction. The World Wide Web is built on hypertext: {Click the hypertext link to learn more}. The prefix hyper- suggests text that goes beyond ordinary text.

Hyperventilate means to breathe abnormally fast and deep, disrupting the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood. This often happens during panic attacks or extreme anxiety: {She started hyperventilating and had to breathe into a paper bag}. Figuratively, to hyperventilate is to react with excessive alarm or excitement: {Critics hyperventilated over the casting announcement}.

Hyperventilates means to breathe abnormally fast and shallow, often triggered by panic, anxiety, or physical exertion. The rapid breathing expels too much carbon dioxide, causing dizziness, tingling, or faintness: {She hyperventilates during panic attacks}. Figuratively, to hyperventilate is to react with excessive alarm or excitement: {The media hyperventilates over every minor scandal}.

Hyperventilating is breathing abnormally fast and shallow, often triggered by panic, anxiety, or physical exertion. The rapid breathing expels too much carbon dioxide, causing dizziness, tingling, or lightheadedness. Figuratively, hyperventilating describes any overwrought reaction: {The internet is hyperventilating over the casting announcement}. The noun is hyperventilation.

Hyperventilation is abnormally rapid or deep breathing that expels carbon dioxide from the blood faster than the body produces it. This can cause dizziness, tingling in the extremities, and lightheadedness. It often occurs during panic attacks or moments of intense anxiety, though it can also result from physical conditions. {The doctor talked her through her hyperventilation until her breathing slowed.} Someone who hyperventilates may be told to breathe into a paper bag to restore normal carbon dioxide levels.

Hypervigilance is a state of heightened alertness and sensitivity to potential threats. The mind scans constantly for danger, often exhaustingly so. It's associated with anxiety disorders, PTSD, and trauma responses: {Her hypervigilance made it impossible to relax in crowds}. The hypervigilant person startles easily and struggles to feel safe even in objectively safe environments.

Hyperviolence is extreme, exaggerated, or stylized violence, typically in film, video games, or other media. The term suggests violence pushed beyond realism into spectacle—graphic, prolonged, or aesthetically heightened: {Critics accused the director of hyperviolence for its own sake}. The word often appears in debates about whether such depictions desensitize audiences or constitute artistic expression.

A hyphen is the short horizontal mark (-) used to join words or parts of words. Compound adjectives before nouns often take hyphens: {a well-known author}, {a five-year-old child}. Hyphens connect prefixes to roots in some formations: {self-aware}, {ex-husband}. They also divide words at line breaks. Unlike the longer dash, hyphens link rather than separate.

Hyping is building excitement or enthusiasm for something, often through exaggerated promotion or publicity. Someone hyping a product, event, or person is generating buzz and anticipation: {The studio has been hyping the film for months}. Self-hyping is boastful self-promotion. The word often implies the reality won't match the buildup.

Hypnosis is a trance-like state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility, typically induced by another person's verbal guidance. A subject under hypnosis may follow suggestions, recover buried memories, or experience altered perceptions. The state has therapeutic uses—treating phobias, managing pain, breaking habits—though claims about its power vary widely. {She quit smoking through hypnosis.}

Hypnotic describes something that induces or relates to hypnosis—a trance-like state of heightened suggestibility. A hypnotic {suggestion} is planted during such a trance. More loosely, hypnotic describes anything that captures attention so completely it seems to entrance: {the hypnotic rhythm of the drums}, {her hypnotic gaze}. As a noun, a hypnotic is a drug that induces sleep.

Hypnotise is the British spelling of hypnotize, meaning to induce a trancelike state in someone, typically through focused attention and suggestion. A hypnotist may hypnotise a subject for therapeutic purposes, entertainment, or to access buried memories. The word extends figuratively to describe anything that captivates or fascinates completely: {The flickering flames hypnotised us into silence}. Someone hypnotised by an idea or person is utterly absorbed by them.

Hypnotised is the British spelling of hypnotized—put into a trance-like state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility. A hypnotist hypnotises subjects for therapy or entertainment. Figuratively, anything captivating can hypnotise: {The audience sat hypnotised by the performance}. {She was hypnotised by the flames dancing in the fireplace}.

Hypnotising is the British spelling of hypnotizing—inducing a trance-like state through focused attention and suggestion. The word extends to anything that holds attention so completely it seems to cast a spell: {The flickering flames were hypnotising}. A hypnotising voice or gaze captures and holds you, making everything else fade away.

Hypnotism is the practice of inducing a trance-like state in which a person becomes highly responsive to suggestion. A hypnotist may guide someone to recall memories, reduce pain, or change habits like smoking. The term covers both the technique and the broader phenomenon: {stage hypnotism}, {hypnotism for weight loss}. Whether hypnotism accesses a distinct mental state or merely heightened suggestibility remains debated.

A hypnotist is a person who induces hypnosis in others—a trance-like state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility. Hypnotists work in therapeutic settings to help with pain management, addiction, or anxiety, or as entertainers who make audience volunteers cluck like chickens or forget their own names: {The stage hypnotist had volunteers convinced they were opera singers}.

Hypnotists are practitioners who induce hypnosis—a trance-like state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility. Some work therapeutically, helping clients quit smoking or manage pain. Others perform as entertainers, making volunteers cluck like chickens or forget their names: {The stage hypnotist had the whole audience laughing}.

To hypnotize is to induce a trance-like state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility. A hypnotist hypnotizes a subject, sometimes for therapeutic purposes, sometimes for entertainment: {The stage hypnotist hypnotized volunteers from the audience}. Figuratively, anything that captivates completely can hypnotize: {She was hypnotized by the flames dancing in the fireplace}.

Hypnotized describes the state of being under hypnosis—a trance-like condition of focused attention and heightened suggestibility, typically induced by a hypnotist. More commonly, hypnotized means captivated or spellbound: {She stood hypnotized by the sunset}, {The audience was hypnotized by his performance}. The figurative sense suggests being unable to look away or think of anything else.

Hypnotizes is the act of inducing a trance-like state in someone, typically through focused attention and suggestion. A hypnotist hypnotizes a subject to access the subconscious mind: {The therapist hypnotizes patients to help them quit smoking}. Figuratively, anything that captivates completely hypnotizes: {The dancer's movements hypnotized the audience}.

Hypnotizing is inducing a trance-like state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility. A hypnotist may use rhythmic speech, repetitive gestures, or fixed visual points: {The therapist was hypnotizing patients to help them quit smoking}. Figuratively, anything captivating or mesmerizing can be hypnotizing: {The flickering flames were hypnotizing}.

Hypochondria is excessive worry about one's health, especially the conviction that minor symptoms indicate serious illness. A hypochondriac interprets every headache as a brain tumor, every cough as lung cancer. The condition involves not imaginary symptoms but catastrophic interpretation of real ones: {His hypochondria has him convinced that mole is melanoma}. The clinical term is now health anxiety disorder.

A hypochondriac is someone who persistently worries about having serious illnesses despite medical reassurance. The concern typically focuses on normal bodily sensations interpreted as symptoms of disease: {Every headache convinces him he has a brain tumor}. As an adjective, hypochondriac describes this tendency: {hypochondriac fears}. The related noun is hypochondria.

Hypochondriacs are people who persistently believe they have serious illnesses despite medical reassurance to the contrary. The term comes from an ancient belief that melancholy originated in organs below the ribs. A hypochondriac interprets ordinary bodily sensations as symptoms of disease: {Every headache convinces him he has a brain tumor}. The condition is now clinically termed illness anxiety disorder.

Hypocrisy is the gap between what someone professes to believe and how they actually behave—claiming virtue while practicing vice. A preacher who condemns adultery while having affairs displays hypocrisy. The word often implies deliberate deception, but hypocrisy can also be unconscious: {It's easy to see hypocrisy in others and miss it in yourself}.

A hypocrite is someone whose actions do not reflect their stated beliefs. Hypocrite is always used negatively. In language about religion or morals, hypocrite is used to characterize someone who puts on an appearance of being pious or virtuous but is discovered to be involved in something unethical or criminal.

Hypocrites is the plural of hypocrite—people who pretend to have virtues, beliefs, or standards they don't actually hold. The word implies a gap between public posture and private behavior: {Politicians are hypocrites who preach fiscal responsibility while running up deficits}. Religious hypocrites profess piety but act otherwise. The accusation stings because it suggests deliberate deception rather than mere inconsistency.

Hypocritical describes behavior or attitudes that contradict one's stated beliefs or standards. A hypocritical person condemns in others what they do themselves, or professes values they don't practice: {It's hypocritical to preach honesty while lying to your kids}. The word carries strong moral judgment—calling someone hypocritical accuses them of insincerity or self-deception.

Hypothermia is dangerously low body temperature, typically below 95°F (35°C). It occurs when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, usually from prolonged exposure to cold: {The hikers showed signs of hypothermia after being stranded overnight}. Severe hypothermia causes confusion, slurred speech, and eventually loss of consciousness. The condition can be fatal without treatment.

Hypotheses is the plural of hypothesis—a proposed explanation or educated guess that can be tested.
