Infantry is the branch of an army that fights on foot, as distinguished from cavalry, artillery, or armored units. The term also refers collectively to foot soldiers themselves: {The infantry advanced under heavy fire}. Though modern infantry may ride vehicles to battle, they're defined by fighting dismounted. An infantryman is a soldier in this branch.

Infants are babies—human children in the earliest stage of life, typically before they can walk or talk. The term appears in medical, legal, and formal contexts where "baby" might seem too casual: {infant mortality rates}, {the infant was placed in foster care}. In law, infant sometimes extends to any minor, though this usage is fading.

Infatuated describes being intensely but often foolishly attracted to someone or something. The feeling is consuming and irrational—more obsession than reasoned affection: {He was completely infatuated with her}. Infatuation typically suggests a passion that will fade or that blinds someone to flaws: {Don't mistake infatuation for love}.

Infatuation is an intense but typically short-lived passion or admiration for someone or something. Unlike mature love, infatuation tends to be obsessive and based more on idealization than genuine understanding: {His infatuation with her faded once he got to know her better}. The word often carries a dismissive tone, suggesting the feeling is shallow or foolish. Someone can also have an infatuation with ideas, hobbies, or trends: {her brief infatuation with cryptocurrency}.

Infatuations are intense but typically short-lived passions or obsessions, often romantic. The word carries a sense of foolishness—an infatuation clouds judgment and may not survive closer acquaintance with its object: {teenage infatuations}, {His infatuation with the actress lasted about six weeks}. Unlike love, infatuations are expected to fade.

To infect is to transmit disease-causing organisms to a person, animal, or plant: {The contaminated water infected hundreds of villagers}. By extension, anything that spreads harmfully infects—a corrupted file infects a computer, panic infects a crowd, cynicism infects an organization. The word implies unwanted invasion and spread from one host to others.

Infected describes something that has been contaminated by disease-causing organisms like bacteria, viruses, or parasites. A wound becomes infected when harmful microbes enter and multiply; a person is infected when pathogens have established themselves in the body. The term extends to computers invaded by malware: {My laptop got infected with a virus}. Figuratively, infected can describe the spread of ideas or emotions: {The whole team was infected with his enthusiasm}.
clues: A wound gone bad with bacteria

definition: Infecting is the present participle of infect—to transmit disease or contamination to a living thing or system. A virus infects cells; contaminated water infects a population. The meaning extends to computers, where malware infects devices. Figuratively, emotions and ideas infect: {His enthusiasm was infecting everyone around him}. Fear infects a crowd; doubt infects a team.

Infection is the invasion of the body by harmful microorganisms—bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites—that multiply and cause disease: {The wound became red and swollen from infection}. By extension, infection describes any spreading influence, especially negative: {The infection of cynicism spread through the department}. In computing, infection refers to malware compromising a system.

Infections are invasions of the body by harmful microorganisms—bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites—that multiply and cause illness. The term covers everything from minor complaints like the common cold to life-threatening diseases. {The wound became red and swollen from infection.} Figuratively, infection describes how ideas or emotions spread person to person: {His enthusiasm was an infection that swept through the team.}

Infectious describes something that spreads from one host to another. An infectious {disease} passes between people through contact, air, or other transmission. The word extends to anything that spreads readily: infectious {laughter}, an infectious {smile}, infectious {enthusiasm}. If someone's mood is infectious, others catch it without trying. The medical and figurative uses share the same logic—contagion that moves through proximity.

Infects is the third-person singular form of infect, meaning to transmit a disease-causing agent to a person, animal, or plant. Pathogens like bacteria and viruses infect hosts by entering and multiplying within them: {The flu infects millions every winter}. The word extends to computers, where malware infects systems by corrupting or compromising them. Figuratively, attitudes and emotions can spread person to person: {Her enthusiasm infects everyone around her}.

To infer is to reach a conclusion from evidence or reasoning rather than from explicit statement. If someone avoids eye contact and gives short answers, you might infer they're upset. {From the muddy footprints, she inferred he'd come through the garden}. Infer is often confused with imply—speakers imply (suggest), listeners infer (conclude from what's suggested).

Inference is a conclusion reached through reasoning rather than direct observation. You make an inference when you deduce something from available evidence: {From the wet umbrella, she drew the inference that it was raining}. The verb is infer. In logic and statistics, inference follows formal rules; in everyday use, it simply means reading between the lines.

Inferences are conclusions drawn from evidence or reasoning rather than direct observation. If you see wet streets and people carrying umbrellas, you infer it rained—that's an inference. The word appears frequently in academic and legal contexts: {The jury was asked to draw inferences from the circumstantial evidence}. In logic and statistics, inference is the formal process of deriving conclusions from premises or data.

Inferior means lower in rank, quality, or position. An inferior product falls short of standards. An inferior officer answers to superiors. The word often carries judgment—calling someone's work inferior is dismissive: {He made her feel inferior}. In anatomy, inferior means situated below: the inferior vena cava lies lower than the superior. As a noun, an inferior is someone of lower rank: {He treated his inferiors with contempt}.

Inferiority is the state of being lower in rank, quality, or importance. Someone in a position of inferiority answers to those above them. An {inferiority complex} is a persistent sense of inadequacy, often compensated for by aggression or withdrawal: {His arrogance masks a deep inferiority}. The word implies comparison—inferior to something or someone else.

Inferiors are people lower in rank, status, or ability relative to someone else. The word implies hierarchy—military officers have inferiors, as do managers and aristocrats. {He treated his inferiors with contempt.} The term can sound dismissive or outdated, since modern workplaces often avoid language that emphasizes status differences.

Infernal means of or relating to hell: {infernal regions}, {infernal fires}. By extension, it describes anything hellish or fiendish: {infernal cruelty}, {an infernal scheme}. In casual speech, infernal is a mild intensifier expressing annoyance or frustration: {That infernal noise won't stop}, {Where did I put those infernal keys?} The word sounds slightly old-fashioned in everyday use.

An inferno is a large, intensely hot fire—the kind that consumes buildings or forests: {The warehouse became an inferno within minutes}. By extension, any place of extreme heat qualifies: {The kitchen was an inferno during the summer}. The word carries connotations of destructive, uncontrollable flames rather than a cozy hearth fire. (Capitalized Inferno refers to Dante's work.)

Infernos is the plural of inferno, a large fire that burns intensely and is difficult or impossible to control. The word comes from Latin for hell, and that association gives inferno a sense of destructive, overwhelming heat beyond an ordinary fire. {The wildfires became raging infernos that consumed entire neighborhoods.} Figuratively, any situation of intense heat, chaos, or suffering might be called an inferno.

Inferred is the past tense of infer—to derive a conclusion from evidence or reasoning rather than from explicit statement. If someone says they're tired and skips dinner, you might infer they're unwell. {I inferred from her silence that she disagreed}. Often confused with implied, but speakers imply while listeners infer.

Inferring is drawing conclusions from evidence or reasoning rather than from direct statement. When you infer something, you read between the lines: {Inferring from her tone that she was upset, he changed the subject}. Inferring differs from implying—speakers imply; listeners infer.

Infertile means unable to produce offspring or support growth. Infertile couples struggle to conceive children; infertile soil won't sustain crops. The word applies to people, animals, land, or ideas that fail to bear fruit: {The negotiations proved infertile}. In medicine, infertility typically means inability to conceive after a year of trying.

Infertility is the inability to conceive children or, in agriculture, the inability of soil to support plant growth. Medical infertility is typically diagnosed after a year of unsuccessful attempts at conception: {They sought treatment for infertility}. The word applies to both males and females, though historically women bore more stigma for it. Figuratively, infertility describes any condition of unproductiveness: {the infertility of his later creative work}.

To infest is to be present in large numbers, typically causing damage or disease. Pests infest—rats, roaches, lice, termites: {The apartment was infested with bedbugs}. The word implies unwanted invasion and suggests something difficult to eradicate. Figuratively, problems or undesirable people can infest a place: {Pickpockets infest the tourist areas}.

An infestation is the presence of pests in troublesome numbers—insects, rodents, or other unwanted creatures that have established themselves where they don't belong: {a termite infestation}, {The building had a severe cockroach infestation}. The word implies not just presence but problematic abundance, suggesting the pests have taken hold and spread. It extends to anything that proliferates harmfully: {an infestation of spam emails}, {a weed infestation in the garden}.
clues: Too many pests have moved in

definition: Infestations are instances of pests or parasites establishing themselves in unwanted numbers. The word typically describes insects, rodents, or other creatures that have invaded a space: {a termite infestation}, {an infestation of bedbugs}. It extends to anything that spreads harmfully: {an infestation of weeds}, {a criminal infestation in the neighborhood}. The word carries connotations of disgust and the need for eradication.

Infested describes a place or thing overrun by pests, vermin, or other unwanted creatures in large numbers. A house might be infested with termites, a dog with fleas, or a warehouse with rats. The word carries strong connotations of disgust and contamination. Figuratively, infested can describe any overwhelming presence of undesirable elements: {The comment section was infested with trolls}. The verb infest means to overrun in this harmful way.

Infesting is the present participle of infest—to overrun or inhabit in troublesome numbers. Pests infest: {rats infesting the subway}, {termites infesting the walls}. The word implies unwanted presence and often harm or nuisance. Figuratively, problems or undesirable people can infest a place: {scammers infesting the comments section}.

To infest is to be present in large numbers, typically causing damage or disease. Pests infest—rats, insects, weeds: {The apartment was infested with cockroaches}. The word implies unwanted presence and often uncontrollable spread. Figuratively, problems or undesirable people can infest a place: {Scammers infest those online forums}.

Infidel is someone who doesn't share a particular religious faith—historically used by Christians for non-Christians and by Muslims for non-Muslims. The word carries hostility: it frames the outsider as not merely different but faithless or treacherous. In secular contexts, infidel sometimes appears ironically or defiantly: {I'm a proud infidel when it comes to their dietary rules}.

Infidelities is the plural of infidelity—acts of unfaithfulness, especially sexual betrayal within a marriage or committed relationship: {His infidelities destroyed the marriage}, {She eventually forgave his infidelities}. The word can also refer to disloyalty more broadly, though marital betrayal dominates modern usage.

Infidelity is unfaithfulness to a commitment, most often sexual or romantic betrayal of a spouse or partner: {She discovered his infidelity through text messages}. The word can also describe disloyalty to any pledge or principle—infidelity to one's vows, to a cause, to a faith. The opposite of fidelity.

Infidels is the plural of infidel—a person who doesn't share your religious faith. The word appears most often in historical or religious contexts, where it carries the perspective of the accuser: medieval Christians called Muslims infidels, and vice versa. {The crusaders marched to reclaim the Holy Land from the infidels.} The term can also mean simply one who lacks religious belief.

The infield is the area of a baseball diamond enclosed by the four bases, as opposed to the outfield beyond. By extension, infield refers to the players stationed there—first baseman, second baseman, shortstop, and third baseman: {The team has a solid infield this year}. In track and field, the infield is the grassy area inside the oval.

An infielder is a baseball or softball player who occupies one of the four defensive positions in the infield: first base, second base, shortstop, or third base. The term distinguishes these players from outfielders and the battery (pitcher and catcher): {The manager shuffled his infielders to cover the bunt}.

Infighting is conflict or rivalry among members of the same group, organization, or faction. It suggests internal power struggles, petty disputes, or competition for influence that happens behind closed doors rather than in public view. {The party's infighting cost them the election.} In boxing, infighting refers to close-range combat where fighters exchange blows at close quarters, which inspired the metaphorical sense of bitter internal conflict.
clues: Bickering between people who should agree

definition: To infiltrate is to pass into or through something gradually, often without detection. Water infiltrates soil; spies infiltrate enemy organizations. The word suggests stealth and patience—{Undercover agents infiltrated the criminal network over several years}. It extends to ideas or influences that spread subtly: {Social media has infiltrated every aspect of modern life}. The noun infiltration describes the process or result.

Infiltrated is the past tense of infiltrate, meaning to enter or pass through something gradually or secretly. Water infiltrates soil; spies infiltrate enemy organizations. The word suggests penetration without detection: {The group had been infiltrated by an FBI informant}. It often carries sinister overtones—something unwanted gaining access to where it doesn't belong.

Infiltrates is the act of entering or penetrating gradually, often without detection. Water infiltrates soil; spies infiltrate organizations. The word suggests slow, covert movement past barriers—whether physical, social, or institutional: {The group infiltrates enemy territory}, {Doubt infiltrates even the most confident mind}. In medicine, substances that infiltrate spread into surrounding tissue.

Infiltrating is entering gradually or secretly, usually to gather information or gain influence from within. Spies infiltrate enemy organizations; water infiltrates soil. The word implies penetration that goes unnoticed: {Government agents were infiltrating the protest group}. Cancer cells infiltrate healthy tissue. Ideas can infiltrate a culture.

Infiltration is the act of entering or penetrating gradually, often secretly. Water infiltrates soil; spies infiltrate enemy organizations. The word applies to military tactics, espionage, and any gradual permeation: {The infiltration of the compound took months of planning}. In medicine, infiltration describes fluid or cells spreading into surrounding tissue where they don't belong.

An infiltrator is someone who secretly enters or gains access to an organization, place, or group—typically with hostile intent or to gather information. The word implies deception: the infiltrator pretends to belong while serving outside interests. {Government infiltrators had been reporting on the group's activities for months.} The term appears in military, espionage, and political contexts, but extends to any covert entry: {corporate infiltrators}, {police infiltrators at protests}.

Infiltrators are people who gain access to a place or organization secretly, often with hostile intent. Spies infiltrate enemy governments; undercover agents infiltrate criminal organizations. The word implies deception—infiltrators pose as members while serving outside interests: {Police infiltrators attended the protest meetings}. In military contexts, infiltrators are soldiers who slip behind enemy lines.

Infinite means without limits or end. Space may be infinite; so is the set of integers. In casual use, infinite often just means very large or seemingly endless: {infinite patience}, {infinite possibilities}, {an infinite number of ways to solve this}. The noun infinite refers to something boundless: {the infinite}. In mathematics, infinite describes quantities that exceed any assignable value.

Infinitely means without limit or bound, or to an extreme degree. In mathematics and physics, it describes quantities that increase without end. More commonly, infinitely serves as an intensifier meaning vastly or immeasurably: {This version is infinitely better than the last}. The casual use often involves hyperbole—few things are truly without limit.

Infinitesimal means immeasurably or incalculably small—so tiny as to approach zero without reaching it. The word originated in mathematics to describe quantities smaller than any assignable value, but now commonly describes anything vanishingly small: {an infinitesimal difference}, {infinitesimal chances of success}. As a noun, an infinitesimal is such a quantity.

Infinities is the plural of infinity, referring to multiple instances or types of boundlessness. In mathematics, different infinities have different sizes—the infinity of counting numbers is smaller than the infinity of real numbers, a counterintuitive concept that mathematicians have rigorously proven. Outside technical contexts, infinities often appears in poetic or philosophical discussions: {The universe contains infinities we cannot fathom.}
clues: Sets larger than any finite number

definition: Infinity is endlessness—quantity or extent without limit. In mathematics, infinity is not a number but a concept representing something that grows beyond any bound: parallel lines meet {at infinity}. In everyday use, infinity suggests vastness: {I could stare at this view for infinity}. The symbol ∞ represents it. Things extend {to infinity and beyond}, or loop {into infinity}. An infinity of something is an endless supply: {an infinity of choices}.

An infirmary is a place where sick or injured people receive medical care. The term typically refers to a medical facility within a larger institution—a school infirmary, a prison infirmary, a military infirmary—rather than a standalone hospital. In older usage, infirmary could name a hospital outright, and some hospitals retain it in their names.

Infirmities are weaknesses or ailments, especially those associated with age or illness. The word carries a somewhat formal or literary tone: {the infirmities of old age}, {despite his infirmities, he remained sharp-witted}. Infirmity can also refer to moral weakness or frailty of character, though this sense is less common today.

To inflame is to set on fire or cause to burn—but the figurative uses dominate. Inflame most often means to intensify emotions or conflict: {inflammatory rhetoric inflamed the crowd}, {The editorial inflamed tensions between the two groups}. Body parts become inflamed when they swell, redden, and hurt: {an inflamed joint}, {inflamed sinuses}. Passions and desires can also be inflamed: {Her words inflamed his jealousy}.

Inflamed describes tissue that is red, swollen, and often painful due to injury or infection: {an inflamed appendix}, {inflamed gums}. The word extends to emotions, especially anger: {Rumors inflamed public outrage}. Inflamed passions burn hot. An inflamed situation has been made worse, often deliberately: {His remarks only inflamed the controversy}.

Inflames is the third-person singular of inflame. To inflame is to intensify or provoke strong emotion, especially anger or passion: {His remarks inflamed the crowd}. It also means to cause physical inflammation—redness, swelling, heat: {The infection inflamed the wound}. Figuratively, to inflame a situation is to make it worse or more volatile.

Inflaming is the present participle of inflame, carrying its senses of arousing strong emotion or causing physical inflammation. Something inflaming can stir up passion, anger, or desire: {inflaming rhetoric}, {inflaming tensions between the factions}. It also describes what causes tissue to become red, swollen, and painful: {an inflaming infection}.

Inflammation is the body's response to injury or infection—the redness, swelling, heat, and pain that signal the immune system at work. Chronic inflammation underlies many diseases: {The doctor said my joint pain was caused by inflammation}. Figuratively, inflammation describes stirred-up anger or tension: {inflammatory remarks}, {inflamed passions}. To inflame is to provoke or intensify.

Inflammatory describes something that provokes strong emotion, especially anger or outrage: {inflammatory rhetoric}, {inflammatory comments}. Politicians and media figures are often accused of inflammatory speech when they stir up hostility. In medicine, inflammatory refers to inflammation—the body's response to injury or infection: {inflammatory bowel disease}, {anti-inflammatory drugs}.

Inflatable describes something designed to be filled with air or gas to achieve its functional shape: an inflatable {mattress}, inflatable {raft}, inflatable {balloon animal}. As a noun, an inflatable is such an object—bouncy castles and pool toys are inflatables. The word implies portability when deflated and temporary use when inflated.

Inflatables are objects designed to be filled with air or gas before use. The term covers a wide range: pool toys, bounce houses, rubber rafts, emergency life vests, advertising balloons shaped like cartoon characters. What unites them is that they're stored flat or compact and inflated when needed: {The kids played on the inflatables all afternoon}.

To inflate is to fill with air or gas, expanding something from a compressed or flat state: {inflate a balloon}, {inflate a tire}. The opposite is deflate. Figuratively, to inflate is to increase artificially or exaggerate: {inflate prices}, {inflate one's ego}, {inflated expectations}. Inflation in economics refers to the general rise in prices over time.

Inflated describes something filled or expanded with air or gas: {an inflated balloon}, {inflated tires}. More often the word is figurative, meaning exaggerated or excessive beyond what's justified: {inflated prices}, {inflated ego}, {inflated sense of importance}. Inflated language uses more words or fancier terms than necessary. The connection is to something puffed up beyond its natural or proper size.

Inflates means to fill with air or gas, causing expansion: {She inflates the balloon}. By extension, to inflate is to increase artificially or exaggerate: {The company inflated its earnings}, {His ego inflates with every compliment}. Inflation in economics—rising prices reducing purchasing power—comes from this sense of artificial expansion.

Inflating is the act of filling something with air or gas, causing it to expand: {inflating a balloon}, {inflating a tire}. Figuratively, inflating means artificially increasing or exaggerating: {inflating prices}, {inflating one's credentials}. The word often carries a negative connotation when applied to numbers or claims—suggesting something has been made to appear larger or more impressive than it actually is.

Inflation is a general rise in prices that reduces the purchasing power of money. What cost a dollar last year might cost $1.05 this year. Economists distinguish moderate inflation from hyperinflation, where currency loses value rapidly. Outside economics, inflation refers to the act of filling something with air or gas: {the inflation of a balloon}, {tire inflation}. Figuratively, inflation suggests exaggeration or artificial enlargement: {grade inflation}, {ego inflation}.

Inflection is a change in the form of a word to express grammatical distinctions—tense, number, case, or mood: {walked} shows past tense, {dogs} shows plural. The term also applies to variations in pitch or tone of voice: {Her inflection rose at the end, turning the statement into a question}. An inflection point in mathematics is where a curve changes direction; in general use, it means a turning point or pivotal moment: {The company reached an inflection point when it went public}.

Inflections are changes in word form that signal grammatical relationships—adding -s for plurals, -ed for past tense, -ing for continuous action. English has relatively few inflections compared to languages like Latin or Russian. In a different sense, inflection refers to variation in pitch or tone of voice: {Her voice rose with an inflection of surprise}. The term also describes points where curves change direction or trends shift: {an inflection point in the company's growth}.

Inflexibility is the quality of being rigid, unyielding, or resistant to change. In physical contexts, it describes materials or body parts that don't bend easily: {The inflexibility of the metal made it unsuitable for the project}. More often, inflexibility characterizes attitudes, rules, or people unwilling to adapt or compromise: {Her inflexibility on scheduling made collaboration difficult}. The word carries connotations of stubbornness when applied to people, though in some contexts—like principles or standards—it can suggest admirable steadfastness.

Inflexible means unable or unwilling to bend. Physically, an inflexible material is rigid: {The splint keeps the joint inflexible}. More often the word describes people or positions that won't adapt or compromise: {an inflexible deadline}, {inflexible in her principles}. The connotation can be positive (steadfast, principled) or negative (stubborn, unyielding), depending on context.

Inflict means to cause something unpleasant or harmful to be experienced by someone or something. The word almost always takes a negative object—you inflict pain, damage, suffering, wounds, or punishment, never joy or benefits. {The hurricane inflicted billions of dollars in damage.} {She didn't want to inflict her problems on anyone else.} To inflict yourself or your company on others is to impose your unwanted presence.

Inflicted is the past tense of inflict, meaning to cause something unwelcome or painful to be experienced by someone: {The hurricane inflicted severe damage on coastal towns}, {wounds inflicted during battle}. The word carries a sense of force or imposition—you inflict punishment, suffering, or harm. Someone can also inflict themselves on others, meaning to impose their unwanted presence: {She inflicted herself on us for the entire weekend}.

Inflow is movement into something from outside—the opposite of outflow. Water inflow feeds a lake; cash inflow sustains a business. The word appears often in technical and financial contexts: {The reservoir depends on seasonal inflow from mountain streams}. Capital inflow describes money entering an economy or investment account.

Influence is the power or capacity to produce an effect. The effect may be seen in a person (You can see the influence of the preacher in all of Pastor Whiting’s children) or in something physical or abstract (the influence of the moon on the tides; the influence of weather on grasshopper populations). As a verb, influence means to impact: Her plea influenced my decision.

Influenced is the past tense of influence, meaning to have an effect on someone's thinking, behavior, or development. A person influenced by a mentor adopts some of their ideas or methods: {Her writing was heavily influenced by Toni Morrison}. Things can also be influenced: {The decision was influenced by budget constraints}. To say someone was {under the influence} usually means intoxicated.

An influencer is someone with a large social media following who can affect their audience's opinions and purchasing decisions. The term emerged with platforms like Instagram and YouTube, where personalities cultivate devoted audiences that brands pay to reach. {She partnered with influencers to promote the skincare line.} The word often carries connotations of superficiality or self-promotion.

Influencers are people who shape others' opinions or behaviors, especially those who have built audiences on social media platforms. The term once applied broadly to anyone with sway—politicians, thought leaders, tastemakers—but now typically means content creators who leverage their following for sponsorships and brand deals: {She partnered with influencers to promote the skincare line}. The word often carries a faintly dismissive tone, suggesting self-promotion over substance.

Influences are forces or factors that shape outcomes, decisions, or behavior. A teacher may be the biggest influence on a student's career. To influence someone is to affect their thinking or actions: {Her arguments influenced the jury}. The word often appears with "under": {driving under the influence} means impaired by alcohol or drugs. As a plural noun, influences can mean the people or ideas that shaped someone's work: {You can hear jazz influences in her music}.

Influential describes someone or something with the power to affect outcomes, opinions, or behavior. An influential {person} shapes decisions; an influential {book} changes how people think. The word often implies indirect power—working through persuasion, reputation, or example rather than direct authority: {She became one of the most influential figures in modern architecture}.

An influx is a flowing in—of people, things, or abstract quantities arriving in large numbers or amounts. A city experiences an influx of tourists during festival season. A company sees an influx of cash after a successful product launch. {The influx of refugees strained local resources.} The word suggests volume and momentum, something pouring in rather than trickling.

Info is a clipped form of information, used casually in speech and writing: {Thanks for the info}, {I need some info on flights to Denver}. It appears in compounds like infographic and infomercial. The word feels informal but is universally understood.

An infodump is a large quantity of background information delivered all at once, especially in fiction where exposition interrupts narrative flow: {The second chapter was just an infodump about the planet's history}. The term is usually critical—good storytelling weaves information in gradually rather than dumping it. Also used outside fiction for any overwhelming delivery of facts or context.

Infodumping is delivering a large amount of information all at once, often more than the listener wants or needs. The term originated in fiction writing, where clumsy exposition bogs down narrative: {The first chapter was just infodumping about the world's history}. It now applies to conversation, where someone unloads specialized knowledge without reading social cues: {He started infodumping about train schedules and couldn't stop}. Common in discussions of autism and ADHD, where infodumping about passionate interests is recognized as a trait rather than a flaw.

Infodumps are passages in fiction where the author delivers large amounts of background information, exposition, or worldbuilding all at once, often awkwardly interrupting the narrative. The term is usually pejorative among writers and critics: {The first chapter was nothing but infodumps about the planet's history}. To infodump is to deliver such exposition: {She infodumped for three pages about the magic system}.
clues: Floods of facts all at once

definition: An infographic is a visual representation of information or data, combining graphics, charts, and minimal text to convey complex material quickly. Infographics appear in journalism, marketing, and education: {The infographic showed vaccination rates by state}. The format favors scannable, shareable content over detailed analysis.

Infographics are visual representations of information, data, or knowledge designed to present complex material quickly and clearly. They combine charts, diagrams, icons, and minimal text to make statistics or processes easier to grasp: {The article included an infographic showing how the vaccine works}. Common in journalism, marketing, and educational materials. Singular: infographic.

An infomercial is a television commercial that runs much longer than typical ads—often thirty minutes or more—and is formatted to resemble regular programming. Infomercials typically demonstrate products, feature testimonials, and urge viewers to call a toll-free number to order: {I stayed up too late watching an infomercial for kitchen gadgets}. The word blends information and commercial.

Infomercials are extended television advertisements, typically running thirty minutes or longer, designed to look like regular programming rather than commercials. They often feature product demonstrations, testimonials, and enthusiastic hosts pitching kitchen gadgets, fitness equipment, or self-help programs: {I stayed up late watching infomercials for ab machines}. The format thrives in late-night and weekend time slots when airtime is cheap.

To inform is to give someone information: {The doctor informed her of the diagnosis}. More formally, it means to shape or give character to something: {His experiences informed his writing}. To inform on someone is to report their wrongdoing to authorities—an informer or informant passes information, often secretly. {She informed on her accomplices to get a lighter sentence.}

Informal describes situations, language, or behavior that is relaxed and casual rather than official or ceremonial. An informal {gathering} lacks rigid structure. Informal {dress} means no suit required. Informal speech includes contractions, slang, and sentence fragments that would be out of place in formal writing. {We kept the meeting informal.}

An informant is someone who provides information, especially to authorities. The word often implies secrecy—police informants report on criminal activity from inside, sometimes in exchange for leniency or payment. In research contexts, an informant is simply a source: {The anthropologist interviewed local informants about village customs}. The term is neutral compared to the more pejorative *snitch* or *rat*.

Informants are people who provide information, especially to authorities. The word often implies secret or privileged knowledge: a police informant supplies tips about criminal activity, an anthropologist's informant shares cultural insights from within a community. The term can carry negative connotations of betrayal—{The gang discovered he was an informant}—or neutral ones depending on context.

Information is any knowledge obtained from study, observation, or research. In a more particular sense, information is something you want to know about a subject: Do you have any information about the holiday public transportation schedule? Information is never pluralized; if you want to talk about multiple instances, you say pieces of information.
clues: Details passed from person to person

definition: Informed means having knowledge or information about something, particularly knowledge that enables good judgment or decision-making. An informed {decision} or informed {choice} is one made with adequate relevant facts at hand. To keep someone informed is to provide them with updates or news as situations develop. Informed {consent} is permission given with full understanding of the risks and implications, especially in medical or legal contexts. The word also characterizes people who stay current on events: {She's a well-informed voter}.

An informer is someone who secretly provides information to authorities, especially about criminal activity. The word carries connotations of betrayal—an informer is typically seen as disloyal to their community or associates: {The gang suspected there was an informer in their ranks}. Police informers trade information for money, leniency, or protection. The term is slightly more formal than synonyms like snitch or rat.

Informers are people who provide information to authorities, especially about criminal activity or the actions of others. The term usually carries a negative connotation—informers betray associates or neighbors, often for money or to avoid punishment themselves. {The police relied on informers within the gang}. Synonyms like snitch, rat, and stool pigeon share this taint of disloyalty.

Informing is the act of giving someone information or knowledge: {Thanks for informing me of the change}. It also means serving as an animating principle or influence: {the values informing her work}. A darker sense is reporting someone to authorities, especially secretly: {He was informing on his neighbors to the police}. An informant informs in this last sense.

Infotainment blends information with entertainment, typically in media that packages news or educational content in an engaging, accessible format: {The morning show is pure infotainment—celebrity gossip mixed with weather updates}. The term often carries a dismissive edge, suggesting style over substance. In automotive contexts, infotainment refers to dashboard systems combining navigation, music, and connectivity features.

An infraction is a violation or breach of a rule, law, or agreement. The term typically applies to minor offenses rather than serious crimes: {a traffic infraction}, {a minor infraction of school rules}. In sports, infractions draw penalties: {The referee called an infraction on the play}.

Infrared refers to electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible red light but shorter than microwaves, making it invisible to the human eye but detectable as heat. Infrared technology appears in thermal imaging cameras, night vision devices, remote controls, and heat lamps. As an adjective, it describes equipment or methods that use this radiation: {infrared sensors detected movement in the dark}. The term comes from Latin infra (below), since its frequency falls below that of visible red light.

Infrastructure is the underlying foundation that allows a system to function—the basic physical and organizational structures needed for operation. Roads, bridges, power grids, and water systems form a nation's infrastructure. The term extends to any essential framework: {digital infrastructure}, {social infrastructure}. Politicians often promise to rebuild crumbling infrastructure, meaning neglected public works.

Infringement is a violation or breach of a law, agreement, or right. The word appears most often in legal contexts: patent {infringement}, copyright {infringement}, trademark {infringement}. To infringe is to encroach on someone's rights or territory: {The new law infringes on free speech}. An infringement of the rules in sports is a foul or violation.

To infuriate is to make someone extremely angry—beyond mere annoyance to genuine rage. The word emphasizes the effect on the person angered: {His smug attitude infuriated her}. Something infuriating provokes this intense response: {The infuriating thing is that he was right}.

Infuriated means extremely angry, enraged to the point of losing composure. Someone infuriated by an insult or injustice has been pushed past ordinary annoyance into fury: {She was infuriated by his dismissive tone}. The word works as both past tense of infuriate and as an adjective describing the resulting state.

Infuriating describes something that provokes extreme frustration or anger: {The hold music was infuriating}, {an infuriating lack of accountability}. The word implies sustained or building annoyance rather than a single flash of irritation—something that makes your blood boil the longer you dwell on it.

To infuse is to introduce something into another substance or entity, allowing it to permeate. Tea infuses when steeped in hot water; the water becomes infused with flavor. The meaning extends to intangibles: {Her presence infused the room with energy}, {a speech infused with passion}. In medicine, to infuse is to introduce fluid into the body, typically intravenously.

Infused describes something that has been soaked, steeped, or permeated with another substance or quality. Tea is infused with hot water; oils can be infused with herbs. The word extends to abstract qualities: {Her voice was infused with warmth}. An infused {cocktail} has absorbed flavors from added ingredients. In medical contexts, infused refers to fluids delivered intravenously.

Infusing is the act of steeping something in liquid to extract its essence, as with tea leaves in hot water. More broadly, to infuse is to fill or pervade with a quality: {Her speech was infused with passion}. The word suggests gradual saturation rather than sudden addition—qualities seep in and spread throughout.

An infusion is something steeped or introduced into something else. Tea is an infusion—leaves steeped in hot water. In medicine, an infusion delivers fluids or medication directly into the bloodstream: {The patient received an infusion of antibiotics}. More broadly, an infusion is any introduction of a new element: {The company needed an infusion of capital}, {an infusion of fresh ideas}.

Infusions are liquids created by steeping something in them—most commonly tea or herbal drinks made by soaking leaves, flowers, or herbs in hot water: {chamomile infusions}, {herbal infusions}. In medicine, an infusion is the slow introduction of fluid into the body, typically intravenously: {The patient received a saline infusion}. Figuratively, an infusion is an addition that strengthens or enlivens: {an infusion of cash}, {an infusion of new talent}.

Ingenious describes something cleverly inventive or resourceful—a solution, device, or approach that shows creative intelligence: {an ingenious workaround}, {an ingenious contraption}. The word emphasizes cleverness in design or method rather than raw intelligence. A person can be ingenious, but more often the word modifies their creations or ideas. Not to be confused with ingenuous, which means naively honest or innocent.

An ingenue is a naive, innocent young woman, especially as a stock character in drama and film. The role typically involves wholesome beauty and inexperience with the world: {She was cast as the ingenue opposite the cynical leading man}. By extension, any guileless young woman may be called an ingenue, sometimes with a hint that the innocence is performed rather than genuine.

Ingenuity is clever inventiveness, the ability to solve problems through creative thinking rather than brute force or obvious methods. It implies resourcefulness—finding unexpected solutions with whatever materials or circumstances are at hand: {The prisoners showed remarkable ingenuity in their escape}. {She admired the ingenuity of the design}.

An inglenook is a recessed space beside a fireplace, often with built-in seating. The word evokes cozy domestic scenes—a nook for sitting by the fire: {We settled into the inglenook with our tea}. The term appears in descriptions of traditional English cottages and arts-and-crafts architecture.

An ingot is a block of metal cast in a standardized shape for storage, transport, or further processing. Gold, silver, and steel are commonly formed into ingots. The shape—typically a bar or brick with tapered sides—makes stacking easy and identifies the metal's purity and origin: {a vault full of gold ingots}.

An ingot is a mass of metal cast into a convenient shape for storage, transport, or further processing. Gold and silver ingots are rectangular bars; steel ingots are typically large blocks destined for rolling or forging. The shape standardizes the material for trade or manufacture: {The refinery produces copper ingots for export}.

Ingrained describes something deeply embedded or firmly established, difficult to change or remove. The image is of dye or dirt worked into the grain of wood or fabric. Most often applied to habits, attitudes, or beliefs: {ingrained prejudice}, {ingrained behavior patterns}. What's ingrained has become part of someone's nature through long exposure or repetition: {Years of training had ingrained the response}.

Ingrates is the plural of ingrate, a person who shows no gratitude—someone ungrateful for kindness or favors received. The word carries a tone of moral judgment, implying the person should know better: {After everything I did for them, the ingrates didn't even say thank you}. The noun is somewhat literary; the adjective ungrateful is more common in everyday speech.

Ingratiating describes behavior calculated to win favor, often through excessive flattery or agreeableness: {an ingratiating smile}, {his ingratiating manner with the boss}. The word carries a faintly negative connotation—suggesting the charm is strategic rather than genuine. Someone ingratiates themselves with powerful people to gain advantage.

Ingratitude is failure to acknowledge or appreciate kindness received. Where gratitude recognizes a benefit and feels thankful, ingratitude dismisses or ignores it: {After everything I did for him, his ingratitude stung}. The word often carries moral weight—ingratitude suggests a character flaw, not just forgetfulness.

An ingredient is one of the components that go into a mixture or combination. Recipes list ingredients—the foods combined to make a dish. The word extends to any contributing element: {the ingredients of a successful marriage}, {a key ingredient in their victory}. In lists of product contents, ingredients typically appear in order of quantity.

Ingredients are the individual components that combine to make something, most often a dish or recipe. A list of ingredients tells you what you need before you start cooking: {Check the ingredients before you go shopping}. The word extends beyond food to anything composed of parts—the ingredients of a successful marriage, the ingredients of a hit song. In product labeling, ingredients must be listed, typically in order of quantity.

An ingroup is a social group to which a person feels they belong—defined by shared identity, values, or characteristics. The term appears in psychology and sociology to describe how people categorize others as "us" versus "them." Ingroup {bias} or ingroup {favoritism} describes the tendency to prefer members of one's own group: {The study measured ingroup loyalty among sports fans}. The opposite is outgroup.

Ingrown describes something that has grown inward. An ingrown {toenail} curves into the surrounding flesh instead of growing outward, causing pain and sometimes infection. Figuratively, ingrown suggests excessive inward focus—an ingrown {community} or ingrown {thinking} is insular, closed off from outside influence or fresh perspectives.

To inhabit a place is to live there—humans inhabit cities, animals inhabit forests, spirits inhabit haunted houses. The word emphasizes ongoing residence rather than mere presence: {Fish inhabit these waters}. Figuratively, ideas or feelings can inhabit the mind: {A strange melancholy inhabited her}. An inhabited place has residents; an uninhabited one is empty of life.

Inhabitants are the people or animals who live in a particular place. A town's inhabitants are its residents; a forest's inhabitants are the creatures dwelling there. The word emphasizes ongoing presence rather than temporary visits: {The island's inhabitants have lived there for generations}. Inhabit works for any place that can be occupied—buildings, regions, ecosystems, or even abstract domains: {the inhabitants of the digital world}.

Inhabited describes a place where people or other creatures live. An inhabited island has residents; an uninhabited one is empty. The word applies to any dwelling place with occupants: {The cabin had clearly been inhabited recently}. In science fiction, inhabited often describes planets capable of supporting life: {an inhabited world}.

To inhale is to draw air or other substances into the lungs—the opposite of exhale. Beyond breathing, inhale often implies deliberate intake: inhaling cigarette smoke, inhaling fumes. Informally, to inhale food is to eat it rapidly and eagerly: {He inhaled three slices of pizza before I finished one}.

An inhaler is a small handheld device that delivers medication directly to the lungs through the mouth. Most commonly associated with asthma treatment, inhalers allow patients to breathe in measured doses of bronchodilators or steroids: {She always keeps her inhaler in her purse}. The term also covers devices used to inhale recreational substances.

Inhalers are handheld devices that deliver medication directly to the lungs, used primarily for asthma and other respiratory conditions. The user breathes in while pressing the device, which releases a measured dose of medicine as a fine mist or powder: {She keeps an inhaler in her purse for emergencies}. Also called puffers informally.

Inhaling is drawing air or other substances into the lungs through the nose or mouth. It's the active half of breathing—the intake that precedes exhaling. The word often appears in contexts involving deliberate or conscious breathing: {inhaling deeply before diving underwater}, {inhaling the scent of fresh bread}. It also describes breathing in harmful or intoxicating substances: {inhaling secondhand smoke}, {inhaling paint fumes}.

To inherit is to receive something from someone who has died—property, money, title, or position: {She inherited her grandmother's house}. Beyond legal succession, inherit describes receiving traits from parents: {He inherited his mother's eyes}. More broadly, to inherit is to come into possession of something left by predecessors: {The new administration inherited a budget crisis}. The word implies reception without effort or choice on the receiver's part.

Inheritance is what passes to someone when another person dies—property, money, or possessions left to heirs: {She received a modest inheritance from her uncle}. The word extends to non-material things passed down: a genetic inheritance, a cultural inheritance, {an inheritance of poverty and hardship}. In object-oriented programming, inheritance is a mechanism where one class derives properties and behaviors from another, allowing code reuse and hierarchical organization.

Inheritances is the plural of inheritance—money, property, or other assets received from someone who has died. The word extends to non-material things passed down: {genetic inheritances}, {cultural inheritances}. In programming, inheritances refer to how objects or classes receive properties from parent classes. {The siblings disputed their inheritances for years.}

Inherited describes something received from a predecessor, typically through death or succession. Children inherit property, titles, or genetic traits from parents: {She inherited her mother's eyes}. The word extends to anything passed down: {inherited traditions}, {inherited debt}, {an inherited mess from the previous administration}. In computing, inherited refers to properties or methods a program element receives from a parent class.

Inheriting is the present participle of inherit—receiving something passed down from a predecessor. Most often this means property or money from someone who has died: {She's inheriting the house from her grandmother}. But you can inherit genetic traits, family traditions, or situations: {He's inheriting a mess from the previous administration}. The word implies receiving without having earned or chosen what comes to you.

Inheritors are those who receive something from predecessors—property, titles, traits, or conditions. The word most often refers to legal heirs who receive estates or wealth after someone's death: {The inheritors divided the family fortune}. But it extends to anyone who comes into possession of what earlier generations left behind: {We are the inheritors of a broken system}.

Inherits is the third-person singular of inherit—to receive property, title, or genetic traits from a predecessor. A child inherits an estate from a parent, or inherits her mother's eyes. In computing, a class inherits properties and methods from a parent class: {The button class inherits from the base widget}. To inherit can also mean to receive something from a predecessor in a role: {She inherited a mess from the previous manager}.

To inhibit is to hold back, restrain, or prevent. A drug may inhibit the growth of bacteria. Social anxiety inhibits some people from speaking up. {His presence inhibited honest discussion}. The related adjective inhibited describes someone restrained by psychological barriers, especially regarding emotions or sexuality: {She was too inhibited to dance in public}.

Inhibited describes someone restrained or held back, especially in expressing emotions or desires. An inhibited person struggles to act freely or spontaneously, often due to self-consciousness or psychological barriers: {She was too inhibited to dance in public}. The word suggests suppression rather than absence—the impulse exists but something blocks its expression.

Inhibition is the holding back of impulses, desires, or actions. In psychology, inhibitions are internal barriers that prevent someone from acting freely or spontaneously: {She lost her inhibitions after a few drinks}. Someone with few inhibitions behaves openly, sometimes recklessly. In biology and chemistry, inhibition refers to blocking or slowing a process: {enzyme inhibition}, {neural inhibition}. The word carries a slight clinical tone—having too many inhibitions suggests repression, while having none suggests poor judgment.

Inhibitions are internal restraints that hold you back from acting on impulses or expressing yourself freely. The word usually appears in contexts about overcoming them: alcohol {lowers inhibitions}, therapy helps people {work through their inhibitions}, dancing requires {letting go of inhibitions}. Someone described as having no inhibitions acts without self-consciousness or social restraint. The singular inhibition can describe a specific block: {an inhibition about public speaking}.

Inhospitable describes places or conditions hostile to comfort or survival: {an inhospitable climate}, {inhospitable terrain}. The word applies equally to people who are unwelcoming or unfriendly to guests: {The locals were inhospitable to outsiders}. An inhospitable environment—whether physical or social—offers no refuge or warmth.

Inhuman describes behavior or conditions so cruel, cold, or extreme as to seem beyond normal human capacity—either for brutality or endurance: {The prisoners suffered inhuman treatment}. It can also mean lacking human qualities entirely: {The figure moved with inhuman speed}. Where inhumane emphasizes cruelty toward others, inhuman suggests something alien to human nature itself.
clues: What monsters show to their victims

definition: Inhumane describes treatment that causes unnecessary suffering or shows no regard for the welfare of living things. An inhumane practice is cruel, brutal, or lacking basic compassion: {inhumane conditions in the prison}, {the inhumane treatment of animals}. The word often appears in contexts of advocacy and reform, where it carries moral weight.

Inhumanity is cruelty or brutal indifference to human suffering. The word implies behavior so callous it seems to lack the compassion expected of human beings: {the inhumanity of the slave trade}, {man's inhumanity to man}. An inhumanity is a specific cruel act: {the inhumanities of war}.

Iniquity is wickedness or gross injustice—sin of a serious, morally corrupt nature. The word carries biblical weight, often appearing in religious contexts: {a den of iniquity}, {the iniquity of slavery}. It suggests not mere wrongdoing but deep moral corruption or systematic evil. The plural iniquities refers to specific wicked acts: {He was punished for his iniquities}.

Initial describes what comes first or exists at the beginning. An initial {reaction} is the one you have right away; initial {findings} are preliminary results before deeper investigation. As a noun, an initial is the first letter of a name, and in the plural, initials refers to the set of first letters from a person's full name, often used as a signature or monogram. To initial something is to sign it with your initials, typically to indicate acknowledgment or approval: {Please initial each page of the contract}.

Initials are the first letters of a person's name, used as a compact form of identification: {Please write your initials here}. People initial documents to indicate they've read or approved them. Initials also appear as monograms on personal items—towels, stationery, jewelry. Three-letter initials typically include a middle name: {His initials are J.F.K.}

Initiate means to begin or set something in motion: {The company initiated a new training program}. As a verb, it also means to formally admit someone into a group, organization, or secret society, often through a ceremony or ritual: {New members are initiated at the annual gathering}. The noun initiate refers to someone who has been newly admitted or is being introduced to specialized knowledge. The adjective sense, now rare, describes someone possessing such insider knowledge.

Initiated describes something that has been started or set in motion, or someone who has been formally admitted into a group, organization, or body of knowledge. {The company initiated a new training program.} When used as a noun, the initiated refers to people who possess special knowledge or have been admitted to an exclusive group: {The jargon was meaningless to anyone but the initiated.} The word carries connotations of deliberate action or formal ceremony, distinguishing it from things that merely begin on their own.

Initiates works as both verb and noun around the idea of beginning or bringing in. To initiate is to start something: {Who initiated the conversation?} It also means to admit someone into a group, often through ceremony or ritual: {The fraternity initiates new members each fall}. As a noun, an initiate is someone newly admitted to such a group, or a beginner learning the basics of something: {The initiates gathered for their first lesson}.

Initiation is the act of beginning something or being formally admitted into a group, organization, or status. A project's initiation is its start. Fraternity initiations involve rituals marking membership: {The initiation included a hazing ceremony}. An initiation into adulthood might be a first job or other rite of passage. To initiate is to begin or to admit someone through such a process.

Initiations are ceremonies or processes marking entry into a group, status, or phase of life. Fraternity initiations welcome new members, often through rituals or ordeals. Religious initiations mark spiritual transformation. The word also covers first experiences that introduce someone to something new: {her initiation into the world of competitive chess}. The singular initiation is more common.

Initiative is the drive to act without being prompted—the quality of someone who starts things rather than waiting for instruction: {She showed real initiative by reorganizing the filing system on her own}. It also names the first move or opening action: {The company seized the initiative in the market}. In politics, an initiative is a process allowing citizens to propose legislation directly: {a ballot initiative to legalize marijuana}. To {take the initiative} is to act first, setting events in motion.

Initiatives are actions taken to address problems or start new efforts, often implying self-direction rather than following orders: {The company launched several green initiatives}. In politics, an initiative is a process allowing citizens to propose legislation directly through petition and vote, bypassing the legislature: {The marijuana initiative passed with 54% of the vote}.

To inject is to introduce something into another thing, typically by force or pressure. The core use is medical—injecting fluid through a needle into the body: {The nurse injected the vaccine into his arm}. The meaning extends to introducing anything into a system or situation: inject {capital} into a struggling business, inject {humor} into a tense conversation. In computing, code injection is inserting malicious commands into a program. The word always implies insertion from outside, often with the sense of adding what wasn't there before.

Injected is the past tense of inject, meaning to force fluid into something, typically with a syringe: {The nurse injected the vaccine into her arm}. By extension, to inject is to introduce something into a situation: {He injected humor into the conversation}, {The government injected cash into the failing bank}. In computing, code injection refers to inserting malicious commands into a program.

Injecting is the act of forcing fluid into something, typically with a syringe: {The nurse was injecting the vaccine when the patient fainted}. Beyond medicine, injecting describes introducing something forcefully into a situation: {injecting humor into a tense meeting}, {injecting capital into a struggling business}. In computing, code injection is inserting malicious commands into a program.

An injection is the act of forcing something into something else, typically a liquid into a body or system. Medical injections deliver drugs, vaccines, or fluids through a needle: {The nurse gave him an injection in the arm}. The term extends to any introduction of substance or resource: a cash injection, a fuel injection system. In computing, code injection is a security attack where malicious code is inserted into a program.

Injections is the plural of injection—the act of forcing liquid into something, typically medicine into the body through a needle: {The nurse prepared the injections}. The term extends to any introduction of substance or element: a {fuel injection} system, an {injection of capital} into a struggling business. In computing, {SQL injection} is a hacking technique that inserts malicious code into a database query.

An injunction is a court order requiring someone to do or refrain from doing something. Unlike money damages, it compels action: {The judge issued an injunction blocking the merger}. A preliminary injunction maintains the status quo while a case proceeds; a permanent injunction follows final judgment. Outside law, injunction means any authoritative command or directive: {parental injunctions against staying out late}.

Injunctions are court orders that require someone to do something or stop doing something. A judge might issue an injunction to halt construction on a disputed property or prevent a former employee from sharing trade secrets. The term also applies more broadly to any authoritative command or directive: {Despite her mother's injunctions against staying out late, she went to the party anyway}.

To injure is to cause physical harm or damage to a person or body part: {She injured her knee playing soccer}. The word extends to non-physical damage—injuring someone's reputation, pride, or feelings. An injury can be accidental or deliberate. The injured party in a legal context is whoever suffered harm. Injure implies less severity than wound but more than hurt.

Injured means harmed or wounded, whether physically or emotionally. An injured {knee} has been damaged; injured {feelings} have been hurt. The injured are those who have sustained harm: {The injured were taken to nearby hospitals}. Injured can also mean wronged or offended: {an injured party}, {an injured tone of voice}.

Injuries is the plural of injury—harm or damage done to a person, animal, or thing. Physical injuries range from minor cuts to life-threatening trauma: {She sustained injuries in the crash}. The word extends to non-physical harm: injuries to one's reputation, to the environment, or to a relationship. In legal contexts, injuries include any violation of rights: {personal injuries}, {compensable injuries}.

Injury is damage or harm, usually to a body: {She sustained a knee injury during practice}. The word extends to non-physical harm—damage to reputation, feelings, or legal rights: {injury to his pride}, {personal injury lawsuit}. To {add insult to injury} is to make a bad situation worse through additional offense. In legal contexts, injury encompasses any violation of another's rights.

Injustice is unfairness or the violation of what is right—the absence or opposite of justice. It can describe a system that treats people unequally {racial injustice}, a specific wrong {The verdict was an injustice}, or the general condition of unfairness {a world full of injustice}. To {do someone an injustice} is to judge or treat them unfairly.

Injustices is the plural of injustice—instances of unfair treatment or violations of rights. The word often appears in discussions of systemic wrongs: {historical injustices against Indigenous peoples}, {the injustices of the criminal justice system}. To {right past injustices} is to correct or compensate for them.

Ink is a colored liquid used for writing, printing, or drawing. Pen ink flows onto paper; printer ink transfers text and images. The substance extends to the dark fluid squid and octopus release as defense. In slang, ink means tattoos: {He's got a lot of ink on his arms}. To ink a deal is to sign it, making it official.

An inkblot is a dark stain or spot made by ink, or a shape created by folding paper over wet ink. The Rorschach test uses symmetrical inkblots to assess personality and psychological states—subjects describe what they see, and their interpretations are analyzed. By extension, anything ambiguous that invites projection may be called an inkblot: {The candidate was a political inkblot onto whom voters projected their hopes}.

Inkblots are irregular shapes made by ink, especially the symmetrical patterns used in psychological testing. The Rorschach test presents standardized inkblots and asks subjects what they see, supposedly revealing aspects of personality or mental state. Outside clinical settings, inkblot has become shorthand for any ambiguous stimulus onto which people project their own interpretations: {The candidate's vague platform was an inkblot—voters saw whatever they wanted}.

Inked is the past tense of ink, meaning to sign or finalize something in ink: {We inked the deal yesterday}. In tattoo culture, inked means tattooed: {She's heavily inked}. Someone who is inked has tattoos. The word also appears in printing contexts for applying ink to a surface.

An inker is someone who applies ink, particularly in comic book production where the inker traces over a penciler's preliminary drawings to create finished, publication-ready art. The role requires skill in line weight, shading, and texture: {The inker transformed the rough sketches into bold, dynamic pages}. In tattoo parlance, an inker is simply a tattoo artist.

Inking is the process of applying ink, whether to a printing surface, a stamp, or artwork. In comics and illustration, inking refers specifically to tracing over pencil drawings with ink to create clean, bold lines—a specialized skill that can dramatically affect the final look of the art. {The inking on that comic gives it a noir feel.} Someone who inks professionally is called an inker.

An inkling is a slight hint or vague idea about something: {I had no inkling they were planning a surprise party}. The word suggests incomplete knowledge—you sense something without fully grasping it. An inkling falls short of certainty or even strong suspicion; it's the faintest stirring of awareness.

Inklings are slight hints or vague notions of something not fully known or understood: {I had no inkling she was planning to leave}, {The first inklings of trouble appeared in the quarterly report}. An inkling suggests the earliest awareness—less than knowledge, more than ignorance. The word almost always appears with qualifiers like "first," "some," or "no."

Inks is the plural of ink—liquid or paste used for writing, printing, or drawing. The word appears in contexts involving multiple types or colors: {The printer uses four inks: cyan, magenta, yellow, and black}. As a verb, inks means signs or finalizes: {She inks a deal with the record label}. In tattoo culture, to ink is to tattoo, so one who inks applies permanent designs to skin.

An inkwell is a small container designed to hold ink for dipping a pen. Before fountain pens and ballpoints, writers kept inkwells on their desks: {She dipped her quill into the inkwell}. School desks once had holes fitted with inkwells. The word evokes old-fashioned writing and penmanship.

Inky means resembling or stained with ink. An inky {darkness} is deep black, like ink. Inky {fingers} are smudged from writing or printing. The word suggests both the color and the liquid quality of ink—something that spreads, stains, or saturates: {The inky water of the harbor reflected no light}.

Inlaid describes a surface decorated by setting pieces of contrasting material—wood, metal, stone, or shell—into shallow recesses so they lie flush: {an inlaid mahogany box}, {a tabletop inlaid with mother-of-pearl}. The technique creates patterns or images within the surface rather than on top of it. Inlaid is the past tense and adjective form of inlay.

Inland means away from the coast or border, toward the interior of a land mass. Water moves inland during floods; travelers head inland from port cities. As an adjective, it describes things situated away from edges: {inland waterways}, {inland cities}. The word contrasts with coastal, maritime, or frontier locations.

A relative by marriage rather than blood: your spouse's parents, siblings, and their families, or the spouses of your own siblings. The term usually appears in compounds—{mother-in-law}, {brother-in-law}, {in-laws}—and often carries connotations of obligation or tension: {We're spending Thanksgiving with the in-laws}.

Inlaws are relatives by marriage rather than blood—your spouse's parents, siblings, and their families. The term usually appears hyphenated or as two words: {My in-laws are visiting for the holidays}. Mother-in-law, father-in-law, and similar compounds specify the relationship. Inlaw relationships are famously fraught territory for jokes and complaints.

Inlay is decorative material set into a surface so it lies flush—wood, metal, stone, or other materials embedded into furniture, floors, or jewelry to create patterns or designs. The technique contrasts with overlay, where material sits on top. To inlay is to create such decoration: {The craftsman inlaid the tabletop with mother-of-pearl}. In dentistry, an inlay is a fitted filling.

Inlays are decorative materials set into a surface—wood, metal, stone—so they lie flush with the surrounding material. The technique creates patterns or images by fitting contrasting pieces into carved recesses: {The table featured mother-of-pearl inlays}. In dentistry, an inlay is a filling shaped outside the mouth and cemented into a tooth cavity.

An inlet is a narrow body of water extending into land from a larger body—a small bay, cove, or arm of the sea: {The boat anchored in a sheltered inlet}. More generally, an inlet is any opening that admits entry, especially for liquids or gases: an air {inlet}, a water {inlet}. The opposite is outlet.

Inlets is the plural of inlet. An inlet is a narrow body of water extending into land from a larger body—smaller than a bay, often between islands or cutting into a coastline: {The boat anchored in a sheltered inlet}. More generally, an inlet is any passage allowing entry, especially for liquids or air into a system: {the air inlet on the engine}.

Inline means positioned within a line or sequence rather than set apart. In computing, inline code runs within the main program flow rather than being called separately; inline styles appear directly in HTML elements. Inline skating uses wheels arranged in a single row. The word often appears hyphenated or as two words: {in-line}, {in line}.

An inmate is a person confined to an institution—typically a prison, but also a psychiatric facility or similar establishment. The word emphasizes residence under constraint: {The inmates were allowed one hour of outdoor recreation daily}. Less commonly, inmate can mean any inhabitant or occupant sharing quarters with others, though this older sense has largely given way to the institutional meaning.

Inmates are people confined to an institution—most often a prison or jail, but also psychiatric hospitals or similar facilities. The term emphasizes their status as residents held against their will: {The inmates were released into the yard for exercise}. Fellow inmates share confinement: {He got along well with his fellow inmates}.

An inn is an establishment offering lodging and often food to travelers. The word evokes a historical or rural setting—a roadside stop with rooms upstairs and a tavern below: {We stayed at a country inn}. Today inn appears in hotel names to suggest quaint hospitality, though the places may be thoroughly modern.

Innards are the internal organs of an animal, especially when removed during butchering or cleaning: {She scooped out the fish's innards}. The word extends to the internal workings of machines or systems: {the innards of a computer}, {the innards of the bureaucracy}. Innards is informal—a folksy alternative to entrails or guts.

Innate describes qualities present from birth or built into something's essential nature, not acquired through experience or learning. An innate {talent} comes naturally. Innate {curiosity} seems hardwired. The word often contrasts with learned: {Is language innate or acquired?} Innate can also mean inherent to a system: {the innate limitations of the technology}.

Inner describes what is inside or closer to the center: the {inner ear}, an {inner pocket}, the {inner city}. It extends to what is private or hidden from others: {inner thoughts}, {inner life}, {inner circle}. Your {inner child} is the emotional part of yourself that remains from childhood. An {inner voice} is intuition or conscience.

Innermost describes what is farthest inward or closest to the center, whether in physical space or in psychological depth. The innermost {room} of a building lies at its core; your innermost {thoughts} or innermost {feelings} are the most private ones, those you rarely share with others. The word emphasizes maximum interiority—not just inner, but the most inner of all.

An innertube is a inflatable rubber tube that fits inside a tire, holding the air that keeps the tire inflated. Once standard in all pneumatic tires, innertubes have been largely replaced by tubeless designs in cars but remain common in bicycles. Inflated innertubes also serve as flotation devices for swimming and tubing down rivers: {We spent the afternoon floating on innertubes}.

Innertubes are the inflatable rubber rings that fit inside tires to hold air pressure. Once standard in bicycle and automobile tires, they've largely been replaced by tubeless designs. The word now most commonly refers to the large inflatable rings used for floating on water—tubing down rivers or being towed behind boats: {We spent the afternoon on innertubes at the lake}.

An innie is a navel that curves inward rather than protruding—the opposite of an outie. Most people have innies. The term extends to anything recessed where an alternative protrudes: {Is your belly button an innie or an outie?}

An inning is a division of a baseball game during which each team has a turn at bat. A regulation game has nine innings. The term extends to opportunities or periods of action: {The reformers had their inning in the 1960s}. In cricket, the singular innings refers to a team's or player's turn batting.

Innings is a division of play in cricket or baseball during which one team bats. In cricket, a single innings (the word is both singular and plural) can last hours or days; in baseball, an inning consists of each team batting once. By extension, a long innings means a full life well lived: {He had a good innings}.

Innit is British slang for "isn't it," used as a tag question seeking agreement or confirmation: {Nice day, innit?} The contraction has expanded beyond its grammatical origins to function as a general-purpose tag after almost any statement: {That was mental, innit}. Associated with working-class London speech, especially among younger speakers.

An innkeeper is the owner or manager of an inn—a small establishment offering lodging and often food to travelers. The term has an old-fashioned ring, evoking roadside lodges and taverns rather than modern hotels: {The innkeeper showed us to our room above the pub}.

Innocence is the state of being free from guilt, sin, or wrongdoing. A defendant maintains their innocence; a child possesses innocence before exposure to the world's harsher realities. The word carries connotations of purity, naivety, and lack of experience: {She spoke with such innocence about the situation}. To {lose one's innocence} is to become aware of evil, cruelty, or complexity—often through direct experience. Innocence can also mean harmlessness: {the innocence of the remark}.

Innocent means free from guilt or wrongdoing: {The jury found him innocent}. It also describes someone lacking experience with evil or corruption—a child's innocent trust, an innocent question asked without ulterior motive. By extension, innocent can mean naive or unsophisticated: {She was innocent of the ways of Wall Street}. An innocent bystander is uninvolved and undeserving of harm. The noun innocent refers to such a person, especially a child or victim: {The bombing killed dozens of innocents}.

Innocents is the plural of innocent used as a noun—people who are blameless, naive, or uninvolved in wrongdoing. The word often appears in contexts of violence or injustice: {The bombing killed dozens of innocents}. It can also describe the naive or guileless: {fresh-faced innocents arriving in the big city}. The Massacre of the Innocents refers to the biblical slaughter of infants by King Herod.

To innovate is to introduce something new—a method, idea, or product that changes how things are done.
