In science, interaction describes how forces, particles, or substances affect each other. In computing, it refers to communication between user and system. The adjective interactive describes things designed for two-way engagement.

Interactions are instances of people, things, or forces acting upon one another or responding to each other's presence. The word covers everything from casual social exchanges {I had a brief interaction with my neighbor} to the way drugs affect each other in the body {dangerous drug interactions}. In computing and design, interactions refer to how users engage with interfaces or systems. The term emphasizes reciprocity—both parties influence or affect the other in some way.

Interactive describes things that respond to user input, creating a two-way exchange rather than passive reception. An interactive {exhibit} lets visitors touch and manipulate displays. Interactive {software} adjusts based on what you do. The word applies to any medium where the audience participates rather than just observes: {interactive storytelling}, {interactive maps}. In education, interactive methods engage students actively rather than having them sit and listen.

Interactivity is the quality of responding to user input rather than presenting fixed content. A video game has high interactivity; a book has none. The term appears constantly in discussions of digital media, education, and design: {The website's interactivity keeps users engaged}. Interactive exhibits, software, and experiences all emphasize this two-way exchange between system and participant.

To intercept is to stop or catch something in transit before it reaches its destination. You can intercept a pass in football, intercept enemy communications, or intercept someone on their way out the door. {The defense intercepted three passes}. In mathematics, an intercept is a point where a line or curve crosses an axis. As a noun in sports, an interception is often shortened to intercept: {He had two intercepts in the fourth quarter}.

Intercepted is the past tense of intercept, meaning to stop or catch something in transit before it reaches its destination. A pass is intercepted when a defender catches a ball meant for an opponent. Communications are intercepted when a third party captures messages between others: {The FBI intercepted their phone calls}. {She intercepted him in the hallway before he could leave}.

Intercepting is the present participle of intercept, used as a verb or adjective. To intercept is to stop, catch, or seize something or someone that is in transit from one place to another. You might intercept a pass in football, intercept a message before it reaches its intended recipient, or intercept an enemy aircraft. The word suggests catching something mid-course: {The defense intercepting that throw changed the momentum of the game.}

Interception is the act of catching or seizing something in transit before it reaches its destination. A defender makes an interception by catching a pass intended for the opponent: {He threw three interceptions in the first half}. Intelligence agencies intercept communications. To intercept someone is to stop them en route: {She intercepted him in the hallway before the meeting}.

Interceptions are acts of catching or seizing something before it reaches its intended destination. In American football, an interception occurs when a defensive player catches a pass meant for the opposing team: {He led the league in interceptions}. The term applies to intercepted communications, missiles, or anything cut off mid-route: {The interception of enemy transmissions proved decisive}.

An interceptor is something that intercepts—that stops, catches, or cuts off something in transit. Most often the word refers to a fast military aircraft designed to intercept and engage enemy planes or missiles before they reach their targets: {Interceptors scrambled to meet the incoming bombers}. In computing and programming, an interceptor is code that catches and handles requests or data before they reach their destination, often for logging or modification.

Interceptors are things designed to stop or catch something in transit. Fighter aircraft tasked with engaging enemy planes before they reach their targets are interceptors, as are missiles designed to destroy incoming warheads. In software, interceptors are components that intercept requests or data flowing through a system, allowing modification or inspection before processing continues. The term applies broadly to anything positioned to cut off or block something mid-course.

Intercepts functions as both verb and noun around the core idea of stopping or catching something before it reaches its intended destination. You intercept a pass in football by catching it before the receiver does; agencies intercept communications by capturing them in transit. {The defender intercepted the ball at the goal line.} In mathematics, an intercept is the point where a line or curve crosses an axis. The noun also refers to the act of interception itself or the thing intercepted: {The intelligence team analyzed the intercepts.}

Interchange involves mutual exchange—two or more parties giving and receiving in turn. Ideas interchange in conversation; highways interchange where traffic flows between them. An interchange is both the act of exchanging and the place where exchange happens: {the interchange of goods between nations}, {a highway interchange}. Parts that interchange are interchangeable—able to substitute for one another: {We interchanged the tires on the car}.

Interchangeable describes things that can be swapped for one another without affecting function or outcome. Interchangeable parts revolutionized manufacturing—any component fits any unit. {The two words are nearly interchangeable}. People or things treated as interchangeable are seen as equivalent and replaceable: {He treats his assistants as interchangeable}.

Interchanges are exchanges or substitutions—of ideas, of goods, of positions. The word often implies reciprocity: {a lively interchange of opinions}. In transportation, an interchange is where highways connect, allowing vehicles to transfer between roads without stopping: {the cloverleaf interchange at Route 95}. The verb interchange means to switch places or exchange mutually.

An intercom is a two-way communication system installed within a building or vehicle, allowing people in different locations to speak to each other: {The secretary's voice came through the intercom}. Intercoms appear in apartment buildings for buzzing visitors in, in offices between rooms, and in aircraft for crew communication. Short for intercommunication system.

Intercoms are communication devices that allow two-way audio between different rooms or locations within a building. Originally wired systems in offices and apartment buildings, the term now covers wireless units, video-enabled doorbells, and baby monitors. {The receptionist buzzed him through the intercom.} Singular: intercom.

Intercontinental means extending or operating between continents: {intercontinental flights}, {intercontinental ballistic missiles}. The word emphasizes vast geographic scope, spanning oceans and landmasses rather than merely crossing national borders. {The hotel chain has intercontinental reach.}

Intercourse is interaction or communication between people or groups: {diplomatic intercourse between nations}, {social intercourse at the party}. The word now most commonly means sexual intercourse—the physical act of sex, especially penetration: {They had intercourse}. The sexual sense has largely overtaken the older meaning of general exchange or dealings.

Interdependence is mutual dependence—a relationship where two or more parties rely on each other. The term appears often in discussions of economics, ecology, and international relations: {The interdependence of global markets means a crisis in one country ripples worldwide}. Unlike one-sided dependence, interdependence implies that each party both gives and receives: {The interdependence between bees and flowering plants benefits both}.

Interdimensional describes movement or existence between different dimensions or planes of reality. The term belongs primarily to science fiction and fantasy, where characters travel through interdimensional portals or encounter interdimensional beings: {The interdimensional rift opened above the city}. In speculative physics, it sometimes appears in discussions of theoretical parallel universes or higher spatial dimensions.

Interest connects to what engages attention or provides advantage. An interest in something is curiosity or concern about it: {She developed an interest in astronomy}. To interest someone is to engage their attention. Something interesting holds that attention. Interest also means a stake or share: {business interests}, {a controlling interest in the company}. Financial interest is money paid for borrowing money, calculated as a percentage: {The loan carries 8% interest}. {In the interest of} means for the benefit of. To act in someone's {best interests} is to do what helps them, whether they recognize it or not.

Interested means having your attention engaged or curiosity aroused: {I'm interested in learning more about that}. It also describes wanting to participate or pursue something: {Let me know if you're interested}. An interested party has a stake in an outcome—financial, personal, or otherwise—which may compromise their objectivity: {All interested parties should recuse themselves from the vote}.

Interesting describes something that captures attention or curiosity. An interesting {book}, {idea}, or {person} engages the mind and invites further exploration. The word is common but vague—it can express genuine fascination or serve as polite filler when stronger opinions go unstated: {That's an interesting theory} may mean remarkable or merely strange. {Interesting times} suggests upheaval rather than boredom.

Interests are the things that engage someone's attention or curiosity—hobbies, subjects, activities they care about: {Her interests include photography and hiking}. An interest in something can also mean a stake or share: {He has a financial interest in the company}. In the plural, interests often refers to what benefits a person or group: {acting in the best interests of the child}. Interest on money—the cost of borrowing or the return on saving—becomes interests mainly in legal or financial contexts involving multiple parties or rates.

An interface is where two systems or entities meet and interact. In computing, it's the point of contact between user and machine—a graphical interface presents visual elements to click; a command-line interface accepts typed commands. More broadly, interface describes any boundary where different things connect: {the interface between science and policy}. As a verb, to interface is to interact or connect: {We need to interface with the marketing team}. The verb sounds corporate and is often mocked as jargon.

Interfaces are points of connection between separate systems—where one thing meets and interacts with another. A computer interface allows user and machine to communicate: a graphical user interface displays icons and menus; an application programming interface lets software components exchange data. Beyond computing, interface describes any boundary where interaction occurs: {the interface between science and policy}. As a verb, to interface is to connect or interact, though this use sounds corporate: {We'll interface with the marketing team}.

Interfaith describes cooperation or dialogue between different religions: {an interfaith service}, {interfaith marriage}, {interfaith council}. The term implies mutual respect across religious boundaries rather than conversion attempts. It became common in the late twentieth century as religious diversity increased in Western societies.

To interfere is to get involved in something in a way that hinders or disrupts it. A meddling neighbor interferes in your affairs. Static interferes with radio signals. The word implies unwanted involvement: {Don't interfere with my plans}. In sports, interference is illegal obstruction of an opponent. In physics, waves interfere when they overlap, either reinforcing or canceling each other.

Interfered is the past tense of interfere—to get involved in something in a way that hinders or alters its course. You interfere with a process, in someone's affairs, or between opposing parties: {The coach interfered with the investigation}. {She interfered in their marriage}. Radio signals interfere when they disrupt each other. In sports, a player interferes by illegally obstructing an opponent.

Interference is the act of getting involved in something that isn't your concern, usually unwelcomely: {I resent your interference in my personal life}. In sports, interference is illegal obstruction of an opponent. In physics, interference occurs when waves meet and combine, either reinforcing or canceling each other. Radio interference is static or disruption from competing signals. To {run interference} is to clear obstacles for someone else—from football blocking.

Interfering describes someone who meddles in others' affairs without invitation. An interfering {neighbor} offers unsolicited opinions about your yard. An interfering {mother-in-law} involves herself in decisions that aren't hers to make. The word carries disapproval—it suggests unwanted involvement rather than helpful concern.

Intergalactic means between or among galaxies—the vast spaces separating these cosmic structures: {intergalactic travel}, {intergalactic dust}. In science fiction and casual use, it often just means outer space or extraterrestrial: {an intergalactic adventure}, {intergalactic beings}. The word suggests immense distances and cosmic scale.

Interim refers to the time between two events or periods—a gap waiting to be filled. An interim {president} serves temporarily until a permanent one takes office. {In the interim} means during that intervening time: {The new system launches in June; in the interim, we'll use the old one}. The word suggests a holding pattern, a pause before the next phase begins.

Interior refers to the inside part of something, contrasted with its exterior or surface. A car's interior includes seats and dashboard; a building's interior is the space within its walls. Interior can describe what lies inland: {the interior of the continent}. It also means inner or private: {interior thoughts}, {interior life}. In government, interior departments handle domestic rather than foreign affairs.

Interiors are inside spaces, especially of buildings: {The interiors were gutted by fire}. Interior design concerns furnishing and decorating such spaces, and interiors often refers to this field: {She works in interiors}. In film and theater, interiors are indoor scenes, contrasted with exteriors. The word also applies to inland regions: {the interiors of Alaska and Canada}.

To interlock is to fit together by overlapping or engaging, like fingers clasping or gear teeth meshing. Things that interlock connect in a way that makes them difficult to separate: {The puzzle pieces interlock}. As a noun, an interlock is a safety device that prevents equipment from operating under dangerous conditions—machinery won't run unless guards are in place, or a car won't start unless the seatbelt is fastened.

Interlocked describes things joined together by overlapping or fitting into one another, like links in a chain or fingers clasped together. The connection implies mutual dependence—neither part easily separates from the other: {Their fates were interlocked}, {interlocked pieces of a puzzle}. Systems or processes interlock when each depends on the others to function.

Interlocking describes things that fit together by overlapping or engaging with each other, like puzzle pieces or linked fingers. The design prevents independent movement: {interlocking gears}, {interlocking directorates} (where board members serve on multiple company boards). As a noun, interlocking refers to a system where components depend on each other's positions—especially railway signals that prevent conflicting routes.

An interloper is someone who intrudes where they don't belong or weren't invited. The word suggests trespass into a space, situation, or group where the person has no right to be: {The cat eyed the new puppy as an interloper in her domain}. It can describe romantic rivals, business competitors encroaching on established territory, or anyone perceived as an unwelcome outsider.

Interlopers are people who intrude where they don't belong or aren't wanted. The word suggests unauthorized presence—someone inserting themselves into a situation, place, or group without invitation: {The old-timers viewed the newcomers as interlopers}. In business, an interloper may be a competitor encroaching on established territory.

An interlude is a period of time between two events or activities—a pause or interval that interrupts the main flow: {a brief interlude of peace between the wars}, {a musical interlude between acts of the play}. The word often suggests something lighter or different in character from what surrounds it: {Their romance was a pleasant interlude in an otherwise difficult year}. In music and drama, an interlude is a short performance filling a gap between longer pieces.

Interludes are intervals or breaks between other events. Originally theatrical—short performances between acts of a play—the word now applies more broadly to any pause or intervening period: {a brief interlude of peace between conflicts}, {musical interludes between speakers}. An interlude often carries a sense of pleasant respite from routine: {a romantic interlude in Paris}.

Intermarriage is marriage between people of different groups—different religions, races, ethnicities, or social classes. The term often appears in discussions of cultural assimilation or community boundaries: {Intermarriage between Jews and non-Jews has increased dramatically}. The related verb is intermarry: {The two families had intermarried for generations}.

Intermediaries are people or entities that act as go-betweens, facilitating transactions or communication between parties who don't deal directly with each other. Banks serve as financial intermediaries between savers and borrowers. Brokers, agents, and middlemen are all intermediaries. {The deal was arranged through intermediaries rather than face-to-face negotiation.}

An intermediary is a person or thing that acts as a go-between, connecting two parties who don't deal directly with each other. A mediator in a dispute is an intermediary, as is a broker arranging a sale: {The bank served as intermediary between buyer and seller}. The word works as both noun and adjective: {intermediary negotiations}, {an intermediary step}.

Intermediate means in the middle between two points, levels, or stages. An intermediate {student} is beyond beginner but not yet advanced. An intermediate {step} falls between the first and last. As a noun, an intermediate is a person at that level or a substance formed during a chemical reaction before the final product. The verb means to act as a go-between: {She intermediated between the feuding parties}.

An intermezzo is a short musical composition between larger sections of an opera, symphony, or other extended work—a brief instrumental piece while the stage is reset or the audience catches its breath. The term extends to any short connecting entertainment or, more loosely, to any interlude: {The weekend was a pleasant intermezzo between grueling work weeks}.

An intermission is a pause or break in the middle of something, especially a scheduled break during a performance: {We got drinks during the intermission}. The word appears most often in theatrical contexts—plays, concerts, operas—where audiences need time to stretch or use the restroom. Outside entertainment, intermission suggests any temporary cessation: {a brief intermission in the rain}.

Intermissions are scheduled breaks during a performance or event. A play, concert, or sporting event pauses at intermission to let the audience stretch, use restrooms, or buy refreshments. The word can extend to any pause in ongoing activity: {We worked through without intermission}. In British English, interval is more common for theatrical breaks.

Intermittent describes something that stops and starts at intervals rather than continuing steadily. An intermittent {noise} comes and goes. Intermittent {rain} falls, pauses, then falls again. The word often appears in medical contexts—intermittent {fasting}, intermittent {fever}—and technical ones: {The car has an intermittent electrical problem}. The opposite is continuous or constant.

An intern is someone gaining supervised practical experience, typically a student or recent graduate working temporarily in a profession: {She's doing a summer intern at the law firm}. Medical interns are newly graduated doctors in their first year of hospital training. To intern someone is to confine them, especially during wartime: {Japanese Americans were interned in camps during World War II}. The confinement sense comes from a different root than the trainee sense.

Internal means situated within or occurring inside something. Internal {organs} are inside the body. Internal {affairs} concern matters within an organization or country rather than external relations. Internal can also describe mental or emotional states—what happens in someone's mind rather than what they express outwardly: {He kept his doubts internal}. The internal workings of a machine or system are its inner mechanisms.

To internalise is to absorb something—a belief, value, or way of thinking—so deeply that it becomes part of your own mental framework rather than something externally imposed: {Children internalise their parents' attitudes toward money}. The word often appears in psychology and sociology, describing how social norms become personal convictions. British spelling of internalize.

Internalization is the process of making something part of oneself—absorbing external ideas, values, or behaviors until they feel natural rather than imposed. A child internalizes social norms; a student internalizes a teacher's criticism. In psychology, internalization explains how cultural expectations become personal beliefs: {She had internalized the message that her worth depended on her appearance}. The term also appears in economics, where to internalize a cost means to incorporate it into a price rather than passing it to others.

To internalize something is to make it part of yourself—absorbing beliefs, values, or knowledge until they become automatic rather than consciously held. A child internalizes social norms. Someone who has internalized criticism carries it as self-doubt: {She had internalized her father's disappointment}. In psychology, internalization contrasts with externalization—directing feelings inward rather than outward.
clues: Let it become part of you

definition: Internalized describes beliefs, values, or attitudes that have been absorbed so thoroughly they feel like one's own rather than externally imposed. A child internalizes parental expectations; an adult may struggle with internalized shame or internalized racism—negative messages about one's own group that have been unconsciously adopted. {She had internalized the idea that asking for help was weakness.}

Internalizing is taking something external and making it part of yourself. A child internalizes values from parents, absorbing them until they feel like personal beliefs rather than imposed rules. In psychology, internalizing emotions means directing feelings inward rather than expressing them: {She internalized her anger instead of confronting him}. The term often carries a cautionary note—internalizing criticism or negative messages can harm self-image.

International describes things involving two or more nations: {international trade}, {international law}, {an international airport}. It can also mean spanning or transcending national boundaries: {an international reputation}, {international waters}. As a noun, an international is a person who has represented their country in sport, especially in British usage: {She's a former England international}.

Internationalism is the principle that nations should cooperate across borders rather than pursue purely national interests. It emphasizes shared concerns—peace, trade, human rights—over sovereignty and self-interest. {The post-war order was built on internationalism}. The term often contrasts with nationalism or isolationism. An internationalist advocates for such cooperation.

Interned has two distinct meanings depending on context. Most commonly, it's the past tense of intern meaning to confine someone, especially during wartime: {Japanese Americans were interned in camps during World War II}. It also means having served as an intern: {She interned at a law firm last summer}.

An internet is any network of interconnected computer networks—multiple separate networks linked together to communicate. Before the global network dominated, the term described various interconnected systems: {The company built an internet linking its regional offices}. The word is now rarely used in this generic sense. (Capitalized Internet is the global network.)

Interning is working as an intern, typically in a temporary position that provides practical experience in a profession or field of study. {She's interning at a law firm this summer.} A separate meaning involves confining or detaining someone, especially during wartime or for political reasons: {The government began interning citizens of enemy nations.} The first sense is far more common in everyday usage.

Internment is the confinement of people, typically during wartime or political crisis. Unlike imprisonment for crimes, internment detains groups based on nationality, ethnicity, or perceived threat: {the internment of Japanese Americans during World War II}. The term carries connotations of injustice—detention without trial or individual evidence of wrongdoing.

Interns are people gaining practical experience in a field, typically students or recent graduates working temporarily at organizations. The arrangement ranges from unpaid positions offering only résumé credit to well-compensated roles at competitive firms: {Summer interns flooded the office in June}. To intern is to work as an intern, or separately, to confine someone—especially during wartime: {Japanese Americans were interned during World War II}.

An internship is a temporary position offering practical experience in a field, typically for students or recent graduates. Internships may be paid or unpaid, lasting weeks to months: {She landed a summer internship at a law firm}. The term increasingly describes any entry-level arrangement where experience substitutes for full compensation.

Internships are temporary positions that give students or recent graduates practical experience in a field. They may be paid or unpaid, and often serve as a bridge between education and employment. Companies use internships to evaluate potential hires; interns use them to build skills and connections: {She landed a job through her summer internship}.

Interplanetary means between or among planets: {interplanetary travel}, {interplanetary space}. The term appears in science fiction and astronomy to describe movement, communication, or distances within a solar system. An {interplanetary mission} travels from one planet to another, as distinct from interstellar travel between star systems.

Interplay is the way two or more things affect or respond to each other—a back-and-forth dynamic where each element influences the others. The word emphasizes mutual action rather than one-sided effect: {the interplay between genetics and environment}, {the interplay of light and shadow}. It appears often in discussions of complex systems where multiple factors work together.

To interpret is to explain or make sense of something not immediately clear. You interpret a dream, a poem, a legal statute, or someone's silence. An interpreter translates spoken language in real time: {She interpreted for the ambassador}. Musicians and actors interpret works by bringing their own understanding to a performance: {His interpretation of Hamlet was brooding and restless}. Data requires interpretation—the numbers don't speak for themselves.

Interpretation is the act of explaining or making sense of something. A translator offers an interpretation of a foreign text; a musician offers an interpretation of a sonata. In law, interpretation determines what statutes or contracts mean: {The court's interpretation of the amendment proved controversial}. An interpretation can be one of several possible readings—your interpretation of events may differ from mine.

Interpretations is the plural of interpretation—explanations or understandings of meaning. A text, event, or artwork may have multiple interpretations: {Scholars have offered competing interpretations of the passage}. In performance, an interpretation is how a musician or actor renders a piece: {Her interpretation of the sonata emphasized its darker passages}. Legal and constitutional interpretations determine how laws apply.

Interpreted is the past tense of interpret—to explain the meaning of something or to understand it in a particular way. A translator interpreted the speech. A court interpreted the law narrowly. {Her silence was interpreted as agreement.} In computing, interpreted code is executed line by line by an interpreter rather than compiled beforehand: {Python is an interpreted language}.

An interpreter translates speech between languages in real time, allowing conversation across a language barrier—distinguished from a translator, who works with written text. In computing, an interpreter is a program that executes code line by line rather than compiling it first: {Python uses an interpreter}. More broadly, anyone who explains or renders meaning: {an interpreter of dreams}, {an interpreter of the law}.

Interpreters are people who translate spoken language from one language to another in real time, enabling communication between parties who don't share a common tongue. Unlike translators, who work with written text, interpreters must process and convey meaning on the spot, whether in courtrooms, hospitals, diplomatic settings, or business meetings. In computing, an interpreter is a program that executes code line by line without first compiling it into machine language, as with Python or JavaScript. {The conference hired interpreters for six languages.}

Interpreting is the act of explaining or making sense of something—a text, a dream, data, or someone's behavior: {I'm not sure how to go about interpreting these results}. It also means translating spoken language in real time between people who don't share a language, distinguished from written translation: {She works interpreting for the UN}. In performance, interpreting a role or piece of music means bringing your own understanding to it.

Interprets is the third-person singular of interpret—to explain or understand the meaning of something. A translator interprets speech from one language to another. A musician interprets a composition through performance choices. A court interprets the law. {She interprets his silence as disapproval.} {The data can be interpreted several ways.}

Interracial describes relationships, interactions, or situations involving people of different races. The term most commonly appears in discussions of interracial marriage, dating, or families, where partners or members belong to different racial groups. {Their interracial relationship faced opposition from both families.} The word gained prominence during debates over anti-miscegenation laws and remains central to conversations about race relations and diversity.

To interrogate is to question someone formally and intensively, typically to extract information. Police interrogate suspects; intelligence officers interrogate prisoners. The word implies pressure and persistence beyond casual questioning: {They interrogated him for hours about his whereabouts}. More loosely, to interrogate an idea or assumption is to examine it critically: {The essay interrogates conventional notions of gender}.

Interrogating is the present participle of interrogate, meaning to question someone thoroughly and often aggressively, typically to extract information. Police interrogate suspects, lawyers interrogate witnesses, and parents interrogate teenagers who came home late. The word carries connotations of pressure and formality that distinguish it from casual questioning. {They spent hours interrogating the witness about what she saw.} In technical contexts, interrogating can refer to querying a system or device for data.

Interrogation is intensive, often aggressive questioning, typically by police or military authorities seeking information from a suspect or prisoner. The word implies pressure and persistence beyond ordinary inquiry: {The suspect broke down after hours of interrogation}. More loosely, any pointed or probing line of questioning: {My mother's interrogation about where I'd been lasted twenty minutes}.

Interrogations is the plural of interrogation, the act of questioning someone intensely and systematically. Police conduct interrogations of suspects. Military and intelligence agencies interrogate prisoners. The word implies persistent, often aggressive questioning aimed at extracting information: {The interrogations lasted for hours}. Extended uses cover any thorough examination: {Her constant interrogations about my personal life were exhausting}.

An interrogator is a person who questions someone intensively, especially in official or adversarial contexts. Police interrogators extract confessions; military interrogators seek intelligence from prisoners. The word carries overtones of pressure, persistence, and power imbalance: {The interrogator leaned in, asking the same question for the fifth time}.

Interrogators are people who conduct interrogations—formal, often intensive questioning. The term most commonly applies to police detectives questioning suspects, military or intelligence officers extracting information from prisoners, or investigators probing witnesses. The word carries connotations of pressure and persistence: {The interrogators worked in shifts, denying him sleep}.

To interrupt is to break into something continuous—a conversation, a process, a flow. You interrupt someone speaking by cutting in before they finish: {Sorry to interrupt, but your car is being towed}. A power outage interrupts service. In computing, an interrupt is a signal that stops normal processing to handle something urgent. The noun interruption is more common than the verb for describing the break itself: {constant interruptions}, {without interruption}.

Interrupted is the past tense of interrupt—to break into or stop something in progress. A conversation is interrupted by a phone call. Sleep is interrupted by noise. An interrupted {pattern} has breaks in it. {Sorry, I interrupted you—please continue.} The word implies something was underway before the disruption occurred.

Interrupting is breaking into someone's speech or activity before they've finished. The word carries a note of rudeness—to interrupt is to cut someone off, to insert yourself where you weren't invited: {Stop interrupting me}. Beyond conversation, interrupting applies to any disruption of continuity: {An emergency broadcast kept interrupting the program}.

An interruption is something that stops a process or activity, or the act of stopping it. A phone call interrupts a conversation; a power outage interrupts work. {Sorry for the interruption.} To speak while someone else is speaking is to interrupt them: {His constant interruptions made discussion impossible}. An interruption in service means a temporary stoppage.

Interruptions is the plural of interruption—instances of breaking into an activity or stopping it before completion. A meeting may have constant interruptions from phone calls. A speaker may ask to be heard without interruption. The word covers both the act of interrupting and the thing that causes it: {Sorry for the interruption}. {She worked late to make up for the day's interruptions}.

Interrupts is usually the verb interrupt in the third person: {She interrupts constantly}. To interrupt is to break into something ongoing—a conversation, a process, a train of thought. The noun interrupt appears mainly in computing, where an interrupt is a signal that temporarily halts a processor to handle a higher-priority task: {hardware interrupts}, {software interrupts}.

Intersect means to cross or cut through, typically at a point or along a line. Two roads intersect where they meet and cross each other; in geometry, lines or planes intersect when they share common points. The word extends naturally to abstract domains: {Their research interests intersect in unexpected ways}. As a noun, an intersect is a point or area of crossing, though intersection is the more common form.

An intersection is where two or more things cross or meet. Most commonly, it's the place where roads meet: {Turn left at the next intersection}. In geometry, an intersection is where lines or shapes overlap. The word extends to any point of overlap or connection: {the intersection of art and technology}, {the intersection of race and class}. What falls within the intersection shares characteristics of both crossing elements.

Intersectionality is a framework for understanding how different aspects of a person's identity—such as race, gender, class, sexuality, and disability—combine to create unique experiences of discrimination or privilege. The term emerged from legal scholarship examining how Black women faced compounded disadvantages that couldn't be understood by looking at race or gender alone. {Her research applies an intersectionality lens to healthcare disparities.} The concept has become central to contemporary discussions of social justice and identity politics.

Intersections are places where things cross or overlap. Roads meet at intersections; so do lines, ideas, and fields of study. The word often highlights productive overlap: {the intersection of art and technology}, {the intersection of race and class}. In math, the intersection of two sets contains only elements common to both.

Intersex describes people born with reproductive or sexual anatomy that doesn't fit typical definitions of male or female. This may involve chromosomes, hormones, genitals, or internal organs. Some intersex traits are apparent at birth; others emerge at puberty or are discovered incidentally. The term replaces older medical language like "hermaphrodite," now considered outdated and offensive. {Many intersex advocates oppose unnecessary surgeries on infants.}

Interstate means between or among states, particularly the states of the United States. An interstate {highway} crosses state boundaries; the Interstate Highway System is the network of such roads. Interstate {commerce} involves trade across state lines. As a noun, an interstate is one of these highways: {We took the interstate to avoid traffic}.

Interstates are the major highways that cross state boundaries in the United States, formally the Interstate Highway System. These divided, limited-access roads connect cities across the country: {We took the interstate from Chicago to St. Louis}. The word functions as noun or adjective: {interstate commerce}, {interstate travel}.

Interstellar means between or among stars: {interstellar space}, {interstellar travel}. The word describes the vast regions of a galaxy outside individual star systems, or objects and phenomena that cross those distances. {Interstellar dust clouds eventually coalesce into new stars.} The term gained wider cultural currency from the 2014 science fiction film of the same name.

To intertwine is to twist or weave together, with each element winding around the others: {Their fingers intertwined}. The word often describes abstract connections—intertwined {fates}, intertwined {histories}, intertwined {economies}. Things that intertwine become difficult to separate, suggesting deep or complicated involvement: {Her personal and professional lives had become hopelessly intertwined}.

Intertwined describes things twisted or woven together, whether literally or figuratively. Vines become intertwined as they grow. Lives, fates, or histories that are intertwined are closely connected and hard to separate: {Their financial interests were deeply intertwined}. The word suggests mutual entanglement rather than one thing wrapped around another.

Intertwining describes the action of twisting or weaving things together so they become entangled or interlocked. Vines intertwine around a trellis; fingers intertwine when holding hands. The word extends naturally to abstractions: {Their lives became intertwining over the years}, {the intertwining of fate and free will}. As a noun or adjective, it characterizes this state of being woven together, whether physical or metaphorical.

An interval is a space between things—in time, distance, or sequence. Musical intervals measure the gap between pitches. In mathematics, an interval is a range of values between two points. Events happen {at regular intervals} or {at intervals of ten minutes}. The word suggests measured separation: {She paused at intervals to catch her breath}.
clues: The stretch from here to there

definition: Intervals are the spaces or gaps between things—in time, distance, or sequence. Events occur {at regular intervals}. Trees stand {at intervals along the road}. In music, an interval is the difference in pitch between two notes. In mathematics, it's a range of values between two endpoints. The phrase {at intervals} means periodically or with gaps between occurrences.

To intervene is to come between—stepping into a situation to alter its course. Someone might intervene in a dispute to restore peace, or a government might intervene in markets to stabilize prices. Medical intervention means treatment that changes what would otherwise happen naturally. {She intervened before the argument turned physical}. The word implies purposeful action to change an outcome, usually by an outside party.

Intervening describes what comes between two things in time or space. The intervening {years} are those that passed between two events. An intervening {wall} separates two rooms. In law, an intervening {cause} is something that disrupts the chain between an action and its consequence. To intervene is to come between, often to prevent or alter an outcome: {The referee intervened before the fight escalated}.

An intervention is an act of stepping in to change the course of events, typically to prevent harm or improve a situation. Medical interventions range from surgery to medication; political interventions may involve diplomacy or military action. The word has a specific informal meaning for a planned confrontation where friends and family urge someone to address destructive behavior, especially addiction: {Her family staged an intervention after she lost her job}. To intervene is the corresponding verb.

Interventionism is a policy or doctrine favoring active involvement in the affairs of other nations or groups, especially through military, economic, or political means. The term typically appears in foreign policy debates: {The administration's interventionism led to military action in three countries}. It contrasts with isolationism, which favors non-involvement. Interventionism can also describe government involvement in domestic markets or private affairs.
clues: Doctrine favoring action in others' matters

definition: An interventionist favors active involvement in the affairs of others—typically a government willing to use military force abroad or regulate domestic markets, rather than pursuing isolationist or laissez-faire policies. {The interventionist wing of the party pushed for sanctions.} Also describes the policies themselves: {an interventionist foreign policy}, {interventionist economic measures}.

Interventions is the plural of intervention—an act of stepping into a situation to alter its course. Medical interventions are treatments or procedures: {surgical interventions}, {early interventions for autism}. In addiction contexts, an intervention is a planned confrontation where family and friends urge someone to seek help: {We're staging an intervention for my brother}. Military or political interventions involve one power acting in another's affairs.

An interview is a formal meeting where one party questions another—typically for a job, news story, or research. The interviewer asks questions; the interviewee answers. Job interviews assess candidates: {She nailed the interview and got the offer}. Journalists interview sources for information. As a verb, to interview is to conduct or undergo such a meeting: {We interviewed six applicants}. Police interview suspects and witnesses.

An interviewer is someone who conducts an interview—asking questions of a job candidate, research subject, or public figure. The word appears in contexts ranging from employment {The interviewer asked about my experience} to journalism {The interviewer pressed the senator on the scandal} to academic research. An interviewer controls the conversation's direction and pace.

Interviewing is the process of conducting or participating in an interview—a formal conversation to assess qualifications, gather information, or explore ideas. Most commonly, interviewing refers to job candidates meeting with potential employers: {She's been interviewing all week}. Journalists interview sources for stories. The word covers both sides: {We're interviewing candidates tomorrow} and {He's interviewing at three companies}.

Interviews are formal meetings where one party questions another—typically to assess qualifications for a job, gather information for a story, or investigate a matter. The word covers both the event and its product: {She gave a great interview} means she performed well; {I read the interview} refers to the published exchange. To interview is to conduct such a meeting or to be its subject: {We're interviewing candidates tomorrow}, {He interviewed with three companies}.

Interweaving is the act of weaving things together, threading elements in and out of one another. The word usually appears figuratively: {The novel's interweaving of past and present creates narrative tension}. It suggests complexity and interconnection—multiple strands becoming inseparable from one another.

Interweb is a humorous or ironic term for the internet, often implying unfamiliarity with technology or mocking those who seem bewildered by it: {My dad finally figured out how to use the interweb}. Sometimes used affectionately for the internet's chaotic, interconnected nature. The plural {interwebs} is equally common.

Interwoven describes things woven together, with strands or threads passing alternately over and under each other. The word extends naturally to anything intertwined or closely connected: {Their lives became interwoven over decades of friendship}. Interwoven suggests elements so thoroughly combined that separating them would be difficult or destructive to the whole.

The intestine is the long, coiled tube in the abdomen where digestion is completed and nutrients absorbed. In humans, it divides into the small intestine (where most absorption occurs) and the large intestine (which processes waste). The plural intestines often refers to the organ generally or to animal entrails: {chicken intestines}, {the intestines of the victim}. Intestinal fortitude is a polite way of saying guts—courage.

The intestines are the long, coiled tube in the abdomen where digestion is completed and nutrients absorbed. The small intestine handles most nutrient absorption; the large intestine (colon) absorbs water and forms waste. Intestinal fortitude is a polite way of saying guts—courage or resolve: {She had the intestinal fortitude to finish the race}.

Intimacy is closeness between people—emotional, physical, or both. Emotional intimacy involves sharing thoughts and vulnerabilities: {Their late-night conversations created a real intimacy}. Physical intimacy ranges from affectionate touch to sex; {intimacy} alone often euphemizes sexual contact: {The relationship became physical, but she wasn't ready for intimacy}. The plural intimacies usually means private acts or exchanges: {the intimacies of marriage}.

Intimate describes what is closest and most personal. An intimate friend shares your deepest confidences. Intimate knowledge of a subject runs deep. An intimate setting is small and private: {an intimate dinner for two}. Intimate relations is a euphemism for sex; an intimate is a close friend or lover. To intimate something is to hint at it indirectly: {She intimated that changes were coming}.

Intimately describes closeness or depth of connection. Two people who know each other intimately share private knowledge or physical closeness: {They had been intimately involved for years}. To be intimately familiar with something is to know it thoroughly, from the inside: {She understood intimately how the system worked}. The word suggests access to what's usually hidden or private.

Intimates works as both verb and noun. To intimate is to hint or suggest indirectly: {She intimated that she might resign}. As a noun, intimates are one's closest friends or confidants—those with whom one shares private matters. Intimates also refers to underwear and other garments worn close to the body: {the intimates department}.
clues: Those who share your deepest secrets

definition: To intimidate is to frighten or threaten someone into compliance or submission. The effect may be intentional—{The lawyer tried to intimidate the witness}—or simply a byproduct of presence or reputation: {His size alone intimidated opponents}. Someone intimidating inspires fear or unease, often through implied power rather than direct threat.

Intimidated means made to feel fearful, timid, or inadequate—often by someone or something perceived as more powerful or impressive. You might feel intimidated by a demanding boss, a complex task, or an unfamiliar social setting: {She was intimidated by the crowd of experts}. The feeling can arise from deliberate threat or simply from being outmatched: {He felt intimidated by her confidence}.

Intimidates means to frighten or threaten someone into compliance or submission. The word suggests using power, size, or force to make others feel small or afraid: {He intimidates witnesses into silence}. Someone can intimidate without explicit threats—mere presence or reputation may suffice: {Her expertise intimidates less experienced colleagues}.

Intimidating describes something or someone that makes others feel fear, nervousness, or inadequacy. An intimidating {person} projects power or hostility. An intimidating {task} seems daunting before you begin. The word often describes situations where confidence falters: {Walking into the interview felt intimidating}. Something intimidating may be genuinely threatening or merely impressive enough to unsettle: {The sheer size of the library was intimidating}.

Intimidation is the act of frightening or threatening someone to influence their behavior. It suggests using fear rather than persuasion: {The witness refused to testify after intimidation from the defendant's associates}. Intimidation can be overt—threats, aggression—or subtle, as when someone's presence or reputation alone creates unease. The word often appears in legal contexts describing witness tampering or workplace harassment.

Two prepositions, in and to, spent so much time together that a union seemed the only respectable thing. In nearly all of its uses, the fusion into suggests movement toward the center or inside, and its most usual position is after a verb of motion: Don’t drive the car into the ditch. She rushed into the room screaming. In literal meanings, into typically denotes entry, introduction, insertion, superposition, or inclusion. Figuratively it is used to talk about resultant states, activities, or conditions: How did you get into stamp collecting? It’s also the preposition used to indicate arithmetic division: How many times will 7 go into 58?

Intolerable describes something so unpleasant, painful, or offensive that it cannot be endured: {The heat became intolerable by midday}. The word implies reaching a threshold—what might be merely unpleasant crosses into what cannot be borne: {intolerable cruelty}, {intolerable working conditions}. Something intolerable demands action or escape.

Intolerance is the unwillingness to accept views, beliefs, or behaviors that differ from one's own. It often manifests as hostility toward particular groups based on race, religion, or other characteristics: {The rally was a response to rising intolerance in the community}. In medicine, intolerance describes the body's inability to process certain substances without adverse effects, as in lactose intolerance or gluten intolerance.

Intolerant describes unwillingness to accept views, beliefs, or behaviors different from one's own: {intolerant of dissent}, {religiously intolerant}. The word often carries moral judgment—calling someone intolerant implies narrow-mindedness. In medicine, intolerant means unable to tolerate a substance without adverse effects: {lactose intolerant}, {intolerant of certain medications}.

Intonation is the rise and fall of pitch in speech, the musical quality that helps convey meaning beyond the words themselves. A rising intonation at the end of a sentence typically signals a question, while falling intonation suggests a statement. {Her intonation made it clear she was being sarcastic.} In music, intonation refers to accuracy of pitch—a singer with poor intonation drifts sharp or flat. The word also applies to the act of chanting or intoning, especially in religious contexts.

Intoxicants are substances that produce intoxication—alcohol, drugs, or other chemicals that alter mental state. The term appears most often in legal and regulatory contexts: {The sale of intoxicants is prohibited on the premises}. It covers anything from beer to hallucinogens, unified by the capacity to impair judgment or induce euphoria.

To intoxicate is to affect someone with alcohol or drugs, impairing their faculties: {He was too intoxicated to drive}. The word extends to any overwhelming influence that clouds judgment or produces euphoria: {intoxicated by success}, {intoxicated with power}. The adjective intoxicating describes things that produce such effects: {an intoxicating perfume}, {the intoxicating rush of victory}.

Intoxicated means drunk or under the influence of alcohol or drugs. The word appears frequently in legal and medical contexts where {drunk} might seem too informal: {The driver was visibly intoxicated}. Figuratively, intoxicated describes being overwhelmed by strong emotion or excitement: {intoxicated by success}, {intoxicated with love}.

Intoxicates means causes intoxication—the impaired state produced by alcohol or drugs. The word extends to any overwhelming effect: {The applause intoxicates him}. Beauty, power, or success can intoxicate as readily as whiskey. What intoxicates clouds judgment and alters perception, whether the source is chemical or emotional.

Intoxicating means capable of causing intoxication—literally through alcohol or drugs, figuratively through intense pleasure or excitement. An intoxicating {perfume} overwhelms the senses. Intoxicating {power} corrupts judgment like drink. {The intoxicating rush of victory}. The word implies something so potent it impairs clear thinking.

Intoxication is the state of being affected by alcohol or drugs—impaired judgment, altered perception, diminished coordination. The word extends to any overwhelming sensation: {the intoxication of first love}, {drunk with power}. Legal contexts specify blood alcohol levels for intoxication: {public intoxication}, {driving under the influence}. The root meaning involves poison (toxic), suggesting substances that alter normal function.

Intramurals are sports competitions between teams from the same school or institution, as opposed to varsity or intercollegiate athletics that pit different schools against each other. The word comes from Latin for "within walls"—games played inside one's own campus boundaries. {I played intramural basketball my freshman year.} Often shortened to IMs.

An intranet is a private computer network accessible only to members of an organization, typically a company or institution. It functions like a miniature internet—using the same underlying technology—but restricted to internal users: {The employee handbook is on the company intranet}. Intranets typically host internal communications, shared documents, and organizational tools.

Intransigence is stubborn refusal to compromise or change one's position. The word implies an unyielding stance that frustrates negotiation or progress: {The union's intransigence brought talks to a standstill}. Unlike mere stubbornness, intransigence often appears in political or diplomatic contexts where flexibility would be expected.

Intrepid means fearless and bold, especially in the face of danger or difficulty. The word carries a sense of adventurous courage rather than mere recklessness: {intrepid explorers}, {an intrepid journalist covering the war zone}. It suggests someone who presses forward despite knowing the risks.
clues: Calm in the face of danger

definition: Intricacy is the quality of being intricate—having many interconnected parts or details that make something complex: {the intricacy of a Swiss watch}, {the intricacies of tax law}. In the plural, intricacies often refers to the specific complexities one must navigate: {She explained the intricacies of the hiring process}.

Intricate describes something with many interconnected parts or fine details that make it complex and difficult to follow or understand. An intricate {pattern} has elaborate ornamentation. An intricate {plot} has many interwoven threads. The word suggests complexity that rewards careful attention rather than confusion that frustrates: {the intricate workings of a watch}, {an intricate web of relationships}.

Intrigue has two main threads. As a noun, it means secret scheming or a clandestine plot: {palace intrigue}, {political intrigue}. It can also mean a secret romantic affair. As a verb, to intrigue someone is to arouse their curiosity or fascination: {The mystery intrigued her}. The noun sense emphasizes hidden machinations; the verb sense emphasizes captivated interest.

Intrigued describes a state of curiosity mixed with fascination—your interest has been piqued by something mysterious or unusual. {I'm intrigued by her theory}. The word implies more than casual interest; something has captured your attention and you want to know more. From the verb intrigue, which can mean to fascinate or to scheme secretly.

Intrigues are secret schemes or plots, often political: {palace intrigues}, {the intrigues of rival factions}. The word suggests covert maneuvering and hidden agendas. As a verb, intrigue means to arouse curiosity or fascination: {The mystery intrigued her}. It can also mean to scheme: {They intrigued against the king}. The noun carries darker connotations than the verb, which usually just means to interest.

Intriguing describes something that arouses curiosity or fascination, usually because it's mysterious, complex, or not immediately understood: {an intriguing possibility}, {The detective found the case intriguing}. Unlike merely interesting, intriguing suggests something that draws you in and makes you want to know more.

Intro is short for introduction—an opening segment that precedes the main content. Music tracks have intros before verses begin, television shows have intros with theme music and credits, and presentations have intros that set context: {Skip the intro and get to the point}. The word works as both noun and verb: {Let me intro you to my colleague}.

Introduce means to bring something or someone into a situation for the first time. You introduce a friend to your parents, a speaker to an audience, or a new policy to an organization. To introduce yourself is to tell someone your name upon first meeting. Introduce also means to present something new: {The company introduced a redesigned model}. In formal contexts, bills are introduced in legislatures. To introduce someone to a subject or activity is to give them their first experience of it: {My uncle introduced me to jazz}.
clues: Make two strangers know each other

definition: Introduced is the past tense of introduce—to bring something or someone into a situation for the first time. A person can be introduced to others at a party, or introduced to a new concept in school. Species introduced to foreign ecosystems may become invasive. Laws are introduced in legislatures. {She introduced me to jazz}. {The company introduced a new product line}.

Introduction is the act of bringing something into use or notice for the first time: {the introduction of vaccines transformed public health}. It also means presenting one person to another: {After a brief introduction, they shook hands}. An introduction to a book or speech sets up what follows. A course titled "Introduction to Philosophy" covers basic principles for beginners.

Introductions are the opening portions of books, speeches, or presentations—the part that comes before the main content and prepares you for it. Introductions are also the acts of presenting people to each other: {We skipped the introductions and got right to business}. An introduction to a subject is a basic or beginner-level treatment: {Introduction to Biology}.

Intros is the plural of intro, a clipped form of introduction. An intro is the opening section of a song, speech, essay, or broadcast—the part that sets up what follows: {The guitar intro goes on too long}. In casual speech, intro also means a personal introduction: {Can you give me an intro to your contact at the firm?}

Introspection is the examination of one's own thoughts, feelings, and mental states. The practice involves turning attention inward rather than outward: {A period of introspection followed his divorce}. Psychology distinguishes introspection from observation—you can observe someone's behavior but only introspect your own mind. The adjective is introspective: {an introspective person}, {introspective lyrics}.

Introspective describes a tendency to examine one's own thoughts, feelings, and mental processes. An introspective person spends time in self-reflection rather than focusing outward on the world or other people. The word often carries positive connotations of depth and self-awareness, though it can shade toward excessive self-absorption. {She became more introspective after the breakup.} Music, writing, or art may be called introspective when it explores the creator's inner life rather than external events.

Introversion is a personality orientation toward one's inner world rather than external stimulation. Introverts typically recharge through solitude and find extended social interaction draining, though this doesn't necessarily mean shyness or social anxiety. {After the party, I needed a day of introversion to recover}. The concept gained wide currency through the Myers-Briggs personality framework, where it contrasts with extroversion.

An introvert is a person who tends toward inner thoughts and feelings rather than external stimulation. Introverts often prefer solitary activities or small groups to large social gatherings, and may feel drained by extensive interaction: {As an introvert, she needed quiet time to recharge after parties}. The term comes from psychology but now describes personality more broadly. The verb introvert means to turn inward.

Introverted describes a temperament oriented toward inner experience rather than external stimulation. Introverted people tend to feel drained by extensive social interaction and recharged by solitude: {She's too introverted for sales work}. The trait exists on a spectrum with extroverted, and most people fall somewhere between the extremes.

Introverts are people who recharge through solitude rather than social interaction. The term comes from psychology, where introversion describes a personality oriented toward inner life rather than external stimulation. Introverts may enjoy company but find crowds draining: {As introverts, we skipped the afterparty}. The verb introverts means turns inward: {She introverts when stressed}.

To intrude is to enter where you're not welcome or wanted. A stranger intrudes on a private conversation; unwanted thoughts intrude on concentration. The word implies violation of boundaries—physical, social, or psychological: {I hope I'm not intruding}. Someone who intrudes is an intruder; the act is intrusion. {Reality has a way of intruding on our fantasies.}

An intruder is someone who enters a place without permission or welcome. The word typically implies unwanted presence—a burglar in a home, a hacker in a computer system, or simply someone who shows up uninvited: {The security system detected an intruder}. Intruder suggests violation of boundaries, whether physical, digital, or social.

Intruders are people who enter where they don't belong—typically a building, property, or space where they have no right to be. The word usually implies unwelcome presence and possible threat: {The alarm system detected intruders}. Security systems, guard dogs, and warning signs all address potential intruders. The term extends to anything that encroaches where it shouldn't: {Invasive species are intruders in native ecosystems}.

Intrusion is the act of entering where you're not wanted or welcome. A physical intrusion violates space: {The security system detected an intrusion}. Social intrusions violate privacy or solitude: {Forgive the intrusion, but I need to speak with you}. In geology, an intrusion is magma that forces its way into existing rock formations. The word carries connotations of unwelcome presence—something that pushes in where it doesn't belong.

Intrusions are unwanted entries or interruptions. A burglar's intrusion violates a home; an intrusion into someone's privacy violates personal boundaries. Geological intrusions occur when molten rock forces its way into existing formations. The word usually carries negative weight—intrusions are rarely welcome: {I apologize for the intrusion, but this is urgent}.

Intrusive describes something that forces itself where it isn't wanted or welcome. An intrusive {neighbor} pries into your business; intrusive {thoughts} are unwanted mental interruptions that arrive unbidden. The word applies to sounds, smells, questions, or presences that disrupt privacy or peace. In geology, intrusive rock forms when magma pushes into existing rock formations and solidifies underground—literally intruding into the surrounding material.

To intuit something is to know or sense it without conscious reasoning—to grasp through instinct rather than logic: {She intuited that something was wrong before anyone spoke}. The word suggests immediate, almost mystical understanding that bypasses evidence or analysis. It's the verb form of intuition, used when someone arrives at knowledge through feeling rather than thinking. (Capitalized Intuit is a software company.)

Intuition is knowledge or understanding that arrives without conscious reasoning—a sense of something that bypasses deliberate thought. You might have an intuition that something is wrong, or trust your intuition when making decisions: {My intuition told me not to take the job}. The word often implies a kind of direct perception, as if truth were felt rather than figured out. Some treat intuition as mystical; others see it as pattern recognition operating below awareness.

Intuitive describes knowledge or understanding that comes without conscious reasoning—you grasp it directly rather than working it out step by step. An intuitive {person} relies on gut feelings. An intuitive {interface} feels natural to use without instruction. {She had an intuitive sense that something was wrong}. The word suggests immediate comprehension rather than learned skill, though what feels intuitive often reflects deep familiarity.

Intuitively describes doing or knowing something through instinct rather than conscious reasoning. If you {intuitively grasp} a concept, you understand it without working through the steps. Something that works {intuitively} feels natural and requires no instruction: {The interface is intuitively designed}. The word often implies that understanding comes easily or automatically.

Inundated means flooded or overwhelmed. Water inundates low-lying areas during storms. More often the word describes being swamped with an excessive quantity of something: {We were inundated with applications}, {inundated by emails}. The suggestion is of being unable to keep up with the volume.

To invade is to enter territory with hostile intent, typically with military force: {Germany invaded Poland in 1939}. The word extends to any unwelcome intrusion—invading someone's privacy, invasive species invading ecosystems, or thoughts invading your mind. Cancer invades surrounding tissue by spreading into it. The noun is invasion.

Invaded is the past tense of invade—to enter a place by force, typically with hostile intent. Armies invade countries; pests invade homes. The word extends to unwelcome intrusion: {Tourists invaded the quiet village}. Privacy can be invaded, and so can personal space. {Cancer had invaded the surrounding tissue.}

An invader is someone or something that enters by force or without permission—typically a military force crossing into another country's territory: {The invaders swept through the countryside}. The term extends to anything unwelcome that intrudes: invasive species are ecological invaders, and viruses are invaders of the body. In video games, Space Invaders established a genre.

Invaders are people or forces that enter a place by force, typically with hostile intent. Armies invade countries, pests invade gardens, and unwanted thoughts invade the mind. The word carries connotations of violation and unwelcome intrusion: {The invaders burned the village}. In science fiction, invaders often means aliens attacking Earth.

Invading is the present participle of invade—entering a place by force, typically with hostile intent. Armies invade countries; pests invade homes. The word extends to unwelcome intrusions generally: {You're invading my personal space}. An invading {army}, invading {species}, or invading {force} represents something entering where it doesn't belong.

Invalid has two distinct pronunciations with different meanings. With stress on the first syllable, an invalid is a person weakened by illness or disability: {She spent years caring for her invalid mother}. With stress on the second syllable, invalid means not valid—legally void, logically unsound, or technically rejected: {an invalid passport}, {an invalid argument}, {invalid data}. The verb invalidate means to render something void or ineffective.

To invalidate is to render something null, void, or ineffective. A court may invalidate a contract found to violate law. New evidence can invalidate a scientific theory. Failing to follow proper procedures might invalidate an election. The word also applies to dismissing someone's feelings or experiences: {Don't invalidate her concerns just because you disagree}.

Invalidated is the past tense and past participle of invalidate, meaning to make something no longer valid or legally binding. Documents, contracts, and agreements can be invalidated by courts or authorities when procedural errors or violations are discovered: {The court invalidated the election results due to widespread fraud}. In technical contexts, data or cache entries are invalidated when they become outdated or unreliable. The term also applies to arguments or theories rendered unsound by new evidence or logical flaws.

Invalidating is the present participle of invalidate, meaning to render something null, void, or without force. Legal documents, contracts, and patents can be invalidated when they fail to meet required standards or when new evidence emerges. In psychology, invalidating describes behavior that dismisses or minimizes someone's feelings: {His response felt invalidating—like my concerns didn't matter}. Test results may be invalidated by procedural errors or contamination.
clues: Proving something to be without merit

definition: Invalidation is the act of rendering something null, void, or without force. A court may order the invalidation of a contract. In computing, cache invalidation removes outdated data. Psychologically, invalidation means dismissing or denying someone's feelings: {Telling someone they're overreacting is a form of invalidation}.

Invaluable means extremely valuable—so precious that its worth cannot be measured: {Her advice proved invaluable during the crisis}. Despite the negative prefix, invaluable doesn't mean "not valuable" but rather "beyond valuation." The word applies to things whose worth exceeds any price: invaluable {experience}, invaluable {contributions}, an invaluable {resource}.

An invasion is the entry of a military force into territory to conquer or occupy it: {the invasion of Normandy}. The word extends to any unwelcome intrusion in large numbers: an invasion of {tourists}, an invasion of {privacy}. Invasive species spread aggressively into new ecosystems. Medical procedures are invasive when they enter the body.

Invasions is the plural of invasion—acts of entering by force, typically military forces crossing into hostile territory: {The invasions of Poland marked the beginning of World War II}. The word extends to unwelcome intrusions of any kind: {invasions of privacy}, {invasions of pests}. In medicine, invasion describes how disease spreads into tissue: {The tumor showed signs of vascular invasion}.

Invasive describes something that intrudes where it doesn't belong or spreads aggressively. An invasive {species} colonizes new territory and displaces native life. An invasive {procedure} enters the body surgically. Invasive {questions} probe into private matters. The word carries connotations of unwelcome encroachment—whether biological, medical, or personal.

To invent is to create something that didn't exist before—a device, method, or concept: {Edison invented the phonograph}. The word implies originality rather than discovery of something already present. Invent also means to fabricate or make up: {She invented an excuse for being late}. An invention can be a useful creation or a lie.

Invented is the past tense of invent—to create something new, whether a device, method, or idea: {Edison invented the phonograph}, {Who invented the wheel?} Invented also describes things fabricated or made up rather than real: {an invented excuse}, {The whole story was invented}. To say someone {invented the game} can mean they originated it or that they excel at it.

Inventing is creating something that didn't exist before—a device, method, or concept: {She's inventing a new kind of solar panel}. The word also covers fabricating stories or excuses: {He's inventing reasons not to go}. Both senses share the idea of bringing something into being from imagination rather than discovery.

Invention is the act of creating something new, especially a device or method that didn't exist before: {The invention of the printing press transformed society}. An invention is also the thing created: {The telephone was Bell's most famous invention}. The word extends to fabricated stories or lies: {His alibi was pure invention}. In rhetoric and music, invention refers to the creative faculty or a compositional exercise.

Inventions are things created or devised for the first time—new devices, processes, or ideas that didn't exist before. The telephone was an invention; so was democracy. Invention also names the act of creating: {Necessity is the mother of invention}. Extended to stories, invention means fabrication: {The whole tale was pure invention}.

Inventive describes someone or something showing creativity and originality, especially in solving problems or creating new things. An inventive person devises clever solutions; an inventive approach finds unexpected ways forward: {She came up with an inventive use for leftover bread}. The word suggests resourcefulness and imagination rather than mere novelty.

An inventor is a person who creates something new—a device, method, or process that didn't exist before. The term typically applies to practical or technical innovations: {the inventor of the telephone}, {a prolific inventor with dozens of patents}. Unlike a discoverer, who finds what already exists, an inventor brings something into being.

Inventors are people who create or devise new things—machines, processes, methods, or ideas not previously existing. The term typically applies to those who conceive original devices or techniques: {Edison was among history's most prolific inventors}. While inventor emphasizes novelty and ingenuity, it often overlaps with innovator, though the latter may improve rather than originate.

Inventory is a complete list of items, especially goods held by a business for sale or use. A store's inventory includes everything on its shelves and in its warehouse. To inventory something is to count and catalog it: {We inventory the stockroom every quarter}. The word extends to any systematic accounting: {a personal inventory of strengths and weaknesses}. When inventory runs low, supplies are nearly depleted.

Invents is the third-person singular of invent, meaning to create something new—a device, method, or concept that didn't exist before: {She invents gadgets in her garage}. It also means to fabricate or make up: {He invents excuses whenever he's late}. The line between creating and fabricating often involves whether the invention serves truth or evades it.

Inverse describes something reversed in position, order, or effect. An inverse relationship means one thing increases as another decreases: {There's an inverse correlation between exercise and heart disease}. In mathematics, an inverse operation undoes another—subtraction is the inverse of addition. The noun refers to the reversed form itself: {The inverse is also true}.

Inversion is a reversal of position, order, or relationship. In grammar, subject-verb inversion creates questions: {Is she coming?} In music, an inverted chord has a note other than the root in the bass. Temperature inversion occurs when warm air traps cooler air below, often worsening smog. Sexual inversion is an outdated term for homosexuality. To invert is to turn upside down or inside out.

Inversions are reversals of normal order or position. In grammar, inversion puts the verb before the subject: {Said he, "I disagree"}. In music, an inverted chord has a note other than the root in the bass. Weather inversions trap warm air above cool air, holding pollution near the ground. In yoga, inversions are poses where the head goes below the heart. The word covers any flip from expected arrangement.

To invert is to turn something upside down or reverse its position, order, or relationship: {She inverted the cake onto a plate}.
