In music, to invert a chord is to rearrange its notes so a different one is on the bottom. An invert is something inverted—in plumbing, the lowest point of a pipe's interior. The word once served as clinical terminology for a homosexual, now archaic and offensive.

Inverted means turned upside down, reversed, or placed in the opposite position or order. An inverted {image} appears flipped. {Inverted commas} is the British term for quotation marks. In grammar, inverted word order puts the verb before the subject: {Never have I seen such a thing}. Something inverted has been flipped from its usual orientation.

To invest is to commit money or resources expecting future returns: {She invested in real estate}, {They invested heavily in tech stocks}. The word extends to non-financial commitments—you invest time, energy, or emotion in relationships, projects, or causes. To be {invested in} something is to care about its outcome. In older or ceremonial usage, to invest someone is to formally confer authority or office: {The bishop was invested with his new responsibilities}.

Invested describes having put resources into something with the expectation of return—money into stocks, time into a project, energy into a relationship. Beyond the financial sense, invested means emotionally committed or having a stake in an outcome: {I'm really invested in how this turns out}. The more invested you are, the more the result matters to you.

To investigate is to examine something systematically to discover facts or establish truth. Police investigate crimes, journalists investigate scandals, scientists investigate phenomena. The word implies methodical inquiry rather than casual looking: {We're investigating reports of fraud}. An investigation can be formal or informal, but it suggests deliberate effort to uncover what isn't immediately apparent.

Investigating is examining something closely to uncover facts or determine the truth. Police investigate crimes, journalists investigate scandals, and scientists investigate phenomena. The word implies methodical inquiry—gathering evidence, questioning sources, following leads: {They're investigating what caused the explosion}. To be {under investigation} is to be the subject of such scrutiny.

Investigation is a systematic search for facts or truth. Police conduct investigations into crimes; journalists investigate corruption; scientists investigate phenomena. The word implies methodical inquiry—gathering evidence, interviewing witnesses, examining records. An investigation can be formal and official or informal and personal: {The committee launched an investigation}, {I did some investigation and found the best price}.

Investigations is the plural of investigation—a systematic effort to find facts or uncover truth. Police conduct investigations into crimes. Journalists pursue investigations into corruption. The word suggests careful, methodical inquiry: {The investigations revealed widespread fraud}. An investigation can be formal (congressional, criminal) or informal (a parent's investigation into who broke the lamp).

Investigative describes work that involves systematic inquiry or examination, especially to uncover hidden facts. Most often applied to journalism or reporting that digs beneath official accounts: {investigative journalism}, {an investigative reporter}. Also describes agencies or procedures focused on inquiry: {investigative powers}, {investigative techniques}. The work implies persistence, skepticism, and following evidence wherever it leads.

An investigator is someone who examines facts to uncover the truth. The word applies across contexts: police investigators solve crimes, private investigators work for hire, and investigators for government agencies probe fraud or misconduct. {The lead investigator questioned witnesses for three hours.} Insurance companies employ investigators to verify claims. In research contexts, principal investigators lead scientific studies.

Investigators are people who examine something systematically to discover facts or information. The term covers police detectives investigating crimes, journalists investigating corruption, and private investigators hired to gather information on individuals. Insurance companies employ investigators to verify claims. {Federal investigators are looking into the company's finances.}

Investing is putting money into something with the expectation of future profit or return. You invest in stocks, bonds, real estate, or a friend's startup. The term extends beyond finance: investing time or energy in a relationship means committing resources to something you hope will pay off. {She's been investing heavily in tech stocks}. {I've invested too much in this project to quit now}.

Investment is the commitment of resources—usually money—with the expectation of future returns or benefits. You make an investment in stocks, real estate, or a business. The term extends beyond finance: {an investment of time and energy}, {an investment in your education}. Something described as an investment justifies its cost through lasting value: {Good shoes are an investment}.

Investments are assets acquired with the expectation of future returns—stocks, bonds, real estate, or other holdings meant to grow in value or generate income: {She diversified her investments across several sectors}. The term extends to anything you put resources into hoping for later benefit: {Education is an investment in your future}. Time, money, and effort can all be investments when spent strategically rather than consumed.

An investor is a person or entity that commits money to something with the expectation of financial return. Investors buy stocks, bonds, real estate, or stakes in businesses, hoping the value will increase or generate income: {Early investors in the company became millionaires}. The term sometimes carries connotations of wealth or sophistication that distinguish investors from ordinary savers.

Investors are people or institutions that commit money to ventures expecting financial returns. The term covers anyone from individuals buying stocks to firms funding startups. An investor typically accepts some risk in exchange for potential profit: {The company is seeking investors for its expansion}. {Investors fled the market when prices collapsed}.

To invigorate is to give energy or vitality to something or someone. A brisk walk invigorates the body; new leadership invigorates a struggling organization. The word suggests not just activation but renewal—restoring vigor that was depleted or dormant: {The cold shower invigorated him}. Invigorating describes things that produce this effect: {invigorating mountain air}, {an invigorating debate}.

Invigorated means filled with energy or renewed strength. Something that invigorates restores vitality—a brisk walk, a cold shower, an encouraging conversation. {She felt invigorated after her morning swim.} {The team came back invigorated from the break.} The word suggests a refreshing boost rather than mere alertness.
clues: Given a new burst of energy

definition: Invigorating describes something that fills you with energy or vitality. A brisk morning walk can be invigorating; so can a cold shower, a challenging debate, or a change of scenery. The word suggests renewal and stimulation: {The mountain air was invigorating}. What invigorates varies by person—some find crowds energizing while others need solitude.

Invincibility is the state of being impossible to defeat or overcome. The word often appears in contexts of fantasy, gaming, or hyperbole: {The power-up grants temporary invincibility}, {He fought with a sense of invincibility}. A feeling of invincibility is the confidence—often misplaced—that nothing can harm you.

Invincible means incapable of being conquered or defeated. An invincible army cannot be beaten in battle. The word often carries hyperbolic force—{She felt invincible after her promotion}—suggesting supreme confidence rather than literal indestructibility. An invincible argument is one that cannot be successfully challenged.

Invincibles refers to a group considered unbeatable or supremely dominant. In sports, it typically describes teams that complete a season without losing: {Arsenal's Invincibles went undefeated in the 2003-04 Premier League}. The term carries both admiration and historical weight—once applied, it tends to stick.

Invisibility is the state of being unable to be seen. The word applies literally to things that don't reflect or absorb visible light, like air or glass, and to fictional powers: {The cloak granted him invisibility}. More often it describes being overlooked or ignored: {the invisibility of homeless people in wealthy neighborhoods}, {She spoke about the invisibility of women's labor}.

Invisible means unable to be seen. Something may be invisible because it's too small, too distant, or transparent: {The bacteria are invisible to the naked eye}. Invisible also describes things that go unnoticed or unacknowledged: {invisible labor}, {invisible to the system}. The invisible hand in economics refers to market forces operating without central direction.

An invitation is a request for someone's presence or participation: {We sent out wedding invitations}, {an invitation to speak at the conference}. To extend an invitation is to offer one; to accept or decline is to respond. Figuratively, something that invites trouble or criticism is an invitation to it: {Leaving your car unlocked is an invitation to theft}.

Invitational describes an event restricted to invited participants rather than open to all comers: an invitational {tournament}, an invitational {track meet}. As a noun, it's shorthand for such competitions: {She qualified for the invitational}. Common in sports, where invitationals bring together selected athletes or teams.

Invitations are requests for someone's presence or participation. A formal invitation to a wedding or gala typically comes printed on quality paper; casual invitations to parties or hangouts might be texted or spoken. The word extends beyond social gatherings: {an open invitation to disaster} suggests circumstances that make trouble likely. Something inviting—appealing or tempting—can be described as an invitation: {The unlocked car was an invitation to thieves}.

To invite is to ask someone to come somewhere or participate in something: {We invited them to dinner}, {She invited questions from the audience}. Invite also means to encourage or make likely: {Leaving the door unlocked invites trouble}. As a noun, invite is casual for invitation: {Did you get an invite to the party?}

Invited is the past tense and past participle of invite, describing someone who has been asked to attend an event, join a group, or participate in something. To be invited suggests welcome inclusion—you don't crash a party if you're invited. The word also works as an adjective: {an invited guest}, {invited speakers at the conference}. When something is described as having invited trouble or criticism, it means the situation provoked or encouraged that response.

Inviting describes something that attracts or tempts you to approach, enter, or participate. An inviting {smile} welcomes you. An inviting {aroma} draws you toward the kitchen. A less inviting prospect is one you'd rather avoid: {The thought of cleaning the garage was not exactly inviting}. The word suggests appeal that pulls you in.

An invocation is a calling upon something for assistance or authority—a deity, a muse, a principle: {The poem opens with an invocation to the gods}. Legal or formal contexts invoke rights or precedents: {an invocation of the Fifth Amendment}. In computing, an invocation is a call to execute a function or program. The opening prayer at a ceremony is also called an invocation.

Invocations are acts of calling upon something for aid or authority. A prayer is an invocation of divine help. A lawyer's invocation of the Fifth Amendment appeals to constitutional protection. In computing, an invocation is a call to execute a function or program: {Each invocation of the script generates a new log file}. The word carries a sense of summoning or activating something powerful.

An invoice is a document itemizing goods or services provided and the amount owed: {The contractor sent an invoice for the repairs}. To invoice is to bill someone or send such a document: {We'll invoice you at the end of the month}. In business contexts, invoices serve as formal requests for payment and records for accounting.

To invoke is to call upon something for aid or authority—invoking a {deity}, invoking the {Fifth Amendment}, invoking someone's {name}. The word suggests deliberate summoning: a lawyer invokes precedent, a speaker invokes the memory of fallen heroes. In computing, to invoke a function or command is to execute it. The noun is invocation.

Invoked is the past tense of invoke, meaning to call upon for aid or authority. You invoke a {deity}, a {law}, or someone's {name} to lend weight to an argument. In computing, to invoke a function or command is to execute it: {The script invoked the database query}. To invoke a feeling is to summon it: {The music invoked memories of childhood}.

Invokes is the third-person singular form of invoke, meaning to call upon something for aid, support, or authority. When someone invokes a law or principle, they cite it as justification: {She invokes the Fifth Amendment}. To invoke a deity or spirit is to summon or appeal to it through prayer or ritual. In computing, invoking a function or command means to execute or activate it. The word often carries a sense of deliberate appeal to something powerful or authoritative.

Invoking is calling upon something for aid, support, or authority. You invoke a deity in prayer, invoke the Fifth Amendment to avoid self-incrimination, or invoke someone's name to lend weight to an argument: {She kept invoking her father's legacy}. In computing, invoking a function or command means executing it. The word carries a sense of summoning—bringing something powerful into the present situation.

Involuntary describes actions or responses that happen without conscious choice or intention. An involuntary {muscle twitch} or {gasp} occurs automatically, beyond one's control. The term also applies to situations imposed on someone against their will: {involuntary manslaughter} involves unintentional killing, and {involuntary servitude} is forced labor. Involuntary can characterize both bodily reflexes and legal or social circumstances where consent is absent.

Involve means to include as a necessary part or consequence: {The job involves a lot of travel}. It also means to draw someone into participation or entanglement: {Don't involve me in your schemes}. To be involved with someone suggests a close relationship, often romantic: {She's involved with a coworker}. An involved explanation is complicated or intricate.

Involved means engaged or participating in something: {She's heavily involved in local politics}. It also describes something complicated or intricate: {an involved explanation}, {involved legal proceedings}. To be involved with someone suggests a romantic or sexual relationship: {They've been involved for months}. Getting involved often implies commitment beyond casual interest.

Involvement is the state of being connected to or participating in something. It often implies active engagement rather than passive presence: {Her involvement in the project was crucial to its success}. The word can suggest varying degrees of commitment, from casual participation to deep entanglement. When someone's involvement in wrongdoing is discovered, it means evidence links them to the act. Romantic or sexual involvement refers to an intimate relationship, sometimes one that complicates other matters.

Invulnerability is the state of being impossible to harm, damage, or defeat. The term appears in discussions of superheroes, video game mechanics, and military technology: {The power-up grants temporary invulnerability}. More abstractly, it describes emotional or psychological imperviousness: {His wealth gave him a sense of invulnerability}. True invulnerability rarely exists outside fiction—the word often signals overconfidence.

Invulnerable means incapable of being wounded, damaged, or harmed. The word often describes mythical heroes or supernatural beings: {Achilles was invulnerable except at his heel}. More commonly it appears in figurative contexts—someone invulnerable to criticism, a position invulnerable to attack, an argument invulnerable to objection. The word suggests absolute protection, though in practice it's usually hyperbole.

Inward describes direction toward the inside or center: {The door swings inward}. It also means toward one's own mind or spirit rather than the external world: {an inward journey}, {inward reflection}. As an adjective, inward describes what lies within: {inward thoughts}, {inward peace}. The adverb form inwardly means privately or mentally: {She smiled inwardly}.

Iodine is a chemical element, a dark purple-gray solid that sublimates into a violet vapor with a sharp odor. Essential in trace amounts for thyroid function, iodine is added to table salt to prevent deficiency. In medicine, iodine solutions serve as antiseptics for wounds: {The nurse swabbed iodine on the cut}. Iodine compounds are also used in photography and water purification.

An ion is an atom or molecule that carries an electrical charge because it has gained or lost electrons. Positive ions (cations) have lost electrons; negative ions (anions) have gained them. Ions are fundamental to chemistry and physics, appearing in contexts from battery technology to biological processes: {Sodium ions cross the cell membrane}. Salt dissolved in water breaks into ions.

The ionosphere is a region of Earth's upper atmosphere, roughly 50 to 600 miles up, where solar radiation ionizes gas molecules and creates layers of electrically charged particles. These layers reflect radio waves back to Earth, enabling long-distance radio communication: {The signal bounced off the ionosphere to reach receivers thousands of miles away}. The ionosphere also produces auroras when solar particles interact with atmospheric gases.

Ions is the plural of ion, an atom or molecule carrying an electrical charge because it has gained or lost electrons. Positive ions (cations) have lost electrons; negative ions (anions) have gained them. Ions are fundamental to chemistry, biology, and physics: {The solution contains sodium and chloride ions}. Ion drives propel spacecraft; ionic bonds hold salts together.

Iota is the ninth letter of the Greek alphabet, but in English it almost always means a tiny amount: {There's not an iota of truth in that story}, {It won't change things one iota}. The sense comes from iota being the smallest Greek letter—a single vertical stroke.

Iridescence is the property of surfaces that appear to shift color when viewed from different angles—like oil on water, soap bubbles, or a hummingbird's throat. The effect comes from light waves interfering with each other rather than from pigment. {The shell's iridescence caught the light as she turned it in her hand.}

Iridescent describes surfaces that shimmer with rainbow-like colors that shift as the viewing angle changes. The effect comes from light interference rather than pigment—soap bubbles, oil slicks, peacock feathers, and abalone shells are iridescent. The word suggests something luminous and slightly magical: {Her dress had an iridescent sheen that caught the light}.

The iris is the colored part of the eye surrounding the pupil, controlling how much light enters. The word also names a genus of flowering plants with showy blooms in purple, blue, yellow, or white—the distinctive petals supposedly resembling the eye structure. In optics and photography, an iris is an adjustable diaphragm that regulates light passage: {The camera's iris opened in low light}. (Capitalized Iris is a proper name.)

Irises is the plural of iris, which names several things united by circular or radiating form. The iris of the eye is the colored ring surrounding the pupil that controls how much light enters. Irises are also showy flowers with sword-shaped leaves and petals that fan outward, often purple or blue but found in many colors. In optics, an iris or iris diaphragm is an adjustable aperture that regulates light passage, mimicking the eye's function.

To irk is to annoy or irritate, typically in a mild but persistent way. What irks you gets under your skin without necessarily enraging you: {It irks me when people don't use their turn signals}. The adjective irksome describes something that produces this nagging annoyance: {irksome delays}, {irksome chores}.

Irked means annoyed or mildly irritated. The word suggests a low-grade frustration rather than serious anger—more a persistent bother than an outburst: {She was irked by his constant interruptions}. Something that irks you gets under your skin without quite provoking rage.

Irks means annoys or irritates, usually in a mild but persistent way. What irks you gets under your skin without rising to real anger: {It irks me when people don't use their turn signals}. The word suggests petty grievances rather than serious offenses.

The strong and durable metal we call iron gives rise to all other meanings of the word. It’s a handy metaphor for things that are strong and hard to resist, in phrases like iron will and iron fist. Some things originally made of iron are called irons, like the household appliance for removing wrinkles from clothes, the golf club, the branding tool, and shackles for the arms or legs. Someone who pumps iron lifts weights for bodybuilding. Irons in the fire is a metaphor relating to blacksmithing, and refers to current activities or projects. As a verb, iron means to make smooth, either literally (iron the dress) or metaphorically (iron out your differences).

Ironclad means protected by iron armor or, more commonly, so firm and unassailable that it cannot be broken or challenged. An ironclad {contract} has no loopholes. An ironclad {alibi} cannot be questioned. An ironclad {guarantee} is absolute. Historically, an ironclad was a 19th-century warship armored with metal plates—the source of the figurative sense of impenetrability.

Ironclads were warships of the mid-19th century protected by iron or steel armor plating, revolutionary in naval warfare because they could withstand cannon fire that would destroy wooden vessels. The term evokes the American Civil War, when the USS Monitor and CSS Virginia famously clashed. As an adjective, ironclad means impossible to break or dispute: an ironclad {contract}, an ironclad {alibi}.

Ironfisted describes harsh, unyielding control—ruling or managing with an iron fist. An ironfisted {dictator} tolerates no dissent. An ironfisted {coach} enforces strict discipline. The image is of a hand clenched in metal, allowing no flexibility or mercy. Also spelled iron-fisted.

Ironic describes situations where outcomes contradict expectations, often with a twist of fate: {It's ironic that the fire station burned down}. The word also applies to speech that conveys meaning through deliberate understatement or reversal: {Nice weather, he said ironically, as rain poured down}. Casual usage has broadened ironic to mean merely coincidental or unfortunate, which irritates purists but reflects how the word actually functions in contemporary speech.

Ironically marks a statement as ironic—expressing the opposite of what's meant, or noting an outcome that contradicts expectations. {Ironically, the fire station burned down}. {He said, ironically, that he just loved waiting in line}. In casual speech, ironically often means merely coincidentally or surprisingly, a usage that irritates purists but has become widespread.

Ironing is the act of pressing clothes or fabric with a heated iron to remove wrinkles. The word also refers to items waiting to be ironed or just ironed: {I have a pile of ironing to do}, {She folded the ironing}. An ironing board is the padded surface used for the task.

Ironman typically refers to an extreme endurance race combining a 2.4-mile swim, 112-mile bike ride, and full marathon run—or to someone who competes in one. More broadly, an ironman is anyone who demonstrates exceptional stamina or toughness: {He's the ironman of the department, never missing a day}. In baseball, an ironman plays every game without rest.

Irons is the plural of iron—metal restraints for the wrists or ankles: {The prisoner was clapped in irons}. A golfer's irons are clubs with metal heads, distinguished from woods. To have {many irons in the fire} is to pursue multiple projects simultaneously. If something is {in the irons}, it's stalled or stuck—from sailing, when a ship faces into the wind and can't move.

An ironwoman is a woman of exceptional strength, endurance, or toughness. The term often refers specifically to a female competitor in Ironman triathlons—grueling races combining swimming, cycling, and running: {She became an ironwoman after completing her first Ironman}. More broadly, it describes any woman who handles demanding circumstances with remarkable stamina.

Ironwork is objects or structures made from iron, especially decorative pieces like gates, railings, fences, and balconies: {The building's ornate ironwork dates to the 1890s}. The term often implies craftsmanship—wrought or forged pieces rather than mass-produced metal. In the plural, ironworks refers to a factory where iron is smelted or processed.

An ironworker is a tradesperson who works with structural iron and steel—erecting frameworks for buildings, bridges, and other structures. The job involves connecting steel beams at heights, often walking narrow beams high above the ground: {Ironworkers bolted the girders into place thirty stories up}. The term also applies to workers in iron foundries or ornamental metalwork shops.

An ironworks is a factory or industrial facility where iron is smelted, cast, or manufactured into products. The word typically appears as a singular noun despite the plural form: {The old ironworks has been converted into a museum}. Historic ironworks were central to early industrialization, producing everything from nails to cannons.

Irony is easily recognizable, but hard to define. The feature that most often characterizes irony is the presence of two contradictory or opposite things, such as when you say one thing but really mean the opposite: There was irony in her voice as she praised the officials for their efforts. Sometimes the contrast in irony is between expectations and reality: Oh the irony! Right after I rented the convertible, it started to rain.

Irrational describes thinking or behavior not guided by reason: {an irrational fear of spiders}, {She became irrational when confronted with the evidence}. The word often implies emotion overriding logic. In mathematics, an irrational number cannot be expressed as a ratio of two integers—pi and the square root of 2 are irrational. The mathematical and everyday senses share the idea of something that doesn't resolve neatly.

Irrationality is the quality of being unreasonable or contrary to logic. It describes thinking or behavior that defies rational analysis: {the irrationality of panic buying}, {the irrationality of his jealousy}. In mathematics, irrationality refers to numbers that cannot be expressed as simple fractions, like pi. The word often carries judgment—calling something irrational implies it should submit to reason but doesn't.

Irreconcilable describes things that cannot be brought into agreement or harmony. Irreconcilable {differences} between spouses are grounds for divorce—conflicts so fundamental that resolution is impossible. Irreconcilable {accounts} of an event contradict each other in ways that can't both be true. The noun form refers to a person or faction unwilling to compromise: {The irreconcilables in the party blocked any deal}.

Irredeemable describes something that cannot be saved, recovered, or made good again. An irredeemable {mistake} has consequences that can't be undone. An irredeemable {person} is beyond moral redemption. In finance, irredeemable bonds cannot be exchanged for cash before maturity. The word often carries a note of finality: {The situation was irredeemable}.

Irrefutable describes something that cannot be denied or disproven: {irrefutable evidence}, {an irrefutable argument}. The word implies such overwhelming force that any attempt at contradiction would fail. It often appears in legal and academic contexts where the strength of proof matters: {The DNA evidence was irrefutable}.

Irregular means deviating from what is regular, standard, or expected. An irregular heartbeat doesn't follow the normal rhythm. Irregular hours vary unpredictably. Irregular verbs don't follow standard conjugation patterns. The word can suggest something improper or unauthorized: {irregular accounting practices}, {irregular troop movements}. As a noun, irregulars are guerrilla fighters operating outside conventional military structure.

Irregularities are deviations from what is standard, expected, or uniform. The word often implies something wrong: {accounting irregularities} suggests financial misconduct, {irregularities in the election} suggests fraud or procedural failures. In medicine, irregularities describe abnormal patterns: {heart irregularities}, {menstrual irregularities}. The term can also simply mean unevenness: {irregularities in the surface}.

Irregularity is deviation from what is regular, standard, or expected. A heart irregularity is an abnormal rhythm. An irregularity in accounting suggests something suspicious or improper: {Auditors discovered irregularities in the company's books}. The word also refers to lack of evenness or uniformity: {irregularities in the surface}. As a euphemism, irregularity means constipation or inconsistent bowel movements.

Irregulars are soldiers or fighters not belonging to a regular army—guerrillas, partisans, or militia operating outside conventional military structure: {The irregulars harassed supply lines throughout the occupation}. In retail, irregulars are goods sold at a discount because of minor flaws or imperfections: {These socks are irregulars—small defects, big savings}.

Irrelevance is the quality of having no bearing on the matter at hand. An irrelevance is something that doesn't connect to what's being discussed or decided: {His personal life is an irrelevance to the question of his qualifications}. The word often carries dismissive force—calling something an irrelevance suggests it shouldn't have been raised at all.

Irrelevant means not connected to or bearing on the matter at hand. Evidence is irrelevant if it doesn't pertain to the case. A detail is irrelevant if it doesn't affect the outcome: {Your personal feelings are irrelevant to the decision}. Something can also be irrelevant in the sense of unimportant or outdated: {Print media has become increasingly irrelevant}.

Irreparable describes damage or harm that cannot be fixed or undone: {irreparable harm}, {irreparable damage to their relationship}. The word appears frequently in legal contexts, where plaintiffs must show irreparable injury to obtain injunctions. Unlike merely serious damage, irreparable damage has no adequate remedy—what's broken stays broken.

Irreplaceable describes something so unique or valuable that nothing else could serve in its place: {The fire destroyed irreplaceable family photographs}. The word emphasizes singularity—an irreplaceable employee has skills or knowledge no substitute could match; an irreplaceable heirloom carries meaning beyond its material worth. Often used for emphasis even when replacement is technically possible.

Irrepressible describes something that cannot be held back or restrained. An irrepressible {laugh} bursts out despite efforts to contain it. An irrepressible {optimist} stays cheerful no matter the circumstances. The word often carries positive connotations—suggesting vitality, spirit, or enthusiasm that refuses to be suppressed: {Her irrepressible energy lifted everyone's mood}.

Irresistible describes something impossible to resist—so appealing, compelling, or powerful that you cannot help but yield to it. An irresistible {urge} overcomes willpower. An irresistible {offer} is too good to refuse. Someone irresistible has overwhelming charm or attractiveness: {She found him absolutely irresistible}. The word often carries a note of pleasurable surrender.

Irresponsibility is the quality of not taking obligations seriously or failing to consider consequences. It can describe a pattern of behavior—{His irresponsibility with money cost him everything}—or a single lapse: {It was an act of pure irresponsibility to leave the children alone}. The word often carries moral judgment, implying someone should have known better.

Irresponsible describes someone who fails to take proper care or consideration for consequences. An irresponsible person neglects duties, makes reckless decisions, or acts without regard for how their actions affect others: {It was irresponsible to leave the children unsupervised}. The word often carries moral judgment—suggesting not just carelessness but a character flaw. Irresponsible can also describe actions or policies: {irresponsible spending}, {irresponsible journalism}.

Irreverence is a lack of respect or seriousness toward things typically treated as sacred, dignified, or important. The word often carries positive connotations—irreverent humor punctures pomposity and questions authority: {The show's irreverence toward politicians made it popular}. But irreverence can also suggest inappropriate flippancy: {His irreverence at the funeral offended the family}.

Irreverent means lacking the expected respect or seriousness toward something usually treated as sacred or important. An irreverent comedian mocks religion; an irreverent biography treats its subject without reverence. The word often carries approval—irreverent humor is bold and refreshing rather than merely disrespectful: {Her irreverent take on royal tradition delighted younger audiences}.

Irreversible describes something that cannot be undone or returned to its original state. The word applies to processes, decisions, and changes that are permanent: {irreversible damage}, {irreversible decline}. Medical contexts use it for conditions beyond recovery: {irreversible brain damage}, {irreversible coma}. What's irreversible admits no remedy or reversal—once done, it's done.

Irrigation is the artificial supply of water to land for growing crops. Most agriculture depends on rainfall, but irrigation allows farming in dry regions and during droughts: {The valley's irrigation system channels water from the river to surrounding farms}. In medicine, irrigation means flushing a wound or body cavity with water or saline solution.

Irritability is a tendency to become annoyed or angered easily. Someone in a state of irritability snaps at small provocations: {His irritability worsened when he was tired}. In medicine and biology, irritability refers to the capacity of tissue or an organism to respond to stimuli—a muscle's irritability, for instance, is its ability to contract when stimulated.
clues: State of being easily set off

definition: Irritable describes a tendency to become annoyed or angered easily. Someone irritable is quick to snap or lose patience: {She gets irritable when she's hungry}. The word often implies a temporary state rather than a permanent trait—fatigue, stress, or illness can make anyone irritable. Irritable bowel syndrome is a digestive condition marked by the gut's oversensitivity to stimuli.

An irritant is something that causes annoyance or discomfort. The word applies equally to physical and emotional provocations: a chemical irritant inflames skin or airways, while a social irritant grates on the nerves. {The new policy was a constant irritant to staff.} As an adjective, irritant describes things that cause irritation: {irritant substances}, {irritant effects}.

Irritants are things that cause annoyance, discomfort, or inflammation. The term applies equally to substances that inflame tissue—chemical irritants, skin irritants—and to people or situations that provoke frustration: {Minor irritants in a relationship can build into major problems}. {Pollen and dust are common respiratory irritants.}

Irritate means to annoy or provoke mild anger: {His constant humming irritated everyone in the office}. The word suggests persistent, low-grade aggravation rather than explosive fury. In medical contexts, irritate describes physical inflammation or sensitivity: {Smoke irritates the eyes}. {The rough fabric irritated her skin}. Something irritating produces this effect; an irritant is the cause.

Irritated describes mild anger or annoyance, often from repeated or persistent provocation: {She was irritated by his constant interruptions}. The word also applies to physical discomfort—skin becomes irritated from friction or chemicals, eyes from dust or allergies. Both senses share the idea of something being rubbed the wrong way.

Irritating describes something that causes mild annoyance or discomfort. An irritating {noise} grates on the nerves; an irritating {habit} wears on patience over time. The word also applies to physical sensation—an irritating {rash}, an irritating {cough}. Something irritating isn't infuriating, just persistently bothersome: {His constant interruptions were irritating}.

Irritation is a state of annoyance or mild anger, the feeling when something bothers you without quite provoking fury: {I couldn't hide my irritation at the constant interruptions}. It also describes physical discomfort—inflammation or sensitivity in body tissue: {skin irritation}, {eye irritation from the chlorine}. The source of either kind of bother is also called an irritation: {The dripping faucet was a constant irritation}.

Ish is a suffix meaning approximately or somewhat: {sixish}, {tallish}, {greenish}. Standalone, ish serves as a hedge—a one-word answer when something is partly true or hard to pin down: {Are you hungry? Ish.} It softens claims and creates flexibility: {The movie was good—ish}.

An island is a body of land entirely surrounded by water, smaller than a continent. The word extends to anything isolated or set apart from its surroundings: a {kitchen island} stands separate from counters, a {traffic island} breaks up the flow of cars. To island something is to make it isolated: {The flood islanded the village for three days}.

An islander is a person who lives on an island, especially a small or remote one. The word often carries connotations of distinct culture or identity shaped by geographic isolation: {The islanders have their own dialect}. It appears in proper names for sports teams and regional identities: {Long Islander}, {Pacific Islander}.

Islanders are people who live on an island, especially when the island is small or remote enough that its residents form a distinct community. The term often carries connotations of a particular lifestyle or culture shaped by geographic isolation and proximity to the sea. {The islanders have maintained traditions that disappeared from the mainland generations ago.} Capitalized, Islanders typically refers to the New York Islanders hockey team.

Islands is the plural of island—land masses surrounded by water on all sides. The word extends to anything isolated or set apart: {islands of calm in a chaotic day}, {traffic islands}. Kitchen islands are freestanding counter units. The Islands, capitalized, often refers to a specific archipelago depending on context—the Caribbean, Hawaii, or elsewhere.

An isle is an island. The word is poetic or literary, appearing in place names like the British Isles or the Isle of Man. In everyday speech, aisle—the walkway between rows—is far more common and frequently confused in spelling. {The tropical isle appeared on the horizon.}

Isles is the plural of isle, a poetic or literary word for island. It appears in proper names like the British Isles or the Isle of Man, and in phrases that evoke romance or mystery: {the isles of Greece}, {distant isles}. In ordinary speech, island is preferred; isles sounds deliberately elevated or archaic.

An ism is a distinctive doctrine, theory, or movement—usually one ending in that suffix: {capitalism}, {feminism}, {Buddhism}. The word often carries dismissive or skeptical overtones, lumping ideologies together as abstract systems rather than lived beliefs: {He's always chasing some new ism}. In casual use, isms can mean prejudices based on group identity: {racism, sexism, and other isms}.

Isms is the plural of ism, referring to doctrines, ideologies, or belief systems—typically ones ending in that suffix: {capitalism}, {feminism}, {racism}. Often used dismissively to lump together various ideologies without engaging them seriously: {He dismissed all their isms and causes}. The word suggests abstract theories rather than practical concerns.

To isolate is to set apart from others or cut off from connection. Scientists isolate variables in experiments; doctors isolate patients with contagious diseases. {The village was isolated by the flood.} You can isolate a problem by identifying it precisely, or feel isolated when lonely or disconnected. As a noun, an isolate is something separated from a larger group—a bacterial strain grown in a lab, or a language with no known relatives.

Isolated means set apart or alone. An isolated {incident} is a single occurrence, not part of a pattern. An isolated {community} has little contact with the outside world. Someone who feels isolated experiences loneliness or disconnection from others. The word suggests separation—whether physical, social, or circumstantial: {The cabin was completely isolated, miles from the nearest road}.

Isolating describes something that separates, sets apart, or cuts off from others. An isolating {experience} leaves you feeling alone or disconnected. An isolating {illness} keeps you confined. In linguistics, an isolating language (like Mandarin Chinese) uses separate words rather than inflections to express grammatical relationships—each word stands isolated from the others.

Isolation is the state of being separate or apart from others. A person in isolation may be quarantined for illness, confined in prison, or simply alone by circumstance or choice: {The cabin's isolation appealed to her}. The word applies equally to physical separation and emotional distance: {He felt a profound sense of isolation despite being surrounded by people}. To isolate something is to set it apart for examination or containment: {Scientists isolated the virus}.

Isolationism is a national policy of avoiding political or economic entanglement with other countries. The term arose in American politics, where it describes opposition to foreign alliances, military intervention abroad, and international commitments: {Isolationism dominated U.S. foreign policy between the world wars}. The word often carries a critical edge, implying narrow self-interest or naïve withdrawal from global responsibilities.

An isolationist advocates for a nation's withdrawal from international affairs, alliances, and foreign entanglements. The term often describes American political figures who oppose military intervention abroad or participation in international organizations: {isolationist senators blocked the treaty}. The stance can extend beyond politics—anyone who advocates avoiding outside involvement might be called isolationist.

Isolationists advocate keeping their country out of foreign entanglements—alliances, wars, and international commitments. The term gained currency in American politics during debates over entering the World Wars: {Isolationists in Congress opposed joining the League of Nations}. The label often carries negative connotations, suggesting naïve withdrawal from global realities, though proponents prefer terms like non-interventionist.

Issue has one meaning as a verb and many meanings as a noun. When you issue something such as a statement, warning, report, or order, you make it known to others. An issue can be the result: Have you seen the latest issue of PC Magazine? A much more common use of issue is synonymous with problem: We continue to experience issues with our new server. When it is said of someone that they have issues, it usually indicates an emotional, attitudinal, or relationship problem.

Issues are matters requiring attention or resolution: {We need to address several issues before launch}. The word often softens harder terms—issues can mean problems without sounding as negative: {The software has some issues}. Personal issues are emotional or psychological difficulties: {He has anger issues}. To take issue with something is to disagree with it. Issues also means offspring, now archaic except in legal contexts, and the copies of a periodical from a particular date: {the March issue}.

An isthmus is a narrow strip of land connecting two larger landmasses, with water on both sides. The Isthmus of Panama connects North and South America; the Isthmus of Corinth links mainland Greece to the Peloponnese. In anatomy, isthmus describes any narrow passage connecting two larger parts: {the isthmus of the thyroid gland}.

Italic refers to a style of type that slants to the right, used for emphasis, titles, foreign words, or to set text apart: {The journal requires titles in italic}. As a noun, usually pluralized: {Set the book title in italics}. The adjective italicized describes text rendered this way. To italicize is to apply this formatting. (Capitalized Italic relates to ancient Italy or its peoples.)

Italics is a style of type that slants to the right, used for emphasis, titles of works, foreign words, and other special purposes: {The book's title should be in italics}. The term comes from Italy, where the style originated. While italic describes the style, italics typically refers to text rendered that way: {Put that phrase in italics}.

An itch is a skin sensation that makes you want to scratch. The verb means to have this sensation: {My back itches}. Figuratively, an itch is a restless desire: {an itch to travel}, {the seven-year itch}. To be itching for something is to want it impatiently: {She was itching for a fight}. Itchy is the adjective: {itchy sweater}, {itchy trigger finger}.

Itched is the past tense of itch. An itch is a skin sensation that makes you want to scratch, and to itch is to feel that sensation: {My mosquito bites itched all night}. Figuratively, to itch for something is to want it restlessly: {She itched to get back on stage}.

Itching is an irritating skin sensation that provokes scratching. The word works as both noun and adjective: {The itching kept me awake}, {my itching scalp}. Figuratively, itching describes restless eagerness: {itching to get started}, {itching for a fight}. An {itching palm} suggests someone eager for bribes or money.

Itchy describes the sensation of skin irritation that makes you want to scratch: {My mosquito bites are so itchy}. Extended to restlessness or impatience: {itchy feet} suggests eagerness to travel or move on. An {itchy trigger finger} implies readiness to shoot—or act impulsively. {I'm getting itchy just sitting here.}

An item is a single thing, especially one among a collection or on a list: {The store carries thousands of items}. News reports are divided into items. In computing, items populate menus, arrays, and inventories. Two people romantically involved are sometimes called an item: {Are those two an item?}

Items are individual things, especially when considered as part of a group or list. A shopping list has items, an agenda has items, a collection has items. The word emphasizes countable units: {The first item on our agenda is budget cuts}. In news, an item is a brief story. Informally, two people who are {an item} are romantically involved.

Iteration is a single cycle in a repeated process. Software developers release iterations of their code, each version building on the last. In computing, iteration refers specifically to executing a set of instructions repeatedly: {The loop runs through ten iterations}. More broadly, any revision or new version counts as an iteration: {This iteration of the design addresses user feedback}.

Iterations are repetitions of a process, each cycle building on or refining what came before. In software development, iterations are successive versions of a product, each incorporating feedback: {We'll address that bug in the next iteration}. The word emphasizes incremental progress—not mere repetition, but repetition toward improvement. Scientists run iterations of experiments; designers produce iterations of prototypes.

An itinerary is a planned route or schedule for a journey, listing destinations, times, and activities: {The travel agent sent our itinerary for the Mediterranean cruise}. It can be detailed or loose, covering anything from a diplomat's official visits to a backpacker's rough plans. The word also refers to the written document itself.

Ivories is informal for piano keys, from the days when they were made of ivory: {She sat down and tickled the ivories}. The term extends to teeth, dice, and billiard balls—all traditionally ivory-colored or once made from actual ivory. The singular ivory refers to the hard white material from elephant tusks.

Ivory is the hard, creamy-white material from elephant tusks, historically prized for carving and piano keys. The color ivory is an off-white with warm undertones: {ivory skin}, {an ivory wedding dress}. An ivory tower is a place of privileged detachment from practical concerns, where academics or artists remain insulated from everyday realities. The international ivory trade is now largely banned to protect elephants. (Capitalized Ivory appears in the soap brand Ivory and in proper names like Ivory Coast.)

Ivy is a climbing or ground-creeping vine with dark, glossy leaves, known for clinging to walls, trees, and fences. English ivy is the most familiar species. The plant suggests old buildings, academic settings, and established tradition. {Ivy covered the stone walls of the library.} Poison ivy, a different plant entirely, causes an itchy rash on contact. (Capitalized Ivy is a given name.)

Ixnay is pig Latin for "nix," meaning to reject, cancel, or put a stop to something. Used as a verb {ixnay that idea} or as an interjection warning someone to stop talking about a sensitive subject: {Ixnay on the surprise party—she's coming!} The word retains a playful, conspiratorial tone from its coded origins.

A jab is a quick, sharp poke or punch—the kind delivered with a straight arm in boxing. Doctors and nurses give jabs (chiefly British for injections). To jab is to thrust something pointed or to poke repeatedly: {She jabbed her finger at the map}. A verbal jab is a pointed remark meant to needle someone.

Jabbed is the past tense and past participle of jab, meaning to poke or thrust something quickly and sharply. You might jab someone with your elbow to get their attention, or jab a finger at a map to indicate a location. In boxing, a jab is a quick, straight punch, so a boxer who jabbed threw such punches. In British informal usage, jabbed also means vaccinated: {I got jabbed last week}.

Jabber is rapid, excited, or incoherent speech—talking quickly without much substance or clarity. The word suggests noise over meaning: {The children jabbered excitedly about their trip}. It can describe any fast, hard-to-follow talk: {technical jabber}, {nervous jabber}. As a noun, jabber is such speech itself: {I couldn't make sense of their jabber}.

Jabbering is rapid, excited, or incoherent talk—speech that comes too fast or garbled to follow easily. The word suggests meaningless chatter or babble: {The monkeys were jabbering in the trees}. Someone might be jabbering nervously, or you might dismiss talk you find pointless: {What are they jabbering about now?}

Jabberwocky refers to nonsensical or meaningless language, especially invented words that sound like they could mean something: {The contract was full of legal jabberwocky}. The term comes from Lewis Carroll's 1871 poem of the same name, which featured invented words like "brillig" and "slithy" that somehow felt meaningful despite having no real definitions. (Capitalized Jabberwocky is the poem itself.)

Jabbing is the present participle and gerund of jab, describing the action of poking or thrusting something sharply, typically with a pointed object or a finger. In boxing, jabbing refers to throwing quick, straight punches. The word often suggests repeated or persistent action: {She kept jabbing at the elevator button}. Figuratively, jabbing can describe verbal attacks or pointed criticism: {He couldn't resist jabbing at his opponent's record}.

Jabroni is a mildly insulting term for a fool, loser, or someone beneath contempt. Professional wrestler The Rock popularized it in the 1990s, though it likely derives from earlier wrestling slang for a jobber—a performer who loses to make others look good. Now used broadly for anyone considered a chump or nobody: {Some jabroni cut me off in traffic}. {Don't be a jabroni}.

Jabronies is the plural of jabroni, a mildly insulting term for a fool, loser, or insignificant person. The word gained wide currency through professional wrestling, where it denotes jobbers—wrestlers who exist mainly to lose to stars. Outside wrestling, it's a casual put-down: {Those jabronies don't know what they're talking about}.

Jabs is the plural of jab—quick, sharp pokes or punches. A boxer throws jabs to keep an opponent at distance. Verbal jabs are pointed criticisms or insults: {She couldn't resist a few jabs at her ex}. In British usage, jabs are vaccinations or injections: {Have you had your flu jab yet?}

A jacaranda is a tropical tree native to South America, prized for its striking clusters of trumpet-shaped purple-blue flowers that bloom profusely in spring. The trees are widely planted as ornamentals in warm climates, where they line streets and fill parks with vivid color. {The jacarandas were in full bloom, carpeting the sidewalks with fallen purple petals.} The wood is also used in furniture making and carving.

Jacarandas is the plural of jacaranda, a tropical tree prized for its spectacular clusters of purple-blue flowers. Native to South America, jacarandas line streets in warm climates from Los Angeles to Sydney, creating carpets of fallen blossoms in late spring: {The jacarandas are blooming early this year}.

Numerous and often unrelated things are called jack, including a device for raising a heavy object (car jack), a face card bearing a picture of a solider, who is also a jack (jack of hearts), a small, six-pronged object used in the game of jacks, and a small flag. To jack something is to raise it with a jack. To jack up prices is to raise them. To jack it up means to ruin something in some way: The hairdresser jacked up my bangs. When Jack is capitalized it is usually a male given name, a nickname for John, or an informal designation for any male.

A jackal is a wild dog native to Africa and Asia, smaller than a wolf, typically hunting in packs and scavenging carrion. Jackals appear frequently in folklore as cunning and opportunistic. Figuratively, a jackal is someone who does dirty work for another or profits from others' misfortune: {political jackals circling a weakened administration}.

A jackalope is a mythical creature of American folklore—a jackrabbit with antelope or deer antlers. The legend originated in the American West, particularly Wyoming, where taxidermied specimens (rabbits with antlers attached) became popular tourist curiosities. The jackalope belongs to a tradition of tall tales and joke taxidermy: {The gift shop sold jackalope postcards}.

Jackalopes are mythical creatures of American folklore—jackrabbits with antelope horns. The legend originated in Wyoming in the 1930s as a taxidermy hoax and tourist attraction. Jackalope postcards, mounted heads, and hunting licenses became staples of Western kitsch. The creature represents a style of American tall tale: the fearsome critter, a fake animal invented to tease gullible outsiders.

Jackals are wild dogs native to Africa and Asia, smaller than wolves and known for scavenging carrion. They hunt small prey but readily feed on kills left by larger predators. Figuratively, a jackal is someone who does dirty work for another or profits from others' efforts: {The dictator's jackals carried out the arrests}.

Jackass means a male donkey, but it's primarily used as an insult for a stupid or obnoxious person: {He made a jackass of himself at the party}. The word also names the MTV franchise featuring dangerous stunts and crude humor.

Jackassery is foolish, stupid, or obnoxious behavior—the kind of conduct you'd expect from a jackass. The word emphasizes repeated or persistent foolishness rather than a single lapse: {I've had enough of his jackassery}. It's informal and mildly vulgar, often used with exasperated affection.
Jackasses is the plural of jackass, meaning male donkeys or, more commonly, stupid or obnoxious people: {The jackasses behind us wouldn't stop talking during the movie}.

A jackboot is a tall military boot reaching above the knee, historically worn by cavalry and later associated with fascist regimes. The word now primarily evokes authoritarian oppression: {jackbooted thugs}, {under the jackboot of tyranny}. To describe tactics or enforcement as jackbooted suggests brutal, militaristic force against citizens.

Jackbooted describes oppressive, brutally authoritarian behavior, evoking the image of military or paramilitary forces in high leather boots. The term almost always appears in {jackbooted thugs} or {jackbooted tactics}, suggesting violent enforcement of power: {Jackbooted agents raided the compound at dawn}. The word is strongly pejorative, implying fascist or totalitarian methods.

Jackboots are tall military boots reaching above the knee, historically associated with cavalry and later with authoritarian regimes—particularly Nazi Germany. The heavy leather boots became symbols of militarism and oppression: {jackbooted thugs}. Figuratively, jackboot represents brutal state power: {under the jackboot of tyranny}, {jackboot tactics}.

A jackdaw is a small crow native to Europe and western Asia, black with a gray nape and pale eyes. Jackdaws are social, intelligent birds known for their curiosity and tendency to collect shiny objects. The name likely comes from the bird's call combined with an old word for crow. {A jackdaw landed on the chimney pot.}

Jacked describes someone with prominent, well-defined muscles—the physique that comes from serious weight training: {He got jacked over the summer}. The word suggests impressive bulk rather than mere fitness. Separately, jacked means stolen: {Someone jacked my bike}. To be jacked up is to be excited, agitated, or under the influence of stimulants.

A jacket is a garment for the upper body, typically extending to the waist or hips and opening at the front. Jackets are lighter or shorter than coats: {a leather jacket}, {a denim jacket}, {a sport jacket}. The meaning extends to outer coverings generally: a book's dust jacket, the jacket of a potato, the insulating jacket around a pipe. To jacket something is to enclose it in a protective layer.

Jackets are outer garments extending to the waist or hips, worn over other clothing for warmth, protection, or style. The term covers everything from suit jackets to leather jackets to windbreakers. A book's jacket is its removable paper cover. To jacket something is to enclose it in a protective outer layer: {jacketed bullets}, {jacketed pipes}.

Jackfruit is a massive tropical fruit—sometimes weighing over fifty pounds—with a bumpy green exterior and sweet, fibrous yellow flesh. Native to South and Southeast Asia, it grows on trees and has a distinctive musky aroma. The unripe fruit has a mild, meaty texture that makes it popular as a plant-based meat substitute: {We made jackfruit tacos for the vegetarians}.

A jackhammer is a powerful pneumatic or electric tool that delivers rapid percussive blows to break up concrete, asphalt, or rock. Construction workers operate jackhammers to demolish pavement or excavate hard surfaces. The verb means to pound repeatedly with similar force: {My heart was jackhammering in my chest}. Also called a pneumatic drill in British English.

Jackhammering is operating a jackhammer—the pneumatic drill used to break up concrete and pavement. The word extends to any aggressive, repetitive pounding motion: {My heart was jackhammering in my chest}. In vulgar slang, it describes vigorous, mechanical sex.

Jackhammers is the plural of jackhammer, a powerful pneumatic or electric tool that breaks up concrete, asphalt, and rock through rapid hammering action. Construction workers use jackhammers to demolish pavement and dig through hard surfaces. The noise is notorious: {The jackhammers outside my window started at seven a.m.} As a verb, to jackhammer is to use one or to pound with similar force.

Jacking is the present participle of jack—raising something with a jack device: {They're jacking up the car to change the tire}. To jack prices is to raise them sharply. In slang, jacking means stealing, especially by force: {He got arrested for jacking cars}. Jacking or jacking off is vulgar slang for masturbating.

A jackknife is a folding pocket knife with a blade that swings into the handle. The word extends to anything that folds similarly: a jackknife is a dive in which the body bends at the waist, touches the toes, then straightens before entering the water. When a tractor-trailer jackknifes, the cab and trailer fold toward each other at the hitch point, usually during a skid. As a verb, jackknife means to fold or bend sharply in this manner: {The truck jackknifed on the icy highway}.

Jackknifed describes something that has folded sharply at a pivot point, like a jackknife blade closing into its handle. Most often used for truck accidents where the cab and trailer swing toward each other at an acute angle: {The semi jackknifed on the icy highway, blocking all lanes}. A diver who has jackknifed bends sharply at the waist before entering the water.

Jackknifing is when a truck and its trailer fold against each other at the hitch, forming a shape like a closing pocketknife. It typically happens when the trailer swings forward during braking or on slick roads: {The semi jackknifed on the icy highway}. The term extends to any similar folding motion—a diver jackknifing in midair, or someone bending sharply at the waist.

Jackknives is the plural of jackknife—a folding pocketknife with one or more blades that pivot into the handle. The word extends to movements resembling a closing knife: a jackknife dive brings the body into a tight V before straightening, and a truck jackknifes when the trailer swings toward the cab at a sharp angle. {The semi jackknifed on the icy highway.}

A jackknife is a large folding knife with a blade that folds into the handle. The word extends to anything that bends sharply at a point: a jackknife dive tucks the body at the waist, and when a truck jackknifes, the cab and trailer fold toward each other, usually in a skid. Also spelled jack-knife or jack knife.

A jackpot is a large cash prize, especially the top prize in a lottery, slot machine, or other gambling game. The term often implies an accumulating pot that grows until someone wins it. To hit the jackpot means to win such a prize, but figuratively it extends to any stroke of exceptional luck or success: {We hit the jackpot with this apartment—great location and cheap rent.}

Jackpots are large cash prizes, especially the top prize in gambling or a lottery. A slot machine's jackpot accumulates until someone wins. The term extends to any big windfall or stroke of luck: {We hit the jackpot with this apartment}. To {hit the jackpot} is to achieve sudden, exceptional success or fortune.

A jackrabbit is a large North American hare with exceptionally long ears and powerful hind legs built for speed. Despite the name, jackrabbits are hares, not rabbits—born fully furred with eyes open, unlike true rabbits. As a verb, to jackrabbit means to move with sudden, bounding starts: {The car jackrabbited away from the light}.

Jackrabbits are large North American hares with long ears and powerful hind legs built for speed. Despite the name, they're hares, not rabbits—born fully furred with open eyes, living above ground rather than in burrows. {A jackrabbit bounded across the desert road}. The name comes from "jackass rabbit," a reference to their donkey-like ears.

Jacks is a children's game played with small six-pointed metal or plastic pieces and a ball. Players bounce the ball and scoop up jacks before catching it: {We played jacks on the sidewalk}. The pieces themselves are also called jacks. In cards, jacks are the face cards ranking between ten and queen. As slang, jacks can mean nothing at all: {You don't know jacks}.

Jackshit means nothing at all, with emphasis on the nothing. It's vulgar but common: {He doesn't know jackshit about cars}, {We got jackshit for our trouble}. Often appears with negatives to stress complete absence or worthlessness. Also spelled jack shit.

Jacuzzi is a brand name for a whirlpool bath or hot tub, now used generically for any such fixture. The tub has jets that circulate warm water for relaxation or therapeutic massage: {We soaked in the jacuzzi after skiing}. Hotels and gyms often advertise jacuzzis as amenities.

Jade is a hard green stone prized for ornamental carving, especially in East Asian cultures. The color jade describes a specific shade of green. As a verb, to jade means to tire or wear out, though this use is rare outside the adjective jaded, meaning dulled or wearied by excess: {jaded by years of disappointment}. An older meaning—a worn-out horse or a disreputable woman—survives mainly in period literature. (Capitalized Jade is a given name.)

Jaded is an adjective used to describe people or opinions that lack enthusiasm or interest. Someone becomes jaded by overexposure to something: This film has something to make even the most jaded moviegoer well up with emotion. Jaded is not related to the stone jade but is from another word that originally denoted an old, worthless, or vicious horse.

A jag is a sharp projection or a period of unrestrained activity: {a crying jag}, {a drinking jag}. The projection sense appears in jagged, meaning having rough, sharp points. The activity sense suggests a bout or spree, often with negative connotations of excess. To jag is to cut or tear unevenly, or to prick. (Capitalized Jag is informal for Jaguar, the car brand.)

A Jagerbomb is a drink made by dropping a shot of Jägermeister into a glass of energy drink, typically Red Bull. The combination of herbal liqueur and caffeine produces a sweet, buzzy effect. It's a staple of college bars and nightclubs, often consumed quickly in groups: {We did three Jagerbombs before hitting the dance floor}.

Jagged describes an edge or surface with sharp, uneven points or notches—the opposite of smooth: {jagged rocks}, {a jagged tear in the fabric}, {jagged mountain peaks}. The word suggests roughness that could cut or snag. Figuratively, something jagged is harsh or irregular: {jagged nerves}, {a jagged melody}.

A jaguar is a large wild cat native to the Americas, the third-largest feline after tigers and lions. Jaguars have tawny coats with distinctive black rosette patterns and are known for their powerful build and strong bite. They inhabit forests and wetlands from Mexico through South America: {We spotted a jaguar crossing the river in the Pantanal}. (Capitalized Jaguar is the British luxury car brand.)

Jaguars is the plural of jaguar, a large spotted wild cat native to the Americas—the third-largest feline after tigers and lions. The jaguar's distinctive rosette markings and powerful build make it an apex predator in Central and South American forests. The Jaguars are also the NFL team based in Jacksonville, Florida: {The Jaguars made the playoffs for the first time in years}.

A jail is a place where people are confined, typically those awaiting trial or serving short sentences. In American usage, jails are local facilities run by counties or cities, distinct from prisons, which hold those serving longer terms. The verb means to put someone in jail: {They jailed him for contempt of court}. Figuratively, anything confining can feel like a jail: {This office is a jail}.

A jailbird is a person who has spent time in prison, especially someone who has been incarcerated repeatedly. The term is mildly contemptuous, suggesting a habitual criminal: {Her uncle was an old jailbird who'd been in and out of prison his whole life}.

Jailbirds is the plural of jailbird, a person who has spent time in prison or who repeatedly ends up there. The term is informal and mildly dismissive, suggesting someone familiar with incarceration: {The bar was full of ex-cons and jailbirds}. The image is of a caged bird—someone confined behind bars.

Jailbreak originally means an escape from prison, whether by force, cunning, or outside help: {Three inmates attempted a jailbreak last night}. In computing, it means bypassing software restrictions on a device to gain unauthorized access or install unapproved applications: {She jailbroke her phone to customize it}. More recently, jailbreak describes attempts to circumvent AI safety guidelines through clever prompting: {He tried to jailbreak the chatbot into ignoring its rules}.

Jailbreakers are people who remove software restrictions imposed by manufacturers on devices like smartphones and gaming consoles. The term borrows from prison escape—breaking out of the "jail" of locked-down operating systems to install unauthorized apps or customize settings. {Jailbreakers voided their warranties but gained full control of their phones.} The word also applies to those who circumvent restrictions on AI chatbots, coaxing them past their programmed limits.

Jailbreaking is removing software restrictions imposed by a device manufacturer, typically to install unauthorized apps or customize the operating system beyond its intended limits. The term originated with Apple's iPhone but applies to any locked-down device: {I jailbroke my phone to install apps that aren't in the App Store}. The metaphor treats factory settings as a prison. In AI contexts, jailbreaking means manipulating a chatbot into bypassing its safety guidelines.

Jailbreaks are escapes from prison, or the acts of helping someone escape. The term extends to bypassing restrictions on electronic devices—removing software limitations imposed by manufacturers so users can install unauthorized apps or modifications: {She jailbroke her phone to customize the interface}. In AI contexts, jailbreaking means circumventing a system's safety guidelines through clever prompting.

Jailbroke is the past tense of jailbreak, meaning to remove software restrictions imposed by a device manufacturer. Originally applied to iPhones and other Apple products, it now covers any device or system where built-in limitations are bypassed: {I jailbroke my old iPad to install apps Apple doesn't allow}. The term extends to AI systems, where jailbreaking means circumventing safety guidelines through clever prompting.

Jailbroken describes a device—typically a smartphone or tablet—whose software restrictions have been bypassed, allowing installation of unauthorized apps or modifications. The term evokes a prisoner escaping confinement: {I jailbroke my iPhone to install apps Apple won't allow}. By extension, jailbroken applies to AI systems whose safety guardrails have been circumvented through clever prompting.

Jailed means put in jail or currently held in jail. The word works as both past tense and adjective: {He was jailed for assault}; {the jailed suspect awaits trial}. Unlike imprisoned, which suggests a formal prison sentence, jailed often implies shorter-term detention or local lockup.

A jailer is a person who runs or works in a jail, responsible for guarding and supervising prisoners. The term applies to anyone from a sheriff overseeing a county lockup to guards in larger facilities. Also spelled gaoler in British English, though that spelling is old-fashioned. {The jailer brought the prisoner his evening meal.}

Jailers are people who run or work in a jail, responsible for guarding prisoners and maintaining order. The term applies to anyone from a medieval dungeon keeper to a modern corrections officer: {The jailers escorted the prisoner to his cell}. Figuratively, anything that confines can be called a jailer: {Addiction became his jailer}.

A jailhouse is a building where prisoners are held, especially a local or county facility rather than a large prison. The word has a folksy, rural feel—you're more likely to hear it in a country song than a legal brief. A {jailhouse lawyer} is an inmate who's learned enough law to help other prisoners with their cases.

A jailor is a person who runs or guards a jail. The spelling jailer is more common in American English, while jailor appears more often in British usage and historical contexts. {The jailor brought the prisoner his evening meal.}

Jailors is the plural of jailor, a variant spelling of jailer—one who guards prisoners or operates a jail. The spelling with -or appears in older texts and legal contexts but has largely given way to jailer in contemporary usage: {The jailors escorted the prisoner to his cell}.

Jails are facilities where people are confined, typically while awaiting trial or serving short sentences. In American usage, jails are local institutions run by cities or counties, distinct from prisons, which hold those serving longer terms. The verb jail means to put someone in such a facility: {They jailed him overnight for disorderly conduct}.

A jalapeno is a small to medium-sized chili pepper, typically green and moderately hot. It's among the most common peppers in Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking, often stuffed, pickled, or sliced raw as a topping: {jalapeño poppers}, {nachos with jalapeños}. The accent mark is often dropped in English spelling.

Jalapenos is the plural of jalapeno, a medium-hot green chile pepper common in Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking. They're often sliced raw on nachos, pickled as a condiment, or stuffed and fried. The pepper takes its name from Jalapa, Mexico. Also spelled jalapeños, with the tilde indicating the Spanish palatal n sound.

Jalopies is the plural of jalopy, an old car in poor condition. The word carries affection alongside deprecation—a jalopy may be beat-up and unreliable, but it's yours: {We piled into his jalopy and headed for the beach}. The term peaked in mid-20th-century American slang but remains understood.

A jalopy is an old, decrepit car in poor condition—the kind that rattles, smokes, or threatens to break down: {He drove up in some rusty jalopy}. The word is mildly humorous and affectionate, suggesting a vehicle kept running despite its sorry state.

The food jam is a concentration of fruit and sugar. Other kinds of jam suggest compression and tight packing, such as a traffic jam (too many cars, too little roadway). If you’re in a jam, you’re in a difficult situation. When you jam things into a place, you fit as many as can be squeezed in. When musicians jam, they play together, often improvising. This is called a jam session.

Jambalaya is a Louisiana rice dish combining meat, seafood, vegetables, and spices in one pot. The dish reflects the region's French, Spanish, and African culinary influences—a Creole cousin to paella. Proteins vary: andouille sausage, chicken, shrimp, crawfish. {We made a big pot of jambalaya for the party.}

Jambalayas is the plural of jambalaya, a Louisiana Creole rice dish combining meat, seafood, vegetables, and spices. The dish typically includes some combination of chicken, sausage, shrimp, and the "holy trinity" of Cajun cooking—onion, celery, and bell pepper. {We ordered three different jambalayas to share.}

A jamboree is a large, lively gathering or celebration, typically involving lots of activity and festivity. The term is most strongly associated with large-scale camping events organized by the Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts, where thousands of young people from different regions come together for outdoor activities and camaraderie. More broadly, jamboree can describe any boisterous party or festive assembly: {The county fair turned into a real jamboree with live music and dancing}.

Jamborees is the plural of jamboree, a large celebratory gathering or party. The word often describes organized events with festive atmosphere: {The town holds jamborees every summer}. Boy Scout jamborees bring together thousands of scouts for camping and activities. More loosely, any boisterous celebration might be called a jamboree: {The wedding turned into quite a jamboree}.

Jammed describes something tightly packed or stuck. A jammed drawer won't open; a jammed gun won't fire. Traffic gets jammed when too many vehicles crowd the road. A room jammed with people is crammed full: {The stadium was jammed for the concert}. In radio, a jammed signal has been deliberately blocked by interference.

A jammer is a device that blocks or disrupts signals—radio jammers interfere with communications, radar jammers confuse detection systems, GPS jammers prevent location tracking. In basketball, a jammer is someone who dunks powerfully. In roller derby, the jammer is the skater who scores points by lapping opponents. Someone who jams musically is also a jammer: {She's a solid jammer on bass}.

Jammers are knee-length swim trunks that fit snugly, worn by competitive swimmers and recreational lap swimmers: {He switched from board shorts to jammers for better speed}. The term also applies to devices that block electronic signals—radio jammers disrupt communications, radar jammers interfere with detection systems. In casual use, jammers can mean pajamas.

Jammies is informal for pajamas, used especially by or with children: {Time to put on your jammies and brush your teeth}. The word has a cozy, affectionate quality that makes it common in family contexts, though adults use it playfully among themselves too.

Jamming covers several kinds of forceful or persistent action. To jam is to push something into a tight space: {She jammed her clothes into the suitcase}. A jam is a blockage or congestion: {traffic jam}, {paper jam}. To jam a signal is to interfere with it deliberately, blocking transmission. In music, jamming is improvising together informally: {The band was jamming in the garage}. A jam session is such an improvised performance.

Jammy is British slang for lucky, especially in a way that seems undeserved: {You jammy bastard, you won again}. The word suggests fortune came too easily—someone who lands a good job without trying or wins at cards repeatedly might be called jammy. Less commonly, jammy means covered with or resembling jam: {jammy fingers}.

Jampacked means extremely full or crowded, with no room to spare. The image is of things compressed together like jam in a jar: {The subway was jampacked during rush hour}. Often written as two words (jam-packed) or hyphenated. The word emphasizes uncomfortable or excessive fullness rather than mere capacity.
