Jams is the plural of jam—fruit preserves made by cooking fruit with sugar until thick. You might have several jams in your refrigerator: {strawberry, apricot, and fig jams}. Jams also refers to difficult situations or traffic congestion: {We've been in some real jams before}. In music, jams are informal improvisational sessions: {The band's late-night jams became legendary}.

Jangle describes a harsh, discordant ringing or clinking sound—keys jangling in a pocket, chains jangling against metal. The word captures sounds that clash rather than harmonize. Figuratively, something can jangle your nerves, grating on them the way the sound grates on the ear: {The constant interruptions jangled her concentration}. In music, jangly describes a bright, trebly guitar tone with ringing overtones.

Jangled describes nerves that are frayed, raw, or on edge—the state of being agitated or unsettled: {Her jangled nerves couldn't take another surprise}. It also describes harsh, discordant sounds—bells or keys that clatter unpleasantly rather than ring clearly: {The jangled chords set everyone's teeth on edge}. Both senses share the quality of grating disturbance.

Jangles is the third-person singular of jangle—to make a harsh, metallic rattling sound: {Keys jangled in his pocket}. Figuratively, something that jangles your nerves irritates or unsettles you. The jangles, as a noun, describes a state of nervous agitation: {I've got the jangles before my interview}.

Jangling describes a harsh, discordant sound—metal striking metal, keys rattling, chains clanking: {the jangling of her bracelets}. The word suggests noise that grates rather than pleases. Figuratively, jangling can describe nerves set on edge: {The constant interruptions left her nerves jangling}.

Jangly describes a harsh, discordant ringing sound—the noise of keys rattling, cheap bracelets clacking, or an out-of-tune guitar. In music, jangly often characterizes the bright, chiming guitar sound of 1960s pop and later indie rock: {that jangly Byrds sound}. The word can also describe frayed nerves: {I'm feeling jangly after too much coffee}.

A janitor is a person employed to clean and maintain a building—emptying trash, mopping floors, fixing minor repairs. The term is standard in American English; British English prefers caretaker. Janitor can suggest low-status work: {He went from janitor to CEO}. The related custodian sounds slightly more dignified.

Janitors are workers who clean and maintain buildings—schools, offices, hospitals, apartment complexes. The job involves sweeping, mopping, emptying trash, and minor repairs. Custodian is a near-synonym that sounds slightly more dignified. {The janitors went on strike for better wages.}

Jank describes something that's poorly made, glitchy, or not working quite right. The word originated in gaming communities to characterize buggy mechanics or clunky controls but has spread to general use for anything janky—shoddy, unreliable, or held together with the digital equivalent of duct tape. {The animation in that game has so much jank.} As an adjective, janky is more common: {My janky old laptop crashes constantly.}

Janky is slang for something that's broken, poorly made, or unreliable. A janky car might break down constantly; a janky website crashes or loads wrong. The word carries connotations of shoddiness and makeshift quality—something that technically works but inspires no confidence. {My laptop's been janky ever since I dropped it.} {That's a pretty janky solution, but it'll do for now.}

A jar is a cylindrical container, typically glass or ceramic, with a wide mouth: {a jar of pickles}, {a mason jar}. The word extends to the contents: {We finished the whole jar}. As a verb, jar means to shake or jolt, or to have a harsh, unsettling effect: {The news jarred her}. Things that jar clash unpleasantly: {His casual tone jarred with the gravity of the situation}. A door left ajar is slightly open—from an unrelated word meaning "on the turn."

Jargon is specialized vocabulary used within a particular profession, group, or field—language that insiders understand but outsiders find opaque or confusing: {medical jargon}, {legal jargon}, {tech jargon}. The word usually carries a negative connotation, implying unnecessarily obscure language that excludes or impresses rather than communicates: {Cut the jargon and tell me what's wrong with my car}.

Jarhead is slang for a U.S. Marine, referring to the high-and-tight haircut that makes the head resemble a jar. Originally mildly derogatory when used by other military branches, Marines have largely embraced the term: {Once a jarhead, always a jarhead}. The word suggests toughness and esprit de corps rather than insult.

Jarheads is slang for U.S. Marines, referring to their high-and-tight haircuts that supposedly make the head resemble a jar. The term originated within military culture and can be used affectionately among Marines themselves or dismissively by outsiders: {A bunch of jarheads were drinking at the bar}. The singular jarhead follows the same pattern.

Jarred is the past tense of jar, meaning to shake, jolt, or disturb. A loud noise jarred her awake. Conflicting information can jar with expectations: {The cheerful music jarred against the somber scene}. Something jarring creates an unpleasant shock or dissonance. Separately, jarred describes food preserved in jars: {jarred tomatoes}, {jarred pickles}.

Jarring describes something that clashes or disrupts with sudden unpleasantness. A jarring {noise} startles. A jarring {transition} feels abrupt and awkward. Jarring {colors} clash disagreeably. The word suggests being jolted or shaken—the way a physical jar rattles its contents: {The ending was jarring after such a gentle buildup}.

Jars is the plural of jar—a cylindrical container, typically glass or ceramic, with a wide mouth: {rows of jars filled with preserved vegetables}, {a jar of peanut butter}. As a verb form, jars means to shake or jolt unpleasantly, or to clash discordantly: {The noise jars my nerves}, {His casual tone jars with the seriousness of the situation}.

Jasmine is a climbing shrub with fragrant white or yellow flowers, widely cultivated in warm regions. The scent is prized in perfumery and flavoring—jasmine tea is green tea scented with jasmine blossoms. The name, from Persian, is also popular as a given name for girls: {Her daughter is named Jasmine}.

Jasper is an opaque variety of quartz, typically red, brown, or yellow, used as a gemstone and in decorative work. The stone's mottled, earthy appearance has made it popular in jewelry and ornamental objects for millennia. {The ring featured a polished jasper set in silver.} (Capitalized Jasper is a given name or place name.)

Jaundice is a yellowing of the skin and eyes caused by excess bilirubin in the blood, typically indicating liver dysfunction or bile duct obstruction. The condition is common in newborns, where it usually resolves on its own. Figuratively, a jaundiced view or eye sees things with bitterness, envy, or cynicism: {He took a jaundiced view of politics after the scandal}.

Jaundiced describes a cynical or resentful outlook, as if viewing the world through yellowed eyes: {a jaundiced view of politics}, {She cast a jaundiced eye on his promises}. The metaphor comes from jaundice, a medical condition that yellows the skin and eyes. A jaundiced perspective assumes the worst, colored by bitterness or disappointment.

A jaunt is a short trip taken for pleasure or leisure, typically brief and lighthearted: {a weekend jaunt to the coast}, {a quick jaunt into town}. The word suggests something casual and enjoyable rather than a serious journey. To jaunt is to take such a trip, though the noun is far more common.

Jaunts is the plural of jaunt, a short trip taken for pleasure or leisure. Jaunts are typically casual excursions rather than serious travel: {weekend jaunts to the coast}, {quick jaunts around the neighborhood}. The word suggests lightheartedness—you take jaunts when you have time to spare and nowhere pressing to be.

Jaunty describes a lively, cheerful manner with a touch of stylish self-confidence: {He wore his hat at a jaunty angle}. There's something carefree and buoyant about jaunty—a spring in the step, a tilt of the cap. The word often applies to physical bearing or dress: {a jaunty wave}, {a jaunty stride}. It can also describe music or speech with similar sprightly energy.

Java is coffee, especially strong or hot coffee: {I need a cup of java to wake up}. The slang term originated in the 19th century from the Indonesian island that exported coffee beans. It remains common in casual American speech: {Let's grab some java}. (Capitalized Java is the Indonesian island or the programming language.)

A javelin is a light spear designed for throwing. In track and field, the javelin throw is an event where athletes hurl the spear for distance: {She won gold in the javelin}. Historically, javelins were weapons of war, lighter than thrusting spears and used by cavalry and skirmishers.

Javelins are light spears designed for throwing. In ancient warfare, soldiers hurled javelins at enemy formations before close combat. The javelin throw remains an Olympic track and field event: {She set a new record in the javelin}. The word also names various missiles and military weapons systems.

The jaw is the bony framework of the mouth—the upper and lower structures that hold the teeth and enable chewing. The lower jaw moves; the upper doesn't. Jaws extend to mechanical devices that grip: the jaws of a vise, the jaws of pliers. To jaw is to talk at length, often tediously: {They jawed for hours about nothing}. To {jaw at} someone is to lecture or scold them.

The jawbone is the bone of the jaw, particularly the lower jaw or mandible—the hinged bone that moves when you chew or speak. As a verb, jawbone means to pressure someone through persistent talk rather than force, often used in political contexts: {The president jawboned the Fed into lowering rates}. The term suggests persuasion through extended conversation or negotiation rather than formal authority.

A jawbreaker is a very hard, round candy designed to be sucked rather than chewed—biting down risks dental damage, hence the name. The candy typically has colorful layers that reveal themselves as it slowly dissolves. Jawbreaker also describes a word that's difficult to pronounce: {That medical term is a real jawbreaker}.

Jawbreakers are hard, round candies designed to be sucked rather than chewed—large enough and dense enough to challenge the jaw if you try to bite through. The name captures both the candy's toughness and its size: {She bought a bag of jawbreakers at the candy store}. Figuratively, a jawbreaker is a word difficult to pronounce: {The medical terminology was full of jawbreakers}.

A jawdropper is something so surprising, impressive, or shocking that it figuratively makes your jaw drop in astonishment: {The plot twist at the end was a real jawdropper}. The term emphasizes dramatic impact—a revelation, performance, or visual spectacle that leaves people stunned.

Jaw-dropping describes something so astonishing that it makes your mouth fall open in amazement: {The view from the summit was jaw-dropping}. Usually positive—spectacular performances, stunning revelations, breathtaking scenery—though it can describe shocking news of any kind. Also spelled jawdropping or jaw dropping.

Jawing is informal talk, especially prolonged or idle chatter. The word suggests conversation that goes on and on: {They spent the afternoon jawing on the porch}. It can also mean scolding or lecturing someone at length: {The coach was jawing at the referee about the call}.

The jawline is the outline of the lower edge of the jaw, from chin to ear. In discussions of appearance, a strong or defined jawline is typically considered attractive: {He has a chiseled jawline}. Cosmetic procedures and exercises sometimes target the jawline to make it more prominent.

Jaws are the bony structures that frame the mouth and hold the teeth—the upper and lower parts that open and close for biting and chewing. The jaws of a tool or machine are the gripping parts that clamp together: {the jaws of a vise}. Figuratively, jaws suggest an inescapable grip: {the jaws of death}, {snatched from the jaws of defeat}. To jaw is to talk at length, often tediously. (Capitalized Jaws is the 1975 Spielberg film.)

A jay is a noisy, colorful bird of the crow family, known for bold behavior and harsh calls. The blue jay is the most familiar North American species. Informally, a jay can mean a naive or gullible person—someone easily fooled, though this usage is dated. To jaywalk is to cross a street carelessly or illegally, from the "foolish country person" sense. (Capitalized Jay is a given name.)

A jaybird is simply a jay—any of the crested, often blue songbirds of the crow family. The extended form appears mainly in American regional speech and in the expression {naked as a jaybird}, meaning completely nude. The phrase's origin is obscure, since jays are fully feathered birds.

Jays are medium-sized, colorful birds in the crow family, known for their intelligence and loud, harsh calls. The blue jay is the most familiar North American species: {A jay landed on the feeder}. Jays cache food and can mimic other birds' calls. In slang, a jay is a naive or gullible person—the source of jaywalking, originally crossing streets like a clueless country bumpkin.

Jayvee is the spoken form of JV, short for junior varsity—the secondary team in high school or college athletics, below the varsity squad. Players on jayvee are typically younger or less experienced, developing skills before advancing: {He played jayvee basketball his freshman year}. Used as noun or adjective: {the jayvee team}.

To jaywalk is to cross a street illegally—outside a crosswalk, against a signal, or otherwise in violation of pedestrian traffic laws. The term emerged in early 20th-century America, when "jay" meant a naive rural person unfamiliar with city ways: {She jaywalked across the busy intersection without looking}.

Jaywalked is the past tense of jaywalk—to cross a street illegally or carelessly, especially outside a crosswalk or against a signal. The term comes from "jay," early 20th-century slang for a naive rural person unfamiliar with city traffic: {She jaywalked across the busy intersection}. Enforcement varies widely; in some cities it's ignored, in others actively ticketed.

A jaywalker is someone who crosses a street illegally—typically outside a crosswalk or against a traffic signal. The term carries mild disapproval: {The driver honked at the jaywalker}. Jaywalking laws vary widely and are often unenforced, but the word persists as a casual label for careless or impatient pedestrians.
clues: One who crosses against the light

definition: Jaywalkers are pedestrians who cross streets illegally—ignoring traffic signals, crossing mid-block, or otherwise violating right-of-way rules. The term comes from "jay," early 20th-century slang for a naive rural person unfamiliar with city traffic: {Jaywalkers darted between honking cars}. The word carries mild disapproval but little real stigma in practice.
clues: People who cross against the light

definition: Jaywalking is crossing a street illegally—typically outside a crosswalk or against a traffic signal. The practice is named for "jay," an old slang term for a naive rural person unfamiliar with city traffic. Laws against jaywalking vary widely; some cities enforce them strictly while others ignore them entirely. {She got a ticket for jaywalking.}

Jaywalks means to cross a street illegally or recklessly—ignoring crosswalks, traffic signals, or oncoming cars: {She jaywalks whenever there's a gap in traffic}. The jay- comes from an old term for a naive rural person, suggesting someone unfamiliar with city traffic rules. Jaywalking laws are unevenly enforced and increasingly challenged as outdated.

Jazz is a genre of American music originating in the early twentieth century, characterized by improvisation, syncopated rhythms, and complex harmonies. It emerged from Black communities in New Orleans, blending African musical traditions with blues and ragtime. Beyond music, jazz can mean liveliness or excitement, and {all that jazz} dismisses accompanying details as unimportant: {romance, flowers, and all that jazz}. To jazz something up is to make it more interesting or lively.

Jazzed means excited or enthusiastic, often with eager anticipation: {I'm totally jazzed about the trip}. The word suggests energized readiness rather than calm contentment. It derives from jazz, whose improvisational energy colors the meaning. Sometimes intensified as {jazzed up}: {We got all jazzed up for the concert}.

A jazzman is a male jazz musician, especially one who plays in a band or combo. The term evokes the classic era of jazz clubs and improvisation: {The old jazzman had played every dive in New Orleans}. It carries a hint of reverence for the craft and lifestyle of jazz performance.

Jazzy describes something lively, bold, or flashy in style. The word comes from jazz music but extends to anything with similar energy or flair: {a jazzy shirt}, {jazzy graphics}. It often suggests something eye-catching or showy, sometimes to the point of being garish: {The presentation was a bit too jazzy for a corporate meeting}.

Jealous describes the fear of losing something you have—especially someone's affection or attention—to a rival: {She was jealous of his friendship with his ex}. The word often extends to envy, wanting what someone else has: {I'm jealous of your vacation photos}. Purists distinguish jealousy (guarding what's yours) from envy (coveting what isn't), but common usage blurs this. A jealous {God} tolerates no rivals. To guard something {jealously} is to protect it fiercely.

Jealousies is the plural of jealousy—instances of resentful suspicion or envious discontent. The word often appears when multiple grievances accumulate: {petty jealousies among coworkers}, {romantic jealousies that festered for years}. Jealousies can also refer to jealous feelings from different sources or directed at different people: {The siblings' jealousies toward each other were obvious to everyone}.

Jealousy is a feeling that may arise when a rival succeeds and you fall short. In love relationships, jealousy is often related to suspicions or fears that your partner prefers someone else. Jealousy is similar to envy, but jealousy arises when two people share a common interest or rank, and envy arises when there is a disparity in rank. Sexual jealousy, professional jealousy, and petty jealousy are the most frequently used phrases.

Jeans are pants made from denim, a sturdy cotton twill fabric, typically blue. Originally workwear for laborers and cowboys, jeans became casual everyday clothing in the mid-twentieth century. They come in countless cuts and washes: {skinny jeans}, {bootcut jeans}, {stone-washed jeans}. The singular jean appears mainly as an adjective: {a jean jacket}.

A jeep is a small, rugged motor vehicle built for rough terrain, originally designed for military use. The term has become generic for any similar off-road vehicle with four-wheel drive: {We took the jeep up the mountain trail}. The word likely derives from the military designation GP (general purpose), though some credit a creature from the Popeye comic strip. (Capitalized Jeep is the trademark.)
Jeepers, a harmless euphemism for Jesus, is used to express surprise or alarm, often in a humorous way.

Jeeps is the plural of jeep, a rugged four-wheel-drive vehicle designed for off-road use. The original Jeep was a military vehicle developed for World War II, and the name became a trademark for civilian versions. Lowercase jeep sometimes refers generically to similar vehicles: {We rented jeeps to explore the back roads}. The word likely derives from "GP" (general purpose).

Jeer is to mock or taunt someone with scornful remarks or sounds: {The crowd jeered the referee}. A jeer is such a taunt. Jeering expresses contempt or derision, often from a group toward an individual—spectators jeering a player, protesters jeering a politician. The word suggests vocal, public ridicule rather than private criticism.

Jeering is mocking or taunting, usually loudly and in a group: {The crowd's jeering grew louder as the referee made another bad call}. Jeers combine derision with hostility—they're meant to humiliate or intimidate. Someone who is jeered at faces open contempt: {He walked off stage to jeering and boos}.

Jeers are mocking or scornful remarks, the vocal expression of contempt or derision: {The politician left the stage amid jeers from the crowd}. To jeer is to taunt or ridicule someone openly: {Fans jeered the referee's call}. Jeers carry more hostility than boos—they're pointed, often verbal, and meant to wound.

Jeez is a euphemism for Jesus, used as a mild exclamation: {Jeez, that was close}. {Aw jeez}. The word allows speakers to express surprise or frustration without explicit blasphemy, though some religious people consider even the euphemism disrespectful.

To jell is to become firm or gel-like, as when a liquid thickens: {The pudding needs time to jell}. More often the word appears figuratively—ideas, plans, or groups jell when they come together into a coherent whole: {The team didn't really jell until midseason}. Also spelled gel.

Jellies is the plural of jelly—soft, semi-solid substances that wobble when touched. Fruit jellies are made from juice and pectin; petroleum jelly is a thick ointment. In British English, jelly means what Americans call Jell-O. Jellies are also a type of soft plastic sandal: {She wore jellies to the beach}. Jellyfish are sometimes called jellies. In slang, jellies can mean jealous feelings: {Don't get the jellies just because she won}.

Jelling is the present participle of jell, which means to take shape or come together. Ideas jell when they solidify into something coherent: {The plan is finally jelling}. A group jells when members begin working well together: {The team took a few weeks to jell}. The spelling gelling, from gel, is equally common.

Jello is a brand name for flavored gelatin dessert—a wobbly, translucent, often brightly colored sweet that sets when chilled. The trademark has become generic for any such product: {She brought lime jello to the potluck}. Jello shots are alcoholic drinks made by mixing liquor into the gelatin. Something described as jello is soft and quivering: {My legs turned to jello}.

Jelly is a soft, wobbly substance that holds its shape but yields to pressure. In American usage, jelly typically means a clear fruit spread made from juice rather than whole fruit—distinguished from jam, which contains fruit pulp. British jelly is what Americans call gelatin dessert. Petroleum jelly is a translucent ointment. Jelly can describe anything with that consistency: {My legs turned to jelly}. As a verb, to jelly is to set into that form. Jellies are also a style of flexible plastic sandal.

A jellybean is a small, bean-shaped candy with a firm sugar shell and a soft, chewy center, typically fruit-flavored and brightly colored. Jellybeans are associated with Easter and often appear in jars for guessing games: {How many jellybeans are in the jar?} Also spelled jelly bean.

Jellybeans are small bean-shaped candies with a firm sugar shell and soft, chewy interior, typically fruit-flavored and brightly colored. They appear in assorted mixes, making them popular for Easter baskets and candy dishes. {I picked out all the black jellybeans}. Also spelled as two words: jelly beans.

A jellyfish is a soft-bodied marine animal with a translucent, umbrella-shaped body and trailing tentacles that can sting. Jellyfish drift with currents rather than swimming with purpose, which gives rise to the figurative sense: a spineless or weak-willed person, someone who lacks backbone or decisiveness. {Don't be such a jellyfish—stand up for yourself.}

A jellyroll is a thin sponge cake spread with jelly or jam and rolled into a spiral, then sliced to reveal concentric layers. The term extends to anything with a similar rolled shape. In jazz slang, jellyroll is the vagina or sexual intercourse—a usage immortalized by early jazz pianist Jelly Roll Morton. {She baked a jellyroll for the church social.}

A jenny is a female donkey, as distinguished from the male (jack). The term extends to other animals: a jenny wren is a female wren. In textile manufacturing, a spinning jenny was an early multi-spindle spinning frame that revolutionized cloth production. {The jenny brayed at the approaching stranger.} (Capitalized Jenny is a given name.)

Jeopardise is the British spelling of jeopardize, meaning to put something at risk of being lost, harmed, or destroyed. The word implies exposing something valuable to danger or potential failure: {Leaking that information could jeopardise the entire investigation}. It typically applies to abstract things worth protecting—careers, relationships, safety, negotiations—rather than physical objects. The construction jeopardise {one's chances} is especially common.

To jeopardize something is to put it at risk of harm or loss: {Smoking jeopardizes your health}. The word implies endangering something valuable through action or negligence: {His reckless spending jeopardized the company's future}. The British spelling is jeopardise.

Jeopardized is the past tense of jeopardize, meaning to put something valuable at risk of being lost, damaged, or destroyed. When you jeopardize something, you expose it to danger or threaten its success: {His drinking jeopardized his marriage}. The word implies that the thing at risk matters—careers, relationships, safety, or opportunities can all be jeopardized by careless or reckless actions.
clues: Threatened with potential loss or harm

definition: Jeopardizing is putting something at risk of harm, loss, or failure. The word implies that something valuable—a relationship, career, safety, or opportunity—faces danger because of an action or circumstance: {He's jeopardizing his health by refusing to see a doctor}. {Don't jeopardize everything we've built}.

Jeopardy is danger or risk, especially of loss, harm, or failure: {The scandal put his career in jeopardy}. The word appears most often in legal contexts—{double jeopardy} is the constitutional protection against being tried twice for the same crime. To jeopardize something is to put it at risk.

To jerk is to make a sharp, sudden movement: {The car jerked forward}. {He jerked his hand away}. A jerk is such a movement, or a contemptible person—someone rude, selfish, or obnoxious: {Don't be such a jerk}. The insult is mild, acceptable in most company. Jerk also names a Jamaican style of spiced, grilled meat: {jerk chicken}. The insult sense may derive from the masturbation meaning of jerk off, implying someone who might as well be masturbating for all the good they do anyone else.
Jerking is the present participle of jerk, meaning moving suddenly or spasmodically: {The fish was jerking on the line}. It can also describe the process of making jerk-style meat.
A jerkoff is a vulgar insult for a contemptible person, implying they're useless or self-absorbed—someone who might as well be masturbating: {Some jerkoff parked in my spot}.

Jerks is the plural of jerk—sudden sharp movements: {The train started with several jerks}. {Involuntary jerks are called myoclonus}. Jerks also means contemptible people: {Those jerks cut in line}. As a verb: {He jerks awake at the slightest noise}. {She jerks the wheel to avoid the dog}.

Jerkwater describes a small, insignificant, or backward place—typically a town so minor it barely registers: {a jerkwater town in the middle of nowhere}, {some jerkwater college nobody's heard of}. The term is dismissive, suggesting a place not worth visiting or taking seriously. It originated from small railroad stops where trains would "jerk" water from trackside tanks.
clues: The kind of town trains skip

definition: Jerky as an adjective means characterized by sudden, abrupt movements: {The ride was jerky}. {His jerky motions betrayed his nervousness}. As a noun, jerky is dried, preserved meat cut into strips: {beef jerky}. The noun comes from Quechua charki, unrelated to the adjective.

A jerrican is a flat-sided metal or plastic container for storing and transporting fuel or water, typically holding about five gallons. The design originated in Germany before World War II—jerry being British slang for German—and Allied forces quickly adopted it for military use. Also spelled jerry can or jerrycan: {We strapped two jerricans to the back of the jeep}.

A jerrycan is a flat-sided metal or plastic container for storing and transporting fuel or water, typically holding about five gallons. The design features a handle on top and a spout for pouring. Originally a German military invention, the container proved so practical that Allied forces copied it during World War II: {We strapped two jerrycans to the back of the jeep}. Also spelled jerry can.

Jerrycans are robust, flat-sided fuel containers, typically holding about five gallons. The design—rectangular with a recessed seam and three handles—originated in Germany before World War II and was widely copied. The name comes from "Jerry," British slang for Germans. Also spelled jerry cans or jerry-cans: {We loaded three jerrycans of diesel into the truck bed}.

A jersey is a knitted garment, typically a pullover sweater or a fitted shirt worn by athletes. The athletic sense dominates in American English: {She bought a Lakers jersey}. Sports jerseys display team colors and player numbers, and fans wear replica jerseys to show allegiance. The fabric jersey—a soft, stretchy knit—takes its name from the garment. (Capitalized Jersey refers to the island or place names.)

Jerseys are knitted garments, typically pullovers or sweaters, or the distinctive shirts worn by athletes to identify their team: {The team wore their home jerseys}. Jersey fabric is a soft, stretchy knit material used in clothing. The plural also refers to Jersey cattle, a dairy breed known for rich milk. (Capitalized Jersey is the island or the U.S. state.)

A jest is a joke or playful remark: {I said it in jest}. The word sounds slightly formal or old-fashioned compared to joke. To jest is to speak humorously or tease: {Surely you jest}. A jester was a court entertainer who told jokes and performed comic routines for royalty.

A jester is a professional entertainer employed by medieval and Renaissance courts to amuse royalty with jokes, songs, acrobatics, and witty commentary. Jesters often wore motley (multicolored clothing) and carried a mock scepter called a bauble. Their role granted unusual license to mock the powerful: {Only the jester dared tell the king the truth}. Today, jester describes anyone who acts the fool for entertainment, or dismissively, someone not to be taken seriously: {He's just the office jester}.

Jesters were entertainers employed by medieval and Renaissance courts to amuse royalty through jokes, tricks, songs, and foolery. They wore distinctive motley clothing and cap with bells. The jester's role granted unusual license to mock even powerful figures: {Only the jester dared tell the king the truth}. Now used figuratively for anyone playing the fool or providing comic relief.

The most frequently encountered jet is an aircraft powered by a jet engine, that is, an engine that produces power by expelling a jet (a forceful stream) rearwards. Any other strong stream of liquid or gas may also be called a jet (jets of water in a fountain). The pervasive wind that flows west to east high in the atmosphere is called the jet stream. A different kind of jet is a dense form of coal that is used in jewelry.

A jetboat is a watercraft propelled by a jet of water expelled from the stern rather than by a propeller. The design allows operation in shallow water where conventional boats would run aground: {We took a jetboat through the canyon rapids}. Jetboats are popular for river tours and thrill rides.

Jetlag is the fatigue and disorientation that follows rapid travel across time zones. Your body's internal clock remains synced to your departure point while local time demands otherwise. Symptoms include insomnia, daytime drowsiness, difficulty concentrating, and digestive upset. {It took me three days to get over the jetlag from Tokyo}. Also spelled jet lag.

Jetlagged describes the state of fatigue and disorientation after traveling across multiple time zones. Your body's internal clock remains set to your origin, leaving you awake at 3 a.m. and drowsy at noon: {I'm still jetlagged from the flight to Tokyo}. Also spelled jet-lagged.

A jetliner is a large passenger aircraft powered by jet engines, typically used for commercial flights. The term distinguishes these planes from smaller private jets and propeller-driven aircraft: {The jetliner touched down at O'Hare}. Most modern commercial aviation relies on jetliners for medium and long-haul routes.

A jetpack is a device worn on the back that uses jet propulsion to lift and move a person through the air. Long a staple of science fiction and futuristic fantasy, working jetpacks exist but remain impractical for everyday use. The word sometimes describes any backpack-style propulsion device: {The jetpack in that old Bond film used hydrogen peroxide}. Figuratively, to {strap on a jetpack} suggests accelerating dramatically or taking bold action.

Jetpacks are wearable devices that propel a person through the air using jet or rocket thrust. Long a staple of science fiction and futuristic fantasy, real jetpacks exist but remain impractical for everyday use—limited by short flight times and high fuel consumption. {Where's my jetpack?} has become shorthand for disappointment that the future hasn't delivered on its promises.

Jets are powerful streams of fluid—water, air, or gas—forced through a narrow opening: {The fountain sent jets of water into the air}. A jet is also an aircraft propelled by jet engines, or the engine itself. To jet is to travel by jet aircraft or to move rapidly: {She jetted off to Paris}. In pool and billiards, jets can mean runs or streaks of successful shots. (Capitalized Jets refers to the New York sports teams.)

Jetsam is cargo or equipment deliberately thrown overboard to lighten a ship in distress. The word pairs with flotsam, which is wreckage floating after a shipwreck. Together, {flotsam and jetsam} refers broadly to debris, discarded items, or displaced people: {the flotsam and jetsam of urban life}.

Jetset, also spelled jet-set or jet set, refers to wealthy, fashionable people who travel frequently by jet aircraft to glamorous international destinations. The term emerged in the 1950s when commercial jet travel was novel and expensive, reserved for the elite. As a verb, to jetset means to travel in this luxurious, globe-trotting manner: {She spent her twenties jetsetting between Paris and Monaco}. A jetsetter is someone who lives this lifestyle. The term now often carries a slightly ironic or aspirational tone.

A jetsetter is someone who travels frequently and glamorously, typically to fashionable destinations around the world. The term evokes wealth, leisure, and a cosmopolitan lifestyle—private planes, resort towns, international social scenes: {She lives a jetsetter lifestyle, splitting her time between Paris and Monaco}. The word emerged when jet travel was novel and exclusive.

Jetsetters are wealthy people who travel frequently to fashionable destinations around the world. The term evokes a lifestyle of luxury, leisure, and international glamour—hopping between Paris, Monaco, and private islands. It originated when jet travel was expensive and exclusive: {The resort caters to jetsetters and celebrities}. Now often used with slight irony or aspiration.

Jetsetting describes a lifestyle of frequent travel to glamorous destinations, typically by jet aircraft. The term evokes wealth, leisure, and cosmopolitan sophistication: {She spent her twenties jetsetting between Paris and New York}. A jetsetter is someone who lives this way. The word can carry a note of envy or mild derision for those with more money than responsibilities.

A jetski is a small recreational watercraft ridden like a motorcycle, propelled by a jet of water rather than a propeller. The rider typically sits or stands astride the craft: {We rented jetskis at the beach}. Originally a trademark (Jet Ski), the word now serves as a generic term. As a verb, to jetski is to ride one.

Jetskiing is riding a jet ski—a small, motorized watercraft that the rider sits or stands on while steering with handlebars. The activity combines elements of motorcycling and water skiing: {We went jetskiing around the bay}. Also spelled jet-skiing or jet skiing.

Jetskis is the plural of jetski, a small motorized watercraft ridden like a motorcycle, typically by one or two people standing or kneeling. The rider straddles the craft and steers with handlebars: {Jetskis buzzed across the lake all afternoon}. The name derives from Jet Ski, a Kawasaki trademark that became generic. Also spelled jet skis.

A jetstream is a narrow, fast-moving current of air high in the atmosphere, typically flowing west to east at altitudes where commercial aircraft fly. Jetstreams influence weather patterns and can speed or slow flights depending on direction: {We landed early thanks to a strong jetstream}. Also spelled as two words: jet stream.

Jetties is the plural of jetty, a structure extending into water. A jetty may be a pier or wharf for mooring boats, or a barrier built to protect a harbor or direct currents: {The fishing boats tied up at the jetties}. Jetties are typically constructed of stone, concrete, or timber pilings.

Jetting is travel by jet aircraft, especially frequent or glamorous air travel: {She spent the summer jetting between Paris and Milan}. The word suggests speed and sophistication. Jetting also describes forceful spurting of liquid or gas: {Water was jetting from the broken pipe}.

Jettison means to throw overboard, especially to lighten a ship or aircraft in distress: {The crew jettisoned cargo to stay afloat}. The word extends to any deliberate discarding of something burdensome or unwanted: {She jettisoned her old beliefs}, {The company jettisoned its failing product line}. The noun jettison refers to the act itself or the material thrown overboard.

Jettisoned is the past tense of jettison, meaning to throw overboard or discard. Originally nautical—a ship's crew jettisons cargo to lighten the vessel in an emergency. The word now applies broadly to anything deliberately abandoned: {The company jettisoned its unprofitable divisions}. {She jettisoned her old beliefs after the experience}.

Jettisoning is throwing something overboard, especially to lighten a vessel in distress. The word comes from maritime emergencies where cargo was sacrificed to save a ship. Extended uses cover any deliberate discarding: {The company is jettisoning unprofitable divisions}. To jettison plans, relationships, or principles is to abandon them decisively.

A jetty is a structure extending into water, typically built of stone, concrete, or wood. Jetties serve as breakwaters protecting harbors, as piers for mooring boats, or as barriers directing water flow at river mouths: {We walked out to the end of the jetty to watch the sunset}. The word also works as an adjective meaning jet-black, though this use is rare and literary.

A jetway is an enclosed, movable walkway that connects an airport terminal directly to an aircraft door, allowing passengers to board without going outside. Also called a jet bridge or passenger boarding bridge. {We waited in the jetway while the crew prepared the cabin.}

A jewel is a precious stone—a diamond, ruby, emerald, or similar gem, especially one cut and polished for ornament: {The crown was set with jewels}. By extension, jewel describes anything or anyone prized for exceptional quality or beauty: {She's a jewel of an assistant}. The jewel of a collection is its finest piece. To jewel something is to adorn it with gems; jeweled means decorated with jewels.

Jeweled describes something decorated or set with jewels: {a jeweled crown}, {a jeweled dagger hilt}. The word often suggests ornate luxury or preciousness. Figuratively, jeweled can describe anything that sparkles or gleams like gems: {jeweled drops of dew}, {the jeweled lights of the city below}. Also spelled jewelled.

A jeweler is a person who makes, repairs, or sells jewelry and often watches. The term covers both skilled craftspeople who design and fabricate pieces and retail merchants who primarily sell them: {The jeweler resized my ring}. Also spelled jeweller in British English.

Jewelers are people who make, repair, or sell jewelry and often watches. The term covers both skilled craftspeople who design and fabricate pieces and retail merchants who primarily sell them. A jeweler's loupe is the small magnifying glass used to examine gems and fine metalwork.

A jeweller is a person who makes, repairs, or sells jewellery—rings, necklaces, bracelets, and other ornamental items. The term also applies to the shop where such work is done: {I took my watch to the jeweller for repair}. Jeweller is the British spelling; Americans write jeweler.

Jewellery is the British spelling of jewelry—decorative items worn on the body, typically made from precious metals, gemstones, or other ornamental materials: rings, necklaces, bracelets, earrings. {She keeps her jewellery in a velvet-lined box.} The word covers both fine pieces and costume jewellery made from less valuable materials.

Jewelry is decorative items worn on the body—rings, necklaces, bracelets, earrings, brooches. The term covers everything from precious gems set in gold to costume pieces worth little. {She inherited her mother's jewelry}. Spelled jewellery in British English.

Jewels are precious or semiprecious stones, especially when cut and polished for ornament: {She wore her finest jewels to the gala}. By extension, jewel applies to anything treasured or prized: {This painting is the jewel of the collection}. The crown jewels are a nation's ceremonial regalia. In watchmaking, jewels are hard stones used as bearings in the movement. Informally, the family jewels means male genitals.

A jezebel is a shameless, scheming, or sexually immoral woman. The term carries strong disapproval, painting its target as manipulative and wicked: {The tabloids called her a jezebel who destroyed his marriage}. The word comes from a biblical queen notorious for her cruelty and idolatry. (Capitalized Jezebel is the biblical figure or a given name.)

A jib is a triangular sail set forward of the mast on a sailing vessel. The phrase {the cut of someone's jib} means their general appearance or manner—originally how a ship could be identified by its distinctive sail shape. Separately, to jib is to balk or refuse to proceed, said of horses and extended to people: {He jibbed at the idea of working weekends}. A jib is also the projecting arm of a crane.

Jibe means to agree or be in harmony: {Her account doesn't jibe with the evidence}. This sense is American and informal. In sailing, to jibe is to shift a sail from one side to the other when running before the wind—also spelled gybe. A separate word jibe means to taunt or mock, though this sense is usually spelled gibe.

Jibes has two distinct sources. One means to agree or be consistent: {Your story doesn't jibe with what she told me}. The other is a taunt or mocking remark, also spelled gibe: {He ignored their jibes about his accent}. In sailing, to jibe is to shift a sail from one side to the other when running before the wind.

A jiffy is a very brief span of time, essentially synonymous with moment or instant: {I'll be back in a jiffy}, {It only takes a jiffy}. The word is informal and cheerful, suggesting quickness without urgency. {Just give me a jiffy to finish this up}.

A jig can be a lively dance or the music that accompanies such a dance. From this, some things that move in a lively way are called jigs, like a fishing device that is jerked up and down in the water, or a device used in processing ore by agitation. To jig can be either to dance a jig or to use a jig in fishing or mining.

A jigger is a small measuring cup used for pouring liquor, typically holding one to two ounces: {The bartender used a jigger to measure the whiskey}. The word extends to various small mechanical devices and gadgets—a jigger might be a golf club, a fishing lure, or any small thing whose proper name escapes you. In this catch-all sense, it overlaps with thingamajig and doohickey.

Jiggers is the plural of jigger, a small measuring cup used for pouring liquor—typically holding 1.5 ounces: {The bartender lined up the jiggers}. A jigger is also a chigoe flea that burrows into skin, or any small mechanical device whose proper name escapes you: {Hand me that jigger over there}.

Jiggle is a small, rapid, back-and-forth or up-and-down movement—a quick shake or wobble. To jiggle something is to shake it lightly: {She jiggled the key in the lock}. Body parts jiggle when they move with a slight bounce: {His belly jiggled when he laughed}. A jiggle is an instance of such movement.

Jiggled is the past tense of jiggle, meaning to shake or move with quick, small, irregular motions. You might jiggle a key in a stubborn lock, jiggle a handle to get it working, or notice something jiggled when bumped: {She jiggled the doorknob but it wouldn't turn}. {The table jiggled when he sat down}.

Jiggles is the third-person singular form of jiggle, describing quick, light shaking movements. When something jiggles, it moves with small, rapid oscillations—like gelatin on a plate or loose change in a pocket. The word often carries playful or slightly comic connotations, particularly when describing body parts: {She jiggles the door handle to get it unstuck}. As a noun, jiggles refers to multiple instances of such movements.

Jiggling is the present participle of jiggle—to shake or move with quick, small movements. Something jiggles when it wobbles or vibrates: {jiggling keys to find the right one}, {jiggling the handle to get the door open}. The word often describes flesh moving under its own momentum: {Her belly was jiggling as she laughed}.

Jiggly describes something that jiggles—shaking or wobbling with small, quick movements. The word typically applies to soft, gelatinous substances or flesh: {jiggly Jell-O}, {jiggly thighs}. It carries a playful, slightly childish tone and often appears in descriptions of desserts or body parts that bounce when moved.

Jiggy means lively, energetic, or uninhibited—often with sexual undertones. The word gained mainstream currency from Will Smith's 1998 hit "Gettin' Jiggy wit It," where {getting jiggy} meant dancing, partying, or hooking up. Outside that phrase, jiggy sees limited use, though it occasionally describes nervous energy: {I get jiggy before job interviews}.

Jigs are lively folk dances, typically in compound time, or the music that accompanies them—associated especially with Irish and Scottish traditions. A jig is also a device that holds work in place or guides a tool: {a drill jig}, {a router jig}. The verb means to dance a jig or to move with quick, jerky motions. To jig something up is to rig or improvise it. {The game is up} was once {the jig is up}—the ruse is over.

A jigsaw is a puzzle made of irregularly shaped interlocking pieces that assemble into a picture. The name comes from the jigsaw—a power tool with a narrow reciprocating blade used to cut curved or intricate shapes, originally used to cut such puzzles from wood. Figuratively, pieces of a jigsaw are fragments that combine to reveal a larger picture: {Investigators assembled the jigsaw of evidence}.

Jigsaws are puzzles made of interlocking pieces that fit together to form a picture. The word also refers to power saws with thin blades that cut intricate curves—the tool's action resembles fitting puzzle pieces together. To jigsaw is to cut with such a saw or to fit together like puzzle pieces: {The schedule was jigsawed to accommodate everyone}.

Jihad is an Arabic term meaning struggle or striving, particularly in service of God. In Islamic tradition, the greater jihad is the internal spiritual struggle against sin and toward moral improvement. The lesser jihad refers to armed struggle in defense of the faith—the sense that dominates Western usage, where jihad typically means holy war waged by Islamic militants: {The group declared jihad against the West}. The adjective is jihadi or jihadist.

Jihadis are people engaged in jihad—Islamic holy war or armed struggle. The term typically refers to militant Islamists who view violent conflict against perceived enemies of Islam as a religious duty. Western media uses jihadi almost exclusively for Islamic extremists and terrorists: {Jihadis claimed responsibility for the attack}. Also spelled jihadist.

Jihadism is a militant Islamic ideology that advocates armed struggle to establish religious governance or defend Muslim lands. The term derives from jihad, an Arabic word for struggle that in mainstream Islam often refers to spiritual self-improvement. Jihadism specifically denotes the violent interpretation embraced by groups like al-Qaeda and ISIS: {The attack was linked to jihadism}. Western usage sometimes applies the label broadly to any Islamic militancy, which critics argue conflates distinct movements and motivations.

To jilt someone is to abruptly reject or abandon them, especially a romantic partner. The word carries connotations of cruelty or callousness—being jilted implies not just rejection but betrayal of expectations: {She jilted him at the altar}. A jilt can also be the person who does the jilting, though this noun use is rare today.

Jilted describes someone who has been suddenly rejected or abandoned by a romantic partner, especially after a promise of commitment: {a jilted lover}, {left jilted at the altar}. The word carries connotations of public humiliation and betrayal—not just a breakup, but being cast aside. To jilt someone is to reject them abruptly after leading them on.

Jilting is the act of abruptly rejecting or abandoning someone, especially a romantic partner. The word typically implies a sudden, callous ending—leaving someone at the altar or breaking off an engagement without warning: {She never recovered from the jilting}. The term carries connotations of betrayal and emotional cruelty.

Jimmied is the past tense of jimmy, meaning to pry open with a tool, typically a crowbar or flat bar used as a lever. The word almost always describes forced entry: {Someone had jimmied the lock}, {The burglar jimmied open the window}. A jimmy is the tool itself—a short crowbar favored for breaking into cars, doors, or windows.

Jimmying is the act of forcing something open, typically a lock, door, or window, using a thin tool as a lever. The word comes from jimmy, slang for a crowbar or pry bar: {Someone had been jimmying the back door}. The term often implies burglary or unauthorized entry.

A jingle is a short, catchy tune designed to be memorable—especially one used in advertising: {I can't get that fast-food jingle out of my head}. The word also describes a light, ringing sound made by small metal objects striking together: {the jingle of keys}, {the jingle of sleigh bells}. To jingle is to make or cause such a sound.

Jingles are short, catchy tunes designed to stick in your head—typically used in advertising to make products memorable: {I can't get that fast-food jingle out of my head}. The word also covers any light, repetitive clinking sound, like keys or small bells: {the jingle of her bracelets}. As a verb, to jingle is to make such a sound: {Coins jingled in his pocket}.

Jingling is the light, high-pitched metallic sound of small objects striking each other repeatedly—keys, coins, bells, or chains: {the jingling of her bracelets as she gestured}. The word can also describe making this sound: {He walked down the hall, jingling change in his pocket}. Jingling suggests a cheerful, rhythmic quality, often associated with holiday bells or loose pocket change.

Jingoism is aggressive nationalism that favors a belligerent foreign policy, especially readiness to go to war. The term carries strong disapproval—it suggests patriotism twisted into hostility toward other nations: {The invasion was driven by jingoism, not legitimate security concerns}. A jingoist beats the drum for military action; jingoistic rhetoric portrays foreign powers as threats requiring forceful response.

Jinn are supernatural beings in Islamic tradition and Arabian folklore, created from smokeless fire and existing in a parallel world to humans. They possess free will, can be good or evil, and may interact with the human realm. A single such being is a jinni, though jinn often serves for both singular and plural. The anglicized genie derives from this word but carries different connotations—wish-granting servants in bottles rather than autonomous spirits. {The story warned of jinn who haunted abandoned places.}

A jinni is a supernatural being in Arab and Islamic tradition—a spirit that can take various forms, influence humans, and possess either good or evil character. The plural is jinn or djinn. Western stories often depict jinn as wish-granting genies in lamps, but traditional belief encompasses a vast spirit world parallel to the human one. {The jinni appeared in a whirlwind of sand.}

Jinns is the plural of jinn, supernatural beings in Islamic and Arabic tradition—spirits created from smokeless fire, capable of good or evil, who exist alongside humans but normally remain invisible. They feature prominently in the Quran and in folklore like the *Arabian Nights*: {The sorcerer summoned jinns to do his bidding}. Also spelled djinns.

A jinx is a person, thing, or circumstance believed to bring bad luck: {He's been a jinx on this team since he arrived}. To jinx something is to curse it or invite misfortune by speaking too confidently: {Don't jinx it by saying we've already won}. The superstition runs deep enough that people genuinely avoid certain statements or behaviors for fear of jinxing outcomes.

Jinxed means cursed with bad luck, as if under a spell that causes things to go wrong. Someone who is jinxed experiences repeated misfortune: {Every project he touches fails—he's jinxed}. Objects or situations can also be jinxed: {That car is jinxed; it breaks down constantly}. The word implies a pattern of bad luck rather than isolated incidents.

Jinxes is the plural of jinx—a curse or hex that brings bad luck. Sports fans avoid jinxes by not mentioning a pitcher's no-hitter in progress. To jinx something is to bring misfortune upon it: {Don't jinx it by saying we've already won}. The word also names the person or thing blamed for the bad luck: {He's a jinx—every team he joins loses}.

Jinxing is tempting fate by speaking too confidently about a favorable outcome before it's secure. If you say {We're definitely going to win} and then lose, someone might accuse you of jinxing it. The superstition holds that expressing certainty invites bad luck—as if the universe punishes overconfidence. {Don't say anything, you'll jinx it.}

Jitter is a nervous, trembling unsteadiness. The jitters are feelings of anxiety or nervousness: {I always get the jitters before a presentation}. Coffee jitters come from too much caffeine. In electronics and telecommunications, jitter is unwanted variation in a signal's timing—small deviations that degrade audio, video, or data quality. To jitter is to shake or fidget nervously.

Jitterbug is a fast, athletic style of swing dance popular in the 1940s, characterized by energetic movements, lifts, and spins. The term also refers to someone who performs this dance: {The jitterbugs cleared the floor with their acrobatics}. By extension, jitterbug can mean a nervous or jittery person, though this sense is dated.

Jitterbugging is dancing the jitterbug, a lively swing dance from the 1930s and 1940s characterized by energetic movements, spins, and lifts. The term can extend to any frenetic activity: {We spent the morning jitterbugging between meetings}.

Jitterbugs is the plural of jitterbug—a fast, energetic swing dance that emerged in the 1930s and 1940s, characterized by acrobatic moves and improvisation. A jitterbug is also someone who performs this dance: {The jitterbugs cleared the floor with their wild moves}. The verb means to dance this way: {They jitterbugged all night}.

Jittering describes rapid, irregular movement or fluctuation—the kind of nervous trembling or shaking that suggests instability. A camera jitters when handheld footage wobbles; a connection jitters when data packets arrive unevenly. In technical contexts, jittering refers to deliberately adding random variation—audio engineers add jitter to reduce distortion, and data scientists jitter points on a graph so overlapping values become visible: {I jittered the scatterplot to show the density}.

Jitters are feelings of nervousness or anxiety, especially before a significant event: {pre-wedding jitters}, {I always get the jitters before a job interview}. The singular jitter is rare except as a verb meaning to act nervously or, in electronics, to experience small rapid variations in a signal. Jittery describes someone in a nervous, agitated state.

Jittery describes a state of nervousness or anxiety, often accompanied by physical restlessness or trembling. Someone jittery before a job interview can't sit still; too much coffee makes you jittery. The word suggests visible agitation—fidgeting, shaky hands, an inability to relax: {Markets were jittery after the announcement}. Jitters is the noun form: {I've got the jitters}.

Jiujitsu is a Japanese martial art focused on grappling, joint locks, and throws rather than strikes. The techniques allow a smaller person to defeat a larger opponent by using leverage and body mechanics. Brazilian jiujitsu, developed in the 20th century, emphasizes ground fighting and submission holds: {She trains jiujitsu three times a week}. Also spelled jujitsu or jiu-jitsu.

Jiujutsu is a Japanese martial art focused on grappling, joint locks, and using an opponent's force against them rather than relying on strikes. The art emphasizes technique over strength, allowing smaller practitioners to defeat larger opponents. Brazilian jiu-jitsu, developed from Japanese jiujutsu, focuses specifically on ground fighting and submissions. Also spelled jujitsu or jujutsu.

Jive covers several loosely related meanings. Originally it named a style of fast, swinging jazz music and the energetic dance that went with it. Jive also became slang for deceptive or nonsensical talk: {Don't give me that jive}. To jive someone is to tease or mislead them. The adjective jive means phony or worthless: {a jive excuse}. Jive is often confused with jibe, which means to agree: {That doesn't jibe with what you said earlier}—though jive increasingly appears in this sense too.

Jives is the verb form of jive—to play or dance to jazz or swing music, or to talk in a teasing, deceptive, or exaggerated way: {He jives her about her cooking}. In African American Vernacular English, jive originally meant empty talk or nonsense. The phrase {that jives with} meaning "agrees with" is a common confusion with "jibes."

Jiving is playful, often exaggerated talk—teasing, joking, or putting someone on: {Quit jiving me and tell me the truth}. The word comes from jive, which originally meant misleading or insincere speech in African American slang. Jiving can also mean dancing to swing or jazz music, though this sense is less common today.

A job is work – work that you perform for compensation (a full-time job), or work that you do to accomplish some end (small jobs around the house). Your job can also be a particular responsibility: It’s your job to make sure no one gets in. Criminal acts are sometimes called jobs, as in a bank job (a robbery). If you’re on the job, you are observant and active at a time when it matters, or you are simply at work.

A jobber is a middleman who buys goods wholesale and sells to retailers—someone who does jobs rather than manufacturing. In wrestling slang, a jobber is a performer whose job is to lose, making featured wrestlers look good: {He spent years as a jobber before getting a real storyline}. In British stock exchange history, jobbers were dealers who traded only with brokers, not the public.

Jobhunting is the process of seeking employment—scanning listings, submitting applications, networking, interviewing. The term frames unemployment as an active pursuit rather than a passive state: {I've been jobhunting for three months now}. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated: job hunting, job-hunting.

Jobless means without a job, synonymous with unemployed. It appears frequently in economic contexts: {jobless claims}, {the jobless rate}. As a noun, {the jobless} refers collectively to unemployed people: {Programs to help the jobless find work}.

Jobs are positions of paid employment: {She applied for three jobs this week}. A job is also any piece of work or task to be done: {Painting the fence was a big job}. In computing, a job is a unit of work processed by a system. To job is to work at odd tasks or buy and sell as a middleman. Something that {does the job} accomplishes what's needed. (Capitalized Jobs typically refers to Steve Jobs.)

A jobseeker is someone actively looking for employment. The term is common in government and bureaucratic contexts, where it often appears in discussions of unemployment benefits, workforce programs, and labor statistics. British English typically writes it as one word, while American English may use job seeker or job-seeker. {The jobseeker's allowance provides temporary financial support while you search for work.}

A jobsworth is a minor official who rigidly enforces petty rules, refusing reasonable requests by citing regulations. The term is British, from the excuse "it's more than my job's worth" to bend the rules: {The jobsworth wouldn't let me in without ID even though she recognized me}. It implies someone who hides behind bureaucratic authority rather than exercising common sense.

A jock is an athlete, especially one who fits the stereotype of being more physically than intellectually inclined. The term often carries connotations of popularity and social dominance in school settings: {The jocks and cheerleaders ruled the cafeteria}. Jock comes from jockstrap, the athletic supporter. In British usage, Jock is informal for a Scottish person.

A jockey is a professional rider in horse races—typically small and light to minimize the burden on the horse. The word extends to anyone who operates or maneuvers something: a {disc jockey} plays records, a {desk jockey} works at a desk. To jockey is to maneuver for advantage: {candidates jockeying for position}. Jockey shorts are close-fitting men's underwear, from the brand name.

Jockeyed is the past tense of jockey, meaning to maneuver skillfully for position or advantage. The word comes from horse racing, where jockeys guide their mounts through crowded fields: {Cars jockeyed for position at the merge}. It often implies competitive or strategic positioning: {She jockeyed herself into the lead role}.

Jockeying is maneuvering for position or advantage, like horse-race jockeys working to get ahead. The word suggests competitive positioning through subtle or strategic moves rather than direct confrontation: {Several candidates are jockeying for the nomination}, {Cars were jockeying for position in the merge lane}. The continuous form emphasizes ongoing struggle rather than a single decisive action.

Jockeys are professional riders in horse races, typically small and light to minimize the burden on the horse. The verb jockey means to maneuver for position or advantage: {Several candidates are jockeying for the nomination}. To jockey something into place is to move it with careful adjustments. A disc jockey plays recorded music.

Jocks is the plural of jock, a slang term for an athlete, especially one who fits the stereotype of being physically strong but not intellectually inclined: {The jocks and the nerds sat at different tables}. Jock can also be short for jockstrap, the supportive undergarment worn during sports. In British usage, Jock is informal for a Scottish person.

A jockstrap is an athletic supporter—an undergarment with a pouch for the genitals and elastic straps around the waist and thighs, worn during sports to protect and hold everything in place. The pouch often accommodates a protective cup. {He forgot his jockstrap and had to sit out practice.}

Jodhpurs are riding pants that fit loosely from the hip to knee and tightly from knee to ankle. The close fit below the knee allows them to slip easily into boots. Named after a city in India, they became standard equestrian attire in the West: {She pulled on her jodhpurs before heading to the stables}.

A joey is a baby kangaroo, wallaby, or other marsupial, especially one still carried in its mother's pouch. The term extends to any young marsupial from birth until it leaves the pouch permanently: {The joey peeked out from its mother's pouch}. In Australian slang, joey can also mean a young animal of other species or a young person.

Joeys is the plural of joey, the term for a baby kangaroo or other marsupial. The word extends to the young of any pouched mammal, including wallabies, koalas, and opossums. Since marsupials are born extremely undeveloped and complete their growth in the mother's pouch, joey specifically refers to this pouch-dwelling stage. {We watched the joeys peeking out from their mothers' pouches.}

Jog refers to a slow, steady run—faster than walking but slower than sprinting: {I jog three miles every morning}. To jog something is to nudge or shake it slightly: {He jogged my elbow}. To {jog someone's memory} is to prompt recall. A jog can also be a sharp turn or irregularity in a line or surface: {The path takes a jog to the left}.

Jogged is the past tense of jog. To jog is to run at a slow, steady pace, typically for exercise: {She jogged three miles this morning}. To jog someone's memory is to prompt recall of something forgotten. A jog can also be a slight shake or nudge, or a brief change in direction: {The path jogged left around the boulder}.

A jogger is someone who jogs—runs at a steady, moderate pace for exercise. The term emerged with the jogging craze of the 1970s and remains the standard word for recreational runners: {Early morning joggers filled the park}. Joggers are also loose-fitting pants with elastic cuffs, designed for athletic or casual wear.

Jogging is running at a steady, moderate pace, typically for exercise rather than speed. It emerged in the 1960s as a fitness activity distinct from competitive running—slower, sustainable, done for health rather than racing. {She goes jogging every morning}. The word also describes any slow, bouncing movement: {the jogging of the cart on the rough road}.

John is one of the most common English male given names, and is a less common surname. When capitalized, it most frequently refers to a person. Some other uses, variably capitalized, include an informal name for a toilet or bathroom (Where’s the john?), and a client of a prostitute. John Doe is a designation for any man, or a substitute name for an anonymous man: The murder victim is a John Doe. John Smith is a placeholder name to represent any man.

A johnboat is a flat-bottomed boat with square ends, typically made of aluminum or wood. Johnboats are designed for shallow, calm waters like rivers, ponds, and swamps, favored by fishermen and hunters for their stability and low draft: {We took the johnboat up the creek to fish for bass}. Also spelled john boat or jon boat.

Johns is the plural of john, an informal term for a toilet or bathroom: {The johns are down the hall}. More commonly, johns refers to the clients of prostitutes—men who pay for sex: {The police arrested several johns in the sting operation}. The term carries a note of anonymity, as if these men are interchangeable.

Join means to bring or come together. You join pieces of wood with glue, join hands with another person, or join a group by becoming a member. Rivers join when tributaries meet the main flow. To join in is to participate: {Join in whenever you're ready}. A join is a place where things connect, especially in woodworking or databases. {Will you join us for dinner?}

A joiner is a woodworker who specializes in making furniture, cabinets, doors, window frames, and other fitted woodwork—distinguished from a carpenter, who does heavier structural work. In British usage especially, the distinction matters: joiners work at a bench with finer pieces, carpenters work on-site with beams and frames. A joiner is also someone inclined to join organizations: {He's a joiner—belongs to every club in town}.

Joinery is the craft of connecting pieces of wood without nails or screws, using interlocking cuts like dovetails, mortises, and tenons. The term also covers the work joiners produce—doors, window frames, staircases, and fitted furniture. In British usage, joinery often distinguishes finer interior woodwork from rougher carpentry: {The joinery in Victorian houses was remarkably precise}.

Joining is the act of coming together or connecting. You might speak of the joining of two rivers, the joining of hands in marriage, or the joining of forces against a common enemy. The word emphasizes the moment or process of union: {The joining of the two companies created a media giant}.

The standard meanings of joint relate to the idea of the verb join. The core meaning of the noun joint is the place where two things meet: finger joint, hip joint. The more common adjective communicated something that is shared: joint venture, joint project. Joint has two common informal meanings: a club or restaurant, especially if it is cheap or disreputable: a great hamburger joint. The other is a marijuana cigarette: Don’t bogart the joint.

Joints are the places where bones meet, allowing movement: {My joints ache in cold weather}. The word extends to any point of connection or junction—where two pipes join, where a plant stem branches. A joint is also a place of business, often seedy or disreputable: {a burger joint}, {a strip joint}. In slang, a joint is a marijuana cigarette. As an adjective, joint means shared or combined: {joint custody}, {joint venture}, {joint account}.

A joist is a horizontal beam that supports a floor or ceiling. Joists run parallel to each other, typically spanning from wall to wall or resting on larger beams, forming the structural framework beneath floorboards or above ceiling panels: {The old joists creaked underfoot}. {We had to sister the damaged joist to reinforce it}.

Joists are horizontal beams that support a floor or ceiling. They run parallel to each other, typically spanning between walls or larger beams, and provide the framework onto which flooring or ceiling material is attached: {The old joists were rotting and needed replacement}. Floor joists, ceiling joists, and roof joists describe their specific locations in a building's structure.

Jojoba is a desert shrub native to the American Southwest and Mexico, cultivated for the oil extracted from its seeds. Jojoba oil closely resembles human skin oils, making it prized in cosmetics and skincare products: {This moisturizer contains jojoba}. The plant tolerates extreme heat and drought.

A joke is something said or done to provoke laughter—a funny story, a witty remark, a prank. {Have you heard the one about the traveling salesman?} A joke can also be something not to be taken seriously: {The exam was a joke}. To joke is to say things in jest rather than earnest: {I was only joking}. A {practical joke} is a prank played on someone. Something {beyond a joke} has become serious or annoying.

A jokebook is a collection of jokes published in book form, typically organized by category or theme. The format ranges from children's riddle books to compilations for amateur comedians: {He brought a jokebook on the road trip to entertain the kids}. Someone described as a jokebook is full of jokes: {My uncle is a walking jokebook}.

Joked is the past tense of joke—to say something humorous or not meant seriously. {He joked about his bad luck}. Someone who joked around was being playful rather than earnest. {She joked that she'd sell the kids if they didn't behave}.

A joker is someone who jokes—a person inclined toward humor or pranks: {He's always been the joker of the group}. In card games, a joker is a wild card, typically depicting a jester, that can substitute for other cards. By extension, a joker can mean an unpredictable element or hidden factor: {There's always a joker in the deck}. The word also dismisses someone as insignificant or foolish: {Who's this joker?}

Jokers is the plural of joker. A joker is someone who jokes—a person prone to humor or pranks: {The office jokers hid my stapler again}. In card games, the joker is a wild card, often depicting a jester. Calling someone a joker can dismiss them as unserious or incompetent: {Some joker cut me off in traffic}.

Jokes are things said or done to provoke laughter—a funny story, a prank, a witty remark. A joke can also be something absurdly inadequate: {The security system was a joke}. To joke is to say something humorous or not meant seriously: {I was only joking}. Someone who {can't take a joke} reacts poorly to teasing. A {practical joke} is a prank. {No joke} emphasizes that something is serious or genuinely impressive: {She ran a marathon—no joke}.

A jokester is someone who tells jokes or plays pranks—a person known for attempting to amuse others. The term is lighthearted and slightly dismissive, suggesting someone who jokes around rather than a skilled comedian: {He's the office jokester, always pulling stunts}. A jokester's humor may or may not land.

Joking describes speech or behavior meant to amuse rather than be taken seriously: {I was only joking}. It signals that what precedes or follows isn't earnest: {Joking aside, we need to talk}. A joking {manner} or joking {tone} suggests lightheartedness. {You must be joking} expresses disbelief—surely this can't be serious.

Jollies is informal for kicks or thrills—pleasure derived from an activity, often mischievous or at someone else's expense: {He gets his jollies from pranking coworkers}. The phrase {get one's jollies} implies indulgence in minor pleasures, sometimes with a hint of disapproval about how the enjoyment is obtained.

Jolly means cheerful and good-humored in a hearty, full-bodied way: {a jolly laugh}, {a jolly old fellow}. The word suggests warmth and conviviality rather than mere pleasantness. British English uses jolly as an intensifier meaning very: {That's jolly good of you}. To jolly someone is to coax them along with good humor: {She jollied him into agreeing}.

Jolt conveys sudden, jarring motion or shock. A physical jolt is an abrupt shake or bump: {The train jolted to a stop}. A jolt of electricity is a sharp shock. Figuratively, a jolt is any sudden surprise or stimulus: {The news gave her a jolt}, {a jolt of caffeine}. To jolt someone is to shake them physically or mentally out of complacency.

Jolted is the past tense of jolt—to shake or jar suddenly, as from impact or shock. A bus jolts when it hits a pothole; passengers are jolted from their seats. The word extends to emotional or mental shocks: {The news jolted her out of complacency}. {He was jolted awake by the alarm}.

Jolting describes sudden, jarring movements or impacts. A jolting {bus ride} bounces passengers roughly. A jolting {realization} strikes with abrupt force—unexpected and unsettling. The word emphasizes the shock of sudden change, whether physical or emotional: {The jolting news left her speechless}.

Jolts are sudden jarring movements or shocks. A train jolts when it starts or stops abruptly. Coffee gives you a jolt of energy. Bad news delivers an emotional jolt. The verb means to shake or startle: {The explosion jolted me awake}. To jolt someone out of complacency is to shock them into awareness.

Jonesing is slang for craving intensely, originally referring to heroin withdrawal but now applied to any strong desire: {I'm jonesing for coffee}, {She was jonesing to get back on stage}. The word comes from jones, slang for an addiction or fixation, possibly from the common surname used to represent an anonymous addict.

Jonquils are spring-flowering bulbs related to daffodils, with clusters of fragrant yellow or white flowers and slender, rushlike leaves. The name comes from a word meaning rush, describing the foliage. In casual use, jonquil often serves as a synonym for any daffodil: {The jonquils are blooming along the fence}.

Jorts are jean shorts—denim pants cut off or manufactured to end above the knee. Once associated with 1980s and 1990s casual fashion, jorts fell out of style before cycling back as both ironic nostalgia and genuine summer wear: {He showed up to the cookout in jorts and flip-flops}.

To jostle is to bump or push against someone, typically in a crowd: {Commuters jostled each other on the platform}. The word suggests repeated contact rather than a single shove. Figuratively, people jostle for position, attention, or advantage—competing in close quarters: {Candidates jostled for the spotlight}. Things that jostle compete for limited space: {Competing priorities jostled in her mind}.

Jostled is the past tense of jostle, meaning to bump, push, or elbow someone, usually in a crowd: {We were jostled by commuters rushing for the train}. The word suggests repeated small collisions rather than a single forceful shove. Figuratively, ideas or priorities can jostle for attention: {Competing demands jostled for space in her mind}.

Jostling is pushing, bumping, or elbowing through a crowd or against others: {jostling for position at the front of the stage}, {commuters jostling on the subway platform}. The word suggests competitive or impatient physical contact rather than accidental bumping. Figuratively, people jostle for attention, power, or advantage without any literal shoving.

Jot captures the idea of something very small. As a noun, it means a tiny amount: {I don't care one jot what he thinks}. The phrase {jot and tittle} refers to the smallest details of something. As a verb, jot means to write something down quickly and briefly, usually as a note or reminder: {Let me jot down your number}. You might jot something on a napkin or in the margins of a book.

Jots is the plural of jot, a tiny amount: {not one jot of evidence}. More commonly, jots appears as a verb—to jot is to write something down quickly and informally: {She jots notes during meetings}, {He jotted down the address}. The phrase {jots and tittles} refers to the smallest details, from marks in Hebrew writing.

A jotter is a small notebook for quick notes or rough work. The term is more common in British English, where it often refers to inexpensive school exercise books: {She kept a jotter in her pocket for stray ideas}. The word suggests informal, provisional writing rather than polished work.

A journal is a record of daily events or reflections—a diary kept for personal use or a log maintained for professional purposes: {She wrote in her journal every night}, {a ship's journal}.
