definition: Lace is a delicate fabric made of threads woven into an open, decorative pattern with holes: {lace curtains}, {a lace collar}. Laces are cords threaded through holes to fasten shoes or garments: {Tie your laces}. To lace is to fasten with such cords, or to add a small amount of something—often alcohol or poison—to food or drink: {coffee laced with whiskey}. A laced story or speech has something woven through it: {a speech laced with profanity}.

Laced describes something threaded or fastened with laces: {laced boots}, {fingers laced together}. More often, laced means something has been added to a drink or food—typically alcohol, drugs, or poison: {coffee laced with whiskey}, {candy laced with fentanyl}. Figuratively, speech or writing can be laced with humor, irony, or profanity: {a tirade laced with obscenities}.

A laceration is a torn or jagged wound, typically caused by blunt trauma or rough contact rather than a clean cut. Doctors use the term to distinguish these irregular injuries from incisions made by sharp objects. {The fall left a deep laceration on his forehead that required stitches.} Laceration also works as a mass noun referring to the act of tearing: {The laceration of tissue was extensive.}

Laces are cords or strings threaded through eyelets to draw edges together and hold something in place—most commonly on shoes, but also corsets, football pads, or any garment requiring adjustable closure. {She bent down to tie her laces.} To lace up is to fasten by tightening and tying the laces. The singular lace also refers to delicate ornamental fabric with an open weave pattern.

Lacewings are delicate flying insects with large, transparent wings marked by a fine network of veins—the "lace" of their name. The adults are harmless, but their larvae are voracious predators of aphids and other small pests, making them valuable in gardens and agriculture. {Green lacewings are sold as biological pest control.}

Lacework is decorative fabric made with intricate patterns of holes and threads, or anything resembling such fabric. The term emphasizes the delicate, openwork quality: {The frost left lacework patterns on the window}. It can describe architecture, metalwork, or natural formations with similar intricacy: {a lacework of bare branches against the sky}.

Lacing is the system of laces threaded through eyelets to fasten something, or the act of threading them: {The lacing on these boots is complicated}. Lacing also means adding a small amount of something, often alcohol or poison, to food or drink: {The punch had a lacing of rum}. A lacing can be a beating or severe scolding.

Lack is the state of not having something, or not having enough of it: {a lack of sleep}, {a lack of evidence}. As a verb, to lack something is to be without it: {He lacks confidence}, {They lack the resources to compete}. What's lacking is what's missing or insufficient. Unlike need or want, lack doesn't imply desire—just absence.

Lackadaisical means lacking enthusiasm or determination, showing a casual indifference where more energy or care would be expected. A lackadaisical {attitude} toward work suggests laziness or apathy. A lackadaisical {effort} falls short of what the situation demands. The word carries mild disapproval—not harsh criticism, but a sense that someone could try harder: {The team's lackadaisical defense cost them the game}.

A lackey is a servant, especially one in uniform who attends a person of high status. The term now mostly appears as an insult for someone who follows orders obsequiously or does another's bidding without question: {He's just a lackey for the party leadership}. The word suggests someone who has surrendered dignity for the sake of pleasing a powerful figure.

Lackeys are servants or followers who do whatever they're told. The word almost always carries contempt—lackeys lack independence and dignity, blindly obeying their masters: {The CEO surrounded himself with lackeys who never challenged his decisions}. In historical usage, a lackey was a liveried footman; the modern sense emphasizes servility over service.
Lacking is a participle that can work as a preposition, usually in a phrase that begins a sentence. It means the same thing as without.

Lackluster describes something dull, uninspired, or lacking brilliance—whether literally or figuratively. A lackluster {performance} fails to impress. A lackluster {economy} shows weak growth. The word suggests falling short of expectations: {The team's lackluster effort disappointed fans}. British spelling: lacklustre.

Lacklustre describes something dull, uninspired, or lacking brilliance—the opposite of shining or vibrant. A lacklustre {performance} fails to impress. Lacklustre {hair} has lost its shine. The word suggests falling short of expected vitality or excellence: {The team put in a lacklustre effort and lost by twenty points}. The spelling is British; Americans write lackluster.

Lacquer is a hard, glossy coating applied to wood, metal, or other surfaces to protect them and give them a shiny finish. Traditional lacquer comes from the sap of certain Asian trees, though modern lacquers are typically synthetic. The verb lacquer means to apply this finish: {The cabinet maker lacquered the dresser to a mirror shine}. Hair lacquer is another term for hairspray, especially the stiff-hold variety that was popular in earlier decades.

Lacquered describes a surface coated with lacquer—a hard, glossy finish that protects and beautifies wood, metal, or other materials. {A lacquered Chinese cabinet} gleams with built-up layers of resin. The word often evokes Asian decorative arts, where lacquerwork is traditional. Figuratively, lacquered can suggest something artificially smooth or overly polished: {her lacquered smile}, {lacquered hair} stiff with spray.

Lacrosse is a team sport in which players use long-handled sticks with netted pouches to catch, carry, and throw a small rubber ball into the opposing team's goal. Originally developed by Indigenous peoples of North America, it's now popular in the United States and Canada at youth, collegiate, and professional levels: {She plays lacrosse for her college team}.

Lactating describes a female mammal producing milk to feed offspring. The term applies during the period after giving birth when mammary glands are active: {lactating mothers}, {a lactating cow}. In human contexts, it often appears in medical or practical discussions about breastfeeding: {The medication isn't recommended for lactating women}.

Lactation is the production of milk by mammary glands, typically following childbirth. The term covers both the biological process and the period during which a mother nurses: {She experienced pain during lactation}. A lactation consultant helps new mothers with breastfeeding difficulties. The verb is lactate.

Lactose is the natural sugar found in milk, composed of glucose and galactose. People who are lactose intolerant lack sufficient enzyme to digest it, causing digestive discomfort from dairy products: {Is this ice cream lactose-free?}

A lad is a boy or young man. The word is common in British and Irish English, where it carries warmth: {He's a good lad}. Among young British men, lad culture celebrates boisterous male bonding—drinking, sports, crude humor. To go out {with the lads} is to socialize with male friends.

A ladder is a device for climbing, consisting of two long parallel supports connected by rungs or steps. Most ladders are portable and lean against a surface, though some are fixed permanently in place. The word extends to anything resembling this structure or suggesting a means of ascent: the corporate {ladder}, the social {ladder}, a {ladder} in a stocking where threads have come undone in a vertical line. To ladder is to climb or to develop such a run in fabric.

Ladders is the plural of ladder—a structure with rungs or steps for climbing up or down. The word appears in contexts involving multiple units {We'll need two ladders to reach the roof} or types {rope ladders, extension ladders}. Figuratively, ladders often suggest hierarchical ascent: {corporate ladders}, {social ladders}. In British slang, ladders are runs in stockings or tights.

Laddie is a Scottish and Northern English term of endearment for a boy or young man, the male counterpart of lassie. It carries warmth and familiarity, often used by older speakers addressing younger males or in nostalgic contexts. Outside Scotland, laddie appears mostly in deliberate evocations of Scottish dialect or culture: {Come here, laddie, and let me show you something}.

Laden means heavily loaded or weighed down. A ship laden with cargo sits low in the water. The word often appears in compounds: {oil-laden tankers}, {debt-laden companies}, {guilt-laden confessions}. Laden typically suggests burden rather than mere fullness—a {laden table} groans under its weight, while trees {laden with fruit} bend their branches.
clues: Like a ship full of freight

definition: Ladies is the plural of lady, referring to women, especially when addressed formally or politely: {Ladies and gentlemen, welcome}. A ladies' room is a women's restroom. {Ladies who lunch} describes wealthy women with leisure time for social gatherings. The term can sound old-fashioned or ironic depending on context: {Listen up, ladies}.

A ladle is a long-handled spoon with a deep bowl, used for serving liquids like soup or stew: {She ladled chili into bowls}. The verb means to scoop and transfer with such a tool, or figuratively to dispense generously: {The coach ladled out praise after the win}.

Ladles are large, long-handled spoons with deep, cup-shaped bowls, used for serving liquids like soup or stew. The verb ladle means to scoop and transfer with such a utensil: {She ladled gravy over the potatoes}. To ladle out can mean to distribute generously: {The organization ladles out grants to struggling artists}.

Lads is the plural of lad—boys or young men. In British and Irish usage, lads often refers to a group of male friends: {I'm going out with the lads tonight}. The word carries connotations of youthful male camaraderie and sometimes rowdy behavior. {Lad culture} describes a masculinity centered on drinking, sports, and banter.

A lady was originally the female counterpart of lord, that is, one having proprietary authority in feudal society. Some of that formal association persists, but today lady is a polite and only slightly formal designation for females, the counterpart of gentleman. Some women find the characterization lady sexist or chauvinistic when it occurs outside the common phrase, ladies and gentlemen. Ladies is a common designation for a lavatory for women in a public place.

A ladybird is a small beetle with a rounded, dome-shaped body, typically red or orange with black spots. The name is chiefly British; Americans usually say ladybug. Both names reflect old associations with the Virgin Mary. Ladybirds are welcomed by gardeners because they eat aphids and other plant pests.

Ladybirds is the British term for the small, dome-shaped beetles Americans call ladybugs. Most species are red or orange with black spots, though patterns vary. Ladybirds are beloved by gardeners because they eat aphids and other pests. The "lady" refers to the Virgin Mary, and the insects have been considered lucky for centuries.

A ladybug is a small, round beetle, typically red or orange with black spots. Ladybugs are considered beneficial insects because they eat aphids and other garden pests. Children often delight in finding them. Also called ladybird, especially in British English.

Ladybugs is the plural of ladybug, a small beetle typically red or orange with black spots. Ladybugs are considered beneficial insects because they eat aphids and other garden pests. Children are often taught to let ladybugs crawl on their hands: {Look, a ladybug landed on me!} Also called ladybirds, especially in British English.

A ladyfinger is a small, light sponge cake shaped like a thick finger, used in desserts like tiramisu and charlottes. The name also applies to several finger-shaped foods: a small banana variety, certain okra pods, and some types of potatoes. In fireworks, a ladyfinger is a small firecracker.

Ladyfingers are light, dry, finger-shaped sponge cakes, slightly sweet and often used as a structural element in desserts like tiramisu or charlotte. They soften when soaked in liquid—coffee, liqueur, or fruit juice—while maintaining enough body to hold layers together. Also spelled as two words: lady fingers.

A ladykiller is a man who is irresistibly attractive to women, often with the implication that he pursues romantic or sexual conquests without serious commitment. The term suggests charm, good looks, and a certain dangerous appeal—the kind of man who breaks hearts. It can be used admiringly or disapprovingly depending on context: {He fancies himself quite the ladykiller}. The compound is sometimes spelled as two words or hyphenated.

Ladykillers is the plural of ladykiller—a man who is irresistibly attractive to women. The term carries a hint of danger or ruthlessness, as if romantic conquest were a kind of predation: {He fancied himself a ladykiller, but women saw through the act}. The word is somewhat dated, more common in mid-twentieth-century usage.

Ladylike describes behavior, manners, or appearance considered proper or refined for a woman—polite, graceful, restrained. The word assumes traditional standards of feminine conduct: {Sit up straight and be ladylike}. It can carry approving or disapproving tones depending on context—sometimes praise for elegance, sometimes criticism implying excessive primness or enforcing gender expectations.

Lag characterizes a time differential or delay, often an undesirable one. Something that lags behind moves or progresses significantly slower. A lag is the delay. The commonest kind of lag is jet lag, when you have traveled a long distance by air and your body isn’t synchronized to your current time zone. A lagging indicator is an economic measure that does not appear until well after some event.

Lager is a type of beer fermented and stored at cold temperatures, producing a crisp, clean taste. Most mass-market beers—Budweiser, Heineken, Corona—are lagers, distinguished from ales by their bottom-fermenting yeast and longer conditioning time. The word comes from German for "storage," referring to the cold cellars where it matures.

Lagers are beers brewed with bottom-fermenting yeast at cooler temperatures, producing a crisp, clean taste. The category includes pilsners, bocks, and most mass-produced American beers. Lagers are typically lighter and more refreshing than ales: {I'll have one of those lagers on tap}. The singular lager names the style or a serving of it.

Lagged means fell behind or failed to keep pace: {The runner lagged behind the pack}. In computing, lagged describes a slow or delayed connection: {The game was so lagged I couldn't play}. Pipes or tanks that are lagged have been wrapped with insulating material to prevent heat loss or freezing.

Lagging is falling behind or moving more slowly than expected. A lagging economy or lagging sales are not keeping pace with projections or competitors. In technology, lagging describes delayed response times: {The game was lagging so badly I couldn't play}. As a noun, lagging refers to insulating material wrapped around pipes or boilers to prevent heat loss. The participle form of lag, lagging often implies something that should be performing better but isn't.

Laggy describes a slow or delayed response, especially in computing and gaming. A laggy connection causes frustrating delays between input and action: {The game was so laggy I kept getting killed}. Laggy video calls stutter and freeze. The word comes from lag, the gap between action and response, with the informal -y suffix marking something characterized by that quality.

A lagoon is a shallow body of water separated from a larger sea or lake by a barrier—typically a sandbar, reef, or strip of land. Coral atolls enclose lagoons, and barrier islands create them along coastlines. The word also applies to shallow artificial ponds, especially those used for sewage treatment: {The wastewater lagoon needed expansion}.

Lagoons are shallow bodies of water separated from a larger sea or lake by sandbars, barrier islands, or coral reefs. The term also applies to the calm water enclosed by a ring-shaped coral atoll. By extension, lagoon describes any shallow pond, especially artificial ones used for sewage treatment or waste settling: {The factory's waste lagoon overflowed during the storm}.

Lags are delays or periods of falling behind, whether in time, speed, or progress. If there's a lag between cause and effect, the effect doesn't happen immediately. In gaming and computing, lag refers to frustrating delays between input and response: {The video lag made the call unbearable}. As a verb, to lag is to fall behind or move slowly: {Production lags behind demand}. In British slang, a lag is a convict, especially one serving a long sentence.

Laid is the past tense of lay—put down, produced eggs, or had sex with: {She laid the baby in the crib}. {The hen laid three eggs today}. {They finally got laid}. To get laid is common slang for having sex. {Laid back} means relaxed and easy-going. {Laid off} means dismissed from a job.

Laidback, also spelled laid-back, describes a relaxed, easygoing temperament or atmosphere, free from tension or urgency. A laidback person doesn't get worked up easily and tends to take things as they come. {The whole vibe at the beach bar was super laidback.} The term can also characterize music, conversation, or any setting with an unhurried, casual feel.

A lair is the den or resting place of a wild animal, especially a predator: {The hunters tracked the wolf to its lair}. By extension, it's any hideout or private retreat, often with sinister overtones: {a villain's lair}, {a criminal's lair}. The word suggests secrecy and seclusion—somewhere deliberately hidden from the world.

Lairs is the plural of lair—a den or resting place of a wild animal, especially a predator: {The hunters tracked the wolves back to their lairs}. By extension, a lair is any hideout or private retreat, often with sinister connotations: {supervillain lairs}, {The detective found the kidnapper's lair}. The word suggests secrecy and concealment.

A lake is a large body of water surrounded by land, bigger than a pond and usually freshwater: {We spent summers at the lake}. The word extends to similar accumulations of other liquids: {a lake of molten lava}, {a lake of spilled wine}. Lake also names a type of pigment made by combining dye with a metalite base, producing rich colors for paints and inks. (Capitalized Lake appears in proper names of specific bodies of water.)

Lakefront refers to the land or area immediately adjacent to a lake's edge: {lakefront property}, {a stroll along the lakefront}. It functions as both noun and adjective, describing real estate, views, or developments situated on a lake's shore. {The city's lakefront attracts joggers and cyclists year-round.}

A lakehouse is a dwelling situated on or near the shore of a lake, typically used as a vacation home or weekend retreat. These properties range from modest cabins to elaborate estates, but all share proximity to water as their defining feature. {We spent every summer at my grandparents' lakehouse.} In computing, lakehouse also refers to a data management architecture that combines features of data lakes and data warehouses.

Lakes are large bodies of water surrounded by land, distinguished from ponds mainly by size—though the line is imprecise. Lakes can be freshwater or saline, natural or artificial. The word extends to any pool of liquid: {a lake of blood}, {a lake of molten lava}. Lake also names a reddish pigment made from dye and metalite compounds.

The land bordering a lake. Lakeshore functions like coastline does for oceans—the strip where water meets land: {We walked along the lakeshore at sunset}. Often appears in place names for waterfront communities and parks. Also spelled as two words: lake shore.

Lallygag, also spelled lollygag, means to spend time aimlessly or to dawdle when you should be doing something productive. It suggests leisurely fooling around rather than attending to responsibilities. {Stop lallygagging and get your homework done.} The word has a playful, slightly old-fashioned quality and is often used by parents or teachers scolding children for wasting time.

A lama is a Tibetan Buddhist monk or spiritual teacher, especially one of high rank. The Dalai Lama and Panchen Lama are the tradition's most prominent figures. {The lama led the monastery's meditation practice.} Not to be confused with llama, the South American animal—one L for the monk, two for the beast.

A lamb is a young sheep, typically under one year old. The meat from such an animal is also lamb: {roast lamb}, {lamb chops}. Figuratively, a lamb is someone gentle, innocent, or easily led—often a victim: {a lamb to the slaughter}. To lamb is to give birth, said of ewes. {Like a lamb} suggests meekness or docility.
clues: What a ewe gives birth to

definition: Lambaste means to criticize or scold someone harshly and at length. If your boss lambastes you for missing a deadline, you're getting a severe verbal thrashing. The word can also mean to beat or thrash physically, though this sense is less common today. {The critics lambasted the film for its weak plot.} {She was lambasted in the press for her controversial remarks.}

Lambasting is harsh, severe criticism—a verbal assault that leaves no doubt about the critic's displeasure. Politicians get lambasted by opponents, movies get lambasted by reviewers, employees get lambasted by bosses. The word suggests public, forceful condemnation rather than private disapproval: {The senator was lambasted for her comments on immigration}. Also spelled lambasting.

A lambchop is a cut of lamb meat taken from the rib, loin, or shoulder, typically including a portion of bone and cooked by grilling, broiling, or pan-frying. The term also serves as an affectionate nickname or term of endearment, similar to calling someone sweetie or honey. {These lambchops need about four minutes per side.} {Come here, lambchop, and give me a hug.}

Lambchops are cuts of lamb meat from the rib or loin, typically served individually with the bone attached: {We're having lambchops for dinner}. The term also refers to sideburns that are wide at the jaw and narrow toward the ear, resembling the shape of the meat cut: {He grew out his lambchops for the costume party}.

Lambda is the eleventh letter of the Greek alphabet (Λ, λ), used across scientific and technical fields. In physics, lambda represents wavelength. In mathematics and computer science, lambda denotes anonymous functions—functions defined without being bound to a name: {Python's lambda expressions let you write quick one-liners}. Lambda calculus is the formal system underlying functional programming. In genetics, lambda phage is a virus that infects bacteria. The symbol appears in various specialized contexts, from cosmology's cosmological constant to linear algebra's eigenvalues.

Lambing is the season or process during which ewes give birth to lambs, typically occurring in late winter or early spring on sheep farms. The term also refers to the work of tending sheep during this period, which often requires round-the-clock attention from farmers. {We hired extra help for lambing season.} As a verb form, lambing describes the act of a ewe delivering her young or a farmer assisting with births.

Lambs is the plural of lamb—young sheep, typically under a year old. The word extends to the meat from such animals: {We're having lambs for the dinner party}. Figuratively, lambs are innocent or gentle people, easy prey for wolves or others who would exploit them. To lamb is to give birth, said of ewes: {The flock is lambing early this year}.

Lambskin is the skin of a lamb, especially when tanned with the wool still attached or processed into soft leather. It's prized for clothing, gloves, and linings because of its suppleness: {a lambskin jacket}. Lambskin also refers to parchment made from lamb hide, historically used for documents and bookbinding.

Lambswool is soft, fine wool from a young sheep's first shearing, prized for its delicacy and warmth. The term usually describes textiles: a lambswool {sweater}, lambswool {yarn}. Because the fibers have never been cut, they're softer than wool from later shearings. Also spelled lamb's wool or lambs wool.

Lame originally described a person or animal unable to walk normally due to injury or disability: {The horse went lame after the race}. {He was lame in one leg from childhood}. This sense remains standard in veterinary and some medical contexts. By extension, lame came to mean weak, unconvincing, or inadequate: {a lame excuse}, {a lame attempt}. In slang, lame means uncool or pathetic: {That party was lame}. Some disability advocates object to the slang usage as perpetuating ableist attitudes, though most speakers are unaware of the connection.

A lamebrain is a stupid or foolish person: {Don't be such a lamebrain}. The word also works as an adjective meaning stupid: {another lamebrain idea from management}. Mildly insulting rather than harsh—the kind of insult you might use with someone you actually like.

To lament is to express grief, sorrow, or deep regret. People lament deaths, losses, and the state of the world: {She lamented the passing of her mentor}. As a noun, a lament is an expression of mourning—a song, poem, or cry of grief. The adjective lamentable describes something regrettable or deplorable: {a lamentable lack of judgment}.

Lamentation is the act of expressing grief or sorrow, often publicly and vocally. A lamentation is also a specific utterance of grief—a wail, a dirge, a mournful cry: {The lamentations of the mourners filled the church}. The word has a formal, literary quality; everyday speech prefers simpler terms like crying or grieving.

Lamentations are expressions of grief, sorrow, or mourning—the outpouring of anguish over loss or suffering. The word carries a formal, almost literary weight: {The lamentations of the bereaved filled the chapel}. It suggests sustained, vocal grieving rather than quiet sadness. (Capitalized Lamentations is a book of the Bible.)

Lamenting is the act of expressing grief, sorrow, or deep regret. Someone lamenting a loss mourns it openly, often with words or sounds of anguish. The term applies both to genuine expressions of pain and to more theatrical displays: {She spent the evening lamenting her failed relationship}. People also lament things they find regrettable without experiencing true grief: {Critics are always lamenting the death of cinema}.

Laments is the plural of lament—expressions of grief, sorrow, or regret. A lament may be spoken, written, or sung: {funeral laments}, {a poet's laments for lost love}. As a verb form, laments means to mourn or express deep regret: {She laments the death of her father}, {He laments his wasted youth}.

To laminate is to bond layers together, typically covering something with a thin protective coating of plastic or similar material: {I laminated my ID card}. Laminate as a noun refers to material made of bonded layers—laminate flooring consists of fused synthetic materials mimicking wood. Laminated surfaces resist moisture and wear. The word applies wherever layers are fused: laminated glass, laminated dough.

Laminated describes something made of thin layers bonded together for strength or protection. Laminated wood consists of sheets glued with grains crossing for stability. A laminated card or document has been sealed in plastic: {I had my ID laminated}. Laminated glass holds together when shattered because of an inner plastic layer.

Laminating is the process of bonding layers together, typically by encasing paper or cardstock between thin sheets of clear plastic film to protect and preserve it. Documents, photos, and ID cards are commonly laminated to make them more durable and resistant to moisture, tearing, and fading. The term extends to manufacturing processes where materials like wood, metal, or glass are layered and bonded: {The countertops are made by laminating sheets of decorative material onto particleboard}.

A lamp is a device that produces light, typically electric but historically fueled by oil or gas. Table lamps and floor lamps are common household fixtures. The word extends to bulbs themselves: {The lamp burned out}. To lamp someone, in older slang, is to look at or stare at them. {She lamped him from across the bar.}

Lamplight is the light produced by a lamp, especially the warm, soft glow of traditional oil or gas lamps rather than electric lighting. The word carries nostalgic or atmospheric connotations: {They dined by lamplight}, {Her face was visible in the lamplight}. It often evokes intimacy or an earlier era.

A lamplighter was a person employed to light and extinguish gas streetlamps, walking a route at dusk and dawn with a long pole. The occupation disappeared with electric lighting but survives in figurative use for anyone who brings illumination or leads the way: {She was a lamplighter for the civil rights movement}.

Lamplighters were workers who lit and extinguished gas street lamps before electric lighting, traveling routes at dusk and dawn with long poles. The term now appears mostly in historical contexts or figuratively for those who bring light or enlightenment to others. {The last lamplighters disappeared from city streets by the mid-twentieth century.}

Lamplit describes something illuminated by a lamp rather than sunlight or electric light, evoking warmth and intimacy: {a lamplit room}, {lamplit streets}. The word carries a nostalgic quality, suggesting scenes from before electric lighting became universal—cozy interiors, quiet evenings, old-fashioned domesticity.

A lampoon is a harsh, mocking attack on someone or something, typically through satire or parody. The word works as both noun and verb: {The late-night show lampooned the senator's speech}. Lampoons exaggerate flaws or absurdities for ridicule, often targeting public figures or institutions. The tone is sharper than gentle teasing—closer to skewering than ribbing.

Lampooning is publicly mocking or ridiculing someone or something through satire, caricature, or parody. The target is usually a public figure, institution, or idea presented as deserving scorn: {The sketch show made its name lampooning politicians}. A lampoon attacks with humor rather than direct criticism, often exaggerating flaws for comic effect.

Lampoons are satirical attacks that mock or ridicule a person, institution, or idea through exaggerated humor. The verb lampoon means to subject someone or something to such mockery: {The sketch show lampoons politicians of all stripes}. Lampoons tend toward broad, pointed comedy rather than subtle wit—closer to caricature than gentle teasing.

A lamppost is a tall pole supporting a street light. Lampposts line roads and pathways, providing illumination after dark. The term appears in expressions about public visibility or drunkenness: {He was so drunk he couldn't find a lamppost to lean on}. In programming and logic puzzles, the lamppost sometimes represents searching where light is available rather than where the answer lies.

Lampposts are tall poles that support street lights, typically lining roads and sidewalks to illuminate public spaces at night. The lamppost is a fixture of urban and suburban landscapes, often appearing in descriptions of evening scenes: {She waited under the lamppost}. In British English, also spelled as two words: lamp posts.

A lamprey is an eel-like aquatic creature with a jawless, circular mouth lined with teeth, which it uses to attach to fish and feed on their blood. Lampreys are among the most primitive vertebrates, predating dinosaurs. {Sea lampreys have devastated fish populations in the Great Lakes.}

Lampreys is the plural of lamprey, an eel-like jawless fish with a circular, sucker-like mouth lined with teeth. Lampreys attach to other fish and feed on their blood and tissue. Some species are parasitic pests in the Great Lakes; others are considered a delicacy in parts of Europe. {The sea lampreys decimated the lake trout population.}

Lamps are devices that produce light, typically consisting of a base, a light source, and often a shade: {a bedside lamp}, {a floor lamp}. The word extends to any light-emitting apparatus: {heat lamp}, {lava lamp}, {lamp post}. In slang, lamps are eyes: {Get a load of those lamps}.

A lampshade is a cover placed over a light bulb to diffuse or direct light and reduce glare. Lampshades come in various shapes—conical, cylindrical, drum—and materials from fabric to paper to glass. {She picked out a new lampshade for the bedroom}. Wearing a lampshade on one's head is a cliché of drunken party behavior.

A lance is a long wooden shaft with a pointed metal head, used as a weapon by mounted knights and cavalry. The knight would couch the lance under his arm and charge, using the horse's momentum to deliver impact. To lance is to pierce, as with such a weapon. In medicine, to lance a boil or abscess is to cut it open to drain fluid. A lance corporal is the lowest rank of noncommissioned officer in some military branches—originally one who served without higher pay. (Capitalized Lance is a given name.)

A lancer is a cavalry soldier armed with a lance—a long spear used in mounted charges. The term evokes 18th- and 19th-century European military units: {Polish lancers}, {Bengal Lancers}. Lancers also names a type of formal quadrille dance popular in the Victorian era. In fantasy games and fiction, lancer often designates a spear-wielding character class.

Lancers is a 19th-century square dance for four or more couples, performed in five figures with specific formations. The name comes from the military cavalry soldiers who carried lances, though the connection to the dance is largely stylistic. {They learned the lancers for the period ball.} The singular lancer refers to a mounted soldier armed with a lance.

Lances is the plural of lance, a long spear used by mounted warriors, especially medieval knights charging in combat. The word extends to similar implements: a lance for spearfishing, a surgeon's lancet. To lance is to pierce, particularly to open an abscess and drain it: {The doctor lanced the boil}. A {freelance} worker originally fought for whoever paid.

The part of the earth that is not water is land. This core meaning inspires all others. Land that is bought and sold is a division of the overall volume of the earth’s land. A country, or a part of the world with a particular characteristic can also be called a land: Her native land is Hungary, but she has traveled to many foreign lands. When you land a fish, you bring it to shore; when you land a job, you acquire it, usually as a result of some effort. When land precedes a noun, it usually refers to some aspect of real estate: land grab, land reform.

A landbridge is a strip of land connecting two larger landmasses, allowing passage between them. The Bering landbridge once linked Asia to North America, enabling human migration during the Ice Age. In shipping, landbridge refers to overland transport connecting sea routes: {Containers crossed the Pacific, then moved by rail landbridge to Atlantic ports}.

Landed describes having arrived at a destination, especially after flight: {The plane landed safely}. It also means possessing land as property: {landed gentry}, {landed wealth}. The landed aristocracy derived status from owning estates rather than earning wages. In casual speech, landed can mean having secured something desirable: {She landed a great job}.

A lander is a spacecraft designed to touch down on a celestial body rather than orbit it: {The lander descended to the lunar surface}. More generally, a lander is someone or something that lands—a fish that's been landed, a plane touching down, a gymnast sticking the dismount. (Capitalized Lander is a city in Wyoming.)

Landfall is the moment when a ship or aircraft reaches land after a journey over water, or when a storm moves from sea onto shore: {The hurricane made landfall near Mobile}. The term emphasizes arrival at land as an event—Columbus's landfall in the Bahamas, a pilot's first landfall after crossing the Atlantic. It can also mean the land itself that is sighted or reached.

Landfalls is the plural of landfall, which denotes the moment when a ship or aircraft reaches land after a journey over water, or when a storm system moves from sea onto shore. Weather reports frequently use the term when tracking hurricanes: {The storm made landfall near Galveston}. For sailors and explorers, landfall historically marked the successful completion of a voyage. The word can also refer to the land itself that is first sighted or reached.

A landfill is a site where garbage and other waste materials are disposed of by burying them in the ground. Modern landfills are engineered facilities with protective liners and systems to manage the toxic runoff that decomposing waste produces. The term also works as a verb: {The city landfilled thousands of tons of debris after the storm}. Landfill can refer to the waste material itself or to land that has been created by filling in low-lying areas with garbage.

Landfills are sites where garbage and other waste materials are disposed of by burying them in the ground. Modern landfills are engineered with liners and drainage systems to prevent contamination of surrounding soil and groundwater, though older or poorly managed sites can leak pollutants into the environment. The term often carries negative connotations in environmental discussions, as landfills produce methane gas and take decades or centuries to decompose. {The city's landfills are nearly at capacity.}

A landgirl was a woman who worked on farms during World War I or World War II, replacing men who had gone to fight. The term refers specifically to members of the Women's Land Army in Britain: {My grandmother was a landgirl in Kent during the war}. Also spelled as two words: land girl.

A landgrab is a swift, aggressive acquisition of territory or resources, often by force or questionable means. Originally literal—seizing land from indigenous peoples or during colonial expansion—the term now applies figuratively to any aggressive takeover: {a corporate landgrab for market share}, {a landgrab for streaming rights}. Also spelled land grab.

A landgrabber is someone who seizes land aggressively or opportunistically, often through questionable legal means or by exploiting weaker parties. The term originated in contexts of colonial expansion and frontier settlement, where speculators or settlers would claim territory belonging to others. Today it applies broadly to anyone—individual or corporate—who acquires land through predatory practices: {International landgrabbers have bought up vast tracts of African farmland}. The related noun landgrab describes the act itself.

Landgrabs is the plural of landgrab—acquisitions of land through aggressive, opportunistic, or dubious means. The term often describes powerful entities seizing territory from less powerful ones: corporations buying up farmland in developing countries, governments appropriating indigenous territory, or developers snapping up urban lots. {International landgrabs have displaced thousands of small farmers.} The word implies that the acquisition is unfair or exploitative, even when technically legal.

A landing is the act of coming down to rest on a surface—an airplane's landing, a gymnast sticking a landing. It also names the place where this happens: a boat landing on a river, a landing strip for aircraft. Inside buildings, a landing is the platform between flights of stairs where you can pause or change direction. As a modifier, it describes things used for coming ashore: {landing craft}, {landing party}.

Landings is the plural of landing, which names the act of coming to rest after flight or travel. Aircraft make landings; so do spacecraft, boats, and troops storming beaches. A landing is also a level area at the top or bottom of stairs, or between flights: {She paused on the landing to catch her breath}. Fish landings are catches brought to shore.

A landlady is a woman who owns property and rents it to tenants, or who runs a boarding house or inn. The term parallels landlord but specifies female ownership or management: {The landlady came by to collect the rent}. In British usage especially, a landlady may also be a woman who manages a pub.

A landline is a telephone connected by physical wires, as opposed to a mobile phone. The term emerged as cell phones became dominant, retroactively naming what had simply been "the phone": {Do you have a landline, or just your cell?} Landlines are associated with home phones, older technology, and reliability during emergencies when cellular networks fail.

Landlines are telephone connections that run through physical wires—as opposed to cellular or satellite phones, which transmit wirelessly. The term emerged only after mobile phones became common; before that, all phones were landlines and needed no distinguishing label. {Does anyone still have a landline?} The word often carries a whiff of obsolescence.

Landlocked describes a place entirely surrounded by land, with no access to the sea: {Bolivia and Paraguay are South America's only landlocked countries}. The term extends to bodies of water cut off from larger ones: {a landlocked bay}, {landlocked salmon} (populations trapped in freshwater lakes). Figuratively, it suggests being hemmed in or isolated from broader connections.

A landlord is someone who owns property and rents it to tenants. The term applies to residential properties {My landlord raised the rent again} and commercial ones. Landlord also means the keeper of an inn or pub, though this sense is now chiefly British. The female equivalent landlady exists but landlord increasingly covers all genders.

Landlords is the plural of landlord, a person who owns property and rents it to others. The term applies to residential housing {My landlord raised the rent again} and commercial real estate. Landlord carries connotations ranging from neutral to negative—the word often appears in complaints about neglected repairs, unfair evictions, or exploitative practices. A landlord may be an individual or a corporation.

A landlubber is someone unfamiliar with the sea or sailing—a person who stays on land rather than venturing onto boats. The term originated as sailors' contemptuous slang for the inexperienced or clumsy: {The landlubbers stumbled around the deck, grabbing anything bolted down}. Now mostly playful or nostalgic, evoking pirate movies and nautical fiction.

Landlubbers is the plural of landlubber—a person unfamiliar with the sea or sailing. The term comes from nautical slang, combining land with lubber (a clumsy person). Sailors use it dismissively for those who lack sea legs or maritime knowledge: {The landlubbers turned green the moment we hit open water}.

A landmark is a prominent feature of a landscape—a building, monument, or natural formation that helps people navigate or identify a location: {The old lighthouse served as a landmark for sailors}. By extension, landmark describes significant events or achievements that mark turning points: a landmark {decision}, a landmark {case}, a landmark {album}. The word suggests something that stands out from its surroundings, whether physically or historically.

Landmarks are prominent features that help identify a location. A landmark may be natural (a distinctive mountain) or built (a famous building). Travelers use landmarks for navigation: {Turn left at the church}. The term extends to significant events or achievements: {a landmark Supreme Court decision}, {a landmark moment in civil rights history}.

A landmass is a large continuous area of land, especially a continent or major portion of one. The term emphasizes size and unbroken expanse: {The Eurasian landmass stretches from Portugal to the Pacific}. Islands are distinguished from landmasses by their smaller scale, though large ones like Australia blur the line.

A landmine is an explosive device buried just below ground, designed to detonate when stepped on or driven over. Landmines remain dangerous long after conflicts end, killing and maiming civilians for decades: {The field was still littered with landmines from the war}. Figuratively, a landmine is any hidden danger that can blow up unexpectedly: {The interview was full of political landmines}.

Landmines are explosive devices buried just below the surface, designed to detonate when stepped on or driven over. Military forces plant them to deny territory to enemies, but they persist for decades after conflicts end, maiming civilians long after wars conclude. Figuratively, a landmine is any hidden danger waiting to be triggered: {The interview was full of political landmines}.

A landowner is a person who owns land, especially a substantial amount of rural or agricultural property. The term often implies wealth or social standing: {The local landowners opposed the new housing development}. In historical contexts, landowners formed a privileged class with political power tied to their holdings.

A landrush is a sudden rush to claim available land, historically referring to government-organized events where settlers raced to stake claims on newly opened territory. The term now commonly describes any competitive scramble for limited resources released simultaneously: {the domain name landrush of the early internet}, {a landrush for beachfront property}. Also spelled land rush.

Lands is the third-person singular present tense of the verb land, meaning to arrive on the ground after traveling through air or water, or to bring something to such arrival: {The plane lands at noon}, {She always lands on her feet}. It also means to succeed in obtaining something desirable: {He lands the job after three interviews}. As a plural noun, lands refers to expanses of territory or property: {The family owns lands throughout the county}, {foreign lands}.

Landscape is a view of natural scenery—hills, fields, forests, water—as seen from a single vantage point. The word extends to paintings or photographs of such views: {a landscape by Constable}. More broadly, landscape describes any field or domain: {the political landscape}, {the media landscape}. In printing and display, landscape orientation is wider than it is tall, mimicking the horizontal sweep of scenic views. To landscape is to modify terrain for aesthetic effect: {They landscaped the backyard with native plants}.

A landscaper is a person who designs, installs, or maintains outdoor spaces—lawns, gardens, patios, and plantings. The term covers both skilled designers who plan elaborate grounds and workers who mow, trim, and haul. {The landscapers arrive every Thursday to cut the grass.} {We hired a landscaper to redesign the backyard.}

Landscapers are people who design, install, or maintain outdoor spaces—lawns, gardens, trees, and hardscape features like patios and walkways. The term covers everyone from crews who mow and trim to professionals who plan elaborate garden layouts: {The landscapers are coming Thursday to put in the new shrubs}.

Landscapes are wide views of natural or outdoor scenery—mountains, valleys, fields, coastlines. The term also covers artistic depictions of such scenes: {a landscape painter}, {a landscape photograph}. Extended uses describe the general state of a domain: {the political landscape}, {the media landscape}. In computing, landscape orientation means wider than tall, as opposed to portrait. To landscape is to modify terrain for aesthetic purposes: {We landscaped the backyard}.

Landscaping is the work of modifying outdoor areas—planting, grading, building paths or walls—to make them more attractive or functional. As a mass noun, it refers to the features themselves: {The new landscaping really improved the property's curb appeal}. Professional landscaping ranges from basic lawn care to elaborate garden design.

A landslide is the sudden collapse and downward movement of a mass of earth or rock on a slope, often triggered by rain, earthquakes, or erosion. The term extends powerfully into politics, where a landslide describes an overwhelming electoral victory: {She won by a landslide}. In both senses, landslide conveys something massive and decisive—ground giving way all at once, or voters shifting dramatically in one direction.

Landslides are masses of rock, earth, or debris that slide down a slope, often triggered by heavy rain, earthquakes, or erosion. The word extends to overwhelming victories, especially in elections: {She won by a landslide}. Both senses share the image of something massive and unstoppable sweeping everything before it.
clues: Slopes that fail all at once

definition: A lane is a narrow path or passageway. On roads, lanes are parallel strips of traffic moving in one direction: {Stay in your lane}, {the left lane is for passing}. Swimming pools and bowling alleys have lanes too. In computing and gaming, {stay in your lane} has become advice to mind your own business or stick to what you know.

Lanes is the plural of lane, a word for a narrow path or road, or a designated strip within a larger road or body of water. Highways are divided into lanes to organize traffic flow; swimmers and bowlers stay in their lanes to avoid interfering with others. The expression {stay in your lane} has become a common way of telling someone to mind their own business or stick to what they know.

Langoustines are small lobster-like crustaceans prized in European cuisine, especially French and Scottish cooking. Also called Norway lobsters or Dublin Bay prawns, they have slender claws and delicate, sweet flesh: {langoustines in garlic butter}, {grilled langoustines with aioli}. They're smaller than true lobsters but larger than most shrimp.

Language is the complex system of symbolic communication that is unique to humans, or this system as used by a single country or population, as in the Burmese language. An even narrower definition is the wording or expressions associated with something, such as the language of the contract. If you are told to watch your language, it is a warning against using profanity. Your native language is the one that you learned first as a child, typically the language spoken by your parents.

Languages are systems of communication—spoken, written, or signed—shared by communities of people. English, Mandarin, and Arabic are languages; so is American Sign Language. The word extends to any specialized system of symbols or rules: {programming languages}, {the language of music}. Someone's language is also their manner of expression: {Watch your language}.

Languid describes a state of relaxed slowness, suggesting someone drained of energy or simply unhurried: {a languid afternoon by the pool}, {She gave a languid wave}. The word can imply pleasant laziness or physical weakness—context determines whether someone is luxuriating or flagging. Languid movements are graceful but slow, as if effort costs too much.
clues: Moving as if through warm honey

definition: Languish means to lose vitality or grow weak, typically from neglect or unfavorable conditions. A prisoner languishes in a cell; a proposal languishes in committee; a plant languishes without water. The word suggests prolonged suffering or decline rather than sudden collapse: {The project languished for years before finally being revived}. Someone can also languish for something they desire, pining with unfulfilled longing.

Languished is the past tense of languish, meaning to grow weak or lose vitality, especially through prolonged suffering or neglect. A prisoner languishes in a cell; a bill languishes in committee; a plant languishes without water. The word suggests slow decline rather than sudden collapse: {The project languished for years before being revived}. It can also mean to pine with longing: {She languished for her distant lover}.

Languishing describes a state of losing vitality, momentum, or spirit. A plant languishes without water; a prisoner languishes in a cell; a project languishes when no one attends to it. The word suggests prolonged neglect or decline rather than sudden collapse: {The bill languished in committee for months}. Someone languishing may also be pining with unmet desire: {languishing for her attention}.

Lanky describes a person who is tall and thin, with an ungainly or loosely jointed quality. The word suggests limbs that seem too long for the body—awkward rather than graceful: {a lanky teenager who hadn't grown into his height yet}. Lanky carries a mild, often affectionate tone, distinct from the harshness of gaunt or scrawny.

A lantern is a portable light source, traditionally consisting of a lamp or candle enclosed in a protective case with transparent panels. The enclosure shields the flame from wind while allowing light to pass through. Lanterns have largely been replaced by electric flashlights for practical use, but they persist in decorative contexts, camping equipment, and cultural celebrations like Chinese lantern festivals. {Jack-o'-lanterns} are hollowed pumpkins carved with faces and lit from within, displayed at Halloween.

Lanterns are portable light sources, traditionally an enclosure with transparent panels protecting a flame from wind. The design varies from paper lanterns at festivals to metal lanterns for camping. By extension, lantern describes lamp-like structures: a lighthouse lantern, or the windowed cupola atop a dome that admits light. {We hung paper lanterns in the backyard for the party.}

A lanyard is a cord worn around the neck or wrist to hold something—an ID badge, keys, a whistle, a phone. Originally a nautical term for short ropes used to secure rigging or weapons, lanyards now appear most often at conferences, schools, and workplaces: {Everyone at the convention wore lanyards with their name tags}.

Lanyards are cords or straps worn around the neck or wrist to hold something—an ID badge, keys, a whistle, a phone. Originally nautical rigging, the term now most commonly refers to the ubiquitous fabric straps at conferences and workplaces: {Everyone at the convention wore lanyards with their credentials}. They often display logos or branding.

Lap is most frequently a noun with two main meanings: the distance around a running track or twice the length of a swimming pool (run a lap, swim laps); and the top of your thighs when you are sitting down: I have a cat in my lap. The verb lap most frequently characterizes the motion of waves on a shore, or the action of taking up a liquid with the tongue, like dogs and cats do. If one thing laps on or over another, it covers or overhangs it.

A lapdance is an erotic performance in which a dancer gyrates on or near a seated customer's lap, typically at a strip club. The dancer may straddle the customer while moving suggestively, though rules about physical contact vary by venue. {He spent two hundred dollars on lapdances that night.}

A lapdog is a small dog suited to being held in a person's lap—breeds like Chihuahuas, Pomeranians, and toy poodles. Figuratively, a lapdog is someone who follows another's wishes without question, eager to please and unwilling to challenge: {The senator accused the media of being the administration's lapdogs}.

Lapdogs are small dogs bred to sit in a person's lap—breeds like Chihuahuas, Pomeranians, and toy poodles. The term extends figuratively to people who follow someone powerful with unquestioning obedience: {The senator surrounded himself with lapdogs who never challenged his decisions}. The figurative use is always dismissive, suggesting servility over independence.

A lapel is the folded flap of fabric on each side of a coat or jacket, extending from the collar down to where the garment buttons. Lapels vary in width and style—notched, peaked, or shawl—and their prominence has shifted with fashion over the decades. A {lapel pin} is a small decorative or symbolic badge worn on this part of a jacket, often to indicate membership, support for a cause, or simply as ornamentation.

Lapels are the folded flaps of fabric on each side of a coat or jacket, extending from the collar down to the chest where the garment buttons. They come in several styles—notched, peaked, or shawl—and vary in width with fashion trends. Wide lapels suggest 1970s style; narrow ones read as modern or conservative. {He grabbed the man by his lapels.}

Lapis is shorthand for lapis lazuli, a deep blue semiprecious stone prized since antiquity for jewelry and pigment. The intense blue of ultramarine paint originally came from ground lapis lazuli. {The necklace featured polished lapis beads}. In gaming contexts, lapis often refers to a blue mineral resource used for crafting or enchanting.
clues: Stone half of a gemstone name

definition: Lapped is the past tense of lap, which has several meanings that converge on the idea of folding or wrapping around. Water laps against a shore, moving in gentle folds. A cat laps milk by curling its tongue to scoop liquid. To lap someone in a race is to complete a circuit around the track and pass them again: {She lapped the slower runners twice}. Something lapped is folded over or wrapped: {lapped siding}, {lapped joints}.

Lapping describes the action of taking up liquid with the tongue, as a cat laps milk, or the sound of gentle waves striking a surface: {water lapping against the hull}. In metalworking and machining, lapping is a precision finishing process that uses abrasive paste to polish surfaces to extreme smoothness and flatness.

Laps is the plural of lap—the flat surface of the upper legs when seated, or a single circuit of a track or pool. To lap someone in a race is to overtake them by a full circuit: {She lapped the slower runners twice}. Water laps against the shore with gentle, repeated waves. A cat laps milk by curling its tongue to draw liquid into its mouth.

A lapse is a temporary failure or slip—a momentary falling away from a standard. A lapse in {judgment}, a lapse in {concentration}, a memory {lapse}. The word implies something brief rather than permanent: {a lapse into old habits}. Time lapses when it passes, especially unnoticed: {Several months lapsed before we spoke again}. A lapsed {membership} or lapsed {Catholic} has expired or fallen away through inaction. In law, rights or offers lapse when they're no longer valid.

Lapsed describes something that has expired, ended, or fallen away through inaction or neglect. A lapsed {membership} wasn't renewed. A lapsed {Catholic} no longer practices the faith. A lapsed {patent} lost its protection. The word implies gradual slipping rather than deliberate termination—things lapse when attention or commitment fades: {After a lapsed silence, the conversation resumed}.

Lapses is the plural of lapse—a temporary failure, slip, or interval. A lapse of memory is a moment of forgetting. A lapse in judgment is a brief failure to think clearly. Lapses can also be gaps in time: {lapses between visits}. As a verb form, lapses means expires or falls away: {The policy lapses if you don't pay}.

A laptop is a portable computer small enough to use on your lap. The screen folds down over the keyboard for transport. Laptops are distinguished from desktop computers by their portability and from tablets by their built-in keyboards. {I left my laptop at the office}. The word works as both noun and modifier: {laptop screen}, {laptop bag}.

Laptops is the plural of laptop, a portable computer small enough to use on your lap. The term distinguishes these machines from desktop computers, which stay in one place. {She brought her laptop to the coffee shop.} {The company issued laptops to all remote employees.}

Larceny is the legal term for theft—taking someone else's property without permission and with intent to keep it. The law distinguishes between petty larceny (minor theft) and grand larceny (theft above a certain dollar amount, varying by jurisdiction). Outside legal contexts, larceny can describe any act of stealing: {The price they charged was practically larceny}.

A larch is a coniferous tree unusual for being deciduous—it drops its needles each autumn. Larches grow in cold northern climates and mountainous regions, valued for their rot-resistant timber. The wood serves in construction, fencing, and boatbuilding. {The larches turned gold before shedding their needles.}

Larches are coniferous trees unusual for shedding their needles in autumn, turning golden before dropping. They grow in cold climates across the Northern Hemisphere and produce durable, rot-resistant wood valued in construction. {The larches on the mountainside blazed yellow against the evergreens.}

Lard is rendered pig fat, traditionally used for cooking and baking. It produces flaky pie crusts and was once the standard frying medium before vegetable oils displaced it. To lard meat is to insert strips of fat before cooking. Figuratively, to lard something is to embellish or pad it: {a speech larded with quotations}.

A larder is a cool room or large cupboard where food is stored, especially in older homes before refrigeration became standard. The word now often refers to one's stock of food generally: {a well-stocked larder}, {The storm left our larder bare}.

Large is the commonest synonym of big, and while not as frequently used as big, it is standard in many expressions and uses, such as clothing sizes, and is also more frequently used as an adverb than big.

A lariat is a rope with a running noose at one end, used to catch horses and cattle. The term is interchangeable with lasso, though lariat emphasizes the rope itself while lasso often emphasizes the act of throwing: {He coiled the lariat and hung it on his saddle}. Cowboys use lariats for roping livestock and tethering horses.

A lark is a small songbird known for singing while in flight, especially the skylark. To be {up with the lark} is to rise early. Separately, a lark is a carefree adventure or bit of mischief: {We drove to the coast on a lark}. To lark about is to fool around playfully.

Larking is playful, carefree activity—having fun in a lighthearted, often mischievous way. The word comes from the bird, whose spirited flight suggested spontaneous amusement. Someone {larking about} or {larking around} is goofing off rather than being serious: {We spent the afternoon larking in the park}. The tone is innocent—pranks and hijinks rather than anything harmful.

Larks are small songbirds known for their melodious singing, especially during flight. The skylark's dawn song gives us the expression "up with the lark" for early rising. A lark is also a carefree adventure or bit of mischief undertaken for fun: {We drove to the coast on a lark}. To lark about is to play or fool around.

Larkspur is a flowering plant with tall spikes of blue, purple, pink, or white blossoms, named for the spur-shaped projection on each flower. Common in gardens and wildflower meadows, larkspurs are toxic to livestock. The related delphinium is sometimes called larkspur, though gardeners often distinguish between them.

To larp is to participate in live action role-playing—a game where participants physically act out characters in fictional scenarios rather than describing actions at a table or through a screen. Players dress in costume, wield prop weapons, and interact in character for hours or days. Extended to mean pretending or putting on an act: {He's just larping as a tough guy}. The noun larp refers to such an event or the activity itself. (Uppercase LARP is the acronym form.)

A larper is someone who participates in live-action role-playing (LARP)—acting out characters in person rather than at a tabletop or on screen. The term extends derisively to anyone perceived as pretending to be something they're not: {Those guys aren't real activists, they're just larpers}. This dismissive sense suggests performative engagement without genuine commitment.

A larva is an immature form of an insect or other animal that looks completely different from the adult. Caterpillars are butterfly larvae; maggots are fly larvae; tadpoles are frog larvae. The larval stage typically involves feeding and growth before metamorphosis transforms the creature into its adult form. Plural: larvae or larvas.

Larvae is the plural of larva—the immature, often wormlike stage of insects and other animals that undergo metamorphosis. Caterpillars are butterfly larvae; maggots are fly larvae. The larval stage typically looks nothing like the adult form: {The larvae feed voraciously before pupating}.

Laryngitis is inflammation of the larynx, the part of the throat containing the vocal cords. The hallmark symptom is hoarseness or complete loss of voice, often accompanied by a dry cough and sore throat. It typically results from viral infection, overuse of the voice, or irritation: {She had laryngitis and could barely whisper}.

Lasagna is a baked Italian dish of wide, flat pasta layered with cheese, meat or vegetables, and tomato sauce. The word also refers to the pasta sheets themselves. Spelling varies: lasagna is standard in American English, lasagne in British. {We're having lasagna for dinner.} {She made a vegetarian lasagne with spinach and ricotta.}

Lasagne is a pasta dish of wide flat noodles layered with sauce, cheese, and usually meat or vegetables, then baked. The noodles themselves are also called lasagne. The spelling lasagna is more common in American English, while lasagne prevails in British English and reflects the Italian plural form: {We're having lasagne for dinner}.

A laser is a device that produces an intense, focused beam of light through stimulated emission of radiation. The acronym stands for "light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation," but the word is now fully naturalized. Lasers appear in everything from surgery and manufacturing to barcode scanners and cat toys. As a verb, to laser something is to cut, treat, or target it with a laser beam: {The surgeon lasered the tissue}. Figuratively, laser describes intense focus: {laser focus}, {laser-sharp precision}.

A laserdisc is an optical disc format for video playback, popular from the 1970s through the 1990s before DVDs made it obsolete. The discs were large—about the size of vinyl LP records—and offered better picture quality than VHS tapes, though they couldn't record. Laserdiscs became a format for serious film collectors and home theater enthusiasts: {He had an impressive laserdisc collection of classic movies}. Also spelled as two words (laser disc) or with a capital D (LaserDisc, the original trademark).

Laserdiscs were optical discs the size of vinyl records that stored video and audio, read by laser rather than a stylus. Popular from the 1980s through the mid-1990s, they offered superior picture quality to VHS tapes but couldn't record and were expensive. DVDs made them obsolete: {My uncle still has a collection of laserdiscs in his basement}.

Lasers are devices that produce intense, highly focused beams of light through stimulated emission of radiation—the acronym stands for "light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation." Lasers range from tiny pointers to industrial cutters to weapons systems. The concentrated beam allows precision: {laser surgery}, {laser engraving}, {laser sights on firearms}. Figuratively, laser describes intense focus: {laser-focused on the goal}.

As a noun, lash may be short for eyelash (lash liner) or it may mean a hit with a whip: The punishment is 50 lashes. The verb lash may refer to hitting with a whip (lashed him on the back) or tying with a rope or cord (lash the spar to the mast). If you lash out at someone, you direct an angry outburst at them. If rain is lashing down, it is falling heavily.

Lashed is the past tense of lash, which means to strike with a whip or to tie down securely. Someone who was lashed received a whipping: {The prisoner was lashed fifty times}. Cargo lashed to a deck is fastened tightly with ropes or straps: {We lashed the kayaks to the roof rack}. In British and Irish slang, lashed means drunk: {We got absolutely lashed last night}.

Lashes are the hairs that grow along the edge of the eyelids, also called eyelashes. The word also refers to strokes of a whip or the flexible part of a whip itself: {The prisoner received twenty lashes}. To lash is to strike with a whip, to tie something down tightly {(lash the cargo to the deck)}, or to move violently: {Rain lashed against the windows}. To {lash out} is to attack suddenly, physically or verbally.

Lashing has two main senses. One involves striking repeatedly with a whip or similar instrument, or with words: {The senator gave his opponents a verbal lashing}. Rain or waves lash against surfaces. The other sense is rope or cord used to bind things together, or the act of securing them: {Check the lashings on the cargo before we sail}.

Lashings means a large amount or plenty of something, used chiefly in British English: {lashings of cream}, {lashings of gravy}. The word appears almost exclusively with food and drink, evoking generous, indulgent portions. Separately, lashings can be the plural of lashing—a beating with a whip, or ropes used to secure cargo.

A lass is a girl or young woman. The word is characteristic of Scottish and Northern English dialects, though it appears throughout English in folksy or affectionate contexts: {a bonny lass}, {Come here, lass}. Lass pairs with lad as its female counterpart.

Lasses is the plural of lass, a word for girls or young women. The term is chiefly Scottish, Irish, and Northern English: {The lasses gathered at the pub after work}. It pairs naturally with lads in casual reference to groups of young people: {The lads and lasses were out celebrating}.

Lassi is a traditional South Asian yogurt-based drink, popular in India and Pakistan. It's typically blended with water and may be sweet, salty, or flavored with fruit—mango lassi being especially common in restaurants. The drink is cooling and often accompanies spicy foods: {I ordered a mango lassi with my curry}.

Lassie is a Scottish and Northern English term for a girl or young woman, the feminine counterpart to lad or laddie: {The lassie couldn't have been more than sixteen}. Outside Scotland, the word sounds quaint or affected, often evoking rural charm or old-fashioned sensibilities.

A lasso is a rope with a running noose at one end, used to catch horses or cattle by throwing it around the animal's neck or legs. The tool is associated with cowboys and ranching in the American West. To lasso is to catch with such a rope: {She lassoed the calf on her first throw}. Figuratively, to lasso something is to capture or secure it: {He's trying to lasso investors for his startup}.

Lassoed is the past tense of lasso—to catch with a rope loop thrown around a target. Cowboys lasso cattle; rodeo performers lasso calves for time. The word extends to any act of capturing or securing: {She lassoed a promotion before anyone else could apply}. {He lassoed the runaway shopping cart.}

Lassoes is the plural of lasso—a rope with a running noose used to catch livestock. Cowboys lasso cattle; rodeo performers lasso calves for sport. As a verb, lassoes means catches with such a rope: {She lassoes the steer on her first throw}. Figuratively, to lasso is to capture or secure: {He lassoed a promotion through sheer persistence}.

Lassoing is catching something with a lasso—a rope with a running noose thrown to snare cattle or horses. The word evokes cowboys and rodeos: {He spent the afternoon lassoing calves}. Figuratively, to lasso is to capture or secure: {She's been lassoing investors for her startup}.

Lassos is the plural of lasso, the rope with a running noose used to catch horses and cattle. Cowboys throw lassos to rope livestock. The word also works as a verb—one lassos a steer by throwing the loop around its neck or legs. {The ranch hands practiced throwing lassos at fence posts.}

Three separately derived words in English have the spelling last—a fact that explains its frequency and versatility. As a verb, last means continue or endure. An old but minor meaning of last as a noun is for an object shaped like a foot, used to build or repair a shoe. As an adjective and adverb, last has the meaning after all others and is the opposite of first. This is its most frequent use.

Lasting describes something that continues for a long time or endures: a lasting {friendship}, a lasting {impression}, lasting {peace}. The word implies durability beyond the moment—what lasts isn't fleeting or temporary. A lasting {legacy} outlives its creator. {The experience left a lasting impact on her}.

Lasts is the plural of last, a foot-shaped form used in shoemaking. The shoemaker builds the shoe around this wooden or plastic mold: {He has lasts for every size}. Separately, lasts is the third-person singular of the verb last, meaning to continue or endure: {The battery lasts about eight hours}.

Lat is gym slang for the latissimus dorsi, the broad muscle that spans the middle and lower back: {I'm working my lats today}. The plural lats dominates because the muscles come in pairs and are typically trained together. Strong lats create the V-shaped torso prized in bodybuilding.
clues: What pull-downs are meant to target

definition: A latch is a fastening device that holds a door, gate, or window closed but can be opened without a key—simpler than a lock. To latch is to close with such a device: {Make sure the gate latches behind you}. To {latch onto} something is to grab hold of it, physically or figuratively: {She latched onto the idea immediately}.

Latching is the act of fastening or securing something with a latch—a simple closure mechanism that catches and holds. The term extends to any firm attachment: {The baby had trouble latching onto the breast}. In electronics, latching describes a circuit or switch that stays in one state until actively reset: {a latching relay}.

A latchkey is a key to an outside door, especially the front door of a house. The term evokes children who let themselves in after school because parents are at work—the {latchkey kid}, a phrase suggesting both independence and mild neglect. The latch in latchkey refers to the door's lock mechanism.

Late means after the expected or usual time: {The train was late}, {Sorry I'm late}. It also indicates the end portion of a period: {late afternoon}, {the late 1990s}. Of a person, late means recently deceased: {my late husband}. As an adverb, late describes timing: {We arrived late}, {She stayed up late}. {Of late} means recently.

A latecomer is someone who arrives after the expected time or after others have already gathered: {Latecomers will not be seated until intermission}. The term extends to anyone who joins a trend, movement, or field after it's well established: {As a latecomer to the smartphone market, they struggled to compete}.
clues: One who shows up behind schedule

definition: Latecomers are people who arrive after the expected or scheduled time. The word often appears in rules or announcements: {Latecomers will not be seated until intermission}. It can also describe those who join a trend, movement, or field after others have established it: {Latecomers to the cryptocurrency boom missed the early gains}.

Lately means in the recent past, covering a period extending back from now: {I haven't been sleeping well lately}, {Have you seen any good movies lately?} The word implies an ongoing or repeated situation rather than a single event—you wouldn't say "I went to the store lately" but might say "I've been going to the store a lot lately."

Latency is the delay between an action and its response. In computing, it measures the time for data to travel from source to destination: {Low latency is crucial for online gaming}. Network latency affects video calls and streaming. The term extends to any system where lag matters—audio equipment, medical devices, financial trading. In psychology, a latency period is a dormant phase before something emerges or develops.

Latent describes something present but not visible or active—hidden, dormant, or potential rather than manifest. A latent {talent} exists but hasn't been developed. A latent {infection} shows no symptoms yet. Latent {heat} is energy absorbed or released during phase changes without temperature change. {His latent hostility finally surfaced.}

Later refers to a time after the present or after a specified point: {I'll call you later}, {We can discuss this later}. It's the comparative form of late, so later can also mean more late: {Each night he stayed out later than the one before}. As a farewell, later is casual shorthand for "see you later": {Later, dude}.

Lateral means to the side or from the side, as opposed to forward, backward, up, or down. A lateral {move} in a career changes position without advancing rank. In football, a lateral is a pass thrown sideways or backward rather than forward. The adjective describes anything positioned at or extending toward the side: {lateral branches}, {lateral thinking}—approaching problems from unexpected angles rather than head-on.

Latest is the superlative of late—the most recent in a sequence. The latest {news} is whatever just happened. {Have you heard the latest?} asks about recent developments or gossip. The latest {fashion} is what's currently in style. {At the latest} sets a deadline: {I need it by Friday at the latest}.

Latex is the milky fluid produced by certain plants, notably rubber trees, that serves as the basis for natural rubber. The word extends to synthetic rubber and rubber products generally: latex {gloves}, latex {paint}, latex {clothing}. In fetish contexts, latex refers to tight-fitting rubber garments. {She wore a latex dress to the club.} (Capitalized LaTeX is a typesetting system.)

A lathe is a machine that rotates a piece of material—typically wood or metal—against a cutting tool to shape it. The operator or an automated system holds the tool steady while the workpiece spins, allowing precise shaping of cylindrical objects: {table legs turned on a lathe}, {lathe-cut brass fittings}. To lathe is to shape something using this machine.

Lather is the frothy foam produced when soap meets water and agitation—the white suds you work up washing hands or shampooing hair. Horses and other animals produce lather as sweat during exertion: {The horse was in a lather after the race}. To lather is to produce or apply this foam. Figuratively, {in a lather} means agitated or anxious: {Don't get yourself in a lather over it}.

Lathering is producing or applying lather—the foam created when soap meets water and agitation. You lather up in the shower, lather shaving cream on your face, or work shampoo into a lather. Figuratively, to get into a lather is to become agitated or worked up: {Don't get yourself into a lather over nothing}.

Latitude is distance north or south of the equator, measured in degrees from 0° at the equator to 90° at the poles. Lines of latitude circle the globe horizontally, parallel to the equator. The word extends to mean freedom or scope for action: {The teacher gave students considerable latitude in choosing their topics}.
