This figurative sense suggests room to move within boundaries, like the range of positions between equator and pole.

Latitudes are imaginary horizontal lines circling the Earth parallel to the equator, measuring distance north or south in degrees. The equator is zero degrees; the poles are ninety. Beyond geography, latitude means freedom or room to act: {The job gives me considerable latitude in how I spend my time}. In the plural, latitudes often refers to regions: {northern latitudes}, {tropical latitudes}.

Latkas are potato pancakes traditional to Ashkenazi Jewish cuisine, especially associated with Hanukkah. Grated potatoes are mixed with onion, egg, and flour, then fried until crispy. They're typically served with sour cream or applesauce: {We made latkas for the first night of Hanukkah}. Also spelled latkes.

A latke is a potato pancake in Jewish cuisine, made from grated potatoes mixed with egg and onion, then fried until crisp. Latkes are traditionally eaten during Hanukkah, where the oil used for frying commemorates the miracle of the temple oil. {We made latkes from my grandmother's recipe.}

Latkes are potato pancakes traditionally eaten during Hanukkah. Grated potatoes are mixed with onion, egg, and flour, then fried until crisp and golden. They're typically served with applesauce or sour cream: {My grandmother's latkes were always the highlight of the holiday}. The dish commemorates the miracle of oil central to the Hanukkah story.

A latrine is a toilet, especially a communal one in a military camp or other basic facility. The word implies something more primitive than a bathroom—often a pit or trench: {The soldiers dug latrines at the edge of camp}. In civilian use, latrine sounds either military or deliberately crude.

Latrines are toilets, especially communal ones in military camps, schools, or other institutional settings. The word typically implies a basic or primitive facility—a pit latrine is simply a hole in the ground. {The soldiers dug latrines at the edge of camp.} Latrine is more common in military and outdoor contexts than in everyday speech.

Lats are the latissimus dorsi muscles—the broad, flat muscles of the back that extend from the armpit down to the lower spine. The term belongs to gym culture, where developing impressive lats is a common goal: {He's been working on his lats}, {Her lats flared out during the pull-up}. Separately, the lat was Latvia's currency before adoption of the euro.

A latte is espresso mixed with steamed milk, typically served in a tall glass or large cup. The word is shortened from Italian caffè latte (milk coffee). A latte has more milk and less foam than a cappuccino. The term extends to similar drinks: {chai latte}, {matcha latte}. In American coffeehouse culture, lattes often come flavored: {vanilla latte}, {pumpkin spice latte}.

Latter refers to the second of two things previously mentioned, contrasting with former: {The menu offered soup or salad, and I chose the latter}. It can also mean near the end of a period: {the latter half of the century}, {in his latter years}. The word is somewhat formal and appears more often in writing than speech.

Lattes are espresso drinks made with steamed milk, the milk-forward alternative to cappuccinos. The word is Italian for "milk," short for caffè latte. In American coffee culture, lattes often come flavored—vanilla, pumpkin spice, caramel—and have become shorthand for upscale coffee habits: {I can't afford lattes every day}. A latte is also an adjective for the drink's characteristic pale brown color.

A lattice is a structure of crossed strips or bars with open spaces between them, forming a regular pattern: {a garden lattice covered in climbing roses}. The design appears in fences, window screens, and decorative panels. In mathematics and crystallography, a lattice is an arrangement of points or objects in a regular, repeating pattern across space. As a verb, to lattice is to form or furnish with such a structure.

Lattices is the plural of lattice, a structure of crossed strips forming a grid pattern with open spaces between. A garden lattice supports climbing plants. In mathematics, a lattice is an ordered set where any two elements have a unique supremum and infimum. In crystallography, it describes the repeating arrangement of atoms in a solid. {Morning light filtered through the lattices of the gazebo.}

Latticework is a structure of crisscrossing strips—wood, metal, or other material—forming a pattern of open spaces. It appears in fences, trellises, and decorative screens, allowing air and light to pass through while providing partial enclosure: {Roses climbed the latticework on the porch}. The pattern itself, or anything resembling it, may be called latticework: {a latticework of shadows on the floor}.

Laudanum is a tincture of opium dissolved in alcohol, once widely used as a painkiller and sedative. It was a common household remedy in the 18th and 19th centuries, prescribed for everything from coughs to insomnia to infant teething. Many notable figures became addicted to it, and its unrestricted availability contributed to widespread opium dependency before modern drug regulations. The word now evokes Victorian-era medicine cabinets and the darker side of patent remedies.

Laugh is the sound people make when something strikes them as funny—a burst of vocal expression showing amusement. The verb and noun share this sense: {She laughed at his joke}, {His laugh echoed through the room}. To laugh something off is to dismiss it lightly. To {have the last laugh} is to succeed after others doubted you. A laugh can also be something amusing: {The movie was a laugh}. Laughable means absurd or ridiculous rather than genuinely funny.

Laughable describes something so absurd or inadequate that it invites ridicule rather than serious consideration. A laughable {excuse} or laughable {attempt} fails to meet basic standards: {The security measures were laughable—anyone could walk right in}. The word carries contempt; what's laughable isn't genuinely funny, just pathetically insufficient.

Laughed is the past tense and past participle of laugh, the vocal expression of amusement or joy characterized by rhythmic sounds and often accompanied by smiling. {She laughed at his joke.} {We laughed until we cried.} Beyond genuine mirth, laughed can indicate derision or dismissal: {They laughed at his proposal.} It also appears in expressions like {laughed off}, meaning to dismiss something as unimportant: {He laughed off the criticism and moved on.}

Laughing is the present participle of laugh, describing the act of making sounds that express amusement or joy. As an adjective, it describes someone or something that laughs or seems to laugh: {laughing children}, {laughing eyes}. The {laughing stock} is a person or thing ridiculed by others. {No laughing matter} means something serious, not to be dismissed lightly.

A laughingstock is a person or thing that becomes an object of ridicule—someone others find absurd or contemptible: {He made himself a laughingstock with that speech}. The word implies public mockery, not private amusement. One can become the laughingstock of a group, institution, or nation: {The team became the laughingstock of the league}.

Laughingstocks are people or things subjected to widespread ridicule or mockery. The word implies public humiliation—becoming an object of general scorn rather than just one person's joke: {The team's losing streak made them laughingstocks}. Someone who becomes a laughingstock has lost credibility or respect in a way that invites open derision.

Laughs is the third person singular and plural of laugh, the vocalization expressing amusement or joy. When something is done {for laughs}, it's done purely for entertainment or to get a reaction. A person who is {good for a few laughs} is entertaining company. In casual speech, laughs often substitutes for fun or amusement generally: {We had some laughs at the party}. The phrase {that's laughs} dismisses something as ridiculous or unserious.

Laughter is the sound humans make when amused—a series of short, rhythmic vocalizations typically accompanied by smiling. It ranges from quiet chuckles to uncontrollable fits: {The room erupted in laughter}. Laughter can also signal nervousness or discomfort rather than amusement. {Laughter is the best medicine} suggests its therapeutic value.

A laughtrack is prerecorded audience laughter added to comedy programs during post-production. The practice became standard in American television sitcoms, cueing viewers when to find something funny. The term often carries skepticism—if a show needs a laughtrack, maybe the jokes aren't landing on their own: {The laughtrack was working overtime on that weak punchline}. Also spelled laugh track.

Launch centers on propelling something into motion or existence. A rocket launches into space; a ship launches into water. You launch a business, a product, a career, or an attack—initiating something substantial. A launch is the act itself or the vessel: {the book launch}, {a motor launch}. To {launch into} a speech or tirade is to begin it energetically. {They're launching a new streaming service next month.}

Launched is the past tense of launch—to set something in motion or send it on its way. A rocket is launched into space, a boat launched into water, a product launched into the market. The word implies a deliberate beginning with forward momentum: {She launched her career in advertising}, {The company launched a new initiative}. To launch into something is to begin it energetically: {He launched into a lengthy explanation}.

A launcher is a device or structure that propels something into motion—a rocket launcher sends missiles skyward, a grenade launcher fires explosives. In computing, a launcher is an application that organizes and starts other programs: {I keep my most-used apps in the launcher}. Game launchers manage downloads and updates for video game libraries.

Launchers are devices or mechanisms that propel something into motion or operation. Rocket launchers fire missiles or spacecraft. Grenade launchers are weapons. In computing, a launcher is software that starts other programs—the home screen of a smartphone is a launcher. {She downloaded a new launcher to customize her Android phone.} The word also applies to people: {The campaign launchers held a press conference.}

Launches covers the act of setting something in motion, whether physical or figurative. A rocket launches when it lifts off; a company launches a product when it introduces it to the market; a ship launches when it first enters the water. The noun launch refers to such an event: {The launch is scheduled for Tuesday}. To launch into something is to begin it with energy or enthusiasm: {She launched into a lengthy explanation of her theory}.

Launching is the act of setting something in motion—a boat into water, a rocket into space, a product into the market, a career into its trajectory. The word captures that initial propulsive moment when something leaves its starting point: {The launching of the new website went smoothly}. A launching pad or launch pad is where rockets begin their ascent; figuratively, any position that enables advancement: {The internship served as a launching pad for her career}.

A launchpad is the platform or facility from which rockets and spacecraft are sent into flight, equipped with the support structures and systems needed to prepare and fire a launch vehicle. The term extends naturally to anything that serves as a starting point for rapid advancement or success: {The internship became a launchpad for her career in tech}. In computing, a launchpad is an interface or application that provides quick access to programs or tools.

Launchpads are platforms from which rockets or spacecraft are launched. The term extends to anything that serves as a starting point for advancement: a job can be a launchpad for a career, a small business a launchpad for larger ventures. {She used the internship as a launchpad into the industry.}

Launder means to wash and iron clothes or linens, though this sense has largely given way to the figurative meaning: to make something questionable appear legitimate. Money laundering is the process of moving illegally obtained funds through legitimate businesses or accounts to disguise their criminal origin. {The cartel laundered millions through shell companies.} The word derives from laundry, connecting the idea of cleaning dirty clothes to cleaning dirty money.

Laundered describes something that has been washed and cleaned—clothes, linens, bedding: {freshly laundered sheets}. The word extends to money that has been processed through legitimate-seeming transactions to disguise its illegal origins: {laundered drug money}, {laundered campaign contributions}. Both senses involve making something dirty appear clean.

A launderette is a self-service establishment where customers wash and dry clothes using coin-operated machines. The term is primarily British; Americans typically say laundromat. {She spent Sunday afternoon at the launderette reading while her clothes tumbled dry.}

Laundering is the process of washing clothes or linens, but the word appears far more often in its extended sense: making illegally obtained money appear legitimate by passing it through banks, businesses, or other financial channels. {Money laundering} is the standard phrase. The metaphor treats dirty money like dirty clothes—something that needs cleaning before it can be used openly.

Launders is the third-person singular of launder, meaning to wash and clean fabric: {She launders the sheets every week}. More commonly, launder refers to disguising the origins of illegally obtained money by passing it through legitimate businesses or accounts: {The organization launders drug money through real estate purchases}. The financial sense dominates contemporary usage.

A laundrette is a self-service laundry where customers wash and dry clothes in coin-operated machines. The term is chiefly British; Americans say laundromat. {She spent Sunday afternoon at the laundrette reading while her clothes dried.}

A laundromat is a self-service facility where customers wash and dry clothes using coin-operated or card-operated machines. The term is a genericized trademark. Laundromats serve people without home washing machines or those handling large loads: {I spent Sunday afternoon at the laundromat}. Also called a launderette in British English.

Laundromats are self-service facilities where customers wash and dry clothes using coin-operated or card-operated machines. The term is primarily American; British English prefers laundrette. Laundromats serve people without home washers or those handling large loads: {I spent Sunday afternoon at the laundromat}.

Laundry is clothing and linens that need washing, or that have just been washed: {I need to do the laundry}, {a basket of dirty laundry}. A laundry is also the place where washing is done—a room in a house or a commercial establishment. To {air dirty laundry} is to discuss private matters publicly: {They aired their dirty laundry in court}.

A laureate is someone honored for exceptional achievement in a field. The word appears most often in compounds: a Nobel {laureate}, a poet {laureate}. The poet laureate holds an official position, appointed to compose verses for state occasions. As an adjective, laureate means crowned with laurel as a mark of distinction—from the ancient practice of honoring victors and poets with laurel wreaths.

Laureates is the plural of laureate, a person who has been honored for distinguished achievement. The term comes from the laurel wreath awarded to victors in ancient Greece. A poet laureate holds an honorary position recognizing poetic excellence. Nobel laureates have received the Nobel Prize: {The ceremony honored laureates in physics and chemistry}.

Laurel is an evergreen shrub or tree with glossy, aromatic leaves. In ancient Greece and Rome, wreaths of laurel crowned victors and poets, making laurel a symbol of achievement and honor. To {rest on one's laurels} is to rely on past accomplishments rather than continuing to strive. {Laurels} often means honors or recognition: {She won laurels for her research}. (Capitalized Laurel is a given name or place name.)

Laurels are the leaves of the bay laurel tree, which in ancient Greece and Rome were woven into wreaths to crown victors and poets. The word now means honors or achievements: {She earned her laurels through years of dedicated research}. To {rest on one's laurels} is to coast on past accomplishments rather than pursuing new ones.

Lava is molten rock that flows from a volcano during an eruption. Once it cools and solidifies, it becomes volcanic rock but may still be called lava: {The hikers crossed an ancient lava field}. Lava extends to similar flowing substances: {a lava lamp}, {lava cake} with its oozing chocolate center.

A lavatory is a room with a toilet and usually a sink—a restroom or bathroom. The word sounds slightly formal or old-fashioned in American English but remains common in British English and in contexts like airline travel: {The lavatory is occupied}. Lavatory can also refer to the sink or basin itself, though this usage has faded.

Lavender is a fragrant plant with pale purple flowers, grown for its scent and used in sachets, soaps, and essential oils. The color lavender is a soft purple with a grayish or bluish tint: {lavender walls}, {a lavender dress}. Lavender has long associations with femininity and, since at least the early twentieth century, with male homosexuality—sometimes used dismissively: {the lavender set}.

Lavish means abundant to the point of excess. A lavish {banquet} features more food than anyone could eat. Lavish {praise} may be effusive. The word can suggest generosity or extravagance depending on context. As a verb, to lavish is to give freely and abundantly: {She lavished attention on her grandchildren}.

Lavished is the past tense of lavish, meaning to give or bestow in generous, even excessive quantities: {She lavished attention on her grandchildren}, {He lavished praise on the team}. The word suggests abundance bordering on extravagance—more than strictly necessary, given freely and without restraint.

A law is a rule that has some official sanction or truth. Statutory law is enacted by legislatures. Common law is not necessarily enacted but is enforced by custom and precedent. A law of nature is something that experience or experiment has proven to be true. A mathematical law is a characteristic of numbers that can be proven or demonstrated as always being true. As an uncountable noun, law (often the law) refers to the entire set of laws that regulate a society or those who enforce them: Under the law he could serve ten years in prison; She got in trouble with the law last month.

Lawfare is the use of legal systems and processes as a weapon against an opponent—filing lawsuits, regulatory complaints, or criminal charges not primarily to win on merits but to exhaust resources, damage reputations, or silence critics. The term blends "law" and "warfare": {The company's lawfare strategy buried the whistleblower in depositions}. Often used critically to suggest abuse of legal mechanisms for political or strategic ends.

Lawful means permitted or recognized by law: {a lawful search}, {lawful permanent resident}. It implies conformity with legal requirements rather than violation of them. Lawful often appears in formal or official contexts where legal status matters. In role-playing games and fantasy settings, lawful describes characters who follow codes and rules, contrasted with chaotic.

A lawgiver is one who establishes or enacts laws for a people or nation. The term carries historical and religious weight, evoking figures like Moses or Hammurabi who delivered foundational legal codes: {Moses is the great lawgiver of the Hebrew Bible}. In broader use, any legislator or legal authority might be called a lawgiver, though the word sounds formal or archaic in modern contexts.

Lawgivers are those who create or establish laws. The term carries weight—it suggests not just legislators passing bills but foundational figures who shape legal systems: {Moses and Hammurabi are among history's great lawgivers}. The word has a formal, often historical or religious flavor, rarely applied to ordinary politicians.

Lawless describes a state without law or regard for it. A lawless {frontier town} has no functioning legal authority. A lawless {mob} ignores the law entirely. The word can describe places, people, or actions: {lawless regions}, {lawless behavior}. It suggests chaos, disorder, or defiance of established rules.

Lawlessness is the state of being without law or order—either the absence of laws altogether or widespread disregard for them. It describes chaos where rules don't apply or aren't enforced: {The region descended into lawlessness after the government collapsed}. The word can characterize places, periods, or behavior: {frontier lawlessness}, {the lawlessness of the mob}.

A lawmaker is a person who makes laws—typically a member of a legislature such as a parliament or congress. The term is common in news coverage: {Lawmakers voted to raise the minimum wage}. It applies to elected officials at any level who have legislative authority, from local councils to national assemblies.

Lawmakers are people who make laws—legislators, members of Congress, parliamentarians. The term is neutral and functional, used heavily in journalism: {Lawmakers voted to raise the minimum wage}. It encompasses elected officials at any level who have authority to create or modify legislation.

Lawmaking is the process of creating laws, typically through legislative bodies like parliaments or congresses. The term covers everything from drafting bills to debating and voting on them: {The lawmaking process can take months or years}. As an adjective, it describes bodies or functions related to creating legislation: {lawmaking authority}, {lawmaking power}.

A lawman is a law enforcement officer, especially in the American West or in contexts evoking that era: {The lawman rode into town at sunset}. The term appears most often in westerns and historical accounts, carrying a nostalgic or romanticized tone. In contemporary usage, it sounds old-fashioned or deliberately evocative compared to neutral terms like police officer.

Lawmen is the plural of lawman, a term for law enforcement officers—sheriffs, marshals, police. The word evokes the American frontier: {lawmen and outlaws}, {a legendary lawman of the Old West}. It appears in historical contexts and Westerns more than contemporary usage, where officers or cops is more common.

A lawn is an area of grass kept mowed and maintained, typically surrounding a house or in a park. The ideal lawn is uniform, green, and weed-free—a suburban standard that requires considerable water and care. {The kids played on the lawn.} Lawn also names a fine, sheer fabric used in clothing, from the French city Laon where it was made.

A lawnmower is a machine with rotating blades that cuts grass to an even height. Most are either push mowers powered by the user or self-propelled models with gasoline or electric motors. Riding mowers handle larger areas. {I need to get the lawnmower serviced before summer}. Also spelled lawn mower.

Lawnmowers are machines that cut grass to a uniform height. The most common type is the push mower, either manual or powered by a gasoline engine or electric motor. Riding mowers handle larger areas. {I need to get the lawnmower serviced before spring}. The singular lawnmower is more common.

Lawns are areas of grass kept short by regular mowing, typically surrounding houses or covering parks and recreational spaces. The lawn emerged as a status symbol—land devoted to appearance rather than agriculture. Maintaining one requires watering, fertilizing, and cutting: {He spends every Saturday on lawn care}. Lawn also modifies related items: lawn {mower}, lawn {chair}, lawn {party}.

Laws are rules established by authority—typically governments—that members of a society must follow or face penalties. The term extends beyond legislation to include natural regularities: the laws of {physics}, the laws of {thermodynamics}. {Murphy's Law} and similar formulations name observed patterns presented as inevitable truths. {The law} collectively means the legal system or police: {He's in trouble with the law}. To {lay down the law} is to state rules emphatically.

A lawsuit is a legal action brought before a court, in which one party claims to have been harmed or wronged by another and seeks a remedy, typically monetary compensation or a court order. Filing a lawsuit initiates formal litigation, distinct from informal dispute resolution. {She threatened to file a lawsuit after the accident.} {The company settled the lawsuit out of court to avoid a lengthy trial.}

Lawsuits are formal legal actions brought before a court, where one party seeks a remedy from another. Someone files a lawsuit claiming they've been wronged—through breach of contract, negligence, discrimination, or other grievances. {The company faces multiple lawsuits over the defective product.} Lawsuits may seek monetary damages, injunctions, or other relief. The threat of a lawsuit often motivates settlement before trial.

A lawyer is someone licensed to practice law—advising clients on legal matters, drafting documents, and representing people in court. The term covers attorneys, solicitors, and barristers depending on jurisdiction. {You should talk to a lawyer before signing anything}. To lawyer is to parse language with excessive precision: {Stop lawyering the contract and just tell me what it means}.

Lawyered describes being outmaneuvered by legal expertise or precise argumentation. Someone who gets lawyered has been defeated by technicalities, careful logic, or rhetorical skill: {He tried to wriggle out of the contract, but she lawyered him into compliance}. The term often carries a note of grudging respect—or resentment—toward the person wielding the legal or argumentative advantage. Popularized by the TV series *How I Met Your Mother*, where a character announces {Lawyered!} after winning an argument.

Lawyering is the work lawyers do—practicing law, handling legal matters, advising clients. The term often carries a slightly dismissive tone, suggesting excessive technicality or adversarial maneuvering: {That's just lawyering—they're looking for loopholes}. Good lawyering means competent legal work; bad lawyering means incompetent or unethical practice.

Lawyers are people licensed to practice law—advising clients, drafting legal documents, and representing them in court. The term covers a range of specializations: criminal defense lawyers, corporate lawyers, divorce lawyers. In American usage, lawyer and attorney are interchangeable, though attorney often sounds more formal. {She hired a lawyer to handle the estate}. Lawyers are frequent targets of jokes and cultural suspicion, cast as mercenary manipulators of language and loopholes.

Lax means not strict, tight, or careful. Lax {security} allows threats through. Lax {standards} permit what stricter ones would reject. A lax {attitude} suggests insufficient concern: {The company was lax about safety regulations}. Muscles or bowels that are lax are loose or slack. The word carries mild disapproval—something lax probably should be firmer. (All caps LAX is the Los Angeles airport.)

A laxative is a substance that promotes bowel movements, used to relieve constipation. The word works as both noun and adjective: {The doctor recommended a mild laxative}; {Prunes have a laxative effect}. Laxatives range from gentle fiber supplements to powerful purgatives.

Laxatives are substances that promote bowel movements, used to relieve constipation. They work through various mechanisms—some soften stool, others stimulate intestinal contractions. Available over the counter or by prescription: {The doctor recommended a mild laxative}. Overuse can cause dependency, so they're meant for occasional rather than regular use.

Lay is a verb meaning to put down or place: {Lay the book on the table}. {The hen lays eggs}. {Lay the foundation before building}. Lay is also the past tense of lie (to recline): {She lay on the bed for hours}. This distinction confuses many speakers. A lay is something's position or arrangement: {the lay of the land}. A lay is also a song or poem, especially a medieval narrative. In slang, a lay is a sexual partner or act of sex: {She was an easy lay}. To lay someone is to have sex with them: {He laid her after dinner}.

A layabout is someone who avoids work and spends their time idling. The word carries clear disapproval—not merely someone resting, but someone habitually lazy: {Her brother is a layabout who's never held a job}. More common in British than American English.

Layaway is a retail purchasing arrangement where a store holds an item while the customer pays for it in installments over time, only releasing the merchandise once it's fully paid off. The practice was common before credit cards became widespread and has seen revivals during economic downturns. {We put the television on layaway for Christmas.} The term can function as a noun or adjective: {layaway plan}, {layaway department}.

A layby is a paved area beside a road where vehicles can pull off to stop—for rest, emergencies, or to let faster traffic pass. The term is primarily British; Americans say {pull-off} or {rest area}. In British and Australian English, layby also means a system of reserving goods with a deposit and paying in installments before taking possession—what Americans call layaway.

A layer is a single thickness of something spread over or under another surface: {a layer of dust}, {layers of paint}. Things arranged in layers stack horizontally—geological strata, cake tiers, clothing worn for warmth. To layer is to arrange in this fashion. In computing and design, layers are stacked planes that can be edited independently. A layer is also a hen that produces eggs.

Layered describes something arranged in layers—distinct horizontal levels or strata stacked upon each other. Layered rock formations reveal geological history. A layered cake has multiple tiers with filling between. Layered clothing allows adjustment for temperature. Figuratively, layered suggests depth and complexity: {a layered performance}, {a layered narrative with multiple meanings}.

Layering is arranging things in layers—stacked horizontal levels or coatings applied one over another. In fashion, layering means wearing multiple garments for warmth or style: {She's mastered the art of layering for unpredictable weather}. In horticulture, layering propagates plants by burying a stem until it roots. Hair layering cuts strands at different lengths to add texture and movement.

Layers are distinct levels or thicknesses stacked on top of one another. Clothing has layers for warmth; cakes have layers separated by frosting; rock formations reveal geological layers. The concept extends to abstraction: layers of {meaning}, layers of {bureaucracy}, layers of {security}. To layer is to arrange in such strata: {She layered the lasagna with cheese and sauce}. A layered approach tackles complexity in stages.

Laying is the present participle of lay—putting down or producing eggs: {She was laying tiles}. {The hens are laying well this spring}. {He's been laying plans for months}. In slang: {He's been laying everything that moves}.

A layman is someone without specialized knowledge or professional training in a particular field. Doctors explain conditions {in layman's terms}—language non-experts can understand. The word originally distinguished ordinary church members from clergy, and this religious sense persists in some contexts. The female form is laywoman, with laypeople or laypersons as gender-neutral plurals.

Laymen is the plural of layman—a person who lacks specialized knowledge in a particular field. Doctors explain procedures {in terms laymen can understand}. The word also refers to someone who isn't ordained clergy: {a church committee of laymen and clergy}. The singular layman and the gender-neutral layperson are more common than the plural.

A layoff is the termination of employees, typically for economic reasons rather than individual performance: {The company announced layoffs affecting 200 workers}. Unlike firing, layoffs often come with severance packages and the possibility of rehiring when conditions improve. The verb phrase is two words: {They had to lay off half the staff}.

Layoffs are terminations of employment, typically when a company eliminates positions due to economic conditions, restructuring, or declining business rather than employee misconduct. Unlike firings, layoffs carry no implication of fault: {The tech sector announced massive layoffs after the market downturn}. A layoff may be temporary, with workers recalled when conditions improve, or permanent. The singular layoff can describe the event or the period of unemployment that follows.

Layout is the arrangement of elements in a space—text and images on a page, furniture in a room, components on a circuit board. The term emphasizes deliberate positioning: {The layout of the magazine was clean and modern}, {We changed the kitchen layout}. In journalism and design, layout often refers specifically to the visual arrangement before final production.

Layouts are arrangements of elements within a space—how rooms are organized in a floor plan, how text and images sit on a page, how components fit on a circuit board. The term applies wherever positioning matters: {The magazine's layouts were clean and modern}, {We reviewed several layouts for the new office}. In publishing and design, layout is both the process and the result.

A layover is a scheduled stop during a journey, especially a wait between connecting flights: {We have a three-hour layover in Chicago}. The term implies a pause rather than a destination—time spent in transit before continuing. Long layovers sometimes allow travelers to leave the airport and explore the stopover city briefly.

A layover is a scheduled stop during a journey, especially a wait between connecting flights at an intermediate airport. The term emphasizes the waiting period rather than the stop itself—passengers endure layovers rather than enjoy them. {We had a four-hour layover in Chicago before the flight to Seattle.} Long layovers sometimes allow travelers to leave the airport and briefly explore the city.

Laypeople are those without specialized knowledge or professional training in a particular field. A doctor explains a diagnosis {in terms laypeople can understand}. The word also distinguishes ordinary members of a religious community from clergy. The singular is layperson, though layman and laywoman remain common.

A layperson is someone without specialized training or expertise in a particular field. Doctors explain procedures {in terms a layperson can understand}. In religious contexts, a layperson is a member of a congregation who isn't ordained clergy. The term avoids the gendered implications of layman.

A layup is a basketball shot made from close range, typically by driving to the basket and banking the ball off the backboard: {She scored on an easy layup}. By extension, a layup is anything easy or requiring minimal effort: {That test was a layup}. In manufacturing, layup refers to the process of arranging composite materials in a mold before curing.

Layups are shots in basketball made from close range, typically by driving to the basket and banking the ball off the backboard. The layup is considered the most basic and highest-percentage shot in the game. Figuratively, a layup is any easy opportunity or sure thing: {That question was a layup}, {The interview should be a layup for someone with her experience}.

Laze means to spend time relaxing or doing nothing in particular: {We lazed by the pool all afternoon}. It suggests pleasant idleness rather than guilty sloth. The noun laze refers to a period of such relaxation: {a Sunday laze}. To {laze away} time is to pass it without effort or purpose.

Laziness is the quality of being unwilling to work or use energy. The word carries moral weight—laziness implies a character flaw rather than simple rest or recuperation. What looks like laziness may be exhaustion, depression, or rational avoidance of pointless effort: {His boss called it laziness, but he was working two jobs}. The lazy person avoids exertion even when effort would benefit them.
clues: The art of avoiding all tasks

definition: Lazing is passing time in idle relaxation, doing little or nothing: {We spent the afternoon lazing by the pool}. The word suggests pleasant, unhurried leisure rather than guilty procrastination. To {laze about} or {laze around} is to move through a space without purpose or urgency.

Lazy describes a reluctance to work or exert effort: {a lazy afternoon}, {too lazy to cook}. The word carries mild disapproval—laziness is a character flaw, though often a forgivable one. Things that move slowly or hang loosely can be lazy: {a lazy river}, {a lazy eye}. To be lazy about something is to neglect it through lack of effort rather than lack of time.

Lazybones is an affectionate or teasing term for someone who is idle or reluctant to exert themselves: {Get up, lazybones, it's nearly noon}. The word treats laziness as a defining characteristic, built into the person's very skeleton. Despite the plural form, it refers to a single person.

To leach is to drain away by percolation—water passing through soil leaches minerals from it, carrying them elsewhere. The word extends to any gradual extraction or loss: {Nutrients leach from overcooked vegetables}. {Years of neglect had leached the color from the curtains}. A leach is also a perforated container used in this process. Not to be confused with leech, the bloodsucking worm.

Leaching is the process of extracting substances by percolating liquid through a material. Water leaches minerals from soil, carrying them deeper underground or into waterways. In chemistry and industry, leaching extracts metals from ore or compounds from plant matter. The word often carries negative connotations—nutrients leaching from soil, chemicals leaching from landfills into groundwater: {Pesticides had leached into the well}.

Lead is double the trouble. It’s two different words with two different pronunciations. Plus, both pronunciations are used for one set of its meanings. The lead that rhymes with bed is a heavy metal and a chemical element. The lead that rhymes with bead is a verb meaning to go before others, to be ahead, or to show the way. The past tense and past participle of lead is lead (rhymes with bed). Lead (rhymes with bead) as a noun means the position at the front, the interval between the leader and the next contender, or the main news story, among other things.

The leader is the one that others follow, typically those in business, government, and sports. Leader can be used to denote anyone or anything that commands or is in first place: The company is a leader in finance and accounting software. Leaders of the Church were not prepared for the reaction to their decision. Another kind of leader is the row of dots that leads the eyes from an entry in a table of contents to its page number.

A leaderboard is a display ranking participants by score or performance, typically in games, competitions, or sales contexts. Video games popularized the term—arcade machines showed high scores, and online games track global rankings. The concept extends to business: {The sales leaderboard updates weekly}. Leaderboards gamify competition, motivating participants to climb higher.

Leaderboards are ranked lists showing top performers in games, competitions, or other scored activities. Originally from arcade games displaying high scores, the term now applies to any public ranking system: {She climbed the leaderboard after her winning streak}, {The sales team checks the leaderboard every Monday}. The singular leaderboard refers to one such ranking.

Leaderless describes a group or organization without anyone in charge: {The movement remained leaderless by design}. It can suggest dysfunction—a ship without a captain—or deliberate structure, as in leaderless resistance movements where independent cells act without central coordination. {After the CEO resigned, the company drifted leaderless for months}.

Leaders are people who guide, direct, or command others—whether formally through position or informally through influence. The word applies across contexts: political leaders, business leaders, community leaders, thought leaders. A leader can head an organization or simply walk at the front of a group: {She was the leader on the hiking trail}. In competitions, the leader holds first place. Leader also names physical things that lead: a fishing leader connects line to hook; a leader in printing is a row of dots guiding the eye across a page.

Leadership is the position or role of leading others, or the qualities that make someone effective in that role: {She showed real leadership during the crisis}. It can refer to a group of leaders collectively: {The party leadership voted to proceed}. Good leadership implies vision, decisiveness, and the ability to inspire others toward common goals.

A leadfoot is someone who drives fast, pressing the accelerator as if their foot were made of lead. The term is mildly disapproving but often affectionate: {My brother's a leadfoot—he's gotten three speeding tickets this year}. As a verb, to leadfoot is to drive with a heavy foot on the gas.

Leadfooted describes someone who drives with a heavy foot on the accelerator, habitually speeding or accelerating aggressively. {He's so leadfooted we got there in half the time.} The term also applies more broadly to anyone who moves clumsily or without grace, as if their feet were made of lead. A leadfooted dancer lacks lightness and finesse. The spelling varies between leadfooted, lead-footed, and leaden-footed.

Leading describes what's out front or most important. A leading {candidate} tops the polls. A leading {role} is the main part. A leading {question} steers toward a particular answer. In printing, leading (pronounced "ledding") is the vertical space between lines of type—from the lead strips once used to create that gap.

Leadoff describes something that comes first or opens a sequence. In baseball, the leadoff batter hits first in the lineup; a leadoff home run comes in the first at-bat of a game. More broadly, leadoff marks whatever begins a series: {the leadoff speaker at the conference}, {a leadoff question in the interview}. As a noun: {She's our leadoff}.

Leads connects to the idea of being in front or guiding. A person leads a group by going first or directing: {She leads the team}. A lead is a position of advantage: {We have a three-point lead}. Leads are also clues or promising contacts: {The detective followed several leads}, {sales leads}. A lead is a leash for a dog, or a wire conducting electricity. In journalism, the lead (sometimes spelled lede) is the opening paragraph. The verb's past tense is led—not to be confused with the metal lead, a different word entirely.

The leadup is the period or sequence of events preceding something significant: {the leadup to the election}, {the leadup to war}. It emphasizes preparation, buildup, or the chain of circumstances that culminate in a main event. Usually hyphenated as lead-up, though increasingly written as one word.

The characteristics of a leaf on a plant or tree give rise to the many other meanings of the word. Most figurative extensions of leaf pick up on a leaf’s characteristics: flat, thin, and tend to come in multiples rather than singles. The leaves of a book are its pages. When you leaf through a book, you turn its pages. Gold leaf is gold in the form of extremely thin sheets. When a tree leafs out, it produces leaves, typically in the spring.

A leafblower is a powered garden tool that produces a strong stream of air to move leaves, grass clippings, and other debris. Most are gasoline-powered or electric, either corded or battery-operated. Landscapers and homeowners use them to clear driveways, sidewalks, and lawns, though their noise has made them controversial in residential areas. {The neighbor's leafblower woke me up at seven on Saturday morning.}

Leafcutters are ants or bees that cut pieces from leaves. Leafcutter ants, found in the Americas, harvest leaf fragments not to eat but to cultivate fungus in underground gardens—the fungus feeds the colony. Leafcutter bees cut circular pieces from leaves to line their nests. Both are named for the distinctive semicircular holes they leave behind.

Leafing is the process of producing or putting out leaves, as plants do in spring: {The trees are leafing out early this year}. It also means turning pages, usually casually or without close reading: {I spent the afternoon leafing through old magazines}. To leaf through something is to browse rather than study it.

A leaflet is a small, printed sheet of paper distributed for information or advertising—often folded but unbound: {Someone handed me a leaflet about the rally}. In botany, a leaflet is one of the smaller blade-like divisions of a compound leaf. The verb means to distribute leaflets: {Volunteers leafleted the neighborhood}.

Leaflets are small printed sheets of paper distributed by hand, typically containing information, advertisements, or political messages: {Protesters handed out leaflets at the rally}. The word also refers to the individual segments of a compound leaf, or the small flaps of tissue in heart valves. The singular leaflet works as both noun and verb—to leaflet an area is to distribute printed materials there.

Leafy describes something covered with or having many leaves: {a leafy canopy}, {leafy greens}. A leafy neighborhood has abundant trees and vegetation, suggesting pleasant residential areas: {They moved to a leafy suburb}. The word often carries connotations of shade, greenery, and natural beauty.

A league is an alliance or association of people, nations, or groups united for mutual benefit or a common purpose: {the League of Nations}, {the Arab League}. In sports, a league organizes teams that compete against each other: {the National Football League}, {a bowling league}. The phrase {in league with} suggests collaboration, often secretive or sinister: {They suspected he was in league with the enemy}. To be {out of someone's league} is to be beyond their level of ability or social standing. Separately, a league is an old unit of distance, roughly three miles—still used figuratively: {twenty thousand leagues under the sea}.

Leagues is the plural of league, a word with two distinct origins. One league is a unit of distance, roughly three miles, now archaic except in literary contexts: {Twenty thousand leagues under the sea}. The other league is an alliance or association—sports teams form leagues, nations join leagues, people {in league with} each other are collaborating, often secretly. To be {out of someone's league} is to be beyond their reach, whether in dating, competition, or ability: {She's way out of my league}.

A leak is an unwanted escape of fluid, gas, or light through a hole or crack: {The roof has a leak}. The hole itself is also a leak. To leak is to escape or allow escape this way: {The pipe is leaking}. Extended to information, a leak is unauthorized disclosure to the press or public: {Someone leaked the memo}. The person who discloses is also called a leak. To {take a leak} is slang for urinating.

Leakage is the act or process of leaking, or the amount that leaks out. A pipe may have leakage; a container may show leakage over time. The word extends to abstract losses: {leakage of classified information}, {revenue leakage from fraud}. In technical contexts, leakage describes unwanted escape of current, heat, or data from a system.

Leaked describes information that was released without authorization, or something that escaped through an unintended opening. A leaked {document} was disclosed by an insider. A leaked {pipe} allowed water to seep out. News organizations report on leaked {emails}, leaked {memos}, leaked {footage}. The word implies both the act of disclosure and the resulting public exposure: {The video was leaked to the press}.

A leaker is someone who discloses confidential information to the public or press without authorization. The term usually applies to government or corporate insiders who reveal secrets: {The administration launched an investigation to identify the leaker}. Leaker carries less heroic connotations than whistleblower—it emphasizes the breach of trust rather than the public interest served.

Leaking describes something that has a leak—allowing contents to escape through a hole or crack: {a leaking pipe}, {a leaking roof}. It extends to information escaping containment: {Someone's been leaking classified documents to the press}. A leaking vessel loses its contents gradually; a leaking organization loses its secrets the same way.

Leaks are unwanted escapes of liquid, gas, or information through gaps or breaches. A pipe leaks water; a tire leaks air; a source leaks classified documents to reporters. The noun names both the escape and the opening that allows it: {We found the leak in the roof}. To spring a leak is to develop one suddenly. A leak can also mean urination: {I need to take a leak}.

Leaky describes something that lets liquid, gas, or other contents escape through holes or gaps: {a leaky faucet}, {a leaky roof}. Extended uses cover anything that fails to contain what it should. A leaky organization lets confidential information slip out. A leaky gut allows substances through the intestinal lining that shouldn't pass. {The administration has been plagued by leaky sources.}

Lean describes something with little fat or excess. Lean meat has minimal fat. A lean person is thin, especially in a fit or sinewy way. A lean budget or operation has been stripped to essentials: {We're running a lean startup}. Lean times are periods of scarcity. To lean is to incline from vertical—against a wall, toward a person, or figuratively toward an opinion: {I'm leaning toward accepting the offer}. A lean-to is a simple shelter that leans against another structure.

Leaning is an inclination or tendency toward something—a preference that falls short of full commitment. Someone with {liberal leanings} tends toward liberal views without necessarily identifying as liberal. The word suggests direction without arrival: {She has leanings toward vegetarianism but still eats fish}. As a present participle, leaning describes the physical act of tilting or resting against something: {He was leaning against the wall}.

Leanings are inclinations or tendencies, especially in opinion or political orientation: {Her socialist leanings were well known}, {a judge with conservative leanings}. The word suggests a tilt rather than a committed position—someone with artistic leanings may not be an artist but feels drawn that way.

Leap, noun and verb, is like jump on steroids: it suggests quick and forceful movement, often upward, usually self-propelled, and often figurative. Quantum leap characterizes sudden and great progress or change. A daring leap is a bold and unexpected move. Things that are said to leap as a characteristic movement include flames, lightning, and of course, frogs. If you leap to a conclusion, you decide or infer something too hastily.

Leapfrog is a children's game where players vault over each other's stooped backs, hands pressing down as they spring past. The image extends to any bypassing maneuver—skipping intermediate steps to advance quickly: {The company leapfrogged its competitors by adopting new technology}. As a verb, to leapfrog is to vault over or surpass: {Startups can leapfrog established firms}.

Leapfrogged is the past tense of leapfrog—to jump over something or someone, as in the children's game where players vault over each other's bent backs. More often figurative: to bypass or surpass by skipping intermediate stages. {The startup leapfrogged its competitors by adopting newer technology.} {She leapfrogged three senior employees to become director.}

Leapfrogging is advancing by jumping over obstacles or intermediate stages. Children leapfrog by vaulting over each other's bent backs. The term extends to any bypassing of sequential steps: {The startup leapfrogged established competitors by adopting newer technology}. Countries may leapfrog older infrastructure entirely, going straight to mobile phones without landlines. In military use, leapfrogging describes alternating advances where units take turns moving past each other.

Leapfrogs is the third-person singular of leapfrog, a children's game where players vault over each other's bent backs. The verb extends to any bypassing or leap ahead: {The company leapfrogged its competitors with new technology}. Military forces leapfrog when units advance past each other in alternating bounds.

Leaping is the act of springing through the air—jumping with force or sudden movement. The word often suggests energy or enthusiasm: {a leaping deer}, {leaping flames}. In phrases like {leaping to conclusions}, it implies hasty or impulsive action. {Her heart was leaping with excitement.}

Leaps is the plural of leap and its third-person singular verb form. A leap is a jump or bound, typically one covering significant distance or height: {The gazelle cleared the fence in two leaps}. To leap is to spring through the air or advance suddenly: {She leaps at every opportunity}. Figuratively, a leap is a dramatic change or progression: {a leap of faith}, {leaps and bounds}.

Leapt is the past tense and past participle of leap, meaning to jump or spring suddenly: {The cat leapt onto the counter}. It shares this role with leaped—both are standard, though leapt is more common in British English and leaped in American. Figuratively, something that leapt can mean it changed abruptly: {Prices leapt overnight}.

Learn is a verb whose meaning is complementary to teach: Teachers teach students in order that students will learn. Many things we learn directly from our experience, as is the case when someone learns a lesson. If you learn a poem or the dialogue of a play, you memorize it. If you learn a dance or a piece of music, you are able to perform it. If you say that someone will never learn, you believe that they won’t benefit from their experience.

Learned functions as both adjective and verb. As an adjective (usually two syllables: LEARN-ed), it describes someone with extensive knowledge, especially scholarly or academic: {a learned professor}, {learned treatises}. As the past tense of learn (one syllable), it simply indicates acquisition of knowledge: {She learned to swim last summer}. A learned behavior is acquired through experience rather than instinct.

A learner is someone who is learning—acquiring knowledge or skill through study, practice, or experience. The word often appears in educational contexts: {a slow learner}, {language learners}, {learner's permit}. A learner's permit allows someone to practice driving before obtaining a full license.

Learning is the process of gaining knowledge or skill through study, experience, or instruction. What you've learned is also your learning: {a person of great learning}. The word often appears in compounds describing how acquisition happens: {distance learning}, {machine learning}, {learning curve}. As an adjective, it describes difficulty with academic skills: {learning disability}, {learning difficulties}.

A lease is a contract for the use of an asset or property, especially real estate and housing, in return for rent. The verb lease can characterize the relationship described in a lease from either party’s point of view. The owner leases property to someone. The rent payer leases the property from the owner. A new lease on something, especially a new lease on life, is an opportunity to regain a former favorable state.

Leases is the plural of lease, a contract granting use of property for a specified time in exchange for payment. Landlords lease apartments to tenants; car dealerships lease vehicles. {The company holds leases on three office buildings}. A lease on life—usually {a new lease on life}—is renewed vitality or opportunity after difficulty.

A leash is a strap or cord for restraining an animal, attached to a collar and held by a person: {She walked the dog on a leash}. Figuratively, to keep someone {on a short leash} is to limit their freedom. To {strain at the leash} is to be eager for release from constraint. The verb means to attach a leash or, more broadly, to restrain.

Leashed means attached to or restrained by a leash—the cord or strap used to control an animal: {The dog must be leashed in public areas}. Figuratively, leashed suggests being held back or under someone's control: {He kept his anger leashed}, {leashed to a desk job}.

Leashes are straps or cords used to restrain or control an animal, typically attached to a collar: {She walked three dogs on separate leashes}. Figuratively, a leash represents any restraint on freedom or independence: {The new regulations kept the industry on a short leash}. To leash is to attach such a restraint; to unleash is to release it.

Leashing is the act of attaching a leash to an animal, typically a dog, for walking or restraint: {She was leashing the puppy when the doorbell rang}. The term extends to any act of tethering or bringing under control: {The new regulations are about leashing corporate excess}.

Leasing is renting property or equipment under a contract for a specified period. A business might lease office space or vehicles rather than buy them. The one who leases out is the lessor; the one who leases is the lessee. {We're leasing a car for three years.} The term covers both sides of the transaction—you can lease something you own to others, or lease something from an owner.

Least is the superlative of little—the smallest amount, degree, or importance: {the least expensive option}, {That's the least of my worries}. As an adverb, it indicates minimum extent: {the least likely outcome}. {At least} sets a floor or offers consolation: {At least no one got hurt}. {Not in the least} means not at all. {Last but not least} introduces a final item while affirming its importance.

Leather is animal hide that has been treated to make it durable and flexible. It's used for shoes, belts, bags, jackets, and furniture upholstery. As an adjective, leather describes things made from or resembling the material: {leather boots}, {a leather-bound book}. In gay slang, leather refers to a subculture associated with BDSM and distinctive clothing: {the leather scene}, {a leather bar}.

A leatherback is a sea turtle distinguished by its leathery, ridged shell rather than the hard plates found on other species. The leatherback is the largest living turtle, reaching weights over a thousand pounds. It ranges across all oceans and dives deeper than any other turtle: {We spotted a leatherback surfacing near the boat}.

Leatherbacks are the largest species of sea turtle, distinguished by their leathery, flexible shells rather than the hard, bony plates of other turtles. They can grow over six feet long and dive deeper than any other turtle. The term occasionally extends to other animals with tough, leather-like skin.

Leatherbound describes a book with a cover made of leather, suggesting quality, durability, or traditional craftsmanship: {a leatherbound edition of Shakespeare}, {leatherbound journals lined the study walls}. The term evokes libraries, heirlooms, and books meant to last generations rather than disposable paperbacks.

Leathernecks is informal slang for United States Marines. The nickname dates to the leather collar once part of the Marine uniform, which protected the neck in combat. The term is affectionate rather than derogatory, used both by Marines themselves and others: {The leathernecks landed at dawn}.

Leatherworking is the craft of shaping, cutting, and treating animal hides to make useful or decorative objects—belts, bags, saddles, armor, book bindings. The term covers techniques like tanning, tooling, stitching, and dyeing. A leatherworker may also be called a leather craftsman or, in specialized trades, a saddler, cobbler, or tanner.

Leave is actually two distinct words: the noun and verb are derived from different sources. Leave the verb is a synonym of depart in its core meaning but also has transitive uses that convey the idea of separation of the subject from something else: Did you leave your bike at school? The verb leave is also interchangeable with let in a few expressions. The noun leave has multiple meanings, including permission, parting, and permitted absence.

Leaven is a substance that makes dough rise—yeast, baking powder, or sourdough starter. The leavening agent produces gas bubbles that lighten and expand the mixture. Figuratively, leaven is any element that transforms or enlivens a whole: {His humor was a leaven to the otherwise dreary proceedings}. To leaven is to add such an element: {She leavened her criticism with praise}.

Leavening is a substance that makes dough rise—yeast, baking powder, or baking soda. The term extends to anything that lightens or enlivens: {The speech needed some leavening humor}. As a verb form, leavening describes the act of adding such an agent: {She's leavening the bread dough}.

Leaves is the plural of leaf—the flat green structures on plants that photosynthesize. {The leaves are changing color.} Leaves also serves as the verb for departing: {She leaves tomorrow}. What remains after someone leaves are the things they {leaves behind}. {Two weeks of paid leave} becomes {two leaves of absence} in the plural, though this usage is uncommon.

Leavetaking is the act of saying goodbye, particularly in formal or emotionally significant contexts. It suggests more ceremony than a casual farewell—the exchange of words, gestures, or rituals that mark a departure: {The leavetaking at the airport was tearful}. Also spelled leave-taking.

Leaving is the act of departing or going away from a place, person, or situation: {I'm leaving in ten minutes}. It also refers to what remains after something is taken away—usually in the plural as leavings, meaning remnants or scraps: {The dog ate the leavings from dinner}. To leave someone or something is to abandon, bequeath, or allow to remain: {She's leaving her husband}, {He's leaving everything to charity}.

Lechaim is a Jewish toast meaning "to life," used when drinking alcohol at celebrations, meals, or gatherings. The Hebrew phrase expresses hope for health and good fortune. Also spelled l'chaim or l'chayim. {They raised their glasses and shouted lechaim!}

A lecher is a man who pursues sexual gratification in an openly crude or excessive way. The word suggests someone ruled by lust rather than discretion: {The old lecher couldn't keep his eyes off the waitress}. Lecherous describes such behavior; lechery is the tendency itself.

Lecherous describes someone who shows excessive or offensive sexual desire, especially in a way that makes others uncomfortable. The word typically applies to men whose interest in sex seems predatory or inappropriate: {a lecherous old man}, {his lecherous gaze}. The related noun is lecher.

Lechers is the plural of lecher, a man who shows excessive or offensive sexual interest in others. The word carries strong disapproval, suggesting someone whose desires are uncontrolled or predatory: {The bar was full of old lechers staring at young women}. Though technically gender-neutral, lecher almost always describes men.
clues: Crude men always on the prowl

definition: Lechery is excessive or unrestrained sexual desire, especially when acted upon indiscriminately. The word carries moral judgment—a lecher pursues sexual gratification without regard for propriety or the feelings of others. {The tabloids catalogued his lechery in lurid detail.} Literary and somewhat old-fashioned, but still current when condemning predatory or compulsive sexual behavior.

A lectern is a tall, narrow stand with a sloped top for holding a book or notes, used by speakers, preachers, or readers. The speaker stands behind it rather than sits: {She approached the lectern to deliver her remarks}. Often confused with podium, which is a raised platform to stand on.

A lecture is a formal talk given to an audience, typically for instruction: {The professor's lecture on quantum mechanics lasted two hours}. The word carries connotations of one-way communication—someone speaks, others listen. This spawns the disapproving sense: to lecture someone is to scold or admonish them at length, often condescendingly: {Don't lecture me about responsibility}. A lecture hall is a room designed for such presentations.

Lectured is the past tense of lecture. To lecture is to deliver a formal talk, typically educational: {She lectured on Renaissance art}. More commonly, lecture means to scold or reprimand at length: {My father lectured me about responsibility}. This sense carries a note of tedium—being lectured implies enduring unwanted criticism or advice.

A lecturer is someone who gives lectures—formal talks on a subject, typically in an academic setting. In universities, lecturer often designates a specific teaching rank, usually below professor: {She's a lecturer in the English department}. The term can also describe anyone who tends to deliver lengthy, instructive monologues, often with a hint of tedium implied.

Lectures are formal talks given to instruct an audience, typically in academic settings: {The professor's lectures on medieval history drew large crowds}. A lecture can also be a lengthy scolding or moralizing speech: {I got a lecture from my mom about staying out too late}. To lecture is to deliver such talks, or to reprimand at length.

Lecturing is the act of delivering a formal talk or educational presentation, typically to students or an audience: {She's lecturing on Renaissance art this semester}. The word often carries a negative sense of speaking at someone in a preachy, condescending, or tediously prolonged way: {I don't need you lecturing me about my choices}. The first sense is neutral; the second implies the speaker has made themselves unwelcome.

Led is the past tense and past participle of lead, meaning to guide, direct, or be in front. Someone led a group, led a meeting, or led the way. A path led somewhere. An investigation led to conclusions. Events led up to an outcome: {One thing led to another}. (All-caps LED is an acronym for light-emitting diode.)

Lederhosen are traditional leather shorts with suspenders, associated with Bavaria and Alpine regions. The garment features a front flap and decorative embroidery, worn historically by workers and now primarily at folk festivals and Oktoberfest celebrations: {He bought lederhosen for the beer festival}. The word is German, literally "leather trousers."

A ledge is a narrow horizontal surface projecting from a vertical face. Mountain climbers rest on rock ledges. Window ledges hold potted plants. The word suggests something you could stand or place things on, but just barely: {He inched along the ledge twenty stories up}. Figuratively, someone on a ledge is in a precarious situation.

A ledger is a book or digital record where financial transactions are systematically recorded and organized. In traditional bookkeeping, the ledger contains accounts showing debits and credits, serving as the authoritative record of a business's finances. The term extends to any formal registry of important information: {The blockchain functions as a distributed public ledger}. In construction, a ledger is a horizontal board attached to a wall to support joists or scaffolding.

Ledgers are books or records for keeping financial accounts. Each transaction gets entered as a debit or credit, allowing businesses to track money flowing in and out. The term extends to any systematic record: {The team kept a ledger of wins and losses}. In construction, a ledger is a horizontal board attached to a wall to support joists or scaffolding.

Ledges is the plural of ledge, a narrow horizontal surface projecting from a vertical one. Window ledges hold potted plants. Mountain ledges offer precarious footing for climbers. {Birds nested on the rocky ledges.} Any shelf-like projection can be a ledge: {She set her coffee on the ledge of the tub}.

Lee is the sheltered side of something—the side away from the wind. Sailors seek the lee of an island for protection from storms. {We anchored in the lee of the cliff.} As an adjective, lee describes this sheltered position: the lee {shore}, the lee {side}. The opposite is windward. (Capitalized Lee is a given name and surname.)

A leech is a blood-sucking worm found in fresh water, historically used in medicine to draw blood from patients. The word extends to anyone who clings to others and drains their resources: {He's a leech who lives off his parents}. To leech is to exploit someone parasitically, or in computing, to download without contributing: {She leeched the entire album without seeding}.

Leeched is the past tense of leech. A leech is a blood-sucking worm once used in medicine, and by extension, a person who drains others of money, energy, or resources. To leech is to cling parasitically or extract something gradually: {He leeched off his parents for years}. In computing, to leech is to download without sharing back: {She leeched the entire torrent without seeding}.

Leeches are bloodsucking aquatic worms, historically used in medicine to draw blood from patients. Modern medicine still uses them selectively to reduce swelling or restore circulation after surgery. Figuratively, a leech is someone who drains others of money, energy, or resources: {He's been leeching off his parents for years}. To leech is to cling parasitically or to extract something gradually.

Leeching is the practice of taking from others without contributing—draining resources, bandwidth, or effort while giving nothing back. In file-sharing networks, a leecher downloads without uploading: {He's just leeching off the torrent without seeding}. More broadly, it describes parasitic behavior: {She's been leeching off her parents for years}. The older sense refers to applying leeches medicinally to draw blood.

A leek is a vegetable in the onion family with a mild, sweet flavor and a distinctive form: a long white cylindrical bulb that transitions into flat, dark green leaves. Unlike onions, leeks don't form a round bulb but grow in overlapping layers that trap dirt, requiring thorough cleaning before cooking. They're essential to dishes like vichyssoise and cock-a-leekie soup, and serve as a national symbol of Wales.

Leeks are vegetables related to onions and garlic, with a milder, sweeter flavor. They have flat green leaves and a white cylindrical stalk, which is the part most commonly eaten. Leeks require thorough washing, as dirt collects between their layers. They appear in soups, stews, and the Welsh national emblem: {potato leek soup}, {braised leeks}.

A leer is a sly, knowing, or lustful sideways glance—the kind that makes the recipient uncomfortable: {He gave her a leer from across the bar}. To leer is to look this way, suggesting sexual interest or malicious amusement. The word carries strongly negative connotations; no one wants to be caught leering.

Leering describes looking at someone in a way that suggests sexual interest or malicious intent—a gaze that lingers too long and makes the recipient uncomfortable. A leer combines a sideways glance with a suggestive or unpleasant expression: {He was leering at her from across the bar}. The word almost always carries negative connotations of predatory or unwelcome attention.

Leers is the plural of leer and its verb form. A leer is a sidelong glance suggesting lust, malice, or sly amusement—the look carries suggestion or threat: {He gave her a lewd leer from across the bar}. To leer is to look this way: {The drunk leered at passing women}. The word almost always implies something unpleasant or predatory in the gaze.

Leery means wary or suspicious, especially about being deceived or getting into trouble: {I'm leery of any deal that sounds too good to be true}. The word suggests cautious distrust rather than outright fear—you're leery of something you suspect might be problematic but haven't confirmed.

Leet is internet slang for elite, originating in early online communities and gaming culture. The term often appears in "leet speak" or "1337 speak"—a style of writing that replaces letters with numbers and symbols (E becomes 3, A becomes 4, T becomes 7). Someone with leet skills is highly proficient, especially at hacking or gaming: {His leet programming skills got him the job}. The style peaked in the 1990s and early 2000s but persists ironically or nostalgically.

Leetspeak is a style of writing that substitutes numbers and symbols for letters they resemble: 3 for E, 4 for A, 0 for O, 1 for I or L. It originated in early internet culture, particularly among hackers and gamers: {h4x0r} for hacker, {n00b} for newbie, {pwn3d} for pwned. The term comes from "elite speak." Once a marker of insider status, it now reads as playful or ironic, sometimes mocking the very subcultures that created it.

Leeward describes the side or direction sheltered from the wind—the opposite of windward. On a ship, the leeward side faces away from where the wind is blowing, providing relative calm. The term extends to islands, coastlines, and any situation where something blocks wind: {We anchored on the leeward side of the reef}. As a noun, leeward refers to this sheltered direction or area. Sailors and meteorologists use it constantly; everyone else encounters it mainly in geography, as in the Leeward Islands.

Leeway is room to maneuver—the margin between where you are and where limits begin. A deadline with leeway allows some lateness. A budget with leeway can absorb overruns. {Give yourself some leeway on the estimate.} The word comes from sailing, where it originally meant a ship's sideways drift from its intended course.

Left is the side opposite to right—the direction of the hand most people don't write with. It also names what remains after something is taken: {There's nothing left}. In politics, the left refers to progressive or socialist positions, from the seating arrangement in the French Revolutionary assembly where radicals sat to the speaker's left. As a verb form, left is the past tense of leave: {She left early}.

A leftfielder is the defensive player in baseball or softball who covers left field—the area of the outfield to the left of center when viewed from home plate. The position requires range, a strong throwing arm, and the ability to read fly balls off the bat: {The leftfielder made a diving catch to end the inning}.

Lefthanded describes someone who uses their left hand as their dominant hand, or something designed for such use: {a lefthanded pitcher}, {lefthanded scissors}. A lefthanded compliment is one that contains an insult within apparent praise—backhanded. The spelling varies: left-handed and left handed are equally common.

Leftie is an informal term for a left-handed person: {Any other lefties at this table need to switch seats?} It also refers, often dismissively, to someone with left-wing political views: {The radio host railed against coastal lefties}. The political sense carries a mildly disparaging tone when used by opponents. Also spelled lefty.
clues: One who writes with other hand

definition: Lefties is the informal plural of lefty—people who are left-handed or, in political contexts, those with left-wing views. The meaning depends on context: {Half the pitchers on the roster are lefties} refers to handedness, while {The lefties in Congress opposed the bill} refers to political orientation. Both uses are casual and sometimes mildly dismissive.

Leftism is the political orientation favoring progressive social change, economic equality, and collective welfare over traditional hierarchies and free-market capitalism. The term covers a spectrum from moderate liberalism to socialism to revolutionary communism. Critics use it dismissively: {His leftism makes him blind to economic realities}. Adherents may embrace or avoid the label depending on context.

A leftist is someone whose political views fall on the left side of the spectrum—favoring social equality, government intervention in the economy, and progressive reform. The term ranges from mild (center-left liberals) to strong (socialists, communists). As an adjective, it describes such politics: {leftist policies}, {a leftist newspaper}. Often used dismissively by opponents: {the leftist media}.

Leftists are people who hold left-wing political views—broadly, those favoring greater social and economic equality, government intervention in the economy, and progressive social policies. The term ranges from neutral description to dismissive epithet depending on who's using it: {Leftists staged a protest outside city hall}. Critics often use it to paint opponents as radical or extreme, while some on the political left embrace it.

Leftover describes what remains after the main use or event has passed. Leftover {food} is what wasn't eaten at a meal. Leftover {funds} are what remains in a budget. As a noun, usually in the plural: {We had leftovers for dinner}. The word can suggest something diminished or secondary—a leftover from an earlier era, a policy that's a leftover from the previous administration.

Leftovers are food remaining after a meal, saved for later eating: {We had leftover turkey for three days after Thanksgiving}. The term extends to anything remaining from a previous use or time: {The policy is a leftover from the Cold War}. Leftovers often carry a slight sense of being secondary or less desirable than the original.

Leftwing describes political positions favoring progressive reform, greater economic equality, and expanded government role in social welfare. The term comes from the seating arrangement in the French revolutionary assembly, where radicals sat to the president's left. Leftwing policies typically support labor unions, environmental regulation, and social safety nets: {leftwing activists}, {a leftwing newspaper}. Often hyphenated as left-wing, especially as an adjective before a noun.

A leftwinger is someone who holds left-wing political views—generally favoring social equality, progressive reform, and government intervention in the economy. The term applies to politicians, activists, or ordinary citizens: {The proposal drew support from leftwingers in the party}. In hockey and soccer, a leftwinger plays on the left side of the forward line.

Lefty is an informal term for a left-handed person, or for someone whose political views lean left—that is, toward liberal or progressive positions. In sports, a lefty pitcher or batter uses their left hand dominantly. The political sense carries mild dismissiveness when used by opponents: {The talk show host blamed lefties for the policy change}. Context usually makes clear whether handedness or politics is meant.

The leg that begins at your hip and ends at your foot inspires the many other uses of the word.
