A listener is someone who listens—to music, to a speaker, to a podcast. The word often implies attentiveness or receptivity: {She's a good listener}. In broadcasting, listeners are the audience for radio or audio content. In computing, a listener is a process that waits for incoming connections or events.

Listeners are people who hear and pay attention to something—a speaker, a broadcast, music. The word often refers to an audience: {The radio show has millions of listeners}. A good listener pays close attention when others speak, making them feel heard. In computing, a listener is a program that waits for and responds to incoming connections or events.

Listening is the act of paying attention to sound, especially speech. It implies more than just hearing—listening suggests active engagement and effort to understand: {Are you even listening to me?} Good listening involves focus and response. {Listening to music} means attending to it with appreciation. In surveillance contexts, a listening {device} or listening {post} captures communications covertly.

A listicle is an article structured as a numbered or bulleted list: {10 Ways to Boost Your Productivity}, {The 25 Best Films of the Decade}. The format dominates online content because it promises digestible, scannable information. The word blends "list" and "article."

Listicles are articles structured as numbered or bulleted lists: {10 Ways to Improve Your Morning Routine}, {The 25 Best Albums of the Year}. The format dominates online journalism because it's easy to scan and share. The word blends list with article. Critics associate listicles with shallow clickbait, though the format itself is neutral.

A listing is an entry in a list or directory—a real estate listing, a job listing, a TV listing. The word emphasizes the item's inclusion in some organized collection: {Check the listings to see what's playing}. In computing, a listing is a printout or display of code. The plural listings often refers to classified advertisements or program schedules as a category.

Listings are items in a list, especially ones published or displayed for public reference. Real estate listings show properties for sale. Job listings advertise open positions. Event listings tell you what's playing at local venues. The term implies organized, searchable information: {I found the apartment through online listings}.

Listless describes a state of low energy and absent motivation—not quite tired, but without the will to engage. A listless person sits around, indifferent to what's happening: {She spent the afternoon in listless boredom, flipping channels without watching anything}. The word suggests apathy more than exhaustion, a kind of spiritless drift.

Lists is an old word for a combat arena—the enclosed field where knights jousted at tournaments. To {enter the lists} is to join a competition or conflict, from the image of a challenger riding into that space. The expression survives mainly in formal or literary contexts: {She entered the lists as a candidate for mayor}.

Lit is the past tense of light—illuminated, ignited, or set on fire: {She lit the candle}. {The room was beautifully lit}. {His cigarette was already lit}. A well-lit space has good lighting; a lit fuse is burning. In slang, lit means drunk, high, or extremely exciting and fun: {The party was lit}. {I got lit last night}. This sense exploded in popularity in the 2010s and can describe both intoxication and general excitement.

Litanies is the plural of litany, a form of prayer consisting of a series of petitions with repeated responses. By extension, a litany is any long, repetitive recitation or tedious list: {a litany of complaints}, {a litany of failures}. The word usually carries a weary or exasperated tone, suggesting the speaker has heard it all before.

A litany is a lengthy, repetitive recitation—originally a form of prayer with a series of invocations and responses. The word now usually describes any tedious enumeration: {a litany of complaints}, {the usual litany of excuses}. The negative connotation suggests weariness with hearing the same grievances or items repeated.

Litchi is a tropical fruit with a rough, reddish shell enclosing translucent white flesh around a dark seed. The flesh is sweet and fragrant, popular fresh or in desserts and drinks. Native to southern China, the fruit grows in clusters on evergreen trees. Also spelled lychee.

Lite is an informal spelling of light, used almost exclusively in marketing and casual writing. It typically describes products reduced in calories, fat, alcohol, or complexity: {lite beer}, {lite mayo}, {a lite version of the software}. The spelling signals something stripped down or less demanding—often with a faintly dismissive tone when applied outside product names: {philosophy lite}, {democracy lite}.

A liter is a metric unit of volume equal to about 1.06 quarts or 0.26 gallons. It measures liquids and gases: {a two-liter bottle of soda}, {The engine displaces 3.5 liters}. In scientific contexts, liter is the standard volume measure. Also spelled litre in British English.

Literacy is the ability to read and write. Basic literacy means functional competence; full literacy suggests fluency. The term extends to competence in other domains: {computer literacy}, {financial literacy}, {media literacy}. These compound forms imply not just familiarity but practical understanding—knowing enough to navigate effectively.

Literal describes something that adheres to the exact, primary meaning of words without metaphor or exaggeration. A literal {translation} renders text word for word rather than capturing its spirit. If you take something literally, you interpret it according to its surface meaning: {I said I was starving, but I didn't mean it literally}. In casual speech, literal and literally have become intensifiers that often contradict their original sense: {I literally died laughing}. This usage irritates purists but is now widespread.

The adverb literally indicates a factual meaning as opposed to a figurative interpretation: They were literally chased out of town by an angry mob. Literally is not successful as an intensifier: Their new album will literally turn the world upside down. If someone translates a work literally, they give a version in the target language that may be truer to the words than to the meaning of the original.

Literary describes writing with artistic ambition beyond mere communication—novels, poetry, essays crafted for aesthetic effect. A literary {style} is polished and deliberate. Literary also means connected to literature as a field: literary {criticism}, literary {journals}. Someone literary reads widely and values books. The word can suggest old-fashioned formality: {a literary way of putting it}.

Literate means able to read and write: {a literate population}, {barely literate}. The word extends to competence in any domain: {computer literate}, {financially literate}. A literate person may also be well-read or culturally educated: {a literate and thoughtful critic}. As a noun, a literate is someone who can read, often in contexts discussing literacy rates.

The literati are the educated class, particularly those engaged with literature, scholarship, and intellectual culture. The term often carries a hint of exclusivity or pretension—the literary establishment as a somewhat self-regarding circle: {The book was praised by the literati but ignored by ordinary readers}. Singular: literatus, though rarely used.

Literature is written work, especially of artistic merit—novels, poetry, drama, essays. The term often implies enduring value: {the literature of the Romantic period}, {American literature}. More broadly, literature means the body of writing on a subject: {medical literature}, {campaign literature}. The adjective literary describes qualities associated with serious writing, sometimes disparagingly: {a literary style that felt overwrought}.

Liters is the plural of liter, a metric unit of volume equal to 1,000 cubic centimeters or about 1.06 U.S. quarts. Liters measure liquids and gases: {The recipe calls for two liters of water}. Outside the United States, the spelling is litres. Engine displacement is often given in liters: {a 3.5-liter V6}.

Lithe describes a body that is supple and graceful, bending easily: {a lithe dancer}, {her lithe figure}. The word suggests fluid, effortless movement—the quality of a gymnast or cat. Lithe carries positive connotations of elegance and flexibility, distinct from merely thin or skinny.

Lithium is a soft, silver-white metal, the lightest of all solid elements. It appears in rechargeable batteries for phones, laptops, and electric vehicles. In medicine, lithium compounds treat bipolar disorder by stabilizing mood: {She's been on lithium for years}. The element's lightness and reactivity make it valuable across industries.

A lithograph is a print made by drawing on a flat stone or metal plate with a greasy substance, then applying ink that adheres only to the drawn areas. The technique was invented in the late 18th century and became important for reproducing artwork and illustrations before photographic methods. As a verb, to lithograph is to produce such prints: {The poster was lithographed in three colors}.

Lithographs is the plural of lithograph—a print made by drawing on a flat stone or metal plate with a greasy substance, then applying ink that adheres only to the drawn areas. The technique produces distinctive prints prized in fine art and commercial illustration: {The gallery specializes in nineteenth-century lithographs}. As a verb, lithographs means produces such prints.

Litigating is the process of taking a legal dispute through the court system. Lawyers litigate cases; parties litigate claims. The word often appears in broader contexts: {They've been litigating this issue in the press for months}. To litigate is to contest something formally, whether in court or in the court of public opinion.

Litigation is the process of taking legal action through the courts. It encompasses everything from filing a lawsuit to the final judgment—the motions, discovery, hearings, and trial proceedings. {The company spent millions on litigation}. Someone engaged in litigation is a litigant; to litigate is to pursue or contest a case in court.

A litigator is a lawyer who specializes in taking cases to court, as opposed to one who handles contracts, wills, or other legal work that stays out of the courtroom. The term emphasizes the adversarial, trial-focused nature of the work: {The company hired an aggressive litigator to fight the lawsuit}.

Litmus is a dye derived from lichen that turns red in acid and blue in base, used to test acidity. The figurative {litmus test} has become far more common than the laboratory one—any single criterion that decisively reveals someone's position or character: {Abortion has become a litmus test for Supreme Court nominees}.

A litre is a metric unit of volume equal to one cubic decimetre—about 1.06 US quarts or 0.26 US gallons. It measures liquids and gases: {a litre of milk}, {engine displacement in litres}. The spelling litre is standard in British English; Americans write liter. Abbreviated L or l.

Litter gathers around the idea of scattered things. Litter is trash strewn in public places: {The park was covered in litter}. A litter of puppies or kittens is a group born together, scattered from the mother. Litter is also material spread on the ground—straw for animal bedding, or absorbent granules in a cat's litter box. To litter is to scatter carelessly: {Empty bottles littered the floor}.

A litterbox is a container filled with absorbent granular material where indoor cats urinate and defecate. The box requires regular cleaning—scooping waste and periodically replacing the litter. {The cat won't use a dirty litterbox.} Also spelled as two words: litter box.

A litterbug is someone who carelessly discards trash in public places rather than disposing of it properly. The word carries mild disapproval and sounds somewhat dated or childish—the kind of term used in anti-pollution campaigns aimed at schoolchildren: {Don't be a litterbug}.

Litterbugs are people who carelessly discard trash in public places rather than disposing of it properly. The term carries a mildly childish or scolding tone, often used in public awareness campaigns: {Don't be a litterbug}. It combines litter with bug in the sense of a person with an annoying habit.

Littered describes a surface covered with scattered objects, usually trash or debris: {The beach was littered with plastic bottles}. It extends to any disorderly scattering: {Her desk was littered with papers}. A field littered with bodies suggests aftermath of violence. For animals, littered means having given birth to a litter of offspring.

Littering is the act of discarding trash or waste in public places rather than proper receptacles. Signs warn against it; fines punish it. The word carries moral weight—littering marks someone as inconsiderate or careless about shared spaces. {The beach was ruined by tourists littering.} Littering also refers to animals giving birth to a litter of offspring.
clues: Leaving rubbish where it shouldn't be

definition: A littermate is one of a group of animals born together to the same mother. Dogs, cats, pigs, and other mammals that give birth to multiple offspring produce litters, and each sibling is a littermate to the others: {The puppy was reunited with one of her littermates after years apart}.

Litters is the plural of litter in its noun senses—scattered trash, a group of animals born together, material spread for animal bedding, or a carried platform. As a verb, litters means to scatter carelessly or to give birth to multiple offspring at once: {She never litters}, {The cat litters twice a year}. {Broken glass litters the street.}

Little, though not as common as its synonym small, is a frequently used word to characterize things as being not big. Usage favors little in a number of common collocations, including little bit, little doubt, little choice, little boy and little girl. In modifier pairs we also commonly say precious little, cute little, and nice little. Little works as an adverb in expressions such as care little and little known.

Littles is an affectionate term for young children, especially in family or parenting contexts: {I'm taking the littles to the park}. The word treats little as a noun rather than an adjective. In age regression and certain subcultures, littles refers to people who adopt childlike personas, often in relationship dynamics with caregivers.

Liturgy is the prescribed form of public worship in a religious tradition, especially the rituals, prayers, and ceremonies of Christian churches. The Catholic Mass and Orthodox Divine Liturgy are liturgies in this formal sense. More broadly, any established ritual order: {the liturgy of a graduation ceremony}, {the familiar liturgy of Thanksgiving dinner}. The adjective is liturgical.

Livable describes a place suitable for living in—meeting basic standards of comfort, safety, and functionality: {The apartment was small but livable}. A livable wage covers essential expenses. Livable weather or conditions are tolerable enough to endure. The word sets a modest bar: not luxurious or ideal, just adequate for human habitation or activity. Also spelled liveable.

The verb live (pronounced with a short vowel) has two main meanings: reside (live in Idaho) and have life (lived to the age of 100). If you live off something, it supports you: Carol lived off her pension. The adjective and adverb live (pronounced with a long vowel) characterizes things that are experienced or captured in real time (live performance, recorded live). Live is similar to alive in some phrases (live birth, live wire). The noun life has the plural form lives.

A liveblog is a running online commentary on an event as it unfolds—a sports match, political debate, or breaking news story. Updates appear in reverse chronological order, with the newest at the top: {I followed the election results through the Guardian's liveblog}. The verb means to provide such coverage: {She liveblogged the trial from the courthouse}.

Liveblogging is posting real-time updates to a blog or social media during an unfolding event—a political debate, a product launch, a sports match. The format creates a running log with timestamps, allowing readers to follow along as events happen: {I'll be liveblogging the election results tonight}. The practice emerged in the early 2000s and remains common for breaking news.

Lived is the past tense of live, but it also functions as an adjective meaning experienced firsthand: {lived experience}, {lived reality}. This adjective use emphasizes direct, personal knowledge rather than theoretical understanding—what someone has actually gone through rather than merely studied or observed.

A livelihood is the way someone earns money to support themselves—their occupation or source of income: {Fishing is the livelihood of most villagers here}. The word often appears when that income is threatened: {The factory closing destroyed their livelihoods}. It carries a sense of basic sustenance rather than wealth.

Livelihoods are means of earning a living—the ways people support themselves and their families. The word emphasizes ongoing sustenance rather than wealth: {Fishing provides livelihoods for coastal communities}. Threats to livelihoods—economic shifts, environmental changes, political upheaval—threaten survival itself: {The factory closure destroyed the livelihoods of hundreds of workers}.

Lively means full of energy, spirit, or activity. A lively {conversation} moves quickly with engaged participants. A lively {neighborhood} bustles with people and activity. A lively {debate} features vigorous exchange. The word suggests animation and vitality rather than mere speed: {The band played a lively tune}. Something can be lively without being loud—a lively {mind} is quick and engaged.

The liver is the large organ in the abdomen that filters blood, produces bile, and processes nutrients. It's essential to metabolism and detoxification. Liver also refers to this organ from animals prepared as food: {liver and onions}, {chicken liver pâté}. As an adjective, liver describes a dark reddish-brown color. A liver is also one who lives: {a clean liver}, {a fast liver}.

Livers is the plural of liver—the organ that filters blood and produces bile. In culinary contexts, livers are prepared as food: {chicken livers sautéed with onions}, {chopped livers}. To be {chopped liver} is to be dismissed as insignificant: {What am I, chopped liver?} A liver is also someone who lives in a particular way: {a clean liver}, {a fast liver}.

Liverwurst is a soft, spreadable sausage made primarily from ground liver, typically pork or calf liver mixed with pork fat and seasonings. German in origin, it's usually eaten cold on bread or crackers: {a liverwurst sandwich on rye}. Also called liver sausage or by its German name, leberwurst.

Livery originally meant the dispensing of food, provisions, or clothing to servants, and from this developed its main modern sense: a distinctive uniform or outfit worn by servants, employees, or members of an organization. {The hotel doormen wore matching livery.} By extension, livery describes any distinctive coloring or marking, including the painted designs on aircraft or vehicles identifying their operator. A livery stable is one where horses are kept and cared for in exchange for payment, or where horses and carriages can be hired—a sense that persists in phrases like {livery service} for car services.

Lives is the plural of life and the third-person singular of live. As a noun, lives are the spans of existence people or creatures have: {The accident claimed three lives}. The verb means to be alive or to dwell: {She lives in Boston}, {He lives for the weekend}. {Nine lives} is the legendary resilience of cats.

Livestock are animals raised on farms or ranches for food or labor—horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, goats. Chickens, turkeys, and ducks are sometimes included but more often called poultry, with livestock reserved for four-legged animals. The word implies groups; a single horse wouldn't count as livestock. {The rancher moved his livestock to higher ground before the flood.}

A livestream is video or audio broadcast in real time over the internet, allowing viewers to watch events as they happen: {I caught the concert on livestream}. The verb means to broadcast this way: {They're livestreaming the press conference}. Unlike recorded video, livestreams offer immediacy—viewers experience events simultaneously with participants, often interacting through chat.

A livestreamer is someone who broadcasts video content in real time over the internet, typically on platforms like Twitch or YouTube. The term usually implies regular streaming as an occupation or serious hobby rather than occasional use: {She quit her job to become a full-time livestreamer}. Most livestreamers interact with their audience through chat while gaming, creating content, or just talking.

Livestreaming is broadcasting video content over the internet in real time, as opposed to uploading pre-recorded material. Viewers watch events as they unfold—gaming sessions, concerts, news coverage, product launches: {She's livestreaming on Twitch right now}. The verb livestream works both ways: you can livestream your content or livestream someone else's broadcast by watching it live.

Livestreams are video broadcasts transmitted in real time over the internet, allowing viewers to watch events as they happen. The term covers everything from professional news coverage to casual gaming sessions on Twitch or YouTube. To livestream is to broadcast this way: {She livestreams her workouts every morning}. Also spelled as two words: live streams.

A livewire is an electrical wire carrying current—dangerous to touch. The figurative sense dominates: a livewire is an energetic, enthusiastic person full of restless vitality: {She's a real livewire—always has three projects going at once}. Also spelled as two words: live wire.

Livid originally describes the bluish-gray color of a bruise, and extends to skin discolored by cold, illness, or death: {His face went livid from the blow}. The more common modern sense is furiously angry: {She was livid when she found out he'd lied}. The connection may be through the pale or flushed appearance of someone in a rage.

Living describes being alive—having life, not dead. As a noun, living means one's livelihood or way of earning money: {She makes a living as a freelance writer}, {It's hard to earn a living in this economy}. The living are those who are alive, as opposed to the dead. A living {language} is still in active use. A living {room} is the main common space in a home. Something can be a {living hell} or a {living nightmare}—intensifiers suggesting ongoing, felt experience rather than mere metaphor.

A lizard is a reptile with a long body, four legs, and a tail—geckos, iguanas, chameleons, and their kin. Unlike snakes, most lizards have visible legs and external ear openings. Informally, lizard describes someone cold-blooded or untrustworthy: {That lizard cheated me out of my savings}. A {lounge lizard} is a man who frequents bars seeking women.

Lizards is the plural of lizard, a typically four-legged reptile with scaly skin and a long tail. Most lizards are small—geckos, skinks, iguanas—though monitor lizards grow quite large. Unlike snakes, most lizards have legs and external ear openings. {The lizards sunned themselves on the rocks.} In slang, a lounge lizard is a man who frequents bars hoping to meet women.

A llama is a South American mammal related to the camel but smaller and without a hump, domesticated for centuries as a pack animal and for its wool. Llamas are known for their calm temperament, though they famously spit when annoyed. In internet culture, llama has become a minor meme, appearing in absurdist humor and as mascots for various platforms. The word also refers to Llama, Meta's family of large language models.

Llamas are large domesticated South American mammals related to camels but without humps. They serve as pack animals in the Andes and are raised elsewhere for their soft wool. Llamas are known for spitting when annoyed. {The farm down the road keeps llamas and alpacas.}

A load is a burden, often a physical one but sometimes abstract. Whatever a cargo or freight vehicle carries is called its load: A semi overturned and dropped its load on the Interstate. In computing and cognitive contexts, load can refer to the amount of information being processed, sometimes with reference to a limit. Load also has many slang meanings. As a verb, load means to add to or create a load: Load the crates into the truck. When something is loaded with a substance of quality, it has a large quantity of it: The new game is loaded with special effects. To say that someone is loaded is an informal way of saying that they are drunk, or rich.

Loadbearing describes a structural element that supports weight from above—a loadbearing {wall} holds up the floor or roof, while a non-loadbearing wall merely divides space. The term matters in construction and renovation: you can't remove a loadbearing wall without replacing its structural function. Figuratively, a loadbearing {assumption} is one that supports an entire argument.

Loaded means carrying a load or full of something: a loaded {truck}, a loaded {gun}. Extended meanings cluster around excess or advantage. A loaded person is drunk or wealthy. Loaded {dice} are weighted to cheat. A loaded {question} contains hidden assumptions that trap the answerer. In computing, a program that has loaded is ready to run. {The question was loaded—any answer would make him look guilty.}

Loading is the process of putting cargo, data, or material into something that will carry or process it: {loading the truck}, {loading the dishwasher}, {the game is still loading}. A loading dock or loading zone is where vehicles receive cargo. In computing, loading refers to transferring data into memory or displaying content: {page loading}. Loading can also mean adding weight or bias to something: {dice loading}, {front-loading a contract with fees}.

A loadout is the specific combination of weapons, equipment, and gear a player selects before entering a game or mission, especially in shooters and tactical games: {I'm still tweaking my loadout for ranked matches}. The term has spread from gaming to military and tactical contexts, referring to how someone has configured their kit for a particular purpose.

Loadouts are the specific configurations of equipment, weapons, and gear that a player selects before entering a game or mission. The term dominates video game contexts—shooters, RPGs, survival games—where choosing the right loadout affects performance: {I'm still tweaking my loadout for ranked matches}. The concept extends to real-world tactical and military contexts, where a loadout is the full set of equipment a soldier or operator carries. The plural form is far more common than the singular, since players typically create and save multiple loadouts for different situations.

Loads means a large amount or many: {There were loads of people at the concert}, {I've got loads of work to do}. The word is informal, common in British English, and functions like lots. It derives from the noun load—a heavy burden or quantity carried—extended to suggest abundance. {Thanks loads} expresses emphatic gratitude.

Loadshedding is the deliberate shutdown of electrical power in parts of a grid to prevent the entire system from failing when demand exceeds supply. Utilities rotate outages through different areas so the burden is shared: {We lost power for two hours during loadshedding}. The practice is routine in countries with unreliable electrical infrastructure, particularly South Africa, where scheduled loadshedding has become a fact of daily life.

A loaf is bread baked in a single shaped mass, typically oblong: {a loaf of bread}, {a sandwich loaf}. The shape extends to other foods molded similarly: {meatloaf}, {a loaf of cheese}. To loaf is to idle or waste time: {He spent the afternoon loafing around the house}. A loafer is someone who loafs, or a slip-on leather shoe.

Loafed is the past tense of loaf, meaning to spend time idly or avoid work: {We loafed around the house all weekend}, {He loafed when he should have been studying}. The word suggests pleasant laziness rather than deliberate shirking.

A loafer is a slip-on leather shoe without laces, typically with a low heel and a moccasin-style upper: {She wore penny loafers with her khakis}. Separately, a loafer is someone who idles or avoids work—one who loafs around: {He spent the summer as a loafer, doing nothing productive}.

Loafers are slip-on shoes without laces, typically leather with a low heel and a flat front. The style suggests casual comfort—easy to slip on and off. {He wore penny loafers with no socks}. Separately, loafers are people who idle or avoid work, from the verb loaf: {a bunch of loafers hanging around the pool hall}.

Loafing is idling or wasting time, avoiding work or responsibility. Someone loafing around the house isn't doing anything productive. The word carries a mild disapproval—not quite lazy, but certainly not industrious: {Stop loafing and help me with these boxes}. {He spent the afternoon loafing on the porch}.

Loam is soil with a balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay—ideal for gardening and agriculture because it retains moisture while draining well. {The tomatoes thrived in the rich loam.} Loamy soil is dark, crumbly, and fertile, the stuff gardeners prize.

A loan is something lent, typically money given with the expectation of repayment: {She took out a loan to buy the house}. Banks make loans; friends loan each other books and tools. The verb loan is interchangeable with lend in American English, though some consider lend more formal. {On loan} means temporarily borrowed: {The painting is on loan from a private collection}.

Loaned is the past tense of loan, meaning to lend something—typically money or objects—with the expectation of return: {She loaned me twenty dollars until payday}. Some consider loan as a verb incorrect, insisting on lend, but loaned has been standard for centuries and appears frequently in American English: {The museum loaned the painting to a gallery in Paris}.

A loaner is something lent temporarily while your own is unavailable—typically a car from a dealership during repairs: {They gave me a loaner while my truck was in the shop}. The term extends to any temporary replacement: loaner {phone}, loaner {laptop}. Less commonly, loaner refers to the person doing the lending.

Loaners are items temporarily provided as substitutes while your own is being repaired or is otherwise unavailable. The term appears most often with cars and phones: {The dealership gave me a loaner while my car was in the shop}. A loaner can also be a person who lends something, though this use is rare.

Loans are sums of money lent to a borrower, typically with the expectation of repayment plus interest. Banks issue loans for homes, cars, and education. The word works as both noun and verb: {She took out a loan for tuition}; {He loaned me fifty bucks}. In American English, loan and lend are often interchangeable as verbs, though some prefer lend for the action and loan for the thing itself.

A loanshark is someone who lends money at exorbitant interest rates, typically operating outside legal banking systems and often using threats or violence to ensure repayment. The term combines the predatory connotations of shark with the lending business. Loansharking has historically been associated with organized crime, though the word now applies to any exploitative lender. {He borrowed five thousand from a loanshark and ended up owing triple that.}

Loansharking is the practice of lending money at exorbitant interest rates, often with threats of violence for non-payment. The term evokes organized crime—loan sharks operating outside legal lending systems, preying on desperate borrowers who can't access conventional credit. The rates compound so aggressively that victims often can never escape the debt: {He got mixed up with loansharking and ended up owing triple what he borrowed}.

Loansharks are people who lend money at exorbitant interest rates, typically operating outside legal banking systems. The term implies predatory practices—high rates, aggressive collection tactics, and borrowers who can't qualify for conventional loans. {He owed money to loansharks and feared for his safety.} Also spelled as two words or hyphenated.

Loathe means to feel intense disgust or hatred toward something: {I loathe getting up early}, {She loathes her ex-husband}. The feeling is stronger than dislike—closer to revulsion. Not to be confused with loath (without the e), which is an adjective meaning reluctant: {He was loath to admit his mistake}.

Loathed is the past tense of loathe, meaning to feel intense disgust or hatred toward something: {She loathed the way he chewed with his mouth open}. The word carries more visceral revulsion than simply disliked—closer to despised or abhorred. {He was loathed by his colleagues for taking credit for their work}.

Loathes is the third-person singular of loathe, meaning to feel intense disgust or hatred toward something: {She loathes getting up early}, {He loathes his ex-wife's new husband}. Loathe is stronger than dislike—it suggests visceral revulsion rather than mere preference.

Loathing is intense disgust or hatred—stronger than dislike, carrying visceral revulsion. You might feel loathing for a person, an idea, or yourself: {She looked at him with undisguised loathing}. Self-loathing is particularly common, describing deep shame or contempt directed inward.

Loathsome describes something that provokes intense disgust or revulsion. A loathsome creature inspires visceral repulsion; a loathsome act offends moral sensibilities deeply. The word carries more weight than merely unpleasant—it suggests something deserving of contempt: {The conditions in the prison were loathsome}. {He found her betrayal loathsome}.

Loaves is the plural of loaf—a shaped mass of bread baked as a single unit: {two loaves of French bread}, {five loaves and two fishes}. The plural extends to other loaf-shaped foods: {meat loaves}. The irregular plural (loaf → loaves, like knife → knives) follows an old English pattern where certain words ending in -f take -ves.

To lob is to throw or hit something in a high, gentle arc—the opposite of a hard, direct throw. In tennis, a lob sends the ball high over an opponent's head. You might lob a ball to a child or lob a crumpled paper toward a trash can. The noun lob describes such a throw or shot: {She hit a perfect lob over the net}. Figuratively, to lob a question or criticism is to deliver it casually or provocatively: {The reporter lobbed a softball question at the candidate}.

Lobbed is the past tense of lob, meaning to throw or hit something in a high, slow arc: {She lobbed the ball over the net}, {He lobbed a grenade into the bunker}. The trajectory is the key—lobbed things travel up before coming down, unlike throws meant for speed or directness. Figuratively, to lob a question or accusation is to toss it out casually or provocatively: {The reporter lobbed a softball question at the candidate}.

Lobbied is the past tense of lobby, meaning to attempt to influence legislators or other officials on behalf of a particular interest. The word comes from the practice of approaching politicians in the lobbies of legislative buildings. {Insurance companies lobbied against the bill}. {She lobbied her congressman for stricter environmental regulations}.

Lobbies is the plural of lobby—entrance halls or waiting areas in buildings like hotels, theaters, and office buildings: {The hotel lobbies were packed with convention guests}. Lobbies also names groups that try to influence legislators or officials: {pharmaceutical lobbies}, {gun lobbies}. As a verb form, lobbies means to attempt such influence: {She lobbies Congress on behalf of environmental groups}.

A lobby is an entrance hall or waiting area, especially in hotels, theaters, or office buildings: {We'll meet in the hotel lobby}. The term extends to groups that try to influence legislators or officials—from the practice of approaching politicians in legislative lobbies. To lobby is to attempt such influence: {Environmental groups lobbied Congress for stricter emissions standards}. A lobbyist does this professionally.

Lobbying is attempting to influence legislators or other public officials on behalf of a particular interest. Lobbyists work to shape policy by meeting with lawmakers, providing information, and advocating positions: {The pharmaceutical industry spends millions on lobbying each year}. The term extends to any organized effort to sway decision-makers: {lobbying the school board for longer recess}.

A lobbyist is someone paid to influence legislators or government officials on behalf of a particular interest—a corporation, industry, union, or cause. Lobbyists work to shape policy through meetings, research, and persuasion: {The pharmaceutical lobbyists pushed hard against price controls}. The term derives from the practice of approaching politicians in the lobbies of legislative buildings.

Lobbyists are people who attempt to influence legislators or other public officials on behalf of specific interests. They work for corporations, trade associations, advocacy groups, or foreign governments, meeting with politicians, providing information, and often contributing to campaigns. The term comes from the practice of waiting in legislative lobbies to catch officials. {Lobbyists for the pharmaceutical industry opposed the bill.}

A lobe is a rounded, projecting part of something larger. The term applies across anatomy, botany, and architecture. Your brain has lobes (frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital), as do your lungs and liver. The fleshy lower part of your ear is its lobe—the part that gets pierced for earrings. Leaves may have lobes, as do some architectural arches. The common thread is a rounded section that bulges outward from a main body.

Lobes are rounded projecting parts of something larger. The brain has lobes (frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital), as do the lungs and liver. The fleshy lower part of the ear is its lobe. Plant leaves may have lobes—rounded divisions that don't extend to the center. {The tumor was located in the right lobe of her liver.}

Lobotomies is the plural of lobotomy, a surgical procedure that severs connections in the brain's prefrontal lobe. Once used to treat mental illness, lobotomies fell out of favor as their devastating side effects became clear—patients often emerged docile but with permanently impaired personality and cognition. Figuratively, something that dulls thinking or removes critical judgment: {Social media is giving us all lobotomies}.

To lobotomise is to perform a lobotomy—a surgical procedure that severs connections in the brain's prefrontal lobe, once used to treat mental illness. The procedure often left patients docile but mentally diminished, which gives the word its figurative force: to lobotomise something is to strip it of vitality, creativity, or critical thinking. {The committee lobotomised the proposal until nothing interesting remained.} British spelling of lobotomize.

Lobotomised is the British spelling of lobotomized, the past tense and past participle of lobotomize. To lobotomise someone is to perform a lobotomy on them—a surgical procedure that severs connections in the brain's prefrontal lobe, once used to treat mental illness. The word now appears almost exclusively in its figurative sense, describing someone or something rendered dull, passive, or incapable of independent thought: {The committee emerged lobotomised, agreeing to everything management proposed.}

Lobotomising is the British spelling of lobotomizing—performing a lobotomy, the surgical procedure that severs connections in the brain's prefrontal lobe. Once used to treat mental illness, lobotomies fell out of favour due to devastating side effects. The figurative sense dominates now: to lobotomise something is to remove its vitality or critical capacity: {Corporate ownership has lobotomised local news}.

Lobotomize means to perform a lobotomy on someone—a surgical procedure that severs connections in the brain's prefrontal lobe, once used to treat mental illness but now largely abandoned due to its devastating effects on personality and cognition. The figurative use is more common today: to lobotomize something is to strip it of vitality, complexity, or intelligence. {The studio lobotomized the script until nothing interesting remained.} {Years of bureaucracy had lobotomized the department.}

Lobotomized describes someone who has undergone a lobotomy—a surgical procedure that severs connections in the brain's prefrontal lobe, once used to treat mental illness. The procedure often left patients passive and emotionally flattened, which gives the figurative sense: rendered unable to think clearly or respond normally. {I felt lobotomized after that meeting}. {The lobotomized protagonist shuffled through the ward}.

Lobotomy is a surgical procedure that severs connections in the brain's prefrontal lobe, formerly used to treat mental illness. Developed in the 1930s and performed widely through the 1950s, lobotomies often left patients docile but cognitively impaired. The practice is now discredited. Figuratively, lobotomy suggests having one's capacity for thought or feeling removed: {Watching that show is like getting a lobotomy}.

Lobs is the plural of lob and the third-person singular verb form. To lob is to throw or hit something in a high, slow arc: {She lobs the ball over the net}. In tennis, a lob clears an opponent at the net. In military contexts, to lob shells is to fire them in an arcing trajectory. The word suggests something tossed casually or lobbed lazily rather than thrown hard.

A lobster is a large marine crustacean with a hard shell, stalked eyes, and large front claws, prized as a luxury seafood. Lobsters are typically bluish-green when alive but turn bright red when cooked. The meat is rich and sweet: {We ordered lobster tails with drawn butter}. In informal use, a lobster is someone with badly sunburned skin: {I forgot sunscreen and came home looking like a lobster}.

Lobstering is the activity or occupation of catching lobsters, typically using baited traps lowered to the ocean floor. The term covers both commercial fishing and recreational harvesting: {He spent his summers lobstering off the Maine coast}. {The family had been lobstering for three generations}.

Lobsters are large marine crustaceans with hard shells, stalked eyes, and large front claws, prized as seafood. They turn red when cooked. The plural often refers to the creatures as food: {We had lobsters for dinner}. A lobster is also someone with badly sunburned skin, from the color: {I forgot sunscreen and turned into a lobster}.

Local means nearby or belonging to a particular place. A local {restaurant} is in your neighborhood; a local {custom} belongs to a specific region. The noun refers to a person from the area: {The locals know the best beaches}. Local can also mean a nearby branch of something larger—a union local, a local anesthetic that numbs only one area. {All politics is local.}

Locale is a place or setting, especially as it relates to events or circumstances occurring there. It carries a slightly formal or literary tone compared to plain "location": {The film's locale shifted from Paris to Prague}. In computing, locale refers to regional settings that determine how software handles language, dates, and currency formats.

Localism is a preference for what's local—local businesses, local governance, local culture. In politics, it advocates shifting power from central authorities to local communities: {The mayor championed localism over federal mandates}. In linguistics, a localism is a word or expression used only in a particular region: {"Pop" for soda is a Midwestern localism}.

Localization is the process of adapting something for a specific place or context. In business and technology, it means modifying products for different markets—translating text, adjusting formats, and accommodating cultural preferences: {The game's localization included new voice acting for each region}. In medicine, localization means identifying where something is situated: {localization of the tumor}. The British spelling is localisation.

To localize is to confine something to a particular place or area: {The infection remained localized in his left foot}. In business and technology, localize means to adapt a product for a specific region or market—translating text, adjusting currencies, or modifying content for local customs: {The software was localized for the Japanese market}.

Locals are the people who live in a particular place, especially as distinguished from visitors or outsiders: {The locals know the best restaurants}. In computing, locals are variables accessible only within a specific function or block of code. At a bar, locals are the regular patrons: {He's one of the locals}.

To locate something is to find it or determine its position: {We finally located the source of the leak}. It can also mean to establish in a particular place: {The company located its headquarters in Denver}. In casual American speech, locate sometimes means simply to settle somewhere: {They located in Texas after the war}.

Location is a place or position—where something is or where something happens. A store's location affects its success. You can share your location with an app. {We're still looking for a location for the wedding}. In film and television, shooting on location means filming at real sites rather than on studio sets.

A locator is something that finds or identifies the position of something else. The term appears in technical contexts: a {store locator} on a website, a {GPS locator} on a vehicle, a {uniform resource locator} (URL) for web addresses. In general use, any device or system that helps you find things qualifies: {The app includes a locator for nearby restaurants}.

A locavore is someone who prioritizes eating food grown or produced locally, typically within a certain radius of where they live. The term emerged in the early 2000s alongside growing interest in sustainable agriculture and reducing the environmental impact of food transportation. {As a locavore, she shops almost exclusively at farmers' markets.}

Locavores are people who prioritize eating food grown or produced locally, typically within a certain radius of where they live. The term blends "local" with the "-vore" suffix meaning eater, placing locavores alongside carnivores and herbivores as a dietary category. The movement emphasizes reducing environmental impact from food transportation, supporting local farmers, and eating seasonally. {As committed locavores, they shop almost exclusively at the farmers market.}

A loch is a Scottish term for a lake or a narrow inlet of the sea. The word appears throughout Scottish geography: {Loch Ness}, {Loch Lomond}. In Irish English, the spelling is lough. The word is rarely used outside place names and Scottish contexts.

Most meanings of lock convey the idea of a barrier (door lock, caps lock, headlock). When you lock something, you prevent access or movement. When two animals’ horns lock, they become intertwined and not easily separable. Locks on a canal control variable water levels using gates. A different lock is about hair: Her golden locks shone in the sun.

A lockbox is a secure container with a lock, used to store valuables or restrict access. Real estate agents use lockboxes to hold house keys for showings. In finance, a lockbox is a bank service where customer payments go directly to a dedicated address for faster processing. Figuratively, putting something in a lockbox means protecting it from interference: {Politicians promised to put Social Security in a lockbox}.

A lockdown is a security protocol confining people to a location during a threat—schools lock down during active shooter situations, prisons during disturbances. The term gained broader currency during the COVID-19 pandemic for restrictions keeping people home: {The city went into lockdown for three months}. Extended, it describes any enforced period of restriction: {My parents put me on lockdown after I crashed the car}.

Lockdowns are emergency measures that restrict movement and activity, typically imposed by authorities during crises. The term gained widespread use during the COVID-19 pandemic to describe orders requiring people to stay home and businesses to close. Schools and other facilities also go into lockdown during security threats, sealing entrances and confining occupants to secure areas. {The city imposed strict lockdowns to slow the spread of the virus.}

Locked means secured or fastened, typically with a lock: {The door was locked}. Something locked is fixed in position or unable to move: {locked in place}, {locked and loaded}. Figuratively, people become locked in conflict, debate, or embrace—held together tightly. To be {locked in} to something is to be committed without easy exit: {We're locked in at that price}. In slang, locked or {locked in} means intensely focused: {He's been locked in all season}.

A locker is a small compartment with a lock, typically in a row of similar compartments, used to store personal belongings in schools, gyms, workplaces, or transit stations. {She kept her gym clothes in her locker}. The term extends to storage compartments on boats and in freezers: {a meat locker}, {Davy Jones's locker} (the ocean floor, where drowned sailors rest).

Lockers are storage compartments, typically in a row of similar units, secured with locks. Schools, gyms, and workplaces provide lockers for personal belongings: {I forgot my combination and couldn't get into my locker}. A locker room is where people change clothes, often near athletic facilities—locker room talk refers to crude conversation, especially among men.

A locket is a small ornamental case, typically worn on a chain around the neck, that opens to reveal a photograph or memento inside. Lockets traditionally hold pictures of loved ones or locks of hair: {She wore a gold locket with her mother's picture in it}. The word suggests sentimental value—lockets are keepsakes, not just jewelry.

Lockets are small ornamental cases, typically worn on a chain around the neck, that open to reveal a photograph or memento inside. The traditional locket holds a picture of a loved one—a child, a spouse, a deceased relative—close to the heart: {She wore a gold locket with her mother's picture}. The singular is locket.

Locking is a style of funk dance characterized by sudden pauses or "locks"—freezing briefly in position before resuming fluid movement. Developed in the late 1960s, it became foundational to street dance and hip-hop culture. The dancer might strike a pose, hold it for a beat, then snap back into motion: {He hit the lock perfectly on the downbeat}.

Lockjaw is a common name for tetanus, the bacterial infection that causes severe muscle spasms—particularly in the jaw, making it difficult or impossible to open the mouth. The term is also used loosely for any condition causing jaw stiffness: {I woke up with lockjaw after sleeping wrong}.

A lockout is a situation where someone is prevented from entering or accessing something. In labor disputes, a lockout is when management shuts out workers to pressure them during negotiations—the employer's counterpart to a strike. In sports, a lockout suspends play when owners and players can't agree on contracts: {The NHL lockout canceled the entire season}. More generally, a lockout occurs when you're shut out of your car, house, or account: {I had to call a locksmith after a lockout}.

Lockouts is the plural of lockout, a situation where workers are prevented from entering their workplace by management during a labor dispute—the employer's counterpart to a strike. The term extends to being shut out of any system or space: {After three failed password attempts, lockouts are automatic}. In sports, a lockout occurs when team owners suspend play during contract negotiations with players.

A lockpick is a tool designed to open locks without the original key, typically a thin metal implement inserted into the keyhole to manipulate the internal mechanism. Lockpicking is associated with burglars, but locksmiths and hobbyists also practice it legitimately. The verb lockpick means to open a lock this way: {She lockpicked the filing cabinet in under a minute}.

Lockpicking is the skill or act of opening a lock without its key, using specialized tools to manipulate the internal mechanism. It's practiced legitimately by locksmiths and security professionals, and illegally by burglars. As a hobby, it has enthusiast communities who practice on locks they own: {I got into lockpicking during quarantine}.

Lockpicks are specialized tools for opening locks without their keys. A basic set includes tension wrenches and picks of various shapes—hooks, rakes, diamonds—each suited to different lock mechanisms. Lockpicking is a legitimate skill for locksmiths and security professionals, though possessing lockpicks may be restricted or illegal in some jurisdictions. {She practiced on padlocks before moving to deadbolts.}

Locks are devices that secure doors, containers, or mechanisms, typically opened with a key or combination. A lock of hair is a strand or curl: {a lock of her hair kept in a locket}. Locks also refers to a system of gates controlling water levels in canals, allowing boats to pass between different elevations. As a verb, to lock is to fasten securely or to become fixed: {Their eyes locked across the room}. To be {locked in} is to be committed or trapped. In wrestling, a lock is a hold that immobilizes an opponent.

A locksmith is a person who makes, repairs, and opens locks. The trade involves cutting keys, installing security hardware, and helping people who have locked themselves out: {We called a locksmith when we lost the house keys}. The word combines lock with smith, the old term for a metalworker.

Locksmiths is the plural of locksmith—a person who makes, repairs, or opens locks. Locksmiths cut keys, install deadbolts, and rescue people locked out of cars and homes. The trade requires knowledge of mechanical and electronic security systems. {We called a locksmith when we lost the house keys.}

Lockstep is a way of marching in very close formation, each person's feet moving in unison with the person ahead. The term extends to rigid conformity or synchronized action: {The party voted in lockstep with its leadership}. The implication is usually negative—mindless uniformity rather than coordinated teamwork: {They moved in lockstep, never questioning orders}.

A lockup is a place of confinement, especially a jail or holding cell: {They spent the night in lockup}. The term also refers to the act of locking something up or a period when things are secured. In finance, a lockup period restricts when investors can sell shares after an IPO. In computing or machinery, a lockup is a freeze or malfunction that renders something unresponsive: {The system went into lockup}.

Loco is Spanish for crazy, borrowed into English slang with the same meaning: {He went loco and started smashing furniture}. The word appears in phrases like {en lo loco} and compounds like {locoweed}—a plant that causes erratic behavior in livestock that eat it. In railroading, loco is informal shorthand for locomotive.

Locomotion is movement from place to place. The term applies to how organisms or machines travel—walking, swimming, flying, crawling: {The injury affected his locomotion}. In biology, it distinguishes self-propelled movement from stationary existence. The word appears in technical contexts more than everyday speech, where {movement} or {getting around} suffice.

A locomotive is the engine that pulls a train—the self-propelled vehicle that provides motive power for railroad cars. The word can also function as an adjective meaning relating to movement or capable of moving: {locomotive power}, {locomotive ability}. In older usage, any self-moving machine might be called a locomotive.

Locomotives are self-propelled railway engines that pull trains. The word comes from Latin roots meaning "moving from place to place." A locomotive hauls freight cars or passenger coaches along tracks: {The steam locomotive pulled into the station}. Figuratively, locomotive can describe anything that drives forward motion or serves as a powerful force.

Locs are a hairstyle in which hair is allowed to mat and coil into ropelike strands, also called dreadlocks or dreads. The style has deep roots in African and Rastafarian culture and has become widely popular across communities. Locs form naturally when hair is left uncombed, though many people cultivate them through specific techniques like twisting or interlocking. {She's been growing her locs for five years.} The spelling *locs* is often preferred over *locks* to distinguish the hairstyle from door locks and to honor its cultural origins.

A locust is a grasshopper that periodically swarms in vast numbers, devouring crops and vegetation across wide areas. The word extends to various large grasshoppers and cicadas. Locust trees—the black locust and honey locust—bear pods resembling the insect. Figuratively, locusts are any devouring horde: {Tourists descended like locusts on the small town}.

Locusts is the plural of locust, a type of grasshopper that periodically swarms in vast numbers, devastating crops and vegetation. Biblical plagues featured locusts as divine punishment. Figuratively, locusts describes any devouring horde: {Locusts of tourists descended on the small town}. The locust tree, with its clustered seed pods, takes its name from the insect.

A lode is a deposit of ore running through rock, typically following a vein or fissure: {The miners struck a rich lode of silver}. The word appears most often figuratively for any abundant source: {a lode of information}, {a rich lode of material for his next novel}. The related lodestar and lodestone use an older sense meaning "way" or "course."

A lodestar is a star used for navigation, especially the North Star. The word extends to anything that serves as a guiding principle or focal point: {Justice was the lodestar of her career}. The spelling loadstar also appears but is less common.

A lodestone is a naturally magnetized piece of iron ore that attracts metal. Before manufactured magnets, lodestones were curiosities and navigational tools. The word extends figuratively to anything that draws people or things powerfully: {The city became a lodestone for artists and dreamers}.

Lodestones are naturally magnetized pieces of the mineral magnetite, capable of attracting iron. Before artificial magnets, lodestones were used in early compasses for navigation. The name comes from an old word meaning "way" or "course"—a stone that leads. Figuratively, a lodestone is anything that powerfully attracts: {She became a lodestone for progressive activists}.

A lodge is a place to stay temporarily, especially while on vacation and near or in a wild place. Some other kinds of buildings are also called lodges (Masonic lodge, Elks lodge). When you lodge someone, you provide them a place to stay. When you lodge something abstract, like a complaint, protest, appeal, or claim, you put it before an authority that can act on it. If something is lodged in a place, it may be stuck there.

Lodged means fixed or stuck in place, often where something shouldn't be: {A bone lodged in his throat}. It also describes temporary residence—you lodge at an inn, or lodge someone for the night. To lodge a complaint or objection is to formally submit it. A bullet lodges in flesh; an idea lodges in memory. The past tense works as both verb and adjective: {The lodged splinter required tweezers}.

A lodger is a person who rents a room in someone else's home, typically with some shared facilities like a kitchen or bathroom. Unlike a tenant who rents an entire property, a lodger lives within the landlord's residence: {She took in a lodger to help with the mortgage}. The arrangement implies a more informal or domestic situation than a standard lease.

Lodgers are people who rent a room in someone else's home, typically paying for accommodation and sometimes meals. The term implies a more informal arrangement than tenant—lodgers share living space with the property owner rather than occupying a separate unit: {The old woman took in lodgers to supplement her pension}. {Three lodgers shared the upstairs rooms}.

Lodges serves as both noun and verb. A lodge is a small house or cabin, often in a rustic or wilderness setting: {a ski lodge}, {a hunting lodge}. It also names the meeting place of fraternal organizations like the Freemasons, or the local chapter itself. As a verb, to lodge is to stay temporarily {(We lodged at a bed and breakfast)} or to become stuck {(A bone lodged in his throat)}. To lodge a complaint is to formally register it.

Lodging is a place to stay, especially temporarily. The word often appears in the plural: {The university provides lodgings for visiting scholars}. A rooming house or inn might advertise lodging available. To find lodging is to secure somewhere to sleep. The word carries a slightly old-fashioned or formal tone compared to alternatives like accommodation or housing.

Lodgings are rented rooms or temporary accommodations, typically in someone else's house rather than a hotel: {He found lodgings near the university}. The term sounds somewhat old-fashioned, evoking an era when boarding houses were common. A single room may be called a lodging, though the plural form predominates even for one space.

Lofi (also lo-fi, short for low fidelity) describes audio with deliberately rough, imperfect sound quality—the opposite of polished studio production. Vinyl crackle, tape hiss, and muffled frequencies become aesthetic choices rather than flaws. The term now primarily evokes {lofi hip-hop}, a genre of mellow instrumental beats often used as background music for studying or relaxing: {I put on some lofi while I work}.

A loft is a space directly under a roof, typically used for storage or converted into living quarters. In buildings, a loft often means an upper floor of a warehouse or factory converted to residential or studio use: {a SoHo loft}. A loft is also an upper level in a church or barn: {choir loft}, {hayloft}. In golf, loft refers to the angle of a club face or the height of a shot—to loft the ball is to hit it high into the air.

Lofted describes something that has been sent high into the air, typically with a graceful arc rather than a flat trajectory. A lofted {golf shot} rises steeply, and a lofted {pass} in soccer curves overhead to reach a teammate. The term comes from the verb loft, meaning to hit or throw something so it travels upward. In golf specifically, lofted also describes clubs with angled faces designed to produce high-arcing shots.

Lofts is the plural of loft—an upper space or room, typically under a roof or in a converted industrial building. A hay loft stores hay above a barn floor. A sleeping loft sits above a main living area. Converted warehouse lofts became desirable urban housing. In golf, loft refers to the angle of a club face, and to loft a ball is to hit it high into the air: {She lofted the ball over the defender's head}.

Lofty describes great height, whether physical or figurative. A lofty {peak} towers above the landscape; lofty {ceilings} create a sense of grandeur. Extended to abstractions, lofty suggests elevated status or ambition: lofty {ideals}, lofty {goals}. The word can carry a negative edge—lofty behavior suggests someone who acts superior or condescending: {She spoke with lofty disdain}.

A log is a section of tree trunk or thick branch, especially one cut for fuel or timber: {We stacked logs by the fireplace}. By extension, log describes any detailed record kept over time—a ship's log, a flight log, a work log. To log is to record systematically or to accumulate: {She logged two hundred hours of flight time}. To {log in} or {log on} is to authenticate access to a computer system; {log out} or {log off} reverses it. To {sleep like a log} is to sleep deeply and immovably.

Loganberries is the plural of loganberry, a dark red berry that is a hybrid of the blackberry and raspberry. The fruit is elongated, tart, and used in jams, pies, and wine. Named after American horticulturist James Logan, who developed the cross in the 1880s: {We picked loganberries from the backyard bramble}.

A loganberry is a dark red berry that's a cross between a blackberry and a raspberry, with the tartness of the former and some sweetness of the latter. Named after the American horticulturist James Logan, who developed it in the 1880s. Loganberries are used in jams, pies, and wine: {The loganberry pie was almost too tart without ice cream}.

A logbook is a record of events, observations, or activities kept in chronological order. Ship captains maintain logbooks documenting voyages—weather, position, incidents. The term extends to any systematic record: a pilot's logbook of flight hours, a truck driver's logbook of miles and rest stops, a scientist's logbook of experiments. {Check the logbook to see who signed in last.}

Logbooks are official records of events, activities, or data kept in chronological order. Ships maintain logbooks documenting navigation, weather, and incidents. Pilots keep flight logbooks recording hours and routes. The term extends to any systematic record: {The maintenance logbook showed the car had been serviced regularly}. Also written as two words: log books.

Logged describes something that has been recorded or entered into a log: {All visitors are logged at the front desk}, {The system logged every keystroke}. Hours or miles get logged when officially tracked. Logged also means having had trees cut down: {logged forest}, {heavily logged hillsides}. To be {logged in} or {logged on} is to have an active session on a computer system.

A logger is a person who cuts down trees for timber, working in forestry or the lumber industry: {Loggers felled the old-growth forest}. In computing, a logger is software that records events or data: {The system logger tracked all user activity}. To log is to record systematically or to harvest timber.

A loggerhead is a large sea turtle with a disproportionately big head. The word also names a tool—an iron ball on a long handle, heated and used for melting tar or warming liquids. The most common use is in the phrase {at loggerheads}, meaning locked in stubborn disagreement: {The two factions have been at loggerheads for months}.

Loggerheads appears almost exclusively in the phrase {at loggerheads}, meaning in stubborn disagreement or conflict: {The two departments have been at loggerheads for months}. A loggerhead was originally a heavy iron tool with a ball-shaped end, heated and used for various purposes—the connection to quarreling is obscure but centuries old.

Loggers are workers who cut down trees and prepare timber for transport, a physically demanding occupation in the forestry industry. The term also refers to software tools or devices that automatically record data over time, such as a {data logger} tracking temperature or a {keystroke logger} monitoring computer input. In programming, loggers are components that capture system events and errors for debugging purposes.

Logging is the business of cutting down trees and transporting timber. The term extends to any systematic recording of data or events: {server logging}, {activity logging}. A log captures what happened and when. To log something is to record it; to log in or log on is to authenticate access to a computer system.

Logic is the study of valid reasoning—the principles that distinguish sound arguments from flawed ones. More loosely, logic refers to any coherent system of thought or the reasoning behind something: {What's the logic of starting a business during a recession?} To say something {defies logic} is to call it irrational. In computing, logic refers to the operations and circuits that process information.

Logical describes something that follows the principles of reasoning or is consistent with what makes sense. A logical argument proceeds step by step from premises to conclusions without contradiction. A logical person thinks clearly and rationally rather than emotionally. Something can be logical without being true—it just means the reasoning holds together internally. {That's the logical next step.} In computing, logical refers to abstract or virtual structures as opposed to physical ones: a logical {drive} may span multiple physical disks.

Login is the act of gaining access to a computer system or website by entering credentials, or the credentials themselves: {What's your login?} As an adjective, it describes related elements: {login screen}, {login page}. The verb form is two words: {log in to your account}.

Logistics is the coordination of complex operations involving people, facilities, and supplies. Military logistics moves troops and equipment where needed. Business logistics manages supply chains—sourcing materials, warehousing, shipping products to customers. The word often appears when someone wants to emphasize practical complications: {We're still working out the logistics of the move}.

A logjam is an accumulation of logs blocking a river, preventing passage. The word extends to any impasse or standstill caused by competing or accumulated obstacles: {a logjam of legislation in Congress}, {traffic logjams during rush hour}. To break a logjam is to resolve what's blocking progress.

Logjammed describes something blocked or stuck, unable to move forward. The image comes from logs piling up and jamming a river during timber drives. A logjammed {highway} is gridlocked with traffic. A logjammed {Congress} can't pass legislation. {The court system is logjammed with cases.}

Logjams are accumulations of logs that block a river or stream, preventing water and other logs from flowing freely. The word extends naturally to any situation where progress is blocked by congestion or accumulated obstacles: {a logjam of legislation in Congress}, {traffic logjams during rush hour}. To break a logjam is to resolve a deadlock.

A logo is a symbol or design that identifies a company, organization, or brand. Logos appear on products, advertisements, uniforms, and websites as visual shorthand for the entity they represent: {The swoosh is Nike's logo}. A logo may incorporate text, imagery, or abstract shapes—often all three. The word is clipped from logotype.
Logos is the plural of logo, a symbol or design that identifies an organization or brand: {Corporate logos plastered every surface of the stadium}. (Capitalized Logos is a philosophical term.)

Logout is the act of ending a session on a computer system, website, or application—the opposite of login. Also spelled as two words: {Don't forget to log out when you're done}. The noun form appears in phrases like {automatic logout} or {session logout}, referring to the moment access terminates.

Logroll combines two related meanings rooted in mutual back-scratching. In politics, to logroll is to exchange votes or favors: {I'll support your highway bill if you logroll for my education funding}. The practice itself is logrolling. The term comes from frontier neighbors helping each other roll heavy logs—cooperative labor that expected reciprocation. Logrolling also names a sport where competitors balance on a floating log, trying to spin or maneuver each other into the water.

Logrolling is the trading of favors, especially among legislators who agree to support each other's bills: {The infrastructure package passed through old-fashioned logrolling}. The term comes from the frontier practice of neighbors helping each other roll heavy logs—mutual assistance that expected reciprocation. In publishing, logrolling refers to authors exchanging favorable reviews of each other's books.

Logs are sections of tree trunk or thick branch, cut for fuel or timber: {We stacked logs by the fireplace}. A log is also a record of events, especially a ship's daily progress or any systematic chronicle: {The captain's log noted rough seas}. To log is to record entries or accumulate: {She logged two hundred flight hours}. To log in or log on is to access a computer system; to log out or log off is to exit.

The loin is the part of the body on both sides of the spine between the ribs and hipbones. In butchery, loin cuts come from this region: {pork loin}, {loin chops}. The plural loins often refers to the groin or reproductive organs, especially in biblical or literary contexts: {the fruit of his loins}, {gird your loins}.

A loincloth is a simple garment covering the groin and sometimes buttocks, wrapped around the hips or suspended from a cord or belt. It's among the oldest forms of clothing, worn in warm climates or by people with minimal material resources: {The tribe wore traditional loincloths}. In modern contexts, loincloths appear in depictions of ancient peoples, jungle explorers, or figures like Tarzan.

Loincloths are minimal garments covering the groin and sometimes the buttocks, worn wrapped or tied around the hips. Among the oldest forms of clothing, loincloths appear across cultures from ancient Egypt to indigenous peoples of the Americas. The loincloth remains associated with primitive or tribal dress: {Tarzan's iconic loincloth}.

Loins are the part of the body between the ribs and hips, roughly the lower back and sides of the abdomen. In butchery, the loin is a cut of meat from this region: {pork loin}, {loin chops}. Biblically and literarily, loins represent procreative power—the seat of strength and sexuality: {fruit of his loins}, {gird your loins}. To {gird your loins} is to prepare for action, from the ancient practice of tucking up robes before exertion.

To loiter is to stand around or move slowly without apparent purpose, lingering in a place longer than necessary. The word often carries a suggestion of idleness or potential mischief: {No loitering signs} warn people not to hang around. Someone might loiter outside a shop, in a doorway, or near a school. {He loitered at the corner, waiting to see if she'd walk by.}

Loitering is lingering in a public place without apparent purpose. The word carries legal weight—loitering laws target people who hang around suspiciously or obstruct others: {He was arrested for loitering outside the convenience store}. The term often criminalizes presence itself, disproportionately applied to homeless people, teenagers, and minorities.

A lolcat is an image of a cat with a humorous caption, typically written in intentionally broken English—misspellings, bad grammar, and baby talk: {I can has cheezburger?} The format spread across the internet in the mid-2000s and spawned countless variations. The captions themselves are sometimes called lolspeak.

Loll means to recline or lounge in a lazy, relaxed manner: {He lolled on the couch all afternoon}. The tongue lolls when it hangs loosely from the mouth, as a dog's does when panting. The head lolls when it droops without muscle control. All uses suggest relaxed heaviness and lack of tension.

Lollies is the British and Australian term for what Americans call candy—sweet confections in general. The word can also refer specifically to lollipops or ice lollies (frozen treats on sticks). In Australian slang, lollies sometimes means money: {He made a few lollies on the deal}.

Lolling is lounging lazily, typically with the body draped loosely: {He spent the afternoon lolling on the couch}. The word suggests relaxed, boneless comfort—limbs splayed, posture abandoned. A tongue lolls when it hangs loosely from the mouth: {The dog sat panting, tongue lolling}. The present participle of loll.

A lollipop is a piece of hard candy mounted on a stick, meant to be licked or sucked rather than chewed. The stick keeps hands clean and lets children enjoy the candy slowly. Lollipops come in various shapes and flavors, from simple spheres to elaborate swirls. {The doctor gave her a lollipop after her shot.}

Lollipops is the plural of lollipop, a hard candy mounted on a stick for holding while you lick or suck it. The form makes them convenient for children and mess-free compared to loose candy. {She handed out lollipops at the party.} Lollipop flavors range from fruit to novelty tastes like root beer or bubblegum.
clues: Round candy you hold and lick

definition: Lolly is British and Australian informal for a lollipop or any piece of candy: {The children spent their pocket money on lollies}. In British slang, lolly also means money: {He's got loads of lolly}. An ice lolly is a frozen treat on a stick—what Americans call a popsicle.

Lollygag is to waste time aimlessly, to dawdle or fool around instead of getting things done: {Stop lollygagging and finish your homework}. The word has an informal, slightly playful tone—a parent might accuse a child of lollygagging, but you wouldn't use it in a business meeting. Also spelled lallygag.

A lollygagger is someone who wastes time or dawdles instead of getting on with things. The word carries a tone of mild, often affectionate exasperation: {Quit being such a lollygagger and help me with these boxes}. It suggests aimless puttering rather than deliberate procrastination.

Lollygagging is wasting time, dawdling, or engaging in aimless activity when you should be doing something productive. The word carries a tone of mild disapproval: {Quit lollygagging and get to work}. It sounds folksy and old-fashioned, more likely from a frustrated parent or coach than a formal setting.

Lollygags means to spend time aimlessly, dawdle, or fool around instead of doing something productive: {Stop lollygagging and get to work}. The word carries a mildly playful tone, suggesting harmless idleness rather than serious laziness. Also spelled lollygag.

A lollypop is a piece of hard candy mounted on a stick, meant to be licked or sucked rather than chewed. The stick keeps hands clean and lets the candy be removed from the mouth and returned. Children are the primary consumers. Also spelled lollipop.

Lollypops is the plural of lollypop, a variant spelling of lollipop—a piece of hard candy mounted on a stick for licking. The spelling with a y appears occasionally but lollipop dominates in standard usage: {The children lined up for lollypops after the parade}.

Lone means single, solitary, or unaccompanied. A lone {wolf} operates without a pack. A lone {gunman} acts without accomplices. The word emphasizes isolation—not just one, but conspicuously one: {A lone figure stood at the edge of the cliff}. Lone often carries a romantic or dramatic quality that *single* or *only* lacks.

Loneliness is the painful awareness of being alone or disconnected from others. It differs from solitude, which may be chosen and enjoyed—loneliness is unwanted isolation. The feeling can strike even in crowds when genuine connection is absent: {She felt a deep loneliness despite being surrounded by people}. Chronic loneliness affects mental and physical health.
