Luck is the force that causes good or bad things to happen by chance rather than through effort or planning. Good luck brings favorable outcomes: {With any luck, we'll finish early}. Bad luck brings misfortune. To luck out is to succeed through chance; to luck into something is to obtain it fortunately. Lucky describes people or things favored by luck, or items believed to attract it: {a lucky charm}.

Lucky characterizes good fortune (lucky winner) and things associated, sometimes superstitiously, with good fortune (lucky charm). A lucky break is an unexpected bit of good luck. If you are lucky enough to do something or for something to happen, the suggestion is that good luck played a part in it. This makes you a lucky one. Someone who is happy-go-lucky seems to experience good fortune most of the time and is not easily discouraged.
clues: On the right side of odds

definition: Lucrative describes something that produces substantial profit or financial gain: {a lucrative career in finance}, {lucrative business opportunities}. The word emphasizes money-making potential rather than mere adequacy—a lucrative deal is notably profitable, not just break-even. Often carries a slightly formal or business-oriented tone.

Lucre is money or profit, almost always with a negative connotation suggesting greed or dishonesty. The word appears most often in the phrase {filthy lucre}, emphasizing that the wealth was gained through disreputable means. Used on its own, lucre sounds literary or ironic: {He wasn't in it for the lucre}.

Ludicrous describes something so absurd or ridiculous that it invites mockery or disbelief: {The idea that he could run a marathon without training was ludicrous}. It suggests foolishness beyond mere error—something laughably unreasonable: {a ludicrous waste of money}, {ludicrous demands}. The word carries contempt rather than gentle amusement.

Lug is most frequently a verb used in relation to heavy things that are difficult to move: I had to lug my suitcase up four flights of stairs. The noun lug describes an instance of lugging or something lugged. A different noun lug is for a variety of things in technical trades that mostly share the quality of being projections, like a ridge that helps provide traction on a shoe or tire. A lug nut bolts a tire onto an axle. Informally, a large, clumsy man may be called a lug.

A luge is a small sled for one or two people, ridden feetfirst in a supine position. It's primarily an Olympic sport where athletes race down an ice track at high speeds: {She won gold in the luge}. The verb means to ride such a sled: {They luged down the course at nearly ninety miles per hour}.

A luger is a person who rides a luge—a small sled ridden face-up and feet-first down an icy track at high speeds. Lugers compete in the Winter Olympics, steering by shifting body weight and applying pressure to the runners: {The luger hit speeds over 90 miles per hour on the final stretch}.

Luggage is the bags and suitcases a traveler carries, containing clothes and personal items. The word is uncountable—you have luggage, not luggages, and a single item is a {piece of luggage}. Luggage suggests bulk and burden, from the verb lug: {We had too much luggage for the overhead bins}.

Lugged is the past tense of lug, meaning to carry or drag something heavy or awkward with effort: {She lugged the suitcase up three flights of stairs}. The word emphasizes the burden—you don't lug something light. {He lugged his equipment across the field}.

Lugging is carrying or dragging something heavy or awkward with effort: {I spent the afternoon lugging boxes up three flights of stairs}. The word emphasizes the burden—you lug a suitcase, not a feather. It can extend to less physical burdens: {She's been lugging that guilt around for years}.

A lugnut is a heavy nut that fastens a wheel to a vehicle's axle. The term comes from lug, meaning a projecting piece that provides a grip or attachment point. Lugnuts are tightened with a wrench in a star pattern to ensure even pressure: {I stripped a lugnut trying to change the tire}.

Lugnuts are the heavy nuts that secure a wheel to a vehicle's axle, tightened onto threaded bolts called lug studs. Changing a tire means loosening the lugnuts, swapping the wheel, then tightening them again in a star pattern: {I can't get these lugnuts off—they're rusted solid}. Sometimes spelled as two words.

Lugs is the plural of lug, which has several meanings united by the idea of something that protrudes or gets pulled. Lugs are projecting pieces that provide a grip or attachment point: the lugs on a tire tread, the lugs on the sole of a hiking boot. A lug is also an ear, especially in Scottish dialect, or a lug nut. To lug something is to carry it with effort: {She lugged the suitcase up three flights of stairs}. A lug can also be a clumsy or slow-witted person: {The big lug finally figured it out}.

Lukewarm describes something mildly warm—neither hot nor cold. Lukewarm water is tepid, around body temperature. The figurative sense dominates: a lukewarm response shows little enthusiasm, a lukewarm reception is unenthusiastic but not hostile. {The proposal received a lukewarm reception from investors.} The word suggests disappointment—you expected heat and got indifference.

Lull captures the idea of temporary calm or quieting. A lull is a pause in activity or intensity: {a lull in the conversation}, {a lull in the storm}. To lull is to soothe or calm, often deceptively: {The steady rhythm lulled her to sleep}. To {lull someone into} a state is to ease them there through false assurance: {lulled into complacency}.

Lullabies is the plural of lullaby—a gentle song sung to soothe a child to sleep. The word evokes soft melodies, quiet voices, and bedtime rituals: {She sang lullabies until the baby's eyes closed}. Figuratively, anything that calms or lulls might be called a lullaby: {the lullaby of rain on the roof}.

A lullaby is a gentle song sung to soothe a child to sleep. The melodies are typically soft and repetitive, the lyrics often nonsensical or dreamlike: {She hummed a lullaby until the baby's eyes closed}. By extension, anything with a similarly calming, soporific quality: {the lullaby of rain on the roof}.

Lulled is the past tense of lull, meaning to calm or soothe into a state of rest or false security. A baby is lulled to sleep by gentle rocking or singing. More often the word suggests being put off guard: {We were lulled into complacency by early success}. The calm before danger is a lull.

Lulling is soothing someone toward sleep or calm, or easing them into a false sense of security. A lullaby lulls a baby. Gentle waves have a lulling effect. {The quiet lulled us into thinking nothing was wrong.} The word suggests gradual, almost hypnotic quieting—reducing alertness through repetition or softness.

Lulls is the plural of lull—a temporary pause or decrease in activity, intensity, or noise: {There was a lull in the conversation}, {a lull in the fighting}. The verb lull means to soothe or calm, often into a false sense of security: {The quiet lulled us into thinking the danger had passed}. A lullaby lulls a child to sleep.

Lulu is an outstanding example of its kind, usually something remarkable or impressive: {That storm was a real lulu}. The word often carries a note of irony or understatement, describing something memorably extreme—whether good or bad: {She came up with a lulu of an excuse}. Informal and somewhat dated.

Lumber is timber that has been cut into boards or planks for building. In American English, you buy lumber at a lumberyard; British English prefers timber. To lumber is to move heavily and clumsily: {The bear lumbered through the campsite}. To be lumbered with something (British) is to be burdened with an unwanted task or responsibility: {I got lumbered with cleaning up after the party}.

Lumbered is the past tense of lumber, which means to move heavily and clumsily: {The bear lumbered through the campsite}. The word suggests bulk combined with awkwardness—elephants lumber, trucks lumber down dirt roads. In British English, to be lumbered with something is to be stuck with an unwanted burden: {I got lumbered with organizing the whole event}.

Lumbering describes movement that is slow, heavy, and awkward—the gait of something large moving without grace: {A bear came lumbering through the campsite}. The word suggests bulk and effort, whether describing an elephant, a truck, or a person hauling themselves out of a chair. Lumbering also refers to the logging industry—the business of cutting and processing timber.

A lumberjack is a person who fells trees and cuts them into logs, typically working in forests as part of the timber industry. The term evokes images of rugged outdoor work with axes and chainsaws, plaid flannel shirts, and life in remote logging camps. Though the occupation has become increasingly mechanized, lumberjack persists in popular culture and in competitive events like log rolling and axe throwing. {He worked as a lumberjack in the Pacific Northwest for twenty years.}

Lumberjacks are workers who fell trees and prepare logs for transport, traditionally associated with North American timber camps of the 19th and early 20th centuries. The term evokes a rugged image: flannel shirts, axes, and life in remote forests. Modern logging uses machinery, but lumberjack persists for competitive wood-chopping and as a cultural archetype: {He ordered the lumberjack breakfast—eggs, bacon, and a stack of pancakes}.

A lumbermill is a facility where logs are cut into boards, planks, and other timber products. The term is interchangeable with sawmill, though lumbermill emphasizes the production of lumber specifically: {The old lumbermill employed half the town}.

Lumbers is the third-person singular of lumber, which has two distinct meanings. One lumber means to move heavily and clumsily: {The bear lumbered through the underbrush}. The other lumber refers to timber—wood processed for building. To lumber is to cut and prepare timber commercially. A lumberjack lumbers; so does anything that moves with awkward weight.

A lumbersexual is an urban man who cultivates a rugged, outdoorsy aesthetic—thick beard, flannel shirts, work boots—without actually doing manual labor or spending time in the wilderness. The term combines lumberjack with metrosexual, suggesting the style is as carefully maintained as any fashion trend: {He's got the full lumbersexual look but has never touched an axe}.

A lumberyard is a place where lumber—boards, planks, beams, and other cut wood—is stored and sold. Contractors, carpenters, and homeowners visit lumberyards for building materials: {I picked up some two-by-fours at the lumberyard}. Larger operations may also stock plywood, hardware, and other construction supplies.

Luminaries are people who have achieved distinction in a particular field—the brightest lights in their domain: {The conference attracted luminaries from across the tech industry}. The word comes from a term for celestial bodies that give off light, and the figurative sense preserves that glow: luminaries illuminate their fields as stars illuminate the sky. A luminary can also be a lamp or light source, though this use is now rare outside of decorative contexts like {paper luminaries} lining a walkway.

A luminary is a person of distinction or brilliance in a particular field—someone who illuminates their domain: {The conference attracted luminaries from across the tech world}. The word comes from light: literally, a luminary is a celestial body, especially the sun or moon. The figurative sense now dominates, describing intellectual or artistic stars who light the way for others.

Luminescence is light produced without significant heat—the glow of fireflies, deep-sea creatures, or phosphorescent paint. Unlike incandescence, where objects glow because they're hot, luminescence comes from chemical reactions, electrical stimulation, or absorbed radiation being re-emitted. The word covers specific types: bioluminescence (living organisms), fluorescence (immediate re-emission), phosphorescence (delayed glow). {The luminescence of the jellyfish lit up the dark water.}

Luminescent describes something that emits light without being heated—the glow of fireflies, deep-sea creatures, or certain chemicals. Unlike incandescence, which produces light through heat, luminescence results from other energy sources: {The luminescent dial of the watch glowed in the darkness}. The word often suggests an ethereal or otherworldly quality: {Her luminescent skin seemed to glow from within}.

Luminosity is the quality or state of emitting light—brightness, radiance. In astronomy, luminosity measures the total energy a star or celestial body radiates per unit of time, distinguishing it from apparent brightness, which depends on distance: {The star's luminosity exceeds the sun's by a factor of ten thousand}. Figuratively, luminosity describes intellectual brilliance or clarity: {the luminosity of her prose}.

Luminous describes something that emits or radiates light: {luminous stars}, {a luminous dial on a watch}. The word extends to things that seem to glow with inner brightness—a luminous complexion, luminous eyes. Figuratively, luminous applies to clarity of thought or expression: {a luminous prose style}, {luminous intelligence}. The word suggests soft, steady radiance rather than harsh brilliance.

A lummox is a clumsy, awkward person—someone physically ungainly or mentally slow. The word suggests a large, bumbling figure who knocks things over or can't quite keep up: {You big lummox, watch where you're going!} It's mildly insulting but often affectionate, the kind of thing you'd call a friend who trips over his own feet.

A lump is a compact mass, typically irregular in shape: a lump of {coal}, a lump of {clay}, a lump in the {throat}. A lump on the body is a swelling, sometimes alarming: {She found a lump in her breast}. To lump things together is to treat them as one group, often ignoring distinctions: {Don't lump all politicians together}. If you don't like it, you can {lump it}—accept it anyway.

Lumpia is a Filipino spring roll—a thin wrapper encasing a savory filling of meat, vegetables, or both, then fried until crispy. Fresh lumpia (lumpiang sariwa) is unfried and wrapped in a soft crepe. The dish came to the Philippines from Chinese immigrants and remains central to Filipino celebrations: {No family party is complete without lumpia}.

Lumps is the plural of lump—irregular masses or swellings. You check for lumps in bread dough or under your skin. {She felt a lump in her breast and scheduled an appointment}. To {take your lumps} is to endure punishment or criticism: {Every rookie takes their lumps}. {Like it or lump it} means accept something whether you want to or not.

Lumpy describes something full of lumps—irregular masses or bumps that disrupt smoothness. Lumpy {oatmeal} has clumps that didn't dissolve. A lumpy {mattress} has uneven spots. Lumpy {gravy} wasn't stirred enough. The word can describe anything uneven or bumpy: {a lumpy pillow}, {lumpy terrain}. Figuratively, a lumpy {performance} is uneven in quality.

Luna is the Latin word for moon, appearing in English primarily as a poetic or literary alternative to moon. It surfaces in scientific terms like lunar and in proper names. Luna commonly appears as a given name for girls and for pets, especially cats. In Spanish-speaking contexts, luna simply means moon.

Lunacy is extreme foolishness or reckless disregard for consequences: {It would be sheer lunacy to attempt the climb in this weather}. The word originally referred to intermittent insanity supposedly caused by phases of the moon—hence the connection to lunar. The older psychiatric sense has faded; what remains is emphatic condemnation of foolish behavior.
clues: Acting without a shred of reason

definition: Lunar means relating to the moon. A lunar {eclipse} occurs when Earth passes between the sun and moon. The lunar {cycle} tracks the moon's phases over roughly 29 days. Lunar {calendars} organize time by these cycles. A lunar {landscape} is barren and cratered, resembling the moon's surface. {The lunar module landed safely.}

A lunatic is a person considered insane or wildly irrational. The word originally tied madness to the moon's phases—people believed lunar cycles triggered mental instability. Today lunatic is informal and often hyperbolic: {My boss is a lunatic}, {lunatic fringe}. It can describe reckless behavior: {a lunatic driver weaving through traffic}. As an adjective: {a lunatic scheme}.

Lunatics are people considered mentally deranged or wildly foolish. The word comes from the ancient belief that the moon caused periodic insanity. Today it's mostly informal, describing people who behave recklessly or irrationally: {The lunatics have taken over the asylum}. As a clinical term for the mentally ill, it's obsolete and offensive.

Lunch is the midday meal, typically eaten between late morning and early afternoon. It falls between breakfast and dinner in the daily sequence: {I packed a lunch for work}, {Let's grab lunch}. As a verb, to lunch is to eat this meal: {We lunched at the café}. {Out to lunch} means absent or, figuratively, mentally disconnected from reality.

A lunchbox is a container, typically with a handle and secure lid, used to carry a packed meal—most often to school or work. Children's lunchboxes frequently feature cartoon characters or bright designs, while adult versions tend toward insulated bags or plain containers. The term sometimes appears in British slang as a vulgar reference to the male genital bulge visible through tight clothing. {She packed her sandwich and apple in her lunchbox.}

Lunchboxes is the plural of lunchbox—a container for carrying a packed meal, typically to school or work. Children's lunchboxes often feature cartoon characters or superheroes. The word sometimes appears as slang for a man's genital bulge visible through tight clothing: {Nice lunchbox in those jeans}.

Lunchbucket refers to a metal pail or box for carrying a packed meal to work, associated with manual laborers and factory workers. As an adjective, lunchbucket describes working-class identity and values: {lunchbucket voters}, {a lunchbucket town}. The term evokes blue-collar authenticity and unpretentious hard work: {He ran on his lunchbucket roots}.

Luncheon is a formal or elaborate midday meal, or simply a slightly elevated word for lunch. The term suggests something more organized than a casual bite—a business luncheon, a charity luncheon, a ladies' luncheon. {The club hosts its annual awards luncheon in May.} Luncheon meat is processed meat sold in cans or loaves, sliced for sandwiches.

A luncheonette is a small, informal restaurant serving light meals and snacks, typically at a counter. The term evokes mid-twentieth-century American diners with stools, soda fountains, and simple fare like sandwiches and soup: {We stopped at a luncheonette for coffee and pie}. The word has a nostalgic quality, as most such establishments have disappeared.

Luncheonettes is the plural of luncheonette, a small informal restaurant serving light meals and snacks, typically at a counter. The term evokes mid-20th-century American diners with soda fountains, booths, and simple fare like sandwiches and coffee: {The old luncheonettes have mostly given way to fast-food chains}.

A lunchpail is a container for carrying a packed meal to work or school, typically a metal box with a handle. The word evokes blue-collar labor—factory workers, construction crews, miners. As an adjective, lunchpail describes unpretentious, hardworking people or attitudes: {a lunchpail approach to the game}, {lunchpail values}. Also spelled lunch pail.

A lunchroom is a room where people eat lunch, typically in a school, workplace, or institution. It may have tables and chairs for eating brought food, vending machines, or cafeteria-style service: {The teachers gathered in the lunchroom between classes}. In American usage, lunchroom and cafeteria overlap considerably.

Lunchtime is the period of day when lunch is typically eaten, usually around midday. The word functions as both noun and adjective: {We met at lunchtime}, {a lunchtime crowd}. In workplace contexts, it often implies a break from work: {I'll call you back at lunchtime}.

A lung is one of the pair of spongy organs in the chest that extract oxygen from inhaled air and expel carbon dioxide. Most vertebrates have lungs; fish have gills instead. To {shout at the top of your lungs} is to shout as loudly as possible. A {lung} in slang can mean a cigarette or the act of smoking one.

A lunge is a sudden forward thrust or movement—with a weapon, a fist, or the whole body: {He made a lunge for the knife}. In fencing, it's the basic attacking move. In exercise, a lunge is a step forward with one leg bent deeply while the other extends behind. The verb means to make such a movement: {The dog lunged at the mailman}.

Lunged is the past tense of lunge, describing a sudden forward movement of the body, typically to attack, reach, or grab something. When someone lunges, they thrust themselves toward a target with force and intent: {He lunged at the intruder with a kitchen knife}. The word often implies aggression or urgency, though it can also describe athletic movements like fencing thrusts or workout exercises.

Lunges are sudden forward movements, typically an aggressive thrust toward a target or an exercise where you step forward and lower your body by bending both knees. In fencing, a lunge is the basic attacking move—extending the sword arm while driving forward with the back leg. {She did twenty lunges across the gym floor.} {He lunges at his opponent.}

A lungfish is a freshwater fish equipped with one or two primitive lungs in addition to gills, allowing it to breathe air and survive in stagnant or drying waters. Found in Africa, South America, and Australia, lungfish can estivate in mud during droughts, remaining dormant until rains return. They represent an ancient lineage linking fish to land vertebrates.

Lunging is the present participle of lunge—a sudden forward thrust or movement. Someone lunging reaches or pushes abruptly toward something: {The dog kept lunging at the fence}. In fencing, lunging is the basic attacking motion. In fitness, lunging refers to performing lunges—exercises where one leg steps forward into a deep bend while the other extends back.

Lungs are the pair of spongy organs in the chest that extract oxygen from air and expel carbon dioxide. Most vertebrates have them. At the top of one's lungs means as loudly as possible: {She screamed at the top of her lungs}. To have good lungs is to have powerful vocal capacity.

A lunkhead is a stupid or slow-witted person—someone whose head might as well be a lunk of wood. The word is mildly insulting but usually affectionate or exasperated rather than cutting: {Don't be such a lunkhead, just read the instructions}.

Lupin is a plant of the pea family with tall spikes of colorful flowers and palmately divided leaves. Lupins grow wild in meadows and are cultivated in gardens for their showy blue, purple, pink, yellow, or white blooms. Some species produce edible seeds, eaten in Mediterranean and Latin American cuisines. Also spelled lupine.

Lupines are flowering plants with tall spikes of colorful blossoms and distinctive palmate leaves that fan out like fingers. They grow wild in meadows and along roadsides, particularly in western North America, and are popular in gardens for their showy purple, pink, blue, or yellow flowers. Some species are cultivated as forage crops or to fix nitrogen in soil.

Lupins are flowering plants of the legume family, known for tall spikes of colorful blossoms in purple, pink, yellow, or white. They grow wild in meadows and are cultivated in gardens. Some species produce edible seeds, eaten as snacks in Mediterranean and Latin American cuisines after soaking to remove bitter alkaloids. Also spelled lupines.

Lupus is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the body's immune system attacks its own tissues, causing inflammation and damage to joints, skin, kidneys, and other organs. The most common form is systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Symptoms vary widely and often include fatigue, joint pain, and a distinctive butterfly-shaped facial rash. {She was diagnosed with lupus after months of unexplained symptoms.}

Lurch is a sudden unsteady movement—a stagger or stumble to one side: {The bus lurched and I grabbed the rail}. Ships lurch in rough seas; drunk people lurch down sidewalks. To {leave someone in the lurch} is to abandon them in a difficult situation. A separate lurch is a decisive defeat in cribbage, when one player scores before the other reaches halfway.

Lurched is the past tense of lurch, meaning to make a sudden unsteady movement. A person lurches when they stagger or stumble: {He lurched toward the door}. Vehicles lurch when they jerk forward or sideways: {The bus lurched to a stop}. The word suggests loss of balance or control, whether physical or figurative: {The company lurched from one crisis to the next}.

Lurches is the plural noun and third-person singular verb form of lurch. A lurch is a sudden, unsteady movement, typically to one side, like the motion of a ship in rough seas or a drunk stumbling home. To lurch is to make such movements: {The bus lurched forward and I nearly fell}. If someone leaves you {in the lurch}, they abandon you in a difficult situation without help or warning.

Lurching describes sudden, unsteady movement—staggering or swaying abruptly from side to side or forward. A drunk lurches down the sidewalk. A bus lurches when the driver brakes hard. The word often suggests loss of control or balance: {The ship lurched violently in the storm}. Figuratively, plans or situations can lurch from one state to another: {The economy lurched toward recession}.
clues: Swaying violently from side to side

definition: A lure is something that attracts or tempts, often toward danger or unwise action: {the lure of easy money}, {the lure of fame}. In fishing, a lure is an artificial bait designed to attract fish. To lure is to entice or draw someone toward something: {They lured him into a trap}. The word usually implies enticement toward something questionable or harmful.

Lured is the past tense of lure—to attract or entice someone toward something, often by offering what they desire. The word carries a suggestion of deception or danger: {She was lured into the alley by promises of easy money}. Fish are lured by bait, customers by discounts, victims by false promises.

Lures are things that attract or entice, often toward something dangerous or unwise: {the lures of easy money}, {the lures of fame}. In fishing, lures are artificial baits designed to attract fish—spinners, flies, plastic worms. The word implies enticement with ulterior purpose; prey doesn't see the hook until too late.

Lurid describes things that are sensationalized, shocking, or gruesome—especially in ways meant to fascinate or horrify: {lurid tabloid headlines}, {the lurid details of the crime}. The word often suggests a morbid or prurient appeal. Lurid can also describe an unnaturally vivid or harsh glow: {the lurid orange of the wildfire sky}.
clues: Shocking in a cheap, vivid way

definition: Luring is drawing someone or something toward you, typically through enticement or deception. The word carries a sense of temptation—you lure with bait, promises, or attractive offers: {luring customers with discounts}, {luring fish to the surface}. What's lured rarely benefits from the encounter.

To lurk is to wait in concealment, often with sinister intent: {A mugger lurked in the shadows}. More loosely, lurk describes anything that remains hidden but present: {Danger lurks beneath the surface}. Online, to lurk is to read forums or chat rooms without participating—observing without revealing yourself: {I've been lurking on this subreddit for months}.

Lurked is the past tense of lurk, meaning to wait or move in a hidden or inconspicuous way, often with sinister intent: {A figure lurked in the shadows}. Online, to lurk is to read discussions without participating—observing a forum or chat without posting: {I lurked on the subreddit for months before commenting}.

A lurker is someone who observes without participating. The term comes from internet culture, where lurkers read forums, social media, or chat rooms without posting or commenting: {I've been lurking on this subreddit for months}. The verb lurk originally meant to lie in wait or move stealthily, suggesting something sinister, but online lurking is usually passive and harmless—just watching from the shadows.

Lurkers are people who observe without participating. The term is most common in online contexts—someone who reads forums, chat rooms, or social media without posting or commenting is lurking. {Most of the group's members are lurkers who never say anything.} The word carries mild disapproval, suggesting someone who watches from the shadows rather than engaging openly.

Lurking is waiting or moving stealthily, often with sinister intent: {A figure lurked in the shadows}. The word suggests concealment and watchfulness—a predator lurks before striking, danger lurks around corners. Online, lurking means reading forums or social media without participating: {I've been lurking on this subreddit for months}. This internet sense carries no negative connotation—lurkers simply observe rather than post.

Lurks is the third-person singular of lurk, meaning to wait in concealment, often with sinister intent: {Something lurks in the shadows}. More broadly, to lurk is to exist unnoticed or barely perceived: {Danger lurks beneath the surface}. Online, lurking means reading forums or chat without participating—present but invisible: {I've been lurking on that subreddit for months}.

Luscious describes something richly pleasurable to the senses, especially taste. Luscious {peaches}, luscious {chocolate cake}. The word suggests sweetness, ripeness, and indulgence. It extends to other sensory pleasures—luscious {colors}, luscious {fabrics}—and to physical attractiveness: {luscious lips}, {a luscious figure}. The connotation is always of abundance and sensual appeal.

Lush describes vegetation that grows thick, green, and healthy: {lush tropical forests}, {a lush lawn}. The meaning extends to anything rich and luxuriant—lush {fabrics}, lush {orchestration}, lush {prose}. Separately, lush is slang for a heavy drinker or drunk, probably from an old slang term for alcohol.

Lust is intense sexual desire—a powerful physical craving for someone: {He looked at her with undisguised lust}. The word extends to any consuming appetite or longing: {lust for power}, {lust for gold}, {bloodlust}. To lust after someone is to desire them sexually; to lust after something is to crave it intensely. In religious contexts, lust is one of the seven deadly sins.

Lusted is the past tense of lust. To lust is to feel intense desire, especially sexual desire: {He lusted after his neighbor's wife}. The word carries connotations of wrongful or excessive wanting—you lust for what you probably shouldn't have. Beyond sex, lust extends to other cravings: {She lusted for power}, {They lusted after fame and fortune}.

Luster is the quality of soft, reflected light—the shine of polished surfaces, healthy hair, or precious stones. A pearl has luster; so does satin. Figuratively, luster is glory or distinction: {His early scandals took some luster off the achievement}. To add luster is to enhance prestige or appeal. The spelling lustre is British.

Lustful describes intense sexual desire or appetite. A lustful {glance} or lustful {thoughts} suggest someone consumed by physical attraction. The word carries moral weight—it implies desire that's excessive or inappropriate, not merely healthy attraction. {He cast a lustful eye at his neighbor's wife.}

Lustre is the British spelling of luster—a soft glow or sheen, especially from reflected light: {the lustre of pearls}, {polished to a high lustre}. Figuratively, lustre means glory or distinction: {Her discoveries added lustre to the university's reputation}. Something that has lost its lustre has become dull or less impressive than before.

Lusts is the plural of lust—intense desires, especially sexual ones. Someone consumed by lusts is driven by powerful cravings: {His lusts led him to ruin}. The word often implies desires that are base or ungoverned. As a verb, lusts means desires intensely: {She lusts after fame}, {He lusts for revenge}.

Lusty means full of vigor, energy, or enthusiasm. A lusty {cheer} is loud and hearty. A lusty {appetite} is strong and eager. The word originally emphasized robust vitality rather than sexuality, though lusty now often suggests strong sexual desire or attraction: {He gave her a lusty look}. The shift toward the erotic has made the older, innocent sense somewhat dated.

A lute is a stringed musical instrument with a pear-shaped body and a neck with frets, plucked like a guitar. It was the dominant instrument of European secular music from the medieval period through the baroque era: {a Renaissance lute}, {lute songs}. The word also names an unrelated clay or cement used to seal joints in laboratory equipment or pipes.

Lutes is the plural of lute, a stringed instrument with a rounded back and angled pegbox, prominent in Renaissance and Baroque music: {The museum displayed several antique lutes}. To lute is also to seal joints with cement or clay, making lutes the third-person singular of that verb: {She lutes the vessel before firing}.

A luthier is a craftsperson who builds and repairs stringed instruments—guitars, violins, cellos, lutes. The term comes from the French word for lute. Luthiers combine woodworking skill with acoustic knowledge, shaping the instrument's body, neck, and components to achieve particular tonal qualities. {She took her violin to a luthier for restoration.}

Luxe means luxury or luxuriousness, often used attributively: {a luxe hotel}, {luxe accommodations}. The word feels slightly more stylish or contemporary than plain "luxury," appearing frequently in fashion, travel, and lifestyle contexts. {The spa offers a luxe experience at budget prices.}

Luxuriated is the past tense of luxuriate, meaning to take deep pleasure in something, especially something sensory or indulgent. The word suggests lingering enjoyment rather than quick satisfaction: {She luxuriated in a hot bath after the long hike}. One luxuriates in comfort, warmth, attention, or freedom—savoring the experience rather than merely having it.

Luxuriating is indulging in something pleasurable with full, unhurried enjoyment. The word suggests taking time to savor comfort or sensory delight: {luxuriating in a hot bath}, {luxuriating in the attention}. It implies not just experiencing pleasure but dwelling in it, letting it soak in.

Luxuries are items or experiences beyond basic necessities—things enjoyed for pleasure, comfort, or status rather than survival. A luxury might be a yacht, a spa day, or simply time to oneself. The word often implies expense or scarcity: {Fresh fruit was a luxury during wartime}. What counts as luxury varies by context and means—one person's luxury is another's routine.

Luxurious describes something characterized by great comfort, elegance, or expense: {a luxurious hotel}, {luxurious fabrics}. The word suggests indulgence beyond necessity—not just comfortable but lavishly so. A luxurious bath isn't quick and functional; it involves hot water, scented oils, unhurried time. Things described as luxurious tend to appeal to the senses and signal wealth or refined taste.

Luxury is comfort or pleasure beyond what's necessary—the extras that make life more enjoyable when basic needs are already met. A luxury {car}, luxury {hotel}, or luxury {apartment} offers high-end quality and amenities. What counts as luxury varies by context: {Running water was a luxury in the cabin}. The adjective luxurious describes anything marked by such indulgence: {a luxurious bath}, {luxurious fabrics}.

Lychee is a small tropical fruit with rough, reddish-pink skin that peels away to reveal translucent white flesh surrounding a large seed. Native to southern China, lychees have a sweet, floral flavor often described as a cross between grape and rose. They are eaten fresh, canned, or dried, and appear in desserts and cocktails. {Fresh lychees are only available for a few weeks each summer.}

Lychees are the plural of lychee, a small tropical fruit native to southern China. The fruit has a rough, reddish-pink shell that peels away to reveal translucent white flesh surrounding a single seed. The flavor is sweet and floral, sometimes compared to grapes or roses. Lychees are eaten fresh, canned, or dried: {We split a bowl of lychees for dessert}.

Lye is a strongly alkaline solution, traditionally made by leaching water through wood ash. The term now usually refers to sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide—caustic substances used in soapmaking, drain cleaners, and food preparation. Lye is corrosive and can cause severe chemical burns: {Keep lye away from children}.

Lying is stating something false with intent to deceive. A lie requires knowing the truth and choosing to misrepresent it: {She was lying about where she'd been}. Lying also serves as the present participle of lie in both senses—reclining and deceiving: {He was lying on the couch}, {They've been lying to us for years}.

To lynch is to kill someone, typically by hanging, through mob action without legal authority. The practice is most associated with the terrorizing of Black Americans in the post-Civil War South, where white mobs murdered thousands with impunity. The term now applies to any extrajudicial mob killing: {The crowd threatened to lynch the suspected thief}.

Lynched is the past tense of lynch, meaning to kill someone by mob action without legal authority—historically by hanging. The term is most associated with the extrajudicial murder of Black Americans, particularly in the South from Reconstruction through the mid-20th century: {Between 1877 and 1950, thousands of Black men were lynched}. The word sometimes extends to any mob killing or vigilante execution.

Lynching is extrajudicial killing by a mob, historically associated with the murder of Black Americans in the post-Civil War South through the mid-twentieth century. Victims were often hanged from trees, though burning and shooting were also common. The killings served as racial terrorism, enforcing white supremacy through spectacle violence. The term now applies to any mob killing: {The film depicted the lynching of an accused thief}. Figuratively, a public lynching describes coordinated attacks on someone's reputation.

Lynchings is the plural of lynching—the killing of a person by a mob without legal authority, typically by hanging. The term is especially associated with the extrajudicial murder of Black Americans in the post-Civil War South, where thousands were lynched through the mid-twentieth century. {Photographs of lynchings were sometimes made into postcards.} The verb lynch extends to any mob killing or vigilante execution.

Lynchpin is an alternate spelling of linchpin—a pin passed through the end of an axle to keep a wheel in place. The figurative sense dominates: a lynchpin is something essential that holds a system together: {She was the lynchpin of the whole operation}. The spelling with y, though common, is technically incorrect—the word derives from an old word for axle, not from lynch.

A lynx is a medium-sized wild cat with distinctive tufted ears, a short tail, and often a ruff of fur around the face. Several species inhabit northern forests and mountains across North America, Europe, and Asia. The Canada lynx and Eurasian lynx are the most widely known. {We spotted lynx tracks in the snow.}

A lyre is a stringed musical instrument of ancient Greece and the Near East, with strings stretched between a U-shaped frame and a crossbar. The player plucked the strings while holding the instrument upright. The lyre is associated with poetry and song—Orpheus charmed beasts with his lyre, and lyric poetry takes its name from verses originally sung to lyre accompaniment.

A lyrebird is a large Australian ground-dwelling bird famous for its extraordinary ability to mimic sounds—other bird calls, chainsaws, camera shutters, car alarms. The male's elaborate tail feathers, spread during courtship displays, resemble the shape of a lyre. {We heard a lyrebird imitating a kookaburra.}

Lyrebirds are large Australian songbirds famous for their extraordinary mimicry—they can reproduce virtually any sound they hear, from other bird calls to chainsaws and camera shutters. The name comes from the male's spectacular tail feathers, which spread into a shape resembling a lyre during courtship displays.

Lyres is the plural of lyre, an ancient stringed instrument with a U-shaped frame and strings stretched from a crossbar to a soundboard. Associated with Greek mythology and classical antiquity, the lyre was played by plucking. {The museum displayed lyres from ancient Greece.} The word appears in poetic contexts evoking classical art and music.

A lyric is a word from a song: {I can't get that lyric out of my head}. In the plural, lyrics means all the words: {She writes her own lyrics}. As an adjective, lyric describes poetry that expresses personal emotion rather than telling a story, or music suited to such poetry: {lyric poetry}, {lyric soprano}. A lyric poem is also called a lyric.
clues: What you read on karaoke screens

definition: Lyrical describes something resembling or appropriate to song—expressing emotion in an imaginative, often poetic way: {lyrical prose}, {a lyrical passage in the symphony}. Someone who {waxes lyrical} speaks enthusiastically and at length about something. In music, lyrical indicates a smooth, melodic quality, especially in singing voices: {a lyrical soprano}. The word overlaps with lyric but tends toward the figurative and evaluative rather than the technical.

Lyricism is the quality of being lyrical—expressing emotion with beauty, imagination, and musicality. The term applies to poetry, prose, music, or any art form that prioritizes feeling and personal expression over narrative or argument: {The film's lyricism elevates a simple story}. A passage marked by lyricism tends toward the rhapsodic, the intimate, the song-like.

A lyricist writes the words to songs, as distinct from the composer who writes the music. The term usually applies to popular music, musicals, and opera rather than poetry set to music after the fact. {Lorenz Hart was the lyricist; Richard Rodgers composed the melodies.}

Lyricists are writers who compose the words for songs. The term distinguishes those who write lyrics from those who compose the music, though some songwriters do both. A lyricist may work with a composer as a team: {Rodgers and Hammerstein}, {Elton John and Bernie Taupin}. The word also applies to poets whose work has a musical, songlike quality.

Lyrics are the words to a song, as distinct from its melody or musical arrangement: {I love the tune but can't remember the lyrics}. The term comes from lyre, the stringed instrument of ancient Greek poets. A lyric, in the singular, is a short poem expressing personal emotion—the kind originally meant to be sung.

Mac is an informal term for a raincoat, especially a mackintosh—a waterproof coat originally made of rubberized fabric. The word is more common in British than American English: {Don't forget your mac, it looks like rain}. Separately, mac is a casual form of address to a man whose name you don't know, now somewhat dated: {Hey mac, you dropped your wallet}. (Capitalized Mac is a prefix in Scottish and Irish surnames, or short for Macintosh computers.)

Macabre describes things characterized by or dwelling on the gruesome, disturbing, or horrifying aspects of death: {a macabre fascination with serial killers}, {The morgue scene had a macabre humor}. The word suggests something unsettling rather than merely sad—death made strange, theatrical, or grotesque. Art, stories, and humor are often described as macabre when they treat mortality with dark relish.

Macadamia is a tree native to Australia, cultivated for its rich, buttery nuts. The nuts have an exceptionally hard shell and are prized in baking and confections: {macadamia nut cookies}, {chocolate-covered macadamias}. The tree genus is named after Scottish-Australian chemist John Macadam.

Macadamias are round, cream-colored nuts with a rich, buttery flavor and hard shells. Native to Australia, they're now cultivated in Hawaii and other tropical regions. The nuts are expensive due to difficult harvesting and processing: {macadamia-crusted fish}, {chocolate-covered macadamias}. Also called macadamia nuts.

A macaque is a medium-sized monkey native to Asia and North Africa, with a stocky build, prominent cheekbones, and often a short tail. Macaques are highly adaptable and social, living in troops near temples, cities, and forests. The rhesus macaque is widely used in medical research. {A troop of macaques raided the tourists' bags.}

Macaques are medium-sized monkeys native to Asia and North Africa, recognizable by their sturdy build and often prominent facial features. They adapt readily to human environments—the rhesus macaque is common in research laboratories, while troops of macaques raid tourist sites across Southeast Asia. {Macaques surrounded the temple, waiting for handouts.}

A macaron is a delicate French sandwich cookie made from almond flour, egg whites, and sugar, with a filling between two round meringue-based shells. The shells have a smooth top, ruffled edge (called the "foot"), and slightly chewy interior. Macarons come in many flavors and colors: {pistachio macarons}, {a box of assorted macarons}. Not to be confused with macaroon, a denser coconut-based cookie.

Macaroni is pasta in the form of short curved tubes, most familiar in macaroni and cheese. The word once had a now-obsolete meaning: an 18th-century dandy who affected Continental fashions—hence "stuck a feather in his cap and called it macaroni" in "Yankee Doodle," mocking American colonists as pretentious rustics.

Macarons are delicate French sandwich cookies made from almond flour, egg whites, and sugar, with a filling between two rounded shells. The shells have a smooth top and ruffled base called a "foot." They come in many flavors and colors: {The bakery displayed rows of pastel macarons}. Not to be confused with macaroons, which are coconut-based.

A macaroon is a small cookie made primarily from coconut or almond paste, egg whites, and sugar. The coconut version—dense, mounded, often dipped in chocolate—dominates American bakeries. Almond macaroons are closer to the original and remain common in Italian and Jewish cuisines. Not to be confused with the French macaron, a delicate sandwich cookie made from almond flour with a filling between two meringue shells.

Macaroons are small, sweet baked goods. The word covers two distinct confections: dense, chewy cookies made primarily from shredded coconut, egg whites, and sugar—common in American bakeries—and the French macaron, delicate sandwich cookies of almond meringue with filling. The spelling macaroon traditionally covers both, though macaron now often distinguishes the French version.

A macaw is a large, brilliantly colored parrot native to Central and South American rainforests, known for its long tail, powerful curved beak, and loud calls. Macaws are often kept as exotic pets and can live for decades: {The scarlet macaw at the zoo is over fifty years old}.

Macaws are large, brilliantly colored parrots native to Central and South American rainforests. They have long tails, powerful curved beaks, and distinctive bare facial patches. Macaws are known for their intelligence and ability to mimic human speech, making them popular—if demanding—pets: {The scarlet macaw spread its wings across three feet}.

A macchiato is an espresso "stained" with a small amount of steamed milk or foam—the name comes from Italian for "stained" or "spotted." The drink preserves espresso's intensity while slightly softening it. A latte macchiato reverses the ratio: steamed milk stained with espresso. Coffee chains have expanded the term to cover various espresso-and-milk drinks that bear little resemblance to the original.

Mace names two unrelated things. One is a medieval weapon—a heavy club with a spiked or flanged metal head, used to crush armor. Ceremonial maces survive as symbols of authority in parliaments and universities. The other mace is a spice made from the lacy covering of nutmeg seeds, with a similar but more delicate flavor. Mace is also a trademark for a pepper spray used in self-defense: {She kept mace in her purse}.

Maced means sprayed with Mace, a brand of tear gas or pepper spray used for self-defense: {She maced the attacker and ran}. The term applies regardless of the actual brand used. Being maced causes intense burning in the eyes and respiratory distress. Separately, maced can mean struck with a mace—the medieval spiked weapon—though this use is rare outside fantasy contexts.
clues: Got a face full of capsaicin

definition: Mach is the ratio of an object's speed to the speed of sound in the surrounding medium. Mach 1 is the speed of sound (about 767 mph at sea level); Mach 2 is twice that. Aircraft traveling below Mach 1 are subsonic, above it supersonic: {The jet broke Mach 3}. Named for physicist Ernst Mach, the term is conventionally capitalized, though lowercase appears in technical contexts.

A machete is a large, heavy knife with a broad blade, used for cutting vegetation and as a weapon. It's the essential tool for clearing jungle paths, harvesting sugarcane, and opening coconuts. In regions where it's common, the machete serves as an all-purpose cutting implement: {He hacked through the undergrowth with his machete}.

Machetes are large, heavy knives with broad blades, used for cutting vegetation or as weapons. The machete is the quintessential tool of tropical agriculture—clearing brush, harvesting sugarcane, opening coconuts. Its effectiveness as an improvised weapon has made it notorious in conflicts and violent crimes: {The attackers came with machetes}. Singular: machete.

A machination is a crafty scheme or plot, usually one designed to harm someone or gain an unfair advantage. The word nearly always appears in the plural, suggesting a web of interconnected schemes: {The novel exposed the machinations of corrupt politicians}. Machinations typically involve secrecy, manipulation, and calculated moves—the kind of plotting associated with villains, rival factions, or ambitious schemers working behind the scenes.

Machinations are scheming plots or crafty maneuvers, usually secret and intended to accomplish some end through underhanded means. The word nearly always appears in the plural and carries a sinister or at least suspicious tone: {corporate machinations}, {political machinations}, {the machinations of her enemies}. Someone engaged in machinations is plotting, not planning.

A machine is a device with moving parts that performs work: a washing machine, a sewing machine, a machine that stamps metal. The word extends to complex systems that function with mechanical efficiency: the political machine, the war machine. A person who works tirelessly or without emotion may be called a machine: {She's a machine—she never stops}. To machine something is to shape it with power tools: {machined aluminum parts}.

A machinegun is an automatic weapon that fires rapidly and continuously as long as the trigger is held down. The term applies broadly to military weapons from mounted belt-fed guns to handheld submachine guns. As a verb, to machinegun is to shoot with such a weapon, or figuratively to do anything in rapid succession: {She machinegunned questions at the witness}. Also spelled machine gun or machine-gun.

Machineguns are automatic firearms that fire continuously while the trigger is held, feeding ammunition from a belt or magazine. The term covers weapons from handheld submachine guns to heavy mounted guns. As a verb, to machinegun is to fire such a weapon at something or someone: {The aircraft machineguned the convoy}. Also spelled machine guns or machine-guns.

Machinery is the collection of machines or mechanical equipment used for a particular purpose: {industrial machinery}, {farm machinery}. The word also refers to the working parts of a machine collectively. Figuratively, machinery describes the system or organization that makes something function: {the machinery of government}, {the machinery of justice}. The term implies complexity and interconnected parts working together.
clues: The cogs that keep things moving

definition: Machines are devices that use mechanical power to perform tasks. The word covers everything from simple levers and pulleys to complex engines and computers. A machine can be any apparatus with moving parts: {sewing machine}, {washing machine}, {slot machine}. Figuratively, machine describes anything that operates with mechanical efficiency: {a well-oiled machine}, {the political machine}. To machine something is to shape it with power tools: {machined aluminum parts}.

Machining is the process of shaping material—usually metal—by cutting, drilling, grinding, or otherwise removing unwanted portions. The term covers operations performed on lathes, mills, and other machine tools: {The part requires precision machining to meet specifications}. A machine shop is where such work is done.

A machinist is a person who operates machine tools—lathes, milling machines, grinders—to shape metal or other materials into precise parts. The work requires reading blueprints, measuring tolerances, and setting up equipment. Machinists work in manufacturing plants, repair shops, and tool-and-die operations: {The machinist cut the replacement gear to exact specifications}.

Machinists are skilled workers who operate machine tools to shape metal and other materials into precise parts. They read blueprints, set up lathes and milling machines, and measure finished pieces to exacting tolerances. The trade requires both technical knowledge and manual dexterity: {The machinists worked overtime to fill the order}.

Machismo is aggressive masculine pride—an exaggerated sense of manhood that emphasizes strength, sexual prowess, and dominance. The word comes from Spanish and often carries a critical edge, implying that the behavior is excessive or compensatory: {His machismo wouldn't let him ask for directions}. The culture of machismo can discourage men from showing vulnerability or emotion.

Macho describes aggressively masculine behavior—tough, dominant, physically strong, emotionally stoic. The word carries a critical edge, suggesting masculinity performed or exaggerated: {He's too macho to ask for directions}. A macho attitude prizes toughness over vulnerability. As a noun, a macho is a man who embodies these traits. The related noun machismo names the attitude itself.

Mackerel is a fast-swimming fish found in temperate and tropical seas, prized for its oily, strong-flavored flesh. The word often appears in compounds: {holy mackerel} is a mild exclamation of surprise, and a {mackerel sky} describes a cloud pattern resembling the fish's striped markings.

Macramé is a craft of knotting cords or strings into decorative patterns, used to make plant hangers, wall hangings, jewelry, and other ornamental items. The technique uses various knots—square knots, half hitches, spiral knots—repeated to create geometric designs. {She learned macramé to make friendship bracelets.} The craft enjoyed peak popularity in the 1970s and has seen periodic revivals.

Macro means large-scale, the opposite of micro. In computing, a macro is a single instruction that expands into a sequence of operations—a shortcut that automates repetitive tasks: {I wrote a macro to format the spreadsheet}. In photography, macro refers to extreme close-up work that reveals fine detail: {macro lens}, {macro photography}. The prefix appears in words like macroeconomics (economy-wide) and macrocosm (the universe at large).

Macros are instructions that automate repetitive tasks, expanding a short command into a longer sequence of actions. In computing, a macro might record keystrokes to replay later: {I wrote a macro to format these reports}. In gaming, macros chain abilities or inputs. In nutrition, macros is short for macronutrients—proteins, carbohydrates, and fats: {I'm tracking my macros}.
clues: Repetitive tasks done with one keystroke

definition: Mad means insane or mentally disturbed, though this sense now sounds old-fashioned or clinical: {a mad scientist}, {go mad with grief}. More commonly, mad means angry: {She was mad at him for forgetting}. Mad also expresses enthusiasm or obsession: {mad about jazz}, {mad for chocolate}. In British slang, mad can mean wild or reckless: {It was a mad night out}. The intensifier mad means extremely: {mad talented}, {mad expensive}—common in youth slang, especially in New York. (Capitalized MAD may refer to the magazine or the Cold War doctrine.)

Madam is a formal term of address for a woman, used without her name: {Right this way, madam}. It parallels sir for men. In correspondence, {Dear Madam} opens letters to unknown female recipients. Madam also denotes a woman who runs a brothel. The informal ma'am is a contraction of madam.

Madame is a formal title of respect for a woman, equivalent to the English Mrs. or ma'am. It comes from French and appears most often in English when addressing or referring to women in French-speaking contexts, or in formal diplomatic and business settings. In historical and literary usage, a madame may also be the woman who runs a brothel. The plural is mesdames, though this form is rare in English. {Madame Ambassador, your car has arrived.}

Madcap describes recklessly impulsive or wildly carefree behavior, often with a sense of zany adventure rather than genuine danger: {a madcap scheme to drive cross-country in three days}, {madcap comedy}. As a noun, a madcap is a person who acts this way. The word suggests foolishness that's more entertaining than harmful.

To madden is to make someone mad—either angry or insane. The anger sense dominates modern usage: {The delays maddened commuters}. Maddening describes things that provoke frustration: {a maddening bureaucracy}, {maddening inconsistency}. The insanity sense survives in literary contexts: {maddened by grief}.

Maddening describes something that provokes intense frustration or exasperation—enough to drive you mad: {the maddening buzz of a mosquito}, {Her maddening habit of interrupting}. The word implies persistent irritation rather than a single offense: a maddening delay drags on, a maddening puzzle refuses to yield.

Made is the past tense and participle of make, one of the most common verbs. It is used in perfect and passive forms in which make is the main verb. Like some other past participles, made has some use as an adjective, particularly as a predicate adjective, as in the beds are all made. As an attributive adjective, made means manufactured or assured of success.

A madeleine is a small French cake baked in a shell-shaped mold, with a distinctive scalloped appearance and soft, spongy texture. The cakes are associated with Marcel Proust's novel *In Search of Lost Time*, where the taste of a madeleine dipped in tea triggers an flood of childhood memories. Because of this famous passage, madeleine has become shorthand for any sensory experience that unexpectedly evokes vivid recollections of the past: {The smell of cut grass was my madeleine, transporting me back to summer afternoons at my grandfather's farm}. (Capitalized Madeleine is a given name.)

Madeleines are small French sponge cakes baked in shell-shaped molds, producing their distinctive scalloped appearance. Light and buttery, they're traditionally flavored with lemon zest or vanilla. The madeleine is famously associated with Proust's *In Search of Lost Time*, where tasting one triggers an extended meditation on memory—making {Proustian madeleine} shorthand for any sensory trigger that unlocks buried recollections.

Mademoiselle is a French title for an unmarried woman or girl, equivalent to Miss in English. It was once standard in French-speaking contexts but has fallen from official use in France, where madame now applies to all adult women regardless of marital status. In English, it appears mostly in period pieces or when affecting French manners: {Mademoiselle, your table is ready}.
clues: How to greet unwed French women

definition: A madhouse is, historically, an institution for the mentally ill—now considered offensive in that sense. The word survives primarily as a figurative term for any chaotic, disorderly place: {It was a madhouse at the mall today}. The implication is noise, confusion, and people behaving erratically.

Madhouses is the plural of madhouse, an old term for an institution housing people considered mentally ill—what would later be called an asylum or psychiatric hospital. The word now appears mainly in figurative use: a place of chaos, noise, or frantic activity. {The office was a madhouse before the deadline.} {It's a madhouse in here!}

A madlad is someone who does something audacious, reckless, or hilariously unconventional—often something technically minor but executed with unexpected boldness. The term celebrates small rebellions and absurd stunts: {He ate cereal with water. Absolute madlad.} Originating from internet culture, it's usually affectionate and ironic, applied to acts that are wild mainly by mundane standards.

Madly means in a wild, frenzied, or uncontrolled manner: {They rushed madly through the streets}. It commonly intensifies romantic attachment: {madly in love}. The word can also mean extremely or to an excessive degree: {I'm madly jealous}, {madly expensive}. In casual speech, madly often conveys enthusiasm: {I'm madly curious about what happened}.

A madman is a person who is insane or behaves in a wild, reckless manner. The term can be clinical or colloquial: {The madman was finally apprehended after a week-long manhunt}. Often it describes someone acting with extreme abandon rather than actual mental illness: {He drove like a madman}, {Some madman bought the company for twice what it was worth}.
clues: Someone clearly not in their senses

definition: Madmen is the plural of madman—a person who is insane or behaves with wild recklessness. The term appears in contexts ranging from clinical to hyperbolic: {The asylum housed dangerous madmen} versus {These madmen are driving like there's no tomorrow}. The word suggests male subjects, though it has been used generically.

Madness is the state of being mentally deranged—what older usage called insanity. More commonly now, madness describes extreme foolishness or recklessness: {It would be madness to invest everything in one stock}. The word also captures frenzied intensity: {the madness of the holiday shopping season}, {March Madness}. In British usage, madness can simply mean absurdity: {This bureaucracy is utter madness}.

Madonnas is the plural of Madonna, a title for the Virgin Mary in Christian tradition, or a representation of her in art: {The museum's collection includes several Renaissance madonnas}. By extension, a madonna is any idealized, pure, or maternal woman—often contrasted with more sexualized figures in the "madonna-whore complex." (Capitalized Madonna also refers to the American pop star.)

A madrasa is an Islamic school, traditionally focused on religious instruction including Quranic study, Islamic law, and Arabic. The term covers institutions ranging from elementary religious education to advanced theological seminaries. In Western media, madrasa sometimes carries connotations of extremism, though most are conventional schools: {He attended a madrasa as a child}. Also spelled madrasah or medresa.

Madrasas are Islamic educational institutions, ranging from elementary schools teaching basic religious instruction to advanced seminaries training scholars in Islamic law and theology. The word is Arabic for "school." In Western media, madrasa often carries connotations of fundamentalist religious teaching, though most are simply ordinary schools: {He attended a madrasa as a boy}.

A madrassa is an Islamic school, typically one focused on religious education and Quranic studies. The term comes from Arabic and can refer to any educational institution in Muslim-majority countries, from elementary schools to universities, though in Western usage it often specifically means a school emphasizing traditional Islamic instruction. {The village madrassa taught children to memorize and recite the Quran.}

A madrigal is a song for several voices singing in harmony without instrumental accompaniment. The form flourished in Renaissance Europe, particularly Italy and England, typically setting secular poetry to intricate vocal arrangements. The term sometimes extends to any elaborate part-song: {The choir performed a selection of Elizabethan madrigals}.

Madrigals are vocal compositions for several voices, typically unaccompanied, that flourished in Renaissance Europe. The form involves intricate harmonies with voices weaving around each other: {The choir performed Italian madrigals}. Madrigal singing persists as a classical tradition, often associated with holiday concerts and Renaissance fairs. The singular is madrigal.

A madwoman is a woman who is insane or behaves in a wild, irrational manner. The term appears in Gothic literature and melodrama—the {madwoman in the attic} has become a critical trope for hidden female rage or suppressed identity. In casual use, it describes someone acting recklessly or with abandon: {She drove like a madwoman to get there on time}.

Madwomen is the plural of madwoman—women who are insane or act with wild abandon. The term carries the same ambiguity as its singular: it can mean clinically insane, furiously angry, or recklessly passionate. {The madwomen in the attic} evokes Victorian literary tropes of confined, mentally ill women. {They danced like madwomen until dawn.}

A maelstrom is a powerful whirlpool—a churning vortex of water that can pull objects under. The word comes from a famously turbulent strait off Norway's coast. Figuratively, a maelstrom is any violent, chaotic situation that threatens to overwhelm: {She found herself caught in a maelstrom of scandal and accusation}. The metaphor emphasizes being drawn into something beyond one's control.

A maestra is a female master or teacher, especially of music. The term appears most often for women who conduct orchestras or lead musical ensembles: {The maestra raised her baton and the orchestra fell silent}. Like its masculine counterpart maestro, maestra implies distinction and expertise.

A maestro is a master musician, especially a conductor or composer of classical music: {The maestro raised his baton}. The Italian word for master has been borrowed into English for distinguished artists generally, often with a hint of playful reverence: {He's the maestro of horror films}. The plural is maestros or maestri.

Maestros is the plural of maestro, a distinguished conductor or composer, or more broadly, a master of any art. The word comes from Italian and retains an Italian flavor: {The maestros of Italian opera shaped centuries of musical tradition}. It applies beyond music to anyone with exceptional skill: {the maestros of Silicon Valley}, {culinary maestros}.

A mafia is any organized criminal network, especially one based on family ties, ethnic solidarity, or regional loyalty. The term extends to any tight-knit group that controls access to power or resources: {the literary mafia}, {Hollywood mafia}. The word suggests secrecy, mutual protection, and ruthless enforcement of loyalty. (Capitalized Mafia refers specifically to the Sicilian or Italian-American crime syndicate.)

Mafiosi is the Italian plural of mafioso—members of the Mafia or similar organized crime groups. The term applies to those involved in the hierarchical criminal organizations originating in Sicily and later established in America: {The FBI surveilled known mafiosi in New York}. It sometimes extends figuratively to any tight-knit group operating by its own rules.

A mafioso is a member of the Mafia—the organized crime syndicates originating in Sicily and Italy, or their American counterparts. The term can apply to any participant in such organizations, from foot soldiers to bosses. More loosely, mafioso describes anyone who behaves like a gangster or operates through intimidation and backroom deals: {He ran the union like a mafioso}. Plural: mafiosi.

A magazine is a periodical publication containing articles, photographs, and advertisements, typically on a specific subject or for a general audience: {fashion magazines}, {I read about it in a magazine}. Magazine also means a storage chamber—the part of a gun holding ammunition before it feeds into the chamber, or a room where explosives or weapons are kept. The storage sense came first: a place where goods are deposited.

Magazines are periodical publications containing articles, photographs, and advertisements, typically printed on glossy paper and issued weekly or monthly: {fashion magazines}, {news magazines}. The word also names the ammunition storage component of a firearm—the detachable container holding cartridges that feed into the chamber. Both senses share the idea of a storehouse: the Arabic root meant warehouse.

A mage is a magician or wizard—someone who practices magic. The word appears almost exclusively in fantasy fiction and gaming, where it typically denotes a character class specializing in spells rather than physical combat: {The mage cast a fireball at the approaching orcs}. Outside these contexts, mage sounds archaic or affected.

Magenta is a vivid purplish-red color, sitting between red and blue on the spectrum. The color was named after the 1859 Battle of Magenta in Italy, where a newly synthesized dye gained fame around the same time. In color printing and digital displays, magenta is a primary color alongside cyan and yellow: {The printer is low on magenta ink}.

Mages is the plural of mage, a person who practices magic—a wizard, sorcerer, or magician. The word appears almost exclusively in fantasy fiction, video games, and role-playing contexts: {The party included two warriors and a mage}, {Mages can cast spells but have weak armor}. It carries a more serious, archaic tone than magician.

A maggot is the soft-bodied, legless larva of a fly, typically found in decaying organic matter where adult flies have laid their eggs. Maggots are pale, wormlike creatures that feed voraciously before pupating into adult flies. The word is used as a strong insult to call someone disgusting or contemptible: {You filthy maggot}. In fishing, maggots serve as popular bait.

Maggots are the larval form of flies—soft, legless, wormlike creatures that hatch from eggs laid in decaying organic matter. They feed voraciously on rotting flesh, garbage, or other decomposing material. In medicine, sterile maggots are sometimes used to clean wounds by consuming dead tissue. The word often carries connotations of filth and disgust: {The garbage was crawling with maggots}.

Magi is the plural of magus, referring to members of an ancient Persian priestly caste known for their expertise in astrology, dream interpretation, and religious ritual. In Christian tradition, the Magi are the wise men from the East who followed a star to visit the infant Jesus, bearing gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh: {The three magi arrived at the manger}. The word gives us magic.

Magic is a power or force that is credited to explain (usually good) things that happen when no logical explanation suffices. If you work magic, the suggestion is that you make something happen that would have seemed impossible. Before another noun, magic usually denotes an imaginary thing that has extraordinary powers (magic wand, magic bullet). Sometimes, magic is used to characterize highly creative and enjoyable works of art or experiences of these: The play was magic; it completed entranced us.

Magical describes things connected to magic—supernatural forces or practices that defy natural laws: {a magical incantation}, {magical powers}. More loosely, magical means enchanting or wonderfully delightful: {a magical evening}, {The light on the water was magical}. This second sense suggests something so special it feels touched by forces beyond the ordinary.

A magician is a person who performs magic. In entertainment, magicians do tricks—card tricks, sleight of hand, making things appear or disappear: {The magician pulled a rabbit from his hat}. In fantasy and folklore, a magician wields supernatural power, casting spells or summoning forces. Figuratively, someone with exceptional skill may be called a magician: {She's a magician with numbers}.

Magicians are people who perform magic. The word covers both entertainers who create illusions—card tricks, disappearing acts, sawing assistants in half—and figures in fantasy and folklore who wield supernatural powers: {Merlin was the most famous magician in Arthurian legend}. Someone exceptionally skilled at something may be called a magician: {She's a magician with numbers}.

A magistrate is a civil officer who administers the law, typically handling minor offenses and preliminary hearings. In the U.S., magistrates often conduct arraignments, set bail, and issue warrants. The term can also refer broadly to any public official with judicial or executive authority: {The local magistrate dismissed the case}. In some countries, magistrate denotes a lower-level judge in a system of tiered courts.

Magistrates is the plural of magistrate, a judicial officer with limited authority, typically handling minor criminal cases, preliminary hearings, or local disputes. In the UK, magistrates are often unpaid volunteers who hear cases in magistrates' courts. In the US, the term usually applies to judges in lower courts or those who issue warrants: {The magistrates dismissed the case for lack of evidence}.

Maglev is short for magnetic levitation, a technology that uses powerful magnets to lift and propel vehicles—typically trains—above a track without physical contact. The absence of friction allows for very high speeds and a smooth ride: {The maglev train connects the airport to the city center in eight minutes}.

Magma is molten rock beneath the earth's surface, held under pressure in the crust or mantle. When it reaches the surface through volcanic eruption, it becomes lava. The word extends metaphorically to any seething, formless source: {a magma of creative energy}, {the magma of political unrest}.

Magnanimity is generosity of spirit, especially toward rivals or those who have wronged you. The word implies rising above pettiness or the desire for revenge: {In victory, she showed magnanimity toward her defeated opponent}. Someone with magnanimity forgives slights, shares credit freely, and doesn't keep score. The quality suggests both moral elevation and a certain largeness of character—being too big to be brought down by small grievances.

A magnate is a powerful figure in business or industry—someone who has amassed great wealth and influence in a particular field: {a shipping magnate}, {a media magnate}, {an oil magnate}. The word implies not just wealth but dominance over an entire sector. It's slightly old-fashioned, evoking the industrial barons of the early twentieth century.

Magnates are powerful figures in business or industry—people who have accumulated wealth and influence in a particular field: {media magnates}, {oil magnates}, {real estate magnates}. The term suggests not just wealth but dominance and control over an entire sector. A magnate shapes markets rather than merely participating in them.

Magnesium is a lightweight metallic element, silvery-white and highly reactive. It burns with an intense white flame, making it useful in flares, fireworks, and photography flash powder. The body requires magnesium for hundreds of biochemical reactions; deficiency causes muscle cramps and fatigue. Magnesium alloys appear in aircraft, cars, and electronics where low weight matters.

A magnet is an object that attracts iron and certain other metals through an invisible force field. Magnets have two poles—north and south—and opposite poles attract while like poles repel. The word extends to anything that draws people or things powerfully: {The beach is a magnet for tourists}. A person with magnetic charm attracts others effortlessly.

Magnetic describes things that attract iron and certain other metals, or that relate to magnetism as a physical force: a magnetic {field}, magnetic {poles}. The word extends naturally to people or qualities that draw others in: a magnetic {personality}, magnetic {charm}. Someone magnetic commands attention and inspires fascination, as if exerting an invisible pull.

Magnetise is the British spelling of magnetize. To magnetise something is to give it magnetic properties—to make it attract iron or align with Earth's magnetic field. Figuratively, a person who magnetises others draws them in with compelling charm or presence: {She magnetised the room the moment she walked in}.

Magnetism is the force by which certain materials attract or repel each other—the invisible pull between a magnet and iron, or between two magnets. The term extends to personal charm or charisma: {Her magnetism drew people to her}. Someone with magnetism commands attention without obvious effort. In physics, magnetism is one of the fundamental forces, closely linked to electricity.

Magnetize means to make something magnetic by exposing it to a magnetic field, allowing it to attract iron or other magnetic materials. The word extends naturally to people and situations: a magnetizing personality draws others in, and a speaker can magnetize an audience. {The screwdriver had been magnetized and kept picking up small screws.} {She magnetized everyone at the party with her stories.}

Magnetized describes something that has been given magnetic properties—able to attract iron or align with magnetic fields. A magnetized needle points north; magnetized screwdriver tips hold screws in place. Figuratively, to be magnetized is to be powerfully drawn: {The crowd stood magnetized by her performance}. The spelling magnetised appears in British English.

A magneto is a small electrical generator that uses permanent magnets to produce current, typically for ignition in internal combustion engines. Before modern electronic ignition, magnetos were standard in automobiles, aircraft, and motorcycles: {The plane's magneto failed on takeoff}. They remain common in lawnmowers, chainsaws, and vintage vehicles because they work without a battery. (Capitalized Magneto is a comic book character.)

Magnets is the plural of magnet—objects that produce magnetic fields and attract iron, steel, and certain other metals. Magnets can be natural (lodestone) or manufactured. Figuratively, anything that draws people or things acts as a magnet: {The beach is a magnet for tourists}. Fridge magnets hold notes and photos to refrigerator doors.

Magnification is the process of making something appear larger than it actually is, or the degree to which something has been enlarged.
