A meltdown is a catastrophic failure in a nuclear reactor where the core overheats and melts, potentially releasing radiation. The word extends to any dramatic collapse or breakdown: a financial {meltdown}, an emotional {meltdown}. When someone—especially a child—has a meltdown, they lose control in a fit of crying, screaming, or rage: {She had a meltdown when they ran out of her favorite cereal}.

Meltdowns is the plural of meltdown, which originally described a nuclear reactor's catastrophic overheating when its core melts through containment. The term now commonly describes emotional breakdowns—intense episodes of distress, frustration, or anger: {She had a meltdown when her flight was canceled}. Financial meltdowns describe market collapses: {the 2008 economic meltdown}.

Melted is the past tense and past participle of melt—to change from solid to liquid through heat. Ice melts, butter melts, chocolate melts. Figuratively, resistance or coldness can melt: {Her anger melted when she saw his face}. {The melted cheese stretched from the pizza to his plate.}

Melting is the process of changing from solid to liquid through heat. Ice melts into water; butter melts in a pan. The word extends to gradual disappearance: {The crowd melted away}. Figuratively, melting describes emotional softening: {Her anger melted when she saw his face}. A melting {pot} is a place where diverse elements blend together.

Melts is the verb melt in the third person singular: ice melts, snow melts, butter melts. As a noun, melts are dishes featuring melted cheese: {tuna melts}, {patty melts}. Melt also refers to the spleen of an animal, especially as used in cooking, making melts its plural.

Meltwater is water produced by melting snow or ice, especially from glaciers, ice sheets, or seasonal snowpack. It feeds rivers and streams during spring thaw and plays a significant role in hydrology and climate science: {Meltwater from the Himalayas supplies rivers across South Asia}. As glaciers retreat, meltwater contributes to rising sea levels.

Melty describes something in a soft, yielding state from heat—not fully melted but getting there: {melty cheese on a burger}, {melty chocolate chips}. The word is informal and evocative, often used for foods at that appealing moment between solid and liquid. It can also describe a warm, soft emotional state: {feeling all melty inside}.

A member is a part of a larger whole—someone who belongs to a group, organization, or body: {a member of the team}, {club members}, {member nations of the UN}. It extends to constituent parts: the members of an equation, a structural member in architecture. Member is also a formal or euphemistic term for the penis, from the sense of a bodily limb or organ.

Members are those who belong to a group, organization, or category. A club has members, a family has members, Congress has members. Body parts are also members: {the members of the body}. In older or humorous usage, member refers to the penis—a euphemism that sounds clinical or deliberately quaint.

Membership is the state of belonging to a group, organization, or institution: {Her membership in the club lapsed}. It also refers collectively to the members themselves: {The membership voted to increase dues}. A membership can be the credential or subscription that grants access: {I renewed my gym membership}.

Memberships is the plural of membership—the state of belonging to a group, organization, or club. It often refers to multiple affiliations: {She maintains memberships at three different gyms}. Memberships can also mean the collective body of members: {The memberships of both unions voted to strike}.

A membrane is a thin, flexible layer that separates, encloses, or lines something. In biology, cell membranes control what passes in and out; mucous membranes line body cavities. The word extends to any thin barrier: {a membrane of ice on the pond}, {the membrane of a drum}. Membrane suggests both separation and selective permeability—keeping things apart while allowing some exchange.

Membranes is the plural of membrane, a thin flexible layer that covers, lines, or separates structures. In biology, membranes enclose cells and organs: {mucous membranes}, {cell membranes}. The term extends to thin sheets in technology and manufacturing: {a semipermeable membrane filters impurities}. Figuratively, a membrane suggests any subtle barrier: {the membrane between waking and sleep}.

A meme is an idea or theme that becomes popular through repetition and spreads from one person or group to another. Today, many memes spread on the Internet, and are often called Internet memes. Some writers make an analogy between memes and genes. They share the qualities of reproducing over time, and sometimes changing or evolving as new groups of people express them.

A memecoin is a cryptocurrency created around an internet meme, joke, or viral trend rather than any technical innovation or practical utility. Dogecoin, featuring the Shiba Inu dog meme, was the original; countless imitators followed. Memecoins are highly speculative, often pump-and-dump schemes where early buyers profit while latecomers lose: {I put fifty bucks into a memecoin and lost it all in a week}.

Memeing is participating in meme culture—creating, sharing, or riffing on internet memes. The word treats meme as a verb: {I spent all morning memeing instead of working}. It can describe both casual sharing and more deliberate comedic creation: {She's been memeing about the election nonstop}.

A memelord is someone with exceptional skill at creating, curating, or deploying internet memes—the humorous images, videos, and formats that spread virally online. The term combines appreciation for meme fluency with gentle mockery of taking that fluency too seriously: {He thinks he's such a memelord because his posts get shared}. Often self-applied with ironic swagger.

A memento is an object kept as a reminder of a person, place, or event: {She kept the ticket stub as a memento of their first date}. Mementos are typically small and portable—photographs, souvenirs, keepsakes. The word emphasizes the object's power to evoke memory rather than its monetary value.

Mementos are objects kept as reminders of people, places, or experiences—souvenirs of personal significance. A concert ticket stub, a dried flower, a photograph: {She kept mementos from every trip she took}. The word comes from Latin for "remember." Plural of memento; also spelled mementoes.

Memes are cultural elements—images, videos, phrases, ideas—that spread rapidly through imitation and sharing, especially online. The term originally described any unit of cultural transmission (fashion, catchphrases, rituals), but now primarily refers to internet content that gets copied and modified: {That format became one of the year's biggest memes}. Memes often layer humor through remixing familiar templates with new captions or contexts.

A memo is a written message, typically brief and internal to an organization. Short for memorandum, it conveys information, instructions, or policy: {The boss sent a memo about the new dress code}. Memos are more formal than emails but less formal than official letters. The plural is memos; memoranda sounds stuffy.

A memoir is a written account of personal experiences, typically covering a particular period or theme rather than an entire life. Unlike autobiography, which aims for comprehensive life history, memoir focuses selectively: {her memoir of growing up in rural Georgia}, {a war memoir}. The plural memoirs often suggests a fuller retrospective, especially by public figures: {He published his memoirs after leaving office}.

Memoirs are a written account of someone's life and experiences, typically composed by that person. Unlike autobiography, which aims to cover an entire life comprehensively, memoirs tend to focus on particular periods, themes, or relationships that shaped the author. The word is almost always plural in this sense, even when referring to a single book: {She published her memoirs after retiring from politics}. Politicians, celebrities, and survivors of notable events frequently write memoirs, though the genre welcomes anyone with a story worth telling.

Memorabilia are objects kept or collected because of their associations with memorable people, places, or events. The word usually implies items connected to popular culture, sports, or history: {Beatles memorabilia}, {World War II memorabilia}, {sports memorabilia}. The singular memorabile exists but is rarely used; memorabilia functions as both singular and plural in practice.

Memorable describes something worth remembering or likely to be remembered: {a memorable performance}, {a memorable vacation}. The word implies positive distinction—experiences, occasions, or achievements that stand out from the ordinary. Something can be memorable for bad reasons too, though {unforgettable} often handles that work: {a memorable disaster}.

Memorial describes something that preserves memory of a person or event: a memorial {service}, a memorial {plaque}, {Memorial Day}. As a noun, a memorial is a structure or ceremony honoring the dead: {the Lincoln Memorial}, {a memorial for victims of the attack}. The word emphasizes remembrance over celebration—memorials typically mark loss or sacrifice.

To memorialize is to preserve the memory of someone or something, typically through a monument, ceremony, or formal tribute: {The statue memorializes soldiers who died in the war}. The word implies deliberate, often public acts of remembrance—naming buildings, establishing holidays, erecting plaques. It can also mean to address a formal petition to an authority, though this sense is rare today.

Memorials are objects, structures, or events that preserve the memory of someone or something—typically the dead or significant historical moments. A memorial can be a monument, a ceremony, a scholarship fund, or a dedicated day: {the Lincoln Memorial}, {a memorial service}, {Memorial Day}. The word emphasizes remembrance rather than celebration.

Memories are mental records of past experiences, the things we remember. A memory can be vivid or hazy, cherished or painful: {childhood memories}, {fond memories of summer camp}. The plural often suggests a collection of recollections from a particular time or place: {sharing memories at a funeral}, {the trip gave us wonderful memories}. To do something {from memory} is to rely on what you remember rather than notes or references.

Memorise is the British spelling of memorize—to commit something to memory so it can be recalled later: {She memorised the poem for class}, {He's terrible at memorising names}. The word implies deliberate effort rather than incidental remembering.

Memorization is the process of committing something to memory through deliberate effort—repeating facts, rehearsing lines, or drilling vocabulary until it sticks. The term often carries a slight negative connotation in educational contexts, implying rote learning without deeper understanding: {The class emphasized memorization over critical thinking}. Still, some knowledge simply requires it: {Memorization of the multiplication tables takes practice}.

To memorize is to commit something to memory so you can recall it later without reference: {I memorized the poem for class}, {She memorized his phone number}. The word implies deliberate effort—you memorize what doesn't stick naturally. What's memorized may be recited verbatim or simply retained as knowledge.

Memorized describes something committed to memory, learned so thoroughly it can be recalled without reference: {She recited the memorized poem without looking at the page}. The word implies deliberate effort rather than casual familiarity—you memorize a speech, a phone number, lines for a play. {He had the directions memorized before leaving}.

Memorizing is the process of committing something to memory through deliberate effort—repeating facts, rehearsing lines, or drilling information until it sticks: {She spent hours memorizing vocabulary for the exam}. The word often implies rote learning rather than deep understanding: {He memorized the formula without grasping the concept}.

Memory is the faculty by which the mind stores and recalls information. It also refers to the information itself: {I have fond memories of that summer}. A good memory retains much; a bad memory loses things. {In memory of} honors someone deceased. To do something {from memory} is to rely on recall rather than reference. In computing, memory is storage capacity for data—the space a device uses to hold information while working.

Men is the plural of man—adult male humans. Beyond the literal, men often stands for humanity generally: {all men are created equal}, {the rights of men}. This generic use, once standard, now strikes many as exclusionary, prompting shifts toward gender-neutral alternatives like people or humans. {The men's room} is the bathroom for males.

Menace is a threat or source of danger: {The abandoned building became a menace to the neighborhood}. As a verb, to menace is to threaten harm or pose a danger: {Storm clouds menaced the coastline}. A person who causes trouble may be called a menace, sometimes affectionately: {That toddler is an absolute menace}.

Menaces are things that threaten harm or danger, or people who behave in a threatening way. The word carries a sense of looming trouble rather than immediate attack: {The abandoned building became a menace to the neighborhood}. A person described as a menace is either genuinely dangerous or, more casually, just annoying and disruptive: {That kid is a menace on his skateboard}. As a verb, to menace is to threaten or intimidate someone.

Menacing describes something that conveys threat or danger. A menacing figure looms with implied violence. A menacing tone suggests harm may follow. The word emphasizes the suggestion of threat rather than its execution—something menacing hasn't struck yet but seems about to: {He took a menacing step forward}. {Storm clouds gathered with menacing speed}.

In a manner that suggests threat or danger. A dog may growl menacingly, a storm cloud may loom menacingly, or a villain may speak menacingly. The word often appears in descriptions of body language or atmosphere: {He leaned menacingly toward her across the table}.
clues: As if about to cause harm

definition: A menagerie is a collection of wild or exotic animals kept in captivity for exhibition. The word often evokes older, less humane forms of display—private collections of aristocrats or traveling shows—before modern zoos emerged. Figuratively, any diverse or motley assortment of people or things: {The office was a menagerie of oddballs and misfits}.

Mend is mainly a verb synonymous with repair, but used in particular contexts. In American English, mend is typically used with non-mechanical things: you can mend clothing, relationships, behavior, or broken hearts, for example. Usage is broader in British English, where you can mend damage to your car. A mend is an act of mending, or the physical evidence of mending. If you’re on the mend, you’re getting better. Mending fences usually means improving damaged relationships.

Mended is the past tense of mend, meaning repaired or restored to working condition. Clothes are mended by sewing, fences by patching, bones by healing. Relationships and hearts can also be mended: {They mended their differences after years apart}. {A mended sock}, {a mended friendship}.

Mending is the act of repairing something, especially clothing: {a basket of mending} refers to items waiting to be patched or sewn. The word implies restoration rather than replacement—fixing what's torn or broken. Relationships can also need mending: {They're on the mend} suggests recovery or reconciliation is underway.

Mends is the verb form of mend—to repair or fix something broken or damaged: {She mends clothes for extra income}. Beyond physical repair, mend applies to relationships and health: {They're trying to mend their marriage}, {He's mending after surgery}. To {mend fences} is to restore good relations after a disagreement. {Mend your ways} means to improve your behavior.

Menial describes work that is lowly, tedious, and requires little skill—tasks like scrubbing floors, washing dishes, or running errands. The word carries connotations of servitude and low status: {menial labor}, {menial jobs}. As a noun, a menial is a domestic servant or someone who performs such tasks: {treated like a menial}.

Meningitis is inflammation of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord. It can be caused by bacterial, viral, or fungal infection, with bacterial meningitis being the most dangerous. Symptoms include severe headache, fever, and stiff neck. {The college required meningitis vaccinations for all dormitory residents.}

Menopause is the permanent end of menstruation, typically occurring in women between ages 45 and 55. The transition often brings symptoms like hot flashes, mood changes, and sleep disturbances. Someone is considered to have reached menopause after twelve consecutive months without a period. {She started hormone therapy to manage her menopause symptoms.}

A menorah is a candelabrum used in Jewish worship. The traditional menorah has seven branches and is an ancient symbol of Judaism, depicted on Israel's state emblem. The nine-branched menorah, called a hanukkiah, is lit during Hanukkah, with one candle added each night: {We gathered around the menorah on the first night of Hanukkah}.

Menorahs is the plural of menorah, a candelabrum used in Jewish worship. The ancient Temple menorah had seven branches. The Hanukkah menorah (also called a hanukkiah) has nine branches—one for each night of the festival plus a helper candle to light the others: {The children placed their menorahs in the window}.

Mensch comes from Yiddish (and German) meaning person, but in English it carries strong connotations of character. A mensch is someone of integrity and honor—a person you can rely on to do the right thing. The word implies warmth, decency, and moral backbone: {He's a real mensch, always helping out}. To call someone a mensch is high praise.

Menstruating describes a woman or girl experiencing menstruation—the monthly discharge of blood and tissue from the uterus. The process typically lasts several days and occurs roughly every four weeks from puberty until menopause. {She was menstruating and didn't feel like swimming.}

Menstruation is the monthly discharge of blood and tissue from the uterus, occurring in women and girls of reproductive age who aren't pregnant. The process typically lasts three to seven days and marks the beginning of the menstrual cycle. Common synonyms include period and, informally, time of the month: {She gets bad cramps during menstruation}.

Mental means relating to the mind—its processes, states, and capacities: {mental health}, {mental arithmetic}, {a mental image}. In British slang, mental means crazy or wildly enthusiastic: {The crowd went mental when the band came on}. A mental note is something you remember without writing down: {I made a mental note to call her back}.

Mentalism is the philosophical position that mental phenomena—thoughts, consciousness, beliefs—are fundamental to reality, not reducible to physical processes. In entertainment, mentalism refers to stage performances simulating psychic abilities like mind-reading, telepathy, or prediction: {The mentalist guessed the card I was thinking of}. A mentalist appears to read minds but relies on psychological techniques, suggestion, and showmanship.

A mentalist is a performer who appears to read minds, predict behavior, or demonstrate other seemingly supernatural mental abilities. The act typically relies on psychological techniques, keen observation, and showmanship rather than actual psychic powers. In British slang, mentalist describes someone who behaves erratically or seems crazy: {He's a complete mentalist on the football pitch}. The term also applies more neutrally to philosophers who study mental phenomena.
clues: One who seems to read minds

definition: Mentalists are performers who appear to read minds, predict outcomes, or demonstrate extraordinary mental powers. The acts typically involve suggestion, psychological techniques, and showmanship rather than claimed supernatural ability. A mentalist might guess what word you're thinking of or reveal the contents of a sealed envelope. The term also applies loosely to anyone focused on mental rather than physical approaches: {He's a mentalist—thinks you can will your way through anything}.

Mentality is a characteristic way of thinking—the mental habits and attitudes that shape how a person or group approaches the world. A {herd mentality} follows the crowd. A {siege mentality} sees threats everywhere. A {winning mentality} expects success. The word often carries slight judgment, implying the mindset is fixed or limiting: {I can't understand that mentality}.

A mentee is a person who receives guidance, advice, or training from a more experienced person—the mentor. The word is a back-formation from mentor, treating the -or ending as if it indicated the one doing the action. Though some consider it awkward or unnecessary, mentee has become standard in professional and educational contexts: {The program pairs mentees with executives in their field}.

Mentees are people receiving guidance from a mentor—someone more experienced in a field, profession, or skill. The relationship typically involves regular meetings where the mentor shares knowledge and advice: {She stays in touch with her former mentees}. The word is a back-formation from mentor, treating the -or ending as if it marked an agent acting upon someone else.

Menthol is a compound derived from peppermint oil that produces a cooling sensation on skin and mucous membranes. It appears in cough drops, topical pain relievers, and cigarettes: {menthol cigarettes}, {a menthol rub for chest congestion}. The cooling effect is a sensory illusion—menthol triggers cold receptors without actually lowering temperature.

To mention something is to refer to it briefly or in passing, without elaborate discussion: {She mentioned that she'd be late}. A mention is such a reference: {The article made no mention of the scandal}. Something {not worth mentioning} is too trivial to bring up. {Don't mention it} dismisses thanks—it was nothing.

A mentor is an experienced person who guides and advises someone less experienced, especially in professional or educational development: {She credits her mentor with helping her navigate the early years of her career}. The word comes from Mentor, the advisor to whom Odysseus entrusted his son. To mentor is to serve in this role: {He mentors young entrepreneurs}.

Mentored is the past tense of mentor, meaning to guide or advise someone less experienced. A mentor shares knowledge and provides support, typically in professional or educational contexts: {She mentored young lawyers at the firm}. Being mentored implies an ongoing relationship rather than a single interaction: {He was mentored by one of the industry's pioneers}.

Mentoring is the practice of guiding someone less experienced through advice, support, and example. A mentor shares knowledge and helps develop skills, whether in careers, academics, or personal growth: {The program pairs new teachers with veterans for mentoring}. The relationship implies ongoing investment rather than one-time instruction.

Mentors is the plural of mentor—a person who guides someone less experienced through advice, support, and example. The word comes from a character in Homer's Odyssey who counseled the young Telemachus. To mentor is to serve as such a guide: {She mentors new employees through their first year}. The term appears frequently in professional and academic contexts: {The program pairs students with industry mentors}.

Mentorship is a relationship in which an experienced person guides someone less experienced, offering advice, knowledge, and support for professional or personal development. The term emphasizes the ongoing nature of the relationship rather than any single act of guidance: {She credited her success to years of mentorship from senior colleagues}. {The program pairs new teachers with veterans for mentorship}.

A menu is a list of options. At a restaurant, the menu shows available dishes and their prices: {Can I see the menu?} In computing, a menu presents choices for the user to select from—a file menu, a dropdown menu. Any set of offerings can be called a menu: {a menu of investment options}.

Menudo is a traditional Mexican soup made with beef stomach (tripe) in a red chile pepper broth, often including hominy. It's considered a comfort food and folk remedy for hangovers, traditionally served on weekends and special occasions: {We had menudo after the wedding}. The dish requires hours of slow cooking to tenderize the tripe. (Capitalized Menudo was a Puerto Rican boy band.)

Menus is the plural of menu, a list of food and drink options available at a restaurant or other eating establishment. The word extends to any list of choices presented for selection, most notably in computing where menus display available commands or options in software applications. {The restaurant updates its menus seasonally.} {Navigate through the dropdown menus to find your settings.}

Meow is the characteristic cry of a cat, and the verb for making that sound: {The cat meowed at the door}. The spelling approximates the sound, with variants like miaow. Figuratively, meow can express catty approval or critique, often drawn out: {Meow, look at that dress}.

Meowing is the vocal sound cats make, or the act of making such sounds. Cats meow primarily to communicate with humans rather than other cats. The word can describe persistent or plaintive calling: {The kitten was meowing at the door}. Figuratively, someone meowing is whining or complaining: {Stop meowing about it and do something}.

Merc is informal for mercenary—a soldier hired to fight for a foreign army or private military force: {The company employed mercs as security contractors}. In gaming and online contexts, merc is also a verb meaning to kill or destroy decisively: {I got merced in the first round}. Merc occasionally shortens Mercury, especially for the defunct American car brand.

Mercenaries is the plural of mercenary—a soldier who fights for pay rather than patriotism or ideology. The term carries connotations of moral indifference: mercenaries fight for whoever pays, regardless of the cause. By extension, mercenary describes anyone motivated purely by money: {a mercenary attitude}, {mercenary lawyers}. {The company hired mercenaries to guard the oil fields.}

A mercenary is a soldier who fights for pay rather than loyalty or ideology, hired by a foreign government or private entity. The word carries connotations of fighting purely for money, without conviction. As an adjective, mercenary describes anyone motivated primarily by financial gain: {His interest in her seemed mercenary}. {The company hired mercenaries to guard the compound}.

Merch is an informal clipping of merchandise, used especially to refer to branded products sold by bands, sports teams, influencers, or entertainment franchises. T-shirts, hats, posters, and other items bearing logos or imagery fall under this umbrella. {I picked up some merch at the concert.} The word also functions as a verb meaning to sell or promote such goods: {They're merching hard on this tour.}

Merchandise is goods available for sale, especially in retail contexts: {The store displayed its merchandise in the window}. The word often suggests commercial products generally rather than specific items. As a verb, to merchandise is to promote or sell goods, or to market something aggressively. Licensed merchandise ({merch} for short) refers to products bearing logos, characters, or branding from entertainment properties.

Merchandising is the promotion and sale of goods, especially through strategic display and presentation in retail settings. It covers how products are packaged, priced, and positioned to attract buyers. The term also refers to the licensing of branded products tied to entertainment properties: {Star Wars merchandising generated billions in toy sales}. As a verb form, merchandising describes the ongoing activity of managing product presentation.

A merchant is a person or business that buys and sells goods, especially one who trades in large quantities or deals in foreign commerce. The term carries a slightly old-fashioned or formal quality in everyday speech, though it remains current in compounds: {merchant marine}, {merchant bank}, {wine merchant}. In modern contexts, merchant often appears in payment processing—the business that accepts credit card transactions.

Merchants are people who buy and sell goods, especially those who trade in quantity or operate businesses. The word suggests commerce at a meaningful scale—not someone selling a used lamp, but someone whose occupation is trade: {The merchants of Venice grew wealthy on Eastern goods}. A merchant {ship} or merchant {marine} carries commercial cargo. In compounds, merchant can specify what's sold: {wine merchant}, {arms merchant}. The term sounds slightly formal or historical in everyday speech, where retailer or seller often substitutes.

Mercies is the plural of mercy—acts of compassion, forgiveness, or forbearance toward those in one's power. The word often appears in religious contexts, where divine mercies are blessings or instances of God's compassion: {His mercies are new every morning}. To be {at the mercy of} or {left to the mercies of} someone or something is to be vulnerable to their treatment, often with ironic implication that little mercy will be shown: {abandoned to the tender mercies of the tax auditor}.

Merciful describes someone who shows mercy—compassion or restraint toward those they could punish or harm. A merciful judge gives a lighter sentence; a merciful God forgives sins. The word implies power held back: {The victor was merciful to the defeated}. By extension, merciful can describe welcome relief from suffering: {Death came as a merciful release}.

Merciless means showing no mercy—cruel, relentless, or unsparing. A merciless {critic} offers no gentleness; a merciless {sun} beats down without relief. The word emphasizes the absence of compassion where it might be expected or hoped for: {The invaders were merciless with the civilian population}.

Mercurial describes rapid, unpredictable shifts in mood or behavior—someone whose temperament changes like quicksilver. The word comes from Mercury, the swift-footed Roman messenger god, and from mercury, the liquid metal that moves erratically when spilled. A mercurial person might be charming one moment and irritable the next: {Her mercurial temperament made her difficult to work with}. The word often carries a note of brilliance alongside the volatility.

Mercury is a silver-white metallic element that remains liquid at room temperature, also called quicksilver. It flows and beads distinctively, historically used in thermometers, barometers, and dental fillings before its toxicity was fully understood. The adjective mercurial, meaning volatile or unpredictable, derives from the planet rather than the element directly. {The mercury rose to 98 degrees.} (Capitalized Mercury is the planet or Roman god.)

Mercy is compassion shown by someone who has authority or power over someone who does not. In this meaning it is often used in religious contexts. As an exclamation, mercy is typically used by older speakers as a spontaneous expression of dismay or shock. It is probably a shortening of “Lord have mercy.”

Mere diminishes what follows—it signals that something is only what it is and nothing more: {a mere child}, {mere speculation}, {a mere formality}. The word emphasizes smallness, insignificance, or insufficiency: {The mere thought of it made her anxious}. Separately, mere is a literary or archaic word for a lake or pond, surviving mainly in British place names.

Merengue is a style of dance music originating in the Dominican Republic, characterized by a fast two-beat rhythm and typically featuring accordion, saxophone, and güira (a metal scraper). The accompanying dance involves partners in close hold moving their hips in sync with the beat: {The band played merengue until midnight}. Not to be confused with meringue, the whipped egg-white confection.

Merfolk are mythical sea creatures with a human upper body and a fish tail below the waist. The term covers both mermaids (female) and mermen (male), useful when referring to the species generally rather than one sex: {The legend spoke of merfolk guarding the sunken treasure}. Common in fantasy fiction and folklore worldwide.

Merge means to combine into a single entity. Traffic lanes merge into one; companies merge to form a larger corporation; two rivers merge at a confluence. In computing, to merge is to combine files, code branches, or datasets: {We need to merge these changes before the release}. The word implies a blending where the original parts lose their separate identity.

Merged describes things that have been combined into a single unit. Separate companies merge to form one; lanes of traffic merge into fewer lanes; files or accounts get merged when consolidated. The word emphasizes that distinct elements have joined together: {The two departments were merged last year}. {Our merged data showed interesting patterns}.

A merger is the combining of two or more entities into one. Most often it describes companies joining together: {The merger created the largest airline in the country}. Mergers differ from acquisitions in that they suggest more equal partnership, though the distinction blurs in practice. The word extends to any joining of separate things into a unified whole.

Mergers is the plural of merger—a combination of two or more companies into a single entity. In business, mergers differ from acquisitions: a merger implies roughly equal partners joining forces, while an acquisition suggests one company absorbing another. {The merger created the world's largest automaker.} {Mergers and acquisitions} is a common phrase in corporate finance.

Merging is the act of combining two or more things into one. Traffic lanes merge when they converge into fewer lanes: {The sign warned of merging traffic ahead}. Companies merge when they combine operations. In computing, merging combines files or code branches: {I spent the morning merging pull requests}. The word emphasizes gradual blending rather than abrupt joining.

Meridian has meanings that cluster around the idea of a defining line or peak. In geography, a meridian is an imaginary line running from pole to pole, marking longitude: {the prime meridian passes through Greenwich}. In astronomy, the celestial meridian is where the sun reaches its highest point at noon. From this comes the figurative sense of a peak or zenith: {the meridian of his career}. In traditional Chinese medicine, meridians are pathways through which vital energy flows.

Meridians are imaginary lines running from pole to pole on a globe, used to measure longitude: {The prime meridian passes through Greenwich, England}. In traditional Chinese medicine and acupuncture, meridians are channels through which vital energy flows in the body. The term suggests lines of connection or pathways, whether geographic or anatomical.

Meringue is a light, airy confection made from whipped egg whites and sugar, baked until crisp on the outside and soft within. It appears as a topping on pies—especially lemon meringue—or shaped into cookies and shells for desserts like pavlova. The texture ranges from marshmallow-soft to shatteringly crisp depending on preparation.

Meringues are light, airy confections made from whipped egg whites and sugar, baked until crisp on the outside. They can be served alone as cookies, used as pie toppings, or shaped into shells for holding fruit and cream: {The lemon meringue pie had peaks of golden meringue}. The texture ranges from crisp throughout to marshmallow-soft inside.

Merino is a type of fine, soft wool prized for high-quality textiles, or the fabric made from it. The wool comes from Merino sheep, a breed known for exceptionally fine fibers: {a merino sweater}, {merino base layers for hiking}. The term often appears in clothing descriptions emphasizing warmth without bulk.

Merit is worth or excellence that earns recognition or reward. A proposal may be {judged on its merits}—its intrinsic qualities rather than who proposed it. To merit something is to deserve it: {The case merits further investigation}. The plural merits often refers to the substantive aspects of a legal case, as opposed to procedural matters.

Meritocracy is a system in which advancement and rewards are based on individual ability and achievement rather than wealth, family connections, or social class. The term often carries an aspirational tone—{a true meritocracy would reward hard work}—but it's frequently used critically to question whether such systems actually exist or whether they merely justify existing inequalities. Someone who believes in meritocratic principles holds that people should rise or fall based on their own talents and efforts.

Meritocratic describes a system where advancement depends on ability and achievement rather than wealth, connections, or inherited status. A meritocratic workplace promotes based on performance; a meritocratic society rewards talent and effort. The word often carries idealistic overtones—critics argue that supposedly meritocratic systems still favor the privileged: {The tech industry claims to be meritocratic, but nepotism thrives}.

Merits are the qualities that make something worthy of praise or reward. To judge something {on its merits} is to evaluate it based on its actual qualities rather than prejudice or irrelevant factors. The verb means to deserve: {The proposal merits serious consideration}. {Her work merits recognition}.

A merlin is a small falcon found across the Northern Hemisphere, known for its swift, agile flight and ability to catch birds on the wing. Compact and fierce, merlins hunt in open country and were historically used in falconry, particularly by noblewomen. {A merlin darted across the meadow in pursuit of a sparrow.} (Capitalized Merlin is the legendary wizard.)

Merlot is a dark blue grape variety used to make red wine, and the wine made from it. The grape produces soft, fruity wines with less tannin than cabernet sauvignon, making it approachable for casual drinkers: {a glass of merlot}, {the merlot was smooth and easy to drink}. Merlot is one of the primary grapes in Bordeaux blends and is widely planted in California, Chile, and Italy. (Sometimes capitalized as Merlot, especially on wine labels.)

A mermaid is a mythical sea creature with a woman's upper body and a fish's tail. Mermaids appear in folklore worldwide, usually as beautiful beings who lure sailors or grant wishes. The word covers the female; the male equivalent is merman. {She dreamed of being a mermaid as a child.}

Mermaids are mythical sea creatures with a woman's upper body and a fish's tail. They appear in folklore worldwide, often as beautiful beings who lure sailors or grant wishes. The male equivalent is a merman. {She dressed as a mermaid for Halloween}. The image persists in children's stories, logos, and coastal kitsch.

A merman is the male counterpart to a mermaid—a mythical sea creature with a human upper body and a fish tail. Mermen appear less frequently in folklore and popular culture than mermaids, though they figure in myths from many traditions. The plural is mermen.

Mermen is the plural of merman, the male counterpart to a mermaid—a mythical creature with a human upper body and a fish tail. Mermen appear in folklore and fantasy as ocean-dwelling beings, sometimes benevolent, sometimes dangerous. {The legend told of mermen who lured sailors to their doom.}

Merpeople are mythical beings with a human upper body and a fish tail instead of legs. They appear in folklore worldwide, from ancient sirens to Disney's Ariel. Merpeople is the gender-neutral alternative to mermaids and mermen: {The novel featured a civilization of merpeople living beneath the waves}.

Merrier is the comparative form of merry—more cheerful, more festive, more full of good spirits. The phrase {the more the merrier} welcomes additional people to join an activity or gathering, suggesting that larger groups enhance enjoyment.

Merriment is cheerful celebration or lively enjoyment, especially in a group: {The merriment continued late into the night}. The word suggests festive good humor—laughing, joking, general high spirits. It sounds slightly old-fashioned, appearing more often in descriptions of holiday gatherings or historical scenes than in casual conversation.

Merry means cheerful and lively, often in a social context involving celebration or drink. A merry {gathering} is festive and full of good spirits. To make merry is to celebrate with enjoyment: {They made merry late into the night}. The more the merrier welcomes additional company. Merry appears in seasonal greetings: {Merry Christmas}. Someone who's had a few drinks might be described as merry—tipsy but pleasantly so.

A merrymaker is someone engaged in lively celebration or festivity. The word suggests active participation in fun—drinking, dancing, laughing—rather than passive attendance: {Merrymakers spilled out of the pub at closing time}. It carries a slightly old-fashioned or literary quality.

Merrymaking is lively celebration and festivity—the activities of people enjoying themselves together: {The merrymaking continued well past midnight}. The word suggests cheerful, often boisterous revelry: drinking, dancing, laughing. It has an old-fashioned quality that evokes holiday gatherings and communal joy rather than solitary pleasures.

Merrymen are the loyal followers of a legendary outlaw, most famously Robin Hood's band in Sherwood Forest. The term evokes a group of jovial companions united in mischief or rebellion: {Robin Hood and his merry men robbed from the rich}. Outside the legend, it occasionally describes any tight-knit group of enthusiastic helpers or accomplices.

A mesa is a flat-topped hill or mountain with steep sides, common in arid regions of the American Southwest. The word comes from Spanish for "table," describing the distinctive tabletop shape. Mesas are smaller than plateaus but share the same flat summit created by erosion of surrounding softer rock. {The trail wound up to the mesa overlooking the desert.} (Capitalized Mesa is a city in Arizona.)

Mesas are flat-topped hills or mountains with steep sides, common in arid regions of the American Southwest. The word comes from Spanish for table, which describes the shape exactly. A mesa is smaller than a plateau but larger than a butte—all three share the distinctive flat summit created by erosion of harder rock layers protecting softer stone beneath.

Mescaline is a psychedelic compound found naturally in certain cacti, especially peyote and San Pedro. It produces vivid hallucinations, altered perception of time and space, and intense sensory experiences. Mescaline has been used for centuries in Native American religious ceremonies and gained countercultural prominence in the 1960s. It is a controlled substance in most countries.

Mesh is a material or structure made of interlocking or woven strands with open spaces between them: {wire mesh}, {mesh fence}, {mesh bag}. The openings themselves are meshes. Gears mesh when their teeth interlock and work together. Figuratively, things mesh when they fit or work well together: {Our schedules don't mesh}. {The flavors mesh beautifully}.

Meshes is the plural of mesh—interlaced structures with regular openings, like nets, screens, or woven fabric: {The meshes of the fishing net were too wide to catch smaller fish}. In computing and 3D modeling, meshes are surfaces built from connected polygons. When gears mesh, their teeth interlock; when ideas mesh, they fit together coherently: {Their plans didn't mesh}.

Meshuga is Yiddish for crazy or senseless, used in English to describe someone acting irrationally or a situation that's absurd: {Have you gone meshuga?} {The whole plan is meshuga}. The word carries affectionate exasperation more often than clinical judgment. Also spelled meshugge, meshugah, or meshuggeneh.

Meshugah is Yiddish for crazy or senseless, used to describe people or ideas that seem absurd or irrational: {Don't listen to him, he's completely meshugah}. The word carries affection or exasperation rather than clinical judgment—calling someone meshugah suggests they're being foolish, not mentally ill. Also spelled meshuga, meshugge, or meshuggeneh.

Meshugga is Yiddish for crazy or senseless, borrowed into English to describe someone or something absurd, foolish, or mentally unhinged: {Don't listen to him, he's completely meshugga}. The word carries affectionate exasperation more often than clinical judgment. Also spelled meshuga, meshugge, or meshuggeneh.

To mesmerise is to capture someone's attention so completely that they seem entranced or spellbound: {The dancer mesmerised the audience}. The word derives from Franz Mesmer, an 18th-century physician who believed he could heal through "animal magnetism"—what we'd now call hypnosis. Something mesmerising holds you transfixed, unable to look away. British spelling; Americans write mesmerize.

Mesmerised (British spelling of mesmerized) describes being utterly captivated or spellbound, unable to look away or think of anything else: {The children sat mesmerised by the fireworks}. The word derives from Franz Mesmer, an 18th-century physician who popularized hypnosis. Something mesmerising holds attention completely, as if by hypnotic power.

Mesmerising describes something so captivating it holds attention completely, as if by a spell: {Her mesmerising performance left the audience breathless}. The word derives from Franz Mesmer, an 18th-century physician whose hypnotic techniques gave us mesmerise. British spelling; Americans write mesmerizing.
clues: So fascinating you cannot look away

definition: Mesmerism is an early theory of hypnotic influence, named after Franz Mesmer, who believed he could cure ailments through "animal magnetism"—invisible forces flowing between bodies. The term now describes any hypnotic or spellbinding influence: {The speaker held the crowd in a state of mesmerism}. To mesmerize is to captivate utterly.

To mesmerize someone is to capture their attention so completely that they become transfixed, unable to look away or think of anything else. The word derives from Franz Mesmer, an 18th-century physician who believed he could heal through what he called "animal magnetism"—a forerunner of hypnotism. Today mesmerize rarely suggests actual hypnosis; instead it describes being utterly captivated: {The dancer's movements mesmerized the audience}. A mesmerizing performance or view holds you spellbound.
clues: Leave someone unable to look away

definition: Mesmerized means captivated or transfixed, unable to look away or think of anything else. The word suggests being held spellbound, as if under a hypnotic influence: {She stood mesmerized by the flames}. Someone mesmerized by a performance or speaker is completely absorbed, their attention locked. The word comes from Franz Mesmer, an 18th-century physician who practiced hypnotism.

Mesmerizes is the third-person singular form of mesmerize, meaning to capture someone's attention so completely that they become transfixed or spellbound. The word derives from Franz Mesmer, an 18th-century physician who popularized hypnosis, though modern usage rarely implies actual hypnotic states. Something that mesmerizes holds you rapt, unable to look away: {The dancer's movements mesmerized the audience}. A mesmerizing performance or view is one that captivates utterly.

Mesmerizing describes something that captures attention so completely you can't look away. A mesmerizing performance holds the audience spellbound; a mesmerizing pattern draws the eye and won't release it. The word suggests being transfixed, almost hypnotized: {The flames were mesmerizing}. From mesmerize, after Franz Mesmer, an 18th-century practitioner of hypnotism.
clues: So fascinating you cannot look away

definition: Mesquite is a thorny shrub or small tree native to the American Southwest and Mexico, common in arid landscapes. The wood burns slowly and produces a distinctive smoky flavor prized in barbecue: {mesquite-grilled steak}, {mesquite chips}. The plant produces edible seed pods once important to indigenous diets.

A mess is an undesirable, disorderly situation (your room is a mess, she got into a mess with the police). If you make a mess, your unskillful action has a bad result. A different mess has to do with communal meals. A mess hall or mess tent is where these happen; a mess kit has cooking and eating utensils. If you mess something up, you make a mess of it. If you mess with someone, you interfere with them in an unwelcome way. If you mess around, you are either behaving in a silly way or are in an adulterous relationship.

A message is information sent from one party to another. Messages can be spoken, written, or transmitted electronically: {I left a message on her voicemail}, {Send me a message when you arrive}. The word extends to underlying meaning or moral: {The movie's message about greed was heavy-handed}. To message someone is to communicate with them, especially digitally. To {get the message} is to understand what's being conveyed, often something implicit.

A messageboard is an online forum where users post text-based messages organized into topics or threads, allowing asynchronous conversation among participants. Unlike real-time chat, messages remain visible for others to read and respond to over time. Messageboards were foundational to early internet communities and remain active today, though the term has largely given way to simply {forum} or {board}. {I found the answer on a vintage car messageboard.}

Messageboards are websites where users post text messages organized by topic, creating threaded conversations that others can read and respond to. Unlike real-time chat, posts remain visible indefinitely, building archives of discussion. Messageboards flourished in the early internet era and still serve niche communities: {I found the answer on a photography messageboard}. Also spelled as two words or as *message boards*.

Messages are communications sent from one person or system to another. The word covers everything from handwritten notes to texts to voicemails: {I left you three messages}. In computing, messages are data packets exchanged between programs or devices. To get the message is to understand what someone means, even if unstated: {After being ignored twice, she got the message}.

Messaging is the activity of sending and receiving messages, especially through digital platforms like texting, email, or apps designed for the purpose. The term encompasses both the technology and the practice: {I prefer messaging to phone calls.} In business and politics, messaging also refers to the strategic crafting of communications to convey a particular image or idea: {The campaign needs to work on its messaging about healthcare.}

Messed is the past tense of mess, carrying its meanings of disorder and bungling. Something messed up is disordered, damaged, or psychologically troubled: {The divorce really messed him up}. To get messed up is to become intoxicated. {I messed around on my phone all morning} means wasting time. {They messed with the wrong person} means provoking unwisely.

A messenger is someone who carries messages or delivers items from one party to another. The role is ancient—royal courts had messengers, and gods sent celestial ones. Today the word often refers to courier services: {The contract arrived by messenger}. Messenger also names communication apps: {Send it to me on messenger}. To {shoot the messenger} is to blame the bearer of bad news rather than its source.

Messengers is the plural of messenger—people who carry messages or deliver communications between parties. The term extends to anyone or anything that conveys information: {The messengers brought news from the front}. In biology, messenger RNA carries genetic instructions. Courier services employ messengers for package delivery. {Don't shoot the messenger} warns against blaming bearers of bad news.

Messes is the plural of mess—states of disorder, dirty conditions, or difficult situations. {The kids left messes everywhere.} {She's gotten herself into some real messes.} In military contexts, messes are dining halls where personnel eat together: {Officers' messes were separate from enlisted quarters.}
clues: Situations that got out of hand

definition: A messiah is a savior or liberator, someone expected to rescue a group from dire circumstances. The term often carries ironic or skeptical undertones when applied to secular figures: {Tech investors are always looking for the next messiah}. Someone with a {messiah complex} believes they're destined to save others. (Capitalized Messiah is the religious title.)

Messiahs is the plural of messiah, a savior or liberator. In Jewish tradition, the Messiah is an anticipated king who will deliver the Jewish people. Christians apply the title to Jesus Christ. Lowercase, messiah extends to any person regarded as a savior of a cause or group: {The tech industry keeps looking for messiahs to solve its problems}. False messiahs have appeared throughout history.

Messianic relates to a messiah—a savior or liberator figure. In Jewish tradition, it describes expectations of a future anointed king; in Christianity, it refers to Jesus Christ as that fulfillment. More broadly, messianic describes zealous belief in a transformative cause or leader: {messianic fervor}, {a messianic vision for social change}. Someone with a {messianic complex} believes they're destined to save others.

Messy describes disorder, untidiness, or lack of cleanliness. A messy room has things scattered about. A messy eater gets food everywhere. The word extends to situations that are complicated or unpleasant to handle: {a messy divorce}, {messy emotions}. Messy implies something that should be tidier but isn't—whether physical clutter or tangled affairs.

Mestizo refers to a person of mixed European and Indigenous American ancestry, particularly in Latin America. The term originated during Spanish colonization to categorize people in the racial hierarchy, ranking below those of pure European descent. Today it remains common in Latin American countries as both demographic category and cultural identity: {Mexico's population is predominantly mestizo}. The word carries different connotations depending on context—neutral census terminology in some countries, contested colonial legacy in others.

Met is the past tense and past participle of meet. Two people who have met have encountered each other: {We met at a conference in 2019}. To have met a requirement or standard is to have satisfied it. To have met with something is to have experienced it: {The proposal met with resistance}. (Capitalized Met refers to the Metropolitan Opera or Metropolitan Museum of Art.)

Meta describes something that refers to or comments on itself—a meta joke is a joke about jokes, a meta movie is a film about filmmaking. The term comes from Greek meaning "after" or "beyond," but in contemporary usage it signals self-reference or self-awareness: {The show got very meta in its final season}. In gaming and competitive contexts, meta refers to the most effective tactics available—the dominant strategies that emerge from how a game is actually played rather than how designers intended: {What's the current meta for that character?} (Capitalized Meta is the technology company.)
clues: When something examines its own nature

definition: Metabolism is the set of chemical processes by which a living organism converts food into energy and builds or repairs tissue. A {fast metabolism} burns calories quickly; a {slow metabolism} stores them. The word extends to any transformative process: {the metabolism of a city}, {the metabolism of ideas}. Metabolic is the adjective: {metabolic rate}, {metabolic disorder}.

Metadata is data about data—information that describes, categorizes, or manages other information. A digital photo's metadata includes the date taken, camera settings, and location. A book's metadata covers author, title, publisher, and ISBN. Email headers, file properties, and database tags are all metadata. The term appears frequently in discussions of digital privacy, since metadata can reveal patterns even when content remains hidden: {They didn't read your messages, but the metadata showed who you called and when}.

Metagame refers to strategy that operates outside or above the game itself. In competitive games, the metagame is the evolving landscape of dominant strategies, popular character picks, and counterstrategies that players must understand beyond the basic rules: {The metagame shifted after the patch nerfed aggressive decks}. More broadly, metagaming means using external knowledge or manipulating situations outside the formal structure: {He was metagaming by using information his character wouldn't know}. The prefix meta- signals this layer of abstraction—the game about the game.

Metagames refers to the strategies and knowledge that exist outside a game's formal rules but shape how it's played. In competitive gaming, the metagame is the current landscape of dominant tactics, popular character picks, and counter-strategies: {The metagame shifted after the patch nerfed that weapon}. More broadly, metagaming means using external information to gain advantage—in tabletop roleplaying, a player metagames when their character acts on knowledge the player has but the character shouldn't: {He's metagaming—his wizard wouldn't know about that trap}.

Metahuman refers to a human with abilities beyond normal human limits—superhuman strength, telepathy, flight, or similar powers. The term appears primarily in comic books, games, and science fiction, where it categorizes characters who have transcended ordinary human capabilities through mutation, accident, or technology: {The metahuman threat required a new kind of response}. Unlike superhero, metahuman is neutral—it includes villains and ordinary people with extraordinary abilities.

Metahumans are humans with superhuman abilities—enhanced strength, flight, telepathy, or similar powers beyond normal human capacity. The term appears primarily in comic books, video games, and superhero fiction as a category distinct from aliens or magical beings: {The city's metahuman population required special containment facilities}. Unlike mutant, which implies genetic origin, metahuman covers any source of powers.

In general use, a metal is a material that is solid, opaque, conducts electricity, and is typically shiny in appearance. Precious metals are those that are relatively rare and command a high price. The hard and durable qualities of metal presumably give rise to the meaning in music: heavy metal is rock music with a strong, loud beat. Metal is infrequent as a British verb; it means to create (a road) using crushed rock or gravel.

Metalcore is a genre of heavy music that fuses hardcore punk's aggression and song structures with heavy metal's technical riffs and breakdowns. The style typically features alternating between harsh screaming vocals and melodic clean singing, along with heavily distorted guitars and intense drumming. {Their new album leans more metalcore than pure thrash.} The genre emerged in the 1990s and reached mainstream popularity in the 2000s with bands like Killswitch Engage and As I Lay Dying.

A metalhead is a devoted fan of heavy metal music. The term embraces the genre's culture—long hair, black clothing, band t-shirts, and enthusiasm for aggressive guitar riffs and thundering drums. Metalheads often identify strongly with the community: {I've been a metalhead since I was fourteen}. The word is affectionate, used by fans to describe themselves.

Metalheads are devoted fans of heavy metal music. The term embraces the culture surrounding the genre—the fashion (black clothing, band t-shirts, long hair), the concerts, the encyclopedic knowledge of bands and subgenres. Metalheads use the term proudly as an identity marker: {The metalheads showed up early to get spots near the stage}.

Metallic describes qualities associated with metal: appearance, sound, or taste. A metallic {sheen} has the reflective luster of polished metal. A metallic {clang} is sharp and resonant. A metallic {taste} in the mouth—often from blood or certain medications—resembles the flavor of metal on the tongue. Metallic colors like gold, silver, and bronze contain reflective particles.

Metals are a class of chemical elements that typically conduct heat and electricity, have a shiny appearance, and can be shaped by hammering or drawing into wire. Most elements are metals—iron, gold, copper, aluminum, zinc. In everyday use, metal often means hard, durable material: {a metal detector}, {metal roofing}. Heavy metal is a genre of loud, aggressive rock music characterized by distorted guitars and powerful rhythms.

A metalsmith is a craftsperson who works with metal, shaping it into functional or decorative objects. The term covers various specializations—blacksmiths work iron, goldsmiths work gold, silversmiths work silver—but metalsmith serves as a general term for anyone skilled in forging, casting, or otherwise manipulating metal: {She trained as a metalsmith before opening her jewelry studio}.

Metalwork is the craft of shaping metal into functional or decorative objects—everything from wrought-iron gates to jewelry to automotive parts. The term covers both the process and the finished products: {The museum's collection includes medieval metalwork}. A metalworker practices the trade; a metalworks is a factory where it happens.

Metalworking is the craft or industry of shaping metal into useful or decorative objects. It encompasses processes like forging, welding, casting, machining, and finishing. A metalworking {shop} might produce anything from jewelry to industrial parts. The term covers both artisanal work and large-scale manufacturing.

Metamorphosis is a dramatic transformation in form or character. In biology, it refers to the developmental process where an animal changes from one distinct stage to another—a caterpillar becoming a butterfly, a tadpole becoming a frog. The word extends to any profound change: {His time abroad triggered a complete metamorphosis}. Kafka's famous story literalizes the metaphor.

A metaphor i language that transfers literal meaning to a context where it cannot apply literally, such as drowning in debt. By combining imagines from different domains, metaphor is commonly used to make language more vivid. It is also common for words develop new meanings and become more frequent than their non-metaphoric use. Ride roughshod, for example, does not bring to mind people riding horses with spiked shoes (the literal meaning), but simply of harsh and insensitive treatment of someone.

Metaphors is the plural of metaphor—a figure of speech that describes one thing as if it were another: {Life is a journey}, {Time is money}. Unlike similes, metaphors don't use "like" or "as." They work by transferring qualities between unlike things, creating fresh ways to understand abstract or complex ideas. {His speech was full of mixed metaphors.}

Metaphysical concerns what lies beyond the physical world—questions about existence, reality, being, and the nature of things. In philosophy, metaphysics asks whether free will exists, what time is, or how mind relates to matter. More loosely, metaphysical describes anything abstract, spiritual, or concerned with ultimate questions: {Her interests turned metaphysical after the accident}. The metaphysical poets of the 17th century used elaborate conceits to explore love and spirituality.

Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy concerned with the fundamental nature of reality—what exists, what kinds of things exist, and how they relate. Questions about time, causation, free will, and the existence of God fall under metaphysics. In casual use, metaphysical often suggests the abstract, spiritual, or beyond ordinary experience: {The conversation turned metaphysical after midnight}. The word can carry a whiff of the speculative or impractical.

Metastasis is the spread of cancer from its original site to other parts of the body. Cancer cells break away from a primary tumor, travel through blood or lymph, and establish new tumors elsewhere: {The cancer had metastasized to his liver}. The verb is metastasize. Figuratively, something harmful that metastasizes spreads insidiously: {Corruption metastasized through the institution}.

Metastasized is the past tense of metastasize, meaning cancer has spread from its original site to other parts of the body through the bloodstream or lymphatic system: {The breast cancer had metastasized to her lungs}. Figuratively, something harmful that metastasizes spreads and takes root elsewhere: {Corruption metastasized throughout the organization}.

Metastasizing is the spread of cancer from its original site to other parts of the body through the bloodstream or lymphatic system: {The tumor was metastasizing to her liver}. Figuratively, it describes any harmful thing that spreads aggressively beyond its origin: {Corruption was metastasizing through the organization}.

The metaverse is a proposed immersive virtual environment where people interact through digital avatars—working, socializing, and transacting in interconnected 3D spaces. The term combines "meta" (beyond) and "universe," suggesting a reality beyond physical existence. Though the concept dates to 1990s science fiction, it gained renewed attention when Facebook rebranded as Meta in 2021: {Companies are investing billions in metaverse development}. Whether the metaverse will become a unified digital realm or remain a collection of separate virtual worlds is still unclear.

A meteor is the streak of light produced when a small piece of space debris burns up entering Earth's atmosphere—commonly called a shooting star or falling star. The object itself, before it enters the atmosphere, is a meteoroid; if any fragment survives to reach the ground, it becomes a meteorite. A meteor shower occurs when Earth passes through a trail of debris, producing many visible streaks: {We stayed up to watch the Perseid meteor shower}.

Meteoric describes something that rises with dramatic speed and brilliance, like a meteor streaking across the sky: {her meteoric rise to fame}, {a meteoric career}. The word emphasizes sudden, spectacular ascent—though meteors actually fall, the image that stuck is their brief, blazing visibility. In astronomy, meteoric refers literally to meteors: {meteoric debris}, {meteoric iron}.

A meteorite is a piece of rock or metal from space that survives passage through Earth's atmosphere and reaches the ground. Before landing, it's a meteor (the streak of light) or meteoroid (the object in space). Meteorites range from pebble-sized to massive: {The meteorite left a crater half a mile wide}. Scientists study them for clues about the solar system's origins.

Meteorites are rocks from space that survive passage through Earth's atmosphere and reach the ground. Most originate from asteroids, though some come from the Moon or Mars. Before landing, they're meteors (the streak of light) or meteoroids (the object in space). Meteorites are prized by scientists for clues about the solar system's formation: {The meteorite contained minerals older than Earth itself}.

Meteoroids are small rocky or metallic bodies traveling through space, ranging from dust-sized particles to objects several meters across. They're distinguished from larger asteroids mainly by size. When a meteoroid enters Earth's atmosphere and burns up, it creates a meteor—the streak of light commonly called a shooting star. Any piece that survives to reach the ground becomes a meteorite.

A meteorologist is a scientist who studies the atmosphere and weather. The term most commonly refers to weather forecasters who predict conditions for the public: {The meteorologist says rain is expected through Thursday}. Research meteorologists study climate patterns, storm systems, and atmospheric phenomena. The field encompasses both the person explaining tomorrow's forecast and scientists tracking long-term climate change.

Meteorologists are scientists who study the atmosphere and weather. Most visible are broadcast meteorologists who deliver forecasts on television and radio, though the field includes researchers studying climate patterns, severe storms, and atmospheric phenomena. {The meteorologists predicted heavy snow for the weekend.}

Meteorology is the scientific study of the atmosphere and its phenomena—weather, climate, and the processes that produce them. A meteorologist analyzes atmospheric conditions to forecast weather: {The meteorology suggested a hurricane was forming}. The field encompasses everything from daily forecasts to long-term climate modeling.

Meter has two main clusters of meaning. One refers to the basic unit of length in the metric system, equal to about 39.37 inches. The other concerns rhythm and measured patterns—the meter of a poem describes its regular arrangement of stressed and unstressed syllables, while musical meter organizes beats into recurring groups. A meter is also a device that measures and records quantity: {gas meter}, {parking meter}, {electric meter}. As a verb, to meter something is to measure or regulate its flow: {The system meters water usage throughout the building}.

Meters is the plural of meter, a unit of length in the metric system equal to about 39.4 inches: {The pool is fifty meters long}. Meters also refers to devices that measure and display quantities: {parking meters}, {electric meters}, {water meters}. In poetry and music, meters are patterns of rhythm or beat. The verb meters means to measure or regulate: {The system meters bandwidth usage}.

Meth is methamphetamine, a powerful and highly addictive stimulant drug. It produces intense euphoria and energy but causes severe physical and mental deterioration with prolonged use: {He lost his teeth to meth}. Crystal meth refers to its crystalline form, typically smoked. Meth is also short for methadone, a synthetic opioid used to treat heroin addiction.

Methadone is a synthetic opioid used medically to treat severe pain and to help people withdraw from heroin or other opioid addictions. It satisfies the body's craving without producing the intense high, allowing patients to function normally: {The clinic dispenses methadone daily}. Like other opioids, methadone itself can be addictive and is tightly regulated.

Methamphetamines are powerful synthetic stimulant drugs that affect the central nervous system, producing intense euphoria, increased energy, and heightened alertness. Highly addictive and illegal in most contexts, meth (as it's commonly called) can be smoked, snorted, injected, or swallowed. Chronic use causes severe physical and psychological damage, including tooth decay ("meth mouth"), skin sores, paranoia, and cognitive impairment. {The town was devastated by methamphetamines in the early 2000s.}

Methane is a colorless, odorless gas—the simplest hydrocarbon, one carbon atom bonded to four hydrogens. It's the main component of natural gas, used for heating and cooking. Methane is also a potent greenhouse gas, released by landfills, livestock digestion, and wetlands. {Cows produce significant methane emissions.}

A methhead is a person who habitually uses methamphetamine, especially one showing visible signs of addiction—gaunt appearance, bad teeth, erratic behavior. The term is derogatory, emphasizing the drug's destructive effects: {The house next door got raided; bunch of methheads living there}. Also spelled meth head.

A method is a way of doing something, especially a systematic or orderly approach: {There's a method to her madness}. In programming, a method is a function belonging to an object or class. The Method (or method acting) is an acting technique where performers draw on personal emotions to inhabit their characters.

Methods are systematic ways of doing things—organized approaches or procedures for accomplishing tasks. A scientist follows research methods; a teacher develops teaching methods. The word often implies deliberate technique rather than improvisation: {There's a method to his madness}. In programming, a method is a function belonging to an object or class.

Meticulous describes extreme attention to detail and precision. A meticulous person notices small things others miss and takes care to get everything exactly right: {meticulous record-keeping}, {a meticulous craftsman}. The word carries approval—unlike fussy or nitpicky, meticulous suggests the attention is warranted and produces quality results.

Metre is the British spelling of meter in most senses. A metre is the base unit of length in the metric system, roughly 39 inches. In poetry, metre is the rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables: {iambic pentametre}. The American spelling meter dominates in both technical and literary contexts worldwide.

Metric refers to measurement or a system of measurement. The metric system uses meters, grams, and liters as base units. More broadly, a metric is any standard of measurement: {What metrics are you using to evaluate success?} In business and tech, metrics are quantifiable indicators tracked over time: {engagement metrics}, {performance metrics}. As an adjective, metric describes things related to the metric system: {metric tons}, {metric units}.

Metrics are measurements used to evaluate or track something. In business, metrics might include sales figures, customer satisfaction scores, or website traffic: {What metrics are you using to measure success?} The singular metric refers to a single measurement or standard: {Customer retention is our key metric}. In technical contexts, metrics can also refer to systems of measurement or mathematical functions for measuring distance.

Metro typically refers to a metropolitan subway or underground rail system: {I took the metro to work}. It also functions as an adjective meaning metropolitan—relating to a large city and its surrounding areas: {the metro area}, {metro Atlanta}. In informal use, metro once described men with refined, urban tastes in grooming and fashion, short for metrosexual. (Capitalized Metro may be a proper name for specific transit systems.)

A metronome is a device that produces regular ticks or clicks at an adjustable tempo, used by musicians to maintain steady time while practicing. Traditional metronomes use a weighted pendulum; modern ones are often electronic or app-based. The tempo is measured in beats per minute: {Set the metronome to 120 BPM}.

Metronomes is the plural of metronome, a device that produces regular ticks or beats at an adjustable tempo, used by musicians to keep time while practicing. Traditional metronomes use a weighted pendulum; modern ones are often digital or app-based. {She set the metronome to 120 beats per minute}. Figuratively, anything that marks time steadily: {His footsteps were a metronome on the pavement}.

A metroplex is a large metropolitan area, especially one formed by multiple cities that have grown together into a continuous urban region. The term is most associated with the Dallas–Fort Worth area in Texas, often called simply {the Metroplex}. It emphasizes interconnected urban sprawl rather than a single dominant city: {Housing prices across the metroplex have risen sharply}.

A metropolis is a very large, important city, especially one that serves as a center of commerce, culture, or political power in a region: {Tokyo is a sprawling metropolis of over thirteen million people}. The word carries connotations of urban density, sophistication, and significance that distinguish it from merely large cities. In formal usage, a metropolis may specifically mean the chief city of a country or region, or the mother city of a colony in ancient Greece.

Metropolitan describes things relating to a large city and its surrounding urban area. A metropolitan {area} includes the central city plus adjacent communities economically tied to it. Metropolitan {life} suggests the bustle, diversity, and sophistication associated with major cities. The word can also function as a noun for a bishop with authority over other bishops in a region.

Metros is the plural of metro, referring to urban rapid transit rail systems: {The metros of Paris and London are among the world's oldest}. Metro can also mean a metropolitan area: {the Dallas-Fort Worth metro}. In either sense, metros describes multiple such systems or regions: {European metros tend to have better public transit than American ones}.

Metrosexual describes a man, typically urban and heterosexual, who takes unusual interest in his appearance, grooming, and fashion—areas traditionally associated with women or gay men. The term emerged in the 1990s and gained currency as a way to describe men who rejected rugged masculine stereotypes in favor of skincare routines, designer clothes, and careful attention to style. {He spends more on hair products than I do—total metrosexual.} The word blends metropolitan with sexual orientation terminology, though it says nothing about actual sexual preference.

Metrosexuals is the plural of metrosexual, a man—typically straight and urban—who takes unusual interest in his appearance, grooming, and fashion. The term emerged in the 1990s to describe men who adopted style habits traditionally associated with gay men or women: {The metrosexuals at his gym spent more time on skincare than weightlifting}. The word combines metropolitan with sexual, though sexuality isn't the point—aesthetics is.

Mettle is a person's capacity to cope well with difficulty—their spirit, courage, or resilience under pressure. To {prove your mettle} or {show your mettle} is to demonstrate you can handle a challenge. Something that {tests your mettle} pushes you to your limits. The word shares an origin with metal, suggesting inner hardness or temper.

A mew is the soft, high-pitched cry of a cat or kitten, or a gull's call. As a verb, to mew is to make this sound: {The kitten mewed plaintively at the door}. Separately, a mew is a cage for hawks, especially during molting, or a row of stables converted to houses—hence the British {mews}, a small residential street.

Mewing is a tongue posture technique popularized online, where you press your tongue flat against the roof of your mouth, supposedly to reshape your jawline over time. Named after orthodontist John Mew, the practice spread through social media as a self-improvement trend, particularly among young men seeking a more defined facial structure: {He's been mewing for six months hoping to get a sharper jaw}.

Mewling describes weak, high-pitched crying or whimpering, like the sounds made by a kitten or an infant. The word carries connotations of helplessness and feebleness, which is why it often appears in dismissive or contemptuous contexts: {mewling complaints}, {a mewling coward}.
