Shakespeare's famous "mewling and puking" from *As You Like It* captures the word's association with infantile weakness. {The kittens were mewling in the box by the door.}

Mews is a row of houses or apartments converted from stables, typically arranged around a courtyard or along a narrow lane. Originally these were service buildings behind grand London townhouses, housing horses and carriages with servants' quarters above. The word is singular despite the -s: {a charming mews in Kensington}, {The mews was quiet at night}. Now mews addresses command premium prices as desirable urban housing.

Mezcal is a Mexican spirit distilled from the cooked hearts of agave plants. Tequila is technically a type of mezcal, made specifically from blue agave in designated regions, but mezcal typically refers to spirits from other agave varieties, often with a distinctive smoky flavor from pit-roasting. {The bartender recommended a mezcal with notes of citrus and earth.}

A mezuzah is a small case containing a parchment inscribed with Hebrew verses from Deuteronomy, affixed to the doorframes of Jewish homes. The word means "doorpost" in Hebrew. Observant Jews touch or kiss the mezuzah when passing through a doorway. The case is mounted at an angle on the right side of the entrance. Plural: mezuzot or mezuzahs.

A mezzanine is an intermediate floor between two main floors of a building, typically a partial level overlooking a larger space below: {The offices were on a mezzanine above the factory floor}. In theaters, the mezzanine is the lowest balcony or its front rows. The term extends to intermediate levels generally—a {mezzanine fund} sits between senior debt and equity in a company's capital structure.

Mezzanines are intermediate floors in a building, typically between the ground floor and the first full story. A mezzanine is usually partial—it doesn't extend across the entire footprint but overlooks the floor below: {The restaurant had additional seating on the mezzanine}. In theaters, the mezzanine is the lowest balcony section. In finance, mezzanine refers to intermediate-risk debt or funding that falls between senior debt and equity.

Mezze is a spread of small dishes served as appetizers or a shared meal in Middle Eastern and Mediterranean cuisines. A mezze spread might include hummus, baba ghanoush, falafel, olives, and flatbread: {We ordered the mezze platter to share}. The style emphasizes variety and communal eating over a single main course.

Mezzo means middle or medium, borrowed from Italian. In music, it modifies volume or voice type: mezzo forte is moderately loud, mezzo piano moderately soft. A mezzo-soprano voice falls between soprano and contralto. Informally, mezzo-soprano singers are called mezzos: {The mezzo was brilliant in the second act}.

Miasma is a noxious atmosphere or influence. The word originally referred to bad air thought to cause disease—the foul smell of swamps and rotting matter before germ theory explained infection. Now it's mostly figurative: {a miasma of corruption hung over the administration}, {the miasma of despair}. The plural is miasmas or miasmata.

Mic is a clipped form of microphone, now standard in casual and technical contexts alike: {Is your mic on?} As a verb, to mic someone is to fit them with a microphone: {The sound crew mic'd the actors before the scene}. The spelling mike, once more common, has largely given way to mic, though both appear. {Drop the mic} or {mic drop} signals a triumphant exit after a decisive statement.

Mica is a mineral that occurs in thin, translucent sheets that can be peeled apart into flexible layers. These sheets have a distinctive sparkle and were historically used in windows, lamp chimneys, and electrical insulation before synthetic alternatives became available. Today mica appears most commonly in cosmetics, where its shimmer adds luster to eyeshadows and body glitters, and in industrial applications requiring heat resistance. {The rock was flecked with bits of mica.}

Mice is the plural of mouse. In its oldest sense, a mouse is a small rodent, and mice are several of them: {The barn was overrun with mice}. Since the 1960s, mouse has also referred to the hand-operated pointing device used with computers, and while mouses is sometimes used for the plural in this sense, mice predominates: {We need to order new mice for the computer lab}.

Mickey has several informal meanings. To {take the mickey} (British) is to mock or tease someone, often good-naturedly. A mickey can also be a small bottle of liquor, typically a flask-sized portion. In the phrase {slip someone a mickey}, it means to secretly drug someone's drink, usually to incapacitate them. The word likely derives from the name Mickey Finn, reportedly a Chicago bartender who drugged and robbed customers.

Micro means very small, often as a prefix: {microchip}, {microorganism}, {micromanage}. In technical contexts, micro- denotes one millionth of a unit: a microsecond is a millionth of a second. Standalone, micro can be a microphone, a microcomputer, or shorthand for anything miniaturized: {She grabbed the micro and started singing}. The opposite is macro.

A microaggression is a subtle, often unintentional comment or action that conveys prejudice toward a marginalized group. Unlike overt discrimination, microaggressions are brief, commonplace exchanges—asking an Asian American {where are you really from?} or telling a Black colleague {you're so articulate}. The term emphasizes cumulative impact: individually minor, collectively wearing. Critics argue the concept pathologizes ordinary social friction.

Microaggressions are subtle slights, snubs, or insults directed at members of marginalized groups, often unintentionally. The term captures everyday indignities that may seem minor in isolation but accumulate: {Where are you really from?} asked of a native-born citizen, or touching a Black person's hair without permission. Critics argue the concept pathologizes ordinary social friction; proponents see it naming something previously invisible. Usually plural.

A microbe is a microscopic organism—bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other life forms too small to see without magnification. The term appears in both scientific and everyday contexts: {antibacterial soap kills microbes}, {gut microbes aid digestion}. Microbe carries less clinical weight than microorganism, making it the common choice in general speech.

Microbeads are tiny plastic spheres, typically less than a millimeter in diameter, added to personal care products like facial scrubs and toothpaste as exfoliants. Because they're too small to be filtered by water treatment plants, they accumulate in waterways and oceans, where marine life ingests them. Many countries have banned microbeads in cosmetics due to environmental concerns.

Microbes are microscopic organisms—bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other life forms too small to see without magnification. The term is informal shorthand for microorganisms, common in discussions of health, disease, and biology: {Your gut contains trillions of microbes}, {antimicrobial soap kills harmful microbes}. Not all microbes cause illness; many are essential to digestion, soil health, and other processes.

A microbiologist is a scientist who studies microorganisms—bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other life forms too small to see without magnification. The work spans medicine, agriculture, environmental science, and industry: {The microbiologist identified the strain responsible for the outbreak}. {She's a microbiologist specializing in soil bacteria}.

Microbiology is the branch of biology concerned with microorganisms—bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other life forms too small to see without magnification. The field encompasses both harmful microbes that cause disease and beneficial ones essential to processes like fermentation, decomposition, and digestion. {She studied microbiology before going into infectious disease research.} Microbiologists work in settings ranging from hospitals to breweries to environmental agencies.

The microbiome is the community of microorganisms—bacteria, fungi, viruses—living in a particular environment, especially the human body. The gut microbiome has received intense scientific attention for its role in digestion, immunity, and even mood: {Research links the gut microbiome to depression}. Each person's microbiome is unique, shaped by diet, environment, and genetics.

Microbiomes are the communities of microorganisms—bacteria, fungi, viruses—that inhabit a particular environment, especially a living body. The human gut microbiome has become a major focus of health research: {Scientists are studying how the gut microbiome affects mood and immunity}. The term extends to any ecosystem's microbial population: {soil microbiome}, {ocean microbiome}.

Microblading is a cosmetic tattooing technique that creates the appearance of fuller eyebrows. A technician uses a handheld tool with fine needles to deposit pigment in thin, hair-like strokes beneath the skin's surface. The results are semi-permanent, typically lasting one to three years before fading: {She got microblading to fill in her sparse brows}.

Microbrew refers to beer produced by a small, independent brewery—typically one making limited quantities with emphasis on quality and distinctive flavor rather than mass-market appeal. The term emerged in the 1980s as craft brewing grew: {The bar features twenty microbrews on tap}. As a verb, to microbrew is to produce such beer. The brewery itself is a microbrewery.

A microbrewer is someone who operates a small-scale brewery, typically producing limited quantities of craft beer with an emphasis on quality, flavor, and traditional brewing methods. The term distinguishes these artisanal producers from large commercial breweries: {The microbrewer experimented with local hops for her seasonal ale}.

Microbreweries is the plural of microbrewery—a small-scale brewery producing limited quantities of beer, typically emphasizing craft techniques and distinctive flavors over mass production. The term emerged in the late twentieth century as alternatives to major commercial brewers gained popularity: {The city's microbreweries offer everything from pale ales to sours}. Microbreweries often sell directly to consumers through attached taprooms.

Microbrewers are people who operate small-scale breweries, typically producing limited quantities of craft beer with emphasis on flavor, quality, and traditional brewing methods rather than mass production. The term emerged in the 1980s as small independent breweries distinguished themselves from large commercial operations: {Local microbrewers have revived interest in regional beer styles}.

A microbrewery is a small brewery producing limited quantities of beer, typically with emphasis on quality, flavor, and traditional brewing methods over mass production. Microbreweries often experiment with styles and ingredients that larger commercial breweries avoid. The term emerged in the 1970s–80s as craft brewing revived: {We visited three microbreweries on our trip through Vermont}.

Microbrewing is the production of beer in small batches, typically by independent breweries emphasizing craft and quality over volume. The practice revived traditional brewing methods and regional styles that industrial brewers had abandoned. A microbrewery produces limited quantities, often for local distribution or on-site consumption: {The microbrewing scene in Portland has exploded}.

Microbrews are beers produced by small, independent breweries—typically those making limited quantities with an emphasis on flavor and craft over mass production. The term emerged in the 1980s as alternatives to dominant commercial brands gained popularity: {The bar has an impressive selection of microbrews on tap}. Microbrews often feature distinctive styles and local ingredients.

A microburst is a sudden, intense downdraft of air from a thunderstorm that spreads outward when it hits the ground, producing damaging winds. Unlike tornadoes, microbursts push straight down and out rather than spinning. They're particularly hazardous to aircraft during takeoff and landing: {The crash was attributed to wind shear from a microburst}.

Microbursts are sudden, powerful downdrafts of air that hit the ground and spread outward, creating intense but localized wind shear. They typically last only a few minutes and affect areas less than a few miles across, but can produce winds exceeding 100 mph. Microbursts pose serious hazards to aircraft during takeoff and landing: {The crash was caused by a microburst the pilot couldn't escape}. Dry microbursts occur without visible precipitation; wet microbursts accompany heavy rain.

A microbus is a small bus, typically seating around a dozen passengers—larger than a van but smaller than a full-sized bus. The term often evokes the iconic Volkswagen Type 2, the compact vehicle that became a symbol of 1960s counterculture: {They loaded the microbus and headed to the festival}.

A microcelebrity is someone who has achieved fame within a limited sphere—typically a niche online community, specific platform, or local scene—rather than mainstream recognition. The term emerged with social media, where someone might have thousands of devoted followers on Instagram or YouTube while remaining unknown to the general public. {She's a microcelebrity in the knitting community.} Unlike traditional celebrities, microcelebrities often cultivate intimate relationships with their audiences and may monetize their modest fame through sponsorships or merchandise.

A microchip is a tiny integrated circuit—a small piece of semiconductor material containing thousands or millions of electronic components. Microchips power computers, phones, and countless devices. The verb means to implant an identifying chip: {We had our dog microchipped}. Often shortened to chip.

Microchipping is the implantation of a tiny electronic chip under the skin, typically for identification purposes. Pet owners microchip dogs and cats so lost animals can be traced back to them: {Make sure your new puppy is microchipped}. The practice extends to livestock and, controversially, to humans for medical records or access control.

Microchips are tiny integrated circuits—semiconductor wafers containing thousands or millions of electronic components. They power computers, phones, and countless devices. The singular microchip also refers to a small identification chip implanted under an animal's skin: {We had the dog microchipped}. To microchip is to implant such a device.

A microclimate is the climate of a small, localized area that differs from the surrounding region. A sheltered garden corner may stay warmer than the open yard; a shaded north-facing slope stays cooler than adjacent sunny ground. Urban areas often form heat islands—microclimates warmer than surrounding countryside. Gardeners and farmers pay close attention to microclimates when deciding what to plant where.

Microclimates are localized atmospheric conditions that differ from the surrounding area. A sheltered garden corner may be warmer than the open yard; a north-facing slope stays cooler than nearby south-facing terrain. Urban areas create microclimates through pavement and buildings that trap heat. Gardeners and farmers pay close attention to microclimates when choosing where to plant: {The vineyard's microclimate produces exceptional grapes}.

A microcosm is a small system or community that reflects the features of a larger one. The word literally means "little world," and that origin captures the idea: a contained version of something vast. {The office was a microcosm of corporate America—complete with politics, cliques, and ambition.} A classroom can be a microcosm of society; a small town can be a microcosm of the nation. The opposite is macrocosm.

Microcosms is the plural of microcosm—a small world that mirrors a larger one. A classroom can be a microcosm of society, a tide pool a microcosm of ocean ecosystems. The word implies that studying the small version reveals truths about the whole: {Her novel uses a small Southern town as a microcosm of American racial tensions}.

Microcredit is the practice of lending small amounts of money to people who lack access to traditional banking—typically impoverished entrepreneurs in developing countries. The loans fund small businesses: a sewing machine, livestock, market inventory. {Microcredit programs have helped millions of women start businesses}. The model relies on group lending and social pressure rather than collateral.

A microdose is a very small quantity of a drug—typically a psychedelic like LSD or psilocybin—taken not to get high but to produce subtle effects on mood, creativity, or focus: {She microdoses mushrooms for anxiety}. The practice gained popularity in Silicon Valley tech culture. The verb is to microdose; the practice is microdosing.

Microdosing is taking very small amounts of a substance—typically a psychedelic drug like LSD or psilocybin—too small to produce obvious effects but supposedly enough to enhance mood, creativity, or focus. The practice gained popularity in Silicon Valley tech culture: {She's been microdosing mushrooms to help with her depression}. The term extends to other contexts where tiny doses are used therapeutically.

A microdot is a photograph reduced to the size of a printed period, used historically to transmit secret information. Spies embedded microdots in ordinary correspondence, invisible to casual inspection but readable under magnification. The term also refers to tiny tablets of LSD, named for their similar size: {He dropped a microdot at the concert}.

A microexpression is a brief, involuntary facial expression that flashes across someone's face, typically lasting only a fraction of a second. These fleeting expressions are thought to reveal concealed emotions—a flicker of contempt, a flash of fear—before the person can consciously suppress them. The concept is popular in psychology and law enforcement training, though its reliability for detecting deception remains debated: {She caught a microexpression of disgust before he smiled}.

Microexpressions are brief, involuntary facial movements that reveal emotions a person may be trying to conceal. Lasting only a fraction of a second, they flash across the face before conscious control can suppress them. The concept figures prominently in discussions of lie detection and emotional intelligence: {Trained investigators learn to read microexpressions for signs of deception}.

Microfiber is synthetic fabric made from extremely fine fibers—typically polyester, nylon, or both. The thinness of the fibers creates a soft texture and high surface area, making microfiber cloths effective for cleaning without chemicals: {Wipe the screen with a microfiber cloth}. Microfiber textiles are also used in athletic wear, upholstery, and bedding for their lightweight feel and moisture-wicking properties.

Microfibers are extremely fine synthetic fibers, typically polyester or nylon, thinner than a human hair. Microfiber cloth is prized for cleaning because the tiny strands trap dust and absorb liquid effectively: {Microfiber towels won't scratch the paint}. The term also refers to these fibers as pollutants—shed from synthetic clothing during washing, they accumulate in waterways and marine life.

Microfilm is a photographic medium that stores documents, newspapers, and other printed materials as highly reduced images on rolls or sheets of film. Before digital archiving, it was the standard method for preserving and compacting large volumes of records, and libraries still maintain extensive microfilm collections. To read microfilm, you use a special viewer that magnifies the tiny images back to readable size. The verb microfilm means to photograph documents onto this medium: {The library microfilmed every issue of the newspaper from the 1800s}.

Microfinance is the provision of financial services—small loans, savings accounts, insurance—to people too poor to access traditional banking. The loans are typically modest amounts enabling recipients to start or expand small businesses: {Microfinance helped her buy a sewing machine and launch her tailoring business}. The model gained prominence in developing countries as a tool for poverty alleviation.

Microgreens are young vegetable or herb seedlings harvested just after the first leaves develop, typically one to three weeks after germination. They're smaller than baby greens but larger than sprouts, prized in cooking for intense flavor and visual appeal: {The chef garnished the dish with peppery radish microgreens}. Common varieties include arugula, basil, and sunflower.

Microgreens are vegetable greens harvested just after the first leaves develop, typically one to three weeks after germination. Smaller than baby greens but larger than sprouts, they're prized for concentrated flavor and nutrition: {a salad topped with microgreens}, {microgreens add color and texture to any dish}. Popular varieties include radish, arugula, and sunflower.

A microloan is a small loan, typically a few hundred dollars or less, extended to borrowers who lack access to traditional banking—often entrepreneurs in developing countries or underserved communities. Microloans fund small businesses, equipment purchases, or basic needs: {She started her textile business with a $200 microloan}. The practice, called microfinance or microlending, aims to reduce poverty by providing capital to those conventional lenders consider too risky or unprofitable to serve.

Microloans are very small loans, typically a few hundred dollars or less, extended to people who lack access to traditional banking. The concept emerged to help entrepreneurs in developing countries start small businesses—buying a sewing machine, livestock, or inventory. {She used a microloan to open her food stall.} Microfinance institutions and some nonprofits specialize in these loans, which often require no collateral.

To micromanage is to control every small detail of someone else's work, leaving them little autonomy or decision-making power. The term is almost always pejorative—micromanagers hover, second-guess, and obsess over minutiae rather than trusting their employees or delegates: {She micromanages everything down to the font size on internal memos}. The noun is micromanagement.

Micromanaged describes being subjected to excessive oversight and control over minor details. A micromanaged employee has their work scrutinized constantly, with little autonomy or trust: {I felt micromanaged—my boss wanted to approve every email before I sent it}. The term implies the management style is counterproductive, stifling initiative rather than improving outcomes.

Micromanagement is a style of oversight that controls every small detail of someone's work rather than trusting them to execute tasks independently. The term is almost always pejorative: {Her micromanagement drove away talented employees}. A micromanager hovers, second-guesses, and demands approval over minor decisions. The verb micromanage works the same way: {Stop micromanaging me}.

A micromanager is someone who controls every small detail of others' work rather than trusting them to handle tasks independently. The term is almost always critical—implying excessive supervision that stifles autonomy and productivity: {My boss is such a micromanager; she reviews every email before I send it}. The verb is micromanage.

Micromanagers are bosses or supervisors who excessively control subordinates' work, monitoring every detail rather than trusting employees to complete tasks independently. The term is almost always pejorative: {Nobody wants to work for a micromanager}. The behavior suggests anxiety, distrust, or inability to delegate—traits that frustrate workers and often reduce productivity.

Micromanages means to control every small detail of someone else's work, leaving little room for independent judgment. A micromanaging boss hovers, second-guesses, and insists on approving minor decisions: {She micromanages her team so closely that nothing gets done without her sign-off}. The term is almost always pejorative, implying distrust and inefficiency.

Micromanaging is supervising with excessive attention to small details, leaving subordinates little autonomy. A micromanaging boss scrutinizes every decision, reviews every email, demands constant updates. The term is almost always pejorative—implying distrust and inefficiency: {Stop micromanaging me and let me do my job}. The noun is micromanagement; the person, a micromanager.

A micronation is a self-declared independent state that lacks recognition from established governments and international bodies. These entities typically claim tiny territories—a backyard, an abandoned platform, a small island—and adopt the trappings of nationhood: flags, constitutions, currency, titles. Most are hobbyist projects, political protests, or artistic experiments rather than serious bids for sovereignty: {He founded a micronation in his apartment and declared himself king}.

Micronations are self-declared entities that claim sovereignty but lack recognition from established governments or international bodies. They range from serious political projects to satirical stunts to hobbyist endeavors. Some exist only online or on paper; others occupy tiny plots of land: {The Principality of Sealand occupies an abandoned sea platform off the British coast}. Unlike separatist movements seeking independence from existing states, micronations typically start from nothing, inventing flags, currencies, and constitutions for territories no larger than a backyard.

A microorganism is a living thing too small to see without magnification—bacteria, viruses, fungi, and single-celled creatures like amoebas. Some cause disease; others are essential to digestion, decomposition, and fermentation. {The gut contains trillions of microorganisms.} Also spelled micro-organism.

Microorganisms are living things too small to see without magnification—bacteria, viruses, fungi, and single-celled creatures. Most are harmless or beneficial; some cause disease. They exist virtually everywhere: in soil, water, air, and inside larger organisms. {The gut contains trillions of microorganisms.} Also called microbes.

A micropayment is a very small financial transaction, typically fractions of a cent to a few dollars, processed electronically. The concept emerged with digital commerce as a way to pay for individual articles, songs, or in-app purchases rather than subscriptions: {The site charges a micropayment of ten cents per article}. Micropayments require low transaction fees to be practical.

Micropayments are very small financial transactions, typically fractions of a dollar, processed electronically. The concept emerged with digital commerce as a way to pay for individual pieces of content—a single article, a song, a few seconds of video—rather than subscribing to entire services. {The platform uses micropayments so readers pay only for what they read.} Despite decades of interest, transaction fees have historically made true micropayments impractical, though cryptocurrency and new payment systems continue to revive the idea.

A microphone is a device that converts sound into electrical signals, used for recording, amplification, or transmission. Singers perform into microphones, podcasters speak into them, and surveillance operations hide them. The word is often shortened to mic (sometimes mike): {Is your mic on?} {She was caught on a hot mic making candid remarks.}

Microphones are devices that convert sound waves into electrical signals. The technology enables recording, amplification, and transmission of audio—from studio vocals to phone conversations to public address systems. Different types (condenser, dynamic, ribbon) suit different purposes. Informally shortened to mic or mike: {Is your mic on?} {She grabbed the microphone and addressed the crowd}.

Microplastics are tiny plastic fragments, typically smaller than five millimeters, that result from the breakdown of larger plastic items or are manufactured small for products like cosmetics and cleaning agents. They accumulate in oceans, soil, and drinking water, entering the food chain and human bodies: {Researchers found microplastics in fish tissue}. The term usually appears in the plural, as the concern is their collective presence rather than individual particles.

Microplastics are tiny fragments of plastic, typically less than five millimeters across, that result from the breakdown of larger plastic items or are manufactured small for products like cosmetics and cleaning agents. They accumulate in oceans, soil, and drinking water, entering the food chain and human bodies: {Researchers found microplastics in fish tissue}. The term emerged as environmental concern about plastic pollution intensified.

A microprocessor is an integrated circuit that serves as the central processing unit of a computer, handling calculations and executing instructions. The "micro" distinguishes it from earlier processors that filled entire rooms—microprocessors fit on a single chip. {Intel's microprocessors powered the personal computer revolution.} The term is now largely synonymous with CPU.

Microprocessors is the plural of microprocessor—an integrated circuit that contains the central processing unit of a computer on a single chip. The microprocessor executes instructions, performs calculations, and manages data flow. Since the 1970s, microprocessors have powered everything from personal computers to smartphones to car engines: {Modern microprocessors contain billions of transistors}.

A microscope is an instrument that magnifies small objects for detailed observation. The basic optical microscope uses lenses to enlarge specimens placed on a glass slide; electron microscopes achieve far greater magnification using beams of electrons. Figuratively, to {put something under the microscope} is to examine it closely and critically.

Microscopes is the plural of microscope, an optical instrument that magnifies small objects for detailed examination. The compound microscope uses multiple lenses to achieve high magnification for viewing cells and microorganisms. Electron microscopes use electron beams rather than light, revealing structures at molecular scale. {The lab's microscopes revealed bacteria in the sample.}

Microscopic means too small to see without a microscope: {microscopic organisms}, {microscopic fibers}. By extension, it describes anything extremely small or detailed: {a microscopic amount of evidence}, {microscopic attention to detail}. The word can suggest thoroughness when examining something closely: {microscopic analysis of the data}.

A microsecond is one millionth of a second. The term appears in technical contexts—computing, physics, electronics—where operations occur at speeds imperceptible to humans. Figuratively, microsecond suggests extreme brevity: {I'll be there in a microsecond}. The prefix micro- comes from Greek for small.

A microsleep is a brief, involuntary episode of sleep lasting a few seconds, often occurring when someone is fatigued but trying to stay awake. The person may appear alert—eyes open, sitting upright—yet the brain momentarily disengages. Microsleeps are particularly dangerous while driving or operating machinery: {He didn't realize he'd been microsleeping until he drifted into the next lane}.

Microsleeps are brief, involuntary episodes of sleep lasting only a few seconds, typically occurring when someone is sleep-deprived but fighting to stay awake. During a microsleep, the brain essentially shuts down momentarily while the person may appear awake—eyes can remain open. The phenomenon is dangerous during driving or operating machinery: {The accident was caused by microsleeps at the wheel}. A single episode is a microsleep.

Microtargeting is the practice of using data analysis to identify and reach very specific groups or individuals with tailored messages, especially in political campaigns and advertising. Voter databases, consumer profiles, and online behavior help craft appeals to narrow demographic slices: {The campaign's microtargeting reached undecided suburban women with ads about education}. The technique raises privacy concerns about how personal data is collected and used.
clues: Reaching narrow groups with tailored content

definition: A microtransaction is a small digital purchase within a video game or app, typically ranging from cents to a few dollars. Players buy cosmetic items, power-ups, or in-game currency: {The game is free but relies on microtransactions}. Though individually minor, microtransactions generate enormous revenue and draw criticism when they create pay-to-win dynamics or exploit compulsive spending.

Microtransactions are small purchases made within video games or apps, typically for cosmetic items, virtual currency, or gameplay advantages. The model lets developers offer games cheaply or free while generating revenue from players who pay incrementally: {The game is free but pushes microtransactions for skins and weapons}. Critics argue the model exploits players, especially when it creates pay-to-win dynamics or targets children.

A microwave is electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths shorter than radio waves but longer than infrared. More commonly, it's the kitchen appliance that uses such radiation to heat food quickly: {Just microwave it for two minutes}. The verb means to cook or heat in this appliance. Microwave ovens work by exciting water molecules, which is why dry foods heat unevenly.

Microwaved describes food or other items heated in a microwave oven: {microwaved leftovers}, {a microwaved cup of coffee}. The word can carry connotations of convenience over quality—microwaved food is quick but rarely as good as other methods: {The restaurant's microwaved entrees tasted rubbery}.

Microwaves are electromagnetic waves with wavelengths between radio waves and infrared light. They're used in radar, telecommunications, and cooking. A microwave is also the appliance that uses these waves to heat food by agitating water molecules: {Just microwave it for two minutes}. The verb means to cook or heat in such an appliance.

Microwaving is cooking or heating food in a microwave oven, which uses electromagnetic radiation to agitate water molecules and generate heat quickly. The word extends to any use of the appliance: {I'm just microwaving some leftovers}. Microwave-safe containers won't melt or release chemicals when microwaved. The verb can suggest convenience over quality: {We microwaved dinner instead of cooking}.

Mics is the plural of mic, the informal spelling of mike—a clipped form of microphone. The spelling mics has become standard in contexts where multiple microphones are involved: {The sound crew set up mics around the stage}. To mic someone is to attach a microphone to them: {They miced up the actors before the scene}.

Mid means in the middle of, typically modifying time periods or ranges: {mid-January}, {mid-career}, {mid-century modern furniture}. It usually appears hyphenated before a noun. Mid can also stand alone in informal speech to mean mediocre or unremarkable: {The movie was mid}—neither good nor bad, just average. This newer slang sense, popular among younger speakers, dismisses something as thoroughly unimpressive.

Midair refers to a point in the air, above the ground, not in contact with any surface. A catch made in midair happens before the ball lands. A {midair collision} occurs between two aircraft in flight. The word usually appears after "in": {The acrobat twisted in midair}.

Midbrow describes culture, taste, or entertainment that falls between highbrow and lowbrow—accessible but not dumbed down, respectable but not intellectually demanding. The term often carries a faint sneer, suggesting something that flatters audiences into thinking they're consuming high culture: {a midbrow biography}, {midbrow literary fiction}. What counts as midbrow shifts with time and context.

Midcentury refers to the middle of a century, typically the 1950s when discussing the twentieth century. The term appears most often in design and architecture contexts, where {midcentury modern} describes a distinctive aesthetic of clean lines, organic curves, and functional simplicity: {a midcentury ranch house}, {midcentury furniture}. Sometimes hyphenated: mid-century.

Midday is noon—the middle of the day, when the sun reaches its highest point. It refers both to the precise moment of twelve o'clock and to the hours around it: {We met for a midday meal}. As an adjective, it describes things occurring at or near noon: {the midday sun}, {midday heat}.

Middle refers to the point or area equidistant from extremes or edges. The middle of a room is its center; the middle of a story is between beginning and end. Middle age falls between youth and old age. A middle child is born between siblings. The middle class occupies the economic space between rich and poor. To middle something is to place it centrally, though this use is uncommon. {She sat in the middle of the row.}

Middlebrow describes cultural tastes or products that fall between highbrow sophistication and lowbrow entertainment—accessible but aspiring to seriousness. The term often carries a faint sneer, implying something that flatters its audience's intelligence without truly challenging it: {middlebrow fiction}, {a middlebrow taste in art}. A middlebrow is a person with such tastes.

The middlegame is the central phase of a chess game, after the opening moves have been played and before the endgame begins. Pieces are developed, tactics unfold, and strategic plans take shape: {Her middlegame play was aggressive, sacrificing a knight for position}. The term extends to any endeavor's middle phase, between initial setup and final resolution.

A middleman is someone who facilitates transactions between two parties—buying from producers to sell to retailers, or connecting buyers with sellers. The term often carries negative connotations, suggesting an unnecessary intermediary who adds cost without adding value: {Cut out the middleman and buy direct}. In other contexts, a middleman is a neutral go-between or mediator: {He acted as middleman in the negotiations}.

Middlemen are intermediaries in a transaction or supply chain—people or businesses who buy from producers and sell to retailers or consumers. The term often carries negative connotations, suggesting unnecessary parties who add cost without adding value: {Cut out the middlemen and buy direct from the manufacturer}. A middleman can also be any go-between or intermediary: {He served as middleman in the negotiations}.
clues: Those who facilitate deals between parties

definition: Middleweight denotes a weight class in boxing and other combat sports, falling between welterweight and light heavyweight—typically around 160 pounds in professional boxing. The term extends to anything of intermediate weight or size: {a middleweight laptop}, {a middleweight contender in the industry}. A middleweight is also a competitor in that class: {The middleweight defended his title}.

Middleweights are boxers or wrestlers in a weight class between welterweight and light heavyweight—typically around 160 pounds in professional boxing. The term extends to any competitors or things of intermediate size or importance: {The company is a middleweight in the tech industry}. As an adjective: {a middleweight contender}, {middleweight division}.

Midfield is the central area of a playing field, especially in soccer, where much of the action takes place between the two goals. A midfielder plays in this zone, typically responsible for both defensive and offensive duties. {She dominated the midfield all game}. The term extends to other sports with similar field layouts.

A midfielder is a soccer player positioned between defenders and forwards, responsible for both attacking and defensive duties. Midfielders control the flow of play, distribute the ball, and link defense to attack. The term extends to similar positions in field hockey, lacrosse, and other sports: {She's played midfielder since high school}.

Midfielders are soccer players who operate in the central area of the pitch, linking defense and attack. They typically cover more ground than other positions, responsible for both winning possession and distributing the ball forward. Different types include defensive midfielders, who shield the back line, and attacking midfielders, who create scoring opportunities. {The midfielders controlled possession throughout the second half.}

A midge is a tiny flying insect, often appearing in swarms near water or in damp areas. The term covers various small flies, some of which bite. In casual use, midge describes any gnat-like pest too small to identify: {The midges were unbearable by the lake at dusk}.

Midges are tiny flying insects, often appearing in swarms near water or in damp areas. The term covers various gnat-like flies, some of which bite. In Scotland and parts of North America, midges are notorious summer pests: {The midges were unbearable at dusk}. Singular: midge.

Midi refers to medium length in fashion, particularly skirts and dresses that fall to mid-calf: {She wore a floral midi skirt}. The term emerged as a contrast to mini and maxi lengths. Midi also describes other medium-sized items: a midi ring sits above the knuckle, and midi controllers are compact music production devices. (All-caps MIDI is the digital music standard.)

Midlife is the middle period of a person's life, typically the years from around forty to sixty. It often carries connotations of reassessment or transition: {a midlife career change}, {midlife crisis}. The term acknowledges a stage between youth and old age when people commonly take stock of their choices and mortality.

Midnight is the moment when one day ends and another begins—twelve o'clock at night, the dividing line between today and tomorrow. It marks the middle of the night, the point of deepest darkness before dawn. {The clock struck midnight.} Midnight often carries associations with mystery, magic, or transformation: Cinderella's deadline, the witching hour. As an adjective, it describes things happening at or associated with this hour: a midnight {snack}, a midnight {swim}, {midnight blue}.

Midpoint is the point exactly halfway between two ends or extremes. In geometry, the midpoint of a line segment lies equidistant from both endpoints. The term extends to time and processes: {We're past the midpoint of the project}. A midpoint can also be a compromise position between opposing views.

Midrange describes the middle portion of a range or spectrum. In audio, midrange frequencies fall between bass and treble—the range where most vocals and instruments sit. Midrange products or options occupy the middle tier between budget and premium: {a midrange smartphone}, {midrange pricing}. In basketball, a midrange shot is taken from inside the three-point line but outside the paint.

The midriff is the middle section of the human torso, between the chest and the waist. The word often refers specifically to the front of this area—the stomach region that becomes visible when wearing a crop top or bikini: {She wore a shirt that exposed her midriff}. Midriff-baring fashion goes in and out of style.

Midriffs is the plural of midriff, the front of the body between the chest and the waist. The word often refers to this area when exposed by clothing: {crop tops that show off midriffs}, {bare midriffs at the beach}. Fashion discussions frequently mention midriffs when describing what garments reveal or conceal.

Midrise describes buildings of intermediate height—typically four to twelve stories, taller than low-rise but shorter than high-rise. The term appears most often in real estate and urban planning: {a midrise apartment complex}, {midrise office buildings along the boulevard}. Midrise development often represents a compromise between suburban sprawl and dense urban towers.

Midseason refers to the middle portion of a defined period, typically a sports season or television broadcast schedule. In sports, midseason trades happen while competition is ongoing: {The team acquired a new quarterback midseason}. In television, midseason replacements fill slots when fall premieres fail. As an adjective: {a midseason slump}, {midseason form}.
clues: When the show takes a break

definition: A midshipman is a naval officer in training, ranking below the lowest commissioned officers. In the United States, midshipmen are students at the Naval Academy; in Britain, the term historically designated young men serving aboard ships as part of their officer training. The word reflects the traditional position of these trainees in the middle section of a ship. {The midshipmen stood at attention during the inspection.}

Midshipmen is the plural of midshipman, a naval rank for officer candidates in training. In the U.S. Navy, midshipmen are students at the Naval Academy or in ROTC programs: {The midshipmen marched in formation at graduation}. The rank historically placed these trainees amidships, between officers and enlisted sailors.

Midst means the middle or central part of something, almost always after "in the": {in the midst of the crowd}, {in the midst of a crisis}. It suggests being surrounded or deeply involved. The word is slightly formal or literary—you might say "in the middle of dinner" casually but {in the midst of battle} for elevated effect.

Midstream is the middle of a stream or river, away from the banks: {The boat stalled midstream}. Figuratively, it means in the middle of an ongoing process or activity: {Don't change horses midstream}, {She switched careers midstream}. The warning against midstream changes reflects the risk of disrupting something already in progress.

Midsummer is the middle of summer, typically late June or early July in the Northern Hemisphere. The word often refers to the summer solstice around June 21, the longest day of the year: {a midsummer festival}, {midsummer madness}. Shakespeare's play gives the word dreamlike, enchanted associations. (Capitalized Midsummer may refer specifically to the holiday or the play.)

Midterm refers to the middle of a defined period. In education, a midterm is an exam given halfway through a course or semester: {I have three midterms next week}. In politics, midterm elections occur halfway through an official's term, especially the U.S. congressional elections held between presidential races: {The party lost seats in the midterms}.

Midterms are examinations given in the middle of an academic term, as distinguished from finals: {I have three midterms next week}. In American politics, midterms are congressional elections held halfway through a presidential term, when all House seats and a third of Senate seats are contested: {The president's party typically loses seats in the midterms}.

Midtown designates the central section of a city, typically between the downtown business district and the residential uptown areas. In American cities, midtown often contains a mix of commercial, entertainment, and office spaces. The term is most strongly associated with Manhattan, where Midtown is a specific district known for landmarks like Times Square and the Empire State Building. {We're meeting for lunch somewhere in midtown.} As an adjective, it describes things located in this area: {a midtown apartment}.

Midway means at or around the halfway point of a distance, process, or time period: {We stopped midway between the two cities}, {She changed her mind midway through the project}. The word functions as both adverb and adjective. A midway is also the area at a fair or carnival where games, rides, and sideshows are located—originally the central walkway running through such attractions. (Capitalized Midway refers to the Pacific atoll or the World War II battle fought there.)

Midweek refers to the middle portion of the week, typically Tuesday through Thursday. As an adjective or adverb, it describes things occurring during this period: {a midweek game}, {We'll meet midweek}. The term often implies a contrast with the busier or more social weekend: {Midweek flights are usually cheaper}.

A midwife is a trained professional who assists women during pregnancy, labor, and childbirth, providing care and support throughout the process. Midwives typically handle uncomplicated deliveries and may work in hospitals, birthing centers, or homes. The word combines elements meaning "with woman," reflecting the midwife's role as a companion through birth. As a verb, to midwife something is to help bring it into being: {She midwifed the project from concept to completion}.

Midwifery is the practice of assisting women through pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period. It encompasses prenatal care, delivery support, and newborn care, traditionally performed by midwives rather than physicians. The field emphasizes natural childbirth and treating pregnancy as a normal process rather than a medical condition: {She studied midwifery before opening her own birthing center}.

Midwifing is assisting in childbirth, the work of a midwife. The term extends to helping bring anything into being: {She spent years midwifing the project through bureaucratic obstacles}. To midwife an idea, movement, or creation is to guide its difficult emergence into the world.

Midwinter is the middle of winter, especially around the winter solstice in late December—the shortest day and longest night of the year in the Northern Hemisphere. The word evokes the coldest, darkest stretch of the season: {a midwinter storm}, {midwinter festivities}. As an adjective: {a midwinter night}.

Midwives is the plural of midwife—a person, typically a woman, trained to assist in childbirth. Midwives provide prenatal care, deliver babies, and support mothers through labor and recovery. The profession predates modern medicine; midwives attended births for millennia before obstetricians existed. {The hospital employs twelve midwives.} {Midwives delivered both of her children at home.}

Miff is a minor irritation or state of slight offense. As a verb, to miff someone is to annoy them in a petty way: {She was miffed that no one remembered her birthday}. The word suggests hurt feelings rather than serious anger—being miffed is milder than being furious.
clues: Give a small cause for sulking

definition: Miffed means slightly annoyed or offended—irritated but not truly angry. The word suggests minor displeasure rather than serious upset: {She was miffed that no one remembered her birthday}. It's informal and somewhat understated, often used when acknowledging that the annoyance is petty or disproportionate.

Might is an important phrasal verb that serves as the past tense, and also a more tentative expression of may. Might can be used to express permission, advisability, probability, or possibility in the past, or in the present or future in a less certain way than other modals: They might be waiting for us now. You might think about wearing that without a belt. The noun might, which suggests power and ability, is derived from the same sources as the verb.

Mightier is the comparative form of mighty, meaning more powerful or stronger: {The pen is mightier than the sword}. The word tends toward the literary or rhetorical, appearing in grand statements about force, influence, or moral strength rather than casual comparison.

Mighty means possessing great power, strength, or force: {a mighty army}, {a mighty river}. It can describe impressive size or extent: {a mighty fortress}. As an adverb, mighty is informal intensification meaning very: {That's mighty kind of you}, {mighty fine work}. The construction feels folksy or Southern in American speech. {The mighty have fallen} refers to the once-powerful brought low.

A migraine is a severe, often debilitating headache typically affecting one side of the head, frequently accompanied by nausea, sensitivity to light and sound, and visual disturbances. Migraines can last hours or days and often recur: {She gets migraines when the weather changes}. The word sometimes loosely describes any bad headache, though medical usage is more specific.

Migraines is the plural of migraine, a severe recurring headache typically affecting one side of the head. Migraines often come with nausea, sensitivity to light and sound, and visual disturbances called auras. The pain can be debilitating: {She gets migraines that leave her bedridden for days}. The word sometimes loosely describes any bad headache.

A migrant is someone who moves from one place to another, typically in search of work or better living conditions. The word applies to people who relocate within a country {migrant farmworkers following the harvest} or across borders. Unlike immigrant or emigrant, migrant emphasizes the movement itself rather than arrival or departure, and often implies temporary or seasonal relocation. Birds and animals that travel seasonally are also migrants.

Migrants are people who move from one place to another, typically crossing national or regional boundaries. The term covers those seeking work, fleeing hardship, or pursuing better opportunities: {migrants crossing the border}, {migrant workers in the fields}. Unlike immigrants or emigrants, migrant emphasizes movement itself rather than arrival or departure, and often implies impermanence or repeated relocation.

Migrate means to move from one place to another, typically over a long distance. The word applies both to animals that travel seasonally between regions {geese migrate south for the winter} and to people who relocate to a new country or area {her grandparents migrated from Poland in the 1920s}. In computing, migrate describes moving data, software, or systems from one platform or format to another: {we need to migrate the database to the new server}. The journey itself is called a migration.

Migrating is the present participle of migrate, describing movement from one place to another. Birds and other animals migrate seasonally, following food sources or favorable weather: {migrating geese flew overhead}. People migrate for work, safety, or opportunity. Data migrates between systems during software upgrades. The word emphasizes the process of movement rather than arrival.

Migration is movement from one place to another, typically over significant distance. Birds migrate seasonally between breeding and wintering grounds. Human migration describes population movements across borders or regions: {migration from rural areas to cities}, {the great migration of African Americans to northern states}. In computing, migration is transferring data or systems from one platform to another: {We're planning a migration to the cloud}.

Migrations are movements from one place to another, typically of groups rather than individuals. Birds make seasonal migrations between breeding and wintering grounds. Human migrations reshape demographics: {waves of migration to the American West}. In computing, migrations move data or systems from one platform to another: {We're planning a database migration next month}.

Milady is an archaic or affected form of address for a woman of high social rank, from "my lady." It appears in historical fiction and period dramas: {Milady, your carriage awaits}. The word often carries ironic or mock-formal overtones when used today: {Well, milady, shall we dine?}

Mild means moderate in intensity, not extreme or harsh. Mild weather is pleasantly warm, neither hot nor cold. A mild {criticism} is gentle, not severe. Mild {cheese} or {salsa} lacks strong flavor or heat. A mild {case} of something is not serious. Mild {soap} is gentle on skin. The word suggests softness, restraint, or lack of aggression: {He had a mild manner that put people at ease}.

Mildew is a thin, fuzzy growth of fungus that appears on damp surfaces, particularly in warm, humid conditions. It typically shows up as white, gray, or black patches on walls, fabrics, paper, leather, and plants. Unlike its close relative mold, mildew tends to grow flat on surfaces rather than penetrating deeply. The word also works as a verb: {The basement flooded and everything mildewed}. Mildew carries connotations of neglect, staleness, and the musty smell that accompanies it.

Mildewed describes something affected by mildew—the fuzzy, discolored growth of fungus that appears on damp organic materials. Mildewed {towels}, mildewed {books}, mildewed {walls}. The word suggests neglect, moisture damage, and a characteristic musty smell. Figuratively, mildewed can describe something old and stale: {mildewed ideas}.

A mile is a unit of distance equal to 5,280 feet or about 1.6 kilometers. It's the standard measure for road distances in the United States and United Kingdom. Figuratively, a mile suggests great distance or degree: {I could see him coming from a mile away}, {She missed the target by a mile}. To {go the extra mile} is to make additional effort beyond what's required.
clues: What runners race in four minutes

definition: Mileage is distance measured in miles, especially as traveled by a vehicle: {What's the mileage on your car?} It also means the rate of fuel consumption: {This hybrid gets great mileage}. Figuratively, mileage is the usefulness or benefit derived from something: {She got a lot of mileage out of that story}. A mileage allowance reimburses travel expenses.

A miler is a runner or horse that specializes in the mile distance. In track and field, milers compete in the 1500-meter or mile event: {She was the top miler in the conference}. The term also applies to racehorses bred for middle-distance races around a mile long.

Miles is the plural of mile, a unit of distance equal to 5,280 feet or about 1.6 kilometers. The word often emphasizes distance or extent: {We walked for miles}. Figuratively, miles conveys a large gap or superiority: {Her performance was miles ahead of the competition}, {We're still miles away from a solution}. (Capitalized Miles is a given name.)

A milestone is a stone marker along a road indicating distance to a destination. Figuratively, it marks a significant stage or achievement in a process: {Turning eighteen is a milestone}, {The treaty was a milestone in diplomatic relations}. In project management, milestones are checkpoints marking completion of key phases.

Milestones are markers of progress or significant points along a journey. Originally stones set at intervals along roads to indicate distance traveled, the word now primarily describes important events or achievements: {reaching developmental milestones}, {a milestone birthday}, {a milestone in her career}. In project management, milestones mark key deadlines or deliverables.

Milieu is the social environment or surroundings in which something exists or develops. The word, borrowed from French, suggests the particular world that shapes a person, movement, or work: {the bohemian milieu of 1920s Paris}, {She thrived in the academic milieu}. It emphasizes cultural and social context rather than physical setting.

Militancy is aggressive pursuit of a cause, typically political or social. The word carries implications of confrontation and unwillingness to compromise: {The union's militancy worried management}. Militant action may involve protests, strikes, or civil disobedience, though the term sometimes shades toward suggesting violence. {Her militancy on environmental issues alienated potential allies}.

Militant describes aggressive advocacy or combativeness in pursuing a cause. A militant {activist} pushes confrontationally for change; a militant {atheist} attacks religion rather than merely disbelieving. As a noun, a militant is someone who fights for a cause, often with implications of violence: {Militants attacked the convoy}. The word sits between passionate and extremist—more forceful than committed, less damning than terrorist.

Militants are people engaged in aggressive action for a cause, typically political or ideological. The word emphasizes combativeness—militants don't just hold beliefs, they fight for them. {Union militants organized the strike}. The term often describes armed insurgents or extremists: {Islamic militants}, {right-wing militants}. Unlike soldiers, militants operate outside formal military structures.

Militarisation is the process of equipping with military resources or giving a military character to something previously civilian. A government may militarise its police force, a border region, or its economy. The word often carries negative connotations, suggesting excessive or inappropriate military influence: {the militarisation of outer space}, {the creeping militarisation of everyday life}. Also spelled militarization.

Militarised is the British spelling of militarized. Something militarised has been equipped with military forces, weapons, or characteristics. A militarised {border} has troops and fortifications. A militarised {police force} uses military equipment and tactics. The term often carries critical connotations—suggesting excessive force or an inappropriate warlike approach: {The response to the protests was heavily militarised}.

Militarism is the belief that a country should maintain strong armed forces and be prepared to use them aggressively. It extends to the glorification of military power, values, and ideals—the view that military strength is the foundation of national security and prestige. {The country's militarism led to conflicts with its neighbors.} Critics use the term to suggest excessive influence of military thinking on civilian policy.

A militarist advocates for military strength and readiness, often favoring aggressive foreign policy or the expansion of armed forces. The term usually carries critical overtones—suggesting someone who sees military solutions where others might prefer diplomacy: {The militarists in the cabinet pushed for intervention}. As an adjective, militarist describes policies or attitudes that prioritize military power.

Militaristic describes an aggressive emphasis on military power and readiness, often implying that a nation or leader prioritizes armed force over diplomacy: {The country's militaristic posture alarmed its neighbors}. The term usually carries negative connotations, suggesting excessive bellicosity or glorification of war: {militaristic rhetoric}, {a militaristic regime}.

Militarization is the process of equipping or organizing something along military lines. A society undergoes militarization when military values, personnel, or equipment increasingly dominate civilian life: {the militarization of police forces}, {the militarization of space}. The term often carries critical connotations, suggesting inappropriate extension of military culture into areas where it doesn't belong.

To militarize is to equip with military forces or give military character to something civilian. A government militarizes a border region by deploying troops. Police forces become militarized when they adopt military equipment and tactics: {Critics decried the militarization of local police departments}. The term often carries negative connotations, suggesting excessive or inappropriate use of military power in non-combat contexts.

Militarized describes something that has been given a military character or equipped with military forces. A militarized {zone} has troops stationed in it. A militarized {police force} uses military equipment and tactics. The word often carries critical connotations—suggesting excessive force or inappropriate military influence: {The border has become increasingly militarized}.

Militarizing is the process of equipping or organizing something along military lines. A government militarizes a region by deploying troops or weapons there. Police forces are criticized for militarizing when they adopt military-grade equipment and tactics. The word often carries negative connotations—suggesting escalation or inappropriate force: {The militarizing of local police departments has drawn widespread criticism}.

Military relates to armed forces and warfare. A country's military is its army, navy, air force, and other branches that conduct combat operations. As an adjective, military describes things connected to these forces: military {base}, military {service}, military {uniform}. Military also characterizes precision, discipline, or strictness associated with armed forces: {He runs his household with military efficiency}.

A militia is a military force composed of ordinary citizens rather than professional soldiers, typically called up in emergencies. In American usage, militia often refers to armed civilian groups organized outside government authority, sometimes with anti-government ideology: {The militia movement gained momentum in the 1990s}. The Second Amendment's reference to "a well regulated Militia" fuels ongoing debate about gun rights.

A militiaman is a member of a militia—a military force composed of ordinary citizens rather than professional soldiers. Militias historically formed for local defense or during emergencies when regular armies were insufficient. The term appears in discussions of colonial America, revolutionary movements, and contemporary armed groups: {The militiamen trained on weekends}.

Militiamen is the plural of militiaman—a member of a militia, which is a military force composed of ordinary citizens rather than professional soldiers. Militias may be organized by governments as reserve forces or emerge independently, sometimes as armed groups outside official control: {The militiamen gathered at the armory}, {Local militiamen patrolled the border}.

Militias are armed groups organized outside regular military forces. In the U.S., the term carries different connotations depending on context: the constitutional militia refers to citizens available for defense {a well regulated militia}, while modern militias are often private paramilitary groups with anti-government ideologies {The militia stockpiled weapons at their compound}. Elsewhere, militias may be tribal, political, or revolutionary forces operating alongside or against state armies.

Milk is the white liquid mammals produce to feed their young. Most milk consumed by humans comes from cows, though goat, sheep, and other animal milks have their uses. The verb means to extract milk from an animal, which extends to extracting anything of value: {He milked the situation for all it was worth}. Plant-based alternatives—oat milk, almond milk, soy milk—have complicated the word's boundaries. To {cry over spilled milk} is to regret what can't be undone.
clues: What cereal bowls get filled with

definition: Milked is the past tense of milk—to draw milk from an animal's udder or a mother's breast. The extended sense dominates: to extract value, money, or advantage from something, often excessively or opportunistically: {He milked the insurance claim for everything he could}. {She milked the applause before continuing}. To milk something {for all it's worth} is to exploit it fully.

Milking is the act of extracting milk from an animal, typically a cow, goat, or sheep. The term extends to any gradual extraction: {milking information from a reluctant witness}, {milking the system for benefits}. To milk something is to draw out its value over time, often exploitatively: {He's been milking that one success for years}.

A milkmaid is a woman who milks cows or works in a dairy. The word evokes pastoral imagery—rural life, simplicity, rosy cheeks from outdoor work. It appears mostly in fairy tales, folk songs, and historical contexts: {The milkmaid carried her pail across the meadow}. The occupation itself has largely disappeared with mechanized dairy farming.

Milkmaids is the plural of milkmaid—a woman who milks cows or works in a dairy. The term evokes a pastoral, pre-industrial past: {The milkmaids rose before dawn to tend the herd}. Milkmaids figure in folk songs, nursery rhymes, and idealized rural imagery, often portrayed as rosy-cheeked and wholesome.

A milkman is a person who delivers milk to homes, typically in the early morning. The occupation was common when fresh milk came in glass bottles left on doorsteps: {The milkman came at five every morning}. Home milk delivery has largely disappeared, making the milkman a nostalgic figure. In jokes, the milkman is a stock character for affairs with housewives.

Milkmen is the plural of milkman, a person who delivers milk to homes, typically in the early morning hours. This occupation was once common when fresh milk in glass bottles was delivered daily to doorsteps, but it has largely disappeared with the rise of refrigeration and supermarkets. The milkman persists in jokes and folklore as a figure of suburban infidelity, the supposed father of children who don't resemble their official fathers.

A milkshake is a cold drink made by blending milk, ice cream, and flavorings—typically chocolate, vanilla, or strawberry: {I ordered a chocolate milkshake with my burger}. In some regions, milkshake refers to flavored milk without ice cream, while the ice cream version is called a frappe or cabinet. The drink is associated with diners and fast food.

Milkshakes are cold drinks made by blending milk, ice cream, and flavorings—chocolate, vanilla, strawberry, or countless variations. The thickness varies by region and establishment; some are thin enough to drink through a straw, others nearly spoonable. {I ordered a chocolate milkshake with my burger.} In diner culture, a milkshake is distinct from a malt, which adds malted milk powder.

Milkweed is a North American plant with thick stems that release a milky sap when broken. Its flowers attract butterflies, particularly monarchs, whose caterpillars feed exclusively on the leaves. The seedpods burst open to release seeds attached to silky white fibers that drift on the wind. {The field was full of milkweed and goldenrod.}

Milky describes something resembling milk—white, pale, or cloudy. A milky {liquid} is opaque and whitish. Milky {skin} is very pale. A milky {sky} is hazy white. The Milky Way is the pale band of stars across the night sky. Milky can also mean containing or yielding milk: {milky sap}, {milky coconut}.

A mill is a place where raw materials are processed into products using machinery, especially machinery that grinds. Wheat is ground to flour in a mill; a steel mill produces steel from raw materials. By extension, any place that turns out great quantities of something in a mechanical fashion can be a mill (puppy mill, rumor mill, diploma mill). A small device for grinding is also a mill (salt mill, pepper mill, coffee mill). If you mill something, you grind or crush it. If people are milling around, they’re walking around aimlessly.

A millefeuille is a French pastry made of thin layers of puff pastry alternating with pastry cream, typically topped with icing or powdered sugar. The name means "thousand leaves," referring to the many flaky layers. Also called a Napoleon in American English: {The bakery's millefeuille was perfectly crisp}.

Millenium is a common misspelling of millennium, which has two n's. A millennium is a period of one thousand years, or specifically the transition from one thousand-year period to the next: {Y2K anxiety peaked as the new millennium approached}. The word also refers to an anticipated age of peace and happiness.

Millennia is the plural of millennium—periods of one thousand years. The word appears in discussions of deep time: {Human civilization spans only a few millennia}. It also describes the singular turning point when one millennium ends and another begins, as with the widely celebrated transition from 1999 to 2000.

A millennial is a person born roughly between 1981 and 1996, coming of age around the turn of the millennium. The term often carries generational stereotypes—tech-savvy, entitled, avocado-toast-eating—though these vary by who's using it. As an adjective, millennial relates to this generation or to a millennium generally: {millennial attitudes toward work}, {millennial celebrations}.

Millennials are the generation born roughly between 1981 and 1996, reaching adulthood around the turn of the millennium. The term often carries connotations—positive or negative depending on the speaker—of being tech-savvy, entitled, or economically burdened: {Millennials killed the diamond industry}. Also called Generation Y.

A millennium is a period of one thousand years. The word often appears in discussions of calendar transitions: {anxiety about Y2K peaked as the new millennium approached}. In Christian theology, the millennium refers to a prophesied thousand-year reign of Christ on earth. Millennia of human history stretch behind us; the plural can be either millennia or millenniums.

A miller is a person who operates a mill, grinding grain into flour. The occupation was once common enough that it became a surname. Miller also names various moths whose dusty wings resemble flour-covered clothing. In fishing, a miller is an artificial fly imitating these moths. {The old miller ground wheat for the whole village.} (Capitalized Miller is a surname.)

Millers is the plural of miller, a person who operates a mill—traditionally one who grinds grain into flour. The term extends to various moths whose dusty wing scales resemble a miller's flour-covered clothing. {The millers worked through the night to meet the order.}

Millet is a small-seeded cereal grain grown widely in Asia and Africa. Several grass species fall under the name, all producing tiny round seeds used for food, animal feed, and birdseed. Millet is drought-resistant and quick-growing, making it a staple crop in arid regions: {The farmers planted millet because it could survive the dry season}.

Millets are a group of small-seeded grasses cultivated as cereal crops, especially in Asia and Africa. They thrive in dry conditions where other grains fail. The term covers several distinct species—pearl millet, finger millet, foxtail millet—united by their hardiness and nutritional density. {Millet porridge is a breakfast staple in many cultures.}

A millilitre is one thousandth of a litre, a small unit of liquid volume. It equals one cubic centimetre. Millilitres measure medicine doses, cooking ingredients, and beverage sizes: {The recipe calls for 250 millilitres of milk}. Abbreviated ml or mL. Also spelled milliliter.

Millilitres is the British spelling of milliliters—units of volume equal to one thousandth of a litre. The measurement appears in medicine, cooking, and science: {The dose is 5 millilitres twice daily}. Abbreviated ml or mL.

A millimeter is one thousandth of a meter, or about the thickness of a dime. In countries using the metric system, millimeters measure small distances and precise dimensions: {The tumor was only three millimeters}. American usage favors inches for everyday measurement but millimeters for technical contexts like firearms and film formats.

A millimetre is one thousandth of a metre, or about 0.039 inches—roughly the thickness of a credit card or a few sheets of paper. This metric unit, spelled millimeter in American English, is the standard measurement for small precise distances in engineering, medicine, and everyday contexts where centimetres would be too coarse. {The tumor measured just three millimetres across.} {Adjust the setting by a couple of millimetres.}

Milling is the process of grinding grain into flour, or more broadly, any cutting or shaping done by a rotating tool. A milling {machine} cuts metal or wood with spinning blades. The ridged edge on a coin is called milling. People milling about are moving in an aimless, circular way, like grain being ground: {Crowds milled around the entrance}.

Million is the number equal to one thousand thousands (1,000,000). It serves as a basic unit for large quantities: {a million dollars}, {millions of people}. Casually, million suggests an indefinitely huge number: {I've told you a million times}. A millionaire has wealth of at least a million in some currency. {One in a million} describes something exceptionally rare or special.
clues: Number after nine hundred ninety-nine thousand

definition: A millionaire is someone whose wealth equals or exceeds one million units of currency—typically dollars. The term once suggested extraordinary affluence, but inflation has diluted its impact; today a millionaire may simply be a homeowner with retirement savings. {He became a millionaire before thirty.} Billionaire now carries the weight millionaire once did.

Millionaires is the plural of millionaire—people whose wealth exceeds one million units of currency, typically dollars. The threshold has shifted in significance; a millionaire in 1900 commanded extraordinary wealth, while today the term often describes the merely affluent: {The neighborhood is full of millionaires}. Billionaire has largely replaced it as shorthand for the truly rich.

Millions is the plural of million, denoting multiple quantities of one million each or an indefinitely vast number. {Millions of people watched the broadcast.} The word often emphasizes overwhelming abundance rather than precise count: {I've told you a million times.} As a noun, {the millions} refers to the masses or ordinary people: {entertainment for the millions}.

Millionth describes the position after 999,999 others in a sequence, or one of a million equal parts. As a noun, a millionth is that fractional portion: {a millionth of a second}. The word often emphasizes tedious repetition: {For the millionth time, clean your room}.

A millipede is a many-legged arthropod with an elongated, segmented body—each segment bearing two pairs of legs. Despite the name suggesting a thousand feet, most species have between 30 and 400. Millipedes are slow-moving and feed on decaying plant matter, curling into a spiral when threatened. They're often confused with centipedes, which are faster, flatter, and have one pair of legs per segment.
clues: Two pairs of legs per segment

definition: Millipedes are elongated arthropods with many body segments, each bearing two pairs of legs. Despite the name (from Latin for "thousand feet"), most species have between 30 and 400 legs. They move slowly, feed on decaying plant matter, and curl into a spiral when threatened. Unlike centipedes, they don't bite.
clues: Curl up when you touch them

definition: A millisecond is one thousandth of a second. The term appears in technical contexts—computing, physics, athletics—where tiny intervals matter: {The server responded in 200 milliseconds}. In casual speech, millisecond often just means an extremely brief moment: {I'll be there in a millisecond}.

A millpond is a body of water dammed to provide power for a mill, typically small and calm. The stillness makes it a standard comparison for tranquil water: {The bay was smooth as a millpond}. The phrase {like a millpond} describes any unusually calm surface, especially the sea on a windless day.

Mills are buildings equipped with machinery for grinding grain into flour, or more broadly, any facility for processing raw materials—sawmills, steel mills, paper mills. The verb means to grind or process: {freshly milled pepper}. To mill about is to move aimlessly in a crowd: {Fans milled around outside the stadium}. A mill is also one-tenth of a cent, used mainly in tax calculations.

A millstone is one of a pair of heavy circular stones used for grinding grain.
