The weight and relentlessness of the grinding process give rise to the figurative sense: a millstone is a heavy burden that weighs someone down or impedes progress. {Student debt has become a millstone around the necks of young graduates.} The biblical image of a millstone hung around someone's neck before drowning suggests inescapable punishment.

Millstones are the heavy circular stones used in a mill to grind grain into flour. One stone rotates against another, crushing whatever passes between them. The word appears most often in the biblical phrase {a millstone around one's neck}—a burden so heavy it would drown you if thrown into the sea.

A millstream is a current of water that flows to or through a mill, powering its wheel. The word evokes rural, pre-industrial landscapes where water mills ground grain: {The old millstream ran behind the farmhouse}. It appears in nostalgic contexts and folk songs, notably "Down by the Old Mill Stream."

A millworker is someone employed in a mill, typically a factory where raw materials are processed or manufactured goods are produced. The term most commonly refers to workers in textile mills, paper mills, or steel mills, though it applies broadly to any mill-based industry. Millworkers historically formed a significant part of the industrial labor force, particularly during the 19th and early 20th centuries. {Three generations of her family were millworkers in the cotton industry.}

Milquetoast describes someone timid, meek, and easily dominated—a person who shrinks from confrontation or assertiveness. The word comes from Caspar Milquetoast, a comic strip character of the 1920s whose name punned on milk toast, a bland invalid's food. {He was too much of a milquetoast to ask for a raise.} The term works as both noun and adjective: {a milquetoast response to the crisis}.

Milquetoasts are timid, unassertive people who avoid confrontation and defer to others. The word comes from Caspar Milquetoast, a comic strip character created in 1924 whose name deliberately evoked milk toast—bland invalid food. {The committee was full of milquetoasts who wouldn't challenge the chairman.} The singular milquetoast works as noun or adjective: {a milquetoast response}.

A mime is a performer who acts out scenes using only gestures and body movements, without speaking. The art form itself is also called mime. To mime is to perform in this silent, gestural way, or more broadly to move your lips without producing sound: {She mimed along to the song}. In computing, MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) standardizes how email attachments and web content are formatted, but in everyday use this appears lowercase in terms like {mime type}. (All-caps MIME is the technical acronym.)

Mimed is the past tense of mime—to act out something using gestures and body movements without speaking. Someone who mimed a phone call held an imaginary receiver to their ear. {She mimed zipping her lips shut.} The word can also mean performed as a mime artist, or lip-synced to recorded music: {The pop star mimed the entire concert}.

Mimes are performers who use gesture and movement rather than speech, typically with exaggerated facial expressions and white face paint. The art form descends from ancient theatrical traditions. A mime also refers to the act itself: {She studied mime in Paris}. To mime is to perform silently or mouth words without sound: {He mimed along to the recording}.

To mimic is to imitate closely, especially in speech, gesture, or appearance. A child mimics a parent's mannerisms; a bird mimics human speech; a harmless snake mimics a venomous species to deter predators. As a noun, a mimic is someone skilled at imitation: {He's a talented mimic who can do any politician}. The adjective describes imitative behavior or appearance: {mimic camouflage}.

Mimicking is imitating someone or something, often to entertain or mock: {She was mimicking the teacher's accent}. Animals mimic for survival—some insects mimic leaves, some birds mimic predator calls. The word suggests close copying of mannerisms, sounds, or appearance rather than general imitation.

Mimicry is the act of imitating something else. In biology, it describes how organisms evolve to resemble other species or their environment—a butterfly mimics a toxic species to deter predators, a stick insect mimics a twig. More broadly, mimicry is any close imitation: {His mimicry of the boss was spot-on}. The word suggests copying appearance or behavior rather than substance.

Mimics is the plural of mimic—a person or creature that copies the appearance, sounds, or behavior of another. A mimic might impersonate celebrities or adopt protective coloring like certain insects. The verb mimic means to imitate, often for comic effect or survival: {She mimics her boss perfectly}. Mimics also serves as the third-person singular present tense: {The bird mimics car alarms}.

Miming is communicating through gesture and expression without words—the art of the mime. Someone miming acts out meaning silently: {She was miming drinking from a cup}. The word also covers lip-syncing to recorded music or pretending to play an instrument: {The band was clearly miming during the TV appearance}.

Mimosa names several things united by delicacy or sensitivity. The mimosa plant (also called sensitive plant) has feathery leaves that fold inward when touched. Mimosa trees bear similar foliage with fluffy, fragrant flower clusters. A mimosa is also a brunch cocktail of champagne and orange juice, named for the flower's color: {We ordered mimosas with our eggs Benedict}.

Mimosas are a genus of plants known for their feathery flowers and sensitive leaves that fold when touched—the so-called sensitive plant. More commonly, a mimosa is a brunch cocktail of champagne and orange juice: {We ordered mimosas with our eggs Benedict}. The drink takes its name from the flower's resemblance to the pale yellow-orange beverage.

A minaret is a tall, slender tower attached to a mosque, from which the call to prayer is traditionally announced. Minarets are distinctive features of Islamic architecture, typically cylindrical or polygonal with a balcony near the top: {The city skyline was punctuated by dozens of minarets}.

Minarets are tall, slender towers attached to mosques, from which a muezzin traditionally calls Muslims to prayer. The distinctive silhouette—often with a balcony near the top and a pointed or onion-shaped crown—has become an architectural symbol of Islam: {The minarets of Istanbul punctuate the skyline}.

Mince means to cut or chop into very small pieces: {mince the garlic and add it to the pan}. Minced meat, or simply mince in British English, is finely ground meat. To mince words is to speak evasively or with excessive delicacy—usually negated: {Let me not mince words: you're fired}. To mince is also to walk with short, dainty, affected steps.

Minced describes food cut into very small pieces, typically by chopping rapidly with a knife or processing in a machine: {minced garlic}, {minced onion}, {minced beef}. In British usage, minced meat or simply mince is what Americans call ground meat. To {not mince words} is to speak bluntly without softening the message.

Mincemeat is a mixture of chopped dried fruits, spices, sugar, and suet, traditionally used as pie filling—especially in British Christmas mince pies. Despite the name, modern mincemeat rarely contains actual meat, though historical versions did. To {make mincemeat of} someone is to defeat or destroy them utterly: {The defense attorney made mincemeat of the witness's testimony}.

Mincing describes movement or speech that is affectedly dainty or delicate—taking small, precise steps or speaking in an overly refined way: {She walked with mincing steps across the stage}. The word often carries dismissive or mocking connotations, suggesting someone is being prissy or effeminate. To {not mince words} is to speak bluntly, without softening or hedging.

We use mind to talk about consciousness. This meaning is reflected in dozens of common expressions, such as change your mind, keep it in mind, speak your mind, cross your mind, and lose your mind. Mind can be contrasted with heart or body, depending on which aspects of the mind are being emphasized. If you mind something, you pay attention to it. If you don’t mind something, you have no objection to it.

A mindbender is something that strains comprehension or challenges perception—a puzzle, paradox, or concept that forces the mind to work hard: {That film's ending was a real mindbender}. The term often describes movies, books, or ideas with unexpected twists or counterintuitive logic. A mindbender can also be a person who manipulates others psychologically, or slang for a hallucinogenic drug.

Mindbending describes something that challenges or overwhelms normal understanding—an idea, experience, or substance that distorts perception or defies comprehension. A mindbending {plot twist} upends everything you thought you knew. Mindbending {drugs} alter consciousness. The word suggests reality itself becoming unstable or strange: {The scale of the universe is mindbending}.

Mindblowing describes something so impressive, surprising, or revelatory that it overwhelms your capacity to process it—as if your mind has been blown apart. The term emerged from 1960s drug culture to describe psychedelic experiences but now applies broadly to anything extraordinary: {The special effects were mindblowing}, {a mindblowing plot twist}. It's often written as two words or hyphenated (mind-blowing) and frequently subject to hyperbole.

Mindblown describes the state of being astonished or overwhelmed by something unexpected or impressive: {I was absolutely mindblown when I saw the final twist}. The term emerged from internet culture, often appearing as a single word or hashtag to react to revelations, coincidences, or information that challenges assumptions. Sometimes rendered as two words or hyphenated.

Mindboggling describes something so extraordinary, complex, or vast that the mind struggles to comprehend it: {The mindboggling scale of the universe}, {mindboggling amounts of data}. The image is of a mind that boggles—hesitates, recoils—when confronted with something beyond easy grasp. Also spelled mind-boggling.

A minder is someone who watches over or takes care of something. A child minder looks after children. In British usage, a minder may be a bodyguard or someone assigned to accompany and monitor another person: {The politician's minders kept reporters at bay}. The word often implies protective supervision that shades into control.

Minders are people who look after someone or something. A child minder watches children; a body minder (or just minder) serves as a bodyguard or escort. In British usage especially, minders handle celebrities or politicians, managing their public interactions: {His minders kept reporters at bay}. The term can suggest protective hovering or control over access.

A mindfuck is an experience that profoundly disorients or destabilizes your sense of reality—a movie twist that makes you rethink everything, a revelation that upends your worldview, or a situation designed to manipulate and confuse: {That ending was a total mindfuck}. To mindfuck someone is to mess with their head, often through psychological manipulation or deception. The term is vulgar but widely used for experiences that leave you questioning what's real.

Mindfucked describes a state of mental disorientation or confusion, typically after encountering something that challenges basic assumptions or defies comprehension: {I was completely mindfucked after that movie's ending}. The term is vulgar but expressive—it suggests your mind has been violated or scrambled, not merely puzzled. Can also describe psychological manipulation: {The cult leader had them mindfucked into believing anything}.

Mindfuckery is the practice of psychologically manipulating, confusing, or disorienting someone, often through deception, gaslighting, or deliberately bewildering behavior. The term is vulgar and informal, carrying connotations of malicious intent or at least reckless disregard for another's mental wellbeing. It can describe anything from elaborate cons to relationship manipulation to media designed to disorient: {I'm done with his mindfuckery—he denies saying things I literally watched him say}. The word emphasizes the cumulative effect of such tactics rather than any single act.

Mindfucking is the act of psychologically manipulating or disorienting someone—deliberately confusing their sense of reality, undermining their confidence, or playing elaborate mental games. It can describe gaslighting in relationships {He's been mindfucking her for years}, or refer to experiences that profoundly challenge perception: {That movie was mindfucking me the whole time}. The term is vulgar but vivid.

Mindfucks are experiences that disorient, confuse, or profoundly alter perception—whether deliberately inflicted or encountered. A film with a shocking twist is a mindfuck. Psychological manipulation that makes someone question reality is a mindfuck. The term suggests something that penetrates and scrambles your thinking: {That ending was one of the biggest mindfucks I've ever seen}. Can describe drugs, revelations, or calculated deception.

Mindful means conscious and attentive, usually with an element of care or concern: {Be mindful of the time}, {mindful of her feelings}. In contemporary usage, mindful often connects to meditation practices—being fully present and aware of one's thoughts and surroundings without judgment: {mindful breathing}, {mindful eating}. The noun is mindfulness.

Mindfulness is the practice of maintaining calm, nonjudgmental awareness of the present moment—one's thoughts, feelings, and surroundings. Rooted in Buddhist meditation traditions, it entered mainstream Western psychology as a stress-reduction technique. {Her therapist recommended mindfulness exercises}. To practice mindfulness is to observe experience without reacting: {I'm trying to approach my anxiety with mindfulness rather than panic}.

Mindless describes action or behavior without thought or purpose. A mindless {task} requires no mental engagement. Mindless {violence} is brutal without reason or reflection. To be mindless {of} something is to be heedless of it: {mindless of the consequences}. The word often carries judgment—that someone should have thought but didn't.

Mindlessness is the state of acting without thought or awareness. It can mean doing something mechanically, without engagement: {the mindlessness of assembly-line work}. It also describes thoughtless or stupid behavior: {The mindlessness of the vandalism shocked the neighborhood}. The word implies either vacancy of attention or absence of purpose.
clues: State of not thinking at all

definition: A mindmap is a diagram that organizes information visually around a central concept, with related ideas branching outward like limbs from a trunk. The format encourages free association and nonlinear thinking, making it popular for brainstorming, note-taking, and planning: {I drew a mindmap to sort out my ideas for the project}. Also written as two words: mind map.

A mindmeld is a merging of thoughts or consciousness between two people, from the telepathic technique in *Star Trek* where Vulcans share minds through touch. Now used loosely for any intense meeting of minds or moment of perfect mutual understanding: {We had a mindmeld about the project direction}. Often spelled as two words or hyphenated.

To mindread is to perceive another person's thoughts without verbal communication—a supposed psychic ability. More commonly, the word describes attempting to infer what someone is thinking: {Stop trying to mindread and just ask her what's wrong}. The noun mindreader and the gerund mindreading follow the same pattern.

A mindreader is someone who claims or appears to know what others are thinking. Stage magicians and mentalists perform as mindreaders, using tricks to simulate telepathy. More commonly, the word appears in denials: {I'm not a mindreader—you have to tell me what you want}. Also spelled as two words.

Mindreaders are people who claim or appear to know what others are thinking. The term covers stage performers who use psychological tricks, purported psychics who claim telepathic ability, and ordinary people with keen intuition: {My wife is a mindreader—she always knows when something's bothering me}. Often used sarcastically when someone expects you to anticipate their unstated thoughts: {I'm not a mindreader; you have to tell me what you want}.

Mindreading is the supposed ability to perceive another person's thoughts directly, without communication. In everyday use, it often describes intuiting what someone is thinking or feeling: {After twenty years of marriage, she could practically mindread}. The term also appears sarcastically when someone expects you to know something they haven't said: {I'm not mindreading here—you have to tell me what you want}.

Minds is the plural of mind—the faculty of thought, awareness, and reasoning. Multiple minds can collaborate or disagree: {Great minds think alike}. To mind something is to object to it or to look after it: {Do you mind if I sit here?} {Mind the children while I'm out}. To be of two minds is to feel conflicted. {Minds were changed after the debate}.

A mindscape is the landscape of someone's mind—the terrain of their thoughts, imagination, or mental state. The word treats consciousness as a place that can be explored or depicted: {The novel takes readers deep into the protagonist's mindscape}. Common in discussions of psychology, art, and speculative fiction where inner worlds become navigable spaces.

Mindscapes are the imagined landscapes of someone's inner mental world—the terrain of thoughts, memories, dreams, and emotions. The word treats consciousness as a place that can be explored or mapped: {The novel takes readers through the protagonist's fractured mindscapes}. Often used in creative or psychological contexts to describe subjective experience as visual or spatial.

A mindset is a person's established set of attitudes or way of thinking about something. It shapes how you interpret and respond to situations: {a growth mindset}, {a fixed mindset}. The word often appears in self-help contexts emphasizing that changing your mindset can change your outcomes: {She approached the challenge with a positive mindset}.

Mindsets are habitual attitudes or mental frameworks that shape how someone interprets and responds to situations. A {growth mindset} sees abilities as developable through effort; a {fixed mindset} sees them as innate. The term often appears in self-help and business contexts: {Changing your mindset can transform your approach to challenges}.

Mindshare is the degree to which something occupies public awareness or attention. Originally marketing jargon for how much mental space a brand claims relative to competitors, it now applies broadly: {Apple has enormous mindshare among tech consumers}. A startup might lack market share but have significant mindshare if people are talking about it. The term treats collective attention as a finite resource that companies, ideas, or movements compete for.

Mine combines two jobs in one; to take the place of a noun or noun phrase already named, and to indicate that the thing referred to belongs to or is associated with you: If your car is still in the shop you can use mine. These two jobs give mine and other words in its class the designation “possessive pronoun.”

Minecars are small wheeled vehicles used to transport ore, coal, or debris through mine tunnels, typically running on narrow-gauge rails. They may be pushed by hand, pulled by animals, or connected in trains behind locomotives. The singular minecar appears in video games like Minecraft, where riding minecars through tunnels is a common gameplay element.

A minecart is a small wheeled vehicle used to transport ore, coal, or debris through mine tunnels, typically running on narrow-gauge rails. The word appears frequently in video games, especially Minecraft and Donkey Kong Country, where minecarts serve as transport or appear in rail-riding sequences: {We loaded the minecart with iron ore}.

Minecarts are small wheeled vehicles that run on rails in mines, used to haul ore, coal, or other materials. The singular minecart appears most often in video games, especially Minecraft, where riding minecarts along player-built rail systems is a core mechanic: {We built a minecart track connecting our bases}.

Mined is the past tense of mine, meaning to extract minerals or other materials from the earth: {They mined coal in these hills for generations}. By extension, to mine is to extract anything valuable from a larger source: {She mined the archives for relevant documents}. Mined also describes areas where explosive mines have been placed: {The harbor was heavily mined during the war}.

A minefield is an area where explosive mines have been buried, creating deadly hazard for anyone crossing it. The figurative sense dominates contemporary usage: any situation full of hidden dangers or potential problems requiring careful navigation. {The interview was a minefield of controversial topics.} {Navigating office politics can be a minefield.}

Minefields are areas where explosive mines have been planted, whether on land or at sea. Soldiers crossing a minefield risk death with each step. Figuratively, a minefield is any situation full of hidden dangers: {The interview was a minefield of potentially offensive questions}. The singular minefield is more common.

A miner is a person who works in a mine, extracting coal, ore, or other minerals from the earth. The term extends to automated mining equipment: {The company deployed underwater miners to harvest seafloor minerals}. In cryptocurrency, a miner is a computer or person that validates transactions and adds them to the blockchain, receiving coins as reward.

A mineral is a naturally occurring inorganic substance with a specific chemical composition and crystalline structure—quartz, felite, copper. Rocks are made of minerals. The term extends to substances extracted from the earth for human use: {mineral rights}, {mineral deposits}. Mineral water contains dissolved minerals. As an adjective, mineral describes things derived from or relating to such substances: {mineral oil}, {mineral wealth}.

Minerals are naturally occurring inorganic substances with a definite chemical composition. In nutrition, minerals are essential elements like iron, calcium, and zinc that the body needs in small amounts. Informally, minerals often means mineral water: {I'll have a gin and minerals}. In British usage, minerals can mean soft drinks generally.

Miners are workers who extract minerals, coal, or other materials from the earth, typically from underground tunnels or open pits. The term extends to those who dig for precious metals: gold miners, diamond miners. In cryptocurrency, miners are computers or their operators that validate transactions and add them to the blockchain, rewarded with new coins for their computational work.

Mines is the plural of mine—an excavation for extracting minerals or an explosive device buried underground or underwater. Coal mines, gold mines, land mines, naval mines. Figuratively, something that's {a mine of information} is a rich source. The possessive pronoun mine ({That book is mines}) appears in some dialects but is nonstandard.

A mineshaft is a vertical or steeply inclined passage providing access to an underground mine. It serves as the main route for transporting miners, equipment, and extracted ore or coal to the surface. Mineshafts typically contain elevators or hoisting systems and ventilation infrastructure. {The old mineshaft had been sealed off for decades.}

Mineshafts are vertical or inclined passages dug into the earth to access underground mines. The shaft serves as the main entry point for miners, equipment, and ventilation, with elevators or hoists moving people and materials between the surface and working levels below: {The old mineshaft had been sealed for decades}.

Minestrone is a thick Italian soup made with vegetables, beans, and pasta or rice. The ingredients vary by region and season, but typically include tomatoes, onions, celery, and carrots in a broth base. {We ordered minestrone and garlic bread.}

A minesweeper is a naval vessel designed to detect and destroy underwater mines, clearing safe passage for other ships. The work is dangerous and methodical, requiring specialized equipment to trigger or disarm explosives before they can damage larger vessels. By extension, minesweeper refers to the classic computer game where players uncover squares on a grid while avoiding hidden mines, using numeric clues to deduce their locations: {I wasted an hour playing minesweeper instead of working}. (Capitalized Minesweeper often refers specifically to the Microsoft Windows game.)

Minesweepers are naval vessels designed to detect and neutralize underwater mines, clearing safe passages for other ships. The work is dangerous and painstaking, requiring specialized equipment to locate explosives hidden beneath the surface. By extension, minesweeper names the classic computer puzzle game where players deduce the locations of hidden mines on a grid: {I used to play minesweeper during slow days at work}.

Minesweeping is the military operation of detecting and removing explosive mines from water or land. Naval minesweepers clear shipping lanes; land-based minesweeping clears fields and roads. The word also describes the practice of finishing other people's unattended drinks at a bar or party: {He was minesweeping at the pub, grabbing any abandoned pint}.

Mingle means to mix or blend together, whether people, substances, or abstract things. At a party, you mingle by moving through the crowd and talking with different people rather than staying in one spot: {She mingled with the guests before dinner}. Things can mingle too—scents mingle in a garden, emotions mingle in a complicated situation. The word suggests combining while still retaining some distinctness, unlike merge or fuse which imply complete blending.

Mingled is the past tense of mingle, meaning to mix or blend together. People mingle at parties, moving through a crowd and making conversation. Feelings can be mingled: {relief mingled with sadness}. Sounds mingle when they blend into one another. The word suggests combination without complete merger—elements remain distinguishable even as they mix.

Mingling is mixing or circulating, especially among people at social gatherings. You mingle at a party by moving through the crowd, making small talk with different groups rather than staying in one spot: {She spent the cocktail hour mingling with potential clients}. Things that mingle blend together: {The smell of coffee mingled with cigarette smoke}.

Mini describes something smaller than usual—a miniature version of a standard item. A mini {skirt} or mini {dress} falls well above the knee. A mini {fridge} fits in a dorm room. The word works as noun or adjective: {She drove a mini} or {a mini vacation}. Mini appears in countless compounds: minivan, miniseries, minigolf. (Capitalized Mini is the car brand.)

Miniature describes something much smaller than the standard version: a miniature {poodle}, a miniature {golf course}, a miniature {replica of the Eiffel Tower}. As a noun, a miniature is a small-scale model or a tiny detailed painting, especially a portrait. {In miniature} means on a reduced scale: {The town was Paris in miniature}.

Miniatures are small-scale representations of larger things. A miniature portrait fits in a locket; a miniature golf course shrinks the game to novelty size. In tabletop gaming, miniatures are small figurines representing characters or units: {He spent the weekend painting his miniatures}. The adjective miniature describes anything unusually small for its type: {a miniature poodle}, {a miniature replica of the Eiffel Tower}.

Miniaturization is the process of making things smaller, particularly in engineering and technology. The term became prominent with the development of electronics, where shrinking components allowed devices like computers and phones to become portable rather than room-sized. {The miniaturization of sensors has revolutionized medical diagnostics.} Beyond technology, miniaturization applies to any systematic reduction in scale, from architectural models to food portions.

To miniaturize is to make something much smaller while preserving its essential form and function. The word arose with modern technology—miniaturized electronics, miniaturized components. Scientists miniaturize devices; manufacturers miniaturize products. The concept extends beyond engineering: {a miniaturized version of the original plan}. The British spelling is miniaturise.

A minibar is a small refrigerator stocked with beverages and snacks, typically found in hotel rooms. Guests help themselves and charges appear on their bill at checkout. The contents are usually overpriced: {I paid eight dollars for a tiny bottle of water from the minibar}. Some minibars have sensors that automatically charge when items are moved.

Minibars are small refrigerators stocked with drinks and snacks, typically found in hotel rooms. Guests help themselves and charges appear on the bill at checkout. The contents are often overpriced: {I paid eight dollars for a tiny bottle of water from the minibar}. Some hotels now use sensors to detect when items are removed.

Minibeast is a British term, mainly used in primary education, for small invertebrates like insects, spiders, worms, and snails. It's a friendly, accessible word that avoids scientific terminology when teaching young children about nature: {We went on a minibeast hunt in the garden}. The term rarely appears in American English or adult scientific contexts.

A minibike is a small, lightweight motorcycle with a low frame, typically designed for off-road recreational use rather than street riding. Originally popular with children and teenagers, minibikes have compact engines and are simpler than full-sized motorcycles: {He learned to ride on a minibike in his uncle's backyard}.

A miniboss is a video game enemy stronger than regular opponents but less powerful than a full boss—a mid-tier challenge encountered between major battles. Minibosses often guard key items or block progress through an area: {There's a miniboss at the end of each dungeon wing}. The term extends to any intermediate obstacle or adversary: {My actual boss is fine, but his assistant is the real miniboss}.

Minibosses are intermediate enemies in video games—tougher than standard foes but less formidable than the main boss of a level or area. They typically guard key items or block progress, serving as skill checks before the final confrontation: {The dungeon has three minibosses before you reach the dragon}. The term extends to any secondary challenge that must be overcome before facing the primary obstacle.

A minicab is a British term for a taxi that must be booked in advance rather than hailed on the street. Unlike licensed black cabs, minicabs are private hire vehicles that operate through a dispatcher or booking office: {I called a minicab to take us to the airport}. The term distinguishes these cars from traditional taxis with their distinctive appearance and right to pick up street fares.

A minidress is a dress with a hemline well above the knee, typically mid-thigh or higher. The style emerged in the 1960s as part of youth fashion's break from conservative dress codes: {She wore a black minidress to the party}. The mini- prefix has spawned related terms like miniskirt.

A minifigure is a small articulated toy figure, particularly the iconic plastic people produced by Lego since 1978. The proportions are distinctive—cylindrical heads, C-shaped hands, stubby legs—and instantly recognizable. Collectors and builders use the shortened form "minifig": {I need a pirate minifig for this ship}. The term sometimes extends to similar small figures from other construction toy brands.

A minifridge is a small refrigerator, typically under four cubic feet, designed for compact spaces like dorm rooms, offices, or hotel rooms. It usually holds beverages and a few small items rather than a household's groceries: {I keep snacks and energy drinks in my minifridge}.

A minigame is a short, simple game embedded within a larger video game. Minigames typically offer a break from the main gameplay, appearing as puzzles, challenges, or diversions: {The fishing minigame became more popular than the main quest}. The term extends to brief activities within apps or websites designed to engage users.

Minigames are small, self-contained games embedded within a larger video game. They typically offer a break from the main gameplay, providing quick challenges with simple mechanics: {I spent hours on the fishing minigame instead of finishing the main quest}. Minigames may be optional diversions or required for progression. The term extends to party games and collections of short competitive activities played in succession.

Minigolf is a recreational version of golf played on a small course with obstacles, tunnels, ramps, and other novelty features that make each hole a puzzle to navigate. Players use putters to guide a ball through these miniature landscapes, typically completing 18 holes in under an hour. The game requires no special skill or athletic ability, making it a popular activity for families and casual outings. Also called miniature golf or putt-putt.

A minigun is a multi-barrel machine gun with rotating barrels, capable of extremely high rates of fire—typically several thousand rounds per minute. The barrels rotate like a Gatling gun, preventing overheating. Despite the name, miniguns are large weapons, usually vehicle-mounted: {The helicopter's minigun tore through the jungle canopy}. The "mini" distinguishes it from larger rotary cannons.

A minigun is a rapid-fire rotary machine gun with multiple rotating barrels, capable of firing thousands of rounds per minute. The design prevents overheating by distributing heat across barrels. Despite the name, miniguns are large weapons typically mounted on helicopters, vehicles, or fixed positions—"mini" only relative to earlier rotary cannons. {The helicopter's minigun tore through the treeline.}

Minimal means the smallest amount or degree possible, or reduced to the barest essentials. Something minimal is stripped down to only what's necessary: {The recipe requires minimal preparation.} {We experienced minimal delays.} In design and art, minimal describes a style characterized by extreme simplicity and the absence of decoration or ornamentation. The word often carries positive connotations of efficiency or elegance, though it can also suggest insufficiency: {The response was minimal at best.}

Minimalism is a style or approach that emphasizes simplicity and the removal of unnecessary elements. In art and design, it favors clean lines, limited colors, and sparse composition. In lifestyle contexts, it describes deliberately owning fewer possessions and reducing consumption: {Her minimalism means she owns only what she truly needs}. The term can apply to music, architecture, writing, or any domain where stripping away excess reveals essential form.

Minimalist describes a preference for the fewest elements, simplest forms, or least amount necessary. In art and design, minimalism strips away ornamentation to emphasize essential structure: {a minimalist aesthetic}, {minimalist furniture}. As a noun, a minimalist practices this approach: {She's a minimalist who owns only what she needs}. The word applies broadly to lifestyle, music, architecture, or any domain where reduction is the goal.

Minimalists are people who favor simplicity and the reduction of elements to essentials. In art and design, minimalists strip away ornamentation to focus on form, space, and basic materials. In lifestyle, minimalists pursue fewer possessions and commitments: {The minimalists sold their house and live in a van}. The term can be dismissive when applied to someone perceived as doing too little.

A minimap is a small map displayed in a corner of a video game screen, showing the player's immediate surroundings, objectives, or teammates in simplified form. It provides spatial awareness without obscuring the main view: {I spotted enemies on the minimap before they came around the corner}. Also called a radar or mini-map.

A minimart is a small retail store that sells a limited selection of everyday items like snacks, beverages, and basic groceries. These compact shops are often found attached to gas stations or in urban areas where full-sized supermarkets aren't practical. The term combines "mini" with "mart" (an old word for market) to emphasize the store's reduced size and inventory compared to a typical grocery store. {I stopped at the minimart for a bag of ice and some sodas.}

Minimise is the British spelling of minimize. To minimise something is to reduce it to the smallest possible amount or degree: {We need to minimise costs}. It also means to downplay or represent as less significant than it really is: {Don't minimise what she went through}. In computing, to minimise a window is to shrink it to an icon or taskbar.

To minimize is to reduce something to its smallest possible amount or degree: {We took steps to minimize risk}. In computing, to minimize a window is to shrink it to an icon or taskbar. Minimize also means to downplay or represent as less significant than it is: {Don't minimize my concerns}.

Minimized describes something reduced to the smallest possible amount or degree: {We minimized our expenses during the lean months}. In computing, a minimized window has been shrunk to an icon or taskbar button, still running but hidden from view: {I minimized the browser to check my desktop}. The word can also suggest downplaying significance: {He minimized his role in the scandal}.

Minimizing is making something as small as possible, or treating it as less important than it is. You minimize a window on your computer screen, shrinking it out of the way. Someone minimizes their role in a scandal to avoid blame: {He kept minimizing his involvement, but the evidence told a different story}. To minimize risk is to reduce it; to minimize an achievement is to downplay it.

Minimum is the smallest amount, degree, or number possible or allowed. A minimum {wage} is the lowest legal pay. {At a minimum}, you should call before showing up. The adjective describes the least acceptable: minimum {requirements}, minimum {effort}. The opposite is maximum. Plural: minimums or minima.

Mining is the extraction of valuable materials from the earth, including metals, coal, gemstones, and other minerals. The process ranges from surface operations like open-pit mines to deep underground excavations. By extension, mining applies to any systematic extraction of resources: {data mining} involves sifting through large datasets for useful patterns, and cryptocurrency mining uses computing power to validate transactions and generate new coins. To mine something is to extract it through such processes: {They've been mining copper in this region for decades}.

A minion is a subordinate who carries out orders, often with excessive eagerness or servility. The word implies someone who exists to do another's bidding: {The CEO surrounded himself with minions who never questioned his decisions}. Minion often carries a mocking or contemptuous tone, suggesting the subordinate lacks independent judgment or dignity. In recent decades, the word has softened through popular culture, sometimes used affectionately for loyal helpers or followers.

Minions are subordinates who carry out someone else's orders, typically with blind loyalty. The word usually carries a negative connotation—suggesting servility or complicity in wrongdoing: {The villain dispatched his minions to do the dirty work}. A minion can also be a favorite or darling, though this older sense is rare. The 2010 animated film *Despicable Me* popularized minions as small yellow cartoon creatures, now ubiquitous in memes and merchandise.

Minis is the plural of mini, a shortening of miniature or minimum. A mini is something small of its kind—a miniskirt, a minibar, a Mini Cooper. In gaming, minis are miniature figures used in tabletop games: {I spent the weekend painting my new minis}. The word functions as both noun and adjective: {mini golf}, {mini fridge}.

A miniseries is a television program that tells a complete story over a limited number of episodes, typically between two and ten, rather than running indefinitely like a regular series. The format became popular in the 1970s and 1980s for adapting novels and historical events, and has seen a resurgence with streaming platforms. {The miniseries covered the entire scandal from start to finish.}

A miniskirt is a very short skirt with a hemline well above the knee, typically mid-thigh or higher. The style emerged in the 1960s as a symbol of youth culture and sexual liberation: {She wore a miniskirt and go-go boots}. Often shortened to mini: {a denim mini}.

Miniskirts are very short skirts with hemlines well above the knee, typically mid-thigh or higher. The style emerged in the 1960s as a symbol of youth culture and sexual liberation: {She wore miniskirts and go-go boots}. The singular miniskirt also works as an attributive: {miniskirt weather}.

A minisode is a short episode of a television series or podcast, typically running a fraction of the standard length. Networks and creators use minisodes as promotional material, bonus content between seasons, or web-exclusive features: {The show released minisodes during the hiatus to keep fans engaged}.

A minister is a member of the clergy, especially in Protestant churches: {The minister led the congregation in prayer}. In government, a minister heads a department or ministry: {the Prime Minister}, {the Minister of Finance}. To minister is to attend to someone's needs, especially in a caring or spiritual capacity: {She ministered to the sick}. The word carries a sense of service—ministers serve their congregations, their governments, or those requiring aid.

Ministers are people who serve in positions of authority. In government, ministers head departments or agencies: {the finance minister}, {the defense minister}. In religion, ministers are clergy who lead congregations, especially in Protestant churches: {The minister performed the wedding ceremony}. To minister is to attend to someone's needs: {She ministered to the sick}.

Ministries is the plural of ministry. In government, ministries are departments headed by ministers: {the ministries of defense, finance, and education}. In religion, ministries are organizations or programs devoted to spiritual work or service: {The church runs several outreach ministries}. The word covers both the institutions themselves and their collective activities.

The noun ministry shows an important difference between American and other varieties of English. Parliamentary governments (as in the UK and many other countries) call their major departments of government ministries (Ministry of Justice). In American English, however, these are simply called departments, and ministry refers to the service, job, or activity of a religious minister: The boy felt called to enter the ministry after high school graduation. The ordained ministry refers collectively to religious ministers.

A minisub is a small submarine, typically designed for specialized tasks rather than military combat—research, underwater exploration, salvage operations, or transporting small crews to depths larger vessels can't reach. The term sometimes appears in contexts of drug smuggling, where cartels use homemade minisubs to move cargo: {Authorities intercepted a minisub off the coast}.

A minivan is a boxy passenger vehicle larger than a station wagon, with sliding side doors and seating for six to eight people. The design prioritizes interior space over style, making minivans practical for families with children: {We piled into the minivan for the road trip}. The word carries suburban-parent connotations that some find unflattering.

Minivans are boxy passenger vehicles designed for families, larger than station wagons but smaller than full-size vans. They typically seat six to eight people, with sliding side doors and fold-flat rear seats for cargo flexibility. The minivan became the suburban family vehicle of choice in the 1980s and 1990s, though SUVs have since claimed much of that market: {We piled the kids into the minivan and headed to soccer practice}.

A mink is a small, semiaquatic mammal prized for its soft, dense fur. Minks are raised on farms specifically for their pelts, which become luxury coats and accessories: {a mink coat}, {a mink stole}. The word often refers to the fur itself or garments made from it: {She wore her grandmother's mink to the opera}.

Minks are small, semiaquatic mammals prized for their soft, dense fur. They belong to the weasel family and are raised commercially on fur farms. The plural also refers to mink fur garments: {She wore her grandmother's minks to the opera}. A mink coat has long signified wealth and glamour, though fur fashion has become controversial.

A minnow is any of various small freshwater fish, often used as bait. The word extends loosely to any tiny fish: {We caught nothing but minnows}. Figuratively, a minnow is a small or insignificant player relative to larger competitors: {a minnow in a sea of corporate giants}.

Minnows are small freshwater fish, typically under a few inches long, belonging to the carp family. The term is used loosely for any tiny fish, especially those used as bait or kept in home aquariums. Figuratively, minnow describes someone or something small and insignificant relative to larger competitors: {In a league of corporate giants, our startup was just a minnow}. Children often try to catch minnows with nets in shallow streams and ponds.

Minor means lesser in size, importance, or seriousness. A minor injury isn't severe. A minor character has a small role. In music, a minor key has a darker, sadder quality than major. A minor is also a person below the age of legal adulthood—typically eighteen in most jurisdictions: {The bar was cited for serving minors}. In education, a minor is a secondary field of study: {She majored in biology with a minor in chemistry}. (Capitalized Minor appears in some proper names.)

Minorities are groups that make up less than half of a larger population. The term typically refers to racial, ethnic, or religious groups that are numerically smaller than the dominant group in a society: {Minorities are underrepresented in corporate leadership}. The word can also describe any smaller faction: {a minority of voters}. Though originally about numbers, minority often implies reduced power or status regardless of actual population size—hence South African blacks were called a minority under apartheid despite being the majority.
clues: Those with fewer in their group

definition: Minority refers to the smaller part of a group—less than half: {A minority of voters supported the measure}. In social contexts, a minority is a group distinguished by race, ethnicity, religion, or other characteristics that differs from the dominant population: {racial minorities}, {religious minorities}. The term implies both smaller numbers and often reduced social power. Minority also describes the state of being under legal age: {He inherited the estate during his minority}.

Minors are people who have not yet reached the age of legal adulthood—typically eighteen in most jurisdictions. The term appears constantly in legal contexts: {The sale of alcohol to minors is prohibited}. In education, a minor is a secondary field of study alongside one's major: {She's majoring in biology with a minor in chemistry}. In music, minor keys and chords have a darker, more melancholy quality than major ones.

A minotaur is a mythical creature with a human body and a bull's head. The original Minotaur of Greek mythology was confined to the Labyrinth on Crete and fed human sacrifices until Theseus killed it. In fantasy games and fiction, minotaurs appear as a species of bull-headed humanoids, typically portrayed as fierce warriors or dungeon-dwelling monsters: {The party encountered a minotaur guarding the treasure room}. (Capitalized Minotaur refers to the specific creature of Greek myth.)

Minotaurs is the plural of minotaur, a creature from Greek mythology with a human body and bull's head. The original Minotaur dwelt in a labyrinth on Crete until Theseus slew it. In fantasy games and fiction, minotaurs appear as a species—often as large, aggressive monsters guarding mazes or dungeons: {The party encountered a band of minotaurs in the underground passage}.

A minstrel was a medieval entertainer who performed songs, poetry, and music, often traveling from court to court or town to town. The word evokes romantic images of wandering musicians with lutes. In American history, minstrel specifically refers to performers in minstrel shows—19th and early 20th century entertainment featuring white performers in blackface (and later Black performers) using racist stereotypes. That legacy makes the word fraught when applied to any performer today.

Minstrels were medieval European entertainers who performed songs, music, and poetry, often traveling between noble courts and public gatherings. The word later attached to a specific American entertainment form: white performers in blackface caricaturing Black people through song and comedy, popular from the 1830s through the early 20th century. This {minstrel show} tradition is now recognized as deeply racist, though its influence shaped American popular music. {Wandering minstrels entertained the court.}

Two words share the spelling m-i-n-t. Mint is the general name for plants in the family Labiatae, many of which are aromatic and used medicinally and for food, such as spearmint or peppermint. Candies with this flavoring are called mints. A mint is also a place where coins or paper money are manufactured. To mint money is to produce the physical tokens of it. If you make a mint, you make a lot of money. Something newly minted has just been produced: The newly minted legislation will take effect on November 1. Something in mint condition is new and unblemished, as if just produced in a mint.

Minted means freshly made or produced, from the original sense of coins being struck at a mint. A {newly minted graduate} has just earned their degree. A {freshly minted phrase} is brand new. In British slang, minted means wealthy—having lots of mint-fresh money: {He's absolutely minted}.

Minting is the process of producing coins by stamping metal, or more broadly, creating something new. The word extends from physical currency to digital assets: {The NFT minting fee was surprisingly high}. Someone minting money is making it rapidly and easily. A freshly minted graduate or executive is newly credentialed: {a freshly minted MBA}.

Mints are candies flavored with mint—the aromatic herb whose oils produce a cooling sensation: {She offered me a mint after dinner}. Breath mints mask odors; after-dinner mints accompany the check at restaurants. Mint also refers to places where coins are manufactured, and things {in mint condition} are pristine, as if freshly minted.

Minty describes the cool, sharp flavor or scent of mint: {minty toothpaste}, {minty fresh breath}. The word often appears in advertising for gum, mouthwash, and dental products. Something minty may taste of peppermint, spearmint, or similar herbs. Figuratively, minty can mean fresh or crisp: {The morning air had a minty quality}.

A minuet is a slow, stately ballroom dance in triple time, popular in the 17th and 18th centuries among European aristocracy. The term also refers to music composed for this dance or in its characteristic style, often appearing as a movement in classical symphonies and sonatas: {The orchestra played a minuet from Mozart}.

Minuets are stately ballroom dances in triple time, popular in 17th and 18th century European courts. The dance features small, precise steps—the name comes from a word meaning small. Minuet also refers to musical compositions written for this dance or in its characteristic rhythm: {The orchestra played a minuet by Mozart}.

Minus, the word for the arithmetic symbol indicating subtraction, is usually interpreted as a preposition when it occurs in text (twenty-three minus five). The symbol form minus is a slightly elongated hyphen but many people just use the hyphen because it is a single keystroke.

The most frequent use of minute by far is the noun, denoting a 60th of an hour, and by extension, a short amount of time: give me a minute, wait a minute. A minute is also a 60th part of a degree in geometric measurement. The plural minutes frequently denotes the official record of the proceedings of a meeting: He seconded the motion to accept the minutes of the last meeting. The adjective minute (second syllable stressed) expresses the concept of very small: The prices were ridiculous and the portions minute.

A minuteman was an American colonial militiaman ready to fight at a minute's notice during the Revolutionary War era. The term evokes readiness and patriotic defense. Minuteman later became the name of U.S. intercontinental ballistic missiles, and various civilian groups have adopted the name, including anti-immigration activists patrolling the U.S.-Mexico border.

Minutemen were American colonial militia members who pledged to be ready for battle at a minute's notice during the Revolutionary War. The term now applies more broadly to any group claiming readiness for rapid response, often with patriotic overtones: {The governor called the volunteer minutemen to assist with disaster relief}. (Capitalized Minutemen may refer to specific organizations or the punk band.)

Minutes are units of time equal to sixty seconds. A meeting's minutes are the official written record of what was discussed and decided: {Who's taking minutes?} To minute something is to record it officially. Something done {to the minute} happens at exactly the scheduled time. A minute amount is tiny, but that sense belongs to the singular form pronounced with stress on the second syllable.

Minutia is a small or trivial detail. The word appears almost exclusively in its plural form, minutiae, referring to the minor particulars of a subject: {She obsessed over the minutiae of wedding planning}. Often carries a dismissive tone—the minutiae are what pedants fixate on while others focus on substance.

Minutiae are the small, precise details of something—the fine points that may seem trivial but often matter: {the minutiae of contract law}, {lost in the minutiae of daily operations}. The word usually carries a hint of tedium, suggesting details that require patience to attend to. Singular: minutia, though rarely encountered.

A minx is a bold, flirtatious, or mischievous girl or young woman. The word carries a tone of playful disapproval—someone might call a woman a minx for being cunning or seductive, but usually with more amusement than censure: {You little minx, you knew exactly what you were doing}. The term sounds somewhat old-fashioned today.

A miracle is an extraordinary event that seems to defy natural laws, typically attributed to divine intervention: {It would take a miracle for him to survive}. Religious traditions center on miracles—healings, resurrections, parting seas. The word extends to any remarkable or improbable occurrence: {It's a miracle we found parking}. This casual use retains a sense of grateful astonishment at unlikely good fortune.

Miracles are events that seem to defy natural laws, typically attributed to divine intervention. A sick person recovers against all medical odds; believers call it a miracle. The word extends to anything remarkably fortunate or improbable: {It's a miracle we found parking}. To {work miracles} is to achieve extraordinary results. The adjective miraculous describes such events or outcomes.

Miraculous describes something so extraordinary it seems to defy natural explanation—as if produced by divine intervention or supernatural forces. A miraculous recovery happens against all medical expectation. The word often carries religious overtones, referring to genuine miracles: {the miraculous healing at Lourdes}. In casual use, miraculous is hyperbole for anything impressively unlikely or fortunate: {It's miraculous we found parking}.

Miraculously describes something happening in a way that seems to defy natural explanation or reasonable expectation. It often signals unexpected good fortune: {Miraculously, everyone survived the crash}. The word can be used loosely for anything surprisingly fortunate: {She miraculously found a parking spot right out front}.

A mirage is an optical illusion caused by atmospheric conditions, typically heat distorting light to create false images—water on a hot road, distant objects floating above the horizon. The word extends to anything illusory or unattainable: {The oasis turned out to be a mirage}. {His promise of reform was just a mirage}.

Mirages are optical illusions caused by atmospheric conditions, typically heat distorting light to create false images—the shimmering water that appears on hot pavement, or distant objects seeming to float above the horizon. By extension, a mirage is anything deceptively appealing but unattainable: {The oasis turned out to be a mirage}. {His promises of reform were just mirages}.
clues: What parched travelers think they see

definition: Mire is deep mud or swampy ground that traps whatever enters it: {The wagon wheels sank into the mire}. To mire is to stick fast in such ground, or figuratively, to become entangled in difficulty: {mired in debt}, {mired in controversy}. The word suggests something that holds you back and is hard to escape.

Mired means stuck or entangled in something that impedes movement or progress. The word comes from mire, meaning mud or swampy ground, so to be mired is literally to be stuck in mud. More often, though, mired describes abstract entanglement: {The project got mired in bureaucratic delays}. A person mired in debt or a company mired in scandal finds themselves unable to move forward. The word nearly always carries negative connotations of being trapped in an undesirable situation.

Mirepoix is a mixture of diced vegetables—typically onion, carrot, and celery—sautéed in butter or oil as a flavor base for sauces, soups, stocks, and braises. The vegetables are usually cut small and cooked slowly until softened but not browned. French in origin, it remains fundamental to classical cooking technique: {Start with a mirepoix and build from there}.

Mires is the plural of mire—a stretch of swampy, boggy ground, or the deep mud itself. To mire is to sink or stick in such terrain: {The truck mired in the soft earth}. Figuratively, to be mired is to be stuck or entangled in difficulty: {mired in debt}, {mired in scandal}, {a project mired in bureaucracy}.

A mirror is a surface that reflects light, typically glass coated with metal, allowing you to see yourself or what's behind you. Mirrors appear in compounds: {rearview mirror}, {mirror image}, {mirror ball}. To mirror something is to reflect or imitate it: {Her expression mirrored his concern}. {The architecture mirrors classical Greek temples}.

A mirrorball is a large sphere covered with small mirrored tiles that rotates and scatters light in all directions, creating moving spots of reflected light across a room. Standard equipment in dance clubs and discos since the 1970s, it evokes nightlife, celebration, and retro glamour: {The mirrorball spun lazily above the dance floor}. Also called a disco ball.

Mirrored describes something that reflects like a mirror or has a mirror-like surface: {mirrored sunglasses}, {a mirrored wall}. It also means duplicated in reverse, as a reflection would be: {The image was mirrored horizontally}. In computing, mirrored data is copied identically to a backup location for redundancy. Figuratively, mirrored suggests correspondence or symmetry: {Her expression mirrored his confusion}.

Mirroring is reflecting or copying something as a mirror does. In psychology, mirroring describes unconsciously imitating another person's gestures, speech patterns, or emotions—a behavior that builds rapport: {She noticed him mirroring her posture}. In computing, mirroring duplicates data across drives or servers for backup. To mirror something is to reflect or replicate it closely: {His anxiety mirrored my own}.

Mirrors are surfaces that reflect images, typically glass coated with reflective metal. A bathroom mirror shows your reflection; a car's mirrors let you see behind. Figuratively, something that mirrors another thing reflects or imitates it: {The child's anxiety mirrored her mother's}. A mirror can be anything that reflects reality: {Art mirrors life}.

Mirth is gladness or amusement expressed through laughter. The word is somewhat literary and old-fashioned, suggesting hearty, unrestrained joy rather than a quiet smile: {The joke provoked general mirth around the table}. Mirthful means full of mirth; mirthless describes hollow or joyless laughter.

Misadventure is an unfortunate incident or unlucky experience—an adventure gone wrong. The word suggests mishap rather than catastrophe: {The camping trip turned into a series of misadventures}. In legal contexts, {death by misadventure} means an accidental death resulting from a lawful but risky act, with no one at fault.

Misadventures are unfortunate or unlucky experiences, typically minor mishaps rather than serious calamities. The word carries a tone of rueful humor—things went wrong, but you can laugh about it later: {She regaled us with tales of her misadventures in online dating}. A misadventure suggests bad luck rather than bad judgment, though the distinction often blurs.

Misandry is hatred or contempt for men, the counterpart to misogyny. The term appears most often in discussions of gender politics, sometimes to describe genuine prejudice against men, sometimes deployed defensively to deflect feminist criticism: {She was accused of misandry for her comments about male behavior}. The adjective is misandrist.

A misanthrope is a person who dislikes or distrusts humanity in general. The attitude isn't hatred of specific individuals but a broader contempt for human nature, motives, or behavior: {He became a misanthrope after years of disappointment}. The adjective is misanthropic; the condition is misanthropy.

Misanthropes is the plural of misanthrope—a person who dislikes or distrusts humanity in general. The misanthrope doesn't necessarily hate individuals but views human nature with contempt or pessimism: {Misanthropes make poor customer service representatives}. The word carries literary overtones from Molière's play of the same name.

Misanthropy is a general dislike or distrust of humankind. Where cynicism doubts human motives, misanthropy goes further—finding the species itself contemptible or unworthy of affection. A misanthrope may withdraw from society or simply regard human contact with weary disdain: {Years of retail work had curdled her into misanthropy}.

Misbehave means to behave badly or improperly, especially by breaking rules or social norms. Children misbehave when they act out; adults misbehave when they violate expectations of conduct: {The kids misbehaved the entire flight}. The word often carries a tone of mild rebuke rather than serious accusation.

Misbehaving is behaving badly or improperly—breaking rules, acting out, or failing to meet expectations of conduct. Children misbehave when they disobey parents or teachers: {The kids were misbehaving all afternoon}. Adults misbehave too, often with a playful or euphemistic sense: {We misbehaved at the office party}.

Misbehavior is conduct that violates rules or expectations—typically minor infractions rather than serious offenses. The word appears most often in contexts involving children or institutions: {The teacher sent him to the principal's office for misbehavior}. Adults misbehave too, though the word carries a slightly juvenile or euphemistic tone when applied to them.

Misbehaviour is the British spelling of misbehavior—conduct that violates rules or norms, especially by children. The word implies actions that fall short of serious wrongdoing but warrant correction: {The teacher sent him to the principal's office for misbehaviour}. It can also describe adult conduct that breaches professional or social standards.

A miscalculation is an error in computing or estimating something: {a miscalculation in the budget}, {a miscalculation of the distance}. More often it refers to a mistake in judgment or planning: {The invasion was a strategic miscalculation}. To miscalculate is to make such an error.
clues: An error in working something out

definition: Miscalculations are errors in judgment or computation. The word applies equally to mathematical mistakes and to flawed assessments of situations: {The invasion was based on serious miscalculations about how the population would respond}. A miscalculation implies the person tried to calculate correctly but got it wrong—distinguishing it from negligence or wild guessing.

Miscarriage is the spontaneous loss of a pregnancy before the fetus can survive outside the womb, typically before twenty weeks. The term carries clinical weight but also deep personal significance: {She had two miscarriages before her son was born}. A miscarriage of justice is a failure of the legal system to reach a fair outcome—an extended sense where something meant to produce good results instead fails catastrophically.

Miscarried is the past tense of miscarry, which has two main senses. Most commonly it refers to the spontaneous loss of a pregnancy before the fetus can survive outside the womb: {She miscarried in her second trimester}. The other sense applies to plans or efforts that fail to achieve their intended result: {The scheme miscarried when their contact failed to show}. Both uses share the idea of something that was underway but did not reach its expected outcome.

To miscarry is to lose a pregnancy before the fetus can survive outside the womb—the spontaneous end of a pregnancy, usually in the first trimester: {She miscarried at ten weeks}. The older and more general sense is to fail or go wrong: {The plan miscarried when the weather turned}. This sense is now rare, displaced by the pregnancy meaning.

Miscast describes an actor poorly suited to a role, or the act of casting such an actor: {He was badly miscast as the romantic lead}. The term extends beyond theater and film to any situation where someone is placed in an ill-fitting position: {She felt miscast as a corporate lawyer when her passion was teaching}.

Miscasting is assigning an actor to a role they're wrong for—whether by appearance, ability, or type. The term implies a judgment call: {The film suffered from the miscasting of its lead}. It extends beyond theater to any poor fit between person and position: {His appointment was a miscasting from the start}.

Miscellaneous describes a collection of varied, unrelated things that don't fit neatly into other categories. A miscellaneous drawer holds random items—tape, batteries, rubber bands. Miscellaneous expenses are the leftovers that don't belong under specific budget lines. The word often signals "everything else": {miscellaneous fees}, {miscellaneous notes}. Sometimes abbreviated misc.

Mischaracterisation is the British spelling of mischaracterization—a false or misleading representation of something. To mischaracterise a person's views is to describe them inaccurately, whether through carelessness or intent: {The article was a gross mischaracterisation of what I actually said}. The word often appears in political and legal contexts where accuracy of representation matters.

Mischaracterization is an inaccurate or misleading portrayal of something—a person's views, a situation, or facts. The prefix *mis-* signals error or distortion: {That's a gross mischaracterization of what I said}. The term often appears in political and legal contexts where accuracy matters and someone stands accused of twisting the truth.

Mischief is playful behavior that causes minor trouble or annoyance without serious harm: {The kids got into mischief while we were out}. It suggests impish troublemaking rather than malice—a child's prank, a pet's antics. {Eyes full of mischief} signals someone is up to something. The phrase {do mischief} or {make mischief} implies stirring up trouble, sometimes deliberately causing discord between people. Legal use retains an older sense of actual harm: {criminal mischief} means property damage or vandalism.

Mischievous describes someone inclined to cause minor trouble or annoyance, usually in a playful rather than harmful way: {a mischievous grin}, {mischievous children}. The word suggests impish behavior—pranks, teasing, rule-bending for fun. Something mischievous may also cause harm without malice: {mischievous rumors}. Often mispronounced with four syllables, but standard pronunciation has three.

A misclick is an unintentional click—hitting the wrong button, link, or target on a screen: {I bought the wrong item because of a misclick}. Common in gaming, where a misclick can waste an ability or attack the wrong target. The verb form works the same way: {I misclicked and closed the whole window}.

Miscommunication is a failure to communicate clearly, resulting in misunderstanding between parties. The prefix *mis-* signals something going wrong—the message sent isn't the message received: {The whole disaster was just a miscommunication about the deadline}. Miscommunication can be minor or consequential, accidental or rooted in deeper failures to listen.

Miscommunications are instances where information is conveyed or understood incorrectly. The word emphasizes the gap between what was meant and what was received: {The project failed due to miscommunications between departments}. Unlike simple misunderstandings, miscommunication often implies fault in the transmission itself—unclear wording, missing context, or assumptions that weren't shared.

A misconception is a mistaken belief or faulty understanding. Unlike a lie, which involves intent to deceive, a misconception is an honest error—you genuinely think you're right: {There's a common misconception that we only use ten percent of our brains}. The word often appears when correcting widely held but inaccurate ideas.
clues: Something mistakenly thought to be true

definition: Misconceptions are mistaken beliefs or wrong ideas about something: {Common misconceptions about evolution persist despite scientific consensus}. The word implies the belief was formed through faulty understanding rather than deliberate deception—you misconceive something by misinterpreting evidence or accepting false information. {She had misconceptions about what the job would involve}.

Misconduct is improper or unacceptable behavior, especially by someone in a position of responsibility or trust. The word usually appears in formal or institutional contexts: {professional misconduct}, {police misconduct}, {sexual misconduct}. A finding of misconduct can lead to discipline, termination, or legal consequences. The verb means to behave improperly or to manage badly: {He misconducted himself at the conference}.

A miscreant is a person who behaves badly or breaks rules—a wrongdoer, scoundrel, or villain. The word carries a slightly old-fashioned or literary flavor, often used with mock seriousness: {The miscreants who egged my car will pay for this}. It can describe anyone from petty troublemakers to serious criminals, though it typically suggests disapproval rather than outrage.

Miscreants are people who behave badly or break rules—wrongdoers, troublemakers, villains. The word carries a literary or slightly archaic flavor, often used with mock seriousness: {The miscreants who toilet-papered my house will pay}. It can describe petty offenders or serious criminals, depending on context.

A miscue is a mistake or error, especially one involving timing or coordination. In billiards, it's a faulty stroke where the cue slips off the ball. More broadly, it's any slip-up in execution: {a miscue in the handoff}, {The miscue cost them the game}. As a verb, to miscue is to make such an error: {The actor miscued and spoke too early}.

Miscues are mistakes or errors, especially in performance. An actor forgets a line, a pool player strikes the cue ball wrong, a fielder misjudges a fly ball—all miscues. The word implies a specific, identifiable moment where something went wrong: {The miscues in the third quarter cost them the game}. To miscue is to make such an error.

A misdeal is an error in dealing cards—giving too many or too few to a player, exposing a card that should stay hidden, or dealing out of turn. The hand is typically voided and redealt. As a verb, to misdeal is to make such an error: {The dealer misdealt and we had to start over}.
clues: When cards go to wrong players

definition: A misdeed is a wrongful or wicked act—something done that shouldn't have been. The word has an old-fashioned, slightly formal quality: {The senator's past misdeeds came back to haunt him}. It suggests moral failing more than legal violation, though the two often overlap.

Misdeeds are wrongful acts—offenses against morality, law, or proper conduct. The word has a slightly formal or literary flavor, often appearing in contexts of accusation or confession: {The politician's misdeeds finally came to light}. Misdeeds tend to be serious but not necessarily criminal; they suggest moral failure as much as legal violation.

A misdemeanor is a criminal offense less serious than a felony, typically punishable by fines, probation, community service, or jail time of less than a year. Common misdemeanors include petty theft, simple assault, trespassing, and minor drug possession. The distinction between misdemeanor and felony varies by jurisdiction, but misdemeanors generally carry lighter sentences and fewer long-term consequences. {He was charged with a misdemeanor for shoplifting.}

Misdemeanors are criminal offenses less serious than felonies, typically punishable by fines or short jail sentences rather than prison time. Petty theft, minor assault, and public intoxication are common examples. The word also applies broadly to any minor wrongdoing or misbehavior: {youthful misdemeanors}, {the usual office misdemeanors}.

A misdemeanour is a minor criminal offence, less serious than a felony but more serious than an infraction. In legal systems that distinguish between the two, misdemeanours typically carry lighter penalties—fines or short jail sentences rather than prison time: {Shoplifting is usually charged as a misdemeanour}. Outside legal contexts, misdemeanour means any minor misbehaviour or wrongdoing: {youthful misdemeanours}. The American spelling is misdemeanor.

Misdemeanours is the British spelling of misdemeanors—minor criminal offenses less serious than felonies. Petty theft, disorderly conduct, and trespassing are typical misdemeanours. The word also applies loosely to minor wrongdoings or misbehavior: {youthful misdemeanours}, {The cat's misdemeanours included knocking glasses off tables}.

To misdiagnose is to identify a condition incorrectly—diagnosing the wrong illness, or failing to recognize the right one: {The doctor misdiagnosed her anxiety as a heart condition}. The term applies beyond medicine to any faulty identification of a problem: {The mechanic misdiagnosed the engine trouble}.

Misdiagnosed means incorrectly identified, especially regarding a medical condition: {She was misdiagnosed with anxiety when she actually had a thyroid disorder}. The error can go either direction—diagnosing disease where none exists, or missing what's actually wrong. Beyond medicine, misdiagnosed applies to any faulty identification of a problem: {The mechanic misdiagnosed the engine trouble}.

Misdiagnosis is an incorrect identification of a disease, condition, or problem. In medicine, it means a doctor has identified the wrong illness or failed to identify the correct one: {The misdiagnosis delayed treatment for months}. The term extends beyond medicine to any situation where the root cause of a problem is wrongly identified: {Their misdiagnosis of the company's troubles led to ineffective reforms}.

Misdirect means to direct wrongly or inappropriately. You can misdirect a letter by addressing it incorrectly, misdirect resources by allocating them poorly, or misdirect attention by drawing it away from what matters. Magicians misdirect audiences to conceal their methods: {While his left hand misdirected, his right palmed the coin}. The word implies intent more often than accident.

Misdirection is the act of drawing attention away from what matters—toward something irrelevant or misleading. Magicians use misdirection to conceal their methods: {While you watch his right hand, his left does the trick}. The word also describes giving wrong directions or guidance: {The witness's misdirection sent police to the wrong address}. More broadly, any deliberate diversion of focus: {The scandal was misdirection from the real policy failures}.

Misdirections are acts of leading attention away from something—often deliberately. A magician's misdirection draws your eye from the sleight of hand. A politician's misdirection shifts focus from an uncomfortable question. The word implies intent to deceive or distract: {The investigation was hampered by misdirections from witnesses}.

Miseducation is education that teaches wrong things or teaches right things wrongly—instruction that leaves someone worse informed than before. The word implies not just inadequate schooling but actively misleading content: {The miseducation of American youth about their own history}. It suggests systematic failure rather than simple ignorance.

A miser hoards money and refuses to spend it, even on necessities. The word implies not just frugality but obsessive, joyless accumulation—counting coins rather than enjoying what they could buy. {The old miser died alone in a mansion full of rotting furniture}. Scrooge is the archetypal literary miser.

Miserable describes a state of great unhappiness or discomfort: {I felt miserable with the flu}. It can characterize conditions that cause such distress: {miserable weather}, {a miserable apartment}. Applied to quantities, it suggests contemptibly small: {a miserable salary}. A miserable person may also be one who makes others unhappy—unpleasant and ill-tempered: {that miserable old crank next door}.
clues: In a state of deep distress

definition: Miserly describes someone extremely unwilling to spend money, even when they have plenty. A miserly person hoards wealth and begrudges every expense: {The miserly landlord refused to fix the heating}. The word carries stronger condemnation than frugal or thrifty—it suggests meanness of spirit, not just careful spending. Miserly can extend beyond money to anything given grudgingly: {miserly portions}, {miserly with praise}.

Misers are people who hoard wealth and hate spending it, even on necessities.
