The word carries strong negative connotations—misers aren't just frugal, they're obsessively stingy to the point of self-denial: {The old miser died alone in a house full of money he never spent}. Dickens's Scrooge is the archetypal miser.

Misery is intense suffering or unhappiness—physical pain, emotional anguish, or wretched living conditions. {The injury caused her constant misery}. A misery can be a specific source of suffering: {the miseries of poverty}. In British informal use, a misery is a persistently gloomy or complaining person. To {put someone out of their misery} is to end their suffering, literally or figuratively—as when finally giving someone news they've been anxiously awaiting.

A misfire is a failure to fire properly—a gun that doesn't discharge, an engine cylinder that doesn't ignite, a rocket that doesn't launch. Extended to any plan or attempt that fails to achieve its intended effect: {The joke misfired badly}. As a verb, to misfire is to fail in this way: {The engine kept misfiring}.

Misfired describes something that failed to fire or discharge properly. A gun misfires when the trigger is pulled but the cartridge doesn't ignite. An engine misfires when fuel fails to combust correctly in a cylinder. Figuratively, a joke or plan that misfired didn't produce the intended effect: {His attempt at humor misfired badly}.

Misfires is the plural of misfire—instances where something fails to fire or ignite as intended. A gun misfires when the trigger is pulled but no shot follows. An engine misfires when fuel fails to combust properly in a cylinder. Figuratively, jokes misfire when they fall flat, and plans misfire when they go wrong: {His attempt at humor misfired badly}.

Misfiring describes an engine or firearm failing to fire properly—the spark plug doesn't ignite the fuel, or the cartridge doesn't discharge. The word extends to anything that fails to work as intended: {The comedy's jokes kept misfiring}. A misfiring plan or strategy goes wrong in execution. In neurology, misfiring neurons send signals erratically, associated with seizures and other disorders.
clues: When the spark comes too late

definition: A misfit is someone who doesn't fit in with their surroundings or social group—awkward, out of place, unsuited to the environment. The word applies to things too: a misfit part doesn't match other components. {She always felt like a misfit in her conservative hometown}. The term can be embraced as identity or used dismissively.

Misfits are people who don't fit in—those who fail to conform to the expectations or norms of a group. The term can be disparaging, suggesting someone awkward or socially inept: {He was always a misfit at school}. But it also carries positive connotations of individuality and creative nonconformity: {Silicon Valley was built by misfits and dropouts}. A misfit can also be something that fits poorly, like an ill-fitting garment.

Misfortune is bad luck or an unfortunate event. It can name the general condition of being unlucky or a specific instance: {a series of misfortunes}, {the misfortune of being born into poverty}. To have {the misfortune to} do something is to be unlucky enough to experience it: {I had the misfortune to witness the whole disaster}.

Misfortunes are instances of bad luck or adverse circumstances—the troubles and setbacks that befall someone: {A series of misfortunes left the family struggling}. The word implies events beyond one's control, distinguishing misfortune from mistakes or failures of judgment. {She bore her misfortunes with remarkable grace.}

To misgender someone is to refer to them using a pronoun or form of address that doesn't match their gender identity—calling a transgender woman "he," for instance. The term emerged alongside growing awareness of gender identity: {The intake form kept misgendering patients}. Usually describes an error, though it can be deliberate.

Misgendered describes someone who has been referred to by the wrong gender—called "he" when they identify as "she," or vice versa, or addressed with gendered terms that don't match their identity. The term emerged from transgender discourse but applies to anyone incorrectly gendered: {The waiter kept calling me "sir" and I felt misgendered}. To misgender someone may be accidental or deliberate.

Misgendering is referring to someone using a gender they don't identify with—wrong pronouns, wrong titles, wrong terms. It can be accidental or deliberate: {I kept misgendering her until I got used to the new pronouns}. Deliberate misgendering is often intended as dismissal or insult. The noun form refers to an instance: {another misgendering}.

A misgiving is a feeling of doubt or apprehension about a future action or decision. Unlike outright opposition, misgivings suggest unease rather than certainty: {She had misgivings about the plan but went along with it}. Usually plural: {Despite his misgivings, he signed the contract}.

Misgivings are feelings of doubt, unease, or apprehension about something—typically a decision, plan, or course of action. The word almost always appears in the plural: {I had misgivings about the merger from the start}. Unlike outright opposition, misgivings suggest lingering uncertainty rather than firm conviction: {Despite her misgivings, she signed the contract}.

Misguided describes actions or beliefs based on faulty judgment or wrong assumptions: {a misguided attempt to help}, {misguided policies}. The word implies good intentions gone astray—someone misguided isn't malicious, just mistaken about the right course. It often carries a note of condescension: calling someone misguided suggests you know better.

Mishandling is managing something badly or carelessly. You can mishandle a package by dropping it, mishandle a situation by making poor decisions, or mishandle funds through negligence or improper accounting. The word implies that something deserved better treatment than it received: {The investigation was botched by mishandling of evidence}.
clues: Dealing with something the wrong way

definition: A mishap is an unlucky accident or minor misfortune—something that goes wrong but typically without serious consequences: {We arrived late due to a mishap with the rental car}. The word suggests bad luck rather than negligence, and usually applies to incidents that are inconvenient rather than catastrophic.

Mishaps are minor accidents or unlucky events—things that go wrong but aren't catastrophic. The word suggests bad luck more than serious harm: {a series of mishaps delayed the trip}, {Despite a few mishaps, the wedding went smoothly}. A mishap is smaller than a disaster but more consequential than a hiccup.

To mishear is to hear incorrectly—to perceive words or sounds differently from what was actually said: {I misheard "flour" as "flower"}. Mishearing often produces confusion or unintentional comedy, especially in song lyrics or names. The past tense is misheard: {Sorry, I misheard you}.

Misheard is the past tense of mishear—to hear something incorrectly, perceiving different words or sounds than what was actually said. {I misheard the address and went to the wrong house}. Misheard lyrics are a common phenomenon, where listeners confidently sing wrong words for years: {For decades I misheard "excuse me while I kiss the sky" as "kiss this guy"}.

A mishearing is an instance of hearing something incorrectly—perceiving different words or sounds than were actually spoken: {The mishearing turned "I scream" into "ice cream"}. Mishearings of song lyrics are common enough to have their own name: mondegreens. The verb mishear follows the pattern of hear: mishear, misheard.

A mishmash is a jumbled mixture of disparate things thrown together without much order or coherence: {The proposal was a mishmash of half-baked ideas}. The word suggests randomness rather than deliberate combination—a hodgepodge. {Her desk was a mishmash of papers, coffee cups, and Post-it notes.}

Mishmashes are confused or jumbled mixtures of disparate things: {The album is a mishmash of genres—folk, electronica, and jazz all thrown together}. The word suggests a lack of coherent organization, though sometimes affectionately: {Her decorating style was a mishmash of everything she'd collected over the years}.

To misinform is to give someone false or inaccurate information, whether intentionally or not. The word emphasizes the effect on the recipient rather than the intent of the speaker: {The report misinformed the public about the actual risks}. Someone who has been misinformed believes something untrue through no fault of their own.

Misinformation is false or inaccurate information, regardless of intent. Unlike disinformation, which is deliberately deceptive, misinformation may spread through honest error or misunderstanding: {Social media accelerates the spread of misinformation}. The term gained prominence in debates about online content and public health messaging.

To misinterpret is to understand something incorrectly—to take a different meaning from words, actions, or events than what was intended. {She misinterpreted his silence as disapproval}. {The data was widely misinterpreted by the press}. Misinterpretation often stems from missing context or projecting one's own assumptions onto ambiguous situations.

Misjudged describes something assessed incorrectly—a person, situation, or action that was understood wrongly. A misjudged {comment} lands badly because the speaker failed to read the room. A misjudged {pass} in sports goes where teammates aren't. To feel misjudged is to believe others have formed an unfair opinion of you: {I've been misjudged my whole life}.

Misjudgment is a faulty assessment or conclusion—getting something wrong when forming an opinion or making a decision. It can be a single bad call {a costly misjudgment} or a pattern of poor evaluation {a series of misjudgments led to the company's collapse}. The word implies error rather than malice. Also spelled misjudgement.

To mislead is to cause someone to believe something untrue or to guide them in the wrong direction. The word suggests leading astray rather than outright lying—you can mislead by omission, selective emphasis, or technically true but deceptive statements: {The ad's fine print was designed to mislead consumers}. Unlike deceive, mislead often implies the victim follows willingly, unaware they're being led wrong.

Misleading describes something that creates a false impression or leads toward wrong conclusions. A misleading {statement} isn't necessarily a lie—it may be technically true while omitting crucial context. Misleading {statistics} can distort reality through selective presentation. {The headline was misleading; the article said something quite different.} The verb mislead means to guide someone toward error or false belief.

Misleads is the present tense of mislead—to guide someone toward a false conclusion or wrong direction. A misleading statement doesn't have to be an outright lie; it can deceive through omission or implication: {The advertisement misleads consumers about the product's effectiveness}. Statistics mislead when presented without context.

Misled is the past tense of mislead—to guide someone toward a wrong conclusion or action, whether through deception or honest error. {The witness misled the jury}. {I was misled by the confusing signage}. The word implies the person who was misled bears less fault than whoever or whatever did the misleading.

Mismanagement is poor or incompetent handling of something, especially an organization, project, or resources. The word typically implies negligence or bad judgment rather than malice: {The company collapsed due to years of financial mismanagement}. Mismanagement often appears in contexts of accountability—someone failed in their duty to manage properly.
clues: When leadership fails its basic duties

definition: A mismatch is a pairing of things that don't go well together or aren't suited to each other: {a mismatch between skills and job requirements}, {The game was a mismatch from the start}. To mismatch is to pair things poorly or inappropriately. Mismatched socks don't match; a mismatched couple seems incompatible.

Mismatched describes things that don't go together well or aren't suited to each other. Mismatched {socks} are different colors or patterns. A mismatched {couple} seems incompatible. Mismatched {expectations} between parties lead to conflict. The word implies things were paired or combined when they shouldn't have been: {The teams were badly mismatched—one had professionals, the other amateurs}.

Mismatches are things that don't go together properly—pairs or combinations where the elements clash or fail to correspond. Socks of different colors are mismatches. A mismatch between supply and demand creates shortages or surpluses. In sports, a mismatch pairs competitors of unequal ability: {The game was a complete mismatch from the opening whistle}.

A misnomer is a name or term that doesn't accurately describe what it refers to. {Koala bear is a misnomer—they're marsupials, not bears}. The word often appears when correcting misconceptions: {Calling it a jellyfish is a misnomer since it's not actually a fish}. Something mislabeled or mischaracterized can itself be called a misnomer.

Misnomers are names or terms that don't accurately describe what they refer to. A koala bear is a misnomer because koalas aren't bears. Calling something a misnomer suggests the label is misleading or historically inaccurate: {Calling it a "free" trial is a misnomer—they charge you immediately}. The singular is misnomer.

Miso is a thick paste made from fermented soybeans, used as a foundation for Japanese cooking. It flavors soups, marinades, dressings, and glazes: {miso soup}, {miso-glazed salmon}. Varieties range from mild white miso to robust red miso. The fermentation gives it a rich, savory depth—a source of umami.

Misogynist as an adjective characterizes a person, remark, or behavior that demonstrates a prejudice against or a dislike for women: A man in the audience was shouting misogynist insults at the performer. A slightly less intense way of suggesting the same tendency is the term male chauvinist.

Misogynistic describes attitudes, behavior, or people that express hatred or contempt toward women. A misogynistic {joke} demeans women; a misogynistic {culture} systematically devalues them. The word applies to both overt hostility and subtler forms of sexism: {The comments section devolved into misogynistic attacks}.

Misogynists are people who hate or hold contempt for women. The term applies to those whose prejudice manifests in beliefs, attitudes, or actions—from casual dismissiveness to systematic discrimination. {The comments section was flooded with misogynists attacking the female CEO}. A single such person is a misogynist; the attitude itself is misogyny.

Misogyny is hatred or contempt for women. The term covers attitudes ranging from active hostility to subtler forms of prejudice and discrimination. A misogynist holds such views. {The company's misogyny was evident in its promotion patterns}. Misogynistic describes things reflecting or promoting these attitudes: {misogynistic lyrics}, {misogynistic jokes}.

To misplace something is to put it somewhere and then forget where: {I've misplaced my glasses again}. The word implies carelessness rather than loss—the item exists somewhere, you just can't find it. Misplaced can also describe things directed at the wrong target: misplaced {trust}, misplaced {anger}, misplaced {priorities}.

Misplaced describes something put in the wrong location or position, often temporarily lost as a result: {I've misplaced my glasses again}. The word extends to abstract things that are inappropriately directed or applied: misplaced {trust}, misplaced {priorities}, misplaced {anger}. A misplaced modifier in grammar attaches to the wrong word in a sentence. The past participle of misplace, it functions primarily as an adjective.

To misplay is to play incorrectly or badly—making a wrong move in a game, mishandling a ball in sports, or bungling a situation that requires skillful action: {The shortstop misplayed the grounder}. As a noun, a misplay is an instance of such an error: {That misplay cost them the game}.

A misprint is an error in printed text—a wrong letter, missing word, or other mistake that escaped proofreading: {The misprint changed "public" to "pubic"}. As a verb, to misprint is to print incorrectly. Misprints range from trivial typos to embarrassing blunders that require corrections or recalls.

To mispronounce a word is to say it incorrectly, either by stressing the wrong syllable, using the wrong vowel or consonant sounds, or otherwise deviating from accepted pronunciation. What counts as mispronunciation depends on context—regional accents aren't mispronunciations, but saying "nuclear" as "nucular" is widely considered one. {I always mispronounce her last name.} People often mispronounce unfamiliar words they've only encountered in writing.

A mispronunciation is saying a word incorrectly—using the wrong sounds, stress, or syllable breaks. Some mispronunciations are common enough to become accepted variants; others mark a speaker as unfamiliar with a word: {Her mispronunciation of "nuclear" as "nucular" drove him crazy}.

To misquote is to quote inaccurately—reproducing someone's words with errors or alterations: {The article misquoted the senator, changing the meaning of her statement}. A misquote is such an inaccurate quotation. Misquotes range from minor errors to significant distortions, and famous quotes are frequently misquoted: "Play it again, Sam" never appears in *Casablanca*.

Misquoted means quoted inaccurately—the words attributed to someone differ from what they actually said or wrote. Famous figures are frequently misquoted: {Einstein never said half the things attributed to him}. Someone may feel misquoted even when the words are exact, if context changes the meaning: {The article misquoted me—I was being sarcastic}.

To misread is to read incorrectly—mistaking one word for another or failing to grasp the meaning of text. The word extends beyond written material to any situation requiring interpretation: {I completely misread the situation}, {She misread his silence as agreement}. A misread is an instance of reading something wrong.

Misreading is reading something incorrectly—mistaking one word for another, or interpreting a text's meaning wrongly. The term extends beyond written words: you can misread a situation, misread someone's intentions, or misread social cues. {I misread the room and made an inappropriate joke.} A misreading is an instance of such error.

To misremember is to remember incorrectly—not forgetting entirely, but recalling details wrong: {I misremembered the meeting time as three instead of two}. The word suggests the memory feels real to the person, even though it's inaccurate. It's sometimes used euphemistically for lying: {The witness didn't lie—he simply misremembered}.

Misremembering is recalling something inaccurately—not forgetting entirely, but getting the details wrong. The word implies the memory feels real to the person, even if it doesn't match what actually happened: {I wasn't lying; I was misremembering}. It's become common in public discourse, sometimes as a polite way to describe what others might call a lie.

To misrepresent something is to describe or portray it falsely or misleadingly. The distortion may be deliberate or careless: {The advertisement misrepresented the product's capabilities}. Lawyers misrepresent facts, politicians misrepresent opponents' positions, and résumés misrepresent qualifications. The noun is misrepresentation.

Misrepresentation is a false or misleading account of something. The word often implies intent to deceive: {The lawsuit alleged misrepresentation of the property's condition}. In legal contexts, misrepresentation can void contracts or establish fraud. More loosely, any inaccurate portrayal qualifies: {That headline is a misrepresentation of what I actually said}.

Misrepresentations are false or misleading statements or portrayals. The word implies distortion rather than complete fabrication—something presented in a way that creates a wrong impression: {The lawsuit alleged material misrepresentations in the prospectus}. In law, misrepresentations can void contracts or constitute fraud if they induce someone to act on false information.

Misrepresented is the past tense of misrepresent—to give a false or misleading account of something. Facts, intentions, or people can be misrepresented, whether through deliberate distortion or careless inaccuracy: {The article misrepresented her views on immigration}. {He felt misrepresented by the documentary}.

Misrepresenting is presenting something inaccurately or falsely, whether through distortion, omission, or outright deception. You can misrepresent facts, intentions, or another person's views: {The article misrepresented her position on the issue}. Someone misrepresenting themselves claims qualifications or identities they don't have. The word implies intent or at least carelessness—not innocent error.

Misrule is bad or unjust governance—the failure of those in power to rule competently or fairly: {years of misrule left the country in ruins}. The word implies not merely poor decisions but a pattern of negligence or corruption. The Lord of Misrule was a figure appointed to preside over Christmas revelries in medieval England, embodying temporary inversion of normal order.
clues: When those in power fail catastrophically

definition: Miss is two different words, usually easily distinguishable by context. To miss is to fail or fail to experience in some way (miss the target, miss a phone call. If you miss someone, either you weren’t available when a meeting was possible, or you are sad for their absence. A miss is an instance of missing, a failure of some kind. Miss is also a title for a young or unmarried woman (usually capitalized), and by extension designates a young woman, or (in the plural, misses) a clothing size for young women: Miss Johnson will be attending the ceremony with her parents.

Missed is the past tense of miss, covering all its senses. You missed the bus if it left without you, missed the target if you failed to hit it, missed a meeting if you didn't attend. To say you missed someone means you felt their absence: {I missed you while you were away}. A missed {opportunity} is one that passed unexploited. {You missed a spot} points out an oversight.

Misses is the plural of miss in its noun senses: failed attempts, absences of contact, or young unmarried women. {He had two hits and three misses}. {Several near misses made her nervous}. As a verb form, misses means fails to hit, catch, or attend: {She misses her old friends}. {The bus misses our stop entirely}.

Misshapen means badly formed or deformed, deviating from normal or expected shape. A misshapen {potato} has irregular lumps and bulges. Misshapen {limbs} may result from injury or birth defect. The word carries connotations of ugliness or wrongness—something that should have turned out differently: {a misshapen lump of clay}, {misshapen by years of resentment}.

A missile is an object propelled at a target. In its broadest sense, any thrown or launched object qualifies: {Protesters hurled missiles at police}. More specifically, a missile is a self-propelled weapon carrying explosives—guided missiles can adjust course in flight, while ballistic missiles follow a fixed trajectory. The word often implies military weaponry: {cruise missile}, {nuclear missile}.

Missiles is the plural of missile—objects propelled at a target. The term covers anything thrown or launched as a weapon, from rocks to arrows, but modern usage centers on self-propelled weapons systems: {cruise missiles}, {ballistic missiles}, {surface-to-air missiles}. In military contexts, missiles typically carry explosive warheads and may be guided or unguided: {The strike involved dozens of missiles}.

Missing describes something or someone absent from where they should be. A missing {person} cannot be located. Missing {pages} have been removed or lost from a document. A missing {ingredient} is one you need but don't have. The word implies incompleteness—something that should be present isn't: {What's missing from this picture?} To {go missing} is to disappear, especially under unexplained circumstances.

A mission is a task or assignment given to someone, often with specific goals: {a rescue mission}, {a diplomatic mission}. Religious missions involve sending people to spread faith or do charitable work in distant places. Mission extends to any purposeful undertaking: {His mission was to find the best tacos in the city}. A mission statement declares an organization's core purpose. The phrase {mission accomplished} signals a goal achieved—sometimes used ironically when success is premature or questionable.

Missionaries are people sent to spread religious faith in foreign lands or among non-believers. Christian missionaries have historically combined evangelism with education, healthcare, and humanitarian work. The term extends to anyone zealously promoting a cause: {dietary missionaries}, {democracy missionaries}. The missionary position—face-to-face sexual intercourse with one partner on top—supposedly reflects what missionaries taught as proper.
clues: They spread religion in foreign lands

definition: A missionary is a person sent to spread religious faith, typically in foreign lands. Christian missionaries have historically combined evangelism with education and humanitarian work. The term extends to anyone zealously promoting a cause: {He approached veganism with missionary zeal}. Missionary position—face-to-face sex with one partner on top—supposedly reflects what missionaries taught as proper.

Missions is the plural of mission—tasks or assignments with specific purposes. Military missions are operations with defined objectives. Diplomatic missions are official delegations or their buildings: {the French mission in Geneva}. Religious missions are efforts to spread faith or the establishments where missionaries work: {Spanish missions dot the California coast}. In video games, missions are discrete objectives players must complete.

To misspeak is to express oneself imperfectly or inaccurately—saying something other than what you meant. Politicians who misspeak often claim their words were taken out of context: {I misspoke when I said we had no plans to raise taxes}. The word can serve as a face-saving way to walk back a statement without fully admitting error.

Misspeaking is saying something incorrectly or inaccurately, especially by accident. Politicians often claim to have misspoken when caught in embarrassing statements—a convenient way to retract words without fully apologizing: {I misspoke when I said the project was fully funded}. The word can describe genuine slips of the tongue or serve as diplomatic cover for lies.
To misspell is to spell incorrectly: {I always misspell "accommodate"}. The word itself is frequently misspelled with only one s. The past tense is misspelled or misspelt.
clues: Get the letters out of order

definition: Misspelled means spelled incorrectly: {The teacher circled the misspelled words}. Also spelled misspelt, particularly in British English. The word itself is frequently misspelled with only one s.
A misspelling is an incorrect spelling of a word: {The document was full of misspellings}. The word itself is often misspelled with only one s.
clues: Getting the letters out of order

definition: Misspent describes time, money, or effort wasted on unworthy pursuits. A {misspent youth} suggests years squandered on frivolous or dissolute activities rather than productive ones. The word carries moral judgment—what counts as misspent depends on who's evaluating: {He considered his years in banking a misspent career}.

Misspoke is the past tense of misspeak—to say something incorrectly or unintentionally. Politicians often claim they misspoke when caught in contradictions: {I misspoke when I said we had no contact with them}. The word can be a genuine acknowledgment of error or a convenient way to walk back statements without admitting to lying.

A misstep is a stumble or awkward step—placing your foot wrong while walking. More often the word is figurative: a mistake or error in judgment, especially one that damages your position or reputation. {One misstep could cost him the election.} {She recovered quickly from her early career missteps.}
clues: An error in judgment or footing

definition: Misstepped is the past tense of misstep, meaning to step wrongly or make an error in judgment. The literal sense—placing a foot badly—is less common than the figurative: {The politician misstepped when she made light of the scandal}. A misstep can be minor or career-ending depending on context.

Missus is an informal term for wife: {I'll have to check with the missus}. It represents the spoken pronunciation of Mrs. and carries a folksy or working-class tone. With "the" it typically refers to one's own wife or the wife of someone contextually understood: {The missus won't let me stay out late}.

Missy is an informal, sometimes condescending term for a young girl or woman. It's often used by adults addressing children in a slightly scolding or teasing way: {Listen here, missy, you need to clean your room}. When directed at adult women, it typically carries a dismissive or patronizing tone, implying the person is acting childish or out of line. The term can also be affectionate in familiar contexts.

Mist is a thin fog—water vapor suspended in air that reduces visibility without obscuring it entirely. {Morning mist hung over the valley}. Mist also describes any fine spray or haze: {a mist of perfume}, {the mist from a waterfall}. Eyes mist over with tears or emotion. To mist plants is to spray them lightly. Something lost {in the mists of time} is obscured by the distant past.

A mistake is an error—something done wrongly or believed incorrectly. You can {make a mistake} in calculation, judgment, or action. To mistake one thing for another is to confuse them: {I mistook her for her sister}. Mistaken as an adjective means wrong: {You're mistaken about that}. {There's no mistaking} something means it's unmistakable.

Mistaken means wrong or in error. A mistaken {belief} or mistaken {impression} is one that doesn't match reality. To be mistaken is to be wrong about something: {If you think I'm paying for this, you're mistaken}. The phrase {mistaken identity} describes confusing one person for another. {Unless I'm mistaken} introduces a tentative claim the speaker believes is correct.

Mistakes are errors or wrong actions, things done incorrectly or poorly judged. A mistake can be minor—a spelling mistake, a mistake in arithmetic—or consequential: {Marrying him was the biggest mistake of my life}. To mistake something is to misidentify it: {I mistook her for her sister}. {Make no mistake} emphasizes certainty about what follows.

Mister is a title of courtesy placed before a man's name, nearly always abbreviated to Mr. It applies to any adult male regardless of status, though it carries slightly more formality than using a first name alone. When used without a name, mister can address a stranger directly: {Hey, mister, you dropped your wallet.} The word also appears in compound titles like {mister chairman} or playfully in {mister know-it-all}.

Mistletoe is a parasitic plant that grows on the branches of trees, drawing water and nutrients from its host. It has leathery evergreen leaves and white berries. In Western tradition, mistletoe is hung as Christmas decoration, and people standing beneath it are supposed to kiss: {They caught each other under the mistletoe}.

Mistook is the past tense of mistake. To mistook someone or something for another is to have wrongly identified them: {I mistook her for my sister from behind}. More broadly, it means to have misjudged: {He mistook my silence for agreement}. {I mistook the address and ended up at the wrong house}.

A mistranslation is a rendering of text or speech from one language to another that contains errors, whether through misunderstanding, carelessness, or limitations in the translator's skill. Mistranslations range from minor inaccuracies to complete reversals of meaning. Some famous mistranslations have had significant consequences, such as diplomatic misunderstandings or biblical passages rendered in ways that shaped centuries of belief. {The treaty's mistranslation nearly caused an international incident.}

To mistreat is to treat someone or something badly, cruelly, or unfairly. The word covers a range of harmful behavior—from neglect to abuse: {The dog had been mistreated by its previous owner}. Mistreat is slightly more formal than its near-synonym treat badly, and slightly less severe than abuse.

Mistreated means treated badly, cruelly, or unfairly. The word suggests ongoing or repeated harm rather than a single incident: {The dog had clearly been mistreated by its previous owner}. It applies to physical abuse, emotional neglect, or unjust treatment: {mistreated employees}, {mistreated prisoners}. Someone mistreated has been wronged by those who should have treated them better.

A mistress is a woman in a position of authority or control—the mistress of a household manages its affairs. The word parallels master but carries additional meanings master lacks. A mistress is also a woman having an ongoing sexual relationship with a married man: {He kept a mistress in the city}. In some contexts, mistress is an archaic or formal title for a woman, surviving in the abbreviations Mrs. and Ms.
clues: Woman in a married man's life

definition: Mistresses is the plural of mistress, a word with several related senses. A mistress is a woman in a position of authority or control—the mistress of a household, the mistress of her craft. It also refers to a woman having an ongoing sexual relationship with a married man: {He kept mistresses throughout his marriage}. The female equivalent of master, mistress has largely fallen out of use except in this romantic sense.

A mistrial is a trial that has been terminated and declared void before a verdict is reached. Common causes include a hung jury that cannot agree, procedural errors, juror misconduct, or prejudicial statements that compromise fairness. When a mistrial is declared, the case may be retried from the beginning: {The judge declared a mistrial after discovering the jury had been tainted}.

Mistrials are trials that have been declared invalid before a verdict is reached, typically because of procedural errors, jury misconduct, or a hung jury that cannot reach agreement. When a judge declares a mistrial, the case may be retried with a new jury rather than being dismissed entirely. {The judge declared a mistrial after learning a juror had discussed the case on social media.}

Mistrust is doubt about someone's honesty, reliability, or intentions. It implies suspicion without necessarily having proof: {Years of broken promises bred deep mistrust}. As a verb, to mistrust is to regard with suspicion: {She mistrusted his motives from the start}. Mistrust suggests wariness rather than outright accusation—you haven't caught them lying, but you're not convinced they're telling the truth either.

Mists is the plural of mist—light fog or fine water droplets suspended in air. The word often suggests something romantic or mysterious: {The valley was shrouded in morning mists}. Figuratively, mists obscure clarity: {the mists of time}, {the mists of memory}. As a verb, mists means becomes misty or sprays lightly: {The window mists over}, {She mists the plants daily}.

Misty describes something covered with or obscured by mist—a light fog or fine spray: {a misty morning}, {misty mountains}. The word extends to anything hazy or indistinct: {misty memories}, {misty recollections of childhood}. Eyes that are misty are slightly tearful, usually from emotion: {She got a little misty during the wedding vows}. (Capitalized Misty is a given name.)

To misunderstand is to fail to grasp someone's meaning correctly—to interpret words, actions, or intentions in a way the speaker or actor didn't intend. {I think you misunderstood me—I meant next Tuesday, not this one.} The noun misunderstanding can be a simple failure of comprehension or a minor disagreement: {We had a little misunderstanding about the bill.}

A misunderstanding is a failure to interpret something correctly. Two people may have a misunderstanding when each takes the other's words differently than intended: {It was just a misunderstanding—I thought you meant next Tuesday}. The word sometimes euphemizes deeper conflicts: calling a bitter dispute a {misunderstanding} minimizes it.

Misunderstandings are failures to understand correctly—instances where meaning, intention, or information is grasped wrongly. The word often implies no one is fully at fault: {It was just a misunderstanding}. Misunderstandings can be minor confusions or the source of serious conflict: {The war began over a series of diplomatic misunderstandings}.

Misunderstood describes someone or something not properly comprehended or appreciated. A misunderstood {artist} produces work others fail to grasp. A misunderstood {instruction} leads to errors. The word often carries sympathy—the misunderstood teenager isn't difficult, just not seen clearly: {He's not mean, just misunderstood}.

Misuse is improper or harmful use of something. You can misuse a tool by using it for the wrong purpose, misuse power by wielding it unfairly, or misuse a word by applying it incorrectly. The noun follows the same pattern: {the misuse of public funds}, {drug misuse}. Misuse suggests deviation from intended or appropriate function rather than mere overuse.

A mite is a tiny arachnid, often microscopic, that lives on plants, animals, or in soil—dust mites trigger allergies, and mites cause mange in dogs. Mite also means a very small amount or a small creature, especially a child: {The poor mite was exhausted}. A mite as an adverb means slightly: {a mite disappointed}.

A miter is a joint where two pieces meet at an angle, typically 45 degrees, forming a corner: {a miter joint in a picture frame}. A miter saw cuts such angles. Separately, a miter is the tall ceremonial headdress worn by bishops and abbots, pointed at the top with two peaks. As a verb, to miter is to join pieces at an angle or to bevel the edge of.

Mites are tiny arachnids, most invisible to the naked eye, that live on plants, animals, and in soil. Some are parasites: dust mites trigger allergies, and chiggers cause itchy bites. The word also means a small amount or a small child: {The poor mite was exhausted}. A widow's mite is a small but heartfelt contribution.

Mithril is a fictional metal invented by J.R.R. Tolkien in his Middle-earth novels—silvery, stronger than steel, and lighter than silk. The word has since become standard fantasy vocabulary, appearing in countless games and stories to denote rare, magical metal of exceptional quality: {I finally found a mithril sword}. Sometimes spelled mythril.

Mitochondria are structures within cells that generate most of the cell's energy supply, converting nutrients into usable fuel through chemical reactions. Often called "the powerhouse of the cell" in biology classes, this phrase has become a meme about the random facts retained from school. The singular is mitochondrion, though mitochondria often serves for both.
clues: Where cells burn fuel for energy

definition: A mitt is a type of glove, especially one with a single compartment for the four fingers together: {oven mitt}, {catcher's mitt}. In baseball, the catcher and first baseman wear mitts rather than fingered gloves. Informally, mitts are hands: {Keep your mitts off my stuff}. The word is a shortened form of mitten.

A mitten is a hand covering with a single compartment for all four fingers together and a separate compartment for the thumb. Mittens keep hands warmer than gloves because fingers share heat: {Don't forget your mittens—it's freezing out there}. Oven mitts and boxing mitts extend the concept to protective padding.

Mittens are hand coverings with a single compartment for the four fingers and a separate one for the thumb, distinguishing them from gloves, which have individual finger slots. Mittens keep hands warmer because fingers share heat: {My mother always made us wear mittens in winter}. The word often suggests childhood or cozy warmth.

Mitts are gloves, especially those without separate fingers or with the fingers cut off: {oven mitts}, {baseball mitts}. In informal speech, mitts means hands: {Keep your mitts off my stuff}. A catcher's mitt in baseball is heavily padded for receiving pitches. Mittens, the full form, typically refers to cold-weather handwear with a thumb compartment but no individual fingers.

A mitzvah is a commandment or good deed in Jewish tradition. The Torah contains 613 mitzvot (plural), covering religious obligations and ethical conduct. In casual use, mitzvah often just means a kind act or favor: {It would be a mitzvah if you could check on her}. A bar mitzvah or bat mitzvah is the coming-of-age ceremony marking when a Jewish child becomes responsible for observing the commandments.

Mix is about combining things that were separate. You mix ingredients when cooking, mix colors when painting, mix sounds when producing music. A mix is the result—a particular combination: {a mix of styles}, {a trail mix}. To mix with people is to socialize: {She doesn't mix well at parties}. To {mix it up} is to fight or compete aggressively. A mix-up is a confusion or mistake.

Mixed describes things combined or blended together: {mixed nuts}, {mixed feelings}, {mixed company}. A mixed {bag} contains varied elements of uneven quality. Mixed {signals} are contradictory messages. Someone of mixed {race} has parents from different racial backgrounds. A mixed {blessing} brings both advantages and disadvantages. To get mixed {up} is to become confused, or to become involved: {He got mixed up with the wrong crowd}.

A mixer is a device or person that mixes things together. A stand mixer blends ingredients; an audio mixer combines sound signals. A mixer is also a non-alcoholic beverage combined with liquor: {tonic water as a mixer for gin}. Socially, a mixer is an event designed for people to meet and mingle: {a freshman mixer}.

Mixers are devices or people that mix things. A stand mixer combines ingredients for baking. An audio mixer blends multiple sound channels. A mixer at a party is someone who mingles easily, or the event itself—a social gathering designed to help strangers meet. In drinks, a mixer is the non-alcoholic component combined with spirits: {tonic water}, {soda}, {juice}. {She's a good mixer} means she's sociable.

Mixes is the plural of mix—combinations or blends of different elements. A DJ's mixes combine tracks; a baker's cake mixes are pre-measured ingredients; a sound engineer's mixes balance audio levels. As a verb, mixes means combines or mingles: {She mixes business with pleasure}, {Oil and water never mixes well together}.

Mixing is combining separate elements into a unified whole. You mix ingredients when cooking, mix paint colors, or mix drinks at a bar. In audio production, mixing balances and blends separate recorded tracks into a final version: {The album took months to mix}. To mix socially is to mingle: {She doesn't mix well with strangers}. A mix-up is a confusion or mistake.

Mixmaster is a brand name for a stand mixer, a kitchen appliance that blends, whips, and kneads ingredients. The term has become generic for any such mixer: {She pulled out the old mixmaster to make cookie dough}. In slang, a mixmaster is a DJ known for skillful blending of tracks, or more broadly anyone who combines disparate elements with expertise.

A mixologist is a bartender, especially one who approaches cocktail-making as a craft. The term emerged in upscale bar culture to distinguish artisanal drink preparation from simple beer-and-shot service: {The mixologist created a custom cocktail using house-made bitters}. Some find the word pretentious—it's bartender with a premium markup.

Mixologists are bartenders who specialize in crafting cocktails, particularly those who approach drink-making as an art or science. The term emerged with the craft cocktail revival and suggests expertise in flavor combinations, techniques, and ingredients beyond standard bar fare: {The mixologists created a custom drink menu for the event}. Some bartenders embrace the title; others find it pretentious.

Mixology is the art or skill of preparing mixed drinks, especially cocktails. The term elevates bartending to a craft, suggesting knowledge of ingredients, techniques, and flavor combinations: {The speakeasy prides itself on its mixology}. A mixologist is someone who practices this craft, though many bartenders find the term pretentious.

A mixtape is a compilation of songs recorded onto a single cassette tape, CD, or digital playlist. Originally, mixtapes were personal creations—someone selecting and sequencing tracks for a friend, a crush, or themselves: {He made her a mixtape for Valentine's Day}. In hip-hop, a mixtape is an unofficial release showcasing an artist's work, often with freestyles over borrowed beats, used to build buzz before a commercial album. The term persists even when no tape is involved.

Mixtapes are compilations of songs recorded onto a single cassette tape, CD, or digital file. Originally, people made mixtapes by recording tracks from the radio or copying from other tapes—a personalized selection for a road trip, a party, or a romantic gesture: {He made her a mixtape of love songs}. In hip-hop, a mixtape is an unofficial release showcasing an artist's work, often featuring freestyles over existing beats. The term persists even though the cassette tape has largely disappeared.

A mixture is a combination of different elements or substances: {a mixture of flour and water}, {a mixture of emotions}. Unlike a compound, the components retain their individual properties and can often be separated. The word suggests variety without uniformity—things brought together but not fully blended: {The crowd was a mixture of locals and tourists}.

A mixup is a confusion or misunderstanding, especially one involving mistaken identities or swapped items: {There was a mixup at the hospital and we got the wrong test results}. The word often implies an accident rather than intention—paperwork errors, scheduling conflicts, miscommunication. Also spelled mix-up.

A mnemonic is a device that aids memory—a phrase, rhyme, or pattern that makes information easier to recall. {"Roy G. Biv" is a mnemonic for the colors of the rainbow.} The adjective describes anything that assists memory: {mnemonic techniques}, {mnemonic devices}. The word comes from Greek for mindful or remembering.

Mnemonics are memory aids—techniques or devices that help you remember information. The classic example is "Every Good Boy Does Fine" for the musical notes E-G-B-D-F. Mnemonics work by connecting unfamiliar information to patterns, rhymes, or images the mind holds more easily: {I learned the planets through a mnemonic about pizza}.

A moan is a low, prolonged sound expressing pain, pleasure, or distress: {She let out a moan as the massage worked the knot from her shoulder}. People moan in grief, during sex, or when sick. The wind moans through empty buildings. To moan is also to complain tediously: {He's always moaning about his job}. British English uses moan for complaint more readily than American.

Moaners are people who complain habitually, often about minor inconveniences. The word carries mild contempt—moaners whine rather than act: {The usual moaners were griping about the new policy}. In sexual contexts, moaners are people who vocalize pleasure audibly during sex.

Moaning is the act of making low, prolonged sounds—whether from pain, pleasure, or complaint. Sexual moaning expresses arousal or climax. Outside the bedroom, moaning often means grumbling or whining: {He's always moaning about his job}. The British use it more readily for habitual complaining: {Stop your moaning and get on with it}.

Moans are low, prolonged sounds expressing pain, pleasure, or dissatisfaction. Someone moans in agony after an injury, moans during sex, or moans about their workload. The verb and noun overlap: {She let out a moan} and {She moaned} describe the same sound. Moaning about something shades into complaining: {He's always moaning about the weather}.

A moat is a deep, wide ditch surrounding a castle or fortified place, typically filled with water to prevent attack. The word extends to any protective barrier: {a moat of lawyers}, {regulatory moats that protect established companies from competition}. In business strategy, a moat is a competitive advantage that shields a company from rivals.

Moats are deep, wide ditches surrounding a castle or fortified place, typically filled with water as a defensive barrier. The word almost always appears in historical or fantasy contexts: {The castle's moat made direct assault nearly impossible}. Figuratively, a moat is any protective barrier that keeps threats at bay—in business, a competitive moat protects market position from rivals.

A mob is a large, disorderly crowd, often with aggressive or violent intent: {An angry mob gathered outside the courthouse}. The word carries connotations of irrationality and herd behavior—a mob mentality. With "the," the mob refers to organized crime, particularly the Mafia: {His uncle had ties to the mob}. In Australian slang, a mob is simply a group or crowd without negative connotations. The verb means to crowd around aggressively or enthusiastically: {Fans mobbed the singer at the airport}.

Mobbed describes being surrounded or crowded by a large group, usually aggressively or enthusiastically. A celebrity gets mobbed by fans; a politician mobbed by reporters. The word implies loss of personal space and control: {We were mobbed the moment we stepped outside}. A place can also be mobbed, meaning extremely crowded: {The mall was mobbed on Black Friday}.

Mobbing is coordinated harassment or bullying, typically by a group against an individual in a workplace or social setting: {The constant mobbing drove her to resign}. In animal behavior, mobbing describes smaller birds attacking a predator en masse to drive it away. The workplace sense emphasizes sustained, organized mistreatment rather than a single incident.

Mobile describes something capable of moving or being moved. A mobile {phone} travels with you; a mobile {home} can be relocated (though rarely is). Mobile {forces} move quickly across terrain. A {mobile face} is expressive, its features shifting easily. As a noun, a mobile is a hanging sculpture with balanced parts that move with air currents, popularized by Alexander Calder. The word also applies to social movement: {upwardly mobile} means rising in status or wealth. (Capitalized Mobile is a city in Alabama.)

Mobiles is the plural of mobile, which has two primary senses. A mobile is a hanging sculpture with parts that move freely in air currents, often hung over cribs: {The baby watched the mobiles spin above her}. In British English, mobile (short for mobile phone) means cell phone: {I left my mobile at home}. The adjective mobile means capable of movement: {mobile units}, {upwardly mobile}.

Mobilisation is the British spelling of mobilization—the process of assembling and preparing resources for action, especially military forces for war. A government orders mobilisation to ready troops and equipment. The term extends to any large-scale organizing effort: {the mobilisation of public opinion}, {mass mobilisation of volunteers}. The verb is mobilise.

Mobilise is the British spelling of mobilize. To mobilise is to organize and prepare resources, people, or forces for action. Armies mobilise for war; activists mobilise support for a cause. The word implies coordinated movement from a state of readiness to one of active engagement: {The government mobilised troops along the border}, {They mobilised voters in key districts}.

Mobilised is the British spelling of mobilized. To mobilise is to organize and prepare resources, people, or forces for action, especially in response to a crisis or goal. The word originated in military contexts—mobilising troops for war—but now applies broadly: {The community mobilised to help flood victims}, {She mobilised her supporters for the campaign}. To mobilise something is to make it active and ready to move.

Mobility is the ability to move or be moved. Physical mobility refers to how well a person can get around—someone with limited mobility may use a wheelchair or walker. Social mobility describes movement between economic classes: {upward mobility}, {downward mobility}. The term extends to flexibility in employment or location: {job mobility}, {geographic mobility}. In military contexts, mobility means the capacity to move troops and equipment quickly.

Mobilization is the act of organizing and preparing resources for action, especially assembling military forces for war: {The mobilization of troops along the border signaled escalating tensions}. The term extends to any large-scale organizing effort: {voter mobilization}, {community mobilization}, {the mobilization of public opinion}. To mobilize something is to get it moving and ready for use.

Mobilizations are acts of organizing people or resources for action, especially military deployment or political campaigns. Troops undergo mobilization before war; activists coordinate mobilizations around causes: {The union planned mobilizations across several cities}. The word implies moving from a static state to active readiness, whether assembling armies or rallying supporters.

Mobilize means to organize and prepare resources for action, especially military forces: {The country mobilized its troops along the border}. The word extends to any coordinated marshaling of people or assets: {Community organizers mobilized voters}, {The company mobilized its legal team}. To mobilize support is to rally it. In medicine, to mobilize a joint is to restore its movement after injury or surgery.

Mobilized is the past tense of mobilize, meaning to organize and prepare for action or movement. Originally military—troops are mobilized for war, reserves mobilized during a crisis. The meaning extends to any coordinated effort: {The campaign mobilized thousands of volunteers}. Resources, support, and communities can all be mobilized. To be mobilized is to be called into active service or readiness.

Mobilizing is organizing people or resources for action, especially urgent or collective action. The word comes from military contexts—mobilizing troops means assembling and preparing them for war—but extends to any coordinated effort: {mobilizing voters}, {mobilizing support for a cause}, {mobilizing emergency response teams}. The emphasis is on moving from static to active, from potential to deployed.

Mobs is the plural of mob—a large, disorderly crowd, often with violent or threatening energy: {Angry mobs surrounded the courthouse}. A mob can also mean any large group: {mobs of tourists}. In organized crime, the Mob refers to the Mafia. In video games, mobs are hostile non-player characters that spawn in groups: {grinding mobs for XP}.

A mobster is a member of an organized crime syndicate, especially the Italian-American Mafia. The term evokes the gangster era of the 1920s and 1930s but applies to contemporary organized crime as well: {The mobster ran gambling operations across three states}. Mobster carries connotations of violence, loyalty codes, and criminal enterprise conducted like business.

Mobsters are members of organized crime groups, particularly the Italian-American Mafia. The term evokes a specific era and style—suited men in smoky rooms, protection rackets, and coded loyalty: {The mobsters ran the neighborhood}. A mobster is a gangster, but with connotations of hierarchy and syndicate membership rather than street-level criminality.

A moccasin is a soft leather shoe, originally made by North American Indigenous peoples, typically constructed from a single piece of hide with the sole turned up and attached to a U-shaped upper. The style has been adapted into casual slip-on shoes. Moccasin also names a venomous North American pit viper, the water moccasin or cottonmouth, which inhabits swamps and waterways of the southeastern United States.

Moccasins are soft leather shoes, originally made by North American Indigenous peoples from a single piece of deerskin with the sole turned up and sewn to a U-shaped upper piece. The style has been widely adopted in casual footwear, often as slip-on loafers: {She kicked off her moccasins by the door}. Water moccasins are venomous snakes, named for their coloring.

Mocha pairs coffee with chocolate. The name comes from Mocha, a port in Yemen that was once the main hub for coffee trade. Today mocha refers to any drink or flavor combining coffee and chocolate: {I'll have a mocha with whipped cream.}

Mochi is a Japanese rice cake made from glutinous rice pounded into a sticky, chewy paste. It appears in many forms—plain, filled with sweet bean paste, wrapped around ice cream, or grilled. The texture is distinctively elastic and slightly stretchy. Mochi is traditional at New Year celebrations but has become popular year-round in various desserts and snacks.

Mock means to ridicule or treat with contempt, often by imitation: {The kids mocked his accent}. It can also mean to mimic derisively or to frustrate expectations: {The locked door mocked our escape plans}. As an adjective, mock describes something simulated or imitation rather than real: a mock {trial}, mock {turtle soup}, a mock {battle}. The noun appears in phrases like {make a mock of}, meaning to make a joke of something serious.

A mockbuster is a low-budget film produced to capitalize on a major studio release, typically with a similar title and premise: {When the studio announced their dragon epic, a mockbuster appeared within weeks}. The term blends "mock" with "blockbuster," suggesting both imitation and inferior quality. Production companies like The Asylum specialize in these films, timing releases to coincide with theatrical premieres and benefit from confused consumers or curious viewers.

Mockery is ridicule or contemptuous imitation—words or actions that hold someone or something up to scorn: {His apology was pure mockery}. A mockery can also be a ludicrously inadequate or futile attempt: {The trial was a mockery of justice}. To {make a mockery of} something is to render it absurd or worthless through poor execution or disrespect.

Mocking describes speech or behavior that ridicules someone, often by imitation: {She repeated his words in a mocking tone}. A mocking smile or laugh conveys contempt. To mock is to make fun of, sometimes by mimicking: {The children mocked his accent}. In software development, mocking creates simulated objects that stand in for real components during testing.

A mockingbird is a gray North American songbird known for its ability to mimic the calls of other birds and various sounds in its environment. The name comes from this imitative behavior—the bird "mocks" other species. Mockingbirds are territorial and sing persistently, often through the night. {A mockingbird was singing outside my window at 3 a.m.}

Mockingbirds is the plural of mockingbird, a gray North American songbird famous for imitating the calls of other birds and sounds in its environment. The bird gives its name to the novel *To Kill a Mockingbird*, where killing one symbolizes destroying innocence: {There were mockingbirds in the oak tree outside my window}.

Mocks is the third-person singular form of mock, meaning to ridicule or imitate derisively: {She mocks his accent behind his back}. In software development, mocks are simulated objects that stand in for real components during testing: {We wrote mocks for the database calls}. Mock exams or trials are practice versions: {The mocks helped her prepare for finals}.

A mocktail is a mixed drink made without alcohol, designed to resemble a cocktail in presentation and complexity. The word blends *mock* with *cocktail*. Mocktails often feature fruit juices, sodas, herbs, and elaborate garnishes: {The restaurant has an impressive mocktail menu for designated drivers}. Also called a virgin cocktail.

Mocktails are cocktails made without alcohol—mixed drinks that mimic the presentation and complexity of their boozy counterparts using juices, sodas, syrups, and garnishes. The term blends "mock" with "cocktail." Bars and restaurants increasingly offer mocktail menus for designated drivers, pregnant women, or anyone avoiding alcohol: {The mocktail list had a virgin mojito and a sparkling berry spritz}.

Mockumentaries are films or television shows that parody the documentary format, presenting fictional content as if it were factual reporting. The style uses handheld cameras, talking-head interviews, and earnest narration to create comic tension between form and content: {This Is Spinal Tap} and {The Office} are classic examples. Singular: mockumentary.

A mockumentary is a film or television show that uses documentary style—interviews, handheld cameras, observational footage—to tell a fictional story, usually for comedic effect. The format mines humor from the contrast between documentary earnestness and absurd content: {The Office}, {This Is Spinal Tap}, {Best in Show}. The term blends "mock" and "documentary."

A mockup is a model or replica made for demonstration, testing, or planning purposes. Architects show mockups of buildings, designers create website mockups before coding, and manufacturers build mockups of products before production. Unlike a prototype, which functions, a mockup typically shows only appearance or layout: {The mockup looked great but had no working parts}. Also spelled mock-up.

Mockups are preliminary models or representations of a design, built to test appearance or demonstrate concepts before final production. In product design, a mockup might be a physical model; in web and software development, mockups show how interfaces will look without functional code: {The designer presented mockups of the new homepage}. Also spelled mock-ups.

Mod is a shortening that has several applications. A mod is a modification, especially to a video game or software that alters or extends its features: {I installed a graphics mod that makes the game look incredible}. In online communities, a mod is a moderator who enforces rules and manages discussions. As a verb, to mod something is to modify it or to serve as a moderator. The word also refers to a British youth subculture of the 1960s characterized by sharp fashion and motor scooters.

Modded describes something that has been modified, especially video games or electronics altered beyond their original specifications. A modded {game} might have new characters, levels, or mechanics added by players rather than developers. A modded {console} can run unauthorized software. The term comes from gaming culture but applies to any customized version of hardware or software: {He's running a heavily modded version of Skyrim}.

A modder is someone who modifies video games, software, or hardware—typically to add features, fix problems, or customize beyond original specifications. Game modders create new levels, characters, or gameplay mechanics: {The modder released a patch that completely overhauled the combat system}. Hardware modders might alter consoles or computers for enhanced performance or aesthetics.

Modders are people who modify video games, software, or hardware beyond their original design. The term comes from "mod" (modification) and describes hobbyists who create custom content, alter game mechanics, or enhance existing products: {The modders released a complete overhaul of the graphics}. Modding communities often extend a game's lifespan well beyond what developers intended.

Modding is the practice of modifying video games, software, or hardware—typically by users rather than original creators. Game modding ranges from small tweaks to complete overhauls: {The modding community created hundreds of new quests for Skyrim}. Hardware modding might mean customizing a car or computer case. The term comes from modification, with the doubled consonant following standard spelling conventions for verbs ending in a short vowel plus consonant.

Mode is a particular way or manner of doing something: {What mode of transportation do you prefer?} In statistics, the mode is the value that appears most frequently in a data set. Mode also describes a state or setting: {The phone is in airplane mode}, {She switched into work mode}. In music, modes are scales with distinct patterns of intervals, like Dorian or Phrygian.

A model is a representation of a thing that is made or used for a particular purpose. A model of a product can be used for testing, in advance of manufacture. A model of climate change can be developed to understand its implications. A fashion model wears clothes for promotional purposes. When you model something, you develop a model of it: Researchers are attempting to model the interactions of these two isomers. As an adjective, model may convey form (a model airplane), or a prototype or ideal (a model legislator).

Modeling is shaping or forming something, especially from a malleable material: {She spent the afternoon modeling clay}. In fashion, modeling is working as a model—displaying clothing or posing for photographers. In science and business, modeling means creating simplified representations of complex systems: {climate modeling}, {financial modeling}. To model behavior is to demonstrate it for others to imitate.

Modelling is the British spelling of modeling. It covers the same range of meanings: working as a model in fashion or art, creating representations of things (such as architectural models or computer simulations), and shaping materials like clay. The word also applies to demonstrating behavior for others to imitate: {The teacher was modelling good listening skills}. In scientific and mathematical contexts, modelling refers to building abstract representations of systems or processes to analyze or predict their behavior.

Models are representations of something else—simplified versions that help us understand, display, or predict. A model {airplane} mimics the real thing at smaller scale. A {computer model} simulates weather or economics. A {business model} describes how a company operates. In fashion and art, a model is a person who poses or displays clothing: {She works as a model}. To model is to create such representations, to pose professionally, or to demonstrate by example: {He models good behavior for his students}. Model as an adjective means exemplary: {a model citizen}, {a model student}.

A modem is a device that converts digital signals to analog and vice versa, allowing computers to communicate over telephone lines or cable systems. The word blends "modulator" and "demodulator." Early modems connected to the internet via dial-up, producing distinctive screeching sounds; modern cable and DSL modems are silent and far faster. {The technician installed a new modem to fix our internet connection.}

Modems are devices that convert digital data to signals suitable for transmission over telephone lines or cable systems, and back again. The word blends modulator-demodulator. Early internet users connected via dial-up modems that made distinctive screeching handshake sounds. Modern cable and DSL modems are faster and silent, often combined with routers in a single device.

Moderate describes something in the middle range—not extreme, not minimal, but somewhere in between. A moderate {climate} is neither too hot nor too cold; moderate {exercise} is neither strenuous nor negligible. As a noun, a moderate is someone whose political views avoid the extremes of left and right. The verb moderate means to preside over a discussion or debate, or to make something less intense: {The medication helped moderate her symptoms}. To do something {in moderation} is to avoid excess.

Moderates are people who hold centrist political views, avoiding extremes of left or right. The term often appears in political commentary: {Moderates in both parties opposed the bill}. As a verb, to moderate is to make less extreme or intense—you might moderate your tone, your drinking, or a panel discussion. A moderator keeps things from getting out of hand.

Moderation is the practice of avoiding extremes or excess, keeping things within reasonable bounds. {Everything in moderation} is common advice about eating, drinking, or any potentially harmful activity. In online contexts, moderation refers to the oversight and management of user-generated content—removing spam, enforcing community guidelines, and keeping discussions civil. A moderator performs this function, whether on a forum, at a debate, or in a panel discussion.

A moderator oversees discussion and enforces rules. In online communities, moderators review content, remove violations, and ban users: {The moderator deleted the post for harassment}. In debates or panels, a moderator guides conversation and keeps participants on topic. In nuclear physics, a moderator is a substance that slows neutrons in a reactor.

Moderators are people who oversee discussions or communities, ensuring rules are followed and civility maintained. Online moderators ({mods}) remove offensive content, ban disruptive users, and shape community culture on forums, social media, and streaming platforms: {The moderators took down the post for violating guidelines}. In debates or panels, a moderator guides conversation and keeps participants on track. In nuclear physics, a moderator is material that slows neutrons in a reactor.

Modern means belonging to the present or recent times rather than the distant past. A modern {building} uses contemporary materials and design; modern {medicine} refers to current scientific practices. Modern can also mean up-to-date or advanced: {modern conveniences}. In historical periodization, the modern era begins roughly with the Renaissance. As a noun, a modern is a person of contemporary times, or someone with progressive views.

Modernism is a broad cultural movement of the late 19th and early 20th centuries that broke with traditional forms in art, literature, architecture, and music. Writers like Joyce and Woolf, painters like Picasso, and architects like Le Corbusier rejected established conventions in favor of experimentation and abstraction. More generally, modernism can mean any embrace of contemporary ideas over traditional ones: {His modernism clashed with the church's conservative teachings}. (Capitalized Modernism often refers specifically to the historical movement.)

A modernist is someone who embraces modern ideas, methods, or styles, particularly in art, architecture, or literature. The term usually refers to the early-to-mid twentieth-century movement that broke with traditional forms: {Joyce and Woolf were literary modernists}, {a modernist building with clean lines and no ornamentation}. As an adjective, modernist describes work or thinking aligned with this sensibility.

Modernists are adherents of modernism—movements in art, architecture, literature, and theology that broke with tradition in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. In the arts, modernists rejected conventional forms in favor of experimentation: {The modernists revolutionized poetry}. In religion, modernists sought to reconcile faith with contemporary thought. The term often contrasts with traditionalists or, later, postmodernists.

Modernity is the condition of being modern—belonging to the present era rather than the past. The term often refers specifically to the period beginning with industrialization, characterized by scientific rationalism, technological progress, and the decline of traditional authority. In academic contexts, modernity describes the social and cultural shifts that distinguish contemporary life from premodern societies: urbanization, secular institutions, individual autonomy. {The tensions between modernity and tradition shape much of the novel's conflict.}

Modernization is the process of updating something to current standards or technologies. A factory undergoes modernization when it replaces old equipment. A country's modernization involves adopting contemporary economic and social institutions. The word often implies progress but can carry ambivalence—{rapid modernization} sometimes threatens traditional ways of life. {The modernization of the rail system took a decade.}

Modernize means to update something to current standards or practices. Buildings are modernized with new infrastructure; industries modernize by adopting new technology; countries modernize their economies or militaries. The word implies bringing something older into alignment with contemporary expectations: {They modernized the kitchen with new appliances}. To modernize can also mean to adopt modern ways: {The company finally modernized its hiring practices}.

Modes is the plural of mode—a way, manner, or style of doing something. Different modes of {transportation} include cars, trains, and planes. A device's modes are its operational states: {airplane mode}, {sleep mode}. In music, modes are scales with distinct interval patterns, like Dorian or Mixolydian. In statistics, a mode is the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.

Modest describes something moderate or unpretentious. A modest {income} is adequate but not lavish. A modest {proposal} doesn't ask for much. A modest person doesn't boast about accomplishments or draw attention to themselves—sometimes genuinely humble, sometimes falsely so. Modest also means not revealing too much of the body: {modest dress}. {She was modest about her achievements}.

Modesty is the quality of being unassuming about one's abilities or achievements—not boasting or drawing attention to oneself: {She accepted the award with characteristic modesty}. The word also refers to propriety in dress and behavior, particularly regarding sexual matters: {Victorian standards of modesty required covering the ankles}. A modest person avoids excess in self-presentation.

Modification is a change made to something, typically to improve it or adapt it to a particular purpose. The word covers alterations ranging from minor adjustments to substantial transformations: {The car has several aftermarket modifications.} In grammar, modification refers to how words or phrases limit or qualify the meaning of other words. Legal documents often undergo modification when circumstances change or parties negotiate new terms.

Modifications are changes made to something, usually to improve it or adapt it to a particular purpose. The word often implies alterations to an existing thing rather than creating something new: {The car had extensive modifications to the engine}. In legal and contractual contexts, modifications are formal amendments: {We agreed to modifications in the contract terms}. Building modifications alter structures; behavioral modifications change habits or conduct.

To modify is to change something, usually in a limited or partial way rather than transforming it entirely. You modify a recipe by adjusting ingredients, modify behavior through feedback, or modify a plan when circumstances shift. In grammar, a modifier is a word or phrase that describes or limits another: in {the red door}, red modifies door. Modified often suggests adaptation for specific needs: {a modified version of the software}.

Mods is the plural of mod, with several distinct meanings. In gaming and software, mods are user-created modifications that alter or extend a program: {The mods for this game add hundreds of hours of new content}. Mods also refers to moderators—people who monitor online communities and enforce rules: {The mods banned him for harassment}. Historically, mods were members of a 1960s British youth subculture known for sharp Italian fashion, motor scooters, and soul music, often contrasted with their rivals, the rockers.

Modular describes something composed of separate, interchangeable units that can be combined, rearranged, or replaced independently. A modular {sofa} consists of pieces that configure in various ways. Modular {design} allows systems to be upgraded part by part rather than replaced entirely. In music, modular {synthesizers} use discrete components patched together. The appeal of modularity is flexibility—swap out one piece without disrupting the whole.

Modulation is the act of adjusting or varying something—typically tone, pitch, or intensity. A speaker modulates their voice to convey emotion or emphasis: {She modulated her tone to sound more reassuring}. In music, modulation is a shift from one key to another. In electronics and broadcasting, modulation is the process of encoding information onto a carrier wave—amplitude modulation (AM) and frequency modulation (FM) are the classic radio technologies.

A module is a self-contained unit that forms part of a larger system. In construction or furniture, modules are standardized pieces designed to fit together: {modular homes}, {modular shelving}. In computing, a module is a section of code that handles a specific function and can be used independently. In education, a module is a unit of study within a course. The underlying idea is always a component that's complete in itself but designed to connect with others.

Modules are self-contained units that form part of a larger system. In education, a module is a discrete section of a course: {The first module covers basic statistics}. In computing, modules are independent pieces of code that can be loaded and reused: {Import the module at the top of your file}. Modular design—whether in software, furniture, or spacecraft—allows components to be added, removed, or replaced without disrupting the whole.

Mofo is a clipped form of motherfucker, used as a noun or intensifier with the same range of meanings but slightly softer impact. It can be hostile {That mofo stole my bike}, affectionate {He's one crazy mofo}, or emphatic {That's one big mofo of a truck}. The abbreviated form appears more often in casual speech and song lyrics where the full word might feel too harsh.

Moggies is the plural of moggy, British informal for a cat—especially an ordinary domestic cat of no particular breed. The word carries affection without pretension: {She has three moggies at home}. Sometimes spelled moggies or moggys.

Moggy is British informal for a cat, especially an ordinary mixed-breed cat rather than a pedigreed one: {The neighbor's moggy keeps coming into our garden}. The word carries affection without pretension—it's the everyday house cat, not the show cat. Also spelled moggie.

A mogul is a powerful or influential person in a particular industry: {a media mogul}, {a real estate mogul}. The word implies wealth and dominance. Separately, moguls are the bumps that form on ski slopes from repeated turns by skiers. (Capitalized Mogul refers to the Mughal dynasty of India.)

Moguls has two unrelated meanings. A mogul is a powerful person, especially in business or entertainment: {a media mogul}, {Hollywood moguls}.
