Separately, moguls are bumps on a ski slope formed by repeated turns carving out the snow, or the sport of skiing down such terrain: {She competed in freestyle moguls at the Olympics}.

Mohair is a lustrous, durable fiber from the Angora goat, or fabric woven from it. The fiber is silky and takes dye well, making it prized for sweaters, suits, and upholstery: {a mohair cardigan}, {mohair blend yarn}. Mohair fabric has a distinctive fuzzy texture and subtle sheen.

A mohawk is a hairstyle in which the sides of the head are shaved and the remaining center strip of hair stands upright, often spiked. Associated with punk rock culture and rebellion since the 1970s: {She showed up with a bright green mohawk}. In figure skating, a mohawk is a turn from one foot to the other while maintaining the same direction of travel. (Capitalized Mohawk refers to the Indigenous people or their language.)

Mohawks are hairstyles in which the head is shaved on both sides, leaving a strip of hair—often spiked upward—running from forehead to nape. The style became iconic in punk subculture during the 1970s and 1980s: {He showed up with a bright green mohawk}. In figure skating, a mohawk is a turn from one foot to the other while maintaining the same edge and direction of travel. (Capitalized Mohawk refers to the Indigenous people or their language.)

Moist describes something slightly wet—damp but not soaking. A moist {towelette} is wet enough to clean with. Moist {cake} has good texture, not dry. Moist {soil} holds water well for plants. The word has acquired a reputation as unpleasant-sounding, which some people find amusing and others genuinely dislike: {Don't say moist around her}.

Moisture is the presence of water or other liquid in small amounts, especially as dampness in the air, on a surface, or within a material. Soil retains moisture; skin loses it. {The cookies went stale from moisture in the air.} Moisturize means to add moisture, typically to skin or hair.

Moisturiser is the British spelling of moisturizer—a cream or lotion applied to skin to prevent dryness. Moisturisers work by trapping water in the outer layer of skin or adding oils to replace what's lost. {She applied moisturiser after her shower.} The term extends to products for hair and other materials that benefit from hydration.

To moisturize is to add or restore moisture to something, especially skin. Moisturizing lotions and creams prevent dryness and maintain suppleness: {I moisturize every morning after showering}. The word applies beyond skincare to anything that benefits from added moisture: {The humidifier helps moisturize the air in winter}.

A moisturizer is a cream or lotion applied to skin to keep it soft and hydrated. Most moisturizers work by trapping water in the outer layer of skin: {She applies moisturizer after every shower}. The term extends to similar products for hair or lips.

Moisturizing means adding or restoring moisture, especially to skin or hair. As an adjective, it describes products designed to hydrate: {moisturizing lotion}, {moisturizing shampoo}. As a verb form, it's the act of applying such products: {She spends ten minutes moisturizing before bed}. The goal is to prevent dryness and maintain suppleness.

A mojito is a cocktail made with white rum, lime juice, sugar, mint, and soda water. The drink originated in Cuba and became popular internationally in the early 2000s. The muddled mint and lime give it a fresh, citrusy character: {We ordered mojitos on the patio}.

Mojitos is the plural of mojito, a Cuban cocktail made with white rum, lime juice, sugar, mint, and soda water. The mint is typically muddled to release its flavor. {We ordered mojitos on the patio}. The drink became widely popular in American bars in the early 2000s.

Mojo is a person's magic charm, talent, or sexual appeal—an ineffable quality that brings success or power. The word entered mainstream English from African American folk magic traditions, where a mojo was a charm or spell. Now it's usually about personal magnetism or effectiveness: {He's lost his mojo}, {She got her mojo back}. In Austin Powers films, mojo became synonymous with masculine swagger and sex appeal.

A molar is one of the large, flat teeth at the back of the mouth used for grinding food. Humans have twelve molars, including four wisdom teeth. In chemistry and physics, molar means relating to a mole—the standard unit for measuring amounts of a substance: {molar mass}, {molar concentration}.

Molars are the large, flat teeth at the back of the mouth used for grinding food. Humans typically have twelve—three on each side of the upper and lower jaws, including the wisdom teeth. The word sometimes appears figuratively for any crushing mechanism: {The bureaucracy's molars ground through the paperwork}.

definition: Molasses is the thick, dark syrup left over when sugar is refined from sugarcane or sugar beets. It has a bittersweet flavor and is used in baking, especially for gingerbread and brown bread. Blackstrap molasses, from the final extraction, is the darkest and most bitter. Something {slow as molasses} moves very slowly: {Traffic was moving like molasses in January}.

Mold (British spelling mould) is a growth of fungus. When something molds, fungus has begun to grow on or in it. A different mold is a container used to give shape to plastic, plaster, or clay that is poured or pressed into it. When you mold something, you form it using a mold. To mold a person or their character is to have great influence in their development.

Molded describes something shaped in or by a mold—a form that gives material its contour. Molded {plastic}, molded {chocolate}, molded {ceiling tiles}. The word also applies to character or behavior shaped by influence: {He was molded by his years in the military}. In British English, spelled moulded.

Moldering describes the slow decay of organic matter—rotting, crumbling, disintegrating over time. Old books molder in forgotten corners of libraries. A corpse molders in its grave. The word suggests neglect and the quiet work of time: {moldering ruins}, {moldering leaves on the forest floor}. Figuratively, something can molder from disuse: {His talents moldered while he worked a dead-end job}.

Molding is decorative trim—strips of wood, plaster, or other material with a shaped profile, used to finish edges where walls meet ceilings, floors, or door frames: {crown molding}, {base molding}. The term also covers the process of shaping material in a mold, or the shaped object itself: {injection molding}, {a plastic molding}. Also spelled moulding in British English.

Molds are hollow forms that shape liquid or soft material as it hardens: {a candle mold}, {a gelatin mold}. The resulting object is also a mold. To mold is to shape something, literally or figuratively: {She molded the clay}, {experiences that mold character}. Separately, mold is the fuzzy fungal growth on damp or decaying matter: {There's mold on this bread}. To mold in this sense is to become moldy.

Moldy describes something covered with mold—the fuzzy fungal growth that appears on food, walls, or other organic matter left in damp conditions: {The bread had gone moldy}. Extended uses suggest staleness or decay: moldy {ideas}, a moldy {old book}. What's moldy has been neglected or left too long.

Mole gathers several unrelated words. The burrowing mammal digs tunnels underground, lending its name to someone who burrows into an organization to spy from within: {They suspected a mole in the intelligence agency}. A mole is also a small dark spot on skin—a pigmented growth. In chemistry, a mole is a unit measuring amount of substance. A mole can also be a massive stone breakwater protecting a harbor. In Mexican cuisine, mole is a rich sauce made with chiles and often chocolate.

A molecule is the smallest unit of a substance that retains its chemical properties—two or more atoms bonded together. Water molecules consist of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. In casual use, molecule suggests something extremely small: {There's not a molecule of truth in what he said}. The adjective is molecular: {molecular biology}, {molecular structure}.

Molecules are the smallest units of a chemical compound, consisting of two or more atoms bonded together. A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. The term extends to any small particle or trace amount: {There's not a molecule of truth in what he said}. In scientific contexts, molecular describes things at this scale: molecular {biology}, molecular {structure}.

A molehill is a small mound of earth pushed up by a burrowing mole. The word appears almost exclusively in the idiom {make a mountain out of a molehill}—to treat a minor problem as if it were a major one.

Molehills are small mounds of earth pushed up by burrowing moles. The word appears most often in the expression {make a mountain out of a molehill}—to treat a minor problem as though it were a major crisis. On its own, molehills suggests trivial matters: {These are molehills, not real obstacles}.

Moles are small burrowing mammals with velvety fur, tiny eyes, and powerful forelimbs adapted for digging. They live underground and are considered pests for the tunnels they create in lawns. A mole is also a dark spot on the skin—a cluster of pigmented cells, usually harmless but sometimes monitored for changes. In espionage, a mole is an undercover agent who infiltrates an organization over a long period: {They discovered a mole in the intelligence agency}. In chemistry, a mole is a unit measuring the amount of a substance, equal to Avogadro's number of particles.

Moleskin is a heavy cotton fabric with a soft, suede-like nap on one side, resembling the velvety fur of a mole. It's used for durable work clothes, jackets, and trousers. In a different application, moleskin refers to soft adhesive padding applied to feet to prevent or cushion blisters: {I always pack moleskin for long hikes}. The fabric and the medical product share the quality of being soft against skin.

A moll is a gangster's girlfriend or a woman associated with criminals. The term comes from early 20th-century American slang and appears frequently in noir fiction and films about organized crime: {The boss showed up with his moll on his arm}. The word is dated but still understood.

Mollusc is the British spelling of mollusk—a soft-bodied invertebrate typically protected by a shell. The category includes snails, clams, oysters, mussels, octopuses, and squids. {The beach was littered with mollusc shells.} Molluscs form one of the largest animal phyla, mostly marine but also freshwater and terrestrial.

A mollusk is a soft-bodied invertebrate animal, typically with a shell. The group includes snails, clams, oysters, mussels, octopuses, and squid. Mollusks are among the most diverse animal phyla, found in oceans, freshwater, and on land. Many are edible: {The restaurant specialized in mollusks—oysters, mussels, and clams}. Also spelled mollusc in British English.

A molly is a small tropical freshwater fish popular in home aquariums, known for being hardy and easy to breed. The name is also slang for MDMA, the psychoactive drug also called ecstasy, typically referring to the powder or crystal form rather than pressed pills: {We took some molly at the concert}. (Capitalized Molly is a given name.)

Mollycoddled means treated with excessive care or protection, pampered to the point of weakness. Someone who has been mollycoddled was shielded from hardship or difficulty, often with the implication they're now ill-equipped for real challenges: {He'd been mollycoddled his whole life and couldn't handle criticism}. The word carries a faintly contemptuous tone toward both the coddler and the coddled.

Mollycoddling is treating someone with excessive care or protection, shielding them from hardship or challenge. The word carries disapproval—it suggests the coddling weakens rather than helps: {Stop mollycoddling the boy and let him figure it out himself}. A mollycoddle is someone who has been pampered into softness.

Molt is what animals do when they shed old feathers, fur, skin, or shells to make way for new growth. Birds molt their feathers seasonally; snakes molt their skin; crabs molt their shells as they grow. The noun molt refers to the process or the material shed: {The chicken coop was full of molt}. Also spelled moult in British English.

Molted is the past tense of molt, meaning to shed feathers, skin, hair, or an outer covering as part of natural growth. Birds molt old feathers to grow new ones; snakes molt their skin; crabs molt their shells. {The parrot molted all summer and left feathers everywhere.}

Molten describes material—usually metal, rock, or glass—that has been liquefied by intense heat: {molten lava}, {molten steel}. The word carries connotations of dangerous heat and fluid movement. Molten is the old past participle of melt, preserved in this specialized sense while melted took over general use.

Molting is the process by which animals shed outer coverings—feathers, fur, skin, or exoskeleton—to allow for new growth. Birds molt feathers seasonally, snakes shed skin as they grow, and crustaceans discard shells that have become too small. The British spelling is moulting. {The parrot is molting and looks a bit ragged.}

Molts is the third-person singular verb form of molt—to shed feathers, skin, hair, or an outer layer as part of a natural growth cycle: {The snake molts its skin several times a year}. Birds molt old feathers to grow new ones. Insects molt their exoskeletons. The noun molt refers to the process or the material shed: {We found owl molts in the barn}.

Mom is an informal word for mother, used especially in American English. It functions both as a term of address {Mom, can I borrow the car?} and as a reference {My mom works nights}. The word carries warmth and familiarity. A {mom and pop} store is a small family-owned business. {Soccer mom} describes a suburban mother devoted to shuttling children to activities.

A momager is a mother who manages her child's career, especially in entertainment. The term blends "mom" and "manager," typically describing mothers who handle business affairs for child actors, musicians, or social media influencers: {Kris Jenner is the ultimate momager}. The word can carry connotations of pushiness or exploitation, suggesting a parent who prioritizes fame and profit over the child's wellbeing.

A momager is a mother who manages her child's career, typically in entertainment or sports. The term blends "mom" and "manager," often carrying a slightly critical edge—suggesting the mother may be overly involved, pushy, or living vicariously through her child's success. Kris Jenner, who manages the Kardashian family empire, is the archetypal momager: {Every young Disney star seems to have a momager hovering backstage}.

A moment is a very brief period of time—shorter than a minute, longer than an instant: {Wait here a moment}, {I'll be with you in a moment}. The word also means a particular point in time: {At that moment, everything changed}. A moment can carry weight or significance: {a moment of clarity}, {this is not the moment for jokes}. In physics, moment refers to a turning force around a point.

Momentary describes something lasting only a moment—brief and fleeting. A momentary {lapse in concentration} passes quickly. {There was a momentary silence before the applause}. The word emphasizes how short-lived something is, often with the implication that it will soon give way to something else: {momentary hesitation}, {momentary relief}.

Momentous describes events of great significance or consequence—moments that mark turning points or carry lasting weight: {a momentous decision}, {a momentous occasion}. The word implies that what happens will matter beyond the immediate present, shaping what follows. Unlike merely important, momentous suggests historical or life-changing gravity.

Moments is the plural of moment, a brief span of time. Moments can signal emotional significance: {One of the happiest moments of my life}. The phrase {has its moments} acknowledges intermittent quality: {The film drags, but it has its moments}. In physics, moment refers to a rotational force—hence {moment of inertia}.

Momentum is the force of movement—what keeps something going once it's started. In physics, it's the product of mass and velocity: a rolling boulder has more momentum than a rolling marble. Figuratively, momentum describes building progress or energy: {The campaign gained momentum after the debate}. To {lose momentum} is to slow or stall. {The momentum of the scandal proved unstoppable}.

Momma is an informal, affectionate term for mother, common in Southern American English and children's speech: {Go ask your momma}. It often carries warmth or nostalgia that the neutral "mother" lacks. In slang, momma can refer to an attractive woman or girlfriend: {She's a fine momma}. Also spelled mama.

Mommas is the plural of momma, an informal and affectionate term for mother. The spelling with double m reflects the pronunciation more closely than mama. {Their mommas raised them right.} The term appears in expressions like {yo momma} jokes and phrases like {momma's boy}, someone overly attached to his mother.

Mommy is a child's word for mother, used by young children or when speaking to them: {Go ask Mommy}. Adults may use it affectionately, nostalgically, or ironically. In sexual contexts, mommy appears in phrases like {mommy kink} or {mommy issues}, referring to attraction shaped by maternal dynamics. The standard British equivalent is mummy.

Moms is the plural of mom, an informal word for mother. The term often appears in contexts addressing mothers as a group: {busy moms}, {working moms}, {soccer moms}. In informal direct address, moms can refer to a single mother: {Hey moms, what's for dinner?}

A monarch is a sovereign ruler—a king, queen, emperor, or similar head of state who typically inherits the position and holds it for life. In constitutional monarchies, the monarch's power is largely ceremonial: {The monarch opened Parliament}. The word also names the monarch butterfly, a large orange-and-black species famous for its long migrations.

Monarchies is the plural of monarchy, a system of government in which a single person—a king, queen, emperor, or similar sovereign—holds supreme authority. The term can refer to nations governed this way: {Several European monarchies have survived into the modern era}. Monarchies range from absolute, where the ruler holds unchecked power, to constitutional, where the monarch serves largely as a ceremonial figurehead.

A monarchist supports monarchy as a form of government—rule by a king or queen rather than elected representatives. The term appears in historical and contemporary political contexts: {Monarchists hoped to restore the deposed royal family}. In countries with existing constitutional monarchies, monarchists typically advocate preserving or strengthening the crown's role.

Monarchs is the plural of monarch, a sovereign ruler such as a king, queen, or emperor who typically inherits the position. The word extends to anyone who dominates a field: {the monarchs of Silicon Valley}. A monarch is also a large orange-and-black butterfly known for migrating thousands of miles: {We watched monarchs pass through on their way to Mexico}.

A monarchy is a system of government in which a single person—king, queen, emperor—holds supreme authority, typically by hereditary succession. The term also refers to a state governed this way: {the British monarchy}, {the fall of the French monarchy}. Modern monarchies range from absolute (the ruler holds real power) to constitutional (the monarch is largely ceremonial while elected officials govern).

Monasteries is the plural of monastery, a building or complex where monks or nuns live in religious community. Monasteries are typically secluded from ordinary society, devoted to prayer, contemplation, and communal religious practice: {Medieval monasteries preserved classical manuscripts through the Dark Ages}. The term applies across religious traditions—Christian, Buddhist, and others.

A monastery is a building or complex where monks live as a religious community, typically following a structured life of prayer, work, and contemplation apart from the wider world. The term applies primarily to Christian and Buddhist traditions, though similar institutions exist in other religions. Monasteries often include a chapel, dormitories, and communal spaces, and historically served as centers of learning and manuscript preservation. {The ancient monastery had been producing wine for centuries.}

Monastic relates to monks, nuns, or the religious communities they form. A monastic {order} follows rules of communal living, prayer, and often poverty and celibacy. Monastic {life} typically involves withdrawal from ordinary society. The word extends to any lifestyle marked by austere simplicity and disciplined routine: {His apartment had a monastic sparseness}.

Monetisation is the British spelling of monetization—the process of generating revenue from something. A website might pursue monetisation through advertising, subscriptions, or sponsored content. The term appears frequently in discussions of digital platforms: {YouTube's monetisation policies have changed again}. More broadly, monetisation describes converting any asset or activity into a source of income: {the monetisation of personal data}.

Monetise is the British spelling of monetize—to convert something into money or a source of revenue. Content creators monetise their videos through advertising. Companies monetise user data by selling it to third parties. The word often carries a slightly cynical edge, implying that something not originally commercial is being exploited for profit: {They'll monetise anything these days}.

Monetization is the process of converting something into a source of revenue. Content creators pursue monetization of their videos through ads and sponsorships. A website monetizes its traffic by selling user data or display advertising. The term appears frequently in discussions of social media platforms: {The app changed its monetization strategy}. Monetization can also mean establishing something as legal tender, though this sense is now rare.

Monetize means to convert something into a source of income. Content creators monetize videos through advertising. A business monetizes its user base by selling data or subscriptions. The word often carries a faintly cynical edge, suggesting that something previously free or uncommercial is being exploited for profit: {They've monetized every aspect of the user experience}.

Monetized describes something that has been converted into a source of revenue. A monetized YouTube channel earns money from ads. A monetized hobby becomes a side business. The term often carries slight cynicism—suggesting that something once free or authentic now serves commercial interests: {She monetized her following by selling courses}. To monetize is to find ways to generate income from an asset, audience, or activity.

Monetizing is the process of converting something into a source of revenue. Content creators monetize videos through advertising. A company monetizes user data by selling it to third parties. The term often carries slight cynicism, suggesting the commercialization of something previously free or authentic: {They're monetizing every aspect of the fan experience}.

Money is a medium for exchange of value, represented concretely by bills and coins (Have you got any money on you?) and abstractly by accounts and credit. The verbs most commonly used with money are raise and make. To raise money is to collect enough of it to do something: They’re trying to raise money for a documentary about hippies. To make money is not to manufacture it, but to receive it in exchange for something, or to realize a profit: Did you make any money when you sold your house? Money is used in common phrases with a related meaning: marry money means marry someone rich. In the money means in a profitable situation.

A moneybag is a bag for holding money, especially coins—the image of a bulging sack that cartoonists draw when depicting wealth. In the plural, moneybags is informal for a wealthy person, often dismissive or resentful: {Some moneybags bought the old factory and turned it into condos}.

Moneybags is an informal, slightly mocking term for a wealthy person, emphasizing their abundance of cash. It often carries a tone of envy or mild resentment: {Hey moneybags, you're buying lunch today}. The word can be used as a noun or as a joking form of address. Though sometimes affectionate among friends, it typically implies the person flaunts or is defined by their wealth rather than other qualities.

Moneyball is a strategy of using statistical analysis rather than traditional scouting to evaluate players and build competitive sports teams on a limited budget. The term comes from the 2003 book about the Oakland Athletics baseball team, whose general manager used data-driven methods to compete against wealthier franchises. Now used broadly for any analytical approach that finds undervalued assets: {They're applying moneyball principles to hiring}.

Moneychangers are people who exchange one currency for another, typically for a fee. The term evokes biblical imagery—Jesus famously drove the moneychangers from the temple. Today it describes currency exchange operators, though the word carries a faintly archaic or disapproving tone: {The moneychangers at the airport offered terrible rates}.

A moneygrubber is someone obsessively focused on acquiring money, especially through petty or undignified means. The term is always disparaging, suggesting greed that overrides other values: {Don't be such a moneygrubber—it's just a few dollars}. The related adjective is moneygrubbing.

Moneygrubbing describes an excessive, often undignified pursuit of money. The term is derogatory, suggesting someone willing to sacrifice principles or dignity for financial gain: {a moneygrubbing landlord who never fixed anything}. A moneygrubber is the person; moneygrubbing is the activity or the adjective describing it.

A moneylender is a person or institution that lends money at interest. The term often implies lending outside traditional banking—sometimes at high rates or to borrowers banks won't serve: {The family borrowed from a local moneylender when the bank turned them down}. In historical and literary contexts, moneylenders appear as figures of both necessity and predation.

Moneylenders are people or institutions that lend money at interest. The term often carries negative connotations, suggesting predatory lending practices or exorbitant rates: {Jesus drove the moneylenders from the temple}. In modern usage, it may describe payday loan operations or informal lenders operating outside mainstream banking.

Moneylending is the practice of lending money at interest. The term often carries negative connotations, suggesting predatory rates or informal arrangements outside mainstream banking: {The family had been in the moneylending business for generations}. A moneylender is someone who engages in this practice.

A moneymaker is something or someone that generates profit or income. A business's moneymaker is its most profitable product or division: {The streaming service became the company's biggest moneymaker}. A person who earns well for themselves or others is also a moneymaker. In slang, moneymaker refers playfully to the body, especially the hips or buttocks: {Shake your moneymaker}.

Moneymakers are people or things that generate profit or income. A successful product line might be a company's biggest moneymaker. A person with a knack for business is a moneymaker. In slang, moneymaker often refers playfully to the buttocks, especially when dancing: {Shake your moneymaker}.

Moneymaking describes activities that generate profit or income: {a moneymaking scheme}, {the moneymaking potential of the franchise}. As a noun, it refers to the pursuit or acquisition of wealth: {He devoted himself to moneymaking}. The word can be neutral or carry a faint suggestion that profit is the primary motive.

A moneyman is someone who controls or provides financial backing—a financier, investor, or the person managing funds for an organization or project. The term often implies power operating behind the scenes: {The candidate's moneymen expected favorable policies in return}. Sometimes used for financial advisors or accountants: {I'll have to check with my moneyman}.

A monger is someone who deals in or promotes a particular commodity or activity. The literal sense survives in compounds like fishmonger and ironmonger (more common in British English). The figurative sense dominates in American usage, usually with negative connotations: a warmonger promotes conflict, a rumormonger spreads gossip, a fearmonger stokes anxiety for effect. The suffix -monger attaches productively to create new compounds: {The senator dismissed his critics as mere hatemongers}.

A mongoose is a small, agile carnivorous mammal native to Africa and Asia, known for its ability to kill venomous snakes. Mongooses are quick and fearless, attacking cobras and other serpents with darting strikes while avoiding fangs. The plural is mongooses, not mongeese: {Mongooses have been introduced to islands to control rats, often with disastrous ecological results}.

A mongrel is a dog of mixed or indeterminate breed, as opposed to a purebred: {The shelter was full of mongrels}. The term extends to anything of mixed origin or composition. Applied to people, mongrel is offensive, suggesting impure ancestry or racial mixing. The word carries connotations of being inferior or lacking pedigree, though some use it affectionately for dogs.

Mongrels are dogs of mixed or unknown breed—the opposite of purebreds. The word extends to any hybrid or mixture: {a mongrel language cobbled together from three others}. Applied to people, mongrel is usually derogatory, implying impure or mixed ancestry. Some reclaim it: {We're all mongrels if you go back far enough}.

A moniker is a name, nickname, or alias—especially one that's informal, self-chosen, or adopted for a particular context: {He goes by the moniker "Big Red"}. The word often suggests something more colorful or distinctive than an ordinary name: {She earned the moniker "Iron Lady" for her tough negotiating style}.

A monitor is a device that displays information or tracks conditions. Computer monitors show visual output; heart monitors track vital signs. The word extends to people who watch or supervise: hall monitors in schools, election monitors at polling places. To monitor is to observe systematically: {We're monitoring the situation closely}. A monitor lizard is a large tropical reptile—the name may derive from a belief that they warn of crocodiles nearby.

Monitoring is the ongoing observation or tracking of something to detect changes, ensure proper function, or gather information. You might monitor a patient's vital signs, monitor network traffic for security threats, or monitor a child's screen time. The word implies sustained attention rather than a single check: {The system requires constant monitoring}. A monitor is both the person or device doing the watching and, separately, a display screen.

Monitors are devices that display information—computer screens showing visual output, or medical equipment tracking vital signs. A monitor is also someone who watches or checks on something: a hall monitor supervises students, an election monitor observes voting. To monitor is to observe systematically: {We're monitoring the situation closely}. Monitor lizards are large reptiles, some exceeding ten feet.

A monk is a man who has withdrawn from ordinary life to devote himself to religious practice, typically living in a community under vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience. Christian and Buddhist traditions are best known for monasticism, though the practice exists in other religions. {The monks rose at dawn for prayer.} Monks often live in monasteries, following strict daily routines of worship, work, and contemplation.

A monkey is a primate, typically smaller than apes and usually having a tail. Monkeys divide into Old World species (Africa, Asia) and New World species (Americas). The word extends to playful mischief: {Stop monkeying around}. To {monkey with} something is to tamper with it. {Monkey see, monkey do} describes mindless imitation. A {monkey on your back} is an addiction or persistent problem. In British slang, a monkey is five hundred pounds.

Monkeying is playful, aimless activity—fooling around or tinkering without serious purpose. Usually appears with "around" or "with": {Stop monkeying around and get to work}. To monkey with something is to tamper or fiddle with it, often unwisely: {Someone's been monkeying with the thermostat}.

Monkeys are primates, typically smaller than apes and usually possessing tails. The term covers a wide range of species across Africa, Asia, and the Americas. To monkey with something is to tamper or tinker: {Stop monkeying with the thermostat}. To {monkey around} is to behave playfully or mischievously. A {monkey on your back} is a persistent burden or addiction.

A monkeywrench is an adjustable wrench with a jaw that moves via a screw mechanism, used to grip nuts and bolts of various sizes. To monkeywrench or {throw a monkeywrench into} something is to sabotage or disrupt it: {The lawsuit threw a monkeywrench into the merger}. Environmental activists who sabotage equipment practice monkeywrenching. Also spelled monkey wrench.

Monkeywrenches is the plural of monkeywrench, an adjustable wrench with one fixed and one movable jaw. The verb form means to sabotage or deliberately disrupt: {Environmental activists monkeywrenched the logging operation by spiking trees}. To {throw a monkeywrench into} something is to cause unexpected problems that derail plans.

Monkfish is a large, bottom-dwelling fish with a broad, flattened head and an enormous mouth. Despite its grotesque appearance, the tail meat is prized for its firm, lobster-like texture: {Pan-seared monkfish with brown butter}. Also called goosefish or anglerfish, it's common in European and American Atlantic waters.

Monks is the plural of monk—men who have withdrawn from ordinary society to live under religious vows, typically in a monastery. The term applies across traditions: Christian monks follow rules like those of St. Benedict, while Buddhist monks may beg for alms. {The monks rose before dawn for prayer.} Monks often take vows of poverty, celibacy, and obedience.

Mono functions as a prefix meaning one or single: monologue, monogamy, monosyllabic. Standing alone, mono usually refers to mononucleosis, the viral infection known for extreme fatigue: {She missed a month of school with mono}. In audio, mono means single-channel sound as opposed to stereo: {The old recording was in mono}.

A monobrow is a single continuous eyebrow formed when hair grows across the bridge of the nose, connecting the two brows. Also called a unibrow. The feature has varied cultural associations—considered attractive in some traditions, unfashionable in others—and is easily removed by plucking or waxing: {He refused to do anything about his monobrow}.

Monochrome means using only one color or shades of a single color. A monochrome photograph uses black, white, and grays rather than full color. In design and fashion, monochrome describes an outfit or palette restricted to variations of one hue: {She wore a monochrome look in shades of blue}. The word also works as a noun: {The film was shot in monochrome}.

A monocle is a single lens worn in front of one eye, held in place by the muscles around the eye socket. Once a fashionable accessory among wealthy men in the 19th and early 20th centuries, it now appears mainly as a costume piece or visual shorthand for aristocratic pretension: {He adjusted his monocle and sniffed disapprovingly}.

Monocles is the plural of monocle, a single corrective lens worn in one eye socket, held in place by the brow and cheek. Once a mark of aristocratic refinement, the monocle is now largely a costume piece or visual shorthand for old-money pretension: {The villain adjusted his monocle and sneered}.

Monoculture is the agricultural practice of growing a single crop over a large area, year after year. This approach maximizes efficiency and yield for that one crop but depletes soil nutrients and makes fields vulnerable to pests and disease. The term extends beyond farming to describe any system dominated by one thing at the expense of diversity: {Critics worry that streaming algorithms create a monoculture of popular content}. A monoculture of thought suggests conformity that stifles innovation or dissent.

Monocultures are agricultural systems where a single crop is grown over a large area, often repeatedly season after season: {The Midwest's corn monoculture stretches for miles}. The practice maximizes efficiency but depletes soil and increases vulnerability to pests. Figuratively, monoculture describes any environment lacking diversity—a workplace monoculture, a cultural monoculture: {Silicon Valley's monoculture of young male engineers}.

Monogamous describes the practice of having only one mate or sexual partner at a time. In zoology, monogamous species pair-bond for mating seasons or for life, as with many birds. Applied to humans, it characterizes someone committed to one romantic or sexual partner: {They've been monogamous for twenty years}. The term contrasts with polygamous, which involves multiple partners. Monogamous relationships may be serial—one partner at a time, but different partners over a lifetime.

Monogamy is the practice of having only one spouse or sexual partner at a time. The term applies both to marriage customs and to mating behavior in animals: {Swans are known for their monogamy}. Serial monogamy describes a pattern of successive exclusive relationships rather than lifelong pairing with one person: {He practices serial monogamy—always faithful, but never for long}.

A monogram is a design made by combining two or more letters, typically someone's initials, into a single symbol: {The towels were embroidered with her monogram}. Monograms appear on stationery, luggage, jewelry, and clothing as marks of ownership or personalization. To monogram something is to add such a design: {a monogrammed shirt}.

Monogrammed describes something decorated with a monogram—a design of interwoven initials, typically representing a person's name. The term usually applies to personalized items suggesting refinement or ownership: {monogrammed towels}, {monogrammed stationery}, {a monogrammed leather briefcase}. Monogramming is common for gifts and luxury goods.

Monograms are designs combining two or more letters, typically initials, interwoven or arranged as a single symbol. They personalize items like towels, stationery, luggage, and jewelry: {The pillowcases were embroidered with her monogram}. To monogram something is to mark it with such a design: {We had the briefcase monogrammed with his initials}.

A monokini is a women's swimsuit consisting of a bottom piece only, leaving the breasts bare—a bikini cut in half. The term plays on a false etymology, as if the *bi-* in bikini meant "two." Monokinis saw brief popularity in the 1960s and remain associated with topless sunbathing at European beaches.

A monolith is a single massive block of stone, either natural or shaped into a monument or pillar. The word extends to anything huge, uniform, and imposing: a corporation can be a monolith, as can a government bureaucracy. The adjective monolithic emphasizes uniformity and resistance to change: {a monolithic political system}, {monolithic architecture}. In computing, a monolithic system keeps all components in one unified structure rather than separating them into modules.

Monolithic describes something massive, uniform, and undifferentiated—like a monolith, a single huge block of stone. A monolithic {organization} operates as one rigid unit without internal variation. Monolithic {architecture} uses enormous single stones. In computing, a monolithic {system} is built as one indivisible whole rather than separate components. The word often carries critical undertones—suggesting inflexibility or lack of nuance: {The party presented a monolithic front on the issue}.

Monoliths is the plural of monolith—a large single block of stone, especially one shaped into a pillar or monument. The term extends to anything massive and uniform: a corporate monolith, a monolith of bureaucracy. In science fiction, monoliths often appear as mysterious alien artifacts. The word implies imposing size and undifferentiated wholeness: {The publishing monoliths have swallowed up the independents}.
clues: Giant rocks carved from one piece

definition: A monolog is an extended speech by one person. In theater, a monolog is a solo speech delivered to the audience or to oneself, distinct from dialog between characters. Outside drama, it describes any prolonged one-sided talk: {His rant about politics turned into a twenty-minute monolog}. Also spelled monologue.

Monologs is the plural of monolog, an alternate spelling of monologue. A monolog is a long speech by one person—whether a character's extended address in a play, a comedian's opening routine, or someone dominating a conversation: {His monologs about work could last an hour}.

A monologue is an extended speech by one person. In theater, it's a character speaking alone or at length while others listen—distinguished from dialogue, which involves exchange. The term extends to anyone holding forth without interruption: {He launched into a monologue about his golf game}. A dramatic monologue in poetry is a poem spoken entirely by a single character.

Monologues is the plural of monologue—a long speech by one person. In theater, a monologue is an extended passage spoken by a single character, often revealing inner thoughts: {She nailed the audition monologue}. More loosely, any one-sided conversation where someone talks at length without interruption: {His monologues about work were exhausting}.
clues: Extended solo addresses to an audience

definition: Monologuing is talking at length without interruption, especially when others might prefer dialogue. The term often carries a mocking edge, particularly for villains in fiction who delay action to explain their plans: {The supervillain was monologuing when the hero escaped}. More broadly, it describes anyone holding forth while others wait: {He was still monologuing about his weekend when I tuned out}.

Monomania is obsessive focus on a single idea, subject, or pursuit to an unhealthy degree. Once a psychiatric term for partial insanity centered on one fixation, it now describes any consuming preoccupation: {His monomania about vintage guitars had taken over the garage}. A monomaniac pursues their obsession with tunnel vision, neglecting everything else.

Monopolies is the plural of monopoly—exclusive control over a commodity, service, or market. A company with a monopoly faces no competition: {Standard Oil's monopolies were broken up by antitrust action}. The word extends to any exclusive possession: {She has a monopoly on his attention}. Monopolies also names the board game, though that's typically capitalized.

Monopolise is the British spelling of monopolize. To monopolise is to gain exclusive control over something—a market, a resource, or a conversation. A company might monopolise an industry by eliminating competitors. Someone who monopolises a discussion doesn't let others speak: {She monopolised the meeting with her complaints}. The word implies dominance that crowds others out.

A monopolist is a person or entity that holds a monopoly—exclusive control over a commodity, service, or market. The term often carries negative connotations, suggesting someone who eliminates competition or exploits their dominant position: {Standard Oil made Rockefeller America's most notorious monopolist}. In economics, monopolist behavior describes pricing and output decisions made without competitive pressure.

Monopolization is the act or process of gaining exclusive control over something. In business, it means dominating a market to eliminate competition: {The company's monopolization of the industry drew antitrust scrutiny}. More broadly, it describes taking over anything to the exclusion of others: {His monopolization of the conversation left no room for other voices}.

To monopolize is to dominate or control completely. A company monopolizes a market by eliminating competition. A person monopolizes a conversation by not letting others speak. The word implies taking more than one's fair share: {He monopolized her attention all evening}. {Tech giants have monopolized the advertising industry}.

Monopolized is the past tense of monopolize, meaning to gain exclusive control over something. A company that has monopolized a market has eliminated or absorbed its competitors. The word extends beyond commerce: someone who has monopolized a conversation has dominated it, leaving others little chance to speak. {She monopolized his attention all evening.}

Monopolizing is taking exclusive control of something, leaving none for others. A company monopolizing a market eliminates competition. A person monopolizing a conversation won't let anyone else speak. {Stop monopolizing the bathroom—other people need to get ready}. The word often carries a note of criticism, implying selfishness or excess.

Monopoly refers to exclusive control over something, especially a market or commodity: {The company had a monopoly on telephone service for decades}. A monopoly exists when one entity dominates to the exclusion of competitors. The term extends beyond economics to any situation of singular dominance: {She has a monopoly on his attention}. (Capitalized Monopoly is the board game.)

A monorail is a railway system in which trains run on a single rail, typically elevated above street level. Monorails appear most often at airports, theme parks, and as urban transit in a few cities. The word also refers to the train itself: {We took the monorail from the parking lot to the terminal}.

Monorails are rail systems where vehicles run on or hang from a single track, typically elevated. The streamlined design makes monorails popular at airports, theme parks, and urban transit systems, where they suggest sleek modernity: {The monorail glided silently above the crowded streets}. Despite decades of futuristic promise, monorails remain novelties rather than mainstream transit.

Monotheism is the belief in a single god, as opposed to polytheism (belief in many gods) or atheism (belief in none). Judaism, Christianity, and Islam are the major monotheistic religions. The term also applies to philosophical positions holding that only one deity exists: {Monotheism emerged gradually in ancient Israel}.

Monotone describes sound that stays on a single pitch without variation: {He read the poem in a monotone}. The word applies to speech, singing, or any sound lacking inflection. Extended uses describe anything tediously uniform or unvarying: {a monotone landscape of gray buildings}. As a noun, a monotone is such a sound or voice: {She spoke in a flat monotone}.

Monotonous describes something tediously uniform, lacking variety or change. A monotonous voice stays at one pitch. A monotonous job repeats the same tasks endlessly. The word carries a negative connotation—sameness that breeds boredom: {The monotonous hum of the engine put me to sleep}. {Days blurred together in monotonous routine}.

Monotony is tedious sameness or lack of variety. The word suggests weariness from repetition: {the monotony of factory work}, {the monotony of suburban life}. A monotonous voice drones on without variation in pitch or tone. Monotony implies not just uniformity but the boredom it produces—the feeling that nothing changes and nothing will.

Monsieur is a French title of respect for a man, equivalent to "mister" or "sir" in English. It appears in English texts when referring to French men or in French-flavored contexts: {Monsieur Dupont will see you now}. The plural is messieurs. In casual English speech, it sometimes carries an air of mock formality or continental flair.

A monsoon is a seasonal wind pattern that brings heavy rainfall, especially in South Asia. The word commonly refers to the rainy season itself or the dramatic downpours that accompany it: {The monsoon flooded the streets within minutes}. Informally, any torrential rain might be called a monsoon: {We got caught in a monsoon on the way home}.

Monsoons are seasonal wind patterns that bring heavy rainfall to tropical regions, especially South and Southeast Asia. The word often refers to the rainy season itself or the torrential rains it produces: {The monsoons arrived early this year}, {We got caught in the monsoon}. Monsoon rains are essential for agriculture but can cause devastating floods.

A monster is a terrifying and threatening creature, often legendary or imaginary. Other meanings that arise from this are someone badly behaved (their children are monsters), something extremely large (monster truck), and a whimsical cartoon or comic character (Cookie Monster). Someone who is a monster in a particular field is very prominent or dominates it: The master chef was a monster in the kitchen. If you create a monster, you inadvertently bring about a situation that is difficult or unmanageable.

Monsters are creatures that frighten—whether from mythology, fiction, or nightmare. Dragons, vampires, and werewolves are monsters. The word extends to anything unnaturally large or threatening: {a monster truck}, {a monster wave}. A person who commits atrocities is called a monster: {The dictator was a monster}. Informally, monster means impressively large: {a monster hit}, {a monster deal}. Children feared for imaginary {monsters under the bed} grow up to use the word casually for formidable challenges or achievements.

Monstrosities are things that are shockingly ugly, deformed, or wrong—violations of natural or aesthetic order. The word often describes architectural eyesores or bureaucratic absurdities: {Those concrete monstrosities ruined the skyline}. It can also refer to acts of cruelty or injustice so extreme they seem inhuman: {the monstrosities committed during the war}.

A monstrosity is something shockingly ugly, malformed, or offensive to the senses. The word often describes buildings or other large creations that violate aesthetic norms: {That new shopping center is an absolute monstrosity}. It can also refer to something outrageously wrong or unjust: {The verdict was a monstrosity of the legal system}. Less commonly, monstrosity describes a deformed creature or birth defect, though this usage now sounds dated and callous.
clues: A creature too horrible to behold

definition: Monstrous describes something unnaturally large, ugly, or horrifying—like a monster. A monstrous {creature} inspires fear; a monstrous {crime} shocks the conscience. The word often emphasizes shocking scale or moral outrage: {a monstrous lie}, {monstrous cruelty}. Informally, monstrous can simply mean enormous: {a monstrous wave}, {monstrous portions}.

A montage is a composite image or sequence made by combining separate elements. In film, a montage compresses time or conveys ideas through rapid succession of shots: {The training montage showed her transformation from novice to champion}. In visual art, montage assembles photographs or other images into a single composition. The technique emphasizes juxtaposition—meaning emerges from how pieces relate to each other.

Montages are composite images or sequences made by combining separate elements. In film, a montage assembles shots to compress time or convey ideas through juxtaposition: {The training montage showed months of preparation in two minutes}. In visual art, a montage combines photographs or other images into a single composition. The technique emphasizes arrangement and contrast over seamless blending.

A month is one of the twelve divisions of the calendar year: January, February, and so on. The word derives from moon—months originally tracked lunar cycles, roughly 29 days each. Modern calendar months range from 28 to 31 days. {I'll be gone for a month}. {She's six months pregnant}. A {month of Sundays} is a very long time.

Monthly describes something that happens once a month or covers the span of a month: a monthly {meeting}, a monthly {subscription}, a monthly {report}. As a noun, a monthly is a magazine published every month. The adverb means every month: {The newsletter comes out monthly}.

Months is the plural of month, a unit of time roughly corresponding to one cycle of the moon—about thirty days. The calendar year divides into twelve months of varying lengths. {It took months to finish the project.} In the plural, months often emphasizes duration: {I haven't seen her in months.}

A monument is a structure built to commemorate a person, event, or achievement—statues, obelisks, arches, and memorial buildings. The term extends to anything that stands as lasting evidence of something significant: {His symphonies are monuments to human creativity}. To make a monument of something is to preserve or honor it. A monument can also be a boundary marker or surveying reference point.

Monumental describes something massive in scale or significance. A monumental {achievement} or monumental {effort} is extraordinarily impressive. Monumental {architecture} is built to impress—think pyramids, cathedrals, war memorials. The word can also mean serving as a monument: {a monumental inscription}. Informally, monumental intensifies negatives: {a monumental failure}, {a monumental waste of time}.

Monuments are structures built to commemorate a person, event, or achievement—statues, obelisks, arches, or buildings designed to preserve memory: {The Lincoln Monument draws millions of visitors each year}. By extension, anything that serves as a lasting tribute or evidence can be a monument: {Her body of work stands as a monument to her genius}. Natural landmarks may also be designated monuments for protection: {a national monument}.
Moo is the characteristic low, prolonged sound made by cattle. As a verb, to moo is to make this sound: {The cows mooed at feeding time}. The word is onomatopoeic—it sounds like what it describes.

Mooch means to get something without paying or working for it, usually by exploiting others' generosity: {He's always mooching cigarettes off coworkers}. A mooch is someone who habitually does this—the friend who never reaches for the check, the roommate who empties your fridge. The word carries judgment: mooching implies taking advantage rather than genuine need. To mooch around (British) is to wander aimlessly or loiter.

Mooched is the past tense of mooch, meaning to get something by asking for it rather than paying or working for it: {He mooched a cigarette off me}. The word implies habitual freeloading or aimless wandering: {She mooched around the house all day}. A mooch is someone who regularly cadges things from others.

A moocher is someone who habitually gets things from others without paying or reciprocating—food, money, rides, lodging. The word carries mild contempt: moochers impose on others' generosity rather than providing for themselves. {He's such a moocher—always bumming cigarettes but never buying his own.} The verb is mooch.

Moochers are people who habitually obtain things from others without paying or reciprocating. The term carries strong disapproval, suggesting someone who exploits the generosity of friends, family, or institutions rather than providing for themselves. {The moochers showed up right at dinnertime, as usual.} While mooch can sometimes be playful between close friends, moochers as a label implies a pattern of freeloading that tests patience.

Mooches is the third-person singular of mooch, meaning to get something by begging or taking advantage of others' generosity: {He mooches cigarettes off coworkers}. A mooch is someone who habitually does this. To mooch around is to wander aimlessly or loiter: {She mooched around the house all afternoon}.

Mooching is getting things from others without paying or reciprocating—bumming cigarettes, crashing on couches, eating someone else's food. The word carries mild disapproval: {He's always mooching off his parents}. To mooch is to obtain things this way, and a mooch is a person who does it habitually.

Mood is a temporary state of mind or feeling—cheerful, melancholy, irritable. Someone {in a mood} is usually in a bad one. If you're {in the mood} for something, you feel like doing it. The mood of a place or work of art is its atmosphere or emotional tone: {The lighting set a romantic mood}. In grammar, mood indicates whether a verb expresses fact (indicative), command (imperative), or possibility (subjunctive).

A moodboard is a collage of images, colors, textures, and sometimes text assembled to establish the visual direction of a creative project. Designers, photographers, and filmmakers use moodboards to communicate aesthetic intentions before production begins: {She put together a moodboard for the album cover}. Also spelled as two words.

Moodboards are visual collages assembling images, colors, textures, and sometimes text to capture a particular aesthetic or feeling. Designers, photographers, and creative professionals use them to establish visual direction before beginning a project: {She created a moodboard for the wedding using Pinterest}. The concept has spread beyond professional design into personal style curation and social media aesthetics.

Moodiness is the tendency to shift between emotional states, especially toward irritability or sullenness. A moody person's temperament is unpredictable—cheerful one moment, withdrawn the next. {His moodiness made him difficult to work with.} The word usually carries negative connotations, suggesting someone hard to please or be around.

Moods is the plural of mood—emotional states or prevailing feelings. A person experiences different moods throughout the day; a room has moods depending on lighting and atmosphere. In grammar, moods are verb forms indicating whether a statement is factual, conditional, or commanding: indicative, subjunctive, imperative. {Her moods shifted unpredictably.} {The painting captures the moods of the sea.}

Moody describes someone whose emotional state shifts unpredictably, often toward gloom or irritability. A moody teenager might be cheerful one moment and sullen the next. The word suggests emotional volatility rather than a single mood: {He's been moody all week}. Moody weather or moody lighting creates an atmospheric, somber effect. (Capitalized Moody is a surname.)

Mooing is the sound a cow makes—a long, low vocalization. The word appears as both noun and verb: {The mooing of cattle carried across the field}, {The cows were mooing at feeding time}. Figuratively, it can describe people making similar sounds or behaving in a herd-like manner.

A mook is a stupid, insignificant, or contemptible person—someone dismissed as a fool or a nobody. The term carries a working-class urban flavor, associated especially with New York Italian-American speech: {Some mook cut me off in traffic}. In action movies and video games, mooks are the disposable henchmen who exist to be defeated by the hero.

Mooks are thugs, henchmen, or low-level criminals—the disposable muscle in crime stories who exist mainly to be defeated by the hero. The word suggests incompetence and interchangeability: {The villain sent his mooks after us, but they were useless}. More broadly, mook can mean any stupid or contemptible person, roughly synonymous with jerk or idiot.

Moolah is slang for money: {I need to save up some moolah before I can afford that trip}. The word is casual and slightly playful, often appearing when someone wants to avoid the plainness of "money" or "cash." Also spelled moola.

The moon is Earth's natural satellite, the luminous object that waxes and wanes through its monthly cycle. By extension, any natural satellite of a planet: {Jupiter has dozens of moons}. To moon is to gaze dreamily or listlessly, as if staring at the moon: {He mooned about the house for days}. In slang, to moon someone is to bare your buttocks at them. A moon is also a month, from the lunar cycle: {many moons ago}. (Capitalized Moon refers specifically to Earth's satellite as a proper noun.)

A moonbase is a permanent or semi-permanent human installation on the Moon's surface. The term appears mostly in science fiction and speculative discussions of space exploration: {The astronauts established a moonbase on the lunar south pole}. Also written as two words: moon base.

A moonbeam is a ray of light from the moon: {Moonbeams filtered through the curtains}. The word carries a soft, romantic, or whimsical quality—more likely to appear in poetry or fairy tales than scientific contexts. Someone called a moonbeam is dreamy or ethereal, perhaps not quite grounded in reality.

Moonbeams are rays of light from the moon, though the word carries a dreamy, fanciful quality that *moonlight* lacks. The singular appears in poetic or whimsical contexts: {a moonbeam fell across her face}. To call something moonbeams is to dismiss it as insubstantial fantasy: {His business plan was all moonbeams and wishful thinking}.

Moonboots are bulky, padded winter boots with thick insulated linings and chunky soles, designed for warmth in snow and cold weather. The name comes from their resemblance to the boots worn by Apollo astronauts—puffy, oversized, and vaguely futuristic. They became a fashion item in the 1970s and have cycled in and out of style since: {She clomped through the snow in her moonboots}.

A moonbounce is an inflatable structure, usually a large enclosed platform, that children jump on at fairs, parties, and playgrounds: {The kids spent hours in the moonbounce}. Also called a bounce house or bouncy castle. Separately, moonbounce refers to a radio communication technique that reflects signals off the moon's surface back to Earth.

Moonbounces are inflatable structures, typically castles or enclosed play areas, that children jump on at parties and carnivals. The bouncy surface comes from air pressure maintained by a constant-running blower. Also called bounce houses, bouncy castles, or jumpy houses. {The kids spent hours in the moonbounce.}

Mooncake is a Chinese pastry traditionally eaten during the Mid-Autumn Festival. Round and dense, mooncakes typically contain sweet fillings like lotus seed paste or red bean, often with a salted egg yolk at the center representing the moon. They're exchanged as gifts and shared among family: {We bought a box of mooncakes for the holiday}.

Mooncakes are dense Chinese pastries traditionally eaten during the Mid-Autumn Festival. They're typically round with ornate designs stamped into the top, filled with sweet lotus seed paste or red bean paste, often containing a salted egg yolk representing the full moon. The pastries are given as gifts and shared among family: {We exchanged boxes of mooncakes with the neighbors}.

A moonchild is someone born under the astrological sign of Cancer, which the moon rules. The term carries dreamy, mystical connotations—suggesting someone sensitive, intuitive, or emotionally attuned. In broader use, moonchild describes anyone with a whimsical or otherworldly quality: {She's always been a moonchild, happiest under the night sky}.

Moondust is the fine, powdery soil covering the lunar surface, composed of tiny rock fragments, mineral grains, and glass particles created by billions of years of meteorite impacts. It clings to everything and posed unexpected challenges during the Apollo missions: {The moondust got into everything}. Figuratively, moondust suggests something ethereal or magical: {Her voice had moondust in it}.

Mooned is the past tense of moon. To moon someone is to expose your bare buttocks as a prank or insult: {He mooned the passing car}. Separately, to moon over someone is to gaze at them dreamily or pine for them: {She mooned over her crush all semester}. The connection is the moon's pale roundness and its association with romantic longing.

Moonflower is a tropical vine with large, fragrant white flowers that bloom at night and close by morning. The name captures both the nocturnal habit and the pale, luminous petals: {The moonflowers opened as the sun set}. Related to morning glories, moonflowers attract night-pollinating moths. The term sometimes applies loosely to other night-blooming plants.

Moonflowers are night-blooming plants, especially varieties of morning glory with large white fragrant flowers that open in the evening and close by morning. The name reflects their nocturnal habit—they bloom under moonlight rather than sun: {The moonflowers opened as dusk fell}. The term sometimes applies to other night-blooming species like datura.

Moonglow is the soft, diffuse light cast by the moon, especially when full. The word evokes romance and quiet nighttime beauty: {We walked along the beach in the moonglow}. It appears in song titles and poetry more often than everyday speech, carrying a dreamy, nostalgic quality.

Mooning is the act of baring one's buttocks at someone, typically as a prank or crude gesture of disrespect: {Some kid mooned us from the back of the school bus}. The term derives from moon as slang for buttocks. Separately, mooning can mean gazing dreamily or pining romantically: {She spent the afternoon mooning over old photographs}.

Moonlight is the light of the moon—actually reflected sunlight, but perceived as its own silvery illumination. The word evokes nighttime romance and mystery: {a walk in the moonlight}, {moonlit gardens}. To moonlight is to work a second job, typically at night: {She moonlights as a bartender}. A {moonlight flit} is a hasty departure to avoid paying rent.

Moonlighted is the past tense of moonlight, meaning to work a second job in addition to one's regular employment. The term originally implied working at night, but now covers any supplementary work regardless of hours: {She moonlighted as a bartender to pay off her student loans}. {He moonlighted for a competitor and got fired when his boss found out}.

A moonlighter is someone who works a second job in addition to their regular employment, typically at night or during off-hours. The term comes from the image of working by moonlight after the day job ends. {She's a moonlighter—teaches during the day and tends bar on weekends.} The practice itself is called moonlighting.

Moonlighting is working a second job, typically in addition to regular full-time employment. The term evokes work done after dark, outside normal hours: {She's been moonlighting as a bartender to pay off her student loans}. The practice may be hidden from the primary employer, though the word doesn't require secrecy.

Moonlights means works a second job, typically at night or in addition to regular daytime employment. Someone who moonlights keeps their primary job while earning extra income elsewhere: {She moonlights as a bartender on weekends}. The term suggests work done quietly or unofficially, sometimes without an employer's knowledge.

Moonlit describes something illuminated by the light of the moon. It functions as an adjective to set a scene with soft, silvery natural light, often evoking romance, mystery, or tranquility: {a moonlit walk on the beach}, {the moonlit garden}. The word appears frequently in poetry and literary description, where nighttime settings benefit from this evocative, atmospheric quality.

A moonquake is seismic activity on the Moon—the lunar equivalent of an earthquake. Moonquakes are generally weaker than earthquakes but can last much longer due to the Moon's dry, rigid structure. They were first detected by seismometers placed during the Apollo missions: {The instruments recorded thousands of moonquakes over several years}.

Moonrise is the moment when the moon appears above the horizon, or the time at which this occurs: {We watched the moonrise from the beach}. Like sunrise and sunset, it names both the event and the hour. A moonrise can be spectacular when the moon appears unusually large near the horizon.

A moonroof is a glass panel in a car's roof that lets in light and can typically slide open for ventilation. The term emerged to distinguish transparent panels from traditional metal sunroofs, though the two words are now often used interchangeably: {I love having a moonroof—it makes the car feel so open}.

Moons is the plural of moon—Earth's natural satellite, or any celestial body orbiting a planet: {Jupiter has dozens of moons}. To moon is to expose one's bare buttocks as a prank or insult: {Someone mooned the camera}. To moon over someone is to gaze or pine dreamily: {He spent the summer mooning over her}.

A moonscape is a barren, desolate landscape resembling the surface of the moon—rocky, cratered, and devoid of vegetation. The word describes actual lunar terrain but more often applies to earthly places with similar stark emptiness: {The volcanic region was a moonscape of black rock and ash}. Bombed cities and strip-mined land become moonscapes.

Moonshine is illegally distilled liquor, especially whiskey made in homemade stills to avoid taxation. The term evokes Appalachian tradition and Prohibition-era bootlegging: {His grandfather used to run moonshine through the mountains}. Moonshine also means foolish talk or nonsense: {That's pure moonshine}. The literal sense—light from the moon—is the oldest but least common today.

A moonshiner is someone who illegally distills liquor, especially in rural areas. The term comes from the practice of working at night to avoid detection: {His grandfather was a moonshiner in the hills of Kentucky}. Moonshine itself is the illicitly produced whiskey, typically unaged and high-proof. The word carries romantic associations with Appalachian independence and defiance of federal authority.

Moonshiners are people who make moonshine—illegally distilled liquor, typically whiskey. The term evokes Appalachian tradition, where homemade spirits were produced in secret stills, often at night to avoid detection: {Revenue agents raided the moonshiners' operation in the hills}. The word can also describe anyone producing alcohol outside legal channels.

Moonshining is the illicit distillation of liquor, especially whiskey, typically done at night to avoid detection—hence the moon. The term evokes rural Appalachian tradition, where homemade corn whiskey was produced to evade taxes or prohibition laws. By extension, moonshining can describe any covert, under-the-table operation: {He's been moonshining auto parts out of his garage}.

A moonshot is an ambitious, groundbreaking project that pushes the boundaries of what seems achievable—originally the Apollo program's mission to land humans on the moon. The term now describes any bold venture with uncertain odds but transformative potential: {The startup's moonshot is to cure Alzheimer's within a decade}. Moonshots accept high risk of failure in pursuit of extraordinary reward.

Moonshots are ambitious, groundbreaking projects that aim for transformative breakthroughs rather than incremental progress. The term derives from the 1960s Apollo missions to land humans on the moon—endeavors that seemed nearly impossible but succeeded through massive investment and coordinated effort. In business and technology, a moonshot is a long-shot venture with potential for enormous impact: {Google's moonshots include self-driving cars and extending human lifespan}. The word implies willingness to risk failure in pursuit of revolutionary change.

Moonstone is a gemstone prized for its adularescence—a soft, glowing light that appears to move across the surface, resembling moonlight. The stone is typically milky white or pale blue and has been used in jewelry for centuries. {She wore a moonstone ring that seemed to glow from within.} In folklore, moonstone is associated with lunar cycles and feminine energy.

Moonstones are gemstones prized for their adularescence—a milky, bluish glow that seems to move across the surface like moonlight on water. They belong to the feldspar mineral group and have been used in jewelry for centuries. The name comes from this lunar shimmer: {Her ring featured a cabochon moonstone set in silver}. In folklore, moonstones were believed to bring good fortune and enhance intuition.

Moonstruck means dazed, dreamy, or slightly crazed—traditionally attributed to the influence of the moon. The word most often describes someone romantically besotted: {She was moonstruck from the moment they met}. The older sense of lunar-induced madness survives in literary contexts but has largely given way to the softer romantic meaning.
clues: Lovesick to the point of madness

definition: Moonwalk names two iconic but unrelated movements. The first is walking on the moon's surface, as astronauts did during the Apollo missions: {We watched the moonwalk on a grainy television}. The second is a dance move popularized by Michael Jackson, where the dancer appears to glide backward while mimicking forward steps. Both noun and verb: {He moonwalked across the stage}.
clues: Dance that looks like floating backward

definition: A moonwalker is someone who has walked on the moon—one of the twelve Apollo astronauts who did so between 1969 and 1972. The term also describes someone performing the moonwalk, the backward-sliding dance move popularized by Michael Jackson: {The kid's a natural moonwalker}.

Moonwalkers are people who have walked on the moon—specifically, the twelve American astronauts who did so during the Apollo missions between 1969 and 1972: {Only moonwalkers truly know what lunar gravity feels like}. The term can also refer to shoes or devices designed to assist walking, or to performers of the moonwalk dance move popularized by Michael Jackson.
clues: People who stepped on lunar surface

definition: Moonwalking is a dance move where the performer appears to glide backward while their legs mime walking forward. Popularized by Michael Jackson in 1983, it creates an illusion of frictionless sliding: {He moonwalked across the stage}. The term also describes the bouncing gait astronauts use in lunar gravity.

Moonwalks names two famous feats of human locomotion. The first is walking on the moon's surface, as astronauts did during the Apollo missions. The second is the dance move popularized by Michael Jackson—a gliding step that creates the illusion of walking forward while sliding backward. Both capture a sense of defying normal physics. As a verb: {He moonwalks across the stage}.

Moony describes someone dreamy, listless, or lost in thought—often with connotations of being lovesick or absent-minded: {She's been moony ever since she met him}. The word suggests a vague, unfocused quality, as if someone is gazing at the moon rather than attending to practical matters. It can also mean resembling the moon in shape or appearance, though this sense is rare.

To moor a boat is to secure it in place, typically by rope or anchor: {We moored at the dock overnight}. A moor is also a tract of open, uncultivated upland, often covered with heather and peat—characteristic of the British Isles: {the Yorkshire moors}, {Wuthering Heights is set on the windswept moors}. (Capitalized Moor is a historical term for North African Muslims.)

Moored means secured in place, typically of a boat fastened to a dock, buoy, or anchor: {The sailboat was moored at the marina}. The figurative sense suggests being anchored or fixed: {She felt moored to her hometown by family obligations}. Something unmoored has come loose or lost its grounding.

A mooring is a place where a boat or ship is secured, or the equipment used to secure it—ropes, chains, anchors, or fixed posts. The plural moorings often refers to the entire arrangement: {The storm tore the yacht from its moorings}. Figuratively, moorings are sources of stability or connection: {She felt cut loose from her moorings after the divorce}.

Moorings are the ropes, chains, anchors, or other equipment used to secure a boat or ship in place: {The storm tore the yacht from its moorings}. By extension, moorings are anything that provides stability or keeps something fixed: {She felt cut loose from her moorings after leaving home}. The figurative sense suggests psychological or emotional anchoring—losing one's moorings means becoming unmoored from familiar certainties.

Moorland is open, uncultivated upland terrain, typically covered with heather, coarse grasses, and low shrubs. The landscape is often boggy, windswept, and treeless—characteristic of parts of Britain, especially Yorkshire and Scotland. {We hiked across the moorland in driving rain.} The word is essentially synonymous with moor but emphasizes the terrain as a type of land rather than a specific place.

Moors are broad stretches of open, uncultivated upland, typically covered with heather, coarse grasses, and boggy ground. The term is especially associated with the British Isles: {the Yorkshire moors}, {Wuthering Heights is set on the moors}. Moorland tends to be windswept, treeless, and somewhat desolate—atmospheric territory for Gothic novels and long walks. To moor a boat is a different word, meaning to secure it in place. (Capitalized Moors refers to the Muslim peoples of North Africa.)

A moose is a large deer native to northern forests of North America, Europe, and Asia—the largest living member of the deer family. Males grow massive palmate antlers shed annually. The plural is also moose: {We saw three moose crossing the road}. In British English, the same animal is called an elk.

As an adjective, moot has contrasting meanings in British and American English. In British English, moot means subject to debate, doubt, or uncertainty, so a moot question is with more than one answer, and about which there is little agreement. In American English, moot means of little or no practical value or importance,
so a moot question is a trivial or irrelevant question. If you moot a subject, you raise it for discussion (British English) or you reduce or remove its significance (American English).

A mop is a cleaning tool with absorbent material at the end of a handle, used wet for washing floors. To mop is to clean with one, or to wipe as if with one: {She mopped her brow with a handkerchief}. A mop can also be a thick mass of untidy hair: {a mop of curls}. To {mop up} is to finish off remaining resistance or clean up the last of something: {mopping up enemy stragglers}.

To mope is to be listless and dejected, often with an element of sulking or self-pity: {He moped around the house for days after the breakup}. A mope is someone who habitually mopes, or an instance of moping: {Don't be such a mope}. The mopes is a state of low spirits: {She's got the mopes}.

A moped is a low-powered motorized bicycle, typically with pedals and a small engine under 50cc. The word blends "motor" and "pedal." Mopeds occupy a middle ground between bicycles and motorcycles, often requiring less licensing than full motorcycles: {She commutes on a moped to save on gas}. Separately, moped is the past tense of mope.

Mopeds are lightweight motorized two-wheelers with small engines and often pedals, designed for low-speed urban travel. The name blends "motor" and "pedal."
