They typically require less licensing than motorcycles and are restricted to lower speeds: {She commutes on a moped to avoid parking hassles}. In casual use, moped sometimes loosely includes any small scooter.

Mopes is a low mood or sulky state, used with "the": {He's got the mopes today}. The word comes from the verb mope, meaning to brood or sulk listlessly: {She moped around the house all weekend}. Someone who mopes is a mope—though this noun more often appears in the plural: {a bunch of sad mopes at the bar}.

Mopey describes someone who is glum, listless, and feeling sorry for themselves. A mopey person sits around looking dejected rather than doing anything about their situation: {He's been mopey ever since she left}. The word carries a hint of impatience with the behavior—moping is passive and unproductive. Also spelled mopy.

Moping is brooding in low spirits, usually with an element of self-pity or sulking. Someone moping wanders aimlessly or sits idle, dwelling on disappointment or sadness: {He spent the weekend moping around the house after the breakup}. The word suggests passivity—not active grieving but listless dejection, often noticed by others who find it tiresome.

Mopping is cleaning a floor with a mop—a long-handled tool with absorbent material at the end, pushed across wet surfaces. The word extends to any wiping or soaking motion: {He was mopping his brow with a handkerchief}. To be {mopping up} is to finish remaining tasks or deal with stragglers after a main effort: {The army spent weeks mopping up resistance}.

A moptop is a hairstyle with thick, shaggy hair that falls over the forehead and ears, resembling a mop. The term became famous with the Beatles in the 1960s, whose bowl-like cuts defined the look: {He showed up with a moptop like he'd stepped out of 1964}. By extension, moptop can describe someone sporting the style.

Moral is used to talk about subjects, behavior, values, or responsibilities that are rooted in a system of right and wrong. A moral person adheres to principles and behaves in ways judged to be good. Morals, as a plural noun, denotes a set of principles that constitute someone’s ethical principles.

Morale is the spirit, confidence, or enthusiasm of a person or group, especially regarding challenges ahead. Military commanders worry about troop morale. Workplace morale affects productivity. {The team's morale was low after three straight losses.} High morale suggests optimism and willingness to persevere; low morale suggests discouragement or defeat.

Moralising is the British spelling of moralizing—lecturing others on right and wrong, often in a way that feels preachy or self-righteous. Someone who moralises draws moral lessons from situations, usually without being asked: {I could do without all the moralising about my lifestyle choices}. The word typically carries a negative connotation, suggesting the speaker is sanctimonious rather than genuinely helpful.

Moralism is the practice of making moral judgments about others' behavior, often in a way that seems excessive, rigid, or self-righteous. Someone given to moralism tends to view situations through a lens of right and wrong rather than with nuance or empathy. The term usually carries negative connotations, suggesting that the moral stance is more about asserting superiority than genuine ethical concern. {His constant moralism about other people's lifestyle choices made him tedious company.}

A moralist is someone who teaches or promotes moral principles, or who comments on questions of right and wrong. The term often carries a critical edge, suggesting someone who moralizes—who lectures others about proper behavior with an air of superiority: {He's such a moralist about other people's drinking habits}. A moralist may also be a philosopher or writer who examines ethical questions: {the French moralists of the seventeenth century}.

Moralists are people who express or promote strong views about right and wrong conduct. The term can be neutral, describing those who study or write about ethics: {the great moralists of the Enlightenment}. But it often carries a negative edge, suggesting someone who judges others harshly or lectures on proper behavior: {The moralists were quick to condemn her choices}.

Morality is the system of principles governing right and wrong conduct. It can refer to a society's shared standards {Victorian morality}, an individual's ethical code {personal morality}, or the quality of being virtuous {a person of questionable morality}. The morality of an action is whether it's right or wrong: {They debated the morality of capital punishment}. Morality often implies standards beyond mere legality—something can be legal but immoral, or illegal but morally justified.

A moralizer is someone who lectures others about right and wrong, typically in a self-righteous or unwelcome way. The term carries a negative connotation—moralizers are seen as preachy and judgmental rather than genuinely ethical: {Nobody likes a moralizer}. The verb moralize and noun moralizing share this disapproving tone.

Moralizers are people who lecture others about right and wrong, typically in a self-righteous or unwelcome manner. The term carries a negative connotation—moralizers presume to know better and impose their judgments rather than offer genuine moral guidance: {The moralizers on social media were quick to condemn her choices}. See also moralize.

Moralizing is lecturing others about right and wrong, especially in a self-righteous or tedious way. The term is almost always pejorative—it suggests the speaker is more interested in displaying virtue than genuinely helping: {I don't need your moralizing; I know what I did was wrong}. To moralize is to draw moral lessons from something, often uninvited.

Morals are principles of right and wrong that guide behavior. They overlap with ethics but tend to be more personal and intuitive—your morals are what you feel is right, while ethics may be codified rules. Someone's morals might forbid lying even when ethics permit it. {She questioned his morals after the affair}. A story's moral is its lesson: {The moral of the fable is that slow and steady wins the race}.

A morass is a stretch of swampy, boggy ground—wet land that's difficult or dangerous to cross. The figurative sense dominates modern usage: a morass is any situation that traps you, slows progress, or proves difficult to escape. {The project became a morass of bureaucratic delays.} {We got lost in a morass of conflicting regulations.}

A moratorium is a temporary suspension of an activity or obligation. Governments declare moratoriums on executions, debt payments, or new construction. The word implies a pause rather than a permanent end: {The city imposed a moratorium on building permits until the infrastructure study was complete}. Plural: moratoriums or moratoria.

A moray is a large eel found in warm seas, typically lurking in crevices and reef holes with its mouth agape to reveal sharp teeth. Morays are generally not aggressive but can deliver serious bites when provoked. The name applies to any of about 200 species in the family Muraenidae: {We spotted a green moray while diving the reef}. (Capitalized Moray is a region in Scotland.)

Morays are eels of the family Muraenidae, found in warm seas worldwide. They have long, scaleless bodies, sharp teeth, and typically live in rocky crevices and coral reefs. Unlike most fish, morays lack pectoral fins and breathe by constantly opening and closing their mouths—a habit that makes them look more threatening than they usually are.

Morbid describes an unhealthy preoccupation with death, disease, or the unpleasant: {a morbid fascination with serial killers}, {morbid curiosity about the accident scene}. The word suggests dwelling on what most people avoid thinking about. In medical contexts, morbid relates to disease or its symptoms: {morbid anatomy} studies diseased tissue. {Morbid obesity} is severe enough to cause health problems.

More is an adjective and adverb used to form comparatives for words that can’t accomplish this with the ending -er; for example, more intelligent. When used alone or followed by a noun, more usually conveys extra, additional, or to a great degree, and is roughly the opposite of less (give me some more, we need more information). The noun mores, meaning moral customs, is construed as plural and does not have a singular form.

Moreish describes food or drink so pleasant that you want more of it: {These cookies are dangerously moreish}. The word is primarily British, capturing that quality of snacks or treats that makes you reach for another before you've finished the first. Something moreish isn't necessarily the finest food—often it's the salty, sweet, or savory things that trigger compulsive nibbling.

A morel is a highly prized edible mushroom with a distinctive honeycomb-patterned cap. Morels appear in spring and are foraged rather than cultivated, making them expensive and sought after: {We found a patch of morels near the old apple orchard}. They have an earthy, nutty flavor and must be cooked before eating.

Morels are prized edible mushrooms with distinctive honeycomb-textured caps, hollow inside and ranging from tan to dark brown. They grow wild in spring, often near dead or dying trees, and are difficult to cultivate commercially—making them expensive. Foragers hunt them eagerly: {We found a patch of morels near the old apple orchard}. The flavor is earthy and nutty, intensifying when dried.

A morgue is a place where dead bodies are kept, typically for identification or before autopsy, burial, or cremation. Hospitals, police departments, and medical examiners maintain morgues. The term extends to newspaper archives of clippings and reference materials—a "morgue" of old stories. {The body was taken to the county morgue}.

A morgue is a facility where dead bodies are kept, typically for identification, autopsy, or awaiting burial or cremation. Hospitals and medical examiners maintain morgues for handling the deceased. The word extends to newspaper and media offices to describe a reference archive of old clippings, photographs, and files—a repository of "dead" stories that might be resurrected for background research. {The detective met the family at the morgue to identify the victim.}

Morning is the early part of the day, from dawn until noon. It begins when night ends and darkness gives way to light. {Good morning} is a standard greeting. {Morning person} describes someone who functions well early. {The morning after} often refers to consequences following a night of excess—hangovers, regrets, or the realization of what happened.

Mornings is the plural of morning, the early part of the day between dawn and noon. As an adverb, mornings means during the morning hours, habitually or repeatedly: {She works mornings at the clinic}. This adverbial use parallels similar time words: {I sleep late Saturdays}, {He jogs evenings}.

Morocco is a type of fine leather made from goatskin, tanned with sumac and typically dyed in rich colors. It has a distinctive pebbled grain and has been prized for centuries in bookbinding and luxury goods: {The first edition was bound in red morocco}. The leather takes its name from the country where it was originally produced. (Capitalized Morocco is the country.)

Moron is a harsh insult for someone perceived as stupid: {What kind of moron leaves their car unlocked in this neighborhood?} The word originated as a clinical term for mild intellectual disability but was abandoned by professionals decades ago. It survives purely as an insult, stronger than *idiot* but less vulgar than profanity-based alternatives.

Moronic means extremely stupid or foolish. The word derives from moron, once a clinical term for mild intellectual disability, now simply an insult for someone acting like an idiot. {That was a moronic thing to say.} {The plan was so moronic it almost worked.}

Morons is the plural of moron—a person of notably low intelligence or poor judgment. The word began as a clinical term for mild intellectual disability but shed that meaning entirely; it now functions as a general-purpose insult for anyone acting stupidly: {The morons in accounting lost the invoice again}. It carries less sting than idiot in most contexts.
clues: People who never quite get it

definition: Morose describes a gloomy, sullen disposition—someone withdrawn into their own dark mood. A morose person isn't just sad but uncommunicative and ill-tempered about it: {He sat morose in the corner, refusing to join the conversation}. The word suggests a brooding quality that pushes others away.

Morph means to transform gradually from one form into another. The word comes from computer graphics, where morphing smoothly blends one image into another: {The werewolf's face morphed into human features}. The term has spread to describe any gradual transformation: {The conversation morphed into an argument}. As a noun, a morph is a variant form, especially in biology where it describes different physical types within a species.

Morphed is the past tense of morph, meaning to transform smoothly from one form into another. The word comes from metamorphosis and gained currency through digital effects that seamlessly blend images: {The actor's face morphed into a wolf}. It now applies broadly to any gradual transformation: {The small startup morphed into a tech giant}.

Morphine is a powerful painkiller derived from opium, used medically for severe pain relief. It's the standard against which other opioids are measured. Morphine produces euphoria and drowsiness, making it highly addictive: {The doctor prescribed morphine after the surgery}. It remains essential in palliative care despite its potential for abuse.

Morphing is the smooth transformation of one image into another through computer animation, where features gradually shift and blend: {The software morphed his face into a wolf}. The term extends beyond digital effects to any gradual transformation: {The company kept morphing into something new}. From metamorphosis.

Morphs is the third-person singular present tense of the verb morph, meaning to change form gradually or seamlessly. The word gained currency with digital technology, where images or sounds could be made to transform smoothly into other images or sounds: {The software morphs one face into another}. Outside technical contexts, morph describes any gradual transformation: {The conversation morphed into an argument}. As a noun, morphs can be plural forms or variants of something, particularly in gaming or biology.

A morsel is a small piece of food, typically one bite's worth: {She savored every morsel of the chocolate cake}. By extension, morsel applies to any small amount or fragment: {a morsel of information}, {not a morsel of evidence}. The word often carries connotations of something choice or delectable.

Morsels are small pieces of food, typically bite-sized: {She fed the dog morsels from her plate}. The word suggests something choice or tasty rather than mere scraps. By extension, a morsel can be any small piece or amount: {a morsel of gossip}, {not a morsel of evidence}. The singular morsel appears in phrases like {a tasty morsel} or {not a morsel left}.

Mortadella is a large Italian cured sausage made from finely ground pork studded with cubes of fat, peppercorns, and sometimes pistachios. It originated in Bologna and is served thinly sliced as cold cuts or in sandwiches. American bologna is a simplified descendant: {The deli had imported mortadella, not just regular bologna}.

Mortal means subject to death—the defining condition of human existence, as opposed to gods or immortals: {We are all mortal}. As a noun, a mortal is a human being: {No mortal could survive that fall}. Mortal also intensifies: a mortal {enemy} threatens your very life, mortal {combat} ends in death, mortal {sin} kills the soul. {She lived in mortal fear of being discovered}.

Mortality is the condition of being subject to death—what separates humans from gods in classical thought. It also refers to death on a large scale: {infant mortality rates}, {mortality from heart disease}. A mortality is a death or the number of deaths: {The war caused massive mortalities}. To confront one's mortality is to reckon with the fact that you will die.

Mortals are human beings, especially as distinguished from gods, immortals, or supernatural entities: {The gods looked down upon the mortals below}. The term emphasizes human vulnerability and finite lifespan. In casual use, mortals can humorously contrast ordinary people with those who seem superior: {Unlike us mere mortals, she never seems to need sleep}.

Mortar has two unrelated meanings. One is a bowl in which substances are ground with a pestle—the mortar and pestle of pharmacies and kitchens. The other is a paste of cement, lime, and sand used to bind bricks or stones: {The mortar between the bricks was crumbling}. A mortar is also a short-barreled cannon that fires shells in high arcs, used for lobbing explosives over walls or into trenches.

A mortarboard is the flat, square-topped cap worn at academic ceremonies—graduations, commencements, and formal university occasions. The name comes from its resemblance to the board used by masons for holding mortar. Separately, a mortarboard is that mason's tool itself: a flat board with a handle underneath for carrying wet mortar.

Mortarboards are the flat-topped caps with tassels worn at graduation ceremonies, named for their resemblance to the board used by masons to hold mortar. The singular also refers to that mason's tool—a flat square board with a handle underneath for carrying wet mortar. {Graduates tossed their mortarboards into the air.}

Mortars are bowl-shaped vessels in which substances are ground or crushed with a pestle—the standard tool for pharmacists, chemists, and cooks preparing spices. The word extends to building materials: mortar is the paste of cement, sand, and water that binds bricks or stones. A mortar is also a short-barreled artillery piece that lobs shells in a high arc: {The position came under mortar fire}. To mortar is to fire such weapons or to apply binding paste between masonry units.

A mortgage is a loan used to buy property, with the property itself serving as collateral. If you fail to make payments, the lender can seize the property through foreclosure. The word also refers to the legal agreement securing such a loan. To mortgage property is to pledge it as security: {They mortgaged the house to pay for her treatment}. Figuratively, to mortgage something is to compromise its future: {mortgaging our children's future}.

Mortgages is the plural of mortgage—a loan secured by real property, typically used to purchase a home. The borrower repays the principal plus interest over years or decades; failure to pay allows the lender to seize the property through foreclosure. {They're comparing mortgages from different banks.} As a verb, mortgages means pledges property as security: {She mortgages her future to pay for the present.}

Mortgaging is pledging property as security for a loan. When you mortgage a house, you give the lender a claim on it until the debt is repaid. The figurative sense suggests trading away something valuable for short-term gain: {He's mortgaging his future by dropping out of school}. {They're mortgaging the children's inheritance to fund their lifestyle.}

A mortician prepares dead bodies for burial or cremation and manages funeral arrangements. The term is more common in American English than British, where undertaker or funeral director prevails. {The mortician applied makeup to give the deceased a peaceful appearance.}

Morticians are professionals who prepare dead bodies for burial or cremation and often manage funeral arrangements. The term is primarily American; undertaker and funeral director cover similar ground, though mortician specifically emphasizes the technical work of embalming and preparing corpses. {The mortician did an excellent job making her grandmother look peaceful.} The word derives from the Latin for death, connecting it to mortuary, mortality, and mortal.

Mortification is deep humiliation or shame—the feeling of wanting to disappear after an embarrassing moment: {Her mortification was complete when she realized she'd been talking to the wrong person for ten minutes}. In religious contexts, mortification means the deliberate suppression of bodily desires through fasting, self-denial, or physical discipline. In medicine, mortification is an old term for gangrene—the death of tissue.

Mortified describes intense embarrassment or shame—the feeling of wanting to disappear after a social blunder or humiliating moment: {I was mortified when I called my teacher "mom" in front of the whole class}. The word suggests embarrassment so acute it feels almost physical. The older sense of mortifying the flesh—subduing bodily desires through discipline—survives mainly in religious contexts.

To mortify is to cause deep embarrassment or shame: {I was mortified when I realized I'd been talking to the wrong person for ten minutes}. The word carries a sense of wounded dignity—stronger than mere embarrassment. In older religious usage, to mortify the flesh meant to subdue bodily desires through discipline or self-denial. Mortified flesh in medical contexts is dead or gangrenous tissue.

Mortifying describes something that causes intense embarrassment or humiliation—the kind that makes you want to disappear: {It was mortifying to realize I'd been talking to her with spinach in my teeth}. The word carries more weight than merely embarrassing; mortifying experiences feel like small deaths to one's dignity. The related verb mortify means to humiliate or, in older religious contexts, to subdue bodily desires through discipline.

A mortuary is a place where dead bodies are kept before burial or cremation—either a funeral home or a room within a hospital or similar institution. As an adjective, mortuary relates to death or burial: {mortuary rites}, {mortuary science}. The word is more clinical than funeral home, suggesting cold storage rather than viewing rooms.

A mosaic is a picture or pattern made by arranging small colored pieces of stone, glass, or tile into a surface. The technique dates to antiquity and remains common in decorative arts. By extension, mosaic describes anything composed of diverse elements: {a mosaic of cultures}, {a genetic mosaic}. In biology, a mosaic organism has cells of different genetic makeup. (Capitalized Mosaic relates to Moses.)

Mosaics are decorative artworks made by arranging small pieces of colored glass, stone, or tile into patterns or images. The technique dates to antiquity and appears in floors, walls, and ceilings of churches and public buildings. Figuratively, mosaic describes anything composed of diverse elements: {a mosaic of cultures}, {a mosaic of farmland seen from the air}.

A mosasaur was a large marine reptile that dominated the oceans during the late Cretaceous period, roughly 100 to 66 million years ago. These predators had elongated bodies, powerful tails, and paddle-like limbs adapted for swimming. They ranged from modest sizes to giants over 50 feet long. Mosasaurs went extinct alongside the dinosaurs.

Mosey means to walk in a leisurely, unhurried way, often with no particular destination in mind: {I think I'll mosey on down to the café}. The word has a distinctly casual, folksy tone—you don't mosey anywhere urgent. {We moseyed around the flea market for an hour}.

Moseyed is the past tense of mosey, meaning to walk or move in a leisurely, unhurried way: {He moseyed over to the bar}. The word suggests ambling without urgency, often with a relaxed or aimless quality. It's informal and distinctly American.

Moseying is walking in a leisurely, unhurried way, often without a fixed destination: {I spent the afternoon moseying around the flea market}. The word carries a casual, slightly old-fashioned charm, suggesting aimless wandering rather than purposeful movement. To mosey along or mosey on over implies taking one's time getting somewhere.

Mosh is to dance aggressively at rock or punk concerts, typically by shoving and slamming into other dancers in a crowd. The area where this happens is the mosh pit: {We spent the whole show in the mosh pit}. Moshing emerged from hardcore punk culture in the 1980s and remains common at metal and punk shows.

A mosher is someone who moshes—participates in the aggressive, pushing style of dancing at punk, metal, and hardcore concerts. The term can also refer more broadly to fans of heavy music and the subculture surrounding it, particularly in British usage: {The moshers hung out behind the science building at lunch}.

Moshers are people who mosh—engaging in the aggressive, physical dancing at rock and metal concerts where participants slam into each other in a crowd. The term can also refer broadly to fans of heavy metal or alternative rock music, identified by their style: band t-shirts, combat boots, long hair. {The moshers formed a pit near the stage.}

Moshing is a form of aggressive dancing at rock and punk concerts, where participants push, shove, and slam into each other in a crowd—typically in an area called a mosh pit near the stage. Despite its violent appearance, moshing follows unwritten rules: you pick people up when they fall. {The show got intense and we ended up moshing for the whole set.}

A moshpit is an area near the stage at a rock or punk concert where audience members engage in moshing—aggressive, often chaotic physical movement including pushing, shoving, and slamming into one another. The activity is consensual chaos: participants expect contact, and there's an unwritten code to help anyone who falls. {I lost my shoe in the moshpit.} Also spelled as two words: mosh pit.

Moshpits are areas at rock or punk concerts where audience members slam into each other, push, and thrash around in an aggressive but usually consensual form of dancing. The activity looks violent from outside, but participants typically help up anyone who falls. {I lost my glasses in the moshpit.} Also spelled as two words: mosh pits.

A mosque is a Muslim place of worship. The building typically features a prayer hall oriented toward Mecca, often with a minaret—a tower from which the call to prayer is announced. Muslims gather at mosques for daily prayers, Friday congregational worship, and religious education: {The new mosque serves the growing Muslim community}.

Mosques are buildings where Muslims gather for worship and prayer. The word comes from Arabic for "place of prostration," reflecting the physical posture of Islamic prayer. A mosque typically features a prayer hall oriented toward Mecca, often with a minaret—a tower from which the call to prayer is announced. {The mosque was filled for Friday prayers.}

A mosquito is a small flying insect, the female of which feeds on blood by piercing skin with a needle-like mouthpart. Mosquitoes are notorious for the itchy welts their bites leave and for transmitting diseases like malaria, dengue, and West Nile virus. The whining sound of a mosquito near your ear is universally dreaded: {I couldn't sleep with that mosquito buzzing around}.

Mosquitoes are small flying insects that feed on blood, leaving itchy bites. The females pierce skin with needle-like mouthparts to draw blood needed for egg production. Mosquitoes breed in standing water and transmit diseases including malaria, dengue, and Zika: {The mosquitoes were relentless at dusk}. They're drawn to body heat, carbon dioxide, and certain scents.

Mosquitos is a plural of mosquito, the small flying insect whose females bite and draw blood from humans and animals. The spelling with -os is less common than mosquitoes but equally correct. {The mosquitos were unbearable near the lake.}

Moss is any of numerous small, soft green plants that grow in dense clumps or mats on rocks, trees, and damp ground. Moss thrives in shade and moisture, making it common in forests and on north-facing surfaces. {The stones were covered in moss.} Figuratively, moss suggests age, stillness, or neglect: {A rolling stone gathers no moss.} (Capitalized Moss is a surname.)

Mosses are small, soft plants that lack flowers and true roots, growing in dense green clumps or mats on rocks, trees, and damp ground. They thrive in shady, moist environments: {The north side of the tree was covered in moss}. A rolling stone gathers no moss—constant movement prevents attachment. To moss over is to become covered with moss, often suggesting age or neglect.

Mossy means covered with or resembling moss—the soft, green plant that grows in damp, shaded places: {mossy stones}, {a mossy bank by the stream}. The word suggests age, neglect, or undisturbed nature: {The mossy old wall hadn't been touched in decades}. Figuratively, mossy can mean outdated or old-fashioned: {mossy traditions}.

Most functions in several parts of speech to express the idea of the greatest amount, limit, or magnitude. It is the superlative of many, some, or any, and it is used to form the superlative of adjectives that don’t inflect with an –est ending, as in the most advanced or the most ridiculous.

A mote is a tiny particle, especially one visible in a shaft of light: {Dust motes floated in the sunbeam}. The word is literary and appears most famously in the biblical injunction about seeing the mote in another's eye while ignoring the beam in one's own—a speck versus a plank, small faults versus large ones.

A motel is a roadside hotel designed for motorists, typically featuring rooms that open directly onto a parking area so guests can park near their doors. The word blends "motor" and "hotel." Motels emerged alongside American car culture and highway systems, offering convenient overnight stays for travelers. They range from budget chains to seedy establishments associated with illicit activities. {We pulled off the interstate and found a cheap motel for the night.}

Motels are roadside hotels designed for motorists, with parking directly outside the rooms. The word blends motor and hotel. Unlike traditional hotels with interior hallways and lobbies, motels typically have exterior entrances and single-story or low-rise layouts: {We pulled off the highway and found a motel for the night}. The term often suggests budget accommodations.

Motes are tiny particles, especially of dust floating in light: {Motes danced in the sunbeam streaming through the window}. The word is literary and evocative, suggesting something almost imperceptibly small. The biblical phrase about seeing {the mote in your brother's eye} uses mote to mean a speck so small it's hypocritical to criticize while ignoring your own larger faults.

A moth is an insect closely related to butterflies but typically distinguished by feathery antennae, nocturnal habits, and a tendency to rest with wings flat rather than upright. Moths range from tiny clothes-eating pests to large, striking species like the luna moth. The phrase {drawn like a moth to a flame} describes an irresistible but potentially dangerous attraction. If clothing is moth-eaten, moths have damaged it by feeding on the fabric.

A mothball is a small ball of pungent chemical—traditionally naphthalene or camphor—placed among stored clothing to repel moths and their larvae. To mothball something is to put it in protective storage or suspend its operation indefinitely: {The Navy mothballed several destroyers after the war}. Something {in mothballs} is inactive but preserved for potential future use.

Mothballed describes something put into long-term storage or suspension, preserved but inactive. The term comes from mothballs—chemical pellets used to protect stored clothing from moths. A mothballed {factory} sits idle but maintained. A mothballed {project} has been shelved indefinitely: {The renovation plans were mothballed when funding fell through}. Military ships are mothballed when decommissioned but kept in reserve.

Mothballing is putting something into long-term storage or suspension while preserving it for possible future use. The term comes from using mothballs to protect stored clothing from insects. Ships, factories, and military equipment get mothballed when not currently needed but too valuable to discard: {The navy is mothballing three destroyers}. Projects and plans can also be mothballed: {We're mothballing the expansion until the economy improves}.

Mothballs are small balls of pungent chemical—traditionally naphthalene or camphor—placed among stored clothing to repel moths and other fabric-eating insects. The strong odor clings to garments and suggests old closets or grandmother's attic. To put something {in mothballs} is to store it indefinitely or suspend its use: {The project has been in mothballs since the budget cuts}.

Moth-eaten describes fabric damaged by moth larvae, which feed on wool and other natural fibers, leaving holes and ragged patches. The word extends to anything shabby, outdated, or decayed from neglect: {moth-eaten furniture}, {moth-eaten ideas}. A moth-eaten argument or theory is one that's been picked apart or no longer holds together.

A mother is a female parent. It is a formal term of address for one’s own mother, and less frequently used than informal words like mom, mum, ma, and mama. Figurative meanings of mother have to do with the idea of causal generation: Necessity is the mother of invention. Before another noun, mother can be a title of respect or authority: mother superior (a senior nun). Before a nonhuman noun, mother may indicate a source: mother ship, mother lode. Someone who mothers supplies the sort of nurturing care that is associated with mothers.

A motherboard is the main circuit board in a computer, containing the central processor and providing connection points for other components—memory, storage drives, graphics cards, and peripherals. Everything routes through it: {The motherboard fried during the power surge}. Also called a mainboard or system board.

Mothered is the past tense of mother, meaning to care for someone in a protective, nurturing way: {She mothered the stray kittens back to health}. It can carry connotations of excessive or unwanted care: {He resented being mothered by his older sister}. To be mothered is to receive such attention.

Motherfucker is a strong vulgar term that can be a contemptuous insult or, paradoxically, express admiration for someone formidable: {He's one bad motherfucker}. It also works as an intensifier: {cold as a motherfucker}, {a motherfucker of a hangover}. Shortened forms include mofo and MF.
Motherfuckers is the plural of motherfucker, used for contemptible people or, with grudging respect, formidable ones: {Those motherfuckers actually pulled it off}.

Motherfuckery is outrageous, contemptible, or absurd behavior—often involving deception, incompetence, or malice: {I'm too old for this motherfuckery}, {The whole situation was pure motherfuckery}. The word conveys exasperated disgust at bullshit, nonsense, or wrongdoing. It functions as the abstract noun form of motherfucker, naming the category of offense rather than the offender.
Motherfucking is an intensive vulgar adjective that amplifies whatever follows: {Get your motherfucking hands off me}. {That was motherfucking delicious.}

Motherhood is the state of being a mother—having borne or adopted children and taken on their care. The word carries strong cultural weight, often idealized: {She embraced motherhood}. It can also refer to mothers collectively: {a victory for motherhood}. The phrase {motherhood and apple pie} describes values so wholesome they're beyond criticism, sometimes used ironically for positions that seem virtuous but lack substance.
clues: The state of having borne children

definition: Mothering is the act of caring for someone as a mother would—nurturing, protecting, and tending to needs. The term applies regardless of the caregiver's gender or relation: {He did most of the mothering while she worked}. Mothering can carry a negative edge when it suggests excessive or unwanted fussing: {Stop mothering me, I can take care of myself}.

Motherland is one's native country, viewed with emotional attachment as a place of origin and belonging. The term evokes patriotic feeling and cultural identity, often appearing in nationalist rhetoric: {They fought to defend the motherland}. It parallels fatherland, though motherland carries softer, more nurturing connotations—the nation as mother rather than patriarch.

Motherless describes someone whose mother has died or is absent: {a motherless child raised by relatives}. The word carries connotations of vulnerability and loss. In Australian slang, motherless intensifies adjectives, especially in {motherless broke}—completely without money.

The motherlode is the principal vein or deposit of ore in a mine—the source from which smaller veins branch. Figuratively, it means any rich source or main supply: {We hit the motherlode of vintage records at that estate sale}. Often spelled as two words: mother lode.

Motherly describes qualities associated with a good mother—nurturing, protective, warm, and caring. A motherly person shows gentle concern for others' wellbeing: {She gave him a motherly hug}. The word applies regardless of whether someone is actually a mother: {The motherly nurse checked on her patients throughout the night}.

Mothers is the plural of mother—women who have borne or raised children. The word often appears in compound phrases: {mothers and fathers}, {single mothers}, {working mothers}. To mother someone is to care for them protectively, sometimes excessively: {Stop mothering me, I can handle it}. Mother can also be a verb meaning to give birth to or originate: {She mothered three children}. {Necessity is the mother of invention.}

A mothership is a large vessel—spacecraft, aircraft, or ship—that carries, deploys, or supports smaller craft. Science fiction popularized the term for alien vessels carrying fleets of smaller ships: {The mothership hovered over the city}. By extension, mothership describes any central hub or headquarters from which operations emanate: {The startup's mothership is in Austin, but they have satellite offices everywhere}.

A mothership is a large vessel that carries, deploys, or supports smaller craft—aircraft, boats, or spacecraft. The term appears in science fiction for alien vessels commanding fleets of smaller ships. Figuratively, a mothership is a central hub or headquarters from which operations extend: {The startup operated from a mothership in San Francisco with satellite offices worldwide}.

Mothman is a creature from American folklore, reportedly sighted in West Virginia in the 1960s—described as a large humanoid figure with wings and glowing red eyes. The legend gained traction after a 1967 bridge collapse was retroactively linked to the sightings, casting Mothman as an omen of disaster. The figure has become a staple of cryptozoology and paranormal culture: {Point Pleasant has a Mothman statue and annual festival}.

Moths are insects closely related to butterflies, typically nocturnal with feathery antennae and drab coloring. They're drawn to artificial light—{moths circling a porch lamp}—which has made them symbols of fatal attraction. Some species damage fabric by laying eggs in wool or silk: {mothballs}, {moth-eaten}. Figuratively, {like a moth to a flame} describes irresistible, often dangerous attraction.

A motif is a recurring element that forms a pattern—in art, music, literature, or design. A floral motif might appear throughout wallpaper or fabric. In storytelling, a motif is an image, phrase, or idea that returns to reinforce theme: {the motif of water and drowning runs through the novel}. In music, a motif is a short melodic or rhythmic figure that recurs and develops.

Motifs are recurring elements in art, literature, music, or design—patterns, images, or themes that appear repeatedly to create unity or reinforce meaning. A novel might use water imagery as a motif; a symphony might return to a four-note motif. In decorative arts, motifs are distinctive design elements: {floral motifs}, {geometric motifs}. The word comes from French, sharing roots with motive—both suggest something that drives or shapes a work.

Motion is movement from one place or position to another: {the motion of the planets}, {set the wheels in motion}. A motion is also a formal proposal put to a vote: {She made a motion to adjourn}. To motion is to direct with a gesture: {He motioned me over}. In law, a motion is a request to a court for a ruling. {Go through the motions} means to do something perfunctorily, without real engagement.

Motionless means completely still, without any movement. A deer stands motionless when it senses danger. {She sat motionless, staring at the wall}. The word emphasizes the absence of motion rather than mere stillness—something motionless has stopped moving or is deliberately holding position.

Motions are movements, whether of bodies, body parts, or objects through space. The word often implies purposeful or directed movement: {She made a motion toward the door}. In formal settings, a motion is a proposal put forward for discussion or vote: {The motion to adjourn was seconded}. To motion is to direct someone with a gesture: {He motioned for us to sit down}. The phrase {go through the motions} means to do something mechanically, without genuine engagement or enthusiasm.

To motivate is to provide someone with a reason or incentive to act: {What motivates you to work so hard?} A motivated person has drive and purpose; an unmotivated one lacks initiative. You can motivate yourself or others through rewards, fear, inspiration, or necessity. The noun motivation refers to the underlying reasons or desires that prompt action.

Motivated describes someone who has a reason or drive to act, whether that reason comes from within or from external rewards and pressures. A motivated {student} works hard because they genuinely want to learn or because grades matter to them. The word often carries positive connotations of energy and determination: {She's one of the most motivated employees I've ever managed}. In compound forms like {self-motivated} or {financially motivated}, it specifies the source of that drive.

Motivation is the reason or drive behind action—what makes you do something. It can be internal desire or external pressure: {Her motivation for studying was a genuine love of learning}. In psychology, motivation explains why organisms behave as they do. Someone's motives are their motivations, usually for a specific act: {Police are still trying to determine a motivation for the attack}. To question someone's motivation is to doubt their sincerity or suspect hidden reasons.

Motivational describes something intended to inspire enthusiasm, determination, or action. A motivational {speaker} aims to energize an audience. Motivational {posters} offer uplifting messages, though the genre has become a target of parody. The word often carries a faint whiff of self-help culture: {He's really into motivational podcasts}.

Motivations are the reasons behind actions or decisions—the internal drives or external factors that prompt someone to do something. When someone asks about your motivations, they want to understand why you acted as you did, often with an implication that your stated reasons might not be the real ones. {Her motivations for joining the company were purely financial.} In psychology, motivation refers more broadly to the processes that initiate and sustain goal-directed behavior.

A motivator is something or someone that provides motivation—a reason or incentive to act. A good boss serves as a motivator for employees. Fear can be a powerful motivator. {Money isn't my primary motivator}. The word often appears in self-help and business contexts, where motivators are distinguished from mere incentives.

A motive is the reason behind an action, especially one that explains why someone did something questionable or criminal: {Police are still trying to establish a motive for the killing}. The word implies purpose driving behavior—detectives seek motives, psychologists analyze them. As an adjective, motive means producing motion: {motive power}, {motive force}.

Motives are the reasons behind actions—the desires, needs, or purposes that drive someone to do something. Police investigate motives for crimes; psychologists explore motives for behavior. The word often implies hidden or questionable intent: {What are his real motives?} {She questioned his motives for helping}. A motive can also be a recurring theme in art or music.

Motley describes a mixture of diverse, often incongruous elements: {a motley crew of musicians and drifters}, {a motley assortment of furniture}. The word carries a slightly dismissive tone—the mix lacks coherence or quality. Historically, motley was the multicolored costume worn by court jesters, which explains its association with varied, mismatched combinations.

Motocross is a form of motorcycle racing conducted on rough, unpaved courses featuring steep hills, sharp turns, and obstacles like jumps and mud pits. The bikes are lightweight and specially designed for the terrain, with enhanced suspension and knobby tires. Riders compete on closed circuits, and races emphasize both speed and technical skill in handling challenging conditions. {He broke his collarbone in a motocross accident.}

Motor refers to a machine that converts energy into mechanical force and motion, powering everything from cars to appliances. The word comes from Latin for "mover," and this sense of causing movement extends beyond machinery: motor skills involve coordinated physical movement, and to motor somewhere is to travel by car. As an adjective, motor describes things relating to engines or vehicles ({motor oil}, {motor vehicle}) or to muscular movement ({motor neurons}).

A motorbike is a two-wheeled vehicle powered by an engine—synonymous with motorcycle, though motorbike often suggests something smaller or lighter. In British usage, motorbike is the everyday term where Americans might say motorcycle. {She commutes to work on her motorbike.}

Motorbikes are two-wheeled vehicles powered by engines—synonymous with motorcycles in most contexts, though sometimes suggesting smaller or lighter models. The term is more common in British English: {He commuted to work on his motorbike}. As a verb, to motorbike is to travel by motorcycle: {We motorbiked through the countryside}.

A motorboat is a boat propelled by an internal combustion engine rather than sails, oars, or paddles. The term covers everything from small recreational craft to larger speedboats and cabin cruisers. As a verb, motorboat has a vulgar slang meaning: to place one's face between someone's breasts and shake one's head rapidly while making a vibrating sound with the lips, mimicking the noise of a boat engine.

Motorboating is the activity of riding in or operating a boat powered by a motor, as opposed to sailing or rowing. In vulgar slang, motorboating refers to placing one's face between someone's breasts and moving the head rapidly side to side while making a sputtering sound with the lips, mimicking an outboard motor. {We spent the afternoon motorboating on the lake.} The slang usage is crude and typically appears in comedy or locker-room contexts.

Motorboats are watercraft powered by engines rather than sails, oars, or paddles. The term covers everything from small outboards to cabin cruisers. To motorboat is to travel by such a boat, or in vulgar slang, to press one's face between someone's breasts and shake rapidly while exhaling—mimicking the sound of an outboard motor.

A motorcade is a procession of motor vehicles, typically escorting an important person such as a head of state or dignitary: {The presidential motorcade wound through downtown}. The term combines "motor" with the "-cade" ending borrowed from cavalcade. Motorcades often include security vehicles, police escorts, and support cars traveling in formation.

A motorcade is a procession of motor vehicles, typically carrying dignitaries or officials and accompanied by security escorts: {The presidential motorcade wound through downtown}. The term suggests formality and protection—police cars clearing the route, flags on fenders, crowds watching from sidewalks. Funeral processions are sometimes called motorcades, though the word most often appears in political contexts.

A motorcycle is a two-wheeled vehicle powered by an engine, straddled by the rider like a bicycle but capable of highway speeds. Motorcycles range from small scooters to heavy touring bikes. The word often shortens to {bike} or {cycle}: {He rides his motorcycle to work}. To motorcycle is to travel by one.

Motorcycles is the plural of motorcycle, a two-wheeled motor vehicle with the rider straddling a saddle. Motorcycles range from small scooters to powerful sport bikes and cruisers. The word can also verb: {She motorcycles to work year-round}. Motorcycle culture carries associations with freedom and rebellion—think leather jackets and open roads.

A motorhead is someone passionate about motors, engines, and vehicles—especially cars and motorcycles. The term suggests hands-on enthusiasm: motorheads typically enjoy working on engines, not just admiring them. {He's been a motorhead since he rebuilt his first carburetor at fifteen.} The word can also refer to someone who uses amphetamines, from "motor" suggesting restless energy.

Motorheads are enthusiasts of motors and engines—people passionate about cars, motorcycles, or anything with horsepower. The term suggests someone who tinkers, races, or obsesses over mechanical performance: {The motorheads spent all weekend rebuilding the transmission}. Also refers to fans of the British rock band Motörhead.

A motorhome is a large vehicle with living quarters built in—typically including beds, a kitchen, and bathroom facilities. Unlike a trailer or camper, the living space and engine are integrated into a single unit. Motorhomes range from modest vans to bus-sized vehicles with full amenities: {They sold the house and traveled the country in a motorhome}.

Motorhomes are recreational vehicles with living quarters built into them—combining transportation and accommodation in one unit. Unlike travel trailers, which are towed, motorhomes have their own engines and can be driven. They range from compact camper vans to bus-sized coaches with full kitchens, bathrooms, and bedrooms: {They sold their house and traveled the country in a motorhome}.

A motorist is someone who drives a car, especially on public roads. The word emphasizes the person's role as a road user rather than as owner or passenger: {Motorists should watch for cyclists}. It appears frequently in traffic reports, news coverage of accidents, and official signage.

A motormouth is someone who talks excessively and rapidly, often without much regard for whether others want to listen: {My sister's such a motormouth—she barely lets anyone else get a word in}. The term is mildly disparaging. As a verb, to motormouth is to talk this way: {He motormouthed through the entire meeting}.

Motormouthed describes someone who talks rapidly and at length, often without much regard for whether others want to listen. The image is of a mouth running like a motor—continuous, mechanical, hard to stop: {Her motormouthed cousin dominated every family dinner}. The noun is motormouth.

Motors are machines that convert energy into mechanical motion—electric motors, combustion motors, outboard motors. The word overlaps with engine, though motors typically emphasize the motion-producing mechanism itself. To motor is to travel by car: {We motored down the coast}. In British English, motor as an adjective relates to cars: {motor insurance}, {motor racing}.

Motorsport is competitive racing involving motorized vehicles—cars, motorcycles, boats, or aircraft. The term encompasses everything from Formula One and NASCAR to motocross and drag racing. British English favors the singular {motorsport}, while American English often uses the plural {motorsports}: {He's been involved in motorsports his whole life}.

Motorsports refers to competitive racing events involving motorized vehicles, including cars, motorcycles, boats, and aircraft. The term encompasses a wide range of disciplines from Formula 1 and NASCAR to motocross and drag racing. Events may take place on purpose-built tracks, public roads closed for competition, or off-road terrain. {He's been a motorsports fan since childhood.} The singular motorsport is more common in British English.

A motorway is a high-speed divided highway designed for through traffic, with limited access points and no intersections at grade. The term is primarily British; Americans say freeway, expressway, or interstate. {Traffic on the M25 motorway was at a standstill.}

Motorways are high-speed divided highways designed for long-distance travel, with controlled access via entrance and exit ramps. The term is primarily British; Americans say freeways or highways. Motorways typically have multiple lanes in each direction, separated by a central barrier: {Traffic was backed up on the motorway for miles}.

Mottled describes a surface marked with irregular spots or patches of different colors or shades: {mottled skin}, {mottled marble}, {the mottled light filtering through leaves}. The pattern suggests unevenness rather than design—blotchy rather than patterned. Mottling often indicates age, disease, or natural variation: {His hands were mottled with age spots}.

A motto is a short phrase expressing a principle, goal, or ideal—often adopted by a person, family, organization, or nation: {The Boy Scouts' motto is "Be Prepared"}. Mottos appear on coats of arms, school crests, and currency. More loosely, a motto is any guiding principle someone lives by: {Her motto was "Never complain, never explain"}.

Mottos is the plural of motto—a short phrase expressing a guiding principle or ideal. Organizations, families, and nations adopt mottos: {The Olympic motto is "Faster, Higher, Stronger"}. School mottos appear on crests and letterheads. Personal mottos capture life philosophies: {Her motto was "No regrets"}. The alternative plural mottoes is also correct but less common.

Mould is the British spelling of mold in all its senses. A mould is a hollow container that shapes liquid or soft material as it hardens: {a jelly mould}, {a mould for casting bronze}. To mould is to shape something, literally or figuratively: {She moulded the clay with her hands}, {experiences that mould character}. Mould is also the fuzzy fungal growth on damp surfaces or decaying matter: {There's mould on the bread}. The spelling mold predominates in American English.

Moulded is the British spelling of molded—the past tense and past participle of mould. Something moulded has been shaped in or as if in a mould: {moulded plastic}, {moulded chocolate}. Figuratively, experiences or influences mould character: {Her years abroad moulded her worldview}.

Mouldering is the British spelling of moldering—slowly decaying or crumbling through age and neglect. Old books moulder in forgotten libraries; abandoned buildings moulder into ruin. The word suggests gradual deterioration rather than sudden collapse: {The manuscript lay mouldering in the archive for centuries}.

Moulding is the British spelling of molding. A moulding is a decorative strip of shaped wood, plaster, or stone used to finish edges or transitions—around door frames, along ceilings, at baseboards: {ornate Victorian moulding}. As a process, moulding means shaping material in a mould or figuratively shaping character: {the moulding of young minds}.

Mouldings is the British spelling of moldings—decorative strips of wood, plaster, or other material used to finish architectural surfaces. Crown mouldings run along ceiling edges; base mouldings cover where walls meet floors. The term also applies to any shaped or cast objects: {plastic mouldings for car interiors}.

Moulds is the British spelling of molds, covering all senses of that word. A mould is a hollow container that gives shape to liquid or soft material poured into it, or the growth of fungus that appears on damp surfaces and decaying organic matter. As a verb, to mould something is to shape it, either literally in a container or figuratively through influence: {The program moulds young athletes into disciplined competitors}. If you break the mould, you do something unprecedented.

Mouldy is the British spelling of moldy—covered with mould, the fuzzy fungal growth that appears on decaying food or damp surfaces: {The bread had gone mouldy}. Figuratively, something mouldy is stale, outdated, or musty: {mouldy old ideas}. In British slang, mouldy can mean unpleasant or worthless: {a mouldy deal}.

To moult is to shed feathers, fur, skin, or an exoskeleton as part of a natural cycle, making way for new growth. Birds moult their feathers seasonally; snakes moult their skin; crabs moult their shells. The noun is the process itself or the material shed: {The dog is in moult}. Spelled molt in American English.

Moulting is the British spelling of molting—the process by which animals shed old feathers, fur, skin, or shells to make way for new growth. Birds moult seasonally, snakes moult their entire skin, and crustaceans moult their exoskeletons as they grow. {The parrot is moulting and looks rather ragged.}

A mound is a pile or heap, typically of earth: {a burial mound}, {a mound of dirt}. In baseball, the mound is the raised area where the pitcher stands. Mound extends to any rounded mass: {a mound of mashed potatoes}. To mound is to form into a pile: {She mounded the rice on the plate}.

Mounds are raised piles or heaps—of earth, sand, snow, or other material. Some are natural formations; others are deliberately built, like ancient burial mounds or pitcher's mounds in baseball. The word extends to any heap-like accumulation: {mounds of paperwork}, {a mound of mashed potatoes}. To mound is to pile into such a shape.

To mount something smaller than you, such as a picture or a bracket, is to fix it in place – on a wall, for example. To mount something larger than you, such as a horse, is to climb up on its back. Mount is also used to describe the act of a male (animal) engaging with a female in sexual intercourse. A mount is an act of mounting, or if an animal, one that you mount: His mount was a dappled gray horse. A different mount is related to mountain, and occurs as the first term in the official names of many peaks (Mount Rushmore, Mount Sinai, Mount Everest).

A mountain is a large natural elevation of land, typically rising steeply and significantly higher than the surrounding terrain. Mountains are distinguished from hills mainly by height and ruggedness, though no universal threshold exists. The term extends to any massive quantity: {a mountain of debt}, {a mountain of paperwork}. To {move mountains} is to accomplish something seemingly impossible. To {make a mountain out of a molehill} is to exaggerate a minor problem.

A mountaineer is someone who climbs mountains, especially as a sport or profession. The term suggests technical skill and serious alpine pursuits rather than casual hiking: {experienced mountaineers attempting Everest}, {a team of mountaineers roped together on the glacier}. As a verb, to mountaineer is to engage in mountain climbing.

Mountaineering is the sport or activity of climbing mountains, especially those requiring technical skill with ropes, ice axes, and specialized equipment. It combines hiking, rock climbing, and navigation through snow and ice. {She took up mountaineering after years of casual hiking}. The word can also describe the broader culture and community surrounding the pursuit.

Mountaineers are people who climb mountains, typically as a sport or recreational pursuit rather than out of necessity. The term suggests someone with technical climbing skills and experience navigating difficult terrain, not merely a hiker on mountain trails. {The mountaineers reached base camp before the storm hit.} As a verb, to mountaineer means to engage in mountain climbing. The word also appears as a team name and demonym for people from mountainous regions.

Mountainous describes terrain characterized by mountains—rugged, elevated, and often difficult to traverse: {the mountainous regions of Nepal}, {mountainous terrain}. By extension, it describes anything enormous or imposing in size: {mountainous waves}, {mountainous debts}, {a mountainous pile of laundry}.

Mountains are large natural elevations of land, typically rising steeply and reaching heights far above surrounding terrain. The term often implies rocky peaks, steep slopes, and significant altitude: {We hiked in the mountains all summer}. Figuratively, a mountain is any enormous quantity or obstacle: {a mountain of paperwork}, {make a mountain out of a molehill}. To {move mountains} is to accomplish something seemingly impossible.

The sloped surface of a mountain, as distinct from its peak or base. Mountainside emphasizes the terrain itself—its steepness, vegetation, or exposure: {Wildflowers covered the mountainside}, {The cabin clung to the mountainside}. Often appears in contexts of climbing, erosion, or scenic views.

Mountainsides are the sloping surfaces of mountains, the terrain between a peak and its base. The word typically appears when describing what covers or occurs on these slopes: {wildflowers blanketing the mountainsides}, {villages clinging to the mountainsides}. Unlike the more technical "slope" or "gradient," mountainsides evokes the visible face of the mountain as landscape rather than as measured incline.

A mountaintop is the highest point or summit of a mountain. The word often carries symbolic weight—mountaintops are places of revelation, achievement, or perspective: {a mountaintop experience}, {shouting it from the mountaintops}. Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I've been to the mountaintop" speech drew on this tradition of elevated vision.

Mountaintops are the highest points or summits of mountains. The word typically appears in contexts emphasizing elevation, remoteness, or dramatic scenery: {Snow covered the mountaintops}. Figuratively, mountaintops suggest achievement or transcendence: {He felt like he was standing on the mountaintop after his victory}.

Mounted means positioned on or attached to something. A mounted {photograph} is fixed to backing; a mounted {TV} hangs on a wall. Mounted police or soldiers are on horseback. The past tense of mount covers climbing onto ({He mounted the horse}), increasing ({Pressure mounted}), and organizing ({They mounted an expedition}). Something that is mounted is secured in place and ready for use or display.

Mounting works as both adjective and noun. As an adjective, it describes something that increases or accumulates over time: {mounting pressure}, {mounting debt}, {mounting evidence}. The word suggests a steady buildup rather than a sudden spike. As a noun, a mounting is a frame, support, or backing on which something is fixed or displayed: {a brass mounting for the telescope}, {the painting's mounting}. The verb mount gives rise to both senses—climbing or increasing, and fixing in place.

Mounts is the plural of mount—things you climb onto or attach things to. A mount can be a horse or other animal for riding, a backing or frame for displaying something {photo mounts}, or a mountain (archaic or in place names). The verb mount means to climb up, get on, or increase: {Pressure mounts as the deadline approaches}. To mount an attack or campaign is to launch it. To mount something is also to attach it to a support: {He mounted the TV on the wall}.

To mourn is to grieve, especially for someone who has died. Mourning involves the outward expression of grief—wearing black, observing rituals, withdrawing from normal activities: {The nation mourned the president's death}. You can also mourn losses other than death: {She mourned the end of her marriage}, {He mourned his lost youth}. The period of mourning varies by culture and relationship.

Mourned is the past tense of mourn—to grieve or express sorrow over a loss, especially a death. {The nation mourned when the president was assassinated.} {She mourned her father for years.} Beyond death, one can mourn the loss of anything valued: {He mourned the end of his marriage.}

A mourner is someone who grieves, especially one attending a funeral or memorial service. The word emphasizes the public or communal aspect of grief—mourners gather, mourners file past a casket, professional mourners were once hired to wail at funerals. {The mourners stood in silence as the coffin was lowered}.

Mourners are people grieving a death, especially those attending a funeral or memorial service. The term emphasizes the collective nature of grief—mourners gather to honor the deceased and support one another: {Mourners filed past the casket}. Professional mourners, hired to weep at funerals, exist in various cultures.

Mournful describes something expressing or suggesting grief or sorrow. A mournful {expression} shows sadness; a mournful {melody} evokes melancholy even without words. The word often describes sounds—a dog's mournful {howl}, the mournful {wail} of a distant train. Something mournful needn't involve actual mourning; it conveys the quality of grief rather than grief itself.

Mourning is the expression of grief, especially after someone's death. It encompasses both the internal experience of sorrow and its outward forms—wearing black, observing periods of withdrawal, holding vigils. {The family is still in mourning.} A mourning {dove} is named for its mournful call. Mourning differs from grief in emphasizing the visible, social dimension of loss.

Mourns is the act of grieving or expressing sorrow, typically over a death: {She still mourns her late husband}. Beyond bereavement, one can mourn any significant loss—a relationship, an era, a way of life: {He mourns his lost youth}. Public mourning may involve rituals, dress, or periods of observance.

A mouse is a small rodent with a pointed snout, large ears, and a long tail—the kind that scurries through walls or gets caught in traps. In computing, a mouse is a handheld device that controls a cursor on screen, named for its shape and tail-like cord. To mouse is to hunt mice, said of cats, or to move timidly. Someone {quiet as a mouse} makes little noise or draws no attention. Plural: mice for rodents, mice or mouses for the device.

A mousehole is a small hole in a wall or baseboard where a mouse might enter or live—the kind often depicted in cartoons with an arched opening. By extension, any cramped opening or confined space: {The apartment was a mousehole, but it was cheap}. In oil drilling, the mousehole is a shallow hole in the rig floor where pipe sections are stored vertically before use.

A mouser is a cat kept for catching mice, or any cat skilled at hunting rodents: {The barn cat was an excellent mouser}. The term emphasizes function over affection—a mouser earns its keep. By extension, mouser occasionally describes other animals or even people who hunt or pursue with cat-like persistence.

A mouser is a cat that catches mice, particularly one kept for that purpose rather than purely as a pet. The term emphasizes function over affection: a good mouser earns its keep by controlling rodents in barns, warehouses, or homes. {The old barn cat was the best mouser we ever had.} By extension, mouser occasionally describes any animal or person skilled at catching or hunting small prey.

A mousetrap is a device for catching or killing mice, typically a spring-loaded mechanism that snaps shut when triggered. The word extends to any trap or scheme designed to lure someone into a compromising position: {The police set up a mousetrap for the smugglers}. To mousetrap is to catch someone this way. A mousetrap can also be something basic but effective—the standard against which improvements are measured: {Build a better mousetrap and the world will beat a path to your door}.

Mousetraps are devices designed to catch or kill mice, typically spring-loaded mechanisms baited with food. The word extends to any trap or scheme: {The police set up a mousetrap for the burglars}. To mousetrap is to lure someone into a trap. The phrase {build a better mousetrap} suggests innovation that improves on existing solutions.

Mousey is a variant spelling of mousy. It describes someone or something resembling a mouse—quiet, timid, and unassertive: {a mousey little man who never spoke up in meetings}. Hair that is mousey is a dull grayish-brown, the color of mouse fur. The spelling with the e is less common but equally acceptable.

Moussaka is a baked Mediterranean dish of layered eggplant, spiced ground meat (usually lamb), and béchamel sauce, associated especially with Greek cuisine. Variations appear throughout the Middle East and Balkans: {We ordered moussaka and spanakopita at the Greek restaurant}.

Mousse is a light, airy preparation with a foamy texture, held together by whipped cream or beaten egg whites. The word comes from French for foam or froth. Chocolate mousse is the classic dessert version, but savory mousses exist: {salmon mousse}, {chicken liver mousse}. Hair mousse is a styling foam that adds volume and hold.

Moustache is the British spelling of mustache—hair grown on the upper lip. The style ranges from thin pencil lines to thick handlebars. A moustache may be grown alone or as part of a fuller beard: {He twirled the ends of his waxed moustache}. To moustache is to grow one.

Moustaches is the plural of moustache—hair grown on the upper lip. The spelling with -ou- is British; Americans typically write mustache. {He admired the waxed moustaches of Victorian gentlemen}. The word covers everything from thin pencil lines to elaborate handlebar styles.

Mousy describes someone or something resembling a mouse—quiet, timid, and unassertive. A mousy {person} shrinks from attention. The word also describes dull, grayish-brown coloring, especially of hair: {Her mousy hair hung limp}. Both senses carry slightly unflattering connotations, suggesting blandness or lack of presence. Also spelled moussy.

The mouth is primarily the opening through which food enters animal bodies. In some contexts, mouth refers to the cavity in which food is chewed. We also use our mouths to form and utter speech, and this function inspires some uses of mouth: You would not believe the things that came out of his mouth. Any opening or terminus that serves an important function may be called a mouth, like the mouth of a cave or river. The verb uses of mouth have to do with speech. Someone who mouths off speaks disrespectfully. If you mouth a word, you silently move your lips as if to pronounce it.

A mouthbreather is someone who breathes through their mouth rather than their nose, often due to congestion or habit. The term is more commonly used as an insult suggesting someone is stupid, slack-jawed, or socially oblivious: {Some mouthbreather cut in front of me at the checkout}. The implication is of someone too dim to perform basic functions properly.

Mouthbreathers is a derogatory term for stupid or oblivious people, evoking the image of someone slack-jawed and dim. The insult suggests someone too dull to breathe through their nose: {The comment section was full of mouthbreathers}. Sometimes spelled as two words or hyphenated.

Mouthbreathing literally describes breathing through the mouth rather than the nose, often due to congestion or habit. The figurative sense dominates online: a mouthbreather is someone perceived as stupid, slack-jawed, or socially oblivious—the image of someone too dim to close their mouth. {The comments section was full of mouthbreathing trolls.}

Mouthfeel is the physical sensation a food or drink produces in the mouth—its texture, weight, and how it moves across the tongue. Wine critics discuss mouthfeel when describing whether a wine feels silky, astringent, or full-bodied. The term appears in food science and brewing: {The oatmeal gives this stout a creamy mouthfeel}. It captures qualities beyond taste—viscosity, temperature, carbonation, grittiness.

A mouthful is the amount that fills or can fit in a mouth: {She took a mouthful of cereal}. Extended, it means a lot to say—either literally, as when a word or phrase is long and awkward {(Hubert Horatio Humphrey is quite a mouthful)}, or figuratively, when someone says something significant: {That last comment was a mouthful}.

Mouthfuls is the plural of mouthful—the amount that fills or can fit in a mouth: {She ate it in three mouthfuls}. A mouthful can also be something difficult to say: {His last name is quite a mouthful}. In informal use, {You said a mouthful} means you've expressed something significant or exactly right.

A mouthguard is a protective device worn over the teeth, typically made of flexible plastic or rubber. Athletes wear mouthguards to prevent dental injuries during contact sports like boxing, football, and hockey: {Don't forget your mouthguard for practice}. Mouthguards are also worn at night to prevent teeth grinding.

Mouthing is forming words with your lips without producing sound, or producing sound without sincerity. You might mouth words across a crowded room: {She mouthed "I love you" from across the table}. To mouth platitudes or pieties is to say them without meaning them—going through the motions of speech without genuine conviction behind it.

A mouthpiece is the part of an instrument, phone, pipe, or other device that goes in or near the mouth. A mouthpiece is also a spokesperson—someone who speaks on behalf of another person or organization, often with the implication that they lack independent views: {The newspaper became a mouthpiece for the regime}. In boxing, a mouthpiece is a guard protecting the teeth.

Mouthpieces is the plural of mouthpiece—the part of an instrument, telephone, or breathing apparatus that contacts the mouth. A mouthpiece can also be a protective guard for teeth during sports. Figuratively, a mouthpiece is a spokesperson, often one who merely relays another's views: {The senator was just a mouthpiece for the oil lobby}.

Mouths is the plural of mouth—the opening in the face used for eating, breathing, and speaking. Rivers have mouths where they empty into larger bodies of water. A mouth can be any opening: {the mouths of caves dotted the cliff face}. As a verb (rhymes with "clothe"), to mouth is to form words with the lips without sound: {She mouthed "I love you" across the room}. To mouth off is to speak rudely or disrespectfully.

Mouthwash is a liquid used to rinse the mouth, typically to freshen breath or kill bacteria. Most mouthwashes contain alcohol and antiseptic ingredients. The term sometimes extends figuratively to anything that cleanses or purifies speech: {He needed some verbal mouthwash after that outburst}.

Mouthwatering describes food so appealing it triggers salivation in anticipation: {The mouthwatering aroma of fresh bread filled the kitchen}. The word extends to anything temptingly desirable: {a mouthwatering real estate deal}, {mouthwatering profits}. Usually hyphenated as an adjective before a noun, often written as one word after.

Mouthy describes someone who talks too much, too boldly, or too rudely—especially when they should keep quiet. A mouthy kid talks back to adults. A mouthy employee challenges the boss inappropriately. The word suggests insolence or excessive opinionatedness: {Don't get mouthy with me}. {She's always been mouthy about politics}.

Move is the verb most closely associated with motion, and that’s what it’s about. Something that moves goes from one place to another. If someone or something moves you, it could mean a number of things. A song that moves you elicits an emotional response. An authority that moves you puts you in a different place: We were moved to a different classroom because of noise. If you move or if a company moves you, you take up residence in a different place. This sense is move house in British English. A move is the act or result of moving. In a competitive or strategic context, a move is some action undertaken with a goal in view: You made a smart move by declining their invitation.

Moved is the past tense of move, covering physical displacement {We moved to California}, emotional impact {I was deeply moved by her speech}, and taking action {The committee moved to adjourn}. When someone is moved, they've been stirred emotionally: {He was moved to tears}. In formal contexts, to have moved means to have proposed something officially: {She moved that the motion be tabled}.

Movement is motion or the act of moving: {the movement of clouds across the sky}, {a dancer's graceful movements}. It extends to organized efforts toward a goal: the civil rights {movement}, the labor {movement}. In music, a movement is a self-contained section of a larger work. A clock's movement is its internal mechanism. Bowel {movement} is the polite term for defecation.

Movements is the plural of movement, covering all its senses. Physical movements are instances of moving or changing position: {The dancer's movements were fluid and precise}. A movement can also be an organized effort by a group working toward a shared goal: {the civil rights movement}, {the labor movement}. In music, a movement is a self-contained section of a larger composition like a symphony or sonata. The word also refers euphemistically to bowel movements—instances of defecation.

A mover is someone or something that moves. Most commonly, movers are workers who transport furniture and belongings during a relocation: {The movers arrive at eight tomorrow}. A mover can also be someone who proposes a motion in a formal meeting. In figurative use, a {mover and shaker} is an influential person who makes things happen. A {prime mover} is the initial source of motion or action—whether a philosophy concept, an engine, or the driving force behind a project.

Movers are people or companies that transport household belongings from one location to another: {The movers arrive at eight tomorrow}. The term extends to anyone who causes movement or change—{movers and shakers} are influential people who drive events forward. A mover can also be something that sells: {That album was a real mover}.

Moves is the plural of move—changes of position, actions taken, or strategic decisions: {She made several moves to consolidate power}. In games like chess, moves are individual turns. Someone's moves can be their dancing style or romantic techniques: {He's got no moves}. If you {make moves}, you're taking action toward a goal. {The movers} are people with influence who get things done.

A movie is a motion picture—a story or documentary recorded on film or video for viewing in theaters or at home. The term is American; British English prefers film. {We saw a movie last night.} {She wants to work in movies.} The movies can mean the theater itself: {Let's go to the movies.}

A moviegoer is someone who goes to movies, especially as a regular habit. The term emphasizes attendance at theaters rather than watching at home: {Moviegoers lined up around the block for opening night}. Someone might watch films constantly at home without being much of a moviegoer.

Moviegoers are people who attend films at theaters.
