The term emphasizes the activity as a habit or identity rather than a single instance—regular moviegoers versus someone who occasionally sees a movie: {Moviegoers lined up around the block for opening night}. The singular moviegoer exists but appears less often.

Movieland is the world of movies and filmmaking, especially Hollywood and its culture of stars, studios, and glamour. The term treats the film industry as a distinct realm with its own customs and inhabitants: {a movieland legend}, {the gossip columns of movieland}. Sometimes used for theme parks or attractions featuring movie-related exhibits.

Moviemaking is the process and craft of creating films, encompassing everything from screenwriting and directing to cinematography, editing, and post-production. The term emphasizes the collaborative, industrial nature of film production rather than the artistic vision alone. {She studied moviemaking at a conservatory in New York.} It can also refer to the film industry as a whole: {Hollywood has dominated moviemaking for over a century.}

Movies are motion pictures—films produced for entertainment, art, or information. The word often refers to the medium collectively: {I love the movies}. It also means the theater where films are shown: {Let's go to the movies}. A movie is a single film: {We watched a movie last night}. The term is more casual than film or cinema.

Moving describes something in motion or causing motion: {a moving target}, {the moving parts of an engine}. More often, moving means emotionally affecting—stirring feelings of sympathy, sadness, or tenderness: {a moving tribute}, {Her speech was deeply moving}. The act of relocating to a new residence is also moving: {Moving is stressful}, {a moving company}.

To mow is to cut down grass, grain, or other vegetation, typically with a blade or machine: {I need to mow the lawn this weekend}. A mower does the mowing. To {mow down} is to kill or destroy in large numbers, evoking the sweeping motion of a scythe cutting through a field: {The gunner mowed down the advancing troops}. A mow (rhymes with "cow") is also an old word for a stack of hay or grain stored in a barn.

Mowed is the past tense of mow, meaning to cut grass or grain with a blade or machine: {I mowed the lawn this morning}. To {mow down} is to kill or destroy in large numbers, as if cutting through a field: {The gunman mowed down the crowd}. The past participle can be mowed or mown.

A mower is a machine or person that cuts grass or grain. Most often it refers to a lawn mower—the motorized device homeowners push or ride across yards: {I need to get the mower out before the grass gets any taller}. Agricultural mowers cut hay or other crops. The word also applies to anyone doing the mowing: {The mowers start at dawn}.

Mowing is cutting grass or grain, typically with a blade or machine. A freshly mowed lawn has that distinctive summer smell. Mowing can also describe cutting down in large numbers: {The machine gun mowed down the advancing soldiers}. A mowing is also a field of grass ready for cutting.

Mown is the past participle of mow, describing grass or grain that has been cut: {freshly mown lawn}, {mown hay drying in the field}. The alternative form mowed works in the same contexts, though mown appears more often as an adjective before a noun.

Moxie is spirited courage and determination—the nerve to take on challenges and see them through. Someone with moxie doesn't back down: {She had the moxie to start her own business at nineteen}. The word carries admiration for boldness and resourcefulness, especially when facing long odds.

Moxy is a variant spelling of moxie—bold determination, nerve, or fighting spirit. Someone with moxy has the courage to take risks or stand up for themselves: {She had the moxy to ask for a raise on her first day}. The spelling with a y is less common than moxie but appears in informal writing.

Mozzarella is a mild, soft Italian cheese with a springy texture, traditionally made from water buffalo milk but now commonly from cow's milk. It melts smoothly and stretches when heated, making it the standard cheese for pizza: {Fresh mozzarella has more moisture than the low-moisture kind used on most pizzas}.

Mph is the abbreviation for miles per hour, a unit measuring speed or velocity. Speed limits, wind speeds, and vehicle performance are commonly expressed in mph: {The highway speed limit is 65 mph}. In countries using the metric system, kilometers per hour (kph) serves the same function.

Muah is a written representation of the sound of a kiss, used playfully or affectionately in text messages and online communication: {Muah! Love you!} It mimics the exaggerated smacking sound of an air kiss or a kiss blown to someone. Sometimes spelled mwah.

Muahahaha is the written form of a stereotypical villain's laugh—deep, theatrical, and sinister. It appears in comics, fiction, and casual writing to signal mock-evil glee or cartoonish menace: {Muahahaha, my plan is working perfectly}. The spelling varies by how many "ha"s the writer includes. Often used ironically to accompany minor mischief or petty victories.

Much indicates a large quantity or degree. It modifies verbs {(I don't sleep much)}, adjectives {(much better)}, and stands alone as a pronoun {(Much remains unknown)}. Much typically appears in negative constructions and questions; in positive statements, *a lot* often sounds more natural. {How much does it cost?} {That's too much.} {Much as I'd like to help, I can't.} As an adjective, much is somewhat formal: {much deliberation}, {much ado}.

Muck is wet, dirty matter—mud, manure, or any foul-smelling filth. Farmers spread muck as fertilizer. To muck out a stable is to clean it. Figuratively, muck is anything degrading or corrupt: {The tabloids love to rake muck}. To muck about (British) is to waste time or fool around. To muck something up is to ruin it through carelessness.

Mucking is digging, clearing, or working with muck—wet dirt, manure, or debris. You muck out a stable by removing soiled bedding. In mining, mucking is clearing broken rock from a tunnel. The word extends to messy or aimless activity: {Stop mucking around and get to work}. To muck something up is to ruin it through carelessness.

To muckrake is to search for and expose misconduct by prominent people or institutions, especially through investigative journalism. The term carries mixed connotations—admirable when revealing genuine corruption, dismissive when implying the investigator is more interested in scandal than truth. A muckraker digs for dirt: {The reporter muckraked her way through city hall records}.

A muckraker is a journalist or writer who investigates and exposes corruption, scandal, or wrongdoing—especially by powerful institutions or public figures. The term emerged in early twentieth-century America for reporters who uncovered corporate abuses and political graft: {The muckrakers revealed unsafe conditions in meatpacking plants}. Though originally dismissive, the label became a badge of honor for investigative journalists.

Muckrakers were early 20th-century American journalists who exposed corruption, scandal, and social injustice in business and government. The term, originally dismissive, became a badge of honor. Their investigative reporting on unsafe food, monopolies, and political machines helped spark Progressive Era reforms. The word now applies to any journalist who digs up institutional wrongdoing: {Modern muckrakers uncovered the company's toxic waste dumping}.

Muckraking is journalism that exposes corruption, scandal, or wrongdoing—especially by powerful institutions or public figures. The term originated in the early 1900s for reporters who investigated corporate abuses and political graft. Though initially disparaging (raking through muck), it became a badge of honor: {Her muckraking brought down the mayor}. The practice continues as investigative journalism.

Mucus is the slippery, viscous secretion produced by membranes lining body passages—the nose, throat, lungs, and digestive tract. It traps dust, bacteria, and other particles, protecting underlying tissues. When you're sick, mucus production increases: {My nose won't stop running}. The adjective is mucous, as in {mucous membrane}.

Mud is wet, soft earth—soil mixed with water to form a thick, sticky substance. Children play in it, vehicles get stuck in it, and it spatters everything. Mud has associations with filth and lowliness: to {drag someone's name through the mud} is to damage their reputation, and {mud-slinging} is making malicious accusations. {Clear as mud} means not clear at all. In cosmetics, a mud mask uses mineral-rich clay for skin treatment.

A mudbath is a treatment in which someone immerses themselves in warm mud, typically at a spa, for therapeutic or cosmetic purposes. The mud is believed to draw out impurities and soothe aching muscles. Figuratively, mudbath describes any situation that becomes extremely messy or dirty: {The rugby match turned into a mudbath after the rain started}. It can also characterize a nasty public dispute involving insults and accusations: {The campaign descended into a mudbath}.

Muddied means made muddy or unclear. Water becomes muddied when sediment stirs up; shoes get muddied on wet trails. The figurative sense dominates: {The scandal muddied his reputation}. To muddy the waters is to make a situation more confusing, often deliberately: {Her testimony only muddied the waters further}.

Muddies is the third-person singular present tense of muddy, used as a verb. To muddy something is to make it muddy—covered or splashed with mud—or to make it unclear or confused: {The new evidence muddies the investigation}. The phrase {muddies the waters} is especially common, describing actions or information that make a situation harder to understand rather than clearer.

Mudding refers to recreational off-road driving through mud, typically in trucks, ATVs, or other rugged vehicles: {We went mudding after the storm}. The activity prizes getting dirty and testing a vehicle's traction. Mudding also describes applying joint compound to drywall seams during construction—smoothing mud over tape to create seamless walls.

Muddle describes a state of confusion or disorder, whether mental or physical. If you're in a muddle, you're bewildered or your affairs are disorganized: {I'm in a muddle about what to do next}. To muddle something is to mix it up confusedly or bungle it. In bartending, however, to muddle means to crush ingredients like mint or fruit in the bottom of a glass to release their flavors. If you muddle through, you manage to cope despite confusion or lack of skill.

Muddled means confused, disordered, or mixed up. A muddled {explanation} lacks clarity. Someone with muddled {thinking} can't reason straight. In bartending, muddled describes ingredients crushed together to release flavor: {muddled mint in a mojito}. To be muddled is to be in a state of mental fog: {I was still muddled from sleep}.

Muddles is the verb form of muddle, meaning to confuse, mix up, or handle clumsily. Someone who muddles through a task manages it despite confusion or lack of skill: {She muddles through the recipe without measuring anything}. To muddle things together is to jumble or blur distinctions between them: {He always muddles the twins' names}. In bartending, one muddles mint or fruit by crushing it in the glass.

Muddling is mixing or mashing ingredients together, especially in cocktail-making where a bartender crushes herbs, fruit, or sugar in the bottom of a glass: {muddling mint for a mojito}. More broadly, muddling is working through something in a confused or disorganized way: {We're muddling through the new software}, {muddling along without a clear plan}.

Muddy describes something covered with or consisting of mud—wet, soft earth: {muddy boots}, {a muddy field}. The word extends to anything lacking clarity or purity: muddy {water} is clouded with sediment, muddy {colors} are dull and brownish, muddy {thinking} is confused. To muddy something is to make it unclear: {The new evidence only muddied the situation}.

Muddying is making something muddy—stirring up sediment in water, tracking dirt across a floor. The figurative sense dominates: to muddy is to make unclear or confused. {Stop muddying the issue with irrelevant details.} To {muddy the waters} is to deliberately obscure a situation that was previously clear.

A mudflat is a stretch of muddy land exposed at low tide, typically found along coastlines or estuaries. Mudflats teem with invertebrates and serve as feeding grounds for shorebirds: {We walked across the mudflat at dawn, watching sandpipers probe the mud}. The surface ranges from firm to treacherously soft.

Mudflats are flat expanses of mud exposed at low tide along coastlines and estuaries. These tidal zones support distinctive ecosystems—shellfish, worms, and the shorebirds that feed on them. The surface appears barren but teems with life beneath. {We walked across the mudflats at dawn, watching sandpipers probe the muck.}

A mudflow is a fast-moving mass of mud, water, and debris flowing downhill, often triggered by heavy rain, volcanic activity, or rapid snowmelt. Mudflows can carry boulders and destroy structures in their path: {The mudflow buried several homes after the wildfire stripped the hillside of vegetation}. Volcanic mudflows are sometimes called lahars.

A mudlark is someone who scavenges in river mud for items of value, particularly along the Thames in London. Historically, mudlarks were among the poorest members of Victorian society, often children, who picked through tidal mud for coal, rope, metal, or anything sellable. Today the term describes hobbyists who search riverbanks for historical artifacts, coins, and curiosities, typically with permits. {The mudlark found a Roman coin embedded in the clay.}

A mudpie is a mound of mud shaped by children at play, imitating the form of a pie or cake: {The kids spent all afternoon making mudpies in the backyard}. The word also names a chocolate dessert—typically a rich, dense confection with an Oreo crust, resembling actual mud in color and texture.

Mudpies are mixtures of mud and water that children shape into pie-like forms during outdoor play. The activity requires no equipment beyond dirt and water, making it a universal childhood pastime: {The kids spent all afternoon making mudpies in the backyard}. Figuratively, something dismissed as worthless or amateurish might be compared to mudpies.

A mudroom is a small room or entryway near a home's exterior door, designed for removing and storing dirty shoes, wet coats, and outdoor gear before entering the main living space. Common in colder climates where tracking in snow, mud, or rain is a concern: {Leave your boots in the mudroom}.

A mudroom is a small room or entryway near a home's exterior door, designed for removing and storing dirty shoes, wet coats, and outdoor gear before entering the main living space. Common in colder climates, mudrooms typically feature hooks, benches, and storage cubbies: {We added a mudroom off the garage to keep the snow and mess contained}.

A mudskipper is a fish that can survive out of water, using its pectoral fins to crawl across mud flats and mangrove shores. These tropical fish breathe through their skin when exposed to air and can even climb low branches. {Mudskippers were flopping across the tidal flat at low tide.}

Mudskippers are small fish that can survive out of water for extended periods, using their pectoral fins to crawl across mud flats and even climb rocks or mangrove roots. Found in tropical and subtropical coastal regions, they breathe through their skin and gill chambers when on land. {Mudskippers were flopping around the tidal pools at low tide.}

A mudslide is a mass of mud and debris sliding down a slope, typically triggered by heavy rain saturating hillsides. Mudslides can be devastating to communities in their path: {The mudslide buried several homes}. A mudslide is also a cocktail made with vodka, coffee liqueur, and Irish cream—named for its brown, creamy appearance.

Mudslides are flows of mud, rock, and debris down a slope, often triggered by heavy rain or earthquakes. The term also names a cocktail made with vodka, coffee liqueur, and Irish cream—sweet, creamy, and often blended with ice: {We ordered mudslides at the beach bar}.

A mudslinger is someone who makes malicious or scandalous attacks on an opponent, especially in politics. The term evokes literally throwing mud—messy, undignified, and meant to soil the target's reputation: {The campaign devolved into mudslinging between the candidates}. The related noun mudslinging describes this practice.

Mudslingers are people who make malicious or scandalous attacks on others, especially in political contexts. The term evokes literally throwing mud—getting someone dirty with accusations whether true or not. {The campaign devolved into a contest between mudslingers.} Mudslinging is the practice; to sling mud is to engage in it.

Mudslinging is the practice of making malicious or scandalous attacks against an opponent, especially in politics. The metaphor suggests throwing dirt to make someone look bad: {The campaign descended into mudslinging}. The word implies the attacks are unfair, exaggerated, or irrelevant to substantive issues. Someone who engages in this is a mudslinger.

Mudwrestling is wrestling in a pit of mud, typically as entertainment rather than serious athletic competition. It became a fixture of bars and novelty events in the late 20th century, often featuring women in bikinis: {The club advertised Friday night mudwrestling}. The mess is the point—spectacle over sport.

Muenster is a mild, smooth-textured cheese with an orange rind, originally modeled on French Munster but developed as a distinctly American variety. It melts well, making it popular for sandwiches and burgers: {a grilled cheese with muenster}. The spelling with "ue" distinguishes the American cheese from its European ancestor. (Capitalized Muenster is a city in Germany.)

Muesli is a breakfast cereal of uncooked rolled oats mixed with dried fruit, nuts, and seeds, typically eaten with milk or yogurt. It originated in Switzerland as a health food. Unlike granola, muesli isn't baked or sweetened: {She soaked her muesli overnight in almond milk}.

A muff is a warm tube of fur or fabric in which to place one's hands: {She carried a fur muff in winter}. To muff is to handle clumsily or bungle: {He muffed the catch}. {She muffed her lines}. In vulgar slang, muff means the female genitals, particularly with pubic hair—perhaps from resemblance to a fur muff: {muff diving} (performing oral sex on a woman).

A muffaletta is a large round sandwich from New Orleans, made on a dense sesame-seeded Italian bread and filled with layers of Italian cold cuts, cheese, and olive salad—a tangy mix of chopped olives, vegetables, and oil that soaks into the bread. The sandwich is typically quartered and served at room temperature: {We split a muffaletta at Central Grocery}.
Muffed is the past tense of muff, meaning bungled: {She muffed the presentation}. {He muffed an easy ground ball}.

A muffin is a small, round baked good, typically sweet and studded with fruit or chocolate chips: {blueberry muffin}, {bran muffin}. American muffins rise into a domed top and are eaten as breakfast or snacks. English muffins are flatter, yeast-leavened, and split for toasting. A {muffin top} is the roll of flesh that spills over tight waistbands—named for its resemblance to the baked good.

Muffins are small, rounded quick breads typically baked in individual cup-shaped molds. American-style muffins are soft and cake-like, often studded with blueberries, chocolate chips, or nuts, and eaten as breakfast items or snacks. English muffins are flatter, denser, and split horizontally for toasting. {I grabbed a blueberry muffin with my coffee.} In British slang, muffin top refers to flesh that spills over tight waistbands.

Muffle means to wrap or cover something to deaden sound, reduce clarity, or provide warmth. A scarf muffles your face against cold; thick walls muffle noise from outside. Muffled sounds are quieter and less distinct: {We heard muffled voices through the door}. Figuratively, to muffle is to suppress or restrain: {The regime muffled dissent}.

Muffled describes sound that has been deadened, dampened, or made indistinct—as if passing through a barrier: {muffled voices through the wall}, {a muffled explosion in the distance}. The word suggests something heard but not clearly, often implying physical obstruction or deliberate suppression. A muffled cry might come through a closed door or a hand pressed over a mouth.

A muffler is a device that reduces noise or provides warmth. On vehicles, the muffler is the part of the exhaust system that dampens engine sound: {The car needs a new muffler—you can hear it coming from a block away}. A muffler is also a warm scarf wrapped around the neck and lower face, now somewhat old-fashioned in this sense.

Mufflers are devices that reduce noise or muffle sound. The primary sense is the component in a vehicle's exhaust system that quiets engine noise: {The car needs a new muffler}. In older or British usage, a muffler is a warm scarf worn around the neck and lower face—something that muffles both cold and sound.

A mug is a sturdy drinking vessel with a handle, typically used for hot beverages: {a coffee mug}, {a beer mug}. Mug is also slang for face: {What a mug!} To mug is to attack and rob someone on the street, or to make exaggerated facial expressions, especially for a camera: {He mugged for the photos}. A mug shot is a police photograph of someone's face.

A mugcake is a single-serving cake mixed and baked in a mug, typically in a microwave. The format allows for quick preparation—a few minutes from craving to eating—without heating an oven or dirtying multiple dishes: {I made a chocolate mugcake while watching TV}. Recipes proliferate online, ranging from basic to elaborate.

Mugged is the past tense of mug, which means to assault someone in a public place with intent to rob them: {She was mugged on her way home from work}. Mugged also describes making exaggerated facial expressions, especially for a camera or audience: {He mugged for the photographers on the red carpet}.

A mugger is someone who attacks and robs people in public places, typically using threats or violence: {The mugger grabbed her purse and ran}. The word implies street crime—an ambush rather than burglary or fraud. Muggers target vulnerable victims in isolated spots. To mug is to commit such a robbery.

Muggers is the plural of mugger—a person who attacks and robs people in public places, typically with violence or the threat of it: {The park became known for muggers after dark}. In South Asian contexts, a mugger is also a broad-snouted freshwater crocodile.

Mugginess is oppressively humid warmth—the quality of air that feels thick, damp, and stifling. The word captures that sticky discomfort when heat combines with moisture: {The mugginess made it hard to breathe}. Summer in humid climates is defined by mugginess.

Mugging is robbery with violence or threat of violence, typically in a public place: {She was mugged on the subway platform}. The crime implies a sudden attack by strangers rather than planned theft. A mugging is an instance of this crime. Separately, mugging means making exaggerated facial expressions, especially for a camera or audience: {The comedian was mugging for the crowd}.

Muggings are attacks in which someone is robbed, typically in a public place and often with violence or the threat of it. The word emphasizes the opportunistic, street-level nature of the crime: {Muggings have increased in the subway system}. A mugging usually involves direct confrontation rather than stealth.

A muggle is someone outside a particular group or subculture who lacks specialized knowledge. The word originated in the Harry Potter books, where it means a person without magical powers. From there it spread to other communities—geocachers use it for non-players who might stumble upon a cache, and various hobbyist groups apply it to outsiders: {We had to wait for the muggles to leave before we could search for the geocache}. The tone ranges from affectionate to mildly dismissive. (Capitalized Muggle appears in Harry Potter contexts.)

Muggles are people without magical abilities, from the Harry Potter series. The term has spread beyond the books to describe anyone outside a particular group or unfamiliar with specialized knowledge: {The technical jargon went right over the muggles' heads}. In geocaching, muggles are non-players who might stumble upon hidden caches.

Muggy describes weather that is warm and unpleasantly humid—the kind of heavy, damp air that makes you feel sticky and uncomfortable: {a muggy August afternoon}. The word almost always refers to atmospheric conditions rather than other forms of heat or moisture.

Mugs is the plural of mug—a sturdy drinking vessel with a handle, typically for hot beverages: {coffee mugs}, {beer mugs}. Mug is also slang for face: {an ugly mug}. The verb mug means to assault and rob someone, or to make exaggerated facial expressions: {mugging for the camera}. A mug shot is a police photograph of someone's face.

A mugshot is a photograph taken by police when someone is arrested, typically showing the face from the front and in profile. The term combines mug (slang for face) with shot (photograph). Mugshots are official records but often surface publicly, carrying connotations of criminality or disgrace: {His mugshot was all over the news}.

Mugshots are photographs taken by law enforcement when someone is arrested, showing the face from the front and in profile. The term extends to any unflattering identification photo: {My driver's license photo looks like a mugshot}. Mugshot websites controversially publish arrest photos, sometimes demanding payment for removal.

Mujahadeen (also mujahideen, mujahedin) are Islamic guerrilla fighters engaged in jihad—holy war or struggle. The term gained prominence during the Soviet-Afghan War (1979–1989), when Western governments supported Afghan mujahadeen resisting Soviet occupation: {The CIA funneled weapons to the mujahadeen}. The word has since applied to various Islamist militant groups across the Middle East and beyond.

Mujaheddin are Muslim guerrilla fighters, particularly those who wage jihad—holy war in defense of Islam. The term gained wide currency during the Soviet-Afghan War (1979–1989), when U.S.-backed Afghan mujaheddin fought Soviet forces: {The mujaheddin controlled the mountain passes}. Also spelled mujahideen or mujahedin.

Mujahedeen are Islamic guerrilla fighters engaged in jihad, or holy war. The term gained wide currency during the Soviet-Afghan War (1979–1989), when U.S.-backed Afghan mujahedeen fought Soviet forces. The singular is mujahid. Various spellings exist: mujahideen, mujahedin, mujahidin. {The mujahedeen controlled the mountain passes.}

Mujahedin are Muslim guerrilla fighters engaged in jihad—armed struggle in defense of Islam. The term gained wide English use during the Soviet-Afghan War (1979–1989), when Western nations supported Afghan mujahedin fighting Soviet occupation. The word carries connotations of holy war and religious duty. Also spelled mujahideen or mujahedeen.

Mujahideen is the plural of mujahid, an Arabic term for those engaged in jihad—armed struggle in defense of Islam. The word gained wide English use during the Soviet-Afghan War (1979–1989), referring to Afghan fighters resisting Soviet occupation: {The CIA funneled weapons to the mujahideen}. It has since applied to various Islamic militant groups. The singular mujahid is rarely used in English.

Mukbang is an online video format where someone eats large quantities of food while talking to the camera. The genre originated in South Korea, where the word combines terms for eating and broadcast. Viewers watch for the sounds of eating, the spectacle of consumption, or companionship during their own meals: {I put on a mukbang while I eat dinner alone}.

Mukbangs are videos or livestreams in which someone eats large quantities of food while talking to viewers. The format originated in South Korea, where eating alone is common and viewers enjoy the virtual companionship. Mukbang hosts often consume enormous portions—whole pizzas, piles of fried chicken, trays of seafood—while chatting, making exaggerated eating sounds, or responding to comments: {I watched mukbangs while eating my sad desk lunch}.

A mukluk is a soft boot traditionally made by Arctic peoples, typically of sealskin or reindeer hide with fur lining. The design keeps feet warm in extreme cold while allowing flexibility for walking on snow and ice. Modern versions use synthetic materials but retain the distinctive soft sole and high ankle: {My mukluks are warmer than any winter boot I've owned}.

Mukluks are soft boots traditionally made by Arctic Indigenous peoples, especially Inuit and Yupik communities. They typically feature sealskin or caribou hide exteriors with fur linings, designed for extreme cold. The term now also applies to commercial winter boots mimicking this style: {She bought a pair of mukluks for the Minnesota winter}.

Mulberries is the plural of mulberry, a fruit resembling an elongated blackberry that grows on trees rather than bushes. The berries range from white to deep purple-black depending on variety. They're sweet when ripe but stain readily: {Her fingers were purple from picking mulberries}. Mulberry trees also famously feed silkworms.

Mulberry is a tree of the genus Morus, cultivated for centuries for its sweet, dark berries and its leaves, which are the primary food source for silkworms. The fruit resembles an elongated blackberry and ranges from white to deep purple-red depending on the species. Mulberry also names the fruit itself and the dark reddish-purple color associated with the ripe berries. {The mulberry tree in our backyard produces more fruit than we can possibly eat.}

Mulch is material spread over soil to retain moisture, suppress weeds, and regulate temperature. Common mulches include wood chips, straw, leaves, and bark. As a verb, to mulch is to apply such a covering: {We mulched the flower beds in spring}. Gardeners also use mulch to improve soil as organic materials decompose.

Mulching is the practice of covering soil with a layer of material—wood chips, straw, leaves, or fabric—to retain moisture, suppress weeds, and regulate temperature. Gardeners mulch around plants in spring or fall: {I spent Saturday mulching the flower beds}. The material itself is mulch; the verb is to mulch.

A mule is the offspring of a male donkey and a female horse—a hybrid animal known for strength, endurance, and stubbornness. Because mules are sterile, the word extends to other hybrids or things that bridge categories. A mule is also a backless slipper or shoe. In drug slang, a mule is someone who transports contraband, especially across borders: {She was arrested as a drug mule at the airport}.

Mules are the offspring of a male donkey and a female horse—sterile hybrids prized for their endurance and sure-footedness. The word extends to other hybrids and to stubborn people: {stubborn as a mule}. A mule is also a backless slipper or shoe. In drug slang, a mule is someone who smuggles contraband, especially by carrying it on or inside their body: {The cartel used mules to move cocaine across the border}.

Mull means to think over at length, to ponder or consider carefully: {She mulled the offer for a week before accepting}, {I need time to mull it over}. The thinking is slow and ruminative rather than decisive. Separately, to mull wine or cider is to heat it with spices and sweeteners—mulled wine is a holiday staple. The two senses are unrelated.

A mullah is a Muslim cleric or religious teacher, particularly in Shia Islam and in regions like Iran, Afghanistan, and South Asia. The title indicates someone learned in Islamic theology and law who may lead prayers, teach scripture, or interpret religious texts. In Western usage, mullah sometimes carries connotations of rigid orthodoxy: {The ruling mullahs banned music from the airwaves}.

Mullahs is the plural of mullah, a Muslim religious leader or teacher, particularly in Shia Islam. The term applies especially to clergy in Iran and other parts of the Middle East and South Asia. In Western usage, it often carries political connotations, referring to religious authorities who hold or influence governmental power: {rule by the mullahs}, {the mullahs in Tehran}.

Mulled describes a beverage that has been heated with spices, sugar, and sometimes citrus: {mulled wine}, {mulled cider}. The preparation typically includes cinnamon, cloves, and nutmeg, creating a warming drink associated with cold weather and holidays. Separately, to mull something over is to think about it carefully: {I mulled over the decision for weeks}.

A mullet is a hairstyle cut short on the top and sides but left long in the back—famously described as "business in the front, party in the back." Popular in the 1980s, it became a cultural punchline but never fully disappeared: {He's still rocking the mullet}. Separately, mullet is a type of thick-bodied fish found in coastal waters worldwide.

Mullets are fish prized as food in many cuisines, found in coastal and brackish waters worldwide. The word also names a hairstyle short on the sides and top but long in back—business in front, party in back. The hairstyle became iconic in the 1980s and has cycled between fashion statement and punchline ever since: {He's still rocking a mullet}.

A mulligan is a do-over, especially in golf—a second shot granted informally after a poor first attempt, not counted against the score. The term has spread beyond golf to mean any second chance: {Life doesn't give you mulligans}. Mulligans are understood as friendly accommodations, not official rules. (Capitalized Mulligan is a surname.)
clues: Pretend that first swing never happened

definition: Mulligans are do-overs, especially the informal golf practice of replaying a poor shot without penalty. The term extends beyond golf to any second chance: {Life doesn't give you mulligans}. In casual card games, a mulligan lets you redraw a bad starting hand. The word carries a sense of forgiveness for mistakes—an unofficial grace period that strict rules wouldn't allow.
Mulligatawny is a spiced soup of Anglo-Indian origin that is sometimes served as a first course.

Mulling is the process of thinking something over carefully, turning it around in your mind: {I've been mulling the offer for days}. Often paired with over: {She mulled over her options before deciding}. Separately, mulling refers to heating and spicing a beverage, especially wine or cider: {mulled wine}, {mulling spices}.

Multicolored means having many colors: {a multicolored scarf}, {multicolored confetti}. The word suggests variety and brightness rather than a specific number—two colors wouldn't typically qualify, but three or more would. Also spelled multicoloured in British English.

Multicultural describes the presence or inclusion of multiple cultural traditions within a single society, institution, or space. A multicultural {neighborhood} has residents from diverse ethnic backgrounds. Multicultural {education} incorporates perspectives from various cultures. The term often carries positive connotations of diversity and inclusion, though critics sometimes use it dismissively to suggest superficial acknowledgment of difference without meaningful integration.

Multiculturalism is the view that different cultures can and should coexist within a single society, each maintaining its distinct identity rather than assimilating into a dominant culture. The term describes both a social reality and a political stance: {Canada embraces multiculturalism as official policy}. Critics use it dismissively to suggest naive tolerance or cultural fragmentation: {Multiculturalism has failed}. The adjective is multicultural: {a multicultural neighborhood}.

Multigenerational means involving or spanning multiple generations of a family or group. A multigenerational {household} includes grandparents, parents, and children living together. Multigenerational {wealth} passes down through successive generations. The term often appears in discussions of family structure, housing, and inherited advantages or trauma.

A multihyphenate is someone who works across multiple creative professions—actor-writer-director, singer-songwriter-producer. The term references the hyphens joining these roles: {She's a true multihyphenate, juggling film, music, and fashion}. The word often carries admiration for versatility, though it can suggest dilettantism when someone spreads themselves too thin.

Multilingual means using or able to use several languages: {a multilingual dictionary}, {multilingual staff}. A multilingual person speaks multiple languages; a multilingual country has several official or commonly spoken languages. The word applies to people, places, documents, or services that operate across language boundaries.
clues: Able to converse in several languages

definition: Multimedia combines multiple forms of content—text, images, audio, video, animation—into a single presentation or product. The term emerged with digital technology, where a multimedia {presentation} or {website} integrates various media types that users can interact with. As an adjective, it describes anything involving this combination: {multimedia journalism}, {multimedia artist}. The word sometimes feels dated, as blending media has become standard rather than novel.

Multinational describes things involving multiple nations or countries. A multinational {corporation} operates across national borders, with subsidiaries or divisions in several countries. Multinational {forces} combine troops from different nations. As a noun, a multinational is a company with operations worldwide: {The multinationals dominate the oil industry}.

Multinationals are corporations that operate in multiple countries, with headquarters in one nation and subsidiaries, factories, or offices in others. The term often carries connotations of vast economic power and influence: {Multinationals have more resources than some governments}. Also called multinational corporations or MNCs.

Multiplatinum describes a music recording that has been certified platinum multiple times, indicating sales of two million or more copies. The threshold varies by country, but the term always signals exceptional commercial success: {Their multiplatinum debut album launched them to stardom}. A multiplatinum artist has achieved this level of sales with one or more releases.

Multiplayer describes games or activities designed for more than one participant, typically connected through a network: {multiplayer online games}, {multiplayer mode}. The term emerged with video gaming but applies broadly to any shared interactive experience. As a noun, it names the format itself: {I prefer multiplayer to single-player campaigns}.

Multiple means more than one, often suggesting several or many: {multiple choice}, {multiple injuries}, {multiple witnesses}. It emphasizes quantity without specifying an exact number. As a noun, a multiple is a number that contains another number a whole number of times—twelve is a multiple of three. {She made multiple attempts before succeeding.}

Multiples are quantities that contain another quantity a whole number of times. Six is a multiple of three; twelve is a multiple of both three and four. In finance, multiples are ratios used to value companies: {The stock trades at a multiple of fifteen times earnings}. In pregnancy, multiples refers to twins, triplets, or more: {She's expecting multiples}.

Multiplex combines the idea of many with the idea of folding or layering. A multiplex cinema contains multiple screening rooms under one roof, and this is now the word's most common noun sense. As an adjective, multiplex describes systems with multiple components or channels operating simultaneously. In telecommunications and electronics, to multiplex is to combine several signals into one for transmission, then separate them at the receiving end. {The theater was an old single-screen that got converted into a multiplex.}

Multiplication is the mathematical operation of combining quantities by repeated addition: three times four means adding three fours together. The notation uses × or · between numbers, or simple juxtaposition in algebra. Beyond arithmetic, multiplication describes any rapid increase: {the multiplication of cells}, {the multiplication of problems}. The verb is multiply.

Multiplied is the past tense of multiply—to increase in number or amount, or to perform multiplication. {The bacteria multiplied rapidly overnight.} {She multiplied twelve by seven.} Something that has multiplied has grown or been calculated: {Our problems have multiplied since then.}

A multiplier is something that multiplies—increases or amplifies an effect. In arithmetic, it's the number by which another is multiplied: in 3 × 4, the multiplier is 3. In economics, the multiplier effect describes how spending ripples through an economy, each dollar generating additional activity. In games and scoring systems, a multiplier increases points earned: {The combo gave me a 2x multiplier}. More broadly, anything that amplifies results: {Social media is a multiplier for both good ideas and bad ones}.

Multipliers are factors that increase or amplify something. In arithmetic, a multiplier is the number by which another is multiplied. In economics, the multiplier effect describes how initial spending generates additional economic activity: {Government investment has a multiplier effect on employment}. More broadly, anything that amplifies results qualifies: {Leverage is a multiplier of both gains and losses}.

To multiply is to increase in number or amount. In arithmetic, multiplying combines quantities: {three multiplied by four equals twelve}. Living things multiply by reproduction: {Bacteria multiply rapidly in warm conditions}. Problems, difficulties, and opportunities also multiply—they grow more numerous: {Our troubles multiplied after the factory closed}. The adverb multiply means in multiple ways: {multiply disadvantaged}.

Multiplying is increasing in number or amount, often rapidly or repeatedly. Bacteria multiply by dividing. Rabbits multiply prodigiously. Problems multiply when ignored. In arithmetic, multiplying is the operation of combining quantities: {What do you get when you multiply six by seven?} The word suggests growth through repetition or reproduction.

Multiracial describes a person whose ancestry includes two or more racial backgrounds, or something that involves or is designed for people of multiple races. A multiracial {family} might include members of different racial identities, while a multiracial {society} encompasses diverse racial groups. The term gained prominence as census categories expanded and more people began identifying with multiple racial heritages rather than checking a single box. {She identifies as multiracial, with Black and Asian heritage.}

To multitask is to handle multiple tasks simultaneously or in rapid alternation. Computers multitask by running several programs at once. People multitask by juggling activities—answering emails while on a conference call, cooking dinner while helping with homework. Research suggests human multitasking often reduces efficiency: {I can't multitask like I used to}.

Multitasking is doing multiple things at once, or switching rapidly between tasks. Computers multitask by running several programs simultaneously. People multitask less efficiently than they imagine—studies suggest the brain handles sequential attention rather than true parallel processing: {I was multitasking during the meeting and missed half of what was said}. The word often appears as a verb: {She multitasked her way through the workday}.

A multitool is a compact device combining several tools in one unit—typically pliers, knife blades, screwdrivers, and other implements that fold into a handle. Swiss Army knives and Leatherman tools are iconic examples. {I always keep a multitool in my glove box.} The term extends to software or games offering multiple functions in one package.

A multitool is a single handheld device combining multiple implements—typically pliers, knife blades, screwdrivers, and other tools folded into a compact body. Leatherman and Swiss Army knives are iconic examples. The term extends to software or systems that consolidate many functions: {This app is a multitool for video editing}.

A multitude is a large number of people or things: {A multitude of factors contributed to the collapse}. The word often suggests an uncountable mass rather than a specific quantity. {The multitude} can refer to ordinary people as a collective—the masses, the crowd: {Politicians who claim to speak for the multitude}.

Multitudes means large numbers of people or things. A politician addresses {the multitudes}. {Multitudes of birds} darken the sky. The word carries slightly more literary or biblical weight than crowds or masses. The phrase {contain multitudes} (from Whitman) describes someone with contradictory or complex aspects: {I contain multitudes}.

The multiverse is a hypothetical collection of multiple universes, including our own, that together comprise all of physical reality. The concept appears in theoretical physics, where it emerges from quantum mechanics and cosmology, and in fiction, where parallel worlds allow alternate versions of characters and events: {In the multiverse, there's a timeline where you made a different choice}. Comic books and films frequently use multiverse storytelling to explore "what if" scenarios.

Multiverses is the plural of multiverse, a theoretical framework proposing that our universe is one of many—possibly infinite—universes existing simultaneously. The concept appears in physics (particularly quantum mechanics and cosmology) and in fiction, where characters traverse alternate realities: {The film explores multiverses where different versions of the protagonist made different choices}.

A multivitamin is a dietary supplement containing multiple vitamins and often minerals in a single pill, tablet, or gummy. People take multivitamins to fill nutritional gaps in their diet: {I take a multivitamin every morning}. Whether they provide meaningful health benefits for people with adequate diets remains debated.

Multivitamins are dietary supplements combining multiple vitamins and often minerals in a single pill, tablet, or gummy. They're marketed as nutritional insurance for people who may not get enough nutrients from food alone: {I take a multivitamin every morning}. Whether they provide meaningful health benefits for well-nourished people remains debated.

Mum means silent or not speaking. To {keep mum} is to say nothing, especially about a secret: {She kept mum about the surprise party}. The phrase {mum's the word} urges secrecy. Separately, mum is British and Australian informal for mother: {I'm visiting my mum this weekend}. A mum is also a chrysanthemum, commonly grown for autumn displays. (Capitalized Mum is a form of address.)

To mumble is to speak indistinctly, with the mouth partially closed or words running together: {He mumbled an apology and left}. Mumbling makes speech hard to understand—the opposite of speaking clearly. As a noun, a mumble is such indistinct speech: {His response was an inaudible mumble}. The word can suggest shyness, reluctance, or simply poor articulation.

Mumbled is the past tense of mumble, meaning to speak in a low, indistinct voice without clearly articulating words. Someone who mumbles keeps their mouth relatively closed or speaks too softly to be understood: {He mumbled an apology and left}. {She mumbled something under her breath}.

Mumbles is speech that's low, indistinct, or hard to understand—words spoken without clear articulation: {I couldn't make out his mumbles from across the room}. As a verb form, someone who mumbles speaks unclearly, often from nervousness, reluctance, or inattention: {She mumbles when she's embarrassed}.

Mumbling is speaking in a low, indistinct voice, often with the mouth partially closed so words run together: {Stop mumbling and speak up}. Someone who mumbles may be nervous, embarrassed, or simply not making an effort to be understood. The word can also describe any low, indistinct sound: {the mumbling of distant thunder}.

Mummers are performers in traditional folk plays or processions, typically wearing masks or costumes and acting out stylized dramas. The tradition survives most visibly in Philadelphia's annual Mummers Parade, where elaborately costumed groups compete in music, dance, and comic performances on New Year's Day. Historically, mummers went door to door performing short plays, often at Christmas.

Mummies is the plural of mummy, which has two distinct meanings. A mummy is a preserved corpse, either through ancient embalming practices like those of Egypt or through natural desiccation. The word also serves as British English for mother, equivalent to American "mommy": {The mummies picked up their children from school}. Context usually makes clear which sense is intended.

Mummification is the process of preserving a body after death, either through deliberate treatment or natural conditions. The ancient Egyptians perfected artificial mummification, removing organs and applying preservatives to prepare bodies for the afterlife. Natural mummification occurs when extreme cold, dryness, or acidic conditions prevent decay: {The desert heat caused natural mummification of the remains}. The word extends to any drying or shriveling that resembles this preservation: {mummification of plant tissue}.

Mummified describes a body preserved from decay, either through deliberate embalming (as in ancient Egypt) or natural desiccation. The flesh dries out rather than rotting: {The desert heat had mummified the corpse}. Figuratively, mummified suggests something dried up, shriveled, or frozen in time: {mummified traditions}, {a mummified bureaucracy resistant to change}.

To mummify is to preserve a body by drying it out, preventing decay. The ancient Egyptians mummified their dead through elaborate processes involving removal of organs and application of resins. The word extends to any extreme desiccation: {The desert heat had mummified the carcass}. Figuratively, something mummified is preserved but lifeless—frozen in an outdated form.

Mummifying is preserving a body by drying it out and treating it to prevent decay. The ancient Egyptians mummified their dead as preparation for the afterlife, wrapping them in linen after removing organs and applying resins. The word extends to any extreme desiccation: {The desert heat had mummified the carcass}. Figuratively, something mummified is preserved but lifeless—frozen in an earlier state.

A mummy is a dead body preserved from decay, either through deliberate embalming (as in ancient Egypt) or natural conditions like extreme cold or dryness. The word also means mother in British child speech and informal usage: {I want my mummy}. To mummify is to preserve a body or become dried and shriveled.

Mumps is a contagious viral disease characterized by painful swelling of the salivary glands, especially those near the jaw. The disease primarily affects children, causing fever, headache, and the distinctive puffy-cheeked appearance. Mumps has become rare in countries with widespread vaccination. The word is grammatically plural but takes a singular verb: {Mumps is no longer common}.

Mums is the plural of mum, the informal British term for mother: {The mums waited outside the school gates}. In American English, mums more often refers to chrysanthemums, the flowering plants popular in fall gardens and decorations: {She planted mums along the front walk}.

Munch is to chew steadily and often audibly, usually on something crunchy or substantial: {She munched on carrot sticks while reading}. The word suggests casual, unhurried eating rather than a formal meal. The munchies, in slang, refers to hunger pangs, especially the craving for snacks associated with marijuana use.

A munchie is a snack food, especially one eaten to satisfy cravings induced by marijuana use. The word appears almost exclusively in the plural: {I've got the munchies}, {We need some munchies for the party}. The munchies refers both to the craving itself and to the snacks that satisfy it.

The munchies are a craving for snack food, especially the intense hunger that follows marijuana use: {I got the munchies and ate an entire bag of chips}. The word also refers to the snacks themselves: {We need to pick up some munchies for the party}. Both senses are informal.

Munching is eating with a continuous chewing motion, often audibly. The word suggests casual, sustained consumption rather than quick bites: {She sat munching popcorn during the movie}, {He was munching on carrots at his desk}. Munching implies a relaxed, almost absent-minded quality to the eating.

A munchkin is a small person or child, used affectionately: {The munchkins are ready for bed}. The term comes from the diminutive inhabitants of Munchkinland in *The Wizard of Oz*. It often implies cuteness or insignificance. In fantasy gaming, a munchkin is a player who exploits rules to gain unfair advantages, prioritizing winning over storytelling.

Munchkins are the small people Dorothy encounters in *The Wizard of Oz*, inhabitants of Munchkinland. The term extends to any small person, especially a child, used affectionately: {The munchkins are finally asleep}. It can also describe anyone notably short or diminutive. Munchkin is also the name of a breed of short-legged cat.

Mundane describes the ordinary, everyday aspects of life—routine tasks, common concerns, earthly matters as opposed to spiritual or transcendent ones. The word often carries a hint of tedium: {I spent the morning on mundane errands like grocery shopping and paying bills}. Something mundane lacks excitement or novelty. In fantasy and science fiction contexts, mundane distinguishes ordinary humans or the non-magical world from those with special abilities.

Mungbean is a small green legume widely cultivated in Asia, used whole in soups and stews or sprouted to produce bean sprouts. The beans can also be ground into flour or made into noodles. Also spelled as two words: mung bean.

Munitions are military weapons, ammunition, and equipment—the material of war. The term usually appears in plural form and often in compounds: {munitions factory}, {munitions depot}, {munitions dump}. As a verb, to munition is to supply with weapons, though this use is rare. The word emphasizes the industrial and logistical side of warfare rather than combat itself.

Muppet is a trademark for the puppet characters created by Jim Henson, combining features of marionettes and hand puppets. In British slang, muppet means a foolish or incompetent person: {Don't be such a muppet}. The insult is mild and often affectionate, suggesting someone is clumsy or dim rather than malicious.

A mural is a large painting or artwork applied directly to a wall or ceiling. Unlike framed paintings, murals are integral to the architecture: {The building's exterior features a mural depicting the neighborhood's history}. Murals range from ancient frescoes to modern street art. As an adjective, mural means relating to walls: {mural decoration}.

A muralist is an artist who paints murals—large-scale works created directly on walls, ceilings, or other permanent surfaces. The term distinguishes these artists from painters who work on canvas or other portable media: {Diego Rivera remains Mexico's most celebrated muralist}. Muralists often work on public commissions, creating art meant to be seen by communities rather than private collectors.

Murals are large-scale artworks painted or applied directly onto walls, ceilings, or other permanent surfaces. Unlike framed paintings that can be moved, murals become part of the architecture itself. They appear in public spaces like building exteriors, subway stations, and schools, often depicting community themes, historical events, or political messages. {The neighborhood commissioned a mural celebrating local heroes.} Indoor murals in homes or businesses typically serve decorative purposes.

A murder is the malicious killing of one person by another or others. Murder (uncountable) characterizes this crime generally. If you murder someone, you commit a murder. Figurative meanings of murder don’t typically involve death. A task described as murder is difficult and challenging: That chemistry test was murder. If you get away with murder, you escape punishment for wrongdoing. To murder an opponent in a competition is to defeat them soundly.

Murderbots are autonomous or semi-autonomous robots designed or imagined to kill humans. The term appears primarily in science fiction, gaming, and tech commentary—often with dark humor about AI gone wrong: {The company's new drone is basically a murderbot}. It also names a popular sci-fiction book series featuring a self-aware security unit. The compound emphasizes lethal intent over the more clinical "autonomous weapons system."

Murdered is the past tense of murder—to kill someone unlawfully and with intent. The word carries moral weight that "killed" doesn't: {He murdered his business partner for the insurance money}. Informally, murdered can mean defeated decisively {(We got murdered in the finals)} or ruined {(She murdered that song)}.

A murderer is a person who commits murder—the unlawful, deliberate killing of another human being. The term carries moral weight beyond legal designation; calling someone a murderer implies not just that they killed, but that they did so with intent and without justification: {The jury found him guilty, but his family refused to call him a murderer}. Serial murderers kill multiple victims over time. Mass murderers kill many at once.

Murderers is the plural of murderer—people who have unlawfully killed others. The word carries moral weight beyond the legal definition, implying deliberate wrongdoing: {The murderers were sentenced to life in prison}. It extends figuratively to those who destroy something valued: {murderers of the English language}.

A murderess is a female murderer—a woman who has committed murder. The word is old-fashioned; modern usage typically applies murderer to people of any sex. {The tabloids called her a cold-blooded murderess.} Like actress and poetess, the -ess suffix marking female gender has largely fallen out of favor.

Murderous describes someone or something capable of or inclined toward murder: {a murderous rage}, {murderous intent}. It extends to anything potentially deadly or extremely dangerous: {murderous heat}, {a murderous climb}. Informally, murderous intensifies difficulty or unpleasantness: {The traffic was murderous}. A murderous look suggests violent hostility, even without actual threat.

Murders is the plural of murder—unlawful killings with intent. A single person can commit multiple murders; a city tracks its annual murders. The verb form means kills unlawfully: {He murders his rival in the first act}. Informally, murders means defeats decisively or ruins: {She murders that song every time she sings it}.

Murk is darkness or gloom, especially when thick or obscuring: {We peered into the murk of the basement}. The word suggests dimness you can almost feel—fog, smoke, deep water. As an adjective (murky), it describes unclear conditions, literal or figurative: {murky waters}, {murky motives}. The noun is literary; the adjective is common.

Murky describes water or air that is dark and cloudy, difficult to see through: {murky pond water}, {the murky depths}. By extension, murky applies to anything obscure or hard to understand: {murky legal language}, {a murky past}. The word often implies something suspicious or concealed: {murky dealings}, {murky motives}.
clues: Too dark and thick to see

definition: Murmur is a soft, indistinct sound—voices too low to make out clearly, or continuous background noise like wind or water: {a murmur of conversation from the next room}. To murmur is to speak quietly, often intimately or complainingly. A heart murmur is an abnormal sound detected through a stethoscope, indicating turbulent blood flow. {She murmured her agreement.}
clues: Speak so only nearby ears catch

definition: A murmuration is the collective swirling flight of starlings—thousands of birds moving in fluid, shape-shifting patterns across the sky. The word comes from the Latin for murmur, evoking the soft rushing sound of countless wings. By extension, murmuration can describe any low, continuous murmuring sound or the act of murmuring itself, though the starling sense now dominates.

Murmurations are the spectacular aerial displays created when large flocks of starlings move in fluid, shifting patterns across the sky. The birds wheel and pivot in near-perfect synchronization, forming shapes that pulse and transform: {We pulled over to watch the murmuration at dusk}. The word comes from murmur—the collective wingbeats and calls create a soft rushing sound. By extension, murmuration can mean any murmuring or the act of murmuring, though these uses are rare.

Murmured is the past tense of murmur, meaning to speak in a low, soft voice that's barely audible: {She murmured something I couldn't quite hear}. The word suggests intimacy, secrecy, or gentleness—lovers murmur endearments, conspirators murmur plans. It also describes continuous low sounds: {The creek murmured over stones}.

Murmuring is the act of speaking in a low, soft voice, often indistinctly or privately. It can suggest intimacy, secrecy, or discontent depending on context. When people murmur among themselves, there's often an implication of complaint or dissatisfaction: {There was murmuring in the ranks about the new policy}. The word also describes continuous soft sounds, like water or wind: {the murmuring of the brook}. As an adjective, murmuring characterizes something that produces such sounds: {murmuring voices in the next room}.

Murmurings are quiet, indistinct sounds—soft voices, rustling leaves, flowing water. The word often suggests discontent expressed in low tones rather than open protest: {There were murmurings of dissatisfaction among the staff}. Murmurings can also be gentle and pleasant: {the murmurings of a brook}, {lovers' murmurings in the dark}.

Murmurs are soft, indistinct sounds—low voices, rustling leaves, flowing water. People murmur when speaking quietly, often intimately or conspiratorially: {She murmured something in his ear}. Murmurs of discontent suggest quiet but spreading dissatisfaction. In medicine, a heart murmur is an abnormal sound detected through a stethoscope, indicating turbulent blood flow.

Muscle is the tissue in animal bodies that contracts to produce movement. It also means physical strength or power: {He's got the muscle to move that furniture}. Figuratively, muscle is force or influence: {political muscle}, {financial muscle}. To muscle your way somewhere is to push through by force. A muscle car is a high-performance American automobile. To {muscle in} is to intrude by force or threat.

Musclebound describes someone whose muscles are so overdeveloped that they've become stiff and clumsy rather than strong and agile. The term carries a mocking edge—implying that excessive bodybuilding has backfired: {He was so musclebound he could barely scratch his own back}. Figuratively, it can describe anything grown rigid through overdevelopment.

Muscled describes having muscles, especially prominent or well-developed ones: {a muscled torso}, {heavily muscled arms}. The word often appears in compound forms: {well-muscled}, {thickly muscled}. As a verb form, muscled means forced through physical strength or aggressive effort: {He muscled his way through the crowd}, {She muscled into the conversation}.

A musclehead is someone obsessed with building muscle, often to the point where it seems to crowd out intellectual pursuits. The term is mildly derisive, implying that weightlifting has replaced thinking: {Don't ask that musclehead—he spends more time at the gym than the library}. Sometimes used self-deprecatingly by fitness enthusiasts.

Muscleheads are people obsessed with building muscle, often at the expense of intellectual development. The term is mildly derisive, implying that someone has prioritized physical bulk over brainpower: {The gym was full of muscleheads grunting at the squat rack}. Sometimes used self-deprecatingly by fitness enthusiasts.

A muscleman is a man with a heavily developed physique, especially one who displays it professionally—a bodybuilder or strongman performer. The term also means an enforcer or thug employed for intimidation or violence: {The loan shark sent his muscleman to collect the debt}. The two senses share an emphasis on physical power over other qualities.

Musclemen is the plural of muscleman—a man with a heavily developed physique, especially one who displays it professionally as a bodybuilder or strongman. The term also refers to hired enforcers who use physical intimidation: {The loan shark sent his musclemen to collect the debt}.

Muscles are the fibrous tissues in animal bodies that contract and relax to produce movement. The human body contains hundreds of muscles, from the large ones that move limbs to the tiny ones that focus eyes. Beyond anatomy, muscles often stands for physical strength or power: {Put some muscle into it}. Someone who muscles their way through a crowd uses physical force; to muscle in on something is to intrude aggressively where you're not wanted. A person who provides muscle for an operation supplies intimidation or enforcement rather than brains.

Muscular describes anything relating to muscles or characterized by well-developed muscles. A muscular {physique} or muscular {arms} suggest visible strength and fitness. The word extends to things that display power or force: muscular {prose} is vigorous and direct, a muscular {foreign policy} is assertive and aggressive. Muscular dystrophy is a group of genetic diseases causing progressive weakness and loss of muscle mass.

To muse is to think about something in a leisurely, contemplative way: {She mused on what might have been}. The word suggests reflective pondering rather than urgent problem-solving. As a noun, a muse is a source of inspiration, especially for artists and writers—someone or something that sparks creative work: {His wife was his muse for thirty years}. (Capitalized Muse refers to the Greek goddesses of the arts.)

Mused is the past tense of muse, meaning to ponder or reflect thoughtfully, often while speaking: {She mused about what might have been}. In dialogue tags, mused signals contemplative speech—someone thinking aloud rather than simply stating: {"I wonder if it matters," he mused}. The word carries a literary quality, appearing more in novels than conversation.

Muses is the plural of muse—sources of creative inspiration. Artists, writers, and musicians speak of their muses, the people or forces that spark their work: {His muses were the women he loved}. To muse is to ponder or reflect quietly, so muses also means thinks deeply: {She muses on the meaning of life}. (Capitalized Muses are the Greek goddesses of the arts.)

A museum is an institution that collects, preserves, and displays objects of cultural, historical, scientific, or artistic significance. Museums range from vast encyclopedic collections like the Louvre to specialized institutions focused on natural history, modern art, or local heritage. {We spent the afternoon at the museum}. The word can describe any place that feels like a preserved collection: {His office is a museum of 1970s memorabilia}.

Museums are institutions that collect, preserve, and display objects of cultural, historical, scientific, or artistic significance. They range from vast encyclopedic collections like national museums to specialized institutions focused on local history, natural specimens, or single artists. {The city's museums draw millions of visitors annually}. To visit museums is a standard tourist activity; to end up in a museum suggests something is outdated or worthy of preservation.

Mush is soft, thick, shapeless matter—food boiled to a pulp, snow turning to slush, anything reduced to a wet mass: {The vegetables had cooked down to mush}. Figuratively, mush is excessive sentimentality: {The movie's ending was pure mush}. As a command to sled dogs, mush means go or move faster. To mush is to travel by dogsled: {We mushed across the frozen lake}.

Mushed is the past tense of mush, which has two distinct meanings. One mush means to travel over snow with a dog sled: {We mushed across the frozen tundra}. The other means to reduce to a soft, pulpy mass: {She mushed the bananas for the baby}. Something mushed together has been compressed or blended into shapelessness.

A musher is a person who drives a dog sled, commanding a team of sled dogs across snow and ice. The term comes from the French *marche* (walk), which became the command "mush" to urge dogs forward. Mushers compete in races like the Iditarod or work in Arctic regions where dog sledding remains practical transport: {The musher called out commands as the team pulled through the blizzard}.

Mushers are people who drive dog sleds, commanding a team of dogs across snow and ice. The term comes from the French *marche* (walk or go), which became the command "mush" shouted to start the dogs moving. Mushing is both a traditional mode of Arctic transportation and a competitive sport: {The mushers lined up for the Iditarod starting gun}.

Mushing is the sport or practice of traveling over snow with a dog sled. The driver, called a musher, stands on the sled runners and commands a team of dogs: {She's been mushing in Alaska for twenty years}. The term extends to recreational dog sledding and competitive races like the Iditarod. "Mush" as a command to start the dogs may come from French *marche*.

Mushroom refers to the fleshy, spore-bearing fruiting body of a fungus, typically with a cap atop a stalk. Some mushrooms are edible delicacies; others are poisonous. The word extends to anything mushroom-shaped: {a mushroom cloud}. As a verb, to mushroom is to spread or grow rapidly: {The small protest mushroomed into a movement}. {Rumors mushroomed after the announcement}.

Mushrooming describes rapid, expansive growth—like a mushroom appearing seemingly overnight. Costs, populations, or problems can be mushrooming: {mushrooming debt}, {mushrooming suburbs}. The word also means gathering wild mushrooms: {We went mushrooming in the forest after the rain}.

Mushrooms is the plural of mushroom—the fleshy, spore-bearing fruiting body of a fungus, typically with a cap and stem. Some are edible delicacies; others are deadly. The verb mushroom means to spread or multiply rapidly: {The town mushroomed after the railroad arrived}. A mushroom {cloud} describes the distinctive shape of a nuclear explosion.

Mushy describes something soft and pulpy, lacking firmness—overcooked vegetables, rotting fruit, wet ground that squishes underfoot: {The bananas had gone mushy}. Figuratively, mushy means excessively sentimental or romantic: {a mushy love story}, {Don't get all mushy on me}. The figurative sense carries mild derision, suggesting emotion that's gone soft and shapeless.

Music is organized sound, typically involving melody, harmony, rhythm, or some combination. It ranges from folk songs to symphonies, from jazz improvisation to electronic beats. Music can accompany words {(set a poem to music)} or stand alone. To {face the music} is to accept consequences. {Music to my ears} describes welcome news. Someone who is musical has talent for or sensitivity to music.

Musical describes things related to or characterized by music. As an adjective, it can mean pleasing to the ear {a musical voice}, naturally gifted in music {she's very musical}, or simply pertaining to music {musical instruments}. The noun musical—short for musical comedy or musical theater—denotes a stage or film production where characters express themselves through song and dance alongside spoken dialogue. {We saw a musical on Broadway.} The form emerged in the early twentieth century and remains a popular entertainment genre.
clues: Play where characters burst into song

definition: Musicality is sensitivity to music—the intuitive grasp of rhythm, melody, and expression that distinguishes a natural performer from a merely competent one. A dancer with musicality moves in ways that feel inevitable to the music. The term extends beyond performance: {The musicality of her prose made it a pleasure to read aloud}. Someone can have technical skill without musicality, hitting every note correctly while missing the soul of the piece.

Musicals are theatrical productions that combine spoken dialogue with songs and often dance. The form spans Broadway shows, film adaptations, and school productions: {We're going to see a musical tonight}, {She loves old Hollywood musicals}. The term can also refer to people with musical talent: {The whole family is musical}.
clues: Theater where actors burst into song

definition: A musician is someone who plays a musical instrument or composes music, whether professionally or as a hobby. The term applies broadly—from orchestral violinists to bedroom guitarists to electronic producers. Professional musicians may perform live, record in studios, or work as session players backing other artists. {She's been a musician since she picked up the piano at age five.} The word carries no implication of skill level; both beginners and virtuosos qualify.

Musicians are people who play musical instruments or sing, especially as a profession or serious pursuit. The term emphasizes skill and practice rather than casual involvement—someone strumming a guitar at a campfire might not be called a musician, but a session player or orchestra member would be. {The musicians tuned their instruments before the concert.}

Musicianship is skill in playing or performing music—the combination of technical ability, interpretive sensitivity, and artistic judgment that distinguishes accomplished musicians. Beyond hitting the right notes, musicianship encompasses timing, dynamics, phrasing, and the subtle choices that bring music to life: {Her musicianship was evident in every phrase}. The term often implies something beyond mere competence—a deeper understanding of musical expression.
clues: Craft of playing an instrument well

definition: Musing is quiet, reflective thought—the kind of contemplation that wanders without urgency. As a noun, it refers to such thoughts expressed aloud or in writing: {Her musings on mortality filled several journals}. The adjective describes someone absorbed in thought: {He stared out the window with a musing expression}. The verb muse means to ponder or reflect: {She mused about what might have been}.

Musings are thoughts or reflections, usually unhurried and somewhat aimless—the mental wandering that happens when you're not trying to solve anything in particular. The word suggests a contemplative quality: {Her musings on mortality filled the later essays}. Often used for written or spoken reflections shared with others: {The blog contains his musings on parenthood}.

Musk is a strong, penetrating scent originally obtained from a gland of the male musk deer, used as a base note in perfumery. The smell is earthy and animalistic—some find it alluring, others overpowering. Synthetic musks have largely replaced the natural substance. The adjective musky describes anything with this heavy, pungent quality: {a musky cologne}, {the musky smell of sweat}.

A musket is a long-barreled firearm that preceded the rifle as infantry's standard weapon. Muskets were loaded through the muzzle with powder and ball, fired by various ignition mechanisms, and were notoriously inaccurate beyond short range. They dominated warfare from the 16th through mid-19th centuries before rifled barrels made them obsolete. {The soldiers formed ranks and fired their muskets in volleys.}

A musketeer is a soldier armed with a musket—a muzzle-loaded long gun used from the 16th through 18th centuries. The term evokes romantic notions of swashbuckling adventure, largely thanks to Alexandre Dumas's novel *The Three Musketeers*. By extension, musketeer describes any loyal companion ready to fight alongside others: {The four of us were musketeers back in college}. (Capitalized Musketeer may refer to team mascots or specific characters.)

Musketeers were soldiers armed with muskets—the long-barreled firearms that dominated European warfare from the 16th through 18th centuries. The word now appears almost exclusively in reference to Alexandre Dumas's novel *The Three Musketeers* and its adaptations: {All for one and one for all, as the musketeers say}. The phrase evokes loyal camaraderie and swashbuckling adventure.

Muskets were the dominant infantry firearm from the 16th through 19th centuries—long-barreled, smoothbore guns fired from the shoulder. They required manual loading of powder and ball, making rate of fire slow but deadly in massed volleys. {The muskets crackled across the field.} Musket appears in historical contexts and period pieces; modern firearms aren't called muskets.

A muskox is a large, shaggy Arctic mammal with curved horns, related to sheep and goats despite its ox-like appearance. Muskoxen form defensive circles when threatened, facing outward with horns ready. Their long outer coat and dense underwool (qiviut) provide insulation against extreme cold. Plural: muskoxen or muskox.

Muskoxen is the plural of muskox, a large shaggy-coated Arctic mammal related to goats and sheep despite its oxlike appearance. When threatened, muskoxen form a defensive circle with horns facing outward to protect calves. {A herd of muskoxen grazed on the tundra.}

A muskrat is a large semiaquatic rodent native to North America, resembling a small beaver with a long, scaly tail. Muskrats live in marshes and wetlands, building lodges from vegetation. The name comes from their musky odor and rat-like appearance, though they're more closely related to voles. Their fur was once prized for coats and hats.

Muskrats are large semi-aquatic rodents native to North America, named for the musky odor they produce. They live in marshes, ponds, and slow-moving waterways, building dome-shaped lodges from vegetation. Despite the name, muskrats are not rats—they're more closely related to voles. Their dense, waterproof fur was historically prized for coats and hats.

Musky describes a heavy, earthy scent—the kind produced by musk, a secretion from certain animals used in perfumery. The smell suggests something primal and slightly wild: {a musky cologne}, {the musky odor of the locker room}. Musky scents can be appealing or off-putting depending on context and intensity.

Muslin is a lightweight, loosely woven cotton fabric. It ranges from sheer to coarse depending on the weave. Fine muslin appears in clothing, curtains, and bandages. Coarser grades serve as backing material or as inexpensive fabric for making test garments before cutting into better cloth: {She made a muslin of the dress pattern first}.
