As a verb, it also means to link computers or devices together.

Neural means relating to nerves or the nervous system: {neural pathways}, {neural tissue}, {neural damage}. In computing and artificial intelligence, neural describes systems modeled on biological nerve networks: {neural network}, {neural processing}. The term appears frequently in discussions of both neuroscience and machine learning.

Neurodivergence is variation in brain function that differs from what's considered typical—encompassing conditions like autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and others. The term frames these differences as natural variation rather than deficits: {Neurodivergence isn't a disorder; it's just a different operating system}. Someone with such differences is neurodivergent; those with typical brain function are neurotypical.

Neurodivergent describes people whose brain function differs from what is considered typical—including those with autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and similar conditions. The term frames these differences as natural variation rather than deficits: {Many tech companies actively recruit neurodivergent employees}. Someone who is not neurodivergent is neurotypical.

Neurodiverse describes people whose brains function differently from what's considered typical—including those with autism, ADHD, dyslexia, or similar conditions. The term reframes these differences as natural variation rather than deficits: {Our company actively recruits neurodiverse candidates}. A neurodiverse group contains people with varied neurological profiles. The related noun is neurodiversity.

Neurodiversity is the concept that neurological differences—autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and similar conditions—represent natural variation in human brain function rather than deficits to be cured. The term reframes these conditions as differences rather than disorders: {The company embraced neurodiversity in its hiring practices}. A person with such differences is neurodivergent; those with typical neurology are neurotypical.

A neurologist is a physician who specializes in disorders of the nervous system—the brain, spinal cord, and nerves. Neurologists diagnose and treat conditions like epilepsy, stroke, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and migraines: {The neurologist ordered an MRI to investigate her recurring headaches}.

Neurologists are medical doctors who specialize in disorders of the nervous system—the brain, spinal cord, and nerves. They diagnose and treat conditions like epilepsy, stroke, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and migraines. Unlike neurosurgeons, neurologists typically treat patients with medication and therapy rather than surgery: {The neurologist ordered an MRI to investigate her recurring headaches}.

Neurology is the branch of medicine concerned with the nervous system—the brain, spinal cord, and nerves. A neurologist diagnoses and treats conditions like epilepsy, stroke, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis: {She was referred to neurology after the seizure}. The field overlaps with psychiatry but focuses on structural and physiological disorders rather than behavioral ones.

A neuron is a nerve cell—the basic unit of the nervous system that transmits electrical and chemical signals. Neurons receive input through branching dendrites, process it in the cell body, and send output along a fiber called an axon. The brain contains roughly 86 billion neurons. In machine learning, artificial neurons are computational units modeled loosely on biological ones.

Neurons are the specialized cells that transmit information through the nervous system. Each neuron receives signals through branching extensions called dendrites and sends them along a fiber called an axon. The brain contains roughly 86 billion neurons, connected in networks of staggering complexity. {The drug affects neurons in the reward pathway.} In casual speech, neurons often stand in for thinking itself: {Get those neurons firing}.

Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections throughout life. This capacity allows the brain to compensate for injury, adapt to new experiences, and strengthen frequently used pathways: {Physical therapy relies on neuroplasticity to help stroke patients regain movement}. The concept overturned older views that adult brains were essentially fixed.

Neuroscience is the scientific study of the nervous system—the brain, spinal cord, and networks of nerve cells throughout the body. The field draws on biology, chemistry, psychology, and medicine to understand how neural structures produce thought, perception, movement, and behavior. {Neuroscience has transformed our understanding of memory and learning.}

Neuroses is the plural of neurosis, a term for mental conditions involving chronic anxiety, obsessive thoughts, or compulsive behaviors without loss of contact with reality. The word was central to Freudian psychoanalysis and mid-twentieth-century psychiatry, though it has largely fallen out of clinical favor. In casual use, neuroses describes persistent anxieties or hang-ups: {We all have our little neuroses}.

Neurosis is a term from psychology for mental disturbance that causes anxiety, obsessive thoughts, or compulsive behavior without loss of contact with reality—distinguishing it from psychosis. The word is now somewhat dated in clinical settings, replaced by more specific diagnoses. In casual use, neurosis describes excessive worry or irrational preoccupation: {Her neurosis about germs makes travel difficult}.

A neurosurgeon is a physician who specializes in surgery on the brain, spinal cord, and other parts of the nervous system. Neurosurgeons treat conditions ranging from brain tumors and aneurysms to spinal injuries and herniated discs. The field requires extensive training beyond medical school, typically a seven-year residency. {The neurosurgeon explained the risks of removing the tumor.}

Neurosurgeons are physicians who specialize in surgery on the brain, spinal cord, and nervous system. They treat conditions ranging from brain tumors to spinal injuries to aneurysms. The field demands extensive training—typically over a decade after medical school. {The neurosurgeons removed the tumor successfully.}

Neurosurgery is surgery performed on the brain, spinal cord, or other parts of the nervous system. It addresses conditions ranging from brain tumors and aneurysms to spinal injuries and epilepsy. The field requires exceptional precision given the delicacy of neural tissue: {The tumor was in a location that made neurosurgery risky}.

Neurotic describes someone prone to anxiety, obsessive worry, or emotional instability. In clinical psychology, neurosis once named a category of mental disorders characterized by distress without loss of contact with reality—distinct from psychosis. The clinical term has faded, but neurotic thrives in everyday speech for anyone who overthinks, frets excessively, or fixates on minor concerns: {She's neurotic about germs}. As a noun, a neurotic is such a person: {a lovable neurotic}.

Neuroticism is a personality trait characterized by emotional instability, anxiety, and a tendency toward negative feelings. Someone high in neuroticism experiences stress, worry, and mood swings more intensely than others: {Her neuroticism made even minor setbacks feel catastrophic}. In psychology's Big Five personality model, neuroticism is one of five core dimensions used to describe human temperament.

A neurotoxin is a substance that damages or destroys nerve tissue. Neurotoxins include snake venoms, certain pesticides, heavy metals like lead and mercury, and some bacterial products like botulinum toxin. Exposure can cause paralysis, seizures, cognitive impairment, or death depending on the toxin and dose: {The pufferfish contains a potent neurotoxin}.

Neurotoxins are substances that damage or destroy nerve tissue. They interfere with the transmission of signals between neurons, causing effects ranging from numbness to paralysis to death. Some occur naturally—in snake venom, puffer fish, or botulinum bacteria—while others are synthetic, developed as pesticides or chemical weapons. {The shellfish were contaminated with neurotoxins from algal blooms.}

A neurotransmitter is a chemical messenger that carries signals between nerve cells. These molecules cross the tiny gaps (synapses) between neurons, triggering or inhibiting electrical impulses in the receiving cell. Dopamine, serotonin, and adrenaline are familiar examples—each associated with different mental states and bodily functions: {Antidepressants work by altering neurotransmitter levels in the brain}.

Neurotypical describes people whose neurological development and functioning fall within conventional norms—those without autism, ADHD, dyslexia, or similar conditions. The term emerged from autism communities as a neutral way to distinguish the majority from neurodivergent individuals: {My neurotypical coworkers don't understand why fluorescent lights bother me}. Sometimes used with gentle irony to flip the usual framing of "normal."

Neurotypicals are people whose neurological development and functioning fall within conventional norms—those without autism, ADHD, dyslexia, or similar conditions. The term originated in autistic communities as a neutral counterpart to "autistic," gently highlighting that "normal" brains are just one variety: {Neurotypicals don't always get our humor}. Sometimes used with light irony.
clues: People whose brains work most commonly

definition: Neuter describes something that is neither one thing nor another, most often applied to grammatical gender (neither masculine nor feminine) or to animals and people lacking functional sex organs. To neuter an animal is to remove its reproductive organs, rendering it incapable of breeding. The word extends figuratively to mean rendering something ineffective or harmless: {The amendment neutered the original bill}. A neutered proposal or argument has had its force or impact removed.

Neutered describes an animal that has had its reproductive organs removed, rendering it unable to breed: {The shelter only adopts out neutered pets}. The verb neuter means to perform this procedure, or figuratively to weaken or render ineffective: {The amendment neutered the bill}. A neutered version of something has had its power or edge removed.

Neutering is the surgical removal of an animal's reproductive organs to prevent breeding. The term usually refers to males (castration), while spaying is the female equivalent, though neutering can cover both. Beyond veterinary contexts, neutering describes any act of removing power or effectiveness: {The amendments neutered the bill}.

Neutral means not taking sides in a conflict or dispute: {Switzerland remained neutral during the war}. A neutral party has no stake in the outcome. Neutral colors like beige and gray don't clash with others. In chemistry, neutral indicates neither acidic nor alkaline. A car in neutral has its gears disengaged. A neutral expression reveals nothing—neither approval nor disapproval.

Neutralise is the British spelling of neutralize. To neutralise something is to cancel out its effect or make it harmless: {The medication neutralises stomach acid}. In chemistry, acids and bases neutralise each other. Military and espionage contexts use neutralise as a euphemism for killing: {Orders came to neutralise the target}. A neutral colour neutralises bolder ones.

Neutrality is the state of not taking sides in a conflict or dispute. Countries maintain neutrality by refusing to join wars or alliances: {Switzerland's neutrality dates back centuries}. The word extends to any impartial stance: {The mediator's neutrality was essential to the negotiations}. Net neutrality is the principle that internet providers should treat all data equally, without favoring certain websites or services.

Neutralization is the act of making something neutral—canceling out its effect, charge, or threat. In chemistry, an acid and base neutralize each other, producing a neutral solution. Military forces neutralize enemy positions by rendering them ineffective. A country's neutralization removes it from conflict: {the neutralization of Belgium in 1839}. The word often appears in clinical or strategic contexts where *eliminate* might sound too harsh.

Neutralize means to cancel out or render ineffective. You neutralize a threat by eliminating it, neutralize an acid with a base, or neutralize an advantage by matching it. In military and espionage contexts, neutralize is often a euphemism for kill: {The target has been neutralized}. The word implies bringing something to a neutral state—neither active nor harmful.

Neutralized is the past tense of neutralize, meaning to render ineffective or harmless. An acid is neutralized by a base. A threat is neutralized when it can no longer cause harm. In military or espionage contexts, neutralized is often a euphemism for killed: {The target has been neutralized}. A neutralized color has been muted by mixing with gray or its complement.

Neutralizing is the act of making something ineffective or counterbalancing its force. You neutralize a threat by eliminating it, neutralize an acid with a base, or neutralize an opponent's advantage by finding a counter. The word appears frequently in military, chemical, and strategic contexts: {The agent was tasked with neutralizing the target}. Neutralizing can be a euphemism for killing.

A neutrino is a subatomic particle with almost no mass and no electric charge. Neutrinos pass through ordinary matter virtually undetected—billions stream through your body every second without interacting. They're produced by nuclear reactions in the sun, stars, and particle accelerators. {The detector captured a handful of neutrinos from the supernova.}

A neutron is a subatomic particle found in the nucleus of atoms, carrying no electric charge—unlike the positively charged proton or negatively charged electron. Neutrons help bind the nucleus together; their number determines an element's isotope. Free neutrons are unstable and decay within minutes. {Neutron stars} are collapsed stellar remnants composed almost entirely of neutrons.

Neutrons are subatomic particles found in the nucleus of atoms alongside protons. Unlike protons, which carry positive charge, neutrons have no electrical charge—hence the name. The number of neutrons in an atom determines its isotope: carbon-12 has six neutrons, carbon-14 has eight. Free neutrons outside the nucleus are unstable and decay within minutes. {Neutron stars} are collapsed stellar cores composed almost entirely of neutrons.

Never is a negating word like no, not, and nor. It is equivalent to not ever. It is often required in negative statements about events in time, and may apply to all time, or only to all time before the present moment: Spike never barks at strangers. I’ve never visited the Prado museum. In statements about the past never is often used with a perfect tense.

Neverending means continuing without end or apparently without end. The word usually describes something that feels interminable rather than something literally eternal: {the neverending stream of emails}, {neverending construction on the highway}. It can be positive when applied to things like love or wonder, but often carries a note of exhaustion. Also spelled never-ending.

Nevermind as a single word is nonstandard but increasingly common, especially in casual writing. It functions as a dismissal—withdrawing a question or statement: {Nevermind, I found it}. The standard spelling remains two words: never mind. The single-word form gained cultural visibility as the title of Nirvana's 1991 album.

Nevermore means never again—at no future time. The word is literary and archaic, rarely used in ordinary speech. Its fame comes almost entirely from Edgar Allan Poe's poem "The Raven," where a bird repeats it as a haunting refrain: {Quoth the Raven, "Nevermore."}

Nevertheless signals that something is true or will happen despite what was just stated. It functions as a connector between contrasting ideas, acknowledging a point while pushing past it: {The evidence was circumstantial; nevertheless, the jury convicted him}. It carries more formal weight than "but" or "still" and often appears at the start of a sentence or after a semicolon. Nevertheless suggests determination or persistence in the face of obstacles.

New is an adjective and adverb that characterizes something that is not old or that has just appeared, just come into existence, or just come to the attention of someone. If you are new to something, you have not experienced it before. If something is new to you, you did not know about it before.

A newbie is someone new to an activity, community, or skill—an inexperienced beginner. The term emerged from internet and gaming culture but has spread to general use: {I'm still a newbie at this job}, {Don't be too hard on the newbies}. It's usually neutral or mildly teasing rather than harsh, unlike the more dismissive *noob*.

Newbies are newcomers or beginners, especially in online communities, gaming, or technical fields. The term carries mild condescension—experienced users might dismiss questions as {newbie mistakes} or create {newbie guides} for the uninitiated. Less dismissive than noob, which implies incompetence rather than inexperience. {We were all newbies once.}

A newborn is a baby in the first weeks of life, typically the first month. The word works as both noun and adjective: {a newborn infant}, {caring for a newborn}. By extension, newborn describes anything very recently created or begun: {a newborn democracy}, {newborn enthusiasm}.

Newborns are babies in their first weeks of life, typically the first month after birth. The term emphasizes how recently they've arrived: {The hospital has a special unit for newborns}. In medical contexts, the newborn period is distinct from infancy, which follows. The word applies to other species as well: {newborn calves}, {newborn kittens}.

A newcomer is someone who has recently arrived or joined—a new resident, employee, or participant: {The newcomers to the neighborhood introduced themselves at the block party}. The word implies unfamiliarity with local customs or established ways: {As a newcomer to the industry, she had much to learn}. It can also describe someone new to an activity or field: {a newcomer to politics}.

Newcomers are people who have recently arrived somewhere or recently joined a group. The word emphasizes unfamiliarity with local customs, established relationships, or how things work: {Newcomers to the neighborhood often struggle to find parking}. It can carry slight condescension from those who arrived earlier, or mark genuine welcome: {We have a mentorship program for newcomers}.

Newfangled describes something new in a way that suggests skepticism or mild disapproval—novelty for its own sake, untested by time: {I don't trust these newfangled gadgets}. The word carries a whiff of the old-timer suspicious of change. It's almost always used by someone who prefers the old way of doing things.

Newfound describes something recently discovered or acquired: {newfound confidence}, {newfound freedom}, {newfound respect}. The word emphasizes the novelty of the discovery rather than when the thing itself came into being—a newfound {friend} may have existed all along, but the friendship is new.

A newlywed is someone who has recently married. The term usually applies during the first year or so of marriage, when the couple is still adjusting to married life: {The newlyweds left for their honeymoon}. Often used in the plural: {newlyweds moving into their first apartment}.

Newlyweds are people who have recently married. The term usually applies during the first year or so of marriage, when the couple is still adjusting to married life: {The newlyweds honeymooned in Italy}. The singular newlywed exists but is less common, since marriage involves two people.

Newness is the quality of being new—recently made, discovered, or experienced. It captures the fresh, unfamiliar character of something: {the newness of the relationship}, {the newness wore off after a few weeks}. Newness often carries positive associations with excitement and possibility, though it can also imply inexperience or untested quality.

News is information about recent events, especially as reported by media: {Have you seen the news?} The word is singular despite its form: {The news is good}. News can be any fresh information: {I have news about the job}. Something that {breaks the news} delivers significant or difficult information. If something is {news to me}, I'm hearing it for the first time.

A newsagent is a British term for a person or shop that sells newspapers, magazines, and often tobacco, candy, and other small goods. The American equivalent is newsstand or newsdealer. {I popped into the newsagent for a paper and some gum.}

Newsagents is the plural of newsagent, a British term for a shop selling newspapers, magazines, cigarettes, and sundries—or the person who runs such a shop. The American equivalent is newsstand or convenience store: {I popped into the newsagents for a paper and some milk}.

A newsboy is a boy who sells or delivers newspapers. The term evokes a historical image—young boys hawking papers on street corners in the early twentieth century: {Extra, extra, read all about it!} The newsboy cap, a rounded cloth cap with a small brim, takes its name from this figure. The role has largely disappeared, though newspaper delivery persists in modified form.

Newsboys are boys or young men who sell or deliver newspapers. The term evokes a historical image—street vendors hawking papers on corners, calling out headlines. Though the occupation has largely disappeared, newsboy persists in {newsboy cap}, a style of soft, rounded cap with a front brim, originally associated with working-class youth.

A newscast is a broadcast of news on radio or television, typically at a scheduled time: {the evening newscast}, {We interrupt this program for a special newscast}. The word combines news with broadcast, following the pattern of other broadcasting terms like telecast and simulcast.

A newscaster is a person who reads or presents news on radio or television. The term emphasizes the broadcast delivery rather than the reporting or gathering of news: {The newscaster announced breaking developments from the scene}. Newscasters may or may not be journalists themselves—some are trained reporters, others primarily read scripts prepared by others.

Newscasting is the broadcasting of news on television or radio. The term emphasizes the delivery aspect—the anchor reading from a teleprompter, the live reports from the field: {She studied journalism but found her calling in newscasting}. A newscaster is one who presents the news, distinct from the reporters who gather it.

A newsfeed is a continuously updated stream of content—news stories, social media posts, or other information—displayed in reverse chronological order or algorithmically ranked. The term emerged with RSS technology but now most commonly refers to the central feature of social media platforms: {I saw your announcement in my newsfeed}. Also spelled news feed.

Newsfeeds are streams of content—news articles, social media posts, or blog updates—delivered automatically to users. The term covers both the technology (RSS feeds, aggregation services) and the familiar scrolling display on platforms like Facebook or Twitter: {I spent an hour doom-scrolling my newsfeed}. Also spelled as two words: news feeds.

A newsflash is a brief announcement interrupting regular programming to report breaking news: {We interrupt this broadcast for a newsflash}. The term sounds somewhat dated, as continuous news cycles have made such interruptions less dramatic. Informally and often sarcastically, newsflash introduces something obvious: {Newsflash: teenagers like to sleep late}.

A newshound is someone who avidly seeks out and consumes news, or a journalist who aggressively pursues stories. The term combines news with hound in its sense of one who hunts or tracks persistently. {The old newshound had sources all over city hall.} It suggests tenacity and nose-to-the-ground determination, whether applied to professional reporters or to civilians who obsessively follow current events.

Newshounds are reporters or journalists, especially those who pursue stories aggressively. The term evokes a hunting dog's relentless tracking instinct applied to news gathering: {The newshounds were already camped outside the courthouse}. It can be affectionate or slightly dismissive depending on context.

A newsie is a person who sells newspapers on the street, especially a young boy hawking papers on a corner—a figure largely historical now but iconic in depictions of early 20th-century urban life: {The newsies shouted headlines to attract buyers}. The word remains familiar from the 1992 Disney musical *Newsies* about the 1899 newsboys' strike.

A newsletter is a regularly distributed publication sent to subscribers, typically covering news and updates about a particular organization, topic, or industry. Originally printed bulletins from clubs and businesses, newsletters now arrive mostly by email: {I subscribe to several tech newsletters}. The format has seen revival as individual writers build audiences through platforms like Substack.

Newsletters are periodical publications distributed to subscribers, typically by email but historically by mail. They contain news, updates, or commentary on a particular topic or from a particular organization: {I subscribe to several tech newsletters}, {the company's monthly newsletter}. The term now often refers to independent email publications by individual writers building audiences outside traditional media.

A newsmaker is a person or event that attracts media coverage—someone whose actions or statements become news. The term often appears in journalism contexts: {The senator has been a newsmaker since her controversial speech}. A newsmaker can be deliberately seeking attention or simply caught up in events that draw public interest.

A newspaper is a publication printed on large sheets of paper, containing news, opinion, advertising, and other content, typically issued daily or weekly. The word extends to the physical paper itself: {I spread newspaper on the floor before painting}. Newspapers may also exist in digital form, though the name persists from print origins.

A newspaperman is a man who works for a newspaper, especially as a reporter, editor, or journalist. The term carries an old-fashioned ring, evoking an era of typewriters, press cards tucked into hatbands, and shouted deadlines: {He was an old newspaperman who'd covered three wars}. The gender-neutral alternative is newspaper journalist or simply journalist.

Newspapers are printed publications issued daily or weekly containing news, articles, opinion pieces, and advertisements. Before the internet era, they were the primary source of current events for most people, and the term still applies to their digital descendants. The newspaper is often simply called {the paper}: {I saw your letter in the paper}. Someone who delivers newspapers to homes has a {paper route}.

Newspeak is language designed to limit thought by restricting vocabulary and eliminating nuance. The term comes from George Orwell's novel *1984*, where the totalitarian government replaces English with a stripped-down language that makes dissent literally unthinkable. Now used broadly for any official jargon that obscures truth or manipulates meaning: {Corporate newspeak turned layoffs into "right-sizing"}.

Newsprint is the cheap, uncoated paper used for printing newspapers—lightweight, grayish, and designed for high-speed printing rather than durability. The paper yellows and becomes brittle with age. By extension, newsprint can refer to newspapers collectively or the ink that rubs off on your fingers: {I got newsprint all over my hands}.

A newsreader is a person who reads the news on television or radio—the British term for what Americans call an anchor or anchorperson. In computing, a newsreader is software for accessing Usenet newsgroups or RSS feeds: {I set up a newsreader to follow several tech forums}.

A newsreel was a short film of news and current events, shown in cinemas before the main feature. From the early twentieth century until television news became dominant in the 1960s, newsreels were how most people saw footage of wars, political events, sports, and celebrities. The term now evokes the grainy black-and-white footage and dramatic narration style characteristic of that era. {The documentary included newsreel footage from World War II.}

Newsreels were short films of current events shown in cinemas before the main feature, a staple of moviegoing from the early 1900s through the 1960s. They delivered news visually—war footage, political events, sports highlights, human interest stories—often with dramatic narration. Before television became widespread, newsreels were how most people saw moving images of world events. {My grandmother remembers watching newsreels about World War II at the local theater.} The format became obsolete as TV news took over.

A newsroom is the central workspace where journalists, editors, and producers gather and process news for publication or broadcast. It's both a physical space—desks, monitors, the hum of activity—and a metonym for the editorial operation itself: {The newsroom decided to hold the story until they had confirmation}. Newsroom culture emphasizes deadlines, accuracy, and the collaborative chaos of breaking news.

Newsrooms are the spaces where journalists work to gather, write, and edit news. The term refers both to physical locations—the bustling floors of newspapers and broadcast stations—and to the editorial teams themselves: {The newsroom decided not to run the story}. A newsroom's culture shapes how news gets reported.

A newsstand is a booth or stall that sells newspapers, magazines, and often snacks, cigarettes, or lottery tickets. Newsstands are typically found on sidewalks, in transit stations, or in building lobbies: {I grabbed a coffee and a paper from the newsstand on my way to work}.

Newsstands are small retail outlets selling newspapers, magazines, and often candy, cigarettes, or lottery tickets. Traditionally found on sidewalks or in transit stations, they serve commuters and passersby seeking quick purchases: {I grabbed a paper from the newsstand on my way to work}. The singular newsstand refers to any such kiosk or counter.

A newswire is a service that gathers and distributes news to subscribing media outlets—newspapers, broadcasters, websites. The term comes from the telegraph wires that originally transmitted these reports. Major newswires like the Associated Press and Reuters supply breaking news that local outlets couldn't gather themselves: {The story came across the newswire this morning}.

Newsworthy describes something significant or interesting enough to merit coverage by news media. A scandal might be newsworthy; a routine meeting usually isn't. The judgment is subjective—what one editor finds newsworthy, another may dismiss: {The protest wasn't considered newsworthy until violence broke out}.

A newt is a small salamander that spends part of its life in water and part on land. Newts have moist skin and slender bodies, returning to ponds to breed. They appear in folklore as witches' ingredients and in modern culture as the amphibian Gingrich jokes inevitably reference. {The pond was full of newts in spring.} (Capitalized Newt is a given name, short for Newton.)

A newton is the SI unit of force—the amount needed to accelerate one kilogram of mass at one meter per second squared. Named after the physicist Isaac Newton, it appears in scientific contexts: {The rocket produced 500,000 newtons of thrust}. Abbreviated N. (Capitalized Newton is the surname.)

Newts are small amphibians related to salamanders, with slender bodies, short legs, and long tails. They live in or near water and have moist, often brightly colored skin. {The pond was full of newts}. In figurative use, newt sometimes suggests something small and slippery, or appears in whimsical contexts—witches' brews famously call for {eye of newt}.

Next functions in various parts of speech to convey the idea of being side-by-side in space, sequential in time, or adjacent in rank or order with nothing intervening: next week, come and sit next to me, take your complaint to the next level of management.

A nexus is a connection or link between things, or a central point where things converge. {The city became a nexus of trade routes.} In legal contexts, nexus refers to a sufficient connection between parties or jurisdictions to establish authority: {The company lacked sufficient nexus with the state to be taxed there.} The plural is nexuses or nexus.

A nib is the pointed tip of a pen—the part that touches paper and delivers ink. Fountain pens have metal nibs; dip pens have replaceable ones. Nib width affects line thickness: {a fine nib for detail work}, {a broad nib for calligraphy}. By extension, any pointed tip may be called a nib.

To nibble is to take small, delicate bites: {She nibbled at her sandwich}. Animals nibble when they gnaw or bite gently. Figuratively, to nibble is to show tentative interest: {Investors are nibbling at the offer}. A nibble is a small bite or a light snack. In computing, a nibble is half a byte—four bits.

Nibbles are small bites or snacks, typically finger foods served before a meal or with drinks: {We put out some nibbles for the guests}. The word suggests casual, light eating rather than a proper meal. In computing, a nibble (also nybble) is half a byte—four bits of data, a playful extension of the "bite" metaphor.

Nibbling is the act of taking small, delicate bites—the way a mouse eats cheese or a person picks at food without real appetite: {She was nibbling at her salad}. The word also covers gentle, affectionate biting: {nibbling on an earlobe}. In the plural, nibbles are small snacks served at parties or gatherings.

Nibs are small pieces or fragments, most commonly referring to crushed cacao beans used in baking and chocolate-making: {She sprinkled cacao nibs on the dessert}. The word also applies to crushed coffee beans or other granular bits. Separately, {his nibs} or {her nibs} is a mildly mocking way to refer to someone who acts self-important: {His nibs wants his coffee now}.

Nice describes things that are pleasant, agreeable, or satisfactory. A nice {day} has good weather; a nice {person} is kind and friendly; a nice {meal} is enjoyable. The word is so common it risks blandness—{nice} can feel like faint praise when stronger words are available. Nice also means precise or subtle: {a nice distinction}. To be {nice} to someone is to treat them well. {Nice work} can be sincere praise or sarcastic. (Capitalized Nice is a French city.)

Niceties are fine points or subtle distinctions—the small details that require careful attention: {the niceties of diplomatic protocol}, {legal niceties}. The word also covers polite formalities and social courtesies: {We exchanged niceties before getting down to business}. Both senses suggest refinement that may be appreciated or dismissed as fussy, depending on context.

A niche is a recess in a wall, often used to display a statue or ornament. From this concrete sense, niche extends to any specialized position or role: an ecological niche describes how a species fits into its environment; a market niche is a specialized segment. To find your niche is to discover where you belong or excel. As an adjective, niche describes something appealing to a small, specialized audience: {a niche podcast}, {niche interests}.

Niches is the plural of niche, meaning specialized positions or recesses. In ecology, a niche is an organism's role in its environment: {Different species occupy different ecological niches}. In business and marketing, niches are narrow market segments: {She found success targeting underserved niches}. Architectural niches are recessed spaces in walls, typically for displaying statues or ornaments.

A nick is a small cut or notch on a surface or edge: {The blade has a nick in it}. To nick something is to make such a cut, often accidentally: {I nicked myself shaving}. In British slang, to nick means to steal or to arrest: {Someone nicked my wallet}, {He got nicked for shoplifting}. The phrase {in the nick of time} means at the last possible moment. (Capitalized Nick is a given name.)

Nicked is the past tense of nick. To nick something is to make a small cut or notch in it: {I nicked myself shaving}. In British slang, to nick means to steal: {Someone nicked my bike}. British police nick suspects when they arrest them: {He got nicked for shoplifting}. A nick is also a small cut or the precise moment: {in the nick of time}.

Nickel is a hard, silvery-white metallic element used in alloys and plating. In American currency, a nickel is a five-cent coin: {Do you have a nickel for the meter?} To nickel-and-dime someone is to drain them through small charges or petty economies: {They nickel-and-dimed us on every fee}.

A nickelodeon was an early movie theater charging five cents admission, popular in the United States from roughly 1905 to 1915. The term also applies to coin-operated player pianos and early jukeboxes—machines that played music for a nickel. Both senses evoke turn-of-the-century popular entertainment: {The old nickelodeon in the corner played ragtime tunes}. (Capitalized Nickelodeon is the children's television network.)

Nickels is the plural of nickel, a US five-cent coin. The word appears in expressions about small amounts of money: {nickels and dimes}, {not worth two nickels}. To nickel and dime someone is to charge for every small thing or to wear them down with petty costs: {They nickel-and-dimed us on fees}.

Nicking is stealing, especially small items or petty theft—British slang that remains common: {Someone's nicked my phone}. To nick also means to make a small cut or notch: {I nicked myself shaving}. In British slang, to get nicked is to be arrested: {He got nicked for shoplifting}. The noun nick appears in {in the nick of time}—at the last possible moment.

A nickname is an informal name used instead of or alongside someone's given name. Nicknames often derive from physical traits, personality, or shortening of real names: {His nickname was Red because of his hair}. They can signal affection, mockery, or group membership. To nickname someone is to give them such a name: {They nicknamed him Tiny, though he was six foot four}.

Nicknames are informal names used instead of or alongside someone's given name. They often arise from affection, physical traits, or inside jokes: {His friends call him Red because of his hair}. Nicknames can be shortened forms of proper names (Bill for William, Peggy for Margaret) or entirely invented. Places, teams, and things also acquire nicknames: {the Big Apple}, {the Windy City}. To nickname someone is to give them such a name.

Nicks is the plural of nick—small cuts, notches, or surface damage: {The blade had nicks along the edge}. Nick also means a police station in British slang, or the act of stealing: {Someone nicked my wallet}. To nick is to make a small cut or, in British usage, to arrest or steal. {In the nick of time} means at the last possible moment.

Nicotine is the addictive chemical compound found in tobacco that makes cigarettes and other tobacco products hard to quit. It acts as a stimulant, raising heart rate and blood pressure while triggering dopamine release in the brain. Nicotine itself is not what causes lung cancer or emphysema—those come from tar and other combustion products—but it keeps smokers coming back. {Nicotine patches help wean smokers off cigarettes gradually.}

A niece is the daughter of one's brother or sister, or the daughter of one's spouse's brother or sister. The relationship extends to great-nieces (a sibling's granddaughter) and so on: {My niece is starting college next fall}. The male counterpart is nephew.

Nieces is the plural of niece, a word for the daughter of one's sibling or the daughter of one's spouse's sibling. The relationship is reciprocal: if someone is your niece, you are their aunt or uncle. Nieces and nephews are often grouped together when referring to this generation of relatives collectively. {I'm taking my nieces to the zoo this weekend.}

Nifty means clever, stylish, or particularly good at what it does. A nifty {gadget} solves a problem elegantly. A nifty {trick} impresses with its ingenuity. The word carries a casual, approving tone—something nifty is pleasing without being grand: {That's a nifty little app}.

To niggle is to find fault in minor, persistent ways—picking at small imperfections rather than addressing larger issues: {She niggled about the font size while ignoring the report's substance}. A niggle is a minor complaint or a small nagging worry: {I have a few niggles about the plan}. Something niggling bothers you in a low-grade, persistent way: {a niggling doubt}.

Niggling describes something small but persistently annoying or troubling. A niggling {doubt} won't go away. A niggling {injury} keeps bothering an athlete without being serious enough to stop play. The word can also describe someone who fusses over trivial details: {Stop niggling and just sign the contract}.

Night is the period of darkness between sunset and sunrise, when the sun is below the horizon. By extension, night means any period of darkness, gloom, or obscurity: {the long night of fascism}. Night also refers to evening activities: {a night out}, {date night}, {movie night}. {Good night} is both a farewell and a wish for restful sleep.

A nightcap is a drink taken before bed, typically alcoholic: {Join me for a nightcap?} The word often serves as a suggestive invitation to extend an evening. Nightcap also refers to a soft cap worn to bed, now old-fashioned. In baseball, the nightcap is the second game of a doubleheader—the one that closes out the night.

A nightcap is a drink taken before bed, typically alcoholic: {Join me for a nightcap?} The term often carries a hint of social invitation or romantic suggestion. Nightcap also refers to the final game in a baseball doubleheader. The original sense—a cloth cap worn to bed for warmth—is now archaic.

A nightclub is an establishment open late at night for drinking, dancing, and entertainment. Unlike bars, nightclubs typically feature a dance floor, DJ or live music, and often charge admission. The atmosphere emphasizes socializing, dancing, and spectacle: {We hit the nightclub around midnight}. To nightclub is to visit such venues: {They spent the weekend nightclubbing}.

Nightclubs are venues for late-night entertainment, typically featuring music, dancing, and alcohol. They range from small bars with a dance floor to elaborate spaces with light shows, DJs, and VIP sections. The culture centers on nightlife—dressing up, going out, and staying out late: {We hit the nightclubs after dinner}. To nightclub is to frequent such places.

A nightcrawler is a large earthworm that emerges from the soil at night, commonly used as fishing bait: {We dug up nightcrawlers before the fishing trip}. The term extends to people who are active at night—prowling, partying, or working late shifts. A nightcrawler might be a club-goer, a nocturnal photographer, or someone with darker purposes.

Nightcrawlers are large earthworms, typically several inches long, that emerge from the soil at night. They're prized as fishing bait and can often be found on lawns and sidewalks after rain or collected by flashlight in the dark. {We went out with flashlights to gather nightcrawlers for tomorrow's fishing trip.} The term sometimes appears in horror or fantasy contexts to describe creatures that hunt or prowl after dark.

Nightfall is the time when daylight fades and night begins—roughly synonymous with dusk or twilight. The word has a slightly literary or poetic quality: {We need to reach the cabin before nightfall}. It emphasizes the arrival of darkness rather than a specific clock time.

A nightgown is a loose garment worn for sleeping, typically by women and girls. It resembles a dress, falling anywhere from knee-length to the floor: {She changed into her nightgown before bed}. The word is sometimes shortened to nightie. Men's equivalents are usually called nightshirts.

Nightgowns are loose garments worn for sleeping, typically by women and children. The traditional nightgown is a long, flowing dress made of lightweight fabric like cotton or silk: {She changed into her nightgown before bed}. The singular nightgown refers to one such garment.

A nighthawk is a nocturnal bird related to the whip-poor-will, known for its erratic flight while hunting insects at dusk. The name extends to people who are active late at night—a synonym for night owl: {He's always been a nighthawk, doing his best work after midnight}. In American cities, nighthawk once commonly meant a late-night taxi driver.

Nighthawks are people who habitually stay up late or are active at night—the human equivalent of nocturnal birds. The word also names several species of night-flying birds related to whippoorwills, known for their erratic flight patterns while hunting insects at dusk. Edward Hopper's 1942 painting *Nighthawks* depicts late-night patrons at a diner, cementing the word's association with urban insomnia and solitary night hours.

A nightie is a woman's or girl's nightgown—a loose, lightweight garment worn for sleeping. The word is informal and slightly diminutive, suggesting something simple or dainty rather than elaborate: {She padded to the kitchen in her nightie}. Also spelled nighty.

Nighties is the plural of nightie, a woman's or girl's nightgown—a loose garment worn for sleeping. The word is informal and slightly diminutive, suggesting something light and feminine: {She packed two nighties for the trip}. The singular is also spelled nighty.

A nightingale is a small brown European songbird famous for its rich, melodious song, which the male often performs at night during breeding season. The bird's nocturnal singing made it a symbol of poetic inspiration and romantic longing in literature: {She sang like a nightingale}. Florence Nightingale, the founder of modern nursing, took her surname from this bird.

Nightingales is the plural of nightingale, a small brown European songbird famous for the male's rich, complex song, often heard at night. The bird's nocturnal singing made it a symbol of poetic inspiration and romantic longing: {The nightingales sang in the garden}. Florence Nightingale, the pioneering nurse, took her surname from the bird.

Nightlife is the entertainment and social activity available in a city or town after dark—bars, clubs, restaurants, concerts, and similar venues. The term implies a scene with energy and options: {The neighborhood has great nightlife}. A city's nightlife is often a measure of its vibrancy and appeal to young people.

A nightlight is a small, dim lamp left on during the night—typically in hallways, bathrooms, or children's bedrooms—to provide just enough illumination for navigation without disturbing sleep. {She plugged in a nightlight so her son wouldn't be scared of the dark.}

Nightlights are small, dim lamps left on overnight to provide just enough light for navigating dark rooms without fully waking. They're typically placed in hallways, bathrooms, or children's bedrooms: {She plugged a nightlight into the outlet near the stairs}. Some nightlights have sensors that turn them on automatically at dusk.

Nightly means happening every night or relating to the night. A nightly {ritual} occurs each evening. The nightly {news} airs once per night. As an adverb, it describes regular nighttime occurrence: {The medication is taken nightly}. In software, a nightly {build} is a version compiled automatically each night from the latest code.

A nightmare is a frightening dream that often wakes the sleeper. The word extends to any terrifying or deeply unpleasant experience: {The airport was a nightmare}. Nightmare also describes worst-case scenarios: {a nightmare situation}, {every parent's nightmare}. As a modifier, it suggests extreme difficulty: {nightmare traffic}, {a nightmare client}.

Nightmares are frightening dreams that wake the sleeper or leave a strong impression of distress. The word extends to any terrifying or deeply unpleasant experience: {The move was a nightmare from start to finish}. Something nightmarish has the dark, surreal quality of a bad dream. {She still has nightmares about the accident.}

Nightmarish describes something resembling or evoking a nightmare—disturbing, terrifying, or surreally unpleasant. A nightmarish {experience} feels like being trapped in a bad dream. The word often describes situations that combine horror with helplessness or absurdity: {The bureaucratic process was nightmarish}, {nightmarish working conditions}. It can intensify to suggest genuine trauma or soften to hyperbolic complaint.

Nights is the plural of night, but it also works as an adverb meaning during the nighttime hours, especially as a regular pattern: {She works nights at the hospital}, {He can't sleep nights}. This adverbial use parallels days, weekends, and other time-period words that double as schedule markers.

A nightscape is a view or depiction of scenery at night, particularly one emphasizing the interplay of darkness with artificial lights, moonlight, or stars. The term parallels landscape and cityscape, but specifically captures nocturnal scenes. Nightscape appears in photography and painting to describe compositions featuring night skies, illuminated skylines, or moonlit terrain. {The photographer waited hours to capture the perfect nightscape of the desert under the Milky Way.}

Nightscapes are scenes or views of the night, especially as subjects for photography or painting. The term parallels landscape but specifies nocturnal settings—cityscapes after dark, starlit wilderness, moonlit seascapes: {She specializes in nightscapes of the desert sky}. In photography, nightscapes often feature long exposures to capture stars or city lights.

Nightshade refers to plants of the genus *Solanum* and related genera, many of which contain toxic alkaloids. Deadly nightshade (belladonna) is notoriously poisonous, lending the whole family a sinister reputation—though tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplants are also nightshades. The name evokes danger and darkness: {The witch's garden was thick with nightshade}.

Nightshades are a family of plants that includes tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, and eggplants, as well as toxic species like belladonna and jimsonweed. The family is notable for containing both common food crops and poisonous plants. Some people avoid nightshades believing they worsen inflammation or arthritis, though evidence for this is limited.

A nightshift is a work period during nighttime hours, typically from late evening through early morning: {She's been working the nightshift at the hospital}. Also refers to the workers on duty during those hours: {The nightshift comes in at eleven}. Often written as two words: night shift.

A nightshirt is a loose, shirt-like garment worn for sleeping, typically reaching to the knees or below. Once standard sleepwear for men, nightshirts have largely given way to pajamas, though they remain in use: {He padded to the kitchen in his nightshirt}.

A nightstand is a small table or cabinet kept beside a bed, typically used to hold a lamp, alarm clock, phone, or book. Also called a bedside table or night table. {She set her glass of water on the nightstand before turning off the light.}

Nightstands are small tables placed beside a bed, typically holding a lamp, alarm clock, book, or phone. The plural of nightstand, which is also called a bedside table or night table. {The matching nightstands flanked the king-size bed.}

A nightstick is a club carried by police officers, typically a straight or side-handled baton used for self-defense or subduing suspects. The name reflects when police walked night beats. {The officer drew his nightstick.} Also called a billy club or truncheon.

Nightsticks are the long, straight clubs carried by police officers, typically made of wood, metal, or hard plastic. The term emphasizes their association with night patrol and maintaining order after dark. They are also called batons or billy clubs. {The officer reached for his nightstick when the crowd turned hostile.}

Nighttime is the hours of darkness between sunset and sunrise. The word functions as both noun and adjective: {nighttime temperatures}, {during the nighttime}. It contrasts with daytime and carries associations of sleep, rest, or activities that happen after dark.

A nightwalker is someone who roams around at night. The word carries sinister or illicit connotations—historically it meant a prostitute or thief who worked under cover of darkness. In fantasy fiction, nightwalker often names undead creatures or vampiric beings that emerge after sunset: {The nightwalkers rose from their graves at dusk}.

Nightwalkers are people who roam about at night. The term carries connotations of illicit activity—historically it meant prostitutes or petty criminals who worked under cover of darkness. In fantasy and horror contexts, nightwalkers are supernatural creatures that emerge after sunset: vampires, zombies, or other undead beings. {The streets belonged to nightwalkers and those who preyed on them.}

A nightwatch is a period of guard duty during nighttime hours, or the person or group keeping watch: {The nightwatch reported nothing unusual}. Historically, nightwatches patrolled cities before modern police forces existed. The term evokes vigilance in darkness—someone staying alert while others sleep.

A nightwatchman is someone employed to guard a building or property during nighttime hours, making rounds and checking for intruders, fires, or other problems. In cricket, a nightwatchman is a lower-order batsman sent in late in the day's play to protect a more skilled batsman from being dismissed before the close: {They sent in the nightwatchman with just three overs remaining}.

Nightwatchmen is the plural of nightwatchman—a person employed to guard premises during the night. The role is largely historical, associated with patrolling streets or buildings before modern security systems: {The nightwatchmen made their rounds every hour}. In cricket, a nightwatchman is a lower-order batsman sent in near the end of a day's play to protect better batsmen until the next morning.

Nigiri is a style of sushi consisting of a small mound of vinegared rice topped with a slice of raw fish or other seafood, sometimes bound with a thin strip of seaweed. The topping—typically salmon, tuna, or shrimp—is pressed by hand onto the rice: {I ordered two pieces of salmon nigiri}. Distinguished from rolls (maki) and sashimi (fish alone).

Nihilism is a philosophy in which traditional values and belief are rejected and human existence is considered to be pointless. Nihilism may also characterize attitudes that arise from such thinking, such as the idea that all established laws and institutions should be abandoned in favor of anarchy. Nihilism has never gained any serious support; the word is typically used to criticize someone’s ideas or actions as being extreme and unworkable.

A nihilist is someone who believes in nothing—no objective meaning, no moral truths, no basis for knowledge or value. The term comes from philosophy but often appears loosely to describe cynics or those who reject conventional beliefs: {He's such a nihilist—nothing matters to him}. In political contexts, nihilists historically advocated destroying existing institutions without proposing replacements.

Nihilistic describes an attitude that rejects meaning, value, or moral principles. A nihilistic worldview holds that life has no inherent purpose and traditional beliefs are groundless. The term often carries negative connotations—suggesting destructive cynicism rather than philosophical inquiry: {His nihilistic outlook made him dismiss any attempt at reform}. In casual use, nihilistic can simply mean darkly pessimistic or indifferent to consequences.

Nihilists are people who believe in nihilism—the philosophical position that life lacks objective meaning, purpose, or value. The term ranges from serious philosophical commitment to casual dismissal: {The nihilists in Dostoyevsky rejected all authority}. In looser use, nihilist describes anyone who seems to believe in nothing or who delights in destruction and negation: {He's such a nihilist—he thinks voting is pointless}.

Nil means nothing or zero. It appears most often in sports scores, especially in British English: {The match ended three-nil}. In other contexts, nil suggests complete absence: {The chances of success are nil}. The word comes from Latin and sounds slightly more formal than zero or nothing.

Nimbies is the plural of nimby, an acronym for "not in my backyard." A nimby opposes local development—housing, shelters, power plants, prisons—while often supporting such projects in principle elsewhere. The term is usually derogatory, suggesting hypocrisy or selfishness: {The nimbies blocked the affordable housing project}.

Nimble means quick and light in movement or action. A nimble {dancer} moves with easy grace; nimble {fingers} work deftly at a task. The word extends to mental quickness: a nimble {mind} adapts rapidly, a nimble {wit} produces clever responses. In business contexts, nimble describes organizations that respond quickly to change: {The startup was nimble enough to pivot when the market shifted}.

A nimbus is a luminous cloud or halo surrounding a supernatural being or saint in art—the golden glow around a holy figure's head. More generally, nimbus describes any atmosphere or aura that surrounds someone or something: {a nimbus of celebrity}, {a nimbus of controversy}. In meteorology, nimbus refers to rain-bearing clouds: {cumulonimbus}, {nimbostratus}.

Nimby is an acronym for "not in my back yard," describing someone who opposes local development projects—housing, power plants, homeless shelters—while often supporting them in principle elsewhere. The term is usually pejorative, implying hypocrisy or selfishness: {Classic nimby behavior—they want affordable housing, just not on their street}. As a noun, a nimby is such a person; as an adjective, it describes this attitude: {nimby opposition killed the project}.

Nimbyism is opposition to development projects in one's own neighborhood—an acronym from "not in my backyard." The term usually carries a negative connotation, implying selfish resistance to things society needs (affordable housing, homeless shelters, wind farms) when they're proposed nearby: {The council accused residents of nimbyism for blocking the halfway house}. Someone who practices nimbyism is a nimby.

A nimrod is a hunter, though this sense is rare outside literary or biblical contexts. In American slang, nimrod means a fool or incompetent person—a shift possibly influenced by Bugs Bunny sarcastically calling Elmer Fudd "nimrod," which audiences unfamiliar with the biblical reference took at face value: {Nice going, nimrod}. (Capitalized Nimrod is the biblical figure.)

A nincompoop is a fool or simpleton—someone lacking sense or judgment. The word sounds comical and old-fashioned, making it a mild, almost affectionate insult: {Don't be such a nincompoop}. It suggests bumbling incompetence rather than malice.
clues: A person notably short on wits

definition: Nincompoops is the plural of nincompoop, a fool or simpleton. The word has an old-fashioned, almost playful quality—more likely to appear in children's stories or gentle mockery than serious insult: {Those nincompoops couldn't organize a picnic}. It suggests bumbling incompetence rather than malice.

Nine is the cardinal number between eight and ten, written as 9 in Arabic numerals and IX in Roman numerals. It appears throughout culture: {a cat has nine lives}, {the whole nine yards}, {dressed to the nines}. In baseball, a team fields nine players; in bowling, knocking down nine pins leaves a spare. {Cloud nine} suggests blissful happiness.

Nineteen is the cardinal number between eighteen and twenty, written 19. It marks the last year of the teenage period: {She's nineteen and starting college}. The Nineteenth Amendment gave American women the right to vote.

Nineteenth is the ordinal form of nineteen, indicating position number nineteen in a sequence: {She finished nineteenth in the race}. As a noun, a nineteenth is one of nineteen equal parts: {Each heir received a nineteenth of the estate}. The nineteenth century spans 1801–1900, though informally people use it for the 1800s.
clues: Ordinal for the number following eighteen

definition: The nineties are the years from 1990 to 1999, or the numbers 90 through 99. Someone {in their nineties} is between 90 and 99 years old. {The nineties} without further context usually means the 1990s: {I grew up in the nineties}. A temperature {in the nineties} falls between 90 and 99 degrees.

Ninety is the number between eighty-nine and ninety-one, or nine times ten. The nineties refers to the years of a decade or century ending in 90-99: {She was born in the nineties}. Someone in their nineties is between ninety and ninety-nine years old. {Ninety percent} often means nearly all: {Ninety percent of success is just showing up}.

A ninja is a covert agent or mercenary in feudal Japan, trained in espionage, sabotage, and assassination. The historical figure has become a pop-culture archetype—black-clad, acrobatic, wielding throwing stars and swords. In casual use, ninja describes anyone with exceptional stealth or skill: {She's a ninja at parallel parking}. {He ninja'd past security without anyone noticing}.

Ninjas is the plural of ninja, a covert agent or mercenary in feudal Japan trained in espionage, sabotage, and assassination. The historical figure has been romanticized into a pop-culture archetype—black-clad, acrobatic, wielding throwing stars and swords. Ninja now describes anyone who moves stealthily or possesses impressive skill: {keyboard ninja}, {spreadsheet ninja}, {She ninja'd past the bouncer}.

Ninjitsu is the traditional Japanese art of stealth, espionage, and unconventional warfare practiced by ninja. The discipline encompasses skills like infiltration, disguise, escape techniques, and combat. In modern usage, ninjitsu often refers to martial arts schools claiming to teach these historical methods: {He's been studying ninjitsu for years}. Also spelled ninjutsu.

Ninjutsu is the traditional Japanese martial art and espionage techniques associated with ninja—covert agents of feudal Japan trained in stealth, sabotage, and unconventional warfare. The discipline encompasses combat skills, disguise, infiltration, and survival tactics. In modern usage, ninjutsu refers to martial arts schools claiming descent from these historical practices: {He studied ninjutsu for years}.

Ninnies is the plural of ninny, a mildly old-fashioned word for a foolish or simpleminded person. The term carries a gentle, almost affectionate quality of condescension rather than real hostility: {Don't be such ninnies—it's perfectly safe}. It suggests naivety or silliness more than stupidity.

A ninny is a foolish or simple-minded person—someone lacking sense or judgment. The word is mild and slightly old-fashioned, more playful than cutting: {Don't be such a ninny}. It suggests harmless stupidity rather than malice.

Ninth is the ordinal form of nine, indicating position number nine in a sequence: {She finished ninth in the race}. A ninth is also one of nine equal parts—one-ninth of something. In music, a ninth is an interval spanning nine notes of a scale, or a chord containing that interval.
clues: Where a relief pitcher often appears

definition: To nip something is to take a small, quick bite or pinch. A nip is an instance of doing this, or the amount taken. If you nip somewhere (especially in British English), you go there quickly and return. To nip it in the bud is to stop the development of some bad thing at an early stage. Nip and tuck is used informally in many situations: to characterize a quick improving activity, as an informal term for cosmetic plastic surgery, and to suggest that two competitors are very close.

Nipped is the past tense of nip—to pinch, bite sharply, or cut off. Frost nips plants, killing tender growth. A dog nips at heels. To nip something {in the bud} is to stop it early. In British slang, to nip somewhere is to go quickly: {I nipped out for cigarettes}. Nipped also means slightly drunk: {He was a bit nipped after the party}.

A nipper is a small child, used affectionately or casually: {The nippers are running around the yard}. More common in British English. Nippers are also small pincers or pliers for cutting or gripping—wire nippers, nail nippers. The tool sense comes from nip, to pinch or bite sharply. A nipper can be anything that nips: a crab's claw, a horse that bites.

Nippers are small pincers or pliers used for gripping, cutting, or pulling—especially for cutting wire or pulling nails. The word extends to the pincers of crabs and lobsters. In British and Australian slang, nippers are young children, probably from the notion of small, grabbing creatures: {The nippers are driving me mad today}.

Nipping describes a sharp, biting quality. Cold weather that nips at exposed skin is nipping: {a nipping wind}, {nipping frost}. The word can also describe quick, pinching actions or remarks that sting: {nipping criticism}. As the present participle of nip, it appears in phrases like {nipping something in the bud}—stopping it early.

A nipple is the small projection at the center of a mammal's breast or udder through which milk is released during nursing. In humans, the surrounding darker area is the areola, though nipple often refers to both together. By extension, nipple describes any small projection resembling one: the rubber nipple on a baby bottle, or a threaded pipe fitting that connects two other fittings.

Nipples are the small projections at the center of the breasts or chest, through which mammals nurse their young. In humans, nipples are sensitive and often erogenous. The word extends to nipple-shaped objects: a rubber nipple on a baby bottle, or a small threaded fitting connecting pipes. {The baby latched onto her nipple}. {He attached the grease nipple to the fitting}.

Nippy describes cold weather that bites at exposed skin—not freezing, but sharp enough to be uncomfortable: {It's getting nippy out there}. The word suggests briskness rather than severity. In British English, nippy also means quick or agile: {a nippy little car}.

A niqab is a face-covering veil worn by some Muslim women, leaving only the eyes visible. It differs from the hijab, which covers only the hair and neck, and from the burqa, which covers the entire face including the eyes behind mesh. The niqab is most common in Gulf states and among conservative communities: {She lifted her niqab to eat}.

Nirvana is a state of perfect peace and liberation from suffering, particularly in Buddhist and Hindu thought—the release from the cycle of rebirth and the extinction of individual desire. In casual use, nirvana describes any blissful or transcendent state: {After a week at the spa, I was in nirvana}. {Finding that rare record was pure nirvana for him.} (Capitalized Nirvana is the rock band.)

A nit is the egg of a louse, typically found attached to hair or clothing fibers. Nit-picking originally meant removing these tiny eggs—tedious, close work—which is why a nit-picker now means someone who fusses over minor details. In British slang, nit is also a mild insult meaning a foolish person: {Don't be such a nit}.

To nitpick is to criticize minor, trivial details—the kind of small flaws that matter little in the larger picture: {Stop nitpicking and focus on the main argument}. A nitpick is such a criticism. The word evokes someone searching for nits (louse eggs) in hair—tedious work requiring excessive attention to tiny things. Nitpicky describes this tendency.

Nitpicked is the past tense of nitpick, meaning to criticize by focusing on trivial faults or minor details. The image is of picking nits—louse eggs—from hair, a painstaking process requiring obsessive attention to tiny things. {The editor nitpicked every comma}. {She nitpicked his proposal until he gave up}.

A nitpicker is someone who focuses on trivial faults or minor details, often to an annoying degree. The word comes from the literal act of picking nits—louse eggs—from hair, a tedious task requiring close attention to tiny things. {Every nitpicker in the office had something to say about the font choice.} The verb is nitpick; the activity is nitpicking.

Nitpickers are people who focus on trivial faults or minor details, often to an annoying degree. The term suggests someone who finds problems where others see none—criticizing small imperfections while ignoring the larger picture: {The nitpickers complained about font choices while the building was on fire}. From the literal picking of nits (louse eggs) from hair.

Nitpicking is finding fault with minor, trivial details—the kind of criticism that focuses on small imperfections while ignoring the larger picture. A nitpicker obsesses over inconsequential errors: {Stop nitpicking my grammar and address my actual argument}. The word carries a dismissive tone, suggesting the criticism is petty or unwarranted.

Nitpicks are small, petty criticisms or complaints—the kind that focus on minor flaws rather than substantive issues: {His nitpicks about the font choice derailed the whole meeting}. The verb nitpick means to find fault with trivial details. The image comes from picking nits (louse eggs) from hair—tedious work on tiny things.

Nitpicky describes someone who fixates on minor details or faults, often to an annoying degree: {Stop being so nitpicky about the formatting}. A nitpicky person finds small flaws others would overlook or forgive. The word carries mild criticism—nitpicking may be thorough, but it's also petty. Related forms: nitpick (verb), nitpicker (noun).

Nitro is a prefix or modifier indicating the presence of nitrogen compounds, especially in explosives and fuels. Nitroglycerin and nitromethane are nitro compounds. In automotive contexts, nitro refers to nitrous oxide used to boost engine power: {He hit the nitro and pulled ahead}. Nitro cold brew coffee is infused with nitrogen gas for a creamy texture. As slang, nitro means explosive or extreme: {That concert was nitro}.

Nitrogen is a colorless, odorless gas that makes up about 78 percent of Earth's atmosphere. It is essential to life—a key component of proteins and DNA—yet most organisms cannot use atmospheric nitrogen directly; it must be "fixed" into compounds like ammonia. {Nitrogen fertilizers have transformed modern agriculture.} In liquid form, nitrogen is used as a coolant for its extremely low temperature.

Nitroglycerin is a highly explosive liquid compound, famously unstable—liable to detonate from shock, heat, or friction. It's the active component in dynamite, where it's stabilized by absorbent material. In medicine, nitroglycerin dilates blood vessels and treats angina and heart conditions: {He keeps nitroglycerin tablets for chest pain}. Also spelled nitroglycerine.

Nitroglycerine is a highly explosive oily liquid, extremely sensitive to shock and heat. It forms the basis of dynamite and other explosives. In medicine, nitroglycerine dilates blood vessels and is used to treat angina and heart conditions, typically as tablets dissolved under the tongue or as patches. Also spelled nitroglycerin.

Nitrous refers to nitrogen compounds, particularly nitrous oxide—a colorless gas used as an anesthetic in dentistry and as a propellant in whipped cream canisters. In automotive contexts, nitrous (short for nitrous oxide systems) boosts engine power: {The car runs nitrous for drag racing}. Recreationally, nitrous means inhaling the gas for its brief euphoric effect: {doing nitrous at a party}.

Nits are the eggs of lice, tiny white specks that cling to hair shafts. Removing them requires meticulous combing, hence {nitpicking}—finding fault with tiny details. In a separate sense, nits are minor complaints or criticisms themselves: {I have a few nits with the proposal, but overall it's solid}.

A nitwit is a foolish or stupid person. The word carries mild contempt without real venom—you might call a friend a nitwit for locking their keys in the car: {Don't be such a nitwit}. It sounds slightly dated, the kind of insult a grandparent might use.

Nitwits is the plural of nitwit, a mildly insulting term for foolish or stupid people. The word suggests thoughtlessness rather than malice: {Those nitwits left the gate open and the dog got out}. It's dismissive but relatively gentle—you might call family members nitwits without causing lasting offense.

Nix means to reject, cancel, or put an end to something: {The studio nixed the sequel}, {Management nixed the proposal}. As a noun, nix is a refusal or nothing at all. The word is informal and punchy, conveying decisive rejection rather than gentle decline.

Nixed is the past tense of nix, meaning to reject, cancel, or put a stop to something: {The studio nixed the sequel}, {Management nixed our proposal}. The word suggests a firm, often abrupt refusal—something gets shut down rather than merely declined.

Nobility refers to people of high hereditary rank—dukes, earls, barons, and the like—who form the aristocratic class in societies with titled hierarchies: {The nobility owned most of the land}. The word also denotes the quality of being noble in character—moral excellence, dignity, and elevated purpose: {There was a quiet nobility in how she faced her illness}. These senses connect through the idea that high birth was once assumed to bring high virtue.
clues: Those born to titles and lands

definition: Noble describes people, actions, or qualities worthy of high respect—characterized by moral excellence, dignity, or generosity of spirit: {a noble sacrifice}, {noble intentions}. Historically, noble refers to aristocratic rank—the nobility being those of high birth: {noble families}, {noble blood}. A noble bearing suggests dignity regardless of actual rank. In chemistry, noble gases are unreactive elements like helium and argon. As a noun, a noble is an aristocrat or a former English gold coin.

A nobleman is a man of noble rank or birth—a member of the aristocracy. The title typically comes with hereditary privileges, land, and social standing: {The nobleman surveyed his estate from horseback}. In historical contexts, noblemen held political power and military obligations; today the term is largely ceremonial or historical.

Noblemen are men of high hereditary rank in aristocratic societies—dukes, earls, barons, and the like. The term belongs to monarchy and feudal systems where nobility held land, titles, and political power by birthright: {The noblemen gathered at court to advise the king}. Singular: nobleman.

Nobles are members of the aristocracy—people who hold hereditary titles and rank above commoners in traditional social hierarchies: {The nobles gathered at court}. The word can also function as an adjective meaning having high moral qualities or impressive character, though noble without the s is more common in that sense. Historically, nobles held land, political power, and legal privileges denied to ordinary citizens.

A noblewoman is a woman of noble rank or birth—a duchess, countess, baroness, or similar aristocratic title. The term appears most often in historical contexts: {The noblewoman hosted lavish gatherings at her estate}. In fantasy fiction and period dramas, noblewomen navigate court intrigue and arranged marriages.

Nobodies is the plural of nobody, meaning people of no importance or influence. The word emphasizes lack of status or recognition: {We were nobodies before the show aired}. It often carries self-deprecating or dismissive force: {Why would they listen to a bunch of nobodies like us?}

Nobody means no person at all: {Nobody answered the door}. As a noun, a nobody is an insignificant or unimportant person: {He was a nobody before the scandal made him famous}. The word carries different weight depending on context—factual in {Nobody was home} but dismissive in {You're a nobody}.

Nocturnal describes activity that happens at night or creatures that are active during darkness. Owls and bats are nocturnal animals. A nocturnal {visit} occurs after dark. The word contrasts with diurnal (active by day): {The cat's nocturnal wanderings kept us awake}.

A nocturne is a piece of music evocative of night—dreamy, contemplative, often melancholic. The term is most associated with piano compositions, particularly those by Chopin, characterized by lyrical melodies over arpeggiated accompaniment: {She played a Chopin nocturne as the evening darkened}. In visual art, a nocturne is a painting of a night scene, a usage popularized by Whistler. The word suggests quietude and introspection rather than the drama of darkness.

Nocturnes is the plural of nocturne, a dreamy musical composition evocative of night. The term applies especially to piano pieces—Chopin's nocturnes are the most famous examples. In visual art, a nocturne is a night scene, particularly atmospheric paintings of moonlit landscapes or cityscapes: {Whistler's nocturnes of the Thames}.

A nod is a quick downward motion of the head, typically signaling agreement, acknowledgment, or greeting. To nod is to make this gesture: {She nodded in approval}. The nod extends to any brief acknowledgment: {The film gives a nod to classic noir}. To nod off is to fall asleep, from the way the head drops when drowsiness takes over.

Nodding is a slight, repeated downward movement of the head—typically signaling agreement, acknowledgment, or drowsiness. A nodding acquaintance is someone you know just well enough to greet with a nod. Nodding familiarity with a subject means shallow knowledge: {I have only a nodding acquaintance with French}. Things that nod move gently up and down: {nodding flowers in the breeze}.

A node is a point of connection or intersection within a larger system or network. In anatomy, lymph nodes are small organs that filter bodily fluids. In botany, a node is where leaves or branches attach to a stem. In computing and network theory, nodes are individual points—computers, servers, or data elements—connected to others in a network. The word suggests both a discrete unit and its relationship to a whole: {Each node in the blockchain stores a copy of the ledger}.

Nodes are points of connection or intersection within a network or structure. In anatomy, lymph nodes filter fluid throughout the body. In computing and telecommunications, a node is any device connected to a network: {The server went down and took three nodes with it}. In botany, a node is the point on a stem where leaves or branches emerge. More abstractly, nodes are key points in any system where elements converge or diverge.

Nods is the plural of nod—a quick downward movement of the head to signal acknowledgment, agreement, or greeting. In plural, nods often refers to instances of recognition or approval: {The film received nods from critics}, {She got nods of agreement around the table}.
