Award nominations are sometimes called nods: {The album earned several Grammy nods}.

Noel is Christmas, or a Christmas carol. The word comes from French and appears most often in seasonal contexts: {The First Noel} is a traditional carol, and noel serves as a poetic or archaic alternative to Christmas in cards and decorations. (Capitalized Noel is a given name.)

A noggin is an informal word for the head: {Use your noggin}. The term is playful rather than crude, often appearing in contexts involving thinking or minor bumps: {I hit my noggin on the cabinet}. Older and now rare meanings include a small cup or a measure of liquor.

Noggins is the plural of noggin, an informal word for the head: {Use your noggins, people}. A noggin is also a small cup or a small measure of liquor, typically a quarter pint. The head sense likely comes from the cup—both are containers of roughly similar size and shape.

A nogoodnik is a person who is no good—a troublemaker, scoundrel, or ne'er-do-well. The word borrows the Yiddish suffix *-nik* (one associated with a thing) and attaches it to the English phrase "no good," creating a playful but pointed term of disapproval: {Her brother was a nogoodnik who couldn't hold down a job}. The tone is usually more exasperated than harsh.

Noir refers to a style of crime fiction or film marked by cynicism, moral ambiguity, and bleak atmosphere. The term comes from French for "black," evoking shadowy visuals and dark themes. Classic noir features hard-boiled detectives, femmes fatales, and urban settings drenched in rain and corruption: {a noir thriller}, {film noir from the 1940s}. The aesthetic has extended beyond its origins: {tech noir}, {neo-noir}. As an adjective, noir describes anything with that brooding, fatalistic quality.

Noise is unwanted sound—loud, discordant, or interfering with what you're trying to hear: {The construction noise made it impossible to concentrate}. The meaning extends to any unwanted signal that obscures information: {static noise}, {background noise in data}. To noise something about is to spread it as rumor or gossip. To {make noise} about something is to complain or draw attention to it. In casual speech, noise can mean meaningless talk: {His promises were just noise}.

A noisemaker is a device designed to produce loud sounds, especially the handheld items used at celebrations—horns, rattles, and clappers brought out at New Year's Eve parties and sporting events. The term extends to any person or thing that makes a racket: {The neighbors complained about the noisemakers next door}.

Noisemakers are devices designed to produce loud sounds, typically used at celebrations like New Year's Eve or sporting events. The category includes horns, rattles, clappers, and party favors: {The kids grabbed noisemakers when the ball dropped}. Figuratively, a noisemaker is anyone who makes a lot of noise or commotion.

Noises is the plural of noise—unwanted or disturbing sounds, or sounds in general: {strange noises in the attic}, {the noises of the city}. To {make noises about} something is to hint at intentions without committing: {She's been making noises about retiring}. To {make the right noises} is to say expected or appropriate things, often insincerely.

Noisy means making a lot of sound, or filled with sound. A noisy {crowd}, a noisy {engine}, a noisy {restaurant}. The word carries a negative connotation—loud suggests volume, but noisy suggests unwanted or excessive volume. A noisy {neighbor} disturbs the peace. Data or signals described as noisy contain interference or unwanted variation: {The readings were too noisy to be useful}.

A nomad is a person with no fixed home, moving from place to place—traditionally following herds, seasonal resources, or trade routes. The word extends to anyone who moves frequently: {After five years as a digital nomad, she'd worked from thirty countries}. Nomadic describes this lifestyle or tendency toward restless movement.

Nomadic describes a way of life involving regular movement from place to place rather than permanent settlement. Nomadic peoples traditionally follow seasonal patterns, moving with herds or toward resources: {nomadic tribes of the steppes}. The word extends to anyone who moves frequently: {She lived a nomadic existence, never staying anywhere longer than a year}.

Nomadism is a way of life based on moving from place to place rather than settling permanently. Traditional nomads follow seasonal patterns—herding livestock to new pastures or tracking game. The term extends to modern lifestyles without fixed residence: {Digital nomadism lets remote workers travel while employed}. The word emphasizes the pattern of movement itself, not just occasional travel.

Nomads are people who move from place to place rather than settling permanently in one location. Traditionally, nomadic peoples followed seasonal patterns for grazing livestock or hunting: {The nomads moved their herds to higher pastures in summer}. The word extends to anyone who lives without a fixed home, whether by choice or circumstance: {Digital nomads work remotely while traveling the world}.

Nominal means in name only, often implying a gap between label and reality: {a nominal democracy with no real elections}, {He's the nominal head of the company}. A nominal fee or sum is so small it barely counts—token rather than substantial: {They charged a nominal fee for admission}. In technical contexts, nominal refers to the designated or expected value: {The engine is running at nominal capacity}. In aerospace jargon, nominal simply means everything is functioning as planned: {All systems nominal}.

To nominate is to formally propose someone for a position, honor, or award: {The president nominated her for the Supreme Court}, {The film was nominated for Best Picture}. A nomination puts a name forward for consideration but doesn't guarantee selection. In politics, to nominate is to select a candidate to represent a party in an election: {The convention nominated him on the first ballot}.

Nominated is the past tense of nominate, meaning to formally propose someone for a position, honor, or award. A political party nominates candidates for office; committees nominate people for prizes: {She was nominated for Best Director}. To nominate can also mean to designate or appoint: {He nominated his sister as executor of his will}.

Nominates is the third-person singular of nominate—to formally propose someone for a position, honor, or award. A president nominates judges; a committee nominates candidates; the Academy nominates films: {The party nominates its candidate at the convention}. To nominate can also mean to designate or appoint: {She nominated Tuesday as the meeting day}.

Nomination is the act of formally proposing someone for a position, award, or honor, or the state of being so proposed: {Her nomination for the Supreme Court surprised everyone}, {The film received six Oscar nominations}. A nomination may also refer to the formal selection itself, as when a political party chooses its candidate: {He secured the nomination after a contested primary}.

Nominations are formal proposals of candidates for positions, awards, or honors. The word covers both the act of nominating and the resulting candidacies: {She received three Oscar nominations}. In political contexts, nominations often follow primaries or conventions: {He secured the party's nomination after a long campaign}. The singular nomination works for both the process and its outcome.

A nominee is a person who has been proposed or selected for something—a position, an award, or a role. In elections, nominees are candidates chosen to represent a party: {the Democratic nominee for president}. In awards, nominees are finalists under consideration: {an Oscar nominee}. In legal and financial contexts, a nominee may be someone designated to act on another's behalf or hold assets in their name.

Nominees are people who have been formally proposed or put forward for something—an award, an office, or a position. The word usually implies selection from a larger field: {The Oscar nominees were announced this morning}. A nominee may also be someone designated to act on another's behalf, as in legal or financial contexts.

Nonaggression is the policy or principle of refraining from attacking or initiating conflict. It appears most often in diplomatic contexts: a nonaggression {pact} or nonaggression {treaty} is an agreement between nations not to attack each other. The term implies deliberate restraint rather than mere absence of hostility.

Nonalcoholic describes drinks containing no alcohol or negligible amounts: {nonalcoholic beer}, {nonalcoholic cocktails}. The term often appears on menus and labels to distinguish options for those avoiding alcohol. In recent years, the nonalcoholic beverage market has expanded well beyond sodas to include sophisticated mocktails and alcohol-free spirits.

A nonapology is an expression that has the form of an apology but doesn't actually accept responsibility or express genuine regret. The classic formula is "I'm sorry if anyone was offended"—which shifts blame to those who took offense rather than acknowledging wrongdoing. Politicians and public figures often issue nonapologies when pressured to apologize but unwilling to admit fault: {His statement was a nonapology that satisfied no one}.

Nonattachment is a state of mind in which one engages with life without clinging to outcomes, possessions, or relationships. Central to Buddhist and Stoic philosophy, it doesn't mean indifference or withdrawal—rather, experiencing things fully while accepting their impermanence: {Nonattachment allowed her to love deeply without fear of loss}. The practice aims to reduce suffering caused by grasping at what cannot be held.

A nonbeliever is someone who doesn't accept a particular belief, especially religious faith. The term usually refers to atheists or agnostics from the perspective of believers: {The preacher warned against the influence of nonbelievers}. It can apply to any doctrine: {nonbelievers in free-market economics}. The word often carries a faint tone of disapproval from those using it.

Nonbelievers are people who don't hold a particular belief, especially religious faith. The term typically appears from the perspective of believers describing those outside their faith: {The missionary sought to convert nonbelievers}. It can sound dismissive or othering, implying the belief in question is the default position. Also spelled non-believers.

Nonbinary describes a gender identity that doesn't fit neatly into the categories of man or woman. A nonbinary person may identify as both, neither, or somewhere along a spectrum between them. The term emerged in the early 21st century alongside growing recognition of gender as distinct from biological sex. {My coworker is nonbinary and uses they/them pronouns.}

Nonchalance is a cool, casual indifference—the appearance of not caring much about something, especially something others might find stressful or important. The word suggests ease and composure: {She accepted the award with studied nonchalance}. It can be genuine calm or a deliberately cultivated pose: {His nonchalance about the deadline worried his teammates}.

Nonchalant describes a casual, unconcerned manner—cool and unbothered, whether genuinely or as a pose. Someone nonchalant about a crisis either doesn't grasp its severity or wants to appear unfazed: {She gave a nonchalant shrug when asked about the deadline}. The word often carries a hint of admiration for someone's composure under pressure.

Nonchalantly means in a casually unconcerned or indifferent manner, as if something requires no special attention or effort: {She nonchalantly tossed the keys on the counter}. The word often suggests studied coolness—appearing relaxed even when circumstances might warrant more reaction: {He nonchalantly mentioned he'd won the lottery}.

Noncom is military slang for a noncommissioned officer—an enlisted member who holds a supervisory rank like sergeant or corporal, as distinct from commissioned officers who hold their rank by formal appointment. {The noncoms kept the platoon running while the lieutenant figured out what he was doing.}

A noncombatant is a person not engaged in fighting during a war or conflict. The term covers civilians, medical personnel, chaplains, and others protected under international law from deliberate attack. Military members who don't directly participate in combat—cooks, clerks, mechanics—may also be called noncombatants: {The treaty required safe passage for noncombatants}.

Noncombatants are people who don't participate in fighting during armed conflict. The term covers civilians and also military personnel not engaged in combat—medics, chaplains, prisoners of war. International law affords noncombatants special protections: {The bombing killed dozens of noncombatants}. The singular noncombatant works as noun or adjective: {noncombatant casualties}, {a noncombatant role}.

Noncommittal describes responses or behavior that avoids taking a definite position or making a commitment. A noncommittal answer neither agrees nor disagrees: {She gave a noncommittal shrug when asked if she'd attend}. The word often suggests deliberate evasiveness—someone staying neutral to keep options open or avoid controversy.

A noncompete is a contractual clause or agreement that restricts someone from working for competitors or starting a competing business after leaving an employer. Typically limited in duration and geographic scope: {She couldn't join a rival firm for two years because of her noncompete}. Often used attributively: {noncompete clause}, {noncompete agreement}. Enforceability varies widely by jurisdiction.

A nonconformist refuses to follow established customs, beliefs, or practices. The term can be admiring—suggesting independent thinking and principled resistance to groupthink—or dismissive, implying stubbornness or contrarianism for its own sake. {She was always a nonconformist, dyeing her hair purple before it was fashionable.} As an adjective: {his nonconformist attitude toward corporate culture}. In British history, Nonconformist specifically designated Protestants who separated from the Church of England.

Nonconformists are people who refuse to follow established customs, beliefs, or practices. The term can be neutral or admiring, suggesting independence of mind: {The tech industry celebrates its nonconformists}. In British religious history, Nonconformists were Protestants who did not conform to the Church of England—Baptists, Methodists, Quakers, and others.

Nonconformity is refusal to follow accepted standards, customs, or practices. The word suggests deliberate deviation rather than mere difference: {Her nonconformity made her unpopular with management}. In geology, a nonconformity is a surface where sedimentary rock overlies older igneous or metamite rock—a break in the expected sequence.

Noncooperation is the refusal to cooperate, especially as a form of protest against authority. The term gained prominence through Gandhi's campaigns against British rule in India, where mass noncooperation—refusing to pay taxes, attend government schools, or buy British goods—became a powerful form of nonviolent resistance. {The workers' noncooperation brought production to a halt.}

Nondescript describes something so ordinary or featureless that it's difficult to describe or remember: {a nondescript office building}, {He drove a nondescript sedan}. The word suggests anonymity through lack of distinguishing characteristics—not ugly or attractive, just unremarkable. As a noun, a nondescript is a person or thing of this sort.

Nondisclosure is the practice of keeping information confidential. The term appears most often in legal contexts: a nondisclosure {agreement} (NDA) is a contract requiring parties to keep certain information secret. {Employees signed nondisclosures before seeing the prototype}. Nondisclosure can also refer to failure to reveal required information: {nondisclosure of assets on a loan application}.

None means not any or no amount of something: {None of the answers were correct}, {I wanted cake but there was none left}. It can refer to people: {None were willing to volunteer}. Despite what some insist, none takes either singular or plural verbs depending on context—both {none of them is ready} and {none of them are ready} are standard. {None other than} emphasizes surprising identity: {The caller was none other than the president}.

A nonentity is a person of no importance or influence—someone who barely registers in the social or professional landscape: {He was treated as a nonentity at the conference}. The word can also refer to something that doesn't exist or has no real substance. Calling someone a nonentity is dismissive, suggesting they lack the presence or significance to matter.

A nonevent is something anticipated that fails to occur or proves anticlimactic: {The much-hyped product launch turned out to be a nonevent}. It can describe an occasion that generates no interest or consequence: {The meeting was a complete nonevent—nothing was decided}.

Nonexistent means not existing—not real, not present, or entirely absent. Something can be nonexistent in fact {Unicorns are nonexistent} or effectively so {Customer service was nonexistent}. The word often emphasizes complete absence rather than mere scarcity: {His chances of winning are nonexistent}.

Nonfiction is writing that presents factual information rather than imagined stories—biography, history, journalism, essays, and similar works. The term defines itself by what it isn't: not fiction. {I mostly read nonfiction these days.} A nonfiction account may still contain errors or bias, but it claims to represent reality.

A nonissue is something that doesn't matter or isn't worth discussing—a topic someone raises that others dismiss as irrelevant or already settled: {Whether she's qualified is a nonissue; she has more experience than anyone}. Often used to shut down debate: {That's a nonissue}. Something can become a nonissue once it's resolved or shown to be unimportant.

Nonjudgmental means refraining from moral criticism or negative evaluation. A nonjudgmental {listener} hears without condemning. The word appears frequently in therapeutic and supportive contexts: {The counselor maintained a nonjudgmental attitude}. Often spelled nonjudgmental (without the second e) in American English.

Nonjudgmental describes an attitude that refrains from criticizing or condemning others for their choices, behavior, or circumstances. A nonjudgmental {therapist} listens without expressing disapproval. The word often appears in contexts involving sensitive topics—addiction, sexuality, mental health—where fear of judgment might prevent honesty: {The hotline offers nonjudgmental support}.

Nonlethal describes weapons, force, or methods designed to incapacitate or deter without causing death. Police may use nonlethal measures like tasers, rubber bullets, or pepper spray for crowd control or subduing suspects. The term is sometimes criticized as misleading since these methods can still cause serious injury or death in certain circumstances; {less-lethal} is an alternative preferred by some agencies. {The officer reached for his nonlethal weapon first.}

Nonmonogamy is the practice of having romantic or sexual relationships with more than one person, typically with the knowledge and consent of everyone involved. The term covers various arrangements: open relationships, polyamory, swinging. {They've practiced nonmonogamy for years.} The prefix distinguishes consensual arrangements from cheating or infidelity.

Nonna is Italian for grandmother, used in English by Italian-American families and increasingly by others as an affectionate term: {Nonna's making Sunday gravy}. The word evokes traditional Italian cooking and family warmth. A nonna figure suggests an older woman who feeds everyone generously and dispenses wisdom.

Nonnegotiable describes something that cannot be changed, compromised, or bargained over. A nonnegotiable demand must be accepted as-is: {Her salary requirements were nonnegotiable}. The term often marks personal boundaries or core principles: {Honesty is nonnegotiable in this relationship}. In finance, a nonnegotiable instrument cannot be transferred to another party.

Nonpartisan means not aligned with or favoring any political party or faction. A nonpartisan {election} doesn't list candidates by party affiliation. Nonpartisan {analysis} aims to be objective rather than ideologically driven. The term often describes organizations, committees, or officials expected to act without political bias: {The Congressional Budget Office is nonpartisan}.

Nonperishables are goods, especially food, that don't spoil quickly and can be stored for extended periods without refrigeration: canned goods, dried pasta, rice, beans. The term appears most often in contexts of emergency preparedness, food drives, and pantry staples: {Stock up on nonperishables before hurricane season}. {The food bank only accepts nonperishables}.

A nonperson is someone treated as if they don't exist or don't matter. The term often describes individuals erased from official records or public acknowledgment, especially under totalitarian regimes: {Stalin had rivals airbrushed from photographs, turning them into nonpersons}. More broadly, it refers to anyone systematically denied recognition, rights, or basic human consideration: {Undocumented workers are treated as nonpersons by the system}.

A nonprofit is an organization that uses its revenue to pursue a mission rather than distribute profits to owners or shareholders. Charities, foundations, and advocacy groups are typically nonprofits: {She works for a nonprofit that provides legal aid}. As an adjective, it describes this status: {nonprofit organization}, {nonprofit sector}. Also spelled non-profit.

Nonprofits are organizations that use revenue to pursue a mission rather than distribute profits to owners or shareholders. Churches, charities, universities, and advocacy groups operate as nonprofits: {She works for a nonprofit that provides legal aid to immigrants}. The term functions as both noun and adjective: {nonprofit sector}, {nonprofit status}. Tax-exempt status comes with restrictions on political activity and financial transparency requirements.

Nonrenewable describes resources that cannot be replenished once depleted, or can only be restored over geological timescales. Fossil fuels—coal, oil, natural gas—are the classic examples: {nonrenewable energy sources}. The term usually appears in environmental and economic discussions contrasting finite resources with renewable alternatives like solar or wind power.
Nonsense, mainly a noun, is used interjectionally to characterize what someone has said as worthless, misleading, untrue, or unacceptable: His premise is nonsense.

Nonsensical means lacking sense or meaning—absurd, illogical, or unintelligible. A nonsensical argument fails to follow logical reasoning. Nonsensical words or sentences are gibberish: {The toddler babbled nonsensical syllables}. The word often carries dismissive force: {His excuses were completely nonsensical}.

A nonstarter is something that has no chance of succeeding or being accepted—an idea, proposal, or plan that fails before it begins. {Raising taxes is a political nonstarter}. The term comes from horse racing, where a nonstarter is an entered horse that doesn't run. In broader use, it dismisses suggestions as not worth considering: {That's a nonstarter for me}.

Nonstarters are things that have no chance of succeeding or being accepted. A proposal that's a nonstarter won't even be considered: {Universal basic income is a nonstarter with fiscal conservatives}. The term comes from horse racing, where a nonstarter is an entered horse that doesn't run. Something dismissed as a nonstarter never gets out of the gate.

Nonstick describes cookware with a coating that prevents food from adhering to the surface: {a nonstick pan}, {nonstick spray}. The coating allows cooking with less oil and makes cleanup easier. By extension, nonstick can describe any surface designed to resist adhesion.

Nonstop means without stopping or pausing. A nonstop {flight} travels directly to its destination without landing in between. Nonstop {rain} continues without interruption. The word works as adjective or adverb: {The baby cried nonstop for an hour}. Also spelled non-stop.

Nonverbal describes communication or expression that doesn't use words. Body language, facial expressions, gestures, and tone of voice are nonverbal cues: {Her nonverbal signals suggested she was uncomfortable}. In developmental contexts, a nonverbal child hasn't yet acquired speech or communicates through other means.

Nonviolence is the practice or principle of refusing to use physical force, especially as a means of political resistance or social change. Associated with figures like Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr., nonviolence treats peaceful protest—civil disobedience, marches, boycotts—as both morally superior and strategically effective: {The movement was committed to nonviolence even when met with brutality}.

Nonviolent describes actions, movements, or people that avoid physical force or aggression. The word often appears in political contexts: {nonviolent protest}, {nonviolent resistance}. A nonviolent offender has committed crimes—typically drug-related—that didn't involve harming others. {The demonstration remained nonviolent despite police provocation.}

Noob is internet and gaming slang for a newcomer or inexperienced person, especially one who makes obvious mistakes or asks basic questions. The term ranges from affectionate to dismissive depending on context: {Don't be such a noob} implies incompetence, while {We were all noobs once} acknowledges the learning curve. Variant spellings include newb and n00b, the latter using zeros for o's in the style of leetspeak.

A noobie is someone new to an activity, game, or community—inexperienced and still learning the basics. The term comes from gaming culture, where it can be neutral or dismissive depending on tone: {Don't be too hard on her, she's a noobie} versus {What a noobie move}. Also spelled noob, newbie, or n00b.

Noobs are newcomers or inexperienced players, especially in online gaming. The term carries condescension—a noob isn't just new but cluelessly so, making obvious mistakes or asking questions easily answered by searching. {Stop feeding the enemy team, noob.} Also spelled newbs or n00bs. Someone who's been playing long enough to know better but still plays badly may be called a noob as an insult.

Noodle has two main clusters of meaning. The first is a strip or tube of pasta, typically made from wheat flour and eggs, boiled and served in soups or with sauce: {chicken noodle soup}, {rice noodles}. The second is informal for head or brain: {Use your noodle}. To noodle is to improvise casually, especially on a musical instrument: {He noodled on the guitar for a while}. To noodle over something is to think about it in an unhurried way.
clues: What ramen bowls are full of

definition: A noodlehead is a fool or simpleton—someone whose head seems as soft and limp as a wet noodle. The word is mildly insulting but often affectionate: {Don't be such a noodlehead}. It belongs to the long tradition of compound insults suggesting empty or defective heads: blockhead, bonehead, knucklehead.

Noodles are long, thin strips of pasta or dough, typically boiled and served in soups or with sauces. The word covers both Italian varieties like spaghetti and Asian types like ramen and rice noodles. To noodle is to improvise casually, especially on a musical instrument: {He noodled on the guitar while we talked}. To noodle something over is to think about it idly. As slang, noodle means head: {Use your noodle}.

Noodling has two distinct meanings. One is catching catfish by hand—reaching into underwater holes and letting the fish bite your arm, then pulling it out. This is a regional practice in the American South and Midwest. The other meaning is casual, improvisatory playing on a musical instrument: {He spent an hour noodling on the guitar}. Both suggest an unstructured, exploratory quality.

A noogie is the act of grinding one's knuckles against someone's scalp, typically while holding their head in a headlock. It's a rough but usually playful gesture, common among siblings and schoolyard friends: {He gave his little brother a noogie}. The word emerged in American slang in the 1970s.

Noogies is the plural of noogie, a playful form of minor torment where someone rubs their knuckles against another person's scalp, typically while holding the victim in a headlock. It's associated with roughhousing among children and siblings: {My older brother used to give me noogies until I cried}. The singular also appears as a verb: {He noogied me in front of my friends}.

A nook is a small, secluded space—a corner or recess set apart from a larger area: {a breakfast nook}, {a reading nook}. The word suggests coziness and shelter. In the phrase {every nook and cranny}, it means every small space or hidden corner: {We searched every nook and cranny of the house}.

Nookie is slang for sexual activity, especially intercourse. The word is playful and mildly vulgar rather than crude: {looking to get some nookie}, {a little nookie on the side}. It suggests casual or recreational sex rather than lovemaking.

Nooks are small, secluded, or partly enclosed spaces—corners, recesses, or out-of-the-way spots: {a cozy reading nook}, {a breakfast nook off the kitchen}. The phrase {every nook and cranny} means every possible place, suggesting a thorough search or complete coverage: {We searched every nook and cranny of the house}.

Nooky is informal slang for sexual activity or intercourse: {looking for a little nooky}, {They snuck off for some nooky}. The word is playful and somewhat coy—less crude than most sexual slang, often used with humor or affection. Also spelled nookie.

Noon is twelve o'clock in the daytime, when the sun reaches its highest point. It marks the middle of the day, dividing morning from afternoon. A noon {meeting}, noon {deadline}, or noon {Mass} happens at this hour. {High noon} emphasizes exactness or dramatic confrontation—from Westerns where gunslingers faced off at midday.

A nooner is sex in the middle of the day, typically during a lunch break: {We snuck home for a nooner}. The word carries a sense of stolen time—a quickie squeezed between work obligations. Less commonly, nooner refers to any midday activity, but the sexual sense dominates.

A noose is a loop of rope with a slipknot that tightens when pulled, used historically for hanging executions. The image carries heavy associations with lynching and racial terror in America, making noose displays threatening rather than merely morbid. Figuratively, a noose represents a trap or inescapable situation: {The noose was tightening around the corrupt politician}.

Nooses is the plural of noose, a loop of rope or cord with a knot that tightens when pulled, historically associated with execution by hanging. The singular noose carries powerful symbolic weight in American culture, where it evokes lynching and racial terror; displaying one is widely understood as a threat or hate symbol. Figuratively, a noose suggests entrapment or impending doom: {I felt the noose tightening as my debts mounted}.
Nope is an informal variant of no and may carry slightly less force of finality than no does.

A noreaster is a powerful storm along the Atlantic coast of North America, characterized by winds blowing from the northeast. These storms typically bring heavy rain or snow, high winds, and coastal flooding, especially in New England and the Mid-Atlantic states. The spelling reflects casual pronunciation of {nor'easter}, though some insist the traditional nautical term is {northeaster}.

Noreasters are powerful storms that strike the eastern coast of North America, named for the northeasterly winds that precede them. These winter storms bring heavy snow, rain, and coastal flooding from the Mid-Atlantic through New England. {Three noreasters hit Boston in two weeks.} Also spelled nor'easters.

Nori is edible seaweed, dried and pressed into thin, dark green sheets. It's the wrapper around sushi rolls and onigiri, and appears shredded as a garnish on rice and noodle dishes. The flavor is briny and faintly sweet. {I picked up some nori at the Asian grocery.}

A norm is a standard or pattern, especially of social behavior—what's considered typical or expected within a group: {Tipping twenty percent has become the norm}. In mathematics, a norm is a function that assigns a positive length to vectors. To violate norms is to behave outside accepted boundaries: {Gender norms are shifting}. The word often appears in plural: social norms, cultural norms, community norms. (Capitalized Norm is a given name.)

The adjective normal is far more frequent and varied in meaning than its related noun norm. What is normal is expected, common, usual, unexceptional. The normal time for something is when it usually or customarily happens. Normal practice is what people usually do in a given situation. The frequent phrase perfectly normal is often used to suggest that some phenomenon should not be regarded as unusual: It’s perfectly normal for the president to defend his legacy. Normal is also the place on a scale where most values occur; outside of this range, values are above normal or below normal.

Normalcy is the state of being normal—the condition of things when nothing unusual is happening. The word gained prominence when Warren Harding campaigned on a "return to normalcy" after World War I. Some consider it a less elegant variant of normality, but both are standard: {Life has returned to normalcy}, {We're all craving some normalcy}.

Normalisation is the British spelling of normalization—the process of making something standard, regular, or acceptable. In diplomacy, normalisation of relations means restoring normal ties between countries: {The two nations began normalisation talks after decades of hostility}. In data processing, normalisation organizes information to reduce redundancy. The word often carries political weight when applied to previously unacceptable conditions: {Critics warned against the normalisation of extremist rhetoric}.

Normalise is the British spelling of normalize. To normalise something is to make it normal or standard—to bring it within expected parameters. Data gets normalised to allow comparison across different scales. Behaviors become normalised when society stops treating them as unusual: {Social media has normalised sharing personal details with strangers}. The word often carries skepticism about whether the thing being normalised should be.

Normality is the state of being normal—conforming to what is typical, expected, or standard. It often appears in discussions of social behavior, where people debate what constitutes normality and who gets to define it. {After months of upheaval, we're finally returning to some sense of normality.} In chemistry, normality is a specific measure of solution concentration. British English sometimes prefers normalcy for the general sense, though both forms are widely understood.

Normalization is the process of making something standard, typical, or acceptable. In social contexts, it describes how unusual or taboo things become ordinary through repeated exposure: {the normalization of violence in media}. In statistics and computing, normalization adjusts data to a common scale or format. In database design, it organizes tables to reduce redundancy. The word often carries concern about gradual acceptance of harmful things: {We can't allow the normalization of hate speech}.

Normalize means to make something standard, typical, or conforming to a norm. In social contexts, to normalize a behavior or condition is to make it seem acceptable or unremarkable: {Society has normalized constant connectivity}. In technical fields, normalizing involves adjusting data or values to a common scale for comparison. The word carries political weight when people argue about whether certain practices should be normalized or whether normalization legitimizes something harmful.

Normalized means made standard or brought into conformity with a norm. Data gets normalized when adjusted to a common scale for comparison. Relations between countries normalize when they return to ordinary diplomatic terms after a period of tension. In casual use, normalized often describes how something once unusual becomes accepted as ordinary: {Social media has normalized oversharing}. The word can carry disapproval when applied to things the speaker believes shouldn't be accepted.

Normalizing is making something standard or acceptable, treating it as normal rather than exceptional or deviant: {Social media is normalizing casual cruelty}. The word often carries disapproval—to accuse someone of normalizing behavior is to say they're making dangerous or harmful things seem ordinary. In metallurgy, normalizing is a heat treatment that refines grain structure in steel.

Normcore describes a fashion trend and aesthetic that deliberately embraces ordinary, unremarkable clothing—think plain t-shirts, dad jeans, and basic sneakers. Rather than standing out through bold or distinctive style choices, normcore finds a kind of anti-fashion statement in blending in. The term combines "normal" and "hardcore," suggesting an ironic commitment to looking aggressively average. {Her normcore wardrobe consisted entirely of gray hoodies and khakis.}

A normie is someone perceived as boringly conventional—a person with mainstream tastes, typical social habits, and no niche interests or subcultural affiliations. The term originated in online communities where enthusiasts of anime, gaming, or internet culture distinguish themselves from the uninitiated masses: {Normies wouldn't get this meme}. Often mildly disparaging, though sometimes self-aware or ironic.

Normies is mildly dismissive slang for ordinary, conventional people—those who follow mainstream tastes and lack interest in niche subcultures, obscure hobbies, or internet communities. The term implies the speaker belongs to a more discerning or unconventional group: {Normies wouldn't get this meme}. Originally from chan culture, now widespread online.

Norms are standards of behavior or expectation that a group considers typical or acceptable. Social norms govern everything from how close to stand to strangers to whether you tip at a restaurant. To violate norms is to behave in ways that others find inappropriate or offensive. In statistics, a norm is a standard or reference point against which measurements are compared. {Test scores were compared against national norms.}

North is the direction toward the top of a map, toward the pole star, or opposite to south. It serves as both direction and adjective: {north wind}, {north side}, {heading north}. In many countries, the North designates a region—in the United States, the states that opposed the Confederacy. {They drove north for hours.} (Capitalized North may refer specifically to a region or proper name.)

Northeast is the direction midway between north and east, or the region lying in that direction. As an adjective or adverb, it describes movement or position toward that point: {The storm is tracking northeast}, {the northeast corner of the property}. In the United States, the Northeast typically means the states from Maine to Maryland or thereabouts.

A northeaster is a storm or strong wind blowing from the northeast. Along the Atlantic coast of North America, northeasters are particularly notorious—powerful winter storms that bring heavy snow, rain, and coastal flooding: {The northeaster knocked out power to thousands of homes}. Also spelled nor'easter.

Northern means situated in, toward, or coming from the north. A northern {climate} is colder; a northern {wind} blows from that direction. The term often describes the upper portion of a region or country: the northern {states}, the northern {coast}. In American contexts, Northern frequently references the Union states during the Civil War era.

A northerner is someone from the northern part of a region or country. In American usage, it often refers specifically to someone from states that opposed the Confederacy during the Civil War: {Northerners flooded into the South during Reconstruction}. The term is relative—a Virginian might be a northerner to someone from Georgia.

Northerners are people from the northern part of a country or region. In American usage, northerners typically means people from states above the Mason-Dixon line, especially in historical contexts involving the Civil War: {Northerners and Southerners still argue about the war}. In England, it distinguishes those from industrial cities like Manchester or Leeds from Londoners. The term often carries cultural assumptions about accent, temperament, or politics.

Northwest refers to the direction midway between north and west, or the region lying in that direction. As an adjective or adverb, it describes movement or position toward that compass point: {We drove northwest for three hours}. A northwest wind blows from the northwest. The term often appears in regional names: {the Pacific Northwest}, {Northwest Territories}. (Capitalized Northwest typically refers to a specific region.)

Northwoods refers to the heavily forested region of the northern United States and Canada, characterized by coniferous and mixed forests, lakes, and cold winters. The term evokes a particular landscape and lifestyle—hunting, fishing, cabins, and wilderness: {We're heading up to the northwoods for deer season}. Sometimes written as two words or hyphenated.

The nose is the part of the face containing the nostrils and the organ of smell. It extends to nose-shaped projections: the nose of an airplane, the nose of a wine (its aroma). To nose around is to pry or investigate. To {nose out} a competitor is to defeat them narrowly. If you {follow your nose}, you go straight ahead or trust your instincts. To {look down your nose} at something is to regard it with contempt. {On the nose} means exactly right.

A nosebleed is bleeding from the nose, usually from dry air, injury, or irritation. As an adjective, nosebleed describes extreme height or elevation: {nosebleed seats} are the cheapest tickets in an arena, so high up the thin air might cause bleeding. Nosebleed prices or valuations are dangerously elevated.

Nosebleeds are episodes of bleeding from the nose, usually from irritated or broken blood vessels inside the nasal passages: {I used to get nosebleeds every winter}. In sports and entertainment venues, the nosebleeds are the cheapest seats—so high up that the altitude might theoretically cause a nosebleed: {We had nosebleed seats but could still see the stage}.

A nosedive is a steep, headfirst plunge—originally of an aircraft dropping with its nose pointed toward the ground. The word extends to any sudden, dramatic decline: {Stock prices took a nosedive}, {His career went into a nosedive after the scandal}. As a verb: {The company's reputation nosedived}.

Nosedived is the past tense of nosedive—to plunge steeply downward. The term comes from aircraft diving nose-first toward the ground. It extends to any sudden, dramatic decline: {The stock nosedived after the earnings report}, {His popularity nosedived when the scandal broke}. The alternative past tense nosedove appears occasionally but nosedived predominates.

Nosedives is the plural of nosedive, a steep downward plunge. The term comes from aviation—an aircraft pointing its nose toward the ground in rapid descent. The figurative use dominates: stocks nosedive, careers nosedive, approval ratings nosedive. As a verb, nosedives is the third-person singular: {The company's reputation nosedives after each scandal}.

Nosediving is plunging steeply downward, like an aircraft dropping nose-first. The term extends to anything in rapid decline: {Stock prices are nosediving}, {His approval ratings have been nosediving since the scandal}. The image captures sudden, dramatic descent rather than gradual decline.

A noseeum is a tiny biting fly, so small it can pass through ordinary window screens—hence the name, a playful respelling of "no see 'em." These insects, also called biting midges or sand flies, deliver painful bites disproportionate to their size. {The noseeums were brutal at dusk.} Also spelled no-see-um.

A nosejob, also spelled as two words, is cosmetic surgery to reshape the nose—technically called rhinoplasty. The term is informal and common in everyday speech: {She's been thinking about getting a nosejob}. People get nosejobs to alter the size, shape, or proportions of the nose, whether for aesthetic reasons or to correct breathing problems.

Noses is the plural of nose—the facial feature used for breathing and smelling. The word extends to nose-shaped projections and the front of things: {the noses of several aircraft}. To say someone {noses around} is to say they pry into others' affairs. {Their noses were pressed against the glass.}

Nosey means overly curious about other people's affairs—prying into business that isn't yours. A nosey neighbor watches your comings and goings; a nosey coworker reads emails over your shoulder. {Don't be so nosey—it's none of your concern.} Also spelled nosy, which is more common.

Nosh means to eat, especially to snack or nibble between meals: {I was noshing on pretzels while watching TV}. As a noun, a nosh is a snack or light meal. The word comes from Yiddish and retains a casual, slightly playful tone. In British usage, nosh can also mean food generally or a full meal.

Noshing is eating, especially snacking or eating casually between meals. The word comes from Yiddish and carries a light, informal tone: {We spent the afternoon noshing on cheese and crackers}. A nosh is a snack or light meal.

Nosiest is the superlative form of nosy—the most intrusive or prying. Someone who is the nosiest asks too many personal questions or shows excessive curiosity about others' affairs: {She was the nosiest neighbor on the block, always peering through her curtains}. {My nosiest coworker somehow knows everyone's salary}.
clues: Least likely to mind own business

definition: Nostalgia is a sentimental longing for the past—often for a time, place, or experience that felt happier or simpler. The feeling blends fondness with melancholy, since what's missed cannot return: {The song filled her with nostalgia for her college years}. Nostalgia can be personal or collective, as when generations share {nostalgia for the '90s}. The adjective is nostalgic: {I get nostalgic whenever I visit my hometown}.

Nostalgic describes a sentimental longing for the past, particularly for a period or place associated with happy memories. Someone feeling nostalgic might revisit old photographs, songs, or places that evoke earlier times: {The smell of fresh bread makes me nostalgic for my grandmother's kitchen}. The word can also describe things that evoke such feelings: a nostalgic {film}, nostalgic {décor}. As a noun, a nostalgic is someone prone to dwelling fondly on the past.

A nostril is one of the two external openings of the nose through which air enters and exits. The nostrils filter, warm, and humidify incoming air. Figuratively, something {right under your nose} might as well be in your nostrils—impossible to miss yet somehow overlooked.

Nostrils are the two external openings of the nose, through which air passes for breathing and smelling. The word usually appears in plural since they come in pairs: {Her nostrils flared with anger}. Flaring nostrils signal strong emotion—rage, fear, or arousal. Animals with prominent nostrils may have them described: {The horse's nostrils steamed in the cold air}.

Nosy means prying into other people's affairs, overly curious about things that aren't your business: {Don't be so nosy}, {nosy neighbors}. The word suggests unwelcome intrusion—someone who asks too many questions or snoops where they shouldn't. Also spelled nosey.

English provides a convenient context clue for negative words: the letter n. Not is the most frequently used, even without counting the words in which not is disguised as n’t, such as can’t and won’t. Not gets its impressive usage statistics from being a general purpose negater: it can make clauses, phrases, and words in every part of speech negative by being prefixed to them. Negating a verb means integrating not into the auxiliary verb of a verb phrase, as in hasn’t seen or won’t come. Not is combined with do to make doesn’t or don’t when no auxiliary is present, but in older and formal English, you can negate a verb with not alone: Judge not that you not be judged.

Notable describes something or someone worthy of attention or remark—standing out from the ordinary. A notable {achievement} deserves recognition; a notable {exception} is one worth pointing out. Notable often suggests importance without claiming greatness: {Several notable figures attended the ceremony}. As a noun, a notable is a person of distinction or prominence in a field.

A notary is an official authorized to witness signatures, administer oaths, and certify documents. The full title is notary public. Notaries verify identity and ensure signers act willingly, adding their seal to make documents legally valid: {The contract requires notarization—find a notary at the bank}.
clues: Stamps documents to make them official

definition: Notation is a system of symbols used to represent information in a specialized field: musical notation, scientific notation, chess notation. The word also refers to a brief written note or annotation: {She made a notation in the margin}. To notate is to write something down using such a system.

A notch is a V-shaped cut or indentation, typically made in an edge or surface. Notches serve practical purposes like keeping things in place or marking measurements, as on a belt or a tally stick. To notch something is to cut a notch in it, or to achieve or record something: {She notched another win}. A notch can also mean a level or degree: {Turn the volume up a notch}. If something is {a notch above}, it's slightly better than what it's compared to.

Notched means having a V-shaped cut or indentation, or a series of them: {a notched belt}, {notched arrow}. The word often describes edges with deliberate cuts for grip or measurement. Figuratively, to have notched something is to have achieved or recorded it: {She's notched three victories this season}.

Notches are V-shaped cuts or indentations, typically made in an edge or surface. A notch on a belt marks where it buckles; notches on a bedpost supposedly tally sexual conquests. A notch can be a level or degree: {Let's take it down a notch}. Mountain passes are sometimes called notches. To notch something is to cut into it or to achieve it: {She notched another victory}.

The many verb and noun uses of note nearly all have to do with documentation or notice (an obviously related word). If you note something, you either observe it, or both observe it and write down something about it. If you ask someone to note something, you want them to pay particular attention. A note is the product of noting: Did you take notes at the lecture? A note can also be a feature of something with a particular quality: She ended her talk on a positive note. There are notes of garlic and rosemary in the sauce. In music, notes are individual tones. #

A notebook is a book of blank or ruled pages for writing notes. Students carry notebooks to class; writers keep notebooks of ideas. The term extends to portable computers small enough to carry like a book: {She pulled out her notebook and started typing}. A notebook can also be a digital document for organizing notes or code.

Notebooks are bound collections of blank or lined pages for writing notes. Students carry notebooks to class; writers keep notebooks for ideas. The word extends to portable computers—a notebook computer, or simply a notebook, is a laptop. In computing, a notebook may also be an interactive document combining code, text, and output: {a Jupyter notebook}.

Noted means recognized or well-known, usually for some particular quality or achievement: {a noted scholar}, {a noted authority on constitutional law}. As a standalone response, noted acknowledges that you've registered what someone said—often with a slightly dismissive or curt undertone suggesting you've heard them but may not act on it: {I need those reports by Friday. —Noted.}

A notepad is a small pad of paper, usually bound at one edge, for jotting quick notes. The pages often tear off cleanly. In computing, a notepad is a basic text-editing application: {I opened Notepad to write a quick memo}. The word also applies to digital note-taking apps generally.

Notes are written records of information—observations jotted during a lecture, reminders to oneself, or annotations in a book's margin. Musical notes are symbols representing pitch and duration, or the sounds themselves: {She hit all the notes perfectly}. A note can be a brief written message: {He left a note on the counter}. To note something is to observe or record it. A note of something is a slight quality: {a note of sadness in her voice}.

Nothing is the absence of anything—no thing at all. It functions as both pronoun and noun: {There's nothing in the box}, {Nothing matters anymore}. As a noun, nothing means something of no importance or value: {Don't worry, it was nothing}, {He came from nothing}. In phrases, nothing intensifies: {nothing less than a miracle}, {nothing short of brilliant}. To say someone is {nothing if not} a quality emphasizes that quality above all others. {Sweet nothings} are whispered endearments. As an adverb, nothing means not at all: {She looks nothing like her sister}.

A nothingburger is something that turns out to be insignificant or disappointing despite initial hype—an event, revelation, or controversy that amounts to nothing: {The scandal was a total nothingburger}. The word suggests deflated expectations, often used dismissively in political commentary when allegations fail to materialize into substance.

Nothingness is the state or quality of being nothing—complete absence, emptiness, or nonexistence. Philosophy uses it to discuss the void or what lies beyond being: {He contemplated the nothingness that preceded creation}. More loosely, nothingness describes insignificance or worthlessness: {Their achievements faded into nothingness}. The word can evoke existential dread or peaceful emptiness depending on context.

Notice centers on the act of becoming aware of something or bringing something to awareness. As a verb, you notice what catches your attention or what you deliberately observe: {I noticed she was limping}. As a noun, notice is information meant to be observed, often a formal announcement or warning: {The landlord gave thirty days' notice}. To give notice is to inform someone officially, especially about leaving a job. If something escapes your notice, you fail to observe it. A noticeable thing is one that readily draws attention.

Noticeable describes something prominent enough to be noticed—detectable, evident, apparent: {There was a noticeable improvement in her mood}. The word often suggests something that stands out against a background or baseline: {a noticeable limp}, {a noticeable difference in quality}. What counts as noticeable depends on context—a scratch noticeable on a new car might go unnoticed on an old one.

A noticeboard is a board mounted on a wall where notices, announcements, and other information can be posted. Common in schools, offices, and community centers: {Check the noticeboard for the meeting schedule}. The term is primarily British; Americans typically say bulletin board.

Notices functions as both verb and noun around the idea of becoming aware or making others aware. To notice something is to observe or pay attention to it: {I noticed you weren't at the meeting}. A notice is an announcement or warning posted for others to see: {eviction notice}, {public notice}. To give notice is to formally announce departure from a job. On short notice means with little advance warning.

Noticing is the act of becoming aware of something—perceiving it, registering it, paying attention to it. The word often implies a shift from unawareness to awareness: {I couldn't help noticing the tension in the room}. In mindfulness contexts, noticing has become a practice in itself—deliberately observing thoughts, sensations, or surroundings without judgment.

A notification is an alert or message informing you of something—an event, update, or required action. The word often appears in digital contexts: phone notifications, app notifications, push notifications. More formally, it can mean official notice: {notification of a lawsuit}, {notification of acceptance}. To receive notification is to be informed.

Notifications are alerts or messages that inform you something has happened or needs attention. In digital contexts, notifications appear on phones, computers, and apps to announce new messages, updates, or activity: {I had to turn off notifications because they were constant}. The singular notification can also mean formal notice of something official: {notification of termination}.

To notify is to inform someone officially or formally, typically about something that requires their attention or action: {Please notify the front desk when you leave}. The word implies deliberate communication rather than casual mention—you notify authorities, employers, or next of kin. A notification is the notice itself or the act of giving it.

A notion is an idea, belief, or concept, often one that's vague or not fully formed: {I had a notion that something was wrong}. It can suggest whimsy or impulse: {She took a notion to learn piano}. In the plural, notions are small useful items sold in stores—buttons, thread, pins, ribbons—miscellaneous accessories for sewing and crafts.

Notions has two distinct uses. In the plural, notions are ideas or beliefs, often ones that are vague, fanciful, or mistaken: {She had romantic notions about country life}. Separately, notions refers to small useful items for sewing—buttons, pins, thread, ribbons—sold together in a shop's notions department or at a notions counter.

Notoriety is fame for something negative—a reputation based on scandal, crime, or bad behavior rather than achievement. A criminal gains notoriety; a hero gains fame. The word carries judgment: {The case brought him unwanted notoriety}. Someone notorious is widely known, but not admirably so.

Notorious means widely known for something bad. A notorious criminal has a reputation that precedes them. The word carries negative weight—you wouldn't call someone notorious for their charity work. {The bar was notorious for its rowdy clientele.} {He was a notorious liar.} The noun notoriety follows the same pattern: fame of the unwelcome kind.

Nougat is a chewy confection made from sugar or honey, egg whites, and nuts—typically almonds or pistachios. The texture ranges from soft and pillowy to dense and tooth-sticking, depending on preparation. Nougat appears as a standalone candy or as a layer in chocolate bars: {The candy bar had a nougat center}.

Nought is the number zero, used primarily in British English: {The score stood at two-nought}. It also means nothing at all: {All their efforts came to nought}. The phrase {noughts and crosses} is the British name for tic-tac-toe. American English typically uses naught for the "nothing" sense and zero for the numeral.

The noughties are the decade from 2000 to 2009—the years beginning with "nought" (zero). The term follows the pattern of twenties, thirties, and so on, filling a gap English lacked until the millennium arrived: {I loved the music of the noughties}. More common in British than American English.

Noughts is the British term for zeros, especially the digit 0. In the game noughts and crosses (American tic-tac-toe), one player marks Os while the other marks Xs. The noughts can also refer to the decade 2000–2009: {Fashion in the noughts was all about low-rise jeans}.

A noun is a name for a person, place, or thing; in fact the words noun and name are related. There are many kinds of nouns that are distinguished by what they designate and by the way they behave in sentences. Nouns can serve as subjects or objects of verbs, and as objects of prepositions. Nouns are by far the most frequent words in most languages, English included.

Nouns are the part of speech that names things—people, places, objects, ideas, qualities. In traditional grammar, nouns serve as subjects and objects: {The dog chased the ball}. English nouns take plurals and possessives but lack the elaborate case systems of languages like Latin or German. The term extends to any word functioning as a noun: {Running is good exercise}.

Nourish means to provide sustenance for growth and health. Food nourishes the body; attention nourishes the mind. The word carries warmth—to nourish is to care for, not merely to feed: {She nourished her garden through the drought}, {Reading nourished his imagination}. What nourishes sustains and strengthens over time.

Nourished describes someone or something that has received sustenance or care. A well-nourished child has been adequately fed; a poorly nourished one hasn't. The word extends beyond food: {nourished by love}, {nourished by hope}. Something nourished has been fostered or cultivated: {She nourished ambitions of becoming a surgeon}.

Nourishing describes food or drink that provides sustenance and promotes health: {a nourishing bowl of soup}, {nourishing meals for growing children}. The word extends to anything that sustains or strengthens: {nourishing conversation}, {a nourishing friendship}. What nourishes feeds something essential—body, mind, or spirit.

Nourishment is food or other substances that sustain life and promote growth. The word carries more warmth than nutrition—it suggests care and sufficiency rather than mere calories. {The soup provided nourishment for the weary travelers.} Figuratively, nourishment extends to anything that sustains or enriches: {intellectual nourishment}, {spiritual nourishment}.

Nouveau is French for "new," borrowed into English as a slightly pretentious or ironic modifier suggesting novelty that may lack substance or authenticity. It appears most often in compounds: {nouveau riche} describes the newly wealthy, implying they lack the refinement of old money. {Nouveau cuisine} was a style of French cooking emphasizing lighter preparations. The word often carries a faint sneer—newness without depth.

A nova is a star that suddenly increases dramatically in brightness, then fades over weeks or months. Unlike a supernova, the star isn't destroyed—it can flare repeatedly. The term extends to anything that bursts onto the scene with sudden brilliance: {She was a nova in the art world}. In casual use, nova sometimes just means new or innovative. (Capitalized Nova is a proper name.)

Novas is the plural of nova, a star that suddenly increases dramatically in brightness before fading over weeks or months. The phenomenon occurs when material from a companion star ignites on a white dwarf's surface. Unlike supernovas, novas don't destroy the star—some recur. {Astronomers have catalogued dozens of novas in our galaxy.}

Novel is more than a book-length fictional story. Indeed, it’s more than a noun. As an adjective, novel means new, with an emphasis originality, as in a novel approach to ending homelessness. Abstractions, such as ideas, approaches, methods, and concepts are most likely to be characterized as novel.

A novelist is a writer who writes novels—book-length works of fiction. The term distinguishes such writers from those who work primarily in short stories, poetry, journalism, or nonfiction: {She's a novelist, not a poet}. {The novelist spent three years completing her latest work}.

Novelists are writers who compose novels—book-length works of fiction. The term emphasizes the craft and profession: {She ranks among the great American novelists}. Unlike authors, which applies broadly, novelist specifies the form. {He worked as a journalist before becoming a novelist.}

A novelization is a novel adapted from a work in another medium—typically a film or television series. Unlike novel adaptations that move from page to screen, novelizations reverse the process: {The novelization of the movie came out the same week as the theatrical release}. They're often published as tie-in merchandise, expanding scenes or adding character depth unavailable in the original format.

A novella is a work of fiction longer than a short story but shorter than a novel—typically between 17,000 and 40,000 words. The length allows more complexity than a short story while maintaining the compression and unity of effect that novels often sacrifice: {Kafka's "Metamorphosis" and Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" are classic novellas}.

Novellas are works of fiction longer than short stories but shorter than novels—typically 17,000 to 40,000 words. The length allows more complexity than a short story while maintaining tighter focus than a novel. Many celebrated works occupy this middle ground: *The Old Man and the Sea*, *Heart of Darkness*, *Of Mice and Men*. The singular is novella.

Novels are book-length works of fiction, typically featuring narrative prose and character development. The form emerged in the 18th century and now dominates literary publishing. A novel is distinguished from shorter fiction by length and complexity: {She's working on her first novel}. The adjective novel, a different word, means new or unfamiliar.

Novelties are new or unusual things, especially small decorative objects, toys, or gimmicks sold as curiosities: {a shop full of novelties}, {novelty items}. The word often implies something amusing but insubstantial—a passing fancy rather than lasting value. Novelty as a singular noun means the quality of being new: {The novelty wore off quickly}.

Novelty is the quality of being new, fresh, or unusual. A novelty is something that has this quality—an item, experience, or idea that appeals because of its unfamiliarity: {The novelty of working from home wore off after a few months}. Novelty items are cheap, amusing objects sold as curiosities or gags: {novelty t-shirts}, {novelty keychains}. When the novelty wears off, initial excitement fades as something becomes familiar.

A novice is someone new to an activity, field, or skill—a beginner who lacks experience. The word often implies someone still learning fundamentals: {a novice driver}, {novice programmers make this mistake constantly}. In religious contexts, a novice is a person who has entered a monastery or convent but has not yet taken final vows.

Novices are people new to an activity, field, or skill—beginners who lack experience. The word often implies someone still learning the basics: {The hiking trail is suitable for novices}. In religious contexts, a novice is someone who has entered a monastery or convent but has not yet taken final vows.

Novocaine is a local anesthetic used to numb tissue during dental and minor surgical procedures. The term has become generic for any dental anesthetic, though the original brand (procaine) has largely been replaced by newer drugs like lidocaine: {The dentist gave me novocaine before drilling}. Figuratively, something that numbs emotionally or intellectually: {Television as novocaine for the masses}. (Capitalized Novocaine is the trademark.)

Now is a busy function word that typically refers to a time that includes the present – where the present can encompass anything from a second to an eon, depending on context. Leave now means this instant, while there are no dinosaurs now means in the current epoch. In conversation, now may have no reference to time and is used instead to change the subject or to direct focus to something: Now what do you want to talk about? Before a verb, now typically signals that the time reference of the verb introduces new information: We now know that there were witnesses.

Nowadays means in the present time, as contrasted with an earlier era: {Nowadays everyone has a smartphone}. The word carries a slight tone of noting change—things are different now than they used to be. It functions the same as "these days" but sounds slightly more formal.

Nowhere means not in or to any place: {The keys were nowhere to be found}. It can describe a remote or insignificant location: {a town in the middle of nowhere}. To {get nowhere} or {go nowhere} is to make no progress. {Nowhere near} means not at all close: {We're nowhere near finished}. Something that {comes out of nowhere} arrives unexpectedly.

A nozzle is a spout or tube fitted to the end of a hose, pipe, or container to direct or control the flow of liquid or gas: {Adjust the nozzle to change the spray pattern}. Nozzles appear on garden hoses, fuel pumps, rocket engines, and spray bottles. The word sometimes refers informally to a nose.

Nozzles is the plural of nozzle, a spout or tube designed to direct or control the flow of liquid or gas. A garden hose has a nozzle to adjust the spray pattern. A fuel pump has a nozzle you insert into your tank. Jet engines and rocket engines use nozzles to direct thrust. {She adjusted the nozzles on the sprinkler system.}

Nth describes something taken to an extreme degree or carried to the highest possible point: {She analyzed the data to the nth degree}. In mathematics, nth represents an unspecified number in a sequence—the nth term, the nth power. The figurative sense dominates everyday usage, suggesting exhaustive thoroughness or ultimate extent: {I've told you for the nth time}.

Nuance is a subtle distinction or shade of meaning. Where others see black and white, someone attuned to nuance perceives gradations: {Her argument lacked nuance}. A nuanced position acknowledges complexity rather than oversimplifying. The word often appears in criticism of reductive thinking: {That take has zero nuance}. As a verb, to nuance something is to add subtle distinctions to it.
clues: What blunt statements tend to lack

definition: Nuanced describes something characterized by subtle distinctions or fine shades of meaning. A nuanced {argument} acknowledges complexity rather than reducing issues to black and white. A nuanced {performance} conveys emotional subtleties. The word often signals intellectual sophistication—or at least the aspiration to it: {We need a more nuanced understanding of the problem}.

Nuances are subtle distinctions or variations in meaning, tone, or quality—the fine shades that separate things otherwise similar. A translator captures the nuances of the original text. A wine has nuances of oak and cherry. The singular nuance works as both noun and verb: {There's a nuance you're missing}; {She nuanced her argument to address critics}. The adjective nuanced describes something showing or requiring sensitivity to fine distinctions: {a nuanced performance}, {a nuanced understanding of the issue}.

A nub is a small lump or knob—a protuberance that sticks out from a surface: {the nub of a broken branch}. The word extends to what remains after something has been worn down: {a pencil worn to a nub}. Figuratively, the nub of something is its central point or essence: {Let's get to the nub of the problem}.

A nubbin is a small lump or stub—something that didn't fully develop or is a remnant of something larger. In agriculture, a nubbin is an undersized ear of corn. The word often describes any small protuberance: {a nubbin of cartilage}, {the nubbin where a branch broke off}. Nubbins suggest incompleteness or diminutiveness.

Nubs is the plural of nub—small lumps, knobs, or protrusions. Fabric may have nubs in its texture. A worn pencil eraser becomes a nub. The nub of something is also its central point or essence: {Let's get to the nub of the matter}. Nubs can refer affectionately to residual limbs or stumps.

Nuclear relates to the nucleus—the dense core of an atom or a cell. In physics, nuclear energy comes from splitting or fusing atomic nuclei: {nuclear power}, {nuclear weapons}. In biology, nuclear refers to the cell nucleus: {nuclear membrane}. The nuclear family is parents and children only, the core unit without extended relatives. To {go nuclear} is to escalate dramatically or resort to extreme measures.

A nucleus is the central, essential part of something around which other parts gather or from which they develop. In biology, it's the membrane-bound structure in a cell containing genetic material. In physics, it's the dense core of an atom, composed of protons and neutrons. In astronomy, the solid core of a comet. The plural is nuclei or nucleuses. {The old city formed the nucleus of the modern metropolis.}

Nude means naked—without clothing. In art, a nude is a depiction of an unclothed human figure: {She posed for a nude}, {classical nudes in oil}. The word carries associations of artistic or aesthetic nudity rather than mere nakedness. Nude also describes colors matching skin tone: {nude lipstick}, {nude heels}. In the nude means unclothed: {He was caught in the nude}.

Nudes are images depicting naked human bodies, especially photographs or artworks shared digitally. The singular nude refers to a naked figure in art or to a naked state: {The model posed nude}. In contemporary usage, nudes typically means sexually explicit photos exchanged privately: {She asked him to send nudes}. The noun also describes a pale beige color resembling light skin tones: {nude lipstick}, {nude heels}.

A nudge is a gentle push, typically with the elbow, to get someone's attention or signal something: {She gave him a nudge when it was time to leave}. To nudge is to push gently or to encourage someone toward action: {I nudged him to apply for the job}. A nudge can also be a person who persistently pesters—from Yiddish, where it rhymes with "could" rather than "judge."

Nudges is the plural of nudge—a gentle push, typically with the elbow, to get someone's attention or hint at something: {She gave him a nudge under the table}. A nudge can also be a subtle prompt toward action: {He needs a nudge to finish the project}. The verb nudges means to push gently or edge gradually: {The cat nudges the door open}.

Nudging is gently pushing or poking someone, usually with an elbow, to get their attention or signal something: {She kept nudging me during the movie}. The term extends to subtle encouragement or persuasion: {He needed some nudging before he'd ask her out}. In behavioral economics, nudging refers to designing choices that steer people toward better decisions without restricting options—placing fruit at eye level in a cafeteria rather than banning cookies.

Nudism is the practice of going without clothes, especially in designated social settings like beaches, resorts, or camps. Adherents view nonsexual communal nakedness as natural, healthy, and liberating. The movement is also called naturism, though some distinguish between the terms: {The resort caters to nudism and clothing-optional lifestyles}.

A nudist is a person who practices social nudity, typically at designated beaches, resorts, or communities. The philosophy holds that nonsexual nakedness is natural and healthy. As an adjective, nudist describes these spaces and practices: {a nudist colony}, {a nudist beach}. The movement is also called naturism.

Nudists are people who practice social nudity, typically at designated beaches, resorts, or camps. The term implies a lifestyle philosophy that views nonsexual nakedness as natural and healthy: {The nudist colony welcomed new members}. Nudist and naturist overlap considerably, though naturist sometimes carries more emphasis on connection with nature.

Nudity is the state of being unclothed—having no clothes on. The word often carries associations with art, sexuality, or vulnerability that *naked* doesn't always share: {The film contains brief nudity}. A nude is a painting or photograph of an unclothed figure: {Modigliani's nudes}. In the nude means naked: {sleeping in the nude}.

A nudnick is a pest or bore—someone who annoys through persistent nagging, complaining, or tedious conversation. The word comes from Yiddish and carries affectionate exasperation as much as genuine irritation: {Stop being such a nudnick and let me finish}. Also spelled nudnik.

A nugget is a small, solid lump of something valuable—originally and especially gold: {They found a nugget in the stream}. The word extends to compact, chunky pieces of food: chicken nuggets, cheese nuggets. Figuratively, a nugget is a small but valuable bit of information or wisdom: {nuggets of advice}, {a nugget of truth buried in his rambling}.

Nuggets are small, solid chunks or lumps of something—most classically gold: {prospectors panning for nuggets}. The word extends to bite-sized pieces of breaded and fried food: chicken nuggets, fish nuggets. Figuratively, a nugget is a compact piece of valuable information or wisdom: {nuggets of advice}, {a nugget of truth}. In sports, the Nuggets are Denver's NBA team.

A nuisance is something or someone that causes annoyance, inconvenience, or minor harm. The word covers a wide range—from a buzzing fly to a neighbor's barking dog to bureaucratic red tape: {What a nuisance to have to fill out all these forms}. In law, a nuisance is an activity or condition that interferes with others' use of property or public spaces.

Nuisances are things or people that cause annoyance, inconvenience, or minor harm. The word covers a wide range—from a neighbor's barking dog to bureaucratic red tape: {Mosquitoes are a nuisance in summer}, {He made a nuisance of himself at the party}. In legal contexts, a nuisance is an activity that interferes with others' use or enjoyment of property.

Nuke is informal for nuclear weapon or nuclear power: {The country is developing nukes}. As a verb, to nuke is to attack with nuclear weapons, or more commonly, to cook in a microwave: {Just nuke the leftovers for two minutes}. The extended sense means to destroy completely: {A virus nuked my hard drive}.

Nuked means destroyed with nuclear weapons, but the word appears far more often in casual contexts. To nuke food is to microwave it: {I'll just nuke some leftovers}. To nuke something in gaming or computing is to wipe it out completely: {I accidentally nuked my save file}. The word captures both the speed and totality of destruction.

Nukes are nuclear weapons—bombs or warheads that derive their destructive force from atomic reactions. The term extends to nuclear power plants and submarines. As a verb, to nuke is to attack with nuclear weapons, or more casually, to microwave something: {Just nuke the leftovers for two minutes}. To nuke also means to destroy utterly: {The update nuked my saved files}.

Nuking is the present participle of nuke. In its literal sense, it means attacking with nuclear weapons: {They're talking about nuking the whole region}. More commonly, it means destroying or eliminating completely: {I'm nuking all my old emails}. In casual speech, nuking often just means microwaving: {I'm nuking some leftovers for lunch}.

Null can function as an adjective, noun, or verb, with the idea of zero or nothing central to its meaning. A null hypothesis, for example, is one where data is insignificant.
