Professional oddsmakers work for sportsbooks and casinos, adjusting lines based on statistical analysis and betting patterns: {The oddsmaking on this fight has shifted dramatically since the weigh-in}. The term extends to any prediction of probabilities: {Political oddsmaking favored the incumbent}.

An ode is a lyric poem, typically one that praises or celebrates its subject. The classical form follows elaborate structures with stanzas and meter, but modern odes are often freer in form while retaining the tone of elevated address: {Keats's "Ode to a Nightingale"}. Informally, any tribute or enthusiastic appreciation may be called an ode: {His essay was an ode to New York pizza}.

Odes are poems, typically lyrical and often elaborate in structure, that address a particular subject with elevated feeling. The classical ode, associated with ancient Greek poets like Pindar, celebrated heroic achievements or public occasions; later poets like Keats wrote odes to abstract concepts or everyday objects {(Ode on a Grecian Urn, Ode to a Nightingale)}. The form suggests serious admiration, though modern usage sometimes applies ode loosely to any tribute or homage: {Her essay was an ode to her grandmother's cooking}.

An odometer is an instrument that measures distance traveled, typically mounted on a vehicle's dashboard. The odometer reading tells you how many miles or kilometers a car has accumulated over its lifetime. To {roll back the odometer} is to fraudulently reduce the displayed mileage, making a used vehicle appear less worn than it is.

Odometers is the plural of odometer, an instrument that measures distance traveled. Every car has an odometer on its dashboard, tracking total miles driven over the vehicle's lifetime. Rolling back odometers to hide high mileage is fraud. Trip odometers can be reset to measure individual journeys: {I reset the odometer before the road trip}.

An odor is a smell—a quality perceived through the nose. The word is neutral but often implies unpleasantness: {a foul odor}, {body odor}. Something {in bad odor} has a poor reputation. Odor can suggest a trace or hint: {an odor of corruption surrounded the deal}. British spelling: odour.

Odorless means having no smell. Carbon monoxide is dangerous partly because it's odorless—you can't detect it without instruments. The word often appears in safety contexts or product descriptions: {odorless paint}, {odorless cleaning solution}. Something truly odorless is rare; the term usually means no *noticeable* or *unpleasant* smell.

Odour is the British spelling of odor—a smell, especially one that is distinctive or unpleasant. Something with no smell is {odourless}. The phrase {in bad odour} means in disfavor: {He was in bad odour with the committee after missing three meetings}. Both spellings share the same range of literal and figurative uses.

Odours is the British spelling of odors, the plural of odor—smells, whether pleasant or unpleasant. The word often leans negative: {Strange odours emanated from the basement}. Body odour, foot odour, and similar compounds typically refer to unwanted smells.

An odyssey is a long, eventful journey marked by adventures and hardships: {Her odyssey from refugee camp to medical school took fifteen years}. The word implies not just travel but transformation through experience—obstacles overcome, lessons learned. Any extended quest or wandering qualifies: {his odyssey through the criminal justice system}. (From the Greek epic about Odysseus's ten-year voyage home.)

Odysseys is the plural of odyssey, a long journey marked by adventure, hardship, or transformation. The word comes from Homer's epic poem about Odysseus's ten-year voyage home from Troy. Any extended, eventful journey qualifies: {Their odysseys through the legal system lasted years}. The term often implies not just distance traveled but obstacles overcome and lessons learned.

Oedipal describes feelings or behavior involving a child's unconscious sexual attraction to the opposite-sex parent and rivalry with the same-sex parent—the pattern Freud called the Oedipus complex, after the mythical Greek king who unknowingly killed his father and married his mother. More loosely, oedipal suggests any fraught parent-child dynamic: {Their relationship had an oedipal intensity}.

Oestrogen is the British spelling of estrogen, a group of hormones that regulate female reproductive development and secondary sex characteristics. Oestrogen levels fluctuate through the menstrual cycle and decline at menopause. The hormones also play roles in bone density and cardiovascular health in both sexes. {Her doctor prescribed oestrogen replacement therapy.}

Off has two core meanings. One is of separation (a restaurant just off the highway, borrow some money off your uncle); the other is of suspension or stoppage (the policeman was off duty at the time). Off is opposite to on in many of its meanings but does not have the same wide range of extended meanings as on has.

Offal is the internal organs and entrails of a butchered animal, used as food or discarded as waste. Liver, kidneys, heart, tripe, and sweetbreads are offal. British cuisine traditionally embraces offal; American tastes have largely rejected it. Figuratively, offal means refuse or rubbish: {the offal of society}.

Offbeat describes something unconventional or departing from the ordinary: {an offbeat sense of humor}, {an offbeat romantic comedy}. The term comes from music, where the offbeat is the weaker, unaccented part of a measure—the "and" between the main beats. What falls on the offbeat stands apart from the expected rhythm.

Offbeats are the weak beats in a musical measure—the counts between the strong downbeats. In 4/4 time, beats two and four are offbeats, emphasized in reggae, ska, and funk: {The guitar hits hard on the offbeats}. Offbeat rhythms create syncopation and groove by stressing where listeners don't expect emphasis.

An offchance is a remote possibility, a slim hope that something might happen despite being unlikely. Almost always appears with "on the": {I stopped by on the offchance she'd be home}. The phrase signals you're acting without much expectation of success but trying anyway.

Offcuts are pieces of material left over after cutting something to size—scraps of fabric, wood, or meat trimmed away from the main piece. In British English especially, butchers sell offcuts cheaply: {She bought offcuts for the dog}. The term extends to any leftover fragments: {offcuts of leather}, {offcuts from the timber yard}.

Offed is the past tense of off used as a verb meaning to kill. The usage is informal and often appears in crime fiction or casual speech about violence: {The mob offed him before he could testify}. It treats "off" as shorthand for removing someone permanently—switching them off, as it were.

Offence is the British spelling of offense. An offence is a violation of rules or law: {a criminal offence}, {a minor offence}. It also means the causing or feeling of hurt or annoyance: {No offence intended}, {She took offence at the remark}. In sports, offence is the attacking side or strategy—the team trying to score.
clues: A violation of law or feelings

definition: Offences is the British spelling of offenses, the plural of offense. An offence is a violation of law or rule: {minor offences}, {criminal offences}. It also means something that causes displeasure or hurt feelings: {I meant no offence}. In sports, offence is the attacking side of play, though this sense more often uses the American spelling.

To offend is to cause displeasure, hurt feelings, or moral outrage: {His remarks offended nearly everyone in the room}. The word covers a spectrum from mild annoyance to deep insult. What offends varies by person and culture—some take offense easily, others rarely. To offend against something is to violate it: {offend against good taste}, {offend against the law}. An offender is someone who commits an offense, especially a crime.

Offended describes the state of feeling hurt, insulted, or resentful after perceiving a slight or disrespect. Someone who is easily offended takes offense at minor provocations. The word can express genuine hurt or signal excessive sensitivity: {She was deeply offended by the accusation}. {Don't be offended—I was only joking}.

An offender is someone who commits an offense—a wrongdoing, crime, or violation. Legal contexts dominate: {first-time offenders}, {repeat offenders}, {sex offenders}. The word implies formal wrongdoing rather than casual error: you're an offender if you break laws or rules, not if you merely annoy someone.

Offenders are people who have committed offenses—violations of law, rules, or standards. The word appears most often in legal and criminal justice contexts: {first-time offenders}, {repeat offenders}, {sex offenders}. Outside legal use, offenders are simply those who cause offense or do wrong: {The worst offenders were the executives who knew and said nothing}.

Offending describes whatever causes offense, harm, or trouble. The offending {party} is the one at fault. An offending {remark} is the one that upset someone. In practical contexts, the offending {item} is simply the problematic one: {The mechanic removed the offending part}. The word often carries a hint of irony or understatement when applied to minor irritants.

Offense centers on wrongdoing or attack. An offense is a violation of rules or laws: {a criminal offense}, {a minor traffic offense}. To cause offense is to upset or insult someone: {I meant no offense}. In sports, offense refers to the attacking side—the team trying to score, opposite of defense. To {take offense} is to feel insulted or hurt by something said or done. The British spelling is offence.

Offenses is the plural of offense. An offense is a violation of law or rules: {minor offenses}, {criminal offenses}. It also means something that causes hurt or anger: {I meant no offense}. In sports, the offense is the team or unit attempting to score. The spelling offences is standard in British English.
clues: Things that land you in trouble

definition: Offensive describes what attacks or causes displeasure. An offensive military strategy advances rather than defends. Offensive remarks or behavior cause anger or disgust: {His jokes were offensive to nearly everyone}. The noun is the attacking posture itself: {The army launched an offensive}, {on the offensive}. In sports, offense and offensive relate to scoring rather than preventing scores.

Offensives are major military attacks or campaigns intended to advance against an enemy: {The spring offensives failed to break through enemy lines}. The word appears almost exclusively in military contexts, often modified by season or location: {the Tet Offensive}, {a series of winter offensives}. Outside warfare, offensive (singular) describes aggressive initiatives: {a charm offensive}, {a marketing offensive}.

When you offer something, you make it available to someone else. If it is something intangible, offer sometimes means you give it without being asked: She’s always offering advice. When you offer to do something, you say that you will do some beneficial thing for someone else. When an institution offers something, that thing is available there: The hotel offers special weekend packages. An offer is the act or result of offering: We had to decline his offer to put us up overnight. An offer can also be associated with an amount of money for buying something: We made a low offer on the house and it was accepted.

An offering is something given or presented, often with a sense of generosity or purpose. The word carries a slightly formal or ceremonial tone: religious offerings to a deity, a company's stock offering, or the offerings at a fundraiser. More casually, it describes what's available: {The restaurant's lunch offerings are limited}. To make an offering is to give something up—sacrifice implied.

Offerings are things presented or made available. The core sense is religious—gifts given to a deity or for sacred purposes: {burnt offerings}, {a collection plate for offerings}. More broadly, offerings are what's on offer: a company's product offerings, a restaurant's seasonal offerings, a university's course offerings. The word suggests items put forward for consideration or acceptance.

Living or operating independently of public utilities, especially electricity and water systems. An offgrid cabin generates its own power through solar panels or generators rather than connecting to the electrical grid. The term extends to lifestyle choices emphasizing self-sufficiency: {They went offgrid for a month—no internet, no phone}. Sometimes hyphenated as off-grid.

Offhand means without preparation or forethought: {I can't give you the figures offhand}. The word suggests casualness—an offhand {remark} is made without much consideration, which can come across as dismissive or rude: {His offhand manner put people off}. As an adverb, offhandedly works the same way.

The most frequent use of office is for designating a place where business or work is done: In some cases, you can get a tax deduction for a home office. Some people say at the office as a way of saying that they’re at their wokplace. A noun or adjective before office typically indicates its function: post office, registry office. An office can also be the position associated with an official job, especially in politics and government: The office of mayor came with many unexpected responsibilities. In some countries, office indicates a large government department, as in Great Britain’s Home Office and Foreign Office.

An officer holds a position of authority or command. In military contexts, officers are commissioned ranks above enlisted personnel: {She was promoted to officer}. Police officers enforce the law. Corporate officers—CEO, CFO, treasurer—hold executive positions. The verb means to staff with officers or to command: {The ship was officered by veterans}. An officer of the court includes judges, lawyers, and court personnel with legal duties.

Officers are people holding positions of authority. In military and police contexts, officers hold formal rank and command responsibilities: {The officers met to discuss strategy}. Corporate officers—CEO, CFO, treasurer—hold executive positions in a company. The term implies official status and duties rather than mere employment. To officer is to command or supply with officers, though this verb form is uncommon.

Offices is the plural of office. An office is a room or building where professional or administrative work is done: {She works in the corporate offices downtown}. Office also means a position of authority or service: {He held office for two terms}, {the office of president}. The offices of a person are services rendered on another's behalf, usually with good or kind: {Through the good offices of a mutual friend, they reconciled}.

Official describes what is formally authorized, recognized, or sanctioned by an authority. An official {statement} comes from someone empowered to speak for an organization. Official {records} are the authoritative version. The official {language} of a country is legally recognized for government use. As a noun, an official is a person holding office or authority: {election officials}, {government officials}, sports {officials} who enforce rules. Something becomes official when it receives formal approval: {It's official—we're getting married}.

Officialdom is the world of officials and bureaucratic administration, often with a slightly dismissive tone suggesting red tape, rigid procedures, and impersonal authority. {After months of battling officialdom, she finally got her permit}. The word groups officials as a collective force—faceless, slow-moving, bound by rules rather than common sense.

Officialese is the stilted, jargon-laden language characteristic of government documents, bureaucratic communications, and official pronouncements. It favors passive constructions, abstract nouns, and unnecessarily complex phrasing where simpler words would do. {The memo was written in such dense officialese that no one could understand what action was required.} The term is mildly derogatory, implying that such language obscures meaning rather than clarifies it.

Officially means in a formal, authorized, or publicly acknowledged way: {The merger was officially announced yesterday}. It contrasts with what's unofficial, informal, or merely rumored. The word often signals that something has crossed from tentative to confirmed: {We're officially engaged}. In casual use, officially can be playful emphasis: {I'm officially exhausted}.

Officials are people holding positions of authority, typically in government, sports, or organizations. Government officials administer public affairs: {elected officials}, {city officials}. In sports, officials are referees or umpires who enforce rules: {The officials reviewed the play}. The word often implies bureaucratic or formal authority: {Immigration officials detained several passengers}.

An officiant is the person who performs a ceremony, especially a wedding or religious rite. The term emphasizes the formal role rather than religious credentials—a friend ordained online to marry a couple is their officiant: {The officiant asked if anyone objected}. Clergy, judges, and justices of the peace all serve as officiants.

To officiate is to perform official duties, especially to preside over a ceremony or sporting event. A judge officiates at a wedding, a priest officiates at a funeral, a referee officiates a basketball game. The word carries formal weight—you don't officiate casual gatherings. {Who's officiating the ceremony?} {She's been officiating NFL games for fifteen years.}

Officiating is presiding over or administering something in an official capacity. A priest officiating at a wedding performs the ceremony. Referees and umpires officiating a game enforce the rules and make calls: {The officiating in last night's game was terrible}. The word implies formal authority to conduct proceedings.

The offing is the distant part of the sea visible from shore—where the horizon meets the water. From this image of something visible but not yet arrived comes the common phrase {in the offing}, meaning about to happen or likely to occur soon: {A promotion is in the offing}. The word rarely appears outside this idiom.

Offline means disconnected from a computer network, especially the internet. You can work offline on a document, then sync changes when you reconnect. The word extends to any unavailability: {Let's take this conversation offline} means to discuss privately, away from the current group or meeting. Someone who's offline may simply be unreachable: {I'm going offline for the weekend}.

To offload is to transfer a burden or load elsewhere. Trucks offload cargo at warehouses. Workers offload tasks to subordinates: {I offloaded the paperwork to my assistant}. In computing, processing may be offloaded to specialized hardware. The word carries a slight sense of relief—you're getting rid of something you'd rather not carry: {He offloaded his old furniture before the move}.

Offloaded is the past tense of offload, meaning to transfer a burden, cargo, or responsibility elsewhere. Trucks offload goods at warehouses. You might offload unwanted furniture at a donation center. The word often implies getting rid of something inconvenient: {She offloaded the tedious paperwork onto her assistant}. In computing, tasks are offloaded to secondary processors.

Offloading is the present participle of offload—to transfer a burden, cargo, or responsibility elsewhere. Workers offload freight from ships and trucks. People offload unwanted possessions at garage sales. Companies offload tasks to contractors. The word implies getting rid of something, often to someone else's disadvantage: {He's always offloading his problems onto me}.

Offloads is the third-person singular of offload, meaning to transfer a burden, cargo, or responsibility elsewhere. You offload cargo from a ship, offload tasks to an assistant, or offload processing to a dedicated server. The word implies getting rid of something that weighs you down: {She offloads her anxieties onto her therapist}. In sports, to offload is to pass the ball while being tackled.

Offputting describes something that creates aversion or discomfort—mildly repellent without being outright disgusting. An offputting {manner} makes someone hard to warm to. An offputting {smell} discourages approach. The word suggests a pushing away, a quality that prevents engagement: {His nervous laugh was offputting}. Also spelled off-putting.

An offramp is a road that allows vehicles to exit a highway or freeway: {Take the next offramp for downtown}. Figuratively, an offramp is any way to exit a difficult situation gracefully—politicians speak of giving adversaries an offramp to de-escalate conflict: {The negotiators offered him an offramp to save face}. Also spelled off-ramp.

Offroad describes travel or activity away from paved surfaces—on dirt, gravel, rocks, or rough terrain. An offroad {vehicle} is built for such conditions, with features like high clearance and rugged tires. As a verb, to offroad is to drive in such terrain: {We spent the weekend offroading in the desert}. Also spelled off-road.

An offroader is a vehicle designed for travel over rough terrain—unpaved roads, trails, sand, mud, or rocky ground. The term covers purpose-built trucks, SUVs, and all-terrain vehicles with features like four-wheel drive, high clearance, and rugged suspension: {We took the offroader out to the desert}. By extension, an offroader can be a person who engages in offroad driving as a hobby or sport.

Offroading is driving a vehicle over rough, unpaved terrain—dirt trails, mud, rocks, sand, or wilderness. It's both a recreational activity and sometimes a practical necessity in remote areas. Vehicles designed for offroading have features like four-wheel drive, high clearance, and rugged tires: {We spent the weekend offroading in the desert}. Also spelled off-roading.

Offscreen describes what happens outside the visible frame of a film, television show, or video. A character who speaks offscreen is heard but not seen. The term extends to actors' lives away from their roles: {They married offscreen after meeting on set}. In computing, offscreen refers to content rendered outside the visible display area.

The offseason is the time of year when a sport or activity isn't in regular play. Teams make trades, players rest or train, and fans wait: {He bulked up during the offseason}. The term extends to any business with seasonal rhythms—tourism, retail, agriculture. As an adjective: {offseason rates at the beach house}. Also spelled off-season.

Offset centers on the idea of counterbalancing or compensating. Gains offset losses; one factor offsets another. An offset is something that balances or counteracts: {The tax break was an offset against higher costs}. In printing and design, offset refers to a technique where ink transfers to an intermediate surface before paper, or to positioning that's slightly displaced from center: {The text was offset to the left}. As a verb, to offset is to counteract or place at an angle: {Solar panels offset our electricity bill}.

An offshoot is something that branches off from a main source. A plant sends out offshoots from its stem or roots. Organizations spawn offshoots: {The splinter group was an offshoot of the original movement}. Ideas, styles, and technologies produce offshoots too: {Jazz has countless offshoots}. The word emphasizes origin and derivation—the offshoot comes from something larger or earlier.

Offshoots are things that branch off from something larger or original. A plant's offshoot is a shoot growing from the main stem. Organizations, movements, or ideas produce offshoots—subsidiary groups or derivative developments: {The splinter party was an offshoot of the original movement}. Family offshoots are descendants or branches of a lineage.

Offshore means away from the shore, in or toward the water: {an offshore breeze}, {offshore drilling platforms}. The term extends to activities conducted in foreign countries, typically for financial advantage: offshore {banking}, offshore {accounts}, offshore {tax havens}. Companies that move operations abroad are said to offshore jobs or manufacturing: {The company offshored its customer service to the Philippines}.

Offshored describes work, jobs, or operations that have been moved to another country, typically to reduce costs: {The company offshored its customer service to the Philippines}. The past tense of offshore, it usually implies relocating business functions from wealthy countries to places with cheaper labor. Compare outsourced, which may stay domestic.

Offshoring is relocating business operations or jobs to another country, typically to reduce costs: {The company offshored its customer service to the Philippines}. Unlike outsourcing, which means contracting work to another company, offshoring specifically involves geographic relocation—though companies often do both simultaneously. The practice became politically charged as manufacturing and service jobs moved overseas.
clues: Relocating business functions to foreign countries

definition: Offside is a violation in sports like soccer and hockey where a player is illegally positioned ahead of the ball or puck relative to opponents. In soccer, you're offside if you're nearer the goal line than both the ball and the second-to-last defender when the ball is played to you. The adjective and adverb describe this position: {The striker was ruled offside}. Figuratively, offside can mean out of line or improper: {His remarks were a bit offside}.

Offsides is a violation in sports where a player is positioned illegally ahead of the ball or a designated line. In American football, offsides occurs when a player crosses the line of scrimmage before the snap. In soccer and hockey, it involves being too far forward when the ball or puck is played. Figuratively, to be offsides is to act prematurely or violate an unwritten rule: {The senator went offsides by announcing before the committee met}. The standard form is offside, but offsides dominates in American speech.

Offsite means away from the main location or premises. An offsite {meeting} or offsite {retreat} takes place somewhere other than the usual workplace. Offsite {storage} keeps materials at a separate facility. As a noun, an offsite is such a gathering: {The team has an offsite next week}. The opposite is onsite.

Offspring are a person's or animal's children or young. The word works as both singular and plural: {Their offspring inherited the estate}, {The mare and her offspring grazed together}. It extends to anything produced or generated by something else: {The album was the offspring of their collaboration}. More formal than kids but less clinical than progeny.

Offstage refers to the areas of a theater not visible to the audience—the wings, backstage, dressing rooms. As an adverb or adjective, it describes action or sound occurring out of sight: {The gunshot was heard offstage}. Figuratively, offstage means private or unofficial, away from public scrutiny: {Offstage, the politician was surprisingly vulgar}.

Offworld means away from Earth or one's home planet, used in science fiction contexts: {offworld colonies}, {offworld mining operations}. The term can function as an adjective or adverb: {They shipped the cargo offworld}. It implies distance not just in space but in accessibility—offworld destinations are remote, often requiring significant travel or technology to reach.

Offworlders are people from another planet or celestial body—extraterrestrials or space colonists viewed from a local perspective. The term appears primarily in science fiction, where it often carries undertones of otherness or suspicion: {The offworlders kept to themselves in the port district}. Someone from Earth visiting Mars would be an offworlder to Martian settlers.

An ofrenda is a home altar constructed during the Mexican Day of the Dead celebration to honor deceased loved ones. The display typically includes photographs of the dead, marigolds, candles, favorite foods, and meaningful objects meant to welcome returning spirits. {She spent hours arranging her grandmother's ofrenda with fresh pan de muerto and marigolds.}

Often means frequently or many times: {I often forget where I put my keys}. It implies regularity without specifying exact frequency—more than occasionally, less than always. {How often do you exercise?} The word sometimes appears as oftentimes, which means the same thing.

To ogle is to stare at someone with obvious sexual interest or desire—an openly leering gaze: {He ogled her from across the bar}. The word carries connotations of inappropriate or unwelcome attention. As a noun, an ogle is such a look: {She caught his ogle and walked away}.

Ogled is the past tense of ogle, meaning to stare at someone with obvious sexual interest or desire. The gaze is typically prolonged and unsubtle: {He ogled her from across the bar}. The word carries a leering, somewhat predatory connotation—ogling suggests the stare is unwelcome or inappropriate.

Ogling is looking at someone with obvious sexual interest or desire—an extended, appreciative gaze that lingers on the body. The word carries a slightly leering quality: {He was ogling the women at the pool}. Unlike a glance or admiring look, ogling implies the gaze is noticeable and possibly unwelcome.

An ogre is a man-eating giant in folklore and fairy tales—ugly, brutish, and fearsome. The word extends to any cruel, intimidating person: {My boss is an absolute ogre about deadlines}. In fantasy games and fiction, ogres are typically large humanoid monsters of low intelligence but great strength.

Ogres are large, hideous humanoid monsters in folklore and fantasy, typically portrayed as man-eating brutes. They appear in fairy tales as villains who threaten heroes and devour children. Figuratively, an ogre is someone cruel, frightening, or tyrannical: {My boss is an absolute ogre}.

Oil is a liquid or liquefiable substance that is not soluble in water and is usually combustible. Oils are used as fuel (heating oil), or for nutrition (coconut oil, fish oil, vegetable oil), in which case they may also be classified as fats. In some contexts, oil is understood to be petroleum: oil spill, oil tanker. As a verb, oil means to apply oil, usually for purposes of lubrication: You need to oil that door; it squeaks. If you oil a pot or other cooking container, you add a small amount of oil to prevent sticking.

An oilcan is a container with a long spout used to apply lubricating oil to machinery, hinges, or other mechanical parts. The classic design has a thumb-operated pump that dispenses oil in controlled drops. {He grabbed the oilcan to silence the squeaky door.}

Oilcloth is fabric treated with oil or a synthetic coating to make it waterproof. Traditionally used for tablecloths, shelf liners, and protective coverings, it wipes clean easily: {She spread the oilcloth over the picnic table}. The material has a slightly shiny, slick surface.

Oiled describes something coated or treated with oil: {oiled leather}, {a well-oiled machine}. The well-oiled machine metaphor extends to any smoothly functioning system. Informally, oiled means drunk—lubricated by alcohol: {He was pretty well oiled by midnight}.

Oilers is the plural of oiler—a person who oils machinery, a ship designed to carry or refuel with oil, or a container for dispensing oil. The word also names sports teams, most notably the Edmonton Oilers hockey franchise and the former Houston Oilers football team.

An oilfield is a region where petroleum deposits lie beneath the surface, typically developed with multiple wells for extraction. The term encompasses both the underground reservoir and the surface infrastructure—derricks, pumps, pipelines—used to bring oil up: {He spent thirty years working the oilfields of West Texas}. Also spelled as two words: oil field.

Oilfields are areas where petroleum deposits exist beneath the ground and can be extracted commercially. The term usually refers to regions with multiple wells and extraction infrastructure: {The oilfields of West Texas transformed the region's economy}. A single oilfield may cover hundreds of square miles.

An oilman works in the petroleum industry, typically as an executive, entrepreneur, or investor rather than a laborer. The term evokes wealth and influence—Texas oilmen, wildcatters who struck it rich: {He made his fortune as an oilman in the 1970s}. The word carries associations with boom-and-bust fortunes and political clout.

Oilmen is the plural of oilman—someone who works in the petroleum industry, especially in exploration, drilling, or executive positions. The term evokes roughnecks and wildcatters as much as boardroom executives: {Texas oilmen dominated the energy sector for decades}. It carries a distinctly American, masculine connotation tied to the oil boom era.

An oilrig is a large structure used to drill for and extract petroleum from beneath the earth's surface or ocean floor. Offshore oilrigs are particularly iconic—massive platforms standing in open water or floating while anchored to the seabed. Also spelled as two words: oil rig.

Oils are greasy liquid substances that don't mix with water. They come from various sources: vegetable oils for cooking, petroleum oils for engines, essential oils for fragrance. As a verb, to oil is to lubricate or apply oil: {He oiled the squeaky hinge}. In art, oils refers to oil paints or paintings made with them: {She works in oils}. To {oil the wheels} is to make a process run smoothly, often through bribery or favor.

Oilskin is fabric treated with oil to make it waterproof, or a garment made from such material. Oilskins are the protective clothing worn by sailors and fishermen against rain and spray: {He pulled on his oilskins before going on deck}. The term evokes maritime work in harsh weather.

Oilskins are waterproof garments made from cloth treated with oil, traditionally worn by sailors and fishermen. The term covers both the fabric itself and the clothing made from it—jackets, pants, and full suits designed to repel seawater and rain: {The crew donned their oilskins as the storm approached}. Modern versions use synthetic materials but retain the name.

Oily describes something covered with, containing, or resembling oil—slick, greasy, or slippery to the touch: {oily skin}, {oily hair}, {oily rags}. Foods can be oily from cooking fat. Extended to behavior, oily describes someone excessively smooth, flattering, or ingratiating in a way that feels insincere: {an oily salesman}, {his oily charm}.

Oink is the sound a pig makes, or a word representing that sound. Children learn it early: {The pig says oink}. As a verb, to oink is to make this sound or to eat greedily like a pig: {He oinked down three helpings}.

Oinking is making the grunting sound characteristic of pigs. The word imitates the noise itself. Children oink when playing farm, and the term extends to any pig-like snorting: {He was oinking with laughter}. Calling someone's eating or speaking oinking suggests piggish behavior.

Ointment is a thick, greasy substance applied to the skin for healing or protection. Ointments typically contain medication mixed with oil or petroleum bases, distinguishing them from lighter creams and lotions. {Apply the ointment twice daily}. A {fly in the ointment} is a small flaw that spoils something otherwise good.

The okapi is a forest-dwelling mammal native to central Africa, related to the giraffe but smaller and with a shorter neck. Its most distinctive feature is the zebra-like stripes on its hindquarters and legs, while its body is dark reddish-brown. Okapis were unknown to Western science until 1901, contributing to their reputation as elusive animals.
Okay is a very useful, short utterance that has now traveled far beyond English to indicate assent, agreement, or understanding.

Okeydoke is a playful variant of okay, used to express agreement or acceptance: {Okeydoke, I'll meet you at noon}. It has a cheerful, slightly folksy quality that makes it common in casual conversation. Also spelled okey-doke or okey-dokey.

Okeydokey is a playful, drawn-out way of saying okay, expressing agreement or acknowledgment with a lighthearted tone: {Okeydokey, I'll see you at noon}. It's casual and slightly goofy, often used to keep things friendly or to signal easygoing acceptance. Also spelled okey-dokey or okiedokie.

Okra is a tall plant cultivated for its edible green seed pods, which become mucilaginous when cooked. This slippery texture thickens gumbo and other stews, though it puts off some eaters. The pods can also be fried, pickled, or roasted to minimize the sliminess. Okra is common in Southern, Caribbean, African, and South Asian cuisines.

The adjective old is itself quite old, first appearing before 900 C.E. Old is generally the opposite of new and characterizes things that began or existed a long time ago. When something new comes along, the thing that it replaces or supplants immediately becomes old. Old can have either positive or negative connotations, depending on the words it appears with: contrast old friend with old ideas.

Olden means belonging to a time long past, appearing almost exclusively in the phrase {olden days} or {olden times}. The word is deliberately archaic-sounding, often used nostalgically or when speaking to children: {In the olden days, people wrote letters by hand}. Outside these set phrases, olden sounds quaint or affected.

Older is the comparative form of old, indicating greater age or longer existence than something else being compared. It applies to people, objects, ideas, and institutions: {My older sister lives in Portland}; {The older version of the software had fewer bugs}. When referring to siblings or generations, older often implies seniority without specifying exact ages. Unlike elder, which is restricted to people and carries formal or familial connotations, older works in any context where age comparison is relevant.

Oldest is the superlative form of old, indicating the greatest age among three or more: {She's the oldest of five children}, {the oldest building in town}. It often carries connotations of precedence or authority: {The oldest son inherited the estate}. Eldest is a near-synonym but typically restricted to people within families.

An oldhead is someone from an older generation, especially one respected for experience or knowledge in a particular scene or culture. The term originated in hip-hop and urban communities to describe veterans who've been around long enough to know how things work: {The oldheads at the barbershop were talking about how music used to be}. It can be affectionate or dismissive depending on context—wisdom or out-of-touch stubbornness: {Don't be such an oldhead about it}.

Oldheads are older people, especially those seen as out of touch with current trends or overly attached to how things used to be. The term originated in hip-hop culture to describe veteran fans or artists from earlier eras: {The oldheads think real rap died in the 90s}. It can be respectful (acknowledging experience) or dismissive (implying irrelevance), depending on context.

An oldie is something old but still valued, especially a song or film from an earlier era that remains popular: {The radio station plays oldies from the sixties and seventies}. The word carries affection rather than dismissal—oldies are classics, not relics. Often appears in the phrase {oldie but goodie}. Can refer fondly to older people: {We oldies remember when phones had cords}.

Oldies are popular songs from an earlier era, typically the 1950s through 1970s rock and roll and pop hits: {The radio station plays nothing but oldies}. The term shifts with time—what counts as oldies keeps getting more recent. More broadly, oldies can refer to old things generally, or affectionately to older people: {a cruise for oldies}.

Oldschool (also old-school or old school) describes attitudes, methods, or styles from an earlier era, often with admiration for their authenticity or proven reliability. Someone oldschool favors traditional approaches over newer trends: {My dad is oldschool—he still balances his checkbook by hand}. In hip-hop, oldschool refers specifically to the genre's foundational era of the late 1970s and early 1980s. The term can signal respect for experience and craftsmanship or gentle teasing about being behind the times.

An oldtimer is someone who has been around a long time—a veteran of a profession, organization, or place: {The oldtimers at the plant remember when it ran three shifts}. It can also simply mean an old person, sometimes affectionately, sometimes dismissively. The word suggests accumulated experience and a connection to how things used to be. Also spelled old-timer.

Oldtimers are people who have been around a long time—veterans of a place, profession, or era. The word suggests experience and longevity: {The oldtimers at the factory remember when everything was done by hand}. It can be affectionate or dismissive depending on context. Oldtimer's disease is a common euphemistic corruption of Alzheimer's disease.

Ole is an informal spelling of "old," representing casual or dialectal pronunciation: {ole boy}, {the same ole story}, {good ole days}. It often appears in folksy expressions or when evoking Southern American speech. The spelling captures a relaxed, familiar tone. Separately, olé (with an accent) is a Spanish exclamation of approval, shouted at bullfights and flamenco performances.

Oleander is an ornamental evergreen shrub with clusters of fragrant flowers, typically pink, white, or red. Native to the Mediterranean region, it thrives in warm climates and lines highways and gardens throughout the American South and Southwest. All parts of the plant are highly toxic—a fact that coexists oddly with its ubiquity in landscaping: {The oleanders along the freeway were in full bloom}.

An oligarch is a member of a small group that holds power in a government or organization. The term derives from oligarchy, a form of government where power rests with a few. In contemporary usage, oligarch most often refers to extremely wealthy individuals, especially Russian businessmen who acquired vast fortunes during the privatization of state assets after the Soviet collapse. {Sanctions targeted oligarchs close to the Kremlin.} The word carries connotations of ill-gotten wealth and corrupt political influence.

Oligarchies is the plural of oligarchy—a system of government in which power rests with a small group of people, typically distinguished by wealth, military strength, or family connections. The term also refers to the ruling groups themselves: {The oligarchies of several former Soviet states consolidated power in the 1990s}. By extension, any organization controlled by a tight inner circle may be called an oligarchy.

Oligarchs are members of a small group that holds power in a government or organization. The term often describes Russian billionaires who accumulated vast wealth during the privatization of state assets after the Soviet collapse: {Western sanctions targeted Russian oligarchs}. More broadly, oligarch labels any ultra-wealthy person whose fortune grants outsized political influence: {tech oligarchs}, {media oligarchs}.

Oligarchy is government by a small group, typically the wealthy or powerful. The term implies that power serves the interests of the ruling few rather than the broader population: {The country had become an oligarchy controlled by a handful of billionaires}. By extension, oligarchy can describe any organization where a small elite holds disproportionate control.

Olive is a small oval fruit, green when unripe and black when mature, prized for eating and for the oil pressed from it. The olive tree, native to the Mediterranean, is ancient in cultivation and symbolic of peace—an olive branch signals reconciliation. Olive also names a dull yellowish-green color, common in military clothing: {olive drab}. As an adjective, it describes skin tone: {olive complexion}. (Capitalized Olive is a given name.)

Olives are small oval fruits of a Mediterranean tree, harvested green (unripe) or black (ripe). Too bitter to eat fresh, they're cured in brine, salt, or oil. Olives are pressed to make olive oil, a staple of Mediterranean cooking. The olive branch is a symbol of peace. {Would you like olives on your pizza?}

An ollie is a skateboarding trick where the rider pops the board into the air without using their hands, achieved by snapping the tail down while sliding the front foot forward. It's the foundational trick for most aerial skateboard maneuvers: {I spent weeks learning to ollie before I could kickflip}. The trick is named after skateboarder Alan "Ollie" Gelfand, who invented it in the late 1970s. (Capitalized Ollie is a given name.)

Ollies is the plural of ollie, a fundamental skateboarding trick where the rider pops the board into the air without using hands. The skater kicks down on the tail while jumping, then slides the front foot forward to level the board. Mastering ollies enables more advanced tricks: {She landed three clean ollies before attempting a kickflip}.

Omakase is a Japanese term for a meal left to the chef's discretion—literally "I leave it up to you." At sushi restaurants, ordering omakase means receiving whatever the chef selects, typically the freshest seasonal ingredients prepared in sequence: {We sat at the bar and did the omakase}. The format implies trust in the chef's expertise and often commands premium prices.

Ombre describes a gradual blending of one color into another, typically from light to dark or vice versa: {ombre hair}, {an ombre sunset}. The effect appears in hair coloring, fabric dyeing, nail art, and design. As a noun, ombre refers to this graduated color technique: {She asked her stylist for an ombre}.

An ombudsman is an official appointed to investigate complaints against organizations, typically government agencies or large institutions. The ombudsman acts as an independent advocate, mediating between individuals and bureaucracies when something goes wrong: {She filed a complaint with the university ombudsman}. The role originated in Sweden and has spread to corporations, newspapers, and public agencies worldwide.

Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, and by extension means the end or final element of something. The phrase {alpha and omega} encompasses everything from beginning to end. In social hierarchies, an omega is the lowest-ranking individual—opposite of alpha. Omega-3 {fatty acids} are essential nutrients. In physics, omega represents angular velocity. {Every story has its omega.} (Capitalized Omega may refer to watch brands, organizations, or proper names.)

An omelet is eggs beaten and cooked in a pan until set, typically folded around a filling of cheese, vegetables, or meat. The dish is a breakfast staple but appears at any meal. Spelling varies: omelet in American English, omelette in British. {I'll have a mushroom omelet with toast.}

Omelets are eggs beaten and cooked in a pan until set, typically folded around a filling of cheese, vegetables, or meat. The dish is a breakfast staple and a test of technique for cooks—a properly made omelet should be tender inside with no browning. Also spelled omelette.

An omelette is a dish of beaten eggs cooked in a flat round and typically folded around a filling—cheese, vegetables, meat, or herbs. The eggs are stirred briefly in a hot pan, then allowed to set. {She made a mushroom omelette for breakfast.} Also spelled omelet, especially in American English.

Omelettes is the plural of omelette, a dish made by beating eggs and cooking them in a pan, typically folded around a filling such as cheese, vegetables, or meat. The spelling omelette is more common in British English, while omelet prevails in American English. A plain omelette contains no filling. {We ordered omelettes with mushrooms and Swiss cheese.}

An omen is a sign or event believed to foretell the future, especially something momentous or fateful: {The crow at the window seemed like an omen}. Omens can be good or bad, though the word alone often suggests something ominous—a dark portent. To omen is rare; the adjective forms ominous and the verb portend are more common.

Omens are signs believed to foretell future events, especially misfortune. A black cat crossing your path, a broken mirror, an owl's call—these are traditional omens. The word often appears with modifiers: {a bad omen}, {an omen of things to come}. Unlike prophecies, omens are read from ordinary events rather than spoken by seers. Something that omens ill bodes badly for the future.

Omerta is the code of silence associated with the Mafia and other organized crime groups—the rule that members never cooperate with authorities or reveal information about criminal activities. Breaking omerta traditionally carried severe consequences, including death. The term extends to any unwritten rule against informing: {The department's omerta protected corrupt officers for years}.

OMFG is an intensified version of OMG (oh my god), with the F standing for fucking. It expresses stronger shock, disbelief, or excitement: {OMFG, did you see what she just posted?} Common in texting and social media, it reads as more dramatic or emphatic than plain OMG.

Omg is a casual written expression of surprise, excitement, or disbelief—short for "oh my god." Common in texting and social media: {omg I can't believe she said that}, {omg this is amazing}. The lowercase form feels more offhand than the emphatic all-caps version. (All-caps OMG is the more emphatic form.)

Omicron is the fifteenth letter of the Greek alphabet (Ο, ο), corresponding to the short "o" sound. In English, the word appears mainly in scientific contexts—naming stars (Omicron Persei), variants of viruses, or in fraternity and sorority names. The COVID-19 variant designated Omicron in 2021 brought the term into widespread use: {The Omicron wave hit just before the holidays}.

Ominous describes something that suggests bad things to come—threatening or foreboding. An {ominous sky} portends a storm. An {ominous silence} precedes bad news. {The letter arrived with an ominous warning}. The word carries a sense of dread without specifying the threat, letting imagination fill the gap.

In a way that suggests something bad is coming. Dark clouds gather ominously before a storm. A character speaks ominously when their words hint at danger or misfortune ahead. {The engine sputtered ominously}. {He was ominously silent when I asked about the test results}.

Omission is leaving something out or failing to do something. An omission can be accidental—a name dropped from a list—or deliberate: {The report's omissions were telling}. In law and ethics, an omission may carry the same weight as an action: failing to report abuse, neglecting to disclose a conflict of interest. {Sins of omission} are wrongs committed by not acting.

Omissions are things that have been left out or not done. An omission may be accidental—a name omitted from a guest list—or deliberate, as when someone withholds information. In legal contexts, an omission can be as significant as an action: failing to report income or neglecting a duty of care. {The report's omissions were more telling than what it included.} The phrase {sins of omission} refers to wrongs committed by failing to act rather than by acting.

Omitted is the past tense of omit, meaning left out or excluded. Something omitted was deliberately or accidentally not included: {Her name was omitted from the guest list}. The word often implies incompleteness—what remains is missing something that might have belonged: {Several key details were omitted from the report}.

Omnipotence is unlimited power—the ability to do anything. The word appears most often in religious contexts, where it describes a divine attribute: {the omnipotence of God}. More loosely, omnipotence can describe any seemingly boundless authority or capability: {the omnipotence of the surveillance state}. The adjective is omnipotent.

Omnipotent means having unlimited or universal power. The word applies most often to God or gods: {an omnipotent deity who created the universe}. It extends to anyone or anything with seemingly absolute authority or capability: {The CEO acted as if he were omnipotent}. The noun omnipotence names this quality. In theology, omnipotence often appears alongside omniscience (all-knowing) and omnipresence (everywhere at once).

Omnipresence is the quality of being everywhere at once. The term traditionally describes a divine attribute—God's omnipresence means no place exists outside divine awareness. More loosely, omnipresence describes anything that seems inescapable: {the omnipresence of smartphones}, {the omnipresence of advertising in modern life}.

Something that is omnipresent can be seen or felt everywhere, all the time. Ubiquitous is a near synonym. Omnipresent is used to characterize both concrete and abstract things, but more often the latter: The omnipresent threat of a terrorist attack is stressful for everyone. In religious contexts, omnipresent is often used to describe a quality attributed to God.

Omniscience is the state of knowing everything—all facts, all thoughts, all possibilities. The concept belongs primarily to theology, where it describes a divine attribute: {Only God possesses true omniscience}. In fiction, an omniscient narrator knows the inner thoughts of all characters. The word sometimes appears ironically for those who act as if they know everything: {He spoke with the omniscience of someone who'd read one article on the subject}.

Omniscient means all-knowing, possessing complete or infinite knowledge. The word applies primarily to God or gods: {an omniscient deity who sees all}. In literature, an omniscient narrator knows the thoughts and feelings of all characters: {The novel uses an omniscient third-person point of view}. Informally, it describes someone who seems to know everything, often with a hint of irony: {My mother was practically omniscient—she always knew when I was lying}.

An omnivore is an animal that eats both plants and other animals. Humans, pigs, and bears are omnivores, in contrast to herbivores (plant-eaters) and carnivores (meat-eaters). The term extends loosely to people with wide-ranging tastes: {She's a cultural omnivore—opera one night, punk rock the next}.

Omnivores are animals that eat both plants and other animals. Humans, pigs, bears, and raccoons are omnivores, distinguished from herbivores (plant-eaters) and carnivores (meat-eaters). The term extends figuratively to people with wide-ranging tastes or interests: {She's an omnivore when it comes to books—fiction, history, science, anything}.

Onboard means aboard or on a vehicle, vessel, or craft: {onboard navigation systems}, {the onboard computer}. Extended to mean part of a team or project: {We need to get everyone onboard before we proceed}. As a verb, to onboard is to integrate a new employee or customer into an organization's systems and culture: {HR will onboard you next week}. Also spelled as two words: on board.

Onboarding is the process of integrating someone new into an organization or system. In workplace contexts, it covers everything from paperwork to training to cultural orientation: {The company's onboarding takes two weeks}. For software and apps, onboarding refers to the initial steps that familiarize users with features: {The app's onboarding walks you through the basics}. The verb is onboard: {We onboarded three new hires this month}.

Once is a busy function word whose meanings arise mainly from the closely related word one. The adverb conveys one time (I went there once) or formerly: They visited the ruins of the once magnificent castle. At once conveys immediacy or concurrence: I can’t do two things at once. Once is used to join clauses to show one thing immediately follows, and may depend upon, another: Once you light the fuse, get out of there.

An oncologist is a physician who specializes in diagnosing and treating cancer. The field divides into subspecialties: medical oncologists administer chemotherapy and other drug treatments, radiation oncologists use targeted radiation, and surgical oncologists remove tumors. {Her oncologist recommended a combination of surgery and chemotherapy.}

Oncoming describes something approaching or moving toward you: {oncoming traffic}, {the oncoming winter}. The word usually implies something unavoidable—you can step aside for oncoming pedestrians, but not for oncoming old age. As a noun, the oncoming of something is its approach: {the oncoming of night}.

One is the written form of the number 1 and works as an adjective in that capacity (one window). One substitutes for a singular noun that has been used already, or when reference is clear from context (buy one, get one free). One is an impersonal and somewhat formal third-person singular pronoun without gender: One should be careful in that situation. Groups of things sharing some characteristic can be designated with an adjective before ones (red ones, lucky ones).

A oneliner is a joke or witty remark delivered in a single sentence: {He's known for his oneliners about married life}. The term also applies to any brief, pithy statement—a memorable quip or a concise piece of code that accomplishes something in one line. Also spelled one-liner.

One-liners are jokes or witty remarks delivered in a single sentence: {He's known for his oneliners about politics}. The term extends to any brief, punchy statement—a memorable quote, a snappy comeback, or a condensed argument. Stand-up comedians who specialize in rapid-fire jokes rather than longer stories are called one-liner comics. Also spelled one-liners.

Oneness is the state of being unified, whole, or singular rather than divided or multiple. In spiritual and philosophical contexts, it often describes a sense of profound connection with the universe, nature, or all living things—the feeling that boundaries between self and other dissolve. More practically, oneness can simply mean agreement or harmony: {The committee finally achieved a oneness of purpose}. The word emphasizes unity as a quality or condition rather than mere numerical singleness.

A onesie is a one-piece garment. For infants, it's a bodysuit that snaps at the crotch for easy diaper changes. For adults, it's a loose-fitting jumpsuit worn as loungewear or pajamas, often with a playful or cozy aesthetic: {I spent Sunday in my onesie watching movies}. The plural is onesies.
clues: Single garment covering torso and legs

definition: Onesies is a one-piece garment, either a snap-crotch bodysuit for infants or a full-body jumpsuit for adults, typically casual loungewear with feet: {She bought a dinosaur onesie for the baby shower}. The adult version gained popularity as ironic comfort wear: {We spent New Year's Eve in matching onesies}. Singular: onesie.
clues: What newborns often come home wearing

definition: Oneupmanship is the practice of gaining or maintaining an advantage over others, especially through subtle competitive tactics. The word suggests a game where each party tries to outdo the other in status, wit, or achievement: {The dinner party descended into oneupmanship as each guest tried to name-drop more impressive connections}. Unlike outright rivalry, oneupmanship often operates through suggestion and implication rather than direct contest.

Ongoing means continuing or in progress, not yet completed: {ongoing negotiations}, {ongoing investigation}, {an ongoing relationship}. The word emphasizes that something started in the past and persists into the present, with no definite end point. {The project is ongoing and expected to take several more months.}

Onigiri is a Japanese rice ball, typically triangular or oval, often wrapped in nori (dried seaweed) and filled with ingredients like pickled plum, salmon, or tuna. A staple of Japanese cuisine, onigiri functions as portable food—sold in convenience stores, packed in lunches, eaten on the go: {I grabbed an onigiri from the konbini}.

Onion is a bulb vegetable with papery outer layers enclosing concentric rings of pungent flesh. Raw onions have a sharp, eye-watering quality that mellows into sweetness when cooked. The layered structure gives rise to the metaphor of peeling back layers to reveal deeper truths or complexities: {The investigation peeled back the onion on years of corruption}. In internet slang, the onion router (Tor) enables anonymous browsing, and .onion addresses exist on the dark web. If you {know your onions}, you're well-informed about a subject.

Onions are pungent bulb vegetables with papery outer layers and concentric rings inside. They're culinary staples across most cuisines, eaten raw, sautéed, caramelized, or pickled. Cutting onions releases compounds that irritate the eyes, causing tears. To {know your onions} is to be knowledgeable about something.

Online means connected to or available through the internet or a computer network. You can shop online, take classes online, or meet someone online. As an adjective, it describes things accessible digitally: {online banking}, {online dating}. The opposite is offline. Something that {goes online} becomes operational or connected: {The new server goes online tomorrow}.

An onlooker is someone who watches an event without participating—a spectator or bystander: {Onlookers gathered at the scene of the accident}. The word often implies passive observation, sometimes with a hint of detachment or voyeurism: {The fight drew a crowd of onlookers}.

Onlookers are people who watch something happen without participating in it. The term typically describes those who gather at the scene of an accident, crime, or public spectacle—present by chance or drawn by curiosity rather than involvement. {Onlookers crowded around the street performer.} Unlike spectators at planned events, onlookers often carry a slightly passive or voyeuristic connotation, as when crowds form around emergencies.
clues: Those who watch but don't participate

definition: It’s significant that the closest relative of only is the word one: only always serves to distinguish one thing, group, or quality from others. As an adverb only limits the application of verbs and adjectives: This area is reserved for members only. Before nouns, only suggests singularity: She’s an only child. Is that the only shirt you have to wear? In writing, only precedes the word it modifies; in speech, the word is emphasized, lessening the importance of position. Listeners who hear, “I could only see three people there,” understand that the only goes with “three” and not with “see.”

Onomatopoeia is the formation of words that imitate sounds: *buzz*, *hiss*, *splash*, *meow*. The term also refers to words formed this way. Comic books are full of onomatopoeia: *pow*, *zap*, *wham*. Languages differ in how they render the same sounds—a rooster says *cock-a-doodle-doo* in English but *kikeriki* in German.

An onramp is a short road that allows vehicles to enter a highway or freeway, typically curving to merge with faster traffic: {We missed the onramp and had to circle back}. Figuratively, an onramp is any entry point or introductory pathway: {Community college can be an onramp to a four-year degree}. Also spelled on-ramp.

An onrush is a powerful forward surge or rush—a sudden, forceful movement toward something: {the onrush of floodwaters}, {the onrush of enemy troops}. The word often describes things that feel overwhelming or unstoppable: {the onrush of technological change}, {the onrush of memories}. It emphasizes momentum and force rather than mere speed.

Onscreen describes what appears on a display—television, computer, or cinema screen: {The onscreen chemistry between the leads was undeniable}. It distinguishes visible screen content from what happens off-camera or behind the scenes. Also spelled on-screen. As an adverb: {The actor first appeared onscreen in 1995}.

Onset is the beginning or start of something, typically something unpleasant or significant: {the onset of winter}, {the onset of symptoms}, {the onset of war}. The word implies a process or condition taking hold rather than a single moment. In linguistics, onset refers to the consonant sound or sounds at the beginning of a syllable.

Onside describes a legal position in sports like soccer and hockey where an attacking player is not ahead of the ball or the second-to-last defender when a pass is made. Being onside means you're eligible to receive the ball and score without penalty. The term extends figuratively to mean being in agreement or on the same team: {We need to get the board onside before announcing the merger}. In American football, an onside kick is a short kickoff designed to be recovered by the kicking team.

Onslaught is a fierce, overwhelming attack—originally military, now used broadly for any intense assault: {The city couldn't withstand the onslaught}. It suggests force arriving suddenly and in quantity: an onslaught of {criticism}, an onslaught of {emails}, an onslaught of {bad weather}. The word carries a sense of being besieged or overwhelmed.

Onstage means on the stage of a theater, in view of the audience: {The actor forgot his lines onstage}. It works as both adverb and adjective: {She walked onstage}, {his onstage persona}. Figuratively, onstage suggests being in the public eye or performing for others, as opposed to one's private self.

Onto is a merger of the prepositions on and to that combines the ideas of both of them. It is often preceded by a verb of motion such as turn, move, or step. In many cases onto is used when the ideas represented by its components are still somewhat separate, as when you log onto a website or hold onto a strap.

Onus is a burden of responsibility or obligation, particularly the duty to prove something or take action. The phrase {onus of proof} (or {burden of proof}) appears frequently in legal contexts, but onus applies broadly: {The onus is on the employer to provide a safe workplace}. The word carries a sense of weight or pressure that falls specifically on someone.

Onward means forward in space, time, or progress—continuing in a direction already established. {The expedition pressed onward despite the storm.} {From that day onward, everything changed.} It often carries a sense of determination or momentum. As an adjective, it describes forward movement: {the onward march of technology}. Onwards is a British variant.

Onyx is a banded variety of chalcedony, a semiprecious stone typically showing parallel layers of black and white. Pure black onyx is most familiar in jewelry: {an onyx ring}, {onyx cufflinks}. The word extends to anything with that distinctive deep black color or lustrous quality.

Oobleck is a mixture of cornstarch and water that behaves as both liquid and solid—it flows when handled gently but resists sudden force. Named after a sticky substance in a Dr. Seuss book, it's a classic science demonstration of non-Newtonian fluids: {The kids made oobleck and watched it ooze through their fingers, then harden when punched}.

Oodles means a large quantity or abundance of something: {oodles of money}, {oodles of time}. The word is informal and lighthearted, often used playfully to emphasize plenty: {She has oodles of talent}.

Oof is an exclamation expressing discomfort, sympathy, or reaction to something painful or awkward. It can respond to physical impact {Oof, that hurt} or to uncomfortable situations: {Oof, that's a rough breakup}. Online, oof often acknowledges someone else's misfortune or embarrassment with mild commiseration: {Oof, sorry that happened to you}.
Ooh is usually a representation of a sound that people make in response to some enjoyable stimulus. A very short ooh with a falling tone may indicate revulsion.

Oohs is the plural of ooh, a vocal expression of wonder, admiration, or delight: {The fireworks drew oohs from the crowd}. As a verb, to ooh is to make this sound, often paired with aah: {The audience oohed and aahed at the baby photos}.

Oolong is a type of Chinese tea, partially oxidized to fall between green and black tea in color and flavor. The leaves are typically rolled or twisted, producing a complex taste that varies from floral and light to rich and roasted depending on processing. {She ordered an oolong at the tea house.}

Oompah is the sound of a tuba or similar brass instrument playing a rhythmic bass line—the characteristic {oom-pah, oom-pah} of German band music, polkas, and beer-hall performances. The word captures both the deep bass note (oom) and the higher chord that follows (pah). As an adjective, it describes this style: {an oompah band}.

Oomph is energy, vigor, or attractive quality—the indefinable something that makes a person or thing stand out. A performer with oomph has charisma and sex appeal. A dish needs more oomph if it lacks punch or excitement. An engine lacks oomph if it doesn't have enough power: {This old truck doesn't have the oomph to make it up the hill}.
People say oops to acknowledge that they—or someone else—have just done something clumsy, made a mistake, or said something awkward or embarrassing.

Oopsie is a playful exclamation acknowledging a small mistake or accident, often used by or around children: {Oopsie, I spilled my juice}. Adults use it ironically or affectionately for minor blunders. As a noun, an oopsie is the mistake itself: {That was a bit of an oopsie}. The word softens errors into something cute rather than serious.
clues: What a child says after spilling

definition: Oopsies is a playful or childish exclamation acknowledging a minor mistake or accident: {Oopsies, I spilled my coffee}. It softens blame and sounds deliberately cute, often used with children or ironically among adults to minimize a blunder. As a noun, oopsies can mean the mistakes themselves: {We all make little oopsies}.

Oopsy is a playful or cutesy way of saying oops, typically used when acknowledging a minor mistake or accident. It softens the admission of error and is especially common in speech directed at or around children: {Oopsy, I spilled my juice}. Adults may use it ironically or self-deprecatingly when they've made a small blunder.

Oorah is a battle cry used by U.S. Marines to express enthusiasm, approval, or solidarity. It functions as a greeting, an affirmative response, or a general expression of esprit de corps: {Oorah, Marine!} The exact origin is disputed, but the cry has been standard Marine vocabulary since at least the 1980s. Sometimes spelled hoorah or ooh-rah.

Ooze is slow, thick movement—liquid seeping gradually through or out of something: {Blood oozed from the wound}, {Water oozed through the cracks}. The word suggests viscosity and unhurried flow. Figuratively, someone can ooze confidence or charm, exuding it so thoroughly it seems to seep from them. As a noun, ooze is soft mud or slime, especially at the bottom of a body of water.

Oozed is the past tense of ooze, meaning to flow slowly and thickly, as liquid seeping through small openings: {Blood oozed from the wound}. Figuratively, someone can ooze a quality they seem to radiate effortlessly: {He oozed confidence}. The word suggests something viscous, gradual, or slightly unpleasant emerging from a source.

Oozes describes slow, thick movement—liquid seeping gradually through small openings or across surfaces. Mud oozes between toes; sap oozes from tree bark. Figuratively, a person oozes qualities they seem to exude effortlessly: {He oozes confidence}; {The place oozes charm}. The word suggests something emerging steadily, almost involuntarily, rather than flowing freely.

Oozing describes something slowly seeping or leaking out, typically a thick liquid like blood, mud, or pus: {The wound was still oozing}. It can also characterize surfaces that release such substances: {oozing blisters}. Figuratively, oozing suggests an excessive or conspicuous display of a quality: {He was oozing confidence}. The word carries connotations of something uncontrolled and often unpleasant, though the figurative sense can be neutral or even positive.

Oozy describes something that oozes—slowly seeping or exuding moisture, mud, or other viscous substances. An oozy wound leaks fluid. Oozy ground is soft and wet, squelching underfoot: {We trudged through the oozy marsh}. The word suggests slow, messy seepage rather than flowing freely.

Opacity is the quality of blocking light—the opposite of transparency. An opaque surface has high opacity; a clear one has none. The term extends to anything difficult to see through or understand: {the opacity of legal language}, {the opacity of his motives}. In graphics software, opacity controls how much underlying content shows through a layer.

Opal is a gemstone prized for its iridescent play of colors—flashes of red, blue, green, and yellow that shift as light moves across the surface. This optical effect, called opalescence, comes from the stone's internal structure of silica spheres. Opals range from milky white to black, with black opals being most valuable. {She wore her grandmother's opal ring.} The adjective opalescent describes anything with similar shimmering, shifting colors.

Opals are gemstones prized for their iridescent play of color—flashes of red, blue, green, and orange that shift as the stone moves. Unlike diamonds or rubies, opals display this internal shimmer rather than brilliance from faceting. {Her grandmother's opal ring caught the light}. Australia produces most of the world's gem-quality opals. Superstition once held opals unlucky, though this belief has faded.

Opaque describes something that blocks light from passing through, making it impossible to see what's behind it. This contrasts with transparent (fully see-through) and translucent (allowing some light but obscuring details). The word extends naturally to anything difficult to understand or penetrate: {The legal language was opaque to most readers}. Opaque prose is dense and unclear; an opaque bureaucracy resists scrutiny. In technical contexts, opacity can refer to how much radiation or other energy a material absorbs.

The core idea of open is the lack of a closing or confining barrier or limit: open door, open discussions. For many meanings, the nearest antonym of open is closed or shut. When you open something, you cause it to be open, as with a door, window, or gate. For something intangible, open can mean to initiate or create something that becomes usable or available, as when you open an account, or when a situation opens a possibility. To open fire means to start shooting. Open is also used intransitively, in which case the thing opening is the subject: The exhibition opens next week.

An opener is anything that opens something else, whether a tool like a bottle opener or can opener, or a person who initiates an action. In sports, the opener is the first game of a series or season. In conversation, an opener is a remark designed to start a dialogue: {He tried a few openers but she wasn't interested}. The opener in a show or concert is the act that performs first, before the headliner.

Openers are things that begin or initiate. A can opener opens cans; a conversation opener starts dialogue. In poker, openers are cards good enough to open betting. The phrase {for openers} means "to begin with" or "as a first point": {For openers, we need to discuss the budget}. An opener is also the first act before a headliner, or the first game of a series.

Openhearted describes someone who is frank, generous, and emotionally available. An openhearted person shares their feelings freely and responds to others with warmth and sincerity: {She gave an openhearted account of her struggles}. The word suggests both emotional transparency and kindness—someone without guile who welcomes connection.

Opening is the act of becoming open or making something open, or the gap or space that results: {an opening in the fence}, {the opening of a new store}. An opening is also a beginning—the opening of a book, a chess opening, opening remarks. By extension, an opening is an opportunity or available position: {a job opening}, {an opening in the schedule}. The adjective describes what comes first: {opening night}, {opening statement}.

Openings are gaps, holes, or opportunities for entry. A job opening is a vacant position. The opening of a film or play is its premiere or first scene. An opening in conversation creates space to speak. In chess, the opening comprises the first several moves. The plural often suggests multiple chances: {There were several openings in the fence}, {career openings in tech}.

Openly means without concealment or secrecy—in a way that others can see or know about. Someone who openly {admits a mistake} doesn't try to hide it. To {live openly} as something is to be public about an identity that might otherwise be concealed: {She was one of the first openly gay athletes}. Openly can also mean candidly: {They spoke openly about their struggles}.

Open-minded means receptive to new ideas, arguments, or perspectives—willing to consider viewpoints different from your own. An open-minded person doesn't dismiss unfamiliar concepts reflexively: {Try to be open-minded about the proposal before rejecting it}. The term often implies intellectual flexibility and a lack of rigid prejudice. Also spelled open-minded and openminded.

Openness is the quality of being receptive, accessible, or unrestricted. A person with openness welcomes new ideas and experiences: {Her openness to criticism made her a better writer}. Openness in communication means transparency and candor: {The company promised greater openness about its practices}. Physical openness describes expansiveness or lack of barriers: {the openness of the prairie}. In personality psychology, openness is one of the "Big Five" traits, measuring curiosity and imagination.

Opera is a dramatic art form combining music, singing, and theatrical performance, with the story told primarily through sung dialogue rather than spoken words: {We have tickets to the opera tonight}. The term also refers to a particular work in this genre: {Carmen is my favorite opera}. Opera can mean the opera house or company: {the Sydney Opera}. In computing, Opera is a web browser. (Capitalized OPERA may be an acronym.)

Operas is the plural of opera, a dramatic art form combining music, singing, and theatrical staging. The word appears in compound terms: {soap operas} are serialized melodramas, {space operas} are epic science fiction adventures, and {horse operas} are Westerns. {The Met stages several new operas each season.}

Operate means to function or to cause something to function. Machines operate when they run properly; surgeons operate when they perform medical procedures; businesses operate when they conduct their affairs. {The elevator operates on a pulley system.} {She operates a small bakery downtown.} To operate on someone is to perform surgery. In military and covert contexts, operatives operate in the field, carrying out missions or gathering intelligence.
