An otherworld is a realm beyond or separate from the ordinary world—the land of the dead, the fairy realm, or some parallel dimension: {Celtic myths are full of journeys to the otherworld}. The term suggests a place that exists alongside our reality but operates by different rules. Often used in fantasy literature and mythology to describe where spirits, gods, or magical beings dwell.

Otherworldliness is the quality of seeming to belong to a realm beyond ordinary earthly existence—something spiritual, ethereal, or simply detached from everyday concerns. A person with an otherworldly air might appear dreamy, mystical, or unconcerned with practical matters. The term can describe genuine spiritual transcendence or simply suggest that someone or something feels strange and removed from normal life: {The otherworldliness of the abandoned cathedral made visitors speak in whispers}.

Otherworldly describes something that seems to belong to another realm—strange, ethereal, or supernatural in quality. An otherworldly {glow} suggests something not quite of this earth. The word applies to experiences, appearances, or atmospheres that feel detached from ordinary reality: {Her voice had an otherworldly beauty}. It can also describe someone so spiritually focused or dreamy they seem disconnected from practical concerns.

An otter is a semiaquatic mammal with a streamlined body, webbed feet, and dense waterproof fur, found in freshwater and coastal habitats. Otters are known for floating on their backs and using rocks to crack open shellfish. Sea otters live in kelp forests along Pacific coastlines; river otters inhabit streams and lakes. {We watched the otters playing in the water.}

Otters are semiaquatic mammals with sleek bodies, webbed feet, and dense waterproof fur. They're known for playful behavior—sliding down mudbanks, floating on their backs, using rocks to crack open shellfish. Sea otters live in coastal waters; river otters inhabit freshwater. {We watched the otters chase each other through the kelp.}

An ottoman is a cushioned footstool or low upholstered seat without a back or arms, often used in living rooms for resting feet or as extra seating. The furniture piece typically accompanies an armchair or sofa: {She put her feet up on the ottoman}. Some ottomans have hinged tops for storage. (Capitalized Ottoman refers to the Turkish empire or people.)

Ottomans are low upholstered seats or footstools, typically without a back or arms. The name comes from Ottoman Turkish furniture styles. An ottoman often sits before a chair or sofa for resting feet, or serves as extra seating: {She propped her feet on the ottoman}. Some ottomans open for storage. (Capitalized Ottoman refers to the Turkish empire or its people.)

An oubliette is a dungeon accessible only through a trapdoor in the ceiling—a place where prisoners were dropped and forgotten. The word comes from French for "to forget." It appears mostly in historical fiction and fantasy: {The castle's oubliette held the bones of forgotten enemies}. Figuratively, any place or situation where people or things are abandoned and neglected: {The proposal languished in a bureaucratic oubliette}.
Ouch and ow are both ways of spelling the sound that people make to express the feeling of pain. People also sometimes say ouch to show that they understand someone else’s experience as painful.

Ouchie is childish or playful language for a minor injury, typically a small cut, scrape, or bruise. It's the kind of hurt that warrants a bandage and a kiss rather than a trip to the emergency room. Adults use it when speaking to children or when being deliberately cute about their own minor mishaps: {I got an ouchie on my finger}. The word can also refer to the bandage itself: {Do you need an ouchie for that?}

Ought expresses obligation, duty, or strong expectation: {You ought to apologize}, {That ought to be enough}. It functions like should but carries slightly more moral weight. Ought typically requires "to" before the following verb, unlike most auxiliaries. In negative constructions, {ought not} sounds formal; {shouldn't} is more common in speech.

The oughties are the years 2000–2009, named for the "ought" (zero) in each year. The term parallels twenties, thirties, and so on, filling an awkward gap in decade nomenclature: {Fashion trends from the oughties are making a comeback}. Also spelled noughties, especially in British English.

An ounce is a unit of weight equal to one-sixteenth of a pound, or about 28 grams. In measuring liquids, a fluid ounce is about 30 milliliters. Ounce often appears in figurative expressions emphasizing small quantities: {She doesn't have an ounce of common sense}. If you give something {every ounce} of your strength or energy, you give it everything you have. The ounce is also a rare name for the snow leopard.

Ounces is the plural of ounce, a unit of weight equal to one-sixteenth of a pound, or about 28 grams. A fluid ounce measures volume rather than weight—one-sixteenth of a pint in the US. Figuratively, ounce suggests a small amount: {He doesn't have an ounce of sense}. {She put every ounce of energy into the project}.

Our is the possessive form of we. You use our before a name or noun phrase to indicate that the thing you name belongs to or is associated with you and others: We sent our Senator a petition. Our daughter is a mechanical engineer. Our is called a possessive because it indicates possession or ownership; different grammarians classify it as an adjective, a pronoun, or a determiner.

An ouroboros is an ancient symbol depicting a serpent or dragon eating its own tail, forming a circle. It represents cyclicality, eternal return, or self-referential systems—things that perpetually consume and regenerate themselves. The image appears across cultures from ancient Egypt to alchemy to modern psychology. Figuratively, anything that feeds on itself or creates an endless loop: {The committee's review process had become an ouroboros, generating more questions than it answered}. Also spelled uroboros.

Ours combines two jobs in one; to take the place of a noun or noun phrase already named, and to indicate that the thing referred to belongs to or is associated with you and others: If your car is still in the shop you can use ours. These two jobs give ours and other words in its class the designation “possessive pronoun.”

You use ourselves as the object of a verb or preposition to refer to yourself and others in a sentence in which we is the subject: We surprised ourselves with the progress we made. Ourselves and other pronouns that end in –self and –selves are called reflexives because they indicate that the action of a verb is reflected back at the subject of the sentence.

Oust means to force someone out of a position or place. The word typically applies to removing people from power or office: {The board voted to oust the CEO}. It can extend to physical removal: {Security ousted the hecklers from the venue}. The ousting is usually decisive and against the person's will.

Ousted is the past tense of oust, meaning forcibly removed from a position or place. Someone ousted from power has been expelled, typically by others acting collectively or through formal process: {The board ousted the CEO after the scandal}. The word implies unwilling departure—you don't oust someone who leaves voluntarily.

Ouster is the act of forcing someone out of a position or place. It typically applies to removal from office, employment, or property: {The board voted for the CEO's ouster}. The word carries a sense of finality—an ouster isn't a resignation or quiet departure but a decisive ejection, often after conflict or misconduct.

Ousting is the act of forcing someone out of a position or place. The word typically applies to removing people from positions of power or authority: {The board voted for the CEO's ousting}, {The ousting of the dictator led to years of instability}. An ousting can be formal or informal, peaceful or violent.

Whether as adverb, preposition, or adjective, out is almost always used as the opposite of in. Like in, out has uses in which the core meaning is not present: Look out for potholes in the road, or We were out $50 because of all the extra fees. The connection of out with the idea of outside and public has given rise to the adjective and verb uses of the word: someone who is out makes no secret about their affiliation or identity, and when you out someone, you reveal something formerly concealed about them.

An outage is an instance of something being not available or used up. The most common kind of outage is a power outage, that is, a loss of electrical power. Most other kinds of outage involve the sudden lack of something that is normally provided at all times, such as water, gas, or Internet or GPS service.

Outages is the plural of outage—periods when something that normally operates continuously stops working. Power outages leave homes dark. Service outages take websites offline. The word implies temporary interruption rather than permanent failure: {Rolling outages affected the city during the heat wave}. {We experienced several internet outages last month}.

Outback refers to remote, sparsely populated rural areas, especially the arid interior regions of Australia. The term evokes vast, dry landscapes far from cities and coastal settlements: {They drove for days through the outback}. By extension, any isolated backcountry can be called outback: {the Nevada outback}. (Capitalized Outback often refers specifically to Australia's interior or the restaurant chain.)

To outbid is to offer more than someone else in a bidding situation—at an auction, for a contract, or when competing for a house: {We were outbid at the last minute}. The word implies competition where the higher offer wins.

Outboard describes position away from the center of a vessel, vehicle, or aircraft—toward the outer edge. An outboard motor mounts on the outside of a boat's stern rather than inside the hull: {We rented a small skiff with a 25-horsepower outboard}. The word works as adjective, adverb, or noun: {the outboard engine}, {mounted outboard}, {fire up the outboard}.

Outboards are motors mounted externally on the back of a boat, as opposed to inboard engines housed within the hull. The term covers both the engines themselves and boats equipped with them: {We rented a couple of outboards for the fishing trip}. As an adverb or adjective, outboard means toward or at the outer edge of a vessel or aircraft: {the outboard engine on the wing}.

Outbound describes movement or travel directed away from a central point, origin, or home base. An outbound {flight} departs from your location; outbound {traffic} flows away from a city center. In business contexts, outbound often characterizes communications or efforts initiated by a company toward customers or prospects, as in outbound {calls} or outbound {marketing}, contrasted with inbound inquiries that customers initiate themselves.

An outbox is a container or folder for items waiting to be sent. In email, the outbox holds messages queued for delivery but not yet transmitted—distinct from the sent folder, which stores messages already delivered. In older office settings, a physical outbox on a desk held papers ready for pickup or mailing: {I left the signed contract in your outbox}.

An outbreak is a sudden occurrence or eruption of something undesirable—disease, violence, or conflict. The word implies rapid spread from an origin point: {an outbreak of cholera}, {an outbreak of fighting along the border}. Outbreak emphasizes the initial emergence; what follows might be called an epidemic or a war.

Outbreaks are sudden occurrences of something unwelcome—disease, violence, or conflict. An outbreak of {cholera} spreads rapidly through a population. An outbreak of {war} or {hostilities} begins abruptly. The word implies something that erupts and spreads: {outbreaks of looting followed the blackout}. Less commonly, outbreak describes any sudden emergence: an outbreak of {laughter}, an outbreak of {creativity}.

An outburst is a sudden release of strong emotion or energy. Someone prone to angry outbursts explodes with little warning: {His outburst shocked everyone in the meeting}. The word applies to any abrupt expression—an outburst of laughter, of applause, of violence. Natural phenomena can have outbursts too: {an outburst of solar activity}.

Outbursts are sudden, uncontrolled expressions of emotion or activity. An outburst of {anger}, an outburst of {laughter}, an outburst of {applause}. The word usually implies something brief and explosive rather than sustained—a momentary loss of composure or a spontaneous eruption: {His outburst shocked everyone in the meeting}.

An outcast is someone rejected or excluded by a group or society. The word suggests being cast out—expelled from belonging: {He lived as an outcast after the scandal}. As an adjective, it describes this state of rejection: {outcast tribes}, {an outcast existence}. The term often carries sympathy for the excluded rather than judgment.

Outcasts are people who have been rejected or excluded from a group or community. The word suggests both the act of being cast out and the resulting social position—someone living on the margins, denied belonging. It can describe literal exile or metaphorical alienation: {The rebels became outcasts, unwelcome in their homeland}. The term often carries sympathy for those rejected.

To outclass is to be so clearly superior that comparison seems unfair: {The visiting team was completely outclassed}. The word implies not just winning but dominating—belonging to a different class entirely. Someone outclassed in a negotiation or debate has been thoroughly bested.

Outclassed means surpassed or defeated by someone clearly superior. The word implies not just losing but being in a different league entirely: {She was outclassed by opponents with years more experience}. Someone outclassed in a competition lacks the skill, resources, or talent to compete meaningfully. The feeling extends beyond contests—you can be outclassed at a fancy restaurant or a job interview where you're clearly out of your depth.

Outclassing is surpassing someone or something so thoroughly that they appear to be in a different class altogether. The word implies not just winning but demonstrating clear superiority: {The veteran outclassed every other competitor in the tournament}. You can outclass rivals in skill, quality, or sophistication.

Outcoached means beaten by superior coaching strategy. A team that loses because the opposing coach made better decisions—adjustments, play calls, personnel choices—was outcoached: {We had more talent, but we got outcoached}. The term appears almost exclusively in sports commentary, often as criticism or grudging admission after a loss.

An outcome is what results from an action, process, or situation—the end state after events have played out. The word emphasizes finality: {We're still waiting to learn the outcome of the election}. In statistics and probability, an outcome is any possible result of an experiment or event. Unlike consequence, outcome is neutral—it doesn't imply good or bad.

Outcomes are results or consequences—what happens after actions, decisions, or processes play out. The word appears constantly in contexts where results matter: {health outcomes}, {learning outcomes}, {election outcomes}. Unlike result, which is neutral, outcome often implies something was at stake: {The outcome of the surgery was uncertain}. In institutional settings, outcomes measure whether goals were achieved.

Outcries is the plural of outcry—loud expressions of protest, anger, or distress. Public outcries follow controversial decisions or revelations of wrongdoing: {The policy sparked outcries from civil liberties groups}. The word suggests collective vocal opposition rather than individual complaint.

An outcrop is rock that emerges visibly at the earth's surface, breaking through soil or vegetation: {granite outcrops dotted the hillside}. Geologists study outcrops to understand underlying rock formations. The word extends to anything that protrudes or emerges unexpectedly: {an outcrop of dissent within the party}. As a verb, to outcrop is to appear at the surface.

An outcropping is a portion of rock that protrudes through the soil or appears at the surface: {Granite outcroppings dotted the hillside}. The word extends to anything that emerges or juts out from its surroundings. Outcrop means the same thing and is more common in technical geological writing.

Outcrops are portions of rock that protrude through the soil surface, exposing what lies beneath. Geologists study outcrops to understand underground formations without digging. The word works as both noun and verb: {Granite outcrops dotted the hillside}; {Limestone outcrops along the riverbank}. Figuratively, anything hidden that surfaces can outcrop: {Old resentments outcropped during the reunion}.

An outcry is a loud shout or cry, especially one of distress, protest, or disapproval. More commonly, it refers to a strong public expression of anger or opposition: {The policy sparked an outcry from civil rights groups}. An outcry suggests widespread and vocal reaction, not just individual complaint.

Outdated means no longer current or useful, superseded by something newer: {outdated technology}, {outdated ideas about gender roles}. The word implies that time has passed something by—what once worked or was acceptable no longer is. {The guidebook was so outdated that half the restaurants had closed.}

To outdo is to surpass or exceed someone else's performance or achievement: {She always tries to outdo her older sister}. The word often implies competitive one-upmanship. To {outdo yourself} is to perform better than you ever have before, sometimes said sarcastically when someone makes an exceptional blunder.

Outdone is the past participle of outdo, meaning to surpass or exceed someone in performance or achievement. To be outdone is to have someone else do better than you: {She refused to be outdone by her rival}. The phrase {not to be outdone} introduces a competitive response: {Not to be outdone, he brought an even bigger gift}.

Outdoor describes things situated, done, or used outside rather than inside a building: {outdoor furniture}, {outdoor activities}, {the outdoor life}. It contrasts with indoor. An outdoors person enjoys nature and open-air pursuits. As a noun or adverb, the form is outdoors: {Let's eat outdoors}, {the great outdoors}.

Outdoors refers to the open air, outside of buildings or enclosed spaces: {The kids played outdoors all afternoon}. As a noun with the definite article, {the outdoors} suggests nature or wilderness as a realm of activity: {She loves the outdoors}. The adjective outdoor describes things suited for or occurring outside: {outdoor furniture}, {outdoor concert}.

An outdoorsman is a man who spends considerable time in wilderness or rural settings—hunting, fishing, camping, hiking. The term suggests competence and comfort in nature: {He was a true outdoorsman who could track deer and build shelter from nothing}. The gender-neutral outdoorsperson exists but sounds awkward; outdoors enthusiast serves better.

Outdoorsmen is the plural of outdoorsman—someone who spends significant time in nature pursuing activities like hunting, fishing, camping, or hiking. The term suggests competence and comfort in wilderness settings: {The lodge catered to serious outdoorsmen}. Though outdoorsman remains common, outdoorsperson and outdoors enthusiast avoid the gendered form.

Outdoorsy describes someone who enjoys outdoor activities—hiking, camping, fishing, and the like. The word is informal and often appears in personal ads or dating profiles: {I'm looking for someone outdoorsy who loves nature}. It can also describe places or things with a rugged, nature-oriented feel: {The cabin had an outdoorsy vibe}.

Outdraw means to draw faster or attract more than another. In Westerns, a gunfighter who outdraws an opponent pulls and fires first: {He outdrew the sheriff in the duel}. More commonly now, it describes drawing larger crowds or audiences: {The opening act somehow outdrew the headliner}. Past tense: outdrew.

Outed is the past tense of out, meaning to publicly reveal someone's secret—most commonly their homosexuality. A closeted person who is outed has their sexual orientation disclosed without consent: {He was outed by a tabloid reporter}. The term extends to exposing other concealed identities or affiliations: {She was outed as a former CIA operative}.

Outer describes what is farther from the center or interior: the outer {layer}, the outer {edge}, outer {space}. It contrasts with inner—the outer surface versus the inner core. Outer can suggest what's visible or peripheral rather than essential: {Her outer calm hid inner turmoil}. In compounds: {outerwear}, {outer limits}.

The outfield is the grassy area of a baseball or softball field beyond the infield dirt, where the left fielder, center fielder, and right fielder position themselves. By extension, outfield refers collectively to those three players: {The team's outfield is among the fastest in the league}. In cricket, outfield similarly denotes the area farthest from the wicket.

An outfielder is a baseball or softball player who fields in the outfield—the grassy area beyond the infield dirt. The three outfield positions are left field, center field, and right field. Outfielders track fly balls, back up throws, and relay the ball to the infield: {The outfielder made a diving catch at the warning track}.

Outfielders are the baseball or softball players positioned in the outfield—the grassy area beyond the infield. The three outfield positions are left field, center field, and right field. Outfielders catch fly balls, field hits that get past the infielders, and throw to bases to prevent runners from advancing: {The outfielders shifted toward right for the left-handed batter}.

An outfit is a set of clothes worn together, chosen to work as a unit: {I love that outfit}. The word extends to any coordinated set of equipment or supplies: {a camping outfit}, {a first-aid outfit}. An outfit can also be a group of people working together, especially a business or military unit: {She joined a small consulting outfit}. To outfit someone is to equip them with what they need: {We outfitted the expedition with supplies}.

Outfits are sets of clothes worn together, chosen to work as a unit: {She planned her outfits for the trip}. The word also refers to groups organized for a common purpose—a business, military unit, or crew: {He worked for a small publishing outfit in Chicago}. As a verb form, outfits means to equip or supply: {The store outfits hikers for backcountry expeditions}.

Outfitted means equipped or supplied with what's needed for a particular purpose. A ship is outfitted for a voyage; a climber is outfitted with gear; a kitchen is outfitted with appliances. {The expedition was fully outfitted before departure.} The word often implies completeness—everything necessary has been provided.

An outfitter supplies equipment and provisions for a particular activity, especially outdoor pursuits like hunting, fishing, camping, or expeditions. The term also applies to stores selling such gear: {We stopped at the outfitter before heading into the backcountry}. In some regions, outfitters provide guided wilderness trips with all necessary equipment and expertise.

Outfitters are businesses or people who supply equipment and gear for specific activities, especially outdoor pursuits like hunting, fishing, camping, or rafting: {We booked a guided trip through a local outfitters}. The term extends to clothing retailers, particularly those selling rugged or outdoor-styled apparel: {I got this jacket at an outfitters downtown}. An outfitter may also provide guides and expertise along with equipment.

Outfitting is the process of equipping or supplying what's needed for a particular purpose. A store outfitting a camping expedition provides gear and provisions. A tailor outfitting a wedding party supplies the formal wear. The word often implies comprehensive preparation: {The outfitting of the research vessel took three months}.

To outflank is to maneuver around the side of an opponent's position, originally a military term for getting troops past the enemy's flank to attack from an unexpected angle. The word extends to any situation where you gain advantage by going around rather than through: {She outflanked the committee by appealing directly to the board}. To be outflanked is to find yourself bypassed or outmaneuvered.

Outflanked means maneuvered around or bypassed, originally a military term for attacking an enemy's side or rear rather than meeting them head-on. The word now applies broadly to being strategically circumvented: {The company was outflanked by competitors who anticipated the market shift}. To be outflanked is to find your position undermined by someone who found a way around your defenses.

Outflanking is moving around the side of an enemy position to gain tactical advantage—attacking where defenses are weakest. The term comes from military strategy but applies broadly to any maneuver that bypasses opposition rather than confronting it directly: {The company outflanked its competitors by targeting an underserved market}. To outflank is to outsmart through positioning.

Outflanks means to get around the side of an opponent, originally a military maneuver to attack an enemy's flank or move past their defensive position. The word now appears mostly in figurative contexts—political, business, or strategic situations where someone gains advantage by circumventing rather than confronting directly: {The startup outflanked established competitors by targeting an overlooked market segment}.

To outfox is to defeat someone through superior cunning or cleverness—to outsmart them as a fox might evade hunters. The word implies winning not through force or resources but through wit: {She outfoxed her competitors by anticipating their moves}. {He thought he could outfox the IRS, but they caught up with him eventually}.

Outfoxed means outsmarted or outwitted, drawing on the fox's reputation for cunning. Someone who has been outfoxed was beaten by a cleverer opponent: {The defense attorney outfoxed the prosecution at every turn}. The word suggests not just losing but being made to look foolish by superior strategy.

Outfoxing is outsmarting or outwitting someone through cunning or cleverness. The fox is proverbially sly, so to outfox is to be even slyer: {She outfoxed the competition by filing her patent early}. The word suggests strategic thinking rather than brute force—winning by being craftier than your opponent.

Outgoing describes movement away from a point of origin: the outgoing {tide}, outgoing {mail}, the outgoing {president} whose term is ending. Applied to personality, outgoing means friendly, sociable, and comfortable initiating conversation with strangers—the opposite of shy or reserved: {She's outgoing enough to talk to anyone at a party}.

Outgrew is the past tense of outgrow. To outgrow something is to grow too large for it: {She outgrew her shoes every few months}. The word extends to interests, habits, or relationships one leaves behind through maturation: {He outgrew his childhood friends}, {I outgrew my fear of the dark}. To outgrow someone or something can also mean to surpass in growth: {The company outgrew its competitors}.

To outgrow something is to grow too large or mature for it. Children outgrow their clothes and shoes. People outgrow habits, friendships, or interests that no longer fit who they've become: {She outgrew her teenage insecurities}. One thing can outgrow another by growing faster: {The city's population outgrew its infrastructure}.

Outgrowing is growing beyond something's capacity or suitability. Children outgrow their clothes and shoes. You can outgrow a phase, a friendship, or a job: {She had outgrown the small-town life}. The word implies natural development rather than deliberate rejection—you don't leave something behind so much as become too large for it.

Outgrown is the past participle of outgrow. To outgrow something is to grow too large or mature for it. Children outgrow their clothes, their toys, their childhood fears. Adults outgrow relationships, habits, or beliefs that no longer fit: {She had outgrown her hometown}. One plant outgrows another by growing faster or larger.

Outgun means to surpass in firepower or weaponry: {The rebels were badly outgunned by government forces}. The meaning extends to any situation where one side has superior resources or capability: {We were outgunned in the bidding war}, {The small firm was outgunned by competitors with deeper pockets}. The word implies being at a serious disadvantage.

Outgunned means outmatched in firepower or resources. Literally, it describes having fewer or inferior weapons than an opponent: {The patrol was outgunned by insurgents with heavier artillery}. Figuratively, it extends to any situation where one side lacks the means to compete effectively: {Our legal team was completely outgunned by their army of corporate lawyers}.

Outgunning is having superior firepower or resources in a conflict or competition. The term comes from literal military contexts—one force outguns another when it has more or better weapons—but extends to any situation where one side overwhelms another through sheer advantage: {We were outgunned in the negotiations}, {The startup was outgunned by competitors with deeper pockets}.

An outhouse is a small structure housing a toilet, typically built over a pit and located away from the main dwelling. Before indoor plumbing became standard, outhouses were the primary form of sanitation in rural areas. The term now evokes rustic or primitive conditions: {The cabin had no running water—just an outhouse out back}.

Outhouses are outdoor toilets, typically small wooden structures built over a pit. Before indoor plumbing became standard, the outhouse was a fixture of rural life: {The old farmhouse still had an outhouse out back}. The word can also mean any outbuilding—a shed, barn, or storage structure separate from the main house—though the toilet sense now dominates.

An outie is a navel that protrudes slightly rather than forming an inward depression—the opposite of an innie. The distinction is a minor anatomical variation with no medical significance, though children often compare: {Are you an innie or an outie?}

An outing is a short trip or excursion, typically for pleasure: {a family outing to the beach}, {a company outing}. The word also means the public exposure of someone's private identity, especially revealing that someone is gay without their consent: {The magazine was criticized for the outing of several politicians}. To out someone is to expose them this way.

Outings is the plural of outing—a short trip or excursion, typically for pleasure: {family outings to the beach}, {a company outing}. An outing can also mean publicly revealing someone's secret, especially their sexual orientation without consent: {The journalist faced criticism for the outing of several politicians}.

An outlander is someone from elsewhere—a foreigner, stranger, or person from a different region. The word carries a slight sense of otherness or not belonging: {The villagers distrusted outlanders}. It appears in fantasy settings where isolated communities view outsiders with suspicion. Less common than foreigner or outsider in everyday speech.

Outlandish describes something strikingly bizarre, unconventional, or far removed from the ordinary. The word suggests excess that goes beyond merely unusual: {outlandish costumes}, {outlandish claims}, {outlandish behavior}. What strikes one person as outlandish may simply be unfamiliar—the word often reveals the speaker's sense of normalcy as much as the thing being described.

Remote or frontier regions far from centers of population or power. The outlands are peripheral territories—wild, sparsely settled, or culturally distinct from the heartland: {Traders ventured into the outlands seeking furs}. The word carries connotations of roughness or otherness, places beyond the reach of civilization's comforts and conventions.

To outlast is to endure longer than something else—to remain when others have faded, broken, or given up. {Their marriage outlasted all predictions}. {These boots will outlast anything else in your closet}. The word implies survival through comparison: you outlast competitors, storms, or difficult circumstances by simply persisting beyond them.

An outlaw is someone who operates outside the law—originally a person stripped of legal protection who could be killed without consequence, now simply a criminal or fugitive. The word carries romantic overtones from Western mythology: outlaws like Jesse James became folk heroes. As a verb, to outlaw something is to ban it: {The treaty outlawed chemical weapons}. As an adjective, outlaw describes things operating illegally or unconventionally: an {outlaw country} singer, an {outlaw motorcycle gang}.

Outlawed means banned or prohibited by law or authority. An outlawed {substance} is illegal to possess or sell. Outlawed {practices} have been officially forbidden. Historically, to be outlawed was to be declared outside the protection of the law—an outlaw could be killed or robbed without legal consequence. Now the term usually just means forbidden: {The treaty outlawed chemical weapons}.

Outlawing is the act of making something illegal or prohibited by law. Governments outlaw substances, practices, or organizations deemed harmful: {The treaty outlawed chemical weapons}. The word can also mean banishing or excluding: {outlawing dissent from public discourse}. The present participle of outlaw, it functions as both verb form and gerund.

Outlaws are people who live outside the law—originally those denied legal protection, now typically criminals or fugitives: {a band of outlaws terrorizing the frontier}. The word evokes romanticized rebels like Robin Hood or Wild West bandits. To outlaw something is to make it illegal: {The city outlawed smoking in parks}. An outlawed practice is banned or prohibited.

An outlet is an opening through which something can escape or be released: {an outlet for water drainage}, {an outlet for creative energy}. In American English, an electrical outlet is a wall socket where you plug things in. An outlet also means a store selling goods at reduced prices, typically from a manufacturer: {outlet mall}, {factory outlet}. A media outlet is a channel for news or information: {The story was picked up by several news outlets}.

Outlets are places where something exits or is released. An electrical outlet provides access to power. A retail outlet sells goods, often at reduced prices: {factory outlet}, {outlet mall}. A media outlet distributes news or entertainment. Figuratively, an outlet is a means of expression or release: {Exercise is my outlet for stress}. Rivers have outlets where they empty into larger bodies of water.

An outlier is something that lies outside the main body or group. In statistics, it's a data point that falls far from the cluster of other values: {The $2 million home was an outlier in a neighborhood of modest houses}. More broadly, an outlier is anyone or anything markedly different from the norm—an exceptional case, an anomaly, a person who doesn't fit the pattern: {She was an outlier among her peers, the only one who hadn't gone to college}.

Outliers are data points or cases that fall far outside the normal range. In statistics, an outlier is a value so distant from others in a dataset that it may skew results or suggest measurement error. The term extends to people or things that don't fit patterns: {She was an outlier among her conservative colleagues}. Malcolm Gladwell's book popularized the word for exceptional achievers whose success defies typical explanations.

An outline is the line marking the outer edge or boundary of something: {the outline of the mountains against the sky}. It also means a general plan or summary showing main points without detail: {an outline of the chapter}, {a rough outline of our strategy}. To outline is to draw such a boundary or to describe something in general terms: {She outlined the proposal in broad strokes}.

Outlined means shown or described in general terms without fine detail. An outlined {plan} presents main points but not specifics. To outline something is to sketch its shape or structure: {She outlined the proposal in three minutes}. Outlined also describes something with its edges marked or visible: {figures outlined against the sky}, {lips outlined in red}.

Outlines are lines marking the outer edges of something, showing its shape without interior detail: {She drew the outlines of the mountains against the sky}. An outline is also a summary or plan showing main points without elaboration: {an outline of the proposal}, {a course outline}. To outline is to sketch boundaries or summarize key elements: {He outlined his strategy for the board}.

Outlining is sketching the main features or boundaries of something. You outline a plan before writing it in detail, or outline a shape before filling it in. {She spent an hour outlining the proposal}. An outlining tool helps organize ideas hierarchically. The word captures the act of drawing edges without filling in substance—establishing structure first.

To outlive someone or something is to live longer than they do: {She outlived her husband by twenty years}. The word extends beyond biological life—ideas, institutions, and objects can outlive their usefulness or relevance: {The policy has outlived its purpose}. To outlive something is often to survive it: {He outlived three heart attacks}.

Outlived is the past tense of outlive, meaning to live longer than someone or something else. A widow has outlived her husband. The word extends to things that persist beyond their expected duration: {The policy outlived its usefulness}. To outlive something is often to survive it: {She outlived two wars and three recessions}.

Outlives means to live longer than someone or something else. A person may outlive a spouse, a pet, or their own expectations. Things outlive their usefulness when they remain after they're no longer needed: {The policy has outlived its purpose}. To outlive a reputation or scandal is to survive long enough that it fades from memory.

Outlook is a view of what lies ahead—either literally or figuratively. A room with a pleasant outlook overlooks something worth seeing. More often, outlook means a perspective on the future: {The economic outlook remains uncertain}, {She has a positive outlook on life}. Someone's outlook is also their general attitude or way of seeing things: {His outlook changed after the accident}. (Capitalized Outlook is Microsoft's email software.)
clues: The lens through which you see life

definition: Outlooks are perspectives or points of view—the mental positions from which people see the world: {Their political outlooks couldn't be more different}. An outlook can also be a forecast or expectation about the future: {The economic outlook remains uncertain}. Less commonly, an outlook is a physical vantage point offering a view.

To outmaneuver is to gain advantage over an opponent through superior strategy or positioning. The word comes from military contexts—troops outmaneuvering enemy forces—but applies broadly to any competitive situation: {She outmaneuvered her rivals for the promotion}, {The smaller company outmaneuvered the industry giant}. Also spelled outmanoeuvre in British English.

Outmaneuvered means defeated through superior strategy or tactics. The word comes from military contexts—armies outmaneuver enemies by positioning troops more cleverly—but applies broadly to any competitive situation: {She outmaneuvered her rivals for the promotion}, {The defense attorney outmaneuvered the prosecution at every turn}. To be outmaneuvered is to lose not through lack of resources but through being outsmarted.

Outmanned means outnumbered in personnel or manpower. A military unit outmanned by the enemy faces superior numbers. The term extends beyond combat to any situation where one side lacks sufficient people: {We were outmanned and outgunned from the start}. Often paired with similar compounds like outgunned or outmatched to emphasize disadvantage.

To outmanoeuver is to gain advantage over an opponent through superior strategy or positioning. The word comes from military contexts—troops outmaneuvering enemy forces—but applies broadly to any competitive situation: {She outmaneuvered her rivals for the promotion}, {The smaller company outmaneuvered the industry giant}. The spelling outmaneuver is American; outmanoeuver is British.

To outmanoeuvre is to gain advantage over an opponent through superior tactics or clever positioning. The word comes from military contexts—troops outmanoeuvring enemy forces—but applies broadly to any competitive situation: {She outmanoeuvred her rivals for the promotion}, {The smaller company outmanoeuvred the industry giants}. Also spelled outmaneuver.

Outmanoeuvred is the British spelling of outmaneuvered, the past tense of outmanoeuvre. To outmanoeuvre someone is to gain an advantage over them through clever or skillful tactics, whether in physical movement, strategy, or negotiation. {The smaller fleet outmanoeuvred the enemy in the narrow strait.} {She outmanoeuvred her rivals by securing key endorsements early.} The word implies not just defeating an opponent but doing so through superior positioning or cunning rather than brute force.

To outmatch is to surpass or defeat by being superior: {The smaller army was outmatched in every engagement}. The word emphasizes the gap between competitors—one side simply has more skill, strength, or resources than the other can counter: {Her experience outmatched his enthusiasm}.

Outmatched means surpassed or defeated by a superior opponent or force. Someone outmatched faces competition they cannot overcome: {The young boxer was clearly outmatched by the veteran champion}. The word implies an imbalance—not just losing, but being overmatched from the start: {Outgunned and outmatched, the rebels retreated}.

To outmuscle is to overpower through superior physical strength or force. Athletes outmuscle opponents for position; corporations outmuscle smaller competitors through sheer resources. {He outmuscled the defender to grab the rebound.} The word implies prevailing not through skill or strategy but through raw power.

Outmuscled means overpowered through superior physical strength or force. Athletes get outmuscled when opponents use size and power to gain advantage: {He was outmuscled under the basket}. The term extends to competitive situations where one party dominates through sheer resources: {The startup was outmuscled by larger rivals}.

To outnumber is to exceed in quantity: {The protesters outnumbered the police three to one}. The word typically appears in contexts of competition or conflict, where numerical advantage matters: {We were badly outnumbered but held our ground}.

Outnumbered describes being faced with superior numbers—having fewer people or forces than the opposing side. A small army can be outnumbered by a larger one; a lone dissenter may feel outnumbered in a room full of agreement. {We were outnumbered three to one}. The word often implies disadvantage but can also set up narratives of heroic resistance against the odds.

To outpace is to move faster than something else, leaving it behind: {The runner outpaced the field in the final stretch}. More often figurative—growth, change, or development that exceeds another rate: {Demand has outpaced supply}. {Technology outpaces our ability to regulate it}. The word implies not just being ahead but actively pulling away.

To outperform is to perform better than someone or something else—a competitor, an expectation, or a benchmark: {The fund has consistently outperformed the market}. The word appears frequently in business and finance contexts, where performance is measured and compared: {Small-cap stocks outperformed large-cap this quarter}.

To outplay is to perform better than an opponent in a game or contest: {We were completely outplayed in the second half}. The word implies superiority in skill or execution rather than mere luck. It appears most often in sports commentary but extends to any competitive situation: {The defense outplayed the prosecution at every turn}.

Outplayed means defeated through superior skill or strategy. In sports and games, to outplay an opponent is to perform better than them throughout the contest: {We were completely outplayed in the second half}. The term extends to any competitive situation where one side demonstrates clear dominance: {The defense outplayed the prosecution at every turn}.

An outpost is a military position stationed at a distance from the main force, typically for observation or defense: {a remote outpost near the border}. The term extends to any distant branch or settlement far from a center of activity: {a trading outpost}, {an outpost of civilization in the wilderness}. Figuratively, anything representing a presence in unfamiliar territory: {The café was an outpost of hipster culture in the suburbs}.

Outposts are remote stations or settlements at a distance from the main body they serve. A military outpost monitors enemy activity far from headquarters. Frontier outposts marked the edge of settled territory. The word extends to any isolated position: {The cafe was an outpost of civilization in the wilderness}. An outpost of a larger organization operates in distant or unfamiliar territory.

An outpouring is a large flow of something released all at once. The word typically describes emotions, expressions, or responses that come forth abundantly: {an outpouring of grief}, {an outpouring of support from the community}. Less commonly, it refers to literal flowing: {the outpouring of lava from the volcano}.

Output is what comes out of a process, system, or effort—the product or result. A factory's output is what it produces; a writer's output is their body of work. In computing, output is data sent from a program or device: {The printer output was garbled}. As a verb, to output is to produce or generate: {The solar panel outputs 300 watts}. Output contrasts with input.

Outrage is intense anger or indignation provoked by something perceived as unjust, offensive, or morally wrong: {The verdict sparked public outrage}. As a verb, to outrage is to provoke such feelings: {His comments outraged the community}. An outrage is also the act itself—a shocking offense or violation: {The massacre was an outrage against humanity}. Outrageous describes things that provoke outrage, though it often softens to mean merely extreme or absurd: {outrageous prices}, {an outrageous outfit}.

Outraged means feeling or expressing intense anger, shock, or indignation—especially at something perceived as unjust or offensive. The word carries moral weight: you're outraged by cruelty, corruption, or violation of standards, not by minor annoyances. {Voters were outraged by the scandal}. {She gave him an outraged look when he suggested she'd lied}.

Outrageous describes something that exceeds acceptable bounds—shocking, offensive, or extreme beyond what's reasonable. An outrageous {insult} crosses lines of decency. Outrageous {prices} are exorbitantly high. The word can also express admiration for bold excess: {Her outfit was absolutely outrageous}. What's outrageous provokes outrage, or at least raised eyebrows.

Outrageously means to an extreme or shocking degree. It can describe something offensively excessive: {outrageously rude behavior}. But it often carries admiration for boldness or extravagance: {outrageously talented}, {outrageously expensive shoes}. The word amplifies whatever follows—whether the excess is condemned or celebrated depends on context.

Outrages are acts of extreme offense, violence, or violation—things that shock the conscience or transgress moral bounds: {The report documented outrages committed against civilians}. As a verb, outrages means to deeply offend or enrage: {The verdict outrages many who followed the trial}. Something outrageous provokes outrage.

To outrank someone is to hold a higher rank or position than they do: {A colonel outranks a major}. The word applies most naturally to military and organizational hierarchies, but extends to any context where things can be ordered by importance or priority: {Safety concerns outrank convenience}.

Outreach is the effort to extend services or assistance beyond usual boundaries, especially to underserved populations: {community outreach}, {voter outreach}. Organizations conduct outreach to connect with people who might not otherwise be reached: {The clinic's outreach program provides care to homeless residents}. As a verb, outreach means to surpass in reaching: {Her influence outreached his}.

An outrider is a person who rides ahead of or alongside a vehicle, group, or procession—historically on horseback, now often on motorcycle. Outriders clear the path, provide security, or announce arrivals: {Police outriders escorted the motorcade through the city}. The term extends figuratively to anyone who scouts ahead or operates at the edges of a group or movement.

An outrigger is a projecting frame or float attached to the side of a boat to prevent capsizing. Canoes with outriggers are traditional in Pacific Island cultures. The term extends to any stabilizing projection: {outrigger scaffolding}, or the brackets that hold fishing rods away from a boat's hull. In aircraft, outriggers are supporting struts extending from the fuselage.

Outriggers are projecting structures that extend from a main body to provide stability or support. On canoes and boats, an outrigger is a float attached by poles parallel to the hull, preventing capsizing—common in Pacific Island watercraft. On cranes and fire trucks, outriggers are extendable legs that brace the vehicle during operation. The term extends to any stabilizing projection: {The scaffolding's outriggers kept it from tipping}.

Outright means completely, without qualification or reservation. An outright {lie} is unambiguous—no partial truth, no shading. An outright {ban} allows no exceptions. To {win outright} is to win decisively, not on a technicality. To {buy something outright} is to pay the full amount at once rather than in installments. The word can also mean immediately or instantly: {The crash killed him outright}.

An outro is the closing section of a song, broadcast, or video—the opposite of an intro. In music, the outro often features a fade-out or a final instrumental passage that signals the end. In podcasts and YouTube videos, the outro typically includes closing remarks, credits, or calls to action like subscribing. {The outro was just the chorus repeating until it faded out.}

Outros is the plural of outro, the closing section of a piece of music, a podcast, or a video—the opposite of an intro. An outro typically wraps things up with credits, farewell remarks, or a musical fade: {The outros on his videos always include a call to subscribe}. {Skip the outros if you're binge-watching}.

To outrun is to run faster or farther than someone or something else: {She easily outran her pursuers}. The meaning extends beyond literal running to any kind of escape or exceeding: {The company's growth outran its infrastructure}. Demand can outrun supply; expenses can outrun income. If something outruns your ability to handle it, it has surpassed your capacity.

Outs is primarily a baseball term for the number of times batters or runners have been retired: {two outs in the ninth inning}. More broadly, outs are ways of escaping a situation: {He's looking for outs on this contract}. The phrase {on the outs} means estranged or in disfavor: {She's been on the outs with her family since the argument}.

To outscore is to score more points than an opponent: {The Warriors outscored the Lakers by twenty in the fourth quarter}. The word belongs to sports commentary and statistics, describing which side accumulated more during a game or period of play.

Outset is the beginning or start of something, typically a process, period, or undertaking. It almost always appears with {at the} or {from the}: {At the outset, no one expected the project to succeed}. {From the outset, she made her intentions clear}. The word emphasizes the initial moment when something is set in motion.

To outshine is to shine brighter than something else, or more commonly, to surpass in excellence or achievement: {Her performance outshone everyone else's}. The word implies comparison—you don't outshine in isolation, but against others. {The younger sister consistently outshone her siblings academically.}

Outshines means to shine more brightly than something else, or figuratively, to surpass in excellence or achievement: {Her performance outshined everyone else's}. The past tense appears as both outshined and outshone. {The moon outshines the stars tonight.}

Outshone is the past tense and past participle of outshine—to shine more brightly than something else, or to surpass in excellence or achievement. {Her performance outshone everyone else's}. {The moon outshone the stars that night}. The word implies comparison: something good was eclipsed by something better.

Outside gained use as a preposition after it was already established as a noun, adjective, and adverb; perhaps because of that, it is often followed by of with no change in meaning. Its core sense is movement to or position on the outer side of something. From this it has acquired other meanings, such as beyond the scope of: Those people operate outside the law.

An outsider is someone who doesn't belong to a particular group—whether by circumstance, choice, or exclusion. The term can be neutral {(an outsider's perspective on the dispute)} or carry connotations of rejection {(She always felt like an outsider at school)}. In competitions, an outsider is a contestant considered unlikely to win: {The outsider came from behind to take the race}.

Outsiders are people who don't belong to a particular group, organization, or community. The term implies exclusion—whether by choice or circumstance: {As outsiders, we weren't privy to their internal disputes}. Someone can be an outsider to a profession, a social circle, or an entire culture. The word often carries connotations of fresh perspective or alienation, depending on context: {The company brought in outsiders to shake things up}.

Outsized means unusually large or disproportionately big: {an outsized influence on policy}, {outsized expectations}. The word suggests something beyond normal scale, often with a hint of excess or imbalance. An outsized personality dominates a room; outsized profits exceed what's typical. Also spelled outsize, especially as an attributive adjective: {outsize ambitions}.

Outskirts refers to the outer edges or peripheral areas of a town, city, or other defined region—the parts farthest from the center. The word appears almost exclusively in the plural and typically follows "on the": {They bought a house on the outskirts of town}. Outskirts suggests a transitional zone where urban development thins out, often carrying connotations of being removed from the action or main activity of a place.

To outsmart someone is to defeat them through cleverness rather than force—finding a way around their defenses or anticipating their moves: {She outsmarted the security system}. The word implies a contest of wits where cunning beats strength or resources: {The smaller company outsmarted its competitors by targeting niche markets}.

Outsmarted is the past tense of outsmart—to defeat someone by being cleverer than they are. The word implies winning through superior thinking rather than force or luck: {She outsmarted the con artist at his own game}. Being outsmarted often carries a sting of humiliation, suggesting you were bested by someone who saw further ahead than you did.

Outsmarting is defeating someone through superior cleverness or cunning rather than force. The word implies a contest of wits where one party anticipates and outmaneuvers the other: {She kept outsmarting the detectives who were tracking her}. You can outsmart opponents, systems, or even yourself: {He thought he was outsmarting the tax code}.

Outsmarts means to defeat someone by being cleverer than they are. The word suggests tactical thinking or cunning rather than brute force: {The detective outsmarted the criminal at every turn}. It implies a contest of wits where one party gains advantage through superior intelligence or strategy.

Outsource means to contract work to an external provider rather than handling it internally. A company might outsource its customer service to a call center or outsource manufacturing to overseas factories. The practice became widespread as businesses sought to reduce costs: {We outsource our IT support to a firm in India}. The word often carries connotations of job displacement or declining quality.

Outsourced describes work or services contracted to an external company rather than handled internally. A business might have outsourced its customer service to a call center abroad, or outsourced payroll to a specialist firm. The term often carries connotations of cost-cutting and, when jobs move overseas, displaced workers: {My position was outsourced to India}.

Outsourcing is the practice of hiring outside contractors or foreign companies to perform work that could be done internally. Businesses outsource to reduce costs, access specialized skills, or focus on core operations: {The company outsourced its customer service to a call center in the Philippines}. The term often carries negative connotations when jobs move overseas, becoming shorthand for domestic job loss.

Outspoken describes someone who expresses opinions freely and directly, even when those opinions might be unwelcome or controversial: {She's been outspoken about corruption in the department}. The word implies boldness rather than tactlessness—an outspoken critic speaks up where others stay silent. {He's outspoken but fair.}

Outstanding means exceptionally good or remarkable: {an outstanding performance}, {outstanding academic achievement}. It also means not yet resolved or paid: {outstanding debts}, {outstanding warrants}. These senses diverge—one praises excellence, the other notes incompleteness. Context usually makes clear which is meant: {She received an outstanding evaluation} versus {The balance outstanding is $500}.

An outtake is footage or recorded material that doesn't make it into the final version of a film, television show, or album. Outtakes may result from mistakes, technical problems, or creative decisions. Collections of outtakes—especially bloopers showing actors breaking character or flubbing lines—are often released as bonus material: {The DVD includes twenty minutes of outtakes}.

Outtakes are portions of a recording—film, video, or audio—that don't make it into the final version. They're often mistakes, flubbed lines, or technical failures: {The DVD includes a reel of outtakes}. Outtakes from comedies frequently show actors breaking character or laughing, released as bonus content. The word sometimes extends metaphorically to any discarded material from a creative project.

Outvoted means defeated by receiving fewer votes than the opposing side. Someone outvoted in a committee or election has lost the decision to the majority: {She was outvoted three to one on the proposal}. The word emphasizes being on the losing side of a formal count rather than simply disagreeing.

Outward means directed toward the outside or external surface. An outward {journey} moves away from a starting point. Outward {appearances} are what others can observe, as opposed to inner reality: {He maintained an outward calm despite his panic}. The adverb form—outward or outwards—describes motion away from a center: {The ripples spread outward}.

To outweigh something is to exceed it in weight, value, or importance. The word appears most often in figurative comparisons: {The benefits outweigh the risks}. {Her experience outweighs her lack of formal credentials}. When making decisions, people weigh factors against each other—what outweighs tips the balance.

Outweighs means to exceed in importance, value, or influence. When benefits outweigh costs, the advantages matter more than the disadvantages: {The risks outweigh the potential rewards}. The metaphor comes from scales—one side literally weighing more than the other. Can also apply to physical weight: {The luggage outweighs the passenger}.

To outwit someone is to defeat them through cleverness rather than force—to be smarter or more cunning than an opponent. The word implies a contest of minds where quick thinking prevails: {The fox outwitted the hounds}. You can outwit a rival, a security system, or your own bad habits.

Outwits means defeats or gets the better of someone through cleverness rather than force. The word implies a contest of minds where quick thinking or cunning prevails: {The detective finally outwits the serial killer}. A smaller animal outwits a predator by using its environment; a negotiator outwits an opponent by anticipating their moves.

Outwitted is the past tense of outwit, meaning to defeat someone through cleverness or cunning rather than force. The word implies a contest of minds where superior strategy prevails: {She outwitted the detective by planting false evidence}. To be outwitted often carries a note of humiliation—you weren't just beaten, you were outsmarted.

Outwitting is defeating someone through cleverness rather than force—staying one step ahead, anticipating their moves, exploiting their weaknesses. The word implies a contest of minds where cunning prevails: {The fox kept outwitting the hounds}. You can outwit an opponent, a system, or even fate itself.

Outwork means to work harder or more productively than someone else: {She consistently outworks her competitors}. The emphasis is on effort and output rather than cleverness or talent. As a noun, an outwork is a defensive fortification beyond the main walls of a castle or fort—a meaning now mostly historical.

Ouzo is a Greek anise-flavored liquor, clear in the bottle but turning milky white when water or ice is added. It is traditionally served as an aperitif, often alongside small dishes called meze. The distinctive licorice taste comes from anise seed, though other herbs and spices may be included. {We ordered ouzo and olives at the taverna.}

Oval describes a shape that is elongated and rounded, like an egg or an ellipse—a circle stretched along one axis. An oval {face}, an oval {mirror}, an oval {track}. As a noun, it names this shape or something having it: {Draw an oval}. The Oval Office is the U.S. president's formal workspace in the White House, often used as shorthand for the presidency itself. (Capitalized Oval typically appears in proper names like Oval Office.)
clues: A circle pulled at both ends

definition: Ovals are closed curves resembling elongated circles—egg-shaped or elliptical forms. The word works as both noun and adjective: an oval {track}, an oval {mirror}, the {Oval Office}. Unlike true ellipses, ovals need not be mathematically precise; any rounded oblong shape qualifies: {She arranged the stones in an oval}.

Ovaries are the pair of reproductive organs in females that produce eggs and hormones. In humans and other mammals, the ovaries release eggs during ovulation and secrete estrogen and progesterone. In flowering plants, the ovary is the part of the pistil containing seeds. {Her ovaries showed multiple follicles on the ultrasound.}

An ovary is a female reproductive organ that produces eggs. In humans and other mammals, ovaries also secrete hormones like estrogen and progesterone. In flowering plants, the ovary is the part of the pistil that contains ovules and develops into fruit after fertilization.

An ovation is enthusiastic applause and cheering from an audience. A standing ovation—when the audience rises to its feet—signals exceptional appreciation: {The performance received a standing ovation}. The word sometimes appears in phrases like {give someone an ovation}, but standing ovation dominates modern usage.

Ovations is the plural of ovation, an enthusiastic show of approval—especially prolonged applause from an audience. A {standing ovation} is the most emphatic form, with the audience rising to their feet. The word sometimes appears in less literal contexts: {The proposal received ovations from supporters across the country}.
clues: What standing audiences give to stars

definition: An oven is an enclosed chamber for heating, baking, or drying. Kitchen ovens cook food; industrial ovens cure materials or fire ceramics. A {Dutch oven} is a heavy pot with a lid. Something {oven-ready} requires no preparation before cooking. A room that's unbearably hot is {like an oven}.

Ovens is the plural of oven—an enclosed chamber for heating, baking, or drying. Kitchen ovens cook food; industrial ovens cure materials or fire ceramics. {The bakery runs six ovens through the night.} Figuratively, a place described as an oven is unbearably hot: {This apartment is an oven in summer.}

As prepositions go, over is busier than most due to its broad range of meanings. When space is the subject, over can mean across or above, or both: a picture over the fireplace, carpets over the floors. In relation to time, over conveys duration: We got to know each other over a period of weeks. Figurative meanings of over also vary widely: We talked about it over dinner. I would take green over pink. They paid over a million dollars for their house. Over can also function as an adverb and an adjective, again with myriad meanings.

To overachieve is to perform beyond expectations, especially academically or professionally. The word often carries a faint note of criticism—implying excessive striving or anxiety about success: {She's such an overachiever}. But it can also simply mean exceeding goals: {The sales team overachieved by fifteen percent this quarter}.

An overachiever is someone who accomplishes more than expected, often through exceptional effort or ambition. The term can be admiring—{She's a real overachiever, graduated top of her class while working two jobs}—but frequently carries a hint of criticism, suggesting someone driven by anxiety or unhealthy perfectionism rather than genuine passion: {He's such an overachiever, always staying late to impress the boss}.

Overachievers are people who accomplish more than expected, often exceeding standards that would satisfy most others. The term carries mixed connotations: it can express admiration for exceptional performance or suggest someone who works excessively hard, possibly at the expense of balance or wellbeing. {The overachievers in class always asked for extra credit.} In competitive environments like schools and workplaces, overachievers may be celebrated or resented depending on how their success affects others.

Overachieving means performing beyond what's expected or required—exceeding standards rather than merely meeting them. The term often carries a hint of criticism, suggesting excessive effort or striving: {She's such an overachiever}. Someone called an overachiever may be seen as anxious about success or unable to relax. The word can also describe genuine excellence: {The team has been overachieving all season}.

To overact is to perform with excessive emotion or exaggerated gestures, beyond what the role or situation calls for. The term applies mostly to theatrical or film performances: {The villain overacted so badly the audience laughed}. It can extend to everyday behavior that seems theatrical or melodramatic: {She overacted her disappointment to make us feel guilty}.

Overacting is exaggerated or excessive performance, especially by an actor who delivers emotions too broadly or dramatically for the material. The term implies a failure of restraint—ham acting that draws attention to itself rather than serving the story: {The villain's overacting turned the thriller into unintentional comedy}. Beyond theater and film, overacting describes any behavior that seems theatrically excessive: {His overacting at the meeting fooled no one}.

Overall describes something considered as a whole, taking everything into account: {The overall effect was stunning}, {What's your overall impression?} As an adverb, it means generally or in total: {Overall, I think it went well}. Overalls are loose-fitting work garments with a bib and shoulder straps, worn over other clothes for protection.

Overalls are loose-fitting trousers with a bib front held up by shoulder straps, typically worn as protective workwear over regular clothes. In American usage, overalls are the bib-and-strap garment farmers and mechanics wear: {He wiped his hands on his overalls}. In British usage, overalls often means any protective outer garment, including what Americans call a jumpsuit or coveralls.

To overanalyse is to examine something so thoroughly that the analysis becomes counterproductive—finding problems that don't exist, missing the obvious while hunting for the subtle, or paralyzing yourself with considerations. {Stop overanalysing every text message}. {We overanalysed the data until we lost sight of the main finding}. The word implies that analysis, normally valuable, has passed the point of usefulness. Also spelled overanalyze.

To overanalyze is to examine something so thoroughly that you miss the point or create problems that weren't there. Someone who overanalyzes a casual remark reads too much into it. Someone who overanalyzes a decision considers so many factors they can't act: {Stop overanalyzing and just pick a restaurant}. The word implies that analysis, usually valuable, has become counterproductive.

Overanalyzing is thinking about something more than necessary or productive, often to the point of paralysis or anxiety. Where ordinary analysis seeks clarity, overanalyzing finds new complications: {Stop overanalyzing the text message—just reply}. The habit tends toward second-guessing decisions already made or reading meaning into insignificant details.

Overarching describes something that encompasses or spans everything else within a category—an overarching {theme}, an overarching {goal}, an overarching {principle}. The image is of an arch that curves over and contains whatever lies beneath it. The word appears almost exclusively in abstract contexts: {The overarching concern was public safety}.

Overbearing describes someone who dominates others through force of personality—pushy, arrogant, and unwilling to consider other viewpoints. An overbearing {boss} micromanages everything. An overbearing {parent} controls every aspect of a child's life. The word suggests someone whose presence feels oppressive, leaving little room for others to breathe or assert themselves.

Overbid means to bid more than something is worth or more than is necessary to win. At an auction, you might overbid on a painting if you get caught up in the excitement and pay far beyond its appraised value. In card games like bridge, to overbid is to bid higher than your hand justifies. The noun overbid refers to such an excessive bid. {The housing market crashed after years of overbidding drove prices to unsustainable levels.}

An overbite is a dental condition where the upper front teeth extend too far over the lower front teeth when the jaw is closed. Some overlap is normal, but a pronounced overbite may affect appearance or cause problems with chewing or speech. Orthodontists correct overbites with braces or other treatments: {She wore braces for two years to fix her overbite}.

Overblown means exaggerated or inflated beyond what's warranted. An overblown {reaction} is disproportionate to its cause. Overblown {rhetoric} uses more force than the subject deserves. {The controversy was overblown}. The word can also describe flowers past their prime, petals blown fully open and beginning to fade.
clues: Given far more weight than deserved

definition: Overboard means over the side of a boat or ship into the water: {The storm swept three sailors overboard}. Figuratively, to go overboard is to be excessive or extreme—to do too much of something: {She went overboard with the decorations}. To throw something overboard is to abandon or discard it: {They threw caution overboard}.

To overbook is to accept more reservations than available capacity—seats on a flight, rooms in a hotel, tables at a restaurant. Airlines routinely overbook, betting that some passengers won't show up: {The flight was overbooked, so they offered vouchers for volunteers to take a later one}. The practice maximizes revenue but risks stranding customers when everyone appears.

Overbooked describes having accepted more reservations or commitments than can actually be accommodated. Airlines routinely overbook flights, betting that some passengers won't show: {We got bumped because the flight was overbooked}. The term extends to any schedule packed beyond capacity: {I'm completely overbooked this week}.

Overbooking is the practice of accepting more reservations than available capacity, common among airlines and hotels that anticipate some no-shows. When everyone actually appears, overbooking becomes a problem: {The flight was delayed while they sorted out the overbooking situation}. The verb overbook works the same way: {They overbooked the hotel by twelve rooms}.

Overcame is the past tense of overcome. To overcome something is to succeed in dealing with or controlling it, especially a problem, obstacle, or negative feeling. {She overcame her fear of public speaking.} {The team overcame a ten-point deficit to win.} It can also mean to overpower or overwhelm someone, as when a person is overcome by emotion or fumes.

Overcast describes a sky completely covered by clouds, with no blue visible: {The day was gray and overcast}. The word also applies to a type of stitching that wraps thread over a fabric edge to prevent fraying. As a verb in sewing, to overcast is to sew such stitches.

To overcharge is to charge too much money for something: {The mechanic overcharged me by fifty dollars}. It can also mean to fill something beyond capacity—overcharging a battery damages it by forcing in more electricity than it can safely hold. As a noun, an overcharge is an excessive charge or the amount by which something exceeds the proper price.

Overcharged describes being charged too much money for something: {They overcharged me by twenty dollars}. A battery that's overcharged has received more electrical current than it should. Figuratively, something overcharged is excessively loaded or intense—an overcharged {atmosphere}, overcharged {rhetoric}. The word suggests excess beyond what's appropriate or safe.

Overcharging is charging too much for something—more than the fair price or more than was agreed upon: {The mechanic was overcharging for basic repairs}. It also means putting too much electrical charge into a battery, which can damage it or reduce its lifespan. Both senses involve excess beyond what's appropriate or safe.

To overclock is to run a computer component—usually a processor or graphics card—faster than its factory-rated speed. Enthusiasts overclock to squeeze extra performance from hardware, accepting trade-offs in heat, power consumption, and stability: {I overclocked my GPU to get better frame rates}. The practice voids some warranties and risks damage if pushed too far.

Overclocked describes computer hardware—typically a processor or graphics card—running faster than its manufacturer-rated speed. Enthusiasts overclock components to squeeze out extra performance, though this generates more heat and can reduce lifespan or cause instability. {My CPU is overclocked to 5 GHz}. Figuratively, overclocked can describe anything pushed beyond normal capacity: {I've been overclocked all week and need a break}.

Overclocking is running a computer component—typically a processor or graphics card—faster than its factory-rated speed. Enthusiasts overclock to extract more performance, though it generates extra heat and may void warranties or reduce hardware lifespan. {I overclocked my CPU to squeeze out a few more frames per second.}

Overcoached describes athletes or performers who have received so much instruction that their natural ability is stifled. The term suggests that coaching has become counterproductive—too many drills, too much analysis, too many corrections: {The quarterback looked overcoached, hesitating on throws he used to make instinctively}. The criticism implies that spontaneity and instinct have been trained out of someone.

Overcoaching is giving too much instruction or guidance, particularly in sports or performance contexts, to the point where it becomes counterproductive. A player who is overcoached may lose confidence, overthink their movements, or fail to develop their own instincts. {The kid had natural talent until overcoaching made him second-guess every swing.} The term implies that sometimes less direction produces better results.

An overcoat is a long, heavy coat worn over other clothing for warmth, typically reaching below the knee. The word emphasizes its function—it goes over everything else: {He buttoned his overcoat against the wind}. Overcoats are associated with formal or professional dress, distinguished from casual outerwear like parkas or jackets.

Overcoats are heavy coats worn over other clothing for warmth in cold weather. The term distinguishes these outer garments from suit jackets or sport coats worn indoors: {He hung his overcoat in the hall closet}. Overcoats are typically long, extending below the waist or to the knees.

Overcome means to succeed against opposition or difficulty. You overcome {obstacles}, {fears}, {challenges}, or {adversity}. The word suggests struggle followed by victory: {She overcame her shyness to become a public speaker}. To be overcome by emotion, heat, or fumes is to be overwhelmed or rendered helpless: {He was overcome with grief}. {Overcome} alone often implies prevailing: {We shall overcome}.

Overcoming is the act of prevailing over obstacles, difficulties, or opposition. The word carries connotations of struggle followed by success: {overcoming adversity}, {overcoming fear}, {overcoming addiction}. It implies effort and persistence rather than easy victory. What's overcome is typically something that initially seemed formidable or resistant to change.

To overcommit is to promise or take on more than you can deliver. Someone overcommits their time by scheduling too many meetings, their budget by pledging funds they don't have, or their energy by agreeing to help everyone who asks. {I overcommitted this week and now I'm drowning.} In computing, memory overcommit allows a system to allocate more memory than physically available, betting that not all processes will need their full allocation simultaneously.

Overcommitted describes having taken on more obligations than you can reasonably fulfill. Someone overcommitted has said yes too many times—to projects, meetings, social engagements, or responsibilities: {I'm completely overcommitted this month and something has to give}. The word implies stress from conflicting demands on limited time or resources.
