Overcommitting is taking on more obligations than you can reasonably fulfill. The word applies to schedules, promises, and resources: {I've been overcommitting myself at work and it's affecting my health}. In computing, memory overcommitting allocates more virtual memory than physical capacity allows. The pattern is common enough that the warning {Don't overcommit} has become standard advice.

To overcompensate is to go too far in correcting a problem or deficiency, creating an opposite imbalance: {He overcompensated for his lack of experience by being overly aggressive}. In psychology, it often describes exaggerated behavior masking an insecurity—the small man who acts tough, the anxious person who seems arrogant. The steering wheel jerks because you overcompensated for a swerve.

Overcompensating is trying too hard to make up for a perceived weakness or failing, often in ways that become obvious or excessive. Someone short might overcompensate by acting aggressive; someone insecure about intelligence might overcompensate by showing off knowledge. The term often carries a note of amateur psychology: {He drives that sports car because he's overcompensating for something}.

Overcompensation is doing too much to make up for a perceived weakness or deficiency. Someone short might overcompensate by acting aggressively dominant. A guilty parent might overcompensate with lavish gifts. The word often carries a critical edge, suggesting the effort is excessive or misdirected: {His sports car feels like overcompensation for something}. In psychology, overcompensation describes exaggerated behaviors masking insecurity.

To overcomplicate is to make something more complex than it needs to be. The word implies criticism—that simpler would be better: {Don't overcomplicate things; just ask her directly}. Engineers overcomplicate designs, writers overcomplicate prose, and planners overcomplicate what should be straightforward tasks.

Overcomplication is the act of making something more complex than it needs to be, or the state of being unnecessarily complex. A simple task suffers from overcomplication when extra steps, rules, or considerations are added beyond what the situation requires: {The project's overcomplication led to missed deadlines}. The word often carries implicit criticism—someone has overthought or overengineered something that should have remained straightforward.

Overconfidence is excessive or unwarranted belief in one's own abilities, judgment, or chances of success. It often leads to poor decisions, inadequate preparation, or dismissal of genuine risks: {His overconfidence cost him the match}. The term implies a gap between perceived and actual competence—someone displaying overconfidence typically doesn't recognize their own limitations. In psychology and economics, overconfidence is studied as a cognitive bias that affects everything from investment decisions to medical diagnoses.

Overconfident means having more confidence than circumstances warrant. An overconfident student skips studying and fails the exam. An overconfident investor ignores warning signs. The word implies that reality will eventually correct the misplaced certainty: {They were overconfident going into the playoffs and got eliminated in the first round}.

Overconsumption is consuming more than is necessary, healthy, or sustainable. The term appears in discussions of resource depletion and environmental damage: {Overconsumption of fossil fuels drives climate change}. It also describes excessive personal intake: {Overconsumption of alcohol leads to liver damage}. The word implies crossing a threshold where consumption becomes harmful rather than beneficial.

To overcook is to cook something too long, resulting in food that's dry, tough, or mushy. The word extends to any situation where excessive effort ruins the result: {Don't overcook the joke by explaining it}. An overcooked {excuse} tries too hard to be convincing.

Overcooked describes food that has been cooked too long, resulting in undesirable texture or taste—dry meat, mushy vegetables, rubbery eggs. Figuratively, something overcooked has been overdone or labored excessively: {The joke was overcooked and fell flat}. {an overcooked metaphor}.

To overcorrect is to adjust too far in the opposite direction when fixing a problem. A driver who overcorrects after drifting right may veer into oncoming traffic. The term applies broadly to any excessive compensation: {After years of being too lenient, the school overcorrected with harsh zero-tolerance policies}. The noun overcorrection describes the result.

Overcorrected is the past tense of overcorrect—to adjust or fix something so much that a new problem emerges in the opposite direction. A driver who overcorrects a skid may spin the other way. {After years of being too strict, they overcorrected and became permissive.} The word often describes well-intentioned changes that go too far.
clues: Swung too far the other way

definition: Overcorrecting is adjusting too far in response to an error, often creating a new problem in the opposite direction. A driver who overcorrects after drifting right may swerve into oncoming traffic. The term applies broadly: {The Fed risks overcorrecting on inflation}. In speech, overcorrecting produces hypercorrections—saying "between you and I" while trying to sound proper.

Overcorrection is adjusting too far in the opposite direction when trying to fix something. A driver who overcorrects after drifting right may swerve left into oncoming traffic. The term applies beyond physical actions: {The company's diversity initiatives felt like overcorrection for past discrimination}. Overcorrection often creates new problems while solving old ones.

To overcrowd is to fill a space beyond comfortable or safe capacity. An overcrowded train has more passengers than it can properly accommodate. Overcrowded prisons create dangerous conditions. The past participle overcrowded functions as an adjective: {The overcrowded classroom made learning difficult}.

Overcrowded describes a space with too many people or things in it for comfort, safety, or function. An overcrowded {train} has no room to move; overcrowded {prisons} strain resources and breed unrest. The word implies not just fullness but excess—more than a space was designed to hold: {The lifeboat was dangerously overcrowded}.

Overcrowding is the condition of having too many people or things in a space. The term implies strain on resources or comfort: {prison overcrowding}, {overcrowding in schools}. A place can be crowded without being overcrowded—the prefix signals excess beyond acceptable limits.

To overdesign is to add unnecessary complexity, features, or robustness beyond what a situation requires. An overdesigned bridge might withstand earthquakes that will never occur in its location. An overdesigned app buries users in options they'll never use. The noun describes this tendency: {The project suffered from overdesign}. Sometimes overdesign wastes resources; occasionally it provides unexpected resilience.

Overdevelopment is excessive or inappropriate building and construction, especially when it strains infrastructure, damages environments, or diminishes quality of life. The term often appears in debates about urban sprawl, coastal construction, or neighborhood density: {Overdevelopment has ruined the character of the old downtown}. In photography, overdevelopment means processing film too long, resulting in excessive contrast or grain.

Overdiagnosed describes a condition identified in someone who would never have developed symptoms or problems from it—a diagnosis that does more harm than good. The term appears most often in medical contexts where screening detects abnormalities that wouldn't have affected the patient's health: {Many early-stage prostate cancers are overdiagnosed, leading to unnecessary treatment}. It can also describe conditions whose prevalence has expanded through broadened criteria: {ADHD may be overdiagnosed in active young boys}.

Overdiagnosing is the act of identifying a condition as a disease or disorder when it would not have caused symptoms or harm during a person's lifetime. This happens particularly with screening tests that detect abnormalities—such as early-stage cancers—that might never progress or cause problems. {Critics argue that widespread PSA testing leads to overdiagnosing prostate cancer.} The concern is that overdiagnosing subjects patients to unnecessary treatment, anxiety, and medical costs.

Overdiagnosis is the detection of a condition that would never have caused symptoms or harm during a person's lifetime. The term is most common in medical contexts, particularly cancer screening: {Prostate cancer screening leads to significant overdiagnosis}. Unlike misdiagnosis, the detected condition is real—but treating it provides no benefit and may cause harm. The concept extends beyond medicine to any system that identifies problems that don't need solving.

To overdo something is to do it to excess—too much, too long, or too intensely. You can overdo exercise, overdo the praise, or overdo the garlic. {Don't overdo it at the gym your first week}. Overdone food has been cooked too long: {The steak was overdone}. Overdone acting or decoration is excessive to the point of seeming false or gaudy.

An overdog is the expected winner or dominant party—the opposite of an underdog. The term describes those who hold power, advantage, or favorable odds: {In this matchup, the defending champions are clear overdogs}. While underdog carries sympathetic connotations, overdog often implies the person or group doesn't need your support.

Overdone means taken too far. Food that is overdone has been cooked too long: {The steak was overdone and tough}. Behavior or style that is overdone is excessive or exaggerated: {The apology felt overdone}, {Her makeup was a bit overdone}. The word suggests something has crossed from appropriate to excessive—whether heat applied to meat or effort applied to performance.

An overdose is a dangerous or lethal quantity of a drug or medication—more than the body can safely process. The term usually implies harm: {She was rushed to the hospital after an overdose}. As a verb, to overdose is to take such an amount: {He overdosed on painkillers}. Figuratively, overdose describes excess of anything: {I've overdosed on Christmas music}.

Overdosed is the past tense of overdose—to take too much of a drug or medication, often with harmful or fatal consequences: {He overdosed on painkillers}. The word appears in both accidental and intentional contexts. Figuratively, overdosed can describe excessive exposure to anything: {I've overdosed on Christmas music this year}.

Overdosing is taking too much of a drug or medication—enough to cause harmful or potentially fatal effects. The word most often appears in contexts of accidental or intentional poisoning: {She was rushed to the hospital after overdosing on painkillers}. Someone can overdose on prescription medications, street drugs, or even over-the-counter remedies. Figuratively, overdosing suggests excessive consumption of anything: {I've been overdosing on true crime podcasts}.

An overdraft is a withdrawal from a bank account that exceeds the available balance, or the amount by which such a withdrawal exceeds the balance. Banks may cover overdrafts as a service, charging fees for the privilege: {I got hit with a $35 overdraft fee}. Overdraft protection links accounts to prevent declined transactions. In British usage, an overdraft can also be a prearranged credit line: {I'm living on my overdraft until payday}.

Overdrafts is the plural of overdraft, which occurs when you withdraw more money from a bank account than it contains. Banks may cover the shortfall and charge a fee: {I got hit with three overdraft fees this month}. An overdraft can also refer to a line of credit that allows such withdrawals: {My checking account has overdraft protection}.

Overdramatic describes behavior or expression that's exaggerated beyond what the situation warrants—making a bigger emotional display than necessary. Someone who weeps over a minor inconvenience or declares a small setback catastrophic is being overdramatic: {Stop being so overdramatic—it's just a parking ticket}. The word often carries a note of dismissal or gentle mockery.

To overdraw is to withdraw more money from an account than it contains, resulting in a negative balance: {I accidentally overdrew my checking account}. Banks typically charge fees for overdrawing. The past tense is overdrew, past participle overdrawn. Extended uses describe exaggeration or excess: an overdrawn {description} embellishes beyond accuracy, an overdrawn {bow} is pulled too far back.

Overdrawn describes a bank account that has had more money withdrawn than it contained, resulting in a negative balance: {My account is overdrawn by fifty dollars}. Banks typically charge fees for overdrawn accounts. Figuratively, something overdrawn is exaggerated or overdone: {The villain in the novel felt overdrawn}.

To overdress is to dress too formally or elaborately for an occasion: {I'd rather overdress than show up in jeans}. The word implies misjudging what's appropriate—wearing a suit to a barbecue or sequins to a casual dinner. An overdress is also a garment worn over another dress or outfit.

Overdressed means wearing clothes too formal or elaborate for the occasion. Someone in a tuxedo at a backyard barbecue is overdressed. The word implies a mismatch between attire and setting: {I felt overdressed in my suit when everyone else wore jeans}. The opposite is underdressed.

Overdrive is a gear in a vehicle that allows the engine to run at lower revolutions while maintaining high speed, reducing fuel consumption and engine wear. The term extends to any state of heightened activity or maximum effort: {The campaign went into overdrive in the final weeks}. In audio, overdrive refers to a distortion effect produced when an amplifier is pushed beyond its clean capacity, creating the crunchy tone prized in rock guitar.

To overdub is to add a new recorded layer—voice, instrument, or effect—onto an existing recording. The technique allows musicians to build up tracks incrementally rather than performing everything at once: {She overdubbed the harmonies after laying down the lead vocal}. As a noun, an overdub is the added layer itself: {The guitar overdubs gave the track its texture}.

Overdubbing is a recording technique where new audio is layered onto an existing track. A singer might overdub harmonies onto a lead vocal, or a guitarist might overdub a solo onto a rhythm track. The technique allows musicians to build complex arrangements one element at a time: {The album took months because of all the overdubbing}. Also appears as overdub (noun and verb).

Overdubs are additional audio tracks recorded over an existing recording. In music production, a band might lay down basic tracks together, then overdub vocals, guitar solos, or harmonies separately: {The producer added string overdubs to sweeten the chorus}. The verb overdub means to record such additions: {She overdubbed her backing vocals last night}.

Overdue means past the expected or required time. A library book becomes overdue when not returned by its due date. A payment is overdue when it should have been made already. The word extends to anything that should have happened sooner: {This conversation is long overdue}. A pregnant woman past her due date is also overdue.

Overeasy describes an egg fried on both sides but with the yolk still runny. The egg is flipped briefly—just enough to set a thin film over the yolk without cooking it through: {I'll have two eggs overeasy with toast}. Also spelled over easy or over-easy. Compare sunny-side up, where the egg isn't flipped at all.

Overeat means to consume more food than your body needs or than is healthy, typically in a single sitting. The word often implies eating past the point of fullness or comfort. {I always overeat at Thanksgiving dinner.} While occasional overeating is common, habitual overeating can lead to health problems. The past tense is overate, and the past participle is overeaten.

Overeating is eating more than your body needs or more than is healthy. It can be occasional—{I always overeat at Thanksgiving}—or habitual, potentially leading to weight gain and health problems. The term implies excess rather than simply eating a lot: a marathon runner loading up on carbohydrates isn't overeating, but someone stress-eating a whole pizza might be.

Overeducated describes someone whose formal education exceeds what their job or circumstances require. The term often carries a dismissive edge—implying that advanced degrees don't translate to practical competence, or that someone is overqualified for available work: {She felt overeducated and underemployed}. Sometimes used self-deprecatingly by those with extensive schooling in fields with limited job prospects.

Overeducation is having more formal education than a job requires or the labor market can absorb. The term usually carries critical undertones—implying wasted credentials, underemployment, or mismatch between training and available work: {a generation facing overeducation and student debt}. Sometimes used to suggest that excessive schooling breeds impracticality or alienation from ordinary life.

Overemotional describes someone who displays or experiences emotions more intensely than a situation warrants. The word implies excess—crying at minor setbacks, flying into rage over small frustrations, or becoming effusively sentimental: {She thought I was being overemotional about the breakup}. Often used dismissively, particularly toward women, to characterize reasonable feelings as excessive.

To overengineer is to design or build something with excessive complexity, precision, or capability beyond what's actually needed. The term implies wasted effort or resources—a solution more elaborate than the problem requires: {The app was so overengineered it took six months to add a simple feature}. Software development uses the term frequently, but it applies to any field where someone builds a tank when a bicycle would do.

Overengineered describes something designed with excessive complexity, features, or specifications beyond what the task requires. An overengineered solution solves problems that don't exist or builds in redundancy nobody needs: {The app is completely overengineered—it took six months to build a glorified to-do list}. The term often implies wasted resources or needless complication, though occasionally suggests impressive-if-impractical thoroughness.

Overengineering is designing or building something with more complexity, features, or robustness than necessary for its purpose. The term implies wasted effort and resources: {The bridge was overengineered for the light traffic it would carry}. In software, overengineering often means anticipating problems that never arise or building elaborate systems for simple tasks. The criticism suggests that simpler solutions would have sufficed.

To overestimate is to judge something as greater than it actually is—more valuable, more likely, more capable. You might overestimate the time needed for a task, overestimate your own abilities, or overestimate someone's interest in your problems. {Don't overestimate how much they care}. As a noun, an overestimate is such a misjudgment: {The budget was an overestimate by half}.

Overestimating is judging something to be greater, better, or more significant than it actually is. You might overestimate how long a trip will take, overestimate your own abilities, or overestimate how much others care about your mistakes. {I was overestimating how much food we'd need}. The error is assuming more rather than less.

Overexertion is pushing yourself too hard physically, resulting in exhaustion, injury, or strain. The term appears frequently in medical contexts and safety warnings: {Heat stroke from overexertion is a serious risk for outdoor workers}. Athletes risk overexertion when training without adequate rest. The word implies exceeding your body's reasonable limits.

Overexplaining is offering more explanation than a situation requires—continuing to clarify, justify, or elaborate when the listener already understands or doesn't need persuading. It often signals anxiety or defensiveness: {She caught herself overexplaining why she'd been late}. The habit can undermine credibility by suggesting uncertainty about one's own position.

To overexpose is to expose too much. In photography, overexposing film or a sensor to light produces washed-out, overly bright images. More broadly, overexposure means too much public visibility: {The band was overexposed after their hit single, and audiences grew tired of them}. A child overexposed to violence may be harmed by it.
clues: Give a photo too much light

definition: Overexposed describes something that has received too much light, particularly in photography where it produces washed-out images with lost detail in bright areas. The term extends to people who have become too visible in media, losing appeal through excessive coverage: {The actor became overexposed after appearing on every talk show that month}. In finance, being overexposed means having too much investment concentrated in one area, creating vulnerability.

Overexposure is too much exposure to something harmful or unwanted. In photography, overexposure means too much light reached the film or sensor, resulting in a washed-out image. Medically, overexposure to sun causes burns; overexposure to radiation causes illness. In media contexts, overexposure describes excessive public visibility that breeds fatigue or contempt: {The constant coverage led to overexposure, and audiences lost interest}.

To overextend is to stretch beyond safe or sustainable limits. The word applies to physical reach, financial commitments, or personal capacity: {The company overextended itself with too many acquisitions}. Military forces overextend their supply lines; individuals overextend their credit. The reflexive form—overextend oneself—is common: {Don't overextend yourself trying to help everyone}.

Overextended describes having taken on more than you can handle—whether commitments, debt, or territory. Someone financially overextended has borrowed beyond their ability to repay. A military force overextended has spread too thin to defend its positions. {We're overextended this month after the car repair.} The word implies vulnerability from excess ambition or poor planning.

Overextension is stretching beyond safe or sustainable limits. The term applies to finances {overextension of credit}, physical strain {muscle overextension}, or commitments {She's overextended herself with too many projects}. Military overextension occurs when forces spread too thin across territory they cannot effectively hold. The word implies vulnerability—what's overextended risks collapse or failure.

Overfished describes a body of water or fish population depleted by excessive fishing. A species is overfished when harvesting outpaces reproduction: {Atlantic cod stocks are severely overfished}. The term appears in conservation and policy contexts, often as a warning that current practices are unsustainable.

Overfishing is harvesting fish faster than populations can reproduce, depleting stocks to unsustainable levels. The practice threatens marine ecosystems and the fishing industries that depend on them: {Overfishing has collapsed the Atlantic cod population}. Regulations like catch limits and seasonal closures attempt to prevent it.

Overflow is excess that spills beyond capacity. A river overflows its banks; a bathtub overflows when left running. The noun names both the excess itself and a channel for it: {a drain overflow}. Figuratively, emotions or crowds overflow: {The stadium was overflowing with fans}. In computing, overflow occurs when a calculation exceeds the maximum value a system can store.

Overflowing describes something so full that its contents spill over the edges: {an overflowing bathtub}, {overflowing trash cans}. The word extends readily to abundance of any kind: {overflowing with gratitude}, {a heart overflowing with joy}. An overflowing crowd exceeds the capacity of a space: {The concert hall was overflowing}.

Overgrazing is the damage to land caused by livestock eating vegetation faster than it can regrow. The result is soil erosion, loss of plant diversity, and degraded pasture: {Overgrazing turned productive rangeland into dust}. The term applies to any situation where animals—domestic or wild—strip an area beyond its capacity to recover.

Overgrow means to grow beyond normal bounds or to cover something with growth. Plants overgrow paths, gardens overgrow with weeds, and vines overgrow abandoned buildings. The past participle overgrown is common: {an overgrown lot}, {overgrown with ivy}. Figuratively, something overgrown has expanded past its proper limits: {an overgrown bureaucracy}.

Overgrown describes something that has grown excessively or beyond intended bounds. An overgrown {garden} is choked with weeds; an overgrown {path} has become impassable with vegetation. The word also characterizes someone or something as larger or more developed than expected while retaining immature qualities: {He's just an overgrown child}. {The overgrown lot hadn't been mowed in years.}

Overgrowth is excessive or uncontrolled growth. Vegetation that has overgrown a space is overgrowth: {The path was hidden by overgrowth}. In medicine, overgrowth describes abnormal tissue proliferation: {bacterial overgrowth}, {bone overgrowth}. The word emphasizes growth beyond normal or desired limits.

Overhand describes a motion where the hand moves from above the shoulder downward—the natural arc of throwing a ball or swinging a hammer. An overhand {pitch} comes from above; an overhand {knot} is tied by passing the end over and through. The opposite is underhand, where the hand swings upward from below.

An overhang is a part that extends or juts out beyond what's below it: {the overhang of the roof}, {a rocky overhang sheltered us from the rain}. In business and finance, an overhang refers to an excess or surplus that weighs on a market—unsold inventory, pending stock options, or accumulated debt that depresses prices or limits future action. To overhang is to extend beyond or loom over: {Branches overhang the path}.

Overhangs are parts that project or jut out beyond what's below them. A roof overhang extends past the walls to shed rain. A cliff overhang creates shelter underneath. In climbing, an overhang is rock that slopes outward, requiring climbers to pull themselves up rather than simply stand. Figuratively, threats or debts overhang—they loom unresolved: {The possibility of layoffs overhangs the department}.

To overhaul something is to examine it thoroughly and make necessary repairs or improvements. Mechanics overhaul engines, taking them apart to fix worn components. The noun refers to this process: {The car needs a complete overhaul}. By extension, overhaul applies to systems and institutions: {an overhaul of the tax code}. In a separate sense, to overhaul is to overtake: {The cruiser overhauled the fleeing vessel}.

Overhauled means thoroughly examined and repaired or renovated. Mechanics overhaul engines, taking them apart to fix or replace worn components. The word extends to any comprehensive revision: {The company overhauled its hiring practices}. To be overhauled can also mean to be overtaken, as one ship overhauling another.

Overhauling is thoroughly examining and repairing something—taking it apart to fix what's wrong and restore it to working order: {The mechanic is overhauling the engine}. The word extends to comprehensive revision of systems or processes: {Congress is overhauling the tax code}. In racing or pursuit, overhauling means catching up to and passing: {The lead boat was overhauled in the final stretch}.

Overhauls is the plural of overhaul, a thorough examination and repair of something: {The engines underwent complete overhauls}. The word implies taking something apart to fix or improve it comprehensively, whether mechanical systems, organizations, or policies: {The tax code needs major overhauls}. As a verb form, overhauls means performs such work: {The mechanic overhauls transmissions for a living}.

Overhead refers to what is above your head or above a reference point: {overhead lights}, {overhead compartments on a plane}. In business, overhead means the ongoing costs of running an operation—rent, utilities, salaries—that aren't tied to producing specific goods: {Our overhead is killing us}. As an adverb: {A plane flew overhead}. An overhead is also a transparency displayed on a projector, or the projector itself.

To overhear is to hear something not intended for you—typically a conversation between others: {I overheard them talking about the layoffs}. The word implies accidental listening rather than deliberate eavesdropping, though the line blurs. What's overheard often shouldn't have been: {She overheard her name and stopped to listen}.

Overheard is the past tense of overhear—to hear something not intended for you, whether by accident or design. You might overhear a conversation through thin walls or overhear your name mentioned at a party: {I overheard them talking about the layoffs}. The word implies the speaker didn't know they were being listened to.

Overhearing is hearing something not meant for you—a conversation, remark, or piece of information you weren't supposed to catch: {I couldn't help overhearing your argument}. Unlike eavesdropping, overhearing is typically accidental rather than intentional. The word often introduces information learned this way: {Overhearing their plans, she decided to act}.

To overheat is to become too hot—hot enough to cause damage or malfunction. Engines overheat when cooling systems fail. People overheat in extreme temperatures. Economies overheat when growth is unsustainably rapid, risking inflation: {The Fed raised rates to cool an overheating economy}. The noun overheating describes the condition itself.

Overheated describes something that has become too hot—an overheated {engine}, an overheated {room}. The word extends to excess intensity or agitation: an overheated {debate}, overheated {rhetoric}. In economics, an overheated {economy} or {market} is growing unsustainably fast, risking inflation or collapse. A person who is overheated may be physically too warm or emotionally worked up.

Overheating is becoming too hot, whether literally or figuratively. An engine overheats when its cooling system fails. An economy overheats when rapid growth triggers inflation. A person overheats from exertion or fever. The term often implies crossing from acceptable warmth into dangerous territory: {My laptop keeps overheating during video calls}.

Overheats is the third-person singular of overheat—to become too hot or to make something too hot. An engine overheats when its cooling system fails. An economy overheats when growth becomes unsustainably rapid, risking inflation. A person who overheats may be physically hot or emotionally agitated: {She tends to overheat during arguments}.

To overhype is to promote something beyond what it deserves, generating expectations that the thing itself can't meet. Movies, products, and events get overhyped when marketing outpaces quality: {The game was overhyped and disappointed everyone}. The noun overhype refers to this excessive promotion: {All the overhype ruined the album for me}.

Overhyped describes something that has received more praise, attention, or excitement than it deserves. The term combines "over" (excessive) with "hyped" (promoted or publicized intensely), suggesting that expectations have been inflated beyond what the thing can deliver. {The movie was so overhyped that the actual experience felt disappointing.} It's commonly applied to products, films, restaurants, or trends that fail to live up to their buildup.

Overincarceration is the imprisonment of more people than necessary or justified—whether through excessive sentences, criminalization of minor offenses, or systemic inequities that funnel certain populations into prison. The term implies that incarceration has exceeded its legitimate purposes: {Critics argue that overincarceration has devastated Black communities}. It often appears in discussions of American criminal justice reform.

Overinvested describes having put too much into something—whether money, time, emotion, or effort. The excess creates vulnerability: {I'm too overinvested in this relationship to walk away now}. In finance, it means holding too much of a portfolio in one asset. Emotionally, it suggests caring more than is healthy or proportionate: {Don't get overinvested in the outcome}.

Overjoyed means extremely happy—joy taken to an intense degree. The word typically describes reactions to specific good news or events rather than general contentment: {She was overjoyed to learn she'd been accepted}. It suggests happiness so strong it's almost overwhelming.

Overkill is excessive force or effort beyond what's needed to accomplish something. The term originated in nuclear strategy, describing destructive capacity far exceeding what would destroy a target. Now it applies broadly to any disproportionate response: {Bringing three lawyers to a traffic court hearing is overkill}. The word often carries mild criticism—suggesting waste, overreaction, or lack of restraint.

Overland means across or by land rather than by sea or air: {They made the overland journey from Missouri to Oregon}. The word emphasizes traveling over terrain, often suggesting a long or arduous route. As an adverb: {We traveled overland through the desert}. The Overland Trail was a major 19th-century emigrant route to the American West.

An overlander is someone who travels long distances overland, typically through remote or rugged terrain, often by vehicle. The term especially describes adventurers who make extended journeys across continents—through Africa, from Alaska to Argentina, or across the Australian outback: {We met overlanders who had driven from London to Cape Town}. Overlanding emphasizes self-reliance and camping along the way rather than staying in hotels.

Overlanding is self-reliant travel to remote destinations where the journey matters as much as the arrival. Unlike off-roading, which emphasizes vehicle capability on difficult terrain, overlanding prioritizes extended travel through wilderness areas, often lasting days or weeks. Participants typically use modified trucks or SUVs equipped for camping and carry supplies for self-sufficiency: {We spent three weeks overlanding through Patagonia}. The term originated with long-distance cattle drives in Australia.

Overlap describes things that extend over and cover part of each other: {The shingles overlap to keep water out}. Schedules overlap when they share common time; interests overlap when they share common ground. As a noun, overlap is the shared portion: {There's considerable overlap between the two job descriptions}. The word captures partial coincidence—not identical, not separate, but sharing territory.

Overlapping describes things that extend over and cover part of each other, like roof shingles or fish scales. The term applies to any partial sharing of space, time, or content: {overlapping shifts}, {overlapping responsibilities}, {overlapping interests}. When schedules or territories overlap, they share common ground without being identical.
clues: Edges crossing into each other's space

definition: Overlaps describes portions that extend over and cover part of each other, like shingles on a roof or schedules that share common hours. The noun overlap names this shared portion: {There's significant overlap between the two proposals}. Things can overlap physically, temporally, or conceptually: {Our interests overlap considerably}. The verb stresses the action of extending across boundaries.

Overlay means to cover or spread over the surface of something, or the covering itself. A map overlay adds information atop a base image; a decorative overlay adorns furniture or fabric. In computing, overlays are interface elements displayed on top of other content, like the chat overlays gamers use while streaming. The word suggests layering—one thing placed upon another without fully replacing what's beneath. {The gold overlay on the frame was starting to wear thin.}

Overload means to burden with too much—more than a system, person, or structure can handle. You can overload a truck, a circuit, or your schedule. As a noun, an overload is the excess itself: {The power grid couldn't handle the overload}. Information overload describes being overwhelmed by too much data. {Don't overload the washing machine}.

Overloaded describes something carrying or handling more than its intended capacity. An overloaded {truck} strains under excessive weight; an overloaded {circuit} trips when too many devices draw power; an overloaded {schedule} leaves no breathing room. The term extends to people who feel overwhelmed by responsibilities or information: {I'm completely overloaded with work this week}. In programming, an overloaded function has multiple definitions that handle different types of input.

Overloading is putting too much load on something—a vehicle, a circuit, a person's schedule. An overloaded truck exceeds its weight capacity; an overloaded outlet trips a breaker. In programming, overloading lets multiple functions share a name but accept different types of input: {The method is overloaded to handle both strings and integers}. Figuratively, information overload overwhelms the mind: {I'm overloading on bad news}.

Overloads means gives too much of something—too much work, too much weight, too much electrical current. An overloaded circuit trips a breaker. An overloaded employee burns out. The noun is the excess itself or the state of being overwhelmed: {information overload}. In programming, to overload a function is to define multiple versions that accept different inputs, letting the same name handle varied situations.

To overlook something is to fail to notice or consider it: {I overlooked one important detail}. The word also means to choose not to punish or address: {We'll overlook the violation this time}. A third sense is to have a view over: {The balcony overlooks the harbor}. As a noun, an overlook is a scenic viewpoint, especially along a highway.

Overlooked means missed or failed to notice: {The investigator overlooked a crucial piece of evidence}. It also means ignored or passed over, often unfairly: {She was overlooked for the promotion}. Something overlooked may be undervalued or underappreciated: {one of the most overlooked albums of the decade}. Less commonly, to be overlooked means to have a view over something: {a balcony overlooking the garden}.

Overlooking works in two directions. To overlook something is to fail to notice it or to choose not to address it: {I overlooked the typo}, {We'll overlook your tardiness this once}. But overlooking also means looking down upon from above: {a balcony overlooking the garden}, {rooms overlooking the bay}. Context usually makes the sense clear.

Overlooks has two main senses that point in opposite directions. To overlook something is to have a view over it from above: {The balcony overlooks the harbor}. But to overlook is also to fail to notice or to excuse: {I overlooked the error}, {We can overlook it this once}. The first meaning implies seeing everything; the second implies missing something.

An overlord is a ruler who holds power over other rulers or lords—a supreme authority in a hierarchy of control. The term evokes feudal systems where lesser nobles owed allegiance to a greater one. In modern use, overlord often appears ironically or in fantasy contexts: {Our new robot overlords}, {She appointed herself overlord of the office coffee supply}. The word suggests dominion that is absolute and possibly tyrannical.

Overlords are rulers or masters who hold power over others, especially those who dominate subordinate lords or territories. The term suggests feudal hierarchy or absolute authority: {The Norman overlords imposed their language on England}. In modern use, overlord often carries ironic or sinister overtones—corporate overlords, robot overlords, alien overlords—implying oppressive control: {Our new tech overlords know everything about us}.

Overmatched describes being outclassed by a superior opponent or challenge—facing something beyond your ability to handle. A boxer may be overmatched against a champion; a small firm may be overmatched competing with industry giants. {The young lawyer was clearly overmatched against the veteran prosecutor.} The word implies the mismatch was apparent, perhaps from the start.

Overmedicated describes someone given too much medication or too many medications, whether by doctors, caregivers, or themselves. The term often appears in critiques of healthcare systems or pharmaceutical culture: {The nursing home kept patients overmedicated and docile}. It can also describe self-medication gone too far: {I felt overmedicated and foggy after doubling my dose}.

Overmedicating is giving or taking too much medication—either excessive doses or too many different drugs. The term often appears in discussions of elderly care, where patients accumulate prescriptions from multiple doctors: {The nursing home was overmedicating residents to keep them docile}. It also describes unnecessary pharmaceutical intervention: {We're overmedicating children for normal behavior}.

Overmedication is the use of more medication than necessary or appropriate—whether too many drugs, too high a dose, or treatment where none is needed. The term often appears in discussions of elderly patients prescribed numerous drugs with overlapping or conflicting effects, or children given psychiatric medications too readily: {The nursing home was cited for overmedication of residents}. To overmedicate is the corresponding verb.

Overnight spans the hours of darkness between evening and morning. As an adverb, it describes something happening during the night: {We drove overnight to get there}. As an adjective, it modifies things lasting or occurring through the night: an overnight {stay}, an overnight {bag}. Figuratively, overnight means suddenly or very quickly: {She became famous overnight}. The verb means to stay somewhere for the night: {We overnighted in Chicago}.

Overnights are things that happen or last through the night. In broadcasting, overnights are preliminary ratings data available the morning after a program airs: {The overnights look promising for the new show}. In finance, overnight rates govern short-term lending between banks. As a verb, to overnight something is to send it for next-day delivery: {We'll overnight the contract to you}.

Overpaid describes someone who receives more money than their work merits: {Most people think CEOs are overpaid}. The word implies a judgment about value—that compensation exceeds contribution. As the past tense of overpay, it simply means paid too much: {I overpaid for that car}.

Overparent is a verb meaning to be excessively involved in managing a child's life, activities, and decisions—often to the child's developmental detriment. The term captures the behavior of parents who hover, intervene unnecessarily, and shield children from normal challenges and consequences. {Teachers complain that overparenting leaves kids unable to handle minor setbacks.} The related noun overparenting describes this pattern of excessive involvement, associated with helicopter parents and snowplow parents.

Overparenting is excessive involvement in a child's life—managing, protecting, and intervening to a degree that prevents the child from developing independence or resilience. The helicopter parent who hovers constantly and the snowplow parent who clears every obstacle exemplify overparenting. {Overparenting can leave kids unprepared for college and adulthood.}

An overpass is a bridge that carries a road or railway over another road. The term emphasizes the structure's function of allowing traffic to pass over an obstacle without intersection: {Take the overpass to avoid the traffic light}. In American usage, overpass is more common than flyover, which prevails in British English.

To overpay is to pay more than something is worth or more than what's owed: {I overpaid for that car}. Someone who is overpaid receives compensation exceeding reasonable value for their work—a charge often leveled at executives and athletes. The noun overpayment appears in billing disputes and tax refunds.

To overperform is to exceed expectations or do better than predicted. The term appears most often in business and finance contexts: {The stock overperformed the market by twelve percent}. Athletes and students can also overperform—delivering results beyond what their track record suggested. The opposite is underperform.

To overplay is to emphasize or exaggerate beyond what's warranted. An actor overplays a role by being too dramatic. To {overplay your hand} is to overestimate your position and act too boldly, often backfiring: {The union overplayed its hand and lost public support}. The opposite of underplay.

Overplayed describes something repeated so often it has lost its impact or appeal. A song becomes overplayed when radio stations exhaust it: {That track was great until they overplayed it all summer}. The word extends to tactics or arguments used too frequently: {The victim card is overplayed}. To overplay your hand is to overestimate your position and push too hard.

Overpoliced describes communities or areas subjected to excessive law enforcement presence and intervention. The term implies that police activity in these places goes beyond what's needed for public safety, resulting in disproportionate stops, arrests, and surveillance: {Black neighborhoods are often both overpoliced and underserved}. The concept suggests that heavy policing itself creates harm rather than preventing it.

Overpopulated describes a place with more inhabitants than its resources can sustainably support. The term applies to cities, regions, or the planet itself: {The island became overpopulated after the tourism boom}. Overpopulated often carries political weight in debates about immigration, development, or environmental limits.
clues: Too many people, too little space

definition: Overpopulation is having more people than an area can sustainably support—exceeding the carrying capacity for resources like food, water, and space. The term applies to regions, countries, or the planet as a whole: {Overpopulation strains infrastructure in rapidly growing cities}. Critics note the concept often masks questions of resource distribution rather than absolute numbers.

To overpower is to defeat or subdue by superior force: {The guards overpowered the prisoner before he could escape}. The word extends to any overwhelming dominance—a smell that overpowers a room, grief that overpowers composure, a flavor that overpowers everything else in the dish. What overpowers doesn't just win; it leaves no contest.

Overpowered means defeated or subdued by superior force: {The guards were overpowered by the mob}. In gaming, overpowered describes a character, weapon, or ability that's too strong relative to others, disrupting balance: {That new hero is totally overpowered—they need to nerf him}. The gaming sense has spread to general slang for anything excessively dominant or effective.

Overpowering describes something so intense it overwhelms resistance or the senses. An overpowering {smell} dominates a room. An overpowering {urge} is nearly impossible to resist. Overpowering {force} defeats opposition completely. The word suggests an intensity that leaves no room for alternatives: {The evidence against him was overpowering}.

To overprescribe is to prescribe medication too readily, too often, or in excessive quantities. The term usually criticizes medical practice rather than individual doctors: {Antibiotics are overprescribed, contributing to resistant bacteria}. {Critics say doctors overprescribe opioids for chronic pain}. The noun is overprescription.

Overprescribed describes medications given more often than medically necessary, or conditions treated with drugs when other approaches might work better. The term carries implicit criticism of medical practice: {Antibiotics are wildly overprescribed for viral infections}. {Adderall has become overprescribed for children who are simply energetic}. Something overprescribed may still help individual patients while causing broader harm—antibiotic resistance, dependency, or side effects across populations.

Overprescription is the practice of prescribing medications more frequently, in higher doses, or for longer durations than medically necessary. The term appears most often in discussions of antibiotics, where overprescription contributes to drug-resistant bacteria, and opioids, where it has fueled addiction crises. {Overprescription of painkillers has been blamed for the epidemic of opioid dependence.} The word implies systemic failure rather than individual error, pointing to patterns across healthcare systems.

Overpriced describes something that costs more than it's worth or more than it should. The judgment is subjective—what seems overpriced to one buyer may seem fair to another: {The drinks at the airport are ridiculously overpriced}. The word implies you're being taken advantage of, not just that something is expensive.

Overproduced describes something made with excessive polish or technical elaboration, often to its detriment. A song can be overproduced when too many layers of instruments, effects, or studio trickery obscure its natural qualities: {The album sounds overproduced—you can barely hear her voice under all that reverb}. The term applies beyond music to films, events, or anything where elaborate production overwhelms content.

To overpromise is to commit to more than you can deliver. The word usually appears alongside underdeliver: {They overpromised and underdelivered}. Politicians overpromise during campaigns. Startups overpromise to investors. The caution against overpromising acknowledges that excessive promises create expectations that damage trust when unmet.

Overpromised describes having committed to more than one can deliver. A politician who overpromised during the campaign faces backlash when reality sets in. A company that overpromised on its product launch scrambles to manage expectations. The word implies a gap between what was pledged and what's possible: {They overpromised and underdelivered}.

Overpromising is committing to more than you can deliver. The word implies a gap between what's pledged and what's possible: {The company has a history of overpromising and underdelivering}. Politicians overpromise during campaigns; salespeople overpromise to close deals. The noun overpromise names the commitment itself.

Overprotective describes someone who shields another person—usually a child—from harm or difficulty to an excessive degree. An overprotective parent might not let children play unsupervised or make their own mistakes: {Her overprotective mother still calls her every night}. The word implies the protection does more harm than good, preventing normal development or independence.

Overqualification is having more education, experience, or skills than a position requires. Employers sometimes reject overqualified candidates, fearing they'll grow bored or leave for better opportunities: {Her PhD was actually a liability—they saw it as overqualification for the entry-level role}. The concept assumes a mismatch between credentials and job demands.

Overqualified describes someone whose credentials, experience, or skills exceed what a position requires. Employers sometimes reject overqualified candidates, fearing they'll be bored, demand higher pay, or leave quickly: {They said I was overqualified for the entry-level position}. The term often frustrates job seekers who would happily accept less demanding work.

Overran is the past tense of overrun. To overrun is to spread over and occupy by force or in overwhelming numbers: {Enemy forces overran the outpost}. Pests or weeds overrun a garden when they take it over. A project overruns its budget or schedule when it exceeds planned limits. Something that overruns a boundary spills past it.

To overrate is to judge something as better than it actually is—to assign too much value, importance, or quality: {I think that restaurant is overrated}. The past participle overrated appears constantly in debates about whether popular things deserve their reputation: {an overrated movie}, {the most overrated player in the league}.

Overrated describes something that receives more praise, attention, or esteem than it deserves. The term implies a gap between reputation and actual quality: {I think The Beatles are overrated} or {The restaurant is overrated—the food is mediocre at best}. It functions as both an adjective and the past participle of the verb overrate. The judgment is inherently subjective; calling something overrated often says as much about the speaker's contrarian stance as about the thing itself.

Overreach means to extend beyond proper limits, typically by attempting more than one can accomplish or by going too far in pursuit of an advantage. When someone overreaches, they defeat their own purpose through excessive ambition or greed: {The company overreached by expanding into too many markets at once}. In legal and political contexts, overreach often describes an abuse of power or authority: {Critics accused the agency of regulatory overreach}. The noun overreach denotes such an instance of going too far.

Overreached is the past tense of overreach, meaning to extend too far or attempt more than one can achieve. Someone who overreached exceeded their grasp—whether in ambition, authority, or physical reach: {The company overreached when it expanded into three new markets simultaneously}. The word often implies failure resulting from excessive confidence or ambition: {The prosecutor overreached and lost the case}.

Overreaching describes going too far in pursuit of an objective, attempting more than one can accomplish or is entitled to. An overreaching {executive} grabs power beyond their authority. An overreaching {argument} extends logic past its breaking point. The word implies ambition that defeats itself—{The prosecution's overreaching claims alienated the jury}. To overreach is to stretch beyond one's grasp.

To overreact is to respond more intensely than a situation warrants—becoming too angry, too worried, or too excited given the circumstances. {I know I'm probably overreacting, but I can't stop thinking about what she said}. The noun is overreaction: {His resignation was an overreaction to mild criticism}.

Overreacting is responding to something with more intensity than the situation warrants—getting too angry, too worried, or too upset. The word often appears in accusations: {You're overreacting}. Whether someone is actually overreacting or responding appropriately is frequently a matter of perspective.

An overreaction is a response disproportionate to its cause—too strong, too emotional, too hasty. The word implies the speaker's judgment that a calmer response would have been appropriate: {Calling the police was an overreaction; the kids were just being loud}. To overreact is to respond this way. What counts as overreaction often depends on perspective—one person's overreaction is another's justified response.

Overreactions are responses disproportionate to what prompted them—excessive in intensity, duration, or consequence. The term implies judgment: what counts as overreacting depends on the observer. {His overreactions to minor criticism made him difficult to work with.} {The market's overreactions to quarterly earnings often correct within days.}

Overreliance is excessive dependence on something, to the point where it becomes a weakness or liability. The word implies that some reliance would be appropriate, but too much creates vulnerability: {Our overreliance on a single supplier left us exposed when they went bankrupt}. Often used in criticism of systems, strategies, or habits that lack backup options.

Override means to use authority to set aside or supersede something—a decision, a rule, or a mechanism. A manager overrides an employee's judgment. Congress can override a presidential veto. In computing, override refers to replacing default behavior with custom instructions. The noun override is the act or means of overriding: {a manual override}, {a congressional override}. To override concerns is to proceed despite them.

Overrides are instances of setting aside or superseding something. A presidential override cancels a congressional veto. In computing, an override replaces default behavior with custom instructions: {The CSS overrides changed the font throughout the site}. Safety overrides allow manual control when automatic systems fail. The word captures any act of asserting authority over an existing rule or setting.

Overriding means more important than all other considerations. An overriding concern takes precedence over everything else: {Safety was the overriding priority}. The word suggests something so significant it eclipses competing factors: {Her overriding goal was to finish the project on time}. In computing, overriding replaces inherited behavior with new code.

Overripe describes fruit or produce that has passed its peak ripeness—soft, mushy, perhaps beginning to ferment or decay. {The bananas had gone overripe and brown}. Figuratively, overripe suggests something past its prime or excessively developed: {overripe prose}, {an overripe performance}. The word implies decay lurking beneath abundance.

To overrule is to reject or set aside a decision, objection, or ruling by exercising superior authority. A judge overrules an objection, allowing the questioned testimony or evidence. A parent overrules a child's protest. When a higher court overrules a lower court's decision, it reverses the outcome. The word implies hierarchy—someone with greater power countermanding someone with less: {The CEO overruled the committee's recommendation}.

Overruled is the past tense of overrule—to reject or set aside a decision, objection, or ruling by exercising superior authority. A judge overrules an objection when allowing the challenged testimony or evidence: {Objection! Hearsay. Overruled.} Parents overrule children, executives overrule subordinates, and appellate courts overrule lower court decisions. To be overruled is to have your position rejected by someone with greater power.

Overruling is the act of rejecting or setting aside a decision, objection, or ruling. A judge overrules an objection when denying it: {Objection! Hearsay. Overruled.} Courts engage in overruling when they reverse precedent: {The overruling of Roe v. Wade sparked protests nationwide}. Someone with authority can do the overruling of a subordinate's decision.

To overrun is to spread over and occupy by force or in overwhelming numbers: {Weeds overran the garden}, {Protesters overran the barricades}. The past tense is also overrun. Something that overruns exceeds its boundaries or limits: {The project overran its budget by millions}. As a noun, an overrun is the amount by which something exceeds expectations, especially costs: {a $2 billion overrun on the construction contract}.

Overruns are instances of exceeding limits—usually budgets, deadlines, or boundaries. A project with cost overruns has spent more than planned: {The construction overruns totaled millions}. In military contexts, an overrun is territory seized by advancing forces. In printing and publishing, overruns are copies produced beyond the ordered quantity.

Overscheduled means having too many commitments or activities packed into available time. The term often describes children whose parents have enrolled them in excessive extracurriculars: {Between soccer, piano, tutoring, and dance, the kids are completely overscheduled}. Adults use it for calendars crammed with meetings and obligations: {I'm so overscheduled this week I can't even grab coffee}.

Overseas means across or beyond the sea—in or to a foreign country, especially one reached by ocean travel. As an adjective, it describes things foreign or international: {overseas markets}, {overseas travel}, {overseas military bases}. As an adverb, it indicates location or movement abroad: {She lived overseas for ten years}. The word often implies significant distance, not just any border crossing.

To oversee is to supervise or watch over work, a process, or people to ensure things proceed correctly: {She oversees a team of twelve engineers}, {A committee will oversee the election}. The word implies authority and responsibility for outcomes, though not necessarily hands-on involvement in the work itself.

Overseeing is supervising or watching over something to ensure it proceeds correctly: {She's overseeing the renovation project}. The word implies responsibility without necessarily doing the hands-on work—a manager oversees employees, a director oversees production. {He was overseeing the transition to the new system.}

An overseer is someone who supervises work or workers. The term appears most often in historical contexts—particularly describing those who managed enslaved people on plantations: {The overseer drove the field hands from dawn to dusk}. In modern use, overseer sounds formal or archaic, largely replaced by supervisor or manager. It survives in some institutional titles and in figurative use for anyone monitoring others' activities.

Overseers are people who supervise or watch over something—workers, operations, or processes. The term historically refers to those who managed enslaved laborers on plantations, a brutal role that makes the word carry harsh connotations in American contexts: {The overseer drove the field hands from dawn to dusk}. In modern use, overseers tend to be officials with monitoring duties: {congressional overseers of the intelligence agencies}.

Oversees is the third-person singular of oversee, meaning to supervise or watch over work, people, or processes to ensure things proceed correctly: {She oversees a team of twelve engineers}. The word implies responsibility and authority rather than hands-on involvement—a manager oversees without necessarily doing the work themselves.

To oversell is to promote something beyond what it can deliver—exaggerating benefits, making promises that won't hold, or pushing too hard. A salesperson oversells a product; a politician oversells a policy. The word implies eventual disappointment when reality falls short: {The movie was good, but the trailer oversold it}. In finance, oversold describes a stock that has dropped sharply and may be undervalued.

Overselling is promoting something more aggressively or extravagantly than the facts warrant. A salesperson might oversell a product's capabilities; a job candidate might oversell their qualifications. The term also applies to literally selling more of something than exists or can be delivered—airlines routinely oversell flights, booking more passengers than seats. {The pitch was good but he was clearly overselling it.} Whether literal or figurative, overselling risks disappointment or backlash when reality fails to match the hype.

Oversensitive describes someone who reacts too strongly to criticism, slights, or emotional stimuli—taking offense or feeling hurt more easily than most people would consider reasonable. The word carries a note of judgment: calling someone oversensitive implies their reactions are excessive rather than justified. {Don't be so oversensitive; I was only joking.} It can also describe physical sensitivity, as when skin is oversensitive to touch or sunlight.

Overserved is a euphemism for drunk, framing intoxication as the bartender's fault rather than the drinker's: {I wasn't drunk—I was overserved}. The word originates from bartender liability—establishments can be held responsible for continuing to serve visibly intoxicated patrons. The passive construction deflects responsibility: {He got a little overserved at the wedding reception}.

Oversexed describes someone with unusually strong or frequent sexual desire—more than is considered normal or healthy. The term carries a judgmental edge, implying excess: {The tabloids portrayed him as an oversexed celebrity}. It can also describe atmospheres or content saturated with sexual themes: {an oversexed advertising campaign}.

To overshadow is to cast a shadow over something, literally or figuratively. A tall building overshadows neighboring structures. More often the word describes something that diminishes another by comparison or draws attention away from it: {Her brother's achievements always overshadowed her own}. Bad news can overshadow good: {The scandal overshadowed the team's victory}.

Overshadowed means cast into shadow by something larger or more prominent. A tall building overshadows nearby houses. More often figurative: a person's achievements may be overshadowed by a sibling's fame, or good news overshadowed by tragedy. The word implies being diminished not through fault but by comparison: {Her early work was overshadowed by her later masterpiece}.

Overshadowing is the present participle of overshadow—to cast a shadow over something, literally or figuratively. Most often it describes something that diminishes another by comparison or draws attention away from it: {Her brother's achievements kept overshadowing her own}. A looming threat or presence can be overshadowing: {The overshadowing possibility of war colored every decision}.

Overshadows means to cast a shadow over, literally or figuratively. A tall building overshadows neighboring structures. More commonly, one thing overshadows another by dominating attention or seeming more important: {Her later scandals overshadowed her early achievements}. A person can overshadow others by outshining them: {The lead actor completely overshadowed the rest of the cast}.

To overshare is to reveal too much personal information, especially in contexts where such disclosure feels inappropriate or uncomfortable for others. The term emerged with social media, where people broadcast intimate details to wide audiences: {She overshared about her divorce on Facebook}. As a noun, an overshare is an instance of such disclosure: {That was a bit of an overshare}.

Overshared is the past tense of overshare—to reveal too much personal information, especially in contexts where such disclosure feels inappropriate or uncomfortable for listeners. The term emerged with social media, where broadcasting intimate details became easy: {She overshared about her divorce on Facebook}. {He overshared at the meeting and made everyone uncomfortable}.

An oversharer is someone who reveals too much personal information, especially in contexts where such disclosure feels inappropriate or uncomfortable for others. The term implies a lack of social boundaries—sharing intimate details about relationships, health problems, or family drama with acquaintances or strangers: {My coworker is such an oversharer—I know way too much about her divorce}.

Oversharers are people who reveal too much personal information, especially in contexts where such disclosure feels inappropriate or uncomfortable for listeners. The term implies a lack of social awareness about boundaries—someone who tells coworkers about their digestive problems or posts intimate relationship details on social media: {My aunt is one of those oversharers who tells strangers her whole medical history}.

Overshares means reveals too much personal information, especially in contexts where such disclosure feels inappropriate or uncomfortable. Someone who overshares might discuss intimate medical details at a dinner party or trauma with near-strangers: {She overshares about her divorce with anyone who'll listen}. The noun overshare describes an instance of this.

Oversharing is revealing too much personal information, especially in contexts where it's unwelcome or inappropriate: {She overshared about her divorce on the first date}. The term emerged with social media, where broadcasting intimate details to wide audiences became easy. What counts as oversharing depends on the relationship and setting—telling a stranger your medical history differs from telling a close friend.

To overshoot is to go past an intended target or limit. A plane overshoots the runway by landing too far down it. You can overshoot a budget, a deadline, or a turn on the highway. {We overshot the exit and had to double back.} The noun overshoot describes the amount by which something exceeds its target: {a population overshoot}, {an overshoot in spending projections}.

Overshoots means to go past an intended target or limit. A plane overshoots the runway by landing too far along it. An economy overshoots when indicators swing beyond sustainable levels before correcting. You overshoot a budget by spending more than planned: {We overshot our estimate by twenty percent}. The noun overshoot names such an excess.

Overshot describes something that has gone past its intended target or limit. A plane that {overshot the runway} went too far. An overshot water wheel is powered by water flowing over the top rather than underneath. As the past tense of overshoot, it applies to budgets, deadlines, or estimates exceeded: {We overshot our budget by twenty percent}.

Oversight has two nearly opposite meanings. The first is watchful supervision: {Congressional oversight of intelligence agencies}, {The board has oversight of financial matters}. The second is an error of inattention—something missed or forgotten: {The omission was an oversight, not deliberate}. Context usually makes clear which sense applies.

Oversights are failures to notice or attend to something. The word carries two distinct senses that context usually clarifies. An oversight in the sense of a mistake is something accidentally missed or forgotten: {The billing error was an oversight}. Oversight in the sense of supervision means watchful care or management: {congressional oversight of intelligence agencies}, {regulatory oversight}.

Oversimplification is the act of making something seem simpler than it actually is, usually by ignoring important complexities or nuances. The word often appears as a criticism: {To say the war was about oil is an oversimplification}. To oversimplify is to reduce something to terms that distort or misrepresent it.

Oversimplified describes something that has been made too simple, stripping away important nuances, complications, or details that matter. When an argument or explanation is oversimplified, it fails to account for the complexity of the actual situation: {That's an oversimplified view of why the war started}. The term often carries a critical tone, suggesting that whoever did the simplifying has missed something essential or is being intellectually lazy.

To oversimplify is to reduce something complex to a version so stripped-down that it becomes misleading or inaccurate. The word implies going too far in pursuit of clarity: {That explanation oversimplifies the causes of the war}. Politicians and pundits are often accused of oversimplifying when nuance matters.

Oversize describes something larger than standard or expected dimensions: {oversize luggage}, {oversize load}. The term appears on shipping labels, clothing tags, and highway warning signs. As a noun, oversize refers to items exceeding normal size limits. Also spelled oversized, with no difference in meaning.

Oversized means larger than standard or expected dimensions: {an oversized sweater}, {oversized luggage that won't fit in the overhead bin}. The word often suggests deliberate excess—oversized sunglasses as a fashion choice, an oversized chair for comfort. Sometimes it implies problematic bulk: {The oversized package required special shipping}.

To oversleep is to sleep longer than intended, typically missing an alarm or appointment: {I overslept and missed my flight}. The word implies sleeping past a point when you should have woken—whether for work, school, or other obligations. Past tense: overslept.

Oversleeping is sleeping longer than intended or beyond a set time. It usually implies missing something—an alarm, an appointment, work: {I overslept and missed my flight}. The word can also describe sleeping more than is healthy or necessary: {Oversleeping on weekends throws off your schedule}.

Overslept is the past tense of oversleep—to sleep longer than intended or beyond a set time: {I overslept and missed my flight}. The word implies failure to wake when one should have, whether from exhaustion, a missed alarm, or simple accident.

Oversold describes something promoted beyond its actual merit or value. A product is oversold when marketing claims exceed what it delivers: {The movie was oversold—critics called it a masterpiece, but it was just okay}. In finance, oversold describes a stock or market that has declined sharply and may be undervalued, suggesting a potential rebound. A flight or venue is oversold when more tickets have been sold than seats available.

Overspecialization is excessive narrowing of focus, skill, or function—specialization taken too far. A species that overspecializes may thrive in one niche but face extinction when conditions change. In careers, overspecialization can make someone highly expert but unemployable outside a narrow field: {His overspecialization in medieval Icelandic poetry limited his job prospects}. The term implies vulnerability through lack of adaptability.
clues: Depth at the cost of breadth

definition: Overspending is spending more money than you should or more than you have. It can describe personal habits {overspending on credit cards} or institutional excess {government overspending}. The word implies crossing some threshold—a budget, an income level, or reasonable limits: {Holiday overspending left them in debt through February}.

Overspent is the past tense of overspend—to spend more money than you have or more than you intended: {We overspent on vacation and had to cut back the next month}. As an adjective, it describes someone who has exhausted their budget: {The overspent department requested emergency funds}.

To overstay is to remain somewhere longer than intended, permitted, or welcome. You can overstay a visa, overstay your welcome, or overstay a visit. The word implies exceeding some limit—official or social: {We overstayed our welcome and they stopped inviting us}. {His visa expired after he overstayed by three months}.

Overstayed is the past tense of overstay, meaning to remain somewhere longer than intended, allowed, or welcome. Someone overstays a visa by remaining in a country past its expiration. A guest who overstays their welcome has lingered until the host wants them gone: {We overstayed by three days and could tell they were ready for us to leave}.

To overstep is to go beyond acceptable limits or boundaries. The word almost always appears with an object indicating what was exceeded: overstep one's {authority}, overstep one's {bounds}, overstep the {mark}. {The manager overstepped by making promises he couldn't keep.} The suggestion is of someone acting presumptuously or exceeding their rightful scope.

Overstepped is the past tense of overstep, meaning to go beyond acceptable limits or boundaries. Someone who overstepped exceeded their authority, violated social norms, or crossed a line: {He overstepped when he criticized her parenting}. The word implies transgression—not just going far, but going too far.

Overstepping is going beyond proper limits or boundaries. The word usually appears with bounds or a similar object: {overstepping his authority}, {overstepping the bounds of decency}. Someone who oversteps has exceeded what's appropriate for their role or position: {The committee felt the director was overstepping by making the decision unilaterally}.

Oversteps means to go beyond acceptable limits or boundaries, typically of authority, propriety, or one's role. When someone oversteps, they exceed what is appropriate or permitted: {She oversteps her authority when she makes decisions without consulting the board}. The word often appears with bounds or mark: {He oversteps the bounds of decency}. The singular overstep functions as both verb and noun, referring to a single instance of going too far.

To overstimulate is to provide too much stimulation, whether sensory, emotional, or mental. The term appears frequently in discussions of child development, where bright lights, loud sounds, or too much activity can overstimulate infants and toddlers, leading to fussiness or meltdowns. Adults can also become overstimulated, particularly in environments with excessive noise, crowds, or information. {The casino's flashing lights and constant noise overstimulated her senses.} The related adjective overstimulated describes someone in this overwhelmed state.

Overstimulated describes a state of excessive sensory or mental input—when sounds, lights, activity, or demands overwhelm the nervous system's capacity to process them. Children become overstimulated at birthday parties; adults at crowded airports. The term appears frequently in discussions of autism and sensory processing: {She left the concert early, completely overstimulated}. The related noun is overstimulation.

Overstimulating describes something that provides too much sensory input, excitement, or mental demand. An overstimulating environment—bright lights, loud sounds, constant motion—can overwhelm the senses and cause anxiety or fatigue: {The casino was overstimulating for her}. The term appears often in discussions of child development and neurodivergence, where sensitivity to stimulation varies widely.

Overstimulation is the state of having too much sensory input, mental activity, or external stimulation to process comfortably. It commonly describes what happens to infants and young children when bombarded with noise, light, or activity, leading to fussiness or meltdowns. Adults use it too, especially in discussions of sensory processing: {The crowded mall left me in a state of overstimulation}. The term also applies to excessive nerve or muscle activation in medical contexts.

Overstock means to supply with more inventory than needed or can be sold. Retailers who overstock tie up capital in goods that may require discounting to move. As a noun, overstock refers to the excess merchandise itself: {The store held a clearance sale to get rid of overstock}. The adjective overstocked describes the resulting condition: {an overstocked warehouse}.

The overstory is the uppermost layer of foliage in a forest—the canopy formed by the crowns of the tallest trees. It contrasts with the understory, the vegetation growing beneath. The term appears in ecology and forestry: {The overstory blocked most of the sunlight from reaching the forest floor}.

To overstretch is to stretch something beyond its capacity or safe limits. Muscles overstretch and tear. Resources overstretch when demands exceed supply. The word often describes institutional strain: {The military is overstretched by commitments on multiple fronts}. To overstretch yourself is to take on more than you can handle.
