The term usually appears in {paleo diet}, an eating approach that mimics ancestral patterns—meat, fish, vegetables, nuts, and fruit while avoiding grains, dairy, and processed foods. As an adjective, paleo describes this lifestyle: {paleo recipes}, {going paleo}.

Paleolithic means of or relating to the earliest period of the Stone Age, when humans first developed stone tools. The era spans from roughly 2.5 million years ago to about 10,000 BCE. In casual use, paleolithic describes anything primitively old or outdated: {His views on women are paleolithic}. The paleo diet claims inspiration from this era. (Capitalized Paleolithic is the standard form in scholarly contexts.)

A paleontologist is a scientist who studies prehistoric life through fossils—the preserved remains and traces of ancient organisms. The work spans dinosaur bones, plant impressions, and microscopic organisms, reconstructing Earth's biological history: {The paleontologist spent years excavating the dig site}. The field bridges biology and geology.

Paleontologists are scientists who study prehistoric life through fossils—the preserved remains and traces of ancient organisms. They reconstruct extinct species, trace evolutionary lineages, and piece together past ecosystems: {Paleontologists discovered a new dinosaur species in Montana}. The field bridges biology and geology, requiring expertise in both living systems and rock formations.

Paleontology is the scientific study of ancient life through fossils—the preserved remains or traces of organisms from past geological periods. Paleontologists examine bones, shells, footprints, and other evidence to reconstruct extinct species and understand how life evolved over millions of years. {The museum's paleontology department recently unveiled a new dinosaur skeleton.}

Pales is the third-person singular of pale, meaning to become less intense or significant by comparison: {Her accomplishments pale next to his}. Things that pale lose color or vitality. The noun pales are pointed wooden stakes forming a fence—the origin of {beyond the pale}, meaning outside acceptable boundaries. A pale was historically a fenced territory under particular jurisdiction.

A palette is a board on which an artist mixes paints, traditionally held in one hand while painting with the other. By extension, palette means the range of colors an artist uses or the range of elements available in any creative domain: {The designer works with a muted palette}. A palette can also be a range of flavors in food and wine. In computing, a palette is a set of available colors or tools in graphics software.

Palettes is the plural of palette, a board on which an artist arranges and mixes paints. By extension, a palette is any range of colors or elements available for use: {The designer works with a muted palette}, {The chef's palette includes Asian and Mediterranean flavors}. In computing, a palette is a set of available colors, tools, or options displayed for selection.

Palimony is financial support paid by one partner to another after the end of a long-term relationship in which the couple was not married. The term blends "pal" with "alimony" and emerged in the 1970s from a famous lawsuit involving actor Lee Marvin. Unlike alimony, palimony has no automatic legal standing and typically requires proof of an agreement between partners. {She sued for palimony after their fifteen-year relationship ended.}

A palindrome is a word, phrase, or sequence that reads the same backward as forward. Classic examples include *madam*, *racecar*, and *A man, a plan, a canal: Panama*. Spaces and punctuation are typically ignored when determining whether something qualifies. The concept extends to numbers: 12321 is a numeric palindrome.

Palindromes are words, phrases, or sequences that read the same backward as forward. Simple examples include "radar" and "noon"; longer ones require ignoring spaces and punctuation: {A man, a plan, a canal: Panama}. The concept extends beyond language to numbers and DNA sequences. Crafting palindromes is a minor literary amusement.

A palisade is a fence of wooden stakes or iron bars set firmly in the ground, forming a defensive barrier. Historically, palisades surrounded forts and settlements for protection against attack. The word extends to any row of tall, narrow objects resembling such a fence: {a palisade of cliffs along the river}. The Palisades along the Hudson River took their name from this resemblance.

Palisades are a row of wooden stakes or iron railings set in the ground to form a fence or defensive barrier. The term also describes a line of steep cliffs, especially those rising along a river or coastline: {The Hudson River palisades are a dramatic sight from Manhattan}. The plural suggests a continuous formation rather than a single point. (Capitalized Palisades often refers to specific geographic features or place names.)

A pall is a cloth draped over a coffin, hearse, or tomb, which gives rise to its figurative meaning: something that covers or hangs over in a gloomy way. {A pall of smoke hung over the city.} {The bad news cast a pall over the celebration.} As a verb, pall means to become dull or less interesting through familiarity or excess: {The novelty of working from home eventually palled.}

A pallbearer is one of several people who carry or escort a coffin at a funeral. The term comes from the pall, a cloth draped over a coffin. Pallbearers are typically chosen from close friends or family members of the deceased: {He was honored to serve as a pallbearer at his uncle's funeral}.

Pallbearers are the people who carry a coffin at a funeral, typically six or eight, walking in formation from hearse to gravesite. The role is usually given to close friends or family members of the deceased as a mark of honor: {His brothers and childhood friends served as pallbearers}. Honorary pallbearers walk alongside without actually bearing weight.

Pallet is most likely to be encountered as a noun designating a platform used for storage and shipment of boxed or wrapped goods. It’s typically made of wood and is moved with a forklift. A different pallet is a small, hard bed, or a hard mattress. A painter’s pallet (also spelled palette) is the colors found in his or her works, or the board that actually holds little blobs of paint while in use.

Pallets are portable wooden platforms used to stack goods for storage and shipping. Forklifts slide underneath to move heavy loads. The word also names a makeshift bed—a thin mattress or pile of blankets on the floor: {She made up a pallet for the overnight guest}. In art, a pallet (usually spelled palette) holds paint for mixing.

The palm is the inner surface of the hand between the wrist and fingers. To palm something is to conceal it in your hand, as a magician palms a card or a basketball player illegally palms the ball. To {grease someone's palm} is to bribe them. To {have someone in the palm of your hand} is to have them under your control. Palm also names a family of tropical trees with fan-shaped or feather-shaped leaves and no branches—the coconut palm, date palm, oil palm. Palm fronds have long symbolized victory and peace; {Palm Sunday} commemorates Jesus's entry into Jerusalem, when crowds waved palm branches. (Capitalized Palm appears in product names like Palm Pilot.)

Palmed is the past tense of palm, meaning to conceal something in the hand. A magician palms a coin; a card cheat palms an ace. The word suggests sleight of hand and deception: {He palmed the stolen ring before anyone noticed}. To {palm off} is to pass something inferior as genuine: {They palmed off cheap imitations as designer goods}.

A palmetto is a type of fan palm with fan-shaped leaves, native to the southeastern United States and Caribbean. The cabbage palmetto is particularly associated with South Carolina, appearing on its state flag: {palmetto-lined beaches}, {a grove of palmettos}. The word comes from Spanish for "little palm." (Capitalized Palmetto often appears in proper names associated with South Carolina.)

Palming is concealing something in the palm of your hand, especially to steal or cheat: {She was caught palming merchandise at the store}. Magicians palm cards and coins to create illusions. In basketball, palming is an illegal move where a player's hand rotates under the ball while dribbling. The word also names an eye relaxation technique where you cover closed eyes with cupped palms.

Palmistry is the practice of reading a person's character or predicting their future by examining the lines and features of their palm. Also called palm reading or chiromancy, it has ancient roots across many cultures but no scientific validity: {She visited a palmist at the county fair}. The adjective is palmistic.

Palmreading is the practice of interpreting the lines, shapes, and features of a person's palm to reveal character traits or predict their future. Also called palmistry or chiromancy. A palmreader examines the major lines—life, heart, head—along with mounts and finger lengths: {She had her palmreading done at the fair}. Often spelled as two words: palm reading.

Palms are the inner surfaces of the hands, from wrist to fingers. To palm something is to conceal it in the hand: {The magician palmed the coin}. To palm off is to dispose of something deceptively: {He tried to palm off the forgery as genuine}. Palm also refers to tropical trees with fan-shaped or feathery leaves, or a branch carried as a symbol of victory. To win the palm is to triumph.

A palomino is a horse with a golden or tan coat and a white or cream-colored mane and tail. The coloring appears across many breeds and is prized for its striking appearance: {She rode a palomino in the parade}. The term comes from Spanish and evokes the romanticized imagery of the American West.

Palominos are horses with a golden or tan coat and a white or cream-colored mane and tail. The coloring occurs across many breeds and is particularly associated with American quarter horses and Western riding. {A palomino stood at the fence, its pale mane catching the light.}

Palpable describes something so intense or present it seems physically touchable. A doctor performs a palpable exam by feeling with the hands—checking for lumps, tenderness, swelling. The figurative sense dominates: {The tension in the room was palpable}. Palpable relief, palpable excitement, palpable fear—emotions strong enough to feel almost tangible.

Palpitating describes a heart beating rapidly, strongly, or irregularly—often from exertion, fear, or excitement: {She stood there, heart palpitating, waiting for the results}. The word extends to any trembling or quivering sensation: {palpitating with anticipation}. Palpitations are the noun form, typically describing the unsettling awareness of one's own heartbeat.

Palpitation is an awareness of one's own heartbeat, especially when it feels rapid, irregular, or unusually forceful. The sensation often accompanies anxiety, exertion, or caffeine intake: {She felt palpitations before the interview}. Usually plural: {heart palpitations}. The word extends figuratively to any trembling or fluttering excitement.

Palpitations are heartbeats you become uncomfortably aware of—racing, pounding, fluttering, or skipping. The heart may actually beat irregularly, or it may beat normally while feeling abnormal. Causes range from caffeine and anxiety to cardiac arrhythmias. {She felt palpitations after her third cup of coffee.} The singular palpitation exists but rarely appears outside medical contexts.

Pals are friends, typically close ones with an easy, familiar relationship. The word suggests warmth without formality: {We've been pals since college}. As a verb, to pal around is to spend time together casually: {They palled around all summer}. Pal can also be a form of address, sometimes friendly, sometimes confrontational: {Listen here, pal}.

Palsy is paralysis, especially partial paralysis accompanied by involuntary tremors. The term appears in medical conditions like cerebral palsy and Bell's palsy. In older usage, palsy could mean any trembling or weakness: {stricken with palsy}. As a verb, to palsy is to paralyze or render helpless: {Fear palsied his limbs}.

Pampas are the vast, treeless grasslands of South America, especially in Argentina and Uruguay. The word is Spanish, borrowed from Quechua. In English, pampas usually appears with the definite article: {gauchos riding across the pampas}. Pampas grass is a tall ornamental plant with feathery plumes, native to these plains but now common in landscaping worldwide.

To pamper is to treat with excessive care and attention, indulging someone's desires and shielding them from discomfort: {She pampered herself with a spa day}, {pampered pets}. The word often implies luxury or spoiling—giving more comfort than is strictly necessary. A pampered child may grow up expecting special treatment.

Pampered describes someone who has been treated with excessive care, comfort, or indulgence—often to the point of spoiling. A pampered {child} gets whatever they want. A pampered {pet} eats better than most people. The word can be neutral or slightly disapproving, suggesting someone unaccustomed to hardship: {She lived a pampered life until the money ran out}. To pamper is to indulge in this way.

Pampering is indulgent care or attention—treating someone (or yourself) with unusual comfort and luxury. A spa day, breakfast in bed, or letting a child skip chores might all count as pampering. The word carries a hint of excess: {After the project ended, she spent a week pampering herself}. What qualifies as pampering depends on what's normal—for some, it's a massage; for others, simply sleeping in.

To pamper is to treat someone with excessive care and attention, indulging their every comfort: {She pampers herself with spa days}. Pampers is the third-person singular form of this verb: {He pampers his grandchildren shamelessly}. The word suggests spoiling or coddling, giving someone more luxury or attention than strictly necessary. (Capitalized Pampers is the diaper brand.)

A pamphlet is a small, unbound booklet—typically just a few pages, stapled or folded—covering a single topic. Pamphlets often present information, arguments, or propaganda: {a political pamphlet}, {health pamphlets in the waiting room}. Historically, pamphlets were a key medium for disseminating ideas before mass media.

A pamphleteer is someone who writes and distributes pamphlets, especially on political or controversial subjects. The term evokes an era when pamphlets were a primary medium for public debate—think Thomas Paine or Jonathan Swift. As a verb, to pamphleteer is to produce such writings: {He pamphleteered against the monarchy for years}.

Pamphleteers are writers or distributors of pamphlets—short printed works typically advocating a political or social position. The term evokes an era before mass media when pamphlets were primary vehicles for public argument: {The pamphleteers of the American Revolution shaped colonial opinion}. Today it often carries a slightly dismissive tone, suggesting partisan zeal over balanced analysis.

Pamphlets is the plural of pamphlet, a small unbound booklet or leaflet, typically covering a single topic. Pamphlets have historically served political, religious, and educational purposes—distributed to spread ideas cheaply and widely: {Revolutionary pamphlets circulated through the colonies}. Today the word often suggests informational brochures: {The doctor's office had pamphlets on diabetes}.

A pan is a dish for cooking food in an oven or over heat (frying pan, roasting pan). A pan is usually shallower than a pot. If you pan for gold, you separate rock from gold in a shallow pan. If you pan something such as a movie or proposal, you criticize it severely. A different verb pan is related to panorama, and describes the movement of a camera: The cinematographer panned across the stage. Finally, pan is an adjective or combining form meaning all: The athlete competed in the Pan-American games.

A panacea is a cure for all diseases or difficulties—a universal remedy. The word appears most often in the negative: {There's no panacea for poverty}. When someone dismisses a proposed solution as {not a panacea}, they mean it won't solve everything, though it may help somewhat.

Panache is flamboyant confidence and style—a distinctive flair that makes ordinary actions seem impressive. Someone who dresses with panache has bold, assured taste. To do something with panache is to do it with verve and showmanship: {She handled the crisis with panache}. The word implies not just competence but a certain swagger in the execution.

A panama is a lightweight hat made from plaited leaves of a Central American plant, traditionally worn in warm weather. Despite the name, the hats originated in Ecuador but gained their name from Panama, where they were widely sold to travelers crossing the isthmus. {He wore a cream panama tilted at a rakish angle.} (Capitalized Panama is the country.)

A pancake is a flat, round cake made from batter and cooked on both sides on a griddle or in a pan. Pancakes are typically eaten for breakfast with toppings like syrup or fruit. The flatness gives rise to figurative uses: something {flat as a pancake} is extremely level, and to pancake is to flatten or collapse: {The building pancaked during the earthquake}.

Pancaked is the past tense of pancake, meaning to flatten or collapse into a compressed layer. Buildings pancake when floors collapse onto each other: {The tower pancaked in seconds}. Aircraft pancake when they drop flat onto a runway or water. In skiing or snowboarding, to pancake is to fall flat: {He caught an edge and pancaked hard}.

Pancakes are flat, round cakes made from batter and cooked on a griddle or pan. The American version is thick and fluffy, typically served in stacks with butter and maple syrup: {We had pancakes for breakfast}. British pancakes are thinner, closer to French crêpes. The word also works as a verb meaning to flatten or collapse: {The building pancaked during the earthquake}.

Pancetta is Italian cured pork belly, similar to bacon but unsmoked. It comes in flat slabs or rolled into a cylinder, sliced thin for sandwiches or diced for cooking. Pancetta adds rich, savory depth to pasta dishes like carbonara: {Render the pancetta until crispy, then add the garlic}.

The pancreas is a large gland behind the stomach that serves two functions: it secretes digestive enzymes into the small intestine, and it produces hormones—including insulin—that regulate blood sugar. Inflammation of the pancreas is pancreatitis. The adjective is pancreatic: {pancreatic cancer}, {pancreatic enzymes}.

A panda is a large black-and-white bear native to China, known for eating bamboo and serving as a symbol of wildlife conservation. The term usually means the giant panda; the red panda is a smaller, unrelated animal with reddish fur and a bushy tail. {We saw the pandas at the zoo.}

Pandas are large bearlike mammals native to central China, with distinctive black and white markings. They eat almost exclusively bamboo. The giant panda is an endangered species and a symbol of wildlife conservation. The lesser-known red panda is a smaller, russet-colored animal more closely related to raccoons. In computing, pandas (often lowercase) is a popular Python library for data analysis and manipulation: {I used pandas to clean the dataset}.

A pandemic is an outbreak of disease that spreads across multiple countries or continents, affecting large populations. Distinguished from an epidemic, which is more geographically contained: {The 1918 flu pandemic killed millions worldwide}. The word gained everyday currency during the COVID-19 pandemic that began in 2020. Figuratively, pandemic describes anything spreading uncontrollably: {a pandemic of misinformation}.

Pandemics is the plural of pandemic, a disease outbreak that spreads across multiple countries or continents, affecting large populations. A pandemic differs from an epidemic mainly in geographic scope: {The 1918 flu and COVID-19 were pandemics; Ebola outbreaks have been epidemics}. The word also works as an adjective: {pandemic influenza}, {pandemic proportions}.

Pandemonium is wild uproar and chaos—noise, confusion, and disorder all at once. The word suggests a scene where control has broken down completely: {Pandemonium erupted when the verdict was announced}. Originally the name of the capital of Hell in Milton's *Paradise Lost*, it now describes any place or situation of tumultuous chaos.

To pander is to gratify or indulge someone's weaknesses, desires, or prejudices—typically for gain or approval. Politicians pander to voters, entertainers pander to audiences: {The film panders to the lowest common denominator}. A panderer caters to base instincts rather than challenging them. The noun pander, now rare, originally meant a go-between in sexual intrigues—a pimp.

Pandered is the past tense of pander, meaning to gratify or indulge someone's weaknesses, desires, or base instincts—often for personal gain. Politicians pander to voters by telling them what they want to hear. Media outlets pander to audiences with sensational content. The word carries disapproval, implying that the pandering sacrifices integrity: {The film pandered to the lowest common denominator}.

Pandering is catering to base desires or prejudices, especially to gain approval or advantage. A politician panders when they tell audiences whatever they want to hear rather than what's true or responsible: {The speech was pure pandering to the base}. The word carries contempt—pandering suggests cynical manipulation rather than genuine responsiveness. In legal contexts, pandering specifically means procuring customers for prostitutes.

Panders means caters to base desires or weaknesses, often in a calculated or cynical way. A politician who panders tells audiences what they want to hear rather than what's true. A movie that panders relies on cheap thrills instead of substance. {The ad campaign panders to fears about crime}. The word carries strong disapproval—it suggests sacrificing integrity for approval or profit.

A pane is a single sheet of glass in a window or door. Windows may have multiple panes separated by frames: {a six-pane window}. The word extends to other flat, framed sections: {a pane of ice}, {the panes of a honeycomb}. In computing, a pane is a bounded section of a window display.

Paneer is a fresh cheese common in South Asian cooking, made by curdling milk with lemon juice or vinegar and pressing the curds into a firm block. Unlike aged cheeses, it's mild and doesn't melt when heated, making it ideal for dishes like {palak paneer} or {paneer tikka}. The texture resembles firm tofu.

Panel has two main meanings. The first is a broad, flat surface or object with a particular purpose (solar panel, instrument panel). This meaning includes broad, flat boards used in building or to line interior walls. The second is a group of people with a particular task (advisory panel, panel of experts). To panel a room is to line its walls with panels; you may end up with an oak-paneled room.

Paneling is wooden boards or other material used to cover walls or ceilings, typically for decoration or insulation. It can refer to the material itself or the finished surface: {The den had dark oak paneling}. Wood paneling was especially popular in mid-twentieth-century American homes. The word also covers the act of installing such material: {We spent the weekend paneling the basement}.

A panelist is a member of a panel—a group assembled for discussion, judging, or decision-making. The term appears most often in contexts of talk shows, academic conferences, and competitions: {The panelists debated healthcare reform}. Game shows feature celebrity panelists who answer questions or evaluate contestants.

Panels are distinct sections or pieces that form part of a larger whole. A door may have raised panels; a dress may be cut from panels of fabric; a comic strip tells its story through sequential panels. A panel is also a group assembled for discussion, judgment, or advice: {a panel of experts}, {a jury panel}. Control panels and instrument panels group switches and displays. To panel a room is to cover its walls with wooden panels.

Panes is the plural of pane, a sheet of glass fitted into a window or door frame. A single window may contain multiple panes: {The old farmhouse had windows with twelve panes each}. By extension, pane applies to any flat section within a larger surface—a panel in a door, or a rectangular area in a software interface: {Drag the file to the left pane}.

Panettone is a tall, dome-shaped Italian sweet bread studded with dried fruit and candied citrus peel, traditionally eaten at Christmas. The dough is enriched with butter and eggs, giving it a light, fluffy texture: {We brought a panettone to Christmas dinner}. Plural: panettoni or panettones.

A panflute is a wind instrument made of graduated tubes bound together, played by blowing across the open tops. Each tube produces a single note, with pitch determined by length. The instrument appears across many cultures—ancient Greece, the Andes, Eastern Europe—and produces a breathy, ethereal sound: {The panflute melody floated over the crowd}. Also spelled pan flute.

A pang is a sudden, sharp feeling of physical or emotional pain. Physical pangs are typically brief and intense—hunger pangs, pangs of labor. Emotional pangs accompany distressing feelings like guilt, remorse, or longing: {She felt a pang of regret when she saw her old house}. The word nearly always appears with "of" followed by the specific sensation, emphasizing the acute but momentary nature of the discomfort.

A pangolin is a scaly mammal native to Africa and Asia, covered in overlapping keratin plates that form protective armor. When threatened, it curls into a tight ball. Pangolins are nocturnal insectivores, using long sticky tongues to extract ants and termites from nests. They are among the world's most trafficked animals, hunted for their scales and meat.

Pangolins are scaly mammals found in Africa and Asia, the only mammals covered entirely in keratin scales. They curl into a ball when threatened and feed almost exclusively on ants and termites. Pangolins are among the world's most trafficked animals, hunted for their scales and meat despite international protections.

Pangs are sudden sharp pains or spasms, physical or emotional. Hunger pangs grip the stomach. Pangs of guilt or remorse strike the conscience. The word almost always appears in the plural and typically with an of-phrase naming the cause: {pangs of jealousy}, {the pangs of unrequited love}.

A panhandle is a narrow strip of territory projecting from a larger region, shaped like the handle of a pan: {the Texas panhandle}, {the Florida panhandle}. The verb panhandle means to beg for money in public places, typically by approaching strangers on the street: {He panhandled outside the subway station}. A panhandler is someone who does this regularly.

Panhandled is the past tense of panhandle, meaning to beg for money in public places, typically on streets or sidewalks: {He panhandled outside the subway station for years}. The term comes from the image of extending a pan to collect coins. Panhandling usually implies direct solicitation from strangers rather than passive begging with a sign.

A panhandler is someone who begs for money in public places, typically on city streets. The term is American and slightly euphemistic—it sounds more active than "beggar," suggesting someone working a stretch of sidewalk: {Panhandlers approached us outside the subway station}. The verb is panhandle: {He panhandled for bus fare}.

Panhandlers are people who beg for money in public places, typically on sidewalks or street corners. The term comes from the image of holding out a pan to collect coins. Panhandling usually involves direct solicitation from passersby: {Panhandlers congregated near the subway entrance}. The word carries a slightly dismissive tone compared to simply calling someone homeless or a beggar.

Panhandles works as both noun and verb. A panhandle is a narrow strip of territory projecting from a larger region, resembling a pan's handle: {the Texas Panhandle}, {the Florida Panhandle}. To panhandle is to beg for money in public places, typically by approaching strangers on the street: {He panhandles outside the subway station}. A panhandler is someone who does this regularly.

Panhandling is begging for money in public places, typically on streets or sidewalks. The term is American and slightly euphemistic—it sounds more official than "begging," which is why it appears in municipal codes and news reports: {The city passed an ordinance against aggressive panhandling}. A panhandler asks strangers for spare change, often with a sign or cup.

Panic is sudden, overwhelming fear that disrupts rational thought. A crowd may panic during a fire; an investor may panic when markets drop. The adjective panicked describes someone in this state: {a panicked expression}. To panic is to succumb to such fear: {Don't panic}. A panic attack is an episode of intense anxiety with physical symptoms. As slang, panic means to make someone laugh uncontrollably: {That comedian panics me}.

Panicked is the past tense of panic—to suddenly lose composure through fear or anxiety. Someone who panicked acted rashly under pressure: {She panicked and slammed the brakes}. The word can also work as an adjective describing the state itself: {panicked investors sold everything}, {a panicked look in his eyes}.

Panicking is the present participle of panic—experiencing or causing sudden, overwhelming fear that overrides rational thought. Someone panicking may freeze, flee, or act erratically: {She was panicking about the deadline}. Markets panic when investors sell frantically. The spelling retains the K to preserve the hard C sound before -ing.

Panicky describes someone gripped by panic—frantic, overwhelmed by sudden fear or anxiety. It can also describe actions or decisions made in that state: {a panicky phone call}, {panicky selling on the stock market}. The word carries a slightly informal or colloquial tone compared to "panicked."

Panics is the plural of panic—sudden episodes of overwhelming fear or anxiety. Financial panics are crises where markets collapse and investors rush to sell. Panic attacks are intense physical episodes of terror. The verb form means to cause or experience sudden fear: {The crowd panics when the lights go out}, {News of the shortage panicked shoppers}.

A panini is a sandwich made with Italian bread, typically grilled or pressed until the bread is crispy and the filling is warm. The word is Italian plural, but in English panini functions as singular: {I'll have a panini}. Some speakers use paninis as the English plural, others stick with panini for both. The sandwiches usually feature ingredients like mozzarella, tomatoes, and cured meats.

Paninis is a common English plural of panini, the Italian pressed sandwich made with bread like ciabatta or focaccia and grilled until the fillings are warm and the exterior is crisp. In Italian, panini is already plural (one panino, two panini), but English speakers treat it as singular: {I ordered a panini}. The double-plural paninis follows naturally: {The café serves excellent paninis}.

Panna cotta is an Italian dessert of sweetened cream set with gelatin, served chilled. The name means "cooked cream" in Italian. It's typically unmolded onto a plate and served with fruit, caramel, or chocolate sauce: {The restaurant's panna cotta was silky and not too sweet}. Also spelled as two words: panna cotta.

Panned is the past tense of pan in its critical sense: to disparage or harshly criticize, especially a creative work. {The film was panned by critics but beloved by audiences.} The metaphor comes from panning for gold—sifting through material and finding nothing of value. Separately, panned describes camera movement sweeping horizontally across a scene.

Panning has several meanings united by sweeping horizontal movement. In film and photography, to pan is to rotate the camera sideways, following action or surveying a scene: {The camera panned across the crowd}. In cooking, panning means cooking in a pan. In gold prospecting, panning is swirling water and sediment in a shallow pan to separate gold. To pan something is also to criticize it harshly: {Critics panned the film}. In audio, panning shifts sound between left and right channels.

A panopticon is a prison designed so that a single guard can observe all inmates without them knowing whether they're being watched—a central tower surrounded by cells. The concept, proposed by philosopher Jeremy Bentham in the 18th century, has become a metaphor for surveillance and social control: {Social media has created a digital panopticon where everyone monitors everyone else}.

A panorama is a wide, unobstructed view extending in all directions: {The summit offered a panorama of the valley below}. Originally, panoramas were large circular paintings viewed from inside, creating an illusion of being surrounded by a scene. The word now applies to any sweeping visual or comprehensive survey: {a panorama of 20th-century art}, {panoramic photographs} that capture wider angles than standard shots.

Panoramas is the plural of panorama—a wide, unobstructed view of a landscape or scene: {The hiking trail offers stunning panoramas of the valley}. The term extends to comprehensive surveys of a subject: {a panorama of 20th-century art}. In photography, panoramas are images stitched together to capture a wider field than a single frame allows.

A panpipe is a wind instrument made of tubes of graduated length bound together, played by blowing across the open tops. The tubes produce different pitches according to their length. Often called panpipes in the plural, the instrument appears in folk music traditions worldwide: {the haunting sound of Andean panpipes}.

Panpipes are a wind instrument made of graduated tubes bound together, played by blowing across their open tops. Each tube produces a different pitch based on its length. The instrument appears across many cultures, from ancient Greece (where myth attributes it to the god Pan) to the Andes. Also called a pan flute.

Pans are broad, shallow cooking vessels, typically metal, used on stovetops for frying, sautéing, and simmering. The word extends to similar containers used for other purposes: a {gold pan} for prospecting, a {bedpan} for the bedridden, or the pan of a toilet. To pan is to wash gravel in search of gold, or to criticize harshly: {Critics panned the film}. In filmmaking, to pan is to rotate a camera horizontally across a scene.

Pansexual describes sexual or romantic attraction to people regardless of their gender or sex. Unlike bisexual, which historically implied attraction to two genders, pansexual emphasizes that gender is not a determining factor in attraction at all. The term gained currency in the early 21st century alongside increased recognition of nonbinary and transgender identities. {She identifies as pansexual because she's attracted to the person, not their gender.}

Pansexuality is sexual attraction that isn't limited by gender—attraction to people regardless of whether they're male, female, nonbinary, or otherwise. Where bisexuality historically implied attraction to two genders, pansexuality emphasizes that gender isn't a determining factor at all: {Her pansexuality means she's open to dating anyone she connects with}.

Pansexuals are people who experience sexual or romantic attraction regardless of gender identity or biological sex. The term distinguishes itself from bisexual by emphasizing attraction to all gender identities, including those outside the traditional male-female binary. {My friend came out as pansexual in college.} The singular pansexual functions as both noun and adjective: {a pansexual person}, {she identifies as pansexual}.

Pansies are garden flowers with velvety petals in varied colors, often with dark central markings that suggest a face. They bloom in cool weather and are popular for borders and containers. Pansy is also a derogatory term for an effeminate man or a weak, timid person: {Don't be such a pansy}. This slur, once common, now sounds dated.

A pansy is a garden flower with velvety, multicolored petals, often displaying a distinctive "face" pattern. The word is also a slur for an effeminate man or a gay man, or more broadly, someone considered weak or cowardly: {Don't be such a pansy}. The insult derives from the flower's delicate appearance and its association with effeminacy.

Pant describes rapid, shallow breathing—the kind that follows exertion or comes with strong emotion. Dogs pant to cool themselves; runners pant after sprints. To pant for something is to desire it intensely: {He panted for recognition}. As a noun, a pant is a single labored breath. Pants, the garment, is a separate word—pant as a modifier ({pant leg}, {pant suit}) is a back-formation from it.

Pantaloons are loose-fitting trousers, typically gathered at the ankle. The term evokes historical costume—the baggy breeches of commedia dell'arte characters or the tight-fitting men's trousers fashionable in the early 19th century. Today pantaloons sounds old-fashioned or theatrical: {The clown wore oversized pantaloons}. Sometimes shortened to pants, which became the standard American word for trousers.

Panted is the past tense of pant, meaning to breathe with short, quick breaths, typically from exertion or heat: {She panted after climbing the stairs}, {The dog panted in the summer heat}. By extension, to pant for something is to yearn for it intensely: {He panted for recognition}.

A pantheon is the collection of gods belonging to a particular religion or mythology: {the Greek pantheon}, {the Hindu pantheon}. By extension, a pantheon is any group of highly respected or influential figures in a field: {She earned her place in the pantheon of jazz greats}. The word suggests a kind of immortal status within a domain. (Capitalized Pantheon is the ancient Roman temple.)

Pantheons are collections of gods belonging to a particular religion or mythology: the Greek pantheon, the Norse pantheon, the Hindu pantheon. By extension, a pantheon is any group of exalted figures in a field: {She belongs in the pantheon of jazz greats}. The Pantheon in Rome was a temple dedicated to all gods, now a model for domed buildings worldwide.

A panther is a large wild cat, though the term applies differently depending on region. In North America, panther usually means a cougar or mountain lion. In other parts of the world, it refers to leopards, especially black leopards—cats whose dark coloration obscures their spots. The Florida panther is an endangered cougar subspecies native to southern Florida. {A black panther stalked through the jungle undergrowth.} (Capitalized Panther often refers to the Black Panther Party or the Marvel superhero.)

Panthers is the plural of panther, a word that covers several large cats. In the Americas, panther usually means a cougar or mountain lion. Elsewhere it typically refers to a leopard, especially a black one—technically a melanistic leopard, though {black panther} has become the common term. The Florida panther is an endangered cougar subspecies. {Panthers prowled the jungle's edge.}

Panties are women's or girls' underpants, typically lightweight and close-fitting. The word carries a slightly informal or intimate connotation compared to the neutral "underwear." In American English, panties is standard; British English more often uses knickers. {She packed three pairs of panties for the trip.}

Panting is rapid, shallow breathing, typically from exertion or heat. Dogs pant to cool themselves; humans pant after sprinting up stairs. The word extends to eager anticipation: {fans panting for the sequel}. As an adjective, it describes breathlessness: {She arrived at the door, panting and flushed}.

Panto is British shorthand for pantomime—a type of musical comedy theater traditionally performed around Christmas. These productions feature fairy-tale plots, audience participation, cross-dressing roles, and broad humor aimed at families: {We're taking the kids to the panto this year}. The word is informal and specifically British.

Pantomime is acting without words, using gestures and facial expressions to convey meaning: {The street performer pantomimed being trapped in a box}. As a noun, it refers to this form of expression or a performance using it. In British English, pantomime (often shortened to panto) is a type of comic theatrical production performed during the Christmas season, featuring fairy tales, audience participation, and cross-dressing actors. More broadly, pantomime describes any exaggerated show or empty display: {The trial was a pantomime of justice}.

Pantomimed is the past tense of pantomime—to act out something using gestures and body movements rather than words. Someone who pantomimed a message conveyed it through exaggerated physical expression: {She pantomimed drinking from a cup}, {He pantomimed confusion with a shrug and raised eyebrows}. The word implies theatrical, silent communication.

Pantomimes are theatrical performances that tell stories through exaggerated gesture, movement, and facial expression rather than spoken words. In British tradition, a pantomime (or panto) is a specific type of comedic holiday stage show featuring fairy tale plots, audience participation, and gender-swapped casting. The verb pantomime means to act something out silently with gestures: {He pantomimed opening a door}. By extension, pantomimes can describe any insincere or empty display: {The hearings were mere pantomimes of accountability}.

Pantomiming is acting out something through gesture and movement without speaking—the silent communication of mime. Someone pantomimes a phone call by holding their hand to their ear, or pantomimes drinking by tilting an imaginary cup. The word applies both to theatrical mime performance and everyday silent gesturing: {She was pantomiming something through the window, but I couldn't make it out}.

Pantries is the plural of pantry, a small room or closet used for storing food, dishes, and kitchen supplies. Historically, pantries were essential features of homes before refrigeration became common. The word now often describes any dedicated food storage space: {She stocked the pantries with canned goods before the storm}.

A pantry is a small room or closet used to store food, dishes, and kitchen supplies. Traditionally located near the kitchen, it keeps dry goods, canned items, and tableware organized and accessible: {The pasta is in the pantry}. A butler's pantry is a service area between kitchen and dining room for storing serving pieces and preparing food for the table.

Pants are a garment covering the body from waist to ankles, with separate sections for each leg. In American English, pants means trousers; in British English, pants means underpants. To pants someone is to yank their pants down as a prank. {She caught him with his pants down} means she found him unprepared or exposed. To {wear the pants} is to be the dominant partner in a relationship.

Pantsed is the past tense of pants, meaning to pull down someone's pants or trousers as a prank or humiliation: {He got pantsed in front of the whole gym class}. The act typically targets someone unaware, exposing their underwear or more. Pantsing is associated with schoolyard bullying and hazing rituals.

Pantsing is yanking someone's pants down as a prank or humiliation, typically from behind: {He got pantsed in the locker room}. The act is associated with schoolyard bullying and hazing rituals. In writing communities, pantsing refers to composing without an outline—flying by the seat of your pants—as opposed to plotting.

A pantsuit is a woman's matched set of jacket and trousers, worn as a coordinated outfit. The term emerged as women adopted tailored suits in professional settings where skirts had been standard. A pantsuit signals business formality: {She wore a navy pantsuit to the interview}. Hillary Clinton's colorful pantsuits became a signature style.

A pantsuit is a woman's coordinated outfit consisting of a jacket and matching trousers, designed to be worn together as a unified ensemble. The term emerged in the 1960s as women began wearing tailored pants in professional and formal settings previously dominated by skirts and dresses. Pantsuits became associated with women in business and politics, symbolizing professionalism and authority. {She wore a navy pantsuit to the interview.} The singular form pantsuit is also common.

Panty is the singular form of panties, women's or girls' underpants. The singular appears mainly as a modifier: {panty liner}, {panty hose}, {panty raid}. On its own, panty sounds either childish or sexualized, depending on context. The plural panties is standard for the garment itself.

Pantyhose are sheer nylon stockings fused to panties, worn as a single garment covering the legs and waist. They emerged in the 1960s alongside miniskirts and largely replaced garter-held stockings. The word is usually plural: {She bought three pairs of pantyhose}. British English prefers tights.

Pantywaist is a dismissive term for a weak, timid, or effeminate man—someone lacking courage or toughness: {Don't be such a pantywaist}. The word originally referred to a child's undergarment that buttoned at the waist, the association with children's clothing giving rise to the insult. Old-fashioned but still used.

A panzer is a German tank, especially from World War II. The word comes from German for "armor" and appears most often in historical contexts discussing Nazi Germany's armored divisions: {Rommel's panzers swept across North Africa}. In gaming and military history discussions, panzer often modifies other nouns: {panzer division}, {panzer corps}, {panzer tactics}.

Panzers are German tanks or armored vehicles, particularly those used in World War II. The word comes from German for "armor" and appears most often in historical contexts about the war: {Rommel's panzers swept across North Africa}. Panzer divisions were armored military units that formed the backbone of Germany's blitzkrieg tactics.

Papa is an informal, often affectionate word for father, used especially by young children or in families where it's the traditional term: {Give Papa a kiss}. In some cultures and regions, papa refers specifically to a grandfather. In the NATO phonetic alphabet, Papa represents the letter P.

The papacy is the office and authority of the Pope, the head of the Roman Catholic Church. It also refers to a particular pope's tenure: {The papacy of John Paul II lasted 27 years}. More broadly, the papacy denotes the system of church government centered on papal authority, often discussed in historical or political contexts: {the medieval papacy's influence on European monarchs}.

A papadam is a thin, crispy Indian flatbread made from lentil, chickpea, or rice flour, typically served as an accompaniment to meals or with chutneys as an appetizer. The discs are dried and then fried or roasted until they puff and crisp. Also spelled papadum, poppadom, or poppadum.

Papadams are thin, crispy Indian flatbreads made from lentil, chickpea, or rice flour, typically served as an appetizer or side dish. They're fried or roasted until brittle and often accompanied by chutneys: {We started with papadams and mango chutney}. Also spelled papadum, poppadom, or papad.

A papadom is a thin, crispy Indian flatbread made from lentil, chickpea, or rice flour, typically fried or roasted and served as an appetizer or side dish. Papadoms often accompany chutneys and pickles at the start of a meal: {We ordered papadoms while we waited for our curry}. Also spelled papadum, poppadom, or poppadum.

Papadoms, also spelled papadums or papads, are thin, crispy Indian flatbreads made from lentil, chickpea, or rice flour. They are typically served as an appetizer or side dish in South Asian cuisine, often accompanied by chutneys or pickles. Papadoms can be fried, roasted, or cooked over an open flame until they puff up and become crunchy. {We started the meal with papadoms and mango chutney.}

A papadum is a thin, crisp Indian flatbread made from lentil, chickpea, or rice flour, typically served as an appetizer or side dish. They're fried or roasted until crunchy and often accompanied by chutneys: {We ordered papadums while waiting for the main course}. Also spelled papadam, poppadom, or poppadum.

Papadums are thin, crispy Indian flatbreads made from lentil, chickpea, or rice flour, typically served as an appetizer or side dish. They're fried or roasted until brittle and often accompanied by chutneys: {We started with papadums and mango chutney}. Also spelled papadum, poppadom, or papadam.

Papal means relating to the pope, the head of the Roman Catholic Church. Papal {authority} is the power vested in the pope to govern church matters. A papal {bull} is an official decree issued by the pope, while a papal {conclave} is the assembly of cardinals that elects a new pope. The word appears almost exclusively in formal or religious contexts discussing Catholic Church governance and tradition.

Paparazzi are freelance photographers who aggressively pursue celebrities to capture candid shots for tabloids and gossip media. The word is Italian, borrowed from a photographer character in Fellini's 1960 film *La Dolce Vita*. A single such photographer is a paparazzo, though paparazzi often serves for both singular and plural: {The paparazzi swarmed the restaurant exit}.

A paparazzo is a freelance photographer who aggressively pursues celebrities to capture candid shots for tabloids and gossip media. The work often involves staking out restaurants, following cars, and invading private moments: {Paparazzi swarmed the actress as she left the hospital}. The plural paparazzi is more common than the singular, reflecting how they typically operate in packs.

Papaya is a large tropical fruit with orange flesh, black seeds, and a soft, butter-like texture when ripe. The fruit grows on a tall, palm-like tree native to Central America but now cultivated throughout the tropics. Papaya is eaten fresh, added to smoothies, or used in cooking—green papaya appears in Southeast Asian salads. The enzyme papain, extracted from papaya, is used as a meat tenderizer.

Papayas is the plural of papaya, a tropical fruit with orange flesh, black seeds, and soft, buttery texture when ripe. The large oblong fruits grow on fast-growing trees native to Central America. Green papayas are used in salads and cooking throughout Southeast Asia. {The papayas at the market were perfectly ripe.}

The core meaning of paper, a manufactured material for writing and drawing, inspires its many extended meanings. The mass noun refers to the substance generally, and paper (countable) or piece of paper denotes a single sheet of it. Some documents printed on paper, such as a newspaper or an academic report on a particular subject, can be called papers. Someone’s papers may be the documents establishing their identity, such as a passport or travel documents—or they may also be the a loosely defined collection of information on paper associated with a person: We found old love letters among her papers. As a verb, the most frequent meaning of paper pertains to wallpaper.

A paperback is a book with a flexible paper cover, as opposed to a hardcover with rigid boards. Paperbacks are cheaper to produce and lighter to carry. The term works as noun or adjective: {I'll wait for the paperback}, {the paperback edition}. Mass-market paperbacks are the small, inexpensive format sold in drugstores and airports; trade paperbacks are larger and pricier.

Paperbacks are books with flexible paper covers, as opposed to hardcovers with rigid boards. They're cheaper to produce and sell for less. A book typically appears first in hardcover, then later in paperback: {I'll wait for the paperback}. Mass-market paperbacks are the small, inexpensive editions sold in drugstores and airports; trade paperbacks are larger and printed on better paper.

A paperboy is a person, traditionally a boy or young man, who delivers newspapers to homes on a regular route. The job was once a common first employment for teenagers, though the role has largely been taken over by adults in cars. {The paperboy tossed the newspaper onto the porch.}

A paperclip is a small bent wire used to hold sheets of paper together. The familiar double-loop design has remained largely unchanged since the late 19th century. To paperclip documents is to fasten them this way: {I paperclipped the receipt to the form}. The word also appears as two words or hyphenated.

Paperclips is the plural of paperclip, a small bent wire device used to hold sheets of paper together. The standard design—a double-looped oval—has remained largely unchanged since its invention. Paperclips also get repurposed for small tasks: picking locks, resetting electronics, scratching unreachable itches. {I need some paperclips for these reports.}

Papercraft is the art of creating objects by cutting, folding, and assembling paper. The term covers a range of techniques from simple origami to elaborate three-dimensional models of buildings, characters, or vehicles constructed from printed templates: {She downloaded a papercraft pattern for a tiny house}. Unlike origami, papercraft typically involves cutting and gluing rather than folding alone.

A papercut is a small wound made by the edge of a sheet of paper slicing the skin. Despite being minor, papercuts are notoriously painful because they're shallow enough to expose nerve endings without drawing much blood: {I got a papercut opening the envelope}. The word also refers to the art of cutting decorative designs from paper.

Papercuts are small cuts on the skin caused by the edge of a sheet of paper. Despite being minor injuries, they're notorious for stinging disproportionately to their size. The term extends to minor but accumulating irritations: {Death by a thousand papercuts}—a situation where small problems compound into serious damage.

Papercutting is the art of cutting decorative designs from paper, typically using scissors or a knife. The craft appears across many cultures—Chinese jianzhi, Polish wycinanki, German scherenschnitte—each with distinctive patterns and techniques. Designs range from simple silhouettes to intricate lace-like compositions. The term also covers the finished artwork: {She framed the papercutting her grandmother made}.

Paperless describes systems or processes that eliminate paper documents in favor of digital alternatives: {a paperless office}, {paperless billing}. The term emerged with computing but gained momentum as environmental concerns made reducing paper use desirable. Going paperless promises efficiency and sustainability, though the fully paperless office remains more aspiration than reality for most workplaces.

Papers are documents, especially official ones establishing identity, status, or authorization: {The officer asked for my papers}. Immigration papers confirm legal residency. Walking papers means dismissal from a job. Divorce papers formalize the end of a marriage. Academic papers are scholarly essays. To paper something is to cover it with wallpaper, or to fill a venue with free tickets: {They papered the house to make the show look popular}.

A paperweight is a small, heavy object placed on loose papers to keep them from scattering. Paperweights are often decorative—glass, metal, or stone—and collected as ornaments. The function requires only weight and a flat bottom, so almost anything dense enough can serve: {She used a rock as a paperweight}.

Paperwork is the documents, forms, and administrative records required for official processes: {I spent the morning doing paperwork}. The term usually carries a tone of tedium—necessary but unexciting clerical tasks. Despite the name, paperwork now includes digital forms and electronic filing: {The paperwork for the loan application was all online}.

Papi is an affectionate Spanish term for father or daddy, borrowed into English primarily through Latino communities. In romantic or flirtatious contexts, it functions like "baby" or "honey" when addressing a man: {Hey papi, looking good}. The term carries warm, familiar connotations—playful when flirting, tender when addressing an actual father or older male figure.

A pappadom is a thin, crispy Indian flatbread made from lentil, chickpea, or rice flour, typically fried or roasted and served as an appetizer or side dish. Often accompanied by chutneys or yogurt-based dips: {We ordered pappadoms while waiting for the curry}. Also spelled papadum, poppadom, or papad.

Pappadoms are thin, crisp Indian flatbreads made from lentil flour, typically served as an appetizer or side dish. They may be fried, roasted, or microwaved until crunchy, and often accompany chutneys and pickles: {We ordered pappadoms while waiting for our curry}. Also spelled papadum, papadam, or poppadom.

A pappadum is a thin, crisp Indian flatbread made from lentil, chickpea, or rice flour, typically served as an appetizer or side dish. Pappadums are usually fried or roasted until they puff and become brittle. They often accompany chutneys and curries: {We ordered pappadums while waiting for the main course}. Also spelled papadum, papad, or poppadom.

Pappadums are thin, crispy Indian flatbreads made from lentil, chickpea, or rice flour, typically served as an appetizer or side dish. They're fried or roasted until brittle and often accompanied by chutneys: {We started with pappadums and mango chutney}. Also spelled papadum, poppadom, or papad.

Pappardelle are broad, flat ribbons of pasta, typically about an inch wide. The noodles are traditionally served with rich, hearty sauces—especially meat ragùs—where their wide surface catches chunks of braised meat: {pappardelle with wild boar ragù}. The word is Italian and usually treated as plural.

Pappy is an informal, affectionate word for father, used especially in rural American dialects: {My pappy taught me to fish}. It can also mean grandfather. The word shares territory with papa and pop but sounds more old-fashioned or regional. Separately, pappy describes food that is soft and mushy, like pap.

Paprika is a spice made from dried, ground peppers—ranging from mild and sweet to smoky or hot, depending on the variety. Hungarian paprika and Spanish pimentón are the most prized. The bright red powder colors and flavors dishes like goulash, deviled eggs, and paella: {She dusted the potatoes with paprika}.

Papyrus is a tall reed that grows in wetlands along the Nile and elsewhere, and also the writing material ancient Egyptians made from it by pressing strips of the plant's pith together. By extension, papyrus refers to any ancient manuscript written on such material: {The museum acquired a papyrus containing fragments of Homer}. Plural: papyri or papyruses.

Par is the standard or expected level—what's normal or acceptable. In golf, par is the number of strokes a skilled player should need for a hole or course: {two under par}, {bogey is one over par}. Something {on par with} another is equal to it. {Below par} or {not up to par} means substandard. {Par for the course} is what you'd typically expect, often said resignedly.

A parable is a short story that illustrates a moral or spiritual lesson. The term is especially associated with the teachings of Jesus—the parables of the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, the Sower. Unlike fables, parables typically involve realistic human situations rather than talking animals. The word sometimes describes any story with an obvious moral: {The film is a parable about greed}.

Parables are short stories that illustrate a moral or spiritual lesson. The term is most associated with the teachings of Jesus—the parable of the Good Samaritan, the parable of the Prodigal Son—but the form appears across religious and philosophical traditions. Unlike fables, parables typically feature human characters in realistic situations, with meaning conveyed through analogy rather than explicit statement: {He spoke in parables, leaving listeners to draw their own conclusions}.

A parabola is a U-shaped curve formed when a cone is cut by a plane parallel to its side. In mathematics, it's the set of points equidistant from a fixed point (focus) and a fixed line (directrix). Parabolas appear throughout physics and engineering—the path of a thrown ball, the shape of satellite dishes and car headlight reflectors. The adjective is parabolic: {a parabolic arc}, {parabolic mirrors}.

Paracetamol is a common pain reliever and fever reducer, known as acetaminophen in North America. It's gentler on the stomach than aspirin or ibuprofen but can damage the liver in high doses. {Take two paracetamol and call me in the morning.}

A parachute is a fabric canopy that opens to slow descent through air. Skydivers and pilots use parachutes to land safely after jumping or ejecting from aircraft. Figuratively, a {golden parachute} is a generous severance package for executives. As a verb, to parachute is to descend by parachute or to insert suddenly: {They parachuted a new CEO into the struggling company}.

Parachuted is the past tense of parachute—to descend using a fabric canopy that slows a fall through air. Soldiers parachute into combat zones; skydivers parachute for sport. Figuratively, to be parachuted into a position is to be dropped there from outside, often implying the person lacks relevant experience: {The CEO was parachuted in from a rival company}.

Parachutes are fabric canopies that slow descent through air by creating drag. Skydivers and cargo drops use parachutes to land safely. A golden parachute is a generous severance package for executives—a soft landing after being pushed out. To parachute in is to arrive suddenly from outside: {They parachuted in a new CEO from a rival firm}.

Parachuting is the activity of jumping from an aircraft and descending by parachute. The sport version is skydiving, which emphasizes freefall before deploying the chute. Military parachuting delivers troops or supplies behind enemy lines. {She took up parachuting after her sixtieth birthday.}

A parachutist is someone who jumps from an aircraft and descends using a parachute. The term covers both military paratroopers and recreational skydivers: {The parachutists landed in the field at dawn}.

Paracord is a lightweight nylon rope originally used in parachute suspension lines. Its strength-to-weight ratio and durability have made it popular for outdoor and survival applications: {She braided paracord into a sturdy bracelet}. The inner strands can be pulled out for fishing line, thread, or other uses when needed.

A parade is a public procession, typically celebratory or ceremonial: {the Thanksgiving Day parade}, {a military parade}. The verb means to march in such a procession, or more broadly, to display something ostentatiously: {He paraded his knowledge at every opportunity}. A parade of things is a series of them: {a parade of witnesses}. To {rain on someone's parade} is to spoil their enjoyment.

Parades is the plural of parade—a public procession celebrating an occasion or displaying military force: {holiday parades}, {victory parades}. The verb means to march in such a procession, or to display something conspicuously: {She parades her wealth}. To parade as something is to pose as it falsely: {He parades as an expert but knows nothing}.

Paradigm has a fairly narrow meaning in grammar, where it denotes a set of forms derived from a common element, such as all the inflections of a verb or adjective. More generally, a paradigm is an influential model or pattern: Mendeleev created a paradigm for chemistry with his periodic table. When people talk about a paradigm shift, they mean a new way of thinking brought about either by theoretical advances, or by an event that disproves or invalidates what has gone before: The tsunami caused a paradigm shift in the way that people thought about the safety of nuclear power.

Paradigms is the plural of paradigm, a model or pattern that serves as an example. In science and philosophy, a paradigm is a framework of accepted theories and methods that shapes how a field thinks: {The discovery forced scientists to question existing paradigms}. More loosely, paradigm means any dominant way of understanding something: {a paradigm shift in how we approach mental health}.

Parading is moving in a showy procession or display. Soldiers parade through streets after victory; protesters parade for visibility. The word often suggests deliberate exhibition: {She was parading around in her new dress}. To parade something is to display it ostentatiously: {He's always parading his wealth}. The continuous form emphasizes ongoing, conspicuous movement.

Paradise refers literally to a place believed in some religions to exist or to have existed: that is, the Garden of Eden, heaven, or a sweet spot that the righteous experience before heaven. In this use, Paradise is most likely to be capitalized. Paradise also designates figuratively any earthly place full of enjoyment and delight, and often has a modifier before it (surfers’ paradise, tropical paradise, lovers’ paradise).

Paradises is the plural of paradise, a place or state of supreme happiness and delight. The word originally meant an enclosed garden, then came to designate heaven or the Garden of Eden. Extended uses describe any idyllic setting: {tropical paradises}, {tax paradises}. The plural often appears when comparing destinations: {Hawaii and Tahiti are island paradises}.

A paradox is an idea or fact that seems to contradict itself. A paradox may be true, in which case it has to be explained by unconventional means, or it may be false because of a failure to take a relevant fact into account. People sometimes use the word to talk about the unusual or counterintuitive, rather than the contradictory: The paradox of human life is the existence of an animal body and instincts with a mind that turns toward the heavens.

Paradoxes is the plural of paradox—statements or situations that seem self-contradictory but may contain truth. {The paradoxes of quantum mechanics challenge intuition}. A paradox can be a logical puzzle ({Zeno's paradoxes}), a surprising truth ({the paradox that less is more}), or an apparent contradiction in someone's character: {She was a paradox—generous yet ruthlessly ambitious}.
clues: Truths that seem to oppose themselves

definition: Paradoxical describes something that seems to contradict itself or defy logic, yet may still be true. A paradoxical situation contains elements that appear incompatible: {It's paradoxical that the busiest people often find time to help others}. The word suggests the contradiction is more apparent than real—that deeper understanding might resolve it.

A paradrop is the delivery of personnel or supplies by parachute from an aircraft in flight. The term functions as both noun and verb: {The military conducted a paradrop of humanitarian supplies}; {They paradropped reinforcements behind enemy lines}. The word compresses parachute drop into a single term used primarily in military contexts.

Paraffin is a waxy, translucent substance derived from petroleum, used in candles, cosmetics, and food preservation. In British English, paraffin also means kerosene—the liquid fuel for lamps and heaters: {The paraffin heater warmed the garage}. Paraffin wax specifically refers to the solid form: {She dipped the strawberries in paraffin wax}.

To paraglide is to fly using a lightweight, free-flying glider—a fabric wing attached to a harness, launched by running off a slope or cliff. The sport emerged in the 1980s from parachute technology. Unlike hang gliders with rigid frames, paragliders pack into a backpack: {We paraglided over the Swiss Alps}. Skilled pilots ride thermal currents for hours.

A paraglider is a lightweight, free-flying aircraft consisting of a fabric wing and harness. The pilot launches from a slope or cliff, riding air currents to stay aloft. Unlike a parachute, which only descends, a paraglider is designed for sustained flight and can travel considerable distances. The word also refers to the person piloting one: {Paragliders circled above the valley}.

Paragliders are lightweight, free-flying aircraft consisting of a fabric wing and harness, launched by running off a slope or cliff. The pilot hangs beneath the canopy and steers by shifting weight and pulling brake toggles. Unlike parachutes, paragliders are designed for sustained flight rather than descent: {Paragliders circled in the thermal updrafts above the ridge}. The word also refers to the pilots themselves.

Paragliding is a recreational sport in which a person glides through the air while suspended from a fabric wing, having launched from a hill or cliff. Unlike hang gliding, the wing has no rigid frame—it's essentially a steerable parachute designed for sustained flight rather than descent. {We went paragliding over the Swiss Alps}.

A paragon is a model of excellence or perfection—someone or something that embodies the ideal of a quality: {a paragon of virtue}, {a paragon of efficiency}. The word implies not just high quality but the highest, a standard against which others are measured: {She was considered a paragon among nurses}.

Paragons are models of excellence or supreme examples of a quality. The word usually appears with a specifying phrase: {a paragon of virtue}, {a paragon of patience}. Someone described as a paragon embodies the ideal form of whatever trait is named—though the term sometimes carries faint irony, suggesting the standard is impossibly high.

A paragraph is a distinct section of writing, typically beginning on a new line and containing sentences that develop a single idea or topic. In casual speech, paragraph can mean any chunk of text: {Read me that paragraph}. The paragraph symbol (¶) marks where one begins or should begin. To paragraph is to divide text into such sections.

Paragraphs is the plural of paragraph—a distinct section of writing dealing with a single idea or topic, typically beginning on a new line and often indented. As a verb, to paragraph is to arrange text into such sections: {She paragraphs her essays carefully to guide the reader}. In casual speech, paragraphs sometimes emphasizes length: {I'm not reading your paragraphs right now}.

A parakeet is a small parrot, typically with bright plumage and a long tail. The term covers many species, but in American usage usually means the budgerigar—the common pet bird sold in pet stores: {The parakeet chirped from its cage}. Parakeets can be trained to mimic speech, though less reliably than larger parrots.

Parakeets is the plural of parakeet, a small to medium-sized parrot with a slender build and long tail feathers. The term covers many species kept as pets, most commonly the budgerigar: {The parakeets chattered noisily in their cage}. Parakeets are known for their bright plumage and ability to mimic human speech.

A paralegal is a person trained in legal work who assists lawyers but isn't licensed to practice law independently. Paralegals conduct research, draft documents, interview clients, and organize case files. The role emerged as law firms sought cost-effective ways to handle routine legal tasks: {She worked as a paralegal while studying for the bar exam}.

Parallax is the apparent shift in an object's position when viewed from different vantage points. Hold a finger before your face and alternately close each eye—the finger seems to jump against the background. Astronomers measure stellar parallax to calculate distances to nearby stars. In photography, parallax error occurs when the viewfinder and lens see slightly different frames. Figuratively, parallax suggests how perspective shapes perception: {The novel explores the parallax between immigrant and native-born experience}.

Two lines are parallel if they are aligned in the exact same direction and if extended in one plane would never meet. When cars are parked parallel, they are side by side at the same angle. Events or other abstractions that parallel each other happen at the same time or proceed in the same way. A parallel is something equal to another thing in essential aspects: There were striking parallels in the two accounts.

Parallelism is the use of similar grammatical structures in a series or pair: {government of the people, by the people, for the people}. Good parallelism creates rhythm and clarity; faulty parallelism jars: {She likes hiking, swimming, and to bike} mixes forms awkwardly. Beyond grammar, parallelism describes any arrangement of corresponding elements—parallel lines in geometry, parallel processing in computing, or parallel developments in history that unfold similarly without direct connection.

Parallels are things that correspond or run alongside each other without intersecting. Lines are parallel when they maintain equal distance. Events or situations are parallels when they share notable similarities: {The parallels between the two cases are striking}. To draw parallels is to point out resemblances. As a verb, to parallel something is to match or correspond to it: {Her career paralleled his in many ways}. Parallel bars are gymnastic equipment; parallel parking places a car alongside the curb.

Paralyse is the British spelling of paralyze—to cause loss of movement or sensation, typically through nerve damage or injury: {The accident paralysed him from the waist down}. Figuratively, to paralyse is to render helpless or unable to act: {Fear paralysed her}. Systems can be paralysed too: {The strike paralysed the city's transit network}.

Paralysed is the British spelling of paralyzed. To be paralysed is to lose the ability to move part or all of the body, typically from nerve damage or injury: {He was paralysed from the waist down after the accident}. Figuratively, paralysed describes being unable to act or function: {paralysed by fear}, {paralysed with indecision}. The spelling extends to paralyse and paralysing.

Paralysing is the British spelling of paralyzing—causing paralysis or the inability to move. The word extends readily to figurative uses: paralysing {fear}, paralysing {indecision}, a paralysing {blow} to the economy. Something paralysing renders you unable to act or function normally.

Paralysis is the loss of the ability to move part of the body, typically from nerve damage or disease. The meaning extends to any state of inability to act or function: {The scandal caused paralysis in the administration}. Economic or political paralysis describes systems frozen by indecision or conflict. {Analysis paralysis} is overthinking to the point of inaction.

To paralyze is to cause loss of muscle function, typically through nerve damage or disease: {The accident paralyzed him from the waist down}. The word extends to any inability to move or act: {Fear paralyzed her}. Systems and processes can be paralyzed—a strike paralyzes transportation, indecision paralyzes an organization. Also spelled paralyse in British English.
clues: Strip away all ability to move

definition: Paralyzed describes the inability to move or act. In its literal sense, a paralyzed limb or body has lost motor function, often from nerve damage or spinal injury: {She was paralyzed from the waist down}. Figuratively, paralyzed means frozen by overwhelming emotion or indecision: {paralyzed with fear}, {The committee was paralyzed by infighting}. Also the past tense of paralyze.

Paralyzes means to cause paralysis—loss of the ability to move. A spinal injury may paralyze someone from the waist down. The word extends to any kind of immobilization: {Fear paralyzed him}. A government can be paralyzed by gridlock, an economy by uncertainty. {The news paralyzed her; she couldn't speak.}
clues: Takes away all ability to move

definition: Paralyzing describes something that causes paralysis—literal inability to move, or figurative inability to act. A paralyzing {injury} damages the spine. Paralyzing {fear} renders someone frozen, unable to respond. Paralyzing {indecision} prevents any choice at all. The word emphasizes completeness: not merely slowing but stopping altogether.

A paramedic is a medical professional trained to provide emergency care outside hospitals—at accident scenes, in ambulances, during transport. Paramedics can administer medications, start IVs, and perform advanced procedures that basic emergency medical technicians cannot. {The paramedics arrived within minutes and stabilized him before the hospital transfer.}

Paramedics are emergency medical professionals who provide care outside hospitals—typically arriving by ambulance to treat injuries, heart attacks, or other acute conditions. They perform procedures like administering medications, inserting IVs, and operating defibrillators. {The paramedics arrived within minutes and stabilized him for transport.} Paramedic training falls between that of EMTs and physicians.

A parameter is a variable that defines the conditions or limits of a system or operation. In mathematics and programming, parameters are values passed into functions that determine their behavior: {The function takes two parameters: width and height}. More broadly, parameters are the boundaries within which something operates: {We need to work within the parameters of the budget}. The word often appears in the plural to mean constraints or guidelines: {What are the parameters of this project?}

Parameters are the variables or limits that define a system's behavior or scope. In technical contexts, parameters are values passed into functions or equations: {The function takes three parameters}. More broadly, parameters are the boundaries within which something operates: {We need to work within the parameters of the budget}. Often interchangeable with boundaries or guidelines in general use.

Paramilitaries are armed groups organized along military lines but not part of a country's official armed forces. The term covers a range: guerrilla fighters, militia groups, death squads, or quasi-official forces that governments use while maintaining deniability. {Paramilitaries carried out attacks on civilian villages}. The singular paramilitary works as both noun and adjective: {a paramilitary organization}, {a paramilitary accused of torture}.

Paramilitary describes groups organized along military lines but operating outside official armed forces. Paramilitary organizations may support or oppose governments—from militia groups to rebel fighters to private security forces. The term often carries sinister overtones, suggesting violence without accountability: {paramilitary death squads}, {paramilitary training camps}. As a noun, a paramilitary is a member of such a group.

Paramount means supreme or of highest importance—above all others in rank or significance. A {paramount concern} takes precedence over everything else. {Safety is paramount} means nothing matters more. The word carries formal weight, often appearing in legal or official contexts: {the paramount duty of the court}. (Capitalized Paramount is the entertainment company.)

A paramour is a person with whom someone has an illicit romantic or sexual relationship, typically outside of marriage.
