A peephole is a small hole you look through to see what's on the other side—typically a lens set into a door that lets you see who's there before opening: {She checked the peephole before unlocking the door}. The word extends to any small opening that permits viewing while remaining concealed.

Peeping is looking furtively or through a small opening—the kind of looking you do when you don't want to be seen doing it. A {peeping Tom} is a voyeur who spies on people in private moments, especially through windows. The phrase comes from the legend of Lady Godiva, where Tom was struck blind for peeking at her naked ride through Coventry.

Peeps is informal for people, especially one's friends or social circle: {I'm heading out with my peeps}. The word carries warmth and familiarity. Separately, peeps are quick, high-pitched sounds—the cries of young birds or similar noises. To peep is to make such a sound, or to look quickly and furtively: {She peeped through the curtains}.

A peepshow is an exhibition viewed through a small opening, traditionally a box with a lens showing pictures or scenes inside. The term now primarily refers to coin-operated booths where customers watch erotic performances or films through a window: {The old Times Square was lined with peepshows and adult theaters}. By extension, any voyeuristic glimpse into private matters.

A peer is someone of equal standing—in age, rank, or status. Classmates are peers; so are colleagues at the same level. In British usage, a peer is specifically a member of the nobility: {a peer of the realm}. To peer is a different word meaning to look closely or searchingly, often with difficulty: {She peered through the fog}.

Peerage is the rank or status of a peer—a member of the nobility holding titles like duke, marquess, earl, viscount, or baron. The peerage also refers collectively to all such nobles: {She was elevated to the peerage}. In Britain, peers historically held seats in the House of Lords. A peerage can be hereditary or granted for life.

Peered is the past tense of peer, meaning to look closely or intently, usually because something is difficult to see. You peer through fog, into darkness, or at fine print. The word suggests straining to make something out rather than casual looking. {She peered through the window to see who was at the door.} {He peered at the map, trying to find the street name.}

Peering is looking intently or with difficulty, often by narrowing the eyes or leaning closer: {She peered through the fog}, {He peered at the fine print}. The word suggests straining to see something not easily visible. In networking, peering is the direct exchange of internet traffic between providers, bypassing intermediaries.

Peers are people of equal standing—in age, rank, status, or ability. Students learn from their peers; professionals seek peer review. {She's well respected among her peers.} In British usage, peers are specifically members of the nobility who hold titles. To peer is a different word meaning to look closely or squint: {He peered through the fog}.

Pees is the plural of pee—instances of urination: {The dog took three pees on our walk}. Also the third-person singular verb: {She pees before every long drive}. The word is mildly childish but common in casual speech.

A peeve is something that annoys or irritates, usually a minor recurring grievance: {Loud chewing is a pet peeve of mine}. The verb means to irritate: {It peeves me when people don't signal}. Peeved means annoyed. The word is a back-formation from peevish, meaning ill-tempered or easily irritated.

Peeved means annoyed or irritated, typically over something minor. It suggests mild displeasure rather than serious anger: {She was peeved that no one remembered her birthday}. The word carries a slightly old-fashioned, almost quaint quality—being peeved sounds less harsh than being pissed off.

Peeves is the plural of peeve, meaning things that annoy or irritate someone. The word appears most often in the phrase {pet peeves}—minor irritations that bother a particular person disproportionately: {One of my pet peeves is people who chew with their mouths open}. As a verb, to peeve is to annoy: {It really peeves me when they're late}.

Peevish means irritable or easily annoyed, especially over small things. A peevish person complains readily and shows displeasure at minor inconveniences: {She grew peevish when the waiter forgot her coffee}. The word suggests a sour, querulous temperament rather than explosive anger—more sulky than furious.

Peewee means very small, especially for its kind. A peewee is a small person or thing, often used affectionately for young children: {the peewee football league}. The word likely imitates a small bird's high-pitched call. As an adjective: {a peewee version of the adult game}.

Peewees are very small things or people, especially young children. In youth sports, peewee designates the youngest age division: {My son plays peewee hockey}. The word derives from the pewee, a small grayish bird named for its call. Informally, peewee can be mildly teasing: {Get out of here, peewee}.

A peg is a device that attaches or binds objects. Tent pegs secure a tent to the ground. Clothes pegs (British English) secure clothes to a line to dry. The pegs of a string instrument hold one end of the strings. When you peg something, you attach it with a peg, but the verb is frequently used to fix one quantity to a certain level: Saudi Arabia’s currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar. To peg someone as something means to identify them as such: I pegged her as a liberal the first time I met her.

A pegasus is a winged horse—a mythical creature capable of flight. The word derives from the Greek mythological horse Pegasus and has become a common noun for any such creature in fantasy literature, games, and art: {The knight rode a pegasus into battle}. Plural: pegasi or pegasuses. (Capitalized Pegasus is the mythological horse or constellation.)

Pegboard is a flat board perforated with evenly spaced holes, used for organizing tools and supplies by inserting hooks or pegs: {He mounted a pegboard in the garage for his wrenches}. The grid pattern allows flexible arrangement. Pegboard also names a children's game where colored pegs fit into holes to create patterns or pictures.

Pegged is the past tense of peg, carrying forward its meanings of fastening, fixing, or identifying. To peg something is to secure it with a peg, or to set a value at a fixed level: {The currency is pegged to the dollar}. To peg someone is to identify or categorize them quickly: {I had you pegged as a lawyer from the start}. In slang, pegged describes a sexual practice where a woman penetrates a man anally with a strap-on dildo.

Pegging has several meanings united by the idea of fastening or fixing. To peg something is to fasten it with a peg—a small wooden or metal pin: {peg the tent to the ground}. Prices or currencies can be pegged to a standard: {The dollar was pegged to gold}. To peg someone is to identify or categorize them: {I had him pegged as a lawyer}. A peg leg is a wooden prosthetic. In cribbage, pegging is moving pegs on the scoring board. In sexual slang, pegging refers to a woman penetrating a man anally with a strap-on dildo.

A pegleg is a wooden prosthetic leg, especially the simple post-style replacement traditionally associated with pirates and sailors who lost limbs. The term extends to anyone with such a prosthesis: {The old pegleg hobbled down to the dock}. As an adjective, it describes someone wearing one: {a pegleg pirate}.

Pegs are small cylindrical or tapered pieces used for fastening, hanging, or marking. A tent peg secures canvas to the ground. A coat peg holds clothing. Cribbage uses pegs for scoring. To peg something is to fasten it with pegs or to fix it at a level: {The currency is pegged to the dollar}. To peg someone is to identify or categorize them: {I had her pegged as a lawyer}. To {take someone down a peg} is to humble them.

A pelican is a large waterbird with a long bill and an expandable throat pouch used for scooping up fish. Pelicans are found near coastlines, lakes, and rivers worldwide. The brown pelican dives from the air to catch prey; white pelicans fish while swimming. {A pelican glided low over the water}.

Pelicans are large waterbirds with long bills and expandable throat pouches used for scooping up fish. They're found near coastlines, lakes, and rivers worldwide, often seen flying in formation or diving for prey. {A squadron of pelicans glided over the bay}. The New Orleans Pelicans are an NBA team. (Capitalized Pelicans typically refers to the basketball team.)

A pellet is a small, rounded mass of compressed material. Animal food often comes in pellets. Guns may fire pellets—small projectiles of metal or plastic. The word extends to any small ball-shaped object: owl pellets (regurgitated indigestible matter), pellets of bread, pellets of ice. To pellet is to form into pellets or to strike with them.

Pellets are small, rounded pieces of material—compressed or naturally formed. Animal feed comes in pellets; so does ammunition for air guns. Owl pellets are regurgitated masses of indigestible bone and fur. Wood pellets fuel stoves. The word suggests something compact and uniform: {The medication comes in tiny pellets}. To pellet is to form into pellets or to strike with them.

A peloton is the main cluster of cyclists in a road race, riding closely together to reduce wind resistance and conserve energy. The word comes from French, where it means a small ball or group. In professional cycling, riders in the peloton take turns at the front, sharing the work of cutting through the air. {She broke away from the peloton with three kilometers to go.} The term has spread beyond cycling to describe any tightly packed group moving together.

A pelt is an animal skin, especially one with fur still attached: {beaver pelts}, {a stack of fox pelts at the trading post}. The fur trade dealt in pelts. To pelt is to strike repeatedly with thrown objects: {Kids pelted the car with snowballs}. Rain or hail pelts a surface when it hits hard and fast. At {full pelt} means at top speed.

Pelted is the past tense of pelt, meaning to throw things repeatedly at a target: {The crowd pelted the speaker with tomatoes}. Rain or hail pelts when it strikes hard and fast. To pelt can also mean to run at full speed: {The kids pelted down the street}. A pelt as a noun is an animal skin with fur attached.

Pelting describes something coming down hard and fast, usually rain or hail: {We ran through the pelting rain}. The word derives from the verb pelt, meaning to strike repeatedly with thrown objects. A pelting storm beats against windows; pelting sleet stings exposed skin.

Pelts are animal skins, especially with fur or hair still attached: {beaver pelts}, {fox pelts}. The fur trade dealt in pelts. A pelt is also a beating or bombardment—rain pelts a window, hail pelts a roof. To pelt someone is to throw things at them repeatedly: {The crowd pelted the speaker with tomatoes}. At full pelt means at top speed.

The pelvis is the basin-shaped bone structure at the base of the spine, formed by the hip bones, sacrum, and coccyx. It supports the spine, protects internal organs, and connects the trunk to the legs. In anatomy, pelvic describes this region: {pelvic floor}, {pelvic exam}. The female pelvis is typically wider to accommodate childbirth.

Pemmican is a concentrated food made from dried meat pounded into powder and mixed with melted fat, sometimes with dried berries. Originally a Native American preparation, it became essential provisions for fur traders and polar explorers because it keeps indefinitely without refrigeration and packs maximum calories into minimum weight: {They carried pemmican for the Arctic expedition}.

One kind of pen is a writing implement that uses ink. When you pen a letter or some other document, you write it. Another pen is an enclosure that prevents escape, such as one for animals (pig pen). When you pen living things, you enclose them in a pen. Pen is also an informal shortening of penitentiary: Her dad’s in the pen. A female swan is called a pen.

To penalize is to impose a penalty or disadvantage on someone for breaking a rule or doing something wrong. Sports officials penalize fouls; tax codes penalize certain behaviors; teachers penalize late work. The word often implies systematic or official punishment rather than informal consequences: {The new policy penalizes workers who take sick days}. Also spelled penalise in British English.

Penalizing is imposing a penalty or disadvantage on someone for breaking a rule or failing to meet a standard. Sports officials penalize fouls; tax codes penalize early withdrawals; teachers penalize late submissions. The word suggests formal or systematic punishment rather than spontaneous retaliation: {The new policy penalizes workers who take unscheduled breaks}.

Penalties is the plural of penalty—punishments or disadvantages imposed for breaking rules or laws. In sports, penalties result from fouls or infractions: {The team committed too many penalties}. In law and finance, penalties are fines or additional charges: {late payment penalties}, {tax penalties}. The death penalty is capital punishment. A penalty kick or penalty shot is awarded after certain fouls.

A penalty is a punishment or disadvantage imposed for breaking a rule or law. In sports, penalties give the opposing team an advantage—a free kick, extra shots, or time in the penalty box. In contracts and finance, penalties are fees for violations: {The early withdrawal penalty was steep}. The death penalty is capital punishment. More loosely, a penalty is any unwelcome consequence: {the penalty of fame}.

Penance is an act of self-punishment or devotion performed to show repentance for wrongdoing. In Catholic practice, penance is assigned by a priest after confession—prayers, fasting, or good works to atone for sins. More broadly, any voluntary suffering undertaken to make amends: {He did penance for his neglect by visiting her grave every week}. To {do penance} is the standard phrase.

Penances is the plural of penance—acts of self-punishment or devotion undertaken to show remorse for wrongdoing. In Catholic practice, penances are assigned by a priest after confession: prayers, fasting, or charitable works. More broadly, any suffering accepted as atonement qualifies: {She did her penances for years of neglect by caring for him daily}.

Pence is the plural of penny in British currency. One hundred pence make a pound sterling: {That'll be fifty pence}, {a few pence short}. The form appears in compound prices: {a fifty-pence piece}. In American English, pennies is the standard plural, and pence sounds distinctly British.

A penchant is a strong liking or inclination toward something, often a particular activity or pursuit. The word carries a sense of habitual attraction rather than passing interest. {She has a penchant for vintage clothing.} {His penchant for risk-taking worried his family.} Unlike a mere preference, penchant suggests something that consistently draws a person's attention or shapes their behavior.

A pencil is a writing or drawing instrument consisting of a thin rod of graphite or colored material encased in wood or held in a mechanical holder. The word also functions as a verb meaning to write, draw, or mark with a pencil; to pencil something in is to make a tentative arrangement: {Let me pencil you in for Thursday}. Pencil appears in compounds like {pencil skirt}, which is narrow and fitted, and {pencil mustache}, which is thin and precisely shaped.

Penciled means drawn, written, or marked with a pencil: {a penciled sketch}, {penciled notes in the margin}. To pencil something in is to schedule it tentatively, as if written in pencil rather than ink and subject to change: {Let me pencil you in for Thursday}. Penciled can also describe thin, delicate lines resembling pencil strokes: {penciled eyebrows}.

Pencils is the plural of pencil, a writing instrument with a core of graphite or colored material encased in wood or a mechanical holder. Unlike pens, pencils can be erased. {She sharpened her pencils before the exam.} To pencil something in is to schedule it tentatively: {Let me pencil you in for Thursday}.

A pendant is an ornament that hangs from a chain worn around the neck, or more broadly, anything that hangs or dangles from something else: {a light pendant}, {a pendant earring}. As an adjective, pendant means hanging or suspended, though this use is literary and rare. The spelling *pendent* sometimes appears for the adjective.
Pending is a participle functioning as a preposition with two specific meanings; one similar to during, and one to until. It is frequent in journalism and law.

A pendulum is a weight suspended from a fixed point so it can swing freely back and forth. The regular motion of pendulums made them essential to early clocks. Figuratively, pendulum describes anything that swings between extremes: {The political pendulum has swung back toward conservatism}. The phrase {swing of the pendulum} suggests cyclical reversals.

Pendulums is the plural of pendulum, a weight suspended from a fixed point so it can swing freely back and forth. The classic example is the swinging weight that regulates a grandfather clock. Figuratively, a pendulum describes anything that shifts between extremes: {The political pendulum swings left and right over generations}. {Public opinion acts like a pendulum.}

To penetrate is to pass into or through something—a bullet penetrates flesh, light penetrates darkness, water penetrates soil. The word implies overcoming resistance or crossing a barrier. Extended uses follow naturally: to penetrate a market is to establish presence there; to penetrate a mystery is to understand it deeply; to penetrate an organization is to infiltrate it. A penetrating gaze seems to see through you; a penetrating analysis cuts to the core. {The cold penetrated his thin jacket}. {She couldn't penetrate his reserved exterior}.
clues: Go where barriers would stop others

definition: Penetrates is the third person singular of penetrate, meaning to pass into or through something. A bullet penetrates flesh; light penetrates darkness; cold penetrates thin clothing. The word extends to understanding: {The meaning finally penetrates}. To penetrate a market is to gain entry; to penetrate a disguise is to see through it. In sexual contexts, penetrate refers to insertion into a body cavity.

Penetrating describes something that enters or passes through, literally or figuratively. A penetrating {wound} pierces deep into tissue. A penetrating {stare} seems to see through surface appearances. Penetrating {cold} cuts through clothing. A penetrating {analysis} gets to the heart of a matter. The word suggests sharpness, depth, and the ability to reach what lies beneath.

Penetration is the act of entering or piercing something. A bullet's penetration depends on its velocity and the material it strikes. Sexual penetration refers specifically to insertion into a body cavity. In military and espionage contexts, penetration means infiltrating enemy territory or organizations: {The agency achieved deep penetration of the terrorist network}. Market penetration measures how much of a potential customer base a product has reached.

A penfriend is someone you correspond with regularly by letter, typically someone you've never met in person. The relationship exists primarily through written exchange, often across countries or cultures. The term is more common in British English; Americans usually say pen pal. {She's had a penfriend in Japan since she was twelve.}

Penguin refers to flightless seabirds of the Southern Hemisphere, recognizable by their black-and-white coloring and upright waddle. They swim expertly but cannot fly—their wings have evolved into flippers. Penguins live in colonies, often in Antarctic or subantarctic regions, though some species inhabit temperate coastlines. {We watched the penguins dive for fish.}

Penguins is the plural of penguin, a flightless seabird native to the Southern Hemisphere. Penguins are distinctive for their black-and-white coloring and upright waddle on land, though they're graceful swimmers. They live in colonies and appear frequently in nature documentaries and children's media: {We watched the penguins huddle together against the Antarctic wind}.

Penicillin is an antibiotic derived from mold, the first of its kind to be widely used against bacterial infections. Discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 and developed for medical use in the 1940s, it revolutionized treatment of wounds, pneumonia, and sexually transmitted diseases. {The doctor prescribed penicillin for strep throat.} Some people are allergic to penicillin, which can cause severe reactions.

A peninsula is a piece of land that projects into a body of water, connected to the mainland by a narrow strip: {the Italian peninsula}, {the Korean Peninsula}. The word captures the idea of being almost an island—surrounded by water on three sides but not quite cut off. Florida and Baja California are peninsulas.

The penis is the male sex organ, used for urination and sexual intercourse. In humans and other mammals, it becomes erect when engorged with blood during arousal. The word appears in clinical, educational, and casual contexts alike: {The doctor examined his penis}. Informally, countless slang terms substitute—cock, dick, dong, johnson, and dozens more.

Penises is the plural of penis, the male sex organ used for urination and copulation. The word appears in anatomical, medical, and sexual contexts: {The study measured penises of three hundred adult males}. The alternative plural penes exists but sounds clinical or archaic.

Penitence is sincere regret for wrongdoing, especially with the desire to make amends. The word carries religious weight—penitence before God, confession and penitence—but applies to secular contrition too: {His penitence seemed genuine, but she wasn't ready to forgive}. Related forms include penitent and the more formal penitential.

A penitentiary is a prison, especially a state or federal facility for serious offenders serving long sentences. The word carries a formal, institutional tone—legal documents and news reports use it more than casual speech, where {prison} or {jail} suffice. {He served fifteen years in a federal penitentiary.}

Penitents is the plural of penitent—people who repent their sins or wrongdoing. The word appears most often in religious contexts, where penitents confess to a priest or perform acts of penance: {The penitents knelt before the altar}. In Catholic tradition, hooded penitents process through streets during Holy Week observances.

A penknife is a small folding knife, originally used for sharpening quill pens. The term now applies to any compact pocketknife with one or more blades that fold into the handle: {He used his penknife to open the package}. The diminutive size distinguishes it from larger utility knives.

A penlight is a small flashlight roughly the size and shape of a pen, designed to clip into a pocket. Doctors use penlights to check pupil response; mechanics use them to illuminate tight spaces. The compact size trades brightness for portability: {She pulled a penlight from her coat to read the map}.

Penmanship is the art or skill of writing by hand. Good penmanship means clear, legible, often elegant handwriting: {Her penmanship was so beautiful that she addressed wedding invitations for extra money}. The word carries an old-fashioned quality now that keyboards have largely replaced handwriting in daily life.

A pen name is a fictitious name used by a writer instead of their real name. Authors adopt pen names for various reasons—privacy, gender concealment, genre separation, or simply a more memorable identity: {She published romance novels under a pen name}. Also spelled as two words: pen name.

A pennant is a long, narrow flag tapering to a point, typically flown from ships or displayed at sporting events. In American baseball, the pennant is the league championship—winning it means advancing to the World Series: {The Cubs won the pennant}. Triangular pennants also appear as decorative banners at car dealerships and fairgrounds.

Pennants are long, narrow, tapering flags. They fly from ships, hang in stadiums, and mark championships—a team that {wins the pennant} takes first place in its league. Pennants also decorate used car lots and children's parties, strung in colorful rows. A single such flag is a pennant.

Penne is a type of pasta cut into short tubes with diagonally sliced ends, resembling quill pens. The ridged surface and hollow center hold sauces well: {penne alla vodka}, {penne arrabbiata}. Like other pasta shapes, penne takes a singular verb when referring to the dish: {The penne is ready}.

Penned is the past tense of pen, meaning to write or compose: {She penned a letter to her grandmother}, {He penned several novels in his youth}. The word carries a slightly literary or formal tone. Separately, penned means confined in an enclosure: {The sheep were penned for the night}, {penned up like animals}.

Pennies is the plural of penny, referring to individual one-cent coins: {She counted out the pennies from her piggy bank}. When discussing monetary value rather than physical coins, the plural is usually pence (British) or cents (American): {It costs fifty pence}. To {pinch pennies} is to be frugal. {Pennies on the dollar} describes buying something far below its value.

Penniless means having no money at all: {She arrived in the city penniless}. The word emphasizes complete poverty, not just being short on cash. A penniless artist lives in destitution; someone who forgot their wallet is merely without funds at the moment.

A penny is a coin of small value—one cent in the United States, one hundredth of a pound in Britain. The word often stands for trivial amounts: {It won't cost you a penny}. A {penny for your thoughts} invites someone to share what they're thinking. {Penny-wise and pound-foolish} describes saving small amounts while wasting large ones. To {pinch pennies} is to be frugal. {A pretty penny} is actually a large sum: {That car must have cost a pretty penny}.

A pennywhistle is a simple wind instrument with six finger holes, producing a high, clear tone. Also called a tin whistle, it's associated with Irish and Celtic folk music. The name reflects its cheap construction—historically costing about a penny. {She learned to play pennywhistle before moving on to the flute.}

A penpal is a person with whom you exchange letters, typically someone you've never met in person. The relationship exists primarily through correspondence, often across long distances or between different countries: {I had a penpal in Japan when I was twelve}. The term emerged when letters were written with pens; despite email and messaging largely replacing postal mail, penpal persists for any correspondent-based friendship.

Penpals are people who maintain a friendship through regular correspondence, traditionally by mail. The practice was especially popular before email and social media, often connecting children across countries: {I had a penpal in Japan when I was twelve}. The term still applies to any correspondence-based friendship, including digital ones. Also spelled pen pals.

A penpusher is someone who does routine paperwork or clerical work—the implication being that their job involves nothing more demanding than pushing a pen across forms. The term is mildly dismissive, suggesting bureaucratic drudgery rather than meaningful work: {He's just a penpusher at the tax office}. Also spelled pen-pusher. The American equivalent is pencil pusher.

Penpushers is the plural of penpusher, a mildly derisive term for someone whose job consists mainly of paperwork—a clerk or bureaucrat. The image is of someone who does nothing but push a pen across forms all day: {The penpushers in accounting rejected my expense report}. More common in British English; Americans tend toward pencil pusher.

Pens is the plural of pen—writing instruments that dispense ink: {She keeps a cup of pens on her desk}. Pen also means an enclosure for animals, so pens can be such enclosures: {The pigs were separated into different pens}. As a verb form, pens means writes or composes: {She pens a weekly column for the local paper}.

A pension is a regular payment made to someone who has retired from work, typically funded by contributions during their working years: {She lives on her pension}. Government and employer pensions provide income after age-based retirement. To pension someone off is to retire them with a pension, sometimes implying they've become useless: {They pensioned off the old equipment manager}. In European usage, a pension (pronounced the French way) is a small hotel or boarding house.

A pensioner is someone who receives a pension—regular payments from a retirement fund, government program, or former employer. The term is more common in British English than American, where {retiree} often substitutes: {The pensioners lined up for their monthly checks}. {A bus full of pensioners toured the countryside}.

Pensioners are people who receive a pension—regular payments from a retirement fund, government program, or former employer. The term is more common in British English, where it often specifically means retirees receiving state benefits: {pensioners queuing at the post office}, {a discount for pensioners}. In American English, retiree is the more usual term.

Pensions are regular payments made to someone who has retired from work, typically funded by contributions during their working years. A pension may come from a former employer, the government, or a private plan. The verb pension appears mainly in {pension off}—to retire someone with a pension, or more broadly, to dismiss as no longer useful: {They pensioned off the old equipment}.

Pensive describes a state of quiet, serious thought—often tinged with sadness or melancholy. Someone pensive is lost in reflection, perhaps troubled by something they can't resolve: {She grew pensive when the conversation turned to her father}. The word suggests inward focus and a certain wistfulness, distinct from mere concentration.

A pentacle is a five-pointed star enclosed within a circle, used as a mystical or magical symbol. It appears frequently in Western occult traditions, Wicca, and various forms of ceremonial magic, where it may be drawn, worn as an amulet, or inscribed on ritual objects. The pentacle is often confused with the pentagram, which is simply the five-pointed star without the surrounding circle. {She wore a silver pentacle on a chain around her neck.}

A pentagon is a five-sided polygon. In geometry, a regular pentagon has equal sides and angles, each interior angle measuring 108 degrees. The shape appears in nature, architecture, and design—from starfish to decorative tiles. {Draw a pentagon and connect all its vertices to form a five-pointed star.} (Capitalized Pentagon refers to the U.S. military headquarters.)

Pentagons are five-sided polygons. Regular pentagons have equal sides and angles; irregular ones vary. The Pentagon, headquarters of the U.S. Department of Defense, takes its name from its distinctive five-sided shape. {The children cut pentagons from construction paper.}

A pentagram is a five-pointed star drawn with five straight strokes, forming a continuous line that creates a pentagon at the center. The symbol has ancient associations with mathematics, magic, and mysticism. In modern use, it appears frequently in occult contexts—upright in Wiccan practice, inverted in associations with Satanism: {She wore a pentagram pendant}.

Pentagrams are five-pointed stars drawn with five straight strokes, each line crossing two others. The shape appears in various contexts: mathematical geometry, national flags, and religious symbolism. In occult traditions, a pentagram enclosed in a circle represents magical protection or elemental forces. Inverted pentagrams—with one point downward—are associated with Satanism and the occult: {The album cover featured pentagrams and skulls}.

A pentathlon is an athletic competition comprising five different events. The modern Olympic pentathlon includes fencing, swimming, equestrian show jumping, pistol shooting, and cross-country running. Ancient Greek pentathlons featured discus, javelin, long jump, a foot race, and wrestling. {She trained for years to compete in the pentathlon.}

A penthouse is a luxurious apartment on the top floor of a tall building, typically featuring premium amenities and panoramic views: {They bought a penthouse overlooking Central Park}. The word originally meant a shed or lean-to attached to a larger structure—the modern sense emerged when rooftop additions to apartment buildings became desirable rather than utilitarian.

Penthouses are luxury apartments on the top floor of a building, typically featuring premium amenities, expansive views, and private outdoor space. The term originally meant a shed or lean-to attached to a building's wall—the "top floor apartment" sense emerged in the early twentieth century as urban high-rises became desirable. {The penthouse sold for twelve million.}

Penumbra is the partial shadow between full shadow and full light—the fuzzy edge where an eclipse isn't total or a lamp's circle fades into darkness. The word extends to any gray zone or ambiguous boundary: {The case falls in the penumbra of the First Amendment}. Constitutional lawyers use it for rights implied but not explicitly stated. In astronomy, the penumbra is the lighter outer region of a sunspot or the partial shadow cast during an eclipse.

A peon is a worker of the lowest rank, especially one doing unskilled or menial labor. The term originally referred to indebted laborers in Latin America bound to work until debts were paid. Now it often describes anyone at the bottom of a hierarchy: {I'm just a peon around here—nobody tells me anything}. The word carries connotations of powerlessness and expendability.

Peonies is the plural of peony, a flowering plant with large, showy blooms in shades of pink, white, red, and yellow. Native to Asia, Europe, and western North America, peonies are prized in gardens and floral arrangements for their lush, fragrant flowers: {The peonies in her garden bloom every May}. They're traditional wedding flowers and symbols of prosperity in Chinese culture.

Peons are workers of the lowest rank, especially laborers bound by debt or obligation to their employers. The term originated in Spanish colonial systems where workers were tied to land or masters. In modern use, peon usually appears figuratively for anyone doing menial work or occupying the bottom of a hierarchy: {The executives flew first class while the peons sat in coach}. The tone is often self-deprecating or sardonic.

A peony is a flowering plant prized for its large, showy blooms that appear in late spring and early summer. The flowers, which range from white to pink to deep red, are known for their lush, layered petals and sweet fragrance. Peonies are popular in gardens and floral arrangements, particularly for weddings. {The peonies in her bouquet were gorgeous.} They're perennials that can live for decades with proper care.

The noun people is used as the plural of person in most contexts, even though the words share no history. People is, however, related to popular and population. In addition to denoting any group of two or more humans, people is used to denote groups that share particular characteristics, as in the German people. Even though people is a plural noun, the pluralized form peoples is also used to talk about multiple groups, each of which has a distinct identity.

Peoples is the plural of people when people itself means a nation, ethnic group, or distinct community: {the peoples of Southeast Asia}, {indigenous peoples}. This distinguishes collective groups from individuals—"people" are persons, but "peoples" are populations with shared identity, culture, or territory.

Peoplewatching is the casual pastime of observing strangers in public places—their appearance, behavior, and interactions. Parks, cafés, and airports are classic spots for it. The appeal lies in idle curiosity about other lives: {We spent the afternoon peoplewatching at the train station}. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated.

Pep is lively energy and enthusiasm: {She's full of pep today}. A pep talk is an encouraging speech meant to boost morale or confidence. A pep rally is a gathering, typically at schools, to generate enthusiasm before a sports event. To pep up is to make livelier or more energetic: {A cup of coffee will pep you up}. (Capitalized Pep may be a nickname or brand name.)

Pepitas are hulled pumpkin seeds, green and flat, eaten as a snack or used in cooking. The term comes from Spanish and appears most often in Mexican and Southwestern cuisines: {salad topped with pepitas}, {pepita sauce}. Sometimes the word refers to any pumpkin seed, hulled or not.

Pepper names two unrelated spices. Black pepper comes from dried berries of a tropical vine, ground to season food. Peppers of the capsicum family—bell peppers, jalapeños, cayennes—range from sweet to fiercely hot. To pepper something is to sprinkle it liberally: {The comedian peppered his routine with profanity}. To pepper with gunfire is to riddle with shots.

A peppercorn is the dried berry of a tropical vine, ground to make pepper. Peppercorns come in varieties—black, white, green, pink—depending on processing and ripeness. In legal usage, a peppercorn rent is a nominal payment (historically an actual peppercorn) that satisfies contract requirements without real exchange of value: {They lease the land for a peppercorn}.

Peppercorns are the dried berries of the pepper plant, ground to produce black pepper. Black peppercorns are picked unripe and dried; white peppercorns have the outer layer removed; green peppercorns are harvested earlier and preserved. A peppercorn rent is a nominal payment—so small as to be merely symbolic: {The building was leased for a peppercorn rent of one dollar a year}.

Peppered is the past tense and past participle of pepper, carrying forward that verb's meanings. If something is peppered with small objects or marks, they are scattered across its surface like peppercorns: {The wall was peppered with bullet holes.} When someone is peppered with questions or criticism, they receive a rapid barrage of them. Food that has been peppered has had pepper applied to it. A peppered {moth} is a species known for its speckled coloring.

Peppermint is a plant in the mint family with a strong, cool flavor from its high menthol content. The flavor itself is also called peppermint, appearing in candies, teas, and toothpaste: {peppermint tea}, {a peppermint candy cane}. The plant yields peppermint oil, used in cooking and medicine for its cooling sensation and ability to soothe digestive issues.

Pepperoncini are mild Italian chili peppers, typically pickled and served as a condiment or garnish. They're pale yellow-green, wrinkled, and slightly sweet with gentle heat. Common on antipasto platters, in salads, and as a topping for sandwiches and pizza: {I always ask for extra pepperoncini on my sub}.

Pepperoni is a spiced, cured sausage made from beef and pork, sliced thin and most familiar as a pizza topping. The word is American, adapted from Italian *peperoni* (bell peppers)—though Italian pepperoni contains no peppers. {A large pepperoni pizza, please.}

Peppers are fruits of plants in the capsicum family, ranging from sweet bell peppers to fiery hot varieties like jalapeños and habaneros. The heat comes from capsaicin, measured in Scoville units. Pepper also names an unrelated spice—black pepper—ground from dried berries. To pepper something is to sprinkle it liberally or bombard it: {The lawyer peppered the witness with questions}.

Peppery describes something with the hot, sharp taste of pepper: {a peppery arugula salad}, {peppery radishes}. Extended to temperament, it means quick to anger or sharp-tongued: {a peppery old colonel who didn't suffer fools}. The word can also describe speech or writing that's sharp and spirited: {peppery commentary}, {a peppery exchange}.

Peppy means lively, energetic, and cheerful. A peppy person radiates enthusiasm; a peppy song has an upbeat tempo that makes you want to move. The word suggests buoyant, bouncy energy rather than intensity: {She gave a peppy introduction}, {The commercial featured peppy music}. Sometimes used dismissively for forced cheerfulness.

Although you can perceive something through any of your senses, people use this verb most often to talk about perception through the eyes or with the mind: We perceived a large, dark shape moving toward us. I perceived a note of disappointment in her voice. Sometimes perceive can refer to the future, in which case its meaning is similar to anticipate or imagine: I perceive difficulties arising when you try to implement this plan without everyone on board.

Percent means per hundred—a way of expressing a proportion as a fraction of one hundred. {Fifty percent of the class passed}. The word functions as noun, adjective, and adverb: {a ten percent raise}, {sales increased five percent}. In casual speech, percent often emphasizes certainty or completeness: {I'm a hundred percent sure}. Also spelled per cent, especially in British English.

A percentage is a proportion expressed as parts per hundred, indicated by the symbol %: {What percentage of voters support the measure?} The word often appears where portion or share would suffice: {A large percentage of the budget goes to salaries}. In the plural, percentages can mean commission or profit margin: {The salespeople work on percentages}.

Percentages are proportions expressed as parts per hundred. A percentage represents a fraction with 100 as the denominator: 25 percent equals one quarter. The word covers both the concept and specific figures: {What percentage of voters turned out?} {The percentages don't add up}. In plural, percentages often refers to statistical odds or probable outcomes: {The percentages favor the incumbent}.

Perception is a verbal noun based on the verb perceive. Perception can refer to the faculty of becoming aware through the senses or mind, as in impaired perception. Perception can also be a particular sense impression: The camouflage is so effective that perception of the octopus is nearly impossible. Perception is used appreciatively to describe an ability to discern things quickly, acutely, or intuitively: She is a therapist of very rare and sensitive perception.

Perceptions are the ways we take in and interpret information through our senses or mind. The word often emphasizes that what we perceive may differ from objective reality: {Public perception of the candidate shifted after the debate}. A perception can also be an insight or observation: {Her perception about the team dynamics proved accurate}. The gap between perception and reality is a common theme in philosophy, psychology, and politics.

Perceptive describes someone quick to notice, understand, or interpret things that others might miss. A perceptive reader catches subtle themes; a perceptive friend senses when something is wrong. The word implies mental sharpness and sensitivity to nuance: {That's a perceptive observation}. Perceptive often suggests emotional intelligence as much as intellectual acuity.

A perch is a place where a bird rests, typically a branch or rod, and by extension any elevated seat or vantage point where someone sits or stands: {She watched the parade from her perch on the balcony}. To perch is to sit or rest in such a position, often suggesting something precarious or temporary. Perch is also a common freshwater fish with spiny fins, popular among anglers. In older usage, a perch was a unit of measurement equal to about five and a half yards.

Perched means sitting or resting on an elevated or narrow spot, the way a bird settles on a branch. A house perched on a cliff occupies a precarious-looking position. A person perched on a stool sits lightly, perhaps temporarily: {She perched on the edge of the desk}. The word suggests height, balance, or readiness to move.

Perches are the elevated spots where birds rest or roost, and by extension any high or precarious position where someone sits or stands: {The lifeguard watched from her perch above the pool}. As a verb, to perch means to settle or rest in such a position, often temporarily or somewhat precariously: {A cat perched on the windowsill}. Perch is also a common freshwater fish with spiny fins, and historically a unit of land measurement equal to about five and a half yards.

Percolate means to filter or seep through a porous substance. Coffee percolates when hot water passes through ground beans. The word extends to gradual spreading or penetration: {News of the scandal slowly percolated through the organization}. Ideas percolate when they develop gradually in the mind: {Let that thought percolate for a while}. To {percolate up} is to rise from below, as when grassroots ideas reach leadership.

Percolated is the past tense of percolate, which means to filter or seep through a porous substance. Coffee percolates when hot water passes through ground beans. More broadly, ideas or information percolate when they spread gradually: {News of the merger percolated through the company}. If something has percolated, it has had time to develop or sink in: {I let the idea percolate for a few days before deciding}.

Percolates means to filter or seep through a porous substance. Coffee percolates when hot water passes through ground beans. Ideas percolate through an organization when they spread gradually. Something percolating in your mind is developing slowly beneath conscious attention: {Let the idea percolate for a few days}. The noun is percolation; the device is a percolator.

Percolating is the process of liquid filtering gradually through a porous substance. Coffee percolates when hot water passes through grounds. The word extends to any slow seepage or spread: {Rumors were percolating through the office}. Ideas percolate when they develop gradually in the mind: {I've been letting the concept percolate for a few weeks}.

Percolation is the process of liquid filtering slowly through a porous material. Coffee percolates when hot water passes through grounds. Water percolates through soil to reach aquifers. The word extends to gradual spreading or seeping: {News of the scandal percolated through the organization}. In physics and mathematics, percolation theory studies how connected pathways form in random systems.

A percolator is a coffeepot that brews by cycling boiling water up through a tube and down through ground coffee. The process repeats until the coffee reaches desired strength. Before drip machines became standard, percolators were the dominant method of home coffee brewing. The word extends to anything that percolates—filters or spreads gradually: {Ideas percolated through the organization}.

Percolators are coffeepots that brew by cycling boiling water up through a tube and down through ground coffee. The process repeats until the coffee reaches desired strength. Before drip machines dominated, percolators were the standard home brewing method. The word extends to anything that percolates—filters slowly, spreads gradually: {Ideas percolate through the culture}.

Percussion refers to the striking of one object against another. In music, percussion instruments produce sound through striking, shaking, or scraping: drums, cymbals, xylophones, tambourines. The percussion section of an orchestra or band plays these instruments collectively. In medicine, percussion is a diagnostic technique where a doctor taps the body to assess underlying structures by the resulting sound. {The percussion was thunderous during the finale.}

A percussionist is a musician who plays percussion instruments—drums, cymbals, xylophones, timpani, and the like. The term typically implies formal training or professional status, distinguishing someone who plays in an orchestra or jazz ensemble from a casual drummer: {The percussionist moved between the marimba and the snare drum throughout the piece}.

Perdition is eternal damnation—the state of being condemned to hell. The word carries a sense of utter ruin and destruction, particularly of the soul: {The preacher warned that sinners faced perdition}. It appears in religious contexts and dramatic speech, often suggesting irreversible spiritual doom. {He believed gambling was the road to perdition.}

Peregrine means wandering or migratory, from a Latin root meaning foreign or traveling abroad. The word is rare and literary, appearing mostly in historical or poetic contexts: {peregrine monks wandering medieval Europe}. Its most common encounter is in peregrine falcon, a bird of prey famous for its global range and spectacular hunting dives. (Capitalized Peregrine is a given name.)

Perennial describes something lasting through the years or recurring regularly. A perennial plant lives more than two years, dying back seasonally but returning from its roots—unlike annuals, which complete their cycle in one season. Extended to other contexts, perennial means enduring or persistent: {a perennial favorite}, {perennial optimism}, {the perennial problem of poverty}. The noun form refers to such a plant: {Hostas are shade-loving perennials}.

Perennials are plants that live for more than two years, returning season after season rather than dying after one growing cycle like annuals. Gardeners prize perennials for their reliability: {The perennials came back strong this spring}. The term extends to anything enduring or recurring: {perennial favorites}, {perennial problems}, {the perennial question of work-life balance}.

Perestroika was the restructuring of the Soviet political and economic system in the 1980s under Mikhail Gorbachev. The Russian word means "rebuilding." Along with glasnost (openness), perestroika aimed to reform the stagnant Soviet state but ultimately contributed to its collapse. The term now sometimes describes any sweeping institutional overhaul: {The company needs its own perestroika}.

Perestrojka was the restructuring of the Soviet political and economic system initiated by Mikhail Gorbachev in the mid-1980s. The Russian word means "rebuilding" or "restructuring." Along with glasnost (openness), perestrojka aimed to modernize the stagnating Soviet economy through limited market reforms and decentralization. The term now evokes that era of dramatic change that preceded the USSR's collapse: {The reforms of perestrojka couldn't save the Soviet system}.

Perfect describes something without flaw or defect—complete in every way. A perfect {score} has no errors. A perfect {circle} meets exact geometric standards. Perfect also means ideally suited: {She's perfect for the role}. The verb, stressed on the second syllable, means to refine until flawless: {He spent years perfecting his technique}. In grammar, the perfect tenses indicate completed action.

Perfecting is the process of bringing something toward an ideal state—refining, polishing, completing. A chef spends years perfecting a signature dish. An artist keeps perfecting brushstrokes. The word implies ongoing effort toward excellence, though true perfection may remain elusive: {She's still perfecting her technique}. In legal contexts, perfecting a claim or lien means completing the formal requirements to make it enforceable.

Perfection is the state of being without flaw or defect—complete, accurate, and excellent in every way. The word often describes an ideal that may be unattainable: {Perfection is the enemy of good}. Something done {to perfection} is done exactly right: {The steak was cooked to perfection}. A person who is {perfection} embodies an ideal: {She was absolute perfection in that role}.

Perfectionism is the refusal to accept any standard short of perfection. A perfectionist holds themselves or others to impossibly high standards, often at the cost of completion or satisfaction: {Her perfectionism kept her revising the manuscript for years}. In psychology, perfectionism can be adaptive (driving excellence) or maladaptive (causing paralysis and anxiety). The word sometimes carries a note of criticism—perfectionists may be seen as difficult to work with or unable to finish projects.

A perfectionist is someone who refuses to accept anything less than flawless. The term usually carries a mild criticism—perfectionists may produce excellent work but at the cost of time, flexibility, or their own peace of mind: {She's such a perfectionist that she rewrote the email six times}. Some wear the label proudly; others recognize it as a polite word for obsessive.

Perfectionists are people who demand flawlessness from themselves or others, often to an unreasonable degree. The trait can drive excellence but also anxiety and procrastination—nothing gets finished if nothing is good enough. {Perfectionists make terrible collaborators.} {She's such a perfectionist that she rewrote the email six times.}

Perforated means pierced with holes, typically in a pattern. Perforated paper tears cleanly along a line of small punctures. A perforated eardrum has a hole or rupture. Perforated metal sheets allow airflow while maintaining structure. The word describes anything deliberately or accidentally punctured: {perforated stamps}, {a perforated ulcer}.

Perforation is a hole or series of holes punched through a surface, typically to allow easy separation or passage. The perforated line on a sheet of stamps lets you tear them apart cleanly. Perforated paper, leather, or metal allows air or liquid through: {perforated eardrum}, {perforated ulcer}. The verb is perforate.

Perforations are small holes punched through a surface, typically in a line or pattern. The rows of tiny holes between postage stamps are perforations, as are the dotted lines on notebook paper that let you tear pages cleanly: {Tear along the perforations}. The term also applies to holes made by puncture wounds or disease, as when an ulcer perforates the stomach wall.

Perform means to carry out an action, task, or function—especially one requiring skill or preparation. Musicians perform concerts, surgeons perform operations, and employees perform their duties. The word often implies an audience or evaluation: {How did the new software perform in testing?} When someone performs, they may also be putting on an act, presenting themselves in a calculated way rather than behaving naturally. A performance is an instance of performing, whether a staged show or simply how well something functions.

Performance is the act of carrying out, accomplishing, or executing something—whether a task, function, or duty. It extends naturally to the execution of artistic works before an audience: a musical performance, a theatrical performance. From there it takes on the sense of how well something or someone functions: {The car's performance exceeded expectations}; {Her job performance has been outstanding}. In contemporary usage, performance often implies a degree of deliberate presentation or artifice, as when someone's behavior seems calculated for effect rather than genuine.

Performances is the plural of performance—instances of presenting entertainment or executing a task. Musicians give performances, athletes have strong or weak performances, and employees receive performance reviews. A single car engine has performance; a concert series has performances. {The orchestra's weekend performances were sold out.}

Performative describes actions that accomplish something merely by being stated. A judge saying {I sentence you to ten years} doesn't describe sentencing—it is the sentencing. Wedding vows, promises, and declarations work this way. More broadly, performative has come to mean done for show rather than substance: {His apology felt performative}, suggesting the gesture was about appearing sorry rather than being sorry.

A performer is someone who performs—acts, sings, dances, plays music, or otherwise presents entertainment before an audience. The word covers professionals and amateurs alike: {She's been a performer since childhood}. Beyond entertainment, performer can describe anyone executing a task, often with a modifier: {a high performer}, {a consistent performer}.

Performers are people who perform—actors, musicians, dancers, acrobats, or anyone who presents entertainment before an audience. The word emphasizes the act of execution rather than creation: a composer writes music, but a performer plays it. {The performers took their bows after the final curtain.} Someone described as a strong performer may simply be effective at their job, not necessarily on a stage.

Performing is doing something in front of an audience—acting, singing, dancing, or playing music. The word extends to any execution of a task: {The car is performing well}. A performing {arts} school teaches theater, music, and dance. To describe someone as performing suggests they may be putting on an act rather than being genuine: {She's always performing for attention}.

Perfume is a fragrant liquid applied to the body for a pleasant scent, typically stronger and longer-lasting than cologne. More broadly, perfume is any sweet or pleasant smell: {the perfume of roses filled the garden}. As a verb, to perfume is to apply fragrance or to fill with scent: {Jasmine perfumed the evening air}.

Perfumed means scented with perfume or a pleasant fragrance: {perfumed soap}, {perfumed stationery}, {the perfumed air of the garden}. The word can suggest something overly scented or artificially fragrant: {Her perfumed presence announced her arrival before she entered}. Figuratively, perfumed may imply something prettified or made artificially pleasant.

A perfumer is someone who creates perfumes—a specialist in blending aromatic compounds to produce fragrances. The term applies both to artisan craftspeople who compose original scents and to those who manufacture or sell perfumes commercially: {The perfumer spent years developing the signature notes for the new fragrance line}.

Perfumery is the art and craft of making perfumes, or a place where perfumes are made or sold. The word covers both the industry and its products collectively: {She studied perfumery in Grasse}, {the perfumery counter at the department store}. A perfumery may also be a factory or shop specializing in fragrances.

Perfumes are fragrant liquids worn on the body, typically applied to pulse points. The word covers both the product and the category of scents generally. As a verb, to perfume is to apply fragrance or to fill with pleasant scent: {Jasmine perfumed the evening air}. Something that perfumes a space suffuses it with aroma, whether literally or figuratively.

A pergola is an outdoor structure consisting of vertical posts supporting an open lattice of crossbeams, typically used to create a shaded walkway or sitting area. Climbing plants like vines or roses are often trained to grow over it: {Wisteria draped the pergola in purple}. Unlike a gazebo, a pergola has no solid roof.

Pergolas are outdoor structures with vertical posts supporting an open overhead framework, typically made of wooden beams or lattice. Unlike gazebos or pavilions, pergolas have no solid roof—they're designed to provide partial shade and support climbing plants like vines or roses: {Wisteria draped over the pergola}. They define garden spaces and outdoor living areas.

Perhaps expresses possibility or uncertainty—something may or may not be true or happen. {Perhaps she's already left}. It can soften statements or requests: {Perhaps you could help me with this}. Perhaps also introduces rough estimates: {Perhaps a dozen people showed up}. The word is slightly more formal than maybe.

Peridot is a bright yellowish-green gemstone, a variety of the mineral olivine. It has been used in jewelry for thousands of years and is the birthstone for August. The distinctive lime-green color comes from iron in the crystal structure. {She wore a peridot pendant that matched her eyes.}

Peril is serious danger or risk of harm. The word carries a slightly literary or formal tone: {The climbers faced great peril on the mountain}, {at peril of one's life}. To peril something is to put it at risk, though the verb is rare. {In peril} and {at your peril} are the common phrases—the latter a warning that proceeding means accepting the consequences.

Perilous means full of danger or risk. A perilous {journey} threatens harm at every turn. A perilous {situation} could easily end badly. The word carries a slightly literary or dramatic flavor—you're more likely to encounter it in adventure stories than casual conversation. {The climbers faced perilous conditions on the mountain}.

Perils are serious dangers or risks that threaten harm. The word carries a slightly formal or literary tone: {the perils of ocean travel}, {financial perils}. To peril something is to put it at risk, though this verb form is rare. {At your peril} warns of danger: {Ignore the instructions at your peril}.

Perimenopause is the transitional phase before menopause when a woman's body begins shifting toward the end of reproductive capacity. It typically begins in the mid-forties and lasts several years, marked by irregular periods, hormonal fluctuations, and symptoms like hot flashes, mood changes, and sleep disruption: {Her doctor said the night sweats were probably perimenopause}.

Perimeter is the outer boundary of an enclosed area, or the total length of that boundary. In geometry, you calculate the perimeter of a shape by adding the lengths of all its sides: {The perimeter of a rectangle is twice the length plus twice the width}. More broadly, perimeter refers to the defended edge of a military position or secured zone: {Guards patrolled the perimeter}. In basketball, the perimeter is the area beyond the lane but inside the three-point line.

Perimeters is the plural of perimeter—the outer boundary or edge of an enclosed area. In geometry, the perimeter is the total length around a shape: {Calculate the perimeters of these triangles}. More broadly, perimeters mark defensive boundaries: {Guards patrolled the perimeters of the compound}. Security perimeters establish controlled zones around sensitive locations.

An idea implicit in many meanings of period is occurrence in cycles—in other words, periodicity. A period is typically a demarcated length of time with particular characteristics: a mating period, a period of calm. If you wonder why the dot at the end of sentence is called a period (in American English), think of that period as punctuating a cycle of sentences. As an adjective, period typically refers to a period of time in the somewhat distant past that is made more specific by context: a new period drama from the BBC; She’s redone her living room in period furniture.

Periodic means recurring at regular intervals. A periodic {checkup} happens on a fixed schedule. Periodic {table} arranges elements by recurring patterns in their properties. The word can also describe something that happens occasionally but not on a strict schedule: {periodic outbursts of violence}. Periodically is the adverb: {The machine needs to be serviced periodically}.
clues: Showing up from time to time

definition: Periods are intervals of time, whether defined by duration, by historical character, or by recurring events: {the medieval period}, {a period of economic growth}, {class periods}. In punctuation, a period is the dot marking the end of a sentence. In menstruation, a period is the monthly discharge of blood from the uterus. Saying {period} at the end of a statement adds finality: {I'm not going, period}.

Peripheral means at the edge or boundary rather than the center. Peripheral {vision} is what you see at the outer edges of your visual field. Peripheral {concerns} are secondary to the main issue. In computing, a peripheral is any device connected to a computer but not part of its core—printers, keyboards, monitors, external drives: {The store sells computers and peripherals}.

Peripherals are devices that connect to a computer but aren't part of its core processing unit—keyboards, mice, monitors, printers, external drives. The term comes from their position at the edge of the system rather than its center. In broader use, peripherals can mean any secondary equipment or accessories: {We packed the tent and all the peripherals}.

Periphery is the outer boundary or edge of something, as opposed to its center: {homes on the periphery of the city}, {the periphery of the retina}. It extends to figurative margins—things at the periphery of a discussion or field receive less attention than what's central. In computing, peripherals are devices connected to but separate from the main computer: keyboards, monitors, printers.

A periscope is an optical instrument with mirrors or prisms that lets you see things not in your direct line of sight. The classic periscope is used in submarines to view the surface while submerged: {The captain raised the periscope to scan for enemy ships}. Periscopes also appear in tanks and trench warfare, allowing observation while staying protected.

Periscopes are optical instruments that allow viewing from a concealed or submerged position. A system of mirrors or prisms lets an observer see over or around obstacles—most famously from submarines looking above the water's surface. The term extends to any device using similar principles: {tank periscopes}, {trench periscopes}. As a verb, to periscope is to extend or peer upward like a periscope: {Prairie dogs periscoped from their burrows}.

Perish means to die or be destroyed, often violently or prematurely: {Thousands perished in the earthquake}. The word carries literary or formal weight—news reports say victims perished rather than died. Things that perish may also decay or deteriorate: {The rubber gaskets had perished with age}. To {perish the thought} is to reject an idea as unthinkable.

Perishable describes things that decay or spoil relatively quickly, especially food: {perishable goods}, {highly perishable items}. The noun perishables refers to foods requiring refrigeration or prompt consumption: {Put the perishables in the fridge first}. The word implies a limited window before something becomes unusable or unsafe.

Perishables are goods that spoil or decay quickly, especially food items requiring refrigeration: {The movers won't transport perishables}. The term appears most often in shipping, grocery, and moving contexts, distinguishing items with limited shelf life from durable goods. Singular perishable functions as both noun and adjective: {perishable cargo}, {a perishable}.

Perished is the past tense of perish, meaning to die or be destroyed, often in circumstances that are violent, sudden, or extreme: {Thousands perished in the earthquake}. The word carries a formal or literary weight heavier than simply "died." In British usage, to be perished means to be extremely cold: {I'm absolutely perished}.

Perishing means dying or being destroyed, often gradually: {The refugees were perishing from cold and hunger}. In British informal use, perishing is an intensifier meaning extremely or damned, especially about cold: {It's perishing outside}, {I'm perishing cold}. The adjective can also describe something causing such discomfort: {a perishing wind}.

Periwinkle names two unrelated things. One is a small sea snail with a spiral shell, eaten in coastal cuisines and found clinging to rocks at low tide. The other is a trailing evergreen plant with blue or purple flowers, commonly used as ground cover. The color periwinkle—a pale blue-violet—takes its name from the flower: {a periwinkle cardigan}, {periwinkle bridesmaid dresses}.

Periwinkles are small edible sea snails found in coastal waters, gathered from rocks and tidal pools. The word also refers to trailing evergreen plants with blue or white flowers, commonly used as ground cover. The two meanings are unrelated—different words that converged on the same spelling. {We picked periwinkles off the rocks at low tide.}

A perjurer is someone who commits perjury—lying under oath in legal proceedings. The term applies to anyone who deliberately gives false testimony after swearing to tell the truth: {The witness was exposed as a perjurer when surveillance footage contradicted her statement}.

Perjury is the crime of lying under oath—deliberately giving false testimony in court or other official proceedings where you've sworn to tell the truth. The charge requires that the falsehood be material to the case, not merely incidental. {He was convicted of perjury after investigators proved he lied to the grand jury.}

Perk is a benefit or advantage that comes with a job or situation beyond the basic compensation: {Free parking is one of the perks}. The word is a shortening of perquisite. As a verb, to perk up is to become more lively or alert: {She perked up when she heard her name}. Coffee perks when it brews in a percolator—the liquid rising and falling through the grounds.

Perked is the past tense of perk, which means to become more lively, cheerful, or alert—often after a period of low energy or spirits. Coffee perks when it brews in a percolator, bubbling up through the grounds. More commonly, people perk up when something improves their mood or energy: {She perked up after hearing the good news.} {A cup of tea really perked him up.}

Perks are benefits or advantages that come with a position, membership, or situation—extras beyond the basic compensation or expectation. The word is short for perquisites: {The job doesn't pay much, but the perks are great}. Company cars, free meals, and gym memberships are typical workplace perks. The word has expanded beyond employment: {One of the perks of living downtown is walking to everything}.

Perky describes someone cheerful, lively, and alert—often with a bounce in their step or brightness in their voice: {She was annoyingly perky for 6 a.m.} The word can carry a hint of excess, suggesting enthusiasm that others find tiresome. Perky also describes things that stick up or out jauntily: {a perky ponytail}, {perky breasts}.

A perm is a chemical treatment that gives hair a lasting wave or curl, short for permanent wave. The curls hold their shape through washing until the treated hair grows out. To perm hair is to apply such a treatment: {She permed her hair for the wedding}. Perms were especially popular in the 1980s. In British usage, a perm is also a permutation, especially in football pools.

A permaban is a permanent ban from an online platform, game, or community—as opposed to temporary suspensions that expire. The term combines "permanent" and "ban." Getting permabanned typically results from severe or repeated violations: {He got permabanned for cheating}, {One more offense and it's a permaban}. As a verb: {The mods permabanned three accounts last night}.

Permabanned means permanently banned from a platform, game, or online community—as opposed to a temporary suspension. The term emerged from gaming and internet culture, where moderators distinguish between time-limited penalties and lifetime exclusions: {He got permabanned from the server for cheating}. {One more offense and you're permabanned}.

Permacrisis describes a prolonged period of instability marked by overlapping crises—economic, political, environmental, or social—that seem to have no clear resolution. The word captures the sense that modern life lurches from one emergency to the next without returning to normal: {Between the pandemic, inflation, and climate disasters, we're living in permacrisis}. Coined in the early 2020s, it reflects exhaustion with constant upheaval.

Permaculture is an approach to agriculture and land use that mimics natural ecosystems, emphasizing sustainability, biodiversity, and closed-loop resource cycles. The term blends "permanent" with "agriculture" (or "culture"). Practitioners design gardens, farms, and communities where elements work together—plants that fix nitrogen, animals that control pests, water systems that harvest rain: {We're converting the backyard to permaculture principles}.

Permadeath is a video game mechanic where a character's death is permanent—no respawns, no reloading saves, no second chances. The player must start over from the beginning or lose that character forever. The feature raises stakes dramatically: {I lost my 40-hour save to permadeath}. Common in roguelikes and survival games, permadeath appeals to players who want meaningful consequences.

Permafrost is ground that remains frozen for at least two consecutive years, found in polar regions and high mountains. It can extend hundreds of meters deep, with only a thin surface layer thawing seasonally. Climate scientists track permafrost because its thawing releases stored carbon: {As permafrost melts, it accelerates global warming}.

A permalink is a permanent link—a URL designed to remain unchanged indefinitely, ensuring the address will still work in the future. The term emerged from blogging, where each post gets its own stable address rather than appearing only on a shifting front page. {I'll send you the permalink so you can bookmark it.} Now used broadly for any persistent web address.

Permanence is the quality of lasting indefinitely, of remaining unchanged through time. It contrasts with the temporary or fleeting: {the permanence of stone versus the impermanence of ice}. The word often carries philosophical weight—questions about what endures and what passes away: {She doubted the permanence of any human institution}.

Permanent describes something that lasts indefinitely or is intended to remain unchanged. A permanent {job} offers ongoing employment rather than temporary work. Permanent {teeth} replace baby teeth and are meant to last a lifetime. A permanent {marker} creates marks that resist washing or fading. The noun permanent, now somewhat dated, refers to a hair treatment that creates long-lasting curls or waves. Despite its meaning, permanent often admits exceptions: even {permanent} residents can sometimes be deported.

Permeate means to spread or flow throughout something, passing through its pores or gaps. Water permeates soil; a smell permeates a room. The word applies equally well to abstractions: {Corruption had permeated every level of government}. When something permeates, it saturates thoroughly rather than merely touching the surface—the influence becomes part of the thing it enters.

Permeated is the past tense of permeate, meaning to spread or pass through something completely. A smell permeates a room by filling every part of it. Ideas permeate a culture by saturating it thoroughly. The word suggests penetration into every corner or layer: {The smell of cigarette smoke had permeated the curtains}. {Corruption had permeated the entire organization}.

Permed describes hair that has been given a permanent wave—a chemical treatment that creates lasting curls or waves in naturally straight hair. The style was especially popular in the 1980s: {She still had the same permed hair from her high school photos}. The term can also describe someone who has received such a treatment: {I got permed for prom}.

Permission is the act of allowing someone to do something, or the state of being allowed. When you have permission, someone with authority has agreed that you may proceed: {She got permission from her parents to stay out late}. Permission can be granted formally through documents or informally through a nod or verbal okay. To ask permission is to request approval before acting, a convention that acknowledges someone else's authority over the matter.

Permissions are authorizations to do something—access a place, use a resource, or take an action that would otherwise be restricted. In computing, permissions control what users can do with files and systems: {read permissions}, {write permissions}, {You don't have permission to access this folder}. The singular permission is the broader concept; the plural permissions typically refers to specific rights that can be granted or revoked.

Permissive describes someone or something that allows behavior others might restrict or forbid. A permissive parent gives children wide latitude; a permissive society tolerates diverse lifestyles. The word often carries a faint disapproval—implying too much is allowed: {Critics blamed permissive attitudes for rising crime rates}. In technical contexts, permissive means optional rather than required: a permissive license allows modification of software.

Permit centers on allowing or authorizing. To permit something is to give consent or make it possible: {The rules don't permit smoking indoors}, {Weather permitting, we'll have the picnic outside}. A permit is an official document granting authorization: a {building permit}, a {parking permit}, a {work permit}. Permit is slightly more formal than let or allow.

Permits functions as both verb and noun around the idea of allowing. To permit is to give permission or make possible: {The rules permit one absence per semester}, {Weather permitting, we'll eat outside}. A permit is an official document granting authorization: a building permit, a work permit, a parking permit. The noun stresses the first syllable (PER-mit), the verb the second (per-MIT).

Permitting is the present participle of permit, used when someone or something allows, authorizes, or makes possible an action or condition. {Weather permitting, we'll have the picnic outside.} In bureaucratic contexts, permitting refers to the process of obtaining official permits: {The permitting phase delayed construction by six months.} The word often implies conditional allowance—something happens only if circumstances or authorities don't prevent it.

Perms is the plural of perm, a hairstyle created by chemically treating hair to hold curls or waves permanently—or at least until the hair grows out: {She got perms throughout the eighties}. The word is short for permanent wave. In computing and gaming contexts, perms is short for permissions: {You need admin perms to access that folder}.

Permutations are the different arrangements possible when ordering a set of things. In mathematics, permutation refers specifically to arrangements where order matters—the permutations of ABC include ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, and CBA. More loosely, permutations are variations or different versions: {The idea has gone through countless permutations since we first proposed it}. The singular permutation appears in both technical and general contexts.

Pernickety means excessively fussy about small details, demanding that things be just so. Someone pernickety might reject a document for a minor formatting error or send back a dish because the garnish is wrong: {She's pernickety about how the towels are folded}. The word is British; Americans usually say persnickety.

A perogi (also pierogi, pyrogy, or varenyky) is a filled dumpling of Eastern European origin, typically made from unleavened dough wrapped around savory or sweet fillings—potato and cheese, sauerkraut, meat, or fruit. They're boiled, then often pan-fried in butter: {We ordered a plate of perogies with sour cream and onions}.

A perogie is a filled dumpling of Eastern European origin, typically made with unleavened dough and stuffed with potato, cheese, sauerkraut, meat, or fruit.
