Photobombed is the past tense of photobomb—to insert yourself into someone else's photograph without their knowledge or consent, typically by appearing in the background just as the picture is taken. The effect is usually comic or mischievous: {I didn't notice the guy until I saw the photo—we got photobombed}. The term emerged with digital photography and social media, where unexpected intruders in the frame became a recognized phenomenon.

A photobomber is someone who deliberately inserts themselves into a photograph, usually without the knowledge or consent of the intended subjects. The act is typically meant to be humorous or disruptive, with the photobomber appearing in the background making faces, striking poses, or otherwise drawing attention away from the main subjects. {A random guy photobombed our wedding pictures.} The term emerged alongside smartphone culture and social media sharing.

Photobombing is the act of inserting yourself into someone else's photograph without their knowledge or consent, typically by appearing in the background just as the picture is taken. The intent is usually humorous or mischievous rather than malicious. {I didn't notice the stranger photobombing us until I looked at the picture later.} The term extends to any unexpected intrusion into a photo, including by animals or objects that disrupt the intended shot.

Photobombs is the verb form of photobomb—to insert oneself into someone else's photograph without their knowledge or consent, typically appearing in the background just as the picture is taken. The act is usually playful or mischievous: {He photobombs every group shot at parties}. A photobomb can also be the resulting image or the person who does it.

A photobooth is a small enclosed kiosk where people take photographs of themselves, typically by inserting coins and posing for a series of automatic shots. Traditional photobooths produce strips of small prints; modern versions at events often include props and digital sharing options. {We squeezed into the photobooth at the wedding reception.}

Photobooths is the plural of photobooth—a small enclosed space equipped with a camera for taking quick portrait photographs. Traditional photobooths dispensed strips of photos after inserting coins; modern versions at weddings and parties often include props and digital sharing. {The photobooths at the reception had a line all night.}

A photocopier is a machine that makes paper copies of documents by projecting light onto the original and transferring the image to blank paper. Office photocopiers handle high volumes; smaller versions are called copiers or copy machines. The verb is photocopy: {Can you photocopy this report for me?}

A photocopy is a duplicate of a document made by a machine that photographs and reproduces the original. To photocopy is to make such a copy: {I need to photocopy my passport}. The word emerged with xerographic technology in the mid-20th century and remains standard despite digital alternatives. A photocopier is the machine that makes them.

Photocopying is making copies of documents or images using a machine that scans the original and reproduces it on paper. The term covers both the process and the activity: {I spent the morning photocopying contracts}. Though digital scanning has reduced its dominance, photocopying remains standard for quick paper duplicates in offices and libraries.

A photofinish is a race ending so close that only a photograph of the finish line can determine the winner. The term extends to any extremely close competition or outcome: {The election was a photofinish, with fewer than a hundred votes separating the candidates}. Also spelled photo finish.

Photogenic describes someone or something that looks good in photographs. Some faces photograph better than others—features that seem ordinary in person can appear striking on camera, while conventionally attractive people sometimes photograph poorly. {She's incredibly photogenic; every shot looks professional.} The word occasionally describes anything that produces or relates to light, but the camera-ready sense dominates.

A photograph is an image created by capturing light on a sensitive surface—originally chemical film, now usually a digital sensor. To photograph is to take such an image: {She photographed the wedding}. Unlike paintings or drawings, photographs record what was actually in front of the camera, giving them evidentiary weight: {The photograph proved he was there}.

A photographer is someone who takes photographs, whether as a profession, serious pursuit, or casual hobby. Professional photographers specialize in areas like portraiture, weddings, journalism, fashion, or wildlife. The term applies equally to someone shooting with expensive equipment in a studio and to anyone snapping pictures with a phone. {The photographer asked everyone to smile.}

Photographic describes anything relating to or produced by photography. A photographic {image} or {record} is one captured by a camera. Someone with a photographic {memory} can recall visual details with unusual precision and clarity, as if they had taken a mental photograph. The word also characterizes qualities that resemble photographs: sharp, detailed, realistic. A photographic {likeness} captures someone exactly as they appear.

Photographs are images created by capturing light on a sensitive surface—originally chemical film, now typically digital sensors. The word often shortens to photos. As a verb, to photograph is to take such images: {She photographs weddings for a living}. Someone who {photographs well} looks attractive in pictures. Photographs serve as evidence, art, and memory: {old family photographs}, {crime scene photographs}.

Photography is the art and practice of capturing images using light. A camera records light onto a sensitive surface—historically film, now typically a digital sensor. The word covers both the technical process and the creative discipline: {She studied photography in college}. {Wedding photography} and {nature photography} name specialized fields. {Aerial photography} captures images from above.

A photojournalist is a journalist who tells news stories primarily through photographs rather than written text. Photojournalists work for newspapers, magazines, and wire services, documenting events from war zones to political protests to human interest stories: {The photojournalist spent three months embedded with troops in Afghanistan}. The work emphasizes capturing decisive moments that convey narrative and emotion.

Photojournalists are journalists who report stories primarily through photographs rather than written text. They document news events, conflicts, and human interest stories for newspapers, magazines, and news websites: {Photojournalists captured the aftermath of the earthquake}. The work often requires being present at dangerous or emotionally intense situations.

A photon is the smallest unit of light or other electromagnetic radiation—a quantum of energy that behaves as both a particle and a wave. Photons have no mass and travel at the speed of light. The term appears in physics, photography, and increasingly in everyday contexts: {Solar panels convert photons into electricity}. {Photons from distant stars take millions of years to reach us}.

Photons are particles of light and other electromagnetic radiation. Unlike matter particles, photons have no mass and always travel at the speed of light. Each photon carries a specific amount of energy determined by its wavelength—shorter wavelengths (like X-rays) carry more energy than longer ones (like radio waves). {The detector registered individual photons striking the sensor.}

Photorealism is a style of visual art—especially painting and drawing—that aims to reproduce subjects with the precision and detail of a photograph. The movement emerged in the late 1960s, often depicting mundane scenes: storefronts, cars, reflections in glass. The term extends to computer graphics striving for lifelike rendering: {The game's photorealism is stunning}.

Photorealistic describes images that resemble photographs in their level of detail and accuracy. The term applies to paintings, digital renderings, and computer graphics that achieve near-photographic fidelity: {The video game's photorealistic graphics blurred the line between animation and live action}. A photorealistic style prioritizes technical precision over stylization or abstraction.

Photos is the plural of photo, an informal shortening of photograph. It refers to images captured by a camera: {I took some photos at the wedding}, {She scrolled through old photos on her phone}. The word dominates casual speech and writing, while photograph sounds more formal or technical.

A photoshoot is a planned session where a photographer takes pictures, typically of a model, celebrity, product, or event. The term implies professional or semi-professional work with deliberate staging: {We did a photoshoot for the new catalog}. Also spelled as two words: photo shoot.

Photoshoots are sessions where a photographer takes planned photographs of a subject—typically a model, celebrity, product, or location. The term implies preparation and intent, distinguishing it from casual snapshots: {The magazine arranged a photoshoot for the cover story}. Also spelled as two words: photo shoots.

Photoshop is image-editing software that became so dominant its name turned into a verb. To photoshop an image is to digitally alter it—removing blemishes, combining elements, or manipulating reality: {That photo is obviously photoshopped}. The verb applies regardless of which software is actually used. A photoshopped image may be subtly retouched or blatantly fabricated.

Photoshopped means digitally altered, from Adobe Photoshop software that became synonymous with image manipulation. A photoshopped image has been edited—retouching blemishes, removing objects, compositing elements, or distorting reality: {That photo is obviously photoshopped}. The term often implies deception or unrealistic beauty standards: {Magazine covers are heavily photoshopped}. Now used generically regardless of which software was actually used.

Photoshopping is digitally altering an image, especially to improve appearance or create deceptive effects. The term comes from Adobe Photoshop software but applies to any image manipulation: {They photoshopped her waist smaller}, {That sunset looks photoshopped}. The practice ranges from minor touch-ups to wholesale fabrication, making photoshopped a synonym for digitally fake.

Photoshops is the verb form of Photoshop, meaning to digitally alter an image using photo-editing software. Though derived from the Adobe trademark, the verb has become generic: {She photoshops all her Instagram photos}. The term often implies deceptive manipulation—removing blemishes, slimming bodies, or fabricating scenes entirely. {That sunset looks photoshopped.}

Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae, and some bacteria convert sunlight into chemical energy. Using light, water, and carbon dioxide, they produce sugars for food and release oxygen as a byproduct. Nearly all life on Earth depends on photosynthesis—directly for food or indirectly through the oxygen it generates.

A phrase is a group of words functioning as a unit within a sentence but not containing both a subject and verb—{in the morning}, {running late}, {the old house on the corner}. To phrase something is to express it in particular words: {Let me phrase this carefully}. How you phrase a question affects what answers you get. In music, a phrase is a short melodic passage forming a distinct unit within a longer piece.

Phrases is the plural of phrase—a group of words forming a unit of meaning smaller than a complete sentence. In grammar, phrases function as single parts of speech: a noun phrase, a verb phrase. In music, a phrase is a short melodic passage. The verb phrases means to express in particular words: {Let me phrase this carefully}. To {turn a phrase} is to express something memorably.

Phrasing is the way something is expressed in words—the particular arrangement and choice of language: {The phrasing of the contract left room for interpretation}. In music, phrasing refers to how a performer shapes melodic lines, grouping notes and managing breath or bowing to create musical sentences. A comedian's timing depends on phrasing as much as content.

Phrenology is a discredited pseudoscience from the 19th century that claimed personality traits and mental abilities could be determined by examining the shape and bumps of the skull. Practitioners believed different brain regions controlled specific faculties, and that these areas grew or shrank based on use, affecting skull contours. Though thoroughly debunked, phrenology influenced early neuroscience and is now invoked as a byword for scientific racism and junk science: {That's just phrenology with extra steps}.

Phyllo is paper-thin pastry dough used in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cooking, most famously in baklava and spanakopita. The sheets are layered with butter or oil between them, creating a flaky, crispy texture when baked. Working with phyllo requires patience since the delicate sheets dry out quickly and tear easily. {She brushed each layer of phyllo with melted butter before adding the next.}

Physical relates to the body and the material world, as opposed to the mind, spirit, or abstract concepts. A physical {exam} assesses bodily health. Physical {labor} requires bodily effort. The physical {sciences} study matter and energy. Physical {contact} involves touching. To {get physical} can mean becoming violent or sexually intimate. A physical is a medical examination: {I need to schedule my annual physical}.

Physicality is the quality of being physical—having bodily presence, tangible form, or material existence. The word often emphasizes the body's involvement in an activity: {The role demanded real physicality from the actor}. In sports, physicality suggests aggressive, body-to-body play: {Their defense relies on physicality rather than speed}. The term can also describe how concrete or tactile something feels: {I miss the physicality of vinyl records}.

Physicals is the plural of physical, most often referring to medical examinations: {Annual physicals are required for student athletes}. The word can also denote physical education classes or physical therapy sessions. In finance, physicals are tangible commodities—actual oil, grain, or metals—as opposed to futures contracts or other derivatives.

A physician is a doctor—someone licensed to practice medicine and treat illness. The term is slightly formal, often appearing in professional and institutional contexts: {primary care physician}, {attending physician}. In everyday speech, doctor is more common, while physician appears on forms, in hospital settings, and in compounds like {physician assistant}.

A physicist is a scientist who studies physics—the fundamental laws governing matter, energy, motion, and the structure of the universe. Physicists work in fields ranging from quantum mechanics to astrophysics, often splitting between theoretical work {a theoretical physicist} and experimental research {particle physicists at CERN}.

Physicists are scientists who study physics—the fundamental nature of matter, energy, space, and time. They investigate everything from subatomic particles to the structure of the universe. Some work theoretically, developing mathematical models; others conduct experiments. {The physicists at CERN discovered the Higgs boson.}

Physics is the science of matter, energy, and their interactions—how objects move, how forces act, how the universe behaves at scales from subatomic particles to galaxies. {She majored in physics}. The physics of something refers to its physical properties or behavior: {The physics of a curveball involves spin and air resistance}.

Physio is an informal shortening of physiotherapy or physiotherapist, common in British, Australian, and New Zealand English: {I've got a physio appointment tomorrow}, {The physio said I need to strengthen my core}. In American English, the full forms or "physical therapy" and "physical therapist" are more typical.

Physiology is the branch of biology dealing with how living organisms function—how bodies work rather than what they're made of. Where anatomy describes structure, physiology describes process: how muscles contract, how nerves transmit signals, how kidneys filter blood. The word extends to particular systems: {the physiology of digestion}, {plant physiology}. Someone's physiology is their body's particular way of functioning: {Her physiology doesn't tolerate caffeine well}.

A physiotherapist is a healthcare professional who treats injury, disease, or disability through physical methods—exercise, massage, manipulation, and other techniques—rather than drugs or surgery. The term is standard in British English and most of the world; Americans typically say physical therapist. {The physiotherapist worked on strengthening her knee after surgery.}

Physiotherapy is the treatment of injury, disease, or disability through physical methods—exercise, massage, heat, manipulation—rather than drugs or surgery. The goal is restoring movement and function. British English prefers physiotherapy; American English tends toward physical therapy. A physiotherapist designs rehabilitation programs for patients recovering from strokes, surgeries, or chronic conditions.

Physique is the form and structure of a person's body, especially regarding muscular development and physical fitness: {He has the physique of a swimmer}. The word typically appears in contexts of athleticism or attractiveness, carrying a slightly more formal or admiring tone than simply saying "body" or "build."

Physiques is the plural of physique—the form, size, and development of a person's body, especially as shaped by exercise or genetics. The word typically appears in contexts involving athletics or physical fitness: {Swimmers and gymnasts have very different physiques}. It suggests overall bodily structure rather than specific measurements.

Pianissimo is a musical direction meaning very soft—quieter than piano. The term comes from Italian and appears in sheet music as an instruction to performers. As an adverb or adjective, it describes passages played at this hushed dynamic level: {The strings enter pianissimo beneath the soloist}. Often abbreviated pp.

A pianist is a person who plays the piano, especially as a profession or serious pursuit. The term typically implies skill or training beyond casual playing: {She's been a concert pianist for twenty years}. {The jazz pianist improvised throughout the set}.

Pianists are people who play the piano, especially as a profession or serious pursuit. The term implies skill beyond casual playing—one might say {My daughter plays piano} but {My daughter is a pianist} suggests commitment or achievement. Concert pianists perform publicly; jazz pianists and classical pianists work in different traditions.

A piano is a large keyboard instrument where hammers strike strings when keys are pressed. The full name, pianoforte, reflects its ability to play soft (piano) and loud (forte)—a revolutionary feature when invented. Grand pianos have horizontal strings; upright pianos stand vertically to save space. Piano also serves as a musical direction meaning softly: {The passage is marked piano}.

Pianos is the plural of piano, the large keyboard instrument with hammered strings. The word covers the full range—grand pianos, upright pianos, electric pianos: {The music school has six pianos}. Piano also serves as a musical direction meaning soft or quietly, from the Italian, but that sense rarely takes a plural.

A piazza is a public square or marketplace, especially in Italian towns. The word entered English through Italian architecture and urban design: {The cafe tables spilled out into the piazza}. In parts of the American South, piazza refers to a covered porch or veranda on a house—a regional usage that puzzles visitors from elsewhere.

Pic is informal for picture, especially a photograph: {I'll send you a pic}. The word thrives in digital contexts—profile pics, pics or it didn't happen. It can also mean a movie, though this use is mostly confined to entertainment industry jargon: {The studio greenlighted the pic}.

Picadillo is a Latin American and Spanish dish of ground meat—usually beef or pork—cooked with tomatoes, onions, and various seasonings. Regional versions add olives, raisins, capers, or potatoes. It serves as a filling for tacos, empanadas, and stuffed peppers, or stands alone over rice: {My grandmother's picadillo had green olives and hard-boiled eggs}.

Piccata is a style of preparing meat—typically veal or chicken—by slicing it thin, dredging in flour, sautéing, and serving with a sauce of lemon, butter, and capers: {chicken piccata}, {veal piccata}. The dish appears on Italian-American restaurant menus. The word comes from Italian, suggesting something piquant or sharp.

A piccolo is a small flute pitched an octave higher than the standard flute, producing the highest notes in an orchestra. Its bright, piercing tone cuts through even full orchestral sound: {The piccolo solo soared above the brass section}. Players typically double on both flute and piccolo.

Piccolos is the plural of piccolo, a small flute pitched an octave higher than the standard flute. The piccolo produces the highest notes in an orchestra, its bright, piercing tone cutting through full ensemble passages: {The piccolos shrilled above the brass section}. The word comes from Italian for "small."
clues: Small flutes pitched an octave higher

definition: The verb pick in many ways combines the ideas of choosing and seizing. Can you pick a winner? If so, you know how to identify one. If you pick a fight, you start it. To pick someone’s brain is to solicit information from them with questions. Someone or something randomly picked is randomly selected. A pick is an instance or the result of picking, but is also the name of a variety of tools (ice pick, hair pick, guitar pick). If you pick at something, you tinker with it to get a desirable result.

A pickax is a hand tool with a heavy metal head mounted on a wooden handle, used for breaking up hard ground, rock, or pavement. One end of the head is pointed, the other typically flattened like a chisel. The tool is associated with mining, construction, and manual labor: {The workers swung pickaxes at the frozen earth}. Also spelled pickaxe.

A pickaxe is a hand tool with a long wooden handle and a head that typically has a pointed end and a chisel end, used for breaking up hard ground or rock. The pointed end loosens material; the chisel end pries it apart. {Workers swung pickaxes to break through the frozen soil.} Also spelled pickax.

Pickaxes is the plural of pickaxe, a heavy tool with a pointed metal head mounted on a wooden handle, used for breaking up hard ground or rock. The head typically has a pick on one end and a chisel or adze on the other. {The miners swung their pickaxes into the coal seam.} Figuratively, to pickaxe is to chip away at something laboriously.

Picked describes something carefully selected or chosen: {a picked team of specialists}, {picked troops}. The word emphasizes deliberate selection rather than random assignment—picked items represent the best or most suitable options from a larger group. As the past tense of pick, it also covers the act of gathering: {We picked apples all afternoon}.

A picker is someone or something that picks. Fruit pickers harvest crops by hand. A picker in a warehouse selects items for orders. Guitar pickers play by plucking strings. The word often appears in combinations: {cherry picker}, {cotton picker}, {nit-picker}. A picker tool extracts or separates things: {ice picker}, {lock picker}.

Pickers is the plural of picker—someone or something that picks. Fruit pickers harvest crops by hand. Guitar pickers play fingerstyle or flatpick. Pickers also describes people who search through items for valuable finds, especially at estate sales, flea markets, or antique shops: {The pickers arrived early to get first look at the garage sale}.

A picket is a pointed stake driven into the ground, used for fencing or tethering animals. The meaning extends to a person stationed outside a workplace during a strike to discourage others from entering: {Picketers blocked the factory entrance}. To picket is to protest in this way. A picket fence is a row of pointed wooden slats, an emblem of suburban domesticity. In military use, a picket is a soldier or group posted to watch for the enemy.

Picketing is the act of standing or marching near a workplace, business, or other location to protest or draw attention to a grievance, typically during a labor dispute. Picketers usually carry signs and try to discourage others from entering the premises or doing business there. {The union organized picketing outside the factory gates.} The term extends beyond labor contexts to any organized demonstration at a specific location: {Animal rights activists were picketing the research facility.}

Pickets are pointed stakes driven into the ground, typically as part of a fence or to secure something in place. The word extends to people stationed outside a workplace during a strike, standing like human stakes to discourage others from entering: {Union members walked the picket line for three weeks}. As a verb, to picket means to stand guard in this way, or to enclose an area with pointed stakes. A picket fence, with its evenly spaced vertical slats, evokes images of tidy suburban domesticity.

Picking is the act of selecting or gathering. You pick fruit from trees, pick items from a list, or pick a winner. Cotton picking and cherry picking are literal harvests; {cherry-picking} figuratively means selecting only what supports your case. Picking also describes plucking motions—picking a guitar, picking at food, picking a lock. A picking is something gathered: {slim pickings} means little worth taking.

Pickings are things available to be taken or chosen, especially what remains after others have had first choice. The word almost always appears with a modifier: slim pickings means little is available; easy pickings means something can be taken with little effort or resistance. Rich pickings suggests abundant rewards: {The unlocked cars were rich pickings for thieves}.

A pickle is a cucumber preserved in brine or vinegar, though other vegetables can be pickled too: {pickled beets}, {pickled onions}. The verb means to preserve food this way. A pickle is also an awkward situation: {We're in a real pickle now}. In baseball, a pickle is a rundown—a baserunner trapped between fielders.

Pickleball is a paddle sport combining elements of tennis, badminton, and ping-pong. Players use solid paddles to hit a perforated plastic ball over a low net on a court smaller than a tennis court. The game has surged in popularity, especially among older adults, for being easier on joints than tennis: {The retirement community added six pickleball courts}.

Pickled describes food preserved in brine or vinegar: pickled {cucumbers}, pickled {herring}, pickled {eggs}. The process gives foods a characteristic sour or tangy flavor. Figuratively, pickled means drunk: {He was thoroughly pickled by midnight}. The connection is immersion—cucumbers soaked in brine, a person soaked in alcohol.

Pickles are cucumbers preserved in brine or vinegar, though the term extends to any vegetable preserved this way: pickled {onions}, pickled {beets}. In British English, pickle (singular) often means a tangy relish or chutney. To be {in a pickle} is to be in a difficult situation. The verb pickle means to preserve in brine: {We pickled the excess cucumbers from the garden}.

Pickling is preserving food in brine or vinegar, creating an acidic environment that prevents spoilage: {pickling cucumbers}, {pickling beets}. The process gives preserved foods their characteristic tangy flavor. In metalworking, pickling means cleaning metal surfaces with acid to remove scale or oxide. To be {in a pickle} is to be in a difficult situation—preserved in trouble, as it were.

A picklock is a tool designed to open locks without the proper key, or a person skilled at using such tools. The word carries connotations of burglary and illicit entry: {The detective found a set of picklocks in the suspect's pocket}. As a verb, to picklock is to open a lock this way, though "pick the lock" is more common.

Picklocks are tools designed to open locks without the proper key, used by locksmiths and burglars alike. The term can also refer to people who pick locks: {The picklocks worked quickly before the guards returned}. A single tool is a picklock; the plural covers either multiple tools or multiple practitioners.

A pickoff is a baseball play where the pitcher or catcher throws to a base to catch a runner off guard, hoping to tag them out before they return: {The pitcher made a quick pickoff throw to first}. The term extends to any quick interception or elimination—in football, a pickoff is an interception, and in military contexts, it describes picking off targets one by one.

A pickpocket is a thief who steals from people's pockets or bags in public places, typically without the victim noticing: {The crowded subway was full of pickpockets}. The verb pickpocket means to steal in this manner: {Someone pickpocketed my wallet at the festival}. The crime requires dexterity and distraction rather than force.

Pickpocketing is the act of stealing from someone's pocket or bag without their awareness, typically in crowded public places. The crime relies on distraction and dexterity rather than force: {Pickpocketing is rampant in tourist areas}. The term covers both the practice generally and specific instances of it.

Pickpockets are thieves who steal from people's pockets or bags in public places, typically using stealth and distraction rather than force. The singular pickpocket refers to a person who does this: {The pickpocket worked the crowded subway platform}. The verb pickpocket means to steal in this manner: {Someone pickpocketed my wallet at the concert}.

Picks is the third-person singular of pick, meaning to select or choose: {She picks the ripest tomatoes}. To pick is also to pluck or gather: {picking berries}, {picking flowers}. You pick at something by pulling at it repeatedly. A pick is a pointed tool for breaking hard surfaces, or a thin piece of plastic or bone for plucking guitar strings. Picks can also mean selections or choices: {These are my picks for the playoffs}.

Pickup covers things that are collected or gathered. A pickup is a small truck with an open bed for hauling. In music, a pickup is a device that captures string vibrations for amplification, or the notes before a downbeat. A pickup game is informal and impromptu—players are picked up on the spot. To pick up speed is to accelerate. A pickup line is an opening gambit to attract a stranger: {He tried some cheesy pickup line at the bar}. The adjective describes things assembled ad hoc: {a pickup band}.

Pickups is the plural of pickup, covering all its senses. A pickup is a small truck with an open cargo bed. In music, pickups are the electromagnetic devices on electric guitars that convert string vibrations to electrical signals. A pickup can be casual sex or the person you pursue for it: {He's looking for a pickup at the bar}. A pickup game is informal and impromptu, organized on the spot rather than scheduled.

Picky describes someone who is excessively selective or hard to please, especially about food: {She's a picky eater}. The word suggests fussiness over small details that others might overlook: {He's picky about which brand of coffee he drinks}. Picky carries a mildly critical tone—being picky is pickier than being selective.

A picnic is a meal eaten outdoors, typically in a pleasant setting like a park or beach, with food brought from elsewhere: {We packed sandwiches for a picnic by the lake}. The word extends to the basket or spread itself: {a picnic of cold chicken and lemonade}. Informally, something described as {no picnic} is difficult or unpleasant: {Raising three kids alone is no picnic}.

Picnicking is eating a meal outdoors, typically in a park, at a beach, or in some other pleasant setting. The activity usually involves bringing food from home in a basket or cooler: {We spent the afternoon picnicking by the lake}. The double k preserves the hard c sound before the -ing ending.

Picnics is the plural of picnic—an outdoor meal, typically informal and eaten in a pleasant setting like a park or beach. The word also serves as a verb: {She picnics by the river every Sunday}. To say something is {no picnic} means it's difficult or unpleasant: {Raising three kids alone is no picnic}.

Pics is the informal plural of pic, itself a clipping of picture. It refers to photographs or images, especially digital ones shared online or via text message. {Send me some pics from the party.} The word is ubiquitous in casual digital communication, where brevity matters. The phrase {pics or it didn't happen} is a joking demand for photographic proof of an unlikely claim.

A pictogram is a symbol or image representing a word, concept, or object—communication through pictures rather than letters. Ancient writing systems like Egyptian hieroglyphics used pictograms. Modern pictograms appear on signs, labels, and interfaces where meaning must cross language barriers: restroom figures, hazard warnings, airport wayfinding symbols. Also called pictograph.

Pictograms are pictures or symbols that represent words, ideas, or information. They appear in signage, statistics, and ancient writing systems. A pictogram of a flame warns of flammability; a row of human figures shows population data. Unlike alphabetic writing, pictograms communicate meaning through visual resemblance to what they represent: {The cave paintings included pictograms of animals and hunting scenes}.

A pictograph is a picture or symbol representing a word, idea, or thing—the earliest form of writing before alphabetic systems developed. Cave paintings and Egyptian hieroglyphics are pictographs. The term also applies to modern statistical charts using repeated symbols to represent quantities: {The pictograph showed car icons, each representing 1,000 vehicles sold}.

Pictographs are pictures or symbols representing words, ideas, or objects—the earliest form of written communication. Ancient cave paintings and Egyptian hieroglyphics are pictographs. The term also applies to modern statistical graphics where small images represent quantities: {The pictograph showed each icon representing 100 voters}. Charts using pictographs make data visually intuitive but can distort scale.

A picture is a visual representation—a painting, drawing, photograph, or image on a screen. The word extends to mental images: {I get the picture}, {Picture this}. A picture can be a film: {motion picture}, {picture show}. To picture something is to imagine it: {I can't picture him as a father}. Someone who embodies a quality is {the picture of health} or {the picture of innocence}.

Pictures are visual representations—photographs, paintings, drawings, or images on screens. The word covers an enormous range, from a child's crayon scribbles to museum masterpieces. To picture something is to form a mental image: {I can't picture him with a beard}. A picture can represent a situation: {The picture isn't as grim as the headlines suggest}. The pictures, especially in British usage, means the cinema: {We're going to the pictures tonight}.

Picturesque describes scenes or places that are visually striking in a charming, quaint, or scenic way—the kind of thing that would make a good picture. A picturesque {village} has cobblestone streets and half-timbered houses. A picturesque {coastline} features dramatic cliffs and hidden coves. The word often suggests beauty that feels composed or idealized: {The inn was picturesque but lacked hot water}.

Piddle means to urinate, used especially with children or pets: {Does the puppy need to go piddle?} The word is deliberately mild and childish. Piddle also means to waste time on trivial matters: {Stop piddling around and get to work}. To piddle away time or money is to squander it in small, insignificant amounts.

Piddling means trivially small or insignificant—too minor to merit serious attention. A piddling {amount} of money barely registers. A piddling {detail} isn't worth fussing over. The word carries dismissive contempt: {They offered me some piddling sum and expected gratitude}.

Piddly means trivially small or insignificant—too minor to merit serious attention. A piddly {raise} barely covers inflation. A piddly {amount} of food leaves you hungry. The word carries dismissive contempt: {They offered some piddly sum and expected me to be grateful}. Also spelled piddling, with the same meaning.

A pidgin is a simplified language that develops when groups with no common tongue need to communicate, typically for trade. Pidgins have reduced grammar and limited vocabulary drawn from multiple source languages. Unlike creoles, pidgins are not native languages—no one grows up speaking one as a first language. {They communicated in a pidgin of Portuguese and Malay.}

A pie is a baked dish with a filling inside a pastry crust—fruit pies, meat pies, savory pies. The filling is enclosed or topped with more pastry. To describe something as {easy as pie} or {a piece of pie} is to call it effortless. {Pie in the sky} refers to promises unlikely to materialize. To have a {finger in every pie} is to be involved in many activities. {Pie chart} names the circular graph divided into wedges. (Capitalized Pie may refer to the mathematical constant pi spelled out, or to a name.)

Piece is a handy noun to denote any of the parts of component things (piece of an engine) or of things that are typically divided (two pieces of cake). Single examples of general nouns denoting a class of things are called pieces (piece of furniture). Products of creative work (writing, composition, painting) are often called pieces. To piece something out is to divide it into parts, usually equal ones.

Piecemeal means done in pieces rather than all at once—gradually, bit by bit, without a unified plan. The word works as both adverb and adjective: {The reforms were implemented piecemeal}, {a piecemeal approach to solving the problem}. It often carries a slightly negative connotation, suggesting something incomplete or haphazard rather than systematic.

Pieces are parts of something that has been divided, broken, or separated: {The vase shattered into pieces}. A piece of something is a portion or segment: {a piece of cake}, {a piece of advice}. Pieces also names the individual units in board games like chess or checkers. To {go to pieces} is to fall apart emotionally. To {pick up the pieces} is to recover after disaster.

Piecework is work paid by the unit produced rather than by time spent. A garment worker might earn per shirt sewn, a picker per bushel harvested. The system rewards speed but can encourage cutting corners: {She preferred piecework because she was fast}. The adjective piecework describes such arrangements: {piecework wages}, {piecework rates}.

Piecing is joining separate parts into a whole. In quilting, piecing is the fundamental technique of sewing fabric patches together to form a design: {She spent the afternoon piecing a quilt top}. More broadly, piecing describes any gradual assembly: {piecing together evidence}, {piecing together what happened}. The word suggests patient reconstruction from fragments.

Piecrust is the pastry shell that forms the outer layer of a pie, made from flour, fat, and water. A good piecrust is flaky and tender. The term appears in {piecrust promise}—one easily made and easily broken, like the delicate pastry itself.

Piehole is slang for mouth, used dismissively or humorously. The image is of the mouth as a hole for shoving pie into. It appears most often in commands to be quiet: {Shut your piehole}. Someone who should {keep their piehole shut} talks too much or says things they shouldn't.

A pier is a structure extending from shore into water, typically supported by pillars. Piers serve as landing places for boats, platforms for fishing, or walkways for strolling: {We walked to the end of the pier}. In architecture, a pier is a solid support between windows or other openings, or a pillar supporting an arch or bridge.

To pierce is to penetrate or make a hole through something, typically with a sharp instrument: {The arrow pierced his armor}. Ears and other body parts are pierced to accommodate jewelry. Figuratively, a scream can pierce the silence, cold can pierce to the bone, or a gaze can pierce through pretense. Something piercing is sharp and penetrating—a piercing wind, a piercing cry, piercing eyes. (Capitalized Pierce is a surname or given name.)

Pierced describes something that has been punctured or penetrated, creating a hole or opening. Body parts are pierced for jewelry: {pierced ears}, {a pierced nose}. The word often appears as an adjective describing someone who has such piercings: {She's heavily pierced}. Figuratively, something can pierce the heart or soul—a pierced heart suggests emotional wounding. A piercing sound or gaze is sharp and penetrating.

Pierces is the third-person singular of pierce, meaning to penetrate or make a hole through something with a sharp point. A needle pierces fabric; a scream pierces the silence. The word often suggests sudden, forceful entry: {The arrow pierces his armor}. Figuratively, something that pierces cuts through resistance or reaches deep: {Her gaze pierces right through me}.

Piercing describes something that penetrates sharply—a piercing {scream} cuts through noise, a piercing {stare} seems to see through you, piercing {cold} goes right to the bone. As a noun, a piercing is a hole made in the body for jewelry: {She got a nose piercing}. The word always suggests intensity and directness, whether physical or metaphorical.

Piercings are holes made in the body to hold decorative jewelry. Ear piercings are most common, but piercings appear on noses, eyebrows, lips, tongues, navels, nipples, and genitals. The word refers both to the holes themselves and the jewelry worn in them: {She has multiple piercings}, {I need to clean my piercings}. Getting pierced ranges from mall kiosks for earlobes to specialized studios for more intimate locations.

Pierogi are Eastern European dumplings—pockets of unleavened dough filled with potato, cheese, sauerkraut, meat, or fruit, then boiled and often pan-fried. Associated especially with Polish cuisine, they appear at holiday meals and as everyday comfort food. The singular is pierog, though pierogi often serves for both: {I'll have one more pierogi}.

Pierogies are filled dumplings from Eastern European cuisine, particularly Polish and Ukrainian traditions. The dough is unleavened, wrapped around fillings like potato and cheese, sauerkraut, meat, or fruit, then boiled and often pan-fried in butter. They're comfort food, served with sour cream or onions: {We had pierogies at the church festival}. Also spelled pierogi, which is already plural in Polish.

Pierogis are Eastern European dumplings—pockets of unleavened dough filled with potatoes, cheese, sauerkraut, meat, or fruit, then boiled and often pan-fried in butter. Associated especially with Polish cuisine, they appear at church suppers and ethnic festivals across the American Midwest and Northeast: {We stopped for pierogis at the Polish diner}. The standard Polish plural is pierogi, but pierogis is common in American English.

Piers are structures extending from shore into water, used for boarding boats, fishing, or strolling: {We walked to the end of the pier to watch the sunset}. The word also refers to vertical supports in architecture—the solid sections between windows or arches, or pillars supporting a bridge. A buttress pier reinforces a wall. (Capitalized Piers is a given name.)

Pies is the plural of pie—a baked dish with a crust and filling. Savory pies contain meat or vegetables; sweet pies hold fruit or custard. The word appears in idioms: {easy as pie}, {pie in the sky}, {a finger in every pie}. To pie someone is to throw a pie in their face, usually as protest or prank.

A pietà is a representation in painting or sculpture of the Virgin Mary cradling the dead body of Christ after the crucifixion. The term comes from Italian for "pity" or "compassion." Michelangelo's marble sculpture in St. Peter's Basilica is the most famous example. The image emphasizes maternal grief and has become an iconic motif in Western art.

Piety is devoted reverence toward God or the sacred—the quality of being deeply religious: {Her piety was evident in daily prayer}. The word extends to dutiful respect for parents, family, or tradition: {filial piety}. Piety can carry a hint of excessive or performative devotion, though the noun for that is usually pietism or the adjective pious.

Pig is the common name for animals in the swine family that are widely raised for food. When used figuratively, pig has more negative associations than its near synonym hog and it is much more frequent. A person called a pig is being called gluttonous, selfish, or offensive. If you pig out, you eat a great quantity of something. Pig is pejorative slang for policeman.

A pigeon is a stout-bodied bird with a small head, common in cities worldwide. Pigeons and doves are the same family—pigeon typically names the larger, urban species. To pigeon someone is to swindle them, and a pigeon is a gullible person easily deceived: {He was a pigeon for every con man in town}. A pigeonhole is a small compartment, and to pigeonhole is to categorize narrowly.

A pigeonhole is one of a set of small open compartments for sorting mail or storing papers—named for the nesting boxes in a dovecote. To pigeonhole something is to assign it to a category, often dismissively or reductively: {Critics pigeonholed her as a romance novelist}. The verb suggests oversimplification—filing something away rather than engaging with its complexity.

Pigeonholed means assigned to a narrow category and kept there. The image comes from the small compartments in a desk or cabinet where papers are sorted and filed away. To pigeonhole someone is to classify them rigidly: {Once you're pigeonholed as a comedy actor, it's hard to get dramatic roles}. The term often carries frustration—being pigeonholed means others refuse to see your full range.

Pigeonholes are small compartments for sorting mail or papers, named for the nesting boxes in a dovecote. The verb means to classify or categorize, often dismissively or reductively: {Critics pigeonholed her as a romance writer}. To pigeonhole something can also mean to set it aside for later, effectively shelving it: {The proposal was pigeonholed indefinitely}.

Pigeonholing is categorizing someone or something in a rigid, often dismissive way: {Critics kept pigeonholing her as a pop singer}. The image comes from the small compartments (pigeonholes) in old desks where papers were sorted and filed away. To pigeonhole someone is to assign them a fixed label that ignores their complexity or potential for change.

Pigeons are stout-bodied birds with small heads, found worldwide in cities and wild areas alike. Urban pigeons descend from domesticated rock doves and thrive on human scraps and architecture. The word also means a person easily deceived or swindled—a mark or sucker: {He was a pigeon for every con artist in town}. To pigeon someone is to swindle them. Clay pigeons are targets launched for shooting practice.

Piggies is a playful, childish word for pigs or toes. The nursery rhyme "This Little Piggy" gives each toe a personality, making piggies the default term when playing with a baby's feet: {Let me see those little piggies}. Outside the nursery, piggies can be affectionate or mocking for pigs, or dismissive for greedy people.

Piggy is a child's word for a pig, often used affectionately or playfully. It extends to anything pig-shaped or pig-related: a piggy {bank}, piggy {toes}. As an adjective, piggy describes greedy or gluttonous behavior: {Don't be so piggy with the cookies}. {Piggy eyes} are small and close-set, like a pig's.

Piggyback describes carrying someone or something on one's back or shoulders, with the carried person's legs wrapped around the carrier's waist: {Give me a piggyback ride!} The word extends to anything that rides along on something else, whether physically or figuratively: a piggyback {trailer} rides atop another on a train, and a company might piggyback {on a competitor's success}. As a verb, to piggyback means to attach or add on to something already in motion or existence.

Piggybacked is the past tense of piggyback, originally describing how a child rides on someone's back with arms around the neck. The meaning extends to anything carried on or attached to something else: {The amendment piggybacked on a popular bill}. In computing, data can be piggybacked on existing transmissions. To piggyback on someone's work is to exploit their effort for your own benefit.

Piggybacking is riding on someone's back with your legs around their waist, the way a child might ride on a parent. The image extends to anything that hitches a ride on something else: a bill piggybacking on popular legislation, a device piggybacking on another's network connection. {She piggybacked on his research to advance her own thesis.} To piggyback is to carry someone this way, or to attach one thing to another for mutual transport.

Piggybacks refers to rides on someone's back, with legs wrapped around the waist and arms around the shoulders: {He gave his daughter piggybacks around the yard}. The term extends to anything that rides along on something else—a bill that piggybacks on popular legislation, a product that piggybacks on another's success. As a verb, to piggyback is to attach or ride along: {The startup piggybacks on existing infrastructure}.

A piggybank is a small container for saving coins, traditionally shaped like a pig with a slot in the top. Children use piggybanks to accumulate spare change: {She's been dropping quarters into her piggybank for months}. The term extends to any personal savings reserve: {I had to break into my piggybank to cover the repair}. Also spelled piggy bank.

Piggybanks are small containers for saving coins, traditionally shaped like pigs with a slot on top for inserting money. The pig shape became standard through folk tradition, though the original connection may have been to "pygg," a type of clay once used for storage jars. {She's been dropping her spare change into a piggybank since January.} Figuratively, a piggybank represents personal savings generally.

Pigheaded means stubbornly refusing to change one's mind or course of action despite good reasons to do so. The word carries a stronger negative charge than merely stubborn—it suggests willful obstinacy that others find exasperating: {He was too pigheaded to admit he was wrong}. {Don't be so pigheaded about this}.

A piglet is a young pig, typically one still nursing or recently weaned. The word emphasizes smallness and youth: {The sow had a litter of eight piglets}. Piglet also names the timid character in A.A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh stories.

Piglets are young pigs, typically those still nursing or recently weaned. The word carries connotations of smallness and cuteness: {The sow had a litter of eight piglets}. Piglet appears as a character name in children's literature, most famously Winnie-the-Pooh's timid companion.

Pigment is a substance that gives color. In biology, pigments are molecules that produce color in living things—melanin in skin, chlorophyll in plants. In art and manufacturing, pigments are finely ground particles mixed into paints, inks, dyes, and cosmetics: {The artist ground her own pigments}. To pigment something is to add color to it.

Pigments are substances that give color to materials by absorbing certain wavelengths of light and reflecting others. Natural pigments come from minerals, plants, and animals; synthetic ones are manufactured. Pigments are mixed into paints, inks, dyes, and cosmetics. In biology, pigments like melanin and chlorophyll determine skin color and enable photosynthesis: {The pigments in autumn leaves emerge as chlorophyll breaks down}.

A pigpen is an enclosure where pigs are kept—a small fenced area or shed on a farm. The word extends to any extremely messy or dirty space: {Your room is a pigpen}. The insult carries the implication of filth and disorder associated with pigs wallowing in mud. Also spelled pig pen or pigsty, which shares the figurative meaning.

Pigs are stout, omnivorous mammals with flat snouts, raised for meat (pork, bacon, ham) or kept as pets. The word extends to people who are greedy, messy, or gluttonous: {He made a pig of himself at the buffet}. Pig is also derogatory slang for police officers. To pig out is to eat excessively.

Pigskin is leather made from pig hide, used for gloves, footballs, and other goods. In American English, pigskin commonly refers to a football itself, even though modern footballs are typically cowhide: {He loved throwing the pigskin around on Thanksgiving}. The term evokes casual, nostalgic football culture.

Pigsties are enclosures where pigs are kept, or rooms and spaces that are extremely dirty and messy: {His apartment was a pigsty}. The figurative sense is far more common than the literal one. Also spelled pigstys. Singular: pigsty.

A pigsty is an enclosure where pigs are kept—typically a small, muddy pen. The word extends to any place that's filthy or chaotic: {Your room is a pigsty}. The figurative use is far more common than the literal one. Also called a pigpen.

A pigtail is a braid or束 of hair hanging from the head. In American usage, pigtails usually means two braids or ponytails, one on each side: {She wore her hair in pigtails}. British usage may refer to a single braid. The word extends to anything twisted or coiled like a braid: a pigtail {connector} in electrical work, or the curly tail of a pig itself.

Pigtails are a hairstyle where the hair is divided and gathered into two bunches, one on each side of the head: {She wore her hair in pigtails}. The style is associated with children, especially girls, though adults wear it too. A single gathering at the back is technically a ponytail, not a pigtail, though usage varies. The name comes from the twisted shape resembling a pig's curly tail.

A pika is a small, round-eared mammal related to rabbits, found in rocky mountain regions of North America and Asia. Pikas are known for their high-pitched calls and habit of gathering vegetation into haypiles for winter. They resemble hamsters but are lagomorphs, not rodents.

Pikas are small mammals related to rabbits, found in mountainous regions of Asia and North America. They have rounded ears, no visible tail, and live among rocky slopes where they gather vegetation into haypiles for winter. Their high-pitched alarm calls echo across alpine terrain: {We heard pikas calling from the talus field}.

A pike is a long wooden shaft with a pointed metal head, used as a weapon by infantry before firearms became dominant. The word extends to sharp-pointed things: a pike position in diving tucks the body with legs straight. A pike is also a large predatory freshwater fish with an elongated body and sharp teeth. In American regional use, a pike is a turnpike or toll road: {We took the pike to avoid traffic}. To pike is to thrust or pierce. (Capitalized Pike is a surname.)

Pikelets are small, thick pancakes popular in Britain, Australia, and New Zealand. Smaller and spongier than American pancakes, they're typically served at tea time with butter, jam, or cream. In some regions, pikelet refers to a type of crumpet. {She made a batch of pikelets for afternoon tea.}

A pikeman is a soldier armed with a pike—a long wooden spear used in infantry formations, especially in European warfare from the 15th through 17th centuries. Pikemen formed dense squares or blocks, their weapons bristling outward to repel cavalry charges: {The pikemen held the center while musketeers fired from the flanks}.

Pikemen were infantry soldiers armed with pikes—long wooden spears typically fifteen to twenty feet in length. They formed the backbone of European armies from the late medieval period through the seventeenth century, standing in tight formations to repel cavalry charges. The term now appears mainly in historical contexts: {The pikemen held their ground as horsemen approached}.

Pikes are long wooden shafts with pointed metal heads, used historically as infantry weapons against cavalry. The word also names several types of fish with elongated bodies and pointed snouts—the northern pike being the most familiar. In American dialect, a pike is a turnpike or toll road: {Take the pike to the next exit}. To come down the pike is to appear or arrive: {the best opportunity to come down the pike in years}.

Pilaf is a rice dish in which the grains are first browned in oil or butter, then cooked in seasoned broth. The technique keeps grains separate rather than sticky. Pilaf often includes meat, vegetables, or dried fruits, and appears across Middle Eastern, Central Asian, and South Asian cuisines. Also spelled pilau or pilaw.

Pilates is a system of exercises emphasizing controlled movements, core strength, and flexibility. Developed in the early twentieth century by Joseph Pilates, it focuses on precise, flowing motions coordinated with breathing. Classes typically use mats or specialized equipment like the reformer: {I do Pilates three times a week}. The name is often lowercased when referring to the practice generally.

A pile is an unorganized mass of things in one place (pile of dirty dishes). Pile may also designate a large amount, especially of money. To pile things means to create a pile of them. If people pile in to a place, they get in quickly. If things pile up, they accumulate. Other meanings of pile are a long column driven into the ground as a support; a surface of thick fur or threads (deep pile carpeting); and (usually plural) hemorrhoids.

To piledrive is to drive something downward with tremendous force, like a piledriver—the heavy machine that hammers posts into the ground. In wrestling, a piledriver is a move where you lift an opponent upside down and drop them headfirst. The term extends to any forceful downward action: {He piledrove the ball into the end zone}.

A piledriver is a machine that hammers heavy posts (piles) into the ground to create foundations for buildings, bridges, and docks. The term extends to anything delivering powerful downward force—a piledriver punch, a piledriver wrestling move where an opponent is driven headfirst into the mat. {He hit him with a piledriver of a right hook.}

Piledrivers are machines that drive piles—heavy posts of wood, steel, or concrete—into the ground to create foundations for buildings, bridges, and other structures. The term extends to a wrestling move where one wrestler drives another headfirst into the mat: {He finished the match with a devastating piledriver}. Anything that hits with similar force might be called a piledriver: {a piledriver of a punch}.

Piledrives is the third-person singular of piledrive, meaning to strike with overwhelming downward force—like the construction machine that hammers posts into the ground. In wrestling, to piledrive is to drive an opponent headfirst into the mat. Figuratively, it describes any crushing attack or dominant action: {The stock market piledrives tech shares}, {She piledrives through her opponents}.

Piledriving is the act of driving piles—heavy posts or beams—into the ground to support structures like bridges or buildings. The term extends to any forceful, repetitive downward motion. In wrestling, a piledriver is a move where one wrestler drives another headfirst into the mat. In sex, piledriving describes vigorous thrusting in a position where one partner's legs are raised overhead: {He was piledriving her into the mattress}.

Piles has two unrelated meanings. One is the plural of pile—heaps, stacks, or large quantities: {piles of laundry}, {piles of money}. The other is an informal term for hemorrhoids—swollen blood vessels in and around the anus that cause discomfort, itching, and sometimes bleeding: {suffering from piles}.

A pileup is an accumulation of things heaped together, often chaotically. The term most commonly describes a multi-vehicle collision where cars crash into each other in succession: {A pileup on the freeway involved twelve vehicles}. More broadly, any backup or accumulation qualifies: {a pileup of dirty dishes}, {a pileup of unanswered emails}.

Pileups are accumulations or backups, especially chain-reaction collisions on highways where multiple vehicles crash into one another: {A pileup on the freeway closed three lanes}. The word extends to any overwhelming buildup: {a pileup of unread emails}, {a pileup of dirty dishes in the sink}.

To pilfer is to steal small amounts or petty items, often repeatedly and surreptitiously. The word suggests taking things of minor value rather than grand theft: {Someone had been pilfering office supplies}. It carries connotations of sneakiness and pettiness rather than boldness or violence.

Pilfered is the past tense of pilfer, meaning to steal small amounts or items of little value. The word suggests petty theft rather than grand larceny—swiping office supplies, filching coins from a jar: {Someone had pilfered snacks from the break room}. It often carries a slightly lighter moral weight than outright stealing.

Pilfering is stealing in small quantities, typically of low-value items. The word suggests repeated, petty theft rather than a single dramatic heist: {Employees caught pilfering office supplies}. Someone might pilfer snacks from a roommate's stash or pilfer coins from a tip jar. The noun form describes both the act and the habit.

A pilgrim is a person who journeys to a sacred place for religious devotion—to a shrine, holy city, or site of spiritual significance: {pilgrims traveling to Mecca}, {pilgrims at Lourdes}. The word extends to any long journey undertaken with purpose or reverence: {a pilgrim in search of meaning}. In figurative use, we are all pilgrims passing through life. (Capitalized Pilgrim refers to the English settlers at Plymouth.)

A pilgrimage is a journey to a sacred place or shrine, undertaken for religious devotion: {Muslims make a pilgrimage to Mecca}, {pilgrimage to the Holy Land}. The word extends to any journey with deep personal significance—visiting a beloved author's home, a musician's grave, or the field where a historic game was played: {an annual pilgrimage to Graceland}. As a verb, to pilgrimage is to make such a journey, though this use is less common than the noun.

Pilgrimages are journeys to sacred places, undertaken for religious devotion or spiritual significance: {Medieval pilgrimages to Canterbury}, {the annual pilgrimage to Mecca}. The term extends to any journey made with reverence or deep personal meaning: {a pilgrimage to Graceland}, {her pilgrimage to her grandmother's birthplace}. The word emphasizes the journey itself as meaningful, not just the destination.

Pilgrims are people who journey to a sacred place for religious reasons—to a shrine, holy city, or site of spiritual significance. The word extends to any travelers on a meaningful quest: {pilgrims seeking a new life in California}. More loosely, pilgrims are people new to a place or undertaking. (Capitalized Pilgrims refers to the English colonists who founded Plymouth.)

Piling refers to heavy posts or stakes driven into the ground to support a structure, especially where soil is soft or unstable. Bridge supports, docks, and buildings in coastal areas often rest on pilings—typically wooden, steel, or concrete columns sunk deep into earth or underwater: {The old pier's wooden pilings had rotted through}. Piling also works as the present participle of pile: {They were piling boxes in the corner}.

Pilings are posts or columns driven into the ground to support a structure. They form the foundation for piers, docks, bridges, and buildings on soft or unstable soil. Wooden pilings line waterfronts; steel and concrete pilings support heavy construction. {The old pilings were encrusted with barnacles.} {Engineers drove pilings sixty feet down to reach bedrock.}

A pill is a small, smooth tablet containing medicine or food supplements that is typically swallowed. A modifier often specifies what is being treated (birth control pill, sleeping pill, vitamin pill). The pill, in proper context, refers to contraception for women by pill. A bitter pill (to swallow) is something unpleasant that must be done or endured. If you call a person a pill, it means they are tedious or unadventurous.

Pillage is the violent seizure of goods, especially during war or civil unrest—troops pillaging a conquered city, looters pillaging stores during riots. The word works as both verb and noun: {The army pillaged the village} or {The pillage lasted three days}. It implies systematic, often brutal taking rather than opportunistic theft.

Pillaged is the past tense of pillage, meaning to plunder or loot, especially during war or civil unrest. Armies pillage conquered towns; rioters pillage shops. The word suggests violent, systematic theft rather than opportunistic grabbing: {The invaders pillaged the countryside}, {Museums filled with artifacts pillaged from colonial territories}.

A pillager is someone who plunders or loots, taking goods by force during war, raids, or civil unrest. The word carries a sense of violent theft and destruction: {Viking pillagers swept through coastal villages}. In gaming contexts, particularly Minecraft, pillagers are hostile characters that raid settlements.

Pillagers are people who plunder and loot, typically during war, raids, or civil unrest. The word evokes violent seizure of goods and valuables: {Viking pillagers descended on the coastal villages}. It carries a sense of lawless destruction beyond mere theft—pillagers don't just steal, they ransack.

Pillages is the verb form of pillage, meaning to plunder or loot, especially during war or conflict. Soldiers pillage conquered towns; raiders pillage coastal villages. The word implies violent theft on a large scale, stripping a place of valuables: {The army pillaged the countryside as it advanced}. Figuratively, someone pillages resources when exploiting them ruthlessly.

Pillaging is the act of plundering or looting, especially during war or civil unrest. Soldiers pillage conquered cities; rioters pillage shops. The word suggests violent, opportunistic theft on a significant scale: {The invading army spent days pillaging the countryside}. Figuratively, it describes aggressive extraction: {corporate pillaging of natural resources}.

A pillar is a vertical structure that supports something above it—a column holding up a roof or bridge. The word extends to anything that provides essential support: a {pillar of the community} is someone whose presence and contributions are fundamental to it. The {pillars of democracy} are its foundational principles. To go from {pillar to post} is to move frantically from place to place seeking help or resolution.

A pillarbox is a freestanding public mailbox, cylindrical and typically painted red, found in Britain and former British colonies. The term comes from their resemblance to architectural pillars. Pillarbox red describes that distinctive bright red color: {She wore pillarbox red lipstick}.

Pillars are vertical structures that support something above them—columns holding up a roof or bridge. The word extends to anything that provides essential support: {She was a pillar of the community}. The {pillars of democracy} are its foundational principles. A {pillar of strength} is someone others rely on in difficult times. To go from {pillar to post} is to move from place to place without settling.

A pillbox is a small container for pills, often with compartments for organizing daily doses. The shape—squat, cylindrical, flat-topped—gives its name to a pillbox hat, a brimless women's hat fashionable in the mid-20th century. In military usage, a pillbox is a small concrete fortification with gun slits, used as a defensive position.

Pillboxes are small containers for carrying pills, typically divided into compartments for organizing daily doses. The word also names small, squat military fortifications with thick concrete walls and narrow slits for firing weapons—their shape resembles the containers. A pillbox hat is a small, flat-topped cylindrical hat without a brim, fashionable in the mid-twentieth century: {Jackie Kennedy's iconic pillbox hat}.

A pillbug is a small crustacean that lives on land, typically found under rocks, logs, and leaf litter. Despite appearances, it's not an insect but related to shrimp and crabs. When disturbed, it curls into a tight ball—hence the name. Also called a roly-poly or woodlouse. {The kids spent the afternoon collecting pillbugs from under the porch.}

Pillbugs are small crustaceans that live on land, found in damp places under rocks, logs, and leaf litter. They have segmented, armored bodies and can roll into a tight ball when disturbed—hence the name. Also called roly-polies, woodlice, or sowbugs, though sowbugs technically cannot roll up. Despite their bug designation, they're more closely related to shrimp and crabs than to insects.

Pilled describes fabric that has developed small fuzzy balls on its surface from friction and wear: {This old sweater is getting pilled}. In internet slang, pilled means having adopted a particular worldview or ideology, from the "red pill" metaphor in *The Matrix*—often combined with a modifier: {blackpilled}, {breadpilled}. Someone who is pilled has been converted to a belief system, for better or worse.

Pilling is the formation of small fuzzy balls on fabric surfaces, caused by friction during wear or washing. Sweaters, fleece, and other soft textiles are prone to pilling: {This cheap sweater started pilling after one wash}. A fabric shaver or pill remover can restore the smooth appearance.

Pillock is British slang for a stupid person, a fool: {Don't be such a pillock}. The word is mildly vulgar—it may derive from an old slang term for penis—but has lost most of its sexual connotation. Calling someone a pillock is dismissive rather than vicious, suggesting they're being thick-headed.

Pilloried is the past tense of pillory. A pillory was a wooden framework with holes for the head and hands, used to publicly humiliate offenders—crowds might jeer or throw things at the immobilized person. The literal punishment is obsolete, but the figurative sense thrives: to be pilloried is to be publicly ridiculed or denounced. {The politician was pilloried in the press for his remarks.}

A pillory is a wooden frame with holes for securing the head and hands, used historically to publicly punish and humiliate offenders. The condemned stood exposed to ridicule and abuse from passersby. The verb means to expose someone to public scorn or ridicule: {The press pilloried the senator for his hypocrisy}. The figurative sense now dominates—few remember the device itself.

A pillow is a soft cushion for supporting the head during sleep, typically filled with feathers, foam, or synthetic fibers. Pillows also serve decorative purposes on sofas and beds. To pillow something is to rest it as if on a pillow: {She pillowed her head on her arms}. A {pillow fight} is a playful battle using pillows as weapons.

A pillowcase is the removable cloth cover that fits over a pillow, protecting it and providing a washable surface to sleep on. Most are simple fabric sleeves open at one end: {I need to change the pillowcases}. Also called a pillowslip.

Pillows are soft cushions for supporting the head during sleep or rest, typically filled with down, foam, or synthetic fibers. Beyond bedding, pillows serve as decorative items on sofas or as support for other body parts: {She propped a pillow under her knees}. To pillow is to rest one's head on something soft: {He pillowed his head on her lap}.

Pills are small solid doses of medicine meant to be swallowed whole. The word extends to anything pill-shaped or pill-like: birth control pills, vitamin pills. To pill is to form into small balls, as when fabric develops those annoying fuzzballs. {A bitter pill to swallow} is something unpleasant you must accept. {On the pill} means using oral contraceptives.

If you pilot an aircraft, you are the pilot. By extension, both the noun and verb are used generally of people who lead or show the way. A different meaning of pilot is a TV program made as a sample for possible future development. From this, a preliminary activity may attract the adjective pilot (pilot project). Sometimes the pilot light that starts a heater or gas appliance is just called a pilot.

Piloting is navigating or controlling the movement of a vessel, aircraft, or vehicle. A pilot does the piloting, whether steering a ship through a harbor or flying a plane. The term extends to guiding anything through difficulty: {She's piloting the legislation through committee}. Piloting also names the skill or practice itself: {He studied piloting before getting his license}.

Pilots are people who operate aircraft, guiding planes through takeoff, flight, and landing. The term extends to those who navigate ships through difficult waters or steer spacecraft. A pilot can also be a trial version of something—a pilot {program}, a pilot {episode}—testing viability before full commitment. To pilot is to guide or steer: {She piloted the company through the merger}.

Pilsener is a pale, golden lager beer with a crisp, hoppy flavor, originally brewed in the Czech city of Pilsen. The style became so influential that most mass-market lagers worldwide are variations of it: {He ordered a pilsener to go with his burger}. Also spelled pilsner.

A pilsner is a pale, golden lager beer with a light body and crisp, hoppy finish. The style originated in the Czech city of Plzeň (Pilsen) in the 1840s and became the template for most mainstream beers worldwide. {I'll have a pilsner}. Also spelled pilsener. (Capitalized Pilsner may refer specifically to beer from Plzeň.)

Pilsners are pale, crisp lagers with a distinctive hop bitterness, originally from the Czech city of Plzeň. The style revolutionized beer in the 19th century and now dominates global brewing—most mass-market beers are pilsner derivatives. Czech pilsners tend toward maltier sweetness; German versions are drier and more assertively hopped: {I'll have whatever pilsner you have on tap}.

Pimento, also spelled pimiento, is a mild, heart-shaped red pepper often found stuffed inside green olives or pureed into pimento cheese, a Southern American spread. The word also refers to allspice, the dried berry of a Caribbean tree—a usage more common in British English. {The olives stuffed with pimento added color to the relish tray.}

Pimentos are mild, heart-shaped red peppers, typically sold jarred or canned. They're the familiar red stuffing in green olives and a key ingredient in pimento cheese spread. The spelling pimiento, closer to the Spanish original, is equally common. Sometimes called cherry peppers for their shape, though they're sweet rather than hot.

A pimp is a man who manages prostitutes and takes a share of their earnings. The term carries connotations of exploitation, flashy dress, and street-level crime. To pimp is to act as a pimp, or more broadly, to promote aggressively: {He's always pimping his new book}. To {pimp out} something is to customize it showily: {pimp out a car with chrome rims}. The adjective pimp means stylish or impressive in slang: {That jacket is pimp}.

Pimped is the past tense of pimp, which in its original sense means to manage prostitutes and take a share of their earnings. More commonly now, pimped describes something that has been customized or upgraded with flashy modifications: {He pimped his car with chrome wheels and neon lights}. The slang sense comes from the MTV show *Pimp My Ride*, where vehicles received extravagant makeovers.

Pimping is the activity of managing prostitutes and taking a share of their earnings. A pimp recruits sex workers, arranges clients, and often provides protection—though the relationship frequently involves exploitation or coercion. In slang, pimping describes ostentatious style or flashy self-presentation: {He was pimping in that gold chain}. To pimp something out is to customize it extravagantly: {pimping out his car with chrome rims}.

A pimple is a small inflamed spot on the skin, typically with a raised center that may contain pus. Pimples result from clogged pores and are especially common during adolescence. Figuratively, something insignificant on a larger surface might be called a pimple: {The town was just a pimple on the map}.

A pimple is an irritated spot on the skin, often on the face, caused by a blocked pore. Pimples are usually the result of a condition called acne, which typically affects teenagers. Pimple is not used very often as a verb but if you pimple someone, you inflict pimples on them.

A pimpmobile is a flashy, ostentatious car associated with the stereotype of a pimp's vehicle—typically a large American luxury sedan with garish customizations like bright paint, excessive chrome, fur interiors, or extravagant wheel rims. The term emerged in 1970s American slang and is used humorously or disparagingly to describe any vehicle that seems designed more for showing off than for practical transportation. {He pulled up in some kind of purple pimpmobile with gold trim.}

Pimps is the plural of pimp—a person who manages prostitutes and takes a cut of their earnings. The word carries connotations of exploitation and control: {Pimps often use manipulation or violence to keep sex workers dependent}. As a verb, to pimp means to act as a pimp, or more broadly to promote aggressively or customize flashily: {He pimped his ride with chrome rims}.

Pins tend to be cylindrical (cotter pin, bowling pin, rolling pin) and may have a pointed end (safety pin, lapel pin) used for attaching or fixing. If you pin one thing to another, you attach it using a pin. If you pin some bad thing on someone, especially if you pin the blame on them, you hold them responsible. To pin down someone or something is to ascertain details or definitive information.

A pinafore is a sleeveless garment worn over a dress or blouse, typically featuring a bib front and tied or buttoned at the back. Originally designed as a protective apron for children to keep their clothes clean, it evolved into a fashion item worn by women and girls. The word combines "pin" and "afore" (in front), describing how the garment was once pinned to the front of a dress. {She wore a white pinafore over her Sunday dress.}

A piñata is a decorated container—traditionally of papier-mâché—filled with candy and small toys, hung up to be broken open with a stick by blindfolded participants. Associated with Mexican celebrations and children's birthday parties, the piñata swings from a rope while the blindfolded person swings at it: {The kids lined up to take turns hitting the piñata}.
