A pomegranate is a round fruit with a tough reddish skin containing hundreds of edible seeds, each encased in juicy red flesh. The seeds cluster in compartments separated by bitter white membrane. Native to the Middle East, pomegranates appear in ancient mythology and religious texts. The fruit is eaten fresh, juiced, or used in cooking: {pomegranate molasses}, {pomegranate seeds scattered over a salad}.

Pomegranates is the plural of pomegranate, a round fruit with a tough reddish rind and compartments of juicy, ruby-colored seeds. The seeds—technically arils—are eaten fresh, pressed for juice, or used in cooking. The fruit appears widely in mythology and religious symbolism, representing fertility and abundance: {The table was piled with figs and pomegranates}.

A pomelo is the largest citrus fruit, native to Southeast Asia, with thick rind and flesh ranging from pale yellow to pink. It resembles a grapefruit but is sweeter and less bitter: {We peeled the pomelo and separated its segments}. The fruit is traditional in Chinese New Year celebrations. Also spelled pummelo.

A pommel is the rounded, raised front part of a saddle, or the knob at the end of a sword handle. In gymnastics, a pommel horse is the apparatus with two handles used for swinging routines. To pommel (also spelled pummel) is to strike repeatedly with the fists: {The boxer pommeled his opponent against the ropes}.

Pommels is the plural of pommel, which has two main senses. A pommel is the rounded front part of a saddle that rises up, or the rounded knob at the end of a sword handle. To pommel someone is to strike them repeatedly with the fists—a variant spelling of pummel: {He pommeled his opponent into submission}. The verb form pommels means strikes repeatedly.

Pomodoro is a time-management technique that breaks work into focused intervals, traditionally 25 minutes, separated by short breaks. Named for the tomato-shaped kitchen timer its inventor used, the method treats each interval as one pomodoro: {I got three pomodoros done before lunch}. The plural is pomodoros or pomodori.

Pomp is ceremonial display and grandeur—the elaborate spectacle of formal occasions. Royal coronations have pomp; so do military parades and state funerals. The word often carries a hint of excess or empty show: {all the pomp and circumstance of graduation}. Pompous behavior inflates self-importance with similar theatrical flair.

A pompadour is a hairstyle in which hair is swept upward from the forehead and back from the face, creating height and volume at the front. The style, named after Madame de Pompadour, mistress of Louis XV, has been worn by both men and women. Elvis Presley's signature look revived it in the 1950s: {He spent twenty minutes perfecting his pompadour}.

Pompadours are hairstyles where the hair is swept up and back from the forehead into a high mound or roll. Named after Madame de Pompadour, mistress of Louis XV, the style has been worn by both men and women across centuries. Elvis Presley's pompadour became iconic in the 1950s: {He spent twenty minutes sculpting his pompadour}.

A pompom is a fluffy decorative ball made of yarn, paper, or similar material. Cheerleaders shake pompoms at sporting events. Smaller versions adorn winter hats, gift wrapping, or craft projects. The word sometimes appears as pom-pom. A pom-pom is also an automatic antiaircraft gun, named for the sound it makes when firing.

Pompoms are fluffy spherical decorations made from gathered strands of material—typically yarn, paper, or plastic strips. Cheerleaders wave large pompoms during routines to add visual flair. Smaller pompoms appear as decorative accents on hats, slippers, or gift wrapping. Also spelled pom-poms or pom pons.

A pompon is a decorative ball of fluffy material—yarn, paper, or fabric strips—used as an ornament on clothing, especially hats, or as a prop by cheerleaders. The spelling pom-pom is equally common. Cheerleaders shake pompons during routines to add visual flair and emphasize movements. The term also applies to certain varieties of chrysanthemum and dahlia with compact, globe-shaped flower heads.

Pompons are decorative balls of fluffed material—yarn, paper, or plastic strips—used for ornamentation or cheering. Cheerleaders shake pompons at sporting events. Smaller pompons adorn hats, gift wrappings, and craft projects. The word also refers to certain chrysanthemums and dahlias with globe-shaped flower heads. Also spelled pom-poms.

Pomposity is inflated self-importance—the quality of behaving as though you're grander or more significant than you are. It shows up in speech, manner, and bearing: {The professor's pomposity made students reluctant to ask questions}. Unlike confidence, pomposity broadcasts itself, demanding recognition it hasn't earned.

Pompous describes someone who takes themselves too seriously, displaying an inflated sense of importance or dignity. A pompous {speech} is full of grand language meant to impress. A pompous {official} acts as if their position makes them superior. The word suggests self-importance that others find tiresome or ridiculous: {He delivered a pompous lecture on proper etiquette while his fly was down}.

A poncho is a simple outer garment—a single piece of fabric with a hole in the center for the head, worn draped over the shoulders. Traditional ponchos from South America are woven wool or alpaca; modern versions are often waterproof plastic or nylon, used as emergency rain gear: {I keep a poncho in my backpack for hiking}.

Ponchos are cloaks made from a single piece of fabric with a hole for the head, worn draped over the shoulders. Traditional ponchos from South America are woven wool; modern ones are often waterproof plastic or nylon, used as rain gear: {I keep a poncho in my backpack for sudden storms}. The loose, flowing shape makes ponchos easy to pull on over other clothing.

A pond is a small body of still water, smaller than a lake though the boundary is imprecise. Ponds are often shallow enough for sunlight to reach the bottom, supporting plant growth throughout. They may be natural or artificial: {a duck pond}, {a garden pond}, {a fish pond}. {The pond} is a humorous term for the Atlantic Ocean, used in phrases like {across the pond}.

To ponder is to think about something carefully and at length, turning it over in your mind: {She pondered whether to accept the job offer}. The word suggests deliberate, unhurried consideration rather than quick judgment. You ponder weighty matters—decisions, mysteries, life's big questions—not what to have for lunch.

Pondering is deep or careful thinking about something, often with no immediate resolution in sight. Where thinking can be quick, pondering suggests sustained consideration: {She sat pondering the decision for hours}. The word carries a meditative quality—you ponder weighty matters, not what to have for lunch.

Pondlife refers to the organisms—plants, insects, amphibians, microorganisms—that inhabit ponds: {We studied pondlife under the microscope}. In British slang, pondlife is a contemptuous term for people considered worthless or despicable, suggesting they rank among the lowest forms of life: {The tabloids called the vandals pondlife}.

Ponds is the plural of pond—small bodies of still water, smaller than lakes. The distinction is imprecise but generally involves size and depth: {The property has several ponds stocked with fish}. Ponds may be natural or artificial, created for irrigation, livestock, fish farming, or decoration: {a koi pond}, {a farm pond}.

Pong is a strong, unpleasant smell: {There's a terrible pong coming from the fridge}. Chiefly British. As a verb, to pong is to stink: {Those trainers really pong}. Separately, Pong was an early video game simulating table tennis, released in 1972—one of the first commercially successful arcade games.

Ponies are small horses, typically standing under 14.2 hands at maturity. The word often suggests a child's mount or a gentle riding animal. In British slang, a pony is twenty-five pounds sterling. In American slang, to pony up is to pay what's owed: {Time to pony up for your share of the bill}. A pony is also a small glass for liquor or a crib sheet for cheating on exams.

Pontificate means to speak in a pompous, dogmatic way, as if one's opinions were beyond question: {He pontificated about wine while everyone else just wanted to drink}. The word evokes someone holding forth with unearned authority. Originally it meant to perform the functions of a pope or bishop—the pontiff—but this sense is now rare outside Catholic contexts.

Pontificates means to speak in a pompous, dogmatic way, as if one's opinions were beyond question. The word evokes someone holding forth at length on topics they consider themselves expert in: {He pontificated about wine while the sommelier stood by silently}. The tone suggests the speaker is more impressed with their pronouncements than the audience is. From the same root as pontiff—the Pope delivers authoritative pronouncements; everyone else just sounds self-important trying.

Pontificating is speaking in a pompous, self-important way, as if delivering authoritative pronouncements from on high. The word suggests someone holding forth at length on matters they consider themselves expert in, often without invitation: {He spent dinner pontificating about wine}. The tone is typically condescending, the audience typically trapped.

Pontification is speaking in a pompous, dogmatic way—holding forth as though your opinions were unquestionable truths. The word derives from pontiff, suggesting someone who speaks with the authority of a pope: {We endured his pontification about the proper way to grill a steak}. To pontificate is to deliver such pronouncements.

Pontifying is speaking in a pompous, dogmatic way—delivering opinions as if they were authoritative pronouncements from on high. The word carries the image of a pontiff (the Pope) issuing decrees, applied mockingly to anyone who lectures others with unearned certainty: {He spent dinner pontifying about wine while the sommelier rolled her eyes}.

A pontoon is a flat-bottomed float used to support structures on water. Pontoon bridges rest on a series of these floats. A pontoon boat has two parallel hulls providing stability for leisurely lake cruising: {We spent the afternoon on the pontoon}. In British usage, pontoon is also the card game Americans call blackjack or twenty-one.

Pontoons are hollow, watertight floats that provide buoyancy—typically cylindrical or boat-shaped structures supporting a bridge, dock, or platform. A pontoon bridge floats on such supports rather than resting on fixed piers. Pontoon boats use two parallel floats to create a stable, flat-decked watercraft popular for recreational cruising: {We rented a pontoon for the afternoon on the lake}.

A pony is a young horse (pony stallion) or a small horse (Shetland pony). Pony is sometimes used to characterize things that are smaller than the standard size, especially alcoholic drinks. The verb pony up is not related to horses and means to pay or put in money, usually in the context of achieving fairness or settling an account.

A ponytail is a hairstyle in which hair is gathered and fastened at the back of the head, hanging down like a horse's tail. The style keeps hair out of the face and ranges from casual to polished depending on placement and tightness: {She pulled her hair back in a quick ponytail before going for a run}.

Ponytails is the plural of ponytail, a hairstyle in which hair is gathered and fastened at the back of the head, hanging down like a horse's tail. The style is practical for keeping hair out of the face during exercise or work: {She always wears ponytails to volleyball practice}. Pigtails are ponytails worn in pairs, one on each side.

Poo is a childish or euphemistic term for feces, or the act of defecating: {I need to go poo}. Common in households with young children and in casual speech where stronger terms feel inappropriate. Also appears as the verb poop. The word is mild and inoffensive—bathroom humor rather than vulgarity.

A poobah is a pompous or self-important official, especially one who holds multiple positions or wields influence across several domains. The term comes from the character Pooh-Bah in Gilbert and Sullivan's operetta *The Mikado*, who held numerous grandiose titles simultaneously. Often used mockingly: {the local poobahs who run the chamber of commerce}. A {grand poobah} or {high poobah} is someone of exaggerated importance, real or imagined.

Poobahs are people who hold positions of power or influence, often with an air of self-importance. The term carries a mocking edge, suggesting the person takes their authority more seriously than others do: {The local poobahs gathered to discuss the zoning change}. Sometimes spelled pooh-bahs. The singular poobah often appears in compounds: {a high poobah of finance}.

Pooch is informal for dog, used affectionately: {I'm taking the pooch for a walk}. The word carries a warm, familiar tone—you'd call your own dog or a friendly neighborhood mutt a pooch, not a show champion or police K-9.

Pooches is the plural of pooch, an informal and affectionate word for dogs: {I'm taking the pooches to the park}. The term carries a warm, slightly playful tone—you'd call beloved pets pooches, not strays or working dogs.

A poodle is a breed of dog known for its curly, dense coat and high intelligence. Poodles come in three sizes—standard, miniature, and toy—and are often associated with elaborate grooming styles, though they were originally bred as water retrievers. The breed's reputation for prissiness makes poodle a mild insult for someone seen as pampered or overly fussy: {He's not cut out for fieldwork—he's a poodle}. As a verb, chiefly British, to poodle means to move in a leisurely, unhurried way: {We poodled around the countryside all afternoon}.

Poodles are a breed of dog known for their curly, dense coat and high intelligence. They come in three sizes—standard, miniature, and toy—and are often associated with elaborate grooming styles, particularly the continental clip with pompoms. Despite a reputation as pampered show dogs, poodles were originally bred as water retrievers: {She trained her poodle for agility competitions}.

Poof is the sound of something vanishing or appearing suddenly, often with a puff of air or smoke: {The magician waved his wand and—poof—the rabbit disappeared}. As an exclamation, it emphasizes how quickly something happened or ceased to exist: {One day the money was just gone, poof}. In British slang, poof is a derogatory term for a gay man, equivalent to American "fag."
Pooh informally expresses a speaker’s disappointment at some turn of events or rejection of someone’s comments.

A poohbah is a pompous official or someone who holds multiple positions of authority—often with the implication that the titles outweigh the actual importance. The term comes from a character in Gilbert and Sullivan's *The Mikado* who held numerous grandiose offices simultaneously. It's usually mildly mocking: {The local poohbahs gathered to discuss the zoning changes}. Also spelled poo-bah or Pooh-Bah.

Poohbahs are people who hold positions of importance, especially those who act self-importantly or pompously. The term carries a mocking edge—it suggests someone who takes their authority more seriously than others do: {The local poohbahs gathered to discuss the zoning changes}. Often used for officials, executives, or community leaders whose influence may be more ceremonial than substantial.

Pool has two distinct origins in English. One pool is a body of still water—a pond, a puddle, or an artificial basin for swimming: {The kids splashed in the pool}. Blood or other liquids collect in pools. The other pool is a shared resource or collective stake. A typing pool shares secretarial work; a car pool shares rides; a gene pool contains a population's genetic material. To pool resources is to combine them. Pool is also a billiards game played on a table with pockets, named for the betting pools once associated with it.

A poolboy is a young man employed to maintain and clean a swimming pool. The role has become a stock figure in sexual fantasy and pornography—the attractive service worker who catches the eye of a bored housewife or wealthy homeowner: {The poolboy fantasy is such a cliché}. Also spelled as two words: pool boy.

Pooled describes resources, money, or efforts that have been combined from multiple sources into a shared collection. When people pool their funds, they contribute to a common pot: {We pooled our money for a group gift}. Pooled data or samples are merged for analysis. The word implies collaboration or aggregation for mutual benefit or greater effect.

A poolhall is an establishment where people play pool—billiards on tables with pockets. Traditionally associated with gambling, idleness, and rough crowds, the word carries working-class or slightly disreputable connotations: {He spent his afternoons in poolhalls instead of looking for work}. Also spelled as two words: pool hall.

Pooling is combining resources, funds, or efforts into a shared reserve. People pool their money for group gifts or investments; companies pool risk through insurance arrangements. {We're pooling our frequent flyer miles for a family trip}. In machine learning, pooling reduces data dimensions by summarizing regions of information. Water pooling means it's collecting in one place rather than draining.

A poolroom is a commercial establishment with billiard tables available for hourly rental. The term can also refer to a room in a private residence containing a pool table. In older American usage, poolroom sometimes meant a place where betting on horse races occurred, since such establishments often had billiard tables: {The cops raided the poolroom on suspicion of illegal gambling}.

Pools is the plural of pool, covering all its senses. A pool is a body of still water, natural or artificial—from a tide pool to a swimming pool. Pool also means a shared resource or collective supply: a car pool, a gene pool, a pool of candidates. The game pool is played on a felt table with cue sticks and numbered balls. To pool resources is to combine them: {We pooled our money for the gift}.

A poolshark is someone highly skilled at billiards who hustles less experienced players for money, often by concealing their ability until bets are placed: {He lost three hundred dollars to a poolshark at the bar}. The term combines the predatory connotation of shark with pool halls' reputation for gambling. Sometimes spelled as two words: pool shark.

Poolside refers to the area immediately adjacent to a swimming pool: {We had drinks poolside}, {poolside loungers}. The word functions as both noun and adjective, evoking leisure, resorts, and summer relaxation. {She spent the afternoon poolside with a book}.

Poop is informal for feces, used especially by or around children: {The dog pooped on the carpet}. As a verb, to poop is to defecate. The poop deck is the raised deck at a ship's stern—an unrelated nautical term. To be pooped is to be exhausted: {I'm too pooped to go out tonight}.

Pooped means exhausted or worn out: {I'm completely pooped after that hike}. The word is informal and mild. Separately, pooped is the past tense of poop, the childish or euphemistic verb for defecating: {The dog pooped on the rug}. In nautical use, a ship is pooped when a wave breaks over the stern.

Poophead is a mild, childish insult suggesting someone is stupid or annoying. It combines two words children find inherently funny—poop and head—making it a favorite schoolyard taunt. Adults occasionally use it for humorous effect or when a stronger insult feels inappropriate. {My little brother called me a poophead when I wouldn't share my candy.}

Pooping is the act of defecating—expelling feces from the body. The word is casual and slightly childish, common in family settings and informal speech: {The baby's pooping again}. It can describe animals too: {The dog keeps pooping on the neighbor's lawn}. Less crude than shitting but too informal for medical contexts.

Poops is the third-person singular of poop, meaning to defecate: {The dog poops in the backyard every morning}. As a noun, poops is the plural of poop, referring to multiple instances of feces: {I had to clean up all the poops before the guests arrived}. The word is mildly childish, common with kids and pet owners.

Poopy is childish slang meaning covered in or resembling feces: {The baby has a poopy diaper}. By extension, it describes anything unpleasant, bad, or disappointing: {I'm having a poopy day}. The word belongs to baby talk and informal speech, often used by or around young children.

Poopyhead is a childish insult, the sort of thing a five-year-old might call a sibling: {You're a poopyhead!} Adults use it ironically or affectionately, often with children or pets. The insult has no real sting—it's playground-level name-calling that combines taboo bathroom language with the satisfying compound structure kids love.

Poor describes a lack of money or resources: {poor families}, {poor countries}. It extends to anything deficient or inadequate: {poor health}, {poor judgment}, {poor visibility}. Poor can express sympathy: {The poor thing looked exhausted}. As a noun with *the*, it refers collectively to people without money: {policies that hurt the poor}. To poor-mouth is to claim poverty, often falsely.

Poorboys is a plural of poorboy, the New Orleans name for a large sandwich on a long roll—what much of America calls a submarine sandwich, hoagie, or hero. The name comes from "poor boy," originally a cheap but filling meal for workers. {We grabbed poorboys from the corner deli.} Also spelled po'boys.

A poorhouse was a publicly funded institution where people unable to support themselves—the destitute, elderly, or disabled—were housed and often required to work. Common in the 19th and early 20th centuries before modern welfare systems: {His grandfather died in the poorhouse}. The word survives mainly in the expression {end up in the poorhouse}, meaning to become financially ruined.

Poorhouses were publicly funded institutions that housed the destitute, common in the 18th and 19th centuries before modern welfare systems. Conditions were deliberately harsh to discourage dependency—residents often worked in exchange for shelter and meager food. The word survives mainly as a rhetorical warning: {Keep spending like that and you'll end up in the poorhouse}.

Poorly means in an inadequate or unsatisfactory way: {The team performed poorly}, {a poorly written essay}. In British usage, poorly also works as an adjective meaning unwell or slightly ill: {She's feeling poorly today}. The adverb sense is standard everywhere; the adjective sense sounds distinctly British to American ears.

The many meanings of pop are hard to summarize, but the imitative origin of the word is a good clue. A pop is a sudden, explosive sound. When you pop something, this sound usually results (pop a balloon, pop popcorn). If you pop pills, you swallow them – probably lots of them. If you pop a question, you ask it, perhaps unexpectedly. Pop is one of the names for sweetened, fizzy beverages. Before another noun, pop is often a shortening of popular (pop culture, pop music, pop star).

A popadam is a thin, crispy Indian flatbread made from lentil, chickpea, or rice flour, typically fried or roasted until brittle. Served as a starter or side dish with chutneys and dips: {We ordered popadams while waiting for the curry}. Also spelled papadum, poppadom, and various other ways reflecting different transliterations from Hindi.

A popadom, also spelled papadum or papadam, is a thin, crispy Indian flatbread made from lentil, chickpea, or rice flour. It is typically fried or roasted until brittle and served as an accompaniment to curries and other South Asian dishes, often with chutneys or pickles. {The waiter brought out popadoms while we studied the menu.}

Popadoms are thin, crispy Indian wafers made from lentil or chickpea flour, typically served as an appetizer or side dish with chutneys and dips. They're fried or roasted until they puff and become brittle. Also spelled papadum, poppadom, or papad: {We ordered popadoms while waiting for the curry}.

A popadum is a thin, crispy Indian flatbread made from lentil, chickpea, or rice flour, typically served as an appetizer or side dish. Popadums are fried or roasted until they puff up and become light and crunchy: {We ordered popadums with chutney while we waited for the curry}. Also spelled papadum, poppadom, or papad.

Popadums are thin, crispy Indian flatbreads made from lentil or chickpea flour, typically fried or roasted until brittle. They're served as an appetizer or side dish, often with chutneys and dips: {The waiter brought popadums while we looked at the menu}. Also spelled papadums, poppadoms, or papads.

Popcorn is a variety of corn whose kernels explode when heated, puffing into light, irregular white shapes. It's eaten as a snack, typically with butter and salt, and is strongly associated with movie theaters. {We made popcorn for movie night.} As an adjective, popcorn suggests light entertainment without much substance: a popcorn {movie}, popcorn {fiction}.

The pope is the head of the Roman Catholic Church, considered by Catholics to be the spiritual successor to Saint Peter. The title applies to the Bishop of Rome, who serves as the supreme authority on matters of faith and church governance. Informally, pope can describe anyone treated as the ultimate authority in a field: {the pope of fashion criticism}. The adjective papal relates to the pope or papacy.

Popes is the plural of pope, the head of the Roman Catholic Church. The word appears in historical discussions spanning multiple pontificates: {The popes of the Renaissance were often patrons of the arts}. It also appears in comparative contexts: {Some popes have been reformers, others conservatives}.

A popgun is a toy gun that makes a popping sound when fired, typically shooting a cork or soft projectile with compressed air. The term extends to any small or ineffective firearm: {That little pistol is just a popgun}. Figuratively, something dismissed as a popgun lacks real power or threat.

A poplar is a fast-growing deciduous tree with soft wood and triangular or heart-shaped leaves that flutter in the slightest breeze. Poplars are common in temperate regions and include cottonwoods and aspens. The wood is used for paper pulp, plywood, and cheap furniture. {A row of Lombardy poplars lined the driveway.}

Poplars are fast-growing deciduous trees of the genus Populus, characterized by their tall, columnar shape and trembling leaves that flutter in the slightest breeze. They thrive near water and are often planted as windbreaks or along roadsides. The wood is soft and lightweight, used for paper pulp and cheap lumber. {A row of Lombardy poplars lined the driveway.} The trees are known for releasing cottony seeds that drift through the air in early summer.

A popover is a light, hollow roll made from an egg batter that puffs up dramatically during baking, creating a crisp exterior and airy interior. The name comes from the batter rising and "popping over" the sides of the baking tin. In computing and interface design, a popover is a small overlay that appears when clicking or hovering over an element: {The settings popover appeared when I tapped the icon}.

Popovers are light, hollow pastries made from an egg-rich batter that puffs dramatically when baked. The same batter baked in a hot pan with beef drippings becomes Yorkshire pudding. The name comes from the way the batter "pops over" the rim of the baking tin. {She served warm popovers with butter and jam.}

A poppadom is a thin, crisp Indian flatbread made from lentil or chickpea flour, typically served as an appetizer or side dish. The discs are dried then fried or roasted until they puff and crisp. They often accompany chutneys and are standard fare at Indian restaurants: {We ordered poppadoms while we waited for our curry}. Also spelled papadum, papadam, and other variants.

Poppadoms are thin, crispy Indian flatbreads made from lentil or chickpea flour, typically served as an appetizer or side dish. They're fried or roasted until brittle and often accompanied by chutneys and relishes. Also spelled papadum, papadam, or poppadum. {We ordered poppadoms while we looked at the menu.}

A poppadum is a thin, crispy Indian bread made from lentil or chickpea flour, typically served as an appetizer or side dish. The discs are dried then fried or roasted until they puff and crisp. Often accompanied by chutneys or pickles: {We ordered poppadums while we waited for our curry}. Also spelled papadum, papadam, or poppadom.

Poppadums are thin, crispy Indian flatbreads made from lentil or chickpea flour, typically served as an appetizer or side dish. They're fried or roasted until they puff and crisp, often accompanied by chutneys or pickles: {We started with poppadums while we waited for the curry}. Also spelled papadums, poppadoms, or papads.

Popped is the past tense of pop. Something popped if it burst with a sharp sound: {The balloon popped}. Eyes or veins pop when they bulge suddenly. To pop somewhere is to go briefly: {I popped into the store}. In slang, to pop someone is to shoot them, and to pop pills is to take them casually. Popped collar describes a shirt collar turned up rather than folded down.

A popper is something that pops. Popcorn poppers heat kernels until they burst. Party poppers release confetti with a bang. In fishing, a popper is a lure that makes a popping sound on the water's surface. Poppers are also small capsules of amyl nitrite or similar inhalants, crushed and sniffed for a brief euphoric rush—popular in club and sexual contexts for intensifying sensation.

Poppers are small capsules of amyl nitrite or similar chemicals, crushed and inhaled for a brief euphoric rush and muscle relaxation. They're associated with club culture and gay male sex, where they enhance sensation and relax smooth muscles. The term also refers to jalapeño peppers stuffed with cheese and fried: {jalapeño poppers}. A popper can be any container or device that pops—a party popper, a fishing lure that makes a popping sound on the water.

Poppet is a British English term of endearment for a child or someone regarded with affection, similar to sweetheart or darling: {Come here, poppet}. The word derives from an older sense meaning a small figure of a human, like a doll or puppet—and in fact shares origins with puppet. In engineering, a poppet is a mushroom-shaped valve that moves up and down rather than rotating, commonly found in internal combustion engines.

Poppets is a British term of endearment for children or loved ones, similar to "sweethearts" or "darlings": {Come along, poppets}. The word derives from puppet, suggesting something small and cherished. In mechanical contexts, a poppet is a valve component that moves up and down, as in an engine's poppet valve.

Poppies is the plural of poppy, a flowering plant with delicate, papery petals in vivid reds, oranges, and yellows. The opium poppy yields narcotic compounds used in painkillers and heroin. Red poppies are symbols of remembrance for soldiers killed in war, especially in Commonwealth countries on Remembrance Day: {She wore a poppy on her lapel}.

Popping describes the action or sound of small explosions or sharp bursts: {popping corn}, {popping sounds from the engine}. It covers quick movements in and out: {popping into the store}, {popping by for a visit}. Eyes can be popping with surprise or intensity. In dance, popping is a style involving sharp, rhythmic muscle contractions. Something popping is also vibrant or exciting: {The colors are really popping}.

Poppy refers to flowering plants known for their showy, papery blooms and seed pods. The opium poppy yields compounds used in narcotics and painkillers. Red poppies are symbols of remembrance for war dead, worn especially on Veterans Day and Remembrance Day in Commonwealth countries: {She pinned a poppy to her lapel}. Poppy seeds appear in baking. (Capitalized Poppy is a given name.)

Poppycock is nonsense or rubbish—empty talk that shouldn't be taken seriously. The word sounds quaint and slightly comical, often used to dismiss something as absurd: {That's absolute poppycock}. It carries less force than bullshit but more dismissiveness than nonsense.

Poppyseed is the tiny, kidney-shaped seed of the poppy plant, used as a flavoring and topping in baking: {poppyseed muffins}, {poppyseed bagels}. The seeds have a mild, nutty taste and add visual texture. Because poppies produce opium, eating poppyseeds can sometimes trigger false positives on drug tests—though the seeds themselves contain negligible opiates.

Pops is an informal, affectionate term for one's father: {Hey pops, can I borrow the car?} It can also address any older man in a familiar way, sometimes condescendingly: {You okay there, pops?} In music, pops refers to popular orchestral concerts or their repertoire: {the Boston Pops}.

A popsicle is a frozen treat on a stick, typically fruit-flavored ice or frozen juice. The word is used generically for any such frozen confection, though it originated as a trademark: {The kids ran after the popsicle truck}. In American summers, popsicles are childhood staples. (Capitalized Popsicle is the trademark.)

Popsicles is the plural of popsicle, a frozen treat on a stick—flavored ice or ice cream meant to be eaten by hand. The word is a trademark but used generically for any such frozen confection: {The kids ran after the popsicle truck}. {We made popsicles from orange juice}.

A popstar is a famous singer or performer of pop music, typically one with widespread commercial success and public recognition. The term implies celebrity status beyond mere musicianship—popstars attract media attention, fan devotion, and cultural influence: {She dreamed of becoming a popstar}. Also spelled as two words: pop star.

Popstars is the plural of popstar, referring to performers who have achieved fame and commercial success in popular music. The term encompasses singers and musicians whose appeal is broad enough to generate hit records, sold-out concerts, and widespread media attention. Popstars often become cultural icons whose influence extends beyond music into fashion, social media, and celebrity culture generally. {The popstars of the 1980s defined a generation's style.}

Populace refers to the people living in a particular area or country, considered as a group. It often carries a slightly formal or literary tone and may suggest the common people as distinct from elites or rulers: {The new policy was unpopular with the general populace}. Unlike population, which emphasizes numbers, populace emphasizes the people themselves as a collective body with opinions, needs, or characteristics.

Popular describes what many people like, know, or participate in. A popular {song} gets heavy airplay; a popular {kid} has many friends; a popular {destination} attracts crowds. The word can also mean "of the people" rather than elite or specialized: {popular culture}, {popular vote}, {popular uprising}. Something done {by popular demand} responds to widespread request.

Popularity is the state of being liked, admired, or supported by many people. A politician's popularity rises and falls with public opinion. A song gains popularity through radio play and streaming. The word can also describe how widespread something is: {the popularity of smartphones}, {the growing popularity of remote work}. Popularity often implies broad appeal rather than critical merit—what's popular isn't always what's best.

Popularize means to make something widely known, liked, or accessible to ordinary people. A scientist might popularize complex theories by explaining them in plain language, or a celebrity might popularize a fashion trend simply by being seen wearing it. {The documentary popularized interest in climate science.} The word implies bringing something from a specialized or elite domain into mainstream awareness, sometimes with the connotation that the original has been simplified or diluted in the process.

To populate a place is to inhabit it or fill it with inhabitants: {Immigrants populated the frontier}. The word extends to filling anything with content or data: {populate a database}, {populate a spreadsheet with values}. In computing, fields that populate automatically fill themselves with default or calculated information.

Populated describes a place where people live. A densely populated area has many inhabitants; a sparsely populated region has few. The word extends beyond humans: {The forest is populated with deer and wild turkeys}. In computing, a populated field contains data rather than standing empty. To populate is to fill with inhabitants or entries: {Immigrants populated the frontier}; {The database populated automatically}.

Population is the total number of people, animals, or organisms living in a particular place: {the population of Tokyo}, {the deer population}. In statistics, a population is the entire group from which samples are drawn for study. The word also describes the act of populating: {the population of the American West}.

Populations is the plural of population—the total number of people or organisms living in a particular area, or the act of populating. Different populations can be compared: {The populations of rural counties have declined while urban populations grow}. In statistics, a population is the entire set from which samples are drawn: {The study examined three distinct populations}.

Populism is a political approach that frames issues as the common people versus a corrupt elite. It can appear across the ideological spectrum—left-wing populists target wealthy corporations and billionaires, while right-wing populists target cultural elites and established institutions. The term is often used dismissively to suggest demagoguery or oversimplification: {His economic proposals were pure populism}. A populist champions ordinary people's interests, or claims to.

Populist describes political movements or figures claiming to represent ordinary people against a corrupt elite. The term is ideologically flexible—populists appear on both left and right, united by appeals to "the people" versus "the establishment." A populist {candidate} campaigns against Washington insiders; populist {policies} promise to return power to regular citizens. The noun identifies someone who takes this stance: {He ran as a populist}. Critics use the term to suggest demagoguery or oversimplification.

Populists are politicians or movements that claim to represent ordinary people against a corrupt elite. The term can be neutral or pejorative depending on context—supporters see populism as democratic accountability, critics see it as demagoguery that oversimplifies complex issues. Populist movements have appeared across the political spectrum: {right-wing populists blame immigrants}, {left-wing populists target corporations}. A populist {appeal} speaks to common grievances rather than policy details.

A popup is something that appears suddenly, especially a window or advertisement that opens automatically on a computer screen: {I installed an ad blocker to stop the popups}. Popup books have illustrations that spring into three dimensions when pages are opened. A popup store or restaurant operates temporarily in a space before moving on. Also spelled pop-up.

Popups are windows or boxes that appear suddenly on a screen, typically without being requested. On websites, popups often display advertisements or requests to subscribe: {I can't read anything with all these popups}. The term extends to popup ads, popup blockers, and popup menus. In baseball, a popup is a fly ball hit high but not far. Popup also describes temporary or appearing-from-nowhere things: popup shops, popup restaurants, popup books with three-dimensional illustrations that rise when pages open.

Porcelain is a hard, white, translucent ceramic made by firing clay at high temperatures. The finest porcelain originated in China, making *china* and *porcelain* near-synonyms for delicate dinnerware. Porcelain appears in decorative objects, dental work, and bathroom fixtures. As an adjective, it suggests smooth paleness: {porcelain skin}. The material's fragility makes it a metaphor for anything delicate or easily damaged.

definition: A porch is a covered structure attached to the entrance of a building, typically with a roof supported by columns or posts. Front porches are traditional gathering spaces in American homes: {We sat on the porch drinking lemonade}. A screened porch keeps out insects while letting in air. Back porches and side porches serve similar functions away from the street.

Porches is the plural of porch—a covered structure attached to the entrance of a building, typically with a roof supported by columns or posts. Front porches are gathering spaces for sitting outdoors while sheltered from sun or rain: {The neighbors sat on their porches and watched the storm roll in}. A screened porch keeps out insects. Back porches tend to be more private.

Porcini are prized edible mushrooms with meaty brown caps and thick white stems, native to forests across Europe and North America. The name comes from Italian for "little pigs," perhaps reflecting their plump shape or the enthusiasm with which they're hunted. Porcini appear frequently in Italian cuisine, dried or fresh, lending an earthy, nutty depth to risottos, pastas, and sauces. {I rehydrated some dried porcini for the soup.}

A porcupine is a large rodent covered in sharp, barbed quills that serve as defense against predators. When threatened, a porcupine raises its quills; contrary to myth, it cannot shoot them, but the quills detach easily on contact and are painful to remove. {The dog learned the hard way to leave porcupines alone.}

Porcupines is the plural of porcupine, a large rodent covered in sharp, defensive quills. When threatened, porcupines raise their quills; contrary to myth, they cannot shoot them, but the barbed spines detach easily on contact. {We spotted porcupines gnawing on the cabin steps.} The animals are nocturnal and found across North America, Africa, and parts of Asia.

A pore is a tiny opening in a surface, especially the minute holes in skin through which sweat passes: {clogged pores}, {open pores}. Plants have pores for gas exchange; rocks and membranes have pores that allow passage of fluids. The verb pore means to study intently: {She pored over the documents for hours}. The verb is almost always followed by "over."

Pores are tiny openings in a surface that allow passage of liquids or gases. Skin pores release sweat and oil; porous materials like sponges absorb water through countless pores. To pore over something is to study it intently: {She pored over the documents for hours}. This verb pore is unrelated to the noun—the spelling pour is a common error.

Pork is the meat of a pig, used as food: {pork chops}, {pulled pork}, {pork belly}. In American politics, pork refers to government spending directed to a particular district primarily to benefit constituents and win votes rather than serve broader public interest: {The bill was loaded with pork}. The verb pork is vulgar slang for having sex.

A porkchop is a cut of pork from the loin, sliced perpendicular to the spine and typically including a rib bone: {grilled porkchops with applesauce}. The cut is a staple of American home cooking. In slang, porkchop can describe someone considered thick or unsophisticated, or in some Black American usage, a person seen as an Uncle Tom—subservient to white authority.
clues: What you might bread and fry

definition: Porkchops are cuts of pork from the loin, sliced perpendicular to the spine and typically including a section of rib bone. They're a staple of home cooking, pan-fried, grilled, or baked: {Mom's porkchops with applesauce}. The singular porkchop sometimes describes something shaped like the cut—a rounded form with a protruding handle.

Porkies is British slang for lies, from Cockney rhyming slang: porky pies = lies. The singular porky appears, but the plural dominates: {He's been telling porkies again}. The term is informal and mildly humorous rather than accusatory—you'd say someone's telling porkies about trivial matters, not about serious deceptions.

A porkpie is a hat with a flat crown and a narrow brim turned up all around, resembling the shape of a traditional pork pie. It became associated with jazz musicians in the mid-20th century and has cycled in and out of fashion since: {He wore a felt porkpie tilted back on his head}. In British rhyming slang, porkpie (or porky) means lie: {Don't tell porkies}.

Porn is short for pornography—sexually explicit material designed to arouse. The word covers everything from magazines to videos to internet content: {He got caught watching porn at work}. As a suffix, -porn describes any content offering visual gratification: {food porn}, {real estate porn}, {disaster porn}. The adjective form is usually porno.

A pornographer is someone who produces pornography—sexually explicit material intended to arouse. The term covers creators across media: filmmakers, photographers, writers, website operators. It can be neutral or derogatory depending on context: {He made his fortune as a pornographer} versus {Just another sleazy pornographer}.

Pornographic describes material depicting sexual acts with the primary purpose of arousing the viewer or reader. A pornographic {film}, {magazine}, or {website} contains explicit sexual content. The word also applies figuratively to anything that exploits or displays something shamelessly: {pornographic violence}, {a pornographic display of wealth}.

Pornography is material depicting sexual activity, intended to arouse. The term covers everything from explicit photographs and videos to written erotica. Porn is the common shortening. What counts as pornography versus art or erotica depends on who's judging—the line has shifted across eras and cultures. {The internet transformed how pornography is distributed and consumed.} Metaphorically, anything that offers visceral gratification without substance may be called pornography: {poverty porn}, {food porn}, {disaster porn}.

A pornstache is a thick mustache without a beard, typically associated with male porn actors of the 1970s and 1980s. The style suggests sleaziness or dated masculinity, often worn ironically: {He grew a pornstache for Movember}. Also spelled porn stache or porn 'stache.

A pornstar is a person who performs in pornographic films or videos, typically as a profession. The term carries less stigma than older equivalents and is often used by performers themselves: {She's one of the most famous pornstars in the industry}. Also spelled as two words: porn star.

Porous describes material with tiny holes or spaces that allow liquids or gases to pass through: {porous rock}, {porous membrane}. A porous border is easily crossed. A porous defense in sports lets opponents through too easily. The word suggests permeability—things flow in and out where perhaps they shouldn't: {The company's porous security allowed the breach}.

A porpoise is a small toothed whale, similar to a dolphin but with a blunter snout and stockier body. Porpoises are found in coastal waters worldwide. The verb porpoise describes the motion of rising and plunging through water—or through air, when an aircraft or vehicle bounces rhythmically: {The plane porpoised down the runway}.

Porpoises is the plural of porpoise, a small toothed whale related to dolphins but typically smaller and stouter, with a blunt snout rather than a beak. Porpoises surface to breathe with a characteristic rolling motion. The verb porpoises describes similar undulating movement: {The boat porpoised through the waves}, {The submarine porpoised to the surface}.

Porpoising is a repeated bouncing motion where something rises and dips like a porpoise breaking the water's surface. In aviation, it describes an aircraft oscillating between climbing and descending during landing or takeoff. In motorsport, particularly Formula 1, it refers to a car's violent vertical bouncing at high speeds caused by aerodynamic instability: {The team struggled with porpoising all season}.

Porridge is a hot cereal made by boiling oats or other grains in water or milk until thick and soft. It's a traditional breakfast food, especially in Britain and Scotland: {a bowl of porridge with honey}. The word appears in the British slang phrase {do porridge}, meaning to serve a prison sentence—from the association of porridge with institutional meals.

The many meanings of the noun port share the idea of an opening or conduit through which something passes, be it cargo, data, or air: What ports do you have on your computer? Chicago is the largest port on the Great Lakes. A separately derived port accounts for the class of sweet wines originally from Portugal. As a verb, port means to carry a weapon, or to send or transmit via a port. In the computer age, the dominant usage for both noun and verb is in relation to the various ports built into hardware devices and the movement of data through or across them.

Portabella is a spelling variant of portobello, the large brown mushroom with a meaty texture popular in vegetarian cooking. The cap can grow several inches across and is often grilled or roasted whole: {a portabella burger}. Also spelled portabello, portobella.

Portabello is a large, mature cremini mushroom with an open cap and exposed gills, typically four to six inches across. The size and meaty texture make it popular as a vegetarian alternative to burgers: {grilled portabello sandwich}. Also spelled portobello.

Portabellos are large, mature cremini mushrooms with broad, flat caps and dark gills. Their meaty texture makes them popular as a vegetarian substitute in dishes where beef might otherwise appear: {a grilled portabello burger}. Also spelled portobello or portabella—the spellings are interchangeable and none is more correct than another.

Portable describes something designed to be carried or moved easily. A portable {radio} or {computer} travels with you. The word implies a tradeoff—portable versions are typically smaller or lighter than stationary ones, sometimes at the cost of power or features. Software is portable when it runs on different systems without modification.

Portage is carrying a boat or its cargo overland between navigable waters, or the route where this happens: {The portage around the falls took two hours}. The word also applies more broadly to the act of carrying or transporting goods. As a verb, to portage is to make such a carry: {We portaged the canoes across the ridge}.

A portajohn is a portable toilet—a self-contained plastic outhouse used at construction sites, outdoor events, and anywhere plumbing isn't available. The name comes from Porta John, a trademark that became generic. Also spelled porta-john or porta john. {The festival had a row of portajohns near the parking lot.}

A portal is a doorway or entrance, especially one that's large or imposing: {the cathedral's main portal}. The word suggests a threshold between spaces or states. In fantasy and science fiction, portals are gateways to other worlds or dimensions. In computing, a portal is a website serving as an entry point to other content—a starting place for browsing.

A portaloo is a portable toilet, typically a self-contained plastic unit found at outdoor events, construction sites, and festivals. The word is British, formed from "portable" and "loo." Americans more often say porta-potty or port-a-john. {The queue for the portaloo stretched halfway across the field.}

Portals are doorways or gates, especially grand or imposing ones: {the portals of the cathedral}. The word suggests a threshold between realms—hence its adoption for website entry points that aggregate content and services: {Yahoo was once the dominant internet portal}. In fantasy and science fiction, a portal is a magical or technological passage to another place or dimension: {a portal opened in the sky}.

Portapotties are portable toilets—self-contained units that can be moved to locations without plumbing. They're ubiquitous at construction sites, outdoor festivals, and public events. The word combines portable with potty, the childish term for toilet. Also spelled porta-potties or porta potties. {The line for the portapotties stretched halfway across the fairgrounds.}

A portapotty is a portable toilet—a self-contained plastic outhouse that can be moved to locations without plumbing. Common at construction sites, outdoor festivals, and public events. Also spelled porta-potty or porta potty, from a trademarked brand name that became generic. {The line for the portapotties stretched halfway across the fairgrounds.}
A portcullis is a security device seen mostly on historical buildings such as castles. It is a grating that can be lowered to completely block a door, gateway, or archway in order to prevent passage.

Ported describes software or games that have been adapted to run on a different platform than originally designed: {The classic RPG was ported to mobile devices}. In computing, ported also means routed through a specific network port. For phone numbers, ported means transferred from one carrier to another while keeping the same number.

A portent is a sign or warning of something momentous, usually something bad: {Dark clouds gathered on the horizon, a portent of the storm to come}. The word carries an ominous weight—portents precede disasters, upheavals, or dramatic change. Something portentous is either full of such significance or, more commonly now, pompously self-important.

Portents is the plural of portent—signs or omens foretelling future events, especially ominous ones. The word carries a sense of weight and significance: {dark portents of war}, {portents of doom}. Unusual occurrences—eclipses, comets, strange weather—have historically been read as portents. The word sometimes appears ironically for lesser premonitions: {The traffic jam was a portent of how the day would go}.

A porter is someone who carries things for others—luggage at hotels and train stations, supplies in hospitals, or goods in markets. The word also names a dark brown beer, supposedly favored by London porters in the 18th century. In buildings, especially British ones, a porter is a doorkeeper or caretaker who manages access and handles deliveries: {The porter signed for the package}. (Capitalized Porter is a surname.)

A porterhouse is a thick cut of beef steak containing both the tenderloin and the strip, separated by a T-shaped bone. It differs from a T-bone only in having a larger portion of tenderloin: {We split a porterhouse for two}. Porterhouse also refers to a pub or chophouse that serves porter and other drinks alongside food, though this sense is now rare.

Porters are workers who carry luggage or goods. At hotels and train stations, porters help travelers with their bags. In hospitals, porters move patients and equipment between departments. The term also applies to workers who carry loads in mountainous regions: {Sherpas work as porters on Himalayan expeditions}. A porter is also a dark beer, supposedly named because London porters favored it.

A portfolio is a case for carrying loose papers, drawings, or documents. From this comes the extended sense of a collection of work samples, especially for artists, designers, or writers seeking employment: {She brought her portfolio to the interview}. In finance, a portfolio is the range of investments held by a person or institution: {a diversified portfolio}. A minister's portfolio is their area of governmental responsibility.

Portfolios is the plural of portfolio. A portfolio is a flat case for carrying documents or artwork. By extension, it refers to a collection of investments held by a person or institution: {She diversified her portfolios across stocks and bonds}. It also means a selection of work samples demonstrating someone's abilities: {The designer showed portfolios to three agencies}.

A porthole is a small, usually circular window in the side of a ship or aircraft. Ship portholes are typically fitted with thick glass and a hinged metal cover that can be sealed against water. The shape distinguishes them from ordinary rectangular windows: {light streaming through the porthole}, {She watched the waves through her cabin's porthole}.

Portholes are small, typically circular windows in the side of a ship or aircraft. The round shape and thick glass help withstand pressure and water. On ships, portholes can often be opened for ventilation: {She watched the coastline recede through the porthole}. The term sometimes extends to any small, round window.

A portico is a covered entrance to a building, supported by columns and often featuring a roof with a pediment. The structure projects from the main building, creating a sheltered walkway or porch: {Visitors gathered under the portico to escape the rain}. Porticos are characteristic of classical architecture, particularly Greek and Roman temples, and appear on grand civic buildings, banks, and stately homes.

Porting is the process of adapting software to run on a different platform, operating system, or hardware than it was originally designed for: {The studio spent months porting the game from console to PC}. The term comes from the verb port, suggesting transfer or carrying across. A clean port preserves functionality; a lazy port introduces bugs or performance issues.

A portion is a part of something larger: {a portion of the proceeds}, {a generous portion of mashed potatoes}. It often implies division or allocation—the share that belongs to someone or gets served to them. To portion something is to divide it into shares: {She portioned out the inheritance among her children}. Portion can also mean one's lot or fate, though this use sounds old-fashioned.

Portions are parts of a larger whole, especially shares divided among people: {The waiter brought generous portions}. A portion of something is an amount set aside or allotted: {A portion of the budget goes to maintenance}. To portion out is to divide into shares: {She portioned the inheritance among her children}. Portion can also mean one's lot or fate, now somewhat literary: {Suffering was his portion}.

definition: A portmanteau is a word formed by blending parts of two other words: *brunch* from breakfast and lunch, *smog* from smoke and fog. The term comes from a type of hinged suitcase that opens into two compartments—the linguistic sense captures how two words are packed into one. {Spork, motel, and emoticon are all portmanteaus.}

Portmanteaus is the plural of portmanteau, a word formed by blending parts of two other words: *brunch* from breakfast and lunch, *smog* from smoke and fog, *Brexit* from Britain and exit. The term originally meant a large traveling bag that opens into two hinged compartments—the linguistic sense captures how two words fold together into one. {Internet culture produces portmanteaus constantly: *chillax*, *frenemy*, *staycation*.}

A portobello is a large, mature cremini mushroom with a broad, flat cap and dense, meaty texture. Portobellos are often grilled or roasted whole and served as a vegetarian main course: {a portobello burger}, {stuffed portobellos}. The name emerged in the 1980s as a marketing term for what had been common brown mushrooms. Also spelled portabella or portabello.

A portrait is a painting, drawing, photograph, or other artistic representation of a person, typically focusing on the face and upper body. The goal is usually to capture not just physical likeness but something of the subject's character or mood. Portrait extends to written descriptions that vividly depict someone: {The biography paints an unflattering portrait of the senator}. In photography and design, portrait orientation means the image is taller than it is wide, as opposed to landscape.

Portraits are paintings, photographs, or other artistic representations of a person, typically focusing on the face. The word emphasizes capturing likeness or character: {The gallery featured portraits of former presidents}. A portrait can also be a written or verbal description that reveals someone's nature: {The biography painted a vivid portrait of the artist}. In printing, portrait orientation means the page is taller than it is wide, like a traditional painted portrait.

Portraiture is the art or practice of creating portraits—representations of specific people, especially their faces. The term covers painted, drawn, or photographed likenesses: {She studied portraiture at art school}. Portraiture can also mean portraits collectively, or the skill of capturing someone's likeness and character: {The photographer was known for her sensitive portraiture}.

To portray is to depict or represent someone or something, whether in visual art, writing, or performance. An actor portrays a character; a novelist portrays small-town life; a painting portrays a battle scene. The word implies interpretation—how something is portrayed shapes how it's understood: {The media portrayed him as a hero}. A portrayal can be accurate, sympathetic, or distorted.

A portrayal is a representation or depiction of someone or something, especially in art, film, or writing: {Her portrayal of the queen earned an Oscar nomination}. The word emphasizes interpretation—an actor's portrayal reveals how they understand the character. Portrayals can be accurate or misleading: {The documentary offered a sympathetic portrayal of the controversial figure}.

Portrayed is the past tense of portray, meaning to depict or represent someone or something. An actor portrays a character by embodying them on stage or screen: {She portrayed Hamlet in the all-female production}. Artists portray subjects in paintings or photographs. More broadly, to portray is to describe or present in a particular way: {The media portrayed him as a villain}.

Portraying is representing someone or something in a particular way. An actor portrays a character by embodying them on stage or screen: {She's portraying Lady Macbeth this season}. A writer or artist portrays subjects through their chosen medium. The word often implies interpretation—how something is portrayed shapes how audiences perceive it: {The film was criticized for portraying the conflict one-sidedly}.

Ports are openings where things pass through. A port is a harbor town where ships load and unload cargo: {The ship arrived at port}. In computing, a port is a socket where cables connect or a virtual endpoint for network traffic: {USB port}, {port 443}. Port wine is a sweet fortified wine from Portugal. To port software is to adapt it for a different system. In nautical use, port is the left side of a vessel facing forward—opposite starboard.

Pose connects the idea of positioning with the idea of presenting. To pose is to hold a position, especially for a photograph or portrait: {She posed beside the fountain}. A pose is that assumed position. Figuratively, a pose is an affected manner meant to impress: {His cynicism is just a pose}. To pose as someone is to pretend to be them: {He posed as a doctor}. To pose a question or problem is to present it for consideration.

Posed is the past tense of pose, which means to position oneself or something else for effect—typically for a photograph, portrait, or artistic representation: {She posed for the camera}. Posed also describes questions or problems that have been put forward: {The detective posed several questions to the suspect}. Something posed can seem artificial or affected rather than natural: {The whole scene felt posed}.

A poser is someone who affects attitudes, behaviors, or styles they don't genuinely hold—pretending expertise or belonging they haven't earned. The word carries contempt: {He's not a real skater, just a poser}. Poser also means a difficult question or problem, though this sense is less common: {The detective faced a real poser}.

Posers is the plural of poser, a person who adopts attitudes, styles, or identities they haven't earned—someone who affects expertise or belonging without the substance: {The regulars dismissed the newcomers as posers}. Common in music and subculture contexts, where authenticity matters: {real punks vs. posers}. The word carries contempt for inauthenticity.

Poses covers both physical positioning and pretense. A pose is a deliberate arrangement of the body—for a photograph, a painting, or in yoga. To pose is to hold such a position: {She posed for the portrait}. But pose also means to present or put forward: {The situation poses a challenge}. When someone poses as something, they pretend to be it: {He posed as a doctor to gain access}. A pose can therefore be an affected manner—behavior meant to impress rather than express: {His cynicism is just a pose}.

A poseur is someone who affects attitudes, behaviors, or styles to impress others without genuine commitment or understanding. The term implies superficiality—a poseur in the punk scene wears the clothes but doesn't grasp the ethos. {He's just a poseur who bought a guitar to look cool.} The word carries contempt for inauthenticity.

Poseurs is the plural of poseur—people who affect attitudes, behaviors, or styles to impress others rather than from genuine conviction. The term carries contempt: {The scene was full of poseurs who'd never heard the band's early albums}. A poseur claims membership in a subculture or expertise in a field without authentic credentials. The French spelling adds a note of irony, as if the affectation extends even to the word itself.

Posh means elegantly luxurious or associated with the upper classes. A posh {hotel} is expensively appointed. A posh {accent} suggests privileged British upbringing. The word carries slight mockery—calling something posh often implies it's pretentious or unnecessarily fancy: {We can't afford anywhere that posh}. To posh up is to make something more elegant or refined.

Posies is the plural of posy, a small bouquet of flowers. The word sounds quaint and old-fashioned: {Ring around the rosie, a pocket full of posies}. Posies suggests something dainty and informal—wildflowers picked on a walk rather than an arranged florist's display.

Posing is assuming a position, typically for artistic or photographic purposes: {She spent hours posing for the portrait}. Extended meanings involve pretense—posing as someone you're not, or adopting attitudes for effect rather than sincerity: {He's just posing as an expert}. Something that poses a threat or challenge presents it: {The storm posed serious risks to coastal towns}.

Meanings of the noun position are frequent and familiar, unlike those of its underlying verb posit; but understanding posit tells you most of what you need to know about position. To posit something is to put it in a place, or to put it forward as an assertion. A position is a place or configuration in space with particular characteristics, or abstractly, a condition or situation with reference to a place: The drill will only operate in an upright position. If you take a position on some matter, you announce or declare your attitude or opinion about it: The committee decided against taking a position on the issue. A position in a hierarchy of any kind is a place in it: What position does she occupy at the bank?

Positioning is the act of placing something in a particular location or arrangement: {The positioning of the cameras gave us full coverage of the room}. In marketing, positioning refers to how a brand or product is perceived relative to competitors—its place in consumers' minds: {The company's positioning as a luxury brand justified higher prices}. The word often emphasizes deliberate, strategic placement rather than random location.

Positions are locations or placements—where something or someone is situated: {She shifted to a more comfortable position}. The word extends to stances on issues: {What's your position on the budget?} In employment, a position is a job or role: {He applied for the position of director}. To position something is to place it deliberately: {Position the camera so it captures the whole room}. In sex, positions are configurations of bodies during intercourse.

Most meanings of positive can be paired with opposites characterized by negative. A positive test result is one finding the presence of something. Positive numbers are those greater than zero. Positive also characterizes what is favorable where negative means unfavorable: The audience gave a very positive reaction to the proposal. These measures will have a positive impact. Finally, positive can convey certainty: I’m positive that I saw her leaving earlier. As a noun, positive most frequently means a positive test result, or a photographic print made from a negative.

Positively means in a positive manner—with certainty, approval, or optimism: {She responded positively to the proposal}. It also serves as an intensifier meaning absolutely or definitely: {The view was positively breathtaking}, {I'm positively certain}. In technical contexts, positively refers to electrical charge: {positively charged particles}.

Positives are favorable or affirmative things—the opposite of negatives. In photography, a positive is an image with tones matching reality, not reversed as in a negative. In grammar, the positive is the base form of an adjective before comparison: {good} rather than {better} or {best}. To {accentuate the positives} is to focus on what's going well. A positive test result confirms the presence of what's being tested for.

Positivity is an optimistic or hopeful outlook—the tendency to focus on what's good rather than what's wrong. The word often appears in self-help contexts: {Try to maintain your positivity during difficult times}. It can also mean simply the quality of being positive: the positivity of a test result, the positivity of an electrical charge.

Posole is a traditional Mexican soup or stew made with hominy—dried corn kernels treated with lime—typically simmered with pork and seasoned with chiles. It's served with an array of garnishes: shredded cabbage, radishes, oregano, lime. The dish is celebratory, often prepared for holidays and special occasions. Also spelled pozole.

A posse is a group assembled for a common purpose, originally a body of citizens summoned by a sheriff to help capture a criminal or keep order. The Old West imagery persists: {The sheriff rounded up a posse to track the outlaws}. In casual use, posse means any group of friends or associates: {He showed up with his whole posse}.

Posses is the plural of posse—a group assembled for a common purpose. Originally a posse was a band of citizens deputized by a sheriff to pursue outlaws: {Posses scoured the hills for the escaped prisoner}. Now it usually means a person's crew or entourage: {He rolled up with his whole posse}.

To possess something is to have it or own it: {She possesses considerable talent}, {He was arrested for possessing a firearm}. Possess often sounds more formal than have or own, appearing in legal contexts ({possessing stolen property}) and descriptions of qualities ({She possesses an unusual grace}). To be possessed is to be controlled by a spirit or demon, or figuratively by an intense emotion: {What possessed you to do that?}

Possessed describes being controlled or influenced by something external—originally a spirit or demon: {She screamed as if possessed}. The word extends to any overwhelming force: {possessed by jealousy}, {possessed by an idea}. To be possessed of something is to have it: {He was possessed of great wealth}. Self-possessed means composed and in control of oneself.

Possession is having or owning something: {The police found drugs in his possession}. In law, possession may differ from ownership—you can possess what you don't own and own what you don't possess. Possessions are belongings: {She packed her few possessions}. In sports, possession is control of the ball. Spiritual possession means a demon or spirit has taken control of someone's body: {The priest performed an exorcism to end the possession}. In grammar, possession is the relationship shown by apostrophe-s or possessive pronouns.

Possessions are things you own or have with you. The word often appears when belongings are considered as a group: {She gathered her possessions and left}. A possession can also be a territory under another country's control: {The island was a British possession}. In supernatural contexts, possession is the state of being controlled by a spirit or demon: {The priest performed an exorcism to end the possession}.

Possessive describes an excessive desire to own or control something, especially a person: {He's possessive of his girlfriend}. In grammar, possessive refers to forms showing ownership—the 's in {John's book}, or pronouns like my, your, his, her, its, our, their. The possessive can signal either literal ownership or looser relationships: {my doctor}, {her birthday}, {its meaning}.

Possessiveness is the tendency to treat people or things as one's own property, often with excessive control or jealousy. In relationships, possessiveness manifests as demanding attention, monitoring a partner's activities, or resenting time spent with others: {His possessiveness drove her away}. The term usually carries negative connotations—suggesting insecurity rather than healthy attachment.

Possibilities are things that might happen or be true—outcomes not yet determined. The word implies openness rather than certainty: {The possibilities are endless}. Someone with possibilities has potential for development or success. To explore the possibilities is to consider options before committing: {Let's discuss the possibilities over lunch}.
clues: The range of potential future states

definition: Possibility is something that could happen or be true. It ranges from the barely conceivable to the highly likely: {There's a possibility of rain}. In the plural, possibilities often suggests potential or promise: {The job has real possibilities}. {We need to consider all the possibilities before deciding}.

Possible describes something that can exist, happen, or be done—not blocked by logic, nature, or circumstance. It sits between impossible and certain on the scale of likelihood. {Is it possible to finish by Friday?} The noun form names a person or thing that might succeed or be chosen: {She's a possible for the promotion}. When someone does {everything possible}, they exhaust all available options. The phrase {as soon as possible} is so common it's often abbreviated ASAP.

Possibly indicates that something may happen or be true, without certainty: {We'll possibly finish by Friday}. It often softens requests or suggestions: {Could you possibly help me with this?} The word ranges from genuine uncertainty to polite hedging to emphatic denial: {I couldn't possibly accept}.

A possum is any of several marsupials, most commonly the Virginia opossum of North America—a cat-sized creature known for "playing possum," feigning death when threatened. The spelling possum reflects casual pronunciation of opossum, though in Australia and nearby regions, possum refers to distinct species. {A possum got into the garbage again.}

Possums are marsupials found in Australia, New Zealand, and nearby regions—furry, tree-dwelling animals with prehensile tails. In American usage, possum typically refers to the opossum, a different marsupial native to the Americas. To {play possum} is to feign death or unconsciousness, as opossums do when threatened.

Three different nouns share the spelling post, and all have spun off different parts of speech. Meanings in one group arise from the post that is like a pole or stake: fence post, goalpost. The verb from this post means to display in a public place: He posted it on the Web. The second group of meanings related to the postal service: Did you send the letter by post? What time did you post it? In the third group, post refers to a place where someone is assigned: He has a new post in the State Department. They posted her to a small regional office.

Postage is the cost of sending something through the mail, or the stamps representing that cost. {The postage for international packages has gone up.} {Did you remember to put postage on the envelope?} Postage paid means the sender has already covered the mailing cost.

Postal relates to the mail system—postal {workers}, postal {codes}, the Postal Service. In slang, {go postal} means to suddenly become violently unhinged, especially in a workplace setting. The expression emerged in the 1990s after a series of shootings by U.S. Postal Service employees.

A postapocalypse is the period or setting after a catastrophic event has destroyed civilization—nuclear war, pandemic, environmental collapse. The term appears most often in fiction describing worlds where survivors navigate ruins and rebuild: {a postapocalypse where water is the only currency}. As an adjective, postapocalyptic is more common: {postapocalyptic fiction}, {a postapocalyptic wasteland}.

Postapocalyptic describes settings, stories, or scenarios taking place after a catastrophic event has destroyed civilization: {a postapocalyptic wasteland}, {postapocalyptic fiction}. The apocalypse in question is usually nuclear war, pandemic, environmental collapse, or similar global disaster. The genre explores survival, rebuilding, and human nature under extreme conditions. Also spelled post-apocalyptic.

A postbox is a public receptacle for depositing outgoing mail, typically a freestanding metal box or a slot in a wall. In British usage, postbox also refers to a private mailbox where incoming mail is delivered. The iconic red pillar boxes in Britain are postboxes. Also called letterbox or mailbox.

A postcard is a small card for sending a brief message through the mail without an envelope, typically with a picture on one side and space for writing and an address on the other. Postcards are associated with travel—tourists send them from vacation spots: {Wish you were here!} A postcard-perfect scene is one worthy of being photographed for such a card.

Postcards are small cards for mailing without an envelope, typically featuring an image on one side and space for a brief message, address, and stamp on the other. Tourists send postcards from vacation destinations: {Wish you were here!} The format implies brevity and informality—a postcard message is short by design. Figuratively, something {postcard-perfect} is scenic enough to appear on one.

A postcode is a sequence of letters and numbers added to an address to help sort mail—the British equivalent of an American ZIP code. British postcodes like SW1A 1AA encode geographic information more precisely than ZIP codes, identifying areas as small as a few dozen addresses. {What's your postcode?}

Postcodes are alphanumeric codes used in mailing addresses to identify delivery areas. The term is primarily British; Americans say zip codes. A postcode typically appears at the end of an address: {London SW1A 1AA}. The singular postcode refers to the code itself or the area it covers: {What's your postcode?} {Property values vary by postcode}.

A postdoc is a researcher who has completed a doctorate and holds a temporary position for further training, typically at a university or research institution.
