The position—formally a postdoctoral fellowship or appointment—bridges the gap between earning a PhD and securing a permanent academic job: {She's doing a postdoc at Stanford}. Also used as an adjective: {postdoc research}, {postdoc years}.

Posted means displayed publicly or sent to a destination. You post a notice on a bulletin board, post a letter in the mail, or post content online. In accounting, to post is to record a transaction: {The payment was posted to your account}. To keep someone posted is to provide ongoing updates. Posted also describes someone stationed somewhere: {guards posted at every entrance}.

A poster is a large printed sheet meant to be displayed on a wall or other vertical surface. Posters announce events, advertise products, or serve as decoration: {a movie poster}, {a concert poster}, {She hung posters of her favorite band}. In online forums, a poster is someone who posts messages: {a frequent poster on Reddit}.

A poster child is someone who perfectly represents or embodies a cause, condition, or quality—originally referring to children featured in charitable campaigns to generate sympathy and donations. The term now applies broadly and often ironically to anyone who exemplifies something, whether positive or negative: {He's the poster child for why you shouldn't skip leg day}. The spelling varies between one word, two words, and hyphenated.

Posterior means situated at or toward the back, the opposite of anterior. In anatomy, the posterior side of the body faces backward: {posterior muscles}, {the posterior lobe of the brain}. As a noun, posterior is a slightly formal or humorous term for the buttocks: {He landed on his posterior}. In time, posterior means coming after: {a date posterior to the founding}.

Posterity means future generations—all the people who will exist after the present time. The word often appears in contexts of legacy and preservation: {We must protect the environment for posterity}, {The letters were saved for posterity}. It can also mean a person's descendants specifically: {He had no posterity to inherit the estate}.

Posterize has two distinct meanings. In image editing, to posterize is to reduce the number of colors or tones, creating flat areas of solid color that resemble a silk-screened poster: {The filter posterizes the photo for a pop-art effect}. In basketball slang, to posterize someone is to dunk on them so dramatically they could appear on a poster as the humiliated defender: {He posterized the center with a two-handed slam}.

Posterized describes a basketball player who has been dunked on so emphatically that the moment could be frozen as a poster—the dunker soaring triumphantly, the defender caught helplessly in the frame: {He got posterized by LeBron}. The term has spread beyond basketball to describe any humiliating defeat captured visually. In image editing, posterized refers to reducing color gradations to create a flat, poster-like effect.

Posterizing is a basketball term for dunking on an opponent so emphatically that the image could become a poster—the defender frozen helplessly as the ball slams through: {He posterized the center with a two-handed jam}. The term has spread to any dramatic domination captured in a memorable image. In digital imaging, posterizing reduces the number of colors in an image, creating flat bands of color that resemble a printed poster.

Posters are large printed sheets designed for public display, typically featuring images and text to advertise events, promote causes, or decorate walls. A movie poster promotes a film; a wanted poster seeks a fugitive. The term extends to anyone who posts—someone who contributes messages to online forums or social media: {The poster asked for advice on home repairs}. To be the {poster child} for something is to typify or represent it prominently.

Postgame refers to the period immediately following a sporting event, or activities occurring during that time: {postgame analysis}, {postgame interviews}, {the postgame show}. The term extends to any activity that follows a main event: {postgame drinks after the concert}. In video gaming, postgame content is what becomes available after completing the main storyline.

Postgraduate describes education pursued after completing a bachelor's degree: {postgraduate studies}, {a postgraduate degree in economics}. As a noun, a postgraduate is a student engaged in such work. The term is more common in British English; Americans typically say graduate student or grad student. Postgraduate work includes master's and doctoral programs.

Posthumous describes something occurring or appearing after death. A posthumous {award} honors someone who has died. A posthumous {novel} is published after the author's death. A posthumous {child} is born after the father has died. The word carries a sense of recognition or continuation beyond the grave: {He received a posthumous pardon fifty years after his execution}.

A postie is a mail carrier—the person who delivers letters and packages to homes and businesses. The term is informal and primarily British, Australian, and New Zealand usage: {The postie comes around eleven}. Americans would say mailman or mail carrier.

Posting is placing something where others will see it—a notice on a bulletin board, content on social media, a message to an online forum. A posting is also a job assignment, especially to a distant location: {She received a posting to the embassy in Berlin}. In accounting, posting means recording transactions to a ledger.

A postman is a person who delivers mail to homes and businesses. The term is more common in British English; Americans typically say mail carrier or mailman. {The postman comes around ten o'clock.} The female equivalent, postwoman, exists but is rarely used.

A postmark is the official stamp applied by a postal service to a piece of mail, showing the date and location of mailing and canceling the stamp to prevent reuse. The postmark establishes when and where something was sent: {The letter bore a postmark from Chicago dated June 3rd}. As a verb, to postmark is to apply such a stamp: {The package was postmarked yesterday}.

Postmarked describes mail that has been stamped by the postal service with an official mark showing the date and place of mailing: {The letter was postmarked Chicago, December 3rd}. The postmark proves when something was sent, which matters for deadlines: {Applications must be postmarked by Friday}.

Postmarks are the marks stamped on mail by postal services, typically showing the date and place of mailing and canceling the stamp to prevent reuse. A postmark serves as proof of when and where something was sent: {The letter bore a Paris postmark dated June 1942}. As a verb, to postmark is to apply such a stamp.

A postmaster is the official in charge of a post office. The term applies to anyone running a local branch up to the head of a national postal service: {She served as postmaster for thirty years}. In computing, postmaster is the standard email address for system administrators handling mail server issues: {Send delivery problems to postmaster@example.com}.

Postmodern describes art, architecture, literature, and thought that reacts against modernism's faith in progress, universal truths, and clean aesthetics. Where modernism sought clarity and grand narratives, postmodernism embraces fragmentation, irony, pastiche, and skepticism toward any single authoritative viewpoint. In architecture, this might mean playfully mixing historical styles; in philosophy, questioning whether objective reality is knowable. {The building's postmodern design clashed columns with neon}. The term often carries either celebratory or dismissive overtones depending on the speaker.

Postmodernism is a broad intellectual and artistic movement that emerged in the mid-twentieth century as a reaction against modernist certainties. It questions grand narratives, objective truth, and fixed meanings, emphasizing instead fragmentation, irony, and the blurring of boundaries between high and low culture. In architecture, postmodernism rejected austere functionalism for playful, eclectic designs. In philosophy and literary theory, it challenged the idea that texts have stable meanings. The term often carries a dismissive edge when critics use it to describe work they find pretentiously obscure or relativistic: {It's just postmodernism—style over substance}. (Capitalized Postmodernism sometimes appears as a proper noun when referring to the movement as a distinct historical period.)

Postmortem means after death. A postmortem examination (or simply a postmortem) is an autopsy—a medical inspection of a corpse to determine cause of death. The word extends to any analysis conducted after something ends: {We held a postmortem on the failed campaign}. In computing and business, postmortems review what went wrong with a project or system failure.

Postmortems are examinations conducted after death to determine cause—autopsies. The term extends to any analysis of something that has ended: {The team held a postmortem on why the project failed}. In business and tech, postmortems review completed projects to identify what went wrong and what worked. The singular is postmortem.

A postnup is a legal agreement between spouses made after marriage, governing how assets and debts would be divided in case of divorce. It's the married counterpart to a prenup (prenuptial agreement): {They signed a postnup after his business took off}. Short for postnuptial agreement.

Postpartum refers to the period following childbirth, typically concerning the mother: {postpartum depression}, {postpartum recovery}, {postpartum care}. The term appears most often in medical contexts, describing physical and psychological changes in the weeks after giving birth. {She struggled with postpartum anxiety for months.}

To postpone is to move something to a later time: {The game was postponed due to rain}, {Let's postpone the meeting until next week}. The word implies intention—events are postponed deliberately, not by accident. Postpone suggests rescheduling rather than canceling entirely; the thing still happens, just not when originally planned.

Postponed means delayed until a later time. Events, decisions, and deadlines get postponed: {The meeting was postponed until next week}, {They postponed the wedding due to illness}. The word implies intention—something actively rescheduled rather than simply late. Indefinitely postponed often signals quiet cancellation.

Postproduction is the phase of filmmaking, video production, or audio recording that happens after principal filming or recording ends. This includes editing, adding visual effects, mixing sound, color correction, and other refinements: {The film wrapped shooting in March but spent six months in postproduction}. As a modifier: {postproduction costs}, {postproduction facilities}.

Postpunk is rock music that emerged in the late 1970s following punk's initial explosion, retaining punk's experimental attitude while expanding its sonic palette. Where punk was raw and stripped-down, postpunk bands incorporated synthesizers, angular guitars, and darker atmospheres: {Joy Division and Siouxsie and the Banshees defined the postpunk sound}. The term also describes the broader aesthetic—art, fashion, literature—associated with this era. Also spelled post-punk.

Postracial describes a society or era supposedly beyond racial divisions—where race no longer determines opportunity or shapes social dynamics. The term gained currency after Barack Obama's 2008 election, when some declared America had entered a postracial phase. Critics argue the concept is premature or naive, masking persistent inequalities: {The idea of a postracial America collapsed under the weight of evidence}. Often used skeptically or in scare quotes.

Posts are upright supports—wooden posts hold up fences, metal posts anchor signs. A post is also a position or station: a military post, a trading post, or someone's post within an organization. To post is to station someone: {Guards were posted at the entrance}. In the digital sense, a post is a message published online—to social media, a forum, or a blog—and to post is to publish one: {She posts daily updates}. To post something physically is to display it publicly or send it by mail (chiefly British): {post a notice}, {post a letter}.

A postscript is an addition to a letter or document, written after the main body has been completed and signed. Abbreviated P.S., it typically adds an afterthought: {P.S. I forgot to mention I'll be late Thursday}. By extension, a postscript is any supplementary comment or concluding remark: {The epilogue served as a postscript to the trilogy}.

Postscripts are additions written after the main body of a letter or document, typically following the signature. The abbreviation P.S. introduces them: {P.S. I forgot to mention the party is Saturday}. Figuratively, a postscript is any afterthought or supplementary remark: {The final chapter serves as a postscript to the author's career}.

Postseason refers to the period of competitive play that follows the regular season in sports leagues. Teams that qualify based on their regular-season performance compete in playoff rounds leading to a championship: {The team's postseason hopes ended with last night's loss}. As an adjective, it modifies related terms: {postseason roster}, {postseason stats}.

Posttruth describes a cultural condition where appeals to emotion and personal belief matter more than objective facts in shaping public opinion. The term gained currency after 2016 to characterize political discourse where verifiable claims carry less weight than tribal allegiances: {We're living in a posttruth era}. Often hyphenated: post-truth.

Posture is how the body is positioned or held. Good posture keeps the spine aligned; poor posture causes slouching. Beyond the physical, posture describes an attitude or stance toward something: {The company adopted a defensive posture toward regulators}. To posture is to assume an attitude for effect, often insincerely: {Politicians posturing for the cameras}.

Postures is the plural of posture—positions of the body, or attitudes and stances taken toward something. Physical postures range from upright to slouched: {The yoga instructor corrected their postures}. Figurative postures are adopted positions, often performative: {Their aggressive postures were meant to intimidate}. The verb means to assume an affected stance: {He postures as a reformer while protecting the status quo}.

Posturing is adopting attitudes or positions for effect rather than from genuine conviction. The word suggests performance over substance—striking poses meant to impress or intimidate: {His tough talk was just posturing}. Politicians engage in posturing when they take symbolic stands without intending action. The term is almost always dismissive, implying the behavior is hollow or theatrical.

Postwar means occurring or existing after a war, especially after World War II: {postwar reconstruction}, {the postwar economic boom}. The term typically refers to the period immediately following a conflict, when societies rebuild and adjust: {postwar Germany}, {postwar baby boom}. Without further specification, postwar usually evokes the late 1940s and 1950s.

A posy is a small bunch of flowers, typically arranged to be held in one hand or worn: {She carried a posy of violets}. The word is somewhat old-fashioned and suggests something dainty or sentimental. Posy once also meant a short verse or motto, especially one inscribed inside a ring—a sense now largely forgotten.

The frequent noun pot refers to any of various containers: for cooking, for holding plants, for making coffee. Cooking metaphors are at work in expression like melting pot, stir the pot, and sweeten the pot. Less frequent but still prominent is as slang for marijuana (legalize pot, pot smoker). The verb pot usually means put in a pot and is used most often of plants: I need to pot my geraniums.

Potassium is a chemical element, a soft silvery-white metal essential to biological function. It regulates fluid balance, nerve signals, and muscle contractions. Dietary potassium comes from bananas, potatoes, leafy greens, and other foods. {Your potassium levels are low.} The element's symbol is K, from the Latin kalium.

A potato is a starchy tuber grown underground, one of the world's most important food crops. Potatoes are boiled, baked, fried, or mashed. The word extends to the plant itself and to other tuber-producing plants: {sweet potato}. A {couch potato} is someone who sits around watching television. A {hot potato} is a controversial issue people avoid handling. {Small potatoes} means something trivial or insignificant.

Potatoes is the plural of potato, the starchy tuber that serves as a dietary staple worldwide. The word appears in countless compound forms: {mashed potatoes}, {baked potatoes}, {potato salad}. {Small potatoes} means something trivial or insignificant. {Couch potato} describes someone who spends excessive time watching television.

Potbellied describes someone or something with a rounded, protruding belly: {a potbellied old man in suspenders}, {a potbellied stove}. The word suggests a paunch that swells outward like a pot. Potbellied pigs are a small domestic breed kept as pets, distinguished by their round midsections.

Potbellies is the plural of potbelly—a rounded, protruding stomach that suggests the shape of a pot. The word usually describes men who have gained weight in the midsection: {Middle age brought potbellies and receding hairlines}. Potbellied pigs are a small breed kept as pets. A potbelly stove is a rounded cast-iron stove.

A potbelly is a round, protruding stomach—the kind that hangs over a belt: {He developed a potbelly in middle age}. The word also names a type of small, bulbous cast-iron stove used for heating: {The cabin had an old potbelly in the corner}. Both uses reference the same rounded shape.

A potboiler is a book, film, or other creative work produced quickly and formulaically to make money rather than for artistic merit—something churned out to keep the pot boiling, to pay the bills. The term carries mild disdain: {He dismissed the novel as a potboiler}. Many respected authors have written potboilers between more ambitious projects.

Potboilers are works of art—typically novels, films, or paintings—produced quickly and primarily to earn money rather than for artistic merit. The term suggests something thrown together to keep the pot boiling, to pay the bills: {He wrote potboilers between his serious novels}. The word carries mild contempt, implying formulaic or hackneyed work, though some potboilers prove more enduring than their creators intended.

Potency is strength or power, especially the capacity to produce effects. A drug's potency determines its dosage requirements. {The potency of his argument convinced the jury}. In men, potency refers specifically to the ability to achieve erection and sexual intercourse—the opposite of impotence. Potent is the adjective form.

Potent means having great power, strength, or effect. A potent drug produces strong results; a potent argument persuades forcefully; a potent leader commands influence. The word often implies concentrated effectiveness: {a potent dose}, {a potent symbol}. In older usage, potent specifically meant sexually capable in men—the opposite of impotent.

Potential refers to something possible that could happen or become real now or in the future: She has the potential to become a great conductor. These chemicals have the potential to cause widespread environmental damage. When followed by a noun, potential means not actual but possible: About 200 potential jurors are called to serve every day. He excused himself because of a potential conflict of interest.

A pothead is a person who smokes marijuana regularly, especially to excess. The term is mildly dismissive but not strongly pejorative—potheads themselves may use it self-deprecatingly: {I was such a pothead in college}. The image is of someone whose life revolves around getting high.

Potheads are people who smoke marijuana habitually. The term suggests someone whose identity or lifestyle centers on getting high, often with connotations of laziness or lack of ambition: {a bunch of potheads playing video games all day}. The word is mildly derogatory but sometimes used self-descriptively by marijuana enthusiasts.

A potholder is a thick pad used to protect hands when handling hot cookware—grabbing pot handles, lifting lids, removing pans from the oven. Typically made of quilted fabric or silicone, potholders hang near the stove for quick access: {Hand me that potholder before I burn myself}.

A pothole is a hole in a road surface, formed when pavement breaks down from water damage, traffic, and freeze-thaw cycles. Potholes range from minor nuisances to tire-damaging hazards: {I hit a pothole and bent my rim}. In geology, a pothole is a cylindrical hole worn into rock by swirling water and sediment.

Potholes are holes or pits in a road surface, formed when pavement breaks down from water damage, traffic stress, and freeze-thaw cycles. They range from minor nuisances to tire-destroying craters: {I hit a pothole and bent my rim}. Cities with harsh winters are notorious for them. Figuratively, potholes are obstacles or setbacks: {a few potholes on the road to success}.

Potholing is the British term for exploring natural underground caves as a recreational activity, called spelunking in American English. The word comes from pothole in its older sense of a deep vertical shaft in limestone terrain. Potholers navigate tight passages, underground rivers, and vertical drops: {We went potholing in the Yorkshire Dales}.

A potion is a liquid mixture intended to have some special effect when drunk—magical, medicinal, or poisonous. The word carries strong associations with fantasy and folklore: {love potions}, {sleeping potions}, {the witch's potion}. In modern use, potion often appears playfully for any concoction: {What's in this potion you're drinking?}

Potions are liquids with magical, medicinal, or mysterious properties—brewed concoctions meant to produce specific effects when drunk. The word belongs primarily to fantasy and folklore: {love potions}, {healing potions}, {a witch stirring her potion}. In video games, potions restore health or grant abilities. Outside fantasy contexts, potion sounds deliberately archaic or whimsical: {What's in this potion you're brewing?}

Potluck is a meal where each guest brings a dish to share. The word combines pot (a cooking vessel) with luck (whatever happens to be available). A potluck dinner might feature casseroles, salads, and desserts from different contributors: {We're having a potluck for the office party—I'm bringing my grandmother's mac and cheese}. Extended to mean whatever is available by chance: {take potluck}.

Potlucks are communal meals where each guest brings a dish to share. The format distributes cooking duties and creates variety—you might end up with five casseroles or a perfect spread. {We're having a potluck for the office holiday party.} The singular potluck can also mean whatever happens to be available: {We took potluck at a roadside diner.}

A potpie is a savory pie with a filling of meat and vegetables in a thick gravy, typically topped with a pastry crust. Chicken potpie is the most familiar variety in American cooking, though beef and turkey versions are common. The dish can be baked in a single large pan or in individual portions. Some regional styles, particularly in Pennsylvania Dutch cooking, feature a stew-like version with squares of dough rather than a crust.

Potpourri is a mixture of dried flower petals, herbs, and spices kept in a bowl to scent a room. By extension, potpourri describes any miscellaneous collection or medley: {The album is a potpourri of musical styles}. The word comes from French, literally "rotten pot"—originally a stew of various meats.

Pots is the plural of pot—containers typically round and deep, used for cooking, storing, or growing plants. A pot of coffee, a flower pot, a pot of gold. In poker, the pot is the accumulated stakes. To go to pot is to deteriorate. Pots can also be marijuana: {He smokes a lot of pots} sounds odd because pot as cannabis is usually uncountable.

A potshard is a fragment of broken pottery, especially one found at an archaeological site. The pieces help date excavations and reveal information about ancient cultures. Also spelled potsherd, preserving the old English word for a broken piece of earthenware.

Potshards are fragments of broken pottery, especially those found at archaeological sites. The word is an alternate spelling of potsherds, with shard being the more common modern form of sherd. Archaeologists study potshards to date sites and understand ancient cultures: {The dig uncovered potshards from the Bronze Age}.

A potshot is an easy or opportunistic shot, originally one taken at game merely to fill the cooking pot rather than for sport. The word now usually means a quick, casual criticism or attack made without much thought or risk: {The senator took potshots at his opponent's record}. Taking potshots suggests hitting an easy target rather than engaging seriously.

Potshots are shots taken casually or opportunistically, without careful aim—originally at game killed merely for the cooking pot rather than for sport. The word now primarily describes cheap criticisms or attacks, especially from a safe distance: {Politicians took potshots at the proposal without offering alternatives}. To {take potshots} is to snipe or criticize without real engagement.

A potsticker is a Chinese dumpling with a thin wheat wrapper enclosing a filling of ground meat and vegetables, pan-fried until the bottom crisps while the top steams. The name describes the cooking method—the dumplings stick slightly to the pot before being loosened. Also called gyoza (Japanese) or jiaozi (Chinese).

Potstickers are Chinese dumplings with a distinctive cooking method: they're pan-fried until the bottom crisps, then steamed in the same pan, creating a texture that's both crispy and tender. The name comes from how the dumplings stick slightly to the pot during cooking. Typically filled with ground pork and vegetables, they're served with a dipping sauce of soy, vinegar, and chili oil. {We ordered potstickers as an appetizer.}

Potted describes something placed or grown in a pot, most commonly plants: {a row of potted herbs on the windowsill}. In British English, potted also refers to food preserved in a sealed pot or jar, like potted shrimp. A potted version of something is a condensed or summarized form: {a potted history of the Roman Empire}. In informal British and Australian usage, potted can mean drunk, though this sense is dated.

To potter is to occupy oneself in a leisurely, unhurried way with minor tasks—puttering around the garden, pottering about the house. The word is more common in British English; Americans typically say putter. A potter is also a person who makes pottery—ceramic vessels shaped by hand on a wheel or by other methods. {She trained as a potter in Japan.} The potter's wheel is the rotating disk on which clay is shaped. (Capitalized Potter typically refers to Harry Potter or the surname.)

Pottering is moving about in an unhurried, aimless way, occupying oneself with small tasks: {She spent the morning pottering around the garden}. The word suggests pleasant idleness rather than productive work—puttering with tools in the garage, tidying shelves without urgency. Chiefly British; Americans prefer puttering.

Potters is the plural of potter—a person who makes ceramic objects by shaping clay, typically on a rotating wheel. The term appears in phrases like {a guild of potters} or {potters at the craft fair}. As a verb form, potters means to occupy oneself in a leisurely, aimless way: {She potters around the garden on weekends}. This sense is more common in British English; Americans tend to say putter.

Pottery is objects made from clay that has been shaped and hardened by heat—pots, bowls, vases, and similar vessels. The term covers both the finished products and the craft of making them: {She took up pottery as a hobby}. A pottery is a workshop or factory where such items are produced.

Potting is the act of placing plants in pots with soil: {She spent the afternoon potting herbs for the windowsill}. It also refers to preserving food in sealed containers, as with potted meat. In billiards and snooker, potting means sinking a ball into a pocket. A potting shed is a garden outbuilding for transplanting seedlings and storing supplies.

Potty is a child-sized toilet or portable seat for toilet training toddlers: {Time to sit on the potty}. The word itself is childish, used when speaking to or about young children. To {go potty} is to urinate or defecate. Separately, potty means slightly crazy in British informal usage: {She's gone a bit potty}.

A pottymouth is someone who uses profanity frequently or habitually, especially a child: {Watch your language, pottymouth}. The term is itself childish, more playground taunt than serious criticism. As an adjective, pottymouthed describes such a person: {her pottymouthed little brother}. Also spelled potty mouth or potty-mouth.

A pouch is a small bag or flexible container, often one that closes or fastens: a tobacco pouch, a mail pouch, a pouch for carrying documents. Animals like kangaroos and pelicans have natural pouches—folds of skin that hold young or catch food. Any pocket-like receptacle or bulge qualifies: {She had pouches under her eyes from lack of sleep}. To pouch is to form into or place in a pouch.

A pouf is a large, firm cushion used as a seat or footrest, typically round or cylindrical and often made of leather or fabric. In British English, pouf (also poof or poofter) is offensive slang for a gay man or an effeminate man. The spelling pouffe emphasizes the furniture sense.

A poultice is a soft, moist mass of material—typically herbs, clay, or meal—applied to the body to relieve soreness, inflammation, or infection. The mixture is usually heated and spread on cloth before being pressed against the skin: {She applied a mustard poultice to his chest for the congestion}. The verb means to apply such a treatment.

Poultry is domestic fowl raised for meat or eggs—chickens, turkeys, ducks, geese. The word covers both the living birds and their flesh as food: {a poultry farm}, {the poultry section of the grocery store}. Unlike beef or pork, the same word serves for animal and meat.

Pounce is to spring or swoop suddenly to seize something, as a cat pounces on a mouse or a hawk on prey. The word extends to any swift, aggressive action: {She pounced on the opportunity}, {Critics pounced on his mistake}. A pounce is an instance of pouncing: {The cat made its pounce}.

Pounced is the past tense of pounce—to spring or swoop suddenly to seize something, as a cat does on prey: {The hawk pounced on the mouse}. Figuratively, to pounce is to act quickly on an opportunity or to attack someone's words: {Critics pounced on the mayor's gaffe}. {She pounced the moment tickets went on sale}.

Pounces is the plural of pounce and the third-person singular verb form. To pounce is to spring suddenly, as a cat on prey: {The kitten pounces on anything that moves}. Figuratively, to pounce is to seize an opportunity or attack a weakness: {Critics pounced on the contradiction in her statement}.

Pouncing is the act of springing or swooping suddenly to seize something. A cat pounces on a mouse; a hawk pounces on prey. Figuratively, to pounce is to seize any opportunity quickly: {She pounced on the job offer}, {Critics pounced on his mistake}. The word suggests predatory quickness—waiting, then striking.

Pound is most frequently a noun denoting a measure of weight in the imperial system equal to just under half a kilo. Another noun meaning is for a unit of currency in the United Kingdom (pound sterling) and in some other countries, notably Egypt. A third meaning of pound is for a place of detention, especially of animals (dog pound). The verb pound is for repetitive, forceful striking. Your heart pounds when you are excited or exerting yourself. You can pound nails with a hammer.

Poundcake is a dense, rich cake traditionally made with a pound each of butter, sugar, eggs, and flour—hence the name. The proportions yield a tight crumb and buttery flavor without requiring leavening agents. Modern recipes often scale down the quantities while keeping the ratios: {She baked a lemon poundcake for the office party}.

Pounded is the past tense of pound, meaning to strike repeatedly with force: {He pounded the nail into the wall}, {Waves pounded the shore}. It extends to heavy, rhythmic movement: {She pounded up the stairs}. In cooking, pounded describes meat beaten thin: {pounded chicken breast}. Informally, to get pounded is to be defeated badly or to drink heavily: {We got pounded in the second half}, {They got pounded at the bar last night}.

A pounder is something weighing or delivering a specified number of pounds—almost always preceded by a number: a {quarter-pounder} is a burger patty weighing four ounces before cooking, a {twelve-pounder} was a cannon firing twelve-pound balls. The pattern extends freely: a fish, a baby, a hailstone. Without a number, pounder usually means something that pounds or strikes repeatedly.

Pounding is heavy, repeated striking—the physical act or its sound. Your heart pounds when racing from fear or exertion. A pounding headache throbs painfully. To give someone a pounding is to beat them badly, whether in a fight or a competition: {Our team took a pounding in the semifinals}. Pounding surf crashes against the shore.

Pounds is the plural of pound, a unit of weight equal to sixteen ounces, or the basic monetary unit of the United Kingdom. Someone pounds on a door by striking it repeatedly and heavily: {He pounded on the table}. Your heart pounds when it beats hard and fast. To pound something out is to produce it with effort: {She pounded out three chapters that night}.

Pour is to cause liquid to flow from a container in a continuous stream: {She poured coffee into mugs}, {Pour the batter into the pan}. Rain pours when it falls heavily. People pour into a space when they arrive in large numbers. To {pour out} feelings is to express them freely and at length. {It never rains but it pours} means troubles come all at once.

Poured is the past tense of pour—to cause liquid to flow from a container: {She poured coffee into mugs}. Rain pours when it falls heavily. People pour into a space when they arrive in large numbers: {Fans poured through the gates}. To pour out feelings is to express them freely: {He poured out his heart to her}.

Pouring describes liquid flowing steadily from a container, or the act of causing it to do so. Rain that comes down heavily is pouring, and we say {it's pouring} when caught in such weather. When people arrive somewhere in large numbers, they pour in: {Fans were pouring into the stadium}. If you pour yourself into something, you give it intense effort and concentration. To pour out emotions or words is to express them freely and abundantly.

A pourover is coffee brewed by slowly pouring hot water over grounds in a filter, allowing it to drip into a cup or carafe below. The method gives precise control over brewing variables like water temperature and pour rate: {I'll make a pourover while you wait}. Also written pour-over or pour over.

Pours is the third-person singular of pour—to cause liquid to flow in a continuous stream: {She pours the coffee}, {Rain pours down}. Figuratively, things pour when they come in overwhelming quantities: {Money pours into the campaign}, {Complaints poured in}. To pour oneself into something is to invest great effort: {He pours himself into his work}.

A pout is a facial expression of displeasure or sulkiness, with lips pushed forward: {She gave a little pout when he said no}. To pout is to make this expression or to sulk generally: {He's been pouting all day about losing}. Full lips may be described as pouty, sometimes admiringly: {pouty lips}. A pout is also a type of fish with a large head.

Pouted is the past tense of pout—to push out the lips in displeasure, sulkiness, or disappointment. Children pout when they don't get their way; adults pout when feeling slighted: {She pouted when he forgot their anniversary}. Pouted lips can also be deliberately sensual, as in fashion photography or flirtation.

Poutine is a Québécois dish of french fries topped with cheese curds and brown gravy. The heat from the gravy softens the curds without fully melting them. Once regional fast food, poutine has spread across Canada and beyond, with restaurants offering variations that add pulled pork, smoked meat, or other toppings: {We grabbed poutine after the hockey game}.

Pouting is sulking or showing displeasure by pushing out the lips and wearing a discontented expression. Children pout when denied something; adults pout when feeling slighted or ignored: {She spent the evening pouting because he forgot their anniversary}. The gesture can also be deliberately playful or seductive: {pouting for the camera}.

Pouts are expressions of displeasure made by pushing the lips forward, typically signaling sulkiness or mild petulance: {She gave him one of her famous pouts}. The word also refers to the lips themselves when positioned this way, sometimes deliberately for photographs or flirtation: {pursing her lips into a pout for the camera}. As a verb, to pout is to make this expression or sulk silently.

Pouty describes lips that are full and protruding, or a facial expression suggesting displeasure or sulkiness—the look of someone pushing their lower lip out in a pout. The word often carries a slightly childish or petulant connotation: {She gave him a pouty look when he said no}. In fashion and photography, pouty lips are desirable, suggesting sensuality rather than sulking.

Pov is internet slang for point of view, used especially as a label on social media videos that invite viewers to imagine themselves in a scenario: {pov: you're the only one who showed up to the party}. The format became ubiquitous on TikTok, where creators use it to frame skits, jokes, and relatable moments. (All-caps POV is the standard abbreviation.)

Poverty is the state of having little or no money, goods, or means of support. It ranges from relative deprivation to absolute destitution: {Millions live in poverty}. Extended uses describe any severe lack: {a poverty of imagination}, {intellectual poverty}. The {poverty line} is the minimum income threshold below which a person or family is officially considered poor.

Pow is an exclamation representing a sudden impact, explosion, or punch: {Pow! Right in the kisser}. It appears in comic books and action contexts to convey the sound of a blow landing. Figuratively, pow suggests sudden forceful effect: {The spices hit you—pow—right away}. (Capitalized POW is a prisoner of war.)

Powder is any substance reduced to fine, dry particles. Talcum powder goes on skin, baking powder leavens bread, gunpowder propels bullets. To powder is to apply powder or reduce to powder: {She powdered her nose}. To {take a powder} is to leave hastily, often to avoid trouble. {Powder your nose} is a euphemism for using the restroom. Powder also refers to fresh, dry snow prized by skiers: {The mountain got six inches of powder overnight}.

A powderkeg is literally a barrel for storing gunpowder—highly explosive if ignited. The figurative sense dominates modern usage: a volatile situation that could erupt into violence or chaos at any moment. {The region has been a powderkeg since the disputed election.} {Ethnic tensions turned the province into a powderkeg.} Also spelled powder keg.

A powderpuff is a soft pad used to apply cosmetic powder to the face or body. The fluffy, delicate object lends itself to figurative use: powderpuff describes anything perceived as soft, weak, or unserious. A powderpuff {question} is easy and unchallenging. Powderpuff {football} is a non-contact game, traditionally played by women.

Powders is the plural of powder—fine dry particles of a substance. The term often appears in contexts involving multiple types: {baking powders}, {protein powders}, {medicinal powders}. As a verb form, powders means to apply powder: {She powders her nose}. The phrase {take a powder} is dated slang meaning to leave quickly or disappear.

Power is mainly a noun used to describe the ability to do something or create an effect: The committee does not have the power to implement these recommendations. There are many specific meanings of power that depend on context, such as electrical power, power of attorney, or an influential country or nation (All the great powers attended the conference). When power is used as a verb, it usually means supply energy to: What powers the aircraft? Before a noun, power typically denotes the availability of mechanical or electrical power, as in power brakes or power steering.

A powerball is a weighted ball used for grip strength and wrist exercises, typically containing a gyroscope that spins when activated by wrist movement. The faster you rotate your wrist, the more resistance builds: {My forearm is burning from the powerball workout}. (Capitalized Powerball is the lottery game.)

A powerboat is a boat propelled by an engine rather than sails, oars, or paddles. The term covers everything from small motorboats to large cabin cruisers: {They spent the weekend on a powerboat in the lake}. Powerboating as a sport involves racing these vessels at high speeds.

A powerbroker is someone who wields influence behind the scenes, arranging deals and shaping outcomes without holding formal authority. The term usually applies to politics or business, where powerbrokers trade favors, control access, or command networks that let them determine who succeeds: {The union powerbroker decided which candidates got endorsed}. Also spelled power broker.

Powerbrokers are people who wield influence behind the scenes, brokering deals and shaping outcomes without holding formal authority. The term typically describes political operatives, wealthy donors, or well-connected figures who determine who gets what: {The real powerbrokers met privately before the vote}. The word implies that visible leaders aren't always the ones making decisions.

Powered describes something supplied with energy or force to operate. A powered {device} runs on electricity, fuel, or another energy source. The word often appears in compounds indicating the power source: battery-powered, solar-powered, nuclear-powered. {The boat is powered by a small outboard motor.} Figuratively, something can be powered by determination or ambition. High-powered suggests exceptional strength or capability: a high-powered {attorney}, a high-powered {rifle}.

Powerful describes something with great strength, force, or influence. A powerful {engine} generates significant output. A powerful {leader} commands authority. A powerful {argument} persuades effectively. The word scales from physical might {(a powerful blow)} to emotional impact {(a powerful film)} to social dominance {(powerful interests)}. Powerfully is the adverb: {The ending affected me powerfully}.

A powerhouse is a source of great energy or strength. Originally a building where electrical power is generated, the word now most often describes a person, team, organization, or nation with exceptional capability or influence: {an economic powerhouse}, {She's a powerhouse in the courtroom}. A powerhouse performance overwhelms with its force and intensity.

Powerhouses are sources of great energy, influence, or productivity. The term originally meant a building housing machinery that generates electrical power. Now it usually describes people, organizations, or nations with exceptional capability or dominance in their field: {Germany is an economic powerhouse}, {She's a powerhouse in the courtroom}. A powerhouse performance is one of extraordinary force or impact.

Powerless means lacking power, strength, or authority to act or influence outcomes. Someone powerless to stop something cannot prevent it despite wanting to: {She felt powerless to help}. The word often describes a frustrating inability to affect circumstances: {Citizens were powerless against the regime}. It can also mean lacking official authority: {The committee was powerless to enforce its recommendations}.
Powerlessness is the condition or state of being without power. In the abstract, it is the opposite of power, which is the ability to act or influence.
clues: The state of being utterly ineffective

definition: Powerlift refers to the sport of powerlifting or the act of performing its three core lifts: the squat, bench press, and deadlift. As a verb, to powerlift is to train in or compete at this discipline: {She's been powerlifting for five years}. A powerlifter focuses on maximum single-repetition strength rather than the explosive technique of Olympic weightlifting.

A powerlifter is someone who competes in powerlifting—a strength sport focused on three lifts: the squat, bench press, and deadlift. Unlike Olympic weightlifters, powerlifters don't perform explosive overhead movements; they aim to lift maximum weight through controlled movements. {She started as a casual gym-goer but became a competitive powerlifter within two years.}

Powerlifters are athletes who compete in powerlifting, a strength sport centered on three lifts: the squat, bench press, and deadlift. Unlike Olympic weightlifters, who perform explosive overhead movements, powerlifters focus on maximal force through slower, controlled lifts. {The powerlifters at our gym train in a separate room with specialized equipment.}

Powerlifting is a strength sport consisting of three lifts: the squat, bench press, and deadlift. Competitors get three attempts at each lift, and their best successful attempts are combined for a total score. Unlike Olympic weightlifting, which emphasizes explosive overhead movements, powerlifting focuses on raw strength through slower, controlled lifts: {She set a state record in powerlifting}.

A powermonger is someone who aggressively pursues power, typically political power, often with the implication of hoarding it or seeking it for its own sake rather than for legitimate purposes. The -monger suffix suggests trafficking in power the way a warmonger traffics in war or a rumormonger spreads rumors: {The committee was stacked with powermongers more interested in influence than policy}.

Powermongers are people who aggressively pursue power, typically political power, for its own sake rather than to accomplish specific goals. The word carries strong disapproval—it suggests someone hungry for control and influence, willing to manipulate or scheme to get it: {The reformers accused the old guard of being powermongers clinging to their positions}.

A powernap is a brief sleep, typically 15–30 minutes, intended to restore energy without the grogginess of longer rest. The term emphasizes efficiency—maximum refreshment in minimum time: {I squeezed in a powernap between meetings}. Also spelled as two words: power nap.

A powerplant is a facility that generates electricity—coal, nuclear, hydroelectric, or solar powerplants convert various energy sources into electrical power for distribution. The term also refers to the engine or motor assembly that propels a vehicle: {The aircraft's powerplant consists of two turbofan engines}. Also spelled as two words: power plant.

A powerplay is a strategic maneuver using strength or advantage to pressure others. In hockey and other sports, it's the period when one team has more players on the field due to an opponent's penalty: {They scored twice on the powerplay}. In business or politics, a powerplay is an aggressive move to gain control or force an outcome: {The merger was a classic corporate powerplay}.

Powerplays are strategic maneuvers that leverage one's authority or advantage to achieve a goal, often at another's expense. In hockey, a powerplay is the advantage gained when the opposing team has a player in the penalty box: {They scored on the powerplay}. More broadly, any aggressive use of position or influence: {corporate powerplays}, {political powerplays}. The word suggests calculated moves rather than brute force.

Powers is the plural of power in its many senses—abilities, authorities, forces, or influential entities. Nations with global influence are {world powers}. Mathematical powers are numbers multiplied by themselves: {two to the third power}. Someone's powers of observation or persuasion are their capabilities in those areas. {The president's powers are limited by Congress.} (Capitalized Powers is a surname.)

Powersharing is an arrangement where political authority is divided among groups that might otherwise compete for exclusive control. The term appears most often in contexts of ethnic, religious, or partisan conflict, where rival factions agree to govern jointly rather than winner-take-all: {The peace agreement established a powersharing government between the two parties}. Also spelled power-sharing.

A powerslide is a controlled skid where a vehicle's rear wheels lose traction while the driver maintains steering control, used in racing and stunt driving: {He hit the gas and threw the car into a powerslide around the corner}. The term also applies to a similar maneuver in skateboarding, rollerblading, or ice skating where the skater turns sideways to brake while sliding forward. In video games, especially racing and kart games, the powerslide is often a core drifting mechanic that builds speed boosts.

A powertrip is an episode of exercising authority for its own sake, deriving satisfaction from control rather than accomplishing anything useful. Someone on a powertrip relishes making others comply: {The new manager is on a total powertrip with all these pointless rules}. Often written as two words: power trip.

A powerup is an item in video games that temporarily enhances a character's abilities—extra speed, invincibility, stronger attacks: {Grab the powerup before the boss fight}. The term extends to anything that boosts performance or energy: {Coffee is my morning powerup}. Also spelled power-up.

Powerups are items or bonuses in video games that temporarily enhance a player's abilities—extra speed, invincibility, stronger attacks, or additional lives. {Grab the powerup before it disappears.} The term extends beyond gaming to anything that boosts performance or energy: {Coffee is my morning powerup.} Also spelled power-ups.

Powerwalk is a form of exercise that involves walking at a brisk, sustained pace, typically faster than a casual stroll but without breaking into a jog. The arms usually swing vigorously to increase intensity and calorie burn. Powerwalking appeals to those who want cardiovascular benefits without the joint impact of running. {She powerwalks three miles every morning before work.} The term also appears as two words: power walk.

Powerwalking is walking at a brisk, sustained pace for exercise, faster than a casual stroll but without breaking into a jog. The arms typically swing vigorously to increase intensity and calorie burn. It emerged as a fitness trend in the 1980s and remains popular as low-impact cardiovascular exercise: {She goes powerwalking every morning before work}. Also spelled power walking or power-walking.

To powerwash is to clean a surface using a high-pressure water spray, typically from a specialized machine. The method strips away dirt, grime, mold, and loose paint from decks, driveways, siding, and vehicles: {We powerwashed the patio before the party}. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated. The noun is power washer or pressure washer.

Powwow originally refers to a Native American ceremonial gathering featuring dancing, singing, and spiritual rituals—events that remain culturally significant today. The word has been borrowed into general American English to mean any meeting or conference, often with a casual or planning-oriented tone: {Let's have a quick powwow about the schedule}. This informal use can strike some as disrespectful to Indigenous traditions.

Powwows are gatherings of Native American peoples for ceremonial dancing, singing, and cultural celebration. The word comes from an Algonquian term for a spiritual leader or healing ceremony. In informal use, powwow means any meeting or conference, especially one involving discussion or negotiation: {Let's have a quick powwow about the project}. This casual sense can strike some as trivializing.

Pox refers to diseases that produce skin eruptions or pustules—smallpox, chickenpox, cowpox. The word often appears as a curse: {A pox on both your houses!} In modern usage, pox usually means syphilis when used alone: {He caught the pox}. To call something a pox is to label it a blight or scourge: {Social media is a pox on civil discourse}.

Pozole is a traditional Mexican soup or stew made with hominy—dried corn kernels treated with lime—and meat, typically pork or chicken. The broth is often seasoned with chiles and served with an array of garnishes: shredded cabbage, radishes, oregano, lime, and tostadas. It's a celebratory dish, common at holidays and family gatherings. Regional variations include red (rojo), green (verde), and white (blanco) versions, depending on the chiles or absence thereof.

Practical means useful in actual application rather than theoretical. A practical {solution} works in the real world. Practical {skills} have everyday value. A practical person focuses on what can be done rather than abstract ideals. Something impractical may be beautiful or interesting but fails to function effectively. Practical also means virtual or near-complete: {a practical certainty}.

The practicalities of something are its concrete, real-world aspects—the details that must be handled to make something work: {We loved the idea of moving abroad, but the practicalities of visas and healthcare gave us pause}. The word often signals a shift from abstract planning to nuts-and-bolts concerns: {Let's discuss the practicalities}.

Practicality is the quality of being useful, sensible, or realistic rather than theoretical or idealistic. It emphasizes what works in real conditions: {I admire the design, but I question its practicality}. In the plural, practicalities are the concrete details that must be addressed: {We'll discuss the practicalities of moving overseas}.

Practice is a noun and, in American English, also a verb (the British spelling of the verb is practise). When you practice something do it: Always try to practice kindness. If you practice a skill, you work at it repeatedly in order to learn or master it: She vowed to practice the piano everyday. As a noun, practice usually denotes an instance of training or rehearsing. Practice can also describe a particular professional business, such as a law practice or a dental practice.

Practiced means skilled through repeated experience: {a practiced eye}, {a practiced hand}. Someone practiced at something has done it enough to become proficient. The word suggests competence gained through repetition rather than natural talent. A practiced {smile} or practiced {ease} may imply rehearsed smoothness—polished but possibly insincere.

Practices are repeated activities done regularly, either as routine or for improvement. A doctor or lawyer practices medicine or law—meaning they work in their profession. Religious practices are observances and rituals. Practice also means rehearsal: {She practices piano daily}. Best practices are methods considered most effective in a field. The verb and noun share this spelling in American English; British English distinguishes practise (verb) from practice (noun).

Practise is the British spelling of the verb meaning to do something repeatedly to improve skill, or to engage regularly in an activity: {She practises piano for two hours daily}, {He practises law in Manchester}. In British usage, practice with a C is the noun, while practise with an S is the verb—a distinction American English doesn't maintain, using practice for both.

A practitioner is someone who practices a profession, skill, or art—especially in fields requiring specialized training or expertise. The term appears most often in contexts involving medicine, law, and other licensed professions: {a nurse practitioner}, {a general practitioner}, {a legal practitioner}. It can also describe anyone who regularly engages in a particular activity or method: {practitioners of yoga}, {a practitioner of nonviolent resistance}. The word emphasizes active, ongoing engagement rather than mere credentials or theoretical knowledge.

Praetorians were elite soldiers in ancient Rome who served as the emperor's personal bodyguard. The term now refers to any group fiercely loyal to a leader, especially one that wields disproportionate political influence: {The president surrounded himself with praetorians who answered to no one else}. The word often carries sinister overtones of unaccountable power.

Pragmatic is a somewhat formal way of saying practical, that is, relating to what is possible or can actually be done, as opposed to what is theoretical or intellectual: Everyone welcomed the new mayor’s pragmatic approach to the city’s long-term problems. More narrowly, pragmatic can refer to the philosophical school called pragmatism, which emphasizes practical application as the main criterion for assessing meaning, truth, or value.

Pragmatism is a practical approach that values results over theory or ideology. A pragmatist asks "Does it work?" rather than "Is it pure?" {Her pragmatism helped the committee reach a compromise}. In philosophy, pragmatism is specifically the American school of thought (James, Dewey, Peirce) holding that the meaning and truth of ideas lie in their practical consequences.

A pragmatist focuses on practical results rather than abstract theories or ideals. In everyday use, someone called a pragmatist approaches problems by asking what works rather than what's philosophically pure: {She's a pragmatist—if it solves the problem, she doesn't care whose idea it was}. In philosophy, pragmatism is a specific tradition holding that the meaning and truth of ideas lie in their practical consequences.

A prairie is a large, flat or gently rolling expanse of grassland, especially in North America. The term typically evokes the Great Plains—treeless terrain once covered in native grasses and wildflowers: {We drove through miles of open prairie}. Prairie can modify related things: {prairie dog}, {prairie schooner}, {prairie fire}.

Prairies are vast, flat grasslands, especially the expansive treeless plains of central North America stretching from Canada through the American Midwest. The word evokes open horizons, tall grasses, and agricultural heartland: {Miles of prairie stretched to the horizon}. Prairie dogs, prairie fires, and prairie schooners all take their names from this landscape.

Praise is expressing approval, admiration, or gratitude—usually toward a person for their actions or qualities. You praise a child for good behavior, an employee for excellent work. Religious praise is directed at God or the divine: {hymns of praise}, {Praise the Lord}. As a noun, praise is what you receive when someone commends you: {The book received widespread praise from critics}. To {damn with faint praise} is to offer such weak approval that it functions as criticism.

Praised is the past tense of praise, meaning to express approval, admiration, or commendation for someone or something. When you are praised, you receive positive recognition for your actions, qualities, or achievements. {She was praised for her quick thinking during the emergency.} {The film was widely praised by critics.} The word carries warm connotations of acknowledgment and validation, whether the praise comes from authority figures, peers, or the public.

Praising is expressing approval, admiration, or commendation. The word functions as both verb form and adjective: {She kept praising his work} describes ongoing commendation, while {praising remarks} describes the character of the remarks themselves. Praising suggests active, voiced appreciation rather than silent approval.

A praline is a confection made from nuts and sugar. In the American South, pralines are creamy, fudge-like candies made with pecans and brown sugar: {New Orleans pralines melt in your mouth}. European pralines typically feature caramelized nuts ground into a paste, used in chocolates and pastries. The pronunciation varies—Americans often say PRAH-leen or PRAY-leen.

Pralines are confections made with nuts and sugar. The word covers two distinct treats: in French cooking and much of Europe, pralines are caramelized nuts or a paste made from them, used in chocolates and pastries. In the American South, especially New Orleans, a praline is a creamy candy made with brown sugar, butter, and pecans: {We bought pralines from a shop in the French Quarter}.

A pram is a four-wheeled carriage for a baby, designed so the infant lies flat. The word is primarily British; Americans say stroller or baby carriage. Pram is short for perambulator. Separately, a pram is a small flat-bottomed boat, also spelled prahm.

Prams are baby carriages—wheeled vehicles for transporting infants, typically with a hood and lying-flat bed. The word is British, shortened from perambulator. Americans more often say stroller or baby carriage. {She pushed the pram through the park.} In Australian slang, prams also refers to small dinghies.

Prance describes a high-stepping, springy way of moving—horses prance when they lift their legs dramatically, and people prance when they walk with exaggerated, showy energy: {She pranced across the stage in her new heels}. The word often carries a note of vanity or self-display. Children prance when playing; adults who prance may seem affected or overly pleased with themselves.

Pranced is past tense of prance—to move with high, springy steps, lifting the knees in an exaggerated or showy manner. Horses prance when excited or restrained. People prance when walking with theatrical self-satisfaction or energy: {She pranced into the room like she owned the place}. The word often carries a note of mockery or amusement at someone's manner.

A prancer is one who prances—moving with high, springy steps, often in a showy or spirited manner. The word most commonly describes horses that lift their legs high and move with exaggerated elegance. It extends to people who walk with theatrical flair or self-conscious pride: {She came in like a prancer, expecting everyone to notice}. Prancer is also famously one of Santa's reindeer.

Prances is the third-person singular form of prance—to move with high, exaggerated steps, suggesting energy or self-display. Horses prance when they lift their legs high in a spirited gait. People prance when walking with theatrical flair or affected dignity: {She prances around like she owns the place}. The word often carries a mocking edge, implying vanity or showing off.

Prancing is a high-stepping, bouncy way of moving—lifting the knees and placing the feet down with exaggerated flair. Horses prance when spirited or restrained; people prance when showing off or moving with theatrical energy: {She came prancing into the room like she owned the place}. The word often carries a note of mockery, suggesting someone is being overly showy or self-important.

A prank is a playful trick designed to surprise, embarrass, or mildly inconvenience someone: {We pranked him by filling his office with balloons}. Pranks range from harmless jokes among friends to elaborate public stunts. The word can also function as a verb: {They pranked the new employee on her first day}. A prank call is a phone call made as a joke, often to strangers.

Pranked is the past tense of prank, meaning to play a trick or practical joke on someone: {We pranked him by filling his office with balloons}. The word has gained currency with the rise of prank videos online, where elaborate setups are staged to fool unsuspecting targets: {She got pranked on camera}.

Pranking is playing tricks or practical jokes on others, often for amusement or to capture reactions. The word gained currency with the rise of internet video culture, where elaborate setups are filmed for entertainment: {He got famous pranking strangers in public}. Pranking ranges from harmless fun to mean-spirited harassment, depending on the target's reaction and the prankster's intent.

Pranks are mischievous tricks played on someone, usually for amusement rather than malice: {The seniors pulled pranks on the freshmen during orientation week}. A prank often involves deception or surprise—hiding someone's belongings, fake spiders, plastic wrap on the toilet. {It started as a harmless prank but got out of hand.} To prank someone is to play such a trick on them.

A prankster is someone who plays pranks—practical jokes or mischievous tricks on others. The word suggests habitual behavior rather than a one-time joker: {He was the class prankster, always hiding the teacher's chalk}. Pranksters range from harmless tricksters to those whose antics cross into cruelty or property damage.

Pranksters are people who play pranks—mischievous tricks or practical jokes meant to surprise, embarrass, or amuse. The term suggests someone who makes a habit of such behavior rather than a one-time joker: {The office pranksters filled his desk drawers with gelatin}. Prankster carries a lighter connotation than trickster, implying harmless fun rather than malicious deception.

A prat is British slang for a fool or idiot, someone who does or says stupid things: {He made a prat of himself at the meeting}. Originally, prat was slang for the buttocks, which survives in the term {pratfall}—a comedy fall landing on one's backside. Calling someone a prat is milder than stronger insults; it suggests foolishness rather than malice.

A pratfall is a comedy fall, specifically one landing on the buttocks (prat): {The clown took a spectacular pratfall}. Figuratively, a pratfall is an embarrassing blunder or humiliating failure: {His speech was one pratfall after another}.

Pratfalling is the act of taking a pratfall—a comic fall landing squarely on the buttocks. The term belongs to physical comedy and slapstick, where pratfalling is a deliberate skill: {The comedian spent years pratfalling on stage before landing a film role}. Figuratively, it can describe public embarrassments or blunders: {The campaign kept pratfalling from one gaffe to the next}.
Pratfalls is the plural of pratfall—comedy falls or embarrassing blunders: {The slapstick routine was full of pratfalls}.

A prattfall is a fall onto one's buttocks, especially a comedic one performed deliberately for laughs. The term belongs to physical comedy and slapstick: {The clown took a spectacular prattfall}. Figuratively, a prattfall can be any humiliating blunder or embarrassing failure: {The CEO's prattfall came when leaked emails revealed his ignorance of the product}.

Prattle is idle, trivial talk—the kind of rambling chatter that goes on without saying much of substance. Children prattle; so do nervous guests and bores at parties. The word suggests harmlessness but also emptiness: {She prattled on about her vacation while I tried to work}. As a noun, prattle is such talk itself: {the prattle of toddlers}, {cocktail party prattle}.

A prawn is a shellfish similar to a shrimp, with a slender body, long antennae, and edible flesh. The distinction between prawns and shrimp is loose—British English favors prawn for larger specimens, American English uses shrimp more broadly. {Grilled prawns with garlic butter.} In Australian slang, to {throw a prawn on the barbie} is quintessential outdoor cooking.

Prawns is the plural of prawn, a shellfish similar to shrimp. In British English and much of the world, prawn is the standard term for what Americans call shrimp, though technically prawns are a distinct species with branching gills. {Prawns on the barbie} is stereotypically Australian. {We ordered garlic prawns.}

To pray is to address a god or spiritual power, typically in petition or thanks: {She prayed for her mother's recovery}. The word extends to earnest requests directed at anyone: {I pray you'll reconsider}. The interjection {pray tell} is an old-fashioned or ironic way of saying "please explain."

Prayed is the past tense of pray—to address words to a deity, ask earnestly, or hope fervently. {She prayed for guidance}. {They prayed the storm would pass}. The word carries religious connotations but extends to any desperate hoping: {I prayed I wouldn't be late}.

Prayer is communication directed toward a deity or spiritual force—expressing gratitude, making requests, seeking guidance, or simply acknowledging the divine. It may be silent or spoken, private or communal, spontaneous or ritualized: {She said a prayer before the meal}. A prayer is also the text of such an address: {the Lord's Prayer}. Figuratively, something that doesn't have {a prayer} has no chance of success.

A prayerbook is a book containing prayers and devotional texts for religious worship, either private or communal. Most major religions have traditional prayerbooks: the Jewish siddur, the Catholic missal, the Book of Common Prayer in Anglican churches. {She brought her grandmother's worn prayerbook to services.}

Prayerful describes a disposition toward prayer or a manner characterized by devotion and reverence. A prayerful person prays regularly or approaches life with spiritual contemplation. The word also describes things done in the spirit of prayer: {a prayerful silence}, {prayerful consideration of the decision}. It suggests earnestness and humility rather than casual thought.

Prayers are words or thoughts addressed to a deity, often in petition, thanks, or worship: {She said her prayers before bed}. The word extends to any earnest hope or wish: {Our prayers are with the family}. Someone who {doesn't have a prayer} has no chance at all. A prayer can also be the act itself: {a moment of prayer}.

Praying is the act of addressing a god, spirit, or higher power—typically to give thanks, seek guidance, or ask for something. The word extends to any fervent hoping: {I'm praying the rain holds off}. A praying mantis holds its forelegs in a position resembling hands clasped in prayer.

Prays is the act of addressing a deity or higher power, typically in worship, petition, or thanksgiving: {She prays every morning before breakfast}. Extended uses include earnest hoping: {He prays the weather holds for the wedding}. To pray tell is an archaic or ironic way of asking someone to explain: {What, pray tell, were you thinking?}

To preach is to deliver a religious sermon or moral instruction: {The pastor preached on forgiveness}. Extended uses suggest unwanted moralizing or repetitive advocacy: {Don't preach to me about my habits}. To {preach to the choir} is to advocate to those already convinced. {Practice what you preach} means live by your own advice.

Preached is the past tense of preach—to deliver a sermon or religious message: {The minister preached on forgiveness}. Extended uses describe advocating earnestly for any cause or belief: {She preached the virtues of early rising}. When someone has {preached to the choir}, they've tried to persuade people who already agree.

A preacher is someone who delivers sermons or religious instruction, typically a minister or clergy member. The word often implies passionate, moralizing speech: {He's preaching to the choir}. Outside religious contexts, preacher can describe anyone who lectures others about how they should behave: {Don't be such a preacher about my diet}.

Preachers are people who deliver sermons or religious messages, typically clergy members speaking to congregations. The term extends to anyone who advocates persistently for a cause or moral position: {He's always preaching about the evils of processed food}. To call someone a preacher outside religious contexts often implies unwelcome moralizing.

Preaches is the third-person singular of preach. To preach is to deliver a sermon or religious message: {The pastor preaches every Sunday}. Extended to any earnest advocacy or moralizing: {She preaches the benefits of meditation}. When someone {preaches to the choir}, they're arguing to people who already agree. Preach often carries a negative tone of unwanted lecturing: {He's always preaching about diet and exercise}.

Preaching is delivering a sermon or religious instruction, typically from a pulpit: {The pastor's preaching drew crowds from across the county}. Extended to any earnest advocacy of beliefs or principles: {preaching the gospel of clean eating}. Often carries a negative sense of lecturing others self-righteously: {Spare me the preaching—I know I shouldn't smoke}.

Preachy describes speech or writing that moralizes excessively, offering unsolicited lessons about right and wrong. A preachy {movie} hammers its message rather than letting viewers draw their own conclusions. A preachy {friend} can't resist turning every conversation into a lecture. The word is always critical—nobody wants to be called preachy.

A preamble is an introductory statement that sets the stage for what follows. The Preamble to the U.S. Constitution opens with {We the people} and announces the document's purposes. More broadly, any preliminary remarks before the main point: {After a long preamble about his credentials, he finally made his proposal}. To preamble is to make such remarks, though the noun dominates.

Preapproval is conditional authorization granted before a formal application or final decision. In lending, preapproval means a bank has reviewed your finances and will likely approve a loan up to a certain amount: {We got preapproved for a mortgage before house hunting}. The term appears in credit card offers, medical procedures requiring insurance clearance, and any process where preliminary vetting precedes final commitment.

Preapprove means to approve something in advance, before a formal application or final decision. Banks preapprove customers for loans or credit cards based on preliminary information: {I got preapproved for a mortgage before house hunting}. The term signals conditional approval—final approval still depends on verification and documentation.

Precarious describes situations that are unstable, uncertain, or dangerously insecure. A precarious {balance} could tip at any moment. A precarious {living} barely sustains you. Someone in a precarious {position} faces risk from multiple directions. The word often implies that disaster looms if circumstances shift even slightly: {The company's financial situation remains precarious}.

A precaution is something done in advance to prevent harm or prepare for danger: {Take precautions against sunburn}. The word implies foresight—acting before a problem arises rather than reacting afterward. {As a precaution, she backed up all her files}. To take precautions during sex usually means using contraception or protection against disease.

Precautions are measures taken in advance to prevent harm or trouble. You take precautions against risks you anticipate: {safety precautions}, {fire precautions}, {Take precautions against identity theft}. The word often appears with qualifiers indicating degree: {reasonable precautions}, {every precaution}, {extra precautions}. Without modification, {take precautions} commonly refers to contraception or safe sex.

Precedence is the condition of coming before others in importance, order, or rank. When something {takes precedence}, it receives priority: {Safety takes precedence over convenience}. In formal settings, precedence governs who enters first, who sits where, and who speaks when. {Order of precedence} establishes hierarchical ranking among officials or dignitaries.

A precedent is an earlier instance that serves as a guide or justification for later ones. In law, precedents are past court decisions that establish how similar cases should be decided: {The ruling set a precedent for future discrimination cases}. More broadly, any prior action can set precedent: {There's no precedent for canceling the event}. Something unprecedented has never happened before. As an adjective (pronounced with stress on the second syllable), precedent means coming before: {conditions precedent to the agreement}.

Precedents are past actions or decisions that serve as examples or standards for future ones. In law, precedents are prior court rulings that guide judges in similar cases: {The Supreme Court set a precedent that lower courts must follow}. More broadly, any established custom or practice can be a precedent: {There's no precedent for canceling the event}. To {set a precedent} is to establish a pattern others may follow or cite.

A precinct is a defined district or bounded area, typically for administrative purposes. In American politics, precincts are the smallest voting divisions: {Which precinct do you vote in?} Police precincts are both jurisdictional zones and the station houses within them: {He was taken to the precinct for questioning}. The plural precincts often means the grounds or environs of a place: {the precincts of the cathedral}, {within the precincts of the university}.

Precincts are bounded areas or districts. In American elections, a precinct is the smallest voting unit—the neighborhood where you cast your ballot: {Which precinct do you vote in?} Police precincts are jurisdictional zones and the stations within them. In British usage, precincts often means the grounds surrounding a building: {within the precincts of the cathedral}. The singular precinct shares all these meanings but appears less frequently.

Precious describes something of great value or cherished deeply. Precious {metals} like gold and silver have high monetary worth. Precious {memories} are treasured emotionally. A precious {few} means very few indeed—emphasizing scarcity. The word can turn negative when describing affected or overly refined behavior: {Don't be so precious about it}. In direct address, precious is a term of endearment: {Come here, precious}.

Preciousness is the quality of being precious—highly valued, cherished, or rare: {the preciousness of time}, {the preciousness of clean water}. It can also describe affected refinement or excessive delicacy in manner or style: {The film's preciousness undercut its emotional impact}. This second sense is usually pejorative, suggesting something too cute or self-consciously artful.
clues: The condition of being dearly loved

definition: A precipice is a very steep or vertical rock face—a cliff edge from which one could fall. The word almost always carries danger or drama: {She stood at the precipice, looking down into the gorge}. Figuratively, a precipice is any point of crisis where disaster looms: {The company teetered on the precipice of bankruptcy}.

Precipitate means to cause something to happen suddenly or prematurely: {The scandal precipitated his resignation}. In chemistry, to precipitate is to separate a solid from a solution; the noun precipitate names this solid residue. As an adjective, precipitate describes hasty, rash action without due consideration: {a precipitate decision}. Rain, snow, and hail precipitate from clouds—they fall as precipitation.
