Pretexts is the plural of pretext, a false reason given to disguise the real one. A pretext provides cover for intentions you'd rather not admit: {The inspection was a pretext for searching the house}. To act {under the pretext of} something is to use it as an excuse: {He visited under the pretext of returning a book, but really wanted to see her}.

Pretty describes something pleasing to look at, usually suggesting delicacy or charm rather than striking beauty: {a pretty face}, {a pretty garden}. As an adverb, pretty means fairly or moderately: {pretty good}, {pretty much done}. The phrase {a pretty penny} means a large sum. {Sitting pretty} means being in a favorable position. To {pretty up} is to make more attractive, often superficially.

A pretzel is a baked bread product twisted into a distinctive knot shape, typically salted on the outside. Soft pretzels are large, chewy, and eaten fresh; hard pretzels are small, crispy snacks. The twisted shape has made pretzel a verb and adjective for contortion: {She pretzel-twisted herself into the yoga pose}, {pretzel logic}.

Pretzels is the plural of pretzel, a baked bread product twisted into a distinctive knot shape. Pretzels come in two main varieties: small, hard, and salted as a crunchy snack, or large, soft, and chewy, often sold at street carts and sporting events. {She grabbed a bag of pretzels from the vending machine.}

Prevail means to prove superior or win out in the end: {Justice will prevail}. It often implies overcoming opposition or difficulty: {Despite the odds, common sense prevailed}. To prevail upon someone is to persuade them, usually after some effort: {She prevailed upon him to stay}. Prevailing conditions or winds are the ones that predominate: {the prevailing winds from the west}.

Prevailed is the past tense of prevail, meaning to triumph or prove stronger: {Common sense prevailed}. It also means to be widespread or dominant: {A sense of optimism prevailed throughout the company}. To {prevail upon} someone is to persuade them, often after effort: {She prevailed upon him to stay}.

Prevailing means most common, widespread, or dominant at a given time: {the prevailing wisdom}, {prevailing winds}, {prevailing attitudes toward marriage}. It suggests what currently holds sway rather than what's permanent. Prevailing winds blow most frequently from a particular direction. A prevailing party in a lawsuit is the one that wins.

To prevail is to prove superior or win out: {Common sense prevailed}, {Justice will prevail}. What prevails is widespread or dominant in a place or time: {the conditions that prevailed in medieval Europe}, {prevailing winds}. To prevail upon someone is to persuade them, often with difficulty: {She prevailed upon him to stay}.

Prevent means to stop something from happening or someone from doing something. You prevent {accidents}, prevent {disease}, or prevent someone from {entering}. The word implies action taken in advance—you can't prevent what has already occurred. Prevention is the noun: {an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure}.

Prevention is the act of stopping something from happening before it does. The word appears most often in contexts of health and safety: {disease prevention}, {crime prevention}, {fire prevention}. The phrase {an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure} captures the idea that stopping problems early costs less than fixing them later.

A preview is a glimpse of something before its full presentation or release. Movie previews show clips to entice audiences; a preview of a book might be the first chapter. To preview is to see or show in advance: {We previewed the exhibit before it opened to the public}. In computing, preview displays how a document will look when printed or published.

Previews are advance showings or glimpses of something before its full release. Movie previews (also called trailers) advertise upcoming films. A preview can also be a showing for critics or select audiences before general opening: {The play is still in previews}. To preview is to see or show something in advance: {Let me preview the slides before the meeting}.

Previous means coming before in time, order, or sequence: {the previous owner}, {a previous engagement}, {the previous chapter}. It often implies immediately before: {She had mentioned it in a previous conversation}. Used informally after a noun, previous can mean premature or hasty: {Aren't you being a bit previous?}—though this British usage sounds old-fashioned to American ears.

Prewar describes the period before a war, especially before World War I or World War II: {prewar architecture}, {prewar prices}, {the prewar economy}. The word usually appears as an adjective modifying nouns, evoking a time before conflict disrupted normal life. Context determines which war is meant.

Prey is an animal hunted and killed by another for food: {The owl swooped down on its prey}. By extension, prey includes anyone vulnerable to exploitation or attack: {con artists and their prey}. To prey on something is to hunt it, exploit it, or weigh heavily on it: {The scandal preyed on his mind}. A predator is one who preys; prey is what gets preyed upon.

Preyed is the past tense of prey. To prey on something is to hunt and kill it for food: {Hawks preyed on the mice in the field}. Extended uses describe exploitation or victimization: {Scammers preyed on elderly homeowners}. Something that {preyed on her mind} troubled her persistently.

Preying is the present participle of prey, describing the act of hunting and killing other animals for food. A hawk preying on field mice is doing what predators do. The word extends to human behavior when someone exploits or victimizes others, particularly the vulnerable: {scammers preying on the elderly}. The continuous form emphasizes ongoing or habitual predatory behavior rather than a single act.

Price is what you pay to get something—usually money, but it can be any cost or sacrifice. A store sets prices; a buyer pays them. The {price of admission} might be literal or figurative. {At what price?} questions whether something is worth its cost. To price something is to set or determine its cost: {We priced the car too high}. {Everyone has their price} suggests anyone can be bought.

Priceless describes something so valuable it cannot be assigned a price—a priceless {heirloom}, a priceless {work of art}. The word often applies to things whose worth is sentimental or irreplaceable rather than monetary: {priceless memories}, {priceless moments with family}. In casual speech, priceless means hilariously funny or absurd: {The look on his face was priceless}.

Prices is the plural of price—what something costs or what someone asks for it. Prices rise and fall with supply and demand. To price something is to set or determine its cost: {Help me price these items for the garage sale}. If you {price yourself out of the market}, you ask more than buyers will pay.

A pricetag is a label attached to merchandise showing its cost. Figuratively, the pricetag of something is what it costs in money, effort, or sacrifice: {The pricetag for the new highway shocked taxpayers}. Also spelled as two words: price tag.
clues: Tells you how much something costs

definition: Pricey means expensive, usually with a note of complaint or hesitation: {The restaurant was good but a bit pricey}. The word suggests something costs more than expected or more than the speaker wants to pay. Also spelled pricy.

Pricing is the process of setting prices for goods or services, or the prices themselves: {competitive pricing}, {dynamic pricing}. The term implies strategy rather than arbitrary assignment—companies develop pricing {models} and pricing {structures}. {The pricing on these apartments is aggressive for the neighborhood.}

To prick is to pierce with a fine point or to cause a sharp localized pain: {She pricked her finger on the needle}. A prick is such a puncture or the sensation it causes. To prick up your ears is to listen attentively, like a dog whose ears rise at a sound. In vulgar slang, prick means penis and serves as a sharp insult for a contemptible man: {Her ex-husband is a real prick}. The insult implies someone mean and penetrating—the puncture sense bleeding into character.

Pricked is the past tense of prick, meaning to pierce or puncture with something sharp: {She pricked her finger on a thorn}. It also describes a sudden sharp sensation: {Tears pricked her eyes}. Figuratively, something that pricked your conscience caused a stab of guilt. {His ears pricked up} means he became suddenly alert and attentive.

Pricking is the sensation of being pierced by something sharp—pins, needles, thorns. The feeling can be literal or figurative: {a pricking sensation in my fingers}, {the pricking of conscience}. The phrase {pricking of my thumbs} (from Macbeth) suggests intuitive foreboding. Pricking also names the act itself: {pricking holes in paper}, {pricking out seedlings}.

A prickle is a small, sharp point on a plant—finer than a thorn, like those on a raspberry cane. The word extends to any sharp tingling sensation: {a prickle of fear ran down her spine}, {the prickle of wool against skin}. To prickle is to cause or feel such sensations: {Her skin prickled with anticipation}. {The hay prickled his bare arms.}

Prickles are small, sharp points that stick out from a surface—the spines on a cactus, the thorns on a rose stem, or the stiff hairs on a hedgehog. The word also describes the sensation of being pricked: {She felt prickles on her skin as she walked through the tall grass}. Figuratively, prickles of fear or excitement are tingling sensations that seem to pierce the skin from within.

Prickliness is the quality of being covered in sharp points or spines: {the prickliness of a cactus}, {the prickliness of a hedgehog's quills}. More often, prickliness describes a person's tendency toward irritability or defensiveness: {His prickliness made him difficult to work with}. A prickly person is quick to take offense, easily provoked by minor slights.

Prickling is a sensation of many small, sharp points pressing into the skin—the feeling of pins and needles, or of hairs standing on end. It often accompanies numbness fading, anxiety rising, or skin reacting to cold: {a prickling sensation spread across her scalp}. Figuratively, prickling describes the early stirring of an emotion: {a prickling of unease}.

Prickly describes something covered with prickles or sharp points: {a prickly cactus}, {prickly brambles}. A prickly sensation is sharp and stinging, like pins against skin. Figuratively, prickly describes someone easily irritated or quick to take offense: {He gets prickly when you mention his ex}. A prickly subject is sensitive and likely to provoke disagreement.

Pricks is the plural of prick—small punctures or, in vulgar slang, penises or contemptible men: {I'm tired of dealing with pricks like him}. It's also the verb meaning punctures: {She pricks holes in the dough before baking}.

Pride is a uniquely human emotion of self-importance or accomplishment, sometimes regarded as good (civic pride, hometown pride), and regarded negatively when it is excessive and combined with prejudice (white pride, nationalistic pride). If you pride yourself on something, you experience a feeling of pride for having done or endured it. Your pride and joy is something you are particularly proud of. The collective noun pride is used for a group of lions.

Prides is the plural of pride—groups of lions living together: {Several prides share territory in the Serengeti}. The word also works as a verb meaning to take satisfaction in something, used reflexively: {She prides herself on her punctuality}. {He prides himself on never missing a deadline}.

Pried is the past tense of pry. To pry is to use leverage to open or move something: {She pried the lid off the paint can}. It also means to inquire intrusively into someone's private affairs: {He pried into her personal life}. {The detective pried answers from reluctant witnesses.}

Pries is the third-person singular form of the verb pry, which has two distinct meanings. One pry means to look or inquire too closely into matters that aren't your business: {She pries into everyone's personal affairs}. The other pry means to move or open something with leverage, as with a crowbar: {He pries the lid off the paint can}. Context usually makes clear which sense is intended.

A priest is a person authorized to perform religious rites, serving as an intermediary between worshippers and the divine. In Christianity, priests lead services, administer sacraments, and provide spiritual guidance—the term applies specifically to Catholic, Orthodox, and some Anglican clergy, while Protestants typically use minister or pastor. Other religions have their own priestly traditions: {a Hindu priest}, {a Shinto priest}. Figuratively, someone deeply devoted to an idea or practice may be called its priest: {a high priest of modernism}.

A priestess is a female priest—a woman authorized to perform religious rites and ceremonies. The term appears most often in reference to ancient or non-Christian religions: {a priestess of Apollo}, {a voodoo priestess}. Some modern pagan and Wiccan traditions use priestess as an official title. In contexts where priest applies to women, priestess may sound archaic or deliberately gendered.

Priestesses is the plural of priestess, a woman who performs religious rites or holds sacred office. The term appears most often in discussions of ancient religions—Greek, Egyptian, Roman—where women served specific deities: {The priestesses of Athena tended the eternal flame}. Some modern pagan and Wiccan traditions also use the title for female spiritual leaders.

Priesthood is the office or status of being a priest, or priests collectively as a group: {He entered the priesthood at twenty-five}, {the Catholic priesthood}. The term can extend to any elite body claiming special authority or access to sacred knowledge: {the priesthood of academic economics}. In some traditions, priesthood refers to specific levels or powers of religious authority.

Priestly means relating to or characteristic of a priest—the rituals, vestments, duties, or manner associated with religious clergy. A priestly {blessing} comes from a priest. A priestly {demeanor} suggests solemnity and spiritual authority. Someone with priestly {ambitions} aspires to the priesthood.

Priests is the plural of priest, a person authorized to perform religious rites and ceremonies. In Christianity, priests serve as intermediaries between congregations and God, administering sacraments and leading worship. Other religions have priests with varying roles: {The temple priests performed the sacrifice}. Figuratively, priests of any domain are its devoted practitioners: {priests of high fashion}.

Prim describes someone excessively formal, proper, or easily shocked by anything improper. A prim {person} purses their lips at crude jokes. Prim {manners} are stiff and correct to the point of prudishness. The word often carries mild disapproval—primness as constraint rather than genuine refinement: {She was too prim to laugh at the joke}.

Primacy is the state of being first in rank, importance, or authority. The primacy of the Catholic Church refers to papal supremacy. In broader use, primacy simply means preeminence: {the primacy of reason over emotion}, {the primacy of shareholder value}. In psychology, the primacy effect describes how we remember earlier items in a sequence better than later ones.

Primadonna—from the Italian for "first lady"—originally meant the lead female singer in an opera company. The term now more commonly describes someone who behaves as if they deserve special treatment, is temperamentally difficult, or throws tantrums when things don't go their way: {The director refused to work with her again—total primadonna}. Also spelled prima donna.
clues: Thinks the world revolves around them

definition: A prima donna is a female opera singer who sings leading parts. By extension, a prima donna is someone who is self-centered, temperamental, and difficult to deal with.

Primal means first or original—relating to the earliest stage of something. A primal {instinct} or primal {fear} reaches back to ancient origins, before civilization shaped behavior. The word suggests something raw and fundamental: {a primal scream}, {primal urges}. Primal often implies powerful, elemental forces beneath the surface of modern life.

Primaries are elections held to select candidates who will represent a political party in a general election. In the United States, primary elections occur at federal, state, and local levels, with presidential primaries receiving the most attention as parties choose their nominees. {The Iowa caucuses and New Hampshire primary traditionally kick off the presidential race.} Beyond politics, primaries can refer to primary feathers on a bird's wing, or more generally to things that are first or most important in a series.

The adjective primary has two main meanings that often overlap: first in importance and first in order. Primary education is education for young children. A primary reason, goal, or objective is the main one. In this meaning, primary is often contrasted with secondary. A primary election is one that happens before a general election, to choose candidates. Such elections are often just called primaries. The outermost feathers on a bird’s wing are primaries and the three primary colors (red, yellow, blue) may also be called primaries.

A primate is a member of the mammalian order that includes humans, apes, monkeys, and lemurs—animals typically characterized by forward-facing eyes, grasping hands, and large brains relative to body size. In religious contexts, a primate is a high-ranking bishop or archbishop: {the Primate of the Anglican Church}. The biological and ecclesiastical senses share no connection beyond the spelling.

Primates are members of the biological order that includes humans, apes, monkeys, and lemurs—mammals typically characterized by grasping hands, forward-facing eyes, and large brains relative to body size. The word also serves as the plural of primate in its ecclesiastical sense, referring to senior bishops or archbishops: {The primates of the Anglican Communion met in London}.
clues: Mammals with grasping hands, forward-facing eyes

definition: Primavera is Italian and Spanish for spring, appearing in English mainly in two contexts. Pasta primavera features fresh spring vegetables—zucchini, tomatoes, peppers—in a light sauce. In furniture, primavera refers to a pale tropical hardwood used for veneer and cabinetry, prized for its fine grain.

Like the related adjective primary, prime means main or first in importance (prime minister, prime suspect). A prime number is only divisible by itself and one; the set of such numbers are called primes. To prime something is to prepare it for use or operation (prime a pump). Sometimes prime means to apply primer, which is a substance that prepares a surface for some further treatment or covering.

Primed means prepared or made ready for action. A pump is primed by filling it with fluid so it can begin operating. A surface is primed with a base coat before painting. A person who is primed has been prepared or briefed: {The witness had been primed to give certain answers}. To be primed for something is to be ready and eager: {She was primed for a fight}.

A primer is an introductory text or course covering the basics of a subject: {a primer on investing}, {a primer on constitutional law}. The word also refers to a substance applied as a preparatory coat—primer on walls before paint, primer on skin before makeup. In ammunition, a primer is the small charge that ignites the main explosive. Pronounced with a short *i* for the coating and ammunition senses, with a long *i* for the introductory text in American English.

Primers are introductory texts or guides covering the basics of a subject: {a primer on constitutional law}, {a primer for new parents}. The word also names substances applied to surfaces before painting to improve adhesion, or small charges that ignite larger explosive compounds. In molecular biology, primers are short DNA sequences that initiate replication. All senses share the idea of something that comes first and prepares for what follows.

Primes functions as both noun and verb. The noun refers to prime numbers—integers greater than one that are divisible only by themselves and one—a fundamental concept in mathematics and cryptography. More broadly, a prime is the best or most vigorous stage of something: {in the prime of life}. The verb means to prepare something for use or action: you prime {a pump}, prime {a surface} before painting, or prime {someone} with information before a meeting.

Primetime is the evening hours when television viewership peaks, typically 8–11 PM. Networks schedule their most popular shows and charge advertisers premium rates during primetime. The term extends to anything operating at peak capacity or importance: {a primetime player}, {ready for primetime}. Something {not ready for primetime} is amateurish or underprepared.

Primeval describes the earliest ages of the world or universe—ancient beyond human history. A primeval {forest} has existed since before recorded time, untouched by civilization. The word carries connotations of raw, elemental power: primeval {forces}, primeval {instincts}. Something primeval feels connected to origins, to a time before things were tamed or ordered.

Priming is preparation that readies something for use or action. You prime a pump by filling it with fluid so it can begin drawing more. You prime a surface before painting so the topcoat adheres properly. You prime a person by giving them information beforehand: {She primed him on what to expect at the interview}. In psychology, priming refers to how exposure to one stimulus influences response to a later one—seeing the word "yellow" makes you faster to recognize "banana."
clues: Laying groundwork before the main event

definition: Primitive describes something basic, early, or undeveloped. A primitive {tool} is simple and unrefined. Primitive {societies} lack modern technology or complexity—though calling people primitive carries condescending overtones. In art, primitive refers to work that appears unsophisticated or childlike, sometimes deliberately. A primitive {instinct} is fundamental and unlearned. In computing, a primitive is a basic building block: {graphics primitives}, {data primitives}.

Primo means first-rate or excellent: {That was some primo weed}. The word comes from Italian and Spanish for "first" and carries a casual, slightly slangy tone. In music, primo indicates the lead or upper part in a duet. Primo also means cousin in Italian and Spanish, occasionally appearing in English contexts referring to family.

Primordial means existing from the earliest times or the very beginning. It describes what was present at the origin of something: {primordial soup}, the hypothetical mixture from which life first emerged; {primordial ooze}; the {primordial universe}. The word suggests ancient, fundamental, and elemental forces: {primordial fears}, {primordial instincts}. Something primordial precedes everything that developed later.

To primp is to groom oneself with fussy attention to appearance—adjusting hair, checking makeup, smoothing clothes: {She primped in front of the mirror before the party}. The word suggests vanity or excessive concern with looking good, often before a social occasion. Someone who primps spends more time on their appearance than strictly necessary.

Primping is fussing over one's appearance—adjusting hair, touching up makeup, straightening clothing. The word suggests minor, somewhat vain grooming: {She spent twenty minutes primping in the bathroom mirror}. Unlike serious grooming, primping implies superficial attention to details that may not need attention.

A primrose is a woodland plant with pale yellow flowers that bloom in early spring, among the first to appear after winter. The {primrose path} is a life of ease and pleasure—attractive but potentially leading to ruin, from Shakespeare's use in Hamlet. Primrose yellow is a pale, delicate shade.

Primroses are flowering plants that bloom in early spring, bearing clusters of pale yellow or other soft-colored flowers. The word evokes innocence and fresh beginnings. The {primrose path} is a pleasant route that leads to ruin—easy choices with bad consequences: {He followed the primrose path of easy credit into bankruptcy}.

A prince is a male member of a royal family, typically a son or grandson of a king or queen. The title extends to rulers of small states (principalities) and is used figuratively for someone preeminent in a field: {a merchant prince}. {The prince will inherit the throne.} (Capitalized Prince may refer to the musician.)

A princeling is a young prince, or more often, a minor or insignificant one—a prince of a small territory or with little real power. The diminutive suffix carries condescension: {The country was divided among squabbling princelings}. In modern use, princeling often describes children of powerful figures who inherit privilege without merit, especially the offspring of Chinese Communist Party elites.

Princelings are minor or insignificant princes—either literally (rulers of small territories) or figuratively (people with modest power who act self-importantly). In Chinese political context, princelings refers to the children of prominent Communist Party officials who leverage family connections for wealth and influence: {The princelings dominated China's business elite}.

Princely means befitting or characteristic of a prince—grand, lavish, or magnificent. A princely {sum} is impressively large. A princely {estate} suggests luxury and scale. The word can describe generous gestures: {He left a princely tip}. Princely bearing or manner suggests noble dignity, though the word sometimes carries ironic overtones when the grandeur seems excessive.

Princes is the plural of prince—male members of a royal family, especially sons of a king or queen. The term extends to rulers of small states and to men of high rank in various hierarchies: {princes of the church}, {merchant princes}. Figuratively, a prince is someone preeminent in a field: {a prince among men}, {princes of industry}.

A princess is a daughter of a king or queen, or the wife of a prince. The term extends to any woman of royal rank. Figuratively, princess describes someone treated with special privilege or who expects such treatment: {She's such a princess—she won't carry her own bags}. The word can be affectionate or disparaging depending on tone. {Daddy's little princess} suggests an indulged daughter.

Princesses is the plural of princess—daughters of monarchs or wives of princes. The word often carries connotations of privilege, delicacy, or entitlement: {She treats her daughters like princesses}. Someone called a princess dismissively is seen as spoiled or demanding: {Don't be such a princess about it}.

As an adjective, principal means most important or first in rank: It’s the principal city in the state, but not the capital. As a noun, principal is typically a person, most frequently the head of a school. However, principal can also represent, for example, the ringleader in a crime or the parties to a contract. Principal is used to designate a sum of money, as in a loan or debt, to which interest is added. Principal is often confused with its homonym principle.

A principality is a territory ruled by a prince or princess, or from which such a title derives. Monaco and Liechtenstein are modern principalities. The term also appears in Christian theology, where principalities are an order of angels—or, in some contexts, malevolent spiritual powers: {We wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities}.

Principals are the people at the head of something. A school principal runs the school. In law, a principal is the primary party in a transaction or the person who authorizes an agent to act on their behalf. In finance, principal is the original sum of money invested or loaned, distinct from interest or earnings: {The monthly payment covers both principal and interest}. The principals in a film or play are the lead actors, as opposed to extras or supporting cast.

Principle is a noun that designates a rule, law, or doctrine. Unlike its homonym principal, principle does not designate a person. Principle is often used in the plural because where there is one, there are others: The course will acquaint students with the principles of modern physics. The common phrase in principle means fundamentally or in essence: I accept your argument in principle but I have a few questions.

Principled describes someone who acts according to strong moral convictions or ethical standards: {a principled stand against corruption}, {She's too principled to accept bribes}. The word implies consistency—a principled person doesn't abandon their values when inconvenient. It often appears in contexts of integrity under pressure: {He made the principled but unpopular decision to resign}.

Principles are fundamental truths, rules, or beliefs that guide behavior or reasoning. Scientific principles explain how things work: {the principle of natural selection}. Moral principles shape conduct: {She refused on principle}. A person of principle acts according to ethical standards. {In principle} means theoretically, even if not in practice: {I agree in principle, but the details concern me}. The plural often refers to someone's core values: {He's a man of principles}.

To print is to transfer words and images to a surface, usually using ink on paper. If you print a document, chances are that you are just sending it to your printer to do the work. The noun print refers to anything that results from this process or one like it (print of a Monet painting, print from a photographic negative). To print also means to write in separate letters by hand. Such writing, whether by hand or machine, is also called print: Be sure to read the fine print.

A printer is a machine that produces text or images on paper, typically connected to a computer. Office printers handle documents; industrial printers produce newspapers and books. The older sense—a person who operates a printing press or runs a print shop—persists in publishing contexts: {The manuscript went to the printer last week}.

Printers are machines that produce text or images on paper or other materials. The term covers everything from home inkjet printers to commercial printing presses. In computing, a printer receives data from a computer and renders it as a physical document: {The printer is out of ink}. Historically, a printer was a person who operated a printing press or ran a print shop—a trade that shaped publishing for centuries.

Printing is the process of reproducing text or images, typically by pressing inked surfaces onto paper. The term covers everything from Gutenberg's movable type to modern laser printers. A printing is also a single production run of a book: {The novel is in its third printing}. Printing as handwriting means forming disconnected letters rather than cursive script: {Please print your name clearly}.

A printout is a document produced by a printer, typically paper output from a computer: {I need a printout of that spreadsheet}. The term emerged with computing to distinguish physical copies from what remains on screen. Also spelled print-out or print out.

Prints are images or text reproduced from a plate, block, or digital file—woodcuts, lithographs, photographs, or copies from a printer. The word also refers to fabric patterns: {a floral print dress}. Prints left at a crime scene are fingerprints. In plural, prints often means printed photographs: {I ordered prints from the drugstore}.

Prior means coming before in time, order, or importance: {a prior engagement}, {prior experience required}. Without prior {notice} means without advance warning. As a noun, a prior is a ranking monk in certain religious orders, below an abbot. In American legal slang, a prior is a previous criminal conviction: {The defendant has two priors}.

Priorities are the things that matter most or demand attention first. To set priorities is to rank tasks or concerns by importance: {We need to get our priorities straight}. When someone says {I have other priorities}, they're explaining why something won't get their attention. The singular priority means the state of being first in importance, or a single item given precedence: {Safety is our top priority}.

To prioritize is to arrange things in order of importance or urgency, deciding what deserves attention first: {We need to prioritize our tasks for the week}. The word often implies choosing some things at the expense of others: {The company prioritized profits over safety}. To prioritize something is also simply to treat it as important: {She prioritizes her health}.

Priority is what comes first or matters most. Something given priority receives attention before other things: {Safety is our top priority}. The plural priorities refers to what someone considers most important: {You need to get your priorities straight}. Priority can also mean the right to precede others: {Emergency vehicles have priority at intersections}. To prioritize is to rank things by importance.

Priors are previous criminal convictions on someone's record. The term appears most often in legal contexts where past offenses affect sentencing: {The defendant has two priors for assault}. Someone with priors faces harsher penalties than a first-time offender. In Bayesian statistics, priors are the probability assumptions you start with before seeing new data.

A priory is a religious house governed by a prior or prioress, ranking below an abbey in the hierarchy of monastic institutions. Priories were common in medieval Europe, particularly among Benedictine and Augustinian orders, and many historic buildings bearing the name still stand today as churches, ruins, or converted private homes. {The old priory has been turned into a boutique hotel.}

A prism is a transparent solid with flat surfaces that refracts light, splitting white light into its spectrum of colors. The classic shape is triangular, but prisms come in various geometries for optical instruments. In geometry, a prism is any solid whose two ends are parallel, congruent polygons. Figuratively, to see something {through the prism of} a particular viewpoint is to have that perspective color your interpretation.

Prisms are transparent objects with flat surfaces that refract light. A triangular glass prism splits white light into a spectrum of colors—the classic rainbow effect. In geometry, a prism is any solid with two identical parallel bases connected by rectangular faces. Figuratively, to see something {through the prism of} a particular viewpoint is to have that perspective shape your understanding.

A prison is a building where people are confined as punishment for crimes. Prisons hold those serving sentences; jails typically hold those awaiting trial or serving short terms, though the words often blur. Prison extends to any confining situation: {Her marriage felt like a prison}. To imprison is to put someone in prison or confine them generally.

A prisoner is someone held in captivity, typically in a jail or prison as punishment for a crime or while awaiting trial. The term extends to anyone confined against their will: a {prisoner of war}, a {prisoner of conscience}. Figuratively, someone trapped by circumstances is a prisoner to them: {a prisoner of his own success}, {held prisoner by chronic pain}.

Prisoners is the plural of prisoner—people held in confinement, typically in a jail or prison. The term extends beyond legal detention: {prisoners of war}, {prisoners of conscience}. Figuratively, anyone trapped by circumstances: {We were prisoners of the weather}, {a prisoner of his own success}.

Prisons are institutions where people convicted of crimes are confined as punishment. The term extends to any place of confinement or captivity: {His own mind became a prison}. To imprison is to confine someone, whether literally in a jail or figuratively in circumstances that trap them: {She felt imprisoned by her marriage}.

A priss is someone who is excessively prim, proper, or easily offended by anything crude or improper. The word suggests fussiness and an air of superiority: {Don't be such a priss—it's just a little mud}. To priss around is to move or behave in a dainty, affected manner. The adjective prissy carries the same sense of being overly fastidious or prudish.

Prissy describes someone excessively concerned with propriety, neatness, or appearing proper—often to the point of being fussy or easily shocked. The word carries a dismissive edge, suggesting the person's standards are uptight or prudish: {Don't be so prissy about a little mud}. Prissy behavior prioritizes appearances over substance.

Pristine describes something in its original, unspoiled condition—untouched by damage, decay, or contamination. A pristine {wilderness} shows no human impact. A pristine {1967 Mustang} looks factory-fresh. The word often implies cleanliness or purity: {The kitchen was pristine}. Pristine can also mean ancient or primitive, though this sense is rare outside academic contexts.

Privacy is the state of being free from observation or intrusion by others. It encompasses both physical seclusion and control over personal information: {The fence gave them some privacy}. Privacy concerns have intensified with digital technology—data collection, surveillance, and online tracking prompt debates about {privacy rights} and {privacy settings}. To invade someone's privacy is to intrude on matters they wish to keep to themselves.

The various meanings of the adjective private mostly suggest a separation of information or privilege in contrast to what is public. The private sector is distinct from the public sector, and private property is owned by an entity, not the government. If you want to go somewhere private or do something in private, you mean where others won’t hear or interfere with you. As a noun, private designates a low rank in the military or other institution. Your privates are your genitalia.

A privateer is a privately owned ship authorized by a government to attack enemy vessels during wartime, or the captain or crew of such a ship. The authorization came through a "letter of marque," which distinguished privateers from pirates—though the line often blurred in practice. {British privateers harassed French merchant ships throughout the war.} The term sometimes extends to anyone who profits from conflict while operating in legal gray areas.

Privateering is the practice of privately owned ships attacking enemy vessels under government authorization during wartime. A privateer carried a letter of marque—official permission to raid enemy shipping and keep a share of captured goods. Distinguished from piracy by this legal sanction, privateering was effectively state-sponsored piracy: {American privateers harassed British merchant ships during the Revolutionary War}. The practice was largely abolished by international agreement in the 19th century.

Privateers were private ships or their crews authorized by governments to attack enemy vessels during wartime. A letter of marque made the distinction between privateer and pirate—one operated with official sanction, the other without. The term extends to the sailors themselves: {The privateers captured three merchant ships off the coast}. By extension, privateer can describe anyone who pursues profit through aggressive but technically legal means.
clues: Armed ships with official raiding licenses

definition: Privately means away from public view or knowledge. A privately held company isn't traded on stock exchanges. To speak privately is to do so without others hearing: {Can we talk privately?} Someone who privately disagrees may not voice their objection openly. Privately also indicates personal funding rather than government: {a privately funded school}.
clues: Where no one else can see

definition: Privates refers to the genitals—the body parts kept covered and private: {The doctor examined his privates}. The term is euphemistic, common when speaking to children or avoiding clinical vocabulary. Separately, privates are soldiers of the lowest rank: {The privates lined up for inspection}.

Privatisation is the transfer of ownership or control from government to private entities. State-owned industries, utilities, or services are sold to private investors or companies: {the privatisation of British Rail}, {privatisation of the postal service}. The term is central to debates about efficiency versus public interest. British spelling; Americans write privatization.

Privatise is the British spelling of privatize, meaning to transfer ownership or control of a business, industry, or service from the government to private individuals or companies. The term emerged prominently during the 1980s as governments began selling off state-owned enterprises like utilities, railways, and telecommunications. {The government plans to privatise the national airline.} Critics argue that privatising essential services prioritises profit over public welfare.

Privatised is the British spelling of privatized, the past tense of privatise. To privatise is to transfer ownership or control of a business, industry, or service from the government to private hands: {British Rail was privatised in the 1990s}. The process often sparks debate about efficiency versus public interest.

Privatization is the transfer of ownership or control from government to private entities. A state-owned airline undergoes privatization when sold to investors. The term often appears in political debate: {Critics argued that privatization of the postal service would hurt rural communities}. The opposite process is nationalization.

To privatize is to transfer ownership or control of something from the public sector to private hands. Governments privatize industries, services, or assets—such as utilities, transportation, or prisons—often with the aim of increasing efficiency or reducing public spending. {The city voted to privatize its water system.} Critics argue that privatizing essential services prioritizes profit over public welfare. The noun is privatization.

Privatized describes something transferred from government or public ownership to private control. Industries, services, and assets can be privatized: {The city privatized its water system}. The term often appears in debates about efficiency versus public accountability: {Critics argued that privatized prisons prioritized profit over rehabilitation}. Sometimes used loosely for any shift from communal to individual control.

Privatizing is transferring something from public or government ownership to private control. Governments privatize state-owned industries, utilities, or services: {The country has been privatizing its railways}. The term often appears in debates about efficiency versus public interest: {Critics argued that privatizing healthcare would leave the poor uninsured}.

Privilege is a special right, advantage, or immunity granted to particular people or groups. The wealthy enjoy privileges unavailable to others; {Check your privilege} asks someone to recognize unearned advantages. A privileged {communication} is legally protected from disclosure. To privilege something is to treat it as more important: {The curriculum privileges Western authors}. As an adjective, privileged describes those who benefit from such advantages.

Privileged describes someone who enjoys advantages or special rights not available to everyone. A privileged {upbringing} means access to wealth, education, or social connections. In law, privileged {information} is protected from disclosure: {attorney-client communications are privileged}. The word increasingly appears in discussions of social inequality, where {privilege} denotes unearned advantages from race, class, or gender: {Check your privilege}.

Privileges are special rights, advantages, or immunities granted to particular people or groups. The word often implies unearned benefits: {Check your privilege} asks someone to recognize advantages they take for granted. In computing, privileges are permission levels controlling what users can access: {The admin has root privileges}. To privilege something is to favor it over alternatives.

Privy means private or secret, now mainly surviving in legal and formal phrases. A {privy council} is a body of confidential advisors. To be {privy to} something is to share in secret knowledge: {Only three executives were privy to the merger plans}. As a noun, a privy is an outhouse—a small outdoor toilet, private in its way.

Prize centers on something of value worth pursuing or possessing. A prize is an award given for achievement or victory: {She won first prize in the competition}. It can be anything captured or seized, especially in war—a prize ship, prize money. As an adjective, prize means outstanding or worthy of a prize: {a prize specimen}, {prize cattle}. To prize something is to value it highly: {I prize these letters from my grandmother}. A prized possession is one you treasure.

Prized means highly valued or cherished. A prized {possession} is one you treasure above others. A prized {student} earns special regard. The word implies something has been singled out for esteem: {Her prized roses won at the county fair}. Prized often suggests rarity or personal significance rather than mere monetary worth.

A prizefight is a boxing match, especially a professional bout fought for money. The term dates from when boxing operated outside legal sanction, with fighters competing for cash prizes. Modern usage retains a slightly rough or old-fashioned flavor: {The prizefight drew thousands to the arena}. The fighters are prizefighters.

A prizefighter is a professional boxer—someone who fights for prize money. The term carries old-fashioned connotations of bare-knuckle bouts and smoky arenas: {He had the battered face of an aging prizefighter}. Prizefighting is the sport itself, sometimes used to distinguish boxing from amateur competition.

Prizefighters are boxers who fight for money, especially professionals. The term evokes the sport's raw, commercial essence—fighters competing for purses and titles: {The old gym had trained prizefighters for three generations}. The singular prizefighter emphasizes individual toughness and skill in the ring.

Prizefighting is boxing for money, especially professional boxing. The term dates from when such bouts were often illegal or barely regulated, fought for a cash prize. Today it sounds slightly old-fashioned or literary, evoking bare-knuckle brawls more than modern sanctioned matches: {He spent his youth in the prizefighting circuit}.

Prizefights are boxing matches fought for money, typically professional bouts with purses for the winner. The term carries an old-fashioned flavor, evoking bare-knuckle brawls and early professional boxing before modern regulation: {He followed the prizefights in the newspaper}. A prizefighter is a professional boxer.

Prizes are awards given for achievement, victory, or luck—trophies, medals, cash, ribbons. A Nobel Prize recognizes exceptional contribution; a lottery prize rewards chance. As a verb, to prize something is to value it highly: {She prized her grandmother's ring above all her possessions}. Prize also works as an adjective: a prize {student}, a prize {pig}. To prize something open is to pry it: {He prized the lid off the crate}.
As a preposition, pro is borrows from Latin and means supporting or in favor of: Are you pro-choice or pro-life?

Proactive means taking initiative rather than waiting to respond to events. A proactive {approach} anticipates problems before they arise. Proactive {measures} prevent rather than react. The word emerged in the mid-20th century as the opposite of reactive, and has become standard in business and self-help contexts: {Be proactive about your career}. Sometimes overused to the point of buzzword status.

Probabilities is the plural of probability—the likelihood that something will happen, expressed as a ratio or percentage. In statistics, probabilities range from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). In everyday speech, probabilities often means odds or chances: {The probabilities favor the incumbent}. {In all probability} means most likely.

Probability measures how likely something is to happen, expressed as a number between zero (impossible) and one (certain). In everyday speech, probability often just means likelihood: {What's the probability he'll show up?} In statistics and mathematics, probability is calculated precisely—the probability of rolling a six on a fair die is one in six. {In all probability} means almost certainly.

Probable describes something likely to happen or be true, though not certain. A {probable cause} of death is the most plausible explanation. {The probable outcome} suggests what you'd reasonably expect. As a noun, a probable is someone likely to be selected: {She's a probable for the Olympic team}. Probable falls between possible and certain on the confidence scale.

Probably expresses likelihood without certainty—more likely than not, but not guaranteed. It hedges predictions and softens assertions: {They're probably stuck in traffic}, {I'll probably regret this}. The word sits between possibly (lower confidence) and certainly (higher): {She's probably right, but I wouldn't bet on it}.

Probation is a period of testing or trial during which someone must prove themselves. In criminal justice, it's a sentence that allows an offender to remain in the community under supervision instead of serving time in prison: {He was given two years' probation for the theft}. In employment and education, probation is a trial period during which performance is monitored and continued participation depends on meeting certain standards: {New hires are on probation for ninety days}.

A probe is something inserted to explore or investigate. Medical probes examine body cavities; space probes travel to distant planets; investigators probe for the truth. The word works as both noun and verb: {The Senate launched a probe into campaign financing}; {Reporters probed the senator's finances}. To probe is to examine thoroughly, often persistently or intrusively.

Probes is the plural of probe—a device or instrument for exploring or examining something not easily accessible. A space probe travels to distant planets. A medical probe investigates wounds or body cavities. The verb probe means to investigate thoroughly: {Investigators probed the company's finances}. {The doctor probed the wound for fragments}. Probing questions search beneath the surface.

Probing describes investigation that goes deeper than surface examination. A probing question seeks information someone might not volunteer. A probing look tries to read what's behind your expression. A probing investigation digs past the obvious. The word suggests persistent, searching inquiry: {The reporter's probing revealed years of financial misconduct}.

Probiotic describes live microorganisms—usually bacteria or yeasts—that provide health benefits when consumed, particularly for digestive function. Probiotic foods like yogurt, kefir, and kimchi contain these beneficial cultures. As a noun, a probiotic is a supplement or food containing such organisms: {She takes a daily probiotic for gut health}. The term contrasts with prebiotic, which refers to fiber that feeds beneficial bacteria.

Probiotics are live microorganisms—typically bacteria or yeasts—consumed for their purported health benefits, especially for digestion. They appear in fermented foods like yogurt and kimchi, or as dietary supplements. The theory is that these "good bacteria" support the gut's natural microbial balance: {She takes a probiotic every morning}. Scientific evidence for specific health claims varies widely.

Problem, a noun, has a handful of related meanings, all of which convey the idea of something that requires effort to solve or put right. The most straightforward kind of problem is one that has a simple mathematical solution. Other kinds of problems are sources of grief, worry, and distress. When problem is used attributively, before another noun, it casts a shadow over the main noun with a suggestion that it is hard to deal with, as in problem child or problem tenant.

Problematic describes something that presents difficulties or raises concerns. A problematic situation is troublesome; a problematic argument has flaws. In contemporary usage, problematic often signals moral or social objection: {His comments about women were problematic}. This newer sense can sound euphemistic—a way of calling something offensive without saying so directly.

Problems are difficulties, obstacles, or situations requiring resolution. A math problem needs solving; a personal problem needs addressing. The word often implies something wrong: {We have a problem with the plumbing}. To say someone {has a problem} with something means they object to it or struggle with it: {Do you have a problem with that?} In slang, {no problem} dismisses thanks or concern.

A procedure is a series of steps followed to accomplish something. Medical procedures, legal procedures, and standard operating procedures all describe established sequences of actions. The word emphasizes method and order: {What's the procedure for filing a complaint?} In computing, a procedure is a set of instructions that performs a specific task.

Procedures are established ways of doing things, typically involving a sequence of steps carried out in a particular order. The word applies across contexts: medical procedures, legal procedures, standard operating procedures in business. When someone asks about procedure, they want to know the accepted or official way something is done. {What's the procedure for filing a complaint?} In computing, a procedure is a named block of code that performs a specific task.

Proceed means to go forward or continue, especially after a pause or interruption: {After the delay, the meeting proceeded as planned}. It often implies moving through steps or stages: {proceed to checkout}, {proceed with caution}. Legal proceedings are formal actions in court. Proceeds (the noun) are money received from a sale or event: {All proceeds go to charity}.

A proceeding is an action or course of action, often official or formal. Legal proceedings are the events that make up a court case or hearing: {The judge halted proceedings}. In the plural, proceedings can mean a published record of a conference or learned society: {proceedings of the Royal Academy}. To proceed is to continue or move forward.

Proceedings are organized events or activities, especially formal ones: {legal proceedings}, {divorce proceedings}, {congressional proceedings}. The word often refers to official records of what happened at a meeting or conference: {The proceedings of the symposium will be published next month}. In legal contexts, proceedings are the steps taken in a court case or other official action.

Proceeds are the money received from a sale, event, or transaction: {The proceeds from the auction went to charity}, {She invested the proceeds from selling her house}. The term is almost always plural and typically refers to the total amount collected, often before expenses are deducted. Proceeds commonly appears in contexts involving fundraising, asset sales, or legal settlements.

Process is a series of actions or steps toward an end result: {the hiring process}, {a manufacturing process}. It also names ongoing activity: {Peace is a process, not an event}. In law, process refers to legal proceedings or a summons. In biology, a process is a projection from a body part. To process is to put through a procedure: {process an application}, {process meat}. {Processed foods} have been chemically altered for preservation or flavor.

Processed describes something that has been put through a series of mechanical or chemical operations to alter, preserve, or prepare it. The term appears most often with food: processed {cheese}, processed {meat}, processed {foods}—products that have been modified from their natural state, often with additives for flavor or shelf life. In broader use, processed can apply to anything that has undergone systematic treatment: processed {applications}, processed {data}. The word sometimes carries negative connotations, implying that something natural has been made artificial or less wholesome.

Processes is the plural of process—a series of actions or steps toward a result. Manufacturing processes, thought processes, legal processes. The word has two pronunciations: PRAH-sess-ez follows the standard English pattern, while proh-SESS-ez (with emphasis on the second syllable) is common in technical and scientific contexts. As a verb form, processes means handles or deals with systematically: {The plant processes thousands of applications daily}.

Processing is the act of handling, treating, or transforming something through a series of steps. Food processing converts raw ingredients into packaged products. Data processing organizes information for analysis. When an application is processing, the system is working on it: {Your request is still processing}. To say you're {processing} news or emotions means you're working through them mentally, absorbing their meaning.

A procession is a group of people or vehicles moving forward in an orderly line, often as part of a ceremony or ritual: {a funeral procession}, {a wedding procession}. The word emphasizes formal, deliberate movement rather than a casual crowd. Figuratively, a procession of events or items suggests a continuous sequence: {a procession of witnesses took the stand}.

Processions is the plural of procession—a group of people or vehicles moving forward in an orderly line, often ceremonial: {funeral processions}, {wedding processions}, {religious processions through the streets}. The word suggests formality and deliberate pace rather than casual movement.

A processor is something that processes—that is, performs a series of operations on something to change or prepare it. In computing, a processor (or microprocessor) is the chip that executes instructions and performs calculations, the brain of a computer: {My laptop has a fast processor but not much memory}. Food processors chop, blend, and mix ingredients. Word processors are software applications for creating and editing text documents. A person who processes applications, claims, or data may also be called a processor.

Processors are devices or systems that handle, transform, or manage something. In computing, a processor (or microprocessor) is the chip that executes instructions—the brain of a computer: {The new laptop has a faster processor}. Food processors chop and blend ingredients. Word processors are software for creating documents. In business, payment processors handle credit card transactions. The term extends to people who process applications, claims, or data.

Prochoice describes the position that women should have the legal right to choose whether to terminate a pregnancy. The term emerged in the 1970s as the affirmative counterpart to prolife in the abortion debate: {prochoice activists}, {a prochoice candidate}. Also spelled pro-choice.

To proclaim is to announce publicly or declare openly, usually with some formality or authority: {The governor proclaimed a state of emergency}. It suggests broadcasting rather than quiet statement—you proclaim victory, innocence, or a new policy. Something that proclaims a quality displays it unmistakably: {His accent proclaimed his origins}.

A proclamation is a formal public announcement, typically issued by an authority figure or government: {The governor issued a proclamation declaring a state of emergency}. Proclamations carry official weight but often lack the force of law—they announce, commemorate, or urge rather than compel. The verb is proclaim.

Proclamations is the plural of proclamation—formal public announcements, typically issued by authorities. A mayor issues a proclamation declaring a holiday; a king's proclamation announces new laws. The word carries official weight: {The governor's proclamation ordered flags at half-staff}. Proclamations can also be emphatic personal declarations: {His proclamations about never marrying proved premature}.

To procrastinate is to delay or postpone action, especially habitually or without good reason: {I procrastinated on the essay until the night before it was due}. The word implies knowing you should act but finding excuses not to. Procrastination often involves substituting easier tasks for harder ones, or simply doing nothing at all.

Procrastinated is the past tense of procrastinate—to delay or postpone action, typically out of laziness, avoidance, or distraction rather than necessity: {I procrastinated all week and had to write the paper overnight}. The word implies knowing you should act but failing to do so: {She procrastinated on the decision until it was made for her}.

Procrastinating is putting off tasks you should be doing, typically in favor of less important or more pleasant activities. The word carries a note of self-reproach—you know you're delaying: {I spent the whole afternoon procrastinating instead of finishing my report}. Someone who habitually delays is a procrastinator.

Procrastination is the habit or act of putting off tasks, especially ones that should be done promptly. The delay is typically voluntary and often irrational—you know you should do it, but you don't: {My procrastination on the tax return cost me the early refund}. The word implies avoidance rather than legitimate postponement.

A procrastinator is someone who habitually delays or postpones tasks, especially ones that require immediate attention. The word carries a mildly self-deprecating tone when used about oneself: {I'm such a procrastinator—I always wait until the last minute}. Unlike someone who is merely lazy, a procrastinator often intends to act but keeps deferring.

Procrastinators are people who habitually delay or postpone tasks, especially ones they find unpleasant or difficult. The word carries mild self-deprecation when used reflexively: {We procrastinators always wait until the last minute}. A procrastinator may intend to act but keeps finding reasons not to—yet.

Procreation is the act of producing offspring—reproduction, especially human reproduction. The word carries a formal or biological tone, often appearing in discussions of sexuality from religious, legal, or scientific perspectives: {Some traditions hold that sex is only for procreation}. Unlike casual terms for having children, procreation emphasizes the biological function itself.

A proctologist is a physician who specializes in disorders of the rectum, anus, and colon. The term is older and less formal than the current medical designation, colorectal surgeon. Proctologist appears frequently in jokes, where the profession serves as shorthand for unpleasant work: {My brother-in-law is a proctologist—he deals with assholes all day}.

A proctor is someone who supervises an examination to prevent cheating: {The proctor walked up and down the aisles during the test}. At some universities, a proctor is an official responsible for student discipline. As a verb, to proctor is to supervise: {She proctored the SAT last weekend}.

To prod is to poke or jab, usually with something pointed like a finger or stick: {She prodded the fire with a poker}. Extended, it means to urge or encourage someone toward action: {His parents prodded him to apply for the job}. A prod is both the act and the instrument—a cattle prod delivers an electric shock to move livestock. {She needed a prod to get started.}

Prodded is the past tense of prod, meaning to poke or jab at something, typically to urge movement or action: {She prodded the fire with a stick}. More often figurative—to nudge someone toward doing something: {His wife prodded him to call the doctor}. {After weeks of prodding, he finally submitted the application}.

Prodding is the act of poking or pushing at something, literally or figuratively. Physical prodding uses a finger, stick, or pointed instrument: {The doctor's prodding revealed tenderness in his abdomen}. More often, prodding means persistent urging or prompting: {After some prodding from his wife, he finally called the doctor}. The word suggests repeated, gentle pressure rather than forceful demand.

Prodigal means wastefully extravagant, especially with money: {a prodigal spender}, {prodigal habits that left him bankrupt}. The word carries connotations of reckless abundance rather than mere carelessness. A prodigal is someone who spends lavishly and unwisely. The phrase {prodigal son} comes from a biblical parable about a wastrel who squanders his inheritance, then returns home penitent—so prodigal often implies eventual return or redemption: {The prodigal daughter came back to the family business}.

Prodigals are people who leave home or abandon their responsibilities, often spending money recklessly, before eventually returning. The word comes from the biblical parable of the prodigal son, who squandered his inheritance then came home to his father's forgiveness. The term usually implies both wastefulness and the possibility of redemption: {The prodigals returned to the family business after years of wandering}.

Prodigies is the plural of prodigy—a person, especially a child, with exceptional talent or ability: {Mozart was among history's great musical prodigies}. The word can also mean a remarkable thing or event, though this sense is less common now: {prodigies of nature}. A child prodigy shows adult-level mastery in a specific domain at an unusually young age.

A prodigy is a person, especially a young one, with exceptional talent or ability: {a child prodigy}, {a piano prodigy}. The word implies natural gifts that seem to exceed normal human capacity. More broadly, prodigy can mean something extraordinary or marvelous—a wonder or portent—though this older sense is now rare.

Prods is the plural of prod—a pointed instrument for goading animals, or a poke or jab meant to urge action: {a few prods with a stick got the cattle moving}. Figuratively, prods are prompts or reminders: {She needed constant prods to finish her homework}. The verb form means to poke or urge: {He prods his team to meet deadlines}.

Produce centers on bringing something forth. Farmers produce crops; factories produce goods; artists produce work. The verb stresses creation or generation: {The region produces excellent wine}. To produce evidence or documents is to present them. In entertainment, to produce is to oversee and finance a project's creation. As a noun (stress on first syllable), produce means fresh fruits and vegetables: {the produce section of the grocery store}.

Produced is the past tense of produce. To produce something is to make it, create it, or bring it into existence: {The factory produced thousands of units daily}. A film or album that someone produced was overseen and guided through creation: {She produced his debut record}. Evidence produced in court is presented or brought forward. As an adjective, produced often appears with modifiers: {a well-produced documentary}, {a cheaply produced knockoff}.

A producer is someone who makes or creates something, especially in quantity. In agriculture and economics, producers grow crops or manufacture goods. In entertainment, a producer oversees and finances the creation of films, music, or television—handling logistics while directors handle creative vision. A music producer shapes a recording's sound: {She brought in a new producer for the album}. In ecology, producers are organisms like plants that create energy from sunlight.

Producers are people or entities that make or create something. A film or theater producer secures funding and oversees production. A music producer shapes the sound of recordings. In economics, producers manufacture goods or provide services—the opposite of consumers. In ecology, producers are organisms like plants that generate their own food through photosynthesis, forming the base of food chains.

Produces is the verb form of produce, meaning to make, create, or bring into existence. A factory produces goods, a farm produces crops, a writer produces manuscripts. To produce evidence is to present it: {The lawyer asked her to produce the documents}. In entertainment, to produce a film or album is to oversee its creation. What something produces are its results or outputs: {The experiment produced unexpected findings}.

The verb produce gives rise to the noun product and the relationship between their meanings is predictable. Anything produced can be called a product: The country has to import most of its food products. He is a product of a very harsh upbringing. An end product is the result of a number of production steps. In chemistry, the product is what results from compounding and chemical reaction of substances. In math, the product is the result of multiplication. Product is usually countable but may be treated as uncountable in business jargon: Our goal is to move more product.

Production is the verbal noun from produce and denotes an instance, the activity, or the result of producing something (gas production, food production). Production is frequent in talk about economics, where it refers to the output of an economy. In the entertainment industry, production is sometimes a count noun and refers to a specific version or presentation of a play, opera, musical, or the like. If you make a production out of something, you give it more importance or complexity than it deserves.

Productions are things produced—especially creative works staged or manufactured for an audience. A theatrical production is a play or musical as realized on stage. A film production encompasses everything involved in making a movie: {The production ran over budget}. The word often emphasizes scale or effort: {Getting the kids ready for school is a major production}. In manufacturing, production refers to the process of making goods: {production costs}, {production line}.

Productive means yielding results, output, or growth. A productive worker accomplishes much; productive land yields abundant crops. The word often implies efficiency: {We had a productive meeting}. In economics, productive activities generate goods or value. Productive can also mean giving rise to something: {a productive cough} brings up mucus; anger may be {productive of} violence.

Productivity is the rate at which work gets done or goods are produced. In economics, it measures output relative to input—labor, time, or resources: {The new machinery doubled our productivity}. In everyday use, productivity describes personal efficiency and the satisfying completion of tasks: {I had a productive morning}. Productivity culture celebrates constant optimization and output, sometimes to unhealthy extremes.

Products are things produced—manufactured goods, agricultural outputs, or the results of any process. A product of one's {environment} or {upbringing} is shaped by those influences. In mathematics, a product is the result of multiplication. In business, products are what companies sell, distinguished from services: {We're launching three new products this quarter}.

Profane describes what lies outside the sacred—the secular, worldly, or irreverent. Profane language is crude or blasphemous: {His profane outburst shocked the congregation}. To profane something sacred is to treat it with irreverence or contempt: {vandals profaned the cemetery}. The word carries judgment—what's profane violates what should be respected.

Profanities are words or expressions considered irreverent, vulgar, or obscene—typically those involving religious blasphemy, bodily functions, or sex. The term covers everything from mild oaths to hardcore obscenity: {The coach let loose a string of profanities}. What counts as profanity shifts with time and culture; words that once shocked may become unremarkable.

Profanity is language considered disrespectful toward sacred things, or more broadly, vulgar or obscene speech. The term covers everything from blasphemy to common swear words: {The movie was full of profanity}. A profanity is a single instance—a curse word or obscene expression: {He muttered a profanity under his breath}.

A profession is an occupation requiring specialized education and training—medicine, law, engineering, accounting. The term carries connotations of expertise, ethical standards, and social status that distinguish professions from ordinary jobs. {She entered the legal profession after law school.} To make a profession of something is to declare it openly: a profession of {faith}, a profession of {love}. The oldest profession is a euphemism for prostitution.

Before a noun, professional imparts the idea that the person, firm, or service designated does work that meets a certain standard: We hired professional landscapers to design the acreage. A professional athlete is one who is skilled enough to earn a living by participating in a sport. A person who is called a professional has a white-collar occupation: The new apartment building is intended to appeal mainly to single professionals who work downtown.

Professionalism designates qualities, practices, or standards that meet a certain standard: The mayor felt that the district attorney’s office lacked the professionalism to obtain convictions. People who are members of a profession are usually eager to develop and maintain professionalism because it enhances their reputation.

Professionals are people who work in occupations requiring specialized training or expertise—doctors, lawyers, engineers, accountants. The term distinguishes those who do something for pay from amateurs who do it for love: {professional athletes}, {professional musicians}. Professional conduct suggests competence and adherence to standards: {She handled the crisis like a true professional}. The adjective describes work-related contexts: {professional development}, {professional attire}.
clues: Those who do it for work

definition: Professions are occupations requiring specialized education and training, typically involving intellectual rather than manual work: law, medicine, engineering, accounting. The term carries connotations of expertise, ethical standards, and social status that distinguish professions from trades or jobs. {She entered the medical profession after years of study.} Someone's profession is simply their line of work: {What's your profession?}

A professor is a teacher at a college or university, typically one who has achieved the highest academic rank in their field. The title often implies expertise, advanced degrees, and involvement in research alongside teaching duties. In American universities, professor designates a specific rank above associate professor and assistant professor, though informally any college instructor may be addressed as professor. {Professor Williams teaches organic chemistry.} The word sometimes appears sarcastically to mock someone acting overly knowledgeable: {Okay, professor, tell us how it's really done.}

Professors are academics holding teaching positions at universities and colleges. The title typically implies both teaching duties and scholarly research. In American universities, professor designates the highest faculty rank, above associate and assistant professors. The term extends loosely to any college instructor: {My chemistry professor canceled class}. To {profess} something is to claim or declare it openly—professors being those who profess expertise in their fields.

A professorship is the position or office of a professor at a college or university. It often refers specifically to an endowed or named chair: {She was appointed to the Hamilton Professorship of Economics}. The term emphasizes the formal academic rank rather than the teaching itself: {He held the professorship for thirty years before retiring}.

Proficiency is competence or skill in a particular area, suggesting more than basic ability but not necessarily mastery: {Her proficiency in Spanish got her the job}. Language learning often uses proficiency levels to mark progress. Someone proficient can perform tasks capably and reliably, though an expert might still outperform them.

A profile is a shorthand representation of another thing that gives essential information. Traditionally, a profile was an outline of the side view of a person’s face. Today, your profile on a social media site tells basic things about you. A profile picture is one that you intend to be representative of you. A profile can also be the general idea of something that exists in the public mind: How can we raise the profile of our company? The verb profile is to make a profile of someone or something. To racially profile someone is to view them with bias because of their race.

Profiled is the past tense of profile, meaning to create a summary of someone's characteristics or to examine them based on observable traits. A journalist profiles a celebrity by researching and describing their life. Law enforcement profiles suspects by matching them to behavioral or demographic patterns—a practice called {racial profiling} when based on ethnicity. {The article profiled three women who escaped the cult.}

A profiler is a person or tool that creates profiles. In law enforcement, a profiler analyzes crime patterns to construct psychological portraits of suspects: {The FBI profiler believed they were looking for a white male in his thirties}. In computing, a profiler is software that measures program performance—tracking memory usage, execution time, and bottlenecks to help developers optimize code.

Profilers are tools or people that analyze patterns to build profiles. In computing, a profiler examines how software runs—measuring memory use, execution time, or performance bottlenecks: {Run the profiler to find what's slowing down the code}. In law enforcement, profilers study crime scenes and behavior to construct psychological portraits of unknown suspects. The term also describes those who engage in racial or demographic profiling—targeting people based on group characteristics rather than individual behavior.

Profiles are outlines or side views—the shape of a face seen from the side, or any silhouette showing an object's edge. The word extends to summaries of essential characteristics: a profile of a company, a criminal profile, a dating profile. To profile someone is to analyze or describe their key traits. A high profile draws attention; a low profile avoids it. Profiling often refers to law enforcement targeting individuals based on demographic characteristics: {racial profiling}.

Profiling is the practice of drawing inferences about someone based on their characteristics or behavior patterns. Law enforcement uses profiling to identify likely suspects—controversially, racial profiling targets people based on ethnicity: {The department was accused of profiling Black drivers}. In computing, profiling analyzes program performance to identify bottlenecks. Psychological profiling builds portraits of criminals from crime scene evidence.
