A proton is a subatomic particle with a positive electric charge, found in the nucleus of every atom. The number of protons determines which element an atom is—hydrogen has one, helium has two, uranium has ninety-two. Protons and neutrons make up atomic nuclei, while electrons orbit around them.

Protons are subatomic particles found in the nucleus of every atom, carrying a positive electric charge. The number of protons defines what element an atom is—hydrogen has one, helium has two, uranium has ninety-two. In chemistry and physics, protons are fundamental: {The proton count determines an element's atomic number}. Protons also appear in discussions of particle accelerators and radiation therapy.

A prototype is an original model from which later versions are developed or copied. In engineering and design, it's an early working version built to test concepts before full production: {The prototype crashed during testing}. The word extends to any first example that establishes a pattern: {She was the prototype of the modern career woman}. In cognitive science, a prototype is the most typical example of a category—a robin being the prototypical bird rather than a penguin.

Prototypes are early models or preliminary versions built to test a concept before full production. Engineers build prototypes to identify design flaws; software developers release prototypes for user feedback. The word extends to first examples of a type—the original after which others are patterned: {The Ford Model T was the prototype of the affordable automobile}. In cognitive science, a prototype is the most typical example of a category: a robin is a prototypical bird in ways a penguin isn't.

Prototyping is building an early model of something to test whether it works before committing to full production. Software developers create prototypes to get user feedback. Industrial designers prototype to check form and function. The process emphasizes learning through iteration—build quickly, test, refine, repeat: {We're still in the prototyping phase}.

A protractor is a semicircular or circular tool marked with degrees, used for measuring and drawing angles. Standard in geometry classes and drafting, it typically spans 180 degrees in a half-circle shape: {Use the protractor to measure the angle between these two lines}.

Proud describes a feeling of satisfaction in one's own achievements, qualities, or possessions—or those of someone close: {I'm proud of what we accomplished}, {a proud father}. Pride can be warranted or excessive; the proud may be dignified or arrogant. A proud moment is one worth celebrating. Proud also means having self-respect: {too proud to ask for help}. Something that stands proud projects slightly above a surface.

Prove means to demonstrate that something is true or valid. You prove a claim by providing evidence or logical argument: {The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt}. In mathematics, to prove a theorem is to establish it through formal reasoning. Prove also means to turn out to be: {The investment proved worthless}. In baking, dough proves when it rises before baking. The exception proves the rule uses an older sense of prove meaning "test"—the exception tests whether the rule holds.

Proved is the past tense and past participle of prove, meaning to demonstrate truth or validity: {The experiment proved his theory correct}. Both proved and proven work as past participles—{has proved} and {has proven} are equally standard—though proven is more common before nouns: {a proven method}, {proven results}.

Proven is the past participle of prove, used interchangeably with proved in most contexts: {a proven track record}, {proven guilty}. Some style guides prefer proved after has or have {(has proved effective)} and proven as an adjective before nouns {(a proven method)}, but both forms appear freely in either position. Proven carries a slightly more emphatic or established quality: {proven results} suggests reliability beyond mere demonstration.

Provenance is the origin or source of something, particularly its history of ownership or custody. The term appears most often in discussions of art, antiques, and manuscripts, where establishing provenance helps verify authenticity and value: {The painting's provenance traces back to a Florentine merchant in 1642}. In computing, data provenance tracks where information came from and how it was processed.

A proverb is a short, memorable saying that expresses a general truth or piece of advice: {A stitch in time saves nine}, {The early bird catches the worm}. Proverbs are passed down through generations and often employ vivid imagery or wordplay. They differ from idioms in that their meaning is usually transparent from the words themselves.

Proverbs are short, memorable sayings that express common wisdom or practical truths: {Too many cooks spoil the broth}, {A stitch in time saves nine}. They tend to be old, passed down through generations, and often employ rhyme or parallel structure to aid memory. A proverb typically offers advice or observation about human nature rather than literal fact. {As the proverb goes, you can lead a horse to water but you can't make it drink.} (Capitalized Proverbs is a book of the Bible.)

Proves is the third-person singular of prove—to demonstrate truth or validity through evidence or argument: {The DNA evidence proves his innocence}. In cooking, dough proves when it rises after leavening: {Let the bread prove for an hour}. The exception proves the rule uses an older sense of prove meaning "test"—the exception tests whether the rule holds.
clues: Shows something to be the case

definition: Provide means make available and strongly overlaps the meaning of the verb give: The resort provides towels and drinking water for all pool visitors. If a law provides for something it stipulates that thing: The new copyright law provides for prison sentences related to illegal copying and distribution. Provided, the past participle of provide, is can also be used as a conjunction: We’ll go provided that we can find a babysitter.

While it is technically a past participle, provided can be used as a conjunction to introduce a condition applying to the main clause: Mr. Balmer can avoid jail time, provided he complies with the terms of his probation.

Providence is foresight and prudent care for the future, especially wise provision against want or misfortune: {Her providence in saving during good years saw them through the recession}. In religious contexts, providence refers to God's protective guidance and care over creation—the divine force that provides for human needs and directs events: {They trusted in providence to see them through}. The word often implies timely or fortunate provision: {By some providence, help arrived just when we needed it}. (Capitalized Providence is the capital of Rhode Island.)

A provider is someone or something that supplies what is needed or wanted. The word appears frequently in contexts involving essential services: {healthcare provider}, {internet service provider}, {childcare provider}. In family contexts, provider often refers to the person who earns income to support dependents, as in {the sole provider for his family}. The term carries connotations of reliability and responsibility, emphasizing ongoing supply rather than a one-time gift or sale.

A province is a principal administrative division of a country, similar to a state: {the Canadian provinces}, {the provinces of China}. Beyond geography, province means a sphere of knowledge or activity: {That's outside my province}. In British usage, {the provinces} refers to areas outside the capital—the regions considered less sophisticated or cosmopolitan than London.
clues: A realm of knowledge or territory

definition: Provinces are administrative divisions of a country, typically the primary subdivision below the national level—comparable to states in the United States. Canada has provinces; China has provinces. In a broader sense, the provinces means areas outside the capital or major cities: {She moved from Paris to the provinces}. This usage often carries connotations of being less sophisticated or cosmopolitan.

Provincial relates to provinces—administrative regions of a country, or areas outside the capital or major cities. A provincial government administers such a region. More commonly, provincial describes attitudes considered narrow or unsophisticated, suggesting someone limited by their local perspective: {His provincial tastes prevented him from appreciating the foreign film}. The noun provincial refers to a person from the provinces, often implying cultural limitations.

Provincials are people from provinces or regions outside the capital or major cultural centers. The term often carries condescension, suggesting unsophisticated outsiders unfamiliar with metropolitan ways: {The provincials gawked at the city's architecture}. In sports, provincials refers to provincial-level championships or tournaments: {She qualified for the provincials in figure skating}.

Proving is the process of establishing truth or validity. You prove a theorem, prove your worth, or prove someone wrong. In baking, proving (also proofing) is letting dough rise before baking: {The bread is proving on the counter}. The proving ground is where something gets tested under real conditions.

Provision is the verbal noun of provide. It can mean the act of providing (a program for the provision of clothing to the homeless) or something that is provided for a purpose, such as food: We do not have enough provisions for a week of camping. A provision can offset a potential liability: There’s a provision in the contract for the death of any of the parties. If you make provision for something, you prepare for it with the expectation that it could happen: The plans make provision for the later addition of air conditioning to the building.

Provisions are supplies, especially food and other necessities for a journey or extended stay: {We stocked up on provisions before the camping trip}. The word also refers to stipulations or conditions in legal documents: {The contract includes a provision for early termination}. To provision is to supply with what's needed: {The ship was provisioned for a six-month voyage}.

A provocateur is someone who deliberately provokes others—stirring up trouble, inciting conflict, or provoking reactions. The word often appears in {agent provocateur}, meaning someone who infiltrates a group to encourage illegal acts that justify crackdowns. More loosely, provocateur describes anyone who courts controversy or pushes boundaries to get a reaction: {He styled himself as a cultural provocateur, delighting in offending mainstream sensibilities}.

Provocateurs are people who deliberately stir up trouble or provoke others to action. The term often appears in {agent provocateur}, someone who infiltrates a group to incite members toward illegal acts that justify crackdowns. More broadly, provocateurs challenge conventions or spark controversy: {artistic provocateurs}, {political provocateurs}. The word carries implications of calculated disruption rather than spontaneous agitation.

Provocation is something that incites a response, usually anger or retaliation. An insult can be a provocation; so can a border incursion. The word often appears in legal contexts where someone claims their actions were responses to being provoked: {He argued the assault was committed under extreme provocation}. Without provocation means unprompted: {The dog attacked without provocation}.

Provocations are actions or statements intended to anger, irritate, or incite a response. The word often appears in contexts of conflict: {He refused to respond to their provocations}. A provocation may be deliberate baiting or simply something that triggers a strong reaction: {The article was full of provocations designed to generate outrage}.

Provocative describes something intended to provoke—to stir up a reaction. The reaction might be anger, argument, or desire. A provocative {remark} is designed to annoy or challenge. A provocative {outfit} is sexually suggestive, meant to attract attention. A provocative {thesis} challenges accepted thinking. The word can carry approval (bold, thought-provoking) or disapproval (deliberately inflammatory), depending on context.

To provoke is to stir someone to action or emotion, often negative. You might provoke {anger}, provoke {a response}, or provoke someone {into making a mistake}. The word suggests deliberate incitement: {He kept provoking her until she snapped}. Things can also provoke without intention—a comment might provoke {thought} or provoke {controversy}. To be easily provoked is to have a short temper.

Provoked is the past tense of provoke, meaning to deliberately stir up a reaction—usually anger or aggression. Someone provoked might lash out in response: {He hit me first—I was provoked}. The word often appears in legal and moral contexts where it mitigates blame: {The attack was unprovoked} suggests greater culpability than {She was provoked into responding}.

Provokes is the third-person singular form of provoke, meaning to deliberately stir up a reaction in someone or something. Most often the reaction is anger or irritation: {He provokes her until she loses her temper}. But provoke can also mean to bring about or give rise to something more neutral: {The announcement provoked widespread discussion}. To provoke someone into action is to goad or incite them, sometimes through deliberate antagonism.

Provolone is an Italian cheese, pale yellow and semi-hard, with a smooth texture and mild to sharp flavor depending on age. Young provolone is creamy and mild; aged provolone develops a stronger, tangier taste. It melts well and appears on sandwiches, pizzas, and cheese boards: {I'll have provolone on that sub}.

The prow is the forward part of a ship or boat—the pointed bow that cuts through water. The word appears most often in literary or nautical contexts: {The prow of the vessel sliced through the waves}. Figuratively, prow can suggest the leading edge of anything moving forward.

Prowess is exceptional skill or ability, especially in battle or competition: {martial prowess}, {athletic prowess}, {his prowess on the basketball court}. The word carries connotations of demonstrated excellence rather than mere potential—prowess is proven through action. It often implies a combination of skill and courage, particularly in older or more literary usage.

To prowl is to move stealthily, typically in search of prey or opportunity. Cats prowl at night; burglars prowl neighborhoods. The word suggests quiet, watchful movement with predatory intent. A prowl is an instance of such movement: {on the prowl for bargains}, {a tiger on the prowl}. A prowl car is a police patrol vehicle.

Prowled is the past tense of prowl, meaning to move stealthily in search of prey or opportunity. Animals prowl when hunting; people prowl when searching with predatory or restless intent: {A cat prowled the alley}, {She prowled the aisles looking for bargains}. The word suggests quiet, deliberate movement with watchful awareness.

A prowler is someone who moves stealthily, typically with sinister intent. The word usually describes a person lurking around property at night, possibly casing it for burglary or peering through windows: {She called the police about a prowler in the backyard}. Animals that hunt by stealth also prowl, making them prowlers of a sort.

Prowlers are people or animals that move about stealthily, typically with predatory or criminal intent. The word often appears in crime contexts—someone lurking outside homes at night: {Police responded to reports of a prowler in the neighborhood}. Animals that hunt by stealth also prowl: {nocturnal prowlers like owls and foxes}.

Prowling is moving stealthily, typically in search of prey or opportunity. Animals prowl when hunting; people prowl when up to no good: {Someone was prowling around the house last night}. The word suggests quiet, purposeful movement with predatory or suspicious intent. A prowl car is a police cruiser patrolling for trouble. {On the prowl} means actively seeking—often sex or a good time.
clues: Silently searching for something to catch

definition: Prowls is the verb prowl in its third-person singular form—to move stealthily, typically while searching for something. Predators prowl for prey; burglars prowl neighborhoods looking for vulnerable homes. The word suggests quiet, purposeful movement with potentially threatening intent: {A cat prowls the garden at night}. Someone {on the prowl} is actively seeking something, often a romantic or sexual partner.

Proxies is the plural of proxy. A proxy is a person or thing authorized to act on another's behalf: {She voted by proxy at the shareholders' meeting}. In computing, a proxy server acts as an intermediary between a user and the internet. Proxy extends to anything standing in for something else: {GDP is often used as a proxy for economic well-being}.

Proximity is nearness in space, time, or relationship. Physical proximity means being close by: {The hotel's proximity to the beach made it ideal}. The word often implies that closeness matters—proximity to a fire hydrant affects where you can park, proximity to power affects who gets heard. {In close proximity} is common but redundant.

A proxy is someone or something that acts in place of another. A proxy vote is cast by one person on behalf of another. A proxy server sits between a user and the internet, handling requests on their behalf. In statistics, a proxy variable substitutes for one that's harder to measure: {They used income as a proxy for social class}. By extension, proxy describes anything done at one remove: a proxy war is fought through surrogates rather than directly between the principal powers.

A prude is someone excessively concerned with propriety, especially regarding sex. The word carries disapproval—it suggests the person's modesty is performative or excessive rather than genuine: {Don't be such a prude}. Prudish describes this quality. The related prudery names the attitude itself.

Prudence is careful judgment about practical matters—the quality of thinking ahead and avoiding unnecessary risks. A prudent person weighs consequences before acting: {Prudence dictated that we save money for emergencies}. The word suggests wisdom applied to everyday decisions rather than abstract philosophy. Prudence can shade into excessive caution: {His prudence bordered on timidity}.

Prudent describes someone who exercises careful judgment, especially in practical matters. A prudent person thinks ahead, weighs risks, and avoids rash decisions: {a prudent investor}, {It would be prudent to wait for more information}. The word suggests caution without timidity—wisdom applied to real-world choices rather than theoretical knowledge.

Prudery is excessive concern with propriety, especially regarding sexual matters. A prude recoils from frank discussion of bodies or desires, finding offense where others see none. The word carries judgment—prudery suggests the squeamishness is unreasonable or performative: {Victorian prudery kept piano legs covered}. The adjective is prudish.

Prudes is the plural of prude—people who are excessively modest or easily shocked by matters relating to sex or nudity. The word carries disapproval, suggesting the person's standards are unreasonably strict or performative: {Don't be such prudes—it's just a nude beach}. Prudish is the adjective form.

Prudish describes someone excessively concerned with propriety, especially regarding sex or bodily functions. A prudish person is easily shocked or offended by things others find unremarkable: {She was too prudish to laugh at the joke}. The word carries a note of criticism—suggesting the sensitivity is excessive or performative rather than genuinely principled.

Prune has two distinct meanings. As a noun, a prune is a dried plum, wrinkled and dark, eaten as a snack or used in cooking. The wrinkled appearance gives rise to informal use describing elderly or shriveled-looking people or skin: {My fingers are all pruney from the bath}. The verb prune means to trim branches or foliage from a plant to encourage healthy growth or shape it. This extends figuratively to cutting away unnecessary parts of anything: {We need to prune the budget} or {prune redundant staff}.

Pruned describes something that has been trimmed or cut back. Trees and shrubs are pruned to remove dead branches or encourage growth: {The roses need to be pruned in late winter}. By extension, anything reduced or streamlined has been pruned: {a pruned budget}, {a pruned guest list}. In computing, a pruned dataset or tree has had unnecessary elements removed.

Prunes are dried plums, dark and wrinkled, often eaten for their laxative effect or used in baking and stews. The verb prune means to trim away dead or overgrown branches from a tree or shrub to encourage healthy growth. By extension, to prune is to reduce or cut back anything excessive: {We need to prune the budget}, {She pruned the guest list}.

Pruning is the cutting away of parts from a plant—dead branches, excess growth, wayward shoots—to improve health, shape, or yield: {The roses need pruning}. The term extends to any selective removal meant to strengthen what remains: pruning a {budget}, pruning a {guest list}, pruning {unnecessary features} from software. In computing, pruning eliminates branches from a decision tree or search algorithm to improve efficiency.

Pruny describes skin that has become wrinkled from prolonged exposure to water, like fingers and toes after a long bath: {My hands got all pruny from doing the dishes}. The word comes from the resemblance to a prune's wrinkled surface. It's informal and typically describes a temporary, harmless condition rather than permanent wrinkling.

Pry means to inquire too closely into matters that aren't your business: {She's always prying into other people's affairs}. A prying person is nosy. Separately, to pry is to use leverage to force something open or apart: {He pried the lid off the crate}. The tool used for this—a flat metal bar—is also called a pry or pry bar.

Prying describes intrusive curiosity about other people's private affairs. Prying eyes watch what's not their business; prying questions dig where they're unwelcome: {She resented her mother's prying}. To pry is to inquire too closely: {I don't mean to pry, but are you two dating?} A separate pry means to lever something open or apart: {pry the lid off}, {pry information out of someone}.

A psalm is a sacred song or hymn, especially one from the Book of Psalms in the Hebrew Bible. The 150 psalms attributed largely to King David express praise, lament, thanksgiving, and petition to God. By extension, any sacred song or poem of worship: {The congregation sang a psalm}. To psalm is to sing psalms, though this verb is rare.

Psalms is the plural of psalm—a sacred song or hymn, especially one from the biblical Book of Psalms. The word often appears in religious contexts referring to multiple such compositions: {The choir sang psalms during the service}, {He memorized several psalms as a child}. (Capitalized Psalms refers to the biblical book.)

Pseudo functions as a prefix and standalone word meaning false, fake, or pretending to be something it's not. As a prefix, it attaches to nearly anything: pseudo-intellectual, pseudo-science, pseudonym. Standing alone, pseudo works as an adjective or noun: {The whole ceremony felt pseudo}; {He's a pseudo who name-drops philosophers he's never read}. The tone is usually dismissive—calling something pseudo suggests it fails to be the genuine article.

Pseudocode is informal notation for describing how a computer program works, written in a mix of programming structure and plain language. It sketches algorithms without committing to the syntax of any particular programming language: {The professor asked us to write pseudocode before coding the solution}. Pseudocode helps programmers plan logic and communicate ideas without getting bogged down in technical details.

Pseudohistory presents itself as historical scholarship but lacks the methodology, evidence standards, or peer accountability that distinguish legitimate history. It typically promotes claims rejected by mainstream historians—ancient aliens building the pyramids, Holocaust denial, lost civilizations like Atlantis. {The documentary was entertaining pseudohistory dressed up with impressive graphics.} Pseudohistory often advances ideological agendas or exploits gaps in the historical record.

A pseudointellectual affects the manner of intellectualism without the substance—dropping references, using jargon, or adopting scholarly airs to seem smarter than they are. The word is almost always an insult, suggesting pretension and shallowness: {He dismissed her as a pseudointellectual who name-dropped philosophers she'd never actually read}. As an adjective, it describes such posturing: {pseudointellectual babble}.

Pseudointellectuals are people who pretend to knowledge or intelligence they don't actually possess. The term is dismissive, suggesting someone who name-drops philosophers without understanding them or uses jargon to sound impressive: {The coffee shop was full of pseudointellectuals debating Nietzsche}. The singular pseudointellectual works as both noun and adjective: {pseudointellectual posturing}.

A pseudonym is a fictitious name adopted by a person, especially a writer or performer, to conceal their identity or create a distinct persona: {George Orwell was the pseudonym of Eric Arthur Blair}. Writers use pseudonyms to separate genres, avoid prejudice, or maintain privacy. The term applies more broadly to any assumed name used in place of one's real identity.

Pseudonyms are fictitious names adopted by writers, artists, performers, or others who wish to conceal their real identities. Authors use pseudonyms for various reasons: to write in multiple genres without confusing readers, to avoid discrimination, or simply to maintain privacy. {Stephen King published several novels under the pseudonym Richard Bachman.} The term covers pen names, stage names, and aliases, though each has slightly different connotations depending on the field.

Pseudoscience is a set of beliefs or practices presented as scientific but lacking the methodology, evidence, or rigor that actual science requires. Astrology, phrenology, and conversion therapy are examples—they adopt scientific-sounding language without subjecting claims to testable hypotheses or peer review. {The documentary exposed the pseudoscience behind the supplement industry.}

Pseudoscientific describes claims or practices that present themselves as scientific but lack the methodology, evidence, or rigor of actual science. Astrology, phrenology, and certain alternative medicine treatments are often called pseudoscientific: {The study's methodology was pseudoscientific at best}. The label implies deception or self-deception—the appearance of science without the substance.

Psi is the twenty-third letter of the Greek alphabet (Ψ, ψ), used in mathematics and physics to represent various quantities, particularly wave functions in quantum mechanics. In paranormal contexts, psi refers to psychic phenomena collectively—telepathy, clairvoyance, psychokinesis: {researchers studying psi abilities}. (Uppercase PSI is pounds per square inch.)

Psilocybin is a psychoactive compound found in certain mushrooms, commonly called magic mushrooms or shrooms. When ingested, it converts to psilocin and produces hallucinations, altered perception, and changes in mood and thought. Psilocybin is a controlled substance in most countries, though research into its therapeutic potential for depression and PTSD has expanded in recent years.

Psionic describes mental powers beyond normal human capability—telepathy, telekinesis, psychic projection. The term belongs almost exclusively to science fiction and fantasy, where it distinguishes mind-based abilities from magic or technology: {psionic abilities}, {psionic warfare}. Characters with such powers are psionics or psions. The word blends "psychic" with "electronic," suggesting a quasi-scientific framework for paranormal mental phenomena.

Psionics refers to mental powers treated as a kind of technology or science—telepathy, telekinesis, precognition, and similar abilities imagined as natural phenomena rather than magic. The term blends "psi" (from parapsychology) with "electronics," suggesting these powers can be studied, measured, and developed systematically. Common in science fiction, role-playing games, and speculative fiction: {The psionics system lets characters develop mental abilities alongside conventional skills}. A psionic character or creature possesses such powers.

Pssst is a hissing sound used to get someone's attention discreetly, often whispered to avoid being overheard by others: {Pssst, over here!} The spelling attempts to capture the sibilant, breathy quality of the sound. It typically signals that the speaker wants a private word or is about to share something confidential.
Psst represents a hissing sound that people make to quietly attract someone else’s attention.

Pst is a sound made to get someone's attention quietly or secretively, often a sharp whisper through barely parted lips: {Pst, over here!} It suggests the speaker doesn't want others to notice. The spelling attempts to capture a sound that's mostly just a hissing sibilant.

Psych functions primarily as a verb meaning to prepare mentally or get into the right state of mind: {I need to psych myself up for this interview}. To psych someone out is to intimidate or unnerve them through psychological tactics: {He tried to psych out his opponent before the match}. As an exclamation, psych! (also spelled sike) reverses what was just said—a gotcha moment: {I got you a new car! Psych!} As a noun or adjective, psych is informal shorthand for psychology or psychiatric: {a psych major}, {the psych ward}.

The psyche is the human mind or soul—the totality of mental and emotional life. Psychology and psychiatry take their names from this concept. In casual use, psyche often means someone's mental state or emotional makeup: {The trauma affected her psyche deeply}. To psych someone out is to intimidate them mentally; to psych yourself up is to prepare mentally for a challenge. (Capitalized Psyche is a figure from Greek mythology.)

Psyched means excited, energized, or mentally prepared for something: {I'm so psyched for the concert tonight}. The word suggests eager anticipation or having worked oneself into a state of readiness. To psych someone out is to intimidate or unnerve them through psychological tactics. To psych oneself up is to mentally prepare: {She psyched herself up before the interview}.

Psychedelia refers to the culture, art, and aesthetic associated with psychedelic drugs and their mind-altering effects. The term encompasses the visual style (swirling colors, kaleidoscopic patterns), music (extended improvisations, unusual sounds), and broader sensibility that emerged from 1960s drug experimentation: {The poster was pure psychedelia—Day-Glo colors and melting lettering}. It can describe anything evoking that era's hallucinogenic experience, whether or not drugs are involved.

Psychedelic describes drugs that alter perception and consciousness—LSD, psilocybin mushrooms, mescaline. The experience typically involves vivid visual hallucinations, intensified colors, and distorted sense of time. The adjective extends to art, music, and design that evokes these altered states: {psychedelic rock}, {psychedelic posters} with swirling patterns and Day-Glo colors. {The sixties were the heyday of psychedelic culture.}

Psychedelics are drugs that alter perception, mood, and thought—producing vivid sensory experiences, distorted sense of time, and sometimes profound feelings of insight or connection. The category includes LSD, psilocybin mushrooms, mescaline, and DMT. {She experimented with psychedelics in college}. The term also works as an adjective: {psychedelic art}, {psychedelic rock}. Recent research explores therapeutic uses for depression and PTSD.

Psyches is the plural of psyche, the human mind or soul—the inner self that thinks, feels, and experiences. Psychology takes its name from this concept. The word often appears when discussing mental states collectively: {The psyches of trauma survivors require careful treatment}. {War damages the psyches of everyone involved}. To psyche someone out is to unnerve them through psychological tactics.

Psychiatric relates to psychiatry—the branch of medicine dealing with mental illness and emotional disorders. A psychiatric {hospital} treats such conditions. A psychiatric {evaluation} assesses mental health. The word describes anything connected to the diagnosis, treatment, or study of mental disorders: {psychiatric care}, {psychiatric medication}, {psychiatric symptoms}.

A psychiatrist is a physician who specializes in diagnosing and treating mental illness. Unlike psychologists, psychiatrists hold medical degrees and can prescribe medication. The term often appears in contexts of serious mental health treatment: {Her psychiatrist adjusted her antidepressant dosage}. Informally, seeing a psychiatrist may carry more stigma than seeing a therapist or counselor.

Psychiatrists are medical doctors who specialize in diagnosing and treating mental illness. Unlike psychologists, psychiatrists can prescribe medication: {Her psychiatrist adjusted her antidepressant dosage}. The term sometimes carries dismissive connotations, as when someone suggests another person needs psychiatric help: {You should see a psychiatrist}.

Psychiatry is the branch of medicine devoted to diagnosing and treating mental disorders. Unlike psychologists, psychiatrists hold medical degrees and can prescribe medication. The field encompasses talk therapy, pharmacological treatment, and sometimes hospitalization for severe conditions: {She went into psychiatry after medical school}. {His psychiatry rotation convinced him to specialize in the field}.

Psychic describes abilities or phenomena that seem to transcend ordinary physical laws—mind reading, predicting the future, communicating with the dead. A psychic is a person who claims such abilities: {She consulted a psychic about her missing sister}. The word also means relating to the mind or soul rather than the body: {psychic wounds that never fully healed}.

Psychics are people who claim supernatural abilities to perceive information hidden from ordinary senses—reading minds, sensing the future, or communicating with the dead. The term often carries skepticism: {She doesn't believe in psychics}. As an adjective, psychic describes these purported abilities: {psychic powers}, {psychic readings}. The noun also names the field itself: {He's interested in psychics and the paranormal}.

Psyching is the present participle of psych, which means to mentally prepare or intimidate. To psych yourself up is to build confidence before a challenge: {She was psyching herself up for the interview}. To psych someone out is to unnerve them through mind games or intimidation: {He kept psyching out his opponents with trash talk}. The word comes from psychology, suggesting mental manipulation or preparation.

Psycho is informal shorthand for psychopath or psychotic, though in casual use it rarely distinguishes between them. It describes someone dangerously unstable or violently irrational: {My ex was a complete psycho}. The adjective means crazy or unhinged: {That was a psycho move}. The word is imprecise clinically but vivid colloquially—it suggests someone whose behavior is frighteningly unpredictable.

Psychoanalyse is the British spelling of psychoanalyze—to examine someone's mind using the methods of psychoanalysis, exploring unconscious thoughts, memories, and motivations. More loosely, it means to scrutinize someone's psychology or motivations: {Stop trying to psychoanalyse me}. The noun is psychoanalysis; the practitioner is a psychoanalyst.

Psychoanalysis is a method of treating mental disorders developed by Sigmund Freud, based on exploring unconscious thoughts, childhood experiences, and repressed desires through techniques like free association and dream interpretation. The term also refers to the broader theory of mind underlying this treatment—the idea that unconscious conflicts shape behavior and emotion. A therapist practicing psychoanalysis is a psychoanalyst: {She's been in psychoanalysis for years}. The approach has influenced psychology, literature, and cultural criticism, though its scientific standing remains contested.

A psychoanalyst is a therapist who practices psychoanalysis—a method of treating mental disorders by exploring unconscious thoughts, early memories, and repressed feelings, typically through extended talk therapy. The approach derives from Freud's theories about the unconscious mind. {She saw her psychoanalyst twice a week for years.}

To psychoanalyze is to examine someone's thoughts, feelings, and behavior through the lens of psychoanalytic theory—probing unconscious motivations, childhood experiences, and hidden conflicts. In clinical settings, it describes formal therapeutic treatment. More loosely, it means attempting to explain someone's actions through psychological interpretation: {Stop psychoanalyzing me—I just don't like olives}. The casual use often carries a note of unwelcome intrusion.

Psychoanalyzed is the past tense of psychoanalyze, meaning to treat or examine someone using psychoanalysis—the method developed by Freud that explores unconscious thoughts, childhood experiences, and repressed emotions to understand psychological problems. In casual use, it often describes any deep probing into someone's motives or mental state: {Stop trying to psychoanalyze me; I just don't like olives}. The term can carry a slightly dismissive tone when used outside clinical settings.

Psychoanalyzing is examining someone's behavior, motives, or personality through a psychological lens—whether professionally or, more often, casually. A therapist psychoanalyzes patients through formal treatment. But the word usually describes amateur attempts to explain why someone acts as they do: {Stop psychoanalyzing me—I just like the color blue}.

Psychobabble is psychological jargon used loosely or pretentiously, especially by non-experts. The term is dismissive, suggesting the speaker is dressing up simple observations in clinical-sounding language: {All that talk about "boundaries" and "inner child" is just psychobabble}. It implies the language obscures rather than illuminates.

Psychodrama is a therapeutic technique in which participants act out emotional situations from their lives, playing themselves or others to gain insight into their feelings and relationships. The term extends to real-life situations marked by exaggerated emotional conflict: {Every family gathering turns into psychodrama with those two}. The adjective is psychodramatic.

Psychodramas are intensely emotional interpersonal conflicts, often characterized by exaggerated reactions and theatrical behavior: {I'm tired of the psychodramas at family gatherings}. The term comes from psychodrama, a therapeutic technique where participants act out emotional situations. In casual use, psychodramas suggests unnecessary drama rooted in psychological issues rather than genuine grievances.

Psychological relates to the mind and mental processes. A psychological {thriller} explores characters' minds rather than relying on action. Psychological {warfare} targets an enemy's morale and thinking. Something psychological originates in the mind rather than the body: {The doctor said my symptoms were psychological}. The {psychological moment} is the perfect time to act on someone's state of mind.

A psychologist studies the mind and behavior. The term covers researchers investigating cognition, perception, or development, as well as clinicians who assess and treat mental health conditions. A psychologist typically holds a doctoral degree but is not a medical doctor—{My psychologist recommended therapy rather than medication}. The word also applies loosely to anyone perceptive about human nature: {She's a natural psychologist}.

Psychology is the scientific study of the mind and behavior—how people think, feel, and act. The field spans clinical practice (treating mental disorders), research (cognition, development, personality), and applied work (industrial, educational, forensic). In casual use, psychology often means the mental characteristics of a person or group: {the psychology of voters}, {I don't understand his psychology}. To {use psychology} on someone is to manipulate them through insight into their thinking.

A psychopath is a person with a personality disorder marked by lack of empathy, shallow emotions, manipulativeness, and disregard for others' rights. The term is clinical in origin but now appears loosely in everyday speech for anyone who seems coldly calculating or dangerously unfeeling: {My ex was a complete psychopath}. Psychopathic behavior may include charm and deception alongside cruelty. The related term sociopath is often used interchangeably, though some distinguish between them based on origin or presentation.

Psychopaths are people with a personality disorder marked by shallow emotions, lack of empathy, manipulativeness, and disregard for others' wellbeing. The clinical term is antisocial personality disorder, but psychopath persists in popular usage for those who seem incapable of genuine remorse or emotional connection: {The documentary explored whether corporate executives are disproportionately psychopaths}. In casual speech, psychopath loosely describes anyone whose behavior seems dangerously unhinged or coldly calculating.

Psychopathy is a personality disorder marked by lack of empathy, shallow emotions, manipulativeness, and disregard for others' rights. Unlike psychosis, psychopaths perceive reality clearly—they simply don't feel moral constraints the way most people do. The term overlaps significantly with antisocial personality disorder and sociopathy, though clinicians draw fine distinctions. {The documentary explored whether corporate culture rewards psychopathy.}

Psychos is the plural of psycho, informal shorthand for psychopath or psychotic person. In casual use, it rarely distinguishes between clinical conditions—it just means someone dangerously unstable or unpredictably violent: {The place was full of psychos}. Often used loosely for anyone who behaves irrationally or intensely: {My ex is a total psycho}.

Psychosis is a mental state in which a person loses contact with reality. Someone experiencing psychosis may have hallucinations, delusions, or severely disordered thinking. The term covers symptoms rather than a single disease—psychosis can result from schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, severe depression, drug use, or medical conditions. {He was hospitalized during an episode of acute psychosis.}

Psychosomatic describes physical symptoms caused or worsened by mental factors rather than purely bodily ones. A psychosomatic illness is real—the pain or dysfunction exists—but originates in stress, anxiety, or emotional disturbance rather than injury or infection: {Doctors found no physical cause; they suspect her symptoms are psychosomatic}. The term sometimes carries dismissive overtones, implying the condition is "all in your head."

A psychotherapist is a practitioner who treats mental and emotional disorders through psychological methods rather than medication—talk therapy, behavioral techniques, and similar approaches. The term covers various specialists: psychiatrists, psychologists, counselors, and clinical social workers may all function as psychotherapists. {She's been seeing a psychotherapist for her anxiety.}

Psychotherapy is the treatment of mental and emotional disorders through psychological methods rather than medication. A trained therapist helps patients explore thoughts, feelings, and behaviors through structured conversation. The term covers many approaches—talk therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, psychoanalysis—all relying on the therapeutic relationship as the primary tool for change. {She's been in psychotherapy for two years.}

Psychotic describes a mental state involving a break from reality—hallucinations, delusions, or severely disordered thinking. The clinical term applies to conditions like schizophrenia or episodes triggered by drugs or trauma. Informally, psychotic gets thrown around loosely to mean crazy or unhinged: {My psychotic ex keyed my car}. A psychotic is a person experiencing psychosis.

Psyop is short for psychological operation—a military or political effort to influence attitudes and behavior through propaganda, disinformation, or strategic messaging. The term has spread from military contexts to describe any manipulation campaign: {That viral story was a psyop to make us distrust the media}. Online, psyop is often used loosely or humorously for anything that seems designed to mess with people's heads: {Daylight saving time is a psyop}.

Psyops is short for psychological operations—efforts to influence the attitudes, emotions, or behavior of a target audience through information, propaganda, or strategic messaging. The term comes from military and intelligence contexts but now applies broadly to manipulation campaigns: {The whole thing was a psyop to make us distrust the media}. Often used half-jokingly to suggest hidden manipulation behind ordinary events.

A pteranodon is a large flying reptile that lived during the Late Cretaceous period, distinguished by its toothless beak and prominent bony crest extending from the back of its skull. Though often grouped with dinosaurs in popular imagination, pteranodons were pterosaurs—a separate order of reptiles. With wingspans reaching over twenty feet, they were among the largest flying animals ever to exist.

Pterodactyl is the popular name for pterosaurs—flying reptiles that lived alongside dinosaurs but were not themselves dinosaurs. The name comes from Greek words meaning "wing finger," describing their membrane wings stretched along an elongated fourth finger. Though scientists prefer the more precise term pterosaur, pterodactyl remains common in casual use: {The museum had a pterodactyl skeleton suspended from the ceiling}.

Pterodactyls is the informal name for pterosaurs—the flying reptiles that lived alongside dinosaurs. Though technically pterodactyl refers to a specific genus, the word serves as the popular catch-all for any of these winged creatures: {The museum has a pterodactyl skeleton with a twenty-foot wingspan}. The image of pterodactyls swooping through prehistoric skies remains a staple of dinosaur media.

A pterosaur is an extinct flying reptile that lived during the age of dinosaurs. Despite the wings and flight, pterosaurs were not dinosaurs but a separate group of reptiles. They ranged from sparrow-sized to the largest flying animals ever known, with wingspans exceeding thirty feet. The name means "winged lizard."

Pterosaurs were flying reptiles that lived during the age of dinosaurs, though they were not dinosaurs themselves. They ranged from sparrow-sized to creatures with forty-foot wingspans—the largest animals ever to fly. Their wings were membranes of skin stretched along an elongated fourth finger. The group went extinct alongside the dinosaurs about 66 million years ago.

Ptooey is a spelling of the sound made when spitting, used to express disgust, contempt, or rejection: {Ptooey! This coffee tastes terrible}. It often accompanies a theatrical spitting gesture, real or imagined. The word appears in comic strips and informal writing to convey emphatic dismissal.

A pub is a bar or tavern, especially in Britain and Ireland, where people gather to drink beer and socialize. Short for "public house," pubs traditionally serve as neighborhood gathering spots: {Let's meet at the pub after work}. The word carries connotations of casual atmosphere, draft beer, and community that distinguish it from more formal establishments.

Puberty is the stage of physical development when a child's body matures into an adult body capable of reproduction. It typically begins between ages 8 and 13 for girls and 9 and 14 for boys, bringing growth spurts, body hair, voice changes, and sexual development. {She started puberty earlier than her classmates.}

Public, originally an adjective that developed noun meanings, has several meanings in which the idea of people—a word that public is distantly related to—figure prominently. The core meaning of public is not private, or open to view or knowledge. From this developed the most common noun sense, namely the people constituting a particular group, such as a community.

Publication is the act of making something publicly available, especially printed material like books, magazines, or journals. A publication is also the thing produced: {a monthly publication}, {scientific publications}. The term extends to any formal release of information: {publication of the findings}, {publication of banns} before a wedding.

Publicise is the British spelling of publicize—to make something widely known or to promote it to the public. Governments publicise policies, companies publicise products, and activists publicise causes. {The charity publicised the event through social media.} The word implies deliberate effort to attract attention or spread information.

A publicist is someone who generates media attention for clients—typically celebrities, companies, or products. The publicist writes press releases, arranges interviews, and manages public image: {Her publicist scheduled three morning shows}. The older sense of a writer on public affairs or international law has largely faded from use.

Publicists are professionals who manage public image and media relations, typically for celebrities, companies, or public figures. They craft press releases, arrange interviews, and work to generate favorable coverage while minimizing negative attention. {Her publicist scheduled a round of talk show appearances to promote the new album.} The singular is publicist.

Publicity is public attention or awareness, especially as generated through media coverage. A company seeks publicity for a new product; a celebrity might shun it. The word often implies deliberate effort: {The stunt was just a publicity grab}. A publicity {campaign} promotes something; a publicity {nightmare} damages a reputation. Bad publicity is still publicity—the word is neutral about whether attention helps or harms.

To publish is to make something available to the public, especially by printing and distributing it: {She published her first novel at twenty-five}. Publishers are companies that produce books, magazines, newspapers, or digital content. The meaning extends beyond print—you can publish a website, a podcast, or research findings. To publish is also to announce formally: {The banns were published in church}.

Published describes work that has been made available to the public, typically through print or digital distribution. A published {book}, {article}, or {study} has gone through some process of production and release. The term implies a degree of formality or legitimacy—self-published work exists but carries different connotations than traditionally published material. {Her findings were published in a peer-reviewed journal.}

A publisher is a person or company that produces and distributes books, newspapers, magazines, or other content for public consumption. Publishers handle editing, printing, marketing, and sales—the business side of getting written work to readers. In digital contexts, any entity that makes content publicly available may be called a publisher: {The website publisher removed the controversial article}. To publish is to make something public, so a publisher is fundamentally one who brings things to light.

Publishers are companies or individuals that produce and distribute written works—books, newspapers, magazines, or digital content. A publisher typically handles editing, design, printing, and marketing: {She submitted her manuscript to several publishers}. The term extends to anyone who makes content publicly available: {The blog's publisher posted daily updates}.

Publishing is the business of producing and distributing written or visual content to the public—books, magazines, newspapers, or digital media. The term covers everything from editorial selection to printing to marketing: {She works in publishing}. Self-publishing bypasses traditional gatekeepers, letting authors produce and sell their own work directly.

Pubs is the plural of pub, short for public house—a British establishment serving alcoholic drinks and often food. Pubs are central to British social life, distinct from bars in their traditional atmosphere: {We visited three pubs in the village}. The word appears in compounds like {pub crawl}, moving from pub to pub in an evening.

A puck is the vulcanized rubber disk used in ice hockey—black, flat, and about an inch thick. Players shoot it across the ice into the goal. The word extends to similar objects in other games like air hockey. To puck something is to hit it as one would a hockey puck. {The puck slid past the goaltender.} (Capitalized Puck is the mischievous fairy.)

To pucker is to draw together into wrinkles or folds, typically by tightening muscles: {She puckered her lips for a kiss}. Fabric puckers when it gathers unevenly. A pucker is the resulting wrinkle or crease. Sour tastes make the mouth pucker involuntarily. {Pucker up} is an invitation to kiss.

Puckered describes something gathered or contracted into wrinkles or small folds. Lips pucker for a kiss. Fabric puckers when stitched too tightly. A face puckers in distaste at something sour. {Her lips were puckered in concentration}. The word suggests a drawing inward, a tightening that creates irregular creases.

Puckers is the plural noun and third-person singular verb form of pucker, which describes the action of drawing together into wrinkles or small folds. Lips pucker for a kiss or in displeasure; fabric puckers when it gathers unevenly. {Her face puckers whenever she tastes something sour.} The noun refers to a wrinkled or gathered spot, as in clothing or skin: {There were puckers in the seam where the stitching pulled too tight.}

Pucks is the plural of puck, most commonly the hard rubber disk used in ice hockey: {The goalie blocked three pucks in rapid succession}. A puck is also a mouse-like input device used with graphics tablets, or any small disk-shaped object. In folklore, Puck is a mischievous sprite—the trickster in Shakespeare's *A Midsummer Night's Dream*.

Pudding is a soft, sweet dessert, though what it means varies by country. In American English, pudding typically refers to a creamy, milk-based dish thickened with starch or eggs: {chocolate pudding}, {banana pudding}. In British English, pudding can mean any dessert {(What's for pudding?)} or specifically a steamed or boiled dish, often dense and rich: {Christmas pudding}, {sticky toffee pudding}. The word also appears in savory dishes like {black pudding} and {blood pudding}, which are sausages. {The proof is in the pudding} means results matter more than promises.

Puddings is the plural of pudding, a term covering different desserts depending on where you are. In American English, pudding usually means a creamy, spoonable dessert made from milk and sugar: {chocolate pudding}, {butterscotch pudding}. In British English, pudding is a broader category that includes steamed or boiled dishes like Christmas pudding, or simply means dessert generally: {What's for pudding?} Black pudding and blood pudding are savory sausages made with blood—not desserts at all.

A puddle is a small, shallow pool of liquid, typically rainwater collected on the ground: {Children splashed through puddles on the sidewalk}. The word extends to any small accumulation of spilled liquid: {a puddle of milk}, {a puddle of blood}. To puddle is to form such pools or to wade through them.

Puddles are small, shallow pools of water, typically formed by rain collecting in depressions on the ground. Children splash in them; drivers avoid them. The verb means to form such pools or to splash about in water: {Rain puddled on the uneven pavement}. To puddle is also to work clay or soil into a watertight mass.

Pudge is informal for a chubby person or for chubbiness itself: {Look at that pudge around my middle}. The word carries affection more than criticism—you might call a pleasantly plump baby or pet a {little pudge}. As a nickname, Pudge suggests someone stocky or round-faced.

Pudgy describes someone or something that is short and somewhat fat in a soft, rounded way. The word often applies to children or body parts: {pudgy fingers}, {pudgy cheeks}, {a pudgy toddler}. It carries a gentler, more affectionate connotation than words like fat or chubby—suggesting endearing plumpness rather than criticism.
clues: Pleasantly plump in a cuddly way

definition: Pueblo comes from the Spanish word for "people" or "village." In the American Southwest, it refers to the adobe or stone communal dwellings built by Indigenous peoples, characterized by flat roofs and terraced levels: {The ancient pueblo at Mesa Verde attracts thousands of visitors}. Pueblo also designates the Indigenous peoples who built and inhabit these structures, including the Hopi and Zuni. In Spanish-speaking regions, pueblo simply means a town or village.

Pueblos is the plural of pueblo, a Spanish word meaning village or town, used in English for the communal adobe or stone dwellings built by certain Native American peoples in the American Southwest: {The ancient pueblos at Mesa Verde draw thousands of visitors}. The word also refers to the peoples who built and inhabit these structures—the Pueblo Indians. In Spanish-speaking regions, pueblo simply means any small town or village.

Puff, a noun and verb, suggests inflation and the movement of air. Various kinds of food that consist mostly of air are called puffs (cheese puffs, corn puffs). Puff pastry rises a lot when baked. When you puff on a cigarette or pipe, you inhale smoke from it; you can also take a puff. Difficult breathing is sometimes called puffing, or huffing and puffing. Food or some other object that is puffed is expanded with air. Something that is puffed up is inflated or exaggerated.

A puffball is a type of fungus with a round, ball-shaped body that releases spores in a dusty cloud when mature and pressed or struck. Children delight in stepping on them. Figuratively, puffball describes anything soft, round, and fluffy: {a puffball of white fur}, {puffball sleeves}.

Puffballs are round fungi that release clouds of spores when mature and disturbed—squeeze one and it puffs. They grow in fields and forests, some species edible when young and white inside. The word extends to anything similarly round and puffy: a puffball skirt billows out, a puffball dog breed has fluffy fur.

Puffed describes something swollen with air or inflated beyond its usual size. Puffed {sleeves} billow outward; puffed {rice} has been expanded by heat and pressure. Someone puffed from exertion is out of breath: {He arrived puffed after climbing the stairs}. To be puffed {up} is to be swollen with pride or self-importance.

A puffer is a fish that inflates itself into a spiny ball when threatened—also called a pufferfish or blowfish. The word extends to anything that puffs: a puffer jacket is quilted outerwear filled with insulating material that gives it a puffy appearance. In slang, a puffer can be an asthma inhaler or someone who smokes.

A pufferfish is a fish that inflates itself into a spiny ball when threatened, deterring predators. Many species contain tetrodotoxin, a potent poison—yet pufferfish is considered a delicacy in Japan (as fugu), where specially licensed chefs prepare it to avoid the toxic organs. {The pufferfish puffed up the moment I touched the tank.}

Puffery is exaggerated praise or promotion, especially in advertising—claims so obviously overblown that no reasonable person would take them literally. {The best coffee in the world} or {nothing runs like a Deere} qualify as puffery rather than false advertising because they're understood as opinion, not fact. The word carries a deflating connotation: calling something puffery dismisses it as empty bluster.

A puffin is a stocky seabird with a large, colorful bill, black and white plumage, and bright orange feet. Puffins nest in coastal cliffs and spend most of their lives at sea. Their distinctive appearance—often compared to a clown or parrot—has made them popular symbols of northern coastal regions: {We saw puffins nesting on the cliffs of Iceland}.

Puffing is breathing in short, labored bursts, as after exertion: {He arrived puffing and out of breath}. It extends to anything that emits air or smoke in bursts—a steam engine puffing along, someone puffing on a cigarette. Puffing also means inflating or promoting extravagantly: {puffing up his credentials}, {puffing a new product}. In legal contexts, puffing is exaggerated sales talk not meant as factual claims.

Puffins are seabirds of the auk family, recognizable by their stocky bodies, black-and-white plumage, and colorful triangular bills that become brighter during breeding season. They nest in burrows on coastal cliffs and spend most of their lives at sea. The Atlantic puffin is sometimes called the "clown of the sea" for its distinctive face markings.

A puffling is a baby puffin—the downy chick of the seabird known for its colorful beak. The word follows the common pattern of adding -ling to form diminutives for young animals. Pufflings are born in burrows and eventually make their way to the sea: {Every year, volunteers in Iceland rescue disoriented pufflings that wander into town}.

Puffs are short bursts of air, breath, or smoke: {She took a few puffs on the cigarette}. The word extends to anything light and airy—a cream puff, a powder puff, a puff pastry. A puff piece is promotional writing disguised as journalism. To puff is to breathe heavily or emit short bursts: {He puffed up the stairs}. To puff up is to swell or inflate, literally or with pride.

Puffy describes something swollen, inflated, or puffed up with air. Eyes get puffy from crying or lack of sleep. A puffy jacket is quilted and filled with insulating material. Puffy clouds look soft and rounded. Puffy {sleeves} billow out from the shoulder. The word suggests temporary inflation rather than permanent bulk.

A pug is a small dog breed with a wrinkled face, short muzzle, and curled tail. The breed originated in China and became popular as a companion dog. Pug also refers to clay that has been mixed and kneaded for pottery, or the act of preparing it: {She pugged the clay before throwing}. A pug nose is short and slightly flattened.

Pugs is the plural of pug, a small breed of dog with a flat face, wrinkled brow, and curled tail. The breed originated in China and became popular as a companion dog. {She has two pugs that follow her everywhere.} The compact, sturdy build and expressive face give pugs a distinctive appearance.

Puke is vomit—the noun and the verb. To puke is to throw up: {I think I'm going to puke}. The word is informal but not particularly vulgar, common among children and adults alike. Puke can express disgust figuratively: {This movie makes me want to puke}. A puke is also, informally, a disgusting person.

Puked is the past tense of puke, meaning to vomit. The word is informal but not vulgar: {He puked all over the bathroom floor}. Like vomit, it extends to disgust or rejection: {The system puked when I tried to upload the file}.

Pukes is the third-person singular of puke, meaning to vomit: {She pukes every time she rides in the backseat}. As a noun, pukes are instances of vomiting or the vomit itself. Puke can also mean a contemptible person: {Those pukes don't deserve your time}.

Puking is vomiting—ejecting stomach contents through the mouth. The word is informal and slightly crude, preferred in casual speech over clinical alternatives: {I was up all night puking}. Someone who looks green or unwell might be described as ready to puke. The sight of something disgusting can make you {want to puke}.

Pull is an important “cause motion” verb, in which the resulting motion is toward the speaker. It is typically the opposite of push: I pulled down a branch and smelled the blossoms. From this, many other meanings arise, such as pulling something behind you so that it moves with you or pulling something out of your pocket toward you. Pull is frequently followed by adverbs of direction, such as pull up in a vehicle or pull off a victory. As a noun, pull represents an act or instance of pulling. Figuratively, it represents influence: She has a lot of pull with the CEO.

A pullback is a withdrawal or retreat, especially of military forces: {The general ordered a pullback from the border region}. In finance, it's a temporary decline in price after a rise: {Traders saw the pullback as a buying opportunity}. The word captures any deliberate stepping back or reduction in activity, intensity, or commitment.

A pulley is a wheel with a grooved rim through which a rope or chain runs, used to lift heavy loads or change the direction of force. Multiple pulleys working together form a block and tackle, which multiplies lifting power: {We rigged a pulley system to hoist the engine out of the car}. The word extends to any similar mechanism in machinery.

Pulleys is the plural of pulley, a wheel with a grooved rim through which a rope or chain runs, used to lift heavy loads or change the direction of force. Simple machines like pulleys reduce the effort needed to raise objects: {The stage crew used pulleys to raise the curtain}. A system of multiple pulleys working together is called a block and tackle.

Pulling is the act of exerting force to move something toward you or in a direction, the opposite of pushing. It extends to drawing or extracting: {pulling weeds}, {pulling a tooth}, {pulling strings} to get favors. In British slang, pulling means successfully attracting a romantic or sexual partner: {He was out pulling last night}. To be {pulling for} someone is to support or root for them.

A pullout is an act of withdrawing or retreating—troops execute a pullout from occupied territory, investors make a pullout from declining markets. It also names removable inserts in publications: {The magazine included a pullout map of the region}. As an adjective, pullout describes things designed to extend or unfold: a pullout {couch}, a pullout {drawer}. In driving, to pull out is to leave a parking space or merge into traffic.

A pullover is a garment, typically a sweater or jersey, that you put on by pulling it over your head rather than buttoning or zipping it: {She grabbed a pullover before heading out}. The term distinguishes these from cardigans and other open-front tops.

Pulls is most often the third-person singular of pull—to move something toward oneself or in a specified direction: {She pulls the door open}, {The tractor pulls the trailer}. A pull is an act of pulling, or something you pull: a {drawer pull}, a {pull tab}. Pull extends to attraction or influence: {The city pulls young people from small towns}, {He has pull with the mayor}. To {pull strings} is to use connections; to {pull off} something is to succeed against odds; to {pull out} is to withdraw.

A pullup is an exercise in which you hang from a bar and pull your body upward until your chin clears the bar: {I can do twenty pullups}. The movement builds upper-body strength, particularly in the back and arms. Also spelled pull-up. A pullup diaper is a disposable training pant that a child can pull on and off like underwear.

Pullups are an exercise in which you hang from a bar and lift your body until your chin clears it, primarily working the back and arms. The term also refers to disposable training pants for toddlers transitioning from diapers: {He's finally in pullups}. In either sense, the word describes something you pull up.

Pulp is soft, wet, shapeless matter—the fleshy interior of fruit, the fibrous material from which paper is made, or anything reduced to mush: {The banana had turned to pulp}. To pulp something is to crush it into this state. Pulp fiction refers to cheap, sensational magazines printed on rough wood-pulp paper, and by extension any lurid or lowbrow entertainment: {a pulp novel}, {pulp horror}. To {beat someone to a pulp} is to pummel them severely.

A pulpit is an elevated platform or lectern in a church from which a minister delivers sermons. The word extends to preaching generally: {He was a powerful voice from the pulpit}. The {bully pulpit} is a position of authority that gives someone a platform to advocate their views—originally describing the U.S. presidency.

Pulpits are raised platforms in churches from which clergy deliver sermons. The pulpit positions the speaker above the congregation, lending authority to religious pronouncements. By extension, {the pulpit} refers to religious teaching or preaching generally: {He used the pulpit to advocate for social justice}. {Bully pulpit} describes any position of influence used to promote views.

Pulps is the verb form of pulp, meaning to reduce something to a soft, wet mass. Paper mills pulp wood; publishers pulp unsold books by grinding them for recycling: {They pulped ten thousand copies of the failed memoir}. The term also names cheap fiction magazines printed on rough wood-pulp paper, popular from the 1920s through 1950s: {He collected old detective pulps}.

Pulpy describes something with the texture or consistency of pulp—soft, moist, and slightly fibrous. Orange juice with pulp is pulpy. Overripe fruit turns pulpy. The word extends to fiction that resembles pulp magazines: sensational, lurid, cheaply entertaining. {The novel had a pulpy noir feel.} A pulpy mass is shapeless and yielding.

A pulsar is a rapidly rotating neutron star that emits beams of electromagnetic radiation from its magnetic poles. As the star spins, these beams sweep across space like a lighthouse, producing regular pulses detectable from Earth—hence the name, from "pulsating star." Pulsars rotate with extraordinary precision, some spinning hundreds of times per second.

Pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation from their magnetic poles. As the star spins, these beams sweep across space like lighthouse beacons, producing regular pulses detectable from Earth. The pulses arrive with such precision that pulsars serve as natural cosmic clocks. {Astronomers discovered the first pulsar in 1967.}

Pulsating describes something that throbs or beats rhythmically, expanding and contracting in a steady pattern. A pulsating heart pumps blood; pulsating music has a strong, driving beat. The word suggests energy and life—something active rather than static: {pulsating lights}, {the pulsating rhythm of the city}. It can describe physical sensation: {a pulsating headache}.

Pulse is two different nouns, plus a verb related to one of them. Your pulse is the rhythmic beat of your heart, as detected in various parts of the body. When your pulse quickens, either it speeds up, or you are a character in a romantic novel getting excited about something. If something pulses (besides your heart), it exhibits rhythmic behavior of some kind. The other noun pulse is a dried legume, such as a lentil or chickpea.

Pulses are the edible seeds of legumes—beans, lentils, chickpeas, and dried peas. The term appears most often in nutrition, agriculture, and international food contexts: {Pulses are a good source of protein}. In everyday American English, people usually say beans or lentils rather than pulses. Separately, pulses is the plural of pulse—rhythmic beats or throbs: {electrical pulses}, {the pulses of light from a strobe}.

Pulsing describes something that beats, throbs, or surges rhythmically. A pulsing vein is visibly throbbing. Pulsing music has a strong, driving beat. Pain that comes in waves is pulsing: {a pulsing headache behind my eyes}. The word suggests vitality and energy—a pulsing city, a pulsing nightclub. Light can pulse: {The cursor sat pulsing on the screen}.

Pulverise means to crush or grind something into fine particles or powder: {The mill pulverises grain into flour}. Figuratively, it means to defeat utterly or demolish: {The team pulverised their opponents 7-0}. British spelling of pulverize.

To pulverize is to crush or grind something into fine particles or powder: {The mill pulverizes grain into flour}. Extended to destruction more broadly—to pulverize an opponent is to defeat them utterly, to pulverize a building is to reduce it to rubble. The word emphasizes thoroughness: what's pulverized isn't just broken but obliterated.

Pulverized means reduced to powder or dust, crushed into fine particles: {The machine pulverized the rocks into gravel}. Figuratively, it means utterly destroyed or defeated: {Our team got pulverized in the semifinals}. The word emphasizes completeness—not just broken, but thoroughly demolished.

Pulverizes means reduces to powder or dust through crushing, grinding, or pounding: {The machine pulverizes rock into fine gravel}. Figuratively, to pulverize is to defeat utterly or destroy: {Our team pulverized the competition}. The word emphasizes thoroughness—what's pulverized isn't just broken but reduced to particles.

Pulverizing is reducing something to powder or dust through crushing, grinding, or pounding. A mortar and pestle pulverizes spices. Industrial machines pulverize rock into gravel. Figuratively, to pulverize is to defeat utterly or destroy: {Our team got pulverized in the playoffs}. The word emphasizes thoroughness—not just breaking but obliterating.

A puma is a large wild cat native to the Americas, also called a cougar or mountain lion. It's the largest cat that can purr but cannot roar. The tawny coat and solitary hunting style make it distinctive among American predators: {A puma was spotted near the hiking trail}. (Capitalized Puma is the sportswear brand.)

Pumas are large wild cats native to the Americas, also called cougars or mountain lions. The plural of puma, these tawny predators range from Canada to South America: {Pumas have been spotted in the foothills recently}. The word comes from Quechua through Spanish.

Pumice is a lightweight volcanic rock, pale and full of holes from gas bubbles trapped as lava cooled rapidly. Its rough, porous texture makes it useful for scrubbing—removing dead skin from feet, cleaning stubborn stains, or smoothing surfaces. As a verb, to pumice is to rub with this stone: {She pumiced her heels in the bath}.

To pummel is to strike repeatedly with the fists, typically in a sustained assault: {The boxer pummeled his opponent against the ropes}. The word extends to any relentless beating—waves pummel a coastline, critics pummel a film. Also spelled pommel, though that spelling more commonly refers to the front part of a saddle or a sword handle.

Pummeled is the past tense of pummel, meaning to strike repeatedly with the fists or other blows: {The boxer pummeled his opponent against the ropes}. Extended uses describe any sustained beating or battering: {Waves pummeled the coastline}, {Critics pummeled the film}. Also spelled pummelled.

Pummeling is the act of striking someone or something repeatedly and forcefully, typically with fists. When a boxer pummels an opponent, she lands blow after blow. The word extends naturally to any sustained assault: {The coastal town took a pummeling from the hurricane}. Sports commentators favor it for lopsided contests where one team thoroughly dominates another. The spelling pummelling is standard in British English.

Pummelled is the past tense of pummel, meaning to strike repeatedly with fists or other blows: {He pummelled the punching bag until his arms ached}. The spelling with double L is standard in British English; Americans typically write pummeled. Figuratively, anything that batters or overwhelms can pummel: {The coast was pummelled by storms all winter}.

Pummelling is the act of striking repeatedly with the fists, or by extension, any sustained beating or battering: {The boxer took a pummelling in the third round}. Figuratively, it describes overwhelming force or criticism: {The stock took a pummelling after earnings}. Also spelled pummeling. The verb is pummel.

A pump is a device that moves fluids using suction, pressure, or a combination of these. Many pumps are natural, like the heart, and many are also made for particular purposes: water pump, gas pump. The verb pump means to use a pump or to move a fluid by means of a pump: Pump the water out of the basement. Pump has taken on figurative meanings. If you move something up and down, as you would the handle of a water pump, the same verb can be used: She said hello and pumped my hand. If you pump someone, you try to elicit information from them.

Pumped describes being filled with energy, excitement, or enthusiasm—like a tire inflated to capacity. Someone who is pumped is ready for action: {I'm so pumped for the concert tonight}. In fitness contexts, pumped describes muscles temporarily enlarged from increased blood flow during exercise: {My arms are totally pumped after that workout}.

Pumpernickel is a dark, dense German bread made from coarsely ground whole rye. It has a slightly sweet, earthy flavor and chewy texture. Traditional pumpernickel is baked slowly for many hours, which gives it its characteristic deep brown color. The American version is often lighter and colored with molasses or cocoa: {a pumpernickel bagel}, {turkey on pumpernickel}.

Pumping is the present participle of pump, covering both literal and figurative uses. Water pumps through pipes; blood pumps through veins; music pumps through speakers. To be pumping means active exertion: {She was pumping iron at the gym}. As an adjective, pumping describes energetic music or atmosphere: {The club was pumping last night}. Pumping also refers to expressing breast milk with a pump.

A pumpjack is the mechanical device used to extract oil from underground wells when natural pressure is insufficient. Its distinctive shape—a pivoting beam that rocks up and down, driving a rod into the earth—dots oil fields worldwide. Also called a nodding donkey, horsehead pump, or beam pump. {Pumpjacks lined the horizon across the Texas plains.}

Pumpjacks are the mechanical devices used to extract oil from underground wells, recognizable by their distinctive rocking motion—a counterweighted beam pivoting up and down like a drinking bird. They dot oil-producing landscapes across Texas, Oklahoma, and other petroleum regions. Also called nodding donkeys, horsehead pumps, or beam pumps: {Pumpjacks lined the horizon as far as we could see}.

A pumpkin is a large, round, orange squash with a thick rind and pulpy interior full of seeds. Native to North America, pumpkins are harvested in autumn and strongly associated with fall traditions, particularly Halloween jack-o'-lanterns and Thanksgiving pie. The word is also used as a term of endearment, especially for children: {Come here, pumpkin}. In informal usage, a pumpkin can describe someone unsophisticated, and {pumpkin spice} has become a ubiquitous autumn flavor profile.
