Regimens is the plural of regimen, a systematic plan or routine followed to achieve a specific goal. The word appears most often in health contexts: a fitness {regimen}, a skincare {regimen}, a medication {regimen}. Any structured course of action can be a regimen: {She follows a strict study regimen before exams}. The word implies discipline and regularity.

A regiment is a military unit, typically consisting of several battalions under a single commander. The word extends to any large, organized group: {a regiment of volunteers}. To regiment is to organize rigidly or impose strict order: {The school regimented every hour of the students' day}. Regimented schedules, environments, or lives follow strict, uniform patterns.

Regimented describes something organized according to strict rules or rigid structure. A regimented {schedule} leaves no room for spontaneity. A regimented {diet} follows precise portions and timing. The word comes from regiment, the military unit, and carries connotations of discipline imposed from above—order that may feel oppressive rather than helpful: {The school's regimented approach stifled creativity}.

Regiments is the plural of regiment, a military unit typically commanded by a colonel, larger than a battalion but smaller than a brigade. The word extends to any large, organized group: {regiments of volunteers showed up to help}. As a verb, to regiment is to organize rigidly or impose strict discipline: {The school regimented every hour of the students' day}. Regimented schedules, lifestyles, or systems leave little room for flexibility or individual choice.

Regimes is the plural of regime, a word for a system of government or administration, often one that is authoritarian or oppressive: {The regime cracked down on dissent}. The term extends to any systematic way of doing things, particularly health-related routines: {exercise regimes}, {dietary regimes}. In scientific contexts, regimes describe prevailing conditions or patterns: {weather regimes}, {flow regimes}. The word carries a slightly formal or clinical tone compared to alternatives like system or routine.

A region is an area distinguished from others by some characteristic—geographic, political, cultural, or administrative. The {Midwest region} shares climate and culture. A {wine region} produces distinctive grapes. In anatomy, a region is a part of the body: {the lumbar region}. Regional means belonging to or characteristic of a particular region: {regional accents}, {regional cuisine}.

Regional describes something relating to or characteristic of a particular geographic area rather than a whole country or the world: {regional dialects}, {regional cuisine}, {a regional accent}. It often implies a scope larger than local but smaller than national: {regional news coverage}, {regional manager}. In medicine, regional anesthesia numbs a specific body area rather than producing unconsciousness.

Regions are areas distinguished from surrounding territory by particular characteristics—geography, climate, politics, or culture. The {Midwest region} shares agricultural identity; {wine regions} share growing conditions. A region of the body is a general area: {the abdominal region}. Regions can be administrative divisions or simply zones with common features: {mountainous regions}, {conflict regions}.

The verb register has some overlap in meaning with record, but register suggests both officialness and endurance. If you register a trademark or a domain name on the internet, you have the sole legal use of it. When voters register, they become part of the official list of voters. The noun register denotes records of registrations. A cash register, in addition to holding money, may keep track of or transmit transactions. The Federal Register is a government publication that disseminates government notices.

Registered means officially recorded or enrolled. A registered {voter} appears on electoral rolls. A registered {nurse} holds certified credentials. Registered {mail} is tracked through the postal system. To be registered for something is to be signed up: {Are you registered for the conference?} The word implies formal documentation that confers status or provides proof.

Registering is the present participle of register, covering its range of meanings. To register is to record officially: {registering voters}, {registering a complaint}. Instruments register measurements: {The thermometer was registering below zero}. Emotions register on faces when they become visible. When something registers, it sinks in or makes an impression: {It took a moment for the news to register}.

Registers covers several related ideas about recording, range, and formality. A register is an official record or list: a {register of voters}, a {cash register} that records sales. To register is to record formally: {register a car}, {register for classes}, {register a complaint}. Something that registers makes an impression: {The news didn't register at first}. In music and linguistics, register means the range of a voice or instrument, or a level of formality in speech—you use different registers talking to your boss versus your friends. Heating vents that control airflow are also registers.

A registrar is an official responsible for maintaining records. At universities, the registrar oversees student enrollment, grades, and transcripts: {Contact the registrar's office to request your transcript}. In hospitals, a registrar may be a senior doctor in training (British) or an admissions clerk. Registrars also record vital statistics like births and deaths, or manage domain name databases.

Registration is the act or process of entering information into an official record or system: voter registration, vehicle registration, course registration. The word also refers to the document or status that results: {Her registration expires next month}. In music, registration is the combination of organ stops selected to produce a particular sound.

A registry is an official record or list where information is systematically recorded: a {gift registry}, a {voter registry}, a {sex offender registry}. The term also applies to the office or system maintaining such records. In computing, the registry is a database storing configuration settings for an operating system. A ship's registry indicates the country under whose flag it sails.

Regressed is the past tense of regress, meaning to return to an earlier or less developed state. A patient's condition may have regressed after initial improvement. In psychology, to regress is to revert to childlike behavior under stress. In statistics, regressed describes data that has been analyzed through regression: {We regressed income against education level}.

Regressing is moving backward or returning to an earlier state. A patient regresses when their condition worsens after improvement. In psychology, regressing means reverting to childlike or less mature behavior under stress: {She found herself regressing to old habits when anxious}. In statistics, regressing refers to performing regression analysis—modeling the relationship between variables.

Regression is movement backward or return to an earlier state. In psychology, it describes reverting to less mature behavior under stress: {The child's regression included thumb-sucking after the new baby arrived}. In statistics, regression analysis measures relationships between variables, predicting one from others. A regression in progress or development is a setback: {The patient showed regression after initially improving}.

Regret is the feeling of sorrow or disappointment over something that happened or failed to happen: {I regret not spending more time with my father}. As a noun, it names this feeling: {She felt a pang of regret}. In formal contexts, regret expresses polite refusal or apology: {We regret to inform you that your application was unsuccessful}. The plural regrets often appears in declining invitations: {Please send my regrets}.

Regretful describes feeling or expressing regret—sorrow or disappointment about something that happened or didn't happen: {She gave a regretful sigh as she turned down the invitation}. Often confused with regrettable, which describes the thing that causes regret rather than the person feeling it. A regretful person made a regrettable decision.

Regrets are feelings of sorrow or disappointment about something that happened or failed to happen: {I have no regrets about leaving that job}. The word often appears in formal contexts for declining invitations: {She sends her regrets}. To have regrets is human; to live without them, rare.

Regrettable describes something unfortunate or worthy of regret—an outcome, decision, or situation that one wishes had been different: {a regrettable mistake}, {a regrettable loss of life}. The word often appears in formal apologies or official statements, sometimes as understatement: {The incident was regrettable} may acknowledge harm without accepting full blame.

Regretted is the past tense of regret—to feel sorrow or disappointment about something that happened or something you did: {She regretted not saying goodbye}. It can also mean to decline politely: {He regretted that he couldn't attend}.

Regretting is feeling sorrow or disappointment about something that has happened or been done, especially something you wish you could change: {I'm already regretting that second slice of cake}. The word often appears in polite formulas: {We are regretting to inform you that your application was unsuccessful}. Someone regretting a decision is experiencing the emotional aftermath of a choice they now see as wrong.

To regroup is to reorganize after a setback or disruption. Military forces regroup after a failed assault, gathering scattered units to try again. The meaning extends to any recovery of composure or coordination: {Let's regroup after lunch and figure out our next steps}. A company might regroup after losing a major client, reassessing strategy before moving forward.

Regrouping is reorganizing after a setback or disruption. Soldiers regroup after a battle scatters their formation. A team regroups after a loss. The word implies gathering strength or composure before trying again: {Let's regroup and figure out our next move}. In arithmetic, regrouping is the process of borrowing or carrying between place values when adding or subtracting.

To regrow is to grow again after being cut, damaged, or lost. Lizards regrow tails, forests regrow after fires, hair regrows after chemotherapy. The noun regrowth describes this process or its result: {The regrowth of native vegetation took several years}.

Regrowth is the process of growing again after damage, removal, or loss. Hair regrowth follows chemotherapy. Forest regrowth occurs after logging or fire. The word appears in medical, ecological, and cosmetic contexts: {The cream promises to stimulate hair regrowth}. Regrowth can also refer to what has grown back: {New regrowth covered the burned hillside}.

The adjective regular suggests things that are usual and predictable – perhaps predictable because they happen on a regular schedule. If you get regular exercise, you do it reasonably often. A regular meeting is one that happens at the same time every day, week, month, and the like. A regular contributor to a publication is one whose work appears in it frequently. The noun regular is an informal designation of a person or thing that is regular, like a habitual customer of a business: Harry was a regular at the neighborhood bar.

Regularity is the quality of occurring at consistent intervals or following a predictable pattern: {the regularity of the tides}, {She exercises with impressive regularity}. It also describes evenness or uniformity in shape or arrangement: {the regularity of his features}. In digestive contexts, regularity means normal bowel function—a euphemism common in laxative advertising.

Regulars are people who frequent a place habitually—the familiar faces at a bar, café, or gym who show up consistently enough to be recognized: {The bartender knew all the regulars by name}. In military contexts, regulars are professional soldiers in a standing army, as opposed to reserves or militia. Regular as an adjective describes what is normal, standard, or occurring at fixed intervals.

Regulate means to control or maintain something according to rules, standards, or desired conditions. Governments regulate industries; thermostats regulate temperature. The word implies ongoing adjustment rather than one-time intervention: {The body regulates its own temperature}. To regulate can also mean to make regular or orderly: {He regulated his habits after the health scare}.

Regulating is controlling or adjusting something to maintain order, consistency, or compliance with standards. Governments regulate industries; thermostats regulate temperature. {The agency is responsible for regulating food safety}. Regulating implies ongoing oversight rather than a one-time fix—keeping something within acceptable limits or ensuring it functions properly.

Regulation is an official rule or directive issued by an authority to control how something is done. Governments create regulations to govern industries, protect public safety, and enforce standards: {environmental regulations}, {banking regulations}. The word also functions as an adjective meaning conforming to rules or of standard issue: {regulation uniform}, {regulation size}. As a general concept, regulation refers to the act or process of controlling or supervising something: {the regulation of blood sugar}, {temperature regulation}.
clues: Imposed order on how things work

definition: Regulations are official rules issued by an authority to control conduct or procedure. Government agencies create regulations to implement laws: {environmental regulations}, {building regulations}, {safety regulations}. The term often implies bureaucratic requirements that may feel burdensome: {We're drowning in regulations}. Regulation as an adjective means standard or required: {regulation uniform}, {regulation size}.

A regulator is a device or mechanism that controls or maintains something at a desired level: a voltage regulator, a pressure regulator, a thermostat regulating temperature. In institutional contexts, a regulator is a person or agency that oversees an industry or activity to ensure compliance with rules: {The financial regulator imposed new restrictions on lending}. The word implies keeping something within acceptable bounds.

Regulators are devices or people that control, adjust, or maintain something within desired limits. A voltage regulator keeps electrical current steady; a pressure regulator controls gas flow. In government and industry, regulators are agencies or officials who enforce rules: {Federal regulators shut down the bank}. The term often carries connotations of bureaucratic oversight: {Regulators are breathing down our necks}.

Regurgitate means to bring swallowed food back up through the mouth. Some birds regurgitate to feed their young. Extended to mental content, it means to repeat information without processing or understanding it: {Students regurgitate facts for the exam and forget them immediately}. The figurative sense usually carries disapproval—mindless repetition rather than genuine thought.

Regurgitated is the past tense of regurgitate, meaning to bring swallowed food back up—as birds do when feeding their young. By extension, it describes information repeated without thought or understanding: {He just regurgitated what the professor said without adding any insight}. The implication is mechanical reproduction rather than genuine processing or original thought.

Regurgitates is the third-person form of regurgitate, meaning to bring swallowed food back up—some birds regurgitate to feed their young. Extended to liquids or substances expelled from an opening: {The drain regurgitated murky water}. Figuratively, to regurgitate information is to repeat it without understanding or originality: {He just regurgitates whatever he reads online}.

Regurgitating is the present participle of regurgitate—to bring swallowed food back up, as when birds feed their young or when someone vomits. Figuratively, to regurgitate information is to repeat it mechanically without understanding or original thought: {He's just regurgitating what he read online}. The word carries dismissive connotations when applied to speech or writing.

Regurgitation is the act of bringing swallowed food back up—what birds do to feed their young, or what happens when you vomit. The word extends to any mechanical repetition without processing: {The essay was just regurgitation of the textbook}. In medicine, regurgitation also describes blood flowing backward through a faulty heart valve.

Rehab is short for rehabilitation—the process of restoring someone or something to good condition. Most often it refers to treatment programs for addiction: {She checked into rehab for alcohol}. It also applies to physical therapy after injury or surgery, and to renovating buildings: {We bought a fixer-upper and rehabbed it ourselves}.

Rehabbed is the past tense of rehab, meaning restored or renovated. A rehabbed {house} has been fixed up for resale. A rehabbed {knee} has undergone physical therapy. A rehabbed {addict} has completed treatment. The word carries optimism about renewed function or value: {They bought a rehabbed Victorian for half the price of new construction}.

Rehabbing is the process of rehabilitating—restoring something to good condition. Most often it describes renovating run-down properties: {She makes a living rehabbing old houses}. It also refers to recovering from injury or addiction: {He's been rehabbing his knee since the surgery}, {She spent six weeks rehabbing at a treatment center}.

Rehabilitate means to restore to a former condition or capacity. A physical therapist rehabilitates injured athletes. Prisons claim to rehabilitate criminals—preparing them for productive life outside. The word extends to restoring reputation: {The documentary sought to rehabilitate Nixon's legacy}. Buildings and neighborhoods can be rehabilitated through renovation. In all uses, the core idea is bringing something damaged back to acceptable function.

Rehabilitated describes someone or something restored to good condition, reputation, or useful function. A rehabilitated criminal has been reformed and prepared for reintegration into society. A rehabilitated building has been repaired and made functional again. {The rehabilitated osprey was released back into the wild.} {His reputation was eventually rehabilitated after the scandal.}

Rehabilitating is restoring someone or something to a former condition or standing. A physical therapist works on rehabilitating an injured knee. A politician rehabilitates a damaged reputation. Old buildings get rehabilitated for new uses. The word applies equally to criminals being prepared for reentry into society and to restoring the good name of historical figures: {Scholars have spent decades rehabilitating her legacy}.

Rehabilitation is the process of restoring someone or something to a former condition or standing. A criminal undergoes rehabilitation to become a productive member of society. An injured athlete rehabilitates a torn ligament. A disgraced politician seeks rehabilitation of their reputation. The word often shortens to rehab, especially for addiction treatment: {She checked into rehab}. Physical rehabilitation restores function after injury or surgery. Buildings in disrepair undergo rehabilitation to become usable again.

Rehabs is the plural of rehab, a clipped form of rehabilitation. Most often it refers to treatment facilities for addiction: {She's been through three rehabs}. It can also mean rehabilitation programs generally—physical therapy after injury, restoration of buildings, or reform programs for offenders. As a verb, rehabs means renovates or restores: {He rehabs old houses for a living}.

Rehash means to present old material again without meaningful improvement or originality. Someone rehashes arguments, ideas, or content that has already been covered: {The sequel just rehashes the plot of the original}. As a noun, a rehash is the result—a warmed-over version of something: {His speech was a rehash of talking points we've heard before}. The word carries a dismissive tone, suggesting laziness or lack of fresh thinking.

Rehashed describes something presented again without meaningful change—old material warmed over. A rehashed argument offers nothing new. A rehashed movie plot recycles familiar elements. The word carries a dismissive tone, suggesting laziness or lack of originality: {The sequel was just a rehashed version of the first film}. From rehash, to rework old material.

Rehashing is going over old material again, usually without adding anything new. The image is of hash—a dish of chopped, reheated leftovers. To rehash an argument is to repeat it without fresh insight: {They spent the whole meeting rehashing the same complaints}. The noun rehash describes the tired result: {The sequel was just a rehash of the original}.

A rehearsal is a practice session before a performance or event. Actors rehearse plays, musicians rehearse concerts, couples rehearse wedding ceremonies. The word implies preparation for something that will happen formally later: {We have dress rehearsal tomorrow}. By extension, any preliminary run-through can be a rehearsal: {The meeting was just a rehearsal for the real negotiation}.

Rehearsals are practice sessions for a performance—actors running through a play, musicians preparing for a concert, speakers refining a presentation. The word implies repetition aimed at polish: {We have rehearsals every night this week}. A dress rehearsal is a final run-through in full costume. Figuratively, something serving as preparation for a larger event may be called a rehearsal: {The skirmish was a rehearsal for war}.

To rehearse is to practice a performance before presenting it—actors rehearse scenes, musicians rehearse concerts, speakers rehearse presentations. The word extends to any preparatory run-through: {Let me rehearse the plan one more time}. To rehearse can also mean to recount or enumerate: {She rehearsed her grievances at length}.

Rehearsed describes something practiced beforehand rather than spontaneous. A rehearsed {speech} or rehearsed {answer} has been prepared and repeated until polished. The word often carries a note of suspicion—that something presented as natural is actually calculated: {His apology sounded rehearsed}. The opposite is unrehearsed or off-the-cuff.

Rehearsing is practicing something before a performance or presentation. Actors rehearse their lines, musicians rehearse pieces, speakers rehearse speeches. The aim is to work out problems and build confidence before it counts. Rehearsing extends to mental preparation: {She kept rehearsing what she would say when she saw him}.

To reheat is to heat something again, especially food that has cooled: {Reheat the leftovers in the microwave}. The word implies returning something to a previously warm state rather than heating it for the first time.

To rehire is to employ someone again after they previously left or were let go: {The company rehired several workers it had laid off during the pandemic}. As a noun, a rehire is a returning employee: {New hires start Monday; rehires start Tuesday}.

To rehome an animal is to find it a new owner and living situation, typically when the current owner can no longer care for it: {We had to rehome our dog when we moved overseas}. The term is gentler than "give away" and implies responsible placement. Animal shelters and rescue organizations frequently use it: {The shelter rehomed over 200 cats last year}.

Rehomed is the past tense of rehome, meaning to find a new home for a pet or animal that can no longer stay with its current owner: {We rehomed the dog after moving to an apartment that didn't allow pets}. The term emphasizes placement with a new family rather than surrender to a shelter. Sometimes used for children in adoption contexts, though this usage is controversial.

Rehoming is finding a new home for something, almost always a pet. When owners can no longer care for an animal, they rehome it—placing it with a new family rather than surrendering it to a shelter: {We had to rehome our dog when we moved abroad}. The term sounds gentler than "giving away" and implies careful placement rather than abandonment.

Reign is the period during which a monarch rules: {the reign of Queen Victoria}, {during the king's reign}. By extension, any dominant period of control or influence: {His reign as champion lasted five years}. To reign is to rule as sovereign, or to prevail as the dominant force: {Chaos reigned after the announcement}. {The reigning champion} is the current titleholder.

Reigning describes whoever currently holds a title or position of dominance. A reigning {monarch} sits on the throne now. A reigning {champion} has not yet been defeated. The reigning {theory} is the one most widely accepted at present. The word emphasizes current status rather than the act of ruling: {the reigning world record holder}.

Reignite means to ignite again—literally to restart a fire or flame that has gone out. The word appears most often in figurative contexts: reigniting a {romance}, reigniting {tensions}, reigniting {debate}. {The comments reignited controversy over the policy.} The sense is of something dormant flaring back to life.

Reignited is the past tense of reignite—to light again something that had gone out, or to revive something that had faded. A fire reignites when embers catch fresh fuel. More often figurative: {The controversy reignited after new evidence emerged}. {Their romance reignited years later}. The prefix re- emphasizes resumption after a period of dormancy.

Reigns is the third-person singular of reign—to rule as monarch or hold dominant position. A king reigns over his kingdom; a champion reigns until defeated. {She reigns supreme in her field.} The noun reign is a period of rule: {during the reign of Elizabeth II}. Figuratively, anything dominant reigns: {Chaos reigns}, {Silence reigned}.

Reiki is an alternative healing practice in which a practitioner channels energy through their hands to promote physical or emotional well-being. Developed in Japan in the early twentieth century, it involves light touch or hovering hands over the body: {She went for a reiki session to help with her anxiety}. The practice has no scientific basis but remains popular in wellness communities. (Capitalized Reiki is the standard form.)

Reimagine means to think about something in a fundamentally new way, envisioning it differently from how it currently exists or has traditionally been understood. The word implies creative rethinking rather than minor adjustment: {The director reimagined the classic fairy tale as a dystopian thriller}. Common in marketing and arts contexts, reimagine can sound grandiose when applied to modest changes.

Reimagining is the act of rethinking or reconceiving something in a fundamentally new way. The word appears frequently in discussions of creative adaptations: a reimagining of a classic film, a reimagining of the healthcare system. Unlike a remake or revision, reimagining suggests a more radical departure from the original—keeping the essence while transforming the form: {The director's reimagining of Hamlet sets the play in a corporate boardroom}.

To reimburse is to pay someone back for money they've spent: {The company will reimburse you for travel expenses}. The word implies restoring funds to someone who paid out of pocket on another's behalf. It's more formal than "pay back" and typically appears in business, legal, or insurance contexts: {Submit your receipts to be reimbursed}.

Reins are the straps attached to a horse's bridle that the rider holds to control direction and speed. This concrete meaning extends to figurative control over anything: if you {take the reins}, you assume control; if you {hand over the reins}, you cede it. To rein something {in} is to restrain or slow it down, like pulling back on a horse. {Free rein} means unrestricted liberty to act. The spelling is often confused with reign, which concerns monarchs rather than horses.

To reincarnate is to be reborn in a new body after death—a belief central to Hinduism, Buddhism, and other traditions. The word applies literally to souls entering new physical forms and figuratively to things that return in transformed versions: {The old theater was reincarnated as a nightclub}. As an adjective, reincarnate describes someone believed to be a soul reborn: {a reincarnate lama}.

Reincarnated means reborn in a new body or form. In religious traditions like Hinduism and Buddhism, souls are reincarnated after death into different physical forms. The word extends to secular rebirth or transformation: {The failed restaurant was reincarnated as a trendy bar}. Someone may joke they were a cat or a king {in a past life}, playing on reincarnation beliefs.

Reincarnates means to be reborn in a new body or form after death. In Hindu and Buddhist traditions, the soul reincarnates across many lifetimes. The word extends to secular rebirth: {The show reincarnates as a podcast}, {She reincarnates herself with each new album}. Someone or something that reincarnates appears in a new version while retaining essential identity.

Reincarnating is being reborn in a new body or form after death, according to beliefs held in Hinduism, Buddhism, and other traditions. The term extends to any dramatic transformation or revival: {The company is reincarnating itself as a tech startup}. Something reincarnating returns in a new guise while retaining essential identity.

Reincarnation is the belief that after death, a soul is reborn in a new body. The concept is central to Hinduism, Buddhism, and other Eastern religions, where the cycle continues until spiritual liberation is achieved. More loosely, reincarnation describes any return in a new form: {The restaurant is a reincarnation of a beloved neighborhood diner that closed in 2019}.

Reincarnations are instances of rebirth into new bodies or forms. In Hindu and Buddhist belief, the soul passes through successive reincarnations until achieving spiritual liberation. The word extends to any dramatic transformation or revival: {The band has gone through several reincarnations since the 1980s}. A reincarnation of someone suggests they embody that person's essence: {She's the reincarnation of her grandmother}.

Reindeer are large deer native to Arctic and subarctic regions, with both males and females growing antlers. They're the same species as caribou, though reindeer typically refers to domesticated or semi-domesticated populations in Europe and Asia, while caribou applies to wild North American herds. Reindeer have been herded for centuries by indigenous peoples for meat, milk, and transport. In popular culture, reindeer pull Santa's sleigh: {Rudolph the red-nosed reindeer}.

To reinforce is to strengthen or support something. You reinforce a structure by adding material, reinforce an argument by adding evidence, or reinforce a military position by sending more troops. In psychology, to reinforce behavior is to encourage its repetition through reward or response: {Praising children reinforces good habits}. The spelling reenforce is rare but acceptable.

Reinforced describes something that has been strengthened or supported, typically by adding material or structure. Reinforced {concrete} contains steel bars or mesh for added tensile strength. Reinforced {stitching} uses extra thread or layers to prevent tearing. The word implies deliberate fortification against stress or failure: {reinforced security measures}, {reinforced packaging}.

Reinforcement is anything that strengthens or supports. Troops sent as reinforcement bolster existing forces. Steel reinforcement inside concrete prevents cracking. In psychology, reinforcement is a consequence that increases the likelihood of a behavior recurring—positive reinforcement adds something desirable {The dog got a treat}, while negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant. The plural reinforcements usually means additional personnel or supplies: {We need to hold out until reinforcements arrive}.

Reinforcements are additional troops, personnel, or supplies sent to strengthen a force already engaged. The word almost always appears in plural: {We need to call for reinforcements}. The singular reinforcement refers to the act of strengthening something or the material used to do so—rebar provides reinforcement in concrete, and positive reinforcement encourages desired behavior through rewards.

Reins are the straps attached to a horse's bridle, held by the rider to guide and control the animal. The word extends to any means of control or direction: {hand over the reins}, {take the reins of government}. To {rein in} something is to restrain or check it: {The company reined in spending}. A {free rein} allows unrestricted action.

To reinstate is to restore someone or something to a former position, condition, or authority. An employee fired unjustly may be reinstated with back pay. A suspended license gets reinstated when conditions are met. {The court ordered the company to reinstate the workers.} {Her membership was reinstated after she paid the overdue fees.}

Reinstated is the past tense of reinstate, meaning to restore someone or something to a former position, rank, or condition. An employee fired unfairly may be reinstated after an appeal. A suspended license gets reinstated when requirements are met. {The court reinstated the original ruling.} {She was reinstated as team captain after the investigation cleared her.}

Reinstatement is the act of restoring someone or something to a former position, condition, or status. An employee fired unfairly may seek reinstatement to their job. A suspended license undergoes reinstatement when the penalty period ends. The word implies returning to a state that previously existed: {The court ordered his reinstatement with back pay}.

Reintegration is the process of bringing someone or something back into a whole from which they were separated. The word appears most often in contexts involving people who have been away from mainstream society—prisoners returning to civilian life, soldiers coming home from deployment, or refugees resettling in their homeland. {The program focuses on the reintegration of former gang members into their communities.} The emphasis is on rejoining and becoming a functioning part of the group again, not merely returning to it.

To reinterpret is to interpret something again, usually arriving at a different understanding than before. A court may reinterpret a statute in light of new circumstances. Artists reinterpret classic works, giving them fresh meaning: {The director reinterpreted Hamlet as a corporate power struggle}. The word implies not just revisiting but actively reconsidering—finding new significance in familiar material.

Reinterpretation is a new or different understanding of something previously interpreted another way. A director offers a reinterpretation of a classic play. A court's reinterpretation of a law changes how it applies. {Her reinterpretation of the data challenged the original study's conclusions.} The word implies the original interpretation was incomplete, outdated, or wrong.

Reinterpreted is the past tense of reinterpret—to understand or present something in a new way. A director reinterprets a classic play for modern audiences. A court reinterprets a statute. Scientists reinterpret data in light of new findings. The word implies revision rather than discovery: {The museum reinterpreted its colonial-era exhibits to include perspectives of the colonized}.

Reintroductions are instances of bringing something back after a period of absence. In conservation, the term typically refers to releasing animals or plants into habitats where they once lived but had disappeared: {Wolf reintroductions in Yellowstone transformed the ecosystem}. The word applies more broadly to any return of something previously withdrawn—a discontinued product, a lapsed policy, or a person rejoining a group after time away.

To reinvent something is to make it over completely, creating a substantially new version: {The company reinvented itself as a tech startup}. To {reinvent the wheel} is to waste effort duplicating something that already exists in good form. When people reinvent themselves, they transform their identity, career, or public image: {She reinvented herself after the divorce}.

Reinventing is finding radically new approaches to something that already exists. You might reinvent a business model, a genre, or yourself after a major life change. The phrase {reinventing the wheel} criticizes wasted effort on problems already solved: {Don't reinvent the wheel—just use the existing template}.

Reinvention is the act of remaking something—or oneself—in a substantially new form. A company might undergo reinvention after near bankruptcy. American culture celebrates personal reinvention: the executive who becomes a yoga instructor, the addict who becomes a counselor. {Madonna built her career on constant reinvention.} The word implies transformation thorough enough that the result feels like something new rather than merely improved.

Reinventions are acts of remaking or transforming something—or oneself—in a fundamentally new way. A company undergoes reinventions to stay relevant; a celebrity's career reinventions keep the public interested. The word emphasizes deliberate, often dramatic change rather than gradual evolution: {Her musical reinventions surprised fans with each album}.

Reinvest means to put money back into something rather than taking it out. Investors reinvest dividends by using them to buy more shares rather than pocketing the cash: {We reinvested our profits into expanding the business}. The term implies a cycle—earnings from an investment become fuel for further investment.

Reinvesting is putting money back into something rather than withdrawing it. Investment earnings can be reinvested to compound growth: {We reinvested the dividends}. The term applies beyond finance—reinvesting time, energy, or resources into a project means committing them again after an initial effort: {She's reinvesting in her education}.

To reissue something is to release it again—a book brought back into print, a stamp reprinted, a passport renewed, a classic album released with new packaging or bonus tracks. The noun reissue names the thing itself: {I bought the remastered reissue of their debut album}. The word implies the original had gone out of circulation or needed updating.

Reissues are new releases of previously published material—books, albums, films, stamps, or other items—often with updates, restorations, or additional content: {The reissue includes bonus tracks and remastered audio}. To reissue is to release again: {The label reissued her debut album on vinyl}.

To reject is to refuse to accept, consider, or use something. A publisher rejects a manuscript; a body rejects a transplanted organ; a suitor gets rejected. The noun reject (stress on the first syllable) is a person or thing deemed unacceptable: {factory rejects sold at discount}, {He felt like a reject after being cut from the team}. Rejection stings because it implies not meeting some standard.

Rejected describes something or someone that has been refused, dismissed, or turned away. A rejected {manuscript} didn't find a publisher. A rejected {suitor} was turned down romantically. A rejected {organ} is attacked by the recipient's immune system. The word often carries emotional weight—feeling rejected implies not just refusal but a blow to self-worth: {He felt rejected after they excluded him from the group}.

Rejecting is the act of refusing, dismissing, or declining to accept something or someone. A body may be rejecting a transplanted organ. A person may be rejecting an offer, an idea, or a suitor: {She's rejecting every candidate we put forward}. The word often carries emotional weight—being rejected stings more than simply being turned down.

Rejection is the act of refusing, dismissing, or turning something away. A job applicant faces rejection when not hired. A romantic rejection means someone declines your advances: {I finally worked up the nerve to ask her out, but the rejection stung}. In medicine, organ rejection occurs when the body's immune system attacks transplanted tissue as foreign. The feeling of rejection—being unwanted or excluded—can cut deep: {He struggled with rejection his whole life}.

Rejections is the plural of rejection—instances of being turned down, refused, or dismissed. The word appears most often in contexts of romantic pursuit, job applications, and creative submissions: {After dozens of rejections, she finally found a publisher}. A rejection can sting whether it comes from a person, an institution, or an immune system rejecting a transplant.

Rejects are things or people that have been refused, discarded, or deemed unacceptable. Factory rejects are products that fail quality standards. Social rejects are people excluded from groups: {The lunch table was full of misfits and rejects}. As a verb (re-JECT), to reject is to refuse or dismiss: {She rejected his proposal}, {The body rejected the transplant}.

Rejoice is to feel or express great joy or delight: {The whole town rejoiced when the team won the championship}. It often appears in religious or formal contexts: {Rejoice, for the Lord is risen}. The word carries more weight than simply being happy—it suggests celebration or exultation, sometimes shared with others.

Rejoiced is the past tense of rejoice, meaning to feel or express great joy or delight. The word carries a note of celebration or triumph: {The crowd rejoiced when the verdict was announced}. It often appears in religious or formal contexts: {They rejoiced at the news of his safe return}.

Rejoicing is the expression of great joy or celebration. It functions as both a noun and a verb form: {There was much rejoicing when the team won} describes the celebratory response, while {The crowd was rejoicing in the streets} captures the act itself. The word has a slightly formal or literary quality, often appearing in religious contexts or ceremonial announcements.

Rejoin means to join again after separation: {She rejoined her friends after the phone call}, {He rejoined the company after two years away}. A separate word spelled the same way means to reply sharply or wittily—a rejoinder. This sense is formal and uncommon: {She rejoined that the criticism was unfair}.

To rejuvenate is to make young again or restore youthful vigor. A vacation might rejuvenate someone exhausted by work. Skincare products claim to rejuvenate aging skin. The word applies broadly to renewal: {The new funding rejuvenated the struggling program}. Cities rejuvenate neglected neighborhoods; rest rejuvenates the spirit.

Rejuvenated means made to feel or look young again, or restored to a former state of vitality. A person feels rejuvenated after a vacation or a good night's sleep. The word applies equally to things: {The downtown area has been rejuvenated by new investment}. The sense is always of renewal—energy, appearance, or function brought back to life.

Rejuvenates means makes young again or restores vitality. The word applies to people, skin, energy levels, or anything that can be refreshed: {A good night's sleep rejuvenates the mind}. Products claim to rejuvenate aging skin. A renovation rejuvenates a tired neighborhood. The effect is renewal—returning something closer to its original vigor.

Rejuvenating describes something that restores youthful energy, freshness, or vitality. A rejuvenating {nap} leaves you feeling restored. Rejuvenating {skincare} promises to reverse signs of aging. The word applies broadly to anything that refreshes or renews: a rejuvenating {vacation}, a rejuvenating {conversation}, a rejuvenating {rain} after drought.

Rejuvenation is the process of making something young again or restoring it to a fresher, more vital state. The word applies to physical restoration—{a facial rejuvenation procedure}—and to broader renewal: {the rejuvenation of a declining neighborhood}, {economic rejuvenation}. Urban planners speak of rejuvenation projects; skincare brands promise it in a bottle.

To rekindle is to light again something that has gone out—a fire, a flame. The word appears most often in figurative contexts: to rekindle a {romance}, rekindle {interest}, rekindle {hope}. The implication is that the original spark never fully died, just needed stirring back to life.

Rekindled is the past tense of rekindle—to light again something that had gone out, or to revive something that had faded. A dying fire can be rekindled with fresh wood. More often the word is figurative: {They rekindled their romance after twenty years apart}. Old friendships, interests, and passions are commonly rekindled.

Rekindling is reviving something that had faded or gone out. The literal sense involves fire: {rekindling the embers of last night's campfire}. More often the word appears figuratively for relationships, interests, or emotions that have lapsed: {rekindling an old romance}, {rekindling her passion for painting}. The image is of coaxing dormant coals back to flame.

Rekt is internet slang for wrecked—utterly defeated, destroyed, or humiliated. It originated in gaming culture to describe crushing losses: {Get rekt, noob}. The deliberately misspelled form intensifies the mockery. Usage has spread beyond gaming to describe any severe defeat or failure: {The stock tanked and I got absolutely rekt}.

Relapse is a return to a worse condition after improvement. A patient relapses when illness returns after recovery seemed underway. The word appears most often in contexts of addiction—someone who had been sober relapses by drinking or using again: {She relapsed after six months clean}. The noun names the event itself: {a relapse into depression}.

Relapsed is the past tense of relapse—to fall back into a previous condition, especially an undesirable one. Most often it describes returning to illness after apparent recovery {She relapsed after six months in remission} or returning to addiction after a period of sobriety {He relapsed and started drinking again}. The word carries a sense of setback or failure to maintain progress.

Relapses are returns to a previous, usually worse condition after a period of improvement. A patient relapses when symptoms return after apparent recovery. An addict relapses when returning to substance use after sobriety: {She had two relapses before achieving lasting recovery}. The word implies setback—ground gained, then lost.

Relapsing means falling back into a former state, especially an undesirable one. Someone recovering from addiction who starts using again is relapsing. A disease that returns after apparent recovery is a relapsing illness. {She was doing well for months before relapsing}. The word implies a return to something one had escaped or overcome.

Relatability is the quality of being easy to identify with or understand through shared experience. A character's relatability makes audiences connect emotionally; a speaker's relatability helps their message land. The word emerged from marketing and entertainment contexts but now appears broadly: {The memoir's relatability comes from its honest portrayal of failure}. Something with high relatability feels familiar rather than distant.

Relatable describes something others can identify with or see themselves in. A relatable {character} feels familiar; a relatable {story} echoes common experience. The word has surged in popularity, especially online, where users declare content relatable when it captures shared feelings or situations: {That meme is so relatable}. Critics sometimes dismiss it as overused, but its spread reflects genuine demand for a word that names this particular resonance.

Relate means to tell or recount: {She related the events of that night}. More commonly, it means to connect or establish a link between things: {How does this relate to what we discussed earlier?} To relate to someone is to understand or empathize with their experience: {I can really relate to that}. Things that relate share a connection; people who are related share ancestry.

Related means connected by blood, marriage, or common origin: {Are you two related?} The word extends to any meaningful connection between things: {related topics}, {related industries}. Something related to a subject bears on it or concerns it: {expenses related to the move}. Distantly related things share ancestry or origin but have diverged considerably.

Relation is a connection between things or people. Two quantities have a relation when one affects or corresponds to the other. People related by blood or marriage are relations: {She's a distant relation on my mother's side}. Relations between countries or groups describes their dealings and attitudes toward each other: {diplomatic relations}, {labor relations}. Sexual relations is a formal term for intercourse. In relation to means concerning or compared with.

Relations are the connections between people, groups, or nations. Diplomatic relations exist between countries; race relations concern how ethnic groups interact. The state of relations can be good or strained: {Relations between the two families had soured}. Relations also means relatives: {She has relations in Ohio}. To have relations with someone is a formal or euphemistic way of saying to have sex.

A relationship is a connection between people or things. The word often implies a romantic or sexual partnership: {Are you in a relationship?} But relationships exist wherever there's a meaningful link—between family members, friends, colleagues, or countries. You might examine the relationship between cause and effect, or between income and happiness. The nature of the connection shapes what kind of relationship it is.

Relationships are connections between people—how they relate to one another. The word covers the full range: family relationships, romantic relationships, professional relationships. Used alone, it often implies romantic involvement: {Are you in a relationship?} {They've been in a relationship for three years}. The plural sometimes refers to interpersonal skills generally: {She's good at relationships}.

Relative describes something considered in relation to something else rather than absolutely: {The relative merits of the two candidates}. What counts as cold is relative—frigid in Texas, mild in Minnesota. A relative is a person connected by blood or marriage: {She's a distant relative on my mother's side}. In grammar, relative pronouns (who, which, that) relate clauses to nouns they modify.

Relatives are people connected by blood or marriage—your family members. The word covers the full range from immediate family (parents, siblings, children) to distant cousins and in-laws: {We're having relatives over for Thanksgiving}. As an adjective, relative means considered in relation to something else rather than absolutely: {The relative merits of each approach}. {Everything is relative.}

Relativism is the view that truth, morality, or knowledge exists only in relation to culture, society, or individual perspective—that there are no absolute or universal standards. Moral relativism holds that ethical judgments vary legitimately across cultures: {What's considered wrong here may be acceptable elsewhere}. Cultural relativism suspends judgment when studying other societies. Critics use relativism dismissively to suggest someone lacks firm principles: {His relativism means he won't take a stand on anything}.

Relativity is the condition of being relative—dependent on perspective or frame of reference rather than absolute. In physics, Einstein's theories of relativity describe how measurements of space, time, and motion depend on the observer's position and velocity. Special relativity addresses objects moving at constant speeds; general relativity extends this to gravity and acceleration. Outside physics, relativity often means that judgments vary by context: {Morality has a certain relativity across cultures}. The casual use can imply that nothing is fixed or universally true.

To relaunch is to launch again—typically a product, brand, campaign, or publication that has been revised, rebranded, or allowed to fade before being brought back: {The magazine relaunched with a new editor and redesigned format}. A relaunch implies more significant changes than a simple restart; it suggests a fresh attempt to succeed where an earlier version struggled or circumstances have changed.

Relax means to become less tense, rigid, or anxious. Muscles relax after exertion; a person relaxes after a stressful day. To relax rules or standards is to make them less strict: {The company relaxed its dress code}. As a command, {relax} tells someone to calm down or stop worrying. A relaxed atmosphere is comfortable and informal.

Relaxation is the state of being free from tension, whether physical or mental. Muscles relax after exertion; people relax after stress. {A hot bath is my favorite form of relaxation.} The word also applies to rules or restrictions that become less strict: {a relaxation of border controls}. In physics, relaxation describes a system returning to equilibrium after being disturbed.

Relaxed describes a state of ease, free from tension or anxiety. A relaxed {atmosphere} feels comfortable and informal. Relaxed {muscles} are loose rather than tight. Someone with a relaxed {attitude} doesn't get worked up easily. Relaxed {rules} or {standards} are less strict than usual: {The dress code is pretty relaxed here}.

Relaxing describes something that reduces tension and promotes calm. A relaxing activity, environment, or experience allows stress to melt away: {After a long week, I just want a relaxing evening at home}. The word functions as both a present participle of relax and as a standalone adjective. What counts as relaxing varies wildly by person—some find a hot bath relaxing while others need vigorous exercise to unwind.

A relay is the passing of something along a chain—runners in a relay race, workers in shifts, signals through a network. To relay information is to receive it and pass it on: {Can you relay a message to her?} A relay is also an electrical switch that uses a small current to control a larger one, fundamental to circuits and early computing.

Relays are devices or acts of passing something along. An electrical relay is a switch activated by a signal from another circuit—a small current controlling a larger one. A relay race has team members taking turns, each handing off to the next: {She ran the anchor leg in the 4x100 relay}. To relay information is to receive it and pass it on: {Can you relay a message to the team?} The word captures any system where something moves through intermediate stages rather than directly.

Relearning is the process of learning something again after having forgotten it or after time away. Skills and knowledge often return faster the second time: {After years without practice, relearning piano took less time than she expected}. The term also applies to replacing old habits or beliefs with new ones: {relearning how to trust after betrayal}.

The noun and verb release denotes a change of condition, typically from captivity to freedom, but with much extended use. To release a prisoner is to set her free. When someone releases a report or statement, it becomes publically available. Musicians release albums when they are ready for sale. A release is the act or instance of releasing, or the product of it (press release, news release).

Released describes something that has been let go, set free, or made available. A prisoner is released from custody. A movie is released to theaters. Information is released to the public. The past tense of release, it implies prior restraint or containment: {The hostages were finally released after months of negotiation}. {The label released her album last Friday}.

Releases covers acts of letting go or setting free. A prisoner is released from custody; a company releases a new product to the public; a musician drops a new release. To release pressure is to relieve it: {She released her grip on the railing}. In legal contexts, a release is a document surrendering a claim: {Sign the liability release before the tour begins}.

Relegated means sent down to a less important or less prominent position. In British football, a team is relegated when it drops from a higher league to a lower one. More broadly, to relegate something is to assign it to an inferior category or status: {The project was relegated to the back burner}. Often implies dismissal or demotion: {She was relegated to a minor role}.

Relegation is the act of moving something to a lower position, rank, or status. In British football and other sports leagues, relegation is the system by which the worst-performing teams drop to a lower division at season's end: {The club faces relegation if they lose tomorrow}. More broadly, to consign something to relegation is to dismiss it as unimportant: {the relegation of her concerns to a footnote}.

To relent is to soften in attitude or determination, yielding after resistance: {She finally relented and let the kids stay up late}. Often implies abandoning a hard stance under pressure or persuasion. Weather or pain that relents eases up: {The rain showed no sign of relenting}. The word suggests giving way reluctantly rather than enthusiastically.

Relented is the past tense of relent, meaning to soften in attitude or yield after initial resistance. Someone who relents abandons a firm position, usually under pressure or persuasion: {After hours of begging, she finally relented and let the kids stay up late}. The word implies giving in reluctantly rather than changing one's mind enthusiastically.

Relenting is yielding after resistance, softening a hard stance. Someone who relents gives in to pressure or shows mercy where they had been firm: {After hours of begging, she finally relented and let the kids stay up late}. Weather or pain that relents eases up: {The rain showed no sign of relenting}.

Relentless describes something that never stops or lets up. A relentless {pursuit} continues without pause. Relentless {rain} falls hour after hour. The word often carries a negative charge—relentless {pressure}, relentless {criticism}—but can be admiring: {Her relentless dedication finally paid off}. The root is relent, meaning to soften or yield, which the relentless thing refuses to do.

Relentlessly means without stopping, letting up, or showing mercy. Someone who pursues a goal relentlessly refuses to quit despite obstacles: {She relentlessly promoted her book until it hit the bestseller list}. The word often carries a sense of exhausting persistence—pressure that never eases: {The sun beat down relentlessly}. It can shade toward admiration or criticism depending on context.

To relent is to soften in determination or severity, often after initial resistance. Someone who relents yields to pressure, pity, or persuasion: {She finally relented and let the kids stay up late}. Weather or pain that relents eases up: {The rain relented toward evening}. The word implies giving way after holding firm.

Relevance is the quality of being connected to the matter at hand. Evidence has relevance to a case; a comment has relevance to a discussion. Something lacking relevance is beside the point: {I fail to see the relevance of your question}. In the digital age, relevance often describes how well search results or content match what someone is looking for.

Relevant is an adjective that shares some meanings with pertinent and germane. Something relevant is connected with and important to the matter at hand: The investigation has not turned up any relevant information. A relevant authority is one that has responsibility for dealing with a situation: The explosion took place in a rural area and there has been some difficulty determining who is the relevant authority.

Reliability is the quality of being dependable—performing consistently and as expected. A car with good reliability starts every morning. A person's reliability means you can count on them to follow through. In statistics and research, reliability refers to how consistently a measurement produces the same results: {The test showed high reliability across multiple trials}.

Someone or something that is reliable can be depended on: This car is the most reliable one I’ve ever had. Josh is not a reliable source of information because he wasn’t there. If something proves reliable or proves to be reliable, it is successful in a previously unknown way: The system received 50% more use than was predicted and still proved to be completely reliable.

Reliance is dependence on or trust in someone or something: {The company's reliance on a single supplier proved costly}. Self-reliance is the ability to depend on oneself. To place reliance on something is to trust it will hold or deliver: {I wouldn't place much reliance on his promises}.

Reliant describes someone or something that depends on another for support, help, or resources. A child is reliant on parents for basic needs; an economy may be reliant on a single industry. The word often appears with a preposition: {reliant on fossil fuels}, {reliant upon government assistance}. Self-reliant, by contrast, describes someone who depends mainly on their own capabilities and resources.

A relic is something that survives from an earlier time. Religious relics are physical remains of saints or objects associated with them, venerated by the faithful: {a relic of the True Cross}. More broadly, relics are artifacts from the past: {relics of the Roman Empire}. The word often carries connotations of obsolescence—calling something a relic suggests it belongs to a bygone era: {That flip phone is a relic}.

Relics are objects surviving from an earlier time, valued for their age or associations. In religious contexts, relics are remains of saints or sacred items believed to hold spiritual power: {pilgrims came to venerate the relics}. More broadly, anything outdated or obsolete becomes a relic: {These policies are relics of the Cold War}. The singular relic works the same way.

The noun relief is more common than its underlying verb relieve and is closely related to it in meaning. Relief is the result when a person is relieved of something. Relief may also be something offered that is intended to make something easier or more bearable: The U.S. offered disaster relief. In some situations, relief may be mainly symbolic, such as in the form of money when an injustice cannot be undone. The three words most likely to pair up with relief are debt, pain, and tax.

Reliefs is the plural of relief, covering its various senses. Physical reliefs are sculptural works where figures project from a flat background: {The temple walls featured intricate reliefs depicting battle scenes}. Geographic reliefs are variations in land elevation: {a map showing the reliefs of the mountain range}. The word also pluralizes the sense of assistance or aid: {disaster reliefs}, {tax reliefs}.

Relieve means to lessen or remove something unpleasant—pain, pressure, anxiety, boredom. A medication relieves symptoms; a joke relieves tension. To relieve someone is to take over their duties: {The night shift will relieve us at midnight}. In military contexts, to relieve a city is to end its siege. To relieve yourself is a euphemism for urinating or defecating. {What a relief} expresses gratitude when burden lifts.

Relieved describes the feeling when anxiety, worry, or discomfort lifts. You feel relieved when test results come back negative, when a missing child is found, when pain subsides: {I was so relieved to hear you're okay}. The word captures that exhale moment—tension releasing. To be relieved of duty is to be removed from a position, sometimes as punishment.

A reliever is someone or something that provides relief. In baseball, a reliever is a pitcher who enters the game after the starter: {The manager called in a reliever in the seventh inning}. Pain relievers are medications that reduce discomfort. Stress relievers are activities or practices that ease tension.

Relievers are things or people that provide relief. Most commonly, relievers are medications that ease symptoms: pain relievers, headache relievers, asthma relievers. In baseball, relievers are pitchers who enter the game after the starting pitcher, typically to protect a lead or keep the score close: {The manager called in his best reliever for the eighth inning}.

Relieving is the act of easing or lessening something burdensome. A relieving {sigh} follows the release of tension. In workplace contexts, relieving someone means taking over their duties: {The night shift is relieving the day crew}. A relieving {officer} temporarily fills another's position. To relieve oneself is a euphemism for urinating or defecating, so relieving can carry that sense too.

Religion is a systematic way of organizing existential beliefs, such as whether there is life after death, how the universe began, and the purpose of existence. Some religions are based on the teachings of a single spiritual leader; this is the case with Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism. Other religions, such as Judaism and Hinduism, do not identify a single historical figure but instead have developed over millennia from widely-held beliefs.

Religions is the plural of religion—organized systems of belief, worship, and practice centered on the divine or sacred. The word often appears in comparative contexts: {world religions}, {the study of religions}. It can also refer to specific traditions collectively: {The Abrahamic religions share common roots}. Someone who {gets religion} has a sudden conversion or newfound commitment to a cause.

Religious describes connection to or concern with religion—systems of faith, worship, and spiritual practice. A religious {person} holds beliefs about the divine; a religious {text} or {ceremony} belongs to a faith tradition. Extended uses suggest devotion approaching worship: {She's religious about her morning run}. Religious can also mean belonging to a monastic order: {a religious community of nuns}.

Religiously means in a manner relating to religion: {She was raised religiously}. More commonly, it describes doing something with faithful regularity and dedication, as if it were a sacred duty: {He religiously checks his email every morning}, {She exercises religiously}. The figurative sense emphasizes unwavering commitment to a routine or practice.

Relinquish means to give up or let go of something, typically with some reluctance. You relinquish control, power, claims, or possessions: {She relinquished her seat on the board}. The word implies voluntary surrender rather than having something taken by force, though the choice may be pressured: {He was forced to relinquish custody of his children}.

Relinquished is the past tense of relinquish, meaning to give up or let go of something—typically power, control, a claim, or a possession: {She relinquished her seat on the board}. The word suggests voluntary surrender, often reluctantly: {He finally relinquished his grip on the company he'd founded}.

Reliquaries are containers for religious relics—the physical remains of saints or sacred objects. These vessels range from simple boxes to elaborate gold-and-jewel encrusted shrines, designed to honor and display their contents: {The cathedral's reliquary held a fragment of the true cross}. The singular is reliquary.

A reliquary is a container for sacred relics—typically bones, clothing, or objects associated with saints or religious figures. These vessels range from simple boxes to elaborate jeweled shrines, designed to house and display items believed to hold spiritual power. Medieval churches competed to acquire relics and commission ornate reliquaries to attract pilgrims.

Relish is hearty enjoyment or keen appreciation: {She ate with relish}, {He told the story with obvious relish}. To relish something is to enjoy it thoroughly: {I don't relish the thought of telling him}. Relish is also a condiment of chopped pickles or vegetables, typically served with hot dogs and hamburgers: {Do you want relish on that?}

Relished is the past tense of relish, meaning to enjoy or take pleasure in something with appreciation: {She relished every bite of the meal}, {He relished the opportunity to prove himself wrong}. The word suggests savoring rather than merely liking—lingering over the experience.

Relishing is taking keen pleasure or satisfaction in something: {She was relishing every bite of the meal}, {He stood there relishing his victory}. The word suggests savoring an experience fully, not rushing through it. You might be relishing a moment, an opportunity, or someone else's discomfort.

To relive something is to experience it again, especially in memory or imagination: {I relive that moment every time I hear the song}. The word usually applies to past events—you might relive a triumph, a trauma, or a childhood summer. Sometimes relive suggests involuntary recall: {She relives the accident in nightmares}.

Relived is the past tense of relive—to experience something again, especially in memory or imagination: {She relived the accident in her nightmares}, {Watching the footage, he relived every moment of the championship game}. The word often suggests involuntary recall of intense experiences, though it can also describe deliberate revisiting of cherished memories.

To relive something is to experience it again, usually in memory or imagination: {She relived the moment of victory over and over}. The word suggests vivid re-experiencing rather than mere recollection—feeling the emotions and sensations anew. Sometimes used for literal repetition: {He relives the same routine every day}.

Reliving is experiencing something again, especially in memory or imagination. You relive a moment by mentally returning to it with vivid intensity: {I keep reliving that conversation, wishing I'd said something different}. The word often appears with traumatic or emotionally charged events—victims relive attacks, athletes relive victories. To relive something is more immersive than merely remembering it.

To reload is to load again—fresh ammunition into a firearm, a new roll of film into a camera, updated content into a webpage. The word implies something was emptied or depleted and needs replenishing: {I had to reload the dishwasher after the kids did it wrong}. In gaming, reload is constant: {Reload! I'm out of ammo}. To reload a prepaid card is to add funds.

Reloaded is the past tense of reload—to load again. You reload a gun with fresh ammunition, reload a webpage to refresh it, or reload a prepaid card with funds. In gaming, reloading restores ammo or a saved game state. The word gained cultural currency from film sequels: {The Matrix Reloaded}. A reloaded version of something is refreshed, updated, or given new energy.

Reloading is putting fresh ammunition into a firearm or fresh supplies into any device that was emptied: {He ducked behind cover while reloading}. In computing, reloading refreshes a webpage or restarts software. The word also names the hobby of making ammunition by hand—assembling bullets, powder, primers, and casings: {Reloading your own shells saves money at the range}.

Relocate means to move to a new place. The word usually implies a significant move—changing cities, countries, or premises—rather than shifting something across a room: {The company relocated its headquarters to Austin}, {We're relocating for my wife's job}. The noun is relocation: {relocation expenses}, {job relocation}.

Relocation is the act of moving to a new place. The term typically applies to significant moves—a company relocating its headquarters, a family relocating for work, wildlife being relocated to a new habitat. {The job offer required relocation to Seattle.} Relocation often implies institutional support or planning rather than a casual change of address.

Reluctance is unwillingness or hesitation to do something. The word implies internal resistance rather than outright refusal—you might comply despite your reluctance: {She agreed with obvious reluctance}, {I sensed his reluctance to discuss the matter}. In physics, reluctance is a property of magnetic circuits analogous to electrical resistance.

If you are reluctant to do something, you don’t want to do it for particular reasons. Often, the reason is an anticipated undesirable outcome: The administration was reluctant to discipline the students, fearing demonstrations. When reluctant is placed before a noun designating a role, it may suggest that a person has had a role thrust upon them that they don’t welcome: The doctor became the reluctant leader of the rescue operation.

Reluctantly means with hesitation or unwillingness. Someone who acts reluctantly does so despite reservations: {She reluctantly agreed to help}. The word signals internal resistance—you comply, but not happily: {He reluctantly admitted he was wrong}.

To rely on something is to depend on it or trust it to perform as expected: {We rely on the weather forecast to plan our trips}. You can rely on people, systems, or facts. The word implies confidence—when you rely on someone, you expect them to come through. {I'm relying on you to be there}.

Remade is the past tense and past participle of remake. Something remade has been made again or reconstructed: {The director remade the classic film for modern audiences}. A remade object may be restored to original condition or transformed into something new: {She remade her grandmother's wedding dress into a christening gown}.

Remain means to stay in the same place or condition after others have gone or changed. {Only three contestants remain}. It can express what's left: {Little remains of the original structure}. To remain also means to continue being: {She remained calm throughout the ordeal}. The remains of something are what's left over, especially a dead body or ruins.

Remainder is what's left over after part of something has been used, removed, or accounted for. In division, the remainder is the amount left when one number doesn't divide evenly into another: {Seven divided by three gives two, remainder one}. In publishing, remainders are unsold books sold at steep discounts. {She spent the remainder of her life in Paris.}

Remainders are what's left over after division or subtraction. In arithmetic, dividing 7 by 3 leaves a remainder of 1. More broadly, remainders are whatever portion survives after the main part is gone: {the remainders of dinner}, {the sad remainders of a lost civilization}. In publishing, remainders are unsold books sold at steep discount to clear inventory: {The novel ended up on the remainder table within a year}.

Remaining describes what is left over after other parts are removed, used, or accounted for: {the remaining slices of pizza}, {her remaining years}. It often implies a reduced quantity from some original whole. As a noun, remains refers to what's left behind—food scraps, ruins, or a corpse: {human remains were found in the woods}.

Remains is what's left over after something has been used, destroyed, or has otherwise disappeared. The remains of a meal are the scraps; the remains of a building are the rubble. When applied to people, remains refers to the body after death: {Her remains were cremated}. In archaeology and history, remains designates artifacts, ruins, or physical evidence of past civilizations or events. The word is almost always plural, though it may refer to a singular thing.

Remake as a verb means to make something again, typically with improvements or updates. As a noun, a remake is a new version of something previously made, most commonly applied to films, songs, or other creative works that are produced again with new elements while retaining the original's essential story or structure. {The studio announced a remake of the 1980s horror classic.} Remakes often generate debate about whether they improve upon or diminish the original.

Remakes is the plural of remake—a new version of something made before, typically a film, song, or other creative work: {Hollywood remakes of foreign films rarely capture the original's magic}. The word can also be a verb: {She remakes the bed every morning}. Remakes range from faithful reproductions to radical reimaginings.

A remark is something said, usually brief and often casual: {She made a remark about the weather}. To remark is to say something, typically as an observation rather than a question or command: {He remarked that the food was excellent}. To remark on something is to comment or take notice: {Several critics remarked on the film's unusual structure}.

Remarkable describes something worthy of notice or comment—standing out from the ordinary. A remarkable achievement exceeds expectations; a remarkable coincidence seems too striking to ignore. The word often carries admiration: {She made remarkable progress}. But remarkable can be neutral, simply noting that something deserves attention: {It's remarkable how quickly rumors spread}.

Remarks are comments or observations, typically brief and often casual: {a few opening remarks}, {He made some remarks about the weather}. The verb remark means to comment or notice: {She remarked on how quiet the house was}. Remarks can be pointed or cutting—{snide remarks}—or merely passing observations. {Remarkable} things are worth remarking on.

Remarriage is a marriage entered into by someone who has been married before. The term applies whether the previous marriage ended by death or divorce: {Her remarriage came three years after the divorce}. Second marriages, third marriages, and beyond all count as remarriages.

Remarried is the past tense of remarry—to marry again after a previous marriage has ended through divorce or death of a spouse. {She remarried two years after the divorce.} {He never remarried after his wife died.}

To remarry is to marry again after a previous marriage has ended through divorce or death of a spouse. The word often appears in discussions of family law, religious doctrine, or social expectations: {She remarried three years after her husband passed away}. {The divorce settlement addressed whether either party could remarry}.

Remarrying is marrying again after a previous marriage has ended through divorce or death of a spouse. The word emphasizes the act of entering into a new marriage: {She's remarrying next spring}, {He waited five years before remarrying}. Questions about remarrying often involve practical and emotional considerations—children from previous marriages, financial arrangements, or readiness to commit again.

To remaster is to create a new master recording or version of existing audio, video, or other media, typically using improved technology or techniques. A remastered album might have cleaner sound, better dynamic range, or enhanced clarity compared to the original release. Remastered video games often feature updated graphics while preserving original gameplay. The noun remaster refers to the resulting product: {I bought the 4K remaster of the film}.
