Remastered describes audio or video that has been processed to improve quality from the original master recording. A remastered album typically has cleaner sound, better dynamic range, or enhanced clarity: {The remastered version of the 1970s recording sounds remarkably crisp}. Remastering updates older media for new formats or modern listening standards without re-recording the performances.

Remastering is the process of creating a new master recording or version from existing source material, typically to improve quality or adapt it to new formats. Audio engineers remaster albums for modern playback systems; film studios remaster movies for high-definition release. Video games get remastered with updated graphics: {The remastered edition includes improved textures and lighting}. The term implies enhancement rather than fundamental recreation—the original content remains, but its presentation is refined.

Remasters are new versions of recordings—typically music albums or films—that have been technically improved from original source materials. The remastering process enhances audio or visual quality using modern technology: cleaning up noise, adjusting levels, sharpening images. {The Beatles remasters sound noticeably better than the original CDs.} Record labels frequently release remasters of classic albums, sometimes controversially when changes alter the original character.

A rematch is a second contest between the same opponents, typically after a close or disputed first meeting: {The champion agreed to a rematch}. The word implies unfinished business—someone wants another chance to prove themselves or settle the score. As a verb, to rematch is to pair opponents again.

Rematches are repeat contests between the same opponents, typically after a close or disputed outcome. Sports leagues schedule rematches; boxers demand them after controversial losses. The word implies unfinished business—someone wants another chance to prove the first result was wrong: {The team wanted a rematch after losing in overtime}.

Remedies is the plural of remedy—solutions that cure, correct, or relieve. Medical remedies treat ailments: {home remedies for a cold}, {herbal remedies}. Legal remedies are forms of relief a court can grant: {The plaintiff sought monetary remedies}. To remedy something is to fix it: {We need to remedy this situation before it gets worse}.

A remedy is something that corrects, cures, or relieves an undesirable condition. In medicine, it refers to a treatment or cure for illness or injury. In law, a remedy is the means by which a right is enforced or a wrong is redressed, such as damages or an injunction. More broadly, remedy applies to any solution that fixes a problem: {The only remedy for this situation is patience}. As a verb, to remedy something is to set it right or provide a cure.

Remember is to bring back to mind something known or experienced. You remember a name, a face, a childhood event. To remember someone to another is to pass along greetings: {Remember me to your mother}. To be remembered is to be kept in memory after death: {He will be remembered for his generosity}. Remember also means not to forget—to keep something in mind for action: {Remember to lock the door}.

Remembered is the past tense of remember—to recall or keep in mind. Something remembered has been retrieved from memory: {I remembered where I left my keys}. To be remembered is to remain in others' thoughts after death or departure: {She wanted to be remembered for her kindness}. {If I remembered correctly, the meeting was at noon}.

Remembering is the act of bringing something back to mind—recalling people, events, facts, or feelings from the past. It can be deliberate {I was just remembering our trip to Maine} or involuntary, triggered by a smell or song. Remembering also implies honoring or commemorating: {a day for remembering the fallen}.

Remembrance is the act of remembering or the state of being remembered. It often carries a ceremonial quality—honoring the dead or commemorating significant events: {a day of remembrance for fallen soldiers}. A remembrance can also be a keepsake or memento: {She kept the ring as a remembrance of her grandmother}. The word suggests something more deliberate and formal than mere memory.

To remind someone is to cause them to remember something: {Remind me to call the dentist}. You can also remind someone of a person or thing they resemble: {She reminds me of my sister}. A reminder is a note, notification, or anything that prompts memory: {I set a reminder on my phone}.

A reminder is something that prompts you to remember—a note, a notification, an alarm, or simply a person or thing that brings something to mind. {Set a reminder for the meeting}. {The scar was a reminder of the accident}. Reminders can be practical (calendar alerts) or emotional (mementos that recall the past).

Reminders are things that cause you to remember something—notes, alerts, or objects that prompt recall. A calendar notification is a reminder of an appointment. A photo can serve as a reminder of happier times. {Set a reminder for the meeting}. {The scar was a constant reminder of the accident}. The word often implies something you might otherwise forget.

Reminding is the act of prompting someone to remember something—an obligation, an event, a fact they may have forgotten. {I'm reminding you about tomorrow's meeting.} The word often implies gentle persistence: {She kept reminding him to call his mother.} A thing can also do the reminding: {The photo kept reminding her of home.}

To reminisce is to indulge in pleasant recollection of past experiences, often aloud with others who shared them: {We reminisced about our college days}. The word carries warmth and nostalgia—you reminisce about good times, not traumas. It suggests lingering enjoyably in memory rather than merely recalling facts.

Reminisced is the past tense of reminisce, meaning to indulge in enjoyable recollection of past events. The word implies fond or nostalgic memory-sharing, often done aloud with others: {We reminisced about our college days}. {She reminisced over old photographs}.

Reminiscence is the act of recalling past experiences, or the memory itself: {She shared reminiscences of her childhood in the country}. The word suggests pleasant, often nostalgic reflection rather than neutral recollection. In the plural, reminiscences are collected memories, sometimes published as informal memoirs. To {indulge in reminiscence} is to linger in the past.

Reminiscences are recollections of past experiences, typically shared aloud or in writing. The word carries a nostalgic quality, suggesting memories that are pleasant or at least meaningful to reflect upon. {Her reminiscences of childhood summers at the lake captivated everyone at dinner.} Reminiscences often appear in memoir titles or as a genre designation for personal recollections: {Reminiscences of a Stock Operator}. The singular reminiscence exists but is far less common than the plural form.

Reminiscent means suggestive or evocative of something else: {The melody was reminiscent of Chopin}. The word implies a resemblance that triggers memory or association. Something reminiscent of the past recalls it without being identical. A person feeling reminiscent is in a mood for recalling memories: {She grew reminiscent over old photographs}.

Reminisces is the verb form of reminisce, meaning to indulge in enjoyable recollection of past events. Someone who reminisces dwells on memories, often sharing them aloud: {She reminisces about her childhood summers at the lake}. The word suggests pleasant nostalgia rather than painful remembering.

Reminiscing is indulging in memories of the past, usually pleasant ones. The word suggests a leisurely, often social activity—friends reminiscing about college days, grandparents reminiscing about how things used to be. {We spent the evening reminiscing over old photographs.} There's warmth in reminiscing that distinguishes it from merely remembering.

Remission is a lessening or abatement of something undesirable. In medicine, remission refers to a period when a disease's symptoms diminish or disappear: {Her cancer has been in remission for three years}. The word also applies to the forgiveness of sins or debts, and to the reduction of a prison sentence. To remit is to send payment or to pardon.

Remittance is money sent as payment, especially across a distance. The word appears most often in formal or financial contexts: bills requesting remittance, or workers sending remittances to family in another country. {Remittances from abroad account for a significant portion of the country's GDP.} The verb is remit.

Remittances are money sent to someone in another place, especially funds that migrant workers send back to family in their home countries. The word carries a formal or financial tone: {Remittances from workers abroad account for a significant portion of the country's GDP}. A remittance can also be any payment sent to settle a debt or bill.

A remix is a new version of a song or recording created by altering the original—adding beats, changing tempo, isolating vocals, or layering new elements: {The DJ dropped a remix of that track}. Beyond music, remix describes any creative reworking of existing material: {His novel is essentially a remix of Greek mythology}. To remix is to create such a version.

Remixed is the past tense of remix—to rework existing material into a new version. Most often applied to music, where a producer takes an original recording and alters it: {The DJ remixed the track with a heavier beat}. The term extends to any creative reworking: {She remixed the classic recipe with modern ingredients}. A remixed version may barely resemble its source or stay close to the original.

Remixes is the plural of remix—a new version of a recorded song created by rearranging, adding to, or otherwise altering the original. DJs and producers create remixes for dance floors, radio play, or fresh artistic interpretation: {The album includes three remixes of the title track}. The term extends beyond music to any creative reworking: {The internet is full of remixes of classic movie scenes}.

Remixing is the process of taking existing material—typically a song—and reworking it into something new. A producer might remix a track by adding beats, changing the tempo, or isolating vocals. The term extends beyond music: {She's remixing her grandmother's recipes with modern techniques}. Remixing celebrates transformation over pure originality, building on what already exists.

A remnant is what's left over after the main part has been used, removed, or destroyed. Fabric stores sell remnants—the end pieces of bolts too small for full projects. The word often suggests something once larger or more significant: {remnants of an ancient civilization}, {the last remnants of the army}. A remnant can be a surviving trace or fragment: {Only remnants of the original forest remain}.

Remnants are what's left over after the main part is gone or used up. A remnant of fabric is the end of a bolt, often sold at discount. Remnants of a meal sit on plates. The word suggests smallness and incompleteness: {remnants of a once-great civilization}, {only remnants of the army survived}. In retail, remnants are discontinued or leftover stock.

Remodel means to change the structure, layout, or appearance of something, most often a building or room. When you remodel a kitchen, you might tear out cabinets, move walls, or install new fixtures—changes more extensive than simple redecoration. The word also applies to reshaping or restructuring in other contexts: {The new CEO remodeled the company's management structure}. A remodel is the project or process of remodeling.

Remodeling is the process of altering or renovating a structure, typically a building or room, to change its appearance, function, or layout. In American English, it most often refers to home improvement projects: {We're remodeling the kitchen next month}. The term extends beyond construction to describe any significant restructuring or reorganization: {The company is remodeling its approach to customer service}. British English typically spells it remodelling.

Remodelling is the act of altering or renovating something, especially a building or room: {They're remodelling the kitchen}. The word also applies to reshaping or restructuring more abstractly: {The company is remodelling its management structure}. This British spelling doubles the L; American English prefers remodeling.

Remorse is deep regret or guilt over a wrong you've committed. It implies more than feeling bad—remorse suggests genuine moral anguish and a wish to undo the harm: {He felt remorse for the way he'd treated her}. Someone who shows {no remorse} appears indifferent to the consequences of their actions, which courts and victims find particularly troubling.

Remorseful describes someone feeling deep regret or guilt over a wrong they've committed. The word implies more than simple regret—it suggests genuine anguish and self-reproach: {He seemed truly remorseful about the harm he'd caused}. A remorseful apology carries emotional weight that a merely apologetic one may not.

Remorseless means without remorse—showing no guilt, regret, or pity. A remorseless killer feels nothing for victims. The word also describes things that continue without letting up: {the remorseless advance of the disease}, {remorseless pressure to perform}. Both senses share an idea of something that won't soften or relent.

To remortgage is to take out a new mortgage on a property you already own, typically to get better terms, release equity, or switch lenders. Common in British English; Americans more often say refinance. {We remortgaged to fund the renovation}. {Interest rates dropped, so they decided to remortgage}.

Remote means far away in space, time, or connection. A remote {village} is isolated and hard to reach. A remote {possibility} is unlikely. Remote {ancestors} lived long ago. The remote {past} is distant history. A remote {manner} is emotionally distant and detached. A remote—short for remote control—is the handheld device for operating electronics from across the room: {Pass me the remote}.

Remotely means from a distance. To work remotely is to work from somewhere other than the main office. A remotely operated vehicle is controlled from afar. The word also serves as an intensifier in negative constructions: {I'm not remotely interested} means not interested at all, not even slightly. {Nothing remotely like this has happened before.}

Remoteness is the quality of being far away or isolated. A place has remoteness when it lies distant from centers of population: {The remoteness of the cabin made it perfect for writing}. The word extends to emotional or psychological distance: {a remoteness in her manner}, {the remoteness of ancient history}. Remoteness can also describe low probability: {the remoteness of the threat}.

Remoulade is a cold sauce based on mayonnaise, typically flavored with mustard, capers, pickles, and herbs. The classic French version accompanies seafood and cold meats. Louisiana remoulade is spicier and more pungent, often served with fried shrimp or crab cakes: {The po'boy came with a generous smear of remoulade}.

Removable describes something designed to be taken off, detached, or separated from a larger whole without causing damage. A removable {cover} can be lifted away for cleaning; removable {storage} can be unplugged and transported between devices. The word often implies that reattachment is possible and intended, distinguishing it from things that are merely breakable or disposable.

Removal is the act of taking something away or eliminating it: {removal of the tumor}, {stain removal}, {removal from office}. A removal can also be a relocation—moving from one place to another: {The family's removal to the countryside happened suddenly}. In some contexts, removal is a euphemism for killing or assassination.

Remove means to take something away from where it is or eliminate it entirely: {Remove your shoes before entering}, {The surgeon removed the tumor}. To remove oneself is to leave or withdraw. Someone removed from a situation is distant or detached from it. In genealogy, removed indicates generational distance: a first cousin once removed shares a great-grandparent with you.

Removed means taken away or eliminated: {The surgeon removed the tumor}. It also describes emotional or social distance—someone removed from a situation is detached or uninvolved: {She seemed removed from the conversation}. In family relationships, removed indicates generational separation: a first cousin once removed is your cousin's child or your parent's cousin.

A renaissance is a revival or renewed interest in something after a period of decline: {Folk music experienced a renaissance in the 1960s}, {The neighborhood is undergoing a renaissance}. The word suggests not just a comeback but a flourishing—cultural, artistic, or intellectual energy returning to something that had faded. (Capitalized Renaissance is the historical period.)

To rename is to give a new name to something: {They renamed the street after the civil rights leader}, {I renamed the file so I could find it later}. The word covers both official changes—cities, buildings, organizations—and casual ones like pet names or computer files. A rename is the act of doing so.

Rend means to tear apart violently or forcefully. The word is literary and somewhat archaic, appearing more often in dramatic or biblical contexts than everyday speech: {a cry that rent the air}, {garments rent in grief}. To rend can also mean to cause emotional anguish: {The news rent her heart}. Past tense: rent.

The literal meaning of render is melt down, and is used with a limited number of nouns: You render fat to remove its impurities. Render has more frequent figurative meanings. When a jury renders a verdict or a court renders a judgment, it delivers it. Render can also mean make: The device was rendered harmless by explosives experts. In some contexts, render is a formal way of saying provide, furnish, or perform: You’ve rendered a great service to your country today.

Rendered is the past tense of render, a verb with several distinct applications. To render something is to cause it to become: {The blow rendered him unconscious}. To render a service or verdict is to deliver it formally. In cooking, rendering extracts fat by heating: {rendered bacon fat}. In computing and design, rendering produces a visual image from data—a rendered image has been processed into viewable form. To render a wall is to coat it with plaster or cement.

Rendering is the act of producing or presenting something. An artist's rendering is a visual representation—a sketch, painting, or digital image showing how something looks or will look: {architectural renderings of the proposed building}. A musical rendering is a particular interpretation or performance. In computing, rendering is the process of generating an image from data: {The video card handles 3D rendering}. Rendering also means extracting fat by melting: {rendering lard from pig fat}.

Renderings are visual representations or interpretations of something. An architect's rendering shows how a building will look when completed. A rendering can also be a performance or interpretation: {her rendering of the national anthem}. In computing, rendering is the process of generating an image from a model or code. The word also applies to translations: {a new rendering of the Greek text}.

Renders is a form of the verb render, which means to cause something to become a certain way: {The blow rendered him unconscious}. To render is also to give or provide something due: {render assistance}, {render a verdict}, {render unto Caesar}. In computing and graphics, renders means produces a visual output from data: {The software renders 3D models in real time}. To render fat is to melt it down for use.

Rendezvous is a meeting at an agreed time and place, or the place itself: {The café was their usual rendezvous}. The word often suggests secrecy or romance—lovers arrange rendezvous, spies meet at rendezvous points. As a verb, to rendezvous is to meet up: {We'll rendezvous at the hotel at noon}. In aerospace, spacecraft rendezvous when they meet in orbit.
clues: Where two parties agree to converge

definition: Rending is the present participle of rend, meaning to tear apart violently or with force. The word appears most often in literary or dramatic contexts: {a rending scream}, {the rending of fabric}. Something rending tears at you emotionally as well as physically—a {heart-rending} sight causes anguish, as if the heart itself were being torn.

Rendition is a particular interpretation or performance of something, especially a song or dramatic piece: {Her rendition of the national anthem brought the crowd to tears}. The word extends to any version or translation of a work. In legal and political contexts, rendition refers to the surrender or transfer of a person from one jurisdiction to another, often controversially applied to the extrajudicial transfer of terrorism suspects to countries where harsh interrogation is permitted.

Renditions are performances or interpretations of something—typically artistic works. A singer's rendition of a song, an actor's rendition of a character, or an orchestra's rendition of a symphony all involve presenting existing material through individual interpretation: {Her rendition of the national anthem moved the crowd}. The word also applies to translations or versions of texts, and in legal contexts, to the surrender of a fugitive between jurisdictions. Extraordinary rendition refers to the extrajudicial transfer of suspects to countries where interrogation methods may include torture.

A renegade is someone who abandons a group, cause, or allegiance to join an opposing side—originally a religious apostate, now more broadly a traitor or defector. The word carries a sense of deliberate betrayal rather than mere departure. In looser use, renegade describes anyone who rejects conventional rules or authority: {a renegade cop who plays by his own rules}. As an adjective, it characterizes rebellious or unconventional behavior: {renegade tactics}. The word often carries romantic connotations of bold independence alongside its negative sense of disloyalty.

Renegades are people who abandon a group, cause, or allegiance to join an opposing one—deserters or traitors. The word carries a sense of defiance: a renegade doesn't just leave quietly but actively rebels against former loyalties. In modern use, renegade often has a romantic edge, suggesting someone who breaks rules or conventions: {a renegade cop who plays by his own rules}, {renegade artists challenging the establishment}. The singular renegade works as both noun and adjective: {a renegade faction}, {going renegade}.

To renege is to go back on a promise or commitment: {He reneged on his agreement to sell me the car}. In card games, to renege is to fail to follow suit when able—a violation of the rules. The word carries connotations of bad faith, suggesting someone who can't be trusted to keep their word.

Reneged is the past tense of renege, meaning to go back on a promise, commitment, or agreement: {He reneged on the deal at the last minute}. The word often appears with "on" to specify what was abandoned. In card games, to renege is to fail to follow suit when able—a violation of the rules.

Reneges means goes back on a promise or commitment. Someone who reneges fails to follow through on what they agreed to do: {He reneged on his promise to help with the move}. In card games, to renege is to fail to follow suit when required and able. The word carries a sense of betrayal or bad faith.

Reneging is going back on a promise or commitment. The verb renege appears most often in card games, where it means to fail to follow suit when able, but the broader sense dominates: {He reneged on the deal at the last minute}. The word carries a tone of betrayal or bad faith—not just changing plans but breaking one's word.

To renew is to make something new again or restore it to a fresh state. You renew a subscription, license, or membership by extending its validity: {I need to renew my passport before it expires}. Renew also means to resume after an interruption: {They renewed their friendship after years apart}. Something renewed gains fresh vigor or energy: {The vacation renewed my enthusiasm for work}.

Renewable describes something that can be replenished or restored. Renewable energy comes from sources like solar, wind, and water that aren't depleted by use: {The country invested heavily in renewable power}. A renewable contract or subscription can be extended: {The lease is renewable annually}. Renewable resources regenerate naturally, unlike fossil fuels which exist in finite supply.

Renewables are energy sources that replenish naturally and won't run out—solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal power. The term almost always appears in discussions of replacing fossil fuels: {The country is investing heavily in renewables}. The singular renewable is less common, typically appearing as an adjective: {renewable energy}, {renewable resources}.

Renewal is the act of making something new again or extending its duration. You renew a subscription, a license, or a lease by paying to continue it: {My membership is up for renewal}. Renewal also means restoration or revival: {spiritual renewal}, {urban renewal}. Something renewed gains fresh life or validity after a period of decline or expiration.

Renewed describes something restored, revived, or begun again after a pause. A renewed {interest} in gardening suggests enthusiasm that had faded. Renewed {efforts} follow earlier unsuccessful attempts. A renewed {sense of purpose} implies one had been lost. To feel renewed is to feel refreshed or reinvigorated: {After the retreat, she returned renewed}.

Renminbi is the official currency of the People's Republic of China, meaning "people's currency" in Mandarin. The yuan is its primary unit, and the two terms are often used interchangeably in casual contexts, though renminbi technically names the currency system while yuan names the denomination: {The renminbi has strengthened against the dollar}.

To renounce is to formally give up or reject something—a claim, a right, a belief, or an allegiance: {She renounced her citizenship}, {He renounced his claim to the throne}. The word carries weight and finality, implying a deliberate, often public declaration. One renounces worldly possessions, renounces violence, renounces a former faith. The noun is renunciation.

Renounced is the past tense of renounce, meaning to formally give up or reject something—a claim, right, belief, or allegiance. The word carries weight and finality: {She renounced her citizenship}, {He renounced violence after years in the movement}. What's renounced is typically something once held or valued, now deliberately abandoned.

Renounces is the third-person singular form of renounce, meaning to formally declare that one is giving something up or rejecting it. A person renounces a claim, a title, a belief, or an allegiance: {She renounces her citizenship}, {He renounces violence}. The word carries weight—renouncing implies a deliberate, often public rejection rather than casual abandonment.

Renouncing is the act of formally rejecting or giving up something—a claim, a right, a belief, or an allegiance. The word carries weight and finality: {He's renouncing his citizenship}, {She's renouncing her family's religion}. You might also speak of renouncing violence, worldly pleasures, or a former way of life. The formality distinguishes renouncing from simply quitting or abandoning.

To renovate is to restore something to good condition, typically a building or room, through repair and updating: {They're renovating the kitchen}, {The theater was renovated in the 1990s}. Renovation usually implies significant work—more than routine maintenance but less than complete reconstruction. The word applies most naturally to structures but extends to other restorations: {renovate your wardrobe}, {renovate your image}.

Renovated describes something that has been restored, repaired, or updated to improve its condition. The term applies most often to buildings, rooms, and spaces that have undergone significant work to modernize them or return them to good repair: {They moved into a beautifully renovated Victorian}. A renovated kitchen might have new appliances and countertops; a renovated hotel might have updated plumbing and décor throughout. The word suggests more substantial improvement than simple cleaning or minor repairs.

Renovating is restoring something to good condition, typically a building or room. The work usually involves repairing, updating, or modernizing: {They spent six months renovating the kitchen}. Unlike remodeling, which changes structure or layout, renovating focuses on refreshing what's already there—new paint, fixtures, flooring. {We're renovating an old farmhouse.}

Renovation is the process of restoring or improving something, especially a building or room: {The kitchen renovation took three months}. Unlike restoration, which aims to return something to its original state, renovation typically involves updating or modernizing. The verb is renovate: {They're renovating the old warehouse into apartments}.

Renovations are improvements or repairs made to a building, restoring it to good condition or updating it for modern use. The word usually implies substantial work—more than routine maintenance: {The kitchen renovations took three months}. Home renovations often involve contractors, permits, and temporary displacement: {We're staying with my parents while the renovations are underway}.

Rent is payment made to use something that belongs to someone else, typically property or equipment, for a specified period. To rent is either to pay for such use or to make something available for such payment—context usually makes clear which direction the transaction flows. {The rent is due on the first.} {We rented a cabin for the weekend.} Something that's for rent is available to be rented. A rent in fabric or another material is a tear or rip, from a different verb meaning to tear apart violently.

Rental refers to the act of renting or something available for rent. A rental {car}, rental {property}, or rental {agreement} involves temporary use in exchange for payment. As a noun, it can mean the amount paid {(Monthly rentals start at $1,200)} or the thing being rented {(We picked up our rental at the airport)}. The adjective describes anything connected to renting rather than owning.

Rentals are things available for temporary use in exchange for payment: {car rentals}, {vacation rentals}, {ski rentals}. The word often appears in compounds describing the business or category: {rental car}, {rental property}, {rental agreement}. A place advertising rentals has items or spaces you can hire rather than buy.

A renter is someone who pays to use property they don't own, typically an apartment or house: {The building has twelve renters}. In American usage, renter and tenant are nearly interchangeable, though tenant appears more often in legal contexts. Renter can also mean one who rents things out, though this sense is rare.

Renters is the plural of renter—people who pay to occupy property they don't own. The word appears frequently in discussions of housing policy: {renters' rights}, {renters insurance}. In contexts contrasting ownership with tenancy, renters stands opposite homeowners or landlords: {The neighborhood is split between renters and owners}.

Renting is paying for temporary use of something owned by another—an apartment, a car, equipment. The term covers both sides of the transaction: a tenant renting from a landlord, or a landlord renting to a tenant. {We're renting until we can afford to buy.} {She's been renting out the spare room.}

Rents is the plural of rent in its noun senses: payments for temporary use of property {The rents in this neighborhood have skyrocketed}, or tears in fabric {The rents in the sail let the wind through}. In slang, rents is a clipped form of parents: {I'm staying at my rents' place for the summer}.

Renunciation is the formal rejection or abandonment of something—a claim, right, belief, or way of life. The word carries weight: you don't renounce trivial things. A prince might issue a renunciation of his claim to the throne. Religious converts may make a renunciation of their former faith. {His renunciation of violence was complete.} The act implies deliberate, often public, giving up.

To reopen is to open again after being closed. A store reopens after renovations; a wound reopens if it hasn't healed properly. Authorities may reopen a case when new evidence emerges. The prefix re- emphasizes resumption: {The restaurant will reopen under new management}. {Peace talks reopened after a three-month stalemate}.

Reopening is the act of opening again after a period of closure. A business reopens after renovation, a case reopens when new evidence emerges, a wound reopens if healing is disrupted. The term gained prominence during pandemic-era debates about when schools, restaurants, and economies should resume normal operations: {The governor announced a phased reopening}.

Reorg is informal shorthand for reorganization, especially a corporate restructuring that reshuffles departments, reporting lines, or staff: {The company announced another reorg}, {I survived three reorgs in five years}. The word carries weary familiarity—reorgs are common enough in business to need their own abbreviation. Also used as a verb: {They're reorging the whole division}.

To reorganize is to arrange something in a new way or restructure how it operates. Companies reorganize departments, governments reorganize agencies, and individuals reorganize closets or schedules. The word often signals significant change rather than minor adjustment: {After the merger, they reorganized the entire sales division}. In legal contexts, a company that reorganizes under bankruptcy protection restructures its debts while continuing operations.

To reorient is to adjust position, direction, or focus—literally or figuratively. You might reorient a satellite dish for better reception, or reorient your career toward a new field. The word often implies finding one's bearings after confusion or change: {After the merger, the company had to reorient around new priorities}. Sometimes spelled re-orient.

Rep is an informal shortening with several sources. Most commonly it's short for repetition in exercise contexts: {I did fifteen reps of bicep curls}. Rep also abbreviates representative, especially a sales rep or congressional rep. In theater, rep is repertory: {a play in rep}. As slang, rep means reputation: {He's got a bad rep around here}.

To repackage is to package something again, often in a new or different form. Products get repackaged for different markets or seasons. The word extends to ideas, proposals, or content presented in altered form: {The administration repackaged its failed policy with new messaging}. The implication is often that the substance remains unchanged despite fresh presentation.

Repackaged means presented in a new form or container without substantial change to the contents. Products get repackaged for different markets or to refresh their appeal. Ideas and policies get repackaged to make them more palatable: {The administration repackaged its failed initiative under a new name}. The word often carries a skeptical tone, implying superficial change: {It's just the same old proposal, repackaged}.

Repackaging is presenting something in a new form without changing its substance. Goods are repackaged when moved to different containers or given new labels. Ideas, policies, or products are repackaged when marketed differently: {The proposal is just a repackaging of last year's failed initiative}. The term often implies superficial change masking sameness.

Repaid is the past tense of repay. To repay is to pay back money owed or return a favor: {She repaid the loan in full}, {How can I ever repay your kindness?} Repaid can also suggest revenge or retaliation: {He repaid the insult with a punch}.

Repair is to fix something that's broken, damaged, or not working properly: {The mechanic repaired the transmission}. As a noun, it's the act of fixing or the work involved: {The roof needs repair}. Something {in good repair} is well-maintained; {beyond repair} means too damaged to fix. To repair a relationship is to mend it after conflict. The formal phrase {repair to} means to go somewhere: {They repaired to the drawing room}—unrelated to fixing, from a different root meaning to return home.

A repairman is a person whose job is fixing things—appliances, machines, equipment. The word typically applies to someone who comes to your home or business: {The repairman said the dishwasher needs a new pump}. Though gendered, repairman remains common; repairperson exists but sounds awkward to most speakers.

Repairs are acts of fixing or restoring something damaged, broken, or worn. The word emphasizes restoration to working condition: {The car is in the shop for repairs}. To make repairs is to do repair work. In the plural, repairs often suggests ongoing maintenance: {The building needs extensive repairs}. Beyond repairs (or past repair) means damaged beyond fixing.

Reparation is the act of making amends for a wrong or injury—restoring what was damaged or compensating for harm done. In the plural, reparations usually refers to payments or other compensation demanded from a defeated nation after war, or more recently, proposed payments to descendants of enslaved people: {The debate over reparations for slavery continues}. The word carries both the practical sense of repair and the moral weight of atonement.

Reparations are compensation for wrongs inflicted, especially payments made by a defeated nation for wartime damage or by governments to groups historically harmed by official policy. The term often refers specifically to proposed payments to Black Americans for slavery and its aftermath: {The city council debated a reparations program for descendants of enslaved people}. More broadly, reparations can mean any amends or restitution: {The company offered reparations to affected communities}.

Reparenting is the psychological process of providing oneself—or receiving from a therapist—the emotional nurturing that was absent in childhood. The concept comes from therapy, where adults learn to meet their own unmet developmental needs: {Reparenting my inner child has been the hardest part of recovery}. In computing, reparenting means reassigning an element to a different parent in a hierarchy: {The window manager reparented the application window}.

Repartee is quick, witty conversation or the skill of engaging in it. The term suggests cleverness and verbal agility—replies that are sharp, timely, and often playful: {Their dinner party repartee kept everyone entertained}. A person known for repartee can produce apt comebacks on the spot.

Repatriated means sent or returned to one's country of origin. Governments repatriate refugees, prisoners of war, or remains of the dead. Museums repatriate artifacts to their countries of origin: {The bronze sculptures were repatriated to Nigeria}. Money is repatriated when moved back to the investor's home country. A person who has been repatriated is also called a repatriate.

Repatriation is the return of someone or something to their country of origin. People may be repatriated after war, displacement, or imprisonment abroad: {The treaty included repatriation of prisoners}. The term applies equally to objects: {the repatriation of stolen artifacts to their home countries}. In finance, repatriation refers to moving money back to one's home country: {corporate repatriation of overseas profits}.

Repatriations are acts of sending or bringing someone or something back to their country of origin. People may be repatriated after wars, refugees returned to homelands, or prisoners of war sent home. The term also applies to returning money, assets, or cultural artifacts: {The museum agreed to the repatriation of looted antiquities}. In finance, repatriations move profits or capital back to a company's home country.

To repay is to pay back what you owe—money borrowed, a favor received, or a debt of any kind: {I'll repay you as soon as I get paid}. The word extends to returning treatment in kind, good or bad: {How can I ever repay your kindness?} {She repaid his betrayal with silence}. Something repays effort if it proves worthwhile: {The view from the summit repays the climb}.

Repayment is the act of paying back money that was borrowed or owed: {The loan requires monthly repayments over five years}. It extends to non-monetary contexts—repaying a favor, kindness, or wrong: {His betrayal was poor repayment for years of loyalty}. The word implies obligation fulfilled or debt settled.

Repeal is the act of revoking or annulling a law, regulation, or official decree, or the verb describing this action. When a legislature repeals a statute, it formally withdraws the law from the books, rendering it no longer enforceable. {Congress voted to repeal the controversial provision.} {Prohibition was repealed in 1933.} Unlike amendment, which modifies existing law, repeal eliminates it entirely.

Repealed is the past tense of repeal, meaning to officially revoke or cancel a law, rule, or policy. Governments repeal legislation when it's no longer wanted or considered effective: {The amendment was repealed after decades of controversy}. {Congress voted to repeal the tax}.

To repeat is to do, say, or occur again. You repeat a word for emphasis, repeat a mistake you should have learned from, or repeat a grade in school. A repeat is a second occurrence: {It was a repeat of last year's disaster}. In broadcasting, a repeat is a rerun. On repeat means playing continuously: {I had that song on repeat all day}. History repeats itself; patterns recur.

Repeated describes something that happens more than once: {repeated attempts}, {repeated warnings}. It suggests recurrence, often with a note of persistence or excess—repeated requests may border on nagging, repeated failures on futility. The word can also describe something said or done again: {a repeated phrase}, {repeated measurements}. To do something repeatedly is to do it many times over.

A repeater is something or someone that repeats. A person who repeats a grade or course is a repeater, as is someone who commits the same offense multiple times: {a repeat offender}, {a three-time repeater}. A repeating firearm—one that fires multiple shots without reloading—is a repeater. In telecommunications, a repeater is a device that receives and retransmits signals to extend their range.

Repeating describes something that occurs again or continues to recur. A repeating {pattern} shows the same elements cycling through. A repeating {decimal} has digits that recur infinitely: 1/3 = 0.333... A repeating {rifle} or {firearm} can fire multiple shots without reloading. {The repeating theme in her novels is loss and redemption.}

Repeats are things that occur again—reruns of television shows, recurring patterns, or second helpings: {no repeats on the playlist}, {The channel runs nothing but repeats}. In music, a repeat is a passage played twice, often marked by repeat signs. As a verb form, repeats describes saying or doing something again: {History repeats itself}, {She repeats everything I tell her}.

To repel is to drive back or away. Armies repel invaders. Insect repellent repels mosquitoes. Magnets with like poles repel each other. The word extends to emotional rejection: something repellent disgusts or repels you, pushing you away psychologically: {The smell repelled me}. A person can repel unwanted advances or attention.

Repelled is the past tense of repel. To repel is to drive back or ward off: {The army repelled the invasion}. It also means to cause disgust or aversion: {The smell repelled her}. In physics, like magnetic poles repel each other. Someone repelled by something finds it deeply off-putting: {I was repelled by his arrogance}.

Repellent describes something that drives away or causes aversion. Insect repellent keeps bugs at bay; a water-repellent jacket sheds rain. The word also describes anything that provokes disgust or strong distaste: {His arrogance was repellent}. As a noun, a repellent is a substance that wards off pests or moisture. Also spelled repellant.

Repelling describes something that drives away or causes aversion. A repelling force pushes objects apart—magnets repel when like poles face each other. A repelling odor makes you turn away. The word often describes something physically or emotionally off-putting: {His repelling manner kept people at a distance}. Water-repelling fabrics shed moisture.

Repels means drives away or pushes back. A force field repels intruders. Insect repellent repels mosquitoes. Magnets with like poles repel each other. The word extends to emotional rejection: {His arrogance repels people}. What repels you disgusts or offends you: {The idea of eating insects repels her}.

To repent is to feel deep regret for wrongdoing and resolve to change. The word carries religious weight—sinners repent before God—but applies to any genuine remorse: {He repented his harsh words}. Repentance implies not just feeling sorry but turning away from the behavior: {She repented of her gambling and never placed another bet}.

Repentance is sincere regret for wrongdoing, coupled with a commitment to change. The word carries religious weight—in Christian theology, repentance is essential for salvation and forgiveness. But secular use is common: {His apology showed no real repentance}. Unlike mere regret, repentance implies turning away from the behavior, not just feeling bad about it.

Repentant describes someone who feels genuine remorse for wrongdoing and wishes they had acted differently. A repentant {thief} or repentant {sinner} acknowledges their mistakes and seeks forgiveness or redemption. The word carries a stronger moral weight than simply being sorry—it implies a change of heart and often a desire to make amends. {He was repentant after realizing how much his words had hurt her.}

Repenting is expressing or feeling sincere regret for wrongdoing. The word carries religious weight—repenting before God, repenting of sins—but applies to secular contexts too: {He died repenting the choices that cost him his family}. To repent is to turn away from past behavior, not merely to feel bad about it.

A repercussion is a consequence or effect, especially an unintended or indirect one that follows from an action: {The decision had repercussions no one anticipated}. Usually plural, repercussions suggest a chain of effects rippling outward: {The scandal's repercussions are still being felt years later}. The word carries a slightly formal tone and often implies negative outcomes.

Repercussions are consequences that follow from an action, usually negative and often unintended. The word suggests effects that ripple outward: {The scandal had repercussions throughout the industry}. Unlike simple consequences, repercussions imply a kind of bouncing back—actions returning to affect their source or spreading wider than anticipated: {She didn't consider the repercussions of her decision}.

Repertoire is the collection of works a performer or group is prepared to present—songs a singer knows, plays a theater company can stage, pieces an orchestra has rehearsed. The word extends to any stock of skills or techniques someone has ready: {a comedian's repertoire of impressions}, {a chef's repertoire of sauces}. In casual use, repertoire can simply mean range of abilities: {Flattery isn't in his repertoire}.

Repetition is the act of doing or saying something again. The word covers both the process and the result: {Repetition is key to learning} refers to repeated practice, while {a repetition of yesterday's mistakes} means another instance. In exercise, a repetition (or rep) is one complete movement in a set: {Do three sets of ten repetitions}. Repetition in speech or writing can be intentional for emphasis or accidental through carelessness.

Repetitions is the plural of repetition, an instance of doing or saying something again. In exercise and strength training, repetitions—usually shortened to reps—refers to the number of times a movement is performed in a set: {Do three sets of twelve repetitions}. The word also applies to repeated elements in music, speech, or writing, where repetition may serve for emphasis or become tedious depending on context.

Repetitive describes something that repeats, often more than necessary or desired. A repetitive {task} is monotonous. Repetitive {strain injury} comes from making the same motion too many times. The word usually carries a negative connotation—repetitive {music} or repetitive {arguments} suggest tedium rather than pleasing rhythm.

To rephrase is to express the same meaning in different words: {Let me rephrase that question}. The term implies restating something for clarity, emphasis, or diplomacy—often when the original wording was unclear, awkward, or poorly received: {She rephrased her criticism to sound less harsh}.

To replace something is to put something else in its position: {We replaced the broken window}. You can replace what's lost, damaged, or inadequate with something new. A person who replaces another takes over their role or function: {She replaced him as CEO}. Replace also means to put something back where it was: {Replace the books on the shelf when you're done}.

Replaceable describes something that can be substituted or exchanged for another of its kind: {The battery is replaceable}. When applied to people, it often carries a dismissive edge—suggesting someone lacks unique value: {No one wants to feel replaceable at work}. The word implies interchangeability, whether of parts, products, or personnel.

Replaced is the past tense of replace—to put something new in the position of something removed or lost. A worn part gets replaced with a fresh one. A retiring employee is replaced by a new hire. To feel replaced is to sense you've been pushed aside for someone or something else: {She felt replaced when her best friend started hanging out with the new girl}.

Replacement is something or someone that takes the place of another: {We need a replacement for the broken window}, {She's looking for a replacement while she's on leave}. The word also names the act of replacing: {The replacement of old pipes took three days}. A replacement {part} substitutes for one that's worn or damaged. In military contexts, replacements are new personnel filling vacancies left by casualties or transfers.

Replacing is putting something new in place of something else. You replace a broken window, a worn tire, or a retiring employee. The thing replaced is usually removed, damaged, or inadequate: {They're replacing the old carpet with hardwood}. To replace can also mean to put something back where it was: {She replaced the book on the shelf}.

Replay means to play again. You replay a recording to watch or hear it once more: {Let me replay that voicemail}. Athletes replay a game mentally, reviewing what happened. In sports broadcasting, a replay shows a moment again, often in slow motion: {The replay confirmed the call}. As a verb, replay also means to repeat an experience or event: {She kept replaying the argument in her head}.

Replays are repeated showings or playings of something. In sports broadcasting, a replay shows an important moment again, often in slow motion: {Let's see that touchdown on the replay}. In gaming, replays are recorded sessions you can watch back. The verb replay means to play again—a game, a recording, or mentally: {I keep replaying the conversation in my head}.

Replenish means to fill something back up or restore it to a former level. You replenish supplies, replenish stock, replenish your energy. The word implies something was depleted and is now being restored: {She replenished her coffee cup}, {The rain replenished the reservoir}. Unlike simply filling, replenish carries the sense of renewal—making full again what had been diminished.

A replica is an exact or close copy of something, typically made at the same scale as the original: {a replica of the Mayflower}, {replica jerseys}. The word implies intentional reproduction rather than accidental similarity. Replicas range from museum-quality reproductions to mass-produced merchandise. Unlike a forgery, a replica doesn't pretend to be the original.

A replicant is a bioengineered artificial human, coined in the 1982 film *Blade Runner*. Unlike mechanical robots, replicants are organic beings grown rather than built, virtually indistinguishable from humans except through specialized testing. The term has spread beyond the film to describe any synthetic being designed to pass as human: {The debate over AI consciousness echoes the replicant question}.

Replicants are bioengineered humanoids in the *Blade Runner* universe—artificial beings designed to be nearly indistinguishable from humans. The term has spread beyond the films to describe any synthetic being that mimics human appearance and behavior: {The robots were so lifelike they seemed like replicants}. The word sometimes appears in discussions of AI and cloning, carrying undertones of existential unease about what makes someone truly human.

Replicas are copies or reproductions of something, typically made to closely resemble an original. The word usually implies intentional duplication rather than accidental similarity, and replicas range from museum-quality reproductions of artworks to mass-produced souvenirs. {The gift shop sold replicas of artifacts from the exhibit.} Unlike forgeries, replicas are generally acknowledged as copies rather than presented as originals.

To replicate is to reproduce, duplicate, or make a copy of something. Scientists replicate experiments to verify results. Viruses replicate inside host cells. The verb often implies precise reproduction: {The study failed to replicate the original findings}. A replicate is a copy or reproduction, particularly in scientific contexts where multiple identical samples are tested.

Replicated means copied or reproduced, especially to create an exact duplicate. Scientists replicate experiments to verify results. Cells replicate their DNA before dividing. Software can be replicated across servers. {The study couldn't be replicated by other researchers.} {The virus replicated rapidly in the host.}

Replicates is the verb form of replicate—to make a copy or reproduce something. Scientists replicate experiments to verify results. Cells replicate by dividing. A study that replicates earlier findings confirms them. As a noun, replicates are the copies themselves, especially repeated trials in an experiment: {We ran three replicates to ensure accuracy}.

Replicating is making a copy or duplicate of something. Scientists replicate experiments to verify results. Cells replicate by dividing. A study that can't be replicated raises questions about its validity. The word implies producing something closely matching the original: {The forger spent years replicating the master's brushwork}.

Replication is the act of copying or reproducing something. In science, replication means repeating an experiment to verify results: {The study's findings await replication}. In biology, DNA replication is how genetic material copies itself before cell division. More broadly, replication can mean any duplication: {replication of the original design}, {data replication across servers}.

A replicator is something that makes copies—of itself or of other things. In biology, genes are replicators, reproducing themselves across generations. In science fiction, a replicator is a device that assembles objects from raw materials or energy: {The crew used the replicator to produce food and spare parts}. The term appears in discussions of nanotechnology and self-reproducing machines.

Replicators are things that make copies of themselves. In biology, genes and viruses are natural replicators. In science fiction, replicators are machines that can reproduce or manufacture objects—most famously the devices in Star Trek that synthesize food and equipment from raw matter: {She ordered a cup of tea from the replicator}. The term appears in discussions of nanotechnology and artificial intelligence, where self-replicating machines raise both promise and concern.

Reply is a response to something said, written, or done. You reply to questions, emails, accusations, or attacks. The word works as both verb and noun: {She didn't reply to my text}, {His reply was brief}. In legal contexts, a reply is a plaintiff's response to a defendant's answer.

Repo is short for repossession—the act of taking back property when a buyer defaults on payments. Cars are most often repossessed: {They came to repo his truck at 3 a.m.} A repo man recovers such property professionally. In finance, repo also means repurchase agreement, a short-term borrowing arrangement where securities are sold with an agreement to buy them back. In software development, repo is short for repository—a storage location for code: {Clone the repo and submit a pull request}.

The central idea of report, whether as noun or verb, is representation of something that has already happened or is happening. Generally, a report is a written or spoken account. A written report is usually understood to be somewhat lengthy and authoritative. When you report something, you tell someone about it, especially someone in authority. This is often implied when no recipient of the information is named: Students are told to report any suspicious activity. Things that are reported, as opposed to merely said or repeated, often take on an idea of importance simply by use of the verb.

A reporter is someone who gathers and presents news for newspapers, television, radio, or online media. The term emphasizes the core task: reporting what happened. {Reporters gathered outside the courthouse}. A reporter may also be someone who takes down official records: a court reporter transcribes legal proceedings verbatim.

Reporters are journalists who gather and report news. The term covers anyone whose job is to investigate events and communicate findings to the public—newspaper reporters, television reporters, court reporters who transcribe proceedings. {Reporters gathered outside the courthouse}. A reporter may also be a person who reports something in a general sense: {The study relied on self-reporters}.

Reporting is the act of giving an account of events, findings, or information. A journalist does reporting when gathering and presenting news. An employee does reporting when conveying results to supervisors. The word often implies a formal or official context: {Her reporting on the scandal won awards}, {quarterly financial reporting}. Reporting also describes hierarchical relationships: {She has three people reporting to her}.

Reports are accounts of events, findings, or information, usually delivered to someone in authority: {The committee submitted its reports to the board}. A report can be a document, a spoken account, or news coverage. To report is to give an account, to present oneself {(report for duty)}, or to inform on someone. A report is also a sharp explosive sound, especially from a gun: {The report of the rifle echoed through the valley}.

A repository is a place where things are stored or deposited, especially in large quantities or for safekeeping: {a repository of ancient manuscripts}, {a nuclear waste repository}. The term extends to people or institutions that hold accumulated knowledge: {She's a repository of local history}. In software development, a repository (or repo) stores code and tracks changes to it.

To repossess is to take back property when the buyer fails to make payments. Banks repossess cars, homes, and other financed goods: {They repossessed his truck after he missed three payments}. The word emphasizes that ownership reverts to the original seller or lender. Less commonly, repossess means to regain possession of something previously owned.

Repossessed describes property taken back by a seller or lender when the buyer fails to make payments. Cars, homes, and furniture are commonly repossessed: {They came to repossess the car after he missed three payments}. The word implies a forced reclaiming—the buyer loses what they thought was theirs.

Repossession is the act of taking back property when a buyer fails to make payments. Banks repossess cars, houses, and other financed goods when loans go into default: {The repo man came for the truck at dawn}. The shortened form repo is common in casual speech. To repossess can also mean simply to possess again, though the legal/financial sense dominates.

Repossessions are acts of taking back property when a buyer fails to make payments. A bank repossesses a car or house when the loan goes into default. The term appears frequently in financial and legal contexts: {The economic downturn led to a wave of home repossessions}. A repossession can also refer to the item itself: {The lot was full of repossessions waiting to be auctioned}.

Repost is to share content that has already been posted, typically on social media: {Sorry if this is a repost, but I just saw it}. The noun refers to the shared content itself. Reposting may credit the original source or not—the latter often draws criticism. On some platforms, the native sharing feature has its own name (retweet, reblog), while repost suggests copying content outright.

Reposting is sharing content on social media that was previously posted, either by yourself or someone else. The practice ranges from legitimate sharing—spreading news or amplifying voices—to low-effort recycling of popular content for engagement: {He's always reposting memes from three years ago}. On some platforms, reposting has a native function (retweet, reblog); on others it requires manual copying or screenshots.

To repot is to transfer a plant from one pot to another, typically a larger one to accommodate growth: {The roots were coming through the drainage holes, so I repotted it}. Repotting refreshes soil and gives roots room to spread.

Repped is the past tense of rep, meaning to represent or act on behalf of someone or something. A salesperson reps a product line; an agent reps talent: {She repped some of the biggest names in Hollywood}. In fitness slang, to rep is to perform repetitions of an exercise: {I repped out twenty pushups}.

Repping is representing—acting on behalf of someone or something, or showing allegiance to a group, brand, or place. Sales reps are repping their companies. Someone wearing their hometown's gear is repping where they're from: {She's always repping Chicago}. In fitness contexts, repping means doing repetitions of an exercise: {He was repping out push-ups}.

Reprehensible describes conduct deserving of strong criticism or condemnation—blameworthy in a way that invites moral judgment. The word carries weight: you might call a minor lapse regrettable, but reprehensible suggests genuine wrongdoing. {The cover-up was reprehensible.} {His treatment of the staff was reprehensible.}

Represent means to stand for or act on behalf of something else. A lawyer represents clients; an elected official represents constituents. Symbols represent ideas: {The dove represents peace}. To represent something is also to depict or portray it: {The painting represents a pastoral scene}. In casual speech, to represent is to proudly embody one's group or origins: {She's out there representing for her hometown}.

Representation is standing in for something else. A lawyer provides legal representation by acting on a client's behalf. Elected officials serve as political representation for constituents. In art, representation depicts subjects recognizably: {figurative representation versus abstraction}. A representation can also be a statement or claim: {The salesman made false representations about the product}. The word often appears in discussions of who gets depicted or included: {diversity in media representation}.

Representations are things that stand for or depict something else. A painting is a representation of its subject; a map is a representation of terrain. In law, representations are statements made to induce agreement: {The seller made false representations about the property's condition}. The word often appears in discussions of how groups are portrayed: {representations of women in media}. In cognitive science and AI, representations are internal models or encodings of information.

Representative describes something that stands for or typifies a larger whole. A representative sample captures the characteristics of a population. A representative government acts on behalf of citizens. As a noun, a representative is a person who speaks or acts for others—a sales representative, a union representative, a member of Congress. {The survey wasn't representative of actual voter opinions.} {She served as the company's representative at the conference.}

Representatives are people who act or speak on behalf of others. In government, representatives are elected officials who serve in a legislative body: {She called her representative about the bill}. Sales representatives work on behalf of companies. A representative sample or example typifies a larger group: {The survey wasn't representative of the whole population}. The word often implies legitimate authority to act for others' interests.

Representing is the present participle of represent, carrying its meanings into ongoing action. Someone representing a client acts on their behalf: {The lawyer representing the defendant requested a continuance}. An image representing something depicts or symbolizes it. In slang, representing means showing pride in one's origins or affiliations: {Just out here representing my hometown}.

Repress means to hold back or suppress. You might repress a laugh, a memory, or a rebellious faction. In psychology, to repress is to push uncomfortable thoughts or feelings out of conscious awareness: {He repressed memories of the accident}. Governments repress dissent; individuals repress emotions. The word suggests forceful containment—what's repressed doesn't disappear but remains under pressure.

Repressed describes feelings, memories, or desires pushed out of conscious awareness or deliberately suppressed. In psychology, repressed material remains in the unconscious, influencing behavior without the person's knowledge: {repressed childhood trauma}. More loosely, a repressed person inhibits natural impulses or emotions, often to unhealthy degrees: {He was so repressed he couldn't express affection}. Repressed can also describe groups kept down by authority: {a repressed population}.

Repression is the act of subduing or holding something down by force. A government engages in repression when it suppresses dissent: {The regime's repression of protesters drew international condemnation}. In psychology, repression is the unconscious exclusion of painful memories or desires from awareness—a defense mechanism that keeps disturbing thoughts buried. The adjective repressed describes both suppressed populations and individuals who have pushed emotions out of conscious reach: {repressed anger}, {a repressed memory}.

Repressive describes actions or systems that control people through force or restriction of freedom. A repressive {regime} suppresses dissent. Repressive {measures} limit speech, assembly, or other liberties. The word carries strong negative connotations—no government calls itself repressive, though critics often apply the label.

A reprieve is a temporary relief from something unpleasant, especially a postponement of punishment. A prisoner facing execution may receive a reprieve—a delay or cancellation of the sentence. More broadly, any brief escape from difficulty counts: {The rain stopped, giving us a reprieve from the heat}. As a verb, to reprieve is to grant such relief.

Reprieved is the past tense of reprieve, meaning to grant relief from punishment, danger, or an unpleasant situation. Originally referring to the postponement or cancellation of a death sentence, it now applies broadly to any temporary or permanent rescue from something dreaded: {The governor reprieved the condemned man}, {The old theater was reprieved from demolition}.

Reprieves are postponements or cancellations of punishment, especially a death sentence. More broadly, a reprieve is any temporary relief from something unpleasant: {The rain gave us a brief reprieve from the heat}. The verb reprieve means to grant such relief: {The governor reprieved the condemned man at the last moment}.

A reprimand is a formal expression of disapproval, typically from someone in authority: {The officer received a written reprimand for misconduct}. To reprimand someone is to rebuke them sharply: {The teacher reprimanded the students for talking during the exam}. A reprimand carries more official weight than a scolding but stops short of punishment.

Reprimands are formal expressions of disapproval, typically delivered by someone in authority to someone who has done something wrong. A boss reprimands an employee for repeated lateness; a judge reprimands a lawyer for courtroom misconduct. The word works as both noun and verb, with the verb suggesting the act of delivering such criticism: {She was reprimanded for violating company policy}. Reprimands are official but usually stop short of actual punishment.

Reprint works as both verb and noun. To reprint is to print again—a book goes back to press, an article appears in a new publication. A reprint is the result: another printing of a work, or a copy from that printing. {The essay was reprinted in several anthologies}. A reprint may be identical to the original or include minor corrections, but substantial revisions make it a new edition rather than a reprint.

Reprints are copies of a publication produced after the original printing. A book that sells well goes into reprints; a scholar orders reprints of their journal article to distribute. As a verb, to reprint is to print again: {The publisher reprinted the classic novel for its anniversary}. A reprint may be identical to the original or include minor corrections.

A reprisal is a retaliatory action taken against someone who has harmed you or your interests. In warfare, reprisals are acts of retaliation against an enemy: {The bombing was a reprisal for the attack on the embassy}. More broadly, any punitive response qualifies: {She feared reprisals from management after filing the complaint}. The word carries connotations of proportional revenge—answering harm with harm.

Reprisals are retaliatory actions taken against someone who has caused harm or offense. The term often appears in contexts of war or conflict, where one side responds to enemy attacks with counterattacks: {The bombing prompted immediate reprisals}. In workplace contexts, reprisals are punitive actions against employees who report misconduct: {whistleblower protections against reprisals}. The singular reprisal is less common but carries the same meaning.

A reprise is a repetition—most often of a musical passage or song, especially one returning later in a performance: {The show ended with a reprise of the opening number}. The word extends to any return or repetition of something done before: {a reprise of last year's successful marketing campaign}. As a verb, to reprise is to repeat, especially a role: {She reprised her award-winning performance}.

Reproach is criticism or blame for a failure or fault: {His silence was a reproach to my carelessness}. To reproach someone is to express disappointment in them, often with an element of sadness rather than anger: {She reproached him for forgetting their anniversary}. Something beyond reproach cannot be criticized—it's faultless. The word carries more sorrow than scold, more disappointment than condemnation.

Reproachful describes an expression of blame or disappointment directed at someone. A reproachful look or tone conveys that someone has failed to meet expectations or done something wrong: {She gave him a reproachful glance when he arrived late}. The word suggests quiet disapproval rather than open anger—more guilt-inducing than confrontational.
clues: A look that says you erred

definition: A reprobate is a morally unprincipled person, someone given to wickedness or vice. The word carries a theatrical quality—calling someone a reprobate suggests disapproval tinged with dark amusement: {The old reprobate gambled away his inheritance}. In theological contexts, a reprobate is someone rejected by God and beyond salvation. As an adjective, reprobate describes depraved or shameless behavior: {his reprobate lifestyle}.
clues: A person given over to sin

definition: Reprobates are people given to immoral or unprincipled behavior—scoundrels, degenerates, ne'er-do-wells. The word carries religious overtones of being rejected by God or beyond redemption: {a den of reprobates and sinners}. In casual use, it's often affectionate rather than truly damning: {I'm meeting the old reprobates for poker tonight}.

Reproduce means to create a copy or likeness of something: {The printer can reproduce the image in high resolution}. In biology, to reproduce is to generate offspring—organisms reproduce sexually or asexually to perpetuate their species. The word also means to recreate conditions or results: {Scientists struggled to reproduce the findings}. A reproduction is a copy, often of artwork or furniture.

Reproduction is the process by which organisms produce offspring, perpetuating their species through biological mechanisms. The word extends to any copying or duplication: {a reproduction of the original painting}, {the reproduction of documents}. In audio and video, reproduction refers to the quality of playback: {The sound reproduction on these speakers is excellent}. As an adjective, reproduction describes copies made to resemble originals: {reproduction furniture}, {reproduction antiques}.

Reproductions are copies of original works—typically art, furniture, or documents. A reproduction of a Rembrandt hangs where the original would be too valuable or unavailable. The word can carry a slight taint of inauthenticity: {It's not an original, just a reproduction}. In biology, reproductions would be instances of reproducing, though the singular form dominates that sense.

Reproductive relates to reproduction—the biological process of producing offspring. Reproductive {organs}, reproductive {health}, reproductive {rights}. The word appears frequently in discussions of biology, medicine, and politics surrounding fertility, contraception, and abortion. In biology, reproductive {success} measures how effectively an organism passes on its genes.

To reprogram is to program again or differently—rewriting the instructions that control how something operates. Computers get reprogrammed when software is updated or replaced. The word extends to minds and behavior: {therapy helped reprogram his response to stress}, {She's trying to reprogram her eating habits}. The metaphor treats human patterns as code that can be rewritten.

Reprogrammed is the past tense of reprogram—to program again or differently. Computers and devices get reprogrammed when their software is updated or replaced: {We reprogrammed the thermostat for the new schedule}. The word extends to changing ingrained patterns of thought or behavior: {She reprogrammed herself to wake up early}, {Years of therapy reprogrammed how he responds to stress}.

Reprogramming is changing the instructions that control something's behavior. Computers are reprogrammed when their software is rewritten. The term extends to any systematic alteration of conditioning or habits: {The cult reprogrammed its members}, {I'm trying to reprogram myself to wake up earlier}. In biology, cellular reprogramming converts specialized cells back to a stem-cell-like state.

Reps is the plural of rep, a word with several unrelated meanings. Most commonly, reps are repetitions of an exercise: {I did three sets of twelve reps}. Reps can also be representatives—sales reps, union reps, customer service reps. In textiles, rep is a fabric with a ribbed surface, making reps varieties of such fabric.

Reptiles are cold-blooded vertebrates with scaly skin—snakes, lizards, turtles, crocodiles, and their kin. Unlike amphibians, they don't need water to reproduce; unlike mammals and birds, they can't regulate their body temperature internally. Calling a person a reptile suggests they're cold, treacherous, or morally repulsive: {That reptile cheated his own mother}.

Reptiles is the plural of reptile—cold-blooded vertebrates with scaly skin that typically lay eggs on land. The class includes snakes, lizards, turtles, and crocodilians. Figuratively, calling someone a reptile suggests they're cold, calculating, or morally repugnant: {That reptile cheated his own grandmother}.

Reptilian describes something relating to or resembling reptiles—the cold-blooded, scaly vertebrates like snakes, lizards, and crocodiles. The word often carries negative connotations when applied to people, suggesting cold, calculating, or predatory qualities: {His reptilian eyes followed her across the room}. In conspiracy culture, reptilian refers to supposed shape-shifting alien beings believed to secretly control human affairs.

Reptilians are humanoid reptile creatures from conspiracy theories—alleged shapeshifting aliens who secretly control governments, media, and other institutions of power. The theory holds that world leaders and celebrities are actually these disguised reptiles manipulating humanity: {He thinks the royal family are reptilians}. The belief is associated with fringe thinking and antisemitic tropes about shadowy elites.

A republic is a form of government where power rests with citizens who elect representatives to govern, rather than with a monarch or hereditary ruler. The term implies rule by law and public institutions rather than by personal authority. In American political discourse, republic often emphasizes constitutional limits on majority rule, distinguishing it from pure democracy: {We're a republic, not a democracy}. (Capitalized Republic may refer to specific political parties or historical states.)

A republican supports or advocates for a republic—a form of government where power rests with citizens who elect representatives rather than with a monarch or emperor. The term describes both the political philosophy and its adherents: {republican ideals}, {a committed republican}. In countries with monarchies, republicans actively oppose royal rule: {Irish republicans sought independence from Britain}. (Capitalized Republican refers to members of the U.S. political party.)

Republicanism is commitment to republican government—a system where power resides in elected representatives rather than a monarch or hereditary aristocracy. The term encompasses both the political philosophy favoring such systems and active support for establishing or maintaining them.
