In American history, republicanism shaped the founders' vision of civic virtue and self-governance: {The Constitution reflects Enlightenment republicanism}. (Capitalized Republicanism refers to support for the Republican Party.)

Republics is the plural of republic, a form of government in which power resides with citizens who elect representatives rather than with a monarch or emperor. The term often implies constitutional protections and rule of law: {The founders established republics across the former colonies}. Banana republics are small nations with unstable governments dominated by foreign business interests.

Repudiation is the act of rejecting or refusing to accept something—a claim, an obligation, a belief, or a relationship. A government might issue a {repudiation of the treaty}. In contract law, repudiation occurs when one party indicates they won't fulfill their obligations, allowing the other to seek remedies. The word carries a sense of formal, emphatic rejection rather than casual dismissal.

Repugnant describes something that provokes strong disgust or aversion—offensive to one's sense of morality or taste: {The idea of eating insects is repugnant to many Westerners}, {repugnant behavior}. In legal contexts, repugnant means inconsistent or incompatible: {a clause repugnant to the Constitution}. The word carries more moral weight than merely unpleasant.

Repulse means to drive back or repel, whether physically or emotionally. An army repulses an attack by forcing the enemy to retreat. A person repulses unwanted advances by firmly rejecting them. The word also describes causing a feeling of intense disgust or aversion: {His table manners repulsed everyone at dinner}. As a noun, a repulse is an instance of being driven back or rejected, often with connotations of defeat or rebuff.

Repulsed means driven back or rejected with force. An army repulses an attack; a person repulses unwanted advances. The word also describes feeling intense disgust or aversion: {I was repulsed by the smell}. This second sense—meaning disgusted rather than physically pushed away—has become the dominant use in everyday speech.

Repulsion is a strong feeling of disgust or aversion—the opposite of attraction. Something repulsive makes you want to pull away: {She felt a wave of repulsion at the sight}. In physics, repulsion is the force that pushes objects apart, as when like magnetic poles or like electrical charges resist each other.
clues: Magnetic poles forcing each other away

definition: Repulsive describes something that provokes strong physical or moral disgust—something so offensive it pushes you away: {a repulsive smell}, {repulsive behavior}. The word is stronger than merely unpleasant; it suggests an instinctive recoiling. In physics, repulsive forces push objects apart, as when like magnetic poles repel each other.

To repurpose something is to adapt it for a different use than originally intended. An old factory gets repurposed as loft apartments. A mason jar becomes a drinking glass. The word often appears in contexts of recycling, sustainability, or creative reuse: {She repurposed the wooden pallets into garden furniture}. Content gets repurposed when adapted for different platforms or audiences.

Repurposed describes something adapted for a new use different from its original purpose. An old factory becomes repurposed as loft apartments. A mason jar gets repurposed as a drinking glass. The term often carries connotations of resourcefulness or sustainability: {repurposed shipping containers turned into affordable housing}, {repurposed content across social media platforms}.

Repurposing is finding a new use for something beyond its original purpose. Old factories get repurposed as loft apartments. A mason jar becomes a vase. The word often carries connotations of resourcefulness or sustainability: {She's repurposing vintage fabric into handbags}. In pharmaceutical contexts, drug repurposing means finding new medical applications for existing medications.
clues: Converting old items for new uses

definition: Reputable describes someone or something with a good reputation—trustworthy, respectable, and well-regarded. A reputable {contractor} does quality work and honors commitments. A reputable {source} can be relied upon for accurate information. The word often appears when distinguishing legitimate operators from questionable ones: {Make sure you use a reputable dealer}.

Reputation is what people generally think or say about someone or something, especially regarding character, ability, or quality. A person's reputation precedes them when others have already formed opinions before meeting them. You can have a reputation {for} something specific: {She has a reputation for being difficult to work with}. Reputation can be good or bad, built over years or destroyed in moments. To {protect your reputation} is to guard how others perceive you.

Reputations is the plural of reputation, the collective judgments and opinions that others hold about a person, organization, or thing based on past behavior or perceived character. People build, protect, damage, or lose their reputations over time. {Politicians live and die by their reputations.} A reputation can be good or bad, deserved or undeserved, and may differ across different communities or contexts.

A request is an act of asking for something: {She put in a request for time off}. To request is to ask, typically with some formality or politeness: {I request your presence at the meeting}. Request implies the asker lacks authority to demand—you request from equals or superiors, but order subordinates. {Available upon request} means you must ask to receive it.

Requests are things asked for—favors, demands, or formal applications: {We've received several requests for refunds}, {at the request of the committee}. To request is to ask, typically more formally than simply asking: {She requested a meeting with the director}. A request can also be a song or piece asked for: {The DJ played my request}.

A requiem is a Mass for the dead in the Roman Catholic Church, or the musical setting of that liturgy. Mozart's Requiem and Verdi's Requiem are among the most celebrated. By extension, requiem describes any solemn piece commemorating the dead, or figuratively, a final tribute to something that has ended: {The documentary served as a requiem for the dying industry}.

Requiems is the plural of requiem, a musical composition or religious service honoring the dead. The word comes from the Latin Mass for the Dead, which opens with "Requiem aeternam" (eternal rest). Famous requiems include those by Mozart, Verdi, and Brahms. Figuratively, a requiem marks the end of something: {The factory closing was a requiem for the town's prosperity}.

Require means to need or to demand as necessary. A job may require certain qualifications; a recipe requires specific ingredients. In formal or legal contexts, require indicates obligation: {Passengers are required to wear seatbelts}. The word carries more weight than need—what's required isn't optional. {This requires your immediate attention.}

Required means necessary or demanded by rule, law, or circumstance. A required {course} must be taken to graduate. Required {reading} is assigned, not optional. The word often appears in bureaucratic or institutional contexts: {All required documents must be submitted by Friday}. Something required is obligatory rather than merely recommended.

A requirement is something that must be met or fulfilled—a condition, qualification, or necessity. {Applicants must meet all job requirements}. Requirements may be formal rules or practical necessities: {entrance requirements}, {system requirements}, {the requirements of the job}. What someone requires becomes a requirement: {Sleep is a basic human requirement}.

Requirements are things that must be met, fulfilled, or possessed—conditions or qualifications necessary for something else to happen. A job has requirements; so does a visa application. {She met all the requirements for graduation.} In software development, requirements specify what a system must do: {The client keeps changing the requirements.} The word often implies official or formal standards rather than mere preferences.

Requisition is a formal demand or request, typically from an authority: {The army issued a requisition for supplies}. As a verb, to requisition something is to demand it officially, often implying seizure or compulsory acquisition: {The government requisitioned private vehicles during the emergency}. The word carries overtones of bureaucratic or military authority—you requisition what you have the power to take.

To reread is to read something again: {I reread the email three times before responding}. The word implies returning to material you've encountered before, whether for clarity, pleasure, or study. Some books reward rereading; others don't survive it.

To rerelease something is to release it again—typically a film, album, or book brought back to market after its initial run. A rerelease often includes new features, restored footage, or updated packaging: {The studio rereleased the classic with a remastered soundtrack}. As a noun, it refers to the product itself: {The anniversary rerelease includes bonus tracks}.

To reroll is to roll dice again, typically after an unsatisfactory result. In tabletop and video games, a reroll lets you discard an outcome and try for a better one: {I used my luck token to reroll the attack}. Extended to any situation where you abandon one random result for another: {I'm going to reroll my character} means generating a new one from scratch.

A rerun is a broadcast of a television program that has already aired: {Nothing but reruns this summer}. The word extends to any repetition of something already done or experienced: {a rerun of last year's debate}. As a verb, to rerun is to broadcast, perform, or execute again: {They reran the experiment with better controls}.

Reruns are repeat broadcasts of television programs that have aired before. A show in its first run consists of new episodes; reruns fill the gaps between seasons or replace canceled programming. The term extends to any repetition of something already experienced: {Summer means nothing but reruns} can describe both TV schedules and the feeling that nothing new is happening.

Resale is the act of selling something previously purchased. The resale market includes used cars, secondhand clothing, and concert tickets bought for profit. Resale {value} is what an item can fetch when sold again: {Toyotas hold their resale value well}. Resale {shops} sell secondhand goods.

To reschedule is to assign a new time or date to something previously planned: {We had to reschedule the meeting for next week}. The word implies the original arrangement still matters—you're moving it, not canceling. Banks and governments reschedule debt payments to extend deadlines or restructure terms.

Rescue is saving someone or something from danger, captivity, or harm. A lifeguard rescues a drowning swimmer; firefighters rescue people from burning buildings. The word works as both verb and noun: {The coast guard performed a daring rescue}. To come to someone's rescue is to help them out of difficulty, literal or figurative: {My sister came to my rescue when I couldn't pay rent}.

Rescued is the past tense of rescue—to save someone or something from danger, harm, or an undesirable situation. A lifeguard rescued a swimmer. Firefighters rescued residents from a burning building. The word extends to less dire situations: {The phone call rescued me from an awkward conversation}. Rescued animals are those saved from abuse, neglect, or euthanasia.

A rescuer is someone who saves another from danger, harm, or difficulty. The word applies to professionals—firefighters, lifeguards, emergency responders—and to anyone who intervenes in a crisis: {Rescuers pulled survivors from the rubble}. It can extend beyond physical danger: {She was my rescuer when I was drowning in paperwork}.

Rescues is the plural of rescue, the act of saving someone or something from danger, harm, or an undesirable situation: {The coast guard performed three rescues that night}. As a verb form, rescues means saves or delivers from peril: {She rescues stray dogs from the streets}. A rescue can be dramatic—pulling someone from a burning building—or mundane: {Thanks for the rescue; that conversation was going nowhere}.

Research can be a noun or a verb whose meanings are connected with investigating in order to gain knowledge: The department’s research is currently focused on how the brain processes spoken language. She has been researching a treatment for a rare genetic disorder. The noun can also mean the results of an investigation, and it is often used with verbs such as indicate, show, suggest, find, and reveal: Research suggests that international visitors want to explore beyond the main tourist attractions.

A researcher is someone who conducts systematic investigation to discover or establish facts. The term spans academic scientists, market analysts, journalists, and anyone methodically gathering information: {She works as a researcher at a biotech company}, {The documentary team hired researchers to dig through archives}. Research can be the activity or the findings themselves.

Resegregation is the return to racial or demographic separation after a period of integration, typically in schools, housing, or public institutions. The term emerged prominently in discussions of American education, where court-ordered desegregation programs were dismantled or circumvented, leading neighborhoods and schools to become racially homogeneous again. {Critics argue that the resegregation of urban schools has accelerated since the 1990s.} The process may occur through explicit policy changes or through demographic shifts like white flight.

To resell is to sell something you previously bought: {She resells vintage clothing on eBay}, {Ticket scalpers resell seats at a markup}. The word emphasizes the transaction chain—someone acquired the item specifically to sell it again, often at a profit. Resale is the noun form.

A reseller buys goods or services from a manufacturer or distributor and sells them to others, typically end consumers or smaller businesses. Unlike retailers who may modify or brand products, resellers often sell items largely unchanged, acting as intermediaries in the supply chain. The term appears frequently in technology and telecommunications, where companies purchase software licenses, hosting services, or phone plans in bulk to resell: {We bought our domain through an authorized reseller}. Resellers may add value through customer support or bundling.

Resellers are people or businesses that buy goods to sell them again rather than use them. The term often carries a negative connotation when applied to those who snap up limited items—concert tickets, sneakers, game consoles—to flip at inflated prices: {Resellers bought up all the PS5s before regular customers had a chance}. In business contexts, resellers are legitimate intermediaries who distribute products from manufacturers to end users.

Reselling is selling something you previously bought, often at a markup. The practice ranges from garage sales to professional operations buying limited-release sneakers or concert tickets for resale at higher prices. Online platforms have made reselling a business model: {She makes a living reselling vintage clothing on Depop}.

Resemblance is similarity in appearance or character between things or people. A child may bear a {strong resemblance} to a parent. Two situations may have enough resemblance to invite comparison. The word often implies visual likeness but extends to any shared quality: {The resemblance between the two cases is striking}.

To resent is to feel bitter or indignant about something perceived as unfair or insulting: {She resented being passed over for promotion}. Resentment often festers—you can resent something for years. The object is typically a person, action, or situation: {He resented his brother's success}, {I resent the implication that I was lying}.

Resentful describes feeling bitter indignation at having been treated unfairly or slighted. The emotion lingers—resentment simmers rather than flares: {She remained resentful for years after being passed over for promotion}. Someone resentful toward a person or situation carries ongoing displeasure about a perceived wrong. {He gave a resentful glare when his brother's success was mentioned.}

Resentment is bitter indignation at having been treated unfairly. Unlike quick-burning anger, resentment simmers—it's the feeling that lingers when you believe you've been wronged and the wrong hasn't been acknowledged or corrected. {She harbored resentment toward her sister for years}. Resentment often poisons relationships precisely because it goes unexpressed.

Resentments is the plural of resentment—bitter feelings held toward someone or something perceived as having caused injury or unfairness. The plural often emphasizes accumulated grievances: {He nursed old resentments for years}. In twelve-step programs, making a list of resentments is a formal step toward recovery: {Her sponsor helped her work through her resentments}.

A reservation is an arrangement to secure something in advance, such as a table at a restaurant or a seat on a plane. The word also names land set aside for a specific purpose, most notably the territories designated for Native American tribes in the United States. When you have reservations about something, you harbor doubts or hesitations: {I have some reservations about this plan}. This sense suggests holding back part of your approval or commitment.

Reservations are doubts or misgivings that hold you back from full commitment: {I have reservations about the plan}. The word also means arrangements to hold something in advance—a table at a restaurant, a hotel room, a seat on a flight: {Do you have a reservation?} In North American history, a reservation is land set aside for Indigenous peoples, often through forced relocation. The singular reservation covers all these uses; the plural simply indicates multiple instances.

Reserve centers on holding something back for future use or a specific purpose. A nature reserve protects land from development. Financial reserves are funds set aside for emergencies. To reserve a table is to secure it in advance. Someone with reserve keeps emotions or opinions guarded—they don't share freely. {She maintained her reserve throughout the interview}. Reserve can also mean a substitute player who waits to enter the game, or military forces not on active duty.

Reserved describes someone who keeps thoughts and feelings to themselves, avoiding open expression or easy intimacy: {He was pleasant but reserved at dinner}. The word suggests self-containment rather than coldness—a reserved person may simply be private or cautious. Reserved also means set aside for a particular use or person: {reserved seating}, {a reserved parking spot}.

Reserves are things held back for future use. A country's oil reserves lie underground until needed. Financial reserves are funds set aside for emergencies. Military reserves are troops not on active duty but available when called: {He served in the Army Reserves}. A nature reserve protects land from development. Reserve also describes restraint in manner—someone who shows reserve is guarded or formal. To reserve is to hold something for later: {I reserved a table for eight}.

A reservist is a member of a military reserve force—someone who has received training and can be called to active duty when needed, but who otherwise lives as a civilian. Reservists typically drill periodically to maintain readiness: {The reservist balanced her weekend training with her regular job}. During major conflicts or emergencies, reservists may be activated to supplement active-duty forces.

Reservists are members of a military reserve force—troops who train periodically but aren't on active duty, available to be called up when needed. Most countries maintain reserves alongside their standing armies: {The army called up reservists after the invasion}. {She serves as a reservist one weekend a month}.

A reservoir is a large natural or artificial lake used to store water for human use—drinking, irrigation, or generating electricity. The word extends to any container or space that holds a supply of something: {a reservoir of talent}, {the body's reservoir of fat}. In medicine, a reservoir host harbors a pathogen that can spread to other species.

Reservoirs are places where something is stored or accumulated. Most commonly, a reservoir is an artificial lake created by damming a river to store water for drinking, irrigation, or hydroelectric power: {The reservoir supplies water to three counties}. The term extends to any container holding liquid—the tank in a toilet, the ink chamber in a fountain pen. Figuratively, a reservoir is a supply that can be drawn upon: {a reservoir of talent}, {a reservoir of goodwill}. In epidemiology, a reservoir is an organism or environment that harbors a pathogen without being affected by it.

Reset means to set again or return to an original state. You reset a clock, a password, or a broken bone. Electronic devices reset when restored to factory settings or restarted after malfunction: {Have you tried turning it off and on again?} Figuratively, to reset is to start fresh: {We need to reset our expectations}. A reset is the act itself or a button that triggers it.

Resets is the plural of reset—instances of returning something to an original state or starting position. In gaming, resets are attempts to restart after failure: {After dozens of resets, I finally beat the boss}. In broader use, resets are fresh starts or recalibrations: {The relationship needed several resets before it worked}. To reset is to restore defaults, clear accumulated changes, or begin again.

Resetting is the act of returning something to its original or default state. You might reset a password, a clock, or a broken bone (which requires manipulation back into proper alignment). In gaming and tech contexts, resetting often means restarting a device or reloading a saved state: {I kept resetting until I got the outcome I wanted}. The word also applies to mental or emotional restoration: {a weekend of resetting after a stressful month}.

To resettle is to settle again in a new place, typically after displacement. Refugees resettle in host countries; populations resettle after wars or natural disasters. The word implies establishing a permanent home rather than temporary refuge: {The family resettled in Canada after fleeing persecution}. Resettle can also mean to return to a previous location: {They resettled in the village after the fighting stopped}.

Resettled is the past tense of resettle, meaning to settle again in a new place. People are resettled after displacement by war, disaster, or government policy: {Refugees were resettled in host countries across Europe}. The word can also describe voluntary relocation: {After retiring, they resettled in a warmer climate}.

Resettlement is the process of moving people to a new place to live, typically after displacement by war, disaster, or persecution. Governments and international agencies manage refugee resettlement programs: {The family awaited resettlement in a third country}. The term also applies to relocating populations for development projects or political purposes, sometimes forcibly.

Reshape means to give new form or structure to something. You reshape clay with your hands, reshape a garment by altering its cut, or reshape an organization by changing how it operates. The word implies the thing already had a shape that's being modified: {The economic crisis reshaped the political landscape}. In computing, reshape changes how data is arranged without altering its content.

To reshoot is to film a scene or sequence again, typically because the original footage was unsatisfactory: {The director ordered a reshoot of the opening scene}. As a noun, a reshoot is such a repeated filming session. Major reshoots on a movie production often signal creative problems or studio interference.

Reshoots are additional filming done after principal photography has wrapped, typically to fix problems, add scenes, or adjust a film's direction. In Hollywood, extensive reshoots often signal trouble: {The reshoots cost an extra twenty million}. But minor reshoots are routine—nearly every major production schedules time for them.

A residence is a place where someone lives. The word carries a formal or official tone—you fill out forms asking for your {place of residence}, and a dignitary's official home is their residence. Residence also refers to the fact of living somewhere: {during her residence in Paris}. In medical contexts, residency is a period of specialized training for doctors after medical school.

Residencies is the plural of residency, which names a period of specialized training or an official place of dwelling. Medical residencies follow graduation from medical school and involve supervised practice in a specialty: {She completed her residency in pediatrics}. Artist residencies provide time and space for creative work, often at dedicated institutions. Residency also means legal domicile—the place where someone officially lives for purposes of taxation, voting, or university tuition rates.

Residency is the state of living in a particular place, often with legal implications: {You need to establish residency before you can vote here}. It also refers to a period of advanced medical training in a specialty, completed after medical school: {She's doing her residency in pediatric surgery}. A residency can also be an artist's temporary appointment at an institution: {a writer's residency at the university}.

A resident is someone who lives in a particular place, whether a house, neighborhood, city, or country. {Residents of the apartment complex share a parking garage.} The term also applies to doctors in training who work at a hospital while completing their specialty education after medical school. As an adjective, resident describes someone or something that lives or is based in a location: {the resident expert on tax law}. In computing, resident describes programs or data that remain in memory rather than being loaded as needed.

Residential describes places where people live, as opposed to commercial or industrial areas: {a residential neighborhood}, {residential zoning}. It also describes things related to living arrangements: {residential treatment} involves patients living at a facility, and {residential real estate} is housing rather than business property.

Residents are people who live in a particular place. A city has residents, as does an apartment building or nursing home. The term often distinguishes permanent inhabitants from visitors or workers: {Parking is reserved for residents}. In medicine, a resident is a doctor in advanced training at a hospital, having completed medical school but not yet fully licensed to practice independently.

Residuals are payments made to performers—actors, voice artists, musicians—when their recorded work is rebroadcast, streamed, or reused: {She still gets residuals from that commercial she shot in 2015}. In statistics and science, residuals are the differences between observed values and predicted values—what's left over after a model accounts for what it can. The thread connecting both uses is something remaining after the main event: ongoing compensation after the original work, unexplained variance after the calculation.

Residue is what remains after a process removes the rest. Chemical reactions leave residue. Evaporation leaves residue. A filter catches residue. The word often suggests unwanted traces: {pesticide residue on vegetables}, {soap residue in the washing machine}. In law, the residue of an estate is what's left after specific bequests and debts are settled.
clues: What clings after the rest goes

definition: Resign means to voluntarily give up a position or office: {She resigned from the board}. The word carries formality—you resign a job but quit a shift. To resign yourself to something is to accept it reluctantly: {He resigned himself to the long wait}. A resigned tone or sigh conveys weary acceptance of circumstances beyond your control.

Resignation is the act of leaving a position, typically a job or office: {She submitted her resignation effective immediately}. The word also names a state of reluctant acceptance—yielding to something unavoidable without further struggle: {He accepted his fate with quiet resignation}. Both senses share the idea of giving something up.

Resignations are formal acts of leaving a position or office. The word covers both the act itself and the documents that formalize it: {The CEO handed in her resignation}. When someone submits a resignation, they voluntarily give up their role—though the voluntariness may be nominal when someone is pressured to resign rather than be fired. Mass resignations can signal organizational crisis or protest.

Resigned describes someone who has accepted something unpleasant or unwelcome without resistance: {She gave a resigned sigh and agreed to help}. The word suggests quiet surrender rather than active protest—you've stopped fighting what seems inevitable. To resign is to formally give up a position or office: {He resigned from the board}. A resignation is the act of resigning or the state of being resigned.

Resigning is giving up a position, office, or responsibility voluntarily: {She's resigning from the board effective immediately}. In chess, resigning means conceding defeat before checkmate, acknowledging the position is hopeless. A person resigning themselves to something accepts it as unavoidable: {He's resigning himself to another year in the job}.

Resigns means to give up a position or office voluntarily: {She resigned from the board after ten years}. The word often implies acceptance of something unpleasant—to resign yourself to a situation is to stop fighting it: {He resigned himself to a long wait}. In chess, to resign is to concede defeat before checkmate.

Resilience is the ability to recover from difficulty or spring back into shape. A resilient material returns to form after being bent or compressed. A resilient person endures hardship and bounces back: {Her resilience after the divorce impressed everyone}. The word implies not just survival but restoration—regaining strength, spirits, or position after setback.

Resilient describes the ability to recover from difficulty or return to original form after being bent, stretched, or compressed. A resilient material springs back; a resilient person bounces back from setbacks: {She proved remarkably resilient after the divorce}. The word implies not just survival but restoration—emerging from hardship without permanent damage.

Resin is a sticky, viscous substance secreted by certain plants, especially conifers like pines and firs. Natural resins harden when exposed to air and have been used for centuries in varnishes, adhesives, and incense. Synthetic resins—manufactured polymers with similar properties—are now more common industrially, appearing in plastics, coatings, and composite materials. In 3D printing, liquid resin cures under UV light to form solid objects: {The printer uses a special resin that hardens layer by layer}.

Resins are sticky, viscous substances that harden when exposed to air, produced naturally by plants—especially conifers—or manufactured synthetically. Natural resins like amber and frankincense have been valued for millennia. Synthetic resins form the basis of many plastics, adhesives, and coatings: {epoxy resin}, {polyester resin}. In cannabis culture, resin refers to the concentrated compounds containing THC.

To resist is to push back against something—force, change, temptation, or authority. You can resist an {attacker}, resist {arrest}, or resist the {urge} to check your phone. Materials that resist wear or corrosion withstand them. A person who {can't resist} something finds it irresistible: {I couldn't resist the chocolate cake}. To resist is not necessarily to prevail—only to oppose.

Resistance is the act of opposing or refusing to accept something. You might meet resistance when proposing change, or offer resistance when someone tries to move you. In physics, resistance is a force that opposes motion: {air resistance}, {electrical resistance}. The Resistance refers to underground movements opposing occupying forces, especially in World War II France. Resistance training builds strength by working muscles against opposing force. {The path of least resistance} is the easiest route through obstacles.

Resistant describes something that withstands or opposes a force, substance, or change. Materials can be water-resistant, heat-resistant, or stain-resistant. Bacteria become antibiotic-resistant through evolution. People resistant to new ideas are unwilling to accept them: {He's resistant to any suggestion that he might be wrong}. The noun form, also resistant, names someone who resists, especially a member of an underground movement opposing occupation.

Resisting is actively opposing or working against something. You might resist arrest, resist temptation, or resist change. The word implies pushback against pressure or force: {She resisted the urge to check her phone}. Materials that resist corrosion or heat withstand those conditions without yielding.

Resistors is the plural of resistor, an electrical component that limits current flow in a circuit. Resistors convert electrical energy to heat and are fundamental to electronics, controlling voltage levels and protecting sensitive components. They're measured in ohms: {The circuit requires two 100-ohm resistors in series}.

To resize is to change the dimensions of something, making it larger or smaller. The word appears most often in computing contexts—resizing windows, images, or files: {Resize the photo before uploading}. Physical objects can also be resized: {The jeweler resized the ring to fit her finger}.

To reskin something is to apply a new visual surface while keeping the underlying structure intact. In gaming and software, reskinning replaces graphics, textures, or interface elements without changing functionality: {They reskinned the character with a dragon theme}. The term extends to any superficial makeover: {The company reskinned their old product and called it new}.

Reskinned describes something given a new surface appearance while keeping its underlying structure or mechanics unchanged. The term comes from video games, where a reskinned character or item uses the same code but different graphics: {It's just a reskinned version of last year's model}. The word often carries a dismissive tone, suggesting superficial change without real innovation.

Reskinning is changing the visual appearance of something—especially software, video games, or vehicles—without altering its underlying structure or function. A reskinned game might feature new characters and graphics while keeping identical gameplay mechanics. The practice is common in mobile gaming, where developers release essentially the same game with different themes: {They just reskinned their puzzle game with a Christmas theme}.

Resolute means firmly determined, unwavering in purpose or belief. A resolute person has made up their mind and won't be swayed: {She remained resolute despite the criticism}. The word suggests admirable steadfastness rather than mere stubbornness—resolution in the face of difficulty or opposition. {His resolute defense of free speech won him allies and enemies alike.}

Resolution is the act of resolving or the state of being resolved. A firm decision or determination: {My New Year's resolution is to exercise more}. The settling of a dispute or problem: {The conflict reached resolution after months of negotiation}. In narrative, the resolution is where plot threads come together after the climax. In optics and imaging, resolution measures the fineness of detail a system can distinguish—higher resolution means sharper images. In music, resolution is the movement from dissonance to consonance, tension releasing into stability.

Resolutions are firm decisions to do or not do something. The word carries a sense of determination—a resolution is stronger than a mere intention. New Year's resolutions are commitments to self-improvement, notoriously abandoned by February. Resolution also means the act of resolving a problem or dispute: {The conflict reached resolution after months of negotiation}. In technical contexts, resolution describes the detail an image or screen can display: {a monitor with 4K resolution}. The plural often refers to formal statements adopted by deliberative bodies: {The committee passed three resolutions}.

Resolve (the verb) has a lot in common with its underlying root solve. To resolve an issue, problem, or conflict is to find a solution for it and thus end it. If symptoms of a disease resolve, they go away. The verbal noun of resolve is resolution. The noun resolve has a different meaning. Resolve is a quality of determination to achieve something, especially when there are obstacles to doing this: I resolve to run for 30 minutes three times each week.

Resolved describes something that has been settled, decided, or worked out. A resolved issue no longer requires attention; a resolved person has made up their mind firmly. In technical contexts, an image or display with high resolution is well-resolved, meaning its details are sharp and distinct. The verb resolve means to find a solution or reach a firm decision: {We resolved our differences over dinner}. Someone who is resolved to do something has committed to that course of action with determination.

Resolving is the act of settling, solving, or determining something. You might be {resolving a dispute}, {resolving technical issues}, or {resolving to do better next year}. The word captures the process of working toward resolution—whether that means finding answers, making firm decisions, or bringing clarity to what was uncertain or contentious.

Resonance is the quality of being deep, full, and reverberating: {the resonance of a cello}, {His voice had a warm resonance}. In physics, resonance occurs when vibrations amplify because frequencies align—a wineglass shattering from a sustained note. Figuratively, resonance describes meaningful connection or significance: {The film had particular resonance for immigrants}. Something resonates when it strikes a chord, echoing beyond its immediate context.

Resonances is the plural of resonance, which at its core describes a quality of deep, full, reverberating sound—the kind that seems to linger and fill a space. From this acoustic sense, resonance extends to anything that evokes a strong response or has lasting significance: {The film's themes had deep resonances with audiences who lived through the war}. In physics, resonance refers to the amplification that occurs when a system vibrates at its natural frequency. Something with resonances carries echoes or meaningful connections to other ideas, experiences, or emotions.

Resonant describes sounds that are deep, full, and continuing to vibrate: {a resonant voice}, {the resonant tone of a cello}. The term comes from physics, where resonance occurs when vibrations amplify at a natural frequency. Figuratively, something resonant strikes a chord or evokes strong response: {Her speech was deeply resonant with the audience}. A resonant image or idea lingers and reverberates in the mind.

Resonate means to produce or amplify sound through vibration—a guitar string resonates when plucked, a voice resonates in a large hall. The figurative sense dominates contemporary usage: something resonates when it strikes a chord, producing an emotional or intellectual response: {Her speech really resonated with the audience}. Ideas, themes, and experiences resonate with people when they feel personally meaningful or familiar.

Resonated is the past tense of resonate, meaning to produce or be filled with a deep, reverberating sound: {The gong resonated through the temple}. More commonly now, it describes when something strikes a chord emotionally or intellectually: {Her speech resonated with voters}. If an idea resonates, it feels meaningful or relevant to the listener—it echoes within them.

Resonating describes something that produces or prolongs sound through vibration, or more commonly, something that evokes a strong response or connection. A speech resonates with an audience when it strikes a chord: {Her message about justice is really resonating with voters}. In its physical sense, a tuning fork resonates at a specific frequency. The figurative use dominates contemporary speech—ideas, experiences, or art resonate when they feel meaningful or personally relevant.

A resonator is a device or structure that amplifies or sustains vibrations at particular frequencies. In musical instruments, resonators enhance sound—the body of a guitar or violin acts as a resonator, as do the metal cones in resonator guitars. In electronics and physics, resonators are components designed to vibrate or oscillate at specific frequencies, used in filters, oscillators, and tuning circuits. The term extends to any cavity or system that naturally reinforces certain wavelengths while dampening others.

Resort centers on going somewhere for relief or solution. A resort is a place people visit for recreation or relaxation: {a ski resort}, {a beach resort}. To resort to something is to turn to it as an option, often reluctantly or as a last measure: {We had to resort to bribery}. A {last resort} is the final option when others have failed. {Recourse} and {resource} share the same root idea of turning back to something for help.

Resorted is the past tense of resort, meaning to turn to something as a course of action, typically when other options have failed or seem unavailable: {She resorted to begging when the money ran out}. The word often carries a note of reluctance or desperation—you resort to measures you'd rather avoid. {They resorted to violence after negotiations collapsed.}

Resorts functions as both noun and verb. A resort is a place people visit for recreation or relaxation—a beach resort, a ski resort, a health resort. To resort to something is to turn to it as an option, often reluctantly or as a last measure: {We had to resort to bribery}. As a {last resort}, you try something when all else has failed. The noun and verb connect through the idea of going to something for help or relief.

Resound means to echo or reverberate with sound: {The hall resounded with applause}. Something that resounds fills a space or lingers: {Her words resounded in his mind for days}. Resounding as an adjective means emphatic or unmistakable: a resounding {victory}, a resounding {success}, a resounding {no}.

Resounding describes something loud and echoing: {a resounding crash}, {resounding applause}. More often it emphasizes completeness or decisiveness: a resounding {victory}, a resounding {success}, a resounding {no}. The figurative sense dominates—when something is resounding, it leaves no room for doubt or ambiguity.
clues: So loud it fills the space

definition: A resource is something useful or available when needed. Natural resources include water, minerals, and timber. Human resources are the people available to work. Financial resources are funds. To be resourceful is to find clever solutions. The plural often suggests wealth or capability: {a country rich in resources}, {We don't have the resources for that project}.

Resourceful describes someone skilled at finding solutions with whatever is available. A resourceful person improvises, adapts, and overcomes obstacles through cleverness rather than superior tools or resources: {She was resourceful enough to fashion a splint from tree branches}. The word suggests practical creativity—making do, thinking on your feet, not giving up when the obvious path is blocked.

Resourcefulness is the ability to find clever solutions with whatever is available. A resourceful person facing a problem doesn't wait for ideal conditions—they improvise, adapt, and make do: {Her resourcefulness during the power outage impressed everyone}. The quality suggests both creativity and practicality, turning limitations into opportunities rather than obstacles.

Resources are assets available for use—money, materials, people, time, or information that can be drawn upon when needed. Natural resources are raw materials like water, timber, and minerals. Human resources refers to personnel, often as a corporate department. Someone {of limited resources} lacks wealth. To be {resourceful} is to manage well with whatever's available.

To respawn is to reappear in a video game after your character has died, returning to play at a designated location: {I'll respawn at the checkpoint}. The term extends to the locations themselves: {Wait for me at the respawn point}. Outside gaming, respawn describes anything that regenerates or reappears after being eliminated: {The weeds respawn faster than I can pull them}.

Respawning is reappearing in a video game after being killed or destroyed. Players respawn at designated locations to continue playing: {I keep respawning at the same checkpoint}. The term extends beyond gaming to describe any return after elimination or failure: {The company keeps respawning under different names}.

Respawns is the third-person singular of respawn, a gaming term for reappearing in the game world after being killed or destroyed. Players respawn at designated points to continue playing: {She respawns at the checkpoint after falling off the cliff}. The concept has spread to figurative use for any return after setback: {The same bad idea respawns every few years}.

As a noun, respect can have a meaning similar to way, part, feature, and other words relating to components: Your analysis is defective in several respects. This meaning is conveyed in phrases such as with respect to and in respect of. A different meaning is roughly synonymous with esteem: Their respect for the famous author prevented them from questioning his work. The verbal use of respect is related to this noun meaning: It is vital that children learn to respect their parents.

Respectability is the quality of being socially acceptable and morally proper. It suggests conformity to conventional standards of behavior and appearance: {a veneer of respectability}, {middle-class respectability}. The word often carries a whiff of judgment—implying concern with appearances over substance, or the stifling norms someone might rebel against: {She traded adventure for respectability}.

Respectable describes someone or something worthy of respect or social approval. A respectable {career}, a respectable {neighborhood}, a respectable {family}. The word often implies conformity to conventional standards rather than genuine admiration—respectable can mean merely acceptable or adequate: {a respectable showing}, {a respectable salary}. Sometimes it carries faint disapproval, suggesting someone overly concerned with appearances: {too respectable to associate with artists}.

Respected describes someone or something held in high regard or esteem. A respected {scholar} has earned admiration through achievement. A respected {tradition} carries cultural weight. The word often appears before titles or roles: {a respected member of the community}, {a respected journalist}. To be respected implies others value your judgment, character, or contributions.

Respectful means showing deference or consideration toward someone or something. A respectful {tone} avoids offense; a respectful {distance} maintains appropriate space. The word implies awareness of another's dignity, authority, or boundaries: {The students were respectful during the ceremony}. To be respectful of someone's wishes is to honor them.

Respecting is a somewhat formal preposition meaning concerning or with regard to: {respecting your earlier question, I have no comment}. It sounds legalistic or old-fashioned in most contexts, where about or regarding would be more natural. Separately, respecting is the present participle of respect: {respecting someone's boundaries}.

Respects appears almost exclusively in the phrase {pay one's respects}, meaning to visit someone as a gesture of honor or courtesy, or to attend a funeral: {We went to pay our respects to the family}. The phrase {in some respects} means in certain ways: {The plan succeeded in some respects but failed in others}.

A respirator is a device worn over the nose and mouth to filter air or supply clean air for breathing. In medical settings, respirators protect against airborne pathogens: {N95 respirators became scarce during the pandemic}. Industrial respirators shield workers from dust, fumes, or toxic gases. The term also applies to mechanical ventilators that assist or replace breathing for patients who cannot breathe adequately on their own.

Respirators are devices worn over the nose and mouth to filter or purify the air being breathed, protecting the wearer from harmful particles, gases, or pathogens. They range from simple disposable masks like N95s to sophisticated apparatus with replaceable cartridges or powered air supply. Medical workers wear respirators during procedures involving airborne diseases, while industrial workers use them around dust, fumes, or toxic chemicals. {The hospital required all staff to be fitted for respirators during the outbreak.}

Respite is a pause or break from something difficult or unpleasant—a temporary relief. A prisoner on death row may receive a respite from execution. A caregiver gets respite when someone else takes over for a few hours. {The rain offered no respite from the heat}. The word suggests the hardship will resume; respite is shelter, not escape.

To respond is to react or reply to something—a question, situation, or stimulus. You respond to an email, respond to criticism, or respond to treatment. The word implies that something came first and your action follows: {She didn't respond to my text}. A response can be verbal, physical, or emotional. First responders are emergency personnel who arrive first at a scene.

A responder is someone who responds—to a question, a situation, or an emergency. The word appears most often in compounds: {first responders} are police, firefighters, and paramedics who arrive at emergencies; {survey responders} answer questionnaires. In medicine, a responder is a patient who shows improvement from treatment: {She was a good responder to the medication}.

Responders is the plural of responder—someone who responds. The term most often appears in compounds: {first responders} are emergency personnel who arrive at crisis scenes; {survey responders} are people who answer questionnaires. In medical contexts, responders are patients who react positively to treatment: {About sixty percent were responders to the new drug}.

Responding is answering or reacting to something—a question, a situation, a stimulus. The word implies that something came first and this is the reply or reaction: {She's not responding to my texts}, {The patient is responding well to treatment}, {First responders are responding to the scene}. It suggests engagement rather than initiation.

A response is what comes back when something is sent out—an answer to a question, a reaction to a stimulus, a reply to a message. The word implies that something prompted it: {Her response to the criticism was measured}. In biology, a response is how an organism reacts to environmental changes. Response time measures how quickly something or someone reacts.

Responsibilities are duties or obligations one is expected to fulfill. The word often implies accountability—if something goes wrong, it falls on whoever had responsibility: {The project's failure was entirely my responsibility}. Responsibilities can be assigned {(job responsibilities)} or assumed {(family responsibilities)}. To {take responsibility} is to accept blame or ownership; to {shirk responsibilities} is to avoid them.

A responsibility is an obligation or burden: It’s your responsibility to report any discrepancy in the figures. Responsibility can also be the state of being responsible: He hasn’t shown that he’s able to deal with ongoing responsibility. If you take responsibility for something, usually something bad, you accept or declare that you are to blame—even if you weren’t actually present. If you claim responsibility for something, you made it happen: No one has come forth to claim responsibility for the bombing.

Responsible means accountable or answerable for something: {Who's responsible for this mess?} A responsible person is trustworthy and makes sound decisions: {She's responsible enough to babysit}. To be responsible for something can mean either causing it {(The storm was responsible for the damage)} or being in charge of it {(He's responsible for marketing)}. A responsible {position} carries significant duties and accountability.

Responsive means reacting readily or appropriately to something. A responsive {audience} engages with a performance. Responsive {customer service} addresses concerns promptly. In relationships, being responsive means attuning to another's needs. In web design, a responsive layout adjusts automatically to different screen sizes. The word implies not just reaction but fitting reaction—responsiveness suggests sensitivity and adaptability.

Two different words are represented by rest. One can act as a noun or verb and relates to the refreshment that comes from stopping activity: Do you need a rest? The engine needs to rest a while or it will overheat. Something at rest is inactive. When rest precedes another noun, conveys this meaning: rest stop, rest period. The other rest is a noun only and is largely synonymous with remainder. It is what is left when some amount or quantity has been used or taken away: She’ll spend the rest of her life in prison. People use the rest in a vague way to mean “all the others” when they assume their listeners will be able to identify what is meant.

Restart means to begin again after stopping. You restart a computer to clear errors, restart a conversation after an interruption, or restart your life after a major change. As a noun, a restart is the act of beginning again: {The server needs a restart}. {After a brief restart, the game continued}.

A restaurant is an establishment where meals are prepared and served to customers. Unlike a café or bar, a restaurant's primary business is food rather than drinks. Restaurants range from fast-food chains to fine dining, and the word covers everything from a neighborhood diner to a Michelin-starred establishment. {We're meeting at the new Italian restaurant downtown.}

Restaurants are establishments where meals are prepared and served to customers. The word covers everything from fast-food chains to fine dining rooms. People go to restaurants for convenience, social occasions, or experiences they can't replicate at home: {Let's try that new restaurant downtown}. The restaurant industry is a major employer in most economies.

A restaurateur is someone who owns or manages a restaurant. The word is borrowed from French and retains its French spelling—no *n* before the *t*, despite the spelling of *restaurant*. {The restaurateur greeted regulars by name.}

Rested describes the state of having had enough sleep or relief from exertion. Someone who is {well-rested} feels refreshed and alert. The word implies recovery from fatigue: {After a week at the beach, she returned feeling rested and ready to work}. Athletes speak of {rested legs} after time off from training.

Restful describes something conducive to rest or relaxation: {a restful afternoon}, {restful colors}. A restful place or activity calms rather than stimulates. The word suggests peacefulness and the absence of stress or disturbance: {The spa had a restful atmosphere}. In computing, RESTful describes web services that follow REST (Representational State Transfer) architectural principles, though this technical sense is usually capitalized. (See RESTful for the technical term.)

Resting describes someone or something at rest—not in motion, not active. An actor between jobs is resting: {She's resting between productions}. A resting heart rate is measured when the body is calm and still. In the phrase {resting bitch face}, it describes the neutral expression someone wears when not consciously animating their features.

Restitution is the act of restoring something to its rightful owner or original state, or compensating for loss or damage. Courts order restitution when criminals must repay victims: {The judge ordered restitution of $50,000 to the fraud victims}. In law, restitution prevents unjust enrichment—if someone gains at another's expense, they must give it back. The word carries a sense of making whole what was broken or taken.

Restless describes an inability to be still or at ease. A restless sleeper tosses and turns. A restless crowd grows impatient. The word suggests both physical movement and mental unease—you might have a restless night because of restless thoughts. Someone with a restless spirit is never satisfied staying in one place or situation: {After three years in the job, she grew restless}.

Restlessness is the state of being unable to rest or remain still—a fidgety, unsettled quality of body or mind. Physical restlessness shows in pacing, shifting position, or an inability to sleep. Mental restlessness manifests as dissatisfaction with the present situation, an urge to be elsewhere or doing something else: {A restlessness came over her, and she knew it was time to move on}.

To restock is to replenish a supply of goods or materials. Stores restock their shelves, anglers restock lakes with fish, hunters restock ammunition. {We need to restock the fridge before the weekend}. The word implies returning inventory to a previous level rather than stocking something for the first time.

Restoration is returning something to its original or proper condition. Art restoration removes centuries of grime from paintings. Dental restoration repairs damaged teeth. The restoration of democracy follows authoritarian rule. A restored classic car is the product of restoration. {The restoration of the old theater took three years.} (Capitalized Restoration refers to the period when English monarchy returned.)

Restorations are acts of returning something to a former condition. A building undergoes restoration to recover its original appearance. A monarch's restoration returns them to power: {the Restoration of Charles II}. In dentistry, restorations are fillings, crowns, or other repairs to damaged teeth. {The restorations on the old paintings took years to complete.}

Restorative describes something that restores health, strength, or well-being: {a restorative nap}, {the restorative powers of nature}. As a noun, a restorative is a tonic or remedy that revives: {The hot soup was just the restorative I needed}. In legal and educational contexts, restorative justice or restorative practices focus on repairing harm rather than punishment.

Restore means to bring something back to a previous condition or state. You restore a building to its original appearance, restore order after chaos, or restore someone's faith after betrayal. In computing, to restore is to recover data from a backup: {I restored my files after the crash}. To restore someone to a position is to reinstate them. The noun restoration covers both the act and, capitalized, specific historical periods of monarchical return.

Restored means brought back to a former or original condition. A restored {painting} has been cleaned and repaired. A restored {building} has been renovated to match its historical appearance. Restored {faith} or restored {confidence} has returned after being lost. {The technician restored the deleted files}. To feel restored is to feel refreshed or revitalized: {A good night's sleep left her fully restored}.

Restores is the third-person singular of restore, meaning to return something to a former condition or position. A technician restores vintage cars; a curator restores damaged paintings. Software restores files from backup. {The treatment restores mobility to damaged joints.} To restore can also mean to bring back: {The election restores hope for reform.}

Restoring is the present participle of restore—bringing something back to a former condition, position, or owner. You might be restoring {an old car}, restoring {order after chaos}, or restoring {someone's faith in humanity}. The word implies returning something to what it was or should be: {They're restoring the painting to its original colors}.

To restrain is to hold back or keep under control. You might restrain a dog from chasing a squirrel, restrain your temper in an argument, or restrain spending during tight times. Physical restraint involves actual holding or binding: {Security guards restrained the man until police arrived}. The word implies force or effort applied against something that would otherwise act freely.

Restrained describes something held back or kept in check. A restrained {response} is measured rather than emotional. Restrained {colors} are muted, not bold. A restrained {performance} shows discipline and control. The word suggests deliberate moderation—someone or something capable of more but choosing less: {His grief was restrained but visible}.

Restraining means holding back or keeping under control. A restraining {order} is a court directive prohibiting someone from approaching or contacting another person. Restraining {hands} physically hold someone in place. The word suggests active effort to limit movement, action, or influence: {She put a restraining hand on his arm before he could speak}.

Restraint is the act of holding back or keeping something in check, whether physically, emotionally, or socially. A person exercising restraint controls their impulses or actions: {She showed admirable restraint by not responding to the insult}. Physical restraints are devices that limit movement, like handcuffs or straps used in medical settings. The word also describes a quality of moderation or self-control in behavior, taste, or expression—someone who dresses with restraint avoids flashiness.

Restraints are devices or measures that restrict movement or freedom. Physical restraints include handcuffs, straitjackets, and seatbelts: {The patient was placed in restraints}. The word extends to any limiting force: legal restraints, budgetary restraints, restraints on free speech. In intimate contexts, restraints often refers to bondage equipment: {silk restraints}, {leather restraints}.

Restrict means to limit or confine within bounds. You might restrict access to a building, restrict someone's diet, or restrict spending. Laws restrict behavior; rules restrict options. A restricted area is off-limits to unauthorized people. The word implies deliberate constraint rather than natural limitation: {The new policy restricts employees to one remote day per week}.

Restricted means limited or confined within boundaries. A restricted {area} is off-limits to unauthorized people. Restricted {access} allows only certain users. A restricted {diet} limits what you can eat. In film ratings, restricted (R) means viewers under 17 require an accompanying adult. The word implies deliberate constraint rather than natural limitation: {Parking is restricted to residents only}.

A restriction is a rule, condition, or limitation that controls or confines what can be done. Restrictions may be imposed by authorities {travel restrictions during the pandemic}, built into agreements {dietary restrictions for the study participants}, or arise from circumstances {budget restrictions forced cutbacks}. The word often implies constraint that is unwelcome but accepted as necessary. To place or impose restrictions is to limit freedom or options in some defined way.

Restrictions are rules, limits, or conditions that control or constrain what can be done. They may be imposed by authorities, laws, institutions, or circumstances: {dietary restrictions}, {travel restrictions}, {age restrictions}. The word often implies that something would otherwise be permitted or possible but for the restriction in place. Restrictions can range from minor inconveniences to significant barriers, and they typically exist to protect, regulate, or maintain order.

A restroom is a room with toilets and sinks for public use—the standard American term for facilities in restaurants, offices, airports, and other public spaces. The word is a euphemism, implying a place to rest rather than to relieve oneself. {Where's the restroom?} British English prefers toilet or loo.

Restrooms is the standard American term for public toilet facilities, typically found in businesses, restaurants, and public buildings. The word is a euphemism—no one rests there—but it has become the neutral, inoffensive default: {Where are the restrooms?} Signs may say "restroom" even when only one toilet is present.

To restructure is to reorganize something's fundamental arrangement or composition. Companies restructure by changing management hierarchies, merging departments, or renegotiating debt: {The firm restructured after bankruptcy}. Governments restructure agencies; individuals restructure their finances or daily routines. The word often signals significant change, sometimes euphemistically implying layoffs or downsizing.

Restructured describes something that has been reorganized or rearranged, usually to make it work better or adapt to new circumstances. Companies restructure when they change their organizational hierarchy, merge departments, or lay off workers: {The restructured firm emerged leaner after bankruptcy}. Debt can be restructured by renegotiating terms. The word often signals significant, sometimes painful, change imposed from above.

Restructuring is the act of reorganizing the structure of something, especially a company or institution. Corporate restructuring typically involves changing operations, ownership, or finances—often through layoffs, mergers, or debt renegotiation: {The company announced a major restructuring that would eliminate 2,000 jobs}. The term often serves as a euphemism for painful cuts.

Rests covers what remains and what pauses. The rest of something is the remainder: {I'll save the rest for later}. To rest is to cease activity, relax, or sleep: {She rested after the long hike}. Something rests where it sits or is supported: {His hand rested on her shoulder}. A case rests when no more evidence will be presented. In music, rests are notated silences between sounds.

Result is what happens because of something else—an outcome, effect, or consequence. Actions produce results; experiments yield results; elections have results. {The result of the vote was a landslide}. To result in something is to cause it: {The accident resulted in three injuries}. To result from something is to be caused by it.

Results are outcomes or consequences—what happens after an action, experiment, or process. Search results show what you found; test results reveal what was measured. In plural, results often implies success: {a coach who gets results}, {I want to see results}. Results can also mean data from research or statistics: {The results of the study were inconclusive}.

Resume spans two words distinguished by pronunciation and usually spelling. With stress on the second syllable, resume means to begin again after interruption: {We'll resume after lunch}, {She resumed her seat}. With stress on the first syllable and typically spelled with accents (résumé), it's a summary of qualifications submitted when applying for jobs: {Send your resume to HR}. The spelling resume without accents is increasingly common for the document.

Resumes is the plural of resume, a summary of qualifications and work history submitted when applying for jobs: {She sent out dozens of resumes before landing an interview}. Resumes also serves as the verb form meaning to begin again after interruption: {Class resumes after lunch}. Context usually makes clear which is meant.

Resupply is to provide fresh supplies to replace what has been used or depleted. The term appears most often in military and expedition contexts: {The troops waited for resupply before advancing}. As a noun, it refers to the supplies themselves or the act of delivering them: {a resupply of ammunition}, {the resupply arrived by helicopter}.

To resurface is to come back up to the surface after being submerged: {The whale resurfaced to breathe}. By extension, things that resurface reappear after a period of absence: {Old rumors resurfaced during the campaign}. Resurface also means to put a new surface on something: {They're resurfacing the parking lot}.

Resurfaced is the past tense of resurface, meaning to come back to the surface after being submerged or hidden. A diver resurfaces after exploring a wreck; a scandal resurfaces years later when new evidence emerges. {Old rumors resurfaced during the campaign.} The word also means to put a new surface on something: {The county resurfaced the highway last summer.}

Resurfaces means to come back into view or awareness after a period of absence. Old rumors resurface during campaigns. A missing person resurfaces years later. The word also has a literal sense: to put a new surface on something. Workers resurface roads, and a submarine resurfaces after diving. {Memories resurfaced when she visited her childhood home.}

Resurfacing is coming back up to the surface, or making something rise again. Physically, a diver resurfaces after being underwater. Figuratively, old memories or scandals resurface when they reappear after being forgotten: {The allegations resurfaced during the campaign}. Resurfacing also means putting a new surface on something: {The crew is resurfacing the parking lot}.

Resurgence is the act of rising again or returning to prominence after a period of decline or inactivity. A political movement experiences a resurgence when it regains influence. A disease sees a resurgence when cases spike after a lull. {The resurgence of vinyl records surprised the music industry.} The word implies something was diminished but never entirely gone.

Resurrect means to bring back to life from the dead, or more commonly, to revive something that had ended or been forgotten. A canceled TV show gets resurrected by a streaming service. An old idea gets resurrected in a meeting. {They resurrected the franchise after twenty years.} The word carries connotations of something dormant being restored to active existence.

Resurrected means brought back to life after death. The word derives from Christian theology about Jesus rising from the tomb, but extends to any revival: a resurrected {career}, a resurrected {franchise}, resurrected {hopes}. Something resurrected has been dormant or abandoned and is now active again: {The band resurrected their 1990s sound for the reunion tour}.

Resurrecting is bringing something back from death or dormancy. The original sense is raising the dead to life, as in Christian accounts of Jesus. More commonly, resurrecting means reviving what had lapsed or been abandoned: {They're resurrecting an old TV series}, {She resurrected her career after a decade away}. The word implies something was truly gone, not merely paused.

Resurrection is the verbal noun of resurrect, which has the notion of bringing back to life. Since this is rare in organisms, the word is typically used figuratively to suggest the return of something abstract to vitality: There was a resurrection of peace talks at the United Nations. When capitalized, Resurrection refers to the return to life of Jesus after he was crucified, as reported in the New Testament. Resurrection also denotes a musical work based on this event.

Resurrections is the plural of resurrection, meaning instances of rising from the dead or being brought back to life. The term originates in Christian theology with Christ's resurrection, but extends to any return from death—literal or figurative. A career can have multiple resurrections; a franchise can see resurrections across decades. {The character has had three resurrections in the comic book series.}

Resurrects means to bring back to life or restore to use. The core sense is religious—Christ resurrected from the dead, and believers may be resurrected at the end of time. More commonly, resurrect applies to revivals of non-living things: {The director resurrects a forgotten play}, {She resurrected her grandmother's recipe}. To resurrect something is to pull it from obscurity or disuse back into active existence.

Resuscitate means to revive someone who has stopped breathing or whose heart has stopped—to bring them back from the brink of death: {Paramedics resuscitated the drowning victim}. The word extends to reviving anything that has failed or gone dormant: {attempts to resuscitate the stalled negotiations}, {resuscitating a dying brand}. The noun is resuscitation, as in CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation).

Resuscitated means brought back to life or consciousness, especially after apparent death or near-death: {The paramedics resuscitated the drowning victim}. The word extends to reviving anything that had faded or failed: {The new director resuscitated the struggling theater company}. A resuscitated career, relationship, or idea has been given new life after seeming finished.

Resuscitating is reviving someone or something from unconsciousness, apparent death, or a diminished state. The term applies literally to emergency medicine—{The paramedics spent ten minutes resuscitating the drowning victim}—and figuratively to revival efforts of any kind: {resuscitating a stalled career}, {resuscitating a dying language}.

Resuscitation is the act of reviving someone from unconsciousness or apparent death. The term most often refers to emergency procedures like CPR: {The paramedics attempted resuscitation for twenty minutes}. Figuratively, resuscitation applies to reviving anything that has failed or faded: {the resuscitation of a struggling company}, {the resuscitation of an abandoned project}.

Retail describes the sale of goods directly to consumers, as opposed to wholesale, which involves selling in bulk to businesses. Retail happens in stores, online, or anywhere individual customers buy products for personal use. As a verb, to retail something is to sell it this way, or more figuratively, to spread information: {She retailed the gossip to anyone who would listen}. The adjective describes this type of commerce: {retail prices}, {retail therapy}.

A retailer is a business or person that sells goods directly to consumers, as opposed to wholesalers who sell to other businesses. The term covers everything from corner shops to department stores to online merchants: {Amazon has become the world's largest retailer}. As a verb form, one who retails goods sells them in small quantities to end users.

Retailers are businesses that sell goods directly to consumers rather than to other businesses. The term distinguishes them from wholesalers and manufacturers further up the supply chain. A retailer might operate physical stores, sell online, or both: {Big-box retailers have struggled against e-commerce}. The singular retailer refers to either the business or a person working in retail sales.

Retain means to keep or continue to hold. You retain {possession} of something, retain {control}, retain {moisture}. A lawyer you retain is one you've hired and kept on. To retain information is to remember it: {I can never retain names}. A retaining {wall} holds back earth or water. The noun is retention.

A retainer is something that keeps something else in place—a dental device that holds teeth in position, a clip that secures a part. In law, a retainer is an advance fee paid to secure a professional's services: {The lawyer required a five-thousand-dollar retainer}. An old-fashioned meaning is a servant or attendant in a wealthy household, especially one who has served for many years: {The family's loyal retainers prepared the estate for the gathering}.

Retainers are things that keep something in place or in service. A dental retainer holds teeth in position after braces. A retainer fee secures ongoing access to a professional's services: {The law firm charges a monthly retainer}. In older usage, retainers were servants or followers attached to a noble household. To retain is to keep or hold onto.

Retaining is the present participle of retain, meaning to keep or hold onto something. A retaining {wall} holds back earth or water. A retaining {fee} secures ongoing professional services. {The soil isn't retaining moisture.} The word emphasizes continued possession or maintenance of something that might otherwise be lost or released.

To retake is to take again—recapturing something lost or repeating something unsatisfactory. An army retakes a city. A student retakes an exam. A film crew shoots a retake when the first attempt doesn't work: {We needed six retakes to get the scene right}. The noun stresses the first syllable; the verb stresses the second.

Retakes are second attempts at something that didn't succeed the first time. A student retakes an exam after failing. A film crew shoots retakes when a scene needs improvement. The word implies the original attempt was inadequate: {After three retakes, the director was finally satisfied}.

To retaliate is to strike back after being harmed or provoked—to return injury for injury. The word implies responding in kind: {When she spread rumors about him, he retaliated by leaking her emails}. Retaliation often escalates conflicts rather than resolving them. The noun is retaliation; the adjective retaliatory.

Retaliates means to strike back or take revenge after being harmed or wronged. The word implies a response in kind—if someone insults you and you insult them back, you retaliate: {When she criticized his work, he retaliated by questioning her credentials}. Retaliation often suggests escalation or a tit-for-tat dynamic.

Retaliating is responding to an injury or offense by inflicting one in return. The word implies a reactive strike rather than an unprovoked one: {He was suspended for retaliating after being shoved}. Retaliation can be physical, verbal, economic, or political—any payback for a perceived wrong.

Retaliation is striking back after being harmed or wronged—returning injury for injury. The word implies proportional response: {The bombing was retaliation for the embassy attack}. In legal contexts, retaliation often describes prohibited punishment of employees who report misconduct: {She sued for retaliation after being fired for filing a complaint}.

Retaliations are acts of revenge or reprisal—responses to injury or offense with similar treatment in return. The word often appears in contexts of escalating conflict: {The bombing prompted retaliations across the border}. Unlike a single retaliation, the plural suggests multiple acts or a pattern of vengeful responses: {The gang war involved retaliations on both sides}.

To retch is to make the involuntary spasmodic movements of vomiting, usually without actually bringing anything up. It's the body's heaving motion when you gag or nearly throw up: {The smell made him retch}. A retch is one such convulsion.
