Retching often accompanies nausea, disgust, or the reflex triggered by something touching the back of the throat.

Retching is the convulsive motion of trying to vomit—the heaving, gagging spasms that may or may not produce anything. Someone retching might be genuinely sick or reacting to something disgusting: {The smell had him retching over the toilet}. Retching can be dry, with no result, or can precede actual vomiting.

Retcon is short for retroactive continuity—changing established facts in a story's past to serve present needs. Comic books and long-running franchises retcon frequently: a dead character was actually alive, a hero's origin gets rewritten. The verb means to make such changes: {They retconned his entire backstory}. The practice draws criticism when it contradicts what fans remember, but it lets storytellers escape continuity traps.

Retconned means retroactively altered in continuity—when established facts in a fictional narrative are changed or reinterpreted by later installments. From "retroactive continuity," the term originated in comics but applies to any serialized fiction: {The sequel retconned the hero's death by revealing it was a clone}. Also used figuratively for revising personal or institutional history: {He retconned his résumé to hide the gap year}.

Retconning is altering previously established facts in a fictional narrative to accommodate new storylines or fix continuity problems. From "retroactive continuity"—the practice of revising a story's past rather than its future. Comic books retcon character deaths; soap operas retcon secret relatives: {The writers retconned his entire backstory}. The term has spread beyond fiction to describe any after-the-fact revision of history: {He's retconning his own statements to seem prescient}.

A retelling is a new version of an existing story, often adapted for a different audience or medium: {a feminist retelling of Cinderella}, {a modern retelling of Romeo and Juliet}. The word emphasizes that the core narrative remains recognizable even as details change. Retellings may update settings, shift perspectives, or reinterpret themes while honoring the original.

Retellings are new versions of stories that already exist, whether myths, fairy tales, classic novels, or historical events. The appeal lies in seeing familiar narratives through fresh perspectives—a villain's point of view, a different cultural setting, or a modern context. {Her novel is a feminist retelling of Bluebeard.} The term appears frequently in publishing and literary discussion, where retellings of public domain works have become a recognized genre.

Retention is the act of keeping or holding onto something. In business, customer retention measures how well a company keeps its clients over time. Memory retention is the ability to store and recall information. Water retention causes swelling when the body holds excess fluid. {The company focused on employee retention after losing several key staff members.}

Rethink means to think again about something, usually with the implication of reconsidering or revising one's position: {The scandal forced the company to rethink its strategy}. As a noun, a rethink is such a reconsideration: {The policy needs a complete rethink}. The noun form is more common in British English.

Reticence is a reluctance to speak freely or reveal one's thoughts. A reticent person holds back, offering little in conversation or keeping opinions private: {His reticence about his past only fueled speculation}. The word suggests restraint rather than inability—someone who could say more but chooses not to.

Reticent means reluctant to speak or share information—reserved, not forthcoming. A reticent {witness} offers little testimony. Someone reticent {about their past} avoids discussing it. The word suggests deliberate restraint rather than shyness. Some use reticent to mean reluctant generally {(reticent to act)}, though purists object to this extension beyond speech.

The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye. It contains cells that detect light and color, converting visual information into nerve signals sent to the brain. {The ophthalmologist examined her retina for signs of damage.} Retinal scans use the eye's unique blood vessel patterns for identification.

Retinas is the plural of retina, the light-sensitive layer of tissue at the back of the eye that receives images and transmits them to the brain via the optic nerve. The word appears in medical contexts {The doctor examined both retinas for signs of damage} and in technology referring to high-resolution displays {retina screens}.

A retinue is the group of attendants, servants, or supporters accompanying an important person. Kings traveled with retinues of advisors and guards; celebrities arrive with retinues of assistants and bodyguards. The word suggests both status and dependence—the important figure needs the entourage, and the entourage needs the patron: {The ambassador arrived with her full retinue}.

When you retire, you stop working at a regular job, either because you have reached a prescribed age or you are ill. You can also retire (that is, stop taking part) from an activity, such as arguing, playing professional tennis, or a board position. When you retire a piece of equipment, you stop using it after a considerable period of service. In cricket and baseball, you retire the batsman or batter when you put him out: The pitcher retired three consecutive batters in the third inning.

Retired describes someone who has left the workforce permanently, typically after reaching a certain age or years of service: {My parents are both retired now}. The word also applies to things withdrawn from active use: a retired {jersey number}, a retired {racehorse}. A retired life suggests quiet seclusion from public affairs. To live retired is to live in withdrawal from society—an older, more literary sense.

A retiree is someone who has retired from work, typically after reaching a certain age or years of service. The word emphasizes the person's current status rather than their former occupation: {The community center offers programs for retirees}. Retirees may receive pensions, Social Security, or other retirement benefits.

Retirees are people who have left the workforce, typically after reaching a certain age or years of service. The term usually implies they receive a pension or have savings to support themselves: {The community attracts retirees from across the country}. {Retirees on fixed incomes worry about inflation}.

Retirement is the period of life after a person stops working, typically in older age. To go into retirement or be in retirement is to have left one's career: {She's been enjoying retirement for five years now}. The word also applies to the act of withdrawing from activity or public life: {The boxer announced his retirement}. A retirement can be a secluded place: {He wrote his memoirs in rural retirement}.

Retires is the third-person singular of retire. To retire is to withdraw from active working life, typically at the end of a career: {She retires next month after thirty years with the company}. Retire also means to withdraw from a place or situation: {He retired to his study}. In sports, to retire a batter is to put them out; to retire a jersey number is to permanently remove it from use. {The pitcher retires the side in order.}

Retiring describes someone who avoids attention and prefers to stay in the background—quiet, modest, unassuming: {She had a retiring disposition that made her uncomfortable at parties}. The word suggests shyness without negative judgment. Separately, retiring can simply mean leaving a job or position permanently: {the retiring CEO}.

Retool means to re-equip with new tools or machinery, especially in manufacturing: {The factory retooled to produce electric vehicles}. More broadly, it means to reorganize or adapt for a new purpose: {She retooled her résumé for tech jobs}, {The comedy retooled after its first season}. The word implies significant restructuring rather than minor adjustment.

Retooled is the past tense of retool, meaning to reequip with new tools or machinery, especially in manufacturing: {The factory retooled to produce electric vehicles}. More commonly, retooled describes overhauling or reorganizing something to make it more effective: {The campaign retooled its message after poor polling numbers}. {She retooled her résumé for tech jobs}.

Retooling is the process of re-equipping with new tools or machinery, especially in manufacturing: {The factory shut down for retooling before launching the new model}. Figuratively, it means restructuring or adapting something for a different purpose: {The campaign is retooling its message after poor polling numbers}. Personal retooling suggests acquiring new skills or changing one's approach.

A retort is a quick, sharp reply, especially one that turns an accusation or criticism back on the speaker: {When she called him lazy, his retort was that she'd never worked a day in her life}. The verb means to reply in this manner. Separately, a retort is a glass vessel with a long downward-pointing neck, used in distillation.

To retouch is to make small corrections or improvements, especially to a photograph or painting. Retouching smooths skin, removes blemishes, adjusts lighting, or otherwise enhances an image: {The photos were heavily retouched before publication}. The noun retouch refers to an instance of such correction. The practice ranges from subtle cleanup to dramatic alteration.

Retouched describes something that has been altered or touched up to improve its appearance. The word applies most often to photographs that have been edited to remove blemishes, smooth skin, or adjust lighting: {The magazine's retouched cover photos set unrealistic beauty standards}. Paintings and other artwork may also be retouched to repair damage or refine details.

Retouching is the process of making small corrections or improvements to an image, typically a photograph. A retoucher might remove blemishes, adjust lighting, or smooth skin tones: {The magazine's retouching made her look ten years younger}. The term carries connotations of subtle enhancement rather than dramatic alteration, though the line between retouching and heavy manipulation is often blurry.

To retrace is to go back over the same path or steps, either literally or figuratively. You might retrace your route looking for a lost item, or retrace the steps of an investigation to find what was missed. {She retraced her steps to the café where she'd left her phone.} The word implies careful, deliberate repetition of a previous course.

Retraced is the past tense of retrace, meaning to go back over the same path or steps: {She retraced her route to find the lost earring}. Figuratively, to retrace is to review or reconstruct a sequence of events or reasoning: {Investigators retraced the suspect's movements that night}.

Retracing is going back over a path or sequence already traveled. You retrace your steps to find something lost, retrace a route to understand where you went wrong. The word extends to mental review: {She spent the afternoon retracing the events that led to their argument}. To retrace is to trace again—whether physically or in memory.

To retract is to pull something back or withdraw it. A cat retracts its claws. An airplane retracts its landing gear. The word extends to statements: to retract a claim is to formally take it back, admitting it was wrong or unfounded: {The newspaper retracted the story after new evidence emerged}. A retraction undoes what was previously put forward.

Retracted means pulled back or withdrawn. A cat retracts its claws; a witness retracts testimony; a newspaper retracts a false story. The word often implies something extended or stated is now being taken back: {He retracted his earlier accusation}. In formal contexts, especially journalism and academia, a retraction acknowledges error: {The study was retracted after data irregularities emerged}.

Retracting is the act of drawing something back or withdrawing it. A cat retracts its claws; a plane retracts its landing gear. When someone retracts a statement, they take it back—formally withdrawing what they previously said: {The newspaper retracted the story after discovering errors}. The word implies deliberate reversal, pulling back something that was extended or put forward.

A retraction is a withdrawal of something previously said or published. Newspapers print retractions when they've reported something false. The word also applies to physical withdrawal—the retraction of a cat's claws, an airplane's landing gear, or a turtle's head into its shell. To retract is to pull back or take back: {He retracted his earlier statement}.

Retractions are formal withdrawals of statements, claims, or publications. A newspaper prints a retraction when it publishes something false. Scientists retract papers when findings prove unreliable or fraudulent. The word also applies to physical drawing back: {the retraction of landing gear}, {muscle retraction during surgery}. In both senses, something extended is pulled back in.

Retraining is teaching someone new skills, typically when their previous job or expertise has become obsolete: {The factory offered retraining programs for displaced workers}. In machine learning, retraining means updating a model with new data to improve its performance or correct its behavior.

Retraumatization occurs when a person who has experienced trauma is exposed to situations, stimuli, or experiences that recall the original traumatic event, triggering a renewed stress response. This can happen through insensitive questioning, medical procedures, legal proceedings, or even well-intentioned therapeutic interventions that inadvertently revisit painful memories. {Survivors of abuse may experience retraumatization when required to recount their experiences repeatedly to different authorities.} The concept is central to trauma-informed care, which seeks to minimize such harm.
clues: When past trauma gets activated anew

definition: To retraumatize is to cause someone to relive or experience fresh psychological harm from a past trauma. Survivors of abuse may be retraumatized by insensitive questioning, graphic media, or being forced to recount their experiences: {The trial retraumatized her}. The term is common in discussions of mental health, victim advocacy, and institutional practices.

Retraumatizing is causing someone to experience trauma again, typically by exposing them to reminders of an original traumatic event. The term appears frequently in discussions of therapy, legal proceedings, and media coverage: {Forcing victims to repeatedly recount their assault can be retraumatizing}. The concern is that well-intentioned interventions may inflict additional psychological harm.

A retread is a tire given new tread after the original has worn down, extending its useful life. The word extends to people or things recycled from earlier use: {The new show is just a retread of the old format}. A military retread is someone called back to service after discharge. To retread a tire is to apply new tread; figuratively, to retread is to go over old ground again.

Retreads are tires that have been given new tread after the original has worn down, extending their useful life at lower cost than new tires. The term extends figuratively to people or things perceived as recycled or unoriginal—a retread film rehashes familiar territory, and calling someone a retread suggests they're past their prime or offering nothing new. {The studio keeps releasing retreads of 80s franchises.} As a verb, to retread means to put new tread on a worn tire.

Retreat is movement backward or away from something, especially withdrawal from an enemy or difficult situation. Armies retreat from battle; people retreat from confrontation. A retreat is also a quiet place for rest or reflection—a mountain retreat, a yoga retreat. The verb can describe gradual recession: {The floodwaters slowly retreated}. To beat a retreat is to withdraw hastily.

Retreating describes movement away from something—typically a withdrawal from danger, conflict, or an untenable position. An army retreats from battle; a person retreats from an argument. The word often implies acknowledging defeat or choosing self-preservation: {retreating floodwaters}, {a retreating hairline}. Retreating can also suggest seeking refuge: {retreating to the mountains for solitude}.

Retreats covers both withdrawal and sanctuary. An army retreats from battle. A person retreats from an argument or difficult position. As a noun, a retreat is the act of withdrawing, or a place of refuge and privacy: {a mountain retreat}, {a yoga retreat}. A retreat can also be a period of seclusion for reflection or spiritual practice: {She went on a silent retreat}. The hairline retreats when it recedes from the forehead.

A retrial is a new trial of a case that has already been tried, typically ordered when the original trial was flawed by procedural error, jury misconduct, or other irregularities: {The judge declared a mistrial and ordered a retrial}. A hung jury—one unable to reach a verdict—often leads to a retrial.

Retribution is punishment inflicted as payback for wrongdoing. Where revenge is personal and justice is systemic, retribution sits between them—punishment that feels deserved, often with a sense of cosmic balance being restored. {The scandal was divine retribution for years of corruption}. The adjective retributive describes punishment focused on payback rather than rehabilitation or deterrence.

Retrieval is the act of getting something back or recovering it from where it was stored. A dog trained for retrieval fetches downed birds. In computing, data retrieval means accessing stored information: {The search engine handles millions of retrievals per second}. Memory retrieval is the cognitive process of recalling what was learned: {His retrieval of names has gotten worse with age}.

The verb retrieve has some overlap in meaning with recover, extract, and fetch. When a computer retrieves information or data, it finds it in a storage space and brings it to the user. Your dog (perhaps she is a retriever!) retrieves a ball that you have thrown. You retrieve your luggage after a flight when it has been separated from you. If divers retrieve something from a buried shipwreck, they bring it out of the water.

A retriever is a dog bred to fetch game that hunters have shot, particularly waterfowl. The name comes from their ability to retrieve downed birds without damaging them. Golden retrievers and Labrador retrievers are among the most popular family pets, prized for their gentle temperaments and trainability. More generally, a retriever is anyone or anything that retrieves: {The software acts as an information retriever}.
clues: Dog bred to bring back birds

definition: Retrievers are dogs bred to retrieve game for hunters, especially waterfowl. The term covers several breeds—golden retrievers, Labrador retrievers, Chesapeake Bay retrievers—all known for soft mouths that carry without damaging. Their trainability and gentle temperament have made them popular family pets: {Golden retrievers are America's most popular breed}.

Retro describes styles, fashions, or aesthetics that imitate or evoke the past, typically the mid-20th century. Unlike merely old things, retro involves conscious revival or nostalgia: {retro furniture}, {a retro diner}, {retro video games}. The word often suggests affection for an earlier era's look or feel rather than authentic vintage items. As a noun, retro is that aesthetic itself: {The whole apartment was done in retro}.

Retroactive describes something that applies to a period before it was enacted or established. A retroactive pay raise compensates for months already worked. A retroactive law punishes acts that were legal when committed. {The tax cut was made retroactive to January 1.} The word often appears in legal and bureaucratic contexts where present decisions must reach backward in time.

Retroactively describes an action or decision that applies to a time before it was made or announced. A law passed retroactively affects events that occurred before its enactment; a pay raise applied retroactively means you receive back pay for the period before the raise was officially granted. {The policy change was applied retroactively to all claims filed this year.} The word often appears in legal and administrative contexts where timing and effective dates matter.

Retrofit means to add new components or features to something already built or manufactured. The term combines "retro" (backward) with "fit," suggesting fitting something into an existing structure after the fact. Buildings get retrofitted with modern insulation or earthquake reinforcement. Older cars can be retrofitted with new technology: {We retrofitted the classic truck with a hybrid engine}. The word works as both verb and noun—the upgrade itself is also called a retrofit.

Retrofits are modifications made to existing equipment, buildings, or systems to add features or capabilities not present in the original design. The term emphasizes updating something already in use rather than replacing it entirely: {The city approved retrofits to make older buildings earthquake-resistant}. A homeowner might install retrofits for energy efficiency; an airline might add retrofits to modernize aging aircraft.

Retrofitting is adding new components or features to something that didn't originally have them, especially updating older buildings, vehicles, or equipment with modern technology: {retrofitting old factories with solar panels}, {The building was retrofitted for earthquake resistance}. The term implies modification rather than replacement—working with existing structures to improve their function or bring them up to current standards.

Retrofuture describes visions of the future as imagined in the past—particularly the optimistic, streamlined futures dreamed up in the mid-20th century with their rocket ships, flying cars, and chrome everything. The term captures both the aesthetic and the poignant gap between what people once expected and what actually came to pass. {The retrofuture exhibit featured illustrations from 1950s magazines predicting life in the year 2000.} Something described as retrofuture or retrofuturistic blends nostalgic design elements with futuristic concepts.

Retrofuturism is a style in art, design, and fiction that imagines the future as people from an earlier era envisioned it—ray guns, chrome rockets, flying cars, robot servants. The aesthetic blends nostalgia with speculation, often drawing on mid-20th-century visions of tomorrow: {The film's retrofuturism gave everything a sleek 1950s space-age look}. Steampunk and dieselpunk are related genres.

Retrofuturistic describes something that evokes past visions of the future—the sleek chrome rockets, bubble helmets, and ray guns that mid-20th-century artists imagined tomorrow would bring. The aesthetic blends nostalgia with speculation: {The diner had a retrofuturistic vibe, all turquoise vinyl and atomic-age signage}. It appears in design, architecture, and fiction that deliberately channels outdated futurism.

A retrogame is a video game from an earlier era of gaming, typically from the 1970s through early 2000s, played on original hardware or through emulation. The term reflects nostalgia for older consoles and arcade machines: {I spent the weekend playing retrogames on my old Nintendo}. Also appears as two words or hyphenated. The verb retrogame means to play such games.

Retrogamers are enthusiasts who play video games from earlier eras—typically those from the 1970s through early 2000s. The hobby involves collecting vintage consoles, cartridges, and arcade cabinets, or using emulators to play classic titles: {Retrogamers swear the original hardware feels different}. The appeal mixes nostalgia with appreciation for older game design philosophies.

Retrogaming is playing video games from earlier eras, typically on original hardware or through emulation. The threshold shifts with time—what counts as retro moves forward as the medium ages. Enthusiasts collect vintage consoles, cartridges, and arcade cabinets: {I've been retrogaming on my old NES lately}. The appeal mixes nostalgia with appreciation for older game design.

Retrograde means moving backward or declining from a better state. Planets in retrograde appear to move opposite their usual direction—an optical illusion that astrology invests with significance: {Mercury is in retrograde}. More broadly, retrograde describes regression or deterioration: {a retrograde step for civil rights}. The verb means to move backward or decline: {The situation has retrograded since last year}.

Retrogrades is the plural of retrograde, a term most familiar from astrology, where planets in retrograde appear to move backward against the stars. Mercury retrograde gets blamed for communication mishaps and technological failures. More broadly, retrograde means moving backward or reverting to an earlier, usually worse state: {retrograde policies}, {a retrograde step for civil rights}. The verb retrograde means to move or appear to move in reverse.

A retrorocket is a rocket engine that fires in the direction of travel to slow a spacecraft down. Used primarily during reentry or landing, retrorockets counter forward momentum: {The capsule fired its retrorockets before splashdown}. The prefix retro- here means backward, not old-fashioned.

Retrospect is looking back on past events or experiences. It appears almost exclusively in the phrase {in retrospect}, meaning when considering something after the fact: {In retrospect, I should have taken the job}. The word implies that understanding or judgment comes more easily with hindsight than it did in the moment.

Retrospective means looking back at the past. A retrospective {exhibition} surveys an artist's career. A retrospective {analysis} examines events after they occurred. As a noun, a retrospective is such an exhibition or review: {The museum is hosting a Picasso retrospective}. In some workplaces, a retrospective is a meeting to reflect on a completed project. Retrospectively applies something to the past: a law applied {retrospectively} affects earlier actions.

Retrospectives are exhibitions or reviews that look back over a body of work, typically an artist's career: {The museum mounted a retrospective of her paintings from the past forty years}. In software development, a retrospective is a team meeting held after a project phase to assess what went well and what could improve. The singular retrospective also works as an adjective meaning backward-looking.

Retrowave is electronic music that evokes 1980s synthesizer sounds and aesthetics—driving beats, analog synth textures, and atmospheric melodies reminiscent of vintage action movies and video games. The term overlaps with synthwave, though retrowave sometimes emphasizes nostalgic visual culture alongside the music: neon grids, sunset gradients, sports cars, VHS artifacts. {The retrowave soundtrack perfectly captured that Blade Runner vibe.}

Retry means to try again after a failure or unsatisfactory result. In computing, retry describes attempting an operation that didn't complete successfully: {The download failed—click retry}. In law, to retry a case is to hold a new trial. The noun refers to an additional attempt: {After three retries, the connection finally worked}.
clues: What perseverance looks like in action

definition: When physical space is involved, the noun and verb return both suggest going back to a point of origin: you return home after a journey, and a fired rocket may return to earth. When abstractions are involved, return suggests reciprocal action, the way you return a favor or return a call in response to one directed at you. If you return an item that you have purchased, you take it back to the store to get your money back. A return is an instance of returning something or something returning. Return on an investment represents the profit you make from it.

Returned is the past tense of return—to go back, come back, or give back. Someone who has returned has come back from somewhere: {She returned from vacation yesterday}. A returned item has been sent back: {returned merchandise}, {returned mail}. In some contexts, returned describes someone who has come back after absence: {a returned soldier}, {returned expats adjusting to life back home}.

Returns means coming or going back. A person returns home after travel; a feeling returns when it resurfaces. Returns also names what comes back: tax returns are forms sent back to the government, and returns on investment are profits that come back to the investor. In retail, returns are items brought back for refund: {The store has a generous returns policy}. The return key on a keyboard goes back to the start of a new line.

Retweet is a Twitter/X term for sharing someone else's post to your own followers. As a noun, it's the shared post itself; as a verb, it's the act of sharing: {That tweet got thousands of retweets}. A retweet can be plain (sharing without comment) or quoted (adding your own text). The abbreviation RT often precedes manually copied tweets.

Retweets are posts on the social media platform X (formerly Twitter) that share someone else's tweet to your own followers. The retweet function lets users amplify content without adding commentary, though quote retweets allow you to add your own text. As a verb, to retweet is to share in this way: {She retweeted the breaking news}. Retweet counts serve as a measure of a post's reach and virality.

Reunification is the process of bringing together what was once divided, typically applied to political entities. Germany's reunification in 1990 joined East and West after decades of Cold War separation. The term appears in discussions of divided nations: {Korean reunification remains elusive}. On a personal scale, reunification describes families or groups coming back together after forced separation.

Reunion is the verbal noun of reunite, which conveys bringing together again. A reunion of people is a meeting of those who are associated but are not normally all together (family reunion, high school reunion). Before another noun, reunion usually designates some activity associated with a reunion of people, such as the reunion tour of a band that separated but then rejoined each other.

Reunions are gatherings of people who have been apart—typically members of a group with shared history. A family reunion brings relatives together, often annually. A class reunion reconnects former schoolmates: {I saw my high school crush at the twenty-year reunion}. The word also applies to any coming together after separation: {a joyful reunion with her long-lost sister}.

Reunite means to bring together again after separation. People reunite with family members, old friends, or former bandmates: {The group reunited for a twentieth-anniversary tour}. Lost pets reunite with their owners. The word implies a prior connection—you can't reunite with someone you've never met. A reunion is the event where reuniting happens.

Reunited means brought together again after a period of separation. People reunite with family members, old friends, or romantic partners: {The siblings were reunited after twenty years apart}. The word carries emotional weight—reunion implies the separation mattered. Things can also be reunited: {The museum reunited the scattered pieces of the ancient vase}.
clues: Found each other after long separation

definition: Reunites means brings together again after separation. People reunite with family after years apart, bands reunite for comeback tours, lost pets reunite with their owners. The word emphasizes the restoration of a previous connection: {The documentary reunites the cast thirty years later}. Something that reunites can also rejoin divided things: {a treaty that reunited the fractured nation}.

Reuniting is the act of coming back together after separation. People reunite with family, friends, or former partners: {The documentary follows a woman reuniting with the daughter she gave up for adoption}. Things reunite too—a band reuniting for a tour, factions reuniting under new leadership. The word carries emotional weight, suggesting restoration of a bond that had been broken or interrupted.

To reup is to reenlist or extend a commitment, originally military slang for signing up for another term of service: {He reupped for four more years}. The meaning has spread to any renewal—subscriptions, contracts, or agreements: {Time to reup my gym membership}. Also spelled re-up.

To reupholster is to replace the fabric, padding, or springs on a piece of furniture: {We had the old armchair reupholstered in blue velvet}. The work typically involves stripping away worn material and rebuilding the seat or cushioning before covering with new fabric. Reupholstering can restore antiques or update furniture to match changing décor.

Reupped means signed up again, especially for military service after an enlistment period ends. The term extends to any renewed commitment or contract: {She reupped with the agency for another two years}. In casual use, it can mean getting more of something: {I reupped my coffee before the meeting started}.

Reusable describes something designed to be used more than once: {reusable shopping bags}, {reusable water bottles}. The term often appears in environmental contexts, contrasting with single-use or disposable items. As a noun, reusables refers to such items collectively: {She switched to reusables to cut down on waste}.

Reuse means to use something again rather than discarding it after one use: {We reuse grocery bags for trash}. The word emphasizes conservation and efficiency—avoiding waste by giving items additional life cycles. Reuse appears frequently in environmental contexts alongside reduce and recycle. As a noun, it names the practice itself: {The container is designed for reuse}.

Rev is short for revolution, specifically of an engine—the number of times the crankshaft rotates per minute. A tachometer measures revs. To rev an engine is to increase its speed, especially while stationary: {He revved the motorcycle at the stoplight}. Figuratively, to rev up is to energize or prepare for action: {The team was revving up for the finals}. Rev also appears as an abbreviation for Reverend.

To revamp something is to renovate or overhaul it, giving it a fresh appearance or improved function: {The restaurant revamped its menu}, {They're revamping the website}. The word carries a sense of significant updating rather than minor tweaks—you revamp something that's become outdated or stale. As a noun, a revamp is such an overhaul: {The show is back after a complete revamp}.

Revamped means renovated, updated, or given a fresh new form. The word implies significant overhaul rather than minor tweaks: {The company revamped its website}, {a revamped menu featuring local ingredients}. Something revamped has been reworked to improve its appeal or function. The underlying image is of replacing worn-out shoe uppers (vamps).

Revamping is the act of renovating or overhauling something to improve it. The word suggests substantial changes rather than minor adjustments: {The restaurant is revamping its menu}, {The company announced a complete revamping of its website}. The root vamp originally meant the upper part of a shoe, and to vamp was to patch it up—revamping implies doing so again or more thoroughly.

Revamps is the plural noun or third-person verb form of revamp—to renovate, update, or give something a fresh new form. A company revamps its logo, a city revamps its downtown, a band revamps old songs for a new album. {The restaurant's revamps included a new menu and modern décor.} The word implies significant overhaul rather than minor tweaking.
clues: Transforms something from the ground up

definition: Reveal is to make something known or visible that was previously hidden or secret. You reveal information by disclosing it: {The investigation revealed widespread fraud}. You reveal something physical by uncovering it: {She pulled back the curtain to reveal the painting}. A reveal is the moment of disclosure itself, especially a dramatic unveiling: {the big reveal at the end of the movie}.

Revealed is the past tense of reveal—to make known something previously hidden or secret. Information gets revealed, truths are revealed, identities are revealed: {The investigation revealed widespread corruption}. In religious contexts, revealed knowledge or truth comes from divine disclosure rather than human discovery: {revealed religion}. The word often carries dramatic weight, suggesting something significant has come to light.

Revealing describes something that exposes what was hidden, unknown, or meant to stay private. A revealing {interview} discloses information the subject might have preferred to keep secret. Revealing {clothing} shows more of the body than typical dress would. A revealing {glance} or {remark} inadvertently betrays someone's true feelings or intentions. The word carries a slight suggestion that what's revealed wasn't meant to be seen.

Reveals is the third-person singular of reveal, meaning to make something known or visible that was previously hidden. {The investigation reveals new evidence}. {Her expression reveals nothing}. In home renovation shows, the reveal (noun) is the dramatic moment when a completed transformation is shown: {The big reveal left them speechless}.

Reveille is a military bugle call or drum signal sounded at dawn to wake personnel and begin the day. By extension, any signal or sound that rouses people from sleep: {The garbage truck at 6 AM served as our reveille}. The word comes from French for "wake up."

Revel is to take intense pleasure or delight in something: {She reveled in her newfound freedom}, {They reveled in the chaos}. The word suggests enthusiastic, sometimes excessive enjoyment. As a noun, revels are lively celebrations or festivities, often with drinking and dancing: {The revels lasted until dawn}.

Revelation is the act of making something known that was previously hidden or secret. A sudden revelation can change how you understand a situation: {The revelation that he'd been lying shocked everyone}. It also describes a surprising discovery or realization: {Seeing her perform live was a revelation}. In religious contexts, revelation refers to divine truth disclosed to humans by God or through sacred texts. (Capitalized Revelation is the final book of the New Testament.)

Revelations are disclosures of previously hidden information, often dramatic or surprising: {The book contains shocking revelations about the president's inner circle}. The word implies something significant being brought to light—secrets exposed, truths uncovered. In religious contexts, revelations are divine truths made known to humans. A personal revelation is a sudden insight or realization: {It was a revelation to discover how much I enjoyed cooking}. (Capitalized Revelations refers to the biblical book.)

Revelatory describes something that reveals or discloses, especially something surprising or previously hidden: {a revelatory documentary about the music industry}, {Her diary entries were revelatory}. The word often suggests significant insight or understanding—not just disclosure but illumination: {a revelatory experience that changed how I saw myself}.

Reveled is the past tense of revel, meaning to take great pleasure or delight in something: {She reveled in her newfound freedom}. To revel is to enjoy oneself thoroughly, often with an element of indulgence or abandon. The word also describes lively celebration or merrymaking: {They reveled late into the night}. Also spelled revelled.

A reveler is someone engaged in lively, boisterous celebration—drinking, dancing, and general merrymaking. The word suggests festive abandon rather than quiet enjoyment: {Revelers filled the streets after the team's victory}. New Year's Eve brings out revelers in every city. Also spelled reveller.

Revelers are people engaged in lively celebration—drinking, dancing, making noise. The word usually describes groups: {New Year's Eve revelers filled the streets}, {revelers spilled out of the bar at closing time}. It carries a sense of boisterous, uninhibited festivity, sometimes with implications of excess.

Reveling is indulging in lively celebration or taking great pleasure in something. The word suggests uninhibited enjoyment—drinking, dancing, merrymaking: {They spent the night reveling with friends}. It can also describe savoring a feeling or situation: {She was reveling in her newfound freedom}. Also spelled revelling.

Revelled is the past tense of revel, meaning to take great pleasure or delight in something: {She revelled in her newfound freedom}. It can also mean to engage in lively celebration or merrymaking: {They revelled late into the night}. This spelling is standard in British English; American English uses reveled.

A reveller is someone engaged in lively, often boisterous celebration—drinking, dancing, making noise. The word suggests festive excess: {Revellers spilled out of the bars at closing time}. It appears frequently in news coverage of holidays and festivals: {New Year's Eve revellers packed the square}. Also spelled reveler.

Revellers are people engaged in lively, often noisy celebration—drinking, dancing, and general merrymaking. The word typically describes groups enjoying themselves at parties, festivals, or nighttime gatherings: {Revellers spilled out of the bars at closing time}. The spelling revelers is standard in American English.

Revelling is indulging in lively enjoyment, often with drinking, dancing, or boisterous celebration: {They spent the night revelling in the streets after the victory}. The word suggests uninhibited pleasure, sometimes to excess. One can also revel in something more quietly—taking deep satisfaction in it: {She was revelling in her newfound freedom}. The spelling with double L is British; American English uses reveling.

Revelries are noisy, boisterous celebrations—drinking, dancing, and general merrymaking: {The revelries continued until dawn}. The word often appears in descriptions of parties that have grown loud or wild, and frequently carries a slightly disapproving or ironic tone, as though the celebration has exceeded reasonable bounds.

Revelry is noisy, boisterous celebration—the kind involving drinking, dancing, and general merriment: {The revelry continued until dawn}. The word suggests uninhibited festivity, often with a hint of excess. Revelers are the people engaged in such celebration: {Revelers spilled out of the bar onto the street}.
clues: What follows when corks start popping

definition: Revels are lively festivities—drinking, dancing, merrymaking. The word suggests uninhibited celebration, often continuing late into the night: {The revels lasted until dawn}. To revel is to take great pleasure in something, especially with abandon: {She reveled in her newfound freedom}. A reveler is someone who joins in such festivities.

A revenant is someone who returns, especially from the dead. The word carries gothic and supernatural overtones—ghosts, vampires, and the undead are revenants. More loosely, anyone who reappears after a long absence might be called a revenant: {He showed up at the reunion like a revenant from our college days}.

Revenants are beings that return from the dead—ghosts, spirits, or reanimated corpses. The word carries a literary or gothic tone, appearing in horror fiction and folklore: {The village lived in fear of revenants rising from unmarked graves}. Unlike zombies, revenants typically retain purpose or personality, often returning to settle unfinished business or seek revenge.

Revenge is harm inflicted in return for a wrong suffered. It's personal retaliation—you get revenge on someone who hurt you: {She plotted revenge against her ex-husband}. The verb means to inflict such harm: {He vowed to revenge his father's murder}. Revenge differs from vengeance mainly in that vengeance sounds loftier and may be impersonal. {Revenge is a dish best served cold} counsels patience before striking back.

Revenue is money received, especially from business activities or taxation. A company's revenue is its total income before expenses are deducted—distinct from profit, which is what remains after costs. Government revenue comes primarily from taxes. The word often appears in compounds: {revenue stream}, {tax revenue}, {annual revenue}.

Reverb is the persistence of sound after its source stops, created by reflections off surfaces. In music production, reverb is an effect that simulates this acoustic phenomenon, adding depth and space to recordings: {Add some reverb to the vocals}. Short for reverberation. As a verb, to reverb is to apply this effect.

Reverberate means to echo or resound, especially repeatedly: {Thunder reverberated through the valley}. Sound reverberates when it bounces off surfaces and returns. The word extends to lasting effects or consequences: {The scandal reverberated through the industry for years}. News reverberates when it spreads and prompts reactions. {Her words reverberated in his mind long after she left.}

Reverberated is the past tense of reverberate, meaning to echo or resound repeatedly. Sound reverberates when it bounces off surfaces: {The thunder reverberated through the valley}. The word extends to effects that spread outward: {The scandal reverberated across the industry}. {Her words reverberated in his mind for days}.

Reverberates means to echo repeatedly, as sound bouncing off surfaces: {Her voice reverberated through the empty hall}. Extended to any effect that spreads outward in waves or has lasting impact: {The scandal reverberated across the industry}. A single decision can reverberate for years, its consequences felt long after the initial event.

Reverberating describes sound that echoes, resounds, or continues in a series of reflections: {His voice went reverberating through the empty hall}. The word extends to anything that produces lasting effects or spreads outward: {The scandal sent reverberating shockwaves through the industry}. A reverberating space amplifies and prolongs sound; a reverberating decision amplifies and prolongs consequences.

Reverberation is sound that persists after its source has stopped, created by waves bouncing off surfaces. A room with hard walls has noticeable reverberation; a carpeted room with soft furniture has little. The word extends to any continuing effect or repercussion: {The reverberations of the scandal lasted for years}. The verb is reverberate.

Reverberations are sounds that persist by bouncing off surfaces—the lingering echo in a cathedral, the rumble of thunder rolling through hills. The word extends to any continuing effects or repercussions: {The reverberations of that decision are still being felt today}. A single event sends out reverberations the way a stone dropped in water sends out ripples.

To revere someone or something is to regard them with deep respect and admiration, often bordering on awe: {She revered her grandmother}, {a revered institution}. The feeling is stronger than mere respect—it suggests veneration, the kind of honor once reserved for saints or sages. (Capitalized Revere refers to Paul Revere.)

Revered means deeply respected and honored, often with a sense of awe or veneration. The word typically applies to people, traditions, or institutions that have earned widespread admiration: {a revered leader}, {the revered tradition of afternoon tea}. Someone revered commands respect through achievement, wisdom, or moral authority rather than mere position.

Reverence is deep respect mixed with awe, the kind of regard you might have for something sacred, ancient, or profoundly admirable: {She spoke of her grandfather with reverence}. The word suggests more than ordinary respect—a sense of wonder or veneration. To revere is the verb; a reverend is a member of the clergy deserving such respect. {He held the old manuscript with reverence}.

Reverend is an honorific title for Christian clergy, used with a name: {the Reverend Martin Luther King Jr.}, {Reverend Jackson}. Informally, reverend serves as a noun meaning a member of the clergy: {The reverend gave a moving sermon}. The underlying adjective meaning worthy of reverence is archaic.

Reverent describes an attitude of deep respect, awe, or veneration—typically toward something sacred, honored, or greatly admired. A reverent {tone} is hushed and respectful. Reverent {silence} greets a solemn moment. The word suggests more than ordinary politeness; it implies something approaching worship or profound admiration: {He spoke of his mentor in reverent terms}.

A reverie is a state of being pleasantly lost in one's thoughts, a kind of waking dream where the mind wanders freely. Someone in a reverie appears distant or distracted, absorbed in daydreams or fantasies rather than focused on their surroundings. {She sat at the window, lost in reverie.} The word suggests a peaceful, somewhat dreamy mental state rather than concentrated thinking or troubled preoccupation.

Reveries are daydreams—pleasant, dreamy states of absorbed thought. The word suggests being lost in imagination rather than focused on the present: {She sat at the window, lost in reveries of her childhood}. A reverie is typically idle and pleasant, distinguished from worry or deliberate planning. The singular reverie works the same way: {His reverie was interrupted by the phone}.

Reversal is a change to the opposite direction, position, or course of action. A court may issue a reversal of a lower court's decision. A reversal of fortune turns success into failure or vice versa. In medicine, a reversal undoes a previous procedure: {vasectomy reversal}. The word implies not just change but complete turnabout: {a reversal of policy}, {role reversal}.
clues: When everything goes the other way

definition: Reversals are turnarounds—changes to an opposite direction, position, or outcome. A court reversal overturns a lower court's decision. A reversal of fortune shifts circumstances from good to bad or vice versa: {The company's reversal stunned investors who had expected continued growth}. In film, a reversal is a plot point that upends expectations.

The verb reverse suggests movement backward in space or in time. When time is involved, the meaning often suggests reverting to an earlier state, or undo: The appellate judge reversed the decision. If you reverse your vehicle, you make it move backwards. If a trend reverses, it begins to move in the direction opposite. The adjective reverse characterizes things that are opposite or contrary to what is usual: Put the files in reverse alphabetical order, from Z to A.

Reversed means turned backward, opposite, or in the contrary direction. A reversed {image} appears as a mirror reflection. A reversed {decision} overturns a previous ruling. Reversed {charges} are paid by the recipient rather than the caller. Something reversed has had its order, direction, or position switched: {The names were reversed on the list}.

Reversible describes something that can be turned back, undone, or returned to a previous state. A reversible {jacket} can be worn inside out, with different fabric or color showing. A reversible {decision} can be changed. In medicine, reversible {damage} can heal; irreversible damage cannot. The word often appears in discussions of whether actions or conditions can be undone: {Is climate change reversible?}

Revert means to return to a previous state, condition, or practice. Property may revert to its original owner. A person reverts to old habits under stress: {She reverted to smoking when the pressure mounted}. In computing, to revert is to restore an earlier version of a file or document. In Indian and Southeast Asian English, revert commonly means to reply: {Please revert at your earliest convenience}—a usage unfamiliar to most American and British speakers.

Reverting is returning to a previous state, condition, or practice. Property reverts to its original owner when conditions are met. A person reverts to old habits under stress. In version control and editing, reverting means undoing changes to restore an earlier version: {I'm reverting to the last save}. The word implies going backward rather than simply changing.

Reverts is the third-person singular of revert, meaning to return to a previous state or condition: {The land reverts to wilderness if left untended}. In legal contexts, property reverts to a former owner when conditions are met. In computing, to revert is to restore an earlier version: {She reverts the document to yesterday's draft}. As a noun, reverts names people who return to a previous religion, especially Islam.

A review is an evaluation or assessment of something—a book, film, product, or performance: {The restaurant got mixed reviews}. To review is to examine or assess: {Let's review the evidence}. Review also means to look over material again, especially before a test: {I need to review my notes}. A review can be a formal inspection ({a military review}) or a retrospective survey ({a year in review}).

A reviewer is someone who examines or evaluates something, then reports on it. Book reviewers, film reviewers, and restaurant reviewers assess works for publication. In professional contexts, reviewers examine documents, code, or applications: {The manuscript was sent to three peer reviewers}. The role implies authority to judge quality or suitability.

Reviewing is examining something again or with critical attention. You review notes before an exam, review a contract before signing, or review your options before deciding. A critic reviews books, films, or restaurants—evaluating them for an audience: {She makes a living reviewing Broadway shows}. Reviewing also describes formal inspection: {The general spent the morning reviewing the troops}.

Reviews are evaluations or assessments of something, typically products, services, performances, or creative works. A book review offers critical commentary on a text; a performance review assesses an employee's work. Reviews range from professional criticism in publications to casual customer feedback online: {The restaurant had mixed reviews on Yelp}. As a verb, to review means to examine or assess something, or to look over material again: {I need to review my notes before the exam}.

Reviled is the past tense of revile, meaning to criticize or attack with harsh, abusive language. Someone who is reviled is despised and spoken of with contempt: {He was reviled by critics during his lifetime but celebrated after his death}. The word suggests sustained, bitter condemnation rather than casual dislike.

Revise means to look over again with an eye toward changing or improving. You revise a draft, a plan, or an estimate: {I revised the manuscript after getting feedback}. To revise an opinion is to change it based on new information. In British education, to revise is to review material before an exam—what Americans call studying.

Revised describes something that has been changed, corrected, or updated from an earlier version: {a revised estimate}, {the revised edition includes new chapters}. The word implies deliberate improvement or correction rather than arbitrary change. To revise is to look over material again and make alterations: {She revised her manuscript before submitting it}.

Revising is the act of examining and improving something—typically written work—by making changes, corrections, or updates. A writer revises a draft to sharpen arguments or fix awkward phrasing. Students revise for exams by reviewing material. To revise can also mean to alter an opinion or estimate: {We revised our projections downward after the quarterly report}.

Revision is the act of revising—examining and changing something to improve or correct it. A revision is also the result: a changed version of a text, plan, or design. {The manuscript went through several revisions before publication.} In British academic usage, revision means reviewing material before an exam: {I need to do some revision for tomorrow's test.}

Revisionism is the practice of reexamining and reinterpreting established views, particularly in history or political ideology. The term often carries negative connotations, suggesting that someone is distorting accepted facts to serve a particular agenda: {Holocaust revisionism is a form of antisemitic denial}. In Marxist contexts, revisionism refers to attempts to modify orthodox doctrine, typically by advocating for gradual reform rather than revolution. A revisionist is someone who engages in such reinterpretation.

Revisionist describes someone who reexamines and reinterprets accepted views, especially historical narratives. The term can be neutral—historians regularly revise interpretations as new evidence emerges—or pejorative, suggesting distortion of established facts for ideological purposes: {revisionist history}, {Holocaust revisionist}. In political contexts, revisionist often implies deviation from orthodox doctrine: {The party accused him of revisionist tendencies}.

Revisionists are people who reinterpret established beliefs, narratives, or historical accounts. The term is neutral in academic contexts—historians regularly revise understanding as new evidence emerges. But revisionist often carries suspicion, implying someone is distorting accepted truth for ideological purposes: {Holocaust revisionists}, {revisionist history}. In Marxist discourse, revisionists are those accused of abandoning orthodox doctrine.

Revisions are changes made to improve, correct, or update something, most often a document, plan, or design. The word emphasizes deliberate reworking rather than starting fresh: {The manuscript went through several revisions before publication}. In academic contexts, revision often means studying material again, especially before an exam—a usage more common in British English. A revision can also refer to the updated version itself: {This is the third revision of the contract}.

To revisit is to visit again or return to something previously encountered. You might revisit a favorite vacation spot, revisit an old argument, or revisit a decision that needs reconsideration. The word often suggests reexamination with fresh perspective: {Let's revisit this proposal after the budget meeting}. A revisit is an instance of returning.

Revisited describes returning to something after time has passed—a place, topic, or work—often with fresh perspective. It appears commonly in titles signaling an update or reexamination: {Brideshead Revisited}, {a theory revisited}. To revisit a decision is to reconsider it: {The committee revisited the policy after complaints}.

Revitalisation is the British spelling of revitalization—the process of bringing renewed life, energy, or vigour to something that has declined. Urban revitalisation restores neglected neighbourhoods. Economic revitalisation rebuilds struggling industries. The word implies not just improvement but restoration of former vitality: {The revitalisation of the historic district brought shops and residents back to empty streets}.

Revitalise is the British spelling of revitalize—to bring new life or energy to something that has declined or stagnated. Cities revitalise neglected neighbourhoods. Companies revitalise aging brands. {The new management team revitalised the struggling department}. The word implies restoration rather than creation from scratch.

Revitalization is the process of giving new life or vigor to something that has declined or stagnated. Cities undergo revitalization when neglected neighborhoods receive investment and development. A revitalization of interest means renewed enthusiasm for something previously ignored: {The documentary sparked a revitalization of folk music}. The term often appears in urban planning, business strategy, and cultural preservation.

To revitalize is to restore vitality, energy, or life to something that has declined or stagnated. Cities revitalize neglected neighborhoods. Companies revitalize aging brands. A vacation can revitalize your spirit. The word implies bringing back vigor that once existed: {The new mayor promised to revitalize the downtown district}.

Revitalized means restored to vigor or vitality. Something revitalized has been given new life or energy after a period of decline: {The downtown area was revitalized with new shops and restaurants}, {She felt revitalized after her vacation}. The word implies not just improvement but a return to a former state of health or strength.

Revival is the act of bringing something back—to life, to consciousness, to use, or to prominence. A patient experiences revival after resuscitation. A revival of interest in vinyl records means renewed popularity. In religion, a revival is a period or meeting aimed at reawakening spiritual fervor: {tent revival}, {revival meeting}. In theater, a revival is a new production of an old play or musical: {the Broadway revival of Oklahoma!}

A revivalist advocates for or leads religious revivals—emotionally charged gatherings aimed at renewing faith and winning converts. The term evokes tent meetings, fiery preaching, and calls to repentance: {a traveling revivalist preacher}. More broadly, revivalist describes anyone seeking to restore or renew something from the past: {architectural revivalists}, {a jazz revivalist}.

Revivalists are people who seek to bring back or renew something from the past, whether religious fervor, artistic styles, or cultural practices. The term most commonly applies to preachers and evangelists who conduct revival meetings aimed at rekindling spiritual commitment among believers. {The revivalists drew thousands to their tent meetings across the rural South.} Beyond religion, revivalists champion the restoration of earlier traditions, movements, or aesthetic forms that have fallen out of fashion.

Revivals is the plural of revival—instances of bringing something back to life or prominence. Religious revivals are gatherings meant to reawaken faith: {tent revivals}, {the Great Awakening revivals}. Cultural revivals restore interest in neglected styles or practices: {the folk music revival}, {Gothic Revival architecture}. Theater revivals are new productions of older plays or musicals: {Broadway revivals of classic shows}.

To revive is to bring back to life, consciousness, or vigor. A paramedic revives a drowning victim; coffee revives you in the morning. The word extends to restoring things that have faded or lapsed: {They're trying to revive the old downtown district}. A Broadway revival brings back a classic show. Interest, hope, and memories can all be revived.

Revived describes something brought back—to life, consciousness, activity, or relevance. A revived patient regains consciousness; a revived economy shows renewed growth; a revived fashion trend returns to popularity. {The paramedics revived him after his heart stopped}. {Interest in vinyl records has revived among younger listeners}. The word is the past tense and past participle of revive.

Revives is the third-person singular of revive—to bring back to life, consciousness, or vigor. A paramedic revives a drowning victim. Coffee revives a tired worker. A director revives a forgotten play by staging it anew. {The rain revives the garden}. {Nothing revives her spirits like a weekend away}.

Reviving is the present participle of revive—bringing something back to life, consciousness, or vigor. A paramedic works at reviving a patient. A company focuses on reviving a struggling brand. {The rain is reviving the garden}. Reviving can also serve as an adjective: {a reviving cup of coffee}, {a reviving breeze after the heat}.

To revoke is to officially cancel or withdraw something previously granted—a license, a privilege, a permission, an offer. The word implies formal authority: governments revoke visas, courts revoke probation, boards revoke certifications. {His driver's license was revoked after the third offense.} In card games, to revoke is to fail to follow suit when able, a penalty-worthy mistake.

Revoked is the past tense of revoke, meaning to officially cancel or withdraw something previously granted. Licenses get revoked for violations, privileges revoked for misconduct, offers revoked before acceptance: {His driver's license was revoked after the third DUI}. The word carries formal weight—things are revoked by authorities, not casually taken back.

Revolt is to rise up against authority—to rebel, mutiny, or refuse submission. A revolt is such an uprising: {The peasant revolt spread across three provinces}. Revolt also means to disgust or repel: {The smell revolted her}. Something revolting causes strong disgust. To be {revolted by} something is to find it deeply offensive or sickening.

Revolted is the past tense of revolt, meaning to rebel or rise up against authority: {The colonists revolted against the crown}. More commonly now, revolted describes a feeling of intense disgust: {I was revolted by the smell}. The two senses connect—both involve rejection and turning away from something intolerable.

Revolting describes something that provokes disgust or strong aversion: {The smell from the dumpster was revolting}. It applies to physical repulsiveness—rotting food, bodily fluids—and to morally repugnant behavior: {His treatment of the staff was revolting}. The word carries more visceral force than merely unpleasant or offensive.

Revolts is the plural of revolt—uprisings or rebellions against authority: {The colonial revolts spread across three continents}. As a verb form, it means either to rise up in opposition or to cause disgust: {The peasantry revolts against the king}, {The smell revolts me}. What revolts someone is what they find deeply offensive or nauseating.

Revolution is the verbal noun of revolve, meaning to go around, so the revolution of the earth is the fact of its going around, or one complete instance of this. Revolution also denotes a fundamental change in the governance of a country, usually sudden and quick, and typically when the people get rid of their current government. Such revolutions are usually capitalized and have a modifier (French Revolution, Russian Revolution, American Revolution). A historical or significant change in the way things are done is also a revolution: Machinery was introduced to manufacturing during the Industrial Revolution.

Revolutionaries are people who advocate or participate in revolution—the overthrow of an established political system or social order. The term can be admiring or hostile depending on one's perspective: {The revolutionaries stormed the capital} might describe heroes or terrorists. Revolutionary as an adjective means radically new or transformative: {revolutionary technology}, {a revolutionary approach to education}.

Revolutionary describes something that brings about fundamental, dramatic change—overturning established systems or ways of thinking. A revolutionary {idea} transforms a field; revolutionary {technology} disrupts entire industries. The word also relates to political revolutions: revolutionary {forces}, revolutionary {movements}. As a noun, a revolutionary is someone who advocates or participates in overthrowing a government or social order: {The revolutionaries stormed the capital}.

Revolutionise is the British spelling of revolutionize—to transform something fundamentally and dramatically. The word implies not gradual improvement but wholesale change: {The smartphone revolutionised communication}. Industries, societies, and ways of thinking can all be revolutionised. The term borrows gravity from political revolution, suggesting upheaval that remakes the old order.

Revolutionised is the British spelling of revolutionized. To revolutionise something is to transform it fundamentally, usually through innovation or radical change: {The smartphone revolutionised how we communicate}. The word implies not mere improvement but a complete overturning of previous methods or systems.

Revolutionize means to fundamentally transform something, bringing about radical and sweeping change. The word derives from revolution in its political sense—the overthrow of an established order—but now applies broadly to any dramatic upheaval in how things work. Technology revolutionizes industries; ideas revolutionize thinking. {The smartphone revolutionized how we communicate.} {Darwin's theory revolutionized biology.} The term often carries positive connotations of progress and innovation, though the changes described may be disruptive.

Revolutions is the plural of revolution. A revolution is a complete turn around an axis—the earth's revolution around the sun takes one year. By extension, revolution means a fundamental change that overturns an existing order: the French Revolution, the Industrial Revolution, {a revolution in how we think about privacy}. Revolutionary means radically new or relating to political overthrow.

Revolve means to move in a circle around a central point or axis. The Earth revolves around the sun; a door revolves on its hinges. Figuratively, things revolve around whatever is central to them: {Her life revolves around her children}. To revolve something in your mind is to turn it over, considering it from different angles.

A revolver is a handgun with a rotating cylinder containing multiple chambers, each holding a single cartridge. Pulling the trigger advances the cylinder, aligning the next round with the barrel. The mechanism distinguishes revolvers from semi-automatic pistols, which feed from a magazine. {He kept an old six-shot revolver in the nightstand.}

Revolvers are handguns with a rotating cylinder containing multiple chambers, each holding a single cartridge. The cylinder advances with each trigger pull, aligning the next round with the barrel. Distinguished from semi-automatic pistols by this revolving mechanism: {He carried a six-shot revolver}. The term occasionally applies to other rotating devices.

Revolving describes something that turns around a central point or axis. A revolving door rotates continuously, allowing entry and exit. Revolving credit renews as you pay it down—the available balance keeps coming back around. {The restaurant's revolving rooftop offered panoramic views}. {She had a revolving cast of roommates}.

Revs is the plural of rev, short for revolution—specifically the rotations of an engine per minute. A tachometer measures revs. To rev an engine is to increase its speed: {He revved the motorcycle impatiently at the stoplight}. Figuratively, to rev up is to intensify or prepare for action: {The campaign is revving up for the final weeks}.

A revue is a theatrical entertainment consisting of loosely connected sketches, songs, and dances, typically satirizing current events or popular culture. Unlike a musical with a single plot, a revue strings together varied acts under a theme or simply for variety: {a Broadway revue}, {a political revue lampooning the administration}.

Revulsion is intense disgust or loathing—a visceral pulling-away from something offensive: {She felt a wave of revulsion at the sight}. The word suggests physical recoil, not just intellectual disapproval. {His betrayal filled her with revulsion}. A sudden revulsion of feeling is an abrupt shift in emotion, though this sense is now rare.

Revved is the past tense of rev, meaning to increase an engine's speed by pressing the accelerator: {He revved the engine before pulling away}. Figuratively, to be revved up is to be energized or excited: {The team was revved up for the championship game}.

Revving is increasing an engine's speed, especially while stationary or in neutral—making it roar without going anywhere: {He sat revving the motorcycle at the light}. Figuratively, to rev up is to energize or prepare for action: {The campaign is revving up for the final weeks}. The word imitates the sound of a racing engine.

A reward is something given in return for good behavior, service, or achievement—the opposite of punishment. Parents reward children for completing chores; companies reward employees with bonuses. A reward may also be offered for specific help: {a reward for information leading to an arrest}. The verb means to give such recognition: {Her patience was finally rewarded}.

Rewarded is the past tense of reward—to give something in return for service, achievement, or merit. Someone rewarded for hard work receives recognition or compensation: {She was rewarded with a promotion}. The word implies deserved return: {His patience was finally rewarded}. To feel rewarded is to experience satisfaction from an outcome: {I felt rewarded just seeing their faces}.

Rewarding describes something that gives satisfaction, fulfillment, or a sense of accomplishment. A rewarding {career} provides more than just income—it offers meaning. A rewarding {experience} leaves you feeling the effort was worthwhile. The word emphasizes emotional or psychological payoff rather than material gain, though both can apply: {Teaching is exhausting but deeply rewarding}.

Rewards are things given or received in return for effort, achievement, or service. A reward can be payment, recognition, or satisfaction: {The job offers financial rewards}, {Seeing her graduate was reward enough}. To reward someone is to give them something for what they've done: {The company rewards loyalty with bonuses}. Reward also names the feeling of satisfaction from accomplishment: {Teaching has its own rewards}.

To rewatch is to watch something again—a movie, a TV series, a video. The word implies deliberate return rather than accidental repetition: {I've rewatched that scene a dozen times}. Some shows reward rewatching with details missed the first time. As a noun, a rewatch is the act itself: {The movie holds up on rewatch}.

Rewild means to restore land to its natural, uncultivated state—removing human intervention and reintroducing native species. Conservation efforts rewild former farmland by planting indigenous vegetation and bringing back wolves or bison. The term extends to personal transformation: {After burnout, she rewilded her life, abandoning schedules for intuition}. Rewilding reverses domestication, whether of landscapes or lifestyles.

Rewilded describes land, ecosystems, or animals that have been returned to a wild or natural state after human intervention or domestication. Conservation efforts may rewild former farmland by reintroducing native species and removing human infrastructure: {The rewilded estate now supports wolves and wild horses}. Animals raised in captivity may be rewilded—rehabilitated for release into natural habitats.

Rewilding is the practice of restoring land to a more natural, uncultivated state—allowing ecosystems to regenerate with minimal human intervention. This may involve reintroducing native species, removing barriers to wildlife movement, or simply stepping back and letting nature reclaim territory: {The foundation is rewilding thousands of acres of former farmland}. The concept extends metaphorically to personal life—shedding domesticated habits for something wilder: {She spent a month in the woods, rewilding herself}.

Rewind means to wind backward—returning tape, film, or other spooled media to an earlier point. With cassettes and VHS, you had to rewind before returning a rental. Digital media eliminated the mechanism but kept the word: streaming services still have rewind buttons. Figuratively, to rewind is to revisit something from the beginning: {Let me rewind and explain how we got here}.

Rewinding is returning something to an earlier point—originally magnetic tape spooled backward to replay audio or video: {I kept rewinding that scene to catch the dialogue}. The word persists even for digital media that has no physical tape: {Let me rewind a bit}. Figuratively, to rewind is to revisit or reconsider: {If we could rewind to last Tuesday, I'd make a different choice}.

Rewinds is the verb form of rewind—to wind backward, returning something to an earlier position. Originally applied to tape in cassettes and VCRs: {She rewinds the movie to watch that scene again}. Now used for any media playback: {He rewinds the podcast thirty seconds}. Figuratively, to mentally revisit: {My brain keeps rewinding to that conversation}.

To rewire is to replace or reconfigure the electrical wiring in a building, device, or system: {The old house needed to be completely rewired}. Figuratively, rewire describes changing ingrained patterns of thought or behavior: {Therapy helped rewire how I respond to stress}. The brain can rewire itself through neuroplasticity—forming new neural pathways.

Rewired is the past tense of rewire—to replace or repair electrical wiring: {We rewired the whole house after buying it}. Figuratively, rewired describes fundamental changes to how something functions, especially the brain or habits: {Therapy rewired how I respond to stress}. {Social media has rewired our attention spans.}

Rewires is the verb rewire in the third person or as a plural noun. To rewire is to replace or redo electrical wiring: {The electrician rewires old houses}. Figuratively, rewiring describes fundamental changes to how something functions, especially the brain or habits: {Meditation rewires neural pathways}. {Therapy helped rewire her response to stress}.

Rewiring is replacing or reconfiguring electrical wires, especially in a building: {The old house needs complete rewiring}. Figuratively, rewiring describes fundamentally changing how something functions—particularly mental patterns or organizational systems: {Therapy helped with rewiring my response to stress}, {The company is rewiring its approach to customer service}.

Rework means to revise or redo something to improve it. A writer reworks a draft, an engineer reworks a design. The noun refers to the process itself or the revised product: {The script needed considerable rework before filming}. In manufacturing, rework specifically means correcting defective items rather than scrapping them.

Reworking is the process of revising, reshaping, or redoing something to improve it or adapt it for a new purpose. The term applies broadly: a musician might release a reworking of an earlier song, a writer might produce a reworking of a classic tale, or a manufacturer might subject defective products to reworking before they can be sold. {The film is a reworking of the 1954 original.} The word emphasizes that substantial effort goes into the revision, distinguishing it from minor tweaks or corrections.

Rewound is the past tense and past participle of rewind. To rewind is to wind something back to an earlier point—originally tape in a cassette or reel: {I rewound the VHS to watch that scene again}. The term persists for digital media even without physical tape: {She rewound the podcast thirty seconds}.

To rewrite is to write something again, typically to improve or correct it: {The editor asked her to rewrite the ending}. A rewrite is the revised version itself. The word implies more than minor edits—substantial reworking of content, structure, or style. In journalism and screenwriting, rewrites are routine: scripts pass through multiple hands, each doing a rewrite.

Rewrites is the plural of rewrite—a revised version of something written. A screenplay may go through dozens of rewrites before filming.
