Rosebud lips are small and delicately shaped. As a term of endearment: {Good morning, rosebud}.

A rosehip is the fruit of a rose plant—the round or oval seed pod that develops after the flower fades. Rosehips are rich in vitamin C and commonly used in teas, jellies, and herbal remedies: {rosehip tea}, {rosehip oil}. They range from red to orange and appear in late summer through autumn.

Rosehips are the rounded fruit of a rose plant, remaining on the stem after the petals fall. They're typically red or orange and rich in vitamin C, used in teas, jams, and herbal remedies: {rosehip tea}, {rosehip oil}. Also spelled as two words: rose hips.

Rosemary is an aromatic evergreen shrub with needle-like leaves, native to the Mediterranean. The herb flavors lamb, chicken, potatoes, and bread. Its piney, slightly bitter taste intensifies when dried. Rosemary has traditional associations with remembrance: {There's rosemary, that's for remembrance}. (Capitalized Rosemary is a given name.)

Roses is the plural of rose, the thorny flowering shrub prized for fragrant blooms and cultivated in countless varieties. Red roses traditionally symbolize romantic love; other colors carry different meanings. To {come up roses} is for things to turn out well. {Stop and smell the roses} advises slowing down to appreciate life. {A bed of roses} describes easy, comfortable circumstances—often in the negative: {Life isn't always a bed of roses}.

A rosette is a decorative element shaped like a rose, with petals radiating from a center. Rosettes appear in architecture, on ribbons awarded as prizes, and in food presentations like piped frosting. In biology, rosette describes circular arrangements of leaves or other structures growing from a central point: {The succulent forms a tight rosette}.

Rosettes are circular ornaments or arrangements resembling roses. Architectural rosettes appear on ceilings and moldings. Ribbon rosettes are awards pinned to prize-winning animals or worn as badges of honor. The word also names the circular cluster pattern in certain plants and the spotted markings on leopards and jaguars. In cooking, rosettes are fried pastries made by dipping a shaped iron into batter.

Rosewater is water infused with rose petals or rose oil, used in cooking, cosmetics, and perfumery. It adds a delicate floral flavor to Middle Eastern and South Asian desserts: {baklava scented with rosewater}, {rosewater lassi}. As an adjective, rosewater describes something excessively sentimental or unrealistically optimistic: {rosewater notions of romance}.
clues: Distilled fragrance for Middle Eastern sweets

definition: Rosewood is a dense, richly colored hardwood prized for fine furniture, musical instruments, and decorative woodwork. The wood comes from several tropical tree species and typically features deep reddish-brown to purple hues with distinctive dark streaking. Its name derives from the faint rose-like fragrance released when the wood is cut. Rosewood's beauty and durability have made it so desirable that several species are now protected due to overharvesting.

Rosin is a solid resin derived from pine trees, used to increase friction or grip. Musicians rub rosin on bow strings to help them catch and vibrate the strings of violins, cellos, and similar instruments: {She rosined her bow before the performance}. Dancers and athletes apply rosin to hands or shoes for better traction. Rosin also appears in soldering flux and adhesives.

A roster is a list of names, typically of people belonging to a group or scheduled for duty. Sports teams have rosters of players; workplaces post rosters showing who works which shifts. The word implies organized membership or rotation: {She checked the roster to see when she was on call}. To roster someone is to add them to such a list.

Rosters is the plural of roster, a list of names—typically people assigned to a team, duty, or organization. Sports teams have rosters of players; workplaces have rosters showing who works which shifts. {The coach announced the final rosters before the season opener.} {She checked the rosters to see when she was scheduled.}

Rosy means having a pink or reddish color, like roses or healthy cheeks: {rosy cheeks from the cold}. Extended to outlook and prospects, rosy means optimistic or promising: {a rosy future}, {rosy predictions}. Someone who sees things through {rose-colored glasses} has an unrealistically positive view. The opposite appears in phrases like {not so rosy} or {less than rosy}.

Rot is a noun and verb that is both older and more frequent than its nearest synonym, decay. To rot is to deteriorate in a natural way, as food rots in your fridge, or dead trees rot in the forest. An instance or outbreak of rotting is also called rot, which serves as a general name for various kinds of fungal or bacterial decay. If someone is talking rot, they are speaking nonsense. The phrase stop the rot usually means to stop some undesirable process that is making things worse.

Rotary describes circular motion or arrangement. A rotary engine has parts that rotate rather than reciprocate. A rotary phone has a circular dial you turn to select numbers. As a noun, a rotary is a traffic circle—an intersection where vehicles move in one direction around a central island. {Take the second exit off the rotary.} The term rotary for traffic circles is mainly used in New England.

To rotate is to turn around a central point or axis. The Earth rotates on its axis; a wheel rotates around its hub. Rotate also means to take turns in sequence: {Employees rotate through different departments}, {We rotate who brings snacks}. Crops are rotated to preserve soil health. A rotating {president} serves a term before the next takes over.

Rotating describes something that turns around a central point or axis. A rotating {fan} sweeps air across a room. Rotating can also mean alternating or taking turns: a rotating {schedule}, rotating {shifts}. {The presidency rotates among member nations annually.}

Rotation is the act of turning around an axis or center point. The Earth completes one rotation every twenty-four hours. The meaning extends to any cyclical sequence: {crop rotation}, {tire rotation}, {The restaurant has a rotating menu}. In sports, a rotation is the order in which players take turns: {He's fifth in the pitching rotation}. To be {in rotation} is to be among items that cycle through use.

Rotations are acts of turning around a center point or axis. The Earth's rotation produces day and night. In agriculture, crop rotation alternates plantings to preserve soil health. Work rotations cycle employees through shifts or positions: {The new nurses are on six-week rotations through different departments}. In sports, a rotation is the order in which players take turns: {He's locked into the starting rotation}.

Rote is mechanical repetition without understanding or thought. Learning by rote means memorizing through sheer repetition rather than grasping underlying meaning: {She learned her multiplication tables by rote}. The word appears almost exclusively in this phrase, carrying a mildly negative connotation—suggesting mindless drill over genuine comprehension.

Rotgut is cheap, low-quality liquor—the kind that burns going down and leaves you feeling wrecked: {We drank rotgut whiskey in the back of his truck}. The word suggests alcohol so harsh it might rot your insides. It can apply to any poorly made or adulterated spirit.

Roti is a round, unleavened flatbread from South Asian cuisine, made from whole wheat flour and cooked on a griddle. It serves as a staple accompaniment to curries and other dishes: {She tore off a piece of roti to scoop up the dal}. In Caribbean cooking, roti also refers to a wrapped sandwich using the flatbread as a vessel for curried fillings.

Rotis is the plural of roti, a round flatbread from South Asian cuisine. Made from whole wheat flour and cooked on a griddle, rotis are a staple accompaniment to curries and other dishes: {We ordered extra rotis to scoop up the dal}. The term appears in Indian, Pakistani, Caribbean, and other cuisines influenced by South Asian cooking.

A rotisserie is a cooking apparatus that rotates meat on a spit before a heat source, ensuring even browning and self-basting: {rotisserie chicken}. The word also names the style of cooking or the prepared food itself. In fantasy sports, rotisserie leagues use cumulative statistics across categories rather than head-to-head matchups—named after the New York restaurant where the format was invented.

Rotisseries is the plural of rotisserie—a cooking apparatus that slowly turns meat on a spit over a heat source, allowing it to cook evenly and baste in its own juices. The term also applies to shops or restaurants specializing in spit-roasted meats: {The neighborhood has two rotisseries known for their chicken}. In fantasy sports, rotisserie leagues use cumulative statistical rankings rather than head-to-head competition.

A rotor is the rotating part of a machine, distinguished from the stationary part (the stator). In helicopters, the rotor is the assembly of spinning blades that provides lift. In engines, generators, and turbines, rotors spin to convert or transfer energy. The word also appears in meteorology for a turbulent horizontal vortex that forms downwind of mountains.

Rotors is the plural of rotor—a rotating component in a machine. Helicopter rotors are the spinning blades that provide lift. In a car's braking system, rotors are the metal discs that brake pads clamp against to slow the wheels: {The mechanic said I need new rotors}. Electric motors and generators have rotors that spin within stationary housings.

A rototiller is a motorized gardening machine with rotating blades that churn and break up soil, used to prepare ground for planting. The blades spin on a horizontal axis, mixing in organic matter and loosening compacted earth: {We rototilled the backyard before putting in the vegetable garden}. Also called a rotary tiller.

Rots is the third-person singular form of the verb rot, meaning to decay or decompose through the action of bacteria and fungi. Organic matter rots when left exposed to moisture and air: {The fallen fruit rots quickly in summer heat}. Figuratively, things rot when they deteriorate through neglect or corruption: {The whole system rots from the inside}. As a plural noun, rots are diseases that cause decay in plants or animals.

Rotten describes organic matter that has decayed and spoiled: {rotten fruit}, {rotten meat}, {rotten teeth}. The smell of rotten eggs is sulfurous and unmistakable. Extended uses convey corruption or poor quality: a rotten {system}, rotten {luck}, a rotten {deal}. Something rotten is thoroughly bad: {I feel rotten about what I said}. To be {rotten to the core} is to be corrupt beyond redemption.

Rotting describes the process of decay—organic matter breaking down through bacterial or fungal action. A rotting {apple} softens and browns. Rotting {wood} crumbles. The word often emphasizes the ongoing, visible nature of decomposition: {the smell of rotting vegetation}, {a rotting corpse}. Figuratively, something rotting is deteriorating or corrupting: {a rotting infrastructure}, {rotting from within}.

A rotunda is a round building or room, especially one topped with a dome. The term typically applies to grand architectural spaces—the rotunda of the U.S. Capitol, a museum rotunda with a domed ceiling. The roundness is essential: {Visitors gathered in the rotunda beneath the painted dome}.

Rotundas is the plural of rotunda, a round building or room, especially one with a dome. The Capitol Rotunda in Washington, D.C., is the most famous American example. The term applies to both grand public spaces and smaller circular rooms: {The museum's rotundas echoed with footsteps}.

The rouble is the basic monetary unit of Russia, divided into 100 kopecks. Also spelled ruble. The currency has experienced dramatic fluctuations in value, particularly during economic crises: {The rouble crashed after sanctions were imposed}. Belarus also uses a currency called the rouble.
Roubles is the plural of rouble, the basic unit of currency in Russia and Belarus. The spelling with -ou- is British; Americans typically write rubles. {The painting sold for twelve million roubles.}

Rouge is a red cosmetic powder or cream applied to the cheeks to create a flushed appearance—what's now more often called blush. The word comes from French for red, and extends to any reddish substance: jeweler's rouge for polishing metal, the rouge on a roulette wheel. In Canadian football, a rouge is a single point scored when a kicked ball is not returned from the end zone.

Rough is most frequently an adjective, typically opposite to smooth in several senses, and often synonymous with harsh. A rough draft or rough estimate is preliminary and requires further work. Someone going through a rough patch is having difficulties. To rough something is to work with it in a preliminary way. To rough someone up is to hurt them physically. If you are roughing it, you’re living with few comforts.

Roughhewn describes something crudely shaped or unfinished, like timber cut with an axe but not smoothed or planed: {roughhewn beams in the cabin ceiling}. The word extends to people or manners that are unpolished or unsophisticated but genuine: {a roughhewn charm}, {his roughhewn features}. Also spelled rough-hewn.

Roughhouse is boisterous, physical play that stops short of actual fighting—wrestling, tumbling, shoving. Kids roughhouse; siblings roughhouse; puppies roughhouse. The word works as both noun and verb: {The boys were roughhousing in the living room} or {That's enough roughhouse for one afternoon}. The play is rowdy but usually good-natured.

Roughhoused is the past tense of roughhouse, meaning to engage in boisterous, physical play—wrestling, shoving, tumbling around. It describes the kind of rowdy horseplay common among children or young people: {The kids roughhoused in the backyard until someone got hurt}. The activity sits between play and fighting, energetic but not genuinely violent.

Roughhouses is the verb form of roughhouse, meaning to engage in boisterous, physical play—wrestling, shoving, tumbling around. It describes the kind of energetic horseplay common among children or young animals: {The kids roughhouse in the backyard until someone gets hurt}. As a noun, a roughhouse is such a session of rowdy play.

Roughhousing is boisterous physical play—wrestling, tumbling, shoving—that stops short of real fighting. Children roughhouse; so do puppies. The activity walks a line between play and aggression: {The boys were just roughhousing, but someone's going to get hurt}. As a verb, to roughhouse is to engage in such play.

Roughing is preliminary or incomplete work that establishes basic structure before finishing: {roughing in the plumbing}, {roughing out a sketch}. In hockey and other contact sports, roughing is a penalty for unnecessary physical contact—shoving or hitting beyond what the rules allow. To go {roughing it} is to live without usual comforts, especially while camping.

Roughly means approximately or without precision: {roughly half the population}, {It costs roughly fifty dollars}. It also means in a crude or unfinished manner: {a roughly sketched outline}, {roughly hewn timber}. When describing physical treatment, roughly means with force or violence: {The guards handled him roughly}.

A roughneck is a worker on an oil drilling rig, performing the physically demanding labor of handling pipes and equipment on the drill floor. More broadly, roughneck describes any tough, rowdy, or uncouth person—someone rough around the edges: {He hung around with roughnecks and troublemakers}. The term suggests working-class masculinity and a readiness for hard work or hard living.

Roughnecks are workers on oil drilling rigs, performing physically demanding labor on the drill floor. The term extends to any tough, rough-mannered person, often with connotations of working-class masculinity and readiness for a fight: {A crew of roughnecks showed up at the bar after their shift}. The word can be affectionate or dismissive depending on context.

Roughness is the quality of being rough—uneven, coarse, or not smooth. A surface has roughness when it catches the hand: {the roughness of sandpaper}, {the roughness of tree bark}. The word extends to harshness in manner or speech: {There was a roughness in his voice that startled her}. In technical contexts, roughness is a measurable property of surfaces, quantifying texture at microscopic scales.

A roughrider is a skilled horseman who breaks and trains wild horses, or more broadly, someone who rides with daring and rough technique rather than polish. The term gained fame through Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders, volunteer cavalry who fought in the Spanish-American War: {He fancied himself a roughrider, though he'd barely been on a horse}.

Roughriders are skilled horsemen who break and train wild horses, or cavalry soldiers trained for rugged terrain. The term evokes frontier toughness and daring. Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders were volunteer cavalry in the Spanish-American War, cementing the word's association with bold, unconventional fighters: {The roughriders charged up the hill}.

Roughshod originally described horses fitted with shoes having projecting nails or points for better traction on rough terrain. The word survives almost exclusively in the phrase {ride roughshod over}, meaning to treat someone or something with brutal disregard: {The company rode roughshod over environmental regulations}. The image is of iron-shod hooves trampling whatever lies beneath.

Roulette is a casino game where a ball is dropped onto a spinning wheel divided into numbered compartments; players bet on where the ball will land. The wheel has slots numbered 1–36 alternating red and black, plus one or two green zeros. By extension, roulette describes any situation left to pure chance: {Russian roulette} involves spinning a revolver cylinder with one bullet and pulling the trigger—a metaphor for reckless gambles with serious consequences.
Round is used as a preposition in British English in nearly all cases where American English uses around. The meaning is the same.

A roundabout is a circular intersection where traffic flows in one direction around a central island—vehicles yield on entry and exit at their desired road. The design keeps traffic moving without signals. As an adjective, roundabout means indirect or circuitous: {She took a roundabout route to avoid traffic}. A roundabout {way of saying something} avoids directness. In British English, a roundabout is also a merry-go-round.

Roundabouts are circular intersections where traffic flows in one direction around a central island, yielding to vehicles already in the circle. Common in Britain and increasingly in America, they reduce the need for traffic lights. The word also names a British amusement park ride—what Americans call a merry-go-round or carousel.

Rounded describes something with curves rather than sharp angles or edges: {rounded corners}, {rounded edges}. A rounded number has been adjusted to a convenient value: {The bill came to $19.87, rounded to $20}. A rounded education or personality is complete and well-developed across different areas: {a well-rounded individual}. Rounded vowels are produced with pursed lips.

A rounder is someone who makes rounds—a person who travels a regular circuit, whether a doctor visiting patients or a drunk making the rounds of local bars. In American usage, rounder often carries a disreputable connotation: a habitual gambler, drinker, or petty criminal who frequents certain establishments. {He was a rounder who knew every card room in town.} In baseball, rounders is a British bat-and-ball game ancestral to the American sport.

Rounders is a British bat-and-ball game played between two teams, similar to baseball but with a smaller bat held in one hand and a softer ball. Players hit the ball and run around four posts (bases) to score a rounder. It's traditionally played in schools and informally in parks: {We played rounders in PE class}. The game is considered a precursor to baseball.
clues: British game with posts, not bases

definition: A roundhouse is a circular building where locomotives are stored and serviced, with tracks radiating from a central turntable. The shape extends to other circular or curved structures. A roundhouse punch or kick swings wide in a sweeping arc rather than traveling straight: {He threw a roundhouse that caught me on the jaw}. In baseball, a roundhouse curve breaks dramatically.

Roundhoused is the past tense of roundhouse, meaning to strike with a powerful swinging blow that travels in a wide arc—typically a punch or kick: {He roundhoused the guy who insulted his girlfriend}. The term comes from the roundhouse kick in martial arts, where the leg sweeps around in a semicircular motion. The word often appears in descriptions of fights or action sequences.

Roundhouses are circular punches thrown with a wide, sweeping arc rather than straight from the body. The term extends to kicks delivered the same way—swinging the leg in a curve to strike with maximum force: {He caught him with a roundhouse to the jaw}. Separately, a roundhouse is a circular building where locomotives are serviced and stored, with tracks radiating from a central turntable.

Rounding is adjusting a number to a nearby value, typically one with fewer digits or decimal places. You round 3.7 up to 4, or 3.2 down to 3. The verb also applies to physical shaping: {rounding the corners of a table}. To round something is to make it rounder or to go around it: {The ship rounded the cape at dawn}.

Rounds covers a lot of ground as both noun and verb. A round is something circular or spherical, or a complete cycle or series: {a round of drinks}, {a round of golf}, {rounds of ammunition}. Medical staff make rounds when they visit patients in sequence. The verb means to make round, to go around something, or to complete: {We rounded the corner}. To round up or round down is to adjust a number to a convenient figure. If you round on someone, you turn and confront them sharply.

A roundtable is a discussion among equals, with no one at the head—from the legendary table of King Arthur, where no knight outranked another. The term now describes any meeting or broadcast format where participants share ideas as peers: {a roundtable on climate policy}, {The Sunday morning roundtable debated the election}. Also spelled round table.

Roundtables are discussions or meetings where participants have equal standing, named for the legendary table of King Arthur where no seat held precedence. The format appears in academic conferences, policy debates, and media programs: {a roundtable on climate policy}, {The experts gathered for a roundtable discussion}. The singular roundtable can name either the event or the group itself.

Roundtrip describes a journey that returns to its starting point: a roundtrip {ticket}, roundtrip {airfare}. The two-word form {round trip} usually functions as a noun: {The round trip takes about four hours}. In computing, a roundtrip is a complete cycle of sending data and receiving a response: {roundtrip latency}.

A roundup is a gathering of scattered things into one place. Cowboys conduct roundups of cattle. Police conduct roundups of suspects. A news roundup collects related stories: {Here's your weekly tech roundup}. The verb phrase is two words: {We need to round up the usual suspects}.

Roundups collect scattered things into one place. The original sense involves gathering livestock, especially cattle, by riding around them and driving them together. This extends to any systematic gathering of people or things: {a roundup of suspects}, {a news roundup}. The word often appears in journalism to describe compilations of related items or summaries of events: {Here's your weekly roundup of tech news}.

Rouse means to wake or stir into action. You rouse someone from sleep, or rouse yourself to get moving. A speaker rouses a crowd to enthusiasm; a threat rouses suspicion. The word suggests bringing something from dormancy to activity: {The smell of coffee roused him from bed}. To be roused to anger is to have it awakened. Rousing as an adjective means stirring or energizing: {a rousing speech}, {a rousing chorus}.

Roused is the past tense of rouse, meaning to wake or stir into action. Someone roused from sleep has been awakened: {She roused him at dawn}. The word extends to stirring emotions or energy: {The speech roused the crowd to action}. To be roused to anger is to have that feeling provoked.

Rousing means stirring enthusiasm or excitement. A rousing {speech} energizes the crowd; a rousing {rendition} of a song brings people to their feet. The word suggests something that rouses people from passivity into engagement or action: {The team got a rousing send-off}. A rousing {success} is emphatic and spirited.

A roustabout is an unskilled laborer, particularly one who works on oil rigs or in circuses. On drilling platforms, roustabouts handle the physically demanding grunt work—moving equipment, cleaning, and general maintenance. In circus life, they set up and tear down tents and equipment. The term suggests someone who does hard manual labor without specialized training, often moving from job to job. {He started as a roustabout before working his way up to driller.}

A rout is a disorderly retreat or overwhelming defeat: {The battle ended in a rout}. To rout an opponent is to defeat them decisively, scattering their forces. The word implies not just losing but collapse—an army breaking and fleeing rather than withdrawing in order. By extension, any lopsided victory: {The game was a 42-3 rout}.

Route is a path or course from one place to another: {the shortest route to the airport}, {a bus route}, {a trade route}. It extends to any planned sequence: {a route to success}. In American English, route rhymes with either "root" or "out"—both are standard. To route is to send along a particular path: {Route the cable through the wall}.

Routed is the past tense of two different verbs. From route: directed along a path {The call was routed through three countries}. From rout: defeated decisively and sent fleeing {The army was routed at the first assault}. Context usually makes clear which is meant—logistics suggests the first, combat the second.

A router is a device that directs data traffic between computer networks, connecting your home or office to the internet and managing communication between devices. Pronounced to rhyme with "outer." Separately, a router (rhyming with "hooter") is a power tool that hollows out grooves or shapes edges in wood: {He used a router to cut the decorative molding}.

Routers are devices that direct data traffic between computer networks. A home router connects your devices to the internet, managing which data goes where. In networking, routers make decisions about the best path for data packets to travel. Separately, a router is a power tool that hollows out or shapes wood and other materials: {He used a router to cut decorative edges on the cabinet doors}.

Routes are paths or courses from one place to another. A bus route connects stops along a fixed path; a trade route links commercial centers. To route something is to send it along a particular path: {They routed the cables through the ceiling}. Route can rhyme with "out" or with "boot"—both are standard. A different word spelled the same, pronounced like "out," means to defeat decisively: {The team was routed in the finals}.

A routine is a regular sequence of actions or a fixed program: {my morning routine}, {a comedy routine}, {a dance routine}. As an adjective, routine means ordinary or standard: {routine maintenance}, {a routine checkup}. What's routine is unremarkable—expected rather than exceptional. In computing, a routine is a set of instructions that performs a specific task.

Routines are regular sequences of actions or established patterns of behavior. A morning routine might include coffee, exercise, and checking email. In computing, a routine is a set of instructions that performs a specific task. In entertainment, a routine is a rehearsed performance: a comedy routine, a dance routine. The word often carries connotations of the mundane or mechanical: {stuck in a routine}, {the same old routines}.

Routing is directing something along a path or course. In computing and telecommunications, routing determines how data travels through networks: {The routing table shows which servers handle each request}. In physical contexts, routing means sending along a specified route: {They're routing all calls to the main office}. Routing also refers to cutting grooves or hollowing out with a router tool. Pronounced either to rhyme with "shouting" or with "looting."

Routs is the plural of rout—a disorderly retreat or overwhelming defeat: {The battle ended in a series of routs}. As a verb form, routs means defeats decisively or drives out: {The underdog team routs the defending champions}. To rout out is to find and force from hiding: {The investigation routs out corruption at every level}.

A roux is a mixture of fat and flour cooked together, used to thicken sauces, soups, and gravies. The fat—usually butter—is melted, flour is stirred in, and the mixture is cooked to varying degrees: a white roux for béchamel, a blonde roux for velouté, a dark roux for gumbo. {Start with a roux and build the sauce from there.}

A rover is one who roves—a wanderer or someone who travels without fixed destination. In sports, particularly Australian rules football, a rover is a player with no set position who ranges across the field. The word also names wheeled robotic vehicles designed to explore terrain, especially on other planets: {The Mars rover sent back images of the surface}. In archery, a rover shoots at targets at varying distances. {He spent his twenties as a rover, never settling anywhere long.} (Capitalized Rover is a brand name or proper noun.)

Rovers is the plural of rover, meaning those who roam or wander without fixed destination. The word often appears in team names—especially British football clubs like Blackburn Rovers—evoking an adventurous, traveling spirit. In planetary exploration, rovers are robotic vehicles designed to traverse extraterrestrial surfaces: {The Mars rovers sent back stunning images}. In some youth organizations, Rovers designates an older age group of scouts.

Roving describes movement without a fixed destination or path—wandering, itinerant. A roving {reporter} covers stories wherever they arise. A roving {eye} wanders appreciatively over potential romantic interests. As a noun, roving is fiber that has been carded and drawn into a loose strand, ready for spinning into yarn.

Row has two distinct meanings from different origins. One is a line of things arranged side by side: a row of {houses}, a row of {seats}, {three in a row}. To row is also to propel a boat with oars: {We rowed across the lake}. The other row (rhyming with "cow") is British for a noisy argument or quarrel: {They had a terrible row about money}.

A rowan is a tree or shrub of the genus Sorbus, especially the European mountain ash, known for clusters of white flowers and bright red berries. The berries have traditional associations with protection against witchcraft and evil spirits in Celtic and Scandinavian folklore. {Rowans lined the path to the old cottage.} (Capitalized Rowan is a given name.)

A rowboat is a small boat propelled by oars, typically seating one to four people. The rower sits facing backward, pulling the oars through oarlocks mounted on the gunwales. Rowboats are used for fishing, recreation, or ferrying short distances: {We rented a rowboat and spent the afternoon on the lake}.

Rowboats is the plural of rowboat—a small boat propelled by oars rather than sails, motor, or paddle. Rowboats are typically open-topped and seat one to several people, used for fishing, recreation, or short-distance transport on lakes and calm waters: {We rented rowboats at the park}.

Rowdies is the plural of rowdy—people who behave in a rough, noisy, or disorderly way. The word often describes troublemakers at public events: {The rowdies in the stands were ejected after throwing bottles}. It can be affectionate or critical depending on context—rowdies at a bachelor party versus rowdies vandalizing property.

Rowdiness is rough, noisy, disorderly behavior—the quality of being rowdy. It suggests boisterous energy that may verge on unruliness: {The rowdiness of the crowd got the bar shut down}. The word often describes groups rather than individuals, implying collective disruption.

Rowdy describes noisy, rough, or disorderly behavior, often involving boisterous energy that disrupts order: {a rowdy crowd}, {rowdy fans}. A rowdy person or rowdy (noun) causes such disturbances. The word carries less menace than violent but more than merely loud—it suggests unruly behavior that might tip into trouble: {Things got rowdy after midnight}.

A rower is someone who rows—propels a boat using oars. The term applies both to casual recreational rowing and to the competitive sport, where rowers train intensively and race in crews: {The rowers glided past in their eight-person shell}. In rowing culture, the word distinguishes serious athletes from occasional paddlers.

Rowers are people who row—propelling boats through water using oars. The term applies to recreational rowers, competitive athletes in racing shells, and anyone manning oars: {The rowers pulled in unison across the lake}. In crew and sculling, rowers train intensively for races measured in meters or miles.

A rowhome is a house sharing side walls with adjacent houses, forming a continuous block of residences. The term is regional, used primarily in Philadelphia and surrounding areas—elsewhere the same structure is called a rowhouse or townhouse. {The brick rowhomes of South Philly date to the early 1900s.}

A rowhouse is a house that shares side walls with neighboring houses, forming a continuous line along a street. Common in older American cities like Philadelphia and Baltimore, rowhouses are typically narrow, two or three stories tall, and nearly identical in design: {We bought a rowhouse in Fells Point}. Also spelled row house. British English prefers terraced house.

Rowhouses are a series of attached houses sharing side walls, built in a continuous line along a street. Each unit has its own entrance and typically spans multiple floors. The style is characteristic of older American cities like Philadelphia and Baltimore, and of British cities where they're called terraced houses: {blocks of brick rowhouses lined the neighborhood}.

Rowing is the act of propelling a boat through water using oars, either as transportation, recreation, or competitive sport. In competitive rowing, athletes sit facing backward and pull oars through the water in synchronized strokes, racing in crews of one, two, four, or eight. The sport demands exceptional cardiovascular fitness and technique. {She took up rowing in college and still rows every morning.} Rowing also refers more casually to any oar-powered boating: {We went rowing on the lake.}

Rows are horizontal lines or arrangements of things placed side by side: {rows of corn}, {rows of seats}, {the back row}. To row is to propel a boat with oars. Separately, row (rhyming with "cow") means a noisy quarrel or disturbance: {They had a terrible row about money}.

Royal means of or relating to a king or queen: {the royal family}, {royal decree}, {royal palace}. By extension, royal describes anything magnificent or fit for royalty: {a royal welcome}, {royal treatment}. It also intensifies certain nouns: {a royal mess}, {a royal pain}. In Britain, the Royals are members of the royal family. A royal is also a paper size (20 × 25 inches) and a sail above the topgallant. (Capitalized Royal appears in proper names of institutions and military units.)

A royalist supports monarchy as a system of government, or specifically supports a royal family's claim to power. The term often appears in historical contexts—English Civil War royalists backed Charles I against Parliament. More broadly, anyone favoring hereditary rule over republican government: {He's a royalist at heart, fascinated by kings and queens}. (Capitalized Royalist often refers specifically to historical factions.)

Royalists are supporters of a monarch or monarchy, especially during periods when royal authority is contested. The term most often appears in historical contexts—English Civil War royalists backed Charles I against Parliament, French royalists opposed the Revolution. More broadly, a royalist favors hereditary rule over republican government: {The country remains divided between royalists and democrats}.

Royals are members of a royal family—kings, queens, princes, princesses, and their relatives. The word appears most often in journalism and casual speech: {The royals attended the charity gala}, {tabloid coverage of the royals}. In card games, royals are the face cards: king, queen, jack. The Kansas City Royals are a Major League Baseball team.

Royalties are payments made to owners of intellectual property—authors, musicians, inventors, or patent holders—for each use or sale of their work. A novelist receives royalties on book sales; a songwriter earns royalties when their song is streamed or performed. The term extends to payments for extracting natural resources: {oil royalties}, {mineral royalties}. Royalty in the singular usually means royal status or royal persons collectively.

Royalty refers to people of royal rank—kings, queens, princes, and their families. The word also means the status or power of being royal: {She was born into royalty}. In business, a royalty is a payment to an owner for use of their property, typically a percentage of revenue: authors receive royalties on book sales, musicians on recordings, landowners on mineral extraction. {The patent holder collects royalties from manufacturers.}

An rpg is a rocket-propelled grenade—a shoulder-fired weapon that launches an explosive projectile. The term appears frequently in military and video game contexts: {The soldiers took cover when they spotted the rpg}. In gaming communities, rpg also refers to role-playing games, though that sense is more commonly written in capitals. (Capitalized RPG is the standard form for both meanings.)

RSVP is to respond to an invitation, indicating whether you'll attend: {Have you RSVPed to the wedding yet?} The noun refers to such a response: {We need an RSVP by Friday}. From the French *répondez s'il vous plaît* (please respond), it appears on invitations requesting confirmation. The lowercase form is less common than the all-caps version. (All-caps RSVP is standard.)

Rub is to move something back and forth against a surface with pressure. You rub your eyes when tired, rub lotion into skin, rub a stain to remove it. Things that rub together create friction: {My shoes rub against my heels}. A rub is an act of rubbing or a difficulty: {There's the rub}. To {rub someone the wrong way} is to irritate them. To {rub it in} is to emphasize someone's failure or mistake. A rub is also a spice mixture applied to meat before cooking.

Rubber is an elastic material that stretches and returns to shape, originally derived from tropical tree sap but now often synthetic. It appears in countless products: tires, bands, gloves, erasers. In British usage, a rubber is an eraser. In American slang, a rubber is a condom. To rubber is to gawk or stare: {rubbernecking at an accident}. To {rubber-stamp} something is to approve it automatically, without real scrutiny.

Rubberneck is to crane one's neck to stare at something, especially an accident or spectacle: {Traffic slowed as drivers rubbernecked at the wreck}. The image is of a neck so flexible with curiosity it might be made of rubber. A rubberneck is also a gawking tourist or any nosy onlooker. The word carries mild contempt for idle curiosity.

Rubbernecked is the past tense of rubberneck—to crane one's neck to stare at something, especially an accident or spectacle. The image is of a neck so flexible with curiosity it might be made of rubber. {Traffic slowed as drivers rubbernecked at the wreck}. The word carries a mildly disapproving tone, suggesting idle or morbid curiosity.

A rubbernecker is someone who stares at something, especially slowing down to gawk at an accident or unusual scene. The word evokes craning one's neck for a better view. Rubbernecking causes traffic delays as drivers slow to look: {Traffic backed up for miles because of rubberneckers}. The term carries mild contempt—curiosity that's intrusive or morbid.

Rubberneckers are people who slow down or crane their necks to gawk at something, especially accidents or disaster scenes. The word evokes the image of stretching one's neck like rubber to see what's happening: {Traffic backed up for miles because of rubberneckers}. The term carries mild contempt—rubberneckers satisfy their curiosity at others' expense, often causing additional problems.

Rubbernecking is craning your neck to stare at something, especially an accident or disturbance. The image is of a neck so flexible it might be made of rubber, stretching to get a better look. Traffic slows when drivers rubberneck at crashes on the opposite side of the highway. The term can extend to any nosy gawking: {Quit rubbernecking and mind your own business}.

Rubbernecks is the verb form of rubberneck, meaning to crane one's neck to stare at something—typically an accident, celebrity, or spectacle. The image is of a neck so flexible with curiosity it might as well be rubber. Traffic slows when drivers rubberneck at crashes. As a noun, a rubbernecker is a gawker: {Rubbernecks crowded around the crime scene tape}.

Rubberstamp, usually written as two words or hyphenated, refers to a stamp with a rubber printing surface used to mark documents with dates, signatures, or standard text. Figuratively, to rubber-stamp something is to approve it automatically without genuine consideration: {The board just rubber-stamps whatever the CEO proposes}. A rubber stamp is also a person or body that gives such perfunctory approval.

Rubberstamped describes something approved automatically, without genuine scrutiny or deliberation. The image is of an official mechanically stamping documents without reading them. A rubberstamped {decision} or {approval} suggests the outcome was predetermined: {The board rubberstamped the CEO's proposal without discussion}. The term carries a whiff of criticism—implying the approving body failed to exercise independent judgment.

Rubberstamping is approving something automatically, without real scrutiny or independent judgment. The image is of an official stamping documents mechanically, not reading them: {The board was accused of rubberstamping the CEO's decisions}. The term implies the approval process is a formality rather than genuine oversight.

Rubberstamps are devices with raised lettering or designs used to make repeated impressions in ink—for official marks, dates, or signatures. Figuratively, to rubberstamp something is to approve it automatically without scrutiny: {The committee just rubberstamps whatever management proposes}. A rubberstamp approval carries no real deliberation. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated.

Rubbery describes something with the texture or consistency of rubber—flexible, resilient, slightly bouncy. Food that's rubbery has an unpleasant chewiness: {The overcooked calamari was rubbery}. Legs that feel rubbery are weak and unsteady, as after exertion or shock: {His legs went rubbery when he heard the news}.

Rubbing is the action of pressing something against a surface and moving it back and forth, or the result of that action. You might give someone a back rub, or notice the rubbing of your shoe against your heel. A rubbing is also an image made by placing paper over a textured surface and rubbing with charcoal or pencil, as in a brass rubbing or gravestone rubbing. {The rubbing of the branches against the window kept me awake.}

Rubbish is waste material or garbage—things thrown away as worthless. British English uses rubbish where American English prefers trash or garbage. Extended to mean nonsense or worthless talk: {That's complete rubbish}. As a verb, to rubbish something is to criticize or dismiss it harshly: {Critics rubbished the proposal}. As an adjective, rubbish means poor quality: {I'm rubbish at tennis}.

Rubble is broken fragments of stone, brick, or concrete—the debris left after a building collapses or is demolished: {Rescuers searched through the rubble for survivors}. The word evokes destruction, whether from earthquakes, bombs, or wrecking crews. Figuratively, rubble can describe anything reduced to ruins: {The scandal left his reputation in rubble}.

A rubdown is a vigorous massage, typically given after physical exertion to relax muscles and stimulate circulation: {The trainer gave him a rubdown after the match}. The term suggests brisk, practical massage rather than spa-style pampering—something athletes get in locker rooms, not on heated tables with ambient music.

Rubdowns is the plural of rubdown, a brisk massage typically given to relax muscles or stimulate circulation. Athletes get rubdowns after workouts or competitions: {The trainer gave him a quick rubdown before the match}. The term can also refer to a thorough wiping or drying: {Give the car a rubdown with a chamois}.

A rube is an unsophisticated person, especially one from a rural area who is easily fooled or impressed by city ways. The word carries condescension—it's what a carnival barker calls the marks, what a con artist sees in an easy target: {Those rubes will believe anything}. The term comes from the name Reuben, once stereotypically associated with country folk.

Rubes is the plural of rube, a derogatory term for unsophisticated country people—rustics easily fooled or impressed by city ways. The word derives from the name Reuben, once stereotypically rural. Carnival workers and con artists historically used it for easy marks: {The rubes lined up to see the sideshow}. It retains a condescending edge: {Those rubes will believe anything}.

Rubies are precious gemstones prized for their deep red color, second only to diamonds in hardness among natural gems. The finest specimens come from Myanmar and command prices rivaling or exceeding diamonds. Ruby is the birthstone for July and traditionally symbolizes passion and vitality. In a figurative sense, ruby describes anything with that characteristic rich red color: {ruby lips}, {ruby wine}. The word also appears in programming as Ruby, a popular scripting language.

The ruble is the basic monetary unit of Russia, divided into 100 kopecks. It has been Russian currency for centuries, surviving the Soviet era and continuing after. The word appears in contexts of Russian economics and exchange rates: {The ruble fell sharply against the dollar}. Also spelled rouble, especially in British English.

Rubles are the basic unit of Russian currency, with each ruble divided into 100 kopecks. The word also applies to currencies in Belarus and historically in the Soviet Union. {The painting sold for twelve million rubles.} Also spelled roubles, especially in British English.

A rubric is a set of criteria for evaluating work, especially in education: {The grading rubric awards points for thesis, evidence, and clarity}. Originally a rubric was a heading or category in a document—from the red ink used in medieval manuscripts to mark sections. That sense persists in formal contexts: {under the rubric of national security}. A rubric can also mean an established rule or custom: {the rubrics of polite conversation}.

Rubrics are guidelines, rules, or categories under which things are organized or evaluated. In education, a rubric is a scoring guide that spells out criteria for grading: {The rubric awards points for thesis, evidence, and organization}. More broadly, rubric means a heading or category: {These items fall under the rubric of office supplies}. The word originally referred to text written in red ink—instructions or headings in medieval manuscripts—which explains its connection to guidance and categorization.

Rubs is the plural of rub and the third-person singular verb form. A rub is an act of rubbing—applying pressure while moving back and forth: {a back rub}, {a foot rub}. A rub is also a spice mixture applied to meat before cooking: {a dry rub for ribs}. Shakespeare's {there's the rub} means there's the difficulty or obstacle. To rub is to apply friction: {She rubbed her eyes}. Things that {rub you the wrong way} irritate you.

Ruby is a deep red precious gemstone, a variety of corundum valued for its color and hardness. The finest rubies rival diamonds in price. Ruby also names the color itself—a rich, vivid red: {ruby lips}, {ruby wine}. In printing, ruby is a small type size (5.5 points). In British slang, a ruby is a curry, from rhyming slang "ruby Murray." (Capitalized Ruby is a given name or programming language.)

Rucking is walking or hiking while carrying a weighted backpack, typically for fitness or military training. The practice originated in military conditioning, where soldiers march with loaded rucks (backpacks). As civilian exercise, rucking offers low-impact cardio with strength benefits: {I've replaced my morning jogs with rucking}. The weighted pack increases calorie burn and builds endurance without the joint stress of running.

A rucksack is a bag carried on the back with shoulder straps—essentially a backpack. The term is more common in British English and among hikers and military personnel: {She packed her rucksack for the trek}. In American English, backpack dominates casual use, while rucksack often suggests rugged or military-style gear.

Rucksacks is the plural of rucksack, a bag carried on the back with shoulder straps. The word is more common in British English, where Americans typically say backpack. Rucksack often suggests hiking or outdoor use: {We loaded our rucksacks and set off up the trail}.

A ruckus is a noisy disturbance or commotion: {The kids were making a ruckus in the backyard}. It suggests loud, disorderly activity rather than serious conflict—more annoyance than danger. {What's all the ruckus about?}

A rudder is a flat piece hinged to the stern of a boat or ship, used for steering. Moving the rudder redirects water flow, turning the vessel. Aircraft have vertical rudders for the same purpose. Figuratively, a rudder is anything that provides guidance or direction: {Without a clear strategy, the company lacked a rudder}.

Rudderless means lacking direction or guidance. A rudder steers a ship; without one, the vessel drifts wherever currents take it. The word almost always appears figuratively: {The company seemed rudderless after the CEO resigned}. A rudderless person or organization has no clear purpose or leadership.

Rudders is the plural of rudder, a flat piece mounted at the back of a boat or aircraft that swivels to steer it. Figuratively, anything that guides direction can be a rudder: {Without clear leadership, the company lacked a rudder}. Someone {without a rudder} drifts aimlessly through life.

Rude describes behavior that violates social expectations of politeness or respect: {Don't be rude to the waiter}. A rude {awakening} is an unpleasant surprise that shatters comfortable assumptions. Rude can also mean primitive or roughly made: {a rude shelter}. In older usage, rude meant unrefined or uncultured—this sense survives mainly in literary contexts.

Rudeness is behavior that shows disregard for others' feelings or social conventions—interrupting, ignoring greetings, speaking harshly. What counts as rude varies by culture and context: {His rudeness to the waiter was embarrassing}. The word can describe a single act or a general quality: {I was shocked by the rudeness of her reply}.

Rue means to feel regret or sorrow over something, typically a past action or decision: {She'll rue the day she crossed me}. The phrase {rue the day} is particularly common, often as a warning or dramatic pronouncement. As a noun, rue is bitter regret: {full of rue}. Separately, rue is also a bitter-tasting shrub with yellow flowers, once used medicinally.

A ruff is a stiff, pleated collar worn in the 16th and 17th centuries, fanning out around the neck like a wheel. The word extends to similar features in nature—the ring of feathers around certain birds' necks, or the frill on a lizard. In card games, to ruff is to play a trump card when you can't follow suit.

A ruffian is a rough, lawless person given to violence or brutality. The word has an old-fashioned, literary quality—you're more likely to encounter ruffians in Victorian novels than on the evening news: {A gang of ruffians accosted him in the alley}. It suggests someone coarse and dangerous but perhaps not organized enough to be a proper criminal.

Ruffians are violent, lawless people—thugs or hooligans who cause trouble through force or intimidation. The word carries an old-fashioned flavor, often appearing in adventure stories or period pieces: {The travelers were set upon by ruffians}. In modern use, it sometimes has a playful edge when describing rough but harmless mischief: {Those little ruffians tracked mud through the house}.

Ruffle describes a disturbance of smoothness. Wind ruffles water or hair; a bird ruffles its feathers. To ruffle someone is to disturb their composure: {The criticism didn't ruffle her}. A ruffle is also a strip of gathered fabric used as trim on clothing or curtains—the gathering creates deliberate irregularity in what would otherwise lie flat.

Ruffled describes something with its smoothness disturbed—feathers, fabric, hair, or water that has been agitated or displaced: {a ruffled collar}, {ruffled feathers on an angry bird}. Applied to people, ruffled means flustered or annoyed: {She seemed ruffled by the unexpected question}. A ruffled garment has decorative gathered fabric along an edge.

Ruffles are strips of fabric gathered or pleated to create a wavy, decorative edge on clothing or furnishings: {a blouse with ruffles at the collar}, {ruffled curtains}. The word extends to anything similarly textured—wind ruffles water, a bird ruffles its feathers. To ruffle someone is to disturb their composure: {His comment ruffled a few feathers}.

Ruffling is disturbing the smoothness of something—feathers, hair, water, fabric. A bird ruffles its feathers when agitated or cold. Wind ruffles the surface of a pond. To ruffle someone is to annoy or unsettle them: {His casual dismissal ruffled her}. Ruffling through papers or pages means flipping quickly: {She was ruffling through the documents looking for the contract}.

A rug is a floor covering, typically smaller than a carpet and not attached to the floor. Rugs add warmth, define spaces, or protect flooring: {an area rug}, {a bathroom rug}. To {pull the rug out from under} someone is to suddenly remove their support or advantage. To {sweep something under the rug} is to conceal it.

Rugburn is skin irritation caused by friction against a rough surface, typically carpet. The abrasion leaves a raw, reddened patch that stings: {I got rugburn on my knees from wrestling with my brother}. The term often carries sexual connotations, suggesting vigorous activity on the floor.

Rugburns are abrasions caused by friction against a rough surface, typically carpet. The skin reddens and may blister from repeated rubbing—commonly during sex, wrestling, or children's roughhousing on the floor: {I've got rugburns on my knees from last night}. Also spelled as two words: rug burns.

Rugby is a contact sport in which two teams advance an oval ball by carrying, passing, and kicking, scoring by touching it down in the opponent's goal area or kicking it through goalposts. Players may tackle ball carriers but cannot pass forward. Two main codes exist: rugby union (fifteen players) and rugby league (thirteen). {He played rugby at university.} (Capitalized Rugby is the English town where the sport originated.)

Rugelach are small crescent-shaped pastries from Jewish baking tradition, made by rolling triangles of cream cheese dough around sweet fillings—typically cinnamon sugar, nuts, jam, or chocolate. The dough is rich and flaky, closer to pie crust than bread. Rugelach appear at holidays and celebrations but are common year-round in Jewish bakeries and delis.

Rugged describes something rough, uneven, and wild—typically terrain or landscapes that are difficult to traverse: {rugged mountains}, {rugged coastline}. When applied to people, especially men, rugged suggests a weathered, strong, outdoorsy appearance that implies toughness and self-reliance. Rugged can also characterize something built to withstand harsh conditions: {rugged equipment designed for extreme environments}. The word carries connotations of durability and resilience rather than refinement or smoothness.

Ruggedness describes the quality of being rough, uneven, or hardy. Terrain with ruggedness features rocks, steep slopes, and irregular surfaces that make travel difficult. When applied to people, ruggedness suggests toughness and the ability to endure harsh conditions: {His ruggedness made him well-suited for wilderness survival}. Products designed for ruggedness can withstand rough handling, extreme temperatures, or demanding environments without breaking down.

A rugrat is a young child, especially a toddler or infant who crawls or plays on the floor. The term is affectionate but informal, often used by parents describing their own kids: {The rugrats are finally asleep}. It suggests the chaos and energy of small children underfoot.

Rugrats is an affectionate or mildly exasperated slang term for young children, especially toddlers—the ones still crawling around on the rug: {I can't make it tonight; I've got to stay home with the rugrats}. The word emphasizes the chaos and ground-level existence of small children. (Capitalized Rugrats is the animated television series.)

Rugs are thick fabric floor coverings, typically smaller than carpets and not wall-to-wall. A rug might cover part of a hardwood floor or define a seating area. Rugs also appear as blankets or wraps: {a lap rug}, {a prayer rug}. In British slang, a rug is a toupee. To {pull the rug out from under} someone is to suddenly withdraw support.

Ruin is destruction or severe damage—the state of being wrecked beyond repair or use. A building falls into ruin; a scandal brings financial ruin. The plural ruins refers to what remains of destroyed structures: {ancient ruins}, {the ruins of the castle}. To ruin something is to destroy or spoil it completely: {The rain ruined the picnic}. A person can be ruined financially, socially, or emotionally. In older usage, a woman's ruin meant loss of virginity or reputation.

Ruined describes something destroyed, spoiled, or reduced to a state beyond repair. A ruined building lies in decay; a ruined reputation cannot recover. The word often carries finality: {The rain ruined the wedding}. In casual speech, ruined can be hyperbolic: {That movie ruined me} means it affected you deeply, not that you're actually destroyed.
clues: Left in a state beyond repair

definition: Ruining is the process of destroying, damaging, or spoiling something beyond recovery. It applies to physical things {(The flood is ruining the carpet)}, abstractions {(You're ruining my reputation)}, and experiences {(Stop ruining the movie for everyone)}. The force can be gradual or sudden, intentional or accidental.

Ruinous describes something that causes or leads to ruin—destruction, collapse, or severe damage. A ruinous {decision} brings disaster. Ruinous {costs} are so high they threaten financial devastation. The word also describes things already in ruins: {a ruinous castle}, {ruinous walls}. {The war proved ruinous to the economy.}

Ruins are the remains of something destroyed or decayed—typically buildings, cities, or structures that have collapsed or fallen into disrepair: {ancient ruins}, {the ruins of a bombed cathedral}. The word extends to any state of destruction or collapse: {His gambling left his finances in ruins}. To be {in ruins} is to be devastated. A single ruin is one such remnant, or the state of being ruined: {The scandal brought about his ruin}.

The ideas that pervade the meanings of the noun and verb rule are standard and authority. As a count noun, a rule is a principle that governs conduct, play, or behavior. As an uncountable noun, rule denotes control by government or some other principle: the rule of Queen Christina. As a verb, rule means to govern or control with authority. When a judge rules, she decides the outcome of a case. When a sovereign rules, he holds responsibility for governing his country.

A rulebook is a book or other document that contains rules, especially rules governing a game or sport. When people talk about the rulebook figuratively, they are referring to rules that govern a particular activity: He threw out the rulebook when he made that decision.

A rulebreaker is someone who violates rules or refuses to follow established conventions. The term can be neutral or admiring—rebels and innovators are often celebrated as rulebreakers: {Every industry needs rulebreakers who challenge the status quo}. It can also be disapproving when applied to those who simply disregard standards others follow.

Ruled describes something governed by authority or marked with lines. A country may be ruled by a king or a constitution. Ruled paper has horizontal lines for writing: {She preferred ruled notebooks for taking notes}. To be ruled by emotion is to be controlled by it. A judge rules on motions; those decisions are rulings.

A ruler is a strip of rigid material marked with units for measuring length, or a straightedge for drawing straight lines. The other ruler is someone who rules—a monarch, dictator, or other person exercising authority over a territory or people: {The ruler of the kingdom demanded tribute}. Both senses share the idea of imposing order.

Rulers are people who govern or control—monarchs, dictators, heads of state: {The rulers of the ancient world wielded absolute power}. A ruler is also a straight-edged measuring instrument, typically marked in inches or centimeters, used for drawing lines and measuring distances: {She used a ruler to underline the heading}.

Rules are established guidelines governing conduct or procedure. Games have rules; so do institutions, religions, and social settings. To rule is to govern or decide authoritatively: {The court ruled in her favor}. A ruler measures straight lines—and also governs. Something that rules is dominant or excellent: {That song rules}. As a {rule}, something happens generally or usually.

A ruling is an authoritative decision, especially one issued by a judge or official body: {The court's ruling struck down the law}, {We're awaiting a ruling from the committee}. As an adjective, ruling describes whoever holds power: the ruling {party}, the ruling {class}. A ruling {passion} is a dominant interest or obsession that governs someone's life.

Rulings are official decisions or judgments issued by authorities—judges, referees, regulatory bodies. A court ruling settles a legal question: {The Supreme Court's ruling struck down the law}. Rulings also come from sports officials, tax agencies, or anyone with power to decide disputes. To ruling as an adjective: the ruling {class}, the ruling {party}.

The noun rum denotes liquor distilled from cane sugar and its products. It stands for alcoholic drinks generally in the expression demon rum. An unrelated adjective rum, mainly British, characterizes things that are strange and slightly suspect: They’re a rum bunch of people.

Rumba is a ballroom dance of Cuban origin characterized by pronounced hip movements and a slow-quick-quick rhythm. The music accompanying it features syncopated beats and percussion. As a verb, to rumba is to perform this dance: {We rumbad until midnight}. Also spelled rhumba.

Rumble is a deep, continuous, rolling sound—thunder rumbling in the distance, a truck rumbling past, a stomach rumbling with hunger. The word captures low-frequency vibration you can almost feel. As a noun, it's that sound itself: {the rumble of the subway}. In dated slang, a rumble is a street fight between gangs. To rumble someone (British) is to discover their secret: {They rumbled our scheme}.

Rumbled is the past tense of rumble, which means to make a deep, rolling sound like thunder or a heavy vehicle: {The truck rumbled past}. Your stomach rumbles when hungry. In British slang, to be rumbled is to be found out or exposed: {We thought we'd gotten away with it, but we were rumbled}.

Rumbles is the third-person singular of rumble and its plural noun. A rumble is a deep, continuous sound like distant thunder or a hungry stomach: {My stomach rumbles when I skip breakfast}. Engines rumble, storms rumble in the distance. To rumble someone (British slang) is to discover their secret or expose their scheme: {The police finally rumbled the gang}. A rumble can also be a street fight between rival groups, now somewhat dated: {The gangs scheduled a rumble for midnight}.

Rumbling describes a low, continuous sound like distant thunder or a heavy truck passing: {We heard the rumbling of the approaching storm}. A rumbling stomach signals hunger. As a noun, rumblings often refers to early signs of discontent or unrest: {There were rumblings of dissatisfaction among the staff}. The word suggests something building or approaching.
clues: Sound of an approaching freight train

definition: Rumblings are low, continuous sounds like distant thunder or a growling stomach. The word commonly appears in figurative use for early signs of discontent or trouble: {There were rumblings of dissent among the staff}. Political rumblings suggest unrest brewing beneath the surface. The singular rumbling works the same way but is less common.

To ruminate is to think deeply about something, turning it over in the mind repeatedly: {She ruminated on what might have been}. The word comes from the literal sense of chewing cud—cattle and other ruminants regurgitate food to chew it again. The figurative sense captures that same quality of returning to something already processed. Rumination can be productive reflection or unproductive dwelling: {He spent weeks ruminating over the rejection}.

Ruminating means chewing over—literally or figuratively. Cows and other ruminants ruminate by rechewing partially digested food brought back up from the stomach. In human contexts, ruminating means turning something over repeatedly in the mind: {She spent the evening ruminating on what went wrong}. The word often carries a negative connotation of unproductive dwelling on problems.

Rumination is the act of turning something over repeatedly—whether food or thought. In digestion, it's the process by which cows and other ruminants regurgitate and rechew their food. In psychology, rumination describes dwelling on the same thoughts obsessively, usually negative ones: {Her rumination about the breakup kept her awake}. The word suggests a slow, circular process that may or may not lead anywhere productive.

Ruminations are prolonged, often repetitive thoughts or reflections. The word carries a sense of turning something over in the mind again and again: {His late-night ruminations kept him awake}. The term comes from the digestive process of cows and other ruminants, who chew, swallow, regurgitate, and rechew their food. Mental rumination can be productive contemplation or unproductive brooding: {She tried to stop her anxious ruminations about the interview}.

Rummage is to search through something by moving contents around, typically in a disorganized way: {She rummaged through the drawer looking for scissors}. The word suggests hurried, messy searching rather than methodical examination. A rummage sale offers secondhand goods, often donated items sold for charity—things someone has cleared out while rummaging through their belongings.

Rummaged is the past tense of rummage, meaning to search through something by moving items around carelessly or unsystematically: {She rummaged through the drawer looking for her keys}. The word suggests digging through clutter or disorganized spaces—boxes, closets, bags—rather than methodical searching.

Rummages is the third-person singular form of rummage, meaning to search through something by moving items around in a disorderly way: {She rummages through the drawer looking for her keys}. The searching is typically hasty and messy, suggesting digging through clutter rather than methodical inspection. As a noun, rummages refers to multiple instances of such searching, or to items collected for a rummage sale—a sale of secondhand goods, often for charity.

Rummaging is searching through something by moving items around, typically in a disorderly way. The word suggests pawing through drawers, bags, or cluttered spaces looking for something specific: {She was rummaging through her purse for her keys}. It implies a hands-on, somewhat messy search rather than a methodical one.

Rummy is a family of card games where players draw and discard to form sets and runs—groups of matching cards or sequences in the same suit. Gin rummy and canasta are popular variants. Separately, rummy is dated slang for a drunkard, from rum: {The old rummy sat at the end of the bar}.

A rumor is unverified information passed from person to person, often about someone's private affairs or about events of public interest. Rumors may turn out true or false—the defining feature is that they circulate before confirmation: {Rumors of layoffs spread through the office}. The verb means to circulate such information, usually passive: {It's rumored that they're getting divorced}. British spelling: rumour.

Rumored describes something reported through unofficial channels but not confirmed: {The company is rumored to be planning layoffs}. What's rumored may or may not be true—the word signals hearsay rather than established fact. {A rumored merger sent the stock price climbing}.

A rumormonger is someone who spreads rumors, especially habitually or maliciously. The word carries clear disapproval—rumormongers traffic in unverified gossip, often stirring up trouble or damaging reputations: {The office rumormonger had everyone convinced layoffs were coming}. Also spelled rumourmonger in British English.

Rumors is the plural of rumor—unverified information passed from person to person. Rumors spread through communities, workplaces, and social media, often gaining or losing details along the way: {Rumors of layoffs circulated through the office}. The word implies uncertainty about truth: {I've heard rumors, but nothing confirmed}.

Rumour is the British spelling of rumor—unverified information passed from person to person: {Rumour has it she's leaving the company}. A rumour may be true, false, or somewhere between. The verb means to spread such information, usually in passive constructions: {He was rumoured to be bankrupt}. Rumours thrive where official information is scarce.

Rumours is the British spelling of rumors—unverified stories or reports passed from person to person: {Rumours of layoffs spread through the office}. Rumours may be true, false, or somewhere between. The word often implies gossip or speculation: {There were rumours about their relationship for months}.

The rump is the hindquarters—the fleshy part of an animal or person where the back meets the legs. In butchery, rump refers to a cut of beef from this area: {rump roast}, {rump steak}. For humans, rump is a slightly humorous or euphemistic term for the buttocks: {She fell flat on her rump}. Figuratively, a rump is what remains of a group after most members have left or been removed: {a rump parliament}, {the rump of the old party}.

To rumple is to wrinkle, crease, or make untidy—typically fabric, hair, or bedding: {She rumpled his hair affectionately}, {rumpled sheets}. A rumpled appearance suggests dishevelment, whether from sleep, exertion, or carelessness. The word works as both verb and noun, though the noun (a wrinkle or crease) is less common.

Rumpled describes something wrinkled, creased, or disheveled from being crushed or disturbed: {a rumpled shirt}, {rumpled bedsheets}. It often suggests a comfortable disarray rather than damage—a rumpled appearance can seem endearing or lived-in: {He showed up looking rumpled after sleeping on the train}. The verb rumple means to make wrinkled or messy.

Rumps is the plural of rump—the hindquarters or buttocks of an animal or person. A butcher sells beef rumps; a rider watches horses' rumps ahead on the trail. Figuratively, a rump is what remains of something diminished: {a rump parliament}, {the rump of the old coalition}. {The dog wagged not just its tail but its whole rump.}

A rumpus is a noisy disturbance or commotion, often playful rather than serious: {The kids were making a rumpus upstairs}. A rumpus room is a space—usually in a basement—designated for recreation and rowdy play, where noise won't disturb the rest of the household.

A rumrunner is someone who smuggles alcohol illegally, especially by boat. The term emerged during Prohibition in the United States (1920–1933), when smugglers transported liquor from ships anchored beyond territorial waters or across borders from Canada and the Caribbean. {Rumrunners made fortunes during the dry years.} The word also applies to the boats themselves.

Rumrunners were people who smuggled alcohol, especially during Prohibition in the United States (1920–1933). They transported liquor by boat, truck, or car to evade federal agents: {Rumrunners brought Canadian whiskey across the Great Lakes}. The term evokes the era of speakeasies and organized crime. Now used historically or for anyone smuggling contraband.

Rumrunning is the smuggling of alcoholic beverages, especially by boat. The term emerged during Prohibition in the United States (1920–1933), when smugglers transported liquor from Canada, the Caribbean, and ships anchored beyond territorial waters. {His grandfather made a fortune rumrunning during Prohibition.} The compound rum-runner refers to both the smuggler and the vessel used.

The core meaning of the verb run, meaning to move very fast on foot, is often lost in more frequent uses of the word. If you run a business, a computer program, or a campaign, you are the controller of it. Something that is running (water, a server, an engine) is operating or moving in a normal and useful way. A run is an instance of running; perhaps on foot (morning run), but also an instance of completing a process (trial run) or the things produced in such an activity (print run). In baseball and cricket, a run is the basis for scoring.

A runabout is a small, lightweight vehicle—typically a boat, car, or aircraft—designed for short trips and general utility rather than specialized tasks. A runabout boat is an open motorboat for casual cruising. The word suggests something nimble and practical: {She keeps a little runabout for errands around town}. As an adjective, it describes casual movement from place to place.

Runabouts are small, versatile vehicles—boats, cars, or aircraft—designed for casual, short-distance travel rather than specialized work. A runabout boat is typically an open motorboat for recreational use on lakes or near shore. The term suggests something nimble and unpretentious: {We took the runabout across the lake}. A person who runs about—a gadabout—is also occasionally called a runabout.

A runaround is evasive or misleading treatment, especially when seeking information or action from someone in authority: {I've been trying to get a straight answer, but they keep giving me the runaround}. The word suggests being shuffled from person to person or excuse to excuse without resolution. Also written as two words: run-around.

A runaway is someone or something that has escaped or fled, especially a child who has left home without permission: {The shelter helps runaways get back on their feet}. As an adjective, runaway describes things out of control—runaway {inflation}, a runaway {train}—or overwhelming victories: a runaway {success}, a runaway {bestseller}. The word emphasizes momentum that can't easily be stopped.

Runaways are people or things that have fled or escaped control. A runaway child has left home without permission; a runaway train has lost its brakes. As an adjective, runaway describes something out of control or overwhelming: {runaway inflation}, {a runaway bestseller}, {a runaway victory}. The word often implies momentum that can't be stopped.

A rundown is a summary or brief overview: {Give me a rundown of what happened at the meeting}. The word also describes something in poor condition from neglect: a rundown {neighborhood}, a rundown {motel}. In baseball, a rundown is when a baserunner gets caught between bases while fielders throw the ball back and forth trying to tag him out.

Rundowns is the plural of rundown, a summary or briefing that covers the main points: {Give me a quick rundown of what happened}. In baseball, a rundown is a situation where a baserunner is trapped between bases while fielders throw the ball back and forth trying to tag them out.

A rune is a letter from ancient alphabets used by Germanic and Scandinavian peoples, carved into stone, wood, or bone. The angular shapes suited carving. Beyond their literal function, runes carried mystical associations—used for divination, magic, and casting spells. This occult sense persists: fantasy games feature runes as symbols of power, and modern pagans use them for fortune-telling. Any mysterious symbol or inscription might be called a rune: {The document was covered in runes I couldn't decipher}.

Runes are the letters of alphabets used by ancient Germanic peoples, including Vikings and Anglo-Saxons. The angular characters were designed for carving into wood or stone. Because runes appear on amulets and in mystical contexts, the word carries associations with magic and divination: {casting runes}, {reading the runes}. In fantasy games and fiction, runes are symbols of magical power: {The sword was inscribed with ancient runes}.

A runestone is a large stone bearing inscriptions in runic alphabets, typically erected by Norse and other Germanic peoples during the Viking Age and earlier. Most commemorate the dead or mark territorial claims. Runestones are found throughout Scandinavia and in areas of Viking settlement: {The runestone near the church dates from the eleventh century}.

Runestones are large stones inscribed with runic alphabets, erected by Norse and Germanic peoples during the Viking Age and earlier. Most commemorate the dead or mark significant events. The term extends to smaller stones or tokens marked with runes for divination: {She cast the runestones to read his fortune}. In fantasy games, runestones often carry magical properties.

A rung is one of the horizontal bars forming the steps of a ladder. By extension, rung describes any level in a hierarchy or progression: {the bottom rung of the corporate ladder}, {climbing the rungs of success}. Separately, rung is the past participle of ring: {The bells have rung}.
