The word usually appears with "good" attached: {A good samaritan stopped to help change her tire}. Laws called Good Samaritan laws protect people who assist others in emergencies from liability. The lowercase form emphasizes the general sense of charitable helper rather than ethnic or religious identity. (Capitalized Samaritan refers to a person from ancient Samaria or a member of the surviving religious community.)

Samba is a Brazilian dance and music genre characterized by syncopated rhythms and lively movement. It emerged from African and Portuguese influences and remains central to Brazilian culture, especially during Carnival: {The streets filled with samba dancers}. The verb means to dance samba: {They sambaed until dawn}.

Sambuca is an Italian anise-flavored liqueur, clear and syrupy-sweet. It's traditionally served with three coffee beans floating on top—representing health, happiness, and prosperity—and sometimes set aflame. {We ordered sambucas after dinner.} The drink is often taken as a digestif or added to espresso.

Same, mainly an adjective, is an extreme version of like: its core meaning is like in every way. It is often followed by a prepositional phrase with as. Same always references at least two things and implicitly involves the ideas of comparison and equality.

Sameness is the quality of being identical or unchanging. Two things that share sameness are alike in relevant ways: {the sameness of their views on politics}. When applied to experience over time, sameness often carries a negative sense of tedious uniformity: {the numbing sameness of suburban strip malls}, {She couldn't bear the sameness of her daily routine}.

Samey describes things that are boringly similar or repetitive, lacking variety or distinctiveness. British informal. The word suggests monotony through resemblance: {The songs on the album all sound a bit samey}. {After a while, the beach towns started to feel samey}.

A samosa is a fried or baked pastry with a savory filling, typically triangular and made with a thin, crispy shell. The filling is usually spiced potatoes and peas, though meat versions are common. Samosas originated in South Asia and the Middle East and are now popular street food and appetizers worldwide: {We ordered samosas to start}.

Samosas are fried or baked pastries with savory fillings, triangular in shape and originating in South Asian cuisine. The crisp outer shell typically contains spiced potatoes, peas, onions, or ground meat. They're served as snacks or appetizers, often with chutneys for dipping: {We ordered samosas while we waited for the main course}.

A samovar is a metal urn, traditionally Russian, used for heating water for tea. It typically has a central chimney for burning charcoal and a spigot for dispensing hot water. The samovar occupies a central place in Russian hospitality and tea culture: {The samovar was always ready for guests}.

A sample is a small portion taken from something larger—enough to show what the whole is like. You might taste a sample of cheese, analyze a blood sample, or survey a sample of voters. In music, to sample is to extract a snippet from an existing recording for use in a new track. As an adjective, sample indicates something representative: {a sample size of 500}, {sample questions from the exam}.

Sampled is the past tense of sample—to take a small portion of something larger to evaluate, test, or experience: {We sampled the wine before ordering a bottle}. In music production, sampled means incorporating a portion of an existing recording into a new track: {The beat sampled a classic funk record}. In statistics, sampled populations have been selected for study.

A sampler is a representative selection or collection of items: {a sampler of local cheeses}, {a sampler platter}. In needlework, a sampler is a piece of cloth embroidered with various stitches, letters, and decorative motifs—traditionally made by young women to demonstrate skill. In music production, a sampler is an electronic instrument that records and plays back snippets of sound, allowing musicians to incorporate and manipulate audio fragments: {He built the beat using a sampler and vintage funk records}.

Samplers are collections that offer a taste of variety—an assortment of chocolates, a compilation of songs, or a selection of craft beers. In music production, a sampler is an electronic instrument that records and plays back audio clips, allowing producers to incorporate fragments of existing recordings. Historically, a sampler was a piece of embroidery demonstrating various stitches, often made by young girls learning needlework: {Her grandmother's sampler hung framed in the hallway}.

Samples are small portions taken from a larger whole to represent or test it: a blood sample, a fabric sample, a free sample at the grocery store. In music, a sample is a snippet of recorded sound repurposed in a new composition: {The track samples an old soul record}. To sample is to take or try such a portion: {We sampled the local cuisine}. In statistics, a sample is a subset of a population used to draw conclusions about the whole.

Sampling is taking a small portion to represent a larger whole. In research, you sample a population to draw conclusions without surveying everyone. In music production, sampling means extracting a snippet from an existing recording to incorporate into a new track: {The song samples a 1970s funk bassline}. A sampling of something is a representative selection: {Here's a sampling of what we'll cover today}.

Samsara is the cycle of death and rebirth in Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions—the continuous wheel of existence through which souls pass until they achieve liberation. The concept implies that life is an endless repetition of suffering unless one breaks free through enlightenment or spiritual practice: {trapped in samsara}, {escape from samsara}. In broader usage, samsara can describe any feeling of being caught in repetitive, unsatisfying patterns: {the samsara of office politics}. (Capitalized Samsara may refer to the 1992 documentary film or various artistic works.)

A samurai was a member of the warrior class in feudal Japan, serving a lord and following a strict code of honor called bushido. The word now evokes disciplined martial skill and loyalty: {He approached his work with samurai focus}. In modern usage, samurai often modifies nouns to suggest Japanese warrior tradition: {samurai sword}, {samurai armor}. The plural is also samurai.

A sanatorium is a facility for treating chronic illness, especially tuberculosis. Before antibiotics, patients with TB were sent to sanatoriums—often in mountainous or dry climates—for rest, fresh air, and medical supervision. The word now applies more broadly to any residential treatment center for long-term recovery: {a sanatorium for nervous exhaustion}. Also spelled sanitarium.

Sanatoriums is the plural of sanatorium, a medical facility for long-term illness, especially tuberculosis in the era before antibiotics. Patients were sent to sanatoriums for rest, fresh air, and supervised care—often in remote or mountainous locations thought beneficial for lung disease. The word now evokes a dated, institutional quality: {The old sanatorium on the hill has been converted to condos}.

Sanctified means made holy or set apart as sacred. In religious contexts, something sanctified has been consecrated for divine purposes: {sanctified ground}, {a sanctified marriage}. The word extends to anything treated with special reverence or given moral authority: {sanctified traditions}, {sanctified by time and custom}. Someone described as sanctified may be genuinely devout or affectedly pious.

Sanctify means to make holy or sacred. A priest sanctifies the bread and wine; marriage sanctifies a union. More broadly, to sanctify something is to give it legitimacy or approval: {Time has sanctified the tradition}. The adjective sanctified describes what has been made holy, and by extension, excessively pious or self-righteous.

Sanctimonious describes someone who makes a show of being morally superior, especially while judging others. The word carries strong negative connotations—a sanctimonious person isn't genuinely devout or ethical but merely performs righteousness: {His sanctimonious lecturing about family values rang hollow after the affair came to light}. The tone is always hypocritical or self-satisfied.

Sanctimoniousness is the quality of making a show of moral superiority while lacking genuine virtue. The sanctimonious person broadcasts righteousness, lectures others, and positions themselves as ethically above reproach—often hypocritically. {His sanctimoniousness about diet vanished when no one was watching}. The word implies that the piety is performed rather than sincere.

Sanctimony is a show of righteousness or moral superiority, especially when hypocritical or excessive. The sanctimonious person makes a display of virtue while judging others: {I couldn't stand his sanctimony about my smoking while he drank himself to sleep every night}. The word nearly always carries disapproval—genuine piety isn't called sanctimony.

Sanction carries opposite meanings that context must resolve. To sanction something is to authorize or approve it: {The board sanctioned the merger}. But sanctions (usually plural) are penalties imposed to punish or coerce: {economic sanctions against the regime}. The shared thread is official action—approval grants permission, punishment enforces compliance. A sanctioned event has backing; a sanctioned country faces restrictions.

Sanctioned carries opposite meanings depending on context. To sanction something is to officially approve or authorize it: {The board sanctioned the new policy}. But sanctions (usually plural) are penalties imposed to punish or coerce, especially in international relations: {economic sanctions against the regime}. A sanctioned country or individual is one facing such penalties. The ambiguity rarely causes confusion—context makes clear whether approval or punishment is meant.

Sanctioning carries two opposing meanings. It can mean giving official approval or permission: {The committee sanctioned the new policy}. But it also means imposing penalties, especially economic or diplomatic ones: {The UN sanctioned the regime for human rights violations}. Context usually makes clear which is meant—approving something desirable or punishing something objectionable.

Sanctions can punish or permit. The punitive sense dominates modern usage: economic or political penalties imposed on a nation to pressure behavior change {The UN imposed sanctions on the regime}. But to sanction something is also to authorize or approve it {The committee sanctioned the new policy}. Context usually clarifies which meaning applies—governments impose sanctions but sanction actions.

Sanctity is the quality of being sacred, holy, or inviolable. Religious contexts speak of the sanctity of {life}, {marriage}, or {the Sabbath}. The word extends to anything treated as deserving ultimate respect or protection: the sanctity of {contracts}, the sanctity of {the home}. To violate something's sanctity is to desecrate or profane it.

Sanctuaries are places of refuge or protection. The word originally meant holy places—the inner chamber of a temple, a church where fugitives could claim asylum. Now it extends to any safe haven: {wildlife sanctuaries}, {bird sanctuaries}, {The library was her sanctuary from the chaos at home}. A sanctuary offers shelter from threat or intrusion.

The sanctuary in a church is the room where worship takes place. This idea of a sacred, quiet, and safe place extends to other meanings. A wildlife sanctuary is a protected home for wild animals. A sanctuary city in the U.S. is one that offers undocumented residents protection from federal immigration authorities. When you give someone sanctuary, you offer them protection from some threat. Where no specific place is involved, sanctuary is the state or condition of being protected from harm.
clues: Protected ground for wildlife or worship

definition: A sanctum is a private space where one is free from intrusion—a personal retreat or inner chamber. The word carries connotations of sacredness, from its origins in temple architecture where the innermost room housed what was most holy. {His study was his sanctum, and no one entered without permission.} An {inner sanctum} is the most private area within an already private space, often where decisions are made by a select few.

Sand is tiny loose grains of rock, typically found on beaches and in deserts. It forms when stone weathers over time. Sand varies in color and texture—from fine white Caribbean sand to coarse volcanic black. To sand is to smooth a surface with sandpaper or a similar abrasive. To {sand down} the rough edges. In the plural, sands often means a beach or desert expanse: {the sands of time}, {the Arabian sands}.

A sandal is an open shoe consisting of a sole held to the foot by straps, leaving much of the foot exposed. Sandals range from simple thong designs to elaborate gladiator styles with multiple straps. They're associated with warm weather, casual wear, and ancient civilizations: {She kicked off her sandals at the beach}. With socks, sandals are a notorious fashion faux pas—or deliberate dad style.

Sandals are open shoes held to the foot by straps, leaving much of the foot exposed. They range from simple flat soles with minimal strapping to elaborate designs with heels and decorative elements. Sandals are ancient footwear, suited to warm climates: {She kicked off her sandals at the beach}. {Sandals with socks} is a fashion choice that draws strong opinions.

Sandalwood is a fragrant wood from trees of the genus *Santalum*, prized for its rich, warm scent. The wood and its extracted oil are used in perfumes, incense, and traditional medicine. Indian sandalwood is considered the finest variety. {The room smelled of sandalwood and jasmine.}

A sandbag is a bag filled with sand, used to build barriers against flooding or as fortification. Sandbags also serve as ballast or improvised weights. To sandbag someone is to hit them with a sandbag, or figuratively, to coerce or bully. In games and competition, sandbagging means deliberately underperforming to gain advantage later—hiding your strength to sandbag opponents who underestimate you.

Sandbagged describes being weighed down or protected by sandbags, as in flood control. More often, it means being treated unfairly or caught off guard: {We got sandbagged by hidden fees}. In games and sports, to sandbag is to deliberately underperform to gain advantage later—hiding your true skill to hustle opponents or secure easier matchups: {He sandbagged his way into the amateur bracket}.

A sandbagger deliberately underperforms or conceals ability to gain advantage later—in golf, hiding skill to inflate a handicap; in poker, slow-playing a strong hand; in business, lowballing projections to exceed them later. The term evokes someone weighed down by sandbags, holding back. {He's such a sandbagger—claims he can't play, then runs the table.}

Sandbaggers are people who deliberately underperform or conceal their abilities to gain an advantage later—common in golf, poker, and other competitions where handicaps or expectations matter. Someone who {sandbagged} their way to a lower handicap, then played their true game in a tournament, is a sandbagger. The term extends to anyone strategically downplaying their skills: {The sandbaggers in our fantasy league always draft last}.

Sandbagging is deliberately underperforming or concealing strength to gain an advantage later. In poker, it means checking with a strong hand to lure opponents into betting. In business or sports, someone sandbags by lowering expectations so they can exceed them: {He's sandbagging—he'll crush those sales targets}. The term evokes weighted bags slowing someone down on purpose.

Sandbags are bags filled with sand, used primarily to build temporary barriers against flooding or as fortification in military contexts. Stacked together, they form walls that redirect water or stop bullets. The verb sandbag means to reinforce with sandbags, but it has extended meanings: to coerce or bully someone, or to deliberately underperform to gain advantage later. {He sandbagged in the early rounds, then crushed his opponents in the finals.}

Sandbanks are ridges or mounds of sand formed by water currents or waves, typically found in rivers, estuaries, or shallow coastal waters. They can shift with changing conditions and pose hazards to navigation: {The boat ran aground on a sandbank}. At low tide, sandbanks may become exposed, creating temporary islands.

A sandbar is a ridge of sand built up by currents in a river, lake, or ocean. Sandbars form in shallow water and may be exposed at low tide or remain just beneath the surface—a hazard to boats. Swimmers sometimes wade out to stand on sandbars: {We walked out to the sandbar at low tide}.

Sandbars are ridges of sand formed by currents in rivers, lakes, or coastal waters. They often lie just below the surface, creating hazards for boats and swimmers. At low tide, sandbars may become exposed, forming temporary islands. {The boat ran aground on a sandbar}.

Sandblast means to clean, etch, or smooth a surface by propelling fine particles at high pressure. The abrasive—originally sand, now often other materials—strips away paint, rust, or grime from metal, stone, or glass. The technique also creates frosted or textured finishes: {sandblasted glass panels}. As a noun, a sandblast is the stream of particles or the equipment that produces it.

Sandblasted describes a surface that has been abraded by a high-pressure stream of sand or similar grit. The process strips away paint, rust, or grime, leaving a clean, often matte finish: {The sandblasted brick looked brand new}. Glass can be sandblasted to create a frosted, translucent effect. Figuratively, something sandblasted has been scoured or worn down: {Her face looked sandblasted by years in the desert sun}.

Sandblasting is a process of cleaning, smoothing, or etching a surface by propelling fine particles at high velocity, typically using compressed air. Despite the name, the abrasive material may be sand, glass beads, walnut shells, or other substances. The technique removes rust, paint, and corrosion from metal, or creates frosted effects on glass: {The crew sandblasted the old bridge before repainting}.

A sandbox is a shallow container filled with sand for children to play in. In computing, a sandbox is an isolated environment where programs run without affecting the larger system—safe for testing untrusted code. The verb means to isolate something in such an environment: {We sandboxed the suspicious file before opening it}. Sandbox also appears as an adjective describing open-ended games or modes without fixed objectives: {sandbox gameplay}.

Sandboxes are enclosed areas filled with sand for children to play in, or in computing, isolated environments where code can run without affecting the broader system. The computing sense captures the same idea—a contained space for safe experimentation: {Test the new feature in the sandbox before deploying}. To sandbox something is to isolate it this way.

A sandcastle is a structure built on a beach by piling and shaping wet sand, typically made by children as play. The word often appears figuratively for something fragile or impermanent: {Their business plan was a sandcastle waiting for the tide}. To build sandcastles {in the air} is to indulge in unrealistic fantasies.

Sandcastles is the plural of sandcastle—a structure built from wet sand, typically on a beach. Children pile and shape damp sand into towers, walls, and moats, knowing the tide will wash it away. The impermanence makes sandcastle a metaphor for fragile or temporary achievements: {All our careful planning turned out to be sandcastles}.

A sander is a power tool that smooths surfaces by abrasion, typically wood. Sanders come in various types—belt sanders for heavy material removal, orbital sanders for finishing work, palm sanders for detail. The tool vibrates or rotates sandpaper against the surface: {I used a sander to strip the old finish off the deck}.

Sanding is the act of smoothing or abrading a surface with sandpaper or a similar material. The term applies to woodworking, auto body repair, drywall finishing, and other contexts where surfaces need smoothing or preparation: {The sanding took longer than the painting itself}. Light sanding between coats helps paint adhere.

A sandlot is a vacant lot or open piece of ground, often sandy or unpaved, where children gather to play informal games. The term is most associated with pickup baseball games played without adult supervision or official rules, evoking a nostalgic image of American childhood before organized youth sports. {We played sandlot baseball every summer until dark.} As an adjective, sandlot describes this informal, amateur style of play: {sandlot football}.

Sandlots are vacant lots or open patches of ground, typically in urban areas, where children play informal games—especially baseball. The term evokes American neighborhood life before organized youth sports, when kids gathered on whatever dusty or weedy ground was available: {He learned to pitch on the sandlots of Brooklyn}. As an adjective, sandlot describes amateur or improvised play: {sandlot baseball}, {sandlot football}.

The sandman is a mythical figure who brings sleep by sprinkling magical sand in children's eyes. Parents invoke him at bedtime: {The sandman is coming, time for bed}. The "sand" explains the gritty residue sometimes found in the corners of eyes upon waking. The figure appears in folklore, lullabies, and popular culture as a gentle bringer of dreams. (Capitalized Sandman may refer to specific fictional characters.)

Sandpainting is the art of creating images by pouring colored sand onto a surface. Among Navajo and other Indigenous peoples of the American Southwest, sandpaintings are ceremonial works made on the ground, often destroyed after use in healing rituals. The technique also appears in secular art, where designs may be fixed with adhesive: {The artist demonstrated sandpainting at the craft fair}.

Sandpaper is paper or cloth coated with abrasive particles, used for smoothing surfaces or removing material. It comes in grades from coarse to fine, measured by grit number—higher numbers mean finer abrasive. To sandpaper something is to rub it with sandpaper: {I sandpapered the table before staining it}. Figuratively, a sandpaper voice or personality is rough and abrasive.

Sandpipers are small to medium-sized shorebirds with long bills and legs, typically seen probing sand and mud for invertebrates along beaches, mudflats, and wetlands. The name covers dozens of species in the family Scolopacidae, many of which migrate vast distances. Their quick, teetering movements along the water's edge make them easy to spot: {A sandpiper darted across the wet sand}.

Sandpipers are small to medium-sized shorebirds with long bills and legs, typically seen probing wet sand or mud for invertebrates. They're known for their quick, teetering movements along beaches and tidal flats. The family includes numerous species—some called sandpipers specifically, others known as godwits, curlews, or snipes. {A flock of sandpipers scattered as the wave rolled in.}

A sandpit is a shallow excavation or container filled with sand, typically for children to play in. The British term corresponds to American *sandbox*. Sandpit also refers to a quarry where sand is extracted: {The old sandpit had filled with rainwater over the years}.

Sands is the plural of sand, referring to expanses of sandy terrain—beaches, deserts, or dunes: {the white sands of the Caribbean}, {the shifting sands of the Sahara}. Figuratively, {the sands of time} evokes an hourglass, suggesting time passing or running out: {The sands are running low}.

Sandstone is a sedite rock formed from compressed sand grains, typically quartz, ceite together over millions of years. It ranges from soft and crumbly to quite hard, appearing in colors from white to red to brown depending on mineral content. Sandstone is widely used in construction and paving: {The old courthouse was built of local sandstone}. Many famous geological formations—canyon walls, natural arches, desert mesas—are carved from sandstone.

A sandstorm is a strong wind that lifts and carries sand or dust across open terrain, reducing visibility to near zero. Common in deserts and arid regions, sandstorms can last minutes or days: {We waited out the sandstorm in the tent}. Also called a dust storm, though sandstorms typically involve coarser particles.

Sandstorms are violent windstorms that lift and carry large quantities of sand and dust, reducing visibility and making travel dangerous. Common in deserts and arid regions, they can darken skies for hours: {The sandstorm forced us to shelter in place}. Metaphorically, any overwhelming onslaught: {a sandstorm of criticism}.

A sandtrap is a hazard on a golf course—a depression filled with sand, strategically placed near greens or fairways to penalize errant shots. Also called a bunker. The term extends figuratively to any situation that's easy to fall into but difficult to escape: {The project became a sandtrap for our budget}.

Sandtraps are hazards on a golf course—shallow pits filled with sand, strategically placed near greens or along fairways to penalize errant shots. Getting out of a sandtrap requires a specialized shot. Also called bunkers. The term extends figuratively to any situation that's easy to fall into but difficult to escape: {The contract was full of legal sandtraps}.

A sandwich is food between two pieces of bread—meat, cheese, vegetables, or combinations thereof. The format extends to variations: {open-faced sandwich}, {ice cream sandwich}. To sandwich something is to insert it between two other things: {The meeting was sandwiched between two calls}. As an adjective, sandwich describes layered structures: {sandwich panel}, {sandwich construction}. (Capitalized Sandwich refers to the English town or the Earl whose gambling habits supposedly inspired the food.)

Sandwiched means positioned or squeezed between two other things. The image comes from the filling pressed between slices of bread. A person can be sandwiched between two others on a crowded bench, or a meeting can be sandwiched between appointments: {I sandwiched a quick lunch between calls}. The word often suggests being uncomfortably compressed or fitted into limited space.

Sandwiches is the plural of sandwich—food consisting of a filling between slices of bread or in a split roll: {We packed sandwiches for the picnic}. To sandwich something is to squeeze it between two other things: {The meeting was sandwiched between two phone calls}. {She sandwiches her workouts into her lunch break}.

Sandwiching is placing something between two other things, like filling between slices of bread. The term applies physically—{sandwiching insulation between layers of drywall}—and figuratively to scheduling or positioning: {She sandwiched a quick lunch between meetings}. In communication, sandwiching criticism between compliments is a common feedback technique.

A sandworm is any of various worms that burrow in sand or sandy soil, including marine polychaetes used as fishing bait. The term gained wider currency through Frank Herbert's *Dune*, where sandworms are colossal creatures inhabiting desert planets, producing the valuable spice melange. {We dug for sandworms at low tide.}

Sandworms are burrowing marine worms found in sandy coastal sediments, commonly used as fishing bait. The term also refers to the colossal fictional creatures in Frank Herbert's *Dune* series—massive desert-dwelling worms that produce the valuable spice melange and can be ridden by the Fremen people. The *Dune* sandworms have become iconic in science fiction: {The sandworm rose from the desert floor}.

Sandy describes things containing, covered with, or resembling sand. A sandy beach is covered in sand; sandy soil contains a lot of it. Sandy hair is a yellowish-brown color, like light sand. A sandy texture feels gritty. {The path grew sandy as we approached the dunes.} {She had sandy hair and freckles.} (Capitalized Sandy is a given name.)

Sane describes a mind in proper working order—rational, sound, able to perceive reality accurately. The word often appears in legal contexts: a defendant found sane can stand trial. More loosely, sane means reasonable or sensible: {That's the only sane approach to the problem}. To {stay sane} is to maintain composure under stress. {No sane person would accept those terms.}

Sang is the past tense of sing. Someone sang a song, a choir sang hymns, birds sang at dawn. The word appears in expressions like {She sang his praises} (spoke highly of him) and {He sang like a canary} (informed to authorities). The alternative past tense sung is less common in standard usage.

Sangria is a Spanish punch made from red wine, chopped fruit, sweetener, and often brandy or other spirits. The fruit—typically oranges, lemons, and apples—steeps in the wine, which is served chilled over ice. White wine versions exist but are less traditional. {We ordered a pitcher of sangria for the table.}

Sanguine is a somewhat literary adjective with a meaning typically overlaps hopeful and optimistic: He is sanguine about being able to avoid litigation. The report expresses sanguine views about the economy. In a different meaning, sanguine suggests a pinkish or reddish color, as in a sanguine complexion.

A sanitarium is a facility for treating chronic illness, especially tuberculosis or mental disorders. The word evokes an earlier era when patients were sent to remote locations for rest cures, fresh air, and isolation: {The doctor recommended six months at a sanitarium in the mountains}. Also spelled sanatorium, with the same meaning.

Sanitariums is the plural of sanitarium, a facility for treating chronic illness or promoting recovery, particularly associated with tuberculosis treatment in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Patients were sent to sanitariums for rest, fresh air, and supervised care: {The mountain sanitariums filled with consumptives seeking a cure}. The word is now largely historical, though it sometimes appears for rehabilitation facilities. Also spelled sanatoriums.

Sanitary means clean and hygienic, especially in ways that protect health by preventing disease or contamination: {sanitary conditions}, {sanitary facilities}. A sanitary {napkin} is an absorbent pad worn during menstruation. Sanitary concerns involve waste disposal, water treatment, and food handling. The word sometimes carries a sterile or clinical connotation: {The hospital room was almost too sanitary}.

Sanitation is the systems and practices that protect public health—sewage disposal, water treatment, garbage collection, and general cleanliness. Poor sanitation spreads disease; modern sanitation dramatically reduced cholera, typhoid, and other waterborne illnesses. The word often appears in official contexts: {sanitation department}, {sanitation workers}. Broader uses cover any effort to maintain hygienic conditions: {food sanitation standards}.

Sanitise is the British spelling of sanitize. To sanitise is to make something clean and hygienic, free from dirt or germs: {sanitise your hands before eating}. Figuratively, to sanitise is to remove objectionable or sensitive content: {The report was sanitised before release}. This second sense often implies making something palatable at the cost of accuracy or honesty.

Sanitised is the British spelling of sanitized, the past tense and participle of sanitize. To sanitise something is to clean it thoroughly, making it hygienic and free from germs or contamination. More commonly, sanitised describes information or content that has been altered to remove anything offensive, controversial, or unpleasant: {The official report was a sanitised version of what actually happened}. A sanitised account often feels incomplete or dishonest because the messy truths have been scrubbed away.

Sanitiser is the British spelling of sanitizer—a substance or product that reduces or eliminates germs on surfaces or skin. Hand sanitisers, typically alcohol-based gels, became ubiquitous during the COVID-19 pandemic: {There's sanitiser by the door}. The term extends to cleaning products for surfaces in kitchens, bathrooms, and public spaces.

To sanitize is to make something clean or free of contamination—disinfecting a surface, sterilizing equipment, or purifying water. The word extends to removing objectionable content: sanitizing a document strips sensitive information, sanitizing a story removes offensive elements. This figurative sense often carries negative connotations, suggesting that important truths have been scrubbed away to make something more palatable: {a sanitized version of history}.

Sanitized means cleaned of germs or contaminants, or more commonly, stripped of anything offensive, controversial, or unpleasant. A sanitized version of history omits the ugly parts: {The documentary presented a sanitized account of colonialism}. Sanitized language avoids profanity or harsh truths. The word often carries a critical edge—suggesting something has been made too clean, losing authenticity or important detail in the process.

Sanitizer is a substance that reduces or eliminates germs on surfaces or skin. Hand sanitizer, typically alcohol-based gel or liquid, became ubiquitous during the COVID-19 pandemic: {There's sanitizer by the door}. Surface sanitizers disinfect countertops, equipment, or other objects. Figuratively, sanitizer suggests something that cleans up or makes acceptable: {The PR team acted as sanitizers for the scandal}.

Sanitizers are substances or devices that reduce contamination, particularly germs on surfaces or hands. Hand sanitizers—alcohol-based gels or liquids—became ubiquitous during the COVID-19 pandemic: {There's sanitizer by the door}. The term extends figuratively to anything that cleans up or makes palatable: {social media sanitizers that filter offensive content}.

Sanitizing is cleaning something to remove germs or contaminants, or making something acceptable by removing objectionable elements. You sanitize {kitchen surfaces} to kill bacteria. A sanitized {version} of events omits uncomfortable truths: {The documentary sanitized the dictator's brutal reign}. The second sense often implies dishonest tidying-up—making something presentable at the cost of accuracy.

Sanity is soundness of mind—the state of being mentally healthy and able to think rationally. Legal contexts use it narrowly: a defendant's sanity determines whether they understood their actions. More loosely, sanity means reasonableness or good judgment: {Working from home has helped me keep my sanity}. To {question someone's sanity} is to suggest they're acting irrationally.

Sank is the past tense of sink. Something that sank went down—a ship beneath the waves, a stone through water, a person into a chair. The word captures the completed downward motion: {The Titanic sank in 1912}. {My heart sank when I heard the news}. {He sank the eight ball to win}.

Sap is the fluid that circulates through plants, carrying water and nutrients—maple sap becomes syrup. By extension, sap refers to vitality or energy: {The heat sapped my strength}. To sap is to gradually drain or undermine: {Constant criticism sapped her confidence}. A sap is also a fool or dupe, someone easily taken advantage of: {Don't be a sap}. Separately, a sap is a small leather-covered club filled with lead, used to strike someone, and to sap means to hit with one. (All-caps SAP is the software company.)

A sapling is a young tree, typically slender and flexible, past the seedling stage but not yet mature. The word extends to young people, especially lanky adolescents: {The boy had grown into a tall sapling of fifteen}. The term suggests something still developing, not yet fully formed or hardened.

Saplings are young trees, slender and flexible, not yet grown to full size. The word often suggests vulnerability or potential: {The saplings bent in the wind but didn't break}. Figuratively, sapling can describe a young person, especially a tall, thin one.

A sapper is a military engineer who builds fortifications, lays or clears mines, and handles demolitions. The term comes from digging saps—trenches used to approach enemy positions. Sappers do the dangerous groundwork of combat engineering: {The sappers cleared a path through the minefield}. In British Commonwealth forces, sapper is also the lowest enlisted rank in engineer units.

Sappers are military engineers who specialize in fortification, demolition, and obstacle clearing. The term comes from digging saps—trenches that approach enemy positions. Modern sappers build bridges, clear minefields, and breach defenses: {Sappers moved ahead of the infantry to neutralize booby traps}. In some armies, all combat engineers are called sappers regardless of specific duty.

Sapphic means relating to romantic or sexual attraction between women. The term derives from Sappho, the ancient Greek poet of Lesbos who wrote love poetry addressed to women. Sapphic serves as a broader umbrella than lesbian, sometimes including bisexual women or anyone who experiences woman-loving attraction: {sapphic poetry}, {sapphic romance novels}, {the sapphic community}. In poetry, sapphic also refers to a specific classical meter Sappho used. (Capitalized Sapphic may appear in formal or classical contexts.)

Sapphire is a precious gemstone, typically deep blue, prized in jewelry for its brilliance and hardness—second only to diamond. Sapphires can occur in other colors (pink, yellow, white), but blue dominates the word's associations: {sapphire eyes}, {sapphire waters}. A sapphire anniversary marks 45 or 65 years of marriage, depending on tradition.

Sapphires is the plural of sapphire, a precious gemstone typically deep blue in color. Sapphires are a variety of corundum, the same mineral as rubies but in different hues—sapphires can also be pink, yellow, or colorless. {The ring was set with diamonds and sapphires.} The blue of sapphires serves as a color reference: {sapphire waters}, {sapphire skies}.

Sappiness is excessive sentimentality—emotion that feels overdone or unearned. A movie's sappiness might involve tearful reunions and swelling music; a greeting card's sappiness lies in its cloying verse. The word carries gentle mockery: {I know it's pure sappiness, but I cried anyway}. From sap in its sense of sticky tree fluid, suggesting something cloyingly sweet.

Sapping is the act of gradually draining strength, energy, or resources. Heat saps your energy; prolonged conflict saps morale; endless meetings sap productivity. {The humid weather was sapping everyone's will to work.} In military contexts, sapping refers to digging trenches or tunnels to undermine fortifications—the origin of the figurative sense of slow, steady weakening.

Sappy describes something excessively sentimental or emotional in a way that feels cloying or unearned: {a sappy love song}, {The movie got too sappy at the end}. The word suggests sweetness without substance—tears or feelings that come too easily. Literally, sappy means full of sap, the fluid in plants, which is where the figurative sense originates: sticky-sweet like tree sap.
clues: So sweet it makes you cringe

definition: Saps is the plural of sap in its various senses. Sap is the fluid that circulates through plants, carrying nutrients. By extension, a sap is a foolish or gullible person—someone whose vitality seems drained: {Those saps fell for the scam}. A sap is also a small leather-covered club filled with lead, used to strike someone. To sap is to gradually weaken or drain: {The heat sapped our energy}.

Sarcasm is saying the opposite of what you mean to mock or convey contempt: {Oh, great job} when someone has blundered, {Thanks for the help} when none was given. The tone signals that the literal meaning should be inverted. Sarcasm differs from irony in its hostile edge—it's meant to sting.

Sarcastic describes speech or manner that uses irony to mock or convey contempt—saying the opposite of what you mean to highlight someone's foolishness or failure: {Oh, great job} when someone spills coffee everywhere. A sarcastic person deploys this tone habitually. The delivery often involves exaggerated intonation that signals the words shouldn't be taken at face value.

Sarcophagi is the plural of sarcophagus, a stone coffin typically adorned with sculpture or inscription. The word comes from Greek roots meaning "flesh-eating"—ancient limestone coffins were believed to decompose bodies rapidly. Sarcophagi are associated with ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome, often displayed in museums: {The museum's collection includes several Roman sarcophagi}.

A sarcophagus is a stone coffin, typically decorated with sculpture or inscriptions. The word evokes ancient burial practices—Egyptian, Greek, Roman—where the elaborate container both preserved and honored the dead: {The museum's Egyptian wing displays a carved granite sarcophagus}. Plural: sarcophagi or sarcophaguses.

A sardine is a small, oily fish typically sold canned in oil or sauce. Several species of small herring and related fish are marketed as sardines. The word appears most often in {packed like sardines}—crammed tightly together, as the fish appear in their tins: {We were packed like sardines on the subway}.

Sardines are small, oily fish typically sold canned in oil or sauce. They're eaten whole, bones and all. The word also names a children's game where one person hides and others join them in the hiding spot until everyone is crammed together—{packed in like sardines}. That phrase describes any crowded space: {We were sardines on that subway car}.

Sardonic describes a grimly mocking or cynical manner—humor with a bitter edge. A sardonic smile or remark conveys scorn or skepticism rather than warmth: {He gave a sardonic laugh at the proposal}. Where sarcastic suggests intent to wound, sardonic implies weary detachment, as if the speaker finds the world's absurdities unsurprising.

A saree is a traditional South Asian garment worn by women, consisting of a single length of fabric—typically five to nine yards—draped around the body, with one end wrapped as a skirt and the other drawn over the shoulder or head. Also spelled sari. {She wore her grandmother's silk saree to the wedding.}

Sarees are the traditional draped garment worn by women across South Asia, particularly India. A saree is a single length of fabric—typically five to nine yards—wrapped around the body with one end tucked into a petticoat and the other draped over the shoulder. The plural appears in contexts like shopping or discussing collections: {She inherited her mother's sarees}. Also spelled saris.

Sarge is an informal term of address for a sergeant, used in military and police contexts: {Hey, sarge, what's the plan?} The clipped form signals familiarity or casual respect. It appears both in direct address and as a nickname.

A sari is a garment worn by women in South Asia, consisting of a long piece of cloth wrapped around the body, typically draped over one shoulder. The fabric may be plain cotton or elaborately embroidered silk. {She wore her grandmother's wedding sari.}

Sarin is a highly toxic nerve agent developed as a chemical weapon. Exposure causes convulsions, paralysis, and death by disrupting the nervous system. Colorless and odorless, it can be inhaled or absorbed through skin. Sarin has been used in terrorist attacks and warfare despite international bans: {The Tokyo subway attack used sarin gas}.

Saris is the plural of sari, a garment worn by South Asian women consisting of a long piece of fabric wrapped around the body, typically with one end draped over the shoulder. The fabric, often silk or cotton, may be elaborately decorated: {The wedding guests wore saris in brilliant colors}.

A sarong is a length of fabric wrapped around the body and tucked or tied at the waist, worn as a skirt or dress. Traditional in Southeast Asia and the Pacific islands, sarongs appear in Western contexts mainly as beach or resort wear: {She threw a sarong over her swimsuit}.

Sarsaparilla is a plant whose root was traditionally used to flavor beverages, and by extension, a sweet carbonated drink flavored with it or something similar. The old-fashioned soft drink became associated with the American West and general stores: {He ordered a sarsaparilla at the saloon}. The word also refers to the tropical vine itself, once believed to have medicinal properties.

A sash is a decorative band of fabric worn around the waist or over one shoulder, often indicating rank, achievement, or ceremonial status: {The beauty queen wore her sash and tiara}. Military officers and dignitaries wear sashes as part of formal dress. Separately, a sash is the frame holding glass panes in a window—a sash window slides up and down within its frame.

Sashay is to walk with exaggerated, swaying movements—a strut that calls attention to itself. The word often implies theatrical confidence or flirtation: {She sashayed across the room}. In square dancing, sashay is a sideways sliding step where partners move past each other. The casual verb sometimes just means to go or proceed: {He sashayed over to the bar}.

Sashayed is the past tense of sashay, meaning to walk with an exaggerated swaying motion, often suggesting confidence or flamboyance: {She sashayed across the room}. The word can imply showing off or moving with deliberate flair. It also means to move casually or glide somewhere: {He sashayed over to the bar}.

Sashaying is walking or moving with an exaggerated, confident swagger—hips swaying, posture bold. The word suggests self-conscious flair, sometimes theatrical or flamboyant: {She came sashaying into the room like she owned the place}. In square dancing, to sashay is a specific sideways sliding step. The term often carries a hint of showiness or attitude.

Sashays is the third-person singular of sashay, meaning to walk or move with an exaggerated swaying motion, often suggesting confidence or showiness: {She sashays into the room like she owns the place}. The word can carry a theatrical or camp quality, sometimes used mockingly: {He sashayed down the hallway in his new outfit}.

Sashes is the plural of sash, which has two distinct meanings. A sash is a decorative band of fabric worn around the waist or over the shoulder, often indicating rank or achievement: {beauty queens wear sashes}, {military officers display medals on sashes}. Separately, a sash is the frame holding the glass in a window, typically the movable part that slides up and down: {The old sashes were painted shut}.

Sashimi is a Japanese dish of thinly sliced raw fish or seafood, served without rice. Unlike sushi, which combines raw fish with vinegared rice, sashimi showcases the fish alone, typically arranged on a plate with garnishes like shredded daikon and wasabi: {The sashimi platter had salmon, tuna, and yellowtail}.

Sasquatch is a large, hairy, ape-like creature said to inhabit forests of the Pacific Northwest. The word comes from Salish languages and is interchangeable with Bigfoot, though sasquatch tends toward the regional and folkloric while Bigfoot sounds more tabloid. Despite thousands of reported sightings, no physical evidence has confirmed its existence: {He claims to have seen a sasquatch while hiking in Oregon}.

Sass is impudent or disrespectful talk, especially from someone in a subordinate position: {Don't give me any sass}. The verb means to talk back: {She sassed her teacher and got detention}. Sassy describes someone inclined to sass—bold, spirited, sometimes admirably so: {a sassy comeback}.

Sassafras is a North American tree with aromatic bark and distinctive mitten-shaped leaves that may have one, two, or three lobes. The root bark was traditionally used to flavor root beer and tea, though the key compound safrole is now banned in commercial foods due to health concerns. {The sassafras trees along the fence line turn brilliant orange in fall.} The wood, lightweight and durable, was once prized for fence posts and small boats.

Sassing is talking back with attitude or disrespect, especially to someone in authority. Children sass parents, students sass teachers: {She got in trouble for sassing the principal}. The word implies impertinence rather than outright hostility—more eye-rolling defiance than genuine confrontation.

Sassy describes someone who is bold, spirited, and slightly impertinent—talking back with confidence and flair rather than deference. The word often carries affection: {I love her sassy attitude}. A sassy remark is cheeky but not truly offensive. The term applies especially to women and children who speak their minds without apology, and to gay men expressing themselves with theatrical confidence.

Sat is the past tense and past participle of sit. You sat in a chair, sat through a lecture, sat for a portrait. A building sits on a foundation; yesterday it sat there too. Food that {sat out overnight} may have spoiled. If something doesn't {sit well} with you, it sat poorly from the start. (Capitalized Sat is the abbreviation for Saturday; all-caps SAT is the standardized test.)

Satanic means relating to or characteristic of Satan, the devil of Christian theology. The word often describes practices or beliefs associated with devil worship: {satanic rituals}, {satanic cults}. More loosely, satanic characterizes anything supremely evil or wicked: {satanic cruelty}. The 1980s saw widespread {satanic panic}—moral alarm about supposed devil worship that proved largely unfounded.

Satanism is the worship or veneration of Satan, or more broadly, any belief system that embraces Satan as a symbol. Some forms involve literal devil worship; others treat Satan as a metaphor for individualism, rebellion against authority, or rejection of religious orthodoxy. The term is often used loosely to describe anything perceived as anti-Christian or darkly transgressive: {The pastor warned that heavy metal music promoted satanism}. (Capitalized Satanism refers to organized religious movements.)

Satanists are adherents of Satanism, a term covering various belief systems that venerate Satan or use Satan as a symbol. Some practice theistic Satanism, worshipping Satan as a deity. Others, like members of the Church of Satan or the Satanic Temple, are atheists who use Satan as a symbol of individualism, rebellion against authority, or opposition to religious orthodoxy: {The satanists filed a lawsuit claiming religious discrimination}.

Satay is a Southeast Asian dish of skewered, grilled meat served with a sauce, typically peanut-based: {We ordered chicken satay as an appetizer}. The meat is usually marinated in spices before grilling. Also spelled saté or sate.

A satchel is a bag with a shoulder strap, typically flat-bottomed with a flap that closes over the top. The word often suggests a bag for carrying books or papers: {She slung her satchel over her shoulder and headed to class}. Satchels are associated with students and messengers, though the style appears in fashion accessories too.

Satchels is the plural of satchel, a bag with a strap worn over the shoulder or across the body, typically with a flap that closes over the top. Satchels are associated with schoolchildren carrying books and with messengers: {She packed her satchels for the first day of school}. The word suggests something sturdier and more structured than a tote or backpack.

Sated means fully satisfied, especially regarding appetite or desire. Someone who has eaten enough is sated; so is someone whose curiosity or lust has been thoroughly gratified. The word suggests satisfaction to the point of having no remaining want: {We left the feast sated and sleepy}. Unlike satiated, which can imply excess, sated tends toward simple contentment.

A satellite is an object that orbits a larger celestial body—the moon is Earth's natural satellite. More commonly, satellite refers to artificial objects launched into orbit: communications satellites, weather satellites, spy satellites. By extension, satellite describes anything dependent on or subordinate to something larger: a satellite {state}, satellite {offices}, satellite {campuses}. Satellite television and radio deliver signals via orbiting transmitters: {We get two hundred channels on satellite}.

Satellites are objects that orbit larger bodies. The moon is Earth's natural satellite; artificial satellites are machines launched into orbit for communication, navigation, weather monitoring, or observation. The term extends to anything dependent on or revolving around something more central: {satellite offices}, {satellite states}. A satellite {dish} receives signals from broadcasting satellites. {The company has satellites in twelve countries.}

Satin is a smooth, glossy fabric with a lustrous face and dull back, made from silk, polyester, or other fibers woven in a particular way. The sheen comes from the weave structure rather than the fiber itself. Satin appears in formal wear, lingerie, and bedding: {satin sheets}, {a satin ribbon}. As an adjective, it describes smooth, lustrous surfaces: {satin finish}, {satin skin}.

Satire is a form of humor that accentuates the weaknesses and shortcomings of a person, institution, or enterprise. The phrases political satire and social satire are both frequent because politicians, and people generally, do and say silly things. A particular work such as a play, poem, or story that uses satire can also be called a satire: The movie is a dark satire about political failure in the wake of a natural disaster.

Satires are works that use humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize human folly, vice, or institutions. The form spans literature, film, television, and other media: {Jonathan Swift wrote some of the sharpest satires in English}. Political satires mock governments and leaders; social satires target cultural norms and behaviors. The term can also describe real situations that seem to parody themselves: {The hearing devolved into a satire of democratic process}.

Satirical describes something that uses irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to expose and criticize foolishness or vice—typically in politics, society, or human behavior. A satirical {article} mocks its subject while making a serious point. Satirical {news} programs like *The Daily Show* blend comedy with commentary. The word often appears with entertainment that looks like straight reporting but isn't: {I thought it was real, but it turned out to be satirical}.

Satirise is the British spelling of satirize, meaning to mock or criticize through satire—using humour, irony, or exaggeration to expose foolishness or vice. Writers satirise politicians, institutions, and social conventions: {The show brilliantly satirises celebrity culture}. The target is held up for ridicule, often to prompt reflection or reform.

A satirist is someone who uses satire—humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize and expose foolishness or vice, especially in politics and society. The term typically applies to writers, cartoonists, or performers: {Jonathan Swift was a master satirist}. A satirist's work aims to provoke reflection, not just laughter.

Satirists are writers or performers who use satire—humor, irony, or exaggeration—to criticize and mock human folly, vice, or political institutions. The term applies across forms: Jonathan Swift was a satirist in prose, *The Onion* employs satirists in journalism, *Saturday Night Live* features satirists in sketch comedy. {The satirists had a field day with the scandal.}

To satirize is to mock or criticize through satire—using humor, irony, or exaggeration to expose foolishness or vice. Writers satirize politicians, institutions, or social norms: {The show satirizes celebrity culture}. The target is held up for ridicule, but the critique usually has a serious point beneath the comedy.

Satirized is the past tense of satirize, meaning to mock or criticize through satire—using humor, irony, or exaggeration to expose foolishness or vice. The target is usually a public figure, institution, or social trend: {The show satirized political corruption}. {Her novel satirized suburban conformity}.

Satirizing is using humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize or mock something—usually human folly, vice, or institutional failings. The aim is exposure rather than mere entertainment: {The show has been satirizing politicians for decades}. {She spent the article satirizing corporate jargon}. Writers, cartoonists, and comedians satirize to provoke thought or change.

Satisfaction is the feeling of fulfillment when a need, desire, or expectation is met: {She finished the project with a deep sense of satisfaction}. It extends to adequate resolution of a complaint or debt: {The refund was offered to their satisfaction}. To {demand satisfaction} historically meant to challenge someone to a duel to restore wounded honor. In legal and formal contexts, satisfaction is the discharge of an obligation.
clues: The pleasure of a job done

definition: Satisfactory describes something that meets requirements or expectations without necessarily exceeding them. A satisfactory grade passes but doesn't shine; a satisfactory meal fills you up without being memorable. The word carries a slightly lukewarm connotation—adequate rather than impressive. {The inspector found the building's safety measures satisfactory.} When someone calls your work satisfactory, you've cleared the bar, but just barely.

Satisfied describes contentment when a need, desire, or expectation has been met. A satisfied {customer} has no complaints. If you're satisfied with an explanation, you accept it as adequate. To be satisfied is to have enough—not necessarily delighted, but no longer wanting: {I'm satisfied with how things turned out}. The word often implies sufficiency rather than excess.

Satisfy means to meet a need, desire, or expectation adequately. If you satisfy your hunger, you eat enough to no longer feel hungry. If you satisfy a requirement, you fulfill what is demanded. {The explanation satisfied her curiosity.} The word carries a sense of sufficiency rather than excess—to be satisfied is to have enough, not necessarily to have everything one might want. Someone who is hard to satisfy has standards that are difficult to meet. In legal contexts, to satisfy a debt or judgment is to pay it in full.

Satisfying describes something that fulfills a need, desire, or expectation. A satisfying {meal} leaves you comfortably full. A satisfying {answer} resolves a question adequately. The word often carries a sense of completeness or closure—there's something satisfying about {finishing a difficult task} or {hearing a door click shut}. What's satisfying varies by person: a satisfying {crunch}, a satisfying {ending}, a satisfying {win}.

Sativa is a classification of cannabis plants, distinguished from indica by tall, narrow-leafed growth and effects typically described as energizing or cerebral rather than sedating. The term appears in strain names and dispensary menus: {I prefer sativas for daytime use}. Botanically, it derives from the Latin for "cultivated," appearing in species names like *Cannabis sativa* and *Avena sativa* (oats).

Satnav is British English for a GPS navigation system, especially the kind mounted in a car: {The satnav kept telling me to turn left into a field}. Short for satellite navigation. Americans typically say GPS.

A satsuma is a small, seedless citrus fruit with loose, easily peeled skin—a variety of mandarin orange. Satsumas are prized for their sweetness and convenience, especially as snacks or in lunchboxes. They're sometimes called "Christmas oranges" in Britain, where they traditionally appear in holiday stockings. {The kids peeled their satsumas at the picnic table.} (Capitalized Satsuma is a place in Japan, or a type of Japanese pottery.)

Satsumas are small, sweet citrus fruits with loose, easily peeled skin and few or no seeds. A variety of mandarin orange, they're named after a former province in Japan. Satsumas are popular as snacks and in children's lunchboxes because they peel so cleanly: {The kids went through a whole bag of satsumas}.

Saturate means to soak something so thoroughly that it can hold no more. A saturated sponge drips when squeezed. The meaning extends to any kind of filling to capacity: {The market is saturated with smartphones}. Saturated colors are rich and intense, free of white or gray. In chemistry, a saturated solution contains the maximum dissolved substance possible at a given temperature. Saturated fats have no double bonds between carbon atoms—they're "full" of hydrogen.

Saturated describes something that has absorbed as much as it can hold, whether literally or figuratively. A saturated sponge can't take on more water; a saturated market can't absorb more products. In chemistry, a saturated solution contains the maximum dissolved substance, and saturated fats have no double bonds between carbon atoms. Colors described as saturated are rich and intense, not washed out or pale. {The rain left my clothes completely saturated.}

Saturation is the state of being completely filled or soaked—unable to absorb more. A sponge reaches saturation when it can hold no additional water. Markets reach saturation when demand is fully met: {The smartphone market is approaching saturation}. In color theory, saturation measures intensity or vividness—how pure a hue is versus how washed out or gray. {Turn up the saturation to make the colors pop.}

A satyr is a creature from Greek mythology—part man, part goat, with pointed ears, a tail, and often goat legs. Satyrs were woodland spirits known for drunkenness, lechery, and revelry in the company of Dionysus. The word extends to any man with excessive or uncontrolled sexual appetite: {The old satyr couldn't keep his hands to himself}.

Satyrs are creatures from Greek mythology—half-man, half-goat beings with pointed ears, horse tails, and perpetual erections. They inhabited wild places, chasing nymphs and indulging in wine. The word extends to any man of excessive sexual appetite: {He had a reputation as a satyr}. In entomology, satyrs are a family of brown butterflies.

Sauce is a liquid or semi-liquid accompaniment to food, adding flavor or moisture: {tomato sauce}, {hot sauce}, {cheese sauce}. The word extends to impudent or cheeky behavior: {Don't give me any sauce}. In slang, sauce means alcohol: {He's been on the sauce again}. To sauce something is to add sauce to it, or informally, to speak impudently to someone.

Sauced means drunk or intoxicated: {We got completely sauced at the wedding reception}. The term is informal and suggests moderate to heavy inebriation. It derives from sauce as slang for alcohol, particularly hard liquor. Separately, sauced describes food served with sauce: {sauced pasta}, {lightly sauced wings}.

A saucepan is a deep cooking pot with a long handle and usually a lid, used on stovetops for heating liquids, making sauces, boiling eggs, and similar tasks. Unlike a skillet, it has high sides; unlike a stockpot, it's small enough for one hand to manage: {She heated the soup in a saucepan}.

Saucepans are deep cooking pots with a single long handle and usually a lid, used on stovetops for liquids and sauces. The singular saucepan is more common; the plural typically appears when discussing cookware sets or kitchen inventory: {The saucepans hang from a rack above the stove}.

A saucer is a small shallow dish, typically round with a slight depression, designed to hold a cup. The cup sits in the depression, and the saucer catches drips or holds a spoon. By extension, anything saucer-shaped: a {flying saucer}, {saucer-eyed} with surprise. {She set the teacup back on its saucer.}

Saucers are small shallow dishes designed to hold cups, catching drips and providing a resting place for spoons. The shape—round, flat, slightly concave—gives us {flying saucers}, the classic UFO silhouette. Wide eyes are sometimes described as {big as saucers}. A saucer is also the singular form: {She set the teacup back on its saucer}.

Sauces is the plural of sauce—liquid or semi-liquid preparations that accompany food to add flavor, moisture, or visual appeal. {The chef prepared three sauces for the tasting menu.} In slang, to sauce or get sauced means to drink alcohol: {He was pretty sauced by midnight.}

Saucy means boldly playful or flirtatious, often with a hint of impudence: {a saucy wink}, {a saucy remark}. It suggests cheekiness without real offense—more teasing than rude. The word can describe someone who talks back with spirit: {Don't get saucy with me}. In older usage, saucy meant impertinent or presumptuous, but modern use leans lighter, even complimentary.

Sauerkraut is finely shredded cabbage fermented in its own juice with salt. The fermentation produces a sour, tangy flavor and extends preservation. A staple of German cuisine, it appears alongside sausages, pork, and in Reuben sandwiches: {I'll have the bratwurst with sauerkraut}.

A sauna is a small room or building designed for dry or steam heat bathing, typically heated to high temperatures. Users sit inside to sweat, believed to promote relaxation and health benefits. The practice originated in Finland, where saunas remain culturally central. The word also refers to a session in such a room: {We had a sauna after swimming}. Informally, any uncomfortably hot space becomes a sauna: {This car is a sauna}.

Saunas is the plural of sauna, a small room or building designed for dry or steam heat bathing. Traditional Finnish saunas use heated rocks to produce intense dry heat; water poured on the rocks creates bursts of steam. The practice involves sitting in high temperatures to induce sweating, often followed by cooling off: {The gym has separate saunas for men and women}. Infrared saunas use radiant heat rather than heated air.

Saunter is to walk in a slow, relaxed manner without urgency or purpose. The word suggests ease and confidence—someone who saunters isn't rushing anywhere: {He sauntered into the meeting ten minutes late}. As a noun, a saunter is a leisurely walk: {an afternoon saunter through the park}.

Sauntered is the past tense of saunter, meaning to walk in a slow, relaxed, unhurried manner. The word suggests casual confidence or leisurely movement without particular purpose: {He sauntered into the room as if he owned the place}. Unlike strolling, sauntering often carries a hint of swagger or nonchalance.

Sauntering is walking in a slow, relaxed, unhurried manner—strolling without apparent purpose or destination. The word suggests ease and leisure, perhaps even a touch of self-satisfaction: {He came sauntering in twenty minutes late, not a care in the world}. Where walking is neutral, sauntering implies you have time to waste.

Sauropods were enormous herbivorous dinosaurs with distinctive body plans: long necks, small heads, massive bodies, and long tails. The group includes the largest land animals ever to exist—Brachiosaurus, Diplodocus, Apatosaurus (once called Brontosaurus). {The sauropod's neck allowed it to reach vegetation other dinosaurs couldn't access.}

Sausage is ground meat—usually pork, beef, or a mixture—seasoned and stuffed into a cylindrical casing. Sausages may be fresh, cured, or smoked: {breakfast sausage}, {Italian sausage}, {bratwurst}. The word extends to anything sausage-shaped: {sausage fingers}, {sausage curls}. In British slang, {silly sausage} is an affectionate term for someone being foolish.

A sausagefest is a gathering or event with a heavy preponderance of men—the sausages being penises. The term is mildly vulgar and usually disparaging, suggesting the gender imbalance makes the event less appealing: {The party was a total sausagefest}. Also spelled sausage fest.

Sausagemaking is the process of grinding meat, mixing it with fat and seasonings, and stuffing it into casings. The term often appears figuratively to describe messy, unappetizing processes that produce acceptable results—especially in politics and legislation: {If you like laws and sausages, you should never watch either one being made}.

Sausages are seasoned ground meat stuffed into casings, typically cylindrical links. The word usually appears as a plural because sausages come in bunches and are eaten multiple at a time: {sausages and eggs for breakfast}. Types vary widely—Italian, breakfast, bratwurst, chorizo. British {bangers and mash} pairs sausages with mashed potatoes.

Sauté is a cooking method where food is fried quickly in a small amount of fat over high heat, typically in a shallow pan. The technique keeps ingredients moving—the word comes from French for "jumped"—to ensure even browning without burning. As an adjective, sautéed describes food cooked this way: {sautéed mushrooms}, {sautéed onions}. A sauté pan has low, sloped sides that make tossing ingredients easier.

Sauteed describes food that has been cooked quickly in a small amount of fat over high heat, typically in a shallow pan: {sauteed mushrooms}, {sauteed spinach with garlic}. The technique keeps ingredients moving to prevent burning while developing flavor through browning. Also spelled sautéed, preserving the French accent.

Sautéing is cooking food quickly in a small amount of fat over high heat, typically in a shallow pan. The technique involves frequent stirring or tossing to brown food evenly without steaming it: {Sauté the onions until translucent}. The word comes from French for "jump," describing how food moves in the pan. Also spelled sauteing.

Sauteing is cooking food quickly in a small amount of fat over high heat, typically while stirring or tossing. The technique keeps ingredients moving in the pan to prevent burning and ensure even browning: {She was sauteing onions and garlic for the sauce}. Also spelled sautéing.

Savage means wild, fierce, or untamed. A savage {attack} is brutal and unrestrained. Savage {criticism} is harsh and unsparing. As a noun, savage was historically applied to indigenous peoples by colonizers—a usage now recognized as dehumanizing and offensive. In contemporary slang, savage describes someone admirably bold or ruthless: {That comeback was savage}. To savage is to attack ferociously: {Critics savaged the film}.

Savaged is the past tense of savage, meaning to attack ferociously. Animals savage prey by biting and tearing: {The dog savaged the intruder}. Critics savage performances or policies with harsh words: {The film was savaged by reviewers}. The word implies not just damage but viciousness—an attack meant to destroy rather than merely wound.

Savagery is violent, brutal, or cruel behavior—the conduct of someone acting without restraint or civilization: {The savagery of the attack shocked investigators}. It can describe physical violence or fierce verbal assault. The word implies something primitive or animalistic, though historically it was applied prejudicially to non-European peoples. {The film depicts war in all its savagery}.

Savages is an old and now offensive term for people considered primitive or uncivilized—typically Indigenous peoples as viewed by European colonizers. A Virginia planter in 1750 might write of {savages on the frontier}. The word also describes anyone who behaves with extreme cruelty or brutality: {The critics were absolute savages}. As a verb, to savage is to attack ferociously: {The dog savaged the intruder}; {Reviews savaged the film}.

Savaging is attacking with violent ferocity, the way a wild animal might tear at prey. Critics savage films, reviewers savage books—the word implies destruction beyond mere criticism: {The press savaged the candidate's record}. A dog savaging a rabbit isn't just biting; it's shaking, tearing, refusing to let go.

A savanna is a flat grassland with scattered trees, found in tropical and subtropical regions where rainfall is seasonal. The landscape supports grazing animals and their predators—the African savanna is famous for lions, elephants, and wildebeest. {Miles of open savanna stretched to the horizon.} Also spelled savannah.

A savannah is a flat grassland with scattered trees, found in tropical and subtropical regions where rainfall is seasonal. The landscape is characteristic of much of Africa, where it supports iconic wildlife like lions and elephants. {The wildebeest migrated across the savannah.} Also spelled savanna. (Capitalized Savannah is a city in Georgia.)

Savannahs is the plural of savannah, a grassland with scattered trees, typically found in tropical and subtropical regions. The landscape is characterized by distinct wet and dry seasons: {the savannahs of East Africa}, {elephants roaming the savannahs}. The spelling savannah (with the h) is less common than savanna but appears in proper names, notably Savannah, Georgia.

Savannas is the plural of savanna, a tropical or subtropical grassland with scattered trees and seasonal rainfall. Savannas cover much of Africa, where they support iconic wildlife like lions, elephants, and zebras. The ecosystem is characterized by distinct wet and dry seasons: {The savannas of East Africa attract tourists from around the world}.

A savant is a person of profound learning or exceptional skill in a specialized field. The term often appears in {idiot savant}, now usually {savant syndrome}, describing someone with developmental disabilities who demonstrates extraordinary ability in a narrow domain—calculating calendar dates instantly, playing complex music by ear, or drawing cityscapes from memory. Outside clinical contexts, savant suggests deep expertise: {a wine savant}, {a political savant}.

Savants are people of profound learning or expertise in a particular field. The term often appears in {idiot savant}, now usually {savant syndrome}—a condition where someone with cognitive limitations displays exceptional ability in a narrow domain like music, math, or memory. Outside clinical contexts, savant can simply mean a learned person or scholar.

As a verb, save preserves (save a historical landmark), protects (save for a rainy day), and prevents (save from disaster). In imperatives, save can express pointlessness (save your breath) or heroism (save the day). Save also has a minor role as a preposition or conjunction in formal writing, where it means the same thing as except or except for: The dinner was a disaster, save for the delicious dessert.

Saved is the past tense of save, covering all its meanings: rescued from danger {The lifeguard saved him from drowning}, preserved for later {I saved some cake for you}, or stored digitally {Have you saved your work?}. In religious contexts, saved means redeemed from sin or granted salvation: {Are you saved?} {He got saved at a revival meeting}.

A savepoint is a marked position in a video game that preserves progress, allowing a player to return there after failure rather than starting over: {I died right before the savepoint}. In databases, a savepoint marks a position within a transaction that can be rolled back to without abandoning the entire operation.

Savepoints are locations in a video game where progress is automatically or manually saved, allowing players to resume from that spot after failure or quitting. The term extends to database transactions, where a savepoint marks a position you can roll back to without undoing everything: {I set a savepoint before running the risky query}. Figuratively, any fallback position: {Let's establish some savepoints before we commit to this plan}.

A saver is someone who saves—typically money, but also time, energy, or other resources. The word often appears in compounds describing things that conserve: {a real time-saver}, {energy-saver mode}, {screen saver}. A saver may also be someone who rescues or preserves: {a life saver}. In finance, savers are distinguished from spenders or investors.

Saves is the third person singular form of the verb save and is used when the subject is a single person or thing (other than I or you). The noun saves is the plural of save, which has several meanings. In some sports, a save is a successful effort to stop the other team from scoring. A save is also the action of capturing data on an electronic device.

Saving conveys rescuing (the paramedics are saving the accident victim) and conservation (the principal is saving money by hiring newer teachers). It is also routinely used in sports (the goalie is saving the game) and computing (saving a data backup). The participle saving has a minor role as a preposition or a conjunction in formal writing, where it means the same thing as except.

Savings is money set aside rather than spent, typically accumulated over time for future use: {She dipped into her savings to cover the repairs}. A savings account holds deposited money that earns interest. The singular saving means a reduction in cost or expenditure: {The new system represents a significant saving in labor}.

A savior is someone who rescues or delivers others from danger, harm, or destruction. The word carries strong religious connotations, particularly in Christianity where the Savior refers to Jesus Christ as the redeemer of humanity. In secular use, savior describes anyone who provides crucial help in a desperate situation: {The firefighter was hailed as a savior by the trapped family}. The term can also be used ironically or critically when someone acts with an inflated sense of their own importance in helping others.
clues: The one who gets you out

definition: Saviors is the plural of savior, one who saves or rescues others from danger, destruction, or difficulty. The word often carries religious weight—Christians call Jesus Christ the Savior. But saviors appear in secular contexts too: {The firefighters were hailed as saviors}. The term can be ironic when someone's help proves unwelcome or self-serving: {He fancied himself the savior of the department}.

A saviour is someone who rescues or delivers others from danger, destruction, or difficulty. The word carries weight—you wouldn't call someone a saviour for minor help. In Christian contexts, the Saviour refers to Jesus Christ as redeemer of humanity. Outside religion, saviour describes anyone who provides crucial rescue: {She was the saviour of the company during the crisis}. The spelling saviour is British; Americans write savior.

Saviours is the plural of saviour, the British spelling of savior. A saviour is someone who rescues or delivers others from danger, harm, or destruction. The word often carries religious weight—Christians call Jesus Christ the Saviour—but applies broadly to anyone who saves the day: {The goalkeeper was our saviour in the final minutes}.

Savor means to taste or smell something with pleasure, lingering over the experience: {She savored every bite of the chocolate cake}. The meaning extends to any deliberate enjoyment: {He savored his victory}. As a noun, savor is the distinctive taste or quality of something: {The dish had a smoky savor}. British spelling: savour.

Savored is the past tense of savor, meaning to taste or enjoy something slowly and thoroughly. Food or drink can be savored: {She savored every bite of the chocolate cake}. The word extends to any pleasurable experience taken in deliberately: {He savored the moment of victory}. What's savored is appreciated rather than rushed through.
