Savoring is the act of enjoying something slowly and fully, drawing out the pleasure. You savor a fine meal by eating deliberately, noticing each flavor. The word extends beyond taste to any experience worth lingering over: {savoring the moment}, {savoring a victory}. To savor something is to appreciate it rather than rush through it.

Savors is the verb form of savor, meaning to taste or smell something with pleasure, or to enjoy an experience fully and deliberately: {She savors her morning coffee}. To savor something is to linger over it rather than rush through. A thing savors of something else when it suggests or hints at it: {His excuse savors of dishonesty}.

Savory describes food that is flavorful and appetizing, especially in a salty or spicy way rather than sweet: {savory snacks}, {a savory pie}. The word suggests rich, satisfying taste—umami rather than sugar. Figuratively, something savory is morally respectable, usually in the negative: {The neighborhood had some unsavory characters}. Savory is also an herb in the mint family used in cooking.

Savour (or savor in American spelling) means to taste or smell something with pleasure, lingering over it: {She savoured every bite of the chocolate cake}. Extended to any experience, savour means to enjoy fully and deliberately: {He savoured the moment of victory}. As a noun, savour is a distinctive taste, smell, or quality: {The scandal gave the affair an unsavoury savour}. Something that {savours of} a quality suggests or hints at it: {His explanation savoured of dishonesty}.

Savouring is the British spelling of savoring—enjoying something slowly and deliberately, extracting full pleasure from the experience. You savour a fine wine, a quiet moment, or a hard-won victory: {She sat savouring her morning coffee}. The word implies lingering appreciation rather than rushing through.

Savours is the British spelling of savors, the third-person singular form of the verb savor. To savour something is to enjoy it fully, lingering over the experience: {She savours her morning coffee}. It can also mean to have a particular quality or hint of something: {His explanation savours of excuse-making}.

Savoury is the British spelling of savory, covering both the adjective meaning pleasantly salty or spicy rather than sweet, and the noun referring to aromatic herbs used in cooking. A savoury dish or snack has a rich, full flavor that satisfies without sweetness: {The menu offered both sweet and savoury options}. In British usage, a savoury may also be a small appetizer or final course served at formal dinners.

Savvy is practical understanding or shrewdness—knowing how things actually work: {She has real political savvy}, {He lacks the tech savvy to set it up}. As an adjective, it describes someone with this quality: {a savvy investor}, {media-savvy politicians}. The verb, now dated, means to understand: {You savvy?}

A saw is a tool with a toothed blade for cutting hard materials—wood, metal, bone. The tooth pattern lets the blade bite and remove material on each stroke. Types include handsaw, chainsaw, circular saw, and hacksaw. To saw is to cut with such a tool, or to move back and forth as if sawing: {He sawed at the rope with his knife}. Separately, saw is the past tense of see. A saw is also an old saying or proverb: {the old saw about early birds and worms}.

Sawbones is informal, often humorous slang for a doctor or surgeon. The term dates from an era when surgery frequently meant amputation, evoking the grim image of a bone saw: {The old sawbones patched me up}. It appears most often in historical fiction or deliberately old-fashioned speech.

Sawdust is the fine particles of wood produced when cutting or sanding lumber. It accumulates beneath saws and in woodworking shops. Sawdust has practical uses—as animal bedding, mulch, or fuel for pellet stoves. Figuratively, something described as sawdust is dry and flavorless: {The overcooked chicken tasted like sawdust}.

A sawfish is a large ray with a long, flat snout edged with tooth-like projections, resembling a saw. These bottom-dwelling fish use the saw to slash through schools of fish and probe sandy seafloors for prey. Found in tropical coastal waters and estuaries, sawfish are now critically endangered due to overfishing and habitat loss.

Sawgrass is a tall sedge with sharp-edged leaves that can cut skin, native to wetlands of the southeastern United States. It dominates the Florida Everglades, forming vast expanses called "river of grass." The name comes from the serrated leaf margins, which resemble saw teeth: {We waded through sawgrass up to our shoulders}.

A sawhorse is a four-legged frame used to support wood for sawing, or to hold planks as a temporary work surface. Sawhorses typically come in pairs: {He set up two sawhorses and laid a sheet of plywood across them}. They're common on construction sites and in workshops, often collapsible for storage.

Sawing is the act of cutting with a saw, moving the blade back and forth through material: {The sawing took all morning}. The word extends to any back-and-forth motion resembling saw use: sawing at a tough steak with a knife, a violinist sawing away at the strings. Loud snoring is sometimes called sawing logs.

A sawmill is a facility where logs are cut into lumber using large power-driven saws. Historically powered by water wheels, modern sawmills typically run on electricity. The term can refer to the entire operation or specifically to the machinery that does the cutting. {The old sawmill by the river closed down decades ago.} Sawmills remain central to the timber industry, processing raw logs into boards, beams, and other wood products for construction and manufacturing.

Sawmills is the plural of sawmill, a facility where logs are cut into lumber. The term covers both the building and the machinery inside it—large circular or band saws that slice timber into boards of standard dimensions. {The old sawmills along the river employed half the town.} Sawmill towns often grew around logging operations, declining when forests were depleted.

Saws is the plural of saw—a tool with a toothed blade for cutting hard materials like wood or metal. {The carpenter keeps his saws sharp.} Saws also refers to old sayings or proverbs: {ancient saws about early birds and rolling stones}. As a verb, saws means cuts with a saw or moves back and forth like one: {She saws through the branch}; {The violinist saws away at the strings}.

Sawtooth describes a shape resembling the teeth of a saw—a series of sharp, angled points rising gradually on one side and dropping steeply on the other. The term appears in technical contexts like electronics, where a sawtooth wave rises linearly then drops abruptly, and in architecture, where sawtooth roofs feature angled sections that maximize natural light. {The oscilloscope displayed a clean sawtooth pattern.} As an adjective it modifies anything with this jagged profile: sawtooth {mountains}, sawtooth {edges}.

Sax is informal for saxophone, the curved brass woodwind instrument with keys and a reed mouthpiece: {She plays sax in a jazz quartet}. The word appears in compounds like {alto sax}, {tenor sax}, {sax player}. Less commonly, sax is a tool for cutting roofing slates.

A saxophone is a brass wind instrument with a single reed mouthpiece, curved body, and keys operated by the fingers. Despite being made of brass, it's classified as a woodwind because of its reed. Invented in the 1840s, the saxophone became central to jazz and also appears in classical music, marching bands, and rock: {She plays alto sax in a jazz quartet}.

Saxophones are wind instruments with a single-reed mouthpiece and a curved metal body, invented in the 1840s. The saxophone family spans soprano to bass, with alto and tenor most common. Though made of brass, saxophones are classified as woodwinds because of how they produce sound. They dominate jazz and feature in concert bands, rock, and classical music: {a wailing saxophone solo}.

A saxophonist is a person who plays the saxophone. The word appears in contexts ranging from jazz clubs to concert halls: {The saxophonist stepped forward for a solo}. Also spelled saxophonist with the stress on the second syllable, though both pronunciations are common.

The three most frequent verbs (be, have, do) earn their status partly because they can be both main and auxiliary verbs. Say is the most frequent verb that doesn’t also have a helping job, probably because we have a predilection for quoting others. Like many frequent verbs, say is irregular, with its inflected form said for the past and past participle. Over the centuries, say has developed figurative uses: The clock says five o’clock. Say can also express a supposition: Let’s say no one responds to your offer; what then?

A saying is a short, familiar expression conveying conventional wisdom or a common observation: {There's an old saying about not counting your chickens before they hatch}. Sayings circulate widely enough that speakers often introduce them with phrases like "as the saying goes" or "you know what they say." The term covers proverbs, adages, and maxims without distinguishing among them.

Sayings are short, well-known expressions that convey wisdom, truth, or advice—often passed down through generations. They overlap with proverbs, maxims, and adages, though sayings is the most general term. {As the old saying goes, you can't teach an old dog new tricks.} People reference sayings to add authority to a point or acknowledge conventional wisdom, sometimes ironically: {You know what they say about assumptions.}

Sayonara is a Japanese word for goodbye, borrowed into English with connotations of finality—a permanent farewell rather than a casual see-you-later. It often signals the definitive end of something: {After that argument, it was sayonara to our friendship}. Sometimes used dismissively: {One more screwup and it's sayonara}.

A scab is the rough crust that forms over a wound as it heals—dried blood and tissue protecting new skin beneath. Picking at scabs delays healing. Extended meanings share the sense of something unwanted or contemptible. A scab is a worker who crosses a picket line or takes a striker's job: {The union called them scabs}. The term is strongly derogatory in labor contexts. As a verb, to scab is to form a crust or to work during a strike.

A scabbard is a sheath for a sword or dagger, typically made of leather or metal and worn at the hip or back. The word appears most often in historical or fantasy contexts: {He drew his blade from its scabbard}. To scabbard a weapon is to return it to its sheath.

Scabbards are sheaths for swords or daggers—protective cases that cover the blade when not in use. Typically made of leather or metal, a scabbard hangs from a belt or baldric, allowing the weapon to be drawn quickly: {He slid the blade back into its scabbard}. The word appears often in historical fiction and fantasy.

Scabbed describes something covered with scabs—the dry, rough crusts that form over healing wounds. A scabbed knee is partway through recovery. The word extends to surfaces with similar rough, patchy textures. Figuratively, scabbed can mean morally corrupt or tainted, though this use is rare. In labor contexts, scabbed work is that done by strikebreakers.

Scabbing is the formation of a scab over a wound as it heals: {The cut on her knee is scabbing over nicely}. In labor contexts, scabbing is working during a strike or taking a striker's job—acting as a scab. The term carries strong disapproval among union workers: {He was accused of scabbing when he crossed the picket line}.

Scabby describes something covered with scabs—the crusty formations over healing wounds: {a scabby knee from falling off his bike}. Extended uses describe anything rough, flaky, or in poor condition: {scabby paint peeling off the walls}. In British slang, scabby means shabby or contemptible: {a scabby little flat}, {That's a scabby thing to do}.

Scabies is a contagious skin condition caused by microscopic mites that burrow into the skin, producing intense itching and a rash. The mites spread through prolonged skin-to-skin contact, making scabies common in crowded living conditions: {The shelter had an outbreak of scabies}. Treatment typically involves prescription creams that kill the mites.

Scabs are the crusty formations that develop over wounds as they heal—dried blood and plasma protecting new skin beneath. Picking at a scab delays healing. The word extends to workers who cross picket lines during strikes, replacing union members: {The factory brought in scabs to keep production running}. The term is strongly pejorative in labor contexts.

A scaffold is a temporary framework of poles and planks providing workers access to high surfaces during construction or repair: {Workers erected scaffolding around the building}. Historically, a scaffold was also a raised platform for public executions. Figuratively, to scaffold is to provide supporting structure—in education, scaffolding means giving learners temporary support that's gradually removed as they gain competence.

Scaffolding is the temporary framework of poles and platforms erected around a building under construction or repair, allowing workers to reach high areas. The term extends to any temporary supporting structure: {The scaffolding of assumptions underlying the theory}. In education, scaffolding refers to instructional support that's gradually removed as learners gain competence.

Scaffolds are temporary structures erected alongside buildings during construction or repair, giving workers platforms to stand on at various heights. Figuratively, a scaffold is any temporary framework supporting development: {The teacher provides scaffolds until students can work independently}. Historically, a scaffold was also a raised platform for executions. As a verb, to scaffold is to provide such support.

Scalability is the capacity to grow or shrink in response to demand. The term dominates technology and business contexts: a scalable system handles increased load without breaking, a scalable business model works whether you have ten customers or ten million. {The startup's main selling point was scalability}. Something that "doesn't scale" works at small volumes but fails when expanded.

Scalable describes something that can be expanded or contracted to match demand. The word dominates technology and business contexts: a scalable {system} handles growth without fundamental redesign; a scalable {business model} works whether you have ten customers or ten million. The underlying idea is that size changes without breaking the essential structure. {We need a solution that's scalable across all our markets.}

Scalawag is a mildly disapproving term for someone who behaves badly or causes trouble, though often with a sense of affection or amusement rather than genuine condemnation. {That little scalawag ate all the cookies.} Historically, scalawag had a sharper edge in the American South during Reconstruction, where it designated white Southerners who supported Republican policies and cooperated with federal authorities—considered traitors by their neighbors.

Scalawags is typically used to describe mischievous or dishonest people, often with a tone of playful disapproval rather than genuine condemnation. {Those little scalawags got into the cookie jar again.} The word carries an old-fashioned, slightly theatrical quality. In American history, scalawag specifically referred to white Southerners who supported Reconstruction after the Civil War—a term used disparagingly by opponents who viewed them as traitors to the South.

Scald means to burn with hot liquid or steam: {She scalded her hand on the boiling water}. To scald milk is to heat it just below boiling. The noun is the injury itself—a scald is a burn from hot liquid rather than flame or contact with a hot surface. Figuratively, scalding criticism or remarks are harshly severe.

Scalded describes something that has been burned by hot liquid or steam. Skin becomes scalded from contact with boiling water; milk is scalded when heated just below boiling. The word often appears in cooking: {scalded milk} has been heated to kill bacteria and improve texture in baking. Figuratively, a scalded feeling suggests sudden, sharp pain or shock.

Scalding describes something hot enough to burn, typically liquid or steam: {scalding water}, {scalding coffee}. The word extends to harsh criticism or rebuke: {a scalding review}, {scalding remarks}. Something scalding inflicts damage—whether physical burns or wounded pride.

Scale has a jumble of uses, owing to its arrival in English from different sources. Meanings fall broadly into three categories: those having to do with the bony plates on fish and some other animals; those connected with the weight-measuring device called a scale or scales; and those referring to a graduated series in which there is usually an understood top and bottom, or upper and lower part. This last group of senses is the most productive as noun and verb. The scale of a drawing or model is its size in relation to the real thing. If you scale something up or down, you make it larger or smaller by adjusting the scale on which it operates.

Scaled describes something that has been adjusted in size, scope, or proportion, typically to fit different contexts or requirements. A scaled {model} or scaled {drawing} maintains the proportions of the original while being larger or smaller. In computing and business, scaled often appears in compounds: a {scaled-up} operation has grown, while {scaled-down} expectations have been reduced. Scaled also describes surfaces covered with scales, as on fish or reptiles, or things that have been climbed: {We scaled the cliff before noon}.

Scales are the small, overlapping plates covering fish, reptiles, and some other animals—protective armor that flexes with movement. The singular scale extends to similar structures: {scales on a butterfly's wing}, {scales of rust}. A scale is also a device for weighing, or the balance pans themselves. The scales of justice symbolize fair measurement. Musical scales are sequences of notes ascending or descending in pitch. To scale something is to climb it {(scale a wall)} or to adjust proportionally {(scale up production)}. When scales fall from your eyes, you suddenly see clearly.

Scaling is adjusting size or magnitude. In computing and business, scaling means expanding capacity to handle growth: {The startup struggled with scaling its infrastructure}. To scale up is to increase; to scale down is to reduce. Scaling also refers to removing scales from fish, or the buildup of mineral deposits: {scaling on the pipes}. In climbing, scaling means ascending: {scaling the cliff face}.

Scallawag (also scalawag) is a rascal or scamp—someone mischievous but not truly wicked. The word often carries affection: {You little scallawag, you ate all the cookies}. Historically, scallawag was a derogatory term for white Southerners who supported Reconstruction after the Civil War, implying they were traitors to their region.

A scallion is a young onion harvested before the bulb fully develops, with a white base and long green leaves. Both parts are edible, used raw in salads or cooked in stir-fries and soups. The term is interchangeable with green onion in American English: {Chop the scallions and sprinkle them on top}.

Scallions are young onions harvested before the bulb fully develops, with long green stalks and small white bases. They're eaten raw in salads, used as garnish, or added to cooked dishes for mild onion flavor. Also called green onions or spring onions: {Chop some scallions for the stir-fry}.

A scallop is a marine mollusk with a distinctive fan-shaped shell, prized as seafood for its sweet, tender muscle. The shell's radiating ridges give rise to the decorative meaning: a scalloped edge has a series of curved projections, like the edge of a scallop shell. To scallop potatoes is to bake them in cream sauce, typically in layers—the connection to the shell being the traditional baking dish.

Scalloped describes an edge cut or shaped into a series of rounded curves, like the shell of a scallop: {a scalloped hem}, {scalloped lace trim}. In cooking, scalloped means baked in a cream sauce, often with breadcrumbs: {scalloped potatoes}. The connection is visual—the overlapping potato slices or sauce bubbles suggest shell-like curves.

Scalloping refers to the activity of harvesting scallops, the edible bivalve mollusks prized for their sweet, delicate meat: {We went scalloping off the coast of Florida}. The term also describes creating a decorative edge with a series of curved projections resembling scallop shells: {She finished the quilt with scalloping along the border}.

Scallopini are thin slices of meat, usually veal, pounded flat and quickly sautéed. The dish typically involves dredging in flour and cooking in butter or oil with a sauce—often lemon, wine, or mushrooms: {veal scallopini}, {chicken scallopini}. The word comes from Italian, where it means "small scallops" for the shape of the cutlets.

Scallops are edible bivalve mollusks prized for their sweet, tender flesh—specifically the round adductor muscle that opens and closes the shell. They're a culinary delicacy, typically seared, grilled, or served raw: {The seared scallops were perfectly caramelized}. Scallops also refers to the decorative wavy edge pattern resembling a scallop shell: {The dress had scallops along the hem}. As a verb, to scallop is to cut such an edge or to bake food in a cream sauce: {scalloped potatoes}.

A scallywag is a mischievous person, especially a child who causes trouble in an endearing way: {You little scallywag, you ate all the cookies}. The word is affectionate rather than harsh—it suggests roguish charm more than genuine wrongdoing. In American history, scallywag (or scalawag) referred disparagingly to white Southerners who supported Reconstruction after the Civil War.

Scallywags are mischievous troublemakers, usually applied affectionately to children or pets causing minor chaos: {Those scallywags tracked mud all over my clean floor}. The word carries a playful, old-fashioned tone—more exasperated than truly angry. Historically, scalawag (the more common American spelling) was a serious insult for white Southerners who supported Reconstruction after the Civil War.

The scalp is the skin covering the top and back of the head, where hair typically grows. Historically, some cultures removed enemies' scalps as trophies—to scalp someone was to cut away this skin. The verb now means to resell tickets at inflated prices: {Scalpers were selling tickets for three times face value outside the stadium}. To scalp can also mean to make small, quick profits through frequent trades.

Scalped is the past tense of scalp, meaning to cut or tear the scalp from someone's head—historically associated with warfare practices among some Native American tribes and American colonists. Extended uses: a ticket scalper has scalped you if they've charged an inflated price. In trading, to scalp is to make quick profits on small price movements: {He scalped the stock for a few cents per share}. To get scalped can also mean to be badly beaten or cheated: {We got scalped in that deal}.

A scalpel is a small, extremely sharp knife used for precise cutting, especially in surgery and dissection. The blade is typically thin and pointed, designed for making clean incisions with minimal tissue damage. Scientists and artists also use scalpels for detailed work requiring fine cuts. Figuratively, scalpel suggests surgical precision: {The editor took a scalpel to the manuscript, excising every unnecessary word}.

Scalpels is the plural of scalpel, a small sharp-bladed knife used for surgery and dissection. The blade is typically thin and pointed, designed for precise incisions. Figuratively, scalpel suggests surgical precision: {The editor took a scalpel to the manuscript}, {budget cuts made with a scalpel rather than an axe}.

A scalper buys tickets or goods at regular prices, then resells them at inflated prices when demand exceeds supply: {Scalpers outside the stadium were asking three hundred dollars for fifty-dollar seats}. The practice thrives around concerts, sporting events, and product launches. In trading, a scalper makes quick transactions to profit from small price movements. The older sense—one who takes scalps—is now rare outside historical contexts.

Scalpers buy tickets or goods at regular prices and resell them at inflated prices when demand exceeds supply. The practice is common with concert tickets, sporting events, and limited-edition products: {Scalpers were asking three times face value outside the stadium}. The term carries negative connotations of opportunistic profiteering. In trading, scalpers make rapid small-margin transactions to profit from tiny price movements.

Scalping is cutting or tearing the scalp from a person's head—historically practiced as a war trophy or proof of killing. The term extends to buying tickets or goods at regular prices and reselling them at inflated rates: {Scalpers were selling concert tickets for triple the face value}. In trading, scalping means making rapid transactions for small profits. To scalp someone figuratively is to exploit or cheat them.

Scalps is the plural of scalp—the skin and hair covering the top of the head. Historically, scalps were cut from enemies as war trophies, particularly associated with conflicts between Native Americans and European settlers: {The raiding party returned with scalps}. In trading and ticketing, scalps are items bought and resold at marked-up prices. The verb scalps means to take a scalp, to resell at inflated prices, or to make quick profits on small price movements: {He scalps concert tickets outside the venue}.

Scaly describes surfaces covered with scales or resembling them in texture—the overlapping protective plates found on fish, reptiles, and certain insects. Skin conditions that produce dry, flaking patches are often called scaly: {My elbows get scaly in winter}. The word extends to anything rough, flaky, or encrusted: {scaly buildup on the showerhead}. In informal British English, scaly can mean unfair or underhanded.

A scam is a fraudulent scheme designed to cheat people out of money or valuables. The word implies deception—victims believe they're getting something legitimate. Scams range from email phishing to elaborate confidence tricks: {That investment opportunity turned out to be a scam}. To scam someone is to defraud them: {He scammed elderly people out of their savings}.

Scammed is the past tense of scam—to defraud or swindle someone through deception. Getting scammed means falling victim to a scheme designed to take your money or information: {I got scammed by a fake tech support call}, {She scammed him out of thousands}. The word carries less gravity than defrauded but more than tricked.

A scammer is someone who deceives others for profit, typically through fraudulent schemes. The term covers everything from email phishers to con artists running elaborate hustles: {The scammer posed as a Nigerian prince}, {Don't give your credit card to phone scammers}. Unlike older words like swindler or grifter, scammer emerged with internet-age fraud and carries a more casual, contemporary tone.

Scammers are people who run scams—fraudulent schemes designed to cheat others out of money, personal information, or valuables. The term covers a wide range of con artists, from email phishers and fake charity operators to romance fraudsters and tech support imposters. {The scammers posed as IRS agents demanding immediate payment.} While scam originally had associations with carnival grifters, scammers now operate predominantly online, making the word ubiquitous in discussions of internet safety and consumer protection.

Scamming is defrauding people through deceptive schemes, typically for money. The word implies deliberate trickery rather than honest misrepresentation: {He's been scamming elderly people out of their savings}, {She got caught scamming insurance companies}. Someone who scams is a scammer; the scheme itself is a scam.

Scammy describes something that feels fraudulent or deceptive, suggesting a scam even if not proven to be one. The word conveys suspicion more than certainty: {That website looks scammy}, {The whole deal felt scammy from the start}. Often applied to dubious online offers, shady business practices, or anything that triggers distrust.

A scamp is a mischievous person, especially a child who gets into minor trouble but remains endearing: {You little scamp, you ate all the cookies}. The word carries affection—a scamp's wrongdoing is playful rather than malicious. Less commonly, to scamp work is to do it carelessly or hastily.
clues: A roguish kid up to something

definition: Scamper is to run with quick, light steps, often playfully or in haste. The word suggests small creatures or children darting about: {Squirrels scampered across the lawn}, {The kids scampered off to the playground}. As a noun, a scamper is an instance of such running: {a quick scamper through the rain}.

Scampered is the past tense of scamper, meaning to run with quick, light steps—the way a small animal or child moves when excited or frightened: {The squirrel scampered up the tree}. The word suggests playful or hurried movement rather than serious flight.

Scampering is running with quick, light steps, usually playfully or in haste. The word suggests small creatures or children moving rapidly: {Squirrels went scampering up the tree}, {The kids came scampering down the stairs}. There's an innocence to scampering—it's hard to imagine anything menacing doing it.

Scampers is the third-person singular form of scamper, meaning to run with quick, light steps—the hurried movement of small creatures or children: {A squirrel scampers across the lawn}. The word suggests playful or nervous energy rather than sustained speed. As a noun, scampers are quick dashes or frolics.

Scampi are small lobster-like crustaceans, or a dish of large shrimp or prawns prepared in garlic butter and white wine. In American restaurants, shrimp scampi typically means shrimp sautéed in this garlicky butter sauce, often served over pasta: {We ordered the shrimp scampi as an appetizer}.

Scamps is the plural of scamp—a mischievous person, especially a child who causes minor trouble in an endearing way: {Those little scamps got into the cookie jar again}. The word carries affection rather than real disapproval, suggesting pranks or antics that amuse more than annoy. Occasionally used for adults behaving roguishly.

Scams are fraudulent schemes designed to cheat people out of money or information. The word covers everything from email phishing to elaborate cons: {I keep getting scam calls about my car's warranty}. To scam someone is to swindle them. A scammer runs such schemes. The line between a scam and aggressive marketing can be blurry.

Scan originally meant to analyze verse by examining its meter, but now more often means the opposite—to look over quickly rather than carefully: {She scanned the headlines}. In computing and imaging, to scan is to pass a sensor systematically across something to capture or read data: scanning a barcode, scanning a document. A scan is the act of scanning or its result: {a brain scan}, {a quick scan of the room}.

Scandal is an event or action that causes public outrage or disgrace, typically involving moral wrongdoing or impropriety by someone in a position of trust: {The financial scandal brought down the company}, {a sex scandal}. The word also covers the outrage itself: {The news caused quite a scandal}. Scandals in politics and celebrity culture often end with the suffix -gate, after Watergate. Something scandalous is shocking or disgraceful.

To scandalize is to shock or offend through improper behavior or violation of moral standards: {Her divorce scandalized the whole town}. The word suggests causing widespread disapproval or outrage, particularly in contexts where reputation and propriety matter. What scandalizes depends heavily on the community—behavior that scandalizes a conservative congregation might barely register elsewhere.

Scandalized describes feeling shock or outrage at something considered improper or morally offensive. The reaction typically involves perceived violations of decency or propriety: {She was scandalized by the explicit lyrics}. Someone scandalized often displays visible disapproval—gasps, raised eyebrows, clutched pearls. The word can be used seriously or with ironic exaggeration: {My grandmother would be scandalized to see me in this dress}.

A scandalmonger is someone who spreads gossip and rumors, especially malicious or damaging ones. The word carries contempt—it's not neutral like "gossip" but suggests someone who traffics in scandal for pleasure or profit: {The tabloids are run by scandalmongers}. The verb scandalmonger and noun scandalmongering follow naturally.

Scandalmongers are people who spread gossip and rumors, especially malicious or embarrassing information about others. The term carries disapproval—scandalmongers don't just repeat what they hear but actively traffic in it, often embellishing for effect: {The tabloids are run by scandalmongers who don't care whose reputation they destroy}.

Scandalous describes something that causes public outrage or moral shock: {a scandalous affair}, {scandalous behavior}. It can refer to actions that violate accepted standards of decency or propriety, or to revelations that damage reputations. The word often carries a whiff of the salacious—scandals tend to involve sex, money, or hypocrisy. Something scandalous may also simply be shockingly bad: {The conditions in that nursing home are scandalous}.

Scandals is the plural of scandal—actions or events that cause public outrage or damage reputations. A scandal typically involves behavior that violates moral standards or public trust: {The administration was rocked by a series of scandals}. Political scandals, financial scandals, and sex scandals dominate news cycles, often ending careers. The word implies not just wrongdoing but exposure—a scandal requires an audience to be scandalized.

Scanned is the past tense of scan. To scan is to look over something quickly, searching for particular information: {She scanned the crowd for her daughter}. Scanning also means to examine systematically, especially with technology—a machine scans documents, barcodes, or body parts to capture or analyze data: {The nurse scanned my wristband}. In poetry, a line scans if its meter is regular.

A scanner is a device that systematically examines something. An optical scanner converts documents or images into digital files: {I need to scan my passport}. A radio scanner monitors multiple frequencies. At airports and hospitals, scanners use X-rays or other technology to see inside bodies or luggage. In computing, a scanner detects malware or vulnerabilities. A person who scans—reading quickly or surveying a crowd—is also a scanner.

Scanning is methodical visual or electronic examination—moving across a surface or through data to detect or extract what matters. Eyes scan a crowd for a familiar face; machines scan documents to digitize them. A medical scan images the body's interior. To scan text is to read it quickly for key points rather than studying every word. In poetry, to scan a line is to analyze its meter: {The verse doesn't scan properly}.

Scans are images produced by machines that systematically examine something, whether a body part via CT or MRI, a document fed through a scanner, or a barcode read at checkout. The verb scan means to look over something quickly but thoroughly, searching for specific information: {She scanned the crowd for familiar faces}. In poetry, a line scans if its meter follows the expected rhythmic pattern. {The doctor ordered brain scans after the accident.}

A scapegoat is a person or group blamed for problems they didn't cause, deflecting responsibility from the actual source. The word comes from an ancient Hebrew ritual where a goat was symbolically loaded with the community's sins and driven into the wilderness. Modern use is almost always figurative: {Immigrants became scapegoats for the economic downturn}. To scapegoat someone is to make them bear undeserved blame.

Scapegoated means made to bear blame for others' failures or misdeeds. The scapegoat was originally a goat symbolically burdened with the sins of the community and driven into the wilderness. Now it's anyone unfairly blamed: {He was scapegoated for the team's poor performance}. {Immigrants are often scapegoated during economic downturns}.

Scapegoating is the practice of blaming one person or group for problems caused by others or by circumstances beyond anyone's control. The term comes from an ancient ritual in which a goat was symbolically loaded with the community's sins and driven into the wilderness. Modern scapegoating typically targets vulnerable or marginalized groups: {Immigrants are often scapegoated during economic downturns}. The scapegoat receives punishment or hostility that should be directed elsewhere—or nowhere at all.

Scapegoats are people or groups blamed for problems they didn't cause or bear disproportionate responsibility for. The term comes from an ancient ritual where a goat was symbolically loaded with the community's sins and driven into the wilderness. Modern scapegoats absorb blame that should fall elsewhere: {Immigrants became scapegoats for the economic downturn}. To scapegoat someone is to make them one.

A scar is a mark left on skin or tissue after a wound heals—the body's permanent record of injury. Scars extend to any lasting trace of damage: {The hillside still bears scars from the wildfire}. Emotional scars are psychological marks left by trauma: {The divorce left scars on everyone}. To scar is to leave such a mark: {The accident scarred her face}, {That experience scarred him for life}.

A scarab is a beetle, especially the dung beetle sacred to ancient Egyptians, who saw its ball-rolling as a symbol of the sun's daily journey. The word now usually refers to carved representations of the beetle used as amulets, seals, or jewelry: {a scarab ring}, {an Egyptian scarab pendant}. Scarabs remain popular in decorative arts.

Scarabs are beetles of the family Scarabaeidae, which includes dung beetles and June bugs. The term most often refers to the sacred scarab of ancient Egypt, where the dung-rolling beetle became a powerful symbol of the sun god and regeneration. Ancient Egyptians carved scarab-shaped amulets from stone or faience, often inscribing them with hieroglyphs and placing them with mummies. {The museum's collection includes several carved scarabs from the New Kingdom period.}

Scarce describes something in short supply relative to demand—not absent, but insufficient: {Water is scarce in the desert}, {Jobs were scarce during the recession}. The word implies difficulty obtaining what's needed. To {make yourself scarce} is to leave quickly or stay away, especially to avoid trouble.

Scarcity is the condition of being in short supply relative to demand. Economics treats scarcity as fundamental—resources are finite while wants are unlimited. The word emphasizes insufficiency: {Water scarcity threatens the region}, {a scarcity of affordable housing}. Scarcity often drives up value, as with rare commodities or limited editions.

Scare is sudden fear or alarm, or something that causes it: {a bomb scare}, {quite a scare}. As a verb, to scare is to frighten: {The noise scared me}. To {scare up} something is to find or gather it with effort: {We scared up enough chairs for everyone}. Scary is the adjective. A scarecrow is a decoy figure meant to frighten birds from crops.

A scarecrow is a humanlike figure set up in fields to frighten birds away from crops, typically made of old clothes stuffed with straw and mounted on a pole. The word extends to anyone dressed in ragged clothing or looking disheveled: {He looked like a scarecrow in that old coat}. Scarecrows appear frequently in folklore and fiction as figures that come to life.

Scarecrows is the plural of scarecrow—a human-shaped figure set up in fields to frighten birds away from crops. The typical scarecrow is made of old clothes stuffed with straw, mounted on a wooden frame. By extension, a scarecrow is any person who looks ragged or gaunt: {He was thin as a scarecrow after months in the wilderness}.

Scared means afraid or frightened. It ranges from mild unease to intense fear: {I'm scared of heights}, {The noise scared me}. To be {scared stiff} or {scared to death} is to be extremely frightened. {Running scared} describes acting from fear of failure or defeat. Scared often implies a more immediate or situational fear than afraid, which can describe a general disposition.

A scarefest is an event or experience packed with frightening content—a horror movie marathon, a haunted house attraction, or a Halloween celebration heavy on scares. The word combines scare with the suffix -fest (from festival), suggesting an abundance or concentration of frights: {The kids turned the basement into a scarefest for trick-or-treaters}.

A scaremonger is someone who spreads alarming or exaggerated warnings, typically to provoke fear or anxiety in others. The term carries a strongly negative connotation, suggesting that the person's warnings are overblown, manipulative, or self-serving rather than genuinely helpful. {Critics dismissed him as a scaremonger for predicting economic collapse.} The related verb scaremonger and noun scaremongering describe the activity itself: {The tabloids have been scaremongering about immigration for years.}

Scaremongering is the deliberate spreading of alarming or exaggerated claims to provoke public fear, typically for political or commercial advantage. The term is almost always pejorative—accusing someone of scaremongering dismisses their warnings as manipulative rather than legitimate: {Critics called the campaign's ads about crime pure scaremongering}. A scaremonger is one who engages in this practice.

Scaremongers are people who spread alarming or exaggerated warnings, typically to manipulate public opinion or create unnecessary fear: {The scaremongers predicted economic collapse that never came}. The term is dismissive—it implies the fears being spread are overblown or self-serving. To scaremonger is to engage in this behavior.

Scares is the plural of scare—a sudden fright or alarm. A series of scares might involve repeated startling incidents: {The neighborhood had several scares with coyotes last summer}. A health scare or bomb scare is a frightening episode that may or may not prove serious. As a verb, scares is the third-person singular: {Nothing scares her}.

Scareware is software that frightens users into paying for unnecessary products or services. It typically displays fake warnings about viruses or security threats on your computer, urging immediate action: {A pop-up told me my system was infected, but it was just scareware trying to sell fake antivirus software}. The tactic exploits panic to override judgment.

A scarf is a length of fabric worn around the neck or head for warmth, fashion, or modesty. Scarves vary from thin silk to heavy wool. To scarf something down (or scarf it up) is to eat it quickly and greedily: {He scarfed down three slices of pizza}. In woodworking, a scarf joint connects two pieces by overlapping tapered ends.

Scaring is the act of frightening someone or something. The word functions as both a verb form and an adjective: {You're scaring me} describes the action in progress, while {a scaring experience} characterizes something as frightening. The related forms scared and scary are more common in most contexts.

Scarlet is a brilliant red with a slight orange tinge—bolder and more vivid than crimson. The color has long been associated with royalty, military uniforms, and sin: {a scarlet cloak}, {the Scarlet Letter}. A {scarlet woman} is promiscuous, drawing on biblical imagery of the Whore of Babylon dressed in scarlet. Scarlet fever is a contagious disease marked by a red rash.

Scarred describes something marked by scars—the visible traces left after wounds heal. Skin becomes scarred from cuts, burns, or surgery. The word extends to lasting damage of any kind: {scarred tissue}, {a landscape scarred by wildfires}. Figuratively, scarred suggests emotional or psychological damage from difficult experiences: {She was scarred by the divorce}, {a generation scarred by war}.

Scarring is the formation of scar tissue, either literally on skin or figuratively on the psyche. Physical scarring results from wounds, burns, or surgery: {The accident left permanent scarring on her arms}. Emotional scarring describes lasting psychological damage: {childhood trauma and its scarring effects}. As an adjective, scarring characterizes experiences that leave such marks: {a scarring defeat}, {a scarring memory}.

Scars are marks left on skin or tissue after wounds heal—the body's permanent record of injury. The word extends to any lasting trace of damage: {The landscape still bears the scars of wildfire}. Emotional scars are psychological wounds that persist: {childhood scars}, {the scars of war}. To scar is to leave such marks, literal or figurative: {The accident scarred her for life}.

Scarves is the plural of scarf—a length of fabric worn around the neck for warmth or style: {She pulled out her winter scarves when the temperature dropped}. The alternate plural scarfs also exists but is less common.

Scary describes something that causes fear or alarm: {a scary movie}, {a scary noise in the basement}. The word works for genuine threats and mild frights alike—a scary diagnosis versus a scary Halloween costume. Informally, scary can mean impressively extreme: {She has a scary amount of energy}. The related noun is scare; the verb is to scare.

Scat has two unrelated meanings. One is animal droppings, especially from wild animals: {bear scat}, {coyote scat}. Wildlife trackers identify species by their scat. The other scat is a style of jazz singing using improvised nonsense syllables instead of words—{scatting} over instrumental passages. As a command, scat means go away quickly, usually directed at animals: {Scat, cat!}

Scathing describes criticism or remarks that are harshly severe and withering: {a scathing review}, {a scathing rebuke}. The word implies words sharp enough to wound—delivered with contempt or bitter disapproval. {Her scathing assessment of his work left him speechless.}

Scatter means to disperse or spread in various directions. You scatter seeds across soil, or a crowd scatters when startled. Things that scatter end up distributed irregularly rather than grouped: {Papers scattered across the desk}. A scattering of something is a sparse, random distribution: {a scattering of applause}, {a scattering of houses along the road}.

A scatterbrain is someone who has difficulty focusing or organizing their thoughts, frequently forgetting things or jumping erratically from one topic to another. The term is mildly critical but usually affectionate, suggesting disorganization rather than stupidity. {She's such a scatterbrain—she left her phone in the refrigerator again.} The adjective scatterbrained describes this quality: {His scatterbrained approach to planning made the trip chaotic but memorable.}

Scatterbrained describes someone who is disorganized, forgetful, or unable to concentrate on one thing at a time. A scatterbrained person might lose their keys constantly, forget appointments, or jump from topic to topic in conversation. The term suggests a mind that scatters its attention rather than focusing it. {She's too scatterbrained to be trusted with the arrangements.} The related noun scatterbrain refers to such a person.

Scattered describes things spread over an area without pattern or concentration. Scattered {showers} occur here and there, not everywhere. Scattered {papers} lie disorganized across a surface. A scattered {population} lives dispersed rather than clustered. Someone who is scattered lacks focus or seems disorganized: {I've been so scattered lately I keep forgetting appointments}.

A scattergun is a shotgun, so called because it fires shot that spreads widely rather than a single projectile. The term emphasizes the weapon's broad, imprecise dispersal pattern. Figuratively, scattergun describes any approach that covers wide ground without precision: {a scattergun marketing strategy}, {scattergun questioning}. The adjective suggests trading accuracy for coverage.

A scattering is a small, dispersed quantity of something—not a concentrated mass but items spread thinly across space or time: {a scattering of houses along the road}, {a scattering of applause from the audience}. The word suggests enough to notice but not enough to constitute a significant amount.

Scattershot describes something wide-ranging but unfocused, like pellets spraying from a shotgun rather than a single aimed bullet. A scattershot {approach} tries many things without clear strategy. Scattershot {criticism} hits multiple targets without precision. The word implies inefficiency—covering lots of ground but lacking direction or coherence.

Scatting is a style of jazz singing that uses improvised nonsense syllables instead of words, allowing the voice to function like an instrument. Singers like Ella Fitzgerald and Louis Armstrong made scatting famous, riffing vocally over chord changes with syllables like "doo-ba-dee-dah." The term also refers to the act of leaving quickly or shooing something away: {The cat went scatting across the yard when it heard the door slam}.

Scavenge means to search through discarded material for something usable. Animals scavenge carrion; people scavenge dumpsters, junkyards, or abandoned buildings: {We scavenged parts from old computers to build a new one}. The word implies resourcefulness in finding value where others see waste. Extended uses cover any opportunistic gathering: {scavenging ideas from competitors}, {scavenging quotes for an essay}.

Scavenged is the past tense of scavenge, meaning to search through discarded material for useful items or to collect food from whatever sources are available. Animals scavenge carrion; people scavenge abandoned buildings or junkyards: {We scavenged parts from old computers to build a new one}. The word suggests resourcefulness amid scarcity.

A scavenger is a person or animal that searches through discarded material for useful items. Vultures and hyenas are scavengers, feeding on carrion. People scavenge at dumps, thrift stores, or curbsides: {He furnished his apartment entirely from scavenging}. The word extends to anything that collects waste or debris—certain cells scavenge dead tissue, and chemical scavengers bind unwanted substances.

Scavengers are creatures that feed on dead or decaying matter rather than hunting live prey. Vultures, hyenas, and certain beetles are classic scavengers. The term extends to people who search through discarded materials for useful items: {Scavengers picked through the dump for recyclables}. In chemistry, a scavenger is a substance that removes impurities or unwanted components from a system.

Scavenging is searching through discarded material for something useful or edible. Animals scavenge carrion; people scavenge dumpsters, junkyards, or abandoned buildings. The word implies picking through what others have left behind: {She spent the afternoon scavenging for spare parts}. In biology, scavengers are organisms that feed on dead matter rather than hunting live prey.

A scenario is a possible sequence of events or an imagined situation. Planners develop scenarios to prepare for various outcomes: {worst-case scenario}, {best-case scenario}. In film and theater, a scenario is an outline of the plot. The word often describes hypothetical situations posed for discussion: {Let's consider a scenario where interest rates rise sharply}.

Scenarios are imagined sequences of events or possible situations. The word often appears in planning contexts: {best-case scenario}, {worst-case scenario}, {doomsday scenario}. In film and theater, a scenario is an outline of a plot. The singular scenario has largely displaced the phrase "in that case" in conversational English: {In that scenario, we'd need more time}.

A scene is a place where something happens: {the scene of the crime}, {the scene of the accident}. In drama and film, a scene is a unit of action in one location—several scenes make an act. To {make a scene} is to create a public disturbance through emotional outburst. A scene is also a sphere of activity or interest: {the music scene}, {the downtown art scene}, {that's not really my scene}. Behind the scenes means out of public view, where the real work or decisions happen.

Scenery is the natural features of a landscape considered in terms of their appearance: {The mountain scenery was breathtaking}. In theater, scenery refers to the painted backdrops and constructed elements that create a stage setting. A {change of scenery} means a shift to new surroundings, often for refreshment or variety.

Scenes is the plural of scene—distinct portions of action in a play, film, or narrative. Extended, scenes are places where particular activities occur: {the music scene}, {the bar scene}. To {make a scene} is to cause a public disturbance. {Behind the scenes} means out of public view. In youth slang, scenes can express enthusiastic agreement or acknowledgment: {Want to grab dinner? —Scenes!}

A scenester is someone conspicuously embedded in a particular cultural scene—music, art, fashion, nightlife. The term often carries a dismissive edge, suggesting someone more focused on being seen and cultivating the right aesthetic than on genuine engagement: {The bar was full of scenesters in vintage jackets}. Compare hipster, which overlaps but emphasizes taste over social positioning.

Scenic describes views or places that are visually striking, especially natural landscapes: {a scenic overlook}, {the scenic route}. Taking the scenic route means choosing a longer path for its beauty—or, figuratively, taking unnecessary time to reach a point. In theater and film, scenic refers to stage sets and backdrops: {scenic design}, {scenic painter}.

Scent is a smell, especially a pleasant or distinctive one: {the scent of roses}, {a faint scent of perfume}. Animals follow a scent trail left by prey or other creatures. To scent something is to detect it by smell, or to sense it figuratively: {She scented trouble}. Scent also means perfume: {She dabbed scent behind her ears}. To throw someone off the scent is to mislead them.

Scented means having a smell, usually a pleasant one. Scented {candles}, scented {soap}, and scented {lotions} have had fragrance added. A {scented garden} features plants chosen for their aroma. The word almost always implies deliberate pleasantness—you wouldn't describe garbage as scented.

Scents is the plural of scent—smells, especially pleasant or distinctive ones: {the scents of pine and woodsmoke}, {a shop selling perfumes and scents}. The word also works as a verb meaning to smell or detect: {The dog scents a rabbit}. To scent danger or trouble is to sense it coming.

A scepter is an ornamental staff held by a monarch as a symbol of royal authority. The object appears in coronation ceremonies, official portraits, and heraldic imagery. Figuratively, the scepter represents sovereign power itself: {to wield the scepter}, {pass the scepter to an heir}. Also spelled sceptre in British English.

Scepters are ornamental staffs held by monarchs as symbols of royal authority. The scepter appears in coronation ceremonies and formal portraits, representing sovereign power: {The king raised his scepter}. Figuratively, to hold the scepter is to reign: {She held the scepter for forty years}.

A sceptic doubts claims that others accept readily, demanding evidence before belief. The word applies especially to those who question religious doctrines, paranormal phenomena, or received wisdom: {He was a sceptic about alternative medicine}. Sceptic is the British spelling; Americans write skeptic. In philosophy, scepticism is the position that certain knowledge is impossible.

Sceptical is the British spelling of skeptical—inclined to doubt or question claims, especially those accepted without evidence. A sceptical person withholds belief until convinced: {She remained sceptical of his excuses}. The word suggests healthy questioning rather than cynical dismissal.

Scepticism is the British spelling of skepticism, denoting a disposition to question claims or withhold belief until sufficient evidence is provided. In philosophy, scepticism refers to doctrines that challenge the possibility of certain knowledge. In everyday use, it describes a healthy wariness toward assertions that lack proof: {Her scepticism about miracle cures kept her from wasting money}. The word often carries positive connotations of critical thinking rather than mere cynicism.

Sceptics are people who doubt or question accepted beliefs, claims, or assertions. The term applies both to those who maintain a questioning attitude generally and to those who doubt specific things: climate sceptics, vaccine sceptics. In philosophy, sceptics hold that certain knowledge is impossible. {Sceptics demanded more evidence before accepting the findings.} This is the British spelling; Americans write skeptics.

A sceptre is a ceremonial staff held by monarchs as a symbol of royal authority. Kings and queens carry sceptres at coronations and other state occasions. The word extends figuratively to mean sovereign power itself: {to wield the sceptre}. Spelled scepter in American English.

Sceptres is the plural of sceptre, the British spelling of scepter—an ornamental staff held by monarchs as a symbol of royal authority. Kings and queens carry sceptres during coronations and formal ceremonies. Figuratively, sceptres represent sovereign power itself: {The sceptres of Europe trembled as revolution spread}.
clues: Staffs held by kings and queens

definition: Schadenfreude is pleasure derived from another's misfortune—a German word adopted into English because no native term quite captures the concept. The feeling ranges from mild satisfaction when an arrogant rival fails to darker enjoyment of genuine suffering: {I felt a twinge of schadenfreude when my smug coworker got passed over for promotion}.

As a noun, schedule is a list of events aligned with anticipated times that serves as a reference. A schedule that lists the times at regular intervals, such as a bus schedule, is the same thing as a timetable. A schedule for things that will happen only once, such a conference schedule, can also be called a program. As a verb, schedule usually means find a time slot for: Have you scheduled a doctor’s appointment yet?

A scheduler is a person or system that arranges times for events, appointments, or tasks. In computing, a scheduler is the component of an operating system that determines which processes get CPU time and in what order: {The kernel scheduler prioritizes interactive tasks over background jobs}. Someone might also be called a scheduler if their job involves coordinating appointments or shifts: {Call the scheduler to book your next visit}.

Schedules is the plural of schedule—a plan that specifies times for events or activities: {class schedules}, {train schedules}, {work schedules}. As a verb, schedules means arranges or plans for a specific time: {She schedules her meetings for mornings}. To be {on schedule} is to proceed as planned; {behind schedule} means delayed.

Scheduling is the process of arranging events, tasks, or appointments into a timetable: {The scheduling of the conference took weeks}. In computing, scheduling refers to how an operating system allocates processor time among competing tasks. The word covers both the act of planning when things happen and the system that governs that timing.

A schema is a mental framework or outline that organizes knowledge and guides understanding. In psychology, schemas shape how we interpret new information: {His schema for "restaurant" includes being seated, ordering, and paying}. In computing and databases, a schema defines the structure of data—tables, fields, and relationships. The word appears in technical contexts where underlying structure matters more than surface content. Plural: schemas or schemata.

A schematic is a diagram showing the elements of a system using simplified, standardized symbols—especially for electrical circuits or mechanical assemblies: {The electrician consulted the schematic before rewiring}. As an adjective, schematic describes something presented in simplified or diagrammatic form: {a schematic overview of the process}. The word can suggest oversimplification: {His understanding of politics is too schematic}.

Schematics are technical diagrams that show how the parts of a system connect and relate to each other. The term applies most often to electrical circuits, where schematics use standardized symbols to represent components like resistors, capacitors, and transistors. Engineers and technicians rely on schematics to build, repair, or understand complex systems. {I can't fix this without the schematics.} The word also extends to any detailed plan showing how parts fit together: {She sketched out the schematics for the new database architecture.}

A scheme is a plan, especially one that's systematic or cleverly devised: {a scheme to defraud investors}, {a get-rich-quick scheme}. The word often carries a whiff of deviousness—to scheme is to plot. In British usage, scheme is more neutral, describing any organized plan: {a pension scheme}, {a colour scheme}. The word also applies to abstract arrangements: {rhyme scheme}, {classification scheme}.

Schemed is the past tense of scheme, meaning to make plans—usually secret or underhanded ones. The word carries connotations of cunning and self-interest: {They schemed to take over the company}, {He schemed his way into her inheritance}. Neutral planning is rarely called scheming; the word implies plotting.

A schemer is someone who makes plans, especially cunning or underhanded ones. The word carries negative connotations—schemers pursue their goals through manipulation rather than honest effort: {Office schemers always seem to get ahead}. A schemer calculates angles others don't see, often at others' expense.

Schemers are people who make plans, usually cunning or underhanded ones. The word carries a negative connotation—schemers plot for personal advantage, often at others' expense: {The schemers had been working behind the scenes for months}. A neutral planner makes plans; a schemer makes schemes.

Schemes are plans or arrangements, often with a suggestion of cleverness or cunning: {a get-rich-quick scheme}, {a scheme to defraud investors}. The word carries a whiff of suspicion in American English—schemes sound underhanded. In British usage, scheme is more neutral, referring to official programs: {a pension scheme}, {a housing scheme}. To scheme is to plot or plan, usually with self-interested motives.

Scheming describes calculated, often underhanded planning to achieve a goal. A scheming person plots strategically, usually for personal gain: {a scheming politician}, {scheming to get the inheritance}. The word carries connotations of manipulation and self-interest—scheming implies cunning rather than straightforward effort.

A schism is a formal split within an organization, typically a religious body, resulting from disagreement over doctrine, leadership, or practice. The Great Schism of 1054 divided Christianity into Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches, and the word still carries ecclesiastical weight. More broadly, schism describes any deep division that fractures a formerly unified group: {The party suffered a schism over immigration policy}. Unlike a mere disagreement, a schism implies a lasting rupture.

Schisms are divisions or separations within a group, especially one that was previously unified. The term most often appears in religious contexts, where a schism occurs when factions break apart over doctrinal disagreements or disputes about leadership. {The Great Schism of 1054 divided Christianity into Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches.} The word extends to any significant split in an organization or movement: {Policy disagreements created lasting schisms within the party.}

Schizophrenia is a severe mental disorder characterized by distorted thinking, hallucinations, delusions, and withdrawal from reality. Symptoms often include hearing voices, paranoid beliefs, and disorganized speech or behavior. The word is frequently misused to mean split personality or internal conflict—{the schizophrenia of American foreign policy}—but the clinical condition involves psychosis, not multiple selves.

Schizophrenic describes someone with schizophrenia, a severe mental disorder marked by distorted thinking, hallucinations, and difficulty distinguishing reality from delusion. As a noun, a schizophrenic is a person with the condition: {Her brother is a schizophrenic who requires daily medication}. Loosely and often offensively, schizophrenic describes anything erratic or contradictory: {The company's schizophrenic pricing strategy confused customers}. This casual use is considered insensitive to those with the actual disorder.

A schlemiel is an awkward, clumsy person who seems destined for misfortune—the one who spills the soup. The word comes from Yiddish and carries affectionate contempt rather than malice. A schlemiel differs from a schlimazel: the schlemiel spills the soup, the schlimazel gets it spilled on him. {Don't be such a schlemiel.}

Schlep comes from Yiddish and means to carry or haul something cumbersome, or to make a tedious journey: {I schlepped groceries up four flights of stairs}, {We schlepped all the way across town for nothing}. The word emphasizes effort and inconvenience. As a noun, a schlep is such a burdensome trip or task: {Getting there is a real schlep}.

Schlepp comes from Yiddish and means to drag or haul something with effort: {I schlepped groceries up four flights of stairs}. It often implies tedious effort or an inconvenient journey: {We schlepped all the way across town for nothing}. As a noun, a schlepp is a tedious trip or a clumsy, incompetent person. Also spelled schlep.

Schlepped is the past tense of schlep, a Yiddish-derived verb meaning to carry or drag something heavy or cumbersome: {I schlepped groceries up four flights of stairs}. It also means to make a tedious journey: {We schlepped all the way across town for nothing}. The word conveys effort and inconvenience.

A schlepper is someone who lugs things around or drags themselves from place to place—a carrier of burdens, often weary or unglamorous. From Yiddish, the word can describe a delivery person or errand-runner, but more often carries a dismissive tone: a nobody, a loser, someone undistinguished. {I'm just a schlepper—I carry the equipment while the talent performs.}

Schlepping is the act of hauling or lugging something, especially with effort or tedium. From Yiddish, the word implies burden—physical or psychological. You schlep groceries up five flights of stairs, or schlep across town for a meeting that could have been an email: {I've been schlepping this laptop around all day}. The noun schlep refers to an arduous journey or task.

Schleps is the third-person singular of schlep, meaning to haul or carry something cumbersome, or to make a tedious journey: {She schleps groceries up three flights of stairs every week}. From Yiddish, the word emphasizes effort and inconvenience. As a noun, a schlep is such a burdensome trip: {Getting to the airport is a real schlep}.

Schlock is cheap, trashy, or low-quality merchandise or entertainment. The word comes from Yiddish and carries affectionate contempt—acknowledging something is bad while suggesting it might be enjoyably so: {We watched schlocky horror movies all weekend}. Schlock horror, schlock fiction, and schlock art deliver guilty pleasures without pretense of quality.

Schlocky means cheap, trashy, or of low quality. The word comes from Yiddish and carries a dismissive tone toward things that are shoddily made or artistically worthless: {a schlocky horror movie}, {schlocky souvenirs from the gift shop}. Something schlocky may have a certain campy appeal despite—or because of—its obvious cheapness.

A schlub is a person who is clumsy, stupid, or socially awkward—someone hapless and unglamorous. The word carries affectionate contempt: {He's a lovable schlub who can't get out of his own way}. From Yiddish, it often describes ordinary, unremarkable people, especially men: {Just another schlub commuting to work}.

Schlubby describes someone or something dowdy, unstylish, or sloppily put together. From Yiddish *schlub* (a clumsy or unattractive person), the adjective suggests rumpled clothes, poor grooming, or general slovenliness: {He showed up in his schlubby weekend sweats}. The word carries mild affection—schlubby is more endearing than insulting.

Schlubs are ordinary, unremarkable people—especially ones perceived as awkward, unfashionable, or slightly slovenly. The word carries affectionate condescension: {Just a bunch of schlubs watching the game}. From Yiddish, it suggests someone lacking polish or ambition, the opposite of someone impressive or put-together. The singular is schlub.

Schlump, from Yiddish, describes a slovenly, lazy, or unkempt person—someone who shuffles through life without much energy or attention to appearance. The word carries affectionate contempt: {He's been lying on the couch all day like a schlump}. As a verb, to schlump is to move or sit in a slouchy, listless way. Also spelled schlub or shlump.
clues: Unkempt person lacking drive or energy

definition: Schlumpy describes someone or something that looks shabby, unkempt, or carelessly dressed. Derived from Yiddish, it suggests a rumpled, sloppy appearance without much concern for style or presentation. {He showed up to the interview in a schlumpy sweater and wrinkled khakis.} A schlumpy person isn't necessarily dirty, just indifferent to looking polished or put-together. The word carries affectionate undertones when self-applied but can be mildly insulting when directed at others.

Schmaltz is excessive sentimentality, especially in music, art, or entertainment—the kind of emotional appeal that feels manipulative or cheap: {The movie was pure schmaltz, with swelling violins and tearful reunions}. The word comes from Yiddish for rendered chicken fat, suggesting something greasy and over-rich. Also spelled shmaltz.

Schmaltzy describes something excessively sentimental or emotionally overwrought—music, movies, or gestures that lay on the feelings too thick. From Yiddish *schmaltz* (rendered chicken fat), suggesting something rich to the point of being cloying: {a schmaltzy love song}, {The movie was entertaining but schmaltzy}. The noun schmaltz works the same way: {pure schmaltz}.

Schmear comes from Yiddish and means a spread or smear, typically cream cheese on a bagel: {I'll have a bagel with a schmear}. The phrase {the whole schmear} means everything, the entire affair—similar to "the whole shebang": {They ordered lox, bagels, the whole schmear}.

A schmo is an ordinary, unremarkable person—often one who's a bit foolish or easily taken advantage of. The word comes from Yiddish and carries mild contempt or affectionate dismissal: {Some schmo from the home office wants to see the reports}. Also spelled schmoe. The related schlemiel and schmuck occupy nearby territory.

A schmoe is an ordinary, unremarkable person—often one who's a bit foolish or easily taken advantage of. The word carries mild contempt or pity: {Some poor schmoe got stuck with the bill}. It suggests someone average, anonymous, perhaps gullible—the guy who doesn't know what's really going on. Also spelled schmo.
clues: Any random dolt off the street

definition: Schmoes is the plural of schmo, a mildly dismissive term for an ordinary, unremarkable, or foolish person. It carries affectionate contempt—not sharp insult but gentle condescension: {just a bunch of schmoes watching the game}, {average schmoes like you and me}. From Yiddish, related to schmuck but softer.

Schmooze means to chat in a friendly, often strategic way—making small talk to build connections or curry favor. The word comes from Yiddish and carries a whiff of insincerity: {He spent the cocktail hour schmoozing potential investors}. A schmoozer works a room. Schmoozing can be genuine socializing, but often implies networking with an agenda.

A schmoozer is someone skilled at friendly, ingratiating conversation—the kind of person who works a room, remembers names, and makes everyone feel important. The term carries a hint of calculation: schmoozers chat not purely for pleasure but to build connections or gain advantage. {He's a natural schmoozer who always leaves with a handful of business cards.}

Schmoozing is friendly, ingratiating conversation, especially to build social connections or advance one's interests. The word comes from Yiddish and carries a slightly cynical edge—schmoozing often implies working a room, cultivating contacts, or buttering someone up: {He spent the cocktail hour schmoozing potential investors}. Someone good at it is a schmoozer.

Schmoozy describes someone or something characterized by friendly, ingratiating conversation—often with an ulterior motive. A schmoozy salesperson works the room with charm and flattery. A schmoozy atmosphere encourages casual networking and deal-making: {The cocktail hour got increasingly schmoozy as people angled for introductions}. The word carries a hint of insincerity.

A schmozzle is a chaotic mess or confused situation—a muddle, a state of disorder: {The whole project turned into a complete schmozzle}. The word is informal and somewhat old-fashioned, more common in British, Australian, and South African English than American. Also spelled schemozzle or shemozzle.

Schmuck is a Yiddish-derived insult meaning a stupid or contemptible person. The word originally meant penis in Yiddish, but that sense has faded in English, where it now functions as a milder put-down than its origin suggests: {Don't be a schmuck}, {I felt like a schmuck for forgetting her birthday}. The word carries a sense of foolishness or social cluelessness rather than malice.
clues: Person who acts without any class

definition: Schmucks is the plural of schmuck, a Yiddish-derived insult for a contemptible or foolish person. The word originally meant penis in Yiddish, but that sense has faded in English. It's milder than it sounds—roughly equivalent to jerk or idiot: {Don't be such schmucks}, {Those schmucks didn't even read the contract}.

Schmutz is dirt, grime, or any bit of filthy matter—borrowed from Yiddish. It often refers to a smudge or spot on a surface: {You've got a little schmutz on your face}. The word carries an affectionate, fussy quality, as when a parent licks a thumb to wipe something off a child's cheek.

Schnapps is a strong alcoholic spirit, typically clear and distilled from grain or potatoes. In German-speaking countries, it refers to any distilled liquor and is often fruit-flavored. In American usage, schnapps usually means sweetened flavored liqueurs like peppermint or peach schnapps: {We did schnapps shots after dinner}.

A schnauzer is a breed of dog originating in Germany, characterized by a wiry coat, bushy eyebrows, and a distinctive bearded muzzle. The breed comes in three sizes: miniature, standard, and giant. Schnauzers were originally bred as working dogs for guarding and ratting. {Their schnauzer barked at every delivery truck.}

Schnauzers is the plural of schnauzer, a breed of dog originating in Germany, characterized by a distinctive bearded muzzle and wiry coat. The breed comes in three sizes—miniature, standard, and giant—each recognized as separate breeds. {She has two schnauzers that follow her everywhere.}
clues: German breed with distinctive facial hair

definition: Schnitzel is a thin cutlet of meat, pounded flat, breaded, and fried until crispy. The dish is German and Austrian in origin. Wiener schnitzel is made with veal; other versions use pork or chicken. {The schnitzel was golden brown and covered half the plate.}

A schnook is a pitifully meek or gullible person—someone easily taken advantage of or pushed around. The word comes from Yiddish and carries affectionate contempt: {Don't be such a schnook—stand up for yourself}. A schnook isn't malicious, just hapless.

Schnookums is a saccharine term of endearment, typically used for a romantic partner, baby, or pet. The word is deliberately cutesy and often deployed ironically or self-mockingly: {How's my little schnookums today?} It belongs to a family of playful pet names like sweetums and snookums.

Schnoz is informal slang for a nose, especially a large or prominent one. The word comes from Yiddish and carries a humorous or affectionate tone: {Look at the schnoz on that guy}. Also spelled schnozz or schnozzle.

Schnozz is informal slang for a nose, especially a large or prominent one. The word has a Yiddish flavor and often carries affectionate humor rather than insult: {Look at the schnozz on that guy}. Comedian Jimmy Durante was famously nicknamed "The Schnozz" for his distinctive nose. Also spelled schnoz or schnozzle.

A scholar is someone devoted to learning and study, especially in academic fields. The word suggests deep expertise and serious intellectual work: {a Shakespeare scholar}, {a biblical scholar}. Scholar can also mean a student, particularly one who holds a scholarship: {Rhodes scholars study at Oxford}. Scholarly describes work characterized by careful research and analysis.

Scholarly describes work, activity, or people characterized by serious academic study and intellectual rigor. A scholarly {article} meets the standards of academic research; a scholarly {person} devotes themselves to learning and careful analysis. The word suggests depth and methodical attention rather than casual interest: {a scholarly examination of Renaissance art}.

Scholars are people devoted to learning and academic study, typically through research and teaching at universities. The word implies deep expertise in a specialized field: {a Shakespeare scholar}, {a biblical scholar}. A scholar can also be a student who holds a scholarship. Scholarly describes work marked by careful research and rigorous standards.

Scholarship is the pursuit of knowledge through serious study and research, or the body of work produced by such effort: {Her scholarship on medieval history is widely cited}. A scholarship is also financial aid awarded to students, typically based on academic merit or need: {She won a full scholarship to the university}. The word carries connotations of rigor and intellectual achievement.

Scholarships are financial awards given to students to help pay for education. Unlike loans, scholarships don't require repayment. They may be based on academic achievement, athletic ability, financial need, or membership in particular groups: {She received a full scholarship to play basketball}. The word also refers to serious academic study: {a work of impressive scholarship}.
