A school is an institution or setting where instruction is given. In American English, school is used generally to designate education from early childhood through university. In British English, school is more likely to refer to places and experiences up to the end of secondary education. When school precedes another noun the resulting compound is usually about an entity or activity closely associated with elementary and secondary education: school lunch, school teacher, school uniform. When someone is schooled in a subject, that are instructed in it, or are very experienced in and knowledgeable about it.

A schoolbag is a bag for carrying books, supplies, and other items to and from school. The term covers backpacks, messenger bags, and traditional satchels—any bag regularly used for this purpose: {She stuffed her homework into her schoolbag}.

A schoolboy is a boy who attends school, typically elementary or secondary. The word often carries connotations of youth and inexperience: {schoolboy error}, {schoolboy crush}. As an adjective, it suggests naive enthusiasm or amateur mistakes: {He made a schoolboy blunder on the contract}.

A schoolbus is a vehicle, typically yellow in North America, used to transport students to and from school. The distinctive color and flashing lights signal other drivers to stop when children are boarding or exiting. Also spelled as two words: school bus.

Schoolbuses is the plural of schoolbus, the yellow vehicles that transport students to and from school in North America. The distinctive color—officially "school bus yellow"—was standardized in 1939 for visibility and safety. {A line of schoolbuses waited outside the gymnasium after the game.}

Schoolchildren are children who attend school, typically ranging from about five to eighteen years old. The word emphasizes their collective identity as students: {Schoolchildren lined up for the bus}, {The museum offers programs for schoolchildren}. The singular schoolchild exists but sounds awkward; most people say schoolboy, schoolgirl, or just student.

Schooldays are the years spent in formal education, typically from childhood through adolescence. The word carries nostalgic weight, evoking memories of classrooms, friendships, and coming-of-age experiences: {I haven't seen her since our schooldays}. Often appears in the phrase {back in my schooldays}. Also spelled as two words: school days.

Schooled means educated or trained, often in a particular skill or discipline: {She was schooled in classical piano from age five}. In informal use, to school someone is to defeat them decisively or teach them a humbling lesson: {He got schooled on the basketball court}. The slang sense carries a note of embarrassment for the one being taught.

A schoolgirl is a girl who attends school, typically referring to primary or secondary students rather than university. The word often evokes images of uniforms, youth, and innocence: {She wore her hair in schoolgirl braids}. As an adjective, schoolgirl describes qualities associated with young female students—sometimes naivety, sometimes enthusiasm: {a schoolgirl crush}.

Schoolgirls is the plural of schoolgirl—a girl who attends school, typically of primary or secondary age. The word often carries connotations of youth, innocence, or naivety: {She giggled like a schoolgirl}. In some contexts, particularly in fashion or certain media, schoolgirl evokes a specific aesthetic of uniforms, plaid skirts, and knee socks.

A schoolhouse is a building where classes are held, especially a small rural building serving as a single school. The word evokes one-room schools of earlier American history, where students of all ages learned together: {the little red schoolhouse}. Modern usage is nostalgic or regional.

Schooling is formal education, especially at the primary and secondary levels: {She had very little schooling}. The word emphasizes the institutional process rather than the knowledge gained. Schooling also means training or discipline: {The horse needs more schooling before competition}. In a competitive sense, to give someone a schooling is to defeat or outperform them decisively, often with an implication of teaching them a lesson.

A schoolkid is a child or adolescent who attends school. The term is informal and slightly more casual than *student* or *pupil*: {The sidewalks were crowded with schoolkids heading home}. It applies broadly from elementary through high school ages.

Schoolkids are children who attend school, typically from elementary through high school age. The term is casual and often appears in contexts about education policy, safety, or childhood experience: {Schoolkids poured out of the building when the bell rang}. Also spelled as two words.

A schoolmarm is a female schoolteacher, especially one working in a rural or old-fashioned setting. The term carries connotations of strictness, primness, and old-fashioned propriety. When used figuratively, schoolmarm describes anyone—regardless of gender—who is excessively prim, pedantic, or moralistic: {Stop being such a schoolmarm about my grammar}. The word has a slightly dismissive or mocking tone, suggesting someone uptight or overly concerned with rules.

Schoolmarms is the plural of schoolmarm, a somewhat dated term for a female schoolteacher, especially one seen as prim, strict, or old-fashioned. The word often carries a faintly mocking tone, suggesting someone overly concerned with rules and propriety: {She scolded him like a schoolmarm correcting grammar}. The singular also appears as schoolma'am.

A schoolmaster is a male teacher, especially the head or principal of a school. The term sounds old-fashioned in most contexts today, evoking images of stern Victorian educators with canes: {The schoolmaster rapped the desk for silence}. It persists in British private school usage and historical fiction. A schoolmaster can also be someone who instructs in a broader sense: {Experience is a hard schoolmaster}.

A schoolnight is a night before a school day, typically Sunday through Thursday. Parents invoke it to enforce early bedtimes or refuse requests: {You can't stay up late on a schoolnight}. Adults use it self-deprecatingly when declining evening plans: {I'd better not—it's a schoolnight}. The term implies responsibility winning over fun.

A schoolroom is a room where classes are taught, especially in elementary schools or in older educational settings. The word evokes traditional education—desks in rows, a chalkboard, a teacher at the front: {The old schoolroom still had its original wooden benches}. Modern usage often favors classroom.

Schools are institutions for teaching and learning, typically for children and adolescents: {elementary school}, {high school}. The word extends to universities and specialized training programs: {law school}, {film school}. A school is also a group of fish or other aquatic animals swimming together. As a verb, to school someone is to educate or train them, or informally, to defeat them decisively while demonstrating superior skill: {He got schooled on the basketball court}. A school of thought is a shared set of beliefs or methods among a group.

Schoolwork is the academic tasks students complete as part of their education—homework, assignments, projects, and studying. The term typically refers to work done outside class hours: {She stayed up late finishing her schoolwork}. It encompasses everything from daily homework to long-term research papers.

A schoolyard is the outdoor area adjacent to a school building where children play during recess and lunch breaks. The term often modifies other nouns to suggest childish or unsophisticated behavior: a schoolyard {bully}, schoolyard {taunts}, schoolyard {antics}. {The argument devolved into schoolyard name-calling.}

Schoolyards are the outdoor areas of schools where children play during recess and before or after classes. The word evokes childhood games, social hierarchies, and the rough-and-tumble of growing up: {schoolyard bullies}, {schoolyard taunts}. As a modifier, schoolyard often suggests something juvenile or unsophisticated: {schoolyard insults}, {schoolyard romance}.

A schooner is a sailing vessel with two or more masts, rigged fore-and-aft rather than with square sails. Schooners were common cargo and fishing ships in the 18th and 19th centuries: {The schooner sailed up the coast carrying lumber}. In some regions, a schooner is also a tall beer glass.

Schooners are sailing vessels with two or more masts, rigged fore-and-aft—the sails run along the length of the ship rather than across it. They were workhorses of 18th and 19th century coastal trade, prized for speed and maneuverability with small crews. A schooner is also a tall beer glass, typically holding a pint or more: {He ordered a schooner of lager}.

Schtick is a performer's signature routine, gimmick, or style—the thing they're known for: {His schtick is playing the confused foreigner}. From Yiddish, the word extends beyond entertainment to describe anyone's characteristic approach or angle: {What's your schtick?} The spelling varies: shtick, schick, shtik.

Schticks is the plural of schtick, a performer's signature routine, gimmick, or comic bit: {His schticks were getting stale}. More broadly, any person's characteristic approach or recurring behavior pattern: {She has several schticks she uses to close deals}. Also spelled shticks.

Sciatica is pain radiating along the sciatic nerve, which runs from the lower back through the hips and down each leg. The condition typically affects only one side of the body and ranges from a dull ache to sharp, burning pain: {Her sciatica flared up after the long drive}. Usually caused by a herniated disk or bone spur compressing the nerve.

Science is the activity of experimentation and observation of the natural world, with a view to understanding how it works and what laws govern it. A key feature of science is the requirement that an experimental result should be replicable. Information and knowledge gained from the conduct of science is also called science. Different branches of science are typically identified by a modifier, such as computer science, medical science, and social science.

Sciences are branches of knowledge based on systematic observation, experimentation, and evidence—typically the natural sciences (physics, chemistry, biology) and sometimes the social sciences (economics, psychology, sociology). The term often contrasts with the arts or humanities: {She's better at sciences than languages}. Someone {has something down to a science} when they've perfected a reliable method.

Scientific describes methods, knowledge, or activities based on systematic observation, experimentation, and evidence. A scientific {approach} follows rigorous procedures to test hypotheses. Scientific {consensus} represents agreement among experts based on accumulated research. The word can also mean precise or methodical: {He brought scientific rigor to his cooking}.

A scientist is someone who studies the natural world through systematic observation and experiment. The term typically implies formal training and adherence to scientific method—forming hypotheses, testing them, analyzing results. Scientists work across disciplines: {a climate scientist}, {a political scientist}, {a data scientist}. The word carries authority; calling someone a scientist suggests rigor and expertise, which is why it gets contested: {Is a social scientist really a scientist?}

Scientists are people who study the natural world through systematic observation and experiment. The term usually implies professional researchers in fields like biology, chemistry, physics, or geology, though it extends to anyone applying scientific method: {citizen scientists tracked bird migrations across the region}. A {mad scientist} is a stock character—the genius whose experiments go dangerously wrong.

A scimitar is a curved sword with a single sharp edge on the convex side, associated with Middle Eastern and South Asian warriors. The blade's curve makes it effective for slashing from horseback. In Western usage, scimitar often serves as a generic term for any curved Eastern sword: {The pirate's scimitar gleamed in the torchlight}.

Scimitars is the plural of scimitar, a curved sword with a single cutting edge on the convex side, associated with Middle Eastern and Central Asian warriors. The distinctive backward curve distinguishes it from European straight swords: {The cavalry charged with scimitars raised}. The word evokes exotic or historical settings in fiction and film.

A scion is a descendant or heir, especially of a wealthy or prominent family: {a scion of the Rockefeller dynasty}. The word carries connotations of inherited privilege and lineage. In horticulture, a scion is a shoot or twig cut from one plant to be grafted onto another—the ancestral meaning from which the figurative use grew.

Scions is the plural of scion, which has two main senses. In horticulture, a scion is a shoot or twig cut from one plant to be grafted onto another: {The scions were carefully selected from the healthiest trees}. More commonly, scions are descendants or heirs, especially of wealthy or prominent families: {scions of old money}, {the scions of a political dynasty}.

Scissor functions as a verb meaning to cut with scissors or to move in a scissor-like motion—legs or blades crossing and recrossing: {She scissored the article from the newspaper}, {His legs scissored through the water}. As an adjective, it describes this crossing action: a {scissor kick} in swimming. The noun is almost always plural: scissors.

Scissoring describes a motion like scissors opening and closing—legs crossing and uncrossing, blades cutting. In sexual slang, scissoring refers to a position where two women interlock their legs and rub genitals together: {They were scissoring on the couch}. The term appears frequently in pornography and casual discussion of lesbian sex, though its prevalence in actual practice is debated.

Scissors are a hand-held cutting tool with two blades joined at a pivot, operated by squeezing the handles together so the sharpened edges slide past each other. The word is typically plural even when referring to a single instrument: {a pair of scissors}, {the scissors are in the drawer}. Scissors can also describe a movement where two things cross like scissor blades, as in a scissors kick in swimming or soccer. To scissor something is to cut it with scissors or to move in a crossing motion.

Scoff means to mock or express contempt, usually through dismissive words or tone: {Critics scoffed at the idea}, {She scoffed when I suggested we could finish on time}. The word implies not just disagreement but derision—treating something as unworthy of serious consideration. In British slang, scoff is also a verb meaning to eat quickly or greedily: {He scoffed the whole pizza}.

Scoffed is the past tense of scoff, meaning to mock or express contemptuous disbelief: {He scoffed at the idea of getting up early}. The word conveys dismissive ridicule—not just disagreement but treating something as absurd or beneath consideration. In British usage, scoff can also mean to eat greedily: {She scoffed the entire pizza}.

Scoffing is mocking or expressing contemptuous disbelief. Someone scoffing at an idea dismisses it as absurd or unworthy: {He scoffed at the suggestion that he apologize}. The word implies superiority—the scoffer considers themselves above whatever they're rejecting. In British usage, scoffing also means eating greedily: {She scoffed the entire cake}.

A scofflaw is someone who habitually ignores or flouts laws, especially minor ones. The term originally targeted those who violated Prohibition laws, but now applies broadly to anyone who treats rules as optional: {The city cracked down on parking scofflaws}. It carries a tone of contempt for the person's disregard of civic duty.

Scofflaws are people who habitually disregard laws, especially minor ones they consider beneath enforcement: {The city cracked down on parking scofflaws}. The word was coined during Prohibition for those who flouted alcohol laws. It now applies broadly to anyone who treats rules as optional—tax evaders, jaywalkers, those who ignore court summonses.

Scoffs means mocks or dismisses with contempt. To scoff at something is to treat it as unworthy of serious consideration: {Critics scoffed at the idea}, {She scoffed when I suggested we could finish by Friday}. The noun scoff is the act itself or a mocking remark. Scoffs often proves premature—people scoff at innovations that later succeed.

To scold is to rebuke someone angrily, typically for a fault or misbehavior: {She scolded him for leaving the door open}. The word suggests sharp, sustained criticism rather than a single correction—often from a position of authority like parent to child. As a noun, scold once meant a habitually nagging person, especially a woman, now dated and offensive.

Scolded is the past tense of scold, meaning to rebuke or criticize sharply, especially for a fault or misbehavior. The word often implies a tone of angry disappointment: {She scolded him for leaving the door unlocked}. Scolding suggests a verbal reprimand rather than punishment—more lecture than consequence.

Scolding is sharp verbal criticism or rebuke, typically from someone in authority to someone who has misbehaved: {The child got a scolding for tracking mud inside}. A scolding is usually brief and pointed rather than prolonged—more a burst of disapproval than a lecture.

Scolds is the third-person singular of scold, meaning to criticize or rebuke someone sharply, especially for a fault or mistake: {She scolds him whenever he leaves dishes in the sink}. The word often implies a nagging or persistent quality to the criticism, and frequently describes how parents or authority figures address children or subordinates.

A sconce is a wall-mounted light fixture, typically decorative, that holds candles or electric bulbs and directs light upward or outward: {The hallway was lit by antique brass sconces}. Historically, a sconce was also a small defensive fortification or earthwork, though this sense is now rare outside historical contexts.

Sconces are light fixtures mounted on walls, typically holding candles or electric bulbs and projecting outward from the surface. They provide ambient or accent lighting in hallways, beside mirrors, or flanking fireplaces: {The brass sconces cast a warm glow in the dining room}. Historically, sconces held candles or torches; modern versions are usually electric.

A scone is a small, lightly sweetened baked good, typically round and served with tea. British scones resemble American biscuits—tender, crumbly, often split and spread with clotted cream and jam. American scones tend to be denser, wedge-shaped, and sometimes studded with fruit or glazed. The pronunciation varies: rhymes with "gone" in Britain, with "bone" in America.

Scones are small, lightly sweetened baked goods, typically round or wedge-shaped, served at breakfast or tea. British scones are plain and often split to serve with clotted cream and jam. American scones tend to be larger, richer, and may contain fruit, chocolate, or other additions. The word rhymes with either "stones" or "cons" depending on region.

Scooch means to move over a short distance, usually while seated: {Scooch over so I can sit down}. It can also mean to slide or shimmy into a tight space: {She scooched through the gap in the fence}. The word is informal and suggests small, shuffling movements rather than standing up and relocating. Also spelled scootch.

Scooched is the past tense of scooch, meaning to move over or slide a short distance, usually while seated: {She scooched over to make room on the bench}. It can also mean to crouch or squeeze into a tight space: {He scooched down behind the couch}. The word is informal and often implies a small, shuffling adjustment rather than a full repositioning.

Scooching is the present participle of scooch, meaning to move over or shift position slightly, usually while seated: {Could you scooch over a bit?} The word suggests small, informal adjustments rather than dramatic movement. Also spelled scootching.

A scoop is a deep, rounded utensil for lifting and transferring loose material—ice cream, flour, coal. The word extends to the quantity held: {two scoops of ice cream}. In journalism, a scoop is an exclusive story obtained before competitors: {The reporter got the scoop on the scandal}. To scoop is to lift with such a motion, to hollow out, or to beat rivals to a story. The informal {What's the scoop?} asks for the latest information.

Scooped is the past tense of scoop—to lift or gather with a curved motion, like a shovel or cupped hands: {She scooped ice cream into bowls}. In journalism, to be scooped is to have a competitor publish your story first: {We got scooped by the Times}. In casual speech, scooped can mean picked up: {I scooped her from the airport}.

Scooping is the act of lifting or gathering with a curved motion, as with a spoon or cupped hands: {She was scooping ice cream into bowls}. In journalism, scooping means beating competitors to a story: {The local paper kept scooping the national outlets}. To be scooping someone up is to gather them quickly, often affectionately: {He was scooping the kids into his arms}.

Scoops is the plural of scoop—a utensil for lifting and transferring loose material, or the amount it holds: {two scoops of ice cream}. A scoop is also an exclusive news story obtained before competitors: {The reporter landed the scoop of the year}. To scoop is to lift with such a motion or to beat rivals to a story. {What's the scoop?} asks for the latest information.

Scoot means to move quickly or hurriedly, often with a sense of darting or sliding: {We need to scoot or we'll miss the train}. It can also mean to shift position slightly: {Scoot over so I can sit down}. A scooter is a small vehicle you propel by scooting—pushing with one foot against the ground.

Scootch means to move a short distance, typically while seated, by sliding or shuffling: {Scootch over so I can sit down}. It can also mean to crouch or squeeze into a tight space: {She scootched down in her seat to avoid being seen}. The word is informal and often implies a small, somewhat awkward adjustment of position. Also spelled scooch.

Scooted is the past tense of scoot, meaning to move quickly or suddenly, often in a hurried or informal way: {She scooted out the door before anyone could stop her}. It also describes sliding oneself along a surface while seated: {He scooted over to make room on the bench}.

A scooter is a small vehicle you stand or sit on. The original scooter is a child's toy—a platform with wheels and an upright handlebar, propelled by pushing one foot against the ground. A motor scooter is a lightweight motorcycle with a step-through frame: {She rides a Vespa scooter to work}. Electric scooters for rent now clutter city sidewalks.

Scooters is the plural of scooter—a small vehicle propelled by pushing one foot against the ground while standing on a narrow platform. Children's scooters have two or three wheels and a handlebar. Motorized versions include mopeds and Vespas. Mobility scooters help people with limited movement get around. {The kids raced their scooters down the sidewalk.}

Scooting is moving quickly or hurriedly, often with a sense of sliding or shuffling: {I'm scooting out early today}, {She scooted across the bench to make room}. The word suggests informal, low-effort movement. When dogs scoot, they drag their rear ends along the ground—usually a sign of irritation or parasites.

Scope is the range or extent of what something covers or addresses: {The scope of the investigation widened}. A project's scope defines its boundaries. Beyond scope means outside those limits. Scope also refers to instruments for viewing—microscope, telescope, stethoscope—and informally to any such device: {Let me take a look through the scope}. To scope something out is to survey or assess it: {We scoped out the competition}.

Scopes is the third-person singular verb form of scope—to examine, assess, or survey something: {She scopes out the competition before making a move}. The phrase {scope out} dominates casual usage, meaning to check out or evaluate: {Let's scope out that new restaurant}. As a plural noun, scopes are instruments for viewing: telescopes, microscopes, rifle scopes.

Scoping is the process of determining boundaries or extent. In project management, scoping defines what work will and won't be included: {We're still scoping the project}. In programming, scoping refers to where variables are accessible in code. Informally, to be scoping something is to be checking it out or sizing it up: {He was scoping the competition}.

Scorch means to burn the surface of something, damaging it with heat without fully consuming it: {I scorched my shirt with the iron}. Plants scorch in intense sun or drought, their leaves turning brown and dry. Scorching heat is oppressively hot. To scorch is also to move at high speed: {The car scorched down the highway}. A scorcher is an extremely hot day.

Scorched describes something burned on the surface, damaged by intense heat without being consumed: {The scorched earth smoldered for days}. Scorching heat is extreme and oppressive. A {scorched-earth policy} destroys anything useful to an advancing enemy—or metaphorically, leaves nothing behind when departing a situation. {The sun had scorched the grass brown}.

A scorcher is an extremely hot day: {Tomorrow's going to be a scorcher}. The word extends to anything intensely hot or powerful—a scorching criticism, a blistering serve in tennis, a devastating remark. In sports, a scorcher is a hard-hit ball or a blazing fast shot on goal.

Scorches is the verb scorch in the third person singular. To scorch is to burn a surface, causing discoloration or damage without destroying completely: {The iron scorched my shirt}. Heat scorches lawns in summer. Figuratively, a scorching {review} or scorching {criticism} is harshly negative. To {scorch the earth} is to destroy everything useful before retreating, denying resources to an enemy.

Scorching describes extreme heat that burns or singes: {a scorching summer day}, {scorching temperatures}. The word extends to anything intense or severe—a scorching {review} is harshly critical, a scorching {pace} is punishingly fast. To scorch is to burn superficially, leaving marks but not consuming: {The iron scorched the shirt}.

Most meanings of score, a noun and verb, arise from the core idea of a record, often written, of some other thing. The score in a competition is a statement of the points won by each competitor. The score of a test is a number representing the correct answers. The score of a musical work is a record of it in musical notation, from which it can be reproduced. When you score something, you assign a score to it, or in more literal use, you make physical markings on it. This meaning arises from the original notion of score, a mark being made to represent the quantity of twenty.

A scoreboard is a large display showing the score and other information during a sporting event or competition. The term extends to any visual tracking of comparative standings: {The company's sales scoreboard showed the western region in the lead}. To {put points on the scoreboard} is to achieve measurable success.

Scoreboards are displays showing the current score in a game or competition. The term extends to any visual tracking of comparative standings: {The company's sales scoreboard showed the Western region in the lead}. A scoreboard may be a physical board, an electronic display, or a screen graphic.

A scorebook is a book used to keep track of scores, typically in sports. Some scorebooks are official and are used to record the scores of several games or even an entire season. Other scorebooks are personal and contain scores of only one game or match.

A scorecard is a card or document for recording scores in a game or competition: {She kept the scorecard during the golf match}. Beyond sports, scorecard refers to any system for tracking performance or comparing results: {The administration's scorecard on environmental policy is mixed}. To {keep score} or {settle the score} uses the same logic of tracking and balancing accounts.

Scorecards are cards or sheets used to record points, performance, or progress. In golf, players mark strokes on a scorecard for each hole. In business, a scorecard tracks metrics against goals: {The company's quarterly scorecard showed improvement in customer satisfaction}. To {keep score} of something is to track it systematically.

Scored is the past tense of score. To score is to earn points in a game or competition: {She scored twice in the second half}. Score also means to achieve or obtain: {We scored tickets to the show}, {He finally scored with that girl}. In another sense, to score is to cut lines or grooves into a surface: {Score the meat before marinating}. Scored can describe something marked with such lines: {The scored surface helped the glue adhere}.

A scorekeeper is a person who records and maintains the score during a game or competition. The term extends to anyone who tracks progress or tallies results: {She appointed herself scorekeeper of his failures}. In figurative use, keeping score suggests monitoring wins and losses in relationships or disputes: {Marriage works better when neither partner is the scorekeeper}.

A scorer is someone who scores—whether putting points on a board in sports, keeping official tallies in competitions, or recording musical compositions. In sports, it can mean a player who scores frequently {the team's leading scorer} or the person tracking the game's statistics. The term extends to anyone who marks or rates: test scorers grade exams.

Scores is the plural of score, meaning recorded points in a game or competition: {The scores were tied at halftime}. Scores also means large numbers, roughly synonymous with dozens: {Scores of people attended the rally}. As a verb, scores means achieves or obtains: {She scores well on standardized tests}, {He finally scores a date with her}.

Scoring is the act of earning or recording points in a game or competition: {The team's scoring improved in the second half}. In broader use, scoring means achieving success—getting something desired: {He had trouble scoring tickets to the show}. As slang, scoring often means obtaining drugs or having sex. In music, scoring is the process of writing or arranging a composition for instruments: {She's scoring the film's soundtrack}.

Scorn is contempt mixed with derision—looking down on someone or something as worthless or beneath consideration. To scorn is to treat with such contempt: {She scorned his apology}. To {scorn to do} something is to refuse it as beneath one's dignity. Scornful means full of scorn; to be scorned is to be rejected contemptuously.

Scorned is the past tense of scorn, meaning to treat with contempt or reject disdainfully. A scorned lover has been spurned or cast aside: {Hell hath no fury like a woman scorned}. Scorned ideas or proposals have been dismissed with disdain. The word carries emotional weight—not just rejected, but rejected with contempt.

Scornful describes someone expressing contempt or disdain, treating something as beneath consideration: {She gave him a scornful look}. A scornful {laugh} mocks openly. Scornful people convey that the object of their scorn deserves derision: {He was scornful of their attempts to apologize}.

Scorns is the verb form of scorn, meaning to treat with contempt or disdain. Someone who scorns something dismisses it as unworthy of attention or respect: {She scorns conventional wisdom}, {He scorns anyone who disagrees with him}. The noun scorn refers to the contempt itself: {They heaped scorn on the proposal}.

A scorpion is an arachnid with a segmented tail ending in a venomous stinger, found mainly in warm climates. Scorpions have pincers like crabs and sting prey or threats by curving the tail over the body. The sting is painful to humans and occasionally dangerous. Scorpius, the scorpion constellation, is one of the zodiac signs.

Scorpions are arachnids with pincers and a curved tail ending in a venomous stinger. They inhabit warm regions worldwide and hunt insects and small prey. The plural often appears in warnings about desert environments: {Check your boots for scorpions}. Scorpio, the zodiac sign, takes its name from the constellation shaped like a scorpion.

To scotch something is to put an end to it or render it harmless—typically a rumor, plan, or threat: {Let me scotch that idea before it spreads}. The word suggests decisive suppression rather than gradual elimination. A scotch is also a wedge or block placed against a wheel to prevent rolling. As an adjective, scotch means frugal or sparing, though this sense is now rare. (Capitalized Scotch refers to whisky or things Scottish.)

Scots refers to the Germanic language or dialect spoken in lowland Scotland, distinct from both English and Scottish Gaelic: {Scots has its own literary tradition dating back centuries}. The word also describes things relating to Scotland or its people, though Scottish is more common in that sense. As a plural noun, Scots means Scottish people collectively: {The Scots have a reputation for thriftiness}. (Capitalized Scots is standard; lowercase scots is rare.)

A scoundrel is a dishonest or unscrupulous person—someone who behaves badly through cunning or moral failing rather than violence: {That scoundrel cheated half the town out of their savings}. The word has an old-fashioned, almost literary quality, and is sometimes used with grudging affection: {He was a charming scoundrel}.

Scoundrels is the plural of scoundrel, a person without moral principles—someone who lies, cheats, or behaves dishonorably. The word has an old-fashioned, almost theatrical quality: {Those scoundrels made off with the treasury}. It can be used affectionately for mischievous rogues: {My brothers were lovable scoundrels}.

Scour means to clean or brighten a surface by rubbing it hard, typically with an abrasive material: {She scoured the pots until they gleamed}. This vigorous action extends to searching thoroughly and systematically: {Police scoured the area for evidence}. Water scours when it rushes over a surface with enough force to erode or wear it away, as a river scouring its banks. The noun scour refers to the act of scouring or the erosion caused by rushing water.

Scoured is the past tense of scour, which has two distinct meanings. The first is to clean or polish by rubbing hard: {She scoured the pots until they gleamed}. The second is to search thoroughly: {Police scoured the area for evidence}. Both senses share an idea of intense, exhaustive effort applied to a surface or space.

A scourge is a cause of widespread suffering or affliction: {Famine was the scourge of the region}, {the scourge of addiction}. The word originally meant a whip used for punishment, and to scourge someone was to flog them. The punitive sense survives in figurative use—a scourge devastates, it doesn't merely inconvenience.

Scourges is the plural of scourge—something that causes widespread suffering or destruction: {the scourges of war and famine}, {Malaria remains one of Africa's greatest scourges}. A scourge was originally a whip used for punishment, and the word retains that sense of relentless affliction. The verb scourges means inflicts suffering upon: {Drought scourges the region every summer}.

Scourging is severe whipping or flogging, especially as punishment or torture. The term appears most often in religious and historical contexts—Christ's scourging before crucifixion, or medieval penitents scourging themselves. Figuratively, any harsh affliction may be called a scourging: {the scourging of the coastline by hurricanes}.

Scouring is vigorous cleaning by scrubbing or abrading: {scouring pots and pans}, {scouring the bathtub}. The word extends to thorough searching: {Police spent the night scouring the woods for the missing child}. In textile manufacturing, scouring removes natural oils and impurities from raw fibers. Water may scour a riverbed, eroding it through constant flow.

Scours means to clean or brighten by vigorous rubbing, typically with an abrasive: {She scoured the pot until it gleamed}. Extended, it means to search thoroughly and systematically: {Police scoured the neighborhood for evidence}. Water scours a channel by eroding it through persistent flow. In livestock, scours is severe diarrhea, especially in calves—a usage that functions as a singular noun: {The calf has scours}.

A scout is someone sent ahead to gather information—originally military reconnaissance, now extended to talent scouts searching for promising athletes, actors, or musicians. To scout is to search or explore: {We scouted locations for the wedding}. A Boy Scout or Girl Scout is a member of youth organizations emphasizing outdoor skills and character development; from this comes the informal sense of someone trustworthy or helpful: {He's a real scout}. (Capitalized Scout refers to the youth organizations or their members.)

Scouted is the past tense of scout—to search an area for information, talent, or resources. A military unit scouted enemy positions. A talent agent scouted nightclubs for promising singers. {We scouted locations for the wedding venue}. To scout something out is to investigate it thoroughly before committing: {She scouted out the neighborhood before signing a lease}.

Scouting is the activity of searching an area to gather information—military scouts assess enemy positions, talent scouts evaluate potential recruits, and location scouts find filming sites. The word also refers to the youth movement founded in the early twentieth century, emphasizing outdoor skills, community service, and character development: {She learned camping through scouting}. To go scouting is to search: {I went scouting for apartments}.

A scoutmaster is the adult leader of a troop of Boy Scouts, responsible for organizing activities, teaching outdoor skills, and supervising youth members. The role combines mentorship with practical instruction in camping, hiking, and citizenship: {He served as scoutmaster for fifteen years}.

Scouts are people sent ahead to gather information—about enemy positions, terrain, or talent. A military scout reconnoiters. A talent scout searches for promising athletes or performers: {The scouts loved his fastball}. To scout is to search or explore: {We scouted locations for the wedding}. If you scout around, you look for something: {I'll scout around for a better deal}. (Capitalized Scouts refers to the youth organization.)

A scowl is an angry or disapproving facial expression, with furrowed brow and downturned mouth. To scowl is to wear such an expression: {She scowled at the interruption}. Unlike a frown, which may indicate puzzlement or concentration, a scowl conveys displeasure or hostility.

Scowled is the past tense of scowl, meaning to frown in an angry or disapproving way. The expression involves furrowed brows and a downturned mouth, conveying displeasure or hostility: {She scowled at the interruption}. {He scowled but said nothing}.

Scowling describes the act of frowning deeply in a way that expresses displeasure, disapproval, or anger. The expression typically involves furrowed brows and a downturned mouth. {He sat scowling at his phone after reading the message.} Someone who is scowling may be genuinely upset or simply concentrating intensely—context usually makes the difference clear.

Scowls are angry or disapproving facial expressions, typically involving furrowed brows and a downturned mouth. As a verb, to scowl is to make such a face: {She scowled at the interruption}. A scowl communicates displeasure without words—darker than a frown, less dramatic than a glare.

To scrabble is to scratch, scrape, or claw frantically, usually while searching for something: {She scrabbled in her purse for her keys}. The word suggests hurried, somewhat desperate movements with the hands or fingers across a surface. Scrabble also means to struggle or scramble: {scrabbling to make ends meet}. (Capitalized Scrabble is the board game.)

Scrabbled is the past tense of scrabble, meaning to scratch, scrape, or claw frantically at a surface: {She scrabbled at the locked door}. It also means to scramble or struggle awkwardly: {He scrabbled up the rocky slope}. The word suggests desperate, clumsy effort—hands or feet working urgently against resistance. {The cat scrabbled for purchase on the tile floor.}

A scrabbler is someone who scrapes, scratches, or scrambles—usually with effort and without elegance. The word often describes someone struggling to get by or clawing their way forward: {He was a scrabbler, always hustling for the next opportunity}. A scrabbler may also be someone who plays the board game Scrabble.

Scrabbles is the third-person singular of scrabble, meaning to scratch, scrape, or claw frantically at a surface: {The cat scrabbles at the door to be let in}. It often suggests desperate or clumsy grasping: {She scrabbles for a handhold on the rock face}. Figuratively, to scrabble is to struggle or scramble: {He scrabbles to make ends meet}.

Scrabbling is frantic, clawing movement—scratching or scraping at a surface, often while struggling for grip or purchase: {I could hear something scrabbling in the walls}, {She was scrabbling at the door handle}. The word suggests desperate or undignified effort: {scrabbling for a foothold on the cliff}, {scrabbling to make ends meet}. It can also mean searching hastily through clutter: {He was scrabbling around in the drawer for his keys}.

Scraggly describes something thin, uneven, and unkempt—growing or hanging in irregular, straggling clumps. A scraggly beard is patchy and poorly maintained. Scraggly bushes are sparse and ragged. The word suggests neglect or natural disorder: {a few scraggly trees at the edge of the parking lot}, {his scraggly hair hadn't been cut in months}.

Scram means to leave quickly, usually as a command: {Scram, kid, you're bothering me}. The word is informal and slightly dated, evoking mid-twentieth-century American speech. In nuclear engineering, scram is an emergency reactor shutdown—either a verb or noun: {The operator scrammed the reactor}; {an automatic scram}.

Scramble involves hurried, often clumsy movement or mixing. You scramble up a rocky slope using hands and feet, or scramble to finish before a deadline. Scrambled eggs have been stirred while cooking. To scramble a signal is to make it unintelligible without a decoder. Fighter jets scramble when launched urgently in response to a threat. A scramble is also a disorderly rush: {There was a scramble for the exit}.

Scrambled describes something mixed up or disordered. Scrambled eggs are beaten and stirred while cooking until the yolks and whites form soft, irregular curds. A scrambled message has been encoded or garbled beyond recognition: {The signal was scrambled to prevent interception}. Scrambled brains suggest confusion or disorientation. Fighter jets scramble when they take off urgently in response to a threat.

Scrambles is the third-person singular verb form of scramble. To scramble is to move awkwardly or urgently, often on hands and knees: {She scrambled up the rocky slope}. To scramble eggs is to stir them while cooking. In military and aviation contexts, jets scramble when they launch urgently in response to a threat. A scramble can also be a competitive rush: {the scramble for concert tickets}. In golf, a scramble is a format where all players hit from the best ball's position.

Scrambling is the act of moving quickly and awkwardly, often using hands and feet to navigate rough terrain or obstacles: {We spent the afternoon scrambling over rocks to reach the summit}. It also describes hasty, disorganized effort to accomplish something under pressure: {There was a lot of scrambling to meet the deadline}. In communications, scrambling refers to encoding signals so unauthorized parties cannot understand them. In cooking, scrambling eggs means stirring them while frying.

Scrap is a small piece or fragment, especially one left over after the main portion has been used: {scraps of fabric}, {scraps of paper}. Food scraps are what remain after a meal. Scrap metal is discarded metal suitable for reprocessing. To scrap something is to discard or abandon it: {They scrapped the plan}. Separately, a scrap is a brief fight or quarrel, and to scrap is to engage in one: {The kids were scrapping in the yard}.

A scrapbook is a blank book for preserving and displaying memorabilia—photographs, newspaper clippings, ticket stubs, letters, pressed flowers. The practice emphasizes personal curation and decoration: {She kept a scrapbook of her travels}. As a verb, to scrapbook is to engage in this craft, which has spawned an industry of specialty papers, stickers, and tools.

Scrapbooking is the hobby of assembling photographs, memorabilia, and decorative elements into albums. Beyond simple photo storage, it involves artistic arrangement with papers, stickers, and embellishments to preserve memories: {She spent the weekend scrapbooking her daughter's graduation}. The practice has spawned a substantial craft industry.

Scrapbooks are blank books for preserving and displaying mementos—photographs, newspaper clippings, ticket stubs, pressed flowers, handwritten notes. The practice involves arranging these items on pages, often with decorative elements. As a verb, to scrapbook is to create such collections: {She spent the afternoon scrapbooking her vacation photos}.

Scrape means to drag something hard or rough across a surface, removing material or making a harsh sound: {She scraped the ice off the windshield}. You scrape a knee when you fall, scrape food off plates, scrape by on a small income. A scrape is the act itself, the sound it makes, or the resulting mark or wound. To get into a scrape is to find yourself in an awkward predicament—minor trouble you'll have to scrape your way out of.

Scraped is the past tense of scrape—to drag something rough or sharp across a surface. You scrape ice off a windshield, scrape a knee falling on pavement, or scrape the bottom of a pot clean. To scrape by or scrape through is to barely manage: {We scraped by on one income}. In computing, scraped data has been automatically extracted from websites: {They scraped thousands of job listings}.

A scraper is a tool for scraping—removing material from a surface by drawing a hard edge across it. Paint scrapers remove old coatings; ice scrapers clear windshields. In computing, a scraper is software that extracts data from websites: {The company built a scraper to harvest pricing data from competitors}. A {sky-scraper} is a building that scrapes the sky.

Scrapers are tools designed to remove material from a surface by dragging a hard edge across it. A paint scraper removes old finish from wood. An ice scraper clears windshields. In computing, a scraper is software that extracts data from websites automatically: {They built scrapers to harvest pricing data from competitor sites}. The singular is scraper.

Scrapes are instances of scraping—drawing something rough or sharp across a surface. A scrape can be a minor skin injury from friction: {She got a few scrapes on her knees}. The word also names difficult situations or minor conflicts: {He got into a few scrapes with the law}. In this sense, a scrape suggests trouble you've barely gotten into—or out of.

A scrapheap is a pile of discarded metal or machinery, typically at a junkyard. Figuratively, to be {thrown on the scrapheap} is to be discarded as useless or obsolete—often said of workers pushed out of jobs or ideas abandoned: {The policy ended up on the scrapheap of history}.

Scrapheaps are piles of discarded metal, machinery, or other unwanted materials. The word often appears figuratively: to be {thrown on the scrapheap} is to be discarded as useless, especially of workers deemed too old or obsolete. {The policy consigned thousands to the scrapheap.}

Scraping is the act of dragging something hard or sharp across a surface, often producing a harsh sound: {the scraping of chairs on the floor}. It removes material by abrasion: {scraping ice off the windshield}, {scraping the bottom of the barrel}. Scrapings are the bits removed this way. In computing, scraping means extracting data from websites automatically: {web scraping}, {data scraping}.

Scrapped means discarded or abandoned, usually because something is no longer useful or a plan didn't work out: {The old machinery was scrapped for parts}, {We scrapped our vacation plans when the car broke down}. The past tense of scrap, it applies to physical objects sent for salvage and to ideas or projects that get cancelled.

A scrapper is someone who fights readily or refuses to back down—a person with combative spirit who punches above their weight: {She's a scrapper who won't quit}. The word usually carries admiration for tenacity rather than criticism of aggression. Separately, a scrapper works in scrap metal salvage, collecting and processing discarded materials for recycling.

Scrappers are people who fight or struggle tenaciously. The word emphasizes grit and willingness to engage rather than skill or size: {The team was full of scrappers who never gave up}. A scrapper may also be someone who collects scrap metal for resale.

Scrappiness is the quality of being combative, tenacious, or willing to fight despite disadvantages. A scrappy team wins through hustle and determination rather than superior talent. The word carries admiration for underdogs who punch above their weight: {What she lacks in experience, she makes up for in scrappiness}.

Scrapping has two distinct sources. From scrap meaning a fragment or leftover, scrapping is the act of discarding or abandoning something: {They're scrapping the old policy}, {The navy is scrapping three destroyers}. From scrap meaning a fight, scrapping is engaging in a scuffle or heated dispute: {The kids were scrapping in the yard}, {rival factions scrapping over territory}.

Scrappy describes someone who fights above their weight—determined, combative, willing to scrap despite disadvantages. A scrappy team lacks talent but compensates with hustle: {The scrappy underdog took the game to overtime}. The word carries admiration for tenacity and resourcefulness. Separately, scrappy can mean consisting of scraps or fragments—disjointed and incomplete: {a scrappy collection of notes}.

Scraps are small pieces or bits left over after the main part of something has been used. Food scraps are the uneaten remains of a meal, often given to pets or composted. Scraps of fabric or paper are remnants that might be saved for later projects. In the plural, scraps can also mean fights or quarrels, usually brief and informal ones: {The kids got into scraps on the playground}. If you scrap something, you discard it or abandon a plan entirely.

A scrapyard is a place where discarded metal, vehicles, and machinery are collected for salvage or recycling. Old cars are crushed, appliances stripped for parts, and metals sorted for resale. Also called a junkyard: {We found a replacement bumper at the scrapyard}.

Scrapyards are places where discarded metal, vehicles, and machinery are collected for recycling or salvage. Old cars get crushed, appliances stripped for parts, and metals sorted for resale. The term evokes industrial landscapes of rusted heaps and heavy equipment: {We found a replacement fender at the scrapyard}. Also called junkyards or salvage yards.

To scratch a part of your body is to relieve the itch that is arising there. To scratch a surface is to leave a rough mark or marks in it, the way a collision scratches a car. To barely scratch the surface is to make only preliminary and perhaps insignificant progress. A scratch is an instance of scratching, or the mark(s) left by doing this. To make or do something from scratch is to start at the very beginning. Something not up to scratch is of less than average quality.

A scratchcard is a ticket with a concealed area that can be scratched off to reveal whether you've won a prize, typically in lotteries or promotional games. The coating is usually a thin metallic or latex layer removed with a coin or fingernail: {I won twenty dollars on a scratchcard}. Also spelled scratch card.

Scratchcards are lottery tickets or game cards with a coating that conceals symbols or numbers underneath. Players scratch off the opaque layer—usually with a coin—to reveal whether they've won a prize: {I bought a scratchcard at the gas station and won twenty dollars}. Also spelled as two words: scratch cards.

Scratched is the past tense of scratch—to drag something sharp across a surface, leaving a mark or relieving an itch. A scratched surface shows damage: {The table was badly scratched}. A scratched item has been removed from competition: {The horse was scratched from the race}. In informal use, scratched can mean hastily assembled: {a scratched-together meal}.

A scratcher is something or someone that scratches. Most commonly it refers to a device for scratching an itch—a back scratcher with its long handle, or a post for cats to claw. Scratcher also means a scratch-off lottery ticket: {I bought a few scratchers at the gas station}. In tattoo culture, a scratcher is an amateur who works without proper training or sanitation, often from home—the term is derogatory among professionals.

Scratchers are lottery tickets you play by scratching off an opaque coating to reveal symbols or numbers underneath: {I bought a few scratchers at the gas station}. The term is informal and primarily American. More broadly, anything that scratches—a back scratcher, a pet scratching at the door—can be called a scratcher.

Scratches are shallow marks or cuts made by something sharp or rough dragging across a surface. A cat leaves scratches on furniture; a key leaves scratches on a car door. On skin, scratches are minor wounds: {He came back from the hike covered in scratches}. To {start from scratch} is to begin with nothing—from the scratch line in a race.

Scratching is the act of scraping with nails, claws, or a rough surface—to relieve an itch, mark a surface, or cause damage. A DJ scratching moves a vinyl record back and forth to create rhythmic sounds: {He started scratching when he was fifteen}. To be scratching the surface is to deal only superficially with something. Lottery tickets require scratching to reveal potential winnings.

A scratchpad is a pad of paper for casual notes, rough calculations, or temporary jottings—things not meant to be kept. The term extends to any space for provisional work: a scratchpad in software holds data temporarily during processing, and a mental scratchpad is where you hold information while thinking through a problem.

Scratchwork is rough, informal calculation or writing done while working through a problem—the kind of notes you make on scrap paper before producing a clean final version. It's disposable by nature: {My scratchwork was a mess of crossed-out equations}. The term appears most often in math and science contexts, where preliminary figuring precedes polished solutions.

Scratchy describes something rough or irritating to the touch or sound. A scratchy wool sweater irritates the skin. A scratchy voice or recording sounds harsh and grating, as if damaged: {The old vinyl had a scratchy quality}. A scratchy throat feels raw and uncomfortable, often signaling a cold coming on.

Scrawl is hasty, careless handwriting—the kind that's barely legible: {I could barely make out his scrawl}. As a verb, to scrawl is to write in this manner: {She scrawled a note and left it on the counter}. The word suggests speed or indifference rather than careful penmanship.

Scrawled is the past tense of scrawl, meaning to write hastily or carelessly, producing messy, barely legible marks: {a note scrawled on the back of an envelope}, {graffiti scrawled across the wall}. The word suggests rushed or sloppy handwriting rather than deliberate penmanship.

Scrawling is writing in a hasty, careless, or illegible manner. The word emphasizes messiness over speed—scrawled handwriting sprawls across the page with uneven letters and poor control: {She was scrawling notes in the margins}. Scrawling can also describe drawing or marking surfaces carelessly: {graffiti scrawled on the subway walls}.

Scrawls are instances of hasty, careless handwriting—messy marks that sacrifice legibility for speed. The word carries a dismissive edge: to call someone's writing scrawls suggests it's barely readable. As a verb, to scrawl is to write this way: {She scrawled a note and left it on the counter}. Graffiti scrawled on walls. Doctors scrawl prescriptions.

Scrawny describes someone or something unattractively thin and bony: {a scrawny kid with knobby knees}, {scrawny chickens pecking in the yard}. The word carries a hint of weakness or malnourishment—you wouldn't call a lean athlete scrawny. It's mildly unflattering but not harsh.

To scream is to cry out loudly, especially in distress. Some things that make a loud noise or attract great attention are also said to scream, such as sirens and headlines, or people talking in a loud, angry way. A scream is an instance of screaming, or the sound made by it. Scream is also used informally to denote someone or something lively and enjoyable: Her new comedy is a real scream.

Screamed is the past tense of scream—to cry out loudly and sharply, usually from fear, pain, or excitement: {She screamed when the spider dropped on her arm}. Screamed also describes things that suggest such intensity: {Headlines screamed the scandal}. To say something screamed a quality means it was unmistakably obvious: {The whole outfit screamed money}.

A screamer is someone or something that screams. In informal use, it often describes something remarkable or extreme: a screamer of a goal, a screamer of a headache. In journalism, a screamer is a sensational headline. Online, a screamer is a video or image designed to lull viewers before startling them with a sudden loud noise and frightening image: {I fell for that screamer and nearly had a heart attack}.

Screamers are things that scream or provoke screaming. In journalism, a screamer is a sensational headline in large type. In slang, something exceptionally intense or impressive earns the label: {That last goal was a screamer}. In printing and computing, a screamer is an exclamation point. Certain South American birds known for their loud calls are also called screamers.

Screaming is loud, high-pitched vocalization typically expressing fear, pain, excitement, or anger. As an adjective, it intensifies: a screaming {headache} is severe, a screaming {deal} is exceptionally good, and screaming {colors} are glaringly bright. Something can be screamingly funny or screamingly obvious. {The baby was screaming all night.} {That jacket is a screaming shade of orange.}

Screamo is a subgenre of hardcore punk and emo that emerged in the 1990s, characterized by chaotic instrumentation and vocals that alternate between melodic passages and raw, high-pitched screaming. The style emphasizes emotional intensity and catharsis, with lyrics often exploring themes of personal anguish, existential despair, or political frustration. {I went through a screamo phase in high school.} Bands like Saetia and Orchid helped define the genre's sound.

Screams is the plural of scream—a loud, sharp cry expressing fear, pain, or excitement. Beyond literal shrieks, screams describes anything that demands attention: {The headline screams scandal}. Something that {screams} a quality displays it unmistakably: {The décor screams money}. In slang, if something {is screams}, it's hilarious: {That video is screams}.

Scree is the loose rocks and debris that accumulate on mountain slopes, typically below cliffs or along steep hillsides. The fragments range from gravel to boulder-sized, creating unstable footing for hikers: {We picked our way carefully across the scree field}. The word often appears in mountaineering contexts where such terrain presents both obstacle and hazard.

Screech is a harsh, high-pitched sound—sharp and unpleasant, like tires on pavement or an owl's cry. The word works as both noun and verb: {The car came to a halt with a screech of brakes}; {She screeched at him to stop}. Unlike a scream, which suggests fear or pain, screech emphasizes the grating quality of the sound itself.

Screeches are harsh, high-pitched sounds—sharp and unpleasant to the ear. Tires screech when braking hard, owls screech in the night, and people screech in alarm or anger. The word captures both the sound itself and the jarring effect it has on listeners: {The train's screeches echoed through the station}. To screech is to produce such a sound, or to bring something to a sudden halt: {The car screeched to a stop}.

Screeching describes a harsh, high-pitched sound—unpleasant and piercing. Tires screech when braking hard, owls screech in the night, children screech on playgrounds. The word emphasizes the grating quality: {The train came to a screeching halt}. Something that comes to a screeching halt stops abruptly and completely.

A screed is a long, tedious piece of writing or speech, usually a rant or harangue: {He launched into a screed about government corruption}. The word carries negative connotations—screeds are tiresome and often angry. In construction, a screed is a leveling tool or a strip of material used as a guide for smoothing concrete or plaster to an even surface.

Our modern age is dominated by the use of screen to refer to a surface on which an image is projected (television screen, cell phone screen), but there are many other kinds of screens, most of them serving protective or decorative purposes. Themes common to these screens are roughly rectangular shape (cinema screen) and portability (folding screen). Verb uses of screen take their cues from the noun. To screen a film is to show it. To screen something from view is to hide it behind a screen.

A screencast is a video recording of a computer screen, typically with voice narration explaining what's happening on screen. Screencasts are commonly used for software tutorials, product demos, and technical support: {I made a screencast showing how to set up the app}. The format lets viewers follow along step by step.

Screened describes something that has been filtered, examined, or shielded. A screened {porch} has mesh panels to keep insects out while allowing air through. Screened {candidates} have passed preliminary evaluation: {All applicants are screened for criminal history}. A screened {film} has been shown to an audience. To be screened for a disease is to undergo testing for it.

A screener is a person or device that screens—examining things to filter, sort, or evaluate them. Airport screeners check passengers and luggage. In hiring, a screener conducts initial interviews to narrow candidates. A screener is also an advance copy of a film sent to critics or award voters before general release: {Oscar screeners leaked online again this year}.

Screening is examining or testing to identify problems, candidates, or suitability. Medical screening detects disease early: {routine cancer screening}. Job screening filters applicants. Airport security screening checks for threats. The word also means showing a film: {a private screening of the documentary}. As a material, screening is mesh used in window screens or sieves.

Screenings are showings of films, typically for preview audiences, critics, or special groups before or outside regular theatrical release: {The studio held advance screenings for press}. Screening also refers to systematic testing or examination—medical screenings check for disease, security screenings check for threats. The plural often appears in contexts where multiple tests or showings occur: {cancer screenings}, {airport screenings}.

A screenname is a username or handle identifying someone online—on social media, in chat rooms, or in gaming. The term emerged in the early internet era, especially with services like AOL, where your screenname was your online identity. It implies a degree of anonymity or persona separate from one's real name: {I don't remember her actual name, just her screenname}.

A screenplay is the written script for a film, containing dialogue, scene descriptions, and camera directions. Unlike stage plays, screenplays use specific formatting conventions—slug lines for locations, sparse prose, dialogue centered on the page. {She sold her first screenplay to a major studio}. The screenplay serves as the blueprint from which a movie is made.

Screenplays are scripts written for film or television, containing dialogue, scene descriptions, and directions for action. The format is highly standardized—slug lines indicate location, dialogue centers on the page, parentheticals guide delivery. A screenplay serves as the blueprint from which directors, actors, and crew build the finished production: {She sold her first screenplay to a major studio}.

Screenprint refers to a printing technique where ink is forced through a mesh screen onto a surface, with a stencil blocking areas that should remain unprinted. The method produces bold, flat colors and is used for posters, T-shirts, and fine art. As a verb, to screenprint is to create such an image: {We screenprinted the band's logo onto fifty shirts}. Also called silk-screen or serigraphy.

Screenprinting is a printing technique where ink is pushed through a mesh screen onto a surface below, with a stencil blocking areas that should remain unprinted. Each color requires a separate screen. The method works on fabric, paper, glass, and other materials: {The band sold screenprinted T-shirts at the merch table}. Also called silk screening or serigraphy.

Screens are flat surfaces for displaying images—television screens, computer screens, phone screens. A screen can also be a barrier that blocks or filters: a window screen keeps insects out, a privacy screen blocks views, and a screen of trees conceals what's behind it. To screen is to filter, test, or examine: {They screen applicants carefully}. A screen test evaluates an actor's suitability for film. In film's early days, the screen was the projection surface; now {the big screen} means cinema generally, while {the small screen} means television.

A screensaver is a program that displays moving images or patterns on a computer monitor after a period of inactivity. Originally designed to prevent burn-in on older monitors—where static images could leave permanent marks—screensavers became decorative, displaying flying toasters, starfields, or family photos. Modern screens rarely need protection, but screensavers persist as visual idle states and light security measures.

Screensavers are programs that display moving images or patterns on a computer monitor after a period of inactivity. Originally designed to prevent burn-in on older CRT displays—where static images could permanently mark the screen—they became largely decorative once LCD technology eliminated the problem. Many featured flying toasters, starfields, or abstract visualizations. The term extends metaphorically to anything that fills dead time without purpose: {Meetings are just screensavers for productivity}.

A screenshot is an image captured from a computer, phone, or other screen, preserving exactly what was displayed at that moment. Screenshots document error messages, save receipts, share conversations, or preserve evidence: {I took a screenshot of the confirmation page}. The verb is interchangeable with the noun: {Screenshot that before it disappears}.

Screenshots are digital images capturing what appears on a screen at a given moment. The term functions as both noun and verb: {I took screenshots of the error messages}, {She screenshotted the conversation as evidence}. Screenshots serve as documentation, proof, or a way to share visual information. The verb form varies—screenshotted and screenshot both appear as past tense.

Screenshotting is capturing an image of what's currently displayed on a screen. The verb covers phones, computers, and other devices: {She was screenshotting the conversation as evidence}. The word often implies preserving something before it disappears—a fleeting social media post, an embarrassing message, a price before it changes.

Screentime is the amount of time spent looking at electronic displays—televisions, computers, phones, tablets. The term emerged with concerns about children's media consumption and has expanded to adult usage: {I'm trying to reduce my screentime}. Parents monitor screentime; apps track it; health experts debate its effects. Also spelled as two words: screen time.

A screenwriter is a person who writes scripts for films or television programs. The work involves dialogue, scene descriptions, and story structure, typically formatted according to industry conventions. Screenwriters may create original stories or adapt existing material: {She worked as a screenwriter in Hollywood for twenty years}.

Screenwriters are writers who create scripts for film and television. The screenwriter develops dialogue, scenes, and story structure, working within the constraints of visual storytelling. In film, screenwriters may adapt existing works or create original material; in television, they often work in writers' rooms collaboratively. {The screenwriters spent months reworking the third act.}

Screenwriting is the craft of writing scripts for film or television. A screenplay structures dialogue, action, and scene descriptions in a specific format that guides directors, actors, and crew. The work involves not just storytelling but understanding visual narrative—what the camera sees, how scenes cut together. {She studied screenwriting at film school.} {The screenwriting process took two years.}

A screw is a metal fastener with a spiral thread, driven by rotating: {I need a screw to hang this shelf}. As a verb, to screw means to fasten with a screw, or to rotate something into place: {Screw the lid on tight}. From the turning motion comes the slang meaning of sex: {They screwed in the back seat}. Screw also means to cheat or take advantage of: {They really screwed us on that deal}. {Screw you} is a dismissive insult, milder than {fuck you}. To screw up is to make a mistake: {I really screwed up this time}. To screw around is to waste time or be unfaithful. The word is vulgar but considerably milder than fuck.

A screwball is an eccentric or crazy person: {Her uncle is a lovable screwball}. In baseball, a screwball is a pitch that curves opposite to a curveball. Screwball comedy is a film genre from the 1930s and 40s featuring zany characters and fast-paced witty dialogue: {Bringing Up Baby is a classic screwball comedy}.
Screwballs is the plural of screwball—eccentric people or, in baseball, pitches that break unexpectedly: {The office is full of lovable screwballs}. {He threw nothing but screwballs that inning}.

A screwdriver is a hand tool with a handle and a shaft ending in a tip shaped to fit into the head of a screw, used to turn screws in or out. The most common types are flathead (with a single blade) and Phillips (with a cross-shaped tip). Screwdriver also names a cocktail of vodka and orange juice, so called because it was supposedly first stirred with an actual screwdriver. {Hand me that Phillips screwdriver.}
clues: Vodka and orange, or toolkit essential

definition: Screwdrivers are hand tools with a handle and a shaft ending in a tip shaped to fit into screw heads—flathead for slotted screws, Phillips for cross-shaped recesses. Power drills often replace them for heavy work. A screwdriver is also a cocktail of vodka and orange juice: {I'll have a screwdriver}.

Screwed is the past tense of screw in all its senses. Something screwed is fastened with screws. Someone who screwed had sex. Screwed also means cheated or ruined: {We got screwed on the contract}. {If they find out, we're screwed}. The word is vulgar but milder than fucked, which it euphemizes.

Screwing is the present participle of screw. It can mean fastening with screws, having sex, or cheating someone: {He was screwing the boards into place}. {They were screwing in the bedroom}. {The company has been screwing its customers for years}.

A screwjob is a situation where someone is cheated or manipulated out of something they deserved, especially through behind-the-scenes scheming. The term gained prominence from professional wrestling, where a match outcome is secretly predetermined against a wrestler's expectations: {The championship ending was a total screwjob}. More broadly, any rigged or unfair result: {The contract negotiation was a screwjob from the start}.

Screws is the plural of screw—metal fasteners or, in slang, acts of sex. It's also the third-person verb: {She screws the panels into place}. In prison slang, screws are guards—from the old practice of applying thumbscrews as punishment, or from the idea of keeping inmates screwed down.

A screwup is a mistake or blunder, or a person who habitually makes them: {The launch was a total screwup}. {He's the family screwup}. The word is a milder euphemism for fuckup, acceptable in contexts where the stronger word would offend.
Screwups is the plural of screwup—mistakes or people who habitually make them: {We've had too many screwups on this project}. {Those screwups in logistics lost the shipment}.

Screwy means crazy, absurd, or not functioning properly: {Something screwy is going on here}. {That's a screwy idea}. The word suggests something off-kilter, like a screw that's gone in crooked. It's dated but still used, with a slightly comic tone.

Scribble is hasty, careless writing or drawing—marks made without attention to legibility or form. Children scribble before they can write properly; adults scribble notes they may struggle to read later. The word suggests speed over care: {I scribbled down her number}. As a noun, a scribble is the messy result: {The page was covered in scribbles}.

Scribbled is the past tense of scribble—to write hastily or carelessly, producing messy or illegible marks. A scribbled note was dashed off without attention to neatness: {She scribbled down the phone number on a napkin}. Scribbled can also describe meaningless marks made by children or in idle moments: {The margins were covered in scribbled doodles}.

A scribbler is someone who writes, usually with the implication that what they produce is hasty, careless, or of little merit. The term often carries a dismissive or self-deprecating tone: {He fancied himself a novelist but was really just a scribbler}. Writers sometimes use it with false modesty to describe themselves. In Canadian usage, a scribbler is also a notebook for schoolwork.
clues: Someone who writes without much care

definition: Scribblers is the plural of scribbler—someone who writes hastily, carelessly, or without much skill. The term often carries dismissiveness: {a café full of scribblers pretending to be novelists}. It can be self-deprecating when writers use it about themselves: {We scribblers have to stick together}.

Scribbles are hasty, careless marks made with a pen or pencil, often illegible or meaningless. Children scribble before they learn to write properly; adults scribble when jotting quick notes or doodling absently. The verb scribble suggests writing done without care for neatness or legibility: {She scribbled her number on a napkin}. Scribbles can also dismiss someone's writing as worthless: {His so-called poetry is just scribbles}.

Scribbling is hasty, careless writing or drawing—the kind that fills margins during boring meetings or covers a toddler's attempts at art. The word suggests something dashed off without much thought or skill: {I found some scribbling in the back of his notebook}. It can also describe the act itself: {She was scribbling notes during the lecture}.

A scribe is someone who writes things down professionally—originally by hand, before printing existed. Scribes copied manuscripts, recorded transactions, and served as literate intermediaries in societies where most people couldn't read or write. The word now appears in historical contexts or humorously for any writer: {The office scribe took notes at every meeting}. As a verb, to scribe is to mark or score a line, especially in carpentry or metalwork, using a pointed tool also called a scribe.

A scribe is someone who copies or writes out documents by hand, a role of considerable importance before printing and digital technology made the job largely obsolete. In ancient and medieval times, scribes were essential for preserving religious texts, legal records, and literary works. The verb scribe means to write or inscribe, though it sounds old-fashioned in most contexts. In woodworking and metalworking, to scribe is to mark a line or pattern on a surface, and the tool used for this is also called a scribe.

A scrim is a loosely woven fabric used in theater—opaque when lit from the front, transparent when lit from behind, creating dramatic reveals or ghostly effects. The word extends to any thin, translucent material: {a scrim of clouds filtered the sunlight}. In video production, scrims diffuse or reduce light intensity. To scrim is to cover with such material.

Scrimmage is a practice game or session, especially in American football, where teams play against each other or split into squads without official stakes: {The coach scheduled a scrimmage for Saturday}. In football, the line of scrimmage is the imaginary line where the ball is placed before each play. More broadly, scrimmage can mean any rough-and-tumble struggle or confused fight.
clues: Informal game before the real one

definition: Scrimmages is the plural of scrimmage—a practice game or informal contest, especially in football or hockey, where teams run plays against each other without official scoring. The word also means a confused struggle or skirmish: {There were scrimmages between protesters and police}. As a verb, to scrimmage is to engage in such practice: {The team scrimmages every Thursday}.

To scrimp is to be very careful with money or resources, spending as little as possible. The word suggests uncomfortable frugality—not wise budgeting but pinching pennies out of necessity or excessive caution: {They scrimped and saved for years to buy a house}. To {scrimp on} something is to provide less than needed: {Don't scrimp on the sunscreen}.

Scrimping is being extremely careful with money or resources, often to the point of deprivation. The word carries a sense of pinching pennies out of necessity rather than choice: {Years of scrimping and saving finally paid off}. To scrimp is to economize severely, cutting corners wherever possible.

Scrimshaw is the folk art of carving or engraving on whale ivory, bone, or baleen—traditionally practiced by sailors on long whaling voyages. The word covers both the craft and the objects produced: {a collection of antique scrimshaw}, {scrimshaw depicting ships and sea creatures}. As a verb, to scrimshaw is to create such work.

Script is writing, especially by hand—the cursive letters themselves or a system of written characters: {Arabic script}, {Cyrillic script}. A script is also the written text of a play, film, or broadcast: {We're still waiting on the final script}.
