Figuratively, serfdom describes any state of bondage or subjugation: {Corporate workers joke about their serfdom to the quarterly report}.

Serfs were peasants in medieval Europe bound to the land they worked, occupying a status between slave and free. They couldn't leave without their lord's permission and owed labor or a share of crops in exchange for protection and the right to farm. {The serfs worked the manor's fields from dawn to dusk.} The term now describes anyone in a condition of servitude or exploitation: {We're just serfs to the algorithm.}

A sergeant is a noncommissioned officer rank in military and police forces, typically supervising a small unit of soldiers or officers. In the military, sergeants form the backbone of enlisted leadership, bridging the gap between officers and lower-ranking troops. Police sergeants oversee patrol officers and handle administrative duties: {The sergeant assigned teams to the night shift}. The rank appears in compounds indicating seniority: staff sergeant, master sergeant, sergeant major.

Sergeants is the plural of sergeant, a noncommissioned military rank above corporal, typically responsible for training and supervising small units of enlisted personnel. The rank also exists in police forces, usually denoting a supervisor of patrol officers. {Three sergeants led the training exercise.} The spelling is often confused with sergent, which is incorrect in English.

Serial describes things that occur in a sequence or series, one after another. A serial {killer} commits multiple murders over time; a serial {number} uniquely identifies an item within a sequence. In media, a serial is a story published or broadcast in regular installments—the format that gave us soap operas and podcast dramas. Serial also has technical meaning in computing, where it describes data transmission one bit at a time rather than in parallel. {She's a serial entrepreneur who's started five companies.}
clues: Told one chapter at a time

definition: To serialize is to produce or publish something in sequential parts rather than all at once. Novels were once commonly serialized in magazines, with new chapters appearing weekly or monthly. Television shows are serialized when episodes form a continuous narrative rather than standalone stories. In computing, to serialize is to convert data into a format that can be stored or transmitted and later reconstructed—turning complex structures into a sequence of bytes.

Serialized describes something released or published in sequential installments rather than all at once. A serialized {novel} appears chapter by chapter; a serialized {podcast} unfolds episode by episode. The format builds suspense and sustains audience engagement over time. In computing, serialized data has been converted into a format suitable for storage or transmission—a sequence of bytes that can be reconstructed later.
clues: Released one chapter at a time

definition: A series is a number of similar things coming one after another. Television shows with recurring characters air in series—seasons of episodes, often simply called {a series}. In mathematics, a series is a sequence of terms following a rule. {A series of unfortunate events} suggests one thing after another, connected by theme or consequence. The word is both singular and plural: {one series}, {three series}.

A serif is the small decorative stroke or line extending from the ends of letters in certain typefaces. Compare the feet on letters in Times New Roman to the clean edges of Arial. Typefaces with these strokes are called serif fonts; those without are sans-serif. {The newspaper uses a serif font for body text.}

Serifs are the small decorative strokes or lines at the ends of letters in certain typefaces. Times New Roman has serifs; Arial does not. Fonts with serifs are called serif fonts; those without are sans-serif. Serifs are thought to guide the eye along lines of text, making them popular for printed books and newspapers.

Serious describes something requiring careful attention or carrying significant weight. A serious {illness} threatens health; a serious {conversation} addresses important matters. Serious people are earnest and not given to levity: {She's serious about her career}. To take something seriously is to treat it as worthy of consideration. {Are you serious?} questions whether someone truly means what they've said. {Serious money} or {serious talent} emphasizes impressive magnitude.

Seriously means in a serious manner—with gravity, sincerity, or genuine concern: {We need to talk seriously about our finances}. It also functions as an intensifier meaning truly or very much: {I'm seriously considering quitting}. As a standalone interjection, it expresses disbelief or demands confirmation: {Seriously? You're moving to Alaska?} The phrase {take seriously} means to regard as important or worthy of attention.

Seriousness is the quality of treating something as important or worthy of careful attention. A person showing seriousness approaches matters with gravity rather than levity: {The seriousness of her expression told me something was wrong}. The word also describes the degree to which something demands concern: {No one doubted the seriousness of the situation}. When someone questions your seriousness, they're asking whether you're genuinely committed or just playing around.

A sermon is a religious talk delivered during a worship service, typically by clergy expounding on scripture or moral teaching. The word extends to any lengthy moralizing lecture: {I asked one question and got a thirty-minute sermon}. To {sermonize} is to preach or lecture tediously. {Spare me the sermon} requests someone stop moralizing.

Sermonizing is lecturing others in a self-righteous or moralizing way, as if delivering a sermon. The word carries a negative connotation—suggesting unwelcome preachiness rather than genuine guidance: {Nobody asked for your sermonizing}. {He kept sermonizing about the evils of social media while scrolling through his phone}.

Sermons are religious addresses delivered during worship services, typically expounding on scripture or moral teaching. The word extends to any lengthy lecture on conduct or duty, often unwelcome: {I don't need a sermon from you about my choices}. To {preach to the choir} is to deliver a sermon to those already convinced.

Serotonin is a chemical compound that acts as a neurotransmitter in the brain, influencing mood, sleep, appetite, and other functions. Low serotonin levels are associated with depression, which is why many antidepressants work by increasing serotonin availability: {SSRIs block serotonin reuptake}. The compound also plays roles in digestion and blood clotting.

A serpent is a snake, especially a large or venomous one. The word sounds more literary or biblical than snake: {The serpent tempted Eve in the garden}. Figuratively, a serpent is a treacherous person—someone who seems harmless but strikes when trusted. The association with deception runs deep in Western culture.

Serpentine means resembling or suggesting a serpent. A serpentine path winds and curves like a snake's movement: {The river followed a serpentine course through the valley}. Serpentine can describe sinuous physical forms or, figuratively, something devious and cunning: {serpentine plotting}. As a noun, serpentine is a greenish mineral with a mottled, snake-like appearance, used in decorative stonework.

Serpents is the plural of serpent, a literary or formal word for snake. The term carries mythological and religious weight—the serpent in Eden, serpents in Greek mythology. Serpent suggests something more sinister or symbolic than the neutral snake: {The serpent whispered temptation}. In heraldry and symbolic art, serpents represent wisdom, danger, or immortality.

Serrated describes an edge with a row of sharp, tooth-like points, like a saw blade. A serrated knife cuts bread without crushing it. Serrated leaves have jagged margins. The word implies deliberate design—nature or manufacture creating teeth for a purpose: {the serrated edge of the steak knife}, {serrated leaf margins help identify the plant}.

Serum is the clear, yellowish fluid that remains after blood has clotted and the cells are removed. In medicine, serum from immunized animals or recovered patients contains antibodies and can be used therapeutically: {antivenom serum}, {immune serum}. The term extends to any watery biological fluid. In skincare, a serum is a lightweight, concentrated liquid applied before moisturizer: {vitamin C serum}.

Serums is the plural of serum. In medicine, serum is the clear fluid that separates from blood after clotting—used for transfusions, testing, and vaccines: {The lab analyzed the blood serums}. In skincare, serums are lightweight liquids with concentrated active ingredients: {She layered serums before moisturizer}. The Latin plural sera appears in technical contexts.

A servant is someone employed to perform duties in another person's household, such as cooking, cleaning, or attending to personal needs. The term carries connotations of a bygone era when domestic service was more common and hierarchical. In broader use, servant describes anyone who serves others, whether literally or figuratively: {public servants} work for the government, and {civil servants} administer its functions. The word often implies subordination or dedication to another's will: {a servant to her ambitions}.

Servants are people employed to perform domestic duties in a household—cooking, cleaning, attending to the needs of others. The term carries connotations of class hierarchy and is now largely replaced by more specific titles: housekeeper, nanny, butler. In older or religious usage, servant suggests devotion or service: {a servant of God}, {public servants}. The word often implies subordination: {He treated his staff like servants}.

Serve centers on acting for the benefit of another. A waiter serves customers, a soldier serves their country, a public official serves constituents. To serve food or drinks is to present them: {Dinner is served}. In tennis and volleyball, to serve is to put the ball in play. A serve is that opening shot. Something that serves a purpose fulfills it: {This will serve our needs}. To serve time is to complete a prison sentence. {Serve someone right} means they got what they deserved.

Served is the past tense of serve—to provide food or drink, perform duties, or fulfill a function: {She served coffee to the guests}, {He served in the Navy}. In sports, served means having put the ball into play: {She served an ace}. Slang use means to deliver a devastating insult or comeback: {You just got served}.

A server is a person or thing that serves. In restaurants, a server brings food and drinks to tables—a gender-neutral alternative to waiter or waitress. In computing, a server is a computer or program that provides data or services to other computers on a network: {The website crashed because the server went down}. In tennis and volleyball, the server is the player putting the ball in play.

Servers are people or things that serve. A server in a restaurant takes orders and brings food. In computing, a server is a computer or program that provides data or services to other computers on a network: {The website crashed because the servers went down}. In tennis and volleyball, the server is whoever serves the ball. Server also names implements for serving food: {a cake server}, {salad servers}.

Serves is the third-person singular form of serve, covering its wide range of meanings. To serve is to work for or attend to someone, as a waiter serves customers or a soldier serves their country. It extends to providing or delivering something useful: {This room serves as my office}. In sports like tennis, to serve is to put the ball in play. The expression {serves you right} suggests someone got the negative consequence they deserved.

The act of serving or an instance of serving is service, and the many meanings of serve often have a closely related service counterpart. Resources that are provided for a society are often characterized as services: health service, postal service. In commerce, service is often contrasted with product to distinguish tangible from intangible things that are bought and sold. Military service is the act or fact of being in the armed forces. A service for a vehicle is an instance of having it worked on my a mechanic. Service also works as a verb: to service an appliance, vehicle, or venue is to take care of or repair it.

A serviceman is a member of the armed forces—army, navy, air force, or marines. The term emphasizes military service rather than rank: {Three servicemen were killed in the attack}. Serviceman also refers to someone who repairs or maintains equipment: {The appliance serviceman came to fix the dishwasher}. The military sense dominates contemporary usage.

A servicemember is a person serving in the armed forces—army, navy, air force, marines, or coast guard. The term is deliberately gender-neutral, replacing older usage like "serviceman": {The bill provides healthcare benefits for servicemembers and their families}. Also spelled as two words: service member.

Servicemen is the plural of serviceman—a member of the armed forces. The term encompasses soldiers, sailors, marines, and airmen: {Thousands of servicemen were deployed overseas}. It often appears in contexts honoring military personnel: {a memorial to fallen servicemen}. The compound *servicemembers* has gained ground as a gender-neutral alternative.

Services are acts of assistance or work performed for others. As a plural, it often refers to professional or commercial offerings: {financial services}, {cleaning services}, {goods and services}. A service is also a religious ceremony: {funeral services}, {Sunday services}. The military services are branches of armed forces. To service something is to maintain or repair it: {service the car}. In breeding contexts, to service means to mate with.

Servicewomen is the plural of servicewoman—a woman serving in the armed forces. The term parallels servicemen and emerged as women took on military roles: {Servicewomen now serve in combat positions that were once closed to them}. The gender-neutral servicemembers increasingly appears in official contexts.

Servicing is the work of maintaining, repairing, or providing ongoing support for something. Vehicles require regular servicing to stay roadworthy. Financial institutions service loans by processing payments and managing accounts. Equipment servicing keeps machinery operational. In a sexual context, servicing means performing sex acts on someone, often with connotations of duty or transaction rather than mutual pleasure: {He paid her for servicing him}.

A serving is a portion of food or drink meant for one person: {The recipe makes six servings}. As an adjective, serving describes someone currently holding a position: {a serving member of Congress}, {the serving president}. A serving dish or spoon is used to distribute food to others at the table.

Servitude is the state of being enslaved or bound to serve another. In its strictest sense, it describes slavery or forced labor: {a life of servitude}. More broadly, it can mean any condition of subjection or lack of freedom: {domestic servitude}, {indentured servitude}. In legal contexts, a servitude is a right that limits how property can be used, such as an easement allowing others passage across land.

Sesame is a plant cultivated for its small, flat seeds, which are rich in oil and used extensively in cooking. Sesame seeds top hamburger buns and bagels, flavor Asian dishes, and are ground into tahini paste. Sesame oil is prized in Asian cuisines for its nutty flavor. {Open sesame}—the magic phrase from Ali Baba—has become a figurative key to access or opportunity.

Sesh is informal for session—a period devoted to a particular activity. Most often it refers to a drinking session or a session of smoking marijuana: {We had a proper sesh last night}, {Come over for a sesh}. The word appears in compounds like {smoke sesh} or {study sesh}. Predominantly British slang, though spreading.

A session is a period devoted to a particular activity, typically with a defined beginning and end. A court is {in session} when conducting business; a {recording session} captures performances; a {therapy session} lasts an hour. In computing, a session tracks a user's interaction with a system between login and logout. The word often implies focused, uninterrupted time: {I need a good session at the gym}.

Sessions is the plural of session—a period devoted to a particular activity. Court sessions, recording sessions, therapy sessions, and legislative sessions all share this sense of bounded time for focused work. Congressional hearings are often called sessions: {The committee held sessions throughout the week}. In fitness, sessions refers to individual workouts: {I've been doing three sessions a week with a trainer}.

Set, a noun and verb, has meanings across a broad range of seemingly unrelated domains. A set is a collection of things that belong together due to a shared characteristic, such as a skill set or a set of dishes. When you set an object somewhere, you place it there. If you set a record, a standard, or a tone, you establish it. If you set an example, you exhibit behavior that others can imitate. Set is often followed by adverbs that result in phrasal verbs with their own meanings, such as set up, set forth, and set out.

A setback is an event or development that delays or reverses progress toward a goal. The word implies temporary rather than permanent defeat—a setback in negotiations, a setback in recovery from illness. {The project suffered a major setback when funding was cut.} In construction and zoning, setback has a technical meaning: the required distance between a building and a property line, street, or other boundary.

Setbacks are reversals of progress or checks to advancement. A project hits setbacks when unexpected problems arise. A recovery suffers setbacks when symptoms return. The word implies temporary rather than permanent defeat—setbacks can be overcome: {Despite early setbacks, the campaign eventually succeeded}. In construction, a setback is the required distance a building must be positioned from a property line or street.

A setlist is the sequence of songs a musician or band plans to perform at a concert: {The setlist leaked online before the show}. Fans trade setlists to track how tours evolve. The term extends to DJ mixes and any planned performance lineup. Also spelled as two words: set list.

Setlists are the ordered sequences of songs a band or musician plans to perform at a concert or show. Artists prepare setlists before performances, balancing crowd favorites, new material, and pacing: {The band posted their setlist backstage}. Fans share and compare setlists online to track what songs were played at different tour stops.

A setpiece is a carefully planned and rehearsed element designed for maximum effect. In sports, setpieces are plays executed from a stoppage—corner kicks, free kicks, or penalty shots: {They scored twice from setpieces}. In film and theater, a setpiece is an elaborate scene or sequence showcasing production values. In writing, it's a passage of heightened craft: {The novel's setpiece is a twelve-page dinner party}. The word suggests something prepared rather than improvised, impressive but perhaps lacking spontaneity.

Setpieces are carefully planned and rehearsed sequences, whether in film, theater, sports, or military operations. In cinema, a setpiece is an elaborate scene designed to showcase spectacle—a car chase, a battle, a heist: {The movie's best setpiece is the zero-gravity fight}. In soccer and other sports, setpieces are plays from a dead ball: corner kicks, free kicks, penalty shots. The term implies preparation and choreography rather than improvisation. Also spelled set pieces or set-pieces.

Sets is the plural of set and third-person singular of the verb. A set is a collection of related things: a chess {set}, a {set} of encyclopedias, a matching {set}. In mathematics, a set is a defined collection of elements. A tennis match comprises sets. To set is to put something in position, establish something, or harden: {The sun sets}, {concrete sets}, {she sets the table}. {He sets a good example for his kids.}

A setter is a dog bred to locate game birds by freezing in position—"setting"—when prey is detected, alerting hunters to the quarry's location. The major breeds are English, Irish, and Gordon setters, distinguished by their silky coats and keen noses. More broadly, a setter is anyone or anything that sets: a {trend setter}, a {record setter}, a {typesetter}. In volleyball, the setter is the player who positions the ball for attackers to spike.

Setters is the plural of setter. A setter is a breed of long-haired hunting dog trained to locate game birds and freeze in position—"setting" to indicate where prey hides. The major breeds are English, Irish, and Gordon setters. Beyond dogs, a setter is anything or anyone that sets: a {typesetter}, a {trendsetter}, a {pacesetter}. In volleyball, the setter positions the ball for teammates to spike.

Setting is the time, place, and circumstances in which something occurs. A novel's setting might be Victorian London; a film's setting could be a dystopian future. The word extends to physical surroundings: {a romantic setting for dinner}. A setting is also a position on a dial or control: {Turn the oven to its highest setting}. In jewelry, the setting is the metal framework holding a gemstone.

Settings are the adjustable parameters that control how something operates—on a device, in software, or on equipment. You adjust settings to customize behavior: {Check your privacy settings}, {The oven's temperature setting was too high}. In fiction, the setting is where and when a story takes place: {The novel's setting is Victorian London}. A setting can also be a surrounding context or physical arrangement: {a gemstone's setting}, {a formal dinner setting}.

Several meanings of the verb settle suggest a transition to a more stable, enduring state. To settle a dispute or a lawsuit means to end it with an agreement. When people settle a geographic area, they go there to live and begin to build a community. When something settles, it comes to rest from a more active state. Dust may settle on surfaces; the contents of a package may settle. When overactive children settle down (or are told to do this), the hope is that they become quieter.

Settled describes something that has come to rest or been resolved. A settled question is no longer in dispute. Settled weather is stable and predictable. A person who feels settled has found stability—in a place, relationship, or state of mind: {After years of moving, she finally felt settled}. To be settled into a chair is to be comfortably positioned. A settled area has established inhabitants, as opposed to wilderness.

Settlement is an arrangement that resolves a dispute, especially a legal case ending before trial: {They reached an out-of-court settlement}. It also means a place where people establish a community, particularly in previously uninhabited or sparsely populated territory: {early European settlements along the coast}. Settlement can refer to the act of settling—paying a debt, colonizing land, or the gradual sinking of a structure into its foundation.

Settlements are places where people establish residence, from small villages to large cities. The word also means the act of settling—resolving a dispute or debt: {They reached a settlement out of court}, {a divorce settlement}. In legal contexts, a settlement is an agreement that ends litigation, usually involving payment: {The company paid a multimillion-dollar settlement}. Settlement can also mean the process of colonizing land: {European settlement of the Americas}.

A settler is someone who moves to a new region to establish residence, especially in previously uninhabited or sparsely populated territory. The word carries historical weight from colonial expansion: {Early settlers faced harsh winters}. In contemporary usage, particularly regarding Israel-Palestine, settler often implies contested legitimacy—someone establishing residence on disputed land: {West Bank settlers}. To settle is to establish such residence, or more broadly, to resolve or come to rest.

Settlers are people who move to a new region to establish residence, typically where few or none of their kind lived before. The word often appears in historical contexts describing colonial expansion: {The settlers pushed westward}. It can carry neutral or loaded connotations depending on perspective—pioneers building communities or colonizers displacing indigenous populations. In the board game Settlers of Catan, players compete to establish settlements.

Settles is the third-person singular of settle, a verb with meanings that cluster around coming to rest or resolution. Dust settles on furniture, a bird settles on a branch, sediment settles to the bottom. A person settles into a chair or settles down for the night. To settle a dispute is to resolve it; to settle a debt is to pay it. Settlers settle land by establishing permanent residence. {She settles her accounts monthly}. {The snow settles on the rooftops}.

Settling is the process of coming to rest or resolution. Sediment settles at the bottom of a glass; dust settles on surfaces. A building settles as its foundation shifts over time. People settle into routines or settle down after excitement. {The house is still settling} explains creaking sounds. To accuse someone of settling suggests they accepted less than they deserved: {Don't settle for mediocrity}. Settling a debt or dispute means resolving it.

Setup is the way something is arranged or organized: {What's your setup for working from home?} It also means the preliminary work to make something ready: {Setup takes about an hour}. A setup can be a scheme to deceive or incriminate someone: {The whole thing was a setup}. In sports and games, a setup is a play that creates an opportunity: {a perfect setup for the winning shot}. The one-word form is the noun; the verb is two words: set up.

Setups is the plural of setup, which refers to arrangements or configurations. A setup can be the way equipment is organized {(nice gaming setup)}, circumstances deliberately arranged {(It was a setup—the cops were waiting)}, or the preparatory portion of a joke before the punchline. In sports, a setup is a pass or play that creates a scoring opportunity.

Seven is the number between six and eight, represented by the numeral 7. It appears throughout culture as a significant quantity: seven days in a week, seven deadly sins, seven wonders of the ancient world. In games of chance, seven is often lucky—rolling a seven in craps wins on the come-out roll.

Seventeen is the cardinal number between sixteen and eighteen, written 17. It holds cultural significance as an age on the cusp of adulthood—old enough to drive in most places, not yet old enough to vote or drink. {She turned seventeen last month.} {Seventeen magazine} targets teenage girls.

Seventh indicates position number seven in a sequence: {She finished seventh in the race}. As a noun, a seventh is one of seven equal parts, or in music, an interval spanning seven scale degrees. {Every seventh customer gets a discount.} {Add a seventh of a cup of flour.}

Seventies refers to the numbers 70 through 79, most commonly applied to years in a century or decades in a person's age. {Disco dominated the seventies} means the 1970s; {She's in her seventies} means between 70 and 79 years old. The term can also describe temperatures in that range: {It'll be in the low seventies this weekend}. Context usually makes clear which seventies is meant.

Seventy is the number between sixty-nine and seventy-one, equal to seven times ten. The seventies refers to a decade: {disco dominated the seventies}. Someone in their seventies is between seventy and seventy-nine years old. As a rough quantity, seventy suggests a large but countable number: {seventy miles per hour}, {seventy dollars}.

Sever means to cut or break apart, especially with force or finality. A sword severs a limb. An accident severs a cable. The word often appears in figurative contexts: {They severed ties with the company}, {The scandal severed his connection to the party}. To sever a relationship is to end it completely and often permanently.

Severance is the act of cutting off or separating, or the state of being cut off. A {severance of ties} ends a relationship or connection. In employment, severance refers to compensation given when someone loses their job: {She negotiated three months' severance}. A severance {package} may include pay, benefits continuation, and other terms. The word implies a clean break rather than gradual separation.

Severe means harsh, strict, or intense to a degree that causes hardship or discomfort. Severe weather brings dangerous conditions; a severe injury requires serious medical attention. A severe person is stern and unsparing: {a severe taskmaster}. Severe punishment is harsh; severe criticism is cutting. The word suggests an extreme that tests endurance: {severe pain}, {severe drought}, {severe consequences}.

Severed means cut off or separated, typically by force. A severed {limb} has been cut from the body. A severed {connection} has been abruptly broken. The word implies a clean, decisive break rather than gradual separation: {The explosion severed the cable}. Severed ties suggest relationships ended definitively, often with finality or hostility.

Severity is the degree to which something is serious, harsh, or intense. A storm's severity determines the damage it causes. The severity of a crime influences sentencing. Severity can describe physical conditions {the severity of her injuries}, punishments {the severity of the penalty}, or manner {He spoke with unusual severity}. Something severe is not mild or gentle.

Severs is the third-person singular form of sever, meaning to cut off or separate completely. A blade severs a rope; a court ruling severs parental rights. The word implies finality—what's severed is fully detached: {The accident severs the nerve}. Figuratively, someone severs ties or severs a relationship when ending it decisively.

Seviche is an alternative spelling of ceviche—raw fish or seafood cured in citrus juice, typically lime or lemon, with onions, chili peppers, and cilantro. The acid in the citrus "cooks" the fish without heat, firming and whitening the flesh. The dish is associated with Peru but appears throughout Latin America and the Caribbean: {We ordered seviche as an appetizer}.

Sew is to join pieces of fabric or other material by passing thread through them with a needle, either by hand or with a sewing machine. The skill extends from basic repairs like {sewing on a button} to elaborate crafts like quilting and tailoring. To sew something up means to close it with stitches, and figuratively to secure or finalize: {They sewed up the deal before competitors could respond}. The past participle sewn is more common than sewed.

Sewage is wastewater and human waste carried through sewer systems. It includes what goes down drains and toilets in homes and businesses, along with industrial discharge. Sewage requires treatment before release into waterways: {The city's sewage treatment plant processes millions of gallons daily}. Figuratively, sewage describes anything foul or worthless: {The internet is full of sewage}.

A sewer is an underground pipe or tunnel that carries wastewater and sewage away from buildings to treatment facilities. The word extends to the whole system: {The city's sewers date back to the 1800s}. Figuratively, a sewer is any place of filth or moral degradation: {a sewer of corruption}. Separately, a sewer is a person who sews.

Sewers are underground systems of pipes and channels that carry wastewater and storm runoff away from populated areas. The word also refers to the pipes themselves: {The city is replacing aging sewers}. Figuratively, a sewer suggests filth or moral degradation: {a sewer of corruption}. Separately, a sewer is a person who sews.

Sewing is the craft of joining fabric or other materials using needle and thread. It encompasses everything from mending a torn seam to constructing garments from scratch. A sewing {machine} automates the stitching process. A sewing {kit} contains needles, thread, and basic supplies. {She took up sewing during the pandemic.}

Sewn is the past participle of sew—to join fabric or other material with needle and thread: {a hand-sewn quilt}, {poorly sewn seams}. It appears after auxiliary verbs: {The button had been sewn on crooked}. Sewed also serves as past participle, though sewn is more common. The phrase {sewn up} means secured or settled: {We've got the contract sewn up}.

Sews is the third-person singular of sew—to join pieces of fabric using needle and thread or a sewing machine: {She sews her own clothes}. The word extends to attaching anything by stitching: {He sews patches onto his jacket}. To {sew up} something is to close it with stitches or, figuratively, to secure it completely: {They sewed up the deal}.

Sex has many definitions connected with its core meaning of animal reproduction. When animals have sex, a male and female engage in intercourse. When people have sex, they typically have recreational sex, which can take place between people of any gender and without the implication of reproduction. In many contexts, sex is another term for gender: Have you determined the sex of the kittens yet? People of the same sex can now marry in many states.

A sexaholic is someone addicted to sex—a person whose sexual behavior feels compulsive and uncontrollable. The term follows the pattern of alcoholic and workaholic, treating sexual activity as a substance-like dependency: {He joined a support group for sexaholics}. Also spelled sexoholic. The clinical term is sex addict.

A sexbot is a robot designed for sexual use—an advanced sex doll with mechanical or AI components that simulate human interaction. The term combines sex with robot, following the pattern of chatbot and similar compounds. Sexbots appear frequently in science fiction exploring themes of intimacy, consent, and artificial consciousness: {The film raised uncomfortable questions about people who prefer sexbots to human partners}.

A sexcapade is a sexual adventure or escapade—typically a casual encounter, affair, or series of them, often with an element of recklessness or indiscretion: {The tabloids detailed the senator's sexcapades}. The word is playful, treating sexual exploits as adventure stories rather than scandals.

Sexes is the plural of sex, referring to the categories of male and female based on reproductive function. The word often appears in phrases emphasizing this division: {the opposite sex}, {the battle of the sexes}, {both sexes were represented}. To say {the sexes} is to invoke men and women as distinct groups: {relations between the sexes}.

Sexiest is the superlative of sexy—the most sexually attractive or appealing among a group: {People magazine's sexiest man alive}. The word applies beyond physical attraction to anything with strong appeal or excitement: {the sexiest new tech startup}, {the sexiest car on the market}. What counts as sexiest shifts with cultural taste.

Sexiness is the quality of being sexually attractive or appealing. It can describe physical appearance, behavior, voice, or attitude—anything that provokes desire: {There's a certain sexiness to confidence}. The word extends beyond people to things with allure or excitement: {the sexiness of a new sports car}, {the sexiness of startup culture}. What counts as sexy varies enormously by era and culture.

Sexism is prejudice or discrimination based on sex, typically against women. It ranges from individual attitudes to systemic patterns in hiring, pay, and opportunity. Sexist assumptions about capabilities or proper roles often operate unconsciously: {The hiring committee didn't realize their questions to female candidates were sexist}. The term emerged from 1960s feminism, modeled on racism.

Sexist describes attitudes, behaviors, or systems that discriminate based on sex, typically against women. A sexist {joke} demeans one sex; a sexist {hiring practice} favors another. The noun identifies someone who holds such views: {He's a sexist}. The word emerged alongside feminism's vocabulary in the 1960s, modeled on racist.

Sexists are people who hold or express prejudiced views based on sex, typically assuming women are inferior to men. The word works as both noun and adjective: {The hiring manager turned out to be a sexist}, {sexist attitudes in the workplace}. Sexist remarks range from casual assumptions about gender roles to overt hostility.

Sexless describes something lacking sex or sexual characteristics. A sexless creature has no distinguishable gender. A sexless relationship or marriage involves no sexual activity: {Their marriage had become sexless}. The word can also mean unappealing or devoid of sexual energy: {The performance was technically perfect but sexless}.

A sexpot is a person, usually a woman, considered exceptionally sexually attractive or seductive. The term suggests someone whose appeal is overt and physical rather than subtle: {She played the sexpot in a string of B-movies}. The word has a slightly dated, mid-20th-century feel, often used now with ironic or campy overtones.

Sexpots is the plural of sexpot, a person considered extremely sexually attractive or seductive. The term combines sex with pot in its older sense of a prized vessel or container—something desirable. It typically describes women and carries a slightly dated, playful tone: {She was one of the great sexpots of 1950s Hollywood}. The word suggests overt, unapologetic sex appeal rather than subtle attractiveness.

Sext is a text message with sexual content—explicit photos, videos, or suggestive language sent electronically. The verb means to send such messages: {They'd been sexting for weeks before meeting in person}. Originally associated with teenagers and cautionary tales about digital permanence, sexting is now mainstream among adults in romantic relationships.

A sextant is a navigational instrument used to measure the angle between a celestial body and the horizon, allowing sailors and aviators to determine their position at sea or in the air. The device uses mirrors and a graduated arc spanning sixty degrees—one sixth of a circle, hence the name. Though largely supplanted by GPS, sextants remain valued as backup instruments and for their elegance: {He took a sextant reading at noon to fix their latitude}.

Sextants are navigational instruments used to measure the angle between a celestial body and the horizon, allowing sailors and aviators to determine their position. The device has a graduated arc of sixty degrees—one-sixth of a circle, hence the name. Before GPS, sextants were essential for ocean navigation: {The captain took a reading with his sextant at noon}.

Sexted is the past tense of sext, meaning to send sexually explicit messages, photos, or videos via text or messaging apps. The term blends sex and text: {They sexted for months before meeting in person}. Sexting ranges from flirtatious messages to explicit images, and has generated legal concerns when minors are involved.

A sextet is a group of six, especially six musicians or singers performing together, or a composition written for such a group: {a jazz sextet}, {Brahms's string sextets}. The term extends to any group of six people or things considered as a unit. In poetry, a sextet is the final six lines of a sonnet.

Sexting is the activity or sending sexually explicit messages or photographs using SMS (on a cell phone, for example). The word is formed from sex and texting. Sexting is usually associated with teenagers and young people, though politicians have occasionally been caught in sexting scandals.

Sextortion is extortion using sexual material as leverage—typically threatening to release intimate images unless the victim pays money or provides more explicit content. The crime often begins with someone obtaining or creating compromising photos through hacking, catfishing, or prior relationships: {He was arrested for sextorting teenage girls he'd met online}. A blend of sex and extortion.

Sexts are sexually explicit text messages, photos, or videos sent electronically, typically between romantic or sexual partners. The verb sext means to send such content: {They'd been sexting for weeks before meeting in person}. Sexting among minors raises legal concerns about child pornography, even when consensual between peers.

Sexual relates to sex in its two main senses: the biological distinction between male and female, and physical intimacy. Sexual {reproduction} involves combining genetic material from two parents. Sexual {attraction} is desire for physical contact with another person. Sexual {harassment} and sexual {assault} describe unwanted advances or contact. The word covers anatomy, behavior, identity, and orientation: {sexual organs}, {sexual activity}, {sexual identity}.

To sexualise something is to make it sexual or view it in sexual terms. The word often carries disapproval, especially when applied to things that shouldn't be sexual: {Critics accused the ad campaign of sexualising children}. Media, clothing, and behavior can all be sexualised. The American spelling is sexualize.

Sexualised (also spelled sexualized) describes something given sexual character or made to seem sexual. A sexualised image emphasizes erotic appeal. To say someone is sexualised suggests they've been presented in a way that foregrounds sexuality—often with implications of inappropriateness: {Critics condemned the sexualised portrayal of teenage characters}. The term frequently appears in discussions of media, advertising, and cultural attitudes toward bodies.

Sexualities is the plural of sexuality, referring to different types or expressions of sexual orientation and desire. The term gained prominence as awareness grew that sexuality isn't binary: {The workshop addressed diverse sexualities including gay, bisexual, and asexual identities}. It also appears in academic contexts discussing how cultures construct and regulate sexual expression.

Sexuality encompasses sexual feelings, attractions, and behaviors. It includes one's orientation—whether attracted to the same sex, opposite sex, both, or neither—as well as broader aspects of identity and expression related to sex. {She's open about her sexuality}. The word also refers simply to capacity for sexual experience: {the sexuality of adolescence}, {a film that explores human sexuality}.

Sexualization is the act of making something sexual or viewing it in sexual terms. The word often carries negative connotations—the {sexualization of children} in media, the {sexualization of women} in advertising. To sexualize is to impose sexual meaning where it doesn't inherently belong, or to emphasize sexuality over other qualities: {The costume sexualized the character unnecessarily}.

To sexualize something is to make it sexual or to view it through a sexual lens. The term often carries negative connotations, suggesting that sexuality has been imposed where it doesn't belong or is inappropriate: {Critics argued the advertisement sexualized young girls}. Media, advertising, and fashion are frequently accused of sexualizing women's bodies or everyday activities. The related noun sexualization describes this process as a cultural phenomenon: {the sexualization of childhood}.

Sexualized describes something that has been made sexual or given sexual characteristics, often when sexuality wasn't inherent to it. The term frequently appears in cultural criticism to describe how media, advertising, or fashion imbues subjects with erotic overtones: {Critics argued the ad campaign sexualized teenage models}. It can also describe behavior or environments charged with sexual energy or suggestion. The related verb sexualize means to render something sexual or to view it through a sexual lens.

Sexy describes someone or something that arouses sexual interest or desire: {a sexy outfit}, {I find confidence sexy}. The word extends to anything exciting or appealing in a way that captures attention: {a sexy new sports car}, {Spreadsheets aren't exactly sexy, but they get the job done}. This figurative use often describes ideas or products that generate buzz or enthusiasm.

Shabbat is the Jewish day of rest, observed from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall. It commemorates the biblical seventh day when God rested from creation. Observant Jews refrain from work, travel, and various activities prohibited by Jewish law, instead focusing on prayer, family meals, and rest: {We light candles every shabbat}. (Capitalized Shabbat is more common in formal or religious contexts.)

Shabby describes something worn, faded, or in poor condition from use or neglect: {a shabby coat}, {shabby furniture}. It extends to people dressed in worn clothing or to places that look run-down: {a shabby motel on the edge of town}. Figuratively, shabby means mean or unfair: {That was a shabby way to treat a friend}.

A shack is a small, crudely built dwelling—typically rundown or makeshift: {They lived in a shack at the edge of town}. The word suggests poverty or improvisation. To {shack up} is to live together, especially as an unmarried couple: {They've been shacking up for a year now}.

A shacket is a garment that blends features of a shirt and a jacket—heavier than a typical button-up shirt but lighter and less structured than a jacket. Usually made of flannel, denim, or wool, shackets work as outerwear in mild weather or as layering pieces: {I threw on a shacket for the bonfire}.

A shackle is a metal restraint, typically a pair of rings connected by a chain, used to bind a prisoner's wrists or ankles. The word extends to any device that fastens or secures, like the U-shaped fitting used in rigging and lifting. Figuratively, shackles are whatever constrains freedom or progress: {the shackles of poverty}, {shackled by outdated regulations}. To shackle someone is to restrain them physically or limit them in some other way.

Shackled means bound with shackles—metal restraints fastened around wrists or ankles: {The prisoners were shackled together}. The word extends to any severe constraint on freedom or movement: {shackled by debt}, {shackled to a job she hated}. The figurative use emphasizes not just limitation but the sense of being trapped against one's will.

Shackles are metal restraints, typically rings connected by a chain, used to bind a prisoner's wrists or ankles. The word almost always appears in plural form, whether referring to literal restraints or figurative ones: {throwing off the shackles of oppression}. To shackle someone is to put them in shackles or, more commonly, to impose severe constraints on their freedom or ability to act. {Budget cuts have shackled the department's ability to respond to emergencies.}

Shackling is the act of putting shackles on someone—binding their wrists or ankles with metal restraints. The word extends to any form of severe constraint: {The country's progress was shackling by outdated regulations}. In poultry processing, shackling refers to hanging birds by the legs on a conveyor line.

Shacks is the plural of shack, a small, crudely built dwelling or shelter. Shacks suggest poverty, impermanence, or makeshift construction: {fishing shacks along the pier}, {The workers lived in shacks at the edge of the plantation}. To shack up is to live with someone, usually a romantic partner, in informal or temporary arrangements.

Shade is an area out of direct sunlight, like the shade of a tree on the ground around it. By extension, a lampshade is placed over a light bulb to reduce the intensity of its light; informally, shades are sunglasses. A shade of something is a form of it slightly different than another: It was a lighter shade of blue. To shade something is to shelter it from the sun or strong light. This use is usually adjectival (shaded patio, shaded window).

Shaded describes something protected from direct light, especially sunlight: {a shaded patio}, {shaded by tall oaks}. In drawing and design, shaded areas are darkened to suggest depth or shadow: {The artist shaded the figure's cheekbones}. Shaded can also mean gradually varied in color or tone: {shaded from pale yellow to deep orange}. Sunglasses and lamps may be shaded—fitted with something that blocks or diffuses light.

A shader is a program that controls how graphics are rendered on a computer screen, determining color, lighting, shadows, and visual effects for each pixel or vertex. Shaders run on graphics processing units and are fundamental to modern video games and 3D applications: {The water shader makes the lake look incredibly realistic}. In simpler contexts, a shader can be any device or material that produces shade.

Shades are sunglasses—eyewear with darkened lenses: {She put on her shades and headed to the beach}. The term is casual and cool-sounding. Shades also refers to variations of color: {different shades of blue}. A shade is something that blocks light—a window shade, a lamp shade—or a slight amount: {a shade too bright}. In literary use, shades are ghosts or spirits of the dead.

Shadiness is the quality of being shady—either literally providing shade or figuratively suggesting something questionable or dishonest. A tree's shadiness offers welcome relief from sun. A business deal's shadiness makes you suspect fraud: {The whole arrangement had an air of shadiness that made investors nervous}. The figurative sense dominates contemporary usage.

Shading is the gradual variation of light and dark in a drawing or painting to create the illusion of depth and form. Artists use shading to make flat surfaces appear three-dimensional. The term extends to any subtle gradation: {There are shadings of meaning I hadn't considered}. To give someone shade—public criticism or dismissal—yields a different sense of shading: subtly dissing someone without direct confrontation.

Like the related word shade, shadow is a noun and a verb. A defined space of shade is a shadow, like that of a pole, a person, or a building. Figuratively, a shadow is a faint quality that accompanies something (shadow of doubt). If you are described as someone’s shadow, the suggestion is that you often accompany that person. To shadow someone is to follow them, perhaps in order to learn their job, or perhaps secretly: The detective shadowed the suspect. In parliamentary government, a shadow cabinet minister is a party official in the opposition.

A shadowban is a form of online moderation where a user's posts become invisible to others without notification—the person continues posting, unaware they've been silenced. Platforms use shadowbans to discourage spammers and trolls who might create new accounts if openly banned. As a verb: {I think I've been shadowbanned—none of my comments are getting replies}.

Shadowbanned describes a user whose posts or comments have been secretly hidden from others by a platform, without notifying the user. The person can still post normally, but no one else sees their content—a kind of invisible exile. Platforms use shadowbanning to discourage spammers and trolls without triggering the complaints that explicit bans invite: {I think I've been shadowbanned—my posts aren't getting any engagement}.

Shadowbanning is a moderation technique where a user's posts are hidden from others without notifying the user. The shadowbanned person continues posting normally, unaware their content is invisible to everyone else. Platforms use it to discourage bad actors without provoking them: {I think I've been shadowbanned—my tweets get zero engagement}. Also called a stealth ban or ghost ban.

Shadowbans are a moderation technique where a user's content is hidden from others without notifying the user. The person continues posting normally, unaware their contributions are invisible to everyone else. Platforms use shadowbanning to discourage bad actors without triggering the retaliation that explicit bans might provoke: {I think I've been shadowbanned—my posts get zero engagement}. Also called stealth bans or ghost bans.

Shadowbox works as both noun and verb. A shadowbox is a shallow display case with a glass front, used to exhibit memorabilia, medals, or collectibles against a decorative background. The verb shadowbox means to practice boxing moves against an imaginary opponent, throwing punches at the air as a training exercise. Figuratively, to shadowbox is to engage in a conflict or debate that lacks a real adversary: {Politicians shadowbox over issues that have already been decided}.

Shadowboxed is the past tense of shadowbox, meaning to throw punches at an imaginary opponent as training or exercise. Boxers shadowbox to warm up, practice form, or work on footwork without a partner. Figuratively, to shadowbox is to go through the motions of fighting without engaging a real adversary: {The candidates shadowboxed on policy without addressing real differences}.

A shadowboxer is someone who shadowboxes—practices fighting moves against an imaginary opponent, throwing punches at the air. Boxers use it for training and warm-up. Figuratively, a shadowboxer fights phantom threats or engages in combat where no real opponent exists: {He's just a shadowboxer, arguing against positions nobody holds}.

Shadowboxes works as both noun and verb. A shadowbox is a display case with a glass front and recessed interior, used to showcase objects with depth—medals, memorabilia, dried flowers: {She arranged her grandmother's thimble collection in a shadowbox}. To shadowbox is to spar with an imaginary opponent, throwing punches at the air as training or warm-up. Figuratively, shadowboxing describes fighting something intangible or avoiding direct confrontation: {The candidates spent the debate shadowboxing rather than engaging each other's positions}.

Shadowboxing is practicing boxing moves against an imaginary opponent, throwing punches at the air to develop technique, footwork, and conditioning. Fighters shadowbox to warm up or train without a sparring partner. Figuratively, shadowboxing describes fighting against something that isn't really there—engaging with phantom threats or rehearsing confrontations that may never happen: {He spent the whole meeting shadowboxing with objections nobody had raised}.

Shadowed describes something that has a shadow cast upon it, creating darkness or dimness: {a shadowed corner of the room}, {her shadowed eyes}. It also means followed secretly: {The detective shadowed him for weeks}. Figuratively, shadowed suggests something darkened by trouble or gloom: {a shadowed past}, {shadowed by grief}.

Shadowing is following someone closely, either to observe or learn from them. A medical student shadows a doctor, watching procedures firsthand. In darker contexts, shadowing means covert surveillance: {The detective had been shadowing the suspect for weeks}. The word captures both legitimate mentorship and secretive trailing—in each case, one person moves in another's shadow.

Shadowland is a realm between light and dark, known and unknown—a liminal space where boundaries blur. It often describes places of ambiguity or obscurity: the shadowland between sleep and waking, between life and death, between memory and forgetting. {The disease had taken her to a shadowland where she recognized no one.} The term appears in fantasy and horror to name literal realms of darkness or the supernatural.

Shadowlands refers to a dim, ambiguous realm between light and dark—often the territory between life and death, or the known and unknown. The term suggests places of uncertainty, transition, or diminished clarity: {After the diagnosis, she entered a kind of shadowlands}. C.S. Lewis used it as a title for his meditation on grief, reinforcing associations with loss and the threshold of mortality. In fantasy and gaming, shadowlands are typically dark regions inhabited by spirits or malevolent forces.

Shadowplay is theatrical entertainment using shadows cast on a screen or wall, typically by hands, puppets, or cutout figures positioned between a light source and the viewing surface. The term extends to any interplay of light and shadow: {The shadowplay of leaves on the bedroom wall}. Figuratively, shadowplay suggests deceptive maneuvering or hidden activity behind a visible facade: {The treaty negotiations were mere shadowplay while the real deals happened elsewhere}.

Shadows are dark areas where light is blocked by an object. Every shadow implies both a light source and something standing in its way. Shadows lengthen at dawn and dusk, shrink at midday. Figuratively, a shadow is anything that follows closely or looms ominously: {living in the shadow of her famous mother}, {a shadow of doubt}. To shadow someone is to follow them secretly. The shadows means darkness or obscurity: {lurking in the shadows}.
clues: Dark forms where light cannot reach

definition: Shadowy describes something dark, dim, or filled with shadows: {a shadowy corner of the room}, {shadowy figures in the alley}. The word often suggests mystery or obscurity—things not fully visible or knowable. A shadowy organization operates in secret. A shadowy past contains hidden or unclear elements. The connotation is usually ominous or suspicious rather than merely dim.

Shady describes a place sheltered from direct sunlight: {a shady spot under the oak tree}. The figurative sense dominates modern usage—shady means suspicious, dishonest, or of questionable character: {a shady deal}, {That guy seems shady}. The connection runs through darkness and concealment: what happens in the shade is hidden from view.

All shafts have roughly the same shape – long and cylindrical – but vary in composition. A long pole that is part of a weapon or tool is often called a shaft (golf club shaft). A shaft could consist of sunlight. A mineshaft is a deep hole dug in the ground for access to ore. Shaft is also a vulgar synonym for penis. If you shaft someone, you treat them unfairly and meanly.

Shafted means cheated, swindled, or treated unfairly—given the short end of a deal. The image is of being impaled or penetrated, with overtones of the vulgar sense of shaft (penis): {I got shafted on that car deal}, {The company shafted its workers when it cut their pensions}. The word is informal but not quite vulgar.

Shafts is the plural of shaft—long narrow poles or passages. Arrow shafts fly toward targets; mine shafts descend into the earth; elevator shafts run vertically through buildings. Shafts of light pierce darkness. To shaft someone is to treat them unfairly: {He really got shafted on that deal}. The noun the shaft means similar mistreatment: {She gave him the shaft}.

A shag is a type of rough, matted texture—shag carpet has long, thick pile; a shag haircut has layered, textured strands: {The room still had its 1970s shag rug}. {She got a shag cut}. A shag is also a type of cormorant (seabird), and the shag is a dance that originated in the Carolinas. In British slang, to shag is to have sex: {They shagged in the loo}. A shag is an act of sex or a sexual partner: {He's looking for a shag}. The British slang is vulgar but common, popularized in American awareness by the Austin Powers films.

Shagged as an adjective describes something with a shag texture—rough and matted: {a shagged wool throw}. More commonly, shagged is British slang meaning had sex with, or exhausted: {We shagged all afternoon}. {I'm absolutely shagged}. The exhaustion sense may derive from the exertion of sex, or from the idea of being worn out like old shag carpet.
Shagging is the present participle of shag—dancing the Carolina shag, or in British slang, having sex: {They were shagging in the back room}. {We spent the weekend shagging}.

Shaggy means covered with rough, matted hair or fiber: {a shaggy dog}, {a shaggy beard}. A shag-dog story is a long, meandering joke with an anticlimactic or absurd punchline—perhaps from the shagginess suggesting untidiness or lack of direction.
Shags is the plural of shag—textured rugs, layered haircuts, seabirds, Carolina dances, or in British slang, acts of sex: {Nice shags on the dance floor}. As a verb: {He shags anyone who's willing}.

A shah is a king or ruler of Iran (formerly Persia). The title was used by Iranian monarchs until the 1979 revolution that deposed Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the last shah. In historical contexts, shah appears in titles like {shah of shahs} (king of kings). The word also names the king piece in chess, from which the game's name derives: checkmate comes from Persian for "the king is dead." {The shah fled into exile.}

Shake describes a motion, one-time or repeated, of quick, oscillating movement. You can shake your head to indicate no, or you can shake from cold or fear. People shake hands in greeting and to signal agreement. To shake off something is to remove it by shaking, or to rid yourself of something unpleasant: I had to shake off any doubts I had. A shake is an instance of shaking. Or it might be a milkshake. If you have the shakes, you are trembling from fear or some pathological condition.

A shakedown is an act of extortion—demanding money through threats or intimidation: {The protection racket was just a shakedown}. It also means a thorough search, especially of a person or cell by police or guards. As an adjective, shakedown describes a trial run meant to test new equipment or reveal problems: {a shakedown cruise}.

Shakedowns are acts of extortion—demanding money or favors through threats or intimidation. A corrupt cop running shakedowns extracts bribes from business owners. The word also means thorough searches, especially of prisoners or cells: {Guards conducted shakedowns looking for contraband}. A shakedown cruise is a test voyage to identify problems in a new ship or aircraft before regular service.

Shaken is the past participle of shake. Something shaken has been moved rapidly back and forth: {a shaken bottle of champagne}. More often, shaken describes emotional disturbance—being rattled or unsettled by an experience: {She was visibly shaken after the accident}. {Shaken, not stirred} is the famous martini instruction from James Bond.

A shaker is a container designed to be shaken—typically for mixing drinks or dispensing seasonings through perforated holes: {a cocktail shaker}, {a salt shaker}. The word extends to anything that shakes or causes shaking. A {mover and shaker} is someone who gets things done and influences events. (Capitalized Shaker refers to the religious sect.)

Shakers are containers with perforated tops for dispensing granular substances by shaking: {salt and pepper shakers}. The term also refers to people who shake things, or to cocktail shakers used for mixing drinks. In the phrase {movers and shakers}, it describes influential people who make things happen. (Capitalized Shakers refers to members of a religious sect.)

Shakes are rapid, involuntary trembling movements of the body or part of it, often caused by cold, fear, illness, or withdrawal from alcohol or drugs. {She had the shakes after coming out of the freezing water.} The phrase {in two shakes} or {two shakes of a lamb's tail} means very quickly. {No great shakes} describes something or someone unremarkable or mediocre: {The restaurant was no great shakes, but it was cheap.}

A shakeup is a sudden, significant reorganization—usually of personnel or structure within an organization. Companies announce shakeups when they replace executives or restructure departments: {The CEO resigned amid a major shakeup at headquarters}. The term implies disruption and change, often prompted by poor performance or scandal.
clues: When the org chart gets redrawn

definition: Shaking is trembling or vibrating movement, whether from cold, fear, excitement, or external force. A person may be {shaking with rage} or {shaking from the cold}. Buildings shake during earthquakes. {She was shaking her head} indicates disagreement or disbelief. {I can't stop shaking} suggests loss of physical control from emotion or chill.

Shakshuka is a dish of eggs poached in a sauce of tomatoes, peppers, onions, and spices like cumin and paprika. Originally from North Africa and popular throughout the Middle East, it's typically served in the pan it's cooked in, with bread for dipping: {We ordered shakshuka for brunch}.

Shaky describes something that trembles, wobbles, or lacks stability. A shaky hand trembles; a shaky table rocks on uneven legs. The word extends to anything uncertain or unreliable: {shaky evidence}, {a shaky alibi}, {shaky finances}. Someone feeling shaky is unsteady on their feet, often from illness, nerves, or shock: {I felt shaky after the accident}.

Shakycam is a filming technique using handheld or deliberately unstable camera movement to create a raw, documentary-like feel. Common in horror films, found-footage movies, and action sequences, it aims for immediacy and realism but can induce motion sickness in viewers: {The shakycam made the chase scene feel intense but gave me a headache}. Also called shaky cam.

Shale is a fine-grained sedimentary rock formed from compressed clay and mud. It splits easily into thin layers along parallel planes. Shale formations often contain oil and natural gas, extracted through hydraulic fracturing: {The company drills for shale oil in North Dakota}. {Shale cliffs crumbled along the shoreline}.

Shall is a modal verb that provides aspectual information about the main verb (which is always a present or perfect infinitive). It is typically used in the first person (with I and we). Shall can be a formal or emphatic way of talking about the future in declarative sentences: We shall be more than happy to accept your invitation. In questions, however, shall indicates a degree of uncertainty and may suggest a request for advice: Shall I wait up for you? When used with second- and third-person subjects or pronouns, shall has emphatic force and can suggest a command: You shall deliver the entire sum tomorrow, under penalty of arrest.

A shallot is a small, mild-flavored bulb in the onion family, often preferred in French cooking for its delicate taste. Shallots grow in clusters like garlic but resemble small onions, with papery copper or gray skin. They're commonly minced for vinaigrettes, sauces, and dishes where raw onion would be too harsh: {The recipe calls for two shallots, finely diced}.

Shallots are small onions that grow in clusters of bulbs rather than as single bulbs. They have a milder, more delicate flavor than common onions, with a hint of garlic. French cooking prizes them for sauces and vinaigrettes: {Mince the shallots finely before adding to the pan}.

Shallow describes limited depth—the opposite of deep. A shallow pool doesn't reach far below the surface. Shallow breathing doesn't fill the lungs. Shallow understanding doesn't penetrate the subject. Applied to people, shallow is dismissive: concerned only with surfaces, lacking intellectual or emotional depth. {She found him charming but shallow.} The shallows are areas of water near shore.

Shallowness is lack of depth—physical or intellectual. Water has shallowness when it's not deep enough to swim in. A person shows shallowness when their thinking or interests don't go beyond surface appearances: {The shallowness of his analysis disappointed everyone}. The word often carries judgment, implying someone is vapid or concerned only with trivial things.

Shallows refers to a stretch of water that is not deep—the opposite of the depths. The word appears almost exclusively in the plural: {We waded through the shallows}, {fish spawning in the shallows}. Figuratively, shallows suggests superficiality: {content that never ventures beyond the shallows of the topic}.

Shalom is a Hebrew word meaning peace, used as a greeting and farewell among Jews. The word carries connotations beyond mere absence of conflict—completeness, wholeness, welfare, and harmony. {Shalom, welcome to our home.} Like its Arabic cognate salaam, shalom appears in religious and secular contexts alike.

A sham is something false presented as genuine—a pretense or counterfeit: {The election was a sham}. A person who pretends to be something they're not is also a sham: {He's a sham and a fraud}. As a verb, to sham is to fake: {shamming illness to avoid work}. The adjective describes things meant to deceive: {sham outrage}, {sham marriages}. A pillow sham is a decorative cover—ornamental rather than functional.

A shaman is a person believed to communicate with the spirit world, typically to heal the sick, divine the future, or guide souls. The role appears across many indigenous cultures, from Siberia to the Americas. Shamans often enter trance states through drumming, chanting, or psychoactive substances. The term has been adopted loosely in New Age contexts: {She consulted a shaman for spiritual guidance}.

Shamanic describes practices, beliefs, or states associated with shamans—spiritual practitioners who enter trances to communicate with spirits, heal the sick, or guide souls. The word appears in anthropology and in contemporary spiritual movements: {shamanic drumming}, {shamanic journeying}, {a shamanic ritual}. It can describe anything reminiscent of such practices: {The music had a shamanic intensity}.

Shamanism is a set of spiritual practices centered on a shaman—a person believed to interact with the spirit world through altered states of consciousness. Found across many indigenous cultures, shamans traditionally heal illness, guide souls, and mediate between human and spirit realms. The term now applies broadly to similar practices worldwide, sometimes loosely: {She studied shamanism in Peru}. In contemporary usage, shamanism often describes neo-spiritual movements drawing on these traditions.

Shamans are people who act as intermediaries between the natural and spiritual worlds, typically in indigenous or traditional cultures. They enter altered states of consciousness to heal, divine the future, or communicate with spirits. The role combines priest, healer, and mystic: {The shaman performed a ritual to cure the sick child}. In looser usage, shaman describes anyone claiming spiritual powers or practicing alternative healing.

Shamble means to walk with a slow, shuffling, awkward gait—dragging the feet rather than lifting them cleanly: {He shambled across the room in his bathrobe}. The word suggests weariness, age, or carelessness. As a noun, a shamble is this kind of walk. The plural shambles, a different word, means a scene of disorder or destruction.

Shambled is the past tense of shamble, meaning to walk with a slow, shuffling, awkward gait—dragging the feet rather than lifting them cleanly: {He shambled across the room in his bathrobe}. The word suggests weariness, age, or physical difficulty. Zombies in horror films characteristically shamble toward their victims.

A shambler is someone or something that shambles—walks with an awkward, shuffling, unsteady gait. The word often describes zombies or similar undead creatures in horror fiction, who move with that characteristic lurching walk: {The shamblers emerged from the fog, dragging their feet}. Outside horror contexts, it can describe any slow, clumsy walker.

Shambles originally meant a slaughterhouse or meat market, now rarely used that way. The modern sense is a state of complete disorder or destruction: {The kitchen was a shambles after the party}. Unlike mess or disaster, shambles often implies wreckage—things knocked over, scattered, or ruined rather than merely untidy. British speakers may use it with a singular verb: {The economy is a shambles}.

Shambling describes a slow, awkward, shuffling way of walking, as if the legs aren't quite coordinated or the person lacks energy to lift their feet properly. It often suggests someone who is exhausted, elderly, or zombie-like in their movement. {The old man came shambling down the hallway.} A shambling gait conveys weariness or physical decline, and the word frequently appears in horror contexts to describe the unsteady walk of the undead.

Shambolic describes something chaotic, disorganized, or utterly lacking in order. The word is primarily British and carries a tone of affectionate exasperation rather than harsh criticism: {The whole operation was shambolic from start to finish}. A shambolic person or situation is messy and confused but often endearingly so, suggesting bumbling incompetence rather than malice.
clues: Like a scene of utter confusion

definition: Shame is the painful feeling of having done something wrong, foolish, or disgraceful—or of being exposed as inadequate. It differs from guilt, which focuses on the act; shame focuses on the self. {She couldn't meet their eyes from shame}. To shame someone is to cause this feeling or to publicly disgrace them. A shame is also something regrettable: {It's a shame you couldn't come}. To {put to shame} is to outclass completely: {Her cooking puts mine to shame}. Shameless means without shame, usually as criticism.

Shamed describes someone who has been made to feel shame—the painful emotion of having done something wrong, inadequate, or dishonorable. To be shamed is to have this feeling imposed by others: {He was publicly shamed for his remarks}. The participial form works as both adjective and verb: {a shamed expression}, {They shamed him into apologizing}.

Shamefaced means embarrassed or ashamed, showing it in one's expression or manner: {He gave a shamefaced apology}. The word suggests visible discomfort—someone caught out or exposed. Despite appearances, the word doesn't come from "shame-faced" but from an older term meaning "held fast by shame," though the spelling has long since shifted to match the apparent meaning.

Shameful describes actions, situations, or behaviors that cause or deserve shame—a sense of disgrace or dishonor: {a shameful display of cowardice}, {shameful working conditions}. The word carries moral judgment, suggesting something falls short of accepted standards. What's considered shameful varies by culture and era. Shameful differs from ashamed, which describes the feeling rather than its cause: {He was ashamed of his shameful conduct}.

Shameless describes someone who acts without shame or embarrassment, even when their behavior would normally warrant it. A shameless {liar} lies boldly and without apparent guilt. Shameless {self-promotion} is aggressive and unapologetic. The word carries disapproval—shameless people transgress social norms and don't seem to care: {She made a shameless grab for the inheritance}.

Shamelessly means without shame or embarrassment, especially when shame might be expected. It often describes bold or brazen behavior that others might find inappropriate: {She shamelessly promoted her own book at the funeral}. The word can carry disapproval or grudging admiration, depending on context: {He shamelessly flirted with everyone at the party}.
clues: Acting without a hint of guilt

definition: Shames is the verb form of shame, meaning to cause someone to feel disgrace or humiliation: {She shames him for his laziness}. To shame someone into something is to pressure them through guilt: {They shamed him into apologizing}. To shame someone out of something works the opposite way. In internet culture, shaming often targets specific behaviors: {body-shaming}, {slut-shaming}, {fat-shaming}.

Shaming is the act of causing someone to feel shame—publicly criticizing or humiliating them for perceived wrongdoing. The word often appears with a modifier indicating what's being criticized: {body shaming}, {slut shaming}, {fat shaming}. Online shaming campaigns can destroy reputations: {The internet shaming went viral within hours}.

Shampoo is a liquid soap for washing hair. The verb means to wash with shampoo: {I shampooed twice to get the chlorine out}. Shampoo also cleans carpets and upholstery. A shampoo is an instance of shampooing: {a cut and shampoo}.

Shampoos is the plural of shampoo, a liquid soap formulated for washing hair. Different shampoos target specific hair types or conditions: {dandruff shampoos}, {volumizing shampoos}, {color-safe shampoos}. The verb shampoos means washes with shampoo: {She shampoos her hair every other day}. Shampoo also applies to cleaning carpets and upholstery.

A shamrock is a small clover with three leaves, used as a symbol of Ireland. The plant is associated with St. Patrick, who supposedly used its three-part leaf to illustrate the Christian Trinity. People wear shamrocks on St. Patrick's Day: {She pinned a shamrock to her lapel}. The word sometimes extends loosely to any three-leafed clover.

Shamrocks are three-leafed plants, typically clover, serving as the national emblem of Ireland. The plant is associated with St. Patrick, who according to legend used its three leaves to explain the Christian Trinity. Shamrocks appear everywhere on St. Patrick's Day—on decorations, clothing, and greeting cards. A four-leafed clover is not a shamrock but a lucky charm.

Shams are things that appear genuine but aren't—fakes, frauds, or pretenses. A sham marriage exists only on paper. A sham trial reaches a predetermined verdict. The word works as noun, adjective, or verb: {The whole investigation was a sham}, {sham outrage}, {He shammed illness to skip work}. A pillow sham is a decorative cover—not deceptive, just ornamental.

Shandies is the plural of shandy, a drink mixing beer with lemonade or ginger beer. The combination produces a lighter, sweeter, less alcoholic beverage than straight beer, popular in summer: {We ordered shandies on the patio}. The drink goes by different names regionally—radler in German-speaking countries.

A shandy is a drink made by mixing beer with lemonade or another soft drink, typically in equal parts. Popular in Britain and Europe as a lighter, more refreshing alternative to straight beer: {I'll have a shandy—it's too hot for a proper pint}. The American version sometimes uses ginger ale instead of lemonade.

To shanghai someone is to coerce or trick them into doing something, originally to kidnap them for service as a sailor. The term comes from the practice of drugging or forcing men aboard ships bound for Shanghai and other distant ports: {They shanghaied him into joining the committee}. The word suggests being pressed into service against one's will. (Capitalized Shanghai is the Chinese city.)

Shanghaied means kidnapped or coerced into service, originally referring to the practice of drugging or tricking men into serving as sailors on ships. The term comes from the Chinese port city, a common destination for vessels needing crew. Now used more broadly for being forced or tricked into any unwanted situation: {I got shanghaied into helping them move}.

Shanghaiing is the practice of kidnapping or coercing people into service aboard ships, historically through drugging, assault, or deception. The term comes from Shanghai, a common destination for vessels that needed crews obtained by force. The verb shanghai now extends to any situation where someone is pressed into unwilling service: {I got shanghaied into organizing the office party}.
