Survivors of such disasters are shipwrecked sailors, cast ashore on islands or left adrift: {The shipwrecked crew survived on coconuts for weeks}. Figuratively, shipwrecked can describe any situation of ruin or abandonment: {shipwrecked dreams}, {shipwrecked by circumstance}.

Shipwreckers are people who cause ships to wreck, especially those who historically lured vessels onto rocks or shoals using false lights, then plundered the cargo and let the crew drown. The term also applies more broadly to anyone who deliberately destroys ships or sabotages maritime ventures: {The coastal villagers had a reputation as shipwreckers}.

Shipwrecks is the plural of shipwreck—the destruction or sinking of a ship, or the remains of such a vessel. Shipwrecks lie on ocean floors as archaeological sites and diving destinations. Figuratively, any ruined endeavor can be a shipwreck: {the shipwreck of his political career}. The verb means to cause or suffer such destruction: {They were shipwrecked on a remote island}.

A shipwright is a craftsman who builds and repairs ships. The term traditionally refers to wooden ship construction, though it extends to modern vessel building. Shipwrights work with hull design, framing, and planking: {The shipwright inspected the damaged keel}. The trade requires knowledge of both carpentry and naval architecture.

Shipwrights are craftsmen who build and repair ships. The term applies to workers in traditional wooden shipbuilding as well as modern vessel construction. A shipwright's skills include carpentry, fitting, and understanding hull design: {The shipwrights worked for months to restore the old schooner}.

A shipyard is a facility where ships are built, repaired, or dismantled. Large shipyards contain drydocks, cranes, and workshops for constructing vessels from keel to launch. The word combines the nautical with the industrial: {The shipyard employed thousands during the war}. Naval shipyards build military vessels; commercial shipyards handle cargo ships and tankers.

Shipyards are facilities where ships are built and repaired. They combine dry docks, cranes, workshops, and storage areas along waterfronts. Major shipyards construct everything from cargo vessels to naval warships, while smaller ones may specialize in repairs or recreational boats: {The old shipyards along the river have been converted to condominiums}.

A shire is a county in England, particularly in traditional or formal usage. The term survives in county names like Yorkshire, Hampshire, and Lincolnshire. In Britain, {the shires} refers to rural hunting country in the Midlands, evoking traditional English countryside. Shire also names an administrative district in some Commonwealth countries. A shire horse is a large draft breed originally from the English shires.

Shires are counties in England, particularly those whose names end in -shire: Yorkshire, Lancashire, Oxfordshire. The word evokes rural England—rolling countryside, market towns, traditional ways of life. In Tolkien's Middle-earth, the Shire is the pastoral homeland of hobbits, drawing on this association. Shire horses are a large English draft breed.

To shirk is to avoid doing something you're supposed to do, especially work or duty: {He shirked his responsibilities as a father}. The word implies laziness or cowardice rather than principled refusal. Someone who habitually avoids their obligations is a shirker. You can shirk a task, shirk work, or simply shirk without an object.

Shirked is the past tense of shirk, meaning to avoid or neglect a duty or responsibility. Someone who shirked their obligations deliberately evaded what they were supposed to do: {He shirked his chores and went fishing instead}. The word carries connotations of laziness or cowardice—shirking work, shirking responsibility, shirking one's duty.

A shirker is someone who avoids work, duty, or responsibility, especially by sneaking away or making excuses. The term carries strong disapproval, suggesting not just laziness but a deliberate effort to dodge obligations while others carry the load. {The team resented the shirkers who disappeared whenever heavy lifting was required.} During wartime, shirker was applied specifically to those who avoided military service.

Shirkers are people who avoid work or responsibility, especially by sneaking away or pretending to be busy. The word carries strong disapproval—shirkers leave others to pick up the slack: {The rest of the team resented the shirkers who disappeared whenever heavy lifting was needed}. In military contexts, shirker historically described those who evaded combat duty.

Shirking is avoiding work or responsibility, especially duties you're supposed to perform. The word implies laziness or deliberate evasion rather than legitimate inability: {He was accused of shirking his duties}. Someone who shirks is a shirker. {No shirking—we need all hands on deck}.

Shirks is the third-person singular of shirk, meaning to avoid or evade duties or responsibilities. Someone who shirks their obligations fails to fulfill them through neglect or cowardice rather than inability: {He shirks his share of the housework}. The word carries connotations of laziness or moral weakness—a shirker lets others carry the burden.

A shirt is a garment covering the torso, typically with sleeves and a front opening or pullover design. The word usually means a button-front dress shirt or a casual top like a T-shirt, distinguished from sweaters, jackets, and underwear. To {lose your shirt} is to lose everything in a failed venture. To {keep your shirt on} is to stay calm.

A shirtdress is a woman's dress styled like an elongated button-front shirt, typically with a collar, cuffs, and a waist that may be belted. The style emerged in the mid-twentieth century as practical daywear: {She threw on a cotton shirtdress for the office}.

Shirtless means not wearing a shirt, with the upper body bare or exposed: {shirtless joggers in the park}, {He answered the door shirtless}. The word applies almost exclusively to men—women without tops are typically described differently.

Shirts is the plural of shirt, a garment covering the upper body, typically with sleeves and a front opening or pullover design. The word appears in compounds describing varieties: {dress shirts}, {T-shirts}, {polo shirts}. To {keep your shirt on} is to stay calm. To {lose your shirt} is to lose everything in a bad investment or gamble. To {give the shirt off your back} is to be extremely generous.

Shirtsleeves are the sleeves of a shirt, but the word usually appears in the phrase {in shirtsleeves}, meaning wearing a shirt without a jacket or coat. The image suggests informality or readiness to work: {The senator rolled up his shirtsleeves and waded into the crowd}. Shirtsleeve as an adjective describes casual, direct approaches: {shirtsleeve diplomacy}.

Shisha is a water pipe used to smoke flavored tobacco, also called hookah or narghile. The tobacco is heated with charcoal and the smoke passes through water before inhalation. Shisha is popular in Middle Eastern cafes and has spread globally as a social activity: {We spent the evening at a shisha lounge}. The word can refer to the pipe itself or the flavored tobacco mixture.

Shishkabob is an alternate spelling of shish kebab—chunks of meat and vegetables threaded on a skewer and grilled. The dish originated in the Middle East but has become standard backyard cookout fare: {We threw some shishkabobs on the grill}. The spelling reflects English speakers' phonetic interpretation of the Turkish.

Shishkabobs are pieces of meat and vegetables threaded onto skewers and grilled. The chunks—often lamb, beef, or chicken alternating with peppers, onions, and tomatoes—cook over open flame or charcoal. The spelling varies widely: shish kebab, shish kabob, and other forms all appear. {We're grilling shishkabobs for the party.}

Shishkebab is meat and vegetables threaded onto skewers and grilled, a dish originating in the Middle East. The chunks are typically marinated before cooking: {We made shishkebabs with lamb, peppers, and onions}. Also spelled shish kebab or shish kabob.

Shishkebabs are pieces of meat and vegetables threaded onto skewers and grilled or roasted. The chunks are typically marinated beforehand and may include lamb, beef, chicken, onions, peppers, and tomatoes. The dish originated in the Middle East and has spread worldwide with countless variations: {We grilled shishkebabs at the cookout}. Also spelled shish kebab, shish kabob, or as two words.

Shishkebob is an alternate spelling of shish kebab—chunks of meat and vegetables threaded onto a skewer and grilled. The spelling reflects English speakers' attempts to capture the Turkish original: {We made shishkebobs on the backyard grill}. The dish appears at cookouts and in Middle Eastern restaurants under various spellings.

Shit is a vulgar term for excrement. As a noun, shit can also mean stuff ({Get your shit together}), nonsense ({Don't give me that shit}), trouble ({He's in deep shit}), nothing ({I don't know shit}), or quality goods ({This is the shit}). As a verb, it means to defecate, but also to deceive ({Are you shitting me?}). To shit oneself is to be terrified. As an exclamation, it expresses frustration, surprise, or dismay. Common expressions include {no shit}, {tough shit}, {holy shit}, {shit happens}, {up shit creek}, and {when the shit hits the fan}.

Shitbag is a vulgar insult for a contemptible or worthless person—someone so useless or unpleasant they're likened to a bag of excrement: {That shitbag stole money from his own grandmother}. In military slang, it often targets soldiers who shirk duties or fail to meet standards. The term also literally refers to a colostomy bag.

Shitbirds is a vulgar insult for contemptible or worthless people. The term implies someone is as lowly and disgusting as a bird that feeds on feces. Common in military slang for incompetent or troublesome subordinates: {Listen up, shitbirds—we move out at 0600}. Also used more broadly for anyone viewed with disdain.

A shitbox is a car or other vehicle in terrible condition—rusty, unreliable, barely running: {My first car was a shitbox I bought for five hundred bucks}. The term is vulgar but affectionate; people often speak fondly of the shitboxes they've owned, acknowledging both the vehicle's worthlessness and their attachment to it.

Shitboxes is the plural of shitbox, a vulgar term for a dilapidated or poorly functioning vehicle—typically an old car that barely runs: {He's still driving that shitbox from college}. The term can extend to any rundown piece of equipment or machinery. Despite the contempt, owners sometimes use it affectionately for vehicles they've kept alive against the odds.

Shitcan is vulgar slang meaning to discard, reject, or fire. You shitcan a bad idea by throwing it out. A company shitcans an employee by terminating them: {They shitcanned the whole department}. As a noun, a shitcan is a garbage receptacle or, in military slang, a latrine. The word conveys blunt dismissal—something isn't just removed but thrown away like trash.

Shitcanned is a vulgar slang term meaning fired from a job or forcibly removed from a position. {He got shitcanned after showing up drunk to the meeting.} It can also mean rejected, discarded, or abandoned—applied to projects, plans, or proposals that have been thrown out. {The whole marketing campaign got shitcanned when the budget was cut.} The term carries a strong sense of dismissal with finality and often contempt.

Shitcanning is the act of firing someone from a job or discarding something completely. To shitcan an employee is to terminate them abruptly; to shitcan a project is to abandon it: {The whole proposal got shitcanned after the budget review}. The term is coarse but common in workplace slang, suggesting disposal without ceremony—tossing something in the garbage.

A shitcoin is a cryptocurrency with little or no value, often created as a joke, scam, or speculative gamble. The term dismisses coins lacking legitimate utility or technological foundation: {I lost money on some shitcoin that promised to revolutionize pet food delivery}. What counts as a shitcoin depends on who's talking—Bitcoin maximalists may consider everything else a shitcoin.

Shitfaced is a vulgar adjective meaning extremely drunk: {We got shitfaced and sang karaoke until 2 a.m.} It belongs to a family of crude intoxication terms that combine an expletive with a body part.

A shitfest is a situation marked by chaos, incompetence, or overwhelming unpleasantness. The word emphasizes scale and intensity—not just bad, but spectacularly so: {The meeting devolved into a complete shitfest}. It can describe events, projects, or any collective disaster where everything seems to go wrong at once.

A shitfit is a vulgar term for an explosive outburst of anger or frustration, typically exaggerated or disproportionate to the situation: {My boss threw a shitfit when he saw the typo}. The word emphasizes the theatrical, uncontrolled nature of the tantrum. Also spelled as two words: shit fit.
Shithead is a vulgar insult for a stupid or contemptible person—someone whose head is full of excrement rather than brains: {Don't be a shithead about this}.

A shitheel is a contemptible person—someone low, dishonest, or morally worthless. The term suggests someone so base they might as well have stepped in shit: {Her ex-husband was a complete shitheel who cheated on her for years}. Vulgar but vivid.
Shithole is a vulgar term for a place that is filthy, run-down, or otherwise awful: {We stayed in a total shithole of a motel}.

Shitkicker is a rough, rural, or working-class person—someone who might literally kick through cow shit on a farm. The term can be dismissive or affectionate depending on context. Shitkickers are also heavy boots suitable for such work: {He wore his old shitkickers to the bar}. As an adjective, shitkicker describes anything aggressively country: {shitkicker music}, {a shitkicker bar}.

A shitlist is an informal list of people one dislikes, distrusts, or wants to punish: {After that stunt, you're on my shitlist}. The term implies grudge-keeping and future consequences—being on someone's shitlist means they're watching for opportunities to retaliate or deny favors. Often used humorously or hyperbolically.

A shitlist is an informal record of people someone intends to punish, retaliate against, or treat unfavorably—those who have earned enmity: {After that betrayal, he went straight to the top of my shitlist}. The term is vulgar but common in casual speech. Unlike a formal blacklist, a shitlist is typically personal and implies grudge-holding rather than institutional exclusion.

A shitload is a very large quantity of something—more than expected, more than manageable, or simply a lot: {I have a shitload of work to do}, {They made a shitload of money on that deal}. Vulgar but common in casual speech. The word emphasizes abundance through crude exaggeration.

Shitloads is vulgar slang for a very large quantity: {They made shitloads of money on that deal}. The singular shitload works the same way: {a shitload of paperwork}. Like similar formations (assload, fuckton), it emphasizes abundance through crude intensification.

A shitpost is low-effort online content posted for amusement rather than substance—often deliberately absurd, nonsensical, or provocative. The term spans everything from meaningless spam to surreal humor that rewards those in on the joke. To shitpost is to produce such content: {He spent the evening shitposting on Discord}. The practice has its own ironic subculture where quality emerges from apparent carelessness.

A shitposter is someone who posts low-quality, provocative, or absurd content online, typically to amuse themselves or annoy others. The posts may be intentionally stupid, inflammatory, or nonsensical—the point is disruption or humor rather than meaningful contribution. {He's just a shitposter, don't take the bait.} The term can be affectionate among those who embrace the practice.

Shitposting is posting low-effort, provocative, or absurd content online, often with no purpose beyond getting reactions or filling a feed with nonsense. The intent ranges from ironic humor to deliberate trolling: {I wasn't trying to make a point, just shitposting}. A shitpost may be an intentionally bad meme, a non sequitur reply, or inflammatory garbage. The term is vulgar but neutral—shitposters often wear the label proudly.

Shitposts are low-effort online content posted for amusement rather than substance—deliberately absurd, nonsensical, or provocative material meant to entertain or annoy rather than inform. The term emerged from internet culture where users flood forums or social media with intentionally worthless content: {The whole thread devolved into shitposts}. To shitpost is to produce such content, often as a form of ironic humor or trolling.

A shitshow is a situation characterized by chaos, incompetence, or spectacular failure. The term emphasizes not just that something went wrong, but that it descended into visible, often public disorder: {The press conference was a complete shitshow}. Originally military slang, now widespread in casual speech to describe any badly mismanaged event or ongoing disaster.

Shitshows is the plural of shitshow—situations or events that are chaotically disorganized, embarrassingly mismanaged, or spiraling out of control. The term is vulgar but common: {Both debates were absolute shitshows}. A shitshow implies not just failure but spectacular, often public failure with multiple things going wrong simultaneously.
A shitstorm is a situation of chaos, controversy, or overwhelming trouble: {His comments created a shitstorm on social media}.
Shitstorms is the plural of shitstorm, describing situations of chaos or overwhelming trouble: {The company faced shitstorms on multiple fronts}.

Shitter is a vulgar slang term for a toilet or bathroom. The word derives from shit and emphasizes the fixture's primary function in crude terms. It can also refer disparagingly to a person, suggesting they are worthless or contemptible: {That shitter owes me money}. In card games, particularly poker, a shitter is a bad hand. The phrase {built like a brick shitter} describes someone with a solid, sturdy physique.

Shitting is the present participle of shit, meaning defecating. In expressions like {shitting bricks} or {shitting oneself}, it conveys extreme fear or anxiety: {I was shitting bricks waiting for the test results}.
Shitty is a vulgar adjective meaning bad, unpleasant, or of poor quality: {I had a shitty day}. {That's a shitty thing to say.}

Shitwork is tedious, unglamorous labor that nobody wants to do but somebody must: filing, data entry, cleaning up after others, the thankless tasks that keep organizations running. The term implies such work is beneath one's abilities or position: {I'm tired of doing all the shitwork while he takes the credit}. Often falls disproportionately on those lowest in a hierarchy.

A shiv is a crude knife or stabbing weapon, typically improvised in prison from available materials—a sharpened toothbrush handle, a filed-down piece of metal. The word carries a strong association with prison violence: {He got shivved in the yard}. Outside prison contexts, shiv appears in crime fiction and slang for any makeshift blade.

Shiva is the seven-day mourning period observed in Judaism following the burial of a close relative. Family members "sit shiva" at home, receiving visitors who come to offer condolences: {We're sitting shiva for my grandmother this week}. The practice involves specific rituals including covered mirrors, low seating, and suspended normal activities. (Capitalized Shiva is the Hindu deity.)

Shiver is an involuntary trembling, usually from cold or fear. The body shivers to generate warmth; the mind shivers at what frightens it. {A shiver ran down her spine.} To shiver is to experience this trembling: {She shivered in the cold rain.} The shivers are a bout of shivering, often from illness or dread: {That story gives me the shivers.}

Shivered is the past tense of shiver, meaning to tremble or shake slightly, usually from cold or fear. The body shivers involuntarily to generate warmth: {She shivered in the drafty room}. Shivered also describes fearful trembling: {He shivered at the thought of what might happen}. Glass or other brittle material that shivered has shattered into fragments.

Shivering is the act of trembling or shaking, typically from cold or fear. The body shivers involuntarily to generate warmth through rapid muscle contractions: {She stood shivering in the rain}. Shivering can also accompany fever, shock, or intense emotion: {He was shivering with anticipation}.

Shivers are trembling movements of the body, usually from cold or fear. {A chill ran through her and she felt the shivers}. To shiver is to tremble this way: {He shivered in the doorway, waiting for someone to answer}. The shivers can also be a state of fearful anticipation: {That movie gave me the shivers}. To {shiver your timbers} is nautical slang, now used only in pirate talk.

Shivs are crude knives or stabbing weapons, typically improvised in prisons from available materials—sharpened toothbrushes, filed-down spoons, broken glass bound with tape. The singular shiv can also be a verb: {He got shivved in the yard}. Outside prison contexts, shiv appears in games and fiction for any makeshift blade.

Shivved is the past tense of shiv, meaning to stab someone with a makeshift blade—typically a weapon improvised in prison from available materials like a sharpened toothbrush or piece of metal. The word carries connotations of desperate, close-quarters violence: {He got shivved in the yard over a gambling debt}.

Shlep comes from Yiddish and means to drag or haul something with effort, or to make a tedious journey: {I don't want to shlep all the way downtown for one errand}. As a noun, a shlep is a tiresome trek or a clumsy, slow-moving person. Also spelled schlep.

Shlepp means to carry or drag something cumbersome, or to make a tedious journey: {I shlepped groceries up four flights of stairs}, {We shlepped all the way across town for nothing}. From Yiddish. As a noun, a shlepp is a tedious trip or an oafish, unappealing person. Also spelled schlep.

Shlepped is the past tense of schlep, a Yiddish-derived verb meaning to carry or drag something heavy or cumbersome, or to make a tedious journey: {I shlepped groceries up four flights of stairs}, {We shlepped all the way across town for nothing}. The word conveys effort and inconvenience. Also spelled schlepped.

Shlepping is carrying or hauling something, especially with effort or reluctance. From Yiddish, the word suggests tedious transport—dragging bags, lugging groceries, moving boxes: {I spent the morning shlepping furniture up three flights of stairs}. To shlep somewhere is to travel there tediously: {We shlepped all the way across town for nothing}. Also spelled schlepping.

A shlub is an ordinary, unremarkable person, often one who is seen as clumsy, awkward, or somewhat pitiable. The word comes from Yiddish and carries connotations of schlumpiness—someone who may be poorly dressed, socially graceless, or simply unimpressive. It's usually mildly disparaging but can also be affectionate: {He's just a regular shlub trying to get by}. The spelling schlub is equally common.
clues: Ordinary person lacking charm or drive

definition: Shlubs is the plural of shlub, a Yiddish-derived term for an ordinary, unremarkable person—someone schlumpy, unstylish, or socially awkward. The word carries affectionate condescension: {Just a bunch of shlubs watching the game}. A shlub isn't necessarily disliked, just unimpressive. Also spelled schlubs.

Shmaltz is rendered chicken or goose fat used in traditional Jewish cooking, prized for its rich flavor in dishes like chopped liver or matzo balls. The word comes from Yiddish and has spawned the more common figurative sense: excessive sentimentality or emotional appeal, especially in music, theater, or writing. {The movie was pure shmaltz, but I cried anyway.} Something dripping with shmaltz is schmaltzy. Also spelled schmaltz.

Shmaltzy describes something excessively sentimental or emotionally overwrought, often to the point of being corny or cloying. The word comes from Yiddish *schmaltz*, meaning rendered chicken fat—the implication being that something shmaltzy is greasy, rich, and laid on too thick. It applies especially to music, films, or speeches that try too hard to tug at heartstrings: {The movie's shmaltzy ending had everyone rolling their eyes}. Also spelled *schmaltzy*.

Shmear is a Yiddish-influenced spelling of schmear, meaning a spread or smear of something soft—most often cream cheese on a bagel: {I'll have a bagel with a shmear}. The {whole shmear} means everything, the entire affair: {They ordered lox, bagels, capers—the whole shmear}.

A shmo is a stupid, boring, or insignificant person—someone unremarkable or slightly pathetic: {Some shmo from accounting}. The word comes from Yiddish and carries mild contempt or dismissal rather than strong insult. Also spelled schmo. The related schmuck is harsher.

A shmoe is an ordinary, unremarkable person—often one who is naive, easily fooled, or slightly pitiable. The word carries affectionate condescension: {Some poor shmoe got stuck with the bill}. From Yiddish, it suggests someone harmless but not particularly sharp. Also spelled schmo or schmoe.

Shmooze, also spelled schmooze, is a verb meaning to chat in a friendly, often ingratiating way, typically to gain favor or make useful connections. It comes from Yiddish and carries connotations of smooth talk and social maneuvering. {She spent the whole party shmoozing with potential investors.} The noun shmooze refers to such a conversation, and someone skilled at this is a shmoozer.

Shmoozing is engaging in friendly, often self-serving conversation—chatting someone up to build rapport or gain advantage. From Yiddish. The word suggests warmth that may be strategic: {He spent the cocktail hour shmoozing potential investors}. A shmoozer is skilled at this kind of social lubrication. Also spelled schmoozing.

Shmuck is a Yiddish-derived insult meaning a foolish, contemptible, or objectionable person. The word literally means penis in Yiddish, though most English speakers use it without awareness of this origin. It falls somewhere between mild and moderately offensive, roughly equivalent to jerk or asshole depending on context. {Don't be such a shmuck.} The spelling schmuck is more common.

Shmucks is the plural of shmuck, a Yiddish-derived insult for a foolish, contemptible, or gullible person. The word literally means penis in Yiddish, though this origin is largely forgotten in English usage. {Those shmucks fell for the scam}. The spelling schmucks is equally common.

Shmutz is Yiddish-derived slang for dirt, grime, or any unwanted substance—especially a small spot or smudge: {You've got some shmutz on your collar}. A parent might lick a thumb to wipe shmutz off a child's face. The word carries affectionate, informal connotations. Also spelled schmutz.

A shoal is a shallow area in a body of water, where the bottom rises near the surface and may pose a hazard to boats: {The ship ran aground on a shoal}. Shoal also names a large group of fish swimming together, synonymous with school: {A shoal of mackerel darkened the water}. As an adjective, shoal means shallow: {shoal waters}.

Shoals are shallow areas in a body of water where the bottom rises near the surface, creating hazards for navigation. A ship may run aground on shoals. The word also means a large group of fish swimming together: {A shoal of herring passed beneath the boat}. Figuratively, shoals suggest hidden dangers or difficulties: {the shoals of academic politics}.

Shock covers a cluster of meanings unified by the idea of sudden, forceful impact. A physical shock is a violent collision or jolt; an electrical shock is current passing through the body. Emotional shock is the stunned state following unexpected news or trauma. In medicine, shock is a dangerous condition where blood pressure drops critically. To shock someone is to disturb or offend them with something unexpected: {The verdict shocked the nation}. A shock of hair is a thick, unruly mass—a different word entirely.

Shocked describes a state of sudden surprise, disbelief, or disturbance. The feeling ranges from mild astonishment to deep emotional distress: {I was shocked to hear about her resignation}, {shocked by the violence in the film}. Someone can be shocked into silence or action. The word often carries moral overtones—{shocked and appalled}—though it's frequently exaggerated for effect: {I'm shocked, shocked to find gambling going on here}.

A shocker is something that shocks—an unexpected event, revelation, or piece of news that startles or disturbs: {The election results were a real shocker}. The word often carries irony, used sarcastically when something is entirely predictable: {He showed up late again—shocker}. In British slang, a shocker is something notably bad or disappointing: {I had an absolute shocker of a day}.

Shocking describes something that causes sudden surprise, dismay, or outrage. A shocking {revelation} upends expectations; shocking {violence} disturbs viewers. The word implies intensity—more than merely surprising, something shocking provokes a visceral reaction. It can also describe things meant to provoke: {shock value}, {shock jock}. Used loosely, shocking expresses mild disapproval: {The prices were shocking}.

Shocks are sudden, jarring impacts—physical or emotional. A car's shocks (short for shock absorbers) cushion against road impact. Electric shocks jolt the body. Emotional shocks arrive as unexpected news: {The diagnosis came as a shock}. To shock is to disturb or offend: {Her language shocked the guests}. Shock can also describe a thick mass of hair: {a shock of white hair}.

A shockwave is a wave of intense pressure that moves through a medium faster than the speed of sound, typically caused by an explosion or supersonic object. The term extends to any sudden, powerful disturbance that spreads outward: {The assassination sent shockwaves through the political establishment}. Also spelled as two words: shock wave.

Shockwaves are intense pressure disturbances that travel through a medium—air, water, or earth—faster than the speed of sound. Explosions and supersonic aircraft produce literal shockwaves. Figuratively, shockwaves describe the spreading impact of dramatic events: {The scandal sent shockwaves through the industry}. Also written as two words: shock waves.

Shoddy describes something poorly made or of inferior quality: {shoddy construction}, {shoddy workmanship}. The word often implies cutting corners or lack of care rather than honest limitation. Shoddy treatment is careless or disrespectful. Originally, shoddy was a noun for cheap fabric made from recycled wool—the material's poor quality gave rise to the adjective.

A shoe is a covering for the foot, typically with a stiff sole and flexible upper. Shoes protect feet from terrain and weather while signaling style, status, or occupation: {running shoes}, {dress shoes}, {work shoes}. To be {in someone's shoes} is to be in their situation. A horseshoe is also called a shoe. To shoe a horse is to fit it with these protective metal plates. {If the shoe fits, wear it} means accept a criticism that applies to you.

A shoebill is a large African wading bird with a massive shoe-shaped bill, standing up to five feet tall with a seven-foot wingspan. Found in swamps of central Africa, it's known for its prehistoric appearance and statue-like stillness when hunting. Also called shoebill stork, though it's more closely related to pelicans.

Shoebills are large wading birds native to East African swamps, named for their massive shoe-shaped bills. Standing up to five feet tall with a prehistoric appearance, they're known for their motionless hunting style and unsettling death stare. They hunt fish, frogs, and small reptiles by lunging suddenly with their powerful beaks.

A shoebox is a cardboard box designed to hold a pair of shoes. Because shoeboxes are sturdy, uniform, and accumulate in closets, they become storage containers for photographs, letters, receipts, and small keepsakes: {I found the old letters in a shoebox in the attic}. As an adjective, shoebox describes cramped spaces: {a shoebox apartment}.

Shoeboxes are cardboard containers designed to hold shoes for retail sale and storage. After their original purpose, they commonly serve as improvised storage for photographs, receipts, letters, and small keepsakes: {I found old love letters in a shoebox in the attic}. A shoebox apartment is cramped and rectangular.

Shoegaze is a style of rock music characterized by heavily distorted guitars, ethereal vocals buried in the mix, and dense layers of sound. The name comes from performers' tendency to stare at their feet—actually watching their effects pedals—rather than engaging the audience. The genre emerged in late 1980s Britain: {My Bloody Valentine basically invented shoegaze}. As a verb, to shoegaze is to perform or listen to this music.

Shoegazing is a style of alternative rock from late 1980s Britain, characterized by layers of distorted guitars, ethereal vocals buried in the mix, and dense walls of sound. The name comes from performers' tendency to stare downward at their effects pedals rather than engage the audience. {My Bloody Valentine pioneered the shoegazing sound.} The term often applies to the introspective, dreamy aesthetic beyond just the music.

A shoehorn is a curved implement, typically made of plastic, metal, or horn, that helps you slip your heel into a shoe without crushing the back. The verb shoehorn means to force something into a tight space or situation where it doesn't naturally fit: {They shoehorned three more passengers into the already crowded van}. The figurative use often implies awkwardness or strain: {The director shoehorned a romance subplot into an already bloated script}.

Shoehorned describes something forced into a space or situation where it doesn't quite fit. From the curved tool used to wedge feet into tight shoes, the term now usually appears figuratively: {The director shoehorned a romantic subplot into an already crowded film}. The implication is awkwardness or strain—the thing inserted doesn't belong naturally.

Shoehorning is forcing something into a space or category where it doesn't quite fit. The image comes from the tool used to squeeze a foot into a tight shoe. You might shoehorn a meeting into an already packed schedule, or shoehorn an irrelevant point into an argument: {He kept shoehorning references to his book into every conversation}. The word implies awkwardness or strain—the thing being inserted doesn't belong naturally.

Shoehorns are curved tools for easing the heel into a shoe without crushing the back. The verb shoehorn means to force something into a tight space: {They shoehorned three more passengers into the back seat}. It often implies awkward or improper fitting: {The director shoehorned a love story into the action film}.

A shoelace is a cord or string threaded through eyelets to fasten a shoe snugly to the foot. Learning to tie shoelaces is a childhood milestone. {Your shoelace is untied.} To do something {on a shoestring} suggests operating with minimal resources—a shoestring being even less substantial than a proper lace.

Shoelaces are the cords threaded through eyelets to secure shoes to feet. They're tied in a bow for easy removal. {Your shoelaces are untied.} Learning to tie shoelaces is a childhood milestone. Velcro and slip-ons have displaced laces on some footwear, but laced shoes remain standard for athletic and formal wear.

A shoemaker is a person who makes or repairs shoes. The trade is ancient, and the term persists even as mass production has largely replaced handcrafting: {The old shoemaker worked from a tiny shop downtown}. A cobbler is similar, though traditionally cobblers only repaired shoes while shoemakers made them.

Shoemakers are people who make or repair shoes. The trade is ancient, and shoemaker appears in countless folk tales and idioms. {The shoemaker's children go barefoot} suggests that professionals neglect their own families while serving others. A cobbler is a shoemaker who specializes in repairs rather than making shoes from scratch.

Shoemaking is the craft or industry of producing footwear. The term covers everything from artisanal cobblers handcrafting bespoke shoes to factory production of mass-market sneakers. {He apprenticed in shoemaking before opening his own shop.}

Shoes are coverings for the feet, typically with a sturdy sole and an upper portion. The word encompasses everything from sneakers to dress shoes to boots. To be {in someone's shoes} is to imagine their situation. {If the shoe fits, wear it} means accept a criticism that applies to you. To {wait for the other shoe to drop} is to anticipate an inevitable consequence.

A shoeshine is the act of polishing shoes, or the polished appearance itself: {He stopped for a shoeshine before the interview}. A shoeshine boy or shoeshine man offers the service, typically from a sidewalk stand. The word can modify other nouns: {shoeshine kit}, {shoeshine stand}.

Shoestring is a lace used to fasten shoes. As an adjective, it describes something done with minimal resources: a shoestring {budget}, a shoestring {operation}. The phrase {on a shoestring} means with very little money: {They started the company on a shoestring}. In baseball, a shoestring {catch} is a ball caught just above the ground.

A shofar is a ram's horn blown as a trumpet in Jewish religious ceremonies, most notably during Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. The sound—a series of blasts ranging from short staccato bursts to long sustained notes—calls worshippers to reflection and repentance. {The shofar sounded at the close of Yom Kippur.}

A shogun was a military dictator who ruled Japan from the late twelfth century until 1868, when the emperor was restored to power. The shogunate held actual political authority while emperors remained ceremonial figures: {The shogun controlled the samurai class}. In modern usage, shogun sometimes describes a powerful behind-the-scenes leader: {He was the shogun of the party machine}.

A shogunate is a Japanese military government headed by a shogun—the supreme military commander who ruled Japan while the emperor remained a figurehead. The term refers both to the institution and to specific historical periods: the Tokugawa shogunate lasted from 1603 to 1868. {The shogunate maintained strict control over foreign trade.}

Shoguns were the military dictators who ruled Japan from the late 12th century until 1868, wielding power while emperors remained as ceremonial figureheads. The title passed through hereditary dynasties, with the Tokugawa shoguns holding control for over 250 years. In contemporary use, shogun sometimes describes any powerful behind-the-scenes leader: {He was the shogun of the department, making all the real decisions}.

Shone is the past tense and past participle of shine, used when the verb means to emit or reflect light: {The sun shone through the clouds}, {Her eyes shone with excitement}. When shine means to polish something, the past tense is shined: {He shined his shoes}.

Shoo is a sound used to drive away animals or people, especially birds or small creatures: {Shoo! Get out of here!} As a verb, to shoo is to chase something away with gestures or sounds: {She shooed the cat off the counter}. A {shoo-in} is someone virtually certain to win or succeed.

Past tense of shoo. To shoo is to wave or gesture at someone or something to make them go away, often with quick hand motions and the word "shoo" itself: {She shooed the cat off the counter}. The action is dismissive but usually not hostile—more nuisance removal than aggression: {He shooed the kids out of the kitchen}.

Shooing is the act of driving someone or something away with gestures or sounds, typically waving hands and saying "shoo": {She was shooing flies from the picnic table}. The word suggests a casual, dismissive urgency—you shoo away pests, stray animals, or people you want gone without ceremony.

Shook is the past tense of shake. As slang, shook means emotionally affected—shocked, disturbed, or deeply moved: {I was shook when I heard the news}, {That movie left me shook}. The usage suggests being rattled or unsettled, as if physically shaken. In older usage, shook up carries the same sense: {all shook up}.

A shoot is new growth sprouting from a plant—a stem, branch, or sprout pushing up: {Bamboo shoots are edible}. {New shoots appeared in spring}. To shoot is to fire a weapon, send forth rapidly, or move quickly: {Shoot the arrow}. {She shot him a glance}. {He shot down the hallway}. A shoot is also a photography or film session: {The shoot lasted all day}. As an exclamation, shoot is a mild euphemism for shit: {Oh shoot, I forgot}. {Shoot, that's too bad}. The euphemism allows frustration without vulgarity.

A shootdown is the act of bringing down an aircraft by gunfire or missile. The term appears most often in military and news contexts: {The shootdown of the spy plane escalated tensions between the two nations}. As a verb phrase, shoot down means to destroy an aircraft in flight, or figuratively to reject something decisively: {They shot down every proposal we made}.

A shooter is someone who fires a weapon—an {active shooter} threatens people in a public place. In sports, a shooter is a player who shoots: {She's one of the best shooters in the league}. A shooter can be a shooting game, especially a video game genre focused on gunplay: {first-person shooter}. A shooter is also a small glass of straight liquor meant to be downed in one gulp.

Shooters is the plural of shooter—one who shoots. A shooter can be a person firing a weapon, an athlete who takes shots at a goal, or a small glass of liquor meant to be downed in one gulp: {We ordered a round of shooters}. In slang, shooters are guns: {He's got shooters in the trunk}. In gaming, shooters are video games centered on gunplay: {first-person shooters}, {third-person shooters}.

Shooting is the act of firing a gun or other projectile weapon. A shooting is an incident where someone is shot: {There was a shooting at the mall}. Shooting also names the sport of target practice or hunting with firearms. Extended uses cover anything propelled rapidly: {a shooting star}, {shooting pains}. In film and photography, shooting is the process of capturing images: {We start shooting next week}.

Shootings are incidents in which firearms are discharged at people. The term most often refers to violent attacks, especially mass shootings at schools, workplaces, or public gatherings: {Another mass shooting dominated the news cycle}. Police shootings involve officers firing at suspects. A shooting can also be a film production: {The shooting wrapped in three weeks}.

A shootout is a gun battle, typically a dramatic exchange of fire between opposing sides: {The shootout left three officers wounded}. In sports, a shootout is a tiebreaker where players take turns attempting to score—penalty kicks in soccer, alternating shots in hockey. By extension, any decisive head-to-head confrontation: {a political shootout over the budget}.

Shootouts are exchanges of gunfire, typically between opposing groups—police and criminals, rival gangs, or military forces: {Three people were killed in the shootout}. In sports, a shootout is a tiebreaker format where players take alternating shots on goal, common in hockey and soccer. By extension, any dramatic head-to-head confrontation can be called a shootout: {a shootout between rival tech companies for market dominance}.

Shoots is the plural of shoot—new plant growth or photography sessions: {The bamboo sends up shoots in spring}. {We have three shoots scheduled this week}. As a verb, shoots means fires, sends forth, or moves quickly: {She shoots hoops after school}. {He shoots from the hip}.

A shop is a place where goods are sold or services are provided—often smaller and more specialized than a store: {a coffee shop}, {a barber shop}, {a print shop}. In British English, shop is the general word where Americans would say store. A shop is also a workspace for making or repairing things: {machine shop}, {wood shop}. To shop is to visit stores looking to buy: {I need to shop for groceries}. To {shop around} is to compare prices or options before committing.

A shopaholic is someone who shops compulsively, treating retail therapy as an addiction. The word blends "shop" with "alcoholic" to suggest the behavior is habitual and hard to control: {She's such a shopaholic—her closet is stuffed with things she's never worn}. The tone is usually light and self-deprecating rather than clinical.

Shopaholics is the plural of shopaholic—a person with a compulsive urge to shop, often spending beyond their means or buying things they don't need. The word blends shopping with alcoholic, suggesting addiction: {The mall was packed with shopaholics on Black Friday}. The term is usually lighthearted rather than clinical.

Shopaholism is compulsive shopping—the inability to resist buying things, often beyond one's means or needs. The term treats shopping as an addiction, parallel to alcoholism: {Her shopaholism left her buried in credit card debt}. The condition blends genuine psychological compulsion with lighthearted self-deprecation about retail indulgence.

The shopfloor is the area of a factory or workshop where production happens—where workers operate machinery and assemble products, as distinct from offices or management spaces. The term often carries class connotations, representing ordinary workers versus executives: {Decisions made in the boardroom don't always make sense on the shopfloor}. Also spelled shop floor.

A shopgirl is a young woman who works in a retail store, typically as a sales clerk. The term is old-fashioned and carries class connotations—shopgirls were working-class women in an era when such employment was one of few respectable options: {She started as a shopgirl and worked her way up to floor manager}.

A shopkeeper is a person who owns or manages a small retail store. The term is more common in British than American English, where {store owner} or {shop owner} is preferred. {The shopkeeper unlocked the door at nine sharp.} The word suggests an independent business rather than a chain or franchise.

Shopkeepers is the plural of shopkeeper—a person who owns or manages a small retail store. The term suggests independent proprietors rather than employees of large chains: {The shopkeepers along Main Street formed a merchants' association}. In British usage especially, shopkeeper carries connotations of the traditional high street and small-scale commerce.

To shoplift is to steal merchandise from a store while posing as a customer. The crime involves concealing items and leaving without paying: {She was caught shoplifting cosmetics}. A shoplifter is one who does this; the act is shoplifting. The term emphasizes the retail context—stealing from shelves rather than from persons or homes.

Shoplifted is the past tense of shoplift—to steal merchandise from a store while posing as a customer: {She shoplifted a pair of earrings}. The word implies concealment and walking out without paying, distinguishing it from robbery or burglary. {He was caught on camera and arrested for what he had shoplifted}.

A shoplifter is someone who steals merchandise from a store while pretending to be an ordinary customer. The term emphasizes the method—concealing items and walking out without paying—rather than the scale of theft: {Store security detained the shoplifter at the exit}.

Shoplifters are people who steal merchandise from retail stores, typically by concealing items and walking out without paying. The term emphasizes the casual, opportunistic nature of the crime—distinct from burglary or armed robbery. {Store security detained two shoplifters near the exit.}

Shoplifting is stealing merchandise from a store while posing as a customer. The crime typically involves concealing items and walking out without paying. Someone caught shoplifting may face arrest, fines, or a ban from the store. {She was charged with shoplifting after security found unpaid items in her bag.}

Shoplifts is the act of stealing merchandise from a store while posing as a customer. The term emphasizes the method—concealing items and walking out without paying—rather than the scale: {She shoplifts makeup from the drugstore}. A person who does this is a shoplifter.

Shopped is the past tense of shop, meaning visited stores to browse or buy: {We shopped for groceries yesterday}. To have shopped around is to have compared options before deciding: {She shopped around for the best mortgage rate}. In British slang, to have shopped someone is to have informed on them to authorities: {He shopped his accomplice to the police}.

A shopper is someone who shops—browsing or buying goods at stores or online. The word often implies browsing rather than committed buying: {Just a shopper, not a buyer}. In retail contexts, a shopper may be a person hired to evaluate customer service by posing as a customer ({mystery shopper}) or a free advertising circular distributed at supermarkets.

Shoppers are people engaged in shopping—browsing stores or websites with intent to buy. The term covers casual browsers and serious buyers alike: {The mall was packed with holiday shoppers}. Retail businesses track shopper behavior to optimize store layouts and marketing. A personal shopper selects items on behalf of clients.

Shopping is the activity of visiting stores or browsing online to look at or purchase goods. It can be a practical errand {I need to do some grocery shopping} or a leisure activity {We spent the afternoon shopping for antiques}. As a modifier, shopping describes places or things related to this activity: shopping {mall}, shopping {cart}, shopping {list}. To {go shopping} is the standard phrase for the activity itself.

Shops are retail stores where goods are sold. The word is more common in British than American English, where store predominates. To shop is to visit such places looking to buy things: {I need to shop for groceries}. A shop is also a workshop or place where things are made or repaired: {auto body shop}, {machine shop}. To {shop around} is to compare options before committing. To {talk shop} is to discuss work matters in a social setting.

Shoptalk is conversation about one's work or profession, especially when it bores or excludes others present: {The dinner devolved into shoptalk about quarterly earnings}. The word implies technical jargon or insider concerns that outsiders find tedious. Also spelled as two words.

A shopvac is a heavy-duty vacuum cleaner designed for workshops, garages, and construction sites. Unlike household vacuums, shopvacs handle wet spills, sawdust, drywall dust, and debris that would clog or damage regular machines. The name comes from Shop-Vac, a brand that became generic: {I need to shopvac the garage after sanding}.

Shore is the land along the edge of a body of water—ocean, lake, or river. The shore is where water meets land: {We walked along the shore at sunset}. To go {ashore} is to leave a boat for land. Shore also functions as a verb meaning to support or prop up, usually with *up*: {They shored up the foundation with timbers}. Figuratively, you can shore up anything that needs reinforcement: {shore up a failing argument}, {shore up public confidence}.

Shorebreak is a wave that breaks directly on or very close to the shore, where the water meets the beach. These waves form when incoming swells hit a steep, shallow bottom and collapse abruptly rather than rolling in gradually. Shorebreak can be surprisingly powerful and dangerous, slamming swimmers and bodyboarders onto hard-packed sand: {The shorebreak at that beach has broken plenty of necks}.

A shoreline is the boundary where a body of water meets the land—the edge of an ocean, lake, or river. The term emphasizes the linear quality of this boundary: {We walked along the shoreline}, {The shoreline was dotted with fishing villages}. Unlike shore, which suggests an area, shoreline refers specifically to the line of contact.

Shorelines are the boundaries where land meets a body of water—the edges of oceans, lakes, and rivers. The term often appears in environmental and coastal management contexts: {Development along shorelines threatens wildlife habitats}. Shoreline can also function as an adjective: {shoreline erosion}, {shoreline property}.

Shores are the land along the edge of a body of water—an ocean, lake, or river. The word often suggests the meeting point of land and water rather than deep inland: {We walked along the shore at sunset}. In the plural, shores can mean a country or region, especially poetically: {distant shores}, {these shores}. As a verb, to shore up is to support or reinforce something at risk of collapsing: {They shored up the sagging foundation}.

Shoring is the system of temporary supports used to hold up a structure during construction, repair, or excavation. Workers install shoring to prevent walls from collapsing, trenches from caving in, or buildings from shifting: {The crew put up shoring before removing the load-bearing wall}. Figuratively, shoring up means reinforcing something weakened: {The CEO's statement was meant to shore up investor confidence}.

Shorn is the past participle of shear, meaning cut or clipped. Most often it describes sheep that have had their wool removed: {freshly shorn sheep}. It extends to hair cut very short or removed entirely: {shorn of his locks}. Figuratively, to be shorn of something is to be stripped or deprived of it: {shorn of power}, {shorn of dignity}.

The meanings of short in all parts of speech derive from its core adjectival meaning, where it is the opposite of long and tall. For spatial uses, short indicates small distance from end to end: short hair. For temporal uses, short indicates little elapsed time from beginning to end: a short break. Short is also frequent as an adverb, where it often has a negative connotation of undesirable: They had to cut their vacation short. His performance came up short. If you short someone, you give them less than they expect or less than they are due, often in a dishonest way.

A shortage is an insufficient supply of something needed or wanted. When demand exceeds availability, there's a shortage: {a housing shortage}, {a shortage of skilled workers}, {food shortages during the war}. The word implies a gap between what exists and what's required—not complete absence, but not enough.

Shortages is the plural of shortage—situations where demand exceeds supply. The word implies insufficiency of something needed: {food shortages}, {labor shortages}, {housing shortages}. Unlike scarcity, which suggests natural rarity, shortages often imply systemic or temporary failures: {Supply chain disruptions caused shortages of computer chips}.

Shortbread is a rich, crumbly cookie made with butter, sugar, and flour—no leavening. The "short" refers to the crumbly texture created by high butter content, as in shortening. Traditional Scottish shortbread is often shaped into rounds or fingers: {She served shortbread with tea}. The simplicity of ingredients makes butter quality essential.

Shortcake is a dessert of sweet biscuit or sponge cake topped with fruit and whipped cream. Strawberry shortcake is the classic version: {We're having strawberry shortcake for dessert}. The cake itself is called shortcake because it contains a high ratio of fat (shortening), making the texture tender and crumbly rather than chewy.

Shortchange means to give someone less than they're owed, originally in the literal sense of returning insufficient change from a transaction. The meaning extends to any situation where someone receives less than they deserve: {The new policy shortchanges rural communities}. A shortchange artist is a scammer who confuses cashiers to steal money.

Shortchanged means cheated out of what you're owed—originally referring to receiving too little change in a transaction, now broadly applied to any situation where someone gets less than they deserve: {I felt shortchanged by the whole experience}. The word implies unfairness, whether through deliberate deception or mere circumstance: {Budget cuts left the schools shortchanged}.

Shortchanging is giving someone less money back than they're owed in a transaction, whether by accident or deliberate cheating. The figurative sense has become more common: to shortchange someone is to give them less than they deserve or were promised. {The city's students have been shortchanged by years of budget cuts.} {I felt shortchanged by the rushed ending of an otherwise great novel.}

Shortcircuited describes something that has been bypassed or interrupted before completing its normal course. In electrical systems, a short circuit occurs when current flows through an unintended path, often causing failure. Figuratively, to shortcircuit something is to circumvent or derail it: {The scandal shortcircuited his political career}. Also spelled short-circuited.

Shortcircuiting is bypassing the normal path or process, often to get results faster. In electronics, a short circuit occurs when current flows through an unintended path, bypassing resistance. Figuratively, to shortcircuit something is to circumvent or undermine it: {The scandal shortcircuited his campaign}. The term also describes mental processes that skip deliberate reasoning: {Fear shortcircuits rational thought}. Also spelled short-circuiting.

A shortcoming is a flaw or deficiency—a way in which someone or something falls short of expectations or standards. The word often appears in the plural: {Despite its shortcomings, the plan was approved}. Unlike more pointed terms like fault or failure, shortcoming suggests incompleteness rather than fundamental wrongness: {He was aware of his own shortcomings}.

Shortcomings are faults, flaws, or failures to meet a standard or expectation. The word implies a gap between what is and what should be—a falling short of some ideal. Unlike defects, which suggest something broken, shortcomings often point to inadequacy rather than malfunction: {The report highlighted shortcomings in the company's safety procedures}. People acknowledge their own shortcomings when admitting personal limitations or weaknesses.

A shortcut is a quicker or more direct route than the usual one: {We took a shortcut through the park}. The meaning extends to any method that saves time or effort: {There are no shortcuts to learning a language}. In computing, a shortcut is a keyboard combination or icon that provides quick access to a function or file.

Shortcuts are quicker routes or methods that bypass the usual process. A shortcut through the park saves time; a keyboard shortcut executes a command without navigating menus. Shortcuts can also mean cutting corners: {There are no shortcuts to mastery}. The singular shortcut works as noun, verb, and adjective: {shortcut the approval process}, {a shortcut key}.

Shorted is the past tense of short, most often appearing in electrical contexts. A circuit shorted when an unintended connection allowed current to flow along an easier path: {The wiring shorted and blew the fuse}. In finance, someone who shorted a stock bet on its price falling: {He shorted GameStop and lost a fortune}. To be shorted means to receive less than expected: {The cashier shorted me five dollars}.

Shorten means to make or become shorter. You shorten a dress by hemming it, shorten a trip by leaving early, shorten the odds by improving your chances. {We need to shorten this article by a thousand words.} The opposite is lengthen.

Shortening is solid fat used in baking to make pastry tender and flaky—it "shortens" the gluten strands that would otherwise make dough tough. Vegetable shortening like Crisco replaced lard in many American kitchens. More broadly, shortening is the act of making something shorter: {the shortening of days in autumn}.

Shortest is the superlative form of short—the least long in distance, duration, or height among three or more things compared. {Take the shortest route}. {She was the shortest person in the room}. {That was the shortest movie I've ever seen}.
clues: Taking the least amount of time

definition: A shortfall is the amount by which something falls short of what is needed, expected, or required. It typically appears in financial and resource contexts: a budget shortfall means revenues don't cover planned expenditures, while a shortfall in supplies means there aren't enough to meet demand. {The company faced a $2 million shortfall after sales dropped.} Unlike deficit, which often implies debt, shortfall emphasizes the gap between what you have and what you need.

Shortfalls are amounts by which something falls short of what's needed or expected. Budget shortfalls mean revenues don't cover expenses. A shortfall in production means output didn't meet targets. The word emphasizes the gap between actual and required: {The pension fund faces a shortfall of two billion dollars}. Unlike deficits, shortfalls can apply to any measurable quantity—staffing, supplies, votes.

Shorthand is a system of rapid writing using symbols or abbreviations instead of standard letters and words, historically used by secretaries and court reporters to transcribe speech in real time. By extension, shorthand means any abbreviated way of referring to something: {The phrase became shorthand for government dysfunction}. As an adjective: {shorthand notes}, {shorthand notation}.

Shorthanded means lacking the usual or necessary number of workers or players: {We're shorthanded today—two people called in sick}. In hockey, a team is shorthanded when a player is in the penalty box, giving the opponent a numerical advantage. A shorthanded goal is scored despite having fewer players on the ice.

Shorties is the plural of shorty, an informal term for someone short in stature or, affectionately, a child or younger person. In hip-hop and urban slang, shorty often means an attractive woman or a girlfriend: {He was out with his shorty last night}. The spelling shawty reflects pronunciation in some dialects. Shorties can also refer to small servings of alcohol or short cigarettes.

Shorting is causing an electrical short circuit, whether accidental or deliberate: {The faulty wiring kept shorting the system}. In finance, shorting means selling borrowed securities with the intention of buying them back later at a lower price—betting that the price will fall: {Hedge funds were shorting the stock heavily}. Both senses involve bypassing the normal path or process.

A shortlist is a reduced list of candidates or options that have made it past initial screening. From a pool of applicants, a committee produces a shortlist of finalists: {Three candidates were shortlisted for the position}. The verb shortlist means to place on such a list. British spelling often hyphenates: short-list.

Shortlisted is the past tense and past participle of shortlist, meaning selected for a final round of consideration. Candidates for jobs, nominees for awards, and proposals for contracts get shortlisted when they survive initial cuts: {She was shortlisted for the position}. More common in British than American English, where "made the short list" often substitutes.

Shortlists is the plural of shortlist—a narrowed selection of candidates or options from a larger pool, typically finalists under serious consideration: {Three novels made the shortlists for both major prizes}. As a verb form, shortlists means to place on such a list: {The committee shortlists five applicants for interviews}.

Shorts are pants that end above the knee, worn in warm weather or for athletics. The word is always plural: {a pair of shorts}. Shorts also names short-term investments or securities, and in film, short subjects—brief movies shown before the main feature. Someone who is {caught short} lacks what they need at a critical moment.

To shortsheet a bed is to fold the top sheet so it doubles back partway down, preventing someone from stretching out their legs fully—a classic prank at summer camps and sleepovers: {We shortsheeeted the counselor's bunk while he was at the bonfire}. The trick is harmless but startling when discovered at bedtime.

Shortsighted describes someone who cannot see distant objects clearly, a condition also called nearsighted or myopic. The word is more common in its figurative sense: lacking foresight or failing to consider long-term consequences. A shortsighted {policy} or shortsighted {decision} may solve an immediate problem but create bigger ones down the road. {It was shortsighted of them to cut the maintenance budget.} The word often carries a note of criticism, implying that better planning was possible.

Shortsightedness is the quality of focusing on immediate concerns while failing to consider long-term consequences: {The shortsightedness of the policy became clear within a decade}. It suggests a lack of foresight or planning. The word also refers literally to nearsightedness—difficulty seeing distant objects clearly—though this sense is less common in American English.

Shortstack is informal for a short person, often used affectionately or teasingly: {Hey shortstack, need help reaching that?} The term comes from a short stack of pancakes—a smaller serving than the full stack. In poker, a shortstack is a player with relatively few chips compared to others at the table.

Shortstop is the defensive position in baseball between second and third base, or the player who occupies it. The shortstop typically has the widest range on the infield and handles the most ground balls. The position is often called simply short: {He plays short for the Yankees}. A shortstop must be quick, agile, and have a strong throwing arm.

Shortstops is the plural of shortstop, the baseball position between second and third base, or the player who occupies it. The shortstop typically handles more fielding chances than any other position and must combine quick reflexes with a strong throwing arm. Great shortstops are often among a team's most valuable players: {The Yankees have had legendary shortstops}.

A shortsword is a blade longer than a dagger but shorter than a standard sword, typically between one and two feet. Historical shortswords include the Roman gladius. The term appears most often in fantasy games and fiction, where it represents a quick, light weapon favoring agility over reach: {The rogue equipped a shortsword for close combat}.

Shortwave refers to radio frequencies between about 3 and 30 megahertz, capable of traveling long distances by bouncing off the ionosphere. Before the internet, shortwave radio was how people tuned in to foreign broadcasts: {listening to the BBC on shortwave}, {a shortwave radio}. The term works as noun, adjective, or verb: {to shortwave a message across the Atlantic}.

Shorty is an affectionate or casual term for someone short in stature, often a child or a woman. In hip-hop and urban slang, shorty refers to an attractive woman or girlfriend: {That's my shorty}. It can also mean a young person generally, regardless of height: {The shorties on the block look up to him}. Also spelled shawty.

Shot gets all of its work by being the past and past participle, as well as the verbal noun, of shoot. A shot is an instance or the result of shooting – a gun, a scene in a movie, or a picture with a camera. A shot is also a small measure of liquid: Give me a shot of whiskey. An injection of a drug with a needle is also a shot in American English. Something described as shot is in a poor or exhausted condition: My nerves are shot.

A shotgun is a firearm with a smooth bore that fires shells containing multiple pellets, spreading on impact—effective for hunting birds and close-range combat. Shotgun extends to things characterized by wide spread or side-by-side arrangement: {shotgun approach}, {shotgun wedding} (hastily arranged, often due to pregnancy). To {ride shotgun} is to sit in the front passenger seat, from the armed guard position on stagecoaches. As a verb, to shotgun a beer is to puncture the can and drink rapidly.

Shotgunning is drinking a canned beverage by puncturing a hole near the bottom, placing your mouth over it, then popping the tab—the rush of air forces the liquid out fast for rapid consumption: {We shotgunned beers in the parking lot before the concert}. The term extends to any rapid, indiscriminate approach: shotgunning job applications means sending many at once without targeting. In cannabis use, shotgunning is blowing smoke directly into another person's mouth.

Shotguns are firearms with smooth bores that fire shells containing multiple pellets or a single slug, spreading on impact. Used for hunting, sport shooting, and home defense. To shotgun a beer is to puncture the can and drain it rapidly. Shotgun also means the front passenger seat: {I call shotgun!} To shotgun something is to do it all at once or scatter efforts broadly.

Shot put is a track and field event in which competitors throw a heavy metal ball as far as possible from a small circle. The ball itself, called a shot, typically weighs 16 pounds for men and about 9 pounds for women in competition. Athletes use a pushing motion rather than an overhand throw, keeping the shot close to the neck before explosively extending the arm. {She set a new school record in the shot put.}

Shots is the plural of shot, covering all its meanings. Shots can be drinks of liquor taken in one gulp: {We did shots at the bar}. Shots are also injections: {The baby needs her shots}. In sports, shots are attempts to score. Gunfire is shots: {Shots rang out}. {Shots fired} signals conflict, literal or figurative—often announcing a verbal attack or challenge online.

Should, a modal verb, has several uses that give aspectual information about the main verb, which is in infinitive form after should. You should go expresses obligation or advisability. You should have gone suggests a failed obligation in the past. In questions, the speaker is seeking advice: Should I make another appointment? The modal verb imparts the idea of reasonable expectation: We should be there by midnight. Should can express an idea of futurity in the past, but this usage is more common in British than American English (where would is more likely): They realized that they should have to sell the farm.

The anatomical position of human shoulders, which effectively form shelves on either side of the neck, is responsible for many figurative meanings. Areas adjacent to a higher, more prominent part can be called shoulders: The road’s shoulders were recently paved. The capacity of shoulders to bear weight inspires the verb shoulder, which most frequently conveys taking on responsibility: She shouldered the burden of hosting the reception. If you cry on someone’s shoulder, you seek sympathy from them. Shoulders figure in idioms like rub shoulders with (associate) and shoulder to shoulder (solidarity).

Shouldered is the past tense of shoulder, meaning to carry or push with the shoulder: {He shouldered his bag and left}, {She shouldered through the crowd}. To shoulder responsibility or blame is to accept it. Shouldered also describes something having shoulders of a particular kind: {broad-shouldered}, {narrow-shouldered}.

Shouldering is the act of pushing with or carrying on the shoulder. You shoulder through a crowd by using your shoulder to make way. You shoulder a burden—literal or figurative—by taking it on: {shouldering the responsibility for the project}. To shoulder someone aside is to push them out of the way. A rifle is shouldered when brought to the shoulder for firing or carrying.

Shoulders are the joints connecting arms to the torso, or the area of the body around them. The word extends to similar structures: the shoulder of a {road} is its edge, a {bottle's shoulder} is where it narrows toward the neck. To shoulder something is to carry it on your shoulders, or to take on responsibility: {She shouldered the burden of caring for her parents}. To {rub shoulders with} someone is to associate with them. A {chip on one's shoulder} signals a combative attitude. To give someone the {cold shoulder} is to snub them.

Shout is to speak or cry out loudly, projecting the voice with force: {She shouted his name across the street}. People shout to be heard over distance or noise, or from strong emotion—anger, excitement, alarm. As a noun, a shout is such an utterance: {I heard a shout from the back room}. In British and Australian slang, a shout is a round of drinks: {It's my shout}.

A shoutcaster is a person who provides live commentary for video game competitions, narrating the action for viewers watching esports events. The term combines "shout"—reflecting the excited, rapid-fire delivery common during intense gameplay—with "broadcaster." Shoutcasters typically work in pairs, with one handling play-by-play and another providing analysis: {The shoutcasters went wild when the underdog team pulled off the upset}.

Shouting is speaking or crying out loudly, typically to be heard over distance or noise, or to express strong emotion. People shout in anger, excitement, warning, or celebration. The word works as both verb form and noun: {Stop shouting at me}, {I could hear shouting from the next room}. To shout someone down is to silence them with louder noise.

A shoutout is a public acknowledgment or expression of thanks, typically brief and informal: {I want to give a shoutout to everyone who helped make this happen}. Common on social media and in broadcasts, shoutouts recognize someone's contribution or simply show appreciation. The term comes from the idea of calling out someone's name to a crowd.

Shoutouts are public acknowledgments or mentions, typically expressing gratitude or recognition: {Thanks for the shoutouts on social media}. Common in broadcasts, podcasts, and online content, a shoutout directs attention to someone or something: {I want to give a shoutout to everyone who helped make this happen}. The word reflects internet-era culture where recognition is currency.

Shouts is the plural of shout—loud, emphatic vocalizations meant to be heard at a distance or to convey strong emotion. People shout warnings, commands, or greetings: {Shouts of joy erupted from the crowd}. The verb form means to call out loudly: {She shouts across the playground}. In British and Australian slang, shouts are rounds of drinks: {The next round of shouts is on me}.

Shove is to push forcefully or roughly: {He shoved past me in the hallway}, {She shoved the papers into her bag}. The push is typically sudden and unceremonious. To {shove off} is to leave, originally nautical—pushing a boat away from shore. {Shove it} is a vulgar dismissal, short for {shove it up your ass}.

Shoved is the past tense of shove, meaning to push forcefully or roughly. A shove is more aggressive than a push—you shove someone out of the way, shove clothes into a suitcase, or shove past people in a crowd. {He shoved the door open with his shoulder.} {She shoved the papers across the desk.}

A shovel is a hand tool with a broad blade and long handle, used for digging or moving loose material like dirt, snow, or coal. To shovel is to move material this way: {I spent the morning shoveling the driveway}. By extension, to shovel food is to eat quickly and carelessly: {He shoveled pasta into his mouth}.

Shoveling is the act of moving material—snow, dirt, coal, gravel—with a shovel. The word implies repeated lifting and throwing motions: {I spent the morning shoveling the driveway}. Figuratively, to shovel something is to move it in large, hasty quantities: {shoveling food into his mouth}, {shoveling money into a failing project}. Also spelled shovelling.

Shovelled is the past tense and past participle of shovel, meaning to move material with a broad-bladed tool: {He shovelled snow from the driveway}. By extension, to shovel is to move anything in large, hasty quantities: {She shovelled food into her mouth}. This spelling is standard in British English; Americans write shoveled.

Shovelling is the British spelling of shoveling—moving material with a shovel or similar tool: {He spent the morning shovelling snow from the driveway}. The word extends to any act of moving quantities hastily or carelessly: {shovelling food into her mouth}, {shovelling money into failing projects}.

Shovels are hand tools with a broad blade attached to a long handle, used for digging, lifting, and moving loose material like dirt, snow, or coal. The verb means to move material with a shovel or, figuratively, to move things quickly and carelessly: {He shoveled food into his mouth}. To {shovel out} after a storm is to dig free from snow.

Shovelware is software produced in bulk with little regard for quality, typically to fill out a product catalog or pad a collection. The term evokes shoveling content onto a disc or platform without curation: {The budget game compilation was pure shovelware}. Originally applied to hastily assembled CD-ROM collections in the 1990s, it now describes any low-effort digital content mass-produced for quick profit.

Shoving is pushing someone or something roughly or forcefully. The word implies aggression or urgency—you shove your way through a crowd, shove someone aside, or shove belongings into a bag when you're in a hurry. {Stop shoving!} {She was shoving clothes into her suitcase.}

When you show something or when something shows, it becomes visible or apparent. To show an abstract quality is to make it evident: She showed no mercy in her judgments. The house showed signs of neglect. Show as a noun characterizes many things that are united by the idea of being visible or watchable. Forms of entertainment that have clear temporal boundaries are often called shows: television show, slideshow, puppet show. More generally, show can be a manifestation of something: show of hands, show of affection. Commercial and informational events centered around a particular thing are also called shows: art show, trade show.

Showbiz is informal for show business—the entertainment industry, especially film, television, theater, and music. The word carries connotations of glamour, celebrity culture, and the performative aspects of the industry: {She's been in showbiz since she was a child}. {That's showbiz} dismisses setbacks as typical of the industry's unpredictability.

A showboat is a river vessel with a theater for traveling entertainment, once common on American waterways. By extension, a showboat is someone who shows off or behaves flamboyantly to attract attention: {He's such a showboat on the basketball court}. The verb means to show off: {She was showboating for the cameras}.

Showboating is showing off, performing ostentatiously to attract attention or admiration. The term comes from the riverboat theaters that traveled American waterways, bringing flashy entertainment to river towns. Athletes showboat after scoring, drawing criticism for unsportsmanlike conduct: {He was penalized for showboating in the end zone}. The word implies the display is excessive or unnecessary.
