Siding is the material covering a building's exterior walls—wood, vinyl, aluminum, or other materials that protect and finish the outer surface: {The old clapboard siding needs replacing}. Siding also refers to a short stretch of railroad track connected to and running alongside a main line, used for passing trains or storing cars.

To sidle is to move sideways, especially in a cautious, furtive, or unobtrusive way: {He sidled up to the bar}. The word suggests approaching indirectly rather than head-on, often to avoid notice or confrontation: {She sidled toward the exit during the boring speech}. A sidle is this kind of sideways movement.

A siege is a military operation surrounding a fortified place to cut off supplies and force surrender. The image of prolonged pressure extends to other contexts: a {siege of illness}, {under siege} from creditors. To {lay siege} to something is to pursue it with sustained intensity. A siege {mentality} is a defensive mindset assuming hostile surroundings.

Sieges is the plural of siege, a military operation where forces surround a fortified place to cut off supplies and force surrender. The term extends to any prolonged effort to overcome resistance: {The city endured multiple sieges during the war}. To {lay siege to} something is to pursue it relentlessly.

Sienna is an earthy pigment ranging from yellowish-brown in its natural state (raw sienna) to reddish-brown when heated (burnt sienna). The color appears frequently in art supplies and interior design: {The artist mixed burnt sienna with white for the skin tones}. As a color term, sienna describes this warm brownish-orange hue. (Capitalized Sienna is the Italian city or a given name.)

Sierra means a jagged mountain range, from the Spanish word for saw—the peaks resembling saw teeth. The term appears in place names throughout the American West and Latin America: the Sierra Nevada, the Sierra Madre. In the NATO phonetic alphabet, sierra represents the letter S. {We could see the sierra rising in the distance.} (Capitalized Sierra is a given name and appears in place names.)

A siesta is a short nap taken in the early afternoon, especially in hot climates where midday heat makes work impractical. The practice is traditional in Spain and Latin America, where businesses may close for several hours after lunch. In English, siesta often suggests any afternoon rest: {I think I'll take a siesta after this meal}.

Siestas is the plural of siesta, a short nap taken in the early afternoon, especially in hot climates. The practice is associated with Mediterranean and Latin American cultures, where midday heat makes rest practical: {The village shut down for siestas}. In English, siesta often suggests any refreshing afternoon nap.

A sieve is a utensil with a mesh or perforated bottom used for straining solids from liquids or separating finer particles from coarser ones. Flour sifters and colanders are types of sieves. The verb sieve means to pass something through a sieve: {Sieve the flour before adding it to the batter}. Figuratively, to sieve is to sort or filter: {We sieved through hundreds of applications}. If someone has a memory like a sieve, they forget things easily.

Sieves are mesh or perforated tools for separating fine particles from coarse ones, or solids from liquids. Flour passes through a sieve; rocks don't. The verb means to pass something through such a device, or to examine carefully: {Police sieved through the evidence}. A {memory like a sieve} retains nothing.

Sift originally describes passing dry ingredients like flour through a mesh sieve to remove lumps and aerate the material. This physical action of separating finer particles from coarser ones extends to any careful sorting process: detectives sift through evidence, researchers sift data for patterns, and beachcombers sift sand for shells. To sift something out is to identify and remove it from a larger mass. {We spent hours sifting through old photos looking for the right one.}

Sifting is the act of passing something through a sieve or fine mesh to separate particles by size. Flour is sifted to remove lumps and aerate it. Beyond the kitchen, sifting describes any careful sorting through material: {Investigators spent weeks sifting through the evidence}. To sift is to examine methodically, separating what matters from what doesn't.

Sifts is the act of passing something through a sieve or filter to separate fine particles from coarse ones: {She sifts the flour before mixing}. By extension, to sift is to examine carefully, sorting the useful from the useless: {Detectives sifted through the evidence}. {He sifts fact from rumor}.

A sigh is a long, audible breath expressing weariness, relief, longing, or resignation: {She let out a sigh of relief when the test results came back negative}. The verb means to exhale this way: {He sighed and closed the book}. Things that make similar sounds may sigh: {Wind sighed through the trees}. A {sigh of relief} has become nearly formulaic for moments when tension releases.
clues: Long breath showing weariness or relief

definition: Sighed is the past tense of sigh—to exhale audibly, usually expressing weariness, relief, longing, or resignation. {She sighed and closed the book}. A sigh often signals emotions words don't capture: {He sighed when he saw the mess}. Things that make similar sounds may sigh: {The wind sighed through the trees}.

Sighing is breathing out audibly, usually expressing weariness, relief, longing, or resignation. The word often appears as a present participle describing someone in that state: {She sat sighing over old photographs}. Sighing can also modify sounds that resemble sighs: {the sighing wind}, {sighing waves}.

Sighs is the plural of sigh—audible exhalations expressing weariness, relief, longing, or resignation. {Her sighs filled the silence between them.} As a verb, sighs is the third-person singular: {He sighs every time I mention her name.} Wind or machinery that sighs makes a similar sound: {The old house sighs in the wind.}
clues: Long breaths showing relief or frustration

definition: Sight is the faculty of seeing—one of the five senses. A sight is something seen, especially something notable or worth seeing: {the sights of Paris}, {What a sight!} It can also mean something unsightly: {I look a sight}. The sights of a firearm are the device you look through to aim. At first sight means upon initial viewing. To sight something is to see it, especially after searching: {We finally sighted land}. Out of sight means not visible, or in slang, extraordinary: {That concert was out of sight}.

Sighted means having the ability to see—the opposite of blind. It often appears in compounds: {a sighted guide helped the blind hikers navigate the trail}. To have sighted something is to have seen or spotted it: {The captain sighted land on the horizon}. A sighted weapon has been adjusted for accuracy at a particular range.

A sighting is an instance of seeing something, especially something rare, elusive, or notable: {a UFO sighting}, {the first sighting of the comet}, {celebrity sightings in Los Angeles}. The word implies the thing seen was glimpsed rather than studied at length. Birdwatchers log sightings; tabloids report them.

Sightings are instances of seeing something notable, rare, or sought after. The word usually implies the thing seen is elusive or unexpected: {UFO sightings}, {celebrity sightings}, {the first robin sighting of spring}. Birdwatchers log sightings; tabloids report them. A sighting confirms presence without necessarily providing proof.

A sightline is an unobstructed line of vision between an observer and what they're looking at. The term appears most often in discussions of theater seating, stadium design, or architectural planning: {The pillars block the sightlines from the cheap seats}. A clear sightline means nothing interferes with the view.

Sightlines are the unobstructed paths of vision from a viewer to what they're watching. The term appears most often in discussions of theater, stadium, and arena design: {The balcony has poor sightlines to stage left}. Architects and planners work to ensure good sightlines from every seat. The concept extends to any context where clear views matter: {Trees along the median block sightlines for turning drivers}.

To sightread is to perform music or read text aloud without prior practice or preparation, encountering the material for the first time: {She can sightread almost anything you put in front of her}. The skill is essential for session musicians and accompanists. Also written as two words: sight-read or sight read.

Sightreading is performing music from a score you haven't seen before, without practice or preparation. Musicians develop sightreading skills to handle unrehearsed material: {The audition included a sightreading portion}. The term extends to any cold reading of notation, including sight-singing for vocalists. To sightread is to perform this way: {She can sightread almost anything you put in front of her}.

Sights are things worth seeing, especially notable attractions in a place: {We spent the day seeing the sights of Paris}. A sight is also a device for aiming a weapon or optical instrument—the part you look through to align your target. To set your sights on something is to make it your goal. To have someone in your sights is to be tracking or targeting them.

Sightseeing is the activity of visiting notable places as a tourist—landmarks, monuments, natural wonders, historic sites. The word emphasizes looking rather than doing: {We spent the morning sightseeing in Rome}. A sightseeing tour takes visitors past attractions, often by bus or boat. The term can carry a whiff of superficiality, suggesting tourists who glimpse rather than engage.

Sightseers are tourists or visitors who travel to look at notable places, landmarks, or attractions. The word emphasizes the visual nature of casual tourism—people who come to see rather than to study, work, or participate: {Sightseers crowded the observation deck}. {The cathedral was packed with sightseers taking photos}.

A sigil is a symbol believed to have magical power. In occult traditions, sigils are created or inscribed to represent entities, intentions, or desires—often used in rituals or worn as talismans. The term appears in fantasy fiction and games for any mystical symbol or seal: {The wizard traced the sigil in the air}. {Each demon had its own sigil.}

Sigils are symbols believed to have magical power. In occult traditions, a sigil is a designed image—often combining letters, geometric shapes, or abstract marks—intended to represent and invoke a specific intention or entity. Practitioners create sigils to focus will or manifest desires: {She drew a sigil for protection}. In fantasy fiction and games, sigils often function as magical seals or emblems of power. The singular is sigil.

Sigma is the eighteenth letter of the Greek alphabet (Σ, σ), used in mathematics and statistics to represent summation or standard deviation. In internet slang, sigma describes a man who supposedly succeeds outside traditional social hierarchies—a lone wolf who doesn't need validation: {sigma male}, {sigma grindset}. The term emerged from online masculinity discourse and is often used ironically. (Capitalized Sigma appears in fraternity and sorority names.)

Sign is the most general term for something that represents, refers to, or indicates something else. It is closely related to signal and shares some meanings with it. A sign of aging is some indication that aging is happening: The wrinkles around his eyes were a sign he had reached the half-century mark. A road sign is an informational marker. A sign that you make by gesturing is intended to communicate a message: He gave the thumbs up sign. Nearly all verbal meanings of sign are about affixing a signature as an indication of agreement or obligation: The contracts are not signed yet. Sign language is a language consisting of gestural signs; when someone uses this language, they are said to sign.

A signal is something that conveys information or triggers action—a gesture, sound, light, or electrical impulse that communicates meaning. Traffic signals control movement; a signal from the coach tells the runner to steal; electronic signals carry data through wires or airwaves. To signal is to send such communication: {She signaled for the check}. Signal also works as an adjective meaning notable or outstanding: {a signal achievement in medicine}. The signal-to-noise ratio, from electronics, now describes any situation where useful information competes with irrelevant clutter.

Signaling is communication through signs, gestures, or indicators rather than explicit statement. Traffic lights signal when to stop and go. In economics and biology, signaling describes behavior that conveys information about hidden qualities: {A college degree serves as signaling to employers}. Virtue signaling is expressing opinions mainly to demonstrate good character rather than effect change.

Signalling is the British spelling of signaling—the act of conveying information through signals. Traffic lights do signalling. A driver signals a turn. In economics and evolutionary biology, signalling describes behaviors that communicate hidden qualities: {Luxury goods serve as signalling of wealth}. The doubled L follows British spelling conventions.

Signals are signs, gestures, or transmissions that convey information or prompt action. A traffic signal controls intersection flow. A signal from a coach tells the batter to bunt. Radio signals carry broadcasts. To signal is to communicate through such means: {She signaled the waiter for the check}. Figuratively, actions signal intentions: {The announcement signals a shift in policy}.

A signature is a person's name written in their own hand, used to authorize documents or indicate authenticity: {Her signature was on the contract}. By extension, signature describes anything distinctive or identifying: a chef's signature {dish}, a musician's signature {sound}. In music, a key signature or time signature appears at the beginning of a staff. In printing and bookbinding, a signature is a folded sheet forming a section of pages.

Signatures are names written in a person's distinctive handwriting, used to authorize documents, authenticate identity, or mark personal correspondence. The way someone signs their name is itself called their signature, and people develop recognizable styles that serve as proof of authorship or agreement. Beyond handwriting, signature extends to anything distinctive or characteristic: a chef's {signature dish}, a musician's {signature sound}. In computing, signatures are blocks of text automatically appended to emails, or unique patterns that identify viruses and malware.

Signed describes something bearing a signature or other mark of authentication. A signed {contract} has been executed by the parties. A signed {copy} of a book bears the author's autograph. In mathematics, signed numbers can be positive or negative, as opposed to unsigned values that are only positive. In computing, a signed {integer} reserves one bit to indicate whether the value is positive or negative.

A signer is someone who signs something—a document, a petition, a contract. The signers of the Declaration of Independence are the Founding Fathers who put their names to it. In contexts involving deaf communication, a signer is someone who uses sign language: {She's a fluent signer}.

A signet is a small seal, especially one set in a ring, used to authenticate documents by pressing into wax or clay. Signet rings bear distinctive designs—family crests, monograms, or symbols—that identify the owner. The word now often refers to the ring itself: {He wore his grandfather's gold signet ring}.

Significance is the quality of being meaningful or important. A discovery of great significance changes how we understand something. Statistical significance indicates results unlikely to have occurred by chance. The significance of an event may not be apparent until later: {We didn't grasp the significance of her resignation at the time}. To look at someone with significance is to convey unspoken meaning.

Significant means large or important enough to matter. A significant {difference} is one worth noting; a significant {other} is a romantic partner. In statistics, significant has a technical meaning: unlikely to have occurred by chance alone. {The results were statistically significant.} The word implies consequence—something significant has effects or implications that deserve attention.

Signing is the act of writing one's signature, especially to authorize or agree to something: {The signing of the contract took place at noon}. A signing is also an event where an author or celebrity signs items for fans: {a book signing}. Separately, signing refers to communication through sign language: {She learned signing to talk with her deaf students}.

Signoff is the act of ending a broadcast, shift, or communication session. Radio and television stations have signoffs when they cease transmission for the night. In workplace contexts, signoff means official approval: {We need signoff from legal before proceeding}. As a verb phrase, to sign off is to conclude or approve: {She signed off on the budget}.

A signpost is a post bearing a sign that gives directions or information, typically found at road junctions or along trails. Figuratively, anything that serves as a guide or indicator: {The economic data were signposts of recovery}. As a verb, to signpost is to mark with signs or to indicate clearly: {The author signposts her argument in the introduction}.

Signposting is the practice of explicitly guiding readers or listeners through an argument or text—announcing what's coming, marking transitions, summarizing what's been covered. Academic writing relies heavily on signposting: {This essay will first examine... then consider... finally argue...} The term comes from literal signposts that direct travelers, extended to verbal navigation aids.

Signposts are markers along a road or path showing directions or distances to destinations. The word extends to anything that provides guidance or indicates what lies ahead: {The survey results are signposts for future policy}. To signpost something is to mark it clearly or indicate its direction: {The author signposts her argument in the introduction}.

Signs are indications or markers that convey meaning. A sign may be a posted notice {No Parking signs}, a gesture {She made the sign of the cross}, or evidence of something {signs of life}. The zodiac divides into twelve signs. To sign is to write your signature or communicate in sign language. {He signed the contract and handed it back.}

Signup is the act of registering or enrolling for something: {The signup process takes five minutes}. As an attributive noun, it modifies related terms: a signup {form}, a signup {bonus}, a signup {page}. Often written as two words (sign up) when used as a verb: {Sign up for the newsletter}.

Silence is the absence of sound or speech. When you ask for silence, you want people to stop talking or making noise. The verb silence means to cause something or someone to become quiet: {The teacher silenced the class with a look}. In a darker sense, to silence someone can mean to prevent them from speaking out, whether through intimidation, censorship, or violence. {Silence is golden} suggests that keeping quiet is often wiser than speaking.

Silenced describes something that has been made quiet or prevented from speaking. A silenced {gun} has a suppressor attached to muffle its report. A silenced {critic} has been shut up, whether through persuasion, intimidation, or force. The word often carries sinister overtones—those who are silenced rarely chose silence themselves.

A silencer is a device attached to a firearm's muzzle to reduce the sound of discharge—also called a suppressor. The term extends to anything that quiets: a silencer on an engine or exhaust system. Figuratively, a silencer is someone or something that stops others from speaking: {The lawsuit was a silencer, meant to intimidate critics}.

Silencers are devices that reduce noise. The term most often refers to attachments for firearms that muffle the sound of gunshots, properly called suppressors: {The assassin screwed a silencer onto the pistol}. Silencers also appear in exhaust systems and other machinery. Figuratively, a silencer is anything that suppresses speech or dissent: {Money is a powerful silencer of criticism}.

Silences is the plural of silence—periods without sound or speech. {The silences between them grew uncomfortable.} {Long silences punctuated the interview.} As a verb, silences means to quiet or suppress: {She silences her phone during meetings.} {The regime silences dissent.} To silence someone can mean to kill them: {The witness was silenced before trial.}

Silencing is the act of causing someone or something to become quiet or to stop making sound. More often it describes suppressing speech, expression, or dissent: {The regime's silencing of journalists drew international condemnation.} In molecular biology, gene silencing refers to mechanisms that prevent a gene from being expressed. The word carries strong connotations of power imbalance—those who do the silencing typically hold authority over those being silenced.

Silent means making no sound or refraining from speech. A silent {room} has no noise; a silent {person} says nothing. Silent can describe things that operate without sound: a silent {film}, a silent {auction}. To remain silent is to withhold comment, often strategically: {She remained silent on the allegations}. A silent {letter} appears in spelling but isn't pronounced: the k in {knife}.

Silently means without making sound: {She crept silently down the hallway}. It extends to communication—reading silently, suffering silently, silently disagreeing. What happens silently goes unannounced or unacknowledged: {The policy silently expired}. Software runs silently when it operates in the background without user notification.

A silhouette is the dark outline of something seen against a lighter background, with interior details obscured: {The trees stood in silhouette against the sunset}. Originally referring to profile portraits cut from black paper, it now describes any shape defined by its outline rather than its features. As a verb, to silhouette is to show as a dark shape: {The figure was silhouetted in the doorway}.

Silhouetted describes something seen or shown as a dark shape against a lighter background, with details obscured and only the outline visible: {The trees were silhouetted against the evening sky}. The word typically appears with against, conveying how light from behind transforms a figure into pure outline: {A lone figure stood silhouetted in the doorway}.

Silhouettes is the plural of silhouette—a dark shape seen against a lighter background, showing outline but no interior detail. The word often describes figures backlit by sunset or window light: {Silhouettes of trees lined the horizon}. As a verb form, silhouettes means to show as a silhouette: {The lighthouse silhouettes against the evening sky}.

Silicon is a chemical element, a metalloid abundant in Earth's crust. Combined with oxygen, it forms silica—the basis of sand, quartz, and glass. Pure silicon's semiconductor properties make it essential to computer chips and electronics, giving rise to {Silicon Valley} as shorthand for the tech industry. Solar panels and silicone rubber also depend on silicon compounds.

Silicone is a synthetic polymer containing silicon, oxygen, and carbon, valued for its flexibility, heat resistance, and water repellency. It appears in sealants, lubricants, medical implants, cookware, and countless industrial applications. {Silicone caulk} seals bathroom fixtures; {silicone implants} augment breasts. Not to be confused with silicon, the element used in computer chips.

Silk is a fine, lustrous fiber produced by silkworms, or the smooth fabric woven from it. The texture gives silk its figurative uses: a {silky voice} is smooth and pleasing, {silky hair} is soft and shiny. In horse racing, silks are the jockey's colorful uniform. To {take silk} in British legal usage means to become a senior barrister.

Silks are garments made from silk fabric, especially the distinctive colored shirts and caps worn by jockeys in horse racing: {The jockeys paraded in their silks before the race}. Each owner registers unique colors and patterns, making their horses identifiable from a distance. By extension, silks can refer to any fine silk clothing or, in British legal usage, the robes worn by senior barristers who have "taken silk" to become Queen's or King's Counsel.

Silkscreen is a printing method where ink is pushed through a mesh stencil onto a surface below—originally silk, now typically synthetic. The technique produces bold, flat colors and is used for posters, T-shirts, and fine art prints. Andy Warhol's famous portraits were silkscreens. As a verb, to silkscreen is to print using this method: {We silkscreened the band's logo onto five hundred shirts}.

Silkscreening is a printing technique where ink is pushed through a mesh screen onto a surface below. Areas of the screen are blocked off to create a stencil, so ink only passes through in the desired pattern. The method works on fabric, paper, glass, and other materials: {The band's t-shirts were silkscreened by hand}. Also called screen printing.

Silkscreens are prints made by forcing ink through a mesh screen onto a surface, with a stencil blocking areas that should remain unprinted. The technique produces bold, flat colors and crisp edges—Andy Warhol's celebrity portraits are iconic examples. As a verb, to silkscreen is to print using this method: {We silkscreened the band logo onto t-shirts}. Also called screen printing or serigraphy.

A silkworm is the caterpillar of a moth that spins a cocoon of fine, lustrous fiber—the source of commercial silk. The insects have been domesticated for thousands of years and can no longer survive in the wild. {Silkworm farming requires careful temperature control.}

Silkworms are caterpillars of the silk moth, cultivated for thousands of years to produce silk thread. The larvae spin cocoons of fine, strong fiber that can be unwound and woven into fabric. Commercial silk production involves killing the pupae before they emerge and damage the continuous thread: {The silkworms were ready for harvesting}.

Silky describes a texture that is smooth, soft, and lustrous like silk: {silky hair}, {silky fur}. The word extends to anything with that quality of effortless smoothness—a silky voice is rich and pleasing, a silky movement is fluid and graceful. {The lotion left her skin feeling silky}.

A sill is the horizontal piece at the bottom of a window or door frame: {She set the plant on the windowsill}. In construction, a sill plate is the lowest horizontal member of a frame, resting on the foundation. In geology, a sill is a flat sheet of igneous rock that has intruded between existing layers.

Silliness is the quality of being silly—foolish, absurd, or lacking seriousness. It can describe behavior, remarks, or situations that are laughably trivial or nonsensical: {Enough silliness—let's get back to work}. The word often carries affection rather than criticism, suggesting harmless playfulness: {The kids dissolved into silliness}.

Sills are the horizontal members at the base of a structure or opening. A window sill is the ledge at the bottom of a window frame, inside or out: {She set plants on the windowsill}. A door sill is the threshold you step over. In construction, a sill plate is the lumber that sits directly on a foundation, supporting the frame above. In geology, a sill is a horizontal sheet of igneous rock intruded between existing layers.

Silly describes behavior or ideas that are foolish, lacking good sense, or absurd: {Don't be silly, of course you can come}. It often carries affection rather than harsh judgment—a silly mistake is minor, a silly joke deliberately goofy. Children acting silly are being playful and giggly. The word has weakened over centuries; it once meant blessed, then innocent, then simple-minded, arriving finally at its current lightness.

A silo is a tall cylindrical structure for storing grain or fodder on a farm. The term extends to any isolated storage system, and figuratively to organizational divisions that don't communicate with each other: {The marketing and engineering teams work in silos}. To silo information is to keep it compartmentalized: {Data gets siloed across different departments}. A missile silo is an underground launch facility.

Siloed describes something isolated or compartmentalized, kept separate from related things that might benefit from connection. The image comes from grain silos—tall structures that store crops in separate containers. Organizations become siloed when departments don't communicate: {Marketing and engineering operated in siloed fashion, never sharing data}. Information, teams, or thinking can all be siloed, implying inefficiency or missed opportunities for collaboration.

Silos are tall cylindrical structures for storing grain, fermented feed, or other bulk materials on farms. The word extends to any isolated storage or containment system. In business and organizational contexts, silos describe departments or groups that operate in isolation, hoarding information rather than sharing it: {Marketing and engineering work in silos}. To silo something is to compartmentalize it: {The data was siloed across multiple systems}. Underground silos house intercontinental ballistic missiles.

Silt is fine sediment—particles smaller than sand but larger than clay—carried by water and deposited where flow slows: riverbeds, lake bottoms, deltas. Silt makes soil fertile but clogs waterways. As a verb, to silt or silt up is to become blocked with sediment: {The harbor had silted up over decades of neglect}.

Silver is a chemical element and precious metal. Sterling silver is at least 92.5% silver and is used in dining utensils and jewelry. In rankings in which metals represent values, silver is usually behind gold and ahead of bronze: The Olympian finished second, and so was awarded the silver medal. As a color name, silver is a bright or metallic gray. Silver is used to mark the 25th anniversary of an occasion and was once a standard of currency. To silver an object is to coat or plate it with silver.

A silverback is a mature male gorilla, typically over twelve years old, named for the distinctive patch of silver-gray hair that develops across the back with age. Silverbacks are the dominant leaders of gorilla groups, responsible for protection and decision-making. The term extends figuratively to any older, dominant male in a group: {The silverback of the department finally retired after thirty years}.

Silverbacks are mature male gorillas, typically over twelve years old, named for the distinctive patch of silver-gray hair that develops across their backs. A silverback leads and protects his troop, making decisions about feeding and travel. The term extends figuratively to dominant older men in any group: {The silverbacks in the boardroom resisted the merger}.

Silverfish are small, wingless insects with silvery scales and a tapered, fish-like body. They move in quick, wriggling motions and thrive in damp, dark places—bathrooms, basements, old books. They're household pests that feed on starchy materials: paper, glue, fabric, wallpaper paste. {We found silverfish in the box of old photographs.}

Silvering is the process of applying a reflective metallic coating to a surface, especially to make mirrors. The term also describes the appearance of something turning silver—whether literally, as metal tarnishes, or figuratively: {the silvering of her hair over the years}. Old mirrors may show degraded silvering as dark spots where the backing has worn away.

A silversmith is a craftsman who works with silver, making or repairing items like jewelry, flatware, and decorative objects. The trade requires skills in shaping, joining, and finishing metal: {The silversmith hammered the bowl into shape}. Historically, silversmiths also served as bankers, since they worked with precious metal.

Silversmiths are craftspeople who work silver into objects—jewelry, flatware, bowls, candlesticks, and decorative items. The trade requires skills in shaping, soldering, engraving, and polishing metal. Historically, silversmiths also served as bankers, since they worked with precious metal and could assess its purity: {Paul Revere was a silversmith by trade}.

Silverware is eating utensils—knives, forks, and spoons—regardless of whether they're actually made of silver. The term persists from when such items were commonly silver or silver-plated: {Set the table with the good silverware}. In broader use, silverware can include any metal tableware: serving pieces, platters, or decorative items. British English prefers cutlery for eating utensils.

Silverwork is the craft of making objects from silver, or the objects themselves produced by this craft. The term encompasses both decorative and functional items—jewelry, tableware, religious artifacts, and ornamental pieces—shaped through techniques like hammering, engraving, and casting. {The museum's collection of colonial silverwork includes candlesticks and serving pieces.} A silverworker or silversmith is someone skilled in this craft.

Silvery describes a light gray color with metallic sheen, like polished silver: {silvery hair}, {the silvery surface of the lake}. The word extends to sounds—clear, light, and ringing: {silvery laughter}, {a silvery voice}. Moonlight is often called silvery for its pale, luminous quality.

A sim is a simulation or simulated version of something, especially in gaming contexts: {The Sims}, {flight sim}, {racing sim}. The word also refers to a SIM card—the small chip in mobile phones that identifies the subscriber and stores data: {I need to swap my sim into the new phone}. In online gaming, sim can describe roleplay focused on realistic scenarios rather than fantasy elements. (All-caps SIM refers specifically to the card technology.)

Similar describes things that share qualities without being identical. Two similar {houses} resemble each other but aren't the same house. Similar can suggest close resemblance {(Their writing styles are remarkably similar)} or loose comparison {(We had a similar experience)}. The word implies enough overlap to invite comparison, but enough difference to prevent calling things the same.

Similarities are features or qualities that things share—the ways in which they resemble each other. The word typically appears in discussions comparing two or more items: {The similarities between the two cases are striking}. To {draw similarities} is to point out shared characteristics. The opposite is differences.

Similarity is the quality of being alike or resembling something else. Two things share similarity when they have features in common: {The similarity between the twins was striking}. The word often appears in comparisons: {There's a strong similarity between their writing styles}. In the plural, similarities names specific shared features: {Despite their differences, the proposals have several similarities}.

A simile is a figure of speech comparing two different things using "like" or "as": {Her eyes sparkled like diamonds}, {He ran as fast as the wind}. The explicit comparison marker distinguishes simile from metaphor, which states the comparison directly. Similes appear constantly in everyday speech: {sleep like a baby}, {clear as mud}, {spread like wildfire}.

Simmer describes liquid heated just below boiling—hot enough for small bubbles to rise gently but not vigorously. You simmer a soup or sauce to cook it slowly without breaking it apart. Figuratively, emotions simmer when they're present but contained: {Resentment simmered beneath the surface}. To {simmer down} is to calm down after agitation.

Simmered is the past tense of simmer, meaning to cook liquid at a temperature just below boiling, with small bubbles rising gently: {The soup simmered on the stove all afternoon}. Figuratively, to simmer is to exist in a state of suppressed activity or emotion: {Tensions had simmered for years before the conflict erupted}. To {simmer down} is to calm down after agitation.

Simmering describes liquid heated just below boiling, with small bubbles rising gently: {Let the sauce keep simmering while you prepare the pasta}. Figuratively, simmering describes emotions held in check but ready to surface—anger, tension, or resentment kept at a slow burn: {simmering rage}, {simmering conflict}. A simmering attraction suggests quiet intensity waiting to ignite.

Simmers is the third-person singular of simmer—to cook liquid at just below boiling, with small bubbles rising gently: {The soup simmers on the stove}. Figuratively, emotions or conflicts that simmer are present but contained, not yet boiling over: {Resentment simmers beneath the surface}. {Tensions between the two countries have simmered for decades}.

Simp is internet slang for someone, typically a man, who shows excessive attention or devotion to another person, usually in hopes of romantic interest. The word implies the attention is unreciprocated and embarrassing: {He's simping for her in the comments again}. To simp is to behave this way. Originally from "simpleton," the word gained currency in hip-hop before spreading online.

Simpatico, borrowed from Italian and Spanish, describes people who get along naturally, sharing similar temperaments or sensibilities. Two people who are simpatico have an easy rapport and mutual understanding: {We clicked immediately—totally simpatico}. The word can also characterize something as agreeable or congenial to one's tastes: {The laid-back atmosphere was simpatico with my vacation mood}. It carries warmer connotations than mere compatibility, suggesting genuine harmony rather than just absence of conflict.

Simped is the past tense of simp, slang meaning to show excessive attention or devotion to someone, typically in hopes of romantic interest: {He simped for her all semester and she barely knew his name}. The term often carries mockery, suggesting the attention is unreciprocated or undignified.

Simpering describes a smile or manner that is affectedly coy, self-conscious, or ingratiating—often with an air of false modesty or silliness. The word carries contempt: {She gave a simpering laugh at his weak joke}. A simpering person seems to be seeking approval through exaggerated sweetness rather than genuine warmth.

Simping is showing excessive attention or devotion to someone, typically a romantic interest, in ways that seem desperate or self-degrading. The term emerged from internet culture and carries mockery—suggesting someone who goes overboard trying to impress someone who isn't reciprocating: {He's simping so hard for her, buying gifts she never asked for}. The related noun simp describes such a person.

Simple is mainly an adjective, roughly synonymous with easy, and opposite to difficult and complicated. A simple task or step is one that can be completed with little effort. A simple answer is easy to understand. Sometimes simple is used to emphasize that something is not special or unusual (simple fact, simple truth). A simple sentence has only one clause. Simple things (in life) is a way to characterize ordinary and accessible experiences.

Simpleminded describes someone lacking intelligence or sophistication—unable to grasp complexity or nuance. The word can be insulting when applied to people: {Don't be so simpleminded about this}. Applied to ideas or solutions, it suggests naive oversimplification: {a simpleminded approach to foreign policy}. Sometimes the word carries a gentler sense of uncomplicated innocence.

A simpleton is a foolish or gullible person, someone easily deceived or lacking basic common sense. The word carries a condescending tone, suggesting the person is naive rather than intellectually disabled: {He fell for the scam like a simpleton}. It sounds somewhat old-fashioned today, more likely encountered in novels than conversation.

Simpletons is the plural of simpleton, a person regarded as lacking intelligence or common sense. The word carries a tone of condescension or dismissal, implying the person is not just uninformed but fundamentally slow-witted. {The con artist preyed on simpletons who believed his outlandish promises.} Unlike words like fool or idiot, simpleton has an old-fashioned quality that makes it sound almost quaint, though still insulting.

Simplicity is the quality of being easy to understand, use, or do. It suggests an absence of complexity, ornamentation, or unnecessary elements. {The simplicity of the design made it elegant.} Something valued for its simplicity is often praised for being straightforward or uncomplicated: {I appreciate the simplicity of her explanation.} Simplicity can also suggest a lack of sophistication, sometimes disparagingly: {He dismissed their simplicity as naïveté.}

Simplification is the process of making something less complex or easier to understand. When you simplify an explanation, a process, or a system, the result is a simplification. The word often carries a slightly negative connotation, suggesting that important nuances have been lost: {That's an oversimplification of the issue}. In mathematics, simplification refers to reducing an expression to its most basic equivalent form.
clues: The act of making less complicated

definition: To simplify is to make something less complex or easier to understand. You simplify instructions by removing unnecessary steps, simplify a fraction by reducing it to lowest terms, or simplify your life by getting rid of clutter. The word often implies stripping away complications to reveal what's essential: {Let me simplify this for you}.

Simplistic describes something that oversimplifies a complex issue, reducing it to false clarity. Unlike *simple*, which is neutral or positive, simplistic carries criticism—the explanation or solution ignores important nuances: {His simplistic view of the conflict ignored centuries of history}. A simplistic answer isn't helpfully straightforward; it's naively inadequate.

To simulate is to imitate or reproduce the conditions, appearance, or effects of something. A flight simulator lets pilots practice without leaving the ground. Scientists simulate climate patterns with computer models. The word can also mean to feign: {She simulated enthusiasm for the project}. Simulated materials imitate costlier ones: simulated {leather}, simulated {diamonds}.
clues: Reproduce conditions in a controlled environment

definition: Simulated describes something made to look or function like something else without being the real thing. A simulated {leather} jacket uses synthetic materials. A simulated {emergency} tests responses without actual danger. Simulated {wood grain} is printed to resemble real wood. The word implies deliberate imitation, often for practice, testing, or cost savings: {simulated combat training}, {simulated flight conditions}.

Simulation is the imitation of a real process or system. Scientists run computer simulations to model climate change; pilots train in flight simulators. The word can suggest something false or pretended: {His concern was pure simulation}. In philosophy, simulation theory proposes that reality itself might be a computer-generated construct. To simulate is to create such an imitation or to feign: {simulate enthusiasm}.

Simulations are imitations of real processes, systems, or situations. A flight simulator lets pilots practice without leaving the ground. Computer simulations model weather patterns, disease spread, or economic systems. In gaming, simulation games replicate activities like city-building or farming. The philosophical sense asks whether reality itself might be a simulation—a programmed construct we mistake for genuine existence.

A simulator is a device or program that imitates real-world conditions or systems for training, testing, or entertainment. Flight simulators let pilots practice without leaving the ground. Driving simulators test vehicle designs. In gaming, simulators recreate activities from farming to surgery: {I've logged hundreds of hours in that truck simulator}. The term extends to any system that models complex processes: {a climate simulator}, {a nuclear reactor simulator}.

Simulators are devices or programs that recreate the conditions of something else—typically for training, testing, or entertainment. A flight simulator lets pilots practice without leaving the ground. Driving simulators teach new drivers. In gaming, simulators model real-world activities: farming simulators, city-building simulators, even goat simulators. The appeal is experiencing something without its costs or consequences.

A simulcast is a broadcast transmitted simultaneously across multiple channels or platforms—radio and television together, or streaming alongside traditional broadcast. The word blends "simultaneous" and "broadcast." As a verb, to simulcast is to transmit this way: {The concert was simulcast on three networks}. {They simulcast the debate online}.
clues: Same program, different platforms, same moment

definition: Simulcasts are broadcasts transmitted simultaneously across multiple channels or platforms—radio and television together, or a live stream alongside a cable broadcast. The word blends "simultaneous" and "broadcast." As a verb, to simulcast is to transmit this way: {The debate was simulcast on all major networks}. The singular simulcast refers to a single such broadcast.

Simultaneous describes things happening at exactly the same time: {The two bombs exploded simultaneously}. It applies to events, actions, or states that coincide: {simultaneous translation}, {simultaneous equations}. The word implies perfect temporal overlap, not merely rough coincidence: {They reached the finish line in a simultaneous tie}.

At the same time. Two things happen simultaneously when they occur together, not one after the other: {The bomb flashes arrived almost simultaneously}. The word often emphasizes coincidence or coordination: {She was simultaneously raising three children and finishing law school}.

Sin is a transgression against divine or moral law—an act that violates religious commandments or ethical principles. The concept is central to Christianity, Judaism, and Islam, where sins range from minor failings to grave offenses requiring atonement. The seven deadly sins (pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, wrath, sloth) catalog fundamental human vices. Outside religion, sin describes any serious wrongdoing: {It would be a sin to let this food go to waste}. To sin is to commit such an act. To {live in sin} is to cohabit without marriage—dated but still understood.

Since is most often an adverb but when followed by a single noun phrase, a date, or a point in time, it acts as a preposition to indicate the starting time of something: We’ve lived here since 1998. As a conjunction, since can introduce a point in time in the form of a clause (since I was five years old), or it can state the reason or justification for something, like because: I worked in the lobby since it’s the only place with free Wi-Fi.

Sincere describes feelings, expressions, or people that are genuine and without pretense. A sincere {apology} comes from real remorse, not social obligation. A sincere {person} means what they say. The word implies alignment between inner feeling and outward expression—the opposite of hypocritical or performative. {I'm sincere when I say I want to help}.

Sincerely means genuinely or without pretense: {I sincerely appreciate your help}. It intensifies earnest statements: {I sincerely hope you're right}. The word appears most often as a letter closing—{Sincerely yours} or just {Sincerely}—now so formulaic that it conveys politeness rather than actual sincerity.

Sincerity is genuineness of feeling or expression—meaning what you say and saying what you mean. A sincere apology comes from actual remorse, not social obligation. {I doubt the sincerity of his offer}. The word often appears when authenticity is questioned: {Her sincerity was never in doubt}. Sincerity implies alignment between inner state and outward presentation.

Sinew is the tough, fibrous tissue connecting muscle to bone—what anatomists call tendon. The word appears most often in its plural or figurative forms. {The sinews of his forearms stood out as he gripped the rope.} Sinews suggest strength and the capacity for exertion: {the sinews of war}, {the sinews of democracy}. Sinewy describes lean, muscular bodies or tough, stringy meat.

Sinews are the tough fibrous tissues connecting muscle to bone—tendons. The word appears most often in its figurative sense: the sinews of something are what give it strength or hold it together. Money is sometimes called {the sinews of war}. A sinewy person is lean and muscular, all tendon and no fat.

Sinewy describes something lean and muscular, suggesting strength without bulk. A sinewy arm shows visible tendons and tight muscle. The word extends to prose or argument that is spare and vigorous: {sinewy writing}, {a sinewy defense of free speech}. Meat that is sinewy has tough, stringy connective tissue—usually undesirable in cooking.

Sinful means wicked or morally wrong according to religious or ethical standards—violating divine law or deeply held principles. A sinful {act}, sinful {thoughts}, sinful {desires}. The word carries religious weight but extends to secular contexts for emphasis or humor: {a sinful amount of chocolate}, {sinfully delicious}. To call something sinful implies not just wrongness but transgression against a higher standard.

To sing is to produce musical sounds with the voice—forming melodies, often with words. Birds sing. So do whales. Beyond literal vocalization, sing extends to any melodious sound: {The kettle sang on the stove}. To {sing someone's praises} is to commend them enthusiastically. In slang, to sing is to confess or inform, especially to police: {He sang like a canary}.

A singalong is an informal gathering where people sing together, typically following lyrics displayed on screen or in a songbook: {The bar hosts a piano singalong every Friday}. As a modifier, it describes events designed for group participation: {a singalong version of the film}, {singalong carols}. Also spelled sing-along.

Singalongs are gatherings or events where people sing together, typically following lyrics displayed on screen or printed sheets. The word also describes songs suited to group singing—simple melodies with repetitive choruses that invite participation: {The camp counselor led singalongs around the fire}. Children's shows often feature singalong segments.

Singe means to burn superficially—scorching the surface without igniting. Hair singes easily near open flame. Fabric singes if an iron is too hot. The smell of singed hair is distinctive and unpleasant. A singe is the mark left by such burning: {The candle left a singe on the tablecloth}.

Singed is the past tense of singe, meaning to burn superficially—scorching the surface without consuming: {The candle singed her hair}. Unlike burned, singed implies slight damage, often just enough to leave a mark or smell: {His eyebrows were singed from leaning too close to the grill}.

Singeing is burning something lightly on the surface, just enough to scorch or remove fine fibers without consuming it. Cooks singe poultry to remove pinfeathers; hairdressers once singed hair ends. The word captures that moment of controlled, superficial burning: {the singeing smell of burnt hair}, {singeing the edges of ribbon to prevent fraying}.

A singer is someone who sings—professionally, recreationally, or as part of a group. The term covers opera divas and shower crooners alike. In bands, the singer usually handles lead vocals: {She's the singer for an indie rock group}. Singer-songwriter specifies someone who writes and performs their own material.

Singers is the plural of singer—people who sing, whether professionally or casually. The word covers opera divas, rock frontmen, shower warblers, and everyone in between: {The singers in that choir have been rehearsing for months}. Lead singers front bands; backup singers provide harmony and support.

Singing is the act of producing musical sounds with the voice, typically by sustaining tones and following a melody. It encompasses everything from casual humming in the shower to professional operatic performance. As an adjective, singing describes something that produces a melodious or ringing sound: {a singing kettle}, {singing wires in the wind}. The word also appears in compounds like {singing voice} and {singing lesson}. Someone might have a {singing sensation} in their ears after exposure to loud noise.

Meanings of the adjective single are united by the idea of only one. A single bed is wide enough for one person. A single parent is not united with the other parent of a child. Conventional meanings of single as a noun include a room for one person, as in a hotel; an unmarried person (a club for singles); a song released for sale by itself (a hit single); and in baseball, a hit ball that puts the batter on base. The verb single is mostly used in baseball to mean a hit that put the batter on first base. Single is sometimes used as an intensifier before a noun: Every single answer was wrong.

Singlehanded means done by one person without help: {She sailed singlehanded across the Atlantic}. The word implies self-reliance and often carries admiration for accomplishing something difficult alone. Also spelled single-handed. The adverb form is singlehandedly: {He singlehandedly turned the company around}.

Singlehandedly means done by one person alone, without help: {She singlehandedly organized the entire fundraiser}. The word emphasizes individual effort against what might normally require assistance or teamwork. Often carries a note of admiration for the accomplishment: {He singlehandedly turned the company around}.

Singlehood is the state of being unmarried or without a romantic partner. The word often appears in discussions of life choices and social expectations: {She embraced singlehood rather than settling for the wrong person}. Unlike the slightly clinical *unmarried* or the potentially pitying *alone*, singlehood frames the condition neutrally or even positively.

Singleminded means focused on one goal or purpose to the exclusion of everything else. A singleminded {pursuit of wealth} ignores other considerations. The word can be admiring—{singleminded dedication}—or suggest dangerous tunnel vision. Also spelled single-minded.

Singles are individual items sold separately rather than in sets or bundles: {The album is available as singles}. In sports, singles matches pit one player against one, as opposed to doubles. Singles also refers to unmarried people as a social category: {a singles bar}, {a singles cruise}. In music, a single is a song released individually, typically to promote an album.

A singlewide is a mobile home built as one unit, typically 14-18 feet wide, designed to be transported on its own chassis. Contrast with doublewide, which consists of two sections joined on-site. The term often carries class connotations in American speech: {They grew up in a singlewide in rural Kentucky}.

Singsong describes a rhythmic, repetitive rise and fall in speech or music—the kind of lilting pattern children use in playground taunts or that makes certain accents distinctive. As a noun, it can mean a casual group singing session, especially British: {We had a singsong around the piano}. The adjective often carries a mildly dismissive tone, suggesting monotony or artificiality in someone's delivery.

Singular means one of a kind or exceptional: {a singular achievement}, {a singular talent}. Something singular stands out from the ordinary. In grammar, singular refers to forms denoting one person or thing, as opposed to plural: {The singular of "mice" is "mouse"}. Singular can also mean strange or peculiar: {a singular way of speaking}.

Singularities is the plural of singularity—the quality of being singular, unique, or unusual. In physics and cosmology, singularities are points where density becomes infinite and ordinary physical laws break down, as at the center of a black hole or at the moment of the Big Bang: {Scientists debate what happens at singularities}. In mathematics, a singularity is a point where a function behaves anomalously. The technological singularity refers to a hypothetical future moment when artificial intelligence surpasses human intelligence, triggering unpredictable change: {Some futurists believe the singularity is near}.

Singularity is the quality of being singular—unique, remarkable, or standing alone. In physics, a singularity is a point where normal rules break down: the center of a black hole, where matter is infinitely dense. {The technological singularity} refers to a hypothetical future moment when artificial intelligence surpasses human intelligence and triggers runaway, unpredictable change. The word often carries a sense of something unprecedented: {the singularity of the event}.

Sinister describes something that suggests evil, harm, or malevolent intent: {a sinister figure lurking in the shadows}, {sinister motives}. The word implies threat through darkness or concealment rather than open hostility—a sinister smile unsettles because you sense hidden danger. In heraldry, sinister means the left side of a shield (from the bearer's perspective), reflecting the old superstition that left-handedness was unlucky or evil.
clues: Quietly threatening in an unsettling way

definition: To sink is to move downwards, particularly in water, and sometimes with dire results, as when a ship sinks. If your hopes sink or your heart sinks, this also suggests a dire outcome. To sink something sharp (teeth, claws, fangs) into a surface is to penetrate it. When something sinks in, it penetrates a surface or your mind. A sink is a basin, supplied with water and with a drain in the bottom. A sink is also a low place where waste or vice is concentrated.

A sinker is a weight attached to a fishing line to make it sink. The term extends to anything that sinks or causes sinking. In baseball, a sinker is a pitch that drops sharply as it reaches the plate. A sinker is also a doughnut, especially a plain one meant for dunking in coffee. The phrase {hook, line, and sinker} means completely or without reservation: {She fell for it hook, line, and sinker}.

Sinkers are weights attached to fishing lines to pull bait or lures underwater. The term extends to anything that sinks: a pitch in baseball that drops sharply as it reaches the batter, or doughnuts dunked in coffee. In the expression {hook, line, and sinker}, swallowing the whole fishing rig means believing something completely.

A sinkhole is a depression or hole in the ground caused by the collapse of surface material into an underground void. Sinkholes form naturally in areas with soluble bedrock like limestone, where water gradually dissolves rock below the surface. They can also result from human activity—broken water mains, mining, or drilling. Sinkholes range from shallow dips to catastrophic collapses that swallow cars and buildings. Figuratively, a sinkhole is anything that consumes resources with little return: {That renovation project became a money sinkhole}.

Sinkholes are depressions or holes in the ground formed when underlying rock dissolves or collapses. They range from shallow dips to dramatic cavities that swallow cars or buildings. Sinkholes occur naturally in limestone regions where groundwater erodes bedrock, but can also result from human activity like mining or broken water mains. {A massive sinkhole opened up in the parking lot overnight.}

Sinking describes downward movement through a medium—a ship sinking beneath waves, feet sinking into mud, the sun sinking toward the horizon. The word extends to gradual decline: {sinking profits}, {sinking hopes}. A sinking feeling is that heavy sensation in the stomach when you sense something has gone wrong: {I had a sinking feeling we'd missed our chance}.

Sinks is the plural of sink—basins with drains and faucets for washing hands, dishes, or other items: {The bathroom has double sinks}. As a verb form, sinks means descends or submerges: {The ship sinks slowly}. Things that sink move downward—objects in water, the sun toward the horizon, spirits when hope fades: {My heart sinks every time I see the news}.

Sinned is the past tense of sin—to transgress against moral or religious law. In religious contexts, sinning offends against God's commandments: {He sinned and begged forgiveness}. More loosely, it means to do wrong or violate standards: {She sinned against good taste with that outfit}.

A sinner is someone who commits sins—actions that violate moral or religious law. The term carries strong religious connotations, particularly in Christianity, where all humans are considered sinners by nature. Outside strictly religious contexts, sinner often appears with ironic or humorous intent: {I've been a sinner—I had three slices of cake}. To call yourself a sinner may signal genuine remorse or playful self-deprecation about minor indulgences.

Sinners is the plural of sinner—people who have committed sins or transgressions against moral or religious law. The word carries strong religious connotations, suggesting violation of divine commandments: {We are all sinners in the eyes of God}. Outside religious contexts, sinner often appears ironically or affectionately: {You old sinner, I knew you'd be here}.

Sinning is engaging in acts considered morally wrong or violations of religious law. The word carries weight in religious contexts—sinning against God, sinning in thought or deed—but extends to secular transgressions: {I know I'm sinning against my diet, but this cake is worth it}. The continuous form often implies ongoing or habitual wrongdoing rather than a single lapse.

Sins is the plural of sin, which in religious contexts refers to acts that violate divine law or moral principles. Christianity speaks of original sin, the fallen state inherited from Adam and Eve. Beyond religion, sin describes any serious wrongdoing or transgression: {His sins caught up with him}. The verb sin means to commit such an act: {We have all sinned at some point}. Informally, something can be {a sin} if it's a waste or shame: {It would be a sin to throw out all this food}.

A sinus is a hollow cavity in the body, most commonly the air-filled spaces in the skull connected to the nasal passages. When people complain about their sinuses, they usually mean congestion or infection in these cavities: {My sinuses are killing me}, {a sinus headache}. In anatomy and medicine, sinus refers to various channels and cavities: the venous sinuses of the brain, the maxillary sinus behind the cheekbone.

Sinuses are hollow cavities, especially the air-filled spaces in the skull that connect to the nasal passages. When people complain about their sinuses, they usually mean these are congested or inflamed: {My sinuses are killing me}. The term extends to any cavity or channel in body tissue, and in medicine describes abnormal passages formed by disease or injury.

To sip is to drink in small amounts, taking liquid into the mouth gradually rather than gulping: {She sipped her tea while reading}. A sip is also the small quantity taken: {He took a sip of water}. The word suggests deliberate, measured drinking—savoring a beverage or being cautious with something hot. {Sip} can extend figuratively to gradual intake of anything: {sipping information from various sources}.

A siphon is a tube that uses atmospheric pressure to draw liquid from a higher container to a lower one, often to empty tanks or transfer fuel: {He siphoned gas from the car}. The verb extends to any gradual transfer or diversion: {Embezzlers siphoned funds from the company over years}. Also spelled syphon.

Siphoned is the past tense of siphon, meaning to draw liquid from one container to another through a tube using atmospheric pressure or suction: {He siphoned gas from the tank}. Figuratively, to siphon is to divert resources gradually and often illicitly: {Executives siphoned millions from the company over several years}.

Siphoning is drawing liquid from one container to another through a tube, using gravity and atmospheric pressure—the classic method for stealing gasoline from a car's tank. By extension, siphoning describes any gradual, often illicit transfer: {He was siphoning funds from the company into offshore accounts}. The word implies steady, quiet extraction rather than sudden theft.

Siphons is the plural of siphon, a tube that moves liquid from one container to another by exploiting differences in air pressure—once flow starts, gravity does the work. To siphon is to transfer liquid this way: {Someone siphoned gas from my car}. Figuratively, siphoning means diverting resources gradually: {The manager had been siphoning funds into a personal account}.

Sipped is the past tense of sip—to drink in small quantities, taking liquid into the mouth a little at a time rather than gulping. {She sipped her tea while reading}. {He sipped the whiskey slowly, making it last}.

Sipping is drinking in small quantities, taking liquid into the mouth gradually rather than in gulps. The word suggests deliberate, unhurried consumption—you sip hot tea, fine whiskey, or a cocktail. {She sat sipping her coffee while reading the paper.} Sipping implies savoring or caution, not thirst.
clues: Taking a drink bit by bit

definition: Sips is the plural of sip—small mouthfuls of liquid, taken delicately rather than gulped: {She took tiny sips of her tea}. As a verb, sips means to drink in this manner: {He sips his coffee while reading the paper}. The word suggests measured, unhurried consumption.

Sir is a respectful form of address for a man, used without his name: {Yes, sir}, {Excuse me, sir}. It appears in formal contexts—military, service industries, classrooms—and sometimes sarcastically: {Well, sir, I don't think so}. In correspondence, {Dear Sir} opens letters to unknown recipients. (Capitalized Sir is a British honorific title.)

Sire is a male parent, especially of a horse or other animal used in breeding: {The stallion sired three champions}. In formal or historical address, sire was a title of respect for a king or lord: {Yes, sire}. The verb means to father offspring, used almost exclusively for animals or, when applied to humans, with archaic or ironic effect.

A siren is a device that produces a loud, wailing warning sound—on emergency vehicles, at factories, or for air raids. The sound itself is also called a siren: {The ambulance siren grew closer}. From Greek mythology, a siren is a creature whose beautiful singing lured sailors to shipwreck, so the word extends to any dangerously alluring woman: {She was a siren who left a trail of broken hearts}. The adjective siren describes something seductively appealing but potentially harmful: {the siren call of easy money}. (Capitalized Siren refers specifically to the mythological creatures.)

Sirens are devices that produce loud warning sounds—on emergency vehicles, air raid systems, or security alarms. The wailing rises and falls to cut through ambient noise and demand attention. In Greek mythology, sirens were creatures whose beautiful singing lured sailors to their deaths on rocky shores. By extension, a siren is any dangerously alluring person or thing: {the siren call of easy money}. A siren song promises pleasure but leads to destruction.

Sirloin is a cut of beef from the back, between the short loin and the round. It's a popular steak cut, less tender than ribeye but flavorful and relatively lean: {I'll have the sirloin, medium rare}. Sirloin can be divided into top sirloin and bottom sirloin, with top sirloin generally considered the better cut.

Sirloins is the plural of sirloin, a cut of beef from the lower back of the animal, prized for its tenderness and flavor. It appears in various preparations: {grilled sirloins}, {sirloin steaks}, {sirloin tips}. The cut sits between the short loin and the round, yielding meat suitable for roasting or cutting into steaks.

Sis is an informal term of address for a sister, or for any woman or girl you feel close to: {Hey sis, can I borrow your car?} Among women, sis functions as a term of solidarity or friendly address, even between strangers: {You dropped your phone, sis}. It carries warmth and familiarity without the full formality of "sister."

Sissies is the plural of sissy, a disparaging term for a boy or man considered weak, timid, or effeminate: {The other kids called him a sissy because he wouldn't fight back}. The word implies failure to meet masculine expectations. It's also used among gay men, sometimes reclaimed as playful self-description, sometimes still stinging.

Sissy is a disparaging term for a boy or man considered weak, timid, or effeminate—someone who doesn't meet expectations of masculine toughness: {Don't be such a sissy}. The word often targets boys who avoid rough play or show fear. It carries strong connotations of cowardice and, frequently, implied homosexuality. As an adjective: {sissy behavior}. Originally a child's word for sister.

Sista is an informal spelling of sister, representing African American English pronunciation. It typically refers to a Black woman, often conveying solidarity, affection, or shared identity: {Hey sista, how you doing?} The term emphasizes community and kinship among Black women, though it can also simply mean a female friend or ally.

A sister is a female sibling—someone who shares at least one parent with you. The term extends to women bound by shared experience or affiliation: {sisters in the struggle}, sorority sisters, nursing sisters. In Black American English, sister (often shortened to sis) is a familiar term of address among women. Sister also designates a nun: {Sister Mary Catherine}. To sister something in construction is to reinforce it by attaching a parallel piece alongside.

Sisterhood is the bond between sisters, or by extension, the connection among women who share common experiences, goals, or solidarity. It can describe a formal organization of women, especially a religious community of nuns or a sorority: {She joined the sisterhood at nineteen}. More broadly, sisterhood invokes feminist ideals of mutual support: {There's a sisterhood among women in male-dominated fields}.

Sisterhoods is the plural of sisterhood, which refers to bonds between women based on shared experiences, goals, or identity. A sisterhood may be a formal organization—a religious order of nuns, a sorority, or a women's group: {She joined several sisterhoods dedicated to social justice}. More broadly, it describes solidarity among women: {The sisterhoods formed during the movement lasted decades}.

Sisterly describes the affection, support, or bond characteristic of sisters. It suggests warmth and loyalty between women who share a close relationship, whether biological siblings or not: {She gave me some sisterly advice}. The word often implies protectiveness or gentle teasing: {a sisterly hug}, {sisterly rivalry}.
clues: The way close sisters treat each other

definition: Sisters are female siblings—daughters of the same parents. The bond between sisters often implies closeness and shared history: {My sister and I talk every day}. Sister extends to women united by common cause, faith, or identity: {sisters in the movement}, {the Sisters of Mercy}. In Black American usage, sister addresses or refers to a Black woman with warmth and solidarity. Sister can modify nouns to indicate parallel or affiliated entities: {sister cities}, {sister companies}.

When you sit, your buttocks are on a flat surface – like a chair or the ground. When a four-legged animal sits, its rear and all feet rest on the ground. One object sits on another when it rests on top of it: The book sits on the shelf. When a deliberative body sits, it is in session and doing work. If you sit someone, you direct them to or provide them with a seat. To sit is also shorthand for babysit, that is, care for someone else’s children.

A sitar is a large stringed instrument from India with a long neck, a gourd-shaped resonating chamber, and movable frets. It typically has six or seven main strings plus a dozen or more sympathetic strings that resonate when the main strings are plucked, giving the sitar its characteristic shimmering sound. The instrument became familiar to Western audiences through 1960s rock music.
Sitars are popular stringed instruments in Indian classical music. They have a large, rounded body and a very long neck with frets. The sitar is played with a plectrum.

A sitcom is a television comedy series featuring recurring characters in familiar settings—typically a home, workplace, or social gathering spot. Short for "situation comedy," the format relies on everyday situations generating humor through character dynamics and dialogue rather than physical gags or sketches. Episodes are usually self-contained, returning characters to their starting situations by the end: {I grew up watching sitcoms like Friends and Seinfeld}.

Sitcoms are situation comedies—television series built around a fixed cast of characters in recurring settings like homes, workplaces, or hangout spots. Episodes typically present self-contained conflicts resolved within thirty minutes, often with laugh tracks or studio audiences. The format dominated American television for decades: {I grew up watching sitcoms after school}.

A site is a place or location, especially one designated for a particular purpose: a construction {site}, a {campsite}, a historic {site}. In computing, a site is a location on the internet—a {website}. The verb means to place or position something: {The factory was sited near the river}. To {site} a building is to choose where it goes.

Sitrep is military and emergency-services shorthand for "situation report"—a concise update on current conditions, typically covering location, status, and any developments. The term has spread to casual use for any quick summary of what's happening: {Give me a sitrep on the project}. {The sitrep from the field was grim}.

Sits is the third-person singular of sit—to rest with weight on the buttocks rather than the feet: {She sits at her desk all day}. Something sits when it occupies a position: {The house sits on a hill}. To sit also means to convene: {The court sits in session}. Things that sit idle remain unused: {The car just sits in the garage}.

A sitter is someone who sits, especially in a specific capacity. A babysitter watches children; a house sitter looks after a home while owners are away. In art, a sitter is someone posing for a portrait: {The painter asked his sitter to hold still}. In sports, a sitter is an easy shot or chance that should be impossible to miss—one you could make sitting down.

Sitters is the plural of sitter—someone who sits, or more commonly, someone who watches over something while another is away. A babysitter minds children; a house sitter looks after a home; a pet sitter cares for animals. In art, a sitter is the subject of a portrait. In sports, a sitter is an easy shot that a player should never miss: {He had an open goal but missed a sitter}.

Sitting is the position of being seated, or an instance of it: {a long sitting at the computer}, {painted in a single sitting}. A sitting of a court or legislature is a session when it meets. As an adjective, sitting describes someone currently holding a position: a sitting {president}, a sitting {judge}. A {sitting duck} is an easy target—stationary and vulnerable.

A situation is the circumstances or state of affairs at a particular time and place: {We need to assess the situation before acting}. It often implies complexity or difficulty: {a delicate situation}, {an awkward situation}. In military and emergency contexts, situation refers to current conditions requiring response. A job or position, especially domestic service, was once called a situation: {She found a situation as a governess}.

Situations is the plural of situation—a set of circumstances at a particular time and place. The word often implies complexity or difficulty: {We've been in similar situations before}. Job listings sometimes appear under "situations wanted" or "situations vacant," a usage more common in British English. A situation comedy (sitcom) puts characters in amusing predicaments.

A situationship is a romantic or sexual relationship that lacks clear definition or commitment. It occupies the space between casual dating and an official partnership—more than friends with benefits, less than boyfriend and girlfriend. The term emerged from dating culture to describe connections where neither party has explicitly defined what they are: {We've been in a situationship for six months and I still don't know where it's going}.

A situationship is a romantic or sexual relationship that lacks clear definition or commitment—more than friendship, less than an official couple. The term captures the ambiguity of modern dating where people may spend significant time together without establishing expectations: {We've been in a situationship for months and I still don't know where we stand}. Unlike friends with benefits, situationships often involve emotional intimacy alongside the uncertainty.

A situp is an exercise for strengthening abdominal muscles, performed by lying flat on your back and raising your torso to a sitting position without using your arms: {I do fifty situps every morning}. Also spelled sit-up.

Situps are an exercise for strengthening abdominal muscles. You lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat, then raise your torso toward your knees and lower it back down. {I do fifty situps every morning.} Also spelled sit-ups.

Six is the number between five and seven, represented by the numeral 6. It appears in countless common expressions: {six of one, half dozen of the other} means two options are equivalent. A {six-pack} is beer sold in groups of six, or well-defined abdominal muscles. {At sixes and sevens} means confused or disorganized. {Six feet under} means dead and buried.

A sixpack is a package of six items sold together, typically cans or bottles of beer or soda: {He grabbed a sixpack from the fridge}. The term also refers to well-defined abdominal muscles that form a visible grid pattern: {He's been doing crunches to get a sixpack}. Usually hyphenated or as two words: six-pack.

Sixpence was a British coin worth six pennies, or half a shilling—a small but useful sum for centuries. The coin was discontinued in 1980 but survives in expressions and traditions: the nursery rhyme "Sing a Song of Sixpence," or the custom of placing a sixpence in a bride's shoe for luck. {He hadn't a sixpence to his name.}

A sixshooter is a revolver with a cylinder holding six cartridges—the iconic handgun of the American West. The term evokes cowboys, gunslingers, and frontier justice: {He drew his sixshooter and fired}. Also spelled six-shooter.
