Slaps is recent slang meaning something is excellent or impressive, especially music or food: {This song slaps}, {Her cooking slaps}. The word suggests impact—something that hits hard in a good way. The usage spread from hip-hop culture into mainstream youth slang around the 2010s.

A slapshot is a powerful hockey shot where the player winds up and strikes the puck with a forceful slapping motion, generating maximum velocity. The stick blade contacts the ice just before the puck, creating a whipping effect: {He wound up for a slapshot from the blue line}. Slower to execute than a wrist shot but harder to stop.

A slapshot is a powerful hockey shot where the player winds up and slaps the stick forcefully against the ice just behind the puck, using the stick's flex to generate maximum velocity. It's the hardest shot in hockey but less accurate than wrist shots: {He unleashed a slapshot from the blue line}.

Slapstick is broad physical comedy—pratfalls, pie-in-the-face gags, exaggerated violence played for laughs. The term comes from a hinged paddle that makes a loud slap when actors pretend to hit each other. {The Three Stooges specialized in slapstick}. As an adjective: {slapstick humor}, {slapstick routines}.

To slash something suggests one of two outcomes: a gaping incision (slash his throats, slash his wrists) or a sharp reduction (slash spending, slash a budget). Slash is frequent in media headlines because of its compactness; there you can read about slashing forecasts, payroll, emissions, and such. Cutting implements (knife, claw, sword) are often the subjects of slash. A slash is an instance of slashing, usually with a weapon, or the cut left by one.

Slashed is the past tense of slash, meaning to cut with a sweeping stroke. A slashed tire has been deliberately cut. Slashed prices have been dramatically reduced. In fashion, slashed sleeves have decorative cuts revealing fabric beneath. A slashed budget has been severely cut: {The department's funding was slashed by forty percent}.

A slasher is a person or thing that slashes—cuts with sweeping strokes. The term most commonly refers to slasher films, a horror subgenre featuring a killer who stalks and murders victims one by one, typically with a blade: {We watched slashers all Halloween weekend}. The killer in such films is also called a slasher. In Australian and New Zealand English, a slasher is a brush-cutting tool or machine.

Slashers are horror films featuring masked killers who stalk and murder victims, typically teenagers, with bladed weapons: {Halloween and Friday the 13th defined the slasher genre}. The term comes from the slashing motion of knives and machetes. Slasher can also mean a person or thing that slashes—someone who cuts budgets, clears brush, or wields a blade.

Slashfic is fan fiction depicting romantic or sexual relationships between characters—typically same-sex pairings not present in the original work. The term comes from the slash punctuation marking character pairings: {Kirk/Spock}, {Harry/Draco}. The genre originated in 1970s Star Trek fandom and remains a major category of online fan writing. Also called simply slash.

Slashing describes cutting with sweeping strokes, often violent or dramatic: {a slashing attack with a knife}, {slashing rain against the windows}. Figuratively, it means severe or drastic: {slashing budget cuts}, {a slashing critique}. In hockey, slashing is a penalty for swinging a stick at an opponent. The word conveys aggressive, broad strokes rather than precise incisions.

A slat is a thin, narrow strip of wood, metal, or plastic, typically one of several arranged parallel to each other: {sunlight filtered through the slats of the blinds}, {the slats of a bed frame}. Slats appear in fences, shutters, benches, and crates—anywhere rigid strips create a structure while allowing air or light to pass between them.

Slate is a fine-grained rock that splits into smooth, flat layers, traditionally used for roofing tiles and chalkboards. The color slate is a dark bluish-gray. A slate is also a list of candidates or items grouped together: {The party announced its slate for the upcoming election}. To slate something is to schedule it: {The meeting is slated for Tuesday}. In British usage, to slate someone is to criticize them harshly: {Critics slated the film}. To wipe the slate clean is to start fresh, forgetting past offenses—from the practice of erasing chalk marks. (Capitalized Slate is a news magazine.)

Slated means scheduled or designated for something: {The building is slated for demolition}, {She's slated to speak at noon}. In British usage, to slate someone is to criticize them harshly: {The film was slated by reviewers}. The word comes from the practice of writing appointments on slate boards.

Slates is the plural of slate, a fine-grained rock that splits into thin, flat pieces used for roofing or writing surfaces. The verb slates means schedules or designates: {The meeting is slated for Tuesday}, {She's slated to become the next director}. In British usage, to slate someone is to criticize them harshly: {Critics slated the film}.

To slather is to spread thickly and liberally: {She slathered sunscreen on the kids before the beach}. The word suggests generous, even excessive application—butter slathered on bread, praise slathered on a mediocre performance. A slather (usually plural) means a large amount: {slathers of mayonnaise}.

Slathered means spread thickly or liberally, usually something wet or viscous: {toast slathered with butter}, {slathered in sunscreen}. The word suggests generous, even excessive application—not a delicate touch but a heavy coating. It can extend beyond physical spreading: {a performance slathered with sentimentality}.

Slathering is spreading something thickly and generously, often messily: {slathering butter on toast}, {slathering sunscreen on the kids}. The word suggests abundance bordering on excess—more than a thin coat, applied without much precision. Figuratively, slathering can mean lavishing excessively: {slathering praise on someone}.

Slathers is an informal plural noun meaning a large quantity, usually of something spreadable or pourable: {slathers of butter}, {slathers of sunscreen}. The word often appears with "on"—{She put slathers of mayo on the sandwich}. As a verb, to slather is to spread thickly or lavishly: {He slathered the bread with peanut butter}.

Slats are thin, narrow strips of material—typically wood or metal—arranged in parallel. Window blinds have slats that tilt to control light. Bed frames use slats to support a mattress. Slatted benches let water drain through. In older slang, slats meant ribs: {so skinny you could count his slats}.

Slaughter is the killing of animals for food, or the brutal killing of many people. A slaughterhouse processes livestock; a battlefield slaughter leaves bodies strewn across the ground. The verb means to kill in either sense: {They slaughtered the hogs in November}; {Civilians were slaughtered by the advancing army}. In casual use, slaughter describes a crushing defeat: {We got slaughtered in the playoffs}.

Slaughtered is the past tense of slaughter—to kill animals for food or to kill people violently and in large numbers: {The villagers were slaughtered by invading forces}. In casual speech, slaughtered describes overwhelming defeat: {We got slaughtered 42 to nothing}. In British slang, slaughtered means extremely drunk: {He was absolutely slaughtered by midnight}.

A slaughterhouse is a facility where animals are killed and processed for meat. The word carries its grim meaning plainly—a house of slaughter. Figuratively, any scene of mass killing or carnage: {The battlefield became a slaughterhouse}.
clues: Building for turning animals into meat

definition: Slaughterhouses are facilities where animals are killed and processed for meat. The term carries industrial connotations—large-scale operations with assembly-line efficiency. Figuratively, any place of mass killing or carnage: {The battlefield became a slaughterhouse}. Also called abattoirs, though that term sounds more clinical or euphemistic.

Slaughtering is the killing of animals for food or the killing of people in large numbers. A slaughterhouse is where livestock are killed and processed. The word extends to decisive defeats: {The team took a slaughtering in the playoffs}. To slaughter can also mean to bungle badly: {He slaughtered the pronunciation of her name}.

Slaughters is the plural of slaughter and the third-person singular verb form. A slaughter is the killing of animals for food, or more broadly, the violent killing of many people: {The slaughters of World War I shocked a generation}. To slaughter is to kill in these ways. In informal use, to slaughter an opponent is to defeat them decisively: {Our team slaughters yours every year}.

A slave is a person owned as property by another, forced to work without freedom or compensation. The institution of slavery has existed across cultures throughout history, though in American context it refers specifically to the race-based chattel slavery of Africans and their descendants. Extended uses describe complete subjection: {a slave to fashion}, {a slave to his appetites}. As a verb, to slave is to work extremely hard: {She slaved over the report all weekend}. In computing, a slave device operates under the control of a master device.

A slavecatcher was a person who pursued and captured enslaved people who had escaped, returning them to enslavement for bounty. In the antebellum United States, slavecatchers operated under legal sanction, particularly after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 required Northern states to cooperate in capturing runaways. The term now appears primarily in historical contexts: {The slavecatchers tracked the family through three states}.

Slavecatchers were people who pursued and captured escaped slaves, returning them to enslavement for bounty payments. The term applies especially to those operating under the U.S. Fugitive Slave Acts, which compelled cooperation even in free states: {Slavecatchers tracked runaways as far as Canada}. The word now appears in historical contexts and as a pointed insult for law enforcement seen as oppressive.

A slavedriver is a person who oversees enslaved workers, enforcing labor through threat or violence. The term now commonly describes any harsh, demanding boss or taskmaster: {My manager is a total slavedriver—she expects us to work weekends without complaint}. The figurative use carries the cruelty of the original meaning. Also spelled slave driver.

Slavedrivers is the plural of slavedriver—originally a person who supervised enslaved workers, often with a whip. The term now typically appears as a hyperbolic complaint about a demanding boss or authority figure: {My manager is such a slavedriver—she expects us to work through lunch}.

A slaveholder is a person who owns slaves—human beings held as property and forced to labor without freedom. The term appears primarily in historical contexts, especially discussions of the antebellum American South: {Many of the Founding Fathers were slaveholders}. Unlike the more clinical "slave owner," slaveholder emphasizes the person's role and identity rather than mere possession.

Slaveholders are people who legally own other human beings as property. The term appears most often in discussions of the antebellum American South, where slaveholders formed a powerful planter class: {Many of the Founding Fathers were slaveholders}. The word carries historical weight—it names the relationship plainly rather than softening it.

A slavemaster is a person who owns or oversees enslaved people. The term appears in historical contexts describing plantation owners and overseers in slave-holding societies: {The slavemaster controlled every aspect of their lives}. Figuratively, it describes anyone exercising absolute, dehumanizing control over others: {Her boss was a real slavemaster about deadlines}.

A slaveowner is a person who legally holds other human beings as property. The term appears primarily in historical contexts, especially discussions of the antebellum American South: {Many of the Founding Fathers were slaveowners}. Also spelled as two words: slave owner.

Slaveowners are people who legally held other human beings as property. The term appears primarily in historical contexts, especially discussions of the antebellum American South: {Many of the Founding Fathers were slaveowners}. The compound emphasizes the possessive relationship central to the institution of slavery.

Slaver has two distinct meanings depending on pronunciation. With a long A, a slaver is a ship used in the slave trade, or a person who deals in slaves: {The slaver carried its human cargo across the Atlantic}. With a short A, to slaver is to drool or let saliva dribble from the mouth. Dogs slaver; so do people who drool with excessive desire: {He slavered over the dessert menu}.

Slavers has two pronunciations for two meanings. With a long A, slavers are people who deal in slaves—those who capture, transport, or sell human beings. The ships used in the slave trade were also called slavers. With a short A, slavers means drools or produces excessive saliva: {The dog slavers at the sight of food}. Figuratively, to slaver over something is to desire it excessively: {Critics slavered over her debut novel}.

Slavery is the condition of being owned by another person as property, forced to work without freedom or pay. The enslaved person has no legal rights and can be bought, sold, or inherited. By extension, slavery describes any situation of extreme subjugation or compulsion: {wage slavery}, {slavery to fashion}. {She escaped slavery through the Underground Railroad.}

Slaves is the plural of slave—people owned as property and forced to work without freedom or compensation. The word appears in historical contexts {slaves built the plantation economy} and in figurative uses suggesting complete domination {slaves to fashion}, {wage slaves}. As a verb, slaves means to work extremely hard: {She slaves away at two jobs}.

A slaveship is a vessel used to transport enslaved people, particularly during the Atlantic slave trade from the 16th through 19th centuries. These ships carried captive Africans in notoriously brutal conditions—packed into holds with minimal space, food, or sanitation. The term evokes this specific historical horror: {the Middle Passage aboard a slaveship}. Also spelled as two words: slave ship.

Slaveships were vessels designed or used to transport enslaved people, most notoriously across the Atlantic during the transatlantic slave trade from the 16th through 19th centuries. The holds were configured to pack human beings in brutal, often fatal conditions: {The slaveship carried over four hundred captives from the Gold Coast to Jamaica}. The word sometimes appears as two words: slave ships.

Slaving is working extremely hard, often at tedious or exhausting tasks: {She's been slaving over that report all week}, {He slaved away in the kitchen for hours}. The term draws on the image of enslaved labor to convey grueling, unrelenting effort. In computing, slaving refers to configuring a device to operate under the control of another: {slaving the secondary drive to the primary}.

Slaw is a salad made from shredded raw cabbage, typically dressed with mayonnaise or vinegar. The most familiar version is coleslaw, but slaws can incorporate other vegetables like carrots, broccoli, or kale. It's a common side dish at barbecues and picnics, often served alongside fried chicken or pulled pork sandwiches. {The fish tacos came topped with a tangy lime slaw.}

Slay means to kill, especially violently or in battle—a word from older English that survives in literary and religious contexts: {David slew Goliath}. The past tense is slew, past participle slain. In contemporary slang, slay means to impress powerfully or dominate: {She slayed that interview}, {You look amazing—slay!} This sense, rooted in drag and Black gay culture, suggests performance so good it figuratively kills the audience.

Slayed is the past tense of slay, used primarily in informal contexts meaning to impress or delight overwhelmingly: {She slayed at the party}, {That outfit slayed}. The standard past tense for the literal meaning of killing is slew, but slayed dominates in figurative usage about performance, appearance, or humor: {The comedian absolutely slayed}.

A slayer is one who kills, especially in a violent or dramatic fashion. The word carries a literary or archaic tone in literal use: {the slayer of dragons}, {the slayer of kings}. In contemporary usage, slayer often appears figuratively or humorously: {a lady-killer is a slayer of hearts}. In slang, to slay is to impress or overwhelm, making a slayer someone who excels spectacularly.

Slayers is the plural of slayer—one who kills, especially in dramatic or violent fashion. The word has an archaic, literary quality when used literally: {dragon slayers}, {slayers of giants}. In modern usage, slayer often appears in fantasy contexts or as hyperbole for someone who dominates: {She's a slayer on the dance floor}. The term gained currency through vampire fiction and the television series *Buffy the Vampire Slayer*.

Slaying is killing, especially in a violent or dramatic way: {The slaying shocked the quiet neighborhood}. In contemporary slang, slaying means performing exceptionally well or looking stunning—dominating so thoroughly you've figuratively destroyed the competition: {She walked in and absolutely slayed}. The phrase {slay queen} celebrates someone who consistently excels.

Slays is the third-person singular of slay, which means to kill, especially in a violent or dramatic manner: {The knight slays the dragon}. In contemporary slang, slay means to impress powerfully or perform exceptionally well: {She absolutely slays in that dress}, {That comedian slays every time}. The slang sense conveys devastating excellence—killing it, metaphorically.

Sleaze is sordid, corrupt, or distasteful behavior, especially involving sex or money: {The tabloids thrive on celebrity sleaze}. A sleaze or sleazebag is a person who embodies such qualities—dishonest, slimy, or sexually predatory. As an adjective, sleazy describes cheap tackiness or moral grubbiness: {a sleazy motel}, {sleazy business dealings}.

A sleazebag is a person regarded as morally repugnant, dishonest, or disgustingly sleazy—someone who inspires contempt through slimy behavior, shady dealings, or general untrustworthiness: {That sleazebag tried to cheat my grandmother out of her savings}. The term is informal and derogatory, often applied to con artists, corrupt figures, or anyone who seems to lack basic decency.

A sleazeball is a person regarded as morally corrupt, dishonest, or generally repugnant. The term combines sleaze—suggesting seediness and low ethical standards—with ball as a suffix of contempt, similar to scumbag or dirtbag. Sleazeballs are typically associated with shady dealings, sexual impropriety, or exploitative behavior. {That sleazeball tried to sell me a car he knew was a lemon.} The word is informal and always disparaging.

Sleazeballs is the plural of sleazeball—a person regarded as dishonest, corrupt, or morally repugnant. The term suggests someone slimy and untrustworthy, often in business or politics: {Those sleazeballs charged her twice for the same repair}. The insult emphasizes contempt rather than specific wrongdoing.

Sleazy describes something cheap, shoddy, or morally disreputable. A sleazy motel has stained carpets and hourly rates. A sleazy salesman uses manipulative tactics. Sleazy behavior suggests corruption or sexual impropriety: {a sleazy politician}, {sleazy pickup lines}. The word often combines physical seediness with moral taint—places and people that feel unclean in more ways than one.

A sled is a vehicle with runners for traveling over snow or ice. Children ride sleds down snowy hills; dogs pull sleds across frozen terrain. The verb means to ride one: {We went sledding after the first snowfall}. In American English, sled and sleigh overlap, though sleigh tends toward larger, horse-drawn vehicles.

Sledding is the activity of riding a sled down a snowy slope, typically for recreation: {The kids went sledding after the first big snowfall}. Figuratively, sledding describes how difficult or easy progress is: {rough sledding}, {easy sledding}, {It's been tough sledding since the layoffs}.

A sledge is a heavy sled used for transporting loads over snow or ice, typically larger and sturdier than recreational sleds. In British English, sledge is the common word for what Americans call a sled: {The children took their sledges to the hill}. A sledgehammer is sometimes shortened to sledge. To sledge is also cricket slang for taunting opponents to disrupt their concentration.

A sledgehammer is a large, heavy hammer swung with both hands, used for breaking concrete, driving stakes, or demolition work. The head typically weighs ten to twenty pounds. Figuratively, sledgehammer describes anything lacking subtlety or finesse: {a sledgehammer approach to diplomacy}. As a verb, to sledgehammer is to strike or destroy with overwhelming force.

Sledgehammers are heavy, long-handled hammers swung with both hands for maximum force—used to drive stakes, break concrete, or demolish walls. The weight does the work. Figuratively, a sledgehammer approach lacks subtlety: {The prosecution took a sledgehammer to the defense's argument}. To {use a sledgehammer to crack a nut} is to apply excessive force to a simple problem.

Sledges is the plural of sledge—a heavy sled used for transporting loads over snow or ice, typically pulled by dogs or horses. In British English, sledge also means what Americans call a sled for recreational sliding. A sledgehammer is sometimes shortened to sledge: {He grabbed the sledges from the truck}. To sledge is to ride a sledge or, in cricket slang, to verbally taunt opponents.

Sledging has two distinct meanings. The first is riding on a sled, typically down a snowy hill: {The children went sledging after the first snowfall}. The second, primarily British and Australian, is the cricket practice of verbally taunting opposing players to break their concentration—trash talk meant to unsettle a batsman: {The bowler was warned for sledging}.

Sleds are vehicles designed to slide over snow or ice, typically with runners or a smooth bottom. Children ride sleds downhill for fun; dogs or horses pull sleds to transport goods across frozen terrain. To sled is to ride one: {We went sledding after the first big snowfall}. In American slang, sleds can mean snowmobiles.

Sleek describes a smooth, glossy surface or streamlined shape. A sleek {cat} has shiny, well-groomed fur. A sleek {sports car} has clean lines and no unnecessary bulk. The word suggests polish and sophistication—sometimes with a hint of slickness or superficiality: {a sleek marketing campaign}. To sleek hair is to smooth it down.

Sleep is the natural state of rest in which consciousness is suspended and the body repairs itself. Most animals sleep daily; humans spend roughly a third of their lives asleep. To sleep with someone usually means to have sex with them. A limb that has {fallen asleep} has gone numb. To {sleep on} a decision is to postpone it until morning. {Let sleeping dogs lie} warns against stirring up trouble.

Sleepaway describes a camp or program where children stay overnight for an extended period, typically a week or more, rather than returning home each day. It functions almost exclusively as an attributive adjective modifying camp: {She spent every summer at sleepaway camp in the Catskills}. The term distinguishes residential programs from day camps, where participants go home each evening.

A sleeper is one who sleeps, especially in a particular way: (sound sleeper, light sleeper). Other things called sleepers include a beam to which rails are attached for trains to travel on; and a railcar that has beds, or an overnight train with these. A sleeper describes a sudden success that is not expected, and a spy whose work is not suspected by others where he or she lives. A sleeper sofa or sleeper couch converts to a bed when it is unfolded.

Sleepers are railroad ties—the wooden or concrete beams laid crosswise beneath the tracks. The term is standard in British English, while Americans say ties. Sleepers are also people who sleep, pajamas for infants, or things that succeed unexpectedly after attracting little initial attention: {The film was a sleeper hit}. A sleeper agent remains dormant until activated.

Sleepiness is the state of wanting or needing sleep—the drowsy feeling that precedes falling asleep. It may come from fatigue, boredom, or the body's natural rhythms: {The sleepiness hit me around 3 p.m.} Sleepiness while driving or operating machinery is dangerous.

Sleeping is the state of being asleep—unconscious rest that humans and animals require daily. As an adjective, it describes someone or something in that state: {a sleeping child}, {let sleeping dogs lie}. A sleeping {partner} (British) or sleeping {bag} or sleeping {car} extends the word to things associated with sleep. {Sleeping around} means having casual sex with multiple partners.

Sleepless describes being unable to sleep or marked by lack of sleep: {a sleepless night}, {sleepless with worry}. It can characterize a person who hasn't slept or a period spent without sleep. By extension, sleepless suggests restless vigilance or ceaseless activity: {the sleepless city}.

Sleeplessness is the state of being unable to sleep, whether for a single night or as a chronic condition. It emphasizes the experience rather than the clinical diagnosis: {The sleeplessness was getting to her}. Unlike insomnia, which sounds medical, sleeplessness fits naturally into ordinary speech about restless nights and exhausted days.

A sleepover is an occasion when a child spends the night at a friend's house, or when a group of children gather at one home to sleep: {My daughter is having a sleepover this weekend}. The term applies mainly to planned social events among children and teenagers, distinct from simply staying overnight somewhere.

Sleepovers are social gatherings, typically among children or teenagers, where guests spend the night at a friend's home. The appeal lies in the combination of late-night activities—movies, games, snacks—and the novelty of sleeping somewhere other than your own bed. {My daughter is having a sleepover for her birthday.} Adults occasionally use the term playfully or euphemistically for overnight romantic visits.

Sleeptalking is speaking while asleep, typically during lighter sleep stages. The speech ranges from mumbled nonsense to coherent sentences, usually with no memory of it afterward: {My roommate says I was sleeptalking about work deadlines}. Also spelled as two words: sleep talking.

To sleepwalk is to walk around while asleep, performing activities without conscious awareness. The condition is also called somnambulism. Figuratively, to sleepwalk through something is to do it mechanically, without full engagement or attention: {He sleepwalked through his morning routine}. {The team sleepwalked into defeat}.

Sleepwalked is the past tense of sleepwalk—to walk around while asleep, performing actions without conscious awareness: {She sleepwalked into the kitchen and opened the refrigerator}. Figuratively, to sleepwalk through something is to do it without engagement or attention: {He sleepwalked through the presentation}.

A sleepwalker is someone who walks or performs other activities while asleep. The condition, called sleepwalking or somnambulism, typically occurs during deep sleep and is more common in children. Sleepwalkers usually have no memory of their nighttime wanderings. Figuratively, a sleepwalker is someone going through life without full awareness: {He moved through his days like a sleepwalker}.

Sleepwalkers are people who walk or perform other activities while asleep, typically during deep sleep stages. The condition, called somnambulism, ranges from sitting up in bed to leaving the house. Figuratively, sleepwalkers are people who move through life unaware or disengaged: {The sleepwalkers stumbled toward disaster without seeing the signs}.

Sleepwalking is walking or performing other activities while asleep. The sleepwalker typically has no memory of the episode afterward. The term extends to doing something mechanically, without full awareness or engagement: {The team was sleepwalking through the season until their star player returned}.

Sleepwalks is the verb for walking or performing activities while asleep, a phenomenon also called somnambulism. The sleepwalker typically has no memory of the episode: {She sleepwalks almost every night}. Figuratively, to sleepwalk through something is to do it mechanically, without awareness or engagement: {He sleepwalked through the entire meeting}.

Sleepy describes the state of wanting or needing sleep: {I'm getting sleepy}. A sleepy {town} or sleepy {village} is quiet and uneventful, as if drowsing. Sleepy can also mean sluggish or slow-moving: {a sleepy economy}. The word suggests peaceful drowsiness rather than exhaustion.

A sleepyhead is someone who is drowsy or has just woken up, used affectionately rather than critically: {Come on, sleepyhead, breakfast is ready}. The term is typically directed at children or loved ones who are slow to wake or reluctant to get out of bed.

Sleepyheads is the plural of sleepyhead, an affectionate term for someone who is drowsy or has been sleeping: {Wake up, sleepyheads!} The word is gentle and playful, typically used with children or loved ones rather than as criticism.

Sleet is precipitation that falls as ice pellets—rain that freezes before hitting the ground, or snow that partially melts and refreezes. It creates a distinctive rattling sound on windows and surfaces: {The forecast calls for sleet turning to snow overnight}. Sleet makes roads treacherous, coating them with ice. As a verb, to sleet means to fall as sleet: {It sleeted all morning}.

Sleeting describes weather in which sleet is falling—precipitation that freezes into ice pellets before reaching the ground, or rain that freezes on contact with cold surfaces. {It's sleeting outside, so the roads will be slick.} Sleeting conditions typically occur when temperatures hover around freezing.

A sleeve is the part of a garment that covers the arm, from shoulder to wrist or somewhere in between. Sleeves vary in length and style: {short sleeves}, {long sleeves}, {rolled-up sleeves}. A sleeve is also a protective covering shaped like a tube: a record sleeve, a cable sleeve. To have something {up your sleeve} is to hold it in reserve as a secret advantage. To {wear your heart on your sleeve} is to display emotions openly.

Sleeveless describes a garment without sleeves—the fabric tubes that normally cover the arms: {a sleeveless dress}, {a sleeveless shirt}. Tank tops, vests, and many summer garments are sleeveless by design.
clues: How halter tops are always made

definition: Sleeves are the parts of a garment that cover the arms, from shoulder to wrist or partway. Styles vary widely: long sleeves, short sleeves, cap sleeves, no sleeves at all. To have something {up your sleeve} is to hold it in reserve, hidden from others. To {roll up your sleeves} is to prepare for work. To {wear your heart on your sleeve} is to display emotions openly.

A sleigh is a vehicle on runners designed to travel over snow or ice, typically pulled by horses or reindeer. The word evokes winter scenes—{a one-horse open sleigh}, Santa's flying sleigh. To sleigh is to travel by sleigh, though the verb is rare. {We went sleighing through the countryside.}

Sleighbells are small metal bells attached to a horse's harness, traditionally used on sleighs in winter. They jingle as the horse moves, warning pedestrians and adding festive charm. The sound is strongly associated with Christmas and winter holidays: {Hear those sleighbells jingling}. Also spelled as two words: sleigh bells.

A sleighride is a journey in a horse-drawn sled over snow, typically for recreation or pleasure: {We took a sleighride through the snowy woods}. The word evokes winter nostalgia—jingle bells, bundled passengers, scenic landscapes. In slang, sleighride can refer to a cocaine high, from the drug's association with snow.

Sleighs is the plural of sleigh, a vehicle on runners designed to travel over snow or ice, typically pulled by horses or reindeer. {Santa's sleighs} in holiday displays multiply the iconic image. As a verb, sleighs means to travel by sleigh: {She sleighs through the countryside each winter}.

Sleight is dexterity or cunning, especially in deceiving. The word appears almost exclusively in {sleight of hand}—the skill of performing tricks so quickly or deftly that observers can't follow what's happening. Magicians use sleight of hand literally; politicians and salesmen use it figuratively to misdirect attention from what they're really doing.

Slender describes something thin relative to its length or height: a slender {waist}, slender {fingers}, a slender {tree}. The word carries a graceful connotation that thin or skinny may lack. Extended uses emphasize smallness or insufficiency: slender {means}, slender {hopes}, a slender {margin of victory}. {The evidence was slender at best.}

Slept is the past tense and past participle of sleep. {I slept poorly last night}. {She had slept through the alarm}. To have {slept with} someone is to have had sex with them. To have {slept on} a decision is to have delayed it overnight: {I slept on it and decided to accept the offer}.

A sleuth is a detective or someone who investigates mysteries. The word carries a slightly playful or literary tone—you're more likely to encounter it in cozy mysteries than police reports: {an amateur sleuth}, {The reporter sleuthed out the truth}. To sleuth is to investigate or track down information.

Sleuthing is detective work—investigating, gathering clues, following leads. The term comes from sleuth, itself shortened from sleuthhound, a tracking dog. Most sleuthing today is amateur or figurative: {After some sleuthing, I found out who had been taking my lunch from the office fridge}.

Sleuths are detectives or investigators, whether professional or amateur. The word carries a slightly literary or playful tone, often evoking fictional investigators: {The amateur sleuths pieced together the clues}. As a verb, to sleuth is to investigate: {She sleuthed around until she found the answer}.

Slew has two distinct origins. One is the past tense of slay: {He slew the dragon}. The other means a large quantity: {a whole slew of problems}, {slews of paperwork}. This informal sense suggests an overwhelming or unmanageable number. As a verb, to slew (or slue) means to turn or swing sideways: {The car slewed across the icy road}.

To slice something is to cut it, with the result that a portion (often small or thin) is removed (slice cake, slice pie, slice salami). A slice is an instance of doing this, or the resulting piece (slice of bacon). In sports such as tennis or golf, to slice suggests a stroke that results in backspin on the ball. A slice in these and other sports is the path of a ball as it curves in the direction of the side from which it was hit.

Sliced is the past tense and participle of slice, describing something that has been cut into flat, thin pieces. {Sliced bread} is so ubiquitous that it serves as a benchmark for convenience and innovation: {the best thing since sliced bread}. Beyond food, sliced applies to anything divided into portions or segments. In sports, a sliced shot curves away from the striker, usually unintentionally.

A slicer is a tool or machine that cuts things into slices—a meat slicer, a bread slicer, an egg slicer. In golf, a slicer is someone whose shots curve sharply away from their body (right for right-handers). In data analysis, a slicer is an interactive filter that lets users segment information: {Add a slicer to filter the dashboard by region}.

Slices is the plural of slice—portions cut from a larger whole. A loaf yields slices of bread; a pizza divides into slices. The word extends to portions of anything: {a slice of the profits}, {a slice of life}. As a verb form, slices means cuts into portions or moves sharply through: {The boat slices through the water}.

Slicing is cutting into thin, flat pieces: {slicing bread}, {slicing tomatoes}. The term extends to any smooth, sweeping cut through something: {The boat sliced through the water}. In golf and tennis, slicing produces a shot that curves away from a straight path. In computing, slicing extracts a portion of a sequence—a slice of an array or string.

Slick describes something smooth and glossy, often with a coating that reduces friction: {slick with oil}, {rain-slicked streets}. The word extends to polished performance—a slick presentation is impressively smooth, though perhaps superficially so. A slick operator is clever and persuasive but not entirely trustworthy. As a noun, a slick is a film of oil on water. To slick hair is to smooth it down, often with product: {He slicked his hair back}.

A slicker is a long waterproof coat, originally oilskin, worn in rainy weather. The word also means a swindler or smooth operator—someone slick enough to deceive others. City slicker describes an urban sophisticate, usually from a rural perspective and often with mild contempt: {Those city slickers don't know a thing about farming}.

Slickers is the plural of slicker, a waterproof coat or jacket—especially the yellow oilskin variety worn by fishermen and sailors. City slicker describes someone from an urban area, implying sophistication but also naivety about rural life: {Those slickers from New York don't know the first thing about farming}. The term carries a hint of distrust—slick suggests smooth-talking or deceptive.

Slid is the past tense and past participle of slide. Something that slid moved smoothly across a surface: {The glass slid off the table}. The word covers both deliberate and accidental motion: {She slid into the booth} describes choosing a seat, while {The car slid on ice} suggests loss of control.

Slide is about smooth movement on a surface with little friction, the way a car slides on ice or a baseball runner slides into a base. By extension, to slide is to move easily through something, to move without others noticing, or to become gradually worse. If you let something slide, you ignore its worsening condition. A slide is an instance of sliding. It is also a piece of playground equipment on which children can slide.

A slider is something that slides. In baseball, it's a pitch that breaks sharply to one side as it reaches the plate. A slider is also a small hamburger, typically two or three inches across, served as an appetizer or in multiples: {We ordered a plate of sliders}. In user interfaces, a slider is a control you drag along a track to adjust a value: {Move the slider to increase brightness}.

Sliders are small hamburgers, typically two to three inches across, served as appetizers or in multiples as a main course. The name suggests they slide down easily. The term originated with White Castle's miniature burgers but now applies to any small sandwich served this way: {We ordered a plate of sliders to share}. In other contexts, a slider is a baseball pitch that breaks laterally, or an interface element—a control you drag along a track to adjust values like volume or brightness.

Slides are smooth, sloped surfaces designed for descending, typically found on playgrounds where children climb up and slide down. The word extends to any controlled descent or lateral movement: a baseball player slides into base, stock prices slide downward, and things slide into place when they fit smoothly. Slides are also individual frames in a presentation, a usage that persists from the era of photographic transparencies projected onto screens. As footwear, slides are backless sandals you slip into without fastening. {She kicked off her slides at the door.}

A slideshow is a sequential presentation of images, text, or other visual content displayed one frame at a time. Originally the term described projected photographic slides shown in order, often accompanied by narration at family gatherings or educational lectures. Now slideshows are almost entirely digital, created with presentation software for business meetings, classrooms, or personal photo collections. {She put together a slideshow of vacation photos for the reunion.}

Slideshows are presentations composed of a sequence of images or screens displayed one after another. Originally these were photographic slides projected onto a screen; now the term usually refers to digital presentations made with software like PowerPoint or Google Slides: {She put together a slideshow for the quarterly meeting}. A slideshow of vacation photos remains a cliché of boring entertainment.

Sliding describes smooth, continuous movement across a surface. A child goes sliding down a hill; a drawer slides open. The word often implies effortlessness or gradual change: a sliding {scale} adjusts based on variables, sliding {doors} move horizontally rather than swinging. {Prices have been sliding all year} suggests steady decline. To let something slide is to neglect it deliberately.

Slight describes something small in degree or importance: a slight {improvement}, a slight {chance}, a {slight delay}. A slight person has a slender, delicate build. To slight someone is to treat them with disrespect or indifference, often by ignoring them: {She felt slighted when they didn't invite her}. A slight is such an act of disrespect: {He never forgot the slight}.

Slighted describes feeling disrespected or snubbed, typically through being overlooked or treated as unimportant: {She felt slighted when they didn't invite her to the meeting}. The slight needn't be intentional—someone can feel slighted by an innocent oversight. The word suggests wounded pride more than deep offense.

Slights are small acts of disrespect or dismissiveness—being overlooked, snubbed, or treated as unimportant. The word captures offenses that may seem minor but accumulate: {She remembered every slight from her childhood}. As a verb, to slight someone is to treat them with such casual disregard: {He felt slighted when they didn't invite him}.

Slim describes something narrow or slight in width or build: a slim {figure}, a slim {volume}. It extends to things that are barely sufficient or unlikely: slim {chances}, a slim {margin of victory}, slim {pickings}. To slim or slim down is to lose weight or reduce: {She's been slimming down for the wedding}. {The company slimmed its workforce}.

Slime is a viscous, slippery substance that's typically unpleasant—think the trail left by a slug or the gunk coating a neglected drain. The word carries strong connotations of disgust, which is why calling someone a slime or saying they're slimy suggests they're morally repulsive or untrustworthy. As a verb, to slime is to coat with slime or, figuratively, to damage someone's reputation through underhanded tactics. In recent years, slime has also become a popular children's craft material—a stretchy, squeezable goo made from glue and other household ingredients.

A slimeball is a despicable or untrustworthy person, someone whose behavior strikes others as slimy—underhanded, sleazy, or morally repugnant. The term evokes something disgusting to the touch, and that visceral quality carries into its figurative use. {Her ex-boyfriend turned out to be a total slimeball.} It's informal and always derogatory.

Slimed is the past tense of slime, meaning to cover with or as if with slime—a viscous, often unpleasant substance. The word gained pop culture currency from Nickelodeon game shows where contestants got doused with green goo: {She got slimed on live TV}. Figuratively, to be slimed is to be smeared or treated in a way that feels gross or degrading: {He slimed his way into her trust}.

Slimes is the plural of slime and the third-person singular verb form. Slime is viscous, often unpleasant matter—mucus, algae, or ooze. To slime is to coat with such substance: {The fish slimed my hands}. In gaming, slimes are common blob-like monsters. To slime someone figuratively is to attack their reputation with false or damaging information: {The campaign slimed her with attack ads}.

Slimming describes something that makes a person appear thinner, or the process of trying to lose weight. A slimming {dress} or slimming {color} creates a leaner silhouette. As a noun, slimming refers to dieting or weight-loss efforts: {She's been on a slimming program for months}. The term is more common in British than American English.

Slimy describes something covered with or resembling slime—wet, slippery, and slightly viscous: {slimy seaweed}, {a slimy slug}. The texture provokes disgust, which carries into the figurative sense: a slimy person is repulsively ingratiating or dishonest, someone who makes you feel like you need a shower after dealing with them.

A sling is a device for hurling stones—a pouch on two cords, swung to build momentum. David killed Goliath with one. The word extends to any strap or band that supports, suspends, or carries: a rifle sling, an arm sling for injuries, a baby sling. To sling is to throw casually or carelessly: {She slung her bag over her shoulder}. To {sling hash} is to work as a short-order cook. A sling is also a cocktail of spirits, sugar, and citrus: {a Singapore sling}.

Slingbacks are women's shoes with a strap that wraps around the back of the heel rather than enclosing it. The design offers more security than a mule while remaining open and elegant, making slingbacks popular for dressy occasions: {She wore black slingbacks with her cocktail dress}.

A slinger is someone who slings—throws or hurls something with force, typically using a strap or device. Historically, slingers were soldiers who hurled stones with leather slings. The term extends to anyone who handles or serves something rapidly: a {hash slinger} works in a cheap restaurant, a {mud slinger} hurls accusations. In construction, a slinger directs crane operators and attaches loads.

Slinging is the present participle of sling—to throw with force or casual motion: {He was slinging rocks at the fence}. It extends to serving or distributing quickly: {slinging drinks at the bar}, {slinging hash} (serving food). In street slang, slinging often means selling drugs: {He got caught slinging on the corner}.

Slings is the plural of sling, which names several devices for throwing, supporting, or carrying. A sling is a primitive weapon—a strap or pouch whirled to hurl stones: {David slew Goliath with a sling}. A sling also supports an injured arm, suspends cargo for hoisting, or carries a baby against the body. To sling is to throw casually or hang loosely: {She slung her bag over her shoulder}. To {sling hash} is to work as a short-order cook. {Slings and arrows} evokes misfortune, from Shakespeare's famous soliloquy.

A slingshot is a Y-shaped device with an elastic band stretched between the prongs, used to launch small projectiles like stones. Children's toy and occasional hunting tool. In American English, slingshot also describes the maneuver of using a planet's gravity to accelerate a spacecraft: {The probe used Jupiter for a slingshot toward Saturn}. As a verb, to slingshot is to accelerate rapidly, often by releasing stored energy: {The car slingshoted past the competition}.

Slingshots is the plural of slingshot, a Y-shaped device with an elastic band for launching small projectiles. Children use slingshots to fling pebbles; the weapon appears in the biblical story of David and Goliath. As a verb, to slingshot is to accelerate rapidly using momentum or gravitational pull: {The spacecraft slingshots around Jupiter to gain speed}.

Slink means to move quietly and furtively, typically to avoid notice or because of shame or guilt: {The cat slinked through the fence}; {He slinked away after the confrontation}. The word suggests sneaky, stealthy movement—someone who slinks is trying not to be seen. As an adjective, slink describes a prematurely born calf, and by extension, the soft leather made from its hide.

Slinkies is the plural of Slinky, a coiled spring toy that "walks" down stairs through a wave-like motion. The word also describes things with slinky qualities—sinuous, sleek, or seductively smooth: {She tried on several slinkies before settling on a red dress for the party}.

Slinking is the present participle of slink, describing movement that is stealthy, furtive, or ashamed. A cat slinks through tall grass stalking prey. A person caught doing something embarrassing slinks away. The word suggests trying not to be noticed, whether from predatory intent or shame: {She saw him slinking out the back door}.

Slinks is the third-person singular of slink, meaning to move in a quiet, furtive, or stealthy manner—often suggesting shame, guilt, or sneakiness: {He slinks away whenever the boss appears}. The word can also describe seductive movement: {She slinks across the stage}. As a noun, slinks refers to prematurely born calves, or their hides used for fine leather.

Slinky describes movement that is sinuous, graceful, and suggestively smooth—often with sexual overtones. A slinky {dress} clings to the body and flows with movement. A slinky {walk} suggests seductive confidence. The word evokes sleekness and fluidity: {She made a slinky entrance in black silk}. (Capitalized Slinky is the toy.)

Slip has substantial overlap in meaning with slide, with the added feature that slip often suggests things that are accidental or undesirable. You can slip and fall on ice; time (or people) can slip away quickly without you noticing them. If something slips your mind, you forget it, often regrettably. A slip is an instance of slipping, and several other things, such as a small piece of paper; a mistake in speech or writing; a development for the worse; and a woman’s undergarment, worn like a dress or skirt.

A slipcover is a removable fabric covering designed to fit over upholstered furniture like sofas and armchairs. It protects the original upholstery from wear, stains, and pet hair while allowing for easy washing or seasonal changes in décor. {We bought a slipcover to hide the worn spots on the couch.} The term can also apply to protective paper or cardboard sleeves for books or media cases.

Slippage is the act or amount of slipping—a gradual loss, decline, or failure to meet expectations. Sales figures show slippage when they fall short of projections. A schedule experiences slippage when deadlines slide. {There's been some slippage in our market share}. The word often appears in business and engineering contexts where precise measurements matter and small deviations accumulate.

Slipped is the past tense of slip—to lose traction or move smoothly and quickly. Someone slipped on ice, slipped out of the room, or slipped a note under the door. Time slipped away. A detail slipped your mind. Standards slipped. {She slipped the ring off her finger}. A slipped disc is a spinal injury where cushioning tissue has shifted out of place.

A slipper is a soft, lightweight shoe worn indoors for comfort. Slippers typically slide on easily without laces or buckles: {She padded around the house in her slippers}. The word can also describe a formal shoe for dancing or evening wear, though this usage is old-fashioned.

Slippers are soft, lightweight footwear worn indoors for comfort and warmth. They typically slide on easily and have flexible soles unsuitable for outdoor use. The term covers everything from plush bedroom slippers to ballet slippers worn for dance. {She padded around the house in her slippers.}

Slippery describes surfaces that are smooth, wet, or otherwise difficult to grip or stand on without sliding: {The roads are slippery after the rain}. By extension, slippery characterizes things that are hard to hold onto or pin down—an eel is slippery, but so is a slippery concept that resists clear definition. A slippery person is evasive and untrustworthy, hard to hold accountable. The slippery slope is a rhetorical warning that one step will inevitably lead to worse ones.

Slipping is the present participle of slip, covering movement without firm grip or control. Something slipping is sliding unintentionally: {The glass was slipping from her hands}. Standards or performance that are slipping are declining: {His grades have been slipping lately}. Time slipping away passes quickly or unnoticed. If something is slipping your mind, you're forgetting it.

Slips is the plural of slip, covering all its meanings. Paper slips are small pieces—receipts, notes, tickets. A slip of the tongue is a minor verbal error. Slips are also undergarments worn beneath dresses, or places where boats dock. The verb slips means loses footing, moves quietly, or declines gradually: {Time slips away}, {She slips out the back door}.

Slipshod means careless or sloppy, lacking attention to detail or proper standards: {slipshod work}, {a slipshod investigation}. The word originally described shoes worn down at the heel—footwear so neglected it barely stayed on. That image of shabby disrepair extends to any task done without care: {The report was slipshod, full of errors and missing data}.

A slipstream is the area of reduced air pressure behind a moving vehicle or object, where following closely requires less effort. Cyclists and race car drivers draft in a competitor's slipstream to conserve energy before overtaking. The verb means to follow in this zone: {She slipstreamed the lead car until the final lap}. Figuratively, to ride in someone's slipstream is to benefit from their trailblazing effort.

Slipstreaming is the practice of following closely behind a moving vehicle or body to take advantage of reduced air resistance in its wake. Cyclists and race car drivers slipstream to conserve energy or gain speed: {He tucked in behind the leader, slipstreaming until the final lap}. In computing, slipstreaming means integrating updates or patches into an installation file so they install together: {I slipstreamed the service pack into the Windows installer}.

Slipstreams are the areas of reduced air resistance behind moving vehicles. A cyclist riding in another's slipstream expends less energy. The concept extends to any advantageous position created by someone ahead: {The startup rode in the slipstream of the tech giants}. As a verb, to slipstream is to follow closely in such a draft.

A slipup is a minor mistake or error, usually careless rather than serious: {It was just a slipup—I accidentally sent the email to the wrong person}. The word suggests something that went wrong despite good intentions, not a fundamental failure. Also spelled slip-up.

A slipway is a ramp sloping into the water, used for launching or hauling out boats and ships. Vessels are built or repaired on slipways, then slid into the water when ready: {The ship was launched from the slipway at the naval yard}. Also called a slip.

A slit is a long, narrow cut or opening: {a slit in the curtain}, {a mail slit in the door}. To slit is to make such an opening, typically by cutting lengthwise: {slit the envelope open}, {slit someone's throat}. A slit skirt has a vertical opening for ease of movement. Slit is also vulgar slang for vulva.

Slither is to move with a smooth, twisting, sliding motion—the way a snake travels across ground. The word suggests something slightly unsettling or sinister: {The snake slithered through the grass}. By extension, people slither when they move in a sneaky or insinuating way: {He slithered out of the room before anyone noticed}.

Slithered is the past tense of slither, meaning to move with a smooth, twisting, side-to-side motion like a snake: {The python slithered across the path}. People slither when moving stealthily or awkwardly along the ground: {He slithered under the fence}. Figuratively, someone untrustworthy slithers away from accountability.

Slithering describes smooth, gliding movement close to a surface, like a snake's locomotion. The word suggests sinuous, side-to-side motion without legs: {A snake came slithering through the grass}. It can apply to anything moving with similar fluid, slightly unsettling grace: {The rope slithered off the dock into the water}.

Slithers is the verb slither in the third person singular. To slither is to move with a smooth, twisting motion, like a snake sliding across ground: {The python slithers through the grass}. The word suggests something sinuous and often unsettling. People slither when they move sneakily or squeeze through tight spaces: {He slithered out the back door before anyone noticed}.

Slithery describes movement like a snake's—smooth, sinuous, and slightly unsettling. A slithery creature slides along surfaces without legs. The word often carries connotations of something unpleasant or creepy: {slithery eels}, {a slithery sensation on the skin}. It can also suggest slipperiness: {The mud was slithery underfoot}.

A sliver is a thin, narrow piece cut or broken from something larger: {a sliver of glass}, {a sliver of cake}. The word suggests sharpness or delicacy—wood slivers can pierce skin, while a sliver of moon is the thinnest visible crescent. To sliver is to cut into such pieces. A sliver of something abstract is a small portion: {a sliver of hope}.

Slivers are thin, narrow pieces cut or broken from something larger. A sliver of wood might lodge painfully under skin; a sliver of glass could cut a finger. The word extends to small portions generally: {a sliver of cake}, {a sliver of hope}. To sliver is to cut into such pieces: {She slivered almonds for the salad}.

A slob is a person who is messy, lazy, or uncouth—someone who neglects personal grooming or keeps their living space in disorder: {He's such a slob, there are pizza boxes everywhere}. The word carries mild contempt, suggesting someone who has let standards slip rather than someone truly offensive.

Slobber is saliva that drips or runs from the mouth. Babies slobber, as do certain dog breeds. To slobber is to drool uncontrollably or to let saliva escape while eating or sleeping: {The baby slobbered all over his bib}. Figuratively, to slobber over something is to show excessive, undignified enthusiasm: {Critics slobbered over the director's latest film}.

Slobbering is drooling or letting saliva run from the mouth, as babies and some dogs do. It extends to excessive, unrestrained displays of affection or enthusiasm: {slobbering praise}, {slobbering all over a celebrity}. The word suggests something undignified or lacking self-control.

Slobbers is saliva that drools or dribbles from the mouth—what babies and certain dog breeds produce abundantly: {The Saint Bernard slobbers all over the furniture}. To slobber is to drool or to kiss sloppily. Figuratively, to slobber over something is to express excessive enthusiasm: {Critics slobbered over her debut novel}.

Slobbery describes something covered with or producing saliva—wet, drooling, messy: {The dog gave me a slobbery kiss}. It can characterize affection that feels excessive or unpleasantly moist: {slobbery sentimentality}. The word carries a slightly comic, mildly disgusting quality.

Slobs are people who are messy, lazy, or lacking in personal standards. The word suggests someone indifferent to cleanliness or appearance: {The apartment looked like slobs lived there}. A slob may also be slovenly in habits or manners more broadly: {Don't be such a slob—use a napkin}.

Slog is an informal noun or verb that connotes hard, tedious work. Something described as a slog implies that it requires effort, patience, and tolerance: Living in the Arctic is a hard slog for a Southern California boy. If you slog through or slog your way through something, you persist until it is finished, despite the effort: For the last 200 yards we had to slog our way through loose gravel.

A slogan is a short, memorable phrase used to promote a product, cause, or idea. Advertising slogans aim to stick in the mind: {Just Do It}, {I'm Lovin' It}. Political slogans rally support or crystallize a position: {Make America Great Again}, {Yes We Can}. The term can carry a dismissive edge—calling something "just a slogan" suggests empty rhetoric over substance.

Sloganeering is the practice of using slogans—catchy phrases or mottos—especially in political contexts. The term is usually dismissive, implying empty rhetoric over substantive argument: {The debate devolved into sloganeering}. Someone who sloganeers relies on memorable phrases rather than genuine engagement with issues.

Slogans is the plural of slogan—a short, memorable phrase used to promote a product, cause, or idea. Advertising slogans aim to stick in the mind: {Just Do It}, {I'm Lovin' It}. Political slogans rally supporters: {Yes We Can}, {Make America Great Again}. The best slogans compress complex appeals into a few punchy words; the worst become empty clichés.

Slogged is the past tense of slog, meaning to work or move with steady, effortful persistence. The word suggests laborious progress rather than quick results: {We slogged through the mud for hours}, {She slogged away at the report all weekend}. Whether physical trudging or grinding mental work, slogging implies determination against difficulty.

Slogging is hard, steady, often tedious work or travel. The word suggests persistence through difficulty rather than speed or grace: {After hours of slogging through the mud, we reached camp}. In cricket and boxing, slogging means hitting hard and wildly. The figurative sense dominates: {slogging through paperwork}, {slogging away at a novel}.

A sloop is a sailboat with a single mast and a fore-and-aft rig—typically one mainsail and one headsail. The design is common for recreational sailing because it's simple to handle: {We spent the afternoon on a little sloop in the harbor}. Historically, sloops also served as small warships.

Slop is liquid waste or spilled mess—watery food, kitchen scraps fed to pigs, or any unappetizing semi-liquid substance. The verb means to spill carelessly: {Water slopped over the edge of the bucket}. Slop extends to anything carelessly made or of low quality: {The movie was pure slop}. Slops, in the plural, are cheap ready-made clothing or a sailor's loose trousers.

A slope is a surface that lies at an angle rather than flat or level, like the slope of a hill or a roof. The word also denotes the degree of such an incline, measured as a ratio of vertical rise to horizontal run: {The slope of the driveway made it treacherous in winter.} In mathematics, slope describes the steepness of a line on a graph. As a verb, slope means to incline or slant in a particular direction. The plural slopes often refers specifically to ski hills: {We hit the slopes every weekend in January.}

Slopes is an ethnic slur for people of East Asian descent, derived from the perceived shape of their eyes. The term is offensive and dates mainly from American military conflicts in Asia. {The platoon used slurs like slopes and gooks.}

Slopestyle is a winter action sports competition where skiers or snowboarders navigate a course featuring rails, jumps, and other obstacles, performing tricks that judges score for difficulty and style. The format emerged from freestyle skiing and snowboarding culture and became an Olympic event in 2014: {She won gold in slopestyle}.

Sloppy describes something messy, careless, or lacking precision. A sloppy room is untidy; sloppy work shows insufficient attention to detail. Sloppy food is wet and unappetizing: {sloppy joe}. Sloppy weather is rainy or muddy. Sloppy clothing is loose and baggy. A sloppy kiss is wet and enthusiastic. {Don't get sloppy with the details.}

Slosh describes liquid moving noisily in a container or underfoot. Water sloshes in a bucket when you walk; boots slosh through puddles. The word captures both the motion and the sound—a wet, splashing movement: {Coffee sloshed over the rim of the mug}. In British slang, sloshed means drunk.

Sloshed is informal for drunk, typically quite drunk rather than merely tipsy: {We got absolutely sloshed at the wedding reception}. The word evokes liquid sloshing around, as if the person were a container of alcohol. British English favors it slightly more than American.

Sloshes is the third-person singular of slosh, describing liquid moving noisily in a container or someone walking through water or mud: {Water sloshes in the bucket as she walks}, {He sloshes through the puddles}. As a noun, sloshes are instances of this splashing movement or sound.

Sloshing is the sound and motion of liquid moving around inside a container or space. Water sloshes in a half-full bucket when you walk. Beer sloshes in a glass carried unsteadily. The word captures both the audible splash and the visible surge: {I could hear liquid sloshing around in the tank}. To slosh through something is to wade noisily: {sloshing through puddles}.

A slot is an opening that is probably wider than a slit, though the words are unrelated. When time is involved, a slot is a fixed period of time among others: I’ll fit your appointment into the three o’clock slot. A slot may also be a position or job (among others) in an institution: We have an open slot for a programmer. Slot machines are sometimes called slots. To slot something is to fit it into a slot, or provide a slot for it: I’ll slot you for 4-5 p.m.

A slotcar is a miniature electric racing car that runs in a grooved track, guided by a pin or blade that fits into the slot. The cars are powered through metal strips in the track and controlled by handheld triggers that regulate speed. Slotcar racing was a popular hobby in the 1960s and remains a niche pursuit: {He spent weekends at the slotcar track}. Also spelled slot car.

Sloth is disinclination to action or labor—laziness elevated to a defining trait. It's one of the seven deadly sins, suggesting spiritual torpor rather than mere idleness: {His sloth kept him from achieving anything meaningful}. A sloth is also a slow-moving arboreal mammal of Central and South America, named for its unhurried movements and long periods of rest.

Sloths, mammals that live in the treetops of Central and South America, sleep a lot and move slowly. They have long arms and claws, and move around upside down. In language, sloth is laziness or a lack of effort.

Slots are narrow openings or positions designed to receive something. A mail slot accepts letters; a time slot accommodates an appointment. Slot machines, often called simply slots, are casino gambling devices: {She lost two hundred dollars playing slots}. To slot something is to place it into position: {They slotted the new player into the lineup}.

Slotted describes something with a slot—a narrow opening or groove cut into it. A slotted spoon has openings that let liquid drain through. A slotted screw has a single straight groove for a flathead screwdriver. The word also works as a verb's past tense: {She slotted the key into the lock}, {He got slotted into the morning shift}.

Slouch is a drooping, relaxed posture—shoulders rounded, spine curved, head forward. To slouch is to stand, sit, or walk this way: {Don't slouch at the dinner table}. The word carries connotations of laziness or poor discipline. A slouch can also mean someone lacking skill or competence, but almost always in the negative: {She's no slouch at chess}.

Slouches names people who lack energy, effort, or skill, most often appearing after a negative: {She's no slouch at tennis}. To call someone {no slouch} is to praise their competence. The verb slouch means to sit, stand, or walk with drooping posture—shoulders rounded, spine curved: {Don't slouch at the dinner table}. A slouch is also a drooping posture or a soft, shapeless hat.

Slouching is sitting or standing with drooped shoulders and a curved spine—the opposite of upright posture. Parents and teachers tell children to stop slouching. The word suggests laziness or poor discipline: {He came slouching into the meeting twenty minutes late}. To slouch toward something is to approach it slowly or reluctantly, evoking Yeats's beast slouching toward Bethlehem.

Slouchy describes a loose, relaxed, or drooping quality. A slouchy {posture} involves rounded shoulders and a curved spine. Slouchy {clothing} fits loosely and hangs without structure: {a slouchy sweater}, {slouchy boots}. The word can suggest comfortable casualness or unflattering sloppiness, depending on context.

Slough has two pronunciations with different meanings. Rhyming with "now," a slough is a swamp or muddy area, or figuratively a state of despair or degradation: {a slough of despond}. Rhyming with "stuff," to slough is to shed or cast off, as a snake sloughs its skin. Extended: {slough off dead cells}, {slough off responsibilities}.

Slow means not fast—taking more time than usual or expected. A slow {walk}, a slow {response}, a slow {learner}. Traffic moves slowly; a watch runs slow when it loses time. To slow or slow down is to reduce speed: {Slow down, you're driving too fast}. Figuratively, someone who is slow may be dim-witted, and a slow {day} lacks activity. {Slow burn} describes anger that builds gradually.

A slowcoach is someone who moves, works, or acts too slowly—holding others back or trying their patience. The term is British; Americans say slowpoke. {Come on, slowcoach, we're going to be late!} The word originally referred to a slow-moving stagecoach.

Slowcoaches is the plural of slowcoach, British slang for a person who moves, works, or thinks slowly. It carries mild impatience or affectionate teasing: {Come on, slowcoaches, we'll miss the train!} The American equivalent is slowpoke.

A slowdown is a reduction in speed, pace, or activity. Economic slowdowns mean reduced growth or productivity: {The housing market slowdown affected construction jobs}. A work slowdown is a labor action where employees deliberately reduce their pace without striking outright. Traffic slowdowns occur when congestion forces vehicles to crawl.

Slowdowns are reductions in speed or pace. Traffic slowdowns occur during rush hour. Economic slowdowns indicate decreased growth or activity. In labor disputes, a slowdown is a deliberate reduction in work pace—less dramatic than a strike but still disruptive: {The union organized a slowdown to pressure management}.

Slowing is the present participle of slow, used as a verb or adjective to describe a reduction in speed or pace. Traffic may be slowing, or economic growth may be slowing. As an adjective, it modifies nouns: {the slowing economy}, {a slowing heartbeat}. The noun slowing refers to the process itself: {a slowing of momentum}.

Slowly means at a low speed or gradual pace, the opposite of quickly. It modifies actions that take more time than usual or expected: {She slowly opened the door}. Slowly can suggest deliberateness or caution: {He slowly backed away from the edge}. It also describes gradual processes: {The economy is slowly recovering}.

Slowness is the quality of moving, happening, or responding without speed. Physical slowness describes unhurried movement: {the slowness of the glacier's advance}. Mental slowness suggests delayed comprehension or reaction: {His slowness to grasp the joke embarrassed everyone}. Slowness can be deliberate—a virtue of careful work—or a frustrating impediment: {The slowness of bureaucracy drove her mad}.

Slowpitch is a variety of softball where the pitcher delivers the ball in a high arc rather than fast and flat. The slow, looping trajectory—typically required to reach a certain height—gives batters time to set up and swing, making the game more offense-oriented than fastpitch. Also spelled slow-pitch or slow pitch. {We play slowpitch on Thursday nights.}

A slowpoke is a person who moves, works, or acts slowly—usually said with mild impatience or affection: {Hurry up, slowpoke!} The term is informal and often playful, common in American English. British English prefers slowcoach.

Slowpokes are people who move, work, or act slowly. The term is mildly teasing rather than harsh: {Hurry up, slowpokes, we're going to be late!} It's most common in American English, where the singular slowpoke appears more often than the plural.

Sludge is thick, soft, wet matter—mud, sediment, or industrial waste with a similar consistency. Sewage treatment produces sludge. Oil sludge accumulates in engines. The word suggests something unpleasant and difficult to deal with: {wading through bureaucratic sludge}. As a music genre, sludge (or sludge metal) combines doom metal's slow heaviness with hardcore punk's aggression.

S-l-u-g represents some unrelated words. A slug is a small creature like a snail without a shell that lives in forests and gardens; a piece of metal shaped like a coin that is used deceitfully in machines that accept coins; and a quantity of liquid swallowed at once (slug of orange juice). A slug is a noun and verb for a violent blow with the fist. A boxer might slug his opponent in the jaw or deliver a slug to his jaw.

A slugfest is a fierce, prolonged contest characterized by heavy blows exchanged between opponents. The term originated in boxing to describe fights where both fighters trade punches relentlessly rather than employing defensive strategy, but it extends readily to any brutal competition: {The playoff game turned into a 12-9 slugfest}. Baseball uses it specifically for high-scoring games with lots of hits. The word emphasizes mutual aggression and endurance over finesse.

Slugfests are prolonged, brutal fights or contests—originally boxing matches where fighters trade heavy blows rather than employing finesse. The term extends to any intense competition: a political slugfest, a legal slugfest, a slugfest at the ballot box. In baseball, a slugfest is a high-scoring game where both teams hit well: {The game turned into a 12-9 slugfest}.

Slugged is the past tense of slug, which has two main verb senses. To slug someone is to hit them hard with a fist or blunt object: {He slugged me in the jaw}. In baseball, to slug is to hit powerfully: {She slugged three home runs last season}. A slugger is a powerful hitter. To slug something back is to drink it quickly: {He slugged back his whiskey}.

A slugger is someone who hits hard—originally a boxer known for powerful punches, now most often a baseball player who hits for power rather than average. The term emphasizes brute force over finesse: {He's not fast, but he's a slugger who can clear the fences}. Informally, a slugger is anyone who fights or competes aggressively.

Sluggers are powerful hitters, especially in baseball—batters known for driving the ball hard and far rather than for finesse or contact hitting: {The team's sluggers combined for twelve home runs}. More broadly, a slugger is anyone who hits hard, whether in boxing or a barroom fight. The singular slugger appears in compounds like {Louisville Slugger}, a brand of baseball bat.

Slugging means hitting hard, especially in baseball where a slugger is a powerful hitter known for extra-base hits. {He's been slugging well this season.} Beyond sports, slugging is fighting with fists or drinking heavily in gulps: {They were slugging it out in the parking lot}, {slugging whiskey straight from the bottle}. In skincare, slugging is coating the face with petroleum jelly overnight to lock in moisture.

Sluggish means slow-moving or lacking energy. A sluggish economy grows at a disappointing pace. A sluggish stream barely flows. Someone feeling sluggish after a heavy meal moves with reluctance: {I felt sluggish all afternoon}. The word suggests not just slowness but a heaviness or resistance to motion—like a slug dragging itself along.

Sluggishness is the quality of being slow, lethargic, or lacking energy and responsiveness. It applies to people, animals, systems, or processes that move or function at less than normal speed or efficiency. {The sluggishness of the economy worried investors.} A person experiencing sluggishness might feel heavy and unmotivated, while a sluggish computer takes too long to respond to commands. The word suggests not just slowness but a kind of resistant inertia.

Slugs are soft-bodied mollusks resembling snails without shells, often found in gardens where they eat plants. A slug is also a bullet or a counterfeit coin used in vending machines. In printing, a slug is a line of type cast as one piece. To slug someone is to punch them hard: {He slugged the guy right in the jaw}. A slug of whiskey is a mouthful swallowed at once.

A sluice is a channel or gate that controls water flow—used for irrigation, mining, or regulating water levels in reservoirs and canals. The verb means to wash or flush with rushing water: {They sluiced the deck clean}. Rain or other liquids may sluice down surfaces: {Water sluiced through the gutters}.

A sluicebox is a long, narrow trough used in mining to separate gold or other heavy minerals from gravel and sand. Water flows through the box, washing lighter material away while riffles along the bottom trap heavier particles. The device dates to the California Gold Rush and remains used by small-scale prospectors: {We set up the sluicebox in the creek and ran gravel through it all afternoon}.

A slum is a densely populated urban area marked by poverty, substandard housing, and inadequate sanitation. The word often appears in the plural: {the slums of Mumbai}, {growing up in the slums}. To slum or go slumming is to visit places or engage in activities considered beneath one's usual social standing, often with condescending curiosity: {slumming it at a dive bar}.

Slumber is a somewhat literary or gentle word for sleep, often suggesting peaceful, undisturbed rest. It works as both noun and verb: {The baby fell into a deep slumber}; {He slumbered through the afternoon}. Slumber carries a softer connotation than sleep, making it common in children's contexts like slumber parties—overnight gatherings where the actual sleeping is often minimal. Something dormant or inactive can also be said to slumber: {ancient volcanoes that slumber for centuries}.

Slumbering means sleeping, especially peacefully or for a long time. The word carries a gentler, more literary quality than sleeping: {the slumbering child}, {a slumbering village}. Figuratively, something slumbering lies dormant or inactive, waiting to be awakened: {slumbering resentments}, {a slumbering volcano}.

Slumberland is a fanciful name for the realm of sleep and dreams—an imaginary place one visits while sleeping. The word appears mainly in children's literature and lullabies: {Off to slumberland with you}. It suggests peaceful, dreamy sleep rather than restless nights. Sometimes used playfully for beds or bedrooms: {I'm heading to slumberland}.

Slumbers is the plural of slumber—periods of sleep, especially peaceful or prolonged rest. The word is literary and somewhat old-fashioned: {She was roused from her slumbers by a knock at the door}. As a verb, slumbers means sleeps: {The village slumbers while the night watch keeps guard}. Figuratively, something that slumbers lies dormant or inactive.

A slumlord is a landlord who owns rundown rental properties, typically in poor urban neighborhoods, and neglects maintenance while extracting maximum rent from tenants who have few housing alternatives.
