Squatting is crouching with knees bent and buttocks near the heels: {She was squatting by the fire}. In property law, squatting means occupying vacant land or buildings without permission or legal right. Squatters may gain certain rights through prolonged occupation in some jurisdictions. In weightlifting, squatting is performing squats—lowering the body while bearing a barbell across the shoulders.

Squawk is the harsh, abrupt cry of a bird—especially a startled or agitated one. By extension, people squawk when they complain loudly or protest: {Customers squawked about the price increase}. The word works as both verb and noun: {The parrot let out a squawk}. In aviation, a squawk is a transponder code assigned to aircraft for identification.

A squawkbox is an intercom or loudspeaker system, especially one used for announcements in offices, schools, or aircraft. The term suggests the tinny, harsh quality of the audio: {The pilot's voice crackled over the squawkbox}. In finance, squawkbox refers to a speaker system broadcasting real-time market commentary from brokers to trading desks.

Squawked is the past tense of squawk, meaning to make a loud, harsh, abrupt cry—the sound of a startled bird or an angry parrot. By extension, people squawk when they protest loudly or complain shrilly: {She squawked when she saw the bill}. A radio squawked if it crackled with sudden noise.

Squawking is the present participle of squawk, which means to make a loud, harsh, abrupt cry like that of a startled bird. People squawk when they complain loudly or protest noisily about something: {The customers were squawking about the price increase}. As a noun, squawking refers to this kind of noise or complaint. In aviation, squawking refers to an aircraft transmitting a specific identification code via its transponder.

Squawks is the plural of squawk, a harsh, abrupt cry like that of a startled bird. By extension, any sharp complaint or protest: {The new policy drew squawks from the staff}. As a verb form, squawks means to make such a sound or to complain loudly: {She squawks every time we change the schedule}.

A squeak is a short, high-pitched sound—the noise a mouse makes, or a door with rusty hinges, or sneakers on a gym floor. To squeak is to make such a sound, or to barely succeed: {She squeaked through the exam}. A {squeaky wheel gets the grease} means those who complain loudly get attention. A {narrow squeak} is a close call.

Squeaked is the past tense of squeak—to make a short, high-pitched sound. Mice squeak, hinges squeak, shoes squeak on polished floors. {The door squeaked when I opened it}. To squeak by or squeak through is to barely succeed: {She squeaked through the exam with a passing grade}.

A squeaker is something or someone that squeaks—a toy, a mouse, a person with a high-pitched voice. More commonly, squeaker describes a competition or contest won by the narrowest of margins: {The election was a squeaker, decided by fewer than a hundred votes.} In sports, a squeaker often refers to a game won by a single point or goal. The word captures both the tension of a close outcome and the relief of barely getting through.

Squeaking is producing or characterized by short, high-pitched sounds—the noise of mice, rusty hinges, or rubber soles on polished floors. Something squeaking by passes narrowly: {The bill squeaked through the legislature}. A squeaking wheel gets the grease—complaints get attention.

Squeaks are short, high-pitched sounds—the noise a mouse makes, a door hinge needs oiling, or sneakers on a gym floor. To squeak is to make such a sound, or to barely manage something: {We squeaked by with a one-point win}. A {squeaky wheel gets the grease}—those who complain loudest get attention. A {narrow squeak} is a close call.

Squeaky describes sounds that are high-pitched and slightly grating, like a rusty hinge or rubber sole on a floor: {The squeaky wheel gets the grease}. Something squeaky clean is spotlessly clean—so clean it squeaks when rubbed—or figuratively, free of any taint or scandal: {His record is squeaky clean}.

Squeal is a high-pitched, prolonged cry or sound—the noise a pig makes, or a child in excitement, or brakes that need replacing. To squeal is to make such a sound: {The tires squealed as the car took the corner}. In slang, to squeal is to inform on someone to authorities: {He squealed to the cops about the whole operation}.

Squealed is the past tense of squeal, meaning to make a high-pitched, prolonged cry or sound. Pigs squeal; so do brakes, tires, and excited children. Figuratively, to squeal is to inform on someone, especially to authorities: {He squealed to the cops about the whole operation}. {She squealed with delight when she saw the puppy}.

A squealer is someone who informs on others, especially to authorities—a tattletale or snitch: {The gang suspected there was a squealer among them}. The term comes from squeal in its slang sense of confessing or betraying secrets. More literally, a squealer is anything that squeals, particularly a young pig.

Squealing is making a high-pitched, prolonged sound—the noise of brakes, pigs, or excited children. The word often suggests involuntary or uncontrolled vocalization: {The tires were squealing as the car took the corner}. Informally, squealing means informing on someone to authorities: {He's squealing to the cops}.

Squeals is the plural of squeal—a high-pitched cry or sound, often expressing excitement, fear, or delight: {squeals of laughter from the children}, {the squeals of tires on pavement}. As a verb form, squeals means to make such sounds or, in slang, to inform on someone: {He squeals to the cops every time}.

Squeamish describes excessive sensitivity to unpleasant sights, smells, or ideas—particularly blood, gore, or bodily functions. A squeamish person might faint at the sight of a needle or turn away during surgery scenes in movies: {I'm too squeamish to watch}. The word extends to moral fastidiousness: {Don't be squeamish about asking for what you're owed}.

Squeamishness is excessive sensitivity to unpleasant sights, smells, or situations—the quality of being easily nauseated or disturbed. Someone with squeamishness about blood shouldn't become a surgeon. The word extends to moral fastidiousness: {His squeamishness about office politics held back his career}. It often carries a hint of judgment, suggesting the sensitivity is excessive or precious.
clues: Tendency to feel faint seeing blood

definition: Squee is an exclamation of intense excitement, delight, or glee—the kind of high-pitched noise someone might make when overwhelmed by something adorable or thrilling: {I saw the puppy and just went squee}. Common in internet culture and fandom contexts, it can also function as a noun or verb: {The announcement produced maximum squee}, {Fans squeeing over the trailer}.

A squeegee is a tool with a rubber blade on a handle, used to wipe liquid from a surface—cleaning windows, spreading ink across a silkscreen, or clearing water from a floor. The blade pushes liquid ahead of it rather than absorbing it. To squeegee is to clean or wipe with this tool: {He squeegeed the shower door after every use}.

Squeegees are tools with a rubber blade for wiping liquid from surfaces—typically a flat blade on a handle used to clean windows or spread ink across a silkscreen. The verb means to wipe with such a tool: {He squeegeed the shower door after every use}. At gas stations, squeegees sit in buckets of soapy water for cleaning windshields.

To squeeze is to apply pressure from two sides, or all around, like you might squeeze a lemon to extract juice. If you squeeze a person, you apply unwelcome pressure, perhaps as a demand for money. A squeeze is an instance of squeezing something tangible, or the result of being pressured. If you’re in a tight squeeze, you’re in a difficult position. To put the squeeze on someone is to pressure them. They will probably feel the squeeze when you do.

A squeezebox is any musical instrument that produces sound by compressing bellows to force air across reeds—accordions, concertinas, and bandoneons. The name captures the playing action: you squeeze the box to make music. {He pulled out the old squeezebox and played a polka.}

Squeezeboxes is the plural of squeezebox, an informal term for any handheld musical instrument that produces sound by compressing bellows while pressing buttons or keys—accordions, concertinas, and bandoneons. The name captures the essential action: you squeeze the box to make music. {He played polkas on an old squeezebox.}

Squeezed is the past tense of squeeze—to press firmly from opposite sides or to extract by pressing: {She squeezed his hand}, {He squeezed juice from the lemon}. Figuratively, squeezed describes pressure or constraint: {squeezed for time}, {squeezed out of the market}. A {squeezed middle} refers to people financially pressured from multiple directions.

Squeezes is the plural of squeeze and the third-person singular verb form. A squeeze applies pressure from opposite sides: {She squeezes the tube from the bottom}. A tight squeeze is a cramped space or narrow margin. In informal use, a squeeze is a romantic partner: {his main squeeze}. To {put the squeeze on} someone is to pressure them.

Squeezing is applying pressure from opposite sides, typically to compress, extract, or force through a narrow space. You squeeze an orange to get juice, squeeze toothpaste from a tube, or squeeze someone's hand in affection or reassurance. To squeeze into a tight space is to fit with difficulty: {We squeezed into the back seat}. A financial squeeze is pressure from limited resources.

Squelch captures the wet, sucking sound made when walking through mud or soggy ground, and by extension any act of forcefully suppressing or silencing something. If you squelch a rumor or squelch dissent, you crush it decisively. {She squelched through the marsh in her rubber boots.} {The CEO squelched speculation about layoffs.} In electronics, squelch refers to a circuit that suppresses background noise when no signal is present.

Squelching is making a wet, sucking sound—the noise of boots in mud, water in shoes, or walking across soggy ground: {We went squelching through the marsh}. The word imitates the sound it describes. Squelching also means suppressing or silencing forcefully: {The government squelched the uprising}, {She squelched his complaints with a look}.

Squelchy describes the soft, wet sound or sensation of walking through mud, soggy ground, or waterlogged material. The word is onomatopoeic—it sounds like what it describes: {My boots made squelchy noises crossing the marsh}. Something squelchy yields underfoot with a sucking, saturated quality: {the squelchy lawn after days of rain}.

A squib is a small firework that hisses and then pops—more noise than spectacle. By extension, a squib is any brief, pointed piece of writing: a short satirical paragraph, a filler item in a newspaper, a quick lampoon. In film, a squib is a small explosive charge used to simulate gunshot wounds. A {damp squib} is something that fails to produce the expected effect—like a firework that fizzles out.

Squibs are small fireworks that burn with a hissing sound before exploding. The term extends to brief satirical pieces or witty attacks in writing. In film and theater, squibs are small explosive devices hidden under clothing to simulate bullet impacts. A {damp squib} is something that fails to meet expectations—promising much but delivering little.

A squid is a marine mollusk with a torpedo-shaped body, eight arms, two longer tentacles, and the ability to squirt ink when threatened. Squid are eaten worldwide—fried calamari being the most familiar preparation. In slang, squid describes an inexperienced or reckless motorcyclist, typically one who rides without proper gear: {Some squid in shorts nearly wiped out on the highway}.

Squids are marine mollusks with elongated bodies, large eyes, eight arms, and two longer tentacles. They move by jet propulsion, squirting water through a siphon. Squid is also common seafood, often fried as calamari. In slang, a squid is an inexperienced or reckless motorcyclist: {Some squid in shorts and flip-flops nearly wiped out on the highway}.

A squiggle is a short, wavy or curly line, typically drawn carelessly or playfully: {The toddler's drawing was just a mess of squiggles}. Squiggles appear in doodles, signatures, and informal notation. The word suggests something without precise form—random, wiggly marks rather than deliberate shapes. As a verb, to squiggle is to make such marks or to move in a wriggling way.

Squiggles are irregular, wavy lines that twist and curve without pattern—the kind a child makes when scribbling, or that appear in someone's illegible handwriting. The word suggests playfulness or disorder: {The doctor's signature was just a series of squiggles}. To squiggle is to draw such lines or to move in a wriggling motion.

Squiggly describes lines or shapes that twist and curve irregularly, like a child's scribble or a worm's path: {squiggly handwriting}, {a squiggly line under the misspelled word}. The word suggests something playful or imprecise rather than geometric. In typography, the tilde (~) is sometimes called a squiggly.

A squillionaire is someone absurdly wealthy—richer than a billionaire, though the exact figure is deliberately vague. The word substitutes the nonsense prefix "squill-" for "bill-" or "mill-" to suggest wealth beyond ordinary comprehension: {Tech founders become squillionaires overnight}. Often used humorously or critically when discussing extreme wealth inequality.

To squint is to partially close the eyes, either to see more clearly in bright light or to focus on something distant or small: {She squinted at the tiny print}. A squint can also be a quick or furtive glance: {He took a squint at the document}. In medical contexts, squint refers to a condition where the eyes don't align properly—one eye turns inward or outward while the other looks straight ahead.

Squinting is partially closing the eyes, either to see more clearly in bright light or to focus on something distant or unclear: {She stood squinting into the sun}. People also squint when suspicious or skeptical, narrowing their eyes as if scrutinizing something: {He squinted at the contract before signing}.

Squints is the verb form of squint—to partially close the eyes, typically to see better or react to bright light: {She squints at the fine print}. A squint is also an informal term for a quick look: {Let me have a squint at that}. In British usage, squint can mean crooked or askew: {That picture frame is squint}.

Squinty describes eyes that are partially closed or narrowed, whether from bright light, poor vision, or suspicion. It can characterize a person's habitual expression or a particular look: {He gave me a squinty glare}. The word sometimes carries unflattering connotations, suggesting someone looks shifty or is straining to see.

A squire was historically a young nobleman serving a knight, training for knighthood himself. The term later came to mean a country gentleman or landowner, especially in rural England: {the village squire}. As a form of address, squire is informal and slightly old-fashioned, used between men: {What can I get you, squire?} To squire someone is to escort them, especially a woman to a social event.

Squires is the plural of squire, a word with historical and informal modern uses. In medieval times, a squire was a young man of noble birth who served a knight, often as an attendant and apprentice in training for knighthood himself. The term later came to designate a country gentleman or landowner, particularly in England. In informal use, squire persists as a friendly form of address between men, especially in British English: {All right, squire?}

Squirm is to twist and wriggle the body, especially from discomfort or restlessness: {The child squirmed in her seat}. The word extends to psychological discomfort—feeling uneasy or embarrassed: {He squirmed when asked about his past}. {The question made everyone squirm}.

Squirmed is the past tense of squirm, which means to twist and wriggle the body, typically from discomfort, embarrassment, or an attempt to escape restraint. A child squirms in a chair during a long lecture; someone squirms under pointed questioning. The word captures both physical movement and psychological unease—you can squirm without actually moving if you feel acutely uncomfortable. {He squirmed when his mother brought out the baby photos.}

Squirming is twisting and wriggling the body, typically from discomfort, restlessness, or an attempt to escape restraint. A child squirms in a dentist's chair; a fish squirms on a hook. Figuratively, squirming describes acute embarrassment or unease: {I was squirming through his entire speech}. The image is of someone who can't sit still under pressure.

Squirms is the third-person singular of squirm—to twist and wriggle the body, typically from discomfort or restlessness: {The child squirms in his seat}. Figuratively, to squirm is to feel acute embarrassment or unease: {She squirms whenever someone mentions the incident}. As a noun, squirms are instances of such movements.

Squirmy describes restless, wriggling movement—the kind of fidgeting that comes from discomfort, impatience, or an inability to sit still. Children are often squirmy during long car rides or boring events. The word can also characterize situations that make someone feel awkward or uneasy: {The interview got squirmy when they asked about my gap year}. Something squirmy might literally writhe, like a bucket of bait worms, or just make you want to look away.

A squirrel is a small, bushy-tailed rodent that climbs trees and hoards nuts. The verb means to hide or store away for future use: {She squirreled away money for emergencies}. To squirrel around is to move erratically or fidget restlessly. Squirrelly describes someone acting nervous, unpredictable, or slightly crazy.

Squirreling is the act of stashing things away for later, like a squirrel hiding nuts. The word usually implies accumulating small amounts over time: {She's been squirreling away money for years}. It can suggest hoarding or secretive saving. Also spelled squirrelling.

Squirrelly means restless, nervous, or unpredictable—like a squirrel's erratic movements. A squirrelly person is jumpy or behaves oddly: {He gets squirrelly when he hasn't had his coffee}. Something squirrelly seems off or suspicious: {The whole deal felt squirrelly}. Also spelled squirrely.

Squirrels is the plural of squirrel—small, bushy-tailed rodents that climb trees and hoard nuts. As a verb, to squirrel something away is to store or hide it for future use, like the animal caching food: {She squirreled away money for emergencies}. To squirrel around is to move in quick, erratic bursts.

Squirrely describes someone or something nervous, jumpy, or erratically unpredictable—like a squirrel's twitchy movements. A squirrely person might be jittery, evasive, or acting suspiciously: {He got squirrely when I asked about the money}. The word can also mean eccentric or slightly crazy: {That's a squirrely idea, but it might work}.

Squirt means to force liquid out in a thin stream or jet: {She squirted ketchup on her fries}, {Water squirted from the hose}. The liquid itself can squirt: {Juice squirted everywhere when I bit into the orange}. A squirt is an instance of squirting or the stream produced. Informally, squirt is a dismissive term for a small or insignificant person, especially a child: {Listen here, squirt}.

Squirting is the present participle of squirt—to eject liquid in a thin, forceful stream: {The ketchup bottle was squirting everywhere}. In sexual contexts, squirting refers to the expulsion of fluid from the vagina during orgasm or intense stimulation, a phenomenon that remains debated in its precise physiology but is widely depicted in pornography.

Squirts is the plural of squirt and the third-person singular present tense of the verb. A squirt is a thin stream of liquid forced out through a small opening, or the act of producing such a stream: {a few squirts of lemon juice}. To squirt is to eject liquid in this way. Squirt is also an informal, slightly dismissive term for a small or insignificant person, especially a child: {Listen here, squirt}.

Squish is to press or squeeze something soft so it deforms or flattens: {She squished the clay between her fingers}, {I accidentally squished a bug}. The word is onomatopoeic—it sounds like what it describes. As a noun, a squish is the act or sound of squishing: {the squish of wet shoes on linoleum}. Something squishy yields easily to pressure.

Squished is the past tense of squish, meaning pressed or crushed so that something flattens, deforms, or oozes: {The tomato got squished at the bottom of the grocery bag}. It suggests soft or yielding material compressed with some force. Squished also describes being packed tightly into a space: {We were all squished together in the back seat}.

Squishing is the act of pressing something soft until it deforms or flattens. The word captures both the action and often the sound—wet, yielding, satisfying: {I love squishing the mud between my toes}. Squishing suggests gentle, playful compression rather than destructive force: {She couldn't stop squishing the stress ball}.

Squishy describes something soft and yielding that compresses when squeezed: {a squishy stress ball}, {squishy mud between your toes}. The word suggests pliability and often moisture or give. Figuratively, squishy means vague or lacking rigor: {squishy logic}, {squishy on the details}. In political contexts, squishy describes someone whose positions seem soft or unreliable: {a squishy moderate}.

Sriracha is a hot sauce made from chili peppers, vinegar, garlic, sugar, and salt. The name comes from a coastal Thai city, though the sauce is now most associated with the American brand featuring a rooster on the bottle. Sriracha has become a ubiquitous condiment, added to everything from eggs to ramen to pizza: {I put sriracha on everything}.

Stab is a verb and noun centered on the sudden piercing of something with a pointed object, typically a knife or blade. A stabbing is usually a violent attack, but the word extends to any sharp, sudden motion or sensation: a stab of {pain}, a stab of {guilt}. If you take a stab at something, you make an attempt at it without much preparation or confidence. To stab someone in the back is to betray them, especially while pretending friendship.

Stabbed is the past tense of stab—to pierce or wound with a pointed weapon, typically a knife: {He was stabbed in the chest}. Figuratively, a sharp sudden pain stabs: {Pain stabbed through her shoulder}. To be {stabbed in the back} is to be betrayed by someone trusted. {She stabbed at the salad with her fork.}

Stabbing describes a sharp, sudden, piercing sensation or action. As an adjective, it most often modifies pain: {a stabbing pain in my chest} suggests something intense and localized, as if caused by a knife. The noun stabbing refers to an attack in which someone is wounded or killed with a pointed weapon. The word carries violence in both uses—whether literal assault or the figurative assault of acute physical discomfort.

Stabbings is the plural of stabbing—acts of piercing someone with a pointed weapon, typically a knife. The word appears most often in news reports about violent crime: {Three stabbings occurred downtown last night}. A stabbing can be fatal or survivable, intentional or accidental.

Stabby describes a mood of irritable aggression—the urge to stab something, though not literally. It's informal slang for feeling hostile or on edge: {I haven't had my coffee yet and I'm feeling stabby}. The word can also describe something that pokes or jabs: {a stabby cactus}, {stabby heels on hardwood floors}.

Stabilise is the British spelling of stabilize. To stabilise something is to make it steady or keep it from changing: {The doctor worked to stabilise the patient's condition}. Economies stabilise after turbulent periods. A stabiliser helps maintain balance or consistency—chemicals that preserve food, devices that steady cameras, or fins that keep ships upright.

Stability is the quality of being stable—steady, firm, not easily changed or disturbed. Physical stability keeps structures standing and objects balanced: {The table lacks stability on uneven ground}. Emotional or mental stability suggests consistent, reliable temperament. Financial stability means secure resources. Political stability implies enduring governance without upheaval. In science, stability describes systems that resist change or return to equilibrium after disturbance.

Stabilization is the process of making something stable—preventing fluctuation, collapse, or deterioration. Economic stabilization aims to control inflation or unemployment. Medical stabilization keeps a patient's condition from worsening: {The paramedics focused on stabilization before transport}. In engineering, stabilization prevents structural movement or soil erosion. The word implies bringing something volatile or precarious into a steady state.

Stabilize means to make or become stable—to steady something that was fluctuating, wavering, or at risk of collapse. Doctors work to stabilize patients in critical condition. Governments stabilize currencies. A relationship stabilizes after a rocky period. The word implies bringing something to a state of equilibrium where it can hold its position: {Her condition has stabilized}.

Stabilized describes something that has been made stable or steady after a period of change or uncertainty. A patient's condition stabilizes when vital signs stop fluctuating. Markets stabilize after volatility. {The medication stabilized her mood}. In technical contexts, stabilized refers to substances treated to prevent deterioration or equipment fitted with devices to reduce unwanted movement: {stabilized camera footage}, {stabilized fuel}.

A stabilizer is something that keeps another thing steady or prevents unwanted change. Aircraft have stabilizers—horizontal and vertical surfaces that maintain flight attitude. Food stabilizers are additives that prevent separation or degradation: {The ice cream contains stabilizers to improve texture}. A mood stabilizer is medication that evens out emotional swings. In photography, a stabilizer reduces camera shake. The spelling stabiliser appears in British English.

Stabilizers are devices or substances that keep something steady or prevent unwanted change. On aircraft, stabilizers are the horizontal and vertical tail surfaces that maintain stable flight. In food chemistry, stabilizers are additives that preserve texture and prevent separation: {The ice cream contains stabilizers to keep it smooth}. Training wheels on a bicycle are sometimes called stabilizers, especially in British English. In any context, stabilizers counteract forces that would otherwise cause instability.

Stable describes something firmly established and resistant to change or disruption. A stable {structure} won't collapse; a stable {relationship} endures; a stable {patient} isn't getting worse. The word implies reliability and equilibrium. As a noun, a stable is a building where horses are kept. To stable a horse is to house it there. A stable of something—{athletes}, {writers}, {products}—is a group under common management.

A stableboy is a young male worker who tends to horses in a stable, handling tasks like feeding, grooming, mucking out stalls, and exercising the animals. The term evokes an earlier era when horses were essential for transportation and agriculture, though stableboys still work at racing facilities, riding schools, and equestrian estates today. The job is entry-level, often performed by teenagers or young men learning horsemanship from the ground up.

A stablecoin is a cryptocurrency designed to maintain a fixed value, typically pegged to a traditional currency like the US dollar. Unlike Bitcoin or Ethereum, which fluctuate wildly, stablecoins aim for price stability—useful for transactions, savings, or as a safe harbor during market volatility. Most are backed by reserves of the pegged currency, though some use algorithmic mechanisms to maintain their peg.

Stablecoins are cryptocurrencies designed to maintain a fixed value, typically pegged to a conventional currency like the US dollar. Unlike Bitcoin or Ethereum, which fluctuate wildly, stablecoins aim for price stability—making them useful for trading, transfers, and as a store of value within crypto markets. Most are backed by reserves of the pegged currency, though some use algorithms to maintain their peg.

A stablemate is a horse from the same stable as another, trained by the same owner or trainer. The term extends to any person or thing from the same organization or source: {The sedan and its sportier stablemate share the same engine}. Colleagues at the same company, athletes on the same team, or products from the same manufacturer can all be stablemates.

Stablemates are horses housed in the same stable, especially racehorses trained by the same person. The term extends to people or things from the same source—athletes on the same team, products from the same company, or artists on the same record label: {The two singers are stablemates at Atlantic Records}. When stablemates compete against each other, there's often speculation about whether one will defer to the other.

Stables is a building or complex where horses are housed, fed, and cared for. The word often appears as a singular noun despite its plural form: {The stables burned down last night}. A racing stable is a collection of horses under one trainer's management. To stable a horse is to keep it in such a facility.

Stabs is the plural of stab and the third-person singular verb form. A stab is a thrust with a pointed weapon or object, or the wound it produces: {multiple stab wounds}. Figuratively, a stab is a sudden sharp sensation: {a stab of pain}, {a stab of guilt}. To {take a stab at} something is to attempt it: {I'll take a stab at fixing it}. A {stab in the back} is a betrayal. To stab is to pierce or thrust: {He stabbed the meat with his fork}.

Staccato describes sounds that are short, sharp, and detached from one another. In music, staccato notes are played crisply, with clear separation between them—the opposite of legato. The term extends to any clipped, abrupt manner of speaking or any rapid succession of distinct sounds: {staccato bursts of gunfire}, {She spoke in staccato sentences}.

A stack is an orderly pile, typically higher than it is wide. A tall chimney can be called a stack or smokestack. In computing, the stack is the part of memory where new things are added on top of the last thing put there. If you blow your stack, you lose your temper. To stack items is to put them in a stack. Stacking chairs are designed to be stacked up when stored. If something is stacked against you, you are at a disadvantage.

Stacked describes things arranged in a pile or layers: {stacked boxes}, {stacked pancakes}. In slang, stacked means having large breasts—the image is of a woman whose chest sticks out in front. To say the deck is stacked or the odds are stacked against you means circumstances have been arranged to favor one side unfairly. In gaming and sports, a stacked team or lineup is loaded with talent.

A stacker is a person or machine that stacks things—arranging items in piles or layers. In warehouses and factories, stackers are forklifts or automated equipment that move and stack pallets or materials. A person who stocks shelves or organizes inventory may be called a stacker. In gambling slang, a stacker is someone who secretly arranges a deck of cards to cheat.

Stacking is arranging things in a pile, one atop another: {stacking boxes}, {stacking firewood}. The term extends to any layered accumulation—stacking advantages, stacking the odds. In gaming, stacking often means combining multiple bonuses or effects: {The buffs don't stack}. To {stack the deck} is to arrange cards dishonestly, or more broadly, to rig an outcome.

Stacks are things piled one atop another: a stack of {books}, a stack of {pancakes}, a stack of {bills}. A smokestack releases exhaust vertically. Library stacks are shelving areas. In computing, a stack is a data structure where the last item added is the first removed. In slang, stacks means large amounts of money: {He's got stacks}. To be stacked against someone means circumstances favor their opponent.

A stadium is a large outdoor venue for sporting events and concerts, typically oval or horseshoe-shaped with tiered seating surrounding a central field or stage. The word comes from an ancient Greek unit of distance—about 600 feet—which became the name for the track where footraces were held. Modern stadiums seat tens of thousands: {The stadium was packed for the championship game}.

Stadiums is the plural of stadium, a large venue with tiered seating surrounding a field or stage for sporting events, concerts, or other spectacles: {The city built two new stadiums for the Olympics}. The Latin plural stadia appears occasionally in formal or technical contexts but sounds pretentious in everyday speech.

Staff has two core meanings. One is a long stick used as a walking aid, weapon, or symbol of authority—a shepherd's staff, a wizard's staff, the staff of office. The other meaning is the people employed by an organization: {The staff meets every Monday}. As a verb, to staff is to provide workers: {We need to staff the front desk}. In music, a staff is the set of five horizontal lines on which notes are written.

A staffer is a member of a staff—someone employed by an organization, especially in a support or administrative role. The word appears most often in journalism and politics: {White House staffers}, {campaign staffers}, {congressional staffers}. It distinguishes employees from principals, executives, or elected officials they serve.

Staffers are the people who work for an organization, especially in support roles rather than leadership positions. The term appears most often in journalism and political contexts: {White House staffers briefed reporters on the new policy}. It carries a slightly informal tone compared to staff members or employees, and implies people who are part of a larger team rather than independent operators.

Staffing is the process of hiring and assigning personnel to fill positions in an organization. It covers recruiting, selecting, and placing employees where they're needed: {The company's staffing needs have doubled since last year}. A staffing agency connects employers with workers, often for temporary or contract positions. As an adjective, staffing describes resources devoted to personnel: {staffing levels}, {staffing budget}, {staffing shortages}.

A stag is an adult male deer, especially a red deer. The word extends to men-only gatherings: a stag {party} or stag {night} celebrates a groom before his wedding. To go stag is to attend an event without a date: {He went stag to the prom}. In finance, a stag buys new share offerings hoping to sell quickly at a profit.

A stage is a raised platform where performances occur—theatrical shows, speeches, concerts. By extension, the stage means the theater as a profession: {She's been on the stage for twenty years}. Stage also means a point in a process or development: {the early stages of pregnancy}, {a stage of grief}. To stage something is to produce it for an audience or to arrange it for effect: {stage a play}, {stage a protest}, {stage a photo op}. A stagecoach was a horse-drawn vehicle traveling in stages between stations.

A stagecoach is a large horse-drawn carriage that historically carried passengers and mail along established routes, stopping at stations to change horses. The stage in the name refers to these segments of the journey. {The stagecoach arrived at noon, covered in dust from the trail.} The word evokes the American West and an era before railroads.

Stagecoaches were horse-drawn passenger vehicles that traveled scheduled routes between towns, the primary means of long-distance land travel before railroads. The name refers to traveling in stages—stops where fresh horses replaced tired ones. {The stagecoach arrived twice weekly carrying mail and passengers.} Stagecoach robberies became iconic in Western lore.

Stagecraft is the art and technique of theatrical production—the practical skills involved in mounting a play or performance. This includes set design, lighting, sound, costumes, and the mechanics of scene changes. The term extends to any skilled management of presentation: {a politician known for stagecraft}, {The CEO's stagecraft kept investors calm during the crisis}.

Staged describes something arranged or performed rather than occurring naturally or spontaneously. A staged {photograph} is posed rather than candid. A staged {robbery} is faked, meant to deceive. In theater, a staged {production} has been mounted for performance. The word often implies artifice or manipulation: {The whole confrontation looked staged for the cameras}.

A stagedive is the act of jumping from a concert stage into the crowd below, trusting the audience to catch you. Associated with punk and rock shows, it's both a performer's gesture of abandon and a fan's act of participation. To stagedive is to make such a leap: {He stagedived during the encore and the crowd carried him to the back}.

Stagediving is leaping from a concert stage into the crowd below, trusting the audience to catch you and pass you along on raised hands. It's a ritual of punk and metal shows, equal parts performer bravado and audience participation: {The singer went stagediving during the encore}. Security guards generally disapprove.

Stagefright is the nervous anxiety that grips performers before or during an appearance—the racing heart, sweaty palms, and mental blankness that come from facing an audience. The condition affects even experienced performers: {She's done a hundred shows but still gets stagefright}. Also spelled as two words: stage fright.

A stagehand is a person who works backstage in a theater, concert venue, or film set, handling scenery, props, lighting equipment, and other technical elements of a production. Stagehands set up before performances, manage scene changes during shows, and strike the set afterward: {The stagehands worked through the night to prepare for opening night}.

Stagehands are the workers who handle scenery, props, lighting, and other technical elements during theatrical productions or live events. They move set pieces between scenes, manage curtains, and ensure smooth transitions—essential but typically unseen by the audience. {The stagehands struck the set after closing night.}

Stages are distinct phases in a process or development: the stages of grief, stages of cancer, stages of a rocket. A stage is also a raised platform where performances occur—actors on a stage, a concert stage. To stage something is to arrange or present it: stage a play, stage a protest, stage a comeback. The stage refers to the acting profession: {She's been on the stage for thirty years}. In compounds, stage appears in stagecoach (a horse-drawn vehicle making scheduled stops) and stage fright (nervousness before performing).

Stagestruck describes someone captivated by the theater and eager to become an actor. The condition typically afflicts young people who dream of performing: {She's been stagestruck ever since her first school play}. The word carries a faintly patronizing tone, suggesting naive infatuation rather than serious ambition.

Stagflation is an economic condition combining stagnant growth, high unemployment, and persistent inflation—a troublesome combination because the usual remedies for inflation tend to worsen unemployment and vice versa. The term emerged in the 1970s when oil shocks produced exactly this scenario in Western economies: {The Fed struggled to address stagflation without making either problem worse}.

Stagger captures the idea of unsteady, lurching movement—the way someone walks when drunk, injured, or overwhelmed. {He staggered out of the bar at closing time.} By extension, if news or a revelation staggers you, it throws you off balance mentally. The verb also means to arrange things in an alternating or overlapping pattern: {staggered work shifts}, {staggered seating}. As a noun, stagger refers to an unsteady gait or, in the plural staggers, a disease affecting livestock that causes them to walk erratically.

Staggered describes things arranged in alternating positions or times rather than aligned. Staggered seating places each row offset from the one ahead for better sightlines. Staggered work hours spread arrivals across time. As the past tense of stagger, it means walked unsteadily or was shocked: {She staggered under the weight}; {I was staggered by the news}.
clues: Arranged in an alternating offset pattern

definition: Staggering describes something so extreme it makes you figuratively lose your balance. A staggering {sum} or staggering {loss} is hard to comprehend. Staggering {incompetence} leaves you reeling. The word intensifies scale, whether of achievement, failure, or sheer quantity: {The staggering cost of the project forced them to reconsider}.

Staging is the process of preparing or arranging something for presentation or use. In theater, staging is how a production is put on—the blocking, sets, and visual elements that bring a script to life. The word extends to any deliberate arrangement: {the staging of a photo op}, {the staging of troops before an invasion}. In real estate, staging means furnishing a home to make it more appealing to buyers. In medicine and oncology, staging determines how far a disease has progressed: {The cancer staging showed it hadn't spread}. In computing, a staging environment is where software is tested before going live.

Stagnant describes water or air that doesn't flow or circulate, becoming foul or stale: {a stagnant pond}, {stagnant air in the basement}. The meaning extends to anything showing no activity, growth, or development: {stagnant wages}, {a stagnant economy}, {His career had grown stagnant}. The word implies not just stillness but deterioration from lack of movement.
clues: Water that sits and grows foul

definition: Stagnate means to stop moving or developing. Water that stagnates becomes foul from lack of circulation. A career stagnates when advancement ceases. An economy stagnates when growth flatlines. The word implies not just stillness but deterioration through inactivity: {Sales have stagnated for months}. What doesn't flow forward tends to decay.

Stagnating describes a state of not moving, growing, or developing. Water that is stagnating has stopped flowing and often becomes foul or stale. The word applies more often to abstractions: a stagnating economy shows no growth, a stagnating career goes nowhere, and stagnating wages fail to keep pace with inflation. {The project has been stagnating for months while we wait for approval.} The implication is always negative—something that should be progressing has come to a standstill.

Stagnation is the condition of not moving, growing, or developing. Water that doesn't flow becomes stagnant; economies and careers can similarly stagnate. {The company fell into stagnation after years without innovation.} The word carries negative connotations—stillness where movement is expected or needed.

Stags is the plural of stag—male deer, especially red deer. The word extends to men attending social events without female companions: {a stags-only poker night}. Stag parties (or stag dos in British English) are pre-wedding celebrations for the groom. In finance, stags are speculators who buy new share issues hoping to sell immediately at profit.

A stain is a discoloration left by a substance that has soaked into a surface: {a coffee stain on the carpet}, {grass stains on her jeans}. The verb means to leave such a mark, or to color deliberately with dye or pigment: {stain the deck}. Figuratively, a stain is something that damages reputation or character: {a stain on his honor}. Stainless steel resists corrosion; a stainless record has no blemishes.

Stained describes something marked or discolored by a substance that has penetrated its surface: {a stained tablecloth}, {coffee-stained teeth}. The word extends to reputation or character—a stained {record} or stained {honor} carries the mark of past wrongdoing. Stained {glass} is colored during manufacture, not damaged, though the word is the same.

Staining is the process of applying color or leaving marks on a surface. Wood staining adds color while preserving grain. In microscopy, staining makes cell structures visible: {The lab tech is staining the tissue samples}. Staining also refers to leaving unwanted marks: {The berries are staining your fingers}. Figuratively, staining means tainting reputation: {allegations staining his career}.

Stainless means without stains or blemishes. A stainless {reputation} is unblemished. Stainless {steel} is an alloy resistant to rust and corrosion—so common that stainless alone often means stainless steel: {The kitchen has stainless appliances}. The word emphasizes purity or durability: {a stainless record of service}.

Stains are marks or discolorations left on a surface, typically from spilled liquids or contact with substances that penetrate or bond with the material: {coffee stains on the carpet}, {grass stains on jeans}. To stain is to leave such a mark, or to apply coloring deliberately: {stain the deck}. Figuratively, a stain is a blemish on reputation or character: {a stain on his record}.

A stair is one of a series of steps for moving between levels. Stairs usually refers to the whole set: {Take the stairs to the second floor}. A staircase or stairway is the structure containing them. {Stair} alone sometimes means the full flight: {the back stair}, {below stairs}.

A staircase is a set of stairs together with its surrounding structure—the walls, railings, and supporting framework that form a complete unit: {a spiral staircase}, {the grand staircase in the hotel lobby}. Where stairs refers to the steps themselves, staircase emphasizes the architectural whole.

Staircases are structures of steps connecting different levels of a building. A staircase includes not just the stairs themselves but the surrounding framework—railings, banisters, and the space they occupy. Grand staircases serve as architectural focal points in mansions and public buildings. {The spiral staircase led to the attic.}

Stairs are a series of steps that allow people to move between different levels of a building or structure. Each individual step is called a stair, though the singular form appears mainly in compounds like {staircase} and {stairwell}. The phrase {up the stairs} or {down the stairs} indicates direction of travel. To {take the stairs} means to walk rather than use an elevator or escalator.

A stairway is a set of stairs providing passage between floors or levels of a building. It includes the steps themselves along with any railings, landings, or enclosing walls. The term is roughly interchangeable with staircase, though stairway more often suggests the passage itself rather than the architectural structure: {The stairway to the basement was dark and narrow}.

A stairwell is the vertical shaft or enclosed space containing a staircase in a building. The term emphasizes the architectural cavity rather than the stairs themselves: {The fire alarm sent everyone rushing to the stairwell}. In emergencies, stairwells serve as evacuation routes when elevators shut down.

A stairwell is the vertical shaft in a building that contains a staircase. The term emphasizes the enclosed space rather than the stairs themselves—the area between floors where the staircase rises. Stairwells in apartment buildings and office towers often double as emergency exits: {She took the stairwell down to avoid the crowded elevator}.

A stake is a pointed piece of wood or metal driven into the ground—for support, boundary marking, or tying something to. To stake a plant is to secure it upright. To stake a claim is to assert ownership, from the practice of marking land boundaries. Stakes are also what you wager in a bet or risk in an enterprise: {The stakes are too high}. When the stakes are raised, more is at risk. To have a stake in something is to have an interest in its outcome. To stake someone is to provide them with money or resources: {She staked him to a new set of tools}.

Staked is the past tense of stake, carrying forward its meanings. Something staked has been fastened with a stake: {The tomato plants were staked and tied}. Money or reputation staked has been wagered or risked: {She staked her career on the project's success}. To have staked a claim is to have asserted ownership or interest: {He staked his claim to the corner office}. In vampire lore, a staked vampire has been killed by a stake through the heart. In cryptocurrency, staked coins have been committed to a network to earn rewards.

A stakeholder is anyone with an interest in how something turns out. In business, stakeholders include shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, and the surrounding community—anyone affected by a company's decisions. The term has spread to any project or initiative: {We need to consult all stakeholders before moving forward}. Originally, a stakeholder held the stakes in a bet or wager until the outcome was decided.

Stakeholders are people or groups with an interest in something's outcome—a project, decision, or organization. The term comes from someone holding stakes in a bet, but now dominates business and policy language: {We need to consult all stakeholders before proceeding}. Stakeholders may include employees, investors, customers, communities, or anyone affected by an entity's actions. The word often signals inclusive decision-making, though critics find it vague corporate jargon.

A stakeout is a period of covert surveillance, typically by police watching a location for criminal activity: {We've had a stakeout on the warehouse for three days}. The term comes from the idea of staking out territory—claiming a position and holding it. By extension, any patient waiting and watching: {Her stakeout of the sale rack finally paid off}.

Stakeouts are periods of covert surveillance, typically by law enforcement watching a location for criminal activity or waiting for a suspect to appear: {The detectives spent three nights on stakeout outside the warehouse}. The term evokes long hours in parked cars with coffee and binoculars. Extended to any patient watching and waiting: {Her stakeout of the mailbox finally paid off when the letter arrived}.

Stakes are what you stand to win or lose. In gambling, stakes are the money wagered: {high-stakes poker}, {The stakes are $100 per hand}. More broadly, stakes are what's at risk in any venture or conflict: {The stakes couldn't be higher—if we fail, the company folds}. Stakes also means pointed posts driven into the ground, from which the gambling sense derives—wagers were once placed on or near a stake marking the finish line.

Staking is the act of marking or claiming territory with stakes, or of supporting something—usually a plant—by tying it to a stake: {staking tomatoes}. To stake out a location is to watch it covertly: {The detectives spent weeks staking out the warehouse}. In gambling and investment, staking means putting up money: {She's staking her savings on this venture}. In cryptocurrency, staking refers to locking up coins to support a blockchain network and earn rewards.

A stalactite is a mineral formation that hangs from the ceiling of a cave, created over thousands of years as water drips through rock and deposits dissolved minerals. Stalactites grow downward like icicles: {The cave was filled with stalactites glistening in the lamplight}. The companion formation growing upward from the floor is a stalagmite.

Stalactites are mineral formations that hang from cave ceilings, created over thousands of years as water drips through rock and deposits dissolved minerals. They grow downward like stone icicles: {The flashlight revealed stalactites covering the cavern roof}. The matching formations that grow upward from cave floors are stalagmites—stalactites hang tight to the ceiling.

A stalag was a German prisoner-of-war camp for enlisted military personnel during World War II. The word is a German abbreviation for Stammlager, meaning main camp. Stalags held millions of Allied prisoners under conditions ranging from harsh to brutal: {His grandfather spent two years in a stalag after being captured at Dunkirk}.

A stalagmite is a cone-shaped mineral deposit that rises from the floor of a cave, formed by the slow dripping of mineral-rich water from above. Stalagmites grow upward, while their counterparts stalactites hang downward from the ceiling. When they meet, they form a column.

Stalagmites are cone-shaped mineral formations that rise from the floor of caves, built up over millennia by dripping water depositing dissolved limestone. They grow upward from the ground, unlike stalactites, which hang from above. When the two meet, they form a column. {The cave tour wound past massive stalagmites taller than a person.}

Stale characterizes negative qualities that arise when something is no longer fresh or new. Stale bread is hard and dry. Stale ideas or news are familiar, known, and offer nothing interesting. Stale things smell or taste unpleasant. The infrequent verb stale means become stale.

Stalemate is a position in chess where the player to move has no legal moves but is not in check—the game ends in a draw. By extension, stalemate describes any deadlock or impasse where neither side can advance: {Contract negotiations reached a stalemate}. The verb means to bring to such a standstill: {The opposing factions stalemated each other}.

Stalemates is the plural of stalemate, a situation where neither side can advance or win. The term comes from chess, where a player not in check has no legal move—the game ends in a draw. More broadly, stalemates are deadlocks or impasses: {The negotiations reached stalemates on several key issues}. As a verb, stalemates means brings to such a standstill.

Staleness is the condition of being stale—no longer fresh. Bread loses its softness, air grows stagnant, jokes lose their humor. The word extends naturally to anything that has lost vitality through age or overuse: {the staleness of their marriage}, {the staleness of recycled talking points}. In chess, staleness appears in stalemate—a drawn position where no fresh moves remain.

definition: Stalk names the stem or main axis of a plant, or any slender supporting structure. Eyes may be on stalks, as with crabs. To stalk is to pursue prey or a person stealthily and persistently; a predator stalks its quarry, and someone obsessively following another person is a stalker engaged in stalking. {She noticed someone had been stalking her social media profiles.} To stalk can also mean to walk stiffly with long strides, often conveying anger or indignation: {He stalked out of the room without a word.}

Stalked describes something that has a stalk—a stem or supporting structure: {stalked celery}, {stalked eyes} on a crab. Separately, stalked is the past tense of stalk: to pursue stealthily or obsessively. A hunter stalked deer through the forest. {She was stalked by an ex-boyfriend for months.} The two words share a spelling but have different origins.

A stalker is someone who pursues another person obsessively and uninvited—following them, monitoring their movements, or repeatedly contacting them despite clear signals to stop. The term carries criminal connotations: {She got a restraining order against her stalker}. More casually, stalker describes someone who monitors another's social media with unusual intensity: {I'm not a stalker, I just looked at his Instagram}. The verb is stalk.

Stalkers are people who pursue or follow others obsessively, often with unwanted and threatening attention. The term applies to wildlife photographers who stalk game, but more commonly describes those who harass, surveil, or fixate on a person—especially celebrities or former romantic partners: {Her stalkers showed up at every public appearance}. In video games, stalker may name an enemy type that hunts the player.

Stalkerware is software secretly installed on someone's device to monitor their activity—tracking location, reading messages, recording calls, or capturing keystrokes. Unlike legitimate parental controls or employee monitoring tools, stalkerware operates covertly and is typically used by abusive partners, jealous spouses, or controlling family members: {Her ex had installed stalkerware on her phone}. Also called spyware or spouseware.

Stalking is the act of pursuing someone persistently and obsessively, typically in a way that causes fear or distress. A stalker may follow, watch, or repeatedly contact their victim, often despite being told to stop. The word also has an older, neutral sense: to stalk game is to approach prey stealthily while hunting. {She filed a restraining order against the man who had been stalking her.} {The lion was stalking a gazelle through the tall grass.}

Stalks is the plural of stalk, which has two distinct meanings from different origins. One stalk is the main stem of a plant, or a slender supporting structure: {celery stalks}, {the stalk of a wineglass}. The other stalk is a verb meaning to pursue prey or a person stealthily, often with sinister intent: {The detective stalked the suspect for weeks}. A person who stalks another obsessively and threateningly is a stalker. To stalk can also mean to walk stiffly or haughtily: {She stalked out of the room in anger}.

One set of meanings of stall can be remembered with reference to install. A stall is a compartment designed to hold something, such as an animal in a barn, the wares of a seller at a market, or a single toilet in a public bathroom. Another use of stall has to do with delay, often intentional. If a process stalls, it stops moving forward. If a person stalls, they deliberately avoid making progress. A stall is an instance of stalling. If an aircraft goes into a stall, it loses lift.

Stalled describes something that has stopped making progress or come to a halt. An engine stalls when it dies unexpectedly. Negotiations stall when they reach an impasse: {Peace talks have stalled over territorial disputes}. A stalled car blocks traffic; a stalled project sits unfinished. The word implies an interruption that wasn't planned—something should be moving but isn't.

Stalling is delaying or buying time, often to avoid commitment or confrontation: {Quit stalling and give me an answer}. The word comes from stall, where an engine loses power and stops—so stalling can mean that mechanical failure, or the deliberate act of causing it: {The plane kept stalling on takeoff}. In negotiations or conversations, stalling is a tactic: {He's just stalling until his lawyer arrives}.

definition: A stallion is an adult male horse that has not been castrated, kept especially for breeding. The word implies strength, vigor, and sexual potency. Informally, stallion describes a man considered sexually attractive or virile: {He thinks he's quite the stallion}.

Stallions are adult male horses that have not been castrated. The term emphasizes the animal's breeding capacity and often connotes power, vigor, or sexual potency. A man called a stallion is being compared to such a horse—strong, virile, sexually impressive: {He thinks he's a real stallion}.

Stalls are individual compartments or booths—spaces partitioned off for a specific purpose. A horse stall houses one animal. A bathroom stall provides privacy. Market stalls are vendor booths. In British usage, the stalls are ground-floor theater seats. As a verb, to stall is to stop progress or delay: an engine stalls when it cuts out unexpectedly; a person stalls when buying time. {She stalled for time while her partner escaped.}

Stalwart describes someone or something loyal, reliable, and unwavering in support or commitment: {a stalwart defender of free speech}, {stalwart allies}. The word also implies physical or moral strength—a stalwart figure is sturdy and resolute. As a noun, a stalwart is a loyal, hardworking supporter: {party stalwarts turned out for the rally}.

Stalwarts are loyal, reliable supporters—people who can be counted on through difficulty or over time. The word often describes committed members of a political party or organization: {party stalwarts}, {stalwarts of the movement}. A stalwart is dependable in a sturdy, unglamorous way—not flashy, but steadfast.

Stamina is the capacity to sustain prolonged physical or mental effort. Athletes build stamina through training; difficult tasks require stamina to complete. The word implies endurance over time rather than burst strength: {She had the stamina to run marathons}, {The job interview tested my stamina}.

To stammer is to speak with involuntary pauses and repetitions, often from nervousness or a speech disorder: {He stammered through his wedding vows}. A stammer is the condition itself or an instance of it: {She has a slight stammer}. Unlike a stutter, which repeats sounds, a stammer suggests halting, blocked speech—though the words often overlap.

Stammered is the past tense of stammer, meaning to speak with involuntary pauses or repetitions, typically from nervousness, excitement, or a speech impediment: {She stammered an apology}. Unlike a deliberate pause, stammering suggests loss of verbal control. The word often appears in dialogue attribution to convey a character's emotional state: {"I—I didn't mean to," he stammered}.

Stammering is speaking with involuntary pauses, repetitions, or prolonged sounds—the same condition Americans usually call stuttering. British English favors stammering. The word also describes halting or uncertain speech from nervousness or confusion: {She gave a stammering apology}. As a noun, it names the condition itself: {His stammering worsened under pressure}.

Stammers is the verb stammer in the third person singular, describing speech marked by involuntary pauses and repetitions of sounds. Someone who stammers struggles to get words out smoothly: {He stammers when nervous}. A stammer differs from a stutter mainly in regional preference—British English favors stammer, American English stutter. As a noun, stammers are instances of such halting speech.

A stamp is a small adhesive label affixed to mail indicating postage has been paid, or a device for impressing a mark on a surface: {a rubber stamp}, {a date stamp}. To stamp is to bring the foot down forcefully: {She stamped her feet in frustration}. To stamp something out is to extinguish or eradicate it: {efforts to stamp out corruption}. A stamp of approval signals official endorsement. Something that bears someone's stamp shows their characteristic influence or style.

Stamped describes something marked or impressed with a design, seal, or official mark: {a stamped envelope}, {stamped approval}. It also means crushed or flattened by forceful stepping: {stamped out the fire}. A stamped {passport} bears official entry marks. {Stamped on my memory} means permanently impressed there. To be {stamped with} a quality is to display it unmistakably.

A stampede is a sudden, panicked rush of animals or people fleeing or charging together. Cattle stampedes were a danger on Western cattle drives; a loud noise could set the herd running. The word extends to any headlong mass movement: {a stampede for the exits}, {a stampede of investors dumping stocks}. As a verb, to stampede is to rush in panic or to cause such a rush: {Don't let them stampede you into a decision}.

Stampedes is the plural of stampede—a sudden, panicked rush of animals or people moving as a mass. Cattle stampede when spooked; crowds stampede toward exits during emergencies. Figuratively, a stampede describes any headlong rush: {a stampede of investors fleeing the market}. The verb means to cause or join such a rush: {Don't let them stampede you into a decision}.

Stampeding is a present participle of stampede, describing the act of rushing headlong in a panicked mass. Cattle stampede when spooked; crowds stampede toward exits in emergencies. The word captures both the collective nature and the loss of individual control: {The fans were stampeding toward the stage}. Figuratively, to be stampeded into something is to be pressured into hasty action.

Stamping is the act of bringing a foot down forcefully, usually to express frustration or make noise: {The child went stamping off to her room}. It also refers to the industrial process of pressing or cutting material with a die: {metal stamping}, {stamping out parts}. A stamping ground is a place someone frequents—their usual haunt.

Stamps are small adhesive labels affixed to mail indicating postage has been paid, or official marks impressed on documents. To stamp is to bring one's foot down forcefully, or to impress a mark: {She stamped her foot in frustration}. Stamps also designate tools that impress marks or cut shapes. Figuratively, something that {stamps} a person or thing leaves a defining mark: {The experience stamped him forever}.

A stan is an extremely devoted fan, often to the point of obsession. The term originated from Eminem's 2000 song about a fan whose obsession turns deadly. To stan is to support someone or something with intense, unwavering enthusiasm: {I stan her so hard}, {We stan a queen who speaks her mind}. The word walks a line between genuine admiration and self-aware irony about excessive fandom. (Capitalized Stan is a given name.)

Stance is how you position your body, especially your feet and legs, when standing or preparing for action: a batter's stance, a golfer's stance. Extended to mean a mental position—your attitude or viewpoint on an issue: {What's your stance on the new policy?} To {take a stance} is to commit to a position, often publicly.

Stances is the plural of stance—a way of standing or positioning the body, especially in sports or combat: {batting stances}, {defensive stances}. More often, stance refers to a mental position or attitude toward something: {What's your stance on the issue?} {The company has softened its stance on remote work}.

Stanchions are upright posts or supports, typically made of metal, used to hold something in place or create barriers. In crowd control, stanchions connected by ropes or retractable belts guide people into orderly lines at banks, airports, and theaters. On ships and docks, stanchions support railings or secure cargo. In farming, stanchions are frames that restrain cattle by the neck during milking or feeding. {The velvet ropes hung between brass stanchions at the museum entrance.}

The many meanings of stand are rooted in the notion of being upright on your feet. As a transitive verb, stand is part of many idioms such as stand a chance, stand trial, and stand your ground. Stand can also mean tolerate, especially when used with a negation: I can’t stand rap music. A stand can be a position you are prepared to defend (take a stand), or it can be a place where a particular thing happens, such as a concession stand or a witness stand.

Standalone describes something complete in itself, not requiring connection to or support from other things. A standalone {app} works without an internet connection. A standalone {film} isn't part of a series. The word applies to software, devices, buildings, or creative works that function independently: {The garage is a standalone structure}. Also spelled stand-alone.

Standard describes what is normal, expected, or widely accepted as a baseline. A standard {size} fits most people. Standard {practice} is how things are typically done. Standard {English} is the variety used in formal contexts. As a noun, a standard is a level of quality {(high standards)}, a flag or banner {(the royal standard)}, or an upright support {(lamp standard)}. A song that becomes a standard enters the permanent repertoire: {jazz standards}. (Capitalized Standard may refer to specific brand names or publications.)

A standardbearer is someone who carries a flag or banner, especially in military contexts or ceremonial processions. More commonly, the term describes a prominent advocate or representative of a cause, movement, or political party: {She became the standardbearer for progressive reform}. The standardbearer embodies and advances what the group stands for.

Standardbearers is the plural of standardbearer, someone who carries a flag or banner—originally in military contexts, where the role required courage under fire. The meaning extends to anyone who leads or represents a cause, movement, or organization: {She became one of the standardbearers of the civil rights movement}. Also spelled standard-bearers or standard bearers.

Standardization is the process of establishing uniform criteria, methods, or specifications. Industries adopt standardization to ensure compatibility: {USB standardization let any charger work with any device}. The term applies to manufacturing, language, testing, and procedures. Standardization enables efficiency and interoperability but can also flatten regional or individual variation: {Critics argue that standardization in education stifles creativity}.

Standardize means to bring things into conformity with a common standard. You might standardize procedures across departments, spelling across a document, or measurements across an industry. The goal is uniformity—eliminating variation so that things work together or can be compared: {The company standardized its software across all offices}. Also spelled standardise in British English.

Standardized means made uniform according to a standard. A standardized {test} uses the same questions and conditions for all test-takers, allowing comparison of results. Standardized {parts} are interchangeable because they conform to fixed specifications. The word often appears in contexts of education, manufacturing, and measurement where consistency matters: {standardized procedures}, {standardized formats}.

Standards are benchmarks for measuring quality, achievement, or behavior. A product meets safety {standards}; a school maintains academic {standards}. The word implies expectations that should be upheld: {She has high standards for herself}. A standard can also be a flag or banner, especially one that rallies troops or represents authority. As an adjective, standard means typical or widely accepted: {standard procedure}, {standard English}.

Standby is a state of readiness—waiting to be called into action. A standby generator activates when power fails. Airline passengers {on standby} wait for unclaimed seats. Electronic devices on standby aren't fully off but consume minimal power, ready to wake. As an adjective, standby modifies things kept in reserve: {standby mode}, {standby crew}. An {old standby} is something reliably useful: {Chicken soup is an old standby when I'm sick}.

Standbys are people or things kept ready for use when needed. A standby is a reliable backup—someone you can count on, or a substitute ready to step in: {Coffee and aspirin are my morning standbys}. In travel, standby refers to waiting for an available seat on a flight: {We flew standby and barely made it}.

Standing describes an upright position—on one's feet rather than sitting or lying: {The standing passengers swayed as the train moved}. A standing ovation requires the audience to rise. Standing also means permanent or ongoing: a standing {army}, a standing {invitation}, a standing {order}. Your standing is your reputation or rank within a group: {Her standing in the community}, {academic standing}. In legal contexts, standing is the right to bring a lawsuit—without it, a court won't hear your case.

Standings are the ranked positions of competitors in a league, tournament, or ongoing competition, based on their win-loss records or accumulated points: {The team moved into first place in the standings}. Unlike one-time rankings, standings track cumulative performance over a season or series and are updated continuously as games are played.

A standoff is a situation where opposing sides are deadlocked, neither able to advance or prevail: {The hostage situation turned into a tense standoff with police}. In sports and games, a standoff is a tie. As an adjective, standoff describes someone aloof or unfriendly—more commonly standoffish: {He has a standoff manner that puts people off}.

Standoffish describes someone who is cold, distant, or unfriendly—keeping others at arm's length rather than engaging warmly. The word often suggests aloofness or reserve rather than outright hostility: {She seemed standoffish at first, but warmed up once we started talking}. Someone standoffish may be shy, snobbish, or simply private.

Standoffs are situations where opposing sides reach an impasse, neither able to advance or willing to retreat. The term comes from competitive contexts—a standoff in a game means neither side gains advantage. In tense confrontations, a standoff may involve armed parties facing each other without attacking: {The hostage situation ended in a three-hour standoff with police}. In hardware, standoffs are small spacers that hold components apart, keeping circuit boards from touching surfaces.

A standout is someone or something that stands out—notably superior or exceptional among others: {She was a standout in her graduating class}. As an adjective, it describes exceptional quality: {a standout performance}, {a standout feature}. The word implies distinction without effort, as if excellence naturally draws attention.

Standouts are people or things that are noticeably superior to others in a group. The word emphasizes visibility—they stand out from the crowd: {She was a standout among the applicants}. In sports, a standout is an exceptional player: {The team's defensive standouts earned all-conference honors}.

A standpoint is a position from which something is viewed or evaluated—a perspective shaped by one's circumstances, beliefs, or role: {From a legal standpoint, the contract is enforceable}. The word emphasizes that conclusions depend on where you stand: {From the customer's standpoint, the policy makes no sense}.

Stands covers positions of stability and endurance. To stand is to be upright on one's feet, or to remain in place: {The offer still stands}. A stand is a position taken: {her stand on immigration}. It's also a structure for holding things ({music stand}, {nightstand}) or selling them ({fruit stand}, {hot dog stand}). A stand of trees is a group growing together. The stands are seating areas at a stadium. To {stand for} something is to represent it or tolerate it: {I won't stand for that behavior}.

A standstill is a complete stop or state of no movement or progress. Traffic comes to a standstill during rush hour. Negotiations reach a standstill when neither side will budge. {The project ground to a standstill after funding was cut}. The word emphasizes motionlessness where motion is expected or desired.

Standup has several meanings united by the idea of standing upright or facing something directly. A standup comic performs alone before an audience, delivering jokes without props or partners: {She's been doing standup for ten years}. As an adjective, standup describes someone reliable and honorable—a {standup guy} won't betray you. A standup meeting is held with participants standing, typically brief. In software development, a {daily standup} is a short team check-in. Something standup is designed to be used while standing: a {standup desk}, a {standup paddleboard}.

Standups are brief daily meetings where team members report progress and obstacles, typically while standing to keep the meeting short. The format originated in agile software development: {We cover blockers in our morning standup}. Separately, standups are standup comedy performances or the comedians who perform them: {She's been doing standups at local clubs}.

Stank is the past tense of stink: {The whole place stank of cigarettes}. In informal speech, stank also works as an adjective meaning foul-smelling or unpleasant: {Get your stank feet off the couch}. The noun stank describes a bad smell or, in slang, a nasty attitude: {She gave me nothing but stank}.

Stanning is intense, devoted fandom—supporting a celebrity, artist, or public figure with passionate enthusiasm. From "stan," which blends "stalker" and "fan" (after the Eminem song about an obsessive fan). The term has softened from its dark origins; now it usually just means being a superfan: {I've been stanning this band since their first album}. {We stan a queen who speaks her mind.}

Stans is the plural of stan, meaning obsessive fans who follow celebrities or public figures with intense, sometimes unhealthy devotion. The term comes from the Eminem song "Stan" about a fan whose obsession turns fatal. Stans defend their favorites aggressively online and attack critics: {Her stans flooded the comments}. The word can be affectionate or mocking depending on context.
clues: Followers who take devotion too far

definition: A stanza is a group of lines in a poem, set off by space from other groups. Stanzas function somewhat like paragraphs in prose, organizing verse into units with consistent patterns of rhyme, meter, or length. Common forms include the couplet (two lines), quatrain (four), and sestet (six). {The final stanza brought the poem full circle.}

Stanzas is the plural of stanza, a grouping of lines in a poem set off by spacing or other visual breaks. Stanzas function somewhat like paragraphs in prose, organizing a poem into units of thought or rhythm. Common forms have names: a couplet is two lines, a quatrain is four. {The poem's final stanzas shift from grief to acceptance.}

Two words share the spelling s-t-a-p-l-e. The first is a fastener, U-shaped and often made of metal, in which pointed ends penetrate layers to bind them together, or in other words, staple them, as you would staple papers together. The second staple is a basic or essential item. Jeans are wardrobe staples. Dietary staples are things you eat regularly: I need to buy milk, eggs, and other staples at the grocery store. Before another noun, staple may refer either to the first (staple gun) or second (staple crop) meaning.

A stapler is a device that fastens sheets of paper together by driving a thin metal staple through them and bending its ends flat. Desktop staplers sit on a surface and are pressed by hand; heavy-duty staplers punch through thick stacks. Surgical staplers close wounds with metal clips. {I need to borrow your stapler.}

Staples are the basic, essential items of a category—the foods you always keep stocked, the supplies a business can't run without: {Rice and beans are staples of many cuisines}. A staple is also a U-shaped metal fastener, whether the small wire kind that binds papers together or the larger kind hammered into wood. To staple is to fasten with such a device. As an adjective, staple means principal or regularly produced: {Corn is their staple crop}.

We use star generally to talk about heavenly bodies visible to us only at night.
