Strife is somewhat literary—conflict, tension, or trouble often substitute in everyday speech.
clues: Deep discord that breeds bad blood

definition: Strike has myriad meanings arising from the core verb meaning of hit forcefully: She struck him on the jaw. When strike is followed by an adverbial directional phrase, it means to go or set off on a course: We’ll strike out through the jungle. Strike can also refer to a work stoppage: Workers at the plant will strike for higher wages and better safety. A strike is an instance of striking: There was a strike at the university and classes were cancelled. Several lightning strikes were reported in the area.

A strikebreaker is someone who works during a labor strike, either a regular employee who refuses to join the walkout or an outsider hired to replace striking workers. The term carries strong negative connotations among union supporters, who view strikebreakers as undermining collective bargaining power and worker solidarity. The more contemptuous term *scab* is often used instead. {The company brought in strikebreakers to keep the factory running.}

Strikebreakers are workers hired to replace employees who are on strike, or existing employees who cross picket lines to keep working during a labor dispute. The term carries negative connotations from the perspective of striking workers and union supporters, who view strikebreakers as undermining collective bargaining power. Also called scabs.

Strikebreaking is the practice of undermining a labor strike, whether by hiring replacement workers, using force against picketers, or pressuring strikers to return to work. Companies have employed professional strikebreakers, private security, and sometimes government forces to break strikes: {The company's strikebreaking tactics turned public opinion against management}.

A strikeout in baseball is when a batter accumulates three strikes and is out. The term extends to any decisive failure: {The product launch was a strikeout}. As a verb phrase, to strike out means to fail completely or, in dating, to be rejected: {I struck out with her at the party}. Also spelled strike-out or strike out.

Strikeouts are instances of striking out. In baseball, a strikeout occurs when a batter accumulates three strikes and is out: {He led the league in strikeouts}. The term applies from either perspective—a pitcher's strikeouts are batters retired, a batter's strikeouts are failures at the plate. Outside baseball, a strikeout is any failed attempt: {After several strikeouts with publishers, she self-published}.

A striker is someone or something that strikes. In soccer, a striker is a forward position focused on scoring goals: {The striker headed the ball into the net}. In labor disputes, strikers are workers who have walked off the job. A striker can also be the hammer mechanism in a firearm or clock, or the metal plate a door latch engages.

Strikers are workers who refuse to work as a form of protest, typically to pressure employers over wages, conditions, or other grievances: {The strikers formed a picket line outside the factory}. In soccer, a striker is a forward whose primary role is scoring goals. More generally, anyone or anything that strikes—a clock's hammer, a tool for igniting matches.

Strikes connects ideas of hitting, stopping, and sudden action. To strike is to hit forcefully: {Lightning struck the tree}, {He struck her across the face}. Workers strike when they refuse to work as protest: {The nurses went on strike}. A strike in bowling knocks down all pins. In baseball, a strike is a pitch the batter swings at and misses, or one that crosses the plate in the strike zone—three strikes and you're out. To {strike a match} is to ignite it by friction. To {strike a pose} is to assume one dramatically. {That strikes me as odd} means it seems odd. To {strike gold} or {strike it rich} is to find sudden fortune.

Strikethrough is a typographic effect that draws a horizontal line through text, like ~~this~~. It indicates deletion, correction, or obsolescence while keeping the original visible. In digital communication, strikethrough often conveys ironic retraction—crossing out what you "didn't really mean" while making sure readers see it: {I think he's an idiot a lovely person}.

Striking describes something that immediately catches attention and makes a strong impression. A striking {resemblance} is one you notice right away; a striking {woman} has features that stand out from the crowd. The word carries positive connotations of distinctiveness rather than mere oddness. As the present participle of strike, it also describes the act of hitting or the state of workers who have walked off the job: {The striking miners refused to negotiate}.

A string is something long, thin, and fairly flexible, like the apron strings used to tie the garment. Strings made of gut, nylon, or metal make the sounds on string instruments, which may be called strings collectively. A string is also a line of continuity, like a performer’s string of hits or the string of characters that make up a password. To string something up is to attach or suspend it with string. To string someone along is to keep them waiting, or to deceive them.

A stringer is a journalist who works freelance for a news organization, typically covering a specific geographic area or beat without being on staff: {The paper relies on stringers for international coverage}. In construction, a stringer is a long horizontal beam supporting a structure—the side pieces of a staircase that hold the treads, or structural members in bridges and aircraft. In fishing, a stringer is a cord or chain threaded through the gills of caught fish to keep them in the water: {He added another bass to the stringer}.

Stringers are long structural supports, typically running horizontally to reinforce or connect other elements. In construction, stringers support stair treads. In journalism, a stringer is a freelance correspondent who contributes stories to a publication without being on staff: {The paper relies on stringers for local coverage}. In fishing, a stringer is a line or chain threaded through the gills of caught fish to keep them in the water.

Stringing is the present participle of string—threading, arranging in a line, or fitting with strings. Someone stringing beads makes a necklace. Stringing a guitar prepares it for play. To be {stringing someone along} is to mislead them with false promises or encouragement, keeping them hopeful without real intention of following through.

Strings is the plural of string—thin cords or threads. In music, strings refers collectively to instruments played by bowing or plucking: violin, viola, cello, bass. An orchestra's {string section} or simply {the strings} provides harmonic foundation. In computing, a string is a sequence of characters treated as a single unit: {Parse the input string}. To pull strings is to use hidden influence: {She pulled strings to get him the job}. {No strings attached} means without conditions or obligations.

Stringy describes something composed of or resembling strings—long, thin, fibrous strands. Stringy {meat} is tough and full of chewy fibers. Stringy {hair} hangs in lank, separated strands, usually from being unwashed or wet. Stringy {cheese} pulls apart in stretchy threads. A person described as stringy is tall and thin, with a lean, sinewy build.

The noun strip is related to stripe and has some overlap in meaning. A strip is something whose greatest dimension is length (landing strip, comic strip, strip mall). A major street is sometimes called a strip. The verb strip is not related to the noun. To strip something (paint, bark, wallpaper, for example) is to remove it. If you strip a person, you remove their clothes. If a person strips, they do the removing themselves.

A stripe is a long narrow band of color or texture contrasting with its surroundings: {a shirt with blue and white stripes}, {the stripes on a zebra}. Stripes can indicate rank—military personnel wear stripes on their sleeves to show grade. By extension, stripe means type or kind: {politicians of every stripe}. The verb means to mark with stripes: {The morning light striped the floor through the blinds}. To {earn one's stripes} is to prove oneself through experience.

Striped means marked with stripes—bands of color or texture that contrast with the surrounding surface. A striped {shirt} has parallel lines running through the fabric. A tiger is striped; a leopard is spotted. The word can be pronounced as one syllable (STRYPED) or two (STRY-pid), with the two-syllable version more common in formal or poetic contexts.

Stripes are long narrow bands or lines that differ in color or texture from what surrounds them. They appear on clothing, flags, animals, and surfaces both natural and designed. A tiger has stripes; so does the American flag. In military and other uniformed contexts, stripes are insignia indicating rank: {She earned her stripes after two years of service}. To earn one's stripes more broadly means to prove oneself through effort or experience.

Striploin is a cut of beef from the short loin, running along the spine behind the ribs. It's a tender, well-marbled steak cut known for rich flavor, sold boneless as New York strip or bone-in as a club steak. The term is most common in butchery and restaurant menus: {grilled striploin with herb butter}.

A stripogram is a novelty greeting delivery where someone, usually hired for a birthday or bachelor party, arrives in costume and performs a striptease for the recipient. The word blends "strip" with "telegram," recalling old-fashioned singing telegram services. Also spelled strippergram. {They hired a stripogram dressed as a police officer.}

Stripped is the past tense of strip—to remove covering, clothing, or components. A stripped bed has had its sheets removed. A stripped car has been dismantled for parts. Stripped can mean reduced to essentials: {a stripped-down version of the software}. Paint stripper leaves wood stripped of its finish. To be stripped of a title or rank is to have it taken away as punishment.

A stripper is a person who performs striptease—removing clothing to music as entertainment, typically in a club setting. The word also applies to tools and chemicals that remove things: a wire stripper strips insulation from electrical cables, paint stripper dissolves old coatings. {She worked as a stripper to pay for law school.}

A strippergram is a novelty gift in which someone hires a performer to arrive at a party or event, often in costume or disguise, and perform a striptease for the guest of honor. Popular for bachelor and bachelorette parties, birthdays, or office pranks: {They hired a strippergram dressed as a police officer for his fortieth birthday}.

Strippers are people who perform striptease—removing clothing to music, typically for entertainment in clubs or at private parties. The term usually refers to women, though male strippers perform for bachelorette parties and similar events. Separately, a stripper is a tool or chemical that removes paint, insulation, or other coatings: {wire strippers}, {paint stripper}.

Stripping is removing an outer layer or covering. You strip paint from furniture, insulation from wire, or bark from a tree. A person strips by removing clothing—which gives the word its association with striptease performances: {She works as a stripper}. In mechanical contexts, stripping means damaging threads so they no longer grip: {He stripped the bolt by overtightening it}.

A strippogram is a novelty greeting delivered by a performer who strips while singing or reciting a message, typically hired for bachelor parties, birthdays, or office pranks. The term combines "strip" with "telegram," evoking the old singing telegram tradition: {They hired a strippogram for his fortieth birthday}. Chiefly British; the American equivalent is usually called a singing stripper or strip-o-gram.

Strips are long, narrow pieces cut or torn from something larger: {strips of bacon}, {strips of cloth}, {a strip of land along the coast}. To strip is to remove a covering or outer layer—stripping paint, stripping bark, stripping clothes. A strip is also a sequence of drawn panels telling a story (comic strip) or a road lined with businesses (the Vegas Strip). To strip someone of rank or privilege is to take it away forcibly.

A striptease is an erotic performance in which someone gradually removes their clothing, typically to music. The art lies in the tease—the slow reveal rather than immediate nudity. Striptease is associated with burlesque shows and strip clubs. As a verb, to striptease is to perform such an act: {She worked her way through college doing striptease}.

Strive means to make great effort toward a goal, often against difficulty or opposition. The word suggests sustained exertion rather than a single attempt: {She strives for excellence in everything she does}. You can strive to achieve something, strive for a result, or strive against obstacles. The word carries a sense of earnestness and determination—striving implies the goal matters deeply.

Strived is a past tense and past participle of strive, meaning to make great effort toward a goal: {She strived for excellence in everything she did}. The form strove is more traditional, but strived has gained acceptance and appears frequently in contemporary usage. Both are correct.

A striver is someone who works hard to achieve something, typically success or advancement. The word often carries a hint of ambition that may be excessive or status-conscious: {She dismissed him as a social striver}. In neutral or positive contexts, it simply means someone making determined effort: {The program rewards strivers who show dedication}.

Strivers is the plural of striver—people who work hard toward goals, usually with connotations of ambition and persistent effort. The word often appears in discussions of social mobility and success: {a neighborhood of strivers and dreamers}. It can carry admiration or faint condescension, depending on context—celebrating determination or implying someone is straining beyond their station.

Striving is the act of making great effort toward a goal, often against difficulty or opposition. The word emphasizes ongoing exertion rather than achievement: {Despite years of striving, success eluded him}. It carries a sense of earnest, sometimes noble struggle: {the striving of artists for recognition}, {human striving for meaning}.

A strobe is a light that flashes rapidly and repeatedly, used in photography, emergency vehicles, and dance clubs. The flashing creates a distinctive effect where motion appears choppy or frozen. As a verb, to strobe is to flash in this manner: {Emergency lights strobed across the wet pavement}. Short for stroboscope.

Strobes are lights that flash in rapid, regular bursts. The word is short for stroboscopic, describing the flickering effect. Strobes appear in photography equipment, emergency vehicles, dance clubs, and aircraft warning systems. As a verb, to strobe is to flash intermittently: {Red lights strobed across the ceiling}. The flashing can induce disorientation or, in some people, seizures.

Strobing describes a rapid, pulsing flash effect—like a strobe light. In video and digital displays, strobing is an unwanted flickering that occurs when frame rates clash with movement or lighting: {The LED lights were strobing badly on camera}. As a makeup technique, strobing uses highlighter to create a luminous, lit-from-within glow on high points of the face, named for the bright, attention-catching quality of strobe lighting.

Strode is the past tense of stride. To stride is to walk with long, purposeful steps, suggesting confidence or determination: {He strode into the room and demanded answers}. The word carries more force than simply "walked"—it implies deliberate, energetic movement.

Stroganoff is a dish of sautéed beef in a sauce of sour cream, onions, and mushrooms, typically served over egg noodles or rice. Named after a 19th-century Russian aristocratic family, the dish became popular internationally through French and American adaptations. {We're having beef stroganoff for dinner tonight.} Variations using chicken or ground beef are common in home cooking.

The core idea of stroke is verbal, and is related to strike but usually has more gentle connotations (except in the case of the cerebral blockage or hemorrhage that we call a stroke). To stroke an object or animal is to caress it with the hand, often in a caring and repetitive way. Stroke is sometimes used figuratively to mean flatter: He stroked her ego. A stroke is also an act or instance of stroking, typically when it denotes a repetitive movement: Children learn all the major strokes in swimming. You can see individual brush strokes in the photograph.

Strokes is the plural of stroke, covering its many senses. A stroke is a single movement—of a pen, brush, oar, or limb in swimming: {She completed the race in powerful strokes}. A stroke of luck or genius is a sudden instance of it. In medicine, a stroke is a sudden interruption of blood flow to the brain, often causing paralysis or death. To stroke is to caress gently: {He stroked the cat's fur}. In slang, to stroke someone is to flatter them, feeding their ego.

Stroking is the act of moving one's hand gently over a surface, typically with affection or to soothe: {She sat stroking the cat's fur}. The word extends to any repeated, caressing motion. In competitive contexts, stroking refers to the technique of moving oars or paddles through water. Informally, stroking someone's ego means flattering them.

A stroll is a leisurely walk taken for pleasure rather than purpose: {an evening stroll through the park}. To stroll is to walk in this unhurried way, with no particular destination or urgency. Someone who strolls through a task approaches it casually, perhaps too casually: {He strolled through the interview like he already had the job}.

A stroller is a lightweight wheeled chair for pushing a small child: {She folded up the stroller and put it in the trunk}. The word also means one who strolls—someone taking a leisurely walk—though this sense is less common now that the baby carriage dominates usage.

Strollers are wheeled chairs for transporting small children, pushed by a parent or caregiver. The British term is pushchair or pram. Strollers also refers to people who stroll—walk in a leisurely way: {Evening strollers filled the boardwalk}.

Strolling is walking in a leisurely, unhurried way—wandering without urgency or fixed destination: {We spent the afternoon strolling through the old quarter}. The word suggests pleasure or aimlessness rather than purpose. A strolling musician or vendor moves slowly through a space, stopping to perform or sell.

Stromboli is a type of Italian-American turnover—seasoned meats, cheese, and sometimes vegetables rolled in pizza dough and baked until golden. Unlike calzones, which are folded and crimped, stromboli is rolled into a log shape: {We ordered a pepperoni stromboli to share}. Named after the volcanic Italian island, though the dish originated in Philadelphia.

The adjective strong overlaps in meaning with sturdy, powerful, and durable, and is the opposite of weak. Strong wind may be damaging. Strong relationships can withstand stresses. Strong support can be relied upon. To characterize a person as strong can refer to physical strength, or the ability to withstand emotional and psychological distress. If you are strong in something, like faith or conviction, those traits are noticeable in you. A strong smell or strong taste is usually a negative characterization, suggesting excess.

Strongarm means using physical force or intimidation to achieve a goal. As a verb, to strongarm someone is to coerce them through threats or violence: {They strongarmed the shopkeeper into paying protection money}. As an adjective, it describes aggressive tactics: {strongarm methods}, {strongarm robbery}. The term implies bullying rather than persuasion—getting compliance through fear rather than agreement.

Strongarmed is the past tense of strongarm, meaning to use force, intimidation, or coercion to achieve something: {He strongarmed the witness into changing her testimony}. The term evokes physical force even when the pressure is purely psychological or financial: {The corporation strongarmed smaller competitors out of the market}.

Strongarming is using force, threats, or intimidation to compel someone to do something. The term evokes physical coercion—twisting someone's arm—but extends to any aggressive pressure tactics: {The company was strongarming suppliers into accepting lower prices}. Politicians, businesses, and bullies all get accused of strongarming when they push too hard.

Strongarms is the verb form of strongarm, meaning to use force, threats, or intimidation to compel someone: {The landlord strongarms tenants into paying illegal fees}. The noun strongarm refers to a person who uses such tactics—an enforcer or intimidator. As an adjective, it describes coercive methods: {strongarm tactics}.

A strongbox is a sturdy, lockable container designed to protect valuables, documents, or money from theft or damage. Typically made of heavy metal with reinforced walls and a secure locking mechanism, strongboxes range from small portable cashboxes to larger safes bolted to floors or walls. {The family kept their jewelry and important papers in a strongbox.} The term emphasizes the container's strength and security rather than its size.

Stronger is the comparative form of strong—indicating greater strength, intensity, or degree than something else. Physical strength: {She's stronger than her brother}. Intensity of feeling or effect: {The coffee could be stronger}. Resilience: {What doesn't kill you makes you stronger}. Arguments, evidence, or cases can be stronger than alternatives. A stronger economy shows more robust growth.

A stronghold is a fortified place—a castle, fortress, or defensible position: {The rebels retreated to their mountain stronghold}. By extension, it's any area where a particular group, belief, or activity dominates: {a Republican stronghold}, {a stronghold of traditional values}. The word emphasizes both strength and the idea of holding ground against opposition.

Strongholds are fortified places—castles, fortresses, or well-defended positions: {The rebels retreated to their mountain stronghold}. The term extends to any area where a group maintains firm control or dominance: {a Republican stronghold}, {a stronghold of traditional values}. The singular stronghold is more common; the plural usually describes multiple such places or competing centers of power.

A strongman is a performer who demonstrates feats of physical strength—lifting heavy weights, bending metal bars, breaking chains. The term extends to authoritarian political leaders who rule through force and personal power rather than democratic institutions: {The country fell under the grip of a strongman}. Strongman competitions test athletes in events like deadlifts and atlas stones.

Strongmen is the plural of strongman. In its literal sense, strongmen are performers who demonstrate feats of physical strength—lifting heavy objects, bending metal bars, breaking chains. The term also describes authoritarian political leaders who consolidate power through force of personality and suppression of opposition: {The twentieth century produced no shortage of strongmen}. The athletic and political meanings share connotations of dominance and intimidation.

A strongroom is a heavily secured room designed for storing valuables, typically in a bank or similar institution. The walls, floor, and ceiling are reinforced, and access is controlled by vault doors or multiple locks: {The bank's strongroom held safe deposit boxes and cash reserves}. Distinguished from a safe by being room-sized rather than furniture-sized.

A strongwoman is a female athlete who competes in strength sports—lifting heavy objects, pulling vehicles, carrying weights for distance. The term parallels strongman and refers specifically to competitive strength athletics rather than general fitness. Figuratively, a strongwoman is a female leader who rules with an iron grip, the feminine counterpart to political strongman: {The province was governed by a local strongwoman}.

Stroopwafels are Dutch cookies made of two thin waffle layers pressed together with caramel syrup in between. The name combines *stroop* (syrup) and *wafel* (waffle). Traditionally served atop a hot drink so the steam softens the caramel: {She balanced the stroopwafel on her coffee cup to warm it}. Singular: stroopwafel.

Stroppy is British slang for bad-tempered, irritable, or argumentative—someone being difficult or contrary: {Don't get stroppy with me}. The word suggests petulant annoyance rather than serious anger: {She got stroppy when I asked her to help}. Uncommon in American English.

Struck is the past tense and past participle of strike. A clock struck {midnight}. Lightning struck the {tree}. Workers struck for better {wages}. Someone struck by beauty or grief is powerfully affected. To be {struck dumb} is to be rendered speechless. {Struck from the record} means officially removed. A struck {match} has been ignited by friction.

Structural describes something relating to or affecting structure—the way parts are arranged or organized to form a whole. A structural {engineer} analyzes how buildings and bridges bear loads. Structural {damage} compromises the integrity of a building's frame or foundation. In more abstract uses, structural refers to fundamental organization rather than surface features: structural {reforms} address underlying systems, not superficial fixes. {The committee identified structural problems in how complaints were handled.}

Structure is the way parts are arranged or organized into a whole. A building has physical structure; an essay has logical structure; a molecule has chemical structure. The word implies that arrangement matters—that components relate to each other in purposeful ways. To structure something is to give it organization: {She structured the course around weekly themes}. Structured environments have clear rules; unstructured time is free of them.

Structured describes something organized according to a deliberate plan or framework. A structured {environment} has clear rules and expectations. A structured {interview} follows a predetermined set of questions. The word often contrasts with free-form or improvised approaches: {The class was too structured for creative exploration}. In computing, structured {data} is organized in defined formats that machines can easily process.

Structures are things that have been built or organized—buildings, bridges, frameworks, systems. The word emphasizes how parts fit together: {the structure of a sentence}, {corporate structure}, {bone structure}. To structure something is to arrange or organize it: {Let me structure my thoughts before responding}. A structured environment has clear rules and organization; an unstructured one is loose or freeform.

Strudel is a pastry made by wrapping thin layers of dough around a filling, then baking. Apple strudel, filled with spiced apples, raisins, and breadcrumbs, is the classic version: {We ordered strudel and coffee at the Viennese café}. Other fillings include cheese, cherries, or savory ingredients. The dough is stretched paper-thin before rolling.

Strudels is the plural of strudel, a pastry made of thin dough wrapped around a filling, typically apple with cinnamon and raisins. The dough is stretched paper-thin before rolling, creating flaky layers when baked. Though apple strudel is most famous, savory versions with cheese or meat exist: {She brought two apple strudels to the potluck}.

Struggle is effort against resistance. You struggle to lift something heavy, struggle to understand difficult material, struggle against an opponent. The word implies difficulty and exertion: {She struggled with depression for years}. A struggle is any hard-fought effort: {the struggle for civil rights}, {a power struggle}. To struggle is also to move with difficulty: {He struggled to his feet}.

Struggled is the past tense of struggle, meaning to make strenuous efforts against difficulty or opposition. Someone who struggled with a decision found it hard to make. A business that struggled faced serious challenges. {She struggled to keep her balance on the ice.} {He struggled with depression for years.} Physical struggling involves forceful movement against restraint: {The suspect struggled as officers handcuffed him.}

Struggles are difficult efforts against resistance or opposition. The word captures both the effort and the hardship: {financial struggles}, {the struggles of daily life}. Someone who struggles with addiction fights an ongoing battle. A company struggles to stay afloat. The plural often emphasizes repeated or various difficulties rather than a single contest: {We all have our struggles}.

Struggling describes effort against difficulty or resistance. Someone struggling with a heavy load strains to carry it. A struggling {business} barely survives. You might struggle to {find the right words} or struggle {with addiction}. The word implies ongoing effort without easy success—not yet failed, but not thriving either.

To strum is to sweep the fingers across the strings of a guitar, banjo, or similar instrument, sounding multiple strings at once rather than plucking them individually: {She strummed a few chords while waiting for the others to tune up}. The word suggests casual or rhythmic playing rather than technical precision. A strum is a single instance of this motion, or the sound it produces.

Strumming is brushing the fingers across guitar strings to produce sound, or the sound produced by doing so. The word captures both the action and its acoustic result: {the strumming of an acoustic guitar in the next room}, {She sat strumming while we talked}. Strumming suggests casual or rhythmic playing rather than precise picking of individual strings.

Strums is the plural noun or third-person singular verb form of strum—to play a stringed instrument by brushing fingers across the strings in a sweeping motion rather than plucking individual notes. Strumming produces chords and rhythm: {She strums her guitar on the porch every evening}. The word can extend to any idle, repetitive finger movement: {He strums his fingers on the desk}.

Strung is the past tense and past participle of string. Something strung together has been connected in sequence: {beads strung on a wire}, {words strung into sentences}. Strung also describes something fitted with strings: a freshly strung {racket}, a strung {bow}. To be {strung out} is to be exhausted, anxious, or addicted to drugs. {High-strung} describes a tense, nervous temperament.

Strut is a proud, confident walk with head high and chest out—the gait of someone showing off or feeling self-important: {He strutted around the office after his promotion}. The word often carries a whiff of arrogance or vanity: {peacocks strutting}, {models strutting down the runway}. To {strut your stuff} is to display your abilities or assets. A strut is also a structural brace that resists compression, as in aircraft wings or automobile suspensions.

Struts are structural supports designed to resist compression—the beams and bars that keep things from collapsing inward. In vehicles, struts are shock-absorbing components in the suspension system. To strut is to walk with exaggerated pride or self-importance, chest out, shoulders back: {He strutted around like he owned the place}. The phrase {strut your stuff} means to display your abilities or assets confidently.

Strutting is walking with exaggerated pride or self-importance—chest out, shoulders back, steps deliberate and showy. A rooster struts around the barnyard; a person struts after a victory or to project confidence: {He came strutting in like he owned the place}. The word often carries a note of mockery, suggesting the pride is unearned or excessive.

Strychnine is a bitter, highly toxic alkaloid derived from the seeds of the strychnine tree. It causes violent muscular convulsions and death by asphyxiation. Once used in small doses as a stimulant and in rat poison, it now appears mainly in murder mysteries and forensic discussions: {The autopsy revealed traces of strychnine}.

A stub is a short remaining piece left after the main part has been used or removed—the stub of a pencil, a ticket stub, a check stub. These remnants often serve as records or receipts. In computing, a stub is placeholder code that stands in for functionality not yet implemented. To stub your toe is to strike it painfully against something, and to stub out a cigarette is to extinguish it by pressing the burning end against a surface.

Stubbed describes something cut short or reduced to a stub. A stubbed {cigarette} has been extinguished by pressing it against a surface. A stubbed {toe} has been painfully struck against something: {I stubbed my toe on the coffee table}. In computing, a stubbed function is a placeholder that stands in for code not yet written.

Stubbies are short glass bottles of beer, typically holding 375ml or less, common in Australia and parts of the American South. The term also refers to a style of very short shorts, particularly the tight-fitting ones popular in Australia during the 1970s and 80s. Both uses derive from the squat, stubby shape—compact and truncated compared to standard lengths. {Grab a stubby from the esky.} {He wore his old stubbies to the barbecue.}

Stubble is the short, stiff remnants of something cut close to its base. After harvest, stubble is the stalks left standing in a field. On a face, stubble is the rough growth of beard a day or two after shaving: {He rubbed the stubble on his chin}. Stubble suggests incompleteness—neither cleanly removed nor fully grown.

Stubborn describes someone who refuses to change their mind or course of action, even in the face of good arguments or evidence. The word carries a negative connotation—stubbornness is persistence without flexibility: {She's too stubborn to admit she was wrong}. A stubborn stain or problem resists removal or solution. Stubborn can shade toward positive when it suggests determination against difficult odds: {his stubborn refusal to give up}.

Stubbornness is the quality of refusing to change one's mind, course of action, or position despite pressure, argument, or good reasons to do so. It carries a negative connotation, suggesting unreasonable persistence rather than admirable resolve. {His stubbornness cost him the deal.} A stubborn person digs in their heels; stubbornness is the tendency to do so habitually. The word can sometimes shade into grudging respect when the resistance proves justified.

Stubby describes something short and thick, often with a blunt end: {stubby fingers}, {stubby legs}, {a stubby pencil}. The word suggests compactness without elegance—functional but squat. A stubby is also Australian slang for a short, squat beer bottle: {He grabbed a stubby from the cooler}.

Stubs are short remnants left after the main part has been removed or used. A ticket stub remains after the usher tears your ticket. A pencil stub is what's left after heavy use. A check stub stays in your checkbook as a record. Tree stumps are sometimes called stubs. To stub your toe is to strike it against something: {I stubbed my toe on the coffee table}. To stub out a cigarette is to extinguish it by pressing. In computing, a stub is placeholder code awaiting full implementation.

Stucco is a plaster material applied to exterior walls, where it dries to a hard, textite finish. Traditional stucco is cement-based; it's common on Mediterranean and Spanish colonial architecture. The surface is often textured—smooth, rough, or patterned. As a verb, to stucco is to coat with this material: {They stuccoed the house last summer}.

Stuck is the past tense and past participle of stick, carrying forward its senses of adhesion and fixedness. Something stuck is unable to move: a drawer stuck shut, a car stuck in mud, a person stuck in traffic. Figuratively, to be stuck is to be unable to proceed: {I'm stuck on this math problem}. If you're stuck with something, you're burdened with it unwillingly: {We're stuck with this old couch}. To get stuck in (British) is to begin energetically.

A stud is an upright post in a wall frame, or a projecting knob or peg—shirt studs, tire studs, studs on a leather jacket. In breeding, a stud is a male animal kept for reproduction, especially a stallion; a stud farm raises horses. By extension, stud is slang for a sexually attractive or virile man: {He thinks he's such a stud}. In poker, stud is a variant where some cards are dealt face up.

Studded means covered or decorated with studs—small raised knobs, buttons, or ornamental pieces. A studded leather {jacket} has metal studs for effect. Studded {tires} have metal points for grip on ice. Figuratively, something can be studded with anything that dots a surface: {a sky studded with stars}, {a career studded with achievements}.

A student is someone who studies, especially one enrolled in a school or taking lessons. The word applies from kindergarten through graduate school: {She's a third-grade student}, {law students}. Beyond formal education, student describes anyone learning systematically: {a student of human nature}, {a lifelong student of jazz}. A student can also be someone under observation or training: {a student teacher}, {a student driver}.

Students are people engaged in study, typically at a school, college, or university. The word applies broadly to anyone learning a subject, whether formally enrolled in an institution or pursuing knowledge independently: {a student of history}, {a lifelong student of human nature}. In American usage, student covers learners at all levels, while British English often reserves it for those in higher education, using pupil for younger children.

A studfinder is a handheld device used to locate wooden or metal studs behind drywall, essential for securely hanging heavy objects: {Use the studfinder before you drill}. The term doubles as a joke about detecting attractive men: {I don't need a studfinder—I married one}.

Studied describes something done with deliberate effort or careful consideration. A studied {response} is carefully thought through rather than spontaneous. A studied {pose} or {indifference} suggests deliberate artifice—the appearance of casualness that actually required effort. The word often implies calculation or even insincerity: {Her studied nonchalance fooled no one}.

Studies are focused efforts to learn or understand something, whether formal academic work or personal investigation: {She completed her studies in biology}, {He's deep in his studies}. A study is also a room designated for reading and work, or a careful examination: {a study of migration patterns}. To study is to apply oneself to learning: {I need to study for the exam}. Something that {studies well} rewards close attention.

A studio is a workspace for creative or technical work—an artist's studio, a recording studio, a photography studio. In film and television, a studio is both the physical space where productions are shot and the company that makes them: {The studio rejected the script}. A studio apartment is a single room serving as both living and sleeping space, usually with a small kitchen.

Studious describes someone devoted to study and learning, or characterized by careful attention: {a studious student}, {studious attention to detail}. The word suggests deliberate, diligent effort rather than casual interest. A studious silence or studious avoidance implies something done with careful purpose, perhaps even conspicuously so.

A studmuffin is an attractive, sexually appealing man—someone regarded as good-looking and desirable. The word is playful and slightly campy, combining stud (a virile man) with the affectionate diminutive muffin: {Check out the studmuffin at the bar}. It peaked in 1980s and 1990s slang but remains recognizable. Also spelled stud muffin.

Studmuffins is the plural of studmuffin, slang for an attractive, sexually appealing man—especially one who's muscular or conventionally masculine. The term is playful and slightly ironic, combining stud (a virile man) with muffin (suggesting something sweet and desirable): {The gym was full of studmuffins working on their biceps}. Often used humorously or affectionately rather than seriously.

Studs are upright posts in a wall frame—the vertical supports to which drywall or paneling attaches. In clothing, studs are decorative metal fasteners or small ornamental buttons, especially on formal shirt fronts. A stud is also a male animal kept for breeding, which extends to slang for a sexually attractive or active man: {He thinks he's such a stud}. Studded means embedded with studs: {a leather jacket studded with metal}, {snow tires with studs}.

Study centers on applying the mind to learn or understand something. You study for an exam, study a foreign language, or study someone's face for clues to their mood. A study is also the product of such effort—a research paper or detailed analysis: {a study on climate change}. In a home, a study is a room devoted to reading and intellectual work. In art, a study is a preliminary sketch exploring composition or technique. To be {a study in contrasts} is to embody opposing qualities.

Studying is the activity of learning or reviewing material, especially for school: {I was up all night studying for the exam}. It can also mean examining something carefully: {She spent hours studying the map}. To be studying a subject is to be formally enrolled in its coursework: {He's studying medicine at Johns Hopkins}.

Stuff is a general, uncountable noun whose closest synonym is things. What stuff refers to is often only made clear by a preceding adjective (cool stuff, fun stuff, weird stuff, crazy stuff). Someone’s stuff may be their personal possessions (get your stuff off the table!) or their personal problems or issues (she’s dealing with relationship stuff). To stuff something is to fill it with a uniform substance, the way you might stuff a pillow. To stuff yourself is to eat too much.

Stuffed describes something filled to capacity. A stuffed animal has soft material inside; a stuffed pepper has rice and meat. After a big meal, you feel stuffed. To get stuffed is British slang for dismissal: {Get stuffed!} In taxidermy, stuffed animals are preserved specimens with their insides replaced. A stuffed shirt is a pompous, self-important person.

A stuffie is a stuffed animal or plush toy—a soft fabric figure filled with cotton, foam, or similar material. The term is affectionate and informal, used especially by children and those who collect plush toys: {She sleeps with her favorite stuffie every night}. Also spelled stuffy.

Stuffies is an affectionate term for stuffed animals or plush toys, used especially by children and adults who collect them: {She sleeps with all her stuffies}. The word carries warmth and attachment—these aren't just toys but companions. In some regional usage, particularly in New England, stuffies can also refer to stuffed clams or quahogs.

Stuffiness describes air that feels close, stale, and poorly ventilated—the kind that makes you want to open a window. The word extends naturally to describe people or atmospheres that are similarly airless in a social sense: formal, pompous, and resistant to fresh ideas. A stuffy {dinner party} or a stuffy {professor} lacks the easy flow of genuine warmth. {The stuffiness of the old library made it hard to concentrate.}

Stuffing is material used to fill something. A pillow or teddy bear contains stuffing—soft material that gives it shape and bulk. In cooking, stuffing is a seasoned mixture of bread, vegetables, and herbs packed inside poultry or vegetables before roasting: {The turkey stuffing had chestnuts and sage}. To {knock the stuffing out of} someone is to defeat or demoralize them thoroughly.

Stuffy describes air that feels close, stale, or poorly ventilated: {The room was stuffy after being shut up all winter}. A stuffy nose is blocked by congestion. Of people or atmospheres, stuffy means excessively formal, old-fashioned, or self-important: {a stuffy professor}, {stuffy Victorian attitudes}. The word suggests a lack of freshness—whether of air, ideas, or manner.

To stumble is to trip or lose your footing while walking: {She stumbled on the uneven pavement}. Extended uses follow naturally—to stumble through a speech is to falter or make mistakes, and to stumble upon something is to discover it by accident: {I stumbled across an old photo in the attic}. A stumble is an instance of tripping, or any misstep or blunder.

Stumbled is the past tense of stumble—to trip or lose one's footing without falling completely: {She stumbled on the uneven pavement}. By extension, to stumble is to speak haltingly or make errors: {He stumbled through his presentation}. To {stumble upon} or {stumble across} something is to discover it by accident: {I stumbled on an old photo while cleaning}.

Stumbling is the present participle of stumble—to trip or lose one's footing while walking: {She went stumbling down the dark hallway}. Figuratively, stumbling means faltering or making mistakes: {stumbling through an apology}, {stumbling over his words}. A stumbling {block} is an obstacle that impedes progress.

A stump is what remains of something after the main part has been removed or destroyed—most commonly a tree trunk left in the ground after the tree is cut down, but also the remnant of a limb or tooth. To stump is to baffle or perplex: {That question really stumped me}. In American politics, to stump means to campaign, especially by traveling and giving speeches—from the old practice of using a tree stump as a makeshift platform. {She's been stumping across the Midwest for weeks.}

Stumped means baffled or unable to proceed—stuck without an answer or solution. The image is of being stopped short, like a tree reduced to a stump. {That last question really stumped me.} {The detective was stumped by the lack of evidence.} In cricket, stumped describes a batsman dismissed when the wicket-keeper breaks the stumps while they're out of their crease.

A stumper is a question or problem that defeats you—one you can't answer or solve: {That last clue was a real stumper}. The word comes from the idea of being stumped, left baffled like a tree reduced to its stump. Stumpers appear in quizzes, riddles, and crossword puzzles where difficulty is the point.

Stumpers are questions or problems that leave someone unable to answer—things that stump you. Quiz shows feature stumpers that contestants can't solve. A stumper in conversation stops someone cold: {That last riddle was a real stumper}. The word comes from the idea of being stopped short, as if hitting a tree stump.

Stumping is campaigning for political office or on behalf of a candidate, from the historical practice of speaking from tree stumps as improvised platforms. Politicians go stumping through swing states; surrogates do stumping for candidates they support: {She spent October stumping for the governor's reelection}. Stumping also means baffling or perplexing: {That question really stumped me}.

Stumps are what remain when something is cut short—the base of a tree after felling, the remnant of a limb after amputation, or the stub of a pencil worn down by use. In cricket, stumps are the three upright posts forming the wicket. To stump is to baffle or perplex: {The riddle stumped everyone}. Politicians stump when they campaign, traveling to give speeches—from the old practice of speaking from tree stumps. {He's out on the stump in Iowa this week.}

Stumpy describes something short and thick, like a stump. A stumpy tail is one that's been docked or is naturally abbreviated. Stumpy legs or fingers are disproportionately short relative to the body. The word carries a slightly disparaging tone when applied to people: {a stumpy little man waddled toward us}.

To stun is to daze or render senseless, typically by a blow to the head or an electrical shock: {The boxer was stunned by the punch}. Stun guns and stun grenades incapacitate without killing. More commonly, stun means to shock or astonish: {The news stunned everyone}. Something stunning can be either shocking or strikingly beautiful: {a stunning revelation}, {a stunning dress}.

Stung is the past tense and past participle of sting. A bee stung you, or you've been stung before. Beyond the literal pierce of an insect or plant, stung describes sharp emotional hurt: {I was stung by her criticism}. To get stung is also to be cheated or overcharged: {We got stung on the hotel price}.

Stunk is the past tense and past participle of stink. Something stunk if it smelled bad: {The garbage stunk up the whole kitchen}. Figuratively, something that stunk was of poor quality or morally offensive: {His excuse stunk}, {The whole deal stunk of corruption}.

Stunned describes being dazed or rendered senseless, either literally or figuratively. A blow to the head can leave someone stunned—unable to think clearly or react. More commonly, stunned describes overwhelming shock or surprise: {I was stunned when she announced her resignation}, {The news left us all stunned}. The effect implies momentary paralysis, a failure to process what just happened.

A stunner is someone or something that stuns, most often by being strikingly attractive or impressive. The word applies especially to people whose appearance makes others take notice: {She walked in and everyone agreed she was a stunner}. It can also describe an unexpected event or outcome that leaves people momentarily speechless, like a stunning upset in sports or politics. In British slang, stunner serves as general praise for anything excellent.

Stunners is the plural of stunner—someone or something strikingly impressive, especially a person of remarkable beauty: {The photos from the gala were full of stunners}. The word can describe anything that astonishes or overwhelms: {The team pulled off a few stunners this season}. In British slang, stunner is enthusiastic praise for anything excellent.
clues: Results nobody saw coming at all

definition: Stunning means striking enough to stun—to overwhelm the senses or leave someone momentarily dazed. A stunning {view} takes your breath away. A stunning {upset} shocks observers. A stunning {dress} commands attention. The word applies to both beauty and surprise: {She looked stunning} describes appearance, while {stunning news} describes impact. Something stunning stops you in your tracks.

Stuns is the third-person singular of stun—to daze or render senseless, typically by a blow to the head or an electrical shock. A stun gun incapacitates without killing. Figuratively, what stuns leaves you momentarily unable to think or respond: {The news of her death stuns everyone who knew her}. Stunning beauty or success overwhelms the senses.

A stunt is a daring feat performed for show—especially in film, where stunt doubles take physical risks for actors. The word extends to any attention-grabbing action: {a publicity stunt}, {a political stunt}. The implication is often that the act prioritizes spectacle over substance. Separately, to stunt something is to prevent its full growth or development: {Malnutrition stunted the child's growth}. A stunted tree remains small and twisted.

Stunted describes something whose growth has been checked or limited, leaving it smaller or less developed than normal. A stunted tree never reached full height; a stunted economy fails to expand. The word often implies deprivation—lack of nutrients, resources, or opportunity: {Malnutrition left the children physically and mentally stunted}. Figuratively, stunted suggests something held back from reaching its potential: {His emotional development seemed stunted}.

Stunting is showing off, especially by flaunting wealth, style, or success. The term comes from hip-hop culture, where it describes ostentatious displays—expensive cars, jewelry, designer clothes: {He's been stunting on Instagram all week}. Separately, stunting refers to impaired growth or development: {Malnutrition causes stunting in children}.

A stuntman is a person who performs dangerous physical feats in place of an actor during film or television production—falls, fights, car crashes, fire gags. The work requires athletic skill and precise choreography to create the illusion that the star is in peril. {The stuntman doubled for the lead in all the action sequences.} Also: stuntwoman, stunt performer.

Stuntmen are performers who execute dangerous or physically demanding actions in film and television, substituting for actors during scenes involving falls, fights, car crashes, or other hazards. The work requires athletic skill and precise choreography to create the illusion that the star performed the action. {The stuntmen rehearsed the explosion scene for hours.}

Stunts are daring or dangerous feats, especially those performed for entertainment: {movie stunts}, {aerial stunts}. A stunt double performs risky scenes in place of an actor. Extended to attention-getting acts: {a publicity stunt}, {a political stunt}. To stunt is to perform such feats. Separately, to stunt something is to prevent its full growth or development: {Malnutrition stunted the children}.

A stuntwoman is a woman who performs dangerous action sequences in film or television, substituting for actors during risky scenes. Stuntwomen execute falls, fights, car chases, and other physical feats requiring specialized training: {The stuntwoman did all the rooftop jumps}. The role demands athletic skill and precise timing to create convincing action while minimizing actual danger.

Stupefied describes being so shocked, stunned, or overwhelmed that you can't think clearly or react normally. The word suggests mental paralysis—your faculties temporarily shut down: {She sat stupefied, unable to process what she'd just heard}. Someone can be stupefied by astonishing news, extreme fatigue, or intoxicants. The adjective comes from stupefy, which means to put someone in this dazed state.

To stupefy is to stun or daze, depriving someone of clear thought or sensation. Alcohol or drugs can stupefy: {He was stupefied by the sedatives}. Shock or astonishment also stupefies: {The news left her stupefied}. The effect suggests a dulling of mental faculties—someone stupefied isn't just surprised but rendered unable to think clearly.

Stupefying means causing mental numbness or astonishment so extreme it leaves someone unable to think clearly. A stupefying {blow to the head} dazes physically. Stupefying {boredom} or stupefying {heat} overwhelms the mind. Stupefying {news} leaves you speechless: {The stupefying scale of the fraud took months to comprehend}.

Stupid describes a lack of intelligence or good judgment. A stupid person doesn't think clearly; a stupid decision shows poor reasoning. The word ranges from clinical assessment to casual insult: {That was a stupid thing to say}. Stupid also means pointlessly annoying: {This stupid printer won't work}. As a noun, stupid addresses someone directly: {Hey, stupid}.
clues: Showing a real lack of sense

definition: Stupidity is the quality of being unintelligent or showing poor judgment. It can describe a permanent trait or a momentary lapse: {I can't believe my own stupidity}. A stupidity is also a particular foolish act or idea: {the stupidities of youth}, {bureaucratic stupidities}. The word carries more bite than foolishness—it suggests someone should have known better.

Stupor is a state of near-unconsciousness or severely reduced mental responsiveness, typically caused by shock, drugs, alcohol, or illness. Someone in a stupor may be awake but barely aware of their surroundings: {He sat in a drunken stupor, unable to respond to questions}. The word also describes mental numbness from exhaustion or overwhelming emotion: {The news left her in a stupor}.

Stupors is the plural of stupor, a state of near-unconsciousness or greatly diminished awareness. A person in a stupor is unresponsive to surroundings, whether from shock, drugs, alcohol, or illness: {He found her in one of her drunken stupors}. The word implies a heavy, dulled condition rather than complete unconsciousness.

Sturdy describes something solidly built and able to withstand stress or rough handling: {sturdy furniture}, {sturdy hiking boots}. Applied to people, it suggests physical robustness or mental resilience: {a sturdy constitution}, {sturdy independence}. The word implies reliability without elegance—functional strength rather than delicacy.

A sturgeon is a large freshwater fish prized for its roe, which becomes caviar. Sturgeons are ancient, bony-plated fish found in rivers and coastal waters of the Northern Hemisphere. They can grow enormous—some species exceed fifteen feet—and live for decades. Overfishing for caviar has made several species endangered.

Stutter is to speak with involuntary repetition or prolongation of sounds, especially initial consonants: {He stuttered badly as a child}. The noun names this speech pattern. Beyond speech, stutter describes any halting, repetitive motion or sound: {The engine stuttered and died}. {The lights stuttered before going out}.

Stuttering is a speech pattern marked by involuntary repetitions, prolongations, or blocks—moments when words won't come out smoothly: {He's been stuttering since childhood}. As an adjective, it describes halting or interrupted motion: {The engine made a stuttering sound before dying}. Figuratively, stuttering progress is uneven and faltering: {The economy's stuttering recovery worried investors}.

Stutters is the third-person singular form of the verb stutter, which describes a speech pattern marked by involuntary repetition or prolongation of sounds, syllables, or words. {He stutters when he's nervous.} The word extends to mechanical contexts where something operates in fits and starts rather than smoothly: {The engine stutters before finally dying.} As a noun, stutters are individual instances of this halting speech or action.

A sty is a pen or enclosure for pigs, typically a small, muddy, foul-smelling structure. By extension, any filthy or cluttered space becomes a sty: {Clean up your room—it's a sty}. A sty (also stye) is separately a small, painful swelling on the edge of an eyelid, caused by an infected gland.

A stye is a small, painful, inflamed swelling on the edge of an eyelid, caused by a bacterial infection of a gland or hair follicle. It typically appears as a red bump resembling a pimple and may fill with pus before draining and healing on its own. {I woke up with a stye that made my eye look swollen.} The spelling sty is also used.

Style is the distinctive way something is done, made, or expressed. A writer's style, a style of architecture, a style of dress. Style often suggests elegance or flair: {She has real style}. To style something is to design or arrange it: {He styled her hair for the wedding}. In fashion and design, to style is to create a particular look. A self-styled expert has given themselves that title without official recognition.

Styled means designed or arranged in a particular way, especially regarding appearance or manner. Hair is styled by a professional. A room is styled for a photoshoot. Cars are styled to look sporty or elegant. To be styled something is to be officially named or designated: {He styled himself a visionary}. Self-styled implies a title someone has claimed rather than earned.

Styles is the plural of style—distinct ways of doing, making, or presenting things. Fashion has styles, writing has styles, architecture has styles. {She tried several styles before finding one that suited her}. In computing, styles are formatting rules applied to documents: {The stylesheet defines heading styles}. To style something is to design or arrange it: {She styles hair for a living}.

Stylin is slang for looking good or displaying impressive style, especially in dress or attitude. Often appears with a dropped g to suggest casual cool: {He rolled up to the party stylin in a new leather jacket}. Sometimes paired with profilin: {stylin and profilin}. The term suggests confident self-presentation that others notice and admire.

Styling is the act of arranging or designing something's appearance—hair, clothes, a car, a webpage. A stylist does styling for a living, whether for fashion shoots or interior spaces. In computing, styling refers to the visual formatting applied to content: {The CSS handles all the styling}. Self-styling means giving oneself a title or designation, often unearned: {a self-styled expert}.

Stylish describes something fashionable, elegant, or showing good taste in appearance or design. A stylish {outfit} looks put-together and current. A stylish {restaurant} has appealing décor and atmosphere. The word suggests not just following trends but doing so with flair: {She always looks effortlessly stylish}.

A stylist is someone who cultivates or creates style. A hair stylist cuts and arranges hair. A fashion stylist selects clothing and accessories for photo shoots, celebrities, or everyday clients. In writing, a stylist is someone with distinctive prose style: {She's more stylist than storyteller}. The term implies attention to aesthetics and presentation.

Stylists are professionals who shape appearance or presentation. A hair stylist cuts and arranges hair. A fashion stylist selects clothing for photo shoots, celebrities, or everyday clients. In writing, a stylist is someone with distinctive prose—or an editor who polishes others' work: {The magazine employed several stylists to clean up submitted articles}. The common thread is crafting how something looks or reads.

Stylization is the process of representing something according to a particular style rather than realistically. In art and design, stylization simplifies or exaggerates features for aesthetic effect: {The stylization of the human figure in ancient Egyptian art}. A stylized portrait emphasizes certain characteristics while ignoring others. The term applies across visual arts, theater, literature, and music—anywhere convention or artistic choice shapes representation away from strict naturalism.

To stylize something is to render it in a deliberate, often simplified or exaggerated manner rather than realistically: {stylized flowers on the wallpaper}, {a stylized portrait}. Stylized art emphasizes design elements—clean lines, bold shapes, distinctive patterns—over naturalistic representation. The term can suggest artificiality when applied to behavior or speech: {Her movements were oddly stylized}.

Stylized describes something rendered in a distinctive, non-realistic manner that emphasizes particular features or follows artistic conventions rather than natural appearance. A stylized {portrait} might exaggerate certain facial features. Stylized {violence} in films is choreographed and aesthetically presented rather than realistic. The term often suggests deliberate artifice: {The dance was highly stylized, with precise geometric movements}.

A stylus is a pointed instrument for writing or marking. The original stylus scratched letters into wax tablets; modern versions include the needle that reads vinyl record grooves and the pen-shaped tool for touchscreens and graphics tablets. {She tapped the screen with her stylus.} Plural: styli or styluses.

Stymie means to block or frustrate progress. Originally a golf term for when an opponent's ball lies between yours and the hole, it now describes any situation where someone or something obstructs your path forward: {Budget cuts stymied the research project}. The word emphasizes being thwarted by circumstances rather than direct opposition.

Stymied means blocked or thwarted—unable to proceed because of an obstacle. Originally a golf term for when an opponent's ball blocks your path to the hole, it now applies to any frustrating impasse: {The investigation was stymied by missing records}. {We're completely stymied on how to fix this}.

Styrofoam is a genericized trademark for expanded polystyrene foam, the lightweight white material used for disposable cups, takeout containers, and packing materials. It's technically a brand name for a specific type of insulation board, but common usage applies it to any foam plastic: {The coffee came in a styrofoam cup}. The material is notorious for being non-biodegradable. (Capitalized Styrofoam is the trademark.)

Suave describes a man who is smoothly charming, sophisticated, and socially confident—often with an undertone of superficiality or excessive polish. A suave manner suggests elegant ease in social situations: {a suave diplomat}, {He was too suave to be trusted}. The word carries mild suspicion that the charm may be calculated rather than genuine.

Sub is a noun and verb that is usually a shortening of several words that begin s-u-b: a submarine; a submarine sandwich (one on a long roll or bun); a substitute, or to substitute for someone, such as a teacher (we had a sub today, subbing for the coach); and a subscription: I billed her for the magazine sub. The prefix and adjective sub conveys below, inferior, or subordinate. A subwoofer produces low bass frequencies. A sub par performance is not very good, except in golf.

Subatomic describes anything smaller than an atom or occurring within atoms. Subatomic particles—electrons, protons, neutrons, quarks—are the building blocks of matter at scales below atomic structure. The term appears in physics contexts: {subatomic physics}, {subatomic realm}. Figuratively, it can suggest something vanishingly small or imperceptibly fine-grained.
clues: At the quark and electron level

definition: The subconscious is the part of the mind that operates below conscious awareness—thoughts, memories, and impulses that influence behavior without being directly accessible. {Subconsciously, she'd been avoiding him for weeks.} The term is looser than the technical unconscious in psychology, often used interchangeably in everyday speech: {My subconscious must have known something was wrong.}

A subcontinent is a large, relatively self-contained landmass that forms a distinct part of a continent. The term most often refers to the Indian subcontinent—India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and neighboring countries—set apart from the rest of Asia by the Himalayas. {The cuisine of the subcontinent features complex spice blends.}

To subcontract is to hire another party to perform work you've been contracted to do. A construction company might subcontract electrical work to a specialized firm. The subcontract is the agreement governing this arrangement. The practice is standard in industries where projects require diverse expertise: {They subcontracted the plumbing to a local outfit}.

Subcontracting is hiring another party to perform work you've been contracted to do. A construction company might subcontract electrical work to specialists. The practice allows businesses to take on large projects without maintaining all necessary expertise in-house: {They're subcontracting the software development to a firm in Austin}. The hired party is a subcontractor.

A subcontractor is a person or company hired by a main contractor to perform a specific portion of a larger project. The general contractor builds the house but subcontracts the electrical work, plumbing, or roofing to specialists. {We're waiting on the subcontractor to finish the HVAC installation.} The arrangement creates a chain: the client hires the contractor, who hires subcontractors, each responsible for their piece.

Subcontractors are individuals or companies hired by a primary contractor to perform specific portions of a larger job. A general contractor building a house might hire subcontractors for electrical, plumbing, and roofing work. The arrangement distances the client from the workers actually doing the job: {The company uses subcontractors for all its deliveries}.

A subculture is a group within a larger culture that distinguishes itself through shared interests, values, or practices: {punk subculture}, {gaming subculture}, {the drag subculture}. The term implies both belonging to the mainstream and standing apart from it. Members often signal affiliation through style, language, or behavior that outsiders don't fully understand.

Subcultures is the plural of subculture—a group within a larger culture that distinguishes itself through shared interests, values, or practices. Punks, goths, skaters, and gamers form subcultures. The term implies both belonging to the broader society and standing apart from it: {The city's drag scene was a vibrant subculture with its own stars and hierarchies}.

A subdivision is a part created by dividing something larger. In real estate, a subdivision is a tract of land divided into individual lots for housing development, often used to describe the resulting neighborhood itself: {They live in a subdivision outside the city}. The term applies broadly to any secondary division: administrative subdivisions of a country, subdivisions of a chapter.

Subdivisions are parts created when something larger is divided, or the act of dividing itself. The word appears most often in reference to land development: a subdivision is a tract of land that has been divided into individual lots for building homes, and by extension, the residential neighborhood that results. {They moved to a subdivision outside the city.} In other contexts, subdivisions are simply smaller units within a larger category or organization, such as administrative subdivisions of a country or subdivisions within a company.

To subdue is to bring under control, typically through force or authority. You might subdue an attacker, an uprising, or a wild animal. The word extends to quieter forms of conquest: subduing your emotions means keeping them in check, and subdued lighting or colors are muted, soft, less intense than usual. A subdued person is quiet and restrained, perhaps because something has taken the fight out of them. {The medication helped subdue her anxiety.}

Subdued describes something quieted, softened, or restrained from its natural intensity. A subdued {voice} is hushed; subdued {lighting} is dim; subdued {colors} are muted. A person who is subdued has been made less lively or assertive, often through defeat, disappointment, or exhaustion: {He seemed subdued after the meeting}. The word implies something held back or tamped down rather than simply absent.

Subduing is the act of bringing something under control, typically through force or sustained effort. You subdue an attacker by overpowering them, subdue a fire by containing it, subdue an urge by suppressing it. The word implies overcoming resistance: {After subduing the suspect, officers placed him in handcuffs}. Subdued can also describe something muted or restrained—subdued {lighting}, subdued {colors}, a subdued {mood}.

Subhuman describes someone or something regarded as less than fully human—inferior in dignity, intelligence, or moral worth. The term has been used to justify atrocities, dehumanizing groups to make violence against them seem acceptable: {Nazi propaganda depicted Jews as subhuman}. It can also describe conditions unfit for human beings: {subhuman living conditions}. As a noun, it labels a person so regarded.

The commonest meaning of the noun subject (stress on first syllable) is similar to topic, something that is the focus of attention or study. In grammar, the subject of a sentence is typically the agent associated with the verb. In a monarchy, a subject is like a citizen. The verb subject (stress on last syllable) means to cause someone or something to have an unpleasant experience: Do not subject the animals to torture.

Subjective means based on personal feelings, opinions, or perspectives rather than external facts. A subjective {judgment} reflects individual taste; a subjective {experience} varies from person to person. The opposite is objective. In grammar, subjective refers to the subject of a sentence or the case of pronouns functioning as subjects: {I}, {he}, {she}, {they}.
clues: Dependent on individual point of view

definition: Subjectivity is the quality of being based on personal perspective, feelings, or opinions rather than external facts. It's the opposite of objectivity. A film critic's review reflects her subjectivity—another critic might see the same movie differently. In philosophy, subjectivity concerns the nature of conscious experience: how things seem from the inside. {The subjectivity of pain makes it hard to measure.}

Subjects are things placed under something else—under discussion, under study, under authority. In school, subjects are branches of knowledge: {math}, {history}, {science}. A subject of conversation is what's being talked about. In grammar, the subject performs the action of the verb. A subject of a ruler or government is someone under their authority. In experiments, subjects are people or animals being studied. To subject someone to something is to expose them to it, often unpleasantly: {They subjected him to hours of questioning}.

To subjugate is to bring under complete control, typically by force or conquest. Nations subjugate other nations; colonial powers subjugated indigenous peoples. The word implies domination and the suppression of autonomy: {The emperor sought to subjugate all neighboring kingdoms}. Figuratively, one might subjugate personal desires to duty or ambition.

Subjugated means brought under control or domination, typically by force. A subjugated people has been conquered and made subordinate to another power: {The subjugated population was forced to pay tribute to their new rulers}. The word implies not just defeat but ongoing subordination—kept in a state of submission rather than merely beaten.

Subjugation is the act of bringing someone or something under control, typically by force. Nations subjugate conquered peoples; dictators subjugate populations. The word implies domination and the loss of autonomy: {the subjugation of indigenous tribes}, {economic subjugation}. It can extend to abstract things: {the subjugation of emotion to reason}.

A sublease is a lease granted by a tenant to a third party, transferring some or all of their rights to the property while the original lease remains in effect. The original tenant becomes a sublessor, responsible to both the landlord and subtenant. To sublease is to grant such an arrangement: {She subleased her apartment for the summer while studying abroad}. Many leases prohibit or restrict subleasing.

Subleasing is renting out property you yourself are renting—becoming a landlord to a subtenant while remaining a tenant to your own landlord. The practice is common when someone needs to leave before a lease ends: {She's subleasing her apartment while she's abroad for the semester}. Many leases prohibit or restrict subleasing without the landlord's consent.

To sublet is to rent out property you're renting from someone else. A tenant with a year-long lease might sublet their apartment for the summer while traveling. The noun sublet refers to such an arrangement or the property itself: {We found a sublet near campus}. The landlord's permission is typically required. Past tense: sublet.

Sublets is the plural of sublet—an arrangement where a tenant rents out their leased space to someone else: {She found a sublet for the summer while studying abroad}. Also the verb form: {He sublets his apartment whenever he travels for work}. Sublets often exist in legal gray areas, as many leases prohibit them without landlord approval.

Subletting is renting out property you yourself are renting, typically with the landlord's permission. A tenant who can't break their lease might sublet to someone else for the remaining months: {She's subletting her apartment while she's abroad}. The person who moves in is a subletter or subtenant. Also called subleasing.

Sublimation is the direct transformation of a solid into a gas without passing through a liquid phase—dry ice sublimating into carbon dioxide vapor, or snow disappearing on a cold sunny day. In psychology, sublimation is the channeling of unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities: {He sublimated his aggression through competitive sports}. Both senses share the idea of something transforming into a higher or more refined state.

Sublime describes something of such excellence or grandeur that it inspires awe—beauty, art, or nature so elevated it transcends ordinary experience: {a sublime sunset over the mountains}, {Mozart's sublime compositions}. The word carries a sense of the overwhelming or transcendent. In chemistry, to sublime is to pass directly from solid to gas without becoming liquid, as dry ice does. The verb also means to elevate or refine something base into something pure or noble. (Capitalized Sublime refers to the text editor or band.)

Subliminal describes something that operates below the threshold of conscious awareness. A subliminal {message} in advertising might flash too briefly to register consciously yet still influence behavior. The word often carries sinister connotations—manipulation that bypasses rational thought: {subliminal persuasion}, {subliminal cues}. The opposite is supraliminal, though that word is rarely used outside psychology.

A submachine gun is a compact, lightweight automatic firearm that fires pistol-caliber ammunition. Designed for close-quarters combat, it can be fired from the hip or shoulder and typically uses a detachable box magazine. The category emerged between world wars and includes iconic models like the Thompson and Uzi. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated: {sub-machine gun}, {submachine gun}.

A submarine is a vessel designed to operate underwater, used by navies for warfare and surveillance, and in civilian contexts for research and exploration. The word also works as an adjective meaning underwater: {submarine cables}, {submarine warfare}. As a verb, to submarine is to undermine or sabotage covertly. A submarine sandwich—a sub—is a long sandwich on a cylindrical roll, named for its shape.

Submarines are vessels designed to operate underwater. Military submarines carry torpedoes and missiles; research submarines explore ocean depths. The word also refers to long sandwiches on oblong rolls—also called hoagies, grinders, or heroes depending on region: {I ordered a meatball submarine for lunch}. As a verb, to submarine is to undermine something covertly, or in baseball, to pitch with an extreme underhand motion.

To submerge is to put or go under water or another liquid: {The submarine submerged beneath the ice}. By extension, anything that gets buried or overwhelmed is submerged: {submerged in debt}, {submerged in work}. A submerged truth lies hidden beneath the surface. To submerge yourself in a subject is to immerse yourself completely in studying it.

Submerged means underwater or covered by liquid: {The submerged wreckage lay on the ocean floor}. By extension, something submerged is hidden or obscured: {submerged tensions}, {submerged memories}. A submerged population or community exists beneath notice, overlooked by mainstream society.

A submersible is a vessel designed to operate underwater, typically smaller and more limited in range than a submarine.
