Sweets are candy, confections, or sugary treats. The term is more common in British English, where Americans would say candy: {The children asked for sweets}. Sweets can also refer more broadly to desserts or sweet foods generally: {She has a weakness for sweets}. As a term of endearment, {sweets} addresses someone affectionately.

A sweetshop is a British term for a small retail store that sells candy, chocolates, and other confections. The American equivalent is a candy store. Sweetshops are often associated with childhood nostalgia and may stock traditional sweets alongside modern treats. {The children spent their pocket money at the village sweetshop.}

Sweetshops are British candy stores—small retail establishments selling confectionery, chocolates, and sweets. The word evokes traditional shops with jars of boiled sweets and penny candy: {The children pressed their faces against the sweetshop window}. In American English, the equivalent would be candy store.

The sweet spot is the optimal point where effectiveness is greatest. Originally from sports—the area on a bat, racket, or club face that produces the best hit: {She caught it right on the sweet spot}. Extended to any ideal combination of factors: {The price hits the sweet spot between affordable and premium}. Also spelled as one word.

To sweettalk someone is to use flattery or charm to persuade them: {He sweettalked his way into the VIP section}. The approach is manipulative but not necessarily dishonest—more coaxing than deceiving. As a noun, sweettalk is the flattery itself: {Don't fall for his sweettalk}. Also spelled sweet-talk and sweet talk.

Sweettalking is using flattery or charm to persuade someone, often with manipulative intent: {He was sweettalking her into lending him money}. The term implies insincerity—the words sound nice but serve the speaker's agenda. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated. A sweettalk is an instance of such persuasion; a sweettalker is someone who does it habitually.

Sweetums is a playful term of endearment, typically addressed to a romantic partner or child. It belongs to the category of cutesy pet names like *honeybunch* or *snookums*, often used with exaggerated affection or gentle irony: {Come here, sweetums}. The -ums suffix adds childish charm to *sweet*.

The noun and verb swell have related meanings connected with expanding or growing larger. To swell is to grow larger, especially from injury or infection. When something abstract swells (swelling crowd, swelling population) it increases quickly. A noise that swells becomes louder. Large waves in the ocean, before they crest or break, are called swells. The somewhat old-fashioned adjective swell is used appreciatively, sometimes ironically, for people and things that are agreeable and enjoyable: He’s a really swell guy.

Swelled is the past tense of swell—to expand, increase, or bulge outward. Water swells wood. A river swells after rain. Ranks swell with new recruits. Pride swells the chest. {His ankle swelled after the fall.} {The crowd swelled to thousands.} As a past participle, swelled competes with swollen, which is more common for physical conditions: a {swollen} ankle rather than a {swelled} ankle.

Swelling is the enlargement of a body part, typically caused by fluid accumulation, injury, or inflammation. A swelling is also the raised area itself: {The swelling on her ankle went down after she iced it}. Beyond the physical, swelling describes any gradual increase in size, intensity, or volume—a swelling {crowd}, swelling {music}, or swelling {emotions}. As a participle of swell, it captures the process of becoming larger or more pronounced.

Swells serves as both noun and verb forms of swell. Ocean swells are long, rolling waves that travel great distances from storms. In older slang, swells are fashionable, well-dressed people of high social standing: {The swells arrived in their carriages}. As a verb: {The river swells after heavy rain}, {Pride swells in her chest}, {The crowd swells as showtime approaches}.

Swelter is a verb, noun, and adjective that all have to do with heat. If you swelter, you suffer from heat. If you swelter through something, you endure it despite the heat. As an adjective, swelter is a bit old-fashioned. The more common form, sweltering, describes a very hot and uncomfortable condition: We had a sweltering summer.

Sweltering describes oppressively hot and humid conditions—the kind of heat that makes you sweat just standing still: {a sweltering August afternoon}, {The apartment was sweltering without air conditioning}. The word emphasizes discomfort more than mere temperature. To swelter is to suffer in such heat.

Swept is the past tense and past participle of sweep. To sweep is to clean a surface with a broom or brush, moving debris away: {She swept the kitchen floor}. The motion extends to anything moving quickly across a space: {His eyes swept the room}, {Fire swept through the building}. A sweeping {victory} or sweeping {changes} are comprehensive and decisive. To be {swept up} in something is to be carried along by it: {They got swept up in the excitement}.

Swerve is a sudden turn or deviation from a straight path. A car swerves to avoid an obstacle; a conversation swerves into unexpected territory. To swerve is to make such a movement: {The driver swerved at the last second}. In slang, to swerve someone is to dodge or avoid them, especially romantically: {She swerved him hard}.

Swerved is the past tense of swerve, meaning to turn sharply or veer suddenly from a straight course: {She swerved to avoid the deer}. Often implies an abrupt, evasive movement—whether literal or figurative: {He swerved away from the topic whenever it came up}.

Swerves is the plural noun and third-person singular verb form of swerve. To swerve is to turn sharply or change direction abruptly, usually to avoid something: {The driver swerved to miss the deer}. The noun swerve is an instance of this sudden change in course. Figuratively, swerve can describe any abrupt departure from an expected path or position: {The plot takes a wild swerve in the third act}. In slang, to swerve someone is to dodge or avoid them.

Swerving is turning sharply to one side, usually to avoid something: {The driver swerved to miss the deer}. The word implies sudden, reactive movement rather than planned course changes. Figuratively, to swerve is to deviate from a path or commitment: {He never swerved from his principles}. In slang, swerving someone means deliberately avoiding or rejecting them.

Swift describes rapid movement or action. A swift {current} moves fast; a swift {response} comes without delay. The word often suggests smooth, effortless speed rather than frantic rushing: {The hawk made a swift descent}. A swift is also a small bird known for its fast, agile flight and its habit of spending most of its life airborne. (Capitalized Swift refers to the singer, the writer, or the programming language.)

Swifts are small, fast-flying birds with long, curved wings, often seen darting through the sky catching insects. They resemble swallows but belong to a different family. Swifts spend most of their lives airborne—eating, sleeping, and even mating on the wing. The word also names a reel for winding yarn: {She wound the skein onto the swift}.

A swig is a large gulp of liquid, especially an alcoholic drink taken directly from the bottle or container: {He took a swig of whiskey}. The verb means to drink this way: {She swigged her beer and slammed the glass down}. The word suggests casual, enthusiastic drinking rather than refined sipping.

Swigging is drinking in large gulps, typically from a bottle or container held to the mouth rather than poured into a glass. The word suggests informal, enthusiastic consumption—you might swig beer at a barbecue but wouldn't swig wine at a formal dinner. {He was swigging whiskey straight from the bottle.} The noun swig denotes a single large gulp taken this way.

Swigs are large gulps of a drink, typically taken directly from a bottle or container rather than sipped from a glass: {He took several swigs from the flask}. The word usually appears with alcoholic beverages but applies to any drink consumed this way. As a verb, to swig is to drink in this manner: {She swigged her coffee and headed out}.

Swill is liquid garbage fed to pigs, or by extension any unappetizing food or drink: {This coffee tastes like swill}. To swill is to drink greedily or in large quantities: {They swilled beer until closing time}. Swill also means to rinse or splash with water: {swill out the bucket}.

Swim is to move through water by moving the body—arms, legs, fins, or tail. Fish swim naturally; humans learn to swim. The word extends to floating or being immersed: {eyes swimming with tears}, {bacon swimming in grease}. To swim in something is to have an abundance of it. If your head swims, you feel dizzy or disoriented. A swim is a session of swimming: {I went for a swim}.

A swimmer is someone who swims, whether for recreation, exercise, or competition. The word applies broadly—from children splashing in pools to Olympic athletes racing for medals. A strong swimmer handles water confidently; a weak swimmer may struggle. In biology, swimmer can describe any creature that moves through water: {Sea turtles are powerful swimmers}.

Swimmers are people who swim, whether for exercise, competition, or recreation. The word also names various creatures adapted for swimming, and in casual speech, refers to sperm cells: {His swimmers were tested at the fertility clinic}. Swimmer's ear is an infection of the ear canal from retained water.

Swimming is propelling yourself through water using movements of the limbs. As an activity, it ranges from leisurely recreation to competitive sport to survival skill. The word also works as an adjective: a swimming {pool}, a swimming {hole}. If your head is swimming, you feel dizzy or disoriented. If something is swimming {in} liquid, it's surrounded by plenty of it: {The pancakes were swimming in syrup}.

Swimmingly means smoothly and successfully, without any problems or obstacles: {The project is going swimmingly}, {Everything proceeded swimmingly until the power went out}. The image is of gliding through water with ease. The word often carries a slightly old-fashioned or playful tone.

A swimsuit is a garment worn for swimming or sunbathing. Women's swimsuits range from one-piece designs to bikinis; men's are typically trunks or briefs. The term covers athletic competition wear and casual beachwear alike: {She packed three swimsuits for the vacation}. Also called a bathing suit or swimming costume (British).

Swimsuits are garments designed for swimming or water activities. The term covers everything from brief bikinis to full-coverage one-pieces to men's trunks. {She packed three swimsuits for the beach vacation}. Also called swimwear, bathing suits, or in British English, swimming costumes.

Swimwear is clothing designed for swimming or beach activities—bathing suits, bikinis, trunks, and the like. The term functions as a retail and fashion category: {the swimwear section}, {swimwear trends for summer}. It's slightly more formal than "bathing suit" and broader than any specific garment.

To swindle is to cheat someone out of money or property through deception: {They swindled him out of his life savings}. A swindle is an instance of such fraud. The word suggests elaborate schemes rather than simple theft—confidence games, fake investments, fraudulent contracts. A swindler is someone who makes a practice of it.

Swindled is the past tense of swindle, meaning cheated or defrauded through deception. Someone who has been swindled was tricked out of money or property: {She was swindled out of her life savings by a fake investment scheme}. The word implies deliberate manipulation rather than simple theft.

A swindler is someone who cheats others out of money or property through deception. The word implies deliberate fraud rather than mere dishonesty—a swindler gains trust, then exploits it: {The swindler convinced retirees to invest their savings in a fake company}. Con artist and grifter are near synonyms.

Swindlers are people who cheat others out of money or property through deception. The word implies deliberate fraud rather than opportunistic theft—swindlers gain trust before exploiting it. {The swindlers posed as investment advisors and disappeared with their clients' savings.}

Swindles are acts of fraud or deception for financial gain. A swindle involves tricking someone out of money or property through false promises or manipulation: {The investment scheme was one of the largest swindles in the company's history}. To swindle is to cheat in this way: {He swindled elderly victims out of their life savings}.

Swindling is the act of cheating someone out of money or property through deception or fraud. The word emphasizes deliberate trickery—a swindler gains trust before exploiting it: {He was arrested for swindling elderly investors out of their retirement savings}. Swindling implies a scheme rather than a single dishonest act.

Swine is the formal or technical term for pigs, used especially in agriculture and veterinary contexts: {swine flu}, {swine fever}. The plural is also swine. As an insult, swine means a contemptible person—greedy, cruel, or morally repugnant: {He's an absolute swine}. The insult sounds slightly old-fashioned or British.

Meanings of swing, noun, verb, and adjective, typically involve motion between two extremes or sides (pendulum swing), or in relation to a fixed point, like the way you swing a golf club or a bat, or the way a door swings open. A swing is an instance of swinging, as well as a piece of playground equipment on which children can swing. A mood swing is a sudden change from elation to depression, or vice versa. Swing voters are those whose votes may decide the outcome.

A swinger is someone who swings—on a playground, at a ball, or through life with carefree energy. The word took on specific meaning in the 1960s for people who engage in partner-swapping or group sex, typically married couples who have sex with other couples by mutual arrangement: {They met other swingers at the club}. A swinger can also simply mean someone fashionable or uninhibited.

Swingers are people who engage in recreational partner-swapping or group sex with other couples, typically as part of an organized social scene: {They met other swingers at a club downtown}. The term emerged in the 1960s and 70s alongside the sexual revolution. Outside this context, a swinger is simply someone lively and uninhibited, though this older sense has largely been eclipsed.

Swinging describes rhythmic back-and-forth motion, like a pendulum or a child on a playground swing. In music, swinging refers to the lilting rhythmic feel of jazz: {a swinging big band number}. As slang, swinging means lively and fashionable, especially evoking the 1960s: {swinging London}. It also describes the practice of couples exchanging sexual partners: {a swinging lifestyle}, {swingers' parties}.

Swings is most often the plural of swing, the playground apparatus or the back-and-forth motion it makes. The verb swing covers this movement and extends to punches thrown in an arc, mood changes, and shifts in opinion or fortune: {The election swings on turnout in three counties}. In music, swing is a jazz style with a driving rhythm that makes you want to move. If something is in full swing, it's at peak activity. The phrase swings and roundabouts suggests gains and losses that balance out.

A swingset is an outdoor play structure consisting of a frame—usually metal or wood—from which one or more swings hang on chains or ropes. Found in backyards, playgrounds, and parks, swingsets often include additional features like slides or climbing bars. The term is sometimes written as two words or hyphenated: {swing set}, {swing-set}. {The kids spent all afternoon on the swingset.}

Swingsets are outdoor play structures featuring suspended seats that children pump back and forth. A typical swingset has a metal or wooden frame supporting two or more swings, often alongside slides or climbing bars. The word usually appears as two words or hyphenated: {swing set}, {swing-set}.

Swipe is a sweeping motion—to strike or move with a broad, quick stroke. You might {swipe at a fly} or {take a swipe at} an opponent, literally or figuratively. To swipe something is also to steal it: {Someone swiped my phone}. On touchscreens, swiping means dragging a finger across the surface to navigate: {swipe right} on a dating app to indicate interest, {swipe left} to pass. To swipe a card is to run it through a reader.

Swiped is the past tense of swipe. To swipe is to move something with a sweeping motion—originally striking or stealing with a quick grab: {Someone swiped my wallet}. The dominant modern sense involves dragging a finger across a touchscreen: {She swiped through the photos}. On dating apps, swiping right signals interest, swiping left rejection: {I swiped right on him but we never matched}.

A swiper is someone who swipes—whether swiping a credit card, swiping through dating profiles, or swiping something in the sense of stealing it. The word gained cultural currency through the cartoon fox Swiper in *Dora the Explorer*, whose catchphrase "Swiper, no swiping!" made it familiar to a generation of children. In interface design, a swiper is a component that allows users to navigate by swiping: {The image swiper lets you browse the gallery}.

Swipes is the plural of swipe, a sweeping motion or stroke. A swipe can be a criticism or verbal jab: {He took swipes at his opponents during the debate}. In digital contexts, swipes are the finger gestures used to navigate touchscreens—scrolling through photos, dismissing notifications, or indicating interest on dating apps: {She got dozens of right swipes on her profile}.

Swiping is the action of moving a finger across a touchscreen to navigate, dismiss, or select. On dating apps, swiping right signals interest while swiping left rejects: {I spent an hour swiping on Tinder}. The older sense—stealing something quickly—persists: {Someone's been swiping lunches from the break room fridge}.

Swirl describes circular or spiral motion—liquid moving in curves, smoke coiling upward, dancers spinning. As a noun, it's the pattern itself: {a swirl of cream in coffee}, {swirls of color}. Things swirl when they move in curving paths or create spiral shapes: {Leaves swirled in the wind}. Figuratively, thoughts or emotions swirl when they feel chaotic or overwhelming: {Rumors swirled around the resignation}.

A swirlie is a prank in which someone's head is forced into a toilet bowl while the toilet is flushed, creating a swirling effect around the victim's head. It is associated with bullying, particularly in school settings, and appears frequently in teen movies and television shows depicting hazing or torment by older students. {The seniors threatened freshmen with swirlies during orientation week.}

Swirling describes circular or spiral motion—liquid moving in a vortex, leaves caught in wind, or fog drifting in curling patterns: {She sat swirling the wine in her glass}. The word extends to confused or chaotic movement: {swirling rumors}, {swirling emotions}. Things that swirl seem to move without clear direction, caught up in their own turbulence.

Swirls is the plural of swirl—circular or spiral patterns of movement or shape. Water swirls down a drain; cream swirls in coffee; decorative swirls adorn a cake. The verb swirls describes this spinning motion: {Dust swirls in the wind}, {Rumors swirled about the merger}. The word suggests graceful, continuous curves rather than sharp angles.

Swirly describes something characterized by swirling patterns or motion—curves that spiral or coil: {swirly handwriting}, {a swirly design on the fabric}. The word has a casual, slightly playful quality. A swirly is also slang for the prank of dunking someone's head in a toilet and flushing: {The bullies gave him a swirly}.

Swish captures the sound of something moving quickly through air or water—a soft, rushing hiss: {the swish of her silk dress}, {windshield wipers swishing back and forth}. In basketball, a swish is a shot that passes through the net without touching the rim. As an adjective, swish means elegantly fashionable, especially in British English: {a swish restaurant}. The word is also dated slang for effeminate or gay, now largely replaced by other terms.

Swished is the past tense of swish, which means to move with a soft rushing or rustling sound: {Her silk dress swished as she walked}. It also describes moving something with a sweeping motion: {The horse swished its tail at the flies}. In basketball, to swish a shot is to sink it cleanly through the net without touching the rim: {He swished the three-pointer at the buzzer}.

Swishes is the plural noun and third-person verb form of swish. A swish is a soft rushing sound, like fabric brushing against itself or a basketball passing cleanly through the net: {Nothing but net—three swishes in a row}. To swish is to move with that sound: {Her skirt swishes when she walks}. Swish can also mean stylishly elegant, or serve as dated slang for effeminate, often applied to gay men.

Swishing is the sound of rapid movement through air or liquid—a soft, rushing, frictional noise: {the swishing of skirts}, {windshield wipers swishing back and forth}. The word is onomatopoeic, imitating what it describes. In basketball, a swishing shot passes through the net without touching the rim.

Swishy describes movement or sound that suggests swishing—a light, brushing, rustling quality. A swishy skirt moves with flowing motion; swishy hair swings and bounces. The word can also mean effeminate, describing mannerisms stereotypically associated with gay men: {He's a little swishy but so what?} This sense ranges from affectionate to derogatory depending on speaker and context.

The idea of two things, and movement or change from one to the other, is inherent in most meanings of switch. If you switch allegiances, suppliers, or phones, you abandon one and start with another. If you switch back to something, you return to a thing that you used before. A switch is an act or instance of switching (make the switch!), or a device that enables some kind of switching: light switch, railroad switch. As a concrete noun, a switch is a flexible whip or rod.

A switcharoo is a sudden or sneaky exchange—swapping one thing for another, often to deceive or surprise: {They pulled the old switcharoo and replaced the real diamond with a fake}. The word is playful and informal, typically appearing in phrases like {pull a switcharoo} or {the old switcharoo}.

A switcharoo is a sudden or sneaky exchange, usually meant to deceive or surprise: {They pulled the old switcharoo and swapped the real diamond for a fake}. The word is playful and informal, often appearing in the phrase {the old switcharoo}. On Reddit, it names a running joke where commenters deliberately misinterpret which noun a statement refers to.

A switchback is a road or trail that zigzags up a steep slope, each segment reversing direction from the one before: {The hiking trail switchbacked up the mountain}. The design reduces the grade, making ascent manageable for vehicles or hikers. In British usage, a switchback can also mean a roller coaster. As a verb, to switchback is to follow such a winding course.

Switchbacks are sharp zigzag turns in a road or trail, typically on a steep slope where a straight path would be too steep to navigate. Mountain roads and hiking trails use switchbacks to gain elevation gradually: {The trail made a dozen switchbacks before reaching the summit}. The term also applies to roller coasters with similar zigzag patterns.

A switchblade is a knife with a blade that springs open at the press of a button, designed for quick one-handed deployment. The mechanism made switchblades popular in mid-20th-century gang iconography, leading to legal restrictions in many jurisdictions: {He pulled a switchblade from his pocket}. Also called a flick knife in British English.

A switchblade is a knife with a blade that springs open at the push of a button, designed for quick one-handed deployment. The mechanism made them associated with street violence and gang culture, leading to legal restrictions in many jurisdictions. {He pulled a switchblade from his pocket.} Also called a flick knife in British English.

A switchboard is a panel or system for routing electrical connections, especially telephone calls. Early telephone switchboards required human operators to physically connect calls by plugging cables into jacks. The term now applies to any central routing system: {The receptionist operates the switchboard}. Figuratively, anything that coordinates multiple inputs functions as a switchboard: {The brain's prefrontal cortex acts as a switchboard for decision-making}.

Switched is the past tense and past participle of switch, covering its various meanings. If you switched something, you changed it, often abruptly or completely: {She switched careers after ten years in finance}. You might have switched places with someone, or switched channels on the television. In electrical contexts, switched describes something controlled by a switch: {a switched outlet}. If someone switched on you, they changed allegiance or, in slang, informed on you to authorities.

A switcheroo is an unexpected or sneaky exchange, substitution, or reversal—typically one intended to deceive or catch someone off guard. The word is informal and often playful, suggesting a trick or sudden change rather than a straightforward swap. {The old switcheroo} is a common phrase describing a classic bait-and-switch maneuver. {They pulled a switcheroo on us at the last minute.}

A switcheroo is a sudden, often sneaky exchange or substitution—swapping one thing for another when no one's looking or expecting it: {They pulled the old switcheroo and replaced the real diamond with a fake}. The plural switcheroos describes multiple such swaps. The word is playful and informal, suggesting trickery or mischief rather than serious deception.

Switches are devices that open or close electrical circuits, or redirect flow from one path to another. Light switches control room lighting; railroad switches direct trains between tracks. To switch is to change or exchange: {She switched seats with me}, {He switched careers}. A switch can also be a thin flexible rod for striking—to switch someone is to hit them with one. In BDSM contexts, a switch is someone who alternates between dominant and submissive roles.

Switching is the act of changing from one thing to another—switching channels, switching sides, switching jobs. In BDSM, switching means alternating between dominant and submissive roles, and a switch is someone who enjoys both. To switch can also mean to strike with a thin flexible rod (a switch), as in old-fashioned corporal punishment: {Grandma threatened to switch our legs if we misbehaved}.

A switchyard is a railroad yard where cars are sorted and assembled into trains, typically using a series of switches and tracks to route cars to different destinations. The term also applies to electrical substations where power lines converge and voltage is transformed or redirected: {The storm damaged the switchyard, causing widespread outages}.

A swivel is a coupling that allows connected parts to rotate independently—a swivel chair spins on its base, a swivel lamp adjusts direction. To swivel is to turn or pivot: {She swiveled around to face him}. {His head swiveled toward the sound.} The word suggests quick, rotational movement rather than full-body turning.

Swivels is the plural of swivel—a device that allows rotation without tangling, like the coupling on a dog leash or fishing line. To swivel is to turn or pivot: {She swiveled in her chair to face him}. Swivel appears in compounds: {swivel chair}, {swivel-hipped}. Figuratively, to {swivel} between options is to shift attention back and forth.

Swole is slang for muscular, describing someone with visibly developed muscles from weight training: {He's been hitting the gym—dude is swole}. The word comes from swollen, suggesting muscles that have expanded from exercise. It carries an approving tone, often used admiringly or as a goal: {trying to get swole for summer}.

Swollen describes something that has expanded beyond its normal size, typically from fluid accumulation, pressure, or inflammation. A sprained ankle swells; so do rivers after heavy rain. {Her eyes were swollen from crying.} Figuratively, swollen can suggest excess or inflation: {swollen with pride}, {swollen ranks of protesters}. The word is the past participle of swell, though swelled also serves that function.

Swoon is to faint or lose consciousness, typically from overwhelming emotion. The word now appears more often in its figurative sense—to be overwhelmed with delight or admiration: {Fans swooned when he took the stage}, {a swoon-worthy performance}. The noun names the faint itself or the state of rapturous absorption: {She fell into a swoon}.

Swooned is the past tense of swoon—to faint or lose consciousness, typically from overwhelming emotion. The word appears most often in historical or romantic contexts: {She swooned when she saw the blood}. In modern use, swoon is usually figurative, expressing intense admiration or desire: {Fans swooned over the actor's performance}.

Swooning is fainting or losing consciousness, typically from strong emotion, heat, or shock. The word now appears more often in its figurative sense—being overwhelmed by romantic attraction or admiration: {Fans were swooning over the lead singer}. The literal faint has become old-fashioned; the metaphorical swoon thrives.

Swoons is the plural noun or third-person verb form of swoon. To swoon is to faint, especially from overwhelming emotion—historically from shock, heat, or tight corsets. The word now more often describes being overcome by romantic or aesthetic feeling without actually losing consciousness: {She swoons every time he walks by}, {Fans swooned over the new album}. A swoon is such a moment of being overwhelmed.

Swoonworthy describes someone or something so attractive, romantic, or appealing that it could make you swoon—overwhelmed with admiration or desire. The word applies most often to romantic interests, celebrity crushes, or moments in fiction: {That scene where he confesses his love is absolutely swoonworthy}. Also used for aesthetic pleasures: {swoonworthy desserts}, {swoonworthy architecture}.

Swoop is a swift, sweeping descent—the motion of a bird diving toward prey or a plane dropping altitude suddenly. The word captures both speed and the curved arc of the movement: {The hawk swooped down on the rabbit}. To swoop in figuratively is to arrive suddenly and take action: {She swooped in and solved the problem}. In {one fell swoop} means all at once, in a single decisive action.

Swooped is the past tense of swoop—to descend rapidly, as a bird diving on prey: {The hawk swooped down and seized the mouse}. By extension, to move suddenly toward something: {She swooped in and grabbed the last donut}. Police or authorities swoop when they conduct sudden raids: {Officers swooped on the warehouse at dawn}.

Swooping describes a swift, curving descent or movement—the motion of a bird diving toward prey, or a hand sweeping down to grab something. The word captures both speed and arc: {A hawk came swooping down from the sky}. Figuratively, someone swooping in arrives suddenly and decisively: {She swooped in at the last minute to save the deal}.

Swoops is the third-person singular of swoop—to descend rapidly, as a bird of prey diving toward its target: {The hawk swoops down on the mouse}. By extension, anything that moves with similar sudden downward motion swoops: {She swoops in at the last minute to claim credit}. A swoop can also be a sweeping grab or raid.

Swoosh is both a sound and a movement—the rush of air or liquid passing swiftly: {The curtain swooshed open}, {He heard the swoosh of skis on snow}. The word imitates what it describes. As a noun, it also refers to a curved shape suggesting motion, most notably the Nike logo: {the iconic swoosh}.

Swooshes is the plural of swoosh—a rushing or rustling sound, or a sweeping movement that produces one: {The swooshes of passing cars kept her awake}. As a verb form, swooshes describes making that sound or motion: {Her skirt swooshes when she walks}. The word is onomatopoeic, imitating the sound itself.

A sword is a weapon with a long metal blade and a handle, designed for cutting or thrusting. Swords were primary weapons in warfare and personal combat from ancient times through the Middle Ages, before firearms made them obsolete on battlefields. They remain important in ceremonial contexts, martial arts, and as symbols of authority or honor. To {cross swords} with someone is to engage in conflict or debate. The {sword of Damocles} refers to imminent danger or a precarious situation.

A swordfight is combat between people wielding swords, whether in historical battle, sport, or staged performance. The term extends to any dramatic blade-to-blade confrontation: {The movie's climactic swordfight lasted ten minutes}. Figuratively, a swordfight is any sharp verbal or intellectual clash: {The debate turned into a swordfight over tax policy}.

Swordfighting is combat or competitive sport using swords. Historical swordfighting encompassed dueling and battlefield combat; modern practice includes Olympic fencing, historical European martial arts (HEMA), and staged combat for film and theater. The word also describes combat in video games and fantasy settings: {The game's swordfighting mechanics feel realistic}.

Swordfights are combat encounters using swords, whether actual battles or staged performances. The word evokes dueling, fencing, or cinematic action sequences: {The movie featured elaborate swordfights}. Figuratively, any sharp verbal or intellectual clash: {The debate devolved into swordfights over policy details}.

A swordfish is a large ocean fish with a long, flat, sword-shaped upper jaw. Prized as a game fish and for its firm, mild flesh, swordfish is commonly served as steaks: {grilled swordfish with lemon butter}. The plural is swordfish or swordfishes.

Swordplay is fighting or fencing with swords, whether in actual combat, sport, or theatrical performance. The word extends to any clever back-and-forth exchange resembling a duel: {The interview featured witty swordplay between host and guest}. Swordplay in film often involves elaborately choreographed sequences.

Swords are bladed weapons with long metal blades and hilts, designed for cutting or thrusting. Before firearms, swords were primary military weapons; now they're ceremonial, collectible, or used in fencing. To {cross swords} is to clash or argue. A {sword of Damocles} is an ever-present threat. {The pen is mightier than the sword} values persuasion over force.

A swordsman is a person skilled in fighting with a sword. The term appears most often in historical contexts, fantasy fiction, and martial arts: {He trained for years to become a master swordsman}. The word typically refers to men, though swordswoman exists for female practitioners.

Swordsmanship is skill in fighting with a sword—the techniques, training, and art of blade combat. The term covers both historical martial traditions and modern competitive fencing. By extension, swordsmanship can describe any display of skillful verbal sparring or intellectual dueling: {His rhetorical swordsmanship was unmatched in debate}.

Swordsmen is the plural of swordsman—a person skilled in fighting with a sword. The term appears most often in historical contexts, fantasy fiction, and martial arts: {The swordsmen clashed on the battlefield}. A swordswoman is the female equivalent, though swordsmen sometimes covers both.

A swordsmith is a craftsman who forges swords. The term distinguishes this specialized work from general blacksmithing, emphasizing the skill required to create functional blades. Swordsmiths appear frequently in discussions of Japanese katana-making, where the craft carries particular cultural prestige: {The swordsmith folded the steel dozens of times}.

Swordsmithing is the craft of forging swords—shaping steel through heating, hammering, and tempering to create bladed weapons. The term distinguishes this specialized metalwork from general blacksmithing, emphasizing the skill required to produce blades that balance sharpness, flexibility, and durability. {He studied traditional Japanese swordsmithing techniques.}

Swordsmiths are craftspeople who forge swords. The term emphasizes traditional metalworking skill—heating, hammering, and tempering steel into blades. Japanese swordsmiths who made katanas are particularly renowned. The word appears in historical and fantasy contexts: {The swordsmith spent weeks folding the steel}.

A swordswoman is a woman skilled in the use of a sword, whether in combat, sport, or ceremonial contexts. The term parallels swordsman but specifies female gender, and appears in historical fiction, fantasy literature, and discussions of martial arts. {The swordswoman defeated three opponents in the tournament.} In fencing and kendo, female practitioners may be called swordswomen, though the gender-neutral fencer or practitioner is more common in competitive contexts.

Swore is the past tense of swear. Someone who swore made an oath or promise: {She swore to tell the truth}. Swore also means used profanity: {He swore when he stubbed his toe}. The past participle is sworn: {They had sworn allegiance}.

Sworn is the past participle of swear, used in contexts involving oaths and solemn declarations. A sworn {statement} or sworn {testimony} is given under oath, with legal consequences for lying. Sworn {enemies} are bound by deep, enduring hostility. A sworn {officer} has taken an official oath of duty. {He was sworn in as president.}

Swung is the past tense and past participle of swing. Something swung has moved in an arc or changed direction: {The door swung open}, {Opinion swung against the war}. In jazz, music that swung had rhythmic drive and groove: {That band really swung}.

A sycamore is a large deciduous tree. In North America, it refers to the American plane tree, with mottled bark that peels in patches to reveal pale inner layers. In Britain, the word typically means a maple species. The biblical sycamore is a fig tree native to the Middle East: {Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore to see Jesus}.

Sycamores is the plural of sycamore, a large deciduous tree with distinctive mottled bark that peels away in patches, revealing pale wood beneath. In North America, sycamore refers to the American plane tree; in Britain, it's a maple species. The biblical sycamore is yet another tree entirely—a fig native to the Middle East. {The sycamores along the riverbank provided welcome shade.}

Sycophancy is excessive flattery or fawning behavior toward someone in power, typically to gain favor or advantage. The sycophant praises indiscriminately, agrees reflexively, and never offers honest criticism. {The CEO surrounded himself with yes-men, and the sycophancy eventually cost the company millions.} The word carries strong contempt—sycophancy implies both dishonesty and weakness.

Sycophant is a term used to negatively characterize someone who cultivates favor with people in power by acting agreeable and servile: The King has always been surrounded by sycophants who tells him what he wants to hear. Sycophant has several synonyms, such as parasite, toady, and leech.

Sycophants are people who flatter others excessively to gain advantage—yes-men, toadies, brownnosers. The word carries strong disapproval: sycophants are insincere, self-serving, and often surround those in power. {The CEO surrounded himself with sycophants who never challenged his decisions.} {She dismissed his compliments as sycophancy.}

A syllable is a unit of spoken language consisting of a single uninterrupted sound, typically containing a vowel with or without surrounding consonants. Words break into syllables: "cat" has one, "kitten" has two, "syllable" has three. Syllables determine rhythm in speech and poetry, and they guide where words can be hyphenated in writing.

Syllables are the basic rhythmic units of spoken language—each one built around a vowel sound, often with consonants attached. Words break naturally into syllables: "cat" has one, "kitten" has two, "syllable" has three. Counting syllables matters for poetry, pronunciation, and teaching children to read. {How many syllables in "banana"?}

A syllabus is an outline of topics to be covered in a course or text. Professors distribute syllabi at the start of a semester detailing readings, assignments, and exam dates: {The syllabus says the final paper is due December 15th}. The plural is syllabi or syllabuses.

Sylphs are slender, graceful spirits of the air in Renaissance and later mythology—invisible beings inhabiting the atmosphere. The word now describes any slender, graceful woman or girl: {She moved like a sylph across the stage}. The adjective sylphlike captures this quality of ethereal delicacy.

Two organisms live in symbiosis when one supplies an essential element to the other, or each supplies an essential element to the other. The organism we call lichens, for example, is actually a fungus and an alga living in symbiosis. People use symbiosis more generally to talk about any relationship in which two things contribute to each other in a way that fosters dependency. The related adjective is symbiotic.

A symbiote is an organism that lives in close physical association with another organism, typically to the benefit of both. The term gained widespread currency through comic books and science fiction, where symbiotes are often depicted as alien life forms that bond with human hosts, sometimes parasitically. In scientific contexts, the preferred term is symbiont. {The alien symbiote granted its host superhuman abilities.}

Symbiotic describes a relationship where different organisms live in close association, typically to mutual benefit. The term comes from biology—lichens are symbiotic partnerships between fungi and algae—but extends to any interdependent relationship: {The two companies developed a symbiotic arrangement, each supplying what the other lacked}. A symbiotic relationship implies that both parties gain from the connection, though in biology, symbiosis technically includes parasitic relationships where only one benefits.

A symbol is something that represents something else by association or convention. A dove symbolizes peace; a skull symbolizes death. Letters are symbols for sounds, and mathematical symbols stand for operations or quantities. The word extends to any object, image, or mark that carries meaning beyond itself: {The ring became a symbol of their commitment}. To symbolize is to serve as or represent through symbols.

Symbolic describes something that represents something else through association or convention rather than literal resemblance. A dove is symbolic of peace; a wedding ring is symbolic of commitment. The symbolic meaning of an act often matters more than its practical effect: {The gesture was purely symbolic}. In logic and mathematics, symbolic refers to the use of symbols rather than words: {symbolic logic}.

Symbolism is the use of symbols to represent ideas, qualities, or concepts beyond their literal meaning. A dove may stand for peace, a skull for death. Writers, artists, and filmmakers employ symbolism to add layers of meaning: {The novel's water imagery carries obvious symbolism about rebirth}. The term also describes the practice of interpreting things symbolically: {Critics have found Christian symbolism throughout the work}. (Capitalized Symbolism is a 19th-century artistic movement.)

To symbolize is to represent something abstract through a concrete image or object. A dove symbolizes peace; a heart symbolizes love. The verb works in both directions—the dove symbolizes peace, and we can say peace is symbolized by the dove. Things that symbolize needn't be physical: {Her resignation symbolized the movement's collapse}.

Symbolizes is the verb form of symbol—to represent something abstract through a concrete image or object. A dove symbolizes peace; a ring symbolizes commitment. The word implies a conventional or widely understood association rather than a personal one: {The torch symbolizes knowledge}. Things can also symbolize unintentionally: {His empty chair symbolized everything we'd lost}.

Symbols are things that represent something else by association or convention. A dove symbolizes peace; a skull symbolizes death. Letters are symbols for sounds, and numbers are symbols for quantities. National flags, religious icons, and corporate logos all function as symbols. In computing, symbols include characters like @ and #. The verb symbolize means to serve as a symbol for something: {The broken clock symbolized their failed marriage}.

Symmetric means having corresponding parts that mirror each other across a dividing line or point. A butterfly's wings are symmetric. In mathematics, a symmetric relation works in both directions—if A relates to B, then B relates to A. The word is interchangeable with symmetrical, though symmetric appears more often in technical contexts: {a symmetric matrix}, {symmetric encryption}.

Symmetrical describes something with parts that mirror each other across a dividing line or point. A symmetrical face has features evenly balanced on both sides. Symmetrical can extend beyond physical form to describe balanced arrangements: {a symmetrical argument}, {symmetrical responsibilities}. The shorter form symmetric appears mainly in technical contexts.

Symmetries is the plural of symmetry, denoting instances or types of balanced, proportional arrangement. In geometry and physics, symmetries describe properties that remain unchanged under certain transformations—rotation, reflection, or translation: {The crystal's symmetries determine its optical properties}. Artists and architects exploit visual symmetries to create harmony and balance. In abstract use, symmetries can refer to correspondences or parallels between different domains: {curious symmetries between their two careers}.

Symmetry is balance achieved through corresponding parts—elements that mirror, repeat, or match across a dividing line or central point. A butterfly's wings have bilateral symmetry; a snowflake has radial symmetry. The concept extends beyond geometry: {the symmetry of their relationship}, {a pleasing symmetry between the book's opening and closing chapters}. In physics, symmetry describes invariance under transformation—properties that remain unchanged when a system is rotated, reflected, or shifted.

Sympathetic describes a feeling of understanding and care for someone else's suffering or misfortune: {She was sympathetic when I told her about losing my job}. A sympathetic person is one who tends to show such feelings. The word extends to things that are agreeable or compatible: a sympathetic {portrayal} presents its subject favorably, and sympathetic {characters} in fiction are ones the audience can root for. In anatomy and physiology, the sympathetic nervous system controls involuntary responses like heart rate and digestion, particularly the "fight or flight" response.

Sympathies is most often encountered in expressions of condolence: {Please accept my sympathies on the loss of your father}. The plural suggests multiple feelings or gestures of compassion directed toward someone in grief or hardship. Sympathies can also mean inclinations or loyalties: {Her political sympathies lie with the left}. One's sympathies are where one's support naturally flows.

Sympathise is the British spelling of sympathize. To sympathise is to share or understand another's feelings, especially their suffering or difficulties: {I sympathise with your frustration}. It can also mean to support a cause or position: {He secretly sympathised with the rebels}. The noun is sympathy; the adjective sympathetic.

Sympathiser is the British spelling of sympathizer—someone who supports or agrees with a cause, movement, or group without necessarily being a formal member: {Communist sympathisers were monitored during the Cold War}. The term often carries a faintly suspicious tone, implying alignment with something controversial or subversive.

To sympathize is to share or understand another's feelings, especially their distress or sorrow: {I sympathize with what you're going through}. It can also mean to support or approve of something: {She sympathized with the workers' demands}. Sympathize emphasizes emotional understanding, while empathize suggests more fully inhabiting another's perspective.

A sympathizer supports or agrees with a cause, group, or belief, often without being a formal member. The term frequently carries political weight, suggesting someone who shares the views of a controversial movement: {Nazi sympathizers}, {communist sympathizers}. While it can be neutral—{I'm a sympathizer with the labor movement}—it often implies suspicion or accusation, as if the person's allegiance is hidden or questionable. The British spelling is sympathiser.

Sympathizers are people who support or feel aligned with a cause, group, or ideology without being full members. The term often carries suspicion—during the Cold War, {communist sympathizers} faced persecution. Someone may be called a sympathizer to suggest hidden allegiance: {Nazi sympathizers}, {rebel sympathizers}. The word implies passive support rather than active participation, though that line blurs under scrutiny.

Sympathy is fellow feeling—sharing in another's emotions, especially sorrow or hardship. To {have sympathy for} someone is to understand and care about their situation. Sympathy often implies emotional distance: you feel for them rather than with them, distinguishing it from empathy. {My sympathies} expresses condolences. In the plural, sympathies can mean allegiances: {Her sympathies lay with the rebels}. Things in sympathy resonate together: {The strings vibrated in sympathy}.

Sympatico describes people who get along easily, sharing similar temperaments or views: {We hit it off immediately—totally sympatico}. The word suggests natural compatibility and mutual understanding, often implying an unspoken connection. Borrowed from Italian and Spanish, it appears in English with a Continental flavor, sometimes spelled simpatico.

Symphonic describes music composed for or characteristic of a symphony orchestra—large-scale, richly orchestrated, and formally structured. A symphonic {poem} is an orchestral work inspired by a narrative or image. The term extends to anything grand and harmoniously complex: {The novel builds to a symphonic conclusion}. Symphonic rock and symphonic metal blend classical orchestration with rock instrumentation.
clues: In the manner of orchestral works

definition: Symphonies is the plural of symphony—a large-scale orchestral composition typically in four movements. Major orchestras build their seasons around symphonies by Beethoven, Brahms, and Mahler. The word extends to anything elaborate and harmonious: {a symphony of flavors}, {the symphony of a city waking up}. A symphony orchestra is one large enough to perform such works.

A symphony is a large-scale orchestral composition, typically in four movements, representing one of classical music's most ambitious forms. The word extends to symphony orchestras—the ensembles that perform such works—and to harmonious combinations generally: {a symphony of colors}, {a symphony of flavors}. Beethoven's symphonies remain touchstones of the form.

A symposium is a formal meeting or conference where experts present papers and discuss a particular subject. Unlike casual gatherings, symposiums typically feature prepared presentations followed by questions and debate among specialists in a field. The word originally referred to a drinking party in ancient Greece where philosophical conversation flowed alongside the wine. Today it retains its association with intellectual exchange, though the drinking is usually confined to the reception afterward.

A symptom is a sign that something is wrong—typically a physical or mental change indicating disease or disorder: {Fever is a common symptom of infection}. Symptoms are what patients report; doctors distinguish these from signs, which they observe directly. The word extends to any indication of an underlying problem: {Rising crime rates are a symptom of deeper social issues}.

Symptoms are signs that indicate something is wrong, especially with health. A symptom of disease is something the patient experiences—pain, fatigue, nausea—as distinct from clinical signs a doctor observes. The word extends beyond medicine: {Rising prices are a symptom of inflation}. Symptoms point to underlying causes rather than being the problem itself.

Synaesthesia is a neurological condition in which stimulation of one sense triggers automatic experiences in another—hearing a sound might produce a color, or seeing a letter might evoke a taste. Those who have it are synaesthetes. The word also describes deliberate blending of senses in art or writing: {a loud shirt}, {a warm color}, {a sharp cheese}. Also spelled synesthesia.

A synagogue is a Jewish house of worship and community gathering. Unlike a temple, which historically referred to the central sanctuary in Jerusalem, synagogues serve local congregations for prayer, study, and social functions. The building typically contains a sanctuary with an ark holding Torah scrolls: {The congregation met at the synagogue for Shabbat services}.

Synagogues are Jewish houses of worship and community gathering. The synagogue serves as a place for prayer, religious study, and social functions within Jewish communities. {The old synagogues of Eastern Europe were destroyed during the Holocaust.} {They attend synagogue every Saturday.}

A synapse is the junction between two nerve cells where signals pass from one to the other. The transmitting neuron releases chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) across a tiny gap, triggering electrical activity in the receiving neuron. Synapses are fundamental to how the brain processes information, forms memories, and learns. The verb synapse means to form such a connection: {neurons synapsing during learning}.

Synapses is the plural of synapse, the junction where nerve cells communicate. Electrical or chemical signals cross the tiny gap between neurons, allowing information to flow through the nervous system. The word appears in both neuroscience and figurative contexts: {The synapses weren't firing that early in the morning}. {New synapses form as we learn}.

Sync is a clipped form of synchronize, used as both noun and verb. To sync devices or files is to update them so they match or coordinate with each other: {Let me sync my calendar with yours}. When things are {in sync}, they're aligned or operating in harmony; {out of sync} means mismatched or poorly timed. The term dominates in computing and electronics but extends to any coordination of timing or content: {The audio wasn't in sync with the video}.

Synced is the past tense and past participle of sync, meaning brought into alignment or harmony with something else. Most commonly it describes digital devices or accounts that have been updated to match each other's data: {My phone synced with the cloud overnight}. It can also describe people or groups operating in coordination: {The dancers moved in synced precision}. The spelling synced prevails over synched in contemporary usage.

Synching is the present participle of sync, itself a clipped form of synchronize. To sync devices or files is to align their contents so both match: {My phone is synching with the cloud}. Audio and video sync when they're properly aligned in time. The spelling syncing is equally common.

Synchronicities are meaningful coincidences—events that seem connected not by cause and effect but by significance. The term comes from psychologist Carl Jung, who proposed that some coincidences carry psychological or spiritual meaning beyond chance: {The synchronicities kept piling up until she couldn't ignore them}. People invoke synchronicities when patterns feel too purposeful to be random.

Synchronicity is the occurrence of meaningful coincidences—events that seem connected by significance rather than cause. The term comes from psychology, where it describes moments when inner experience and outer events align in ways that feel purposeful but lack causal explanation: {Meeting her felt like synchronicity—I'd just been thinking about her}. The word often carries a mystical or spiritual connotation, suggesting the universe arranges meaningful patterns.

Synchronisation is the British spelling of synchronization—the act of causing things to happen, operate, or move at the same time or rate. Clocks are synchronised to show identical times. Swimmers perform synchronised routines. In computing, synchronisation keeps files or databases matched across devices: {The app handles synchronisation between your phone and laptop}.

Synchronise is the British spelling of synchronize. To synchronise is to cause things to happen or operate at the same time or rate: {We synchronised our watches before splitting up}. Clocks synchronise, dancers synchronise their movements, and devices synchronise data to match across platforms. The noun is synchronisation.

Synchronised is the British spelling of synchronized, meaning coordinated in time or movement. Swimmers perform synchronised routines; clocks are synchronised to show identical time. The spelling with -ised follows British convention, while American English uses -ized. {The synchronised divers entered the water as one.}

Synchronization is the act of making things happen at the same time or in coordination with each other. Clocks are synchronized to show identical time. Swimmers perform synchronized routines. In computing, synchronization keeps files or databases matched across devices: {The app runs a background sync}. Audio and video must be synchronized or lips won't match words. The shortened form sync dominates casual use: {out of sync}, {sync your calendar}.

Synchronize means to cause things to happen or operate at the same time or rate. You synchronize watches so they show identical times. Swimmers synchronize their movements to perform in unison. In technology, to synchronize is to update files or data across devices so they match: {My phone syncs with my laptop automatically}. The shortened form sync dominates casual use.

Synchronized means happening at the same time or moving in unison. Clocks are synchronized when they show identical time. Synchronized {swimming} features coordinated movements among multiple swimmers. To synchronize devices is to update them so their data matches: {My phone synchronized with the cloud}. The British spelling is synchronised.

Synchronizing is coordinating things to occur or operate in unison. You might synchronize watches before a mission, or synchronize dance moves with a partner. In computing, synchronizing means updating files or data across devices so they match: {My phone is synchronizing with the cloud}. The word implies bringing separate elements into alignment—whether in time, rhythm, or content.

Syncing is the process of synchronizing data between devices or systems so they match. When you sync your phone with the cloud, files update to reflect the latest versions in both places: {My photos are syncing right now}. The word appears constantly in computing contexts—syncing calendars, contacts, music libraries. Outside technology, syncing describes any coordination: {The dancers had trouble syncing their movements}.

Syncopated describes music or rhythm that emphasizes beats normally unstressed, creating a sense of surprise or swing. Jazz, ragtime, and funk rely heavily on syncopated rhythms: {The syncopated piano line gave the tune its infectious bounce}. More broadly, syncopated can describe any pattern with unexpected accents or irregular timing.

Syncopation is a rhythmic technique in music where emphasis falls on normally weak beats or between beats, creating an off-kilter, propulsive feel. Jazz, funk, and reggae rely heavily on syncopation to generate groove and swing. The effect catches listeners slightly off guard, making rhythms feel more dynamic and less predictable. {The drummer's syncopation gave the song its distinctive bounce.}

Syncs is the verb form of sync, short for synchronize. To sync devices is to make their data match: {My phone syncs with the cloud automatically}. Things that sync up align or coordinate: {Our schedules finally synced}. As a noun, syncs are instances of synchronization: {The app performs automatic syncs every hour}.

A syndicate is a group of individuals or organizations that join together for a common purpose, typically business or criminal. News syndicates distribute content to multiple outlets; crime syndicates coordinate illegal operations across territories. In finance, syndicates of banks share the risk of large loans. To syndicate content is to sell it for publication across multiple platforms: {The column is syndicated in over two hundred newspapers}.

Syndicated describes content—articles, comic strips, radio programs, television shows—that is sold or licensed to multiple outlets for simultaneous publication or broadcast. A syndicated {columnist} appears in dozens of newspapers. Syndicated {reruns} air on local stations across the country. The arrangement allows creators to reach wider audiences while outlets share costs. In finance, a syndicated {loan} is funded by multiple lenders.

Syndicates is the plural of syndicate—a group organized around a shared purpose, usually business or crime. A crime syndicate coordinates illegal operations across territories. A media syndicate distributes content to multiple outlets. In gambling, a syndicate pools money for larger bets: {The lottery syndicate split the jackpot twelve ways}. As a verb, to syndicate is to distribute widely: {The column is syndicated to newspapers nationwide}.

Syndication is the sale or licensing of content—television shows, newspaper columns, comic strips—to multiple outlets simultaneously. A syndicated columnist appears in dozens of newspapers; a syndicated sitcom airs on local stations after its network run. The term extends to any distribution through a network of partners: {radio syndication}, {web syndication}. In finance, syndication means pooling resources among multiple lenders or investors to fund a large transaction: {The loan was syndicated among twelve banks}.

A syndrome is a group of symptoms that occur together and characterize a particular condition or disease: {chronic fatigue syndrome}, {Down syndrome}. Medical syndromes are named for their discoverers, symptoms, or affected populations. The word extends to any set of characteristics that typically appear together: {empty nest syndrome}, {imposter syndrome}. In casual use, syndrome can describe any recognizable pattern of behavior: {middle child syndrome}.

Syndromes is the plural of syndrome, a group of symptoms that consistently occur together or a condition characterized by such a set: {The patient presented with symptoms consistent with several known syndromes}. Beyond medicine, syndrome describes any pattern of behaviors or traits that tend to cluster: {empty nest syndrome}, {impostor syndrome}. The word often carries clinical or diagnostic overtones even in casual use.

Synergy is a beneficial effect that emerges when two or more things add up to greater than the sum of their parts. The term has strict technical uses, as in physiology (two muscles working in synergy), but people use it most often to talk about human enterprises: The interaction of the team members creates a synergy that enables the team to do more work. The related adjective is synergistic.

Synesthesia is a neurological phenomenon in which stimulation of one sense triggers automatic experience in another—hearing a sound might produce a color, or seeing a letter might evoke a taste. People with synesthesia might perceive the number 5 as red or experience Tuesday as having a particular texture. The term extends loosely to any blending of sensory modes: {The music had a synesthetic quality, all purples and golds}.

A synonym is a word with the same or a similar meaning to another word. Synonyms must be the same part of speech. Some synonyms can substitute for each other in a sentence without significantly changing the meaning. More often, each of a set of synonyms has a slightly different connotation. English has a large vocabulary with many sets of synonyms that give writers and speakers the opportunity to create very subtle distinctions in meaning.

Synonyms is the plural of synonym—words that share meaning with other words. Happy and joyful are synonyms; so are big and large. Perfect synonyms are rare; most differ in connotation, register, or context. {Can you think of any synonyms for "angry"?} The concept is fundamental to thesauruses and vocabulary instruction.

A synopsis is a brief summary of a longer work—a book, film, article, or event. It captures the main points or plot without full detail: {The back cover provides a synopsis of the novel}. In publishing and film, a synopsis is often required when pitching a project to agents or producers.

Syntax is the arrangement of words into phrases and sentences. In language, syntax governs word order and grammatical structure—why {the dog bit the man} means something different from {the man bit the dog}. In computing, syntax refers to the rules for writing valid code; a syntax error means the program can't parse what you wrote. The word extends to any system with structural rules: {the syntax of a musical composition}.

Synth is short for synthesizer—an electronic instrument that generates and manipulates sound waves to produce music. Synths dominated 1980s pop and remain central to electronic genres: {The track opens with a pulsing synth}. The word also works as an adjective: {synth-pop}, {synth-heavy}. In science fiction, synth sometimes means a synthetic human or android.

Synthesis is the combining of separate elements into a unified whole. In chemistry, synthesis creates compounds from simpler substances. In philosophy, synthesis resolves thesis and antithesis into a new understanding. More broadly, any work that pulls together diverse sources or ideas performs a synthesis: {Her book is a synthesis of recent scholarship on the topic}. The verb is synthesize.

Synthesise is the British spelling of synthesize. To synthesise is to combine separate elements into a coherent whole: {The report synthesises data from multiple sources}. In chemistry, to synthesise a compound is to produce it through chemical reactions. In music, a synthesiser generates sounds electronically rather than acoustically.

Synthesiser is the British spelling of synthesizer. An electronic instrument that generates and manipulates sound waves to produce music. Early synthesisers used analog circuits; modern ones are typically digital. The word extends to any device that combines elements into a whole: {a speech synthesiser}. To synthesise is to combine parts into something new.

Synthesisers is the British spelling of synthesizers—electronic instruments that generate and manipulate sound. A synthesiser produces tones through oscillators, filters, and modulators rather than acoustic vibration: {The band's sound relied heavily on synthesisers}. The term extends to any device that combines elements to create something new, as in speech synthesisers.

Synthesize means to combine separate elements into a coherent whole. A researcher synthesizes findings from multiple studies into a unified theory. {She synthesized insights from biology, chemistry, and physics}. In chemistry, to synthesize is to produce a compound through chemical reactions: {Scientists synthesized the drug in the lab}. The word implies active construction—not just gathering parts, but integrating them into something new.

Synthesized describes something created by combining elements into a unified whole. In chemistry, a synthesized compound is produced artificially rather than extracted from nature: {synthesized hormones}, {synthesized fibers}. In music, synthesized sound is generated electronically rather than by acoustic instruments: {The track features synthesized drums and bass}. More broadly, synthesized information or ideas have been assembled from multiple sources into a coherent form.

A synthesizer is an electronic instrument that generates and manipulates sound, typically through keyboards, oscillators, and filters. Musicians use synthesizers to create tones ranging from imitations of acoustic instruments to entirely novel sounds: {The synthesizer dominated 1980s pop music}. Often shortened to synth. Beyond music, any device that combines elements into a unified output may be called a synthesizer.

Synthesizers are electronic instruments that generate and manipulate sound, producing tones through oscillators, filters, and other components rather than acoustic vibration. They range from keyboard instruments to modular systems with patch cables. The singular synthesizer often shortens to synth: {She plays synth in a new wave band}. Synthesizer also applies to anything that synthesizes—combines elements into a unified whole.

Synthesizing is combining separate elements into a unified whole. In chemistry, it means producing compounds through reactions: {synthesizing aspirin from salicylic acid}. More broadly, synthesizing applies to integrating ideas, information, or sources: {The essay does a good job of synthesizing competing theories}. The word emphasizes creation through combination rather than mere assembly.

Synthetic describes something made artificially rather than occurring naturally. Synthetic {fibers} like nylon and polyester are manufactured, unlike cotton or wool. Synthetic {chemicals} are laboratory creations. The word can suggest inferiority to the natural—a synthetic {smile} is fake, not genuine. In philosophy, a synthetic statement combines concepts not inherently connected, requiring evidence beyond the definitions themselves.
clues: Made by chemical process, not nature

definition: Synthetics are materials made artificially rather than occurring in nature—synthetic fibers like nylon and polyester, synthetic rubber, synthetic diamonds. The term often appears in fashion and textiles: {I prefer natural fabrics over synthetics}. In finance, synthetics are derivative instruments that replicate the behavior of other assets without holding them directly.

Synthpop is a genre of electronic pop music that emerged in the late 1970s and early 1980s, characterized by synthesizers as the dominant instrument, drum machines, and often robotic or emotionally detached vocals. Acts like Depeche Mode, New Order, and Soft Cell defined the sound. The term blends synthesizer and pop: {That playlist is pure synthpop}.

Synths is the plural of synth, a clipped form of synthesizer—an electronic instrument that generates and manipulates sound. The term dominates in music contexts: {The synths on that track are incredible}, {80s pop was defined by synths}. Synth also works as an adjective: {synth pop}, {synth wave}. In gaming and science fiction, synths are synthetic humans or androids: {The synths in that game are nearly indistinguishable from humans}.

Synthwave is a genre of electronic music that emerged in the late 2000s, drawing heavy inspiration from 1980s film soundtracks, video games, and synth-pop. The sound emphasizes analog synthesizers, drum machines, and pulsing basslines that evoke a nostalgic, often neon-tinged vision of retro-futurism. Synthwave has expanded beyond music into a broader aesthetic movement encompassing visual art, fashion, and film. {I've been listening to synthwave while working late nights.}

Syphilis is a sexually transmitted bacterial infection that progresses through stages if untreated, eventually causing serious damage to the heart, brain, and other organs. The disease was widespread and often fatal before the development of antibiotics. {He tested positive for syphilis}. The adjective is syphilitic.

Syphon is a variant spelling of siphon—a tube that uses atmospheric pressure to draw liquid from one container to another, or the act of transferring liquid this way. The spelling with y is more common in British English: {He syphoned petrol from the tank}. Figuratively, to syphon funds is to divert them, often illicitly.

Syrah is a red wine grape variety producing full-bodied, dark wines with notes of black fruit, pepper, and smoke. The grape thrives in warmer climates and is central to wines from France's Rhône Valley. In Australia and South Africa, the same grape is called shiraz: {a bold syrah from California}, {Australian shiraz tends toward riper, jammier flavors}.
clues: Dark grape behind Northern Rhône reds

definition: A syringe is a device for injecting or withdrawing fluids, typically a tube fitted with a plunger and a hollow needle. Medical syringes deliver medications or draw blood. Other syringes lack needles—a bulb syringe clears an infant's nose, a turkey baster bastes meat. The verb means to wash or spray with a syringe: {The doctor syringed my ears to remove wax}.

Syringes are tube-shaped medical devices with a plunger mechanism, used to inject fluids into or withdraw them from the body. A syringe typically attaches to a hollow needle for penetrating skin. Beyond medicine, syringes appear in cooking for injecting marinades and in crafts for precise glue application. {The nurse prepared the syringes for the vaccination clinic.}

Syrup is a thick, sweet liquid made by dissolving sugar in water or by reducing plant juices. Maple syrup comes from tree sap; corn syrup from processed corn starch. Cough syrup is medicine in a sweetened liquid base. Figuratively, something syrupy is cloyingly sweet or sentimental: {His syrupy compliments made everyone uncomfortable}.

Syrupy describes something with the thick, sweet consistency of syrup: {syrupy cough medicine}, {syrupy pancake topping}. The word extends to anything cloyingly sweet or sentimental: {a syrupy love song}, {syrupy dialogue}. The figurative use usually carries a negative charge—excessive sweetness that feels artificial or nauseating.

Sysadmin is short for system administrator—the person responsible for maintaining and operating computer systems, servers, and networks. Sysadmins handle everything from user accounts to security patches to keeping servers running at 3 a.m.: {The sysadmin finally tracked down the memory leak}. The role blends technical expertise with constant troubleshooting.

A system is a set of connected parts working together as a whole. The body has systems—circulatory, nervous, digestive. Governments and institutions are systems. A stereo system combines components. {The system} often means established power structures: {fighting the system}, {working within the system}. To {get something out of your system} is to purge an impulse or emotion by indulging it.

Systematic describes a way of doing something that is ordered, logical, and thorough, such as a systematic search of the entire building. A systematic approach is one that is methodical and all-inclusive. Sometimes, systematic is confused with systemic, as in systematic abuse or a systematic problem.

Systemic is an adjective describing something that is present throughout an entire system. Something that affects the entire body, for example, can be called systemic, as in systemic pain. A systemic risk is inherent to a system’s design. A systemic pesticide is one that is harmless to the plant but toxic to pests that feed on the plant.

Systems is the plural of system—organized sets of connected parts working together. The word often appears in contexts involving infrastructure or procedures: {computer systems}, {healthcare systems}, {systems failure}. In technical fields, systems thinking emphasizes how components interact rather than examining them in isolation. Someone who works in {systems} typically handles technology or organizational processes.

Tab’s numerous and varied meanings must be discerned from context. Online, a tab is a clickable link that opens a separate page, or a separate display page in your browser. The tab key on your keyboard creates an indentation (a tab), or advances to the next available field. That kind of tab is inspired by the physical one, a projecting piece of something that allows you to identify it, close it, or pull it out. A tab at a restaurant or business is a line of credit. If you keep tabs on someone, you monitor their actions and movements. Tab may also be short for tablet when it refers to a pill.

Tabbies is the plural of tabby, a cat with a distinctive coat pattern of stripes, spots, or swirling marks, typically in brown or gray. The term comes from a type of striped silk fabric. {Three tabbies lounged on the porch.} Tabby can also mean an older woman, usually one given to gossip—now dated and mildly disparaging.

Tabbouleh is a Middle Eastern salad made primarily of finely chopped parsley, bulgur wheat, tomatoes, mint, onion, and dressed with olive oil and lemon juice. The herb-forward dish originated in Lebanon and Syria, where parsley dominates rather than grain: {We ordered hummus and tabbouleh as appetizers}. Also spelled tabouli or tabouleh.

A tabby is a domestic cat with a distinctive coat pattern of stripes, swirls, or spots, typically in gray or brown with darker markings. The tabby pattern is one of the most common in cats, appearing across many breeds. The term can also describe the coat pattern itself: {a tabby coat}, {tabby markings}. Historically, tabby referred to a type of wavy-patterned silk fabric, which likely inspired the cat terminology.

A tabernacle is a place of worship, particularly in certain Christian denominations like Mormon and some Protestant churches. The word originally referred to a portable sanctuary—the tent that housed the Ark of the Covenant during the Israelites' wilderness wanderings. In Catholic and some other Christian contexts, a tabernacle is the ornate container on an altar where consecrated bread is kept. The term can also mean any temporary dwelling or shelter: {The festival-goers made tabernacles of their tents}. (Capitalized Tabernacle often refers to a specific building, such as the Mormon Tabernacle in Salt Lake City.)

Tabernacles is the plural of tabernacle, a word for a dwelling place or tent, especially one used for worship. In Jewish tradition, the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot) commemorates the temporary shelters Israelites used during their wilderness wanderings. The Tabernacle, capitalized and singular, refers specifically to the portable sanctuary described in Exodus that housed the Ark of the Covenant. In broader religious use, a tabernacle may be any house of worship or a container for sacred objects.

Tabla is a pair of hand drums used in classical Indian music and other South Asian musical traditions. The set consists of two drums of different sizes and pitches: the smaller, higher-pitched daya played with the dominant hand, and the larger, bass-toned baya.
