Tap also names a device controlling liquid flow—a faucet or spigot. To tap a resource is to access it: {tap into savings}, {tap a phone line}. A tap in this sense draws something out. In dance, tap involves metal-soled shoes striking the floor rhythmically. To tap someone for a job is to select them: {She was tapped to lead the committee}.

Tapa is a Spanish appetizer or snack, typically served in small portions alongside drinks. The plural tapas has become the standard English form, referring both to the dishes and the style of eating: {We shared tapas at the bar}. Tapas range from olives and cured ham to more elaborate preparations, and the word now appears in restaurants worldwide.

Tapas are small dishes of Spanish origin, served as appetizers or combined to make a meal. The style emphasizes variety and sharing—a table might hold plates of olives, cured ham, fried potatoes, and grilled shrimp. {We ordered a dozen tapas and split everything}. The concept has spread globally, influencing how restaurants serve small plates meant for grazing.

Tapdance is a style of dance in which the performer wears shoes fitted with metal plates that click rhythmically against the floor. The dancer creates percussive patterns with heel and toe strikes: {She tapdanced her way through the audition}. Figuratively, to tapdance is to improvise evasively or perform verbal acrobatics to avoid a direct answer: {He tapdanced around the question about his finances}.

A tapdancer is someone who performs tap dancing—a style of dance where rhythmic sounds are produced by metal plates on the heels and toes of the dancer's shoes striking the floor. The term applies to both professionals and amateurs: {She trained as a tapdancer from age five}. Also spelled as two words: tap dancer.

Tapdancing is a style of dance in which the performer wears shoes fitted with metal plates that click rhythmically against the floor. The dancer creates percussive patterns with the feet, essentially becoming both dancer and drummer. Also spelled tap dancing or tap-dancing. To tapdance around something is to avoid addressing it directly: {The senator tapdanced around the question of funding}.

Tape is a narrow strip of material—fabric, paper, plastic, or adhesive-backed film—used for binding, fastening, sealing, or marking: {masking tape}, {duct tape}, {measuring tape}, {police tape}. Magnetic tape once dominated audio and video recording, so tape became shorthand for recordings themselves: {Did you get that on tape?} The verb means to fasten with tape or to record: {Tape the box shut}, {We taped the interview}.

Taped is the past tense of tape—to fasten, bind, or record using tape. Something taped is secured with adhesive tape: {I taped the box shut}. A taped conversation or performance has been recorded: {The interview was taped yesterday}. In sports, athletes get taped up when trainers wrap their joints for support. {I've got it taped} (British) means having something figured out or under control.

A tape deck is a device for playing and recording audio cassettes or reel-to-reel tapes, typically as a component in a stereo system rather than a standalone player. Before digital formats, tape decks were standard home audio equipment: {He recorded the album from vinyl onto his tape deck}. The term persists in car audio, where cassette players were once standard.

Tapenade is a Provençal spread or condiment made from finely chopped olives, capers, and anchovies, typically blended with olive oil and seasonings. The paste ranges from coarse to smooth and appears most often as an appetizer spread on bread or crackers. Black olive tapenade is traditional, though green olive versions have become common. {We served tapenade with crostini before dinner.}

Taper describes a gradual narrowing toward one end, or the process of becoming gradually smaller. A candle tapers to its wick; a taper is itself a thin candle. Fingers, columns, and trouser legs may taper. The verb extends to any gradual decrease: {The medication dosage tapers over two weeks}. To {taper off} is to diminish slowly: {Her enthusiasm tapered off after the first month}.

Tapered describes something that gradually narrows toward one end. A tapered candle is thicker at the base than the top. Tapered jeans fit more closely at the ankle than the thigh. The verb taper means to narrow progressively: {The trail tapered to nothing}. Figuratively, things taper off when they diminish gradually: {Interest tapered off after the first week}.

Tapering describes something that gradually narrows toward one end, like a candle or a sharpened pencil. The word also applies to gradual reduction: {a tapering off of enthusiasm}, {tapering your medication dosage}. In fitness, tapering refers to reducing training intensity before competition to optimize performance.

Tapers are the plural of taper—slender candles or wax-coated wicks used for lighting other candles or carrying flame. The verb taper means to narrow gradually toward one end, like a candle's shape: {The road tapers to a single lane}. Extended to any gradual reduction: {Her medication dosage tapers off over two weeks}. Athletes taper training before competition, reducing intensity to peak on race day.

Tapes is the plural of tape—strips of material used for binding, fastening, or recording. Adhesive tapes stick things together. Magnetic tapes store audio or video: {I found some old tapes in the attic}. To tape is to record or to fasten with tape. {She tapes every episode of that show.}

Tapestries is the plural of tapestry—a heavy textile with woven designs, traditionally hung on walls or used as furnishing. Tapestries often depict scenes, figures, or patterns: {The medieval tapestries showed hunting scenes}. Figuratively, tapestry describes anything richly interwoven: {the tapestry of urban life}, {a tapestry of cultures}.

A tapestry is a heavy textile with decorative designs woven into it, traditionally hung on walls. Tapestries were both ornamental and functional in medieval castles, providing insulation and depicting scenes from history or mythology. Figuratively, tapestry describes anything composed of diverse interwoven elements: {the rich tapestry of urban life}, {a tapestry of cultures}.

A tapeworm is a parasitic flatworm that lives in the intestines of humans and other animals. Tapeworms attach to the intestinal wall and absorb nutrients from their host, sometimes growing to remarkable lengths. Infection typically comes from eating undercooked meat containing larvae: {The patient had a tapeworm from eating raw pork}.

Tapeworms is the plural of tapeworm, a parasitic flatworm that lives in the intestines of humans and other animals. Tapeworms attach to the intestinal wall and absorb nutrients from their host, sometimes growing to considerable length. Infection typically comes from eating undercooked meat containing larvae: {The pork was contaminated with tapeworms}.

A taphouse is an establishment that serves beer on tap, typically offering a wide selection of draft beers. The term emphasizes the tap system over bottled options and often suggests a casual atmosphere focused on craft or specialty beers: {The new taphouse downtown has twenty local brews on draft}. Taphouse overlaps with bar, pub, and alehouse but carries a slightly more beer-centric connotation.

Taphouses are establishments that serve beer directly from taps, typically offering a wide selection of draft beers. The term emphasizes the tap system over bottled options, often suggesting craft beer focus and a casual atmosphere: {The neighborhood has three new taphouses}. Singular: taphouse.

Tapioca is a starchy substance extracted from cassava root, used as a thickener and in puddings. Tapioca pudding contains small pearls of the starch that become translucent and chewy when cooked: {The tapioca pudding had that distinctive texture she remembered from childhood}. Larger tapioca pearls appear in bubble tea.

A tapir is a large, pig-like mammal native to Central and South America and Southeast Asia, with a distinctive flexible snout resembling a short trunk. Tapirs are herbivores related to horses and rhinoceroses, though their stocky build and snout give them an appearance all their own. They're shy, mostly nocturnal, and often found near water.

Tapirs are large, pig-like mammals native to Central and South America and Southeast Asia. They have stout bodies, short legs, and a distinctive flexible snout resembling a truncated elephant trunk. Tapirs are herbivores, typically inhabiting forests near water. Despite their bulk, they're surprisingly agile swimmers and can use their prehensile snouts to grab foliage.

Tapout is the act of tapping an opponent or the mat to signal surrender, originating in wrestling and martial arts where a fighter concedes to escape a painful hold: {He got caught in an armbar and had to tapout}. More broadly, it means quitting or giving up when you've had enough: {I'm at my tapout point with this project}. The term appears as both noun and verb, sometimes spelled tap out or tap-out.

Tapped is the past tense of tap, covering all its senses: struck lightly {He tapped me on the shoulder}, accessed a resource {They tapped the maple trees for syrup}, or selected for a role {She was tapped to lead the committee}. In slang, tapped or tapped out means exhausted or depleted: {I'm tapped—can't lend you anything}. To get tapped can mean to be wiretapped or, vulgarly, to have sex.

Tapping is repeated light strikes or touches. You might hear a tapping at the window or feel someone tapping your shoulder. Tapping a resource means drawing from it: {tapping into reserves}, {tapping a phone line}. In dance, tap dancing involves tapping shoes against a hard floor. To tap someone for a position is to select them: {She was tapped to lead the committee}.

A taproom is a bar or room where beer is served on tap, typically attached to or located within a brewery. Unlike traditional bars that stock various brands, taprooms primarily serve beers made on the premises, giving customers direct access to fresh drafts. The term has seen renewed use with the craft beer movement, as small breweries often open taprooms as their main public-facing space. {The new brewery's taproom opens this weekend.}

Taprooms are bars or rooms where beer is served on tap, typically attached to a brewery. The term emphasizes draft beer over bottles or cans. Modern craft breweries often operate taprooms where customers sample beers directly from the source: {We spent the afternoon visiting taprooms along the brewery trail}.

A taproot is a plant's primary root, growing straight down and giving rise to smaller lateral roots. Carrots, dandelions, and oak trees have taproots. Figuratively, a taproot is a central source or origin: {The taproot of her anxiety was never addressed}.

Taproots is the plural of taproot, the main root of a plant that grows straight down and from which smaller lateral roots branch off. Carrots, dandelions, and parsnips are familiar examples—the edible part is the taproot itself. The term extends figuratively to mean a central source or origin from which other things develop: {The taproot of her success was years of disciplined practice}. Plants with taproots are often difficult to transplant or eradicate because the root reaches deep into the soil.

Taps is the plural of tap—devices controlling liquid flow, light touches or strikes, or acts of tapping. A bartender works the taps. The taps of a dancer's shoes click against the floor. Phone taps are surveillance devices. To be {on tap} is to be available: {We have several candidates on tap for the position}. (Capitalized Taps is the military bugle call.)

A taqueria is a Mexican restaurant or food stand specializing in tacos and related fare—burritos, quesadillas, tortas. The word is Spanish, and taquerias range from street carts to sit-down establishments: {We grabbed lunch at the taqueria on the corner}.

Taquerias is the plural of taqueria, a Mexican restaurant or stand specializing in tacos and related fare like burritos, quesadillas, and tortas. The word comes from Spanish and retains its Spanish plural. Taquerias range from roadside stands to sit-down restaurants: {The best taquerias in the city are cash-only}.

A taquito is a small rolled tortilla filled with meat, cheese, or other ingredients, then fried until crispy. The name is Spanish for "little taco." Taquitos are typically served as appetizers or snacks, often with salsa, guacamole, or sour cream for dipping: {We ordered taquitos to start}.

Taquitos are small rolled tacos, typically filled with seasoned meat or cheese, then fried until crispy. The tortilla becomes a crunchy shell around the filling. They're served as appetizers or snacks, often with salsa, guacamole, or sour cream for dipping: {We ordered taquitos and margaritas}. Also called flautas, though flautas are sometimes distinguished as larger or made with flour tortillas.

Tar is a thick, dark, sticky substance derived from organic materials like coal, wood, or petroleum. It's used for waterproofing and paving: {The roofers spread hot tar over the surface}. Cigarette tar refers to the residue that accumulates in lungs. To tar someone is to coat them with tar—historically as punishment ({tarred and feathered})—or to damage their reputation: {Don't tar us all with the same brush}. A tar is also old-fashioned slang for a sailor.

A tarantella is a lively Italian folk dance in rapid 6/8 time, characterized by whirling movements and increasing tempo. The dance is traditionally performed by couples and associated with southern Italy, especially Naples. Legend held that the frenzied dancing could cure the bite of a tarantula spider—both words derive from the city of Taranto. The term also refers to music composed for or in the style of this dance: {Chopin's Tarantella in A-flat major}.

A tarantula is a large, hairy spider. The name originally referred to a European wolf spider associated with the Italian city of Taranto, where its bite supposedly caused frenzied dancing (tarantism). Today it typically means the bigger, stockier spiders of the family Theraphosidae, kept as exotic pets and featured in horror films. Despite their fearsome appearance, most tarantulas are relatively harmless to humans.

Tarantulas is the plural of tarantula, a large hairy spider found in warm regions. Despite their fearsome appearance, most tarantulas are relatively harmless to humans—their bite is painful but rarely dangerous. They're popular as exotic pets: {She keeps tarantulas in terrariums}. The name comes from Taranto, Italy, where a different spider's bite was once blamed for a dancing mania.

Tarballs are clumps of crude oil that wash up on beaches after spills or natural seepage, weathered into sticky black masses by sun and seawater. In computing, a tarball is an archive file created by the Unix tar utility, often compressed: {Download the tarball and extract it}. The name comes from "tar archive," with the playful suffix matching the petroleum sense.

Tardigrades are microscopic animals, also called water bears or moss piglets, known for their remarkable ability to survive extreme conditions—intense radiation, the vacuum of space, temperatures near absolute zero, and decades without water. When threatened, they enter a dehydrated state called a tun, reviving when conditions improve. Despite their resilience, they're fragile in ordinary environments, living only a few months under normal circumstances.

Tardy means late or delayed, arriving after the expected time. The word appears most often in school contexts, where students receive tardy slips for showing up after the bell: {She was marked tardy three times this week}. Tardy can also describe slow movement or action: {a tardy response to the crisis}.

A target is something at which you aim a weapon or something that you establish as a goal. If you achieve a target, you reach the goal: They met their sales target. Before another noun, target characterizes the goal: target audience, target date. In military contexts, a target is the thing aimed at with the goal of destroying it. As a verb, target means to take aim at something. If an audience is targeted, it is identified as a group to address or win over. If something is on target, it is meeting expectations or is otherwise accurate, valid, and on course.

Targeted means selected as a specific object of attention or action. Targeted {advertising} aims at particular demographics. A targeted {attack} focuses on a chosen victim rather than striking randomly. {Targeted sanctions} apply to specific individuals or entities. The word often implies deliberate selection based on certain characteristics: {She felt targeted because of her beliefs}.

Targeting is directing attention, effort, or resources toward a specific objective. Marketing campaigns target demographics; missiles target locations; policies target problems. The word implies deliberate selection and focus: {The ads were targeting young professionals}. In online contexts, targeting often refers to using data to reach specific audiences: {behavioral targeting}, {targeted advertising}.

Targets are things aimed at—literally or figuratively. A target is what you shoot at, what you're trying to hit or reach: {sales targets}, {target audience}, {target date}. To target something is to select it for attention or attack: {The ads target young adults}. A target can also be someone singled out for criticism or harm: {She became a target of online harassment}.

A tariff is a tax on imported goods, charged when they cross a border. Governments use tariffs to generate revenue or protect domestic industries from foreign competition: {The new tariffs on steel raised prices for manufacturers}. Extended from trade, tariff can mean any schedule of rates or charges: {The hotel's tariff includes breakfast}.

Tariffs are taxes imposed on imported goods, making foreign products more expensive relative to domestic ones. Governments use tariffs to protect local industries, raise revenue, or as leverage in trade disputes: {The administration announced new tariffs on steel imports}. Tariff can also mean any schedule of rates or charges: {the hotel's tariff for room service}.

Tarmac is a paved surface, especially at an airport where planes taxi, load, and unload: {The plane sat on the tarmac for two hours}. The word comes from tarmacadam—a road surface of crushed stone bound with tar. Though technically distinct from modern asphalt, tarmac now serves as a general term for any paved runway or apron area.

A tarn is a mountain lake, typically small and formed in a cirque—a bowl-shaped hollow carved by glacial ice. The word is used especially in Britain's Lake District: {We hiked up to the tarn beneath the summit}. Tarns are often deep relative to their size, with cold, clear water.

Tarnation is a mild oath expressing surprise, frustration, or emphasis, a euphemism for damnation: {What in tarnation is going on here?} The word sounds old-fashioned and rural, associated with American frontier speech. It appears almost exclusively in the phrase {what in tarnation} or {where in tarnation}, functioning like "what the hell."

Tarnish is the dull film that forms on metal surfaces when they react with air or moisture—silver tarnishes to gray or black, copper to green. To tarnish is to lose or cause to lose luster: {The silverware had tarnished over the years}. Figuratively, tarnish means to damage or sully: {The scandal tarnished his reputation}. A tarnish on someone's record is a blemish that diminishes their standing.

Tarnished describes something that has lost its shine or luster, typically through oxidation or exposure: {tarnished silver}, {tarnished brass}. The word extends naturally to reputation or honor that has been damaged or diminished: {His tarnished reputation never fully recovered}. Something tarnished still exists but has lost the brightness it once had.

Tarnishes is the third-person singular of tarnish. Metal tarnishes when it loses its luster through oxidation or corrosion: {Silver tarnishes if left exposed to air}. Figuratively, something tarnishes a reputation or image by diminishing its quality or purity: {The scandal tarnishes his legacy}. As a noun, tarnishes are instances or patches of discoloration on metal surfaces.

Tarnishing is the process of losing luster or becoming dull, typically through oxidation or chemical reaction. Silver tarnishes when exposed to air; brass tarnishes over time. The word extends to reputation and honor: {The scandal succeeded in tarnishing his legacy}. Something tarnishing is actively losing its shine, literally or figuratively.

Taro is a tropical plant cultivated for its starchy, edible root. The corm is a dietary staple across Pacific Islands, Asia, and Africa, prepared by boiling, steaming, or pounding into paste. In Hawaii, mashed taro becomes poi. Taro root has a mildly sweet, nutty flavor and must be cooked to neutralize irritating compounds. The large heart-shaped leaves are also eaten.

Tarot is a deck of 78 cards used for fortune-telling and divination. The deck includes 22 major arcana cards depicting archetypal figures like the Fool, the Lovers, and Death, plus 56 minor arcana in four suits. A tarot reading interprets cards drawn or laid out in patterns: {She consulted the tarot before making her decision}. Originally a Renaissance card game, tarot's occult associations developed later.

A tarp is a large sheet of waterproof material—typically canvas or plastic—used to cover and protect things from weather. Tarps shield firewood, camping gear, truck beds, and construction sites: {We threw a tarp over the woodpile before the rain}. The word is a clipped form of tarpaulin, now more common than the full word in everyday speech.

Tarpaper is a heavy paper impregnated with tar, used as a moisture barrier in building construction. It typically goes beneath shingles on roofs or behind siding on walls to keep water from penetrating the structure. A tarpaper shack is a crude dwelling, often associated with poverty, where tarpaper serves as both the exterior wall covering and the only protection from the elements.

A tarpaulin is a large sheet of waterproof material—canvas treated with tar or wax, or modern plastic—used to cover and protect things from weather. Tarps shelter cargo, construction sites, camping gear, or anything left outdoors: {We threw a tarpaulin over the woodpile}. Usually shortened to tarp.

A tarpit is a natural deposit where tar or asphalt seeps to the surface, trapping animals that become preserved as fossils: {the La Brea Tar Pits}. Figuratively, a tarpit is anything that ensnares and immobilizes: {The project became a tarpit that consumed resources for years}. In computing, a tarpit is a server deliberately slowed to trap spammers or attackers, wasting their time and resources.

Tarpits are natural pools of thick, sticky asphalt that have trapped animals for millennia—the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles famously preserved prehistoric creatures. Figuratively, a tarpit is anything that ensnares and holds fast: {The project became a tarpit that consumed resources for years}. In computing, a tarpit is a server deliberately slowed to trap and waste the time of spammers or attackers.

Tarpon are large, powerful fish prized by sport fishermen for their spectacular leaps when hooked. Found in warm Atlantic waters, they can exceed two hundred pounds. Their silvery scales flash dramatically as they fight: {He spent three hours landing that tarpon}. Though edible, they're almost always released—the battle is the point.

Tarps is the plural of tarp, itself a clipping of tarpaulin—a large sheet of waterproof material used to cover and protect things from weather: {We threw tarps over the firewood before the storm}. Tarps cover boats, construction materials, camping gear, and anything else that needs shielding from rain or sun.

Tarragon is an aromatic herb with slender, slightly anise-flavored leaves, used especially in French cooking. It flavors vinegar, mustard, and béarnaise sauce: {chicken with tarragon}, {tarragon butter}. The plant grows in bushy clumps and is best used fresh, as drying mutes its distinctive flavor.

Tarred is the past tense of tar—to coat with tar, the dark, sticky substance derived from wood or coal. Roads were once tarred for weatherproofing. To be {tarred with the same brush} is to be unfairly associated with others' faults. {Tarred and feathered} was a humiliating punishment in which hot tar and feathers were applied to the body.

Tarring is the application of tar—a thick, dark, sticky substance derived from wood or coal. Roads are tarred to seal and preserve them. The word appears most often in {tarring and feathering}, a historical punishment where hot tar was poured on someone before covering them with feathers. Figuratively, tarring means smearing someone's reputation: {tarring all politicians with the same brush}.

Tart describes a sharp, acidic taste—the sourness of unripe fruit or lemon: {tart green apples}, {a tart vinaigrette}. Extended to speech or manner, tart means cutting or caustic: {a tart reply}. As a noun, a tart is a small open pastry with fruit or custard filling. In British slang, tart is a mildly offensive term for a promiscuous woman or prostitute. To {tart up} is to dress or decorate gaudily.

Tartan is a pattern of intersecting horizontal and vertical stripes in multiple colors, forming a distinctive plaid. The pattern is strongly associated with Scotland, where specific tartans identify clans, families, or regions: {the Black Watch tartan}, {wearing the family tartan}. Tartan appears on kilts, scarves, and other textiles. The word also describes fabric woven in this pattern.

Tartar has two main meanings. One is the hard deposit that forms on teeth from plaque—what dentists scrape off during cleanings. The other is a fierce or formidable person: {She's a real tartar when crossed}. This sense comes from the Tartars, Central Asian warriors known for their ferocity. Cream of tartar, used in baking, is an unrelated substance—a byproduct of winemaking.

Tartare describes raw meat or fish prepared as a dish, typically finely chopped or minced and served with seasonings: {steak tartare}, {tuna tartare}. The preparation usually includes capers, onions, and a raw egg yolk. Tartare sauce (or tartar sauce) is a mayonnaise-based condiment with pickles and herbs, traditionally served with fried fish.

Tarts are small pastries with a filling—fruit, custard, or savory ingredients—in an open-faced shell: {apple tarts}, {jam tarts}. A larger version is simply a tart rather than a pie when it lacks a top crust. Separately, tart means sharp or acidic in taste: {tart cherries}, {a tart lemonade}. By extension, a tart remark is cutting or biting. In British slang, a tart is a promiscuous woman or prostitute, though the word can be used more loosely for any woman dressed provocatively. To {tart up} something is to dress it up gaudily or cheaply.

To tase is to shock someone with a Taser, a brand of electroshock weapon used to incapacitate: {The officer tased the suspect}. The word gained notoriety from a 2007 viral video in which a student shouted "Don't tase me, bro!" Also spelled taze.

Tased means struck with a Taser, a brand of electroshock weapon that fires barbed probes delivering an incapacitating electrical current. Police commonly tase suspects to subdue them without lethal force: {The officer tased him when he refused to drop the knife}. The spelling tazed also appears.

A taser is a weapon that delivers an electric shock to incapacitate someone, typically used by police for subduing suspects without lethal force. The device fires two small darts connected by wires that deliver a disabling jolt: {The officer drew his taser when the man refused to comply}. As a verb, to taser someone is to shock them with such a device. The lowercase form has become generic for any similar electroshock weapon. (Capitalized Taser is the trademark.)

Tasered means struck with a Taser, a brand of electroshock weapon that fires barbed darts connected to wires, delivering an incapacitating electric current. Police use Tasers to subdue suspects without lethal force: {The officer tasered him when he refused to drop the knife}. The verb has become generic, applying to any similar stun device regardless of brand.

Tasers are handheld electroshock weapons that fire barbed darts connected by wires, delivering an electric current that temporarily incapacitates the target through neuromuscular disruption. Originally a brand name now used generically, tasers are standard equipment for many police forces as a less-lethal alternative to firearms: {The officer drew his taser when the suspect refused to comply}. To taser someone is to shock them with one.

A task is a piece of work to be done—something assigned or undertaken: {I have a few tasks to complete before lunch}. Tasks are typically discrete and finite, smaller than projects but more substantial than errands. To task someone is to assign them work, often with a sense of burden: {She was tasked with organizing the event}. To {take someone to task} is to criticize or reprimand them.

A taskbar is a strip along the edge of a computer screen—typically the bottom—showing open applications, system status, and navigation controls. Windows popularized the term; other operating systems use similar bars with different names. {I pinned the browser to my taskbar for quick access.}

A taskforce is a temporary group assembled to address a specific problem or objective. The term originated in military contexts—a naval taskforce combines ships for a particular mission—but now appears widely in government and business: {The mayor appointed a taskforce on homelessness}. Also spelled task force.

A taskmaster is someone who assigns work and demands it be done, especially with strict or exacting standards. The word often carries connotations of harshness: {Her new boss was a real taskmaster}. You can be your own taskmaster, holding yourself to rigorous expectations. The term appears in contexts ranging from workplace supervision to self-discipline.

Taskmasters are people who assign and oversee work, especially demanding supervisors who push others hard. The term often carries connotations of strictness or severity: {Her piano teacher was a real taskmaster}. A taskmaster need not be a formal boss—anyone who imposes discipline or exacting standards qualifies: {Hunger is a cruel taskmaster}.

Tasks are pieces of work that need to be done, usually discrete assignments with defined goals or deadlines. The word implies something that has been assigned or accepted as a responsibility: {I have several tasks to complete before the meeting}. To task someone is to assign them work or burden them with responsibility. If you take someone to task, you criticize or reprimand them for a failing.

A tassel is a bunch of threads or cords bound at one end and hanging loose at the other, used as decoration on clothing, curtains, graduation caps, or furniture: {The tassel on his mortarboard swung as he walked across the stage}. Corn produces tassels—the pollen-bearing flowers at the top of the stalk. To tassel is to form or put forth such flowers.

Tassels are decorative bunches of threads or cords bound at one end and hanging loose at the other. They adorn curtains, graduation caps, throw pillows, and clothing: {The scarf had silk tassels at each end}. Tassel also refers to the pollen-bearing flower cluster at the top of a corn plant. As a verb, to tassel is to form or put forth such clusters: {The corn is starting to tassel}.

Taste is the sense that perceives flavor through the tongue—sweet, salty, sour, bitter, savory. A taste is also a small sample: {Just a taste of the soup}. Extended, taste means preference or discernment: {She has expensive taste in clothes}, {That joke was in bad taste}. To taste something is to perceive its flavor or to experience it briefly: {He tasted freedom for the first time}. A taste for something is an inclination toward it: {He developed a taste for adventure}.

Tastebuds are the small sensory organs on the tongue and elsewhere in the mouth that detect flavors—sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami. The word is often used figuratively to refer to someone's flavor preferences or palate: {My tastebuds crave something spicy}. When food is described as pleasing or offending your tastebuds, it means you find it delicious or unpleasant. Also spelled as two words: taste bud.

Tastebuds are the sensory receptors on the tongue that detect flavor—sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami. The word often appears figuratively for one's sense of taste or flavor preferences: {My tastebuds aren't ready for anything that spicy}. Also spelled as two words: taste buds.

Tasted is the past tense and past participle of taste. It most often describes having perceived flavor through the mouth: {I tasted garlic in the sauce}. It can also mean sampled or tried: {She tasted freedom for the first time}. When something tasted a certain way, it had that flavor quality: {The water tasted metallic}. In older or literary use, tasted could mean experienced or underwent: {He had tasted defeat before}.

Tasteful describes choices that show good aesthetic judgment and restraint. A tasteful {outfit} is well-coordinated without being showy. Tasteful {décor} suggests elegance and refinement. The word often implies knowing what to leave out—avoiding excess, vulgarity, or ostentation. {The memorial was simple and tasteful.} Tasteful can sound faintly condescending when applied to others' choices.

Tasteless describes something lacking flavor or aesthetic merit. Bland food is tasteless. So is decor that shows no sense of style. The word extends to behavior that offends good judgment or sensitivity: {a tasteless joke about the accident}, {a tasteless display of wealth at the funeral}. What registers as tasteless varies by culture and context.

A tastemaker is someone whose preferences and choices influence what others consider stylish, desirable, or culturally relevant. The term applies to critics, celebrities, influencers, and industry insiders who shape trends in fashion, food, music, art, or design. {Magazine editors were once the primary tastemakers in fashion.} Being a tastemaker implies not just having good taste but having the cultural authority to establish what good taste means for others.

Tastemakers are people whose preferences influence what becomes popular or fashionable. They shape trends in fashion, music, food, or culture—not through formal authority but through social influence. Critics, celebrities, and influential bloggers often serve as tastemakers: {The magazine's editors are tastemakers who decide what's stylish each season}. The term implies both cultural power and a certain arbitrariness about whose taste gets elevated.

Tastemaking is the activity of influencing what becomes popular or fashionable. Tastemakers—critics, editors, influencers, curators—shape cultural preferences by highlighting certain music, fashion, food, or art: {The magazine's tastemaking power launched countless designers' careers}. The term can carry a whiff of elitism, suggesting that some people's opinions matter more than others.

A taster is someone who tastes food or drink professionally—evaluating quality, checking for poison, or sampling products before sale: {a wine taster}, {a royal taster}. The word extends to small samples meant to give a preview: {The article offers a taster of what's in the book}. A taster can also be a small cup or spoon used for sampling.

Tastes is the verb form of taste—to perceive flavor or sample something: {She tastes the soup before serving}. More often it appears as a noun plural referring to personal preferences and sensibilities: {His tastes run toward the exotic}. Someone with expensive tastes prefers costly things. {Tastes differ} acknowledges that preferences vary. {There's no accounting for tastes} suggests preferences defy explanation.

Tasting is sampling food or drink to assess its flavor: {a wine tasting}, {a cheese tasting}. The word names both the act and the event organized around it. As an adjective, tasting describes the faculty: {tasting notes}, {tasting menu}. A tasting portion is small—enough to evaluate, not to satisfy.

Tastings are events where small samples of food or drink are offered for evaluation or enjoyment: {wine tastings}, {cheese tastings}, {beer tastings}. The format allows sampling multiple varieties without committing to full portions. Professional tastings involve systematic assessment; casual ones are social occasions centered on sampling and comparison.

Tasty describes food or drink that has a pleasing flavor: {a tasty meal}, {tasty snacks}. It implies satisfying rather than refined—you'd call street food tasty, not a Michelin-starred tasting menu. Informally, tasty can describe anything appealing: {a tasty profit}, {a tasty goal}. In British slang, a tasty person is sexually attractive.

Tat refers to cheap, tasteless, or low-quality goods—the kind of trinkets sold at tourist traps or cluttering thrift store shelves: {The market was full of tat}. Primarily British. Tat is also the verb for making lace by tatting, a technique using a small shuttle to create intricate knotted patterns. As slang, a tat is a tattoo: {She got a new tat on her shoulder}.

Tatami are the thick woven straw mats used as flooring in traditional Japanese rooms. They're made from rush grass over a rice straw core, giving a firm but slightly cushioned surface. Room sizes in Japan are often measured in tatami: {a six-tatami room}. The mats also appear in martial arts training areas.

Tater is informal for potato, common in rural and Southern American speech: {tater tots}, {mashed taters}. The clipped form appears in casual cooking contexts and comfort food marketing. In baseball slang, a tater is a home run—the ball leaving the park like a potato being launched.

Tatted describes someone who has tattoos, typically many or prominent ones. The word comes from tattoo and functions as an informal adjective: {He showed up tatted from neck to knuckles}. Being tatted up or tatted out suggests extensive coverage. Tatted also has an older, unrelated meaning in needlework: lace made by tatting, a technique of knotting thread into decorative patterns.

A tatter is a torn scrap or shred, especially of cloth or paper. The plural tatters describes something badly torn or in ruins: {His reputation lay in tatters}. Clothes reduced to tatters are ragged and barely holding together. The adjective tattered describes anything worn, frayed, or falling apart: {a tattered flag}, {a tattered copy of the book}.

Tattered describes something torn, ragged, or worn to shreds through age or hard use: {a tattered flag}, {tattered clothes}. The word extends to things damaged or diminished figuratively: {a tattered reputation}, {tattered hopes}. Something tattered hangs together but just barely—still recognizable but degraded.

Tatters are torn, ragged pieces of cloth or clothing. Something {in tatters} is badly torn or, figuratively, ruined: {His reputation was in tatters after the scandal}. The singular tatter appears mainly in the phrase {tattered and torn}. A person dressed in tatters wears worn-out, ragged clothes.

To tattle is to report someone's misbehavior to an authority—a child telling a parent about a sibling's wrongdoing, or an employee informing a boss about a coworker's violation. The word carries a childish connotation; adults who tattle are often seen as petty or untrustworthy. A tattletale is someone who habitually tattles. {Don't tattle on your sister.}
clues: Let adults know who did it

definition: Tattled is the past tense of tattle, meaning to report someone's wrongdoing to an authority figure. The word carries childish connotations—children tattle on siblings or classmates: {She tattled to the teacher about who broke the window}. Adults who tattle are acting like children, informing on others for petty violations rather than keeping quiet.

A tattler is someone who reveals secrets or reports others' misdeeds, especially a child who tells on playmates: {Don't be a tattler}. The word carries childish connotations—adults who inform are more likely called informants or snitches. Tattler also names certain shorebirds known for their alarm calls that alert other wildlife to danger.

Tattles is the verb tattle in the third person singular: to report someone's wrongdoing to an authority, especially a child telling on another child to a parent or teacher. {She tattles on her brother whenever he breaks the rules.} The word carries a childish or petty connotation—adults who tattle are acting like children.

A tattletale is someone who reports another person's wrongdoing to an authority—a child who runs to tell the teacher, an employee who informs management. The word carries childish connotations and implies the reporting is petty or self-serving rather than principled: {Don't be a tattletale}. As an adjective, tattletale describes things that reveal what someone wanted hidden: {tattletale signs of a late night out}.

Tattletales are people who report others' misdeeds to authority figures—children who run to teachers, employees who inform on coworkers. The word carries childish connotations, suggesting the reporting is petty or self-serving rather than principled: {Nobody likes a tattletale}. Adults using it often mock the behavior as immature.
clues: Those who inform on their peers

definition: Tattling is reporting someone's misbehavior to an authority, especially when done by children seeking to get a peer in trouble: {Stop tattling on your sister}. The word carries connotations of pettiness—tattling is distinguished from legitimate reporting by its trivial nature or self-serving motive. Adults who tattle are seen as childish or untrustworthy.

Tattoo has two origins. One is a signal—originally a drumbeat calling soldiers to quarters, now also a military display with music and marching. The other is a design made by inserting pigment under the skin. To tattoo is to mark the skin this way: {She got a butterfly tattooed on her shoulder}. Figuratively, something tattooed is permanently marked: {The image was tattooed in my memory}.

Tattooed describes skin that bears permanent designs made by injecting ink beneath the surface: {His tattooed arms told the story of his Navy years}. The word often appears attributively to characterize people: {a tattooed biker}, {heavily tattooed musicians}. It can suggest countercultural identity or, increasingly, mainstream fashion.

Tattooing is the practice of inserting ink under the skin to create permanent designs. The process uses needles to deposit pigment in the dermis layer, where it remains visible through the outer skin. Tattooing encompasses both the craft itself and its cultural traditions: {She studied tattooing in Japan}, {Traditional Polynesian tattooing uses hand-tapped tools}. The word also describes the act in progress: {The tattooing took six hours}.

A tattooist is a person who creates tattoos by injecting ink under the skin to produce permanent designs. The term is interchangeable with tattoo artist, though tattooist has a slightly more traditional or workmanlike connotation while tattoo artist may emphasize the creative or aesthetic aspect of the craft. {She's been a tattooist for fifteen years and specializes in Japanese-style work.}

Tattoos are permanent designs made by inserting ink under the skin with needles. Once associated with sailors, prisoners, and counterculture, tattoos have become mainstream body art: {She has tattoos covering both arms}. The verb tattoo means to mark the skin this way: {He tattooed a dragon on her back}. A military tattoo is something else entirely—an evening drum signal or ceremonial performance.

Tatty means worn, shabby, or in poor condition: {a tatty old cardigan}, {tatty furniture}. More common in British than American English. The word suggests something that has seen better days—not ruined, but visibly deteriorated through age or neglect. A tatty neighborhood looks rundown; tatty decorations seem cheap or faded.

Tau is the nineteenth letter of the Greek alphabet (Τ, τ), corresponding to the English T. In mathematics and physics, tau represents various quantities—most notably the mathematical constant equal to 2π (approximately 6.28), which some mathematicians argue is more natural than pi for describing circles. In biology, tau proteins help stabilize cellular structures; their malfunction is associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Taught is the past tense and past participle of teach. Someone taught you to read; you were taught manners. The word sometimes emphasizes instruction received rather than given: {She's self-taught on guitar}. {He taught high school for thirty years.}

To taunt is to mock or provoke someone with insulting remarks, often to get a reaction: {The older kids taunted him about his stutter}. A taunt is the insult itself. Taunting implies repeated or sustained mockery rather than a single jab—there's cruelty in it, an intent to wound or goad.

Taunting is mocking or provoking someone with insulting remarks, gestures, or challenges designed to humiliate or goad them into reaction: {The taunting from the stands grew louder as the opposing team took the field}. It carries a sense of cruelty or aggression—not playful teasing but deliberate needling meant to wound or provoke.

Taunts are mocking remarks intended to provoke, humiliate, or wound. The word covers both the act and its content—someone hurls taunts, and those taunts sting: {The crowd's taunts grew louder as he walked off the field}. To taunt is to deliver such provocations: {She taunted him about his failure}. Taunting often aims to goad someone into a reaction.

Taupe is a grayish-brown color, roughly the shade of a mole's fur—the word comes from the French for mole. The exact hue varies; some taupes lean gray, others brown, and decorators distinguish warm taupe from cool taupe. The color is popular in interior design for its neutrality: {taupe walls}, {taupe upholstery}.

Taut means pulled tight, with no slack or looseness: {a taut rope}, {taut muscles}. The word extends to anything showing tension—a taut expression reveals strain, a taut thriller maintains suspense without wasted moments. Taut prose is lean and controlled, with nothing extraneous. The opposite is slack or loose.

A tavern is an establishment that serves alcoholic drinks and sometimes food—essentially a bar or pub. The word has an old-fashioned ring in American English, where it often evokes colonial-era inns or appears in deliberately quaint business names: {The Old Town Tavern has been serving locals since 1847}. In some regions, tavern remains the standard term for a neighborhood drinking establishment.

Taverns is the plural of tavern, a place that serves alcoholic drinks and sometimes food. The word evokes an older style of establishment—the roadside inn where travelers stopped for ale and lodging, or the colonial meeting house where revolutionaries plotted. Modern usage tends toward deliberate nostalgia: {The historic district has cobblestone streets and old taverns}.

Tawdry describes something cheap and gaudy—showy but of poor quality. A tawdry {dress} might feature too much glitter and synthetic fabric. The word extends to anything trashy or sordid: {tawdry gossip}, {a tawdry affair}. What distinguishes tawdry from merely cheap is the failed attempt at elegance or respectability.

Tawny is a warm brownish-orange color, like a lion's coat or autumn leaves. The word most often describes animal fur, skin tones, or wine: {a tawny owl}, {tawny port}. It suggests earthiness and warmth rather than bright or vivid color.

Tax is money that governments require people and businesses to pay, calculated as a portion of income, property value, or the price of goods and services. Taxes fund public services like roads, schools, and defense. The verb tax means to impose such a levy: {The state taxes cigarettes heavily}. Beyond money, tax extends to anything that strains or burdens: {The climb taxed his endurance}. If you tax someone with something, you accuse them of it, though this use is somewhat formal and old-fashioned.

Taxation is the system by which governments collect money from citizens and businesses to fund public services and operations. The word covers both the practice itself and the amount collected: {Taxation without representation sparked the American Revolution}. Heavy taxation draws complaints; tax policy shapes economies. The power to tax is among a government's most fundamental authorities.

Taxed is the past tense of tax, meaning a government levy was imposed: {Income is taxed at different rates}. Beyond finance, taxed means strained or burdened: {The crisis taxed our resources}. To be taxed is to feel depleted: {I'm completely taxed after that meeting}. To tax someone with something is to accuse them: {She taxed him with neglecting his duties}.

Taxes are compulsory payments to governments, levied on income, property, transactions, or goods. The word usually appears as a plural because multiple types exist: income taxes, property taxes, sales taxes. To tax something is to impose such a levy: {The state taxes cigarettes heavily}. Figuratively, something that taxes you strains your resources or patience: {The journey taxed her strength}.

A taxi is a car for hire, usually with a driver, that takes passengers where they want to go for a fare. Also called a taxicab or cab. The verb means to travel by taxi or, for an aircraft, to move along the ground under its own power before takeoff or after landing: {The plane taxied to the gate}.

A taxicab is an automobile for hire, typically summoned on the street or at a stand, that takes passengers to a destination for a metered fare. Usually shortened to taxi or cab: {We grabbed a cab outside the hotel}. Yellow taxicabs are iconic in New York City. The taxi- comes from taximeter, the device that calculates the fare.

Taxidermied describes an animal that has been preserved and mounted through taxidermy—the skin stuffed or stretched over a form to create a lifelike appearance. {A taxidermied deer head hung above the fireplace.} The word functions as both past tense verb and adjective: {He taxidermied the fish himself} or {a taxidermied owl}.
clues: Dead animal made to look alive

definition: A taxidermist is a person who practices taxidermy—the art of preserving and mounting animal skins to create lifelike representations. Taxidermists work for museums, hunting lodges, and private collectors, turning game trophies or specimens into permanent displays: {The taxidermist mounted the deer head above the fireplace}.

Taxidermists are people who practice taxidermy—the art of preserving and mounting animal skins to create lifelike representations. They work with hunters' trophies, create museum specimens, or restore damaged mounts. The craft requires knowledge of anatomy, sculpture, and painting: {The taxidermist positioned the deer as if it were mid-leap}.

Taxidermy is the art of preserving and mounting animal skins to create lifelike representations. A taxidermist poses the specimen over a form, reconstructing the animal's appearance for display in museums, homes, or trophy collections. {The deer head above the fireplace was his grandfather's taxidermy.} The practice requires knowledge of anatomy and sculpture alongside preservation techniques.

Taxiing is what aircraft do when moving on the ground under their own power—rolling along runways and taxiways before takeoff or after landing. {The plane spent twenty minutes taxiing before reaching the gate.} The term extends to any vehicle maneuvering slowly into position.

Taxing describes something that demands significant effort, energy, or resources. A taxing job drains you physically or mentally. A taxing conversation leaves you exhausted. {The hike was more taxing than I expected.} The word draws on the sense of taxation as something that takes from you, depleting what you have.

A taxiway is a paved path at an airport that aircraft use to move between runways, terminals, and hangars. Pilots taxi along these routes after landing or before takeoff: {The plane turned off the runway onto the taxiway}. Taxiways are marked with yellow lines and designated by letters to guide ground movement.

A taxman is a person who collects taxes, especially one who works for the government's revenue agency. The term often carries a slightly adversarial tone—the taxman is who comes after your money: {The taxman takes a third of my paycheck}. British English uses it more than American, where {IRS agent} is more common.

Taxonomy is the science of classification, especially the systematic categorization of living organisms into hierarchical groups—kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. More broadly, any scheme for organizing things into categories: {the taxonomy of literary genres}, {a taxonomy of user behaviors}. The plural taxonomies often refers to competing classification systems for the same domain.

A taxpayer is a person or entity that pays taxes to a government. The term often appears in political rhetoric emphasizing accountability: {taxpayer dollars}, {hardworking taxpayers}. It frames government spending as money belonging to citizens rather than the state: {Is this really the best use of taxpayer money?}

Taxpayers are people or entities that pay taxes to a government. The term appears constantly in political discourse, where it frames government spending as coming directly from citizens' pockets: {taxpayer dollars}, {taxpayer-funded programs}. Politicians invoke taxpayers to argue for fiscal restraint or against policies they oppose: {Hardworking taxpayers shouldn't foot the bill for this}.

Tazed is a past tense spelling of tase, meaning to shock someone with a Taser stun gun: {The officer tazed the suspect during the arrest}. The more common spelling is tased, following the brand name Taser, but tazed appears frequently in informal writing.

A tchotchke is a small decorative object of little value—a trinket, knickknack, or curio. The word comes from Yiddish and often carries a slightly dismissive tone, suggesting clutter or kitsch: {Her shelves were crowded with tchotchkes from every vacation}. Tchotchkes may also be cheap promotional items companies give away at trade shows.

Tchotchkes are small decorative objects or trinkets, often of little value—the knickknacks that accumulate on shelves, mantels, and desks. The word comes from Yiddish and carries a slightly dismissive tone, suggesting clutter or kitsch rather than meaningful possessions: {Her apartment was full of tchotchkes from her travels}. Also spelled tsotchkes or chachkas.

The main use of tea is to designate the beverage made from the leaves of Camellia sinensis, but tea can also denote the plant itself, or the dried leaves before they are brewed in water. Tea is also used to designate any other beverage made by infusion of leaves, seeds, or spices in water, as in ginger tea or fenugreek tea. In the UK and some other countries influenced by British culture, tea also designates an afternoon or evening meal that may feature tea as a beverage.

A teabag is a small porous pouch containing tea leaves, designed to steep in hot water. The bag allows brewing without loose leaves. As a verb, teabag has a vulgar slang sense: to lower one's scrotum onto another person's face, the motion resembling dipping a teabag. This may be sexual or a prank, especially in gaming culture where it mocks defeated opponents.

Teabags are small porous pouches containing tea leaves for steeping. They offer convenience over loose-leaf tea—just dunk in hot water and remove. The verb teabag has a vulgar slang sense: to lower one's scrotum onto someone's face, the motion resembling dipping a teabag. In video games, teabagging a defeated opponent is a taunt.

A teacake is a small, lightly sweetened bread or cake served with tea. In Britain, it typically refers to a round yeast bun containing dried fruit, often toasted and buttered: {We had teacakes with our afternoon tea}. In the American South, teacakes are simple sugar cookies, a traditional homemade treat.

Teacakes are small, lightly sweetened baked goods served with tea. In Britain, a teacake is typically a round yeast bun containing dried fruit, often toasted and buttered. In the American South, teacakes are simple, soft cookies resembling sugar cookies, traditionally made for children: {My grandmother's teacakes were famous at church socials}.

To teach is to help someone learn—passing on knowledge, skills, or understanding through instruction or example. Teachers teach students; parents teach children right from wrong. The word extends beyond formal education: {Life taught her to be cautious}. To teach someone a lesson is to give them a punishing experience they won't forget. {That'll teach you} means the consequence should prevent repetition.

Teachable describes someone willing and able to learn—open to instruction rather than resistant to it: {She's smart and teachable, a coach's dream}. The word can also apply to subjects or skills that can be taught: {Is creativity teachable, or is it innate?} A teachable moment is an unplanned opportunity for instruction that arises naturally from circumstances.

A teacher is someone who instructs others, typically in a school setting. The word applies broadly—from kindergarten teachers to university professors, from piano teachers to driving instructors. Good teachers don't just transmit information; they help students understand: {She was the teacher who made me love science}. Teacher also appears in spiritual contexts: {a Buddhist teacher}, {Jesus as teacher}.

Teachers are people who instruct others, typically in schools or educational settings. The word usually implies a profession—someone paid to educate students in subjects from arithmetic to art. But teacher extends beyond classrooms: life can be a teacher, experience can be a teacher, and anyone who shows you something becomes one. {My piano teacher canceled our lesson.} {Failure is the best teacher.}

Teaches is the third-person singular of teach—to impart knowledge or skill to someone. A professor {teaches organic chemistry}. Experience {teaches humility}. The word often appears in proverbs and generalizations: {History teaches us that empires fall}. {Who teaches your daughter piano?}

Teaching is the work of instructing others—passing on knowledge, skills, or understanding. The word covers both the profession {She went into teaching after college} and the act itself {His teaching style emphasizes discussion}. In religious contexts, teachings (usually plural) are doctrines or principles: {the teachings of Buddha}, {biblical teachings}.

Teachings are ideas, principles, or doctrines passed down by a teacher, philosopher, or religious figure. The word typically appears in contexts of wisdom or guidance: {the teachings of Buddha}, {her grandmother's teachings about kindness}. Unlike lessons, which can be practical or mundane, teachings usually implies moral, spiritual, or philosophical content meant to shape how one lives.

A teacup is a small cup designed for drinking tea, typically with a handle and often paired with a saucer. Teacups are generally smaller and more delicate than coffee mugs. {A storm in a teacup} is a disproportionate fuss over something trivial.

Teacups are small cups designed for drinking tea, typically with a handle and often paired with a saucer. The word also names an amusement park ride where passengers sit in cup-shaped vehicles that spin: {The kids wanted to ride the teacups three times in a row}. A {tempest in a teacup} is a minor dispute blown out of proportion.

A teahouse is an establishment serving tea and light refreshments. In East Asian cultures, teahouses are traditional gathering places with elaborate tea service rituals: {We stopped at a teahouse in Kyoto}. In Western contexts, the term often evokes these Asian traditions or refers to cafés specializing in tea rather than coffee.

Teahouses are establishments serving tea and light refreshments. In East Asian cultures, particularly China and Japan, teahouses are traditional gathering places with elaborate customs around tea preparation and consumption. In Western contexts, teahouses tend to be cafés specializing in tea rather than coffee: {We spent the afternoon at a little teahouse downtown}.

Teak is a tropical hardwood prized for its durability and water resistance. The tree is native to South and Southeast Asia. Teak's golden-brown color and natural oils make it ideal for outdoor furniture, boat decks, and flooring: {The patio set was solid teak}. It weathers to a silvery gray if left untreated.

A teakettle is a covered container with a handle and spout, used for boiling water on a stovetop. Traditional teakettles are made of metal and often have a whistle that sounds when the water reaches a boil. The word is sometimes shortened to kettle, though kettle can also refer to other pot-like vessels. {Put the teakettle on and I'll make us some tea.}

Teal is a blue-green color, named after the colored patch on the wing of the teal duck. The shade sits between blue and green on the spectrum: {teal walls}, {a teal sweater}. The teal duck itself is a small freshwater bird found across the Northern Hemisphere.

A tealight is a small candle in a thin metal or plastic cup, designed to burn for several hours. The shallow container holds the wax as it melts completely. Tealights are used in decorative holders, under food warmers, and in aromatherapy diffusers: {She scattered tealights around the bathtub}.

Tealights are small, squat candles in thin metal or plastic cups, typically burning for several hours. The name comes from their original use warming teapots, but they now serve mainly as ambient lighting or decoration: {She scattered tealights around the bathtub}. Also spelled tea lights.

A team is a group working together toward a common goal. Sports teams compete as units; work teams collaborate on projects. The word extends to any coordinated pairing: a team of horses, a team of oxen. To team up is to join forces: {She teamed up with her rival to win the competition}. As an adjective, team describes collective effort: {team spirit}, {team player}.

Teambuilding refers to activities or exercises designed to improve cooperation, communication, and trust among members of a group—typically coworkers. The term often carries a slightly dreaded connotation, suggesting mandatory fun: {The retreat included a teambuilding exercise where we had to build a tower out of spaghetti}. Also spelled as two words: team building.

A teammate is someone who plays on the same team as you, whether in sports, games, or collaborative work projects. The term implies shared goals and mutual cooperation—your teammates are the people you work alongside rather than compete against. {My teammate passed me the ball right before I scored.} In workplace contexts, teammate has become a popular alternative to coworker, emphasizing collaboration over mere proximity.

Teammates are people on the same team—in sports, work, or any collaborative effort. The word emphasizes shared purpose and mutual reliance: {She passed to her teammate for the winning goal}. In gaming, teammates may be strangers matched together: {My teammates kept dying in the first round}.

Teams are groups of people working together toward a shared goal. The word applies to sports ({the home team}), workplaces ({our marketing team}), and any collaborative effort. To team up is to join forces: {We teamed up to finish the project}. Team can also describe matched pairs: {a team of horses}.

A teamster is someone who drives a truck for a living. The term originally meant a driver of a team of horses or draft animals pulling a wagon, and that sense persists in historical contexts: {The teamster guided his mules along the mountain trail}. The word now almost always refers to professional truck drivers: {The teamsters hauled freight across three states}. (Capitalized Teamster refers to a union member.)

Teamsters are drivers of trucks or other commercial vehicles, especially members of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, the large American labor union. The word originally referred to drivers of teams of draft animals—horses or oxen pulling wagons. {The teamsters threatened to strike if wages weren't raised.} The union expanded beyond trucking to represent workers in warehouses, airlines, and other industries.

Teamwork is cooperative effort by a group toward a shared goal. The word emphasizes coordination and mutual support rather than individual achievement: {Good teamwork won us the game}. It appears constantly in workplace and sports contexts, sometimes to the point of cliché: {There's no "I" in teamwork}.

A teapot is a vessel for brewing and serving tea, typically with a handle, spout, and lid. The shape is so familiar it becomes metaphorical: a {tempest in a teapot} is an overreaction to a trivial matter. In computing, the Utah teapot is a standard 3D test model, referenced in the HTTP error code 418: "I'm a teapot."

Teapots is the plural of teapot, a vessel for steeping and serving tea. A teapot typically has a handle, spout, and lid, designed to keep tea warm while allowing easy pouring. {She collected antique teapots from England and Japan.} A {tempest in a teapot} is a disproportionate fuss over a trivial matter.

Tear represents two different English words that have settled on the same spelling. One is the drop of liquid from the eye—tears flow when we cry, and we speak of {tears of joy} or being {moved to tears}. The other tear means to rip or pull apart forcefully: {She tore the letter in half}. To tear also means to move with violent haste: {He tore down the street}. A tear is the resulting rip: {a tear in the fabric}. To be {torn} is to feel conflicted between options. The two words are distinguished by pronunciation: the eye produces a "teer," while ripping creates a "tare."

A tearaway is a reckless young person who behaves wildly or causes trouble—British slang for what Americans might call a hellion or juvenile delinquent. The word suggests youthful rebellion rather than serious criminality: {He was a bit of a tearaway in his teens but settled down after university}. As an adjective, it describes such behavior: {tearaway youth}.

A teardown is the systematic disassembly of something to examine its components. Engineers perform teardowns on competitors' products to analyze design and manufacturing: {The teardown revealed cheaper materials than advertised}. In real estate, a teardown is a property purchased not for its existing structure but for the land—the building will be demolished: {They bought the old bungalow as a teardown}. In testing and software, teardown refers to cleanup after a process completes.

Teardowns are the acts of completely disassembling something to examine its components, common in technology analysis where experts take apart devices to study their construction: {The teardown revealed the phone's battery was glued in place}. In real estate, a teardown is a property purchased specifically to demolish the existing structure and build something new: {They bought the old bungalow as a teardown}.

A teardrop is a single drop of the salty liquid produced by crying—the tear itself, or the shape it makes: rounded at one end, tapering to a point at the other. The teardrop shape appears in jewelry, guitar picks, and camper trailers. {A teardrop rolled down her cheek.}

Teardrops are drops of the salty liquid that flows from the eyes when crying. The word is slightly more poetic or deliberate than *tears*: {A teardrop rolled down her cheek}. Teardrop also describes a shape—rounded at one end and tapering to a point at the other: {teardrop earrings}, {a teardrop trailer}.

Tearful describes someone who is crying or close to tears: {She gave a tearful goodbye at the airport}. It can also describe things marked by weeping: a tearful {reunion}, a tearful {apology}. The word suggests visible emotion without implying the intensity of sobbing—more restrained, often mixed with other feelings like relief or gratitude.

Teargas is a chemical weapon that irritates the eyes and respiratory system, causing tears, pain, and temporary blindness. Despite being banned in warfare, it's commonly used by police for riot control and crowd dispersal: {Police fired teargas into the crowd}. As a verb, to teargas is to attack with such chemicals. Also spelled tear gas.

Teargassed is the past tense of teargas, meaning to attack with tear gas—a chemical agent that irritates the eyes and respiratory system, causing tears, pain, and temporary blindness. Police and military forces teargas crowds to disperse them: {Protesters were teargassed outside the capitol}. Also spelled tear-gassed.

Tearing describes something that moves with violent speed or intensity: {He went tearing down the street}. It also describes pain that feels like flesh being ripped: {a tearing sensation in my shoulder}. As the present participle of tear, it covers the act of ripping: {She was tearing the letter into pieces}.

A tearjerker is a movie, book, song, or other work designed to provoke strong emotions, especially sadness: {The film is an unabashed tearjerker}. The term carries a slight note of criticism—implying the emotional manipulation is obvious or excessive—but is often used affectionately for works that deliver a satisfying cry.

Tearjerkers are movies, books, songs, or other works designed to provoke strong emotional responses, particularly sadness or sentimentality. The term carries a slightly dismissive tone, suggesting the emotional manipulation is obvious or heavy-handed rather than earned through genuine artistry. {She dismissed the film as just another tearjerker, but I cried anyway.} Despite the faint criticism implied, people often seek out tearjerkers deliberately, finding catharsis in a good cry.

Tearjerking describes something designed to provoke tears or strong emotion, especially through sentimental or manipulative means: {a tearjerking movie}, {a tearjerking reunion scene}. The word often carries a hint of criticism—suggesting the emotional response is being manufactured rather than earned. A tearjerker is the thing itself: {That film was a real tearjerker}.

A tearoom is an establishment serving tea and light refreshments, typically with a genteel or old-fashioned atmosphere: {We stopped at a tearoom for scones and sandwiches}. In gay slang, tearoom refers to a public restroom used for anonymous sexual encounters between men—a usage that emerged in the mid-twentieth century.

Tearooms are establishments serving tea and light refreshments, typically with a genteel or old-fashioned atmosphere: {We stopped at a tearoom for scones and clotted cream}. The term also refers, especially in older slang, to public restrooms used as meeting places for anonymous gay sex—a usage that has faded as gay culture has become more open.

Tears are the drops of salty liquid that flow from the eyes during crying or irritation. They may signal grief, joy, frustration, or physical pain: {She wiped away her tears}. Tears also form reflexively—from onions, wind, or dust. To be {in tears} is to be crying. To {tear up} is to begin crying. Separately, tears (rhyming with "airs") is the plural of tear, meaning rips or holes.

Teary describes eyes filling with tears or a person on the verge of crying: {She got teary during the speech}. It suggests emotion welling up rather than full-blown weeping—the precursor to actual tears. Teary-eyed works the same way: {a teary-eyed goodbye}.

Teas is the plural of tea—the beverage made by steeping dried leaves in hot water, or the plant itself. Multiple varieties are teas: {green teas}, {herbal teas}, {black teas}. In British usage, teas can mean multiple instances of the light afternoon meal: {We hosted several teas for visiting relatives}. In slang, tea means gossip, so teas would be multiple pieces of gossip, though the singular dominates: {spill the tea}.

Tease centers on playful provocation. To tease someone is to mock them good-naturedly or tantalize them: {She teased him about his haircut}, {The trailer teases the upcoming season}. A tease is someone who arouses interest or desire without satisfying it—often sexual: {He's such a tease}. To tease out something is to extract it carefully: {teasing out the meaning of the poem}. Teasing hair involves backcombing it for volume.

Teased is the past tense of tease. To tease someone is to make fun of them playfully or mockingly: {She teased him about his haircut}. Teasing can be affectionate or cruel depending on context. To tease also means to comb or backcomb hair for volume, or to pull apart fibers: {She teased her hair before the party}. To tease something out is to extract it gradually: {teasing out the implications of the data}.

A teaser is something that stimulates curiosity without fully satisfying it. A teaser for a film or TV show reveals just enough to generate interest: {The studio released a teaser trailer}. A teaser can be a puzzle or riddle, a provocative advertisement, or a person who teases. In journalism, a teaser is a brief item promoting a story to come.

Teasers are things that tease—short previews designed to spark curiosity without satisfying it. Movie teasers hint at coming attractions. Article teasers on a magazine cover entice you to read inside. A teaser rate on a loan starts attractively low before rising. The word also applies to difficult puzzles: {brain teasers}. A person who teases others playfully or provocatively is also a teaser.

Teases is the verb form of tease—to mock playfully, provoke, or tantalize. Someone teases a friend about a crush, or teases a cat with a string. Hair that's teased is backcombed for volume. A teaser is a preview meant to tantalize: {The studio released teases of the upcoming season}. As a noun, teases are instances of teasing or people who tease: {She's such a tease}.

A teashop is a small café or restaurant serving tea and light refreshments, typically pastries, sandwiches, and scones. The term evokes a quaint, old-fashioned British establishment: {We stopped at a teashop in the Cotswolds for cream tea}. In American usage, teashop may also refer to a retail store selling tea and tea accessories.

Teashops are small establishments serving tea and light refreshments. The term is primarily British, evoking a quaint atmosphere of scones, cakes, and afternoon tea. American English more commonly uses tearoom or tea house. {We stopped at a teashop in the Cotswolds for cream tea.}

Teasing is playful provocation—mocking, poking fun, or making light of someone, usually without malicious intent: {She was teasing him about his haircut}. The line between affectionate teasing and hurtful ridicule depends on relationship and tone. Teasing also means to tantalize or withhold something desired: {Stop teasing and tell me the answer}. Hair that's teased has been backcombed for volume.

A teaspoon is a small spoon used for stirring beverages and eating soft foods. It's also a unit of measurement in cooking, equal to about 5 milliliters or one-third of a tablespoon: {Add a teaspoon of vanilla extract}. Abbreviated tsp.

Teaspoons are small spoons used for stirring beverages and measuring ingredients. As a unit of measurement, a teaspoon equals about 5 milliliters—one-third of a tablespoon. Recipes often call for teaspoons of spices, extracts, or leavening agents: {Add two teaspoons of vanilla}. The teaspoon is the smallest spoon in a standard flatware set.

A teat is a nipple, especially the projection on a mammal's breast or udder through which milk is drawn by nursing young. The word extends to artificial nipples on baby bottles. Teat sounds slightly more clinical or agricultural than nipple: {The calf searched for the teat}. In British usage, teat is the standard term for a bottle nipple.

Teatime is the customary hour for drinking tea, typically late afternoon in British tradition. The word evokes a ritualized break—cups, saucers, perhaps biscuits or sandwiches: {We'll discuss it at teatime}. By extension, teatime can mean any regular daily pause or the light meal accompanying it.

Teats are the nipples of mammals, particularly the projections through which young suckle milk. The word applies to humans but more often describes animals: {The piglets fought for position at their mother's teats}. Teats also refers to the rubber nipples on baby bottles or similar devices designed for feeding.

Tech is an informal shortening of technology or technical. It often refers to the technology industry as a whole: {She works in tech}, {a tech startup}. As an adjective, it describes things related to technology: {tech companies}, {tech support}. A tech is also a technician: {The lab tech drew my blood}.

A techie is a person with expertise in or enthusiasm for technology, especially computers and electronics. The term can be affectionate or dismissive depending on context—either praising technical skill or suggesting someone is overly absorbed in gadgets and gear: {Ask one of the techies to fix the projector}. Also spelled techy.

Techies are people with technical expertise, especially in computing and electronics. The term is informal and mildly affectionate, suggesting enthusiasm as much as skill: {The techies in IT fixed my laptop}. A techie might be a professional programmer, a hobbyist who builds computers, or anyone notably comfortable with technology.

Techlash is a public backlash against major technology companies, particularly regarding concerns about privacy, market dominance, misinformation, and social harms. The term blends "technology" and "backlash," emerging in the late 2010s as sentiment shifted from Silicon Valley enthusiasm to skepticism: {The techlash has prompted calls for regulating social media platforms}.

Technical relates to the specific methods, skills, or knowledge required in a particular field. A technical {manual} explains how something works. Technical {expertise} means specialized competence. In sports and arts, technical {skill} refers to precision and control of fundamentals rather than creativity or expression. A technical {foul} in basketball penalizes procedural violations rather than physical contact. Something technical in the strict sense may differ from practical reality: {Technically, he's still employed here, but he hasn't shown up in months}.

Technicalities are minor details of rules, laws, or procedures—often ones that seem to matter more on paper than in spirit. A case dismissed {on a technicality} fails not because of innocence but because of procedural error. The word usually carries a dismissive tone, suggesting that strict adherence to rules has overridden common sense or substantive justice: {He got off on a technicality}.

A technicality is a minor detail or fine point, especially one that carries legal or procedural weight despite seeming trivial: {He got off on a technicality}. The word often implies frustration—a small rule overriding what seems like obvious justice or common sense. More neutrally, technicalities are the specific details of a craft or field: {the technicalities of contract law}.
