The main uses of the singular noun term are for either a word or group of words, usually considered a noun as a whole, that designates something (What’s the term for someone who is habitually tardy?) or a period of time with fixed ends, (term in office). In the plural, terms are the provisions of an agreement or understanding. Even more generally, terms denotes the general standing you have with someone or something: She’s on good terms with her in-laws. Fields such as law, mathematics, and logic have specific meanings for term. As a verb, term means to label with a word or phrase: Art that is loosely termed “post-modern.”

The meanings of terminal overlap largely with some meanings of end. In expressions of time, terminal means at or near the end (terminal cancer). The noun terminal denotes a building or place that is a destination or is at the end of a transportation route (truck terminal, train terminal). In computing, terminal usually designates one end of an information exchanging process – the end where the user is found.

Terminals are endpoints or final points in a system. In transportation, a terminal is where journeys begin or end: an airport terminal, a bus terminal. In electronics, terminals are connection points where wires attach: {Connect the positive terminal first}. A computer terminal is a device for entering and receiving data from a system. As an adjective, terminal describes something at the end or leading to death: a terminal {illness}, a terminal {patient}. {The diagnosis was terminal.}

Terminate means to bring something to an end. A contract terminates when it expires or is canceled. Employment terminates when someone is fired or quits. In harsher usage, to terminate someone can mean to kill them—a euphemism favored in espionage and action films: {The agent was ordered to terminate the target}. A bus route terminates at its final stop. A pregnancy may be terminated through abortion.

Terminated means ended or concluded, often abruptly or definitively. A contract can be terminated, a pregnancy can be terminated, or an employee can be terminated—a formal way of saying fired. In science fiction and action contexts, terminated became a euphemism for killed: {The target has been terminated}. The word carries finality that "ended" lacks.

Termination is the act of ending something or the state of being ended. A contract reaches termination when it expires or is canceled. Employment termination means someone has been fired or laid off: {The company offered severance packages with all terminations}. In more clinical contexts, termination refers to ending a pregnancy. The word carries a formal, often bureaucratic tone—people say termination when they want to avoid saying fired, ended, or aborted.

A terminator is something or someone that ends, limits, or finishes something. In astronomy, the terminator is the boundary line between the illuminated and dark portions of a celestial body like the moon: {The terminator crept across the lunar surface as the sun set}. In genetics, a terminator is a DNA sequence that signals the end of transcription. In electronics, a terminator is a resistor at the end of a transmission line that prevents signal reflection. The word also serves as general slang for anything that definitively ends or destroys something: {That last exam was a real terminator}. (Capitalized Terminator refers to the film franchise.)

Terminators are things that end or conclude something. In astronomy, the terminator is the line dividing the illuminated and dark portions of a celestial body—the boundary between day and night on the moon or a planet. In genetics, a terminator is a DNA sequence that signals the end of transcription. The word gained pop-culture currency from the *Terminator* film franchise, where it names robotic assassins: {He walked toward us like a terminator}.

Terminology is the set of specialized terms used in a particular field, discipline, or subject area: {medical terminology}, {legal terminology}, {the terminology of linguistics}. The word can also refer to the study of such terms and their proper use. When someone objects to your terminology, they're questioning your word choice rather than your underlying point.

Terminus is the final point or end of something—especially the last station on a transportation line: {The train terminates at Grand Central, the line's terminus}. A terminus can be any endpoint: the terminus of a nerve, the terminus of a glacier. The word retains its Latin flavor and often appears in formal or technical contexts. Plural: termini or terminuses.

Termites are small, pale insects that live in colonies and feed on wood and other plant matter. Often called white ants, they're not actually ants but are more closely related to cockroaches. Termites cause billions of dollars in structural damage annually by eating wooden buildings from the inside: {The inspector found termite damage in the basement}. A termite can also describe someone who quietly undermines from within.

Termites are small social insects that live in colonies and feed on wood and other plant matter. They cause significant structural damage to buildings by eating wooden components from the inside out, often undetected until the damage is severe. Termites are sometimes called white ants, though they're more closely related to cockroaches. {The inspector found termite damage in the basement.}

Terms are the conditions or provisions of an agreement: {the terms of the contract}, {terms of surrender}. To {come to terms} is to reach agreement, or to accept something difficult: {She came to terms with her diagnosis}. Terms also means the relationship between people: {on good terms}, {on speaking terms}. In specialized contexts, terms are words with specific meanings: {legal terms}, {technical terms}. A school term is a division of the academic year.

A tern is a seabird related to gulls but typically smaller and more slender, with a forked tail, pointed wings, and a sharp bill. Terns are graceful fliers that dive headfirst into water to catch fish. The Arctic tern makes the longest annual migration of any bird, pole to pole. {A tern hovered above the waves before plunging after its prey.}

Terns are seabirds related to gulls but typically more slender and graceful, with pointed wings, forked tails, and sharp bills. They are found worldwide near coastlines, lakes, and rivers, where they dive headfirst into water to catch fish. Common species include the Arctic tern, famous for its pole-to-pole migration—the longest of any bird. {A flock of terns wheeled above the pier.}

A terrace is a raised flat area, especially one cut into a hillside for cultivation or a paved outdoor space adjoining a building: {We had drinks on the terrace}. In British usage, a terrace is a row of connected houses sharing side walls. At stadiums, terraces are standing sections with tiered steps. To terrace land is to shape it into level platforms: {terraced rice paddies}.

Terraced describes something arranged in a series of flat levels rising one above another, like steps. Terraced hillsides allow farming on steep slopes: {terraced rice paddies}. In British English, terraced houses are row houses sharing side walls in a continuous line: {a terraced street in Manchester}.

Terraces are flat, level areas cut into a slope, creating a series of step-like platforms. In agriculture, terracing prevents erosion and allows farming on hillsides: {rice terraces in the Philippines}. In architecture, a terrace is an outdoor patio or balcony, or a row of connected houses sharing side walls. In British usage, the terraces are standing sections at football stadiums where fans gather: {singing from the terraces}.

Terracing is the practice of cutting flat steps into a hillside to create level surfaces for farming or construction. The technique prevents erosion and allows cultivation on steep terrain: {Rice terracing has shaped Asian mountainsides for centuries}. Terracing also refers to the resulting landscape or the process of installing tiered levels in gardens and yards.

Terracotta is a brownish-orange clay, or objects made from it—pots, tiles, sculptures, architectural ornaments. The material is fired but unglazed, porous and earthy. As a color term, terracotta describes that distinctive reddish-brown: {terracotta walls}, {a terracotta sunset}. The word comes from Italian for "baked earth."

Terraform means to transform a planet or moon to make it habitable for Earth life—altering atmosphere, temperature, and terrain to resemble Earth conditions. The concept comes from science fiction but appears in serious discussions of Mars colonization: {It would take centuries to terraform Mars}. In computing, Terraform is infrastructure software, and the verb means to provision or configure systems automatically: {We'll terraform the new servers tonight}.

Terraformed describes a planet, moon, or other celestial body that has been artificially modified to support Earth-like life. The process involves altering atmosphere, temperature, and surface conditions to make an otherwise hostile world habitable: {Mars in the novel had been terraformed over centuries, with breathable air and flowing rivers}. The term comes from science fiction but appears in serious discussions of space colonization.

A terraformer is a person, organization, or device that transforms a planet or moon to make it habitable for Earth life—adjusting atmosphere, temperature, and surface conditions. The term belongs primarily to science fiction, where terraformers are colonizers reshaping alien worlds: {The terraformers spent generations greening Mars}. By extension, anyone dramatically reshaping an environment might be called a terraformer.

Terraformers are people or entities that terraform—transform a planet's environment to make it habitable for Earth life. The term belongs almost entirely to science fiction, where terraformers might be engineers, colonists, or machines working to give Mars breathable air or liquid water: {The terraformers had spent three generations warming the planet}. By extension, anyone radically reshaping an environment for human use.

Terraforming is the hypothetical process of modifying a planet's atmosphere, temperature, and surface to make it habitable for Earth life. The concept appears most often in science fiction and speculative discussions about colonizing Mars or other planets: {Terraforming Mars could take centuries}. The verb is terraform: {We'd need to terraform before establishing permanent settlements}.

Terraforms means to transform a planet or moon to make it habitable for Earth life—adjusting atmosphere, temperature, and surface conditions to resemble Earth. The concept belongs to science fiction and speculative planetary science: {In the novel, colonists terraform Mars over centuries}. Figuratively, to terraform is to radically reshape any environment to suit one's needs.

Terrain is the physical character of a stretch of land—its elevation, slope, vegetation, and surface features. The word implies land considered from a practical standpoint: {The terrain made hiking difficult}. Military strategy depends heavily on terrain. Figuratively, terrain describes any area of activity or knowledge: {familiar terrain for a veteran negotiator}.

A terrapin is a freshwater or brackish-water turtle, especially the diamondback terrapin of North American coastal marshes. The word occupies middle ground between sea turtles and land tortoises, though usage varies by region—in British English, terrapin often applies broadly to small freshwater turtles kept as pets.

Terrapins are freshwater or brackish-water turtles, especially the diamondback terrapin of North American coastal marshes. The term sits between turtle (the broad category) and tortoise (land-dwelling species), though usage varies regionally. In British English, terrapin often covers what Americans call turtles. {We spotted terrapins sunning on a log.}

A terrarium is a sealed or partially enclosed glass container for growing plants or keeping small land animals. The enclosure creates a miniature ecosystem, trapping moisture that cycles through condensation: {She built a terrarium with moss and succulents}. For animals like lizards or frogs, terrariums simulate natural habitats with controlled temperature and humidity.

Terrariums are glass containers housing small plants or animals in a controlled environment. A terrarium for plants creates a self-sustaining ecosystem where moisture recycles through condensation. For reptiles or amphibians, a terrarium replicates natural habitat with appropriate heat, humidity, and substrate: {She keeps her gecko in a terrarium with a heat lamp}. The singular is terrarium.

Terrazzo is a flooring material made by embedding chips of marble, granite, or glass in cement or resin, then grinding and polishing the surface smooth. The result is a durable, speckled finish popular in commercial buildings, schools, and mid-century modern design: {The old hospital had terrazzo floors throughout}.

Terrestrial means relating to Earth or to land as opposed to water or air. A terrestrial {planet} is rocky like Earth, distinct from gas giants. Terrestrial {animals} live on land rather than in water. The word contrasts with aquatic, aerial, and celestial: {terrestrial life} versus life in the heavens. In broadcasting, terrestrial refers to signals transmitted from ground-based towers rather than satellites.

Terrible means causing terror or dread: {a terrible accident}, {terrible news}. The word often softens to mean simply very bad or unpleasant: {terrible weather}, {a terrible movie}, {I'm terrible at math}. In casual speech, terrible functions as an intensifier suggesting extremity without necessarily implying badness: {a terrible shame}, {terrible beauty}. Someone who looks terrible appears unwell or exhausted.

A terrier is a type of small, energetic dog originally bred to hunt vermin by digging them out of burrows—the name comes from a word meaning earth. Terriers are known for their feisty, tenacious temperament: {She has the determination of a terrier}. The group includes many breeds: Jack Russell, Scottish, Yorkshire, pit bull.

Terriers are small, energetic dogs originally bred to hunt burrowing animals—the name comes from a word meaning earth. The group includes dozens of breeds: fox terriers, Jack Russells, Scottish terriers, pit bulls. They share a reputation for feistiness and tenacity. {Terriers were bred to dig rats out of their holes.}
clues: Dogs bred to dig out prey

definition: Terrific originally meant causing terror—a terrific storm was one to fear. The word has flipped almost entirely to mean wonderful or excellent: {The food was terrific}, {She did a terrific job}. It can also mean very great in size or intensity: {a terrific explosion}, {terrific speed}. The older frightening sense survives mainly in literary contexts.

Terrified means extremely frightened—fear at its most intense. Where scared suggests discomfort and afraid suggests worry, terrified implies overwhelming dread: {She was terrified of losing her job}, {The children stood terrified as the storm approached}. The word carries physical connotations—being frozen, unable to think or act.
clues: Unable to move from sheer fright

definition: Terrifies is the third-person singular of terrify—to fill with terror or intense fear. The word implies fear strong enough to paralyze or overwhelm: {The thought of public speaking terrifies her}. What terrifies can be real threats or irrational anxieties: {Heights terrify me}, {The news terrifies investors}.

To terrify is to fill with terror—intense, overwhelming fear. The word implies more than ordinary fright; something that terrifies produces a visceral, paralyzing dread: {The thought of speaking in public terrifies me}. Terrifying describes things that inspire such fear: {a terrifying scream}, {terrifying news}. Terrified describes the state of experiencing it: {The children were terrified during the storm}.

Terrifying describes something that causes intense fear or dread. A terrifying {experience} leaves you shaken. A terrifying {thought} is one you can barely bring yourself to consider. The word implies fear strong enough to overwhelm—not merely scary or unsettling, but paralyzing: {The storm's approach was terrifying}.

Territorial describes anything relating to land or geographic areas, especially those controlled or claimed by a person, animal, or political entity. Animals exhibit territorial behavior when they defend their home range from intruders; humans do much the same with property lines and national borders. {The dog gets territorial when strangers approach the yard.} A territorial dispute involves competing claims over land. In political contexts, territorial often refers to regions that belong to a country but lack full statehood or provincial status.

Territoriality is the instinct or behavior of defending a territory. Animals display territoriality through marking, vocalizing, or aggression toward intruders. The concept extends to humans: {Office territoriality makes people possessive about their desks}. In law and politics, territoriality refers to jurisdiction based on geographic boundaries rather than personal status.

Territories is the plural of territory—areas of land under particular jurisdiction or control. Countries have territories; animals defend territories against intruders. In sports, a team's territory is the part of the field they're defending. Sales representatives have territories they cover. {The company divided the region into territories for its salespeople.} In politics, territories are regions that belong to a country but aren't full states or provinces: {the U.S. territories of Puerto Rico and Guam}.

Territory is an area of land, especially one under the control of a ruler, government, or military force: {disputed territory}, {enemy territory}. Animals defend territory against intruders of their own species. Figuratively, territory is any domain of knowledge or activity: {We're in unfamiliar territory here}. In some countries, a territory is an administrative region that lacks the full status of a state or province. Something that {comes with the territory} is an unavoidable part of a situation.
clues: Area claimed by state or beast

definition: Terroir is the complete natural environment in which wine or other agricultural products are produced—the soil, climate, topography, and surrounding vegetation that give a product its distinctive character. The concept is central to French winemaking philosophy, where wines from specific regions are valued for expressing their terroir: {You can taste the terroir in this Burgundy}. The term has expanded beyond wine to coffee, cheese, and other foods where place of origin affects flavor.
clues: What makes regional wines taste different

definition: Terror is intense, overwhelming fear—the kind that grips and paralyzes. A terror is something that causes such fear: {the terrors of war}, {that dog is a terror}. The word often appears in political contexts: {reign of terror}, {war on terror}. A holy terror is someone, especially a child, who causes constant trouble through wild or uncontrollable behavior.

Terrorise is the British spelling of terrorize. To terrorise is to fill with terror through threats, violence, or intimidation: {The gang terrorised the neighbourhood for months}. It can describe systematic campaigns of fear or individual acts of cruelty: {He terrorised his younger siblings}. The word implies sustained or repeated frightening, not a single scare.

Terrorised is the British spelling of terrorized, the past tense and past participle of terrorize. To terrorise is to fill with terror or to coerce through fear and intimidation: {The gang terrorised the neighbourhood for months}. Someone terrorised has been subjected to systematic frightening or violent threats.

Terrorising is the British spelling of terrorizing—to fill with terror or to coerce through fear and intimidation. Someone terrorises a neighbourhood by threatening violence. A bully terrorises classmates. The word implies sustained or repeated acts that keep victims in a state of fear: {The gang had been terrorising local shopkeepers for months}.

Terrorism is the practice of violent, destructive acts against innocent people. Terrorism has existed in nearly all periods of human history. Its motive is sometimes to induce fear in order to bring about submission, though this does not usually succeed. People who carry out terrorism are typically connected with radical political or religious organizations, though many acts of terrorism have also been committed by people acting alone, usually in a state of extreme mental unbalance.

A terrorist is a person who uses violence or the threat of violence against civilians to advance political, ideological, or religious goals. The intent is typically to create fear and compel governments or populations to act. The term is politically charged—one side's terrorist is often another's freedom fighter. {The bombing was claimed by terrorists}. Terrorist also works as an adjective: {terrorist attack}, {terrorist organization}.

Terrorists are people who use violence or threats of violence against civilians to advance political, religious, or ideological goals. The term implies intent to create fear beyond the immediate victims—bombings, hostage-taking, assassinations designed to terrorize a wider population. {The terrorists claimed responsibility for the attack.} The label is politically contested; governments and insurgents often disagree on who qualifies. One side's terrorist may be another's freedom fighter, though the word itself carries strong condemnation.

To terrorize is to fill with terror or to coerce through fear and intimidation. Invading armies terrorize civilian populations. A bully terrorizes the playground. The word implies sustained or repeated acts of frightening behavior, not a single scare: {The gang terrorized the neighborhood for months}. Someone who terrorizes doesn't just frighten—they dominate through fear.

Terrorized is the past tense of terrorize, meaning to fill with terror or to control through fear and intimidation. Someone terrorized by a bully lives in constant dread. A neighborhood terrorized by crime feels unsafe. The word implies sustained or repeated threat rather than a single frightening moment: {She was terrorized by her ex-husband for years}.

Terrorizes means to fill with terror or to control through fear and intimidation. A dictator terrorizes a population; a bully terrorizes classmates. The word implies sustained or repeated threats rather than a single frightening incident: {The gang terrorized the neighborhood for months}. Someone can also terrorize in a less serious sense—a toddler who terrorizes the household with tantrums.

Terrorizing is creating intense fear through threats or violence. A bully terrorizes classmates; an invading army terrorizes civilians. The word implies sustained intimidation rather than a single frightening moment: {The gang had been terrorizing the neighborhood for months}. Casual use describes anything persistently annoying or distressing: {My cat has been terrorizing the houseplants}.

Terrors is the plural of terror—instances of extreme fear or things that cause it. The word often appears in set phrases: {the terrors of war}, {the terrors of the deep}. {Night terrors} are episodes of intense fear during sleep, distinct from nightmares. A person who causes trouble, especially a misbehaving child, may be called {a terror}: {Their toddler is an absolute terror}.

Terry is a type of fabric with uncut loops on one or both sides, giving it a soft, absorbent texture. It's the standard material for towels and bathrobes: {terry cloth}, {a terry robe}. The loops create more surface area, which is why terry absorbs water so well. (Capitalized Terry is a given name.)

Terse describes speech or writing that is brief and to the point, using no unnecessary words. A terse {reply} may be admirably efficient or may feel curt and unfriendly—context determines which. {His terse "no" ended the discussion.} The word often carries a slight edge, suggesting someone is being short with you rather than simply concise.

A tesla is the SI unit of magnetic flux density, measuring the strength of magnetic fields. One tesla equals one weber per square meter. The unit is used in physics, engineering, and medical imaging—MRI machines typically operate at 1.5 to 3 teslas. {The Earth's magnetic field is about 50 microteslas.} (Capitalized Tesla refers to the inventor or the car company.)

Tessellation is a pattern of shapes that fit together perfectly without gaps or overlaps, like tiles covering a floor. The term comes from geometry, where it describes how polygons can repeat to fill a plane: {The honeycomb is nature's most famous tessellation}. Tessellations appear in art, architecture, and mathematics, from ancient mosaics to M.C. Escher's interlocking figures.

A tesseract is a four-dimensional analog of a cube—a hypercube. Just as a cube is bounded by six square faces, a tesseract is bounded by eight cubic cells. The concept exists in mathematics and geometry, though it can only be represented in three dimensions as a projection or unfolded net. The term gained wider recognition through Madeleine L'Engle's novel *A Wrinkle in Time*, where it describes a method of folding space-time for interstellar travel.
clues: A cube with extra spatial depth

definition: A test is a procedure to evaluate quality, performance, or knowledge: {a math test}, {a blood test}, {a stress test}. To test something is to subject it to such evaluation. Test can also mean challenge: {The climb tested our endurance}. A {test of character} reveals someone's true nature under pressure. To {put something to the test} is to see if it holds up.

A testament is evidence or proof of something: {The building stands as a testament to Victorian architecture}. More formally, a testament is a will—a legal document directing disposition of property after death, which is why the phrase "last will and testament" exists. In religious contexts, the Old Testament and New Testament are the two main divisions of the Christian Bible. (Capitalized Testament refers specifically to biblical divisions.)

Testaments are things that serve as evidence or proof: {The ruins stand as testaments to the city's ancient glory}. The word often appears in the phrase {a testament to}, indicating something demonstrates a quality or achievement. In legal contexts, a testament is a will—a document declaring how property should be distributed after death. Capitalized, the Old Testament and New Testament are the two main divisions of the Christian Bible.

Tested describes something that has been examined, tried, or proven through experience. A tested {method} has demonstrated its effectiveness. A tested {friendship} has survived challenges. {Time-tested} means proven reliable over a long period. In medical contexts, tested indicates having undergone examination: {Have you been tested for allergies?} Battle-tested suggests proven under difficult conditions.

A tester is someone or something that tests. A software tester checks programs for bugs. A product tester evaluates goods before release. The word also names devices that perform tests: a circuit tester, a battery tester. In another sense, a tester is a small sample of a product—especially cosmetics or perfume—provided for customers to try before buying.

Testers are people or devices that test things. Software testers check programs for bugs. Product testers evaluate items before release. A tester can also be a small sample: {The store offered perfume testers}. In historical contexts, a tester was a canopy over a bed—from the same root as "test" meaning a shell or covering.

A testicle is one of the two oval organs in the male scrotum that produce sperm and testosterone. The word is anatomical and neutral, appearing in medical contexts and everyday speech alike: {He was hit in the testicles}. The informal equivalent is ball or balls.

Testicles are the pair of male reproductive glands that produce sperm and testosterone. They hang in the scrotum outside the body. The singular testicle appears in expressions about courage or audacity: {He didn't have the testicle to say it to my face}, though balls is far more common in such contexts.

Testified is the past tense of testify, meaning to give evidence or make a formal statement, especially under oath in a legal proceeding: {She testified before the grand jury}. More broadly, it means to serve as evidence or proof: {The ruins testified to the city's former grandeur}. In religious contexts, to testify is to declare one's faith or spiritual experience publicly.

Testifies is the third-person singular form of testify—to give evidence or bear witness. In legal contexts, a person testifies under oath in court: {She testifies tomorrow about what she saw}. More broadly, something that testifies to a fact serves as evidence of it: {The ruins testify to the city's former grandeur}. In religious usage, to testify is to publicly declare one's faith or spiritual experience.

Testify means to give evidence or bear witness, most formally in a legal setting where a person testifies under oath about what they know or observed. The word extends beyond courtrooms: you can testify to someone's character or testify that a product works as advertised. In religious contexts, to testify is to publicly declare one's faith or share a personal spiritual experience. {Several witnesses testified against the defendant.} {I can testify to her honesty.}

Testifying is giving testimony—making a formal statement, especially under oath in legal proceedings: {She spent three hours testifying before the grand jury}. The word extends to any solemn declaration of truth or belief: {He's been testifying to the power of exercise for years}. In religious contexts, testifying means bearing witness to one's faith or spiritual experiences.

A testimonial is a statement praising someone's character, abilities, or a product's effectiveness. Companies use testimonials from satisfied customers to promote their goods: {The website features glowing testimonials}. A testimonial can also be a formal tribute—a dinner or gift honoring someone's service: {The retiring coach received a testimonial from former players}.

Testimonials are statements praising or recommending something, typically a product, service, or person's character. Companies collect customer testimonials for advertising: {The website features glowing testimonials from satisfied users}. In professional contexts, a testimonial may be a formal letter attesting to someone's qualifications or conduct. The word often carries a whiff of marketing—testimonials are selected for their enthusiasm, not their balance.

Testimonies is the plural of testimony, referring to formal statements or declarations, especially those given under oath in legal proceedings. Beyond courtrooms, testimonies often appear in religious contexts, where believers share personal accounts of spiritual experiences or transformations: {Several church members gave testimonies about how their faith helped them through difficult times}. The word carries weight and solemnity, implying statements meant to be taken seriously as evidence or witness to truth.

Testimony is a formal statement, especially one given under oath in legal proceedings: {The witness's testimony contradicted the defendant's account}. Beyond courtrooms, testimony refers to any evidence or proof supporting a claim: {His success is testimony to years of hard work}. In religious contexts, testimony means a public declaration of faith or spiritual experience: {She shared her testimony at the revival}.

Testing is the act of examining something to assess its quality, performance, or condition. Students take tests; software undergoes testing before release; doctors order testing to diagnose illness. {We're still in the testing phase}. As an adjective, testing means difficult or challenging: {It's been a testing few weeks}.

Testosterone is the primary male sex hormone, responsible for developing masculine characteristics like facial hair, deeper voice, and muscle mass. Women produce it too, in smaller amounts. Beyond biology, testosterone often stands for aggressive or competitive male behavior: {Too much testosterone in the boardroom}. Low testosterone ({low T}) is marketed as a treatable condition in aging men.

Tests are procedures to evaluate knowledge, ability, or quality. Students take tests to demonstrate learning; doctors order tests to diagnose conditions; engineers run tests to check whether something works. To test is to examine or try out: {Let's test the water before diving in}. {That really tested my patience.} A test can be any challenge that reveals character or capability.

Testy describes someone who is easily irritated or quick to take offense. A testy {reply} snaps back with impatience. The word suggests a short fuse rather than deep anger—someone testy is prickly and prone to small flare-ups: {He gets testy when he's hungry}. The mood is often temporary rather than a fixed personality trait.

Tetanus is a serious bacterial infection that causes severe muscle spasms and stiffness, particularly in the jaw—hence its common name, lockjaw. The bacteria typically enter through wounds, especially deep punctures. Tetanus shots are routine vaccinations that prevent the disease: {When did you last have a tetanus shot?} {She stepped on a rusty nail and went to get a tetanus booster.}

A tether is a rope, chain, or line that fastens something to a fixed point while allowing limited movement: a dog on a tether, a tethered balloon. To tether is to fasten with such a line. Figuratively, to be {at the end of your tether} is to have exhausted your patience or resources. Tethering a phone shares its internet connection with another device.

Tetherball is a playground game in which two players strike a ball attached by a rope to the top of a pole, each trying to wind the rope completely around the pole in their direction. The game requires no court or equipment beyond the pole and ball: {We played tetherball at recess}. The word also names the ball itself.

Tethered means tied or fastened to something, restricted in movement or range. A tethered {goat} can only graze as far as its rope allows. The meaning extends to anything constrained: a phone tethered to a {charger}, a worker tethered to their {desk}. In computing, tethering connects a device to another for internet access: {I tethered my laptop to my phone}.

Tethering is connecting a mobile device to another device—typically a laptop or tablet—to share its internet connection. Your phone becomes a wireless hotspot, letting other devices access the network through it: {I was tethering my laptop to my phone during the train ride}. The term comes from tether, suggesting the invisible link binding the devices together.

Tethers are ropes, chains, or similar restraints that secure something while allowing limited movement—a goat tethered to a post, a spacecraft tethered to a station. Figuratively, tethers are any binding connections: {the tethers of responsibility}. To be at the {end of one's tether} is to have exhausted patience or resources. The verb tether means to fasten with such a restraint: {She tethered her horse outside the saloon}.
clues: Ropes that limit an animal's range

definition: Tetris is a puzzle video game where players rotate and position falling geometric shapes to complete horizontal lines, which then disappear. The game, created in 1984 by a Soviet programmer, became one of the most popular and recognizable video games ever made. As a verb, to tetris means to fit objects together efficiently in tight spaces: {I tetrised all our luggage into the trunk}.

Tetrominoes is the plural of tetromino—a geometric shape made of four squares joined edge to edge. The seven distinct tetrominoes (I, O, T, S, Z, J, L) are the falling pieces in Tetris, where players rotate and position them to complete horizontal lines. The term comes from combining "tetra" (four) with "domino."

Text is language in written form. Text can also refer to the specific wording of anything that is printed: Alterations to the text of the document were being proposed right up to the last minute. In the context of computing, text may refer to a particular kind of file in which the information is encoded in ASCII and is readable by nearly any computer without the use of special programs. The relatively recent verb text is used for the activity of sending SMS between small devices, usually mobile phones: I texted you and you never texted me back.

A textbook is a book designed for formal study of a subject, used in schools and universities: {The professor assigned three textbooks for the course}. As an adjective, textbook means perfectly typical or exemplary—exactly as described in instructional materials: {a textbook case of fraud}, {textbook technique}. The adjective often carries slight irony, since real situations rarely match textbook descriptions.

Textbooks are books designed for formal study of a subject, used in schools and universities. They present information systematically, often with exercises and review questions. {The professor assigned three textbooks for the semester.} As an adjective, textbook describes something that perfectly matches established standards or expectations: {a textbook example of poor leadership}, {textbook technique}.

Texted is the past tense of text, meaning to send a written message electronically, typically via mobile phone: {She texted me the address}. The word emerged with SMS technology in the 1990s and quickly became standard despite initial resistance to verbing the noun. {I texted him back but never heard anything}.

Textile refers to fabric or cloth, especially woven material. The word covers the full range from raw fibers to finished goods: {the textile industry}, {textile workers}, {textile mills}. As an adjective, it describes things related to fabric production or fiber arts: {textile design}, {textile art}. The plural textiles often refers to the industry or to fabric goods collectively.

Textiles are woven or knitted fabrics, or the fibers and yarns used to make them. The term covers everything from cotton and silk to synthetic materials like polyester. In industry and commerce, textiles refers broadly to the cloth trade: {She works in textiles}. The textile industry encompasses spinning, weaving, dyeing, and finishing processes.

Texting is sending written messages via mobile phone or messaging app. The term emerged with SMS technology in the 1990s and now covers any typed conversation on a phone: {I was texting my sister when the bus arrived}. Texting while driving is illegal in many places. The noun texting refers to the activity itself: {Too much texting is ruining kids' spelling}.

Texts are written works, especially those studied for their content: religious texts, literary texts, legal texts. A text is also the main body of a book apart from notes or illustrations. In education, a text is a textbook. Most commonly now, texts are messages sent between phones: {I'll send you a text when I get there}. The verb means to send such a message: {She was texting during dinner}.

Textspeak is the abbreviated, informal writing style that emerged from SMS messaging and spread to other digital communication. It favors short forms, acronyms, and phonetic spellings: {u} for you, {2nite} for tonight, {lol} for laughing out loud. The style developed when phone keypads made typing tedious and character limits costly. Though smartphones removed those constraints, textspeak persists in casual contexts: {ty for the info}, {omw}.

Texture is how something feels to the touch—smooth, rough, grainy, silky. The word extends to any surface quality perceived through senses: the texture of a painting's brushstrokes, the texture of a voice. In food, texture describes mouthfeel: {The soup needed more texture}. Figuratively, texture means richness or complexity: {The novel has real texture}.

Textured describes something with a surface you can feel or see variation in—not smooth or uniform. A textured {wall} has deliberate roughness; textured {fabric} has a weave you can sense under your fingers. The word extends to experiences with depth or complexity: {a textured performance}, {textured flavors}. Food products labeled "textured" have been processed to simulate another texture: {textured vegetable protein}.

Textures is the plural of texture—the feel or appearance of a surface. A fabric has texture; so does skin, wood, or stone. In music and writing, texture describes the layered quality of sound or prose: {The symphony's rich textures}. In computing, textures are images applied to 3D surfaces to simulate material appearance: {loading high-resolution textures}. As a verb form, textures means to give surface variation: {She textures the clay with her fingertips}.

To thank is to express gratitude: {I thanked her for the gift}. The noun thanks means an expression of gratitude: {Many thanks for your help}. Thanks also serves as an interjection equivalent to "thank you": {Thanks, I appreciate it}. {Thanks to} attributes cause, often sarcastically: {Thanks to the rain, the picnic was ruined}. {No thanks to you} emphasizes someone's lack of help.

Thankful describes feeling or expressing gratitude: {I'm thankful for my health}, {thankful to be alive}. The word often appears around Thanksgiving, when people enumerate blessings. Thankful emphasizes the emotional state of gratitude, while grateful tends toward the response or action that follows: you feel thankful, then act grateful.

Thankfully is an adverb with two distinct uses. The older sense means in a manner expressing gratitude: {She thankfully accepted the gift}. The more common modern use is as a sentence adverb expressing relief or satisfaction about a situation: {Thankfully, no one was injured in the crash}. This second use, parallel to fortunately or mercifully, once drew criticism from usage purists but is now standard.

Thankfulness is the state of feeling grateful or appreciative. It suggests a warm awareness of benefits received: {Her thankfulness for their support was evident}. The word often carries a sense of relief—thankfulness that something difficult has passed or that circumstances aren't worse: {He felt profound thankfulness just to be alive}.

Thankless describes tasks or roles that earn no gratitude despite effort: {a thankless job}, {the thankless work of organizing volunteers}. The word implies that appreciation is deserved but withheld. Less commonly, thankless describes a person who fails to show gratitude—ungrateful: {a thankless child}.

Thanks is an expression of gratitude, a casual alternative to "thank you": {Thanks for the ride}, {Thanks, I appreciate it}. The noun form refers to gratitude itself: {She expressed her thanks}. {Thanks to} attributes cause, often sarcastically: {Thanks to you, we missed the train}. {No thanks} declines an offer: {Coffee? No thanks}.

Thanksgiving is the expression of gratitude, especially to God: {a prayer of thanksgiving}, {a thanksgiving service}. The word emphasizes the act of giving thanks rather than simply feeling grateful. {They offered thanksgiving for the safe return of their loved ones.} (Capitalized Thanksgiving is the American and Canadian holiday.)
clues: The act of expressing grateful praise

definition: Thataway is informal or dialectal for "in that direction," often accompanied by a pointing gesture: {The trail goes thataway}. It mirrors thisaway (this way) and suggests casual, folksy speech. The word appears in Western films and rural dialogue, sometimes humorously: {They went thataway!}

Thatch is a roof covering made of straw, reeds, or similar plant material layered to shed water. Thatched cottages evoke rural England and preindustrial life. The word extends to any thick, matted covering resembling such a roof: {a thatch of unruly hair}. To thatch is to apply or make such a covering.

Thatched describes a roof covered with thatch—dried plant material like straw, reeds, or palm leaves bundled and layered to shed water. The word evokes rustic or traditional architecture: {a thatched cottage in the English countryside}, {thatched huts along the beach}. Thatched can also describe hair that lies thick and unruly, resembling straw.

A thatcher is a person who makes or repairs thatched roofs—roofs covered with straw, reeds, or similar plant material. The trade is ancient but still practiced, especially in rural England and other regions where traditional buildings are preserved: {The thatcher spent three weeks replacing the cottage roof}. (Capitalized Thatcher typically refers to British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.)

Thatching is the craft of covering roofs with dried plant material—typically straw, reeds, or palm fronds—layered and bound to shed water. The technique is ancient and still practiced in parts of Britain, Africa, and the Pacific. Thatching also refers to the material itself or the finished covering: {The cottage's thatching needed repair after the storm}.

Thaw is the process of frozen things becoming unfrozen—ice melting, ground softening, food warming to usable temperature. A spring thaw ends winter's grip. To thaw meat is to bring it from frozen to workable: {Let the chicken thaw overnight in the fridge}. Figuratively, thaw describes warming relations or softening attitudes: {Relations between the two countries began to thaw}. A person who thaws becomes friendlier after initial coldness.

Thawed describes something frozen that has warmed enough to become soft or liquid again. Meat thawed overnight in the refrigerator is ready to cook; a thawed pipe can flow water again. The word extends to emotional states: relations between estranged family members may have thawed after years of silence. {The thawed chicken sat in a pool of its own juices.} {Their thawed friendship picked up where it left off.}

Thawing is the process of warming something frozen until it softens or liquefies. Frozen food thaws before cooking; ice thaws in spring. The word extends to emotional warming: {Relations between the two countries are finally thawing}. A thawing period follows prolonged coldness, whether of temperature or temperament.

Thaws is the verb form of thaw—to melt or warm after being frozen. Ice thaws in spring, frozen pipes thaw when heated, and a person thaws when their coldness or reserve softens: {She thaws a little once you get to know her}. As a noun, thaws are periods of warming: {The January thaws brought flooding}.

Theater is a building where performances are staged or films are shown. More broadly, theater is the art form itself—dramatic performance as a medium: {She studied theater in college}. A theater of war or operations is a region where military action occurs. Theatrics or theatrical behavior treats real life as if it were a stage performance: {His resignation speech was pure theater}.

Theaters are buildings designed for performances—plays, musicals, operas, and other live entertainment. The word extends to movie theaters, where films are shown. Theater also names the art form itself: {She studied theater in college}. A theater of war is a region where military operations occur. In British English, spelled theatre.

Theatre is the British spelling of theater—the art form of staged dramatic performance, or the building where such performances occur. Both spellings work for all senses: a theatre of war, a surgical theatre, theatrical behavior. American English strongly prefers theater; British English uses theatre almost exclusively.

Theatres is the British spelling of theaters—buildings where plays, films, or other performances take place. The word covers everything from grand Victorian playhouses to small cinema screens. Theatre also means the art form itself: {She's devoted her life to the theatre}. A theatre of war is a region where military operations occur. In medicine, an operating theatre is where surgeries are performed.

Theatrical describes what relates to theater or dramatic performance: {theatrical productions}, {theatrical lighting}. More often, it characterizes behavior that seems exaggerated or designed for effect—dramatic in a way that feels performed rather than genuine: {She made a theatrical sigh}. The word can be neutral or critical depending on context. As a noun, theatricals are dramatic performances or, dismissively, overdone displays of emotion.

Theatricality is the quality of being theatrical—dramatic, exaggerated, or designed for effect. The term can be neutral when describing stage performance: {The production embraced its theatricality}. More often it carries a whiff of criticism, suggesting behavior that feels staged or overwrought: {His theatricality made it hard to take his apology seriously}.

Theatrics are dramatic, exaggerated behaviors designed to attract attention or create an emotional effect. The word usually carries a dismissive tone—suggesting the display is excessive or insincere: {Save the theatrics for someone who cares}. Less commonly, theatrics refers neutrally to theatrical techniques or stagecraft: {The play's theatrics were impressive}.

Theft is the act of taking someone else's property without permission or legal right, intending to keep it permanently. The word covers everything from shoplifting to embezzling millions: {He was charged with theft}. Identity theft involves stealing personal information to commit fraud. Unlike robbery, theft doesn't require force or confrontation—it can happen without the victim knowing.

Them is the objective form of they. You use it to refer to two or more people that you have already named so that you don’t have to repeat their name or names: Please give this to Todd and Kim when you see them.

Thematic means relating to or organized around a theme—a central subject or idea. A thematic {analysis} examines recurring motifs. A thematic {approach} to teaching groups material by topic rather than chronology. {The exhibition takes a thematic rather than biographical view of the artist's work.}

A theme is any identifiable characteristic that can be observed throughout something. A musical theme, for example, might occur multiple times in a work of many movements. A theme can also be a main idea, or an idea closely associated with someone or something: She repeatedly emphasized the themes of dedication and hard work to bring good results. When theme precedes a noun, it is usually to identify something as having an obvious motif, as in a theme party or a theme restaurant. As a verb, theme means provide an ambience to.

Themes are the central ideas or subjects running through a work—the underlying meanings a story, film, or piece of music explores: {The novel's themes include loss and redemption}. In computing, a theme is a preset visual style: {I changed my phone's theme to dark mode}. Theme also works as a verb: {a Vegas casino themed around ancient Egypt}.

Theming is the practice of applying a consistent visual or conceptual style to something—a party, a website, a retail space. A {themed restaurant} might evoke a rainforest or the 1950s. In software, theming refers to customizing the appearance of an interface: {dark mode theming}, {custom theming options}. The goal is cohesive aesthetic identity across all elements.

Whether referring to a time other than now or communicating a sequence, then is your go-to adverb. Then works for both temporal and spatial sequences: Let’s eat and then go to the movie; The photo shows the happy couple in the middle, then the parents, then the bridesmaids. In indicating things that happen later, then has acquired the meaning of as a consequence: If you’ve spent all your money then you’ll have to go home.

Theocracies is the plural of theocracy—a system of government in which religious authority rules, or claims to rule, on behalf of God or gods. In a theocracy, religious law serves as civil law, and clergy hold political power: {Medieval Europe saw theocracies where popes wielded authority over kings}. The term often carries critical connotations, implying that secular governance has been subverted by religious doctrine.

A theocracy is a government in which religious authorities hold political power, or in which the state claims to govern according to divine law. The clergy may rule directly, or secular leaders may derive their authority from religious sanction: {Iran is often described as a theocracy}. The term sometimes describes any society where religion dominates public life: {Critics warned the country was sliding toward theocracy}.

A theocrat is a ruler who governs in the name of God or a deity, or someone who advocates for religious authority over civil government. The term often carries critical connotations, suggesting dangerous fusion of political and religious power: {The ayatollahs ruled as theocrats}. {Critics called him a theocrat who wanted to impose biblical law on everyone}.

Theocrats are people who advocate for or exercise religious authority over government. A theocrat may be a religious leader who holds political power, or someone who believes divine law should supersede civil law: {The theocrats pushed to make blasphemy a crime}. The term often carries negative connotations, implying authoritarian imposition of religious doctrine on society.
clues: Those who govern by divine mandate

definition: A theologian is a person who studies or is an expert in theology—the systematic study of the nature of God, religious belief, and religious practice. Theologians may work within a particular faith tradition, interpreting sacred texts and doctrines, or they may take a comparative or philosophical approach across religions. The term applies both to academic scholars and to religious thinkers whose writings shape doctrine. {Augustine was one of the most influential theologians in Christian history.}

Theologians are scholars who study religion, religious belief, and the nature of the divine. The term typically refers to those working within a faith tradition—Christian theologians, Islamic theologians—though it can include academic study of religion more broadly. {Medieval theologians debated how many angels could dance on the head of a pin.}

Theology is the study of God, gods, or religious belief—the systematic examination of divine nature, religious doctrines, and spiritual questions. Someone studying theology might analyze scripture, debate the problem of evil, or compare how different traditions understand salvation. The word often implies Christian thought specifically, though it applies to any religion's intellectual tradition: {Islamic theology}, {Hindu theology}. A theology can also mean a particular system of religious beliefs: {liberation theology}, {process theology}.

A theorem is a statement in mathematics or logic that has been proven true through rigorous demonstration from accepted axioms and previously established theorems. Unlike a hypothesis or conjecture, a theorem carries the weight of proof: {The Pythagorean theorem relates the sides of a right triangle}. In casual use, theorem sometimes refers to any general principle or rule that seems reliably true, though mathematicians reserve the term for formally proven propositions.

Theoretical concerns ideas, concepts, and abstract reasoning rather than practical application or direct experience. A theoretical physicist works with mathematical models; a theoretical possibility exists in principle but may never occur. The word often implies a gap between thought and reality: {That sounds good in theory, but will it work?} Theoretical knowledge comes from study and reasoning; practical knowledge comes from doing.

Theoretically describes what should happen according to theory, logic, or principle—as opposed to what actually happens in practice. {Theoretically, the plan should work} acknowledges doubt about real-world execution. The word often signals skepticism: {Theoretically, anyone can become president}. It can also mean in terms of theory rather than application: {theoretically sound but practically useless}.

Theories is the plural of theory. A theory is an explanation for how or why something works—a framework of ideas meant to account for observed facts. In science, a theory is well-tested and widely accepted: {the theory of evolution}, {quantum theory}. In everyday speech, theory often means speculation or guess: {I have a theory about why she left}. {In theory} means according to principle, if not always in practice.

Theorise is the British spelling of theorize—to form theories or speculate about something: {Scientists theorised that the extinction was caused by an asteroid impact}. It often implies reasoning without conclusive evidence: {We can only theorise about what happened}. The noun is theory; the adjective theoretical.

A theorist develops or works with theories—systematic frameworks for understanding phenomena. The term appears across disciplines: political theorists, music theorists, conspiracy theorists. Unlike a practitioner who applies knowledge directly, a theorist focuses on underlying principles and explanations: {She's more of a theorist than an experimentalist}. The word can carry dismissive undertones, implying detachment from practical reality.

Theorists are people who develop or study theories—systematic explanations of how things work. The term appears across disciplines: political theorists, music theorists, conspiracy theorists. {Theorists have long debated whether language shapes thought}. The word can carry mild dismissiveness, implying someone more concerned with abstract ideas than practical realities: {That's fine for theorists, but it won't work in the real world}.

To theorize is to form theories or speculate about explanations for something: {Scientists theorized that the extinction was caused by an asteroid impact}. The word implies intellectual speculation rather than proven fact—you theorize when you don't yet have definitive answers. {She theorized about why he'd left so suddenly}.

A theory is an idea that is proposed to explain something. A theory can be very simple (My theory is that she decided to leave him a long time ago) or extremely complex—like the theory of quantum mechanics. In science, researchers propose a theory and then devise experiments that will prove the theory is correct (that it explains the phenomenon), incorrect (fails to explain what happens experimentally), or occasionally incomplete (explains some aspects satisfactorily, but not others).

Theorycraft is the practice of analyzing game mechanics through mathematics and simulation to optimize performance—calculating damage output, comparing equipment, or determining ideal character builds. The term originated in gaming communities, especially around strategy and role-playing games: {The theorycraft says this weapon is best, but it doesn't account for player skill}. As a verb, to theorycraft is to engage in such analysis: {I spent hours theorycrafting my raid build}.

Therapeutic describes something that heals or promotes health and wellbeing. Medical treatments are therapeutic, but so are activities that restore mental or emotional balance: {I find gardening therapeutic}. A therapeutic conversation helps someone process difficult feelings. The word often implies relief or restoration rather than cure—something that makes you feel better even if it doesn't fix the underlying problem.
clues: Having a curative or restorative effect

definition: Therapies is the plural of therapy—treatments intended to heal, relieve, or improve a condition. The word spans medical interventions {radiation therapies for cancer}, psychological approaches {cognitive behavioral therapies}, and alternative practices {massage and aroma therapies}. When someone is exploring their options, they might ask about {available therapies} or compare {different therapies} for effectiveness.

A therapist is a person trained to treat physical or mental conditions. Physical therapists work with the body—restoring movement, reducing pain. Psychotherapists and talk therapists treat mental and emotional issues through conversation rather than medication: {I've been seeing a therapist for my anxiety}. The word often stands alone for the psychological kind: {My therapist says I need better boundaries}.

Therapists are professionals who provide therapy—treatment for physical, mental, or emotional conditions. The term most commonly refers to psychotherapists or counselors who help people work through psychological issues: {She's been seeing a therapist since the divorce}. It also applies to practitioners of physical therapy, occupational therapy, massage therapy, and other specialized treatments. A therapist is distinct from a psychiatrist, who holds a medical degree and can prescribe medication.

Therapy is treatment intended to heal or relieve a condition, especially through non-surgical means. Physical therapy restores movement after injury. Radiation therapy targets cancer cells. Used alone, therapy often means psychotherapy—talk-based treatment for mental or emotional problems: {I've been in therapy for years}. {She started therapy after the divorce}. Therapeutic describes anything with healing properties or effects.

While it shares pronunciation with another high-frequency word (their), there is so distinct from its sound-alike that even a computer program can pinpoint errors. There can function as four or five parts of speech but it does most of its work as an adverb. Its easiest job is to be the counterpart of here for things that are more remote in space or time from the speaker. Its more sophisticated role is to introduce a sentence that tells you whether or not something exists or is available: There’s a supermarket just around the corner. There isn’t any soup left. As an interjection, the meaning of there depends on context but usually suggests an idea of finality: There! I finally finished my paper. There, there, that’s enough.

Therefore signals a conclusion drawn from what preceded. It introduces a result, consequence, or logical inference: {The bridge is unsafe; therefore, we must find another route}. More formal than "so," therefore appears frequently in academic writing, legal documents, and philosophical arguments. {I think, therefore I am.}

A theremin is an electronic musical instrument played without physical contact. The performer moves their hands near two antennas—one controlling pitch, the other volume—creating an eerie, wavering tone associated with science fiction films and Halloween soundtracks: {The theremin gave old horror movies their spooky atmosphere}.

Thermal relates to heat, whether describing its presence, production, or retention. A thermal blanket keeps you warm; thermal energy is heat energy; thermal imaging detects heat signatures. As a noun, a thermal is a rising column of warm air that gliders and birds ride to gain altitude without expending energy. In casual use, thermals refers to insulated undergarments worn in cold weather: {I wore my thermals under my jeans for the ski trip}.

Thermals are columns of rising warm air that birds and gliders use to gain altitude without expending energy. Pilots and hawks circle within thermals to climb. The word also refers to thermal underwear—insulating garments worn in cold weather: {I packed thermals for the ski trip}. Both senses connect to heat retention or movement.

Thermite is a pyrotechnic mixture of metal powder (usually aluminum) and metal oxide that burns at extremely high temperatures—hot enough to melt through steel. Used industrially for welding railroad tracks and cutting metal, it also appears in incendiary weapons. Once ignited, thermite cannot be extinguished with water: {The thermite cut through the lock in seconds}.
clues: Burns hot enough to melt steel

definition: A thermometer is an instrument for measuring temperature. The familiar kind uses liquid—mercury or alcohol—that rises or falls in a glass tube marked with a scale. Digital thermometers have largely replaced these in medical and household use. {The thermometer read 102 degrees.}

Thermometers are instruments for measuring temperature. The most familiar type uses a glass tube containing mercury or colored alcohol that expands or contracts along a calibrated scale as temperature changes. Digital thermometers have largely replaced these in medical and household use. Beyond the everyday versions pressed under tongues or mounted on walls, thermometers serve specialized purposes in cooking, laboratory work, and industrial processes. {The thermometer read 102 degrees, confirming her fever.}

Thermonuclear describes reactions or weapons involving the fusion of atomic nuclei at extremely high temperatures—millions of degrees. A thermonuclear bomb (hydrogen bomb) uses a fission explosion to trigger fusion, releasing vastly more energy than fission alone. The term applies to processes powering stars and to the most destructive weapons ever built: {thermonuclear war}, {thermonuclear device}.

A thermos is an insulated container that keeps beverages hot or cold for extended periods. The double-walled vacuum design prevents heat transfer, making it useful for coffee, soup, or cold drinks: {She packed a thermos of hot cocoa for the hike}. Originally a trademark, the word has become generic for any vacuum flask. (Capitalized Thermos is the brand name.)

A thermostat is a device that automatically regulates temperature by switching heating or cooling systems on and off. Most thermostats let you set a target temperature: {Set the thermostat to 68}. Programmable thermostats adjust temperatures on a schedule. Figuratively, anything that maintains equilibrium might be called a thermostat: {The Federal Reserve acts as a thermostat for the economy}.

A thesaurus is a word reference book that groups words according to their semantic relations. The most common relation, and the one for which people often consult a thesaurus, is synonymy: words that share a similar meaning, sometimes representing various parts of speech, are grouped together in a thesaurus. Other relations that may be discoverable in a thesaurus include antonymy (opposites), hypernymy and hyponymy (relations between more general and more specific words), and meronymy (relations of parts to wholes).

A thesis is a proposition put forward for consideration or proof. In academic contexts, a thesis is a substantial research paper required for a degree—especially the extended work submitted for a doctorate. The thesis of an essay or argument is its central claim: {Her thesis is that economic factors drove the revolution}. In classical rhetoric and music, thesis also refers to the stressed or downbeat position.

A thespian is an actor, especially one who performs on stage. The word comes from Thespis, the ancient Greek credited with inventing tragedy. Thespian often carries a whiff of pretension or gentle mockery: {Our community theater thespians take themselves very seriously}. It can also function as an adjective meaning theatrical or dramatic.

Thespians are actors, especially stage actors. The word comes from Thespis, an ancient Greek credited as the first person to appear onstage as a character rather than as himself. The term has a slightly formal or theatrical flavor: {The local thespians are staging Hamlet this weekend}. High school drama clubs often call themselves thespian societies.

Theta is the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet (Θ, θ), used in English primarily as a mathematical and scientific symbol. In trigonometry, theta conventionally represents an angle: {Find theta when sin θ = 0.5}. In statistics, it often denotes an unknown parameter. Theta also names specific concepts in finance (options time decay) and neuroscience (a type of brain wave). (Capitalized Theta may be a fraternity name.)

You use they to designate multiple people or things that you have already referred to with a noun or nouns: The students wrote reports about the field trip they went on. In modern speech, they is also often used to refer back to an indefinite singular pronoun such as whoever, someone, or anybody to avoid the problem of appearing to be sexist by using he or she, and to avoid the awkwardness of using he/she: If anyone wants the extra tickets they should call me.

Thick, mainly an adjective, characterizes a dimension from side to side or front to back. A thick book has many pages. After a unit of measure, thick typically specifies a dimension through something solid (walls 15 inches thick). Abstract things described as thick are hard to understand. People described as thick are being called stupid. If air is thick, it is not fresh and may be polluted with something. Generally, thick characterizes abundance and density (thick hair, thick fog, thick forest).

Thicken means to make or become thicker—more dense, more viscous, or less transparent. You thicken gravy with flour. Fog thickens as visibility drops. A plot thickens when complications arise and things get more interesting: {The plot thickens—now her ex-husband is involved}.

Thickening is the process of becoming thicker or making something thicker: {The thickening fog made driving dangerous}. In cooking, a thickening is a substance added to liquids to increase viscosity—flour, cornstarch, or roux: {Add the thickening gradually while stirring}. The word also names a thickened area or mass: {a thickening in the arterial wall}.

A thicket is a dense growth of shrubs, bushes, or small trees—vegetation too tangled to walk through easily. The word extends to any dense tangle: {a thicket of regulations}, {a thicket of legal complications}. Something described as a thicket is difficult to navigate or sort through.

Thickets is the plural of thicket—a dense growth of shrubs, bushes, or small trees, difficult to pass through: {We pushed through the thickets along the riverbank}. Figuratively, a thicket is any tangled or complicated mass: {a thicket of regulations}, {lost in a thicket of legal arguments}.

Thickheaded means slow to understand or stubbornly resistant to new ideas—as if the skull were too thick for anything to penetrate. The word is blunter than *dense* but milder than *stupid*: {Don't be so thickheaded—just read the instructions}. A thickheaded person may be intelligent but unwilling to grasp what seems obvious to others.

Thickness is the distance through something from one side to the other, the third dimension after length and width: {a wall of six-inch thickness}. It also describes the quality of being thick—density or viscosity: {the thickness of the fog}, {adjust the thickness of the batter}. In plural, thicknesses can mean layers: {several thicknesses of cardboard}.

A thief is someone who steals—takes property belonging to others without permission. The word covers everything from petty shoplifters to professional burglars: {The thief made off with her purse}. Figuratively, anything that deprives you of something valuable: {Time is a thief}. Plural: thieves.

Thievery is the act or practice of stealing. The word carries a slightly literary or old-fashioned tone compared to plain *theft*, and often suggests repeated or habitual stealing rather than a single incident: {The shop owner blamed his losses on employee thievery}. It can extend to any form of dishonest taking: {corporate thievery}, {intellectual thievery}.

Thieves is the plural of thief—people who steal. The word appears in contexts ranging from petty crime to organized robbery: {Thieves broke into the warehouse overnight}. The phrase {thick as thieves} describes people who are very close or conspiratorial, like partners in crime sharing secrets.

Thieving describes the act of stealing or a person inclined to steal: {thieving bastards}, {a thieving little rat}. As a noun, it refers to theft itself: {The thieving had been going on for months}. The word carries strong disapproval, often appearing in angry accusations or colorful insults.

The thigh is the upper part of the leg, between the hip and the knee. It contains the body's largest bone (the femur) and some of its most powerful muscles. Thighs appear in cooking as cuts of poultry: {chicken thighs}, {turkey thighs}. The word carries mild erotic charge when referring to human anatomy: {her bare thighs}.

Thighs are the upper portions of the legs, between the hip and the knee. They contain the body's largest muscles and are associated with strength and power in athletics. In cooking, chicken thighs are prized as darker, more flavorful meat than breast portions. The thigh also carries erotic connotations given its proximity to the genitals; showing too much thigh has historically been considered immodest. {She felt the burn in her thighs after climbing the stairs.}

A thimble is a small protective cap worn on the fingertip when sewing, preventing the needle from pricking the skin as you push it through fabric. Thimbles are typically made of metal, plastic, or leather. The word extends to any small cup-shaped fitting, such as a metal ring used in rigging to protect rope from chafing.

Thimbles are small protective caps worn on the fingertip while sewing, allowing you to push a needle through fabric without pain. The classic thimble is a metal dome with a dimpled surface to grip the needle. The word extends to any small cap-shaped object: a thimble-sized amount is very little. In rigging, a thimble is a metal ring that protects rope where it loops around a hook or eye.

Thin, mainly an adjective, is the opposite of thick but it does not have the dimension-specifying functions that thick has. Things that are thin have a narrow or scant dimension from top to bottom, front to back, or side to side (thin layer of snow). Thin air is air at a high altitude, except in the expression out of thin air (where it is meaningless). To thin something is to dilute it, or reduce its density or dimensions.

Thing is the most general singular noun in English; it rarely refers to people but it can refer to any other object, abstraction, matter, case, situation, quality, or characteristic that can also be designated with a noun. In the plural, thing can refer to circumstances in general or to a situation that has been indicated otherwise: How are things? Aunt Nell is trying to get things settled with Uncle Frank’s estate.

A thingamabob is a thing whose name you don't know or can't recall: {Hand me that thingamabob over there}. It belongs to a family of placeholder words—thingamajig, whatchamacallit, doohickey—used when pointing or context makes the referent clear enough. The word sounds playful and slightly old-fashioned.

Thingamabobs is the plural of thingamabob, a placeholder word for something whose name you can't recall or don't know: {Hand me that thingamabob over there}. It belongs to a family of similar terms—thingamajig, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same function of naming the unnameable.

Thingamajig is a placeholder name for something whose actual name you can't recall or don't know: {Hand me that thingamajig over there}. It belongs to a family of similar nonsense words—thingamabob, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same function of pointing at an object while admitting you've forgotten what it's called.

Thingamajigs are objects whose names you can't recall or don't know. The word is a playful placeholder, interchangeable with thingamabob, whatchamacallit, or doohickey: {Hand me that thingamajig over there}. It typically refers to small mechanical parts or gadgets whose proper names escape you in the moment.

Thingamebob is a placeholder word for an object whose name you can't recall or don't know: {Hand me that thingamebob over there}. It belongs to a family of similar terms—thingamajig, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same purpose of filling in when the real word escapes you.

Thingamejig is a placeholder word for something whose name you can't recall or don't know: {Hand me that thingamejig over there}. It belongs to a family of similar terms—thingamabob, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same purpose of naming the unnamed. The word sounds playful and informal, often accompanied by vague pointing.

Thingamybob is a placeholder word for an object whose name you can't recall or don't know: {Hand me that thingamybob over there}. It belongs to a family of similar terms—thingamajig, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same function of naming the unnameable. The spelling thingamabob is equally common.

Thingamyjig is an informal placeholder noun for an object whose actual name you can't recall or don't know. It belongs to a family of similar terms—thingamabob, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same function of letting conversation continue without the precise word. {Hand me that thingamyjig on the counter.} The spelling thingamajig is more common.

A thingmabob is a thing whose name you can't recall or don't know—a placeholder word for any object: {Hand me that thingmabob over there}. Interchangeable with thingamajig, whatchamacallit, doohickey, and similar terms. The word is casual and often affectionate, suggesting mild exasperation at one's own forgetfulness.

Thingmajig is a placeholder word for an object whose name you can't recall or don't know: {Hand me that thingmajig over there}. It belongs to a family of such terms—thingamabob, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same function of naming the nameless. The word often appears when pointing at something specific but unnamed.

Things is the most general noun in English for referring to objects, matters, or circumstances. It can mean physical objects {(Put your things away)}, situations {(Things are getting complicated)}, actions {(I have things to do)}, or abstract matters {(Let me explain a few things)}. The word's vagueness makes it useful when precision isn't needed or possible: {One thing led to another}. Your things are your belongings. {The thing is} introduces an explanation or excuse. To {do your own thing} is to act independently.

Thingumajig is a placeholder word for something whose name you can't recall or don't know: {Hand me that thingumajig over there}. It belongs to a family of similar fill-in words—thingamabob, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same function of pointing to an unnamed object. The spelling varies: thingamajig, thingumajig, thingummy.

Thingummybob is a placeholder word for something whose name you can't recall or don't know: {Hand me that thingummybob over there}. It belongs to a family of similar terms—thingamajig, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same function of letting speech continue when the precise word escapes you.

Thingy is a placeholder word for something whose name you can't recall or don't bother to specify: {Hand me that thingy over there}, {The thingy on the car is broken}. It's casual and vague, often accompanied by pointing or gesturing. Variants include thingamajig, thingamabob, and whatchamacallit.

Thingymajig is a placeholder word for an object whose name you can't recall or don't know: {Hand me that thingymajig over there}. It belongs to a family of similar terms—thingamabob, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same function of pointing to something nameless. The word is casual and often accompanied by a vague gesture.

It’s all in your mind.
