The word extends to any powerful, sweeping movement: {a tide of public opinion}, {the tide of history}. To {turn the tide} is to reverse momentum. Something that {tides you over} sustains you temporarily until conditions improve.

Tidewater refers to water affected by tides—coastal areas where rivers meet the sea and water levels rise and fall with tidal cycles. The term often describes low-lying coastal regions: {tidewater Virginia}, {tidewater plantations}. In American usage, Tidewater specifically names the coastal plain of Virginia and Maryland along the Chesapeake Bay.

Tidiness is the state of being neat and orderly, with things in their proper places. It applies to physical spaces {the tidiness of her desk}, personal appearance, or habits of organization. Someone who values tidiness keeps their environment uncluttered and arranged. The quality suggests care and discipline, though excessive tidiness can imply rigidity.
clues: When nothing is out of place

definition: Tidings is news or information, typically about events of significance. The word sounds old-fashioned or literary in modern usage, appearing most often in set phrases: {glad tidings}, {tidings of great joy}. Outside religious or deliberately archaic contexts, news has largely replaced it: {What tidings do you bring from the front?}

Tidy means neat, orderly, and well-arranged: {a tidy desk}, {a tidy appearance}. A tidy person keeps things in order. To tidy is to make something neat: {I need to tidy up before guests arrive}. In British usage, a tidy sum or amount is considerable: {She earned a tidy profit on the sale}.

Tidying is the act of making a space neat and orderly, typically by putting things in their proper places, straightening up, or clearing away clutter. It suggests lighter, more routine organizing rather than deep cleaning—you might tidy a desk before a meeting or tidy the living room when guests are expected. {I spent the morning tidying before my parents arrived.} The term gained fresh currency through Marie Kondo's popular decluttering philosophy centered on tidying up.

To tie something is to unite it with or connect it to another thing: you can tie a rope to a vehicle or tie performance to pay. To tie a knot is to create the knot using something like string or rope, but to tie the knot is a figurative way to express entering into marriage. When scores are tied, or when you tie the score, the scores are equal. To tie a record is to achieve the same level as that achievement. Among other things, a tie can be an instance of tying in competition (the game ended in a tie), a strip of material worn and tied around the neck (necktie), or a connection between things: The two countries enjoyed close diplomatic ties.

A tiebreak is a method for determining a winner when competitors are tied. In tennis, a tiebreak is a special game played when a set reaches 6-6, with points counted numerically until one player wins by two with at least seven. More broadly, any procedure that resolves a deadlock: {The coin flip served as a tiebreak}. Also spelled tie-break or tiebreaker.

A tiebreaker is a method for determining a winner when competitors are tied. In tennis, a tiebreaker is a special game played when sets are tied at six games each. More broadly, any deciding factor can be called a tiebreaker: {The candidate's experience was the tiebreaker}. Also spelled tie-breaker.

Tiebreakers are methods or additional contests used to determine a winner when competitors finish equal. In tennis, a tiebreaker is a special game played when a set reaches 6-6. In tournaments and elections, tiebreakers resolve deadlocks through extra rounds, coin flips, or predetermined criteria: {The committee used head-to-head record as the first tiebreaker}.

Tied is the past tense of tie, covering all that verb's meanings. Something tied is fastened or bound: {Her hands were tied behind her back}. A tied game or election has equal scores or votes—neither side ahead. To be tied up is to be busy or unavailable: {I'm tied up in meetings all afternoon}. To have your hands tied is to be prevented from acting.

A tier is one of a series of rows or levels arranged one above another, like the tiers of a wedding cake or stadium seating. The word extends naturally to any hierarchical ranking system: {The company offers three tiers of service}. In gaming and competitive contexts, tier often designates quality or power rankings, with top tier meaning the best and bottom tier the worst. As a verb, tier means to arrange in levels or ranks. The adjective tiered describes something with multiple levels: {a tiered pricing structure}.

Tiered describes something arranged in tiers—horizontal levels stacked one above another. A tiered {wedding cake} has multiple layers of decreasing size. Tiered {seating} rises in rows so each has a clear view. The word extends to abstract levels: tiered {pricing} offers different rates for different service levels, and a tiered {system} has distinct grades or ranks.

Tiers are levels or ranks arranged in a hierarchy, each above or below another: {The stadium has three tiers of seating}, {a two-tier pricing system}. The word implies structured gradation—premium tiers offer more than basic ones, upper tiers sit above lower ones. Subscription services commonly use tiers to differentiate access levels. To tier is to arrange in such levels.

Ties are things that bind, fasten, or connect. A tie secures something: you tie your shoes, tie a knot, tie up a package. Railroad ties are crossbeams holding tracks together. Ties are also connections between people—family ties, business ties. In competitions, a tie means equal scores: {The game ended in a tie}. A tie is also a necktie: {He loosened his tie after the meeting}.

A tiff is a minor quarrel or petty disagreement, typically between people who are otherwise close: {They had a tiff over whose turn it was to cook}. The word suggests something brief and not seriously damaging to the relationship—more a spat than a fight. (All caps TIFF is an image file format.)

The tiger is the largest species of cat and generally thought of as a fierce and dangerous animal. Things called tiger that are not large, fierce cats attract the name because of some feature reminiscent of the real thing. A man described as a tiger is probably virile, successful, and strong. The tiger moth, tiger lily, and tiger prawn are all organisms with striped markings like those of a tiger. Tiger stripes are markings of black or another dark color on a lighter color.

Tigers are large striped cats native to Asia, the largest of the wild cat species. The word appears in various figurative uses: a {paper tiger} is something that appears threatening but isn't, while to {have a tiger by the tail} is to be in a situation difficult to control or escape. In sports, numerous teams bear the name Tigers. {The tigers prowled their enclosure.} (Capitalized Tigers typically refers to a specific team.)

Tight describes something firmly fixed, stretched taut, or fitting closely with little room to spare. A tight {lid} won't come off easily. Tight {jeans} hug the body. A tight {deadline} leaves no margin. Money is tight when funds are scarce. A tight {game} is closely contested. Someone who is tight with money is stingy; someone tight with a friend is close. Tight also means drunk: {He got tight at the party}. In slang, tight means excellent or cool: {That new album is tight}.

Tightarse is British and Australian slang for a stingy person—someone reluctant to spend money even when they easily could. The image is of someone so cheap their buttocks clench at the thought of parting with cash. Also spelled tight-arse or as two words. The American equivalent is tightwad or cheapskate. {Don't be such a tightarse—it's your round.}

A tightass is someone excessively uptight, rigid, or unwilling to relax—the sort who insists on following every rule and can't take a joke. The image is of someone clenching so hard they can't loosen up: {Don't be such a tightass, it's just a party}. As an adjective, tightassed describes the same quality. Mildly vulgar.

Tighten means to make or become tight—to increase tension, reduce slack, or secure more firmly. You tighten a bolt, a belt, or your grip. Muscles tighten with exertion or anxiety. Rules and restrictions tighten when they become stricter: {The government tightened border controls}. To {tighten your belt} is to reduce spending during hard times.

Tightfisted means unwilling to spend or give money—stingy, miserly: {Her tightfisted uncle never tipped more than five percent}. The image is of a fist clenched around coins, refusing to open. The word carries mild disapproval but is less harsh than cheapskate or miser.

Tightknit describes a group whose members are closely connected through strong bonds of loyalty, affection, or shared purpose: {a tightknit family}, {a tightknit community}. The metaphor comes from fabric woven with threads close together, suggesting unity that's hard to penetrate or pull apart. Also spelled tight-knit.

Tightlipped means reluctant to speak, especially about a particular subject. Someone who is tightlipped keeps information to themselves: {Officials remained tightlipped about the investigation}. The image is of lips pressed firmly together, refusing to let words escape. Also spelled tight-lipped.

Tightness is the quality of being tight—firm, secure, or constricted. It describes physical sensations: {tightness in my chest}, {tightness in my hamstrings}. It applies to fit: the tightness of a seal, the tightness of jeans. Tightness in markets or budgets means scarcity or constraint. In relationships, tightness suggests closeness: {the tightness of their bond}.

A tightrope is a rope or wire stretched taut high above the ground, walked by acrobats and circus performers. The word extends naturally to any precarious situation requiring careful balance: {Walking a tightrope between honesty and diplomacy}, {The negotiations were a tightrope act}. To {walk a tightrope} is to navigate a situation where missteps in either direction bring trouble.

Tightropes are ropes or wires stretched taut between two points, high above the ground, for acrobats to walk across. The singular tightrope appears more often in figurative use: to {walk a tightrope} is to navigate a situation requiring careful balance between competing demands or dangers: {Parents walk a tightrope between protecting children and letting them take risks}.

Tights are a snug-fitting garment covering the legs and usually the torso up to the waist, made of stretchy material like nylon or spandex. They differ from stockings by being a single piece rather than two separate leg coverings. Dancers and gymnasts wear opaque tights; sheer tights serve as women's hosiery. In British usage, tights covers what Americans call pantyhose.

A tightwad is a person who is excessively reluctant to spend money—stingy beyond what circumstances require. The word is mildly contemptuous: {Don't be such a tightwad; it's her birthday}. A wad is a roll of bills, and a tightwad keeps that wad held tight.

Tightwads are people who are excessively reluctant to spend money. The term carries mild contempt—tightwads aren't just frugal, they're stingy to the point of annoyance: {Those tightwads won't even split the check fairly}. The image is of someone clutching their wad of cash so tightly nothing escapes.

A tigress is a female tiger. The term extends figuratively to describe a woman who is fierce, aggressive, or formidable, especially in protecting her interests or loved ones: {She turned into a tigress when anyone threatened her children}. The figurative sense emphasizes qualities traditionally associated with tigers—ferocity, power, and fearlessness—applied to human behavior.

A tiki is a carved wooden or stone figure representing a Polynesian deity or ancestor, typically featuring a stylized human form with large eyes and exaggerated features. The term extends to the mid-20th-century American aesthetic inspired by Pacific Island culture: tiki {bars}, tiki {torches}, tiki {mugs}. This style evokes an idealized tropical escapism with bamboo, thatch, and rum drinks. {The backyard was decorated with tiki torches for the luau.}
Tikis, a borrowing from Maori, is a design motif inspired by Polynesian art and culture. It is often in the form of a humanoid figure.

Tikka refers to pieces of meat (usually chicken) marinated in spices and yogurt, then grilled or roasted. The word comes from South Asian cuisine and appears most often in {chicken tikka} or {chicken tikka masala}—the latter a dish of tikka pieces in a creamy, spiced tomato sauce that became a British staple.

Tilapia is a mild-flavored freshwater fish, popular worldwide as an inexpensive protein source. Native to Africa and the Middle East, tilapia are now farmed extensively on every continent. The flesh is white, lean, and adaptable to many cooking styles: {grilled tilapia with lemon}, {blackened tilapia tacos}. The fish's rapid growth and tolerance for crowded conditions make it ideal for aquaculture.

A tilde is the wavy horizontal mark (~), used in Spanish over the letter n (ñ) to indicate a palatal nasal sound, and in Portuguese over vowels to indicate nasalization. In computing, the tilde appears in URLs, file paths, and programming languages with various technical functions. Informally, tildes flanking a word add a playful or ironic tone: {~vibes~}.

A tile is a flat, thin piece of hard material—ceramic, stone, or clay—used to cover surfaces like floors, walls, and roofs. Tiles are laid in patterns, with grout filling the gaps between them. The word extends to similar units: {ceiling tiles}, {carpet tiles}, {Scrabble tiles}. In computing, to tile windows is to arrange them edge-to-edge without overlapping.

Tiles are flat, thin pieces of hard material—ceramic, stone, or plastic—used to cover surfaces like floors, walls, and roofs. They're typically arranged in patterns and fitted together: {bathroom tiles}, {roof tiles}, {subway tiles}. In games, tiles are the playing pieces in Scrabble, mahjong, and dominoes. To tile is to cover with tiles or, in computing, to arrange windows side by side on a screen.
clues: Scrabble has a hundred of these

definition: Tiling is the process of covering a surface with tiles, or the tiles themselves once installed: {The bathroom tiling took three days}, {Victorian tiling in the entryway}. In mathematics and computing, tiling refers to covering a plane with shapes that fit together without gaps or overlaps, like a tessellation. Window tiling arranges application windows side by side on a screen.
Till is identical in meaning to until. It is used in conversation and in poetry or lyrics where a word of one syllable rather than two is required.

Tilled describes soil that has been prepared for planting by turning, breaking up, and loosening the earth. Land that has been tilled is ready to receive seeds: {The freshly tilled fields stretched toward the horizon}. The opposite of tilled ground is fallow or untilled land left unworked.

A tiller is a lever or handle used to steer a boat, attached to the rudder. By extension, someone {at the tiller} is in control of any enterprise. Separately, a tiller is a shoot growing from the base of a plant, especially a cereal crop, or a person or machine that tills soil: {The garden tiller broke down before we finished}.

Tillers are people who till soil—farmers or agricultural workers who cultivate land by plowing, turning, and preparing it for planting. The word carries a slightly literary or historical quality: {tillers of the earth}. Separately, a tiller is a lever or handle used to steer a boat, attached to the rudder. On plants, tillers are shoots that sprout from the base of a stem, especially in grasses and grains.

Tilling is the practice of turning and breaking up soil to prepare it for planting. Farmers till fields before sowing crops, loosening compacted earth and mixing in organic matter. The word covers various methods—plowing, harrowing, cultivating—that disturb the soil surface: {Spring tilling begins as soon as the ground thaws}.

There are two tilts, each represented as a noun and verb. First, to tilt something is to move it out of horizontal. If something tilts, it does this. A tilt is an instance of tilting or the angled state resulting from tilting (tilt of the head). Second, to tilt is to engage in a competition on horseback, using lances or spears against an opponent. This competition is called a tilt. At full tilt refers to doing something as fast as possible.

Tilted describes something inclined or slanted from its usual position: {a tilted picture frame}, {She held her head at a tilted angle}. In gaming and poker slang, tilted means emotionally agitated or frustrated to the point of impaired judgment: {After losing three hands in a row, he was completely tilted}. The gaming sense has spread to general use for being off-balance or rattled.

Tilting is the act of angling or inclining something from vertical or horizontal. A tilting platform shifts position; a tilting windmill adjusts to the wind. In medieval jousting, tilting was the sport itself—knights tilting at each other with lances, giving us {tilting at windmills} for futile attacks on imaginary enemies. In gaming and poker slang, tilting describes playing emotionally after a frustrating loss: {He's tilting hard after that bad beat}.

Tilts is the third-person singular and plural form of tilt. To tilt is to lean or tip at an angle: {The tower tilts slightly to the north}. A tilt is an inclined position or a tendency toward something: {a tilt toward conservatism}. To go {full tilt} is to move at maximum speed or intensity. In gaming slang, tilt describes an emotional state—usually frustration—that impairs judgment: {He went on tilt after losing three hands in a row}.

Timber is wood prepared for use in building or carpentry—logs, beams, planks. Standing trees destined for harvest are also timber: {old-growth timber}, {timber rights}. As an exclamation, "Timber!" warns that a tree is falling. Figuratively, timber suggests raw material or potential: {presidential timber}, {She's starter timber}.

Timberland is forested land, especially land covered with trees suitable for commercial logging. The term emphasizes the economic potential of the trees rather than ecological or recreational value: {The company owns thousands of acres of timberland in the Pacific Northwest}. In real estate and forestry, timberland is bought, sold, and managed as a long-term investment.

The timberline is the elevation on a mountain above which trees cannot grow, marking the boundary between forested slopes and alpine terrain. Also called the tree line. Climate, temperature, and exposure determine where this boundary falls: {We hiked past the timberline into bare rock and tundra}. The word also applies to the latitudinal limit of tree growth in polar regions.

Timbers is the plural of timber, referring to large pieces of wood used in construction, especially as structural supports in buildings, ships, or mines. The nautical exclamation {shiver me timbers} expresses surprise or disbelief, evoking the image of a ship's wooden frame shaking from impact—though it's now used almost exclusively in pirate-themed contexts or as playful exaggeration. In forestry, timbers may refer collectively to standing trees suitable for lumber.

Timbre is the distinctive quality or character of a sound that distinguishes it from other sounds of the same pitch and volume. It's what makes a violin sound different from a trumpet playing the same note, or one person's voice recognizable from another's. Musicians and audio engineers speak of timbre when describing whether a sound is warm, bright, harsh, or mellow. {The rich timbre of her voice filled the concert hall.}

Every language finds ways to divide time into past, present, and future, so it’s no surprise that the word time is itself a high-frequency word. It appeared first in English as a noun and is related to the word tide, which gives us a glimpse into our ancestors’ sense of time. Like many nouns, time has both countable and uncountable meanings. Uncountable time communicates the concept of the continuum in which all things happen (since the beginning of time), or for a slice of the continuum (the time of the colonization). Countable time relates to occasions, events, and specific hours: The times of the meetings have changed. When is the best time for me to call you? Several times I tried to stop her.

A timebomb is an explosive device set to detonate at a predetermined time. Figuratively, any situation likely to become dangerous or disastrous if left unaddressed: {The pension shortfall is a timebomb waiting to explode}. In computing, a timebomb is code designed to trigger at a specific date—whether malicious or a trial software expiration. Also spelled time bomb.

Timebombs is the plural of timebomb, a bomb set to detonate at a predetermined time. Figuratively, a timebomb is anything that threatens future catastrophe: {The pension deficit is a timebomb waiting to explode}. A person described as a timebomb is dangerously volatile, likely to snap. Also spelled as two words: time bombs.

A timecard is a record of when an employee starts and finishes work, used to calculate wages or track attendance. Originally a physical card punched by a time clock, timecards are now often digital: {Don't forget to submit your timecard by Friday}. To punch a timecard or be on the clock suggests hourly wage work rather than salaried employment.

A timeclock is a device that records when employees arrive at and leave work, typically by stamping times on a paper card or logging entries electronically. To {punch the timeclock} is to record one's arrival or departure—and by extension, to work a conventional job with fixed hours: {I'm tired of punching a timeclock}.

Timed describes something measured, regulated, or constrained by time. A timed {exam} must be completed within a set period. A timed {release} medication dissolves at controlled intervals. To say something was {well-timed} or {poorly timed} is to judge whether the moment was right: {Her announcement was perfectly timed to maximize impact}.

A timekeeper is a person or device that tracks time. In sports, a timekeeper monitors game duration and records how long events take. In workplaces, timekeepers track employee hours. The word also describes clocks and watches, especially regarding accuracy: {This old watch is still a reliable timekeeper}. Someone who is habitually punctual or late may be called a good or bad timekeeper.

Timekeepers are people or devices that track time. A timekeeper at a sporting event monitors how long play has lasted. Watches, clocks, and stopwatches are timekeepers. Someone who is a good timekeeper arrives punctually and meets deadlines: {She's always been a reliable timekeeper}.
clues: People or devices measuring elapsed time

definition: Timekeeping is the measurement and recording of time, whether by clocks, watches, or official observers. In sports, timekeeping determines race results and game duration. In workplaces, it tracks hours worked: {The company uses digital timekeeping for payroll}. Good timekeeping also means punctuality—arriving when expected.

Timelapse is a photographic technique that compresses long periods into short sequences by capturing images at intervals and playing them back at normal speed. A flower blooming over days becomes seconds of footage; clouds race across the sky. As a modifier: {timelapse photography}, {timelapse video}. Also spelled time-lapse or time lapse.

Timeless describes something unaffected by the passage of time—enduring, ageless, or eternally relevant. A timeless {classic} remains appealing across generations. Timeless {beauty} doesn't fade. Timeless {wisdom} applies regardless of era. The word often carries a tone of admiration: {Her style is timeless}. Something timeless transcends its moment of creation.

Timelessness is the quality of being unaffected by time's passage—remaining relevant, beautiful, or true across eras. A work of art achieves timelessness when it speaks to generations beyond its own: {the timelessness of Shakespeare's themes}. The word can also describe moments that feel suspended outside ordinary time: {the timelessness of a summer afternoon}.

A timeline is a visual or conceptual representation of events arranged in chronological order along a line, typically with dates marked to show when things occurred. Timelines help illustrate the sequence and relative spacing of historical events, project milestones, or personal histories. In social media contexts, timeline refers to the stream of posts and updates that appears on a user's feed: {I scrolled through my timeline for an hour}. As a verb, to timeline something means to plot it out chronologically or schedule it across time.

Timelines are chronological representations of events, showing when things happened in relation to each other: {The timeline of the investigation revealed crucial gaps}. Project managers use timelines to track deadlines and milestones. In science fiction and discussions of time travel, timelines are alternate versions of history: {In that timeline, the war never happened}. The singular timeline often refers to the sequence of posts in a social media feed.

A timelock is a mechanism that prevents access until a specified time has passed. Bank vaults use timelocks to ensure they cannot be opened outside business hours—even by someone with the combination. In cryptocurrency and computing, a timelock restricts when funds can be spent or data accessed: {The smart contract has a 48-hour timelock}. The concept extends to any delayed-release restriction.

Timely means happening at the right moment or without undue delay. A timely {warning} comes soon enough to be useful. A timely {arrival} is neither too early nor too late. {The rain was timely—the crops were about to fail}. Something timely is also relevant to current events: {a timely discussion of election security}.

Timeout is an enforced pause or break. In sports, teams call timeouts to stop the clock and strategize. With children, timeout is a disciplinary measure—a period of isolation to calm down: {Go sit in timeout for five minutes}. In computing, a timeout occurs when a system stops waiting for a response after a set interval: {The connection timed out}. As a verb (usually hyphenated or two words), to time out is to exceed an allowed duration.

Timeouts is the plural of timeout. In sports, a timeout is a brief stoppage of play requested by a team to strategize or rest: {The coach called two timeouts in the final minute}. For children, a timeout is a disciplinary pause—time spent sitting quietly away from activity. In computing, a timeout occurs when a system stops waiting for a response: {The connection failed after repeated timeouts}.

A timepiece is any device that measures or displays time—clocks, watches, sundials, hourglasses. The word often suggests something well-crafted or antique: {a handsome timepiece on the mantel}, {He consulted his pocket timepiece}. It sounds slightly formal or old-fashioned compared to simply saying clock or watch.

A timer is a device or mechanism that measures time intervals. Kitchen timers count down cooking minutes; athletic timers measure race durations. In computing, timers trigger events after specified delays. Someone who times things—a race official, a coach with a stopwatch—is also a timer: {The timer signaled the end of the round}.
Times is the word we use to express the multiplication symbol. It is interpreted as a preposition: seven times four is 28.

A timesaver is something that reduces the time needed to complete a task—a shortcut, tool, or method that increases efficiency: {Meal prepping on Sundays is a real timesaver}. The word often appears in productivity advice and marketing for appliances or software.

A timescale is the span of time over which something happens or is measured: {On a geological timescale, human civilization is a blink}. It often appears in planning contexts to indicate expected duration: {What's the timescale for this project?} Also spelled as two words: time scale.

A timeshare is a vacation property arrangement where multiple owners share rights to use a property, typically for designated weeks each year. The concept emerged from resort condominiums: {They bought a timeshare in Hawaii}. Timeshares are notorious for aggressive sales tactics and difficulty reselling: {We sat through a two-hour timeshare presentation to get free tickets}.

Timeshares are partial ownership arrangements for vacation properties, where multiple buyers each purchase the right to use a unit for a specific period each year. The model promises affordable access to resort accommodations but has a reputation for aggressive sales tactics and difficulty reselling: {We sat through a two-hour timeshare presentation to get the free tickets}. The singular timeshare refers to one such arrangement or property.

Timesheets are records of hours worked, typically filled out by employees for payroll or billing purposes. They track when work started and ended, breaks taken, and tasks performed. Once paper forms, timesheets are now usually digital: {Don't forget to submit your timesheets by Friday}. The singular timesheet refers to one such record or the document itself.

A timesink is an activity that absorbs far more time than intended or than it's worth. Video games, social media, and elaborate hobbies are common timesinks: {I meant to check one email and fell into a two-hour timesink}. The term carries mild self-reproach—you know you're wasting time but can't stop. Also spelled as two words.

A timeskip is a narrative device that jumps forward in time, skipping over intervening events. Common in fiction, film, and television, it allows storytellers to bypass uneventful periods or show characters years later: {After a ten-year timeskip, the protagonist has become a seasoned warrior}. In fan communities, timeskip often refers specifically to a story's later arc featuring older versions of characters.

A timestamp is a record of when something occurred—a date, time, or both, attached to data or documents. Computers generate timestamps automatically: file creation times, message send times, transaction records. In video, a timestamp marks a specific moment: {Skip to timestamp 3:42}. As a verb, to timestamp is to mark something with its time of occurrence.

Timestamps are markers indicating when something occurred or was recorded. A timestamp might show the date and time a file was created, when a message was sent, or when a specific moment appears in a video: {Skip to the timestamp at 14:32}. In digital contexts, timestamps enable sorting, searching, and verifying the sequence of events.

The timestream is the continuous flow of time conceived as a current or river. The word appears almost exclusively in science fiction, where characters may travel through, alter, or branch the timestream: {Changing the past could disrupt the entire timestream}. It treats time as something with direction and momentum that can be navigated or disturbed.

A timesuck is an activity, website, or task that consumes far more time than intended or warranted: {Social media is such a timesuck}, {I meant to check one email and fell into a two-hour timesuck}. The word implies the time was wasted or at least unproductive—something that pulls you in and doesn't let go.

A timetable is a schedule showing when events occur, especially for transportation or academic purposes: {Check the train timetable for departures}. School timetables list class periods and subjects. The verb means to schedule: {The meeting is timetabled for Thursday}. In British English, timetable often appears where Americans would say schedule.

A timewarp is a hypothetical distortion in the flow of time, allowing movement between different eras—a staple of science fiction. More commonly, it describes a place or situation that feels stuck in the past: {Walking into that diner was like entering a timewarp}. The Rocky Horror song "Time Warp" names a dance. Also spelled time warp.

Timewarps are distortions or disruptions in the normal flow of time—moments when time seems to speed up, slow down, or fold back on itself. The concept comes from science fiction, where a timewarp might transport someone to another era: {We stepped through the timewarp into Victorian England}. More loosely, a timewarp describes places or situations that feel frozen in the past: {The diner was a timewarp to the 1950s}. The Rocky Horror Picture Show made "Time Warp" a dance craze.

A timezone (usually two words: time zone) is a region of the Earth that observes a uniform standard time for legal, commercial, and social purposes. The world is divided into roughly 24 time zones, each offset from Coordinated Universal Time (UTC): {What timezone are you in?} In computing, timezone often refers to a setting that determines how timestamps display: {The server's timezone was set to UTC}.

Timid describes a tendency toward fear or hesitation, especially in social situations or when facing risk. A timid person shrinks from confrontation, avoids bold action, and may be easily startled or intimidated: {She gave a timid wave from across the room}. The word suggests a disposition rather than a momentary state—someone who is timid by nature, not just afraid in the moment.

Timidity is the quality of being timid—fearful, hesitant, or lacking confidence. It suggests a disposition to shrink from challenges or confrontation: {His timidity kept him from speaking up in meetings}. The word often implies excessive caution where boldness would serve better.

Timing is the selection or control of when something happens. Good timing means choosing the right moment; bad timing means choosing the wrong one: {His timing was perfect—he asked for a raise right after landing the big account}. In performance, timing is the rhythm and pace of delivery—a comedian's timing determines whether jokes land. In mechanics, timing refers to the synchronization of engine components: {The car runs rough because the timing is off}.

Timpani are large bowl-shaped drums with heads that can be tuned to specific pitches, typically played in sets of two to four. A staple of orchestral percussion, they provide both rhythmic foundation and dramatic emphasis: {The timpani thundered through the finale}. Also called kettledrums. The singular timpano is rarely used; timpani serves for one or many.

Tin is a chemical element and an abundant, widely used metal. Some things made or formerly made of tin are called tins, especially in British English (where the corresponding American term is can or pan), such as muffin tin, cake tin, or tin of sardines. So-called tin foil is today more likely to be made of aluminum. To tin something, in British English, is to seal it in a tin (or can in American English): We’ll tin tomatoes to use in the winter.

A tincture is a solution of a substance in alcohol, especially a medicinal extract: {tincture of iodine}, {herbal tinctures}. The word extends to any slight trace or hint of something: {a tincture of sadness in her voice}. In heraldry, tincture refers to the colors and metals used in a coat of arms.

Tinctures are liquid extracts, typically made by soaking herbs or other substances in alcohol to draw out active compounds: {She takes a tincture of echinacea for colds}. In heraldry, tinctures are the colors and metals used in coats of arms. The verb tincture means to impart a trace of some quality: {His optimism was tinctured with caution}.

Tinder is dry, flammable material used to start fires—paper, dry leaves, small twigs, or specially prepared substances that catch a spark easily. The word extends metaphorically to anything that could ignite conflict or passion: {The economic crisis was tinder for revolution}. A tinderbox was originally a container for tinder and flint; now it means a volatile situation ready to explode. (Capitalized Tinder is a dating app.)

A tinderbox is a container holding tinder and the implements for striking a flame—historically flint and steel. Before matches, tinderboxes were essential household items. The word now appears almost exclusively in its figurative sense: a volatile situation ready to ignite. A region with ethnic tensions is a tinderbox; so is a relationship on the verge of explosive conflict. {The disputed territory remained a tinderbox for decades.}

Tinderboxes is the plural of tinderbox, a small container holding tinder and flint for starting fires—essential before matches existed. The figurative sense dominates modern usage: a volatile situation ready to ignite. A region, relationship, or political climate can be a tinderbox: {The prison was a tinderbox waiting to explode}.

Tinfoil is thin, pliable metallic sheeting, originally made of tin but now almost always aluminum. It's used to wrap food for storage or cooking and to line baking pans. The term persists despite the material change, much like we still "dial" phones. In conspiracy culture, a {tinfoil hat} supposedly blocks mind-control signals, making "tinfoil hat" shorthand for paranoid or outlandish beliefs: {That's some real tinfoil-hat thinking}.

A tinge is a slight trace of color or quality: {a tinge of pink in the sky}, {a tinge of sadness in her voice}. The word suggests something barely present but noticeable—enough to affect the whole without dominating it. To tinge is to impart such a trace: {Regret tinged his memories of that summer}.

Tinged means slightly colored or flavored with something. A sky tinged with {pink}, a voice tinged with {sadness}, coffee tinged with {cinnamon}. The word suggests a trace or hint rather than full saturation—something present but not dominant: {His compliment was tinged with envy}.

Tingle is a prickling or stinging sensation, often from cold, excitement, or restored circulation: {My fingers tingled as they warmed up}. The feeling suggests thousands of tiny pinpricks. Anticipation or strong emotion can make your skin tingle: {The suspense made my spine tingle}. As a noun, it's the sensation itself: {a tingle of excitement}.

Tingled is the past tense of tingle, describing a prickling or slightly stinging sensation, often from cold, excitement, or restored circulation: {My fingers tingled as they warmed up}. The sensation can be pleasant or unpleasant. Figuratively, anticipation or strong emotion produces tingling: {She tingled with excitement}.

Tingles is a prickling or slightly stinging sensation, often pleasant, spreading across the skin or through the body. The word suggests anticipation or excitement: {I get tingles just thinking about it}. ASMR enthusiasts use tingles specifically for the pleasant scalp or spine sensations triggered by certain sounds. As a verb, to tingle is to experience this sensation: {My fingers tingled in the cold}.

Tingling describes a prickling, slightly stinging sensation on the skin, often compared to pins and needles. It can result from physical causes like reduced blood flow when a limb "falls asleep," or from emotional states like excitement or anticipation: {I felt a tingling in my fingers as the announcement approached}. The word functions as both an adjective and a noun, capturing that distinctive electric-like feeling that hovers between pleasant and uncomfortable.

Tingly describes a prickling, slightly electric sensation on the skin or in the body—the feeling of a limb waking up from numbness, or the excited flutter before something happens. It can be physical: {My fingers are tingly from the cold}. Or it can describe anticipatory excitement: {I get tingly just thinking about the concert}.

A tinker is an itinerant mender of pots, pans, and other metal household items—a trade now nearly vanished. The word survives mainly in the verb: to tinker is to make small adjustments or repairs, often amateur or experimental: {He tinkered with the engine all afternoon}. To tinker with something can suggest aimless fiddling rather than serious work: {Congress keeps tinkering with the tax code}.

Tinkered is the past tense of tinker, meaning to make small adjustments or repairs, often in an experimental or unskilled way: {He tinkered with the engine all afternoon}. The word suggests casual, exploratory work rather than systematic repair—fiddling with something to see if it improves: {She tinkered with the recipe until it tasted right}.

A tinkerer is someone who makes small adjustments or repairs, often in an experimental or amateur fashion. The word suggests hands-on curiosity rather than formal expertise—someone who opens things up to see how they work, fiddles with mechanisms, or improvises fixes: {He's a tinkerer who spends weekends in the garage rebuilding old radios}. Tinkerer can carry either admiration for resourcefulness or mild dismissal of unsystematic dabbling.

Tinkerers are people who tinker—who fiddle with mechanisms, adjust things experimentally, or make small repairs and modifications. The word suggests amateur enthusiasm rather than professional expertise: {Weekend tinkerers in their garages have launched billion-dollar companies}. Tinkerers work by trial and error, learning through hands-on experimentation rather than formal training.

Tinkering is making small adjustments or repairs, often in an experimental or unskilled way. Someone tinkering with an engine tries minor fixes without systematic knowledge. The word suggests puttering—working without a clear plan: {He spent Saturday tinkering in the garage}. Tinkering with a system means making incremental changes rather than overhauling it: {Congress keeps tinkering with the tax code}.

Tinkers is the plural of tinker, an itinerant metalworker who mends pots, pans, and other household items. The word carries associations with wandering and improvisation. To tinker is to fiddle with something, making small adjustments without a systematic plan: {He tinkers with old radios in his garage}. The expression {tinker's damn} (or dam) means something worthless—so cheap even a tinker wouldn't value it.

Tinkle is a light, high-pitched ringing sound, like a small bell or ice cubes in a glass: {the tinkle of wind chimes}. As a verb, to tinkle is to make such sounds. In informal British English, tinkle is a childish or euphemistic word for urination: {I need to go for a tinkle}. To {give someone a tinkle} is to phone them.

Tinkles is the plural of tinkle—light, high-pitched ringing sounds like small bells or ice cubes in a glass: {the tinkles of wind chimes on the porch}. As a verb form, it means makes such sounds: {The fountain tinkles in the courtyard}. In childish or euphemistic speech, tinkles can mean urinates: {She tinkles before bed}.

Tinkling describes a light, high-pitched ringing sound, like small bells or ice cubes in a glass: {the tinkling of wind chimes}, {tinkling laughter}. The word suggests something delicate and pleasant. As a noun, a tinkling is the sound itself: {We heard a faint tinkling from the piano}.

Tinnitus is the perception of sound—usually ringing, buzzing, or hissing—when no external sound is present. It's a symptom rather than a disease, often resulting from hearing damage, ear infections, or age-related hearing loss. {The tinnitus in his left ear made it hard to sleep}. Severity ranges from occasional mild annoyance to constant and debilitating.

Tinny describes a thin, high-pitched, metallic sound—the quality of cheap speakers, old recordings, or small devices: {The music sounded tinny through the laptop speakers}. It also describes things resembling tin: flimsy, insubstantial, or cheaply made. A tinny taste is unpleasantly metallic. In Australian slang, a tinny is a can of beer or a small aluminum boat.

Tinpot describes something cheap, inferior, or lacking real authority—suggesting the flimsiness of thin metal compared to solid construction. It typically modifies leaders or regimes: a tinpot {dictator} rules with pretensions of power but little legitimacy. A tinpot {operation} is amateurish and unimpressive. The word carries contempt for things that aspire beyond their actual worth.

Tins is the plural of tin—metal containers, especially for food: {rows of tins on the pantry shelf}, {tins of sardines}. More common in British than American English, where cans predominates. Tins also names shallow metal baking pans: {muffin tins}, {cake tins}. As a verb form, tins means coats with tin or preserves in tins.

Tinsel is thin strips or threads of shiny metallic material used for decoration, especially on Christmas trees. The glittering effect extends figuratively to anything superficially attractive but lacking substance: {the tinsel of Hollywood}, {all that glitters is tinsel}. As an adjective, tinsel describes gaudy showiness: {tinsel dreams of fame}.

A tint is a slight coloring or shade, typically a pale or delicate variation of a color: {a pinkish tint}, {tinted windows}. To tint is to apply such coloring: {She tinted her hair auburn}. A tint can also be a trace or hint of something: {a tint of sadness in her voice}. In color theory, a tint is a color mixed with white, as opposed to a shade (mixed with black).

Tints are shades or varieties of color, especially lighter variations created by adding white: {The walls came in various tints of blue}. To tint is to apply a slight color to something: {She tinted her hair}, {tinted windows}. A tint differs from a dye in being lighter or more subtle—a wash of color rather than a transformation.

A tintype is a photograph made by creating a direct positive image on a thin sheet of metal coated with dark lacquer or enamel. Despite the name, tintypes were usually made on iron, not tin. Popular from the 1860s through the early 1900s, they were cheap, durable, and quickly produced—common at carnivals and boardwalks. {An old tintype of my great-grandparents hung in the hallway.}

Tintypes are photographs made on thin iron plates coated with dark lacquer or enamel—not actually tin. Popular from the 1860s through early 1900s, they were cheap, durable, and produced quickly at fairs and studios. The phrase {not on your tintype} was slang for "absolutely not," now archaic. {She found a tintype of her great-grandmother in the attic.}

Tiny means extremely small—smaller than small, approaching the minimum. A tiny {apartment} barely fits its furniture. A tiny {amount} of salt won't affect the recipe much. Tiny often carries affectionate connotations, especially for living things: {a tiny kitten}, {tiny fingers}. The word intensifies well: {a tiny bit}, {the tiniest hint of jealousy}.
clues: What a grain of sand is

definition: Nouns and verbs with different meanings are represented by tip. A tip is a piece of practical information or advice. If you tip someone off, you give them useful information. A tip is also the end of something, like the tip of a knife or the tips of your toes. To tip something is to give it a (sharp) tip. Finally, a tip is an amount of money given in appreciation of service; to tip someone is to provide this.

A tipi is a cone-shaped tent traditionally used by Indigenous peoples of the North American Great Plains, made of animal hides or canvas stretched over wooden poles. The design allows for quick assembly and disassembly, suited to nomadic life following buffalo herds. Also spelled teepee or tepee. {We stayed in a tipi at the campground.}

Tipis is the plural of tipi, the conical tent traditionally used by Indigenous peoples of the North American Plains. Made of animal hides or canvas stretched over wooden poles, tipis were portable dwellings suited to nomadic life. The spelling tipi reflects the Lakota word more accurately than tepee, though both are common: {The tipis were arranged in a circle at the encampment}.

A tipline is a phone number or communication channel where people can report information, especially about crimes or misconduct. Law enforcement agencies operate tiplines to receive anonymous leads: {Call the FBI tipline if you have information}. News organizations and companies may also maintain tiplines for receiving confidential information from sources or whistleblowers.

A tipoff is advance warning or secret information, especially about something illicit: {Police received a tipoff about the drug shipment}. The word also names the opening play in basketball, when the referee tosses the ball and players jump to tap it to teammates. As a verb (tip off), it means to give such warning: {Someone tipped off the press}.

Tipoffs is the plural of tipoff. A tipoff is advance warning or secret information, especially about something illicit: {Police received tipoffs about the drug operation}. In basketball, the tipoff is the initial jump ball that starts play—hence figuratively, the beginning of something: {The press conference was the tipoff to campaign season}.

Tipped describes something with a tip or end of a particular kind: {gold-tipped arrows}, {a white-tipped tail}. It also means having received a tip—either gratuity or information: {a well-tipped waiter}, {police tipped off about the raid}. Something tipped has been tilted or overturned: {The canoe tipped and spilled us into the water}.

Tipping is the practice of giving a gratuity for service—at restaurants, hotels, salons, or for deliveries. The custom varies widely by country and context: {Tipping culture in America expects 20 percent}. Tipping also refers to the act of tilting or overturning: {The boat was tipping dangerously}. A tipping {point} is the threshold where change becomes unstoppable.

Tippy describes something that tips easily or feels unstable, likely to overturn with slight pressure or uneven weight distribution. A {tippy canoe} requires careful balance; a {tippy chair} wobbles dangerously. The word is informal and often appears in warnings or descriptions of precarious situations. In some dialects, tippy-toes is a variant of tiptoes, describing the act of walking on the balls of one's feet.

Tips are pointed ends or summits—the tip of a finger, the tip of an iceberg. More commonly in everyday speech, tips are small sums of money given for service: {She left a generous tip for the waiter}. Tips also means pieces of advice or inside information: {stock tips}, {betting tips}, {helpful tips for new parents}. As a verb, tips means tilts or overturns: {The canoe tips easily}, {He tips his hat in greeting}.

A tipster is someone who provides tips—inside information, predictions, or confidential advice. In gambling contexts, a tipster offers picks on races or games, sometimes for a fee: {The tipster's horse came in last}. In journalism and law enforcement, a tipster supplies leads or confidential information: {An anonymous tipster alerted police to the location}.

Tipsters are people who provide tips—usually predictions about horse races, sports outcomes, or stock picks, often for a fee or subscription. The term carries a slightly disreputable air, suggesting insider knowledge of uncertain reliability: {The tipster promised a sure thing in the third race}. Tipster also means someone who provides information to authorities: {A tipster alerted police to the hideout}.

Tipsy describes being slightly drunk—enough to feel the effects of alcohol but not severely impaired. The word suggests a pleasant, mildly unsteady state: {She was tipsy after two glasses of wine}. Tipsy carries a lighter connotation than drunk, often implying cheerful looseness rather than serious intoxication.

Tiptoe is the tips of the toes, or the posture of standing on them: {She stood on tiptoe to see over the crowd}. To tiptoe is to walk quietly on the balls of the feet, minimizing sound: {He tiptoed past the sleeping baby}. Figuratively, to tiptoe around something is to approach it cautiously or avoid addressing it directly: {They tiptoed around the subject of money}.

Tiptoeing is walking on the balls of your feet with heels raised, either to move quietly or to reach something high: {She tiptoed past the sleeping baby}. Figuratively, to tiptoe around something is to approach it cautiously, avoiding direct confrontation: {He's been tiptoeing around the issue for weeks}.

Tiptoes are the tips of one's toes, and to tiptoe is to walk on them—quietly, carefully, or to gain height. {She tiptoed past the sleeping baby.} Figuratively, to tiptoe around something is to approach it cautiously, avoiding direct engagement: {He tiptoed around the subject of money.} To be {on tiptoes} is to be in eager anticipation.

A tirade is a long, angry speech of criticism or denunciation. The word suggests sustained verbal attack rather than brief complaint: {She launched into a tirade about the state of modern politics}. Tirades are typically one-sided—the speaker vents while others endure.

Tirades is the plural of tirade, a long, vehement speech expressing criticism, anger, or disapproval. A tirade is typically one-sided and emotionally charged: {She launched into one of her tirades about the neighbors}. Unlike a rant, which may wander, tirades usually maintain focus on a target: {His tirades against the media were legendary}.

Tiramisu is an Italian dessert made of layered espresso-soaked ladyfingers and mascarpone cream, dusted with cocoa powder. The name means "pick me up" in Italian, referring to the caffeine lift. Rich and creamy with a coffee-bitter edge, it became a staple of Italian restaurant menus worldwide in the 1980s and 90s.

Tire connects to ideas of weariness and encirclement. To tire is to lose energy or become fatigued: {The long hike tired us out}. Something that tires you can also bore you: {His constant complaints tire me}. A tire is also the rubber covering around a wheel—spelled tyre in British English. To tire of something is to grow weary of it: {I never tire of watching the sunset}.

Tired describes the state of needing rest or sleep, whether from exertion, lack of sleep, or mental strain: {I'm too tired to think straight}. The word extends to things that have lost freshness or effectiveness—a tired {argument}, a tired {joke}. To be tired of something is to have lost patience or interest: {I'm tired of hearing excuses}. Tires, the rubber rings on wheels, give us a different tired—fitted with tires.

Tiredness is the state of feeling weary or fatigued, wanting rest or sleep. It can be physical—from exertion or lack of sleep—or mental, from sustained concentration or emotional strain. {The tiredness hit her as soon as she sat down.} Unlike exhaustion, tiredness suggests a milder, more ordinary depletion that rest can remedy.

Tireless describes someone or something that continues without fatigue or flagging effort: {a tireless advocate for reform}, {tireless dedication to the cause}. The word emphasizes sustained energy and persistence rather than literal inability to tire. It often carries admiration for someone's commitment: {She was tireless in her pursuit of justice}.

Tires are the rubber coverings fitted around wheels, providing traction and cushioning the ride. Most tires are pneumatic—inflated with air and mounted on rims. {I need to rotate my tires}. {The car skidded on bald tires}. As a verb, tires means to grow weary or cause fatigue: {The long hike tires me out}. {She never tires of that song}.

Tiresome describes something that causes weariness or annoyance through prolonged exposure. A tiresome {task} is tedious; a tiresome {person} tests your patience. The word emphasizes the draining effect rather than the cause: {His tiresome complaints wore everyone down}. Unlike tiring, which suggests physical exhaustion, tiresome implies mental or emotional fatigue.

Tiring describes something that depletes your energy or patience. A tiring {day} leaves you exhausted. A tiring {conversation} wears you out. The word applies equally to physical exertion and mental strain: {The hike was tiring}, {Dealing with bureaucracy is tiring}. What's tiring for one person may not be for another.

Tissue is a soft, thin paper used for wiping or wrapping—facial tissue for noses, tissue paper for gifts. In biology, tissue is a mass of cells forming a structural material: {muscle tissue}, {scar tissue}, {tissue samples}. A {tissue of lies} is an elaborate fabrication, suggesting something woven together. {She handed him a tissue.}

Tissues are soft, thin sheets of absorbent paper used for wiping noses, cleaning surfaces, or other disposable tasks: {She grabbed a tissue to blot her tears}. In biology, tissue is a mass of cells forming a structural material in living organisms: {muscle tissue}, {nerve tissue}. The plural tissues often appears in both contexts.

A tit is a small songbird common across Europe and Asia—blue tit, great tit, coal tit. The name has nothing to do with the vulgar sense that dominates American awareness. Tit is also crude slang for a breast, and in British usage, an insult for a foolish person: {You silly tit}. The phrase {tit for tat} (retaliation in kind) comes from an older expression meaning blow for blow, unrelated to either birds or anatomy.

A titan is someone of extraordinary size, strength, or achievement in their field: {a titan of industry}, {literary titans}. The word evokes immense power and influence, often applied to business leaders, athletes, or creative figures who dominate their domains. The original Titans were primordial Greek gods who preceded the Olympians—their overthrow by Zeus became a symbol for any clash of great powers. (Capitalized Titan is Saturn's largest moon or a member of the mythological race.)

Titanic means enormous in size, strength, or power—suggesting something of mythic proportions. The word comes from the Titans of Greek mythology, primordial deities of immense might. A titanic {struggle} involves forces of extraordinary magnitude. A titanic {effort} pushes human capacity to its limits. {The project required a titanic investment of resources.} (Capitalized Titanic usually refers to the ship.)

Titanium is a silver-gray metallic element prized for being both lightweight and exceptionally strong. These properties make it ideal for aerospace components, medical implants, and high-performance sporting goods. Titanium resists corrosion remarkably well, even in seawater. The adjective titanium often emphasizes durability or premium quality: {titanium credit cards}, {titanium-strength coating}.

Titanosaurs were massive herbivorous dinosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous period, representing the last surviving group of long-necked sauropods. Some species rank among the largest land animals ever to exist, with estimates suggesting lengths over 100 feet and weights exceeding 70 tons. The name means "titan lizard," reflecting their enormous size. {The titanosaur skeleton barely fit in the museum's main hall.}

Titans are beings of enormous size, strength, or influence. The word derives from Greek mythology's Titans—primordial gods who ruled before the Olympians. In modern use, titans are dominant figures in their fields: {titans of industry}, {tech titans}. The word suggests not just power but a kind of foundational, era-defining importance. (Capitalized Titans may refer to the mythological beings or sports teams.)

A titbit is a small, choice morsel of food, or by extension, an interesting piece of information or gossip: {She shared a few titbits about the upcoming merger}. The word is the British spelling; Americans use tidbit. Both suggest something pleasingly small and select—a taste rather than a full serving.

Titbits is the British spelling of tidbits—small, choice morsels of food or, more commonly, interesting pieces of information or gossip. {She shared a few titbits about the upcoming merger.} The word suggests something appetizing but minor, a sample rather than a full serving. In American English, the spelling tidbits predominates.

A tithe is a tenth of one's income or produce, traditionally given to support a church or clergy. The practice originated as a religious obligation in ancient times and remains part of some faiths today: {Members are expected to tithe ten percent of their earnings}. The verb tithe means to pay or collect such a portion. Extended loosely, tithe can mean any regular contribution to a cause.

Tithes are contributions of one-tenth of income or produce, traditionally given to support a church or clergy. The practice has roots in ancient religious obligation but now extends to any regular giving to religious institutions: {The congregation pays tithes every month}. To tithe is to give such a portion, or to levy it: {They tithed their harvest}.

Tithing is the practice of giving one-tenth of one's income to a religious institution, rooted in biblical tradition. Many churches still expect or encourage members to tithe: {Our family has been tithing since I was a child}. The term extends to any regular proportional giving. Historically, a tithing was also an English administrative division of ten households.

Titillated means pleasantly excited or aroused, often with a hint of the forbidden or risqué. The word suggests mild, teasing stimulation rather than deep engagement: {The tabloid headlines titillated readers with hints of scandal}. Something titillating appeals to prurient curiosity or provides a thrill of the slightly naughty.

Titillating describes something that arouses mild sexual interest or pleasurable excitement. The word suggests a teasing, superficial stimulation rather than deep engagement—{titillating gossip} or a {titillating glimpse}. It often carries a slightly disapproving tone, implying the appeal is cheap or shallow: {The documentary promised insight but delivered only titillating footage}. The related verb titillate means to excite in this way, and titillation is the resulting state.

Titillation is a feeling of mild excitement or arousal, often with sexual overtones. The word suggests a teasing, superficial kind of stimulation rather than deep engagement—tabloids offer titillation, not journalism. Something titillating tickles interest without fully satisfying it. {The movie promised titillation but delivered nothing memorable.} The related verb titillate means to excite or arouse in this pleasantly superficial way.

The title of a document, presentation, or work of art is its name. When a person holds a title, it is something they have won in competition (a heavyweight title) or that has been given to them on the basis of some quality or distinction they possess (he inherited the title of marquess). In law, title may refer to a section of a long statute (Title IX of the Higher Education Act) or to the right to property as represented by a document: I’ve lost the title to my car. As a verb, titled usually appears as the participle titled and means called a certain thing: an exhibition aptly titled “Lumps and Bumps”.

Titled describes something or someone that has a title. A titled {book} or {article} has a particular name: {a documentary titled "March of the Penguins"}. A titled {person} holds a noble rank—duke, earl, baron: {She married into a titled family}. The word often implies aristocratic status: {titled landowners}, {titled nobility}.

Titles are names that indicate rank, office, or distinction: {Doctor}, {President}, {Duke}. They precede or follow personal names to show status or achievement. Title also means the name of a creative work—a book, film, or song: {What's the title of that movie?} In property law, title is legal ownership or the document proving it: {The title to the house was in her name}. In sports, a title is a championship: {He's fighting for the heavyweight title}. To title something is to give it a name.

A titmouse is a small, crested songbird common in North American woodlands, known for its gray plumage and acrobatic movements at bird feeders. The name has nothing to do with mice—it comes from an Old English word for small bird. Plural: titmice.

Tits are small songbirds of the family Paridae, common in European gardens. The word is also vulgar slang for breasts: {nice tits}. This sense is crude but common—less clinical than breasts and less childish than boobs. {Tits up} means failed or dead: {The whole plan went tits up}. To get on someone's tits (British) is to annoy them greatly.

A titter is a nervous, suppressed laugh—quieter and more restrained than a giggle, often with a hand covering the mouth. It suggests embarrassment, awkwardness, or trying not to laugh openly: {A titter ran through the audience when his voice cracked}. The verb means to laugh this way: {The students tittered at the innuendo}.

Tittering is a particular kind of laughter—light, nervous, and often suppressed or half-stifled. It suggests amusement tinged with embarrassment or self-consciousness, the kind of giggling that ripples through a classroom when someone says something accidentally suggestive. {The audience tittered at the actor's wardrobe malfunction.} Unlike hearty laughter, tittering carries connotations of immaturity or inappropriate amusement, as if the person knows they probably shouldn't be laughing.

Titters are small, partly suppressed laughs—nervous, self-conscious, or slightly mocking. The word suggests giggling held back, often inappropriate to the moment: {Her comment drew titters from the back row}. To titter is to laugh this way, with a restrained, high-pitched quality that distinguishes it from open laughter.
Titties is the plural of titty, an informal term for breasts: {She flashed her titties at the concert}. The word is vulgar but playful, common in casual speech and hip-hop lyrics.

A tizzy is a state of nervous agitation or flustered excitement, usually over something minor: {She got into a tizzy about the seating arrangements}. The word suggests overreaction—being more worked up than the situation warrants. Informal and slightly dated.

A toad is a tailless amphibian similar to a frog but typically stockier, with warty skin and shorter legs adapted for walking rather than hopping. Toads prefer drier habitats than frogs and secrete toxins through their skin. Calling someone a toad suggests they're repulsive or contemptible: {That little toad betrayed us}.

A toadie is a person who flatters and fawns over someone more powerful, hoping to gain favor or advantage. The word implies servile, insincere behavior—agreeing with everything, laughing at bad jokes, running errands without being asked: {He surrounded himself with toadies who never challenged him}. To toadie or toadie up to someone is to behave this way.

Toadies is the plural of toady—a person who flatters and fawns over someone powerful to gain favor. The word suggests servile, sycophantic behavior: {The executive surrounded himself with toadies who never challenged his decisions}. To toady is to behave this way: {She toadied to the boss shamelessly}.

Toads are squat, warty amphibians related to frogs but typically with drier, bumpier skin and shorter legs suited to walking rather than hopping. They're found worldwide and often appear in folklore as ugly or magical creatures. Figuratively, toad describes an unpleasant or repulsive person: {That little toad sold us out}.

A toadstool is a mushroom, especially one that is poisonous or inedible. The word evokes the classic fairy-tale image: a rounded cap on a stem, often red with white spots. There's no scientific distinction between toadstools and mushrooms—the terms overlap—but toadstool carries connotations of danger or folklore: {Don't eat that, it's a toadstool}.

Toadstools are mushrooms, especially poisonous or inedible ones. The word evokes the classic image of a wild mushroom with a rounded cap on a stem—the kind found in forests and fairy tales. There's no scientific distinction between toadstools and mushrooms; the terms reflect folk tradition rather than biology. {Don't eat those toadstools growing in the yard.}

A toady is a person who flatters and fawns over someone in power, hoping to gain favor. The word carries strong contempt—a toady has no dignity or independent judgment, only servile eagerness to please: {He surrounded himself with toadies who agreed with everything he said}. As a verb, to toady is to behave this way: {She toadied to the boss shamelessly}.

Toast is bread browned by heat, typically in a toaster or under a broiler: {buttered toast}, {toast and jam}. To toast is to brown food this way, or to warm oneself: {toasting by the fire}. A toast is also a ritual of raising glasses to honor someone or something: {a toast to the bride and groom}. To be toast is slang for being doomed or finished: {If the boss finds out, you're toast}.

Toasted describes bread or other food browned by dry heat: {toasted bagel}, {toasted almonds}. The verb toast means to brown food this way, or to raise a glass in someone's honor: {Let's toast the happy couple}. A toast is both the browned bread and the celebratory gesture. Informally, toasted means drunk or high: {We got completely toasted last night}.

A toaster is a small kitchen appliance that browns slices of bread by exposing them to radiant heat. Most toasters have slots that hold the bread vertically and a lever or button that lowers it into the heating chamber. {The toast popped up from the toaster.} Toaster ovens are larger countertop appliances that can toast, bake, and broil.

A toastie is a grilled sandwich, typically with cheese and other fillings pressed between slices of bread and heated until the outside is crispy and the inside melted. The term is chiefly British; Americans would say grilled cheese or panini. {I grabbed a ham and cheese toastie for lunch.}

Toasties are grilled or toasted sandwiches, typically with melted cheese and other fillings pressed between two slices of bread. The term is chiefly British: {I made ham and cheese toasties for lunch}. A toastie maker or sandwich press creates the characteristic sealed edges and crispy exterior.

Toasting is heating bread or other food until browned and crisp: {The smell of toasting bagels filled the kitchen}. It also refers to the act of raising glasses in honor of someone or something: {After much toasting, the wedding guests were thoroughly drunk}. In Jamaican music culture, toasting is a style of rhythmic chanting over beats, a precursor to rap.

A toastmaster is the person who presides over a banquet or formal dinner, introducing speakers, proposing toasts, and keeping the event moving. The role requires a mix of charm, timing, and crowd control: {The toastmaster called for silence before the bride's father spoke}. Toastmasters International is an organization devoted to public speaking skills.

Toasts is the plural of toast in all its senses. Slices of bread browned by heat: {She made toasts with butter and jam}. Ceremonial drinks honoring someone: {We raised our glasses for toasts to the bride and groom}. The verb form covers both browning bread and drinking in honor: {He toasts his bagel every morning}; {She toasts her colleagues at every company dinner}.

Toasty means pleasantly warm, with a connotation of coziness: {The fire made the cabin nice and toasty}. It suggests warmth that's comfortable rather than excessive—the temperature of being wrapped in a blanket or sitting near a hearth. The word is informal and often affectionate in tone.

Tobacco is a plant whose dried leaves are smoked, chewed, or snuffed for their stimulant effects. The nicotine in tobacco is highly addictive, making it among the most harmful legal substances: {He quit tobacco after thirty years}. Tobacco also refers to the product itself—loose leaf, cigarettes, cigars, or chewing tobacco. The tobacco industry has faced decades of litigation and regulation over health effects.

A tobacconist is a person who sells tobacco products, or the shop where such products are sold. The term evokes an older retail tradition—a specialty store selling cigars, pipe tobacco, cigarettes, and smoking accessories: {The tobacconist recommended a milder blend}. The word has become less common as tobacco sales shifted to convenience stores and supermarkets.

A toboggan is a long, flat-bottomed sled without runners, traditionally made of thin boards curved up at the front. Used for sliding downhill over snow or ice: {The kids took the toboggan to the steepest hill in the park}. In some American dialects, toboggan also means a knit winter cap—the kind you'd wear while sledding.

Tobogganing is the activity of riding a toboggan—a long, flat-bottomed sled without runners—down snow-covered slopes. The sport ranges from casual recreation to competitive racing on specially constructed chutes: {We went tobogganing in the park after the first big snowfall}.

Toboggans are long, flat-bottomed sleds without runners, designed for sliding downhill over snow or ice. The front curves upward to glide over obstacles. Multiple riders typically sit in a line: {We piled onto the toboggan and flew down the hill}. In some Southern U.S. dialects, a toboggan is a knit winter cap—the kind you'd wear while sledding.

Tock is the second half of a clock's sound, paired with tick. Where tick represents the sharper, higher sound, tock is the deeper, answering beat: {tick-tock, tick-tock}. The pair suggests the steady passage of time, and tock rarely appears alone.

Today is the current day—the one you're in right now: {I have a meeting today}, {today's weather}. It extends to the present time or era: {Today's smartphones are more powerful than yesterday's computers}. As a noun, today names this day: {Today is my birthday}. The adverb yesterday and tomorrow complete the immediate temporal trio.
clues: What the calendar shows right now

definition: Toddies are hot drinks made with liquor, water, sugar, and spices. A hot toddy typically combines whiskey or brandy with honey, lemon, and hot water, often served as a remedy for colds or a warming winter drink: {She made toddies for everyone after they came in from the snow}.

To toddle is to walk with short, unsteady steps, as a young child does when first learning to walk: {The baby toddled across the room}. By extension, toddle describes any unhurried, casual movement: {I'll toddle off to bed now}. A toddler is a child at the toddling stage, roughly one to three years old.

Toddled is the past tense of toddle, meaning to walk with short, unsteady steps like a small child learning to walk. The word extends to casual, unhurried movement by adults: {She toddled off to the shops}. British speakers use it for leisurely departures: {Well, I'd better toddle along}.

A toddler is a young child who has learned to walk but hasn't yet mastered the skill—typically between ages one and three. The word captures the unsteady, tottering gait characteristic of this stage: {The toddler wobbled across the room}. By extension, toddler describes products and services aimed at this age group: {toddler bed}, {toddler classes}.

Toddlers are young children who have recently learned to walk, typically between one and three years old. The word captures their unsteady gait—they toddle rather than stride. {The toddlers chased each other around the playground.} The toddler stage is marked by rapid development, tantrums, and the word "no."

Toddling is walking with the short, unsteady steps characteristic of a young child just learning to walk. The word captures that distinctive gait—slightly wobbly, determined, not quite in full control: {The baby came toddling across the room}. Adults who walk slowly or aimlessly may also toddle: {I'm just toddling off to the shops}.

A toddy is a drink made by mixing spirits (usually whiskey or rum) with hot water, sugar, and spices. The hot toddy is a classic cold-weather remedy and comfort drink: {She made him a hot toddy when he came in from the snow}. In South and Southeast Asia, toddy also refers to the fermented sap of palm trees, drunk fresh or distilled into arrack.

A toe is any of the digits at the end of your foot. The part of a sock or shoe that covers your toes is also the toe. Toe also describes the lowest part of something, or something shaped like a toe. From head to toe is a way of saying thoroughly or throughout, suggesting that no part is overlooked. If you’re on your toes, you are alert and ready to act. To toe the line is to obey rules and conform to expectations.

A toehold is a small ledge or crevice just large enough to support the toes when climbing: {She found a toehold in the rock face}. Figuratively, it's any minimal but secure position from which to advance: {The company established a toehold in the Asian market}. In wrestling, a toehold is a hold in which the foot is bent or twisted.

Toeholds are small footholds or grips just big enough for the toes, used in climbing: {She found toeholds in the rock face}. Figuratively, a toehold is any initial position from which to advance—a first foothold in a market, a minor advantage that might grow: {The company gained a toehold in Asia}.

A toenail is the hard protective plate covering the upper surface of a toe, equivalent to a fingernail. In carpentry, to toenail is to drive a nail at an angle through one piece of wood into another: {He toenailed the stud to the floor plate}.

Toenails are the hard, protective plates covering the tips of the toes, equivalent to fingernails on the feet. They grow slowly and require periodic trimming. In carpentry, to toenail is to drive a nail at an angle through one piece of wood into another: {He toenailed the stud to the plate}.

Toes are the digits at the end of the foot—humans have five on each. To toe a line is to stand with toes touching it, hence to comply with rules or expectations: {He refused to toe the party line}. To be {on your toes} is to be alert and ready. To {toe the water} is to test something cautiously. As a verb, to toe is to touch or kick with the toe: {She toed the ball into the goal}.

Toffee is a chewy candy made by boiling sugar and butter together until it caramelizes and hardens. British toffee tends to be softer than American versions, which are often called taffy. {She made a batch of toffee for the holidays}. Someone who {can't do something for toffee} (British) is utterly hopeless at it.

Toffees is the plural of toffee, a chewy candy made by boiling sugar and butter together. British English uses toffees as countable units—individual pieces of the confection: {She unwrapped one of the toffees from the tin}. American English more often treats toffee as a mass noun, making toffees less common.

Toffs is the plural of toff, British slang for wealthy, upper-class people, often with connotations of snobbery or entitlement. The word carries mild derision—it's what working-class people call those born into privilege: {The toffs in their country estates have no idea how ordinary people live}.

Tofu is a soft, bland food made from coagulated soy milk pressed into blocks. It originated in East Asia and is a staple protein in vegetarian and vegan cooking. Tofu absorbs flavors from marinades and sauces, making it versatile despite its neutral taste: {The stir-fry had crispy tofu with garlic and ginger}. Textures range from silken to extra-firm.

Tofurkey is a tofu-based meat substitute shaped and seasoned to resemble turkey, typically served at Thanksgiving or other holiday meals as a vegetarian or vegan alternative: {We're having tofurkey this year since my sister went vegan}. The word blends tofu and turkey. Tofurky is a trademarked brand name for such products.

Tofurky is a brand name for a turkey-shaped roast made from tofu and wheat protein, typically served as a vegetarian or vegan alternative at Thanksgiving: {We're having tofurky this year since my sister went vegan}.
