The word has become somewhat generic for any meatless turkey substitute, and carries mild cultural associations with earnest vegetarianism.

A toga is the loose outer garment worn by citizens of ancient Rome—a single piece of cloth draped over the body and around one shoulder. The toga symbolized Roman citizenship and formal occasions. Today, toga appears mainly in {toga party}, where people wrap themselves in bedsheets in imitation of the ancient garment.

Togas is the plural of toga, the draped outer garment worn by citizens of ancient Rome. The toga was a marker of Roman citizenship and status—different styles indicated social rank. Today, togas appear mainly at costume parties, where bedsheets serve as approximations: {a toga party at the frat house}.

The useful adverb together suggests union of things that can or did exist separately. To put something together is to assemble its parts, or for abstract things, draw connections among them. To work together is to work cooperatively or harmoniously. If you ask whether two people are together, you want to know if they are a couple. If you take two things together, you consider them as one, or closely related. When people come together, they either gather in one place, or unite in a cause.
clues: At the same time or place

definition: Togetherness is the feeling of closeness and connection that comes from being with others—family, friends, or community. It emphasizes shared experience and emotional warmth rather than mere physical proximity: {The holidays are about togetherness}. The word often appears in sentimental contexts celebrating bonds between people.

Toggle is a fastener or switch that moves between two positions—a coat toggle pushed through a loop, a light switch flipped on or off. In computing, toggle describes any control that alternates between states with each activation: {Toggle the setting to enable dark mode}. The verb means to switch back and forth: {I keep toggling between tabs}.

Toggles is the third-person singular of toggle. A toggle is a switch that alternates between two states—on and off, open and closed: {She toggles between dark mode and light mode}. The word comes from a pin passed through a loop to fasten something, which could only be in or out. In computing, toggles are ubiquitous interface elements. To toggle is to switch back and forth: {He toggles between tabs while working}.

Toil is hard, exhausting labor—work that drains and wears you down: {Years of toil in the fields left his hands calloused}. The word carries connotations of drudgery and thanklessness. As a verb, to toil is to work strenuously: {She toiled through the night to finish the report}. To {toil away} emphasizes the grinding persistence of such effort.

Toiled is the past tense of toil, meaning to work extremely hard, usually for a long time and often with little reward. The word carries connotations of exhausting, grinding labor: {She toiled in the fields from dawn to dusk}. {He toiled for years on a novel that never found a publisher}.

A toilet is a fixture for urinating and defecating, consisting of a bowl with a seat and a mechanism for flushing waste away with water. The room containing this fixture is also called a toilet, especially in British English, where Americans more often say bathroom or restroom. Toilet formerly referred to grooming and dressing, which is why toiletries are personal care items like soap and toothpaste. {The toilet's clogged again.} {Where's the nearest public toilet?}

Toiletries are personal care items used for grooming and hygiene—soap, shampoo, toothpaste, deodorant, razors, and the like. The word typically appears when packing for travel or shopping for bathroom supplies: {Don't forget to pack your toiletries}. Hotels often provide basic toiletries for guests.

A toiletry is an item used in washing and grooming—soap, shampoo, toothpaste, deodorant, razors, and the like. Usually plural: {Don't forget to pack your toiletries}. The word derives from toilet in its older sense of the process of dressing and grooming oneself.

Toilets is the plural of toilet—a fixture for urinating and defecating, typically a bowl connected to plumbing that flushes waste away. The room containing this fixture is also called a toilet, especially in British English: {Where are the toilets?} Toilet once meant the process of grooming oneself, surviving in {toiletries} and {toilet water} (a light perfume).

Toiling is working hard, especially at physically demanding or tedious labor. The word carries connotations of sustained effort and weariness: {farmers toiling in the fields}, {She spent years toiling away at a job she hated}. Toiling suggests not just work but struggle—effort that extracts a cost.

Toils are snares or traps, usually figurative: {caught in the toils of bureaucracy}, {escape the toils of addiction}. The word suggests entanglement—being wrapped up in something difficult to break free from. Literary and somewhat old-fashioned, toils appears almost exclusively in this plural form with this meaning. (The verb toil, meaning to labor hard, is a different word.)

A toke is a puff on a cigarette or pipe, especially one containing marijuana: {She took a long toke and passed the joint}. The verb means to take such a puff: {They were toking in the parking lot}. The word belongs almost exclusively to cannabis culture.

A token is a small object or an idea that in either case symbolically represents something else. Physical tokens may be used like money, to give you access to something. A gift of flowers may be a token of love. Token has many uses in computing, some having to do with authenticating the way computers communicate with each other. The adjective token is often used disparagingly, suggesting that something is done of the sake of appearance: It was a meaningless token gesture.

Tokenism is the practice of making only a symbolic effort toward inclusion—hiring one woman, featuring one minority character—to deflect criticism rather than achieve genuine diversity or equality. The token presence creates an appearance of fairness while leaving existing power structures intact: {The company's single Black executive felt like tokenism rather than progress}.

Tokens are objects or symbols that stand for something else. A subway token grants passage. A token of appreciation represents gratitude. In computing, tokens are the smallest meaningful units that software processes—words, numbers, or symbols parsed from text. As an adjective, token describes minimal or symbolic efforts: a {token gesture}, a {token minority hire}. The phrase {by the same token} means correspondingly or for the same reason.

Tokes is the plural of toke, a puff or drag on a marijuana cigarette or pipe: {He took a few tokes and passed it along}. The singular toke also works as a verb meaning to smoke marijuana: {They were toking in the parking lot}. The word emerged from 1960s drug culture and remains casual slang.

Toking is smoking marijuana, typically by taking a drag from a joint, pipe, or bong. The term comes from toke, slang for a puff or drag: {We spent the afternoon toking on the back porch}. Less commonly, toking can refer to smoking anything, but the marijuana association dominates.

Told is the past tense of tell. You told someone something when you communicated it to them: {I told you so}, {She told me a secret}. {All told} means in total, counting everything: {There were fifty people all told}. {I told you} often carries a note of vindication—you warned them and were right.

Tolerable means bearable or acceptable, though not ideal. Something tolerable can be endured without too much discomfort: {The pain was tolerable with medication}. It also describes things that are adequate but unremarkable—passable, good enough: {The food was tolerable, nothing more}. {How are you feeling? —Tolerable.}

Tolerance is the capacity to accept or endure something, especially opinions or behaviors different from one's own: {religious tolerance}, {tolerance for dissent}. In medicine and pharmacology, tolerance is the body's diminished response to a substance after repeated exposure: {He had built up a tolerance to the painkillers}. Engineering uses tolerance for the allowable deviation from a standard: {manufacturing tolerances}. To have a high or low tolerance for something is to handle more or less of it before reaching your limit: {I have zero tolerance for rudeness}.

Tolerant describes a willingness to accept differences—in beliefs, behaviors, or people—without interference or complaint. A tolerant society allows diverse viewpoints. Tolerant can also mean able to endure or withstand: plants tolerant of {drought}, patients tolerant of {a medication}. The word sometimes carries faint criticism, implying passive acceptance rather than genuine embrace: {He was tolerant of her habits but never quite approved}.

To tolerate something is to allow or endure it without interference, even if you don't approve: {I tolerate his messy habits but I don't like them}. The word implies reluctant acceptance rather than enthusiasm. You might tolerate a noise, a person's behavior, or an opposing viewpoint. In medicine, to tolerate a drug or treatment is to endure it without adverse reaction: {She tolerates the medication well}.

Meanings of toll are split in two groups, each represented by a noun and a verb. First, a toll is an amount collected for some service, such as crossing a bridge. By extension, a toll is the burden resulting from something, like a heavy toll on people who suffer a disaster. A death toll is the number of deaths associated with an adverse event. To toll someone is to charge them a toll. Second, a toll is the sound that a bell makes. When a bell tolls it makes its characteristic sound.

A tollbooth is a small structure at a bridge, highway, or tunnel where drivers stop to pay a fee for passage. The attendant inside collects the toll or the driver deposits coins into a machine: {We slowed down as we approached the tollbooth}. Many tollbooths have been replaced by electronic collection systems.

Tolled is the past tense of toll. A bell tolls when it rings slowly and solemnly, typically marking deaths or calling people to worship: {The church bells tolled for the fallen soldiers}. Time or events toll when they pass with weighty significance. In another sense, authorities toll fees from travelers: {The bridge tolled five dollars per crossing}. In legal contexts, to toll a statute of limitations is to pause or suspend its running.

A tollgate is a barrier across a road where travelers must pay a fee before proceeding. Historically these were physical gates at bridges, turnpikes, or town entrances; modern tollgates are often automated stations on highways. In business contexts, tollgate refers to a checkpoint in a process where approval is required before moving forward: {Each phase of the project has a tollgate review with stakeholders}.

Tolling is the slow, measured ringing of a bell, especially to mark a death or funeral. Church bells toll to announce solemn occasions, each stroke separated by silence: {The tolling of the bells signaled the king's passing}. Figuratively, something tolling suggests an ominous warning or approaching end. In legal contexts, tolling refers to suspending or pausing a time limit: {The statute of limitations was tolled during his absence from the state}.

Tolls are fees charged for using a road, bridge, or other passage, or the act of collecting such fees. The verb toll has a separate meaning: to ring a bell slowly and repeatedly, typically to mark a death or solemn occasion. {The church bells tolled for the fallen soldiers.} When something takes its toll, it causes gradual damage or wear: {Years of stress took their toll on his health.} The phrase {for whom the bell tolls} reminds us that every death diminishes the living.

A tom is a male cat, short for tomcat. The term extends to other male animals: a tom turkey is a male turkey. The word suggests the roaming, territorial nature associated with unneutered male cats. {The old tom prowled the neighborhood at night.} (Capitalized Tom is a given name.)
clues: What you call a male cat

definition: A tomahawk is a light ax traditionally used by Native Americans of eastern North America, with a straight handle and a head that may be stone or metal. The word entered English from Algonquian languages. To tomahawk is to strike or kill with one. In sports, a tomahawk describes an overhead chopping motion: {a tomahawk dunk}, {a tomahawk chop}.

Tomahawks are light axes originally used by Native American peoples as tools and weapons. The word entered English from Algonquian languages. A tomahawk has a straight handle and a head that may be bladed, spiked, or clublike. To tomahawk is to strike or kill with one. The tomahawk steak, a thick ribeye with an extended bone, resembles the weapon's silhouette.

A tomatillo is a small, round, green fruit enclosed in a papery husk, used in Mexican cooking. Related to tomatoes but tart rather than sweet, tomatillos are the base of salsa verde and various sauces. The husk is removed before cooking: {Peel the tomatillos and roast them until slightly charred}.

Tomatillos are small, round fruits enclosed in a papery husk, used extensively in Mexican and Central American cooking. Related to tomatoes but with a distinctly tart, citrusy flavor, they form the base of salsa verde and other green sauces. The husk must be removed and the slightly sticky surface rinsed before cooking. Unlike tomatoes, tomatillos are typically used while still green and firm rather than allowed to fully ripen.

A tomato is the red, fleshy fruit of a vine plant, eaten raw in salads and sandwiches or cooked into sauces. Botanically a fruit, it's treated as a vegetable in cooking. Tomatoes range from small cherry varieties to large beefsteaks. The plural is tomatoes. In dated slang, a tomato was an attractive woman.

Tomatoes is the plural of tomato, the red fruit of a nightshade plant, eaten as a vegetable in salads, sauces, and countless dishes. {She sliced tomatoes for the sandwiches.} In older slang, tomatoes meant attractive women—dated now and likely to sound odd or offensive.

A tomb is a place of burial, especially one that is built rather than simply dug—a vault, chamber, or monument housing the dead. Tombs range from ancient stone structures to elaborate mausoleums: {the tomb of the unknown soldier}, {Egyptian tombs filled with treasures}. Figuratively, any silent, dark, or deathly still place may be called a tomb: {The house was a tomb after everyone left}.

A tomboy is a girl who enjoys activities, clothing, or behaviors traditionally associated with boys—climbing trees, playing rough sports, rejecting dresses. The term carries mild approval or neutrality, suggesting spirited independence rather than transgression: {She was a tomboy who preferred building forts to playing with dolls}. As gender norms shift, the word appears less frequently.

Tomboys are girls who prefer activities, clothes, or behaviors traditionally associated with boys—climbing trees, playing rough sports, rejecting dresses. The term carries less weight than it once did as gender expectations have loosened, but it still describes girls whose energy and interests don't fit conventional feminine molds: {She was a tomboy who spent summers catching frogs and building forts}.

Tombs are burial chambers or vaults for the dead. A tomb may be an underground room, a stone structure above ground, or a carved-out space in rock. The word often suggests something grander than a simple grave: {the pharaoh's tomb}, {a family tomb}. Figuratively, any dark, silent, or confining place: {The house was a tomb after she left}.

A tombstone is a stone marker placed at a grave, typically inscribed with the deceased person's name and dates: {We found our ancestor's tombstone in the old cemetery}. The word extends to anything resembling such a marker in shape or finality. In finance, a tombstone is a print advertisement announcing a completed deal—so called because of its plain, rectangular format listing participants. In computing, tombstone can refer to a placeholder marking deleted data.

Tombstones are stone markers placed at graves, typically inscribed with the deceased's name, birth and death dates, and sometimes an epitaph: {We wandered through the old cemetery reading tombstones}. In finance, a tombstone is a print advertisement announcing a completed deal—the blocky, text-heavy format resembles a grave marker. The verb tombstone means to dive into water feet-first with arms at your sides, body rigid like a tombstone.

A tomcat is an adult male cat, especially one that roams and hasn't been neutered. The word emphasizes the animal's wandering, territorial, and mating behaviors. By extension, a man who tomcats around pursues casual sexual encounters: {He spent his twenties tomcatting through Europe}.

Tomcats is the plural of tomcat, a male cat. The word distinguishes the male from females (queens) and neutered males. Tomcat also describes a man who pursues casual sexual encounters: {He spent his twenties tomcatting around}. The verb tomcat means to seek such encounters, usually said of men behaving promiscuously.

Tomcatting is pursuing casual sexual encounters, typically said of men who are promiscuous or unfaithful. The word comes from the male cat's reputation for roaming in search of mates: {He spent his twenties tomcatting around the city}. The tone is usually disapproving or ruefully self-aware.

A tome is a large, heavy book, often one volume of a larger work. The word carries connotations of scholarly weight and physical heft: {dusty tomes lined the library shelves}. It's frequently used with gentle irony for any imposing book: {I'm halfway through that tome on Roman history}.

Tomes is the plural of tome, a large or scholarly book. The word often carries a hint of weight or seriousness—dusty tomes in a library, ancient tomes of forbidden knowledge. It can be used ironically for any thick book: {I'm halfway through that tome she recommended}.

Tomfool means foolish or silly, with a suggestion of absurdity: {tomfool ideas}, {tomfool behavior}. The word is old-fashioned, appearing mainly in set phrases like {tomfool scheme} or {tomfool stunt}. As a noun, a tomfool is a person who acts foolishly. The related tomfoolery means silly or foolish behavior: {Enough of this tomfoolery}.

Tomfoolery is foolish or silly behavior, usually harmless but annoying: {Enough tomfoolery—let's get back to work}. The word suggests playful mischief rather than serious misconduct, often used by adults scolding children or by anyone tired of nonsense.

Tomorrow is the day after today. It functions as both noun and adverb: {Tomorrow is my birthday}, {I'll call you tomorrow}. Beyond the literal, tomorrow represents the future generally: {the leaders of tomorrow}, {tomorrow's technology}. The phrase {tomorrow never comes} observes that postponed tasks remain undone, since tomorrow perpetually recedes.

Tomorrows are future days, used poetically or rhetorically to mean the times ahead: {All our tomorrows depend on the choices we make today}. The plural emphasizes an accumulation of future moments rather than a single next day. {She's saving her money for her tomorrows.}

A ton is a unit of weight. In the US, a short ton equals 2,000 pounds; in Britain, a long ton equals 2,240 pounds. A metric ton (or tonne) is 1,000 kilograms. Beyond measurement, ton commonly means a large quantity: {I have a ton of work to do}. {That must have cost a ton.} In British slang, a ton is a hundred, especially £100 or 100 mph.

Tone designates a value on a scale. In music, a tone is a particular pitch. In sound generally, different tones have different uses, like the ring tone on your phone. Different tones of color have slightly different appearances. Tone can also refer to a quality of emotion or intent, like an angry tone in conversation. Muscle tone is the desirable quality of a muscle’s being fit. To tone something is to give it the desired quality or tone.

A tonearm is the pivoting arm on a turntable that holds the cartridge and stylus, allowing the needle to track the record's grooves. It balances tracking force against the need to move freely across the disc. Quality tonearms minimize vibration and maintain consistent contact between stylus and vinyl.

Toned describes something with firmness, definition, or a particular quality. A toned body has visible muscle definition from exercise: {She has incredibly toned arms}. Skin can be toned—even in color and texture. In combinations, toned indicates degree or type: {a sepia-toned photograph}, {his measured, even-toned response}. To tone down is to moderate; to tone up is to strengthen.

Toner is a fine powder used in laser printers and photocopiers to form text and images on paper. The powder adheres to electrically charged areas and fuses to the page with heat. Separately, toner is a liquid applied to skin after cleansing to remove residue and prepare for moisturizer: {She uses toner morning and night}.

Tones are variations in sound, color, or manner that convey distinct qualities. A musical tone has a specific pitch and duration; a {harsh tone} in someone's voice signals displeasure. In visual arts, tones refer to gradations of color or light and dark. To tone something is to give it a particular quality or to moderate it: {tone down the rhetoric}. If you're toned or {well-toned}, your muscles are firm from exercise. A toner is ink for printers or a skincare product meant to improve skin tone.

Tongs are a gripping tool with two arms joined at one end, used to pick up objects without touching them directly. The word is almost always plural, like scissors or pliers. Kitchen tongs lift hot food; fireplace tongs handle burning logs; ice tongs grip slippery blocks. {She used the tongs to flip the steaks on the grill.}

The tongue is an organ in the mouths of humans and most vertebrates. Because of the obligatory involvement of the tongue in producing speech, it is a metonym for language itself: Her mother tongue is Swahili. Several idioms in which tongue features are about speech: hold your tongue, on the tip of one’s tongue, slip of the tongue. Some inanimate objects with an analogous shape or function are also called tongues, like the flap in the middle of a shoe or the clapper of a bell.

Tongues is the plural of tongue—the muscular organ in the mouth used for tasting, swallowing, and speech. Languages are also tongues: {She speaks in foreign tongues}. In religious contexts, {speaking in tongues} refers to glossolalia—uttering sounds or words believed to be divinely inspired, especially in Pentecostal worship: {The congregation spoke in tongues}.

Tonic connects to tension and restoration. In music, the tonic is the first note of a scale—the home base that resolves tension. A tonic is also something that restores vigor or well-being: {The vacation was a tonic for her spirits}. Tonic water is a carbonated mixer with quinine, traditionally paired with gin. In medicine, tonic describes sustained muscle contraction, as in a tonic seizure.

Tonics are substances believed to restore or invigorate health and vitality. The word often appears in compounds: a gin and {tonic} is a cocktail, {tonic water} is carbonated water with quinine. In music, the tonic is the first note of a scale, the home base to which melodies resolve. Hair {tonics} were once popular grooming products promising to strengthen or stimulate hair growth. The adjective tonic describes something that produces or restores physical, mental, or moral vigor.

Tonight refers to the present night or the night following the current day. As an adverb, it indicates when something happens: {I'm staying home tonight}. As a noun, it names this particular evening: {Tonight is the night we've been waiting for}. The word assumes shared temporal context between speaker and listener.

Toning is the process of firming or strengthening, especially muscles through exercise: {She's been toning her arms with light weights}. In photography and printing, toning adjusts color balance or adds a color cast to an image. Hair toning neutralizes unwanted brassiness after bleaching. The common thread is subtle adjustment toward a desired quality—firmer, warmer, cooler, more even.

Tonkatsu is a Japanese dish of breaded, deep-fried pork cutlet, typically served sliced into strips alongside shredded cabbage and a thick, sweet-savory sauce. The cutlet is coated in panko breadcrumbs, giving it a distinctively light, crispy texture: {We ordered tonkatsu and cold beer at the izakaya}.

Tonkotsu is a Japanese style of ramen featuring a rich, creamy, opaque broth made by boiling pork bones for many hours until the collagen and fat emulsify into the liquid. The name literally means "pork bone" in Japanese. The broth is typically milky white and has an intense, savory flavor that distinguishes it from lighter soy-based or miso ramens. {I'm craving tonkotsu—nothing else hits the same on a cold night.}

Tons is the plural of ton, a unit of weight equal to 2,000 pounds (short ton) or 2,240 pounds (long ton). More commonly, tons is an informal intensifier meaning a great deal: {I have tons of work to do}, {Thanks tons}. The casual usage far outpaces the precise measurement in everyday speech.

Tonsils are masses of tissue at the back of the throat, one on each side, that help fight infection. They're most discussed when inflamed—tonsillitis often afflicted children before tonsillectomies became routine: {The doctor said her tonsils need to come out}. To be {down to the tonsils} in something is to be deeply immersed in it.

Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils, the two oval-shaped tissue masses at the back of the throat. Usually caused by viral or bacterial infection, it produces sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and swollen glands. Recurring cases once led routinely to surgical removal of the tonsils, though this is now less common: {The doctor said her tonsillitis would clear up with antibiotics}.

Tonsils are two masses of tissue at the back of the throat, part of the immune system's first line of defense against inhaled or swallowed pathogens. They're most famous for becoming infected—tonsillitis was once treated almost routinely by surgical removal: {She had her tonsils out when she was seven}.

The adverb too has two core ideas: one use signifies excess or extremes: this room is too cold. The other idea is conjunctive. Reflecting this, too is almost always used near a conjunction or in a sentence that has a parallel in a previous sentence or clause: We saw the Palmers, and the Tysons were there, too. In this sense, too is a close synonym of also.

Toodles is a playful, casual goodbye—lighter and more whimsical than a simple "bye." It often carries a slightly ironic or campy tone: {Toodles, I'm off to get coffee}. The word sounds deliberately silly, making it useful for softening departures or adding levity.

Took is the past tense of take. All the meanings of take appear with took in past contexts: {She took the keys}, {He took offense}, {The project took three months}, {They took a walk}. Took sometimes appears where taken would be standard: {I should have took the other road}—this is common in casual speech but considered nonstandard in formal writing.

Tookus is a slang term for the buttocks, borrowed from Yiddish. It's informal and mildly humorous rather than vulgar: {Get off your tookus and help me}, {She slipped and landed right on her tookus}. Also spelled tuchus, tuchas, or toches.

A tool is an implement used to accomplish a task—hammers, screwdrivers, saws. The meaning extends to anything that serves a purpose: {Language is a tool for communication}. Software tools help users perform specific functions. To tool is to drive casually: {tooling around town}. In slang, a tool is a person easily manipulated or one who's obnoxiously trying too hard—an insult suggesting someone lacks independent thought: {Don't be such a tool}.

A toolbar is a row of buttons or icons on a computer screen that provide quick access to frequently used commands or functions. Most software applications display toolbars near the top of the window: {The formatting toolbar has buttons for bold, italic, and underline}. Users can often customize which tools appear or hide toolbars entirely.

A toolbelt is a belt with loops, pouches, or holders for carrying tools while working—worn by carpenters, electricians, and other tradespeople to keep equipment within reach. Figuratively, a toolbelt is a collection of skills or resources someone has available: {Add this technique to your toolbelt}. Also spelled tool belt.

A toolbox is a container for storing and transporting tools, typically with compartments or trays for organization. Figuratively, a toolbox is a set of skills, resources, or techniques available for a particular purpose: {We need to expand our diplomatic toolbox}. In computing, a toolbox is a collection of software utilities or a panel of icons representing available functions.

Toolboxes is the plural of toolbox—a container for storing and organizing tools, typically with compartments or trays: {He grabbed the toolboxes from the garage}. Figuratively, a toolbox is a set of skills, strategies, or resources available for a particular purpose: {Therapists need diverse toolboxes to help different clients}.

Tooled describes leather that has been decorated with impressed designs using special implements: {a tooled leather belt}, {hand-tooled cowboy boots}. In bookbinding, tooled covers feature ornamental patterns pressed into the material. Separately, tooled is slang for drove or traveled, often at speed: {We tooled around town in his convertible}. To get tooled up is to equip oneself, especially with weapons.

Tooling refers to the process of designing, making, or equipping with tools, especially the specialized machinery and equipment needed for manufacturing. In industrial contexts, tooling includes dies, molds, jigs, and fixtures required to produce parts: {The tooling costs for a new car model run into millions}. The term extends to software development, where it describes the suite of programs and utilities that support coding, testing, and deployment: {Modern JavaScript tooling has become increasingly complex}. Tooling can also mean decorative impressions made on leather or bookbindings using heated tools.

A toolkit is a collection of tools kept together for a particular purpose: {a plumber's toolkit}, {a first-aid toolkit}. The word extends naturally to software—a set of programs or functions bundled for developers. Figuratively, a toolkit is any set of resources or skills: {emotional toolkit}, {parenting toolkit}.

Toolkits are collections of tools or resources assembled for a particular purpose. A carpenter's toolkit contains hammers, saws, and screwdrivers. In software, a toolkit is a set of programming components for building applications. The word extends to any curated set of methods or resources: {a toolkit for managing stress}, {a teacher's toolkit for classroom engagement}.

A toolmaker is a skilled craftsman who makes and repairs precision tools, dies, jigs, and fixtures used in manufacturing. The trade requires expertise in metalworking, measurement, and machine operation. More broadly, toolmaker describes any creature that fashions implements: {Early humans were toolmakers long before they developed language}.

Tools are implements used to accomplish tasks—hammers, saws, wrenches, and the like. The meaning extends to anything that serves as a means to an end: {Language is a tool for communication}. Software applications are tools. In slang, a tool is a person easily manipulated or used by others, or someone obnoxiously dim: {Don't be such a tool}.

A toon is an animated cartoon character, especially one from classic animation or video games: {The toons in that movie interact with live actors}. The word emerged from animation industry slang and gaming culture. Toon can also refer to a cartoon itself: {I watched Saturday morning toons as a kid}. In online gaming, toon often means a player's character or avatar.

Toons is informal for cartoons—animated characters or the shows featuring them: {Saturday morning toons}, {classic Looney Toons}. The word carries affection and nostalgia, evoking childhood entertainment. In gaming, a toon is a player's character or avatar: {I'm leveling up my toon}.

Toot is a short blast of sound from a horn, whistle, or similar instrument: {The train gave a toot as it approached the crossing}. To toot is to make such a sound. To {toot your own horn} is to boast or draw attention to your achievements. In slang, a toot can be a snort of cocaine or a drinking spree. On the social media platform Mastodon, a toot is a post—their playful term for what Twitter calls a tweet.

Tooted is the past tense of toot—to make a short sound on a horn, whistle, or similar instrument: {He tooted the car horn twice}. By extension, to toot one's own horn is to boast. In slang, tooted can mean snorted cocaine: {They tooted a few lines at the party}. On the social platform Mastodon, tooted means posted a message, since posts there are called toots.

A tooth is one of the hard, bony structures in the mouth used for biting and chewing. Teeth appear throughout nature and machinery wherever something grips or cuts: the teeth of a {comb}, a {saw}, a {gear}. To have a {sweet tooth} is to crave sugary foods. To fight {tooth and nail} is to struggle fiercely. Something with {teeth} has real power to enforce: {The new regulation has no teeth}.

A toothache is pain in or around a tooth, typically caused by decay, infection, or damage to the tooth or gum. The ache can range from mild sensitivity to severe throbbing. {I couldn't sleep because of my toothache.} Toothache has long been a byword for misery—few pains feel as insistent or distracting.

A toothbrush is a small brush with a handle, used to clean teeth. The bristles are typically nylon, mounted on a head small enough to reach all areas of the mouth. Electric toothbrushes rotate or vibrate the head mechanically. {I need to replace my toothbrush.}

Toothless means lacking teeth, whether literally or figuratively. A toothless {smile} comes from an infant or elderly person who has lost their teeth. A toothless {law} or toothless {regulation} lacks enforcement power—all gums, no bite. {The amendment rendered the bill toothless.}

Toothpaste is a paste or gel applied to a toothbrush for cleaning teeth. It typically contains mild abrasives, fluoride, and flavoring. {I'm out of toothpaste}. Figuratively, something that {can't be put back in the tube} refers to information or actions that can't be undone once released.

A toothpick is a small pointed sliver of wood, plastic, or metal used to remove food particles lodged between teeth. Toothpicks also serve as miniature skewers for hors d'oeuvres or to test whether baked goods are done: {Insert a toothpick—if it comes out clean, the cake is ready}.

Toothpicks are small, pointed sticks used to remove food lodged between teeth. They're typically made of wood, though plastic and metal versions exist. Toothpicks also serve as miniature skewers for appetizers or as tools for applying small amounts of glue or paint. Figuratively, something as thin as a toothpick is extremely slender: {Her legs were like toothpicks}.

Tooting is making short sounds on a horn, whistle, or similar instrument: {a car tooting its horn}, {tooting on a recorder}. The word suggests brief, often cheerful blasts rather than sustained notes. In the phrase {tooting one's own horn}, it means boasting or self-promotion. Tooting also appears as a mild intensifier in expressions like {you're darn tootin'}, meaning emphatically yes.

Toots is an informal, mildly affectionate term of address, typically directed at a woman: {Hey, toots, how's it going?} The word feels dated and can come across as condescending or patronizing, especially from men to women. It occasionally appears in nostalgic or ironic contexts evoking mid-20th-century American speech.

Tootsie is an affectionate term for a person, especially a woman or child, similar to sweetie or honey: {Hey, tootsie, come give me a hug}. The word has a slightly dated, playful quality. Tootsies, in the plural, is baby talk or informal speech for toes or feet: {My little tootsies are freezing}. (Capitalized Tootsie is a trademark for candy or refers to the film.)

Tootsies is an affectionate or playful term for toes or feet, used especially when speaking to or about children: {Wiggle your tootsies}. Adults use it humorously to refer to their own feet: {My tootsies are freezing}. The singular tootsie can also be a term of endearment for a person, though this sounds dated.

As a noun or quasi-adjective, top has the connotation of being highest, uppermost, and the opposite of bottom. The use of top with physical things (top of the building) is extended to abstract things to mean most important or prominent (top of the charts, the top earner). Though infrequently applied in temporal contexts, top usually means first: the top of the fourth inning. This cluster of meanings is carried over to the verb top, whose most frequent meaning is be at the top: The song topped the charts for twenty weeks. With physical things, top can mean add or remove a lid or cover.

Topaz is a hard, transparent gemstone, typically yellow or amber but occurring in other colors including blue, pink, and colorless. It ranks 8 on the Mohs hardness scale, making it suitable for jewelry. Topaz is the traditional birthstone for November: {She wore her grandmother's topaz ring}. The word also names the yellowish-brown color of the classic stone.

A topcoat is an outer coat worn over other clothing for warmth or weather protection—heavier than a jacket but typically lighter than an overcoat: {He grabbed his topcoat on the way out}. In painting and finishing, a topcoat is the final layer applied over primer or base coats: {Let the topcoat dry completely before handling}.

A tophat is a tall, flat-crowned formal hat with a narrow brim, traditionally made of silk or beaver felt. Once standard formal wear for men, it now appears mainly at ceremonial occasions like weddings and horse races, or as a symbol of old-fashioned elegance and wealth. Also spelled top hat.

Tophats is the plural of tophat, a tall cylindrical hat with a flat top and narrow brim, traditionally made of silk or beaver felt. Once standard formal wear for men, tophats now appear mainly at ceremonial occasions, in period costumes, or as symbols of old-fashioned elegance and wealth: {The magician pulled a rabbit from his tophat}. Also spelled top hats.

Topheavy describes something with too much weight or bulk at the top relative to its base, making it unstable or prone to tipping: {The bookshelf was topheavy and wobbled dangerously}. The term extends to organizations with too many executives relative to workers, or to women with disproportionately large breasts. Also spelled top-heavy.

Topiaries are shrubs or trees trimmed into ornamental shapes—geometric forms, animals, spirals. The art requires patience; a topiary garden takes years to develop. The word can also refer to the practice itself: {She studied topiary at the botanical institute}. {The estate's topiaries included peacocks and chess pieces}.

Topiary is the art of trimming shrubs and trees into ornamental shapes—geometric forms, animals, spirals. The word also refers to the shaped plants themselves: {The garden featured elaborate topiary}. As an adjective, it describes this style of gardening: {topiary hedges}, {topiary animals}.

A topic is a subject of discussion, study, or conversation: {What's the topic of your essay?} Any matter that people consider or talk about is a topic. A topic can be broad or narrow, serious or trivial. Something {off topic} strays from the subject at hand. {Hot topic} suggests a matter of current interest or controversy.

Topical describes something relating to current events or matters of immediate interest: {a topical debate}, {topical humor}. News and commentary are topical when they address what's happening now. In medicine, topical means applied to a specific area of the body surface rather than taken internally: {topical ointment}, {topical anesthetic}. The two senses share the idea of something localized—to a moment or a place.

Topics are subjects of discussion, study, or writing—the specific matters being addressed. A conversation has topics; a research paper has a topic; a meeting agenda lists topics. The word often implies discrete, bounded areas of focus: {We covered several topics in today's class}. {Let's change the topic.} In online contexts, topics organize forum threads or content categories.

A topknot is a knot or tuft of hair worn at the crown of the head. The style appears across cultures and eras—from traditional Japanese coiffures to the contemporary man bun. Topknot also refers to a crest of feathers on a bird's head: {The cockatoo raised its topknot}.

Topless describes a woman whose breasts are exposed, or a place where such exposure occurs: {a topless beach}, {topless dancers}. The word applies almost exclusively to women—a shirtless man is rarely called topless. Topless also describes things lacking a top: {a topless convertible}, {a topless tower}.

Topline refers to the highest or most important level of something. In business, the topline is gross revenue before any deductions—the first line on an income statement: {We need to grow the topline before worrying about margins}. As an adjective, topline means premier or most significant: {topline talent}, {topline results}. To topline is to headline or be the main attraction: {She toplined the Vegas show for three years}.

Topography is the physical features of a land area—its hills, valleys, rivers, and elevations—or the study and mapping of such features. A region's topography determines where roads can be built and water will flow. The term extends to any detailed description of surface features: {the topography of the brain}, {the political topography of the region}.

Topped describes something with a covering, addition, or finishing element on its surface: {a sundae topped with whipped cream}, {mountains topped with snow}. It also means surpassed or exceeded: {Last year's sales figures can't be topped}. In British slang, to top oneself is to commit suicide, making topped a past tense for that grim act.

A topper is something that goes on top. A hat is a topper. A decorative piece crowning a cake or Christmas tree is a topper. In casual speech, a topper is something that surpasses what came before—a joke funnier than the last, a story more outrageous: {Just when I thought he couldn't top that, he had another topper}. A top hat may also be called a topper.
clues: What sits at the very peak

definition: Topping is something placed on top of food—cheese on pizza, whipped cream on pie, sprinkles on ice cream: {What toppings do you want on your burger?} In British usage, topping is an old-fashioned adjective meaning excellent or first-rate. To top something is to surpass it, so a topping performance outdoes others.

Toppings are items added on top of a base food—cheese on pizza, sprinkles on ice cream, croutons on salad. The word almost always appears in plural: {What toppings do you want on your burger?} A topping bar lets customers customize their own.

Topple means to fall over or cause to fall, typically from an upright position: {The statue toppled into the square}. The word suggests instability—something top-heavy losing its balance. Figuratively, topple describes the overthrow of those in power: {The revolution toppled the government}. What topples usually seemed secure before it fell.

Toppled is the past tense of topple, meaning to fall or cause to fall from an upright position: {The statue toppled during the earthquake}, {Protesters toppled the monument}. Extended to power structures, topple means to overthrow or bring down: {The scandal toppled the government}, {A coup toppled the regime}.

Topples is the third-person singular of topple, meaning to fall or cause to fall from an upright position, usually by becoming top-heavy or unbalanced: {The stack of books topples over}. Extended to power structures, topples means to overthrow or bring down: {The revolution topples the regime}. What topples doesn't just fall—it tips, loses balance, comes down from a height.

Toppling is the act of falling or causing to fall, usually from an upright position. A stack of books topples when bumped; a statue is toppled by protesters. The word often describes the overthrow of those in power: {the toppling of the regime}, {toppling the dictator}. What topples was typically standing or dominant before its fall.

Tops are the uppermost parts or highest points of things: {mountain tops}, {treetops}, {the top of the page}. A top is also a garment covering the upper body: {She bought three new tops}. In the plural, tops can mean the best or most excellent: {This restaurant is tops}. At tops, something reaches its maximum: {The job will take two hours, tops}. In BDSM contexts, tops are the dominant partners. A spinning top is a toy that rotates on a pointed base. To top something is to exceed or surpass it, or to put something on top: {topped with whipped cream}. (Capitalized Tops may be a brand name or proper noun.)

Topside refers to the upper surface or deck of a ship, as opposed to below deck: {The captain ordered all hands topside}. More broadly, it means the upper part or top of anything: {the topside of the roast}. In British English, topside is also a lean cut of beef from the thigh. As an adverb, it means on or toward the top: {Let's head topside}.

Topsoil is the uppermost layer of soil, typically the top few inches, where most plant roots grow and organic matter concentrates. It's darker and richer than the subsoil beneath it. Gardeners buy topsoil to improve planting beds: {We spread fresh topsoil before laying the sod}. Erosion and construction can strip away topsoil, leaving less fertile ground.

Topspin is forward rotation applied to a ball, causing it to dip faster and bounce higher than it otherwise would. In tennis, table tennis, and other racket sports, players use topspin to keep aggressive shots in play while making returns more difficult for opponents. The ball is struck with an upward brushing motion that sets it spinning forward. {She hit a heavy topspin forehand that kicked up off the court.}

Topsyturvy means upside down or in complete disorder—everything reversed from its proper position. A room left topsyturvy has been thoroughly ransacked or chaotically rearranged. The word extends to abstract confusion: {The news turned my world topsyturvy}. Often hyphenated as topsy-turvy.

A toque is a close-fitting brimless hat. In North America, the word has two distinct uses: in Canada, a toque (also spelled tuque) is a knitted winter cap, often with a pompom: {Don't forget your toque, it's freezing out}. In professional kitchens, a toque is the tall white hat worn by chefs.

A torch is a handheld light source—originally a burning stick or bundle of materials, now typically a battery-powered flashlight in British English. Americans say flashlight; Brits say torch. A blowtorch produces a hot flame for welding or cutting. To torch something is to set it on fire, often deliberately: {Rioters torched the building}. To {carry a torch} for someone is to harbor unrequited love.

A torchbearer carries a torch, literally or figuratively. The term evokes ceremonial processions—Olympic torchbearers relay the flame from Greece to the host city. More often, torchbearer describes someone who leads or champions a cause, movement, or tradition: {She became the torchbearer for criminal justice reform}. The image suggests carrying light forward through darkness.

Torchbearers are people who carry torches, whether literally in ceremonies and processions or figuratively as carriers of tradition, knowledge, or a cause. The torch suggests something that must be kept alive and passed on: {She became one of the torchbearers of the civil rights movement}. Athletes who carry the Olympic flame are torchbearers in both senses.

Torched is the past tense of torch, meaning to set fire to something deliberately: {Someone torched the abandoned warehouse}. The word often implies arson or intentional destruction. Informally, torched can mean defeated badly or criticized harshly: {The critics torched his new film}.

Torches is the plural of torch—a portable light source, traditionally a burning stick or bundle, now often a battery-powered flashlight (the standard British term). People carry torches through darkness, and mobs carry them to express menace. To {carry a torch} for someone is to maintain unrequited love. {The villagers grabbed torches and pitchforks.}

Torching is the act of setting something on fire, usually deliberately: {The torching of the warehouse was ruled arson}. It can describe controlled burning or criminal destruction. Figuratively, torching means to criticize harshly or destroy completely: {Critics are torching the new policy}.

Torchlight is the light cast by a torch—whether a flaming brand or a flashlight. The word evokes searching in darkness: {They made their way by torchlight through the cave}. A torchlight {procession} or {parade} features participants carrying flames, often for ceremony or protest.

Tore is the past tense of tear, meaning to rip or pull apart: {She tore the letter in half}. It extends to moving with force or speed: {He tore down the street}. To be {torn} between options is to feel pulled in opposite directions.

A toreador is a bullfighter, particularly one who fights on horseback or plays a prominent role in the spectacle. The word comes from Spanish and appears frequently in opera, literature, and figurative use: {He entered the boardroom with the swagger of a toreador}. In technical bullfighting terminology, matador is more precise for the principal fighter who kills the bull, but toreador remains common in English for any bullfighter.

A torii is a traditional Japanese gate marking the entrance to a Shinto shrine. The structure typically consists of two upright pillars topped by two horizontal crossbars, often painted vermilion. Torii mark the transition from ordinary space to sacred ground: {We passed through the torii and entered the shrine complex}. The plural is torii or toriis.

Torment is intense suffering—physical pain or mental anguish that persists and gnaws. The noun emphasizes prolonged distress: {the torment of chronic illness}, {the torments of jealousy}. As a verb, to torment is to inflict such suffering or to harass persistently: {Stop tormenting your sister}. Children torment each other; guilt torments the conscience. A tormentor is one who causes such suffering.

Tormented describes someone suffering intense anguish—physical, mental, or emotional. A tormented {soul} is wracked by inner demons; a tormented {artist} channels pain into creation. The word suggests ongoing distress rather than a single moment of pain: {He was tormented by guilt for years}. To be tormented is also to be harassed or plagued: {tormented by mosquitoes}, {tormented by doubts}.

Tormenting describes causing severe physical or mental suffering, or the state of being subjected to it. A tormenting {memory} won't leave you alone. A tormenting {itch} demands attention. The word suggests persistent, nagging distress rather than a single blow: {The tormenting uncertainty of waiting for test results kept her awake}.

A tormentor is someone who inflicts suffering on another—physical pain, psychological cruelty, or persistent harassment: {The bully became her daily tormentor}. The word implies ongoing or repeated torment rather than a single act. In theater, tormentors are the curtains or flats at the sides of a stage that mask the wings from the audience.

Tormentors are people or things that cause prolonged suffering or anguish. The word typically describes those who inflict pain deliberately and repeatedly: {She finally confronted her childhood tormentors}. In theater, tormentors are the curtains or flats at either side of a stage, masking the wings from the audience.

Torments are sources of severe suffering or anguish, whether physical or mental: {the torments of chronic pain}, {the torments of jealousy}. The word suggests ongoing affliction rather than a single moment of pain. To torment is to inflict such suffering, or to tease and annoy persistently: {Stop tormenting your sister}.

Torn is the past participle of tear, describing something that has been ripped or pulled apart: {a torn shirt}, {torn pages}. Figuratively, torn describes emotional conflict—being pulled in opposing directions: {I'm torn between staying and leaving}. A country can be {torn apart by war}, a family {torn by disagreement}.

A tornado is a violently rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm to the ground, forming a distinctive funnel shape. Tornadoes can destroy buildings, uproot trees, and hurl debris at deadly speeds. The word extends to any similarly destructive force: {She tore through the office like a tornado}. Tornado Alley refers to the central United States where tornadoes are most frequent.

Tornadoes is the plural of tornado—a violently rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm to the ground. Tornadoes form when warm, moist air meets cold, dry air, creating powerful updrafts that can spin into funnel clouds. They range from brief, weak twisters to devastating storms that level entire neighborhoods: {The tornadoes that struck the Midwest left thousands homeless}.

Tornados is a plural of tornado, a violently rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm to the ground. Tornadoes form most frequently in the central United States, where warm and cold air masses collide: {Tornados touched down across three counties}. The spelling tornadoes is more common, but both are standard.

A torpedo is a self-propelled underwater missile designed to detonate on impact with a ship or submarine. The weapon revolutionized naval warfare by allowing smaller vessels to threaten larger warships. Extended uses include the torpedo sandwich (a long submarine-style sandwich) and the verb meaning to deliberately sabotage or destroy something: {The scandal torpedoed his chances at reelection}. In older usage, torpedo referred to electric rays that stun prey, which inspired the weapon's name.

Torpedoed means struck or sunk by a torpedo—an underwater explosive projectile: {The submarine torpedoed the cargo ship}. Figuratively, to torpedo something is to destroy or sabotage it decisively: {The scandal torpedoed his campaign}, {Budget cuts torpedoed the project}. The metaphor emphasizes sudden, devastating destruction of plans or efforts.

Torpedoes is the plural of torpedo, a self-propelled underwater weapon designed to detonate on contact with a target: {The submarine fired torpedoes at the convoy}. The verb form means to destroy or wreck, literally or figuratively: {The scandal torpedoed his campaign}. A torpedo can also be a submarine sandwich in some regional American usage.

Torpedoing is attacking or destroying with a torpedo—the self-propelled underwater explosive. More often, the word appears figuratively: to torpedo something is to sabotage or deliberately wreck it. {The senator torpedoed the bill with last-minute amendments.} {His outburst torpedoed any chance of reconciliation.}

Torpedo is a noun that can also be used as a verb, mainly in the context of a plan or idea to mean cause to fail. The noun torpedo can mean different things that all have in common some aspect of danger. The earliest usage of torpedo is for a kind of fish that produces an electric current in its body. Later, torpedo was used to designate an explosive device for naval warfare. Finally, a torpedo is a cigar that is pointed at one end.

Torpor is a state of sluggishness or inactivity, physical or mental. Someone in torpor lacks energy or motivation: {The summer heat induced a pleasant torpor}. In biology, torpor is a controlled reduction in metabolic activity—what hibernating animals enter to conserve energy. Figuratively, torpor describes institutional or social stagnation: {The company had fallen into bureaucratic torpor}.

Torque is rotational force—the twisting power that causes something to spin around an axis. In physics and engineering, torque measures how effectively a force produces rotation: {The engine delivers impressive torque at low RPMs}. A wrench applies torque to a bolt; a car's torque determines acceleration. The verb means to apply such force: {Don't torque it too tight or you'll strip the threads}.

Torqued means twisted or rotated with force, from the physics term for rotational force. A mechanic torques bolts to specification. Extended to emotional states, torqued means angry or agitated: {He was really torqued about the parking ticket}. In bodybuilding and fitness, a torqued position involves rotational tension: {Keep your spine torqued through the movement}.

Torquing is applying rotational force, especially when tightening bolts or fasteners to a specific tension: {Make sure you're torquing the lug nuts to spec}. Mechanics and engineers torque components to precise measurements using a torque wrench. Informally, torquing can mean twisting or wrenching something with force.

A torrent is a violent, rushing stream of water—the kind that appears during heavy rain or snowmelt. The word extends to any overwhelming flow: {a torrent of abuse}, {a torrent of emails}. In computing, a torrent is a file shared through peer-to-peer networks, downloaded in fragments from multiple sources simultaneously: {I downloaded the album as a torrent}.

Torrential describes rain or water that falls in overwhelming quantities, as from a torrent—a violent, rushing stream. A torrential downpour doesn't just rain; it pours with such force that visibility drops and streets flood within minutes. The word extends to anything that comes in an overwhelming rush: {a torrential outpouring of grief}, {torrential abuse on social media}.

Torrenting is downloading files using BitTorrent protocol, which distributes data across many users rather than from a single server. Each downloader simultaneously uploads pieces to others, making large files transfer efficiently. The term often implies pirating copyrighted content—movies, music, software—though the technology itself is neutral: {I spent the weekend torrenting the entire series}.

Torrents are rushing streams of water, especially violent ones caused by heavy rain: {Torrents poured down the mountainside}. The word extends to any overwhelming flow: a torrent of {abuse}, a torrent of {words}. In computing, torrents are files shared through BitTorrent protocol, which distributes data across many users: {I downloaded the album from torrents}.

Torrid means intensely hot, either literally or figuratively. A torrid climate is scorching and dry. More commonly, torrid describes passionate intensity: a torrid {love affair}, a torrid {romance}. In sports, a torrid {streak} or torrid {pace} suggests exceptional, heated performance: {The team went on a torrid run through the playoffs}.

The torso is the trunk of the human body—everything except the head, arms, and legs. In art, a torso is a sculpture of a body without limbs or head, whether by design or because the original broke: {the torso of Apollo}. The word extends to anything truncated or incomplete: {the torso of an unfinished novel}.

Torsos is the plural of torso, the trunk of the human body—everything from shoulders to hips, excluding head, arms, and legs. The word often appears in contexts involving anatomy, sculpture, or violence: {The museum displayed classical torsos}. A torso can also be any incomplete or fragmentary work.

A tort is a wrongful act that causes harm to someone, for which the injured party can sue for damages. Unlike crimes, which are prosecuted by the state, torts are civil matters between private parties. Common torts include negligence, defamation, and trespass: {The company faced a tort claim after the accident}. Tort law forms the basis of most personal injury litigation.

A torte is a rich, dense cake, typically made with ground nuts or breadcrumbs instead of flour and layered with cream, jam, or ganache. European in origin, tortes are often more elaborate than standard cakes: {a Sachertorte from Vienna}, {a chocolate hazelnut torte}. The word is sometimes used loosely for any fancy layered cake.

Tortellini are small ring-shaped pasta filled with meat, cheese, or vegetables, folded and pinched to form a distinctive navel-like shape. They originate from the Emilia-Romagna region of Italy and are typically served in broth or with cream sauce: {We ordered the tortellini in brodo}. Smaller than tortelloni, which use the same folding technique but come with different fillings.

Tortelloni are large ring-shaped pasta, folded and pinched to form a distinctive navel or hat shape. They are the bigger sibling of tortellini, typically stuffed with cheese, spinach, or meat fillings: {The tortelloni came in a light butter and sage sauce}. Like other filled pastas, they're served in broth or with sauce rather than baked.

Tortes is the plural of torte, a rich cake typically made with ground nuts or breadcrumbs instead of flour and layered with cream, jam, or ganache. European in origin, tortes tend to be denser than American layer cakes: {The bakery displayed chocolate tortes and fruit tortes in the window}.

A tortilla is a thin, flat round of unleavened bread, fundamental to Mexican and Central American cuisine. Corn tortillas are the traditional form; flour tortillas became common in northern Mexico and the American Southwest. Tortillas wrap fillings in tacos, burritos, and enchiladas, or accompany meals as bread. In Spain, a tortilla is something different: a thick omelet typically made with potatoes and onions.

Tortillas are thin, round flatbreads fundamental to Mexican and Central American cuisine. Corn tortillas are made from masa (nixtamalized corn dough); flour tortillas use wheat flour and are more common in northern Mexico and Tex-Mex cooking. Tortillas wrap tacos, burritos, and enchiladas, or accompany meals as edible utensils: {She scooped up beans with a warm tortilla}.

A tortoise is a land-dwelling reptile with a high-domed shell, into which it can retract its head and legs for protection. Tortoises are known for their slow, deliberate movement and exceptional longevity—some species live well over a century. The word often evokes patience or persistence: {slow and steady wins the race}, from Aesop's fable of the tortoise and the hare.

Tortoises is the plural of tortoise, a land-dwelling reptile with a high-domed shell and sturdy, column-like legs. Unlike their aquatic relatives the turtles, tortoises live entirely on land and move slowly—hence the fable of the tortoise and the hare. {The Galápagos tortoises can live over a hundred years.} Some speakers use tortoise and turtle interchangeably, though technically tortoises are a subset.

Tortoiseshell is a mottled pattern of brown, amber, and black, originally from the shell of hawksbill sea turtles, historically used for decorative objects like combs and eyeglass frames. Now the term mostly describes cats with this coloring—nearly always female due to genetics—or anything imitating the pattern: {tortoiseshell glasses}, {a tortoiseshell cat}. Also spelled tortoise-shell.

Torture is the deliberate infliction of severe pain or suffering, typically to extract information, punish, or intimidate. Governments torture prisoners; captors torture hostages. The word extends to intense mental anguish: {Waiting for the test results was torture}. As a verb, to torture someone is to subject them to such treatment. Figuratively, anything agonizingly unpleasant may be called torture: {That movie was absolute torture}.

Tortured describes someone who has been subjected to torture, or something marked by intense suffering: {a tortured prisoner}, {a tortured expression}. Extended uses suggest painful strain or excessive complexity: {tortured logic}, {a tortured metaphor}. A tortured artist or soul suffers inner anguish, often romantically portrayed as fuel for creativity.

A torturer is a person who inflicts severe pain on others, typically to extract information, punish, or terrorize. The term applies both to those who torture professionally—interrogators, executioners—and to anyone who causes extreme suffering: {The regime's torturers operated in secret prisons}. Figuratively, anything that causes prolonged anguish can be called a torturer: {Insomnia was his nightly torturer}.

Tortures is the plural of torture—instances of inflicting severe pain as punishment, coercion, or cruelty: {The tortures of the Inquisition are well documented}. As a verb, tortures means causes extreme suffering: {The uncertainty tortures him}. Extended uses cover any source of anguish: {the tortures of unrequited love}, {the tortures of a guilty conscience}.

Torturing is the present participle of torture—inflicting severe pain or suffering, typically to extract information, punish, or terrorize. The word extends to causing intense mental anguish: {Stop torturing yourself over what you said}. It also describes prolonged frustration or anticipation: {The suspense was torturing me}.

Torturous describes something that inflicts or involves torture—extreme pain or suffering: {a torturous interrogation}, {torturous back pain}. By extension, anything agonizingly slow, difficult, or unpleasant qualifies: {a torturous commute}, {torturous negotiations}. Often confused with tortuous, which means winding or complex rather than painful.

Toss means to throw something lightly or casually, often with an upward or sideways motion: {She tossed her keys on the counter}. You can toss a salad by mixing it, toss and turn in bed when you can't sleep, or toss back a drink by downing it quickly. To toss something out is to discard it. A coin toss decides matters by chance. In British slang, if you don't give a toss, you don't care at all, and a tosser is a contemptible person.

Tossed is the past tense of toss, meaning thrown lightly or casually: {He tossed the keys onto the counter}. A tossed salad has been mixed by lifting and turning the ingredients. To have {tossed and turned} is to have slept restlessly. In British slang, tossed off means masturbated.

Tosser is British slang for a contemptible or pathetic person. The word derives from toss, British slang for masturbate ({toss off}), making tosser literally "one who masturbates"—roughly equivalent to wanker: {Don't be such a tosser}. {That tosser cut me off in traffic}. The insult implies someone useless and self-absorbed. Less familiar to Americans.

Tossers is the plural of tosser, British slang for contemptible or pathetic people. From toss off (masturbate), it suggests people too busy pleasuring themselves to be useful: {The tossers in management have no idea what's happening}.

A tossup is a situation where either outcome is equally likely—too close to call. The term comes from flipping a coin, where heads or tails have equal chances: {The election is a tossup}. In quiz competitions, a tossup is a question either team can answer first. Also spelled toss-up.

A tostada is a Mexican dish consisting of a flat, crispy fried or toasted tortilla topped with various ingredients—typically refried beans, meat, lettuce, cheese, and salsa. The word is Spanish for "toasted." Unlike tacos, tostadas are eaten flat rather than folded: {I ordered two chicken tostadas and a horchata}.

Tostadas are a Mexican dish consisting of flat, crispy fried or toasted tortillas topped with various ingredients—typically beans, meat, lettuce, cheese, and salsa. The word is Spanish for "toasted." A single tortilla prepared this way is a tostada: {I'll have two tostadas and a side of rice}.

Tostones are twice-fried plantain slices, a staple of Caribbean and Latin American cuisine. Green plantains are sliced, fried until soft, flattened, then fried again until crispy. They're typically served as a side dish or snack, salted and sometimes accompanied by garlic sauce or mojo: {We ordered tostones with our rice and beans}.

A tot is a very young child, typically a toddler: {The tots played in the sandbox}. The word also means a small amount, especially of liquor: {a tot of rum}. To tot up is to add figures together: {Let me tot up the bill}.

Total emphasizes completeness or entirety—the whole amount with nothing left out. A total of the numbers is their sum. Total {silence} is absolute silence. A car that's totaled is damaged beyond economical repair: {The crash totaled his truck}. To total something up is to add it: {Let me total the bill}. {A total stranger} is someone completely unknown to you.

Totaled means destroyed beyond practical repair. A car is totaled when the cost to fix it exceeds its value—the insurance company writes it off as a total loss: {Some drunk driver totaled my Honda}. The word applies to any vehicle or object wrecked completely. Separately, totaled is the past tense of total, meaning added up: {I totaled the receipts}.

Totalitarian describes a political system in which the state holds absolute authority over all aspects of public and private life. A totalitarian regime typically features one-party rule, suppression of dissent, state-controlled media, and intrusive surveillance: {totalitarian governments}, {totalitarian control}. The noun totalitarianism names this system of governance. The word emerged in the twentieth century to describe fascist and communist states.

Totalitarianism is a system of government that demands complete control over public and private life, permitting no opposition or independent institutions. The state regulates everything—economy, education, media, family—and typically enforces conformity through surveillance and terror. The term emerged in the twentieth century to describe regimes like Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia: {Totalitarianism crushes individual liberty in the name of the collective}. Distinguished from mere authoritarianism by its ambition to reshape society entirely rather than simply maintain power.

Totalitarians are people who support or practice totalitarianism—a system of government that demands complete control over public and private life, tolerating no opposition. The word usually carries condemnation: {The totalitarians crushed all dissent}. It applies to both rulers who impose such systems and citizens who embrace them.

Totality is the state of being complete or whole—everything included, nothing left out. {The totality of the evidence points to his guilt.} In astronomy, totality is the phase of an eclipse when one celestial body completely obscures another: {We drove six hours to witness two minutes of totality.}

Totalled is the British spelling of totaled. It means added up to a sum: {The bill totalled £47.50}. In informal use, especially American, to total a vehicle is to wreck it beyond economical repair—the repair cost totals more than the car's value. {He totalled his dad's car last weekend.}

Totally means completely or entirely: {I totally forgot about the meeting}. In casual speech, it serves as enthusiastic agreement or emphasis: {Are you coming? —Totally!} This emphatic use, especially common among younger speakers, can intensify almost any statement: {That's totally unfair}. The word sometimes carries a Valley Girl association, though it's thoroughly mainstream.

Tote is both a verb and a noun centered on carrying. To tote something is to carry it, especially something bulky or heavy: {She toted her laptop everywhere}. A tote or tote bag is a large, open-topped bag with handles, typically used for carrying everyday items like groceries or books. The word has an informal, practical feel and appears frequently in compounds like {gun-toting} to describe someone who habitually carries a firearm.

A totem is an object—typically an animal or plant—serving as a spiritual emblem for a group, especially among Indigenous peoples of North America. The totem represents ancestral connection and identity. A totem pole is a carved wooden column depicting such figures. Figuratively, anything symbolizing a group's identity or values: {Homeownership became a totem of the American dream}.

Totems are objects—typically animals or plants—that serve as spiritual symbols or emblems for a group, clan, or individual. In Indigenous North American cultures, a totem represents ancestral connection and may be carved into a totem pole. More broadly, totem describes anything treated as a sacred emblem or symbolic representation: {The company logo became a totem of corporate identity}. A personal totem might be an animal one feels spiritually connected to.

Toting is carrying something, usually something substantial or cumbersome: {toting a rifle}, {toting groceries}, {toting a heavy bag through the airport}. The word has a rural or informal flavor. Gun-toting describes someone who carries firearms, often with connotations of readiness for conflict.
clues: Schlepping something from place to place

definition: Tots are very young children, roughly toddler age—old enough to walk but still small: {The playground was full of tots}. The word is informal and affectionate. Tots also names small pieces of something, especially tater tots—fried cylinders of shredded potato: {We ordered tots with our burgers}. As a verb, tot means to add up, usually with "up": {Let me tot up the bill}.

Totter means to move unsteadily, as if about to fall. A toddler totters across the room; an elderly person totters down the stairs. The word suggests weakness, imbalance, or the fragility of age. Figuratively, institutions or systems can totter: {The regime tottered on the brink of collapse}. A totter is an unsteady gait or movement.

Tottering describes unsteady, wobbling movement that suggests imminent collapse. A toddler totters on new legs; an elderly person totters with a cane. The word extends to unstable situations: {a tottering regime}, {a tottering economy}. Something that totters sways precariously but hasn't fallen yet.

A toucan is a tropical American bird with brilliantly colored plumage and an enormous, lightweight bill that can be as long as its body. Toucans live in rainforest canopies and nest in tree hollows. The oversized bill, despite its cartoonish appearance, helps the bird reach fruit on branches too thin to support its weight.

Toucans are tropical American birds known for their enormous, brightly colored bills. Despite their size, the bills are lightweight and help regulate body temperature. Toucans eat mainly fruit and nest in tree cavities. Their distinctive appearance makes them popular in zoos and advertising: {A toucan mascot has sold breakfast cereal for decades}.

Touch has mainly to do with physical sensations that arise because of our sensitive nerve endings. The sense of touch enables us to feel these. When you touch someone or something (literally), a part of your body, usually a hand or finger, contacts them. To touch someone figuratively is to affect their emotions, usually in a positive way. When physical objects touch, they are in contact with each other. A touch can also be a small thing you do to improve something: The scratch in the wood needs a touch up.

A touchback in American football occurs when the ball becomes dead behind a team's own goal line after being put there by the opposing team—typically on a kickoff or punt that lands in the end zone. The receiving team gets the ball at a designated yard line (usually the 25) without having to return it. {He let the kick sail into the end zone for a touchback.}

A touchdown is a score in American football worth six points, achieved when a player carries or catches the ball in the opponent's end zone. The term comes from rugby, where the ball must literally touch down, though in American football it need only cross the goal line. Extended to any successful completion: {The spacecraft made a safe touchdown on Mars}. In casual speech, touchdown celebrates any win or accomplishment: {Got the promotion—touchdown!}

Touchdowns are scoring plays in American and Canadian football, worth six points, achieved by carrying or catching the ball in the opponent's end zone. The term comes from rugby, where the ball must touch the ground to score—a requirement football dropped but the name kept. Figuratively, a touchdown is any successful completion: {The product launch was a touchdown for the team}.
Touche is an anglicized spelling of touché

Touched describes being emotionally moved or affected: {I was touched by her kindness}. Something that touches you reaches your feelings. Touched also means slightly mentally unstable or eccentric—{touched in the head}—suggesting someone lightly affected by madness. In both senses, touched implies contact with something that leaves a mark, whether tender or troubling.

Touches is the plural of touch—physical contacts or light strokes: {a few touches of the brush completed the portrait}. It also names small additions or modifications: {The room needs a few finishing touches}. Someone who {has the touch} possesses a knack or skill. To say someone is {touched} can mean emotionally moved or slightly crazy.
Touching is a participle that works as a preposition, as is the case with many of its synonyms, such as concerning and regarding.

The touchline is the boundary line running along each side of a soccer or rugby field, marking the edge of play. When the ball crosses the touchline, it goes out of bounds. Coaches and substitutes stand along the touchline during matches: {The manager paced the touchline nervously}.

A touchpad is a flat, touch-sensitive surface that detects finger movement and translates it into cursor motion on a screen. Standard on laptops as an alternative to a mouse: {Use two fingers on the touchpad to scroll}. Touchpads also appear on other devices—game controllers, music equipment, smart home panels.

A touchscreen is a display that responds to finger contact, allowing users to interact directly with what's on screen rather than through a keyboard or mouse. Touchscreens dominate smartphones, tablets, and many ATMs and kiosks. The technology has made swiping, tapping, and pinching standard gestures: {The touchscreen on my phone is cracked but still works}.

Touchscreens are display surfaces that detect and respond to finger contact or stylus input, allowing users to interact directly with what they see rather than through a separate keyboard or mouse. The technology transformed mobile phones and tablets into intuitive devices: {She tapped the touchscreen to select her order}. Touchscreens now appear on everything from ATMs to refrigerators.

A touchstone is a standard by which something is judged or evaluated: {Her first novel remains the touchstone against which her later work is measured}. The word comes from a black stone once used to test gold and silver—rubbing metal against it left a streak that revealed the metal's purity. The figurative sense now dominates: a touchstone is any reliable test or benchmark.

Touchstones are standards by which things are judged or evaluated. The original touchstone was a dark stone used to test gold and silver—rubbing the metal against it revealed its purity by the color of the streak.
