By extension, trumping means outdoing or defeating someone with a superior move or advantage: {His experience trumped her enthusiasm}. To trump up charges or evidence is to fabricate them: {The accusations were trumped up to discredit her}.

Trumps is a card game, or the suit designated to beat all others in such games. A trump card outranks cards of other suits regardless of face value. Figuratively, a trump card is any decisive advantage held in reserve: {She played her trump card and won the negotiation}. To trump is to outdo or defeat: {His offer trumped all the others}. {To come up trumps} (British) is to succeed unexpectedly.

A truncheon is a short, thick stick carried as a weapon, especially by police officers. The term is more common in British English; Americans typically say nightstick or baton. Truncheons are used for striking or subduing: {The officer drew his truncheon}. The word can suggest blunt force or heavy-handed authority.

Truncheons are short, thick clubs carried by police officers, especially in Britain. The word suggests official authority—a truncheon is a sanctioned weapon for crowd control or subduing suspects, distinct from improvised clubs. {The bobby raised his truncheon.} The verb means to strike with one: {Protesters were truncheoned by riot police.}

Trundle means to move slowly and heavily, often with a rolling or rumbling quality: {The cart trundled down the cobblestone street}. It suggests something wheeled or round moving steadily but without speed or grace. A trundle bed is a low bed on casters that slides under a larger bed for storage. To trundle along is to proceed at an unhurried, plodding pace: {We trundled through the day's tasks}.

Trundling is the present participle of trundle, meaning to roll or move along heavily or slowly. A cart trundles down a cobblestone street; a toddler trundles across the room. The word suggests steady but ungainly motion: {The old bus came trundling up the hill}. To trundle off is to depart in this unhurried way.

A trunk is the main stem of a tree, the thick central column from which branches grow. The meaning extends to other central structures: the trunk of the human body is the torso, excluding head and limbs. A trunk is also a large rigid container for storage or travel, and in American English, the rear storage compartment of a car. An elephant's trunk is its long prehensile nose. Trunks are loose shorts worn for swimming or boxing.

Trunks are short pants worn for swimming or boxing, covering the waist to mid-thigh: {He packed his swim trunks for the beach}. The word is always plural for this garment—you don't wear a trunk. Trunks is also the plural of trunk, referring to tree stems, elephant noses, storage chests, or car compartments.

A truss is a physical object that supports another. In construction, trusses are often visible only during the building process because they support from within. A truss on a bridge is more likely to be visible. If you are wearing a truss, it is probably to treat a hernia. To truss something may mean to support it with a truss, but it can also describe binding with a cord, as you truss poultry before roasting.

Trust is confidence that something or someone is reliable and honest. This core meaning gives rise to other meanings, like a charitable trust or investment trust, both of which handle money devoted to charity or investment. Trust may also refer negatively to a cartel, that is, a group of companies that cooperate to limit competition. To trust someone is to judge them dependable and to rely on them. To trust something abstract means that you think it dependable: I’ve learned to trust my instincts.

A trustafarian is a young person from a wealthy background who adopts the lifestyle, appearance, or politics associated with countercultural movements—dreadlocks, bohemian dress, anti-capitalist rhetoric—while being financially supported by family money. The term blends "trust fund" with "Rastafarian," highlighting the contradiction between affected rebellion and actual privilege: {The coffee shop was full of trustafarians talking about fighting the system}.

A trustbuster is someone who works to break up monopolies and large business combinations that stifle competition. The term emerged in early 20th-century America when the federal government began aggressively enforcing antitrust laws, with President Theodore Roosevelt becoming the most famous trustbuster of that era. Today it applies to regulators, politicians, or advocates who pursue legal action against corporations deemed to hold excessive market power. {The trustbusters have their sights set on Big Tech.}

Trustbusting is government action to break up monopolies and large corporate combinations that restrict competition. The term dates to the early twentieth century, when U.S. presidents like Theodore Roosevelt pursued antitrust lawsuits against powerful industrial trusts: {Roosevelt earned his reputation as a trustbuster by taking on Standard Oil}. The word still appears in discussions of corporate regulation and market concentration.

Trusted describes someone or something that has earned confidence through reliability or proven loyalty. A trusted {friend} can be counted on. A trusted {source} provides dependable information. Trusted {advisors} have access others don't. The word implies a track record—trust that has been tested and confirmed rather than merely hoped for.

A trustee is a person or organization legally responsible for managing property or assets on behalf of another. The trustee holds legal title but must act for the beneficiary's benefit, not their own: {The bank serves as trustee for the estate}. Trustees also serve on governing boards of institutions like universities and hospitals: {a board of trustees}, {She was appointed trustee of the foundation}.

Trusting describes someone who readily believes in the goodness or reliability of others. A trusting {child} accepts what adults say. A trusting {nature} makes someone vulnerable to deception. The word often carries a note of naivety—to be too trusting is to be insufficiently guarded: {She was trusting to a fault}.

Trustless describes systems designed so that participants don't need to trust each other or a central authority. The term comes from cryptocurrency and blockchain technology, where transactions are verified by code and consensus rather than institutions: {Bitcoin is trustless—you don't need to trust a bank}. Despite the negative-sounding prefix, trustless is typically positive in this context, implying security through design rather than faith.

Trusts is the verb form meaning to have confidence in someone or something: {She trusts her instincts}, {He trusts you with his life}. As a noun, trusts are legal arrangements where property is held by one party for another's benefit—hence {trust fund}. In business, trusts were combinations of corporations acting as one entity, often to limit competition: {antitrust laws}.

Trustworthiness is the quality of being reliable, honest, and deserving of confidence. Someone with trustworthiness keeps promises, acts with integrity, and can be counted on in difficult situations: {Her trustworthiness made her the obvious choice to manage the estate}. The word applies to people, institutions, and information sources alike.
clues: What makes someone safe to confide in

definition: Trustworthy describes someone or something deserving of confidence—reliable, honest, and unlikely to deceive or fail you. A trustworthy friend keeps secrets. A trustworthy source provides accurate information. {Is he trustworthy enough to handle the money?} The word implies proven dependability, not just good intentions.

Trusty describes something or someone reliable and proven over time: {a trusty steed}, {my trusty old backpack}. The word carries a slight old-fashioned or affectionate quality, often applied to tools, companions, or objects that have served well. As a noun, a trusty is a prisoner granted special privileges for good behavior.

Truth is the the quality of being true, mainly as opposed to false. It is most often an uncountable noun (tell the truth, truth will out), and is typically used with the, implying that for a given situation there is only one truth. When used as a countable noun truth designates a single statement or utterance regarded as being true (we hold these truths to be self-evident). We usually think of truth as being expressed in language, but it is often used with verbs that suggest we can become aware of the truth through any of our senses (uncover the truth, realize the truth). #

A truther is someone who believes an official account of a major event is false and that the "real truth" has been suppressed. The term gained currency with 9/11 truthers, who reject the mainstream explanation of the September 11 attacks. It now applies to various conspiracy adherents: {COVID truthers}, {election truthers}. The label is often pejorative, implying credulity rather than skepticism.

Truthers are people who reject official explanations of major events, believing instead in conspiracy theories—particularly that governments or powerful institutions are hiding the real story. The term gained prominence with 9/11 truthers, who dispute the established account of the 2001 attacks: {The truthers insisted it was an inside job}. The label now extends to other conspiracy movements: COVID truthers, election truthers. Often used dismissively by those outside the movement.

Truthful describes someone who habitually tells the truth or something that accurately represents reality. A truthful {person} doesn't lie; a truthful {account} doesn't distort facts. The word emphasizes character or reliability: {She's always been truthful with me}. Truthful carries more weight than honest—it suggests not just avoiding lies but actively conveying what's true.

Truthfulness is the quality of being honest and accurate in what one says. It suggests a habitual disposition toward truth rather than a single instance: {Her truthfulness made her a trusted witness}. Truthfulness implies sincerity—not just avoiding lies but genuinely representing one's beliefs and knowledge.

Truthiness is the quality of something feeling true, even if it has no basis in fact. The word first appeared in the 19th century but was little used until 2005, when U.S. satirist Stephen Colbert brought it to life again. Colbert defined it as “the truth we want to exist.” Today, it carries a negative connotation, to label a widespread false belief put forward as a convenient truth.
clues: When something feels factual but isn't

definition: Truths is the plural of truth—facts, realities, or statements that accord with what is actual. People speak of {universal truths}, {hard truths}, or {uncomfortable truths}. The word often carries weight beyond mere facts, suggesting deeper or more significant insights: {She told him some truths he didn't want to hear}. To {speak truth to power} uses the singular; to catalog multiple insights requires truths.

Truthy describes something that feels true or seems true without actually being true. The word emerged in American political commentary to characterize claims that appeal to intuition or emotion rather than facts: {It's not true, but it's truthy}. In programming, truthy has a technical meaning: a value that evaluates as true in a boolean context even if it isn't literally true—like a non-empty string or nonzero number.

Try is a frequent word that is difficult to define without referring to its less frequent synonym, attempt. While try can act as both a noun and verb, the noun trial is in fact derived from it and is closely related in meaning. Try can be followed by a noun phrase (try the peaches), a to infinitive (try to sleep), or a gerund (try topping that), with construction suggesting a slightly different sense of the verb.

A tryhard is someone who puts in excessive effort, especially in competitive contexts where others are playing casually. The term is mildly derogatory, suggesting the person cares too much about winning or impressing others: {Don't be such a tryhard, it's just a pickup game}. Common in gaming culture, where it describes players who use every possible advantage in casual matches. Sometimes spelled as two words or hyphenated.

Tryharding is putting excessive effort into winning or succeeding, especially in casual contexts where such intensity seems inappropriate. The term emerged from gaming culture, where a tryhard pursues victory with sweaty determination in matches meant for fun. The word carries mild derision—implying someone cares too much: {Stop tryharding, it's just a friendly match}. It can extend beyond games to any situation where someone's visible effort exceeds the stakes.

Trying describes something that tests your patience, endurance, or composure. A trying {day} is exhausting and difficult to get through. A trying {person} wears on your nerves. {These have been trying times for everyone}. The word captures the sense of being stretched or strained by circumstances.

A tryout is a test of someone's abilities, typically for a spot on a team, a role in a play, or a job: {She has tryouts for the soccer team tomorrow}. The word emphasizes competitive evaluation—multiple candidates trying out for limited positions. As a verb phrase, try out means to test or audition: {He's trying out for the lead role}.

Tryouts are competitive evaluations where people demonstrate their abilities to earn a place on a team, in a cast, or in some selective group. Athletes try out for sports teams; actors try out for roles. The word implies that selection isn't guaranteed—you're being tested against others or against a standard: {Tryouts for the basketball team start Monday}.

Trypophobia is an aversion to clusters of small holes or bumps—honeycombs, lotus seed pods, certain corals, or skin conditions with grouped lesions. The sight triggers discomfort, disgust, or anxiety in those affected. Whether it qualifies as a true phobia is debated, but the visceral reaction is well-documented: {Those images of holes in skin triggered my trypophobia}.

A tryst is a private romantic meeting, especially a secret one between lovers: {They arranged a tryst at a hotel across town}. The word carries connotations of illicit romance or clandestine affairs. As a verb, to tryst is to meet secretly, though this use is rare and literary.

Trysts is the plural of tryst, a secret meeting between lovers: {Their trysts took place in a cheap motel outside of town}. The word carries a romantic or illicit flavor, suggesting assignations that must be hidden. Less commonly, tryst can mean any private appointment, but the romantic sense dominates.

A tsar is a Russian emperor, the title used by rulers of Russia from the 16th century until the 1917 revolution. By extension, tsar refers to anyone with great power or authority over a particular domain: a {drug tsar}, a {manufacturing tsar}. In American government, czar is the more common spelling for appointed officials overseeing specific policy areas. {The president named a new border tsar.}

A tsarina is the empress of Russia—either the wife of a tsar or a woman ruling in her own right. Catherine the Great was the most famous tsarina. The word is sometimes spelled czarina. Figuratively, tsarina can describe any woman wielding absolute authority: {She was the tsarina of the fashion department}.

Tsarist describes things relating to the rule of the tsars, the emperors who governed Russia until the 1917 revolution: {tsarist Russia}, {tsarist policies}. The word often carries connotations of autocratic or repressive governance. Sometimes spelled czarist. (Capitalized Tsarist appears at sentence beginnings but has the same meaning.)

Tsars is the plural of tsar, the title of Russian emperors from the sixteenth century until the 1917 revolution. The word derives from Caesar. Tsar extends to anyone with supreme authority over a domain: a {drug tsar}, a {media tsar}. In American government, czar (the more common spelling in the US) designates officials appointed to coordinate policy: {the border czar}, {the climate czar}.

Tsk is a clicking sound made with the tongue against the roof of the mouth, expressing disapproval, annoyance, or mild rebuke. Often doubled or tripled for emphasis: {Tsk tsk, you should know better}. The spelling attempts to capture a sound that isn't really pronounceable as written—it's more cluck than word.

A tsunami is a series of ocean waves caused by underwater disturbances—typically earthquakes, but also volcanic eruptions or landslides. These waves travel at high speeds across open water, then surge to devastating heights when they reach shallow coastal areas. Figuratively, tsunami describes any overwhelming force or flood: {a tsunami of criticism}, {a tsunami of debt}.

Tsunamis are massive ocean waves triggered by underwater disturbances—earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or landslides. Unlike wind-driven waves, tsunamis move the entire water column, traveling across open ocean at jet speed before piling up catastrophically as they reach shallow coastal waters. {The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed over 200,000 people.} Figuratively, a tsunami is any overwhelming surge: {a tsunami of emails}.

A tub is a wide, open container, typically round and used for holding liquids or washing: {a washtub}, {a tub of ice cream}. A bathtub is often shortened to tub: {I'm going to soak in the tub}. Hot tub names the heated outdoor variety. Tub can describe anything tub-shaped, including boats (often disparagingly): {that old tub}.

A tuba is the largest and lowest-pitched brass instrument, producing deep bass tones through a wide bell and long coiled tubing. The player buzzes their lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece. Tubas anchor brass sections in orchestras and marching bands: {The tuba player lugged his instrument onto the field}.

Tubas is the plural of tuba, the largest and lowest-pitched brass instrument. Tubas form the bass foundation of orchestras and marching bands: {The tubas thundered through the finale}. A tuba player wraps the instrument's coiled tubing around their body, with the bell facing upward or forward.

Tubby describes someone short and somewhat fat, with a rounded belly—like a tub. The word is mildly insulting but often affectionate, especially for children: {He was a tubby little kid}. As a noun, tubby can be a nickname or mild taunt: {Hey, tubby, save some for the rest of us}.

A tube is a hollow cylinder, typically for conveying liquids or gases: {a tube of toothpaste}, {breathing tube}, {test tube}. The London Underground is {the Tube}. In American slang, {the tube} once meant television, from the cathode ray tube. Anatomically, tubes are cylindrical passages: {fallopian tubes}, {bronchial tubes}. To tube is to float down a river on an inflated inner tube.

A tuber is a thickened underground stem or root that stores nutrients for a plant—potatoes and yams are tubers. The word extends to any swollen, fleshy plant structure. In anatomy, a tuber is a rounded projection or swelling, particularly on a bone.

Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection that primarily attacks the lungs, causing coughing, fever, weight loss, and if untreated, death. Once called consumption because patients seemed to waste away, it remains a leading cause of death worldwide despite being largely curable with antibiotics. Abbreviated TB: {She tested positive for TB}.

Tubers are thickened underground plant structures that store nutrients—potatoes and yams being the most familiar examples. They develop from stems or roots and allow plants to survive dormant periods. Unlike bulbs, tubers lack the layered structure of onions. The word sometimes extends loosely to any starchy root vegetable: {a bin of tubers at the farmers market}.

Tubes is the plural of tube—hollow cylindrical structures for containing or conveying something. Beyond physical pipes and containers, tubes has specific slang meanings. {The tubes} can mean television: {What's on the tubes tonight?} In anatomy, {getting your tubes tied} refers to tubal ligation for sterilization. {Down the tubes} means ruined or wasted: {All that work went down the tubes}.

Tubeworms are marine invertebrates that live inside protective tubes they secrete, anchored to rocks, coral, or the ocean floor. The most dramatic species cluster around hydrothermal vents in the deep sea, where they can grow several feet long and survive without sunlight by hosting bacteria that convert chemicals into energy. Smaller varieties encrust ship hulls and pier pilings, sometimes becoming a nuisance. {The dive revealed giant tubeworms swaying near the volcanic vent.}

Tubing is hollow cylindrical material, typically flexible: rubber tubing, plastic tubing, copper tubing. The word also names a recreational activity—floating down a river or being towed behind a boat while sitting in an inflated inner tube: {We went tubing on the Guadalupe River}.

Tubthumping is vigorous, noisy promotion of a cause or viewpoint—the kind of emphatic advocacy that pounds the point home. The image is of someone beating on a tub like a drum to draw attention. A tubthumper engages in such promotion: {He's been tubthumping for tax reform for years}. The term often carries a whiff of self-righteousness or excessive zeal.

Tubular describes something shaped like a tube—hollow and cylindrical: {tubular steel}, {tubular pasta}. In anatomy and biology, tubular structures abound: {tubular glands}, {tubular flowers}. In surfer slang from the 1980s, tubular became an exclamation of enthusiasm, from the tube-shaped curl of a perfect wave: {Totally tubular, dude!} The slang now sounds dated or ironic.

Tuchas is Yiddish-influenced slang for the buttocks: {Get off your tuchas and help me}. The word appears in American English, especially in Jewish communities and regions with Yiddish heritage. It's informal but not vulgar—more playful than crude. Also spelled tuchus, tuchis, or toches.

Tuchus is Yiddish-derived slang for the buttocks: {Get off your tuchus and help me}. The word appears in American English with many spellings—tuchis, tush, tushy—reflecting its oral transmission from Yiddish speakers. It's informal but not vulgar, often used affectionately or humorously.

Tuck means to fold, push, or gather something into a compact or concealed position. You tuck a shirt into pants, tuck blankets around a child, tuck hair behind an ear. To {tuck in} or {tuck into} food is to eat heartily. A tuck is also a fold sewn into fabric to adjust fit, or in diving and gymnastics, a position with knees drawn to the chest. A {tummy tuck} is cosmetic surgery to flatten the abdomen.

Tucked is the past tense of tuck, meaning to fold, push, or secure something into a snug position. You tuck a shirt into your pants, tuck a child into bed, or tuck your legs beneath you. {She tucked the letter into her pocket.} A tucked-away place is hidden or secluded. To be {tuckered out} is to be exhausted.

Tucker means to tire out or exhaust, usually in the passive: {I'm all tuckered out after that hike}. The word is informal and often folksy. A tucker is also a piece of lace or cloth worn around the neck and shoulders, now mainly historical—surviving in the expression {best bib and tucker}, meaning one's finest clothes. (Capitalized Tucker is a surname or given name.)

Tuckered means exhausted or worn out, almost always appearing as {tuckered out}: {The kids were completely tuckered out after the hike}. The word has a folksy, informal quality and often describes physical tiredness from activity rather than mental fatigue. It's especially common when talking about children or after a long day.

Tucking is the act of folding or pushing something into a secure or concealed position: {She was tucking the sheets under the mattress}. Parents tuck children into bed. You might tuck your shirt in or tuck a strand of hair behind your ear. In transgender contexts, tucking refers to concealing male genitalia to create a flatter appearance under clothing.

Tuckus is informal slang for the buttocks, borrowed from Yiddish. The word appears in various spellings—tuchus, tuchis, tokus—all representing the same Yiddish term. It's milder than ass, often used affectionately or humorously: {Get your tuckus off the couch}.

A tuft is a bunch of threads, fibers, hairs, or grass held together at the base and loose at the other end: {a tuft of hair}, {tufts of grass between the paving stones}. As a verb, to tuft means to furnish with tufts or to secure padding by stitching through at intervals, as in tufted upholstery or a tufted mattress.

Tufting is a textile technique where yarn or thread is pushed through a backing fabric to create loops or cut pile, producing textured surfaces like rugs, carpets, and upholstery. The process can be done by hand with a tufting gun or industrially. Tufting also describes decorative buttons or stitches that create the dimpled pattern on mattresses and upholstered furniture: {The tufting on the headboard gave it a classic look}.

Tufts are small clusters or bunches of something soft or flexible—threads, hair, feathers, grass—growing or held together at the base: {tufts of hair poked out from under his cap}, {tufts of grass between the paving stones}. The verb tuft means to form or secure with tufts, as in tufted upholstery where buttons create dimpled patterns. (Capitalized Tufts is the university.)

Tug is a short, sharp pull: {She gave his sleeve a tug}. To tug is to pull with effort or force: {The child tugged at her mother's hand}. A tug is also a powerful boat that pulls or pushes larger vessels—a tugboat. Figuratively, a tug is an emotional pull: {He felt the tug of nostalgia}. A {tug of war} is a contest where two sides pull opposite ends of a rope, or any struggle between competing forces.

A tugboat is a small, powerful boat designed to push or pull larger vessels—guiding ships into harbor, maneuvering barges through channels, or towing disabled craft. Despite their size, tugboats have oversized engines relative to their hulls, giving them exceptional pushing power. {Two tugboats nudged the tanker toward the dock.}

Tugboats are small, powerful boats designed to push or pull larger vessels—guiding ships into harbors, towing barges, or maneuvering cargo vessels through tight spaces. Their strength relative to their size makes them essential in ports and waterways where large ships can't navigate alone: {Tugboats nudged the tanker toward the dock}.

Tugged is the past tense of tug, meaning to pull with effort or force. A tug is sharper and more insistent than a gentle pull: {She tugged at his sleeve to get his attention}. The word suggests resistance—you tug on something that doesn't yield easily: {He tugged the suitcase free from the overhead bin}.

Tugging is pulling with short, sharp movements or sustained effort. A child tugs at a parent's sleeve for attention. A boat tugs a barge. The word often implies resistance or difficulty: {She kept tugging at the stuck drawer}. Figuratively, conflicting desires tug at someone: {Duty and desire were tugging him in opposite directions}.

Tugs is the plural of tug and the third-person singular verb form. A tug is a sharp pull: {She felt tugs on her sleeve}. A tugboat, often shortened to tug, is a powerful vessel that pulls or pushes larger ships. To tug is to pull with effort or persistence: {He tugs at his collar when nervous}. {Heartstrings} are tugged when emotions are stirred.

Tuition is the money paid for instruction, especially at a school or university: {Tuition has risen faster than inflation for decades}. In older or British usage, tuition means the teaching itself rather than its cost: {She received private tuition in mathematics}. The American sense of tuition-as-payment now dominates.

A tuktuk is a small three-wheeled motorized vehicle used as a taxi, common throughout South and Southeast Asia. The name imitates the sputtering sound of its engine. Tuktuks weave through congested streets where cars can't easily navigate: {We hired a tuktuk to get to the temple}. Also spelled tuk-tuk.

A tulip is a spring-flowering bulb plant with cup-shaped blooms on a single stem, cultivated in countless colors and varieties. Native to Central Asia, tulips became famously associated with the Netherlands after sparking speculative mania there in the 1630s. {The tulips are up early this year.} A tulip glass has a curved bowl resembling the flower's shape.

Tulipmania refers to the speculative frenzy in 17th-century Holland when tulip bulb prices soared to extraordinary heights before collapsing. The term now describes any speculative bubble driven by irrational exuberance rather than underlying value: {Critics called the cryptocurrency surge tulipmania 2.0}. Also spelled tulip mania.

Tulips are bulbous flowering plants with cup-shaped blooms on tall stems, typically appearing in spring. Native to Central Asia, they became famously associated with the Netherlands, where "tulip mania" in the 1630s saw single bulbs trading for extraordinary sums. Tulips come in virtually every color and are popular in gardens and as cut flowers: {She planted tulips along the walkway}.

Tulle is a fine, lightweight netting fabric, often made of silk, nylon, or rayon. It appears most commonly in wedding veils, ballet tutus, and formal gowns, where its sheer, delicate quality creates volume without weight: {layers of white tulle cascading from the bodice}. The fabric takes its name from Tulle, a city in France.

Tumble means to fall in an uncontrolled way, often rolling or turning: {She tumbled down the stairs}. The word suggests motion without grace—clothes tumble in a dryer, acrobats tumble deliberately, stock prices tumble suddenly. To {tumble to} something is to grasp it belatedly: {It took me a while to tumble to what she meant}. A tumble is a fall, or informally, a casual sexual encounter: {They had a tumble in the hay}.

Tumbled is the past tense of tumble—to fall, roll, or move in an uncontrolled way: {She tumbled down the stairs}, {The kids tumbled out of the car}. Prices or values tumble when they drop sharply. Tumbled stones have been polished smooth by rotating in a drum with abrasives. To {tumble to} something is to suddenly understand it.

Tumbledown describes buildings or structures in a state of disrepair, ready to collapse or already partly fallen: {a tumbledown cottage at the edge of the property}, {tumbledown walls overtaken by ivy}. The word suggests picturesque neglect rather than dangerous ruin—more charming decay than imminent hazard.

A tumbler is a drinking glass with a flat bottom and no handle or stem, typically used for water or spirits. The name comes from early versions with rounded bottoms that would tumble over if set down—forcing you to finish your drink. A tumbler is also an acrobat who performs flips and somersaults, or the rotating drum of a clothes dryer. In locks, tumblers are the pins or levers that must align for the mechanism to open.

Tumblers are drinking glasses with flat bottoms and no stem or handle—the ordinary glasses most people reach for daily. The name comes from early versions with rounded bottoms that would tumble over if set down, encouraging drinkers to finish their contents. In locks, tumblers are the internal pins or levers that must align correctly for a key to work. Tumblers also names acrobats who perform flips and rolls, tumbling through the air.

Tumbles is the third-person singular of tumble—to fall or roll in an uncontrolled way: {She tumbles out of bed every morning}. Things that tumble move with chaotic motion: {Clothes tumble in the dryer}. Prices tumble when they drop sharply. Tumbles also works as a noun for such falls: {The toddler took a few tumbles learning to walk}.

A tumbleweed is a dried plant that breaks from its roots and rolls across open ground, dispersing seeds as the wind pushes it. Several plant species form tumbleweeds, most iconically in the American West. Figuratively, tumbleweed evokes emptiness or awkward silence—when a joke falls flat, someone might say {nothing but tumbleweeds} to describe the dead air.

Tumbleweeds are dried, bushy plants that break off at the root and are blown across open landscapes by the wind, iconic in depictions of the American West. They symbolize desolation, abandonment, and awkward silence—when someone says {tumbleweeds are rolling by}, they mean a joke fell flat or a situation became uncomfortably quiet. The most common species is Russian thistle, despite its association with American deserts.

Tumbling is the act of falling, rolling, or performing acrobatic movements—somersaults, flips, cartwheels. Gymnasts practice tumbling on mats. Outside athletics, tumbling suggests uncontrolled falling or rapid decline: {Stock prices came tumbling down}. A tumbling stream moves with churning motion over rocks. Hair that tumbles falls loosely and abundantly.

Tummies is the plural of tummy, an informal and affectionate word for stomach or belly. The term belongs to the speech of children and those addressing them: {Do you have a tummy ache?} Adults use it playfully or when being deliberately cute: {too many cookies for our tummies}.

Tummy is a childish or affectionate word for stomach or belly. Adults use it when speaking to children or in casual, playful contexts: {Does your tummy hurt?} {I've got butterflies in my tummy}. The word sounds too informal for medical or serious discussion.

A tumor is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells multiply uncontrollably. Tumors may be benign (noncancerous) or malignant (cancerous and capable of spreading). The word appears in both medical contexts and figurative use: {The corruption was a tumor on the organization}. Also spelled tumour in British English.

Tumors are abnormal growths of tissue in the body. A tumor forms when cells multiply uncontrollably, creating a mass. Tumors may be benign (not cancerous) or malignant (cancerous and capable of spreading). The word often carries alarming connotations: {The doctor found a tumor on the scan}. In figurative use, tumor can describe any unwanted growth or corruption within a system.

A tumour is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells multiply uncontrollably. Tumours may be benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous and capable of spreading). The word appears in medical contexts and everyday speech: {The scan revealed a tumour on her lung}. British spelling; Americans write tumor.

Tumours is the British spelling of tumors—abnormal growths of tissue in the body. A tumour forms when cells multiply uncontrollably, creating a mass that may be benign (harmless) or malignant (cancerous). {The scan revealed a tumour on her kidney.} The word applies both to specific growths and to the condition generally: {tumour growth}, {tumour suppression}.

Tumult is a loud, chaotic disturbance—the uproar of a crowd, the clamor of battle, or any scene of noisy confusion: {The announcement caused a tumult in the courtroom}. It extends to inner turmoil: {a tumult of emotions}. The adjective tumultuous describes things marked by such disorder: {a tumultuous reception}, {tumultuous applause}.

Tumultuous describes something marked by chaos, uproar, or violent agitation. A tumultuous {crowd} surges and roars. A tumultuous {period} in history is full of upheaval and disorder. The word often applies to emotions: a tumultuous {relationship} is stormy and turbulent, marked by intense highs and lows. {The announcement was met with tumultuous applause.}
clues: Like a crowd in angry protest

definition: Tuna are large, fast-swimming ocean fish prized for their meat. The flesh ranges from pale pink to deep red depending on species, and is eaten fresh, canned, or raw in sushi and sashimi. Canned tuna is a kitchen staple: {tuna salad}, {tuna casserole}. Bluefin tuna command extraordinary prices at Japanese fish markets.

Tundra is a vast, flat, treeless arctic region where the subsoil is permanently frozen. The landscape supports only low-growing vegetation—mosses, lichens, and hardy shrubs. Tundra conditions also occur at high altitudes below the tree line. The word extends figuratively to any barren, inhospitable expanse: {The office felt like an emotional tundra}.

Tundras is the plural of tundra, the vast treeless plains of arctic and subarctic regions where the subsoil remains permanently frozen. The landscape supports only low-growing vegetation—mosses, lichens, and hardy shrubs. The word extends to any cold, barren expanse: {The northern tundras stretched endlessly before them}.

A tune is a melody—a sequence of musical notes forming a recognizable piece: {She hummed a familiar tune}. To tune an instrument is to adjust it to proper pitch. To tune a radio or TV is to adjust it to receive a particular station. To {tune in} is to watch or listen; to {tune out} is to stop paying attention. Something {in tune} is at correct pitch or in harmony; {out of tune} is the opposite. To {change your tune} is to shift your attitude or position. {To the tune of} introduces a large sum: {repairs to the tune of ten thousand dollars}.

Tuned describes something adjusted for optimal performance or reception. A tuned instrument produces correct pitches. A tuned radio receives a specific frequency. A tuned engine runs efficiently. {Stay tuned} means keep watching or listening. To be tuned in is to be aware and attentive: {She's really tuned in to office politics}. Tuned out is the opposite—disengaged or ignoring something.

A tuner is a device or person that adjusts something to proper pitch or frequency. A piano tuner adjusts string tension for correct pitch. An electronic tuner helps guitarists tune their instruments. In audio equipment, a tuner is the component that receives radio signals and selects stations: {an AM/FM tuner}. A tuner can also be an aftermarket part that modifies engine performance: {a performance tuner for his truck}.

Tuners are devices or people that adjust pitch or frequency. A piano tuner brings the instrument's strings into proper pitch. An electronic tuner helps guitarists tune by displaying whether notes are sharp or flat. In electronics, a tuner is the component that selects radio or television frequencies: {The old stereo had a separate tuner and amplifier}. Car tuners modify vehicles for better performance.

Tunes is the plural of tune—melodies or songs. Someone who {calls the tunes} controls what happens. To {change your tune} is to shift your position or attitude. {Stay tuned} means keep watching or listening. In informal use, tunes often just means music: {We listened to some tunes on the drive}.

A tuneup is routine maintenance performed on an engine to keep it running smoothly—replacing spark plugs, adjusting timing, checking filters. The term extends to any minor adjustment or preparation: {The team had one last tuneup game before the playoffs}. A tuneup can also mean a brief, easy contest before a more serious one.

Tuneups are routine maintenance procedures to keep something running smoothly. The term originated with automobiles—adjusting the engine, replacing spark plugs and filters—but extends to any system needing periodic optimization: {The piano needs a tuneup}, {I'm going in for my annual tuneup} (a medical checkup). A tuneup can also be a warm-up or practice session before a main event.

Tungsten is a dense metallic element with the highest melting point of any metal, making it essential for high-temperature applications. It forms the filaments in incandescent light bulbs and hardens steel for cutting tools. The element's symbol W comes from its alternate name, wolfram. {Tungsten carbide drill bits can cut through almost anything.}

A tunic is a loose-fitting garment extending to the hips or knees, typically sleeveless or short-sleeved. In ancient Rome and Greece, tunics were basic dress for both sexes. The style persists in various forms: military dress uniforms, clerical vestments, and modern fashion tops worn over pants or leggings. {She paired a belted tunic with skinny jeans.}

Tunics are loose garments extending to the knees or below, typically sleeveless or short-sleeved. The tunic was standard dress in ancient Rome and Greece, worn by both sexes. Modern tunics are women's tops that fall past the waist, often worn over leggings: {She paired a flowy tunic with skinny jeans}.

Tuning is the process of adjusting something to optimal performance. Musicians tune instruments to correct pitch: {The orchestra spent ten minutes tuning before the concert}. Mechanics tune engines for better performance. In broadcasting, tuning means selecting a frequency: {tuning the radio to a different station}. To {tune in} is to watch or listen; to {tune out} is to stop paying attention. {Fine-tuning} involves small, precise adjustments. In machine learning, tuning adjusts model parameters to improve results.

A tunnel is a passage cut through or under an obstacle—earth, rock, or water. Tunnels carry roads, railways, and utilities through mountains and beneath rivers. Animals tunnel through soil. To {tunnel} is to dig such a passage. Figuratively, {tunnel vision} describes narrow focus that excludes peripheral awareness. {Light at the end of the tunnel} suggests hope after difficulty.

A tunneler is someone or something that digs tunnels. The word applies to workers who excavate underground passages, to machines designed for boring through earth or rock, and to animals like moles and gophers that burrow beneath the surface: {The tunnelers broke through to the other side after months of drilling}.

Tunneling is the process of digging or constructing a tunnel—an underground or underwater passage. The word extends to any movement through a confined space: {The mole was tunneling through the garden}. In computing, tunneling sends data through a network by encapsulating it within another protocol, creating a secure pathway. In physics, quantum tunneling describes particles passing through barriers they shouldn't classically be able to penetrate. Also spelled tunnelling.

Tunnelling is the British spelling of tunneling—the act of digging or boring a passage through or under something. Workers engage in tunnelling to create subways, mines, or underground passages. In physics, quantum tunnelling describes particles passing through barriers they classically shouldn't penetrate. Animals tunnel through soil; prisoners tunnel to freedom.

Tunnels are underground or underwater passages, typically constructed for transportation, utilities, or mining. Roads and railways pass through mountain tunnels; subway systems run through urban tunnels. The verb means to dig such a passage: {They tunneled under the prison wall}. Figuratively, to tunnel through something is to work through it with narrow focus: {She tunneled through the paperwork}. Tunnel vision describes this narrowed attention.

Tupelo is a North American tree that grows in swampy areas, known for its soft, light wood and the honey produced from its flowers. {Tupelo honey has a distinctive mild flavor.} The wood resists splitting, making it useful for furniture and crates. (Capitalized Tupelo is a city in Mississippi.)

Tuppence is British for two pence—a tiny sum, now essentially symbolic. The word appears mainly in expressions emphasizing insignificance: {I don't care tuppence what he thinks}. To {put in your tuppence worth} (or {two cents}) is to offer an opinion, often unsolicited. Also spelled twopence.

Tupperware is plastic food storage containers with tight-fitting lids, originally a brand name that became generic. The word often applies to any such containers regardless of manufacturer: {I need some tupperware for these leftovers}. A tupperware party is a home sales gathering where the products are demonstrated and sold. (Capitalized Tupperware is the trademark.)

A turban is a head covering made by winding a long cloth around the head. Turbans are traditional dress in parts of South Asia and the Middle East, and are religiously significant for Sikh men, who wear them to cover uncut hair. The word also describes women's close-fitting hats that resemble wrapped turbans: {She wore a silk turban to the cocktail party}.

Turbans are head coverings made by wrapping a long cloth around the head. They hold religious significance in Sikhism, where they're worn by observant men, and appear in various forms across South Asian, Middle Eastern, and North African cultures. The style of wrapping and fabric often indicates regional origin, religion, or social status. {He adjusted his turban before entering the temple.}

A turbine is a machine that extracts energy from a moving fluid—water, steam, or gas—by directing it against angled blades mounted on a rotating shaft. The spinning shaft drives generators, pumps, or propellers. Turbines power hydroelectric dams, jet engines, and wind farms: {The wind turbine's blades turned slowly in the breeze}.

Turbines are machines that extract energy from moving fluid—water, steam, or gas—by channeling it through a wheel of angled blades. The fluid pushes the blades, spinning a shaft that drives generators or other machinery. Turbines power most electricity generation, from hydroelectric dams to natural gas plants. Wind turbines capture energy from moving air. Jet engines use gas turbines for propulsion.

Turbo is short for turbocharger—a device that forces extra air into an engine to boost power. The word extends to anything enhanced for speed or intensity: {turbo mode}, {turbo-charged growth}. As an adjective or prefix, turbo suggests amped-up performance: {Let's turbo this project}. In casual speech, turbo can modify almost anything to mean faster or more powerful.

To turbocharge is to boost power or performance dramatically. The literal meaning involves fitting an engine with a turbine-driven compressor that forces more air into combustion, increasing output. Figuratively, turbocharge means to intensify or accelerate anything: {The tax cut turbocharged the economy}, {Coffee turbocharged my morning}. The adjective turbocharged works similarly: {a turbocharged campaign}.

Turbocharged describes an engine fitted with a turbocharger—a device that forces extra air into the combustion chamber, increasing power output. The term extends to anything enhanced or intensified beyond normal capacity: {a turbocharged economy}, {turbocharged growth}. The figurative use suggests something supercharged, accelerated, or operating at maximum intensity.

A turbocharger is a device that forces extra air into an engine's combustion chamber, increasing power output. It's driven by exhaust gases spinning a turbine, which compresses incoming air—essentially recycling waste energy. {The turbocharger kicked in and the car surged forward.} Often shortened to turbo.

Turbocharges is the verb form of turbocharge—to equip an engine with a turbocharger, a device that forces more air into combustion for greater power. Figuratively, to turbocharge something is to dramatically boost its speed, intensity, or effectiveness: {The new funding turbocharges our expansion plans}. {Coffee turbocharges my mornings}.

Turbocharging is using a turbine-driven compressor to force more air into an engine, increasing its power output. The term extends to any dramatic boost or acceleration: {turbocharging the economy}, {turbocharging your productivity}. The figurative use emphasizes adding force or speed to something already in motion.

Turbos is the plural of turbo, a turbocharger—a device that forces extra air into an engine to boost power. Cars with turbos accelerate faster: {The new model comes with twin turbos}. Turbo also works as an adjective meaning high-powered or accelerated: {turbo mode}, {turbo charging}. In gaming, to turbo is to use rapid-fire button pressing.

Turbulence is irregular, chaotic motion in air or fluid, marked by eddies and unpredictable changes in pressure and velocity. In aviation, turbulence causes aircraft to shake or drop: {We hit some turbulence over the Rockies}. The word extends to any state of disorder or instability: {political turbulence}, {emotional turbulence}, {the turbulence of adolescence}.

Turbulent describes violent, chaotic motion—especially in fluids. Turbulent {water} churns unpredictably; turbulent {air} makes for a rough flight. The word extends to any disorder or upheaval: a turbulent {period} in history, a turbulent {relationship}. A turbulent person is prone to causing disturbance or unrest: {The turbulent crowd surged toward the gates}.

A turd is a piece of excrement, specifically a solid one: {The dog left a turd on the sidewalk}. As an insult, turd describes a contemptible or worthless person: {That little turd stole my lunch}. The word is vulgar but almost comically blunt—its Anglo-Saxon directness gives it a certain crude charm. It appears in the phrase {turd in the punchbowl}, meaning something or someone that ruins an otherwise good situation: {He was the turd in the punchbowl at every meeting}.
Turds is the plural of turd—pieces of excrement or, as an insult, contemptible people: {Clean up your dog's turds}. {Those turds in accounting rejected my expense report again}.

Turducken is a dish consisting of a deboned chicken stuffed inside a deboned duck, which is then stuffed inside a deboned turkey—three birds nested together and roasted as one. The name blends turkey, duck, and chicken. It's associated with elaborate holiday meals and Cajun cooking: {We're doing a turducken for Thanksgiving this year}.

A tureen is a deep, covered serving dish, typically oval or round, used for bringing soup or stew to the table. The lid keeps the contents warm while the handles allow passing. Tureens range from plain to ornate, with fancy ones displayed as part of formal dinnerware: {She ladled the bisque from a silver tureen}.

Turf is grass and the layer of earth held together by its roots. A patch of turf can be cut and transplanted as sod. Artificial turf mimics grass for athletic fields. Turf also means territory—the area someone controls or claims as their own: {gang turf}, {Don't step on my turf}. To turf someone out (British) is to eject them forcibly.

Turfs is the plural of turf—grass and the soil beneath it, or areas of ground covered with grass. The word extends to territory someone controls or claims expertise over: {rival gangs defending their turfs}, {bureaucrats protecting their turfs}. In British English, turfs also works as a verb form: {He turfs out the old newspapers}.

A turkey is a large game bird native to North America, domesticated and raised for meat. Turkey is the centerpiece of American Thanksgiving dinners and common at Christmas. In bowling, a turkey is three consecutive strikes. Informally, a turkey is a failure or flop: {That movie was a real turkey}. Calling someone a turkey means they're foolish or inept. To {talk turkey} is to speak frankly about practical matters. To go {cold turkey} is to quit something abruptly, especially an addiction. (Capitalized Turkey is the country.)

Turkeys is the plural of turkey—the large North American bird domesticated for food, especially associated with Thanksgiving. The word extends to failures or flops: {The movie was a turkey}. In bowling, a turkey is three consecutive strikes. Calling someone a turkey means they're foolish or inept: {Don't be such a turkey}. (Capitalized Turkey is the country.)

Turmeric is a bright yellow-orange spice ground from the root of a tropical plant related to ginger. It gives curry powder its distinctive color and appears in South Asian and Middle Eastern cuisines. The root can be used fresh or dried. Turmeric has become popular as a dietary supplement, promoted for anti-inflammatory properties: {turmeric lattes}, {turmeric supplements}.

Turmoil is a state of confusion, agitation, or disturbance—circumstances churning with uncertainty or conflict. A country may be in political turmoil, a mind in emotional turmoil: {The news threw the family into turmoil}. The word suggests disorder that's disorienting rather than violent, though violence may accompany it.

The core meaning of the verb turn involves motion, either around an axis (the world turns), or in a way that results in a change of direction (turn left at the next intersection). However, many phrasal verbs in which turn appears may not involve motion, such as turn up, turn down, or turn out. The noun turn most commonly represents an alternation between two or more people sharing an activity, as in the phrase take turns. Turn also represents an instance of turning in any of its senses.

Turnabout is a reversal or change to an opposite position, direction, or course of action: {The company's turnabout on remote work surprised employees}. The phrase {turnabout is fair play} suggests that retaliating in kind is justified—if someone tricks you, you're entitled to trick them back. A turnabout can also be a circular area for vehicles to reverse direction.
clues: Going back the way you came

definition: Turnaround is a reversal or dramatic change, especially from bad to good: {The company's turnaround surprised investors}. It also means the time needed to complete a process and return results: {a 48-hour turnaround on lab tests}. In transportation, a turnaround is a space for vehicles to reverse direction. To turn something around is to reverse its fortunes or direction.

Turnarounds are reversals of direction, fortune, or condition. A business turnaround rescues a failing company. A turnaround in a game shifts momentum from one side to the other. In transportation, a turnaround is the time or space needed to reverse direction, unload, reload, and depart again: {The airline improved its turnaround time between flights}. A turnaround can also be a U-shaped driveway for reversing vehicles.

A turncoat is someone who switches allegiance—abandoning a cause, party, or group to join the opposition. The term carries strong disapproval, implying betrayal rather than principled change of mind: {The senator was branded a turncoat after voting with the other party}. Unlike a mere defector, a turncoat often actively works against former allies.

Turncoats are people who switch allegiance, abandoning their original side to join the opposition. The term carries strong disapproval—turncoats aren't just changing their minds but betraying former allies: {The party's turncoats voted with the opposition on the spending bill}. The image is of someone literally turning their coat inside out to display different colors.

Turned is the past tense of turn, covering all that verb's meanings—rotation, change of direction, transformation. Something that has turned has changed state: milk turns sour, leaves turn colors, conversations turn serious. A turned ankle has twisted painfully. A well-turned phrase is elegantly crafted. {She turned thirty last week.} {The tide had turned against them.}

Turning is the act of rotating, changing direction, or shifting position. A turning in the road is a bend or junction where one can change course; in British usage, it specifically means a side street or path branching off: {Take the second turning on the left}. The word also describes a pivotal moment or shift: {a turning in the conversation}. Turnings are the waste shavings produced when shaping wood or metal on a lathe.

A turnip is a root vegetable with white or cream-colored flesh and a purple-tinged top where it grows above ground. It has a mildly peppery, slightly bitter taste and is eaten cooked or raw. The leafy greens attached to the top, called turnip greens, are also edible and popular in Southern cooking. The phrase {fell off the turnip truck} suggests someone is naive or unsophisticated, as if they just arrived from rural farm country.

Turnips are round root vegetables with white or cream-colored flesh and a slightly bitter, peppery taste. They grow quickly and store well, making them a traditional cool-weather crop. The leafy greens are also edible: {turnip greens}. Rutabagas are sometimes called Swedish turnips or yellow turnips. {She roasted turnips with the other root vegetables.}

Turnkey describes something complete and ready for immediate use. A turnkey system, solution, or project requires no further work—just turn the key and go: {The contractor delivered a turnkey home}. The term appears frequently in business and technology contexts: {turnkey software}, {a turnkey operation}. As a noun, a turnkey is an archaic term for a jailer—one who turns the key.

A turnoff is a road or exit that branches off from a larger one: {We missed the turnoff and had to double back}. Figuratively, a turnoff is something that kills interest or attraction, especially romantic or sexual: {Bad breath is a major turnoff}. The verb phrase is two words: {turn off the lights}, {His attitude really turns me off}.

Things that cause loss of interest, attraction, or arousal. The word applies to both sexual and nonsexual contexts: {Bad breath is a major turnoff}, {The long commute was a turnoff for potential buyers}. A turnoff is also a road or ramp that branches from a main route: {We missed the turnoff and had to double back}.

Turnout is the number of people who show up for something—an election, a rally, a performance: {Voter turnout was higher than expected}, {We had a good turnout for the fundraiser}. In ballet, turnout is the outward rotation of the legs from the hips. A turnout can also be a widened section of road where vehicles can pass or pull over.

Turnouts are the numbers of people who show up for something—an election, a rally, a performance: {Voter turnout was historically low}, {We had a good turnout for the fundraiser}. In railroads, a turnout is a track switch allowing trains to move from one line to another. In ballet and dance, turnout refers to the outward rotation of the legs from the hips. Turnouts can also be wide spots on narrow roads where vehicles can pull aside to let others pass.

Turnover is the rate at which things cycle through—employees leaving and being replaced, inventory selling and restocking, or money flowing through a business. A high turnover rate at a company means staff don't stay long. In sports, a turnover is losing possession to the opponent. A turnover is also a pastry made by folding dough over a filling: {apple turnover}.

Turnovers are pastries made by folding dough over a filling—fruit, meat, or cheese—creating a half-moon or triangular pocket: {apple turnovers}, {beef turnovers}. In sports, a turnover is loss of possession to the opponent through error or interception: {The team committed three turnovers in the fourth quarter}. In business, turnover refers to the rate at which employees leave and are replaced, or the total volume of sales in a period.

A turnpike is a toll road—a highway where drivers pay fees to use it. The term comes from the spiked barrier (a turning pike) that blocked passage until tolls were paid. In the northeastern United States, turnpike remains common in official road names: {the New Jersey Turnpike}, {the Pennsylvania Turnpike}. Elsewhere, toll road or tollway is more typical.

Turnpikes are roads, especially highways, where travelers pay tolls. The original turnpikes had barriers—spiked poles that turned—to block passage until fees were paid. Now the word simply means a toll road: {Take the turnpike to avoid local traffic}. In American usage, major interstate toll roads often carry the name: the New Jersey Turnpike, the Pennsylvania Turnpike.

Turns is the plural of turn and the third-person singular verb form. A turn is a rotation, a change of direction, or an opportunity in sequence: {Take turns}. The verb means to rotate, reverse, or transform: {She turns the key}, {Milk turns sour}. Turns appears in idioms: {turns out} (proves to be), {turns up} (appears), {turns down} (rejects). {The plot turns on a single decision.}

A turnstile is a mechanical gate with rotating horizontal arms or a revolving door that allows only one person to pass through at a time, typically after inserting a coin, ticket, or transit card. Turnstiles control access to subways, stadiums, amusement parks, and other venues where entry must be monitored or paid for. {She swiped her MetroCard and pushed through the turnstile.} The mechanism ensures people enter single-file and prevents unauthorized entry or exit.

Turnstiles are rotating barriers that allow one person to pass at a time, typically after paying a fare or presenting credentials. The mechanism counts entries and controls access—common at subway stations, stadiums, and amusement parks. {She pushed through the turnstile and hurried to the platform.}

Turnt is slang for being in a heightened state of excitement, energy, or intoxication—typically at a party or social event. It emerged from African American Vernacular English as a past tense of "turn up," meaning to get wild or hyped: {The club was turnt last night}. Sometimes intensified as {turnt up}. The word suggests uninhibited fun, often with alcohol or drugs involved.

A turntable is a circular rotating platform. The term most commonly refers to the platter on a record player that spins vinyl records: {She placed the LP on the turntable}. DJs use turntables to mix and scratch records. The word also applies to rotating platforms for trains, vehicles, or display items, allowing them to be turned around or repositioned.

Turntables are rotating platforms, especially the circular platter on which vinyl records spin during playback. In DJ culture, turntables became instruments—scratching, mixing, and beat-matching transformed record players into tools for creating new sounds: {She learned to spin on turntables before switching to digital}. The word also applies to rotating platforms for trains or display items.

Turntablism is the art of manipulating vinyl records on turntables as a musical instrument rather than just a playback device. DJs scratch, beat-juggle, and mix records to create new sounds and rhythms: {The competition showcased turntablism at its finest}. The practice emerged from hip-hop culture in the 1970s and elevated the DJ from selector to performer.

A turntablist is a DJ who uses turntables as musical instruments rather than simply playing records. Through techniques like scratching, beat juggling, and mixing, turntablists create new sounds and compositions from existing recordings. The practice emerged from hip-hop culture in the 1970s and 80s: {The turntablist competed in the DMC World Championships}.

Turpentine is a pungent solvent distilled from pine resin, used to thin oil-based paints and clean brushes. The sharp, distinctive smell is immediately recognizable to anyone who has painted with oils: {The studio reeked of turpentine}. By extension, turpentine can refer to various pine-derived resins and oils. To turpentine trees is to tap them for resin.

Turquoise is a blue-green mineral prized as a gemstone, or the color of that stone—a distinctive blend of blue and green suggesting tropical waters or desert skies. The stone has been valued for millennia in jewelry and ornamentation, particularly in Native American and Middle Eastern traditions. As a color term, turquoise describes things in that blue-green range: {turquoise waters}, {a turquoise dress}.

A turret is a small tower, typically one projecting from a corner of a larger building or fortification. In military contexts, a turret is a rotating armored structure housing guns on a warship, tank, or aircraft: {The tank's turret swiveled toward the target}. In machining, a turret lathe holds multiple cutting tools that rotate into position.

Turrets is the plural of turret, a small tower projecting from a building, especially a castle or fortress. Military turrets are rotating armored structures housing guns on tanks, warships, or aircraft: {The tank's turret swiveled toward the target}. In fantasy games and fiction, turrets often appear as defensive towers that automatically fire at enemies.

A turtle is a reptile with a protective shell into which it can withdraw its head and limbs. In American English, turtle covers both land and aquatic species; British English reserves turtle for sea-dwelling types and uses tortoise for land species. To {turtle} or {turn turtle} is to flip upside down, like a capsized boat. In computing, turtle graphics teach programming by moving a cursor that draws lines as it goes.

A turtledove is a small wild dove with a soft, purring coo, found across Europe and Asia. The name has nothing to do with turtles—it comes from the bird's call. Turtledoves appear frequently in poetry and scripture as symbols of devoted love, and {two turtle doves} feature in the Christmas carol "The Twelve Days of Christmas."

Turtledoves are small wild doves known for their soft, purring coo and their devoted pair bonds. The name comes from the Latin for their call, not from turtles. Because mated pairs stay close and seem affectionate, turtledove became a term of endearment for a sweetheart: {Hello, my turtledove}. They appear in the song "The Twelve Days of Christmas."

A turtleneck is a close-fitting, high collar that folds over on itself, or a sweater or shirt featuring such a collar: {She wore a black turtleneck under her blazer}. The style covers the neck completely, unlike a crew neck or V-neck. In British English, the same garment is often called a polo neck.

Turtlenecks is the plural of turtleneck, a sweater or shirt with a high, close-fitting collar that folds over and covers the neck. The style provides warmth and a sleek silhouette: {She packed three turtlenecks for the ski trip}. In British English, the garment is called a polo neck.

Turtles is the plural of turtle, a reptile with a protective shell encasing its body. Turtles include land-dwelling tortoises, freshwater species, and sea turtles. The phrase {turtles all the way down} describes infinite regress—from the cosmological myth of a world-supporting turtle standing on another turtle, endlessly. {We saw sea turtles nesting on the beach.}

Turtling describes withdrawing into a defensive position, like a turtle retreating into its shell. In gaming, it means adopting an extremely defensive strategy—building fortifications, refusing to attack, waiting out opponents: {Stop turtling and fight!} More broadly, turtling can mean curling up protectively or hunkering down to avoid engagement: {She spent the weekend turtling under blankets}.

Tushie is a playful, mild term for the buttocks, typically used with or around children: {Go wash your tushie}. It comes from Yiddish and sounds affectionate rather than crude. Adults sometimes use it for humorous effect: {Get your tushie off the couch}. Also spelled tushy.

Tushy is an informal, mildly childish word for the buttocks. It appears most often in speech directed at or about children, though adults use it playfully among themselves as well. {The toddler fell right on her tushy.} The word avoids the vulgarity of ass while being less clinical than buttocks or bottom.

A tusk is a long, pointed tooth that extends outside the mouth of certain animals, most notably elephants, walruses, and wild boars. Unlike regular teeth, tusks grow continuously throughout the animal's life and serve purposes ranging from digging and defense to social display. Elephant tusks are made of ivory, which has historically made these animals targets for poaching. {The walrus used its tusks to haul itself onto the ice.} To tusk is to dig or gore with tusks.

Tusks are elongated teeth that project beyond the mouth, found on elephants, walruses, wild boars, and some other animals. They serve as weapons, tools for digging, or displays of dominance. Elephant tusks are prized for their ivory, driving centuries of poaching: {The poachers were caught with a truckload of tusks}. Figuratively, anything long and tooth-like may be called a tusk.

A tussle is a vigorous struggle or scuffle, typically brief and not seriously violent: {The kids got into a tussle over the remote}. The word suggests physical grappling but extends to any spirited contest or dispute: {a tussle with bureaucracy}, {a legal tussle over property rights}. To tussle is to engage in such a struggle.

Tussled is the past tense of tussle, meaning to engage in a brief, rough struggle or scuffle. The fight is usually not serious—more wrestling than combat: {The kids tussled over the remote}. Hair that is tussled has been mussed or disheveled, as if someone had been in a scrap: {His tussled hair gave him a boyish look}.

Tussles are brief, vigorous struggles or scuffles—physical or figurative. The word suggests something less serious than a fight: {The kids had a tussle over the remote}. Political opponents engage in tussles over legislation. A tussle with a problem implies grappling with difficulty: {After a tussle with the instructions, I assembled the shelf}.

Tussling is engaging in a rough physical struggle or scuffle, typically without serious intent to harm. Children tussle on the playground; siblings tussle over the remote. The word extends to any vigorous contest: {The two candidates have been tussling over the same voters for months}. A tussle is usually brief and scrappy rather than a full-blown fight.

A tutor is a private instructor who teaches one student or a small group, typically supplementing formal education: {She hired a math tutor for her son}. The verb means to provide such instruction: {He tutors high school students in chemistry}. In British universities, a tutor is a faculty member who advises and instructs students individually.

A tutorial is a lesson that teaches a specific skill or concept, typically through step-by-step instruction. Originally describing a session with a tutor, the word now most often refers to instructional guides—especially in software and gaming: {I watched a tutorial on video editing}, {The game starts with a tutorial level}. As an adjective, tutorial describes anything relating to instruction or tutoring.

Tutorials are instructional guides that walk you through a process step by step. They teach practical skills—how to use software, play an instrument, or complete a craft project. Video tutorials dominate online learning: {I watched a tutorial on how to braid hair}. In academic settings, a tutorial is a small-group session with an instructor, common in British universities.

Tutoring is one-on-one or small-group instruction, typically supplementing formal education. A tutor helps a student with specific subjects or skills: {She's been tutoring him in calculus}. Tutoring can be remedial, helping struggling students catch up, or enrichment for those seeking advancement. The word covers both providing and receiving such instruction: {He earns money tutoring on weekends}.

Tutors are people who provide individual or small-group instruction, typically outside formal classroom settings. A tutor might help a struggling student catch up or push an advanced one further. The verb means to give such instruction: {She tutors high school students in math}. College athletes sometimes have academic tutors to keep them eligible.

Tutting is making a disapproving clicking sound with the tongue against the roof of the mouth, often written as "tut-tut." The sound expresses mild disapproval, impatience, or disappointment without words: {She tutted at the mess in the kitchen}. British speakers tut more readily than Americans, who might just sigh or shake their heads.

A tutu is a short, stiff skirt worn by ballet dancers, typically made of multiple layers of tulle or net fabric that project outward from the waist. The classic tutu creates a disk-like silhouette that allows audiences to see the dancer's leg movements: {She adjusted her tutu before the performance}.

Tutus are the short, stiff skirts worn by ballet dancers, made of multiple layers of tulle or netting that project outward from the waist. The classic tutu creates a disk-like silhouette that allows audiences to see the dancer's leg work. Longer, softer versions are called romantic tutus: {The corps de ballet entered in matching white tutus}.

A tux is a tuxedo—formal evening wear for men consisting of a black jacket with satin lapels, matching trousers, and typically a bow tie: {He rented a tux for the wedding}. The clipped form is standard in casual speech. (Capitalized Tux is the Linux penguin mascot.)

A tuxedo is formal evening wear for men, consisting of a black jacket with satin lapels, matching trousers with a satin stripe, and typically worn with a bow tie and formal shirt. Distinguished from a full tailcoat by its shorter jacket, the tuxedo occupies the middle ground of men's formal dress—appropriate for black-tie events but not the most formal occasions. Often shortened to tux: {He rented a tux for prom}.

Tuxedos is the plural of tuxedo, a man's formal evening suit distinguished by satin or grosgrain lapels on a black or midnight blue jacket, worn with matching trousers and a bow tie. The tuxedo occupies the tier below white tie in formal dress codes: {The invitation specified tuxedos}. Americans often shorten it to tux.

Twaddle is foolish, trivial, or pretentious talk or writing—nonsense that wastes the listener's time: {The article was pure twaddle}. The word carries mild contempt, suggesting the speaker finds the content beneath serious consideration. As a verb, to twaddle is to talk in this empty way, though the noun is far more common.

Twang is a sharp, vibrating sound—the release of a taut string or the resonance of certain regional accents: {the twang of a banjo}, {a Texas twang}. The word imitates the sound it describes. As a verb, to twang is to make or cause this sound: {She twanged the guitar string}.

Twanging is the present participle of twang and is used to characterize a sound with a sudden, high-pitched beginning and a quickly dropping pitch, like that of a plucked string on a musical instrument.

Twangs is the plural noun and third-person singular verb form of twang. A twang is a sharp, vibrating sound like that of a plucked string on a guitar or banjo, or a nasal quality in someone's speech often associated with regional accents: {She spoke with a Southern twang}. To twang is to make such a sound or to pluck something that produces it: {He twangs the bowstring nervously}.

Twangy describes sounds that have a sharp, vibrating quality, like a plucked string or a taut wire snapping back. It most often characterizes voices or accents with a nasal, resonant quality associated with country music or certain regional American dialects: {She spoke with a twangy Southern accent}. Guitars, banjos, and other stringed instruments can sound twangy when their strings produce that distinctive resonant ping.

Twat is vulgar slang with a transatlantic split. In British English, it's a term for the female genitals and a strong insult for a stupid or contemptible person: {You absolute twat}. In American English, it refers to genitals but as an insult is less common and sounds almost quaint—more foolish than vicious. British speakers use twat more freely; Americans might find it jarring.

Twats is the plural of twat, referring to female genitals or, as an insult, stupid people. The insult is common in British English: {Those twats have no idea what they're doing}. In American usage, it's less frequent and sounds somewhat dated.

Tweak is a small adjustment or fine-tuning: {I made a few tweaks to the recipe}. To tweak something is to adjust it slightly, often to improve performance: {She tweaked the settings until the picture looked right}. To physically tweak is to pinch and twist: {He tweaked her nose playfully}. In slang, tweaking describes erratic behavior from methamphetamine use, or more loosely, acting agitated or irrational: {He's been tweaking all day}.

Tweaked is the past tense of tweak, meaning to make small adjustments or fine-tune something: {I tweaked the settings until the picture looked right}. It can also mean pinched or twisted sharply: {She tweaked his ear}. In slang, tweaked describes someone high on stimulants, especially methamphetamine, or acting jittery and erratic: {He's been up for three days—totally tweaked}.

A tweaker is someone who uses methamphetamine, especially habitually. The term references the drug's effects—obsessive, repetitive behaviors and jittery movements: {Some tweaker stole the catalytic converter off my truck}. More broadly, tweaker can describe anyone who tinkers obsessively with something, adjusting settings or code endlessly: {He's a total audio tweaker}.

Tweakers are people who use methamphetamine or other stimulants, especially habitually. The term comes from tweaking—the jittery, compulsive, often erratic behavior characteristic of stimulant use: fidgeting, obsessive tinkering, inability to stay still. {The tweakers were up all night taking apart a lawnmower.} The word is dismissive or contemptuous.

Tweaking is making small, precise adjustments to improve something: {She spent hours tweaking the design}. Software developers tweak code; musicians tweak settings on equipment. The word suggests fine-tuning rather than major overhaul. In drug slang, tweaking describes the jittery, obsessive behavior of someone on methamphetamine or other stimulants: {He's been up for days, tweaking}.

Tweaks are small adjustments or fine-tunings, usually to improve something that's already mostly working: {a few tweaks to the recipe}, {The software needs some tweaks before release}. To tweak is to make such adjustments, or to pinch and twist sharply: {She tweaked his nose}. In slang, tweaking means behaving erratically, especially from stimulant drugs like methamphetamine: {He was up all night tweaking}.

Twee describes something excessively dainty, quaint, or cutesy—often to the point of being affected or cloying. A café with too many doilies and vintage teacups might be dismissed as twee. The word carries a note of British disdain: {The décor was unbearably twee}. In music criticism, twee pop refers to a deliberately precious, jangly indie sound.

Tweed is a rough-textured woolen fabric, typically woven in mixed colors to produce a flecked or heathered appearance. Associated with rural Britain and outdoor pursuits, tweed suggests country estates, hunting, and academic life: {a tweed jacket with leather elbow patches}. Harris tweed, from Scotland's Outer Hebrides, is particularly prized.

Tweedledee refers to one of two things so alike as to be virtually indistinguishable, usually paired with tweedledum: {The candidates are tweedledee and tweedledum on economic policy}. The names come from Lewis Carroll's *Through the Looking-Glass*, where Tweedledee and Tweedledum are identical twins. The pairing suggests a distinction without a meaningful difference.

Tweeds are garments made from tweed—a coarse, durable woolen fabric with a flecked appearance, traditionally associated with British country wear. The plural usually refers to a suit or outfit: {He wore his tweeds for the hunt}. The fabric and style suggest rural aristocracy, academia, or old-fashioned formality.

Tween is an informal, shortened spelling of between that may be used in poetry where a word of one syllable is required. As a noun, it is a shortened form of tweenager, used informally to refer to an adolescent or young teenager.

Tweens are children between childhood and adolescence—roughly ages nine to twelve. The term blends "between" and "teen," capturing that transitional phase when kids are no longer little but not yet teenagers. Marketing often targets tweens as a distinct demographic: {tween fashion}, {tween entertainment}. The singular tween refers to one such child.
clues: Kids on the cusp of teenhood
