The word works as both past tense verb and adjective: {I upgraded my phone last week} or {the upgraded model has more storage}. Upgrading often implies modernization or enhancement rather than complete replacement.

Upgrades are improvements or enhancements to something already in place. You upgrade software to a newer version, upgrade a plane ticket to first class, or upgrade your phone. The word works as both noun and verb: {The system needs upgrades}, {We upgraded our internet plan}. In gaming and tech contexts, upgrades are often incremental improvements to equipment, abilities, or services: {unlocking weapon upgrades}, {paying for premium upgrades}.

Upgrading is improving something by replacing it with a better version or adding enhanced features. You upgrade software, hardware, airline seats, or hotel rooms. The word implies moving up a scale of quality or capability: {We're upgrading our internet to fiber}, {She got upgraded to first class}. Upgrading can also mean improving skills or qualifications: {He's upgrading his certification}.

Upheaval is violent disruption or dramatic change—the kind that overturns established conditions. The word suggests something forced upward from below: geological upheaval raises mountains; political upheaval topples governments. It applies to personal life too: {The divorce caused tremendous upheaval for the whole family}. The scale is always significant—upheaval implies fundamental displacement, not minor disturbance.
clues: When the ground shifts beneath you

definition: Upheavals is the plural of upheaval—a violent or sudden disruption that overturns an existing state of affairs. The word suggests forces thrusting upward from below, whether geological or social: {The political upheavals of the 1960s transformed American society}. Upheavals can be personal as well as collective: {She faced several upheavals in her first year of marriage}.

Upheld is the past tense and past participle of uphold. To uphold is to support, maintain, or defend something—usually a principle, decision, or standard: {The court upheld the lower court's ruling}. {She upheld the family's traditions}. The word appears frequently in legal contexts when judges affirm previous decisions.

Uphill describes movement or direction toward higher ground: {The trail runs uphill for two miles}. Figuratively, an uphill {battle} or uphill {struggle} requires sustained effort against resistance—like climbing a slope. As a noun, an uphill is an ascending stretch: {We hit a steep uphill near the summit}.

To uphold is to support, maintain, or defend something against challenge or opposition. Courts uphold rulings when they affirm them on appeal: {The Supreme Court upheld the lower court's decision}. You can uphold principles, traditions, or standards by continuing to honor them: {She upheld her family's reputation for honesty}. The word suggests active preservation rather than passive acceptance.

Upholding is maintaining, supporting, or defending something—typically a principle, law, decision, or standard. Courts uphold rulings when they affirm them on appeal: {The Supreme Court upheld the lower court's decision}. One upholds traditions by continuing to observe them, or upholds values by acting in accordance with them: {upholding the constitution}, {upholding democratic norms}.

Upholstery is the soft covering on furniture—the fabric, padding, and springs that make a chair or sofa comfortable to sit on. The word also refers to the craft of applying these materials: {The couch needs new upholstery}. Car interiors have upholstery too: {leather upholstery}, {cloth upholstery}.

Upkeep is the work and cost of maintaining something in good condition: {The upkeep on an old house can be substantial}. It covers routine maintenance, repairs, and the resources required to keep things functioning properly. The word applies to property, equipment, or even people: {He pays child support for the upkeep of his kids}.

Upland refers to elevated terrain—higher ground as opposed to lowlands, valleys, or coastal areas. As an adjective, it describes things found in or characteristic of such regions: {upland meadows}, {upland birds}. The plural uplands often names a specific elevated region: {the Scottish Uplands}. In ecology, upland distinguishes drier elevated areas from wetlands.

Uplift carries the idea of raising something up. Physically, geological forces uplift land masses. Emotionally or spiritually, something uplifts you by improving your mood or elevating your spirit: {The music was genuinely uplifting}. As a noun, uplift refers to this elevation—moral uplift, spiritual uplift, or the geological raising of terrain. A bra provides uplift in the most literal sense.

Uplifted describes something raised up, either physically or emotionally. A face {uplifted toward the sky} is tilted upward. More often the word refers to spirits or mood: {I felt uplifted after talking with her}. The past participle of uplift, it suggests elevation toward something higher or better—improved morale, renewed hope, or spiritual elevation.

Uplifting describes something that raises the spirits or improves mood: {an uplifting speech}, {uplifting news}. The word implies emotional elevation—hope, inspiration, or encouragement. Music, stories, and experiences are commonly called uplifting when they leave you feeling better than before: {The documentary was surprisingly uplifting despite its heavy subject matter}.

Uplifts is the third-person singular of uplift, meaning to raise up—physically, emotionally, or spiritually. Music uplifts the soul. A bra uplifts the breasts. As a noun, an uplift is something that elevates: {The news gave her an uplift}. In geology, uplift refers to the rising of land masses through tectonic forces.

An uplink is a transmission sent from Earth to a satellite or spacecraft, or the equipment and channel used for such transmission. The term contrasts with downlink, which travels the opposite direction. By extension, uplink describes any data transfer from a local device to a central or remote system: {The field team uplinked their findings to headquarters}.

Upload means to transfer data from a local device to a remote system, typically a server or cloud service: {I need to upload these photos to the website}. The opposite of download. As a noun, an upload is either the act of uploading or the file being transferred: {The upload took forever on this slow connection}.

Uploaded is the past tense of upload, meaning to transfer data from a local device to a remote system—typically a server or cloud storage. The opposite of download. {I uploaded the photos to the shared drive}. {The video was uploaded yesterday}. Something uploaded exists on a remote system, accessible to others or retrievable later.

Uploading is the process of transferring data from a local device to a remote system—the opposite of downloading. You upload files to cloud storage, photos to social media, videos to streaming platforms: {I'm still uploading the footage from last night}. The noun upload refers to either the act or the content transferred: {The upload failed halfway through}.

Uploads are files transferred from a local device to a remote server or network location. The term covers both the act of transferring and the files themselves: {Check your uploads folder}, {The upload failed halfway through}. To upload is to send data outward—the opposite of download. Upload speed, often slower than download speed on home internet connections, determines how quickly you can share files, post videos, or back up data to the cloud.

Upmarket means appealing to or designed for affluent consumers with sophisticated tastes: {an upmarket boutique}, {upmarket cosmetics}. The term positions products, services, or neighborhoods on a scale of price and prestige. To {move upmarket} is to target wealthier customers or improve quality. More common in British English; Americans often say upscale.

Upon is an old preposition that is now largely replaced by on. It can still be used instead of on to bring an air of formality, or when two syllables rather than one are required in poetry or lyrics. Upon survives in many fixed phrases and quotations because of this: When you wish upon a star…

Upped is the past tense of up used as a verb, meaning to increase or raise something: {They upped the price}, {She upped her game}. The phrase {upped and left} means departed suddenly or unexpectedly: {He just upped and left without saying goodbye}.

Upper means higher in position, rank, or status. The upper {floors} of a building are above the lower ones. The upper {class} occupies a higher social position. Upper {management} holds more authority. As a noun, an upper is the part of a shoe above the sole, or slang for a stimulant drug that elevates mood or energy—the opposite of a downer.

An upperclassman is a student in the later years of high school or college—typically a junior or senior. The term distinguishes these students from underclassmen (freshmen and sophomores), who are newer to the institution. {The upperclassmen got first pick of dorm rooms.} The word is American and increasingly replaced by the gender-neutral upperclassman or simply upper-level student.

Upperclassmen are students in the later years of high school or college—juniors and seniors, as opposed to freshmen and sophomores. The term implies seniority and experience within the institution: {Upperclassmen get first pick of dorm rooms}. The singular upperclassman traditionally used the masculine suffix, though upperclassman now serves as gender-neutral for many speakers.

An uppercut is a punch delivered in an upward arc, typically aimed at an opponent's chin or body. The fist swings from below, rising sharply—distinct from hooks or jabs that travel horizontally. A signature move in boxing, it's most effective at close range: {He landed a devastating uppercut in the third round}. The term works as both noun and verb: {She uppercut him cleanly}.

Uppercuts are punches thrown in an upward arc, typically aimed at an opponent's chin or body. The motion comes from below, with the fist driving upward—distinct from jabs or hooks. In boxing, a well-timed uppercut can end a fight: {He dropped his guard and took two uppercuts to the jaw}. The term extends to any sharp upward blow.

Uppercutting is delivering an uppercut—a punch that travels upward, typically aimed at an opponent's chin or torso. The term belongs primarily to boxing and combat sports: {He was uppercutting with his left while blocking with his right}. Figuratively, it can describe any sharp upward strike or sudden aggressive move from below.

Uppers are stimulant drugs—amphetamines, cocaine, caffeine—that increase alertness and energy, contrasted with downers that sedate. The term comes from the lifting effect on mood and activity. Separately, uppers are the parts of shoes above the sole: {The uppers were leather, but the soles were rubber}. To be {on one's uppers} is to be destitute, from worn-out shoes with nothing left but the upper portion.

Uppity describes someone who doesn't accept their expected place in a social hierarchy—acting above their station, asserting themselves when deference is expected. The word carries a history of racial condescension, frequently used by white Americans to disparage Black people who refused subservience: {That uppity Negro thinks he's as good as us}. Today it's applied more broadly to anyone seen as presumptuous or self-important, but the racial undertone lingers, especially in American usage.

Upright means vertical or erect—standing straight up rather than leaning, tilted, or lying down: {The fence posts must be perfectly upright}. An upright piano stands vertically against a wall, unlike a grand piano. Figuratively, an upright person is honest and morally correct: {an upright citizen}, {upright conduct}. The noun refers to a vertical structural element: {the uprights of a goal post}.

Uprights are vertical structural elements—the posts that support a goal in football, the vertical bars of a fence, the standing beams in a frame. An upright piano stands tall rather than lying horizontal like a grand piano. The term emphasizes the vertical orientation: {The ball sailed between the uprights}.

An uprising is a rebellion or revolt against established authority, typically involving collective action by a group against those in power. The word emphasizes the act of rising up—people who were subjugated asserting themselves against oppression. {The uprising was brutally suppressed by government forces.} Unlike revolution, uprising doesn't imply success or complete overthrow.

Uprisings are rebellions or revolts against authority, typically involving collective action by groups seeking political change. The word suggests organized resistance that rises up from below—citizens against a government, workers against employers, colonized peoples against occupiers: {The Arab Spring sparked uprisings across the Middle East}. An uprising may be violent or peaceful, successful or crushed.

Uproar is loud, chaotic noise or commotion, often from a crowd: {The announcement caused an uproar in the courtroom}. It extends to any intense public reaction or controversy: {The policy change sparked an uproar on social media}. Despite its spelling, uproar has no connection to roaring—it comes from a Dutch word meaning tumult or rebellion.

Uproarious describes something that provokes loud, unrestrained laughter or noise. An uproarious {comedy} has the audience howling. An uproarious {crowd} is boisterous and unruly. The word emphasizes volume and abandon—quiet amusement doesn't qualify. {The dinner party grew uproarious after midnight.}

To uproot is to pull something up by the roots—a plant, a tree, a weed. The word extends naturally to displacing people from where they've settled: {War uprooted millions from their homes}. You can also uproot abstractions like traditions or corruption, suggesting removal at the deepest level. The noun is uprootedness.

Uprooted describes something torn from the ground, roots and all: {The storm uprooted several old oaks}. More often figurative—displaced from home, community, or familiar surroundings: {The war uprooted millions of families}. To feel uprooted is to feel disconnected from where you belong: {After the move, she felt completely uprooted}.

Uprootedness is the state of being displaced from one's home, culture, or familiar environment. It suggests not just physical relocation but a deeper disconnection—the loss of roots that once anchored identity and belonging: {The uprootedness of refugee life left her longing for the village she'd never see again}. The word carries more emotional weight than displacement alone.

Uprooting is the act of pulling something up by its roots, whether literally with plants or figuratively with people and institutions. When you uproot a tree, you remove it entirely from the ground; when families are uprooted, they're forced to leave their homes and communities, often abruptly. The word carries connotations of disruption and displacement: {The war caused mass uprooting of civilians}. Uprooting can also mean eliminating something entrenched, like corruption or tradition.

Uproots means to pull something up by the roots, literally or figuratively. You uproot a plant from the ground or uproot a family by forcing them to leave their home: {The war uprooted millions of refugees}. To uproot a problem or practice is to eliminate it completely: {efforts to uproot corruption in the department}.

Ups are instances of rising or improving—the opposite of downs: {Life has its ups and downs}. The verb ups means to increase or raise: {The company ups its prices every year}, {She ups the ante}. To up and do something is to do it suddenly or unexpectedly: {He ups and leaves without a word}. (All-caps UPS is the shipping company.)

Upsadaisy is an exclamation used when lifting a child or helping someone who has fallen: {Upsadaisy, up you go!} The word is playful and reassuring, typically addressed to toddlers being picked up or encouraged to stand. Also spelled upsy-daisy, ups-a-daisy, or oopsy-daisy.

Upscale describes something associated with wealth, high quality, or elevated social status: an upscale {restaurant}, an upscale {neighborhood}, upscale {clientele}. The word often implies expensive but tasteful—luxury without ostentation. As a verb, to upscale is to make something more refined or expensive: {The hotel upscaled its amenities to attract wealthier guests}.

Upscaling is increasing the resolution or quality of an image or video, typically using software that interpolates pixels to make low-resolution content appear sharper on high-resolution displays: {The TV's upscaling makes old DVDs look better on a 4K screen}. More broadly, upscaling means improving or upgrading something to a higher standard: {The hotel underwent upscaling to attract wealthier guests}.

Upsell is a sales technique where a seller encourages a customer to buy a more expensive version or add extras to their purchase: {The waiter tried to upsell us on the premium wine}. As a noun, it's the upgraded item itself or the act of offering one. The practice is ubiquitous in retail, hospitality, and online commerce—every {Would you like fries with that?} is an upsell.

Upselling is the sales practice of encouraging a customer to buy a more expensive version of what they're already purchasing, or to add extras: {The waiter tried upselling us on the premium wine}. It differs from cross-selling, which promotes related but different products. The verb is upsell: {They upsell every customer on the extended warranty}.

Upset covers disturbance of normal states—emotional, physical, or competitive. An upset stomach is queasy. An upset person is distressed or angry: {She was upset about the news}. To upset something is to knock it over or disturb its equilibrium: {The cat upset the vase}. In sports, an upset is a victory by the underdog—a disruption of expected order: {The unknown boxer pulled off a stunning upset}.

Upsets are disturbances to expected order or emotional equilibrium. A stomach upset is digestive distress. An emotional upset leaves someone distressed or agitated. In sports, an upset occurs when an underdog defeats a favored opponent: {The tournament was full of upsets}. The word captures both the internal turmoil and external disruption of things going wrong.

Upsetting describes something that causes emotional distress or disturbance: {The news was upsetting to everyone}. It can range from mildly disappointing to deeply disturbing. The word also has a technical sense in metalworking—upsetting is the process of shortening and thickening metal by hammering or pressing on its end.

The upshot is the final result or outcome of a series of events or discussions: {The upshot was that we decided to move forward with the merger}. It often introduces a summary after complications: {We argued for hours, but the upshot is nothing changed}. The word implies cutting through details to reach the bottom line.

Upsidaisy is an exclamation said when lifting a child or helping someone up, especially after a stumble or fall: {Upsidaisy, there you go!} The word is playful and encouraging, making the motion feel like fun rather than correction. Also spelled upsy-daisy, ups-a-daisy, or oopsie-daisy.

Upside is used informally and in speech with the same meaning as against or on. It is rarely used with this meaning except in the phrase upside the head. Upside can also refer to the perceived advantage of something, typically in comparison to an implied disadvantage: We were late, but the upside was that we didn’t have to listen to a boring speech.

Upsize means to increase in size, scale, or quantity. In fast food contexts, to upsize is to order a larger portion: {Would you like to upsize your meal?} More broadly, it applies to expanding anything—homes, vehicles, investments: {They upsized to a four-bedroom when the twins arrived}. The opposite of downsize.

Upskirting is the act of taking photographs or video under someone's skirt or dress without their consent, typically using a concealed phone or camera. The practice is a form of voyeurism and sexual harassment, now criminalized in many jurisdictions: {He was arrested for upskirting on the subway}.

Upspeak is a speech pattern in which declarative statements end with rising intonation, making them sound like questions. It's particularly associated with younger speakers and certain regional dialects, notably in California and Australia. While sometimes criticized as conveying uncertainty or seeking approval, upspeak serves various conversational functions, including checking that a listener is following along or signaling that more information is coming. {So I went to the store? And they were completely out of milk?}

Upstage originally refers to the back of a theater stage, away from the audience. An actor positioned upstage forces others to turn their backs to the audience to face them—a trick that steals focus. From this comes the common meaning: to divert attention from someone by outshining them. {The bride's sister upstaged her by announcing her pregnancy at the reception.} As an adjective, upstage can mean haughty or aloof.

Upstaged means overshadowed or outshone by someone else's performance or presence. The term comes from theater, where an actor moving upstage (toward the back) forces others to turn away from the audience. Now it applies broadly: {She felt upstaged by her sister's announcement at the party}. To be upstaged is to have attention stolen from you.

Upstages means draws attention away from someone else, typically by outshining or outperforming them: {The supporting actor completely upstaged the lead}. The term comes from theater, where moving upstage (toward the back) forces other actors to turn away from the audience. To upstage can also mean to treat someone dismissively or make them feel less important.

Upstaging is drawing attention away from someone who should be the focus. An actor upstages another by positioning themselves to force the other to turn away from the audience. More broadly, anyone who overshadows another at their moment—a guest wearing white to a wedding, a sibling announcing an engagement at your birthday—is upstaging: {She accused the bridesmaids of upstaging her}.

Upstairs refers to the upper floor or floors of a building: {The bedrooms are upstairs}. As an adjective, it describes things located above: {the upstairs bathroom}. As a noun, it means the upper level itself: {The upstairs needs painting}. Informally, upstairs can mean the brain or mental faculties: {not quite right upstairs}. To {kick someone upstairs} is to promote them to a position with less real power.

Upstanding describes someone of strong moral character—honest, responsible, and respected in their community: {an upstanding citizen}, {an upstanding member of society}. The word suggests someone who stands up straight, both literally and figuratively, meeting obligations and behaving honorably. In formal contexts, {all rise} may be announced as {be upstanding} to request that people stand.

An upstart is someone who has risen quickly to a position of wealth, power, or prominence—especially one perceived as presumptuous or lacking the credentials traditionally expected. The term carries a note of resentment from established figures: {The tech upstart threatened the industry giants}. As an adjective, it describes such people or their enterprises: {an upstart competitor}, {upstart ambitions}.

Upstarts are people or organizations that have recently risen to prominence or success, often in ways that challenge established players or conventions. The term carries a slightly dismissive tone, suggesting that the newcomer lacks the experience, credentials, or refinement of those already in power. {The tech upstarts threatened to disrupt the entire industry.} Someone called an upstart is often seen as presumptuous or overly ambitious, though the word can also convey grudging respect for scrappy ambition.

Upstate refers to the northern or inland regions of a state, especially in contrast to major urban centers typically located downstate. The term is most commonly associated with New York, where upstate encompasses everything north of New York City and its suburbs. As an adjective, adverb, or noun, upstate conveys distance from metropolitan areas: {She moved upstate for college}; {My grandparents have an upstate cabin}. The boundary between upstate and downstate varies depending on who you ask.

Upstream means in the direction from which a river or stream flows—against the current: {We paddled upstream for hours}. The opposite is downstream. In technical and business contexts, upstream refers to earlier stages in a process or supply chain: {upstream suppliers}, {upstream production}. In computing, upstream changes flow back to the original source code repository.

An upswing is an upward movement or trend, especially in economic conditions or business activity: {The economy is on an upswing}, {an upswing in housing sales}. It can also describe improvement in mood or fortune: {Her spirits took an upswing after the good news}. The word often implies recovery from a low point.

Upswings is the plural of upswing—a movement or trend in an upward direction. The word appears most often in economic contexts: {The market has seen several upswings this quarter}. It also describes improvements in mood, health, or fortune: {Her career has had its upswings and downturns}.

Uptake is the act of taking something in or absorbing it. In biology, cells have uptake of nutrients; lungs have oxygen uptake. The word appears most often in the idiom {quick on the uptake} (or {slow on the uptake}), meaning fast or slow to understand: {She's quick on the uptake—I only had to explain it once}.

Uptalk is a speech pattern in which statements end with rising intonation, as if asking a question. Common among younger speakers, it can signal uncertainty, seek confirmation, or simply mark conversational style: {So I went to the store? And they were out of milk?} Critics sometimes dismiss it as unconfident, though linguists note it serves legitimate communicative functions.

Uptalking is speaking with a rising intonation at the end of statements, making them sound like questions. The pattern—sometimes called uptalk or high rising terminal—became associated with California speech in the 1980s and has since spread widely. Critics find it tentative or annoying; linguists note it often serves to check whether listeners are following: {So I went to the store? And they were totally out?}

Uptempo describes music with a fast, lively beat: {an uptempo jazz number}, {The band shifted to something more uptempo}. The term contrasts with ballads and slower pieces. In broader use, uptempo can characterize anything energetic or brisk: {an uptempo campaign speech}.

An uptick is a small increase, especially in something measured over time: {an uptick in sales}, {an uptick in violent crime}. The term comes from stock trading, where an uptick is a transaction at a higher price than the previous one. The word implies modest, incremental movement rather than dramatic change.

Uptight describes someone who is tense, anxious, or unable to relax—often excessively concerned with rules, propriety, or control. An uptight person may be rigid about small matters or easily offended: {Don't be so uptight about it}. The word suggests someone who would benefit from loosening up. {She's too uptight to enjoy a spontaneous road trip}.

Uptime is the period during which a system, machine, or service is operational and available. The term originated in computing—servers and websites are measured by their uptime percentage, with "five nines" (99.999%) being the gold standard. {The site had 99.9% uptime last quarter.} The concept extends to any continuous operation: factory uptime, personal productivity. The opposite is downtime.

Uptown refers to the northern or residential part of a city, as opposed to downtown's commercial center. The distinction originated in Manhattan, where uptown meant toward the higher-numbered streets. As an adverb or adjective, it describes direction or location: {heading uptown}, {an uptown apartment}. Uptown often connotes wealth or sophistication: {uptown tastes}, {moving on up to the uptown side}.

An upturn is a shift toward improvement or increase, especially in economic conditions: {an upturn in the housing market}, {Business showed an upturn in the second quarter}. The verb means to turn upward or over: {upturned faces watched the fireworks}, {The plow upturned the soil}. An upturned nose tilts upward at the tip.

An upvote is a click or tap indicating approval or agreement, used on social media platforms and forums like Reddit. Posts and comments accumulate upvotes, which increase their visibility. The verb means to cast such a vote: {I upvoted your comment}. The opposite is downvote.

Upvoted is the past tense of upvote, meaning to register approval of a post or comment on a website by clicking an arrow or button that increases its visibility score. The term originated on social platforms like Reddit and has spread to forums, news aggregators, and Q&A sites: {Your comment got upvoted to the top}. The opposite is downvoted.

Upvotes are votes of approval on social media platforms and online forums, used to signal agreement, appreciation, or quality. On Reddit, upvotes push content higher in rankings; on other platforms they may be called likes or similar. The verb means to cast such a vote: {I upvoted your comment}. High upvote counts confer visibility and informal credibility.

Upvoting is clicking a button to express approval or agreement with online content—a post, comment, or answer. On platforms like Reddit, upvotes increase a post's visibility and contribute to a user's reputation score. The opposite action is downvoting. {I've been upvoting every comment in this thread.}

Upward indicates movement or direction toward a higher position: {The balloon drifted upward}. It extends to increases in quantity or degree: {Prices moved upward}, {upward of fifty people}. As an adjective, it modifies nouns directly: an {upward trend}, an {upward glance}. The variant upwards is interchangeable in most contexts, though upward is preferred before nouns.

Upwelling is the movement of deep water rising toward the surface, especially in oceans where cold, nutrient-rich water ascends to replace warmer surface water pushed aside by winds. These zones support abundant marine life. Figuratively, an upwelling is any surge from below: {an upwelling of grief}, {an upwelling of popular anger}.

Upwind means in the direction from which the wind is blowing—the opposite of downwind. To stand upwind of something is to have the wind carry its scent away from you: {Stay upwind of the campfire smoke}. Hunters approach game from upwind so their scent won't alert the prey. As an adjective: {the upwind side of the island}.

Uranium is a dense, silvery-white metallic element, atomic number 92. It is radioactive and fissionable, making it the primary fuel for nuclear reactors and the core material in nuclear weapons. Enriched uranium has a higher concentration of the isotope uranium-235, which sustains chain reactions. {The country was accused of enriching uranium for weapons development.}

Urban describes things relating to cities or densely populated areas, as opposed to rural or suburban environments: {urban development}, {urban poverty}, {the urban landscape}. Urban can suggest the culture and lifestyle associated with city living—fast-paced, diverse, cosmopolitan. In music marketing, urban became a category label often applied to Black artists, a usage criticized as a euphemism; many organizations have dropped it.

Urbanisation is the process by which populations shift from rural areas to cities, or by which areas become more urban in character. The term covers both demographic movement and physical transformation—farmland giving way to housing developments, villages growing into towns. {Rapid urbanisation has strained the city's infrastructure.} Also spelled urbanization.

Urbanism encompasses the study, planning, and character of city life and urban environments. It examines how cities develop, function, and affect their inhabitants—covering everything from street layouts and building density to social dynamics and economic patterns. Urban planners practice urbanism when they design neighborhoods or transit systems. The term also describes a lifestyle or sensibility shaped by city living, with its emphasis on walkability, density, and public spaces. {New urbanism advocates for mixed-use development and pedestrian-friendly design.}

An urbanite is a person who lives in a city, especially one who seems thoroughly adapted to urban life. The word often carries connotations of sophistication or cosmopolitan sensibility: {As a lifelong urbanite, she found the quiet of the countryside unsettling}. It contrasts with rural dwellers or suburbanites.

Urbanites are city dwellers—people who live in urban areas rather than rural or suburban ones. The term often carries connotations of sophistication, cultural engagement, or cosmopolitan lifestyle: {Young urbanites flocked to the neighborhood's new restaurants and galleries}. It can also imply a disconnect from rural life or nature.

Urbanization is the process by which populations shift from rural areas to cities, or by which areas become more city-like in character. The term describes both demographic movement and physical transformation—farmland giving way to housing developments, villages growing into towns. {Rapid urbanization has strained the city's infrastructure.} The adjective urbanized describes places that have undergone this change.

An urchin is a mischievous or ragged child, especially one who is poor or neglected—the kind found darting through crowded streets in Victorian novels. The word also names sea urchins, the spiny marine animals that look like living pincushions on the ocean floor. The connection between scruffy children and spiky sea creatures traces back to hedgehogs, which were once called urchins for their bristly appearance.

Urchins is the plural of urchin, a word with two main meanings. A sea urchin is a spiny, globe-shaped marine animal. An urchin is also a mischievous or ragged child, especially a poor one living on the streets: {Dickensian urchins begging for coins}. The child sense carries a note of pity or affection rather than disapproval.

Urge is a strong impulse or desire pushing toward action: {I felt the urge to laugh at the worst possible moment}. As a verb, to urge is to advocate strongly or press someone toward something: {She urged him to reconsider}, {They urged caution}. You can urge a horse forward or urge a bill through committee. The word carries a sense of pressure—internal when it's a feeling, external when it's persuasion.

Urgency is the quality of requiring immediate attention or action. An urgent matter presses for resolution now, not later: {The urgency in her voice made me drop everything}. Urgency can be genuine—a medical emergency—or manufactured to pressure someone: {Don't let the salesman's false urgency rush you into a decision}.

Urgent describes something requiring immediate attention or action. An urgent {message} demands a quick response; an urgent {need} cannot wait. The word implies time pressure—delay could mean missed opportunity or harm. Urgent often appears in medical contexts ({urgent care}) and business communications, where it signals priority over routine matters.

Urges are strong impulses or desires pushing toward action, often ones that require effort to resist: {She fought the urge to laugh}, {He had sudden urges to check his phone}. The word often implies something primal or difficult to control—urges to eat, to flee, to speak out. As a verb, to urge is to push or encourage strongly: {They urged him to reconsider}, {She urged caution}.

A urinal is a plumbing fixture designed for men to urinate into while standing, typically wall-mounted in public restrooms. The word also applies to any receptacle for urine, such as a portable container used by bedridden patients. {The restroom had a row of urinals along one wall.}

Urinals are plumbing fixtures designed for urination, typically wall-mounted in men's restrooms. They allow standing use without a full toilet stall. The singular urinal refers to one such fixture: {The restroom had three urinals and two stalls}. Urinal can also mean any receptacle for urine, including portable containers used in medical settings.

Urine is the liquid waste product that the kidneys filter from blood and that the body expels through urination. It consists mainly of water along with dissolved salts and organic compounds the body needs to eliminate. In medical contexts, urine samples provide diagnostic information about health conditions, drug use, and hydration levels. The word appears in compounds like {urine test} and {urine sample}, and informally people often substitute pee or piss.

An urn is a large decorative vase, especially one with a pedestal base, often used to hold the ashes of a cremated person. Urns also serve as planters or purely ornamental vessels. A large metal container for making and dispensing hot beverages may also be called an urn: {a coffee urn}.

Urns are decorative vases, typically with a pedestal base and often featuring handles. The most solemn use of an urn is to hold the ashes of a cremated person. In classical and neoclassical art, urns appear frequently as ornamental motifs on buildings, in gardens, and on monuments. A large container for serving hot beverages may also be called an urn: {a coffee urn}. The word occasionally appears in poetic contexts evoking mortality or antiquity.

Uroboros is a circular symbol depicting a serpent or dragon eating its own tail, representing cyclicality, eternal return, or self-renewal. The image appears across ancient cultures and features prominently in alchemical imagery. It serves as a metaphor for anything that perpetually recreates itself or returns to its origin: {The project became a uroboros, each solution generating the problem it was meant to solve}. Also spelled ouroboros.

Usability is how easy something is to use—particularly software, websites, and designed objects. Good usability means users can accomplish tasks efficiently without confusion or frustration. The term is central to user experience design: {We conducted usability testing before launch}. Usability considers learnability, error prevention, and satisfaction alongside basic functionality.

The two parts of speech that use represents—noun and verb—are usually distinguished by pronunciation, with the s getting an /s/ sound in the noun, a /z/ sound in the verb. The common phrase used to, however, usually has the /s/ sound. Whether noun or verb, use involves the application of attention or effort toward some object or person to achieve something. As a noun use is generally neutral in meaning but a verb there can be negative connotations when the object is a person: They were just using me to get to the Senator.

Used describes something that has had a previous owner or has been employed before: a used {car}, used {clothing}, used {books}. The word often implies wear or reduced value compared to new items. To be {used to} something is to be accustomed to it: {I'm used to the noise by now}. {Used to} also indicates past habits or states that no longer apply: {I used to smoke}, {There used to be a theater here}.

Useful describes something that serves a practical purpose or helps accomplish a task: {a useful tool}, {useful advice}. It implies genuine utility rather than mere availability—something useful actually gets used. To {make yourself useful} is to contribute helpfully rather than stand idle. {Come in useful} means prove valuable when needed: {That extra key might come in useful someday}.
clues: Not just sitting there looking pretty

definition: Useless describes something that serves no purpose or provides no benefit: {This broken umbrella is useless}. It can describe people who fail to contribute: {He's useless in a crisis}. The word often expresses frustration or dismissal: {It's useless to argue with her}. Something useless lacks utility entirely, while something merely unhelpful might still have some value.

Uselessness is the quality of having no practical function, value, or purpose. It describes the state of being unable to serve any useful end or produce any worthwhile result. The word often carries emotional weight beyond mere description—to call something useless is usually dismissive or contemptuous. {The uselessness of the committee became apparent when nothing changed.} A sense of uselessness can afflict people who feel they have nothing meaningful to contribute.

A user is someone who uses something, most commonly a product, service, or system. In computing and technology, user refers to a person who operates software, accesses a website, or has an account on a platform: {The app has over two million active users}. User can also carry negative connotations when it describes someone who exploits others for personal gain: {He turned out to be a user who only called when he needed something}. In the context of drugs, a user is someone who takes illegal substances.

A username is a name that identifies someone on a computer system or online service, typically chosen when creating an account: {Pick a username and password}. Usernames may be real names, pseudonyms, or invented handles. On social platforms, your username is often how others find and address you: {My username is @darkwolf99}.

Usernames are the names people choose to identify themselves on websites, apps, and online services. A username is typically paired with a password to log in: {I forgot my username}. Unlike real names, usernames are often creative, anonymous, or pseudonymous: {Her username was xX_DarkAngel_Xx}. Some platforms use email addresses as usernames instead.

Users are people who use something—a product, service, system, or substance. In computing, a user is anyone who operates software or accesses a platform: {The app has millions of active users}. User often implies a relationship of consumption rather than creation. With drugs, user is a neutral alternative to addict: {a longtime heroin user}. The word can carry slight condescension when contrasted with makers or builders.

An usher is someone who guides people to their seats—at weddings, theaters, stadiums, or churches. The role involves greeting arrivals and directing traffic. As a verb, usher means to escort or guide: {She ushered us to our table}. To {usher in} is to introduce or inaugurate: {The treaty ushered in a new era of cooperation}.

Ushered is the past tense of usher, meaning to guide or escort someone somewhere: {The host ushered us to our seats}. It often suggests formal or ceremonial movement. Figuratively, to usher in is to mark the beginning of something new: {The invention ushered in a new era of communication}.

Ushers are people who guide others to their seats in theaters, churches, stadiums, or at weddings. The verb usher means to escort or guide: {She ushered us to our table}. More broadly, to usher something in is to mark its beginning or arrival: {The new policy ushered in an era of reform}.

Usual describes what normally happens or what you typically encounter—the expected, customary, or standard state of things. {I'll have my usual}, meaning the regular order. {It's business as usual} suggests nothing out of the ordinary. {The usual suspects} are the predictable candidates. As usual means as is customary: {As usual, she was running late}.

To usurp is to seize power, position, or rights without authority or legal claim. A usurper takes what belongs to another, typically through force or cunning: {The general usurped the throne}. The word extends beyond political power—anything that wrongfully displaces something else usurps it: {Television usurped radio's place in American living rooms}.

Usurpation is the act of seizing power, position, or rights without legal authority. A military coup is usurpation of government; taking credit for someone else's work is usurpation of recognition. The word implies illegitimacy—the usurper has no rightful claim to what they've taken: {The general's usurpation of the presidency sparked international condemnation}.

Usurped is the past tense of usurp, meaning to seize power, position, or rights without authority or legal right. The word typically applies to thrones, titles, or roles taken by force or illegitimate means: {The general usurped the presidency in a coup}. It can extend to less dramatic contexts: {The new software has usurped the role of traditional spreadsheets}.

A usurper is someone who seizes power, position, or rights without legitimate authority. The word implies illegitimacy—a usurper takes what rightfully belongs to another: {The general was denounced as a usurper after the coup}. In historical contexts, usurpers typically claimed thrones through force rather than succession. The term extends beyond politics: {Social media has become the usurper of traditional news}.

Usurpers are people who seize power, position, or rights without legitimate authority. The word carries strong connotations of illegitimacy—usurpers take what isn't theirs by force or cunning: {The usurpers overthrew the rightful king}. Beyond political contexts, anything that displaces what properly belongs can be called a usurper: {Streaming services became usurpers of traditional television}.

Usurping is seizing power, position, or rights without legitimate authority. A usurping general takes control of the government by force. The word implies illegitimacy—the usurper has no rightful claim to what they've taken: {The prince accused his uncle of usurping the throne}. Extended uses cover any encroachment on another's domain: {Technology is usurping traditional skills}.

Usurps means seizes power, position, or rights without legal authority. A general usurps the throne by coup. The word implies illegitimate takeover of what belongs to another: {The vice president usurped the president's authority while she was hospitalized}. Extended uses describe anything that inappropriately displaces something else: {Work had usurped every other part of his life}.

Usury is lending money at excessive or exploitative interest rates. The term originally meant any interest charged on loans—medieval Christians and Muslims considered all such charges immoral. Modern usage restricts it to predatory lending: {The payday loan industry has been accused of usury}. Laws against usury set caps on permissible interest rates.

A utensil is a tool or implement, especially one used in the kitchen for preparing or eating food: {cooking utensils}, {eating utensils}. The word covers knives, forks, spoons, spatulas, ladles, and similar handheld equipment. Outside the kitchen, utensil appears in phrases like {writing utensils} for pens and pencils, though this sounds slightly formal.

Utensils are tools or implements, especially those used for eating or cooking. The word typically refers to forks, knives, and spoons—{plastic utensils}, {a drawer full of utensils}—but extends to kitchen tools generally: {cooking utensils} like spatulas, whisks, and ladles. The singular utensil sounds slightly formal; people more often say {fork} or {spatula} than {utensil}.

The uterus is the organ in female mammals where offspring develop before birth—the womb. It's a muscular, pear-shaped structure in the pelvic cavity where a fertilized egg implants and grows. Medical terms use the Latin form: {uterine cancer}, {uterine lining}. The plural is uteri or uteruses.

Utilitarian describes things designed for practical use rather than beauty or comfort: {utilitarian furniture}, {utilitarian architecture}. The word often implies a no-frills, function-first approach. In philosophy, utilitarianism is the ethical theory that the right action is whatever produces the greatest good for the greatest number. A utilitarian in this sense judges choices by their consequences for overall well-being.

Utilitarianism is an ethical theory holding that the right action is the one producing the greatest good for the greatest number. Associated with philosophers Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, it measures morality by outcomes rather than intentions or rules. {Her utilitarianism led her to support policies that maximized overall welfare, even when they disadvantaged a few.}

Utilities are essential services—electricity, gas, water, sewage—delivered to homes and businesses through infrastructure networks. The term also refers to the companies providing these services or the bills they send: {My utilities run about two hundred a month}. In computing, utilities are small programs that perform system maintenance tasks. More broadly, utility means usefulness or practical value: {The utility of this approach remains unclear}.

Utility is usefulness—the quality of serving a practical purpose. In economics, utility measures the satisfaction derived from consuming goods or services. A utility is also a public service company providing electricity, gas, or water: {The utility raised rates again}. In computing, a utility is a small program that performs a specific task. As an adjective, utility describes something functional rather than decorative: a utility {knife}, a utility {vehicle}.
clues: Essential service like gas or electricity

definition: Utmost means the greatest or most extreme degree possible. It typically modifies abstract nouns: {utmost importance}, {utmost care}, {utmost respect}. To do your utmost is to try as hard as you can. The word combines "out" and "most"—the outermost point, the furthest extent: {We pushed our resources to the utmost}.

A utopia is an imagined perfect society where everything works harmoniously—no poverty, no injustice, no conflict. The word often carries a tinge of skepticism, implying such perfection is unattainable: {His vision of a classless society was dismissed as utopia}. Utopian thinking can be idealistic dreaming or genuine social philosophy. (Capitalized Utopia is the fictional island from Thomas More's 1516 book.)

Utopian describes an idealized vision of society—perfect, harmonious, but unrealizable. A utopian scheme sounds wonderful in theory but ignores practical obstacles: {His utopian plans for universal peace went nowhere}. The word often carries a note of naïve optimism, suggesting dreamers who underestimate human nature. As a noun, a utopian is someone who holds such ideals. (From Thomas More's 1516 book *Utopia*, describing an imaginary island society.)

Utopianism is belief in or pursuit of an ideal society—one free from the flaws of existing arrangements. The term carries both aspirational and dismissive connotations: reformers may embrace utopianism as necessary vision, while critics use it to suggest naïve impracticality. {His utopianism blinded him to political realities.} The word derives from Thomas More's 1516 *Utopia*, itself a pun on Greek words meaning "good place" and "no place."

Utopians are people who believe in or advocate for an ideal society—one free from the flaws and injustices of existing systems. The term can be admiring or dismissive: visionaries pursuing worthy goals, or naive dreamers ignoring human nature and practical constraints. {The utopians among us still believe we can eliminate poverty.} A utopian (adjective) scheme is idealistic to the point of impracticality.

Utopias is the plural of utopia, an imagined place or state where everything is perfect—social conditions, government, human nature itself. The word was coined by Thomas More for his 1516 book describing an ideal island society. Because such perfection proves impossible, utopia often carries ironic weight: {Their utopias always seem to require someone in charge}. Dystopia is the opposite.

Utter as an adjective means complete or absolute, emphasizing the extreme degree of something: {utter nonsense}, {utter chaos}, {an utter failure}. It intensifies negative qualities more often than positive ones. The verb utter means to speak or produce sounds: {She didn't utter a word}. To utter counterfeit currency is to put it into circulation—a legal term for passing off fakes as genuine.

The uvula is the small, fleshy projection that hangs from the back of the soft palate at the entrance to the throat. It's visible when you open your mouth wide: {The doctor pressed down my tongue to see my uvula}. The uvula plays a role in speech, swallowing, and triggering the gag reflex.

Vacancies is the plural of vacancy—empty positions or unoccupied spaces. Job vacancies are positions waiting to be filled: {The company posted three vacancies last week}. Hotel vacancies are available rooms, famously advertised on roadside signs. The word can also describe mental emptiness: {He stared with a vacancy that suggested he wasn't listening}.
clues: Jobs or rooms not yet filled

definition: Vacancy is an unfilled position or unoccupied space. A job vacancy awaits an applicant; a vacancy at a hotel means rooms are available. The word extends to emptiness of mind or expression: {He stared with vacancy in his eyes}. A vacancy rate measures how much rental property sits unoccupied in a given market.

Vacant means empty or unoccupied. A vacant {lot} has no building on it. A vacant {apartment} has no tenant. A vacant {position} awaits someone to fill it. Extended to people, vacant describes an empty expression—a vacant {stare} suggests no one's home mentally, a look of blankness or inattention.

To vacate is to leave a place empty—you vacate a hotel room, an apartment, a position. The word implies more than simply leaving; it suggests making something available for others: {We need to vacate the premises by noon}. In legal contexts, to vacate a judgment or ruling is to nullify it, rendering it void: {The court vacated the conviction}.

Vacating is leaving a place or position, making it empty and available: {We're vacating the apartment at the end of the month}. Courts vacate judgments when they nullify them, as if clearing the decision from the record. The word implies formal or complete departure rather than stepping out briefly.
clues: Making a place no longer occupied

definition: A vacation is a period away from work or routine, typically for rest or travel: {We're taking a vacation to the coast}. Americans vacation; the British take holidays. The verb means to go on vacation: {They vacation in Maine every summer}. School vacations are breaks between terms. To vacate a place is to leave it empty—vacation originally meant freedom from occupation.

A vacationer is someone taking a vacation—a person traveling for leisure rather than business or necessity. The word emphasizes the temporary status: {The beach was crowded with vacationers}. British English prefers holidaymaker.

Vacations is the plural of vacation—periods of time away from work or school for rest and recreation. {Summer vacations stretch longest for students.} The verb form means to take such time off: {She vacations in Maine every August.} In British English, holiday serves where Americans say vacation.

To vaccinate is to administer a vaccine—a preparation that stimulates the immune system to develop protection against a specific disease. The word comes from the Latin for cow, after the cowpox material used in the first smallpox vaccine. {Have you been vaccinated against measles?} {The clinic vaccinates children for free.} Vaccination has become contentious in public discourse, with anti-vaccination movements questioning safety and mandates.

Vaccinated describes someone who has received a vaccine—a preparation that stimulates immunity against a disease. The term gained everyday prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic, when vaccination status affected access to travel, venues, and workplaces: {Are you vaccinated?} {The restaurant requires guests to be fully vaccinated}. To vaccinate is to administer such a preparation.

Vaccination is the administration of a vaccine to stimulate immunity against a disease. The term covers both the act and the resulting protection: {Vaccination rates have dropped in some communities}. A vaccination may be given by injection, oral dose, or nasal spray. The word often appears in debates about public health policy and personal choice.

Vaccinations are doses of vaccine administered to produce immunity against diseases. The word typically refers to the act or process of receiving vaccines: {childhood vaccinations}, {COVID vaccinations}. A vaccination record documents which vaccines someone has received and when. The term often appears in debates about public health policy and individual choice.

A vaccine is a preparation administered to stimulate the immune system to produce protection against a specific disease, typically containing weakened or killed pathogens, or components of them. Vaccines are usually given by injection but may also be oral or nasal. The term also applies figuratively to preventive measures against non-medical threats: {The best vaccine against misinformation is critical thinking}. To vaccinate someone is to give them a vaccine.

Vaccines are preparations that stimulate the immune system to produce protection against specific diseases. They typically contain weakened or killed pathogens, or components of them, training the body to recognize and fight future infections. {The polio vaccine virtually eliminated the disease in developed countries}. Vaccines can also target non-infectious conditions: {a cancer vaccine}. The verb vaccinate means to administer a vaccine.

A vacuum is a space entirely devoid of matter—or more practically, a space with much less air pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. Nature {abhors a vacuum}, filling empty spaces. The word extends to any void or emptiness: {His death left a vacuum in her life}. A vacuum cleaner (or just vacuum) removes dirt by suction; to vacuum is to clean with one. In vacuum-packed goods, air has been removed to preserve freshness.

Vacuuming is cleaning with a vacuum cleaner—a machine that sucks up dust and debris from floors, upholstery, and other surfaces. The word functions as both a verb form and a noun describing the activity itself: {I spent Saturday morning vacuuming}, {The vacuuming can wait until tomorrow}. The task has become synonymous with routine household cleaning.

Vacuums is the plural of vacuum—a space empty of matter, or more loosely, any space from which air has been removed. The word extends to emptiness generally: {a power vacuum}, {a vacuum in leadership}. A vacuum is also a vacuum cleaner, and to vacuum is to clean with one: {I need to vacuum the living room}. {She bought two new vacuums for the office}.

A vagabond is a person who wanders from place to place without a fixed home or regular work. The word carries romantic connotations of freedom and adventure, but historically implied disreputability—someone on society's margins. {He spent his twenties as a vagabond, drifting through Europe}. As an adjective, vagabond describes anything wandering or unsettled: {a vagabond life}, {vagabond thoughts}.

Vagabonding is traveling without fixed plans or destination, typically for an extended period and on a modest budget. The word suggests freedom from routine obligations and openness to wherever the road leads: {She spent a year vagabonding through Southeast Asia}. Unlike tourism, vagabonding emphasizes the journey over destinations and immersion over sightseeing.

Vagabonds are people who wander from place to place without a fixed home or regular work. The word carries romantic connotations of freedom and adventure, but historically it described those on society's margins—drifters, tramps, or itinerants viewed with suspicion: {Medieval laws punished vagabonds as potential criminals}. As a verb, to vagabond is to live or travel as one: {He vagabonded across Europe for a year}.

The vagina is the muscular canal in female mammals extending from the uterus to the external opening, serving as the birth canal and the receptacle for the penis during intercourse. In casual speech, vagina often refers to the entire external female genitalia, though anatomists distinguish between the internal vagina and the external vulva.

Vagrancy is the state of wandering from place to place without a fixed home or employment. Historically, vagrancy laws criminalized homelessness and unemployment, giving police broad power to arrest people for simply having no visible means of support: {He was picked up on vagrancy charges}. Such laws have largely been struck down as unconstitutional, though the concept persists in related offenses like loitering.

A vagrant is a person without a settled home or regular work, wandering from place to place. The word carries legal weight—vagrancy laws historically criminalized homelessness and idleness. As an adjective, vagrant describes things that wander or stray: {vagrant thoughts}, {a vagrant breeze}. The term suggests aimlessness more than simple poverty.

Vagrants are people who wander from place to place without a fixed home or regular employment. The term carries legal weight in many jurisdictions, where vagrancy laws historically criminalized being homeless or unemployed in public spaces. {Police rounded up vagrants sleeping under the bridge.} The word has a somewhat dated, official feel compared to more neutral terms like homeless people, and can imply judgment about someone's lifestyle or choices.

Vague describes something unclear, indefinite, or lacking precise boundaries. A vague {answer} doesn't commit to specifics. A vague {memory} is hazy rather than sharp. A vague {shape} in the fog can't be identified. Someone who is vague may be evasive or simply uncertain: {She was vague about her plans for the weekend}.

Vaguely means in an imprecise or unclear way: {I vaguely remember meeting him once}. It can indicate slight degree—not quite reaching full awareness or feeling: {The name sounds vaguely familiar}, {I felt vaguely uneasy}. Something vaguely resembling another thing shares only loose or approximate similarity: {a vaguely Mediterranean flavor}.

Vagueness is the quality of being unclear, imprecise, or indefinite. A statement has vagueness when its meaning or boundaries aren't sharply defined: {The vagueness of the contract led to disputes}. Vagueness can be accidental or strategic—politicians sometimes cultivate vagueness to avoid commitment. In philosophy, vagueness refers to concepts with fuzzy boundaries, like "tall" or "bald," where no precise cutoff exists.

Vain describes excessive pride in one's appearance or abilities—someone vain spends too long at the mirror or fishing for compliments. The word also means futile or unsuccessful: {a vain attempt}, {in vain}. To {take someone's name in vain} is to use it disrespectfully, especially God's name in casual oaths.

A valedictorian is the student with the highest academic standing in a graduating class, typically delivering the farewell speech at commencement. The honor carries significant prestige in American high schools and colleges: {She was named valedictorian of her class}. The title comes from a Latin word meaning to say farewell.

Valedictorians are students who deliver the valedictory address at graduation, typically those with the highest academic standing in their class. The honor usually goes to whoever earns the top grade point average: {She was named valedictorian of her high school class}. Some schools now name multiple valedictorians to avoid cutthroat competition over fractions of a point.

A valentine is a card or gift given on Valentine's Day, February 14th, expressing affection or romantic interest: {She received a dozen valentines from secret admirers}. The word also refers to the person who receives such a token or to a sweetheart in general: {Will you be my valentine?} The association with love dates to medieval traditions linking the feast day with courtship. (Capitalized Valentine is a given name or the saint.)

Valentines are cards, gifts, or messages exchanged on Valentine's Day, February 14th, expressing affection or romantic interest. The term also refers to the people receiving such tokens—a sweetheart or loved one: {She's been my valentine for twenty years}. Children exchange valentines at school parties, while adults might send flowers or chocolates to their valentines. (Capitalized Valentines typically appears in Valentine's Day.)

A valet is a personal attendant who handles clothing, grooming, and related duties for a wealthy employer—the gentleman's gentleman. The word extends to hotel employees who park guests' cars: {The valet brought the car around}. As a verb, to valet is to perform such services. A valet is also a stand for holding clothes and accessories.

Valets is the plural of valet, a person who performs personal services for another—originally a manservant who attends to clothing, grooming, and travel arrangements. The word now most commonly refers to someone who parks cars at hotels, restaurants, or events: {The valets were backed up because of the wedding reception}. As a verb form, valets means provides such service: {He valets at the country club on weekends}.

Valiant means brave and determined, especially in the face of danger or difficulty. The word carries a somewhat formal or literary tone, often describing heroic effort: {a valiant warrior}, {a valiant attempt to save the company}. A valiant effort may fall short but still earns respect for its courage and determination.

Valid means sound, well-grounded, or legally binding. A valid {argument} follows logical rules. A valid {passport} hasn't expired and will be accepted by authorities. A valid {point} deserves consideration. Valid {criticism} has merit. In computing, valid input meets required format specifications: {Please enter a valid email address}. The opposite is invalid.

To validate is to confirm something is legitimate, accurate, or acceptable. You validate a parking ticket to avoid paying, validate data to ensure it meets requirements, or validate a theory through testing. In emotional contexts, to validate someone is to acknowledge their feelings as real and reasonable: {I just needed someone to validate my concerns}. Validation often implies official approval or endorsement.

Validated is the past tense of validate, meaning to confirm something as true, accurate, or acceptable. Documents get validated by officials, parking tickets get validated by merchants, and scientific findings get validated through replication. In emotional contexts, to feel validated is to have your feelings or experiences acknowledged as legitimate: {I just needed someone to listen—I felt so validated}.
clues: Checked and found to be accurate

definition: Validating is confirming something's accuracy, legitimacy, or worth. You validate a parking ticket to avoid paying, validate data to ensure it meets requirements, or validate a theory through testing. In psychological contexts, validating someone means acknowledging their feelings as real and reasonable: {She felt better after her therapist validated her concerns}. The word implies official or authoritative confirmation.

Validation is the act of confirming something is correct, legitimate, or acceptable. Documents require validation to prove authenticity. In technical contexts, validation checks that data meets specified requirements: {The form failed validation because the email field was empty}. Emotionally, validation means acknowledgment that someone's feelings or experiences are reasonable: {She just needed validation that her anger was justified}. To seek validation is to want approval or confirmation of one's worth.

Validity is the quality of being sound, well-grounded, or legally binding. A valid argument holds up to scrutiny; a valid passport is current and properly issued; a valid excuse is one that others accept as legitimate. In logic and statistics, validity has technical meanings related to whether conclusions follow from premises or whether a test measures what it claims to measure. {The court questioned the validity of the contract.} {Scientists debated the validity of the study's findings.}

A valkyrie is a female figure from Norse mythology who chooses which warriors die in battle and carries the worthy to Valhalla. The word literally means "chooser of the slain." In modern use, valkyrie often describes a fierce, formidable woman, especially one associated with battle or determination: {She swept through the office like a valkyrie on a mission}. The image appears frequently in fantasy games, heavy metal iconography, and opera—Wagner's "Ride of the Valkyries" being the most famous example. (Capitalized Valkyrie may be a proper name or title.)

Valkyries are figures from Norse mythology—female spirits who choose which warriors die in battle and escort the worthy to Valhalla. The word literally means "choosers of the slain." In modern use, valkyrie often describes a fierce, powerful woman: {She descended on the meeting like a valkyrie}. Wagner's "Ride of the Valkyries" has made the term synonymous with dramatic, thunderous arrivals. (Capitalized Valkyries refers to the mythological beings specifically.)

A valley is a low area of land between hills or mountains, typically with a river flowing through it. Valleys form through erosion by water or glaciers over time. The word extends to any elongated depression: {the valley between two waves}. In anatomy, a valley is a groove or depression between raised areas. {We hiked down into the valley at sunset.}

Valleys is the plural of valley—low areas of land between hills or mountains, typically with a river or stream running through them. Valleys often shelter communities and agriculture: {The valleys were green with spring crops}. Figuratively, valleys represent low points between peaks: {the peaks and valleys of economic cycles}.

Valor is courage in the face of danger, especially in battle. The word carries a formal, elevated tone—you're more likely to encounter it in military citations and historical accounts than everyday speech: {medals awarded for valor}, {acts of valor on the battlefield}. Valor suggests not just bravery but nobility of spirit.

Valour is the British spelling of valor—courage in the face of danger, especially in battle. The word carries a formal, almost ceremonial tone: {medals for valour}, {acts of valour}. It suggests not just bravery but nobility of spirit, the kind of courage worthy of honor and remembrance.
clues: Courage in the face of peril

definition: Valuable describes something worth a lot—whether in money, usefulness, or importance. A valuable {painting} commands a high price. Valuable {advice} proves genuinely helpful. Valuable {time} shouldn't be wasted. As a noun, valuables are possessions worth protecting: {She locked her valuables in the hotel safe}.

Valuables are possessions worth significant money—jewelry, electronics, important documents, cash. The term appears most often in warnings and insurance contexts: {Don't leave valuables in your car}. A hotel safe protects valuables. What counts as valuable varies by context; at a beach, your phone and wallet qualify.

Valuation is the process of determining what something is worth, or the figure arrived at through that process. Financial professionals perform valuations on companies, real estate, and assets to establish fair market prices for buying, selling, or taxation purposes. {The startup's valuation exceeded one billion dollars after the latest funding round.} Unlike value, which can be abstract or subjective, valuation typically implies a formal assessment expressed in monetary terms.

Value is what something is worth, expressed either in numbers or in something of comparable worth: Does a college education have value equal to its cost? In math, value is a magnitude or quantity that can be represented by a number. In the plural, values refers to the beliefs and views that a person or group holds about what is right and wrong. The verb value can mean place a value on, but more often it means to regard or esteem highly: I really value the time I had with my grandparents.

Valued means considered important or precious: {a valued member of the team}, {valued customers}. Something valued has worth assigned to it, whether emotional or monetary. The word implies appreciation and esteem—to be valued is to matter to someone. In technical contexts, valued simply means having a value assigned: {a null-valued variable}.

Values are the principles or standards a person or group considers important—beliefs about what is right, good, or worthwhile that guide behavior and judgment: {family values}, {traditional values}, {Our company values integrity above all}. The word often appears in political and moral discourse: {voters concerned about values}. Values also serves as the plural of value in its other senses: the values of variables, the values of properties.

Valuing is the act of determining worth or holding something in esteem. An appraiser valuing a house assesses its market price. Someone valuing honesty considers it important: {She's always valuing loyalty above all else}. The word carries both the calculating sense of appraisal and the emotional sense of appreciation.

A valve is a device that controls the flow of liquid, gas, or loose material through a passage—opening, closing, or partially blocking it. Heart valves regulate blood flow between chambers. Valves in brass instruments alter pitch by changing the path of air. The word extends to any mechanism that permits flow in one direction only: {a safety valve}, {a pressure-relief valve}. Figuratively, a valve is an outlet for releasing pressure: {Exercise serves as a valve for stress}. (Capitalized Valve is the video game company.)

Valves are devices that control the flow of liquids or gases through a pipe or channel, opening or closing to regulate passage: {a heart valve}, {the valve on a radiator}. In brass instruments, valves redirect air through different tube lengths to change pitch. The term extends to any structure that permits flow in one direction while preventing backflow: {The veins have valves that keep blood moving toward the heart}.

Vamoose means to leave quickly, often to avoid trouble or detection: {Let's vamoose before the cops show up}. The word has a slightly comic, old-fashioned flavor, evoking Westerns and cartoon escapes. It comes from Spanish *vamos* (let's go).

Vamoosed is the past tense of vamoose, meaning to leave quickly or make a hasty departure. The word comes from Spanish *vamos* (let's go) and carries a playful, slightly old-fashioned tone: {By the time the cops showed up, he'd already vamoosed}. It suggests slipping away rather than formal departure.

The noun vamp can be one of the following: a woman who seduces men to gain advantage; a repeated set of notes or chords in music; the top part of a boot or shoe that is sewn onto the sole; or a vampire. To vamp is to act like a seducing vamp, or to make something fresh and interesting by adding new parts: I’m going to vamp up my wardrobe.

Vamping is the act of improvising or filling time, especially in music where a performer repeats a simple chord progression or rhythmic pattern while waiting for a cue or another musician. The term extends beyond music to any situation where someone stalls or ad-libs: {The host kept vamping until the guest arrived}. In a different sense, vamping describes seductive behavior, derived from vamp as a femme fatale who uses charm to manipulate others.

A vampire is a mythical creature that rises from death to drink the blood of the living, typically by biting the neck. Vampires in folklore and fiction are associated with immortality, nocturnal activity, and aversion to sunlight, garlic, and crucifixes. The word extends to people who drain others emotionally or financially: {an emotional vampire who exhausts everyone around her}. A vampire bat actually drinks blood, lending biological reality to the myth.

Vampires is the plural of vampire—mythological creatures that rise from the dead to drink blood from the living. In folklore and fiction, vampires are typically immortal, nocturnal, and repelled by garlic, sunlight, or crucifixes: {The castle was said to be haunted by vampires}. Figuratively, a vampire is anyone who drains others' energy or resources: {emotional vampires who exhaust everyone around them}.

Vampirism is the practice or condition of being a vampire—surviving by drinking blood. The word covers both the mythological phenomenon and, in clinical contexts, a rare delusion or fetish involving blood consumption. Figuratively, vampirism describes any parasitic draining of another's resources or vitality: {corporate vampirism}, {emotional vampirism}.

Vamps is the plural of vamp, which has two distinct meanings. A vamp is the upper front part of a shoe or boot covering the instep. Separately, a vamp is a seductive woman who uses her attractiveness to manipulate men—short for vampire in its figurative sense: {silent film vamps like Theda Bara}. To vamp is to improvise an accompaniment or repeat a simple musical figure while waiting: {The pianist vamped until the singer was ready}.

Vampy describes a style that's darkly seductive and glamorously predatory—think deep red lipstick, smoky eyes, and an air of dangerous allure. The word draws on the femme fatale sense of vamp (a woman who uses her sexuality to manipulate), not the bloodsucking creature. {She went for a vampy look with black nails and a plunging neckline.}

A van is a boxy motor vehicle larger than a car but smaller than a truck, designed for carrying passengers or cargo: {delivery van}, {moving van}, {minivan}. The rear typically opens for loading. In British usage, van often specifically means a cargo vehicle, while Americans use it for passenger vehicles too: {soccer mom in her van}. (Capitalized Van is a name or name prefix.)

A vandal is someone who deliberately damages or destroys property, especially public property or things of beauty. The word carries connotations of senseless destruction rather than theft or purposeful damage: {Vandals spray-painted graffiti on the memorial}. The term extends to anyone who defaces or ruins something through carelessness or malice: {Some vandal scratched my car in the parking lot}. (Capitalized Vandal refers to the ancient Germanic tribe.)

To vandalise is to deliberately damage or deface property, especially public property: {Someone vandalised the bus shelter with spray paint}. The word carries connotations of senseless destruction rather than theft—damage for its own sake. Vandalise is the British spelling; Americans use vandalize.

Vandalised is the British spelling of vandalized, past tense of vandalize—to deliberately damage or deface property: {The bus shelter had been vandalised with spray paint}. The word derives from the Vandals, a Germanic tribe notorious for sacking Rome, though historians note their destruction was exaggerated.

Vandalising is the British spelling of vandalizing—deliberately damaging or defacing property, especially public property: {Someone's been vandalising the bus shelters again}. The word implies senseless destruction rather than theft, often targeting things like buildings, vehicles, or monuments.
