In manufacturing, waterjet cutters slice through metal, stone, and other materials using water forced through a narrow nozzle, sometimes mixed with abrasive particles. Waterjets also appear in cleaning equipment, dental tools, and boat propulsion systems: {The sculptor used a waterjet to shape the granite}.

Waterlilies are aquatic plants with large floating leaves and showy flowers that grow in ponds and slow-moving water. The round leaves, called lily pads, rest on the surface while roots anchor in mud below. Monet's paintings made waterlilies iconic in art: {The museum has three of his waterlilies}. Also spelled water lilies.

A waterlily is an aquatic plant with large flat leaves that float on the surface and showy flowers that rise above the water. The leaves are round or heart-shaped, and the flowers—white, pink, yellow, or blue—open during the day or night depending on species. Waterlilies grow rooted in mud at the bottom of ponds and slow streams: {The pond was covered with waterlilies}.

The waterline is the level where water meets the hull of a boat or ship. A vessel sits lower when heavily loaded, higher when light—the waterline shifts accordingly. Ships often have marks painted on their hulls showing safe loading levels. The term extends to any boundary between water and air: {The waterline on the bathtub showed how high the flood had risen}. It also refers to the margin where fingernails meet skin at the base.

Waterlogged describes something so saturated with water that it can barely function. A waterlogged boat sits dangerously low, heavy with absorbed water. Waterlogged soil can't drain; waterlogged wood has lost its structural integrity. The word often implies damage or uselessness from prolonged exposure: {The field was too waterlogged to play on}.

A watermark is a faint design visible in paper when held to light, created during manufacture to indicate origin or prevent counterfeiting. Currency and official documents bear watermarks as security features. The term extends to digital marks embedded in images or documents to establish ownership: {The photographer's watermark appeared across every preview}. To watermark is to add such a mark.

Watermarking is embedding an identifying mark or pattern into something—typically digital content like images, audio, video, or documents. The mark may be visible or invisible, designed to prove ownership, prevent counterfeiting, or track unauthorized distribution: {The studio watermarks screeners to trace leaks}. The term extends from traditional watermarks pressed into paper during manufacture.

Watermarks are faint designs or patterns embedded in paper, visible when held to light, originally used to identify the papermaker and now commonly seen in currency to prevent counterfeiting. Digital watermarks are invisible codes embedded in images, audio, or video to track ownership or detect unauthorized copying: {The stock photo still had watermarks on it}. To watermark something is to apply such a mark.

Watermelon is a large fruit with a hard green rind and sweet, juicy flesh—typically red or pink with black seeds, though seedless and yellow varieties exist. The flesh is mostly water, making it a summer staple: {We brought watermelon to the picnic}. The word also names the trailing vine that produces the fruit.

Watermelons is the plural of watermelon, the large fruit with green rind, red flesh, and black seeds—a summer staple at picnics and barbecues. {We bought three watermelons for the Fourth of July party.} The word also appears in the crude expression {carrying watermelons}, a nervous excuse for being somewhere you don't belong, from the film *Dirty Dancing*.

A watermill is a mill powered by flowing water, historically used for grinding grain into flour. A water wheel captures the current's energy to turn millstones or drive machinery. Watermills were essential infrastructure before steam and electric power: {The village watermill ground wheat for the whole county}.

A waterpark is a recreational facility featuring water-based attractions—pools, slides, wave machines, lazy rivers, and splash areas. Most waterparks are outdoor summer destinations, though indoor versions operate year-round: {The kids spent all day at the waterpark}. Also spelled as two words: water park.

Waterparks are recreational facilities built around water-based attractions—pools, slides, wave machines, and lazy rivers. They range from modest outdoor complexes to massive indoor resorts. The term also applies to the attractions themselves: {The kids want to spend the whole day at the waterpark}. Also spelled as two words: water parks.

Waterproof describes something that doesn't allow water to penetrate: a waterproof {jacket}, waterproof {mascara}. The word functions as a noun for a garment that repels water and as a verb meaning to make something resistant to water: {We waterproofed the deck before winter}. Water-resistant suggests partial protection; waterproof implies complete.

Waterproofing is the process of making something resistant to water penetration, or the material used to achieve this: {The basement needs waterproofing}, {We applied waterproofing to the deck}. The term covers both the act and the substance—sealants, membranes, or coatings that prevent water damage.

Waters is the plural of water, used when distinguishing among bodies of water or types: {international waters}, {territorial waters}, {the waters of the Caribbean}. To {test the waters} is to gauge a situation before committing. {Muddy the waters} means to confuse an issue. A woman's {waters break} when amniotic fluid releases before childbirth. (Capitalized Waters is a surname.)

A watershed is the ridge of high land dividing two drainage basins—water falling on one side flows to one river system, on the other side to another. By extension, watershed names the entire drainage area feeding a river: {the Mississippi watershed}. The figurative meaning dominates in everyday speech: a watershed moment or watershed event marks a turning point where things change decisively, like water dividing to flow different directions. In British broadcasting, the watershed is the time (usually 9 PM) before which adult content cannot air.

A watershed is the ridge of high land dividing two drainage basins—rain falling on one side flows to one river system, on the other side to another. By extension, a watershed is a turning point or dividing line between two phases or conditions: {The discovery of penicillin was a watershed in medical history}. The term also refers to the entire drainage basin itself—all the land whose water flows to a single river or lake.

To waterski is to glide across water on one or two long narrow boards while being towed by a motorboat, gripping a handle attached to a rope. The boards themselves are waterskis. The activity combines elements of skiing and surfing: {We spent the afternoon waterskiing on the lake}. Also spelled as two words: water ski.

A waterskier is someone who skis on water, pulled behind a motorboat while standing on one or two skis. The term covers both recreational enthusiasts and competitive athletes who perform slalom, jumping, or trick skiing: {The waterskier carved through the boat's wake}.

Waterskiing is being towed behind a motorboat while standing on one or two skis, gliding across the water's surface. The sport requires balance, arm strength, and a driver who knows what they're doing: {We went waterskiing every summer at the lake}. Variants include barefoot skiing and slalom skiing on a single ski.

A waterskin is a container for carrying water, traditionally made from animal hide or bladder that has been treated to hold liquid without leaking. Before the invention of plastic bottles and canteens, waterskins were essential gear for travelers, soldiers, and anyone venturing far from reliable water sources. The term now appears mostly in historical contexts or fantasy settings: {The ranger filled his waterskin at the stream before continuing into the desert}.

Waterskins are containers for carrying water, made from animal hide or bladder sewn into a pouch. Before canteens and plastic bottles, travelers and soldiers relied on waterskins for portable hydration: {The hikers filled their waterskins at the stream}. The word now appears mostly in historical fiction and fantasy settings.

Waterskis are a pair of long, narrow boards strapped to the feet for gliding over water while being towed by a motorboat. The sport requires balance and grip strength as the skier holds a tow rope and leans back against the pull: {She slalomed expertly on a single waterski}. To waterski is to engage in the activity.

A waterslide is a slippery chute or track with flowing water, used for recreational sliding into a pool or splash area. Waterslides range from backyard plastic sheets to elaborate amusement park structures with twists, drops, and enclosed tubes: {The kids spent all afternoon on the waterslide}. Also spelled as two words: water slide.

Waterslides are recreational chutes or channels with water flowing through them, designed for sliding down into a pool or splash area. They range from simple backyard versions to elaborate amusement park attractions with twists, drops, and tunnels: {The kids spent all afternoon on the waterslides}. Also spelled as two words.

A waterspout is a tornado that forms over water, appearing as a rotating column of air and mist extending from a cloud to the water's surface: {We watched a waterspout form over the bay}. Waterspouts are usually weaker than land tornadoes but can still be dangerous to boats. Separately, a waterspout is a pipe or spout that discharges water, as on a fountain or roof gutter.

Waterspouts are rotating columns of water and spray that form over bodies of water, essentially tornadoes over seas or lakes. They descend from storm clouds in a funnel shape, drawing water upward: {We watched a waterspout form over the bay}. The term also refers to pipes or spouts that discharge water, as from a roof gutter.

Watertight describes something sealed so completely that water cannot enter or escape: a watertight {container}, a watertight {seal}. The figurative sense dominates: a watertight {alibi} has no gaps; a watertight {argument} cannot be refuted; a watertight {contract} leaves no room for dispute. The common thread is impermeability—nothing gets through.

A waterway is a navigable body of water—a river, canal, or channel used for travel or transport: {The Erie Canal opened a waterway from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic}. The term emphasizes the water's function as a route rather than its natural features. Inland waterways connect ports and facilitate commerce where roads cannot.

Waterways are navigable bodies of water—rivers, canals, channels, or coastal routes used for transportation or commerce. The term emphasizes the water's function as a passage: {The Mississippi was once America's most vital commercial waterway}. Waterways may be natural or artificial, like the canals connecting the Great Lakes.

A waterwheel is a large wheel fitted with paddles or buckets around its rim, positioned so that flowing or falling water turns it. The rotation powers machinery—historically for grinding grain, sawing lumber, or driving bellows. Waterwheels were the primary source of mechanical power before steam engines: {The old mill's waterwheel still turns, though it no longer grinds flour}.

Waterwheels is the plural of waterwheel, a large wheel turned by flowing or falling water to generate power. For centuries, waterwheels drove mills for grinding grain, sawing lumber, and other mechanical work: {The old waterwheels along the river have been restored as historical landmarks}. They represent an early form of renewable energy, largely replaced by turbines.

Water wings are inflatable armbands worn by children learning to swim, providing buoyancy to keep them afloat: {She put water wings on her daughter before they got in the pool}. The term sometimes extends to other flotation devices for beginners. Also spelled as two words.

Waterworks refers to a system of reservoirs, pipes, and pumps that supplies water to a city or region: {The city's waterworks dates to the 1890s}. In informal British usage, waterworks means the urinary system: {The doctor asked about my waterworks}. To turn on the waterworks is to start crying, especially theatrically or manipulatively: {She turned on the waterworks when the cop pulled her over}.

Watery describes something containing or resembling water. Watery eyes produce tears; watery soup is too thin. A watery {grave} is death by drowning. Watery colors are pale and washed out. The word often suggests dilution or weakness: {watery coffee}, {a watery smile}. {Her eyes grew watery as she read the letter.}

A watt is a unit of power measuring the rate of energy transfer—one joule per second. Named for Scottish inventor James Watt, it quantifies electrical consumption {a 60-watt bulb}, mechanical output {a 250-watt motor}, and other energy flows. Kilowatts and megawatts scale up for larger applications. {The space heater draws 1500 watts.}

Wattage is electric power measured in watts, indicating how much energy a device consumes or produces: {Check the wattage before plugging in multiple appliances}. The term extends to intensity or impact generally: {Her stage presence has serious wattage}. Higher wattage means more power—literally for lightbulbs, figuratively for star quality.

Wattle has two unrelated meanings. One is a fleshy growth hanging from the head or neck of certain birds, especially turkeys and roosters—the red dangly bit. The other is a construction method using interwoven sticks and branches, often plastered with mud or clay: {wattle and daub}. In Australia, wattle refers to various acacia trees and shrubs, whose flexible branches were traditionally used in wattle construction.

Wattles are the fleshy, often reddish lobes that hang from the throat or chin of certain birds, especially chickens and turkeys. The term extends to similar structures on other animals. Separately, wattles are rods or stakes interwoven with branches to form fences or walls—wattle and daub being an ancient building technique using this framework plastered with mud or clay.

Watts are units of power in the International System, measuring the rate of energy transfer. One watt equals one joule per second. The term appears constantly in discussions of electricity and appliances: {a 60-watt light bulb}, {The microwave uses 1200 watts}. Watts measure how much energy something consumes or produces per unit of time. (Capitalized Watts is a surname.)

Wave describes a kind of movement, like the one resulting from a disturbance in water in which a ridge moves toward shore. This inspires other designations, like rhythmic movements of the hand in greeting or farewell, or a recurring and regular oscillation, like radio waves. The repeating swells of water caused by tides are called waves, and by extension, anything that suddenly swells and then dissipates is also a wave: wave of sadness. The verb wave characterizes movement that oscillates or that varies in a limited way: a flag waving in the breeze, wave to the fans, wave a magic wand. If you make waves you disrupt the regularity of a state or process.

Waved is the past tense of wave. To wave is to move something back and forth in the air, typically a hand in greeting or farewell: {She waved goodbye from the platform}. Hair that is waved has gentle curves or undulations, either natural or styled: {Her waved hair fell softly around her shoulders}.

A waveform is the shape of a wave when represented visually—typically as a graph showing amplitude over time. The term appears most often in audio and electronics: {The waveform showed a clean sine wave}. Sound editing software displays audio as waveforms, letting users see volume and patterns. Different wave shapes (sine, square, sawtooth) produce distinct sounds in synthesizers.

Wavelength is the distance between successive peaks of a wave—whether light, sound, or radio. Different wavelengths of light produce different colors; different wavelengths of radio carry different stations. Figuratively, people on the same wavelength think alike or communicate easily: {We're just not on the same wavelength}.

Waver means to fluctuate or show uncertainty. A person wavers between options, unable to commit: {She wavered on whether to accept the job}. Physical wavering is unsteady movement—a flame wavers in the breeze, a voice wavers with emotion. Something unwavering is firm and resolute. Not to be confused with waive, meaning to forgo a right or requirement.
clues: Cannot seem to make up mind

definition: Wavered is the past tense of waver, meaning to fluctuate or show indecision. Someone who wavered moved back and forth between choices or commitments: {She wavered between accepting the job and staying where she was}. It can also describe physical unsteadiness—a voice that wavered, a flame that wavered in the wind. {His resolve never wavered.}

Wavering describes unsteady movement or uncertain resolve. Something that wavers physically oscillates or flickers: {The candle flame wavered in the draft}. More often, wavering applies to hesitation or indecision: {Her wavering commitment worried the team}. A wavering voice trembles with emotion or uncertainty. To be unwavering is to hold firm without doubt or fluctuation.

Wavers is the plural of waver, a moment of hesitation or unsteadiness: {His voice had wavers in it}. More commonly wavers is a verb—to fluctuate, hesitate, or show uncertainty: {She wavers between acceptance and rejection}. Something that wavers moves unsteadily: {The candle flame wavers in the draft}. Not to be confused with waiver, a legal release of rights.

Waves are ridges of water moving across a surface, caused by wind or disturbance. The ocean's waves crash on beaches; smaller waves ripple across ponds. Wave extends to any undulating motion or pattern: {waves of grain}, {radio waves}, {heat waves}. A wave of something is a sudden surge: {a wave of nausea}, {waves of immigrants}. To wave is to move the hand in greeting or signal, or to move back and forth: {flags waving in the breeze}. Hair that waves has gentle curves. (Capitalized Waves or WAVES was the women's naval reserve in World War II.)

Waving is the act of moving a hand back and forth as a greeting, farewell, or signal: {She was waving from the platform as the train pulled away}. It also describes anything moving with a similar undulating motion: {flags waving in the breeze}, {fields of waving grain}. In hair styling, waving creates soft, flowing curves.

Wavy describes something with waves or wave-like curves: {wavy hair}, {wavy lines}. The pattern suggests gentle undulation rather than sharp angles or tight curls. Wavy can describe physical surfaces, visual patterns, or motion: {The flag hung wavy in the breeze}. In slang, wavy means cool or stylish, suggesting smooth, effortless appeal.

Substances designated as wax share several qualities: solid at room temperature, melting at about 40 °C, and often occurring naturally, like beeswax or earwax. To wax something is to apply a protective coat of wax to it. A different verb wax means to increase in size or intensity and is most typically used of the moon from new moon to full moon. If someone waxes poetically, lyrically, or eloquently, for example, they express themselves in those ways.

Waxed is the past tense of wax in its two distinct senses. One meaning is to apply wax—a waxy coating, a waxed floor, waxed paper. The other is the older verb meaning to grow or increase: {The moon waxed full}. This second sense survives mainly in {wax and wane} and in phrases like {wax poetic} or {wax nostalgic}, meaning to become increasingly so: {He waxed eloquent about his hometown}.

Waxes covers both verbs. From wax meaning to apply wax: {She waxes her car every month}, {He waxes his legs}. From the older wax meaning to grow or increase, now literary or archaic except in set phrases: the moon waxes and wanes, {to wax poetic}, {to wax nostalgic}. The noun plural refers to waxy substances: {candle waxes}, {ear waxes}.

Waxing is the process of applying and removing wax—most commonly to remove body hair. Hot wax is spread on skin, allowed to harden, then stripped away, pulling hairs from the roots: {She gets a waxing before vacation}. Waxing also means applying wax for shine or protection: {waxing the car}, {waxing skis}. A waxing moon is one growing fuller, approaching full—the opposite of waning.

A waxwing is a crested songbird with silky plumage, named for the waxy red tips on some wing feathers. Three species exist worldwide, including the cedar waxwing and Bohemian waxwing of North America. They travel in flocks and feed heavily on berries: {A flock of waxwings stripped the holly bush in an hour}.

A waxwork is a lifelike figure made of wax, typically depicting a famous person. The term usually appears in the plural—waxworks—referring either to a collection of such figures or the museum housing them: {We visited Madame Tussauds and saw the waxworks of celebrities}. Figuratively, someone standing unnaturally still might be compared to a waxwork.

Waxworks is a museum or exhibition of wax figures, typically depicting famous people or scenes from history. The figures are life-sized sculptures made from wax, often startlingly realistic: {We visited the waxworks to see the royal family}. Madame Tussauds is the most famous example. The singular waxwork refers to an individual figure.

Waxy describes something resembling wax in texture, appearance, or feel—smooth, slightly shiny, and pliable. Waxy {leaves} have a protective coating. Waxy {skin} looks pale and unnaturally smooth, often suggesting illness. A waxy {buildup} is a film of accumulated residue. Waxy {potatoes} hold their shape when cooked, unlike starchy varieties that fall apart.

Way is one of the oldest and still one of the most useful nouns in English. It has dozens of meanings that have arisen out of its oldest and most central idea: a thoroughfare for travel. Today’s most frequent use of way is to designate a manner, mode, or method, especially one for achieving a goal. Way appears in dozens of fixed expressions with one of its core meanings, such as give way, by the way, lead the way, make one’s way, and by way of.

A wayfarer is a person who travels on foot, especially over long distances. The word is literary and old-fashioned, evoking pilgrims, wanderers, and solitary journeys: {The wayfarer rested beneath an oak tree}. It suggests someone without a fixed destination or home, moving through the world rather than toward a particular place.

Wayfarers are people who travel on foot, especially those journeying long distances. The word is literary and old-fashioned, evoking pilgrims, wanderers, and travelers of earlier eras: {The inn offered shelter to weary wayfarers}. Wayfarer also names a classic style of sunglasses with thick, trapezoidal frames.

Wayfaring means traveling on foot, especially over long distances. The word is literary and old-fashioned, evoking journeys made by pilgrims or wanderers rather than modern tourists: {a wayfaring stranger}, {wayfaring folk of the Middle Ages}. A wayfarer is one who travels this way.

A wayfinder is a person skilled in navigation, especially one who guides others through unfamiliar territory. The term appears in Pacific Islander traditions, where wayfinders navigate vast ocean distances using stars, waves, and wildlife. More broadly, it describes anyone who helps others find their way—literally or figuratively: {She became a wayfinder for first-generation college students}.

Wayfinders are people who navigate, especially using traditional methods like reading stars, waves, or landscapes rather than modern instruments. The term often refers to Polynesian navigators who crossed vast Pacific distances by observing natural signs. More broadly, a wayfinder is anyone who finds or charts a path forward: {The early wayfinders of the civil rights movement}.

Wayfinding is the process of navigating through an environment—figuring out where you are and how to get where you're going. The term appears most often in architecture and urban planning, where it describes signage systems, landmarks, and spatial layouts that help people orient themselves: {The airport's wayfinding could use improvement}. It also applies to natural navigation skills and digital interfaces.

Waylaid is the past tense of waylay, meaning to ambush or intercept someone, typically to rob or attack them: {Bandits waylaid the travelers on the mountain road}. More often now, it describes being stopped or delayed unexpectedly: {I was waylaid by my neighbor on the way out the door}. The word suggests being caught off guard while in transit.

To waylay is to ambush or intercept someone, typically to attack, rob, or delay them: {Bandits waylaid travelers on the mountain road}. The word suggests lying in wait along someone's path. Figuratively, it means to stop someone unexpectedly, often to make demands on their time: {She was waylaid by reporters outside the courthouse}.

Waylaying is lying in wait to ambush or intercept someone, typically to rob or attack them: {Bandits were waylaying travelers on the mountain road}. More loosely, it means stopping someone to make demands on their time: {She kept getting waylaid by colleagues on her way to the meeting}. Present participle of waylay.

A waypoint is a designated stopping point or reference location along a route. In navigation—whether hiking, flying, or using GPS—waypoints mark specific coordinates to guide travel: {We set waypoints every few miles along the trail}. The term extends to any intermediate goal or milestone in a journey or process.

Waypoints are specific locations along a route, used for navigation. In aviation and maritime contexts, waypoints are coordinates that define a flight path or course: {The pilot programmed the waypoints into the GPS}. Hikers and drivers use waypoints to mark stops or turns along a journey. In video games, waypoints often appear as on-screen markers guiding players to objectives.

Ways is the plural of way, covering all its meanings: methods, directions, distances, and customs. It appears in many fixed expressions: {mend your ways} means reform your behavior; {parting of the ways} marks a separation; {ways and means} refers to methods, especially for raising money. In nautical contexts, ways are the tracks on which a ship slides during launching. The suffix -ways forms directional adverbs like sideways, lengthways, and always.

Wayside refers to the edge or side of a road or path. It appears most often in the expression {fall by the wayside}, meaning to fail to continue or to be abandoned before completion. The phrase originates from biblical parable about seeds that fell on the path and failed to grow. Something that falls by the wayside drops out of contention or gets left behind while others progress: {Many promising projects fell by the wayside during budget cuts}.

A waystation is a stopping point along a route—originally a place where travelers could rest and resupply between destinations. The term extends to any intermediate stage in a journey or process: {The hostel served as a waystation for migrants heading north}. A waystation implies temporary pause rather than final destination.

Waystations are stopping points along a route, places where travelers can rest, resupply, or transfer between stages of a journey. The term originally referred to stations along stagecoach or railway lines. Now it often appears figuratively for intermediate steps in any process or progression: {The job was just a waystation on her path to something better}. Also spelled as two words: way stations.

Wayward describes someone or something that resists control or follows an unpredictable, self-willed course. A wayward {child} defies authority; a wayward {curl} won't stay in place. The word carries a sense of straying from what's expected or proper—not necessarily rebellious, but difficult to guide or govern: {Her wayward impulses led her far from the path her parents had planned}.

The adjective weak is the opposite of strong and has some overlap in meaning with poor and vulnerable. The weak point in a process, argument, or physical object is the place most vulnerable to attack. Physically weak suggests an inability to resist force. A weak economy is not growing and has poor prospects. A weak signal is hard to distinguish or interpret. The weak refers collectively to groups unable to defend themselves. A weak verb inflects according to a predictable pattern.

Weaken means to make or become less strong. Physical structures weaken under stress; resolve weakens under pressure; arguments weaken when evidence contradicts them. {The disease had weakened him considerably.} {Her confidence weakened as the interview went on.} To weaken a position is to undermine it; to weaken in resolve is to waver.

Weakened describes something that has lost strength, force, or effectiveness. A weakened {immune system} is more vulnerable to infection. A weakened {argument} has been undermined by counterevidence. {The storm weakened as it moved inland}. The word implies a previous state of greater power or resilience that has diminished.

A weakling is a person or animal lacking physical strength or stamina. The word often carries contempt—calling someone a weakling suggests they're pathetically feeble: {Don't be such a weakling; pick up the box}. It extends to moral or emotional weakness: {He was a weakling who couldn't stand up to his overbearing mother}.

Weaklings are people who lack physical strength, courage, or force of character. The word carries contempt—it's not a neutral description but a judgment: {The coach had no patience for weaklings}. Someone might be called a weakling for failing to stand up for themselves or for being easily overpowered. The singular weakling applies to one such person.

Weakness is the state of lacking strength, power, or effectiveness. A weakness in a structure is a vulnerable point; a weakness in an argument is a flaw. Personal weaknesses are shortcomings or deficiencies: {Public speaking is my weakness}. The word also describes fondness that undermines resolve: {I have a weakness for chocolate}. In this sense, weakness implies susceptibility to temptation.

Weaknesses is the plural of weakness—areas where someone or something falls short or is vulnerable. A person's weaknesses might be character flaws, gaps in knowledge, or susceptibilities: {Chocolate is my weakness}. In strategic contexts, weaknesses are points that can be exploited: {The report identified weaknesses in the company's cybersecurity}. The word often pairs with strengths in assessments of people, plans, or organizations.

Wealth is an abundance of valuable resources or possessions. In its most concrete sense, wealth means money and property: {She inherited great wealth from her uncle}. More broadly, wealth describes any plentiful supply: {a wealth of experience}, {a wealth of information}. The wealthy are those who have accumulated substantial riches. Wealth often carries implications of prosperity beyond mere sufficiency—not just having enough, but having more than enough.

Wealthy means having a great deal of money or valuable assets. The word suggests established, substantial riches rather than a sudden windfall: {a wealthy family}, {a wealthy neighborhood}. Wealthy can also describe abundance beyond money: {a region wealthy in natural resources}. The noun {the wealthy} refers collectively to rich people as a class.

To wean is to gradually transition a young mammal from mother's milk to other food: {The puppies were weaned at six weeks}. By extension, wean means to detach someone from a habit, dependency, or source of comfort: {She's trying to wean herself off social media}, {He was slowly weaned from painkillers after the surgery}. The process implies gradual withdrawal rather than abrupt separation.

Weaned is the past tense of wean, meaning to transition a young mammal from mother's milk to other food: {The puppies were weaned at six weeks}. By extension, weaned describes being gradually detached from any dependency or habit: {She was weaned off painkillers}, {He was weaned on classic rock}—raised with early, formative exposure to it.

Weaning is the process of transitioning a baby or young animal from breast milk or formula to other food sources. The term extends to any gradual withdrawal from dependence: {weaning yourself off caffeine}, {weaning the economy off fossil fuels}. The process implies a shift toward independence, whether physical or psychological.

A weapon is anything used to attack or defend in combat—from knives and guns to clubs and fists. The word extends to anything deployed against an opponent: {Humor was her best weapon}. Nuclear weapons, biological weapons, and chemical weapons are categories of mass destruction. To weaponize something is to turn it into a means of attack: {They weaponized social media}.

Weaponisation is the process of converting something into a weapon or using it as one. A pathogen can be weaponised for biological warfare; uranium is weaponised to make nuclear bombs. Figuratively, weaponisation describes turning ordinary things into tools of attack: {the weaponisation of social media}, {weaponising someone's past against them}. British spelling of weaponization.

To weaponise something is to convert it into a weapon or adapt it for military use: {They weaponised the drone}. More often figurative—turning something benign into a tool for attack or harm: {weaponised incompetence}, {weaponising social media}, {She weaponised his own words against him}. The spelling with -ise is British; Americans write weaponize.

To weaponise something is to convert it into a weapon or adapt it for military use: {weaponised anthrax}, {weaponised drones}. More broadly, it means to exploit something as a tool for attack or advantage: {They weaponised social media to spread disinformation}, {She accused him of weaponising their children in the divorce}. British spelling of weaponized.

Weaponising is the British spelling of weaponizing—turning something into a weapon or using it as one. The term applies literally to military development {weaponising drones} but more often appears figuratively: weaponising information, weaponising social media, weaponising the justice system. The implication is that something neutral or benign has been converted into a tool for attack or coercion.

Weaponization is the process of turning something into a weapon or using it as one. Nuclear material undergoes weaponization when made into bombs. More often the term is figurative: the weaponization of {information}, of {social media}, of {the justice system}. The implication is that something neutral or benign has been repurposed for attack: {the weaponization of victimhood}, {weaponized incompetence}.

To weaponize something is to adapt it for use as a weapon or turn it into a means of attack. Military programs weaponize biological agents or nuclear material. Figuratively, anything can be weaponized—information, social media, legal processes: {They weaponized the court system to bankrupt their opponents}. The term implies deliberate transformation of something neutral or benign into something harmful.

Weaponized describes something converted into or used as a weapon. A weaponized {virus} has been modified for military use. The term extends beyond literal armaments: weaponized {rhetoric}, weaponized {social media}, weaponized {incompetence}. In these figurative uses, something ordinarily neutral becomes a tool for attack or manipulation: {They weaponized his past mistakes against him}.

Weaponizing is turning something into a weapon or using it as one. The literal sense applies to military contexts: {weaponizing anthrax}, {weaponizing drones}. More often the word appears figuratively—exploiting something for attack or advantage: {weaponizing social media}, {weaponizing the justice system}, {weaponizing someone's past against them}. The implication is that something neutral or benign has been converted into a tool for harm.

Weaponry is a collective noun for weapons, especially military weapons considered as a group. The term emphasizes the arsenal aspect—the full range of arms available to a fighting force or nation. {The country's nuclear weaponry remains a closely guarded secret.} {Medieval weaponry included swords, crossbows, and siege engines.} Unlike the simpler weapons, weaponry often carries connotations of organized military capability or technological sophistication.

Weapons are objects designed or used to injure, kill, or destroy. The term covers everything from knives and clubs to firearms and nuclear missiles. Weapons can also be figurative—anything deployed to gain advantage: {Her sharp wit was her most effective weapon}. To weaponize something is to turn it into a weapon or use it as one: {They weaponized social media to spread disinformation}.

A weaponsmith is a craftsman who forges weapons—swords, axes, spears, and similar arms. The term appears most often in fantasy fiction and video games, where weaponsmiths sell or upgrade equipment: {I need to find a weaponsmith to repair my blade}. In historical contexts, the work overlapped with blacksmithing and armoring.

The verb wear usually takes an item of clothing as its object and is used to describe the state of being dressed in that item of clothing: What are you going to wear? I’m wearing a tux. Some items worn are not garments, but the same verb is used because they adorn or protect the body: wear a badge, wear a seatbelt. If you wear an expression, such as a smile, you are displaying it. When something other than a human is the subject, wear has different meanings. Something that wears off loses its effectiveness or appeal. Something that wears out becomes unusable through fatigue or overuse. The noun wear can describe the process of deterioration through use, or in combination, a particular kind of clothing, such as outerwear.

Wearable describes something designed to be worn on the body: {wearable art}, {wearable technology}. As a noun, wearables are electronic devices worn as accessories or clothing—fitness trackers, smartwatches, health monitors: {She tracks her sleep with a wearable}. The term emerged with miniaturized computing but applies broadly to anything suitable for wearing.

Wearables are electronic devices designed to be worn on the body—smartwatches, fitness trackers, heart monitors, smart glasses. The term emerged with the rise of portable computing and health-tracking technology: {My wearables sync to an app on my phone}. In fashion contexts, wearables may simply mean clothing or accessories that can actually be worn, as opposed to avant-garde pieces meant only for display.

Wearily is an adverb describing actions done with fatigue, exhaustion, or a lack of energy. Someone who speaks wearily sounds tired and possibly discouraged. {She wearily climbed the stairs after her double shift.} The word can suggest physical tiredness but often carries overtones of emotional or mental depletion—a weariness born from repetition, frustration, or resignation rather than simple lack of sleep.

Weariness is the state of being weary—tired, fatigued, or drained of energy. Physical weariness follows exertion: {weariness after a long hike}. Mental or emotional weariness comes from prolonged stress, monotony, or frustration: {a weariness with politics}, {the weariness in her voice}. The word carries a sense of heaviness that simple tiredness doesn't quite capture.

Wearing describes something that causes fatigue or gradual erosion. A wearing {day} leaves you exhausted. A wearing {journey} depletes your energy. The word captures slow depletion rather than sudden impact—the cumulative effect of sustained effort or stress. {Her constant criticism was wearing on everyone.}

Weary means exhausted or drained of energy, whether physical or mental. You might be weary after a long hike or weary of constant demands on your attention. The word suggests a deeper fatigue than simply tired—often tinged with resignation: {She grew weary of his excuses}. As a verb, to weary is to make or become tired: {The endless meetings wearied everyone}.

A weasel is a small, slender carnivorous mammal with short legs and a long body, known for hunting rodents and rabbits. The weasel's reputation for cunning and evasiveness gives rise to figurative uses: a weasel is a sneaky, untrustworthy person. To weasel is to evade or escape from something: {He weaseled out of his promise}. Weasel words are deliberately vague language meant to mislead without technically lying.

Weaseled is the past tense of weasel, meaning to evade or escape from a situation through cunning or deceit. To weasel out of something is to avoid an obligation or commitment by sneaky means: {He weaseled out of paying his share}. The verb draws on the weasel's reputation for slipperiness and slyness.

Weaseling is the act of evading responsibility, commitment, or direct answers through evasive or underhanded means. Someone weaseling out of a promise finds excuses to avoid fulfilling it: {He's weaseling out of helping us move}. The term draws on the weasel's reputation for sneaky, slippery behavior. Weaseling can also mean inserting oneself somewhere through cunning: {She weaseled her way into the meeting}.

Weaselling is evading or escaping from a commitment or responsibility through cunning or deceit. The image comes from the weasel's reputation for slipperiness and its ability to squeeze through tight spaces. Someone weaselling out of a promise finds clever excuses to avoid keeping it: {He's weaselling out of paying his share}. Also spelled weaseling.

Weaselly describes behavior that is evasive, sneaky, or dishonestly indirect—like a weasel slipping through narrow spaces to avoid capture. A weaselly answer dodges the question. A weaselly person avoids commitment or responsibility through slippery maneuvers: {His weaselly excuses fooled no one}. The word carries strong contempt for cowardly dishonesty.

Weasels are small carnivorous mammals with long slender bodies, short legs, and keen hunting instincts. They're known for pursuing prey into burrows and killing animals larger than themselves. The singular weasel also describes a sneaky, untrustworthy person. To weasel is to evade or escape through cunning: {He weaseled out of his commitment}. Weasel words are deliberately vague expressions used to avoid saying something directly.

Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a given time and place—temperature, precipitation, wind, clouds. {What's the weather like?} Climate is long-term patterns; weather is day-to-day. To weather something is to endure it: {weather a storm}, {weather criticism}. Wood or stone that weathers shows effects of exposure to the elements. {Under the weather} means feeling unwell.

Weatherbeaten describes something worn, roughened, or damaged by prolonged exposure to sun, wind, rain, and other elements. A weatherbeaten face shows deep lines and leathery skin from years outdoors. A weatherbeaten barn has faded paint and warped boards. The word suggests endurance through harsh conditions: {the weatherbeaten fishing boats in the harbor}.

Weatherbound means unable to proceed or depart because of bad weather. Ships stay weatherbound in harbor during storms; travelers find themselves weatherbound at airports when flights are grounded. {We were weatherbound for three days waiting for the snow to clear.} The word applies to any situation where weather prevents planned movement or activity.

A weathercock is a weather vane in the shape of a rooster, mounted on a rooftop to show wind direction. The cock swivels freely, always pointing into the wind. Figuratively, a weathercock is someone who shifts opinions or loyalties readily: {He's a political weathercock, changing positions with every poll}.

Weathered describes something worn, changed, or aged by exposure to the elements. Weathered wood has been bleached and roughened by sun, wind, and rain. Weathered stone shows the erosion of centuries. A weathered face bears the marks of time spent outdoors—lined and leathery. Figuratively, weathered suggests having endured difficulty: {a weathered veteran of political campaigns}. To have weathered something is to have survived it: {They weathered the crisis}.

Weathering is the gradual breakdown of rock, stone, or other materials through exposure to the elements—wind, rain, frost, and sun. The process shapes landscapes over millennia and erodes buildings over decades. Figuratively, weathering means enduring or surviving difficulty: {She's weathering the crisis well}. The adjective weathered describes something worn or aged by exposure: {a weathered face}, {weathered wood}.

A weatherman is a person, typically on television or radio, who presents weather forecasts. The term remains common despite being gendered; *weather forecaster* or *meteorologist* serves as a neutral alternative. {The weatherman says it's going to rain all week.}

Weathermen is the plural of weatherman, a person who forecasts and reports weather conditions, typically on television or radio. The term has fallen somewhat out of favor as the profession has become less male-dominated, with {weather forecaster} or {meteorologist} now preferred. {The weathermen are predicting snow for the weekend.}

Weatherproof means resistant to damage from rain, wind, sun, or other weather conditions: {a weatherproof jacket}, {weatherproof sealant for the deck}. As a verb, to weatherproof something is to treat or modify it for weather resistance: {We need to weatherproof the windows before winter}.

A weathervane is a device mounted on a rooftop or high point that pivots to show wind direction, typically featuring an arrow or decorative figure like a rooster. Figuratively, a weathervane is someone whose opinions shift with prevailing sentiment: {Critics called the senator a political weathervane}.

Weathervanes are devices mounted on rooftops or poles that rotate to show wind direction. Typically featuring a pointer or decorative figure—a rooster is traditional—they pivot on a vertical axis so the arrow or figure faces into the wind. Figuratively, a weathervane is someone whose opinions shift with prevailing sentiment: {Politicians are weathervanes, turning whichever way the wind blows}.

Weave is to interlace threads or strips to create fabric or a structure—the fundamental process behind textiles, baskets, and wicker furniture. The pattern of interlacing is also called a weave: {a tight weave}, {a loose weave}. Extended meanings involve combining elements into a whole: {She wove the anecdotes into a compelling narrative}. To weave through traffic or a crowd is to move by threading between obstacles. A weaver is one who weaves; a loom is the apparatus.

A weaver is someone who interlaces threads to make fabric, working at a loom or by hand. The term extends to creatures that construct by similar methods: weaverbirds build elaborate nests from interwoven plant fibers, and weaver ants bind leaves together with silk. Figuratively, a weaver crafts something from disparate elements: {a weaver of tales}, {a weaver of conspiracies}.

A weaverbird is a small African or Asian bird known for constructing elaborate nests woven from grass, leaves, and other plant fibers. The intricate, often globe-shaped nests hang from tree branches and demonstrate remarkable architectural skill. Males typically build the nests to attract mates. Also called weaver.

Weavers are people who weave—interlacing threads on a loom to create cloth. The term extends to anything that weaves: weaver {ants} construct nests from leaves, weaver {birds} build elaborate woven nests. Figuratively, weavers create complex things from disparate elements: {weavers of tales}, {weavers of dreams}.

Weaves is the plural of weave—patterns or methods of interlacing threads to create fabric: {The shop displayed textiles in various weaves}. It's also the verb form: a basket maker weaves reeds, a storyteller weaves tales, a drunk driver weaves through traffic. Hair weaves are extensions woven into natural hair for added length or fullness.

Weaving is the craft of interlacing threads or strips to create fabric or other materials. Vertical warp threads are held taut while horizontal weft threads pass over and under them. The term extends to any similar interlacing: {basket weaving}, {weaving palm fronds into a roof}. To weave through something is to move by threading between obstacles: {She was weaving through traffic}. The past tense is wove for fabric, weaved for movement.

A web is a network: either a tangible one, such as spiders weave, or an intangible one, such as the World Wide Web, which is now increasingly just called the web. Most instances of web before another noun have to do with the World Wide Web (website, web design, web address). A web of deceit or web of lies is an interconnected pattern of them. If an animal’s feet are webbed, there is a membrane of skin between its toes.

Webbing is strong woven fabric made in flat strips, used for belts, straps, and structural support in furniture and equipment: {The lawn chair's webbing had started to fray}. The term also describes any web-like membrane or structure, particularly the skin between the toes of ducks, frogs, and other aquatic animals.

A webcam is a small video camera connected to or built into a computer, used for video calls, streaming, or recording. The word combines web and camera. Webcams became standard equipment during the rise of remote work and video conferencing: {Turn on your webcam for the meeting}. {She covers her webcam with tape for privacy}.

Webcams are small video cameras designed to stream or capture images for transmission over the internet. They're built into laptops and phones or attached externally to computers for video calls, livestreaming, and security monitoring. The singular webcam combines "web" and "camera": {Turn on your webcam for the meeting}. {She covers her webcam with tape for privacy}.

Webcasts are broadcasts transmitted over the internet, typically audio or video content streamed live or made available on demand. The term blends "web" and "broadcast," distinguishing internet delivery from traditional radio or television. Companies webcast conferences, universities webcast lectures, and musicians webcast performances: {The keynote will be webcast for remote attendees}.

A webcomic is a comic strip or graphic narrative published online rather than in print. Webcomics range from simple daily strips to elaborate serialized stories, and the format allows creators to bypass traditional publishing: {I've been reading this webcomic for years}. Many webcomic artists build audiences through social media and support themselves via subscriptions or merchandise.

Webcomics are comics published online rather than in print. The format ranges from simple strips to elaborate graphic narratives, often serialized on dedicated websites or social media. The medium allows creators to bypass traditional publishing: {I've been following that webcomic since 2008}. Many successful webcomics have later been collected in print editions.

A webinar is a seminar conducted over the internet, typically featuring a presenter or panel speaking to a remote audience who can watch, listen, and sometimes submit questions. The format became ubiquitous during the COVID-19 pandemic: {I have three webinars scheduled this week}. Most webinars are business or educational presentations, often recorded for later viewing.

Webinars is the plural of webinar, a seminar conducted over the internet. Webinars typically combine video presentation with interactive features like chat, polls, and Q&A sessions. They're standard fare in corporate training, marketing, and online education: {I sat through three webinars today}. The word blends web and seminar.

A webisode is an episode of a series made specifically for online distribution rather than television broadcast. The term blends "web" and "episode." Webisodes may be original content or supplementary material tied to a TV show, offering bonus scenes or spin-off storylines. {The show released webisodes between seasons to keep fans engaged.} They typically run shorter than traditional episodes, often just a few minutes.

A webmaster is the person responsible for maintaining a website—managing its content, functionality, and technical operation. The term emerged in the early days of the World Wide Web when a single person often handled everything from coding to content updates: {Contact the webmaster if you find broken links}. Now somewhat dated, as web responsibilities have fragmented into specialized roles like developer, content manager, and SEO specialist.

A webnovel is a novel published online, typically in serial installments rather than as a complete book. The format emerged from Asian platforms—particularly Chinese, Korean, and Japanese sites—and often features fantasy, romance, or cultivation genres with hundreds of chapters. Webnovels are frequently amateur works, sometimes later adapted into published books, comics, or television series: {I've been reading this webnovel that updates daily}.

A webpage is a single document on the internet, viewable through a browser. Websites consist of multiple webpages linked together. The term emerged in the 1990s as the World Wide Web developed, though *page* now often suffices: {I bookmarked the page}. Also spelled as two words: web page.

A webpage is a single document on the World Wide Web, displayed in a browser. Websites consist of multiple webpages linked together. The term emphasizes the document itself rather than the site it belongs to: {The webpage wouldn't load}, {I bookmarked that webpage}. Also spelled as two words: web page.

Webs is the plural of web—structures of interlaced threads or filaments. Spiders spin webs to catch prey. By extension, any interconnected network: {a web of lies}, {a web of intrigue}. The World Wide Web shortened to {the web}. As a verb, webs means creates such connections or becomes entangled: {Conspiracy theories webbed through the forum}.

A website is a collection of related pages on the internet, accessed through a single address. Websites serve countless purposes—news, commerce, entertainment, personal expression. The word is sometimes styled as two words (web site) but the single word dominates: {I found it on their website}. Also shortened to site.

Websites are locations on the internet, collections of pages accessible through a browser. A website might belong to a business, a government, a publication, or an individual. The word emerged in the 1990s as the World Wide Web became public: {Have you seen their new website?} Often shortened to site.

A webslinger is someone who shoots webs, virtually always referring to Spider-Man or characters with similar powers. The term combines the superhero's signature ability with the Old West connotation of "slinger"—someone quick and skilled with their weapon. {The friendly neighborhood webslinger swung between buildings.} Used affectionately by fans and in comic book discourse.

A webtoon is a digital comic designed for reading on smartphones and computers, typically formatted as a single vertical strip that readers scroll through rather than flip pages. The format originated in South Korea and has become globally popular for serialized stories across genres—romance, fantasy, horror, action: {I binge-read that webtoon in one night}. (Capitalized Webtoon is the platform.)

Webtoons are digital comics designed for reading on smartphones and computers, typically published in long vertical strips that readers scroll through rather than page through. The format originated in South Korea and has spread globally through platforms like LINE Webtoon and Tapas. {I've been binge-reading webtoons all weekend.} The term can refer to the format, individual comics, or the platforms hosting them.

Wed means to marry—to join in matrimony: {They wed in a small ceremony last June}. The past tense is wed or wedded, with wed more common in casual speech and wedded in formal contexts. Wedded also serves as an adjective meaning married or devoted: {wedded bliss}, {wedded to tradition}. Wed appears in wedding, the ceremony itself.

Wedded means married or joined in marriage: {his wedded wife}, {wedded bliss}. Beyond matrimony, wedded describes deep attachment or commitment to something: {wedded to tradition}, {wedded to the idea}. Someone wedded to a belief holds it stubbornly, for better or worse. The word carries a formal, slightly old-fashioned tone compared to married.

A wedding is a ceremony in which two people get married, along with the associated celebration: {They're planning a June wedding}. The word extends to describe things connected with the event: wedding {dress}, wedding {cake}, wedding {reception}. Figuratively, a wedding can be any union of two things: {a wedding of art and technology}.

Weddings are ceremonies marking the formal union of two people in marriage. The word covers both the legal ritual and the surrounding celebration—the reception, toasts, dancing, and cake. Wedding serves as an attributive noun for the whole event: wedding {dress}, wedding {cake}, wedding {ring}, wedding {party}. A wedding {anniversary} commemorates the date.

A wedge is a piece of material thick at one end and tapering to a thin edge at the other—the shape that lets you split wood, prop open doors, or hold wheels in place. The shape extends to food: a wedge of {cheese}, a wedge of {lemon}. In golf, a wedge is a high-lofted iron for short shots. To wedge something is to force it into a tight space: {She wedged herself between two passengers}. A wedge can also be something that divides: {The issue drove a wedge between them}.

Wedged means fixed tightly in place, as if held by a wedge—a triangular piece used to secure or split things. Something wedged is jammed into a narrow space: {The ball got wedged under the couch}. People get wedged between objects or into tight spots: {I was wedged between two large passengers on the flight}. Figuratively, wedged suggests being stuck or squeezed in: {a small country wedged between two superpowers}.

Wedges are tapered pieces—thick at one end, thin at the other—used to split, secure, or lift. A wedge of wood holds a door open; a wedge driven into a log splits it. The shape extends to food: {a wedge of cheese}, {lemon wedges}. Wedge shoes or heels have soles that form a single sloping piece rather than a separate heel. To wedge is to force into a tight space: {She wedged herself between the seats}. A wedge can also be something that divides: {The issue drove a wedge between old allies}.

A wedgie is the uncomfortable condition of having underwear or other clothing ride up and bunch in the crack of the buttocks. As a prank, giving someone a wedgie means grabbing their underwear from behind and yanking upward: {The older kids gave him a wedgie in the locker room}. An atomic wedgie pulls the waistband over the victim's head.

Wedgied means having received a wedgie—the prank where someone yanks another person's underwear upward from behind, jamming the fabric into the buttocks. The term appears in schoolyard contexts and comedy: {He got wedgied in the locker room}. As an adjective, it describes the uncomfortable state of having one's underwear bunched up: {I've been wedgied all day from these briefs}.

Wedgies is the plural of wedgie, referring either to an uncomfortable condition where underwear rides up between the buttocks, or to the prank of deliberately yanking someone's underwear upward to cause this: {The older kids gave him wedgies in the locker room}. Wedgies also names a style of women's shoes with wedge-shaped heels.

Wedlock is the state of being married. The word sounds old-fashioned or formal in most contexts, surviving mainly in the phrase {born out of wedlock}—meaning born to unmarried parents. {They were joined in holy wedlock.}

Weds is the third-person singular present tense of wed, meaning to marry: {She weds her longtime partner next month}. The word appears frequently in headlines, where its brevity makes it useful: {Royal Heir Weds Commoner}. In extended use, weds can mean to unite or combine: {The design weds form and function}.

Wee means very small or tiny: {a wee bit of sugar}, {the wee hours of the morning}. The word is common in Scottish and Irish English and sounds quaint or playful elsewhere. Separately, wee is childish or euphemistic for urination: {I need to have a wee}, {The dog weed on the carpet}.

Weeaboo is a mildly derisive term for a non-Japanese person obsessively devoted to Japanese pop culture—anime, manga, video games—often to the point of affecting Japanese mannerisms or speech. The term implies cringe-worthy overcorrection: preferring Japanese versions of everything, inserting Japanese words into English sentences, or romanticizing Japan unrealistically. {He's such a weeaboo—he insists on saying "kawaii" instead of "cute".} Often shortened to weeb, which can be self-deprecating or affectionate among fans.

Weeaboos are non-Japanese people, typically Westerners, obsessively devoted to Japanese pop culture—anime, manga, video games—often to the point of fetishizing Japan itself. The term is dismissive, implying someone who idealizes Japanese culture based on shallow media consumption rather than genuine understanding: {He's such a weeaboo—he thinks living in Tokyo would be like an anime}. Sometimes shortened to weeb, which can be either self-deprecating or affectionate among fans.

A weeb is someone obsessively interested in Japanese culture, especially anime and manga. The term began as an insult (shortened from weeaboo) but has been partially reclaimed by fans themselves: {I stayed up all night watching anime like the weeb I am}. It implies someone whose enthusiasm crosses into cringe territory—collecting figurines, learning Japanese phrases, adopting anime mannerisms. Some distinguish weeb (casual fan) from weeaboo (insufferable obsessive), though usage varies.

Weed is any plant growing where it isn't wanted, typically one that spreads aggressively and competes with cultivated plants. Gardeners spend considerable time pulling weeds. The word extends to aquatic plants that choke waterways and, informally, to tobacco or marijuana: {You got any weed?} As a verb, to weed means to remove unwanted plants, or figuratively to eliminate undesirable elements: {They weeded out the weakest candidates}. A person may be called a weed if they're tall and gangly.

Weeded is the past tense of weed—to remove unwanted plants from a garden or lawn: {She weeded the flower beds all morning}. Extended to removing unwanted elements generally: {The hiring manager weeded out unqualified applicants}. Something described as weeded has had its weeds removed: {a freshly weeded vegetable patch}.

Weeding is the act of removing unwanted plants from a garden or cultivated area: {I spent Saturday morning weeding the flower beds}. The term extends to any process of removing unwanted elements: {weeding out unqualified applicants}, {weeding the collection of damaged books}. The work is tedious but necessary—left unchecked, weeds overwhelm what you're trying to grow.

Weedkiller is a substance used to destroy unwanted plants. The term is slightly more common in British English, where Americans tend to say herbicide. Most weedkillers are chemical sprays applied to lawns, gardens, or agricultural fields: {She sprayed weedkiller along the fence line}.

A weedman is a marijuana dealer, typically someone who sells relatively small quantities for personal use rather than a large-scale trafficker: {I need to text my weedman}. The term is casual and familiar, suggesting an ongoing customer relationship rather than a one-time transaction.

Weeds are plants growing where they're not wanted—in gardens, lawns, or fields, competing with cultivated plants for resources. The word extends to anything unwelcome that spreads aggressively: {Misinformation is a weed in public discourse}. To weed is to remove unwanted plants, or figuratively to eliminate undesirables: {weed out the underperformers}. In the plural, weeds can mean widow's mourning clothes, now archaic: {She wore her weeds for a year}. {In the weeds} means overwhelmed or mired in details, from restaurant slang for a server who's fallen behind.

A weedwacker is a handheld power tool with a rotating plastic line that cuts grass and weeds in areas a lawn mower can't reach—along fences, around trees, against walls. Also called a string trimmer or weed eater. The motor spins the line fast enough to slice through vegetation: {I need to weedwack along the back fence}.

To weedwhack is to cut down weeds, tall grass, or overgrown vegetation using a string trimmer—a handheld power tool with a rapidly spinning nylon cord. The term comes from Weed Eater, an early brand name that became genericized. {I spent Saturday morning weedwhacking along the fence line.} Also spelled weed-whack or weed whack.

A weedwhacker is a handheld power tool with a rapidly spinning plastic line that cuts grass and weeds in areas a lawnmower can't reach—along fences, around trees, at the edges of flower beds. Also called a string trimmer or weed eater. The verb form describes using one: {I spent the morning weedwhacking along the driveway}.

The noun week arose to designate the seven-day cycle in which humans arbitrarily chose to subdivide time. Week may designate a calendar week, beginning on Sunday or Monday, or any consecutive period of seven days. In context, week is used synonymously with work week, where the understanding is that any event referred to will take place on a regular workday: Let’s have a meeting next week. Week has spawned the adjective and adverb weekly.

A weekday is any day from Monday through Friday—the days when most people work, as opposed to the weekend. {The museum offers discounted admission on weekdays}. Banks, government offices, and schools typically operate on weekdays. {I prefer to schedule appointments for weekdays}.

Weekdays are the five days of the week that fall between the weekend: Monday through Friday. In most Western cultures, these are the standard working and school days, as opposed to Saturday and Sunday when businesses often close and people rest. {The office is open weekdays from 9 to 5.} The singular weekday functions as both noun and adjective: {Is Thursday a good weekday for you?} {We offer weekday rates.}

The weekend is Saturday and Sunday, the two days at the end of the week when most people don't work. A long weekend includes an adjacent holiday. As a verb, to weekend somewhere is to spend that time there: {We weekended at the lake house}. The adjective form describes activities or schedules tied to those days: {weekend warrior}, {weekend getaway}.

A weekender is a person who visits a place only on weekends, often implying an outsider or part-time resident: {The beach town doubles in population when the weekenders arrive}. The word also refers to a small travel bag sized for a short trip, or to an activity or event spanning a weekend: {a jazz weekender}, {a gaming weekender}.

Weekends is the plural of weekend—the period from Friday evening through Sunday, when most people don't work. The word also functions as an adverb meaning on weekends generally: {She works weekends at the hospital}. To weekend somewhere is to spend a weekend there: {They weekended at the lake house}.

Weekly means once a week or every week: a weekly {meeting}, a weekly {newsletter}. As a noun, a weekly is a publication that appears once per week: {The village weekly covered local politics and high school sports}. Weekly also describes pay periods: {She gets paid weekly}.

A weeknight is any night from Monday through Friday, as distinguished from weekend nights. The term usually implies the evening hours when people have work or school the next morning: {I try not to stay out late on weeknights}. Weeknight television programming and restaurant specials reflect the assumption that people are home and available.

Weeknights are the evenings of Monday through Friday—the nights bracketed by workdays or school days. The term implies routine obligations rather than leisure: {I can't stay out late on weeknights}. Weeknight activities tend toward the practical or restful, saving adventure for the weekend.

Weeks is the plural of week, the seven-day period that structures most calendars and schedules. It often measures duration: {The project took weeks}, {I haven't seen her in weeks}. The plural can suggest an indefinitely long time: {We've been waiting for weeks}. {Weeks went by before we heard anything}.

Weenie is informal for a frankfurter or hot dog. It's also a mild insult for someone timid, ineffectual, or annoying: {Don't be such a weenie}. The word can mean penis in childish or euphemistic contexts. As an adjective, weenie describes something small or insignificant: {some weenie little town in the middle of nowhere}.

Weenies are hot dogs or frankfurters, especially in casual or childish speech: {We roasted weenies over the campfire}. The word also means timid or weak people, carrying a dismissive tone: {Don't be such a weenie}. Less commonly, weenie is childish slang for penis.

Weeny means very small or tiny, a playful diminutive often used with children or in informal speech: {a weeny little spider}, {just a weeny bit more}. The word carries a childish or affectionate tone. It appears in compounds like teeny-weeny and itsy-bitsy-teeny-weeny, intensifying the smallness. Weeny can also be short for weenie.

Weep means to cry, shedding tears from grief, pain, or strong emotion. It sounds more literary than cry: {She wept at the funeral}. Things that leak or ooze liquid also weep: {The wound wept fluid}. A weeping willow has branches that droop downward like a grieving figure. To weep for something is to mourn its loss.

Weeping is crying, especially prolonged or intense crying: {She found him weeping in the garden}. The word carries more gravity than crying—you weep at funerals, over losses, in grief. Things that drip or ooze may weep: {The wound was weeping}. A weeping willow or weeping cherry has branches that hang downward, as if in sorrow.

Weeps is the third-person singular of weep, meaning to cry or shed tears. Someone weeps from grief, joy, or overwhelming emotion: {She weeps whenever she watches that film}. Wounds weep when they discharge fluid. Willows weep—their branches hang downward as if in sorrow.

Weepy describes someone prone to crying or tearful at the moment: {She gets weepy at weddings}, {I've been feeling weepy all day}. It also describes things designed to provoke tears—a weepy {movie}, a weepy {ballad}. The tone is mildly dismissive, suggesting excessive or sentimental emotion rather than dignified grief.

A weevil is a small beetle with an elongated snout, typically a pest that damages stored grain, cotton, and other crops. The boll weevil devastated American cotton farming in the early twentieth century. Weevils in flour or rice are unwelcome but harmless: {I found weevils in the pasta}.

Weevils are small beetles with elongated snouts, notorious for infesting stored grains, flour, rice, and other dry goods. The larvae develop inside seeds and kernels, making infestations hard to detect until adult beetles emerge. Finding weevils in your pantry means discarding contaminated food: {The rice was crawling with weevils}.

Weft is the horizontal threads woven through the vertical warp threads on a loom. The warp provides structure; the weft creates the fabric's pattern and texture. The term extends metaphorically to anything interwoven: {the weft of social connections}, {threads woven into the weft of daily life}.

Weigh is to measure how heavy something is, typically using a scale: {She weighed the package before mailing it}. Extended uses involve careful consideration: {weigh the options}, {weigh the evidence}. To weigh on someone is to burden them: {The decision weighed heavily on her conscience}. To {weigh in} is to offer an opinion or, for athletes, to be officially measured before competition. {Weigh anchor} means to raise it before sailing.

Weighed is the past tense of weigh. Something weighed is measured for heaviness: {The package weighed three pounds}. Weighed also applies to careful consideration: {She weighed her options before deciding}. To be {weighed down} is to be burdened, physically or emotionally: {He was weighed down by guilt}.

Weighing is the act of determining how heavy something is, or the process of careful consideration. You might be {weighing ingredients for a recipe} or {weighing your options before deciding}. The word often appears in phrases like {weighing in} (offering an opinion or, for athletes, being officially measured before competition) and {weighing on} (pressing heavily, as a burden): {The decision was weighing on her}.

Weighs is the verb for determining or having a particular weight: {She weighs the produce before pricing it}, {The package weighs three pounds}. To weigh options or evidence is to consider them carefully before deciding. Something that {weighs on} you is a burden or source of worry: {The decision weighed heavily on her}. To {weigh in} is to offer an opinion or, literally, to be weighed before a competition.

When you weigh something, you determine its weight: The weight of the package is seven pounds. A person’s weight is how much they weigh: Haven’t you put on some weight? Just as weigh can mean consider, weight can also mean importance: Our argument carried weight with the senators. Units of heaviness or mass are called weights: weights and measures. In a gym, weights are the heavy objects people use in for body-building or weight training. The comparatively infrequent verb weight usually means to bias something in a particular way: Boston teachers’ salaries are weighted for the higher cost of living there.

Weighted means adjusted to give certain elements more influence or importance than others. A weighted {average} counts some values more heavily. A weighted {vote} assigns different power to different voters. Weighted {blankets} are heavy by design, filled with materials to add pressure. Something weighted toward a particular outcome favors that result: {The system is weighted against newcomers}. Literally, weighted simply means having weight added: {a weighted fishing line}.

Weightless describes the state of having no apparent weight, as experienced in orbit or freefall when gravity's pull is balanced by motion: {Astronauts floated weightless through the cabin}. By extension, something weightless feels extremely light or unburdened: {The silk was almost weightless in her hands}. Figuratively, a weightless mood suggests freedom from worry or heaviness: {She felt weightless after quitting the job}.

Weightlessness is the condition of experiencing no apparent gravitational pull—the sensation of floating freely. Astronauts experience weightlessness in orbit, not because gravity is absent but because they're in continuous free fall around Earth. The term extends to any feeling of lightness or buoyancy: {a momentary weightlessness at the top of a roller coaster}, {the weightlessness of diving into water}.

A weightlifter is someone who lifts heavy weights, either as competitive sport or for fitness training. In the strict sense, a weightlifter competes in Olympic weightlifting, performing the snatch and clean-and-jerk. More broadly, the term applies to anyone who trains with barbells, dumbbells, or weight machines to build strength or muscle. {She's been a serious weightlifter since high school.}

Weightlifters are athletes who lift heavy weights, either competitively or for fitness. In competitive weightlifting, athletes perform standardized lifts like the snatch and clean-and-jerk. More broadly, anyone who trains with weights at a gym might be called a weightlifter: {The gym was packed with weightlifters in January}.

Weightlifting is the sport or practice of lifting heavy weights, either competitively or for exercise. In competition, athletes attempt maximum lifts in specific movements like the snatch and clean-and-jerk. More broadly, weightlifting refers to any strength training with barbells, dumbbells, or weight machines: {I started weightlifting to build muscle}. Also spelled as two words.

Weights are heavy objects used for exercise, measuring mass, or holding things down. In fitness, weights include dumbbells, barbells, and kettlebells: {She lifts weights three times a week}. On a scale, weights provide standard units for comparison. Figuratively, weights are burdens or factors given importance: {The committee assigned different weights to each criterion}. In machine learning, weights are numerical values that determine how much influence inputs have on outputs.

Weighty describes something heavy, but more often appears in figurative contexts where it means significant, serious, or demanding careful consideration. A weighty {decision} or weighty {matter} carries substantial consequences and shouldn't be taken lightly. Weighty {arguments} have force and substance behind them. The word can also describe prose or speech that feels ponderous or burdensome: {The professor's weighty lectures put students to sleep}.

Weird is a general-purpose adjective to characterize anything that is unexpected or not easily explained: Where are those weird noises coming from? When someone’s behavior is described as weird it suggests that it does not conform to norms: It was weird that she didn’t acknowledge the invitation but then showed up. A weird look is one that is clearly expressive, but unclear as to what it expresses: He gave me a weird look when I asked about his plans for the evening.

Weirdness is the quality of being strange, unusual, or difficult to explain. It can describe anything from minor oddities to deeply unsettling experiences: {There's a certain weirdness to that town}, {I can't get past the weirdness of seeing my ex at work every day}. The word carries less judgment than strangeness—weirdness can be appealing or off-putting depending on context.

A weirdo is a strange or eccentric person. The word carries mild contempt—it's what you call someone whose behavior or interests strike you as off-putting or inexplicable: {That weirdo keeps staring at us}. It can also be playfully affectionate among friends: {You're such a weirdo}. Less commonly, weirdo works as an adjective: {weirdo art films}.

Weirdos is the plural of weirdo—people considered strange, eccentric, or socially off-putting. The word ranges from affectionate to dismissive depending on tone: {Theater kids? Total weirdos, but I love them} versus {Some weirdo followed me home from the bus stop}. Self-identifying weirdos often wear the label proudly.

Welcome expresses pleasure at someone's arrival or presence: {Welcome home}, {Welcome to the team}. As an adjective, it describes something gladly received: {a welcome change}, {welcome news}. To welcome is to greet or receive favorably: {They welcomed the guests at the door}. You're welcome responds to thanks, acknowledging that no debt is owed. Something is welcome to happen if it's permitted or invited: {You're welcome to stay as long as you like}.
