A winger is a player positioned on the wing—the outer edges of the field in soccer, hockey, rugby, and similar sports. Wingers typically attack down the sidelines, delivering crosses or cutting inside toward goal. In political slang, a winger is someone on the extreme end of the spectrum: {a right-winger}, {a left-winger}. The political sense often carries dismissive connotations.

Wingers are players positioned on the sides of the field in sports like soccer, hockey, or rugby—attacking from the flanks rather than the center. The term also refers to people with strong political views: {left-wingers}, {right-wingers}. In informal British usage, a winger can be someone who improvises or acts without preparation, from "wing it."

Winging is the present participle of wing, used as a verb meaning to fly or to travel by air: {Birds were winging their way south}. More commonly, winging appears in the phrase {winging it}—improvising or proceeding without preparation: {I hadn't studied, so I was just winging it on the exam}. The idiom suggests relying on instinct rather than planning.

A wingman is a pilot flying beside and behind the leader of a formation, providing support and protection. The term extends to social situations, especially dating: a wingman helps a friend approach potential romantic partners, running interference or talking them up. {I need you to be my wingman tonight.} The role implies loyal backup rather than personal agenda.

Wingmen is the plural of wingman—originally a pilot flying beside and slightly behind a lead aircraft to provide support and protection. The meaning has shifted to social contexts: a wingman helps a friend pursue romantic interests, typically by engaging others in a group or talking up the friend's qualities. {I need you to be my wingman tonight.}

A wingnut is a nut with two flat projections that allow it to be tightened or loosened by hand without tools. The shape resembles wings, hence the name. In American political slang, wingnut is a dismissive term for someone with extreme views, especially on the right: {The comment section was full of wingnuts ranting about conspiracies}. The slang sense plays on the hardware meaning—implying a screw loose.

Wingnuts are nuts with two flat projections for gripping, allowing hand-tightening without tools. Figuratively, a wingnut is a person with extreme political views, especially on the right: {The comment section filled with wingnuts ranting about the deep state}. The political sense suggests someone whose thinking has gone off-kilter. Singular: wingnut.

Wings are paired appendages that enable flight in birds, insects, and bats—or the analogous structures on aircraft. The word extends to things that flank a central body: the wings of a building, the wings of a stage (offstage areas), or the wing of a political party (its left or right faction). In sports, a wing is a player positioned near the sideline. Chicken wings, often just called wings, are a popular food item, typically fried and sauced. To wing it is to improvise without preparation: {I hadn't studied, so I just winged it}. To take someone under your wing is to mentor or protect them.

Wingspan is the distance from wingtip to wingtip when wings are fully extended. The term applies to birds, aircraft, and insects: {The albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird}. For aircraft, wingspan affects lift and maneuverability. The word extends to anything with outstretched lateral reach: {He demonstrated the wingspan of his new desk}.

Wingspans is the plural of wingspan—the distance from wingtip to wingtip when wings are fully extended. The term applies to birds, aircraft, and insects: {The albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird}. Figuratively, wingspan can suggest reach or scope: {the wingspan of her influence}.
clues: How wide birds stretch their arms

definition: A wingsuit is a specialized jumpsuit with fabric panels between the arms and legs that create wing-like surfaces, allowing skydivers and BASE jumpers to glide horizontally through the air before deploying a parachute. The suit transforms the human body into an airfoil, dramatically increasing flight time and enabling precise aerial maneuvering. {She flew her wingsuit through the narrow canyon at over 100 miles per hour.}
clues: Jumpsuit with arm and leg webbing

definition: Wingsuiting is the sport of gliding through the air using a wingsuit—a jumpsuit with fabric membranes between the arms and torso and between the legs that creates a wing-like surface. Participants typically exit from aircraft or cliff edges, achieving horizontal movement and controlled descent before deploying a parachute to land. {She took up wingsuiting after years of traditional skydiving.} The sport demands extensive skydiving experience and carries significant risk.

Wingsuits are jumpsuits with fabric panels stretched between the arms and legs, creating wing-like surfaces that allow skydivers or BASE jumpers to glide horizontally through the air before deploying a parachute. The design transforms a vertical fall into controlled flight, letting jumpers cover significant horizontal distance: {She flew through the canyon in her wingsuit}.

A wingtip is the outer end of a wing—on a bird, aircraft, or insect. In aviation, wingtips often feature specialized designs to reduce drag: {The plane's curved wingtips improve fuel efficiency}. Wingtip also names a style of dress shoe with a pointed, perforated toe cap that extends backward along the sides, resembling a bird's wing: {He wore polished wingtips to the interview}.

Wingtips are a style of leather dress shoe with a pointed toe cap that extends along the sides in a shape resembling wings, typically decorated with perforated patterns called broguing. The term also refers to the outermost ends of an aircraft's wings: {The plane's wingtips nearly scraped the hangar walls}. In both cases, the word describes the extremity of something that spreads outward.

A wingwalker is a person who performs acrobatic stunts on the wings of an airplane in flight. The practice originated in early aviation barnstorming shows, where performers would climb out of the cockpit onto the wings, sometimes transferring between planes or hanging from struts: {The wingwalker waved to the crowd as the biplane banked over the fairground}.

A wingwoman is a woman who assists a friend in romantic or social pursuits, typically by helping them meet potential partners at bars or social events. The role involves providing support, facilitating introductions, or making the friend look good: {She agreed to be my wingwoman at the party}. The term mirrors wingman, from fighter pilot terminology where a wingman flies alongside to provide backup.

To wink is to close and open one or both eyes quickly. It differs from blink in being assumed to be intentional, and often in conveying information. A wink is an instance of this. A wink of sleep, used with a negative, is a small amount of sleep. A sly wink suggests secret or implicit information aimed at its recipient. To wink at something, an indiscretion for example, is to ignore the implications of it.

Winked is the past tense of wink—to close and open one eye quickly, usually as a signal of shared understanding, flirtation, or playful conspiracy: {She winked at me across the room}. A light that winked flickered briefly. To wink at something is to pretend not to notice it: {The authorities winked at the violation}.

Winking is closing and opening one eye quickly, usually as a signal of shared understanding, flirtation, or playful conspiracy: {She caught him winking at her across the room}. The gesture suggests something unspoken between people—a secret joke, a hint not to take something seriously, or romantic interest. Winking can also be involuntary, as with a nervous tic.

Winks is the plural of wink—brief closures of one eye, typically signaling complicity, flirtation, or playful intent: {She gave him a few winks across the room}. To catch {forty winks} is to take a short nap. As a verb form, winks describes the action: {He winks at the camera whenever he tells a joke}.

Winless means having no wins, typically describing a team or competitor that has failed to win any games or matches in a period: {The team remained winless through October}. The word emphasizes futility—a winless streak carries more weight than simply saying a team hasn't won yet.

A winner is someone or something that wins—a competition, contest, or conflict. The word extends to anything notably successful: {That recipe is a winner}. In sports, a winning goal or shot is also called a winner: {She hit a backhand winner down the line}. To {pick a winner} is to identify something destined for success, often used ironically when someone has chosen poorly.

Winners are those who win—victors in competitions, conflicts, or pursuits. The word extends beyond contests to anything successful or excellent: {That new restaurant is a real winner}. A lottery winner hits the jackpot; a winner in life achieves happiness or success by whatever measure applies. In casual speech, calling something a winner endorses it: {I think this plan is a winner}.

Winning is achieving victory or success—the opposite of losing. A winning {team}, a winning {strategy}, a winning {lottery ticket}. The word also describes qualities that attract favor or approval: a winning {smile}, a winning {personality}. As a noun, winnings are money or prizes gained from gambling or competition: {She collected her winnings from the poker table}.

Winningest means having the most wins, used almost exclusively in American sports journalism: {the winningest coach in college football history}, {the winningest franchise in the league}. The word is informal and often avoided in formal writing, but it fills a gap—no elegant alternative exists for "having won the most games."

Winnings are money or prizes won through gambling, competition, or games of chance: {She collected her winnings from the poker table}, {He spent his lottery winnings on a new car}. The word is almost always plural—a single prize is typically called the winnings rather than a winning. Winnings often implies luck or chance rather than earned income.

Winnow originally means to separate grain from chaff by throwing it in the air and letting the wind blow away the lighter debris. The word now appears mostly in figurative uses: to winnow is to sift through a larger set to find what's valuable or to reduce something to its essence. {We winnowed the applicant pool down to three finalists.} {She winnowed out the weak arguments.}

Winnowing is the process of separating grain from chaff by tossing it in the air and letting the wind blow away the lighter husks. The term extends to any process of sifting through options to separate what's valuable from what isn't: {After winnowing the applicants, we had three strong candidates}. A winnowing {process} or winnowing {down} suggests gradual elimination toward a final choice.

A wino is a person, typically homeless or destitute, who drinks cheap wine to excess. The term is dismissive and often contemptuous, reducing a person to their addiction: {Some wino was sleeping on the bench}. It evokes skid row imagery—someone clutching a bottle in a paper bag.

Winos is the plural of wino, a disparaging term for a person addicted to cheap wine or alcohol generally—someone visibly down on their luck due to drinking: {The park bench was occupied by a couple of winos}. The word conjures images of shabby figures clutching bottles in paper bags.

Wins is the plural of win—victories or successes. In sports, wins are tallied against losses: {The team has twelve wins this season}. The verb wins means to achieve victory or obtain through effort: {She wins every argument}, {He wins their trust}. A win-win is a situation where all parties benefit.

Winter is the coldest season of the year, falling between autumn and spring. In the Northern Hemisphere, it runs roughly from December through February; in the Southern Hemisphere, from June through August. Winter suggests short days, bare trees, and in many regions, snow and ice. Figuratively, winter can mean a period of decline or dormancy: {the winter of one's life}. To winter somewhere is to spend the cold months there: {They winter in Florida}.

Wintergreen is a low-growing North American plant with aromatic leaves and red berries, or the sharp, minty flavor derived from it. The distinctive taste—cool and slightly medicinal—appears in chewing gum, candies, and topical pain relievers: {wintergreen mints}, {wintergreen oil}. The flavor comes from methyl salicylate, chemically related to aspirin.

Wintering is spending the winter in a particular place, especially to escape harsh weather or find resources. Birds winter in warmer climates; wealthy families once wintered in Florida or the south of France. The word also describes the care of livestock through winter months: {The sheep are wintering in the lower pastures}. As a noun, wintering names this seasonal practice or period.

Winterize means to prepare something for winter conditions. You winterize a house by insulating pipes, sealing drafts, and servicing the heating system. You winterize a car by checking antifreeze and switching to winter tires. You winterize a pool by draining and covering it. {We need to winterize the cabin before the first frost.}

Winterized describes something that has been prepared for cold weather. A winterized cabin has insulation, heating, and protected pipes. Vehicles get winterized with antifreeze, snow tires, and cold-weather fluids. {The cottage wasn't winterized, so we couldn't use it after October.} The verb winterize means to make these preparations.

Winterizing is preparing something for cold weather. You winterize a house by insulating pipes, sealing drafts, and servicing the heating system. You winterize a car by checking antifreeze and switching to winter tires. You winterize a boat or pool by draining water and adding protective chemicals before storage: {We spent the weekend winterizing the cabin}.

Winters is the third-person singular verb form of winter, meaning to spend or pass the winter season somewhere: {The geese winter in the south}, {She winters in Florida}. As a plural noun, it refers to multiple winter seasons: {After three harsh winters, they moved to a warmer climate}. (Capitalized Winters is a surname.)

Wintry describes weather or conditions characteristic of winter—cold, bleak, and harsh: {a wintry mix of snow and sleet}, {wintry winds}. The word extends to anything cold or unwelcoming: {a wintry stare}, {a wintry reception}. Also spelled wintery.

Wipe is to clean or dry a surface by rubbing it with something: {She wiped the counter with a cloth}, {He wiped his hands on his jeans}. To wipe something away or off is to remove it by rubbing: {wipe away tears}, {wipe off the dust}. To {wipe out} is to destroy completely or, in surfing and skateboarding, to fall dramatically. To {wipe the slate clean} is to start fresh. A wipe is a single rubbing motion or a disposable moistened cloth for cleaning: {baby wipes}, {disinfecting wipes}.

Wiped is the past tense of wipe—to clean or dry a surface by rubbing: {She wiped the counter}. To wipe something out is to destroy it completely: {The storm wiped out the village}. In slang, wiped means exhausted: {I'm completely wiped after that hike}. To get wiped out can also mean to fall hard, especially in surfing or skateboarding.

Wipeout is a dramatic fall or crash, especially one that sends a surfer tumbling off their board or a skier sprawling across the slopes. The term extends to any spectacular failure or total defeat: {The party suffered a wipeout in the midterm elections}. In finance, a wipeout describes the complete loss of an investment's value. As a verb phrase, wipe out means to destroy completely or exhaust utterly: {The pandemic wiped out small businesses across the country}.

Wipeouts are dramatic falls or crashes, especially in surfing and other board sports where a rider loses control and tumbles into the water or onto the ground. The term extends to any spectacular failure or total defeat: {The stock market wipeout destroyed his retirement savings}. A wipeout can also describe something being completely eliminated or erased. In casual use, wipeouts often carry a note of dark humor, particularly when no serious injury results.

A wiper is something that wipes—most often the rubber blade on a windshield wiper that clears rain or snow: {Turn on your wipers}. The term extends to any device or cloth used for wiping surfaces clean. In fishing, wiper refers to a hybrid striped bass.

Wipers are devices that clear water, snow, or debris from surfaces—most commonly the rubber blades that sweep across a vehicle's windshield: {Turn on the wipers, it's starting to rain}. Rear wipers handle back windows. The term extends to any blade or cloth used for wiping: {The machine's wipers keep the sensor clean}.

Wipes are disposable cloths, usually pre-moistened, designed for cleaning surfaces or skin. Baby wipes clean infants during diaper changes; disinfectant wipes sanitize countertops and hands. As a verb form, wipes means to clean or dry by rubbing: {She wipes down the table after dinner}. To wipe something out is to destroy or eliminate it completely. If you wipe out while skateboarding or surfing, you fall dramatically.

Wiping is the act of cleaning or drying a surface by rubbing it with cloth, paper, or the hand: {She was wiping down the counter}. In computing, wiping means erasing data completely from a storage device. The phrase {wiping the floor with} someone means defeating them decisively.

Wire is a flexible strand of metal with various purposes: binding things, making fences, and carrying electrical current or digital information. The wire is used informally for the finish line of a race, or a deadline or endpoint: The student finished the essay, but went down to the wire. A wire is also a clandestine listening device, or a telegram. To wire something, such as a message or money, to a destination is to send it there electronically. To wire a device is to connect functional wires to it. Wired is sometimes used to distinguish some devices that can also operate wirelessly, like headphones, computer mice, or microphones.

Wired means connected by wires, especially to an electrical system or network: {The house is wired for sound}. Someone who is wired is nervously energetic or overstimulated, often from caffeine or drugs: {I had three espressos and I'm completely wired}. To be wired into something is to be deeply connected to it: {She's wired into the local art scene}. Wired can also mean innately predisposed: {Humans are wired to seek social connection}. (Capitalized Wired is the technology magazine.)

A wireframe is a skeletal outline of a design, showing structure without surface detail. In web and app design, wireframes map layout and functionality before visual elements are added: {Let's review the wireframe before we start on graphics}. In 3D modeling, wireframe rendering displays objects as networks of lines representing edges, without solid surfaces.

Wireless describes technology that transmits signals without physical cables—through radio waves, infrared, or other electromagnetic means. {The café has free wireless.} As a noun, wireless can mean a wireless network or, in older British usage, a radio: {listening to the wireless}. The term gained new currency with WiFi and mobile technology.

Wires is the plural of wire—thin, flexible strands of metal used to conduct electricity or bind things together. The word often appears in contexts involving electrical systems: {The wires in this old house need replacing}. To {pull wires} or {pull strings} is to exert hidden influence. Someone who is {wired} is nervously energetic or electronically connected. {Cross wires} suggests miscommunication: {We got our wires crossed about the meeting time}.

A wiretap is a concealed listening device placed on a telephone line or other communication channel to secretly monitor conversations. The term comes from the early practice of physically tapping into telegraph and telephone wires. As a verb, to wiretap means to install such a device or conduct such surveillance: {Federal agents wiretapped the suspect's phone for six months}. Wiretapping by law enforcement typically requires a court order, though the word now extends to any covert electronic surveillance of communications.

Wiretapped describes a communication line or device that has been secretly monitored, typically by law enforcement or intelligence agencies. A wiretapped phone transmits conversations to eavesdroppers. The term comes from the original method of tapping into telegraph and telephone wires, though modern surveillance rarely involves physical wires: {The FBI wiretapped his cell phone for six months}.

A wiretapper is someone who intercepts communications by connecting to telephone lines or other transmission channels. The term comes from the original method of physically tapping into wires. Now it covers anyone who secretly monitors calls or data traffic, whether through hardware, software, or legal surveillance: {The FBI deployed wiretappers to monitor the suspect's calls}.

Wiretapping is secretly monitoring telephone or electronic communications, typically by law enforcement or intelligence agencies. The term comes from physically tapping into telephone wires, though modern surveillance intercepts digital signals: {The FBI obtained a warrant for wiretapping the suspect's phone}. Illegal wiretapping is a crime in most jurisdictions.

Wiretaps are devices or methods for secretly monitoring telephone or electronic communications, typically used by law enforcement or intelligence agencies. The term evokes its origins in physically tapping into telephone wires, though modern surveillance is largely digital. As a verb, to wiretap is to conduct such monitoring: {The FBI wiretapped his phone for six months}. Wiretapping usually requires a court order, making unauthorized wiretaps a serious crime.

Wiring refers to a system of electrical wires and connections that distribute power or signals through a building, vehicle, or device. The term also applies to the act of installing such a system: {The electrician finished wiring the new addition}. Figuratively, wiring describes how something is internally configured or predisposed to function, especially the brain or nervous system: {His wiring makes him naturally optimistic}. Faulty wiring is a common cause of electrical fires.

Wiry describes something thin, lean, and tough—like wire. A wiry person has a spare, sinewy build with visible muscle definition but little bulk; such physiques often suggest surprising strength and endurance. {He had the wiry frame of a long-distance runner.} Hair that is wiry is coarse, stiff, and springy, resistant to lying flat or being styled. The word can also describe textures or materials that have a similar tough, flexible quality.

Wisdom is the quality of having good judgment, deep understanding, and insight gained through experience. It differs from mere knowledge—wisdom involves knowing how to apply what you know: {With age comes wisdom}. Conventional wisdom refers to widely held beliefs, which may or may not be accurate. Wisdom teeth are the third molars, so called because they emerge in early adulthood when a person is supposedly wiser.

Wise is the adjective associated with wisdom; it is roughly opposite to ignorant and shares some meaning with intelligent and prudent. A wise decision or choice brings good results; a wise investment brings a good return; wise words and sayings incorporate useful information. The wise is used collectively to designate people who are wise. Wise can be used disparagingly in some expressions like don’t get wise with me (where it means insolent). To wise up is to become informed or aware.

A wiseass is someone who makes clever, sarcastic, or mocking remarks, often at inappropriate moments. The term is mildly vulgar and usually conveys annoyance with the person's attitude rather than genuine offense. It functions both as a noun {Don't be such a wiseass} and as an adjective {I'm tired of your wiseass comments}. The related wisecrack refers to the kind of remark a wiseass makes.

A wisecrack is a clever, flippant remark—often sarcastic or mocking: {He couldn't resist a wisecrack about her cooking}. The term suggests quick wit deployed for humor rather than substance. To wisecrack is to make such remarks: {She wisecracks her way through meetings}. A wisecracker is someone who does this habitually.

A wisecracker is someone who habitually makes clever, flippant remarks—the person in the group always ready with a quip or sardonic comment. The term carries a hint of annoyance; wisecracks can wear thin: {Every meeting has one wisecracker who thinks he's hilarious}.

Wisecrackers are people who make wisecracks—clever, often sarcastic remarks delivered for humorous effect. The term suggests someone quick with quips, more concerned with getting a laugh than being helpful or serious: {The back row was full of wisecrackers who wouldn't let the teacher finish a sentence}.

Wisecracking means making clever, flippant remarks—the kind of quick verbal jabs associated with old Hollywood comedies and hard-boiled detectives. A wisecracking sidekick keeps up a steady stream of quips. The word describes both the act and the person: {a wisecracking cabbie}, {She spent the whole dinner wisecracking about her ex}.

Wisecracks are clever, often flippant remarks meant to be funny or show off wit. The word implies speed and sharpness—a wisecrack lands quickly, sometimes at someone's expense: {He couldn't resist making wisecracks during the meeting}. To wisecrack is to make such remarks. A wisecracker is someone known for them.

A wiseguy is a person who makes smart-aleck remarks or acts like a know-it-all: {Don't be a wiseguy}. The term carries mild annoyance rather than genuine hostility. In a separate sense, wiseguy is slang for a member of the Mafia or organized crime—someone who's "wise" to how the underworld operates: {He was a wiseguy in the Gambino family}.

Wiseguys is the plural of wiseguy, a term with two distinct meanings in American English. In general slang, a wiseguy is someone who makes clever or sarcastic remarks, often annoyingly so: {Don't be a wiseguy—just answer the question}. In mafia contexts, wiseguys are members of organized crime families, particularly the Italian-American mob. The term carries connotations of street smarts and criminal sophistication, popularized through films and television depicting organized crime.

A wisenheimer is a person who makes smug, clever remarks or acts as if they know everything—a smart aleck. The word carries a mildly mocking tone, treating the behavior as annoying rather than genuinely offensive: {Some wisenheimer in the back row kept interrupting the lecture with sarcastic comments}. The pseudo-German suffix gives it a playful, old-fashioned quality.

A wisewoman is a woman credited with knowledge of traditional medicine, midwifery, or folk magic—the village healer or herbalist consulted before doctors were accessible. The term carries connotations of age and accumulated practical wisdom: {The wisewoman knew which herbs would ease the fever}. In historical contexts, wisewomen were sometimes accused of witchcraft.

A wish is a desire for something, especially something unlikely or impossible: {I wish I could fly}, {Make a wish and blow out the candles}. To wish is to want something to be true or to happen. You can wish someone well, wish them a happy birthday, or wish them dead. A wish can be a polite request: {It is my wish that you leave}. To get your wish is to have your desire fulfilled.

A wishbone is the forked bone between the neck and breast of a bird, formed by fused collarbones. By tradition, two people each grip one end and pull until it snaps; whoever gets the longer piece may make a wish. The shape gives its name to a football formation and various Y-shaped objects.

Wishbones are the forked bones found in birds, formed by the fusion of the two clavicles. The name comes from a tradition: two people each grip one side of a dried wishbone and pull until it snaps, and whoever ends up with the larger piece supposedly gets their wish granted. The term extends to anything Y-shaped: a {wishbone offense} in football splits receivers wide.

Wished is the past tense of wish, expressing a desire for something—often something unlikely, impossible, or contrary to fact. {She wished she had studied harder}. {He wished them well}. To wish for something is to want it: {I wished for a bicycle every birthday}. {Be careful what you wish for} warns that getting what you want may disappoint.

Wishes is the plural of wish—desires or hopes for something, especially things beyond one's immediate power to obtain: {She kept her wishes to herself}. Wishes often appear in greetings and blessings: {best wishes}, {birthday wishes}, {get-well wishes}. To send {warm wishes} is to express goodwill. The verb form means to want or hope: {He wishes he'd studied harder}.

Wishful describes thinking or feeling shaped by desire rather than reality. A wishful {hope} or wishful {thought} reflects what someone wants to be true, not what evidence supports. The phrase {wishful thinking} is especially common, suggesting self-deception or unfounded optimism: {It's wishful thinking to believe he'll change}.

Wishing is wanting something to be true or to happen, often with little expectation of bringing it about. The word carries a sense of longing or hope rather than active pursuit: {wishing for better days}, {wishing you were here}. A wishing well is where people toss coins while making wishes. {Wishing won't make it so.}

A wishlist is a collection of desired items, typically maintained for gift-giving occasions or future purchases. Online retailers let customers save wishlists of products they hope to buy or receive: {I added the book to my wishlist}. The term extends to any set of hoped-for outcomes: {Universal healthcare is at the top of progressives' wishlist}. Also spelled wish list.

Wishlists are lists of desired items, typically maintained on shopping websites or apps. Users add products they want but aren't ready to buy, creating a personal catalog for future reference or to share with gift-givers: {I added it to my wishlist for my birthday}. The term extends beyond commerce to any collection of hoped-for things: {a wishlist of travel destinations}.

A wisp is a thin, delicate strand or streak of something: {a wisp of smoke}, {a wisp of hair}. The word suggests something barely there, on the verge of dissolving. A wisp of a person is slight and frail. Will-o'-the-wisp, a flickering light over marshes, extends to anything elusive or deceptive.

Wisps is the plural of wisp—thin, delicate strands or fragments of something: {wisps of smoke rose from the chimney}, {wisps of hair escaped her braid}. The word suggests lightness and insubstantiality. A {wisp of a girl} is slight and fragile. {Will-o'-the-wisps} are elusive lights over marshes, or by extension, any misleading goal.

Wispy describes something thin, delicate, and insubstantial—like fine strands barely there. Wispy hair is sparse and flyaway. Wispy clouds are light streaks across the sky. A wispy voice is faint and breathy. The word suggests fragility and impermanence: {wispy threads of smoke}, {a wispy mustache}, {wispy memories of childhood}.

Wisteria is a climbing vine with cascading clusters of fragrant flowers, typically purple, blue, or white. The plant is prized for covering pergolas, arbors, and walls, its hanging flower clusters creating dramatic displays in spring: {The wisteria draped over the garden wall}. Wisteria can be aggressive, requiring careful management to prevent it from damaging structures.

Wistful describes a gentle, melancholy longing—usually for something past or unattainable. A wistful expression suggests quiet yearning mixed with sadness: {She gave a wistful smile when she saw the old photographs}. The word carries a soft, reflective quality rather than acute grief: {He grew wistful thinking about his college days}.

Wistfulness is a gentle, melancholy longing, often directed toward something in the past or something unattainable. Unlike sharper forms of sadness, wistfulness has a dreamy, reflective quality—a bittersweet awareness of what was or what might have been. {There was a wistfulness in her voice when she talked about her childhood home.} The feeling often surfaces when contemplating old photographs, revisiting familiar places, or remembering people no longer present.

Wit is quick, clever intelligence—the ability to make sharp, often humorous observations or connections. Someone with wit can turn a phrase memorably: {Her wit kept the dinner party lively}. A witty remark is both clever and amusing. Wit also means mental faculty more broadly, as in {scared out of my wits} or {gather your wits}. To {have your wits about you} is to be alert and ready. {At wit's end} describes exhausted mental resources.

A witch is a person, especially a woman, believed to practice magic or sorcery. In folklore and fairy tales, witches cast spells and brew potions, often depicted as malevolent: {The witch cursed the princess}. Historically, accusations of witchcraft led to persecution and execution. Modern witches may practice Wicca or other nature-based spiritual traditions. The word also serves as an insult for an unpleasant woman: {The old witch next door complained again}. To witch is to bewitch or enchant.

Witchcraft is the practice of magic, especially magic associated with evil or supernatural powers. Historically, accusations of witchcraft led to persecution and execution, particularly of women. The term now encompasses modern pagan practices like Wicca, which adherents don't consider evil: {She's been studying witchcraft for years}. Figuratively, witchcraft describes any skill so impressive it seems magical: {Her cooking is pure witchcraft}.

A witchdoctor is a traditional healer or medicine man in certain cultures, believed to use magic, spirits, or ritual practices to cure illness, ward off evil, or divine the future. The term carries colonial-era condescension, implying primitive superstition rather than legitimate practice: {The missionaries dismissed the village witchdoctor as a fraud}. Also spelled witch doctor.

A witcher is a monster hunter in the fantasy universe created by Polish author Andrzej Sapkowski, popularized globally through video games and a Netflix series. Witchers are humans mutated through alchemical processes to gain supernatural abilities—enhanced reflexes, resistance to disease, and magic—used to hunt creatures for pay. The term has become shorthand for morally ambiguous mercenary heroes: {He's giving witcher energy—brooding loner who kills monsters for coin}.

Witchery is the practice of witchcraft or magic, or the quality of being bewitching. The word often carries a sense of enchantment or irresistible charm: {the witchery of her smile}, {the witchery of the moonlit forest}. It suggests something captivating that seems to work by supernatural means, whether literal sorcery or figurative spell-casting.

Witches is the plural of witch—people, traditionally women, believed to practice magic or sorcery. In folklore and history, witches were feared as servants of evil; witch hunts and trials led to executions. Modern usage includes practitioners of Wicca and other pagan traditions. Figuratively, witch describes a malicious woman: {The old witch next door complained about everything}.

A witchfinder was a person who identified suspected witches, especially in 16th- and 17th-century England and colonial America. Witchfinders used dubious methods—searching for "devil's marks" on the body, extracting confessions through sleep deprivation, or observing whether suspects floated when thrown in water. The term now appears figuratively for anyone conducting ideological purges or hunting for heretics: {The committee devolved into a witchfinder's court}.

Witchfinders were people who identified and exposed suspected witches, particularly during the witch trials of the 16th and 17th centuries. The term evokes zealous persecution of innocent people based on superstition and hysteria. In modern use, it describes anyone who hunts for hidden enemies or heretics within a community: {The committee had become witchfinders, rooting out ideological impurity}.

A witchhunt is a campaign to identify and punish people accused of holding unacceptable views or engaging in subversive activity. The term invokes the historical persecution of alleged witches, when accusations spread through communities and evidence mattered less than suspicion. Modern witchhunts target political enemies, social deviants, or anyone deemed threatening: {The hearings became a witchhunt against suspected communists}. Often spelled as two words: witch hunt.

A witchhunter is someone who hunts witches—originally, an official or zealot who sought out and prosecuted people accused of witchcraft. The term now applies figuratively to anyone who pursues supposed enemies with righteous fervor and flimsy evidence: {The senator styled himself a witchhunter rooting out communists}. Also spelled witch-hunter or witch hunter.

Witchhunting is the pursuit and persecution of people accused of witchcraft, or more commonly today, a campaign to expose and punish people accused of holding unpopular views or committing social transgressions. The modern sense carries criticism—implying the accusers are driven by hysteria, moral panic, or political motives rather than evidence: {The committee's investigation devolved into witchhunting}. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated.

Witchhunts, also spelled as two words, originally referred to organized campaigns to identify and punish people accused of practicing witchcraft, most notoriously in early modern Europe and colonial America. The term now primarily describes aggressive investigations or persecutions targeting individuals or groups based on flimsy evidence, ideological suspicion, or mass hysteria rather than genuine wrongdoing. {The senator dismissed the ethics inquiry as a political witchhunt.} The word carries connotations of unfairness, mob mentality, and scapegoating.

Witching describes the time or atmosphere associated with supernatural activity, especially magic or sorcery. The {witching hour} is traditionally midnight, when witches and spirits are most active. The word evokes an eerie, magical quality: {a witching moonlit night}. As a verb form, witching means practicing witchcraft or casting spells.

Witchy describes something suggestive of witches or witchcraft—mysterious, magical, or slightly eerie. It often carries affectionate rather than sinister connotations: {She has a witchy vibe with all those crystals and tarot cards}. The word can describe aesthetic choices, personal style, or an intuitive, slightly supernatural quality: {witchy décor}, {a witchy laugh}.
clues: Having an air of dark magic

definition: To withdraw is to pull back or remove. You withdraw money from an account, withdraw troops from a position, or withdraw a statement you regret. The reflexive use suggests retreating into oneself: {She withdrew after the argument}. Withdrawal describes the process, and also the physical symptoms when stopping an addictive substance: {heroin withdrawal}.

Withdrawal is the act of removing or taking back. You can make a withdrawal from a bank account, withdraw troops from a battlefield, or withdraw a comment you regret. Withdrawal from a competition or agreement means pulling out. In medicine, withdrawal describes the physical and psychological symptoms that occur when someone stops using an addictive substance: {He went through heroin withdrawal}. The word also describes emotional retreat—becoming less engaged or communicative: {Her withdrawal from family life worried everyone}.

Withdrawals is the plural of withdrawal, the act of taking something back or removing oneself. Bank withdrawals are money taken from an account. Troop withdrawals remove military forces from a region. In medicine, withdrawals refers to the physical and psychological symptoms that occur when someone stops using an addictive substance: {The withdrawals from heroin were brutal}. This sense often appears with a singular verb: {Withdrawals is the hardest part of getting clean}.

Withdrawing is pulling back or removing from a place, position, or situation. Money is withdrawn from accounts, troops from battlefields, candidates from races. Someone withdrawing from a conversation becomes quiet and disengaged: {She's been withdrawing from friends lately}. Withdrawing also describes the process of stopping an addictive substance: {He's withdrawing from opioids}.

Withdrawn describes someone who has pulled back from social contact—quiet, reserved, uncommunicative: {She became increasingly withdrawn after the divorce}. The word suggests emotional retreat rather than mere shyness. As the past participle of withdraw, it also describes things that have been removed or taken back: {withdrawn funds}, {a withdrawn application}.

Withdrew is the past tense of withdraw. To withdraw is to pull back or remove—withdrawing troops from a position, withdrawing money from an account, withdrawing a hand from a flame. One can withdraw from a competition or withdraw support. To withdraw into oneself is to become quiet and uncommunicative: {She withdrew after the argument and wouldn't speak to anyone}.

Wither means to dry up, shrivel, or lose vitality. Plants wither from lack of water; hopes wither from neglect. A withering {look} or withering {criticism} is scornful enough to make someone shrink. The phrase {wither on the vine} describes something that dies from inattention before reaching fruition: {The proposal withered on the vine when no one championed it}.

Withered describes something that has dried up, shriveled, or lost vitality—typically plants or body parts: {withered leaves}, {a withered arm}. The past tense of wither, it often functions as an adjective for things that have decayed through age, disease, or lack of nourishment. Figuratively, it applies to anything that has lost its former strength or promise: {withered hopes}, {a withered reputation}.
clues: Like a leaf in late autumn

definition: Withering describes something that shrivels, weakens, or declines—like plants drying up from lack of water. A withering {glance} or withering {criticism} is devastatingly scornful, causing the recipient to shrink as if scorched: {She fixed him with a withering stare}. Withering {fire} in military contexts is intense enough to destroy enemy forces.
clues: Fading away from lack of care

definition: The withers are the ridge between a horse's shoulder blades, the highest point of its back. Horse height is measured from ground to withers: {a mare standing fifteen hands at the withers}. The term applies to similar anatomy in other four-legged animals. The unrelated verb wither means to shrivel or decline.

Withheld is the past tense and past participle of withhold—to hold back or refuse to give. Information can be withheld from the public, taxes withheld from a paycheck, affection withheld as punishment. {The witness withheld key details from investigators.} {His name was withheld pending notification of family.}

To withhold is to hold back or refuse to give something. You might withhold information, withhold payment, withhold judgment, or withhold affection. The word implies deliberate restraint—keeping something that could be given or released: {The company withheld his final paycheck}. Taxes withheld from a paycheck are deducted before you receive it.

Withholding is money taken from wages before the employee receives them, typically for taxes, insurance, or retirement contributions. The employer withholds these amounts and sends them directly to the government or other institutions: {Check your withholding if you're getting a huge refund—you're giving the IRS an interest-free loan}. The term also applies to the act of holding back anything: {the withholding of evidence}.

Within has the same meaning as inside but is slightly more formal, and often preferred in writing. It indicates a limit in time, space, or scope: The matter was handled within the department. Be back within an hour. That amount of money is not even within my imagination.

Without is the opposite of with when it means including: a cabin without modern plumbing. In Scottish English, or when it is accompanied by within, it can also mean outside: There are several good accommodation choices both within and without the city.

Withstand means to resist or endure something that threatens, pressures, or challenges. The word typically applies to forces that would otherwise cause damage, defeat, or collapse: {The bridge was built to withstand earthquakes}, {She withstood intense criticism without backing down}. What distinguishes withstand from simply endure is the implication of successful resistance—whatever is withstood does not prevail.

Withstood is the past tense of withstand—to resist, endure, or hold out against pressure or attack. Buildings withstand earthquakes, arguments withstand scrutiny, and people withstand hardship: {The old bridge withstood decades of heavy traffic}. {Her testimony withstood cross-examination}.

A witness is someone who sees an event firsthand, especially one that may require testimony: {Several witnesses saw the accident}. In legal contexts, a witness gives evidence under oath. To witness something is to observe it: {We witnessed history being made}. A witness can also be someone who signs a document to verify another's signature. Religious usage extends the meaning to one who testifies about faith: {bearing witness to God's love}.

Witnessed is the past tense of witness—to see or observe something firsthand, especially something significant: {I witnessed the accident from across the street}. It also means to formally attest to something's authenticity by signing: {The document must be witnessed by a notary}. What gets witnessed tends toward the momentous—crimes, miracles, historic events, legal signings.

Witnesses is the plural of witness—people who observe events or give testimony. In legal contexts, witnesses appear in court to provide evidence: {The prosecution called three witnesses}. Witnesses also attend ceremonies to verify their occurrence: {We need two witnesses for the marriage license}. The verb witnesses means observes or attests to: {She witnesses the signing of contracts daily}.

Witnessing is observing something happen, especially something significant or noteworthy. The word carries weight beyond casual seeing—you witness accidents, crimes, ceremonies, or historic events. In legal contexts, witnessing means formally observing the signing of a document and adding your own signature to verify it occurred. Religious usage extends this further: witnessing can mean sharing one's faith or testifying to spiritual experiences. {I'll never forget witnessing the birth of my first child.}
clues: Observing an event as it unfolds

definition: Wits are mental faculties—the capacity for thinking, reasoning, and responding quickly. Someone who {lives by their wits} relies on cleverness rather than steady employment. To {gather your wits} is to collect yourself mentally. {Scared out of my wits} means terrified beyond rational thought. A {battle of wits} is a contest of intelligence. To be {at your wit's end} is to have exhausted your mental resources and not know what to do next.

A witticism is a clever or humorous remark, typically one that demonstrates verbal dexterity or insight: {He was known for his witticisms at dinner parties}. The word carries a slightly formal or literary tone—in casual speech, people more often say "joke" or "quip." A witticism aims to be clever first, funny second.

Witticisms are clever, humorous remarks—the kind that display quick intelligence and verbal dexterity. The word carries a slightly formal or literary flavor; in casual speech, people more often say {jokes} or {quips}. A witticism aims to amuse through wordplay or sharp observation rather than slapstick or absurdity: {Oscar Wilde's witticisms still circulate today}.

Witty describes someone or something marked by quick, clever humor—the ability to make unexpected verbal connections that amuse: {a witty remark}, {a witty conversationalist}. Wit implies mental sharpness rather than broad comedy; witty observations tend toward the pointed or sardonic. {She's too witty for her own good sometimes.}

Wives is the plural of wife, a woman to whom someone is married. The word appears in contexts ranging from domestic to legal: {Both wives attended the ceremony}, {He outlived three wives}. The phrase {old wives' tale} refers to a superstitious belief passed down through generations, typically by women—now used dismissively for any unfounded popular notion.

Wiz is informal for wizard—someone exceptionally skilled at something: {She's a wiz at crossword puzzles}, {a computer wiz}. The spelling whiz is more common and carries the same meaning. Both suggest natural talent or impressive ability in a particular domain.

A wizard is a person with magical powers, especially a man who practices sorcery in fantasy and folklore: {The wizard cast a powerful spell}. By extension, wizard describes someone with exceptional skill in a particular area: {a financial wizard}, {a wizard with computers}. In software, a wizard is a step-by-step guide that walks users through a complex process. British slang uses wizard as an adjective meaning excellent, though this sounds dated: {That's wizard!}

Wizarding describes things related to wizards or the practice of magic: {the wizarding world}, {wizarding school}. The word gained wide currency through the Harry Potter series, where it distinguishes magical society from the non-magical world. Before that, it was rare, with *wizardly* being the more traditional adjective.

Wizardry is the art or practice of a wizard—magic, sorcery, enchantment. The word extends readily to any impressive skill that seems almost magical: {Her wizardry with numbers saved the company millions}. Technical wizardry suggests mastery of complex systems: {The film's special-effects wizardry won three Academy Awards}.

Wizards are figures with magical powers, appearing throughout mythology, fantasy literature, and games. A wizard typically masters arcane knowledge and casts spells: {The wizard summoned fire from his staff}. By extension, wizard describes anyone with exceptional skill: {a financial wizard}, {a wizard at computers}. In British slang, wizard means excellent: {That's wizard!}

Wobble describes unsteady movement—a rocking or swaying motion that suggests instability or lack of firm support. A table wobbles when its legs are uneven; a toddler wobbles while learning to walk; a politician wobbles when wavering on a position. The noun wobble is an instance of such movement: {There's a wobble in the front wheel}. Something wobbly is prone to wobbling or currently doing so.

Wobbles is a plural noun and third-person verb from wobble—to move unsteadily from side to side. A table wobbles on uneven ground; a toddler wobbles learning to walk. {The chair wobbles on its broken leg.} The wobbles, as a noun phrase, describes a state of unsteadiness or nervous uncertainty: {I got the wobbles before my presentation.}

Wobbling is moving unsteadily from side to side, rocking or swaying without firm balance. A top wobbles as it slows down. A table wobbles on uneven legs. The word extends to uncertainty or wavering: {She's still wobbling on whether to accept the job}. A wobbling voice trembles with emotion or weakness.

Wobbly describes something that moves unsteadily from side to side, lacking stability or firmness. A wobbly table rocks on uneven legs; a wobbly toddler hasn't quite mastered walking. The word extends to anything uncertain or unreliable: a wobbly economy, a wobbly argument, or feeling wobbly after standing up too fast. In British slang, to {throw a wobbly} means to have an emotional outburst or tantrum.
Woe is mainly a noun denoting grief, loss, or sorrow. As an interjection it expresses any of these in a somewhat literary way.

Woebegone describes someone visibly affected by sorrow or misery—looking dejected, forlorn, or pitifully sad: {The dog gave me a woebegone look when I picked up my keys}. The word suggests an almost theatrical quality of sadness written on the face or bearing. It appears in Garrison Keillor's fictional Lake Wobegon, "where all the women are strong, all the men are good-looking, and all the children are above average."

Woeful means full of woe—sorrowful, grieved, or pitiable: {a woeful expression}, {woeful tales of hardship}. It extends to anything deplorably bad or inadequate: {woeful ignorance}, {a woeful performance}. The adverb woefully often emphasizes insufficiency: {woefully underprepared}, {woefully short of funds}.

Woes are troubles, misfortunes, or sources of grief. The word is the plural of woe, an old term for deep sorrow or distress. Woes often appear in phrases describing categories of difficulty: {financial woes}, {marital woes}, {the team's defensive woes}. The word carries a slightly literary or dramatic flavor.

A wok is a round-bottomed cooking pan with high, sloping sides, used especially in Chinese and Southeast Asian cuisine. The shape allows food to be tossed and stirred quickly over high heat: {She stir-fried the vegetables in a hot wok}. Woks work best on gas burners; flat-bottomed versions exist for electric stoves.

Woke began as African American vernacular for being alert to racial injustice and systemic oppression: {Stay woke}. The term spread through social justice movements to mean aware of broader inequalities. By the late 2010s, critics adopted it dismissively for progressive politics they consider excessive or performative: {woke culture}, {go woke, go broke}. The word now carries opposite connotations depending on who's using it.

Wokeness is awareness of social injustice, particularly regarding race, gender, and systemic inequality. The term emerged from Black American slang where being "woke" meant staying alert to racism and its mechanisms. In contemporary usage, wokeness often carries a negative connotation, deployed by critics to mock what they see as performative or excessive concern with progressive causes: {The company's wokeness felt like marketing rather than genuine commitment}. Defenders use it neutrally or positively to describe heightened social consciousness.

Woks are bowl-shaped cooking pans with high, sloping sides, used especially in Asian cuisine. The shape allows food to be tossed and stirred quickly over high heat, making woks ideal for stir-frying. {She seasoned her new wok before using it.}

A wolf is a large wild canine that hunts in packs, native to wilderness regions of North America, Europe, and Asia. The wolf figures prominently in folklore and idiom: a {wolf in sheep's clothing} is a dangerous person disguised as harmless, and to {cry wolf} is to raise false alarms. To wolf food is to eat it ravenously: {He wolfed down his dinner}. A wolf can also be a man who aggressively pursues women.

Wolfbane is a poisonous plant of the genus Aconitum, also called aconite or monkshood. The name comes from its historical use as a poison for wolves. In folklore and fiction, wolfbane wards off werewolves: {The old woman hung wolfbane above her door}. Also spelled wolfsbane.

Wolfdogs are hybrid animals bred from wolves and domestic dogs. The term covers both deliberate crosses and their descendants, which vary widely in temperament and wolf-like traits depending on generation and percentage of wolf ancestry. Ownership is restricted or banned in many jurisdictions due to their unpredictable behavior: {The sanctuary takes in wolfdogs whose owners couldn't handle them}.

A wolfhound is a large, powerful dog bred originally to hunt wolves. The term usually refers to the Irish wolfhound, among the tallest of all dog breeds, though Scottish deerhounds and Russian borzois are sometimes called wolfhounds. Despite their imposing size, they're typically gentle and even-tempered: {The wolfhound barely fit on the couch}.

Wolfhounds are large, powerful dogs originally bred to hunt wolves and other large game. The term typically refers to the Irish wolfhound, one of the tallest dog breeds, or the Russian wolfhound (borzoi). Despite their imposing size and hunting heritage, wolfhounds are generally gentle and calm: {The wolfhounds sprawled across the entire sofa}.

Wolfing is eating rapidly and greedily, like a wolf devouring prey: {He was wolfing down his breakfast before the bus came}. The word suggests consuming food with more speed than manners, barely chewing. Someone wolfing a meal isn't savoring it—they're making it disappear.

Wolfish describes qualities associated with wolves—hungry, predatory, or fierce. A wolfish {grin} suggests menace or aggressive desire. A wolfish {appetite} is ravenous. The word often carries sexual undertones, implying predatory interest: {He gave her a wolfish look across the bar}.

A wolfman is a man who transforms into a wolf or wolf-human hybrid, synonymous with werewolf. The term evokes classic horror films more than folklore: {The Wolfman stalked the misty moors}. Unlike werewolf, wolfman emphasizes the human side of the creature—a man cursed or afflicted rather than a supernatural beast.

A wolfpack is a group of wolves that hunt and live together. The term extends to any coordinated group operating as a unit, especially in military contexts: German U-boats hunting in wolfpacks during World War II. More loosely, wolfpack describes any gang or crew moving together with shared purpose: {a wolfpack of fraternity brothers roaming the bars}.

Wolfpacks are groups of wolves hunting together, or by extension, any coordinated group operating as a unit. The term gained military currency for German U-boat squadrons in World War II that attacked Allied convoys in formation. More loosely, wolfpack describes any aggressive group acting in concert: {a wolfpack of reporters descended on the courthouse}.

Wolfsbane is a highly poisonous plant of the genus Aconitum, with hooded purple or blue flowers. The name reflects old beliefs that it could ward off wolves—or kill them. In folklore and fiction, wolfsbane protects against werewolves: {She hung wolfsbane by the door during the full moon}. Also called aconite or monkshood.

A wolverine is a stocky, powerful mammal of northern forests and tundra, the largest land-dwelling member of the weasel family. Despite its modest size, the wolverine is famously fierce and can drive much larger predators from kills. Its thick fur resists frost, making it valuable in cold climates. The animal's reputation for tenacity and ferocity has made it a popular mascot and nickname. (Capitalized Wolverine is the Marvel Comics character.)

Wolverines are stocky, powerful mammals of the weasel family, native to cold northern regions. Despite their modest size—roughly that of a medium dog—wolverines are remarkably fierce and strong, capable of driving larger predators from kills. They have thick dark fur and a reputation for ferocity disproportionate to their build: {The wolverine dragged the caribou carcass a surprising distance}. (Capitalized Wolverines typically refers to University of Michigan athletics.)

Wolves is the plural of wolf—large wild canines that hunt in packs and figure prominently in folklore and idiom. {Wolves howled in the distance}. To {throw someone to the wolves} is to abandon them to hostile forces. A {wolf in sheep's clothing} disguises predatory intentions. {Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995}.

Woman designates a female human. The word is derived from an older word related to wife, and man. Unlike man, woman has not developed much use before nouns to designate things that are for women, and the possessive form women’s is still preferred.

Womanhood is the state of being a woman, particularly as distinguished from girlhood: {She had just entered womanhood when she left home}. The term also refers to qualities considered characteristic of women, or to women collectively: {a triumph for womanhood}. Unlike manhood, womanhood rarely implies courage or toughness, reflecting older cultural assumptions about feminine virtues.

To womanise is to pursue casual sexual relationships with many women, typically said of men who do so habitually and without serious intent. The word carries a disapproving tone, suggesting superficiality or exploitation: {He spent his twenties womanising and drinking}. Also spelled womanize. A womaniser is a man known for this behavior.

A womaniser is a man who pursues casual sexual or romantic relationships with many women, typically without serious commitment. The term carries disapproval, suggesting manipulation or insincerity: {He had a reputation as a womaniser}. Also spelled womanizer.

Womanize means to pursue casual sexual relationships with many women, typically used of men who do so habitually and without serious romantic intent. The word carries a disapproving tone, suggesting behavior that treats women as conquests rather than partners. {He spent his twenties womanizing before finally settling down.} A man who does this is called a womanizer.

A womanizer is a man who pursues casual sexual relationships with many women, typically without emotional commitment or regard for their feelings. The term carries disapproval, suggesting manipulative or predatory behavior: {He had a reputation as a womanizer}. The verb womanize describes this pattern of conduct.

Womanizers are men who pursue casual sexual relationships with many women. The term carries moral judgment—it implies manipulation, insincerity, or treating women as conquests rather than people. A womanizer seduces and moves on: {He had a reputation as a womanizer who left broken hearts across three continents}. The singular is womanizer.

Womanizing is pursuing casual sexual relationships with many women, typically by a man who does so habitually and without commitment. The word carries connotations of treating women as conquests: {His womanizing eventually cost him his marriage}. A womanizer is someone known for this behavior.

Womankind refers to women collectively, as a group or category of humanity: {a victory for womankind}. The word parallels mankind but specifies the female portion of the human race. It appears in contexts discussing women's shared experiences, rights, or characteristics: {She dedicated her life to advancing womankind}.

Womanly describes qualities traditionally associated with mature women—grace, nurturing warmth, emotional depth, or physical curves. The word carries old-fashioned overtones and implies approval: {her womanly composure}, {a womanly figure}. Unlike feminine, which can describe objects or styles, womanly applies specifically to women themselves.

The womb is the organ in female mammals where offspring develop before birth—the uterus. Figuratively, womb suggests any place of origin or nurturing enclosure: {the womb of civilization}, {safe in the womb of the earth}. To return to the womb is to seek comfort and protection from the outside world.

A wombat is a stocky, burrowing marsupial native to Australia, roughly the size of a medium dog. Wombats are known for their powerful digging claws and backward-facing pouches, which prevent dirt from entering while they burrow. Their cube-shaped droppings, unique among animals, help mark territory without rolling away.

Wombats is the plural of wombat, a stocky burrowing marsupial native to Australia. These sturdy animals dig extensive underground tunnels and are known for producing cube-shaped droppings. {Wombats emerged from their burrows at dusk to graze.}

Wombs is the plural of womb, the organ in female mammals where offspring develop before birth. The word appears in discussions of reproduction, fertility, and pregnancy: {The embryos were implanted in surrogate wombs}. Figuratively, a womb is any place of origin or nurturing development: {the wombs of great civilizations}.

Women is the plural of woman—adult female humans. The word appears in compounds emphasizing female participation or perspective: {women's rights}, {women's studies}, {women's health}. {The women in my family are all teachers.} Calling a group "women" rather than "ladies" or "girls" is generally the neutral, respectful choice.

Won is the past tense and past participle of win. You won a game, won an argument, won someone's trust. {She won by three points.} {He's won every match this season.} Won also names the currency of North and South Korea.

Wonder is a feeling of amazement and curiosity, often tinged with admiration: {The children gazed at the fireworks in wonder}. It can be the thing that provokes this feeling—the seven wonders of the ancient world, a one-hit wonder. To wonder is to feel curiosity or uncertainty: {I wonder what she meant by that}. {No wonder} means it's not surprising: {No wonder he's tired—he worked all night}. Wonder as an adjective suggests remarkable effectiveness: {wonder drug}, {wonder boy}.

Wonderboy is an informal term for a young man who achieves remarkable success or displays exceptional talent, often with an implication of precocity or overnight fame: {the wonderboy of Silicon Valley}, {Wall Street's latest wonderboy}. The term can carry admiration or subtle mockery, suggesting the person's achievements may be overhyped or short-lived. Also spelled wonder boy.

Wondered is the past tense of wonder, meaning to feel curiosity or ask oneself questions: {I wondered where she had gone}, {He wondered if it would rain}. It can also express marvel or amazement: {They wondered at the beauty of the cathedral}. The tone often carries uncertainty or contemplation rather than active inquiry.

Wonderful describes something that inspires wonder or delight—remarkably good, excellent, or pleasing: {We had a wonderful time}. The word has softened from its original sense of awe-inspiring to general enthusiasm. It works as a warm, sincere compliment: {You've been wonderful}. In sarcastic use, wonderful expresses the opposite: {Oh wonderful, now the car won't start}.

Wondering describes a state of curiosity or contemplation—the mind actively questioning or marveling at something. {I was wondering if you'd like to join us} softens a request into polite inquiry. {She sat wondering what went wrong} shows quiet reflection. A wondering {look} or wondering {tone} conveys visible curiosity or amazement. The word captures the mind in motion, not yet arrived at an answer.

A wonderkid is a young person who achieves remarkable success or shows exceptional talent, especially in sports, music, or business. The term carries admiration tinged with amazement—this isn't just a talented child but one performing at levels that surprise adults: {The sixteen-year-old wonderkid scored twice on his debut}. Also spelled wonder kid.

Wonderkids are young people, typically children or teenagers, who display exceptional talent or ability in a particular field. The term appears most often in sports and entertainment, where prodigies emerge early: {The club signed several wonderkids from their youth academy}. In gaming, particularly football management simulations, wonderkids are highly sought-after young players with enormous potential for development. The singular wonderkid functions the same way.

A wonderland is a place of magical beauty, enchantment, or delight—real or imaginary. The word evokes Lewis Carroll's fantastical realm in *Alice's Adventures in Wonderland*, and that dreamlike quality colors most uses: {The garden was a wonderland of exotic flowers}. A winter wonderland is a snow-covered landscape of particular beauty. The term often carries a note of childlike amazement or, sometimes, irony when applied to places that dazzle but may deceive.

Wonderment is a state of awed surprise or admiration—the feeling that arises when encountering something marvelous or inexplicable. It suggests a quiet, contemplative quality distinct from mere excitement: {She gazed at the northern lights in wonderment}. The word often describes childlike openness to mystery: {His eyes were wide with wonderment}.

Wonders are things that inspire awe, amazement, or admiration—the {seven wonders of the ancient world}, the {wonders of modern medicine}. To wonder is to feel curiosity or uncertainty: {I wonder what she meant by that}. It also means to marvel: {We wondered at the beauty of the canyon}. {No wonder} means it's unsurprising: {No wonder you're tired—you've been up since dawn}. To {work wonders} is to achieve remarkable results.

Wonderstruck means filled with sudden wonder or amazement—stopped in your tracks by something astonishing or beautiful. The word suggests being struck as if by a physical force: {She stood wonderstruck before the northern lights}. It carries a sense of speechless awe, often in response to nature, art, or the unexpected.

Wondrous means inspiring wonder or amazement—marvelous, extraordinary. The word is literary and somewhat archaic, lending a fairy-tale or poetic quality: {a wondrous sight}, {wondrous beauty}. As an adverb (also literary), it means remarkably: {wondrous strange}.

A wonk is someone who studies a subject with intense, detail-oriented focus—especially policy or technical matters. The term often appears with a modifier: {a policy wonk}, {a budget wonk}, {a health-care wonk}. It can be mildly dismissive, suggesting someone more interested in arcane details than practical results, but many wonks embrace the label proudly. To wonk out is to dive deep into technical specifics.

Wonks are people deeply absorbed in the details of policy or technical subjects. The term carries affection and mild mockery simultaneously—wonks know more than anyone needs to about tax codes or healthcare reform, and they're eager to tell you about it. {The budget wonks in the office spent hours debating marginal tax rates.} Policy wonk is the most common pairing.

Wonky means slightly off, unstable, or not quite right. A wonky table wobbles; a wonky argument doesn't hold together. In British usage especially, something wonky is crooked or askew: {The picture frame looks wonky}. In American political slang, wonky describes someone deeply immersed in policy details—from "policy wonk": {She gave a wonky answer about tax reform}.

A wonton is a small dumpling in Chinese cuisine, made of thin dough wrapped around a filling of seasoned meat or seafood. Wontons are typically boiled and served in soup or fried until crispy: {wonton soup}, {fried wontons}. The word comes from Cantonese, meaning "swallowing clouds"—a reference to their shape floating in broth.

Wontons are Chinese dumplings made of thin dough wrapped around a filling, typically pork or shrimp. They appear in soup, fried as appetizers, or steamed. {The wonton soup came with six plump dumplings}. The wrapper is thinner than most dumpling doughs, giving wontons their delicate, slightly slippery texture.

Woo is to seek someone's favor or affection, especially romantically: {He wooed her with flowers and poetry}. The word extends to courting anyone's approval: politicians woo voters, companies woo investors. Wooing implies deliberate effort to charm or persuade. The adjective is wooing, the past tense wooed.

Wood is the hard, fibrous matter found under the bark of trees and that composes most of their bulk. In this use, it is uncountable. As a count noun and also as a plural, wood or woods designates a growth of trees larger than a copse or grove but usually smaller than a forest: lost in the woods. Different objects fashioned from wood use the same name, such as a golf club or a wooden wind instrument. Before another noun, wood means using it (a wood stove) or made of it (wood flooring). The verb wood has little active use and appears mainly as the participle wooded, meaning covered in trees.

A woodblock is a block of wood with a design carved into its surface, used for printing. The artist carves away the areas that should remain blank, leaving raised portions that receive ink and transfer the image to paper. Woodblock also refers to a print made this way: {Japanese woodblocks from the Edo period}. In music, a woodblock is a small rectangular percussion instrument struck with a mallet.

A woodcarver is a person who shapes wood into decorative or functional objects using hand tools like knives, chisels, and gouges. The craft ranges from folk art and whittling to fine sculptural work: {The woodcarver spent months on the intricate relief panel}. {Local woodcarvers sell their work at the craft fair}.

Woodcarving is the art or craft of shaping wood by cutting away material with knives, chisels, or gouges. The term covers both the activity and the objects produced: {She took up woodcarving as a hobby}; {The mantelpiece was decorated with intricate woodcarvings}. Unlike woodturning, which uses a lathe, woodcarving is done by hand on stationary wood.

A woodchipper is a machine that reduces branches and tree limbs to small chips, typically by feeding them through rotating blades. Landscapers and tree services use woodchippers to dispose of debris. The device has a grim cultural association from the film *Fargo*, where it disposes of a body—giving rise to dark jokes about "woodchipper accidents."

A woodchuck is a stocky North American rodent that burrows in the ground, also called a groundhog. Woodchucks hibernate through winter and emerge in early spring—hence Groundhog Day, when the creature supposedly predicts the season's length. The tongue-twister {How much wood would a woodchuck chuck?} plays on the name, though woodchucks don't actually chuck wood.

Woodchucks are stocky North American rodents that dig extensive burrows and hibernate through winter. Also called groundhogs, they're the subject of the tongue-twister {How much wood would a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck wood?} Despite the name, woodchucks don't chuck wood—they're burrowers, not lumberjacks.

A woodcock is a plump, short-legged game bird with a long bill, found in woodland habitats across Europe and North America. Woodcocks are prized by hunters and known for their erratic, zigzagging flight pattern, which makes them challenging targets. The American woodcock performs an elaborate aerial courtship display at dusk, spiraling upward before plummeting back to earth.

Woodcraft is skill and knowledge related to living, working, or surviving in forests and wild areas. It encompasses practical abilities like tracking animals, building shelters, identifying edible plants, and navigating through wilderness terrain. The term also applies to the craft of working with wood—carving, whittling, and fashioning useful or decorative objects from timber. {The scout leader taught us basic woodcraft during our camping trip.}

A woodcut is a print made from an image carved into a block of wood. The artist cuts away the areas meant to remain blank, leaving raised lines that receive ink and transfer to paper. The technique produces bold, graphic images with distinctive texture: {a medieval woodcut of the plague}, {Japanese woodcuts influenced the Impressionists}. A woodcut is also the block itself or the technique as an art form.

Woodcuts are prints made from carved wooden blocks, or the blocks themselves. The artist carves away areas that should remain unprinted, leaving raised surfaces that receive ink. The technique dominated European printmaking before metal engraving and remains valued for its bold lines and stark contrasts: {medieval woodcuts of religious scenes}, {Japanese woodcuts influenced the Impressionists}.

A woodcutter is a person who cuts down trees or chops wood, typically for fuel or timber. The term evokes a traditional occupation from folklore and fairy tales—the woodcutter who finds Hansel and Gretel, or who rescues Little Red Riding Hood. In modern use, it may describe anyone who cuts firewood: {He spent the morning working as a woodcutter for the family cabin}.

Woodcutters are people who cut down trees or chop wood, typically for fuel, timber, or clearing land. The term evokes a traditional occupation from before industrial logging: {The woodcutters worked from dawn until dusk}. In fairy tales and folklore, woodcutters often appear as humble forest-dwellers who encounter magical events.

Wooded describes land covered with trees: {a wooded hillside}, {wooded acres}. The term suggests natural forest rather than planted orchards or groves. A wooded area has enough trees to create shade and undergrowth, distinguishing it from merely having scattered trees.

Wooden describes things made of wood: a wooden {chair}, a wooden {fence}. The figurative sense captures the qualities of wood as a material—stiff, inflexible, lacking life. A wooden {performance} is awkward and unnatural. A wooden {expression} shows no emotion. Someone described as wooden seems robotic or unable to convey feeling: {His delivery was wooden and unconvincing}.

Woodgrain is the pattern of lines and textures visible in cut wood, created by a tree's annual growth rings. The term often describes surfaces that imitate this pattern: {woodgrain laminate}, {woodgrain vinyl}. As an adjective, it modifies materials designed to look like wood: {a woodgrain finish on the dashboard}.

Woodland is land covered with trees—less dense than forest but more than scattered groves. The word often appears as an adjective: {woodland creatures}, {woodland paths}. Woodlands typically have enough canopy to shade the ground but enough gaps for undergrowth. In British usage, woodland and forest overlap more than in American English.

Woodlands are areas covered with trees—less dense than forests but more substantial than scattered groves. The term often appears in place names and real estate marketing, suggesting natural beauty: {a housing development backing onto protected woodlands}. As an adjective, woodland describes things associated with such terrain: {woodland creatures}, {woodland trails}.

Woodlice are small crustaceans that live on land, typically found in damp places under logs, stones, or leaf litter. Despite their name, they're not lice but relatives of crabs and lobsters. Gray and segmented, they curl into balls when threatened—a defensive posture that gives them the alternate name "pill bugs" or "roly-polies." {The garden was full of woodlice when I lifted the flowerpot.}

Woodlore is knowledge about forests and wilderness survival—how to track animals, identify plants, build shelter, find water, and navigate without modern tools. The word evokes traditional outdoor skills passed down through generations: {The old trapper's woodlore kept them alive through the winter}. Sometimes spelled as two words.

A woodlot is a small area of woodland, typically privately owned and maintained as a source of firewood, timber, or maple syrup. The term is chiefly North American: {The family harvested firewood from their woodlot each fall}. Unlike managed forests, woodlots are usually modest parcels on farms or rural properties.

A woodlouse is a small crustacean with a segmented, armor-like body, found in damp environments under logs, stones, and leaf litter.
