A writeup is a written account, report, or description of something—typically a summary or evaluation: {The restaurant got a great writeup in the local paper}, {I need to finish the writeup of our findings}. In workplace contexts, a writeup often means a formal disciplinary report documenting an employee's misconduct: {One more incident and you'll get a writeup}. Also spelled write-up.

Writhe means to twist and contort the body, typically in response to intense physical sensation—pain, discomfort, or sometimes pleasure. {She writhed in agony on the hospital bed.} The word suggests continuous, involuntary movement rather than a single twist. Figuratively, writhe can describe emotional torment: {He writhed with embarrassment at the memory.} Snakes and worms writhe as their natural mode of movement, which gives the word its squirming, serpentine connotation.

Writhed is the past tense of writhe, meaning to twist or squirm, typically from pain, discomfort, or intense emotion. The movement suggests contortion—the body turning on itself: {She writhed in agony on the floor}. Figuratively, someone can writhe with embarrassment or shame, suggesting inner torment made visible through restless movement.

Writhing describes twisting, contorting movements of the body, typically from pain, discomfort, or intense emotion. A person writhes on the ground after being kicked; snakes writhe as they move. The word suggests continuous, uncontrolled motion: {She lay writhing in agony}. Figuratively, someone can writhe with embarrassment or shame—squirming inwardly even if still outwardly.

Writing is the act of forming letters, words, or symbols on a surface—or the result of that act. It covers everything from handwriting to composing text: {Her writing is illegible}, {He's working on his writing}. Writing also means written works collectively: {the writing of James Baldwin}. The phrase {the writing on the wall} refers to an ominous sign of what's to come. As a modifier, writing describes tools or activities: {writing desk}, {writing sample}.

Written is the past participle of write, used with auxiliaries to form perfect tenses: {I have written three letters today}. As an adjective, it describes something set down in words rather than spoken: a written {exam}, written {permission}, a written {statement}. What's written carries weight—it's documented, official, on the record. {The written word} suggests permanence compared to speech.

The adjective and adverb wrong is the opposite of right in multiple senses. It overlaps in meaning with incorrect and false. If something goes wrong, it develops in an undesirable or unworkable way. If you go in the wrong direction, you turn or proceed in a way that will not end well. To be on the wrong side of something brings disadvantage or defeat. If you wrong someone, you treat them immorally or unethically. A wrong is an act of wronging someone.

Wrongdoing is behavior that violates moral or legal standards—misconduct, sin, or crime. The word is broad enough to cover anything from petty dishonesty to serious offenses: {The investigation found no evidence of wrongdoing}. A wrongdoer is someone who commits such acts.

Wrongdoings are acts that violate moral or legal standards—sins, crimes, or ethical breaches. The plural emphasizes multiple instances or a pattern of behavior: {The investigation uncovered years of financial wrongdoings}. Often used in formal or legal contexts where specific offenses are being catalogued or condemned.

Wronged is the past tense and past participle of wrong, used as a verb meaning to treat someone unjustly or unfairly. When you've been wronged, someone has done you harm or violated your rights in some way. {She felt wronged by the company's decision to pass her over for promotion.} The term often carries a sense of moral injury rather than just practical harm, suggesting the person deserved better treatment than they received.

Wrongfooted means caught off guard or put at a disadvantage, from the sports image of having your weight on the wrong foot when you need to move. To wrongfoot someone is to surprise them or put them in an awkward position: {The question wrongfooted the candidate}. Someone who has been wrongfooted is unprepared to respond effectively.

Wrongfooting is catching someone off guard or putting them at a disadvantage, typically by doing something unexpected. The term comes from sports, where forcing an opponent onto the wrong foot disrupts their balance: {The sudden policy reversal wrongfooted the opposition}. To wrongfoot someone is to leave them unprepared to respond effectively.

Wrongheaded describes thinking or behavior that is misguided despite stubborn conviction—someone who persists in error while convinced they're right. The word emphasizes not just being wrong but being obstinately so: {a wrongheaded approach to the problem}, {wrongheaded policies that made things worse}. It carries a tone of exasperation at someone's refusal to see reason.

Wrongs are acts that violate someone's rights or cause unjust harm. The word carries moral weight—wrongs demand acknowledgment or redress: {We must right the wrongs of the past}. To wrong someone is to treat them unfairly or harmfully: {She felt deeply wronged by his betrayal}. Legal wrongs are actionable injuries; personal wrongs may fester without remedy.

Wrongthink is holding opinions or beliefs deemed unacceptable by a dominant group or authority. The term derives from George Orwell's *1984*, where "thoughtcrime" described forbidden ideas. In contemporary use, wrongthink often appears sarcastically to criticize perceived ideological conformity: {Expressing any wrongthink gets you canceled these days}. The word implies that certain views are treated as inherently illegitimate rather than merely incorrect.

Wrote is the past tense of write. Where write covers the present act of putting words on a page or composing text, wrote places that action in the past: {She wrote him a letter}, {He wrote three novels before turning forty}. The word extends to any form of composition: {Who wrote this song?}

Wrought is an old past tense and past participle of work, surviving mainly in set phrases. Wrought {iron} has been worked by hand. {What hath God wrought?} asks what God has made or accomplished. Havoc is wrought, not worked: {The storm wrought destruction across the coast}. Something overwrought has been worked up to excess—agitated or elaborate beyond measure.

Wrung is the past tense and past participle of wring. To wring is to squeeze and twist, typically to extract liquid: {She wrung out the wet towel}. Figuratively, to wring something from someone is to extract it with effort: {They wrung a confession from the suspect}. To wring your hands is to twist them together in distress or anxiety.

Wry describes something twisted or bent to one side, especially a facial expression: a wry {smile}, a wry {grin}. The twist suggests ironic amusement or dry humor—acknowledging life's absurdities without complaint. Wry {humor} is understated and slightly mocking, often self-directed: {He made a wry observation about his own failures}. A wry {comment} finds dark comedy in difficult situations.

Wunderkind is a German borrowing meaning a child prodigy—someone who achieves remarkable success or displays extraordinary talent at an unusually young age. The term applies especially to children who excel in music, chess, mathematics, or other fields requiring exceptional ability. In broader use, wunderkind describes any young person who rises quickly to prominence in their field: {The tech wunderkind sold his first startup at nineteen}. The plural may be either wunderkinder (German) or wunderkinds (English).

A wuss is a weak or timid person—someone who lacks courage or physical toughness. The word carries mild contempt: {Don't be such a wuss}. It often appears when someone backs down from a challenge or complains about minor discomfort. The verb wuss out means to chicken out: {He wussed out at the last minute}.

Wusses is the plural of wuss, a person considered weak, timid, or lacking courage. The word carries mild contempt, implying someone who backs down from challenges or complains excessively: {Don't be such wusses—it's just a little cold water}. Often used in casual teasing rather than serious insult.

Wussy is a mildly insulting term for someone perceived as weak, timid, or overly sensitive—a wimp or coward. It functions as both noun and adjective: {Don't be such a wussy}, {That was a wussy move}. The word likely blends wimp with pussy, carrying similar connotations but slightly softer. Also spelled wuss.

A wyvern is a mythical creature resembling a dragon but typically depicted with only two legs and a barbed tail. Where dragons have four legs, wyverns walk on their wings like bats. The creature appears frequently in heraldry, fantasy literature, and video games: {The kingdom's banner bore a golden wyvern}. Also spelled wivern.

Wyverns is the plural of wyvern, a dragon-like creature from European heraldry and legend. Unlike traditional dragons, wyverns have only two legs rather than four, with their front limbs forming wings. They appear frequently in fantasy literature, video games, and coat of arms designs: {The wyverns circled overhead before diving toward the castle}.

Xenomorph refers to an alien life form, especially one with a biology radically different from Earth organisms. The term gained wide currency from the *Alien* film franchise, where it names the predatory creature with an elongated head and acidic blood: {The xenomorph stalked the crew through the ship's corridors}. In broader science fiction, xenomorph describes any extraterrestrial organism whose form is truly alien rather than humanoid.

Xenomorphs are the fictional extraterrestrial species from the *Alien* film franchise—parasitic creatures with elongated heads, acid blood, and a multi-stage life cycle involving hosts. The term combines Greek roots meaning "strange form." In broader science fiction usage, xenomorph can refer to any alien life form: {The planet's xenomorphs ranged from microscopic to massive}.

A xenophobe is someone who fears or dislikes foreigners, foreign cultures, or things perceived as foreign. The term carries strong negative connotations—to call someone a xenophobe is to accuse them of irrational prejudice: {The candidate's anti-immigrant rhetoric appealed to xenophobes}. The related noun is xenophobia, the adjective xenophobic.

Xenophobes are people who fear or hate foreigners, foreign cultures, or things perceived as foreign. The term carries strong negative connotations—calling someone a xenophobe implies irrational prejudice rather than legitimate concern: {The new immigration policy was crafted by xenophobes}. See also xenophobia.

Xenophobia is fear or hatred of foreigners, foreign cultures, or things perceived as foreign. The term combines Greek roots for "stranger" and "fear," but in practice it describes hostility more than anxiety: {xenophobic immigration policies}, {a campaign fueled by xenophobia}. Unlike racism, which targets specific racial groups, xenophobia focuses on national origin or cultural outsider status—though the two often overlap.

Xenophobic describes fear or hatred of foreigners, foreign cultures, or things perceived as strange or alien. The attitude often manifests as hostility toward immigrants or suspicion of outside influence: {xenophobic rhetoric about closing borders}, {The party's xenophobic platform blamed outsiders for economic problems}. The noun is xenophobia.

Xerox began as a trademark for photocopying machines but became a generic verb meaning to photocopy: {Can you xerox this for me?} The company vigorously defends its trademark, but casual usage persists. As a noun, a xerox is a photocopy itself: {Make me a xerox of that document}. The word is fading as digital scanning replaces paper copying. (Capitalized Xerox is the company.)

Xoxo represents hugs and kisses, used as an affectionate sign-off in messages and letters. The x's symbolize kisses (lips pursed for a kiss) and the o's represent hugs (arms encircling). Common in informal correspondence between friends, family, or romantic partners: {Talk soon, xoxo}. Often written in all caps or with varying repetition: {XOXO}, {xo}, {xoxoxo}.

X-ray refers to a form of electromagnetic radiation that can pass through solid objects, used in medicine to image bones and internal structures, and in security to scan luggage. As a verb, to x-ray is to examine using this radiation: {They x-rayed my ankle to check for fractures}. In the NATO phonetic alphabet, X-ray represents the letter X.

X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation that can pass through soft tissue but not bone or metal, making them useful for medical imaging: {The x-ray showed a fracture}. The term works as noun or verb—you can get an x-ray or x-ray a patient. Airport security x-rays luggage. Also spelled X-rays or x rays.

A xylophone is a percussion instrument consisting of wooden bars arranged like piano keys, struck with mallets to produce tones. Each bar is tuned to a specific pitch, with longer bars sounding lower notes. The xylophone appears in orchestras, marching bands, and children's music education: {She played a simple melody on the xylophone}.

Xylophones is the plural of xylophone, a percussion instrument with wooden bars arranged like piano keys and struck with mallets. The bars are graduated in length to produce different pitches. Xylophones appear in orchestras, marching bands, and elementary music classrooms: {The children took turns playing the xylophones}.

A yacht is a boat used for pleasure rather than commerce or fishing. The term typically implies something larger and more luxurious than a simple sailboat or motorboat: {They spent the summer on a yacht in the Mediterranean}. Yacht can function as a verb meaning to sail or cruise in one, though this use is uncommon. The word carries connotations of wealth and leisure.

Yachting is the activity of sailing or racing yachts—typically for recreation or sport rather than commercial purposes. The term suggests leisure and often wealth, as yachts are expensive vessels: {They spent summers yachting in the Mediterranean}. Yacht racing has been an Olympic sport since 1900.

Yachts is the plural of yacht, a recreational boat or ship used for pleasure cruising or racing rather than commercial purposes. Yachts range from small sailboats to massive luxury vessels with full crews: {The harbor was full of yachts}. The word often connotes wealth: {billionaires and their yachts}.

Yack is informal for talk, especially idle or excessive chatter: {We yacked on the phone for hours}. As a noun, it's the talk itself or someone who talks too much. Also spelled yak. Separately, yack can mean to vomit, though this sense is less common.
Yahoo is like wahoo, a cry of excitement and exaltation.
clues: An oafish, unrefined sort of person

definition: Yahoos are crude, uncouth, or rowdy people—the sort who might start a fight at a bar or shout obscenities at a sporting event. The word comes from Jonathan Swift's *Gulliver's Travels*, where Yahoos are brutish humanoid creatures contrasted with the rational Houyhnhnms. {A bunch of yahoos were tailgating in the parking lot.} The term is mildly contemptuous but often used with humor.

A yak is a large, shaggy-haired ox native to the high plateaus of Tibet and Central Asia, domesticated for milk, meat, and transport. Separately, to yak is to talk at length, often tediously: {She yakked on the phone for hours}. The noun yak means such chatter. Also spelled yack.

Yakisoba is a Japanese stir-fried noodle dish made with wheat noodles, vegetables, and meat—typically pork—seasoned with a sweet and savory sauce similar to Worcestershire. Despite the name containing *soba* (buckwheat noodles), yakisoba uses wheat noodles. It's a popular street food and festival staple: {We grabbed yakisoba from a food stall at the matsuri}.

Yakitori is a Japanese dish of skewered chicken pieces grilled over charcoal, typically seasoned with salt or a sweet soy-based sauce called tare. The skewers often feature different cuts—thigh, breast, skin, liver—and may include vegetables. Yakitori bars are casual drinking establishments where the dish is a staple: {We grabbed some yakitori and beers after work}.

Yakking is talking at length, often about trivial matters. The word suggests chatter that's excessive or annoying to others: {They spent the whole meeting yakking about their weekend plans}. Sometimes spelled yacking. The noun yak (or yack) means idle chatter, and to yak is to engage in it.

Yaks are large, shaggy-haired bovines native to the high plateaus of Central Asia, especially Tibet. They serve as pack animals and sources of milk, meat, and fiber in mountainous regions. As a verb, to yak (also yack) is to talk persistently about trivial matters: {They yakked for hours about nothing}.

Yakuza refers to organized crime syndicates in Japan, or a member of such a group. Similar to the Mafia, yakuza organizations are hierarchical, involved in gambling, extortion, and other illegal enterprises, though they have historically operated semi-openly in Japanese society. The word can be singular or plural: {a yakuza boss}, {the yakuza control this district}.

A yam is a starchy tuber grown in tropical regions, with rough brown skin and flesh ranging from white to purple. In American usage, yam often refers to orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, though true yams are a different plant entirely. {candied yams}, {yams and greens}. Yams are a dietary staple across West Africa, the Caribbean, and parts of Asia.

Yammer means to whine, complain, or talk at length in an annoying way. The word suggests persistent, repetitive speech that grates on listeners—someone who yammers doesn't just talk, they go on and on without seeming to notice others have tuned out. {He yammered about his problems for an hour.} {Stop yammering and get to the point.} As a noun, yammer refers to this kind of tiresome talk or the sound of it.

Yammering is persistent, annoying talk—whining, complaining, or going on at length about something trivial: {I couldn't concentrate with all that yammering in the background}. The word suggests both volume and tedium. Someone who yammers doesn't know when to stop.

Yams are starchy, edible tubers grown in tropical regions, with rough brown skin and flesh ranging from white to purple. In American English, yam often refers to orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, though true yams are a different plant entirely: {candied yams at Thanksgiving}. True yams can grow several feet long and are a dietary staple in West Africa and the Caribbean.

A yamulka is a small, round skullcap worn by Jewish men, especially during prayer or religious ceremonies, though many Orthodox Jews wear one at all times as a sign of reverence before God. Also spelled yarmulke or kippah: {He placed the yamulka on his head before entering the synagogue}.

Yamulke is a variant spelling of yarmulke, the small circular cap worn by Jewish men, especially during prayer or religious services. Orthodox Jews often wear it at all times as a sign of reverence before God. Also called a kippah.

Yamulkes is the plural of yamulke, a small round cap worn by Jewish men, especially during prayer or religious services. Orthodox Jews often wear one at all times as a sign of reverence before God. Also spelled yarmulke. {The men put on their yamulkes before entering the synagogue.}

Yang is the active, bright, masculine principle in Chinese philosophy, always paired with its complement yin. Yang represents light, heat, movement, and assertiveness—the sun side of a mountain. The two forces are interdependent, not opposed: {The balance of yin and yang governs health}. In casual use, yang can mean the positive or active element of any pair. (Capitalized Yang is a common Chinese and Korean surname.)

To yank is to pull with a sharp, sudden motion: {She yanked the door open}, {He yanked his arm free}. The noun is the pull itself: {Give it a good yank}. The word suggests more force or abruptness than a simple pull. (Capitalized Yank is informal for an American.)

Yanked is the past tense of yank, meaning to pull something with a sudden, sharp motion: {She yanked the door open}, {He yanked his arm free}. The word suggests force and abruptness rather than gentle tugging. Figuratively, to be yanked from a situation is to be removed suddenly: {The show was yanked after three episodes}.

Yanking is pulling with a sharp, sudden motion. The word emphasizes abruptness rather than sustained effort: {She was yanking weeds from the garden}, {Stop yanking my arm}. To yank someone's chain is to tease or provoke them, usually in fun.

Yanks is the plural of yank, a sharp tug or pull: {He gave the cord several yanks before it started}. As a verb form, it means pulls suddenly: {She yanks the door open every morning}. (Capitalized Yanks is informal for Yankees.)

Yap is a verb and noun for the sharp, high-pitched bark of a small dog, or by extension, annoying chatter from a person who won't shut up. If someone tells you to {quit your yapping}, they want you to stop talking. A yap can also mean a mouth: {Keep your yap shut}. The word captures both the sound and the irritation it produces.

A yapper is someone who talks excessively or annoyingly, or a small dog prone to shrill, persistent barking. Both uses suggest noise without much substance: {That little yapper next door won't shut up}. The word carries dismissive connotations—yappers are more irritating than threatening.

Yapping is persistent, high-pitched barking—the sound small dogs make: {The neighbor's Chihuahua won't stop yapping}. Extended to people, it means talking incessantly about trivial matters: {She's been yapping on the phone for an hour}. The word carries dismissive connotations, suggesting the talk is as annoying and insignificant as a small dog's bark.

Yappy describes a dog that barks frequently in short, high-pitched yelps—typically small breeds like Chihuahuas or terriers: {Their yappy little dog won't shut up}. Extended to people, yappy means talkative in an annoying way, chattering on about nothing: {She got yappy after a few drinks}.

Yaps is the third-person singular of yap, meaning to bark in short, high-pitched sounds—the noise small dogs make. By extension, yaps describes someone talking noisily or foolishly: {She yaps on the phone for hours}. As a plural noun, yaps are those sharp barks themselves, or mouths in dismissive slang: {Shut your yaps}.

A yard is a piece of ground adjacent to a building, especially the area around a house: {front yard}, {back yard}. In American English, yard typically means any outdoor space belonging to a residence; British English prefers garden. Yard also denotes enclosed areas for specific purposes: {shipyard}, {junkyard}, {rail yard}, {prison yard}. Separately, a yard is a unit of length equal to three feet or about 0.91 meters. On a sailing vessel, a yard is a horizontal pole that supports a sail.

Yardage is length or distance measured in yards: {What's the yardage on this hole?} In American football, yardage refers to ground gained or lost: {The running back averaged five yards per carry but his total yardage was disappointing}. In textiles, yardage is fabric sold by the yard.

A yardarm is either end of a yard—the horizontal spar that supports a square sail on a sailing ship. The phrase {the sun is over the yardarm} signals that it's late enough in the day to start drinking, from the naval tradition of the first rum ration when the sun rose past the yardarm.

Yardbird is slang with two distinct meanings. In military and prison contexts, it refers to someone assigned to menial outdoor work—cleaning yards, picking up trash: {The new recruits were yardbirds for their first month}. In jazz, yardbird means a musician, especially a saxophonist, from Charlie "Yardbird" Parker's nickname. A yardbird is also simply a chicken—a bird kept in the yard.

Yards is the plural of yard, a unit of length equal to three feet or about 0.91 meters. The term appears in measurements of fabric, distance, and athletic fields: {She bought three yards of silk}, {a hundred-yard dash}. Yards also names enclosed outdoor areas attached to buildings: {front yards}, {back yards}, {prison yards}. In nautical use, yards are horizontal spars supporting sails.

A yardstick is a measuring stick one yard (three feet) long, used for measuring length. Figuratively, a yardstick is any standard of comparison or evaluation: {Profit is not the only yardstick of success}. The figurative sense dominates in contemporary usage.

Yardsticks are standards used for comparison or evaluation: {Test scores have become the yardstick for measuring school performance}. The figurative sense comes from the literal one—a flat measuring stick one yard long, used in sewing, carpentry, and general measurement before tape measures became common.

Yardwork is the labor of maintaining a residential yard—mowing the lawn, raking leaves, trimming hedges, pulling weeds, and similar outdoor chores. The term is American; British English prefers gardening even for basic maintenance. {I spent Saturday doing yardwork.}

A yarmulke is a small round cap worn by Jewish men, especially during prayer or religious study. Orthodox Jewish men typically wear one at all times as a sign of reverence before God. Also spelled yarmulka or yamaka; also called a kippah.

A yarmulke is a small, round cap worn by Jewish men, especially during prayer or religious study. Orthodox Jews often wear one at all times as a sign of reverence before God. Also spelled yarmulka or called a kippah: {He placed a yarmulke on his head before entering the synagogue}.

Yarmulkes is the plural of yarmulke, a small round cap worn by Jewish men, especially during prayer or religious services. Some observant Jews wear one at all times as a sign of reverence for God. The word comes from Yiddish; the Hebrew term is kippah. {The men donned yarmulkes before entering the synagogue.}

Yarn is fiber spun into long strands for knitting, weaving, or crocheting: {a ball of yarn}, {She bought yarn for a sweater}. The verb means to spin fiber into thread. Separately, a yarn is a long, often exaggerated story, especially one involving adventure or tall tales: {He spun a yarn about his days at sea}. To yarn is to tell such stories.

Yarning is the act of telling stories or engaging in informal, often lengthy conversation. In Australian and New Zealand English, yarning has particular cultural significance among Indigenous communities, where it describes a traditional form of storytelling and knowledge-sharing. More casually, yarning means spinning tales or chatting at length: {We spent the evening yarning about the old days}. The term comes from the expression "spin a yarn," which suggests the drawn-out, winding nature of storytelling.

Yarns are long continuous strands of fibers twisted together, used for knitting, weaving, or sewing. The word extends naturally to long, winding tales—especially informal stories of adventure or exaggeration that someone spins out for entertainment: {He spun yarns about his days at sea}. As a verb, to yarn means to tell such stories, often in a leisurely, rambling way. {We sat on the porch yarning until midnight.}

A yarnspinner is someone who tells stories, especially long, entertaining, or embellished ones. The term evokes folksy oral tradition—tales spun out leisurely, often with colorful exaggeration: {My grandfather was quite the yarnspinner}. The image connects storytelling to the craft of spinning thread, both requiring skill to draw out material into something continuous and coherent.

Yarrow is a flowering plant with feathery leaves and flat clusters of small white or pink flowers, found in meadows and roadsides throughout temperate regions. It has a long history in folk medicine for treating wounds and reducing fever. The plant's pungent, slightly bitter aroma makes it useful in herbal teas and as a companion plant in gardens.

Yaw is rotation around a vertical axis—the side-to-side swinging of a ship, aircraft, or spacecraft. A plane yaws when its nose moves left or right while its wings stay level, distinct from pitch (nose up/down) and roll (wings tilting). The term extends to any vehicle or projectile deviating from its intended course: {The rocket began to yaw during ascent}.

A yawn is an involuntary deep breath with the mouth wide open, typically from drowsiness or boredom. The action is famously contagious—seeing or reading about yawning often triggers one. To yawn is to produce this reflex. Figuratively, a yawn is something tedious: {The movie was a yawn}. A yawning gap or chasm is wide open.

Yawned is the past tense of yawn—to open the mouth wide and inhale deeply, usually from tiredness or boredom. The action is involuntary and contagious: {She yawned, and soon everyone in the room was yawning}. Figuratively, things that gape open may yawn: {A chasm yawned before them}.

Yawning is the act of opening the mouth wide and inhaling deeply, usually from tiredness or boredom. The gesture is famously contagious—seeing or even reading about yawning can trigger it. Figuratively, yawning describes something wide open: {a yawning chasm}, {a yawning gap between rich and poor}.

Yawns are involuntary gaping breaths, mouth opening wide, typically from tiredness or boredom. The singular yawn extends to anything tedious: {The movie was a total yawn}. As a verb form, yawns describes the action: {She yawns every time he starts talking}. Things that gape open may also yawn: {A chasm yawned before them}.

Yawp is a loud, harsh cry or yelp—the sound a dog or bird might make. By extension, it means to speak loudly or complainingly, or the noise itself: {Stop your yawping}. Walt Whitman gave the word literary life: "I sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world." Also spelled yawl or yaup.

Yay is an exclamation of enthusiasm, celebration, or approval: {Yay, we won!} It expresses simple delight, often with childlike energy. As an adverb, yay indicates approximate size or amount, usually accompanied by a gesture: {The fish was about yay big}.

Yea is a formal or archaic word for yes, now mostly confined to voting contexts: {All in favor say yea}. The yeas and nays are the affirmative and negative votes. Yea also serves as an adverb meaning to this extent, often with a gesture: {The fish was yea big}. In casual speech, yeah has largely replaced yea for simple affirmation.
Yeah is an informal way of saying yes in all of its uses. It may be considered disrespectful to answer someone in authority with yeah rather than yes.

English gets its smallest time divisions—second, minute, and hour—from French and Latin, but the bigger chunks—day, month, and year—have been around since Old English and have cognates in Germanic languages. Of these six time divisions, year is the most frequently used, and like day it represents an observable phenomenon: the 365¼ days that it takes for the earth to circuit the sun. For the first 500 or so years that people used the word year they knew it only as the complete cycle of seasons. When Copernicus posited the idea of the earth orbiting the sun, the word already in use easily adapted to the more technical definition.

A yearbook is a book published annually by a school or organization documenting the year's events, activities, and members. School yearbooks typically feature student photographs, club activities, sports teams, and memorable moments from the academic year. Students often sign each other's yearbooks with messages: {Will you sign my yearbook?}

Yearbooks are annual publications documenting a year's events, typically produced by schools to chronicle the academic year with photographs of students, faculty, and activities. High school and college yearbooks serve as keepsakes: {We spent hours signing each other's yearbooks}. Organizations and institutions also publish yearbooks as annual reports or reference compilations.

A yearling is an animal between one and two years old, most commonly referring to horses and cattle. In horse racing, yearlings are often bought and sold before they begin training: {The yearling sold for two million at auction}. The term applies to any young animal in its second year of life.

Yearly means once a year or every year: a yearly {checkup}, yearly {dues}, the yearly {migration of birds}. As an adverb, it describes frequency: {The festival is held yearly}. Yearly and annual are interchangeable in most contexts, though annual appears more often in formal or institutional settings.

Yearn is to long for something with deep, persistent desire—often something distant, lost, or unattainable. The word carries emotional weight that want and wish lack: {She yearned for her homeland}, {He yearned to see his children again}. Yearning suggests an ache, a pull toward something that feels essential but out of reach.

Yearned is the past tense of yearn, meaning to feel a deep, persistent longing or desire for something. The word carries emotional weight beyond simple wanting—it suggests an ache or wistfulness, often for something distant, lost, or difficult to attain. {She yearned for the simplicity of her childhood.} {He yearned to see his homeland again.} Yearning typically involves sustained emotional intensity rather than fleeting desire.

Yearning is a deep, persistent longing—stronger and more aching than mere wanting. You yearn for things felt as distant or lost: a homeland, a former lover, a life not lived. {She felt a yearning for the simplicity of childhood}. The word suggests emotional weight and duration, a desire that sits heavy rather than passes quickly.

Yearnings are deep, persistent longings—desires that pull at you over time. The word suggests emotional intensity and often impossibility or distance: {yearnings for home}, {unfulfilled yearnings}. Where a wish might be fleeting, yearnings imply sustained ache. The word appears most often in literary or reflective contexts.
clues: What the heart keeps reaching for

definition: Yearns means to long for something with deep, persistent desire. The word suggests emotional aching—a pull toward what's absent or unattainable: {She yearns for the simplicity of childhood}, {He yearned to see his homeland again}. Yearning carries more wistfulness than wanting, more tenderness than craving.

Years is the plural of year, a unit of time measuring one complete orbit of Earth around the sun—roughly 365 days. Beyond counting time, years often emphasizes long duration or aging: {It's been years since we talked}, {The stress aged him years}. {Years} can stand alone for an indefinite but substantial period: {I've known her for years}.

Yeast is a microscopic fungus that ferments sugars, producing carbon dioxide and alcohol. This makes it essential for baking bread (where the gas creates rise) and brewing beer and wine (where the alcohol is the point). Yeast also appears as a dietary supplement. Figuratively, yeast is anything that causes ferment or activity: {the yeast of revolution}.
Yech is a representation of a sound that people make when they are disgusted; it may be imitative of retching.

Yeehah is an exclamation of excitement, triumph, or exuberance, associated with cowboys and the American West. It's the sound someone makes riding a bucking horse or celebrating wildly: {Yeehah! We won!} The spelling varies—yeehaw, yee-haw, yahoo—but the spirit is the same: uninhibited enthusiasm.

Yeehaw is an exclamation associated with cowboys, rodeos, and the American West—a shout of excitement or exuberance, often while riding a horse or bull. It conveys rowdy enthusiasm and has become shorthand for rural Southern or Western culture, sometimes affectionately, sometimes mockingly: {Yeehaw, let's go!}

Yeesh is an exclamation expressing exasperation, dismay, or mild disgust—a reaction to something unpleasant or tiresome: {Yeesh, not this again}. It conveys weary disapproval rather than shock, often at someone else's behavior or an annoying situation. The tone is informal and slightly theatrical.

Yeet is an exclamation accompanying a forceful throw or movement, emphasizing power over accuracy: {She yeeted the ball across the field}. The word emerged from internet culture in the 2010s and quickly became a verb meaning to throw something with vigor or reckless abandon. It extends to any sudden, forceful action: {I yeeted myself out of that conversation}. The past tense is contested—yote appears alongside yeeted.

Yeeted is the past tense of yeet, a slang verb meaning to throw something with force or enthusiasm: {He yeeted the ball across the field}, {She yeeted her phone into the pool}. The word emerged from internet culture and carries a playful, exaggerated energy. Some speakers use yote as an alternative past tense.

Yeeting is the present participle of yeet, a slang verb meaning to throw something with force and enthusiasm, often recklessly: {He's yeeting his backpack across the room}. The word emerged from internet culture and emphasizes vigor over accuracy—you don't yeet something gently or carefully. Extended use covers any forceful expulsion or departure: {I'm yeeting myself out of this conversation}.

Yell is to cry out loudly, usually from strong emotion—fear, anger, excitement, or urgency: {She yelled for help}. Unlike scream, yell doesn't necessarily imply a high pitch. A yell is also such a cry. In American universities, a yell is a coordinated chant led by cheerleaders: {the school fight yell}.

Yelled is the past tense of yell—to cry out loudly, typically in anger, excitement, or to be heard across distance: {She yelled at the kids to come inside}. Yelling suggests more volume and urgency than speaking loudly, often with emotional intensity behind it.

Yelling is speaking or crying out in a loud voice, typically from strong emotion—anger, excitement, fear, or urgency. {Stop yelling at me!} {The fans were yelling for their team}. Yelling can also mean calling to someone at a distance: {She yelled across the yard}.

Yellow is a primary color, the color of lemons, that falls between orange and green on the visible spectrum. It has several associations in English that may not be shared in other languages. Applied to people, yellow suggests cowardice and fear, or it may be used disparagingly and offensively to characterize Asians. Yellow journalism is overly sensational. A yellow light stands for caution and the need to be alert. To yellow is to turn yellow or fade, often the result of aging or exposure to the sun.

A yellowbelly is a coward—someone lacking courage or nerve. The term draws on the old association of yellow with cowardice: {Don't be a yellowbelly; just ask her out}. In some regional uses, yellowbelly refers to various fish or animals with yellow undersides, but the cowardice sense dominates in everyday speech.

Yellowcake is a powdered uranium concentrate produced during the early stages of uranium processing, named for its typically yellow color though it can range to orange or greenish. It contains mostly uranium oxide and serves as the raw material for enriching uranium, whether for nuclear reactor fuel or weapons. The term gained broader public awareness during debates over weapons of mass destruction, particularly claims about Iraq seeking yellowcake from Africa in the lead-up to the 2003 Iraq War.

Yellowed describes something that has turned yellow over time, typically from age, exposure to light, or chemical change. Paper yellows, as do teeth, fabric, and old photographs. The word implies deterioration or neglect: {yellowed newspaper clippings}, {yellowed lace curtains}. What was once white or bright has faded toward dingy amber.

Yellowface is the practice of non-Asian actors portraying Asian characters, typically through makeup, prosthetics, and stereotyped mannerisms. The term parallels blackface and carries similar connotations of racist caricature. Historical examples include Mickey Rooney's exaggerated Japanese landlord in *Breakfast at Tiffany's*. The practice is now widely condemned: {The casting of a white actor in yellowface sparked immediate backlash}.

Yellowfin usually refers to the yellowfin tuna, a large fish prized for sashimi and seared steaks, distinguished by its bright yellow dorsal and anal fins. The term also applies to other fish with yellow fins, including certain croakers and sole: {We caught some yellowfin off the coast}.

Yellowing is the process of becoming yellow or yellowish, typically through age, decay, or exposure to light. Paper yellows over time; teeth yellow from coffee and tobacco; leaves yellow in autumn. The word usually implies gradual deterioration: {yellowing photographs}, {yellowing newspaper clippings}, {the yellowing pages of an old book}.

A yellowjacket is a wasp with black and yellow markings, known for its aggressive behavior and painful sting. Unlike honeybees, yellowjackets can sting repeatedly and often nest in the ground or wall cavities. They're particularly aggressive around food in late summer: {The picnic was ruined by yellowjackets}. Also spelled yellow jacket.

Yellowjackets are social wasps with distinctive black and yellow striped markings, known for aggressive behavior when their nests are disturbed. Unlike bees, they can sting repeatedly. They build papery nests underground or in cavities and are attracted to sweet foods and meat at outdoor gatherings: {The picnic was ruined by yellowjackets swarming the soda cans}.

Yellowtail refers to several species of fish with yellow tail fins, most commonly the Japanese amberjack prized in sushi restaurants: {The yellowtail sashimi was incredibly fresh}. In American waters, yellowtail usually means the California yellowtail, a popular game fish. The name also applies to certain snappers and flounders with similar coloring.

Yells is the plural of yell—loud, sharp cries or shouts. School yells are organized cheers at sporting events: {The cheerleaders led the crowd in fight yells}. As a verb, yells is the third-person singular: {She yells at the kids to come inside}. To yell can express anger, excitement, or urgency, or simply project the voice across distance.

A yelp is a short, sharp cry of pain, alarm, or excitement—the kind a dog makes when startled or hurt: {The puppy let out a yelp when I stepped on its tail}. People yelp too, usually involuntarily: {She yelped in surprise}. The verb and noun are interchangeable: you can give a yelp or simply yelp. (Capitalized Yelp is the business review platform.)

Yelps are short, sharp cries—the kind a dog makes when startled or hurt, or a person emits in sudden pain or surprise: {The puppy let out a series of yelps when I stepped on its paw}. To yelp is to make such a sound. The word suggests something involuntary and high-pitched, more startled than sustained.

Yen is a longing or craving, an urge to do or have something: {I have a yen for Chinese food}, {She felt a sudden yen to travel}. The word suggests a persistent but not desperate desire. Separately, yen is the basic monetary unit of Japan, divided into 100 sen. The currency sense appears constantly in financial contexts: {The yen weakened against the dollar}.

A yenta is a gossip or busybody—someone who meddles in others' affairs and spreads rumors. From Yiddish, the word carries affectionate exasperation more than harsh judgment: {My aunt is such a yenta, she knows everyone's business}. The term sometimes extends to anyone who plays matchmaker or offers unsolicited advice about others' lives.

Yentas are gossips or busybodies—people who pry into others' affairs and spread what they learn. The word comes from Yiddish and carries a Jewish cultural flavor, though it's used more broadly: {The yentas in the neighborhood knew everyone's business}. Sometimes spelled yentes.

A yente is a gossip or busybody—someone who meddles in others' affairs and spreads rumors. From Yiddish, the word carries the connotation of an older woman who can't resist prying into neighbors' business: {My aunt is such a yente, she knows everyone's secrets}. The term is sometimes confused with "yenta" as a matchmaker, though traditionally yente implies nosiness rather than matchmaking.

A yeoman was historically a farmer who owned and worked his own land—a step above a peasant but below the gentry. The word survives mainly in the phrase {yeoman's work} or {yeoman service}, meaning diligent, effective labor: {She did yeoman's work organizing the conference}. A yeoman of the guard is a ceremonial bodyguard at the British royal court.

Yep is an informal way of saying yes, conveying casual agreement or affirmation: {Yep, that's the one}. It's slightly more relaxed than yes but less emphatic than yeah. Common in everyday speech and texting.
clues: What a nod might sound like

definition: Yes is the standard adverb and interjection to signal agreement, understanding, and acceptance. It is also a polite way to acknowledge direct address.

A yeshiva is a Jewish school devoted to the study of traditional religious texts, particularly the Talmud and Torah. These institutions range from elementary schools to advanced academies for young men. In Orthodox communities, yeshiva education emphasizes intensive textual study and religious scholarship: {He spent years at yeshiva before becoming a rabbi}. The plural is yeshivas or yeshivot.

A yesman is someone who agrees with everything a superior says, regardless of their own opinion. The word implies spinelessness or careerism—agreeing not from conviction but to curry favor: {The CEO surrounded himself with yesmen who never challenged his ideas}. Also spelled yes-man or yes man.

Yesmen is the plural of yes-man, a person who agrees with everything a superior says in order to curry favor or avoid conflict. The term is disparaging, suggesting someone lacks independent judgment or the courage to voice disagreement. {The CEO surrounded himself with yesmen who never challenged his decisions.} The word implies sycophancy and is often used to criticize leadership that discourages honest feedback.

Yessir is an emphatic or deferential form of "yes sir," compressed into a single word. It signals agreement, compliance, or enthusiasm: {Yessir, I'll get right on it}. The tone ranges from genuine respect to casual affirmation to ironic mockery, depending on context. Also spelled yes sir or yessiree.

Yessirree is an emphatic, folksy way of saying yes, often used to express wholehearted agreement or enthusiastic confirmation: {Yessirree, that's the best pie I've ever tasted}. The word has a deliberately old-fashioned, down-home quality and frequently appears in humorous or exaggerated contexts. Also spelled yessiree.

Yesterday is the day before today. It also refers to the recent past more broadly: {Yesterday's technology is today's landfill}. As an adverb, it means on that day: {I saw her yesterday}. {Born yesterday} suggests naïveté: {I wasn't born yesterday—I know what you're up to}.

Yesteryear means the past, especially a nostalgically remembered earlier time: {the fashions of yesteryear}, {heroes of yesteryear}. The word has a literary, slightly old-fashioned quality—you're more likely to encounter it in headlines or nostalgic writing than everyday speech. It evokes a romanticized view of times gone by.

Yesteryears are times past, especially those remembered with nostalgia or viewed as a distinct era: {the fashions of yesteryears}, {heroes of yesteryears}. The word carries a slightly literary or sentimental tone, often evoking a romanticized past rather than simply referring to previous years.
Yet introduces a contrasting clause with slightly more emphasis than but does: We asked them repeatedly to quiet down yet they still ignored us.

A yeti is a large, ape-like creature said to inhabit the Himalayan mountains—the "abominable snowman" of Tibetan folklore. Like Bigfoot in North America, the yeti occupies cryptozoology: reported sightings persist despite no confirmed evidence. The word extends to anything elusive or legendary: {Finding good help around here is like hunting for a yeti}.

Yetis is the plural of yeti, the legendary ape-like creature said to inhabit the Himalayas. Also called the Abominable Snowman, the yeti occupies the same cryptozoological space as Bigfoot or Sasquatch—a large, elusive humanoid whose existence remains unproven: {expeditions searching for yetis}, {yetis and other mythical beasts}.

A yew is an evergreen tree or shrub with dark needles and red berries, known for its longevity and dense, fine-grained wood. Yews are commonly planted in churchyards and cemeteries throughout Britain. The wood was historically prized for making longbows: {English archers drew yew bows at Agincourt}. All parts of the tree except the berry flesh are poisonous.

Yews are evergreen trees or shrubs with dark green needles and red berries. The wood is dense and flexible, historically prized for making longbows. Yews are often planted in churchyards and cemeteries, giving them associations with death and mourning. Most parts of the tree are poisonous to humans and livestock.

Yield has many meanings as a verb, most of which involve the idea of producing, or of change of possession. If an experiment or analysis yields results, it produces something that is useful and wanted. An investment that yields a return earns money for the investor. When you yield to someone, you give them precedence, either by letting them go first or letting them have their way. The yield of something is the quantity that it gives back. The yield of a crop is how much is harvested, for example, per acre. The yield of an investment is how much it earns.

Yielding describes giving way under pressure or force. A yielding surface is soft and pliable: {The yielding mattress molded to her body}. A yielding person is compliant or submissive, quick to defer to others' wishes. In driving, yielding means allowing others the right of way. The word suggests accommodation rather than resistance—sometimes admirably flexible, sometimes too easily bent.

Yields means to produce or give forth. A field yields crops, an investment yields returns, a search yields results: {The experiment yielded surprising data}. To yield is also to give way—surrendering to force, pressure, or authority: {She yielded to their demands}. A yield sign requires drivers to give way to other traffic. In finance, yield is the return on an investment, expressed as a percentage: {a bond with a 5% yield}.
Yikes is associated with fear but sometimes in an ironic way, where they thing reacted to is not actually frightening but merely something to be avoided.

Yin is one half of the complementary pair in Chinese philosophy, representing the passive, dark, feminine, and receptive principle of the universe. It exists in dynamic balance with yang, its active, bright, masculine counterpart: {the yin and yang of work and rest}. The familiar circular symbol shows each force containing a seed of the other. By extension, yin describes anything characterized by these qualities—coolness, stillness, shadow, or introspection: {She brought yin energy to the hectic office}.

Yin and yang are the two complementary forces in Chinese philosophy—yin being dark, passive, and feminine; yang being light, active, and masculine. Together they represent balance and interdependence: {the yin and yang of work and rest}. The familiar black-and-white circular symbol depicts their interplay. In slang, yinyang is a euphemism for anus or buttocks: {a swift kick in the yinyang}.

Yip is a short, sharp bark or cry, typically from a small dog or a coyote: {The puppy yipped at the mailman}. As an exclamation, yip expresses excitement or triumph, often doubled: {Yip yip!} The word is onomatopoeic—it sounds like what it describes.
Yipe, like yikes, is associated with fear but sometimes in an ironic way, where they thing reacted to is not actually frightening but merely something to be avoided.
People say Yippee! when they are doing or thinking about doing something very exciting.

Yipping is making short, high-pitched barks or cries—the sound of small dogs, coyotes, or excited puppies: {The chihuahua kept yipping at the mailman}. By extension, people who complain or chatter in an annoying, high-pitched way may be said to be yipping.

The yips are involuntary muscle spasms or tremors that disrupt fine motor skills, especially in golf putting or baseball throwing. The term captures a specific athletic affliction: a player who once performed smoothly suddenly can't execute basic movements: {He had the yips so bad he couldn't sink a three-foot putt}. The condition is partly psychological—anxiety about missing feeds the problem. Beyond sports, yips describes any nervous inability to perform a once-automatic task.

A yob is a rude, loud, or aggressive young man—British slang for the type who causes trouble in public, drinks too much, and picks fights: {A gang of yobs smashed up the bus shelter}. The word is "boy" spelled backward, capturing the idea of masculine energy gone wrong. The adjective is yobbish.

Yobs is the plural of yob, British slang for a rude, rowdy, or loutish young man. The term carries strong connotations of antisocial behavior, often associated with drunkenness, vandalism, or public disturbances. {The yobs were thrown out of the pub for fighting.} Yob is backslang—"boy" spelled backward—though this origin is largely forgotten in everyday use.

Yodel is a style of singing that rapidly alternates between the normal voice and a high falsetto, producing a distinctive warbling sound. It originated in the Alps as a way for herders to communicate across mountains and valleys. The technique appears in folk music worldwide and occasionally in country and pop: {She learned to yodel from her Swiss grandmother}.

Yodeled is the past tense of yodel, a style of singing that involves rapid alternation between the chest voice and a high falsetto. The technique originated in the Alpine regions of Europe, where herders used it to communicate across mountains. In American country and western music, yodeling became a distinctive vocal flourish. {She yodeled through the chorus of the old cowboy song.}

Yodeling is a style of singing that rapidly alternates between the normal voice and a high falsetto, producing a distinctive warbling sound. The technique originated in the Alps, where it served as a way for herders to communicate across mountain valleys. It appears in Swiss and Austrian folk music, American country and western songs, and occasionally pop music: {She learned to yodel from her grandmother}.

Yodelling is a style of singing that involves rapid alternation between the normal chest voice and a high falsetto, producing a distinctive warbling sound. The technique originated in the Alpine regions of Europe, where it served as a way for herders to communicate across mountain valleys. {The yodelling echoed through the hills.}

Yodels are vocalizations that rapidly alternate between a low chest voice and a high falsetto, creating a distinctive warbling sound. The technique is associated with Alpine folk music and American country singing. To yodel is to produce this sound: {She yodeled across the valley}. Figuratively, any wavering or fluctuating vocal sound might be called yodeling.

Yoga is a Hindu spiritual discipline involving breath control, meditation, and physical postures aimed at attaining union with the divine or higher consciousness. In Western usage, yoga usually refers to the physical practice—a series of poses and stretches performed for flexibility, strength, and stress relief: {I do yoga three times a week}. Hot yoga, power yoga, and other variations have proliferated as exercise trends. {She rolled out her yoga mat}.

Yoghurt is a variant spelling of yogurt, the thick, creamy dairy product made by fermenting milk with bacterial cultures. This spelling is more common in British English and in countries influenced by British conventions, while yogurt predominates in American English. The fermentation process gives yoghurt its characteristic tangy flavor and smooth texture. {I picked up some Greek yoghurt at the shop.}

A yogi is a practitioner of yoga, particularly someone devoted to its spiritual and meditative disciplines rather than just physical postures. The term suggests serious commitment: {He lived as a yogi in an ashram for ten years}. In casual use, yogi may describe anyone who practices yoga regularly: {She's become quite the yogi since joining that studio}.

Yogis is the plural of yogi, a practitioner of yoga—particularly one devoted to its meditative and spiritual disciplines rather than just physical postures. The term comes from Hindu tradition but now applies broadly to anyone seriously committed to yoga practice: {The yogis gathered at dawn for meditation}. A yogi may also be someone regarded as having achieved spiritual insight through such practice.

Yogurt is a thick, creamy dairy product made by fermenting milk with bacterial cultures. The fermentation process gives yogurt its characteristic tangy flavor and smooth texture. It can be eaten plain or flavored with fruit, honey, or other additions, and serves as both a standalone food and an ingredient in cooking. Greek yogurt is strained to remove whey, resulting in a thicker consistency and higher protein content.

Yoink is an exclamation accompanying the swift grabbing of something: {Yoink! That's mine now}. The word imitates a cartoonish snatching motion. As a verb, to yoink is to snatch or steal quickly: {Someone yoinked my parking spot}. The tone is playful rather than seriously accusatory.

Yoinked is the past tense of yoink, slang for snatching or grabbing something quickly, often with playful mischief: {He yoinked the last slice of pizza before anyone noticed}. The word is onomatopoeic, evoking the swift motion of taking something. It can describe theft but more often suggests harmless opportunism: {She yoinked his phone to see the photo}.

Yoinking is the present participle of yoink, a playful verb meaning to grab or snatch something quickly, often with a sense of gleeful opportunism. The word is onomatopoeic, mimicking the sound of a swift grab, and originated in cartoon and internet culture. {He was yoinking fries off my plate before I could stop him.} Yoinking suggests a casual, good-natured theft rather than anything serious or malicious.

Yokai are supernatural creatures from Japanese folklore—a broad category encompassing monsters, spirits, demons, and shapeshifters. Unlike Western ghosts or demons, yokai range from malevolent to mischievous to benign: a kappa drowns swimmers, a tanuki tricks travelers, a zashiki-warashi brings household prosperity. The term appears frequently in anime, manga, and video games: {The game features dozens of yokai to collect}.

A yoke is a wooden beam fitted across the necks of two draft animals, binding them together to pull a load. From this concrete meaning comes the figurative sense of something that binds or burdens: {the yoke of oppression}, {throw off the yoke of colonialism}. A yoke also names the fitted upper part of a garment across the shoulders or hips. To yoke is to harness animals together, or to join things in general: {yoked in marriage}, {yoked to a tedious job}. A yoke of oxen is a pair.

Yoked originally describes animals joined by a yoke—a wooden frame linking oxen for plowing. By extension, people yoked together are bound or united: {yoked in marriage}, {yoked to a demanding job}. In gym slang, yoked means extremely muscular, particularly in the neck and shoulders—built like an ox: {He got yoked over the summer}.

A yokel is a person from a rural area, especially one portrayed as unsophisticated or ignorant of city ways. The word is mildly insulting, suggesting someone naive, slow-witted, or out of place in modern settings: {Some yokel in a pickup truck nearly ran me off the road}. It often carries class condescension from urbanites toward country folk.

Yokels are unsophisticated rural people, especially as viewed condescendingly by city dwellers. The word implies backwardness, naivety, and lack of worldly knowledge: {The locals dismissed the tourists as yokels who didn't know how to dress for the weather}. Often used humorously or disparagingly to suggest someone is a country bumpkin.

The yolk is the yellow part of an egg, surrounded by the white. It provides nutrients for a developing embryo and is the fattier, richer portion when eaten: {She likes her yolks runny}. Yolk extends to any similar substance, especially the oily secretion in sheep's wool.

Yolks are the yellow centers of eggs, surrounded by the white. The yolk contains most of the egg's fat and nutrients, serving as food for a developing embryo. In cooking, yolks provide richness to sauces, custards, and baked goods: {Separate the yolks from the whites}. Figuratively, yolk can mean the essential or central part of something.

Yolo is an acronym for "you only live once," used to justify impulsive or risky behavior: {I bought the plane ticket—yolo}. The term rose to prominence in the early 2010s and quickly became both sincere rallying cry and self-aware joke. It can preface a decision or stand alone as explanation.

Yonder means over there—at a distance but within sight. The word is old-fashioned or dialectal, surviving mainly in rural American and British regional speech: {What's that building yonder?} It works as an adverb or adjective: {the yonder hills}. The phrase {the wild blue yonder} means the sky or a remote, unknown place.
clues: Where the horizon meets your gaze

definition: Yonks is British slang for a very long time: {I haven't seen her in yonks}, {It's been yonks since we went there}. The word is informal and casual, appearing almost exclusively in the phrase "for yonks" or "in yonks."

Yoo-hoo is a call to get someone's attention, especially when you suspect someone is nearby but can't see them: {Yoo-hoo, is anyone home?} The call carries a cheerful, slightly old-fashioned quality. Also spelled yoo-hoo.

Yore means long ago or former times, appearing almost exclusively in the phrase {of yore}: {knights of yore}, {in days of yore}. The word is literary and deliberately old-fashioned, evoking a romanticized past. Outside the set phrase, yore sounds archaic or playful.

A yorker is a cricket delivery that pitches directly at or just inside the batsman's crease, aimed at the base of the stumps or the batsman's feet. It's one of the most difficult balls to defend against or hit, prized for its ability to sneak under the bat: {He bowled a perfect yorker to shatter the stumps}.

You is the only official second person pronoun in English for subjects and objects. Because it stands for both singular and plural, several unofficial plural pronouns exist to overcome ambiguity, such as you all, y’all, youse, you guys, and so forth. You is used both when directly addressing a person or group, or as an informal way of talking about people in general: You never know how many fans might turn up.

Young characterizes both living and inanimate things that are in the early stages of growth, development, or existence. It is the opposite of old in most of its uses. As a noun, young is usually construed as a plural and denotes the offspring of animals.
clues: Having existed only briefly so far

definition: Youngblood refers to a young person, especially one bringing fresh energy or new perspective to an established group or field. The term emphasizes vitality and inexperience as assets rather than limitations: {The team needs some youngblood to shake things up}. Often used to address or describe a younger man, sometimes with slight condescension from an older speaker: {Listen here, youngblood}.

Younger is the comparative form of young, describing someone or something less old than another: {my younger sister}, {the younger generation}. As a noun, younger often appears in the plural to mean children or youth collectively: {The youngers don't remember life before smartphones}. In naming, younger distinguishes a child from a parent with the same name, less formally than Junior.

Youngest is the superlative form of young—the one with the least age in a group. It typically appears with *the*: {She's the youngest of four children}, {the youngest player on the team}. Without an article, it functions as an adjective: {my youngest daughter}, {their youngest son}.

A youngin is a young person—a child, teenager, or someone noticeably younger than the speaker. The term is informal and often affectionate, used especially in Southern American speech: {These youngins don't know how good they have it}. Also spelled young'un or young'n.

Youngins is informal or dialectal for young ones—children or young people generally. The word appears in Southern American English and African American Vernacular English, often carrying affectionate or folksy connotations: {Get the youngins to bed}, {Back when I was a youngin}. Also spelled younguns or young'uns.

Younglings are young creatures or children. The word has an old-fashioned or literary flavor, suggesting small beings not yet grown: {The mother bird fed her younglings}. It gained pop-culture currency through *Star Wars*, where it refers to children training as Jedi. Outside that context, it remains quaint and slightly precious.

A youngster is a young person, typically a child or teenager. The term carries a slightly old-fashioned or affectionate tone, often used by older speakers referring to those much younger than themselves. {The youngsters in the neighborhood organized a lemonade stand.} It can also apply more broadly to anyone relatively young in a given context, such as a rookie athlete or new employee among veterans.

Youngsters are young people, typically children or teenagers. The word carries a slightly old-fashioned or affectionate tone, often used by older speakers referring to those much younger: {The youngsters were running around the yard}. It can also describe anyone notably younger in a given context: {At sixty, she was surrounded by youngsters in their forties}.

Yours combines two jobs in one; to take the place of a noun or noun phrase already named, and to indicate that the thing referred to belongs to or is associated with the person you’re speaking to, or with people in general: If my car is still in the shop can I use yours? If you’ve got $5.5 million to spare, this house can be yours.

You use yourself as the object of a verb or preposition to refer a second time to the person you are addressing, or to people in general: Did you injure yourself playing football? Always give yourself extra time for the Friday commute. Yourself and other pronouns that end in –self and –selves are called reflexives because they indicate that the action of a verb is reflected back at the subject of the sentence.

Youth is the period of life between childhood and full adulthood, or the quality of being young. A youth is a young person, especially a young man: {Three youths were arrested outside the stadium}. The youth refers collectively to young people: {the youth of today}. Youth carries connotations of energy, inexperience, and potential: {the enthusiasm of youth}, {misspent youth}. As a modifier, it describes things designed for or involving young people: {youth sports}, {youth culture}, {youth hostel}.

Youthful describes qualities associated with being young—energy, freshness, vitality, or appearance. A youthful {face} looks young; a youthful {enthusiasm} suggests the vigor of youth. Unlike young, youthful can apply regardless of actual age: {She maintained a youthful outlook well into her eighties}. The word carries positive connotations, implying desirable qualities rather than immaturity.

Youthquake describes a significant cultural, political, or social shift driven by young people. The term combines youth with earthquake to suggest seismic change originating from a younger generation: {The 1960s youthquake transformed music, fashion, and politics}. It resurfaces whenever youth movements reshape the status quo—voting patterns, protest movements, or cultural trends.

A yowl is a loud, prolonged, mournful cry—the sound a cat makes when distressed, territorial, or in heat. Dogs, wolves, and humans yowl too. The verb means to make such a sound: {The cat yowled outside the door all night}. A yowl is rougher and more drawn-out than a yell, suggesting animal complaint.

Yowled is the past tense of yowl, meaning to produce a long, loud, mournful cry. Cats yowl; so do dogs, wolves, and humans in distress or protest. The sound suggests something more drawn-out and plaintive than a yelp or bark: {The cat yowled at the door until someone let her in}.

Yowling is the present participle of yowl, meaning to produce a loud, drawn-out cry of distress or complaint—typically associated with cats in heat or fighting. The sound is more sustained and mournful than a yelp or screech: {The yowling cats kept us awake all night}. People can yowl too, usually in pain or protest.

Yowls are prolonged, mournful cries—the sound a cat makes when distressed, in heat, or fighting. The word captures something more drawn-out and plaintive than a meow, closer to a wail: {The tomcat's yowls kept the neighborhood awake}. People can yowl too, usually in pain or protest.

Yowza is an exclamation of enthusiasm, surprise, or impressed reaction—similar to wow but more emphatic and playful: {Yowza, look at that car!} The word has an old-fashioned, vaudeville quality, sometimes used ironically or for comic effect. Also spelled yowsa.

A yoyo is a toy consisting of two connected disks with a string wound around the axle between them. You hold the string's end and let the yoyo drop, then flick your wrist to make it climb back up. The term extends to anything that fluctuates up and down: {yoyo dieting}, {yoyo prices}. To yoyo is to move erratically between states. Calling someone a yoyo means they're foolish or incompetent.

Yoyoed is the past tense of yoyo, meaning to move repeatedly up and down or back and forth like the toy on a string. Stock prices yoyo. Weight yoyos when dieting fails. Emotions yoyo during a breakup. {Her mood yoyoed between hope and despair.} {Gas prices have yoyoed all summer.}

Yoyoing is moving repeatedly back and forth or up and down, like the toy on a string. Weight can yoyo between diets. Prices yoyo with market volatility. {My energy levels have been yoyoing all week.} The word captures not just fluctuation but the sense of returning to where you started, only to swing away again.

Yoyos is the plural of yoyo, a toy consisting of two connected disks with a string wound around an axle between them. You hold the string's end and let the yoyo drop, then flick it back up. Figuratively, a yoyo is someone who fluctuates or can't make up their mind: {The stock market yoyos between gains and losses}.

Yuan is the basic unit of currency in China, equivalent to ten jiao or one hundred fen. In international contexts, it's often called the renminbi (RMB), though yuan refers specifically to the unit of account: {The exchange rate is about seven yuan to the dollar}. Financial discussions frequently reference yuan in debates about currency manipulation and trade policy.

Yuca is a starchy root vegetable, the edible tuber of the cassava plant. A staple food across Latin America, Africa, and Asia, it's typically boiled, fried, or mashed: {The restaurant serves yuca fries with garlic sauce}. The spelling yuca reflects Spanish-language usage; cassava and manioc name the same plant. Not to be confused with yucca, a spiky ornamental plant native to the Americas.

Yucca is a plant native to hot, dry regions of the Americas, characterized by stiff, sword-shaped leaves and tall clusters of white flowers. Several species are common in desert landscaping and as houseplants. The yucca root is edible and appears in Latin American cooking, though this is often confused with yuca (cassava), a different plant entirely.
Ick expresses a reaction to something that is repugnant to the senses.

Yucky describes something disgusting or unpleasant—food that tastes bad, textures that repel, situations that feel wrong: {This oatmeal is yucky}. The word is childish or deliberately playful, the kind of thing a toddler says about vegetables or an adult says with ironic exaggeration: {Monday meetings are yucky}.

Yuk is an exclamation of disgust or distaste, reacting to something unpleasant: {Yuk, this milk has gone off}. Also spelled yuck. As a noun, yuks are laughs or jokes: {We got some yuks out of it}. To yuk it up is to joke around or laugh boisterously.

Yuletide is the Christmas season, from late December through early January. The word sounds old-fashioned and literary, evoking traditional celebrations: {yuletide carols}, {yuletide cheer}. It appears most often in holiday marketing and nostalgic contexts: {Wishing you a joyous yuletide}. (Capitalized Yuletide is an equivalent variant.)
People say yum or yum-yum in response to something that tastes or looks good.

Yummy means delicious or appealing to the taste: {These cookies are yummy}. The word is informal and slightly childish, often used by or around children. It extends to anything pleasurable or attractive: {That's a yummy shade of pink}. The noun yummy or yummies refers to tasty treats.
Yup is like yeah, an informal version of yes. It may be considered impolite when used with someone in authority.

Yuppie is a mildly derisive term for a young urban professional—someone in their twenties or thirties with a well-paying white-collar job and conspicuous consumption habits. The word emerged in the 1980s to describe ambitious city dwellers more interested in career advancement and material comfort than social causes: {The neighborhood filled with yuppies and overpriced coffee shops}.

Yuppies is the plural of yuppie, a young urban professional—someone in their twenties or thirties with a well-paying white-collar job and conspicuous consumption habits. The term emerged in the 1980s, often used disparagingly to suggest materialism and self-absorption: {The neighborhood filled up with yuppies and their overpriced coffee shops}.

Yuppy is a mildly disparaging term for a young urban professional—someone in their twenties or thirties with a well-paying white-collar job and conventional aspirations toward career success and material comfort. The word peaked in the 1980s but remains in use: {The neighborhood filled up with yuppies and their expensive strollers}. Also spelled yuppie.

A yurt is a portable, round tent traditionally used by nomadic peoples of Central Asia. The structure consists of a collapsible wooden frame covered with felt or skins, designed for easy assembly and transport. Modern yurts appear as alternative housing, glamping accommodations, or backyard structures: {We stayed in a yurt in Mongolia}. {The retreat center has yurts for guests}.

Yurts is the plural of yurt, a portable tent dwelling traditionally used by nomadic peoples of Central Asia. The structure consists of a collapsible wooden frame covered with felt or skins, designed for easy assembly and transport. In Western usage, yurts have become popular as alternative housing, glamping accommodations, and backyard retreats: {We stayed in yurts at the eco-resort}.

Yuzu is a citrus fruit from East Asia with a distinctive tart, floral flavor somewhere between lemon, grapefruit, and mandarin. The aromatic zest and juice appear in Japanese cuisine—ponzu sauce, desserts, beverages—and increasingly in Western cooking and cocktails: {The chef finished the dish with a yuzu vinaigrette}.

A zaddy is an attractive man, typically older, who exudes style, confidence, and sex appeal. The term blends "daddy" with an intensifying z-sound, suggesting someone who's not just good-looking but radiates swagger: {Did you see him in that suit? Total zaddy}. Common in social media and celebrity culture, often applied to well-dressed men in their thirties and beyond.

Zag is a sharp change in direction, typically one of several in a zigzag pattern. The verb means to make such a turn: {The rabbit zagged left and escaped}. Often paired with zig: {when everyone else zigs, zag}—meaning do the unexpected or go against the crowd.

Zagged is the past tense of zag, meaning to make a sharp turn or change direction, especially as part of an erratic or zigzag path: {The rabbit zagged left and disappeared into the brush}. Often paired with zigged: {We zigged when we should have zagged}.

Zagging is the present participle of zag—to make a sharp change in direction, especially as part of an erratic or evasive path. Usually paired with zigging: {The rabbit went zigging and zagging across the field}. Figuratively, to zag when others zig is to choose a contrarian or unconventional approach: {Everyone else pivoted to video; we zagged and doubled down on text}.

Zags is the plural of zag, meaning sharp changes in direction, especially alternating ones. Zigzags are made of zigs and zags. The verb zag means to make such a turn: {When everyone else zigs, zag}. The expression suggests contrarian thinking—going the opposite way from the crowd.

Zany describes something or someone amusingly unconventional or wildly comical, often with an element of absurdity or eccentricity. A zany {comedy} features exaggerated silliness; a zany {idea} is entertainingly bizarre. The word carries affection rather than criticism—calling someone zany suggests they're delightfully off-kilter rather than genuinely strange. As a noun, a zany is a comical person, though this use is now rare outside theatrical contexts.

Zap captures the idea of sudden, energetic action—originally the sound of a ray gun or electrical discharge in comic books. To zap something is to destroy or disable it quickly: {The laser zapped the target}. In computing, zap means to delete or erase: {I accidentally zapped the whole folder}. Microwaving food is often called zapping: {Just zap it for thirty seconds}. As a noun, a zap is a jolt or burst of energy. The word conveys speed and decisiveness across all its uses.

Zapped is the past tense of zap, which means to strike or destroy with sudden force or energy—originally the blast of a ray gun in science fiction, now extended to microwaves, electrical shocks, or swift elimination: {I zapped the leftovers}, {The surge zapped my computer}. Zapped also means exhausted: {I'm completely zapped after that meeting}.

A zapper is a device that zaps—delivers a sudden jolt of electricity or energy. Bug zappers electrocute insects attracted to their light. TV zappers are remote controls, from the act of zapping through channels. In video games, light guns that "shoot" at screens are sometimes called zappers. {Hand me the zapper, I want to change the channel.}

Zapping is the act of destroying, killing, or hitting something with sudden force or energy—often suggesting electricity, radiation, or weaponry: {The laser kept zapping the invaders}. In casual use, zapping means changing TV channels rapidly with a remote, or heating something quickly in a microwave: {I'm just zapping some leftovers}. The word carries a sense of speed and decisiveness.

Zaps is the plural of zap and the third-person singular verb form. A zap is a sudden burst of energy, electricity, or radiation: {The zaps from the faulty outlet were alarming}. To zap is to strike with such energy, destroy quickly, or move fast: {She zaps through emails every morning}. Zaps also names the electric-shock sensations from antidepressant withdrawal: {brain zaps}.
